title: Tom Brady's Super Bowl LX neutrality strikes a nerve with Patriots fans
text:
For many New England Patriots fans, Tom Brady’s neutral stance ahead of Super Bowl LX landed harder than expected.

“I don’t have a dog in the fight in this one,” Brady told Jim Gray on the “Let’s Go!” podcast, speaking about the Patriots-Seahawks matchup. “May the best team win. And in terms of the Patriots, this is a new chapter in New England, and I’m glad everyone’s embraced the Mike Vrabel regime, all the amazing players that have worked so hard to get their club to this position.”

While Brady framed his comments as part of a new chapter — one shaped by broadcasting and minority ownership with the Raiders — a large majority of readers told us it didn’t sit right.

When we asked Boston.com readers to weigh in, nearly 700 respondents voted, revealing a fan base split between disappointment, understanding, and indifference — all tied to the complicated reality of seeing a Patriots icon speak like an outsider during the franchise’s biggest moment in years.

“Tom prob should be speaking a little warmer toward the fan base that supports him no matter what for 20+ years,” wrote Keith from Medford.

Sean R. of Chelmsford echoed that sentiment more bluntly: “His biggest fans are New Englanders. This was a slap in the face to his biggest fans.”

Still, not everyone was upset. Some readers emphasized perspective, pointing to everything Brady already gave the franchise.

“He helped us win 6 Super Bowls and stayed loyal throughout all those years, despite Bill. He doesn’t owe anything,” Roberto V. of Haverhill wrote.

Others landed somewhere in the middle, wishing Brady would acknowledge his legacy without demanding full-throated fandom. “He’s entitled to his opinions, but loyalty to the legacy would be nice,” said Chris.

Below, readers react to Brady’s neutral support for the Patriots ahead of the Super Bowl.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

How much does Tom Brady’s lack of support for the Patriots in Super Bowl LX bother you?

Yes, I’m bothered!

“After the unveiling of the statue, didn’t we hear from Tom that he is a Patriot for life? He is a phony.” — Steve, Franklin

“New England is the team that made Tom Brady. His statue sits outside of Gillette stadium, he spent the majority of his career there, and he once stated that he is a Patriot for life! It’s ridiculous that he can’t support this team in the Super Bowl. Shame on you, TB!” — David H., Chelmsford

“Having been a devoted fan for over 50 years, I found Tom’s statement to be an insult to a team that he himself said that he was a Patriot for life. The fans elevated him to GOAT status as did I, bought his merchandise, and supported him for 20 years. Even though now it is hard for me to say this, maybe it was never the team that mattered to him, but himself and his glory and accomplishments.” — Susan G., Winthrop

“Brady is in a new career with broadcasting the games. While always remembering the past, when they jump into the sportscasting role they become more neutral in their thoughts on teams. Growing up in St. Louis, Joe Buck did the same thing in regards to the Cardinals. We were all miffed with him going national and not announcing to Cardinals nation only, like his father Jack Buck had done his whole career. We hurt too as fans.” — Jenn H., Acton

“He was part of something special, he gave so much joy to Pats fans and we loved and supported him. He should be rooting the Pats because we’ve always rooted for him. Very disappointed.” — B., North Reading

“Tom can’t say he’s a ‘Patriot for life’ and not support the team with which he made his name, regardless of his ownership stake in a team that won’t be in the playoffs for at least another five years, during which time the Pats will have made at least one other Super Bowl appearance. Loyalty means something.” — John, Worcester

A little bit.

“As much as I’d like Tom Brady to show his support for the Patriots, I sort of understand his position. It is similar to how I felt when Tom left New England for Tampa Bay. I didn’t want him to win a Super Bowl with another team. I never understood why some Patriots fans turned into Buccaneers fans just because Tom played for them. I am a Patriots fan through and through. They are my team, good or bad and there have been plenty of both as I grew up in the 80’s. I felt like Tom was ours and it hurt when he left and succeeded elsewhere (without us). I imagine he’s feeling the same way now.” — Rob R., Franklin

“He has no obligations to support the team. But just the way that many fans still rooted for him during his run with Tampa Bay, it would be nicer if he showed his pride for all the years of donning the Patriots uniform.” — Anonymous reader, West Roxbury

“Tom has every right to remain impartial or not choose a side, but it seems lately he is trying to further and further his identity away from the Pats. A team and fan base that absolutely adore him, so of course it’s annoying a bit. He won’t support the Pats but what can you do?” — Jacob, Cambridge

“Brady is now his own brand. He obviously calculated that being neutral is better for ‘the brand.’ Other Boston sport heroes like Ted Williams, Bill Russell, Larry Bird and Bobby Orr always spoke of their love for their respective teams and teammates. It seems like Brady will measure what it will do for his brand first.” — Michael I., Princeton

“I mean, I’d like for him to be all Pats, but imagine he’s trying to keep his options open. Doesn’t want to seem like he’s diehard Pats fan, should he get into coaching or become a bigger owner of the Raiders.” — Andrew D., Lakeville

“I understand that he is in a different phase of his life now. So is Gronk, Bruschi, Woody, and all the others that played and won with him. But I don’t understand how, after all of this, he can have no emotions about this game! How disappointing! Maybe he is being sensitive to business ramifications. But geez!” — Karen R., Bellingham

Not bothered. He’s still the GOAT.

“He’s a grown a** man. He’s on to another phase in his life. I’ve been a fan of the Patriots since I was a kid (I had a John Hannah poster over my bed). Tom has given us enough that he has as much leeway as he wants with me.” — Gerry, Hinesburg, Vermont

“Brady gave us so much, and then moved on. And that’s fine. He went on to win a Super Bowl with a new team, and now has an ownership interest in a different team. Thank you, Tom, and let’s go, Maye and team!” — Richard, Dorchester

“Doesn’t change the happiness he brought to me for 20 years.” — Steve, Medford

“He’s playing it smart! Team owner plus a broadcaster keeping his thoughts to himself.” — Paul, Boston

“Who cares? Get over it people. He gave you the best 20 years of dominance the NFL has ever seen! The guy now owns part of the Raiders. His Patriots pom poms have been put away. He owes us nothing!” — Kevin, Weymouth

“He is a partial owner in another team and a commentator, so I like to think he is just being neutral. He may also not be ready to be ‘replaced’ in the hearts of Pats fans.” — Elizabeth, Littleton

It doesn’t matter much to me.

“Professional athletes tend to put the past behind them. Tom’s time with the Patriots will always be special, but he’s not a Patriot any longer and not close to this team. In addition, he is now an unbiased analyst, plus a part owner with another team!” — Alan

“He’s not obligated to be a Patriot for life if he’s over it — Kraft did him dirty at the end. But let’s get rid of that over-the-top giant statute if it’s a one-sided love affair!” — Nancy L., Hanover, New Hampshire

“He’s in the public eye as a broadcaster, so if people see him as biased I think it would hurt the perception of how much people would value his opinion. You see the same thing with sports writers who want to be seen as objective. Even if personally they root for a particular team they think their opinions will be suspect if they are viewed as a fan.” — Richard G., Londonderry, New Hampshire

“He has done enough for us, I don’t feel like he owes us anything, especially not rooting for a team considering he is announcing it. It’s not personal, it’s just business. I still love him and he still loves us.” — Jeremy H., Watertown

“Tom Brady has always done what he believed was best for him. He took team-friendly deals because he wanted to win. He left to prove he could do it somewhere else. And honestly, we’re all like that — you’re loyal to your company, but in the end you’ll do what’s best for you. I wish him nothing but luck and I’m grateful for what he gave us. But at the end of the day, he’s gone now, and he deserves to live his own life.” — Kevin, Walpole

title: More than 400 readers voted: $240K in-office Boston job or $120K remote?
text:
A viral workplace question has been circulating online: Would you rather take a $240,000 in-person job or $120,000 remote one?

That got us thinking — what if the in-office job is located in Boston, where commuting time and cost of living can be significant?

So we asked readers to weigh in on the modern workplace dilemma: higher pay in the office, or lower pay with the flexibility of working from home?

More than 400 readers responded to our informal poll. While the higher paycheck came out ahead, the results show a workforce still split on what matters most.

In total, 56% of readers said they would take the $240,000 in-person Boston job, compared to 40% who chose the $120,000 remote role. Another 4% said neither option worked for them, with many in that group saying a hybrid setup would be their ideal scenario.

Why some chose the $120K remote job

Readers who chose the lower-paying remote role mostly cited time and flexibility — especially parents and longtime commuters.

“3 kids under 8 — commuting plus the cost of it is horrible. You can’t get the time back,” one anonymous reader wrote.

Erica from West Roxbury said working from home allows them to juggle school schedules and appointments “without hiring additional childcare or paying for before or after-school programs.”

For many, the commute was the deal breaker.

“An in-person job adds at minimum two hours to my work day,” RM from Arlington wrote, saying their mental and physical health is “so much better without the hassle of a commute.”

Others argued that once you factor in commuting costs and higher expenses living near the city, the salary gap shrinks — even feeling “close to the same.”

Why others picked the $240K in-office Boston job

Readers who chose the $240,000 in-person job largely pointed to the salary — and, for some, a desire to get back to pre-pandemic norms.

“$120K isn’t much these days. Especially around Boston,” Dan from Winchester wrote.

Others said the pay gap made it simple: “The extra $120K is life changing,” wrote Michael from Arlington, citing housing costs, retirement savings, and childcare.

Several also said they prefer being around colleagues.

“I like working in an office environment and having interactions with other humans. Remote work is isolating,” Douglas from Dorchester wrote.

“I worked 5 days a week for 30 years — remote work only started in the last five,” said Shaun from Weymouth, while another added, “People need to get out of the house and get used to in-person interactions again.”

The split underscores an ongoing tension in today’s job market: Is doubling your salary worth giving up remote flexibility — especially in a city like Boston?

Below, see a sampling of reader responses.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

Would you rather have a $240K in-person job (in Boston) or a $120K remote one?

$240K in-person

“$120K really doesn’t buy much these days. I’d take the $240K job and find some cheap hole-in-the-wall accommodations near the office during the week, then return home on the weekends.” — Trevor M., Great Barrington

“Boston is a very dynamic city with lots of perks. $240K is still a great salary and for that I would drive 2 hours each way to collect it.” — Julian V., Leominster

“I like the office and having to get dressed I think it makes you more productive.” — Lisa, Taunton

“Boston is so expensive that I would make it work. If I had children, my choice might be different.” — Molly, Somerville

“I’m a single mom with a 9-year-old boy. Every penny counts. With $240K, I can hire the tutor, nanny, take him on vacations, and provide financial security which would be almost not feasible with $120K living in Boston.” —Sara, Chinatown

“As long as the job was on public transportation. It’s not a big deal. More money, please!” — John, Medford

“Double the money to commute and build in-person relationships is a no brainer.” — Rodger, Medford

“I like the social aspect of being in the office. Being at home is great in some ways but it gets old sitting alone in my home office.” — Serena, Cambridge

“I worked 5 days a week for 30 years, remote work only started in the last 5.” — Shaun C., Weymouth

“I’m doing the remote thing for this month. Not a fan. Being home all day is not all it’s cracked up to be. I like the people in my office and being social on a daily basis.” — Kerri, Whitman

“I’m tired of remote work and lack of community.” — A Boston.com reader from Holliston

“MONEY!!!!!!!!!!” — Rosemary, Watertown

$120K remote

“Hours lost in traffic are never recovered. Most meetings are virtual anyway. Why drive to sit on the screen!” — CJ, Braintree

“Freedom/time is more important than money especially as you get older.” — DL, New Haven, Conn.

“As someone with friends across the world, a remote job would allow me time/opportunity to travel, visit friends, have new experiences, and still make a decent salary.” — Anthony, Jamaica Plain

“Commuting is a treacherous waste of time and office life is mentally suffocating (noise, politics, gossip, atmosphere, infrastructure…), whereas remote work enables the best possible work-life balance for those of us that must still work for a living but cherish flexibility and our freedom.” — A Boston.com reader from Somerville

“3 kids under 8, commuting plus the cost of it is horrible, can’t get the time back.” — Emily

“An in-person job adds at minimum two hours to my work day — my commute is ‘work’ whether the company likes calling it that or not, which means now I’m working 50 hours a week (more if you count time wasted on packing lunch, dressing up fancy, etc.). It means I can’t be with my dog, so I have to deal with the fallout of that, both financial and just lost time with her. It means I can’t let the dishwasher run while I’m working. It means I put wear on my body, vehicle, or bicycle, or deal with the misery that is depending on public transit … My health — mental and physical — is so much better without the hassle of a commute.” — RM, Arlington

“Working from home allows me to bring our kids to school and appointments without hiring additional childcare or paying for before/after-school programs. Remote work is more family-friendly; the trade-off is the isolation from my peers.” — Erica J., West Roxbury

“As a mom of a toddler and 2 dogs, I need the flexibility of being home as much as I can.” — MJ, Plymouth

“Covid was bad for the world but great for my work life. Working from home allowed my to save almost 3 hours/day commuting.” — Francine M., Wenham

“MBTA public transportation is horrible, trains always late, the Red Line is a mess. I don’t miss any of that.” — A Boston.com reader

“I have actually turned down a $210K base salary role that required 3X a day in the office for a $150K base, fully remote role.” — A Boston.com reader from Sudbury

Neither

title: Readers agree: Build a new Madison Park to benefit Boston’s youth
text:
Boston.com readers are weighing in on the future of parcel P-3 in Roxbury — and many say the long-vacant site represents an opportunity the city can’t afford to miss.

Last week, we asked readers what should happen to the 7.7-acre, publicly owned Tremont Street parcel after the expiration of a mixed-use development plan and the city’s pivot toward potentially rebuilding Madison Park Technical Vocational High School there.

More than a dozen readers responded to our poll, with the majority in agreement: support for investing in vocational education triumphed over the parcel’s initial mixed-use development.

Several readers said a new Madison Park high school would be a concrete public benefit on land that has sat idle for decades.

“It’s a real win for Boston’s youth for Madison Park to be built on the P-3 Parcel,” Pip L. from Jamaica Plain said.

“The new Madison Park School will be a state-of-the-art career tech school that will have the important role of giving PBS students many paths to rewarding, well-paying careers in the trades (electricians, plumbers, auto mechanics, hair dressers, etc.) without the burden of the need to attend college. Many of our students will not be in a position to take on the debt and time of a college education. Very important for Boston to get this done,” he added.

Others echoed the call to update school infrastructure across Boston Public Schools more broadly.

“BPS buildings are old and inadequate to deliver a 21st century educational experience,” David H. from Dorchester argued. “Indeed, this is part of the reason young families move out of the city. It’s time to prioritize the implementation of a comprehensive school building plan.”

The emphasis on trades and workforce development came up repeatedly among readers. Collette of Brighton pointed out that Madison Park is the city’s only vocational high school and suggested students should have a clearer pathway into union jobs after graduation.

John S., a Dorchester youth coach of more than 30 years, argued that strengthening vocational education is critical and expressed frustration that promised affordable housing “consistently falls through the loopholes of this city’s rules and regulations.”

Still, even among those who acknowledged the need for housing, there was recognition that the original plan’s reliance on life sciences funding may no longer be viable in today’s market.

As debate continues at City Hall and in Roxbury, readers made one thing clear: whatever happens on parcel P-3, they want the decision to reflect both the city’s fiscal realities and its commitment to the next generation of Boston’s students.

Below, readers share why they want a new Madison Park vocational high school at parcel P-3 in Roxbury.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

What should the city do with parcel P-3 in Roxbury?

“It’s a real win for Boston’s youth for Madison Park to be built on the P-3 Parcel.

The new Madison Park School will be a state-of-the-art career tech school that will have the important role of giving PBS students many paths to rewarding, well-paying careers in the trades (electricians, plumbers, auto mechanics, hair dressers, etc.) without the burden of the need to attend college. Many of our students will not be in a position to take on the debt and time of a college education. Very important for Boston to get this done.

Building on the adjacent P-3 site will allow the new school to move faster and may be less expensive than a slow, cumbersome, painful phased renovation project. Costly swing space for auto shops, etc. will be avoided.

Then the vacated Madison Park site could be made available for affordable housing, perhaps even lab space if that market rebounds. But remember that the housing was to be made affordable from subsidies from the life-sciences portion of the P-3 proposal. With no life sciences, no subsidies. This could make the housing a lot less affordable in the end unless other subsidies are found.” — Pip L., Jamaica Plain

“Education needs to be key in Boston and surrounding areas. Better educational facilities should facilitate better learning opportunities for students. Keep some of what Boston has been built on like Madison’s ORC which teaches out children trades like electricity, construction and journalism. The housing that is always promised seems to always turn less affordable than affordable as it consistently falls through the loopholes of this city’s rules and regulations. I’ve watched the transition through the years and am not impressed by how it has affected our youth at all. These words are spoken by a youth coach for 30+ years!” — John S., Dorchester

“BPS buildings are old and inadequate to deliver a 21st century educational experience. Indeed, this is part of the reason young families move out of the city. It’s time to prioritize the implementation of a comprehensive school building plan.” — David H., Dorchester

“I’m voting to build a brand new and improved campus. Included a football field, score field, baseball and softball field. A state of the art basketball court, fitness gym, swimming, dance studio, as well as all of the vocational programs.” — Rasheedah A., Dorchester

“Madison Park is the only vocational high school in the city. Not every child wants, or is able, to go to college, so this is a very valuable educational resource for students. Young people can graduate with a viable employment skill. I’m not sure if they already have a program for this, but they should have a direct path into union trades upon graduation.” — Collette, Brighton

“My name is Robert J., class of 1978. When we moved to that space in 1977, the space was not even completed… Fast forward 50 plus years later we still do not have a complete building, because we have to share the space with John D O’Bryant … Parcel 3 is the best option right now for us to get a brand new building without looking for any other space that is not available at this time. We have the only vocational school in the city of Boston that serves students to have the opportunity of an education and vocation experience which will make them more marketable when they graduate. But you need a state-of-the-art facility to turn this initiative into a great investment.” — Robert J., Mattapan

“Madison is growing and will house 7th and 8th graders in coming years. There is a need for students to be trained in trades and this decrepit building is vastly undeserving the students.” — E.A., Dorchester

“The city, and Roxbury, desperately need housing. However, it is absolutely true that a life science / lab company isn’t going to be there to fortify the investment. Because of this, the developer should try to find a different set of investors for the commercial space. Surely some industry exists that needs space and can wait for the build-out.” — Firma F., Mattapan

title: 'Boston is a better place because of you:' Readers share heartfelt farewell messages to Jaylen Brown
text:
Jaylen Brown’s decade-long run with the Celtics is coming to an end, but his connection to Boston is far from over.

Brown, who arrived in Boston as the No. 3 pick in the 2016 NBA Draft, established himself as a key player in the Celtics’ storied history. Over 10 seasons, he became a five-time All-Star, helped Boston win the 2024 NBA championship, and became a prominent presence in the city well beyond the basketball court.

Brown was traded to the Philadelphia 76ers this summer, ending his Boston tenure unexpectedly for many fans. Before he begins the next chapter of his career, Brown is giving Boston fans a chance to say goodbye and celebrate his tenure.

Brown will host “741 Frequency Fest” on Sunday, Aug. 30, at Boston Common. The free, public event will run from 2 to 7 p.m. at the Charles Street entrance and will feature music, games, giveaways, back-to-school activities, surprise performances and a special concert.

The celebration is also a thank-you from Brown to the city and fans who supported him throughout his Celtics career.

And Boston fans had plenty to say in return.

After we asked readers to share their farewell messages to Brown, over a hundred responses poured in from across the region and beyond. Many readers thanked him not only for what he accomplished as a Celtics player, but also for the work he did in the community and the example he set away from the court.

“You became the heart and soul of Boston. Thank you for all you’ve done for the Celtics and for the city,” said Melissa T. of Watertown.

For some readers, Brown’s departure was especially difficult because of the player and person they watched him become during his time in Boston.

“One of the greatest Boston Celtics in their storied history. A source of inspiration to many Celtic fans. Poised, confident, consistent and a leader both on the basketball court and in the community. Thanks Jaylen!” said Bobby A. of Acton

Others are already looking ahead to the celebration at the Common, seeing it as one more opportunity to honor Brown before he puts on a 76ers uniform.

“It’s definitely going to be bittersweet to see you go. You contribute so much to the Celtics and we appreciate all the time that you spent with our incredible team. Thank you for everything, forever a Jaylen Brown fan!” said Michelle F. of Fall River.

Below, readers share their full farewell messages to Brown.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

What’s your farewell message to Jaylen Brown?

“I have been a fan since you came to the Celtics. You were the heart of the team. You were a wonderful example and teacher to the new players and for the people of Boston. I wish you all the best. If you take the title The Sixers I will be celebrating you. Thank you for all you have done for Boston.” — Joyce J., Beverly

“I appreciate how much you embraced the communities of color of Boston. A lot of people ignore the true diversity of the city and we felt seen by you. We’ll miss you and don’t be a stranger! You always have a home here.” — Brandi, Dorchester

“JB, you have given your heart to Boston. Don’t think for one second that Boston will ever forget that. You will always be a Bostonian, in our eyes. We will be watching. Best of luck.” — Chuck G., Mattapan

“Jaylen Brown, you dog, you absolute jaw dropping beast. Every time I watched you play on the court it was like watching a master at a craft, sculpting themselves into my life. You inspired me to watch my home team more when you were drafted with JT. Off the court, your intellect, maturity, and humbleness resonate deeply with me-and have been ever since I was a little kid. I’ll be going up to Boston on my birthday on the 29th to move into college and I’ll be at that party on the 30th.” — Gabriel R., Woods Hole

“Thank you Jalen for being what a true Boston Celtic is all about. Giving it your all every game, Volunteering in multiple events for the people of Boston, being a true professional on and off the court, adding an 18th title to our list of victorious moments and of course your loyalty to the organization. It still stings a lot that you will be playing for another team. At the end of your career, I do hope to see your name and number up in our rafters. You truly truly deserve to be placed up there. You may be playing for the 76’ers now, but we all know inside that you’ll be Bleeding Green. Hope you make your way back some day. I wish you the best!” — Rey R., Gardner

“This one hurts. JB has been my favorite player through all the ups and downs, and watching him grow, prove people wrong, and ultimately help bring another championship to Boston made it that much better. I never thought I’d see the day he’d be wearing another jersey, especially a Philly one. I’ll always be a Celtics fan, but I’ll always be a Jaylen Brown fan too. Thank you for everything, 7uice.” — Javid M., Queens, New York

“JB, Your contributions to the Celtics and the city of Boston are immeasurable. You showed us to always give your best effort, keep a positive attitude and have fun. Thanks for the memories and thanks for being awesome. You’re a class act.” — Bobby D., Winthrop

“Watching you play basketball with the Celtics was so much fun. Thank you. But, watching you and reading about what you do off the court is who I admire more. You are so much more than a great basketball player. You are a beautiful, kind, caring human being. Basketball is fun, but caring and taking care of people you love and those you don’t even know, is so much more important. Thank you for all you do outside of basketball. I will continue to watch you in Philly, but more importantly, I will continue to follow you as you continue to make this world a little better for so many who need people like you.” — Michelle A., Pembroke

“I’ve so enjoyed watching you play and appreciate all of the wonderful things you’ve done for our city. What a rare and wonderful combination you possess: Athletic, intelligence, altruism — amazing! My son and I have already made plans to travel to Philly to watch you shine in the City of Brotherly Love! Best of luck to you.” — Alison V., Hingham

“Thank you, Jaylen Brown, for your work and continued work in the Black neighborhoods of Boston. Thank you for being a Player that the Black Communities of Boston could look up to … I wish you the best of luck. I look forward to watching you succeed with the 76ers and know that you still have fans in the Black Communities of Boston. Go 76ers.” — Sherrod, Roxbury

“Jaylen: Writing this is incredibly tough, but I just want to say thank you. Not seeing you on the roster this season is going to hurt deeply. For nine years, you gave absolutely everything to this city. You put your head down, embraced every challenge, and led us to Banner 18. Watching you win Finals MVP was the perfect reward for your relentless grind and grit. Boston is a better place because of you, both on and off the court. Your work in the community and your heart for the youth here will leave a lasting impact long after your basketball days are over. I am so incredibly grateful for the memories, the passion, and the championship. I will miss seeing you wear the green and white, but I wish you nothing but the absolute best in this next chapter. You will always be a champion in Boston. Thank you, JB.” — Mary P., Methuen

“This is not good bye because your legacy will live on throughout New England. Here in our corner of Maine, your example of hard work, tenacity and grit is a frequent topic among friends and families. You led a team last season to reach far better heights utilizing all those things and more. It was a fun year to see you lead a team counted out by the NBA pundits. And no one, and I mean no one presently on the squad will, duplicate what you brought to the Celtics. Thanks for the memories. You are irreplaceable and will be sorely missed come fall.” — Ellie M., Midcoast Maine

“You will be more deeply missed than you can imagine for your great heart, compassion and help for others, being a great inspiration and role model and of course a joy to watch and root for on the court. With so much sadness and admiration from a 76-year-old granny/fan/ season ticket holder. I wish you and your family all the best.” — Pam J., Boston

title: Readers overwhelmingly support capping ticket resale prices. Here's why.
text:
Boston.com readers overwhelmingly support a proposal to cap resale ticket prices in Massachusetts – a measure that has been taken up by lawmakers and New England musicians alike.

The amendment, No. 20, titled “To make music affordable by reining in predatory ticket scalping,” was filed by Sen. Dylan Fernandes, a Falmouth Democrat representing Plymouth and Barnstable. It was one of 595 amendments attached to the Senate’s $325 million economic development bill (S. 3187), which senators passed on Thursday.

The amendment, based on “Noah Kahan” legislation he filed in June, would cap the resale price of concert tickets at 110% of the original ticket’s face value, and limit service fees charged by resale platforms to no more than 10% of the total price. It would also ban the sale of “speculative tickets,” tickets a reseller lists or advertises without actually possessing, and prohibit resale websites from deceptively marketing themselves as official or affiliated with a venue, team, or artist. The attorney general’s office would be authorized to bring enforcement actions against violators.

The push to rein in resale prices gained momentum last week when Gov. Maura Healey picked up the legislation, dubbing it “The Great Divide Act.” Announcing the bill, Healey said she wanted to make sure “Massachusetts fans can better afford to see their favorite performer or team.”

Noah Kahan, who made history this summer as the first artist to headline four consecutive sold-out shows at Fenway Park, joined Healey’s announcement virtually and endorsed the measure, saying “I love my fans and want to protect them however I can.”

Over 40 New England-based artists, including the Dropkick Murphys, the Pixies, and MGMT, joined the Vermont-native in signing a letter Thursday throwing their support behind the amendment.

“Live performance should not be a luxury. Our art is not a commodity to be bought and resold at extreme markups against our wishes,” the letter read.

Ahead of the Senate’s session, Fernandes told Boston.com his amendment is simply about “making music more affordable for people.”

“[This is about] making sure the money stays in the pocket of Massachusetts residents and doesn’t just go to these massive private equity-backed ticket scalping software companies,” he said. “We need to take art back and give it back to artists, give it back to fans, and rein in this multi-billion-dollar ticket scalping marketplace in the United States,” he added.

We asked Boston.com readers where they stood on the issue and if they would support capping resale ticket prices in Massachusetts. Of the 165 readers who responded to our poll, 85% said yes, while 15% said no.

Many readers who supported a cap said they’ve been priced out of shows entirely.

“Concert tickets have become cost prohibitive. I’ve been a life long concert goer and I rarely can afford to go anymore,” said Michelle of Needham.

Other readers chimed in with personal experiences of losing out on the opportunity to go to concerts because of sky-high ticket costs.

“I wanted to take my daughter to see Noah Kahan for her 13th birthday,” Michelle H. of Norfolk explained. “I got a presale code but didn’t have any luck getting tix to any of the four Fenway shows. I can’t afford the $600 resale tix so now we aren’t going. That was the only thing on her birthday list.”

Readers opposed to a cap generally argued the market should be left alone.

“I believe in a supply and demand driven market. Yes, some tickets have high resale prices, but I’ve also gone to a lot of shows for cheap,” argued Ric M. of Winchester.

Dave K. from Cambridge agreed, saying “high ticket prices are a function of economic reality here,” and that “the high prices are not a ‘problem,’ they are a functioning market signal of this reality.”

Here’s what else readers had to say.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

Would you support capping resale ticket prices in Massachusetts?

Yes

“The average person should be able to enjoy someone’s music and not have to be price gouged so much when the artist himself didn’t want this to happen. It’s gotten out of control for many artists these days.” — Christina, Ashburn

“It’s nearly impossible to get tickets as a regular fan of an artist and it’s infuriating to see tickets for resale before the regular sale has even begun. The artists don’t get that money — it all goes to the reseller and Ticketmaster (or Live Nation or whoever the platform is). Artists need to be able to reap the benefits of a grueling tour schedule and fans should be able to see the show without fighting off big business.” — Jenny, Southern New Hampshire

“It’s not right that scalpers buy a surplus of tickets and take advantage of people that are desperate to see their favorite artist. Tickets should be accessible to everyone.” — Meghan, Worcester

“High ticket prices propagated by resellers reduce the number of shows we can see live, and reduces the number of performing artists we can support.” — Mark W., Newton

“I’ve been going to concerts for over 40 years and price increases have simply gotten out of control. You expect ticket prices to increase a little bit each year but over the past 10 years the increases have been enormous. Even the ‘cheap seats’ are over $100 for a big show with better seats pushing upwards of $350+. Then tack on a massive fee which is based on the cost of the ticket, not the cost to issue it. Years ago the fee was the same regardless of the seat location or price and it was actually printed on paper by a human being. Now it’s all automated with digital tickets issued by a computer and somehow it costs more?” — Jack, Lynn

“Noah Kahan resale ticket market is financially gouging. Resellers are fleecing the public because they are allowed to and there is demand from buyers.” — Scott S., Boston

“It has been impossible to get tickets for shows because they are sold out in minutes, only to later see tickets for those same shows go up online the next day for 2-3x the price! Tickets should be for the fans, not the scalpers.” — A.B., South Shore

“I don’t consider myself poor, but funflation has made going out a rare occurrence as LiveNation/Ticketmaster, a de facto monopoly, continues to abuse their position to gouge consumers … Greedy corporations would rather have empty stadiums than price things fairly (and profitably). The arts for everyone, not just the 1%!” — Peter G., Roxbury

No

“The idea of restricting the free market economy in this way is obscene. A person who buys a concert ticket must be able to legally re-sell it for whatever another person is willing to pay for it. I refuse to have my tax money spent by the government enforcing idiotic (and probably unconstitutional) restrictions upon honest business transactions in which citizens agree to participate. If ticket sellers place, by the contracts of ticket purchases, restrictions upon how their tickets can honestly be resold, concertgoers should refuse to purchase those tickets.” — Lyman O., Cambridge

“Because the primary seller (usually Ticketmaster) would then have the ability to increase face value even more than it already is. Tickets to concerts are a want, not a need. Everyone is not entitled to a ticket to a show, and if they want to go they can go to a secondary resale site and purchase a ticket (safely and securely) that reflects the true market value of said ticket. Resale caps will block a seller for selling at its true value and force sales to less secure sites like craigslist, etc. This will 100000% increase scams and bad actors. People who make these ridiculous laws are the same that didn’t get a Taylor Swift ticket, and while it might seem like a harmless idea, you would be creating a black market for any show that has more demand than supply. That is not good for anyone.” — Kevin, Wilmington

“Resellers will likely figure out loophole(s) which will inevitably make the experience of live entertainment even worse when buying tickets second hand. There is no way this proposed legislation will have the teeth necessary to make price gauging go away, and Massachusetts doesn’t have the resources to enforce this law either.” — Alex, Swampscott

“It’s a private enterprise, the government should stay out of it. It should be between a willing buyer and willing seller. If you don’t want to pay, don’t go.” — Stan, Jamaica Plain

“Why does this state feel the need to legislate everything? Focus on making everyday life more affordable than worrying about concert tickets.” — Gus

title: 'I saw the dorsal fin': Readers recall close encounters with sharks
text:
Massachusetts waters are known for their beauty — and, occasionally, for their predators.

After the first great white shark of the season was spotted off the coast, we asked Boston.com readers to share their own encounters with these ocean visitors.

From fleeting glimpses of dorsal fins slicing through the waves to near-miss moments that left hearts racing, readers’ stories reveal a surprising mix of fear, fascination, and even humor.

Some recounted close encounters while fishing or kayaking; others watched from a boat or while wading, only to realize that the “rock” beneath their feet was actually a shark. A few reported unexpected moments of awe, like sharks appearing to guide them to safety rather than menace them.

Whether they took place off the Massachusetts coast or during travels farther afield, the tales reveal the many ways sharks can leave a lasting impression on the people who cross paths with them. Here’s what our readers had to say.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

Readers share their most memorable shark encounters

“While fishing on the seawall of Langone Park in the North End about 10 years ago, just before sunrise and not too long after low tide, I saw the dorsal fin of a 5 foot shark, about 50 feet from the seawall. It had a dark to black tip.” — John W., North End

“I was kayaking off Plum Island in Newburyport a few years ago when the rip tide took me out to sea. I tried paddling back to shore with no success. I prayed to get back to shore. I was very, very scared. And then, a shark swam underneath me to create a current back to shore under the kayak. I successfully managed to get back to shore. It wasn’t there to eat me, it was there to answer my prayer.” — Sergei D., Newburyport

“Nearly stepped on an angel shark at Seabrook Beach [in New Hampshire] in 2002. Was wading in about 3 feet of water and it looked like a rock.” — A.R., Cambridge

“Not a scary encounter, but I was on a whale watch tour out of Plymouth. As our boat was returning, and I was standing on the side of the boat, I watched a shark swim right under.” — Paul, Mashpee

“While scuba diving in Key Largo [in Florida] there were a few nurse sharks, probably 5 or 6 feet long, that were quite annoyed by us swimming in their water. We were told by our guide to keep our fingers close to the body and to not hit them in the face. No worries at all; they were quite rude at times, bumping into us.” — Ben M., Roxbury

“In Florida at S. Augustine Beach a 6-foot black tip shark swam right by me following a group of bait fish.” — Jon, North Andover

“While returning to the shore at Waterlemon Cay on Saint John [in the U.S. Virgin Islands] a 5-foot shark swam about 2 feet in front of my mask in about 2 feet of water.” — Alan P., Deerfield, New Hampshire

title: Readers say political debates should be mandatory. Here’s why.
text:
As Massachusetts heads into the November general election, a wave of Democratic incumbents are declining or have yet to accept a debate with their Republican challengers, which Boston.com readers say is ‘disrespectful to voters.’

State Treasurer Deb Goldberg has turned down several debate invitations from GOP challenger Elizabeth Dionne, including one from GBH, according to the Boston Herald. Attorney General Andrea Campbell has similarly avoided committing to a debate against Republican Michael Walsh, pointing to a signature-collection dispute that temporarily knocked him off the ballot before an appeal restored his spot.

And in the 6th Congressional District, Democratic nominee Dan Koh recently pulled out of two scheduled debates against Republican Micah Jones, telling the Herald through a spokesperson that he’s already done 11 debates and hundreds of community events this cycle.

Not every Democratic incumbent is dodging debates, though. Gov. Maura Healey has locked in two October debates against Republican Mike Minogue. It is not clear when those debates will be held. Boston.com reached out to Healey and Minogue’s campaigns, but did not hear back in time for publication.

In the U.S. Senate race, the Massachusetts Republican Party said in a Facebook post Wednesday that nominee John Deaton has accepted all four televised general-election debate invitations from Massachusetts television stations WWLP-22News in Springfield, Boston 25, WCVB, and WBZ.

“Every one of these invitations should be honored, especially Western Massachusetts,” Deaton said in the Facebook post, adding that if Sen. Ed Markey “wants to pick Boston stages and skip Springfield, that is his choice. It will not be mine.”

Markey’s campaign did not respond to Boston.com’s request for more information in time for publication, but told the Herald a debate is still coming, with details expected “in the coming weeks.”

The stakes may be higher than usual in a state where so many voters don’t enroll with either party. According to the Independent Voter Project, Massachusetts has the highest share of unenrolled voters of any state in the country. State data show that in the 2026 state primary earlier this month, roughly 67% of more than 5.1 million registered voters were unenrolled (“independent”), compared to about 24% registered Democratic and 8% Republican.

When we asked readers if political candidates should be required to debate their opponents before an election, the overwhelming majority (88%) of the 95 respondents said yes.

“It’s the only way to understand how the candidates differ on issues,” said reader James V. of the South End.

Another argued that skipping a debate shows a “lack of skills needed to do the job.”

“We need to know how they stand on issues and challenges to their stances. It is what they run for,” argued Damian M. of Plymouth.

A few readers pushed back, with one framing it as a free-speech issue; candidates, they said, have the right not to speak just like anyone else, while another argued debates don’t do much good without real-time fact-checking.

Still, for most respondents, the message to candidates was simple: show up and present your platform to voters.

“Informed voters are the best voters,” said Dan of Charlestown.

Below, readers share why they want political candidates to debate their opponents.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

Yes

“Candidates should debate their opponents at least once each election cycle, and honestly, more often is better. Debates give voters a chance to hear where candidates stand, see how they think on their feet, and evaluate them without the filter of ads, endorsements, or campaign signs. Signs don’t vote, people do, and if we’re trusting someone with that much responsibility, we should have the opportunity to hear them discuss the issues that matter most to voters.” — Corey D., South Boston

“We need to hear their views and answer questions from us, the media, and the other candidates. Understanding how they think and how they answer tough questions also gives insight into their character.” — Matilda, Westford

“Yes. Debate is necessary for a healthy democracy. As we saw with President Biden’s performance during the 2024 Presidential Election, debate performances can change everything. Candidates should earn their seats by presenting why they are a better alternative to their challengers. Failure to participate in a debate shows a sense of entitlement, particularly for the incumbent; that defending their platform is beyond them. It’s offputting and is disrespectful to the voters.” — Jordan F., East Boston

“A candidate unwilling to discuss, explain and defend their positions should be a major red flag for all voters. But sadly, politics has become largely tribal. However, we should make debates mandatory for undecided, independent voters. Candidates should have to stand up in front of the state and defend prior comments, clarify position points, and pitch their case.” — David, Wakefield

“Debate’s are important to help educate the voters on the positions of each candidate. They make sure they choose someone who best represents them in the elected office.” — Andrew, Chatham

“We need the ability to look beyond the party lines of Democrat and Republican, and really hear their viewpoints on all subjects, local, and national. Get a better understanding of their plans (if they have any), how rational and realistic they are. We need more than attack ads to go by when voting.” — Justin, Cape Cod

“The debate is literally the job interview for public office. Anyone who is not willing to debate their opponent has no business at all running for office.” — Nick, Lynn

“It’s public office, not a private role hidden from discussing your goals and vision. Massachusetts has one of the highest percentages of unenrolled voters that use debates as a way to decide to vote for. Candidates that reject an invite to debate, I almost never vote for.” — James, Quincy

No

“Candidates have free speech protection just like the rest of us. That includes not speaking or choosing where to speak. It is incumbent on the opponent to highlight this flaw/fear and lead the public to believe what they want them to about the refusal to debate.” — Alex, Roxbury

“Because there is no fact check on the candidates. Anyone can lie.” — Nancy, Peabody

“I don’t care if they do or don’t – but if they don’t they lose my vote.” — Philip D., Quincy

title: ‘Outrageous’: Here’s how much readers’ electric bills have been this summer so far
text:
Electric rates jumped for Massachusetts customers on Aug. 1, and while the increase should only directly hit a portion of the state’s residents, many Boston.com readers say they’re already feeling squeezed by their summer electric bills.

Ahead of the rate change, we asked readers whether they were worried about the hike and asked them to share what they’ve actually been paying each month this summer. The response was clear: Readers are concerned, and many say their bills already feel unaffordable.

Of 103 people who answered Boston.com’s poll question, “Are you concerned about the Aug. 1 electric rate increase?,” 88% of respondents said yes, they were concerned. Eleven said they weren’t, and one reader said they weren’t sure.

The rate change applies to “basic service” customers, who buy their electricity supply directly from their utility rather than through an alternative arrangement. According to the Massachusetts Department of Public Utilities, roughly 27% of customers served by Eversource, National Grid and Unitil were on basic service as of April 1. The remaining 73% get their power either through a municipal aggregation plan, in which a city or town negotiates supply rates on residents’ behalf, or through a contract with a competitive supplier selected on their own.

Basic service prices are set through a competitive bidding process and, by state law, are required to change at least twice a year. For Eversource East customers on basic service, bills are projected to rise by about 4.75%; Eversource West customers could see an increase of about 6.68%. National Grid customers on basic service face an estimated 3.08% increase, while Unitil customers could see bills rise by about 5.88%.

By contrast, municipal aggregation plans — now offered in more than 240 Massachusetts cities and towns — tend to lock in supply prices for longer stretches, sometimes multiple years, giving residents more pricing stability than basic service typically offers.

Some readers pointed to their own experience with local power arrangements.

Matt of Winthrop said the promise that most bills won’t change doesn’t match what he’s already paying: “[I pay] 550-600 a month already … Utilities here in MA are already way too high and above the national average.”

Michael W. of Mansfield noted that his town isn’t on municipal aggregation at all — it has its own municipal light plant, a separate arrangement in which the town itself owns and runs the local utility.

“I am on a muni – Mansfield Municipal Electric Department. Why are people not signing on to community solar?” he asked.

Below, in their own words, readers share how much they’ve actually been paying for electricity this summer.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

How much have your electric bills been per month for summer 2026?

“Average of at least $700 a month. Absolutely outrageous. We are conscious of usage and have an ‘energy efficient’ home — LED everything, Hue lighting, Nest products, Emporia Energy monitoring system etc.” — B.G., Beverly

“$700.” — Steve, Melrose

“$500 due to the transportation and adding for clean energy initiatives. Outrageous!” — Joe, Brighton

“$500+.” — Sean, Barnstable

“I’m on an estimated plan that goes all year and I pay $411 per month.” — V., Waltham

“$400+ in June. Can’t wait to see the July bill.” — Kathy C., Westborough

“In 2026: July not received yet, $350 in June, $281 in May. We have heat pumps/AC (whole house) & two EVs. In 2025: $427 in July, $292 in June, and $210 in May.” — Rick W., Brookline

“Typically my monthly electric is between $40-$50 until we hit June with the hot and humid heatwaves, running the two window AC units consistently. June payment was $238.” — Suzy Q., Lynn

“I just paid one for $207 in a 1200 sq. ft. apartment. Of course more than half is in so-called delivery charges.” — Peter, Dorchester

“$200 or more.” — Sarah S., Fitchburg

“I was out of town for six weeks this summer. My electric bill was still $150 for the one month I was gone entirely. All I left running at home was my fridge and two dehumidifiers set to 50%. That to me is absurd and another example as to why our state is becoming even more unaffordable for anyone but the wealthy.” — Alex B., Bedford

“June 2026: $84.76. July 2026: $110.62.” — T.J., Roxbury

“Typically $40 to $50 per month in summer since my wife and I don’t use window AC units.” — Tim S., Acton

“$0. I have rooftop solar panels sized to my usage. The higher the rates go, the more money I’m saving!” — Tom, Haverhill

Boston.com occasionally interacts with readers by conducting informal polls and surveys. These results should be read as an unscientific gauge of readers’ opinion.

title: 'Foolish not to use it': Readers want ShotSpotter back in Cambridge
text:
Cambridge has been grappling with renewed scrutiny of its decision to drop ShotSpotter after the July 4 killing of city worker Xavier Bautista.

Authorities say Bautista, 32, was shot during an early-morning overtime shift and that his body wasn’t found for more than an hour. Prosecutors have charged one man, Rayquon R. Brown, 29, of Canton, in connection with the killing and said the attack appears to have been random, carried out by a group who allegedly set out looking for someone to shoot. Brown was charged on Monday and pleaded not guilty to murder, illegal gun possession, and being an armed career criminal. He was ordered held without bail.

Police unions have argued that the absence of the gunshot-detection system, which the City Council voted to discontinue in May, delayed the discovery of Bautista and the response to the scene.

“It is plausible that an active ShotSpotter system could have resulted in first responders arriving on-scene to render aid to the victim more quickly, particularly in this case when the shooting was not reported via 9-1-1,” Cambridge Police Department spokesperson Sgt. Robert Reardon told CambridgeDay.

The case has reignited a debate that split the council earlier this year, and Boston.com wanted to know where readers stood. We asked if Cambridge City Council should bring back the use of the technology. Of 117 readers who weighed in, the response was overwhelmingly in favor (91%) of bringing back ShotSpotter. Nine percent said no, and just one reader was unsure.

Many who favor bringing the technology back pointed directly to Bautista’s death as proof of what’s lost without it, arguing that faster detection could have meant a faster response.

As one reader, Alex of Roxbury, put it, “It is not perfect, but this technology is useful in quickly identifying very serious and time sensitive incidents.”

Another reader, A.A. of Cambridge, was more blunt: “Common sense to use such technology to safeguard the residents. Foolish not to use it.”

A smaller group of readers pushed back, questioning whether the system actually improves outcomes and whether its cost – $50,000 per year, covered by a federal grant, according to GBH – is justified, given that it may flag gunfire that doesn’t correspond to any reported crime.

Below, readers share their thoughts on reinstroducing ShotSpotter in Cambridge.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

Cambridge City Council voted to end the use of ShotSpotter in May. Should the city bring it back?

Yes, Cambridge should bring ShotSpotter back

“A gunshot is a gunshot, no matter which neighborhood it happens in, and every resident deserves a rapid response. Concerns about police bias are serious, but they should lead to reform – not to throw away a system that can quickly alert to the discharge of a weapon. Our community’s response to gun violence is only as strong as our ability to know a threat exists in the first place.” — Colin F., Cambridge

“It is beyond ridiculous to remove a type of technology that alerts law enforcement to shots fired in our neighborhoods. There is no logical reason to take that away from us, and I say that as someone who lives in a neighborhood where ShotSpotter is used. Cambridge needs to reconsider this misguided policy.” — CeeCee, Boston

“I voted ‘yes’ to bring ShotSpotter back because the recent tragedy showed what can happen when a gunshot goes undetected for nearly an hour. Even if no single technology guarantees prevention, acoustic detection gives first responders a chance to reach victims faster, especially when no one calls 911. And for what it’s worth, if it saves even one life through quicker notification — the same standard often used when debating gun laws — then restoring it strengthens public safety and closes a gap we now know exists.” — A.J.M., Goffstown, New Hampshire

“It’s possible that Xavier’s life could have been saved or comforted in the last moments of his life if the ShotSpotter technology hadn’t been turned off. This technology would have given the police the right tools to support their investigation by allowing them to reach the crime scene within minutes. Cambridge City Council, you’re sworn to uphold the law and protect citizens by ensuring a safe, secure quality of life. We are all watching. We want a full reversal! And while you’re at it, put back the Flock Cameras. Do what is right! Protect our police and citizens; give them the proper tools so this doesn’t happen again. Xavier deserved better. His family deserves better. Cambridge deserves better.” — Carrie P., Cambridge

“I abhor government and corporate tracking such as license plate readers, flock safety cameras, even Apple family sharing (or is it tracking) but ShotSpotter is different. The tech simply helps to identify where a gunshot has occurred; it’s not surveillance of a person or specific spot but an acoustic device that identifies gunshots which are most often illegal in city settings. Never underestimate the Cambridge City Council’s penchant for making terrible decisions.” — Dan, Boston

No, Cambridge should not bring ShotSpotter back

“Shot Spotter isn’t going to stop anyone from pulling the trigger. Let’s see the metrics on how much faster law enforcement responds to gunfire with ShotSpotter versus witness phone calls, and then show me the metrics of how many more suspects are apprehended because of ShotSpotter; then show me the metrics of the deterrent effect of the use of Shot Spotter. I promise you none will pass the sniff test.” — Robert, Somerville

“How many times did ShotSpotter detect a gunshot and officers were deployed, but there was no gunshot and no crime, and those resources were wasted? The city shouldn’t waste money on ineffective and expensive programs.” — Sarah, Brighton

Boston.com occasionally interacts with readers by conducting informal polls and surveys. These results should be read as an unscientific gauge of readers’ opinion.

title: 'Keep the party going': Readers want bars and restaurants to stay open later
text:
The debate over Massachusetts’ nightlife just got a fresh jolt from the State House.

Late Thursday, the Massachusetts Senate passed a $575.4 million economic development bond bill that, among its many provisions to boost small businesses and fund housing and research, includes a slate of measures its sponsors have dubbed the “fun agenda.”

Included in the agenda was an amendment letting cities and towns opt-in to bring back “happy hour” discounted drink specials for the first time since the 1980s, and a separate provision permanently allowing municipalities to designate “Conviviality Districts” where the public can drink outdoors in specified areas. Both amendments were adopted, and the bill now heads back to the House for further consideration.

The Senate’s vote lands just as the clock is running out on a related, more immediate question: whether Massachusetts should keep bars and restaurants open later.

Back in June, lawmakers approved a temporary pilot letting participating cities and towns push last call to 3 a.m. through the end of July, timed to a summer packed with World Cup matches in Foxborough, 250th anniversary celebrations, and Sail Boston. With that pilot set to expire in less than two weeks, Healey has made clear she wants the later hours to stick around.

In a WEEI radio interview last week, the governor said of the extended last call, “I’d like that to continue,” describing the push as “about vibe and energy.” She’s also said she expects the summer to have “a lasting positive economic impact” on Massachusetts.

We asked Boston.com readers whether they’d support making later bar and restaurant hours permanent, and the responses were clear: no later last call, no party.

Of the 233 respondents to our poll, a whopping 70% said they would support keeping bars and restaurants open later, while just over a quarter were against it. Just 4% were unsure.

Many readers who favored keeping the later hours pointed to what other major cities offer and argued Massachusetts’ current rules feel outdated.

“Every other major city does this and the nightlife and culture are better for it. Being so puritanical is just shooting ourselves in the foot,” reader A.N.C. said.

Craig of Middleton said he remembers having access to late-night bars and restaurants when he was younger and doesn’t understand why his own kids don’t have that “privilege” now.

“Personally, I think it is lame our bars aren’t open until 2-3 am,” he said.

But not every reader was on board. Kristen of Melrose said the risks outweigh the benefits, warning that later hours could mean “too many additional drunk drivers on the roads later into the night, more fights, more assaults, and not enough police resources.”

Below, see how readers responded in full.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

Would you support keeping later bar and restaurant hours in Massachusetts?

Yes

“Any opportunity we have to assist our locally owned, independent businesses is an opportunity that should not be missed. Also, the Governor should seriously consider relinquishing the State’s oversight of liquor licenses and give municipalities full ownership of licenses and issuance.” — Courtney O., Somerville

“100% Yes. Boston has been joyful and fun during the World Cup, let’s keep evolving into a world class destination for living and visiting!” — Bill C., Downtown Boston

“Good for the economy, tourists, keeping young people here who are already paying an exorbitant amount to live here. People use ride share apps to get around so no big deal if the T stops earlier.” — Sean H., West Roxbury

“I have seen in many forums that Boston is considered a boring city as far as nightlife goes. And the fact that we don’t have happy hour because of some silly antiquated law also really kills the vibe. I am not saying we have to be the next Las Vegas, it just would be nice to have more nightlife options and bring a little more life to the city. Young people are mostly moving out of the city/Massachusetts due to the cost of living, but it certainly wouldn’t hurt if we offered a little more fun too.” — K.T., Westford

“Growing up in Boston, it was always unclear to me why our city did not allow longer hours for both bars and public transportation. With all the universities and now gentrified areas, it seems as though the state is missing out on significant revenue opportunities by not allowing businesses to run late.” — N.D.W., Roslindale

“Why not? People don’t have to stay out late if they don’t want to, but to be a fun city we need to have the choice” — Joe M., South Boston

“This state already has enough outdated and ridiculous laws, particularly regarding alcohol. It’s time for MA to join the 21st century.” — Brian

“When I go to other cities in the US and abroad, I enjoy the options and energy of late night options and culture in general.” — James L., Provincetown

“It will be good for the economy and Uber drivers like myself!” — Nick K., Boston

No

“Later bar hours will result in more young people getting drunk and causing trouble. More noise, more litter, more accidents causing damage to property and vehicles, injuries and death to people. Potential problems on public transportation. Disturbances in residential neighborhoods statewide. If the state wants to increase revenue, there are other, better ways to do it.” — Jacqueline L., Brighton

“If people cannot restrain themselves from still using their cell phone while driving, you cannot be sure that the same lack of common sense will not prevail when it comes to happy hour or extended hours.” — Sue K., Centerville

“More inebriated drivers on the road increasing Speed, wrong way driving, overall impairment.” — Gina

“Nothing good will come of it. It will likely increase public safety issues and over drinking by patrons.” — Michael S.
