title: Is the U.S. the greatest country in the world? Readers are deeply divided.
text:
As the country hurtles toward its 250th anniversary on Saturday, Boston.com asked readers a simple but loaded question: Is the United States the greatest country in the world? More than 150 answered, and the results reveal a readership — and by extension, perhaps, a country — deeply divided.

Of the 159 respondents, 41% said yes, the U.S. remains the greatest country on Earth. Just under a quarter (23%) landed in the middle, arguing the country is not the greatest, but is still pretty good. And 36% said the U.S. is not the greatest country at all.

“America has been and still is the land of opportunity. No other country can compare,” wrote Robert P. Durham of Connecticut, echoing the sentiment of many “yes” voters who pointed to opportunity, freedom, and the enduring pull the U.S. has on people around the world.

Others weren’t ready to go that far, but weren’t ready to give up on the country either.

“A bad day in the US can still be a good day in a lot of places. But compared to our similar counterpart countries and who we used to be we have fallen far off the pedestal,” wrote Beth of Ayer.

But for many respondents, the answer was a hard “no.”

“America is number one at infant mortality, child obesity, arms sales, pollution, and medical bankruptcy. It remains the greatest country in its widespread military bases. Its remaining exports are social discord, avarice, and gratuitous violence,” wrote Cam B. of Worcester.

The mixed verdict comes at a strange moment for national pride. This summer, the World Cup has brought millions of visitors streaming into U.S. cities — including Boston, where kilted Scotland supporters have been a fixture downtown — for a monthlong celebration that’s injected a burst of community and goodwill into the country.

But scratch the surface of readers’ responses, and that goodwill runs up against deeper, more entrenched anxieties about democracy, inequality, and, for many respondents, about the direction the country has taken under the Trump administration.

Reader after reader cited the current political climate as the reason their faith in American exceptionalism has cracked, even as many of the same respondents said they still believe in the country’s underlying promise of freedom and equality formed 250 years ago.

Below, readers share their thoughts on the United States’ place on the world stage.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

Do you think the US is the greatest country in the world?

Yes

“In spite of Trump, MAGA and the last few years, I still believe that the US can restore its position as leader of the free world and model for third world countries struggling to be democracies.” — Andrew F.

“People take for granted all of the freedoms we have. They trivialize it. In many other countries they would be jailed or worse for expressing their views.” — Tom W., North Shore

“My parents are both immigrants. They had to leave their country due to extreme poverty and hardship. They immigrated to the US and built a foundation from absolutely nothing for my brother and I to have a roof over our heads, food on the table, clothes and shoes, and a good education. My brother and I are now a medical doctor and an engineer, respectively. I don’t think there’s any other country in the world where this could have been pulled off successfully. It saddens me that so many Americans have such a negative view of the country, almost to the point of hatred. It’s far from perfect, but it’s still the greatest. I think it’s okay to be proud to be an American while still recognizing the imperfections.” — Alain M., Waltham

“The US has been a global force for liberty for 250 years. What other power has stood stronger against the scourge of socialism and saved Europe twice?” — Dave, North Shore

“We are still the land of opportunity and that’s why millions of people want to come and live here. We have the most powerful military in the world.” — Tim S., Acton

“The US may not be perfect, but it beats any other country in the world in terms of freedom, education, women’s rights, quality of living, and a myriad of other factors. The grass is always greener, but at the end of the day, the US beats any other country by a country mile.” — Megan

“We have advanced technology and the best fighting forces. We have many educational institutions and medical advances. Look at all the professional sports teams we have, and forms of entertainment. People all over the world want to come here. If you work hard and make wise choices you can be successful. We have many freedoms that people don’t appreciate. They are conditioned to complain about everything that is not perfect. People take for granted that we have clean water, sanitation, many modes of transportation, the internet that allows us to have products and food delivered without leaving home, all kinds of services for the elderly, and free programs for the less fortunate. We have a legal system. We can practice our religion. We are able to make choices of what we want to do and where we can travel. Granted, other countries may have similar situations but I have no wish to live in another country. My relatives fought for this country in wars to preserve what we have. We have something worth protecting. That’s why I feel we are the greatest. People and leaders from other countries recognize our strengths as well.” — K.D.J., North of Boston

“Right now it is tarnished, facing its greatest threat from a con man and charlatan. But it is my belief that the constitution will win, that democracy will survive and the current administration will be nothing but a disease that was cured by American strength through the vote!” — Celeste H., Boston

No, but it’s pretty good

“Jingoism is a pretty destructive mindset. And I absolutely hate a certain administration running the show right now. But I do think that there are plenty of reasons to enjoy the United States for its nationhood and its cultures.” — J.H.B., Medford

“We have such dramatic differences in living standards, healthcare access, food security, and education standards in the US that it’s tough to call us the greatest in the world. We are so great in many things — setting the standard for the world in technology, research, culture and innovation — yet so pig-headed, selfish, and short-sighted in other ways. We could choose to be the greatest, but even asking the question results in name-calling, vitriol, and suspicion! With our political environment so awash in money and splintered interests, it’s almost impossible for genuine discourse, respect, and a commitment to a shared vision of what could make us great to happen. The ingredients for our success and demise are in our collective hands. We need leaders who can rise above and appeal to enough of us to come together. Or we need to go our separate ways and Balkanize, admitting we gave it a good run, but our model of government just won’t work anymore. I choose the positive outlook that we can cure what ails us, but it’ll be painful.” — Tim O., Saco, Maine

“I’ve lost my pride. I’m embarrassed to be an American on the world stage. We are openly more corrupt than ever before, we refuse to believe in facts or science, and cozy up to dictators rather than fight for democracy. We are willing to ban books but not guns.” — Todd B., Brookline

“The wheels are falling off. Corruption is rewarded instead of punished. Trump has succeeded in rolling back all the wrong things. The system is unfair, especially to those who should benefit most.” — Michael G., West Roxbury

“It currently is definitely NOT the greatest country in the world and, in fact, arguably one of the worst. What does potentially and to varying degrees make it one of the best is that the majority recognizes the current fraud and many are willing to stand up and fight it.” — Greg L., Hyde Park

“I have faith in our ability to restore our place as the greatest country in the world but I don’t think that’s possible in the age of Trump. I’m old enough to remember the Reagan era and despite living under multiple Democratic and Republican presidents I have never seen anything as acrimonious and dysfunctional as the Trump era.” — Jack, Lynn

Not at all

“The US is in serious decline. Democracy is under assault. We are a violent, frightened people. Any country that values profit above human well-being will eventually collapse, as we saw in the Civil War. There is a great spirit of generosity in the American people, but too many politicians and wealthy people are corrupt and in control.” — Robert B., Cheshire

“Because we are losing top talent, limiting research funding, removing environmental protections that prevent cancer and other harms to citizens, and losing our standing as an ally.” — Candace, Brookline

“Where do I start? If one standard for the best in the world is defined as quality of life, equality for all, sense of happiness and freedom, then we are lagging far far behind. Most of the Scandinavian countries beat us in almost every category. I think the fact that we have the administration we do says what this country values: money. Greed. Selfishness. That’s nothing to be proud of.” — Leslie M., Quincy

“The government has become completely bastardized from what our founding fathers intended. This is no longer a representative democracy. We’ve made politician an occupation, and we are ruled by men who’ve never worked a day in their lives. Men who don’t know what a gallon of milk costs. What minimum wage is. How it feels to get fired. We’ve allowed the most greedy and ignorant among us to ascend to positions they shouldn’t even be adjacent to, and since they have no dignity nor respect for the offices, they use them to grab all the wealth and power they can.” — Anonymous reader, Shrewsbury

“Gen Xer here. I watched an upswing during the course of my lifetime for women and minorities, and now I am watching the conservative courts and corrupt government take us back in time and dismantle all progress and civility brick by brick. I am truly ashamed.” — Mich S., Hyannis

“We are exceptional, all right. But in the wrong ways. We have once again become international bullies. We are seeing many of our Bill of Rights freedoms dissolve and evaporate. We have lost our ability to have civil discourse. We have lost respect, as a country, for those who are different. We are now ruled by fear, anger, and myopia.” — Peter F., Marblehead

Boston.com occasionally interacts with readers by conducting informal polls and surveys. These results should be read as an unscientific gauge of readers’ opinion.

title: Should Massachusetts use automated speed cameras? Here's what 600+ readers said.
text:
Massachusetts lawmakers are weighing a proposal that would allow cities and towns to install automated cameras to ticket drivers for speeding, running red lights, blocking intersections, and other traffic violations. But Boston.com readers largely oppose the measure.

Asked whether they would support the bill, most respondents said they would not. Of the 633 readers who responded to our poll, 74% said they oppose the proposal, 24% said they support it, and just 2% said they were unsure.

Readers who opposed the legislation frequently described it as an invasion of privacy and questioned whether automated cameras should replace police officers in enforcing traffic laws.

“It’s dystopian. A person should be ‘ticketed’ by a human not a machine,” argued Coach from Norwood.

Patrick from Tewksbury went further, calling for “comprehensive legislation to ban this and other types of automated law enforcement.”

Supporters, meanwhile, said dangerous driving has become commonplace across Massachusetts and argued cameras could provide more consistent enforcement where police cannot.

“Running red lights is a constant. I see it multiple times every day. It’s way out of control. It’s dangerous and has to be stopped,” Dave N. from Cambridge said.

Peter from Roxbury agreed and said he has “never felt less safe as a driver, pedestrian, and cyclist.”

It’s clear without meaningful enforcement drivers no longer feel responsible for how they drive. If there are no consequences for breaking the law and endangering others, people will do it without a second thought just for mere convenience,” he said.

The bill, S.2344, remains under further consideration by the Senate’s committee on Ways and Means.

Below, readers share their thoughts on automated speed cameras in Massachusetts.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

Opponents worried about privacy and government surveillance

“I am very concerned and not a fan of the proposed ‘An Act relative to traffic regulation using road safety cameras.’ It’s a major breach of privacy and the honor system of data collection can and will be used against towns and cities. … We don’t need another ‘big brother’ watching our driving patterns. If safety is the main concern, find an alternative solution to recording our every move in public.” — Dan

“We do not need to add to our public data surveillance state.” — A.R., Arlington

“It’s an invasion of privacy and a step in the wrong direction towards a police state.” — Jeff, Needham

Some said human officers should issue tickets, not cameras

“Computers do not understand human needs. The patrolman understands the difference between my impatience, an honest mistake, and if my kid needs a doctor right away. Do not require me to take a day off to litigate my case if human interaction would have prevented it to begin with.” — Bob, Chelmsford

“As in any case involving penalties, the accused is entitled to face his accuser. A machine is incapable of nuance. A cop at an empty intersection who sees a car run through on a yellow-changing-to-red may let the driver off with a friendly reminder and warning, while an automated camera means an automatic trip to traffic court. I’ll learn from another human being 7 days a week and twice on Sunday before taking penalties from a lifeless machine.” — Ed T., Worcester

Some feared the cameras would prioritize revenue over safety

“I do not view this as a way to improve traffic safety, but rather as a way to increase revenue by penalizing even good drivers for minor or trivial issues.” — Jeff, Framingham

“I would support the implementation of cameras if it was specifically for ‘hot zones’ that have a higher rate of fatality or severe accidents, only in an effort to save lives and make the streets safer. But simply for getting additional revenue on a speeder here and there is absurd.” — Joe B., Hingham

“I don’t condone running red lights but give the people a break. Traffic cameras don’t always tell the whole story. What were the road conditions? Was someone tailgating a driver? All this would do is generate more revenue for the state and town levels and impact people’s driving records.” — Chris C., North Andover

Others cited practical concerns

“They installed ticketing cameras here in Middletown, RI, and neighboring Newport within the past year. They have been a nightmare! I have received multiple $50 fines, typically for exceeding the 10 mph buffer over the posted limit by a single mile per hour. Even if I was in the process of slowing down to the proper speed, if I was just that hair too fast as I entered (or exited) the slow zone — bingo! — a ticket in the mailbox came a week later. There have been cases of residents receiving over $1,000 in fines for similar offenses. Don’t do it, Massachusetts!” — Jonathan, Middletown, Rhode Island

“I own multiple cars. Some are primarily used by other family members but registered in my name. That would leave me liable for someone else’s infraction without proof of who is driving.” — P.R., Dracut

Supporters said dangerous driving has become too common

“As a pedestrian, I watch daily as drivers (and cyclists!) blow through red lights, and it has gotten worse since the Covid era and the reduction of enforcement. With absolutely no repercussions to stop this behavior, I would favor this tool to make intersections safer for all users, especially pedestrians.” — C.L.S., Cambridge

“Massachusetts roads have never been more unsafe. As someone involved in privacy related work, I never would have supported something like this in the past. The scales have shifted and the public safety risks on MA roads have become far too great. We must do this responsibly and with proper safeguards within the limits of the forming Mass Data Privacy Act … We need adequate enforcement that has gone beyond law enforcement. I’m a huge supporter of law enforcement officers, but the problem has become bigger than them in my opinion.” — Joe B., Hanover

“Pre-COVID, I would not support this. But lately, drivers have been poor in following speed limit thresholds, distracted driving despite governing laws against it, relying on car sensors too much, rapid delivery drivers, and general impatience. We now have a baby in our car and that’s changed a lot of perspective on safety — and there isn’t going to be an officer at the corner all day to monitor motor traffic, unless humanoid robots take over some of that one day!” — Bob, Natick

Some argued automation is ‘the only way’ to address the issue

“I lived in DC for a couple years, and it definitely pushed folks to follow the traffic laws, though not as much as you would think it would. As long as the speed traps allow for a little leeway (I think DC allows for around 8-10mph leeway). If we are not going to pay for additional law enforcement officers to enforce the law, then we need to automate the enforcement.” — Andrew, South Boston

“In my city it’s become common for cars to speed through red lights, with many sounding their horns to warn drivers and pedestrians. It’s got to stop. And with police defunded, automation is the only way.” — Jorge G., Lowell

“Car operators violate laws and kill pedestrians and cyclists. Ticketing will reduce incidents of law violation and save lives. Concerns about privacy are red herrings. Roadways are public; if you are concerned, don’t drive your car on them.” — Bob F., Bedford

“Absolutely necessary not only to save continued unnecessary private and public property damage, but to save lives from an over abundance of distracted speeding motorists and unaware pedestrians/cyclists.” — John C., Brookline

title: Readers overwhelmingly support a new data center ballot initiative. Here's why.
text:
A new ballot initiative could change how Massachusetts data centers get approved. The measure, filed by West Springfield resident Jim Fleming after residents near Holyoke and Westfield raised concerns about nearby projects, would bar local permitting boards from signing off on a data center until developers meet several conditions. Among them would be a plan to protect ratepayers from higher electric bills and proof that water needs can be met during a drought. Even then, the project would still need approval from two-thirds of local voters to be green-lit.

The proposal is one of several responses to a wave of data center development moving through cities and towns statewide, some of which have already passed their own limits on size or power use. It also arrives alongside two bills in the Legislature addressing electricity costs and environmental requirements tied to the facilities. Fleming’s petition is now awaiting review by the attorney general, who is expected to rule by Sept. 2 on whether it can move forward toward the 2028 ballot.

We asked readers where they stood, and most were in favor. Of 57 people who responded to our informal poll, 46 said they’d support the measure, while 10 said they would not.

Many “yes” respondents framed the initiative as a matter of local control and fairness, arguing that residents — not developers — should bear the final say over projects that could strain infrastructure.

“It’s common sense,” Ted of Belmont said. “Residents’ energy costs shouldn’t have to subsidize data centers, and we need to know the impact on our neighborhoods and environments before more data centers can be built,” he added.

Others pointed to specific concerns close to home. “I live in Lowell and do not like the way the data center here has affected the community,” wrote Joseph S. In April, a group of Lowell residents sued the city’s data center and the state’s environmental regulation agency over concerns about negative impacts to the community.

Jim of Somerville added that any new facility “should not be allowed until they prove they can acquire their own power and soundproof the location so existing neighborhoods are not adversely impacted.”

Readers who opposed the measure mostly zeroed in on the two-thirds voter threshold, calling it too high and not a feasible path to approval.

“The killer is the 2/3 threshold. That will never be met, so it’s effectively a ban,” wrote Jake, of Boston.

Below is a sampling of what readers had to say.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

A new Mass. initiative would prevent local permitting agencies from approving a data center until several conditions are met and two-thirds of local voters approve the project. Do you support?

Yes

“Residents should have more control over their communities, especially when they are the ones suffering the negative impacts of these data centers.” — Sullivan, Nahant

“It’s horrific to see these monstrosities being built in neighborhoods or anywhere, the mass deforestation, the pollution, noise and, most importantly the water and electricity suck that will impact all our sparse wallets. We don’t need data centers. The American people are not considered or respected in this massive invasion for the rich techs. We deserve a vote and I hope we are heard.” — Leslie G., Lexington

“It seems to be a way for local residents to have a real say in this particularly intrusive kind of development in a city or town. It also requires the developer to deal with the real burden this kind of development causes on local infrastructure which often is not addressed because it is not a direct cost, but has been traditionally borne by third parties.” — Dan, Belmont

“Data centers are being constructed way too fast, with very little input from local communities, and minimal forethought about the lasting environmental, economic, and social impacts related to their construction. Communities should have a say in what gets constructed in their back yards and there should be strong regulations that limit the data centers from indirectly making people’s lives more expensive and more difficult. People are quick to jump on the data center band-wagon right now because they’re a hot subject and it seems like the AI boom is unstoppable, but the industry changes so fast and there’s no telling what the need will be in 3-5 years from now as technology progresses and needs adapt. Data centers can’t easily be converted into different types of infrastructure and buildings and we should be cautious about how we approve these buildings that have very little positive impact on local economies just because they’re currently a hot trend.” — Martinez, Boston

“The breakneck push to build AI data centers is largely driven by billionaire CEOs and Wall Street, with little regard to local residents, or even consumers. There needs to be more of a structured, analytical approach to new data center builds to allow for impact assessments to water and electricity capacity.” — Alex, Bedford

“Local voter approval is key. So many Flock contracts and data center contracts are being signed by town/city executives, often hidden behind NDAs, despite strong opposition by the majority of residents. As technology improves and corporate money pours in, these installations and constructions will accelerate beyond control, and voter disapproval is the only brake we have left to avoid a crash.” — Scott J., Boylston

No

“More regulations aren’t the answer. Keep it simple to ensure power and water conservation needs are met.” — Anonymous reader, West Roxbury

“This is such a nanny state. Let them build their data centers.” — Michael S., Lee

“They will be necessary to keep up with the continual growth of communications and the networked world. If not here then where? If the communities where they are built can extract more tax dollars from the business investor then what is the down side?” — Bob B., Milford

“The measure structure basically allows a few to dictate to the majority.” — Chuck H., North Adams

title: 'The cost of living is just too high': Why some Mass. residents want out
text:
Massachusetts remains a draw for many residents because of its schools, health care, and quality of life. But for many Boston.com readers, the state’s rising costs have prompted serious thoughts about moving elsewhere.

In a recent Boston.com poll, we asked readers if the state’s taxes and/or high cost of living made them consider leaving. Sixty-six percent of 512 respondents said taxes and/or the cost of living in Massachusetts had made them consider leaving the state. Another 22% of respondents said they had already left, while 12% said they had not considered leaving.

The poll came as a new survey from the Mass Opportunity Alliance (MOA) examined why some former Massachusetts residents have relocated elsewhere. MOA, a pro-business nonprofit formed in 2024, surveyed 1,151 people who voted in Massachusetts in the 2024 election but have since moved to New Hampshire, Florida, or North Carolina. The survey found that taxes and housing costs were among the most frequently cited reasons respondents gave for leaving.

Among Boston.com readers who said they had considered leaving, taxes were one of the most common concerns. Some readers pointed to rising property taxes, utility costs, and what they described as an increasing overall financial burden.

“Our taxes keep going up and keep getting increases in fees and monthly costs. The cost of living is just too high in this state,” said MaryAnn M. of Amesbury.

Nationally, Massachusetts ranks among the top 10 states with the highest income tax, according to TurboTax. The state has a 5% tax on both earned and unearned incomes, as well as an 8.5% tax on certain capital gains. Plus, individuals who make over $1 million pay a 4% surtax on their income.

Others said the cost of remaining in Massachusetts — particularly the price of either buying a home and/or paying real estate taxes — had become a deciding factor. Several readers said they planned to stay while their children were in school but expected to move afterward.

“I am here for the schools. Once my kids are out of school, I intend to move so I have less of a tax burden,” said Deb D. of Wayland.

According to Rocket Mortgage, Massachusetts narrowly missed the top 15 ranking of states’ property taxes. The Comonwealth took the No. 16 spot, with a property tax rate of $6,352.52, based on the state’s median home value ($635,252).

For some retirees and empty nesters, the combination of taxes, housing costs, and fixed incomes has made other states more appealing.

“I don’t plan to stay here in retirement. Taxes, especially property taxes (which have doubled on my home since the start of the pandemic), are way too high to survive on a fixed income,” said Alex of Roxbury.

Among readers who had already left Massachusetts, many said lower taxes and a reduced cost of living influenced their decisions. Some cited moves to states including Florida, New Hampshire, North Carolina, and South Carolina.

“I left for Florida for better taxes. No property tax and lower cost of living even near the water is so much nicer,” said Mark of Naples, Florida.

But not all readers viewed Massachusetts’ taxes as a reason to leave. Some said they were willing to pay more because they believed the state’s public services, including education and health care, were worth the cost.

“Massachusetts excels in a high standard of living: education, and health care, to name a few, these are worth paying more in taxes,” said Cynthia K. of Amherst.

Others said the state’s investments in public services were exactly why they planned to stay.

“Quality education, health care, safety, and worker rights protected in a blue state as an island against Trump era policies and overreach make it worth it,” said Joe of Millis.

Below, see how readers responded.

Responses have been lightly edited for grammar and clarity.

Have taxes and/or the cost of living in Massachusetts ever made you consider leaving the state?

Yes, I have considered leaving

“Besides the taxes, the unaffordable cost of renting and the completely impossible ability to own a home is forcing me to leave MA. You can not find any homes within a reasonable distance from Boston for under $500,000. There is no way my children will ever be able to live here.” — John, Woburn

“Unfortunately, I am considering leaving the state after 64 years. Taxes are the main reason and I believe that the root cause of the tax issue is one party rule with few or no checks and balances. The recent implementation of the ‘millionaire’s’ tax is yet another example of the insatiable appetite for more revenue and power.” — Peter, Newburyport

“Nearing retirement and can’t imagine staying in this state with its ultra-high cost of living. Decades of failed housing policies (like in my town of Lincoln) have resulted in a severe housing shortage which has driven the cost of housing exorbitantly high. All other costs follow naturally.” — Wayne K., Lincoln

“Massachusetts offers some of the best education, sports, innovation, and quality of life in the country. I live in North Andover, have children in the public schools, and appreciate much of what the state offers. However, the tax burden has become increasingly difficult to justify. We pay roughly $13,000 a year in property taxes on top of state income, sales, meals, fuel, and other taxes. Meanwhile, the Legislature continues expanding ‘free’ programs while looking for new sources of revenue to fund them. Sadly, once my children are out of the public schools, I can no longer justify the cost of living here and intend to leave my home state. We don’t have a taxation problem, we have a spending problem and something needs to change.” — Chris C., North Andover

“It’s becoming more and more challenging for me and my surrounding neighbors to make ends meet. Utility cost, property and real estate tax, all the taxes on gas, items in Massachusetts make that you have to get a second job to survive. I have several friends and co-workers who have sold their homes and have moved out of state and encourage others to follow.” — J.R., Barnstable

“Almost an empty nester and the millionaires tax adds substantially to my taxes. I’m lucky to have that problem, but it makes New Hampshire look pretty attractive. I travel a ton anyway, it wouldn’t be hard to be out of Massachusetts for more than half the year.” — D.F., South End

“We are working so hard to maintain staying here, but we will leave very soon. I will take my company as well and go to a business-friendly state.” — Jonathan, South Boston

“This state was affordable at one time. Today, the taxation on everything makes it unaffordable. Seniors are being taxed out of their family homes. We plan to leave as well, once our children are off to college. For what we pay, I don’t see a reasonable return anymore. Raising our children, yes, the state is great for raising children to experience the history and culture. We have looked at the three states notes, and Tennessee too. As a soon to be retired couple, selling our house and taking the proceeds and our retirement money with us will ensure we live more comfortably somewhere else.” — Jose Q., Milford

“I own property in New Hampshire. Looking to make it my primary residence in the next five years to lower income tax and reduce regulatory pressure on my wife’s small business.” — David P., Needham

“Tax burden, including real estate taxes. People used to pay off their mortgage and be debt free. Now taxes are a mortgage. And utilities are a second mortgage.” — Al B., Brockton

Yes, I have left the state

“We sold our home in Plymouth last year and are now full time Florida residents currently vacationing in Massachusetts for 2 months to see family and friends. We were snowbirds (and Florida residents 4 or 5 years before that) but could no longer justify the cost of maintaining our Plymouth condo. The main motivation for us initially was taxes. MA was the worst state in the country at the time for the inheritance taxes. With sky high property values it didn’t take much else to get over the inheritance tax threshold. Add in the cost of living, state income taxes, the weather, the traffic — why stay?” — Dan, Plymouth

“I left for Florida in 2023 and will be returning to Massachusetts in the next few months. Yes, Florida has no state income tax, however, living here on the west coast of Florida is not inexpensive. There are higher sales taxes and home prices are up 50% since we purchased here in 2022. It is extremely crowded, even during the summer. Healthcare is sub-par compared to Massachusetts. The summer heat is unbearable. Far worse than anything a New England winter throws at you. And then there’s hurricane season. Lived through three of them. Not for me. The winters here are nice for 3-4 months. If you ever thought the drivers in MA were bad, try living in Southwest Florida. Can’t wait to be back in New England.” — Wayne C., Englewood, Florida

“I left in 2022 after selling my home in Medfield, MA. Property taxes on that home were $15,000 per year. I live in Hilton Head Island, South Carolina, a beautiful resort island in a new build that is larger than my Massachusetts home, and the annual property taxes are $3,100 per year. That’s free money and only part of the savings. Gas is on average $.75/gallon cheaper as is electricity and water. I love New England but it’s not worth it when you’ve reached retirement age.” — C.H., Medfield

“We left MA for North Carolina in 2013 and high real estate taxes was one of the top two reasons, with the winter weather being the other. Just figured we couldn’t live comfortably in retirement while paying such high income taxes and also paying very high heating bills in the winter months.” — Jeanne Y., Durham, North Carolina (formerly of Granby, MA)

“I left at the end of 2025. I have no hard feelings towards Massachusetts and I’m glad that I spend a portion of my life living there. That said, since leaving, our quality of life has never been higher after moving to New Hampshire. Our paychecks are heavier, our expenses are lighter, and our lives are happier. Plus, I’m still within an hour drive of the friends I made in MA. It really was a no-brainer to pack our bags.” — Melanie C., formerly of Fitchburg

“We had a 2,400-square-foot house in Leominster, an $8,000-a-year property tax bill, $600+ for oil, and $250+ for electricity each month. We moved to North Carolina in 2022 into a 1,700-square-foot house; $2,000 a year property tax bill, no oil, and $150 a month for electric, which includes our heat. That’s about $14,000 a year cheaper.” — Tom, formerly of Leominster

“With the income tax, the millionaire tax, and raising the sales tax I thought NH was a much better option and gives me more money to invest:spend on my family.” — Jeff H., Exeter, New Hampshire

“Saved thousands of dollars a year by moving to New Hampshire. No income tax, no sales tax, no interest/dividend taxes, no excise taxes. Add in cheaper home and auto insurance, no car inspections. Yes, property taxes are higher, but only by a few thousand and Mass. property taxes are going up constantly, closing that gap. Overall, we still save $8-10k per year over my tax burden in Massachusetts.” — Neil, Alton, New Hampshire

No, I have not considered leaving

“Would Massachusetts taxes cause me to leave the state? Never! Taxes in Massachusetts support a critical state infrastructure unmatched by any other region in the country. Travel around the nation sometime and check out other states like New York, Florida and Nevada. They’re littered with dilapidated homes, crumbling highways and endless poverty and crime. I know. I lived in Las Vegas, Nevada for a year. Horrible! Streets were full of homeless people and drug dealers. Neighborhoods were replete with abandoned and vandalized houses. And there was no quality healthcare. So go ahead, leave Massachusetts. You’ll regret it and you’ll be back. Especially during your first medical or financial emergency.” — Tommy Z., Holliston

“Why would I ever leave? I enjoy being surrounded by intelligent, healthy people. Great education and great healthcare and the other shared services that we all rely on aren’t cheap. I’m very happy to pay my taxes knowing it contributes to the greater good.” — Robert, Amherst

“Taxes provide services — teachers, infrastructure, free community college, public safety — that are critical. You cannot have services without some way to fund them.” — Maya, Wayland

“Having lived in Georgia, where the taxes were lower than Massachusetts, I would say I found that you get what you pay for with taxes. However, I am not living paycheck to paycheck. That might make me think differently.” — Ezra S., Princeton

“Massachusetts has neither the highest nor the lowest tax rates in the country and we get an awful lot of benefits for the taxes we do pay. Yes, cost of living is a concern (and could be best addressed by building more housing). But I’m not sure how useful it is to know that people who are ideologically opposed to paying income taxes have moved to states that don’t have them. Miss you guys! Those of us you’ve left behind will just have to console ourselves with being a national leader in education, health care, public safety, etc.” — Mitch, Bellingham

“We moved here to be near our daughter. We are in our 80s. We moved from Florida. The political climate and healthcare here is so much better.” — Susan B., Hudson

Boston.com occasionally interacts with readers by conducting informal polls and surveys. These results should be read as an unscientific gauge of readers’ opinion.

title: These are the best New England destinations, according to local celebs
text:
Apple Maps “Hyperlocal” series recently partnered with a few New England celebs for their favorite spots around the region.

Want to visit Noah Kahan’s hometown general store or the skateboard shop Cousin Stizz recommends in the North End? How about Elin Hilderbrand’s favorite Nantucket jewelry shop or chef Brad Leone’s favorite Connecticut restaurants?

Below, we share their Apple Maps itineraries. We also want to know: What did the itinerary get right – or wrong? Did they miss your favorite spot? Share with us.

Boston | New Hampshire & Vermont | Nantucket | Connecticut

Cousin Stizz’s Boston Spots

Cousin Stizz is an American rapper and songwriter from Dorchester, Massachusetts. His debut mixtape “Suffolk County,” released in 2015, received over 12 million listens on SoundCloud, and he received the “Artist of the Year” award at the 2018 Boston Music Awards. His “Hyperlocal” Boston recommendations cover everything from shopping to dining to relaxing in nature.

For shopping, Cousin Stizz listed two locations for sneaker lovers: Bodega (6 Clearway St.), a Jamaica Plain-based shoe, cap and sports retailer disguised behind a convenience store; and Concepts (18 Newbury St.), a shoe store in the Back Bay. He also recommended Orchard Skateshop (149 North St.) in the North End for skate shoes and skate supplies.

“I’ve been going to Bodega since they opened up back in ‘06. It’s definitely one of the dopest sneaker spots in the country, let alone Boston. It’s a real community spot and something everybody gotta experience first hand,” he said.

His favorite destinations for spending time in nature include Franklin Park in the Jamaica Plain, Roxbury, and Dorchester neighborhoods of Boston, and the Muddy River Dock.

“This is where we came up at, we created our dreams sitting there. If you wanna go look up at the sky and see the city from a different angle go there; it’s a dreamer’s paradise,” he said of the dock.

For food, Cousin Stizz had plenty of great recommendations from a variety of cuisines and across several neighborhoods. For a high-end steakhouse, he listed Davio’s as his favorite. Everything on the menu is great, he said, but “they got these egg rolls they be doing that are crazy.” The restaurant has several locations, including in the Seaport (26 Fan Pier) and the Back Bay (75 Arlington St.) neighborhoods in Boston.

For more casual dining, he recommended Dino’s Cafe (141 Salem St.) in the North End; P&P Restaurant and Ice Cream Parlor (1284 Blue Hill Ave.) in Mattapan for Jamaican fare (specifically, patties with coco bread and cheese, and grape nut ice cream); JP Roti Shop (482 Washington St.) in Dorchester for Caribbean food; and Bred Gourmet (2255 Dorchester Ave.) for hamburgers.

“[Bred] got the official Cousin Stizz fries there! Shoutout AB, that’s his brother’s spot. Great burgers too, great food in general. We love Bred,” Cousin Stizz said.

Noah Kahan’s New England Spots

Noah Kahan hails from Strafford, Vermont and has seen immense commercial success since the release of his second album, Stick Season (2022). In 2023 he was nominated for the Grammy Award for Best New Artist for the album. He offered up local recommendations for food, fun, and scenic views across Vermont and New Hampshire.

First up is Coburns’ General Store (216 VT-132, South Strafford, Vermont), which Kahan called the hub of his hometown.

“The folks working the counter have been there since I was born, and it is the epitome of a family-run business. It feels like home,” he said.

For food, Kahan had picks ranging from national chains Buffalo Wild Wings at 555 Shelburne Rd, Burlington, Vermont; and The Bagel Place at 1166 Williston Rd, South Burlington, Vermont) to local spots. Among these were Koto Japanese Steakhouse (288 N Plainfield Rd., West Lebanon, New Hampshire); Gusanoz (410 Miracle Mile, Lebanon, NH); and Worthy Burger (56 Rainbow St, South Royalton, Vermont).

His favorite New England hobby destinations include the Carter Country Club (327 Mechanic St., Lebanon, New Hampshire) where he learned to play golf and Hanover Strings (34 S Main St., Hanover, New Hampshire) where he learned to play the guitar.

For nature, Kahan said Miller Pond (Orange County, Vermont) and Ledyard Bridge (W Wheelock St., Hanover, New Hampshire) were among his childhood favorites.

Elin Hilderbrand’s Nantucket Spots

Elin Hilderbrand is a Nantucket icon whose summer beach reads have reached readers worldwide. The author offered her favorite Nantucket spots, ranging from seafood restaurants to bookstores to local historical landmarks.

She listed Green Point Lighthouse and the Museum of African American History (27 York St., Nantucket) among her favorite landmarks to visit on the island.

For a beautiful place to stay, she recommended The Nantucket Hotel (77 Easton St., Nantucket), and for beautiful gifts, Jessica Hicks Jewelry (2 Union St., Nantucket).

For the “best lobster roll and the best lobster bisque on Nantucket”, try The Seagrille (45 Sparks Ave., Nantucket), and Sconset Market (4 Main St., Siasconset) for groceries.

For a night on the town, she recommends The Chicken Box (16 Dave St., Nantucket) for drinks and live music, Sandbar (4 Bathing Beach Rd. #2234, Nantucket) for a great beach bar, and Cisco Brewers (5 Bartlett Farm Rd., Nantucket).

And last but not least, there are two bookstores on the island she loves: Mitchell’s Book Corner (54 Main St., Nantucket) – “the grand dame of Main Street” – and Nantucket Bookworks (25 Broad St., Nantucket).

Brad Leone’s Connecticut Spots

Brad Leone is an American chef and YouTuber known for his work with Bon Appétit and its YouTube channel, as well as his own shows “Local Legends” and “Makin’ It.” He provided his favorite spots in southeastern Connecticut, including plenty of noteworthy restaurants and places to enjoy nature.

For a nature fix, he recommends heading to Lantern Hill Pond (New London, Connecticut), the Pachaug State Forest, andStone Acres Farm (393 N Main St., Stonington, Connecticut).

For family-friendly spots, check out the Essex Steam Train & Riverboat (1 Railroad Ave., Essex, Connecticut) and Lee’s Toy & Hobby (935 Poquonnock Rd., Groton, Connecticut).

title: Should Boston rebuild Madison Park at Roxbury’s P-3 site?
text:
A long-debated plan to redevelop a 7.7-acre vacant parcel in Roxbury is once again in flux — and city leaders, developers, and community members are divided over what should happen next.

The publicly-owned Tremont Street site, known as parcel P-3, has sat empty for decades. Several redevelopment efforts have fallen through, including a large retail and residential complex in 2019.

In 2023, the Boston Planning & Development Agency designated HYM Investment Group and My City at Peace to lead a mixed-use project with housing, commercial, and a life-sciences lab space. But shifting market conditions — particularly a steep drop in demand for lab space — stalled the project. The tentative designation expired Jan. 31 and is no longer active, according to the Boston Planning Department.

Mayor Michelle Wu’s administration is now considering a different path: rebuild Madison Park Technical Vocational High School — Boston’s only vocational high school, which serves about 1,000 students — on the site. In December, the school was selected for the Massachusetts School Building Authority’s Core Program Eligibility Period, the first step toward securing state funding for a major rebuild.

On “Boston Public Radio” last month, Mayor Wu said the original redevelopment struggled to move forward because of the economics, not the Madison Park proposal, calling the idea of subsidizing affordable housing with lab space as a “pipe dream” in today’s market.

“The economics do not work. Lab spaces are at 30% vacancy and this project for multiple years now was not able to advance or make meaningful progress towards a groundbreaking,” she said.

The shift has divided the development team.

OnyxGroup Realty & Development said it is stepping back from the original plan, writing in an open letter that “the economic landscape has changed” and that “the life sciences investment is not coming,” according to the Boston Herald.

HYM and other development partners, however, are pushing to keep their mixed-use vision alive. At a Roxbury community meeting Monday, HYM’s Thomas O’Brien said he remains committed to the project.

“While we care deeply about the high school, we care deeply about the Boston Public School system, we also care deeply about this community, and we’ll continue to care about this mission and this potential opportunity,” he said.

We want to hear from you: What should the city do with P-3 in Roxbury?

Would you support building a new Madison Park High School on the site? Do you think the mixed-use housing and life sciences proposal deserves more time or consideration? How do you feel about the city changing course?

Tell us by filling out the form or e-mailing us at [email protected], and your response may appear in a future Boston.com article.

Sorry. This form is no longer available.

title: A sweet treat for your mailbox
text:
It’s Monday, Boston.

🥰 We’re coming to the cottage TONIGHT. And by cottage, we mean Cisco’s “Heated Rivalry” lookalike contest in Fenway at 5:30 p.m. today, where two winners will get a $50 Cisco gift card (and hottie bragging rights).

👀 What’s on tap today:

‘Tis the allergy season

AI friendmaking apps

Gillette went bananas

Up first…

OUT & ABOUT

These artists slid in your DMs mailbox

Image and illustration: Kelly Chan.

Snail mail is having a *moment*. Many New England artists are kickin’ it old-school, hopping on the trend of launching snail mail print clubs. The result? A fun passion project that makes their work more accessible.

Here’s what to know:

🖼️ It works like other monthly subscriptions. Customers pay ~$5-$10 per month, and get a little piece of artwork in the mail. Sometimes it’ll be paired alongside other things like stickers, word searches, recipes, or even plantable seed paper.

💻 ‘Cause let’s face it, everyone wants to get offline. We already know analog is so back (think: vinyls, handwritten letters, film cameras), and this is another way that people are looking to find joy, community, and connection without a screen.

🤝 And it’s a win-win for artists and consumers. Artists commit to consistently growing their passion and skills (and also adding a revenue stream), while consumers regularly get a new piece of art that probably costs the same as a latte.

💌 Subscribers even call it “happy mail.” Which is basically anything that’s not a bill or an advertisement. These print clubs add that perfect touch of *whimsy* and something special to look forward to.

✨ Plus, exclusivity and shopping small sweeten the deal. Every send almost always contains work that can’t be found elsewhere — a big draw for those who want something *extra* special. One subscriber’s mindset: Why buy stickers at Michael’s when you can get even cooler ones from artists directly?

🫶 The best part? Building relationships with subscribers. Artists LOVE when subscribers connect back with them, sharing memories, asking them questions, and even sending photos of where they put the prints on their walls. Christine Tyler Hill, a Burlington, Vt.-based artist behind The Cloud Report, even met up with a subscriber in London during her travels.

✍️ Their goal really isn’t about a big following. Yes, there are some artists worldwide who’ve gone viral and make this their 9-5. But for many, these clubs aren’t necessarily big income drivers. In fact, they probably have other jobs, do commissions, sell work at pop-up markets, or even have print vending machines. So working with a smaller audience each month is often a lot more manageable, while still maintaining genuine connections with subscribers.

🙌 Wanna dig deeper? Read the full story.

ADVERTISEMENT

TOGETHER WITH VISIT NH

Mentally, it’s already October

🍁🍂 Summer had its fun. Now, we’re ready to start planning our weekends around fall foliage in New Hampshire. Head north this fall for crisp hikes, scenic drives, apple picking, and local sips. In New Hampshire, it’s easy to pack a lot of fall into a single weekend, with charming towns, mountain views, and plenty of scenic detours all within reach. Start planning your fall getaway early.

CITY

Quick & dirty headlines

Image: Suzanne Kreiter/The Boston Globe.

🚣 The Charles is now giving … dirtier water. The city expanded its initial cyanobacteria algae bloom advisory on Aug. 27, asking locals to avoid the Charles River Lower Basin from the Zakim Bridge area allllllll the way to the BU Jenga Tower (here’s a map). Reminder: It can make you (and your dog) pretty sick, so don’t plan any kayaking days here or in the other 20+ spots on the no-go list. But a little bit of good news: The West Roxbury part of the Charles is now clear.

🤧 Bad news: Allergy season isn’t going anywhere. Raise your hand if you’ve been sneezing all summer! Here’s what happened: We went from cool weather to 90-degree temps FAST, which led to an *explosion* of tree pollen, and then the heat and humidity kept the pollen count high. Heading into fall, we still have some warmer weather in front of us … but now also a longer pollen season (hello, ragweed!). So let’s just say, you’ll wanna buy another box of tissues.

🤖 Gen Z is using AI to find new besties. Young people in Boston are turning to apps that use AI algorithms to match people and even plan activities, without any swiping (see: 222place, Timeleft, RealRoots). And they’re actually working. Users are building real connections through them after struggling to click with anyone here organically. Why is it so hard? Many feel there’s less social infrastructure to meet people nowadays post-grad, but TBH, experts say growing up in the digital age and the pandemic probs didn’t help either …

☕ Add these two new spots to your caffeine rotation. Newbury Street is now home to Japan’s biggest matcha cafe chain, Nana’s Green Tea. And they don’t just do your OG whisked matcha — they serve up matcha sodas, floats, frappes, espresso shots, you name it. Not to mention they’ve also got soft serve, rice bowls, curry plates, and more. Then there’s Grey’s Coffee, which just opened a brick-and-mortar in Quincy, and their menu looks BOMB. We needed this Almond Joy latte yesterday.

THINGS TO DO

Weekday plans

Image: Lane Turner/The Boston Globe.

🍸 Taste three top-tier cocktail bars in one night. Here’s your excuse to grab a drink tonight: PVD’s Loma and DC’s Press Club are taking over Wig Shop for the *ultimate* collab ONLY on Aug. 31.

🎥 Reunite with your fave shows. First up, head to the Grove TONIGHT for the “Love Island USA” reunion episode (here’s a taste of the drama). Then go to The Anchor on Wednesdays every week to watch the newest season of “Ted Lasso.”

🍝 Carbo-load on a budget. Pazza on Porter in Eastie is offering $10 pasta dishes every Tuesday with six classic options, including aglio e olio, cacio e pepe, and alla vodka. Dine-in only!

💬 Trade small talk for real talk. Join Trident Booksellers’ Skip the Small Talk Night on Sept. 2 for guided prompts and deep, meaningful convos with your besties or someone new. Get tickets here!

🍿 Don’t throw away your shot at this screening. Bring a blanket to City Hall Plaza for a FREE outdoor movie night of “Hamilton” on Sept. 3. Bonus: There’ll be free popcorn!

🤳 Meet content creator Chris Olsen IRL. Remember his videos flying to deliver coffee to celebs? Harvard Book Store is hosting Chris on Sept. 3 at First Parish Church to chat about his memoir, “I Think My Therapist Hates Me.”

☕ Spice up your Friday work routine. Norinori in Brookline just launched their new WFH deal: $25 for endless joe (cold brew included!), plus an entree and miso soup. Note: It’s only from 11-3 on Fridays.

🍕 Become a pizza connoisseur.* Chow down on the best slices at Boston Pizza Festival, New England’s biggest ‘za festival on Sept. 19-20, ft. 30+ pizzerias at City Hall Plaza. Tickets are $10 and include two slices to start you off right — but B-Side Members receive $5 entry!

Start an annual membership here to get the discount code!

*This listing was presented in partnership with Boston Pizza Festival.

ONE LAST THING

Gillette went bananas

Image: Barry Chin/The Boston Globe. Illustration: Kelly Chan.

BOOM, BABY! The Savannah Bananas just played the Loco Beach Coconuts at two *sold-out* shows this weekend at Gillette Stadium — and they were a BLAST.

Pats tight end Hunter Henry threw out the first pitch (a strike btw that counted for the game), Keith Urban gave an epic surprise performance, and even 2013 Red Sox champ Shane Victorino made a pinch-hit cameo. But TBH, the energy was unreal before the game even started, with massive crowds dancing outside the stadium HOURS beforehand.

For banana ball newbies, imagine a glammed up version of baseball with choreographed dances, lots of backflips, wacky costumes, and even players on stilts.

But our fave part of all this? Banana Ball owner Jesse Cole, a Mass. native who’s *obsessed* with the Pats, said selling out Gillette means everything to him. This was the league’s first time at Gillette after selling out Fenway last year.

“I never could imagine we’d be playing here,” Cole wrote.

— Written by Kelly Chan

🍌 Thanks for reading! Mom, can they come back soon please?

💜 Special shoutout to today’s sponsor, Visit NH, for supporting local journalism and reminding us why fall is New England’s best season.

🎶 The results are in: 45% of B-Siders said “Jolene” is their fave Dolly song. One reader wrote: “Kinda chic to lament another hot babe.” First in our bloodline to say this …

🍕 We made an oopsie! Boston Pizza Festival is the official event name, not Pizza Fest. Our bad!

title: The best things to do over marathon weekend
text:
Happy Friday, Boston!

⛽ A free tank of gas was not on our April bingo card. But Jeffrey Glassman Injury Lawyers is covering $7,777 at the pump at John’s Gas in Dorchester today at 8 a.m. Drive! Don’t walk!

🥳 And happy birthday to B-Side Member Amundam Mancho! We’d gas you up … but it seems like Jeffrey Glassman’s got you covered.

👀What’s on tap today:

Skip Logan’s TSA line!

An indie bookstore crawl

Boston Marathon: impossible mode

Up first…

BOSTON MARATHON

Your guide to marathon weekend

Image: Suzanne Kreiter/The Boston Globe. Illustration: Gia Orsino.

The runners are coming! The runners are coming! The Boston Marathon might not be till Monday, but the pregame starts NOW.

Here’s how to do marathon weekend right:

🏃 Start with the expo and fan fest. They’re the heartbeat of the weekend’s activities. Running nerds will love the marathon expo at Hynes Convention Center, which is chock-full of marathon merch, panels, and even a freebie or two. Here’s the schedule. For folks who don’t care about their VO2 max, you can find free workout classes, a pop-up pub, food, and live podcast recordings at the fan fest at City Hall Plaza. Here’s the full lineup!

🤑 Take advantage of some DEALS. Everyone can enjoy $10 AYCE pancakes at South Street Diner on April 19 from 4 to 11 p.m., and complimentary cold brews all weekend at Adidas’ Hyperboost Hub at Dick’s House of Sport (if you try on their shoes!). As for our marathon runners, don’t pay for a THING this weekend. Our picks: Free sauna sessions at Moki and free Levain cookies. Here’s a full deal roundup.

📝 Do a little homework … Your assignment: Check out the city’s looooong list of street closures and parking restrictions and the MBTA’s station closures, consult the BAA’s spectator guide (which includes protected times to see the pro runners), and set up the B.A.A. Racing App to track your faves on the course.

👀 Lock down your spectating plans. We suggest the One Mile to Go Block Party at Kenmore if you’re looking for a watch party. If not, we’re partial to the relatively calm stretch of Beacon Street between Washington Square and Coolidge Corner in Brookline. But TBH, the best seat in the house is a restaurant on the route. Here are some spots to try — make a res if you can!

📅 Still have free time? Here’s how we’d fill it:

Party with Heartbreak Hill Running Co. The certified cool kids of the running world are throwing down all weekend with block parties, a cheer zone, after parties, and a shakeout run.

Shop Pinterest-approved activewear. You can shop small, aesthetic brands IRL that you’d normally only find online at pop-up boutique Rec Room. See: Trendy Swedish brand Unna.

Catch a live podcast recording. “Ali on the Run” is taping live at WBUR’s CitySpace on April 17 with a TBA special guest.

Hit up a sober mixer. Sip on some (free!) NA bevs and mingle with fellow runners at Dray’s Sober Social Mixer on April 18.

Want more? Here’s a list of (basically) every activation happening throughout the weekend.

ADVERTISEMENT

TOGETHER WITH MARKETPLACE

Your new pre-flight ritual

✈️✨ Show up early, eat something good, and relax before takeoff. At Boston Logan International Airport, MarketPlace Logan turns waiting at the gate into something better — whether it’s a burger from Shake Shack, ramen from Gachi Sushi & Noodles, or a quick browse through ink by Hudson. Suddenly, you’re not passing time…you’re actually enjoying it. Explore options in your terminal and start your trip before you even board.

CITY

Quick & dirty headlines

Image: Handout

✈️ Your ride to Logan just got WAY cheaper. Enter: Massport’s new airport shuttle service from Uber and Lyft. Uber will run two routes to and from Logan — one in Boston and one in Cambridge — every 30 minutes from 2 p.m. to midnight. Bonus: This week, it’s just $3! Lyft’s route runs through Camberville every hour. The best part? Both will cost $16 or less, and shuttle riders get to skip the TSA line! You can book seats on both through the apps. Here are allllll the deets. Happy travels!

🏃🏾 There’s another Boston marathon this weekend. The 26.TRUE Marathon will be back for its sixth year on April 18 with its biggest race ever (400 runners!) and a new half marathon option. ICYMI: The unsanctioned race is a grassroots, community-focused alternative to the Boston Marathon, launched by the Pioneers Run Crew. The course runs through Roxbury, Jamaica Plain, Dorchester, and Mattapan, and welcomes runners who aren’t white, wealthy, or super-athletic (a.k.a. the Boston Marathon’s target demo). Wanna check it out? Here’s what to know.

🌷 We’re calling it: Spring has officially sprung! The proof: The Public Garden’s lagoon is full and its iconic swan boats are setting sail for the season April 18 with rides open from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Here’s a peek at their pre-launch prep. Meanwhile, the annual Golden Strong Marathon Weekend Meetup is Sunday at noon, where oodles of very good golden retrievers and their humans will gather on the Common for the cutest meetup of all time (here’s a peek). Pets are highly encouraged!

📚 Get in loser, we’re going on the Metro Boston Indie Bookstore Crawl. Now through April 25, you can get prizes just for stopping by your fav indie bookstores. You can visit any one of these 25 bookstores across Greater Boston and pick up a passport to play. After collecting stamps by April 25, you can redeem the passport for prizes at each spot, and be entered to win grand prizes like gift cards, private events, and merch (if you visit them all!). Here are the rules!

THINGS TO DO

Weekend checklist

📀 Party like it’s 1975. Vinyl Index’s annual Record Store Day is taking over Bow Market with a vinyl party on April 18. Think: DJ sets, music-inspired food and drinks, and TONS of records.

🤑 Shop vintage for $1. Yes, we said $1! Buffalo Exchange is ringing in Earth Day on April 18 with a $1 cash-only sale at each of its Greater Boston locations to benefit the Plastic Pollution Coalition.

🍩 Meet the doughnut-eating champion. Some of the world’s top competitive eaters will face off at a doughnut eating contest at the Great American Beer Hall on April 18.

🪩 Get down on the dance floor. The L Club, nathálie wine bar’s sapphic dance party series, is back April 18 with hyperpop music and a packed dance floor. This month’s theme: Spring fever.

🖍️ Pregame your marathon cheering. Trident is screening “Good Will Hunting” and hosting a marathon poster-making sesh on April 18. We’d recommend something like this.

🍵 Try the hottest matcha in town. This weekend only, Levain Seaport is bringing back its viral cookie milk matcha. Be there at 10 a.m. on April 18 and 19 to get it while supplies last!

🌸 Ring in spring with Molly’s Bookstore. They’ll be getting in the spirit by decorating bookmarks and tiny flower pots on April 18. Plus: You’ll get seeds to plant at home!

🎤 Ugly cry to “Someone You Loved.” Sadboy king Lewis Capaldi is coming to MGM Music Hall on April 19, and there are plenty of tickets under $60.

COMMUNITY ANNOUNCEMENT

🩷 💫 No plans this Sunday? Rise & Thrive Women’s Conference is taking over The Cyclorama April 19. Think inspiring speakers, women-owned vendors, and a crowd you’ll actually want to meet — plus music, fashion, and more. Not your typical conference. Grab a ticket here and we’ll see you there!

ONE LAST THING

Boston Marathon: Impossible mode

Image: The Boston Globe. Illustration: Gia Orsino.

These Boston marathoners are giving “running it back” a whole new meaning. Like, they’re planning to run the marathon twice … in a ROW.

30,000+ runners will make the 26.2 mile trek from Hopkinton to Boston on Monday. But for seven of those runners, it’ll be their second marathon of the day. A group from Boston’s Trail Animals Running Club is waking up at 1 a.m. to run the course backwards first, just to turn around and run it back with everyone else. That’s a total of 52.4 miles.

If all of this leaves you wondering: Why? As one runner told Marathon Handbook: “Accomplishing something you’re not sure you can do is one of life’s great joys.” If you say so, bestie!

— Written by Gia Orsino and Emily Schario

🏃 Thanks for reading! Leave it to Bostonians to find a way to make marathoner runners look like slackers.

💜 Special shoutout to today’s sponsor, MarketPlace Logan, for supporting local journalism and making airport dining something to look forward to.

📲 The results are in: 37% of B-Siders said they use social media for less than two hours a day. One reader said: “Depends on how boring work is that day.” Lol.

Boston’s moped crackdown

A chicken finger lawsuit

THINGS TO DO

Skating, strawberries, and shadow daddies

Illustration: Gia Orsino

Step aside, Paris. This weekend, Boston is the city of love. Or, at the very least, it has a lot of fabulous Valentine’s events going on.

Here’s are our picks:

🍕 Give a pizza your heart. Keep your V-Day takeout on-theme with this cute heart-shaped pie from Ducali in the North End. They also have a Heated Rivalry-themed pie with Canadian bacon … if you’re into that.

👠 Grab the Samantha in your life. All weekend long, Boston Landing is hosting a “Sex and the City”-themed Galentine’s bash at Broken Records. Think: Free flowers, karaoke, brunch, permanent jewelry, and SATC screenings, obv.

🍩 Decorate a doughnut! At BlackBird’s Feb. 13 Galentine’s Day event, $65 a pop will get you a box of mini doughnuts, decorating supplies, a girl dinner of caesar salad, fries, and Diet Coke, unlimited hot cocoa, AND BlackBird swag. Now that’s a deal.

📀 Listen to *your song* on vinyl. On Feb. 13, Aeronaut will have a V-Day-themed pop-up vinyl shop in its taproom. Or, head over on Feb. 16 for a board game speed-dating sesh!

⛸️ Skate with your sweetheart. On Feb. 14, Tall Ship’s The Rink is offering two tickets for $14 with code LOVE14. Bonus points if you reserve this hot cocoa and floral arrangement bundle beforehand.

🏒 Heat up your Valentine’s night. Fruitstand is throwing a “Heated Rivalry”-themed queer bash in Harvard Square on Feb. 14, with drag, dancing, and, hopefully, “All the Things She Said” on repeat.

📚 Buy a book for your boo. Harvard Book Store is hosting its first-ever Valentine’s Day book swap on Feb. 14. Bring a partner or pal, secretly buy each other books (at 20% off!), wrap them up, and have a grand reveal!

🍓 Try fancy strawberries for FREE. Luxe strawberry company Oishii is handing out packs of their boujee berries (which retail for up to $20) plus flowers on Feb. 14 at the Greenway Ferris wheel from 4:30 to 7:30 p.m.

⚔️ Spend the night with a shadow daddy. Obviously, we’re talking about Trident’s romantasy trivia on Feb. 14, where you and up to five friends will answer questions about fated mates, faes, and forced proximity.

🥣 Show your community some love. The Super Bowl didn’t go our way, but we can guarantee that Haley House’s annual SOUPer Bowl on Feb. 15 will. Grab a ticket, show up, and slurp soup from top restaurants while supporting Haley House.

ADVERTISEMENT

TOGETHER WITH MEET BOSTON AND THE MASSACHUSETTS OFFICE OF TRAVEL AND TOURISM

Dining in = OUT. Dine Out = IN.

🍽️ 🍷Look, we love a good introverted winter moment — but not enough to miss this. Dine Out Boston returns Feb. 22–March 7, bringing two glorious weeks of prix fixe menus from top restaurants across the city. Lunch or dinner, splurge-y or budget-friendly, you choose. Hosted by Meet Boston in partnership with the Massachusetts Office of Travel and Tourism, this is Boston’s official restaurant week (and it fills up fast). Lock in your table now and thank yourself later.

CITY

Quick & dirty headlines

Image: David L. Ryan/The Boston Globe

🛵 Your Doordash driver might need a new ride. ‘Cause City Councilor Ed Flynn is proposing an all-out ban on delivery drivers using mopeds and e-bikes due to complaints of reckless driving. TBH, he has a point: Delivery drivers have been involved in some pretty serious crashes lately. Though the city has attempted to crack down on the issue, Flynn says residents still complain, and given the sheer number of drivers, police can’t handle it on their own. Now, his proposal will be sent to committee for review.

🚲 Bike down Comm Ave. lately? Thank these cyclists. Last week, over 20 fed up volunteers from the Boston Cyclists Union and BU Urbanism Club teamed up to clear snow off a stretch of the road’s bike lane — and send a message to the city. Per the group, parts of the lanes were completely blocked off by snow several days after the storm, and complaints to 311 and city councilors weren’t moving the needle. So, on Friday, they took matters into their own hands, harnessing their community to clear the path themselves.

🤤 It’s a BIG week for Boston foodies. Why? Three reasons. 1. The 11,000-square foot Eastern Edge Food Hall is opening its doors in Kendall Square, offering several local concepts, from coffee to tacos to wine and beer. Here’s the lineup. 2. On Feb. 14, Boston’s latest Instagram-friendly candy shop, Pic & Mix, will be open for biz in Kenmore Square with an arsenal of trendy sweet treats. And 3. Copley Place announced high-end Italian marketplace Casa Tua Cucina and Greek restaurant Estiatorio Milos will be replacing the building’s Neiman Marcus. Bon appétit!

🚇 This weekend, the Orange Line is acting like your ex … unavailable. From Feb. 14 to 16 (that’s Monday!), the line is shutting down between Jackson Square and Forest Hills for signal upgrades. Per usual, shuttle buses will replace service, but riders can also take the commuter rail fare-free between Forest Hills and South Station. And that’s not all: Riders should brace for another nine-day OL shutdown later this month between Back Bay and Forest Hills, and a weekend shutdown on the Red Line. Now THAT is heartbreaking.

ONE LAST THING

This lawsuit smells like chicken

Illustration: Gia Orsino

Can a chicken shop smell … too much like chicken? Apparently, yes, according to a lawsuit between Raising Cane’s and its Back Bay landlord. Long story short, the landlord recently sent the chicken chain an eviction notice on the grounds that it … “smells like chicken fingers.”

Apparently, the chicken-y scent has been an ongoing issue, with Cane’s claiming to have spent over $200,000 to investigate it. But it all came to a head on Jan. 5, when the shop informed its landlord it wouldn’t be yielding to the “unreasonable demands” anymore. Cue the eviction notice.

But the plot thickens: Now, Cane’s is arguing that the stench is just a means of forcing them to give up their exclusive rights to sell chicken on the property, since the landlord wants to open a Panda Express next door.

You can read about all the messiness here.

— Written by Gia Orsino

🍗 Thanks for reading! Hey, at least this time they know what the smell is.

💜 Special shoutout to today’s sponsor, Meet Boston, for supporting local journalism and giving us all a very good reason to leave the house.

📝 Programming note: We’ll be off on Monday for Presidents’ Day, but we’ll see you back in your inbox on Tuesday. Enjoy the long weekend!

Films, fútbol, and food fests
