title: ‘I don’t know what I’m going to do’: Patients and staff in Dorchester are devastated by Carney Hospital closure
text:
For Lyle and several other regular Carney patients interviewed by the Globe, the news that Steward Health Care, embroiled in bankruptcy turmoil, would be closing Carney on Saturday came as a devastating shock. The announcement, made in late July, gave patients, employees, and advocates barely a month’s notice to prepare, fight the decision, or find new work or primary care doctors.

The closing has caused an uproar among hospital staff and political leaders, who say the hospital is a critical fixture of the community and an essential resource for a diverse and historically underserved patient population. Despite calls for the state to intervene and keep Carney open as it plans to do with six other Steward hospitals — including by using eminent domain to take over St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center — Carney Hospital is still set to shut its doors.

“I don’t know what I’m going to do. . . . I have nowhere else to go,” said Lyle. “This is the only community hospital around here. The ambulance takes you here if you get sick. And people like me, older people like me, what am I, what they’re going to do?”

Carney Hospital, founded in 1863, sees around 2,600 emergency department visits every month, according to a state dashboard.

Stephen Wood, an acute care nurse practitioner in the emergency medicine department, said a significant portion of those patients have high needs, and many struggle with homelessness, substance abuse, or psychiatric issues.

He’s worked at Carney for nearly 10 years because, he said, he’s passionate about serving the people who need help the most. His colleagues feel likewise, he said.

“There’s a deep commitment to serving that patient population, and a lot of them are literally my neighbors,” said Wood, who lives in Dorchester. “We are such a tight-knit group that care for each other . . . that I’ve never experienced anywhere I’ve worked previously.”

He said Carney staff go “above and beyond” to also tackle social justice and health equity issues, in addition to providing emergency medical care. That often included helping patients enroll in Medicaid, get access to substance abuse treatment programs, or ensure their children were up to date on vaccinations. They also have diverse staff and robust language support services to ensure the hospital’s many Haitian, Vietnamese, and other immigrant patients don’t have to worry about a language barrier, he said.

Wood said many of his colleagues “immediately broke down” when they learned the hospital would be closing. In the weeks since, many have loudly advocated for the state to keep the hospital open, to no avail.

“They’re not investing in these low-income communities, and that’s a huge problem in this state, is that we haven’t invested our health care dollars equitably,” said Wood. “You’re now leaving an absolute health care desert in Dorchester, Roxbury, Mattapan, with no thought to what’s going to happen to those communities when this hospital goes away.”

A representative for Steward and Carney Hospital declined to comment. Governor Maura Healey has said Steward determined the hospital did not have a “qualified bid” from an operator interested in taking over the hospital.

To Wood, that sounds like an excuse. “This is an absolute atrocity that she would let this kind of thing happen to this community,” he said.

For Mary Ann Rockett, 62, an emergency room nurse at Carney, the closure “feels like deja vu.”

Rockett had previously worked at the Quincy Medical Center beginning in 2008, until Steward Health Care shut the hospital down in 2020. Quincy was also a very community-oriented hospital, she said.

“It was one of the saddest things that I’ve lived through,” Rockett said. “We know these people so well, we know their limited access to primary care, and we know that we’re the fill-in a lot of times for their access to primary care. . . . When they come through that door, we already know their allergies, their meds, their diagnoses half the time, we know what they’re coming in to complain about before it’s written down.”

When Quincy closed, she said, she remembers hearing about some of her patients passing. Others went to Carney.

“Carney services a true need. . . . What is going to happen to these people when we close?” said Rockett.

Other health centers in the area are also bracing for the hospital’s closing, anticipating they may have to absorb patients.

Michelle Nadow, chief executive of DotHouse Health, a federally qualified health center in Dorchester about 2 miles from Carney, said her organization already sees about 22,000 patients a year, reflecting similar demographics to Carney’s patient population. About 60 percent are on public health insurance, 50 percent prefer to speak a language other than English, and around 85 percent are at or below the poverty line.

Many of their patients prefer to go to Carney for specialty or emergency care, in part because of proximity, as well as language services, Nadow said. And with the health care system in Massachusetts already as fragile as it is, Carney’s closure “most certainly will impact health outcomes and health equity.”

“Places like DotHouse were formed because there wasn’t good access to care for underserved populations, and so these health centers and hospitals were firmly anchored in communities to address those challenges,” Nadow said. “When a piece gets pulled away, it’s like if you shortened a leg of a stool. . . . And then how do you balance that out?”

DotHouse Health’s walk-in urgent care has already seen thousands more patients so far this year than expected, Nadow said. When the wait time exceeds two hours, the urgent care has to pause taking in new patients, which has already happened several times in August. With resources spread so thin, and Carney’s closure just days away, she’s worried that’s only going to continue.

“It’s hard for us to think how we can fill some of those gaps, because we’re a health center, we’re not a hospital,” she said.

Dr. Guy Fish, chief executive of Codman Square Health Center in Dorchester, said his organization is in a similar position. He particularly worries about the loss of Carney’s inpatient psychiatric beds.

“Those patients are not going to go away,” Fish said. “Losing the psychiatric services in a community that has a long history with trauma, a long history with being underserved in and stressed, is going to be devastating.”

Last week, Lyle made the trip to Carney — when she’s feeling well enough she can walk there from her house — to say goodbye to her favorite nurse, who works in the hospital’s community clinic. On the way in the door, she ran into a phlebotomist she knows and stopped to chat.

These days, she said, she cries whenever she’s on the bus and passes Carney.

“Carney is supposed to be a fixture in this community. . . . They saved St. Elizabeth’s, and they saved the other hospitals, why can’t they save this one?” said Lyle, who added she’s still hoping for a miracle. “It breaks my heart to know that Carney is closing.”

title: Dorchester charter school closes, leaving families scrambling to find alternative options
text:
A long-struggling Boston charter school, the Helen Y. Davis Leadership Academy, won’t reopen this fall after failing to enroll enough students to remain financially viable.

The Board of Trustees quietly voted July 17 to shut its doors permanently, surrender its state operating license, and cancel the upcoming school year. Although the Dorchester middle school notified families this summer about the decision, it made no public announcement about it. The move left families scrambling to find new schools for their children with only weeks before the new year was supposed to begin.

Enrollment in Grades 6-8 had fallen to 56 students in July, well below the 216 students the charter is supposed to serve under its operating license with the state Department of Elementary and Secondary Education.

“This was a difficult decision, but one necessitated by the school’s financial condition due to low enrollment, which was no longer sufficient to support the school’s mission and vision,” Sophia Stephney, the school’s executive director, said in a statement. “The staff and leadership team at Helen Y. Davis Leadership Academy has facilitated the transfer of our students to local schools to help ease the stress with the school closing.”

The independent charter school, which is not affiliated with Boston Public Schools, had been struggling with low enrollment for the last few years, fueled by a variety of factors, including a shrinking school-aged population in Boston.

Another independent charter school, City on a Hill in Roxbury, is preparing to close next June.

The declining enrollment at Davis was increasingly creating financial problems for the school, which operates mostly on per-student state aid.

According to a financial audit previously obtained by the Globe, the school racked up nearly $1 million in operating losses during the 2022-23 school year, representing more than 20 percent of its $4.4 million in annual spending.

Davis failed to rein in spending to compensate for a massive cut in per-student state aid — caused by fewer students enrolling than anticipated — and then it overspent its budget by $260,000, including by hiring more staff.

The state Board of Elementary and Secondary Education placed the school on probation in May due to its enrollment and financial problems, and state education officials warned that the school might have to close in the coming months if it failed to enroll enough students. It was the second time since 2018 that the board placed Davis on probation due to financial problems.

The board will need to vote on whether to accept Davis’s decision to surrender its operating license. The board’s next meeting is Sept. 24.

James Vaznis can be reached at james.vaznis@globe.com. Follow him @globevaznis.

title: Federal prosecutors announce drug, fraud busts of two separate Boston gangs
text:
In a separate case, financial fraud charges were brought against nine associates of the Mission Hill Gang, which is anchored in the Mission Main and Annunciation Road housing developments in the city.

If convicted, those charged in both cases could face decades behind bars.

“These are individuals who do not value life, they have terrorized and wreaked havoc in our city,” said Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox in a statement. “These investigations were intricately designed and carried out and there is no doubt that all of those in law enforcement who were involved, have put themselves in danger to get to this point.”

The probe of H Block, which originated as the Humboldt Raiders in Roxbury during the 1980s, according to prosecutors, started in 2021 in response to an increase in gang related drug trafficking and violence, according to the US Attorney’s office. Investigators allege at least a dozen incidents involving firearms and gunfire can be attributed to tensions involving H Block associates during the last three years.

On Thursday, law enforcement officials arrested six H Block associates, charging them with drug dealing in Greater Boston. An additional four H Block associates were already in state custody.

Three of the H Block associates are also charged with a conspiracy to smuggle illegal drugs into a state prison, by allegedly spraying 14 sheets of paper with PCP and a synthetic cannabinoid and mailing the paper to inmates behind bars.

Prosecutors alleged that a single sheet of such drug-laced paper would be worth as much as $80,000 inside the prison.

“The fight to keep our streets safe from dangerous gangs and drugs is an ever-constant struggle and, as this case shows, extends to our state’s prison facilities,” said Acting United States Attorney Joshua S. Levy in a statement. “Today’s arrests are an important step forward in making our streets and prisons safer.”

In a separate case, charges were filed Thursday against a nine Mission Hill Gang associates for a fraud scheme underpinned by stolen checks from postal collection boxes that are then chemically washed and rewritten to various bank accounts. Six of the associates were arrested, three more were already in custody.

Thursday’s announcement followed a law enforcement bust earlier this year that resulted in more than 40 suspected associates of the Jamaica Plain-based Heath Street Gang facing federal charges tied to an alleged racketeering scheme linked to three murders, the wounding of a 9-year-old girl, drug and gun trafficking, and some $900,000 in pandemic unemployment fraud.

title: Glenn Loury wrestles with contradictions on race and in his own life
text:
In the spirit of conservative individualism, he believes that top-down governmental fixes to address inequality can only go so far. He thinks Black communities’ challenges can be solved not with sweeping institutional redistributions like reparations but with internal cultural change and government policies that would promote economic uplift regardless of race. And while Loury has been a critic of mass incarceration, he rebukes progressive narratives about systemic racism that imply American society is purposely keeping Black people in the Jim Crow era. He writes that he believes there needs to be more focus on issues like “the state of the black family, the black victims of violent crime, and the necessity of building social capital within black communities.”

Loury recounts his political evolution in his tell-all memoir, “Late Admissions,” where he also details falling prey to — and overcoming — many of the vices he cites as plaguing Black communities. Loury has mended his relationship with the son he abandoned to a single mother, he’s beaten his addiction to cocaine, and he has gone from being a self-proclaimed “player” and philanderer to a pensive grandfather living in a sleepy part of Providence. The individualism that makes him critical of dynamics he sees in Black communities also makes him hopeful. “I was raised by some of the most industrious people I had ever met,” he writes. “If I believed that black people were lazy or incompetent, it would have made no sense for me to expend so much energy championing the development of their skills and abilities.”

Sitting in his home this summer, Loury and I discussed the apparent contradictions in his life. Some of the quotes that follow have been condensed.

Glenn Loury makes it sound like being a Black conservative is the most natural thing in the world — though not the easiest.

“I talk a little bit about this in the book — about disappointing family members because of my politics and feeling torn between wanting to be an independent thinker and go where my mind leads me on the one hand and feeling that I am in one way or another perhaps being used by people on the right because I’m a rare representative as an African American conservative of a certain type. Or that I’m betraying in some way or another my people and then I’m losing authenticity as a member of the community by sticking [with] a position that so many in the community reject.

“I’m a neoliberal economist and somewhat conservative culturally. I was a born-again Christian at a point in my life. I am no longer a practicing religious follower, but I have great respect for those traditions and for some of the cultural conservatism that comes out of that. But mainly, I think ‘Black conservative’ is a label that sticks to me because I’m a person who believes in personal autonomy and responsibility, and I think African Americans need — we do collectively as a group — to take control of our lives and to not be dependent upon the benefits and transfers and whatnot that come from people who are trying to make up for the past. And I think the imperative in front of African Americans today is an imperative of development, of realizing the potential that has been created by the success of the civil rights movement and the opening up of American society. And that makes me conservative in the sense of the Booker T. Washington side of the Washington-DuBois debate about the future of Black Americans from 125 years ago. I’m on the Booker T. Washington side. In the contemporary times, that’s a relatively conservative position. The way I’ve put it on occasion is to ‘seize the reins.’ The ball is in our court. The train is leaving the station, America is a great open society.

“I think as I get older, it becomes less of a problem to be a Black conservative. Is it lonely sometimes? Yeah. Is it liberating? Sometimes, yeah. So it’s a mixed bag.”

In the aftermath of George Floyd’s death, how did he feelabout the ensuing protests and the Defund the Police movement?

“The radicals had control of the agenda. I think there was a kind of moral panic, in which everybody felt that they needed to demonstrate their solidarity with a moral position, which is anti-racism, and took the relatively few incidents of police mistreatment, which were egregious, like the George Floyd incident, and [built them] into a general case against the necessity of policing broadly.

“So you end up with this slogan, and that’s all it is, a slogan about defunding the police. It’s not a coherent vision of how you’re going to secure public safety for people who live in dangerous circumstances. So I thought the rhetoric was not well matched to the reality, and I think the history since 2020 of the Defund the Police movement shows that a) the police haven’t been defunded in many places, although the police have been hampered. But b) the politics of Defund the Police has backfired on the progressives and now Democrats are running away from it. ‘We never said that. That’s not what we meant.’ As well as the fact that the crime issue is going to be not helpful to the progressive candidates politically. I think it’s one of the reasons why Trump is doing as well as he is doing. And I think that some of the problems in major cities across the country, in Los Angeles and in Chicago and New York, in Philadelphia and Washington, D.C., and Atlanta and other places where at the local level they’re seeing spikes in violent crime and property crime, people who have to live with that are expressing their disquiet.” [Editor’s note: Loury is right that violent crime was higher nationwide in 2023 than in 2019, but not all property-related crimes have increased.]

“I think it is in keeping with the commonsense observation that if you attack police officers, you can expect to get less out of the police officers, and the community actually depends upon the police for security and safety. I find it interesting that if I were to be talking about another set of public employees — teachers — and I were to say the conditions under which they work and the extent to which they get affirmed by the society affects their ability to perform their jobs, most people would have no problem with me saying that. And I think something like that is also true about policing.”

In Loury’s memoir, he describes an early 1980s House Judiciary Committee hearing held by John Conyers Jr., a Black Democratic representative from Detroit, about police brutality. Having grown up in Chicago, Loury understood how threatening crime can be for residents of Black neighborhoods and felt that Conyers’s focus on policing was missing the main problem.

“The brutality issues of policing in Detroit were minor compared to the criminal victimization issues that his constituents had to confront. There was an outbreak of rapes of teenage girls trying to get to school in the early morning hours. I use that as an anecdote in the book, to say what was spurring me to question the party line about race and inequality, which Representative Conyers was an exponent of — police brutality, systemic racism. And I was saying, ‘Yeah, but what about criminal behavior? And don’t we owe something to the people who have to deal with the consequences of it?’”

Why did he tell Coretta Scott King that the civil rights movement was over during a meeting with Black leaders in 1984? Does he still believe that?

“The civil rights movement of the 1950s and ’60s and ’70s, if you like, was successful. It was successful at getting the Civil Rights Act and the Voting Rights Act and the Fair Housing Act and so on. It was successful in promoting an ethos that was very different and much more sympathetic to the aspirations of African Americans than was the case in decades earlier. I think the civil rights movement won.

“But let’s say I take the overrepresentation of Blacks amongst criminal defendants — is that a civil rights problem? I don’t think so. I don’t think that’s a civil rights problem that can be remedied by protest demonstrations or the identification of ‘racist’ laws and then getting them off the books.

“Unfortunately, I think it’s a much tougher problem. This is Glenn Loury here, not everybody’s going to sign on to this: that the root of that problem is the behavior of the people who are being brought under the sway of the law enforcement. And that has to do with a lot of things. It has to do with culture and with their family backgrounds and what kind of values are instilled. I’d accept that it also has to do with economic opportunity and what’s going on in the schools and so on. But I don’t think those, either, are largely civil rights issues — that is, issues turning on African Americans being deprived of the full benefits of citizenship.”

While equality under the law may have been achieved, Black communities still face major challenges. Does he see any place for protest? Yes, he tells me — but when the goals are narrow and targeted.

“I don’t mean to pretend that there aren’t some questions about the way in which certain police departments carry on their duties, that there aren’t certain elements within policing that are racist and so on. And you can talk about what kind of accountability and responsibility police officers who abuse their authority or misuse the awesome powers of their office should be confronted with. Citizens review panels about what happens with policing in a particular place — I’m not necessarily opposed to any of that. But I don’t see a major role for protests unless it’s aimed at ‘OK, the schools in the city aren’t working, we want reform. We have an idea about what that reform should be.’ Let’s say it’s a charter school movement or people who want to try to help parents have more voice in what’s going on in the classroom. ‘We are organizing ourselves in order to make our position known and to make the people who are in positions of responsibility accountable.’

“To say there was no role for protests would be partly like saying that the First Amendment isn’t doing us any good. It can be a vehicle for people to express themselves to the institutions of power. I think that the populist upsurge that we see in the Donald Trump phenomenon is a kind of protest. It’s a kind of way that people without voices are trying to get their voices heard, and I wouldn’t be against that categorically.”

One of Loury’s most controversial views is his opposition to affirmative action. Though he has been the beneficiary of affirmative action programs and believes they have been useful tools in the past, he believes that these programs make the recipients doubt their own worth.

“In the fall of 1970, I was enrolled as an undergraduate with a full scholarship at Northwestern and, of course, that was affirmative action. I probably could have been admitted to MIT [for a PhD] even without a special program because my record was just that stellar. I was taking PhD-level courses as a senior at Northwestern in mathematics and in economics, and I was doing very well in those classes. I was an outstanding prospect regardless of my race, but there’s no way that I can ever know whether or not my admission to Northwestern would have happened even if I hadn’t been Black. Just like there’s no way for me to deny that my appointment as a tenured professor of economics at Harvard in 1982 — just 10 years after I graduated from Northwestern, and only six years after I completed my PhD — full professor, the first Black to have that position in economics at Harvard.

“Well, OK, they brought me in as a joint appointment in economics and Afro-American studies. They wanted to beef up their Black Studies Group. If I weren’t an African American working to some degree on those issues, I’m quite sure that I would not have been offered that position. I had difficulty dealing with the pressures of that position in part because I wasn’t sure that I was ‘good enough’ to pull it off. I was afraid that I was going to fail, and that paralyzed me and I ended up changing the direction of my career in part because of that.

“I think as a historical matter, there was a necessity for something like affirmative action coming out of the period of the Second Reconstruction, out of the post-1960s civil rights environment. But that was 60 years ago. It’s not something that we want to be doing in the second third of the 21st century.”

If systemic approaches like reparations and affirmative action aren’t the right way to go, what is?

“The messages that I would put out within the community’s larger cultural matrix — church basements, popular culture, and things like that — I would want to see be more a message of responsibility and development. Biden goes to Morehouse College and gives a commencement address, and he reminds the students there that this is still America where racism can rear its ugly head at any moment. And he basically says, ‘Support me and I’ll protect you from the racists,’ when what might have been said is ‘You stand on the threshold of greatness. This is an open society. Anything is possible here, hit the ground running, go forth, there are Black billionaires, start a business, etc.’ Affirmative to the possibilities of what can be done in this country and accepting our responsibility to seize the reins of opportunity and to make something of our lives.

“Another thing that I would want to see is transracial politics. I don’t like the reparations stuff. I don’t want to parse the country up into racial enclaves and then get into a quid pro quo negotiation of who’s going to do what for whom. I’d much rather see a transracial, or, if you like, class-based [approach]. So if I take the schools [that] are not working: That’s a problem for everybody. It’s not just a problem for Blacks. If I think that the police are disrespectful, that’s a problem for everybody. It’s not just a problem for Blacks. What about inflation? What about taxes being too high? What about what are we going to do about the climate? These are not racial issues.

“A transracial politics for the larger public space, and an empowerment and seizing opportunity and accepting personal responsibility for the more communal space, is the way I think about it.”

title: Two Steward hospitals and their communities await their sad fate
text:
As for Nashoba Valley, the area has suffered from chronic underinvestment in both health care services and basic infrastructure such as transportation, which is an important social determinant of health. The community is already bracing for dire impacts on health, public safety, and municipal finances in a rural region that is stretched thin, with few options for a largely working-class and aging population.

Once the Ayer hospital closes, it will be difficult to reopen it or to repurpose the building for other types of health care uses as the physical plant further deteriorates and workers leave the region for jobs elsewhere.

The time is now for the state to engage the Nashoba Valley community in exploring options and identifying funding to protect health in the region. Investments in primary care and in nonmedical factors that influence health are likely to have the greatest return on investment.

All communities are worthy of the state’s attention and investments to survive, rebound, and thrive after the crisis brought on by Steward Health Care’s collapse.

Amie Shei

President and CEO

The Health Foundation of Central Massachusetts

Worcester

The writer holds a doctoral degree in health policy.

The small, family-friendly hospital seems destined to go the way of “MD” license plates, home visits, chitchat with your doctor, and that good feeling you get from having the entire hospital watching your back in times of extreme duress. I remember when a doctor would ask to see your wallet before taking any money to be sure you could afford it.

Wow. What has happened?

When the Steward-run (and I say that loosely) Carney Hospital in Dorchester is shut down, another gem will be lost. Everyone will be split up, and another health care desert will be left behind.

I am honored to consider Dr. Martin Williams my dearest friend. Giving his lifeblood to serve, he is irreplaceable, as are the nurses, wound care specialists, anesthesiologists, psychologists, and many others.

I contacted Representative Stephen Lynch and received what came off as a form letter. Beacon Hill does not care. Someone has to.

With sadness,

Heidi Vogel-Marquis

Warwick, R.I.

While I deplore what Steward Health Care has done to once well-respected community hospitals, the outcry that Dorchester, Roxbury, and Mattapan will become a “health care desert” is overblown (“Impending Carney closure hits longtime patients hard,” Page A1, Aug. 29). The same could be said for East Boston, Revere, Winthrop, and Chelsea, communities that also have no hospitals. But all these communities are in close proximity to hospital care available in Boston. Not so for Ayer. The Nashoba Valley Medical Center really should be saved.

What I think is really needed are more urgent care centers and primary care centers. Emergency departments are overwhelmed with patients who could be treated at more local, less expensive facilities.

I hope the Legislature also steps up to regulate for-profit systems. Health care should not be a for-profit business.

Kate Murphy

Woburn

I enjoyed reading Jon Chesto’s commentary looking back at the Market Basket battle of 2014 (“10 years later, Market Basket’s feel-good story,” Page A1, Aug. 28). Arthur T. Demoulas’s successful fight for control of the company is an inspiring example of stakeholder capitalism working. Arthur T.’s vision is to run a business for the benefit of all stakeholders, not just the financial owners. Market Basket provides good service, selection, and prices to its customers and serves its employees with good jobs with good pay, benefits, and a retirement plan, all while delivering returns for its owners.

One can’t help but notice the contrast between this story and that of Steward Health Care that has played out in the same pages — a story in which the financial owners extracted maximum value for their personal benefit while leaving their community and employee stakeholders with nothing (“Fight to forestall hospital closures: Rally demands Healey save Carney, Nashoba,” Business, Aug. 29). The extent to which the patients and staff of Steward’s hospitals recover will be up to the largesse of taxpayers. This story is a sad one, and unfortunately, I feel it’s the kind that is more likely to be repeated in our current economic system.

Don McDaniel

North Andover

title: ‘Everything is so expensive’: For many Boston families, back-to-school shopping is still a big expense
text:
Backpacks alone would likely run her $200, she said, since they had increased from $25 each a few years ago to $40 to $60 now. She had to temporarily leave her job as a ramp agent at Logan International Airport over the summer, as she lacked child care. So back-to-school shopping will make a sizable dent in her savings, she said.

“It will set me way behind on other things,” she said.

That’s a common situation for many families in the Boston area, said Marguerite Dowd, senior director of operations at Cradles to Crayons, a Newton-based charity that provides children’s essentials for low-income families. The nonprofit will provide 75,000 backpacks and more than 1 million school supplies to Massachusetts students this year.

“With the effects of inflation and increased cost of living, so many families are asking themselves how they’re going to afford any of these basic needs for school,” Dowd said.

At $39 billion nationwide, projected back-to-school spending for all K-12 families is down from last year’s $41 billion, according to the National Retail Federation, which surveyed 7,533 consumers in July.

College students, meanwhile, are expected to spend a total of $84 billion this year, down from $94 billion in 2023. Back-to-college spending is projected to be $1,365 per household, only $2 less than last year, according to the retail federation.

This year’s projections, lower than last year but still high, reflect that consumer spending overall is starting to moderate, though consumers still prioritize what’s important to them, said Katherine Cullen, vice president for industry and consumer insights at the National Retail Federation.

“For families with kids in K through 12 or folks heading off to college, there’s nothing more important or more essential than being ready for that first day of class,” Cullen said.

In Massachusetts, higher inflation and costs compared to the rest of the country could hurt profitability for both small and large businesses and raise costs for consumers, compared to the nationwide projections, said Jon Hurst, president of the Retailers Association of Massachusetts. The goal for businesses is to beat the prior year’s sales at least by the rate of inflation, so the recent plateaus and projected drops in spending are concerning for stores, Hurst said.

“That’s showing a bit of exhaustion from the consumers,” he said. “That’s a direct response to price increases through inflation.”

To be able to purchase the necessary back-to-school items, 47 percent of low-income families will have to cut back on other expenses, Dowd said.

Mangie Beverly, a hospital industry customer service employee from Roxbury, said she saves money on school supplies for her daughters Shayla, 12, and Mikaili, 8, by looking for last-minute sales. But shopping just before school starts means some of the supplies her daughters need are gone, she said.

Since clothes and school supplies are necessary expenses, she said, she generally tries not to think about the price increases.

“I just spring for it, because I have to,” she said.

Consumers who took the National Retail Federation’s survey reported being budget-conscious while shopping for school essentials, Cullen said.

A loyal Target Circle rewards member, sale-savvy Natalia Menard ordered notebooks online because her job in the career center at Tufts University earned her a discount. She seeks out sales and turns to reliable staples, gesturing one recent evening inside Target to a pile of colorful, folded T-shirts with sequins and designs that she’s been buying her daughter, Aili, for years for $6 to $8. This year, though, they’re $12.

“That’s intense,” she said. “How do they justify that?”

With her son, Zeke, starting preschool and Aili entering first grade, Menard said, the back-to-school shopping list is much longer than last year’s and includes some expensive items like headphones. She recalled how her own back-to-school shopping strained her family’s budget when she was growing up.

“It was a really rough time,” she said.

title: A raccoon breaks into a tiki bar, an 18-wheeler drives the wrong way into a Burger King drive-through, and MBTA buses are vandalized
text:
Every day, police officers respond to reports of all sorts of events and nonevents, most of which never make the news. Here is a sampling of lesser-known — but no less noteworthy — incidents from police log books (a.k.a. blotters) in our communities.

On Aug. 16, a prowler was found lounging in the rafters of a bar at the Sunset Tiki Bar and Grill in Westford. This was not a two-legged prowler, but a four-legged, furry one. It was a Friday afternoon, and Animal Control Officer Kirsten Hirschler and Officer James Antonelli responded to the call reporting that an “angry raccoon” was refusing to leave the bar. The manager reported that a few employees had tried to scare the creature out and “this had caused the animal to become agitated,” Hirschler said. “At the time of the call, there were approximately 150 people at the establishment so the manager was rightfully a little nervous about the whole situation.” When Hirschler and Antonelli arrived, they were told that keg taps were open and beer had spilled everywhere. Several bottles were moved out of the way and Hirschler was able to climb up, secure the raccoon, and place him safely into a crate. “He definitely wasn’t happy about being moved from his little nook and was soaked in beer,” Hirschler said. “The raccoon was then released beyond a fence on the property where he quickly shot out of the crate into the woods. I think he learned his lesson and won’t be looking to tap the keg anytime soon.”

At 10:02 a.m. Aug. 12, Wakefield police checked out some suspicious activity on Audubon Road, where a woman with blonde hair was reportedly seen walking around with a pair of scissors and a samurai sword. Police discovered that the situation wasn’t as bizarre as it appeared, since the item the woman was carrying was just a “wooden walking stick that looked like a sword.”

At 4:50 p.m. Aug. 24, police were called to Burger King on Route 1 in Norwood after employees reported that an 18-wheeler truck went through the drive-through the wrong way. “After being confronted by employees, the operator became agitated,” the log entry stated. Police reported that the truck was sent on its way, and there was no damage caused to the restaurant.

At 11:50 a.m. Aug. 23, Duxbury police were notified of a missing child in the town forest off Mayflower Street. A command post was established and four officers began searching on foot, along with an officer riding an ATV. The Duxbury Fire Department was requested to come to the scene to help, and Kingston police notified dispatch that it also was available to assist. Soon after the search started, Officer Michelle McDonnell located the child a half mile into the woods. The child was then reunited with its family. “Great job by all Officers and assisting departments involved,” police wrote on Facebook.

A lot of anger has been directed at MBTA buses lately. One recent example occurred around 6 p.m. July 22, when an MBTA bus had to be taken off its route in the area of Washington Street and Forest Hills in Boston after a man kicked and broke one of the door windows. According to Transit Police, he was angry because the bus driver would not pick him up at a non-designated stop and decided to express his frustration by kicking the window, causing a spiderweb crack to form. There were slight delays as the bus was removed from service, police said, and the man fled the scene.

At 11:45 p.m. July 27, someone outside Nubian Station in Roxbury threw a metal object at an MBTA bus that shattered the back window. Service was delayed as the bus was taken out of service for repairs, police said, but no injuries were reported.

At around 10 p.m. Aug. 24, a similar scenario unfolded in Chelsea, when a juvenile male on Cabot Street punched a door window of a bus, causing it to break. Once again, service was delayed. Transit Police said they would be conducting a follow-up investigation.

title: Deep and determined, Weymouth girls’ cross-country is all in to make a run at a Division 1 title
text:
“Our whole senior class wants to get back to that place we’ve been so close to,” said coachMike Miller, who was recently named a 2024 Hall of Fame inductee by the Mass. State Track Coaches Association. “There’s a feeling that the one thing we haven’t done is win an All-State title. And so I think there’s some hunger there.”

Richard, Galusha, and Carnes first teamed up as eighth graders, and have risen together . While Richard was already the team’s second-best runner as a freshman, both Galusha and Carnes had to work their way from further down the depth chart as underclassmen.

“I think the fact that we’ve all improved together and pushed each other for years has helped us each move to the next level,” said Carnes. “And this being our senior season, I feel like that just adds to the motivation to do well.”

The three seniors were the catalysts for team workouts six days per week, totaling 30-plus miles. From the start of the preseason, Miller said the entire team’s commitment to physical conditioning was evident — and not just the top three.

“I think all three set the tone by example. They each put in outstanding training summers, and have come into the season in great shape,” Miller said. “And that translates to everyone else. We don’t want to waste such a good front three, and I think that’s the mind-set a lot of the rest of the team has.”

Junior Leah Glavin and sophomore Natalie McInnis, who finished 93rd and 122nd, respectively, at 2023 All-States, along with junior Mia Manfedi, are candidates for the 3-6 spots.

Weymouth also returns senior Emma Daley, who ran an impressive 19:20 three-mile and finished 44th at All-States as a freshman in 2021, but missed the past two seasons with an injury.

“Toward the end of last season, our gap after number three was just a little bigger than we would want it to be,” Miller said. “With the work that’s been put in, I feel we’ve absolutely closed the gap this summer.”

While repeating as Bay State champions — arguably the state’s toughest conference — remains a goal, the Wildcats hope their performance at the divisional and All-State meets is where they are ultimately measured. Galusha believes that the entire lineup’s big-race experience will pay off come November.

“I think this time around, we know how to not put a ton of pressure on ourselves or create a lot of anxiety [for the postseason races],” Galusha said. “I think we’ve seen how that can lead to not our favorite outcomes, but now we know how to handle it and we’re ready for it.”

Richard, who still looks up to the senior leaders of Weymouth’s 2021 team that won the Division 1A title and was the All-State runner-up, knows the rarity of returning an entire starting line — and the opportunity this unique season presents.

“As a program, we know that we’ve been there before, and that we can do it again,” Richard said. “It’s almost like I’m following those footsteps, that we did it freshman year and just trying to bring it over to this season and this team. And we have everything we need to do it.”

▪ Even after graduating its top three runners, two-time defending state champion Brookline will be among the top Division 1 boys’ squads again this season.

Seniors Altamo Aschkenasy and Lysander Duffield, who each finished in the top 20 at All-States last year, will slide up from the Warriors’ fourth and fifth spots. Brookline’s third spot will be handled by junior Theodore Butty, who comes off a monster outdoor track season in which he placed sixth in both the mile and 2-mile at the Division 1 championship meet.

A number of talented reinforcements will compete for the fourth and fifth spots. Sophomore Liam Hartmann is expected to take a leap following a stellar freshman campaign, while a group of tightly-packed seniors will contend for contributing roles.

“They’ve all been sitting in the wings and seeing the group in front of them do so well,” said coach Michael Glennon. “With that comes pressure, so we’ll have to see how they respond to that. But since we have such a big group, I’m counting on some of them stepping up to it.”

Glennon, head coach at Brookline since 1995, is officially a volunteer assistant coach this fall because of a family trip to Ireland planned in September. Dave Fleming, who coaches Revere track in the winter and spring, is serving as interim head coach, before Glennon plans to resume formally as head coach next fall.

▪ A number of teams kick things off this week with regular season league meets, while other conferences get underway the following week. Among the intriguing opening-week matchups is No. 2 Weymouth vs. No. 7 Newton North, who will square off along with Milton in a Bay State tri-meet on Wednesday.

Some highlights of the early-season invitational schedule include the MSTCA Relays on Saturday, Sept. 7 at Highland Park in Attleboro, and the Frank Kelly Invitational — the first major stop for many teams — on Saturday, Sept. 21 at Wrentham Development Center.

title: These landlords have vacant apartments for homeless families but the paperwork required by the state is driving them away.
text:
Now, with such a staggering influx of families seeking a place to live, the bureaucracy simply can’t keep up. Landlords and advocates describe having to navigate a labyrinth of paperwork, with applications sometimes taking months to get processed. It’s resulted in lost units as frustrated landlords decide that waiting for the paperwork to clear is not worth the forgone income, advocates say, though the exact number is uncertain.

It also leaves vulnerable families in limbo.

“Families are suffering because they don’t have a place to go,” said Geralde Gabeau, the executive director of the Immigrant Family Services Institute, which helps mostly Haitian migrants get connected to essential services.

Families show up at Gabeau’s Mattapan office at all hours looking for a place to stay, she said. Her staff has been working overtime to help connect them with HomeBASE, But while eligible families and landlords line up their paperwork and ready themselves for move-in, the approval process sometimes jams up — the result, she said, of so many people trying to access the program.

In July, Governor Maura Healey’s administration announced plans to sharply limit stays for families in the overflow shelters, leaving migrant families four options: they can accept a ticket to travel elsewhere, they can find a place on their own, such as with family or friends, they can find housing through the HomeBASE program, or, if all else fails, they’ll be put out on the street.

The situation comes as Healey grapples with a system overflowing with more than 7,000 families and costing the state an estimated $1 billion.

A spokesperson for the state’s housing office, Kevin Connor, said in a statement that the Healey administration “will continue to work on improving the HomeBASE program to reduce the time that it takes to re-house families.”

“Connecting families to stable housing is our ultimate goal,” he added.

Advocates working on the front line of the migrant crisis consider HomeBASE to be the best of the available options.

“They are not on the street and they are in a safe place for at least two years,” Gabeau said.

Increasing demand for the program, however, has translated into increasingly frequent delays for families, advocates say.

For years, groups such as Gabeau’s have found landlords through Zillow, real estate databases, and homeowners’ associations. These advocates have kept relationships with those property owners willing to be part of the program.

The Mattapan organization has at times had some HomeBASE applications fully processed within two weeks, but others have dragged on for as long as three months.

The program is helping many, with 384 families who were in shelters now placed in subsidized apartments since July 1, a significant increase from the same time frame last year.

The Healey administration also beefed up HomeBASE, raising the subsidy families receive from $20,000 to up to $30,000 over two years with the possibility of a third year of help. And landlords who rent to a HomeBASE family get an additional one month’s rent as a bonus.

Families contribute 30 percent of their income toward rent and the state pays the rest. Participating landlords generally receive market-rate rents for their units, similar to federal subsidized housing programs.

The state’s housing office doesn’t directly process HomeBASE applications, a spokesperson said. Instead, it contracts with 11 regional agencies across the state, which are responsible for meeting the demand for the program. A spokesperson said that since January, the average statewide wait time for a HomeBASE application is 12.6 days, but that average varies by agency.

One of those agencies, Metro Housing Boston, said in a statement that while it is behind in assigning case workers, it doesn’t have a backlog of cases, and is hiring more staff to speed up processing times.

While HomeBASE has been more effective than the state’s “reticketing program,” which has given 51 families plane tickets to relocate out of the state, advocates say the steps involved — submitting paperwork to a sometimes backed-up system, pulling together the necessary identification for families to sign a lease, having a landlord go through on online portal — still move too slowly.

Jeff Thielman, who leads the International Institute of New England, said that while he is starting to see the strain easing on the shelter system, HomeBASE is still not moving fast enough. His group and other resettlement agencies have a contract with the state to move 400 families out of shelters by the end of the year.

So far, his organization has placed about 10 families in apartments since the contract started in March.

One Brazilian family — a mother and five children — was in a shelter in Roxbury for months while waiting for the HomeBASE paperwork to clear. They were desperate to move because the mother had been raped in a home where the family had previously stayed, said Fernanda Silveirao, their case worker with Fall River nonprofit Source Hub.

Ashley Ferreira, a longtime landlord and property manager in Fall River who owns the apartment the Brazilian family moved into, said the process involved “a lot of runaround” and proved “extremely complicated.”

“The lack of communication and lengthy process is definitely very discouraging,” said Ferreira.

Adam Hoole, a senior paralegal at Greater Boston Legal Services, who helped Silveirao navigate the case in Fall River, has been working with HomeBASE for years. He said the process isn’t straightforward, with copious paperwork requirements for landlords.

HomeBASE works for families who have the resources to move in and start their lives, he said. But it’s not a substitute for emergency shelter or, better, public housing.

“I don’t think it’s the magic solution [the state] thinks it is,” Hoole said. “It’s just a referral of the problem down the road.”

In the meantime, families wait.

The family from Brazil, for example, was matched with a different apartment in Fall River in mid-April, but that landlord pulled out three weeks into the process, feeling overburdened by the paperwork, according to Silveirao. The family stayed in Boston, on edge due to the trauma they had endured in their last living situation.

Silveirao matched them with Ferreira, who persisted with the process for more than a month — forgoing rent that would help with her mortgage payments — until the family could move in early June.

Silveirao said the experience was so daunting she never wants to deal with HomeBASE again.

“It was always more and more and more. Every week that went by, it was another piece of documentation or another certificate that [state officials] needed,” said Silveirao, who said she exchanged more than 80 emails during the process. “I know the caseload is huge, but [the process] makes it so much worse for the family that was involved.”

title: Mass. lawmakers announce deal to add 225 new liquor licenses for Boston
text:
The deal they filed Tuesday would add 195 new restricted licenses for 13 ZIP codes in Boston — with five distributed per year, per ZIP code, over three years. Of the five licenses, three would be for all alcohol sales, and two would be for sales of beer and wine, according to lawmakers.

A dozen other new permits would be unrestricted licenses, meaning they can be used anywhere in Boston and sold for a profit. Moran called those permits “pocket licenses” because it allows the city to parcel them out for specific projects.

The bill would also set aside 15 licenses for nonprofits, small theaters, and outdoor spaces for all alcohol sales, while three others would go to Oak Square in Brighton, which Moran represents and doesn’t have a single sit-down restaurant with a full liquor license, he said.

The decision to root the vast majority of new permits in specific neighborhoods — and require they remain in the ZIP codes to which they were allotted — is crucial to create new economic opportunities in neighborhoods starving for them, said state Representative Chris Worrell, a Dorchester Democrat and lead sponsor of the legislation in the House.

“I see more tourist dollars. Instead of stopping at Newbury [Street], at the Seaport, at Back Bay, I see them coming to Roxbury, Mattapan, and Hyde Park and being amongst the locals,” Worrell said.

The bill has been eyed as a boon for communities of color and small business owners, who have not always had the luxury of affording a liquor license, which can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars.

License holders in the new batch of permits would also be required to sell food.

“People want more restaurants, they want more options for food,” said Moran, a Brighton Democrat. “This bill was about underserved areas.”

Senator Liz Miranda said the bill would go far in closing the racial wealth gap across the city, particularly in Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, and Hyde Park. She said Blue Hill Avenue was once a “cultural mecca” with Black-owned restaurants and nightlife, but that the cost of purchasing a liquor license on the secondary made it difficult, if impossible, for many to launch a business.

“[A cost of] $500,000 to $700,000 to a million dollars is inaccessible to most people. It’s not just neighborhood folks. It literally shatters dreams,” said Miranda, a Roxbury Democrat. “This is more than just about liquor licenses.”

House and Senate leaders both said they hope to send the bill to Governor Maura Healey by the end of the week. Both chambers have informal sessions scheduled for Thursday.

Mayor Michelle Wu said in a statement that each of the new licenses “represents new life and economic prosperity for an entrepreneur, a business, a neighborhood, and families throughout our city.”

The bill was one of several still locked up in closed-door negotiations when lawmakers wrapped up formal sessions on the morning of Aug. 1.

The Senate had passed its version just days prior, proposing to give Boston 264 new liquor licenses — more than the 250 number proposed in a home rule petition from the Boston City Council. The bill also sought to bring discounted licenses to 13 ZIP codes from Mattapan to the South End, with the aim of increasing access for owners of restaurants and bars in neighborhoods of color, who are often priced out of buying their own permits.

The House passed its own version in May, seeking to add 205 permits, mostly in underserved neighborhoods across the city.

The Legislature has long limited the number of liquor licenses that can be issued in most cities and towns, including Boston. The city hit its cap of roughly 1,200 permits two decades ago, and acquiring one usually requires buying one from another restaurant or bar that has closed. The asking price to pour wine, beer, and cocktails can top $600,000.

The soaring costs have concentrated many licenses in well-to-do neighborhoods, such as the Back Bay and the Seaport.

The agreement’s emergence on the day of the state primary continues the slow drip of major legislation to emerge during what is typically a quiet period on Beacon Hill. In the weeks since ending formal sessions, lawmakers have passed agreements to expand access to midwives and improve maternal health care in Massachusetts, and increase oversight of long-term care in the state.

Legislative leaders have said they’re also prepared to call lawmakers back to the State House for another formal session to pass a multibillion-dollar economic development bill that collapsed on the final, chaotic day of formal sessions this week.

Lawmakers have yet to announce a deal on that legislation, however, leaving it unclear when they could return for a formal vote. To pass a bill that authorizes borrowing, such as the economic development bill, lawmakers are constitutionally required to take a roll-call vote, which occurs in formal sessions.

Other legislation, such as the bill to expand liquor licenses, can typically pass in an informal session as long as there isn’t opposition.

Niki Griswold, Diti Kohli, and Shirley Leung of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: When the market speaks, it does not demand health care equity
text:
Explaining the state’s initial decision to accept the closing of Carney Hospital in Dorchester and Nashoba Valley Medical Center in Ayer, Secretary of Health and Human Services Kate Walsh said in July, “The market has spoken.”

While the bluntness of that statement was shocking, the principle behind it is not. Whether they are for profit or technically nonprofit, hospitals are businesses. Like any business, they need customers — for hospitals, that means patients — and the revenue they generate for a healthy bottom line. Steward Health Care decided that five hospitals it operated met that criteria. Steward has reached deals with other operators to run four of those hospitals. The state seeks to take control of another one — St. Elizabeth’s Medical Center in Brighton.

Without a rescuer, the two hospitals that did not make the cut will disappear. When the market speaks — and people listen to it — that’s what happens.

Get College Town

A weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns.

Enter Email

All kinds of businesses disappear. Convenience stores and hardware stores. Bakeries and coffee shops. Banks, supermarkets, drug stores — and hospitals.

Economies of scale — defined as the advantages that can happen when a business increases in size — are part of the big cultural shift that has occurred, one that moves away from local businesses and toward large operations that are supposed to provide more efficient service and savings for consumers.

There’s no more Jordan Marsh or Filene’s and no Bank of Boston. John Hancock Financial Services is owned by Toronto-based Manulife. Large hospital networks like Mass General Brigham and Beth Israel Lahey Health dominate the health care landscape. When the market spoke, it said bigger is better, the strong will survive, and the weak will not.

The collapse of the for-profit hospital network operated by Steward , driven by the extraordinary greed of its CEO, Ralph de la Torre, is an exceptionally ugly part of that big economic picture. Meanwhile, the state’s initial acquiescence to the closing of Carney Hospital in Dorchester as a result of that collapse represents an acceptance of a common outcome: Businesses that don’t survive are often the ones located in low-income areas, which means the poorest and most marginalized suffer the most.

“As a business model, it’s just not succeeding,” said Larry DiCara, a former Boston city councilor and longtime political observer who grew up in the Carney neighborhood. “The constituency for the hospital is now people on the margins of society. As a business, it’s just not lined up to succeed.”

If Carney Hospital closes, leaving what social justice advocates call a health care desert, it won’t be the only potential desert in the Dorchester, Roxbury, and Mattapan communities it serves.

As the Globe recently reported, after the fourth Walgreens shut down, there’s a growing drug store desert in the predominantly Black and Latino neighborhoods of Roxbury and Mattapan. That happens when a chain like Walgreens comes in, and through economies of scale, squeezes out small, independent pharmacies by offering more variety and lower prices. However, if Walgreens or another large chain decides it’s not making enough money in a specific location, it feels free to shut it down, leaving behind people who no longer have a place nearby to pick up prescriptions.

People in those communities must also fight for food access. According to a city report issued in 2021, when it comes to availability of food through supermarkets and convenience stores, sections of Dorchester, Roxbury, Mattapan, and Hyde Park are more than a half-mile from a grocery store — a distance that can be a barrier for elderly people or those with disabilities, and for those relying on public transportation.

Last April, it took a judge’s decision to put the Edgar P. Benjamin Healthcare Center, a Mission Hill nursing and rehabilitation home that has prioritized care for Black patients, into receivership to give it a chance to survive. A new administrator took over in May, after the previous administrator was ousted amid allegations of financial mismanagement. Whether it’s a winning business model is still unknown.

In Massachusetts, political leaders talk a lot about “health equity.” In January, the Healey administration announced what it said was a new approach to reducing health disparities across the state through “community-based interventions.” That was the same month that the Steward Health Care crisis began to publicly unfold, and when the Healey administration began to wrestle with the fallout.

In July, Boston Mayor Michelle Wu also announced a new health equity agenda aimed at improving life expectancy and reducing racial health disparities across the city of Boston

But when the market speaks, it does not demand equity. Unless political leaders intervene to make that happen, communities like the one served by Carney Hospital pay the price.

Joan Vennochi is a Globe columnist. She can be reached at joan.vennochi@globe.com. Follow her @joan_vennochi.

title: Federal prosecutors detail how reputed street gang members allegedly perpetrated a mail theft scheme in Boston suburbs
text:
In an affidavit filed Aug. 27, ATF Special Agent E. Austin Wozniak wrote that the men allegedly perpetrated the fraud between July 2023 and February 2024. Their alleged behavior is called “card cracking,” he wrote.

“Card cracking schemes are fueled by checks that are stolen from U.S. Postal Service (’USPS’) collection boxes,” Wozniak wrote. “The ink from stolen checks [is] chemically washed and rewritten to various recruited bank account holders. These washed checks are deposited into checking accounts for cash withdrawal or laundering through money transfers and other means, such as the purchase of postal money orders.”

Once the parcels are purloined, Wozniak said, “offenders wash stolen checks with chemicals that erase handwritten ink, leaving the check otherwise intact. This process allows for the blank check to be rewritten to any intended payee in any amount.”

Straw account holders are typically recruited through social media and word of mouth and get compensated with a cut of the ill-gotten cash, according to the affidavit.

“Account holders essentially allow for a card cracking suspect to take control of their bank account,” Wozniak wrote. “Stolen, washed checks are deposited into account holders’ bank accounts via ATM deposits or mobile deposits, the account balance is monitored, and cash is withdrawn at ATM machines as soon as it is made available by the bank.”

He wrote that during the summer of 2023, Wellesley police and surrounding law enforcement agencies started receiving numerous check fraud reports pertaining to checks placed in the mail in June and July of last year.

There were 21 such incidents during that time period reported in Wellesley, Brookline, West Roxbury, Newton, Needham, Sherborn, Brockton, and Braintree, the affidavit said.

“Wellesley Police had detectives assigned to this long running investigation, and we are obviously very pleased at the results with these charges,” said Wellesley Police Chief Scott Whittemore in a statement. “Our officers and detectives have invested a great deal of time and effort investigating this case, as well as the many other mail theft cases that have occurred.”

The fraudulent check cashing “unfortunately continues however,” Whittemore said.

He said Wellesley and other communities “continue to experience theft from blue mailboxes. These thefts, usually by suspects with keys, occur during the overnight and early morning hours. We’ve noted the thefts are prevalent after hours on the weekends as well. I would continue to stress that citizens avoid using blue mailboxes, and instead go inside the Post Office to mail letters. I would strongly suggest never mailing a letter after the posted collection times, or in a case where the letter would potentially sit overnight in a mailbox.”

And the stolen cash fuels devastating violence, according to agent Wozniak.

“I learned that some Mission Hill members and associates use the proceeds from the target offenses to purchase weapons, which facilitates violent crime within the gang,” he wrote in the affidavit, adding that the gangsters also allegedly “sell stolen checks to further profit from their mail theft.”

Such theft has been a longstanding issue in Massachusetts.

In January, Needham police warned residents of mailbox “phishing” and urged them to bring outgoing mail into a post office instead of trusting public boxes. Thieves had allegedly been using keys to open mailboxes at mail drop-off locations and stealing mail inside, police said at the time.

In late 2022, Needham, along with other neighboring communities, was targeted for mail thefts by people looking to steal checks, authorities said. In December 2022, cops in Dedham said they had received “multiple reports of mailbox fishing,” and in September 2022, two members of the Newton Police Department took part in a sting operation that resulted in the arrest of an alleged mailbox thief. In August of that year, after receiving multiple reports of checks being stolen from mailboxes and altered (for amounts totaling more than $250,000), police in Mattapoisett arrested two 18-year-olds from Dorchester who were allegedly seen mailbox fishing.

Then, last November, police arrested two men and recovered more than 1,000 pieces of mail allegedly stolen in Wellesley after thieves crashed a vehicle in Brookline.

Some thieves have been even more brazen, robbing letter carriers at gunpoint.

In late December, Boston police responded to a radio call reporting an armed robbery at Talbot and Welles avenues, police said in a statement. Officers located a postal worker who said his mail key was stolen at gunpoint, the statement said.

Another robbery of a mail carrier by a gun-toting assailant was reported in December 2022 in Melrose.

Junior TE/MLB Felix Wood (5-11, 185) should show his effectiveness on both sides of the ball. Senior quarterback Dominic Matteodo returns under center after a solid season and 5-11 senior RB/LB Ben Squarcia returns to the Rams as a powerful runner between the tackles.

Monomoy is poised to make it back to the playoffs despite the lack of depth. “Our team has 26 players right now ... 26 hard-working dedicated student-athletes wanting to compete,” said Sliney.

Graduates included star running back/defensive back Montavius Zollarcoffer and lineman and former captain Isaiah Apperwhite. Zollarcoffer scored 23 touchdowns in 10 games. The Tigers will look to replicate that leadership with Keyshon Wright, a senior who rose from third-string signal-caller to starter in short order. Tight end/linebacker Luke Maffeo (6-0, 210) will provide help on both sides of the ball. Perhaps their biggest challenge will be rebuilding the lines.

Lining up next to Cohello in the Canalmen’s 4-3 defense will be senior Isaiah Rodrick, who’s as athletic as they come. Bourne loses starting quarterback Ty Kelley to graduation.

Outlook: Although the Bengals graduated 17 students, “we have a nice group of returning starters and lettermen who are ready to step up,” said coach Randolph Abraham, who has been on the Brighton coaching staff since 2004. Key returnees on the line include senior Jeremiah Reed (6-2, 275), junior Ernesto Rodriguez (6-2, 287), and senior Jullian Duarte (5-9, 285). They lead an experienced group on both sides of the ball and provide exceptional leadership. On offense, the team is highlighted by the senior running back duo James Burrell (5-9, 170) and Eugune Vanburen III (5-11, 180). Junior quarterback Dontay Gillis-Rayne (6-3, 180) is ready to call plays for the Bengals. “We need to improve defensively and on special teams to reach [the team’s] goals,” said Abraham. “We have had a great preseason and are looking to be competitive in our league and in our division.”
