title: Too many students whose first language isn’t English are struggling. Here’s a plan to help them.
text:
Despite that, Alaia now primarily speaks English. In fact, while both of her parents mostly speak to Alaia in Spanish — and always have — the 8-year-old has lost her ability to easily understand and speak Spanish. “It is sometimes very hard to speak with her,” González said. “She’d say, in Spanish, ‘mami, no entiendo lo que me dices, ¿cómo se dice en inglés?’ And I repeat it to her in Spanish but she insists that I tell her in English.”

Alaia has struggled to learn because she has never been taught in Spanish — her biggest asset, her primary language — at Orchard Gardens, according to her mom, whose proficiency in English is limited. González and her husband are now in the process of switching Alaia to the Hurley K-8 School, one of BPS’s eight schools that offer bilingual education for English language learners, which the couple said they didn’t know was an option in the district. “It’s very hard for me to help her with homework because I don’t understand,” González said. “I had to put her in an after-school program so they can help her with homework because I can’t.”

Educating students whose first language isn’t English, like Alaia, is one of the most urgent challenges facing the Boston Public Schools.

A third of students in the district — or about 16,800 — are classified as English language learners. At the younger grades, the ELL numbers are even higher:47 percent of kindergartners and 51 percent of pre-kindergarteners are non-native English speakers.

For this group of students, the district has to juggle two tasks: teaching them to speak and write English, as required by federal law, while at the same time teaching them academic subjects like math and science.

It’s a daunting challenge — one the district hasn’t always met.

Consider the district’s latest test scores, which paint an abysmal picture for English language learners. Only 4 percent of ELLs in grades 3-8 and 2 percent of ELLs in grade 10 met or exceeded expectations on the English MCAS test in 2024, while 8 percent of ELLs in grades 3-8 and 6 percent of ELLs in grade 10 did so on the math MCAS test.

Academic research suggests that the best way to serve these students is through bilingual education programs that deliver some instruction in their native language, while also teaching them English — like the one at the Hurley. Decades ago, bilingual education was controversial — Massachusetts even banned it for a time.

Now, though, legal restrictions are gone and the barriers are staff and money. Bilingual education is expensive, qualified bilingual teachers are hard to find, and Boston’s bilingual education offerings are relatively scarce.

There’s no magic formula to solve those problems. But there’s also no question that expanding the district’s bilingual education offerings for families like González’s would be a far better use of money than keeping underutilized school buildings open. Boston needs to consolidate schools so that it can direct as many of its resources as possible into closing gaps that have festered for far too long.

For English language learners, the recent history in Massachusetts has been bleak. A political movement in the late 1990s and early 2000s spearheaded by conservative Silicon Valley millionaire Ron Unz drove voters in Arizona, California, and Massachusetts to pass restrictive language laws — so called English-only laws — which severely limited the use of the native language in the education of English learners. The Commonwealth’s voters approved English-only education in a 2002 referendum.

In Boston, the impact was immediate. A University of Massachusetts Boston study found that, from 2003 to 2006, high school dropout rates for English learners almost doubled and that MCAS test score gains for them were lower than those of other student populations; as a result, achievement gaps between ELL students and other BPS groups widened.

In the next decade, things didn’t improve — despite federal intervention, task forces appointed to address the needs of ELL students, and, in 2017, state legislation that effectively repealed the 2002 law. “The district has not created equitable conditions to ensure that all English learners progress both academically and in English language development,” read a comprehensive audit of BPS by state education authorities released in spring 2020, just as the COVID-19 pandemic began.

In 2018, the four-year graduation rate for English learners was the second-lowest among all student groups at 63 percent. Between 2015 and 2018, the dropout rate for English learners grew by roughly 34 percent and was the highest among all groups.

Recent BPS data show that the graduation rates of multilingual learners in Boston are much lower than the average; their dropout rates are nearly double the average.

At the crux of these poor outcomes is the insufficient amount of bilingual education the district offers.

Research shows that programs that use English learners’ primary language in instruction — like dual-language programs, which form part of what is known as bilingual education — are more likely to close achievement gaps. A large-scale, longitudinal study published in 2017 found “that English-only and transitional bilingual programs of short duration only close about half of the achievement gap between English learners and native English speakers, while high-quality, long-term bilingual programs close all of the gap after 5–6 years of schooling.”

And yet, according to figures provided by the district, only 7 percent of English learners — or about 1,200 students — are currently enrolled in the district’s dual-language programs. The rest, including Alaia, learn under what is dubbed an English immersion approach, where teachers teach academic subjects in English with limited support in students’ native languages. Lessons are typically taught in English, but the teacher can use various tools or techniques — like speaking slowly, using simple words, or offering visual aids like pictures and videos — to help students follow along even if their English proficiency is low.

English learners are often described as the fastest-growing student segment in K-12 education nationwide. About 1 in 10 American K-12 students is an English language learner. In the Bay State, the share of public school students with ELL status more than doubled between 2003 and 2018 — from 6 percent to 14 percent.

Additionally, many English language learners have special needs, which further complicates the challenge of educating them. In Boston, nearly 1 in 4 English learners has a disability.

The majority of English learners in the district are native Spanish speakers. But ELLs who speak Haitian Creole as a first language are an emerging demographic — Boston has the third-largest population of Haitians in the country. Small numbers of native Portuguese, Vietnamese, Chinese, Arabic, and Somali speakers attend BPS, according tolast year’s data from the district.

In an ideal world, all ELLs would be enrolled in bilingual programs — which could also serve as attractive options for English-speaking families who may want their child to learn a second language. But Boston only has eight verbal dual-language programs (it also has an American Sign Language program). Dual-language programs include the Mario Umana Academy K-8 in East Boston (Spanish-English), the Mattahunt Elementary School in Mattapan (Haitian Creole-English), the Rafael Hernández K-8 School in Roxbury (Spanish-English), and the Margarita Muñiz Academy in Jamaica Plain, the district’s first and only dual-language high school (Spanish-English).

Building these bilingual education programs requires money, primarily to hire certified bilingual teachers. But there is fierce competition nationwide to hire qualified teachers since so many districts are also contending with rising numbers of ELL students. In fact, the national shortage of bilingual teachers is the main reason why districts across the country aren’t expanding bilingual and dual-language education, according to a recent paper from The Century Foundation, a public policy research nonprofit.

Many school systems have been offering targeted cash incentives like hiring or retention bonuses for bilingual educators — for example, up to $8,000 in Houston for new hires. In Boston, though, according to a district spokesperson, bilingual teachers’ pay is not differentiated from non-bilingual educators’ pay. The spokesperson said BPS would like to explore bonuses for bilingual educators and had discussed the idea with the teachers union.

Rebuilding all the infrastructure needed for bilingual education in Massachusetts takes time, given that the pipeline of bilingual teachers withered during the time the policy was illegal. More than anything, it will take millions of dollars — for sustained investment in curriculum, training and certification of specialized teachers and staff, professional development, and even emerging AI tools to support bilingual education.

In an interview, a BPS spokesperson said the district submitted to state education authorities nine new program proposals to teach multilingual learners. Of those, two are dual-language programs. “That’s a big first step and we want to continue to grow that,” the spokesperson said. “But we are trying to balance doing this well and doing this quickly.” (In the spring, state officials rejected 17 out of 19 new program proposals for multilingual learners the district wanted to implement this fall because they fell short of state criteria.)

Boston does have a program to train bilingual educators: The Bilingual Educators and Accelerated Community to Teacher Program, launched during the 2023-2024 school year, is a 12-month program that’s free to accepted applicants. The district’s spokesperson said the program had 18 graduates last year and the current cohort has 89 participants. Graduates are not required to teach in BPS, but they are strongly encouraged to. BPS is also offering a new bilingual inclusive education initiative, in which graduates of the accelerated teacher program can apply to be a teacher resident next school year at one of the district’s bilingual schools and earn a discounted master’s degree through a partnership with Stonehill College, the spokesperson said.

The district should launch more grow-your-own programs. These programs could help bilingual paraprofessionals or school staff become licensed teachers and create a career pathway for multilingual high school students to become educators.

To the disappointment of many experts and community leaders in Boston, though, the district doesn’t seem to be going all-in on bilingual education.

Last fall, Boston officials announced a new model to educate multilingual students. The approach involves educating non-native speakers in full-immersion general education classes. The idea is that they will have access to multilingual services but not guaranteed instruction in their native language.

Nine of the 13 members of the task force appointed to advise the Boston School Committee on multilingual education resigned in protest.

“The current plan is incomprehensible in its ignorance of what constitutes optimal educational practice,” Miren Uriarte and Rosann Tung, two of the members who resigned, wrote in a Globe op-ed. Indeed, the district could not point to research or studies that would support the plan.

“This is an English-only dumping operation,” Roger Rice, executive director of Multicultural Education, Training and Advocacy, said of the plan last year.

“We are trying to do something very different than we have in previous years. This is the first year of rolling out inclusion differently,” the district’s spokesperson told the Globe last week. “We are on month two of doing that and we’re doing it at very specific grades. We have to give it some time.”

BPS insists that the plan allows multilingual learners to be taught in the least-restrictive environment. They borrow that terminology from the special education world, where inclusive practices are encouraged, such as teaching students with disabilities in a general education classroom.

Mainstreaming special education students leads to better academic outcomes, social skills development, and many more benefits for students with disabilities. But students with disabilities and English language learners are two different populations, and what works for one isn’t necessarily best for the other. The way a former district official put it, BPS’s definition of inclusion, in the context of English learners, is misguided. The definition of inclusion, the former official said, should be celebrating different cultures and different languages and fully embracing multilingualism.

It remains to be seen how the district’s new approach will fare. But it is clearly not ideal. In the long term, increasing bilingual offerings — by attracting more bilingual teachers and rebuilding the pipeline to train them — is the most promising way to give non-native English speakers the education they need.

title: With new zoning rules, Mattapan’s Blue Hill Avenue is poised for a rebirth
text:
After years of underinvestment, the neighborhood is showing new life. Apartment buildings have sprung up, especially near stops on the Commuter Rail’s Fairmount Line. New bus lanes are coming too, to be installed in the center of Blue Hill Ave. A long-discussed neighborhood plan is now official, with zoning that aims to spur along new multistory, mixed-use buildings and support smaller, locally owned businesses. And there’s hope that a tranche of new liquor licenses designated for Mattapan will bring more restaurants and places to linger.

That sounds a bit like the Mattapan Square Ali-Salaam grew up in. Back then there were two movie theaters, bakeries, and a Brigham’s ice cream shop.

“There were places that, if you were a young teen, you could walk down to the square and sit down and have an ice cream sundae,” she said. “Now it’s not that type of atmosphere.”

There’s a lot at play, but one shared goal of the various plans is for business and development to radiate up Blue Hill Ave., creating opportunities for residents and entrepreneurs alike. Today, the road can feel like a mini-highway, with 40,000 cars a day, many of which are simply cutting through Mattapan on their way somewhere else. Those who do often double park in front of businesses and takeout joints, only clogging traffic further.

The zoning changes aim to encourage more housing and even office space. Taller buildings, yes, but also a more pedestrian-friendly sidewalk with room for street-level businesses. A few have already arrived.

Just this month, Marcia Satchell opened a new location of her Blue Mountain Jamaican Restaurant in The Wellington, a new 39-unit apartment building on Blue Hill Avenue in the Wellington Hills section of Mattapan. She’s already welcoming regulars, and she’s excited to contribute to a vibrancy she feels is long overdue here.

“Some of what’s happening throughout other parts of Boston are now happening in Mattapan,” Satchell said. “I think the continuation of development and building is going to be key, and ensuring that Mattapan gets equal opportunity for business growth as other communities.”

New housing is a key ingredient to all that, said Dariela Villon-Maga. The developer and Mattapan native is working on three projects along Blue Hill Avenue, has a bid in for a city-owned parcel on Cummins Highway parcel, and is proposing a mixed-use building near Mattapan Square that would also house an arts complex.

In each project, Villon-Maga says she’s hoping to prioritize the neighborhood’s values. That means emphasizing affordable homeownership over rental units — so that residents will know they can stay. She’s also created a community board to vet occupants of ground-floor space, which those businesses, too, would ultimately own, not rent. All of it, again, aims to enliven Blue Hill Ave.

“The community has really been vocal about their want for more activation along Blue Hill Avenue: More destinations, more places for them to go, whether it’s cafes, restaurants, or art galleries,” Villon-Maga said. “It’s the ability to kind of walk to a destination versus having to go downtown or having to go kind of outside of their neighborhood.”

That’s part of what the city aims to do as well. Five years in the making, Plan:Mattapan aims to enable more buildings that can both bring more residents and a wider variety of commercial spaces to Blue Hill Ave.

Some, yes, would likely be taller than what’s there now. But the idea isn’t to remake the corridor entirely, said Aimee Chambers, who leads planning and zoning at the Boston Planning Department. It’s to make the most of what’s already there.

“We want to make sure that we’re not encouraging demolition of buildings or anything like that,” Chambers said. “Rather, we want to create circumstances where we can work with existing building owners to think about ways to be more creative.”

Still, even among supporters of that vision, there are concerns about growing pains from all this change. Villon-Maga hears a lot of worry about traffic and the new bus lane project that’s now under public review. The $44 million plan would create three miles of designated center bus lanes, 2.25 miles of protected bike lanes, between nine and 11 new pairs of raised bus stops, and more than 14 new crosswalks.

All of the potential construction is on the minds of local entrepreneurs who have invested in the neighborhood, too.

“I’m concerned about the thriving businesses around here,” said Denise O’Marde, the owner of Cafe Juice Up, a juice bar that sits across the street from the Blue Mountain restaurant.

O’Marde sees herself as part of the change: She opened her business in 2018 to bring a healthy food option to a section of Mattapan where convenience stores reigned supreme. The business survived the pandemic, but she’s now worried construction on Blue Hill Ave. could result in more traffic and congestion — and less foot traffic into her shop. “While I support a change for the future — and I understand that it’s so our children will have a nice Blue Hill Ave. for the next 50 years — I’m scared,” she said. “I have anxiety when I think about that.”

Then there’s that perennial concern that comes with new development in working-class neighborhoods: displacement.

Rising rents and home prices have already pushed many Black families out of this part of Boston, something the Rev. Willie Bodrick sees every Sunday when he looks out at his congregation at 12th Baptist Church in Roxbury.

“There are families who come from Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan,” he said. “Now they’re living in Canton, Randolph, Brockton.”

Along with being a pastor, Bodrick’s also a housing developer, work he sees as deeply intertwined with his goal of building community. He and his brother Winston cofounded Ambry Development and are launching three residential buildings, including one on a parcel they acquired from the city, off Blue Hill Avenue near Harambee Park. It’ll be 18 units, all set at affordable prices for lower- and middle-income buyers. And it will be all for sale, not rentals, so that not just current residents but also their children and grandchildren can have a place to call home.

“We know there’s a lot of movement in this neighborhood. And we know we’re in the midst of a housing crisis,” Willie Bodrick said. “We want people to be able to stay in this neighborhood.”

Staying and being part of the evolution of Mattapan is important to small business owners like Derick Foster-Toney, whose family has owned the Chez-Vous roller rink for four decades. The rink, which sits on the border of Mattapan and Dorchester and has been in business since 1933, is one of the few entertainment venues in the area, and has long served a rare role in the neighborhood: a community gathering place. “The fabric of what Boston truly is,” he said, “is defined by places like Chez-Vous.”

Foster-Toney said he’s been buoyed to see new development crop up along the Blue Hill Ave. corridor, and he’s hopeful to be part of it, saying he hopes to obtain one of the new liquor licenses that will be distributed to the neighborhood.

“This area that was forgotten and overlooked because of stigmas,” he said. “It wasn’t the fault of the people,” he noted, but rather a lack of city support. “We have the greatest opportunity to change that narrative and restore a sense of pride.”

title: How a six-year ‘situationship’ built love to last a lifetime
text:
“The difference is that Sam and I were genuine friends. I don’t think people understand that’s part of a situationship,” Winston says. “Because before it was the ‘situationship,’ it was called ‘friends with benefits.’ And I emphasize the friend part.”

Their friendship began when Samantha (who goes by Sam) was 27 and living in Revere. She swiped right and messaged Winston: “Do you even lift, bro?” (Three of his four Tinder photos were shirtless gym selfies.)

“I was not a ‘message first’ kind of gal,” she says, “but I was just in it that day for whatever reason.” The message, she explains, was at least partly “a test of whether he had a good sense of humor.”

They met that evening at the former Living Room in the North End. There were fruity drinks, flirty vibes, and a friendly kiss before they left for their respective homes.

At the time, Winston, then 27, lived in Miami and would start an MPH-PhD in Kinesiology program at Oregon State University that fall. She was a spa director in the North End and loved the excitement of being single and young — afterwork dinner and dates with endless possibilities. They agreed to keep things casual, reuniting during his visits with family in Dorchester. The relationship was label-less, the terms were transparent, but above all, their dynamic was consistent.

Sam described him at the time as: “this cute guy I see once a month.”

They texted near-daily, though, swapping career, life, and even romantic advice, the conversations growing deeper and topics more intimate as time went by. They dated other people and promised to be honest if something became more serious. Each sent the eyes emoji when the other let the text chain go dry.

“I didn’t have many people to talk to the way I used to talk to her. I never had an opportunity to process and be like, what does this mean to me?” says Winston of this time. “Then I realized that when you don’t do that and reflect, it’s hard to appreciate the things that you have.”

Sam was the first to sense a change — she had caught feelings; she wanted more. She bravely broached the topic in 2019 and was met with a gentle rebuff, a reality check on geography and time. A few months later, Winston texted Sam: To be honest, I love you, too, but this won’t work.

“We had very serious feelings for each other, but there wasn’t much to do about it because of the circumstances,” she says. “It was this common understanding, but neither of us wanted to give up on it. So we lived in this limbo of not wanting to stop talking but not wanting to move forward either.”

Just before Christmas 2021, Sam told Winston she couldn’t speak to him anymore. She wanted a full romantic relationship — not a situational one. With heartbreak on both sides, Winston understood her decision.

“It was very respectful, but I was so devastated,” she remembers.

That March, Winston texted — he was moving back for a postdoctoral fellowship at Merrimack College in North Andover. When Sam told him she had a new boyfriend, he was prepared.

“That’s OK,” he told her. “I can wait it out.”

Their friendship resumed after Sam ended the other relationship that summer. She would head to Merrimack’s campus when her schedule allowed; their conversations were now held in real time, over taco salads and two extra-long-twin beds pushed together to make one.

”My life started getting better, just having someone to talk to, someone who cares about you and thinks about you,” says Winston. “It was just me and her — and if it wasn’t for her, I don’t know if I would have made it through my post-doc or been able to muster up the ability to just do the stuff I needed to do.”

By February 2023, Winston was spending nearly every night at Sam’s East Boston apartment, waking up at 5 a.m. to get back to North Andover. (”He’s an early riser, anyway,” says Sam.)

In June 2023, Sam and Winston bought a home in West Roxbury. The decision came after he accepted a role at Northeastern University, where he is currently an assistant professor with the Bouvé College of Health Sciences.

“At this point in my life, I got what the expectation was — I knew, black and white, what she wanted from me,” he says. He proposed the following February.

“Winston will say that the big lifelong commitment was buying this house together, and obviously that’s a huge deal, but I’ve always been vocal about the fact that marriage meant something to me,” says Sam. “If we hadn’t gotten married, I don’t think it would really matter too much to me, but I did still want it.”

Sam and Winston wed at Dearly Studio in Somerville on Sept. 7 with 20 of their family members and friends.

The couple, now both 34, had initially planned for a large wedding, but changed lanes after joyfully discovering their family of two would become three. Their first child is due on Christmas Eve.

“Even when we were not [romantically] together, we had talked about kids and families and our own family dynamics,” says Sam. “That’s one of the things that was attractive to me about him — he always talked about wanting to have kids … and we were so often on the same page about what our approach to parenting would be.”

Dearly’s owner Jusmine Martin and Sam are best friends who met as freshmen at Emerson College. Sam’s father, Samuel Frandino, a professional carpenter, had built the micro-chapel’s altar where the pair wed with Jusmine as officiant.

The party continued at Tony and Elaine’s, Sam’s favorite North End restaurant, where guests cheered the newlyweds. They dined on plates of chicken parmesan and meatballs, and cut into quirky vintage-inspired cookies and cream cake from Buttercream Boston. Frosting was piped into the words “double trouble” — the couple’s “catch phrase” for themselves.

Sam asked that the restaurant keep out their signature checkerboard tablecloths and red tea lights for the family-style meal. She said the classic and “cozy” atmosphere felt familiar to her Italian-American upbringing: “I automatically just felt at home there.”

During the ceremony, Winston recited what he called “Wedding Vows: The Trilogy” in sequential order, a three-part declaration of gratitude and commitment to his wife and family:

“I’m sorry for all the bullshit in the past. Truly. You are teaching me what freedom is and I can never repay you for this. So I’ll give you everything else. I always have and always will always love you. It was already written.”

title: Remembering Jack Connors, Ethel Kennedy, Seiji Ozawa and others we lost in 2024
text:
Boston mayors come and go, each leaving their stamp on the city. But one figure outside of City Hall wielded wide influence for more than half a century: Jack Connors.

The history books will note that the legendary advertising-CEO-turned-philanthropist never held public office, but he didn’t need to. He built a constellation of relationships that reshaped business, health care, education, politics, and philanthropy.

When Connors died in July at 82 after a battle with cancer, it marked the passing of an era. He was a construct of his time, a rare blend of corporate savvy and civic passion, coming along when Boston needed a champion.

He was, at times, everywhere at once: running advertising agency Hill Holliday; chairing the board of the state’s biggest hospital system, Partners HealthCare (now Mass General Brigham); serving as trustee of his alma mater, Boston College; and raising millions of dollars for his beloved Camp Harbor View, which assists struggling city kids and their families.

Connors was as generous with his time as he was with his own money, giving away nearly $100 million of the fortune he made in the business world.

Perhaps his greatest contribution has been left unsaid: Connors helped Boston get back its swagger. It’s not often you hear Bostonians lament how great New York City or Silicon Valley is.

There will never be another Jack Connors — nor does Boston need one anymore. That’s part of his legacy: leaving behind a place confident to stand on its own and fulfill its destiny of being that enviable city on a hill. – Shirley Leung

Long before Pedro Martinez and David Ortiz became icons at Fenway Park, there was Luis Tiant.

During an era when Latino players were gaining a foothold in the Major Leagues, Tiant captivated Red Sox fans with his twirling delivery, Fu Manchu mustache, and charisma.

The righthander from Cuba joined the team as a free agent in 1971 and went on to win 122 games over eight seasons. What “El Tiante” lacked in physical stature, he made up for with determination to work deep into games.

“Tiant was a fierce competitor,” said Hall of Fame catcher Johnny Bench, whose Cincinnati Reds beat Tiant and the Red Sox in an epic seven-game World Series in 1975. “He never backed down.”

After a 19-year career and 229 wins, Tiant returned to Boston to work for the Sox. His titles changed from time to time but he was essentially a resident sage, always available to counsel players — especially fellow pitchers from Latin American countries.

“He was Mr. Tiant, our friend,” Martinez said. “There was respect.”

From the fans, there was love. Tiant was a regular at Fenway, posing for photos and signing autographs. Sunburnt New Englanders would gather around his golf cart during spring training in Florida as he patiently signed baseball cards and teased them with jokes.

Tiant was 83 when he passed away in October after a series of illnesses. Fenway won’t be quite the same next season. – Peter Abraham

Few can forget that iconic photo of Ethel Kennedy, in a black veil and pregnant with her 11th child, at the funeral of her husband, Robert F. Kennedy, just days after he was killed by an assassin while running for president in 1968.

More anguish lay ahead. Two of her sons would die, one of a drug overdose, another in a skiing accident.

But Ethel Kennedy, who died October 10 at the age of 96, was more than the sum of her suffering. She was also known as athletic and funny, charming and loyal. She started what is now the Robert F. Kennedy Human Rights nonprofit organization, championing her husband’s causes. She marched with labor leader Cesar Chavez, sat with Native Americans at Alcatraz, and visited unjustly convicted prisoners in Mexico.

She had deep ties to the Cape, spending much of her later years at the Kennedy compound in Hyannis Port. She enjoyed sailing and golfing, and was an avid supporter of the John F. Kennedy Hyannis Museum.

She encouraged her children to look beyond their privileged lives. At her memorial service in Washington, D.C., her youngest daughter, Rory, recounted a day in 1984 when she was a teenager, sitting next to her brother Douglas, watching TV coverage of anti-apartheid protests and arrests at the South African Embassy. So moved by the cause, they turned to each other and said, “Let’s get arrested.” When they told their mother of this plan, her response was unflinching: “Great, I’ll drive.”

At the service, Rory said her mother influenced so many inside and outside the family because she “loved people.”

“She believed in people, in everyone’s innate potential,” she said. – Patricia Wen

“We’re in the ‘yes’ business.” “Don’t tell me no; show me how.” “It can be done.”

Larry Lucchino — who served as the president and CEO of the Red Sox from 2002 to 2015 and was chairman of both the Jimmy Fund and the Triple-A WooSox when he died in April — often spoke in aphorisms. His favored phrases revealed an idealist’s unrelenting belief in possibility married to a pragmatist’s attention to the minutiae necessary to give form to blueprints.

By the 1990s, Lucchino’s visionary ambition, meticulousness, and doggedness had established him as a legendary baseball executive. Unconstrained by industry convention, he transformed the ballpark experience as the mastermind behind the construction of Oriole Park at Camden Yards in Baltimore.

After Lucchino helped form the Red Sox ownership group led by John Henry and Tom Werner and became the team’s CEO and president in 2002, he took on a different responsibility: The transformation of a team and ballpark that increasingly seemed trapped by their pasts. Conversations about replacing Fenway were scrapped in favor of stunning renovations, most notably the iconic “Monster seats” above the park’s famed left-field wall.

Generations of on-field despair and an 86-year title drought were vanquished through boldness and pugnaciousness embodied by Lucchino’s characterization of the New York Yankees as “the evil empire.” The championship of 2004 ushered in a new era where titles became regular occurrences.

Those championships as well as five ballparks — also including Petco Park in San Diego, JetBlue Park at Fenway South in Fort Myers, Florida, and Polar Park in Worcester — stand as monuments to Lucchino’s ability to turn sandcastles into sandstone. – Alex Speier

When influential Boston music critic Michael Steinberg first saw Seiji Ozawa conduct in the 1960s, he described “an incredible current of energy” that emanated from the Japanese conductor’s body “all the way to the point of the stick, and into the air beyond. It was a beautiful thing to watch.”

During his lengthy career, which included a 29-season tenure as music director of the Boston Symphony Orchestra, Ozawa channeled that energy into classical music in Boston and beyond.

Preferring turtlenecks to tuxedos and wearing his hair long and shaggy, Ozawa was a distinctly approachable and relatable foil to the European elder statesmen of the podium when he arrived on the scene. Like his mentor Leonard Bernstein, he became an inescapable presence not only in the relatively small classical music cultural sphere, but among the general public.

Ozawa recorded extensively with the BSO, and excelled in leading performances of monumental works for orchestra and chorus, such as Mahler’s Symphony of a Thousand, Schoenberg’s Gurre-Lieder, and Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9. For the opening ceremony of the 1998 Winter Olympics in Nagano, Japan, he conducted the fourth movement of that Beethoven work with a live orchestra and chorus while also leading simulcast vocal ensembles (including the Tanglewood Festival Chorus) on five different continents.

Even after he stepped down at the BSO, his ties to the city persisted. He was a regular presence at Fenway Park and in Foxborough, and when traveling abroad, he often visited the local American embassy to catch a Boston sports broadcast.

“‘Seiji,’ not ‘maestro,’” wrote music critic Andrew Pincus in The Berkshire Eagle after the conductor’s death in February. “That’s what musicians, fans, backers, critics, even strangers called him.” – A.Z. Madonna

The odds may have seemed stacked against Gloria Fox’s success in life. She bounced around foster homes as a girl in the 1940s, then became a single mother raising two sons in a Boston housing project.

But when she began volunteering as a community organizer in Roxbury, local leaders spotted her passion for social justice and knack for leadership. Soon she was running antipoverty programs, and helping teens apply for summer jobs or families obtain fuel assistance. “I just became the woman that got busy,” she said in a 2009 interview.

Then, in her early 40s, she heard the pivotal words: “OK kid, it’s time.”

This came from two of Roxbury’s political elite: Mel King, the first Black candidate to reach a Boston mayoral general election, and former state lawmaker Doris Bunte.

Fox would run for — and eventually win in 1985 — the legislative seat representing Roxbury and parts of Dorchester, a position she held for more than 30 years. Fox, who died in November at the age of 82, would become the longest-serving woman in the Massachusetts State House when she announced her retirement in 2016.

Roxbury today is full of vivid reminders of her influence, from the Reggie Lewis Track & Athletic Center, which she helped open, to Malcolm X Boulevard, which she pushed to rename from New Dudley Street. And what is absent is also related to her: She and other leaders in the 1970s stopped a controversial extension of Interstate 95 that would have run through the neighborhood, uprooting housing and businesses.

Sometimes called the “Queen of Roxbury,” she was known to speak up forcefully for affordable housing, improved health care, foster care reform, and other causes she held dear. Upon news of her death, state Senator Lydia Edwards told the Globe: “She never apologized for doing the right thing.” – Patricia Wen

A chef, a reinventor, a mensch. That was Jasper White, who died in May after a career that shined new light on American — and specifically New England — cuisine.

It’s funny that it took a Jersey boy to bring national attention to Boston’s restaurant scene, but that’s what White did — with longtime friend and collaborator Lydia Shire at Seasons in the Bostonian Hotel, then with Restaurant Jasper, opened in 1983. Chef-owners were a rarity at the time, and French tradition still dominated local menus. White’s influences were as likely to be Chinese or Portuguese. Rather than relying on heavy sauces, he focused on local, seasonal ingredients and more modern preparations. Located on the waterfront, Jasper’s also paid particular attention to seafood, from oysters to the pan-roasted lobster that became a favorite of luminaries such as Julia Child.

White influenced home cooks, authoring volumes such as Jasper White’s Cooking From New England. As a progenitor of New American cuisine, he helped change the course of fine dining in this country.

And then he turned the game on its head, launching Jasper White’s Summer Shack in Cambridge in 2000. A tribute to seafood shacks, it was casual, fun, and accessible in a way upscale restaurants were not. Soon there were multiple locations. This trajectory — from fine dining to relaxed, replicable concepts — was one countless other chefs would follow. As usual, White was ahead of the curve. – Devra First

Bostonians of the Year: The do good, feel good Boston Celtics

A home-grown star, a climate innovator, the team behind new liquor licenses, and other Bostonians who made a difference

title: ‘Seeing the way he showed up … it just felt like family’
text:
He had sent his classmate Ashia Aubourg a new song on Facebook Messenger nearly every day, since June — tracks by Little Brother, Outkast, 9th Wonder — followed by chatting and flirting. The two were part of the same friend group at Cambridge Rindge and Latin School, but despite growing closer each year, neither felt confident the other reciprocated their feelings.

“I had told one of my friends … ‘Yeah, I’m talking to Ashia a little bit,’ and he was like, ‘You’ve got no chance,’” Dominic remembers.

But in August, one of Ashia’s friends texted Dominic, advising him to ask Ashia out.

Despite living walking distance apart — both grew up in Cambridge, Ashia in the Coast, Dominic in Area 4 — summer obligations relegated their interactions to DMs. Dominic’s family owns The Daily Catch restaurants; he grew up busing tables, and working the host stand in the North End location. Ashia was in a Harvard summer program for high school students, in a culinary arts track.

On their first date, they walked along the Charles River, crossing the Western Avenue Bridge into Boston. Then, up the Esplanade to the Massachusetts Avenue Bridge to Cambridge. It ended with their first kiss.

The 16-year-olds declared Fridays as date night — a nonnegotiable in their crowded school year schedules. Their first “official” date was at the Catch on a Friday — Sept. 28 — which they’d celebrate as their anniversary for over a decade. They shared fried calamari and twirled black linguini flavored with squid ink in Alfredo sauce.

They bonded over their love for food and discovered a joint talent for playing host — rolling sushi and cooking steaks for their friends. Other evenings were spent at Dominic’s, listening to albums, before he walked Ashia home.

“I would make sure my steps matched hers even though I’m taller, says Dominic. “But we’re the perfect height, [where] my arm fits right around her and I would keep her warm.”

They broke up their senior year, as college plans crystallized. Ashia had long had “tunnel vision” for culinary school, ultimately deciding on Syracuse University, for a joint major in food and policy studies. Dominic would study business at DePaul University in Chicago — a 10-hour drive to Syracuse, in upstate New York. By mid-fall their freshman year, though, they were back together.

In 2015, Ashia lost her father, her aunt, and her grandmother within months of each other. Dominic traveled to Cambridge to be by her side; cooking for family attending her grandmother’s funeral.

“Seeing the way he showed up, not just being there for those really unexpected moments, but following up after and supporting me, it just felt like family,” says Ashia. “I didn’t expect people in college to have that level of emotional maturity.”

Back at school, they met as often as their travel budgets allowed and had Friday date nights via FaceTime, before they discovered DePaul offered a study abroad program in Italy, hosted by Syracuse. They reunited for five months in Florence where they lived with host families and took inexpensive flights to Paris, Morocco, and the Canary Islands.

After graduating, the couple moved into their first apartment together — a studio in Chicago’s River North neighborhood. Ashia began a job in experiential education, working in high schools throughout the city; Dominic worked as a kitchen manager for a commissary.

Growing responsibilities and expenses, and the COVID-19 pandemic, brought new challenges. In 2021, Ashia’s food blog transitioned into a side hustle; the couple acquired a cottage license and sold Caribbean-inspired baked goods at the South Loop Farmers Market. Conversations around marriage had hummed in the background as they transitioned through careers and neighborhoods. In 2022, Dominic added bartending shifts on the weekends to his full-time job. Ashia would wake at 2 a.m. to warm the food she’d saved for him; unbeknownst to her, he was saving for the salt-and-pepper diamond ring he designed with San Francisco jeweler Gem Breakfast. Months later, while on vacation in St. Lucia, he proposed as the sun went down.

They began calling venues and making guest lists. With large families — Dominic is the youngest of seven brothers, Ashia is the middle of four siblings — “at minimum, we were looking at 150, and that would be cutting a lot of important people out,” says Ashia.

A career opportunity for Ashia sent them to Brooklyn in 2023. When his father was diagnosed with a health condition, Dominic joined the family’s business. Life in New York was expensive, but he could commute home easily and frequently. But by 2024, the term “forever fiancé” was starting to get old. Dom asked Ashia: “Do we want to have a house or a wedding first?”

On Dec. 11, 2024, they tied the knot at Cambridge City Hall.

“It’s the middle point between our houses, where Dom would walk past to bring me home,” says Ashia.

Ashia wore a Tojhà dress from clothing rental service Nuuly and carried a bouquet by Rouvalis Flowers. Dominic bought new Clarks Wallabee boots — he’d worn the brand for both their junior prom and the proposal.

They went to The Daily Catch in the North End for a celebratory lunch, prepared by Chef Jimmy Lee, who had helmed the kitchen on their first date. Dominic’s mother made custom placemats for them from the since-retired curtains that had hung that day. Chef Lee sent photos of the newlyweds to his own wife from the kitchen.

They split clams casino and the Lobster Fra Diavolo — finishing with a two-person guava-strawberry cake from West Roxbury baker Get Your Brownies.

The restaurant keeps a strict “walk-ins only” policy, and Dominic and Ashia were there during normal lunch service.

“Even we have to wait in line when we want to go there,” says Dominic. “But if it had been busy that day … no, that was the one day where I could pull out the card. This is my wedding card. Sorry, guys; this table is reserved.”

Read more from The Big Day, The Boston Globe’s new weddings column.

title: 10 new restaurants to try in the new year
text:
In 2020, husband-wife team Aaron and Shanna Chambers opened Salem restaurant Settler, where the menu takes its cues from Mediterranean cuisine and New England farmers and fishermen. Bernadette, their follow-up, focuses on France while continuing to make use of ingredients from the North Shore and beyond. The menu is like a capsule wardrobe for your stomach, stocked with really good versions of staples you want to return to again and again: endive salad, mussels, Parisian gnocchi with mushrooms, roast chicken. Come for l’apéro, the tradition of pre-dinner drinks and snacks; stay for desserts like mille-feuille with quince and brown butter cream.

65 Washington St., Salem, 978-224-2976, www.bernadettesalem.com. Appetizers $8-$28, entrees $28-$48.

Desnuda Cocina & Bar

Japan-inspired listening lounges are gaining ground here, and this latest spot from Mazí Food Group (Gigi, Ilona, Kava Neo-Taverna) gets in on the action with a downstairs sound bar. Come hang out and listen to vinyl after eating ceviche, pork belly bao buns and tacos, miso eggplant, and grilled steak with chimichurri sauce. Chef Jesus Preciado’s menu draws from Asia and Latin America (including his native Colombia). On the cocktail list, find drinks like Beet the Heat (made with spicy pisco and beet syrup) and Amarillo Passion (in which tequila meets yuzu liqueur, passion fruit syrup, and the aji amarillo chile).

647 Tremont St., South End, Boston, 617-286-2333, www.desnudacocina.com. Smaller plates $6-$18, larger plates $18-$32.

Kaia

The latest from Xenia Greek Hospitality, which brought us Bar Vlaha, Krasi, and more. This time, culinary director Brendan Pelley and team whisk diners to the Aegean (with a South End mind-set) via dishes like sea bream crudo with fermented squash broth; barley toasts with beets, pears, and vegan feta; black truffle spanakopita; and grilled whole fish. The wine list is devoted solely to selections from the Aegean and Eastern Mediterranean islands.

370 Harrison Ave., South End, Boston, 617-514-0700, www.kaiasouthend.com. Dishes $16-$44.

Masons Steakhouse

Here’s what happens when a group of powerhouse South Shore culinary pros (including Jimmy Liang of JP Fuji Group and Kevin Long of Tosca) join forces. This swank Quincy steakhouse is located in a former Masonic temple and serves up lobster bisque, oysters Rockefeller, pappardelle bolognese, salmon with spiced cauliflower — and, of course, beautiful steaks. The also-beautiful, creative desserts are from pastry chef and Masons co-owner Robert Gonzalez, who is behind Quincy’s Niveaux Pâtisserie. In a landscape (increasingly) stocked with steakhouses, it is nice to see a new one open with local ownership.

1170 Hancock St., Quincy, 617-689-8818, www.masonssteakhouse.com. Appetizers $14-$32, entrees $29-$45, steaks $52-$160, sides $6-$14, desserts $12-$19.

McGonagle’s Pub

If you appreciate the Dubliner, bringing excellent fish and chips and Irish hospitality to downtown Boston, you will likely feel the same about McGonagle’s in Dorchester. Pigs in a blanket made with sausage from Adams Village Butcher Shop, smoky seafood chowder with Irish soda bread, shepherd’s pie, bangers and mash, and other pub favorites are here, along with wood-fired pizza, brunch (yes, full Irish breakfast), and festive cocktails. Or just drop in for live music and a proper pint of Guinness.

367 Neponset Ave., Dorchester, 617-514-4689, www.mcgonagles.com. Appetizers $8-$16, pizza $18-$19, entrees $18-$34.

Mikiya Wagyu Shabu House

If you’re starving, cold, and enjoy wagyu beef, Mikiya is calling you. This Chinatown restaurant serves all-you-can-eat wagyu hot pot at a variety of price points; you have 90 minutes to cook a variety of cuts in the broths of your choosing, while eating specialty dishes such as sweet shrimp sashimi and wagyu bone marrow, plus fruit and ice cream for dessert. Mikiya is a project from Chubby Group, whose Kevin Liu is also behind Matsunori Handroll Bar.

Wagyu sets $45-$98 (less with annual membership; free or half-price for kids).

Russ & Mimi’s

Named for the parents of owner Kelly Walsh (Sweet Cheeks, Tiger Mama), this Roslindale market offers wine (it’s in the former Solera space), olive oil, hot sauce, and other must-haves. But it’s the food that has the neighborhood most excited. Start the morning with egg wraps, overnight oats, cheesy grits, and cumin-spiced black beans with fried egg, salsa, and avocado; then segue into the “Cubano, veggie grinder, muffuletta, charred broccoli Caesar” part of the day. Chef Stephen Marcaurelle (the Nautilus Pier 4, Tres Gatos) helped design the menu.

16 Birch St., Roslindale, 617-833-6950, www.russandmimis.com. Dishes $8-$16.

Soul on Shawmut

Roxbury-raised chef Aadam Abdul-Musawwir began serving prepared meals and pop-up dinners as Aadam’s Halal Meals. Now, he and two siblings have opened Soul on Shawmut to feed their community. Lightly updated soul food classics are on the menu, along with Buffalo chicken egg rolls, grilled cheese burgers, and more. Fried chicken with Old Bay honey, smoked mac and cheese, slow-cooked collard greens with sauteed cabbage, sweet potato cheesecake, and hibiscus watermelon juice sounds pretty unbeatable for dinner tonight.

722A Shawmut Ave., Roxbury, 617-238-7525, www.soulonshawmut.com. Sandwiches $10-$18, fried chicken $7-$18, sides $5, desserts $3-$6.

Standard Italian

Where others fail, there is Italian food, everyone’s favorite. Standard Italian, in the Eastern Standard complex looming over Fenway, replaces the former All That Fish + Oyster, and it’s a smart move. Lasagna bolognese, porchetta, and espresso martinis could just get us all through the winter. Culinary director Brian Rae is in his element, having previously worked at Coppa, Faccia a Faccia, and Rialto.

771 Beacon St., Fenway, Boston, 857-305-3095, www.standarditalian.com. Appetizers $5-$20, entrees $28-$42, desserts $9-$12.

Zurito

It’s named for the small glass of beer that often accompanies pintxos, the Basque take on tapas, of which this Beacon Hill restaurant serves up plenty: Gildas, skewers of anchovies, peppers, and olives; griddled shrimp with garlic and chile oil; mini croissants stuffed with jamon iberico; squid ink risotto. Cocktails such as the sherry-based Perfect Bamboo and fizzy glasses of tzakolina are perfect accompaniments. Zurito, located in the longtime Bin 26 space, is run by chef Jamie Bissonnette, Babak Bina, and Andy Cartin of BCB3 Hospitality, also behind Somaek, Temple Records, and Sushi @ Temple Records.

26 Charles St., Beacon Hill, Boston, 857-305-3177, www.zuritoboston.com. Pintxos $4.50-$12, raciones $9-$19, platos especiales $17-$125.

title: 50 fun things to do in and around Boston this winter
text:
BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA The BSO’s big-ticket item in the near future is undoubtedly the concert performance of Korngold’s “Die tote Stadt,” presented in collaboration with Boston Lyric Opera and featuring Christine Goerke and Brandon Jovanovich in leading roles under the baton of music director Andris Nelsons (Jan. 30 and Feb. 1). Other coming attractions include Herbert Blomstedt conducting symphonies by Schubert and Brahms (Feb. 13-15); Giancarlo Guerrero leading a dramatic program of Gabriela Ortiz and Tchaikovsky with cellist Alban Gerhardt and vocal ensemble The Crossing (Feb. 27-March 1); the BSO debut of South Korean conductor Eun Sun Kim (March 6-8); and an orchestra tribute to John Coltrane arranged and curated by BSO composer chair Carlos Simon (March 21 and 22). Symphony Hall. 617-266-1200, www.bso.org

BOSTON YOUTH SYMPHONY ORCHESTRAS Under the direction of Federico Cortese, BYSO routinely punches above its weight with regard to repertoire, and the annual opera in concert is a reliable highlight. The young players tackle Verdi’s “Don Carlo,” a sweeping epic of love and duty amidst the terrors of the Spanish Inquisition, in a production stage-directed by Joshua Major with tenor Bruce Sledge in the title role. Jan. 26, 3 p.m., Sanders Theatre, Harvard University. 617-353-3348, www.bysoweb.org

BLUE HERON The sterling early-music focused vocal ensemble stages a 15th-century Mass by Johannes Regis, notable for being one of the first pieces to be based on “L’homme armé”, an explosively popular song of the late Middle Ages. Feb. 1, 3 p.m. First Church in Cambridge. 617-960-7956, www.blueheron.org

NEW GALLERY CONCERT SERIES This small but mighty local series, now in its 25th season, marries contemporary music and visual art. February’s “Rekindle” program includes a world premiere from violinist Abigale Reisman, a new composition by Anthony R. Green, and an appearance by saxophonist Jonathan Suazo and his band alongside the playful paintings of Emily Parent. Feb. 1, 7 p.m. Pickman Hall, Longy School of Music, Cambridge. www.newgalleryconcertseries.org

BROOKLYN RIDER The intrepid Grammy-nominated string quartet makes its Isabella Stewart Gardner museum debut with a spread of music from four centuries; Purcell, Mozart, Brahms, Arvo Pärt, and Betsy Jolas. Feb. 9, 1:30 p.m. Calderwood Hall, Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum. 617-566-1401, www.gardnermuseum.org

STAVE SESSIONS Think of it as Celebrity Series’s fringe festival; unpredictable, experimental, and always a lot of fun. This year’s lineup includes vocalist Courtney Swain of artistic rock band Bent Knee, two-cello string quartet Owls, cellist/vocalist Seth Parker Woods, and brass quartet The Westerlies. Good luck picking just one! Hope you don’t have to. Feb. 11-14. Crystal Ballroom, Somerville. 617-482-6661, www.celebrityseries.org

BOSTON PHILHARMONIC British soprano Claire Booth joins the Philharmonic and conductor Benjamin Zander for Strauss’s pensive “Four Last Songs” and Mahler’s Symphony No. 4, with its final movement depicting a child’s vision of heaven (Feb. 16). Then, the Boston Philharmonic Youth Orchestra takes its own run at a monumental Mahler symphony, the tragic and towering Symphony No. 6 (March 2). Symphony Hall. 617-236-0999, www.bostonphil.org

VÍKINGUR ÓLAFSSON AND YUJA WANG These two pianists are top-shelf recitalists and orchestral soloists on their own, so what happens when they share the stage? With a four-hands program that covers ground from Berio to Brubeck before the grand finale of Rachmaninoff’s “Symphonic Dances” arranged for two pianos, you can expect the timbers to tremble. Feb. 21, 8 p.m. Symphony Hall. 617-482-6661, www.celebrityseries.org

WINSOR MUSIC Director emerita Peggy Pearson begins the evening by taking the spotlight in J.S. Bach’s Concerto for Oboe d’amore. From there it’s onward through the centuries, tracing the legacy of Papa Bach from Mendelssohn (both Felix and Fanny) to Schumann (both Robert and Clara) to Kurt Weill, ending with a piece by Boston violinist/composer Shaw Pong Liu and a world premiere by the students of Winsor’s Opus 1 project. March 1, 7 p.m. St. Paul’s Church, Brookline. 781-999-2477, www.winsormusic.org

THE SEASONS As spring approaches, Boston Lyric Opera presents a new work co-conceived by playwright Sarah Ruhl (“Eurydice,” “The Clean House”) and countertenor Anthony Roth Costanzo, which draws on arias and instrumental pieces by Vivaldi — including “The Four Seasons” — to tell an original tale of passions amid climate chaos. Zack Winokur stage directs, with choreography by Pam Tanowitz and music direction by lutenist Stephen Stubbs. March 12-16. Emerson Paramount Center, Robert J. Orchard Stage. www.blo.org

– A.Z. Madonna

MARK MORRIS DANCE GROUP: “THE LOOK OF LOVE” This evening-length 2022 piece pays tribute to the late Burt Bacharach and his longtime lyricist, Hal David. The music, arranged by MMDG musical collaborator Ethan Iverson, will be performed live by Broadway star Marcy Harriell and an ensemble of piano, trumpet, bass, and drums. The lineup includes “Walk on By,” “I Say a Little Prayer,” “Do You Know the Way to San Jose,” “Always Something There to Remind Me,” and “What the World Needs Now.” MMDG presented “The Look of Love” at Jacob’s Pillow in 2023, but this is the troupe’s first visit to Boston in six years. Jan. 23-26. Emerson Cutler Majestic Theatre. www.globalartslive.org

OMAYRA AMAYA FLAMENCO DANCE COMPANY: “ANTES DEL FIN (BEFORE THE END)” Founded in 1994 by the daughter of flamenco dancers Olga and Curro Amaya, and based in Miami, the Omayra Amaya Flamenco Dance Company combines traditional and contemporary. Featuring live music and guest artists from Spain, its new 75-minute show, “Antes del fin (Before the End),” looks to explore the human condition. The company last performed here at Central Square’s Dance Complex in 2023. Jan. 31–Feb. 2. Arrow Street Arts, Cambridge. www.arrowstarts.org

CALEB TEICHER & CONRAD TAO: “COUNTERPOINT” In 2020, the Celebrity Series brought us tap prodigy Teicher and composer-pianist Tao in the thought-provoking “More Forever,” in which the pair just about kept time at bay. Now they’re back with “Counterpoint,” whose score includes music from George Gershwin’s “Rhapsody in Blue,” the Aria from Bach’s “Goldberg Variations,” stride piano from Art Tatum, and Arnold Schoenberg’s ironic take on the Viennese waltz. Feb. 7-8. Boston Arts Academy Theater. www.celebrityseries.org

TRINITY IRISH DANCE COMPANY: “JIG” Founded by Mark Howard in Chicago in 1990, this “Riverdance” precursor updates traditional Irish stepdancing. You might hear electric guitar alongside the fiddles; you might see stepdancing to pop songs, or dancers hitting the floor with sticks, or women singing a Scottish Gaelic waulking song to the accompaniment of body percussion. You can definitely expect the traditional footwork fireworks. Trinity made its Boston debut in 1998, Global Arts Live hasn’t presented the company here since 2016. Feb. 8 at 8 p.m. Berklee Performance Center. www.globalartslive.org

JENNY OLIVER AND STEPH DAVIS: “GRAY SPACE/BLUE SKIES” This free Neighborhood Arts offering from the Celebrity Series pairs dancer and choreographer Jenny Oliver with marimbist and composer Steph Davis for an afternoon of new choreography and commissioned music. Oliver serves as the head of Dance Performance at Tufts University; in 2019 her “Hot Water over Raised Fists” was presented at the Boston Canter for the Arts. Davis has been awarded residencies at the Goethe-Institut Boston and the Boston Center for the Arts and teaches music theory at Boston Conservatory; their work draws on traditions from across the African diaspora. Feb. 22 at 3 p.m. Free. Cambridge Multicultural Arts Center. www.celebrityseries.org

ANIKAYA DANCE THEATER: “CONFERENCE OF THE BIRDS” This 70-minute multimedia movement theater work from Boston-based ANIKAYA Dance Theater takes its name from a work by 12th-century Iranian poet Farid ud-Din Attar in which the birds of the world gather to decide who will be their sovereign. Directed by ANIKAYA founder and choreographer Wendy Jehlen in collaboration with an international ensemble of dancers-choreographers, “Conference of the Birds” will gather stories from modern-day refugees and other migrants. Feb. 27–March 9. Arrow Street Arts, Cambridge. www.arrowstarts.org

BOSTON BALLET: “SWAN LAKE” Distinctive features of artistic director Mikko Nissinen’s well-received version of the Tchaikovsky/Petipa classic include a prologue that depicts the abduction of Odette and the beginning of Rothbart’s curse transforming her into a swan, and then, in the final act, a brief duet in which Siegfried repents and Odette forgives. Created for the 2014 premiere, Robert Perdziola’s sets and costumes were inspired by the late Gothic and early Renaissance period. Boston Ballet last presented “Swan Lake” in 2022; it’s a measure of the work’s popularity that the company is giving this production 17 performances. Feb. 27-March 16. Citizens Opera House. www.bostonballet.org

WAMPANOAG NATION SINGERS & DANCERS “Please come prepared to dance and sing in the ways that you are able” is the message from the Wampanoag Nation Singers & Dancers, who “prefer to dance with the people instead of for the people” as they celebrate 12,000 years of ongoing Wampanoag and Eastern Woodlands culture. Wearing traditional dress, the performers will accompany themselves on water drums and handcrafted rattles as they reflect on our connections with the world around us. March 8 at 2 and 4 p.m. Free. Cambridge Multicultural Arts Center. www.celebrityseries.org

BOSTON DANCE THEATER: “RED IS A FEELING” The centerpiece of this evening of short dance works focusing on the color red is a new BDT commission by Iranian-Hispanic choreographer Roya Carreras Fereshtehnejad, who was diagnosed with two forms of cancer in her early 30s. Her piece “recalls the sensations where the experience of fighting for your life, holding on to each minute, and letting go all collide into the here and now.” Filling out the evening are BDT founder Jessie Jeanne Stinnett’s “Fifties,” which is set to pop tunes from that decade, and two works that the company presented here this past May, Itzhak Galili’s “If As If” and Marco Goecke’s “Firebird Pas de Deux.” March 14–15. Institute of Contemporary Art. www.globalartslive.org

BOSTON BALLET: “WINTER EXPERIENCE” Two very different works by George Balanchine bookend this attractive Boston Ballet bill. Set to Tchaikovsky’s Orchestral Suite No. 4, the serene, romantic “Mozartiana” is one of the master’s last works; the company hasn’t presented it here since 2003. “Symphony in Three Movements” is another animal altogether, jiving, jitterbugging, and lindy-hopping to World War II–era Stravinsky. In between we get Claudia Schreier’s “Slipstream,” which premiered on the company’s 2022 “choreograpHER” program, and “Vestris,” a seven-minute solo that Soviet choreographer Leonid Yakobson created for Mikhail Baryshnikov in 1969. March 20–30. Citizens Opera House. www.bostonballet.org

– Jeffrey Gantz

070 SHAKE In 2023, this MC and singer-songwriter had her pop breakthrough with a gripping verse on the dark night chronicle “Escapism.” by the British belter RAYE. Last year, she released “Petrichor,” a dense yet expansive collection that shows off her to-the-bone lyricism and flair for veering into far-flung sonic territory. Jan. 29, 7 p.m. doors. House of Blues Boston. 888-693-2583, houseofblues.com/boston

SOMETHING IN THE WAY FEST Local label Run For Cover Records and concert promoter The Bowery Presents jointly celebrate their 20th anniversaries with a pair of all-day shows headlined by shoegaze titans Slowdive, emo stalwarts American Football, cavern-dwelling riffers Balance and Composure, and indie-rock revivalist Soccer Mommy. (Don’t miss Enumclaw, whose poppy 21st-century take on slacker-grunge will have even the crabbiest record-store-clerk type flying their flannel.) Main shows Feb. 1 and 2, 1:45 p.m., Roadrunner Boston; auxiliary shows Jan. 31 and Feb. 1 at The Sinclair, Cambridge. somethingintheway.net

TIM HEIDECKER The prolific comedian gets serious on his latest album, “Slipping Away,” an unflinching look at middle age. It opens with the blithe-sounding yet uneasy dive into writer’s block “Well’s Running Dry,” and veers toward the brink with tracks like the heartbreaking “Hey, Would You Call My Mom For Me?” and the lonely “I Went Into Town.” Feb. 10, 8 p.m. Royale. 617-338-7699, royaleboston.com

LAUREN MAYBERRY “Vicious Creature,” the first solo album from the voice of electro-gloom collective CHVRCHES, flaunts her soprano’s versatility and vulnerability on cuts like the elliptical “Punch Drunk,” the mosh-pit-ready “Sorry, Etc,” and the shimmering Britpop throwback “Sunday Best.” Feb. 11, 8 p.m. Royale. 617-338-7699, royaleboston.com

KELSEA BALLERINI Boasting a twangy alto and a penchant for deftly exploring the gray zone between “pop” and “country,” this Tennessee-born singer-songwriter digs deep into her psyche on her 2024 album, “PATTERNS,” which includes the gently blooming growing-pains missive “Sorry Mom” and the anxiety-riddled breakup chronicle “WAIT!” Feb. 13, 7 p.m. TD Garden. 617-624-1000, tdgarden.com

LATIN MAFIA The genre-melding family band from Mexico City hit it big on TikTok in the early ‘20s with the sumptuous single “Ciudad de las Luces.” Their debut full-length “TODOS LOS DÍAS TODO EL DÍA,” released last year, showcases their omnivorous approach to music-making on heady, hooky songs that draw on reggaeton, Latin trap, new wave, and bedroom pop while spinning into their own orbits. Feb. 16, 7 p.m. doors. House of Blues Boston. 888-693-2583, houseofblues.com/boston

PINK SWEAT$ Reveling in sweetness and rooted in R&B classicism, this Philadelphia singer-songwriter crafts songs — like his latest single, the heart-eyed acoustic ballad “Coffee” — that are as comforting as the soft pants he’s named after. Feb. 17, 8 p.m. Shubert Theatre. 866-348-9738, bochcenter.org

KIM DEAL It came out at the tail end of 2024, but “Nobody Loves You More,” the debut solo full-length from this alt-rock legend, crash-landed into contention as one of the year’s best upon arrival. Deal’s rasp is familiar from college-radio staples like Pixies’ “Gigantic” and the Breeders’ “Cannonball,” but here she frames it in mirrorballs (the mournful slow dance “Are You Mine?”), brass bands (the loose-limbed “Coast”), and insistent samples (the scuzzed-out “Crystal Breath”). The album shows Deal spreading her creative wings in thrilling, daring fashion. March 10, 8 p.m. The Wilbur. 617-248-9700, thewilbur.com

DROPKICK MURPHYS The Boston brawlers’ annual run of St. Patrick’s Day celebrations includes a Saturday-afternoon family concert that benefits their charitable foundation The Claddagh Fund and a House of Blues throwdown on the holiday itself. March 14, 7 p.m., March 15, 2 and 7 p.m., and March 16, 6:45 p.m., at MGM Music Hall at Fenway; also March 17, 6 p.m., at House of Blues Boston. dropkickmurphys.com

TOMMY RICHMAN Last spring, this DMV-repping singer-songwriter lit up the charts with his blown-speakers boast “MILLION DOLLAR BABY.” “COYOTE,” his debut full-length, followed in the fall, and continues his explorations of lo-fi funk. March 21, 7 p.m. Paradise Rock Club. 617-562-8800, crossroadspresents.com

– Maura Johnston

PETER PAN The well-known musical adaptation of Sir J.M. Barrie’s 1904 play, with additional material by indigenous dramatist Larissa Fasthorse. (Earlier versions of “Peter Pan” have been criticized for their stereotypical depictions of Native Americans.) Starring Nolan Almeida as Peter, the boy who refuses to grow up; Hawa Kamara as the intrepid Wendy; and Cody Garcia as the villainous pirate, Captain Hook. Directed by Lonny Price, with songs by Mark Charlap (music) and Carolyn Leigh (lyrics) that include “I’m Flying,” “I Won’t Grow Up,” “Neverland,” and “I Gotta Crow.” Jan. 21-Feb. 2. Broadway In Boston. At Citizens Opera House, Boston. Tickets at www.BroadwayInBoston.com

HAUNTED The premiere of a horror comedy, written and directed by Tara Moses, that focuses on Indigenous siblings Ash (Bradley Lewis) and Aaron (Chingwe Padraig Sullivan). Dead for two decades, they’ve been haunting the families who have attempted to move into their house. Now, they’re hoping for admission to the Spirit World while they’re wondering, according to press materials, “if they’ll ever be free from the shackles of racist stereotypes.” To relax, the siblings dance to the songs of Britney Spears and Mariah Carey. Jan. 24-Feb. 15. Company One Theatre in partnership with the Boston Public Library. At Rabb Hall, Boston Public Library. Tickets are “pay what you want,” at 617-292-7110 or www.companyone.org

THE PIANO LESSON In August Wilson’s Pulitzer-winning drama, two siblings are locked in a fierce contest of wills over what to do with the family’s antique piano, on which an ancestor had carved the faces of family members. Boy Willie (Omar Robinson) wants to use the money to purchase the land where their ancestors were enslaved. But Berniece (Jade Guerra), who sees the piano as a deeply meaningful part of the family’s history, wants to keep it. Directed by Christoper V. Edwards. Jan. 23-Feb. 13. Actors’ Shakespeare Project, in partnership with Hibernian Hall. At Hibernian Hall, Boston. Tickets at 617-241-2200 or ActorsShakespeareProject.org/Piano-Lesson

SPACE Created by LM Feldman and Larissa Lury, written by Feldman, and directed by Lury, “Space” was inspired by the true story of a group of skilled and experienced female pilots, known as the Mercury 13, who underwent rigorous training in a privately funded research project in the early 1960s to become astronauts in America’s first human spaceflight program. But they were denied the chance to become astronauts, because at that time, NASA refused to consider women as candidates. Jan. 30-Feb. 23. Central Square Theater, Cambridge. Tickets at 617-576-9278 x1 or CentralSquareTheater.org

THE GROVE The second play in Mfoniso Udofia’s nine-play Ufot Family Cycle, following a Huntington production late last year of “Sojourners,” the cycle’s origin story. Set in 2009, “The Grove” focuses on Adiaha Ufot (Abigail C. Onwunali), a young gay Nigerian-American who aspires to be a writer and faces a stark choice in her personal life: follow her heart or fulfill the desires of her tradition-minded parents, Abasiama (Patrice Johnson Chevannes) and Disciple (Joshua Olumide). Directed by Awoye Timpo, who helmed “The Bluest Eye” at the Huntington in 2022. Feb. 7-March 9. The Huntington. At Wimberly Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion, Boston Center for the Arts. Tickets at 617-266-0800 or huntingtontheatre.org

THE ODYSSEY Playwright Kate Hamill is known for her contemporized, women-centered stage adaptations of 19th-century novels such as Jane Austen’s “Sense and Sensibility” and “Pride and Prejudice.” With “The Odyssey,” Hamill goes back much further in time, to ancient Greece, for a reimagining of Homer’s epic poem about Odysseus (Wayne T. Carr) and his wife, Penelope (Andrus Nichols.) A premiere directed by Shana Cooper. Feb. 9-March 16. American Repertory Theater. At Loeb Drama Center, Cambridge. Tickets at 617-547-8300 or TicketServices@amrep.org

A MAN OF NO IMPORTANCE Paul Daigneault has enlisted a blue-chip cast for the final production he’ll direct as artistic leader of SpeakEasy Stage Company, which he founded 33 years ago. A musical created by “Ragtime” collaborators Terrence McNally (book), Stephen Flaherty (music), and Lynn Ahrens (lyrics), “A Man of No Importance” stars Eddie Shields as Alfie, a closeted bus driver in 1964 Dublin who is involved with an amateur theater troupe housed in a local church. When Alfie proposes that the troupe stage Oscar Wilde’s racy “Salome” rather than its usual production of Wilde’s “The Importance of Being Earnest,” church authorities try to shut it down. Cast also includes Aimee Doherty, Kerry A. Dowling, Jennifer Ellis, Will McGarrahan, Billy Meleady, Meagan Lewis Michelson, Keith Robinson, Rebekah Rae Robles, Eddie Shields, Sam Simahk, and Kathy St. George. With choreography by Ilyse Robbins and music direction by Paul S. Katz. Feb. 21-March 22. SpeakEasy Stage Company. At Roberts Studio Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion, Boston Center for the Arts. 617-933-8600 or www.speakeasystage.com

WHERE WE BELONG A one-person play, written by Madeline Sayet and directed by Tara Moses, about Achokayis, described as “an indigenous theatre-maker who journeys across international borders, personal history, and cultural legacies in search of a place to belong.” Feb. 28-March 23. Umbrella Stage Company. At Umbrella Arts Center, Concord. Tickets at 978-371-0820 or TheUmbrellaArts.org/WWB

ART After the wealthy, smoothly polished Serge (Michael Kaye) pays more than $100,000 for a work of art — or is it? — that consists entirely of a blank white canvas, he shows it to his friends Marc (John Kuntz) and Yvan (Remo Airaldi). Their reactions — and his reactions to their reactions — put their friendship and their values to a major test. This play by French dramatist Yasmina Reza, probably best-known for “God of Carnage,” is directed by Courtney O’Connor from a translation by Christopher Hampton. Feb. 21-March 16. Lyric Stage Company of Boston. Tickets at 617-585-5678 or lyricstage.com

PARADE A musical inspired by the 1913 case of Leo Frank, the Jewish superintendent of a pencil factory who was wrongfully accused of murdering 13-year-old Mary Phagan. With sensationalistic newspaper coverage fanning the flames of antisemitism, Frank was convicted and sent to prison. Then, in 1915, he was kidnapped by a mob and lynched. Featuring Max Chernin as Leo Frank; Talia Suskauer as Leo’s wife Lucille; and Olivia Goosman, currently a student at The Boston Conservatory at Berklee. With music and lyrics by Jason Robert Brown, and a book by Alfred Uhry. Directed by Michael Arden. March 11-23. At Emerson Colonial Theatre, Boston. Tickets at 888-616-0272 orwww.emersoncolonialtheatre.com

– Don Aucoin

FUTURE FOSSILS A hindsight view of our current moment from the far-flung future, this exhibition brings together a stellar roster of artists — Ai Weiwei, Nari Ward, Rachel Whiteread, Sanford Biggers — to imagine what might remain of the fractured world we now live in when all we know is gone. Jan. 23-April 13. MassArt Art Museum, 621 Huntington Ave.. 617-879-7333, maam.massart.edu

OHAN BREIDING: BELLY OF A GLACIER In 2019, Iceland built a memorial marking the death of the Okjökull glacier, the first of many funereal events held for glaciers worldwide as ice continues to puddle away amid ongoing climate change. As they melt, history is unleashed: millennia of geological events preserved in their strata reveal themselves, from natural disaster marked by deposits of volcanic ash all the way up to man-made impacts like industrial residue. Breiding, an Icelander, presents a documentary film and photographic installation that mourns the melting glaciers, and explores the faint hope around efforts to preserve them. Feb. 1-Dec. 14. Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art, 1040 Mass MoCA Way, North Adams. 413-662-2111, massmoca.org

SOVEREIGN MEMORY: PHOTOGRAPHY, REMEMBRANCE, AND DISPLACED HISTORIES Photography and modernity go hand in hand — the upheavals of a world remade first by colonialism and then industrialization ran right into the new technology, able to capture it firsthand. This exhibition seizes on the medium’s ability to record, but also deceive and reshape collective memory — and, finally, through these artists’ various pieces, be stitched together into something resembling whole. Feb. 7-June 1. The Davis Museum at Wellesley College, 106 Central St., Wellesley. 781-283-2051, www1.wellesley.edu/davismuseum

WITNESSING HUMANITY: THE ART OF JOHN WILSON Bostonians might be most familiar with Wilson, born and raised in Roxbury, through “Eternal Presence,” the monumental, enigmatic bust that’s stood sentinel-like at the National Center of Afro-American Artists (NCAAA) in Roxbury since 1987. But Wilson, who died in 2015, spent decades before and after crafting socially conscious work around the pervasive issue of racial injustice in America that he experienced all his life. This exhibition, co-organized with New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, is the most substantial display of Wilson’s oeuvre ever assembled, and an opportunity for Boston to reckon with a powerful voice that echoes through generations of its social history. Feb. 8-June 22. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, www.mfa.org

SARAH CWYNAR Using film, video, photography, and installation, Cwynar creates dizzying cascades of overlapping images that capture —and critique — the contemporary reality of an image-saturated consumer culture in hyperdrive. Art imitates life: Her work is as disorienting as it is seductive, a dark mirror to the smartphone-and-social media world that dominates contemporary society. Her show at the ICA will feature a brand-new two-part photo installation in collaboration with — how else to put it? — the whims of search-engine algorithms. Feb. 13-Aug. 3. Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100, icaboston.org

WATERS OF THE ABYSS: AN INTERSECTION OF SPIRIT AND FREEDOM A full-scale “takeover” of the Gardner Museum by Fabiola Jean Louis — which means all three of the Gardner’s temporary exhibition spaces, including its billboard-size facade commission, will be in her hands — this show plumbs the depths of Haitian liberation, Vodou faith, and the artist’s roots in all of it. Feb. 27-May 25. The Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, 25 Evans Way. 617-566-1401, www.isgm.org

EDVARD MUNCH: TECHNICALLY SPEAKING I know, I know: “The Scream,” right? There’s no getting around the cultural oversaturation of Munch’s most famous work, but recent efforts have done much to broaden our understanding of Norway’s most-loved artist beyond his all-time smash hit. In the summer of 2023, “Edvard Munch: Trembling Earth,” the Clark Art Institute’s voluminous presentation of the artist’s deep affinities with — and anxieties for — the natural world opened a universe of difference for all but the most devoted Munch fan. “Technically Speaking,” at Harvard, takes a different tack, exploring the artist’s material genius and almost manic enthusiasm for media across painting, drawing, and every manner of printing. With it, a view of an artist too long seen as one-note broadens. March 7-July 27. Harvard Art Museums, 32 Quincy St., Cambridge. 617-495-9400, harvardartmuseums.org

NATIVE PROSPECTS: INDIGENEITY AND LANDSCAPE PAINTING Thomas Cole, the de facto leader of the Hudson River School of painters, depicted the American landscape with both the deep affection he felt for its majestic beauty and the anxiety that gripped him as 19th-century industry advanced deeper into its unspoiled heart. This exhibition presents Cole’s visions alongside historic and contemporary works by Native American artists, bringing Indigenous perspective, and its vital import to the land and its preservation, to the fore. March 8-July 6. Farnsworth Art Museum, 16 Museum St., Rockland, Maine. 207-596-6457, farnsworthmuseum.org

J.M.W. TURNER: ROMANCE AND REALITY Conceived to mark the beloved, bombastic British painter’s 250th birthday, this exhibition at the Yale Center for British Art brings together dozens of works from the Yale collection, which is the richest in North America. Comprising an array of Turner’s beguiling watercolors alongside major oil paintings such as “Dort or Dordrecht: The Dort Packet-Boat from Rotterdam Becalmed,” 1818 (he had a knack for titles), it’s the biggest airing of the Yale collection in more than 30 years. March 29-July 27. Yale Center for British Art, 1080 Chapel St., New Haven. 877-274-8278, britishart.yale.edu

VAN GOGH: THE ROULIN FAMILY PORTRAITS Vincent van Gogh met few successes in his short, unhappy life, but between 1888 and 1889, he might have been as content as he’d ever been.
