That time, spent in the Southern French town of Arles, was where he found peace and satisfaction in the genuine friendship of Joseph Roulin and his wife and three children. Van Gogh’s portraits of them reflect an artist, who was struggling with his mental health, in a moment of rare safety and calm. A collaboration with the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, the show brings together some 20 portraits made in that moment, and a glimpse of a famously tortured artist momentarily calmed. March 30-Sept. 7. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, www.mfa.org

– Murray Whyte

title: Remembering MLK’s 1965 March on Boston
text:
On Monday, Boston, along with the rest of the country, celebrates King, whose historic demonstrations against legally sanctioned segregation in the South often overshadow the civil rights leader’s strong connection to the city. Yet, King’s time in Boston, particularly during the April 23, 1965, march, highlights his commitment to combatting what was commonly called “de facto” segregation in the North.

That day, King visited tenement housing in Roxbury, which he described as a “deplorable outrage,” according to Globe reporting from the time. He tried and failed to have an audience with the Boston School Committee, chaired at the time by Louise Day Hicks, a staunch opponent of school desegregation efforts whom King likened to a modern-day “pharaoh.” He successfully met with Massachusetts Governor John Volpe and Boston Mayor John Collins, urging them to act against northern “de facto” segregation, which he had described in an address to the Massachusetts Legislature the day before as “a new form of slavery covered up with certain niceties.”

When Glynnette Byron (now Scott), first laid eyes on King from the Common’s bandstand, she recalled being “happy, amazed, elated.”

“I was so glad ... our father wanted to take us with him; I think he knew how important that moment was going to be in our lives,” she said.

The Byron sisters grew up in Boston at the tail end of the Great Migration, a period when a massive number of Black people migrated from the Jim Crow South to northern industrial cities. Although most northern states lacked the formally legal kind of segregation practiced in the South, racist attitudes and policies such as redlining, which limited where racial minorities could rent or buy homes, still relegated Black people to the status of second-class citizens.

In the 1960s, the majority of Black Bostonians lived within a few overcrowded neighborhoods poorly serviced by the city, with their children attending overcrowded and underfunded schools. The threat of racially motivated harassment or violence, though diminished compared with the South, was still ever-present.

“We didn’t go to Charlestown, we didn’t go to South Boston,” Beverly Byron said. “Even in the ‘60s, my mother was teaching in South Boston, and it was awful. The little kids were calling her the N-word when she’d drive down the street.”

Marchers who attended the April 1965 demonstration and modern scholars look back on the event with a mixture of pride, joy, and apprehension, from the perspective of a 21st-century Boston and United States, where racially based inequities are still alive and well.

Ed Forry, an Irish Catholic raised in Dorchester and founder of the Dorchester Reporter newspaper, grew up on the other side of that racial divide. Forry was a 21-year-old English student at Boston College when he attended King’s march as a member of the Catholic Interracial Council of Boston, a group that advocated for civil rights through the lens of Catholic social teaching.

He called King’s speech on the Common “a rallying call for all of us who listened.”

“I’m proud I chose that day to bear witness to Martin Luther King’s message,” he said.

Jeanne Theoharis, a professor of political science at Brooklyn College of the City University of New York, described King’s march through Boston as “a site of contradiction.” A Globe article published the day of the march claims that while, “Dr. King was ever solemn and unsmiling in Selma and Montgomery,” up north “he could laugh as he walked the Boston streets.”

Theoharis clarified the historical record: “The day he gets to Boston, there are so many death threats, so he’s not free. Let’s start there.”

Theoharis said the rosy depiction of the march in newspaper columns from that day — juxtaposing King’s warm welcome from Bostonians with the harsh reprisals civil rights demonstrators often faced down South — played into a convenient narrative white Northerners enjoyed telling themselves about race relations in the region at that time.

“Many white Bostonians are very opposed to the idea that Boston is systematically segregated, and they’re very angry at King for trying to shine a light on that,” Theoharis said. “There’s this kind of self-congratulatory sense of ‘King is here,’ and at the same time, this real rejection of what he’s actually saying.”

Glynnette Scott recalled feeling an immense sense of hope growing up during that period. Both she and her sister agreed that as they grew older, especially in the aftermath of King’s assassination, that optimism began to fade.

Reflecting on her lifetime spent witnessing the evolution of American race relations, Glynnette offered her perspective.

“I get a sense now that they’re heading back in the wrong direction. … There’s some talk about Black history not being taught. There’s a push against some of the history that’s part of America being taught. So that’s why I feel things are changing,” she said.

Correction: Because of a reporting error, Glynnette Scott’s last name was omitted in a previous version of this story.

title: ‘They’re everywhere’: Boston losing fight against spread of used drug needles
text:
While long a problem, the proliferation of discarded needles has reached crisis levels since city officials abruptly ended a popular program last June that paid drug users to collect them. The number of 311 service requests for needle pickups surged nearly 50 percent in the final six months of last year, compared with the same period in 2023. Needle-pickup requests last year reached the highest level since the program’s inception in December of 2020 — with an average of 1,125 requests a month during the second half of last year, according to a review of 311 requests.

City crews and community groups that run needle exchange programs are scrambling to contain the problem, which has been exacerbated by a surging homeless population and persistently high rates of illicit drug use. The needles have become so widespread that they have become a major public health concern, as accidental stabbings can result in the spread of blood-borne infections such as HIV and hepatitis C.

Two years ago, a 9-year-old boy from Roxbury was rushed by ambulance to the hospital after he was pricked by a dirty needle while practicing with his Pop Warner football team. Increasingly, tourists have to navigate around the discarded syringes, with their distinctive orange caps, as they walk Boston’s Freedom Trail.

“We’re talking about thousands and thousands of syringes in places where children play and people congregate,” said Mario Chaparro, program director of low-threshold housing at Elliot Community Human Services, a nonprofit that provides mental health and housing services. “It’s only a matter of time before someone gets stuck.”

Street outreach groups trace the worsening problem to the end of a needle-for-cash program that, in just a few years, took 5 million dirty needles off Boston’s streets.

The program, known as the Community Syringe Redemption Program, gave drug users an incentive to collect their own needles by offering them 20 cents per syringe, with a limit of $10 a day per person. It wasn’t much, but it was enough of an incentive for people struggling with addiction and others to collect 25,000 to 35,000 used needles per week and hand-deliver them to one of the program’s vans, which parked early each weekday morning outside of areas of Boston with high concentrations of drug users.

Some months, the program was responsible for collecting nearly 80 percent of the total volume of used needles removed from Boston’s city streets.

But the program’s impact extended far beyond needle collection. The outreach workers in the mobile vans would offer people overdose-reversal drugs and would connect them with treatment programs and housing services to help them overcome addiction. And for many, the $10 in cash from collecting needles was enough for a meal and a “sense of pride” that they were contributing to the city’s safety, said Allie Hunter, cofounder of the company, Addiction Response Resources, that ran the program.

“People felt like they were part of something bigger than themselves, and that was a beautiful thing,” Hunter said.

Gobbi credits the needle-collection program with possibly saving his life.

He encountered the van nearly two years ago while he was homeless and using heroin near a troubled area known as Mass. and Cass, long the epicenter of the city’s homeless and opioid crises. He started bringing in more than 100 needles a day that he picked up from area parks and streets. Then one of the outreach workers told him about a nearby clinic that provides methadone treatment, which helped alleviate the agonizing pangs of withdrawal he felt every time he stopped taking heroin.

“If it wasn’t for that van, I swear to God that I’d either be dead or in prison,” said Gobbi, who is now sober and this month moved into an apartment of his own in Dorchester.

But the federal pandemic relief funds that covered the program’s roughly $1.2 million annual cost dried up last year, and the Boston Public Health Commission decided to focus on other initiatives.

In a statement, the health commission said it continues to maintain a mobile sharps team that last year responded to 10,736 requests through 311 to remove needles. The city fulfills 99.9% of all requests with a median response time of 28 minutes. The outreach team also proactively checks schools and parks for discarded needles, the commission said.

City and public health commission officials also said they have decided to try a different model of syringe removal — one focused on ending open-air drug use and expanding workforce opportunities for people who have struggled with addiction. The city last June expanded a contract with the Newmarket Business Improvement District, which hires former drug users to pick up 300 to 350 needles in city parks and squares with high concentrations of illicit drug use.

“The city is committed to ending outdoor substance use and drug dealing on city streets,” said Kellie Young, director of the city’s coordinated response team. “We will quickly respond to any 311 calls for needles, but we know that outdoor drug use undermines quality of life in our neighborhoods and we are committed to ending it in Boston.”

Yet city and nonprofit outreach teams have not kept pace with the volume of needles being discarded on city streets.

For most of the past four years, the city has collected more discarded needles than it has given out through various programs that dispose of used syringes and provide access to sterile ones. But that changed dramatically late last year. In December, city programs took in 132,463 used needles, while giving out nearly 190,000. That’s a sharp change from last April, when the city took in 250,931 needles and gave out 97,754, according to a city dashboard.

“There are a lot of folks out in the community using drugs — and they don’t have as much incentive now to pick up,” said Katie Weixler, deputy director of prevention at Victory Programs, a Boston nonprofit that offers a range of support services for people who are homeless and struggling with substance use disorders.

On a cold and windy weekday morning, it did not take long for a duo of street outreach workers with Victory Programs to spot a slew of dirty needles near its drop-in center along Massachusetts Avenue. They were scattered on busy sidewalks, behind fences, and under bushes, the needles glistening in the sun. In their backpacks, the workers carried dozens of clean needles and other harm-reduction supplies that they offered to people on the streets.

At one point, the two outreach workers — Dinay Von Johnson and Azzy-Mae Ní Mháille — stopped to scrutinize a forlorn patch of dirt-and-gravel along Melnea Cass Boulevard that was littered with hundreds of bright-orange syringe caps. Yet amid the refuse, the pair couldn’t find a single discarded needle — an encouraging sign, they said, that people who had injected drugs at the site had picked up their needles.

“People sometimes think that people out here don’t care, but they do,” Von Johnson said. “They just need options.”

title: During a nine-hour City Council hearing, Boston residents voice opposition to White Stadium plan
text:
Just five voiced support for the project.

“Boston students deserve a renovated White Stadium – they deserve a public White Stadium, not a private sports and entertainment complex built to enable private profits,” said Jean McGuire, resident of Roxbury and longtime civil rights advocate. “It’s clear that this entire process is being driven by the needs of private investments, not the needs of Boston students. The process has been launched, the state reviews having been conducted, and community members’ concerns about public access and transportation impacts are being ignored, all in a mad rush to next March for White Stadium in order to be a soccer team’s desired opening day.”

In addition to committee chair Julia Mejia, the other councilors there for the duration were District 6 Councilor Ben Weber, whose district abuts Franklin Park, and At-Large Councilor Erin Murphy and District 2 Councilor Ed Flynn. Both Flynn and Murphy have voiced their support for at least pausing the demolition in the interests of the council getting, in part, a better handle on the project’s costs.

In response to a question, Dion Irish, the city’s chief operating officer, upped the city’s share of the project from the $91 million that had emerged last month to “roughly $100 million.”

The soccer team’s share remains unknown, except that it will exceed the city’s share, which elevates the total cost above $200 million.

The meeting was split into two parts, with the morning and early afternoon devoted to discussions of finances and facilities, including the Madison Park high school renovation, and the latter session devoted to community engagement.

Mejia, a councilor at-large, said she would file a resolution for councilors to be polled on their support or lack of support for both White Stadium and Madison Park at the next City Council meeting on Jan. 29.

Diana Fernandez Bibeau, the deputy chief of urban design for the city, pushed back on the notion that the community was not part of the process.

“Our work without a doubt has been impacted by the community feedback that we’ve received today,” said Fernandez Bibeau. “I certainly understand that there is reservation of a particular type of partnership being able to sort of deliver on this project, but we have responded, and we have tried to sort of meet the community where they are in terms of where they are, in terms of where those concerns are, and try to address them every step of the way.

“I also want you to know that it’s hard to do this right, that it’s the reason why no other mayor has taken on the renovation of White Stadium, why no other administrations have taken on the hard work to go ahead and make an improvement at White Stadium and deliver on this promise for historically disinvested communities.”

Also on hand for portions of the meeting were District 7 Councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson, whose district encompasses Franklin Park and District 4 Councilor Brian Worrell, whose district also abuts the park. Also in attendance for portions of the meeting were Councilors John Fitzgerald, Enrique Pepén, Sharon Durkan, and Henry Santana.

Anderson expressed concern with the degree of engagement from the city with citizens.

“The administration should have told the community what planning and engagement would look like,” said Anderson. “We have not done enough to engage the community.”

Weber said he has heard both support and opposition for the plan from his constituents. He found it “disturbing” to hear that there has not been a community process. As for opponents like the Emerald Necklace Conservancy, who have filed a lawsuit that will go to trial in March, he said, “I hear a lot of rhetoric, I don’t hear much about solutions.”

“Some of the rhetoric around the opposition is not tied to the facts, and I wish that it was more tied to the facts, I think we could have a more constructive conversation,” Weber said.

Stevan Kirschbaum, a former BPS bus driver, described the White Stadium plan as “appalling and criminal.”

“We should be chaining ourselves to those trees – this is a criminal rush to judgment.”

Ann Walsh, a Dorchester resident, expressed the belief that the presence of the women’s professional team would be an inspiration to BPS student-athletes.

“My expectation is that a professional women’s soccer team is going to be a good commercial partner like the Red Sox are and offer mentorship and internships.”

title: ‘Our job is not to make people comfortable.’ Local religious leaders support Episcopal bishop’s sermon before Trump.
text:
The exchange triggered a national debate over the role of religious political advocacy during the second Trump administration. Some places of worship that presented themselves as sanctuaries for migrants during Trump’s previous term may have to consider their roles now after the president rescinded longstanding policy to not conduct immigration raids on places of worship.

In Boston, religious leaders overwhelmingly said they were proud of Budde’s sermon.

“I am sure it was uncomfortable for him and he was a guest in her cathedral and she preached the word she felt called to preach,” said the Right Rev. Julia E. Whitworth, who was chosen last year as the new leader of the Massachusetts Episcopal diocese. “Our job is not to make people comfortable, especially when there is a status quo that is unjust.”

Whitworth said that Budde’s sermon was thoughtful and respectful and that now more than ever, religious leaders need to use their voices. But there’s more to do than just sermonizing, Whitworth said.

“We have some tremendous exemplars of religious leaders from many faith backgrounds who have put their bodies on the line for justice in the name of their faith,” she said.

Already some Massachusetts communities are on edge, anticipating that Trump will soon make good on his new pledges to conduct mass deportations by targeting so-called sanctuary cities in blue states. And some ministers in the state say they are prepared to offer what resistance they can.

At the Twelfth Baptist Church in Roxbury, which was once called the “Fugitive Slaves’ Church,” the Rev. Willie Bodrick II said religious leaders have “not only a right, but the responsibility” to speak up about political and social issues. Bodrick said Budde’s comments reminded him of a long line of religious leaders throughout history who have helped advocate for change, such as during the civil rights movement in the 1960s.

“Historically, it’s been the Black church and the Black preaching tradition that has continued to shape and mold not only justice and equality and advocacy in this country, but the world,” he said.

Because of this history, Bodrick said he’s “never been able to separate the Gospel from the lived experiences of people in my city, community, country, and world.”

Thomas Groome, a professor of theology at Boston College, said that, “People of faith have to represent their values in the public forum.” He said both the left and the right use the trappings of religion to try to lend moral credence to their arguments, such as the advocacy around abortion from conservatives, and around civil rights from progressives.

So in her sermon, Groome said, Budde “was representing core foundational Christian values,” such as to love one’s neighbor.

Groome handed the phone to his wife, Colleen M. Griffith, who is also a theology professor at BC. She was getting ready to head out to teach a graduate school class where she planned to talk about Budde’s sermon.

“I think sometimes people feel like a certain type of activism and politics doesn’t belong in our sermons,” she said. “But there is indeed a Christian politics and it’s a politics that’s grounded in the politics of mercy.”

Not everyone agreed with Budde’s sermon. The issue split parishioners after midday Mass at St. Anthony’s Shrine in downtown Boston.

“I disagree with what [Budde] said about Trump being insensitive to the concerns of the LGBTQ [community], and I also don’t think it was appropriate for her to include that in her blessing at that point,” Bob Berluti, 70, said.

Robert Matarazzo, 60, said Trump’s demand for an apology from Budde was a disgusting look.

“You’re at a service and she’s speaking for people who really need the most help,” he said.

His wife, Lisa, 57, agreed.

“I feel she had every right to speak out, and Jesus would want us to do that,” she said.

Material from the Associated Press was included in this story.

title: Josh Kraft wants to be mayor. Where does he stand on the issues facing Boston?
text:
For about a year, Kraft, who is also chair of the Urban League of Eastern Massachusetts, a civil rights organization based in Roxbury, has been running something of a shadow campaign, where he shows up at events, often in communities of color, and then posts about it on social media. According to the Boston Herald, last week he also showed up at a Dorchester neighborhood meeting on the hot-button topic of bike lanes.

On its own, the anti-bike crowd is not big enough to defeat an incumbent mayor who is also the first woman, person of color, and mother to win election to that office in Boston. But put that constituency together with other Boston voters who are turned off by Wu’s often stubborn style of governing and there is a potential anti-Wu coalition for someone with a lot of money and charisma to theoretically harness. Kraft definitely has money, but his charisma quotient is known only to those who frequent the local charity circuit, and his political beliefs remain a mystery. The family connection to President Trump — Robert Kraft contributed $1 million to Trump’s 2017 inauguration — hardly seems like a plus in Boston.

Josh Kraft is running as a Democrat, and last fall he said he was supporting the Democratic ticket for president. However, as I previously reported, in past years he has also contributed to a small group of very conservative Republican lawmakers. They include Representative Bob Latta of Ohio, who supported a constitutional ban on same-sex marriage; Representative Mike Bost of Illinois, who voted against a bill to protect marriage equality; Representative Buddy Carter of Georgia, who sponsored the Sanctity of Human Life Act, which protects life from conception with no exceptions; and Representative Glenn Grothman of Wisconsin, who in a speech on the House floor last July attacked government programs such as subsidized child care for taking “the purpose out of the man’s life because now you have a basket of goodies for the mom.”

Asked about those contributions, a spokesperson said at the time, “Josh is Jewish, is pro-Israel and has family and friends there. And that is why he has supported policy makers who are pro-Israel.” The spokesperson also noted that Kraft supports LGBTQ+ rights and abortion rights.

Whether Kraft’s past contributions matter in a Boston mayoral election remains to be seen. These are strange political times. After all, Massachusetts, including Boston, tilted rightward last November.

As tracked by the Dorchester Reporter, Trump increased his 2024 showing in Boston to 20.2 percent of the vote, up from 15.4 percent in 2020 and 13.7 percent in 2016. Now that Trump is in office, resistance will likely stiffen to actions he takes, for example, regarding immigration.

Yet Massachusetts is not immune to the anti-immigrant fever that is breaking out across the country. Governor Maura Healey, who as attorney general battled Trump immigration policies, is now pushing policies that limit shelter stays and could ultimately restrict shelter resources to residents. And Representative Stephen Lynch, whose district includes parts of Boston, recently voted in favor of The Laken Riley Act, which requires Immigration and Customs Enforcement to issue detainers and take custody of undocumented immigrants charged with theft and other crimes.

Wu, meanwhile, faces critics on several fronts. Property taxes are up. There’s the lingering problem of drug use and homelessness that is centered at the South End encampment known as Mass. and Cass but has also shifted to other neighborhoods. North End restaurant owners are still angry at Wu over on-street dining prohibitions in that neighborhood.

After her plan to move the John D. O’Bryant School of Math & Science from Roxbury to West Roxbury was met with stiff resistance, Wu dropped it, along with efforts to upgrade the facility. She recently released plans to close some Boston schools, a necessary but thankless mission.

Wu also faces community resistance to her plan to demolish White Stadium in Franklin Park and replace it with a stadium for a professional women’s soccer team that would be shared with Boston Public Schools. (Globe CEO Linda Henry has a small, noncontrolling ownership stake in the team.)

Out of that, can Kraft cobble together a coalition of the disgruntled? Perhaps. But first, he has to pick a side on those issues and more. Then he has to build and run a winning campaign by November.

That puts him and the Patriots on the same tight timetable.

title: The late Cecile Richards left behind a call to action
text:
Cecile Richards was an inspiration for women all over the globe (“Cecile Richards, former president of Planned Parenthood; at 67,” Obituaries, Jan. 21). She inspired me so much that I named one of my daughters after her. She has been on my mind for some time as she has been battling for us while battling cancer. We lost her on Monday. I think it is fitting that she died just hours before the swearing in of the president, because her passing reminds us all that we can never give up. I call on everyone to honor her by heeding the call from this excerpt from her book, “Make Trouble”:

“There is no doubt in my mind that we are bold enough, brave enough, and powerful enough. Creating the kind of massive change we need is going to take every single one of us — whether you’re a lifelong activist or you’ve been observing from the sideline until now. So ask yourself: What can I do right now to make my community, my workplace, or my school a better place for everyone? Then … go out, and do it. Consider this your official invitation to make trouble — because we don’t have a moment to waste.”

title: Trump order warning private employers to ‘end illegal DEI discrimination’ has local companies on edge
text:
The striking directive from Trump to eliminate DEI practices on the federal level and “combat illegal private-sector DEI preferences” has added fuel to the DEI backlash already sweeping the country and is causing consternation among some local employers.

“Clients are concerned, as they should be,” said Christie Lindor, founder of the DEI-focused firm Tessi Consulting in Boston.

Some companies have discussed altering the names of their antidiscrimination initiatives to remove “DEI” from the title, or changing language from “diverse” to “inclusive,” workplace experts say, while others have considered dropping programs specific to race and gender.

Trump’s directives don’t have immediate ramifications for most private employers, but his actions are still causing some to reconsider programs intended to create welcoming workplace environments for people of all backgrounds and preferences. They also have been shown to help retain talent, broaden companies’ reach, and improve the bottom line.

His actions could also have a major impact on companies that do business with the government, such as federal aerospace and defense contractors, as well as businesses owned by women and people of color that are prioritized for federal funding.

Governor Maura Healey addressed the DEI backlash at an Associated Industries of Massachusetts event Thursday and urged business leaders not to back away.

“There’s an attempt to bully and scare people,” she said. “It’s pretty blatant what’s happening out there, OK? Just stay strong. Do what’s right. Do what works. And we know these programs work.”

The office of Attorney General Andrea Campbell said it is working on guidance clarifying that DEI efforts are in fact “both legal and essential.”

In the meantime, though, some local businesses are unsure what the future holds.

John B. Cruz III, president of Cruz Companies, a third-generation Black-owned construction firm in Roxbury, said diversity goals in federal contracts gave companies like his, which may not have the connections that white-owned businesses do, a shot to participate in bids. He worries the new rules will hurt his business.

“If I don’t get on a bid list, I can’t grow,” said Cruz. “That’s the most important thing it did for us. It opened doors and allowed us to bid where people weren’t opening the doors.”

At the Community Foundation of Western Massachusetts in Springfield, which funds nonprofits dedicated to education, arts, and social justice, president Megan Burke said she is concerned about the potential impact on organizations with DEI-related missions if they lose federal funding that residents count on. But her organization is still firmly committed to advancing equity.

“We are not backtracking,” she said. “We’re not taking down our DEI commitment statement.”

But some organizations have been doing just that, said David Glasgow, executive director of the Meltzer Center for Diversity, Inclusion, and Belonging at New York University’s law school.

“The strongest trend is not actually organizations explicitly abandoning or retreating DEI, but rather just going quiet and doing DEI work by stealth,” Glasgow said.

Despite the “illegal discrimination” cited in Trump’s orders, many employers aren’t doing anything unlawful, employment lawyers say. Companies tend to know, for example, that hiring quotas are against the law. And most corporate DEI initiatives are focused on combating just that sort of preferential treatment with tools that root out discrimination, such as implicit bias training and pay equity audits.

There are gray areas, such as mentorship programs that are only open to certain groups, and impermissible practices, such as employers considering a person’s race or gender alone as a “plus” when hiring or promoting as a way to diversify workforces that have historically been largely white, employment lawyers note.

But Trump’s actions go far beyond challenging those types of actions. He revoked a 1965 order signed by President Lyndon Johnson banning the discrimination of workers employed by federal contractors and upended the interpretation of longstanding civil rights statutes that have encouraged private employers to counteract discrimination.

“This executive order I think is really significant in that it shifts that paradigm,” said Jennifer Cormier, an employment lawyer at Ropes & Gray in Boston. “The order is really suggesting that DE&I practices are inherently unlawful, and there really isn’t a basis for that in the law.”

Regardless, the Trump administration has already started carrying out the new directives.

On Wednesday, federal workers focused on DEI initiatives were put on leave while their programs were dismantled. Other federal employees were told via email to report colleagues who defied orders to eliminate DEI efforts from their agencies and warned not to “disguise these programs by using coded or imprecise language,” according to news reports.

“These programs divided Americans by race, wasted taxpayer dollars and resulted in shameful discrimination,” the message said.

The directives have gone beyond the scope of DEI-specific programs. A contractor for the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services told The New York Times that the agency was ordered to stop collecting demographic data on gender and race.

The orders also contain multiple references to private employers. One that references cracking down on “dangerous, demeaning, and immoral race- and sex-based preferences” directs the US attorney general to submit a report recommending measures that will “encourage the private sector to end illegal discrimination and preferences, including DEI.” It goes on to compel government agencies to each identify up to nine publicly traded companies, large nonprofits, or other organizations to investigate for compliance.

The fact that the order directs the AG to go after possible offenders means big public companies and other organizations targeted now have much greater legal risk, said Richard Morrison, a senior fellow at the Competitive Enterprise Institute, an anti-regulatory public policy organization in Washington, D.C.

“I expect many large employers to announce revised policies and new commitments to race-blind hiring and promotion in the days and weeks ahead,” he said in an email.

Trump’s directives will likely strengthen the cultural shift away from diversity and inclusion efforts that ramped up when the Supreme Court struck down affirmative action in college admissions in 2023. Last year, 66 percent of US companies said they were increasing investments in DEI, down from 77 percent the previous year, according to a study by the executive search firm Bridge Partners.

In left-leaning Massachusetts, the ripple effects from the federal changes may be muted, workplace observers said, noting that enforcement is often left up to local officials. But they could still have a chilling effect.

Clients with longstanding DEI programs are committed to keeping them, while looking to assess their practices to minimize risks, according to leaders of the DEI Solutions practice group at the Boston law firm Foley Hoag. But organizations that implemented “performative” programs in the wake of George Floyd’s murder in 2020 are more likely to ditch their diversity efforts, said Rosa Nunez, the law firm’s chief DEI officer and consultant.

“There’s a lot more risk there on people pulling the plug because they really do not understand the benefit of the work,” she said.

Trump’s executive orders may be “the first salvo in what I think is going to be a fairly relentless attack on DEI programs,” said Chris Hart, cochair of the Foley Hoag DEI Solutions practice.

A Supreme Court decision or legislation aimed at curtailing workplace diversity and inclusion programs, both of which are possible in the current climate, DEI Solutions cochair Chris Feudo noted, would be truly devastating blows to DEI.

This story was produced by the Globe’s Money, Power, Inequality team, which covers the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston. You can sign up for the newsletter here.

Anjali Huynh and Jon Chesto of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: White Stadium’s rebirth is coming soon, and that’s good news
text:
“All three of these communities are ones who have been long ignored and underserved,” Wu told me recently. “I felt a lot of pressure to make sure to get this right, because these communities have faced disappointment so many times already.”

The White Stadium project is a partnership between the city and a professional women’s soccer team, BOS Nation, slated to begin play in 2026.

From the outset, the project has drawn controversy, including a lawsuit from the nonprofit Emerald Necklace Conservancy, and ongoing complaints from a related advocacy group, the Franklin Park Defenders, which includes neighborhood stalwarts Jean McGuire and Louis Elisa.

Just this week, opponents of the project spearheaded a nine-hour City Council hearing to give full voice to their dissent.

That the city’s share of the project has ballooned in cost - from an early estimate of $50 million to roughly double that - has not helped quiet the criticism.

But I think the critics are wrong. Building a new White Stadium is one of Wu’s boldest ideas, and one that could eventually help shape her legacy.

Unlike some people who have just recently found their passion for Franklin Park - like the Emerald Necklace people - I have been a public advocate of renovating White Stadium for well over a decade. As many people will tell you, the facility—which opened in the 1940s—has been a dump for a whole lot longer than that.

Everyone agrees, or claims to agree, that White Stadium absolutely should be renovated. They just don’t like the price tag. Or the plan. Or the traffic professional soccer will bring. Or the idea that this whole project hinges on the support of a well-heeled group of soccer investors who will have dibs on the facility for 40 days a year. (Globe CEO Linda Henry is a minority investor in the soccer team.)

Forgive me, but I’ve spent years listening to people talk about how much they care about Franklin Park, while never getting behind any proposal to actually improve it. Obviously, renovating White Stadium is just one piece of bringing Franklin Park to its full potential. But it is an important piece, and letting this moment slip away is a terrible idea.

Wu told me she has become a bit obsessed with Franklin Park and its legendary designer, Frederick Law Olmsted, over the two years this project has been germinating. It’s led her to think a lot about what the park can and should be.

“He was basically the first person to say that parks should be for real people, not just, you know, manicured fancy bushes in shapes that you’re not supposed to touch,” she said. “The idea that you could feel a sense of connection to people whose name you might not know, but who you felt were part of your same community because you were in these same spaces.”

One frequent complaint has been that the soccer team will displace the high school football teams who use the stadium for much of their season. But that’s a trade-off for having a facility that can be used for things it cannot accommodate now - soccer, track and field, after-school programs. I love high school football, but why is it the only activity that counts?

Fixing White Stadium is an idea that comes around roughly once a decade. But the naysayers have always won, as Wu points out.

“As you’ve seen over the years, there are many reasons not to do something, and each time this has been promised in the past has fallen apart, either for funding or crumbling political will or voices from outside the city who don’t use the park or stadium, who were listened to,” she said.

The project is a great opportunity to reject the politics of “no”. Which, in this case, is exactly what should happen.

title: BPS has closed dozens of schools since 1980. Despite declining enrollment, the district has held on to most of the buildings.
text:
Some city leaders, including City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune, want the city to make use of more former school buildings for projects such as the Pryde, an affordable apartment building for LGBTQ+ seniors that opened last year in Hyde Park’s former Rogers Middle School. Louijeune plans to file legislation that would make affordable housing the default option for surplus district buildings, by giving the Mayor’s Office of Housing the first pick.

But the Rogers is a rarity, the only 21st-century closure to become housing to date.

A handful of closed schools, such as the Jackson-Mann K-8 andthe West Roxbury Education complex, remain largely unoccupied. A few more have been turned into other city and school facilities, including the district’s central kitchen and a police academy. At least four became private or charter schools, although one has since closed and is back in district hands.

But transforming a BPS school into another BPS school is more of the norm. Edwards Middle School is temporarily housing the Horace Mann School. Fifield Elementary became the Lee Academy. The Tileston School was torn down — and the Ellison-Parks Early Education School was built in its place.

The latest proposed closures, which require school board approval, would affect three schools, Excel High, Dever Elementary, and Mary Lyon Pilot High, and merge two others, the Roger Clap and Winthrop elementary schools, at the end of next school year. Already, district leaders are considering other schools for three of the campuses: Excel High’s campus would become a “new anchor high school,” Dever Elementary would be part of the Ruth Batson Academy rebuild, and the Mary Lyon lower school could take over the Lyon High building.

In some cases, remaining a school was the natural option. Some closed schools shared a building with others — Excel High’s closure would be the third in its building since 2011. Other closures were temporary: Mattahunt Elementary, shut in 2017 to avoid a state takeover, reopened the next school year.

Superintendent Mary Skipper has said the system cannot afford to offload too many buildings: it needs them as “swing spaces” to house schools while home campuses are renovated or rebuilt.

“For us to do the big capital projects, it’s very hard to do it when students are in the building,” she noted at last week’s School Committee meeting.

Skipper was responding to member Brandon Cardet-Hernandez, who advocated for the district to consider selling the buildings and investing that money back into education of BPS students.

“Is there a reason we’re not thinking more aggressive around the assets we have?” he asked. “We have to get cash back so we can spend it in much smarter ways so we can see achievement.”

The district is emphasizing caution this time. Spokesperson Sujata Wycoff said that in the past the district has let go of buildings it ended up needing.

“This is why we have committed to prioritizing BPS use until there is no viable educational use of a building,” she said.

That means while the district may not have yet identified uses for the Winthrop and Clap schools, which the district intends to merge and relocate, it doesn’t plan to let go of them soon. Buildings may also be leased out temporarily — as two currently are to nondistrict schools.

If leaders followed Cardet-Hernandez’s proposal, it would be similar to what happened to many BPS schools closed in 1980. About a dozen schools closed that year were converted into condominiums, including the Prince School on Newbury Street, Brighton’s Oak Square School, and East Boston’s Sheridan School.

Bob Kenney, head of Kenney Development Co., has worked on multiple school-to-housing conversions, including turning the South End’s Bancroft School into the Dartmouth Square condominiums. Many of Boston’s campuses are well-suited to housing, he said — particularly older ones like the Winthrop and Clap.

“People really like the old feeling of the schools,” Kenney said, but the layout also works: “Typically they were built with very wide corridors, and those were very convenient for things like bathrooms and kitchens. Then the windows are good for living areas.”

Matthew Kiefer, a land use attorney with Goulston and Storrs, agreed, adding that neighborhood elementary schools tend to be located in residential areas and some have parking lots. Their compact, multistory buildings divide up well into separate homes.

“These are very good candidates for residential conversion,” he said. “They’re in residential neighborhoods, surrounded by housing.”

For schools closed later in the 1980s, housing conversions tended to resemble the Rogers, aligning with Louijeune’s vision. Properties including the Michelangelo School and the Peter Faneuil School were converted into forms of income-restricted housing.

Louijeune emphasized school closures are traumatic for their communities, and said the district should improve its communications and ensure closures lead to better academic outcomes and facilities. But, she said, if the school district doesn’t need buildings, they should become housing.

“We’re in the middle of a housing crisis in this city and this Commonwealth,” she said.

Others warned any housing conversion should not eliminate important neighborhood assets. Brandy Brooks, head of the housing and education nonprofit Higher Ground, said her organization surveyed families and staff at a handful of schools about a planned new Roxbury elementary school BPS doesn’t have a site for yet. While none of those schools were named for closure or merger this month, the survey asked community members what they’d like potential closed campuses to become.

There was significant community interest in seeing closed schools become affordable housing, Brooks said, but residents were also worried about losing amenities, she said.

“When you [close schools], what other things still exist in this community?” she asked. “How far do people have to go for access to an outdoor playground?”

Kiefer, the land use attorney, warned against one option: holding onto empty buildings, as the district has often done in recent years with sites like the still-vacant West Roxbury Education Complex, which closed in 2019. Even if demographic trends reverse and the city comes to need schools near sites that used to have them, Kiefer predicted, they would be better off building new schools than retrofitting long-vacant 150-year-old buildings.

“Hanging on to it for future use is problematic,” he said. “They own it, they have to maintain it, and it can be a safety hazard.”

title: More than a dozen ways to celebrate Black History Month
text:
From historical plays to intimate concerts to films and children’s activities, here are 13 ways to take part in Black History Month in and around Boston this year.

BLACK PANTHER ON THE GIANT SCREEN AT MUSEUM OF SCIENCE As a part of its Black History Month programming, the Museum of Science Boston brings 2018’s “Black Panther,” starring Chadwick Boseman, to its Omni theater’s IMAX screen. Preregister for free tickets on the museum’s website, where you can find info on the day’s other Black history events. Feb. 1, movie screenings at 5 and 8 p.m. Mugar Omni Theater, 1 Science Park. Preregister at mos.org

BLACK HISTORY IN HOLLYWOOD AT THE COOLIDGE Coolidge Corner Theater celebrates Black filmmakers and actors with its monthlong “Black History in Hollywood” series. Starting Feb. 2 with 1954’s “Carmen Jones,” starring Dorothy Dandridge, the theater will screen six notable titles, including “Super Fly”(1972) and “In the Heat of the Night” (1967). Varying showtimes. 290 Harvard St., Brookline. Buy tickets at coolidge.org/programs/icons or roxfilmfest.com.

SOFAR SOUNDS BLACK ARTIST CELEBRATION AT BOW MARKET Sofar Sounds kicks off Black History Month at Somerville’s Bow Market with a night of live music by local Black artistsperforming hip-hop, R&B, and soul. Between sets, take a walk through Bow Market’s vendors, or purchase cocktails Upstairs at Bow. Feb. 1, 7:30 p.m. $27. 1 Bow Market Way, Somerville. Reserve at sofarsounds.com

WEE GOT THE JAZZ CHILDREN’S EVENT Wee The People teams up with several Boston Public Library branches for a program focused on the phenomenon of jazz and its impact on Black America. The educational program will be available at the Roslindale, Parker Hill, Grove Hall, and Chinatown BPL locations. Children ages 6 and up will enjoy an hour of storytelling, music, and art-making. Feb. 3-6, at 11 a.m. See the schedule of locations at weethepeopleboston.org

MFA FIRST FRIDAYS CELEBRATION This monthly series brings museumgoers together for a night of art, dancing, and specially crafted cocktails. Black History Month’s initial First Friday will center on “Power of the People: Art and Democracy,” an exhibit representing civilizations’ use of art in expressing democratic ideals. Advance tickets required. Feb. 7, 6-9 p.m. Free for members; $27 for non-members. 465 Huntington Ave. mfa.org

BLACK-OWNED BUSINESS MARKETPLACE POP-UP The Cambridge-Somerville Black Business Network invites community members to support Black businesses during its marketplace pop-up. Valentine’s goodies, soaps, accessories, vintage fashion, fragrances, and hand-crafted gifts will be available for purchase from more than a dozen Black-owned businesses. Feb 7 and 8. Times vary. 1 Brattle Square, Cambridge. RSVP for a free ticket at www.sbnmass.org/blackbusinessmarket

SOJOURNER TRUTH: SEWING THE SEEDS OF JUSTICE QUILTING EVENT “Make your own block” with the Sisters in Stitches Joined By The Cloth at Boston’s Museum of African American History. Each participant will make two quilt squares, one to be added to a larger community project in honor of abolitionist Sojourner Truth and one to keep. Feb. 8, 1-4 p.m. 46 Joy St. Suggested $20 donation. Reserve your spot at maah.org

(G)RACE SPEAKS’ A REVOLUTIONARY ENCOUNTER IN LONDON PLAY (G)RACE Speaks at Old South and Boston-based playwright Debra Wiess stage a dramatic reading of “A Revolutionary Encounter in London” at Old South Church. The play centers on a conversation between Phillis Wheatley, the first Black woman to publish a collection of poetry in the United States, and founding father Benjamin Franklin. title: Boston becomes first city to launch fund for families of drug overdose victims
text:
Boston residents who have lost relatives to drug overdoses will be able to apply for financial assistance to ease the strain resulting from the untimely deaths, through a first-of-its-kind initiative funded through legal settlements with the pharmaceutical industry that flooded the nation with highly addictive opioids.

The Boston Public Health Commission last week announced the launch of the “Family Overdose Support Fund,” with $250,000 to cover child care, therapy, funeral expenses, legal services, and other financial burdens. Money for the fund will come from a portion of the multibillion-dollar payouts that opioid manufacturers have made to states and cities for their role in a relentless epidemic that has claimed more than 20,000 lives in Massachusetts in just the past decade.

The fund, which will cover up to $5,000 in expenses per family, is the first municipal fund in the nation dedicated specifically to families of overdose victims — an often overlooked population who can be emotionally and financially devastated by the loss of a close relative to the opioid scourge.

The fund culminates more than a year of planning and community meetings over how to spend money from opioid legal settlements and comes as both Boston and the state show signs of progress in the decades-long fight to stem the tide of overdose deaths.

The commission reported preliminary numbers last week showing that opioid-related overdose deaths declined 39 percent citywide between May and August of last year — after rising the previous year. In 2023, 377 people died of overdoses in Boston, up from 353 the previous year, despite a decline in overdose fatalities statewide, according to the state Department of Public Health.

“If we’re going to use the opioid settlement dollars in any way that’s most meaningful, then we need to allocate money, first and foremost, to families with lost loved ones — mothers, fathers, children, parents who were left behind and suffering from loss," said Dr. Bisola Ojikutu, Boston’s public health commissioner, who announced the fund at an event at Nubian Square in Roxbury.

The new support fund also reflects greater awareness of the devastation wrought by the opioid epidemic and a lessening of the stigma that has long been associated with opioid use. More than 40 percent of adults nationwide say they personally know at least one person who died from a drug overdose, and about one-third of those individuals say their lives were disrupted by the death, according to survey findings published early last year by the nonprofit research institute RAND Corp.

In recent years, parents who have lost children to overdoses have become more outspoken and organized — testifying at state houses for new prevention strategies and often starting charitable funds of their own to support grieving families. In Massachusetts, years of grassroots lobbying by families played a role in the passage of a far-reaching opioid bill that will mandate insurance coverage for overdose-reversal medications such as Narcan as well as addiction recovery services.

Yet the needs of families impacted by the epidemic are immense.

“A lot of times, the children of overdose victims are forgotten,” said Joanne Peterson, the founder and executive director of Learn to Cope, a nationwide support network for those affected by substance use disorder. “The list of what they need goes on and on and on.”

Peterson’s group recently donated $20,000 to families of 26 children who have lost at least one parent to an overdose, or whose parents are absent because of addiction. Money went to pay for children’s clothing, therapy, day care, summer camps, and even the cost of burying a parent, she said.

To qualify for Boston’s new support fund, an applicant must live in Boston and have lost their family member within two years. The deceased must be a spouse, father, father-in-law, brother, sister, child, grandparent, grandchild, legal guardian, or other member of the applicant’s immediate household. Those who are approved will not receive the cash directly; instead, the fund will pay service providers directly, limited to $5,000 per invoice.

Some of the expenses that the fund will cover include funerals, burials, and cremation services for a relative who died of an overdose, as well as clinical therapy for surviving family members. It will also cover activities for surviving children, such as sports, music lessons, and summer camp.

More than 50 families will receive assistance through the fund, which is expected to last two years. The fund is administered by the Boston BullPen Project, a nonprofit that partners with social service agencies to provide assistance to vulnerable communities.

As of November of last year, Boston has received $12.4 million from legal settlements with the opioid industry. The city expects to receive more than $1 million each year through 2038.

title: Does Josh Kraft have a chance against Mayor Wu? 4 writers react.
text:
Meaning, it could happen. But he’s definitely the underdog, and if I had to place a bet right now, my money is on incumbent Michelle Wu coasting to a second term.

Of course, Kraft does have strengths most challengers lack — money and name recognition.

And there are plenty of Wu-haters ready to vote for any opponent with a pulse — though not nearly as many as Twitter and the comments sections might lead you to believe.

But Wu has the advantage of incumbency. She can also boast of Boston’s exceptionally low crime on her watch. And her base of white progressives shows no sign of abandoning her.

In my view, to win Kraft would have to do three things, all at once:

First, in 2024 20 percent of the city’s electorate backed Trump. For those Republican-leaning voters, there’s often no point in voting in municipal elections, since the two finalists are almost always both Democrats. Kraft will need to motivate those voters to show up and vote for him. The trick is, he can’t court them too explicitly without alienating the rest of the city.

Second, Kraft needs to peel away Black voters. He has spent a lot of time wooing the Black community, but it’s an open question whether his philanthropic record will translate into votes.

Third, “the business community” whose complaints about Wu we keep hearing about will need to show that it’s not all bark. I don’t necessarily mean downtown businesses so much as local businesses in the neighborhoods. When every bodega and dry cleaner in the city has a Kraft sign in the window, I’ll believe he’s got a shot.

To be clear, all three are possible. But making all three happen in the same election would be a political feat.

By Joan Vennochi

During nine hours of testimony at a recent Boston City Council hearing about Mayor Michelle Wu’s grandiose renovation plan for White Stadium, several dozen residents spoke out against it. Only five residents expressed support.

In that well of citizen discontent is an opening for Josh Kraft, the philanthropist son of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. The grumbling about Wu is about more than one project. It’s about what critics see as a top-down style of governing, whether the issue is bike lanes or the stadium renovation plan, which calls for a partnership with a professional women’s soccer team and at least $100 million in taxpayer money.

“I understand that in politics, you make decisions,” Jacquetta Van Zandt, a political analyst and host of the Politics and Prosecco podcast, told me. But Wu, she said, took office “with the idea that she would be collaborative with the community. That has not happened.” Van Zandt, who lives in Roxbury, contends that Wu’s approach makes her especially vulnerable in communities of color.

The city’s website on the stadium project lists 13 public meetings and another 15 commission meetings where it was discussed. But in politics, perception is reality. And with Wu’s critics, the perception is that rather than first asking residents what they want, she comes to them with her vision of what she wants – and won’t budge.

Because of what developers contend is her refusal to mingle with their crowd, her ban on outdoor dining in the North End, and a proposal, which ultimately failed, to raise commercial property taxes, Wu also has detractors in the business community.

Out of such discontent, a smart, savvy challenger who knows Boston well could cobble together a credible challenge to Wu. But is Kraft that person? He is a political neophyte, who is known to few voters. He’s a rich white guy, who comes from a family that may not be super popular in Boston right now. Can he beat an incumbent mayor who has a serious political operation? Under the best case scenario – maybe?

By Carine Hajjar

Unseating an incumbent isn’t a common occurrence in Boston mayoral politics. But lately, politics have been anything but conventional. Yes, Josh Kraft’s bid to unseat Mayor Wu is going to be an uphill battle, but don’t write it off in a city struggling with progressive policies.

Who can forget the death, violence, and addiction that the city allowed to fester at Mass. and Cass in the name of “harm reduction” until enough public outcry led to a crackdown? And what about Wu’s message that “we want immigrants to know that it is safe for everyone, to be able to feel comfortable reaching out for emergency services, to report a crime,” as the state continued to conceal alleged rapes and assaults in shelters?

Kraft is likely to run to the right of her, but still as a Democrat in a city where an R next to your name will kill any and all chances. His ties to both the business and nonprofit worlds might be a boon if his campaign focuses on affordability and the revival of Boston’s business, while underlining the social causes that matter to the city.

That won’t make his path to victory easy, but it’s not impossible. The country is in new political territory. Voters in blue cities like Portland, Los Angeles, and San Francisco have started to reject certain progressive policies, and a correction might be due in Boston. Will Kraft be able to capitalize on the vibe shift?

By Marcela García

Anne Chatfield, whose three sons attend Boston Public Schools, has become increasingly disillusioned with the state of the district. And she lays the blame squarely at the feet of Mayor Michelle Wu.

I first connected with Chatfield at the beginning of the school year, when she was dealing with repeated issues of late and no-show buses for her fifth grader at the Murphy K-8 School in Dorchester. While the timeliness of buses has reportedly improved somewhat, the frustrations haven’t disappeared. Last week, Chatfield texted me about yet another no-show bus — this time on the coldest morning of the year. With temperatures below freezing, she had no choice but to drive her son to school herself for the second consecutive day. “I couldn’t let him be outside,” she said.

Her frustrations go beyond the buses. “I’m so happy there is someone running against [the mayor] this fall,” she said, referring to mayoral challenger Josh Kraft. Chatfield said she has lost confidence in Wu’s ability to manage Boston Public Schools effectively and believes many families with children in her South Boston neighborhood feel similarly.

Although Chatfield admitted she doesn’t yet know much about Kraft’s stances on education or transportation, she said she’s “very excited about having a viable alternative and perhaps someone who’s going to bring something different to the table.”

That’s an obvious lane for Kraft to seize. He has plenty of time to articulate his positions and vision for BPS; after all, his campaign hasn’t officially launched. Whether his policies will resonate with disillusioned voters like Chatfield remains to be seen, but one thing is certain: Parents like her are tired of waiting for solutions and are ready to listen to someone new who promises to deliver.
