title: Free events this week: Blind dates with a book, Bachelor nation, and more
text:
What feels like the thousand-day-long month of January has finally come to a close. Next up: February, the month of love, the Super Bowl , and hopefully, those New Year’s resolutions we’re definitely keeping up with. (Not likely.) No matter how you choose to spend your February, there are plenty of fun ways to do so for cheap. Here’s our roundup for no-cost things to do around Boston for the week of Feb. 3-9.

WILL YOU ACCEPT THIS ROSE? “The Bachelor” is back for another season and, once again the resounding question of who will get the final rose is reverberating across Bachelor Nation. For those who don’t want to watch the show alone — or just want to refresh their recap group chat — Lamplighter Brewing hosts a watch party of new episodes every Monday. Feb. 3, 8-10 p.m. 21+ Free. 284 W Broadway. lamplighterbrewing.com

CREATIVE CONNECTION Inspiration doesn’t appear out of thin air for Boston’s creative community. Artist circles are a great way to share your project and get the juices flowing with some back-and-forth conversation. Any medium of choice can join in at the Parker Hill branch of the Boston Public Library’s Craft & Chat, where artists can work on and share their projects, whether painting or fiber arts. Feb. 5, 4:30-5:30 p.m. Free. 1497 Tremont St., Roxbury. bpl.bibliocommons.com

PULL UP YOUR BOOTSTRAPS Despite being a wee bit north of Nashville, New England sure does love its country music. Looking to mix up your playlist? Loretta’s Last Call in Fenway hosts its Country Money Tour with singer Louie Bello every Thursday, presenting up-and-coming and new artists for a night of upbeat live music and line dancing. Feb. 6, 9:30-11:30 p.m. Free. 1 Lansdowne St. lorettaslastcall.com

DIY 4 ALL Puts your kid on the front page with this zine-making workshop at Cambridge Public Library’s O’Neill branch in North Cambridge. The event provides materials and guidance in making colorful and personalized zines for children ages 7 and up — plus, there will be snacks. Registration recommended. Feb. 7, 4-5 p.m. 70 Rindge Ave., Cambridge. cambridgepl.libcal.com/event/13870429

LOVE IS BLIND Keeping an open heart this February is best with keeping an open mind. Community organization Roslindale Village Main Street’s Blind Date with a Book event wants to help readers do both. . Participants can pick from a selection of plainly wrapped books, each with a short description and genre for what’s inside. In return, those who take a book are encouraged to bring a book from their own collection, leaving it with the library to wrap and be set up with someone new. Feb. 8, 10 a.m.-1 p.m. Boston Public Library, Roslindale Branch. 4246 Washington St. roslindale.app.neoncrm.com

MUSIC BE THE FOOD OF LOVE With Valentine’s Day on the horizon, opera is one way to get into the romantic spirit. The Maenad Theatre Troupe will present “Crimes of Passion,” sponsored by the Friends of the Thomas Crane Public Library, a two-act performance featuring classical compositions from “Carmen,” “The Barber of Seville,” and “The Magic Flute.” Following intermission, the troupe will present an abridged performance of “Ruddigore,” a satirical opera about witches, curses, and weddings. Feb. 8, 2-4 p.m. Thomas Crane Public Library. 40 Washington St., Quincy. Registration via Eventbrite required.

Marianna Orozco can be reached at marianna.orozco@globe.com.

title: At Boston supermarkets, shoppers brace for Trump tariffs to spike prices
text:
On Saturday, Trump announced the imposition of sweeping tariffs on goods from Mexico, China, and Canada, to take effect on Tuesday. Mexican and Canadian imports will be subject to a 25 percent tariff, with a lower 10 percent tariff on energy resources from Canada. All products from China will be hit with a 10 percent tariff.

The tariffs fulfill promises made by Trump on the campaign trail, and the Trump administration says they are intended to pressure Canada, Mexico, and China to crack down on fentanyl production and trafficking. But experts say the immediate effects will be felt by consumers, as the tariffs and retaliatory measures from the targeted countries raise the prices of imported goods.

Can Erbil, a professor of economics at Boston College, said most economists — even those who supported Trump — did not think he would actually carry out his pledge on tariffs once in office.

“Everyone was agreeing that this was a bad idea,” Erbil said. “The argument was yeah, this is not going to happen. He’s using this as a bargaining chip, it’s a tactic.”

On Tuesday that tactic will become a reality, and Erbil said grocery shoppers can expect prices to increase on a range of goods frequently imported from Mexico and Canada. More than 50 percent of fresh vegetables in American stores are imported from Mexico, Erbil said. The United States is less dependent on Canada for food stock, but some niche products will be affected, according to Erbil. More than three quarters of frozen fries sold in America are imported from Canada, Erbil said.

Former president Joe Biden’s administration also raised tariffs on China. But those increases were more surgical and targeted specific sectors like electric vehicles and solar cells. Trump’s tariffs, by contrast, are a blunt instrument — one that could have long term effects if not swiftly undone, according to Erbil.

“I think this is going to have an impact, and the impact may be pretty quick,” he said.

Price increases for specific products will depend on how much demand there is for them as the cost rises, Erbil said — a concept in economics known as elasticity. Luxury goods, or those with easy to find substitutes, will see lower increases; necessities and products difficult to replace will likely see increases closer to the full 25 percent tariff, Erbil said.

Nancy Sobel said she rarely shops at large grocery stores, but went to the Fenway Star Market Sunday morning to stock up on bags of cat food and bulkier items like toilet paper that she can’t haul home without the assistance of her friend’s car.

The 70-year-old likes to buy her produce at the Haymarket farmers’ market, finding it less expensive and easier to access from her home in downtown Boston. There, the 10 heads of lettuce she buys for $1 from local farmers won’t be impacted by Trump’s order to impose hefty tariffs on products originating from Mexico, Canada, and China.

Like several others shopping at Star Market Sunday, Sobel was frustrated by the president’s order that will present financial hurdles for those shopping for everyday necessities like eggs, poultry, and produce.

“I’m not a political person, but you can’t help but to pay attention to this, especially with how quickly it’s going on,” she said.

Kenton Jacobs, a 75-year-old retiree from Roxbury, was shopping at the neighborhood’s Price Rite supermarket Sunday afternoon. Jacobs said he lives alone, and typically spends about $50 per week on groceries — a figure that’s jumped significantly over the last few years. He said the tariffs will make things difficult for families, and he is worried that prices may not return to normal even if the policy is reversed.

“It’s gonna be a lot of gouging,” Jacobs said. “Once they come up, they don’t go back down.”

Kathy Guild, a Roxbury mother of seven, exited the Price Rite with a hefty cart of groceries. Inflation has pushed her weekly grocery bill to $400, she said, and she expects Trump’s tariffs will lead to further increases.

“The man came here saying that he’s going to lower things, and all I see is a rise in prices,” Guild said. “This is a man of broken promises.”

Chad Redd and his fiancée buy all food products for their family of five at Star Market, and carefully craft grocery lists before they head to the store for their weekly shopping, hoping to keep their bill below $150.

“I think it’s ridiculous,” Redd said of Trump’s order, adding that he’s already alarmed by the rising price of eggs due to the spread of avian flu threatening the country’s poultry flocks.

Redd pointed not only to eggs, which the store currently prices at nearly $7 a dozen, but also to produce like avocados, which are shipped in from Mexico.

Rebecca Ade felt similarly about Trump’s actions, though she wasn’t as surprised as some of the other shoppers.

“It’s not unexpected given everything he’s done,” she said. “He said he was going to do all this and this is the consequence of electing him.”

Ade, 30, is from Nigeria and studies at Harvard while working part-time in international development. Though she doesn’t plan her shopping ahead of time and tends to pay attention to nutritional value over prices, she said that practice will change when her 2-year-old son soon comes to live with her.

“When my kid is around, I’m going to shop more often and be more cautious about prices,” she said.

title: In looming mayor’s race, who has the Black vote: Michelle Wu or Josh Kraft?
text:
My sense, after months of conversations with Black leaders, is that the Black vote is up for grabs — and that as Black voters go, so goes the election.

From Mattapan to Roxbury, there’s a recurring strain of unhappiness. Wu has not only failed to deliver on her promises to stabilize rents and improve schools, but they feel that the city is not on the right track with rising property taxes, an influx of bike lanes, and a controversial renovation of White Stadium.

This disenchantment with Wu is perhaps why Kraft, the former longtime leader of the Boys & Clubs of Boston and board chair of the Urban League of Eastern Massachusetts, thinks he has a shot at winning. While he’s the son of a billionaire — dad is New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft — the younger Kraft has spent three decades working to uplift youth in Boston and Chelsea’s Black and Latino communities. There’s even a teen center in Mattapan named after him!

But this doesn’t mean unhappy Black voters will automatically flock to Kraft. He will have to earn their vote. Which is why he has spent the better part of a year on a listening tour, meeting with hundreds of civic leaders, small business owners, politicians (current and former), and voters — many in communities of color.

Jacquetta Van Zandt, a Roxbury resident and host of the “Politics and Prosecco” podcast, said she’s upset with the Wu administration’s handling of residential property taxes, the persistent homelessness problem at Mass. and Cass, and the city’s decision to spend $100 million redeveloping the city-owned White Stadium for a new professional women’s soccer team.

“There are some missteps that the Wu administration has done in terms of alienating and not collaborating with the Black community,” said Van Zandt, who met Kraft for the first time last year and described him as “respected” in Black circles.

Van Zandt, who voted for City Councilor Annissa Essaibi George in the 2021 mayoral race, hasn’t decided who she will vote for this time but added, “If the election were held today, I would not vote for Michelle.”

Chanda Smart, who lives in Roxbury and runs her own real estate development and brokerage firm, voted for Wu in 2021 — first in the preliminary and then in the final. But Smart is not sure she’s going to back Wu again. She has also met with Kraft and feels heard. Smart believes he grasps not only how development can boost the local economy but also what it will take to get projects moving along.

“Democracy is alive, and everyone needs to fight for their seat,” she said. “At this point, we are beyond identity and party politics. It’s time for action to match policies that reflect this moment.”

And while every vote matters, votes in the Black community could prove decisive in a close race.

Here’s why: In November 2021, Wu captured 64 percent of Boston’s electorate to become the first woman and person of color elected mayor. In the general election, she won all the majority-minority neighborhoods in the middle of the city that had gone to one of the three Black candidates in the six-way preliminary election, according to an analysis by the MassInc Polling Group.

The only two wards she didn’t win in the city encompass South Boston.

This time around, let’s assume Wu hangs onto her loyal progressive base, voters who support her to fulfill her policy agenda that includes rent stabilization, a Green New Deal, and fare-free transit. Then figure Kraft picks up more conservative white voters who largely backed Essaibi George in the 2021 runoff, and before her Mayor Marty Walsh in 2013 and 2017.

In November 2021, about 144,000 people voted in the mayor’s race, and Wu won by nearly 41,000 votes. That means roughly 22,000 votes swinging the other way is the difference between winning and losing. And that is the approximate size of the Black electorate in Boston.

“More than ever, this year’s mayoral election is going to come down to Black voters,” observed state Representative Christopher Worrell, a Dorchester Democrat, who is Black. “Voters are going to be looking for the candidate who is consistently in the community and delivering tangible results. All too often, my community sees politicians who only show up when they are looking for votes during the campaign. Our next mayor must demonstrate a firm commitment to supporting residents of Dorchester, Roxbury, and Mattapan.”

I expect Kraft and Wu to start courting Black leaders and elected officials for endorsements. Keep a close eye on who endorses early on and who chooses to hold out.

Worrell is keeping an open mind. Wu endorsed him on the front steps of his parents’ home in Dorchester in 2022 when he first ran for state representative. Kraft wrote a check and showed up last November at a Thanksgiving turkey drive he and his brother Brian Worrell, a city councilor, sponsor every year.

Like other groups, Black voters are not a monolith. Homeowners might feel differently from renters, older voters care about issues that young people do not. And the race is just beginning.

Nia Grace, a Roxbury resident and restaurateur, said she’s well aware of criticisms of Wu coming from the Black community, but her experience is that Wu’s administration has been responsive whether it’s addressing concerns about bike lanes to providing grants to help small businesses open storefronts.

“Any administration is going to have critics,” said Grace. “No administration is infallible, and I think that the Wu administration has had a lot more good efforts than not.”

Grace knows Wu. She’s met Kraft before too — his daughter is a singer and performs at Grace’s jazz club in the Seaport District. Still, Grace is not ready to share who she will cast a ballot for come November.

“I am a supporter of the Wu administration as it is currently,” said Grace. “The Wu administration is what I know. I don’t know a Josh Kraft administration.”

We’ll know soon enough what a Kraft candidacy looks like — and whether Boston wants a change in City Hall.

The story has been updated to reflect that Michelle Wu in 2021 won all but two wards in the city.

Shirley Leung is a Business columnist and host of the Globe Opinion podcast “Say More with Shirley Leung.” Find the podcast on Apple, Spotify, and globe.com/saymore. Follow her on Threads @shirley02186

title: Sixty-somethings get a second chance at romance after a loss
text:
He texted back: “Of course I’m real. Why wouldn’t I be?”

“The fraught thing with online dating is having these non-human-beings reach out to you, bots or whatever,” explains Carolyn MacNeil, now 62.

Her New Year’s Day morning featured a phonebook purge; deleting texts and numbers that need not follow her into the new year. She texted Brian anyway, vaguely remembering their short-lived attempt to set up a date earlier that year. She had sent warm condolences when he explained the circumstances, but, also wondered if it was actually a snub.

“I had thought, alright, she’s not going to believe it,’” remembers Brian, who is now 61. His mother had passed in September and much of his time since had been occupied with grieving and sorting her estate.

The texts turned into a phone call that lasted several hours. The chemistry was mutually apparent, but there was one catch. Since they had first connected, Brian, an avid skier, had moved from North Reading to Franconia, N.H.

Carolyn, who lives in West Roxbury, had mentioned distance as a potential dealbreaker on her dating profile. Remembering this, Brian promised to compromise. He volunteered to drive to Massachusetts for their first date — and possible follow-ups. He was frequently in the area for work and to visit one of this three daughters, who was in boarding school in the area.

They had dinner later that month at Not Your Average Joe’s in Waltham. Carolyn recalls Brian entering the restaurant in a sport coat with jeans and “a nice white button-down Oxford shirt.”

They connected on shared values — the importance of family, giving back to their communities in “time, talent, or treasure” — and active, outdoor lifestyles. They both worked in education; between his consulting work, Brian was an adjunct professor at Bentley University while Carolyn, at the time, worked for Boston Public Schools. Both were single parents and had been married before; they were interested in companionship, conversation, and someone to share the many adventures to come.

They continued to meet up for lunch or dinner whenever Brian came through the area, about once every two weeks. After parting ways on their third date, Carolyn called Brian before she got onto the Mass. Pike.

“How about turning around?” she said. “I want to kiss you.”

They shared their first kiss in a Natick parking lot, just off exit 117.

Brian, an only child, had the challenging task of clearing out his late parents’ home in Watertown, Conn. Carolyn joined him on weekends from April through June. They sorted through Brian’s family relics and childhood memories.

“You don’t often get this opportunity to see where someone grew up and their family pictures and sentimental items in their parents’ house. I got to know so much more about him,” says Carolyn. Plus, she was efficient: “I’m very decisive, while he sort of [overthinks] about throwing out the smallest thing. I’m like, ‘No, there are 15 umbrellas from this bank. You don’t need 14 of them.’”

Their days were soon filled with long weekends and day trips, families and lives merged, love notes were tucked between pillows.

“I thought [the relationship] was gonna be kind of, you know, a summer romance,” says Brian. “But that turned into a fall, which turned into a winter into another spring, and what really happens is that one day you wake up, and you realize that you’re a part of each other’s lives. And that you don’t want to be without the other person.”

In May 2023, Carolyn was Brian’s first call when there was a family emergency. He would need to travel to Utah as soon as possible; she booked tickets for two for the first flight out the following morning.

“She dropped everything,” he says. “It was that trip that solidified to me how important and integral she was in making my life better.”

Brian proposed that New Year’s Eve near the Dufferin Terrace in Old Quebec City, overlooking the St. Lawrence River. Carolyn, who remembers being “shocked,” exclaimed, “Of course, yes!”

Wedding planning was laced with sadness. Carolyn’s father, Dan Crane, had been diagnosed with cancer that previous December. As Carolyn and her three siblings arranged his care, Brian took on a role as chauffeur, home cook, and confidant, filling time between medical appointments to learn history and family lore from Dan. (”He was in a shot put contest with Wilt Chamberlain when he was in high school.”) The family said their final goodbyes in August.

Their late parents were on Carolyn and Brian’s minds as they approached their New Year’s Eve wedding. Their small ceremony at the Franconia Inn in Franconia, N.H. would be family only — 14 guests, including Brian’s three daughters, Carolyn’s daughter and son, and their families. It was officiated by Carolyn’s friend, the Rev. Edward M. Cardoza. Carolyn wore her mother’s opal ring and Brian’s mother’s fur stole. One week before the wedding, Carolyn found a small box beneath their bed. Inside was a velvet pouch containing his parents’ gold wedding rings, presumed lost before.

On Dec. 31, 2024, Brian and Carolyn exchanged his parents’ rings. The rings were symbolic placeholders while their custom bands were made. South End jeweler Michele Mercaldo used metal from his parents’ bands to create Brian’s.

The ceremony, which took place in the inn’s dining room, was not religious. However, it included a hand-fasting ritual, a Celtic tradition in which a couple’s hands are wrapped together and freed from a strip of fabric, forming a knot. (Thus the phrase, “Tying the knot.”)

Carolyn carried a bouquet made by Emily Herzig of EH Floral that included lilies of the valley, which symbolize a return to happiness, a journey Brian documented in his vows, down to the hour.

“Three years, 364 days, and 19 hours after we talked that New Year’s Day,” he says, “we married.”

Read more from The Big Day, The Boston Globe’s new weddings column.

title: Josh Kraft claims Mayor Wu hasn’t delivered — but can he?
text:
Kraft is a newcomer to electoral politics but his maiden appearance made his strategy clear. He is hoping to leverage his three decades in community service and frustration with what some perceive as Wu’s distant leadership style to build a coalition of those who feel shut out of City Hall.

To that end, Kraft claimed he will be the mayor who can make rent control a reality, while also building enough housing to make Boston more affordable. A mighty tough trick for anyone, much less a complete political ingenue.

His summary of Wu’s broken promises takes some liberties with the truth. She never promised everyone a lifetime free ride on the MBTA: she said she would advocate for it, beginning with demanding a seat for Boston on the MBTA board — a fight she won.

As for rent control, that was killed — as it has been for nearly 30 years — at the State House, where developers have a virtually undefeated record on this issue.

Kraft says he will offer tax breaks to landlords who agree to a 10-year cap on rent increases. Setting aside the question of whether his version of rent control can be enacted without State House approval, it would have to be an awfully enticing tax cut for landlords to agree to a deal of that length.

Kraft assailed Wu as a leader who doesn’t listen to the community.

“Too often, Mayor Wu acts as if she alone has all the answers,” Kraft said.

Listening to his announcement, I was surprised that Kraft was so negative about Wu at the very start of his campaign. Conventional political wisdom is that challengers begin on a positive note as they introduce themselves to voters who don’t know much about them. Attacks have more credibility, the theory goes, when they come from a candidate voters know more about.

But Kraft and his team seem to be banking on the idea that there is a substantial reservoir of frustration with Wu personally — that she doesn’t meet with enough people, or listen to a big enough circle of people, or ever change her mind about an issue.

The biggest cheer of the event, by far, came when Kraft said he would shut down the push for more bike lanes in the city. To Wu’s adversaries, bike lanes have (absurdly) become the ultimate symbol of her intransigence.

Kraft told me later Tuesday in a phone conversation that for years he brushed aside suggestions that he should run for office someday. “Five or six years ago, running for office wasn’t on my mind,” he said. “People would throw it out there, and I’d say, ‘I don’t know if that’s for me.’ ”

Kraft said he’s running because he thinks the city is headed in the wrong direction. But I was struck by how closely his priorities — more affordable housing, rent control, better schools — mirror Wu’s. Kraft doesn’t say he will push for different things — he claims he will push for them more effectively.

Maybe it was no accident that he announced in Grove Hall, a neighborhood at the border of Roxbury and Dorchester that feels perpetually shut out of power. Before and after Kraft’s speech, Miles Davis’s classic album “Kind of Blue” wafted from the speakers — easily the best campaign-kickoff music I’ve ever heard.

Wu swept into office four years ago on a pledge to bring the voices of the voiceless into City Hall. Now, a son of one of the region’s most prominent families is promising something similar.

Can Kraft convince voters that he can deliver what he claims Wu hasn’t? His prospects could well turn on that question.

title: ‘A win-win for the community’: Vicente’s Supermarket, a Brockton-based grocery store, to replace Warren St. Walgreens in Roxbury
text:
The Walgreens closure in January 2024 prompted pushback from residents and elected officials who said it would threaten residents' access to over-the-counter medications, life-saving prescription, and pharmacists' advice.

The news of the supermarket drew mixed reaction from Roxbury residents, who disagreed on what would be the best business to take Walgreens’ place. Nevertheless, the feedback was resounding: a drugstore void in the surrounding neighborhood needs to be filled.

“There’s a major gap here,” said Louis Elisa, president of the Garrison-Trotter Neighborhood Association. “Four or five miles doesn’t seem like a lot to us, but [for elders], there are a lot of challenges.”

Segun Idowu, the city’s chief of economic opportunity and inclusion, said Vicente’s owners are exploring how to include a pharmacy inside the property.

“I expressed to them the desire of the community that there needs to at least be a pharmacy element in there, and they said, ‘If that’s what the community wants, we will find a way to make it work,‘” Idowu said.

He added, “It’s a win-win for the community: fresh food and access to needed medication.”

The Rev. Miniard Culpepper, of Pleasant Hill Missionary Baptist Church said he would “100 percent” support any supermarket that would incorporate a pharmacy into their store. He said doing so removes the burden for residents at the nearby Martin Luther King Towers, a public development comprised of mostly elderly and disabled tenants.

“If they could walk across the street again [for their prescriptions], that would be amazing,” Culpepper said.

Denise Hogan, a Roxbury resident who once received her prescriptions from the now-closed Walgreens, is skeptical the store will include a pharmacy. She said the neighborhood already has a Price Rite as well as a Stop & Shop.

“We don’t need another supermarket,” Hogan said. “We need something different.”

It is not clear when the store would open, but JP Plunkett, principal for Dorchester-based Red Dome Realty, said “it shouldn’t be too far out.”

“It’s going to be wonderful for the Roxbury community, given the dearth of grocery options there,” he said. “The neighbors are going to be super excited about this.”

As of Tuesday afternoon, 416 Warren St. was included among the supermarket’s locations on Google. The city also issued a permit to renovate the space on Jan. 30, though it doesn’t name Vicente’s Supermarket, according to a building permit database.

Vicente’s Supermarket has pursued health-focused endeavors in the past, though none related to pharmaceuticals.

In 2015, the local chain partnered with the Brockton Neighborhood Health Center to introduce a full-time nutritionist and a teaching kitchen next to the grocer. Through the collaboration, customers would have “hands-on experience with healthy habits‚" and the nutritionist would guide the store’s in-house recipes.

While Red Dome Realty did not confirm how long Vicente’s has committed to staying at Warren Street, Plunkett said the store signed a long-term lease, meaning it is “making a strong commitment to that neighborhood.”

Founded in 1994 by Manuel Vicente, Vicente’s Supermarket specializes “in a delightful array of Brazilian products,” according to its website. The store is now run by Vicente’s two sons, Brian and Jason Barbosa. It has four locations spread across Brockton, New Bedford, and Pawtucket, R.I., each cities with sizable Cape Verdean communities.

Vicente’s Supermarket could introduce a fresh food option in an area with few alternatives. A Price Rite supermarket is a four-minute walk away, and a handful of convenience stores are peppered in the area. A Popeyes and McDonald’s are also in close proximity.

The space is owned by Four16 Warren Street Limited LP, and is valued at roughly $4.5 million, according to city assessment records.

When Walgreens announced its Warren Street location plans in late 2023, it sparked public outrage from elected leaders, clergy, and neighborhood residents alike. Dozens of dissatisfied residents picketed at the drugstore, Boston City Council convened a hearing to assess the closure on the surrounding community, and local congressmembers penned letters to the drugstore giant demanding accountability.

Many charged Walgreens with contributing to local “pharmacy deserts,” parts of Boston where the majority of residents live more than a half-mile from the closest drugstore and don’t have adequate car access.

The neighborhood surrounding the Warren Street store is nearly half Black and one-third Hispanic, according to census data. Residents age 65 and over make up 15 percent of the population. Almost a third of families live below the poverty line.

At least 47 pharmacies closed across Massachusetts in 2024 — the most since 2018, according to a Globe analysis of drugstore registration data. The data also shows that at least two pharmacies have closed since the start of the year, although some announced closures, such as a Walgreens in North Quincy, aren’t included.

With the amount of attention elected officials drew to the Walgreens' closure, Hogan said she wished there would have been more official community engagement on what would replace the drugstore.

These days, Hogan takes the 42 or 44 bus to the Columbus Avenue Walgreens a mile away, or pitches in gas money to have a friend take her. The money and time spent getting her prescriptions makes her long for what she once had a few blocks away.

“We need to find another pharmacy that will open up there,” she said.

Elisa of the Garrison-Trotter Neighborhood Association is relieved that the new shop is “something progressive, [something] other than a shoe store,” referencing the Foot Locker that replaced another Walgreens in nearby Nubian Square.

He said he welcomes a supermarket that would welcome the cultural needs of the surrounding neighborhood, but worries that it might not offer the same medical assistance a standalone drugstore would.

“It’s not a bad idea, but it doesn’t close the gap,” Elisa said.

Elisa said he’d like to see a drugstore open a satellite at 416 Warren St., or have a community health center provide pharmaceutical and other healthcare services.

This story was produced by the Globe’s Money, Power, Inequality team, which covers the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston. You can sign up for the newsletter here.

title: John Wilson left a monumental legacy. The museum world is finally carving out a place for it.
text:
“Friends would ask about my dad,” recalled his daughter Erica Wilson, “and I would say: ‘Well, he has paintings in most of the major museums, some internationally, but nobody knows him.”

That may be about to change: On Saturday, the MFA unveiled “Witnessing Humanity: The Art of John Wilson,” the largest-ever retrospective of his work. The show features more than 100 of Wilson’s creations, including prints, drawings, paintings, and sculpture. It will later transfer to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, which co-organized the exhibition.

Edward Saywell, chair of Prints and Drawings at the MFA, was explicit that “one of the goals of the show” is to help elevate Wilson’s national reputation.

“He’s still not on the national platform he should be,” said Saywell. “That’s despite work of extraordinary skill, importance, and prescience today.”

That’s not to say that Wilson, who died in 2015 at age 92, isn’t revered in his hometown. His large sculpture “Father and Child Reading” stands at Roxbury Community College. The deCordova Sculpture Park and Museum, the Museum of Fine Arts, and Brookline’s Town Hall all display smaller works. Meanwhile, his monumental sculpture “Eternal Presence” keeps vigil over the National Center of Afro-American Artists in Roxbury, where neighbors know it as the “Big Head.”

But compared to his contemporary Black artists, including Jacob Lawrence, Elizabeth Catlett, and Charles White, he never achieved the sort of national profile his supporters believe is his due.

Over the past several years, Saywell and his MFA colleagues have worked with Wilson’s family, his gallery, and the NCAAA to acquire a reservoir of works that spans the full breadth of the artist’s career. The museum now holds roughly 90 objects, an attempt to develop what Saywell called the “collection of record” for Wilson’s work.

“We wanted to commit to somebody we felt was one of the most important Boston artists of the 20th century, somebody we felt was much undervalued nationally,” he said. Saywell added that the Wilson acquisitions are part of a broader effort by the museum to ensure that traditionally underrepresented artists “in the collections have a much more significant place within our acquisition strategies.”

For the artist’s widow, Julie Wilson, the concerted interest in her late husband’s work has been exhilarating.

“He would have been thrilled,” she said, surrounded by Wilson’s work while visiting the museum. “I don’t know how else to put it.”

The couple had three children, whom Wilson often featured in his work. Their eldest daughter, Rebecca, died in 2014. For the surviving two children, Roy and Erica, the experience of their father’s revival has been more complicated.

“It’s about time,” said Roy Wilson, who marveled at what his father would think to see his work on a banner outside the museum.

“I literally cannot imagine how he would respond to that,” he said, adding that he was “a little in awe at the courage” his father showed to remain true to his artistic vision throughout his career. “I also feel grateful that the world is seeing, or potentially seeing, what I see in the work.”

What emerges from “Witnessing Humanity” is an artist who sought to portray Black life in its totality.

“I am a black artist. I am a black person,” Wilson, who admired the work of novelists Ralph Ellison and Richard Wright, told the Globe in 1995. “To me my experience as a black person has given me a special way of looking at the world and a special identity with others who experience some injustices.”

In one early work on paper, “Deliver us from Evil” (1943), Wilson juxtaposes the horrors of Nazi Germany with the racial terror of lynchings in the United States. On the left, Nazi soldiers march near a pile of corpses, while on the right, crowds of people mill around a lynching. At the center of the work is a Black man (almost certainly a self-portrait) who regards the viewer directly as his wife kneels to embrace their child.

But Wilson portrayed Black people as more than victims. Family members and curators said he viewed his art as a necessary corrective to a culture awash in malign caricatures, and he produced a steady stream of portraits — often of himself, family, and friends — that assert their subjects’ essential humanity.

“I’m not simply trying to make a likeness of an individual,” Wilson told the Globe during the 1995 interview, a preview to a joint show with Joseph Norman at the MFA. “I’m trying to use the head as a metaphor of what human beings are about.”

In one early painting, Wilson presents himself in a collared shirt and red sweater vest as he looks warily out at the viewer. In another, “Streetcar Scene” (1945), a muscular Black worker is surrounded by white passengers as he looks out at the viewer, his hands folded atop his lunch pail.

Given Wilson’s lifelong project to present Black life in all its complexity, abstraction was never an option, said Edmund Barry Gaither, director and curator at the NCAAA.

“John felt that there was something that could be said in figurative language that really wasn’t available to the artist in other vocabularies,” he said. “He knew figurative imagery has the capacity to excite empathy.”

Born in Roxbury in 1922, Wilson entered the School of the Museum of Fine Arts on a scholarship in 1939. He was aware from an early age of the negative portrayals of Black people in various media, and that only a handful of artworks at the MFA itself featured Black subjects.

“None of these people looked like me and just by omission the implication was that black people were not capable of being beautiful and true and precious,” he told the Globe.

In 1947, Wilson traveled on an SMFA fellowship to France, where he studied with famed modernist Fernand Léger. He returned two years later and married Julie Wilson, a white woman, in 1950. The couple decamped for Mexico later that year, traveling south in separate vehicles.

The couple stayed in Mexico City for nearly six years, as Wilson absorbed the populist lessons of the Mexican muralists and made prints at the Taller de Gráfica Popular.

After stints teaching and working as an illustrator in Chicago and New York, Wilson returned with his family to Greater Boston in 1964. Settling in Brookline, Wilson would teach at Boston University for the next two decades.

Wilson had brushes with national success throughout his career. Both the Smith College Museum of Art in Northampton and the Museum of Modern Art in New York bought work from him while he was still a student. He repeatedly took top honors at the Atlanta University Art Annuals, a national competition for Black artists, and his work was showcased over the years by numerous galleries and museums, including the Met, the Studio Museum in Harlem, the Philadelphia Museum of Art, among many others.

He also landed some prominent commissions, including a bust for an MLK memorial in Buffalo, N.Y. But his biggest success came in 1985, when he earned a commission to create the King bronze at the US Capitol building.

Delivering it by hand was a moving experience for Wilson, who later recounted the expedition to the Globe.

“Somehow it seemed like the epitome of the seat of power, and it alienated me,” Wilson, who came to sculpture later in his career, told the paper in 1986. “I never felt part of it. But when I delivered the sculpture, that changed. I felt, ‘A piece of me is in that building.’”

Despite these achievements, Wilson remains relatively unknown outside of New England and select art circles. Perhaps that’s because he spent the bulk of his career outside of New York. Perhaps it was due to his race, or his commitment to figurative artwork in an age of abstraction. Wilson was also a devoted father who worked as a teacher for much of his life, meaning his overall output was modest compared to other artists.

Martha Richardson, whose eponymous Back Bay gallery will open a show of Wilson’s self portraits and spot drawings on Feb. 15, said it was likely a combination of these factors.

“John has just remained under the radar,” said Richardson, comparing Wilson to other Black artists from his era. “These are all artists who, crudely speaking, bring much higher prices in the market, but they also have been given much more public notice than John.”

Over the past several years, Richardson, Gaither, and museum curators have worked closely with the family, which has loaned and donated several works to the MFA in advance of the show.

Erica Wilson said her parents’ Brookline home had always overflowed with her father’s creations, describing how he stashed his artworks under beds, stuffed them into closets, and hung them on walls.

“It was the stuff I grew up with, just everywhere,” she said, recalling how she would play in the dining room. “I always thought he was fantastic, but you know it was just like, regular. … That’s what dad does.”

Now, after inspecting the exhibition design and seeing her father’s artwork cataloged and contextualized, Erica said she’s developed a new appreciation for her father, and learned things about herself, as the show has taken shape.

“They send me stuff, and I’m literally crying on my couch because I just cannot believe how beautiful it is,” she said, describing various notes she’s received from curators. “They have just completely changed our world.”

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
LIP CRITIC This New York band’s latest album, “Hex Dealer,” is well-matched to the moment, its yelped vocals and runaway-train doubled drums anchoring electro-punk chaos. They open for the Austin, Texas, thrashers Rickshaw Billie’s Burger Patrol, whose tremendous riffs feel designed to reduce brick walls to rubble. Feb. 7, 7 p.m. Deep Cuts, Medford. 781-219-3815, deepcuts.rocks

RAHEEM DEVAUGHN The soul crooner — who recently began hosting the radio show that, nearly 50 years ago, brought the chilled-out romanticism of Quiet Storm to the masses — sets the mood for Valentine’s week with songs like the slickly besotted “I Don’t Care” and the celebratory “Woman.” Feb. 8, 6 and 9:30 p.m. City Winery Boston. 617-933-8047, citywinery.com/boston

DUA SALEH: I SHOULD CALL THEM WORLD TOUR “I Should Call Them,” the high-concept debut from this pop adventurer, is curious and playful, with their fizzy voice floating above the insistent snares of “Coast” and winding around the serpentine rhythms of “Bo Peep.” Feb. 8, 7 p.m. Brighton Music Hall. 617-779-0140, crossroadspresents.com

MAURA JOHNSTON

SAN MIGUEL FRASER Fresh off being one of the awardees in the first round of Brian O’Donovan Legacy grants, San Miguel Fraser, which brings together Castilian and Celtic in players Maria San Miguel and Galen Fraser (son of famed fiddler Alasdair), make their debut at this Somerville venue. Feb. 12, 7 p.m. $30. The Burren, 247 Elm St., Somerville. 617-776-6896. www.burren.com

AMERICAN AQUARIUM This North Carolina outfit has been making music for 20 years, and they continue to unapologetically hew to their alt-country template — equal parts twang and crunch — most recently on 2024’s “The Fear of Standing Still.” It’s worth making the effort to arrive early enough to see opener William Matheny. Feb. 13, 8 p.m. $18. The Sinclair, 52 Church St., Cambridge. 888-929-7849. www.axs.com

HIGH HORSE/ITAY DAYAN Describing themselves as “four friends, three bows, and one pick,” Boston stringband High Horse meld together bluegrass, old-time, and Celtic in their music. There’ll be klezmer as well Thursday evening, courtesy of Itay Dayan and his quartet. Feb. 13, 7:15 p.m. $15. The Lilypad, 1353 Cambridge St., Cambridge. 617-955-7729. www.lilypadinman.com

STUART MUNRO

HARVEY DIAMOND WITH DOMINIQUE EADE & PHIL GRENADIER Seasoned piano eminence Diamond is joined by virtuosic vocalist Eade and topflight trumpeter Grenadier for an evening of imaginative improvisations on jazz and American Songbook standards. Feb 8, 8 p.m. $20. The New School of Music, 25 Lowell St., Cambridge. music.jondreyer.com

PAUL RISHELL & ANNIE RAINES: The W.C. Handy Award-winning blues duo of finger-style guitar master Rishell and ace harmonica player Raines (both fine singers to boot!) leads a masterclass on 1920s country blues recordings and stories, followed by a concert performance including some of their own stories. Feb. 9, 2 p.m. $25. First Parish in Wayland, 225 Boston Post Road, Wayland. artswayland.com

KENDRICK SCOTT Berklee’s spring Signature Series opens with renowned drummer, composer, and band leader Scott — who’s played and toured with the likes of Herbie Hancock, Charles Lloyd, Terence Blanchard, and The Blue Note All-Stars — performing pieces from across his recording career with an ensemble of seven selected Berklee students. Feb. 13, 7 p.m. $15-$18. Red Room at Cafe 939, 939 Boylston St. college.berklee.edu/events/cafe-939

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA Atlanta Symphony Orchestra music director Nathalie Stutzmann makes her Boston Symphony Orchestra debut with violinist Veronica Eberle soloing in Beethoven’s Violin Concerto, and two early-20th-century orchestral pieces: Ravel’s “Alborada del gracioso” and Stravinsky’s “The Firebird” (Feb. 7 and 8). Next week, 97-year-old Swedish conductor Herbert Blomstedt leads the BSO in symphonies by Schubert and Brahms (Feb. 13-15). Symphony Hall. 617-266-1200, www.bso.org

HANDEL AND HAYDN SOCIETY Valentine’s Day arrives a week early with “Love, Handel,” featuring the Handel and Haydn Orchestra in two passionate cantatas and one concerto grosso, conducted by artistic director Jonathan Cohen with guest soloist soprano Joelle Harvey. Feb. 7, 7:30 p.m.; Feb. 9, 3 p.m. NEC’s Jordan Hall. 617-262-1815, www.handelandhaydn.org

CASTLE OF OUR SKINS The local Black cross-disciplinary arts institution puts a bow on its fourth annual college fellowship program, as Black student musicians from Boston-area music schools such as Longy School of Music, Berklee College of Music, and New England Conservatory collaborate and curate a “Renaissance”-inspired program. Feb. 8, 7 p.m. The BCA Plaza Theater. www.castleskins.org

A.Z. MADONNA

AIN’T NO MO’ Broadway doesn’t always have the last word on the merits of a new play. And a good thing, too. Otherwise, Boston theatergoers might not have a chance to see a wildly inventive work like Jordan E. Cooper’s “Ain’t No Mo.’” But they do, and they should. Under the sure-handed direction of Dawn M. Simmons, “Ain’t No Mo’” delivers a combination of knockabout comedy, stiletto-sharp satire, and scalding fury — the kind of abrupt transitions where your laugh dies in your throat. Through Feb. 8. SpeakEasy Stage Company and the Front Porch Arts Collective. At Roberts Studio Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion, Boston Center for the Arts. 617-933-8600, www.bostontheatrescene.com

THE PIANO LESSON An outstanding production, directed by Christopher V. Edwards, of August Wilson’s inquiry into history, heritage, and the scars left by racism. Siblings Boy Willie (a tour de force by Omar Robinson) and Berniece (an excellent Jade Guerra) are at odds over the family’s antique piano, on which an ancestor had carved the likenesses of enslaved family members. Boy Willie is determined to sell it and use the money to buy the plantation land on which the ancestors had been enslaved. Berniece is implacably opposed, saying “Money can’t buy what that piano cost.” Through Feb. 23. Production by Actors’ Shakespeare Project in partnership with Hibernian Hall. At Hibernian Hall. 617-241-2200, actorsshakespeareproject.org/piano-lesson

THE GROVE The second play in Mfoniso Udofia’s nine-play Ufot Family Cycle, following a Huntington production late last year of “Sojourners,” the cycle’s origin story. Set in 2009, “The Grove” focuses on Adiaha Ufot (Abigail C. Onwunali), a young gay Nigerian-American who aspires to be a writer and faces a stark choice in her personal life: Should she follow her heart or fulfill the desires of her tradition-minded parents, Abasiama (Patrice Johnson Chevannes) and Disciple (Joshua Olumide)? Directed by Awoye Timpo, who helmed “The Bluest Eye” at the Huntington in 2022. Feb. 7-March 9. The Huntington. At Wimberly Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion, Boston Center for the Arts. 617-266-0800, huntingtontheatre.org

SPACE Created by LM Feldman and Larissa Lury, written by Feldman, and directed by Lury, “Space” was inspired by the true story of a group of skilled and experienced female pilots, known as the Mercury 13, who underwent rigorous training in a privately funded research project in the early 1960s to become astronauts in America’s first human spaceflight program. But they were denied the chance to become astronauts because NASA at that time refused to consider women as candidates. Through Feb. 23. Central Square Theater, Cambridge. 617-576-9278 x1, CentralSquareTheater.org

THE ODYSSEY Playwright Kate Hamill is known for her contemporized, woman-centered stage adaptations of 19th-century novels such as Jane Austen’s “Sense and Sensibility” and “Pride and Prejudice.” With “The Odyssey,” Hamill goes back much further in time, to ancient Greece, for a reimagining of Homer’s epic poem about Odysseus (Wayne T. Carr) and his wife, Penelope (Andrus Nichols.) A premiere directed by Shana Cooper. Feb. 9-March 16. American Repertory Theater. At Loeb Drama Center, Cambridge. 617-547-8300, TicketServices@amrep.org

DON AUCOIN

COUNTERPOINT This innovative collaboration between celebrated tap choreographer-dancer Caleb Teicher and pianist-composer Conrad Tao showcases the popular duo’s artistic individuality as well as their creative synergy. Together, they explore the interplay of rhythm, harmony, and theatricality across a variety of musical genres, from J.S. Bach’s “Goldberg Variations” to Tao’s original “More Forever.” Presented by the Celebrity Series of Boston. Feb. 7-8. $44-$98. Boston Arts Academy Theater. www.celebrityseries.org/productions/counterpoint/

TRINITY IRISH DANCE COMPANY Founded in 1990 by choreographer Mark Howard, the progressive Irish-American company has been at the forefront of bringing an inventive contemporary spirit to a traditional art form. The company’s production “JIG,” presented by Global Arts Live, continues the mission of bringing a fresh take to the form’s rhythmic vitality and explosive movement, anchored by a live band. Feb. 8. $42-$65. Berklee Performance Center. www.globalartslive.org

LET’S TALK ABOUT IT This new production, the result of a two-year collaboration between Tess Saoirse Dance Company and Collective Moments Dance Company, focuses on topics that we sometimes fear to address, like mental health issues, neurodiversity, negative self-talk, suicide. Viewers can attend in person or get tickets to watch virtually. Feb. 8. $25-$35. The Dance Complex, Cambridge. (Virtual tickets $15-$20.) www.dancecomplex.org/event/lets-talk-about-it/

KAREN CAMPBELL

WITNESSING HUMANITY: THE ART OF JOHN WILSON Bostonians might be most familiar with Wilson, born and raised in Roxbury, through “Eternal Presence,” the monumental, enigmatic bust that’s stood sentinel-like at the National Center of Afro-American Artists (NCAAA) in Roxbury since 1987. But Wilson, who died in 2015, spent decades before and after crafting socially conscious work around the pervasive issue of racial injustice in America that he experienced all his life. This exhibition, co-organized with New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, is the most substantial display of Wilson’s oeuvre ever assembled, and an opportunity for Boston to reckon with a powerful voice that echoes through generations of its social history. Feb. 8-June 22. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, www.mfa.org

OHAN BREIDING: BELLY OF A GLACIER In 2019, Iceland built a memorial marking the death of the Okjökull glacier, the first of many funereal events held worldwide as ice continues to puddle away amid ongoing climate change. As they melt, history is unleashed: Millennia of geological events preserved in their strata reveal themselves, from natural disaster marked by deposits of volcanic ash all the way up to man-made impacts like industrial residue. Breiding, an Icelander, presents a documentary film and photographic installation that mourns the melting, and explores the faint hope around efforts to preserve the glaciers. Through Dec. 14. Massachusetts Museum of Contemporary Art, 1040 Mass MoCA Way, North Adams. 413-662-2111, massmoca.org

JEAN-MICHEL BASQUIAT AND OUATTARA WATTS: A DISTANT CONVERSATION Basquiat, as most know, was a giant of American art in the 1980s, his superstardom cut short at just 27 when he died of a heroin overdose in 1988. Watts, a New York-based painter, met Basquiat just seven months before he died, but their friendship was quick and deep and forged through their shared passion for painting. In this exhibition, Watts reflects on the creative bond that has transcended death. Through Feb. 23. Currier Museum of Art, 150 Ash St., Manchester, N.H. 603-669-6144, currier.org

MURRAY WHYTE

ALMOST SOMEWHERE: VAGUE RECOLLECTIONS OF A PLACE I MIGHT HAVE BEEN Some people have granular memories of a cherished place. Others recollect more by how they felt when they were there. In this show, 14 artists offer work that blends razor-sharp details with image, tone, and form that defies specificity. In effect, these pieces stir up the idylls and shadows of imagined places, resonant with different meanings for each viewer. Through March 30. Gallery at Atlantic Wharf, 290 Congress St.

CATE McQUAID

BIG BANG STAND-UP The Nova Comedy Collective presents this Boston comedy showcase, with Tooky Kavanagh, Andrew Mayer, Anthony Zonferelli, Kristina Feliciano, and Rob Crean, hosted by David Thomas at The Rooted Café in Somerville’s Arts at the Armory.Feb 8, 8 p.m. $15. Arts at the Armory, 191 Highland Ave, Somerville. www.thenovacomedy.com

JERROD CARMICHAEL The last time Carmichael released a special, it was 2022’s “Rothaniel” on HBO, in which he came out. Last year, he explored his sexuality and relationships in the “Jerrod Carmichael Reality Show.” That puts him in an interesting place to talk about where he is now, as a comedian and as a person, at his Laugh Boston shows.Feb 11-12, 7 p.m. $35. Laugh Boston, 425 Summer St. 617-725-2844, www.laughboston.com

DEMETRIUS FIELDS “I went on a date recently, and within five minutes of the date starting, she was like, ‘How much money do you make?’” says the New York comic. “And I was like, ‘I’m doing pretty good. I make like 75k a year.’ And she looked me in my eyes and told me that that was not enough money. And that was really hard to hear. Especially when you consider the fact that I was already lying.” With Chase Abel and host Trent Wells. Feb. 12, 8 p.m. $25. The Comedy Studio, 5 John F. Kennedy St., Cambridge. www.thecomedystudio.com

NICK A. ZAINO III

WEE WEAR THE CROWNS! Celebrate Black History Month at the Fuller Craft Museum and enjoy a variety of activities and exhibits. The main event is crown making, inspired by Jean-Michel Basquiat, an incredibly prominent and expressive contemporary artist. Families can create their own crowns, decorated with gems, pompoms, and African scrapbook patterns. Feb. 20. 2 p.m.-4 p.m. Free admission, registration required. Fuller Craft Museum. fullercraft.org

LET THE CHILDREN SING! A TRIBUTE TO WILLIAM COOPER NELL Enjoy a performance by the Eastern Mass. Youth Ensemble and City Strings United. The concert will honor abolitionist and author William Cooper Nell, and the historical and contemporary movement of civil rights activism. Programming will include traditional spirituals as well as modern pieces of music to fully embody the breadth of history and the art within it. Feb. 9. 3 p.m.-4:30 p.m. General admission tickets are $7 for children, $15 for adults. Museum of African American History. eventbrite.com

OWL PROWL Take a nature walk at the Broadmoor Wildlife Sanctuary and learn how to find owls hidden in the trees! Guides from the Sanctuary will teach guests how to identify owls by their call and will take guests through the woods to identify the wings, skulls, talons, and feathers. Feb. 15. 4:30 p.m.-6:30 p.m. Tickets are $20-25, registration required. Broadmoor Wildlife Sanctuary, Natick. massaudubon.org

HALEY CLOUGH

title: Josh Kraft is officially running for mayor of Boston. Can he win?
text:
This year’s race for Boston mayor has the makings of an ideological showdown. Josh Kraft, the longtime nonprofit leader and son of billionaire Patriots owner Robert, seems poised to run as a more moderate, business-friendly Democrat against Mayor Michelle Wu, a first-term progressive.

It’s true that Kraft’s policy proposals span the political spectrum. “This campaign is not about ideology, it’s about getting results,” he said while announcing his candidacy in Dorchester yesterday. But his references to his work outside of government and collaboration with business owners, his accusation that Wu is overspending, and his claim that he wants to conserve voters’ “hard-earned tax dollars” were pretty big hints.

Wu, by contrast, won four years ago on a raft of progressive policy goals, including a municipal-level Green New Deal, rent control, free bus service, and raising property taxes on commercial real estate. She’s the daughter of Taiwanese immigrants, a Harvard-educated lawyer, and a protégé of Senator Elizabeth Warren, as well as the first woman and person of color elected to lead the city.

If Kraft does run as a more moderate alternative, his strategy will fit a national pattern. In recent years, moderate Democrats have won high-profile mayoral races in major US cities. Today’s newsletter explains why Kraft may fit that mold — even as his bid to unseat Wu could fall short.

Since 2020, mayoral moderates have been on a winning streak, including in New England. Like Kraft, some come from wealth (Kraft’s father is worth $11.8 billion) or are political outsiders. Consider this list:

In 2021, New Yorkers elected Eric Adams, a former police captain who pledged to tackle crime.

In 2022, Brett Smiley, a relative moderate, became mayor of Providence after vowing to address housing and public safety.

In 2023, a Democrat who favored forcibly removing homeless people and said he wanted to make the City Council more conservative won in Portland, Maine.

Last November, San Franciscans ousted their incumbent mayor, London Breed, in favor of Daniel Lurie, a centrist businessman and heir to a large fortune.

Portland, Oregon also elected a businessman, Keith Wilson, who campaigned against crime and homelessness.

Moderate Democrats have also clinched mayoral races in Houston and Philadelphia, and came close to winning in Los Angeles and Chicago.

The reason for this electoral success is straightforward: The country became more conservative during Joe Biden’s presidency. In last fall’s election, Trump’s support increased from 2020 in almost every Massachusetts community. Nationally, even liberal cities have swung right, sometimes turning against progressive ideas on illegal immigration, homelessness, crime, and education.

Kraft appears to be angling to run on similar issues. In his speech yesterday, he faulted Wu for her handling of housing, public transit, and public education (although neither Kraft nor his children attended Boston Public Schools).

But even if Kraft campaigns in the style of other moderate mayoral candidates, there are a few reasons to think he may struggle to replicate their success.

Ideology. Boston has been an exception to the recent centrist victory parade. It elected Wu in a 28-point landslide in 2021. Like most politicians, Wu has had successes (like lower violent crime rates and the city’s youth summer jobs program) and setbacks (like her property tax plan and BPS). But unlike other liberal mayors, polls taken within the past year suggest she remains relatively popular.

Incumbency. Incumbent mayors are hard to dislodge, particularly in Boston. The last to lose re-election was James Michael Curley in 1949. (The fact that he’d served time in federal prison probably played a role.)

A murky political history. Kraft donated to Wu in 2021 and supported Kamala Harris last November. But he has also voted for Republicans and given money to some who oppose gay marriage and abortion rights. (A spokesperson told the Globe that Kraft, who is Jewish, gave to them “singularly because of their strong public support for Israel.”)

“ Voters know the name Kraft, but they don’t know Josh Kraft,” Mary Anne Marsh, a Democratic strategist, told me. “And they certainly don’t know him as a candidate.”

The national mood. Trump and the Republicans, not Biden and the Democrats, now control Washington. Trump’s 2016 win quickly sparked a backlash, fueling liberal and progressive victories around the country. The chaos of the last two weeks makes another backlash seem likely.

Kraft may also have to navigate his own family’s ties to Trump, a decades-long friend of his father. Kraft, who says he never supported the president, yesterday asked voters “to set aside any ideas they might have about me based on my last name.”

Kraft understands the difficulty of what he’s attempting. “I enter this race as an underdog, and I know this is going to be an uphill fight,” he told supporters. “But I’m excited for the challenge.”

Wu, who is expected to seek re-election, has likewise hinted at how she may run against Kraft, who registered to vote in Boston less than two years ago and recently moved from Chestnut Hill to the North End. “I welcome Josh Kraft to the city,” she said in a statement yesterday.

Read more:

Kraft has led the Boys & Girls Club of Boston and chairs the board of the Urban League of Eastern Massachusetts, a civil rights organization in Roxbury. My colleague Emma Platoff recently profiled him.

Some Black voters have soured on Wu. Kraft hopes to win them over, columnist Shirley Leung explains.

Kraft has embraced some more progressive positions, like calling for rent control and elected members on the school committee. Here’s more from his announcement.

From “strengths most challengers lack” to “maybe?,” Globe Opinion writers debate Kraft’s chances.

Boston and New England

Be prepared: State officials are asking department heads to identify steps to “protect” the state if the Trump administration tries to freeze federal funding again.

Music to somebody’s ears: A 1714 Stradivarius violin that the New England Conservatory is putting up for auction could become most expensive music instrument ever sold. (AP)

Lobsters in trouble: A board that regulates the lobster industry gave in to angry Maine lobstermen and repealed a rule designed to conserve dwindling lobster populations. (Portland Press Herald)

The Nation

FBI lawsuit: Agents who investigated Trump or the Jan. 6 Capitol rioters are suing the Justice Department to stop it from releasing the names of FBI agents involved in the sensitive cases. (CBS News)

Nominees update: The Senate approved Pam Bondi as attorney general. (Politico) The controversial nominations of Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for health secretary and Tulsi Gabbard to lead intelligence will go before the full Senate after Republican holdouts caved to Trump.

Crash recovery: Investigators have retrieved the remains of all 67 victims of the plane crash in D.C. last week. (Fox 5 DC)

Build back better: Maryland officials unveiled plans for a taller, more stable bridge to replace the one that collapsed after a ship struck it last year. (Baltimore Banner)

Missing monarchs: The number of monarch butterflies that spend the winter in the western US has dropped precipitously. Culprits include heat and a lack of milkweed plants. (AP)

A pay raise might work: Faced with a dearth of teachers, the Charlotte-Mecklenburg school district in North Carolina is subsidizing their rent and will build its own housing. (The 19th)

The World

Mass killing: A shooting at an adult education center in Sweden killed at least 11 people, including the gunman, in what officials said was the country’s worst mass shooting. (AP)

Facing his attacker: Author Salman Rushdie will take the witness stand in the trial of the man accused of stabbing him 33 times on stage in upstate New York in 2022. (The Times of London)

📸 Scenes from a life: In her moody series “Pestka,” a Polish photographer captures 11 years in the life that she made with the daughter she raised alone.

😋 Winter Soup Club: Sign up here for the Globe’s cozy newsletter for anyone who loves to make (and eat) soup.

📽️ At the Somerville Theatre: Nearly a century after it premiered, a silent movie with an all-Black cast still exhilarated our critic.

🧙🏽 Holding space: Harvard’s Hasty Pudding club will honor “Wicked” star Cynthia Erivo as its 2025 Woman of the Year today with a parade and a roast.

🏒 Thin ice: With the playoffs looming, Kevin Paul Dupont says it’s time for the Bruins to put up or shut up.

💔 Heartbreak: A teenager’s first can feel enormous. Parents can help.

🧛‍♀️ She’s back: “Buffy the Vampire Slayer” may get a Hulu reboot.

🪦 Epilogue: The Aga Khan became the spiritual leader of the world’s millions of Ismaili Muslims while still a Harvard undergraduate. He died at 88.

title: What’s happening at CATS Academy and Newman School, where they’re suddenly turning out elite basketball prospects?
text:
The court was flush with future Division 1 talent Saturday as the host Griffins (18-3), ranked No. 9 in the national prep coaches poll, captured a 73-61 win over No. 4 Newman School, another program that has emerged from obscurity into a national power.

“I just think there was a need for schools in New England that are willing to offer a year-round, high-level training, basketball-specific space,” said Newman coach Jackson Johnson. “A lot of the prep schools, it’s a little more holistic. Our kids are really trying to chase something specific at a high level.”

Each school’s transformation started from the top down. After coaching the Boston-based Expressions Elite AAU team on the Nike EYBL circuit, Cary Herer took the reins at CATS in 2021, seeking to turn the program into a prep power.

Former longtime Northfield Mount Hermon coach John Carroll had a similar vision for Newman, a small school in Back Bay, when he arrived as an advisor in 2022 and hired Johnson, his former assistant at NMH.

Before he was tapped to build the program, Carroll hadn’t heard of Newman. But he liked the idea of a prep school in downtown Boston.

“Boston is a hotbed for basketball,” Carroll said. “And I thought the combination of that with the social piece, where kids are walking around and they’re seeing themselves all day long because Boston is such a college town.”

When Carroll and Johnson arrived, Newman had a NEPSAC Class D team that was in the Mass Bay Independent League. None of the players from that group made the Cardinals’ new top squad, which is in Class AAA and practices and plays at the New Balance headquarters in Brighton.

Instead, Carroll and Johnson recruited 17 new players, a mix of local kids and prospects from around the country. Among them were 6-foot-6-inch forward Ryan Mela, a former Natick standout who is now a freshman at Providence, and point guard Luka Toews, who transferred from Northfield Mount Hermon and now plays at Boston College.

Those initial recruits trusted the track record of Carroll, who sent more players to the Ivy League than any other coach in the country at NMH. Once high-profile prospects like Mela and Toews made the leap, others followed.

“I had been playing with [Mela] growing up,” said Timmy Bollin, a 6-foot-6-inch wing from Raynham, who played one year at Bridgewater-Raynham and two at St. Sebastian’s before arriving at Newman. “I watched a couple of games and thought it’d be a great fit.”

Like Newman, CATS, now playing in NEPSAC Class AA, quickly attracted talented players, several of whom Herer had coached at Expressions Elite.

One recruit was Harrell, a Providence College-bound senior from Boston who considered brand-name preps like Brewster Academy (N.H.) and Montverde Academy (Fla.) but was intrigued by what CATS could offer.

“The fact of them being so new . . . you can kind of build your own program, in a way,” said Harrell, who is averaging 24 points, 9.7 rebounds, and 10.3 assists. “That’s what they would tell me, and I trusted that.”

Herer’s focus on individual improvement attracted 6-7 Jaylin Williams-Crawford, a defensive stopper who transferred to CATS after leading Charlestown to the MIAA Division 3 title last year, and Leo Curtis, a 7-1 center from Iceland who is committed to Arizona State, among others.

Williams-Crawford primarily played center as the tallest player at Charlestown. CATS has allowed him to play on the wing. Curtis, on the other hand, sought the chance to play other big men his size.

“The pitch has always been development,” said Herer, who led the Atlantic-10 in assists as a senior at UMass for second-year coach John Calipari in 1989-90. “We do not guarantee playing time. We do not guarantee college scholarships. But what we do guarantee is you’re going to get better.”

Such is the aim at both CATS and Newman — to foster development and prepare players for the next level, above all else.

“Obviously, our goal is to always win every game, and we’re going to fight all the time to win games,” Herer said. “But ultimately, the goal is to help these kids attain their goals.”

title: Six juveniles charged in attack of 13-year-old at Forest Hills station
text:
Six juveniles, one as young as 12, and an 18-year-old have been charged in last month’s assault of a 13-year-old boy at the Forest Hills MBTA station, the Suffolk district attorney’s office said Thursday.

The boy was hospitalized and treated for multiple cuts on his forehead and bruising on his body, prosecutors said in a statement.

Lucas Goncalves-Depina, 18, and the six juveniles were detained when they returned to the Forest Hills station, prosecutors said.

The boy told police a girl instigated the Jan. 14 attack when she sat next to him on a bus heading to Forest Hills and said she wanted to fight because he was “spreading rumors” about her, prosecutors said.

The boy said the girl followed him off the bus and punched him in the face multiple times. He got away, but another boy put his arm around his shoulder and walked him toward the bike path, where a group of kids jumped him, punching and kicking him to the ground, authorities said.

Two adults broke up the assault, with one using his bike to separate the attackers. All but one ran away. The juvenile who remained “would not stop kicking the victim,” prosecutors said.

Surveillance video showed eight to 10 juveniles striking the boy, prosecutors said.

Investigators pulled still images from the video and used them to identify the alleged attackers.

Goncalves-Depina has been charged with assault and battery and assault and battery with a deadly weapon (his foot), prosecutors said. At a hearing on Jan. 15 in Boston Municipal Court in West Roxbury, he was released on personal recognizance. His next court date is Feb. 21.

Five teenagers, ages 14 to 16, face the same charges in Dorchester Juvenile Court. They have been arraigned and are scheduled to return to court March 14, prosecutors said.

A 12-year-old has also been charged but has not been arraigned, prosecutors said.

“I thank the Transit police for their quick work in identifying the juveniles involved in this frightening assault, and I’m grateful for the witnesses who assisted this young victim,” District Attorney Kevin Hayden said. “It’s easy for any caring person to imagine the fear this boy must have felt during such a vicious attack.”

title: On being a Pats fan on Super Bowl Sunday
text:
Send questions or suggestions to the Starting Point team at startingpoint@globe.com. If you’d like the newsletter sent to your inbox, sign up here.

What has the incredible run of football excellence by the NFL’s Kansas City Chiefs done to us, as New England Patriots fans?

Bad things. Two weeks ago, we actually rooted for the Buffalo Bills to dethrone the Chiefs in the AFC Championship game.

For anyone who recalls the frequent curb-stompings the pre-Brady/Belichick Patriots suffered at the hands of Jim Kelly, Thurman Thomas, and the Bills of the 1990s, cheering for Buffalo was, well, unnatural, like a weekend getaway to the Island of Doctor Moreau.

But in the interest of defeating Kansas City and protecting New England’s legacy as the greatest football dynasty of the current millennium, we swallowed hard and pulled for a hated division rival (just sports hate, of course. We love Bills fans; there’s nobody with whom we’d rather body slam a flaming table or do some hard liquor shots from the thumbhole of a bowling ball).

And, alas, all we single-day Bills supporters got the full Buffalo fan experience — a brief hope for victory by a superbly talented team that yet somehow managed to fall just short in the most agonizing manner possible. In the AFC title game, it was a fourth down call so close it could have gone either way, so naturally it went against the Bills.

Social media bloomed with AI-generated photos of NFL officials dressed in Chief’s gear, and, yes, it does seem like KC gets the breaks. But remember: During New England’s reign, we made fun of fans in other cities who whined that their defense drew roughing penalties for just thinking unkind thoughts about Tom Brady. Maybe it wasn’t quite that bad, but let’s acknowledge that when the Patriots were good, they had a reputation for calls going their way.

New England won six Super Bowls from 2002 to 2019, but have made the playoffs just twice since then, eliminated in the wild card round both times: In 2020 they lost to Mike Vrabel’s Titans, and in 2022 they were trampled by ... the Bills.

It doesn’t get any easier this weekend for Patriots fans who feel the Chiefs uncomfortably nipping at the heels of New England’s dynasty.

KC is chasing its fourth championship since 2020, and trying to win its third in a row, which is something New England never did. It’s something no NFL team has ever done.

The NFC Champion Philadelphia Eagles are Patriots fans' last hope to stiff-arm the Chiefs’ momentum, at least for this season. It won’t be easy to root for Philly, with memories of Super Bowl LII, in 2018, still fresh in our heads — a 41-33 Eagles win over New England. The Patriots would have won three championships in a row if not for Eagles quarterback Nick Foles swapping brains with Joe Montana and improbably shredding New England all night long.

When President Trump is done declassifying the secret JFK files, how about releasing the contract Foles signed with the Devil to play the most clutch game of his life?

There is nothing wrong with rooting against a team, though I used to think players and coaches from the 1972 Miami Dolphins took it too far. The members of the only undefeated squad in NFL history are known for literally popping champagne every season when the last undefeated team suffers its first loss. They don’t want anyone matching their legacy.

I get it now. I may even ice some bubbly for the Super Bowl this weekend. Whatever the outcome, it will come in handy. As Napoleon supposedly said about champagne, “In victory one deserves it, in defeat one needs it.”

Progress: Two years ago, Patrick Mahomes and Jalen Hurts made headlines as the Super Bowl’s first pair of Black starting quarterbacks. This year, they’re just competitors.
