title: Fletcher ‘Flash’ Wiley, who pushed ‘open doors to rooms we were never in,’ dies at 82
text:
Mr. Wiley, who with his wife, Benaree Pratt Wiley, formed one of Boston’s most important power couples for diversity and activism, died Thursday in hospice care at Spaulding Hospital in Cambridge. He was 82 and had divided his time between Boston and West Tisbury, on Martha’s Vineyard, after having lived for many years in Brookline.

“He was an innovator,” said his longtime friend Duane Jackson, a managing member for Alinea Capital Partners LLC, a real estate investment company.

“Flash was brilliant and committed to what he did and what he believed,” Jackson said. “He was extraordinarily optimistic and always believed there was a light at the end of the tunnel, regardless of the circumstances and conditions.”

Mr. Wiley was a charter participant in the gifted child program in the Indianapolis schools and initially its only Black pupil.

He went on to become the first Black football player recruited to play at the US Air Force Academy, its fifth Black graduate, and the school’s first Black Fulbright scholar.

After launching his legal career in Boston, Mr. Wiley cofounded law firms including Budd, Reilly and Wiley, which became the region’s largest minority-dominant firm and a springboard for the careers of his partners — future US attorney Wayne Budd and future state attorney general Thomas Reilly.

Mr. Wiley often focused on economic development initiatives and had “a nose for finding good deals,” Budd said.

“He did things for clients on a very ethical and upscale basis,” Budd said. “Many others would miss the whole point of the deal, and he would find ways to make it happen in a way that was positive not only for the client, but for our firm as well.”

Mr. Wiley, Budd added, also had a talent for quickly turning cantankerous situations into burgeoning friendships. If someone in a negotiation turned combative, “within a minute or two Flash would have them laughing at him or at themselves,” Budd said.

“A few words from Flash and the next thing you know they had their arms around each other’s shoulders and they were best friends,” he said. “I marveled at that.”

Along with high-level work as a lawyer, Mr. Wiley formerly was director of Boston’s Economic Development Industrial Corp. and had founded and formerly chaired the Governor’s Commission on Minority Business Development.

He also formerly chaired The Dimock Center’s board and helped guide it to become “a premier health center” in Greater Boston, said Dr. Myechia Minter-Jordan, the center’s former president and chief executive who is now chief executive of AARP.

The two had partnered on a capital campaign that revitalized Dimock’s detox center, whose services are “now a beacon of hope to the Roxbury community and beyond,” she said.

In all he did, Minter-Jordan said, Mr. Wiley had an eye on the future and ensured a deepening impact “that will last a lifetime.”

Fletcher Houston Wiley was born in Chicago on Nov. 29, 1942, the son of Mildred Norton Fleming, a beautician, and Fletcher Wiley, a janitor.

Mr. Wiley’s parents divorced. He was an infant when he and his mother moved to Indianapolis to live with his maternal grandmother, Florence Norton, a nurse at Crispus Attucks High School, the city’s all-Black high school.

His grandmother “was pretty much a stickler for the studies,” he said in a video interview for the Air Force Academy. He was chosen for the gifted child program that “opened new vistas for me. It gave you some vision that you had, maybe, some talents that ought to be developed.”

The congressman for his district did not offer Mr. Wiley an appointment to the academy, which instead mailed him information about a prep school. Dejected, he threw it away.

“My grandmother came home, she pulled it out of the trash can, she looked at it,” he recalled. “She said, ‘Let me make a call.’ ”

That led to a year at prep school for potential military academy cadets, where a classmate dubbed him “Flash” for his speed on the football field. Admitted to the Air Force Academy, he played football until an injury ended his football days, and then became the chief cheerleader.

After graduating from the academy and spending his Fulbright year studying in France, he was assigned to a project at the Pentagon when he began dating Benaree Pratt, who is known as Bennie.

They married in 1970 and moved to Greater Boston, where she graduated from Harvard Business School and became the founding chief executive of The Partnership, the Boston nonprofit dedicated to promoting and advancing professionals and executives of color and the places where they work.

The couple was often honored, individually and together for their extensive work professionally and in the community. In 2023, the Boston Bar Foundation gave them its annual Public Service Award “for their many years of selfless leadership, philanthropy, and commitment to community service.”

The Wileys had two children. Their daughter, B.J. Wiley Williams, who lives in Arlington, Va., is founder and chief executive of SoHookd, and their son, Pratt Wiley, lives in Boston and is The Partnership’s current president and chief executive.

Flash Wiley received a master’s degree in public policy from the Harvard Kennedy School and graduated from Harvard Law School. He was a founder of the Black alumni associations for both schools, and a founder of the Massachusetts Black Lawyers Association, which has named a scholarship in his honor.

Advocating for the appointment of Black judges and for inner-city development in his wide-ranging roles, Mr. Wiley also was a pioneering Black entertainment attorney in Boston and a founding member of the Black Entertainment and Sports Lawyers Association.

A lifelong singer, he joked — though often in seriousness — about his hope that The Temptations would someday ask him to join the group.

For his 50th birthday, he produced and was among the performers at a fundraising extravaganza in the Berklee Performance Center that raised tens of thousands of dollars for the Crispus Attucks Children’s Center, which provides early childhood education.

He retired in 2008 as vice president and general counsel of PRWT Services, one of the country’s largest minority-owned businesses.

“Flash was really a Renaissance man and was able to push boundaries and open so many doors for us,” said Carol Fulp, a longtime friend and a former chief executive of The Partnership.

“As African-Americans, we saw him really lead,” said Fulp, who is chief executive of her consulting firm, Fulp Diversity. “We saw him use these incredible skills and navigate and push open doors to rooms we were never in.”

In addition to his wife, son, and daughter, Mr. Wiley leaves his brother Keith of Chicago. A gathering to celebrate his life and work will be announced.

Mr. Wiley’s health had been failing due to multiple medical issues, and his wife held him in his last hours in hospice care.

For all his professional accomplishments, he was always equally known for his love of his family.

“I’ve said this before, that it’s better to be born lucky than good,” Mr. Wiley’s son said.

“And both my sister and I recognize how lucky we were to have grown up and lived in a family where we’ve had a role model of what it means to be a father, a husband, a partner, a fighter — someone who brings joy and humor to everything he does, while at the same time is fiercely committed to helping those who are less fortunate, and helping those who are facing difficulty, and helping those who are in need.”

And that, Pratt said, “is the greatest legacy that any child could ever ask for.”

title: Warming temperatures in Boston appear to have another drawback, study says: More rats
text:
Boston’s human population grew about 9 percent between 2011 and 2020, according to US census data, a bigger increase than the prior decade. Since scientists started keeping records around the turn of the 20th century, the city’s temperature has risen by more than 3 degrees Fahrenheit, giving rats more days each year to forage, have offspring, and become unwelcome and potentially dangerous houseguests, Richardson said.

“People can get sick; there’s a public health component there,” Richardson said. “There are also mental health burdens that come from proximity to rats.”

Biologists looked at 16 cities around the world and based rat population calculations on sightings, complaints, and inspections.

There are far more rats in urban than rural areas, the study said, because the animals rely on human resources. Rat activity is also dependent on temperature, researchers said.

“Warming temperatures resulting from climate change or urban heat islands may extend the seasonal window for aboveground foraging and active breeding period for rats, supporting population growth,” researchers wrote.

The study found “cities that had a greater rise in temperature over time had larger increases in rat sightings.”

City officials have practically no control over the changing climate, Assistant Commissioner of Environmental Services John Ulrich told the Globe, so communities and city government must work harder to mitigate the main driver of rat activity: food waste.

“We don’t get to decide how cold it gets or how much snow falls, but we do have control over sanitation,” Ulrich said Friday.

Warmer temperatures in the past three years allowed Boston’s rat families to get one or two more breeding cycles in, Ulrich said, which “obviously has a huge impact.”

“It feels like the last three winters were pretty warm,” Ulrich said.

“Every year it seems like we see rat populations increasing in the Greater Boston area,” said Joe Dingwall, president of Catseye Pest Control, which opened its office in downtown Boston about 10 years ago.

Dingwall said rats have offspring during most of the year, except the coldest times, when they’re “hunkering down.” But as spring and fall have fewer frigid days, rat populations will grow, he said.

“If we expand those times, their birthing period is longer,” he said, noting Boston’s downtown areas and the dense residential neighborhoods of Dorchester, Roxbury, and Jamaica Plain make the most calls to his pest control service.

This winter’s snow storms and stretches with temperatures dipping below the teens could be working in Boston’s favor by preventing some rats from breeding.

“I’m hoping the recent weather is going to benefit us,” Ulrich said.

Of the 16 cities studied, 11 had rat populations that “significantly increased” during the study timeframe, the report says. Boston ranked ninth out of the 11 cities with more rats, followed by Kansas City and Cincinnati.

There is no definitive way to calculate a city’s total rat population, Richardson said, so the study relied on the best data available: complaints and inspections.

The rudimentary way to count rats across a small geographic area is to assume one rat family’s nest, or burrow, usually has three holes in the ground, Ulrich said. Each rat family has about eight members, he said. So count the number of holes, divide by three and multiply by eight, Ulrich said. However, he noted, a small change in conditions, like food availability, can spur a female rat have more babies quickly.

Researchers don’t use the burrow-counting method because it’s not accurate enough for an entire city, Ulrich said.

All cities need stronger data to calculate their total rat populations, Richardson said, and future warming will make it easier for Boston’s rats to grow their numbers further, creating more problems for residents, he said.

“We’d expect those damages and risks associated with rats to increase,” he said, pointing to the economic costs of rats burrowing under sidewalks and gnawing car wiring.

Boston was one of the denser cities studied, with roughly the same number of people per square kilometer as Amsterdam, which saw a greater increase in rats.

Washington, D.C., had the greatest spike in its rat population, followed San Francisco, Toronto, and New York City.

“That’s definitely not an indictment of the efforts of the rodent control people, it’s an uphill battle,” Richardson said.

New Orleans, Tokyo, and Louisville, Ky., saw significant decreases in rat populations, according to the study. In New Orleans, which had the greatest drop, researchers said monitoring efforts that proactively keep tabs on rats’ whereabout likely contributed to successful mitigation. In Tokyo, social media campaigns highlighting unsanitary conditions and rat sightings played a role, researchers said.

Two cities, Dallas and St. Louis, had rat populations that more or less held steady during the study timeframe.

Food waste is the biggest driver of rat activity, no matter the temperature, Ulrich said, and the city is incorporating multiple ideas into its overall rodent control strategy.

Rats are opportunists, Dingwall said, and will thrive on a neighborhood’s trash and debris if allowed.

Fewer opportunities to burrow into garbage bags means fewer rats around — no matter the temperature or human density, Dingwall, 44, said. Local officials everywhere should focus on hauling trash away as quickly as possible, to reduce the time it’s sitting out available to rats, he said.

“If we see this coming and we stay ahead of it, with good waste practices, it can be controlled to a degree,” he said.

The Boston Rodent Action Plan, which Mayor Michelle Wu launched last year, has started using infrared motion sensors to see where rats are active, Ulrich said. They also partnered with MIT to create an algorithm that predicts where rats will show up. Those tools will help officials measure the effectiveness of waste management strategies, like new rat-proof trash barrels in the North End, Ulrich said.

In 2023, Jamaica Plain residents launched their own rat birth control strategy, working with the nonprofit WISDOM Good Works to set out rat food containing simple contraceptive technology.

Ulrich met with the team in JP and said he hopes the strategy works, although some residents have reported seeing an increase in rat activity, he said.

Citywide, Ulrich’s team is eliminating the use of some common rodenticides, which can lead to “secondary poisoning” in predatory birds, mainly hawks, he said. In the past three years, the city started pumping carbon monoxide into rat nests, which has no risk of secondary effects because it’s a gas, he said.

If future data shows the birth control project is effective in Jamaica Plain, the city is considering rolling it out elsewhere, Ulrich said Friday.

“Fertility, it’s a real challenge with rodents, they’re really incredible breeders, so we’re open to all the tools — especially ones that don’t have a negative impact.”

title: Boston Globe’s Black History Month Film Festival celebrates five years — and ‘multitudes of Black experience’
text:
The late artist Nelson Stevens once said that the murals he painted in Springfield in the 1970s were like “creating stained-glass windows for our community.”

Beauty and excellence are among the themes for the Boston Globe’s fifth annual Black History Month Film Festival, which continues with in-person and virtual events through the end of the month.

On Thursday, the Alamo Drafthouse Cinema hosts a special 25th anniversary screening of Gina Prince-Bythewood’s “Love & Basketball,” the beloved romantic sports drama starring Omar Epps and Sanaa Lathan. Next Wednesday, A Beautiful Resistance Live, a celebration anchored by Globe culture columnist (and the founding curator of the BHM film fest) Jeneé Osterheldt, takes place at the Museum of Science, part of the institution’s yearlong focus on “Being Human.”

With help from partners including Lisa and Alison Simmons at the Roxbury International Film Festival, other festival events include an invitation to stream “Three Kings,” a new documentary about the three Dominican superstars — Pedro Martinez, David Ortiz, and Manny Ramirez — who helped lead the Red Sox to their historic 2004 World Series championship, and a panel discussion on the short documentaries collected in “Legacies: Stories of Black History in the 413.” Those short films about Black Americans in Western Massachusetts include “AfriCOBRA & Nelson Stevens: Art for the People,” which captures a community reclamation project revolving around the work of the late University of Massachusetts Amherst professor, featuring his friend and former colleague, the Roxbury-based multimedia artist Napoleon Jones-Henderson.

“So often we’ve seen Black history as a caveat to American history, when in fact we are very central to that history,” said Erika Slocumb, a history scholar who hosted the “Legacies” shorts block for New England Public Media, with support from Mass Humanities. “It’s important to not only see ourselves on major media platforms, but also on platforms where the history is highlighted very specifically, in an intentional way. It’s an opportunity to witness the multitudes of Black experience.”

title: Robert Terrell, architect of Boston’s key fair housing rule, dies at 73
text:
“I think we have to even go beyond the concept of civil rights and talk about human rights,” he said. “You’ll see the slogan every once in a while, ‘Housing is a basic human right.’ And I think it is. We need to expand that concept into all areas of our economy, because you cannot have a political democracy unless you have economic democracy. The two have to go together.”

Mr. Terrell, a key architect of what city officials have called a first-in-the-nation fair housing amendment to Boston’s zoning codes, was 73 when he died Jan. 29. Diagnosed with cancer in November, he had lived for decades in Roxbury, a neighborhood he loved.

The executive director of Boston’s Office of Fair Housing and Equity, Mr. Terrell had held past roles that included serving as the fair housing, equity, and inclusion officer in the Boston Housing Authority’s Office of Civil Rights, and with several neighborhood civic organizations.

He spoke of his fair housing work “as a sacred trust,” said Boston Mayor Michelle Wu.

“I think he embodied that — a complete commitment to the community and making sure our city could be a home for everyone,” she said in an interview.

He was such a committed activist that many elected officials met him at community meetings long before they were first elected. Mr. Terrell formerly was a leader or board member of organizations including the Madison Park Development Corp., the Roxbury Neighborhood Council, and the Washington Street Corridor Coalition.

The Boston Globe endorsed his candidacy when he sought the District 7 City Council seat in 1997, though his campaign fell short on Election Day.

His background then included serving as an aide to a city councilor. He also held leadership roles with Boston’s branch of the NAACP.

“There wasn’t a room that involved the fair housing movement and civil rights, but also concrete planning and policy, that Bob wasn’t a part of,” said state Senator Lydia Edwards, an East Boston Democrat and former city councilor who previously directed the city mayor’s Office of Housing Stability.

“If I had an idea about housing or I was excited about something in housing, I wanted to talk with Bob,” said Edwards, the Senate chair of the Legislature’s Joint Committee on Housing.

In past years, Mr. Terrell served on the Policy Leadership Council of the Citizens’ Housing and Planning Association, a Boston nonprofit. He also sat on the planning committee for the annual Fair Housing and Civil Rights Conference in Massachusetts.

Those experiences were part of what led to his key role in crafting the historic fair housing measure. The City Council voted to approve it in December 2020 and add it to the zoning code.

“Affirmatively Furthering Fair Housing,” as the measure was known, was inspired by an Obama-era federal rule that had been designed to strengthen the 1968 Fair Housing Act.

Boston’s fair housing measure was created to step beyond simply working to prevent housing discrimination. It requires developers to study existing housing discrimination patterns and determine how they can “do more to fight displacement and create housing for all,” Martin J. Walsh, who was then Boston’s mayor, said in a statement when it was passed.

Two years later, when Mr. Terrell was appointed to direct the city’s Office of Fair Housing and Equity, he promised to be vigilant about enforcement and to reach out to residents who might not realize they have recourse if they have been discriminated against.

“All too often, when people file a fair housing complaint, there’s another six or seven people who have not,” Mr. Terrell told The Tufts Daily, the student newspaper at Tufts University, where he was a part-time lecturer in the Department of Urban and Environmental Policy and Planning.

“They don’t do so either because they fear retaliation, or they don’t have the time, or they are just disgusted, or they don’t know their rights under the law,” he said in that early 2023 interview, adding that “we want to spread the word as much as possible.”

Robert L. Terrell III was born on June 12, 1951, in the South End, the only child of Robert II, a Merchant Marine, and Mildred Samuels Terrell, a community activist in the South End and Roxbury.

Mr. Terrell drew inspiration from his mother’s civic involvement, said Roxanne Hoke-Chandler of Boston, whom Mr. Terrell considered a sister. Activism was “in his blood, she said. She was part of a family beyond his biological relatives that he embraced as his own in the decades after his youth.

She survives him, as does her mother, Roberta Hoke of Boston, and Roxanne’s sister, the Rev. Robyn Franklin-Vaughn of Bowie, Md., both of whom Mr. Terrell also considered family in later years.

Mr. Terrell graduated from Boston Latin School and received a bachelor’s degree in government and sociology from Bowdoin College in Maine. Years later, he graduated from Tufts with a master’s in public policy.

Dion Irish, chief of operations in Boston city government, said Mr. Terrell was his mentor for many years and “took me under his wing and really taught me a lot.”

“I can’t remember Bob ever being angry or ever raising his voice,” Irish said. “He was soft-spoken, but you could still feel his passion and perseverance with the work he was trying to accomplish.”

Mr. Terrell was a calming presence, Wu said, even at the most heated neighborhood meetings.

“His smile always made everyone feel at ease — that we were doing something important, but that we were still all on the same team, moving the city forward,” she said.

His death leaves an absence that will be impossible to fill, Edwards said.

“I think about the wealth of institutional knowledge we don’t have now because Bob is gone, and I’m very sad about that,” she said.

“So much of that knowledge is because of the fights he took on in a Boston that I never knew,” Edwards added. “The Boston I know today is better because Bob was here. It’s better for women, it’s better for people of color, it’s better for poor people, and that’s the legacy people should think about. I didn’t have to fight anywhere near as hard as Bob did.”

A celebration of Mr. Terrell’s life will be held at 11 a.m. Thursday in the Church of St. Augustine and St. Martin in Roxbury. The church plans to livestream the service.

At the end of Mr. Terrell’s life, he asked Hoke-Chandler to contact other activists to ensure they would continue their work.

“He was telling me who to call and who to reach out to and saying, ‘You tell everybody I have faith and trust in them to carry on,’” she said. “He said, ‘I’m not afraid and I have faith it will all continue.’ "

title: Beyond bargains: The social impact of free-stuff groups
text:
For Allende, and other members of groups with names like “Nothing for Sale” and “Buy Nothing,” it’s a point of pride to furnish entire homes — or at least rooms — with goods found for free online. Devotees of the groups say they’re bringing home high quality goods, saving useful items from landfills, and forging meaningful connections with neighbors while they’re at it.

It’s also a great way for home sellers to purge belongings they don’t want lugged into moving vans.

Allende said that when she moved out of her New Jersey apartment to attend graduate school in the Boston area, her mother told what she’d left on the street just sat there. That felt wasteful, said Allende, who joined the Everything is Free Medford Facebook group as a way to reduce duplicate items among her roommates. But when it was time to plan what she called a “microwedding” at Hammond Castle in Gloucester, her decor budget quickly added up. One important item would have cost $300 purchased new — and her total decor budget was $500. So, Allende took to the group and collected wedding tablecloths, an ornate gold mirror, and the dress itself, which she picked up from a neighbor at a local MBTA station.

Allende repurposed many of the items into her home decor after the wedding, but she relisted others back into the group. From time to time, she sees them reappear as posts, continuing their journey upstream to their next, though maybe not final, owner.

For Ginnette Powell of Dorchester, exchanging free home goods was a response to homebound pandemic boredom.

“All we could do was sit around, and then we started to Marie Kondo … our places,” she said. She picked up a futon and jettisoned other belongings.

Instead of spending money on new goods, Powell has reallocated that budget for movers, using an app called Dolly. The futon, worth $500 at retail price, was free, and moving cost $250 from West Roxbury to Dorchester. Allende noted that one of her favorite acquisitions, a book shelving unit, would retail at $400 as sold new.

For the uninitiated, it’s important to pay attention to group and site rules across such Facebook groups, as well as the site Freecycle, which can be specific. Some offer a range of options for choosing a taker, such as “first come, first served,” or random lottery selection, and posts should follow designated formatting rules. (The Buy Nothing Boston Facebook group blocked this journalist after I tried to post a message soliciting member experiences, and Freecycle.org also refused such a post because, said moderators, it did not explicitly further the group’s mission of keeping items out of landfills.)

Altruistic reasons appeal to members, too, who see the groups as potential platforms for mutual aid in their neighborhoods. For instance, Powell said she was able to team up with neighbors to match Hurricane Maria evacuees from Puerto Rico with home furnishings. And during in-person pickups, conversations have offered clues into new ways to help. Powell helps rescue cats, and a neighbor at another pickup offered cat-care supplies. And she sometimes acts as a matchmaker of the potentially useful, obtaining items that might be helpful to others in the future. An aquarium setup came in handy in such a way recently, as did a microscope.

“You’re keeping [items] out of the landfill, and you might even be making connections with people,” Powell said.

In Roslindale, Anne Hernandez has successfully furnished her sunny, art- and plant-filled home with items she said speak to her soul — found mostly on Craigslist and Facebook.

“I am intentional about how I decorate my home, which is my place of peace and calm in such a chaotic world,” she said.

“The thought that all the items my neighbors have gifted me would have been trashed otherwise is sad,” Hernandez continued. “I love the community that is built through exchanging possessions with others. We live in a materialist world, so I appreciate that we can let go of things so that others can enjoy them.“

Stepping outside mainstream retail commerce is a money-saving effort, but in more ways than one, some see it as a radical act. Supporting free-stuff groups reduces waste and demand for item production, but the value of strengthening neighborly ties may outweigh that of anything being traded. Members argue that there is, if you know where to look, enough to go around — including good will.

Allende said some of her pickups turned into long visits, including mothers reminiscing with her about their children’s weddings, and another who surprised her with celebratory champagne.

Laurel Oberstadt-Petrik, a Brighton-based graduate student, said they have sourced hundreds worth in goods from the group, as well as used it to host an in-person clothing swap. But they said the social ties matter the most in the exchange. The groups can double as places to share news of potlucks and other community events, especially valuable in reaching a large and diverse membership.

“A group like this doesn’t necessarily exist to further political connections,” said Oberstadt-Petrik, “but it does act as infrastructure that already exists, in a system that already exists, that can be reformed or changed or shifted or utilized for political action.”

title: Has John Wilson’s time arrived? He’s been here all along.
text:
Wilson died in 2015, having spent much of his career teaching drawing at Boston University with relatively little interest from major museums like the MFA. Displaying more than 100 works from the 1940s onward, the exhibition embraces the whole of Wilson’s artistic evolution and the force of his fiery, justice-driven worldview. In his rough gestural swipes of charcoal and oil stick, charged with dynamic fury, you can feel him in the room with you, spectral, urgent, defiant. I don’t hesitate to call the show a landmark; it pays respect, definitively, to an underacknowledged master of his form, and to his irrepressible devotion to justice. In its intense, often dark beauty, it leaves no question about Wilson’s consequence — only about how long it took to get here.

As a first take on Wilson’s broader legacy, it will no doubt be an introduction for many. The exhibition’s conventional timeline reveals both his consistent devotion to his priorities and his profound creative evolution.

Wilson’s ability was clear even in high school; his teachers at an after-school drawing program in Roxbury encouraged him to apply to the School of the Museum of Fine Arts and helped get him admitted in 1939. A suddenly wider world helped Wilson see how art could advocate for social change; it also made him viscerally aware of the inhumanity with which Black subjects were portrayed.

The show begins with works made mostly in the 1940s — his first attempts to convey the dual injustice of ugly representations and of simply being that seethed within him. “My Brother,” 1942, one of the earliest pieces here, is elegant redress: an image of Frederick, his younger sibling, serene and contemplative. As affectionate and ennobling a portrait as you’ll find, Wilson imagined it more broadly as “a portrait of my neighborhood,” imbued with the frank dignity so many portrayals denied.

Wilson’s explorations were rarely so subtle, often addressing discrimination in blunt fashion: In “Breadwinner,” 1943, a Black man slumps on a park bench like a deflated balloon, a scene of inherent exhaustion and constant struggle. “Black Despair,” 1945, a coda to “My Brother,” is a withering portrayal of Frederick, head buried in forearms, crumpled by his time serving in the army in the Jim Crow South.

Wilson’s obvious talents meant opportunities; in 1947, after graduating from Tufts University, a fellowship from the SMFA funded further studies in Paris, where he worked with the proto-Cubist Fernand Léger. After the war, Léger had abandoned the lofty notions of quasi-abstraction and embraced depictions of working class Parisians. Wilson found affinity with Léger’s social justice priorities, and inspiration in his practiced hand. A lovely little collection of works from that time notes the influence: With their broad swipes of color and rough-hewn semi-cubist figures, they’re almost what you’d imagine an AI image engine would produce if you asked it to fuse Léger and Wilson together.

What Wilson also took from his time in Paris was an aching sense of absence; vast ethnographic collections at museums in the French capitol introduced him to African art, a void in America of which he became keenly aware. With its priority on European art, America was missing other elements he had come to value, too; in 1950, supported by another fellowship, he debarked for Mexico City, where artists like Jose Clemente Orozco and Diego Rivera had forged a socialist-realist movement rooted in justice for common folk.

Wilson had reckoned with injustice all his life. Growing up in Roxbury, his father, a member of the Universal Negro Improvement Association, would share with him progressive Black newspapers filled with images of racial terror — lynchings of Black people in the South, and the more casual brutalities of segregation.

He wanted to bring racial terror to light at the same grand scale that Orozco and Rivera had made famous with their politically driven murals all over the city. Driving from Boston to Mexico through the segregated South, he and his wife, Julia, who was white, traveled in separate cars. The Ku Klux Klan, reinvigorated by the civil rights movement, made their marriage a risk that Wilson could be lynched himself.

The product of that journey is Wilson at his most explicit, enraged, and harrowing: “The Incident,” he called it, a 10-foot-high mural of hooded Klansmen armed with whips and rifles dragging an unconscious Black man to fiery gallows behind them. The violence is seen from inside a home, where a Black woman shields an infant from the atrocity just outside, while her husband clutches a rifle. A small study for the mural is here, seething in vibrant color; in a 1952 photo, Wilson, glaring defiantly, poses with the mural itself — an artist arrived at a purpose that would define his life.

He would depart stylistically from “The Incident,” a clear homage to Orozco, his idol. Drawing became the medium he mastered, often in charcoal and oil stick, coarse and intuitive media that matched the gravitas of his intent. “The Incident” occupies a slim gallery that serves almost as a passageway to the eruption that lies beyond it. Into the 1960s and ‘70s, Wilson found his footing as a champion of civil rights; his every picture boils with resolve, decrying injustice while celebrating defiance.

In “The Oracle,” 1966, a figure arches upward against bands of cascading crimson, arms flung overhead in a stance of defiant power; in “Oracle,” 1965, its precedent, Wilson zooms in, anchoring the figure in thick strokes of gray-black rising up from a crowd. Heavy with gesture, Wilson’s treatment of such scenes matches the weight of their moment: From the shadow of oppression, an uprising of brash, exuberant dissent.

Wilson could also be tender; a 1969 lovely oil stick drawing of Becky, his daughter, is soft and adoring, but it still simmers with ambiguity, as though threat was ever a breath away. I might read it that way because nearby hang four studies for his 1990 “Father and Child Reading” bronze at Roxbury Community College. They are a masterclass in drawing: Dark figures shrouded in with black oil stick read as bundles of sinew and flesh; in two, arms are bound tight around a tiny figure held close to the chest. They are nothing like the sculpture, a loving tribute Wilson made to his father. No, the drawings are urgent, wary; in Wilson’s world, love meant protection. They were one and the same.

A final gallery nods to perhaps Wilson’s most-seen work, his bust of Martin Luther King Jr. commissioned for the Capitol Rotunda in Washington, D.C., in 1986. A maquette of it is here, with a like-size version of “Eternal Presence,” which the MFA acquired recently and showed in 2022.

Here, the irony is all but spent. The show has established what the viewing public hardly knew but needed to see: that Wilson, primarily known for stoic bronze, drew with a ferocity like no other and captured an America too often left unseen. “Eternal Presence” speaks to that very thing: The piece was “my answer to all the omissions, the things I did not see at the Boston Museum of Fine Arts,” Wilson said in a 1995 interview. “I wanted to make a Black image you could not ignore.”

I thought about those words as I watched a video the MFA made for the occasion, of the annual Roxbury ritual of washing down “Big Head” at summer’s end. Seeing families from the neighborhood playfully sudsing up its bronze hide and hosing it down, I thought of legacy — real legacy, intractable and meaningful and without end.

Of course, museum shows matter. This one, with a later date at the Metropolitan Museum in New York, finally establishes Wilson in a canon, where he rightly belongs. But his legacy was cemented decades before. The community he cared for most has felt the dignity and grace of his work for generations; it’s in their DNA. Wilson didn’t live to see this exhibition. But he didn’t need to, to know he mattered.

WITNESSING HUMANITY: THE ART OF JOHN WILSON

Through June 22. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, www.mfa.org

title: Boston issues 37 new liquor licenses for restaurants and community groups from Mattapan to East Boston
text:
Flush with new liquor licenses to give out, the Boston Licensing Board has issued alcohol permits to 37 restaurants and community organizations across the city from Mattapan to East Boston, the bulk of them approved on Thursday.

Typically, the board has few available licenses, but state legislation passed last September created 225 new ones for Boston, perhaps the biggest expansion of alcoholic permits since the end of Prohibition. All these licenses are free, and the board has been inundated with applications.

Most of the new licenses are restricted to 13 ZIP codes in parts of the city that could benefit from the economic boost of sit-down restaurants — including Mattapan, Roxbury, and Hyde Park. These so-called restricted licenses cannot be bought or sold and must be returned to the city when no longer needed.

Among those getting approvals on Thursday include Blue Mountain Jamaican Restaurant in Mattapan, Caffe Dello Sport Eastie in East Boston, La Parada Dominican Kitchen in Roxbury, and community organizations The Huntington Theatre and Franklin Park Zoo. Their applications are being forwarded to the state Alcoholic Beverages Control Commission for final approval before they can begin serving alcohol.

The Boston licensing board decided to postpone voting on whether to award 12 unrestricted licenses the new law created. These licenses can be used anywhere in the city and are far more valuable than neighborhood-based licenses, with a price that can reach $600,000 on the secondary market because they are so rare and can even be used as collateral on loans.

At Thursday’s hearing, licensing board chair Kathleen Joyce said the board wanted to delay voting on the unrestricted licenses to allow more establishments to apply and to avoid a “first come, first served” process. Fourteen applicants are vying for unrestricted licenses.

“I just don’t think it should be first come, first served. I don’t think that’s the right way to make this decision,” Joyce said. “I think we will be seeing a lot of other great applications that would qualify for these 12 as well. So I’d like to hit pause and wait to see what those other applications look like before we make final decisions on these 12 unrestricted licenses.”

The board has been reviewing applications in batches, setting the first deadline in December. The next deadline for applications is May 23.

The new licenses are expected to ease a shortage that has been growing for two decades since Boston hit its state-imposed cap on liquor licenses. Alcohol is a critical profit center for the low-margin restaurant business.

Restaurateurs have had to spend hundreds of thousands of dollars to buy a license on the secondary market or leave Boston to open a restaurant. The scarcity has created a culture of haves and have-nots, favoring deep-pocketed chains and restaurant owners in the Back Bay and the Seaport District and pricing out mom-and-pop restaurants in far-flung neighborhoods.

title: BPDA board OKs new plan for Roslindale Square
text:
The Boston Planning and Development Agency board on Thursday approved five projects with 226 residential units in Dorchester, Downtown, East Boston, Fenway, and Roxbury, along with a plan that aims to bring additional housing and retail to Roslindale Square.

The Roslindale Squares + Streets plan outlines opportunities for multistory buildings, development at intersections, and outdoor amenity space, and recommends updated zoning to allow for mixed-use and apartment projects in and around Roslindale Square.

BPDA board member Matt O’Malley recalled the late Mayor Thomas Menino as encouraging more restaurants in Roslindale Square during his time as a District 5 City Councilor.

“My word, how Roslindale Square has changed in that time — for the better,” said O’Malley, himself a former City Council member.

Projects approved by the BPDA board on Thursday include 63-unit all-affordable project proposed by the Madison Park Development Corp. on vacant parcels in Roxbury that had formerly been targeted by urban renewal; a 22-unit, seven-story project at 2-8 Bowdoin St. in Dorchester; a 20-unit project at 141 Addison St. in East Boston; and an 85-unit, six-story residential building at what’s now a two-story parking garage on the border of Boston and Brookline at 142-146 St. Mary’s St. That project will create a pedestrian pathway to the Fenway MBTA Green Line station.

The board also approved a change to 69-81 Kilmarnock St. in the Fenway from 77 units to 89, including 44 apartments and another 45 units slated to be managed by Boston Children’s Hospital for patient and family housing.

Cruz Development Corp. won approval for a notice of project change for the second phase of its mixed-use residential and commercial project off Warren Street in Roxbury. The project’s first phase, a 55-unit residential building with office space, is named for Roxbury native, state representative and civil rights leader Michael E. Haynes and now serves as the Cruz Cos. headquarters. The approved second phase will be a 52-unit all-affordable apartment building with ground-floor commercial space at 1 Waverly St.

“We try to leave the neighborhoods more empowered than we found them,” said Daniel Cruz, Jr., senior vice president of Cruz Development Corp. “Affordable housing is great. We do a lot of it. But if you don’t empower the neighborhoods and leave them better than you find them, you’re just recycling the status quo.”

BPDA board member Kate Bennett commended Cruz’s commitment to minority and women-owned business participation in their projects, which “set a standard that more and more developers need to be able to achieve.”

The BPDA board also approved a 36-unit office-to-residential conversion at 4 Liberty Square, a seven-story office building at Batterymarch and Water streets in downtown Boston. Developer Greg McCarthy intends to keep the current ground-floor restaurant, the city said.

title: Man pleads not guilty in hit-and-run crash that killed Fisher College student
text:
A man accused in a hit-and-run crash that killed a 20-year-old woman in Roxbury last month pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and other charges at his arraignment Thursday and was held on bail, according to court records.

Christopher Baker, 36, is also facing charges of motor vehicle homicide, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, leaving the scene of a crash that caused personal injury and death, and crosswalk violation, among others.

Police identified the woman who was killed as Taylor Wilkinson. Her sister, 23, suffered minor injuries in the crash, police said.

Baker, who is homeless, was committed to the Suffolk County Jail in lieu of posting $150,000 bail, according to court records.

He was arrested Wednesday after police obtained a warrant charging him in the crash, which occurred Jan. 18 on a busy stretch of Washington Street in the Roxbury area, according to police.

The two women were crossing the road in the area of 1829 Washington St. just before 8:30 p.m. when they were hit by a vehicle police described as a small Mercedes SUV.

An online fundraiser to help Wilkinson’s family had raised more than $23,500 as of Thursday afternoon. On the fundraising page, Wilkinson’s family described her as a “a radiant light in this world.”

“Taylor was more than a daughter, a sister, and a friend—she was a force of nature,” her family wrote. “She lit up every room she entered with her infectious laughter and boundless energy. Whether she was singing her heart out at karaoke or dancing like no one was watching, Taylor’s joy was contagious. A cheerleader for fun and for life itself, she lifted everyone around her with her love and unwavering positivity.”

Wilkinson was a sophomore at Fisher College, where she studied management with a concentration in fashion merchandising. The college’s president, Steve Rich, issued a statement last month mourning Wilkinson’s death, calling her “one of our cherished students.”

“Our hearts go out to her family, friends, and all who had the privilege of knowing and loving her,” Rich wrote.

Wilkinson graduated from the Edward M. Kennedy Academy for Health Careers in June 2023, according to Fisher’s statement.

Baker is due back in court on March 12. His lawyer could not immediately be reached for comment.

Material from previous Globe coverage was used in this report.

title: Boston is set to host the first weeklong Big Queer Food Fest. James Beard winner Karen Akunowicz shares what to expect.
text:
“We need to make sure to continue to hold and create space, and to keep speaking out and showing up and being our loud and vibrant selves, not just for each other but for an entire generation of folks who are coming up,” Akunowicz says.

Akunowicz, 46, and I chatted about the festival, reflected on Boston’s evolution as a food city, discussed her favorite hangout near her home in West Roxbury, and reminisced about our favorite college-era tacos.

Why Boston?

[Founders] David Lewis and Chad Hahne started this as a series of pop-ups across the country, with queer chefs coming together in a very grassroots kind of way, as queer movements often do.

Last year, it was so well-received. We did the event at High Street Place. It sold out so quickly, and it was packed. I’d like to say that this a testament to the folks who live in the city and the folks who work in the city — not only queer folks, but the community that we have here.

I think that, in talking to the City of Boston and Meet Boston about coming back, the city wholeheartedly came in 100 percent. BAGLY is part of it as well, as well as our national sponsor, which is GLAAD. I think that it just goes to show this is not just a welcoming city but a city that’s all in for its LGBTQIA community.

This year’s event is bigger and longer: What’s the plan?

It isn’t just one panel featuring LGBTQIA voices. It’s not a gathering on the sidelines. It’s an entire, four-day festival that’s dedicated to showcasing, amplifying, and uplifting queer voices. There are dinners, discussions, cooking demos, and immersive experiences that are going to highlight the depth and diversity of queer contributions to the culinary world. I think it’s about creating space for our stories to be front and center, not just an afterthought.

The culmination of the event is a huge dine-around at High Street Place. Leading up to that, we’re hosting a dinner with visiting guest chefs at Bar Volpe. There are other dinners, experiences, and panels. If you can’t join on the last day for the grand tasting, there are so many other events that you can come out and support.

Can we talk a bit about your evolution in Boston as a queer chef? What was your journey like?

I’ve been working in restaurants since I was 17 years old, which is 30 years now. I’ve been working in Boston for 20-plus years. When I was coming up, whether I was working front of the house or when I started cooking, I didn’t see folks like me in leadership roles.

Restaurants, historically, have been places where those of us who have felt othered can find a home. It’s a place where we can feel like we fit, and there’s a lot of acceptance. However, we have not necessarily seen ownership and leadership by women, queer folks, or people of color in the past.

Little by little, that’s changing. The industry has historically been tough, hierarchical, male-dominated. Being a queer woman in the kitchen meant navigating spaces that weren’t necessarily built for me or built with me in mind.

Over time, you find your people. You find mentors, friends, and colleagues to support you, lift you up, and then you work to turn around and do the same for others. Change doesn’t come about quickly, and it often doesn’t come in leaps and bounds. It’s about making the small changes, walking forward, crawling forward, continuing to push forward, even when there are setbacks, even when it’s two steps forward and one step back.

What’s the difference between when you started out versus now? How has Boston changed culturally and culinarily?

I think Boston is an amazing, vibrant food city: One of the things I always say is that Boston is a city of neighborhoods, and I think that you need to dive into different neighborhoods to experience all of the different restaurants, food, and culture that the city has to offer.

I remember somebody writing to me and saying — this was a few years ago — that they can’t believe they could walk down West Broadway in South Boston and see Fox & the Knife with LGBTQIA flags in the window, celebrating pride. They said, “I would have never seen this in South Boston 10 years ago.” The fact that our city is changing in this way is heartening and important.

I think we’ve been a bit overlooked in the past. I think that little by little, nationally, we have begun to see more light shining on our food scene. Folks who wouldn’t necessarily have been able to open restaurants are opening restaurants that are amazing and are changing the food scene.

Really? Because I hear it from others: ‘It’s still so hard; the rents are too high.’

All of those things remain true. The rent is incredibly high. It’s a really high threshold to open a restaurant. … It’s an astronomical fee to get a liquor license to open a restaurant. It is not the easiest, but I think that there are folks who are continuously chipping away at it. Look at restaurants like Comfort Kitchen in Dorchester that have received national acclaim.

What was the turning point, and what has to happen to keep this momentum going?

I think what’s happening is that we’re releasing more affordable liquor licenses in different communities. I feel like I just read something that said there are more liquor licenses that have just been issued so parts of the city can continue to grow and become vibrant. I think restaurants are the fabric of our community, right? [We need to] create opportunities for more restaurants across the city and not just in places like the Seaport.

What’s new and amazing? Or where would you like to eat if you could?

I think that Jamie Bissonnette’s new restaurant, Somaek, is an amazing addition to our culinary scene, as well as his Temple Records. I go to a lot of the same places that I’ve gone to for years. I think that one of the things that’s also important is that it’s not about the newest, brightest, and shiniest thing. It’s restaurants like Sarma that have been open for over a decade. They opened in a neighborhood [in Somerville] where there wasn’t much of anything else.

It’s [those] restaurants that I’m also so proud of and that I continue to go back to. We stand on the shoulders of folks like that.

What drew you to Boston?

I’m originally from New Jersey. I did my undergrad in social work at UMass Amherst. The summer before I graduated, I worked as an intern at the State House for Representative Ellen Story of Amherst. I lived here that summer, and I just became enamored with it. I loved how walkable the city was. I didn’t have a car. I took public transportation, and I walked everywhere.

I continue to live in Boston proper. I raise my family here. I live in West Roxbury, and then my restaurants are in South Boston as well as at Logan Airport. I’ve lived in Jamaica Plain, Allston, Brighton, Brookline, Bay Village, and Roslindale, all over 20 years.

I was at Mount Holyoke when you were in Amherst, and I really miss Cha Cha Cha in Northampton.

It was so good! And then it turned into a Bueno Y Sano — I loved the original Bueno Y Sano, the tiny little one in Amherst Center. I still remember my order. I used to get a chicken taco with yogurt and black beans.

I always got the yogurt, never the sour cream.

Always the yogurt.

Last but not least: What’s your neighborhood hangout?

Porter Cafe in West Roxbury. I’ve known the guys who own it forever. It’s a great little bar. After having my daughter, I’m like: ‘OK, can we go to a restaurant? Can we take this tiny baby to a restaurant that’s not Fox & the Knife?’ Everyone was so kind. We walk there from our house. Everyone’s always welcoming and inviting. I don’t want to say it’s a dive bar, but it’s a hole in the wall spot that has been there for a long time, and it’s one of those places that make the neighborhood great.

Interview has been edited and condensed.

title: With federal funding in limbo, Salem State grapples with how to best serve its Latino students
text:
The designation opens universities to receive federal funding that aims to help students of color achieve the same outcomes as their whiter and more well-to-do peers. That money can prove essential for the survival of minority-serving institutions themselves, many of which are public schools already grappling with underfunded budgets. MSIs typically rely on federal funding to support as much as a quarter of their total revenue, said Jessica Colorado, a policy analyst at the State Higher Education Executive Officers Association, and per-student federal funding for Hispanic-serving institutions is 25 percent less than other degree-granting schools.

Since 2020, Department of Education records show MSI funding has supported “culturally responsive programming” at Bunker Hill Community College, science education for Latino students at Springfield Tech, and $1 million in funding over four years for Roxbury Community College, the state’s only predominantly Black institution.

Now that money is under threat. Even as Salem State is looking to finalize its HSI designation, the Trump administration is eliminating benefits for minority-serving institutions through executive order, part of a broader pullback of diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives in higher education.

Peter Wood, who heads the right-leaning National Association of Scholars, said that while historically Black institutions and the tribal colleges “long predate the rise of DEI” and should have their funding maintained, Hispanic-serving institutions fall into a newer category.

“You just have to be an institution that gets really aggressive on its admission of contemporary Hispanic students, so it’s much more DEI-like than historically rooted,” Wood said.

More broadly, White House threats to federal funding also jeopardize longstanding academic programs and financial aid Salem State already offers its roughly 6,000 students. To university president John Keenan, the federal funding freeze announced, and then paused, in January had echoes of the first days of the COVID pandemic.

“It felt like full crisis mode all over again,” Keenan said.

Yet Salem State has no plans to change course. Its HSI “Roadmap to Servingness” outlines dozens of goals for the next few years: Create an alumni Latino email listserv. Launch a center for Hispanic students. Involve more Latino students in research. Hire staff members who are knowledgeable about immigration paperwork.

The university also kept on Elisa Castillo as the assistant vice president for HSI-MSI initiatives, a position that Salem State says is the first of its kind in the state.

Castillo spends her days brainstorming classroom supports for Latino students and coordinating events, including an appearance by John Quiñones from “What Would You Do?” in 2023. Much of her focus lies in creating “high-impact opportunities,” such as paid internships and study-abroad trips to China or Puerto Rico — Castillo’s family homeland — for students who feel that sort of thing may be out of reach. If MSI funding goes away, it will likely be her job to find philanthropic funding and state grants instead.

“We’re in it to do the work, regardless of whether the presidential administration or the federal grants shift,” Castillo said. “We are here to serve our community and students.”

Those students reflect the demographic shifts of the nation as a whole, and the North Shore in particular. Salem State draws many of its students from expanding Latino enclaves north of Boston, including Chelsea, Lynn, and Lawrence. Today, 25 percent of Salem State students identify as Hispanic or Latino, many of them Puerto Rican or Dominican; 8 percent are Black.

Keenan, the president, calls his students “gritty” as a compliment. Roughly half the students at Salem State are the first in their families to attend college, and many hold down jobs in addition to their course load. What’s more, he notes, most stick around after graduating; 80 percent of Salem State grads stay in Massachusetts, becoming the teachers, social workers, and nurses the state needs desperately.

By one measure, nearly 80 percent of all new workers joining the American labor force over the next five years will be Latino, cementing themselves as a core driver of the economy, said Antonio Flores, president of the Hispanic Association of Colleges and Universities.

“If these institutions are not designed to prepare a diverse workforce that is much more savvy about technology, math, and science-based fields, the entire country will suffer,” he added. “Regions like Massachusetts will be in pain without their labor.”

Massachusetts has eight other HSIs — community colleges and smaller private schools — and they already have a big impact. Half of the students at those HSIs are awarded Pell Grants, a rate twice as high as non-HSIs, and the institutions award more than half of associate’s degrees earned by Latinos statewide, according to MSI Data Project. Now with a sizable four-year-public school joining Cambridge College, Fisher College, and Benjamin Franklin Cummings Institute of Technology on the state’s HSI list, administrators expect they’ll award more bachelor’s degrees as well.

HSIs also promote higher upward mobility for Latino and Black students than predominantly white institutions and can teach in ways that better suit those demographics, by providing targeted tutoring and multilingual support, for example, said Marybeth Gasman, associate dean for Research at Rutgers Graduate School of Education.

Critics point to research showing that funding for HSIs is often simply funneled into universities’ general budgets, rather than to programs targeted at underserved students. A Rutgers study that examined 70 abstracts for funding from fiscal year 2022 found that only three recipients directed all of the money to student-specific initiatives — two of which were actually “Latino centered.”

“When you see those numbers, it can be discouraging,” said Rebecca Perdomo, an author of the study and a higher education consultant. “It’s not going to targeted supports as often as you would it to be.”

But that may partly be because the schools that qualify for HSI are broadly underfunded, Perdomo added. A report last spring by the US Government Accountability Office found an alarming range of infrastructure needs and backlogs of delayed repairs at HSIs, and some schools may prioritize pressing issues, like fixing broken buildings, upgrading poor broadband connections, or buying new computers, over new ventures.

“People get their expectations high about HSI funding. Then when you have to distribute, something goes to academic affairs over here, something goes to the library over there. That money runs out before you know it,” said Lorna Rivera, Director for the Mauricio Gastón Institute for Latino Community Development and Public Policy at UMass Boston. “They use it to plug up holes where there have been gaps already.”

Even without any HSI funds to date, Salem State has made do. It hosted a two-day conference for Hispanic and Minority Serving Institutions in July, whichsold out, and the student chapter of the Society of Advancement for Latinos, Chicanos, and Native Americans in Science recently received official recognition.

For Morelia Morel Diaz, a 21-year-old biology major and president of the Latin American Student Organization, those small steps count for a lot. Her family moved from the Dominican Republic to Mississippi a decade ago, and she chose to go to college 1,500 miles away at attend Salem State because of its promises of small classes and diversity. The burgeoning HSI program is only adding to her feeling that she made the right choice.

“Hispanic students can be discouraged by the lack of representation we see in our fields, but to see so many of us here together doing it and killing it, achieving those goals, and breaking those barriers, is amazing,” she said. “A lot of the time, that potential has not been properly supported.”

Hilary Burns of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

This story was produced by the Globe’s Money, Power, Inequality team, which covers the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston. You can sign up for the newsletter here.

title: Ice seems to be everywhere in Boston. And pedestrians are paying the price.
text:
Normally, the hospital sees three or four patients a day who have fallen, Mostofi said. But since bitter cold descended on the region this week, the litany of injuries in the emergency room has “run the gamut,” Mostofi said, including broken ankles, pelvises, and legs, lower-back compression, and a collapsed lung.

That’s not counting the sprains, bumps, and bruises that have been treated at Tufts, which Mostofi said is operating at full capacity this month amid a surge of the flu.

“In my experience, some of these falls are preventable,” Mostofi said. “Some choices people make put them at high risk, such as riding a scooter on the street. That’s not a good idea,” Mostofi said.

In addition, extreme caution should be taken by the elderly, people who use canes and other mobility aids, and those on blood thinners, Mostofi said.

“If somebody is on blood thinners, and they slip and fall and hit their head, that can be a life-threatening emergency,” he said.

With temperatures in Boston not expected to rise above freezing until the weekend, the need for common sense and uncommon precaution could remain for several more days.

“As we continue to experience this challenging stretch of winter weather, we urge everyone to take necessary precautions and look out for one another,” said Caitlin McLaughlin, a spokeswoman for Boston Emergency Medical Services. “The combination of snow, ice, and extreme cold temperatures can create hazardous conditions, and it’s important to stay safe. Please take extra care when traveling, dressing warmly, and checking on vulnerable neighbors.”

Physicians at Massachusetts General Hospital also have seen a rise in fractures and falls this week. Dr. Thuan Ly, chief of its Orthopaedic Trauma Center, said the hospital has seen about 15 ankle fractures over four days, which he estimated is at least 25 percent more than would appear in a typical four-day period. Most of those fractures will require surgery, Ly added, which usually requires about three months of recovery time.

“With this ice, there’s been an increase in intake, and it hasn’t slowed down,” Ly said. “When you get that below-freezing temperature, and you get this ice that’s been sitting around, people have been slipping.”

Pedestrians, cyclists, and motorists have experienced that first-hand this week. At Southwest Corridor Park in Roxbury, Ladybird Aibangbee gripped a railing for balance as she approached a perilous stretch of sidewalk covered in ice and frozen snow.

“It’s dangerous, and it’s scary,” Aibangbee said. Not only in Southwest Corridor Park, but on sidewalks and bike paths across the city that remain iced over after a snowstorm was followed by pelting rain, then bitter cold.

Aibangbee, who lives in Roxbury, was among a number of city residents who said they had fallen in recent days due to uncleared sidewalks coated in ice.

Zack Morrison of the Back Bay said he crashed his bicycle Wednesday on Beacon Street after going over a patch of black ice.

”It’s terrible,” Morrison said of the conditions. The bike lane “was completely iced over.”

Morrison said he had noticed piles of snow being pushed off the street and into bike lanes, where the snow can freeze over despite appearing safe to ride through.

In Nubian Square in Roxbury and along Malcolm X Boulevard, some sidewalks appeared not to have been cleared at all, with lumps of frozen ice sitting atop a layer of thick snow.

In Dorchester, Minnie Pham, a student at Northeastern University, said she was walking to the bus Wednesday morning when she encountered a “pretty dangerous” intersection at Bowdoin and Adams streets near Coppens Square.

Ly, the MGH physician, offered a few words of caution for this week’s foot soldiers.

“My advice is to give themselves time in the morning to go to work, and to give themselves time to get from one place to another,” he said. “Go slow is what I would recommend, and not be in a hurry. Look at the ground.”

Otherwise, the view might be looking up.

title: Will bike and bus lanes be an issue in the Boston mayoral election?
text:
Running for mayor in 2021, Mayor Michelle Wu didn’t exactly conceal that she intended to expand bus lanes and bike infrastructure. In fact, it was a campaign promise.

And she won by a commanding margin.

Bus and bike lanes may well turn into an issue in her reelection campaign, but if so, it’ll cut both ways. Yes, there are lots of voters who find bike lanes annoying, and may gravitate to challenger Josh Kraft as a result.

There are also people enjoying a faster bus commute or a safer bike ride. They vote, too.

Or at least, so Wu should hope.

The problem is that it’s going to be a different conversation this year than it was in 2021. At that point, promising more bike lanes was a pledge to an interest group — bike-riding progressives who cared intensely about what to most people was still a niche issue. There were votes to be gained promising bike and bus lanes, and not many to be lost.

It’s not a niche issue anymore.

Everyone seems to have an opinion about bike lanes that have sprung up around the city. And that makes sense: Streets are one of the very few city services that virtually every city resident uses every day. Unless you happen to be a BPS parent, the state of the schools can feel like a distant concern; streets affect almost everyone, and affect them every day.

Frankly, I hope the election does turn into a slugfest over bike lanes. That would turn the outcome into a verdict of sorts and maybe provide some democratic legitimacy to whatever direction the next mayor takes.

As I wrote last year in my “Are we there yet” newsletter, one of the defining characteristics of bike lane disputes is that both sides tend to view themselves as speaking for an embattled silent majority, and that sense of grievance just deepens the rancor.

So let’s put it to a vote and find out, once and for all, what residents really want.

By Joan Vennochi

Fifty years ago, the battle tearing Boston apart was over a federal court order requiring the busing of students to integrate Boston Public Schools. Today, the big controversy is over an expanded network of dedicated bus and bike lanes promoted by Mayor Michelle Wu.

These are very different fights, fought in very different ways, with rocks thrown at school buses, versus the angry words of today. I guess that’s progress. But the two battles share some common threads: hostility towards elites who think they know better than everyone else, and what might be characterized as a deep-seated resistance to change.

In an election year, are such forces strong enough to propel Josh Kraft to victory over Wu? At his announcement of a mayoral run, Kraft’s criticism of bus and bike lanes drew loud applause. Judging from Wu’s subsequent call for the removal of a controversial bus lane on Boylston Street and a citywide review of all bus and bike lanes, she is taking those cheers seriously.

As she should. “This one unites people on different [political] sides of the street,” Larry DiCara, a former Boston city councilor, former mayoral candidate, and longtime Jamaica Plain resident, told me in an interview. “It’s not just one neighborhood. It’s controversial in the Back Bay and in West Roxbury.” He added that people think of cyclists as a distinct class: young, single and white. “If you’ve got three babies, you’re not going to be biking to the Aquarium,” DiCara said.

To Jim Aloisi, a former state secretary of transportation and strong advocate for bus and bike lanes, opposition to the lanes has deep roots of a different kind in the city’s DNA. “Historically, there is a strange and persistent view among many Bostonians that somehow they have a special privilege to use public streets any way they like. Hence the legendary fights over parking spaces after winter snow storms, or the double or triple parking often blocking bus stops or other cars,” Aloisi, who currently lives in South Boston, told me via email. So it’s not surprising that some Bostonians see bus and bike lanes as “interfering with their unfettered right to exploit the streetscape,” he said.

To DiCara, the struggle over bus and bike lanes is also a version of what historian Theodore H. White called the “urban ballet” — the ever-changing dance that shifts a city’s cultural makeup over time.

Busing, for example, drove white resisters out, altering Boston’s racial demographics.

Could bus and bike lanes drive an incumbent mayor out? If they did, it would be another kind of earthquake.

By Carine Hajjar

Going into her reelection campaign, Michelle Wu needs some political wins. So it seemed unsurprising that she would eliminate the bus lane on Boylston Street that has been the bane of many a commuter’s and business owner’s existence in a city already plagued by bad traffic.

“We have heard from community members that this needs to be changed,” she said recently. (Curiously, when she heard — loud and clear — from North End restaurant owners that they wanted to have outdoor dining, she responded with far less alacrity. But then again, it wasn’t an election year, and they are less likely to vote for her than the Boylston crowd).

Recall that Wu was the gung-ho voice behind creating the Boylston bus lane in the first place. So if getting a political win requires paring back your own policy, it means you’re probably in hot water. Especially if you’re taking cues from your opponent Josh Kraft, who criticized bus and bike lanes and called for a pause in bike lane construction when he announced his run.

And even though Wu’s move is a clear improvement for anyone driving down Boylston, it isn’t going to be enough to avert tough questions on the rest of her record. On the homeless people at Mass. and Cass, on the city’s skyrocketing housing prices, on a T that isn’t getting better fast enough, and on a city still shouting “sanctuary” while migrants are being assaulted in nearby shelters.

And on the poorly placed bike and bus lanes in neighborhoods beyond Back Bay.

Curated by Jim Dao

FROM THE RIGHT: The Wall Street Journal editorial board says no – at least not yet. “The real crisis would come if Mr. Trump defies a Supreme Court ruling. If that happens, and it could, the left may wish it hadn’t squandered its credibility by crying wolf so often about crises that didn’t exist. Readers can relax in the meantime.”

FROM THE LEFT: The New Republic says we’re really, really close. “We are at the very beginning of an administration that already has been marked by far greater levels of hubris and outright lawlessness than any in our lifetime and probably the lifetime of the Republic.”

FROM THE CENTER: David French, a center-right columnist for The New York Times, is pretty worried. “Trump isn’t merely issuing orders and enacting policies; he’s launching a constitutional revolution. The object is nothing less than the transformation of the American presidency.”

By Christopher Weyant

Trivia by Gwen Egan

This column first appeared in Right, Left, and Center, Globe Opinion’s free weekly newsletter about local and national politics. If you’d like to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.

title: US moves backward amid steps to close racial gap in homeownership
text:
Housing experts say it doesn’t have to be that way. The road to homeownership runs uphill for many prospective buyers, but for those of color, the grade is steeper. The good news is: with hard work, discipline, patience, and the right coaching, many renters who don’t think they can achieve their goal of becoming homeowners actually can, giving them access to the many financial benefits of owning property.

Bob Credle is the director of community programs for Urban Edge, a nonprofit community development organization with a mission to strengthen neighborhoods and families. One of the ways the Roxbury-based organization does that is through a comprehensive educational program that meets prospective home buyers where they’re at and coaches them through the process, which could take years. The biggest hurdle for his students, Credle said, is information.

Credle and his colleagues look at the prospective buyers' overall financial picture and coach them on how to save money, improve their credit scores, and get low-rate mortgages and down payment assistance. Many of their successful clients were people who thought they could never own a home because they just didn’t know where to turn for help.

“We’re able to help a lot of people get into down payment-assistance programs, [like] the ONE mortgage program, because we know about them,” he said. “I don’t know how pervasive that information is in the Black community that isn’t associated with organizations like us” and the Massachusetts Affordable Homeownership Alliance.

OneUnited, one of the largest Black-owned banks in the country, recently launched a down payment-assistance program that grants up to $50,000 for qualified, first-time home buyers of color.

Gercide Luc, Urban Edge’s associate director of community programs, said the next biggest obstacle is affordability, especially in Boston. Not only are costs and interest rates high, but properties that are in her clients’ price range are often in need of major repairs.

“As counselors, we’re taking money from a lot of different sources to patch together a down payment with whatever they’ve saved,” Luc said. “Maybe it’s the minimum to actually get into the market. They find a property, and now there’s even more cost that’s involved for repairs to get the property. It makes it very, very difficult.”

David Gasser, programs director at the Citizens' Housing and Planning Association, said that a lot of what has been done to address the racial gap in homeownership has been successful, but to make real progress, Massachusetts communities need to build a lot more housing.

“We have generational wealth being created by those who had access to homeownership,” Gasser said. “And all the economic benefit that comes from that system perpetuates itself, and unless you’re going to create the supply necessary to create affordable new entry points, it’s going to be very difficult to narrow the racial homeownership gap.”

The SHIBA report found homes in majorityBlack neighborhoods are more likely to be appraised for less money than similar homes in majoritywhite neighborhoods. This can have a cascading effect, as homes that are appraised for less than they are worth might sell for less than they are worth, bringing down the value of neighboring properties.

“The appraisal bias issue is a very stark example of a complicated problem, because those appraisals are so individual and the way appraisers are trained and regulated is somewhat difficult to address, but we do participate in some of those efforts,” Gasser said.

Melvin A. Vieira Jr. of RE/Max Destiny is a Black real estate agent who has had many clients of color throughout his career. He said he has successfully challenged low appraisals in Black neighborhoods by sending the appraiser recent comparable sales and asking them to reconsider.

He said many of his clients of color come from families that never owned a home, so growing up, they never heard anything about the home-buying process and had no one to ask about it. He said people like himself and organizations like Urban Edge and MAHA can’t reach enough people by themselves to narrow the racial homeownership gap. He said an updated version of the old home economics course should be part of every public high school curriculum.

“It’s not about cooking and cleaning; it should be talking about checkbooks, talking about savings,” he said. “They should explain how interest works and how to invest in the stock market. How to make yourself financially fit so you can achieve your financial goals after you leave high school. Because the majority of people who come out of high school don’t even have a checking account.

“If you give a person knowledge, it can’t be taken away,” he said. “When you teach a person how to fish, they’ll always know how to fish.”

title: As estimated costs balloon to $700m, Boston will now seek state funds to rebuild Madison Park
text:
“Madison Park is a monster project,” said Greg Maynard of the Boston Policy Institute, who follows school construction closely. “Madison Park is a really old school, it’s in an urban environment, and it’s just expensive to build things in cities. . . . There 100 percent could be cost escalations, especially with the tariffs that are being proposed.”

Over the last decade, the average cost to build a new school in the state has more than doubled, to $650 a square foot, according to the Massachusetts School Building Authority, while the cost of renovations has grown nearly as fast. And school projects in Boston are consistently among the most expensive.

Moreover, many school districts have not been able to resist the allure of state-of-the-art campuses dating to 2010 when Newton shattered spending records with a $200 million high school. This expansive vision of a modern high school often entails arts complexes, high-tech labs, gymnasiums, and classrooms with plenty of space to rearrange for lectures, seminars, and group projects.

But the potential cost of a new Madison Park is now so high that Wu said she would seek funding from the state, a reversal of her previous plan to have Boston build Madison Park with its own money, and to have construction begin this year.

At an event earlier this month, Wu said the city has worked with community members to envision a “modern, updated, beautiful Madison Park campus. . . . We’re taking the first steps in decades to make that a reality by putting forth some of the designs and feedback and then entering a process to apply for funding from the state.”
