“We have a construction boom but none of the Bostonians are getting the jobs,” he said. “The entry point is Madison Park, but we’re not feeding the system.”

Boston school officials have recently been exploring funding strategies for a $700 million rebuild of the Madison Park school, the city’s sole vocational high school. The school’s enrollment this academic year is 1,121 students, according to state data.

Across the Boston school system, DaRosa said more should be invested in students' experiences beyond the standard lessons taught in the classroom.

“We need to be able to provide these kids with resources such as swimming, arts, music, extracurricular activities, school sports,” he said. “We’ve lost a lot of that in BPS, especially at the high school level.”

DaRosa has also been active in raising the alarm about the opioid crisis and conditions at the intersection known as Mass. and Cass, an area near the border of Roxbury and the South End where an open-air drug market has persisted for years despite efforts by city leaders to clean up the area and help people suffering from addiction to access recovery services.

He said he knows as well as anyone how the addiction crisis has affected the community in the vicinity of Mass. and Cass. As a Pop Warner football coach in nearby Clifford Park, DaRosa and other coaches would walk the field before practices to pick up dirty needles.

DaRosa was the longtime head of the Boston Bengals Pop Warner program, but he said the program ended after the 2022 season due to unsanitary conditions on their practice field and ongoing drug activity around it.

“There was no way [it could continue] like that,” he said.

DaRosa said he has long been a proponent of reopening the Long Island recovery campus that shuttered after the bridge that connects Moon Island in Quincy to Long Island was closed in 2014. Boston officials have sought to place a large addiction-recovery campus on Long Island and have been inching toward rebuilding the bridge.

“We can do things as a city to get Long Island back in order,” he said. “It hasn’t really gotten off the ground, while other plans have. So we want to see things like that actually roll out.”

DaRosa is in the early stages of forming his campaign. He said he will soon launch campaign pages on social media and create a website. He said he hopes that “working folks” will support him and volunteer to help get the word out about his candidacy.

“These are folks who are working a 7 to 3, a 9 to 5, and they’re willing to help and support me because they’ve watched me put in the legwork over the years,” he said.

title: Another challenger for Michelle Wu? Developer Thomas O’Brien considering jump into mayoral race.
text:
A person close to O’Brien said he has been fielding calls from residents and business leaders expressing concerns about the city’s fiscal health, rising property taxes on seniors and homeowners, the lack of affordable housing, and the quality of Boston Public Schools, and that they have encouraged him to consider putting his hat in the ring.

Typically, business leaders, especially real estate developers, back the incumbent because they have to work closely with the sitting mayor and need approvals from City Hall for their projects. Indeed, HYM is currently leading the massive Suffolk Downs redevelopment on the East Boston-Revere line, which is still in early phases, and has buildings remaining to go on its redo of the Government Center Garage. HYM also won the bid to develop the city-owned Parcel 3 on Tremont Street in Roxbury into life sciences labs and housing.

But this election cycle could be different, with the commercial real estate community so frustrated by Wu’s policies that some say they will do anything to make sure she doesn’t get reelected — even apparently running against her.

Developers have opposed Wu’s efforts to increase affordable housing requirements and expand green building codes, as well as her attempts to cap residential rent hikes and raise commercial property tax rates. Taken together, developers have said her policies are driving up building costs and discouraging new construction.

While it had been an open secret for a year that Kraft was eyeing a mayoral challenge, news of O’Brien’s potential candidacy took many people by surprise. Like Kraft, O’Brien has never run for public office before.

It is likely O’Brien has been waiting in the wings to see how Kraft would fare.

Wu’s first major challenger was off to a solid start, collecting close to $300,000 in donations in February, and the first independent poll by Emerson College conducted in late February indicated that Wu was far from a shoo-in. The mayor led Kraft with 43 percent support to his 29 percent, while a significant proportion of voters, 24 percent, were undecided.

But then last week Kraft lost momentum after Wu had the best week of her political life after appearing before a Republican-led Congressional committee to defend Boston’s sanctuary city status. She, by many accounts, not only represented the city well but created viral moments of her own clapping back at anti-immigrant sentiment.

That could create an opening for O’Brien if voters think Kraft may have peaked. Kraft and O’Brien would likely vie for moderate voters who want the city to show more fiscal restraint and not raise taxes. And like Kraft, O’Brien could tap his vast network, both in the business community and in neighborhoods around the city where he has built projects, to fundraise and build support.

“Wow,” observed Larry DiCara, a Boston real estate attorney who served as a longtime city councilor before running unsuccessfully for mayor in 1983. “He’d be a very substantial candidate if he decides to run. It makes it more difficult for Kraft to put the pieces together … this changes the entire ballgame.”

A spokesperson for the Kraft campaign declined comment. But a Wu campaign spokesperson took aim at both challengers, tying them together as candidates favored by big real estate interests.

“It is clear some developers are willing to do whatever it takes to buy this office,” according to a statement from the Wu campaign. “It seems like Josh Kraft is not turning out to be what they expected and now they are shopping for a new option.”

Like Kraft, O’Brien is well known in business and civic circles in Boston. A father of five and a Brown University graduate, he serves on the board of the Pine Street Inn and Rose Kennedy Greenway Conservancy. He is also a member of the Global Leadership Council of the Anti-Defamation League of New England. O’Brien grew up in Scituate and Andover and now lives in downtown Boston. And his brother, Bill O’Brien, is head football coach at Boston College.

Thomas O’Brien spent five years in the 1990s working under Menino at the city planning and development agency, then known as the Boston Redevelopment Authority, including two years as its director. O’Brien resigned following a scandal involving a top BRA aide who purchased a subsidized condo intended for low-income families.

Since then, O’Brien has remade himself into one of the region’s most prolific developers and a business leader. He helped launch HYM in 2009, and the firm has played a key role in major, complicated projects, including Boston Landing in Brighton, NorthPoint in Cambridge, Bulfinch Crossing in downtown Boston, and Suffolk Downs.

Still, unseating an incumbent is no easy feat. That hasn’t happened in Boston since 1949, when Mayor James Michael Curley lost to John B. Hynes. Curley had just served time in federal prison for mail fraud, and instead of resigning, he chose to run for reelection.

Wu, a Harvard graduate and mother of three, is a savvy politician who has won multiple citywide elections, first as a city councilor at large and later as mayor in 2021. The Roslindale resident and progressive Democrat has shattered political barriers, becoming the first woman of color to serve as City Council president and the first woman and person of color elected as mayor of Boston.

O’Brien has not openly criticized Wu during her term as mayor. But in offering a statement to the Globe shortly after Kraft’s announcement, he seemed to outline the contours of a potential campaign.

“Boston is facing real challenges — rising taxes, a growing budget, and a housing shortage that needs action. Investments should reflect community priorities, like ensuring our students’ educational priorities are balanced with the need for high-quality sports facilities and other competing issues. Thoughtful planning and engagement matter,” said O’Brien. “We need someone who leads the way, but also is collaborative and works with residents and businesses to shape Boston’s future.”

title: Zoning board made wrong call in rejecting Roxbury birth center
text:
No one — including the neighbors — is questioning the value of the proposed Neighborhood Birth Center. Birth centers provide prenatal, childbirth, and postpartum care in a more homey setting than a hospital, with midwife-centered care that prioritizes natural birth options and fewer medical interventions. Birth centers have been shown to have positive outcomes for women at a lower cost than hospitals. The Legislature recognized this when it passed a bill last session making it easier for birth centers to open, with better-tailored regulations and a framework to license certified professional midwives.

Today, the state’s only operating birth center is in Western Massachusetts, after centers on the North Shore and in Cambridge closed.

A maternal health clinic that is culturally and racially sensitive could also address disparities in maternal health, with statistics showing that Black women are nearly twice as likely as white women to die during pregnancy or within one year postpartum. Neighborhood Birth Center executive director Nashira Baril said the center expects 50 percent of patients will have Medicaid; staff will be multilingual and reflect community demographics; and the center will commit to training student midwives. Around 300 babies a year would be born at the center, which would serve 1,000 families annually with clinical care and programming.

“This birth center is a life-saving investment in our families, ensuring more individuals in our community can give birth safely, with dignity, in an environment that reflects their values and their culture,” state Senator Liz Miranda, who represents Roxbury, said at a zoning board hearing. Miranda told the editorial board she wants the center in Roxbury so it can serve the people of Roxbury, a low-income community with poor birth outcomes. According to a 2023 Boston Public Health Commission report, Roxbury has high rates of preterm births and low-birth weight births.

The proposed site, at 14 Winthrop St., is in the heart of one of Boston’s predominantly Black neighborhoods, near public transportation, and less than 10 minutes by ambulance to Boston Medical Center if a patient needs an emergency transfer. Project organizers say they prefer a residential environment to a storefront since a birth center should provide a home-like feel.

One factor that adds complexity is the birth center partnered with five other nonprofits to buy the property. Sisters Unchained, Matahari Women Workers’ Center, Center for Economic Democracy, Movement Sustainability Commons, and Resist all plan to colocate there. Baril said the partnership was necessary to make the finances work. While neighbors have legitimate concerns about allowing an office building to replace a residential property, the nonprofits — all of which do work in Boston — have responded by scaling back an earlier proposal. The current proposal is relatively modest: 10,550 square feet across two floors, with green space and 11 parking spots. The first floor would house the birth center, and the five nonprofits are expected to employ about 15 staff, with gathering space for around 35 visitors.

The main argument against the center is the neighbors would prefer housing. The plan calls for demolishing one single-family home and one three-family home. Both were built in the mid-1800s. Both are vacant, one deemed structurally unsound.

“Who wants to live across the street from an office building? We’re a neighborhood,” neighbor Nadine Riggs told the editorial board.

While the parcel is zoned residential, the neighborhood is mixed. There are two schools and four churches within a couple of blocks, and the site is steps away from a laundromat, which is on a commercial street that also has a barber shop, public library, and Boys & Girls Club.

City officials received around 100 letters opposing the project and more than 350 supporting it, with opinions split among immediate neighbors and elected officials. Ultimately, the zoning board split, with four members supporting the project and three opposing it, with five votes needed for approval.

The project is not about gentrification but about providing needed services to the local community, and the nonprofits have shown a willingness to work with neighbors on project size and details. The zoning board should reconsider and approve the project. If it doesn’t, city officials should work closely with the birth center to expeditiously find new land that meets its needs.

title: Today in History: March 11, massive earthquake and tsunami in Japan kill nearly 20,000
text:
Today is Tuesday, March 11, the 70th day of 2025. There are 295 days left in the year.

Birthdays: Media mogul Rupert Murdoch is 94. Former ABC News correspondent Sam Donaldson is 91. Musician Flaco Jimenez is 86. Singer Bobby McFerrin is 75. Actor Elias Koteas is 64. Actor Alex Kingston is 62. Actor John Barrowman is 58. Singer Lisa Loeb is 57. Actor Terrence Howard is 56. Actor Johnny Knoxville is 54. Basketball Hall of Famer Becky Hammon is 48. Rock musicians Benji and Joel Madden (Good Charlotte; The Madden Brothers) are 46. Singer LeToya Luckett is 44. Actor Thora Birch is 43. Actor Jodie Comer is 32.

In 1988, one of the most ferocious storms to hit New England blasted the region with 80 miles per hour winds and up to four feet of snow in some areas. Called “The White Hurricane,’’ the storm created drifts that reached to the second floor of many buildings and halted deliveries of food and fuel, accelerating the push for utility wires to be buried underground.

In 1918, what were believed to be the first confirmed US cases of a deadly global flu pandemic were reported among Army soldiers stationed at Fort Riley, Kan.; 46 soldiers would die. (The influenza outbreak would ultimately kill an estimated 20 million to 40 million people worldwide.)

In 1941, President Franklin D. Roosevelt signed the Lend-Lease Act, which provided war supplies to Allied countries during World War II.

In 1965, James Reeb, a Unitarian Universalist minister in Dorchester and Roxbury, died from a beating from a white gang in Selma, Ala., two days earlier. Reeb had joined a large group of ministers and lay workers who answered Martin Luther King Jr.’s call for clergy across the nation to come to Selma to rally against the attack on marchers at the Pettus Bridge earlier in the month.

In 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev was chosen to succeed the late Konstantin Chernenko as general secretary of the Soviet Communist Party.

In 2004, three days before general elections in Spain, 10 bombs exploded in quick succession inside commuter trains in Madrid, killing 193 people in an attack linked to al-Qaida-inspired militants.

In 2006, former Serb leader Slobodan Milošević was found dead at age 64 of a heart attack in his prison cell in the Netherlands, abruptly ending his four-year UN war crimes trial.

In 2010, a federal appeals court in San Francisco upheld the use of the words “under God” in the Pledge of Allegiance and “In God We Trust” on US currency.

In 2011, a magnitude 9 earthquake and resulting tsunami struck Japan’s northeastern coast, killing nearly 20,000 people and severely damaging the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power station.

In 2012, US Army Staff Sergeant Robert Bales shot and killed 16 Afghan villagers — mostly women and children — as they slept. (Bales later pleaded guilty and was sentenced to life in prison without parole.)

In 2021, President Joe Biden signed into law a $1.9 trillion COVID relief package that he said would help defeat the virus and nurse the economy back to health. Lower-income Americans would receive up to $1,400 in direct payments, along with extended unemployment benefits.

title: Years in the making, a new home for formerly homeless people opens in Jamaica Plain
text:
These days, though, Montanino is calling Jamaica Plain home. He’s one of the new residents at 3368 Washington St., a five-story, $105 million residential building celebrating its grand opening on Wednesday. Developed by Boston-based The Community Builders and homeless services provider Pine Street Inn, the building — to be named “The Lyndia” in honor of Pine Street Inn executive director Lyndia Downie — is the largest permanent supportive housing development in New England. The 202-unit building includes 140 studios for formerly unhoused people referred by Pine Street in one wing, and 62 affordable units for families in another.

The city of Boston provided some $17.3 million to the project, and supported it amid a lengthy lawsuit that challenged its zoning.

“To solve homelessness, you have to tackle the roots of the problem, which is making sure that people can have a home, and have support in living in their homes,” said Boston Mayor Michelle Wu. “You really have to have a plan for homes to be accessible and supportive for everyone.”

Downie has long championed permanent supportive housing, which is basically an apartment with social services on site, and Pine Street has gradually grown its inventory of such buildings in recent years. Advocates say tackling the roots of homelessness requires more than just handing out grants, and instead making sure individuals have both a roof over their heads and access to health and wellness support systems to guide them through a world-upending transition. Montanino said he is frequently connected with security and outreach personnel, case managers, a personal landlord, and property managers, all of whom helped him move — and stay — off the streets.

“They’re all hands on deck here,” he said.

The 3368 Washington project includes support services like onsite mental health counseling, 24/7 security, and key fob-activated elevators. Residents are directly referred by Pine Street Inn. On a recent tour of the building, fliers for workforce development programs with Pine Street and Roxbury Community College were available for anyone to read.

The property was formerly a low-slung warehouse, which Pine Street bought in 1997 and over the years used for a variety of functions, including office space for case workers and a small woodworking program. As Pine Street ramped up its housing development efforts, the site stood out, particularly given its proximity to the Green Street Orange Line station. Most developers responded to Pine Street’s bid for proposals with pitches for around 40 to 60 units, Downie said. But Bart Mitchell, CEO of The Community Builders, aimed higher.

“Bart and I went over to look at the site, and Bart, even that day, said, ‘Look, if we can get some height relief, we can do something really sustainable here. We can get some scale,’” Downie said. “That was what, for us, was so exciting. ... The more long-term people you can move out, the better chance you have of meeting shelter demand.”

The project hasn’t been without its challenges. The landlord of a neighboring property sued in 2020, alleging the zoning process to allow the project was flawed. Though the lawsuit eventually settled, the delay cost “multiple millions” of dollars, said Andy Waxman, Community Builders’ senior vice president of real estate.

Pine Street and The Community Builders are collaborating on similar projects, including 900 Morrissey Blvd. in Dorchester, which is under construction now. While many community groups in Jamaica Plain, including the Egleston Square Neighborhood Association and the Jamaica Plain Neighborhood Council, supported 3368 Washington, other projects across the city have seen fierce pushback from neighborhoods.

“It’s an unknown for a lot of people, so I think it creates more anxiety for people — in an understandable way — not knowing exactly what it is,” Waxman said. “Permanent housing with the level of support that Pine Street Inn provides — that combination is great. And so it takes people some time to learn that.”

Potential residents apply through the Boston Housing Authority, and then are screened by Pine Street. Folks have moved in gradually over the past few months, Downie said, and the building is expected to be full by June.

With a gentle demeanor and a quick smile, Montanino proudly showed off his new home last week. He’s learning to cook, and there are spices and oil next to his stove — he’s done steaks and chicken, burgers, and salads. He’s volunteering, and has lined up a job — he starts in April. He dreams of adopting a child, as his mother did him.

“My life’s back,” Montanino said. “I get up early in the morning. I count my blessings, for sure.”

title: When owning a Tesla means always having to say you’re sorry.
text:
At times, Segall said, she’s felt almost desperate to sell the car. But the dealer offered her so little for it — a 2023 Model 3, in excellent condition — that she has decided to try and sell it herself on Facebook Marketplace, albeit at a loss.

“I’m willing to lose $5,000 for emotional betterment,” Segall said, noting that while she awaits a buyer, she’s reduced to taking the only action she can — adding ever more anti-Musk magnets.

Alas, she may need a bigger bumper.

On Tuesday, Trump trolled “Radical Left Lunatics” by buying a Tesla himself. He shopped for the car on the White House lawn, and bought a Model S, for about $80,000. It’s also possible to get a Tesla for less. The cheapest model, Model 3, starts at $42,490, according to Carfax.

In this upside down world — in which Trump supporters who used to harass Tesla drivers for caring about the climate are now the ones who support them — it’s hard to say where things will go. One thing’s for sure: Some Tesla owners willing to sell at a loss are wealthy enough that they won’t feel a thing. But for others, the loss hits hard, but feels better than the alternative.

In February, Kelley Blue Book reported that Tesla sales were falling globally. Locally, the market for used Teslas is lackluster (more on this in a moment). And beyond the numbers, emotions are getting so ugly it’s hard to keep up.

In Littleton, in early March, Tesla charging stations were set on fire, and officials are calling it arson. Over the weekend, fire damaged four Tesla Cybertrucks in Seattle. Three vehicles were vandalized overnight Tuesday at a Tesla dealership in Dedham, police said. Locally and across the country, protests are erupting at Tesla dealerships. In Brookline, a man was arrested for allegedly vandalizing Teslas with stickers.

In Plymouth, Sandy Markowitz, a retiree who, to her chagrin, has two Teslas she can’t find buyers for, has been on an apology tour.

On a recent call, she felt compelled to make the case for herself: she volunteers, she said, has run marathons for charity, and started a book club. But even so, there was her long-ago college roommate on the phone the other day, revealing that she’s angry with Markowitz for owning Teslas.

“You work for big pharma,” Markowitz thought to herself when they got off, “but I’m not mad at you.”

But by their very nature, cars are public. And that means virtue-signaling is part of the game, said local psychologist and executive coach Thierry Guedj.

“I’ll give you an example,” he said. “I know a couple of families who fly private jets — which have a huge carbon footprint — but both families drive Teslas and they act as though they are very environmentally conscious. They show off their left-wing credentials.”

But now, of course, having the Tesla “makes them look bad,” he said, estimating that the wealthy, who paid handsomely for Teslas to begin with, are now willing to take a financial hit to maintain their progressive reputations.

“This kind of virtue-signaling is only available to the rich,” he said.

But in red states, virtue-signaling — signaling MAGA virtues, that is — is becoming more affordable.

Charlie Karyanis, president of City Motor Group, a Cambridge firm that buys and sells used and new cars, said that the local market for used Teslas is so weak that he’s buying them here and shipping them to dealers in the South or Midwest.

That means someone who is willing to overlook Musk’s alleged atrocities — or conversely, likes what he is doing — can pick up a bargain.

For example, Karyanis said, he recently sold a 2022 Tesla Model Y with 26,000 miles to a dealer in Fort Lauderdale for $27,400. Before Musk’s reputational dive, he said, that car would have gone for nearly $40,000.

“There is a lot of opportunity there for someone who wants a pretty sophisticated car,” Karyanis said.

People selling locally, of course, don’t want to act like they’re dumping a toxic asset. So when Scott Oran, a housing developer from Newton, listed his 2018 Model 3 on Craigslist, he played up a different angle — at his wife’s suggestion:

“My wife says sell!” his post read. “My loss, your gain.”

He initially listed the car at $24,900. Then, after two weeks with no offers, he lowered the asking price to $20,900, and eventually, after being told that there was no local market for used Teslas, making it hard to sell to an individual on Craigslist, he sold it to a national used car dealer for $18,000.

Like Sheryl Crow, who in February posted footage of her Tesla being hauled off on a flatbed truck while she waved goodbye, Oran took video of the happy day. “Buh-bye,” he says, off camera, as a truck carts the car off to redder climes.

In liberal circles, Tesla shame can run so deep that Tesla drivers look down on other Tesla drivers. That includes Karen Kaufman of West Roxbury, a retired social worker who drives a 2020 Tesla she’d love to sell, but she prefers not to take the monetary hit.

“When I see those Cybertrucks, that for me is a symbol of a real Trumper,” she said, judging herself for her own judgment. “I know that’s not fair.”

title: Teenagers shot man after argument outside Roxbury library branch, police say
text:
A pair of unrelated shootings in the heart of Roxbury over eight hours starting Tuesday evening left two men wounded and two teenagers facing charges.

The two boys, 17 and 15, face an array of charges after allegedly shooting a 29-year-old man shortly before 5 p.m. by Roxbury’s Nubian Square, police said. Then, a police officer rushed to Malcolm X Park around 12:30 a.m. Wednesday, after hearing roughly a dozen gunshots to find a male victim suffering gunshot wounds to his foot and shoulder.

Both victims were taken to Boston Medical Center and are expected to survive, police said.

Wei Cong, who works at the Peking House Chinese restaurant on Harrison Avenue near Dudley Street and the site of the first incident, said it was the first time he had heard a shooting while on the job.

“I heard four shots,” he said. Police say they recovered five shell casings from the scene.

Police were first alerted to the Nubian Square shooting by a ShotSpotter activation at 4:56 p.m. Officers rushed to the corner of Warren and Dudley Streets, where they found the victim lying on the floor of a neighboring smoke shop with a bullet wound to the leg.

“While processing the scene, detectives launched an investigation and obtained surveillance footage capturing two suspects involved in the incident,“ police said in a statement. ”Detectives disseminated images and broadcasted descriptions of the suspects to responding officers.”

Police accessed nearby camera footage, which showed two people arguing with the victim in front of the Boston Public Library branch on Warren Street, according to a police report. They then appeared on camera sprinting up Warren Street after ShotSpotter registered gunfire, the report said.

Responding officers were given descriptions from the footage and soon saw two teenagers who matched, police said. The 17-year-old was arrested without a struggle, while the 15-year-old was captured after a brief foot chase, police said.

Police are not identifying the suspects because they are minors. Both were scheduled for arraignment Wednesday in Boston Juvenile Court on charges of armed assault with intent to murder, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, trespassing, and several gun law violations.

The 15-year-old was also charged with drug possession after officers allegedly found a bag of crack cocaine in his sock.

About eight hours later, an officer was patrolling near Paulding Street when she heard the crack of about 12 gunshots, according to a police report. In Malcom X Park, near the corner of Dale and Paulding Streets, she found the 24-year-old victim with another male standing over him.

The second man fled, according to a police report, leaving the officer with the bleeding victim. EMTs arrived and placed the victim in an ambulance.

Officers found two guns near the scene and stopped two people for questioning but made no arrests, the police report said.

So far this year, at least 19 people have been shot in Boston, five fatally, including a man shot dead in the Back Bay by an off-duty police officer while allegedly threatening people with a knife. The night’s shootings were the third and fourth in Roxbury this year, none of which have been fatal.

This year is off to a more violent start than 2024, which saw a historically low level of gun violence in the city. There had been nine shootings in Boston by this point last year.

title: MIAA Board of Directors looks ahead, discussing future of Division 1A/Super 8 and lots more
text:
“This is the message being delivered to you,” Baldwin said. “To us, it’s exciting to make [the MIAA] even better. Maybe some of this sticks. Maybe some of it doesn’t. We want to be proactive, not reactive.”

While the possibility of bringing back Division 1A tournaments was one of the five main areas of conversation, it produced very little discussion.

The Division 1A/Super 8 tournament is eligible to return after July 1, a date set by the Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights. For the tournament to return, it would need to follow, at minimum, these four guidelines:

Tournament must be conducted for both genders of a sport.

Must use the same power ranking system for scheduling and seeding.

The champion and runner-up must play five games.

Venues need to be the same or similar between Division 1A and other divisions.

Arlington Catholic athletic director Dan Shine, who was at the helm of the AC hockey program for 40-plus seasons, was one of just a few to offer thoughts.

“I think the reasons given for the 1A format 30 years ago when hockey started it are different from what the reasons would be today,” he said. “Everything has changed over that period of time. I think it’s a great thing to talk about. I think what we have now is fabulous. But I think we’re really going to have to get into the weeds of this and how a 1A tournament benefits the association overall.”

It was revealed that on Tuesday, the MIAA’s football committee voted, 11-0-1, to rescind its proposed 2025 tournament format, which moved all playoff games after Thanksgiving. Instead, this fall football will be played under the same format that has been used the past decade.

Baldwin laid out three requirements for any future football playoff format: 1. All regular season contests should matter; 2. Thanksgiving matters; 3. Super Bowls must conclude the second weekend after Thanksgiving.

“We’re not going [another] week into the winter season, or extending the spring season,” Baldwin said. “Can you build this mousetrap with those parameters? They now have direction.”

The board also heard discussion on standardizing the annual calendar, delineating start dates, first contest dates, cutoff dates, bracket release dates, tournaments, and state finals for the entire school year.

A committee, led by Medfield athletic director Eric Scott, has started to map out a calendar with a suggested start date of the second Monday preceding Labor Day and an end date on the third weekend of June.

“This is the first step,” Scott said. “We have to go to every district and get their input and sit down, hopefully soon, and do a second draft and bring it to different committees. We’re still a ways away from bringing it to this group [for approval].”

Most of the discussion centered on the spring season, with athletic directors expressing difficulty fitting enough games in between when fields become playable and the Memorial Day cutoff date.

“I love fall and winter, but I hate spring,” said Quabbin AD Mark Millville. “It’s not realistic for us to play until a couple of weeks into April. The [cutoff] date is a tough one to swallow being before Memorial Day when you have a month to play baseball and softball.”

While two of the “areas for conversation” received little to no discussion — power ranked vs. hybrid sports and standards for number of divisions per sport — an option was presented that would make the process of adding or removing sports more objective.

“If a sport is gaining momentum or losing momentum, wouldn’t it be better for us to quantify that and make an objective determination?” Baldwin asked the membership.

The proposal, which was not voted on, would have three tiers:

School-sponsored sport. Baldwin noted any school can offer any sport it wishes without needing approval from the MIAA.

Emerging status. For sports played by at least 10 percent of the membership (approximately 38 teams, with co-ops counting as one team). Sports would remain at the Emerging level for two years.

Championships status. After two years at the Emerging level, sports could be deemed worthy of championship status if they reach 15 percent participation among member schools (approximately 57 teams).

The board also previewed two rule changes that will be voted on in May — one restricts schools from submitting eligibility waivers for students who have chosen to repeat a grade and the other would penalize teams that overschedule by forfeiting two games.

Among the final topics were co-op programs in which the host school offers fewer grades (9-12) than a guest school (7-12). The co-op’s eligibility would be determined by the host school.

Lastly, a vote on adding a Massachusetts Charter School Conference was tabled until the board receives more data on the number of non-association games those schools typically schedule.

The 17-school conference, which would be placed in District 6, would feature two divisions, North and South, and include Boston Collegiate in Dorchester, Collegiate Charter of Lowell, Community Charter of Cambridge, Excel Academy in East Boston, Pioneer Charter in Everett, Pioneer Charter II in Saugus, Prospect Hill in Cambridge, Salem Academy, Academy of the Pacific Rim in Hyde Park, Argosy Collegiate in Fall River, Boston Prep in Hyde Park, Codman Academy in Dorchester, Neighborhood House in Dorchester, New Heights in Brockton, Roxbury Prep in Hyde Park, and South Shore in Norwell.

title: Metco president Milly Arbaje-Thomas to step down
text:
“Leading an organization of such significant and historical impact has been one of my greatest honors,” Arbaje-Thomas said in a statement. “I feel privileged to have had the opportunity to leave a meaningful imprint on an organization that I value, cherish, and love.”

Metco, which started in 1966, sends more than 3,000 Boston students to dozens of suburban districts that voluntarily participate in the program, with nearly $30 million per year in state funding. There is also a small Springfield program that sends about 100 students to four suburban communities.

According to the Tufts study, Metco students from 1990 to 2020 were more likely to attend college and went on to earn more money than their peers in Boston Public Schools, adding to a body of research supporting the program’s academic benefits.

Metco has had just two leaders in the last fifty years, with Jean McGuire, who helped found the program spearheading it for more than four decades at the helm before Arbaje-Thomas took over. Arbaje-Thomas previously spent 15 years managing neighborhood antipoverty programs for Action for Boston Community Development.

A search committee featuring board members, as well as Metco families and staff, will be formed and is expected to appoint a new president and CEO by September. Arbaje-Thomas said she is focused on supporting Metco and ensuring a smooth transition and has not begun exploring her next options.

In a statement, Board Chairman Darnell Billings praised Arbaje-Thomas’s leadership and her advocacy for the program.

“She never missed an opportunity to meet with national and state legislators and community leaders, fostering outstanding collaborations and making clear the significant social impact of METCO on the lives of those involved,” Billings said. “We are so proud of the many accomplishments achieved during her tenure and wish her the very best in the future.”

During Arbaje-Thomas’s tenure, the organization opened a new headquarters in Roxbury and transitioned from a first-come-first-serve enrollment process to a lottery system, with a goal of making the program fairer. And the state has added about $8 million to the program’s annual budget.

Dan Gutekanst, the superintendent of Needham Public Schools and a member of the Metco board who was involved in hiring Arbaje-Thomas, said she has been critical in securing legislative support and increased funding for the program.

“Milly has transformed Metco in ways that have been very positive for students,” he said. “All the work that she has done needs to be continued and deepened.”

With rising costs, particularly for transportation, recent increases in state funding have not been enough for Metco to grow its enrollment, which has long sat a bit over 3,000. Each year, Arbaje-Thomas said in 2023, they have about 1,200 applicants and space for 300 new students. Per-pupil costs to participating districts can be more than double the state reimbursement rate.

Vanesa Morales, a Dorchester mother whose son attends ninth grade in Wellesley through Metco, praised the program and Arbaje-Thomas’s work promoting it.

“She was always pushing forth for Metco and encouraging parents to advocate,” Morales said.

But she worried about any vacuum at the organization in a time when diversity efforts in education are under threat from the federal government. Metco is open to all Boston children and includes white students, but was founded with an explicit goal of racial integration and most participants continue to be students of color.

Kemeisha Daley, another Dochester parent whose daughter attends Reading Public Schools as part of the Metco program, said her daughter has benefited from the academic environment, but has experienced racism. Daley said she would like Metco’s central leadership to play a bigger role in supporting families at the ground level.

“At least at the start of the school year or end of the school year, we could have a meeting to talk about what’s going well, what could work better for our children, and what we think should change ... at each district,” Daley said.

Parents and advocates have reported increasing incidents of racism to Metco students from classmates and educators in recent years, and the organization has developed an “Antiracism Road Map,” Metco 2.0, to support district-level inclusion in the wake of the 2020 racial reckoning.

title: Nine Walgreens in Massachusetts are set to close by the end of April. Here’s where they are.
text:
“Increased regulatory and reimbursement pressures are weighing on our ability to cover the costs associated with rent, staffing, and supply needs,” the spokesperson said. “It is never an easy decision to close a store, and we know how important they are to the communities we serve, and therefore do everything possible to improve their performance.”

The Massachusetts stores set to shut their doors are located at 38 W Main Street in Norton, closing on March 17; 525 Boston Post Road E in Marlborough, closing on March 18; 85 Huttleston Avenue in Fairhaven, closing on March 19; 99 Westfield Street in West Springfield, closing on March 20; 32 Union Street in Easthampton, closing on March 25; 625 Massachusetts Avenue in Cambridge, closing on March 27; 757 Gallivan Boulevard in Boston and 800 River Street in Haverhill, both closing on April 28; and 256 Pleasant Street in Methuen, closing on April 29.

In recent months, Walgreens locations in West Roxbury, Quincy, Weston, Hyannis, Athol, and Springfield have also shut their doors.

This is not the first time the Boston area has seen a number of Walgreens locations disappear in quick succession. In recent years, a spate of the chain’s closures in predominantly Black and Latino areas — Mattapan, Hyde Park, and Roxbury — prompted backlash and protests from community members and elected officials.

A Globe analysis last year found that, at the time, almost 15,000 Boston residents lived in a ‘pharmacy desert’ — parts of the city where residents lack easy access to a place to pick up their prescriptions. These areas tended to be low-income, with large Black or Latino populations and below-average vehicle ownership.

The Walgreens spokesperson said that patients of the stores that are closing will be notified by mail. Their prescriptions will automatically be transferred to another nearby Walgreens store, or they can opt to fill them at any of the chain’s locations. Affected pharmacy customers will also be offered free medication delivery for 90 days after the closures, the spokesperson added.

Patients of the Central Square location are being directed to the Walgreens location at 330 River Street in Cambridge, about a half-mile walk away. Customers of the Dorchester location will have their prescriptions transferred to the Walgreens at 825 Morton Street, 2.5 miles away by foot — though there is another location, at 585 Washington Street, that is only a 1.8 mile walk away.

In the October earnings call in which he announced the mass store closures, Walgreens Boots Alliance CEO Tim Wentworth said that the company planned to “follow our historic practice to redeploy the majority of the workforce in those stores that we close.” Walgreens has also said it expected the closures to contribute about $100 million to the company’s adjusted operating income for fiscal year 2025, which ends on Aug. 31.

“Over time, these actions should also enable us to fund the investments we plan to make in higher performing stores as we look to improve our customers’ in store experience,” Manmohan Mahajan, the global chief financial officer of Walgreens Boots Alliance, said in the October earnings call. “For this year, we’re prioritizing investment in those stores that should be the recipient of the scripts, merchandise, and the foot traffic from the stores we’re closing.”

Walgreens Boots Alliance’s most recent quarterly earnings report saw a sales uptick to $39.5 billion, though operating losses — fueled by the costs involved in store closures — swelled to $245 million, compared to $39 million in the same period the year prior.

Just last week, Walgreens Boots Alliance announced it would be acquired by Sycamore Partners, a private equity firm, in a deal with an equity value of just shy of $10 billion.

Due to incorrect information provided to the Globe, an earlier version of this story misstated the number of Walgreens locations scheduled to close in Massachusetts.

title: Dancer Ananth Udupa roots his philosophy in the Natyashastra, an ancient Sanskrit treatise on the performing arts
text:
When Ananth Udupa was 7 and growing up in Phoenix, he underwent a Hindu rite of passage for boys of higher castes called an Upanayana. The ceremony, which goes back millennia, in some ways delineates what it means to be a responsible Hindu man. He plans to perform his work-in-progress “Upanayana Project” at Danza Orgánica’s “We Create 2025: The Movements that Free(d) Us,” which takes place April 4 and 5.

“There are parts of the ritual where it’s the last time, technically, your mother is allowed to feed you,” Udupa said. “The messages are very clear. To eat in silence, to live a life of solitude, to dedicate yourself to the religion.”

It didn’t all sit right with Udupa, who specializes in Bharatanatyam, an Indian dance style historically associated with female courtesans. He was already studying it in dance school, the only boy among dozens of girls.

The “Upanayana Project” blends “that history and my lived experience as a queer child being asked to renounce his femininity, his queerness,” Udupa said.

Where to find him: www.instagram.com/ananth._udupa

Age: 25

Lives in: Medford

Making a living: Formerly a cultural planner at the Metropolitan Area Planning Council, Udupa is pursuing a master’s degree in city planning at MIT, where he’s a research assistant.

Studio: The Dance Complex in Cambridge.

How he started: The choreographer didn’t consider himself an artist until after college, at a program run by the dance nonprofit Monkeyhouse. He found himself thinking, “‘Wait, no, I’m proud of this,’” he recalled. He began “acknowledging my background in dance as of value for myself and also for the world.”

What he makes: He looks to the Natyashastra, an ancient Sanskrit treatise on the performing arts.

“Emotions, or rasa, which translates to ‘the eternal nectar,’ is the tool through which the dancer attains enlightenment, and in that moment shares it with the audience,” Udupa said. “It is in communicating story through gesture, through movement, and in community that we heal.”

How he works: With “Upanayana Project,” Udupa said, “it’s been a process of ‘I have an idea, but I don’t have the words for it,’ and then slowly starting to find words. Working on a little bit of movement, maybe finding some music and then taking a pause.”

In the pause, he researched the ritual’s history and interviewed scholars and initiates. From there, it’s back to the studio. “Now I have all this material that’s circling in my brain that I can begin to create with,” Udupa said.

That might entail writing an improvisational score or drawing out movements. “Sometimes it’s just moving and letting the body do the work,” he said.

Advice for artists: “Pause and listen to what comes from the spirit,” he said, “and trust its truth.”

WE CREATE 2025: THE MOVEMENTS THAT FREE(D) US

At Hibernian Hall, 184 Dudley St., Roxbury, April 4 and 5. Presented by Danza Orgánica. www.danzaorganica.org/we-create-festival.php

Cate McQuaid can be reached at catemcquaid@gmail.com. Follow her on Instagram @cate.mcquaid.

title: Myechia Minter-Jordan heads to D.C. to lead the AARP, advocate for Social Security
text:
Minter-Jordan started in the chief executive job in November, taking over for Jo Ann Jenkins, leading an organization with around 39 million members, about 2,700 employees, and annual revenue of $1.7 billion. She said she took the job in part because it would allow her to have an even broader national impact than where she previously worked, the CareQuest Institute for Oral Health. But doing so means she’ll leave Boston: She already has a home in Washington, where AARP is headquartered, and is putting her family’s West Roxbury home on the market.

She’ll miss the incredible network she established in Boston, led by other prominent people of color such as Bennie Wiley and Carol Fulp. Minter-Jordan moved here in 2007 from Baltimore to be chief medical officer at the Dimock Center in Roxbury, and eventually became its chief executive. She also became a mover and shaker in Boston, and helped launch the New Commonwealth Fund for racial equity and social justice in 2020.

Boston, she said, can be a hard place to break into as an executive, because it’s a city with a firmly entrenched power structure.

“I’m grateful for all the support I received from many of those people,” Minter-Jordan said of her Boston network. “When you have that network, it really supports you as a leader.”

The grand opening of a 202-unit apartment building in Jamaica Plain last week marked a big victory for Lyndia Downie, her team at the Pine Street Inn, and her development partners at The Community Builders.

After all, with 140 apartments for people who will continue to receive support from Pine Street Inn as they move out of homelessness, the project represented the largest such development in New England.

It also represented a victory for Corporate Boston — by showing what can happen when many of the city’s largest employers band together. Corporate donors kicked in more than $6 million toward a $10 million initiative known as the Way Home Fund, providing financial support for services at the JP building that range from helping people establish credit scores to ensuring they’re current with medical appointments.

The initiative began as then-mayor Martin J. Walsh started his second term as mayor in 2018. He led the effort to prod some big names to open their checkbooks, Downie said. Five committed to $1 million each: MassMutual, Bank of America, Liberty Mutual, Mass General Brigham, and Suffolk Construction. Other donors included TD Bank, Eastern Bank, Eversource, Related Beal, and Natixis. (Separately from the fund, developer HYM Investment Group kicked in $5 million as a linkage payment to the city, to help win approval for its massive Government Center project called Bulfinch Crossing.)

While he knows of examples in other US cities, The Community Builders chief executive Bart Mitchell said this is the first time he’s seen a corporate fund-drive of this scope for a project like this in Boston.

TCB developed the $105 million project and assembled the financing, which included money from federal tax credit investors as well as state and city subsidies. Formerly homeless residents in the 140 units pay one-third of their income for rent; the 62 remaining units in the building (dubbed “The Lyndia” in honor of Downie’s career fighting homelessness as Pine Street Inn’s president) are available at subsidized rates to lower-income earners. The 166,000-square-foot building at 3368 Washington St. opened in November, but the principals waited until many tenants moved in before holding a public celebration.

“The opening of the JP building, it really was a huge community effort,” Downie said. “It is the best of who we are, in my opinion, when we can make all these things happen, and get at a really sticky problem. The fact that the corporations are willing to support this, it gives us a lot of confidence in the model and confidence that maybe we can replicate this.”

Ron Dickerman always figured he would return to Massachusetts after leaving for business school at Columbia University in the 1980s. Instead, he stayed in New York, first working in investment banking, and then in private equity.

But the Lexington native does return for one important reason: to shop for real estate investment opportunities.

Dickerman just inked a deal for his private equity firm, Madison International Realty, to buy a 50 percent stake in Legacy Place, the nearly 500,000-square-foot open-air shopping center in Dedham. Dickerman’s firm acquired the stake held by Nuveen in the partnership that owns Legacy Place, for an undisclosed amount. The other partners are WS Development and the Redstone family’s National Amusements Inc., which jointly developed the project more than 15 years ago. (Madison and WS are also partners in MarketStreet Lynnfield, and Madison also is investing in lab developer IQHQ’s Fenway Center project.)

Despite the rise of online shopping, Dickerman is still a big believer in bricks-and-mortar. He notes that Legacy draws regular customers from as far away as 30 miles, because of the tenant mix — it’s essentially full — and the experience. The retail sector appears to be stabilizing, particularly because so few new shopping centers were built across the country in recent years.

“There’s been so much dislocation with Amazon and home delivery,” Dickerman said. “In our view, retail is finally starting to catch an equilibrium.”

Scratch X, formerly known as Twitter, off the list of social media sites for local publicity firm John Guilfoil Public Relations.

JGPR sent out an email last month announcing it would no longer recommend the site to its public safety clients. The reason? It has nothing to do with the controversies surrounding owner Elon Musk and his chaotic attempts to dismantle much of the federal government. Instead, the site simply isn’t getting anywhere near the engagement levels it once did.

Founder John Guilfoil said a survey by his firm drew responses from nearly 150 police, fire, and municipal government agencies across the country, along with 17 news outlets, from mid-December to mid-February. Nearly 40 percent said their use of Twitter/X has greatly decreased in the past two years, and roughly three-fourths said they interact with a member of the public on it less than once a month. “We would have been measuring that in a matter of minutes or hours with a client five years ago,” he said.

One big reason: In early 2023, soon after Musk’s buyout, Twitter announced it would no longer grant users free access to its Application Programming Interface platform, making it more difficult to use, particularly with other digital tools.

Guilfoil still recommends that clients use Facebook, and LinkedIn is helpful because it’s usually not blocked by workplace firewalls. While he said the survey has been accused of being part of a left-wing conspiracy, he simply wants to be an effective communications rep for clients.

“History tells us,” Guilfoil says, “that every one of these internet services will eventually disappear and die.”

title: Free things to do this week: An Alvin Ailey dance class, game and trivia nights, folk music, and more
text:
If you spent Sunday cheering on the St. Patrick’s Day parade and/or hitting up your local Irish pub, you may be in the mood for some quieter cultural events. Thankfully, the Boston scene offers plenty of wallet-friendly ways to mellow out this week. From dance classes to folk performances, here are some free things to do this week in Boston.

YOUTH ART AT CITY HALL The next great American painter may have an original piece hanging at Boston’s City Hall. The building’s walls have been filled with artwork from K-12 Boston Public School students, bringing colorful, youthful energy to the Boston landmark. This is the 31st annual Youth Art Month exhibition, this time displaying pieces from more than 300 of the city’s students. Mondays-Fridays, 9 a.m.-5 p.m. 1 City Hall Square. boston.gov

INDIE TRIVIA Boston’s local trivia scene is active, with many bars devoting nights to contests. At Aeronaut Brewery’s Indie Trivia Night on Tuesdays, the twist is that anyone can assume the role of host. As host, you supply your own set of questions — whether themed or spanning multiple genres — and watch as the competition unfolds in the brewing room. Join Aeronaut’s Facebook group for the chance to curate a future game. March 18, 8-11 p.m. 14 Tyler St., Somerville. aeronautbrewing.com

BINGO, YAHTZEE, UNO! LiteWork Events hosts old-school monthly game nights at Piano Craft Gallery for community members, providing card and board games, ping pong, and more multi-player activities to encourage connection through friendly competition. “Through its events and special programs, LiteWork highlights the power of social interaction within the young, urban demographic,” as the group’s website explains it.March 19, 6-10:30 p.m. 793 Tremont St. pianocraftgallery.com

SHARE THE LOVE Romance novels have come into their own, and the chance to attend book signings and Q&As are plentiful throughout Boston — no tickets required. All She Wrote, a Somerville-based book shop, is teaming up with Emerson College to host a talk and book signing with author TJ Alexander, whose newest historical romance, “A Gentleman’s Gentleman,” centers trans identity in Regency England. March 20, 6 p.m. Emerson Bill Bordy Theater, 216 Tremont St. allshewrotebooks.com

REVELATIONS The Alvin Ailey American Dance Theatre was founded on the principle that everyone can dance — an ideology they’re bringing to Boston with the help of Celebrity Series. The Manhattan-based dance studio will be on site at four Boston community centers — Hyde Park, Mattapan, Roxbury, and Dorchester — to teach locals the company’s signature performance, “Revelations.” This weekend, dancers of all experience levels (including zero) can join former company dancers Renee Robinson and Amos Machanic Jr. and percussionist Roderick Jackson for a day of learning and movement. March 22 and 23, class times vary. Register at celebrityseries.org

KIDS GATHER ‘ROUND This Saturday, Lovestruck Books in Harvard Square will be holding its first children’s storytime event with author Christine Carlucci Evans. Evans will read from her book “Worry Cloud,” an early readers book created to help children acknowledge and manage their stress. Evans will also introduce her newest book, “Breathe In, Breathe Out. It’ll All Work Out” another calming, interactive book for children. March 22, 10:30 a.m. 44 Brattle St., Cambridge. lovestruckbooks.com

CREATING NEW TRADITIONS Reclaiming Folk, a Massachusetts-based organization centering POC folk musicians, returns with its second year of programming. Performances by Mass. artists Naomi Westwater, Grace Givertz, and Kim Moberg will be held at the Boston Public Library in Copley Square. Then, Boston’s Poet Laureate Porsha Olayiwola will lead a talk with the performers about their experiences and artistry. March 22, 1-3 p.m. Boston Public Library, Rabb Hall, 700 Boylston St. bpl.bibliocommons.com

Marianna Orozco can be reached at marianna.orozco@globe.com.

title: Cleanup underway at Roxbury debris facility after 8-alarm fire
text:
Cleanup work began at a construction and demolition debris facility in Roxbury on Monday, a day after an eight-alarm fire caused millions in damage.

The cause of the fire at ReSource Waste Services of Roxbury on Gerard Street, is under investigation, said Brian Alkins, a fire department spokesperson.

Five firefighters were taken to the hospital Sunday with injuries that were not life-threatening. They have since been released from the hospital, Alkins said.

Fire officials said the blaze caused an estimated $4 million in damage. About 150 firefighters responded to the facility and faced windy conditions and limited visibility as large plumes of smoke rose into the air.

Fire officials urged residents Sunday to close their windows and doors to keep the smoke out. On Monday, the city’s public health commission said it was safe to reopen windows and turn HVAC systems back on.

“This morning, our environmental health team conducted an air quality sweep of the Orchard Garden area & surrounding blocks. Air quality has returned to normal with no odors or particulate matter present,” the commission wrote on social media.

Firefighters left the facility around 8 a.m. Monday, nearly 24 hours after the fire broke out.

The fire was contained to a warehouse building where construction debris, including wood, metal, and concrete, was burning inside, said Dave Newman, a spokesperson for ReSource Waste Services, which owns the Roxbury transfer station and several other facilities in New England.

The company’s website says it handles a “wide variety of solid, non-hazardous construction and demolition materials from waste handlers, contractors, roofers, landscapers, property managers, clean-out companies and homeowners.”

Newman said workers were let back into the facility on Monday morning after the fire was finally extinguished and began removing debris, which will be sorted and hauled to sites outside of Boston.

“As the building is cleared, inspectors and structural engineers will assess damage and recommend next steps,” Newman said in an email.

“ReSource is grateful that no one was seriously hurt and for the support they have received from the community,” he added.

In a statement on Sunday, ReSource Waste Services chief executive Jack Canty thanked firefighters for their response.

“We’re thankful that no one was hurt and appreciate the Boston Fire Department’s response in getting the incident under control,” Canty said.

The facility was closed on Sunday, so there was no need for evacuations, he said.

Nick Stoico can be reached at nick.stoico@globe.com.

title: Mass. schools relied on federal aid to buy farm-fresh foods for students’ meals. Then Trump cut it.
text:
But the Trump administration earlier this month suddenly slashed the federal funding for the program, which boosted the amount of fresh produce schools provided to students. Massachusetts was due to receive another $12 million in fiscal 2026 for local schools before it was canceled, leaving school nutrition officials scrambling to find alternative funding or risk a reduction of fresh fruits and vegetables served with school meals.

“It was a catalyst to provide local fresh produce to students at a capacity we had never done before,” said Brandon Rabbitt, a board member of the School Nutrition Association of Massachusetts, which represents more than 900 school administrators. “It’s a large blow for next year, we’re scrambling to figure out what we’re going to do.”

Districts across the state already are facing stark financial outlooks as they grapple with inflation, the loss of federal pandemic aid, and increased costs for transportation. As many are weighing staff cuts or asking voters to approve a property tax override, it’s unlikely the schools can pay for the produce on their own.

Simca Horwitz, the co-director of Massachusetts Farm to School, a nonprofit that works to help farms sell fresh produce directly to local schools, said the abrupt end to the program forces schools to try to find other sources of funding to buy farm-fresh food.

“It just makes it a lot more difficult,” Horwitz said.

Yrmaris Matias, 39, whose son attends the John D. O’Bryant School of Mathematics and Science in Roxbury, said she’s worried about the end of the grant program.

Matias is a member of the school’s parent council, and said some migrant families are afraid of going to food banks due to Trump’s immigration crackdown, and rely on their kids getting healthy food in school. Some other families who rely on food stamps also worry BPS could be forced to scale back its healthy offerings, and their budgets won’t be able to make up the difference, she said.

“It doesn’t make sense for them to take [the grant] away, because we have to think about these families that are really having difficulties,” Matias said.

On March 7, the US Department of Agriculture announced more than $1 billion in funding cuts for a pair of programs that helped schools, food banks, and child care centers cover the cost of locally produced fresh foods.

The decision to end the short-lived program came after the USDA’s Agricultural Marketing Service determined it “no longer effectuates agency priorities,” according to a copy of the termination letter for the grant agreement with the state education department.

A USDA spokesperson told the Globe in a statement the grant program was a pandemic-era program, and the agency would “return to long-term, fiscally responsible” initiatives rather than short-term programs like the Local Food for Schools program, which had no plan for longevity.

The USDA already has 16 nutrition programs in place, the spokesperson said, and remains committed to its core mission of “strengthening food security, supporting agricultural markets, and ensuring access to nutritious food.”

The grant cut is separate from the state’s universal free school meals program and the National School Lunch Program, which remain intact. However, the Local Food for Schools provided districts with additional money for healthy food purchases, the state’s K-12 education department has said.

In Massachusetts, it was used in coordination with the state’s universal free meals program, which was implemented in 2023 to permanently make breakfast and lunch available to all students without cost.

The grant previously allowed schools to buy more fresh fruits and vegetables from local growers like Joe Czajkowski, whose family farm in Hadley supplies fresh produce to public schools in Boston, Chicopee, Springfield, and Greenfield, plus several area food banks.

Big sellers for schools include carrots, butternut squash, black beans, onions, apples, and potatoes, Czajkowski said. And the grant supports the local economy of the Connecticut Valley, where his 400-acre farm is located, he said.

“The money stays in the local community, the jobs are local, more land stays open for agriculture,” he said. Food has to travel less distance to customers, saving on fuel. “It’s better for the environment,” he said.

BPS spends about 15 percent of its $16 million food budget locally, and is working to increase that to 30 percent, according to the district. Before it ended, the district was expecting an additional $250,000 for next year, administrators said. Despite the cancellation, the district said it is confident it can continue providing fresh, nutritious meals daily.

At the Baldwin school in Brighton, Alexis Assad, the BPS culinary manager, lists off locally sourced menu items, including potatoes, broccoli, and black beans.

When it’s in season, the school also offers a veggie burger made from locally-sourced kelp. Even the pizza is local, produced by Sal’s Pizza. (The recipe is adapted for schools, so the dough, sauce, and cheese used in the pizzas meet the schools’ nutritional standards, Assad said.)

“If something just comes out of a bag, it’s not what we’re looking for,” Assad said. “We’re always looking to push the boundaries, and use something as fresh as can be.”

Min-Jen Taylor, the principal, has seen a dramatic improvement in the quality of school meals during her 25 years as an educator, she said.

“Healthy food keeps the kids healthy, so they will come to school regularly, and they’ll be ready to work,” Taylor said. “That’s important for teachers and for families.”

title: Amid zoning debate, advocates press for Roxbury birth center
text:
Tracy Rich

Jamaica Plain

I was glad to see your editorial about the proposed Neighborhood Birth Center near Nubian Square. I am a longtime Roxbury resident and was extremely disappointed when I heard that the Zoning Board of Appeal had turned down the center’s request for a variance.

I live in the Highland Park neighborhood, about a mile from Nubian Square. I have visited the proposed site and to me it seems appropriate for the center. The area is mixed use, it’s close to public transportation, and it would offer a much-needed option to women facing an important event and turning point in their lives.

It would be a point of pride for us in Roxbury to see such a facility become available, and I think it would be a tremendous addition to the overall sense of community that is developing around Nubian Square. There have been many obstacles in the effort to revitalize the area. The birth center would be a positive force in the neighborhood.

Eleanor Foote

Roxbury

Proponents of the Neighborhood Birth Center purchased properties within the Moreland Street Historic District, a nationally recognized residential community governed by Article 50 of the Boston Zoning Code. Article 50-28 explicitly lists clinic and office spaces as forbidden uses, ensuring the district remains residential.

This is not about opposition to a birthing center but, rather, about preserving zoning integrity. Approving this variance would set a dangerous precedent, encouraging further commercial encroachment into residential areas. Zoning laws exist to protect communities from disruptive land-use changes that could erode neighborhood stability, increase traffic congestion, and strain local infrastructure.

Granting the request would have not only violated existing regulations but also undermined any trust between residents and city planning authorities. It would disregard the voices of longstanding residents who have worked to maintain the district’s historical and residential integrity.

The Roxbury Neighborhood Council strongly appreciates the Zoning Board of Appeal’s decision to uphold the integrity of residential zoning regulations and protect the community’s future.

Connie Forbes

Chair

Roxbury Neighborhood Council

The Zoning Board of Appeal hearing on Feb. 25 wasn’t the first time the Matahari Women Workers’ Center has been edged out of Roxbury. In 2018, we moved into a small office at 996 Tremont St. for its proximity to Melnea Cass Boulevard, a landmark honoring a movement ancestor who fought for domestic workers’ rights. At $1,150 per month, it became a hub for our staff and members. Since rising rents forced us to close our doors in 2022, we’ve been “desk surfing” for free at one of our funders’ offices in Boston, but this is temporary.

The Community Movement Commons project that includes the Neighborhood Birth Center and other organizations would provide us with a stable home, including a 200-square-foot office and a larger community room for healing circles, contract negotiations, and workers’ rights trainings, critical resources for the working-class, migrant women of color we organize. With a fixed office cost of $2,000, this would be an affordable, sustainable option given Boston’s rising rents.

We urge Mayor Michelle Wu and other city officials to meet with the Community Movement Commons and create a path forward. Matahari and its partners would build on Roxbury’s legacy of social movement led by women of color, expanding access to health care and advancing justice.

Laura González

Co-director

Matahari Women Workers’ Center

Boston

I became a maternal health advocate the day I became a mother, more than 21 years ago. After experiencing an unexpected and potentially life-threatening postpartum hemorrhage following the birth of my daughter, I have dedicated my life to advancing maternal health both in the United States and globally.

In 2010, I founded the nonprofit organization Every Mother Counts with the vision to make the maternal health journey safe, equitable, and respectful for every mother, everywhere. For the last 15 years, the organization has worked to advance community-based, evidence-driven maternal health solutions, including midwifery-led birth center care, and has been a proud supporter of the Neighborhood Birth Center since 2022.

Midwifery-led birth centers provide high-quality, person-centered, and cost-effective care and are a critical solution to ending the maternal health crisis in our country. Massachusetts families deserve access to the full range of maternity care options, including the culturally responsive midwifery care the Neighborhood Birth Center plans to offer, informed by nearly 10 years of intentionality, expertise, and vision.

Christy Turlington Burns

Founder and president

Every Mother Counts

New York

title: The Boston Harbor cleanup showed the power of the EPA — when it’s willing to use it.
text:
For veterans of environmental campaigns in New England, the harbor cleanup is a poignant reminder of what the EPA can do when it’s well-funded, has strong political backing, and is committed to confronting polluters. A weakened and underfunded EPA, they fear, won’t be so willing and instead might let long-running water quality projects, such as the cleanup of the Charles River, lapse.

“You have to have both the will and the ways to enforce the law,” said John DeVillars, who was the regional EPA administrator in New England in the late 1990s. “Sadly, for the next four years, it doesn’t look like we’re going to have that.”

President Trump’s EPA administrator, Lee Zeldin, has promised to slash the agency’s total spending by 65 percent, and last week it was reported that the agency’s scientific research and development office could be eliminated. The EPA did not respond to questions about what programs would be cut. However, Trump officials are almost certainly eyeing cuts to water quality and pollution control projects that were funded by congressional spending packages passed during the Biden administration.

“We don’t want the extra money, and we don’t need it,” Zeldin said in a recent video on social media.

In Boston, a long-held goal to make every section of local rivers clean enough for public swimming remains just out of reach, and former EPA regulators told the Globe dramatic cuts could jeopardize efforts to stop stormwater and wastewater pollution from entering Boston-area watersheds.

Despite the decades of improvements, some old and problematic sewage systems remain in place. And, when heavy rainstorms overwhelm those systems, pollution spills into rivers and streams.

“Environmental protection doesn’t come cheap, but it pays enormous dividends,” said DeVillars, who oversaw several major cleanups across Massachusetts.

Boston Harbor was essentially used as a sewer for more than a century before a 1983 lawsuit brought by the Conservation Law Foundation and the City of Quincy forced a cleanup. The EPA became a plaintiff in the case that forced Massachusetts to act.

At the time, hundreds of millions of gallons of sewage and 100 tons of sludge poured into the harbor every day. Oil, heavy metals, and other pollutants came with that sludge: 441 pounds of lead per day.

“It was horrific,” said Kathy Abbott, chief executive of Boston Harbor Now who worked as a park ranger in the Boston Harbor Islands in the early 1980s. “Imagine several million toilets worth of excrement bubbling up into the harbor.”

When she lived on a small island working for the park, Abbott saw and smelled the effects each evening. Each morning, as Abbott made her island rounds, she would pick up hundreds of tampon applicators that had washed ashore overnight.

The cleanup, overseen by Federal Judge A. David Mazzone, required a massive, new sewage-treatment plant on Deer Island. The cost was $3.7 billion, financed by increased water rates, state funds, and federal EPA grants.

“Even though the state — and me, specifically — were on the other side of the lawsuit, it immediately became a collaborative effort to get the job done,” said James Hoyte, who was Massachusetts secretary of environmental affairs at the time. He later led the Massachusetts Water Resources Authority, the entity ordered by Mazzone to complete the cleanup.

Cleaning up the harbor “seemed almost inconceivable,” Hoyte said, and “it could not have happened” without the EPA’s involvement.

“Where was the money going to come from?” Hoyte said. “The magnitude of the cost really demanded federal participation.”

Meanwhile, further inland, the Charles River was so polluted that anyone who fell into the water was advised to immediately go to a hospital for a tetanus shot. Public beaches on the Charles have been closed since 1949.

The transformation of the harbor came about not just because of more investment, but from tighter regulations. Under Trump, the EPA is instead moving to weaken dozens of national environmental rules, including those for development in wetlands and wastewater discharges from power plants. Those rules will have to be changed through a lengthy administrative process that involves a public comment period.

Zeldin said in a statement that “we remain committed to clean air, land, and water,” but believes deregulation will reduce costs.

Prior to Trump taking office, the New England EPA office proposed new rules on local businesses to better control stormwater runoff that pollutes the Charles, Mystic, and Neponset River watersheds.

The Charles is now safe to swim in much of the time, thanks to regulatory crackdowns on illegal dumping and sewage overflows, and some experts believe water quality has improved enough that Boston can plan for reopening its beaches. Still, concentrations of E. coli spike after rainstorms and blue-green algae blooms sometimes occur in the summer. Reducing stormwater pollution, regulators had hoped, would prevent recurrences.

The EPA’s legacy in Boston also includes cracking down on air pollution, trash burning, and abandoned hazardous waste. It forced businesses, municipalities, and states to clean up toxic substances and often helped finance those efforts. In the last 30 years, the EPA has spent more than $200 million cleaning so-called brownfield pollution sites in Massachusetts, including more than a dozen in Boston, mostly in Roxbury and Dorchester.

Some cleanups were politically charged. When New England’s EPA office began to pressure GE to clean up the Housatonic River in Western Massachusetts in the 1990s, Jack Welch, the company’s powerful chief executive, rang DeVillars, then the EPA regional administrator.

“Before we go to war, we should talk,” Welch told him, DeVillars recalled.

The talk didn’t go far. Welch visited his office; DeVillars reiterated the EPA had to enforce the law. That’s when Welch apparently called friends in Washington.

US Senators John Kerry and Edward M. Kennedy called, concerned the EPA was playing too tough with the powerful GE executive, DeVillars said.

“Welch and GE put every ounce of legal and political pressure that they could,” DeVillars said. He told the senators: “We’re enforcing the law.”

GE has since spent hundreds of millions of dollars on the Housatonic River cleanup, removing toxic industrial chemicals called PCBs and restoring wetlands. Cleanup efforts downstream of Pittsfield continue to this day.

“This all came from strong enforcement action and holding the line against one of the most influential companies in the country,” DeVillars said.

Hoyte, the former state environmental secretary, also pointed out that budget cuts at the EPA could weaken state agencies such as the Massachusetts Department of Environmental Protection, which receives one-third of its funding from the federal government.

On a recent sunny March day in downtown Boston, in a scene unfathomable before the cleanup effort, several tourists sat on benches overlooking the harbor at Christopher Columbus Waterfront Park. Unaware of the putrid smells that once came from these waters, the visitors told the Globe that the water looks “nice and welcoming.”

Nearby, a welcome center for the Boston Harbor Islands National Recreation Area encourages visitors to “take a dip at the beach” on Spectacle Island, once a rat-infested garbage dump.

“After all,” the promotional sign notes, “Boston has one of the cleanest urban harbors in the nation.”

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
TOMMY RICHMAN: THE COYOTE TOUR The man behind last summer’s lo-fi-funk left-field hit “MILLION DOLLAR BABY” comes to town in support of his 2024 album “COYOTE,” where he offers up 21st-century updates of roller skating jams (the glitchy “WHITNEY”) and Quiet Storm balladry (the pleading “THOUGHT YOU WERE THE ONE”). March 21, 7 p.m. Paradise Rock Club. 617-562-8800, crossroadspresents.com
