BLUSHER This Melbourne pop trio’s new single “Racer” is a sweetly sour confection, with atmosphere-shrouded verses that give way to a brisk, declarative chorus. They open for the Swedish EDM duo NOTD. March 22, 9:30 p.m., Big Night Live. bignight.com

AN EVENING WITH IDA & TSUNAMI: COIN TOSS TOUR 2025 The methodical, harmony-rich New York band Ida and the exuberantly riff-heavy D.C. outfit Tsunami were two gems of the ‘90s independent rock scene, with Tsunami’s label Simple Machines releasing records by both acts back in the day. In celebration of the archival label Numero Group reissuing their music, they’re embarking on a collaborative tour where they’ll sit in on each others’ songs and welcome special guests as they play selections from their top-quality catalogs. March 23, 7 p.m. Crystal Ballroom at Somerville Theatre, Somerville. crystalballroomboston.com

MAURA JOHNSTON

CIMARRON 615 They are a Nashville band with SoCal lineage, with members having done time in various editions of Poco and the Flying Burrito Brothers. Their name incorporates both roots, “615” standing for Nashville, and “Cimarron” pointing to one of Poco’s signature songs, “Rose of Cimarron.” March 21, 7:30 p.m. $50. Firehouse Center for the Arts, 1 Market Square, Newburyport. 978-452-7336. www.firehouse.org

LOGAN LEDGER I’ve been waiting a long time to do a show pick on this guy — ever since the early days of the pandemic put the kibosh on a scheduled appearance. He (finally) brings his Orbisonesque croon and country noir sensibilities to the area to play solo this Wednesday. Ex-Old Crow Medicine Show member Mason Via opens. March 26, 8 p.m. $25. Club Passim, 47 Palmer St., Cambridge. 617-492-7679. www.passim.org

SIRIYA ENSEMBLE This Afro-Persian group hails from Bushehr, Iran, and is guided by the intention of reimagining the traditional folk music of South Iran by fusing it with contemporary sounds. The group comes to Cambridge as part of its debut tour of the US. March 27, 8 p.m. $49. Sonia, 10 Brookline St., Cambridge. www.ticketweb.com

STUART MUNRO

JAVON JACKSON QUARTET The acclaimed tenor saxophonist and his band celebrate the legacy of the late, great American poet Nikki Giovanni. They’ll be performing Hollywood-associated numbers from the Great American Songbook, as featured on Jackson’s second collaborative recording with Giovanni, 2024’s “Javon And Nikki Go to the Movies.” March 22, 7 p.m. $48.05-$64.85. Scullers. scullersjazz.com

KNICKERBOCKER ALL-STARS The acclaimed horn-driven, 9-piece band includes some of New England’s most seasoned blues players, who have performed and recorded with everyone from Freddie King to Marcia Ball to Jimmie Vaughan. March 22, 8 p.m. $22.50-$25. Spire Center, 25½ Court St., Plymouth. spirecenter.org

NEWTON PIANO SUMMIT The free concert series continues with two more sets by two more pianists. Cuban-born Camila Cortina Belo’s work masterfully reconfigures the melodies and rhythms of her heritage through jazz, classical, and world music perspectives. Remarkable rising keyboard virtuoso Anastassia Petrova hails from Kazakhstan, and her music is influenced by the likes of Chick Corea, Thelonious Monk, and the folk tunes of her native country. March 23, 3 p.m. Free. Second Church in Newton, 60 Highland St., West Newton. next-arts.org

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA This weekend (March 21 and 22) the BSO presents a program arranged and curated by composer chair Carlos Simon featuring the music of jazz giant John Coltrane, conducted by Edwin Outwater with soloist Terence Blanchard, a veteran jazz trumpeter as well as composer of film scores (“Da 5 Bloods,” “BlackKklansman”) and operas (“Champion, “Fire Shut Up in My Bones”). Next week, conductor Dima Slobodeniouk leads the ensemble and the Tanglewood Festival Chorus in Mozart’s Requiem, paired with Arvo Pärt’s haunting “Tabula Rasa” featuring BSO violinists Alexander Velinzon and Lucia Lin (March 27-29). Symphony Hall. 617-266-1200, www.bso.org

BOSTON BAROQUE Soprano Erin Morley joins Boston Baroque for various concert arias by Mozart, and the Boston Baroque Orchestra plays Mozart’s “Haffner” Symphony and Beethoven’s Symphony No. 2, all under the leadership of music director Martin Pearlman. March 21, 8 p.m., Jordan Hall; March 22, 8 p.m., GBH Calderwood Studio, Brighton. 617-987-8600, www.baroque.boston

CALIDORE STRING QUARTET The New York-based quartet, which recently released the third and final installment of its Beethoven string quartet cycle on Signum Classics, visits Jordan Hall with a program that includes Beethoven’s String Quartet No. 10, “Harp,” as well as pieces by Schubert, Korngold, and Jessie Montgomery. Presented by Celebrity Series of Boston. March 23, 3 p.m. Jordan Hall. 617-482-2595, www.celebrityseries.org

A.Z. MADONNA

THE ADDAMS FAMILY A musical about the madcap and macabre clan created by New Yorker cartoonist Charles Addams, in which a now-grown-up Wednesday falls in love with a fellow from a “respectable” family. That’s not an adjective you’d apply to the Addamses. As you may have heard, they’re creepy and they’re kooky, mysterious and spooky, not to mention altogether ooky. So there’s a lot riding on the dinner the Addamses host for him and his parents. March 21-23. At Boch Center Wang Theatre. 800-877-7575, bochcenter.org

PARADE There’s an urgency to this sadly timely musical, which unfolds rapidly, as if there’s not a word, note, or moment to spare as it tells the story of Leo Frank (a superb Max Chernin). A Jewish superintendent at an Atlanta pencil factory, Frank was convicted in 1913 — wrongly, in the view of most historians — for the rape and murder of 13-year-old employee Mary Phagan. Amid an ugly atmosphere of antisemitism, Frank was kidnapped by a mob in 1915 and lynched. Book by Alfred Uhry, music and lyrics by Jason Robert Brown, and direction by Michael Arden. Through March 23. At Emerson Colonial Theatre. emersoncolonialtheatre.com

A MAN OF NO IMPORTANCE In and of itself, this production of the Terrence McNally-Lynn Ahrens-Stephen Flaherty musical is a small gem, traversing an emotional range from buoyant high spirits to the depths of melancholy, expertly performed by a cast that is equally persuasive in either mode of expression, and helmed by Paul Daigneault with his trademark vigor and flair. Beyond that, the production registers as a vivid reminder of what Daigneault and the theater company he founded 34 years ago have meant to the cultural life of the city. Season after season, SpeakEasy Stage Company has had the best batting average of any theater company in town. “A Man of No Importance” is the last show Daigneault will direct while leader of SpeakEasy before stepping down June 30. Through March 22. At Roberts Studio Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion, Boston Center for the Arts. 617-933-8600, www.SpeakEasyStage.com

DON AUCOIN

OUROBOROS Titled after an ancient healing symbol, Nejla Yatkin’s immersive, evening-length solo dance explores memory, cyclical time, and cultural paradox. Presented in the round, the work interweaves contemporary and Middle Eastern dance with multicultural storytelling and live cabaret-style song. The set is a nomadic-style tent and audiences are greeted with rosewater and Turkish delights. March 22-23. $17.85-$55.20. Dance Complex, Cambridge. www.dancecomplex.org/event/ouroboros

WORLD FIGURE SKATING CHAMPIONSHIPS Dancing across the floor is one thing, but dancing while flying across the ice takes a whole other skill set that can be breathtaking to watch. This year, the competition, which determines entry into the 2026 World Championships and the 2026 Winter Olympics, returns to Boston, and enthusiasts can buy tickets for a range of sessions, some of which are selling out fast. March 26-30. $36.50-$280. TD Garden. https://isuworlds2025.com/single-session-tickets/

LOOSE Laila Franklin’s new multidisciplinary work, created in collaboration with composer-sound designer David Dogan, reflects on the religious upbringings of Black, queer, and femme people in Black churches. Franklin says the work acts as both reckoning and intervention for “intersecting identities and formative experiences,” exploring the discomfort of bucking traditional practices and expectations as well as the freedom self-acceptance can bring. March 21-22. $15-$40. SomArt Space at the Hive, Somerville. https://somartspace.org/

NEWPORT CONTEMPORARY BALLET The company’s upcoming program, “Mystical Ways,” aims to unlock the power of secrets and evoke the magic of the mysterious. The mixed bill features world premieres by choreographers Marika Brussel, Shane Farrell, and the company’s artistic director, Danielle Genest. March 21-23. $32-$58. Keats Theatre/St. Andrew’s School, Barrington, R.I. https://newportcontemporaryballet.org/

KAREN CAMPBELL

WITNESSING HUMANITY: THE ART OF JOHN WILSON Bostonians might be most familiar with Wilson, born and raised in Roxbury, through “Eternal Presence,” the monumental, enigmatic bust that’s stood sentinel-like at the National Center of Afro-American Artists (NCAAA) in Roxbury since 1987. But Wilson, who died in 2015, spent decades before and after crafting socially conscious work around the pervasive issue of racial injustice in America that he experienced all his life. This exhibition, co-organized with New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, is the most substantial display of Wilson’s oeuvre ever assembled, and an opportunity for Boston to reckon with a powerful voice that echoes through generations of its social history. Through June 22. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, www.mfa.org

SARAH CWYNAR Using film, video, photography, and installation, Cwynar creates dizzying cascades of overlapping images that capture —and critique — the contemporary reality of an image-saturated consumer culture in hyperdrive. Art imitates life: Her work is as disorienting as it is seductive, a dark mirror to the smartphone-and-social media world that dominates contemporary society. Her show at the ICA features a brand-new two-part photo installation in collaboration with — how else to put it? — the whims of search-engine algorithms. Through Aug. 3. Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100, icaboston.org

WATERS OF THE ABYSS: AN INTERSECTION OF SPIRIT AND FREEDOM A full-scale “takeover” of the Gardner Museum by Fabiola Jean Louis — which means all three of the Gardner’s temporary exhibition spaces, including its billboard-size facade commission, will be in her hands — this show plumbs the depths of Haitian liberation, Vodou faith, and the artist’s roots in all of it. Through May 25. Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, 25 Evans Way. 617-566-1401, www.isgm.org

MURRAY WHYTE

MARTHA SCHNEE: RESERVED CHANNEL In the 18th century, much of Boston was a peninsula. The 19th century saw a boom in landfill and development. In this show, Schnee imagines the area in and around the Distillery Gallery had it never been filled in. What would be in the office? The boiler room? She creates a speculative species, the Tuning Fish, and takes viewers underwater in drawings, rubbings, prints, and sounds. Through April 12. Distillery Gallery, 516 East 2nd St., South Boston. www.distillery-gallery.com/exhibitions/2025/reservedchannel

CATE McQUAID

ROSLINDALE QUEER COMEDY NIGHT “My dad is Iranian, he taught me how to drive, and then I took driving classes at school that was primarily taught by Russian teachers,” says host Nora Panahi. “So I drive like an enemy of the state.” She welcomes Rita Mookerjee, LJ James, Marilyn Malibu, Shruti Datari, and Kathleen Meditz for this monthly showcase. March 21, 7:30 p.m. $18.40. The Rozzie Square Theater, 5 Basile St. 617-318-6376, www.rozziesquaretheater.com

FOIL ARMS & HOG: SKITTISH The Irish sketch comedy trio, known for their weekly YouTube videos on everything from the conversations the food stuffs in your fridge might have with each other to the problems an Englishman might have playing Risk, return to Boston with an all-new show. March 21, 8 p.m. $57.50. Boch Center Shubert Theatre, 265 Tremont St.www.bochcenter.org

JAYE MCBRIDE “I like a guy who tells me what he wants,” says McBride. “I love that. One of the best dates I ever had, he told me what he wanted. It was great. He just kept yelling, ‘Untie me and let me get back to my family!’ Oh, it was magical.” Hosted by Brieana Woodward, with Alex Giampapa. March 23, 7 p.m. $15-$20. The Comedy Studio, 5 John F. Kennedy St., Cambridge. www.thecomedystudio.com

NICK A. ZAINO III

FAMILY YOGA AT DECORDOVA SCULPTURE PARK AND MUSEUM Bring your mat and a water bottle, and hone your yoga skills at deCordova Sculpture Park and Museum. Led by instructors from On The Mat Yoga in Concord, this family-friendly class will combine “the imaginative world of the child” with teachings of “mindfulness, self-regulation and joy,” according to the event’s website. After class, guests can peruse the sculpture park, grab a bite at the Twisted Tree Café, or snag a souvenir at the gift shop. March 23, 10:30 a.m. $20/$10 for nonmember adult/child, $18/$16 for member adult/child. 51 Sandy Pond Road, Lincoln. thetrustees.org

SPRING EQUINOX ART FAIR Kick off the spring season and celebrate the Boston area’s arts community. Sponsored by the Stow Area Guild of Artists (SAGA) and the FPC Arts Committee, local artists of SAGA will display and sell their creations, including paintings, photography, pottery, needle felt, and more. Stow musician Alex Rosiewicz will be on hand as well to play folk, rock, and Celtic music throughout the event. March 22, 10 a.m., and March 23, noon. Free admission. 353 Great Road, Stow. fpc-stow-acton.org

BROOKLINE MUSIC SCHOOL 100TH ANNIVERSARY CONCERT The Brookline Music School faculty will perform Camille Saint-Saëns’ “Carnival of the Animals,” a humorous musical suite, in celebration of the school’s 100th anniversary. Three concert times are available for audiences to attend and enjoy a century of music from Brookline’s oldest and largest cultural institution. March 22, 2 p.m., 2:45 p.m., 3:30 p.m. RSVP required. Hunneman Hall, Brookline Public Library, 361 Washington St., Brookline. bmsmusic.org

HALEY CLOUGH

title: Mass. veterans worry about cuts to VA medical research
text:
“It’s been an incredibly rewarding experience, knowing that I am giving back to my fellow veterans,” said Bruno, 69, of Arlington, who served in the Army and Massachusetts Air National Guard in the 1980s.

Now, both veterans have watched with alarm as the Trump administration has taken an ax to the VA, imperiling the agency’s status as a national powerhouse of scientific innovation. Sweeping layoffs and a federal hiring freeze threaten to eviscerate hundreds of research studies and clinical trials conducted through the VA’s Office of Research and Development — an incubator for such pioneering health advances as the implantable cardiac pacemaker, the CT scan, and the nicotine patch.

Already, the Trump administration’s cuts have disrupted years of research into suicide prevention, post-traumatic stress disorder, and spinal cord injuries among veterans, according to veterans service organizations and unions representing VA workers.

At the VA medical center in Bedford, where both Crocker and Bruno volunteer, nearly all the researchers are employed on term agreements that typically renew every three years based on the availability of research funds. Since early February, scores of researchers reaching the end of their contracts have not been rehired under the federal hiring freeze, with job losses rolling in waves through VA research sites across the country, from New England to the Pacific Northwest.

Last week, the VA’s chief of research and development emailed employees saying that those with certain appointments set to expire would be given 90-day exemptions. However, the email did not say what would happen to the employees after the 90-day reprieve, leaving many workers uncertain.

If the cuts continue, the Bedford center could lose more than half of its researchers within the next year and be unable to continue clinical studies that not only benefit former military service members but also the broader public, according to researchers and supervisors who work at the Bedford VA medical center.

In a separate move, the Trump administration disclosed last month that it plans to slash more than 80,000 jobs at the VA as part of an agency-wide reorganization, while assuring the public that the cuts would not jeopardize veterans’ health care.

Some government watchdog groups say efforts to rein in surging costs and inefficiencies at the VA, the second-largest federal agency, are long overdue.

Under the Biden administration, staffing at the agency rose 18 percent to 458,212 employees from 388,971, while the agency’s budget swelled nearly 40 percent to $336.3 billion. The Biden-era surge in costs was driven by a wave of new enrollees in the VA’s sprawling health care system and more than 1.3 million claims from veterans exposed to toxins, who saw expanded benefits under a 2022 law known as the PACT Act. Despite the increased outlays, the agency continues to struggle with a massive backlog of disability claims and significant delays for medical appointments at its hospitals, according to the VA’s website.

The VA’s chief of staff, Christopher Syrek, told top-level officials at the agency this week that it had an objective to cut enough employees to return to 2019 staffing levels of just under 400,000.

Pete Kasperowicz, the VA’s press secretary, said in an emailed statement that the agency had laid off 2,400 probationary employees in “non-mission-critical” positions, which represents less than half of 1 percent of the agency’s total workforce. More than 300,000 VA workers are in positions that are exempt from the federal hiring freeze and layoffs, he said. “So the notion that these layoffs are causing widespread issues across the department is not credible,” Kasperowicz said.

“Disappointingly, it seems government union bosses, the legacy media, and some in Congress don’t want us to reform anything,” Kasperowicz said. “They are working together to use rumor, innuendo, and disinformation to spread fear in the hopes that the department will just keep in place the status quo.”

The cost-cutting, combined with a barrage of menacing emails from the Trump administration — encouraging workers to leave and find “higher productivity jobs” in the private sector or ordering them to produce “5 bullet points” of what they accomplished in the past week — have led many to resign even before their contracts expire.

“We are hacking away at the foundation of one of the most innovative, knowledge-generating institutions in the world,” said Christian Helfrich, a former research investigator at the VA medical center in Seattle, who was terminated last month under the federal layoffs. “At some point, we’re going to damage that foundation so fundamentally that we cannot restore what was there.”

In late February, VA Secretary Douglas Collins took to social media to tout that he was scrapping some contracts, saving the VA nearly $2 billion. Researchers scrambled to download all their patient surveys amid reports that vital IT contracts were among those canceled and the data might vanish. After an outcry, the VA reversed course and paused the sweeping contract cancellations.

Yet major research studies continue to be disrupted.

On March 7, researchers at Boston University’s National Center for Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder learned that its research contract with the VA had been abruptly canceled. Three days later, the contract was restored, according to university officials. Similarly, the VA canceled a contract last month with Minuteman Technology Services in Marblehead, which had spent the past five years researching methods for preventing veterans’ suicide in 22 states. The contract was restored two weeks later after US Representative Seth Moulton of Salem learned of the cancellation and began asking questions of the VA, his office said.

“It’s criminally reckless,” said Moulton, a Democrat and an Iraq War veteran, of the contract cancellations. “Those of us who are younger veterans are counting on this research to be able to address some of the unique concerns and new challenges that veterans face.”

The VA is unusual in that it regularly appeals to its own patients — past military service members — to participate and even design clinical research studies. At the Bedford VA center, veterans are engaged in a multiyear project, known as Whole Health, that seeks to empower veterans to take control of their medical decisions.

“The goal is to shift veterans’ mental focus away from taking orders from above,” said Crocker, 80, the Navy veteran, who has helped design some of the materials for the project.

The center is also engaged in studies on Alzheimer’s disease, chronic pain, schizophrenia, substance abuse, and a host of other ailments that disproportionately affect veterans.

Many veterans worry that the turmoil will harm the health care they receive. Coast Guard veteran Joe Bykowski, 46, who frequents the VA medical center in Northampton, said he is already seeing the effect of the cuts on nurses and other staff and fears the waits for care will get worse.

“Everybody’s petrified of losing their jobs,” he said. “I’ve heard it described as a sniper in a tower picking off people and nobody knows who’s next.”

After weeks of silence, the nation’s leading veterans’ advocacy groups have started to mobilize against the workforce reductions. Both the American Legion and the Veterans of Foreign Wars, two politically influential groups that together boast about 3 million members, have publicly condemned the job cuts in congressional testimony and have called on the Trump administration to reinstate those fired.

On a Saturday afternoon, a fierce wind was whipping the regimental flags outside the Beachmont VFW Post 6712 in Revere when the parking lot began to fill with vehicles. More than 100 veterans — including those who served in Vietnam, Iraq, and Afghanistan — had come to see the VFW’s national commander and Vietnam War veteran, Alfred Lipphardt, deliver a rousing call to action.

“We have to speak out for ourselves,” Lipphardt told the crowd. “This new administration, they say leave no comrade behind. By God, they better stick with it.”

As the crowd dispersed, Grady Durden, a 74-year-old veteran from Roxbury who served 42 years in the Army, recounted all his injuries that were repaired by VA doctors. There was the left arm that was nearly blown off during a gunfight in Vietnam. A right knee that was replaced.

“We’ve got to push back,” he said, “because any country that turns its back on its veterans has lost its way.”

title: White Stadium trial, Day 2: Judge allows new plaintiffs' complaint as city details how plan addresses BPS needs
text:
Before three defense witnesses testified during the second day of the White Stadium trial, the plaintiffs succeeded in introducing a new complaint intended to buttress their legal case.

Superior Court judge Matthew Nestor allowed a motion filed just as the trial resumed Wednesday morning that allows “the petition of not less than 10 taxable inhabitants” of Boston to object to the building of new structures on park land and the city spending taxpayers’ dollars on those structures.

The case will still hinge on the plaintiffs being able to prove that the new stadium actually sits on protected park land, a violation of Article 97, versus the defense’s claim that the stadium parcel has sufficient legal and legislative backing to show that it is exempt from being proper Franklin Park park land.

No new facts or evidence are being introduced, the plaintiffs said.

The defendants strenuously objected to the motion.

Nestor ruled that even though the trial is well underway, there was not enough serious prejudice incurred by the defendants to prevent him from ruling for the plaintiffs.

The defendants said they needed time to read the complaint in order “to ponder” whether they will introduce new evidence or witnesses.

Much of the testimony from the witnesses for the defense focused on how the design of the current White Stadium renovation proposal changed to meet the needs of Boston Public Schools' athletics department and students, as well as keep the project aligned with the original design goals of Frederick Law Olmsted.

Liza Meyer, the chief landscape architect and interim commissioner of the Boston Parks Department, recounted her concerns over initial plans and renderings for the stadium put forth by the expansion NWSL soccer team.

The parks department objected to the team’s plans to use park pathways for delivery vehicles, to fence off an area in front of the park’s Playstead area, build a restaurant too close to the Overlook area, and to use digital lighting on the back of a scoreboard that faced the Playstead.

All the objections were addressed, said Meyer, who is also an ex officio director of the lead plaintiff, the Emerald Necklace Conservancy.

Diana Fernandez Bibeau, deputy chief of urban design for the city, explained how community and design concerns led to modifications that resulted in building wings on each end of both the East and West grandstands. The grandstands’ wings will include space for BPS district coaches, office and storage space, conference rooms, a student lounge, sports medicine, strength and conditioning, a community kitchen, and ADA accessible locker rooms. Public restrooms will be part of each grandstand.

Part of the plaintiffs’ case concerns the project’s impact on areas in Franklin Park that are not located within the 14-acre stadium parcel — these include pathway improvements, utilities work, and lighting.

Avery Esdaile, senior director of athletics for Boston Public Schools, was asked by the defense about how the use of the stadium by the professional women’s soccer team will displace BPS football.

“There are some limits on when we can host games that the stadium usage agreement has identified as after the NWSL season but there are provisions to ask for permission outside that window,” said Esdaile.

Beginning this past season, Esdaile said the two affected schools, Boston Latin Academy and Boston Latin School, essentially moved out of the stadium. BLS has been practicing and playing games at Clemente Field in the Fens, with BLA holding the majority of its practice in the Playstead area just south of the stadium and playing games at the old West Roxbury High School.

Esdaile also provided glimpses of the decrepit state of White Stadium, which was built in 1949. The athletic department’s un-air conditioned offices on the second floor of the West Grandstand were “extremely hot” in the summer, said Esdaile, cold in the winter, plus certain offices endured leaks in the ceiling.

“We made the best of it, but it was not an ideal place to work,” said Esdaile.

The issue of alcohol sales in the stadium during soccer games and outside in the planned restaurant was ruled to be off-limits in the trial by the judge. But because Esdaile was asked by the defense about how the athletic department issued permits for stadium use, the judge allowed the plaintiffs to question Esdaile about how BPS-issued permits forbid alcohol possession.

Linda Henry, CEO of Boston Globe Media Partners, announced last month she is withdrawing from the investor group behind the soccer team.

Michael Silverman can be reached at michael.silverman@globe.com.

title: In ‘Night Side Songs,’ finding ways to talk about illness through song
text:
“Night Side Songs” debuts in the Boston area this month, produced by the American Repertory Theater in association with the Philadelphia Theatre Company (where it ran earlier this month). The show will be performed at the Cambridge Masonic Temple from March 27-April 6, before moving to Hibernian Hall in Roxbury, from April 9-20. The cast includes veteran Broadway star Mary Testa (“Xanadu,” “Oklahoma!”) along with Jordan Dobson (“Hadestown”), Brooke Ishibashi (“Into the Woods”), Jonathan Raviv (“The Band’s Visit”), and Robi Hager.

Drawing its title from famed cultural critic Susan Sontag’s observation that “Illness is the night side of life,” the show reminds audiences to appreciate the ordinary moments — and momentousness — of everyday existence. “[Our show] is about finding the beauty in the smallness and quotidian specificity of life, in these things that happen to us every day. Me sitting here on the ground talking to you, the couch behind me,” said Patrick in an interview over Zoom from his Brooklyn apartment.

Thornton Wilder’s “Our Town,” specifically David Cromer’s acclaimed 2009-10 production that ran off-Broadway, was a particular inspiration, say the Lazours. A version of that production was mounted at the Huntington in 2012 and featured an intimate, immersive staging, with the audience sharing playing space with the actors, and a third act coup-de-théâtre that underlines the necessity of living in the here and now.

While there are several narratives woven into “Night Side Songs,” the main story focuses on the character of Yasmine, who gets diagnosed with cancer at a young age, goes through treatment, and eventually gets a clean bill of health. We learn about her relationship with her mother and watch her marry Frank, a guy she once dated briefly. But Yasmine has stared death in the face, so she’s been given a visceral reminder of her own mortality.

Because of this new awareness of how fragile life can be and how quickly it can pass, “Yasmine goes through her life with this new understanding. Everything takes on this whole new meaning,” Patrick said. “These very simple things are much deeper for her now. Life is more vivid and saturated.”

When the Lazours first began working on the show nearly a decade ago, it was conceived as a more straightforward book musical (developed and commissioned by the ART). The brothers had read a New Yorker article about Vincent T. DeVita’s memoir “The Death of Cancer,” exploring how maverick National Cancer Institute researchers Dr. Emil Freireich and Dr. Tom Frei developed the first successful chemotherapy cocktails to kill tumors in the 1960s.

The brothers had previously written the musical “We Live in Cairo,” set during the Tahrir Square mass protests that toppled Egyptian dictator Hosni Mubarak. The show had its world premiere at the ART in 2019 and ran in New York last fall. “I think we were drawn to the [cancer doctors] because we were just coming off of working on ‘We Live in Cairo’ and were interested in young revolutionaries making change,” Daniel said.

They had watched family members grapple with cancer, and Magar had also been touched by the disease. “I lost my father when I was 25 to colon cancer, and I was his primary caretaker,” Magar said. “Then over the course of this project, my mother was diagnosed with, was treated for, and later died from cancer. So we had a lot to talk about because [the brothers] were going through it for the first time.”

During the show’s development process, they saw how people would talk about their own personal bouts with cancer or the experiences of loved ones. “We realized that we had to write a different kind of show,” said Daniel, of the genre-breaking form that eventually emerged.

Their script was inspired in part by interviews they did with patients, caregivers, and health professionals, including from Harvard Medical School, along with watching the experiences of their own family members. Remnants of doctors Frei and Freireich’s story remain, and there’s also the story of a poor medieval English innkeeper, Prudence of Dursley, whose illness is blamed on the devil.

The seed for the show’s communal singing was planted in the electrifying protest anthem “Genealogy of Revolution” from “We Live in Cairo,” whose staging at ART featured a call-and-response section that was eventually discarded. “Many of the songs in this show,” Daniel said, “are experiments in, ‘How do you get the audience to sing along and find a way to make them participate in a way that’s authentic and not corny?’”

Indeed, to coax the audience to sing along, the creative teams use several different strategies, including call-and-response, teaching the lyrics, and humming the simple melodies. “It’s a gentle way to introduce this idea,” Daniel said. “We’re slowly wading you into the water.”

The show’s music is rooted in folk and musical theater flavors, but the Lazours also cite the Catholic hymns that they grew up listening to in church as an influence. Another big inspiration: a live recording of a 1970s concert by folk-rock singer and humanitarian activist Harry Chapin that their father loved to listen to when they were kids. Daniel said he vividly recalls the power of the live performance recording and hearing the audience unabashedly singing along to the lyrics in the background.

“Night Side Songs” is ultimately “lyric-driven music,” Daniel said. “How can you write a show without bells and whistles, that’s really stripped down and simple?”

Ultimately, the Lazours believe that the show can open up a space to have difficult conversations around illness and mortality. “I hope it can offer a little bit more dimension to this really confusing mystery of life that we don’t usually want to talk about,” Patrick said, “and make these things slightly less scary.”

The Lazours credit Susan Block, a palliative care specialist in Boston, with providing the show’s ultimate takeaway. “We get through these impossible times in our lives by going through them together,” Patrick said.

Indeed, Magar points out that the audience at “Night Side Songs” is a reminder of the need for community when someone is suffering through illness or grief. At one of the talk-backs in Philadelphia earlier this month, she recalls someone saying, “‘I felt like I was singing to help all the characters through this journey.’ And that is kind of a poem for the whole piece. It’s this extension of empathy. It’s how we can show up for each other in tough times.”

NIGHT SIDE SONGS

title: New Dana-Farber cancer hospital wins key state approval, despite Mass General Brigham concerns
text:
Dana-Farber has long provided outpatient cancer treatment at its current campus on Brookline Avenue and more than a half dozen satellite sites, sending patients to its Longwood neighbor, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, which has 30 licensed cancer beds, for inpatient treatment.

But in September 2023, Dana-Farber said it was ending its nearly 30-year alliance with Brigham and Women’s and teaming up with Beth Israel Deaconess to build a new free-standing inpatient hospital for adult cancer care.

Dana-Farber issued a statement after Thursday’s vote saying the review by regulators, including the state Department of Public Health, will “ensure that world-class cancer care is available to everyone who needs it.

“This is an extraordinary opportunity for Boston and the Commonwealth,” said Dr. Benjamin L. Ebert, the Dana-Farber president and chief executive officer. “While the incidence of cancer is rising, what we do now will determine our ability to meet the pace of the disease here and across the region.”

As the state’s population ages, cancer diagnoses are climbing. Officials project a 28 percent increase in the number of cancer cases involving residents aged 75 and over between 2023 and 2028, said Dennis Renaud, director of the determination of need program for the public health department.

Dana-Farber officials have estimated a need for 384 more inpatient cancer beds in the Boston area over the next seven years, Renaud said. The cost to commercial insurers will depend on where patients get care now and where they will get it in the future as more beds are added across the region.

The council’s approval was provisional. It is expected to take effect 30 days after the state Health Policy Commission completes a cost and market impact review. In a preliminary report on Feb. 27, the commission said the Dana-Farber plan would likely boost insurer spending on cancer care, though some aspects of the plan could result in cost savings by funneling more patients to the new hospital from the higher-priced Mass General Brigham hospitals.

But a clinical representative from Mass General Brigham, the state’s largest hospital and health system, called on state regulators to impose a condition, limiting the new cancer hospital to 126 beds, arguing 300 more beds had the potential to increase health care costs, worsen traffic in the Longwood hospital district, and create more stress on area hospital emergency rooms.

Dr. David Ryan, chief of hematology and oncology and clinical director of Mass General Cancer Center, said more patients with cancer-related conditions will gravitate to already strained emergency departments in the Longwood area in hopes of getting admitted to the new cancer hospital.

“To add cancer beds to the Longwood area ... without a simultaneous increase in emergency room beds, will create even more patients at our Boston institutions at 7 a.m. every morning,” said Dr. David Ryan, chief of hematology and oncology and clinical director of Mass General Cancer Center.

Ryan also disputed a notion at the heart of state regulatory reviews: that large numbers of older patients would defect from Mass General Brigham, where many are being treated by specialists for heart and other conditions in addition to cancer.

He estimated that no more than 30 percent of cancer patients would leave Mass General Brigham, which will be renovating floors at Brigham and Women’s and constructing a new tower at Mass General to expand its own cancer care. The rest of the patients will be channeled to Dana-Farber from lower-priced community hospitals, increasing health costs, he said.

Speakers from the neighborhoods surrounding the Longwood Medical Area, densely packed with medical centers, turned up to support a new hospital.

“Here in Boston, there is a dire need for more cancer beds,” said state Representative Chynah Tyler, a Democrat whose district includes Longwood as well as Mission Hill and Roxbury. She said Dana-Farber’s proposal to add 2,400 jobs at the hospital will create “opportunities for people in my district.”

Also backing the plan was state Representative Ann-Margaret Ferrante, a Democrat who represents Essex, Rockport, and Manchester by the Sea, and has been treated at Dana-Farber since she was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in 2021.

“For us as patients, it’s about the level of care...” Ferrante said. “The data clearly shows that a dedicated cancer hospital saves more lives from cancer. And we must move quickly, as the state’s older population is increasing.”

title: Boston School Committee to decide on proposed building closures, merger Thursday night
text:
“There are going to be a lot of people not happy with the decision,” said Jeri Robinson, the committee chairperson, who supported the plan. “But in the long run, I think the people that we have to think most about are our students. [And] our number one job is here to improve student outcomes.”

For months, scores of parents and educators have protested the proposal and staged demonstrations outside schools. On Tuesday, dozens marched around district headquarters in Roxbury and demanded the School Committee leave the schools open and preserve the communities — teachers, students, and staff — inside those buildings.

“We ask you and we implore you, do not take the school away from us,” said Zoila Alvarado, a teacher at the Dever school, during Thursday’s meeting.

BPS administrators have said the buildings are not capable of offering a full range of student services, including special education inclusion, and most have too few students for the size of their buildings. They also do not have enough room to provide a high quality student experience, which includes physical spaces that support learning and are accessible to all students, according to the district.

More than a third of students affected by the proposed closures and merger are multilingual learners, according to Delavern Stanislaus, the district’s chief of capital planning.

“Closing these schools will create pathways for students to transition into schools that are more fully enrolled, with more resources, and offering a higher-quality student experience — often closer to home,” Stanislaus said in a memo to the School Committee earlier this month.

During a January School Committee meeting, administrators said they intended to close about one-fifth of the district’s school buildings by 2030, and have the goal of moving their students into larger buildings that can better serve their needs.

The proposed rollback of buildings comes as the district expects enrollment to level off over the rest of the decade after it had dropped for several years. Enrollment in 2030 is expected to be around 47,000 students, which is about 3 percent less than now.

Superintendent Mary Skipper said the closures and merger approved Thursday will save the district about $20 million, which will be reinvested into schools and classrooms.

On Thursday night, the sole vote against the plan was by School Committee member Rafaela Polanco Garcia, who argued that the district should preserve the schools and their communities.

“It is my position today to encourage you — let’s keep fighting, let’s keep working together,” Polanco Garcia said in Spanish through an interpreter.

Several of her fellow board members, including Stephen Alkins, appeared to be grappling with the issue shortly before voting for the school closures and merger. Alkins acknowledged that the decision was tough.

“The data and the research does show that closures negatively impact student outcomes and performance,” Alkins said. “That same research also shows that when you move students to higher quality educational opportunities, you actually see them perform better.”

A few minutes earlier, a few dozen parents and educators addressed the Committee, calling on them to leave the schools alone.

Among them was Yanery Diaz, whose son attends Dever. She praised the work of educators and staff at the school, and the strong communication the school maintains with families.

“The Dever community is a very united community with a lot of humanity,,” Diaz said in Spanish through an interpreter.

Dermot Kiernan, whose children attend the Clap school, said the school’s teachers are committed to their community, and make students and families feel like they belong.

“ We prefer to stay at the Clap,” Kiernan said.

But not all speakers favored keeping the buildings as they are. Nachelle Gordon, the head of Excel High School, said she supported closing the school.

“As long as the district supports the transition of every student, staff, family member, and community partner, I’m at peace with the closing,” Gordon said.

Maria Barbosa, whose child attends the Clap school, said she supported the merger, but hoped the current faculty are included in the transition.

“We we would love to see our faculty move forward with us,” she said.

Stanislaus noted there are other schools in the district that meet the same criteria for closures and mergers, but did not name them.

Skipper told School Committee members in January that announcing proposed school closures too early would have a detrimental effect on those communities. Students and staff wouldn’t choose that school, and cause a “drain down” of that school, she said.

title: Bit of a spinout in the Tesla community
text:
Although we were happy to be interviewed for the article about conflicted Tesla owners (“Guilty as charged: Liberals with Teslas are now willing to take a hit just to unload them,” Page A1, March 13), we felt that a few important points were not addressed.

When we bought our cars, it was to reduce our carbon footprint, and since the Tesla infrastructure was so good, we each decided to go with the Model 3. We are sold on electric vehicles since we remain committed to a cleaner and more sustainable environment, but in the future, our EVs will not be Teslas. Ditching Amazon Prime (over some of Jeff Bezos’s recent moves) has taught us that convenience is overrated and we can make do with universal charging stations.

However, for now, rather than take a hit by selling our Teslas at a loss to feel better from a political standpoint, we can put our money to better use by donating to the progressive causes we wish to support.

title: High school notebook: Duane Sigsbury steps down as Billerica football coach after 11 seasons
text:
Duane Sigsbury has resigned as head football coach at Billerica after 11 seasons, but will continue in his role as a physical education teacher at the high school.

Sigsbury led Billerica to a 110-48 record, most recently earning a trip to the Division 3 state quarterfinals. He resigned Thursday, citing family reasons; his son, Dylan, is slated to graduate from Billerica this spring and hopes to play football at Endicott this fall.

“It was totally my decision,” said Sigsbury. “I love Billerica. I always have. I know for a fact that I’ll miss it. But after all those years putting everybody else before yourself, it’s time to put me and my family first, and that’s what I’m doing for now. Hopefully I’ll be back coaching someday.”

Sigsbury has coached basketball at Manchester Essex and Austin Prep, and coached softball at Woburn for eight seasons, retiring from that post in 2023 along with his wife, Courtney, who was the head coach of the Tanners for 24 seasons.

▪ David Clay is stepping down after three seasons as the basketball coach at St. John’s Prep.

A 2003 Newburyport graduate, Clay led his alma mater to a 74-26 record over five seasons before becoming Prep’s fourth basketball coach of the 21st century when he was hired in 2022. The Eagles struggled this past season with a 2-18 record after going 13-30 over the previous two seasons.

“Coach Clay was a great representation of St. John’s Prep, leading our basketball program with the utmost respect and humility,” said Prep athletic director Jameson Pelkey.

“His impact was felt beyond the court, as game officials, opposing coaches, and players alike consistently praised his professionalism and character. He has been a respected leader.”

CATS Academy senior Jaylen Harrell has repeated as the state’s Gatorade Boys’ Basketball Player of Year.

The 6-foot-6-inch, 200-pound wing led the Griffins to a 28-7 record and a runner-up finish in the NEPSAC Class AA tournament. Committed to Providence College, Harrell averaged 22.1 points. 8.5 rebounds and 7.2 assists per game. He was a two-time first team Class AA selection and a first team All-New England Basketball League selection this winter.

Harrell has volunteered locally at the Tobin Community Center in Roxbury. “He had them playing at a high level,” said Brewster Academy coach Jeff Gore. “He reminds me of (former Celtics player) Antoine Walker. He can go inside, outside, has a good body and plays a physical style. He has performed well against the best teams, and that’s what I look at.”

Harrell has maintained a B average in the classroom.

title: Watch for the changes: A jazz scene rises in Roxbury
text:
The Thursday night series at Long Live Beerworks, running for just over a year, has become a hotbed of jazz in Boston, helping fill a void created by the retrenchment of the area’s top jazz clubs.

The Regattabar and Scullers once packed patrons into their hotel jazz clubs six nights a week. Like everything else, they closed when the pandemic hit, and they’ve never fully returned, hosting shows only two or three nights a week these days. Both clubs showcased local acts early in the week, but no more. Ryles Jazz Club, a popular spot for local jazz musicians, closed in 2018.

That’s not to say jazz has disappeared from Greater Boston. Wally’s Jazz Cafe on Mass. Ave. is going strong after 78 years, providing Berklee College of Music students with a spot to workshop. The Lilypad in Inman Square has a full calendar of local and national jazz musicians. The Mad Monkfish in Central Square and The Beehive downtown showcase local jazz talent.

But something special is happening in Roxbury, and it started because Michael Feldman wanted to see live jazz and bring new life to his neighborhood.

“Roxbury and jazz,” he says, “they just go together.”

Feldman is the CEO of Feldman Geospatial, a company that was founded by his grandfather in 1946 as a land surveyor and has grown into a high-tech construction engineering firm.

In 2016, Feldman Geospatial bought into the former home of the Boston Piano Co., a three-story brick factory in disrepair. Feldman rehabbed the 162-year-old building, moved into the top two floors, and now rents the bottom floor to Long Live Beerworks, a brewery that started in Providence and operates its second taproom here.

Feldman, who grew up listening to the Brazilian and Afro-Cuban records his father played at home, says he dreamed of bringing music into the Hampden Street building and initially thought he would try to recruit Berklee students to perform. But it became apparent he could think bigger.

In January 2024 he began hiring local jazz groups to play on Thursday nights — Feldman’s firm pays the musicians, even though they bring business to the brewery — and started with a trio led by bassist John Lockwood. Three weeks later Lockwood was back with The Fringe, saxophonist George Garzone’s trio that has been playing around Boston since 1971.

“Boston’s in bad shape,” Lockwood says, referring to the jazz scene. “When I first came here, there were all kinds of clubs here — stuff in Boston, stuff in Cambridge. It kind of fizzled out, and when the pandemic hit it got kind of weird.”

The Long Live jazz series has “snowballed,” he says, thanks to the strong lineup, free admission, easy parking, and great beer.

“Boston needs places like this,” says Lockwood, who is a bass professor at Berklee.

Sue Auclair, the longtime Boston jazz publicist, happened to come to one of those first shows. Lockwood introduced her to Feldman, and soon she was marketing and promoting the series.

Feldman and Auclair say they have been pleasantly surprised by how easy it has been to lure musicians here.

“We’re booked for the year already,” says Auclair, who has done publicity over the years for Scullers, the Newport Jazz Festival, Miles Davis, and countless other jazz venues and artists.

Long Live’s 2025 lineup is a who’s who of Boston jazz, with a particular focus on Latin jazz. The next shows feature singer-pianist Zahili Gonzalez Zamora (March 27), Brazilian mandolinist Ian Coury’s quartet (April 3), Israeli pianist Alon Yavnai (April 10), keyboardist Matt Jenson (April 17) and Puerto Rican saxophonist Edmar Colón (April 24). The Fringe has more gigs here, the next one being May 22.

Alex Alvear has three shows booked in May with different lineups, including his Boston-based Latin ensemble Mango Blue. Feldman saw that band years ago, became a fervent fan, and flies Alvear in from Ecuador to perform at Long Live.

“What Mike is doing is exceptional for a city that has lost its way when it comes to appreciation for live music culture,” says Alvear, who came to Boston in 1986 to study at Berklee and spent nearly 30 years here before moving back to Ecuador in 2015.

By organizing and funding the music series at Long Live, Feldman is doing “something absolutely out of this world for the Boston music scene,” Alvear says.

“The scene was really literally dying in Boston,” he says from his home in Ecuador. “I was heartbroken when I found out that all of these really emblematic music venues had been dying and closing. The city, when I arrived in the ‘80s, was full of music. Live music was an essential component of the city’s identity.”

Feldman wants to make it part of Roxbury’s identity. The potential effect on this part of town is as important to him as is the music.

“Kids who live in this neighborhood don’t always feel good about their neighborhood because of the way people talk about Roxbury,” he says. “I really hope that we impact this neighborhood.”

Bailey lives in the neighborhood herself, just a few blocks down the street. She came to Boston from New York in 2000 to teach at Berklee, where she is assistant chair of the guitar department.

She started coming to Long Live on Sundays for the beer and now performs in the room.

“Look at this space,” Bailey says. “It’s a beautiful space. There are cool people who come here, and the beer is great.”

Most of the seats are occupied by the time her quartet launches into “Old and Young Blues,” a medium-tempo bop tune she wrote. It’s an appropriate song: A young couple, clearly on one of their first dates, chat near the back of the room, while an older couple pay strict attention to the musicians. A middle-age woman taps her toes alone to the rhythm, and a group of five professionally dressed women sip beers at a hightop.

For two and a half hours on Thursday evenings, this is in fact a jazz club — a big, jolly room on the ground floor of a building that had sat derelict for years, used as storage for old vehicles and construction equipment, now alive with A-list music and friends.

“It’s just good for our community,” Feldman says. “It’s good for our spirits. It’s something that’s needed.”

title: My mom, a nurse, treated me through childhood illnesses. In her final days, it was my turn to step up.
text:
When I contracted bronchial pneumonia at age 4, my fever soared so high she dipped me in an ice bath. At 8 years old, I came down with viral pneumonia and she introduced me to breathing exercises with a spirometer. Later that same year, lobar pneumonia struck, so she guided me to the edge of the bed, belly down, allowing postural drainage to flush my lungs.

“You’re my best patient, John,” she told me. After she splurged on a stylish camel-hair coat to keep me warm, I imagined myself her only patient.

The physical and emotional stress and strain of nursing took the best of my mother’s health. Over the years she developed diabetic retinopathy, underwent heart bypass surgery, and suffered a compression fracture in her spine. Through it all, my father, Paul Maddock, remained by her side, until his unexpected passing in 2010. Unable to drive, shop, cook, or organize medications for herself, assistance resulting from my father’s military service was just enough to afford us what many families can’t manage. Single with no children, I left the workforce to be her at-home caregiver.

Before switching to modern devices, we relied on the same tools she’d used with me. She taught me to shake down the mercury in an under-the-tongue thermometer; what to listen for with a stethoscope pressed to her chest, abdomen, and back; how to feel her pulse with two fingers on her wrist while following the second hand on a watch; and when a blood pressure cuff was pumped to exactly the right level.

“Nurses call them vital signs for a reason, John.”

Perhaps she was preparing me for the inevitable when sharing stories about the joy, commitment, and sorrow inherent to her field. On New Year’s Day 1967, her picture appeared in the newspaper for the annual first baby born in Boston: “A TIE,” the caption read, between the St. Margaret’s infant and another newborn at St. Elizabeth’s Hospital. During the Blizzard of ’78, she shuttled to work up the steep climb of Jones Hill in a snowplow truck. And all manner of life-and-death situations nurses everywhere know too well.

Time grew precious when I had to accept the limits of at-home care. The tiniest cut, while on a blood thinner for a congestive heart, hemorrhaged, masking an aggressive UTI. Her temperature plummeted. Renal failure and debilitating dialysis soon followed. After a decade in my care, in the midst of the COVID pandemic, emergency care at the Beth Israel Deaconess Hospital – Milton became the mercy of comfort care at South Shore Hospital. She was 88.

The last time my mother saw home, if given the gift of reprieve, we would have resumed our journey. The sun beckoning and so her vision more favorable, she would have asked me to take her for another “ride down memory lane.” To the house in West Roxbury where she was born; to Roslindale where she was raised, learned to ice skate on Fallon Field, and met my father; along the scenic byways of the South Shore where she had lived.

We would have done so together, anticipating our return, optimistic that we still had some control over the wheel.

John Maddock writes from the South Shore. Send comments to magazine@globe.com. TELL YOUR STORY. Email your 650-word unpublished essay on a relationship to connections@globe.com. Please note: We do not respond to submissions we won’t pursue.

title: Here’s what leading Bostonians like to read, eat, and do in the city
text:
Send questions or suggestions to the Starting Point team at startingpoint@globe.com. If you’d like the newsletter sent to your inbox, sign up here.

Confession time: I wrote this newsletter from a place that is not Boston.

I’ll be there soon, it’s true. But I’ve felt some self-consciousness about writing about a city before actually moving there. Don’t worry: I’m no stranger. Growing up in Maine, I visited Boston often as a kid, and lived there for a year before college. Still, I’m anxious to get to know it better.

So to help me get a jump start, I reached out to elected officials, business and community leaders, university presidents, sports figures, and other influential Bostonians for recommendations. I asked them to tell me something they’ve read, eaten, heard, seen, or visited that helped them get to know the city they inhabit. Today’s newsletter shares their responses.

I often understand a place better when I read about it, and several people I reached out to recommended books.

Gayatri Patnaik, the director of Beacon Press, suggests “Dark Tide,” about a 1919 industrial accident that flooded the North End with millions of gallons of molasses, killing 21 people.

Jessica Tang, who leads American Federation of Teachers Massachusetts, recommends “Chain of Change,” a 1981 book about Boston’s Black communities by Mel King, the late activist and community leader. As WBUR has reported, book clubs across the state still read his book.

If you prefer fiction, Governor Maura Healey admires the novels of Dennis Lehane, a Boston native “whose deep connection to the streets of Boston shines through in his storytelling.”

Tiya Miles, a Harvard historian, recommends “Contending Forces,” a 1900 novel by Pauline Hopkins about Black Bostonians struggling to escape the legacy of slavery. “Walking the streets with Hopkins’s characters brings historical Boston to life and also reveals the existence of a color line,” Miles told me.

Boston is synonymous with American history.

James Rooney, president of the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce, recommends the Tea Party Museum, where you can walk the decks of full-scale replicas of the ships that helped spark the American Revolution — and even toss crates of tea into the harbor.

Marcelo Suárez-Orozco, the chancellor of UMass Boston, recommends reading the Declaration of Rights in the Massachusetts Constitution, which established fundamental freedoms and was a model for the US Constitution.

But the city didn’t stop making history in the 1700s. Mayor Michelle Wu recommends the City of Boston Archives, which contains documents, photos, blueprints, and maps that offer glimpses of the city over centuries. As Wu wrote, “We may think of history in grand moments captured in books and movies, but there’s also magic in feeling the yellowed pages of real life.” You can browse the archive online or visit the Mary C. Beaudry Community Archaeology Center in West Roxbury to see artifacts in person.

If museums and archives sound too dusty, try getting your history on Instagram instead. Vickie Alani, a senior principal at CBT Architects, recommends streetscapecurator, an account that features commentary about Boston’s many historic buildings.

Boston boasts more than a dozen art museums, but several people pointed me to the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum. Even if you’ve already been, as I have, museum director Peggy Fogelman suggests taking another look at an 1888 portrait of Gardner, the collector who started the museum. “Mrs. Gardner’s bare arms and a plunging neckline sparked salacious rumors among her contemporaries,” Fogelman wrote.

The museum, which the eclectic Gardner designed to mimic a Venetian palace, is itself a work of art. In the atrium, “soaring glass ceilings and immaculate, lush gardens reflect the passionate vision of a woman ahead of her time,” Susan Goldberg, the president of GBH, told me. “Sitting in the garden,” says Matthew Teitelbaum, who directs the Museum of Fine Arts, “restores the soul.”

Others suggest going outside. Lee Pelton, who runs The Boston Foundation, recommends The Embrace, a bronze sculpture on Boston Common that honors Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King, who met in Boston. (The foundation helped install it.)

Instead of feasting your eyes, maybe you’re just looking to feast.

Alex Cora, the manager of the Red Sox, praised chef Massimo Tiberi’s award-winning Arya Trattoria in the North End as his favorite go-to spot in the city. Other diners spotted there include Melissa McCarthy and the Rock.

For something lower-key, David Nagahiro of CBT, the architecture firm, recommends Bow Market in Somerville, which features shops and dining around an open-air courtyard.

For an auditory experience, Sally Kornbluth, MIT’s president, recommends the Boston Pops, an orchestra that performs both classical and popular music. “They’re a great mixture of playful and serious — sort of a good microcosm of Boston,” she says. Upcoming shows include a screening of “Jaws” accompanied by a live performance of the iconic score and a sold-out event featuring Cynthia Erivo, the star of “Wicked.”

Every list is partial, and now it’s your turn to add more. Send your ideas about what to read, watch, eat, and do around the city to startingpoint@globe.com and I’ll feature them in a future newsletter. And if you want more now, my colleague Dana Gerber has compiled a list of other Boston-inspired pop culture.
