After Harvard Law, his sister became an assistant district attorney in Middlesex County and went on to serve as a staff attorney and executive director for the Massachusetts Commission on Judicial Conduct. She died in December 2020, without seeing justice for her mother.

In 2023, detectives from the Boston Police Department’s unsolved homicide unit appealed to the public for help.

“Any piece of information, no matter how small or seemingly insignificant, could make a tremendous difference in the course of this decades-long investigation,” police said.

Police also released a poster featuring photos of Pearson and her Camaro that they shared on social media.

“The victim was known to frequent bars/restaurants in the Copley Square area and the City of Cambridge,” the poster read. “The victim appeared younger than her years and she often went by her middle name, Bayla or Francesca.”

Police in Boston and the Suffolk district attorney’s office said the investigation remains active.

“In just the past year we have secured convictions in two homicide cases that were decades old, which is an indication that neither we nor police investigators ever give up on a case, no matter how many years have passed,” James Borghesani, a spokesperson for the Suffolk district attorney’s office, said in a statement. “Breaks in unsolved homicides can come in any number of ways and at any time, so our wish is that the family and friends of Ruth Pearson never give up hope despite their years of sadness.”

Pearson holds out hope that justice can be found for his mother.

“She didn’t deserve to be murdered ... and you can’t bring her back,” Pearson said. “It’s all about justice. It’s a pursuit of justice for a woman who dedicated her life to the upbringing of her three kids.”

Police have asked anyone with information about Pearson’s whereabouts around the time of her death to contact the unsolved homicide unit at 617-343-4470. Those who wish to remain anonymous can call the CrimeStoppers Tip Line at 1-800-494-TIPS or 1-800-494-8477, or text the word ‘TIP’ to CRIME (27463).

Jeremiah Manion of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: ‘I don’t know about tomorrow.’ Hundreds in Boston seek citizenship aid amid Trump’s immigration crackdown.
text:
Beneche said she hopes to complete the process before she graduates from college next year.

“I’m just scared of what the government and the president might do,” said Beneche. “A lot of us just want better futures for ourselves.”

The city’s Office for Immigrant Advancement and Project Citizenship, a nonprofit organization in Boston, hosted the annual event, which started in 2014. Organizers said they screened potential applicants in advance and scheduled appointments for people who qualify for citizenship, meaning they’ve had a green card for five years or three years if they’re married to a US citizen, are age 18 or older, and can speak conversational English.

Gail Breslow, Project Citizenship’s executive director, said the organization has seen immigrants grow anxious as the Trump administration reshapes immigration policy. The federal government has recently initiated deportation proceedings against some immigrants with legal authorization to be in the country, including lawful permanent residents and student visa holders.

“We have so many clients reaching out to Project Citizenship who are anxious and fearful now, and yet are determined to go through this process because they see that even lawful permanent residents who have green cards are being subjected to deportation proceedings or being stopped at borders and not allowed reentry to the United States,” Breslow said. “Our phones have been ringing off the hook over the past several weeks.”

Citizenship applications are also about to change next month, she said.

Under an executive order signed by Trump on the first day of his second term, he ordered the federal government to require applicants for citizenship to divulge more information about their backgrounds. Trump has said the changes are intended to keep terrorists out of the US.

The updated citizenship application is expected to require immigrants to provide information covering the past 10 years, rather than the previous requirement of five years, and seek details about applicants’ parents, siblings, and children, Breslow said.

She said the mandates for information about applicants’ relatives will subject those family members to government scrutiny without their consent.

“It is unduly invasive, it is burdensome, and it’s probably illegal,” Breslow said.

Project Citizenship is also feeling the impact of Trump’s budget cutting, she said. Last month, the organization lost a $150,000 federal grant, which pays for 5 percent of the nonprofit’s budget, Breslow said.

Mayor Michelle Wu attended the event, and discussed her memories of her parents applying for US citizenship. Wu’s parents moved to the US from Taiwan.

“We know that the whole application process is going to change under this federal administration even in the next few weeks and so there’s been a huge demand of residents wanting to make sure they’re getting their forms in and getting this done,” she said.

Beneche, who lives in Everett, said she knows people from Haiti who have been arrested and returned to that country since Trump took office.

“It’s very heartbreaking,” she said. Haiti “is not really a safe place to go back to.”

Oscar Herrera, 42, went to the event with family members who met with volunteers to fill out citizenship applications.

Herrera, who is from Honduras, said he plans to take his citizenship exam next month and watches test prep videos on his phone to get ready.

He said he’s approaching his citizenship application with urgency.

“Today is today. I don’t know about tomorrow,” said Herrera, who works as a custodian. “I need to become a citizen.”

Maria Hemry Joseph said she came to the US from Haiti eight years ago and works as a certified nursing assistant.

Speaking in French, she said she wants to become a citizen so she can vote.

Adeline Mendes, another immigrant from Haiti who also works as a certified nursing assistant, said she’s been living in the US for nine years. She said Trump’s immigration policies don’t figure into her desire to become a citizen.

“I want to vote,” said Mendes, who lives in Everett.

Mendes said living in the US has made her more independent and offered opportunities for her to work and provide for her two children.

“I never stop working,” she said.

Ronald St. Jacques, 43, attended the event with his father, Peter, 77, who is applying for citizenship.

The younger St. Jacques said he doesn’t expect his father to encounter any difficulties because of Trump’s policies. Both are immigrants from Haiti. Ronald St. Jacques said he became a US citizen in 2013.

“I don’t think I have to worry about it because he’s not illegal,” he said.

Claudia Castro attended the event with her husband, who is applying for citizenship. Castro, who is from Honduras, said she became a US citizen after getting help from Project Citizenship.

She said she loves the US, but Trump has changed it.

“It’s different,” Castro said. “Everybody is scared now.”

Muller Mortume and his father, Jean, both moved to the US from Haiti. The younger Mortume is already a citizen and now his father is applying.

The elder Mortume has been in the US for about 15 years, his son said, and he worries about his relatives who have been authorized to stay in the country under humanitarian parole or temporary protected status protections extended to Haitians.

The Trump administration has sought to end humanitarian parole protections for migrants from Haiti, Cuba, Nicaragua, and Venezuela, though a federal judge in Boston has blocked any changes for now. Another form of temporary immigration protections for Haitians is scheduled to end in August.

“Everything happens so fast,” said Muller Mortume. “Things are shifting too quick.”

title: Alex Hassan’s major league career may have been only three games, but now he’s a rising star in the Twins’ front office
text:
Hassan singled off Erik Bedard in the fourth inning and came around to score on Brock Holt’s double.

“One of the greatest days of my life,” Hassan said. “I have the ball from my first hit and the lineup card.”

Later that season, he pinch hit for Ortiz after Big Papi was 4 for 4 with a home run.

“He hit four of the loudest balls I’ve ever seen hit and then they sent me up there and I grounded out,” Hassan said.

It proved to be his last major league game. There are no regrets.

“I made it to the majors, and it was such a good experience with the Sox,” Hassan said. “I was able to see how Terry Francona managed when I was called up for games in spring training, and I was around a lot of special players.”

Hassan tried to make it back, but after two seasons with four other organizations in Triple A, he decided it was time to go in another direction.

“The writing was on the wall,” Hassan said. “It was clear my playing career was winding down. My Triple A manager with the Dodgers, Bill Haselman, was encouraging me to potentially pursue a career in baseball.

“He would talk to me about his lineup decisions and how he handled certain situations. I learned a lot being around him.”

Another former Red Sox player, Gabe Kapler, was with the Dodgers as director of player development. Hassan also got to know assistant farm director Jeremy Zoll.

Those connections led to a six-month internship with the Dodgers front office in 2017 while he was completing his degree from Duke.

“It was a stroke of luck,” Hassan said. “I knew what playing was like and I was able to see it from the other side. It was an immersive experience.”

But once the internship was over, it was time to step away from baseball and come home.

With their first child on the way, Hassan and his wife, Carolyn, decided to settle down in West Roxbury. He put his new degree to use and entered Dell’s sales and marketing training program.

“It’s what made sense for our family,” Hassan said. “Dell was a good company with good people. It was a great experience. I learned a lot.”

But baseball hadn’t given up on Hassan.

Zoll took a job with the Twins as director of minor league operations in 2018. He offered Hassan a position as his assistant.

Had the Twins viewed Hassan as a better fit coaching one of their minor league teams, he likely would have stayed in the corporate world.

But a front-office position intrigued him and Hassan accepted the job.

“Being a coach would have been hard for me at that moment, jumping back into the minor league lifestyle with a young child,” Hassan said. “Going into the front office was something different.”

Hassan and his family moved to Minnesota. He was assistant director of minor league operations for two seasons, then director of player development from 2020-22 before moving up to vice president of hitting development and acquisitions in 2023.

His latest promotion came in January, when he was named assistant general manager under Zoll.

“Alex has been a great addition,” president of baseball and business operations Derek Falvey said. “He’s brought something to every role he’s had with us.”

In an information-driven industry, Hassan is one of those valued executives who can effectively blend major league playing experience with the data.

“I’ve tried to broaden my areas of focus,” Hassan said. “Whether it’s scouting amateur players, MLB roster discussions, free agency or trades, there’s a lot to learn.

“In terms of player development, it’s not just the plan you have for the player. It’s the person, too. You have to consider that. I try to put myself in the shoes of the player who is trying to execute that plan at 7 p.m. You have to find the best balance.”

At 37, Hassan naturally hopes to advance as an executive, though he doesn’t have any particular job in mind. Maybe he will be a general manager someday, but his goals aren’t that specific.

“If you work hard, good things generally will happen. That’s always been the best mentality for me. I don’t have long-term goals. I just want to get better and see where that takes me,” he said.

“I’ve had different roles and enjoyed them all. It seems silly to say, but I really just want to help as many players as I can because I had a lot of people do that for me.

“That’s all I can ask. I think about all the times I was in the minor leagues in the cage trying to figure it out. You don’t do that just because you want to be rewarded. You do that because you love it. I love being in baseball.”

The Red Sox have enviable depth in the outfield, at shortstop, at second base, and even in the rotation, for the first time in a few years.

They also addressed their catching depth by signing veteran Yasmani Grandal to a minor league contract.

What they lack are options at first base beyond Triston Casas.

Utility player Romy Gonzalez is the only other first baseman on the major league roster. Triple A Worcester is using catcher Nathan Hickey there and trying middle infielder Vaughn Grissom to see how that looks.

Casas is off to a slow start, but the Red Sox will give him plenty of runway. The bigger concern is injury. If Casas lands on the injured list, Gonzalez and his 23 games of major league experience at first base are the only choice.

Alex Cora has said Rafael Devers will not play the field this season. It might not be a bad idea to have him take some grounders at first base and see what it looks like.

Maybe the Sox could have Marcelo Mayer give it a shot in Worcester.

A few other observations on the Red Sox:

⋅ The Sox took advantage of the Brewers’ desperate need for pitching with the trade of Quinn Priester last week.

In addition to a legitimate prospect in 19-year-old outfielder Yophery Rodriguez, the Sox received a competitive-balance draft pick, No. 33 overall.

Now the Sox will pick 15th, 33rd, 75th, and 87th in the draft, making up for the pick they lost to the Astros for signing Alex Bregman.

The Sox took Michael Kopech the last time they had the 33rd pick. That was in 2014.

That the Sox were willing to trade Priester speaks to the much better job they’ve done building starter depth under Craig Breslow.

⋅ Entering the weekend, the Red Sox had nine players with at least one stolen base. The only team with more was the Mariners with 12.

⋅ Here’s another one you didn’t expect. There are only three Red Sox pitchers in the last 30 years who pitched at least five innings in each of their first six major league games. They are Daisuke Matsuzaka (2007), Justin Masterson (2008), and Richard Fitts (2024-25).

⋅ Roman Anthony, who turns 21 on May 13, is the youngest player in Triple A, which is roughly 850 players at a given time. Mayer, 22, is the 15th youngest.

⋅ Kristian Campbell reached safely in his first 13 career games. He was 14 of 44 (.318) with 10 runs, eight walks, six extra-base hits, and five RBIs.

Since 1920, only two Red Sox players age 22 or younger had longer streaks.

Ted Williams reached in 15 straight games in 1939. He went on to drive in 145 runs, have a 1.045 OPS, and finish fourth in the MVP voting behind Joe DiMaggio, teammate Jimmie Foxx, and Bob Feller.

The other was George Scott, who reached in his first 26 games in 1966. The Boomer was an All-Star and finished third in the Rookie of the Year voting behind Tommie Agee and Jim Nash.

⋅ Campbell’s brother, Kayden, is a junior infielder at Pope High in Marietta, Ga. He’s receiving recruiting attention from several Division 1 schools, TCU among them.

Kayden made it up to Boston for the press conference announcing his brother’s new contract despite having played a game the night before.

⋅ Sam Bregman, Alex’s father, is running for Governor of New Mexico as a Democrat. He will oppose former Secretary of the Interior Deb Haaland in the June 2026 primary.

Bregman is the District Attorney of Bernalillo County.

Vladimir Guerrero Jr. had all the leverage and he sure used it.

After taking a shot but failing to sign free agents Shohei Ohtani and Juan Soto when they were available, the Blue Jays had little choice but to retain their homegrown star first baseman who was born in Canada.

Guerrero and his agents knew he was worth more to the Blue Jays than any other team. They also knew the Jays couldn’t take the chance of allowing Guerrero to become a free agent at a time the Yankees and the Red Sox could use a power-hitting first baseman.

His age — the deal begins next season, when Guerrero will be 27 — also made the deal more palatable.

That led to a 14-year, $500 million contract with no deferrals. Guerrero also landed an incredible $325 million signing bonus spread out over 15 installments.

The structure of the contract protects Guerrero in several ways. Under an international tax agreement, signing bonuses are taxed at a far lower rate in Canada than salary is. (Guerrero saves further as a resident of Florida, which has no state income tax.)

He also would receive the signing bonus payments even in the event of games being canceled because of a work stoppage.

That could prove important with the league and the Players Association already preparing for a fight for when the collective bargaining agreement runs out after the 2026 season.

It speaks to how much baseball has changed that Vladimir Guerrero Sr. made $125.5 million over his 16-year Hall of Fame career. His son will make that every 3½ years through 2039.

The other winner in this deal is Cubs outfielder Kyle Tucker, who now will be the premier hitter on the free agent market this winter.

If the Cubs hope to retain Tucker, it might be wise to act soon. The price is only going to go up.

Octavio Dotel, who died in the nightclub collapse in the Dominican Republic, was one of those players who always seemed to be having a good day. From New York to Los Angeles and 10 cities in between, he arrived with a good fastball and a big smile. Junior Pepén, who calls Red Sox games in Spanish on the radio, said the Jet Set nightclub was a popular spot for Dominican players during the offseason. Dotel and former Nationals player Tony Blanco were among the dead. Blanco reportedly saved the life of former major leaguer Esteban Germán by pushing him away from the collapse … The Twins went into the weekend not having won three consecutive games since Aug. 15-17, 2024 … Javy Baéz played center field for two innings against the White Sox last Sunday. He’s become a utility player for the Tigers at 32 and still has $48 million due from 2026-27 … The “Don’t Call Us Sacramento” Athletics sold out their first home game, then drew fewer than 9,600 for three of the next five games. The team is set to break ground on its new stadium in Las Vegas in June. Plans are for it to open in 2028 … Mike Trout played every inning of the first 12 games for the Angels. He hit only .205, albeit with an .895 OPS, five home runs, and 11 RBIs. “It’s Mike Trout,” manager Ron Washington said. “It will get better. The more he sees pitches, the better it’s going to get. I’m not worried about Mike. As long as we can keep him on the field and keep his presence around here, he’s going to be Mike.” Trout played only 266 games from 2021-24 because of injuries … The Yankees and Adam Ottavino seem to have arrived at a mutually beneficial agreement. Ottavino signed with the Yankees on April 1, appeared in two games, and was designated for assignment on April 4. He elected free agency and was signed again on April 7. He pitched that day, was designated for assignment the next day, and became a free agent. How long before he signs again? … Ian Seymour could soon be making his major league debut with the Rays. The 26-year-old lefthander from St. John’s of Shrewsbury is off to a good start with Triple A Durham, using an effective changeup to complement his modest (90-93-mile-per-hour) fastball … Kaiden McCarthy of Chester, Vt., is one of the best high school players in the Class of 2027, according to Baseball America. The righthander at Vermont Academy has a mid-90s fastball with a curveball and occasional changeup … The annual ALS Awareness Game will be at Fenway Park on April 27 at noon when Boston College hosts Miami. The game has been played annually to honor former BC captain Pete Frates, who died of ALS in 2019. Go to redsox.com/alsgame to purchase tickets … Major League Baseball held a baseball development camp at the Jackie Robinson Training Complex in Vero Beach, Fla., on Friday and Saturday for girls ages 12-14. Participants included Clara Ciampa (Newton), Joanne Nunes (Sandwich), Lilly Silva (Providence), and Mia Sodre (Dracut) … Happy birthday to 2018 World Series MVP Steve Pearce, who is 42. The Red Sox acquired Pearce from the Blue Jays on June 28, 2018. He had a .901 OPS over 50 games and drove in 26 runs. Pearce was then 11 of 38 with six extra-base hits and 11 RBIs over 10 postseason games. He homered twice and drove in three runs in Game 5 of the World Series as the Sox clinched the championship. A knee injury limited Pearce to 29 games in 2019, and he retired before the 2020 season. Also happy birthday to the founding father of this column, Peter Gammons. He turned 80 on Wednesday. “Legend” as Alex Cora appropriately calls him.

title: ‘I remember, I reclaim, I restore, I reimagine’
text:
All of her work is reparative, but the art most of all.

“We were disconnected by a continent and moved,” she said of Black Americans. “That middle passage didn’t stop our DNA. It did not stop our relocation of culture. I’m always trying to put the parts back together, to re-member them.”

As the federal government targets Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion initiatives and cultural organizations such as the Smithsonian’s National Museum of African American History and Culture, she is clear-eyed.

“This is another cycle for me,” Frazier said. “It’s an ongoing struggle since 1492.”

Where to find her: www.lmerchiefrazier.org

Age: When asked her age, Frazier said “We don’t do that.”

“It’s not because I’m ashamed of my age. It’s because you get put in these categories where people don’t see you anymore,” she said. “Excuse me. Probably I can work circles around certain people who are young.”

Originally from: Jacksonville, Fla.

Lives in: Dorchester

Making a living: “I work as a matter of life subsistence and to feed my art,” she said.

Studio: Frazier has been a resident artist with Northeastern University’s African American Master Artists-in-Residency Program for more than two decades. Her quilts hang on the walls in her large space in AAMARP’s Jamaica Plain studio building. She describes the overhead lights as “minimal,” and keeps her big sewing machines at home. Her living room and dining room, she said, “are a one-person sweatshop.”

How she started: “My grandfather was a tailor in the hills of West Virginia,” the artist said. “My mom followed in his footsteps.”

“She just was a genius,” Frazier said. “She could master woodwork, anything that came in front of her. She was like her dad. That’s the legacy I represent.”

What she makes: Quilts in Frazier’s studio depict people like 19th-century abolitionist, suffragist, and public speaker Frances Ellen Watkins Harper and Ethiopian activist Lale Labuko; they relate stories of racial violence, oppression, and the struggle for civil rights. Shimmering layers of nylon let light pass through and suggest the porousness of time — a technique she developed after learning holography.

“I remember, I reclaim, I restore, I reimagine,” Frazier said. “That’s my life work.”

How she works: “Check me out at two o’clock, three o’clock in the morning,” she said. “I have ancestors and some kind of angels visiting me in my sleep, and I get up and do something.”

Question for artists: “Are you firm in your stance as a human being?” she asked. “Then everything else will flow.”

title: Boston City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune moves to bypass special election process if Fernandes Anderson resigns
text:
But Louijeune and her council colleague Liz Breadon on Monday announced they plan to file a home rule petition to cancel that process, after hearing concerns about turnout and public awareness from elected officials and community leaders in Fernandes Anderson’s district.

The home rule petition would also allow the winner of the race for Fernandes Anderson’s seat in the November election to assume the role as soon as officials certify the election results rather than waiting until the start of the new year, according to a press release from the two councilors.

The councilors also noted that the state’s Supreme Judicial Court has previously ruled that the council does not have the power to remove a councilor from office unless they have been sentenced for a crime, which has not happened yet in Fernandes Anderson’s case.

If Fernandes Anderson does resign, and the council and Beacon Hill approve Louijeune and Breadon’s proposal, that would leave Fernandes Anderson’s seat vacant until November.

“It is our collective responsibility to ensure that every voice in our community is acknowledged and represented,” Louijeune said in a statement Monday. “Given the accelerated timeline, the risk of excluding residents from the process is significant. With the general election approaching later this year, it would be inequitable to ask the public to participate in such a hastened process that will leave voices out.”

Breadon said in a statement that she’s heard from residents in Fernandes Anderson’s district who worry about whether a special election would be in “the best interests of public awareness, civic engagement, or the effective administration of our municipal elections.” She called forgoing the special election “the responsible course of action.”

As the District 7 councilor, Fernandes Anderson represents some of the most historically diverse neighborhoods in Boston, including Roxbury, Dorchester, part of the South End, and the Fenway.

Councilor Erin Murphy pointed to the past marginalization of those neighborhoods as a reason for the city to hold a special election to replace Fernandes Anderson as soon as possible.

But Louijeune and Breadon emphasized that Secretary of State William F. Galvin also opposes a special election in the city in such a tight timeframe. Galvin took the city’s elections department under state oversight earlier this year after reports of a variety of problems during last November’s election, including widespread ballot shortages and communication failures.

In a phone interview with the Globe Monday, Galvin called the idea of holding a special election for Fernandes Anderson’s seat “particularly ridiculous,” arguing it would compromise the efforts to fix the issues the city’s elections department experienced last year. He also said a special election this summer would likely come after the council votes on the budget for the next fiscal year, and the body does not historically meet much in July or August.

“The representation gained is, I think, very limited,” Galvin said. “The cost in terms of potential lost opportunity to correct the bigger problem is greater, and obviously the cost in terms of confusion is greater. ... There’s no good reason to do it, it’s a bad idea.”

Several District 7 residents, community advocates, and other elected officials, including state Senator Liz Miranda and state Representatives Chynah Tyler, John Moran, and Christopher Worrell, also said they support bypassing a special election.

Emma Pettit, a spokesperson for Wu’s office, said in a statement the city’s elections department is ready to hold a special election, but the mayor will review any legislation the council passes, and has directed more staff to help District 7 constituents maintain access to services.

The last time the city held a special election was during the summer of 2023, when Sharon Durkan won the race to replace former Councilor Kenzie Bok after Mayor Michelle Wu appointed Bok to lead the Boston Housing Authority.

Fernandes Anderson did not immediately return the Globe’s request for comment.

At least five candidates so far have filed paperwork with the state to run to replace Fernandes Anderson on the council — Said Abdikarim, Said Ahmed, Mavrick Afonso, Tchad Cort, and Samuel Hurtado.

Federal authorities arrested Fernandes Anderson in December on federal wire fraud and theft charges. Prosecutors allege she paid a staff member, who was also a relative, a $13,000 bonus and later pocketed $7,000 of it as a kickback. Fernandes Anderson initially pled not guilty to the charges.

Last week, she announced she signed a plea agreement and will plead guilty to two of the six federal corruption charges against her, and intends to resign. Fernandes Anderson will appear in federal court for her plea hearing on May 5.

title: Don’t let Shattuck plan languish in limbo
text:
So hopefully, the update will be a new blueprint for services on the site. But if not — if the state has lost interest — better to know that now. Letting the project twist in the wind isn’t fair to residents, service providers, and neighbors. They deserve a concrete update, especially as the relocation date of the hospital patients to the South End nears.

The site, in the corner of Franklin Park, has been used as both a public hospital and shelter for decades. The relocation of the hospital facilities will leave behind a shelter, an addiction treatment clinic, and a slew of buildings nearing the end of their useful lives. This opens a perfect opportunity to build out housing services.

Asked for an update, state officials said they remain “committed to redeveloping Shattuck.” It took a personal visit to the low-barrier Pine Street Inn Shelter to find out that residents there must find other housing options by October as the facility transitions to an overnight-only shelter. The website regarding the hospital relocation, meanwhile, is updated biweekly.

The planning for the 13-acre campus’s post-hospital future began in 2018 with community outreach. But by late 2023, the Healey administration had backed away from the BMC proposal, citing its massive scope. A five-hour City Council meeting in April 2024 garnered negative community feedback, and subsequent updated plans were never shared with the City Council. In February 2025, a source indicated to the Editorial Board that the project was dead.

The original Shattuck plan was admittedly ambitious, offering 400 clinical and shelter beds and 400 supportive housing units. The state’s original request for proposals had only required 75-100 beds, but the plan’s architects argued their vision simply matched the need.

This could very well be true. Boston’s safety net has been stretched thin for years, and an expanded Shattuck campus could be a pressure relief valve, especially in the arena of longer-term housing. It also presents a unique opportunity to ensure that homeless people with coexisting substance use disorders or mental health diagnoses have one-stop access to a variety of support systems.

The campus borders Roxbury to the north, Jamaica Plain to the west, and Roslindale and Mattapan to the east, opening it up to criticism from all sides. Many residents and advocates voiced concerns that problems on the campus would spill into neighboring Franklin Park and the surrounding residential neighborhoods. And they wondered why their communities should be saddled with handling a regional problem.

But it’s also hard to argue against the necessity of adding homeless services. Shattuck, in many respects, is an ideal location. It’s slightly removed from residential areas, bordered by a major thoroughfare, a public park, and a cemetery. The area is zoned for public health purposes and already provides a laundry list of addiction, mental health, and transitional housing programs, and has done so for decades. Most of the community feedback and concern surrounding the project are simply debating matters of scale.

The campus has also been useful for other short-term housing projects. An 18-unit cottage village introduced in 2022 ran until July 2024, when pandemic-era funds dried up. The cottages still stand empty at the site, but no proposals have addressed either reusing or tearing down the structures, despite the program’s touted success.

After seven years of talk, the basic pros and cons of the site aren’t going to change. It’s time to get an update and move the plan forward — or, if the proposal is really dead, to acknowledge that so the search for alternatives can begin. After all, the need remains as real as ever.

title: The politics of representation and belonging in Roxbury
text:
The district includes iconic Black strongholds like Roxbury but also parts of Dorchester, the South End, and the Fenway. Of the roughly 78,000 people who live there, about 25,000 are Black, 20,000 Hispanic, and another 20,000 white, according to Census Reporter, an independent US Census Bureau data visualization platform.

The area’s council seat is opening up because the incumbent, Tania Fernandes Anderson, has pleaded guilty to federal corruption charges and has said she will resign.

According to paperwork filed with the Office of Campaign and Political Finance, there are now at least six candidates seeking to take her place: Said Abdikarim and Said Ahmed, both Somali immigrants who came to the United States as children and declared their intentions to challenge Fernandes Anderson last year; Hurtado; Mavrick Afonso, a Cabo Verdean American who works for Governor Maura Healey’s administration on housing policy; Tchad Cort, a Black woman born and raised in Roxbury who works for the Boston Public Schools transportation department, according to her website; and Miniard Culpepper, a well-known Roxbury pastor who ran for state Senate in 2022.

Hurtado, who works now as the business manager for the city’s supplier diversity department, told me he’s not running as a Latino candidate but rather as someone who wants to represent everybody. In the early 2000s he created South Boston en Acción, a nonprofit to help public housing residents advocate for tenant rights and education access.

First as Janey’s chief of staff when she was the District Seven councilor and then as a senior adviser when she was interim mayor, Hurtado got to know city government. As highlights of his time there, Hurtado mentioned constituent services, working on the cannabis ordinance that Janey authored, and securing funding for the Malcolm X Park, which, Hurtado said, “was the first park that included goals to utilize minority women subcontractors.” (Janey contributed $500 to Hurtado’s campaign, one of the first individuals to do so, he said. She did not respond to a request for comment for this column.)

“This race will be a huge statement if I can build a coalition that’s truly representative of all parts of this district — new voices, people who haven’t been heard, who don’t feel hopeful about change,” Hurtado said.

Still, it took years for Black leaders in Boston to acquire the political power that they have, and the onus will be on Hurtado to prove that his election would be a new chapter in that history — not a retreat from it.

Not that any of the candidates starts off a clear favorite. As wide and multiethnic as the field of contenders is, Jacquetta Van Zandt, a political strategist and host of the “Politics and Prosecco” online show, is not impressed. “There are really no formidable candidates who have had enough of a history in politics to really bring about change,” Van Zandt, who is a homeowner in the district, told me. “A lot of times these community advocates think that they can come with the same kind of piss and vinegar that they bring to the streets and bring that into City Hall, and I think that’s what we’re seeing now.”

Van Zandt said this district is “very mistrustful” because it’s “often the first sought out for votes but the last to get resources.” That’s the reason why the district has some of the lowest voter turnout rates in Boston municipal elections. She said she’s afraid the race will turn into ”just a bunch of community activists screaming and shouting and trying to out community each other, instead of actually talking about governing and what that looks like and what could help this district.”

Hurtado’s candidacy challenges the notion that political representation in District Seven must come only from within the Black community, even as he insists he isn’t running as a Latino candidate. The question is whether he can convince voters to give him a chance.

Correction: An earlier version of this column mischaracterized Samuel Hurtado’s two roles working for former mayor Kim Janey. Hurtado was Janey’s chief of staff when she was the District Seven councilor and senior adviser when Janey was interim mayor.

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
WONDERFUL & STRANGE: A TRIBUTE TO DAVID LYNCH New York-based singer and composer Annie Hart leads this show honoring the late visionary whose view of America was singularly strange yet motivated by a sense of innate goodness. Hart’s synth-romantic act Au Revoir Simone were part of 2017’s “Twin Peaks: The Return,” Lynch’s final love letter to the bucolic yet cursed Washington town he created in the early ’90s. April 19, 6:30 p.m. doors. Crystal Ballroom at Somerville Theatre, Somerville. crystalballroomboston.com

SPIRITBOX: TSUNAMI SEA NORTH AMERICAN TOUR This British Columbia-formed band — whose lead wailer, Courtney LaPlante, joined Houston MC Megan Thee Stallion onstage at Coachella last weekend — specializes in hulking, yet melodic, rock. April 19, 6:30 p.m. MGM Music Hall at Fenway. crossroadspresents.com

LUCY DACUS: FOREVER IS A FEELING TOUR The singer-songwriter released “Forever Is a Feeling,” her latest collection of deeply felt, quietly vibrant folk-pop, in March. April 20 and 21, 7:15 p.m. MGM Music Hall at Fenway. crossroadspresents.com

MAURA JOHNSTON

EBO TAYLOR AND PAT THOMAS A visit — and a farewell, apparently — from a man, now 90 years of age, who has been making his mark on African music for over 50 years and is truly a legend of highlife and Afrobeat. He’s joined by longtime collaborator Pat Thomas, an iconic singer in his own right, and will be showcasing the just released album he made with West Coast impresario Adrian Younge. April 18, 8 p.m. $49.25. Paradise Rock Club, 967 Commonwealth Ave. 617-876-4275. www.globalartslive.org

LA LOM A.k.a. the Los Angeles League of Musicians, this buzzworthy instrumental trio travels coast to coast to offer up a singular musical concoction that pulls in everything from bolero to cumbia, chicha to West Coast country, rockabilly to vintage soul, music that they’ve grounded in some way in the city they call home. April 18, 6:30 p.m. $25. Royale, 279 Tremont St. 888-929-7849. www.axs.com

JIM LAUDERDALE The prolific Jim Lauderdale, who seems to release at least a couple of albums every year, was scheduled to do two area dates last November, but illness intervened. He’s making them up this week with a full band he’s dubbed “the Game Changers,” one that includes the marvelous Lillie Mae, who will play a set to open, then sing with Lauderdale and company. You can catch them in North Andover Saturday and Providence Sunday. April 19, 8 p.m. $35. Crossroads Music Series, 190 Academy Road, North Andover. www.crossroadsmusicseries.org; April 20, 7 p.m. $28.33. The Parlour, 1119 North Main St., Providence. 401-383-5858. www.theparlourri.com

STUART MUNRO

THE BOSTON PROGRESSIVE JAZZ FESTIVAL This eclectic two-night jamboree presents local improvisers playing boundary-bending music. Saturday’s offerings include The New Jazz Orchestra, Brazilian singer-songwriters Caio e Jess, electronic music duo Shwesmo, and more; Sunday’s roster features post-rockers Voodoo Baby Aliens, adventurous collective boyarin/hofbauer/djikstra/mark, and avant-guitarist David Fiuczynski’s KiF, plus additional acts. April 19 and 20, 5-11 p.m. $25 for one night, $40 for both. Arts at the Armory, 191 Highland Ave., Somerville. artsatthearmory.org/events

THE EDMAR COLÓN QUINTET The accomplished Puerto Rican saxophonist, pianist, and composer — who has collaborated with the likes of Wayne Shorter, Teri Lyne Carrington, and the Boston Pops — fronts a first-rate band, previewing pieces for an upcoming album. April 24, 6 p.m. No cover. Long Live Roxbury, 152 Hampden St. longlivebeerworks.com/boston

ERIC BIBB WITH MICHAEL JEROME BROWN The acclaimed acoustic folk blues singer, songwriter, and guitarist is a three-time Grammy Award nominee and two-time Blues Music Award winner, with over 29 solo albums to his credit, and nearly as many collaborations. With fellow blues guitar and vocal ace Brown. April 25, 8 p.m. $35. Club Passim, 47 Palmer St., Cambridge. clubpassim.org

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA The BSO and music director Andris Nelsons continue their end-of-season Shostakovich marathon. This weekend brings Symphony No. 15 paired with Beethoven’s Piano Concerto No. 4, with the redoubtable Mitsuko Uchida as soloist (April 18 and 19); next weekend brings Symphony No. 6, Stravinsky’s Symphony of Psalms, and Aleksandra Vrebalov’s new “Love Canticles” (April 26 and 27; note Saturday and Sunday performances) — but before that, catch a screening of Grigori Kosintsev’s “Hamlet” with score by Shostakovich at the Coolidge Corner Theatre, with pre-concert talk by local Soviet history authority Harlow Robinson (April 23). Symphony Hall. 617-266-1200, www.bso.org

BOSTON PHILHARMONIC Founder Benjamin Zander leads the Philharmonic in Mahler’s titanic Symphony No. 2, featuring Swedish soprano Miah Persson, English mezzo-soprano Dame Sarah Connolly, and Boston’s own Chorus pro Musica. April 18, 8 p.m. Symphony Hall. 617-236-0999, www.bostonphil.org

BOSTON BAROQUE Martin Pearlman puts a bow on five-plus decades of leading Boston Baroque with Handel’s “Ariodante”; Eve Summer stage-directs a cast including mezzo-soprano Megan Moore and soprano Robin Johannsen making company debuts as the title role and Dalinda respectively, opposite soprano Amanda Forsythe as Ginevra. April 24 and 25, 7:30 p.m.; April 27, 3 p.m. GBH Calderwood Studio. 617-987-8600, www.baroque.boston

A.Z. MADONNA

A MIDSUMMER NIGHT’S DREAM The place of “A Midsummer Night’s Dream” in the Bard-iverse is so secure that the first job for any new production is to justify its existence. Director Maurice Emmanuel Parent clears that bar by capitalizing on the anything-goes flexibility built into one of Shakespeare’s most accessible plays. Parent amps up the physicality in a propulsively on-the-move production rife with visual, verbal, and musical allusions to pop culture. Through May 4. Actors’ Shakespeare Project. At Mosesian Center for the Arts, Watertown. 617-241-2200 or actorsshakespeareproject.org/midsummer

THE SQUIRRELS Call it a tale of Haves and Have-nots — or, perhaps, Have-nuts and Have-nots. In this satirical allegory of economic inequality and political polarization by Robert Askins, an epic conflict erupts when a group of fox squirrels, near starvation, asks a group of gray squirrels to share their hoard of nuts. Any resemblance to us present-day humans is purely intentional. Directed by Brooks Reeves. April 18-May 18. Apollinaire Theatre Company. At Chelsea Theatre Works, Chelsea. 617-887-2336, www.apollinairetheatre.com

SHUCKED In telling its tale of a rural community struggling to figure out why its all-important corn crop is dying, side-by-side with a story of love lost, regained, and relocated, “Shucked” leaves no pun unspoken, no entendre un-doubled. The pacing gets a bit sluggish at times, but for the most part “Shucked” careens from scene to scene like “Hee-Haw” on acid. Directed by Jack O’Brien, with a very funny book by Robert Horn, and a score by Brandy Clark and Shane McAnally. Through April 20. Presented by Broadway In Boston. At Citizens Opera House, Boston. broadwayinboston.com

DON AUCOIN

Dance

ALVIN AILEY AMERICAN DANCE THEATER Always a dance harbinger of spring, the company returns for five Celebrity Series performances. The engagement encompasses classics from the company’s storied seven-decade repertoire as well as four Boston premieres. Highlights include interim artistic director Matthew Rushing’s “Sacred Songs,” a new work by Lar Lubovich, “Many Angels,” and a new production of Ronald K. Brown’s classic “Grace,” which the company premiered 25 years ago. April 24-27, $25-$120. Boch Center Wang Theatre. www.celebrityseries.org

ZOÉ DANCE COMPANY The company’s latest production, “O,” reflects a five-year collaboration between dancer-choreographer Callie Chapman and artist Christopher Konopka. The creators call the work a “retro-futuristic narrative” that examines how media and technology shape our perspectives and understanding of reality. The central character is a woman who studies the flight patterns of birds to decipher the hidden lives of those around her. Seating is limited. April 18-19, $20-$25. SomArt Space @ the Hive, Somerville. https://zoedance.org/

TRIVENI ENSEMBLE The company mines India’s rich cultural history with the production “Yatra: Journey Through India.” This show integrates the Indian classical dance forms of Bharatanatyam, Kuchipudi, and Odissi with the music and poetry of classical-era composers. All proceeds benefit the American India Foundation. April 19, 2 and 7 p.m., $25-$50. Boston University Dance Theater. www.trivenidance.org

GOODTHANG 2025 The next installment of Paul Kafka-Gibbons’s “THANG” series is titled “Bizzy Bunny Edition.” The free daylong event features performances by a rolling cast of dancers, musicians, and poets, including veteran dancer-choreographer Kelley Donovan. April 18, 10 a.m.-4 p.m., Free. SomArt Space @ the Hive, Somerville. www.thangthang.org

KAREN CAMPBELL

CHRISTIAN MARCLAY: DOORS Just opened: Marclay is likely best known for “The Clock,” his 2010 magnum opus: a 24-hour long film that actually tells the time using 60-second clips from decades of movie history that track, minute by minute, real time in the real world. “Doors,” made in 2022, follows similar logic, though not so rigorous temporal demands. An amalgam of movie scenes of doors opening and closing, the piece leaves the viewer forever on the tortured edge of unknowing — an in-between world of what was and what’s next. Through Sept. 1. Institute of Contemporary Art/Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100, www.icaboston.org

WITNESSING HUMANITY: THE ART OF JOHN WILSON Bostonians might be most familiar with Wilson, born and raised in Roxbury, through “Eternal Presence,” the monumental, enigmatic bust that’s stood sentinel-like at the National Center of Afro-American Artists in Roxbury since 1987. But Wilson, who died in 2015, spent decades before and after crafting socially conscious work around the pervasive issue of racial injustice in America that he experienced all his life. This exhibition, co-organized with New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, is the most substantial display of Wilson’s oeuvre ever assembled, and an opportunity for Boston to reckon with a powerful voice that echoes through generations of its social history. Through June 22. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, www.mfa.org

EDVARD MUNCH: TECHNICALLY SPEAKING I know, I know: “The Scream,” right? There’s no getting around the cultural oversaturation of Munch’s most famous work, but recent efforts have done much to broaden our understanding of Norway’s most-loved artist beyond his all-time smash hit. In the summer of 2023, “Edvard Munch: Trembling Earth,” the Clark Art Institute’s voluminous presentation of the artist’s deep affinities with — and anxieties for — the natural world opened a universe of difference for all but the most devoted Munch fan. “Technically Speaking,” at Harvard, takes a different tack, exploring the artist’s material genius and almost manic enthusiasm for media across painting, drawing, and every manner of printing. With it, a view of an artist too long seen as one-note broadens ever more. Through July 27. Harvard Art Museums, 32 Quincy St., Cambridge. 617-495-9400, harvardartmuseums.org

MURRAY WHYTE

WEAVING AN ADDRESS Patriots Day, April 19, marks the 250th anniversary of the Battle of Lexington and Concord and the start of the Revolutionary War. This exhibition, curated by artist Marla McLeod, explores the lives of Concord’s Black community in Walden Woods back then with an outdoor installation along the Thoreau Trail focusing on Brister Freeman, a soldier in the war and one of the first enslaved people in the area to gain his freedom. Indoors, fiber artists examine the struggles of tracking Black ancestry. Through Oct. 18. Umbrella Arts Center, 40 Stow St., Concord. www.theumbrellaarts.org/weaving-address

CATE McQUAID

ALEX DRAGICEVICH The New York comic grew up with a policeman for a father, and leans left politically. “I had a few reasons to go to the protests,” he says. “People were like, ‘They’re not trained well, too many guns.’ I’m like, ‘And they … never hugged me.” April 18-19, 7 p.m., 9 p.m., and 11 p.m. $25. Goofs Comedy Club, 432 McGrath Highway, Somerville. 617-718-7200, www.goofscomedy.com

JOE LIST The former Boston comic is at a creative peak at the moment, about to play both stage and screen in theaters. He’s at the Wilbur on the 19th, while his new special “Small Ball” and his documentary tribute to friend and fellow comic “Tom Dustin: Portrait of a Comedian,” are both set for release in movie theaters in May. April 19, 7 p.m. $33-$43. The Wilbur, 246 Tremont St. www.thewilbur.com

SARAH TOLLEMACHE Savings accounts are boring and predictable. That’s why Tollemache prefers to put her money in stocks. “In the stock market, it’s going up, and then it’s going down, and it’s doing that all throughout the day,” she says. “You’re just like, ‘Oh my God! Look how much fun my money is having in there! It had more fun than I did today.”April 20, 7 p.m. $15-$20. The Comedy Studio, 5 John F Kennedy St., Cambridge. www.thecomedystudio.com

NICK A. ZAINO III

SWAN BOATS OPENING DAY Spend Saturday morning at the Boston Public Garden lagoon for the 148th opening of the Swan Boats. Mayor Michelle Wu will speak at 11 a.m. to kick off the festivities, and community members can enjoy Swan Boat rides throughout the day. The three-ton paddle boats were created by Robert Paget, who was inspired by the opera “Lohengrin,” where the story’s hero crosses a river in a swan-drawn boat. April 19, 11 a.m. Tickets are $3.25-$4.75. 4 Charles St., Boston Public Garden. boston.gov

MOSSY MANDRAKES Families and little ones can learn the Japanese art of Kokedama, the process of growing plants in a ball of moss and soil that’s wrapped in string. These creatively stored mandrakes can be hung or potted as decoration. Instructor Aiden Duffy from the youth education team will lead visitors through a lesson on the benefits of growing houseplants and how to care for them. April 20, 1:30 p.m.-3 p.m. Tickets are $36 child, $20 adult, $28 member child. New England Botanic Garden at Tower Hill, 11 French Drive, Boylston. purchase.nebg.org

BEDTIME ADVENTURE TALES Father-daughter duo Dirk and Azaria Rose will perform several stories using puppets this weekend, including a bedtime tale featuring a dog and a cat, and another story of two siblings looking for imaginative ways to quell their boredom. After enjoying the performances, visitors can take part in puppet decorating and meet the performers. April 18 and 19, 10:30 a.m. and 1 p.m. Tickets are $18 for 10:30 a.m. shows, $16 for the April 18 1 p.m. show, and pay what you can for the April 19 1 p.m. show. Puppet Showplace Theater, 32 Station St., Brookline. puppetshowplace.org

HALEY CLOUGH

title: Top Spots to Live in Boston and Cambridge 2025
text:
Median home price: $658,331

Increase since 2019: 42.2%

Pat Tierney moved to Hyde Park for the space. After growing up in densely packed South Boston, she was delighted to find a home in Boston that had a sizable lawn and even horses grazing across the street. In the half-century since she arrived, the horses have gone, but the appeal of the neighborhood’s tree-shaded lots remains, says Tierney, an agent with Insight Realty Group.

“You have bigger yards here” compared with some other parts of Boston, she says. “It’s a more suburban, country feel.”

There’s plenty more to love about Hyde Park as well. Two commuter rail lines and proximity to the Red Line make it easy to get into the heart of the city for work or entertainment, while restaurants, shops, Roundhead Brewing Co., and the thriving Menino Arts Center all make it easy to stay in the neighborhood. An indoor sports complex hosts soccer games and pickleball matches, a well-regarded golf course welcomes the public, and the nearby Neponset River offers opportunities for canoeing and kayaking.

Hyde Park’s housing stock includes many single-family, detached homes — some updated, some in need of a little TLC — and a smaller number of condos, mostly located in renovated houses. The area is also home to Boston’s first LGBTQ, affordable senior housing complex, The Pryde.

Word seems to be getting out about the appeal of the once-overlooked neighborhood. Sales were up last year over 2023, and Tierney sees a wide range of buyers, from city employees and teachers to young professionals, drawn to a rare, relatively affordable area. “Everyone is coming in,” she says.

Median home price: $741,710

Increase since 2019: 37.5%

Roslindale has everything that makes for a vibrant neighborhood: thriving local businesses and eateries, cultural diversity, and plenty of outdoors spaces where the community can connect. Yet it remains something of a hidden gem, with less buzz than some other areas, and condos and some single-family homes still available at comparatively accessible prices by Boston standards.

Median home price: $712,483

Increase since 2019: 27.4%

Boston’s largest neighborhood, culturally rich Dorchester has shaken off much of its past reputation as an unsafe place. Today it offers a diversity of people, places, and price points that make it a dynamic and compelling place to live (and eat — the City of Boston lists more than 200 restaurants in the neighborhood).

Median home price: $993,400

Increase since 2019: 28.6%

Aileen Gorman, 43, has never considered moving out of Charlestown. She grew up in the waterfront Boston neighborhood, made her First Communion and attended school there. When it came time to start her own family, she wanted to raise her children in the walkable, welcoming community she says is unfailingly supportive of its residents, old and new.

“Family and community and a sense of pride are very much part of the makeup of Charlestown,” says Gorman, who volunteers with several local organizations. “We all just take care of each other.”

Boston’s oldest neighborhood, Charlestown is tucked into the corner of Interstate 93 and Route 1. The area’s deep history is evident in ways both big (the 221-foot-tall Bunker Hill Monument) and small (cobblestones and gas street lamps), but the community has not remained stagnant. Once an enclave of working class, Irish-American families, new residents have been renovating traditional red-brick row houses and helping attract a mix of independent businesses and restaurants. Today, the market is dominated by condos and a few single-family homes with prices north of $1 million, though smaller units — and even the occasional houseboat — can be found for less.

Even as Charlestown changes, Gorman says, she has every intention of sticking around for whatever comes next.

“There’s no replicating what we have here,” she says. “Why leave?”

Median home price: $764,463

Increase since 2019: 28.5%

West Roxbury combines the tree-lined streets, grassy lawns, and community vibe of the suburbs with the urban energy and walkable stores and restaurants of the city. That makes it hard to beat. Housing options include single-family homes and condos in renovated houses and newer developments, many with price tags lower than $800,000 (some even come in under $500,000, though they tend to move fast).

Median home price: $801,556

Increase since 2019: 22.7%

Even as home prices have increased in JP, the neighborhood has so far managed to hang on to its bohemian reputation with its annual Porchfest music event, strong arts community, and significant LGBTQ population. It is also home to iconic green spaces, including Jamaica Pond and the Arnold Arboretum, Frederick Law Olmsted’s iconic 281-acre preserve.

Median home price: $1,400,786

Increase since 2019: 70.1%

Even Boston locals would be forgiven for not knowing the exact boundaries of Cambridge’s Riverside neighborhood. The diminutive, densely packed district along the Charles River largely comprises parts of what are otherwise known as Harvard Square and Central Square, as well as a web of smaller residential roads.

Whatever you call it, however, there is no confusion that it is one of the most in-demand areas in Cambridge, with median home prices soaring more than 70 percent over the past five years. Real estate agent Charles Cherney, of Compass, recalls a single-family home recently listed for nearly $1.9 million that quickly garnered multiple offers.

“There are a handful of residential streets and a few lucky people who call this neighborhood home,” Cherney says.

The appeal of the area has a lot to do with the proximity to Harvard Square, Harvard University, and the businesses and restaurants along Massachusetts Avenue, Cherney says. It is also an attractive spot for families, with several well-kept parks and playgrounds scattered throughout, as well as one of the city’s most highly-rated elementary schools, the Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. School.

The future of the neighborhood is less clear. A recent city vote will allow four-story homes to be built on residential properties without special permits or variances, with six stories permitted on some lots, as long as they include affordable housing. Whether this density increase will change the popularity of Riverside — or simply create more of it to love — remains to be seen.

“It will be fascinating to see how it plays out,” Cherney says.

Median single-family price: $1,862,594

Increase since 2019: 52.2%

Downtown Boston conjures images of office buildings and parking garages, it’s true. But the business-oriented district has been popular with home buyers drawn to the neighborhood’s central location and the stunning views and luxury amenities offered by the high end condos that generally dominate the market.

Median single-family price: $1,523,781

Increase since 2019: 46.9%

The appeals of Cambridgeport are numerous: elegant houses, the waterfront beauty of Magazine Beach Park, and easy access to the food, culture, and shopping of both Boston and Cambridge. Would-be residents will have to be patient and willing to pay. There are rarely many listings in the neighborhood and they come with hefty price tags. But what around here doesn’t?

West of Boston

North of Boston

South of Boston

Methodology: To arrive at this annual list, we relied on the finite — but meaningful — wisdom of supply and demand: Significantly increasing prices in these communities are a signal that many buyers are eager to call them home. We analyzed median home prices from 2019 and 2024 to find the biggest five-year increases across three price tiers for each region. In the Boston suburbs, we looked at single-family data from The Warren Group, excluding communities with fewer than 50 sales in 2024. For Boston and Cambridge neighborhoods, we used median home price data — including both single-family and condo sales — from Redfin. Three journalists with real estate expertise collaborated to select our “May We Suggest” entries, our admittedly subjective picks of communities to consider.

title: Boston School Committee to vote on proposed teacher contract Wednesday
text:
“This contract affirms our shared commitment to strengthening teaching and learning, supporting our educators, and building a bright future for every BPS student,” Mayor Michelle Wu said in a statement released shortly after the committee’s vote.

While the City Council must still approve the agreement, district administrators and union representatives said it would raise the wages of some of the district’s lowest paid workers, like classroom paraprofessionals, and guarantee additional staffing for inclusive classrooms with large numbers of students enrolled in special education.

It would also eliminate a requirement that general education teachers obtain a license so they can work with students with disabilities.

“Our district has dedicated public servants on all sides of the [negotiating] table who care deeply about our students and equally understand the importance of our work,” Superintendent Mary Skipper told School Committee members.

Under the terms of the agreement, Boston Public Schools’ teachers, who earn an average of about $120,000, would receive between a 9 percent to 11.5 percent pay increase over the three-year agreement.

Classroom paraprofessionals, who on average earn about $45,000, could see a dramatic boost in pay of about 30 percent over the period. Staff like health paraprofessionals and family liaisons, who earn an average of about $59,000, would see a 12 percent raise.

Sign language interpreters, who earn an average of $63,000, would get a roughly 9 percent raise.

The new agreement is retroactive to Sept. 1.

Lou Mandarini, a senior adviser for Wu who served as part of the district’s negotiating team, said a key initiative was raising the salaries of the city’s lowest-paid workers.

“Over the decades, [contracts have] just given a straight percentage, whether you make $120,000 a year or you make 40 and frankly, that’s something that we’ve sought to correct,” Mandarini told the School Committee. “And the opportunity to do it in the largest collective bargaining agreement in the city is a major win for us” and school employees.

Under the contract, classes with special education students will have new requirements. Inclusive pre-K classrooms will be limited to 15 students. In kindergarten through Grade 6 classes with large numbers of students with individualized education plans, teachers will have the help of another educator.

Additional special education teachers will be assigned to classes in Grades 7 through 12 that have more than eight students with IEPs.

Caitlin Gaffny, a representative of the Boston Teachers Union, praised the new contract, and said it would stabilize staffing in schools and reduce vacancies. By eliminating the dual license requirement, teachers won’t be overwhelmed doing two jobs at once.

“There will be supports for students with disabilities in general education classrooms,” she said. “There are many other improvements which will increase staff well being and allow for a more sustainable career in Boston Public Schools.”

Under the contract, the total cost of union pay would increase by $181 million over three years. That hike is 28 percent more than the $141 million increase included in the last contract, which was reached in 2022. The district did not provide the total cost of the contract.

However, according to the district, the total cost of union salaries under the new contract’s first year in fiscal 2025 would be $815 million. That figure would grow to $843 million in fiscal 2026, then reach $868 million by fiscal 2027.

The union contract would be a sizable chunk of the district’s budget. Last month, the School Committee approved a $1.6 billion budget for fiscal 2026.

To help fund the contract, the School Committee is seeking supplemental budget appropriations from the City Council, including $33.3 million in fiscal 2025 and $55.9 million for fiscal 2026, according to the district’s chief financial officer, David Bloom.

The council must still vote for that additional funding, a decision that could come in May.

Martha M. Walz, the interim president of the Boston Municipal Research Bureau, has raised concerns about the size of the contract’s cost, and focus on wages rather than student outcomes. It appears to do little for English learners, who make up roughly one-third of Boston’s 48,000 students, she has said.

“As BPS stakeholders consider the contract’s substantial costs, the touchstone must be whether and how the contract will lead to improved academic outcomes for Boston’s students,” Walz said in a statement last week. “It is not clear how the limited changes included in the contract will drive improvements in teaching and learning.”

title: A novel for kids tells the true story of a newspaper for dogs
text:
One part of the book that Lobenstine invented was her character’s job at the Globe. She made up that detail, she says, “because it’s such a Boston story and I’m a huge fan of the Boston Globe.” In reality, she adds, “probably the Barking Puppy is the biggest paper I’ve worked at, besides my fourth-grade newspaper.”

When Lobenstine decided to write a children’s novel about their adventures, the real Sophie, now a student at Emerson, jumped right in. “She’s so creative,” says Lobenstine. “I talked to her a little bit about it, and then we decided to do an artist retreat — some friends of ours own a farm in Vermont and they invited us to come. I was working on the book and she was really into being a filmmaker in high school so she made these two short documentaries. She continues to be this amazingly creative person and I’ve seen her really come into her own.”

“The Barking Puppy” is meant to entertain and delight, like any other middle-grade novel — Lobenstine says she was “just smitten with how fun the story could be” — but the author also hopes it inspires its readers, if not to start their own newspapers, to at least “lean into their passions.”

“I wanted the book to model a lot of different ways to be yourself,” she adds, “and to show how a community can be a place where we have room for each other, where we hold each other up.”

Lori Lobenstine will read at 6 p.m. on Thursday, April 24, at the Frugal Bookstore, 57 Warren St., Roxbury.

And now for some recommendations ...

Lydia Millet is one of our finest fiction writers, a cool chronicler of an overheating planet and a master at melding history in humor in novels like “Oh Pure and Radiant Heart” and “A Children’s Bible.” “Atavists” (Norton) is the latest collection of her short fiction, and a perfect introduction to Millet’s work for those who haven’t yet discovered her laser wit and enormous heart.

Tech-driven visions of the future have always had a high error rate (I am still looking around for the robot housemaid promised to me by “The Jetsons”). But as Silicon Valley grows in political influence, the fantastic plans promulgated by industry leaders have begun to influence policy and government budgets. This isn’t great, as science journalist Adam Becker points out in “More Everything Forever: AI Overlords, Science Empires, and Silicon Valley’s Crusade to Control the Future of Humanity” (Basic), a clear-eyed assessment of today’s pie-eyed prophets.

In “Notes to John” (Knopf) readers are given excruciatingly intimate access to the mind of Joan Didion — these collected “notes” comprise the journal she wrote to her husband, John Gregory Dunne, to convey and explain the conversations she had with her therapist over the first decade of the 21st century. They are extraordinary. Didion’s voice is undiluted, bold, open, and the topics she discusses range from childhood to motherhood, from work to money to fame. And yet reading these entries can feel a little invasive, a bit of an intrusion; much as I adore Didion’s work and have learned from her over the years, I kept asking whether we really need to see into her soul, after her death.

This story has been updated to correct an error in the spelling of “The Barking Puppy” author’s last name.

Kate Tuttle edits the Globe’s Books section.

title: How to celebrate Earth Day in Greater Boston
text:
The origins of Earth Day go back to 1970 when concerns about industrialization’s effect on environmental and public well-being sparked national protests and demonstrations demanding government protections for the environment.

Fifty-five years later, Earth Day is a worldwide event. In 2025, the official celebration falls on April 22, but throughout the month, organizations, groups, and individuals gather to mobilize and raise awareness about sustainable practices. This year’s global theme, Our Power, Our Planet, aims to emphasize the strength in numbers, encouraging collective strides toward a healthy planet.

But whether you’re celebrating Earth Day by mobilizing or helping protect and grow the city’s natural landscape, Greater Boston will host diverse opportunities for locals to immerse themselves in communal and educational practices that support the cause. From eco-cleanups with fellow community members to vibrant sustainable markets, here’s how to celebrate Earth Day in 2025.

Fellow tree-huggers and good Samaritans can unite for the Hub’s parks, forestry, and rivers by spending this week helping to repopulate forestry or caring for our waterways. Planting trees promotes biodiversity in these areas, improving conditions for inhabiting critters and the air quality of the local community. Our rivers, too, need a helping hand, being vital recreational spaces for city dwellers and the habitat of local wildlife. Here are some local tree-planting and river cleanup initiatives accepting volunteers in honor of Earth Day:

ARBOR DAY TREE PLANTING Volunteers can register for Speak for the Trees Boston’s annual Arbor Week tree planting featuring tall and leafy additions to Mount Hope Cemetery and Roxbury Community College. The local organization will provide tools and guidance for participants, so all they have to bring is their green thumb — and probably some gardening gloves to avoid splinters. Other nature-based events will take place throughout the week, including seedling bagging and giveaways, a “Mural Making with Nature Workshop,” and a tree giveaway in Jamaica Plain. April 23-May 3, times and locations vary. treeboston.org

PLANT TREES WITH MYRWA The Mystic River Watershed Association is organizing various tree-planting events across the Boston area. With supplies and guidance provided by the organization, volunteers will help sustain the tree canopies in local parks by adding to their population of bare-root trees. April 24-29. Locations vary. mycsticriver.org

CHARLES RIVER CLEANUP Though the Charles River is an iconic natural landmark, it remains susceptible to litter and invasive species. Every year, environmental organizations invite volunteers to revitalize the Charles during their Earth Day cleanup. The effort is statewide, spanning two days, 80 miles, and over 1,000 acres with plenty of volunteer opportunities for Massachusetts residents. April 25 and 26. Times and locations vary. charlesrivercleanup.org

NEPONSET RIVER CLEANUP The Neponset River, the slightly less famous Western Massachusetts river, is also being given special care this Earth Day. The annual cleanup, organized by the Neponset River Watershed Organization, brings together hundreds of volunteers to revive the 29-mile waterway. April 26, 9 a.m.-noon. Free. Locations vary. neponset.org

While Earth Day is historically a day of advocacy, it’s also a cause for celebration. Those hoping to enrich their appreciation of the Earth can learn more about sustainable practices in an upbeat, high-energy environment while partying eco-consciously.

PARTY FOR THE PLANET This Earth Day, the Stone Zoo is shining a light on the captivating lives of wildlife with its Party for the Planet celebration. Visitors can attend educator chats given by zookeepers and explore the unique stories of sloths, barn owls, and cougars. Families can bring their kids along for crafting activities, including painting wooden bee-themed ornaments and wooden magnets. April 22, 9 a.m.-1 p.m. Ticket prices vary. zoonewecngland.org

FOUND VINTAGE EARTHFEST If you haven’t heard, shopping secondhand is in. When shoppers see overpriced retail items, now more than ever they react with “I can just thrift this for cheaper.” Celebrating the growing community of thrifters and vintage shoppers, FOUND Vintage Market is organizing a secondhand outdoor market with dozens of local vendors in attendance. A DJ and food trucks will also be available for attendees. April 26, noon-5 p.m. 222 Jacob’s St., Cambridge.

EARTH DAY N NIGHT FESTIVAL Whether it’s day or night, there are no limits when it comes to celebrating the Earth, which is why the Great American Beer Hall will be hosting a 12-hour event to raise funds for the Clean Water Fund. The day will begin with a New England vendor market, putting the region’s art and artisanal goods on display for purchase. Then, the event will transform into an indie music festival with artists spanning genres, from surfer rock to EDM. April 26, 1 p.m.-1 a.m. posh.vip/earth-day-n-night

BOSTON PUBLIC MARKET EARTH DAY The Boston Public Market will host a five-day Earth Day celebration, beginning with Earth-themed cookie decorating and nature puppet stories geared toward the kiddos. Other events include workshops, grounding yoga classes, and organic smoothies. The programming will end on April 25 with a plant pot workshop, where attendees will sculpt their own planter. April 22-26. 100 Hanover St. bostonpublicmarket.org

Marianna Orozco can be reached at marianna.orozco@globe.com.

title: Used by many, but in need of a ‘complete overhaul.’ At 30, where does the Reggie Lewis Center go from here?
text:
“We’re doing everything we can to maintain it and take care of it as best we can, but it needs a complete overhaul,” said Michael Turner, executive director of business development and marketing for the Reggie.

And there are stark fiscal realities. The center costs between $3.5 million and $4 million to run annually. It’s operating at an annual average deficit of about $2 million, which is covered by Roxbury Community College’s state appropriation. (The site is managed by the college.) Officials at the Reggie, which is also state-funded, hope the center’s separate state appropriation is increased so that it no longer operates in the red.

As the center now celebrates its 30th anniversary, administrators are hoping to reintroduce the center to the communities it serves.

Jennie McDonald-Brown, RCC’s vice president of institutional advancement and the college’s foundation, put it bluntly: The 123,000-square-foot building is a testament to the notion that Roxbury, historically the heart of Black Boston and a neighborhood that has suffered from systemic racism and disinvestment over the decades, deserves nice things, too. It was a world-class facility when it opened and people like McDonald-Brown want to return it to that status.

“This for us is a springboard to bring it back to that place,” she said of the anniversary.

But she and Turner are forthright about the work that needs to be done. The capital needs are significant, and the state is allotting $22 million for center renovations, which, after state fees, will fund $15.3 million worth of improvements in coming months. Turner expects big upgrades to happen over the next two years: a new roof, a new HVAC system, and a new track.

Central to the Reggie’s mission, said Turner and McDonald-Brown, is reducing the life expectancy gap between Roxbury, where more than 80 percent of residents are people of color, and Back Bay, one of Boston’s wealthier, and whiter, neighborhoods, where residents, on average, live much, much longer.

More exercise and healthy programs can help cut into the public health crisis, which reflects structural racism, they say.

When the center first opened, the Globe marveled at the banked, eight-lane 200-meter high school track. But the center’s construction and opening was also imbued with the spirit of its namesake: a basketball legend for both the Celtics and the Northeastern Huskies who was also known locally for his philanthropic work, which included giving away turkeys to those in need at Thanksgiving. Lewis died of cardiac arrest in 1993 at age 27.

At the center’s 1995 opening ceremony, then-governor William Weld said: “Generations of young athletes will use this facility to make their own dreams come true. The name Reggie Lewis will keep them attuned that the real immortals have more than talent and strength. The ones that we remember forever have the biggest hearts.”

Since its inception, the Reggie has had many faces. It is the home to high school indoor track and field in the state, it’s the home to Roxbury Community College Athletics, and it also serves as host to myriad programming, from senior aerobics to AAU basketball to volleyball camps to youth golf lessons to dance classes to political rallies.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, it was the site of a mass vaccination distribution center. Both Turner and McDonald-Brown want residents to think of the facility as much more than a track.

But in recent years, much of the friction regarding the facility has focused on how the center balances those various identities.

Despite the droves who come to the center each year, Turner considers the facility to be underutilized. That’s because the bulk of the 300,000 people who use the facility — about 250,000 — walk through the doors during indoor track season, which runs roughly from late November to late March. During that period, there are on average two track meets every weekday afternoon, not to mention invitationals on the weekends. But for a good stretch of the year, the facility is simply not as busy.

And in recent years, there has been controversy. City councilors raised concerns about use of the track, pushing for more time for city high school indoor runners who were forced to practice in school hallways instead of on the track and questioning how much time is allotted for high school students from the suburbs.

But Turner said recently that the allotted time for city high school students to use the track for practice has not changed in 30 years.

It is a state facility, funded with state money. And as a state facility, it has obligations to host track meets from high schools throughout Massachusetts,according to the state legislation that enabled the creation of the center. But no one uses the facility more than Boston Public Schools, Turner said. He chalked up the recent political friction to “lack of understanding and communication.”

“We do everything in our power to make sure they have access,” he said of serving the city’s public school students.

Officials behind the Reggie agree that the center can do a better job of promoting itself. Too many residents see school buses parked outside the building from well-heeled suburbs and assume that is what the facility is all about.

“We can do a much better job with storytelling,” McDonald-Brown said.

Concurrently with the center’s planned facelift, the Reggie is amid a push to offer more programming, which officials hope will bring in more residents.

Those behind the Reggie hope to raise more than $5 million in the coming years to achieve that. A partnership with the Boston Athletic Association, the organization that puts on the Marathon, has been successful, allowing the center to hire more fitness instructors, which has increased the number of fitness sessions it can offer from three a week for seniors to more than 20 a week for all ages in recent months.
