title: Feeling alone? Go to the Y. YMCA launches campaign to fight loneliness.
text:
“It’s the first time the Y is putting its weight behind a marketing and storytelling effort that is not about membership or signing up for swimming or any of those things,” Shapiro said. “The tagline is ‘See You At the Y,’ but it’s really about being seen and belonging and what it means to be seen.”

The program is backed by a $100,000 grant from the Newton-based Highland Street Foundation, which will support YMCA programming for 2,050 families, sponsor 1,755 free summer memberships for teens, and provide 510 new senior memberships. The funds will also go toward new programs that focus less on physical fitness and more on creating healthy relationships. Think sightseeing tours for seniors, programs to get teens off screens, and more movie and date night events to bring families together (or give parents an occasional break).

To promote the launch, the Y plans to set up oversize Connect Four boards strategically throughout Greater Boston. Each game piece will have a conversation prompt to encourage engagement.

Shapiro said the idea for this new focus stems from a shift he saw in public life as we’ve emerged from the COVID pandemic.

“You can see it in the data: We’re going to libraries less, to the office less, and we’re less invested in public schools and public places,” he said. “We’re not seeing each other as much, and at a higher level, we’re not seeing people different from us. The Y felt like a place where we had a fighting chance,” to prove that such connections were still possible.

Tara Murphy, a YGB board member and vice president of public affairs at Wellesley College, said the impetus for the campaign also stemmed from how the Y adapted during the pandemic to respond to the needs of its members, be it rolling out child care programs for first responders or launching food distribution efforts.

“We started really thinking about the Y as a problem-solver on some of the big things. What are we about and what are the challenges we’re bringing the full force and our scale to solve?” she said. “It showed us that we could think a little bit bigger.”

Calling it both a “catalyst” and a “call to action,” Murphy said the goal of the effort was to give a name to a problem that too often goes unrecognized. And she’s hoping it will help major players in the city to reframe their missions and be more intentional about building community.

“I think a lot of community-building organizations might not think of themselves as being ‘We-fight-loneliness organizations,’” Murphy said.

So far, more than a dozen local nonprofits and civic institutions have signed on, including the Boston Public Health Commission, Boston Police Department, and Boston Public Schools. The City of Boston’s Office of Youth Engagement and Advancement is also taking part, as is the Boston City Council. Nonprofits Catholic Charities, Embrace Boston, and the Red Sox Foundation are all engaged in the effort, with Mass General Brigham and NeighborHealth joining as health care partners.

Boston Public Health Commissioner Dr. Bisola Ojikutu said she’s thrilled that the campaign will help destigmatize conversations about social isolation and mental illness.

“I know my patients don’t necessarily come out and say, ‘I’m lonely,’ even though loneliness is an experience that most of us face in our lives,” she said. “Loneliness is a critical public health issue, and we believe that creating space and opportunity for people to feel connected is a high priority” in an increasingly digital world.

She hopes to partner with the Y to help bring culturally and linguistically appropriate behavioral health specialists into communities across the city and normalize the idea that you can not only go to the Y to lift weights, but also to lift your spirits.

“Just how amazing would it be if people could step into a YMCA and feel like there was someone they could talk to?” Ojikutu said.

Boston’s YMCA was the first in the nation, and Shapiro said he hopes the Greater Boston Y can also be a national leader in shaping these conversations.

“Institutions need to be stickier, there aren’t as many as there used to be,” he said. “We want to demonstrate that there are places where this is happening and those places need to work harder, including us, as we’ve never faced such headwinds. We want Boston to be the most relationally connected city.”

title: Josh Kraft releases plan for BPS, featuring more exam school seats, hybrid School Committee, central office changes
text:
The state and the district are allowing that plan to expire in June. Wu and BPS Superintendent Mary Skipper argue the district has made significant progress toward its goals, pointing to an improved transportation system, updated programs for English learners and special education students, and a new long-term facilities plan.

But critics argue there’s still significant room for improvement, concern the Kraft campaign appears to have taken into account when drafting his education platform.

Kraft’s plan features several proposals that take aim at areas of frustration for BPS families.

Kraft, for instance, says he is committed to seeing the School Committee transition to a hybrid model in which part of the board would comprise members elected by voters.

The idea has proven popular with Boston voters. Currently, the body’s members are appointed by the mayor, but nearly 79 percent of Boston voters in 2021 voted in favor of having a fully elected School Committee. Wu vetoed that proposal in 2023, despite having said on the campaign trail on 2021 that she supported a hybrid model, arguing the switch could bring instability at a time when the district is working to address its significant challenges.

Kraft also said he would reevaluate the current exam schools admissions process, which many parents have found frustrating and unfair in recent years — some arguing the current system locks out high-achieving students from some wealthier neighborhoods and schools, while others say it fails to create opportunities for some of the low-income students it is supposed to benefit.

Kraft’s plan pledges to add more coveted seats to the city’s most competitive and highly desired exam schools, including by possibly creating satellite campuses to accommodate more students.

Kraft is also proposing to change the district’s leadership structure, taking Skipper’s job and splitting it into two superintendent roles — one focused on operations, the other on academics.

He proposed cutting redundant positions at the district’s central office, with the intention of streamlining bureaucracy and sending more resources toward the schools themselves, rather than administration.

Kraft also pledged to issue a comprehensive long-term facilities plan within one year of assuming office should he win in November’s election, so families are not “blindsided by abrupt announcements of of school closings on short notice,” according to the plan.

School closures, which administrators acknowledge are necessary but painful, are historically a politically fraught endeavor, often drawing protests and demonstrations by the impacted families and communities.

The district’s current long-term facilities plan aims to close 17 percent of BPS buildings by 2030 to consolidate resources amid dropping enrollment to provide students with higher quality educational experiences and activities. The plan, however, does not outline which schools could be on the chopping block to avoid influencing students and staff to flee those schools before additional, high-quality seats in the remaining schools are ready. But that’s meant recent school closure announcements have left some families feeling blindsided.

Other elements of Kraft’s education platform include:

Prioritizing boosting the district’s literacy rates by 10 percent through high-dosage tutoring and community partnerships.

Renovating Madison Park Technical Vocation High School through a “community-oriented, efficient process.”

Creating more vocational opportunities for students.

Creating an “Office of Parents” in City Hall to oversee clear communication between families, BPS, and the mayor’s office.

Promoting transparency on districtwide projects by making key data and information for each goal publicly available, including cost and key staff and contact information.

In a lengthy statement to the Globe, Wu slammed Kraft’s plan as evidence he is out of touch with what is best for BPS, in contrast with herself, who is personally invested in the district as a mother of two BPS students.

“Just as we’ve seen in his other campaign proposals, it’s easy to throw rocks without taking the time to learn how budgets, contracts, facilities, and community needs all fit together,” Wu said. She also noted that Kraft’s plan failed to mention or offer a solution for how to better educate and support students and teachers from diverse backgrounds.

“In a district where 1 in 3 students has an IEP and 1 in 2 are a current or former multilingual learner, it’s clueless and irresponsible to leave out any mention of bilingual education, students with disabilities, students experiencing housing insecurity, and pipelines for diverse educators,” she continued.

Wu emphasized recent successes that the district has achieved under her leadership -- including rising attendance, lower chronic absenteeism, strong teacher retention, ongoing facility construction and renovation, and expanded high-quality pre-K programs.

Paul Reville, former state secretary of education and a professor at the Harvard Graduate School of Education, pointed to those metrics as “bright spots” of improvement in the district, and said Kraft’s claim that Wu and school leadership have “failed” BPS students and parents is “unfair.” Reville is not affiliated with Wu’s campaign though he has on occasion offered the mayor advice on education policy.

Still, there’s plenty of room, and need, for more progress, he said. Kraft’s education platform, though, doesn’t necessarily detail how he plans to achieve the lofty goals he’s laid out, Reville said.

“It’s a value statement ... an outline, it’s a sketch of priority areas,” Reville said. “But ultimately, in the campaign, he’ll have to be judged by what kind of meat he puts on the bones here.”

Mary Tamer, a former Boston School Committee member and executive director of education nonprofit MassPotential, said she thought splitting the superintendent job into two roles “makes really good sense,” considering the range of problems that schools leaders are trying to fix in the district.

“Recognizing that these are two very distinct sets of skills, academics and operations, folks that are finely skilled in those areas, makes perfect sense instead of expecting one person to be omniscient,” Tamer said. She is not affiliated with Kraft’s campaign, but said Kraft has previously asked for her opinions and concerns about BPS, which she shared with him.

While she would not say who she trusts more between Kraft and Wu to lead BPS, Tamer did express frustration with the status quo.

“Our data outcomes speak for themselves,” she said. “I do not see the sense of urgency that we should be seeing given how poor our outcomes are for the vast majority of the kids in the Boston Public Schools.”

John Hilliard and Christopher Huffaker of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Raw milk fans hope for easier availability under RFK Jr.
text:
Rumley just wishes he didn’t have to go so far out of his way for what to him should be a routine milk run. “I would much prefer to go to my local grocery store and pick up my raw milk,” he said.

That’s not possible right now in Massachusetts — or in most of the United States. But Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who in February became the nation’s top health official, has pledged to roll back regulations on raw milk and reportedly tapped Mark McAfee, chief executive of the nation’s largest raw milk producer, to advise the Food and Drug Administration “on raw milk policy and standards development.”

“Raw milk,” simply, is milk that hasn’t been pasteurized, which heats milk to kill harmful bacteria and viruses and, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, “is crucial for milk safety.” Before pasteurization became widespread in the early 1900s, milk was linked to about 25 percent of all outbreaks of food and waterborne diseases in the United States. Since 1987, the FDA has banned the interstate sale of unpasteurized milk.

Kennedy’s ideas dovetail with recent trends, with more than a half-dozen states loosening restrictions on raw milk sales in the past five years. The popularity of raw milk is also growing online, with social media posts ranging from the educational to the conspiratorial racking up millions of impressions; some spread mis- and disinformation that raw milk is significantly more nutritious than pasteurized milk or can “cure” conditions such as asthma and autism. Those claims have not been supported by any major health or safety body.

The US Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to multiple requests for comment. But local health officials are alarmed. The Massachusetts Department of Public Health said in a statement that expanding access to raw milk would pose an “unnecessary risk” because “scientific studies have shown that states allowing raw milk sales experience more frequent outbreaks of illness.” Between 1998 and 2018, there were 202 infectious disease outbreaks in the United States linked to raw milk, according to the CDC, including ones caused by Salmonella, E. coli, and Listeria.

Dr. Dennis D’Amico, a dairy food safety specialist at the University of Connecticut, attributes the increased popularity to broader shifts driven by social media and distrust in traditional institutions, as well as by efforts of small dairy farms to stay afloat.

“Raw milk has become kind of a fad. There are lots of places to hear people talk about its virtues, discount what we do know about the risks, and inflate what we do or don’t know about the potential health benefits,” said D’Amico.

Many raw milk producers and consumers who spoke to the Globe described the taste as richer, creamier, and more “natural” than store-bought pasteurized milk. It also comes at a premium: a gallon can sell for $10 or more.

Massachusetts occupies a middle ground in regulating raw milk. Some states ban all sales for human consumption; a few, like California, allow it in grocery stores. Here, raw milk can only be sold at farms licensed by the Massachusetts Department of Agricultural Resources. There are 27 such dairies in the state, the department said, most in rural and western areas.

For the past three legislative sessions, however, advocates have introduced bills to loosen those restrictions, including one by Anne Gobi, a former state senator who is now director of rural affairs for the Healey administration. The bill would have allowed licensed farms to sell directly to consumers off-site, such as at farmer’s markets and via delivery.

Raw milk producers frame the issue as one of consumer sovereignty and regulatory overreach.

“I could start selling alcohol, tobacco, marijuana, and lottery tickets, and there’s risks associated with all those things, too,” said Bill Coutu, owner of Paskamansett Farms in Dartmouth. “So why are we picking on raw milk?”

Producers also argue their milk is just as safe, if not safer, than pasteurized milk because of strict health and safety standards. In Massachusetts, licensed raw milk farms are inspected monthly by the agricultural department and must meet more rigorous bacterial testing requirements than pasteurized milk producers.

But D’Amico, the food safety specialist at UConn, said that comparison isn’t so simple.

“Once a month the state will come in and test one tank, that’s it,” said D’Amico. “They open your bulk tank, take a small sample, go test it, it’s free of pathogens. All the gallons in that lot are associated with that test, but the ones that were produced the next day and the next day that are also hitting the shelf have not been tested. So those are complete unknowns.”

By contrast every gallon of pasteurized milk comes with a near-100 percent guarantee it has undergone a process to kill E. coli, and other pathogens.

Meanwhile, among raw milk producers, there is deep skepticism of what they call “Big Dairy.”

“Big Dairy controls everything, and they hate the fact that raw milk people are out there,” said David Sears, owner of Clover Luck Farms in Pepperell.

The dairy industry has been struggling for years, with fewer than 100 dairy farms left in Massachusetts from more than 5,000 in the 1950s. Nationwide much of the industry has been consolidated under fewer, larger operators.

“The difference between cost of production and your potential income just shrunk and shrunk over the years,” said Sam Shields, a third-generation dairy farmer in Middleborough.

For Shields and others, the premium they get for raw milk is a way to survive.

“Now we can set the price we need to be sustainable,” Sam Shield’s wife, Sue, said, noting they sell raw milk for $10 a gallon — well above prices for pasteurized milk. “But when you’re in the commodity market, you take what they give.”

Proponents of expanding access often cite as a model California, where McAfee runs Raw Farm. He has advocated for a national raw milk ordinance, similar to the existing standard for pasteurized milk, that would set minimum safety standards based on guidelines promoted by his organization, the Raw Milk Institute, and permit interstate sales.

Health and safety experts across the country have spoken out against the proposal.

McAfee also claimed Kennedy is a regular. “He buys my raw milk in Los Angeles,” McAfee said. ”It’s helped him a lot, and he wants more people to have access to it.”

But McAfee’s Raw Farm has had recalls of its products and quarantines over the years; in 2024 it had to recall all its raw milk and cream produced in mid-November after tests detected the presence of the H5N1 bird flu virus in samples.

Alarm bells about raw milk from bodies like the CDC and FDA mean little to consumers like Matt Rumley, who see the choice to drink the product as an act of rebellion against public health institutions they lost trust in years ago.

“There is an incentivization to demonize raw, because this grass-roots upcoming of raw milk in the recent past has probably scared them,” he said.

And if Kennedy’s push to expand access falls short, Rumley said, “it’s still not going to stop me from drinking it. I’ll drive however far I need to drive to continue this lifestyle.”

title: Last meals for the Daily Table, as Dorchester-based nonprofit grocer is set to close
text:
A decade ago, Doug Rauch had a novel idea. The longtime president of Trader Joe’s had spent over 30 years in the grocery industry, but had always been bothered by a sobering statistic: 40 percent of the items on supermarket shelves eventually go to waste. Rauch also knew another fact: That 40 percent of families who qualified for food banks didn’t use them because they were too ashamed. The two facts, taken together, didn’t make sense.

So in 2015, after attending the Advanced Leadership Initiative at Harvard,Rauch opened a new nonprofit grocery store in Dorchester that aimed to solve both problems. The Daily Table worked with a network of growers, manufacturers, and other suppliers to source high-quality food and sell it at a price that people on federal food assistance could afford. The stores were bright and open to all, and in time, the concept expanded to several locations in Greater Boston, eventually serving over 3 million customers and providing them over $16 million in savings.

But on Friday, Rauch and his board announced that due to ongoing financial pressure, the stores were suspending operations. All four Daily Table locations will close within the week. Rauch called the decision devastating, and said it stemmed from a cascading set of factors.

“The decision is entirely economic,” he said. “There is no shortage of people who want to work for us and suppliers who want to work with us. It’s a shortage of funds, and we ran out of funds.”

Problems started during the COVID-19 pandemic, when sales dropped 40 percent, Rauch said. They didn’t layoff staff at the time, he continued, because “we felt that part of our mission was to provide affordable nutrition and good jobs and uplift our community.” The stores were eventually able to bounce back and saw record sales, but then faced another challenge as food prices skyrocketed.

“Food inflation really clobbered us,” he said.

Rauch said a typical grocery store would pass along rising prices to consumers, but that didn’t match The Daily Table’s ethos. The combined pullback of USDA programs that subsidized their work and the slowdown of food-focused philanthropy efforts made the math even harder. The final straw, Rauch said, was the IRS’s delay in paying out a $1.4 million tax credit designed to pay back companies that kept their employees on payroll during the pandemic.

Rauch said he’s been waiting over two years for the funds, and he and his board has been using their own money in the interim to keep the stores afloat.

“If we had [those funds] right now, we probably woudn’t be having this conversation,” he said.

In a letter to customers Friday, The Daily Table’s board noted that the “heartbreaking” decision weighed heavily on them, knowing that “this comes at a time when other food access resources and organizations are at risk.” They steered customers to other local food resources in the Greater Boston area.

The stores will remain open and sell off their merchandise in the coming days. The Dorchester, Roxbury, and Salem stores will close at the end of the day on Sunday, while the Cambridge store may remain open through Monday.

“While I personally, and my team and staff are really devastated and sad to have to be ceasing this operation and closing down the business, the amount of support gratitude and love that our communities and customers have shown our suppliers, vendors and funders is truly humbling and overwhelming,” Rauch said. “I have a feeling of immense gratitude for ten years and am deeply grateful.”

title: A new pathway to vocational training is an alternative to school wait-lists
text:
Add in a hefty dose of local politics for those regional vocational schools, where the costs are allocated among several communities, and you have a prescription for stalemate. Witness the demise of a $445 million proposal for a new Whittier Tech, now looking for a partnership with Northern Essex Community College instead.

But there’s another more modest solution — one the Massachusetts Senate has just given its approval to — a pilot program to encourage career and vocational technical “annexes” adjoining comprehensive high schools and offering vocational programs aimed at juniors and seniors.

“We’re offering this to kids who are at a different point in their lives than the eighth-graders who apply to vocational schools,” said Senator John Cronin, a chief proponent of the concept. “This is the most important work we’re doing right now — to create an opportunity for young people to be able to enter the workforce.”

The Senate set aside $15 million of a $100 million line item for vocational education in a $1.3 billion spending bill passed Thursday. The money was generated through the state’s 4 percent income surtax on incomes over $1 million generated by the 2022 voter-approved Fair Share amendment.

There is no comparable line item in the version passed earlier by the House, but the idea is not without its fans in the other branch, Cronin said.

The model is the MVP (Montachusett Vocational Partnership) Academy in Cronin’s Senate district. It’s a program run by Monty Tech, located in a newly rehabbed warehouse in Fitchburg, and now able to accommodate 120 juniors and seniors from its partner high schools in Fitchburg, Gardner, and the Narragansett Regional School District.

The students stay enrolled in their home districts, thus eliminating any financial disincentive to the sending district. They take academic classes for one full week, followed by vocational training the following week, alternating for the entire year.

The “annex” is just a mile from the main Monty Tech campus. Its schedule allows students to continue to participate in sports or other after-school programs.

It offers programs in carpentry, electrical, and plumbing work and on-the-job training in a co-op program for seniors.

But MVP Academy was borne of a hodge-podge of state grants, including a $1.2 million grant from the Massachusetts Clean Energy Center, and a good deal of local vision.

It shouldn’t have to be that hard to advance such a sound idea.

Cronin estimates modest annexes of some 3,000 to 5,000 square feet would cost from $3 million to $5 million and accommodate 50 to 100 students each. The Senate-passed pilot would prioritize communities where vocational schools have wait-lists of students — as so many do — and where the education department has identified projects that address an “opportunity gap.”

“It represents a sea change to allow students into the voc-tech world, which opens the way to real career paths,” Cronin said. “And this is a funding model that is something we can actually sustain. You get a lot more bang for the buck and it delivers programs to the right target population.”

Lawmakers have too often squabbled over admission requirements — and, yes, the House has managed to resurrect that debate in its budget this year — when they should be working harder to expand opportunities that would make that debate irrelevant.

Career vocational annexes provide a low-cost alternative to those never-ending wait-lists. And they provide opportunity to those ready to work for it. This pilot program deserves a chance to show the way.

title: ‘Devastating’ closure of Daily Table leaves affordable fresh food ‘desert’ in Greater Boston neighborhoods
text:
Daily Table, a nonprofit local grocery chain that offered shoppers fresh food they could more easily afford, announced Friday that it is closing its doors after a decade in business. Residents of Cambridge, Boston, Roxbury, and Salem are already beginning to feel its loss.

Molly Warner, a Dorchester-based dietician and owner of Hand in Hand Nutrition, said she was saddened to hear that Daily Table is ceasing operations.

“In a season when Boston residents are under financial and political stress, the loss of a community gem like Daily Table will not go unnoticed, especially for our most vulnerable residents,” Warner said.

Daily Table’s board of directors said the closure was “heartbreaking” and “not an easy decision” in a letter to customers on Friday. “We are proud to have served over 3 million customers, returning over $16 million in savings to the community while removing the barriers to healthy food.”

The grocery chain cited a number of reasons for its closure, including challenges brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic, “historically high levels of food price increases,” and a lack of sufficient funding to stay afloat.

Jonathan Berk, resident of downtown Salem, said the closure will be tough to bear considering the rising cost of living.

“Everything seems like it’s continuing to rise every day. For folks that are living on tight budgets, not being able to stretch their grocery dollars every week is just gonna cut down on how much food they’re able to provide for their families,” Berk said. “It’s gonna have a major impact on folks’ ability to just put food on their table.”

Berk said Daily Table’s closure is also a great loss for members of the downtown Salem community as there are no other options for fresh produce within walking distance.

“This store served a much larger purpose than just lower costs, it also served a fresh food desert out here,” Berk said. “[Daily Table] was really the only place in downtown or near downtown where you could get fresh bananas or fresh fruits and veggies for that day.”

V. Saragoni, a resident of Salem, shared similar worries.

“I think about many friends and neighbors who may or may not drive or have access to a car,” Saragoni said. “Many folks will have to ride share to the grocery store, which will only add further financial strain to those shopping.”

Teddy Beamer, a former resident of Cambridge, said he shopped at Daily Table’s Central Square location a handful of times as a college student on a budget.

“The only other options for groceries in my neighborhood were H Mart and Whole Foods, which are more expensive. And Target, which can be cheaper but has a limited selection of produce,” Beamer said.

Along with the combination of affordability and quality, Beamer said no other store in his neighborhood had the same genuine sense of community.

“I think that there should be more programs that bring healthy and affordable food to people that need it,” Beamer said. “It’s a shame that [Daily Table] is closing, it had a really strong community feeling to it.”

Daily Table’s four locations will be selling their remaining inventory over the next several days and all items will be deeply discounted until operations close.

title: A grieving mother’s tale of reconciliation
text:
The organizer of this walk for nearly three decades has been Chaplain Clementina Chéry, mother of Louis. In 1993, Louis was a 15-year-old straight-A student at West Roxbury High School. In the most deadly of ironies, a bullet to the back of his head ended his promising life right before Christmas as he was on his way to a gathering of Teens against Gang Violence.

While the killing was still under investigation, Chéry didn’t stop to mourn. The next year she formed the peace institute and became what she has described as a “wedding planner for funerals” — helping suffering neighbors deal with reporters’ loaded questions, plan a meaningful service, and figure out how to go on. In the 30 years since, the institute has become the most important support system in Boston for families of the victims of violence. Today, it’s become a national anti-violence model and is halfway toward the $25 million needed to build a proposed center for healing, just blocks from where Louis was killed.

Three years after Louis’s murder, police arrested a suspect. Charles Bogues was, by his own account, in the neighborhood to do a drug deal armed with a .45-caliber handgun. At some point, he acknowledges, he fired it during a shootout. When his lawyer told him that police had proof he was responsible, Bogues assumed it was true. He later told me that his father, a Boston police officer, said to him, “if you think you did it, do the right thing and plead guilty.” So, based on that advice and his attorney’s dubious representation, he did. What Bogues says his lawyer didn’t tell him was much more consequential than what he did.

But given the chaos of that night, how could police know he fired the deadly shot? From the outset, Chéry was skeptical about the police narrative. The day of the plea, Chéry says she turned to her then-husband, Louis’s father, and said: “God said he didn’t do it. People will think I’m really crazy, but he didn’t kill Louis.” Evidence is emerging that her instincts might have been right.

In 2012, after about 16 years in prison, Bogues was granted parole after Chéry and prosecutors declined to oppose it. Not long after, he appeared onstage with Chéry at the Mother’s Day walk. Together, they joined me for an interview on GBH 2 later to discuss their budding relationship. I asked Chéry why she sought to connect first with Bogues’s mother, Doris, then with Bogues himself. She replied: “It could’ve been my son on the other end of that gun. … No winners here.” Bogues, who more than once told me he hoped his own son would grow up to be like Louis, said he’d asked the chaplain for forgiveness.

In late 2021, Chéry, who relentlessly continued to fight to reform a system she argues revictimizes and retraumatizes survivors, suggested that I watch a nearly hour-long video titled “I didn’t kill Louis Brown.” In it, Bogues convincingly contends that he did not receive effective legal representation and that if all the facts had come out, there would have been more than reasonable doubt that he was guilty.

He maintains that the police and prosecutors were guilty of misconduct for a host of reasons. First, they failed to tell the grand jury there were at least two guns involved — that is, there was more than one .45-caliber shell casing with a unique marking at the scene. They did not ask their own witness about a photo lineup in which she picked out someone other than Bogues. And they failed to call an eyewitness who identified the shooter as someone who looked very different than Bogues.

These are not simply the assertions of a man seeking exoneration; they were also confirmed through rigorous investigation by a team of Northeastern law students.

“I just want to know who killed my son,” Chéry said when I called her after watching the video. Why, she wondered, was Bogues the only one from the multi-person shootout who had been arrested?

Every attempt to reopen the case has failed. Most recently, in 2022, the office of the Suffolk County district attorney wrote Chéry saying it was not persuaded that Bogues’s plea was “either unreliable or unjust.”

If history is prologue, when Chéry, a force of nature, takes the stage on Sunday in Dorchester, she’ll make a deep connection to people like her who have suffered unimaginable loss, while giving a special shout-out to people with a loved one whose killing remains unsolved. Most will think she is not in that group. She would disagree.

While the legal system remains resolute in saying justice was done, the people most intimately involved make a compelling case that it was not. Here’s hoping the mother of Louis D. Brown and the son of Doris Bogues finally get the fair hearing they deserve.

title: Boston wasn’t always a progressive bulwark. Then came Ray Flynn.
text:
In January of 1975, a Black hospital janitor named James Bowden was fatally shot by two white Boston police officers. The Police Department exonerated the officers, but a federal jury found them at fault and awarded the family a settlement of $250,000 five years later. Mayor Kevin White refused to pay the damages, allowing some $600,000 in interest to accrue by the time his successor arrived at City Hall.

In March 1984, Ray Flynn — sworn into office weeks earlier — hand delivered the overdue check to Bowden’s widow, Patricia, in Roxbury. For Flynn and the city he was leading, it was a defining moment. “I hope in a small way this is a symbol of Boston’s commitment to deal with this tragedy,” Flynn told Patricia Bowden.

It also signaled a commitment to fairness, justice, and equality that I saw up close while serving in Flynn’s administration for nearly 10 years. Though sometimes misunderstood, his tenure laid the foundation for the city to become the progressive bulwark it is today.

Revisiting his time in office for my book, The Battle for Boston: How Mayor Ray Flynn and Community Organizers Fought Racism and Downtown Power Brokers, I was reminded of how deeply rooted his principles were. When, in a public housing development, he announced his candidacy for mayor, he signaled his focus would be on poor people. This went beyond policy: When he encountered a homeless person, he would sometimes bring them to a shelter or his own home, he told me.

As a community organizer, I was tapped to lead community engagement for the integration of Charlestown’s all-white Bunker Hill public housing development. Within weeks of Flynn taking office and through collaboration with tenants, religious leaders, community members, and police, Black families began moving into Bunker Hill without incident. This was a sign of what could be accomplished by working with the community. Similar progress occurred several years later in his home neighborhood of South Boston.

Flynn took office during a period of racial unrest, which stemmed from the 1974 federal court-ordered busing. Flynn said his anti-busing stance echoed the concerns of many Black and white parents regarding safety and their authority over their children’s education. He saw schools as a pathway out of poverty, believing they were failing all students.

His position upset his critics, but the racial tensions struck a personal chord. Flynn had grown up in South Boston playing basketball, including on the Roxbury Moulton basketball team, on which he was the first white player. In 1969, he helped launch the Boston Neighborhood Basketball League, which continues to foster peace in the city to this day. Amid the busing crisis, he helped facilitate meetings among leaders of youth sports leagues.

As mayor, he visited the victims of hate crimes reported to the Community Disorders Unit, which was established to address the racial turmoil, and fostered public dialogue through regular reports detailing the unit’s work. With consistent enforcement of civil rights by the police and courts, Boston saw hate crimes drop from 607 in 1978, the year the CDU was created, to 150 by 1987.

Flynn also confronted the downtown power brokers who wielded influence in City Hall: developers, real estate agents, landlords, and bankers. He required developers to fund hundreds of affordable housing units and challenged banks to eliminate racially discriminatory lending practices. He gave neighborhood leaders a seat at the table, and brought down a $40 million deficit and balanced the budget, allowing the city to focus on parks, playgrounds, police, and fire stations. Additionally, he constructed a new Boston City Hospital and renovated public library branches.

At a time when such services were rare in cities across America, Flynn also led by creating an immigrant rights unit, which provided free health care and legal advice to the city’s growing immigrant population. In one case, he provided refuge for 13 Polish defectors fleeing oppressive conditions, a couple of whom slept on couches in the mayor’s office.

No mayorship is without challenges, and Flynn faced criticism for his handling of the Charles Stuart case, which once again heightened racial tensions in the city. Stuart, who killed his pregnant wife, blamed the act on a Black man, setting off a manhunt in the Black community. In 2023, Mayor Michelle Wu would issue an apology to two men falsely linked to the slaying. (Flynn did visit the family of one of those men to apologize, but the meeting did not go well.)

Flynn’s overall legacy, however, has been particularly relevant in the era of Donald Trump, who has sought to rewrite our history as a nation of immigrants. Mayor Marty Walsh fought against Trump’s threats to the immigrant community. More recently, Wu issued a fiery challenge to the federal administration to protect Boston’s immigrant families.

Some may take Boston’s progressivism for granted, but we must not forget how far we’ve come. Mayor Flynn helped establish its enduring foundation, and subsequent leaders have carried the torch. Today, the city embodies equity, fairness, and equality. Let’s keep it that way.

Don Gillis’s book, The Battle for Boston: How Mayor Ray Flynn and Community Organizers Fought Racism and Downtown Power Brokers, was released by Fordham University Press on May 6. Gillis will give book talks at Boston library branches in June. For more information, visit battleforboston.com. Send comments to magazine@globe.com.

text:
New York Times

The credentials committee of the Democratic National Committee voted Monday to void the results of the internal party vote that made David Hogg a party vice chair, ruling that the election had not followed proper parliamentary procedures.

The decision -- which came after roughly three hours of internal debate and one tie vote -- will put the issue before the full body of the Democratic National Committee. It must decide whether to force Hogg and a second vice chair, Malcolm Kenyatta, to run again in another election later this year.

Hogg, 25, an outspoken survivor of the 2018 school shooting in Parkland, Florida, has prompted a fierce backlash over his plans to spend up to $20 million through another organization he heads, Leaders We Deserve, on primary campaigns against incumbent Democrats. Ken Martin, the party chair, has said it is inappropriate for Hogg to meddle in primaries while serving as a party official, and has recommended changing the party’s bylaws to force him to sign a neutrality pledge.
