It hits a home run on “Black & White,” a sumptuous duet with R&B singer Muni Long that recalls the best ‘70s and ‘80s soul-star team-ups. May 30, 7:30 p.m. The Stage at Suffolk Downs. stageatsuffolkdowns.com

KING MALA “And You Who Drowned in the Grief of a Golden Thing,” the stunning debut project from Los Angeles avant-pop artist Areli Castro, is a high-concept piece about power and femininity that drives home the enormity of its central conflicts with all-enveloping electronics and intricate arrangements. She opens for the Canadian synthpop adventurer Lights. June 3, 7 p.m. Brighton Music Hall. 617-779-0140, crossroadspresents.com

MAURA JOHNSTON

K.C. JONES K.C. Jones has Cajun music pedigree, but she’s busy carving a career that moves way beyond the borders of that genre with ample amounts of country and other roots music, as even a cursory listen to her first record, “Queen of the In Between,” reveals. She was here just a week ago as part of the new “Cajun-country-cozy” supergroup Allumé and returns on her own for this show. June 3, 7 p.m. $20. Club Passim, 47 Palmer St., Cambridge. 627-492-7679. www.passim.org

SUZANNE VEGA The veteran folk-rock singer-songwriter is touring in support of “Flying With Angels,” her first album of original music in 11 years, which runs the gamut from addressing free speech and its complications to an ode to Lucinda Williams to a refit of Bob Dylan’s “I Want You.” June 5, 8 p.m. $47.50 and up. The Cabot, 286 Cabot St., Beverly. 978-927-3100. www.thecabot.org

FAHIR ATAKOGLU AND ARA DINKJIAN Turkish pianist and composer Fahir Atakoglu and Armenian-American oud master Ara Dinkjian combine forces to produce their own fusion of Western and global styles. June 5, 7:30 p.m. $30-$50. City Winery, 80 Beverly St. 617-933-8047. www.citywinery.com/boston

STUART MUNRO

SETH WALKER The acclaimed blues and Americana guitarist and singer-songwriter, who has an even dozen albums to his credit, returns to the Fallout Shelter for the first time in over a decade. May 31, 7:30 p.m. $41.29. The Fallout Shelter, 61 Endicott St., Norwood. extendedplaysessions.com

THE NEW BLACK EAGLE JAZZ BAND Among the planet’s most acclaimed traditional jazz bands, the seasoned septet plays early New Orleans, 1920s Chicago, and 1930s small group jazz idioms, and their wide-ranging repertoire encompasses blues, rags, spirituals, and much more. June 1, 7 p.m. $39. Groton Hill Music Center, 122 Old Ayer Road, Groton. grotonhill.org

VANCE PROVEY QUARTET Creative Music Series presents accomplished Connecticut-based trumpeter Provey, who joined the Black Music Division at Bennington College in the early 1980s, teaching alongside the free jazz icon Bill Dixon, the influential multi-instrumentalist and composer. His band includes adventurous improv heavy-hitters Eric Zinman (piano), Scott Samenfeld (bass), and John Loggia (drums). June 5, 8 p.m. $15-$18. The Lilypad, 1353 Cambridge St., Cambridge. lilypadinman.com

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

TRISTAN TRIO The Boston-based trio of pianist Aljoša Jurinić, violinist Thomas Lee Cooper, and cellist Tyler Michael James makes a public debut as a group, with a program of music by Debussy, Mendelssohn, and Saariaho. May 31, 7:30 p.m. Goethe-Institut Boston. Presented by Fermata Chamber Soloists. www.fermata.live

A PILGRIMES SOLACE Soprano Kendra Comstock and lutenist-guitarist Charles Iner team up for a program of religious songs and instrumental pieces by John Dowland and William Byrd, both Roman Catholics who lived and worked in England during times when Catholicism was persecuted and outlawed. June 1, 2 p.m. Cathedral of the Holy Cross. Free.

A.Z. MADONNA

LEARNING HOW TO READ BY MOONLIGHT Natsu Onoda Power directs the premiere of Gaven D. Trinidad’s drama about the struggles of an undocumented Filipino family in 2017-18 as they try to stay afloat in a hostile political environment shaped by two presidents: Rodrigo Duterte in the Philippines and Donald J. Trump in America. We see the story through the eyes of a 6-year-old boy who is learning English from an imaginary friend. Coproduction by Company One Theatre and CHUANG Stage features original songs composed by Trinidad. Pao Arts Center, Boston, from May 29-June 1. Then at The Umbrella Arts Center, Concord, from June 5-8. www.companyone.org

MRS. WARREN’S PROFESSION British actress Imelda Stanton has said of this George Bernard Shaw play that it “asks ever-pertinent questions about the role of women in society, and the choices they make for survival.” Melinda Lopez plays the title character, a former prostitute who is now the madam of a brothel, and Luz Lopez plays Vivie, her daughter, newly graduated from college and really not a fan of how mom makes a living. Also featuring Nael Nacer, Barlow Adamson, Wesley Savick, and Evan Taylor. Directed by Eric Tucker. May 29-June 22. Central Square Theater, Cambridge. 617-576-9278 x1, CentralSquareTheater.org

HELLO, DOLLY! Nobody goes to see this Jerry Herman-Michael Stewart musical in the expectation of a life-changing experience. They go to have some frivolous, escapist fun. (There’s a lot to escape from at the moment.) And that’s what director Maurice Emmanuel Parent delivers in his delightful production, with matchmaker and “marriage broker” Dolly Gallagher Levi winningly portrayed by Aimee Doherty, and an entertainingly stuffy Joshua Wolf Coleman as Horace Vandergelder, “the Yonkers half-a-millionaire” whom Dolly is trying to reel in for herself. Through June 22.Lyric Stage Company of Boston. 617-585-5678,lyricstage.com

THE LIGHT IN THE PIAZZA The eye and the ear are mostly well-served by “The Light in the Piazza.” The rules of dramatic logic? Not so much. In any case, what this quasi-operatic musical is ultimately after is the heart. If you can accept those trade-offs, you’ll be in a position to savor this “Light in the Piazza,” directed by Loretta Greco, with music and lyrics by Adam Guettel and a book by Craig Lucas. In particular, you’ll have a chance to experience the stunning vocal power of Sarah-Anne Martinez as Clara, a young woman who falls for a young man named Fabrizio (Joshua Grosso) while on vacation in Florence with her mother, Margaret (Emily Skinner), in the summer of 1953. Through June 15. Production by The Huntington. At the Huntington Theatre, Boston. 617-266-0800, www.huntingtontheatre.org

DON AUCOIN

SALVAGE In her latest dance/theater work, Alexandra Nunweiler/NunweilerTanz tackles some of the practices of non-denominational American Christianity — from loving to harmful to absurdly ridiculous. Setting the new work in a fictional megachurch, Nunweiler aims to playfully deconstruct the “consumerism, perfectionism, and patriarchy” of the religion as it unearths sometimes unseen, deep-seeded beliefs. The informal work-in-progress showing features music by Calvin Hitchcock and will be followed by a moderated Q&A session with the choreographer and dancers. May 31. $10-$25. Dance Complex, Cambridge. www.dancecomplex.org

ROMÉO ET JULIETTE Boston Ballet finishes its season with the Boston premiere of Jean-Christophe Maillot’s “Roméo et Juliette.” Set to Sergei Prokofiev’s glorious score, performed live by the Boston Ballet Orchestra, Maillot reimagines Shakespeare’s beloved tragedy through the eyes of the well-meaning Friar Laurence, and his adaptation features minimal sets and costumes to sharpen the focus on the dancing and choreography. May 29-June 8. $32-$232. Citizens Opera House. www.bostonballet.org

KAREN CAMPBELL

LEONORA CARRINGTON: DREAM WEAVER Last chance: Carrington’s life story could be a movie: Spirited away from her drudgerous bourgeois life in the UK as a teen by Max Ernst to the heart of the Surrealist movement in Paris, Carrington would endure the Nazi invasion of France, fascist Spain under Franco, and a hurried escape to the United States before landing in Mexico City as a young adult. It was the place, and the life, she was meant for: Working in the Surrealist mode she had learned from Ernst, she quickly made it her own, crafting fantastical worlds spun from personal dream- and nightmare-scapes from her own life, she became one of Mexico’s most-loved artists. This show is the most significant airing of her work ever in New England, and puts on plain view her talent, imagination, and deeply personal approach to both. Through June 1. Rose Art Museum at Brandeis University, 415 South St., Waltham. 781-736-3434, www.brandeis.edu/rose

STANLEY WHITNEY: HOW HIGH THE MOON? This 50-year retrospective of Whitney’s resolutely consistent abstract painting — for decades, he has blocked out grids in patches of color, never the same way twice — arrives as the 74-year old artist gains broad recognition for the first time as the American canon broadens to bring artists like him, a Black abstractionist, into the frame. Through Sept. 1. Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100, www.icaboston.org

WITNESSING HUMANITY: THE ART OF JOHN WILSON Bostonians might be most familiar with Wilson, born and raised in Roxbury, through “Eternal Presence,” the monumental, enigmatic bust that’s stood sentinel-like at the National Center of Afro-American Artists in Roxbury since 1987. But Wilson, who died in 2015, spent decades before and after crafting socially conscious work around the pervasive issue of racial injustice in America that he experienced all his life. This exhibition, co-organized with New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, is the most substantial display of Wilson’s oeuvre ever assembled, and an opportunity for Boston to reckon with a powerful voice that echoes through generations of its social history. Through June 22. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300,www.mfa.org

MURRAY WHYTE

BIANCA FIELDS: ENDSHIPS Fields’s expressionist paintings spring from a lineage that includes Philip Guston and Francis Bacon, with raw, awkward figures coalescing from a welter of messy paint. The Boston painter explores femme archetypes, invoking inner life, embodiment, and ferocity. Along with “Women Who Run from the Wolves,” Fields takes inspiration from “Moby-Dick.” Both texts suggest an embrace of the epic, the dark, and the magical. Fields gives a gallery talk at 1:30 p.m. on Saturday, May 31, in conversation with artist Brittany Miller. Through June 7. LaMontagne Gallery, 450 Harrison Ave. 617-487-3512,www.lamontagnegallery.com

CATE McQUAID

RYAN DAVIS In his new self-produced special, “Underrated,” Davis questions why a woman would want to look through her significant other’s phone. “You tell us that you go through the phone because you’re looking for evidence of another women, and that’s why we think you’re crazy,” he says. “Because you think two women like us.” May 30 at 7 p.m. and 9:30 p.m., May 31 at 6:30 p.m. and 9 p.m., and June 1 at 7 p.m. $40.46-$52.83. Laugh Boston, 425 Summer St. 617-725-2844, www.laughboston.com

WBUR RADIO’S 75th ANNIVERSARY FESTIVAL COMEDY SHOW There are other shows going on in conjunction with WBUR’s anniversary fest, but this one features Boston stand-ups Alex Giampapa, Dan Boulger, Tooky Kavanagh, Orlando Baxter, Emily Ruskowski, and possible special guests. Hosted by Bethany Van Delft. May 31, 9:30 p.m. $35. 5 John F. Kennedy St., Cambridge. www.thecomedystudio.com

I’VE HEARD IT BOTH WAYS: A COMEDY ROCK SHOW A rock ‘n’ roll and stand-up mashup featuring comedy from this year’s Boston Comedy Festival champ Liam McGurk, Gabby Hajos, Nate Hanet, and Kenny Sparrow with music from Monument Hill. June 5, 8 p.m. $15. Upstairs at Hennessy’s Bar, 25 Union St.www.eventbrite.com

NICK A. ZAINO III

HUNDRED ACRE WOOD Take a trip to Hundred Acre Wood with the Boston Children’s Museum for a weekend of fun with Winnie-the-Pooh, Piglet, Tigger, and their pals. Families can visit iconic locations from the franchise like Winnie-the-Pooh’s house or Owl’s Library, as well as learn the history behind these timeless stories. May 30-Sept. 28. Cost of ticket included in general admission, $22. 308 Congress St. bostonchildrensmuseum.org

NEW ENGLAND HONG KONG FESTIVAL Close out AAPI Month with a community celebration at the Hong Kong Festival. Individuals of all backgrounds are welcome to enjoy live performances from Woo Ching White Crane Institution lion dance team, Canto-Pop cover band Juk Sing, and vendors like PureniTea, Not Too Sweet Treats, So Guys, and Clay Lounge. There will be an assortment of games and demonstrations, like pottery throwing, which will teach the audience how to shape clay on a pottery wheel. May 31, 11 a.m.-5 p.m. Free admission. Seven Hills Park, by 78 Meacham Road, Somerville. newenglandhkfest.com

FAMILY FUN FESTIVAL Attendees of the fest can enjoy a variety of food vendors like South Shore Taco Guy, Sarcastic Swine BBQ, an ice cream truck, and concessions of snacks and drinks. There will be arts and crafts, a bouncy obstacle course and inflatable slide, games with wildlife-themed prizes, and more. Live music and performances will accompany the festivities, with Toe Jam Puppet Band at 11 a.m., a lion dance by Kwong Kow School at 12:30 p.m., and DJ Iz.e.real Productions throughout the day. June 1, 11 a.m.- 4 p.m. Free admission. CATS Academy, 2001 Washington St., Braintree. joshuakayefoundation.org

HALEY CLOUGH

title: Boston-area restaurants that accommodate gluten-free diners
text:
Anna’s Taqueria

Look for the Natick location of this homegrown burrito chainlet to roll out gluten-free homemade tortillas in the coming weeks; soon, they’ll introduce the tortillas at each restaurant. 1265 Worcester St., Natick, 508-318-8960, www.annas.com

Bartaco

A user-friendly taco chain with Cali vibes and convenient locations from the Fenway to Fort Point, Bartaco’s menu offers modifications for gluten, dairy, nut, shellfish, and soy allergies, plus an intuitive online interface for pre-orders. Various locations, www.bartaco.com

Bistro 781

The place to go when you need to please a crowd, with salads, bowls, seafood, steaks, and nachos — almost all of ‘em available gluten-free. Plus, there’s a kids’ menu. 336 Moody St., Waltham, 781-899-0297, www.bistro781.com

Bom Dough

This mellow Brazilian café sells sumptuous gluten-free cheese bread, pão de queijo, and a well-labeled roster of gluten-free waffles, egg dishes, parfaits, muffins, and more. 1271 Cambridge St., Cambridge, 617-945-1179, www.bomdough.com

Boston Ale House

An affable ale house that caters to gluten-free guests, with modifications for snacks like potato skins, poutine, even lobster-and-bacon grilled cheese and ice cream. 1885 Centre St., West Roxbury, 617-477-3298, www.bostonalehousegroup.com

Burtons Grill & Bar

This approachable, something-for-everyone chain offers a gluten-free version of its entire menu; this month, they’re also donating a portion of dessert sales to Boston Children’s Hospital Celiac Program. Various locations, www.burtonsgrill.com

Buttermilk & Bourbon

Chef Jason Santos’s free-wheeling parlor of deep-fried indulgence just rolled out a gluten-free rendition of its signature fried chicken: wings, thighs, and tenders. Various locations, www.buttermilkbourbon.com

Capo and Prima

A favorite of gluten-free social media influencers (yes, this is a thing), sibling Italian restaurants Capo and Prima host gluten-free nights; Prima’s is Monday, while Capo’s is Tuesday. Most everything on the menus is gluten-free, from meatballs to pasta to arancini. 443 West Broadway, Boston, 617-993-8080, www.caposouthboston.com; 10 City Square, Charlestown, www.primaboston.com

Cask & Pig

A barbecue-oriented, comfort-food-focused pub with gluten-friendly options for baby back ribs, beef brisket, pulled pork, and more. 780 State Road, Dartmouth, 774-992-0183, www.caskandpig.com

Crave

This North Shore duo, with locations in Beverly and Salem, lives up to its name with husky egg sandwiches, available on gluten-free cheese-and-herb bread. Various locations, www.cravenorthshore.com

Danvers Pizza

North Shore pizza-goers in the know rely on Danvers Pizza for an admirable roster of gluten-free pies with all your favorite toppings, plus gluten-free subs, calzones, and fries. The menu is well-labeled and easy to navigate. 136 Andover St., Danvers, 978-880-7959, www.danverspizza.com

Davio’s

This Italian stalwart, now celebrating 40 years, has changed with the times to offer a full, pasta-laden, gluten-free lunch and dinner menu. Various locations, www.davios.com

Dishon

This cozy, dedicated gluten-free bakery focuses on bread: fresh-baked and fermented for 24 hours, along with gluten-free provisions like pastas and sweets. 915 Elm St., Manchester, N.H., 603-600-1773, www.dishonbakery.com

Faccia a Faccia

Chef Ken Oringer is known for his celiac-friendly dishes (he even wrote a cookbook with his daughter, Verveine, spotlighting kid-focused, gluten-free recipes); at this stylish Newbury Street lair, gluten-free offerings are clearly labeled on the menu, and housemade pasta modifications are available. 278 Newbury St., Boston, 857-991-1080, www.facciabruttaboston.com

Farthest Star Sake

Sip craft sake — gluten-free, made with rice, koji, yeast, and water — alongside gluten-safe cocktails and mocktails. Pop-up food vendors are required to offer both gluten-free and vegetarian choices. 120 N. Meadows Road, Medfield, 508-242-5416, www.fartheststarsake.com

For Pizza

A Medford favorite, For Pizza lets guests build their own gluten-free pies with safe, house-made dough; there’s plant-based pizza, too. 51 High St., Medford, 781-219-3139, www.forpizza.com

Gustazo

At these celebratory four-star Cuban spots in Cambridge and Waltham, the food is shareable and arrives quickly. Happily, most of the menu is gluten-free, including tacos made with plantain shells instead of typical tortillas. Pair them with ceviche and pan-seared shrimp. Various locations, www.gustazo-cubancafe.com

Inna’s

A Newton staple for gluten-free, dairy-free, nut-free, and Kosher Pareve provisions, including gluten-free challah and sought-after latkes. 547 Commonwealth Ave., Newton, 617-795-2626, www.innaskitchen.com

Jennifer Lee’s

This popular Worcester-based bakery specializes in sweets safe for nut-free, gluten-free, and shellfish-free snackers; now, there’s a branch at the Boston Public Market. It’s a prime spot for allergy-friendly bespoke birthday cakes, too. Various locations, www.jenniferleesshoppe.com

Kane’s

This doughnut shop serves 12 gluten-free varieties daily, made in a gluten-safe kitchen, in fun flavors like maple bacon and blueberry blast. Various locations, www.kanesdonuts.com

Libertine

At this North End restaurant, all pasta (except ravioli) has a gluten-free alternative. 125 Salem St., Boston, 857-233-4500, www.libertinenorthend.com

Loco Taqueria & Oyster Bar

This lively taco parlor with Fenway and South Boston outposts offers a dedicated gluten-free fryer and a clearly marked menu. Various locations, www.locotacoshops.com

Mass Ave Diner

Feast on breakfast bowls and gluten-free brioche French toast at this allergy-sensitive diner, with a dedicated gluten-free and meat-free fryer. 906 Massachusetts Ave., Cambridge, 617-864-5301, www.massavediner.com

Mochiko Hawaiian

The menu at this fried chicken and bubble tea destination — which resembles a 1980s arcade game — is more intuitive to navigate than a throwback round of Pac-Man, with a helpful allergy chart and plenty of celiac-safe options, including gluten-free rolls. 324 Walnut St., Newton, 617-433-8882, www.mochikohawaiian.com

Poke by Love Art

The artful poke bowls at this West End Hawaiian takeout spot are crafted in a gluten-free kitchen, which uses tamari instead of traditional soy. 103 Beverly St., Boston, 617-588-0889, www.loveartpoke.com

Post 1917

The kitchen at this chic Reading steakhouse, with a Lexington sibling on the way, can modify almost their entire menu for gluten-free diners by request. 136 Haven St., 781-942-0001, www.post1917.com

Stillwater and Sloane’s

Sarah Wade’s comfort food restaurants offer gluten-free nights every Monday (Stillwater) and on the first Monday of every month (Sloane’s), serving soothing plates like mac-and-cheese and spicy Nashville hot chicken. 197 North Harvard St., Allston, 617-693-8220, www.sloanesboston.com; 120 Kingston St., Boston, 617-936-3079, www.stillwaterboston.com

Sugar and Spice Thai

A Porter Square haven for students on a budget, with a long menu of gluten-free alternatives that don’t compromise on spice or flavor. 1933 Massachusetts Ave., 617-868-4200, www.sugarspices.com

Verveine Cafe & Bakery

Another hit from Ken Oringer (Faccia a Faccia), this time with pastry chef Monica Glass, with a fully gluten-free menu of morning-to-midday curiosities like miso-whipped ricotta toasts and honey-chili tuna melts. 298 Massachusetts Ave., Cambridge, 617-395-3125, www.verveinecafe.com

Violette

This is Cambridge’s go-to, gluten-free bakery, with a focus on special occasion cakes and cupcakes. 1782 Massachusetts Ave., Cambridge, 857-500-2748, www.violettegf.com

Prowling for even more resources? Visit the ever-popular, niche Facebook hit Phil Hates Gluten for unvarnished reviews of local restaurants, and follow Instagram’s Dear Gluten for a treasure trove of gluten-friendly tips. Roaming far from home? Download the Find Me Gluten-Free app for a database of accommodating restaurants.

title: T has to electrify its bus fleet by 2040. Amid delays and soaring costs, some are skeptical.
text:
“There’s no way they are going to meet it,” said Brian Kane, executive director of the MBTA Advisory Board.

He posed a question many are now wondering: “What’s the plan?”

A confluence of factors seemed to have doomed the MBTA’s efforts from the start. As with past big projects, the new garages planned in Quincy and North Cambridge were quickly hampered by blown budgets, design issues not worked out ahead of time, and the scrapping of initial construction plans after bids came in too high — kicking off a series of delays before work had even begun.

Deadlines set by the agency for the facilities to be completed continued to be pushed back, attributed to issues with the supply chain and rising costs. And state lawmakers did not attach dedicated funding to the bold mandate, leaving it to the beleaguered agency, already struggling to afford basic expenses, to come up with the cash for the procurement of new battery electric buses and the garage electrification projects.

Under the state’s clean energy law, passed in 2022, the T has to stop renting and buying buses that emit tailpipe emissions by the end of 2030, and must only operate nonpolluting buses by the end of 2040.

“Well-off folks are getting their EV chargers. The less well-off are supposed to get new buses that don’t pollute their neighborhoods or make them sick,” said state Senator Mike Barrett, chair of the Joint Committee on Telecommunications, Utilities, and Energy. “That was the deal.”

By now, the T was supposed to be operating its new facilities in Quincy and North Cambridge and the Arborway garage in Jamaica Plain in 2027. Combined, they would house around 355 new battery electric buses. Over the following years, the T’s remaining six aging garages would also have to be revamped.

As of March, the majority of the T’s 1,020 buses were belching fumes: 922 are hybrids and 90 use diesel.

As costs steadily increase, some transit advocates wonder how the cash-strapped agency can afford to take on expansion projects without more help from the state.

Further complicating the financial picture, the Trump administration is threatening big cuts to federal transportation funding, particularly for projects that boost mass transit.

Karissa Hand, a spokesperson for Governor Maura Healey, said in a statement that Healey is confident T general manager Phil Eng and his team are “evaluating the current situation, including damaging actions from the Trump administration, to make the best decisions for the success of the system.”

Right now, most of the T’s limited dollars go to making badly needed repairs and maintenance.

In an interview, Eng did not say whether transit officials are considering asking the state to push back the electrification deadlines but said the agency needs to balance building the decarbonized fleet with ensuring “our existing fleet can run safe and reliable.”

Industry headwinds, including tariffs, increasing costs, and just two manufacturers producing battery electric buses in North America — GILLIG and New Flyer — are affecting agencies nationwide, Eng said.

“Those are very aspirational and really good goals,” he said. “At the same time, the industry is challenged in being able to deliver and meet those needs.”

In the meantime, the T is looking to invest in its facilities. A new operational team is evaluating just how big the Arborway garage should be and whether it was planned and scoped right the first time, Eng said. The agency is also exploring options like en-route charging for battery electric buses.

Delayed by a year, the retrofitted North Cambridge garage is now expected to open at the end of 2025. The project budget is $44 million. The garage in Quincy is slated to open in summer 2027, three years behind schedule. The 120-bus facility has an eye-popping price tag: $476 million. And the Arborway garage, the largest with a capacity to accommodate 200 buses, no longer has a projected opening date. The project was allocated $8.3 million in the T’s capital plan — a sliver of its current estimated budget of about $440 million.

Combined, that puts the cost of upgrading the three facilities at nearly $1 billion. In 2017, the T said it expected to spend $808 million to modernize or replace all nine facilities.

Many in the transit and climate world said the crawling progress is troubling and expressed frustration over the agency’s lack of transparency about how it plans to meet its targets amid the setbacks.

“If we are very, very serious about transportation contributing less to pollution, buses are the way to go,” said Reggie Ramos, executive director of the advocacy group Transportation for Massachusetts. “We’re not seeing investments being poured on that.”

Transportation is the largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in Massachusetts, accounting for 38 percent in 2021. The T was responsible for just 1 percent of those sector emissions, according to the agency’s climate assessment published last fall. Although a small piece of the pie, researchers say shifting more trips away from cars to clean buses is critical for curbing climate change.

“We would like the T to not walk back on plans for forward-looking investments in our transit system,” said Vick Mohanka, chapter director at the Massachusetts Sierra Club. “If we can do that all right here — that sets an example for basically every other city in the country.”

More than a dozen of the largest public transit agencies in the United States have mandates for a full bus fleet transition to zero-emission buses, according to a report published last year by the WSP Center for Clean Transportation, a Canadian consulting firm. None have met that goal yet.

Battery electric buses emit significantly fewer emissions than hybrid and diesel buses, studies have found. However, to be truly clean, the power that electric buses use to charge must come from clean, renewable sources — and right now, half of New England’s grid is powered by natural gas.

While the average electric transit bus comes with a much steeper price tag, they can deliver long-term savings through lower maintenance and fuel costs, according to the Department of Transportation.

The bus is used more than any other mode of public transport, and most riders are low-income and people of color from neighborhoods such as Roxbury and Dorchester.

Higher volume roads were historically placed in communities of color. That means that in Massachusetts, Black, Latino, and Asian residents are disproportionately exposed to air pollution from vehicles, including diesel buses, compared with white residents, according to an analysis from the Union of Concerned Scientists. This can lead to serious health impacts, including an increased risk of premature death, cardiovascular disease, and higher rates of asthma.

“Every delay in getting that infrastructure built ... means dirtier air and more delayed rides,” said Seth Gadbois, an attorney at the Conservation Law Foundation, an environmental advocacy organization with headquarters in Boston.

To serve more riders, the bus fleet needs to grow. And so do the size of the garages.

That might mean having to compromise, such as by bringing the facilities, some dating back to the Great Depression, up to this century first — and pausing electrification efforts until money is available, said Katie Calandriello, interim executive director of TransitMatters, a Boston-based advocacy group.

“We need to take a whole government approach to this,” Kane said. “We also have to figure out a way to build these things for less than a billion dollars — and get them done faster.”

State Senator William Brownsberger, who represents parts of Cambridge and Boston, said state lawmakers will likely need to set new deadlines for the T’s bus electrification targets.

“I was a huge fan of setting our 2020 and 2050 greenhouse gas reduction targets and setting interim targets,” he said. “But those are all turning out to be difficult to achieve, so I’ve kind of become disillusioned with that way of approaching our goal-setting.”

title: New and coming soon: 13 new restaurants and bars in R.I. to try this summer
text:
Sometime this spring, Maggie McConnell and Josh Finger, two Per Se alums who fell in love while cooking in Thomas Keller’s kitchens together, will open Claudine in downtown Providence. During an exclusive interview with The Boston Globe earlier this year, McConnell and Finger offered a few details about their vision: Creating a high-end, 26-seat restaurant serving an eight-course tasting menu focused on hyper-local ingredients. An eight-course tasting will cost $165 per person.

Claudine’s menu will evolve daily, and focus on hyper-local ingredients. They’ll work closely with a network of farms, and dry age their own fish and meat in-house for menu items that may include a sashimi of dry-aged bluefin tuna. While there won’t be any “standard” items on the menu that will remain, each course will begin with a daily oyster dish.

Claudine, 225 Weybosset St., Providence, claudinepvd.com.

The restaurant space inside the Wayfinder Hotel, which was seriously damaged by a four-alarm fire in 2022 and then restored, has been empty since the property went up in flames. Now, new restaurant Little Clam is finally moving in. The seafood-heavy restaurant is expected to pay homage to the humble yet iconic clam, and will open in early June.

Antonio Wormley, a Philadelphia native who graduated from nearby Johnson & Wales University in 2012, will serve as Little Clam’s executive chef. After Wormley graduated, he worked as the chef de cuisine at shuttered Vanity and then as executive chef at Milk Money, where he was serving catfish with roasted corn, collard greens, and hot sauce he made in-house. After leaving New England in 2018, he ultimately returned in 2023 to help chef Chris Viaud, a lauded James Beard nominee and Top Chef alum, run Pavilion in Wolfeboro, N.H.

Dovetail & Co., the Wayfinder’s owner and development company, brought in Jake Rojas, who previously ran the since closed Tallulah on Thames, and is now the proprietor of Tallulah’s Taqueria, as the property’s consulting chef.

Little Clam, 151 Admiral Kalbfus Road, Newport, R.I. wayfindernewport.com.

There may be a new pizza shop opening on Block Island this year. Sadie Flateman, the owner of oyster company Great Salt Pond Oyster Co. on the island, is working on opening Virginica Pizza. She plans on serving Neapolitan-style pizza with local produce and shellfish from the island. A sample menu says they’ll offer Block Island clam pizza, three kinds of oysters, littleneck clams, and soft serve ice cream.

“While Crassostrea virginica is the scientific name for the Atlantic oyster, Virginica Pizza brings together oyster service and pizza,” wrote Flateman, the oyster fisher, in a letter to town officials about the pizza shop.

The building is not yet winterized, but Flateman said she wants to stay open for as long a season as possible to serve Block Island natives.

Virginica Pizza, 125 Corn Neck Road, New Shoreham, R.I.

Cocktail wiz Jesse Hedberg and chef Robert Andreozzi, the two owners of Pizza Marvin, are soon opening Club Frills, a bar that will focus heavily on unique cocktails, like a Jell-O shot in the form of a deviled egg. Nikhil Naiker, who is a finalist for the Emerging Chef award from the James Beard Foundation, will lead kitchen operations as a manager, while continuing his NIMKI pop-up at Courtland Club.

“Rob and I have been wanting to open a space together for the last three years,” said Naiker. “This will help me really see and experience a full opening of a restaurant and bar.”

They’ll plan to experiment with plays on classic bar food, like a signature burger, a tuna melt with raw tuna, and a mozzarella stick-onion ring concoction. “It’s all a little ridiculous,” said Andreozzi.

Old bartending techniques, such as clarification and carbonation, and using equipment such as a freeze dryer (usually used for garnishes, but can also be used for spirit infusions) will be a focal point to their cocktail list. They’ll also have a robust zero-proof cocktail menu.

Ed Davis has opened Debbie’s, named for his mom, on Washington Street in downtown Providence. Next to Frisky Fries and across from The Strand theatre, he is serving hot dogs (not hot wieners, the classic Rhode Island food staple) with topping combinations like broccoli rabe, provolone, and relish. It’ll run as a counter service, with a few tables and chairs inside. Davis previously worked at fine-dining and upscale restaurants across Providence, including Birch, the Dorrance, Farmstead, and Oberlin. He’s trading that lifestyle for something more casual.

“I’m good with just making hot dogs,” said Davis. “All of the moves I’ve made are lateral. Only difference is how you put food on a plate.”

Order one of the dog specials — like the “Raab” (broccoli rabe, red pepper relish, provolone, and yellow mustard). Or a grinder, like the “high brow” (mortadella, pistachio tapenade, marinated tomatoes, salsa verde) or the chicken cheesesteak with onions, banana peppers, cooper sharp, provolone, mayonnaise, and some hots. Their vegetable sides, such as the asparagus salad, source ingredients from local farms and producers.

Debbie’s, 100 Washington St., Providence, R.I. Stay updated by checking the restaurant’s Instagram.

David Fierabend of the Groundswell Design Group is opening his second restaurant this week: The Franklin. A highly anticipated restaurant opening for at least a year, The Franklin will be a sophisticated French brasserie. Fierabend is no stranger to the food and beverage space. In 2020, he opened Groundswell at Tiverton Four Corners, which is a bakery and cafe, the Table and Provisions store, and a home and garden store. The Franklin, which is opening in a location that used to be a private club, will be a restaurant, cocktail bar, and patisserie.

The Franklin, 195 Franklin St., Bristol, R.I., groundswellguild.com/the-franklin.

The space that once held Chantarelle/Bouchard Restaurant on Thames Street, has been re-envisioned as Audette by the same team behind Mission, the burger joint in Middletown, and Newport’s TSK, a steakhouse, and Utility, a kitchen goods store for the party host and home chef. Audette, however, focuses on French cuisine. While many other restaurants shy away from fine dining, the creators of Audette have embraced white tablecloths, tableside lamps, and caviar presentations.

The new group — run by Anna Burnley, Tyler Burnley, Chad Hoffer, and Carmen Ratoi — took over Chanterelle in 2024 from the Bouchard family, who ran the establishment for three decades.

If you go, expect a menu of escargot; quail; seared foie gras with rhubarb vanilla purée; quenelles with turnip, halibut, and lobster. For dessert, absolutely order the Grand Marnier soufflé with creme anglaise.

Audette, 505 Thames St., Newport, R.I., audettenewport.com.

The Dean Hotel has undergone a rebrand and become Neptune, named for the farthest planet from the sun. As part of the rebrand, a new restaurant and bar concept is slated to launch this summer in partnership with restaurant industry veteran Michael Lester. Lester previously owned The Dorrance restaurant, and that restaurant’s reopening may have been the largest question mark of all in the last few years.

The Dorrance was an iconic restaurant in downtown Providence a few blocks from City Hall since 2010. It was a breeding ground for kitchen and bar talent, and was known as one of the best restaurants in the state. When the pandemic hit, the restaurant intermittently closed. The Lester family promised to reopen the restaurant in an old pub space, Griswold’s Tavern, in Newport. But those plans fell apart in 2024.

It’s unclear what Lester plans to do in the hotel’s restaurant space. For now, he’s running “d.n/a café,” which serves a list of cocktails, out of the former Dean Bar space.

d.n/a café, 122 Fountain St., Providence, R.I.. Stay updated on Instagram.

Located inside the Newport Harbor Island Resort, which is fresh off a $50 million renovation, the 1639 restaurant recently opened and serves typical coastal dishes like grilled octopus and a Rhode Island striper with summer succotash, Parisienne-style gnocchi, and ratatouille purée. Under executive chef Ryan Connors, they’re also offering three pasta dishes: lobster alla arrabbiata with a squid ink fettuccine, bolognese with cavatelli, and a tableside cacio e pepe where cracked black pepper pasta is folded in a wheel of parmigiano reggiano right in front of you.

1639, 1 Goat Island Road, Newport, R.I., newportharborisland.com.

Opened in March 2025, Bar Lazio is a new Italian bar in the heart of Knightsville, known as Cranston’s “Little Italy.” This is owners Vincenzo Mazza and Christopher Maselli’s first restaurant, and they are specializing in classic Italian desserts, aperitivo, espresso drinks, antipasto boards featuring imported meats and cheeses, and seasonal accompaniments.

Bar Lazio pays homage to the Lazio region of Italy, which is where Mazza and Maselli say many families in their neighborhood can trace their roots back to. They pour wines from Lazio, Itri Olives on their boards that are imported from Itri (which is part of Lazio), and pasta dishes that include guanciale (cured Italian pork jowl or cheek), which is a meat native to Lazio.

Bar Lazio, 1669 Cranston St., Cranston, R.I., barlaziori.com.

The Chapel Grille, a popular restaurant in Cranston located in an old church building, closed earlier this year. Known as a place for movers and shakers, politicians would regularly host fundraisers and victory parties. Now, the restaurant space is in the hands of the Circe Group, which just opened the doors to Circe Prime. It’s an Italian steakhouse and banquet facility by Carlo Carlozzi and Kyle Poland, who already operate Circe restaurants in downtown Providence and East Greenwich. Expect cuts of steak, pasta dishes, Italian dumplings, and olive oil cake for dessert.

Circe Prime, 3000 Chapel View Blvd., Cranston, R.I., cranston.circerestaurantandbar.com.

Earlier this year, Remy’s Loose opened inside The Chanler, the historic and award-winning hotel along Newport’s famed Cliff Walk. Alongside Cara, the menu-less fine dining restaurant inside the property, Remy’s Loose is slightly more casual, offering for dinner a caviar service, a daily crudo with fish from North Atlantic waters dressed in lemongrass and citrus, wagyu steak, housemade pasta, and snapper. They’re also open for lunch, with tuna steak salads, bouillabaisse, and a cheeseburger. Their kitchen is led by executive chef Jacob Jasinski, who joined the property in 2019. He previously staged at several restaurants in the US and Europe, including Eleven Madison Park and Le Bernardin. He’s also held high-level positions at hotels and restaurants across the country, including White Barn Inn in Kennebunkport, Maine; Castle Hill Inn in Newport; Ocean House in Westerly; and Joel Robuchon in Las Vegas.

Remy’s Loose’s beverages celebrate garden-inspired cocktails accented with seasonal ingredients, and both Old and New World wine producers. Paying homage to The Chanler’s tradition around family, the restaurant is named after the hotel’s proprietress Lani Shufelt’s niece — who is Cara’s sister.

Remy’s Loose, 117 Memorial Blvd., Newport, R.I., thechanler.com.

Yellow Door Taqueria, which is owned in part Dropkick Murphys frontman Ken Casey, is opening its first location outside of Massachusetts soon. The taco shop, which has three locations in the Greater Boston area, will open a restaurant in a space currently under construction in the Aloft Hotel in downtown Providence. While a menu for their Providence location has not been finalized, their taco list for their existing shops offers birria, and tacos with meats like chili barbecue roasted duck, coconut shrimp, and confit pork. Posts about the space say the restaurant will open sometime this summer.

Yellow Door Taqueria, 191 Dorrance St., Providence, R.I., yellowdoortaqueria.com.

Know of another great restaurant or bar opening in Rhode Island? Email alexa.gagosz@globe.com.

title: Oh, c’mon, West Roxbury, make way for a family shelter
text:
Re “An uproar over a homeless shelter in West Roxbury” (Marcela García, Opinion, May 24): I’ve lived a short walk from the site of a planned family shelter for nearly a decade, and I welcome the use of the abandoned building there to house homeless families. I understand people are frustrated with the process around community engagement, but the other concerns that have been raised are absurd.

Parking? There is never any parking on Redlands Road.

Safety, trash, and smoking areas? There are multiple commercial establishments, including bars and restaurants, around the corner.

Traffic? The vacant property sits at the corner of Centre Street, which is always busy, and Redlands Road, which is a one-way residential street.

I don’t remember these being major concerns when the building was used as a nursing home.

New things can be scary, but helping people in need is not new to West Roxbury. After all, it was once home to the famous abolitionist and reformer Theodore Parker. A road and church named for him are located near the shelter.

I foresee the residents and staff of the shelter attending our churches, being educated at our schools, supporting our local businesses, and hopefully finding permanent housing nearby. I believe that my friends and neighbors are good people, and I appeal to West Roxbury’s better angels to make sure these families and the employees of the new shelter are welcomed with open arms.

Katie Forde

West Roxbury

title: Family sues BPS bus contractor after driver runs over 8-year-old
text:
Video of the Jamaica Plain crash shows the driver of the school bus asleep at the wheel just moments before abruptly waking and starting the bus during dismissal, when large numbers of students and staff were outside the Curley school. Almost immediately, the bus swerved onto the sidewalk and hit the boy and a school aide, according to videos of the incident.

The 8-year-old boy, who has a diagnosis of autism, suffered a fractured femur that required several surgeries and two months in a hospital and rehabilitation center, according to the complaint.

“This frightening event almost took my child’s life. It is shocking to read the string of lies that the driver gave to the police. This should never happen. The videos don’t lie,” Cynthia Davis, the boy’s guardian, who has raised him for most of his life, said in a statement. “Transdev must be held to account to protect our children and prevent this from ever happening again.”

The school aide with the boy suffered injuries to his left leg and left shoulder, and a laceration behind his left ear, according to police.

The lawsuit comes just weeks after Mayor Michelle Wu and Superintendent Mary Skipper announced an independent investigation of Transdev, which has provided school bus drivers to Boston since 2013. On April 28, 5-year-old Lens Arthur Joseph, a kindergartner at UP Academy Dorchester, was struck and killed by a school bus that he had just exited on Washington Street in Hyde Park.

The driver, Jean Charles, reportedly struck two cars in Mattapan shortly before he allegedly hit Joseph in Hyde Park. He resigned on May 14, shortly before a scheduled termination hearing. He not been charged in the Hyde Park crash.

After that crash, community members complained to city leaders at a public meeting about school buses that speed, hit cars, and drive unsafely through the neighborhood.

Boston officials have said there are about 400 “incidents” per year involving a BPS school bus. Most cause minimal damage, they have said.

According to the lawsuit filed Tuesday against Transdev, both the driver, Vitony Laguerre, 62, of Taunton, and a monitor on board were asleep while the bus was parked outside the school just before the crash occurred.

Laguerre, Transdev, and BPS did not respond to a request for comment.

The school aide injured in the crash also did not respond to an interview request.

Wu on Tuesday said the city is working closely with Transdev and has put in place additional checks and is reviewing every incident.

“But for the families who are grieving or for a family who has had to go through a horrible recovery over an extended period of time, that never should have happened,” Wu said. “And we need to make sure things like that don’t happen.”

In the video released by the family’s lawyers, Laguerre appeared to be napping for at least 45 seconds before suddenly lurching up in his seat. He immediately started driving the bus along a side street, Pershing Road, and lost control. The bus drove up onto the sidewalk. The exterior camera captured the precise moment the student and the school aide were caught between the bumper and a wooden fence.

According to a police report, the boy was run over by the bus, while the aide was pinned to the fence behind him. Briefly, the aide could be seen trying to shield the boy before they disappeared behind the nose of the bus.

The bus then plowed through the fence and came to a stop on school property.

Laguerre is also named as a defendant in the lawsuit filed Tuesday.

Lawyers for the family of the injured boy also released video recordings of the crash that show Laguerre appearing “to smile and laugh about the accident and shrugs his shoulders as if he was unsure of what happened,” according to a police report.

Laguerre gave different explanations about the cause of the crash, according to Boston police reports included with the complaint. Initially, he told officers at the scene that a vehicle had cut in front of him and he was forced to swerve out of the way, but mistakenly hit the gas pedal.

Laguerre subsequently told police he was waiting on the street with the brake activated when he began to move forward, and his foot hit the wrong pedal, according to a supplemental police report written 10 days after the crash. The bus accelerated onto the sidewalk and struck the boy and the school aide, that report said.

A few days after the crash, Laguerre then told police the accident occurred because of a mechanical issue with the steering.

But video of the crash, from a dashcam that recorded the bus’s interior, along with an exterior camera that looked out over the vehicle’s hood, showed there was no other car cutting in front of the bus. And police determined that any mechanical problem with the bus was caused by the crash itself, according to the police report.

The child “suffered great pain of body and anguish of mind, significant medical expenses have been incurred and will be incurred for his care and treatment, and he has suffered and will suffer a substantial loss of his ability to engage in the normal enjoyment of life,” the complaint said.

City and school officials did not respond to questions about whether Laguerre is still employed as a driver.

He was arraigned on May 7 on a misdemeanor charge of negligent operation of a motor vehicle in West Roxbury District Court, according to court filings. He was also charged with unsafe operation of a motor vehicle, which is a civil infraction. Laguerre pleaded not guilty to the charges and was released on personal recognizance. He is is due in court for a pretrial hearing on June 24.

In a statement, Marc Breakstone, one of the lawyers representing the injured child’s family, said Transdev has a systemic safety problem.

“When you’re a multi-billion-dollar international company getting paid millions of dollars a year to keep the children of Boston safe, you must be held accountable,” Breakstone said. “This is obviously not the first time that Transdev has hurt innocent people, but we are working to make sure it does not happen again.”

title: Billy Corgan on playing Smashing Pumpkins songs solo, and Pope Leo XIV being a White Sox fan
text:
“I think that’s the great hubris of a creator,” Corgan said on a Zoom call from his home in Chicago. “You feel these are your sculptures and your paintings, and you have the ability to once more reframe and re-illuminate why they’re attractive to you.”

His “A Return to Zero” solo tour begins this weekend in Baltimore, then heads to the Paradise Rock Club on Monday — a much cozier environment than Corgan’s most recent gig in Boston, when the Smashing Pumpkins performed at Fenway Park with Green Day last summer. The intimate club shows will thread together some of Corgan’s prior solo material, as well as music from different eras of the Smashing Pumpkins: the “Mellon Collie” period circa 1995, which yielded hits like “1979” and “Bullet With Butterfly Wings”; portions of their 2000 concept record “Machina/The Machines of God”; and songs from the band’s latest release, 2024’s “Aghori Mhori Mei.”

Altogether, Corgan will draw from a pool of over 100 songs for the tour, although he won’t necessarily cull enough material for a grandiose three-hour performance, as he’s done in the past with the Smashing Pumpkins.

“I’m 58 now, so I do have to temper myself,” he said with a laugh.

To Corgan, enmeshing the different eras in one setlist felt like “coming home,” and “more resonantly consistent” with the band’s first era, before their — in his words — “quote-unquote breakup” in 2000 and quasi-reformation around 2007. Following a rotation of lineup changes over the years, the band currently performs with three of the four founding members. Guitarist James Iha and drummer Jimmy Chamberlin are back in the saddle with Corgan, while original bassist D’Arcy Wretzky has not rejoined.

From an outside perspective, Corgan’s claim to the Smashing Pumpkins’ two album anniversaries might look like a catalyst for another fallout within the band. But the frontman said he’s been chatting with his bandmates “for years” about how to honor anniversaries in a way that was personal, rather than an opportunistic cash grab.

“One thing we’ve done successfully, I think, in this decade of our knowing each other, is if there’s not an even consensus, we don’t persist,” he said. “That was some of the problems in the ’90s — not taking into account, let’s call it, a balanced view of everybody’s take.”

So when the band had unspecified “differing views” on the two upcoming anniversaries, Corgan took the reins with his new solo group, which includes the Smashing Pumpkins’ touring guitarist, Kiki Wong.

“The fact that these significant anniversaries were going to go by with no particular unified voice of how to present them, I said, ‘Well, I’m just gonna do it myself,’” Corgan said.

Add that to the list of sizable projects that Corgan has taken on in recent years. Directly prior to this interview, Corgan described himself as occupying a “12-year-old brain space” while working on his memoir. (Per his wife Chloé Mendel Corgan, he said, he’s tried to write it on four separate occasions since they met, and “as far as I’m concerned, this [time] is the last.”) Corgan has also owned the National Wrestling League since 2017, and this year launched a podcast called “The Magnificent Others,” in which he interviews fellow cultural bigwigs like Gene Simmons and Sharon Osbourne.

Corgan’s extracurriculars involve his local community, too. Alongside his wife, he runs a plant-based tea shop and cafe called Madame Zuzu’s Emporium in Highland Park, located about 25 miles outside of his hometown of Chicago. (For the record, Corgan has complex feelings about fellow Chicagoan Pope Leo XIV being a White Sox fan instead of rooting for the Cubs; “The joke I’m telling now is, ‘it’s good he was named pope ‘cause that’s the kind of help that they need.’”)

With a daily routine that typically involves 12 to 14 hours of work across his various projects — fueled by an average of six hours of sleep — Corgan has continued to expand his identity as an artist and cultural figure. But that complexity sometimes gets muddled within the public’s narrower perception of Corgan and his role in the Smashing Pumpkins.

“One has to deal with the complication of, I’m so closely identified with the band that most people don’t really understand who I am without the band,” he explained.

“The band’s history after 2001 is rife with incredible external pressures on who the band needed to be in, let’s call it, this second era: a greatest hits band, an artistic band, a mixture of both,” he added. “Not that you’d want to, but you could find a voluminous treasure trove of material of people criticizing me for not being the band that people want me to be in. And me saying, over and over again, ‘The band you think I was in, I was never in. So why would I be in that band now?’”

To Corgan, the name under which he performs is “sort of inconsequential.” But in this case, performing with the Machines of God — especially to revisit some of his older work within the Smashing Pumpkins — casts off many of those notions about how he and the band should operate.

The freedom is the ultimate trade-off for any nitpicks the public might have about him striking out on his own.

“It’s very attractive to me to present this material without dilution — meaning, I don’t really care in this setting for that pressure,” he said.

“If you don’t embrace the freedom, then you’re kinda wasting, let’s call it, ‘the upside of the downside,’” he concluded.

BILLY CORGAN AND THE MACHINES OF GOD

title: ‘Our moment to evolve’: A nonprofit that launched after George Floyd is now navigating a DEI backlash
text:
But racism wasn’t the only crisis gripping the country in those days. There was also COVID-19. And when the face masks started to come off in 2022, McCreary saw how society was ready, even eager, to move on from both Floyd and the pandemic.

It was a familiar, vicious, cycle for Black America — progress, followed by painful setbacks. There was emancipation, then Jim Crow laws; the Civil Rights Act, then a generation of men jailed in the War on Drugs; equal opportunity laws, then a Supreme Court striking down affirmative action in college admissions.

And now America has gone from electing its first Black president to having a White House that is openly dismantling diversity, equity, and inclusion.

The New Commonwealth Fund hasn’t been immune to the sea change. The group is shifting how it raises money, depending less on corporations and more on individuals. And just after the November election, the nonprofit removed the “Racial Equity and Social Justice” part of its name from its website.

McCreary made this decision after counterparts around the country began receiving physical threats because of their work. She worried about the safety of her staff and people at other local organizations they work alongside. She wanted to set an example of how the organization could stay committed to racial equity while also practicing self-preservation.

“What we haven’t done is we haven’t changed our mission,” she said.

From its headquarters in an industrial part of Roxbury, NCF provides about $3 million a year to nonprofits that are lifting communities of color, whether it be through justice reform or the arts. Since its launch, NCF has given out 448 grants to more than 250 organizations in Massachusetts, over $16.3 million in all.

And even as the very idea of eliminating racial inequities feels under attack, the five-year anniversary of Floyd’s death came at a time when organizations like NCF see their work as more essential than ever.

“How do we convince folks that this is the work for the long haul?” McCreary pondered. “This is not a moment. This has to be a movement.”

At first, Damian Wilmot wasn’t as shaken by Floyd’s murder as he had been by the killing of 17-year-old Trayvon Martin in 2012.

Martin was the unarmed Black teen shot and killed in Florida by a neighborhood watch volunteer, George Zimmerman, who thought he looked suspicious. His death was the worst nightmare for every Black parent of a teenager.

“I sort of saw my son in him,” said Wilmot.

But when Floyd was killed, it was Wilmot’s children doing the worrying. Floyd, who was killed by a white Minneapolis police while handcuffed, was 46 years old, and well over 6 feet tall.

Wilmot, with a similar build, had just turned 50 at the time. His children saw Floyd in him.

“Daddy, it’s not safe for you,” his son and daughter warned.

Floyd’s murder sparked discussions for Wilmot, both at home and at work as an executive at Vertex Pharmaceuticals, about what can be done to make sure no Black person dies like that again in police custody.

“Every company was making these proclamations about supporting social justice and doing something, but candidly I didn’t think anyone really knew exactly what to do,” recalled Wilmot, who today serves as board chair of NCF.

Vertex, like so many other corporations and organizations, issued a public statement vowing to fight racism and committed $4 million to nonprofits supporting that effort. All told, at least 20 Greater Boston foundations, organizations, and corporations pledged $1 billion in grants, scholarships, and other investments to end injustice for Black communities.

But Wilmot and other Black leaders in Boston wanted to do more. They called each other daily, and soon a group was regularly convening by Zoom. They felt a need to talk, to organize, and to use their hard-won collective power to do something they could call their own.

It was a who’s who’s of the Black community, including Eastern Bank president Quincy Miller, Fidelity Investments senior vice president Pamela Everhart, Rapid7 CEO Corey Thomas, and State Street chief diversity officer Paul Francisco.

The prospect of starting their own nonprofit to end systemic racism was energizing. “We all agreed, yes, but let’s do it together ... and let’s lead this,” Wilmot recalled.

The money began to pour in, with initial commitments of $20 million, which has grown into about $45 million today.

From the get-go, NCF wanted to disburse the money to grassroots organizations in sums that would be transformative for them.

One of the first recipients was Elevated Thought, a Lawrence nonprofit that uses art to drive social justice. When the group received a $50,000 grant from NCF in 2020, founder Marquis Victor was the only staffer. But the money sparked what Victor called a “Cambrian explosion” — enabling him to tap NCF’s expertise and donor network. Today, Elevated Thought has 17 full-time staffers, with new programs and a budget three times as large as it once was.

Similarly, NCF has been critical to supporting emerging nonprofits like Vital Connections (CxNs), which was founded in December 2020 to improve access to healthcare, including Black maternal health in Boston.

“We’ve had a really, really successful start as an organization, and NCF is one of the anchors of why that was possible,” said Ariel Childs, executive director of Vital CxNs, which so far has received about $667,000 from NCF.

NCF’s launch generated national headlines and inspired Black leaders in other cities to start similar foundations, such as the Houston Equity Fund. But no one could have imagined just how far the pendulum would swing for this sort of work between 2020 and today.

It didn’t happen overnight, and NCF saw today’s challenges coming. McCreary engaged four law firms to review the nonprofit’s grant-making processes and assess whether they could withstand legal challenge, especially after the activist who sued Harvard to overturn affirmative action in college admissions began targeting organizations engaged in racial equity work. NCF’s lawyers concluded its work would pass legal muster because its mission is focused on eliminating racial inequities, but not at the exclusion of other groups.

For Eastern Bank’s Miller, an NCF founder and board member, the legal threats underscore why the organization matters more than ever. He’s confident it can weather the backlash against DEI — with a staff of 12 and millions of dollars committed. But smaller nonprofits focused on racial justice work don’t have that luxury and could use NCF’s help. Corporate support has slowed to a trickle, and there’s only so much private money to go around, even as the needs keep growing.

“The work in 2025 is more important than the work in 2020,” Miller said. “I don’t even think it’s close.”

If anything, he views this moment as a chance to adapt.

“We have to evolve and change to keep supporting this work just like companies during COVID had to evolve and change,” Miller added. “This is our moment to evolve.”

title: How our photographer captured the image that summed up the Celtics’ dispiriting season
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

We all know a picture is worth a thousand words. But sometimes the story behind a photo — especially one that many of us have already seen — merits a few more. The above image is one of those photos, and this is one of those stories.

Last month, Globe photographer Danielle Parhizkaran was perched on a platform behind the Celtics bench at Madison Square Garden, watching the team play the Knicks in Game 4 of the NBA Eastern Conference semifinals.

The stakes were high. The Celtics, last year’s NBA champions, already trailed 2-1 in the series and were behind as the final minutes of the fourth quarter ticked down. Seeking a better vantage point to capture the disappointment on the bench and on the face of head coach Joe Mazzulla, Danielle left her assigned spot and moved higher up in the arena.

And then, as every Boston sports fan knows by now, disaster struck.

As Knicks forward OG Anunoby ran past Celtics star Jayson Tatum with a loose ball, Danielle kept her camera, a Canon R3 with a 400mm 2.8 lens, trained on Tatum as he fell — “not thinking it was something serious,” she said, “but just in case he had a reaction that would illustrate the Celtics’ overall frustration.” But as Tatum turned, the look Danielle saw on his face told a different story. Tatum had ruptured his Achilles’ tendon, ending his season and potentially sidelining him well into next year’s. The Knicks went on to win the game, and then the series.

“I don’t like photographing injuries because it’s so sad to watch,” Danielle said of the photo she captured (1/1600, f3.2, ISO 4000). Tatum was curled on the court floor, left arm framing his face, grimacing in pain and frustration. But it turned out to be the signal image of the team’s season this year.

“In the end, I feel like the photo summed up the Celtics’ playoff run,” she said.

Danielle’s is one of 20 images that the Globe’s photo editors deemed the best that the paper captured in May. Besides a bitter end to the Celtics’ season, the month included graduation ceremonies unfolding in a new political climate, remembrances of fallen soldiers, the fifth anniversary of George Floyd’s murder, the return of outdoor concerts, and a lot of rain.

Below are a few more of the paper’s top photos from last month. Peruse the rest of them here.

Andrea and Nahomy Chavarría arrived in Vermont with their family last year from Nicaragua. They came legally, but President Trump’s changes to immigration policies convinced them to self-deport. At Champlain Valley Union High School, teachers and administrators scrambled to put together an early graduation ceremony for the sisters, who were both seniors.

As Nahomy and her father left the school for the last time, Globe photographer Jessica Rinaldi captured them walking by a giant American flag that the sisters’ classmates had painted and adorned with quotes from American icons. My colleague Giulia McDonnell Nieto del Rio told the family’s story in an article published last month.

April showers brought May flowers — but also more showers. As this newsletter has documented, the city has endured 12 straight weekends of rain, and a 13th looks to be in the offing. Globe photographer David L. Ryan braved the weather to capture an umbrella-toting pedestrian on storm-dampened Boylston Street.

College commencement ceremonies in Greater Boston have taken place in Trump’s shadow as his efforts to cut research funding and bar or deport foreign students hit Harvard, Tufts, and other schools. But there’s still plenty of joy. Photographer Pat Greenhouse captured newly minted BU graduates celebrating in a hail of confetti.

May marked five years since a Minneapolis police officer knelt on George Floyd’s neck, sparking a national conversation about on racism and policing. Globe photographer Erin Clark found an echo of that reckoning outside the Massachusetts State House last month as a singing group made up of formerly imprisoned Black men — from left, Robert Rose, Albert Brown, and Jabir Pope — performed during a rally for criminal justice reform.

Jessica Rinaldi was there as Lilah Bilotta, 7, ran with outstretched arms through a sea of American flags on Boston Common ahead of Memorial Day. To mark the holiday, volunteers with the Massachusetts Military Heroes Fund and Home Base created a garden of more than 37,000 flags — one for every service member from Massachusetts who has given their life since the Revolutionary War.

In between deluges, it finally started to feel like summer last month. Erin Clark captured Brad Shultz, the guitarist for the alt-rock band Cage the Elephant, playing outdoors among the crowd on the second day of this year’s Boston Calling music festival.

🧩 8 Across: Bright students’ org. | ⚡️ 80° Showers and storms

Boston and Massachusetts

Karen Read retrial: A 70-pound German Shepherd mix named Chloe was at the center of the proceedings this week.

Triumphant return: Marco Sturm, who played five seasons with the Bruins from 2005-10, is the team’s new head coach.

Housing: The Healey administration awarded over $7 million to help convert two downtown Boston office buildings into apartments.

Power surge: Data centers to power AI are coming to Massachusetts. Are they an economic opportunity or an energy crisis in waiting?

New England

Gun control: Rhode Island’s House of Representatives passed a ban on assault-style weapons, sending it to the Senate.

Trans rights: New Hampshire Senate Republicans passed legislation that would ban hormone treatments and puberty blockers for minors, bringing it closer to becoming law.

Trump administration

Then vs. now: In Trump’s first term, his ban on travelers from Muslim-majority countries sparked protests at airports and legal pushback. His new travel ban has drawn less resistance.

Russia-Ukraine war: Germany’s chancellor urged Trump to pressure Vladimir Putin to seek peace. Trump said it might be better to let the countries “fight for a while.” (Guardian)

Chelsea arrest: A Boston civil rights group accused immigration agents of unlawfully detaining a father of three on Mother’s Day, seeking $1 million in damages for smashing his wife’s car window and traumatizing their children.

The Nation and the World

Boulder attack: Prosecutors in Colorado charged the suspect with 118 counts, including attempted murder. (AP)

Unanimous decisions: The Supreme Court ruled for a straight woman who lost out on jobs to gay colleagues, saying she doesn’t have to meet a higher standard than minorities to sue for workplace discrimination. (Politico) The justices also said Mexico cannot sue US gunmakers for violence that Mexican drug cartels commit using US-made weapons. (SCOTUSblog)

Diddy trial: The judge threatened to eject the music mogul from the courtroom for making faces at the jury. (NBC)

Will Ukraine’s drone attacks change the war?

Yes, says Bernard-Henri Lévy in the Wall Street Journal, calling Ukraine’s daring raid, which neutralized important Russian planes, “a further step on the path to victory.” (🎁)

No, Jennifer Kavanagh counters in UnHerd. Despite their shock value, the attacks will harden Russia’s resolve and won’t help Ukraine regain lost territory.

Whether or not it turns the tide, Ukraine’s ingenuity has transformed warfare, exposing the threat that cheap drones pose to standard militaries — including the US’s, Max Boot argues in the Washington Post. (🎁)

By Teresa Hanafin

💘 Blind date: She’s a kind and genuine person who plays the cello; he’s into mixology and breathing fire (literally). Did their relationship ignite?

💰 Stash: Americans are getting close to saving what they’re supposed to in order to not run out of money in retirement. Here’s how much that is. (WSJ 🎁)

🏙️ Beautiful buildings: This year’s Boston Preservation Alliance achievement awards have gone to City Hall and its plaza, the Curley Community Center in South Boston, the Twelfth Baptist Church in Roxbury, and more. (BPA)

📺 Tony weekend: Here’s how to watch two stage productions that are nominated for Tony Awards this year, as well as five past winners. The awards show airs at 8 p.m. Sunday on CBS and Paramount+, and Christopher Wallenberg has some predictions. Interestingly, among the 29 plays or musicals vying for Broadway’s most coveted honor, the subject of death is central or ancillary to the story in a dozen of them.

🏠 Home again: She couldn’t have guessed where new love and a new marriage would take her: back to her old house.

🟣 No love: Sherwin-Williams has announced its loneliest color. It’s not that friendless people should use it; it’s the tint that it sold the least last year. (BH&G)
