“They’re part of this community,” John Pregmon, president of North End Cares, which helped to organize the event. “We’re both focused on the same thing, how can we make the North End better and safer.”

In a speech, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin R. Hayden thanked first responders but emphasized the importance of community partnerships and collaboration.

“You’re the reason we do what we do,” Hayden said, speaking to dozens of residents. “But you’re also the reason we’re successful in what we do.”

In an interview, Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox said National Night Out is an opportunity to acknowledge residents who help law enforcement keep the city safe.

“We ask them for so much, to partner with us to provide public safety.” Cox said. “This is an opportunity to go around the city and say ‘Thank You,” to all the residents that work so hard to keep the city safe.”

Danny Coakley, who has lived in the neighborhood for four years, said the North End “full of passion.”

“You won’t meet a group of individuals more invested in their community,” Coakley said.

“An engaged community is a safe community,” Cox said.

Coakley believes police in the North End help the community as much as neighbors help each other.

“They really do a good job of making themselves visible and really want to make sure that they are available to any of the community organizations,” Coakley said.

Mayor Michelle Wu arrived to greet residents. The city’s National Night Out celebration brought together kids, seniors and others to get to know their neighbors.

“Boston is a city that sees safety not only as numbers and statistics and charts, but as community,” Wu said in an interview. “We’re all in this together to keep our communities safe.”

Sharon Verrocchi, who was born and raised in the North End, attended to show her support for law enforcement.

“I love the cops. They do a great job,” Verrochi said.

Michelle Topor chatted with her friend, Mary Ann D’Amato, about the joys of seeing the neighborhood come together.

Topor, who has lived in the North End for 54 years, said “I’m blessed to be able to be here. I could never be anywhere else.”

D’Amato, who’s lived in the neighborhood for 62 years, agreed saying she feels “very safe here.”

title: Boston City Council moves ahead on ordinances for rat-resistant trash bins, Office of Pest Control
text:
“This is an issue that is critical to our city,” Councilor Ed Flynn said in his statement before the council. “If this isn’t a public health issue, a public safety issue, I don’t really know what is.”

The council’s actions come after New York City made national headlines for creating the position of “rat czar” with a hefty $155,000 salary in 2023 to combat its own rodent problem. Boston announced it would tackle its rat issues with a “Boston Rodent Action Plan” the following year.

Now, the councilors want to take their attack plan a step further. Flynn and Councilor Erin Murphy, who both introduced the ordinances for the office and the anti-rat trash cans, warned that the pest problem goes beyond stomach-turning run-ins with rodents on the streets. A six-year study by Tufts University researchers found that most rat populations in Boston carry leptospirosis, a type of bacteria that can infect humans, causing flu-like symptoms and, in rare cases, multiorgan failure and death.

“Our pest control crisis poses public health concerns,” Flynn said. “How about an office dedicated to the public health and quality of life on pest control?”

The pest control office would develop specific response plans for rat-heavy neighborhoods and educate residents on pest prevention, including how to properly dispose of trash and seal openings to their homes. It would “streamline” the work currently split between the Public Works Department, the Inspectional Services Department, and the Water and Sewer Commission, according to the ordinance’s text.

The rat-resistant trash bins would be introduced in neighborhoods with the highest numbers of rodent complaints, such as Allston-Brighton, Dorchester, Chinatown, South End, Roxbury, East Boston, and South Boston. The other plan would create same-day put-out and pickup for uncontained residential waste and containers for commercial trash.

If the rat-resistant trash can ordinance goes through, the Public Works Department would have one year to hand out hard plastic or metal containers with closed lids to prevent rats from entering. The cans may be subsidized, discounted, or reimbursed for low-income houses and small businesses.

Councilors John FitzGerald, Julia Mejia, Henry Santana, and Benjamin Weber added their names to sponsor the trash container ordinance following Flynn and Murphy’s remarks.

Murphy said rodent “hotspots” pose an elevated health risk to working families and seniors living in dense housing and are a mental health concern for some of her constituents, who have told her they are afraid to leave their houses or use their backyards because of the rats.

“Boston’s rodent problem is getting worse, not better,” she said. “Residents are fed up.”

Boston’s Rodent Action Plan contained specific strategies for parks, sewers, public housing complexes, and construction sites. It recommended rat poisons that don’t pose a risk to other wildlife, and a working group of city departments involved in rat mitigation efforts.

The plan, which was composed by “urban rodentology” expert Bobby Corrigan, also endorsed appointing a “rat czar.”

Flynn said on Wednesday that the problem remains rooted in how residents dispose of their trash. He called for a “massive public awareness” campaign and strict enforcement of trash removal policies to solve the rat problem, urging the city to provide bait boxes, compost containers, and language services to residents.

An order for a hearing to explore how the city can collect trash on the same day residents take it out is intended to fix this. Councilor Sharon Durkan, who sponsored the order, said she’s tired of passing heaps of rodent-infested trash left overnight on street corners in her district, which includes Fenway and Back Bay.

“We’ve all walked down a block like that this summer,” Durkan added. “We know that less food waste on the streets means less rats.”

The ordinances for a pest control office and rat-resistant trash bins will be reviewed by the Committee of Government Operations for effectiveness. The same-day trash pickup order will move forward to the Committee on City Services and Innovation Technology.

title: Man who killed teenager in 1989 Roxbury botched robbery granted parole for sixth time from life term
text:
A man who killed a teenager in a botched drug robbery in Roxbury in 1989 has been granted parole from his life term for a sixth time, having been sent back to prison on each prior occasion for violating the terms of his release.

On Tuesday, the state Parole Board granted release to Charles Hughes, 60, according to a ruling.

He was convicted in 1990 of second-degree murder for the fatal shooting of 18-year-old Derek Twitty on April 22, 1989, the ruling said.

Second-degree murder carries a life sentence upon conviction with parole eligibility after at least 15 years behind bars.

Following his conviction, Hughes was paroled in 2005, 2009, 2016, 2019, and 2022, only to return to prison each time due to his “ongoing struggles with substance use disorder,” the board said.

Remaining substance-free is a typical requirement of parole.

“Despite his numerous parole revocations, Mr. Hughes has never been charged with a crime while on parole, nor has he absconded from supervision at any time,” the board said.

Hughes and another man, Mac Hudson, fatally shot Twitty and a second person, who survived the attack, the ruling said.

It said Hughes and Hudson pretended they wanted to buy drugs from the victims but then “drew guns and demanded both drugs and money.”

Twitty and the other person fled, but the assailants gave chase and opened fire, the report said. Hudson was also convicted of second-degree murder, records show.

The Globe reported in 1990 that Twitty was fatally shot in the head, while the second victim was wounded in the chest. The assailants were attempting to rob them of seven to 10 bags of heroin, officials said at the time.

In Tuesday’s ruling, the board said a plan is in place to help Hughes succeed on the outside.

“The conditions set by the Board, which include a Long-Term Residential Program, a recovery coach, and mental health counseling, will assist Mr. Hughes in maintaining sustained remission from his substance use disorder,” the ruling said.

The board said it considered the testimony of Assistant Suffolk District Attorney Montez Haywood, who spoke in opposition to granting a sixth release to Hughes.

“The Board concludes by unanimous decision that Charles Hughes has demonstrated a level of rehabilitation that would make his release compatible with the welfare of society,” the ruling said.

It said he’ll be released within two weeks to a halfway house, and that he’ll have to abide by a number of conditions, including maintaining a nightly curfew, abstaining from drugs and alcohol, submitting to electronic monitoring, and having no contact with Twitty’s family.

Hughes remained incarcerated Wednesday, according to a state Department of Corrections database.

Jerry Manion of the Globe Staff contributed.

Travis Andersen can be reached at travis.andersen@globe.com.

title: ‘He casts a wide swath.’ Sheriff Steven Tompkins has long loomed large in Boston, Democratic political circles
text:
Tompkins’s indictment, and subsequent arrest Friday in Florida, quickly sent reverberations through Boston and Massachusetts Democratic circles, where Tompkins has been a longtime fixture and one of its most prominent Black elected officials.

“He casts a wide swath,” said Joyce Ferriabough Bolling, a longtime Boston political strategist. “There was a time when people would hope he would helm the Democratic Party. . . . He’s not political from the standpoint of a governor or a mayor. But he has his own kind of fiefdom [of public safety officials of color], in which he really stands at the top.”

It’s in part why Ferriabough Bolling said she was “pretty much shocked” by the indictment, which charged that Tompkins — a onetime opponent of marijuana legalization — allegedly pressured the company to sell him stock before it want public before demanding a refund on his $50,000 in late 2021 and early 2022 as his reelection campaign costs mounted.

“This just doesn’t sound like him,” she said of the allegations. “Something’s not right.”

Tompkins, now nearly 12 years into his tenure, began his rise in the sheriff’s office, serving as its chief communicator and marketer before Governor Deval Patrick tapped him to lead it in 2013.

At his swearing-in ceremony, Tompkins said he grew up on public assistance in a single-parent household in public housing in Harlem, recounting going through the “school of hard knocks” and pointing to his own backgroundvwhen talking to young people about staying out of trouble.

His appointment almost immediately took on political shades, tapped as he was to replace his own boss and longtime friend, Andrea Cabral, whom Patrick simultaneously named the state’s secretary of public safety. A year earlier, Tompkins was also an adviser to Warren’s first US Senate campaign. (Aides to Warren did not respond to requests for comment Friday.)

“By the way, it’s a political job,” Patrick told reporters that day in 2013 of the sheriff’s post. “So the folks that are criticizing it as a political hire, tell them: They’re right.”

Eight years later, on an episode of his podcast in which Cabral was a guest, Tompkins described the ceremony as “one of the best days of my life.”

“What a terrific day to be standing next to my best friend on the planet and being sworn into these offices of importance and offices that really do have an effect on other people’s lives,” Tompkins said.

The indictment of Tompkins unsealed Friday morning does not name the cannabis company he is charged with extorting, but a person familiar with the matter confirmed to the Globe that it’s Ascend Mass, a company once run by Cabral and cofounded by Frank Perullo, a longtime political consultant whose old firm worked for Tompkins’s campaign from 2013 to 2015.

Efforts to reach Cabral or Perullo were not successful Friday.

Tompkins has faced accusations before of leveraging his office for personal benefit. In 2015, he agreed to pay a $2,500 fine after he walked into several shops in Boston’s Egleston Square in August 2013, identified himself as sheriff, and flashed his identification before requesting the removal of his opponent’s campaign signs.

“I’ve learned from the experience, and I’ve moved on,” he told the Globe in 2015. “It won’t happen again.”

A year later, Tompkins ran, then suspended, only to then reactivate his bid to be the chair of the state Democratic Party, reentering the race after the death of his wife. He ultimately lost, despite having the backing of then-Mayor Martin J. Walsh.

Two years ago, Tompkins again admitted to violating state law after he created a no-bid job for his niece and repeatedly asked his subordinates to run personal errands for him. His niece had moved into his house to help care for Tompkins’s children after the death of his wife, before Tompkins later named her as a public information officer in his office, regulators said.

All the while, Tompkins has stood as a major figure in Boston. His list of endorsements in his last race reads like a who’s who of Boston and Massachusetts politicos, including Governor Maura Healey and Warren. He has served as chair of Roxbury Community College’s board of trustees since 2019, after then-Governor Charlie Baker, a Republican, tapped him to head the panel. (A college spokesperson declined to comment Friday, citing the federal investigation.)

Tompkins also built a reputation for embracing innovative ways to help pave paths of reentry for those in jail. He was credited with creating the sheriff department’s Common Ground Institute program, which teaches those incarcerated vocation skills in a classroom setting.

Another initiative: Partnering with Ascend so it could hire people recently released from jail as workers at its facilities.

“It’s incumbent on us to do these types of things and not just say to people when they leave jail, ‘Good luck, hope you don’t come back,’” Tompkins told the Globe at the time.

In his 2021 podcast episode with Cabral, which was recorded in August 2021 and posted online that October, Tompkins did not say that he at one point had, or still had, shares in the company, as prosecutors alleged.

But he signed off wishing Cabral well, saying he hoped she enjoys her new position, and “make[s] lots and lots and lots and lots and lots of friends.”

“And money!” he added.

Sean Cotter and Samantha J. Gross of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Sheriffs aren’t supposed to get indicted. But Steve Tompkins just landed on the wrong side of the cell.
text:
According to the indictment, the company initially refused Tompkins’s push to invest. But he aggressively pushed for a piece of the action, insisting that he held sway on whether the company could operate in Boston, and it eventually relented.

The charges against Tompkins came as a surprise to many in local political circles. He has forged a reputation as a low-key convivial leader who runs his races, supports his political allies, and otherwise keeps his head down. He’s also involved in community activities; for example, serving for years on the board of Roxbury Community College.

Tompkins’s attempted shakedown of the marijuana business — identified in the indictment as “Company A” — began in 2020. Around that time, Tompkins told an unnamed company official that he wanted to buy into the company, though it wasn’t yet publicly traded.

Those were the heady, gold-rush days of the Massachusetts cannabis industry, a time of optimism before a combination of oversaturation and heavy regulation made the legal weed business far less lucrative than it once looked on paper.

Alas, Tompkins’s investment tanked. His $50,000 share in the company was worth $138,403 the day the company went public, but it wouldn’t stay there.

By the time he was running for reelection in 2022 — in an unexpectedly competitive race — his stock was under water. Tompkins demanded his initial investment back, in part to help finance his reelection campaign. Though there was no requirement to do so, the company returned his cash, in a series of checks that were included in the indictment.

The indictment does not identify the company that Tompkins allegedly invested in. But the date of the approval of the company’s license and other details seem to align with one company in particular: Ascend Cannabis, a significant national player in the industry seeking to move into the Massachusetts market. At the time, its local operation was led by Andrea Cabral, Tompkins’s predecessor as Suffolk County sheriff and former boss. (To be clear, sources tell the Globe Cabral is not the Ascend official Tompkins allegedly tried to shake down.)

You might be wondering why a sheriff would have any leverage over a cannabis company. His only actual duties are to operate the Suffolk County House of Correction and the much smaller Nashua Street Jail.

But to ensure equity in the cannabis industry, the state requires companies granted licenses to show they were having a positive impact on communities that could have been adversely affected by the advent of the cannabis industry. The company in question demonstrated its “positive impact” by hiring recently released inmates to work in its stores. That was a program that Tompkins, presumably, could have terminated whenever he wanted. So they had incentive to play ball.

Or so the government alleges.

Suffolk County sheriff is an odd job. It’s one of those posts where one is seldom challenged once elected. Making headlines is strictly optional.

Decades ago, it was viewed as a potential political stepping stone, because sheriffs were viewed as overseeing an army of political hacks who could act as a campaign army. Now, it’s one step removed from witness protection.

But low-profile offices can be breeding grounds for corruption — in part, because no one pays attention to them. To be clear, I have no idea whether Tompkins did any of what the government alleges. But it’s the kind of office where scandals sometimes occur without notice.

The one saving grace for Tompkins was that he was arrested in Florida. Friday might have been the worst day of his professional life.

But at least he wasn’t booked into one of the jails he runs.

title: Five things to know about Suffolk County Sheriff Steven Tompkins
text:
Here are five things to know about Tompkins and past troubles he has faced since becoming sheriff more than a decade ago.

Tompkins has served as sheriff in Suffolk County since he was appointed by then-Governor Deval Patrick in 2013. He won election campaigns in 2014, 2016, and 2022, when he beat his former chief of external affairs, Sandy Zamor-Calixte, in a Democratic primary.

As sheriff, Tompkins oversaw the state’s largest county correctional system, which includes the Suffolk County House of Correction, the Nashua Street Jail, and the Civil Process Division.

At the time of his initial appointment, Tompkins succeeded Andrea J. Cabral, for whom he had served as an aide. Cabral was leaving the sheriff’s department after Patrick appointed her as secretary of public safety and security in his administration.

Tompkins worked in Cabral’s office for more than 10 years and had served as her chief of external relations, responsible for her media relations and connections with elected officials, businesses, and community and neighborhood groups.

Patrick at the time defended his appointment of Tompkins as sheriff, saying he was not concerned Tompkins could be viewed as a political hire. Patrick said he looked at other candidates outside of Cabral’s inner circle but that Tompkins was “the right man at the right time.”

Two years ago, Tompkins paid a $12,300 fine levied by the state’s Ethics Commission after he admitted to violating state law by creating a no-bid job for his niece several years earlier and by repeatedly asking his subordinates to run personal errands for him.

Tompkins, at the time, defended the hiring of his niece as a communications staffer in 2017 and told the Globe that he did not create the position for her, a claim that contradicted the agreement he signed with the Ethics Commission. The agreement said he had simply informed his chief of external affairs that his niece — who was not vetted — would soon begin working for the department.

The Ethics Commission also fined Tompkins $2,500 in 2015 after he asked store owners in Roxbury to remove his election opponent’s campaign signs from their windows while invoking his position as sheriff. To settle that case, Tompkins acknowledged that he violated a conflict-of-interest law that prohibits state employees from using their office to secure anything of “substantial value” that is not available to other “similarly situated individuals.”

He acknowledged the wrongdoing in an interview with the Globe in 2015.

“If that’s the rules, that’s the rules,” he said at the time. “I’ve learned from the experience, and I’ve moved on. . . . It won’t happen again.”

Tompkins also faced controversy during his campaigns for re-election to the sheriff’s office.

A 2016 investigation by Boston 25 described a “pay to play” culture at the sheriff’s department where employees frequently donated to Tompkins’ election campaigns. A 2021 report by Common Cause, a government accountability think tank, documented political donations to Tompkins by vendors hired by the department.

Tompkins is well connected in Boston’s political circles and the state Democratic Party. He served as an adviser to Elizabeth Warren’s Senate campaign and has maintained strong political relationships in the state for years.

When Tompkins launched his 2022 re-election campaign, Warren showed up at the kick-off event. A year earlier, then-city councilor Michelle Wu, now the mayor of Boston, trumpeted Tompkins’ endorsement in her mayoral campaign.

Tompkins was also a candidate for chairman of the state’s Democratic Party in 2016 but was eliminated after the first round of voting.

The Suffolk sheriff’s office ended a controversial relationship with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement in 2019, after years of housing ICE detainees at the Suffolk County House of Correction.

The jail was housing about 1,200 detainees, 200 of whom were ICE detainees, Tompkins said at the time.

He said the decision was made so his department could provide rehabilitative services to more women, as the jail was due to begin receiving pretrial and sentenced women under a new agreement with Essex, Norfolk, and Plymouth counties.

“This is not about ICE, this is not about Trump, this is not about the federal government, this is about saving lives,” Tompkins said at the time.

The decision was grounded in helping people get back on their feet, he said.

“To do that, I need space,” he said.

Material from previous Globe coverage was used in this report.

title: Boston neighborhoods face gentrification. Wu has a plan to fight back.
text:
Mayor Michelle Wu has a plan to do something about it. “We benefit from growth,” she said in an interview, “but it’s very real to see investments coming in without guardrails in place, and then the very community members who hung on and believed in the area are the first to get pushed out.”

Released last month, the mayor’s two-year “anti-displacement action plan” includes more than 40 new or enhanced initiatives aimed at stabilizing homes, businesses, and cultural spaces in neighborhoods vulnerable to the predations of the market. The city’s Condominium and Cooperative Conversion Ordinance, which currently protects tenants in buildings with four or more units from the sudden loss of their rental apartments, will expand to include two- and three-unit buildings, where most conversions take place. The city’s program to convert office space into housing has expanded to include student dormitories, easing the competition for neighborhood apartments. In a pilot program, developers in the zoning process will be asked to disclose any potential displacement of residents. And more.

The plan is full of wonky technical details, but that’s the work of city government: methodical, incremental, and focused on the levers that will improve the lives of its people.

One distinctive tool is an interactive map predicting the risk of displacement in every census tract, based on demographics (the percentage of renters, for example, or residents with limited English); the turnover rate among property owners; past evictions; and other indicators. An area in East Boston just behind the glitzy new waterfront condo developments is among the highest at risk, with a large immigrant population, homes flipped at a rate three times the citywide average over two years, and rents rising more sharply than citywide. And though new residential development applications are also rising, the map suggests that supply alone is not enough to keep housing stable and affordable. Along with East Boston, the map identifies Roxbury, Mission Hill, and Dorchester as the neighborhoods most at risk of displacement.

The mayor also has set aside $12 million to help buy and preserve homes in vulnerable neighborhoods. One recent example is Fairlawn Estates in Mattapan, where last month the city and civic partners protected 347 units of housing with deed restrictions that will keep them permanently affordable. Sometimes, taking homes out of the private market completely is the best way to prevent displacement.

Some of the items in the plan, like expanded property tax breaks, still need approval by the Legislature under the antiquated home rule requirements that handcuff cities and towns as they try to control their own fates. A provision to fund legal aid to tenants facing eviction is part of larger statewide legislation. This is vital in Massachusetts, where, according to trial court data, fewer than 10 percent of tenants in eviction proceedings had access to legal counsel last year, while 90 percent of landlords did.

A frustrating paradox of urban growth is that neighborhood improvements can often result in rising prices. The term “green gentrification” describes how new parks or pollution cleanup can beautify neighborhoods but also raise housing costs. Wu rejects the idea that lower-income neighborhoods can’t have nice things. “We cannot accept that it has to be either/or,” she said. The idea is to welcome growth, but carefully and with eyes open to unintended consequences.

In the formerly condemned industrial space on East Boston’s waterfront that is now the Institute of Contemporary Art’s Watershed annex, the current exhibition explores the meaning of home, especially salient in a neighborhood of immigrants. Museum curators recruited East Boston’s schools and civic centers to contribute material for the exhibit: People sent old family portraits, pictures of saints, items given to them for their journey to America by relatives left behind. It’s a beautiful and moving display of longing and belonging — a promise to be a home for everyone that this mayor intends to keep.

Renée Loth is a contributing Globe Opinion writer.

title: Will Sheriff Steven Tompkins keep his job? The answer may lie in a decades-old old court case.
text:
“We hold that where the sheriff is an elected official, the Governor was not an ‘appointing authority’ and, accordingly, lacked the power to suspend” him under the law, wrote Paul J. Liacos, then the chief justice.

More than three decades later, this case provides the precedent for Governor Maura Healey and Attorney General Andrea Campbell as the state confronts the indictment of another elected county official, Suffolk County Sheriff Steven W. Tompkins. Neither can suspend him, though they can file a petition for his removal.

The 67-year-old sheriff for the county that includes Boston, a ubiquitous and influential politician in state and local Democratic circles, was arrested Friday in Florida on charges of extorting a cannabis company for early access to stock — and then allegedly extorting the company again to get his money back after the value of his investment tanked.

For the second consecutive day, Tompkins did not respond to requests for comment, including whether he’s going to resign. He was reelected for a six-year term in 2022.

The sheriff’s office did not respond to requests for comment on Saturday. Healey and Campbell also have not commented on the matter, including whether they plan to ask the SJC to remove him, as Weld and Hashbarger did with McGonigle.

In McGonigle’s case, despite prevailing against the governor and AG, the Middlesex sheriff was still ultimately suspended by the SJC as it weighed whether to remove him entirely. Before the high court reached a final decision about removing him from office, federal courts made the point moot: McGonigle was convicted of tax fraud and racketeering and sentenced to prison.

Any elected official sentenced to state or federal prison time is deemed to have vacated their seat, according to state law. If Tompkins is convicted, each charge of extortion carries a sentence of up to 20 years in federal prison.

Under state law, if the six-year term isn’t up, the governor can appoint an interim replacement to a vacant seat and call a special election in the next even year. Tompkins, as a top aide in the sheriff’s department, was appointed by Governor Deval Patrick in 2013 when then-Suffolk County Sheriff Andrea Cabral was appointed state secretary for public safety.

On Friday, Tompkins was released on $200,000 bail after making an initial appearance in Florida. He is required to return to Massachusetts and report to federal court in Boston by Friday, Aug. 15, and be arraigned at a later date.

On Saturday, the Massachusetts Sheriffs’ Association said in a statement, “Given the active nature of this investigation, the Massachusetts Sheriffs’ Association will respect the parties in this case, and allow the legal process to play out.”

So far, there’s been no major outcry among other Boston politicians for Tompkins to step down. Mayor Michelle Wu, an ally of Tompkins, called the charges “very serious” but said she’d need to know the specifics before commenting further.

Other politicians, including City Councilors Ed Flynn and Erin Murphy, gave statements similar to Wu’s, not taking a stance on resignation.

“Ethical and positive leadership, honesty and integrity must be demonstrated by elected officials and public servants,” Flynn said on Saturday.

That stands in sharp relief to the arrest in December of then-Boston City Councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson. After the councilor was indicted on bribery charges, several of her colleagues, including Flynn and Murphy, as well as Wu, called on her to resign. She resisted for months, but ultimately stepped down in July after pleading guilty in May.

Since his 2013 appointment, Tompkins has overseen the jails in the county that includes Boston, Winthrop, Chelsea, and Revere.

He’s also well known for his influence in city and state Democratic circles, an old-school retail politician, heavily involved in a range of local organizations, including chairing the board of Roxbury Community College. He’s typically eager to pick up a phone call from the media to opine on issues ranging from state politics to the drug crisis at Mass. and Cass near one of his jails.

At times over his tenure, his influence-peddling has run afoul of the law. In 2015, he paid a $2,500 ethics fine and acknowledged wrongdoing after he invoked his position as sheriff while asking store owners in Roxbury to remove the campaign signs of his election opponent from their windows.

At the time, he told the Globe he’d learned from the experience and would follow ethics rules. He added, “It won’t happen again.”

But, it did.

In 2023, he paid a $12,300 fine and admitted to violating state ethics laws by creating a no-bid job for his niece and repeatedly asking subordinates to run his personal errands.

In their indictment released Friday, prosecutors did not name the cannabis company he allegedly leaned on, but a person familiar with the matter said it is Ascend Mass, part of Ascend Cannabis, a multistate retailer. Ascend’s local operations were once run by Cabral, Tompkins’ former mentor and close friend whose ascension had led to his own.

But Cabral is not the Ascend official who was allegedly extorted, according to the source.

In Massachusetts, cannabis companies applying for annual licenses need to show how their business will have a “positive impact,” especially on communities adversely affected by the nation’s war on drugs. For Ascend, the answer ran through Tompkins, with whom they partnered on a program to train and hire people recently released from jail.

This partnership gave Tompkins leverage; without it, according to prosecutors, company officials feared they would not have their license renewed to operate a shop downtown.

As it moved through the licensing process, Tompkins allegedly pressured Ascend to sell him stock before it went public. Tompkins allegedly told a member of the company he “wanted to get in on the stock so [he] could make some cannabis money.”

The company rebuffed him at the time, but Tompkins persisted, according to the indictment, telling the company official Ascend needed his cooperation to renew its license.

So in 2020, the person facilitated the sale of some 28,000 shares, before Ascend went public, for $50,000, according to the indictment. After the company went public in 2021, Tompkins’s stock was worth $138,403, the indictment states.

But when Ascend’s share price sank and Tompkins’ holdings were underwater, he allegedly demanded a refund of his $50,000. Tompkins was up for reelection in 2022 and told the company officials he needed money for “his campaign and personal expenses.”

Tompkins had not signed any agreement that would have guaranteed a refund on his initial investment, according to the indictment, but the official paid him back anyway.

In the 2022 election, Tompkins handily beat his one opponent, a former colleague, in the September primary and then breezed to reelection unopposed, capturing nearly all of the votes cast for sheriff.

title: How New England built the Plains
text:
But something shifted quickly and irrevocably that night he wrote about in 1854. It began with a man named Anthony Burns.

Burns had stowed away for weeks in the belly of a ship to escape enslavement in Virginia. By the time he stepped ashore in Boston, he had become both free and criminal — property that had, under the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, escaped its rightful owner. When federal marshals arrested him on false pretenses, hoping to sneak him back into bondage before the public noticed, Boston erupted.

The courtroom became a spectacle. The public was barred. Burns’s own lawyer was rendered powerless — forbidden to object, speak, or protect his client in any meaningful way. And in a final insult, a government agent tricked Burns into dictating a letter affirming his status as an enslaved person. The judge empathized with Burns but nonetheless ruled against him.

Slavery, it turned out, didn’t need Southern soil. It could be enforced right in the cradle of abolition, in close proximity to the Boston Common.

The city’s Black residents, who had always known the fragility of their freedom, mobilized first. The pastor of the Twelfth Baptist Church demanded Burns’s release. Protests filled the streets. Fearing an uprising, the federal government fortified the courthouse even before the trial had concluded. President Franklin Pierce ordered troops to secure the building. Soldiers lined the entrances, and chains were fastened across the courthouse doors.

What changed wasn’t just policy. It was perception. The moral quarantine in which elite white New Englanders had sequestered themselves failed. Slavery had entered their bubble. Henry David Thoreau, speaking just weeks after Burns’s trial, demanded that his fellow citizens choose moral clarity over legal comfort. “Is it not possible that an individual may be right and a government wrong?” he asked. “Are laws to be enforced simply because they were made?”

Amos Lawrence and others like him — well-heeled, genteel, cloistered — took notice. Eventually they also took action, albeit moderated and carried out on their own terms.

Calls for a more direct confrontation with slavery were not only imaginable at the time — they were already echoing through New England’s streets, pulpits, and newspapers. In the wake of Burns’s arrest, some abolitionists demanded open defiance of the Fugitive Slave Act. Many had supported similar efforts just three years earlier, when Shadrach Minkins, who had fled enslavement in Norfolk, Va., was forcibly rescued from a Boston courthouse by Black activists and white allies. With the help of the Boston Vigilance Committee, Minkins escaped via the Underground Railroad and reached safety in Canada. Figures like Wendell Phillips and William Lloyd Garrison urged moral suasion and civil disobedience; others, including activists in Boston’s Black community, proposed disrupting the legal process altogether. In this atmosphere of mounting urgency, even violence in the name of freedom was discussed.

But rather than confronting slavery where it stood and calling for direct abolition or cutting off commercial interaction with the American South, Lawrence chose to abolish only the chances for slavery’s expansion. He became treasurer of the New England Emigrant Aid Company, a joint-stock corporation chartered by the Massachusetts Legislature with one aim: to raise funds to send free-soil settlers west to Kansas, in order that they might outnumber pro-slavery forces and tip the future of the American West toward freedom.

Boston didn’t send revolutionaries out west. It sent Congregationalists. Missionaries. Schoolteachers. Families armed with shovels, hymnals, rifles, and righteous intent. The Emigrant Aid Company raised funds through an exhaustive network of some 3,000 churches, many of them Quaker or Congregationalist. “For Religion,” their circulars promised. “For Education. For Temperance.” They were advocating a version of abolition that didn’t disturb Boston’s own social order. It was freedom as export. Righteousness at a distance.

The ask was modest — $20 per settler, roughly $700 today. Enough to transport and equip a family to settle Kansas on behalf of abolition.

Donations flooded in. The Rev. Horace James from Worcester sent $23.37, boasting of his congregation, “Never did fingers and thumbs move more nimbly in the performance of any good work.” To him that meant that “verily there is hope for Kansas.” Others weren’t so flush with cash. The Rev. W.C. Jackson from Lincoln, Mass., whose flock scraped together $15, reported, “Your circular for the Emigrant Aid Society came rather inopportunely for us farmers.” Some ministers like Jonathan Lee from Salisbury, Conn., apologized for the frugality of their flock: “From my scanty purse a single dollar must be accepted in testimony of my interest in the cause of truth and freedom,” because, Lee wrote, “I am without pastoral charge or salary.” Others enclosed neat bundles of cash with effusive letters, grateful for a moral cause that could be joined without leaving home. Lawrence threw himself into the effort. He wrote President Pierce — his cousin by marriage — to chide him for failing to protect free-staters. He tracked weapons shipments. He personally funded churches, schools, and armories. He, along with many others, made Kansas a proxy battlefield, a place to perform conviction while sidestepping a harder reckoning with what could be done to stop slavery entirely.

And Kansas, as it turned out, bled.

Missourians — armed and incensed — flooded across the border. Ballot boxes were stuffed. Pro-slavery militias burned pressrooms. In 1856, just as the violence crested, Senator Charles Sumner of Massachusetts delivered a searing speech comparing Kansas to a raped virgin and accusing Southern politicians of barbarism. In a more familiar scene, days later, a South Carolina congressman, Preston Brooks, stormed into the Senate chamber and beat Sumner unconscious with a metal-tipped cane.

This was the war New England had hoped to fund rather than fight. But the borders were dissolving. Eventually, the South seceded. And when Kansas did enter the Union as a free state in 1861, its fate had been sealed not by New England idealism but by the absence of Southern senators in Congress.

When the Civil War gave way to a fractured Reconstruction, Kansas endured not as a solution crafted by New England elites but as a promise seized by Black Americans themselves. As Reconstruction’s guarantees faltered, many formerly enslaved people fled the South for the Plains, becoming known as Exodusters. Others, like Edward McCabe, envisioned Kansas not just as a sanctuary but as a staging ground — a terrain on which to build something autonomous and Black. For McCabe, Kansas — and later, Oklahoma — offered a second chance.

And the names live on. The college town of Lawrence, Kan., bears Amos A. Lawrence’s name, a monument to abolitionism at arm’s length. In Langston, Okla., the Black town McCabe helped found, street names like “Massachusetts” signaled to Black settlers that they were heirs to a longer freedom struggle — one rooted in, but no longer dependent on, New England’s conscience.

The West that New England built was funded by abolitionists who had converted not to revolution but to strategy. They filtered their moral convictions through propriety.

It’s worth asking what their legacy means now.

We live in a moment when the very institutions Amos Lawrence once stood for — elite philanthropy, intellectual inquiry, and cautious reform — have come under fire. Harvard, a beacon of New England liberalism, finds itself besieged by accusations from both right and left. Elsewhere, DEI offices are shuttered. History curricula are rewritten. Librarians contend with what books to put on their shelves. Even here, in the bluest of blue states, there’s talk of “indoctrination,” “wokeness,” and “elites out of touch.” And here too, migrants are detained often without the norms and sorts of protections we assumed would be durable.

In the 1850s, Lawrence and his cohort were shaken into action by a single courtroom scene on Court Street. But their response came with a caveat: They would confront injustice without addressing it at home.

Today, Court Street is quieter, humming more predictably with foot and car traffic — but the moral decisions we must make haven’t gotten easier. Who we detain, whose histories we erase, which freedoms we underfund — all still happen in that old Boston bubble.

The difference now is that there’s no Kansas to send our convictions to.

title: As Washington axes aid for the most vulnerable, legislation in Mass. would tackle inequities
text:
It’s vital work, and many of its recommendations are worth enacting.

This proposed legislation comes at a time when the Trump administration is seeking to limit diversity, equity, and inclusion programs and racial preferences. The work of the Health Equity Compact is not that. It’s about finding practical solutions to address the health needs of places like Brockton, where the average life expectancy is 64 — compared to a statewide average life expectancy of 80, according to the Atrius Health Equity Foundation.

One of the Compact’s specific proposals, for which this editorial board has advocated, is using state Medicaid money to support residency slots. Massachusetts is one of only seven states that doesn’t use Medicaid money to help finance graduate medical education. The state is leaving federal match money on the table, which could support residencies in targeted specialties that Massachusetts needs, like primary care.

In general, anything the state can do to advance career ladders for health care workers is valuable. For example, UMass Chan Medical School just launched a program letting college graduates with unrelated bachelor’s degrees train to become master’s level registered nurses in just 16 months.

The health equity bill allows the public health commissioner to have a role in creating “stackable” credentials for health care workers, where one credential can be added to the next, creating a career path.

Another intriguing idea in the proposed bill is the creation of a trust fund to give grants to “health equity zones,” specific communities with poor health outcomes. This is a model used in Rhode Island, where community organizations in each zone assess local needs and determine how to meet them, with funding available to support those efforts. Rhode Island communities have taken steps as varied as passing a bylaw prohibiting smoking in town parks, delivering nutritious meals to residents, expanding community gardens and farmers markets, and creating a drop-in space for children with behavioral health needs. Establishing health equity zones could build on work Massachusetts is already doing through a program that creates public-private partnerships prioritizing 30 communities with health inequities to address issues like maternal health.

The 45-page bill incorporates the recommendations a Health Equity Task Force made in 2021. But not all of its provisions should make their way into the final legislation.

In particular, at least for now, lawmakers should resist the temptation to pass new health insurance mandates.

The bill would require insurance coverage for interpreters, community health workers, and patient navigators. It is important for hospitals and health centers to be able to employ staff who help patients, including non-English speakers, navigate a complex health care system. These positions are typically funded through grants and, in some cases, by insurance under negotiated agreements or payment models.

But a wide-ranging insurance mandate like the one in this bill would increase premiums for all payers — including those who can least afford them. In 2023, the Division of Insurance published a list of 47 services that state-regulated health insurance is required to cover, and the Legislature has since added another seven, according to the Massachusetts Association of Health Plans. The cost of each mandate can seem small. But they add up. According to the association, state mandates account for more than 17 percent of premium costs, or nearly $2.5 billion in annual spending.

The bill would also require insurers to reimburse equally for telehealth and in-person care for primary care and chronic disease visits. There is ongoing debate over reimbursement rates for telehealth, which exploded in popularity during the pandemic. It’s worth studying the costs and benefits of telehealth in specific specialties before mandating payment parity because ideally, telehealth would provide opportunities for cost savings.

Those quibbles aside, the proposed health equity bill would move the state in the right direction. At a time when the federal government is cutting health care spending and eliminating benefits that help the poorest citizens, it would be a strong statement if Massachusetts were to take the lead in passing a bill to improve the health of people in communities that today suffer the most.

title: City of Boston to celebrate New Edition’s 42nd anniversary on Aug. 30
text:
After a one-year delay, the city of Boston is hosting a block party celebrating New Edition and the R&B group’s formation in Roxbury more than 40 years ago.

The festivities, which include a street naming ceremony, are scheduled for Aug. 30, in Roxbury, where the group was founded in 1978. At the ceremony, Dearborn Street will be renamed “New Edition Way,” and that day will also be declared as “New Edition Day” in Boston, Mayor Michelle Wu announced Monday morning.

“Boston is where it all began for us. This honor means the world to me,” said Bobby Brown, vocalist of New Edition, in a press release.

New Edition received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2017, and in 2022 and 2023, the group was inducted into the Black Music Hall of Fame and the National Rhythm & Blues Hall of Fame.

The celebrations were originally scheduled for last September, but were postponed due to “unforeseen scheduling conflicts,” according to the city’s website.

“It is an honor to welcome home Roxbury natives New Edition to celebrate their global impact, from our communities here in Boston to the music industry worldwide,” Wu said in a press release.

The street naming ceremony will kick off the celebrations, followed by a block party at Orchard Gardens Boys & Girls Club with music, food, and activities for attendees. The event will also feature a backpack giveaway for local youth.

The location of the celebrations, Orchard Gardens formerly known as Orchard Park, is in honor of where the band members grew up.

The group dedicates its success to the support from their fans, affectionately known as the #NE4LIFERS.

“I am truly grateful for the privilege of being made a permanent fixture in our city that has played such a significant role in shaping our lives and career,” Ricky Bell, one of the members of New Edition, said in a press release. “It brings me immense joy to think that future generations of my family, friends, and #NE4Lifers from all over the world will be able to walk and drive down New Edition Way. This honor is mind-blowing in the most awesome way. 02119 IS and WILL always be my home.”

The street naming is scheduled for 10 a.m. Aug. 30 at the corner of Ambrose and Albany streets in Roxbury; the community block party follows at 11 a.m. at the Orchard Gardens Boys & Girls Club, 2 Dearborn St. New Edition will also make a special appearance.
