title: Justin Won didn’t go to Harvard as planned, but now he runs a food stall at MIT
text:
How did you get the chance to open a restaurant at MIT?

It’s at the [Stratton] Student Center, second floor — more like a food court. They invited me because the students had a choice to pick any restaurant.

Did you always want to be a chef?

Well, I had an office job for 19 years. I was a market data analyst: finance, the stock market. But I always wanted to do a food truck on the side.

I don’t want to brag, but I had some cooking talent, cooking my mom’s recipes. Every time I had a party or something, my friends would be like, “Well, just start a restaurant!”

I actually got laid off from work in 2015-ish. With the package they gave me, after they laid me off, I was like, “This is probably a good time to start a food truck.”

I didn’t want to start a restaurant right away, because more than 50 percent fail. The truck was actually pretty busy. I started with MIT and Roxbury Crossing, and slowly it’s growing.

Tell me about the food.

Every recipe is Korean food: barbecue, Korean rice bowls. I grew up eating Korean food, and that’s all I know how to cook — my mom’s recipes. I was born in South Korea, and I moved to the United States when I was 10 years old.

What brought your family here?

Well, I have two brothers. There are three boys. My parents’ dream was to have everyone go to Harvard. But unfortunately, that didn’t happen. The main reason we emigrated from Korea was for education. I grew up in Andover.

Seems like things turned out OK. What do you do when you’re not trying to run a food business? Where do you eat?

I love eating Chinese food in Chinatown. I love Peach Farm restaurant.

Do you have any favorite hidden gems in Canton?

I go to the Italian place in Randolph, La Scala.

Coming from Canton, were you caught up in the Karen Read drama?

I followed a little bit, but not too much.

What does Boston do well, and what food do we need more of?

I think Boston is good, but not as good as New York. But I notice people from Massachusetts who move to Florida, they’re like, “Oh, I miss Boston food!” That’s when I realized that Boston actually has good food.

We do very well with roast beef, North Shore roast beef. We do good good steak and cheese, but not as good as Philly. And Chinese food, too.

Where could we improve?

You know, you can’t compare [New York] pizza to any other place. I don’t know how they do it, but they say it might be the city water.

If you were to eat pizza around here, where would you go?

Santarpio’s in East Boston.

Where did you grow up eating? Do you have any food memories from growing up in Andover?

We used to go to a Chinese place called Andover Jade. It’s not there anymore. And also a steakhouse called Grassfield’s.

My parents used to love Grassfield’s.

We used to go there a lot. I think it’s still there, as a matter of fact.

How did you end up finding a location in Roxbury?

I got an email from MBTA to bid on it. It’s the perfect location, very diverse, 600 people walk through that station every day. That’s what attracted me, the foot traffic.

What’s your favorite dish on the menu? What do you tell people to order?

We specialize in bibimbap, the Korean rice bowl with assorted vegetables. You get to choose any protein, like beef, chicken, pork, tofu, and then it comes with a fried egg on top and six different types of dressings. I’d get beef with gochujang dressing.

When you’re eating at home, what do you snack on? What do you eat for yourself?

A lot of fruit. I eat a lot of watermelon and blueberries. I’m trying to lose weight, too.

What do you do for fun?

I have a family. I have wife and two kids. Normally, when I’m home, I’m actually doing yard work in my house.

Are your kids good eaters?

They are — especially my son. My son is 19 years old and goes to Ole Miss. And my daughter is 17 and going to be a senior at Canton High School. She wants to go to an Ivy League. She’s a smart cookie.

If you could eat anything for your last meal, what would it be?

Barbecue food. Steak.

Is there any food that you hate, that you just never want to eat again?

Organ meats, like liver.

What’s your guilty pleasure?

Smart Food popcorn.

If you had to describe the Boston food scene in a sentence, what would you say?

I would say that it’s fantastic. My customers are mainly young working people and college students.

Is your current job more fun than what you were doing before, in the corporate world?

Definitely. I’d never go back to the corporate world, really.

I bet leaving a corporate job feels like a big risk to some people. What would you say to someone who wants to open a restaurant?

Nothing’s easy. What you see is not actually what you see. There’s hard work behind it. When my wife and I started this, we worked 80 hours a week. We did everything on our own. She still works with me: She runs MIT, and I run the food truck.

If you could have dinner with anyone in the world, who would it be?

Larry Bird. He’s my favorite basketball player. Actually, could I change it to Tom Brady?

Interview was edited and condensed.

title: Boston’s ‘For the Culture Week’ to celebrate HBCUs, R group New Edition
text:
The city of Boston is hosting a weeklong celebration of Boston-based R&B group New Edition, and the legacy of Historically Black Colleges and Universities, known as HBCUs.

“The City is proud to celebrate the historic impact of New Edition while bringing the spirit of HBCUs to the region. We look forward to welcoming residents, families and visitors from across the country for a week of celebration, pride, and community,” said Mayor Michelle Wu in a press release.

The multi-day festivities, which the city has dubbed “For the Culture Week,” comes at a time when city councilors are pushing to bring an HBCU Satellite Campus to Boston. A satellite campus is a site associated with a main campus, but is in a different location, while offering a similar curriculum for students. On Tuesday, Councilor Brian Worrell and the City Council Committee on Education will hold a hearing to explore the possibility.

The United States has more than 100 HBCUs, the majority based in the South where Jim Crow laws prohibited Black Americans from attending almost all of the region’s universities. HBCUs were established to provide opportunities for Black Americans, and are credited with expanding the Black middle class.

Boston is home to more than 24 colleges and universities — but that number does not include a single HBCU or an HBCU satellite campus. According to the order for the hearing, sponsors of the measure believe having an HBCU in Boston would “create a magnet for Black students to attend and later settle in the area.”

City councilors cite a need for an HBCU presence, pointing to persistent educational inequalities. Fifty years after Boston was ordered to desegregate its public schools, the legacy of busing leaves the district scarred, as academic outcomes continue to show racial disparities. For example, Black students go to college at a lower rate than their white peers.

“[It] would also send a message that the city, once marred by the busing battles of the 1970s, has moved forward to a new era,” reads the order for the hearing.

As the city considers drawing an HBCU presence, Culture Week will host events celebrating the schools. On Thursday, The Mix, a restaurant in Dorchester, will have a “Hella Black Trivia,” where attendees will be tested on their knowledge of HBCUs. The next day, The Mix will welcome the Harvard Black Graduate Alliance and local professionals for a mixer featuring food, music, games, and networking.

A highlight of Culture Week is the football game between Johnson C. Smith University and Morehouse College — both HBCUs — at Harvard Stadium, set for Saturday at 4 p.m. Tickets are priced at $30 each.

Ahead of the game, Wu, representatives from the two schools, and the City of Boston Marching Band will host a pep rally at City Hall on Friday at 4 p.m. For those who cannot make the game in person, The Mix will put on a game day watch party, followed by an afterparty.

“When the game ends, the real turn-up begins! 🎶💃🏽 Rock with us late into the night,” The Mix wrote on Instagram.

Other events of the week include parties, music performances, and sports games. Sunday’s Boston Red Sox v. Pittsburgh Pirates game, which starts at 1:35 p.m., will recognize HBCU alumni.

In addition to HBCUs, festivities will celebrate the music and arts scene. On Sunday at 5 p.m., Boston will host the 25th Annual Boston Gospel Fest, New England’s largest Gospel music celebration, at Leader Bank Pavilion. John P. Kee, who was inducted into the Gospel Music Hall of Fame in 2005, will be the headliner.

Culture Week will pay tribute to New Edition, which formed in Roxbury in 1978. The city is set to rename Dearborn Street to “New Edition Way,” and throw a community block party at Orchard Gardens Boys & Girls Club on Saturday. Wu will also declare that day — August 30 — to be “New Edition Day.”

The Grammy-nominated group is known for hits, like “Candy Girl,” “Cool It Now,” and “Mr. Telephone Man” that garnered attention not just in Boston but also across the country. New Edition gained popularity in the 1980s, and topped the Billboard R&B chart throughout that decade.

“Boston is where it all began for us. This honor means the world to me,” said Bobby Brown,a member of New Edition, in a statement.

“From the Roxbury streets to the Harvard Stadium stands, we are showing the world what it looks like when a city comes together for culture and for one another,” City Councilor Ruthzee Louijeune, who is also pushing for HBCU presence in Boston, said in a statement.

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
BLUSH On their just-released full-length, “Beauty Fades, Pain Lasts Forever,” this Singaporean band threads twang-tinged guitars and bummed-out vocal melodies through plush layers of cathartic, speaker-filling fuzz. Aug. 29, 8 p.m. The Lilypad, Cambridge. get2thegigbos.com

NINE INCH NAILS The long-running electro-noise project of Trent Reznor — who’s now enlisted his frequent movie-score collaborator Atticus Ross as a full-time member — boasts a catalog filled with heavy beats and maximized anguish, with cuts like the thrashing “Wish” and the brain-rattling “The Perfect Drug” still possessing an unnerving electricity decades after their release. Aug. 29, 8 p.m. TD Garden. 617-624-1000, tdgarden.com

BENSON BOONE In early 2024, this rock belter’s neo-power ballad “Beautiful Things” began what would become a stranglehold on the pop charts; it’s still at No. 17 on the Hot 100 as of this writing. Since then, he’s released two whole other albums including this year’s “American Heart,” which frames his muscular voice in radio-ready sonics. (You’ll have to head to the show if you want to catch his much-discussed acrobatic abilities.) Sept. 2, 8 p.m. TD Garden. 617-624-1000, tdgarden.com

MAURA K. JOHNSTON

STEVE EARLE It’s been a half-century since the hardcore troubadour helped to blow up what passed for country music with his debut release, “Guitar Town.” Now, weathered but unbowed, he’s looking back with his solo acoustic “Fifty Years of Songs and Stories” tour. Make sure you arrive early enough to catch songbird Laura Cantrell beforehand.Aug. 29, 8 p.m. $49. Blue Ocean Music Hall, 4 Oceanfront North, Salisbury. 800-745-3000. www.ticketmaster.com

NOELINE HOFMAN Ms. Hofman is an up-and-coming, unalloyed-country purveyor from western Canada (Alberta, to be exact). She’s only released an EP so far, but it’s as full of promise for the future as it gets. Think Corb Lund and Colter Wall territory and you won’t be far off.Sept. 3, 8 p.m. $20. Brighton Music Hall, 158 Brighton Ave.www.livenation.com

SHANNON LAY Garage punk turned murmuring folkie Lay hasn’t released an album of original music since 2021’s superb “Geist,” but her latest release, the simply named “Covers, Vol. 1,” serves as a series of signposts to her influences, among them Elliott Smith, Nick Drake, and Vashti Bunyan. Sept. 3, 7 p.m. Free. Myrtle, 134 Waterman Ave., East Providence. www.givemyrtle.com

STUART MUNRO

JIM CONNOLY: WAR IS A RACKET The trombonist, composer, and US Marine Corps veteran debuts his searing new suite on the anniversary of the US withdrawal from Afghanistan. Featuring trombone, string quartet, and jazz trio, the composition is named after the 1935 antiwar manifesto by General Smedley Butler, among the most decorated Marines in history. Aug. 30, 8 p.m. $15. The Lilypad, 1353 Cambridge St., Cambridge. lilypadinman.com

SEVENTH SUN The rising saxophonist who goes by the name “Seventh Sun” returns to the Roxbury venue where he celebrated the release of his self-named debut album last year, this time with his current band comprising guitarists Sasha Zucker and Gabe Kuchan, bassist Maurice Allen Jr., and drummer Chris Napo. Sept. 4, 6 p.m. No cover. Long Live Roxbury, 152 Hampden St. www.longlivebeerworks.com/boston

SONNY LANDRETH & CINDY CASHDOLLAR DUO Slide guitarist Landreth, whose fans include Eric Clapton and Mark Knopfler, and dobro and lap steel specialist Cashdollar, who’s played with everyone from Bob Dylan to Ryan Adams, convene a blues summit. Sept 5. $40. Bull Run Restaurant, 215 Great Road, Route 2A, Shirley. bullrunrestaurant.com

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

BERKSHIRE OPERA FESTIVAL The musicians of the Boston Symphony Orchestra are taking a well-deserved break after running the Tanglewood gauntlet, and concert options in Boston are in short supply on Labor Day Weekend — but there’s still one more chance to catch Berkshire Opera Festival’s 10th anniversary mainstage production of Verdi’s “La Traviata,” starring Vanessa Becerra as Violetta opposite Joshua Blue as Alfredo. Jonathan Loy stage directs. Aug. 29, 7:30 p.m. Mahaiwe Performing Arts Center, Great Barrington. www.berkshireoperafestival.org

THE KNIGHTS The Brooklyn-based chamber orchestra assembles at Williamstown’s Clark Art Institute to celebrate the museum’s exhibition “A Room of Her Own: Women Artist-Activists in Britain, 1875-1945”; they present an outdoor concert with music by Dame Ethel Smyth and Ralph Vaughan Williams (Aug. 30) and a lunchtime family program designed with young children in mind (Aug. 31). Clark Art Institute, Williamstown. www.clarkart.edu

A.Z. MADONNA

INTO THE WOODS: Stephen Sondheim’s fractured fairy tale follows some classic characters who must face the consequences when their wishes come true. Includes the heartbreaking songs “Children Will Listen,” “No One Is Alone,” and “Last Midnight.” Through Sept. 7. Presented by Seacoast Repertory Theatre, Portsmouth, N.H. www.seacoastrep.org/into-the-woods

WHEN ELVIS MET THE BEATLES Based on the true story of the meeting of the two legendary musical acts, this world-premiere musical fills in the gaps around that one night at Elvis’s Los Angeles mansion, when Elvis broke out guitars and the musicians had a jam session. Written by Colin Carberry and Glenn Patterson. Presented by Ogunquit Playhouse. Aug. 28-Sept. 22. www.ogunquitplayhouse.org/show/2025-when-elvis-met-the-beatles

TERRY BYRNE

THE 7 FINGERS The acclaimed Montréal nouveau cirque troupe returns to Boston bringing back its provocative and colorful “Passengers.” Directed by company founder and award-winning Cirque du Soleil choreographer Shana Carroll, the work plays off our fascination with train travel, creating a community of strangers on the move — literally and metaphorically — who express their emotions through an eclectic fusion of dance, dazzling acrobatics, theater, illusion, and music. Sept. 2-26. $35-$158. American Repertory Theater at Loeb Drama Center, Cambridge. https://americanrepertorytheater.org/

THE SOUND OF MEMORY This evening of dances curated by choreographer Annmaria Mazzini explores the passage of time as we move through life and where memory is held in the body, both haunting and sustaining us. In addition to Mazzini, a former dancer with the Paul Taylor Dance Company, the concert features dances created and performed by Jennifer Chin, Jennifer Mabus, Brynt Beitman, and Amanda Stevenson, with music created and performed by Paula Jeanine Bennett and Brittani Nearing. Aug. 28-29. $20-$30. Windhover Center for the Performing Arts, Rockport. www.windhover.org

KAREN CAMPBELL

2025 JAMES AND AUDREY FOSTER PRIZE Opening Thursday: This biannual showcase at the ICA devoted to Boston (and Boston-adjacent) artists arrives into a veritable renaissance of local contemporary art. With the Boston Triennial in full swing with its slate of local creatives — fully a quarter of its projects are by Boston artists, including Alison Croney Moses, also a Foster Prize recipient this year — it feels fair to say that Boston is having a moment. The Foster Prize was established in 1999 with the cultivation of that very moment in mind, making this year’s installment feel like a particular triumph. Artists honored are Moses, Yorgos Efthymiadis, Damien Hoar de Galvan, and Sneha Shrestha (a.k.a. IMAGINE). Through Jan. 19. Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100, www.icaboston.org

DAVID C. DRISKELL: COLLECTOR Opening Friday: Driskell, known more as an educator and advocate for centuries — yes, centuries — of lineage of Black art in America than for his own paintings, died in 2020 with an art collection that reflected his deeply held priorities. This exhibition, drawn from those personal holdings, puts on view for the first time since his death works that served as touchstones over a lifetime of advocacy and artistic production. Paintings from the 19th century onward by Black artists like Edward Mitchell Bannister, Loïs Mailou Jones, Romare Bearden, and Elizabeth Catlett hang with Driskell’s own, and help frame a legacy as much rooted in those he held up as his work itself. Through March 1. Portland Museum of Art, 7 Congress Square, Portland, Maine. 207-775-6148, www.portlandmuseum.org

VAN GOGH: THE ROULIN FAMILY PORTRAITS Final week: Vincent van Gogh met few successes in his short, unhappy life, but between 1888 and 1889, he was as content as he’d ever been. In the French town of Arles, he found peace in the friendship of local postman Joseph Roulin and his family. A collaboration with the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, the show brings together some 20 portraits made in that moment, and a glimpse of a famously tortured artist momentarily calmed. ThroughSept. 7. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, mfa.org

MURRAY WHYTE

SPACE ODYSSEY One of visual art’s puzzles is how to convey the distance between things, and perhaps the greatest challenge is portraying an inconceivable distance that communicates how vast the universe is and how small a human being. For this show, 25 artists contemplate that epic span, along with the mysteries the cosmos stir within us. The slate includes Lindsey Kocur, Boriana Kantcheva, CJ Lori, and Joe Keinberger. Through Sept. 12. 13FOREST Gallery, 167A Massachusetts Ave., Arlington.www.13forest.com/space-odyssey

CATE McQUAID

TCS PRESENTS: CASEY CRAWFORD “So I’m 45 years old, and my mom still buys my underwear,” says Crawford, in a bit that helped him win the Boston Comedy Festival stand-up competition in 2024. “I’m not sure what she’s doing with them but I need the money.” Aug. 29, 9:30 p.m. $20-$25. MEN IN COMEDY: A TATTOO SHOW AND TELL This comedy collective does things differently. First, despite their name they are an all-femme-presenting troupe. POPCORN COMEDY This monthly stand-up show is back at the Somerville Theatre with headliner Carolyn Plummer, plus Raoul Biron, Katy Coughlin, Mike Vabner, Lloyd “Legacy” Sharp, and Jeremy Pearson, with hosts Peter Liu and Jason Fishman. Sept. 4, 7:30 p.m. $23.18. The Somerville Theatre, 55 Davis Square, Somerville. www.eventbrite.com

title: Some city councilors are pushing to bring an HBCU satellite campus to Boston
text:
“These industries determine who’s building and designing our homes, who’s teaching our children, who’s providing medical care to our families, and who’s shaping public policy, and in every one of these sectors, we see underrepresentation at every level,” Worrell said. “These gaps begin in our classrooms. That’s what we need to change, and that’s what an HBCU presence in Boston can help us address.”

While more than two dozen colleges and universities are already based in Boston, none of them are HBCUs. HBCUs, as defined by the Higher Education Act of 1965, are nationally accredited, historically Black colleges that were established prior to 1964, for the purpose of educating Black Americans at a time when many universities discriminated against, or did not admit, Black students.

Many HBCU graduates, and some current HBCU students, spoke passionately in favor of the idea of bringing a satellite HBCU campus to Boston, citing their own personal experiences.

Sixty-five year old Edwin Sumpter told the councilors he has lived in Boston his entire life, except for the two years he spent as a student at Johnson C. Smith University, an HBCU in Charlotte, N.C.

“I had no idea how those two years would really shape me as an individual, as an African American, and instill a pride in me and show me a side of African American life that I only read about, or occasionally saw on TV,” Sumpter said, emphasizing that he supports Worrell’s proposal to bring an HBCU satellite campus to Boston.

Considering “the rich history we do have in this city, around the African American experience and education, the needs that I do feel we do have, especially in my neighborhoods where I’ve grown up, in terms of impacting our young folks, [it] makes more and more sense,” he continued.

Autumn Souto, who works as an enrollment and outreach coordinator with the METCO program, said a lot of METCO and BPS students right now are leaving Boston to attend HBCUs.

“It’s really a pivotal moment in their lives to really feel welcomed in an institution where they feel seen, where they have the space to be their authentic selves,” Souto said. ”For them to have the opportunity to have something right here in Boston, where they have their roots, where they have their families, where they’ve built their communities, can be very pivotal in their education, their careers, and whatever they choose to do in their futures.”

But some residents expressed concern about establishing an HBCU satellite campus in the city, without first investing the necessary resources into supporting Black students and improving educational outcomes in BPS.

“How are you going to place that in the city of Boston with the progress that needs to be done?” asked Russell Glover, a lifelong Bostonian who said he lived through the busing era. “How are we going to benefit from this HBCU coming to Boston? Is it going to be for outsiders? Because how is that going to serve our purpose?”

Others worried about bringing an HBCU satellite campus to Boston with the Trump administration in the White House, when HBCUs could face severe financial harm from federal funding cuts to Pell Grants. Some asked about whether such a proposal would involve financial support for students, especially considering Boston’s high cost of living.

Jonathan Jefferson, the president of Roxbury Community College, emphasized that had RCC been founded just a few years earlier, it would have had the formal HBCU designation. In practice, with a student body that is 80 percent Black, RCC is Boston’s HBCU, he said.

“Please understand that if you want your HBCU, then build it at the one that you already have,” Jefferson said. “We are bringing in the HBCUs to the Commonwealth. Let us do that, work with us, support us, and let’s build a bigger, better HBCU.”

Worrell told the Globe he’s been having conversations and meetings with stakeholders for some time now to explore how to move forward on the idea. But he wanted to hold Tuesday’s hearing to get community feedback, and use it to shape how the city approaches the issue. He fully intends to incorporate all the ideas in concerns into his plan, including making existing stakeholders key parts of the effort.

“There’s no one way, right, on how to get the results that we’re looking for,” Worrell said. “My whole vision of this is to make sure that there’s community at the table, there’s institutions at the table, while we’re creating or formulating this idea.”

title: New Edition reflects on Orchard Park roots and the Roxbury community that inspired them
text:
“It could have been New Edition Street, it could have been New Edition Lane, but at the end of the day, we’ve done this the New Edition way,” said DeVoe, “and we’re continuing to do it.”

For the members of New Edition, “Orchard Park will always be Orchard Park,” according to Bivins, although it was transformed in the late ’90s into the Orchard Gardens public housing development. While the special day and street dedication are a celebration of New Edition’s legacy, the festivities are also a way for the group to honor the people from Roxbury who made a difference in their lives growing up. Brown credited Bill Marshall, then a director of an Orchard Park recreation center, for pushing him to pursue his dreams, “whether it be sports, whether it be entertainment.”

“He was just a big inspiration to me,” said Brown. “He was a father figure of most of the kids in the neighborhood. He was just a good cat.”

Bivins echoed Brown’s praise of Marshall, noting how the director would do everything from referee basketball games to serve food at the center. The space played a pivotal role in the group’s upbringing and the lives of many residents in the neighborhood.

“After school, we would go in there, Bob would do boxing, some of us would go do basketball,” said Bivins. “But by six o’clock, if you were still in the gym, you could go into another room and get a real meal. … And sometimes that one dinner might have been somebody’s dinner at home they didn’t get.”

Bivins later added, “That gym is like the golden nugget” to fully understanding the New Edition story.

Bivins noted that the soon-to-be christened New Edition Way will “run across in front of Bobby’s building,” since he used to live the closest to the gym. The Orchard Gardens Boys & Girls Club, which will host this weekend’s block party, is now located on the street. The festivities begin and 11 a.m. and will include a backpack giveaway for kids, plus free food and activities.

“The block party that we’re doing on Saturday after our street naming is just as important as the street naming,” said DeVoe. “It’s New Edition being able to give back and to pay it forward and to do all of the things that I think we’re ultimately blessed to do.”

In addition to Marshall and the center, Brown pointed to the “many talent shows” hosted in the neighborhood back then, “where the kids had something to do on the weekends.”

“I would join any and every talent show trying to be successful as an entertainer,” said Brown. “I was a big Michael Jackson fan. I was a big Prince fan.”

The group started out as Bivins, Bell, and Brown, with Tresvant joining soon after. Longtime manager and choreographer Brooke Payne (DeVoe’s uncle) would also help them work on their moves.

A Hollywood Talent Night showcase hosted by producer-songwriter Maurice Starr at the Strand Theatre in 1981 would lead to the group’s big break. According to Boston Magazine, a recording contract was on the line for the winner, with New Edition coming in second place after singing a medley of Jackson 5 tunes. However, they impressed Starr so much that he signed the group anyway. DeVoe joined as they recorded their first hit song, “Candy Girl,” and their debut album of the same name.

“The Strand Theatre is still monumental to us,” said Brown. “It’s still the place that gave us that start. And Maurice Starr … kudos to him. We didn’t even win the competition, but we were able to go into the studio the next day and record.”

The song would reach No. 1 on the Billboard Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs chart in May 1983, edging out Michael Jackson’s “Beat It.” The group would go on to grow up in tandem with their musical prowess, as they dropped other hits like “Mr. Telephone Man” and “Jealous Girl,” and established their signature new jack swing style.

Bivins said it was the group’s embrace of hip-hop, even in the early years, as well as their dance skills, that helped them stand out against the pop and R&B acts of the early ’80s.

“That’s a part of New Edition’s legacy as well, the fact that we were rapping on the first song, we were rapping on the first album,” said Bivins. “And then the guys in the group were good pop lockers. Naturally, they could go do street battles and do all that.”

“So, New Edition was like the perfect group. Maurice Starr was like the perfect situation,” he added. “And ‘Candy Girl,’ with Ralph launching it, à la Michael Jackson, was the perfect record.”

Like their old neighborhood, New Edition has evolved over the years, later adding Gill, from Washington, D.C., as a member in 1987 after Brown’s departure in 1985. Brown and other members would go on to establish acclaimed careers outside of the group, with Bell, Bivins, and DeVoe notably spinning off into their own eponymous trio, Bell Biv DeVoe, among other projects.

Brown explained that it’s their deep bonds — formed all the way back in Orchard Park — that have kept them connected throughout all the ups and downs.

“We have a kinship that is just amazing,” said Brown. “It’s the brotherhood that keeps the glue together.”

Back performing together in recent years, the group has been noticeably active, particularly in the wake of the successful 2017 BET miniseries “The New Edition Story,” which set a network record by drawing in more than 29 million unique viewers. New Edition also earned a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 2017, was inducted into the Black Music Hall of Fame in 2022, and honored by the National Rhythm & Blues Hall of Fame in 2023. The group recently had a Las Vegas residency at the Wynn’s Encore Theater as well.

New Edition appreciates the accolades and attention they’ve received in recent years, but they aren’t done building New Edition’s legacy. Noting the lack of Emmy nods for the BET series and the group’s lone Grammy nomination, Bivins admitted that they have a little bit of a chip on their shoulders.

“We still don’t own a Grammy … and we still have aspirations of being in the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, to put that under our legacy,” said Bivins. “But I think Saturday will be a defining moment, something that’s going to create itself.”

But awards can’t compare with the knowledge that their fans have been the most vocal about celebrating the group’s impact on music and the city.

“Sometimes, celebrities do things because they have a movie coming out, an album coming out,” said Bivins. “But it’s good that when you do something and the regular folks say, ‘It’s about time.’ That’s probably one of the most powerful lines you could ever hear as an artist.”

The weekend will also provide the members an opportunity to teach their children and families about “where they come from, where their fathers have evolved from,” said Brown. “It’s gonna be a beautiful situation.”

And while New Edition has come a long way from Orchard Park, Bivins is “just thankful for the things that we have been given,” he said, and the fact that Boston still has as much love for them as they do for their hometown.

“We are a very special group,“ Bivins said. “And honestly, in closing, I’m happy that our Irish city has realized what’s been going on in the hood for 43 years.”

title: ‘It’s where our heart is.’ New Edition to be honored in Roxbury.
text:
Bell and the five other members of New Edition, which formed in 1978 in Roxbury, will be honored with a street renaming ceremony and block party on Saturday, which Mayor Michelle Wu will also declare “New Edition Day” in Boston.

The event is part of “For the Culture Week,” which also celebrates Historically Black Colleges and Universities, or HBCUs. The multiday festivities come at a time when city councilors are exploring bringing an HBCU to Boston via a satellite campus.

Boston is home to more than 24 colleges and universities — but that number does not include a single HBCU or an HBCU satellite campus. As the city considers drawing an HBCU presence, For the Culture Week will host events celebrating the schools.

On Thursday, The Mix, a restaurant in Dorchester, will have a “Hella Black Trivia,” where attendees will be tested on their knowledge of HBCU culture and traditions. The next day, The Mix will welcome the Harvard Black Graduate Alliance and local professionals for a mixer featuring food, music, games, and networking.

For New Edition Day on Saturday, the city is set to rename Dearborn Street to “New Edition Way” at 10 a.m. A community block party will kick off an hour later at Orchard Gardens Boys & Girls Club, which used to be the Orchard Park Community Center, where the band members first met each other. As residents of the Orchard Gardens Housing Project, the six boys, Ronnie DeVoe, Bobby Brown, Ricky Bell, Michael Bivins, Ralph Tresvant, and Johnny Gill, used to gather and play basketball and music, leading to them forming the group.

“It’s the place that New Edition really met each other on the basketball courts, on opposing teams,” said DeVoe. “And for the Boys & Girls Club to be able to come in there and establish some type of partnership with the community. It’s just a full circle situation.”

The event was originally scheduled for September 2024, but was postponed because of scheduling conflicts, according to Dion Irish, Wu’s chief of operations, who helped plan the event.

The block party will include a backpack giveaway for back to school, free food, and activities for the community.

Additionally, a mural honoring the group will be announced by Wu at the block party. The mural was originally scheduled to be painted on the Boys & Girls Club last year, but will now be painted on the Strand Theatre because of its significance to the group.

”That’s actually where the talent shows were held back in those days, where [New Edition] actually ... became first runner-up and led to them getting a recording contract,” Irish said.

While the group has found success outside of the confines of their hometown, they are still dedicated to giving back to the city that raised them and allowed them to grow, the band members said.

Additionally, New Edition, along with the New Commonwealth Fund, an organization that works to address systemic racism through community investment and development, will be making a $25,000 donation to Orchard Gardens Resident Association to benefit youth and senior programs.

“It’s intentional what we’re looking to do,” said DeVoe. “To a certain extent, the world is our home because we’re entertainers, but the foundation was made in Boston, and we want to make sure that we’re pouring back into our city in a number of different ways.”

The event itself will not only showcase the success of New Edition, but also the potential that everyone in Boston has to do something great.

“One of the things we’re hoping to come out of this is just to make sure that the members of the community, the kids in Boston, realize the potential that they have,” Irish said. “So it’s just making it full circle to show the talent and capability of youths in the city of Boston.”

Along with New Edition Day, another highlight of For the Culture Week is the football game between Johnson C. Smith University, located in Charlotte, N.C., and Morehouse College, located in Atlanta — both HBCUs — at Harvard Stadium, set for 4 p.m. Saturday. Tickets are priced at $30 each.

Ahead of the game, Wu and representatives from the two schools will host a pep rally at City Hall at 4 p.m. Friday. For those who cannot make the game in person, The Mix will also put on a game-day watch party, followed by an afterparty.

Other events of the week include parties, music performances, and sports games. Sunday’s Boston Red Sox v. Pittsburgh Pirates game, which starts at 1:35 p.m., will recognize HBCU alumni.

In addition to HBCUs, festivities will celebrate the music and arts scene. On Sunday at 5 p.m., Boston will host the 25th Annual Boston Gospel Fest, New England’s largest Gospel music celebration, at Leader Bank Pavilion. John P. Kee, who was inducted into the Gospel Music Hall of Fame in 2005, will be the headliner.

For the group members, the street renaming and the block party are not only an honor as a group, but also as community members. When they first started rehearsing in basements and recording albums, they never expected to have a physical dedication to them on the streets they called home.

“It’s like when we first started, that was probably one of the furthest things from our minds or in our plans to one day have a street named after New Edition. But to leave a mark in history as a part of your legacy, something that your children’s children and years beyond us and our families can continue to see. [We are] beyond excited,” Bell said.

Now they have the opportunity to return to their hometown and give back to their neighborhood, in partnership with the city, to donate money and resources for the youth and elderly, is an honor for the group.

“It’s just the stuff that dreams are made of,” DeVoe said.

title: What New England’s warmer-than-average summer portends for fall
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

We may mark the seasons in highly definitive ways, but the reality is the elements of one blend into another, especially in New England. Although meteorological summer comes to an end Sunday, the effects of our warmer-than-average summer will linger well into autumn.

Our autumn leaves are affected by summer weather to a great degree. A very wet and humid summer often leads to fungus and other bacterial diseases that can result in a more dull and muted foliage season. This past June and July in New England were hot and somewhat humid, but despite some rainstorms, they were on the drier side. August has been cooler than average, yet also still dry. So could we still see a robust and vibrant canopy of colors unfold this fall?

There’s also ongoing drought conditions to contend with. As our drought worsens and continues to spread across parts of New England, trees will want to conserve moisture and drop leaves early if they remain under stress. This can lead to rather spotty color among the changing leaves.

The yellows and orange pigments are present in the leaves all season. When the foliage finally begins to change, it’s because the trees stop manufacturing chlorophyll — the pigment in plants and trees that gives leaves their deep green color — and we’re left with the brilliant yellows and oranges. This process of Mother Nature can accelerate rather quickly after a dry summer like the one we just had. For the reddish hues, it’s a different story. They’re produced in autumn, and if the leaves are under stress, then we could see a less vibrant red palette.

There are still a few weeks left for the trees to recover if we get more rain, but the long-term pattern doesn’t look very moist.

Don’t worry: The leaves will change color. Every foliage season has some brilliant displays. So, although this may not be the best, it’s still going to look like autumn.

The lack of heat and the dry weather in August have been a blessing in the garden, contributing to one of the best tomato seasons possible. Without prolonged rainfall or humidity, tomato diseases are being kept in check a little better. This doesn’t mean that the lower leaves of your tomato plants might not look pretty terrible, but overall, there are reports of a great tomato season.

Stone fruit, such as nectarines and peaches, are also faring quite well this year, with highly concentrated sugars.

As the calendar turns to September, there’s still time to plant. Summer warmth lingers in the ground, and this is a great opportunity to start a lawn or grow quick-maturing crops, such as lettuce, kale, Asian greens, radishes, and perhaps even baby beets if we get enough warmth to stick around through October.

With rainfall at a premium, you’ll have to augment Mother Nature with your own watering. The good news is the sun is not as strong as it was a month ago, so the soil can stay moist a little bit longer.

This is a good time of the year to divide perennials and move them. It’s also a sweet spot for putting in new trees and shrubs. Because it’s been so dry the past few months, I highly advise moistening the soil before planting. Also, if you move perennials, be sure to water them the day before you move them so that they’re not under stress. Garden centers may also have trouble keeping up with watering, so check the plants you buy and give them the moisture they might need.

There’s not a lot of correlation between summer temperatures and moisture levels and what will happen this winter. The winter pattern is based on bigger global phenomena, such as El Niño, La Niña, and other oscillations, such as the Arctic and North Atlantic. We will definitely have more data on that in the coming weeks.

Meanwhile, my colleague Ken Mahan looked back at four recent summers that were warm and dry like this year, and what the winters that followed were like. You can read his findings here.

title: ‘Allston Christmas’ is coming — here’s what Boston says you can (and can’t) do
text:
“It can feel a little hectic in our neighborhoods,” Wu said at Thursday’s press event. “That’s why our administration has been hard at work to make sure that our students and families can move in as smoothly as possible.”

“Allston Christmas” begins the days leading up to Sept. 1, when thousands of leases in Boston turn over. People moving out of their homes leave furniture and various knick-knacks on street corners, primarily in the student-heavy Allston-Brighton neighborhood, for passersby to take. Oftentimes, students walk around in groups “shopping” for new items for their homes.

Yet, the holiday presents a challenge for municipal workers tasked with maintaining the city’s streets. Last year’s move-in weekend saw more than 3,400 permits issued and inspectors dispatched across student-heavy neighborhoods.

This year, Boston is deploying extra inspectors, sanitation crews, and parking enforcement officers to handle the surge of students and moving trucks. More than 2,500 moving permits have already been issued for this weekend alone, and officials emphasized that residents must pay close attention to trash collection schedules, mattress disposal rules, and parking restrictions.

For many residents, that means knowing exactly when trash can go out. With the Labor Day holiday, most neighborhoods will see pickup delayed by one day, though parts of Fenway, the North End, and Roxbury will remain on schedule. Anything left on the curb outside of those times could lead to a citation.

“Everything dumped on a sidewalk this weekend is subject to a code violation,” said Dennis Roache, superintendent of waste reduction for Boston Public Works. Code enforcement officers in yellow uniforms will be patrolling neighborhoods and answering questions about proper disposal.

Mattresses are another perennial headache. The city is reminding residents that curbside pickup must be scheduled in advance through the city’s website, and that the free service only applies to buildings with six units or fewer.

For larger apartment buildings, tenants are required to work with their property manager or hire a private hauler, said Conor Newman, deputy director office neighborhood services.

In addition, Wu highlighted a new furniture pickup pilot program launched earlier this year. More than 50 discarded items were collected earlier this week by the nonprofit Household Goods, which will redirect items to new homes rather than letting them pile up on sidewalks.

The curb will be just as contested as the sidewalks, as parking enforcement is another major focus. Nick Gove, deputy chief of streets for transportation and BTD commissioner, said residents should be mindful of temporary restrictions in student neighborhoods and use moving zones quickly.

“We don’t want to ticket and tow, so please pay attention to posted signs and do not double-park or block streets,” Gove said.

Residents are also encouraged to use the 311 hotline or mobile app to report illegal dumping, rodent activity, or missed trash pickups. Wu noted that the city has been installing rat-proof trash cans and expanding mattress recycling to cut down on waste.

Boston may not be handing out partridges or pear trees, but officials say following the rules on trash and parking could be the best gift students give themselves and their neighbors this “Allston Christmas.”

title: Boston city councilors, other elected officials, write letters for Tania Fernandes Anderson ahead of sentencing
text:
If prison is part of the sentence, Fernandes Anderson’s court-appointed lawyer asked that his client serve no more than six months.

In May, Fernandes Anderson pleaded guilty to federal wire fraud and theft charges for taking a $7,000 kickback inside a City Hall bathroom from a relative who worked on her staff.

The 46-year-old Democrat made history in 2021 as the first Muslim elected to the council. She attended her final council meeting in June.

Included among the letters of support filed with Fernandes Anderson’s memo were submissions fromcity councilors, Julia Mejia, Liz Breedon, and Brian Worrell, as well as two state representatives, Christopher Worrell and Russell Holmes, and State Senator Liz Miranda.

None sought to excuse Fernandes Anderson’s actions.

Worrell said Fernandes Anderson was a trailblazer as the council’s first African immigrant and Muslim woman and applauded her public service and dedication to the advancements of equity and justice.

“While not without missteps, her intentions have always been rooted in service,” Worrell wrote.

Mejia also commended her former colleague’s impactful advocacy.

“It is crucial to emphasize the heart and intention behind Ms. Anderson’s efforts in the community,” Mejia wrote. “Her work has not only uplifted individuals, but also has strengthened the fabric of the community as a whole.”

Breedon asked the judge to consider house arrest rather than imprisonment. She said Fernandes Anderson has opened her home to vulnerable youth as a foster mom and as the parent of an adopted child.

“While Tanya (sic) has undoubtedly fallen short in our expectations of a public servant, she has also demonstrated a heartfelt commitment to effectively serve the most vulnerable populations in our city,” Breedon’s letter said.

Miranda said she has had the honor of knowing Fernandes Anderson since they were classmates at John D. O’Bryant School of Mathematics and Science in Roxbury.

Over three decades, they have bonded as fellow Cape Verdeans and sisters in community leadership, Miranda wrote.

Miranda asked the judge to “consider an alternative to incarceration that allows her to make restitution, continue her healing, and remain present for her children and the community.”

“A prison sentence would not only punish her, but deeply harm the children who depend on her daily — emotionally, financially, and spiritually,” Miranda’s letter said.

Holmes said Fernandes Anderson’s activist spirit has benefitted businesses and constituents and brought meaningful differences to the community and the children she nurtures.

“While I do not excuse any mistakes she has made, I do believe that Tania is a good and kind person who has shown remorse and a sincere desire to take responsibility for her actions,” Holmes wrote.

Worrell said he knows what a “second chance in life” can do for a person’s soul and being.

“I know personally what it means to be offered the opportunity to learn, to grow, and to serve in a greater capacity,” Worrell wrote.

Fernandes Anderson is “a woman of immense compassion, cultural understanding, and an unrelenting desire to serve her community” and deserved a chance to redeem herself.

Fernandes Anderson’s son, mother, and husband, also wrote in support, as did numerous civic and community organizers, activists and constituents.

Assistant Federal Public Defender Scott Lauer wrote that state sentencing guidelines did not require time behind bars.

Fernandes Anderson’s actions were “an aberration that will not be repeated,” Lauer wrote.

Federal prosecutors wrote that Fernandes Anderson had failed to demonstrate remorse and exhibited an “unwillingness to embrace true contrition” and ought to be sentenced to one year and a day in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release. They also asked that she be ordered to pay $13,000 in restitution.

“Fernandes Anderson undoubtedly overcame substantial personal hardships to win election to the City Council,” Leah B. Foley, US Attorney for Massachusetts, wrote in the sentencing memo. “Fernandes Anderson’s perseverance is commendable, but despite overcoming such challenges, Fernandes Anderson, repeatedly, resorted to criminal and unethical conduct.”

“The pattern and repeated instances of misconduct show this case cannot simply be characterized as a one-off mistake or accident,” Foley wrote.

Shelley Murphy of the Globe Staff contributed to this report.

title: Visibility and accessibility at the heart of Boston’s HBCU Classic between Morehouse College and John C. Smith University
text:
Borders and the city are working to create a narrative for HBCU education and sports that reflects Boston’s growth.

“When Howard played University of Maryland Eastern-Shore at Harvard in 1971, the city did not look like this,” he said. “There weren’t these restaurants, there weren’t these businesses, the population density did not look like this, there was not a woman in the corner office making decisions as mayor. There was not a Black woman as the AG, there was not a woman governor.”

From ribs fresh off the grill at tailgate parties to seeing the pageantry of the cheerleaders and marching bands, the HBCU Classic represents an opportunity to showcase not only the unique flavor of HBCU sports but also the city’s development.

Boston is catching up with the rest of the country in hosting out-of-state HBCU matchups. Neutral-site football games have been an instrumental part of HBCU sports.

New Orleans has the Bayou Classic, which is televised on NBC, at the Superdome. Atlanta has the Celebration Bowl, the de facto HBCU national championship game, featuring the champions of the MEAC and the SWAC conferences. Miami kicks off Labor Day weekend with the Orange Blossom Classic.

Now it’s Boston’s turn.

Tome Barros, the Celtics’ community engagement manager, believes the city is long overdue for its own classic.

“I think a lot of the times people forget Boston has a rich history,” he said. “To be the messengers of the importance of a Historically Black College, Boston’s a perfect place.”

Barros, an HBCU alumnus from Hampton University, has been a consistent advocate for Black higher education and led each of the Celtics’ HBCU Nights.

“This event is a living tribute to the scholars, the athletes, the musicians that play in the band, all the organizers that are trying to break barriers and really put athletics on a bigger platform,” Barros said.

There has been consistent growth for HBCU athletics in Boston in recent years. In 2022, Hampton and North Carolina Agriculture and Technical State University joined the Coastal Athletic Association. The switch allowed the schools to compete against Northeastern in conference games. Harvard has completed a home-and-home series with Howard University and Morehouse in football and basketball recently.

Barros has attended each basketball game his alma mater has played against Northeastern the past two seasons, looking to grow the network across alumni and students and also bring HBCU sports to a higher light.

“I was in the stands and it was nice to just see folks with Hampton gear on in Boston — in Northeastern’s area," he said.

From Olympian Alice Coachman from Tuskegee to Celtics legend Sam Jones from North Carolina Central, Barros believes HBCU athletes fly under the radar.

Deion Sanders made headlines when he became head football coach at Jackson State, bringing eventual Heisman Trophy winner Travis Hunter with him, before the pair left for Colorado.

NFL Pro Bowlers Michael Vick and DeSean Jackson, who were teammates with the Eagles, will coach against each other at Lincoln Financial Field on Oct. 30, when Norfolk State plays Delaware State. Numerous Pro Football Hall of Famers, including Jerry Rice, Walter Payton, and Michael Strahan, are HBCU alums.

Away from the line of scrimmage, Saturday’s game will bring a new level of exposure to a generation of Boston youth, said Tate Ross, the education coordinator at the Yawkey Boys & Girls Club of Roxbury.

They’ll get to see representation from Morehouse, the nation’s only historically Black private liberal arts college for men, whose alumni include Spike Lee, Samuel L. Jackson, and Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.

They’ll get a glimpse of Johnson C. Smith, which is North Carolina’s top private HBCU, according to U.S. News and World Report, all without having to head south.

“You never know the next time they’ll be on campus or at an event where an HBCU team shows up,” Ross said. “It’s that time now for them.”

Some local organizations, such as the Yawkey Club, organize bus tours giving students the chance to see such schools.

Chase English, a sophomore at Morgan State University who attended BC High, said he wished more opportunities to learn about HBCUs in Boston were available for him.

He found out about Morgan State through friends who attended. His decision to take a chance on a public HBCU in Baltimore was a relatively uncommon one for someone who went to a private high school in Boston.

“There was not really much introduction or showcasing, so I kind of had to find it on my own way,” English said.

title: ‘It’s an honor’: Hundreds gather for New Edition celebration, street renaming
text:
New Edition, a legendary R&B group that has been honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and a Grammy, was formed in Roxbury in 1978 right at the site of Saturday’s celebration. The Boys & Girls Club building at the intersection of Ambrose and Albany streets was previously called the Orchard Park Community Center, where the six bandmates first met each other while living in the Orchard Gardens Housing project.

Saturday’s celebration took place during Boston’s “For the Culture Week,” which honored Black excellence and the legacy of Historically Black Colleges and Universities, or HBCU’s. Saturday was the first time in five decades that two HBCUs — Johnson C. Smith University and Morehouse College — faced off in a game of football. The week of events will wrap on Sunday with a HBCU day at Fenway Park and a Gospel Fest featuring notable musicians like John P. Kee, among other celebrations.

Notable local leaders, including Wu and US Representative Ayanna Pressley, joined all six of the bandmates to share remarks about the influence the community and the band have had on each other.

“Everything we learned, every wave, the way we are, our attitude, our swag — is all from you. We got that here,” Ralph Tresvant, lead singer of New Edition, said to the cheering crowd.

The band members — Tresvant, Bobby Brown, Johnny Gill, Michael Bivins, Ronnie DeVoe, and Ricky Bell — reminisced on their upbringing in Boston and thanked fans for their support throughout the years.

“We just want to say thank you. And I want us all to look that way to that building,” Bivins said, pointing to the Boys & Girl’s Club building as the crowd turned around to face it, “In that building is where it all started.”

Acknowledging the occasional internal conflicts that afflicted the band throughout its 42 years, Bell said it was the bandmates’ common roots that kept them together.

“We were friends and brothers before we started singing,” Bell said. “So we can’t get away from each other.”

At the end of his speech, Bell presented the Orchard Gardens Resident Association with a $25,000 check. Later, Gill gave a check of the same amount to the Boston Arts Academy Foundation, which supports the city’s only public high school for visual and performing arts.

Frank Farrow, executive director of the mayor’s Office for Black Male Advancement, highlighted the impact the band — widely considered the pioneers of the modern boy band — made on the R&B and music scene.

“They have been trendsetters and role models for Black men and boys in Boston and across the United States, demonstrating resilience, creativity, and the power of brotherhood,” Farrow said.

Highlighting the importance of preserving Black history, Pressley presented the band with a congressional citation.

“Who we monumentalize — it matters,” Pressley said. “Equity in street names, statues, buildings, and the representation that comes with it — it matters.”

Wu thanked the band for the attention they have brought to Roxbury and said the city is “proud” to “brag about you and honor you on our streets.”

After the street renaming ceremony, the crowd dispersed for a block party. People danced and sang along to music by Black artists, including Michael Jackson, Mary J. Blige, and, of course, New Edition. Others took pictures in front of large white letters spelling out “New Edition Way” before heading over to grab free food. Kids enjoyed a large bounce house and prepared for back-to-school with a backpack giveaway.

Rudy Bienaime, 59, was sporting a 2022 New Edition tour t-shirt. He attended the group’s Boston leg of The Culture Tour, held at TD Garden. Like many attendees, Bienaime has been a fan since the very start.

A Roxbury resident for most of his life, he said he “always did like New Edition, and they ended up making it big.”

“They could’ve given us a free concert,” Bienaime said, laughing.

Michele Frazier, 65, was watching as an LED screen truck flashed through photos of the band in its early days. Frazier, a Roxbury resident, has known the band members since before they blew up and has supported them from day one.

“It’s an honor to see this, to see someone come back and give a lot back to the community,” she said.

title: Double Up Food Bucks savings program expands to Roxbury market
text:
Her dollars may stretch further thanks to the Boston Double Up Food Bucks program, which provides a discount on fruits and vegetables to low-income residents at some grocery stores.

Chance, a Roxbury native who now lives in Dorchester, celebrated the expansion of the Double Up Food Bucks program last month to Nubian Markets, a locally owned grocery store in Roxbury that celebrates the African diaspora.

With the addition of Nubian Markets, Boston now has six “Double Up” locations, with other stores located in Dorchester and East Boston.

Introduced in 2018, the Double Up program is funded by the city and the USDA Gus Schumacher Nutrition Incentive Program, according to Mayor Michelle Wu’s office.

Each day, people who use SNAP benefits can get up to $20 in discounts at participating stores to purchase fresh fruits and vegetables. Customers can get double the amount of produce for half the cost, but cannot exceed the daily $20 discount limit.

Wu, who attended the program’s expansion at Nubian Market, said the goal is to provide access to fresh food at an affordable price for Boston families.

“[We can] now add to the list of local grocery stores where residents can use these Double Up Food Bucks and get more value,” Wu said in an interview. “This is making sure everybody has the full range of options available, no matter your income level [or] where you live in the city.”

The Double Up program does not require any additional sign-ups; users simply pay with their EBT card and let the cashier know they would like to receive the Double Up discount.

Chance, along with her friend Gwendolyn Mitchell, shared their frustrations with food costs in Boston.

“The prices have gotten out of control,” Mitchell said. “But you do the best you can with what you have, you have to just calculate.”

A recent Globe report comparing the cost of breakfast staples at five different grocery stores showed that ten items cost between $38 and $50.

In Mitchell’s experience, three bags of groceries at a chain store can cost her up to $200, which isn’t enough for her large household in Roxbury.

Mitchell has a habit of letting extended family and friends stay with her. She said it’s in her nature to “take everyone in.” But her budget for groceries has to remain in the $100 range.

“What I could get before for $150 is now $300, it’s insane,” Mitchell said. “It’s not an option at all.”

Boston has 143,000 residents receiving SNAP benefits, and since the program’s founding, $850,000 in discounts have been applied through the Double Up program, according to Emily Sinsky, Double Up Food Bucks program manager.

Since 2021, the program has been funded by a federal grant of $500,000 from the US Department of Agriculture through the Gus Schumacher Nutrition Incentive Program, as well as a $500,000 match from the city.

Wu noted that the program benefits local retailers, making it so residents can shop at neighborhood stores with more flexibility.

“Our communities are beautiful and diverse and reflect so many cultures, and it’s in stores like this where the owners are from and are connected to the community ... there’s the ability to provide a specific kind of product or to connect with a cultural need,” Wu said.

Yusuf Yassin, co-owner of Nubian Markets, sees many of the same Roxbury residents come through the door every day.

The produce and food, which aims to “give a platform to the amazing foods and flavors of the African diaspora,” serves as a community staple for its cultural offerings.

“It’s spaces like this where people are seen in the fullness of who they are and have every resource to be able to take care of their families,” Wu said.

Now, residents can make a one-stop shop for cultural groceries and fresh produce.

“With food costs going up, every little bit helps. People come here and shop a small amount, but with the program, they would definitely be motivated to grab more items, and particularly fresh produce,” Yassin said.

Levi Caldwell, who is from the Caribbean but now lives in Roxbury, said that he comes to Nubian Markets because they sell a particular type of fish he ate growing up.

Now, he can shop at Nubian Markets for produce too, rather than going to chain grocery stores.

“This is amazing, I’ll definitely be back for more,” Caldwell said.

Emmanuel Moore, from Dorchester, is diabetic and said he has trouble staying healthy on a budget of $50 a week for groceries.

Moore prioritizes eating food that is good for him, but some weeks, it isn’t feasible.

He’s only been to Nubian Markets a few times, but with the program, he plans on making it his new favorite store.

“I think this is great to have a market like this that is so easy and convenient for people like us [EBT users],” Moore said.

title: Guns made me leave the evangelical church. When will the church leave guns?
text:
The truth took a few seconds to sink in. John had come to practice with a SIG Sauer semiautomatic handgun.

I must have looked as dumbfounded as I felt, because he quickly assured me he had a license to carry a weapon. But that’s not what had me shaken. Moments earlier, we’d been singing about divine mercy and grace. Suddenly, a beautiful space in my life was reduced to a jarring juxtaposition of God’s peace and John’s piece.

Soon after, I realized John wasn’t the only one showing up armed at the altar. John’s wife carried a pistol in her purse, and several of the congregation’s men possessed concealed firearms. I left that church, but the weapons are surely still there — along with a bewildering marriage of faith and firearms that is fueling our uniquely American gun scourge.

Leaving Evangelicalism was no small thing. Before my exodus, I had served as a full-time lay missionary for an evangelical denomination, and in Vienna — where I worked as a foreign correspondent for the Associated Press — I led worship at an English-language Evangelical parish attended by United Nations diplomats and other expatriates. I even joined the board of an international Christian relief and development agency.

But something tectonic was shifting beneath my feet. It was the 2010s, and it seemed to me that most of my fellow white evangelicals, who had always leaned conservative, were tilting hard to the right politically. They were adopting intolerant stances on immigrants and LGBTQ+ people that I didn’t share. Nor could I grasp their fear that the culture beyond the church doors was conspiring to strip them of their religious freedoms and deny them their way of life. Most troubling of all: their inexplicable fervor for firearms.

At the same time, my own views on guns were evolving. I was New England bureau chief for the AP when a gunman armed with a military-style assault rifle massacred 20 first-graders and six adults at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Newtown, Connecticut. Our teams spent more than six gut-wrenching weeks intensively covering the story.

My church dimmed the sanctuary lights and convened a somber prayer meeting. We wept for Sandy Hook’s children and our own, and we cried out for healing and mercy. We, like so many in the aftermath of such tragedies, sent our thoughts and prayers to the families and survivors of the tragedy.

And then we spoke of it no more.

But we need to talk about guns, including guns in the church.

What few realize is how many weapons are owned, concealed, and carried by those who profess to uphold life as sacred and most readily offer pointless thoughts and prayers when it’s taken: white evangelical Christians. Fifty-four percent of white evangelical Protestants keep guns in the home, according to a 2022 survey by the Public Religion Research Institute, compared with about a third of the general population.

Evangelicals also own and operate some major gun manufacturers. The AR-15-style rifle used to slaughter 21 innocents in Uvalde, Texas, in 2022 was made by Georgia-based Daniel Defense, established by an evangelical entrepreneur on a trinity of values: faith, family, and firearms. The company also manufactured some of the rifles used five years earlier in what is still the deadliest single mass shooting in US history: a sniper’s massacre of 60 concert revelers on the Las Vegas Strip.

Guns and God form “a complex relationship that may be impossible to disentangle,” Jessica Dawson, a researcher at the US Military Academy at West Point, concluded in a study published in 2019. Polls consistently suggest a sort of white evangelical inferiority complex: a fear that their influence is waning and their religious beliefs are under fire.

So how can we counter the myth that the answer to our gun problem is more guns? The Rev. Abigail Henrich is attempting it one gun — and one evangelical — at a time.

Henrich, who pastors the progressive Grace Community Boston and Stratford Street United Church in West Roxbury, founded Christians United Against Gun Violence in 2022. She’s among a small but spirited group of Christians who are challenging the white evangelical embrace of gun culture head-on. Henrich organizes gun buybacks, offering Target gift cards to people who turn in their weapons. And she shares gun safety liturgy that churches can use to make their case that guns have no place in the Gospel.

“Someone in the Christian church has to stand against this,” she says.

She’s right. “Thoughts and prayers” may seem to absolve us from doing anything to make sure such a horrible event never happens again. But if you really give a damn, you do something.

title: State’s first human case of West Nile virus in 2025 reported in woman in Middlesex County, officials say
text:
State health officials on Tuesday announced that a woman in her 70s has become the first person to test positive for West Nile virus in Massachusetts this year, after being exposed in Middlesex County.

The announcement comes as the risk of exposure to West Nile virus remains elevated across several Massachusetts communities, officials said, warning that residents should take extra precautions to prevent mosquito bites when spending time outdoors.

“The Massachusetts Department of Public Health today announced the first human case of West Nile virus in Massachusetts this year in a woman in her 70s who was exposed in Middlesex County,” the department said in a press release on Tuesday.

The press release did not provide more details about where in Middlesex County the woman was exposed, or when.

Mosquitoes, which carry the virus and spread it to humans and animals through their bites, first started returning positive test samples in Massachusetts on June 17, The Boston Globe reported. About a month later, a goat in Lunenburg became the first animal to test positive for the virus in the state this year.

In August, the risk of exposure to West Nile virus in Boston was elevated to “high,” the Globe reported, after multiple samples of mosquitoes in the city came back positive, including in Hyde Park and West Roxbury.

“West Nile virus can be a very serious disease and its presence in mosquitoes remains high right now in Massachusetts,” Public Health Commissioner Robbie Goldstein said in a press release.

Even though the weather is cooling down in the region, the prevalence of West Nile Virus among the region’s mosquitoes “is going to be elevated for some time,” Goldstein said.

The release also said there have been more than 300 positive tests conducted on mosquitoes across 12 of the state’s 14 counties.

In the past month, the risk of contracting West Nile virus has been elevated in Acton, Bedford, Billerica, Boston, Brookline, Carlisle, Chelmsford, Dracut, Lowell, and Newton, according to the DPH.

In 2024, there were 19 human cases of the virus in the state reported, according to the DPH dashboard.

Massachusetts residents can reduce their risk of exposure by applying mosquito repellant with an EPA-registered ingredient, such as DEET or oil of lemon eucalyptus, the Health Department said.

Other key precautionary steps include avoiding spending time outdoors during the early morning and evening, and wearing long sleeves and pants to protect against bites.

“The hours from dusk to dawn are peak biting times for many mosquitoes,” the DPH said.

Even though the news of this year’s first positive human case in the state comes as summer turns to fall, “the mosquitoes will be with us until the first hard frost,” state epidemiologist Catherine M. Brown said in the release.
