title: Boston mayoral hopefuls compete for support at candidate forum
text:
It was hosted by the Greater Boston Interfaith Organization in collaboration with the Black Ministerial Alliance TenPoint Coalition.

Organizers sought to extract commitments from the candidates to fund renovations to Madison Park, protect Boston’s immigrants in the face of Trump administration threats, and narrow the gap in homeownership between white families and families of color. The candidates spoke one by one, facing identical questions that exposed relatively few shades of difference.

DaRosa, Kraft, and Wu all pledged to support long-sought renovations for Madison Park, despite the challenges of securing the funding; expressed support for immigrant families amid unprecedented challenges; and addressed the city’s housing crisis, which has left deep racial disparities.

DaRosa, who is a graduate of the city’s only vocational school, said, “Madison is the gem and will be the gem.”

He said his devotion to the school long precedes his political campaign; he has spent years recruiting students to his alma mater.

“For me, it’s not just the funding,” he said. “It’s about giving our young people the inspiration to go to Madison — to get rid of the stigma that Madison is the worst school in Boston, cause it’s not.”

The format gave candidates few opportunities to swipe at each other, something of a rarity in a race that started off ugly and has only grown more so. For months, Kraft and Wu in particular have traded jabs over everything from their personal financial backgrounds to their policies.

On Tuesday, though, both stayed focused on the narrow set of issues posed by organizers. The forum gave Kraft the opportunity to tout his housing plan, which has been the top priority of his campaign.

“We have a housing crisis in the city. First and foremost, we need more homes,” Kraft said. He said he would jumpstart production on thousands of units that are still in the pipeline, and then use the resulting tax revenue to increase eligibility for first-time home buyers.

For Wu, the event was a chance to highlight the work she is already doing and lay out promises for a potential second term.

Asked about how she will respond to the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, she said, “We are fighting for to make sure that Boston continues to be a home for everyone.”

“For me, this is not theoretical,” she said, describing her background as the daughter of Taiwanese immigrants who later became US citizens. “Unlike the Trump administration, Boston follows the law at the city, state, and federal level. We are going to continue to do so and not cooperate with mass deportations.”

Robert Cappucci, who will also appear on the ballot next week, did not attend Tuesday’s forum. He told the Globe this week he is out of town due to a family emergency.

The preliminary election will narrow the field from four candidates to two. Based on public polls, Kraft and Wu are expected to proceed to the general election in November. With mail-in ballots already being returned, and early voting underway, this week marks the final sprint to Election Day.

Wu and Kraft will have at least one more opportunity to spar this week, at another candidate forum Wednesday evening. DaRosa and Cappucci are not included in that event.

Shea Thompson, 24, said Tuesday’s forum helped him narrow down his choices for mayor, though he is still deciding whether he will back Wu or DaRosa.

Wu impressed him with her record, said Thompson, who is a student at Boston University School of Theology, adding of DaRosa that “because of his own personal background, he understands what needs to be fixed.”

title: For Boston City Council: Let’s start with the candidates who won’t embarrass us
text:
Members of the Boston City Council do actually wield power. After all, despite the council’s seemingly low profile, it was worth somebody’s time to give councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson kickbacks in 2023, the latest chapter in the story of a council that’s been marred by scandals both serious and petty over the last few years.

So while the preliminary elections for contested City Council seats on Sept. 9 may not feature much drama, they’re still important. With Fernandes Anderson’s premature retirement as the backdrop — she’s due to be sentenced Friday — it’s important to winnow the field down to candidates who can serve honorably if elected.

There are 10 candidates for at-large City Council vying for eight spots in the general election. Some, but not all, district seats are also contested. The race to fill Fernandes Anderson’s seat representing Roxbury and parts of the South End is the busiest, with 11 candidates running for two spots in the general election.

Get College Town

A weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns.

Enter Email

The Globe editorial board is not going to endorse council or mayoral candidates at this stage of the race; we’ll save that for the general election after the candidates have had more time to campaign. But we are going to make a pitch to voters to factor personal integrity into their choices in this early stage of the race. As a threshold matter, ask yourself: Would I entrust this candidate with my finances?

Because that is just what you’re doing when you select a counselor. Among their other responsibilities, councilors vote on the budget that directs how your tax dollars are spent or misspent. The mayor does hold most of the cards in that process, but the council can veto budgets.

Second to integrity in the list of desirable attributes is independence. In a strong-mayor system of government, there’s a lot of pressure on councilors to act as team players — the team being the mayor’s office. But their job is to represent their constituents, and that inevitably means sometimes butting heads with City Hall.

It’s as much a question of temperament as it is of political leanings: Do candidates seem like the march-in-lockstep type, or do they make and stick to their own decisions based on their assessment of what their constituents need?

Finally, as much as the term “diversity, equity, and inclusion” has become a political lightning rod, the last word on that list is particularly important. Inclusion just means trying to represent all your constituents. In the past, Boston has had politicians who seek to divide, inflame racial or religious differences, or scapegoat vulnerable groups. It doesn’t need them again now.

Turnout in preliminary elections tends to be low, especially when there’s no mayor’s race to whip up interest. While there nominally are four candidates for mayor on next week’s ballot, it’s so widely expected that incumbent Mayor Michelle Wu and philanthropist Josh Kraft will make the general election that the race isn’t generating much heat at this stage.

Hopefully, the preliminary election will yield a field of candidates who can let the voters focus on the issues in the general election. There’s plenty to talk about: property taxes, bike lanes, crime, housing, rats, schools, and ... more bike lanes.

Two years ago, the voters used the preliminary election to remove two scandal-plagued incumbent councilors from contention. That result didn’t just represent accountability, it also opened the way for general elections that seemed focused in the right places, and not on candidates’ personal issues. And the last two years have certainly been more functional than the two “clown show” years that preceded them.

Of course, in sizing up first-time candidates for low-rung political offices, there’s no perfect way to predict which ones will be on the wrong side of a federal indictment someday, or will otherwise become an embarrassment to the city. But the more voters weigh those considerations in their choices, the more likely the city is to avoid future scandal. And if we get it wrong — well, there’s always 2027.

Editorials represent the views of the Boston Globe Editorial Board. Follow us @GlobeOpinion.

title: The bike lane debate continues
text:
But jokes aside, Jacoby’s attempt to conflate I-93 with our city’s main thoroughfares clearly demonstrates one of the key problems in this debate: Massachusetts Avenue is not an interstate. Yes, it cuts a long path through the city, and through Cambridge, Arlington, and beyond. Along its route it serves as a main street for many neighborhoods — with residences, shops, and restaurants lining it. People get to these locations in different ways, and most of the local travel is not by car. To the extent that bike lanes slow traffic, which is questionable, isn’t that actually a good thing?

Statistics abound supporting the fact that death and injuries to cyclists and pedestrians increase dramatically with faster vehicle speeds. Also, most bike lanes aren’t changing the configurations of city streets. What was previously one lane in each direction is still one lane in each direction. It’s a fallacy to claim that every bike lane removes a travel lane, somehow slowing travel time. Bike lanes don’t cause traffic, and if you’re stuck in your car, you’re not in traffic, you are traffic.

So let’s make a deal. Keep I-93 and the Mass Pike bike-free. As for the rest of the city, let’s keep working to create safe, people-friendly streetscapes for all.

Richard Freierman

Cambridge

I always appreciate Jeff Jacoby’s columns whether I agree or disagree with him.

In reading today’s on bike lanes in Boston I was struck by his very interesting perspective that Boston’s arterials were “built for cars, trucks, and buses.” The article cites Massachusetts Avenue and Beacon Street as examples. To my understanding these roads were designed to accommodate pedestrians; horse-drawn carriages, wagons, and omnibuses; and perhaps trolley traffic, albeit traveling at much slower rates of speed than currently exist today.

It is also important to point out a major difference between a highway like I-93 and a roadway like Beacon Street. A highway like I-93 is designed to accommodate traffic speeds much higher than a city street. Speeds of 50 to 70 miles per hour are typical cruising speeds. Beacon Street was neither intended to be, nor designed for, speeds anywhere near that level. I suspect city streets were largely designed to accommodate city pedestrians and other, slower traffic, not suburban commuter traffic. After all, that’s why the I-93’s of the world were built.

Remember also that train, trolley, and horse-drawn transport were the main commuting vehicles to come into the city when many of our city streets were designed. Perhaps bikes are analogous to the horses of yesteryear — although bikes are less odious in their waste output than horses.

Joseph Impellizeri

West Roxbury

Jeff Jacoby correctly chastises the hordes of cyclists who did not belong in the O’Neill Tunnel on I-93. In all fairness, he perhaps should have next chastised the Amazon and FedEx drivers who regularly block bike lanes across the city while they make deliveries, or the many other drivers who regularly endanger their fellow road users on bicycles by improperly driving into or blocking bike lanes.

Instead, Jacoby rants, “how can it it be good policy to carve [bike lanes] into the hectic surface roads that keep roads alive,” claiming incorrectly that bike lanes take space from motor vehicle lanes and cause increased traffic congestion.

In fact, the opposite is true. As reported by Canada’s CBC News, Paris saw a 54 percent increase in bike use from 2018 to 2019, and car use decreased by five percent during the same time period. The city of Copenhagen reported that its support of bicycle transport meant that “the large number of bicycles, for example, makes it easier for necessary basic motor transport such as tradesmen, goods transport and buses to get through more easily.” In fact, there is so much bike use that the city has had to add more bike corridors to cut down on bicycle congestion.

Jacoby cannot say that replicating Europe’s success is impossible here — the same CBC report shows that before New York City installed its bike lanes, it took the average car 4.5 minutes to travel from 96th to 77th street. After the bike lanes were installed, it took just three minutes — a 35 percent decrease. Jacoby is entitled to his opinions, but he is not entitled to call them facts.

Andrew Fischer

Brookline

title: Parent picking up U-Haul truck for college trek left waiting near Mass. and Cass
text:
The guard, Idlebrook said, seemed to avoid making eye contact with him and he did not approach him. Idlebrook just wanted to get his truck and get out of there. Fast.

But he couldn’t leave quickly because U-Haul had given him incorrect information. Most U-Haul locations offer customers 24-hour self-service: You book a vehicle and pick it up at any hour, including while the U-Haul outlet is closed.

But the outlet at 985 Mass. Ave., where Idlebrook had arranged to pick up his truck , was an exception: no 24-hour self-service. Nevertheless, when Idlebrook was making final arrangements a day earlier, U-Haul told him he could pick up his truck there at 6 a.m., an hour before the outlet opened.

He complained to a U-Haul representative on the phone about the wait. “What am I supposed to do until then?” he asked.

“Sorry, we have no further information,” U-Haul told him.

The dispute: Idlebrook thinks U-Haul acted irresponsibly when it gave him wrong information. Its lapse, in his view, exposed him to danger, he said. Though no harm came to him, Idlebrook said U-Haul should be publicly called out to help prevent a recurrence of what happened.

If he had been thinking clearly he would have taken a rideshare to get out of Mass. and Cass, he said. Instead, he walked about a quarter of a mile to a coffee shop at South Bay shopping center, returning at 7 a.m. for his truck.

Idlebrook, 49, a freelance editor and writer, said he understands that mistakes happen, especially at this time of year, when U-Haul trucks and vans are at peak demand from parents packing their children off to college.

What he objects to is U-Haul providing no help once it realized it had stranded him and for taking little responsibility for its mistake after the fact, he said.

U-Haul has a policy of refunding customers $50 when their vehicle isn’t ready at their scheduled pick-up time. And, in fact, U-Haul did refund him $50 of the $285 he was charged for the 110-mile, one-way trip to Amherst.

But Idlebrook wants the full amount refunded. And he thinks U-Haul should take more responsibility, beyond what it said in an email: “We apologize for the inconvenience.”

Idlebrook told me he made several fruitless attempts to discuss with U-Haul how it planned to “fix this issue so someone doesn’t end up in a similar situation.”

The resolution: I contacted U-Haul on Idlebrook’s behalf. I pointed out Mass. Ave. wasn’t his first choice. He originally arranged to pick up his truck at the U-Haul location in West Roxbury, far from Mass. and Cass. But U-Haul later called him to say no truck was available there, but one would be available at the Mass. Ave. location for pickup at 6 a.m.

U-Haul responded to me by acknowledging its mistake: “Unfortunately, our team did not have the truck ready by 6 a.m. … That was our fault, and it resulted in the customer having a 7 a.m. departure.”

But this wasn’t a case of U-Haul not having a truck ready because of a late return by another customer or a mechanical breakdown. This was a U-Haul representative giving Idlebrook erroneous information.

In a follow-up email, after I asked U-Haul to clarify the cause of the delay, it acknowledged it gave Idlebrook wrong information — and promised to do better.

“Our reservation system should not have allowed a 6 a.m. pick-up to be scheduled” at Mass. Ave., U-Haul said. “That was our oversight. Our system has been updated to ensure no other … reservations during non-business hours can be made at our Mass Ave center."

Asked why the Mass. Ave. location didn’t allow 24-hour self-service, U-Haul said it was a decision left to “each local team.”

In its communications, U-Haul seemed to imply that Idlebrook’s complaint was primarily about a one-hour delay. It wasn’t. It was about being stranded.

U-Haul also said customers with concerns about the location where they are picking up their vehicle should tell U-Haul beforehand. That’s good advice. But this wasn’t the issue either. Idlebrook knew the neighborhood he was going to. He intended to zip in and zip out. The problem was U-Haul made it impossible for him to do so.

The takeaway: What happened to Idlebrook wasn’t especially egregious. Some may say, “Get over it.” But Idlebrook came to me to demand accountability. I believe he was motivated by a concern for others who might be thrust into similar circumstances.

I think he should be proud that his persistence yielded a pledge from a major corporation to do better.

title: Boston City Council to hold public hearing Thursday over Mass. and Cass safety issues
text:
“Open substance use in any part of Boston is illegal and unacceptable,” the memo said. “As we have built up a coordinated citywide response to shut down encampments, decrease overdose mortality, and continue to strengthen the continuum of care, our focus is now on ending outdoor substance use in Boston and the criminal activity that supports it.”

Last month, District 2 Councilor Ed Flynn filed a resolution to declare the area a public safety emergency after frustration grew in the abutting South End neighborhood over continuing open drug use and homeless people occupying their steps.

“It’s long overdue for the Boston City Council to have this conversation,” Flynn told his colleagues last month. “If this is not a public health crisis, I don’t know what it is.”

District 8 Councilor Sharon Durkan scuttled Flynn’s resolution, saying she did not believe the resolution represented “the right steps forward,” the Globe reported.

“For starters, what funding would an emergency declaration provide? None,” Durkan said at a council meeting last month.

Flynn’s resolution was sent to committee, often where resolutions go to die. In this case, however, the chair of the council’s public health committee, District 3 Councilor John FitzGerald, who represents part of the South End, promised a hearing.

According to the memo, the Boston Police Department has conducted 467 drug-related arrests so far this year in the South End, Roxbury, and other impacted neighborhoods, an 85% increase from 2024.

Efforts to tamp down drug activity in the area are being supported by the addition of nearly 100 new officers, new bicycle patrols, enhanced street lighting, frequent street cleaning, and the installation of portable cameras for real-time monitoring in high-impact areas, the memo said.

The city’s Coordinated Response Team reported that in the last six months it has, on average, transitioned 55 people per week to treatment or recovery services, or transported them back to their “place of origin” to reunite with relatives.

The Boston Public Health Commission reported that outreach teams are ending outdoor syringe distributions, increasing collection of discarded needles, and referring users to indoor locations and day spaces. The commission also is decentralizing treatment and recovery services away from the Mass and Cass vicinity, the memo said.

In the last six months, the commission has transported 785 people to treatment services, made 1,185 treatment referrals, and reconnected 76 people with family and friends, the memo said.

The area surrounding Mass and Cass has long been the epicenter of the intertwining crises of homelessness and substance abuse in the city.

More than a dozen South End residents previously told the Globe that they regularly see discarded needles and drug paraphernalia on their streets, as well as people openly injecting, smoking, and exchanging substances.

Flynn echoed their concerns in his resolution, which, if passed by the council, is purely symbolic.

“As well-intentioned as some of the City’s efforts have been, it is wholly appropriate to finally acknowledge that the City of Boston’s current plan at Mass and Cass has been an abject failure by any standard,” Flynn wrote.

“Any reasonable person who visits the area will say unequivocally that what has taken place there on a daily basis for over a decade now — an open air drug market and dealing, public drug use, the trafficking of women, acts of serious violence, public defecation and urination, among others — is completely unacceptable,” he continued.

Flynn called for law enforcement to make arrests and have “zero tolerance” for public drug use and dealing. He also pushed for the city to prioritize creating a new treatment facility where people struggling with addiction can receive services.

Residents and business groups have told Boston city councilors that drug use and other illegal activity spread into their neighborhoods after Mayor Michelle Wu in late 2023 instituted a camping ban in the city, which resulted in the dismantlement of a large crime-ridden encampment around Mass and Cass.

Wu has acknowledged residents’ concerns about the persistent issues around Mass. and Cass and in the South End, and said the city has more work to do to address those challenges. She has also highlighted the city’s efforts to respond to the problems, including more police patrols, city outreach workers who connect people struggling with addiction to services, and the Boston Public Health Commission’s needle pickup crew.

Globe staff reporter Niki Griswold contributed to this report.

title: Boston City Council candidate faces complaints after first days of early voting in crowded District 7 race
text:
Ahmed was “harassing any Somali voters who was [sic] not voting for” him according to Jabril’s report, which was obtained by the Globe. He was also allegedly acting as a translator for Somali voters. Eventually, election officials removed him from the voting location, Jibril said.

Jibril filed another police report on Sunday after Ahmed was allegedly warning people at a Dunkin’ Donuts and outside the Islamic Society of Boston Cultural Center to stay away from Jibril, claiming that she worked for the FBI (Jibril received a community leadership award from the FBI in 2019, but has never worked for the federal government).

On Sunday, the police officer recommended Jibril seek a harassment prevention order.

Jibril, who ran for city council herself in 2021, said the harassment has been going on since January 2017, and has involved Ahmed spreading rumors about her sexuality, posting defamatory comments on Facebook (and later deleting them), and telling other members of the Somali community that she is “not a good Muslim.”

Jibril said she is not involved in the District 7 race.

“He’s going too far,” Jibril told the Globe in an interview. “I want my peace of mind. I don’t have time for harassment.”

Ahmed, a Roxbury track coach who ran a failed campaign for the State House in 2024, said he first heard of the police reports from a Globe reporter.

“That is her right [to file a police report], and she can exercise that,” he said. “It’s a he-said, she-said.”

Ahmed is one of eleven candidates vying for the District 7 seat on the Boston City Council to replace disgraced former councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson.

A campaign manager for another District 7 candidate, Said Abdikarim, made similar complaints to the Secretary of State, who oversees elections.

In an email Tuesday, consultant Anthony Morse wrote that Ahmed’s campaign failed to keep the proper distance from the Shelburne Community Center voting location. He also alleged that the translators hired by the city were related to Ahmed, that the Abdikarim campaign had “concerns about what [Ahmed’s campaign] are saying to voters at the polls,” and that Ahmed was “texting people filled in ballots on how to vote.”

Abdikarim told the Globe he stopped by the voting location twice, and both times observed law enforcement and Boston Election Commissioner Eneida Tavares telling the Said campaign to back away from voters and stand across the street from the polling location.

State law prohibits all campaign-related activities within 150 feet of a polling place or early voting site during voting hours.

A spokesperson for the Boston Elections Commission did not immediatly respond to requests for comment.

Abdikarim said “if you were there, you would have thought we are not in the US, the way this gentleman and these people were acting.”

“You cannot intimidate and bully your way to convince someone to vote for you,” he said. “That is not how democracy works.”

title: Meet the four candidates vying for Boston mayor
text:
You can check early voting locations here, and check your Election Day polling place here.

Age: 80

Neighborhood: East Boston

Key Issues: Ending the Boston Trust Act, closing methadone clinics, no affordable housing or other benefits for undocumented immigrants

Favorite place in Boston: The Dunkin’ Donuts on One Harbor St. in the Seaport

Favorite Boston food: Legal Seafoods

Robert Cappucci, 80, is a perennial political candidate and lifelong resident of East Boston. He’s run for office at least 13 times, between many unsuccessful bids for Boston mayor, Boston City Council, the Massachusetts House, and Congress. Cappucci successfully won election to the Boston School Committee in 1987, and was reelected to the position in 1989. His time in the post was cut short when then-Mayor Ray Flynn moved to transition the city’s elected school committee to a body with only mayoral appointees in 1991. He has not held elected office since.

Cappucci was born in a Cambridge hospital and raised in East Boston in a family comprising his parents and five children, he told the Globe. Cappucci’s father, Enrico Cappucci, represented East Boston in the Massachusetts House from 1937 to 1948. He graduated from Boston State College, which was absorbed into UMass Boston, with a degree in political science in 1968. He then enlisted in the Navy, served on active duty for two years, and was in the reserves for several more years, according to the National Personnel Records Center.

Cappucci spent roughly 10 years employed with the East Boston Community Development Corporation, working on housing and development issues, he said. He also worked as a Boston police officer for 13 years. In that time he earned a master’s degree in criminal justice from Anna Maria College. Cappucci retired in 2010 from the force, after a lifetime of being a “workaholic,” he told the Globe.

Cappucci is running as a Democrat, and said he is more concerned with economic and job issues over social issues. But Cappucci espouses conservative positions on many topics that he said are key priorities for him. He emphasized that as mayor he would end all so-called sanctuary city policies — a politicized term that immigration critics, most often on the right, frequently use to refer to municipalities that limit local officials’ cooperation with federal immigration enforcement efforts. He opposes Boston’s local ordinance known as the Trust Act, which only allows local officials to comply with federal immigration authorities’ requests to detain people for possible deportation if the person is also wanted for a serious crime.

He told the Globe he would move to close all methadone clinics, where people struggling with opioid addiction receive treatment and assistance reducing withdrawal symptoms. He also opposes Mayor Michelle Wu’s project to redevelop Franklin Park’s White Stadium for Boston Public Schools students in partnership with a professional women’s soccer team. He said he would move to ensure that no undocumented immigrants are able to access affordable housing programs or other social benefits, and would not allow any new homeless shelters in the city.

“I have a platform that I think reflects the voters, and so the voters will decide, you know, do they want to keep the status quo,” Cappucci told the Globe. “I believe there are people out there, hopefully the majority, will give me an opportunity.”

He emphasized that he supports “law and order,” “peace through justice,” and assistance for veterans, seniors, and people with disabilities. Cappucci describes himself as a “lifelong bachelor” and practicing Catholic. He lives alone.

Age: 48

Neighborhood: Hyde Park

Key Issues: Boston Public Schools, public safety, and the economy/displacement

Favorite place in Boston: On the field at Clifford Park, coaching football

Favorite Boston food: Clam chowder

Whether it’s gun violence in the city’s Cape Verdean community or needles strewn on athletic fields located near Mass. and Cass, Domingos DaRosa is known for his outspokenness — a reputation earned by not pulling punches when it comes to criticizing the city’s powers-that-be, including the mayor’s City Hall administration and Boston police.

The 48-year-old Hyde Park community activist has made his name in city political circles as a thorn-in-the-side of those in power. Now, for the fourth time, he is seeking public office.

His previous three attempts — all campaigns for an at-large City Council post — were unsuccessful. This time around, he’s running for the top job in municipal government: the mayoralty.

And while City Hall observers characterize his current campaign as a long-shot bid for the fifth-floor City Hall corner office, DaRosa projects optimism.

“Folks are tired of the same old politics,” he said.

His candidacy, he said, stands in contrast with those of front-runners Michelle Wu, the incumbent, and Josh Kraft, a nonprofit leader who has publicly jousted with the mayor for months. He gives voters another option: a product of Boston Public Schools, a renter, and someone who has been a victim of the city’s gun violence.

“I’m a survivor of Boston,” he told the Globe recently over the phone.

DaRosa said humanity is missing from city politics. People don’t treat each other well and the city is being sold to “the highest bidder,” he said.

“We talk a good game, but we don’t deliver,” he said.

For too many Bostonians, the city is becoming unlivable, thanks to the rampaging housing and cost-of-living crises, he said.

Failure to fix quality-of-life problems, such as mold, at public housing units over the years, has led to systemic and pricey overhauls of such developments, he said. Government should do a better job when it comes to maintaining such properties, he said.

DaRosa said the city should simply be building more public housing. He said he would favor capping rental increases year-to-year.

“We’ve lost so many of our neighbors because of the policies that are coming out of this administration,” said DaRosa. “We can’t continue to allow those families to be displaced because of those policies. It’s not an equitable city for all communities.”

Central to his campaign is the notion that Boston is simply not working for too many people.

Boston Public Schools, he said, is a failing system. Too many students in the district won’t be able to get into prestigious local colleges because their schooling is lacking, he said.

He said he understands the plight of immigrants because he is one. He was 10 months old when he came to the US from Cape Verde. At the time, he said, he was undocumented. It’s important for the city to educate immigrants on their rights and what the law entails, including what is and is not covered under a city ordinance that spells out how and when police officers should interact with federal immigration authorities.

Regarding White Stadium, he is against the city’s current plan, saying the structure should have never been demolished. He said he favors the plan put forward by the Franklin Park Defenders. The $64 million alternative proposal calls for a roughly 5,000-seat facility, compared to the 11,000-seat stadium of the current project. It would have fewer amenities — such as no professional-grade media and medical rooms or a beer garden.

Public safety is another major issued for DaRosa, who works in property maintenance. DaRosa has experienced street violence firsthand: a bullet grazed his leg outside his mother’s house in Dorchester in 2018. Two other men, including DaRosa’s brother, were shot in the incident.

While homicides are at historically low levels in the city, DaRosa said that even one murder is too many.

Mass. and Cass, the epicenter of the city’s homelessness and opioid epidemics near Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard, also continues to be top of mind for DaRosa. In recent years, DaRosa has objected to the preponderance of dirty needles at Roxbury’s Clifford Park, located down the street from Mass. and Cass.

The conditions were so bad at one point Boston Bengals Pop Warner football program, which used the field for practice, merged with another team so that they could move their practice location.

Open drug-dealing and use on the streets of Boston, as well as quality of life issues on Mass. and Cass including public lewd acts, continue to be a problem, he said.

Additionally, not enough city jobs are going toward city residents, said DaRosa. He noted the income gap between Black and white households locally remains stubbornly large. And while the city has laws on the books requiring construction sites to meet certain diversity and residency quotas, projects have historically failed to meet such standards, he said.

Age: 58

Neighborhood: North End

Key issues: Housing, schools, Mass. and Cass

Favorite place in Boston: Rose Kennedy Greenway, particularly where the mural is, near South Station

Favorite Boston food: Pino’s Pizza in Brighton, because the college kids in the area breathe so much culture into our city

Josh Kraft is best known for two things: his decades as a nonprofit leader in the city, and his privileged background as the third son of billionaire Patriots owner Robert Kraft. Josh Kraft has never had an operational role in the family business, though he did for years lead the family’s philanthropic efforts as head of the New England Patriots Foundation. A graduate of Williams College and the Harvard Graduate School of Education, Kraft worked for more than three decades at the Boys and Girls Club of Boston, including 12 years as its leader. His interest in nonprofit work started young; loved ones say he followed closely in the footsteps of his mother, Myra Kraft, who was beloved for her philanthropy work.

Kraft, 58, grew up in the nearby suburbs in Chestnut Hill and has lived most of his life just outside city limits. He moved in October 2023 to Boston, where he now lives on the waterfront in the North End with his partner, Michelle Perez Vichot. He has two grown daughters from a past marriage.

Kraft is a political newcomer; this is his first run for office. He’s involved himself in past races, however, as a political donor to Democrats — including Michelle Wu in 2021 — as well as Republicans, donations that his staff said were motivated by his support for Israel. Kraft is registered as a Democrat, though over the years he has voted in some GOP primaries.

As a candidate, Kraft has fought to define himself as his own person, distinguishing himself from his father, who has at times been a close friend and supporter of President Trump. The younger Kraft says he has never supported or voted for Trump and believes the president is unfit for office. Still, Kraft has benefited from his wealthy background and his family’s connections; he has put millions of dollars into his own campaign and received donations from associates of his father’s, including NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell.

Kraft has focused his campaign largely on housing, which polling shows is the top issue for most Boston voters.

“I’m running for mayor because Boston has become the most expensive city in America to raise a family,” Kraft said in a recent ad. “As mayor, I’ll listen — not lecture.”

Kraft says as mayor he would prioritize building more homes; he has blamed some Wu administration policies for blocking or delaying construction. He and Wu are split on a number of policies, including the idea of a real estate transfer tax, which would impose a small fee on high-dollar real estate sales to support housing efforts. Wu supports it, Kraft opposes it. They’re also divided on the issue of rent control, which Wu has championed as a signature issue for years. Kraft has proposed an alternate, opt-in form of the policy that would offer landlords tax breaks if they agree to cap annual rent increases. Wu has rejected that plan as “fake rent control.”

One of the candidates’ sharpest divides is over White Stadium, a decades-old facility that Wu is rebuilding into a home for BPS athletes as well as a professional women’s soccer team. Kraft argues the city should not be pouring tens of millions of taxpayer dollars into a project that will also benefit private interests. He has called Wu’s handling of the renovation a “catastrophic failure,” particularly because the mayor has not shared a recent cost estimate for the pricey project.

On immigration, Kraft, like Wu, supports the Boston Trust Act. Kraft has also called for the city to provide more support for individuals returning from incarceration. On transportation, Kraft has said he would immediately pause the construction of city bike lanes, and called for an audit of existing ones. His plan for Boston Public Schools would add more seats in coveted exam schools, change the district’s leadership structure, and transition from a fully appointed School Committee to a partially elected body.

Age: 40

Neighborhood: Roslindale

Key Issues: Community safety, housing affordability, education and youth opportunities

Favorite place in Boston: Franklin Park

Favorite Boston food: Roxbury Russet apples

Michelle Wu is the mayor of Boston and a groundbreaking politician in the city’s history, as the first woman, person of color, and mother to be elected to City Hall’s top job. Wu has served as the city’s chief executive since she won the open mayoral race in 2021, after then-Mayor Martin J. Walsh left the role to serve as former president Joe Biden’s secretary of labor.

Wu, 40, was born in Chicago to Taiwanese immigrant parents, and is the oldest of four children. She attended Harvard College and worked as a consultant before moving back to Illinois to care for her two young sisters and her mother, who was struggling with mental illness. Wu often credits her experience opening and running a tea shop in Chicago — specifically, having to navigate the cumbersome city permitting process — as her inspiration for getting involved in local government. Wu later moved back to Boston with her mother and youngest sister to attend Harvard Law School, where she met her longtime mentor, US Senator Elizabeth Warren.

She worked in then-Mayor Thomas M. Menino’s administration, then on Warren’s first Senate campaign in 2012, before winning election to the Boston City Council as an at-large member in 2013. During her eight years on the council, she earned a reputation as an effective, policy-oriented workhorse and spearheaded several notable policy changes, including implementing a parental leave policy for municipal employees, and regulations on short term rentals such as Airbnbs.

As a first-time mayoral candidate in 2021, Wu ran an unapologetically progressive campaign, championing rent control, free public transit, and a municipal “Green New Deal,” among other issues. Now that she’s an incumbent running for a second term, some say she has evolved, focusing on a more pragmatic version of her earlier vision. Whereas she once supported reducing funding for BPD, Wu this year accepted the endorsement of the city’s largest police union, and touts the city’s low violent crime rates as one of her top accomplishments from her first four years as mayor.

In making her case for reelection, Wu also points to her expansion of pre-K and child-care seats, guaranteeing paid summer jobs for Boston Public Schools students, and efforts to increase the city’s affordable housing stock and promote home ownership opportunities for low-income families. Wu often says her goal is to “make Boston a home for everyone,” emphasizing her personal stake in the city’s future as a Boston Public Schools parent. Wu lives in Roslindale with her husband, Conor Pewarski, their three children — 10-year-old Blaise, 8-year-old Cass, and 7-month-old Mira — and Wu’s mother.

She’s also faced criticism and controversy over her administration’s implementation of bike lanes across the city, and her plan to redevelop Franklin Park’s White Stadium for Boston Public Schools students in partnership with a new professional women’s soccer team.

In recent months, she’s gained national attention over her fierce defense of the city’s diverse communities and immigrant-friendly public safety policies in the face of the Trump administration’s mass deportation efforts. From Capitol Hill, to City Hall plaza, and the set of “The Daily Show,” Wu has defied pressure and threats from the Trump administration to roll back the city’s ordinance that limit local officials’ cooperation with federal immigration enforcement efforts.

The resulting spotlight has earned her a reputation of being an example of successful Democratic leadership in the resistance to Trump’s White House.

“At a time when this federal administration is already causing so much fear and harm in our communities, these threats are serious and consequential, but our same communities have told me loud and clear that silence in the face of oppression is not an option,” Wu proclaimed at an August press conference.

“The Trump administration seeks to divide, isolate, and intimidate cities and make Americans fearful of one another,” she continued. “But Boston is proof of something far more powerful than lies and intimidation; that safety and community come from loving your neighbor as yourself.”

title: State’s second human case of West Nile virus in 2025 reported in woman in Essex County, officials say.
text:
Two more people are confirmed to have West Nile virus in Massachusetts, bringing the total number of cases to four, state public health officials announced Friday.

A man in his 40s, who was exposed in Hampden County, and a man in his 80s, who was exposed in Middlesex County, are the latest in humans cases to be announced by the state Department of Public Health.

Risk levels for the virus have been elevated to high in Ashland, Framingham, Marlborough, Natick, Sherborn, Southborough, Sudbury, and Wayland

“Given how many mosquitoes have been found carrying West Nile virus this summer, we expected that there would be human infections this year,” the state’s public health commissioner, Robbie Goldstein, said in a press release.

News of the cases in Hampden and Middlesex counties came days after the other two human cases were confirmed.

State health officials announced Wednesday that a woman in her 60s, who was exposed in Essex County, has tested positive for the virus.

The first woman who tested positive for the virus is in her 70s and was exposed in Middlesex County, officials said.

Mosquitoes, which carry the virus and spread it to humans and animals through their bites, started returning positive test samples in Massachusetts on June 17.

About a month later, a goat in Lunenburg became the first animal to test positive for the virus this year in Massachusetts.

In August, the risk of exposure to the West Nile virus in Boston was elevated to “high,” after multiple samples of mosquitoes in the city, including in Hyde Park and West Roxbury, came back positive.

“West Nile virus can be a very serious disease, and its presence in mosquitoes remains high right now in Massachusetts,” the state’s public health commissioner, Goldstein, said in a press release.

Even though the weather is cooling down, the prevalence of West Nile virus among mosquitoes “is going to be elevated for some time,” Goldstein said.

There have been more than 300 positive tests from mosquitoes across 12 of the state’s 14 counties, officials said.

In the past month, the risk of contracting West Nile virus has been elevated in Acton, Bedford, Billerica, Boston, Brookline, Carlisle, Chelmsford, Dracut, Lowell, and Newton, according to the DPH.

In 2024, there were 19 human cases of the virus reported in the state, according to the department’s dashboard.

Residents can reduce their risk of exposure by applying mosquito repellent with an EPA-registered ingredient, such as DEET or oil of lemon eucalyptus, officials said.

Other precautionary steps include avoiding spending time outdoors during the early morning and evening, and wearing long sleeves and pants to protect against bites.

“The hours from dusk to dawn are peak biting times for many mosquitoes,” health officials said.

“The mosquitoes will be with us until the first hard frost,” state epidemiologist Catherine M. Brown added in the release.

The Skippers boast a balanced veteran lineup after graduating just three seniors on both sides of the ball. Senior quarterback Michael Wildfire returns as a three-year starter, with seniors Max Monahan and Nolan Flaherty back as his favorite targets in the passing game. Senior Gus Greene will anchor the ground game behind an O-line that is led by seniors Dan Baker (6-6, 230), JT MacDonald (6-3, 230) and Ian Kondrat (6-0, 185). “They have high expectations,” said 20th-year coach Pete Afanasiw. “They want to start by trying to win the league and get back to the final four if possible. Our biggest concern is staying healthy because we don’t have a lot of depth.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 7 p.m., at Norwell

Playoff alignment: Division 7

League: Boston City

Coach: John Parziale (16th season). Career: 81-72.

Last year’s record: 2-8

Strengths: Three-year starting quarterback

Concerns: Four new starters on O-line

Offense: Wing T

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: The Jets will feature new faces at key positions on both sides of the ball as they look to rebuild after graduating 11 seniors. The departure of leading rushers Chris Testa and Steven Chiappa presents the biggest hole to fill, though the cupboard isn’t bare with junior quarterback Caden Pelosi returning for his third season as the starting quarterback. Juniors Luigi Acone and Brian Munoz will spearhead the rushing attack behind an offensive line that lost four starters and returns junior Jason Taft (6-1, 220). “We’re going to try to throw the football a little more than we normally have on offense,” said coach John Parziale, entering his 16th season. “We lost a lot of seniors and our numbers are very low, but we have a strong junior class we are hoping will take a big leap this year.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 6 p.m., vs. Latin Academy

Playoff alignment: Division 7

League: Cape Ann

Coach: Mike Flynn (1st season). Career: 37-8-2 in five seasons at Pingree.

Last year’s record: 3-8

Strengths: Size and strength on O-line

Concerns: Getting acclimated to new systems

Offense: Spread

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: The Generals have a new leader with Super Bowl experience. Former Baltimore Ravens Super Bowl champion and 11-year NFL veteran Mike Flynn takes over at Hamilton-Wenham after previously serving as an assistant at Masconomet. Flynn led the Pingree to three first-place finishes in the Evergreen Division of the NEPSAC while serving as head coach from 2018-23. Hamilton-Wenham is undergoing big changes under the former pro, most notably a switch from the Wing-T to a spread offense. Flynn is turning to his upperclassmen to help set the culture, as he’ll rely on seniors Caden Schrock (RB/LB), Luke Molitano (WR/DB), Griffin Hawkins (TE/DE), and Robbie Bozarjian (OL/DL, 6-2, 265) to help turn the tides. Junior OL/DL Harrison Esker (6-0, 225) will also be an anchor on the line for the Generals, who are set to debut a new turf field after playing all of their games on the road last fall. “It’s been a big transition,” Flynn said. “We’ll be a lot better in Weeks 4 and 5 than we are now.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 6:30 p.m., vs. Triton

Playoff alignment: Division 7

League: Cape Ann

Coach: Zack Lamkin (5th season). Career: 9-35.

Last year’s record: 3-8

Strengths: Experienced offensive line

Concerns: Consistency and staying healthy

Offense: Wing T

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Following three rebuilding years, Ipswich finally feels ready for a breakout season. The Tigers have taken their lumps in recent years as underclassmen were thrown into the fire, but fifth-year coach Zack Lamkin is confident his squad can contend with a veteran group. “I have six kids that are in their fourth year starting varsity football,” said Lamkin. “That’s unheard of.” Three-year starting QB Vin Winter returns for his senior season behind a veteran offensive line that includes seniors Luke Wile (5-11, 215), Hank Latorella (6-2, 260) and Brady Merry (6-3, 230) and juniors Kervin Domingo (5-10, 215) and Jake Stevens (5-11, 225). Senior tailback James Dick and senior fullback Pace Capone anchor a backfield that will also feature junior Cullen Courville and sophomore Ethan Bolesky, while senior tight end/linebacker Will Gromko will be a playmaker on both sides of the ball. “I think we can be a ferocious team,” Lamkin said.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 6 p.m., vs. Chelsea

Playoff alignment: Division 7

League: Boston City

Coach: Rocco Zizza (18th season). Career: 105-73.

Last year’s record: 7-4

Strengths: Talent at skilled positions

Concerns: Depth on the line

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: Dynamic dual-threat quarterback Jack Shapiro, a senior, will bring a steady presence to the huddle during his fifth and final season with the program. Shapiro will be flanked by plenty of talent in the backfield as seniors Micah Nichol (RB/LB), Toan Chau (RB/WR) and Zach Berneus (FB/LB) return from a season highlighted by a 20-14 victory over Thanksgiving rival O’Bryant. Senior Milan Kambampati (6-4, 215) will be a favorite target for Shapiro in the passing game, in addition to anchoring the front seven at defensive end, while senior Timothy Lewis (6-5, 225) sets the tone up front at tackle and defensive end. “We have a tremendous amount of depth at skill positions, but we lack depth with the guys inside,” said longtime coach Rocco Zizza. “We have good numbers and good talent, we just need some more experience.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 6 p.m., at East Boston

Playoff alignment: Division 7

League: Commonwealth

Coach: Zack Swale (1st season). Career: 0-0.

Last year’s record: 4-7

Strengths: Experience and talent at skill positions

Concerns: Offensive line chemistry

Offense: Wing T

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Although the Crusaders are under new leadership with first-year coach Zack Swale, the culture will be familiar to the returning players. Swale, who works as Lowell Catholic’s Director of Operations, wants to maintain the same mind-set the team employed while he served as an assistant under coach Joe Cavanaugh, now at Wilmington, the past two seasons. “These kids have had three different head coaches in the last four years so we want to try to keep some similarities,” said Swale. The Crusaders boast a deep junior class that gained varsity experience last year, including senior QB Shawn Hines and senior Divine Burroughs (RB/DE). Junior Jimmy McGonigle is expected to shine at WR/RB and seniors Kamron Luciano (5-11, 210), Gabe Cuartas (5-10, 220), Isaac Clark (6-0, 200), and Yuniel Nieves-You (5-8, 260) provide veteran leadership on the offensive line. Notre Dame Academy joins Community Charter School of Lowell as a part of Lowell Cathoic’s co-op.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 12, 6 p.m., at Chelsea

Playoff alignment: Division 7

League: Cape Ann

Coach: Joe Grimes (5th season). Career: 27-16.

Last year’s record: 7-4

Strengths: Veteran offensive line

Concerns: New faces on defense

Offense: Wing T

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Led by a deep group of veterans with varsity experience, the Hornets had the luxury of running preseason camp with limited questions to answer. Senior Zach Hurd returns at quarterback after demonstrating his dual-threat abilities as a junior, while senior wideouts Charlie Thurlow and Felix Wood are familiar faces in the passing game. Hurd will be protected by a seasoned group up front, with senior Tony Brown (6-0, 235) and Walker Valeo (6-2, 220) setting the tone for an O-line with ample chemistry. “Some of that [O-line] group has been together now for three years, but most of them were at least together last year,” fifth-year coach Joe Grimes said. “They have seen a lot together and have a good understanding of making calls, which has helped camp go a little easier.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 6:30 p.m., vs. West Bridgewater

Playoff alignment: Division 7

League: South Shore

Coach: Matt Triveri (21st season). Career: 168-56.

Last year’s record: 9-4

Strengths: Big, physical linemen

Concerns: Depth and inexperience

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: The Falcons look to rebuild on the fly after graduating 22 seniors from the team that suffered a 42-20 loss to Uxbridge in the Super Bowl. “We lost a ton,” said longtime coach Matt Triveri. “I think we dressed 25 kids for our first scrimmage, so it’s not a great situation.” Senior Daniel Alade takes over as the starting tailback and will look to lead the offense behind classmate Brenden Andrade (FB/LB). Triveri is optimistic that the Falcons have enough size and strength to boast a formidable offensive line, with seniors James Serafini (6-0, 215) and Shea Taylor (5-11, 280), and juniors CJ Jennings (6-0, 310) and Coti Wieden (6-0, 250) anchoring the unit. “We do have some guys returning up front that know what they are doing and we have size for this level, but they are still young,” Triveri said.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 6:30 p.m., vs. Dennis-Yarmouth

Playoff alignment: Division 7

League: Boston City

Coach: Kevin Gadson (18th season). Career: 101-70.

Last year’s record: 4-6

Strengths: Experienced wide receivers

Concerns: New quarterback and linemen

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Longtime coach Kevin Gadson is looking to reestablish a winning culture after the Tigers graduated most of their starters from last year’s team, which took a step back after winning the Boston City League in 2023. Sophomore quarterback Atticus Bent takes over the quarterback reins, replacing graduated Keyshon Wright. The underclassman will count on seniors Gementri Williams (WR/LB) and Malaki Powell (WR/CB) to ease his transition as the team’s top targets behind an entirely new offensive line. Gadson expects some growing pains for the Tigers, but he’s hopeful a youth movement will set the foundation for years to come. “We are very, very young,” he said. “We have a lot of young kids coming up from JV and middle school that have got to work harder to learn how to compete at the varsity level.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 12, 4 p.m., vs. Roxbury Prep/Boston Prep/Neighborhood House Charter

Playoff alignment: Division 7

League: South Shore

Coach: Nick Liquori (9th season). Career: 56-29.

Last year’s record: 1-10

Strengths: Passing game cohesion

Concerns: Lack of depth

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: Despite winning just one game during an injury-plagued 2024 campaign, Rockland enters this fall with optimism after graduating just six seniors. Ninth-year coach Nick Liquori said the Bulldogs hit the ground running to begin preseason camp returning starters at key positions. Senior quarterback Hayden Hatch provides a veteran presence behind center after gaining valuable experience as a junior, while junior JoMo Bayer (WR/DB) and sophomore Patrick McDonagh (WR) return to the passing game after getting their feet wet last season. Junior Marvelous Pleasant will anchor the ground game behind a young offensive line led by senior Brody Nicholson (6-1, 195). “We’re still fairly young but they’ve done a really good job melding together,” Liquori said. “All summer we had about 75 percent participation in the weight room, passing league and some of the smaller camps we’ve done, so we’ve been happy with the work they are putting in.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 12, 6 p.m., at Dennis-Yarmouth

Playoff alignment: Division 7

League: South Coast

Coach: Matt Brown (1st season). Career: 0-0.

Last year’s record: 6-5

Strengths: Talent at skill positions

Concerns: Depth on the line and at linebacker

Offense: Spread

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: After serving as an assistant at Seekonk the past 16 seasons, Matt Brown will make his head coaching debut for the Warriors after taking over for Jason Azulay. Brown inherits a strong core of experienced seniors, including QB Nico Bonafiglia, who has moved from wide receiver. Bonafiglia will rely on 6-foot-2-inch senior WR Evan Menard as a big target in the passing game, while fellow seniors Austin Motta (WR/CB) and Ben Figueiredo (RB/LB) also bring experience to Seekonk’s skill positions. Up front, seniors Sam Figueiredo (5-8, 180), Jack Bryce (5-11, 200), and Eddie Formigoni (5-10, 215) will anchor a veteran offensive line. Although Brown is the new voice leading the Warriors, he’s hopeful to build on the foundation Azulay set the past four seasons. “My motto is it’s more of the same,” said Brown. “It’s a different guy on the sideline calling plays and calling timeouts, but the culture stays the same.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 6:30 p.m., vs. Warwick (R.I.)

Playoff alignment: Division 7

League: Mayflower

Coach: Matt Doyle (7th season). Career: 34-29.

Last year’s record: 4-7

Strengths: Veteran edge rushers

Concerns: Young linemen, running backs

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: With a pair of senior defensive ends -- Beah Johnson (6-1, 190) and Gavin Meinhold (6-1, 185) -- anchoring the front seven, the Vikings are determined to wreak havoc on opposing quarterbacks this fall. Johnson and Meinhold will be fixtures for South Shore Tech’s defense in front of senior middle linebacker John O’Connor, who returns to the heart of the defense after a knee injury ended his junior season early. O’Connor has switched from the offensive line to fullback and will pave the way for sophomore tailback Dillon O’Brien, the team’s leading returning rusher. Senior QB Tyler Holmes will lead an inexperienced offense with plenty of youth on the line and in the backfield. “We lost some really good seniors, but I’ve been really impressed with the leadership we’ve had and the way the kids have stepped into their roles,” said seventh-year coach Matt Doyle.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 12, 7 p.m., vs. Hull

Playoff alignment: Division 7

League: South Coast

Coach: Justin Kogler (7th season). Career: 99-40 overall, including 45-16 at West Bridgewater.

Last year’s record: 5-5

Strengths: Veteran experience and leadership

Concerns: Consistency on defense

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: With just two graduated starters from a year ago, cohesiveness and experience are two of the Wildcats’ biggest strengths. West Bridgewater oozes veteran talent throughout its offense, led by senior QB Ryan Nunes and senior tailback Ty Holmes, who rushed for more than 1,300 yards in both his sophomore and junior seasons. Nunes will be throwing to familiar targets in senior wideouts Colin O’Neil and Sam Popotte as well as junior Kevin Kearton, while senior Thomas Polidori (FB/LB) adds veteran leadership on both sides of the ball. The O-line is also experienced, with seniors Ben Dowdall (5-11, 185), Patrick Stanton (5-10, 280) and Christian Sanchez (5-10, 310) partnering with juniors Cole Seckinger (5-10, 205) and Ben Kneeland (5-10, 210). “We look to be better, hopefully, this year than we were last year,” said seventh-year coach Justin Kogler. “A lot of these guys have been starting for me for the past three years, so we should be pretty senior-laden and experienced.”

League: Mayflower

Coach: Kazeem Adediran (4th season). Career: 11-18.

Last year’s record: 4-6

Strengths: Experienced group and strong developmental coaching

Concerns: Losing stars to surrounding schools

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Fourth-year coach Kazeem Adediran’s “Triple H” — not to be confused with the famous wrestler — and “Triple F” mantras have the Tritons motivated for a huge season. On defense, senior Dasan Rooks and linebacker Jacob “JJ” Aponte have bought into the “hunt, hit, hurt” mentality, looking to follow up their stellar 2024 seasons. On offense, where they abide by the “Triple F” (fast, focused, finish) mantra, the Tritons will be led by sophomore quarterback Kaleb Pacheco who replaces Anthony LeRoux after he transferred to Diman. The Tritons will also be without Marvins Antoine who transferred to Durfee after totalling 803 yards and eight TDs last year. “We are an amazing development program that teach kids the game of football ... I can’t let things out of my control, control me,” Adediran said. In addition, Atlantis enjoys an experienced wide receiver corp with seniors Collyn Viveiros and Nathaniel Benevides. Sophomore Seraun Pitt could get some work at running back and Matheus DeSouza could see tight end snaps. “We’re building something,” Adedrian said. “This is not the old Tritons from years back . . . This team knows I have high expectations.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 6 p.m., at Monomoy/JP II

League: South Coast

Coach: John McIntyre (16th season). Career: 70-100.

Last year’s record: 7-4

Strengths: An experienced group with 14 seniors

Concerns: Lack of offensive line depth

Offense: Double wing

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: Coming off back-to-back seven-win seasons, coach John McIntyre expects to lead his Canalmen back to the playoffs thanks to an experienced squad with 14 returning seniors. The run-heavy scheme with senior running backs Drew Kelley and Ethan Fox following junior 6-foot-5-inch, 230-pound fullback Malachi Coelho between the tackles should be a tough matchup for opposing defenses. Senior linemen Caden Doherty (6-0, 240) and Max Beals will provide interior blocking on offense and stop the run game on defense. “This team has great senior leadership which was shown by a very successful offseason conditioning program,” said McIntyre. Despite a lack of depth up front, the Canalmen have the experience to make a postseason run.

Season opener: Saturday, Sept. 6, 12 p.m., at Upper Cape

League: Boston City

Coach: Randolph Abraham (14th season). Career: 72-59.

Last year’s record: 3-7

Strengths: Disciplined preparation and strong work ethic

Concerns: Young at skill positions

Offense: Double wing

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Since joining the program in 2004 and ascending into the head coaching role in 2012, Randolph Abraham has emphasized enthusiasm, focus, and a strong work ethic as the foundation for team success. The offense will be built around returning senior quarterback Dontay Gillis-Rayne, who also provides help at free safety. Protecting him will be senior tackle Ernesto Rodriguez (6-2, 287) and senior guard Onil Vasquez (6-0, 250) as they look to set up senior running back Edwin Noncent (6-0, 190) who possesses great size and three-down potential. Junior Edward Veras will block out of the backfield and play linebacker. “We’re looking to be competitive in the league this season,” said Abraham. “With a strong core of returning players and a promising group of underclassmen stepping into bigger roles, we’re aiming to continue their development and contend each week.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 7 p.m., at Nashoba Valley Tech

League: Mayflower

Coach: Calvin Castillias (3rd season). Career: 7-14.

Last year’s record: 3-8

Strengths: Athletic, strong, youthful core

Concerns: Lack of experience, depth

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: The Crusaders will have their hands full trying to replace 15 seniors, including quarterback Sean Gillette, lineman Aiden Giacobbi, and 1,000-yard rusher Peyton Morris. Junior quarterback Daniel Handville will be joined by junior running backs Thomas Allen and Chaz Thomas, junior receiver Anthony Bartlett and senior tight end Amani Cole. While the Crusaders likely enter a rebuilding year, they possess an athletic and strong core of upperclassmen, most of whom will see increased playing time.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 6 p.m., at Tri-County

League: None

Coach: Derrick Beasley (8th season). Career: 23-37.

Last year’s record: 5-5

Strengths: Second-year quarterback, talented wide receivers

Concerns: Lack of experience

Offense: Spread

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Following a playoff berth and second-round exit at the hands of Nashoba Valley Tech, coach Derrick Beasley returns for his eighth season. Senior quarterback Xavier Roman should continue to find speedy wide receiver Ta’Qaire Bell often. Senior defensive lineman Theodore Clark (6-3, 230) registered four tackles for loss last season. Senior nose guard and defensive tackle Clarck Charlotin (6-2, 245) stuffs the middle.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 12, 6 p.m., at Greater Lawrence

League: Boston City

Coach: Ryan Conway (10th season). Career: 33-54 at English.

Last year’s record: 3-6

Strengths: Aggressive skill players

Concerns: Lack of depth

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Senior Lovenson Pierre is back behind center, just the second time in the last nine years the Eagles have returned their quarterback. Wide receiver Isaiah Peoples and running back Manuel Carrion-Miranda will be key skill players and Zion Dejesus, Emanuel Santana, and Nick Ambrose are sturdy pass protectors and create holes for the run game. “These kids compete against each other at the same time they’re learning from each other,” said coach Ryan Conway. “The coaching staff is excited to see these competitions, as these kids grow and develop. They get better and better every single day. They work hard and are tough physically and mentally.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 6:30 p.m., vs. Somerville

League: Mayflower

Coach: Fran Cass (2nd season). Career: 49-71, including 37-43 at Holbrook (two stints).

Last year’s record: 0-7

Strengths: Experienced coaching staff

Concerns: Small roster with depth concerns

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Coming off a season in which they scored just 19 points, Holbrook/Avon will need to improve in all aspects of the game. Coach Fran Cass is in his second stint with the Bulldogs and acknowledged that the team is in rebuilding mode. “I most look forward to teaching football to the young men,” he said. “I knew what an extreme challenge the job will be . . . I’d love to see the school have a competitive football team.” In addition to the varsity squad, Cass and the rest of the staff are looking to further develop the program at all stages, starting with a freshman team. “It is a long road back,” said Cass.

Season opener: Saturday, Oct. 4, 11 a.m., at Upper Cape

League: South Shore

Coach: Michael O’Donnell (9th season). Career: 50-38.

Last year’s record: 4-7

Strengths: Experienced linebacker core

Concerns: Lack of size and overall depth

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: The Pirates missed the playoffs last season, but that hasn’t deterred them from a plan to return to the postseason. Junior Regan Bellew will take over at quarterback following the graduation of Luke Dunham. Sophomores Nick Perry (ILB/OG) and Mason Delgallo (DT/OT) will have prominent roles as two-way players. Despite lacking physicality and depth, O’Donnell is determined to “improve on both sides of the ball.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 7 p.m., vs. Wareham

League: CMAC

Coach: Michael Luks (1st season). Career: 0-0.

Last year’s record: 2-8

Strengths: Solid young core

Concerns: Overall depth

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: First-year head coach Mike Luks takes over the Broncos for Mark Grocholski. Luks, who played at Framingham State, was formerly the offensive coordinator at West Boylston, a prolific offense that beat top-seeded Randolph in last season’s D8 Super Bowl. Luks’ main goal “is to help turn the program around by creating a culture of consistency and high expectations that can lead to putting a winning product on the field.” This starts with senior quarterback Joey Secatore and wideout Shaun Kilgallen, who will be at the heart of Luks’ offensive playbook.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 6:30 p.m., at Murdock

League: Commonwealth

Coach: Jim Rabbitt (9th season). Career: 50-31.

Last year’s record: 5-4

Strengths: Experienced dual-threat QB and team speed

Concerns: Lack of offensive line depth

Offense: Spread

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Ahead of his ninth season at the helm of KIPP Academy, Jim Rabbitt noted his squad is going to be hard to handle. The Panthers’ priorities haven’t changed -- they are determined to capture a Commonwealth title after winning it in 2023. A player to watch is 6-foot-5-inch, 200-pound junior quarterback Elai Machado, a league All-Star last season. Joseph Beato (6-2, 230) will be a mainstay on both sides of the ball as he looks to plug the middle on defense, and open gaps for the running game on offense. Machado will frequently look in the direction of senior wideout Joan Ortiz, whose blazing speed (4.5 second 40-yard dash) will provide a major deep threat and versatile option in the passing game. The hardest challenge will be to replace more than 150 tackles that came from graduated linebackers Mikey Stackpole and Wilfred Campos as they look to improve on their first-round playoff exit last season.

Season opener: Saturday, Sept. 6, 5:30 p.m., vs. Salem

League: Commonwealth

Coach: James Runner (16th season). Career: 61-71.

Last year’s record: 4-4

Strengths: Young but solid team chemistry

Concerns: Lack of experience

Offense: Wing T

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: James Runner enters his 16th season at the helm of a Lynn Tech team that saw its season end via first-round exit against Carver last fall. What’s the goal this year? “To make the playoffs,” Runner said. In order to play postseason football, they’ll need continued production from their top returnees. Elusive sophomore quarterback Jadiel Ortega, a member of the USA Football junior flag football national team, starred as a freshman, accounting for 11 touchdowns and three interceptions on defense. His top target will be wideout Colin McGough, who excels at yardage after the catch. Beefing up the offensive line will be 6-foot, 300-pound junior center Jeffrey Moore-Thayer..

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 12, 7 p.m., vs. Malden

League: Tri-Valley

Coach: Don Shumaker (1st season). Career: 0-0.

Last year’s record: 4-6

Strengths: Seniority and leadership

Concerns: Lack of depth

Offense: Spread

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: The Mohawks enter the season with a new coach, Don Shumaker, who last served as an assistant for Tri-Valley League foe Medway. Shumaker hopes to flip last year’s 4-6 mark under coach Bob Martellio and reach the playoffs with a winning record. Senior captain Pat Halloran returns as a versatile piece on both sides of the ball. He’ll play alongside fellow captain Chuck Smith, who will be a key part of the offensive and defensive lines. Junior quarterback Owen Caulfield will command the offense for a third season and look to snap a six-game losing to end last season.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 12, 6 p.m., vs. Blackstone-Millville/Hopedale

League: Commonwealth

Coach: Rob Flynn (2nd season). Career: 3-5.

Last year’s record: 3-5

Strengths: Strong freshman class, returners in key positions

Concerns: Replacing middle linebacker and running back

Offense: Spread

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Coach Rob Flynn enters his second year with the Mustangs following a 3-5 initial campaign. Following standout Sebastian Joseph’s graduation, Flynn admits his team’s biggest concern will be replacing his production at both the linebacker and running back positions. With Gus Stillman under center, Mattheus Andrade will likely be filling Joseph’s roles on offense and defense. Alex Filip is expected to line up in the slot and contribute defensively. Jackson Wight returns as an edge rusher and Stillman’s blind-side protector as the Mustangs look to clinch a playoff berth for the first time under Flynn.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 6 p.m., vs. Roxbury Prep/Boston Prep/Neighborhood House Charter

League: Commonwealth

Coach: Danny Kelly (4th season). Career: 26-10.

Last year’s record: 11-1

Strengths: Experienced offensive line, returning defensive starters

Concerns: Young at the skill positions

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Coach Danny Kelly returns for his fourth year at the helm of a Vikings squad that won 11 games last season when he was the Globe’s Division 8 Coach of the Year. Sophomore running back Zack Deschenes will make his presence felt behind senior linemen Miguel and Christian Montalvo out of the Vikings’ spread and two-back systems. Junior wideout Dylan Hall and quarterback Nick Sloboda will get the starting nod to steer the Vikings downfield. “Teams will have to account for Deschenes every week with his big-play ability,” said Kelly. “This should give our passing game a chance to attack the field vertically when we need to rely on a steady passing game with a good core of receivers.” They’ll have to make up for the loss of key graduates Chase Carney, Colby Catterton, and KJ Hardin, among others, in hopes of repeating last season’s results, but double-digit wins are still firmly in the cards.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 5, 7 p.m., vs. Brighton

League: Mayflower

Coach: Brandon Mendez (11th season). Career: 68-38.

Last year’s record: 5-4

Strengths: Physical OL/DL, aggressive defensive play

Concerns: Lack of defensive line depth, young secondary

Offense: Double wing

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: Following a first-round playoff departure last season, the Cougars are poised for a deeper postseason run. The team is anchored by three-year starter and senior captain Dylan Mendez (5-8, 250) who will be an impact player on both sides up the middle. The Cougars sport talented junior quarterbacks Aidan Anderson, who’s strong in the run game, and southpaw Cole Correia. On the defensive side, senior linebacker Carmine Cambra should rack up tackles and senior cornerback Ryan Manchester will look to lock down top receivers. “We will play physical and disciplined football, as we always do,” said coach Brandon Mendez. “We have a great group of student-athletes that play together and compete every day.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 12, 7 p.m., at Greater New Bedford

League: South Shore

Coach: Jonathan Marshall (6th season). Career: 26-22.

Last year’s record: 10-2

Strengths: Returning top-end skill talent

Concerns: New-look offensive line
