title: A.R.T. and ProBlak team up to lead creative workshops for upcoming mural
text:
Earlier this summer, the American Repertory Theater announced that it had commissioned a 200-foot mural by Roxbury artist Rob “ProBlak” Gibbs to adorn its new campus in Allston. And now, both Gibbs and the A.R.T. want your input.

The collaborative initiative plans to tap locals for inspiration and ideas for the upcoming artwork. The idea is a community-inspired mural, created with the help of the Bostonians the new creative space will serve, said Dayron J. Miles, the A.R.T.’s associate artistic director.

“We didn’t want to just put another mural up,” Miles said. “We wanted the art that enveloped our building to emanate from stories that reflected our community.”

Before the mural’s installation — which is scheduled for this spring, according to Miles — the A.R.T. and Gibbs will partner with local artists to host conversation-driven creative workshops across the city throughout September. At each, attendees will be encouraged to share their personal stories as Bostonians and their ideas for Boston’s future. These lived narratives and hopeful visions, in turn, will help shape the mural’s final outcome.

The A.R.T. enters its 2025-26 theater season this fall with its Allston relocation on the horizon. Its new home base, the David E. and Stacey L. Goel Center for Creativity & Performance, began construction last summer; once complete, the 70,000-square-foot building will expand the organization’s performance, teaching, and public spaces. Gibbs’s mural, which is set to be completed between late spring and early fall of 2026, according to Miles, will be featured on the Goel’s north-facing exterior wall.

The mural workshops kick off Sept. 6 in Cambridge with additional sessions in Malden, East Boston, Allston-Brighton, Roxbury, Dorchester, and Back Bay. Artists and non-artists are invited to participate.

Gibbs — one of the founders of Artists for Humanity, a nonprofit that supports young creators in Boston — will co-lead each workshop session alongside a fellow local artist.

“Art is typically categorized as two- or three-dimensional — for me, there is a fourth dimension: the shared story. That is what makes the mural or theatrical experience live on, long after it’s created,” Gibbs said in a statement issued by the A.R.T.

The community engagement efforts emulate the Goel’s intended function to “not just be a culture palace for artists and theater makers, but rather be a place where the community could come and investigate their own creativity,” said Miles.

“The mural [will be] another line of respect that can be shown to the community, since the art of storytelling is not from one person [or] one narrative. It’s all of our stories combined,” Gibbs told the Globe in an interview. “I want to show how much we’ve got in common.”

During each two-hour session, Gibbs and the local artist will facilitate conversation between attendees, using the session to stimulate ideas for the city’s future, and, in turn, the future mural. Each guest artist brings their own method for ideation to the experience, whether that be hands-on activities or conversation prompts. (All supplies will be provided.)

Muralist Gina Latham — who co-leads the Cambridge Public Library session on Sept. 6 from 2-4 p.m. — says the opportunity allows her to “flex [her] creative muscles.” She believes community engagement is “the most important piece of the puzzle.”

Interdisciplinary artist Phoebe Warner will co-lead the series’ final workshop at the Harvard Ed Portal in Allston. They said their involvement in the session is especially meaningful to them, as Allston-Brighton is where they first found a home in Boston’s arts scene.

“I’m really hoping that I can honor the community that accepted me and brought me in. That’s my hood, in a way,” Warner said. “I am really grateful and excited that I get to [lead] that space.”

To attend a workshop, find details and locations at americanrepertorytheater.org.

This story has been updated to correct a reporting error in Dayron J. Miles’s comments about the Goel Center’s purpose.

Isabella Bernstein can be reached at isabella.bernstein@globe.com.

title: Yves Salomon-Fernández launches fund-raising campaign for Urban College of Boston
text:
“We are now at a time in our evolution where we need to be much more concerned about the future ... and really solidifying the legacy of the college and broadening our community of supporters to make sure the college continues to exist in perpetuity,” she said.

The school, she said, has grown quickly in recent years, and now has 1,100-plus students, attending classes online or in person, with a focus on early childhood education and social services training.

Salomon-Fernández is starting her third academic year as president. She arrived in the United States at age 12 when her family moved here from Haiti and went to Boston Latin School and then UMass Boston. She received her doctorate from Boston College and eventually became a college administrator, most recently working in a top role at Southern New Hampshire University before becoming Urban College’s president two years ago.

“[Urban College students] are often members of the family going to college for the first time in their family’s history, they might be struggling, they might be new to this country,” said O’Brien, a longtime supporter of the college. “Those are exactly the kinds of families we have to support. Yves represents that on so many levels.”

Walsh has been a frequent Urban College commencement speaker, starting with previous president Michael Taylor. Salomon-Fernández asked Walsh to get more involved, and he said he would do whatever he could to help.

“She’s not afraid to ask, which is half the battle,” said Walsh, who currently heads up the National Hockey League Players’ Association. “Michael Taylor was a great leader but Yves is somebody now who can take it to the next level.”

This probably wasn’t the housewarming party that Ernestine Tiongson and George Giunta originally anticipated when they decided to lease a new apartment at 281 Franklin St. in downtown Boston.

They had just moved in over Labor Day weekend when the crowd showed up last Tuesday morning — not friends and family, but reporters and City Hall staffers. Then the building’s developer, Adam Burns, and the mayor, Michelle Wu, stepped forward.

Wu handed Tiongson, an associate manager at Keurig Dr Pepper, and Giunta, a digital product manager at Manulife, a snake plant as a housewarming gift and asked them some questions about their new place in front of the cameras. The reason for Wu’s visit: It was the first completed project in her tax break program meant to spur office-residential conversions.

So far, the city has received 17 applications to convert 655,000 square feet of offices to residences across 22 buildings, totaling up to 824 new units — should they all be completed. But construction has moved slowly, for various reasons, and work has only started on a few of them (including another project of Burns’s, in Fort Point). This Franklin Street project, led by Burns’s Boston Pinnacle Properties, carved out 15 apartments from what used to be five floors of offices.

Burns said the building had several characteristics that made it a prime candidate for conversion: a smaller floor plan, for example, and operable windows. Even with those traits, he said, the tax break proved critical to making the numbers work.

Coming next: a much bigger office-residential conversion at 44 Bromfield St. However, this one did not take advantage of the city’s program. Thibeault Development considered it but calculated that it made more sense to renovate without participating in the program, attorney Richard Lynds said. The project’s 56 apartments are slated to open in the coming weeks.

Wu said she recognizes these conversion projects are relatively small compared with the city’s overall need for more housing. But she said every little bit helps, particularly when it comes to bringing more life to downtown streets and revenue to downtown businesses.

“Every new home matters,” Wu said. “The only way we’re going to have everything come back fully downtown is to convert it into more of a residential neighborhood.”

For nearly all of the time the Boston Public Market has been open, it’s been led by one person, Cheryl Cronin.

But that’s about to change: Cronin announced on Thursday that she’s stepping down from the job as chief executive of the Boston Public Market Association in January. Cronin says she fully anticipated leaving the job as she approached her 10-year mark with the nonprofit, a milestone that lines up with her announced departure date.

The association’s board, led by chair Dave Clark, has started the search for Cronin’s successor.

When Cronin came to the job in early 2016, the market had opened around a year earlier in a spot above the Haymarket T station and was led by founding chief executive Liz Morningstar.

Today, the market’s roughly 30 stalls are essentially full, primarily with food vendors from around Massachusetts. The market is still rebounding from a major loss in foot traffic during the COVID-19 pandemic, and Cronin has tried to make it more reliant on tourists and less on office workers. Early in the pandemic, the Kendall Foundation gave $750,000 to help keep the market afloat, while Cronin had cut back rents to ensure the stalls could stay occupied.

Rents now make up close to half of the association’s $2.5 million budget — including the costs of a 6.5-person staff — with state funds and philanthropy filling in most of the rest.

“This has been the most gratifying experience of my professional career,” Cronin said. “I’m feeling a little teary or bittersweet. I’ll really miss the team.”

You might notice something different about the Boston skyline Thursday night: Some of the office towers will be lit up in blue.

This will be the second year that the people who died in the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks are honored in Boston in this way, thanks in large part to Gogi Gupta. The founder of Back Bay marketing firm Gupta Media was moved by the “Tribute in Light” that takes place in downtown Manhattan every Sept. 11 and wanted his city to show some solidarity.

Working with his brokers, Ben Heller and Bryan Sparkes of JLL, as well as Mike Simonelli of Structure Tone, the firm that built out Gupta’s new Back Bay office, Gupta and his associates have roped in landlords such as BXP, Fortis Property Group, and Chiofaro Co.

“I don’t think we should leave it on New York’s shoulders,” Gupta said. “I think everybody has to remember that day.”

This year, the Massachusetts Department of Transportation is getting involved, by lighting up the Zakim bridge, as is the city of Boston, by illuminating City Hall and the Bolling Building in Roxbury. Last week, the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce encouraged its members to get involved in the cause. (And Gupta said he has colleagues in Cleveland and Minneapolis starting similar efforts in those cities.)

A whole generation is joining the workforce that wasn’t even born when the World Trade Center towers fell. Gupta worries that the horrors of 9/11 are fading from public consciousness and that the significance of that day is starting to be forgotten. Maybe illuminating more than a dozen buildings in Boston can help prevent that from happening.

“If everyone takes a second and just remembers the lives lost,” Gupta said, “I will have achieved what I wanted to achieve.”

title: AI in the classroom? These Latino teens want Boston schools to do more training — now.
text:
“I was saying to myself, ‘Oh my God, my English isn’t getting better, what am I going to do?’” she says, in a Spanish-language interview.

Enter ChatGPT.

For a week, Guzmán relied on the artificial intelligence chatbot as her teacher, mentor, and study partner. She quizzed it on subjects likely to appear on the exam, and practiced her short response and essay questions, using the chatbot to fine-tune her grammar. By the time exam day rolled around, her nerves had settled — and her score showed it.

“It turned out my results had gone up by a lot from the last time I took it,” she says. “So I said, ‘Wow, maybe I am learning English. Little by little, but I’m learning it.’ I’m still nervous speaking, but at least I can write in it now, I can read, so I feel good.”

Guzmán says her experience highlights one of the ways AI can be harnessed for good in the classroom — English-language learners, after all, make up one-third of the Boston Public Schools population. But they’re far from the only students feeling the impacts of the radical shift in education: Studies show that a majority of students across backgrounds are more than willing to use AI tools for help with schoolwork.

And not all of those uses are so innocuous.

Across the country, the rapid spread of generative AI is upending decades-old teaching philosophies and making existing lesson plans obsolete. Educators warn that students are leveraging chatbots to cheat, answering questions in the blink of an eye and producing written assignments out of thin air. And that deprives them of the critical thinking central to the learning process.

Students say it’s not that simple. While most of her peers are more than willing to use AI for their assignments, Guzmán says, many of them aren’t trying to be academically dishonest. To them, it’s simply a tool — one that doesn’t come with a how-to manual.

At the core of the AI debate is the fact that students — and educators — don’t always know what is and isn’t considered out of bounds. And that’s something that Guzmán and some of her peers are trying to change.

In 2021, Sociedad Latina set out to find a new campaign for its membership. The Roxbury-based nonprofit, which offers after-school and summer enrichment programs primarily for Latino students in Boston, has run awareness campaigns dealing with everything from sexual health to environmental sustainability.

“In all of our history, we’ve always seen [that] change comes from young people,” says Alexandra Oliver-Dávila, the group’s executive director. “We feel like we have not done our job if young people do not understand how important it is for them to be involved in their community, to be engaged, to be able to identify a problem and to know that they can solve it.”

Youth leaders in the group highlighted their concerns surrounding the effects of technology and social media on mental health, particularly in the wake of the pandemic. “They didn’t know what to do, they didn’t know what to feel,” says J.J. Eliassaint, a junior at New Mission High School in Hyde Park who is also part of Sociedad Latina. “They needed some type of guidance. And they weren’t getting that.”

That’s when the group launched its Teens and Tech campaign. Since then, Sociedad Latina has organized various workshops and events, connecting its youth with experts and counselors. What organizers call “digital wellness” habits, Eliassaint says, is simply “teaching kids and parents on ways to use social media for good, or ways to use AI.”

All along, the plan was for the youth to take action.

Sociedad Latina has extended its mission beyond the red-brick walls of its Tremont Street center in Roxbury. Youth members have appeared before the Boston School Committee several times, as well as presented to the Boston City Council’s education committee, calling for increased transparency and visibility in policy decisions on technology use in the classroom, including AI.

Among the group’s recommendations are the development of a certification program for students before they can access AI, aimed at making them “responsible digital citizens,” along with similar workshops for parents.

“Just like we have a class teaching how to use a computer, we should have a class on AI,” Guzmán says. “Something to teach us how to use it for good, and not for ill. Because the world is advancing, and AI is advancing right along with it. It’s not like we can defeat it or treat it like an enemy; we have to know how to use it. We can’t let it use us.”

The current status quo, the group contends. “There are rules and implementations in different schools that are being rolled out, kind of like test trials,” says Stephanie Aguayo, Sociedad Latina’s manager of civic engagement, in a late August interview. “With the AI side of things, some teachers say they can use it, some teachers double-check and run their papers through AI checkers. But there’s no policy to say, ‘What is ethical? What should we be doing?’”

Until recently, Boston Public Schools offered parents and educators relatively few detailed instructions on what made for appropriate AI use, offering virtually no hard-and-fast rules or specific examples for students.

That changed in August, when the district released a spate of updated policies ahead of the 2025 – 26 school year. BPS now also maintains a list of “approved” AI tools, though ChatGPT, the most popular generative AI chatbot, is restricted to faculty use on BPS devices and remains blocked for students. (Gemini, a similar chatbot developed by Google, is now available to students in the seventh grade and up.)

Still, the guidelines leave considerable room for interpretation. “Just as a calculator may be appropriate for completing some math assignment but not for others, AI use is a case-by-case decision that must be made by the teacher based on the learning goals of the assignment,” the guidelines state.

Notably absent is any sort of dedicated course or certification program training students to use ChatGPT or other chatbots — one of the key proposals by Sociedad Latina.

The new guidelines state they reflect “input from staff, educators, and students” gathered over the past few months.

That came as a surprise to Sociedad Latina executive director Oliver-Dávila. Although the group has repeatedly reached out to BPS on the issue, it was not notified of the new policies, despite its testimony before the School Committee and with the superintendent’s team. (A BPS spokesperson said the district appreciated Sociedad Latina’s “participation and collaboration,” adding that the new guidelines were developed with staff input, student focus groups, and “a comprehensive review period.”)

“I wish that, as we had been testifying and making these recommendations, BPS would have responded and let us know they were working on this,” Oliver-Dávila says, adding that the Sociedad Latina students “were clearly interested in having input. I’m disappointed that did not happen.”

Even as students continue to use AI in the classroom, they say they are keenly aware of the negative effects it can have on their social fabric. More than a few are uneasy about it.

“I do think that on some level, yes, we are cheating,” says Ana Baez, a junior at Margarita Muñiz, “if we’re not learning on our own merit, but just through artificial intelligence.” It’s not just cheating on the academic level, she clarifies; it’s cheating yourself out of the experience of learning itself.

Take group projects, for example, one of the most common types of assignment for high school students, and, according to Baez, one of the most undermined by AI. Now, she says, there’s barely any “group work” involved at all — classmates can just type their individual prompts into a chatbot, without even the pretense of coordination.

“We used to go to each other’s houses to work on assignments,” Baez says in Spanish. “Now it’s just, ‘You do your part, I’ll do mine,’ and that’s it. So we’re not actually socializing with our classmates, we’re just using artificial intelligence and that’s it.”

It speaks to a deeper concern: how AI use has frayed even the most basic elements of the classroom ecosystem. “You can’t help each other anymore,” Baez says. “You can only say, ‘I can’t explain this to you, so I won’t.’ If my teacher asks me to help my classmates on an assignment,

I can only tell them, ‘I don’t know how to help you, I did it with ChatGPT.’”

It’s a fine line to draw, says Sociedad Latina manager Aguayo: Students need to know how to use AI responsibly, but there also needs to be guardrails to ensure it doesn’t come at the cost of building formative in-person relationships — even those as perfunctory as a high school study group.

“Fifty percent of life is your social skills,” Aguayo says. “School should be preparing us for the future after you graduate, and in most jobs, you’re going to need some social skills. ... If our schools aren’t setting us up to do that, then yeah, that’s going to have detrimental effects.”

Even with her MCAS scores in hand, Guzmán can see the pitfalls of the technology all too well.

“My dream is to be a lawyer,” she says. “And my teacher always tells me, what happens when you’re in court and you can’t defend your client? You’re not going to be able to ask ChatGPT, ‘What’s such-and-such a word in English’ and expect to go before a judge like that.”

The effect of the district’s new policies remains to be seen. BPS officials say they will continue conversations with parents and students to “ensure flexibility” with AI policy going forward.

“Binding rules can limit the ability to adapt as technology and best practices change,” says Samara Pinto, a district spokesperson. “Instead, BPS has taken a collaborative approach to strengthen our guidelines and ensure AI is used responsibly to support teaching and learning.”

Robbie Torney, senior director for AI programs at San Francisco-based nonprofit Common Sense Media, described the BPS framework as a “good first step” for a comprehensive policy, which manages to balance both the benefits and risks of AI. But the guidelines, he added, “do feel general.”

“I appreciate the age developmental consideration, thinking about how younger students need different protections and guidelines,” he says. “I’m just curious, how is this going to be implemented? How is this going to actually come to life?”

Success will depend in large part on how parents and students react. “Having a policy is a start, and then engaging your community with that policy is another component of that,” Torney says.

Sociedad Latina is especially concerned about the effect on students of color, who make up over 80 percent of the Boston Public Schools population. Research shows that students of color are more likely to use AI tools, both inside and outside the classroom — and are less likely to have clear guidance on how to do that.

Latino teens already use certain generative AI tools at higher rates than their white counterparts, according to a Common Sense Media study published last year: 16 percent of Latinos reported using chatbots and text generators at least once a day, compared with 8 percent of white teens. Latino youth are also much more likely to use generative AI for writing a document or email, especially if that document involves translation from one language to another, the study found.

The same study also found that, among parents of Latino youth, an overwhelming majority said they had not received any communications from their children’s schools about generative AI.

Without adequate guardrails, Oliver-Dávila says, “We’re going to have this huge digital divide of the haves and the have-nots that we already have, and it’s just going to get bigger and bigger and bigger.”

But the students at Sociedad Latina remain optimistic that, with training and transparency, the culture surrounding AI will change for the better.

For the time being, Guzmán says, it will be up to the students to not get swept away by the technological tide. Because teens “understand each other,” she reasons the best way to spread awareness of responsible AI use is through students, like those at Sociedad Latina, sharing their perspectives with their peers.

“Until we’re able to go to a class with teachers who can truly explain how AI works, what you can use it for and what you can’t — that’s how, little by little, there can be a change,” Guzmán says.

title: Bostonians from neighborhoods of color nearly 4 times more likely to be struck by cars across city, data show
text:
The study from Boston’s EMS department and MIT found residents of Boston’s predominantly nonwhite neighborhoods face higher risks of being hit not only in areas demographically similar to their own, but in predominantly white neighborhoods, according to the data.

The researchers divided neighborhoods into categories based on the proportion of residents identifying as white, ranging from under 8.8 percent in the least white areas to 77.9 percent in the whitest.

The findings werepublished in the journal Cities & Health in June. The study is believed to be the first in the country to look at the home addresses of pedestrians and cyclists struck by cars, in addition to analyzing where the crashes happened.

“Nationwide, cities don’t really deal with who is getting hit by cars — they deal with where,” said study author Mark Brennan, a professor at Rutgers University in New Jersey who recently earned a data science PhD from MIT. “We were the first people, to my knowledge, to get at this.”

Researchers said one factor giving rise to the disparity is that residents of predominantly Black, Latino, and Asian neighborhoods are less likely to have access to a car — and more likely to live far from where they work because of a lack of affordable housing.

In Boston’s whitest neighborhoods, 24 percent of residents lacked access to a car, compared to 36 percent of residents in the least white neighborhoods, according to the study.

Forced to walk more between bus stops and train stations as part of longer commutes, Boston’s residents of color are at greater risk of being hit by cars, Brennan said, compared to people who have to walk less, or not at all.

“This is a clear unevenness within the city, it’s extremely troubling,” he said.

Combining US Census data with EMS crash data, researchers found there were nearly three times as many pedestrians and cyclists struck in car crashes in Boston’s “least white” neighborhoods “compared to the whitest neighborhoods” from 2016 to 2021, Brennan said.

When looking at all crashes in Boston, the disparity widened when researchers examined who was hit, he said. Overall, crash victims were much more likely to be from neighborhoods of color.

Because people of color are less likely to have health insurance or jobs that allow them to take time off work, serious injuries from car crashes can have more dramatic economic impacts in households and neighborhoods of color, researchers said.

“The Blackest neighborhoods have 4.1 times as many people struck by cars living in them,” Brennan said.

Because of how racial, economic, and health inequalities are intertwined, the most effective crash-prevention policies “are likely antipoverty ones: ready and flexible access to transport, daycare and afterschool care, primary health care, and housing,” the study said.

Sitting at Nubian Station, retired Boston Public Schools administrator Victoria Mitchell said she always looks “left, right, and left again” before crossing streets, but still ends up having to “jump back” from speeding cars nearly once a week.

“If a car is stopped, another car will try to go around them and not see me at all,” said Mitchell, 77.

Even in Boston’s predominantly white neighborhoods, pedestrians from communities of color accounted for 5 in 10 car crash victims, the study said.

“It’s a deeply disturbing number,” said study author Justin Steil, an MIT urban planning professor who also works as a paramedic.

In Hyde Park, which is among the predominantly non-white neighborhoods analyzed, residents feel Hyde Park Avenue is “extremely dangerous,” said Nathan Eckstrom, an organizer with Boston Better Streets Coalition. Without a shoulder on the road, big trucks zoom past inches away from where people walk, making the study’s findings “ring true,” he said.

“It’s a horrifying statistic of how much more dangerous it is to be from a nonwhite neighborhood in Boston,” Eckstrom said.

A spokesperson said Mayor Michelle Wu’s office aims “to continue our progress as the safest major city in the country,” and has seen crash numbers go down over the past four years.

“Through full reconstructions of larger corridors like Cummins Highway [in Mattapan] or adding speed humps to smaller neighborhood streets, we are investing resources to curb speeding, reduce crashes, and make our streets safer for everyone,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

The MIT and EMS study adds to a growing body of research on how race, poverty, and commuting methods intersect to create health and economic inequities, researchers said.

Brennan said Boston’s neighborhoods of color have a higher share of people who work night and early morning shifts. When they commute before sunrise or after sunset, they may be less visible to tired drivers, he said.

Steil said workers from neighborhoods of color are also more likely to have to commute in unfamiliar neighborhoods far from their own. The logistical challenges of navigating new routes on foot could make pedestrians more vulnerable to oncoming cars, he said.

Boston’s EMS department worked with researchers to compile the data and has already been using it to make infrastructure improvements “through a lens of equity and inclusion,” spokesperson Caitlin McLaughlin said in an email.

“We are committed to not only serving the emergency medical service needs of our residents, but also addressing health inequities,” she said.

Back at Nubian station, de la Cruz said she was worried about winter, when icy or snowy streets may be even more dangerous.

Still, she said in Spanish, she always “does things right” so she can get return customers and keep working — even if the commute takes her farther away.

“Me gusta dar un buen servicio,” she said, which translates to, “I like to provide good service.”

title: At-large, District 7 Boston City Council races decided, according to unofficial city results
text:
With all precincts reported, the four incumbents — Ruthzee Louijeune, Julia Mejia, Erin Murphy, and Henry Santana — and Frank Baker, a former district councilor from Dorchester, finished in the top five slots.

The remaining three positions were secured by Alexandra E. Valdez, Marvin Dee Mathelier, and Will Onuoha, according to unofficial city tallies.

Valdez, Mathelier, and Onuoha have not held elected office in Boston before.

The results indicated that Santana, a freshman councilor, made it through the first round of voting. He needed help from the robust political apparatus of Mayor Michelle Wu, his former boss, to collect enough signatures to appear on the ballot.

Baker represented Dorchester for a decade and was a thorn in the mayor’s side before he declined to run again for his former seat.

Louijeune and Santana are staunch supporters of the mayor. Mejia has at times criticized Wu from the political left, and Murphy has been one of Wu’s most significant adversaries on her right.

Given that a successful at-large run requires broad support and a functional political operation, these seats can be a springboard for a run for mayor or another higher office. Wu was an at-large councilor for a decade, and she defeated another at-large councilor, Annissa Essaibi George, to win the top job. Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley also was an at-large councilor for a decade, and now represents about two-thirds of the city in Washington.

The council is composed of the four at-large seats plus nine district councilors, who are elected to represent geographic regions of the city.

All councilors serve two-year terms, meaning dynamics on the body can and do change quickly. During the first two years of Wu’s term, a fractured council included many critics of the mayor, but it has become more friendly during the latter half of her four-year term. In recent years, the council has successfully pushed for more budgetary authority, but has had trouble exercising it.

The most high-profile of the district council races is the contest to succeed Tania Fernandes Anderson, who was recently sentenced to one month in federal prison after pleading guilty to federal corruption charges.

Eleven candidates campaigned to represent District 7, which is anchored in Roxbury and includes parts of Dorchester and the South End. Tuesday’s election narrows the field to two for the November election.

With 100 percent of the vote counted Wednesday morning, Said Ahmed, a former track and field star and current track coach, and The Rev. Miniard Culpepper, a well-known senior pastor at the Pleasant Hill Missionary Baptist Church, were the top two finishers.

Ahmed received 15.72 percent of the votes cast followed closely by Culpepper with 15 percent, results show.

The next three top vote getters — Mavrick Afonso, Samuel Hurtado, and Said Abdirahman Abdikarim — each collected around 14 percent, results show.

District 7 is among the most diverse of the City Council areas in Boston, with many residents feeling the squeeze of the city’s housing and cost-of-living crises, and a handful of the council hopefuls from the district debated housing, reparations, and ethics reform at a forum last month.

The majority of residents in Roxbury, where the district is rooted, are people of color: 41 percent Black and 30 percent Latino, according to city statistics. The neighborhood’s median household income is $42,000, well below the citywide median of $94,000.

Whoever succeeds in the general election will look to bring stability to a post that has had scandal swirling around it for months. Indeed, for a City Council engulfed in controversy in recent years, Fernandes Anderson’s indictment represented a legal nadir.

She was the first Boston councilor to be indicted by federal authorities since Chuck Turner in 2008, who at the time represented District 7 as well. He was convicted in 2010 of attempted extortion and three counts of providing false statements to FBI agents for accepting $1,000 in cash in exchange for helping a nightclub owner win a liquor license.

Fernandes Anderson had succeeded Kim Janey in representing District 7. Janey became acting mayor when Martin J. Walsh was tapped to become US labor secretary. Janey then ran for a full term as mayor and lost.

The mayor’s race has dominated coverage of this election cycle, and that is to be expected. Wu and her challenger Josh Kraft, a former nonprofit leader whose family owns the New England Patriots, advanced to the November general election, surpassing two lesser-known candidates. Polling has shown Wu in the driver’s seat as she seeks a second term.

Niki Griswold and John R. Ellement of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Polls close in Boston mayor’s race as Michelle Wu fends off three challengers, including Josh Kraft
text:
Wu celebrated in a spirited address to supporters at Adams Park in Roslindale, where purple lights illuminated the trees and upbeat music from a live band filled the air.

“Voters across our city left no doubt: In Boston, wins can’t be bought,” Wu said in a reference to the millions of dollars Kraft and a political action committee have spent against her so far.

“The next eight weeks are about more than the remaining two names on the ballot,” Wu said. “It’s a test of who we are. It’s a test of whether we believe in our city as a place of possibility and promise, whether Boston will keep going as a home for everyone.”

“Today,” she continued, “you answered those questions loud and clear. You sent a message to Josh Kraft, to Donald Trump, and to all their enablers: Boston is not for sale.”

In South Boston, Kraft appeared at Ironworkers Local 7 Hall, home to one of the unions that backed him. Flanked by supporters and family — including his father, billionaire Patriots owner Robert Kraft — Josh Kraft promised a hard fight for the remainder of the campaign.

“Let me be clear: We are still in this race,” Kraft said. “We’re gonna push forward harder, louder, and stronger than ever. We know the road ahead is not going to be easy, but neither is life in Boston right now for too many families.”

“The only poll that matters is in November,” he added. Supporters chanted, “We want Josh!”

The first woman and first person of color elected mayor of Boston, Wu, 40, has a long record in city government and a vast network of supporters. She has also embraced her role as a high-profile antagonist to Trump, positioning herself as Boston’s chief defender in the face of threats and lawsuits from the administration, drawing local support and national attention.

Meanwhile, Kraft, 58, has had to contend with his father’s longtime friendship with Trump, prompting the candidate to disavow the president. Josh Kraft says he has never supported Trump and believes him unfit for office.

Ahead of Tuesday’s vote, Kraft sought to manage expectations, saying he hoped to finish within 15 percentage points of Wu; a strong showing could help him reshape the final months of the campaign and persuade donors to get behind him. Meanwhile, large advantages in public surveys — one recent poll found Wu leading Kraft by 50 percentage points — have set sky-high expectations for the mayor, meaning a smaller margin of victory could be seen as a sign of weakness.

On Tuesday night, some Kraft supporters kept their expectations modest.

“Michelle Wu is way up there. That’s what we hear,” said Vincent Coyle, business manager of Local Ironworkers 7. “But let’s see where we land tonight. It’ll give us a good picture of boots on the ground coming up before the bigger launch.”

The mayor’s race so far has been ugly and expensive. Kraft has poured millions of his own money into the campaign, much of it on ubiquitous television ads. An aligned super PAC has also spent millions on attack ads against the mayor, criticizing her record on housing, as well as the cost of a controversial renovation of White Stadium, which the city is making into a new home for a professional women’s soccer team, as well as Boston Public Schools athletes.

Kraft argues Wu is out of touch and has failed to address the city’s most pressing challenges, such as rising rents and underperforming schools.

Wu’s rhetoric has been just as sharp. She has called Kraft a carpetbagger who is trying to “buy” his way into office, noting he has been a Boston resident for less than two years. (He moved to the North End in October 2023 after living most of his life in the nearby suburbs, though he spent decades working in the city with the Boys and Girls Club of Boston.) She argues he lacks the government experience necessary to lead a city under siege from the White House.

The candidates reiterated those criticisms Tuesday.

“In Boston, wins can’t be bought. They’re built, day after day,” Wu said in her victory speech.

Kraft, meanwhile, said “Wu has shown she doesn’t want to talk about her record. She wants to talk about Donald Trump.”

But “Bostonians deserve better than what they have now,” he said. “They deserve a mayor who listens. A mayor who is accessible and on their side. Not one that cares about the next step in their political career.”

The Boston Elections Department — which has been taken over by state authorities after they found “unacceptable” lapses last fall — released just a fraction of the vote total late Tuesday.

A lopsided result would be nothing new for the city. In 2017, when then-Mayor Martin J. Walsh sought his second term, he won 63 percent of the vote in the September preliminary, besting his nearest competitor by 34 percentage points.

Candidates and strategists were also watching closely for precinct-level data showing where each candidate is weakest and strongest. Kraft has made a point of prioritizing outreach to Boston’s Black voters, for example, and argued Wu has lost touch with the city’s communities of color.

Turnout, of course, was a major factor. According to voting tallies posted on the city’s website on Wednesday, 92,430 votes had been cast.

Some voters told the Globe on Tuesday that they went to the polls because they were motivated to show Kraft the city is not behind him.

“I think Mayor Wu is doing an incredible job, and I am offended at what I’ve heard Kraft saying,” said Amy Battisti-Ashé, a nurse from Jamaica Plain. “I just wanted to be super sure that she would crush him like a bug.”

Taylor Marble, 45, had the national political environment weighing heavily on his mind when he cast his vote for Wu Tuesday.

“I’m very proud of Mayor Wu and her resistance to Trump and ICE and the deportations,” Marble said, praising her “gumption.”

As for Kraft, he added, Marble said, “we don’t need any more billionaires in government.”

Kraft did find pockets of support elsewhere in the city.

Patrick Mogan, a 46-year-old landscaper who lives in South Boston, said he was backing Kraft’s campaign because he believes Wu is not doing enough to address addiction in the city.

“It’s been bad,” Mogan, who is in recovery himself, said outside the polling place at the James F. Condon School.

“We’re the ones that need the help,” he said. “Stop throwing the money around the way people want, and put it to where people need it.”

Joanie Tobin, 45, said she voted for change early Tuesday at the Yawkey Boys and Girls Club in Roxbury. When casting her ballot for mayor, she said she specifically considered housing and development.

“I did not vote for Mayor Wu,” Tobin said. “Primarily because of Mass. and Cass and her ability to handle the day-to-day operations of the city. And Franklin Park, White Stadium, the over-policing.”

Niki Griswold, Mara Kardas-Nelson, Spencer Buell and John R. Ellement of the Globe staff, and Globe correspondents Sadaf Tokhi and Katarina Schmeiszer contributed to this report.

title: There’s an election in Boston today. Here’s what’s on the ballot.
text:
In some races, there is little mystery about who those top vote-getters will be. Polls indicate Wu is poised to cruise to the November general election, when she is likely to face Josh Kraft, the longtime nonprofit leader and New England Patriots heir. That means that for many, the election is functioning more like a high-stakes survey, where the biggest question is what the margin of victory will be between the two top vote-getters.

Tuesday’s election is a particularly crucial test of legitimacy for Kraft, who has poured millions of dollars of his own money into his campaign but has drawn minimal support in public polls.

Also on the ballot for mayor are activist Domingos DaRosa and perennial candidate Robert Cappucci.

At a Roslindale polling place, Wu walked in to vote around 8:30 a.m., holding her daughter, Mira. After casting her vote, she framed Boston as an aspirational place.

“This is a city that people look to when they want to understand what’s possible,” the mayor said. “We are proof of what’s possible when people come together.”

Later, Wu gathered with her three children to make a short video. She held up her phone. “Get out there,” she said. “Make sure your voice is counted.”

Voters across the city had varied takes on the mayoral race.

Joanie Tobin, 45, voted at the Yawkey Boys and Girls Club in Roxbury early this morning. As a Nubian Square resident, Tobin said one of her most important issues is displacement within her neighborhood.

When casting her ballot for mayor, she said she specifically considered housing and development.

“I did not vote for Mayor Wu,” Tobin said. “Primarily because of Mass and Cass and her ability to handle the day to day operations of the city. And Franklin Park, White Stadium, the over-policing.”

Also in Roxbury, Shaun Lynch, 69, had a different take.

“I didn’t want to vote for Kraft. I don’t trust him, and I just want Wu to get back in [office],” Lynch said.

Denise Malis, 69, echoed that sentiment, and said that she “didn’t appreciate the aggressive campaign Kraft did against Wu.”

She said she had a lot of questions about his campaign and said there were many things she “didn’t like” about his campaign.

Lynch also said that he agrees with Wu’s support of immigrants in Boston, which influenced his vote.

Wu’s appearance before Congress earlier this year was on the minds of some casting ballots Tuesday.

Laura Catanzaro and her wife, Laura Pattison, are Roslindale residents and longtime supporters of Wu.

Catanzaro said she finds Wu strategic and smart. “She doesn’t just know what to do, she knows how to do it. You don’t go into a China shop like a bull. You go into a China shop knowing every single piece, and how to walk around every single piece, and keep it from shattering.”

“And that’s how she testified in front of the federal government,” Pattison interjected, emphasizing, “we need her now more than ever given what’s happening at a federal level.”

Jamaica Plain resident Alfonso Denson, 81, said he voted for Wu because he believes she’s done a really good job as mayor, particularly in the face of the Trump administration.

“Especially with everything going on in Washington, with threats of sending the National Guard here, the fact that she’s handled things so well might be the reason they didn’t,” he said.

David Benman, 29, said headed to the polls today with a clear idea of who he wanted to vote for — and why. A few months ago, he was hit by a car while riding his bike, which has brought bike lanes and traffic safety to the fore.

“There were a couple organizations, that put out a list for who the pro-bike lane candidates are, I just kind of followed that,” he said at a Brighton polling place, adding he voted for Wu.

Less predictable than the mayor’s race are the contests for City Council — particularly the open seat for District 7, and the crowded slate for councilor at-large.

In Roxbury-based District 7, 11 candidates are vying to replace disgraced former Councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson, who was recently sentenced to one month in prison on federal corruption charges. Voters and candidates in that race are focused on housing, among other issues.

In the at-large race, the field of 10 candidates will be narrowed to just eight who will face off in November for four spots, in a contest that could shift the city’s political dynamic. All four incumbent at-large councilors — Ruthzee Louijeune, Julia Mejia, Erin Murphy, and Henry Santana — are seeking reelection, while a former Dorchester councilor, Frank Baker, seeks to return to the body. City politicos will be watching to see not only who proceeds to the next round in November, but who gets the most votes on Tuesday, as an indication of their strength in the more competitive final round.

Of course, as in any off-year local race, the big question on Tuesday will be turnout. After a sleepy summer — where most of the political attention was focused at the national, not local, level — how many voters will even show up to cast ballots?

Four years ago, in a historic open-seat race for mayor, just 108,731 voters participated in the September preliminary election, a turnout of just under 25 percent.

Those low numbers mean Tuesday’s results will depend heavily on which candidates manage to get their voters out to the polls. In the final days, both Wu and Kraft have been hitting the campaign trail to motivate supporters, as well as participating in forums on the major issues in the race.

Kraft got a little burst of momentum on Monday, when he won the endorsement of Annissa Essaibi George, the former city councilor who lost the 2021 mayor’s race to Wu.

Kraft said Tuesday he is spending his day visiting polling locations throughout the city and feels good about the state of the race.

“I feel great because every neighborhood we go to, regardless of socioeconomics, race, ethnicity, we hear and feel the same thing. People want change, and we hear them, and we want to capitalize on that,” Kraft said at a polling place in South Boston.

Voters approached Kraft, shaking his hand and telling him that they voted for him or that they were planning on voting for him.

“I’m gonna put residents first,” he said. “And I’ll be accessible, accountable. transparent. It’s all about being neighborhood faced, neighborhood based, and I work for the residents as mayor.”

Still, he came into Tuesday on the back foot. Polls have consistently shown Wu leading Kraft by double digits; an Emerson College survey released last week put her ahead by a staggering 50 percentage points. For both candidates, the final margin of victory on Tuesday will be crucial.

With the bar set sky-high for Wu, a more modest margin of victory could be seen as a sign of weakness for the incumbent. For Kraft, meanwhile, finishing closer than expected behind Wu could bring much-needed momentum to his campaign, even if he still trails her by a significant amount.

Kraft has said he aims to finish within 15 percentage points of Wu.

But some voters, like Amy Battisti-Ashé, a nurse from Jamaica Plain, were inspired to try and thwart his efforts.

“I think Mayor Wu is doing an incredible job, and I am offended at what I’ve heard Kraft saying, so,” she said, “I just wanted to be super sure that she would crush him like a bug.”

Mara Kardas-Nelson and Niki Griswold of the Globe staff and correspondents Sadaf Tokhi and Katarina Schmeiszer contributed to this report.

title: Nobody heals alone, says Rev. Liz Walker in her new book about the power of community
text:
“We could call this an era of mass grief,” Walker writes, as people face not only individual losses but also the collective damage of climate change, inequality, and political instability. And yet as she points out in the book, and in an interview punctuated by the laugh many Bostonians remember from her years as the evening anchor at WBZ-TV, Walker finds hope in the communal. “If you can find that community, or restore it, or lift it up — that’s how you get through. That’s exactly how you get through.” Walker, who stepped down from her role at Roxbury Presbyterian in 2021, spoke with us by phone from her home in Florida.

Q. After graduating from Harvard Divinity School and leaving journalism, you landed as a pastor in Roxbury. How did praying at Cory Johnson’s memorial service affect you?

A. I had covered stories like this as a journalist. We cover shootings all the time, but this was like going back and seeing it from a different perspective. I’d covered funerals of shooting victims, but then you move on. Well, the family doesn’t move on. I was really thrust into the middle of this family’s courage and their grief. It just brought something alive to me.

Q. Tell me more about Cory’s family.

A. Everybody talks about resilience, but I think there’s something more than resilience going on in Cory’s family. They’re just the most wonderful people and to have to go through this horrible pain with such dignity was a real gift to me. They’re not public figures and they don’t want to be. Yet they were willing to open up all their wounds. Deborah, Corey’s mom, you know she’ll never get over the loss of her son but watching her kind of come out of her own darkness has been a gift, too.

Q. Your book isn’t just about the nuts and bolts of running a program or leading a church. You explore a lot of deeper topics about trauma and loss, with a particular emphasis on Black life. Can you tell me a little bit about the research you did?

A. It was what I love to do! I was surprised at all the information out there about systematic trauma, in books like “Weathering” by Arline T. Geronimus, “The Body Keeps the Score” [by Bessel van der Kolk], and “My Grandmother’s Hands” [by Resmaa Menakem]. It was like breadcrumbs of information. You want people to know, “it’s not all you, it’s not because you’ve done this,” it’s bigger than that.

Q. What were the biggest lessons you learned from working with your congregation to build Can We Talk…?

A. The biggest lesson I learned, or maybe the most surprising, was my own trauma. I just never even thought about it until I began, over the years, to listen to other people’s stories. I know firsthand when you do not attend to those kinds of extreme events in your life, they can come back up to haunt you. Just as I was ending the book, my older brother — my only brother — died. He had struggled all his life with alcoholism and a lot of issues, and before he died, by the grace of God, he and I got to talk about his trauma and my trauma. We both lost our parents young, which I talk about in the book, and at that time you just went on, you didn’t talk about it. That’s one thing I learned and probably the biggest lesson. I’m so glad because I’m old now and I want to figure out some things before I go to glory!

Q. What do you hope readers will take away from your book?

A. That we all have pain. I hope that people can see that the idea of listening, treating each other a little bit softer, is a way of healing. Our little gatherings are open to anybody and everybody — in Boston, we’ve had people come from all over, different cultures, different races. And people begin to try to earnestly listen to each other and hear the pain in another person, and somewhere that can touch what’s going on with you. We learn a little bit more about each other, which is important, especially now.

Q. You’re based in Florida now. Has that been a culture shock after living in Boston for four decades?

A. It’s weird! I had people calling me like, “What’s wrong with you? What are you doing?” But I came down here because I love this ocean. I found some really good people who are doing some really courageous things down here.

Q. You’re coming back to Boston soon for another event. What’s it like when you’re back here?

A. Every once in a while, I go to the Chestnut Hill Mall and somebody will say “Liz Walker!” It feels pretty good! It has been really fun to get back and to be able to speak to something that is really in my heart. It’s a gift.

Liz Walker will talk about her book with Chaplain Clementina Chéry at 6 p.m. Friday, Sept. 12 at Just Book-ish, 1463 Dorchester Ave., Dorchester; www.wordsasworlds.org/events.

Interview has been edited and condensed.

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
PULP: HERE COMES MORE “More,” the first album in 25 years from Britpop’s wryest superstar act, tackles getting older with a self-aware grace that adds shine to cuts like the besotted “Farmers Market” while giving dancefloor-appropriate (not to mention festival-grounds-ready) urgency to neo-bangers like “Got to Have Love.” Sept. 13, 7 p.m. The Stage at Suffolk Downs. stageatsuffolkdowns.com

UNCLE CHARLIE’S R&B COOKOUT One of two multi-artist soul fests happening in Boston on Saturday night — the other is headed up by sweet-voiced Y2K sensation Ashanti — this night of R&B is headlined by powerhouse singer Charlie Wilson and rounded out by hit-making crooner Babyface, silk-voiced smoothie El DeBarge, and gospel-influenced belter K-Ci Hailey. Sept. 13, 7:15 p.m. Leader Bank Pavilion. 617-728-1600, livenation.com

MARY IN THE JUNKYARD This London trio’s spectral, shambolic tunes echo the griminess and potential for wonder implied by its name. They open for kindred spirits Wet Leg, whose muscular yet expansive second album, “moisturizer,” came out in July. Sept. 14, 8 p.m. Roadrunner Boston. roadrunnerboston.com

MAURA K. JOHNSTON

ROCKPORT CELTIC FESTIVAL It’s another weekend full of words and music at this annual Celtic festival, from Friday’s opening performance featuring Quebec powerhouse Le Vent du Nord to a capstone on Monday that includes the premiere of a collaborative work composed by Liz Knowles and Ben Shattuck and commissioned in memory of Brian O’Donovan. Sept. 12-14, various start times and ticket prices per event; see website for details. Shalin Liu Performance Center, 37 Main St., Rockport. 978-546-7391, www.rockportmusic.org

THE ARAB BLUES Middle East meets Midwest with this collaboration, which pairs Rami Gabriel on guitar, oud, and buzuq and Karim Nagi on riqq, tublah, and drum kit to produce a singular sonic fusion of Chicago blues and traditional Arabic music. Sept. 12, 8 p.m. $38.15. Arts at the Armory, 191 Highland Ave., Somerville. 617-718-2191, www.artsatthearmory.org

DWIGHT YOAKAM/THE MAVERICKS It’s hard to think of a better lineup than this, at least if you’re a fan of what country music was before the bros took over. Yoakam rode in on the wave of neo-traditionists in the 1980s, the Mavs arrived with their capacious version of the music at the turn of the next decade and, decades later, both continue to make vital music. Sept. 13, 7 p.m. $35 and up. MGM Music Hall at Fenway, 2 Lansdowne St. 800-653-8000, www.ticketmaster.com

STUART MUNRO

THE MAKANDA PROJECT FEATURING RICKY FORD The invaluable Boston-based big band concludes its 20th season of summer concerts with an appearance by Boston-born, expatriate tenor sax master Ford, plus a string section from Roxbury’s own City Strings United, and more. Sept. 13, 1 p.m. Free. First Church in Roxbury, 10 Putnam St. (John Eliot Square). makandaproject.com

WAYNE BAKER BROOKS The youngest son of noted bluesman Lonnie Brooks, the Chicago native grew up amid such masters as Muddy Waters, Buddy Guy, and Jr. Wells. A soulful singer and fiery guitarist, he learned his lessons well, playing at first in his late father’s band, and now fronting his own house-rocking outfit. Sept 16, 7:30 p.m. $30-$35. Haymarket Lounge, City Winery, 80 Beverly at One Canal. citywinery.com/boston

MARY HALVORSON: AMARYLLIS A MacArthur “genius” Grant awardee and DownBeat Critics Poll winner, the adventurous guitarist and composer’s sextet includes trumpet, trombone, vibraphone, bass, and drums for a stirring, ever-shifting synthesis of composition and improvisation. And she’s from Brookline! Sept. 18, 7:30 and 9:30 p.m. $24.33-$35.97. Regattabar. regattabarjazz.com

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

ISABELLA STEWART GARDNER MUSEUM The high-spirited baroque band ACRONYM lands at the Gardner Museum with not one, but two runs through Bach’s complete Brandenburg Concertos. Sept. 13 and 14, 1:30 p.m. www.gardnermuseum.org

MISTRAL MUSIC Music by composers in the orbit of the legendary pedagogue Nadia Boulanger including her students Piazzolla, Bernstein, and Copland; her sister Lili Boulanger, a composer who sadly died at the age of 24; and her own mentor Fauré. Sept. 13, 4 p.m., Andover; Sept. 14, 5 p.m., Brookline.

LUDOVICO ENSEMBLE A portrait program of composer, singer, and pianist Judith Berkson, featuring electronically enhanced takes on songs by Schubert and Schumann as well as Berkson’s searing original music for voice, percussion, synthesizers, and other gadgets. If you liked “Switched-On Bach,” this might be for you. Sept. 15, 8 p.m. Goethe Institut Boston. 170 Beacon St. ludovicoensemble.org

A.Z. MADONNA

RENT Jonathan Larson’s Pulitzer-winning musical, inspired by “La Boheme,” about a group of bohemian friends finding, losing, and then re-finding love in New York’s East Village in 1989-90, when the scourge of AIDS was taking its toll. Directed by Marcos Santana. Featuring Aaron Alcaraz as Mark, Austin Turner as Roger, Didi Romero as Mimi, Isaiah Rose Garcia as Angel, Aaron Arnell Harrington as Tom Collins, Kat Rodriguez as Joanne, Cate Hayman as Maureen, and Kristopher Stanley Ward as Benjamin. Sept. 16-28. North Shore Music Theatre, Beverly. 978-232-7200, www.nsmt.org

SILENT SKY Set in Cambridge at the beginning of the last century, this drama by the prolific Lauren Gunderson focuses on Henrietta Leavitt (Jenny S. Lee), an early astronomer who encountered and overcame gender discrimination in an overwhelmingly male field. Leavitt discovered more than 2,400 variable stars, roughly half of those known during her lifetime, during her career at Harvard College Observatory. The cast also includes Lee Mikeska Gardner, Erica Cruz Hernandez, Kandyce Whittingham, and Max Jackson. Directed by Sarah Shin, who helmed the exquisite 2022 production of Lloyd Suh’s “The Chinese Lady.” Sept. 11-Oct. 5. Central Square Theater, Cambridge. 617-576-9278, www.centralsquaretheater.org/shows/silent-sky/

FEATHERBABY The protean Paul Melendy returns to Greater Boston Stage Company as the title character in the co-premiere of David Templeton’s comedy about a potty-mouthed and territorial Amazon parrot. When Featherbaby’s beloved owner, a crime-scene photographer named Angie (Liv Dumaine), begins to date Mason (Gabriel Graetz), a jigsaw puzzle expert, feathers start to fly. Directed by Weylin Symes. Greater Boston Stage Company, Stoneham. Sept. 12–28. 781-279-2200, greaterbostonstage.org

DON AUCOIN

A TASTE OF IRELAND Boasting a roster of world champion Irish dancers (including Gavin Shevlin and Callum O’Neill) with live music, the show comes to multiple cities in New England as part of its 2025 tour. (It debuted in the US in 2024 off-Broadway and has been making stops around the world.) Billed as a high-energy performance, the show features not just modern Irish dance, tap, and contemporary dance, but storytelling and reimagined Irish musical classics to bring cultural traditions to life. Through Sept. 28. Prices vary by location. www.atasteofirelandshow.com

IN EACH OTHER’S ARMS This new original production by Everett Company draws from true, personal stories to explore our rituals of death and dying — how we mourn, remember, and make meaning of life’s final passage. The work blends dance with storytelling and theater as it aims to open a conversation about death not just as an ending, but as a process to teach us about life. Sept. 19-20 (Brown University) and Sept. 26-Oct. 5 (Everett Stage). Free or pay what you can. Providence. https://everettri.org/

EAST BOSTON MUSIC AND DANCE FESTIVAL This annual event celebrates the rich diversity and resilience of East Boston’s Latin American communities with a day of music, food, free family-friendly fun, and dance performances, ranging from folkloric traditions to ballet, tango, hip-hop, and other genres. The celebration promises nonstop performances on two stages. Many of East Boston’s local restaurants will offer free tastings, and local artists will offer face painting, handcrafted jewelry, vintage fashion, and an array of visual art. Sept. 12, 3-9 p.m. Free. East Boston Memorial Park. www.zumix.org/event/east-boston-latin-music-dance-festival-2025/

FESTIVAL VIVA MÉXICO BOSTON 2025 A celebration of culture and community, this family-friendly festival commemorates Mexico’s Independence Day and the country’s rich heritage. Presented by the Veronica Robles Cultural Center, the event features dance, music, games, a variety of activities, local artisans, and a guest appearance by Consul General Alberto Fierro from the Consulate General of Mexico in Boston. KAREN CAMPBELL

FRED WILSON: REFLECTIONS Just opened: Wilson, a pioneering Black artist who made his name in the 1990s with the simple recontextualizing of objects to reveal neglected elements of American history (a real Ku Klux Klan hood placed in a fancy early-20th-century baby carriage; an actual 19th-century whipping post from a Maryland jail positioned in front of a cluster of ornate Victorian chairs, as though the subject of genteel spectatorship). This show, Wilson’s first solo museum exhibition in a decade, groups together two important series: his works using Murano glass, which he debuted at the 2003 Venice Biennale, of blacked-out ornate mirrors; and his flag paintings, a rereading of African national flags in black and white. The exhibition will also debut “Black now!,” a new installation of objects Wilson has collected over decades — books, T-shirts, posters, DVDs, perfume bottles, and so on — that cobble together a fractured view of Black identity and history. Through Jan. 4. Rose Art Museum at Brandeis University, 415 South St., Waltham. 781-736-3434, www.brandeis.edu/rose

MING FAY: EDGE OF THE GARDEN Closing soon: Fay, who died earlier this year, was best known for his fanciful, outsize papier-mâché sculptures of botanical forms — past works include a lychee, a walnut, a pear, a maple twirler — that he gathered together into fantastical hothouses conjured by his vivid imagination. An associated exhibition at the Pao Arts Center in Chinatown will put Fay’s work in league with the photographer Mel Taing and artist Yu-Wen Wu in an exploration of Boston’s Chinatown gardens. Through Sept. 21. Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, 25 Evans Way. 617-566-1401, www.isgm.org

MAKING HISTORY: 200 YEARS OF AMERICAN ART Closing soon: With nearly 100 works from the collection of the Pennsylvania Academy of Fine Arts, this exhibition offers a retrofit of the standard American art-historical tale with a broader, more inclusive story of the country’s diverse cohort of creative giants who shaped — and continue to shape, and expand — the very notion of American creativity. Featuring such artists as Edward Hopper, Winslow Homer, Gilbert Stuart, Barkley Hendricks, Georgia O’Keeffe, Horace Pippin, Thomas Hart Benton, Mary Cassatt, and Stuart Davis, among many others. Through Sept. 21. Peabody Essex Museum, 161 Essex St., Salem. 978-745-9500, www.pem.org

UN PRESAGIO, BOSTON PUBLIC ART TRIENNIAL Rhode Island-based artist Adela Goldbard built a quarter-scale replica of a 17th century colonial tallship -- the likes of which transported countless thousands of Europeans to the Americas as their empires expanded-- out of invasive weeds that grow in nearby New England marshes. If that’s not explicit enough for you, she’ll light it on fire at Boston City Hall Plaza Friday night after a performance fictionalizing a “first encounter” between colonists and Indigenous peoples -- which, if you hadn’t guessed, ends badly for the colonists in an inferno of retribution. And then there’s the title, translated for non-Spanish spearkers: “They invaded by sea, we responded with fire. An Omen.” Any questions? 7 PM Friday, Sept. 12, Boston City Hall Plaza, 1 City Hall Square. Free public event. www.thetriennial.org.

CHRIS GUSTIN: WILD THINGS This veteran ceramicist pushes limits. Gustin’s new show features undulant closed vessels from his “Cloud” and “Spirit” series, some up to 4 feet tall, that evoke fluidity, clouds, and figures. The wood-fired works, at once sleek and voluptuous, are marked by the artist’s original glazes and the fine settling of ash within the kiln, which melts in the firing process and washes downward. title: She’s a Brazilian in Boston. Now, she says, ‘I feel more Latina than ever.’
text:
From Boston to Worcester, Brazilian culture is infused in the places where Brazilians live and work throughout the state.

When they immigrated to the United States, they brought with them a culture that is now woven into many of Boston’s neighborhoods and nearby towns. The food, music, and warmth of the Brazilian people are easily found in restaurants, bakeries, hair salons, churches, bars, and everywhere in between.

Boston started seeing an influx of Brazilian immigrants in the 1970s, with larger numbers arriving in the 1980s as the country — geographically bigger than the continental United States — faced economic instability.

Many came to the area because they knew someone already living here, says Gabrielle Oliveira, an associate professor of education and Brazil studies at Harvard Graduate School of Education. It’s what researchers call “network migration,” when an immigrant moves knowing they’ll have support in a new country.

In this case, the network began in Minas Gerais, a mineral-rich state that provided mica to the United States during World War II, Oliveira says. A lot of families from the Brazilian city of Governador Valadares (population about 280,000) came to Massachusetts after the war. Even now, the two places remain intertwined, with families sending money and moving back and forth.

The Brazilian diaspora in the United States is the largest, with Greater Boston home to the most Brazilian immigrants per capita, though New York has the largest population.

“Brazilians in Massachusetts are much more visible,” Oliveria says. “In many parts of the state, a day doesn’t go by without people hearing some Portuguese.”

Lately, with the recent crackdown on immigration in Massachusetts and nationwide, some of those conversations have been fearful. The arrest of Marcelo Gomes da Silva, a Brazilian teenager from Milford who was detained by ICE while driving to volleyball practice, shocked many in the community.

From Milford to Everett, many Brazilian business owners say they suffered from fewer customers when the new administration came into office. But, as Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations increase in the state, many in the community say it’s time to come together and find strength in one another.

Community spaces are more important than ever, says Heloísa Galvão, 77. Born on an island in the state of Rio de Janeiro, Galvão moved to Boston in 1988 — and every Brazilian in the region seems to know and look up to her.

At a Brazilian Independence Day event in Medford in mid-August, Brazilian flags were hung all around City Hall, where children spent the afternoon playing games outside and running around in their Brazilian soccer jerseys.

Synthia Guzikowski, 41, ran into Galvão there and asked, “Do you remember me?” At first, Galvão didn’t seem to recognize Guzikowski, but Guzikowski quickly refreshed her memory: Galvão had helped to enroll her in Madison Park High School, when Guzikowski had just moved to Roxbury from Brazil at age 16.

She’s one of hundreds of Brazilian students Galvão assisted when she worked as a field coordinator for Boston Public Schools, serving specifically as a liaison between the schools and Brazilian families.

While working in the school system in 1995, Galvão started organizing get-togethers for Brazilian women. They started out small, in schools and public libraries in Somerville, meeting to discuss their experiences as immigrants in the United States. They’d talk about missing home, struggling with the English language, and all the challenges that come with raising children in a new country. It grew into the nonprofit organization Brazilian Women’s Group, formalized in 2002.

As the executive director of the group and an anchor in the Brazilian community, Galvão seems to have unlimited energy as she labors to support women in abusive relationships and raise money for families struggling financially, among other efforts. She says she dove into this work with “my whole body and soul” — and fell in love with it.

She studied journalism in college and never meant to occupy this role in her adopted homeland. But after moving to the United States, she realized how much the immigrant community needed help with navigating life in a new country.

Proud of her Brazilian heritage and culture — an ambassador in her own way — Galvão wants other Brazilians to feel the same. “I don’t want to know if you came here swimming or on a first-class flight. You’re a human being and you have rights,” she says. For her, arranging events for Brazilians to gather is one way to remind people of their roots. She’s in charge of organizing the region’s largest Brazilian Independence Day event — the 30th anniversary of this celebration. (Originally scheduled for Sept. 7, it was rained out; a new date has not yet been set.)

Like Galvão, many Brazilian immigrants will quickly tell you they don’t speak Spanish. They’re tired of the assumption, and relieved when someone else states correctly that Brazilians speak Portuguese.

The language divide between Brazilians and other immigrant groups from Latin America is one that not only confuses Americans, who often assume Spanish is the first language in all Latin American countries, but that also raises questions about identity — ethnic, racial, and cultural — among Brazilians, who come from Latin America’s largest country, speak a Latin language, and share similar culture, customs, and history with Mexicans, Colombians, and Ecuadorians.

But are Brazilians Latinos? It depends on whom you ask.

“Coming from Brazil, you are labeled as Hispanic. We’re not Hispanic,” says Guzikowski, the Waltham resident who has lived in the area since the early 2000s. “We’re Latinos, but we’re not Hispanic.”

When she moved to the United States, her school had a bilingual Portuguese program that helped her learn English and more easily adapt to her new culture. The program no longer exists.

Guzikowski soon noticed classmates wanted to understand her cultural and ethnic background, yet they were quick to label her as Hispanic. As a young person, she made sure to correct people every time. “We don’t speak Spanish. We’re not colonized by the Spanish,” she says.

Over time, the Hispanic label stopped bothering her. At age 41, she now knows who she is, she says, and labels don’t matter as much.

Many Brazilians, like Guzikowski, think of themselves as Latinos but not Hispanic, a classification found nowhere in the US Census. The census uses the terms Latino and Hispanic interchangeably with a definition that dates back to 1997. The government applies the labels to those of “Spanish culture or origin,” such as those from Cuba, El Salvador, or Chile, regardless of race. When Brazilians reported themselves as Latino or Hispanic in the 2020 Census, they were later recategorized as neither Latino nor Hispanic, according to the Pew Research Center.

In 2020, a coding error in the American Community Survey didn’t recategorize Brazilians, leading to nearly half a million, or 70 percent, of Brazilians checking the Latino and Hispanic box, showing that the government’s definition doesn’t match their experience.

These identity questions are particular to the immigrant experience. While in Brazil, most Brazilians just think of themselves as Brazilians. That is also the case for other people in other Latin American countries. In Brazil, there isn’t a strong sense of a Latino identity, despite learning in school that the country forms part of Latin America and shares borders, cultures, and histories with Spanish-speaking neighbors.

But as soon as a Brazilian person moves to the United States, they are confronted with a multitude of labels they hadn’t thought about before: Latino. Hispanic. Person of color.

Brazilians are often mixed race due to the country’s Colonial history, where miscegenation was often encouraged — not unlike many other Latin American countries.

Some continue to identify themselves as Brazilian only, and don’t think of the term Latino much, even after living in the United States for decades.

José Mário de Oliveira, a Brazilian immigrant from the state of Minas Gerais who moved to the United States in the early 2000s, says in his experience Brazilians and Spanish-speaking Latinos work together at job sites, but tend to live separate lives. While there may be solidarity and community among them while working in construction, retail, or in the restaurant industry, Oliveira says, each community tends to seek their own people when looking for a church to attend, for example.

And they often celebrate their own cultures separately too. Oliveria also helps Galvão in organizing the annual Brazilian Independence Day event in September. For him, it’s important to bring the community together, especially at a time when many are afraid to leave their homes due to current immigration enforcement policies.

When he first moved here, Oliveira says, there weren’t as many community organizations providing services for immigrants, and everything felt harder because of language barriers. Signing some government forms, for example, is easier today, he says, because instructions are offered in Portuguese.

But language isn’t always what divides different immigrant groups; sometimes discrimination comes from within a group or from other immigrants, Oliveira points out. During a recent trip to Home Depot, a worker told him he and his colleague should be deported, after learning they were from Brazil. The worker, a Cape Verdean immigrant who also spoke Portuguese, later said he was joking.

Oliveira didn’t like the joke. Despite being a US citizen, he is looking out for those who aren’t and thinks people should treat each other with respect.

Most of the time, the solidarity between Brazilians and Spanish-speaking Latinos comes from a shared struggle as they are often hustling for jobs that accept limited English-speaking skills.

Brazilian immigrants in the Boston area are overrepresented in low-wage industries, such as construction and food service, while underrepresented in other industries often associated with higher wages, including finance and manufacturing, according to a report by the Latino Equity Fund and Instituto Diáspora Brasil.

Working in the kitchen of a country club, Kamilla Teles says, most waiters never acknowledged her and co-workers with similar jobs — they’d speak to the chefs and act like everyone else didn’t exist. Her co-workers were all Latino immigrants. Once she heard a waiter call them “dumb,” which reminded her of a constant sense of inferiority she says many immigrants — Brazilian and otherwise — often feel. “Our English is never sufficient enough, our skin color is not sufficient. ...No matter how good we are, it’s difficult to get a good job,” she says. “I’m working on my self-esteem to understand that I’m not lesser than anyone else because I’m an immigrant.”

In Brazil, Teles had a career in the pharmaceutical industry, but since moving to the United States, she has worked in restaurants, food delivery, and baby-sitting.

And it’s not for the lack of proper documentation. With the right to work legally in the country, it’s still difficult to find jobs as an immigrant, she says.

It’s an experience that separates Brazilians from Americans, Teles says, but that brings Brazilians closer to other Latinos.

“At the end of the day, we’re all here seeking something. Sometimes we don’t even know exactly what we’re seeking, but we are all here with a dream,” she says. “I think that’s what unites all of us. It’s a line that connects us all — a dream.”

Despite the language barrier or census definitions, Teles believes Latinos must be united. “Living in the United States,” she says, “I feel more Latina than ever, actually.”
