title: It’s ridiculously hard to open a restaurant in Boston
text:
At first glance, District 7 Café in Roxbury looks tiny: a takeout coffeehouse with no tables. Then a bookshelf in the corner, a secret door, rolls to the left, revealing a speakeasy with a newly stocked bar. Hundreds of pennies encased in the bar top — some shining bright, some burnt black — form the name “Roxbury” and its ZIP code, 02119. Above windows looking out on Warren Road, italic letters spell a translation of the neighborhood’s 1800s Latin motto: “In this rocky borough, by God’s right, we are confident.”

It’s late September, and District 7 Café, which just got its liquor license, is rolling out its first boozy Sunday brunch. “Home of the $7 mimosa,” the owner, Royal Smith, declares as he serves waffles with chicken. He sits to chat with customers at one of the six tables. Jazz is playing: Herbie Hancock, John Coltrane. Abstract art by a local painter lines one wall: sunny yellows, earthy greens.

It’s a success story — but it’s a fragile one, because serving his restaurant’s first mimosa has taken Smith a lot longer than he’d hoped.

District 7 Café is among the dozens of Boston restaurants now serving alcohol thanks to a new state law that finally put liquor licenses within reach of entrepreneurs in more parts of the city. But uptake has been slow in the neighborhoods where it was most eagerly anticipated: Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan, the heart of Black Boston.

Restaurateurs like Smith who’ve gotten the first new licenses think they know why: The biggest problem now isn’t liquor regulation. It’s that the city makes it too hard to open a new restaurant at all.

For too long, aspiring restaurateurs in Boston faced an unjust barrier: Massachusetts’ antiquated liquor laws created an artificial scarcity of liquor licenses in the city. Restaurateurs usually had to buy one for $500,000 or more from an existing business — and that didn’t include the cost of a lawyer to negotiate the purchase and navigate the licensing system. The law tended to hold back entrepreneurs of color especially, because liquor licenses in the city cost 100 times more than in the suburbs, where town halls usually had plenty of licenses available.

Finally in August 2024, the Legislature passed a law creating 225 new Boston liquor licenses, 195 of them nontransferable and earmarked for neighborhoods outside downtown, Back Bay, and the Seaport. This year, the city and state have approved about 50 new neighborhood licenses.

This should be a boost to neighborhood prosperity. The restaurant industry has razor-thin margins and a high rate of startup failure. A liquor license helps bring more customers and more profits and supports a business model built on sit-down visits, conviviality, and community — not just takeout.

“Anywhere that has a bar, it enhances people’s dining experience, because it brings a socialization aspect to that restaurant, where people congregate,” says Marcia Satchell, owner of Blue Mountain Jamaican Restaurant in Mattapan. She just added liquor at the six-table eatery on Blue Hill Avenue, painted in floor-to-ceiling deep blues that evoke Caribbean sky and sea.

But Blue Mountain is the only Mattapan restaurant that’s applied for a new neighborhood liquor license so far. East Boston and Jamaica Plain restaurants have made the most use of the new law.

So what’s going on?

Although the new liquor licenses have opened up new opportunities, restaurateurs of color often have fewer resources to tap when they deal with the city’s slow, confusing process for opening a new business.

When Royal Smith signed the lease for District 7 Café in January 2024, the Legislature hadn’t yet approved the neighborhood liquor license bill. He was betting that lawmakers soon would, and they did.

But Smith — who’s also a cofounder of the Boston Black Hospitality Coalition — thought he’d be able to open his restaurant in 12 months. Instead, it took 18.

Smith says he spent months bouncing between City Hall and the Boston Inspectional Services Department at 1010 Massachusetts Ave. “You’re going back and forth: It’s A to B, come back to A, then go to C, come back to A, to go to D.” From January to June 2025, he says, he waited for a plans examiner to sign off on his café. During the long wait, says the café’s general manager, Carolyn Rigueur, she came close to looking for a different job.

“The Roxburys, Dorchesters, Mattapans cannot just sit idle and pay rent and insurance and labor for areas that aren’t being used,” Smith says. “The communities don’t have the deeper pockets like the bigger, established restaurant groups.” Bigger businesses often hire representatives to deal with the city’s red tape — but owner-operators like Smith have to figure it out themselves.

In 2022, the Institute for Justice, a think tank, found that out of 20 cities around the country, Boston is the hardest place to open a restaurant. The report counted 92 required regulatory steps to start a restaurant here, compared with 52 in New York City and 43 in New Orleans. “In Boston, the cost, delays, and complexity created by the regulatory process for small businesses make it difficult — or sometimes even impossible — for entrepreneurs to start their ventures,” the report said.

The process hasn’t gotten much better since. “It takes absolutely forever to open a restaurant in Boston,” says Nick Korn, a longtime bartender turned hospitality consultant and advocate for restaurateurs.

If regulation “were a for-profit business or product, or if there were something like a restaurant liaison or small restaurant advisory board,” says Korn, they’d be “identifying pain points and motivations and optimizing for the user.”

Mayor Michelle Wu has hired senior advisors to focus only on permitting reform, says Segun Idowu, Wu’s chief of economic opportunity and inclusion. An August press release from Wu points to new online systems for requesting inspections and paying for permits. Next steps include new technology. “The departments’ systems don’t talk to one another,” Idowu notes; a new platform should fix that. “We’re looking forward in 2026 to a lot more of these reforms being rolled out,” Idowu says.

Maya Mukhopadhaya opened Jadu, a Jamaica Plain coffeehouse and wine bar, in December 2024, adding the wine thanks to acquiring a neighborhood liquor license in June 2025.

In her six months seeking city permits — related to health, plumbing, and fire codes — she got contradictory instructions about which permits had to come first.

“If you ask five different people in the City of Boston what the order [is], you’ll get five different answers,” she says. “How can we expect the poor unsuspecting souls going through the process to know?”

Most city workers whom Mukhopadhaya talked to were “pleasant people who wanted to help out and not be a roadblock,” she says. But not all.

She discovered that the city’s health department and plumbing division have different rules. The health department’s website says restaurants must install either a commercial dishwasher or a three-bay sink. She chose the commercial dishwasher. Then, she says, a plumbing inspector told her no, she needed a three-bay sink; it took three plumbing inspections and her call for help to the health department to get the dishwasher approved.

“Very begrudgingly, the plumbing inspector came and signed off on our final [inspection],” she recalls. “But as a parting shot, the person — who was I think a little upset at me — said, ‘Who opens a coffee shop next to a Dunkin’ Donuts? I hope your wine bar does better.’”

City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune, who advocated for the neighborhood liquor license law, agrees the city needs to make inspections and permitting more coordinated and efficient. Sometimes “it takes pressure to move things along,” she says.

“The margins in the food industry are very, very thin,” she says. “These liquor licenses, that can help,” but “we do need more systemic reform to make it easier to speed up the process.”

While the city struggles to issue restaurant permits quickly, it’s doing better at opening the liquor license process to smaller restaurants. Until a year ago, says Korn, the hospitality consultant, nearly all restaurant owners who wanted a Boston liquor license hired lawyers. That’s no longer necessary. “The city’s done a really great job of reaching out to these small-business owners, trying to support everybody, doing more outreach than they ever had before,” he says.

Still, Boston restaurateurs have plenty of ideas that could make it easier to open new bars and restaurants:

Boston is so into giving residents every chance to express an opinion about neighborhood change — liquor licenses, new housing — that the process can become a choke point, even when there’s no opposition.

In Jamaica Plain, Jadu had to hold three “abutters meetings” with three neighborhood groups to get its liquor license. “So this four-to-five-block radius around Jadu got flyers from me three separate times about the same thing,” says Mukhopadhaya. “I asked the groups, ‘Hey, can’t we consolidate this? I feel like I’m harassing my neighbors, putting stuff on their doors.’ And it was sort of a ‘Sorry, no can do.’”

She had to go to each house three times with tape and flyers, take photos of each flyer on each door, and upload the photos to a Google Drive to send to City Hall.

In the end, she says, “There was a lot of overlap in who was in those meetings, so it just kind of felt I was meeting the same people three times about the same thing. And they weren’t anti having us in the neighborhood or anything. It was just an extremely arduous process.”

Boston’s Licensing Board and Massachusetts’ Alcoholic Beverages Control Commission use the same application form. But they don’t process applications at the same time, and they often ask different questions about them. So approval can take several months.

“It is quite common that the city will provide edits and requests and ultimately approve an application,” says Korn, “only to have the ABCC come back in a few months with some additional edits or requests.”

Last November, the Legislature passed a law that makes it easier for legal immigrants to qualify for liquor licenses as owners, partners, or managers. The little-known change could help restaurants in Mattapan and other neighborhoods popular with immigrants.

Restaurant owners praise City Hall’s technical assistance program, which connects small businesses to consultants for help with websites, staff training, and more. “I can’t really say enough about the City of Boston in terms of making sure that small businesses are supported,” says Satchell.

Mattapan has a shortage of rentable storefronts for would-be restaurants. “Residents in Greater Mattapan have consistently asked for sit-down, family-style restaurants,” says Fatima Ali-Salaam, chair of the Greater Mattapan Neighborhood Council. “A lot of landlords, because it’s easier to do, may want a convenience store.”

​Too many neighborhood storefronts aren’t zoned for restaurants or don’t have a hood-and-exhaust system for a full kitchen, Korn says. He thinks the city should rezone to allow more restaurants and work with community development and nonprofit Main Streets organizations to identify vacant spaces and help get them move-in ready for restaurants.

Boston neighborhoods also need developers to build new restaurant spaces. For years, says Korn, “new buildings were built expecting a bank or a day care or a dentist’s office, not a restaurant.” One reason: Developers knew getting a liquor license was not financially possible for startups in certain parts of town.

Market forces may eventually address that problem, but Korn thinks the city can help it happen faster. He says City Hall could encourage developers and existing landlords to accept a percentage of a restaurant’s revenue as rent instead of a flat monthly rate, to invest in the tenant and the neighborhood’s long-term success. “Occupied street-level retail spaces, especially ones like restaurant spaces that extend beyond sunset, create foot traffic and more vibrant, more safe commercial districts and neighborhoods,” he says.

Of course, raising startup money can still be harder for entrepreneurs in neighborhoods that have suffered from decades of disinvestment. Louijeune, the City Council president, says she wants to help restaurateurs get access to funds for development of new food concepts. She’s hoping to see community development financial institutions accept liquor licenses as soft collateral for loan underwriting.

Meanwhile, District 7 Café’s Smith is working on a road map to the city’s permitting process, so that it’s easier for future startups than it was for his. A growing neighborhood restaurant scene fits the times we’re in, Smith says. After COVID, he says, “community is where it’s at.” And amid cost-of-living concerns, he says, people want “cheaper eats and food while things skyrocket everywhere else.”

title: Celtics star Jaylen Brown talks decade in Boston, off-the-court impact at charity bowling tournament
text:
On a rare night off the court, Celtics stars traded in their basketball sneakers for bowling shoes as they hit the lanes for a charity fund-raising tournament hosted by Jaylen Brown on Thursday.

The first-ever The BOWL, put on by Brown’s 7UICE Foundation, took over Kings Dining & Entertainment in Back Bay, with proceeds from the festivities going to support the foundation’s work in partnership with the Yawkey Boys & Girls Clubs of Roxbury. The private event was emceed by WEEI’s Meghan Ottolini and featured Boston sports notables competing alongside Boys & Girls Clubs members.

Attendees from the Celtics included president of basketball operations Brad Stevens, head coach Joe Mazzulla, plus players Luka Garza, Anfernee Simons, and Derrick White. Former Red Sox players Lenny DiNardo and Steve Lyons also joined the fun.

“Education is important to me. Sustainability is important to me. The wealth disparity is important to me,” Brown told the Globe during Thursday’s event. “So to have people that are here that want to support that as well — and we can have fun bowling — it’s a beautiful thing."

Get Starting Point

A guide through the most important stories of the morning, delivered Monday through Friday.

Enter Email

During his introduction speech on Thursday night, Brown noted that he’s lived in Boston for a decade, and throughout that time, has remained focused on “trying to use my platform to make a difference in the community.”

“It really takes everyone coming together, collaborating, just finding those spaces to share ideas and innovate and think about what the future of Boston can be,” Brown told the crowd while praising the team behind 7UICE Foundation, which “partners with institutions, organizations and social change leaders to bridge the opportunity gap for youth in traditionally underserved communities,” according to its website.

Brown’s mother, Mechalle, who serves as the foundation’s president, noted during her opening remarks that contributions from the evening’s fund-raiser will also benefit 7UICE Foundation’s upcoming educational fair and the expansion of its Bridge Program — a STEAM-focused youth summer program — across Boston.

“I’m 29. This is my 10th year. So I’ve been here for a third of my life here in Boston,” Jaylen Brown told the Globe. “It is home. So to be able to build with the community, make friends, make family, and all that, and be able to have people grow with you, is pretty spectacular.”

And while Brown has already left quite the legacy on the court — winning a championship, being named NBA Finals MVP, All-Star honors, just to name a few — the Celtics star doesn’t quite know yet what kind of mark he wants to leave outside of basketball. But he knows that helping “impact as many people as” possible in Boston and beyond will always remain a top priority.

“I just want to use my platform and help as many people along the way as I can,” Brown said.

title: Day care should be a place for nurturing, not ICE arrests
text:
Last week in Chicago, armed immigration agents entered the Rayito de Sol Spanish Immersion Early Learning Center during morning drop-off. They forcibly removed a teacher in front of the children she nurtured every day. Children cried. Educators froze. Parents looked on in disbelief. A trusted center of learning became a scene of fear and trauma.

As leaders of Boston institutions devoted to children’s health, learning, and well-being, we feel a deep responsibility to speak out. Our organizations share one foundational promise: When a child walks through our doors, they enter a place of safety, care, and belonging.

What happened in Chicago broke that promise.

For decades, early childhood programs, schools, museums, and youth centers have been recognized as “sensitive locations.” That longstanding federal policy, grounded in common sense, acknowledged that children who feel unsafe cannot learn; parents who fear separation stop seeking care; educators who fear intrusion cannot teach or heal. This year the federal administration rescinded that policy, leaving families and educators vulnerable to exactly what unfolded in Chicago.

Get College Town

A weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns.

Enter Email

Early learning spaces are not just buildings. They are where children build the social and emotional skills that shape their futures as citizens and neighbors. When armed agents cross these thresholds, it endangers not only individuals but the moral foundation of public life.

Here in Massachusetts, we can lead. Every child-serving organization should review its safety protocols and reaffirm its commitment to keeping children’s spaces free from fear. City and state leaders should stand publicly for those protections and ensure that trauma-informed supports are available when trust is broken. All of us — parents, educators, neighbors — must raise our voices when sacred spaces for children are violated.

No child should ever witness the removal of a beloved teacher. No parent should fear drop-off. Our children are watching. Let them see adults who stand up — together — for safety, dignity, and hope.

Carole Charnow

President and CEO, Boston Children’s Museum

Sandra McCroom

President and CEO, Children’s Services of Roxbury

Robert Lewis Jr.

Nicholas President and CEO, Boys & Girls Clubs of Boston

title: For Bostonians of color, wealth is often beyond reach: ‘There’s more survival thinking than investment thinking’
text:
Cox shared her experience with a group of people in Roxbury this summer as part of a series of conversations about wealth at a time when poor and middle-class Bostonians are struggling as wages stagnate and the cost of living soars. Over the course of 26 small-group discussions in Dorchester, Mattapan, Roxbury, the South End, South Boston, Downtown Crossing, East Boston, and Cambridge, 153 community members shared stories of financial hardship and of gentrification and displacement, and a hunger for the financial freedom to spend more time with loved ones. The conversations were led by moderators trained by the RealTalk Network, a Greater Boston nonprofit coalition that holds conversations in underserved communities, in partnership with MIT’s Department of Urban Studies and Planning, and held in collaboration with the Globe.

As one participant in Roxbury put it: “When you are wealthy … you have access to a different schedule than everyone else.”

Running through many conversations was an overwhelming frustration with not having the financial literacy to build enough wealth to live a comfortable life.

A middle-age Latino woman in East Boston said she had inherited a “culture of debt” from her family because of their reliance on credit cards.

In Dorchester, an older Black woman recalled that when she was growing up, she didn’t learn how to write a check or open a bank account.

“Money is funny with Black folks,” a woman in Roxbury said. “I think within our community, money is kind of, like, evil.”

Many participants in the conversations — which were recorded and analyzed for common themes — didn’t want to be identified, as the details they shared were personal, often about their own finances. But some agreed to speak to the Globe afterward in more detail.

Cox, a lifelong Bostonian, owns a house in Uphams Corner. She’s a visiting nurse, an occasional substitute teacher, and CPR instructor, and she recently opened a thrift shop as part of her nonprofit,DAC Enterprises, that supports women and families.

Financially, she said, she’s surviving. But she will always regret not getting more advice — or trying to go in with family members to do something with the Codman Square lot — before she relented to the nonstop calls from developers who wanted to buy it. And she’s determined to help others learn from her mistakes.

“Why is it so difficult for us as Black folks to pool our funds to build our own community institutions?” she asked at a small-group discussion in Roxbury in early August.

Sometimes, Cox said, people don’t want to talk about money because they don’t want others to know what they have — or don’t have. “You get a leg up, and that’s your own little world,” she said. You get “protective of your little nest and afraid somebody’s going to ask you for it.”

A number of people brought up their families’ reluctance to discuss money, saying it was considered impolite, or even taboo.

Makai, who attended a conversation held at a Boston agency for at-risk youth, said he recently learned the budgeting rule about using 50 percent of your income on needs, 30 percent on wants, and 20 percent on savings.

“I never knew that was a thing that existed,” he said. “I just thought, you know, as long as you get your basic necessities, everything else is whatever ... you have left over.”

People who don’t have much money to begin with may not have the time, training, networks, or family resources to establish traditional pathways to financial stability, said Stefanie DeLuca, director of the Poverty and Inequality Research Lab at Johns Hopkins University and coauthor of a new study examining credit access by race and class. Paying bills late can lead to lower credit scores, for instance, which can inhibit access to loans that could be used to buy a car or take a class that could improve income potential.

“Based on 20 years of field work, I’ve observed that there’s more survival thinking than investment thinking going on among low-income families,” DeLuca said, especially for people who don’t have stable employment, live in high-crime neighborhoods, and have family members who rely on them. “It’s like a daily game of whack-a-mole to stay afloat.”

And parents pass their habits down to their children whether they intend to or not, said Ron Bell, a civic engagement organizer in Boston who helped facilitate the community conversations.

“If you see your father or your mother or your family members are going to the check cashers to cash their check, that’s what you think is normal.”

Jose, an Afro-Latino man who attended a conversation in Roxbury, said that many people in his community didn’t know they needed to have “proof of your existence as an adult.”

“If you don’t have tenant history, if you don’t have references, if you don’t have some of these things that you built along the way in this country, they don’t know who you are,” he said. “You can’t even get in the door without some type of proof of your ability to be a citizen.”

A number of immigrants and children of immigrants who took part in the conversations, four of which were held in Spanish, expressed frustration with their inability to build a better life for themselves here. Francisco, in East Boston, had hoped that the “American Dream” would allow him to establish well-being, if not wealth. But neither has come to pass.

“After so many years working, I began to think that the American Dream wasn’t meant to be experienced personally, but rather to be experienced by others, in my case, by my children,” he said in Spanish. “I think I had the wrong idea of the American Dream.”

Some people of color simply don’t trust the government or financial institutions, said Carole Montgomery, who lives on the Roxbury/Dorchester line, and that can inhibit their ability to grow their money.

“African Americans, we have a fear of actually putting our money in the bank. You still have folks who will keep their money in their house,” she said.

Montgomery, who is in her 60s, worked in commercial property management and is partially retired, owns a three-family home, and is doing OK financially. But she lost her husband five years ago and still doesn’t have a will of her own — and worries about not having her affairs in order. She also worries about a recent $600 a month increase to her mortgage payment after her property taxes and insurance both went up.

People from disadvantaged neighborhoods who break out of poverty are sometimes pulled back by the “undertow” of deep need in their community, DeLuca said, whether it’s because they are asked for financial help or they feel an obligation to offer it.

During research for her book “Coming of Age in the Other America,” about poor Black teens in Baltimore, DeLuca was told by a woman that people who found success were often clawed back down by less fortunate members of their community: “It’s kind of like crabs in a bucket.”

Bad credit can also pull people down, and the average credit score for Black individuals is about 100 points lower than it is for white people, said Nathan Hendren, an MIT economics professor who coauthored the credit study with DeLuca.

This isn’t necessarily a result of poverty or bad choices as an adult, he said. Behaviors learned in childhood can lead to low credit scores early in life. By the age of 25, nearly 70 percent of Black borrowers have late payments of more than 90 days on their credit report, research shows, twice as many as whites and more than four times as many as Asians. People with a history of late payments are given lower credit scores because they indicate a likelihood of falling delinquent in the future, Hendren said. And low scores are difficult to undo — and generate higher interest rates that make things cost more.

“It is so hard to claw your way back out,” Hendren said.

Being poor is also traumatic, said Wilbur Brown, director of the Roxbury nonprofit Transitional Remedies Solutions, which helps people recover from addiction, sexual assault, and other forms of trauma. One woman at a Dorchester conversation said that when her paycheck was deposited in her bank account just a few hours late, the experience scared “the hell out of me.”

People are hungry to escape this reality, even if it means spending beyond their means, Brown said.

“If you don’t have a lot of money, you tend to spend it on things that will help you present yourself in a way that you’re probably not, like expensive clothes or jewelry,” said Brown, 70, following his participation in a group conversation in Roxbury.

For people without much money, wealth can be a dirty word, especially when it comes to well-off buyers purchasing property in low-income neighborhoods and upending well-established community support networks.

In East Boston, Sarah, a paraprofessional for the Revere public schools, and her husband, an HVAC technician in Cambridge, have been living in a three-bedroom apartment with their three sons since 2008, when the rent was $1,875 a month. Now it’s more than twice that.

They’ve been trying to buy a home for years, but they make too much to qualify for many first-time homeownership programs, and the $700,000 loan they were approved for isn’t enough to buy a home in Boston, where they are enmeshed in the community — bringing in their neighbors’ mail, riding the T, and sending their youngest sons to vocational school.

“When you’re in that middle class, you’re stuck, and there’s nowhere to go,” said Sarah, who came to the United States from Vietnam when she was a baby.

“It becomes a vicious cycle,” said Jamie, who attended the same session in East Boston. “If you are in this income bracket where you can’t afford to live in the city where there are social services like the train, like access to Boston public schools … then you move to the suburbs where you have less services available to you, then it’s harder to live that way.”

In Roxbury, “the incredible shrinking neighborhood,” as 40-year resident Laura Younger put it, properties close to the border of the South End or Jamaica Plain tend to be described as part of those more well-to-do communities. Roxbury, she said, is often portrayed as a less-desirable area filled with crime and poverty, ignoring the many middle-class residents who live there.

“It’s just what happens when you don’t have a stable, influential, wealthy community,” she said.

And this erosion has an impact, said Younger, 75. Residents feel devalued, unity fades, and the rich history of the community’s struggles and achievements gets lost as more outsiders move in.

“I think there’s no question that wealth is used to quash people, quash ideas in community,” she said during a group conversation in early August. “It’s almost as if when you talk about, ‘How do we make Roxbury wealthier,’ it’s almost like people want to laugh. It’s like, OK, well, the way is when the new people come in, they’ll be wealthy, and you won’t be here.”

This story was produced by the Globe’s Money, Power, Inequality team, which covers the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston. You can sign up for the newsletter here.

title: Share your thoughts on this story: We asked 150 Bostonians about wealth and financial security
text:
Over the summer, more than 150 Boston area residents sat down for a series of small-group community conversations to answer a question: What does wealth mean to you?

During the course of the discussions in Dorchester, Mattapan, Roxbury, the South End, East Boston, Cambridge, and other communities, people shared stories of financial hardship and missed opportunities for wealth building, the impacts of gentrification and displacement, and how the thing they often yearn for most is the financial freedom to spend more time with their families and friends.

title: Is Harvard to blame for the public’s turn against universities? Inside Trump’s war on the school.
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

Harvard University holds a unique place in American society. The school, 140 years older than the country it’s in, has educated more US presidents and produced more Nobel laureates than any other. When a fictional character is supposed to seem smart, like the lawyers in “Suits” or the protagonist of “The Da Vinci Code,” they go to Harvard.

Yet as you’ve probably seen, Harvard has come under pressure in recent years. “The Harvard Plan,” an award-winning podcast from the Globe and WNYC’s “On The Media,” has been documenting those struggles. Its first season focused on Claudine Gay, the school’s former president, who resigned last year over criticism of her response to reports of antisemitism on campus and allegations of plagiarism. Season Two has explored President Trump’s efforts to force Harvard and many other schools to change their policies by freezing billions of dollars in federal research funding.

This season’s final episode dropped over the weekend, so I called up Ilya Marritz, the journalist who hosted the series, to discuss a few of the questions it left me with.

Ian: Conservatives often describe Harvard and other elite universities as liberal bastions. But as your series notes, those schools have also produced leading conservatives, including Trump officials. Is that a contradiction?

Ilya: I’ve even seen a term for it: elite defectors. I interviewed May Mailman, who attended Harvard Law School and is basically the quarterback of Trump’s pressure campaign on higher education. Mailman doesn’t have a lot of nice things to say about Harvard, but the credential obviously made a big difference in her life. So the argument that there’s no room for conservatives at Ivies is a little belied by the fact that so many prominent conservatives have come out of them.

But I don’t think it’s a complete contradiction because many have also been clear that being conservative on campus wasn’t a comfortable experience. I spoke to Kit Parker, a Harvard professor whose course on policing was canceled in 2021 and who was investigated by the university. There’s no doubt that Parker really cares about Harvard. But his view is that Trump’s pressure campaign, while distasteful, is the only way to get badly needed changes at an institution he feels is deeply broken.

While fighting Trump’s pressure campaign, Harvard has also gotten rid of programs and policies aimed at serving transgender students and students of color. Do people there feel responsible for some of the public backlash toward higher education?

Mailman would say the administration is giving universities cover to do things they knew they had to do but were afraid to. Even professors and administrators who consider themselves on the left feel that woke culture has gone too far and that censoriousness has been bad for campus discourse.

But I also got audio of Claudine Gay, Harvard’s former president, speaking in the Netherlands, where she was asked a direct question about this. She said, ‘No. Academia is not to blame. The agenda here is about destroying knowledge institutions because they are centers of independent thought and information.’ So I think it’s possible to feel that campus culture has drifted off course and yet not feel that it was of such great import that the federal government had to cancel billions in research grants.

Season One examined Gay’s leadership. Season Two focuses on Harvard’s current president, Alan Garber. How did that leadership change Harvard?

I attended Gay’s inauguration in the fall of 2023, when I was a Harvard Nieman fellow. It had such Obama 2009 vibes. It celebrated Gay’s immigrant background, pointing to her as the school’s first Black president but not particularly to her scholarship or thinking.

Garber has a lot more people on his side. People generally like him, speak highly of him, and feel that he listens. That may be the grace afforded to a white man who, to some, feels more familiar and less jarring. Gay was partly a victim of bad timing. But Garber served under three Harvard presidents before becoming president and is a medical doctor who sees himself as somebody who can help. It’s pretty close to a universal view that when the presidency landed in Garber’s lap, there was a sense of relief.

title: Finding beds for the homeless in West Roxbury
text:
Credit where it’s due: The easy way out for Mayor Michelle Wu would have been to fight a planned homeless shelter in West Roxbury, which has aroused considerable ire in the neighborhood. But she hasn’t done so, and now the facility appears to be closer to opening at the site of an abandoned nursing home.

The shelter is a state project, designed to house up to 40 families that have become homeless due to floods or other natural disasters, domestic violence, no-fault eviction, unsafe housing, or other causes. The location was already zoned for congregate housing, meaning there was little the city or neighbors could really do to stop it.

“The city is not in the role to decide whether this project moves forward or not,” Wu said last month. The property is going to become a shelter “one way or another,” she noted.

Which is not to say that Wu and her administration couldn’t have spent time that homeless families don’t have battling the state and hoping that the resulting delay would kill the project. The Zoning Board of Appeals, for instance, could have withheld its blessing, which likely would have forced more wrangling over the site.

Get College Town

A weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns.

Enter Email

Instead, last month the board voted 6-1 in favor of the developers.

The win for Making Opportunity Count, the group that will operate the shelter on a contract with the state, was short-lived. It took less than half an hour for the neighboring homeowners to file a lawsuit and a request to immediately halt on the project, as Universal Hub first reported. A judge denied the neighbors’ request for an injunction last week, finding that their request was premature, but left the door open for them to fight the project at a later stage in the process.

That would be unfortunate. Massachusetts, including Boston, is facing a housing crisis — and the most extreme manifestation of that crisis is homelessness. Though shelter numbers have increased due to the arrival of foreign migrants, about three-quarters of the families seeking shelter, as of April, were longtime Massachusetts residents, according to the state.

The people who would live at the West Roxbury site are not the kind of people traditionally associated with homelessness — single men living on the street or people struggling with substance use issues (not that they don’t need places to live, too). The shelter would serve homeless families with children and pregnant women.

In a decent society, homeless families have to live somewhere. And a residential neighborhood in a relatively affluent area — near grocery stores, pharmacies, and public transportation — is much preferable to the out-of-the-way hotels where the state previously housed families.

It’s certainly legitimate for West Roxbury, or any other neighborhood that’s being asked to accept a homeless shelter, to expect the state to make reasonable accommodations to their concerns. The state should be held to its promises to be a good neighbor, which include round-the-clock security, regular trash collection, and rodent control. Officials have also said that shelter applicants will have to pass background checks and that people with serious criminal convictions or pending charges will not be placed there.

What is not reasonable for neighbors to ask, though, is to stop the shelter altogether. The sad reality is that we’d have very few homeless shelters anywhere if neighbors got a veto.

Instead, the city’s emphasis should be on making the shelter work. In fact, there’s potentially an upside for the city taxpayer if homeless families originally from Boston can stay local rather than being moved to a far-flung shelter outside the city. Under federal law, kids from homeless families can continue to be educated in their home district, and it would be cheaper for the district to bus kids from a Boston shelter than from a site far from Boston.

“We will do our very best to support these families and to support the neighbors in welcoming them as part of our community,” Wu said.

With the holiday season approaching, that is the right way for public officials to talk about those in need.

Editorials represent the views of the Boston Globe Editorial Board. Follow us @GlobeOpinion.

title: At Harvard’s Carpenter Center, performance as pollination — and pollination as performance
text:
CAMBRIDGE — Tourmaline is a queer, Black, trans woman. It’s important to note these facts about her because they do so much to define her work as a photographer, video artist, activist, and author.

“Tourmaline: The Lives of a Pollinator” runs through Dec. 21 at Harvard’s Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts. The exhibition, which has been curated by the center’s Kate McNamara with Danni Shen, is an across-the-Charles homecoming. Now based in New York, Tourmaline was born and raised in Roxbury.

The most important word in the title is, of course, the artist’s name. But “pollinator” matters a lot, too. Pollination of many sorts — artistic, social, political — is central to what Tourmaline does. Even her name, shared with a gemstone, is a form of pollination, crossing mineral and human, beauty and strength.

“Pollinator” is the title of the show’s centerpiece, a five-minute video that follows the artist, sumptuously gowned, walking through the Brooklyn Botanical Garden and Edwardian period rooms in the Brooklyn Museum. That portion of the video is in a notably handsome, even dreamlike black-and-white. The image of her staring at the camera, one eye concealed by a floral headdress, is indelible.

Get Starting Point

A guide through the most important stories of the morning, delivered Monday through Friday.

Enter Email

Interspersed with those flower-filled scenes is color footage of the activist Marsha P. Johnson — Tourmaline’s biography of her was published earlier this year — and home video of the artist’s late father. His presence lends “Pollinator” a nice flourish.

Also in the exhibition is another Tourmaline video, “Atlantic is a Sea of Bones.” The title comes from a Lucille Clifton poem. Seven minutes long, the video pays tribute to the performer-activist Egyptt LaBejia. In feeling, it’s far removed from “Pollinator.”

The show includes half a dozen Tourmaline photographs. In several, we see her, a la “Pollinator,” lavishly dressed in vernal settings. Those are in black-and-white. A color photograph shows her on a terrace at the Beverly Hills Hotel. The image has a striking subtext. Overseeing a late 1940s renovation of that outpost of La La Land luxe was the architect Paul R. Williams, who was Black.

Text, sub- and otherwise, matters to Tourmaline. In a fitting touch, the show includes a Pollination Station. Intended for “reading, research, rest, and exchange,” it includes a table, benches, and stools to go with a community bulletin board and 40 books. One of them is that Johnson biography. In the gallery showing “Pollinator,” there’s a photograph taken in 1978 of Johnson, bullhorn in hand, beaming. What a grin she had. The photograph is unframed and unmatted, emphasizing a sense of immediacy. Clearly, hers was a highly active activism.

TOURMALINE: LIVES OF A POLLINATOR

At Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts, 24 Quincy St., Cambridge, through Dec. 21. 617-496-5387, carpenter.center

title: ‘You’re not alone’: Families of homicide victims find strength in community
text:
The ceremony marked the start of Survivors of Homicide Victims Awareness Month, an annual nationwide effort to educate the public, appeal to policymakers and empower grieving families. It lasts from Nov. 20 to Dec. 20. Advocates said it’s held around the holidays because this can be an especially difficult time for families.

“There’s an empty seat at our table,” said Clementina Chéry, president and CEO of the Louis D. Brown Peace Institute, which is named after her son who was 15 when he was shot and killed outside the Fields Corner MBTA station. Chéry founded the Dorchester organization in the wake of her son’s death.

“Instead of leading with my anger, I lead with my love, my faith, my hope … in making sure my child’s name is not a number,” she said.

Dozens of people attended the ceremony, where speakers endorsed proposed legislation that would create a statewide system to address unsolved homicides and increase access to bereavement leave, among other changes.

In the audience, Christine Coppin wiped away tears with a crumpled tissue. Her son was shot to death in Dorchester five years ago, but suddenly she was reliving the pain like it was yesterday.

From a few seats away, Anne Murphy noticed her neighbor’s distress and understood immediately. She slid closer and placed an arm around Coppin’s shoulders. They stayed like that for several minutes.

In an interview after the event, Coppin said the interaction brought her some unexpected peace. She said she’s still haunted by memories of her son’s death. Watching her granddaughter grow up without a father, she keeps reliving the loss.

“I’m just trying to move through it,” she said.

Even with time and distance, the grief is always there, Murphy added. Her son was killed in a 2002 stabbing in Wareham.

“Be patient with yourself,” she told Coppin, wrapping her in a hug. “Hang in there.”

Spurred to action after losing her son, Murphy now leads the Southeastern Massachusetts Chapter of Parents of Murdered Children, which supports families in her region. She said that even though Massachusetts has a low homicide rate compared to other states, these families can’t be forgotten.

“When you go through that and look at the landscape, you know things have to change,” she said. “Because as survivors, we don’t always get listened to.”

Turning pain into power means making their voices heard, said Lisa Randolph, whose brother died in a 1991 shooting in Roxbury. She placed a framed photo of him on the podium before beginning her speech.

“I would keep my grief in the shadows so that no one would know what I was going through,” she said. But that changed over time with healing and community support.

“Now, when the word beats me down, I stand my ground,” she said.

State Representative Chris Worrell said homicide survivors play an important role in anti-violence activism, calling them “the front-line workers of peace.”

“Their strength doesn’t always appear in headlines. Their leadership isn’t always seen from a podium, but it’s seen in community centers, in classrooms, in circles of grieving families,” he said. “They are holding communities together. They are interrupting the cycles of retaliation.”

The state must continue doing more to support them, said Liam Lowney, executive director of the Massachusetts Office for Victim Assistance, whose sister was a victim of gun violence.

“You’re not alone,” he told the audience. “We are all in a club that we didn’t choose to be in,” he said, but it’s a powerful community.

title: Small businesses are drowning in hidden energy costs
text:
Massachusetts residents and businesses pay some of the highest energy costs in the country: We rank the second-highest in the continental United States for electricity and first for natural gas. So Governor Maura Healey is right to be discussing energy costs and casting a wide net on solutions to a complex problem with few easy answers.

High energy costs permeate our entire economy, increasing prices for everyday items and acting as a hidden tax on health care, housing, and more, hampering the state’s competitiveness.

The 4,000 members of the Retailers Association of Massachusetts pride themselves on their commitment to sustainable business practices and believe in making a difference in their communities while managing rising business costs. But that balancing act gets tougher every day.

For example, RAM member Tropical Foods is a small independent grocer with 100 employees that has been serving diverse families in Roxbury for more than a half century. Owner and president Ronn Garry sees the impact of rising costs every day on the vulnerable population he serves. Like many other small businesses, he is constantly weighing the needs of his company with maintaining affordability for his customers.

Consuming more than 100,000 kilowatt-hour of electricity in an average month, Tropical Foods faces an annual electricity bill topping $300,000. A closer look reveals what is driving its high electric bills — and what the governor could do to help businesses like Tropical Foods.

In addition to the cost of purchasing and delivering electricity, Tropical Foods’ bill contains a number of charges — five separately listed — related to advancing the Commonwealth’s electrification and climate goals. Two charges listed subsidize solar energy, another supports electric vehicle charging, and two more pay for renewable energy and energy efficiency. Collectively these add nearly $3,000 to the business’s bill every month.

Other charges not itemized include costs for its electricity supplier to comply with the Regional Greenhouse Gas Initiative to reduce carbon emissions and to subsidize the state’s Renewable Portfolio Standard, which requires a percentage of electric power to be derived from certain renewable sources. Together, these add an additional $4,000 per month. By next year, hidden and opaque charges on Tropical Foods’ bill could total more than $80,000 per year — more than 20 percent of its total bill.

These charges — totaling billions of dollars annually for ratepayers — are a big reason Massachusetts electricity costs have nearly doubled over the past decade, far exceeding inflation.

That’s why RAM supports Healey’s increasing focus on affordability and her “all-of-the-above” approach to energy as a hopeful sign for small businesses like Tropical Foods. These include her recent openness to increasing our supply of natural gas and nuclear power and recent request to the Department of Public Utilities for cost transparency and examining charges on customers’ bills.

A House energy bill recently advanced by committee chair Mark Cusack of Braintree starts an equally important conversation. With still only 15 percent of the electricity on New England’s grid renewable and our short-term emissions target almost certainly out of reach, the bill would shift our statutorily mandated 2030 target of reducing emissions 50 percent below 1990 levels to an advisory goal. It’s based on a fundamental question: Should small businesses and their customers continue to bear these cost burdens? Or would these resources be better used to lower prices directly?

Like state health care mandates — which by some estimates now constitute a quarter of small business premiums — energy mandates are a double whammy for retailers because they not only make it harder for small businesses to employ people in Massachusetts, but they also make it harder for customers to afford living here.

Small businesses are engines of the Massachusetts economy and the anchors of some of our communities’ most vulnerable populations. With so many costs that are out of control — from tariffs to the resurgence of inflation — policy makers must act urgently and decisively on the issues we can control and seek a fairer, more cost-effective path forward. For the sake of our economy and communities, let’s begin with reliable, affordable energy.

title: Is your bus route one of the slowest in Boston? A new study shows the worst performers.
text:
Is your bus route one of the slowest in Boston? A new study shows the worst performers.

The T’s slowest buses only got slower last year, according to a study published this fall by research and advocacy group TransitMatters.

The MBTA’s 10 slowest bus routes clocked an average speed of 6.52 miles per hour in October 2024, a slight decline from 6.83 miles per hour the year prior.

The slowest high-ridership bus in New York City, by contrast, registered an average speed of 5.25 miles per hour, according to city research and advocacy groups.

Bunching — when buses on the same route travel closer together than their schedules dictate — also worsened. Bunching can undermine bus reliability and the broader efficiency of a bus system, experts warn. The percentage of bunched buses among the worst-performing routes increased from 14.1 percent to 15.8 percent between October 2023 and October 2024, the most recently analyzed time frame in the study.

The causes are manifold, says TransitMatters: worsening road congestion, rule-flouting cars, and inadequate bus infrastructure. So too are the consequences, namely, slow and sporadic bus service for some of the city’s least-privileged communities.

“MBTA bus riders are disproportionately people of color, low-income, and transit-dependent, making improvements to bus service a critical equity issue,” the report noted.

The T wrote in a statement to the Globe that “improving the speed and reliability of our bus service is one of our top priorities.”

Insulating buses from frequent and dense thickets of traffic is, transit advocates stress, among the most effective and intuitive ways to speed them up. Dedicated bus lanes, they say, do the job.

The T and Boston have publicly committed to expanding bus lanes throughout the city. Over 45 miles of dark red bus-only lanes wind through Roxbury, downtown Boston, and other nearby municipalities, the T says. Other lanes are in the works, while others have been removed.

Often in Boston, a bus lane is little more than a paint job. The city’s drivers habitually slip through or stop in them.

The T plans to begin spotting and punishing these scofflaws with bus-mounted enforcement cameras next year.

Reconfiguring traffic signals to reduce wait times at intersections could also help, advocates and experts note. The T says it has activated “transit signal priority,” as the adjustment is known, at 118 locations.

The T itself could do more to improve bus performance, TransitMatters said, namely by better managing vehicle intervals. TransitMatters observed, for instance, that the 22 bus route experiences severe bunching, despite traveling through dedicated bus lanes along Columbus Avenue. The group noted that “much of this route’s bunching can be attributed to poor operations.”

Route 1, coincidentally, claimed the top spot (for the second year running), clocking an average speed of 6.03 miles per hour. One of the T’s most popular routes, Route 1, travels from Harvard’s campus along Mass. Ave. until it hooks toward its southern terminus at Nubian in Roxbury.

The CT3 line links the Longwood medical district to Andrew Station in South Boston, cutting through Roxbury. The average CT3 bus traveled 6.42 miles per hour.

Despite being categorized as “bus rapid transit,” the SL4 and SL5 buses connecting downtown, the South End, and Roxbury are among the T’s slowest. They registered an average speed of 6.49 miles per hour, according to the study, 6 percent slower than in 2023.

Route 19, which connects Kenmore to Fields Corner in Dorchester, making stops throughout Roxbury in between, also clocked an average speed of 6.49 miles per hour.

The 66 bus, another very popular route, links Nubian to Cambridge through a more roundabout route that passes through Brookline and Allston. The 66 bus averaged 6.57 miles per hour last year.

The 45 bus, which connects Ruggles, near Northeastern University, to the northeastern edge of Franklin Park, services much of Roxbury. It registered an average speed of 6.62 miles per hour last October.

Route 91 links Sullivan Square, just east of Somerville, to Central Square in Cambridge. The 91 bus averaged 6.63 miles per hour.

The 23 bus, one of the T’s most used lines, links Ashmont to Ruggles, passing through the hearts of Dorchester and Roxbury. Buses traveling the route averaged 6.63 miles per hour last October. The 23 bus is one of three routes that are free to ride until early 2026.

The 10 bus, which loops from Back Bay to City Point in South Boston, registered an average speed of 6.65 miles per hour.

Route 28 buses, some of the T’s most popular, clocked average speeds of 6.7 miles per hour. The 28 bus connects the heart of Roxbury to Mattapan, and spends much of its route trudging up and down Blue Hill Avenue. The 28 bus is one of the three routes that are free to ride until early 2026.

Many of the T’s slowest bus routes also experienced the most bunching, according to TransitMatters. The research group defined the “bunching rate” as the share of buses where the time interval between vehicles (the headway) was less than 25 percent of the scheduled interval.

Route 23 had the highest bunching rate of 19.3 percent.

Route 111, which connects downtown Boston to Chelsea, had a bunching rate of 18.9 percent, a 14 percent increase from the year prior.

Route 1 had a bunching rate of 17.6 percent, a minuscule improvement from 2023.

The 39 bus, a popular route that connects Back Bay Station to Forest Hills, had a bunching rate of 15.9 percent.

The 32 bus, which runs a roughly straight path between Hyde Park and Forest Hills, had a bunching rate of 15 percent.

The SL4 and SL5 had a bunching rate of 14.7 percent.

The 22 bus, which also connects Ashmont to Ruggles, had a bunching rate of 14.6 percent.

Route 66 had a bunching rate of 14.4 percent.

The 28 bus had a bunching rate of 14.2 percent.

Route 57, which connects Watertown to Kenmore, had a bunching rate of 13.2 percent.

title: ‘A five-alarm fire’: Pressley demands federal action as job losses among Black women rise
text:
Her struggle mirrors a trend documented in recent federal employment data, which show the unemployment rate for Black women rising for three consecutive months.

On Monday, Inniss joined a roundtable and press conference hosted by congresswoman Ayanna Pressley in partnership with YW Boston, bringing together impacted Black women, economists, civil rights leaders, mental-health providers, and community members to highlight what Pressley called a “five-alarm fire” in the labor market.

The Democratic congresswoman from Boston has raised the issue of high unemployment among Black women in recent months, writing to Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell, as well as questioning him during congressional hearings on the Civil Rights history of the Fed policies.

Pressley Monday continued to press the central bank and federal agencies to address what she calls a “growing pushout” of Black women from the workforce.

“The feds have a statutory mandate of full employment. We need you to study the data, we need you to come up with a plan,” she said, speaking at the YW Boston Kuumba Library.

According to September’s jobs report, the unemployment rate for Black women remains almost twice the national rate of 4.4 percent.

Black women make up 12 percent of the federal workforce, nearly double their share in the overall labor force. Pressley said recent federal layoffs by the Trump administration have eliminated many jobs historically held by Black women, including roles in student aid processing, fair housing enforcement, and consumer protection.

“Nearly 70 percent of Black women are the primary breadwinners in their households,” she said. “When we lose work, it reverberates far beyond ourselves. Black women are economic ecosystems.”

Pressley also stressed how stark the crisis would appear if another demographic were affected at the same scale. “If white women were being pushed out of the labor force at the rate that Black women are, we’d be looking at the equivalent of three million white women unemployed — the entire female workforce of Pennsylvania,” she said. “If that were happening, the country would be paying attention. That’s exactly why we are calling on the fed to do their job.”

Other speakers detailed the barriers Black women face in the current job market — delayed unemployment benefits, shrinking grant and contract opportunities, and hiring processes they fear may rely on algorithms that replicate bias. Inniss said the speed of her rejection emails made her question whether automated systems were screening her out before a human ever saw her résumé.

“We all know that it’s not legal for companies to engage in racist hiring practices when the decision is happening on a human level, but my sense is that AI is playing a role in discrimination with the algorithms,” she said.

Aba Taylor, president and CEO of YW Boston, said the 7.5 percent unemployment figure only scratches the surface of what many Black women are experiencing.

“We are America’s expendables,” she said. “Overlooked, pushed down, exploited — and yet we still show up, anchor our families, and hold our communities together.”

Economist Anna Gifty Opoku-Agyeman warned that the crisis does not stop with Black women. “Don’t ignore your neighbor when their house is on fire,” said Opoku-Agyeman, a doctoral candidate at Harvard. “What’s happening to Black women economically is now reaching all women. It’s only a matter of time before it reaches other groups.”

Mental-health providers said the economic instability adds to longstanding stressors. Helen Joseph, a licensed mental-health counselor, urged employers to create trauma-informed workplaces and invest in mental-health care rooted in cultural understanding. “Everything happening in this country is creating trauma,” she said. “Our communities will feel these impacts for generations.”

For Inniss, the loss is also personal. Her great-grandmother owned a laundry service in Roxbury in the 1920s and managed to buy two homes. Today, despite multiple degrees, Inniss is still struggling to find stable work. “I look at my life and think, how is it that I have less opportunity than she did in 1926?” she said.

title: Why does a Roxbury Community College graduate earn nearly $15,000 less than a Bunker Hill grad?
text:
There are differences between the Boston colleges. Roxbury is smaller than Bunker Hill and serves students who are more likely to be low-income, Black, or entering college as an adult. The schools offer different academic programs. But are there lessons Roxbury can learn from Bunker Hill about how to better support graduates in entering the workforce?

Amid an ongoing debate over the value of higher education, the Department of Higher Education for the first time released data on post-graduation earnings of public college graduates. The data is available through the state’s Performance Measurement Reporting System and in a report released Nov. 19.

As Americans are increasingly questioning whether college is worth the money, the answer provided by this report — a resounding yes — is important. The report finds that five years after graduation, the typical Massachusetts public college graduate with an associate’s degree will earn approximately $20,000 more a year than a typical high school graduate, while a bachelor’s degree holder will earn $30,000 more.

As Governor Maura Healey said at a State House press conference, college degrees can be tools of economic mobility. “They’re equalizers, tickets to the middle class and far beyond,” Healey said.

But equally important is the report’s nuances, which suggest the value of a degree also depends on what you study and where.

Higher education leaders and policy makers should dig into the data to figure out where improvements are needed. How do colleges ensure more students complete, not just start, college? Do universities adequately inform students about the wage implications of their chosen major? How do schools expand course offerings in high-wage and high-demand majors while doing a better job connecting students in low-wage majors to jobs? Colleges can learn from one another about what works.

Unsurprisingly, one predictor of post-graduation wages is field of study. Someone who earns an associate’s degree from a Massachusetts public college who majored in health sciences will earn a median salary of $76,480 five years after graduation, while the median salary of someone with an associate’s degree in education is $45,400. The median salary for someone with a bachelor’s degree in health care or a STEM field (science, technology, engineering, and math) is more than $85,000, while those with bachelor’s degrees in arts and humanities or education will earn a median salary under $60,000, the report found.

Of course, high wages aren’t the only reason someone enters a field. Massachusetts desperately needs more early educators and special educators, and someone who loves teaching children should be encouraged to study education. But it’s also important that students choosing a major know the wage data and can make an informed decision.

Additionally, the data could be a tool for colleges to shape their programs. Perhaps colleges seeking to be engines of economic mobility could expand programs in health care, the trades, and STEM. College administrators running programs in arts and humanities could redouble their efforts to craft experiential learning experiences, allowing students to gain real-world skills and connections that make it easier to find jobs.

Bunker Hill Community College, for example, got a grant to fund internships for 300 liberal arts students. Bunker Hill president Pam Eddinger (who holds a degree in Japanese literature) said there is a need for students trained in both sciences and liberal arts. “The goal is not that you choose one or the other but how to get the liberal arts grads connected into career in a more meaningful way,” Eddinger told the editorial board.

Massachusetts Maritime Academy has the highest median wage five years after graduation for all public colleges, $98,418. The college is unique because of its focus on maritime trades along with engineering, emergency services, and STEM. Mass Maritime President Rear Admiral Francis McDonald said every degree is aimed at making students employable upon graduation. Every student does a six-month work experience, and they participate in military-style leadership training.

Beyond that, the University of Massachusetts, which is more selective in admissions than other public colleges, generally has the highest post-graduation wages, ranging from $73,000 to $81,000 depending on the campus. The other colleges’ post-graduation earnings range from a median salary of around $54,000 five years post-graduation at the Massachusetts College of Liberal Arts, Holyoke Community College, and Bristol Community College to a median salary of more than $70,000 at Berkshire and Bunker Hill community colleges and Worcester State University.

The report also found that simply enrolling in postsecondary education doesn’t drive a meaningful gain in earnings; only completing a degree does.

As this board has argued previously, public colleges and universities must do more to help students graduate. In addition to the significant financial aid Massachusetts already offers, schools should provide services like academic advising, tutoring, and help with unexpected financial expenses. Colleges can work to schedule classes at convenient times for students and ensure students can easily enroll in required courses.

The new data suggest that attending public college can provide a strong return on investment. But colleges should always be seeking ways to enhance that payoff.

title: Mass. Maritime Academy outpaces other public colleges in the state in graduate earnings, study finds
text:
Graduates of the Massachusetts Maritime Academy earned more than their counterparts at the state’s other public colleges and universities, according to a new study.

A report released earlier this month from the state’s Department of Higher Education culled data from public college graduates in Massachusetts between 2014 and 2018.

The median salary for a Mass. Maritime alum five years after graduation was $98,418, according to the report. That was followed by the University of Massachusetts Lowell at $81,050, UMass Amherst at $80,441, UMass Boston at $74,042, and Bunker Hill Community College at $73,433.

The report found that graduating from a public college or university often served as a springboard to a solid profession.

“Our data suggests that postsecondary pathways may play a significant role not only in improving earnings outcomes for all graduates, but also in reducing income gaps across lines of economic and racial/ethnic backgrounds,” the report said. “For example, gaps in median earning levels across races/ethnicities are roughly half as large among those holding associate degrees from a Massachusetts public college as compared to those holding only a high school diploma.”

Governor Maura Healey, a Democrat, emphasized that finding.

“The data is clear — Massachusetts degrees deliver,” Healey said in a statement. “When students graduate from our community colleges and public colleges, they get paid more, they have more opportunities for upward mobility, and they provide a skilled workforce for our employers.

“This is why, working with the Legislature, we have prioritized making college more affordable in Massachusetts,” the statement continued. “When we lower barriers to pursuing higher education, our students succeed and our economy succeeds.”

Ranking at the bottom of the list of the state’s 28 public postsecondary schools was Springfield Technical Community College at $59,721, Roxbury Community College at $58,807, Bristol Community College and Holyoke Community College at $53,932, and the Massachusetts College of Liberal Arts at $53,627, according to the data.

There are gaps in the data, according to the report. Information about graduates who work out of state, part time, or are in the military is not included.

“Our earnings data and analyses are not without limitations,” the report said. “As examples, the data to which we have access does not include self-employed individuals, military personnel, federal government workers, or persons employed out of state, nor does the earnings data source include hours worked.”

The report omitted graduates who worked part time, and noted that surveying salaries at the five-year mark “may not fully account for varying, long-term earnings growth trajectories by field of study.”

One factor that could explain Mass. Maritime’s leading position could be its focus on STEM-related fields, which are typically more lucrative.

“Massachusetts Maritime Academy is a top-ranked university with seven undergraduate degree programs focusing on science, engineering, technology, math, and business,” the school says on its website. “Our unique blend of academics and experiential learning allows students to learn theory, put that theory into practice, and graduate with both the knowledge and experience needed for a successful career.”

The Bourne academy offers undergraduate coursework in emergency management, energy systems engineering, facilities engineering, international maritime business, marine engineering, marine science, safety and environmental protection, and marine transportation, according to its website.

“Our 14:1 student to faculty ratio and average class size of 20 allows for personalized and direct access to our amazing professors,” the site says. “State-of-the-art labs and simulators create an immersive teaching experience that replicates real life scenarios within practice environments.”

Material from previous Globe stories was used in this report.
