title: Boston hospitals, nonprofits use cooking classes to fight rising hunger
text:
King, who sells popcorn at TD Garden in the evenings, cooks like many home chefs raised on hearty New England comfort food. Meatballs with gravy are a Sunday night staple. But he’s enjoyed the cooking classes and plans to keep coming back.

“I like this a lot,” he said, shaping patties with purple-stained gloves. “I learned something new, and it wasn’t as hard as I thought to make a vegan meal — and it smells good, too.”

King is one of a growing number of patients in Greater Boston who are being “prescribed” cooking classes as part of their medical care. From Revere to Chelsea to Roxbury and the South End, hospitals and nonprofits are leaning into the idea of “food as medicine,” teaching people with diabetes, hypertension, obesity, and other chronic conditions how to cook healthy, affordable meals, often using only what they can get from food pantries.

At MGB Revere Community Health Teaching Kitchen, two free classes a week draw a diverse group of patients, with interpretation in Arabic and Spanish. All the recipes are designed for people receiving food pantry produce — a pantry just off the kitchen serves only plant-based food and currently supplies about 150 families a week.

About 15 patients gathered for last Thursday’s class, taking turns shredding beets, chopping onions, and turning soaked cashews into a creamy garlic aioli. When the cooking was done, they sat and ate together at long tables, swapping stories like old friends.

Food insecurity is surging in Massachusetts. The Greater Boston Food Bank’s latest Food Access Report found that about 2 million adults — over 1 in 3 residents — struggled to afford food in 2024. An estimated 37 percent of households faced food insecurity, nearly double the 19 percent rate in 2019. The most severe form, where people skip meals or go a whole day without eating, has nearly quadrupled in that time, rising from 6 percent in 2019 to 24 percent in 2024.

Dr. Elsie Taveras, chief community health and equity officer at Mass General Brigham, said screening for food insecurity is becoming standard practice at doctors’ offices. She said it’s essential as food insecurity is linked to higher rates of chronic conditions such as diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease.

Across the room from King, Saida Mahjoubi said she comes as much for the camaraderie as the recipes. Participants know each other by name, and they listen as chef Elliot Kephart, a hospital dietitian, teaches about probiotics, prebiotics, and gut health.

Mahjoubi often cooks Moroccan food at home, but she has embraced unfamiliar ingredients like tatsoi, a leafy green vegetable similar to kale and bok choy.

“We’ve learned how to cook squash in the oven and use different ingredients,” she said. “If we don’t normally use it ... in Moroccan food, that’s OK. It gives us ideas that we take back home and make our own.”

Across town, Boston Medical Center’s Teaching Kitchen has become a hub for hands-on nutrition education with produce from the hospital’s expansive rooftop garden, which yields more than 5,000 pounds of food each year. There are 14 monthly in-person and eight virtual classes, free and open to any patients wanting to learn how to turn what the garden produces into soups, stews, and simple sides that can stretch for several meals.

The teaching kitchen launched in 2008 and has grown significantly as physicians focus more on treating the root causes of chronic disease through nutrition, said Olivia Thomas, a dietitian and BMC’s director of nutrition innovation and implementation.

“We have food that’s appropriate for people who are managing their blood sugar, blood pressure, and especially, those who are pregnant,” Thomas said. “We have to give people confidence to eat healthy foods we provide, because the alternatives are ultra-processed foods that are just so cheap but not as nourishing.”

Patients are typically connected through BMC’s social needs screener, which flags food insecurity and refers them to services. The hospital’s food pantry requires a prescription, and patients can visit up to twice a month. The rooftop garden supplies the food pantry, the teaching kitchen, and BMC’s cafeteria.

Beyond the hospital system, the local soup kitchen Haley House has a similar model through its Take Back the Kitchen program, where community cooks teach participants ages 9 and up everything from basic knife skills to preparing meals with produce from the organization’s one-acre farm in Roxbury. Some classes are offered for free at the Roxbury Library and the Hawthorne Community Center, while others are held in the group’s former bakery café in Nubian Square at a cost of $500 per class.

Each two-hour class brings 12 to 15 people into the kitchen to cook, share a meal, and talk about where their food comes from.

“We ask for people’s favorite recipes, and make them in a much healthier way,” said Alexander Bezek, operations director at Haley House.

Earlier this year, Mass General Brigham and La Colaborativa Community Care launched Bridge to Health/Puente a la Salud, a partnership based at La Colaborativa’s Survival Center on Sixth Street. The initiative is designed to link health care with the free, market-style food distribution and cooking support the organization already offers.

That includes expanding its teaching kitchen and inviting families to practice making affordable, culturally familiar dishes. Classes often double as community gatherings, where participants exchange recipes, swap ingredients, and leave with the groceries they need to recreate the meals at home.

“It’s food as medicine — and what does that mean in a food desert or without access to a refrigerator or kitchen because you’re subleasing?” said Dinanyili Paulino, executive vice president at La Colaborativa.

Meanwhile, back in Revere, King was planning his Thanksgiving. Although he enjoyed his first class at MGB, he grinned and said that he still planned to make meatballs and gravy part of his holiday meal. “But now I know I can do things a different way, too,” he said.

title: Robert Kraft and the Patriots continue tradition of helping local families celebrate Thanksgiving
text:
“How lucky are we all?” Kraft said. “Living in this country, even with our problems — and we’re trying to fix the problems of hate and bigotry and pushing back with our Blue Square Alliance — but we’re still the greatest country in the world. I just hope we all keep working together and make it even better.”

Among the players in attendance were quarterback Drake Maye and his wife, Ann Michael, tight end Hunter Henry and his wife, Parker, cornerback Christian Gonzalez, tight end Austin Hooper, guard Mike Onwenu, running back Rhamondre Stevenson, punter Bryce Baringer, quarterback Joshua Dobbs, and linebacker Marte Mapu.

Tackle Thayer Munford Jr., whom the Patriots signed to their 53-man roster earlier in the day, made the trip, as well. As did defensive tackle Isaiah Iton, who is on injured reserve, and two practice squad players, cornerback Miles Battle and offensive tackle Sebastian Gutierrez.

Core special teamer Brenden Schooler, who left Paycor Stadium in a walking boot after Sunday’s 26-20 win over the Bengals, also was present — sans boot — and did not have a noticeable limp. Former Patriots offensive line coach Dante Scarnecchia and Hall of Fame linebacker Andre Tippett made appearances, too.

Kraft, who has been organizing this event for 32 years, expressed appreciation for the large turnout of Patriots past and present.

“I pinch myself when I drive into Patriot Place and see Gillette and think about how I dreamt of owning this team,” Kraft said. “If the good Lord gives you health and you can live and do what you love, to come here for 32 straight years, this really is the symbol of everything we wanted to do with the team.”

Kraft called this time of year an opportunity for players to reflect on their careers and the opportunities that are aided by those around them.

“It’s just a time for everybody to pause,” Kraft said. “It’s the one time I speak to the team and just tell them I’ve been involved in a lot of businesses and there’s nothing like the NFL. Because you can care about your community, you care about winning, you’re competitive, but these guys are getting paid to do what they love. Don’t take it for granted.

“Appreciate the men on your left and right and the coaches and the effort. Because football is the true team effort. You can’t win consistently if you don’t have the right team concept, which we need in America even more now.”

As for his 10-2 Patriots? Kraft is undoubtedly excited. After back-to-back 4-13 seasons and two coaching changes, the Patriots sit atop the AFC and are in contention for the conference’s top seed and first-round playoff bye.

“I can’t tell you how much I’m enjoying this season,” he said. “It can’t get better than this. The expectations were so low. We had to make some hard decisions. Look, our family looks like we are custodians of a public asset. We are trying to manage it on that basis in putting fans first. Sometimes we make mistakes, but we want to win and know how important this team is to the whole community. That’s what drives us.”

The Patriots will practice Wednesday before having Thanksgiving off. They will then practice Friday and Saturday ahead of their “Monday Night Football” matchup against the Giants.

Although Kraft is optimistic after the team’s strong start, he knows the real tests are yet to come.

“We have the best record,” Kraft said. “I hope we have the best team. You know what we always say, ‘The real season starts after Thanksgiving.’ ”

title: Boston’s hardcore scene brings its intensity to a holiday tradition
text:
On Dec. 6 and 7, Boston’s For the Children toy drive takes over Big Night Live for two all-day, all-ages shows. It’s a big leap from the Middle East in Cambridge, where the first local events took place: Big Night Live can accommodate as many as 2,000 people. (Two-day passes are currently sold out.)

More than a dozen bands, including Haywire, Fiddlehead, Bane, Colin of Arabia, and Twitching Tongues, will take the stage each day. Each attendee is expected to bring a new, unwrapped toy for the toy drive. (Two-day attendees are required to bring a toy for each concert.) Volunteer members of the hardcore community will distribute the toys at an event at the Roxbury YMCA on Dec. 10.

The Boston FTC shows are the brainchild of Austin Sparkman, frontman for Haywire. That band has been on a roll of late: Following the 2024 release of their frenetic “Conditioned for Demolition” (11 songs in 19 minutes), they’ll be on tour in early 2026 with the Dropkick Murphys.

“Kudos to Austin,” said Pat Flynn, the high school history teacher and frontman for Fiddlehead. “He’s really kind of revived the Boston hardcore scene in a lot of ways.”

As a young man growing up in small-town Ohio, Sparkman went all-in for hardcore, booking shows out of his home. When he moved to the Boston area 13 years ago, he was adopted by the local scene, as he explained on the phone from a tour stop in the Netherlands. On the day he arrived, 30 members of the community threw a dinner to welcome him.

For a few years, Sparkman helped run Anchors Up, a hardcore venue in Haverhill. In 2015, the city shut it down after a violent incident.

Hardcore, with its rigorous mosh pits and strong-willed, sometimes warring ethical codes, might seem an unlikely community to host an annual toy drive.

“I find it so fascinating from an anthropological and sociological standpoint,” said Flynn, who counts his own band as one of the “softer” hardcore groups in Boston (“I wear, like, sweaters”). “The ethos [of hardcore] is, there kind of is no ethos.”

Sparkman agrees, noting that there are different factions that coexist under the “hardcore” umbrella — punks, skinheads, metalheads. As it has been in LA for years, For the Children is an annual opportunity for them all to come together for a good cause.

Not that they love the idea of being congratulated for doing “charity.”

“We’re not trying to be ‘do-gooders,’ at least in my interpretation,” said Flynn. “We try to stray from moral sanctimony.”

Nevertheless, two years ago Sparkman launched a fund-raiser for the family of Jimmy Flynn, the beloved Quincy hardcore promoter who died after an illness at age 40. The effort raised nearly $50,000.

In July, Haywire headlined the Back to School Skate Jam, a live music event and skateboard competition at the Lynch Family Skatepark in Cambridge. Admission was free with a donation of school supplies.

“We’re all not great people by any means,” said Sparkman of the hardcore community. “But when there is an objective, everyone can come together and make something like this happen.”

Toy donations from the FTC shows will be distributed at an upcoming event at the YMCA and members of the hardcore community will be wearing reindeer outfits, Sparkman said. Brockton’s Colin Campbell, the burly frontman for Colin of Arabia, is scheduled to dress as Santa Claus.

Campbell has had plenty of practice. For years, he said, he has “ho-ho-ho’d over the phone for my friends’ children.”

“I love Christmas, and the spirit of giving,” said this snarling hardcore singer, an Army veteran who named his band’s latest EP “Trauma Dump.” “I’m almost there with my hair and beard combo.”

FOR THE CHILDREN

Dec 6 and 7. Big Night Live, 110 Causeway St, Boston. Starting at $51. ticketmaster.com

title: Boston should return to the neighborhood school
text:
The current “home-based” method has not met its goals for academics or racial diversity, and its confusing and complex design likely hurts the city’s most needy families. The mayor and Boston Public Schools should scrap the current assignment system, consider a return to “neighborhood schools,” and focus their energy on providing access to more high-quality schools, rather than a lottery for a few.

The current system dates back more than a decade. The late mayor Tom Menino inherited a system based on “zones” for elementary and middle schools, a legacy of court-ordered desegregation starting in the 1970s. But in 2012, at the height of his political power, Menino pulled together a committee and charged it with creating a new student assignment system. After years of analysis and public meetings, a novel solution — designed by an MIT graduate student — arose.

Rather than using large zones, families would receive school lists based on where they lived and how closely they lived to schools that were deemed high-quality. Assignment, however, was still up to fate, as families ranked their schools and awaited lottery results. Coined the home-based assignment system, families were promised “higher-quality schools, closer to home,” and shorter bus rides to boot.

It was a bold move then — but that system hasn’t worked as its creators hoped. A rigorous study by MIT’s Blueprint Labs, involving Nobel Prize-winning researchers, found that the changes in assignment did not lead to a boost in test scores, graduation rates, or college access. Nor did the system make a meaningful dent in diversity: 86 percent of Boston children still attended a segregated or intensely segregated school (defined as a population of at least 71 percent white or non-white students) in 2024.

Meanwhile, busing has only gotten more expensive. Boston school transportation spending is the highest in the nation, $189 million this year even though there are 9,000 fewer children riding buses than 10 years ago. Whatever gains the home-based system captured in shortening bus distances have been lost to the snarl of Boston’s traffic, which studies place as among the worst in the country.

The city is spending a lot of money supporting an approach that simply has not worked.

So it is time to radically rethink how our schools are enrolled to deliver on the promise of high-quality schools. The city should start by creating a commission to study the best ideas and generate public engagement to build political support for a final plan.

Here is one approach worth considering: Boston could assign elementary school students in their neighborhoods (secondary schools, grades 7-12 and 9-12, could remain citywide), similar to other big cities like Chicago and Washington, D.C. “Neighborhood schools,” as they are known, is a loaded term, conjuring images of racism and strife, and of a time when schools were built to exclude children.

But a new vision of neighborhood schools is quite different and potentially progressive, allowing the system to invest more heavily in areas of greater need, literally meeting families and students where they are. It also has the added benefit of enabling children and families to develop or deepen relationships where they live, which has proven elusive in a fractured school-choice environment.

A move to neighborhood schools would result in some Boston schools becoming less racially diverse. This could be ameliorated through voluntary magnet programs or strategic siting of new buildings. But we must also be clear-eyed about the data. The fact that about 75 percent of students in the district are Black or Latino makes the math impossible to create a large number of schools balanced across all races. That was a factor cited when the federal desegregation order was lifted from Boston four decades ago.

Although research indicates that racial diversity does have positive impacts on student achievement, it is not a required ingredient for school success. Some of the most successful schools I have worked in or visited, or that operate in Boston today, have an overwhelmingly Black and/or Latino student population. Whether it is the Brooke charter network, the O’Bryant, or the Henry Grew, there are many examples of schools in the city proving that students of color can achieve at the highest levels. Implying that students of color need to be proximal to white or Asian students to be successful is incorrect and dangerous thinking.

No assignment plan can retire busing completely. State law and special education requirements will still demand a daily fleet, but even a diminished one could save tens of millions of dollars annually — money that could be reinvested in schools. Fewer buses would also reduce traffic and carbon emissions.

Critics will argue that some families will not have access to high-quality schools because all the schools in their neighborhood are deemed low performing. That is a problem. But students under the current system also attend low-performing schools. The answer is not to stick with that status quo system but to find ways to improve those schools. We should stop offering families algorithms as a substitute for what they really want.

One approach is to expand seats in high-quality schools. In my decade at Boston Schools Fund, we helped to open thousands of high-quality seats in schools in every neighborhood in Boston. Whether it was supporting the expansion to middle school for New Mission High School in Hyde Park, helping smaller but very effective elementary schools like the Nathan Hale in Roxbury add sixth grades, or working with all neighborhood schools to create a high-quality pre-K-12 pathway for every family in East Boston, the path to more quality school access was simply more quality schools.

With talented educators and a commitment to overhauling facilities, this goal has never been more possible. With a mayor who has experienced this assignment system as a parent, and with a city councilor, Ruthzee Louijeune, who served on the assignment committee in 2012, we have many political leaders with the experience and expertise to tackle this issue.

This is a deeply complex and political topic, with trade-offs and real potential benefits. Who wouldn’t want less time and money spent on buses, more money spent on academics and after-school programs, and the opportunity to go to school with your friends and neighbors?

Even the few high-level suggestions offered here will spark responses and would require immense study and debate. So let’s have it. Surely, all of the public schools in Boston deserve just as much attention for how they are enrolled as the city’s three exam schools.

We may end up back where we are, but at least we would not have accepted a status quo that we know is not working.

title: Assessing Roxbury Community College’s success
text:
Your editorial on the earnings of graduates from public higher education (“Why does a Roxbury Community College graduate earn nearly $15,000 less than a Bunker Hill grad?” Opinion, Nov. 24) was a great explanation of this data. The suggestion of sharing school, and particularly program-specific, data with students is well placed. Thank you for mentioning that financial outcomes are not the only ones that matter and stressing the need for students to have the info to make informed decisions and define their own priorities.

I worry that highlighting final outcomes of Bunker Hill and Roxbury Community Colleges might lead one to think that RCC is not doing a good job. It is certainly possible RCC is an equally effective institution if measured in terms of its contribution to student earning.

If we considered a sample of students at the two schools, with the factors that make them college ready and socioeconomically likely to earn in the future, and could compare where they would be with and without community college, we might find that the increase of earnings for the population who benefited from an RCC education is comparable. It’s a thought to consider.

Get College Town

A weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns.

Enter Email

Sterling Giles

Jamaica Plain

Higher education institutions can, and should, learn from each other. This is particularly important for community colleges, which are crucial engines of opportunity.

To that end, quantifying earnings outcomes can be useful in identifying top performers. The Massachusetts Department of Higher Education recently released a report doing just that, and a Globe editorial focused on the fact that Bunker Hill Community College graduates earn, on average, $15,000 more than Roxbury Community College graduates. This is a striking comparison, but it’s only part of the story: In a broader analysis, Roxbury outperforms Bunker Hill in student earnings.

The biggest piece of the puzzle is which students’ earnings are counted. The DHE report compares the earnings of graduates. To make the key point that earning a degree matters, that’s sound. But if you want to compare which institution is doing a better job, one should look at everyone who enrolls, as does the American Council on Education’s Access and Earnings Classification.

If you include only graduates, an institution would look better even if most students drop out while a few graduate to high earnings. When you look at earnings for everyone who enrolls, Roxbury emerges as a strong performer.

Boston is fortunate to have both of these robust community colleges, and no one benefits from a misleading comparison. But everyone can benefit by examining the practices of colleges that are serving most effectively as levers of economic mobility, which is why the organization I lead, Public Agenda, has been sharing research findings on exactly that question.

Andrew Seligsohn

Boston

The author is president of Public Agenda, a national research organization.

title: Pharmacy deserts make staying healthy harder
text:
For example, someone living in an apartment building with a package drop-off area may avoid using mail order because their package could get stolen. Someone who lacks internet access or doesn’t speak English may struggle to order prescriptions. Someone with strep throat can’t wait three days for an antibiotic to arrive.

A 2019 study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association found that adults over 50 taking cardiovascular medications were less likely to take their medication consistently after the pharmacy where they previously filled a prescription closed. That drop persisted a year after the closure. A 2024 JAMA study in Colorado similarly found that patients filled fewer prescriptions for anticonvulsant medications — which are prescribed to treat epilepsy, some types of chronic pain, and other illnesses — after their pharmacy closed.

Additionally, amid a shortage of primary care doctors, many people rely on pharmacies for vaccinations. For older residents with Medicare Part D insurance plans, physicians may encourage patients to get vaccinated at a pharmacy because it simplifies billing.

In Massachusetts, pharmacists can also prescribe birth control and order medication-related lab tests.

“They are central health hubs and are arguably one of the most accessible health care providers,” said Kaley Hayes, associate director of Pharmacoepidemiology at Brown University’s Center for Gerontology and Healthcare Research. When pharmacies close, Hayes said, “It’s taking another health care provider out of the equation.”

The largest proportion of Massachusetts pharmacy deserts (47 percent) are in urban areas, and deserts created since 2019 include neighborhoods in Boston, Springfield, Worcester, and New Bedford. Generally, urban pharmacy deserts are in areas where people have lower incomes. But pharmacy deserts are spread throughout the state, including in some rural parts of Western Massachusetts, the Health Policy Commission found. The commission defines a pharmacy desert as a census block that’s more than one mile from a pharmacy in an urban area, two miles in a suburban area, or five miles in a rural area, with an adjustment for areas with low vehicle ownership or low-income households.

One way to prevent closures is through payment reform to ensure that insurers compensate pharmacists — regardless of whether they are independent or part of a chain — a fair amount for dispensing drugs.

The Federal Trade Commission issued a report last year that documented ways in which pharmacy benefit managers (middlemen that negotiate drug prices and formularies with insurers, drugmakers, and pharmacies) negotiated higher prices for the same drug for pharmacies affiliated with the benefit managers than for unaffiliated pharmacies. The companies also use tactics like offering lower copays to steer customers to affiliated pharmacies.

Todd Brown, executive director of the Massachusetts Independent Pharmacists Association, estimated based on anecdotal reports from pharmacists that independent pharmacists lose money on about 70 percent of the drugs they dispense. “They’re left to try to eke out enough money to stay in business with the remaining amount of claims that are over the acquisition cost, but that’s becoming smaller and smaller, and PBMs are steering more claims to their own pharmacies,” Brown said.

Congress has been considering ways to regulate pharmacy benefit managers, including through an outright prohibition on the companies or insurers owning pharmacies. The Massachusetts Independent Pharmacists Association is pushing state legislation that would require insurers and pharmacy benefit managers to pay all pharmacies for drugs at a rate no lower than the rate paid by Medicaid. New York passed legislation prohibiting pharmacy benefit managers from penalizing consumers for not using pharmacies affiliated with the companies. Some states set rules around the rates that pharmacy benefit managers in Medicaid managed care programs can use to reimburse pharmacies.

But payment reform can’t be the only solution, since the decline in pharmacies is not unique to independent pharmacies. There have also been closures of chain pharmacies, retail-based pharmacies, and grocery-based pharmacies.

The Health Policy Commission research didn’t delve into the reasons for closures. Mike Tocco, president of Integrated Pharmacy Solutions, which provides pharmacy management services, said causes can include reimbursement challenges, a switch to mail order, the proliferation of shoplifting in inner cities, and the overwork of pharmacists in chain stores, which causes pharmacists to leave the field and fewer to enter.

Insurers could be part of the solution by expanding “preferred pharmacy” networks so consumers have more options to find a new pharmacy. Insurers could also cover medication for a larger number of days if a prescription is filled at a pharmacy that’s about to close, so that patients have more time to find an alternative. Community Health Centers could contribute by expanding pharmacy services in underserved communities.

One open question is whether there’s a systemic way for an insurer, pharmacist, or medical provider to reach out to customers who have filled prescriptions with a closing pharmacy to help them transition to a new pharmacy or method of ordering medication.

Legislation passed in 2024 established a state Office of Pharmaceutical Policy and Analysis. Its priorities should include figuring out how to support customers when pharmacies close — and how to shore up pharmacies so fewer close in the first place.

title: For Wu, growing Boston’s economy starts with people, not cranes
text:
“It is clearly a driver of where she spends her time and focus,” said Dr. Elsie Taveras, chief community health and health equity officer at Mass General Brigham, the state’s largest employer.

It’s not as splashy as groundbreakings and ribbon cuttings, but the shift has defined the economic development strategy of Wu’s first term. That work begins in Boston Public Schools with a push to guarantee a summer job for every student, and it extends into training and placing thousands of adults in skilled jobs. Administration officials say Wu has poured more city dollars into workforce development and secured more than $100 million in public and private grants to support it.

That focus has served Wu well, with Hasbro and other marquee companies drawn by Boston’s ability to attract, retain, and develop talented people. From early 2022, when Wu took office, through early 2025, the number of jobs in the city grew 2.7 percent, according to the most recent data from US Bureau of Labor Statistics, a pace that is faster than the rest of Massachusetts if slower than the United States as a whole.

“It’s a recognition that human capital is the bedrock on which urban success in the 21st century rests, and it is also the most plausible path to make sure that we have a more economically inclusive city,” said Harvard economist Edward Glaeser, who is known for his research on urban economies. “We don’t just want people who have PhDs from MIT or Harvard or Stanford to be able to thrive in those places. We want these to be places where lots of other people can work.”

Perhaps the emphasis on workforce development comes out of economic necessity: High office and lab vacancy rates, coupled with high interest rates, have stalled new construction. Jump-starting development would likely require giving out more tax breaks, which Wu is not apt to do. Instead, she leaned into her comfort zone: building an equitable economy, one resident and one family at a time.

While Wu’s predecessors have championed youth jobs and offered workforce training, she has gone bigger — creating a record number of summer jobs and devoting more resources to help 20- and 30-somethings who’ve felt shut out of growing industries including health care, life sciences, and clean energy. That’s led to two new signature programs: Good Jobs Metro Boston Coalition and the Life Sciences Workforce Development Initiative.

“She sees education and workforce development as a continuum,” said Neil Sullivan, the longtime executive director of the Boston Private Industry Council who has worked with six mayors. “It’s grounded in the public schools, but the commitment has to extend beyond.”

Her administration has been able to deftly tap federal money and philanthropy to create workforce development programs. In 2022, during Wu’s first full year in office, the city won a three-year, $23 million federal grant to train and place people in about 4,600 jobs in Greater Boston. The city expects to meet that goal by August; some 3,250 individuals have already trained or landed jobs as child care teachers, HVAC technicians, and EMTs, with many earning anywhere from $18 to $36 an hour.

Then, in June 2023, during the BIO convention that brought thousands of biotech executives and investors to Boston, Wu unveiled a life sciences initiative to get 1,000 city residents trained and hired at area research labs by the end of 2025.

Since then, the city has invested over $5.7 million in that effort, including a new collaboration with the Massachusetts Biotechnology Council, the state’s life sciences trade association. But the life sciences slowdown means Wu won’t meet her goal this year. Only 126 residents have completed training, with 73 placed in jobs; the city is now retooling the program to offer additional training and educational opportunities so that residents can find similar roles in health care, where labor shortages still exist.

“We have to make sure that all Bostonians have access to those jobs up and down the pipelines,” said Trinh Nguyen, the city’s chief of worker empowerment, a Cabinet-level position Wu created. “And if they don’t, we have to create ramps for them.”

Still, the heart of the mayor’s workforce development will always be with BPS students.

Since coming into office, Wu has tripled the amount of money for youth summer jobs to about $21 million annually and raised another $10 million from philanthropy. In her 2024 State of the City address, Wu promised to “guarantee a summer job offer to every BPS student who wants one.” And this past summer, a record 10,511 students enrolled in the program, up from 6,455 in in 2022.

Summer jobs are a start, but the goal is to help young people build careers. That’s why the city has been working to develop stronger partnerships between employers and schools such as Roxbury Community College, Bunker Hill Community College, and University of Massachusetts Boston.

Perhaps the best example has been the expansion of the Edward M. Kennedy Academy for Health Careers, a BPS vocational high school that prepares students for health care jobs. Early last year, the city won a $37.8 million grant from Bloomberg Philanthropies that will pay to double the number of students it enrolls to 800. It is the largest philanthropic donation ever to BPS, and the money will allow EMK Academy to expand career pathways to include medical imaging and biotech lab sciences in roles that earn upward of $100,000 annually.

Some students, in their EMK maroon scrubs, are already a regular presence at hospitals such as Brigham and Women’s and Massachusetts General, where they have paid internships. A few times a year, students visit the hospitals for hands-on training, from how to insert intravenous lines to how to deal with patient falls.

To Taveras, the MGB executive whose community health portfolio includes working with EMK Academy, the expanded partnership “is a perfect coming together of solving a pain point” that addresses labor shortages for hospitals and helps “some students see themselves in a career that can break the cycle of poverty.”

Whether Wu can maintain momentum on her workforce development initiatives remains to be seen.

Hiring has started to slow, a trend that is expected to continue amid economic headwinds. Grant money for some programs is running out, even as commercial property taxes — a key source of revenue for the city budget — slump. That may ultimately force Wu to reckon with her rocky relationship with developers.

“With housing starts slowing, cranes scarce, and too many local businesses expanding in places other than Boston, it is not clear that the right balance has been found yet,” said Dan Dain, a Boston attorney whose firm focuses on the commercial real estate industry.

The through line for Wu has been creating a city that is a desirable place to live and work — not just for the best and brightest, but for everyone. Companies will need talent at all levels to grow, and it’s that growth that ultimately will fuel the need for more office towers and housing.

That’s the case she made in victory-lap speech at a Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce forum shortly after winning the September primary.

“They’re choosing Boston because of our people,” Wu said. “Competitiveness in this economy and in this moment means working together to nurture, recruit, and promote top talent, building up the community and workforce that any company would want to consider relocating to join,” she added. “So when I say I’m fighting to make Boston a home for everyone, I’m talking about making Boston the human capital of the world, the talent capital of the world.”

Do that, she believes, and the cranes will follow.

title: Burna Boy visits Boston Arts Academy before TD Garden show
text:
Last year, Nigerian artist Burna Boy made history when he became the first African artist to sell out TD Garden. “Boston is now a part of me, Boston is now my home,” he announced at his concert on March 2, 2024, which Boston City Council declared “Burna Boy Day” throughout the city.

Now, amid his ongoing “No Sign of Weakness” tour, it’s apparent that those strong ties to Boston haven’t faded.

Burna Boy — born Damini Ebunoluwa Ogulu — made a surprise visit to the Boston Arts Academy on Tuesday, one day before his next show at TD Garden.

“If you don’t know, I’m from Boston now, because Boston is the first place to show me the kind of love that I have never seen from any city,” Burna Boy said to the crowd of over 100 students, most of whom were seniors. “I intend to give that love back 100-fold.”

Burna Boy briefly addressed the students, and announced that he planned to sponsor BAA’s community bodega, a free, donation-based store within BAA that launched in November as a way to manage food insecurity among students. This is not Burna Boy’s only initiative to fight food insecurity; he is also a partner with Reach Every Available Communal Household (R.E.A.C.H.) Nigeria, a nonprofit that distributes food and hygiene products to vulnerable populations in Burna Boy’s home country.

“Talent is evenly distributed, but opportunity is not,” he told the crowd at BAA. “So I’ve taken it upon myself to, you know, do as much as I can to make sure we all get to where we need to be.”

“It’s important for students not to feel insecure asking for help,” said Edily Perez, 17, a senior at BAA and president of BAA’s student government. She and BAA’s student government facilitated the opening of the bodega.

Perez called herself a huge fan of Burna Boy’s music. As a 13-time Grammy nominee, and one-time Grammy winner for his 2020 album “Twice As Tall,” Burna Boy is one of the most globally-recognized artists from Nigeria. His most recent album, “No Sign of Weakness,” and his song “Love” have been nominated at the 2026 Grammy Awards.

“With an international star’s support, people might feel comfortable asking for what they need,” Perez said.

Burna Boy also gave students 20 free tickets to his TD Garden show, took pictures with BAA staff and students, and restocked some items in the bodega.

Roxbury-based DJ duo SuperSmashBroz and Boston City Council president Ruthzee Louijeune facilitated the school visit.

“Burna Boy means a lot to the Nigerian community — and the Black community — in Boston,” said Louijeune. She will attend Wednesday’s concert, and noted that it will be her fourth time seeing Burna Boy perform.

According to Louijeune, Massachusetts has one of the largest Nigerian populations in the country, and the UMass Donahue Institute estimates that there are approximately 14,300 people from Nigeria living in the state.

But Burna Boy and his music represents more than just one country, Louijeune said.

“There is a diverse Black population at [Burna Boy’s] concerts,” she said. Louijeune recalled fans touting flags from Nigeria, Ghana, Haiti, and more at Burna Boy’s 2024 Boston concert, noting how the crowd felt unified by African heritage and Burna Boy’s music.

“It’s beautiful to see yourself reflected in Burna Boy,” she added.

After his appearance at the BAA, Burna Boy sat courtside for the Celtics’ win against the Knicks Tuesday night.

title: Man injured after stepping off stopped Orange Line train near Roxbury Crossing
text:
A man was injured Wednesday afternoon when he stepped off an Orange Line train that had stopped just outside the Roxbury Crossing station, MBTA officials said.

Transit Police are investigating why the train halted at that location and how a door opened, allowing the man to exit, according to Richard Sullivan, a spokesperson for the department.

The incident occurred at about 3:40 p.m. “The train door opens and an adult male intentionally steps/jumps off the train,” Sullivan said in an email.

One passenger, 14-year-old Dioni Acosta said he saw the man on the ground outside the train lying “motionless.” But Acosta did not see him fall out.

The man was not trapped beneath the train and did not require a technical rescue, according to Sullivan. His injuries are not considered life-threatening.

By 6:30 p.m., Orange Line service had resumed with delays of about 10 minutes.

No further details were available Wednesday evening.

Claire Thornton of the Globe Staff contributed to this report.

title: ‘These schools should remain open’: BPS families, staff protest proposed building closures
text:
But many families and staff who demonstrated Wednesday — first outside BPS headquarters before the meeting, then packed inside the board’s hearing room — argued that the changes would damage local school communities, particularly those of special education students.

Amanda Roberto, a parent of a student at Another Course to College, one of three facilities eyed for closure, said her son and other students have thrived in the school’s small setting. The staff works tirelessly to make sure the students are successful, she told the School Committee.

“You guys need to come up with a plan ... instead of closing down, these schools should remain open,” Roberto said.

Rayshawn Miller, a math teacher at Community Academy of Science and Health, another school to be closed, asked the School Committee to leave the school open.

“Everyone who has stepped foot in the CASH has seen and felt how well we play the cards we are dealt,” Miller told the committee, referring to the school by its nickname. “We do not lose because of our efforts. We lose because you stacked the decks for us.”

The demonstration came just over two weeks after Mayor Michelle Wu and Superintendent Mary Skipper announced the latest round of closures and reconfigurations of school buildings. The proposal called for closing the CASH, ACC, and Lee Academy.

The proposal would also cut the high school grades at the Henderson K-12 Inclusion School, converting it into a pre-kindergarten through eighth-grade school. The seventh and eighth grades would be eliminated from the Tobin Elementary School.

The closures and reconfigurations would be in place by the 2027-2028 school year.

The plan also called for the William E. Russell School, a pre-K through Grade 5 building, to add a sixth grade starting in fall 2026.

The district, in a statement released Wednesday night by spokesperson Samara Pinto, said administrators “are fully committed” to working directly with students, staff, and families if the proposal is approved by the School Committee.

“We will ensure that every student affected by this set of recommendations has a pathway to a high-quality seat at a welcoming school community,” the statement said.

BPS’s building footprint is too large for the number of students enrolled in the district. Enrollment as of Oct. 15 was 46,824, a steep drop from the 53,000 students attending BPS in 2019.

And while new migrant students helped level off the decline in recent years, with about 48,000 attending schools last year, enrollment has fallen further amid federal ICE crackdowns.

The district has a long-term facilities plan that includes a goal of shuttering nearly a fifth of BPS school buildings by 2030. BPS currently operates 109 schools, down from 114 in 2023-2024.

An earlier round of closures — approved by the School Committee in March — will reduce the total number of BPS facilities to 104. The goal is to reach around 95 by 2030, according to the district.

That facility plan serves as the district’s roadmap to 2030 by matching the number of schools in BPS to enrollment projections, the district said in its statement.

“Each of these recommendations aligns with our vision of building a district where all our school facilities are delivering the high-quality educational experience our families and students expect and deserve,” the district said.

School Committee member Brandon Cardet-Hernandez asked district administrators for more information, including whether feedback from parents and staff had led to any revisions in the proposal or transition support for kids who transfer to other schools.

“We heard obviously overwhelmingly emotional testimony from students, families, educators asking us to delay or reject the closure,” Cardet-Hernandez told his colleagues.

Ahead of Wednesday’s meeting, many families and educators waited near the meeting room’s doors, some held signs with messages supporting the schools. The demonstrators hollered “Save our schools!” as Superintendent Skipper and School Committee members walked past to enter the room and take their seats.

Families and educators rallied outside BPS headquarters in Roxbury before they entered the building. Several people gave speeches that described the importance of the schools, and they urged people to oppose the planned closures and school changes.

As they spoke, drivers of passing cars and a BPS school bus honked their horns or yelled out their support from their vehicles.

Emily Frank, a visual arts teacher at the Henderson, told demonstrators that the school’s staff are dedicated to serving students with all levels of abilities. Closures don’t realign resources, “they shatter communities,” Frank said.

“We’re not asking for special treatment, we’re asking for honesty, stability, and an educational environment where inclusion is a lived practice, not a falsely advertised promise,” Frank told the crowd.

title: MBTA investigating after Orange Line train doors open outside of station
text:
MBTA officials said investigators are interviewing an Orange Line train operator after a man was injured when he stepped off a train that had stopped just outside the Roxbury Crossing station on Wednesday.

Train doors opened on the platform side even though the train had not fully reached the station around 3:45 p.m., the MBTA said. The train did not move while the doors were open, the agency said.

Officials said they are investigating what caused the door to open but have ruled out an issue with the train itself or a mechanical problem. It is not clear why the train stopped short.

Two people got off the train as it sat in place, the MBTA said. That section of track is outdoors.

An MBTA spokesperson said they did not fall out but exited on their own.

One man was taken to a local hospital with minor injuries, officials said.

“The train door opens and an adult male intentionally steps/jumps off the train,” said Richard Sullivan, superintendent of the MBTA Transit Police.

The second person who got off the train was not injured, according to the MBTA.

One passenger, Dioni Acosta, 14, said he saw the man on the ground lying “motionless.” He did not see him get off the train.

The man was not trapped beneath the train and did not require a technical rescue, Sullivan said.

According to a Globe reporter who was on the train, it was stopped for about an hour before proceeding to Roxbury Crossing, where the remaining passengers got off. The train was then sent to Wellington Yard for inspection, the MBTA said.

The Globe reporter estimated the drop from the doors to the ground was about five feet.

Orange Line service was paused during the incident. Trains were back in service by about 5:15 p.m., according to an MBTA alert.

Claire Thornton of the Globe staff and Globe correspondent Rita Chandler contributed to this report.

title: I’ve been sucked into the Hallmark movie cult
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

I started watching because I wanted in on the joke. So I clicked on a Hallmark Christmas movie, and sure enough the most formulaic, sappy, saccharine story I’d ever seen played before my eyes for one hour and 24 minutes. I clicked on another one. Then another one, all trying to figure out the strange feeling coming over me. Was it ... satisfaction?

That was two Christmases ago. For a while, I pretended it was a joke, my Hallmark-ness, but I wasn’t fooling anyone. So this year, I found myself becoming so excited for Christmas that I had to install a brake, which was: no Hallmark movies until after Thanksgiving.

Which is now, and I’m frankly out of control. On Black Friday, I immediately signed up for the new Hallmark-Plus streaming channel and entered the predictable-feelings factory that always ends with the main characters sharing a kiss.

Soon, I was deep in subreddits trying to find the best ones from the past, parsing the various genres, where I discovered Hallmark movie factions. Was I a time-travel romance kinda guy? Or a royal princess who finds Prince Charming in flannel in a small town kinda guy? Or the career woman who finds magic and romance in a small town after she comes to shut down/write about/redevelop the local Christmas fair/Christmas tree farm/Christmas whatever kinda guy? I think the latter, but really all of them.

It’s hard to keep up, because they drop a new one every day in December, perhaps every minute. Just this week, I’ve plowed through “Christmas Land” and “Christmas Getaway,” which were aaaamazing, as well as “Melt My Heart This Christmas,” which I thought was just so-so until everyone got all nice and kissy at the end and I clapped.

Then came the nostalgia hit of “A 90’s Christmas,” where an overworked, lonely big city lawyer gets transported back to her childhood home, and, wouldn’t you know it, realizes she should have married the guy next door; and the adorable “Holiday Touchdown: A Bills Love Story,” because nothing is more adorable than Bills fans.

Kurt Vonnegut said that a good story should have an ending that is both surprising and yet inevitable. Hallmark movies skip the surprise; you’re just waiting for the inevitable, which is that the holiday festival will be saved, the couple will fall in love, and it will be the best Christmas ever.

Sure, the characters are caricatures. The women wake up in perfect makeup and manage to stay trim despite subsisting on fresh-baked cookies and hot chocolate. The men wear flannel and drive vintage pickups and, oh, hey miss, do you need help with that flat tire? Why yes, I am the owner of the hardware store that you’ve come to foreclose on, but that’s no matter, I’ve got a wrench in the truck next to my dog and we’ll get you back on your way.

It feels like this is the part where I’m supposed to say it’s indefensible to watch such cookie-cutter shlock when there are so many other things I could be doing with my time, so many truly great films I could be enjoying. But those require an effort that a Hallmark movie does not. I can pop one on at night when I’m winding down, that window when I would typically tell myself I’m going to read a book but instead end up doom-scrolling on my phone, and that soft Hallmark nostalgia will lull me into feeling all is right, that everything I need already surrounds me, and a princess could suddenly appear from Zelarnia (not a real place, I checked, but definitely the real plot of “A Royal Montana Christmas,” which I also just watched) to change everything in one hour and 24 minutes.

And yes, when I recently mentioned to my wife that I wanted to get a sherpa-lined coat, she thought she was calling me out when she accused me of wanting to look like a Hallmark guy. Wanting to? No, honey, I am a Hallmark guy.

Now let me help you with that flat tire. By calling AAA.

title: New Balance shows how inclusion is just good business
text:
It’s market intelligence.

For years, companies treated inclusion as a moral gesture instead of an economic reality. They argued about ideology while ignoring the most important force shaping their future: the customer. But diversity, equity, and inclusion never needed rescuing — it needed better analytics.

Business runs on metrics — profits, market share, viewership. And for years, many companies refused to measure the economic power of Black and brown consumers, even as we shaped the very markets they relied on. In a 2021 McKinsey Podcast, McKinsey partner Shelley Stewart III stated that businesses were missing out on a $300 billion market. Outside of Black Enterprise magazine, few bothered to count our dollars or track our influence with the rigor applied elsewhere.

Contrast that with the blockbuster data fueling the rise of women’s sports — sold-out stadiums, soaring ratings, and investment flowing into everything from women’s rugby to softball and baseball. Metrics drove belief. Metrics drove investment. Metrics are driving change.

The same economic power has always existed in Black and brown communities, but stereotypes kept companies from seeing it. Tiger Woods was treated as an anomaly. And despite Serena Williams’s undeniable dominance, her white counterparts long earned more endorsements and higher appearance fees. The star power and profitability of Black and brown audiences were were obvious; the industry simply refused to acknowledge them.

The awakening started after the police killing of George Floyd in 2020. From Misty Copeland redefining ballet to Coco Gauff electrifying tennis to Black snowboarder Zeb Powell winning gold at the 2020 X Games, companies are no longer guessing. They’re following the culture, the viewership, and the purchasing power of Black and brown communities.

I have lived the shift from an industry that once struggled to imagine me — or people who look like me — as part of their customer base. I am a proud member of the National Brotherhood of Snowsports, a 50-year-old movement that rewrote who belongs on the mountain. My first ski outfit was a canary yellow one-piece Bogner — bought when the brand’s aspirational image was European, white, and exclusive. Yet there we were: thousands of Black skiers nationwide, not asking permission to participate but expanding the market and looking good.

Timberland tells a similar story. Its boots became iconic in cities with large Black populations in the early 1990s, long before the company understood why. Biggie, Nas, Tupac, and the Wu-Tang Clan took them far from New England construction sites. Only later did Timberland follow the culture that had already embraced them.

Nike grasped the economic potential of Black and brown communities early. It built an empire around Black athletic excellence — from Michael Jordan to Williams to LeBron James — and didn’t flinch in backing Colin Kaepernick, who took a knee in 2016 to protest police brutality. Critics warned Nike to stay out of politics; Nike simply followed the market. Culture drives consumption, and culture has long been led by Black and brown consumers.

My friend Ross captured it perfectly, telling me: “Black folks don’t wait for a sale. Status is having it first.”

That is not vanity. That is predictable market behavior — the kind companies pay consultants millions to understand.

Boston has its own version of this evolution. In 2016, New Balance faced backlash after its vice president of public affairs came out in support of Donald Trump in the presidential election, and a neo-Nazi website called New Balance sneakers “the official shoes of white people.” Many of us stopped buying. The business felt out of step with the city we live in.

Fast forward eight years. New Balance now sponsors Gauff — brilliant, bold, beloved — whose presence electrifies every tennis court she touches. It sponsors Sydney McLaughlin-Levrone, an Olympic track and field marvel. It has invested in Historically Black Colleges and Universities. It has expanded its designs. And now it is supporting Sportsmen’s Tennis, a community where Boston’s athletic, cultural, and demographic future is already vibrant and visible.

New Balance didn’t change its politics. It changed its marketing to be in sync with the marketplace, because inclusion is simply the work of seeing, engaging, and honoring all the customers who shape your future.

This is not a diversity initiative. This is a business pivot — toward the consumers who shape the culture and drive the market.

The company I stopped buying from is not the company I see today. It’s following the market. It’s following the money. And it’s smart to do so.

Customers first. Profit follows. Inclusion isn’t charity. It’s reality.

Companies can rebrand DEI, reorganize it, or declare it over. It doesn’t matter. The sneaker companies know who is buying. The apparel companies know who sets the trends. The entertainment companies know who creates cultural gravity.

There’s no need to rescue DEI. It’s alive and well in the customers who are buying products. The market has already moved, and the companies that follow their consumers, not the politics, will be the ones that win.

title: Dedham pastor stands by nativity scene protesting ICE, even as Archdiocese of Boston asks for removal
text:
“There are so few voices that seem to come out and say ‘no’ to this administration,” Josoma, 70, said Tuesday in an interview at St. Susanna’s rectory. “I don’t get that. I don’t understand that.”

Outside the church’s doors, the nativity scene does not include the centerpiece figures of Jesus, Mary, and Joseph. In the empty space they ordinarily occupy are these words: ‘’ICE WAS HERE.“

“The Holy Family,” the sign’s text continues, “is safe in the sanctuary of our church.” A phone number to report activity by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents is listed at the bottom of the sign.

The Archdiocese of Boston has asked that the sign be removed because of its “divisive political messaging,” according to a statement issued last week by spokesman Terrence Donilon.

But in Josoma’s view, “any divisiveness is a reflection of our polarized society, much of which originates with the changing, unjust policies and laws of the current US administration,” the pastor said at a news conference Monday.

Josoma said he is waiting for an opportunity to discuss the issue with Archbishop Richard Henning.

In the meantime, disparaging calls and emails, many of which Josoma described as “disturbing,” are being received at the rectory and on his personal phone, the pastor said. But if he is rattled, Josoma didn’t show any signs of it Tuesday.

Dressed in a sweater and smiling broadly, Josoma recalled his upbringing in a two-family home in Brighton and how he found role models among the priests in St. Columbkille’s Parish. As a seminarian in 1976, he said, Josoma cycled across the country with a fellow student.

Along the way, “I realized anyone can be a priest, just like anyone can run a marathon. But I said to myself, ‘I want to be a good priest,’ ” Josoma said. “If it’s meant to be, it’s meant to be. Go and find out.”

The liberalizing reforms of the Second Vatican Council for the Catholic Church in the 1960s also played a key role in his path toward the priesthood, Josoma said.

Calling attention to the plight of fearful immigrants is an organic outgrowth of his mission, Josoma said. Moments before he spoke with the Globe, the pastor wrapped up a meeting about a refugee Ukrainian family that will arrive in the area this week and needs support.

The family will be the latest of many helped by St. Susanna’s and other local churches as part of an interfaith effort in Dedham.

“It’s always about compassion,” said Josoma, who decided on the nativity display after consulting with the Parish Council.

In 2017, he used a wall of the nativity scene to decry gun violence by listing locations of mass shootings and the numbers of deaths at each. Killings at Newtown, Conn.; Virginia Tech University; San Bernardino, Calif.; and the Washington Navy Yard were among them.

“This can’t be a way of life,“ he said of his motivation for the display.

The following year, he placed a cage around the infant Jesus to call attention to the detention and separation of migrant children from their families at the southern border.

“How do you feel when they put human beings in a cage?” Josoma said of the message. “I just don’t think that people like to see that acknowledgment. It’s easier to deny a reality.”

Outside the rectory Tuesday, parishioners stopped by to view the crèche in subfreezing temperatures. The parish attracts worshipers from dozens of ZIP codes, Josoma said, adding with a laugh that “we’re like the Island of Misfit Toys.”

As parishioners from Needham, Watertown, and West Roxbury dropped by, all expressed support for Josoma’s ministry.

“He’s a wonderful pastor,” said Pat Ferrone, a local leader of the Pax Christi peace movement. “He listens to everyone. He participates in everything. You can say what you need to say.”

Jeannie Connerney recalled Josoma’s kindness after her mother died in January. The pastor organized the funeral, and continues to keep in touch with her father, who is in his 90s.

Concerning the crèche, “this in my mind is what a parish should be doing,” she added.

Phil Mandeville, a parishioner and friend of Josoma’s, said the display “is not a stunt,” adding the figurines are not sacred artifacts, in any event.

“We feel compelled to make this statement. How can you sit back?” Mandeville said.

When Josoma preaches, Mandeville said, he usually ends his sermons with a challenge. One frequent theme, he said, is, “How can you remain quiet when you see people suffering?”

To Josoma, being a good priest itself comes with a mix of challenges. Among them, he said, are these: “Be true to your vocation. Be true to the Gospel. The call, I think, is from God.”

Globe correspondent Truman Dickerson contributed to this story.

title: Out of prison, Tania Fernandes Anderson is still speaking her mind
text:
“Enough of this safe politics of this pretty diplomacy thing in Boston,” she said. “It is extremely depraved.”

Fernandes Anderson spoke in the heart of the council district she once represented about three weeks after completing a monthlong sentence at FCI Danbury in Connecticut, a low-security facility with more than 1,200 inmates, according to federal records.

In May, she pleaded guilty to two of six federal wire fraud and theft charges she faced for taking a $7,000 kickback inside a City Hall bathroom from a relative who worked on her staff.

According to an indictment, Fernandes Anderson hired her relative, then gave her a $13,000 bonus with a caveat: She had to funnel more than half of it back to the councilor.

Prosecutors said Fernandes Anderson arranged the kickback when she was struggling financially, missing rent and car payments, and facing bank overdraft fees and a $5,000 fine from the state Ethics Commission for previously hiring relatives to her council staff.

Fernandes Anderson, a 46-year-old Democrat who came to the US From Cape Verde at age 10, was once a rising star in city politics. She made political history in 2021 on multiple fronts. She was the first Muslim, the first formerly undocumented immigrant, and the first African immigrant to serve on the city’s legislative body. On the council, she represented District Seven, which covers neighborhoods including Roxbury, Dorchester, the South End, and Fenway.

Her political rise came with a compelling backstory, punctuated by stints of homelessness, an eviction as a teenager, racism at school, and immigration complications.

But her political career came crashing down last year when the FBI arrested her at her Dorchester home.

She attended her final council meeting in June, and officially resigned in July of this year.

On Monday night, she spoke at an event hosted by New Beginnings Reentry Services at the Bruce C. Bolling Municipal Building. Among the crowd were local luminaries including former Boston mayoral candidate Josh Kraft, City Council President Ruthzee Louijeune, and Fernandes Anderson’s elected successor, the Rev. Miniard Culpepper.

Known for calling out racism on the City Council floor during the days as a lawmaker, Fernandes Anderson on Monday railed against the perpetuation of “intentional, systemic oppression.”

“We think about how do we defend ourselves?” she said. “We never think of the offensive plan, and we’re never ready. We’re always chasing the carrot.”

She also described her political style.

“To every battle, you need a barbarian and you need a diplomat,” she said. “And I’m no diplomat.”

She continued, “I just don’t fit in that stage, in that place where we still believe in politics and we still say ‘We should lobby the politicians’ or ‘We should go to Mayor [Michelle] Wu and tell her to move money.’ Well, there isn’t enough money, when you do the math.”

She lamented that too many people in Boston are beholden to a “government that holds the purse.” She described the city as a place “where no one dares to speak, where pretty politics take place.”

“No one will open their mouth and say ‘This is [expletive]. This is not working,’” she said.

The crowd applauded.

“If you have a contract with the city, you’re not going to say anything, if you work for the city, you’re not going to say anything,” she said. “If you are cousin, wife, son, whatever of somebody that works for the city you’re not going to say anything.”

Black people, said Fernandes Anderson, need to organize.

“We’ve just been so inundated by our stressors, by our headaches, by our problems, that we can’t organize. And then we wonder why they won’t listen,” she said.

Fernandes Anderson featured on a panel that included others who were formerly locked up, including Sean K. Ellis, who served 22 years in prison before his murder conviction was overturned because of police and prosecutorial misconduct.

The discussion was emceed by Rickey “FuQuan” McGee, who was released in October from prison after prosecutors declared he did not receive a fair trial for a 1997 murder.

During the discussion, Fernandes Anderson appeared to allude to her recent legal troubles.

“I’m very grateful for my journey,” she said. “There ain’t no shame in this game,” meaning there’s no shame in taking accountability.

She added, “It’s a book some day.”

Shelley Murphy of the Globe staff contributed.

title: President Trump has denigrated immigrants before. But calling Somalis ‘garbage’ represents a new front, historians say.
text:
Those dual actions shook both Somali communities around the United States and those who’ve tracked Trump’s history of embracing xenophobic commentary.

Trump, they said, has already adopted a mass deportation agenda, pursued a more autocratic approach to governance, and surrounded himself with fewer people willing to challenge him. To then cast an entire ethnic group as “garbage” is “just beyond the pale,” said Thomas Whalen, a Boston University professor and presidential historian.

“This is a whole new ball game,” Whalen said. He added that Trump is “sounding more authoritarian,” the very type of freedom-limiting governance that many immigrants fled in moving to the United States.

“And this plays into it,” Whalen said, “this extremist rhetoric, because all authoritarian types want scapegoats. People of color are so vulnerable, he can say, ‘This is why we have a bad economy, it’s them.’ That, to me, is concerning — and a little frightening.”

The Trump administration has defended the president’s remarks, pointing to reports about social services fraud rooted in parts of Minnesota’s Somali community, which has spurred dozens of convictions. The state is home to roughly 80,000 people of Somali descent; most of those residents are US citizens.

“President Trump is absolutely right to highlight the problems caused by the radical Somali migrants,” said Abigail Jackson, a White House spokesperson. “While the media feigns outrage, Americans who have suffered at the hands of these schemes will celebrate the president’s comments and strong support for American citizens.”

Somali immigrants represent only the latest group Trump has criticized while his administration carries out mass immigration raids in Minnesota and beyond. In public and private life, the president has routinely made racist comments and at times adopted prejudiced policies dating to the 1970s, when the federal government sued Trump for discriminating against Black people seeking to rent apartments.

Presidents in the modern era have tended to keep discriminatory remarks behind closed doors, Whalen said, such as Lyndon Johnson using racial slurs in private.

But upon entering the political arena, Trump embraced not being “politically correct,” especially on race, using his first 2015 campaign speech to accuse Mexico of sending criminals and “rapists” to the United States.

After he took office, his first administration attempted to ban travel from several Muslim-majority countries. He at times referred to groups of immigrants as “animals.”

William Roberts, senior vice president for rights and justice at the left-leaning Center for American Progress, said Trump has already shown a “pattern of egregious, outright racist statements.”

But his comments attacking Somalis felt “different and dangerous,” he said, in part because he believes “the rhetoric is coupled with a really authoritarian crackdown across the government.”

“Donald Trump has always said [things] previously under the guise of ‘I’m not going to be politically correct.’ He has always wanted to push the envelope on racism,” Roberts said. “He is feeling free to go as far as he wants to go.”

Trump has directly attacked Omar before. In 2019, he suggested that she and three other Democratic congresswomen of color, including Massachusetts’ Ayanna Pressley, should “go back” to “the totally broken and crime-infested places from which they came.” All four women are American citizens, and all but Omar were born in the United States.

Trump again targeted her last week, saying in his Cabinet meeting that she is a “real terrible person.”

Omar has repeatedly defended Minnesota’s Somali community, telling reporters on Wednesday, “We are not, and I am not, someone to be intimidated, and we are not gonna be scapegoated.”

Pressley has also come to her defense, saying that while Trump’s attacks aren’t new, “they are no less dangerous.”

“This vile hate speech toward women, people of color, and immigrant communities puts lives at risk,” Pressley said in a statement to the Globe.

Trump criticizing immigrants without American citizenship is “a very old pattern” for which “each iteration is worse,” said Jennifer Hochschild, a Harvard University political science professor. But his comments on Somali immigrants appear to be more overt, which she attributed in part to his being term-limited and surrounded by more allies.

During the Cabinet meeting when Trump attacked Somalis, Vice President JD Vance banged on the table in support. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt told reporters afterward that Trump’s remarks were an “epic moment.” And Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem later claimed without evidence that half of Minnesota’s immigration visas are fraudulent.

“There were enough people in the room during his first term who he could plausibly expect not to approve of what he was saying, so there may have been a little bit of self-discipline as a consequence of that,” Hochschild said. “Now you’ve got Vance and Noem saying the same stuff.

“There’s a very deep continuity here of real hatred,” she added of Trump, “but there’s an increasing willingness or an increasing capacity to make that explicit verbally.”

She likened Trump’s attacks on Somali people, along with recent comments about immigrants “poisoning the blood of our country,” to those used by Nazi Germany to dehumanize groups of people in the 1930s.

Trump is unlikely to see backlash over his comments from his Republican base, which has long supported his views on race and immigration, public surveys indicate. Fewer Republicans this year than last said they believed there was discrimination against racial and ethnic minority groups, according to Pew Research.

But it’s less clear how Trump’s remarks may affect gains he made among Latino and Black voters during the 2024 election, many of whom said they turned to him for his economic promises.

Whalen, the Boston University professor, said Trump’s Cabinet speech “causes all sorts of problems domestically for the Republican Party, who showed signs in the last presidential election of expanding beyond the white and Southern male base they’ve enjoyed now for several election cycles.”

Democratic elected officials have quickly rallied around the Somali community in places like Minnesota, as Somali residents have responded to the president’s latest attacks with anger and frustration.

Abdirahman Yusuf, director of the Somali Development Center in Roxbury, said in an email the organization is a “non-profit macro-social service provider” that does not engage in national politics. But, he added, “from my experience, Somali people are far from ‘garbage.’”

“Most of those I know are decent, hardworking, law-abiding citizens,” he said, “and permanent legal residents of the United States.”
