Dec. 12, 7:30 p.m. $21. Taffeta Music Hall, 122 Western Ave., Lowell. taffetamusic.com

AARDVARK JAZZ ORCHESTRA: 53rd ANNUAL CHRISTMAS CONCERT The venerable band’s holiday tradition continues, with the usual mix of carols, spirituals, and original compositions by bandleader Mark Harvey, including “The Prophet,” a musical portrait of Kip Tiernan, founder of The Greater Boston Food Bank (beneficiary of this year’s concert), and doubling as a tribute to the late, great Sheila Jordan, who sang it at the 25th annual concert. Dec. 13, 7:30 p.m. $20. Church of the Covenant, 67 Newbury St. aardvarkjazz.com

JOHN LOCKWOOD’S JAZZED UP CHRISTMAS The ubiquitous bass man’s big sound will buoy a bevy of holiday chestnuts. With keyboardist Maxim Lubarsky, drummer Ivanna Questa Gonzalez, and vocalist Nadia Washington. Dec. 18, 6 p.m. No cover. Long Live Roxbury, 152 Hampden St. longlivebeerworks.com/boston

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

A FAR CRY They’re doing one thing and (if reputation is any indicator) doing it well; a chamber ensemble from musician-led orchestra A Far Cry offers afternoon performances of Schubert’s Octet in F Major. No need to push yourself out of the house when it’s already dark to get there. Dec. 13, 3 p.m., St. John’s Church, Jamaica Plain; Dec. 14, 3 p.m., First Church, Cambridge. www.afarcry.org

MUSICIANS OF THE OLD POST ROAD This long-running period-instrument ensemble welcomes a quartet of guest vocalists for “Christmas in the Bach Workshop,” a spread of musical holiday treats composed by J.S. Bach and members of his family and its extended circle. Dec. 13, 4 p.m., First Unitarian Church, Worcester (livestream available); Dec. 14, 4 p.m., Old South Church. www.oldpostroad.org

HANDEL AND HAYDN SOCIETY H+H’s cozy holiday tradition unites the organization’s orchestra and chorus — and the Handel and Haydn Youth Choruses — at Jordan Hall, with a program of German Baroque Christmas music including Graupner’s dazzling “Magnificat.” H+H resident conductor Scott Allen Jarrett leads. Dec. 18, 7:30 p.m.; Dec. 21, 3 p.m. (sold out, waitlist available). NEC’s Jordan Hall. 617-262-1815, www.handelandhaydn.org

A.Z. MADONNA

CHARLES DICKENS’ A CHRISTMAS CAROL Will Lyman, a towering figure in Boston theater whose portrayal of King Lear on Boston Common a decade ago lives vividly in the memory, now tackles the monarch of all misanthropes, Ebenezer Scrooge. Damon Singletary plays Marley, Scrooge’s former partner and fellow miser, with Robert St. Laurence as the beleaguered Bob Cratchit. Other familiar faces include Jared Troilo and Kayla Shimizu. Adapted by Steve Wargo and replete with traditional 19th-century carols, and directed by Steven Maler. Through Dec. 23. Commonwealth Shakespeare Company. At Emerson Cutler Majestic Theatre. Commshakes.org/scrooge25

BLACK NATIVITY One of the most vibrant and cherished holiday traditions hereabouts, “Black Nativity” tells the Nativity story through the lens of the Black experience, with a cast of more than 75 performers. At the helm once again is Roxbury native Voncille Ross, who has been directing “Black Nativity’’ for nearly two decades. The production combines the “song-play” of legendary poet and playwright Langston Hughes with the music of Boston composer-arranger John Andrew Ross. All of it is gloriously sung by talented sopranos, baritones, and tenors, punctuated by percussion and expressive dance under the leadership of ballet mistress and principal dancer Desiree Springer. Narrating the show is Milton Wright, who also serves as the adult chorus director, working with his associate Marilyn Andry, while Steven Hunter Sr. is the orchestral director. Through Dec. 21. Presented by the National Center of Afro-American Artists at Robert J. Orchard Stage, Emerson Paramount Center. 617-824-8400, www.blacknativity.org

SWEENEY CLAUS: THE DEMON FATHER OF SLEET STREET It says something heartening about our fair city that so many Bostonians make room on their holiday calendars for Ryan Landry’s brand of inspired mayhem. His new show is a marriage of the Santa Claus story with “Sweeney Todd,” the 1979 Stephen Sondheim-Hugh Wheeler classic about a vengeful barber whose dotty helpmeet turns his victims into meat pies. While incorporating video more prominently than he has in the past, Landry blends the melodies of musical-theater classics with his own deranged lyrics, in a combination of homage and desecration. Directed by Kiki Samko and featuring a stellar performance as Sweeney by Thain Bertin in his first outing with Landry’s Gold Dust Orphans. Playing Sweeney’s accomplice, Mrs. Leaveit, is Landry himself. Through Dec. 21. Production by Ryan Landry and the Gold Dust Orphans. At Iron Wolf Theatre, South Boston Lithuanian Citizens’ Association, South Boston. Age guideline is 18-plus. www.tickettailor.com/events/thegolddustorphans/1732579/

DON AUCOIN

TAFUTA: A YOUNG CHILD’S SEARCH FOR THE TRUE MEANING OF KWANZAA OrigiNation Cultural Arts Center presents this annual holiday production, which portrays the story of a child overcoming bullying for their family’s belief in the traditions of Kwanzaa. The family-friendly show combines dance, music, and poetry, and it features an ensemble of Boston-area youth alongside adult performers to illuminate the joy and meaning of the pan-African holiday and its seven core principles. Dec. 12. $25. Roxbury Community College Media Arts Center Auditorium. www.originationinc.org

ANTHONY WILLIAMS’S URBAN NUTCRACKER Now in its 25th anniversary season, this lively production is quintessential Boston, with Williams setting his version of the holiday ballet amid iconic landmarks, from the Citgo sign to the State House. Fusing Tchaikovsky’s original music with Duke Ellington’s jazzy “Nutcracker Suite,” the score fuels choreography that embraces not just ballet but also hip-hop, jazz, breakdance, tap, even flamenco as it celebrates the city’s rich diversity. Dec. 13-21. $29-$125. Boch Center Shubert Theatre. www.urbannutcracker.com

ANNE PLAMONDON PRODUCTIONS The Canadian contemporary dance company makes its Boston debut with “Myokine.” Named for the feel-good proteins released by muscles during physical activity (sometimes called “molecules of hope”), the 2023 work for seven performers explores dance’s powerful ability to help the body release tension and anxiety, promoting resilience and well-being. And who couldn’t use a shot of that right about now? Dec. 13-14. $66 and up. Global Arts Live at ICA/Boston. www.globalartslove.org

FUNNY UNCLE CABARET Sweet, whimsical, and often touching, Peter DiMuro’s alternative holiday show uses dance, choirs of singing children, and cabaret to celebrate the magic and joy of the season with the families we choose, not just those we are born into. Presented by DiMuro’s Public Displays of Motion, the show celebrates a landmark 25 years of LGBTQIA+ themes and variations. Dec 13–14. $21.05 and up. The Dance Complex, Cambridge. www.dancecomplex.org

KAREN CAMPBELL

ARSHILE GORKY: REDRAWING COMMUNITY AND CONNECTIONS Just open: The Armenian-American artist Arshile Gorky arrived in the United States in 1920 as a teenager, having survived the Armenian genocide in 1915 and then a dark period in Russia where his mother died of starvation. Arriving in Watertown, the young Gorky found his way to Boston’s New England School of Art in 1923, where his professional arc as a foundational member of Abstract Expressionism, the very first bonafide international art movement made in America, would begin. This show, at Watertown’s Armenian Museum of America, includes works made between 1925 to 1947, and a significant number of his early portraits — the artist’s attempt to capture the community in his new home that helped to make his shattered life more whole. Dec. 12-April 30. Armenian Museum of America, 65 Main St., Watertown. 617-926-2562, armenianmuseum.org

RITUALS FOR REMEMBERING: MARÍA MAGDALENA CAMPOS-PONS AND ANA MENDIETA María Magdalena Campos-Pons and Ana Mendieta never met, which seems odd on many counts: Of similar age, both were exiled dissidents from Cuba living in the United States, making art about the alienation of displacement, often in the elemental language of earth, air, water, and fire. Mendieta, born in 1948 (she died in 1985) was a key member of a cadre of artists in New York who used performance to communicate visceral truths; in her “Silueta Series,” she embedded female forms — and sometimes her own body — in the landscape, emphasizing human connection to something larger than ephemeral political systems. Campos-Pons, born in Cuba in 1959 and now working in Nashville, works with a myriad of materials, from ceramic and clay to video and sound, to conjure deep cultural connection that endures political trauma; her “A Town Portrait,” 1994, now installed at the MFA, evokes the legacies of the colonial sugar industry. Through Feb. 15. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, mfa.org

FINDING MAINE: THE WYETH FAMILY OF ARTISTS Ending soon: With this exhibition, the Farnsworth presents three generations of Wyeths at once: N.C.; his son, Andrew; and his son, Jamie. The Wyeths’ longstanding presence in and around Port Clyde is the stuff of local legend and considerable pride, but this is also an extended family affair, with works by Henriette Wyeth Hurd, John McCoy, Merle James, and others. Through Dec. 31. Farnsworth Art Museum, 16 Museum St., Rockland, Maine. 207-596-6457, www.farnsworthmuseum.org

MURRAY WHYTE

A ÉL MISMO: CHRISTIAN HERNÁN DE RESTREPO What if the Spanish had never colonized Latin America? This Boston artist known for sculptural weavings here reimagines history. De Restrepo, a first-generation Colombian, reflects on his family’s 1985 journey north through Mexico with ritual objects that honor Indigenous pre-Hispanic cultures and wonder how the people, the culture, and the land would look today if the Spanish had never come. Heather McGrath curates. Through March 7. Mills Gallery, Boston Center for the Arts, 551 Tremont St. 617-426-5000,www.bostonarts.org

CATE McQUAID

NICO CATTANEO AND FRIENDS Boston native Cattaneo headlines Goofs for the first time, with fellow comics Laith, Emily Ruskowski, Tooky Kavanagh, Ryan Howe, and Isabel Thurston, plus musical guest Madoc. Dec. 12-13, 7 p.m., 9 p.m., and 11 p.m. $25. Goofs Comedy Club, 432 McGrath Highway, Somerville. www.goofscomedy.com

FRUITCAKES Wicked Queer Comedy presents this fund-raiser for The Network/LaRed, an organization led by survivors working to end partner abuse, hosted by Mel Moscoso and Shelby LeCuyer, with comedy from Sky Nockels and El Kennedy and drag from Tilda Watersclear and Kiera Knox. Dec. 12, 8 p.m. Donation suggested. Democracy Brewing, 35 Temple Place, Boston. www.eventbrite.com/e/fruitcakes-a-holiday-comedy-and-drag-fundraiser-tickets-1977154063026

JOE WONG “Trump wants to build a wall to stop immigrations,” says Wong, who spent some of his early years honing his comedy in Boston. “I’m from China. So I know a lot about walls. They don’t work. And centuries later, it’s just going to become a huge tourist attraction. With Dan Boulger. Dec. 14, 7 p.m. $40.46. Laugh Boston, 425 Summer St.. 617-725-2844, www.laughboston.com

FOOD FOR THOUGHTS Hard to beat the lineup for this Greater Boston Food Bank fund-raiser, with Tony V headlining, plus Tooky Kavanagh, Caroline Moore, Liam McGurk, Corey Rodrigues, and Brieana Woodward. Ticket discount for those who bring three food items. Dec. 15, 8 p.m. $13.95-$23.95. The Comedy Studio, 5 John F. Kennedy St., Cambridge. www.thecomedystudio.com

NICK A. ZAINO III

title: Boston Children’s Hospital plans new $640m pediatric psychiatric hospital with historic Hale donation
text:
The 116-bed building, to be located on the over 10-acre campus of Franciscan Children’s, will house several services beyond inpatient psychiatric care. Those offerings include a partial hospital program and intensive outpatient program, a 14-bedroom acute treatment program, a dental suite, four operating rooms, a pharmacy, outpatient rehabilitation programs, and five outdoor play spaces. The first building is expected to break ground in 2026 and open by 2029, an executive said.

The hospital system will relocate inpatient units from Waltham to Brighton, though medical psychiatric beds will remain in Longwood. In all, the project will nearly double Children’s inpatient psychiatric capacity, hospital officials said.

The Hales’ donation, which includes naming rights to the building, materializes a vision that hospital executives have had for the campus since Children’s announced its acquisition of Franciscan in 2021. This project is only the start.

“We envision, ultimately, over the next 10 to 20 years, continued development of that site,” said Dr. Kevin Churchwell, chief executive of Boston Children’s Hospital. He touted the project as both an expansion of clinical services and a place to teach the next generation of pediatric caregivers and clinicians.

Hospital leaders also envision new research opportunities to develop objective measures of when children are improving or worsening as they grapple with mental illness.

There has been a longstanding shortage of mental health care availability for children, which was exacerbated by the pandemic. Pediatric patients were sometimes spending days to weeks “boarding” in emergency rooms as they waited for an inpatient psychiatric bed to open up. At one point in May 2023, Children’s saw more than 90 children in its emergency room in one day needing psychiatric care.

“That was our pandemic,” Churchwell said.

The hospital and the state have worked to better care for those children, triaging them and sending them to the right kind of care sooner. But still there is a need for more services, hospital officials say.

A state snapshot of surveyed hospitals in November showed there were 48 pediatric patients boarding at hospitals throughout the state. In November 2024, that number ranged from 48 to 71 in weekly reports.

Even as Children’s has worked to improve access to care, Churchwell said the volume of children needing psychiatric support has remained high.

Dr. Stacy Drury, psychiatrist in chief at Boston Children’s, said suicide is the second-leading cause of death in children. And despite increased recognition of psychiatric illness and treatment, she said, there is often a gap of eight to 12 years before parents recognize symptoms in their children and act to get them care.

“Mental health services in Massachusetts are fractured,” Drury said. “This will allow us to have kids go between different intensities of treatment faster without going to ERs.”

“By building a beautiful campus centering mental wellness, it will be one of the most powerful tools we have against stigma,” she added.

Danna Mauch, chief executive of the nonprofit Massachusetts Association for Mental Health, welcomed the news of Children’s investment. She said pediatric psychiatric services see a lot of seasonal fluctuation, which can be hard for smaller institutions to manage. Additionally, the size of Children’s operation could help it retain a talented team of clinicians, whereas other programs have struggled to recruit.

Having a mix of inpatient and outpatient care is also key.

“What they are doing is the right thing, in terms of what we know about kids and families, of their needs, and what we know from research literature about what is optimal,” Mauch said. “And not everyone can pull that off.”

The donation is the latest from the philanthropic couple, who have given regularly to Boston Children’s in particular for years.

In 2018, the Hales announced two donations totaling $100 million to Boston Children’s and Brigham and Women’s Hospital. Before that, they also gave $5 million in 2013 to establish the Hale Family Center for Families at the hospital.

In 2022, the couple gave away $1 million a week in surprise donations to nonprofits across the state, including one to Children’s.

All told, inclusive of this recent donation, the couple’s given away $500 million of their wealth, amassed through Rob’s successful Quincy-based company Granite Telecommunications, which manages telecommunication services for large businesses.

In an interview, the couple said that at least a dozen friends reached out during the pandemic, asking the Hales to help connect them with hospital resources for mental health care. As Boston Children’s and Franciscan came together and embarked on a larger project, the couple was keen to get involved.

The Hales, who have three children, are particularly loyal to Children’s. Rob recalled touring the hospital in 2011 and seeing a child the size of two tennis balls in the neonatal intensive care unit. He teared up recalling the visit, and the fact that because of the hospital’s care, the child would survive.

“We thought then, and now, that if you help Children’s Hospital, you’re helping the world,” Rob said. “Like, hey, is it going to help your kid, our kid, some kid in Roxbury, some kids from Western Mass. and everywhere? Yes, which is wonderful. But as you learn more about Children’s Hospital, is it going to help kids from Bangladesh and Bangalore and everywhere between? Yes. So it’s the idea that you can help not just your community, but the whole world.”

The project, and the donation, comes at a perilous time for health care. Looming federal funding cuts will significantly reduce the money the state receives for Medicaid, the government insurer for the poor and disabled, which insures nearly half of all children in Massachusetts.

“We do think that America needs help right now, perhaps more so than ever,” Rob said. “And, yes, hopefully we can catalyze other leaders [to give].”

Simultaneously with pending cuts, the wealth gap in the United States has only grown.

The Hales are aware of their own fortune. Rob ranked 630th on the Forbes list of the wealthiest people, with a net worth of $6 billion. The couple plans to give away the majority of their wealth.

Karen said giving publicly motivates other people to join a fund-raising campaign. The Hale name already adorns the awning of the front of the main Children’s building and is emblazoned throughout the lobby, the Hale building is an entire section of the hospital, and the Hale Family Center for Families offers a place for families to relax between appointments or find hospital resources.

Karen said the Hales receive emails from friends and acquaintances who come into the hospital and see their name, thanking them for their support. As they embarked on the biggest donation they’ve made to any institution, it felt good to give more, they said.

“Helping this institution gives you joy,” Rob said. “When you sit here, you see the kids coming in, and it tugs at your heartstrings. But you see the kids going out, and you know a bigger percentage of them are going to go out because you’re able to help.”

title: Boston Medical Center public safety officer stabbed, sustains life-threatening injuries, officials say
text:
Branden Bannister, 37, of Roxbury, was arrested at the scene. He was arraigned in Boston Municipal Court on Wednesday, where he pleaded not guilty to charges that include assault and battery with a dangerous weapon resulting in serious bodily injury and cocaine trafficking, according to a statement from the district attorney’s office.

Bannister’s bail was set at $50,000, and Judge Richard Sinnott ordered him to “stay away from all Boston hospitals unless strapped to a gurney,” the district attorney’s statement said.

Bannister is scheduled to return to court for a probable cause hearing on Jan. 12.

“It’s deeply disturbing that this defendant turned a workplace focused on healing people into a place of violence,” District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in the statement. “I wish the security guard a full and fast recovery, and I’m grateful to all those who helped ensure a quick arrest.”

Police responded to a fight at the hospital’s Yawkey Center around 2 a.m. Homicide detectives responded as well.

When officers arrived, Bannister was handcuffed, bleeding from his face, and had been pepper-sprayed, prosecutors said.

According to a police report, Bannister was visiting a patient and left the hospital with items belonging to that person. A public safety officer stopped Bannister outside the hospital to retrieve the items, the report said.

“Video footage captures Bannister walking towards and getting into the face” of the public safety officer, the report said. The officer shoved Bannister, at which point Bannister allegedly “clutched his right hoodie pocket, as if to grip and conceal a weapon,” according to the report.

An altercation ensued during which Bannister allegedly threw punches at public safety officers and allegedly stabbed one of them in the right leg, the report said.

The officers pepper-sprayed Bannister and struck him multiple times, according to the report.

After Bannister was put into handcuffs, one officer noticed an eight-inch slash mark on his ballistic vest carrier, the report said.

The public safety officer who was stabbed hopped on one leg into the hospital and took himself to a trauma unit, leaving “a trail of blood from the initial altercation,” the report said.

Bannister was taken to a hospital with facial lacerations and pepper spray exposure, according to the report.

Officers found approximately 26 grams of crack cocaine after searching Bannister, the report said.

The hospital is “open and operating normally” on Wednesday, Gardner said.

“Boston Medical Center takes incidents such as these very seriously, and the safety and well-being of our patients and staff are always our priority,” he said.

It was not immediately clear if Bannister had a lawyer.

In 2019, Bannister was arrested and charged with distributing class B drugs before the case was dismissed in 2021, according to court documents.

Bannister was also arrested in 2018 and charged with distributing drugs before the case was again dismissed in 2021, according to court documents.

In 2016, Bannister was arrested and charged with assault and battery on a police officer before the case was dismissed in 2021, according to court documents.

title: When grandparents become parents again, and problems add up
text:
One grandmother wrote that she is raising her 11-year-old grandson on her own. The boy has autism, ADHD, PTSD, trauma, and depression.

“[He] is a loving, outgoing boy who loves school and sports,” she wrote. “I am very proud of [him].”

He lost his mother when he was only 2 years old. He receives Social Security survivor benefits but no disability or child support.

The recent government funding cuts, she wrote, means there are “no longer outside options for our family.” Still, she tries to be positive at this time of year.

“As many others on Christmas Day, my gift to myself is his child[‘s] smile [and] excitement,” she wrote. Being remembered by Globe Santa “is the most precious gift you could give to my family.”

US Census Bureau Data from 2024 found a decline in the number of grandparents living with and caring for their grandchildren in the first part of the 2020s compared to the last part of the 2010s, the Associated Press reported.

Many grandparents have written Globe Santa asking for help for their families over the years — and this year is no different.

“It’s very rarely for positive reasons that grandparents find themselves in this situation,” Susan Kelley, a professor emerita at Georgia State University, told the AP. “Usually, it’s a tragic situation in an adult child’s life, either a death, incarceration or mental health issues which correlate with substance abuse. Many grandparents thrive in that role, but there are still socioeconomic and emotional burdens on the grandparents.”

These burdens include their own health struggles and navigating their own well-being while also looking after grandchildren who may have complex medical issues, other grandparents wrote Globe Santa.

One grandmother wrote that she adopted her now 8-year-old granddaughter “who has a lot of her own health issues.” The granddaughter has recently had to get X-rays and MRIs, in addition to physical therapy twice a week, “for as long as insurance will have her.”

“[My granddaughter] is a happy, smart child who loves music [and] books and dance,” she wrote to Globe Santa.

They live on her disability income. The grandmother had a stroke in 2013 — but is “OK as long as I keep my stress level down,” she wrote.

“With all the above, low-income, health issues with both of us, we are grateful to have what we have,” the letter continued. “Anything Globe Santa can bring is much appreciated for this little girl.”

Another grandmother wrote of her myriad health issues — lupus, COPD, emphysema, a major heart attack — “the list goes on.”

Nevertheless, she is the sole provider for her family, including her 5-year-old grandson whom she has custody of.

To make matters worse, the grandmother had to take a leave of absence from work to care for her grandson whose short life has already been marked by neglect, child abuse, custody “battles” between his parents, and witnessing domestic violence.

Traumatized by these events, he is now in therapy and speech therapy, and she is working to help him get “on the right track of where he should be with speech, potty training, and many other milestones he had not reached yet due to [not] being taught.”

The stress of the bills prevents her from providing the holiday season any grandparent would love to give.

“I’m not asking for much,” she wrote. “Just something to give this little angel a Christmas he deserves after all that he has been through.”

These families will join thousands of others across the state in receiving gifts for the holiday season thanks to those who donate to Globe Santa, allowing them to focus on what matters most — their health and each other.

P.S. “Walter’s Run” for Globe Santa is Sunday.

The Parkway Running Club of West Roxbury hosts its 31st annual 5k road race on Sunday, Dec. 14, to raise money for Globe Santa. Named “Walter’s Run,” it honors a beloved member, Walter Burgess, who died in 2023 at the age of 40, after completing a triathlon. This year, under the motto WE Run Inspired, the group is also honoring longtime member Eddie Hastings, who died in 2023. “They both had that giving spirit,” said Jim Sweeney, the running club’s president. Race information is available at: www.WaltersRun.org

For 70 years Globe Santa, a program of the Boston Globe Foundation, has provided gifts to children in need at holiday time. Please consider giving by phone, mail, or online at globesanta.org.

title: Patriots mailbag: Drake Maye vs. Tom Brady on deep passes, and shouldn’t Marcus Jones also be returning kickoffs?
text:
Only in emergency situations. Punt returner and kickoff returner are vastly different jobs with little crossover, particularly at an elite level. Punt returning is more about short-area quickness and creating separation, while kickoff returning is more pure speed and angles. Not saying Jones couldn’t do both, but his burst and acceleration make him ideal for returning punts. Unless you lose a couple of kickoff returners during a game and need him in a pinch, I’d keep him as a punt returner only.

Is it likely that if we held on to the first pick of the 2024 NFL Draft, Drake Maye would have been the pick?

— Sheila McVay, West Roxbury

Tough call. I’d lean toward yes, but you’ve got to keep in mind that a large part of the success or failure of a young quarterback depends on those around him, both personnel and coaching. To that point, it’s a safe bet that we know he would have been very good, but there’s no way of telling how things would have turned out for Maye in Chicago or Washington. (You could argue the growth of Maye and Caleb Williams was stunted in their first seasons because of coaching.) In New England, the coaching staff and personnel around Maye has allowed this season for an organic development that has proven beneficial for all involved.

Why do the Patriots ground and pound in the middle of the line at the goal line? This is far from one of their strengths. What are their strengths? Wheel routes? QB rollouts?

— Edward Hozubin, Northborough

Addressed some of this last week, but it’s worth reiterating that a lot depends on the opponent and defensive scheme, as well as your roster. I’m still a little puzzled as to why there aren’t more jump balls offered to pass catchers such as Hunter Henry, Austin Hooper, and Mack Hollins. Or leaning on Maye’s athleticism with designed rollouts or bootlegs.

In the end, it can come down to a question of efficiency and execution, particularly having all 11 guys on the same page. Over the last couple of weeks, Mike Vrabel and Josh McDaniels have addressed this topic, and I was struck by how they both stressed that execution and precision remain paramount. “Precision is critical — that space is limited,” Vrabel said Monday. “Things happen so much quicker down there.” Regardless of how you do it, it’s something that needs sharpening between now and the playoffs.

Maye’s knack for the long ball is the best I’ve seen in a while. This was one of the few areas Tom Brady did not excel in. How do their numbers compare on passes over 20 yards?

— Bob Granese, Chino Hills, Calif.

Tried to comb through some advanced stats, but there was little definitive information. So I turned to my favorite numbers guy, Aaron Schatz.

“I can tell you Maye, this year, is third with 16.3 yards per pass on passes of 20-plus air yards behind Sam Darnold and Jayden Daniels, and he has a 50 percent completion rate (not including defensive pass-interference calls), which is also second in the league behind Darnold,” said Schatz, who created Football Outsiders and is now the chief analytics officer at FTN Fantasy.

“For Brady, it’s tough to gauge over the breadth of his career, so I decided to look at his peak, which I defined as 2007-12. Obviously, he had plenty of other good seasons, but that’s right at his peak, plus you get two seasons (part of the third) with Randy Moss, who might be the greatest deep-ball receiver ever.

“Clearly, 2007 was Brady’s best season; he had 17.6 yards per pass on passes of 20-plus air yards, and had a completion rate of 44 percent. The numbers for Brady did fall off from 2009-12, eventually bottoming out at 31 percent in 2012. Ultimately, we’re only talking about Maye for one season, so the sample size needs to be taken into consideration.”

With the UNC football season now ended, do you foresee or have you heard rumors about any NFL teams going after Bill Belichick for an open head coaching role? I noted how carefully Belichick recently addressed this question when he said, “I am not pursuing any NFL positions,” which doesn’t preclude an NFL team going after him.

— Chip Huckins, Westmoreland, N.H.

Not at this time, although that’s a great catch by you reading between the lines. I did find it interesting that his longtime second-in-command Berj Najarian, who moved on to Boston College after Belichick left the Patriots, recently left his position at The Heights. If he joins Belichick in Chapel Hill, my guess is he’ll bring some stability to a situation that was anything but for much of the last year. Najarian’s presence would likely serve as an indicator Belichick could demonstrate a renewed commitment to UNC for an extended period.

title: Potential $700 million Madison Park school rebuild wins support from state funding agency
text:
“Thank you to the MSBA for this momentous decision to partner with us for a transformational investment in Madison Park that will redefine the opportunities for our students and the trajectory of our economic future,” Mayor Michelle Wu said in a statement. “This is long overdue to deliver nation-leading facilities to train and support the next generation of our workforce, bringing our entire community into the opportunities of world-class vocational education.”

The city estimated in January that the project could cost as much as $700 million.

That exceeds even the $660 million high school rebuild Lexington voters recently approved and Revere’s $500 million high school project.

Boston is not alone in facing potentially record-breaking costs. Brockton is facing a similar estimated cost for its hoped-for high school replacement. School building costs have surged in recent years due to rising material and labor costs and higher interest rates. President Trump’s tariffs could raise costs even more.

The state’s School Building Authority provides partial reimbursement of construction costs, with the percentage of costs covered based on factors such as the property value and demographics of a school district.

For example, the authority agreed to reimburse Boston about 64 percent of eligible costs, or about $30 million, for the Carter School, which opened this fall. In an effort to rein in costs, the authority limits payments for some features and excludes expenses for features it considers optional. The Carter School’s total cost was more than $100 million.

The proposed new vocational school could be more than a half-million square feet, and serve 2,200 students, according to a prior city planning study. That would include about 800 students enrolled in newly added Grades 7 and 8, doubling the overall enrollment. The expansion would also allow the school to add additional state-approved vocational pathways.

Currently, the school has 20 such programs, from carpentry to nursing. Wu in May signed an agreement with the Greater Boston Building Trades Unions to create a direct pathway for the school’s graduates into the unions’ Building Pathways pre-apprenticeship program.

The campus would feature new facilities and include an auditorium, performing arts spaces, and a media center. The current school, built in 1972, is in terrible condition, with out-of-date facilities and an energy efficiency score of 0 out of 100, according to BPS data.

Madison Park, the district’s only vocational high school, shares a campus with the O’Bryant School of Math and Science. The MSBA application applies to Madison Park; the future of the O’Bryant remains up in the air.

Whether the district renovates existing structures or builds a new Madison Park school on the same campus, the cost would be about $700 million, according to earlier city estimates. Initially the city undertook years of planning and community engagement as part of plans to fund the school without aid from the state agency, but officials switched gears once the potential costs came into view.

The next step for the city will be a feasibility study, where the district and the MSBA explore options for the school’s design. That could partially duplicate work done before the city opted to seek state funding.

Long term, Boston has not been a major recipient of MSBA assistance, as suburban school districts have tended to get a disproportionate share. Under Wu, the district has done better: This is the third year in a row the city has won initial approval from the state agency, after the Ruth Batson Academy last year and the Shaw-Taylor elementary school merger the year prior.

Both of those projects are still in planning stages, and none of the three is likely to be completed until the 2030s.

“We are proud of our ongoing collaboration with the City of Boston on multiple facilities and look forward to continuing our partnership with the invitation of the Madison Park High School project into the MSBA’s Capital Pipeline,” said Mary Pichetti, executive director of the authority, in a statement. “We are pleased to support this investment in the City’s vision for the transformation of Madison Park project which will directly benefit students pursuing career and technical training.”

The MSBA Board also approved funding agreements Friday for BPS on several smaller projects. The agency will pay up to almost $5 million for windows, doors, and roofs at four schools.

The good news on the school building front comes as school officials are also grappling with the less-pleasant task of closing schools. On Wednesday, the Boston School Committee is set to vote on a proposal to close three schools serving about 850 students.

title: Boston leaders tout the city’s low crime rate in 2025, pledge to keep improving public safety
text:
With the New Year approaching, Boston leaders touted the city’s low crime rates in 2025 and pledged to redouble their public safety efforts.

While gun violence has increased slightly this year after reaching a historic low in 2024, Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox said the numbers are still a significant accomplishment.

During a news conference Monday morning at a new Boston EMS training center in West Roxbury, he said the city has recorded 31 homicides so far in 2025, compared to 24 the same time last year. The 2025 tally represents a 16 percent decrease from the city’s five-year average, Cox said.

Other big cities have also seen declines in gun violence following a widespread pandemic surge.

Aside from ongoing violence reduction efforts, Cox said the department has focused on organized retail theft, quality of life crimes, especially around the downtown area, and traffic safety issues involving the reckless operation of scooters.

“The Boston Police Department continues to rely on community policing as our most valued partner in public safety in the city,” Cox said. He praised the agency for building relationships with residents and taking their concerns seriously.

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu thanked local first responders, calling the city a “shining example for the rest of the country” when it comes to public safety.

“This is what it means to be a home for everyone, and to be fighting every day for the residents in every single neighborhood to live in the safest city in America,” she said.

She also acknowledged recent mass tragedies, including the weekend shooting at Brown University.

“It is unthinkable that we live in a world where you don’t even have time to process one major, horrific incident of violence before the next takes place,” she said. “And all the more reason why it is important for us to focus on safety.”

Wu said ongoing efforts will continue as Boston looks forward to hosting a number of large events in the coming months, including the 2026 World Cup games.

Elected officials have sought to reassure residents that local and state law enforcement agencies have things under control in the Boston area, especially after President Trump cited a recent series of so-called “street takeovers” in criticizing the mayor’s leadership. Trump suggested he could move the games elsewhere because of public safety issues, a familiar talking point for the president as he often attacks Democrat-led cities.

Boston officials announced a key arrest in the street takeovers earlier this month. A man from Connecticut was charged with throwing a firework at a Boston police cruiser in an October incident in the South End. The car meetups unfolded in several Massachusetts cities and towns, with large groups of drivers blocking traffic and performing dangerous stunts.

Still, officials said Boston’s overall crime trends are positive.

The recent drop in homicides follows decades of work involving city leaders, police, and community organizations. In 1990, Boston’s most violent year on record, there were 152 homicides.

Officials said they’ll continue taking a public health approach to reducing violence. That means tackling the problem from all angles, including a new initiative that trains hairstylists and barbers to recognize signs of domestic violence and human trafficking, said Isaac Yablo, the city’s senior advisor for community safety and director of the Boston Public Health Commission’s Office of Violence Prevention.

“The main goal will be primary prevention, preventing the violence from happening in the first place,” Yablo said.

Lea Skene can be reached at lea.skene@globe.com. Follow her on X @lea_skene.

title: Anxious, resigned, exhausted: Parents react to the Brown University shooting
text:
Addie Wyman-Battalen is director of counseling at Brandeis University in Waltham. She knows that this news makes parents feel helpless, because she is one. Talking with your child about campus resources — downloading campus safety apps, reviewing a school’s medical amnesty policy (useful if a student is in danger from binge-drinking but peers are afraid to call for help) can impart a measure of control in risky situations.

“I would encourage parents to begin discussing with their children before they get to campus who is or who can be part of their support team if needed, such as counseling on campus or spiritual life,” Battalen says. “We live in a world that is scary, and we can’t control everything, but identifying what you can do to help keep your kid safe can be a good start.”

Meanwhile, seniors eagerly awaited admissions news from Brown, which had originally planned to release decisions on Monday. That process has been delayed up to 48 hours.

“I feel sadness and understanding of the delay. As a parent, I think I’m more anxious than my son. It’s a strange place to be, holding the knowledge of the awfulness of what happened with the anxiety of the results release. It feels a bit surreal,” says one parent of a Brown candidate, requesting privacy for her son.

I talked to parents of college students, and those who are in the application process, about their dual senses of excitement and dread. Though the sentiments varied, one message was universal: Nobody feels completely safe.

Innocence has been taken away, one more time

“I live on Martha’s Vineyard and am the mom of a 13-year-old boy. I went to the Wheeler School on the East Side of Providence for high school, and this latest shooting feels too close to home. Many friends share the mind-set that the Vineyard is a safe place to raise children. What has become abundantly clear is that no community is safe or immune to this type of massacre. Nowhere. A friend’s son attends Brown and happened to be home during the shooting. Was it luck? I don’t know how to resolve this issue but I know that it is not possible to shelter our son from the potential of gun violence, and that feels too vulnerable.” - Kate, Vineyard Haven

“I feel like I’m drowning after this news. My daughter was accepted into Wellesley at 10 a.m. on Saturday. She found out during a debate tournament. We were with her when she opened her email, and we were all ecstatic.

“The next day was the anniversary of Sandy Hook. When that tragedy occurred, she was in preschool in Providence. We routinely played on the Brown campus on nice days, and the East Side is so near and dear to us. I can’t believe we have made no progress since then. She will be studying political science at Wellesley, and while I’m so hopeful for her future and so glad she’ll be on a women’s college campus near us, I am darkly shadowed by these events. - Keri, Winchester

“I’m the parent of a Providence College freshman as well as a lecturer in a program at MIT that offers English Language Studies courses to both undergraduate and graduate international students.

“This weekend’s horrific events in Providence hit even closer to home than all the other school shootings of the past few decades because the PC campus, where my daughter is a freshman, is only a six-minute drive from Brown University.

“I’m lucky because my daughter was actually on her way back home from Rhode Island when the shooting happened on Saturday, and, as of now, she’s still back home, debating when to go back to campus …

“It makes me absolutely mad and incredibly sad that our kids grow up with active shooter drills at their schools, and we all have to live in constant fear. As a parent, the loss of our children’s innocence and an entire generation’s childhood taken away feels just devastating. I also find living with the frequent occurrence of mass shootings draining as an educator, and it’s often hard to explain to my international students that this is our reality, and as a consequence of them having decided to study in the US, now it’s theirs, too.” - Olivia, Arlington

We need put down our phones and look out for one another

“My daughter just started her freshman year at Brown. I am a Brown alum myself. She is safe, and we picked her up last night.

“I know the university will likely respond in many ways prior to student return, likely enhancing building security and video coverage. I find that reassuring. I know my daughter will benefit from the support the university will provide.

“The Brown community is strong and engaged in picking up the vulnerable and marginalized in our society. We know we need to look out even more vigilantly for each other, but we must continue the mission.

“My daughter is a fiercely independent person. She thrives in communities and has completely been absorbed into Brown. She has already told me she knows things haven’t sunk in quite yet, but she will not let this event define her, and she wants to really make the most of the education and experience Brown is giving (and already has given) her.

“How to better look out for each other? By caring. By realizing your fellow students are your family, like your brothers and sisters. By talking to people, by listening to people, especially those who are different from you. By looking up from your phones and the sidewalk to see the people around you.” - Patty, Acton

This has now become routine

“I have a freshman at college at Endicott. We lived in Tucson when [Gaby] Giffords was shot and knew the judge who was killed. A college friend, her first year of teaching, was at Columbine. [She] still talks about hiding under her desk. My kids have also lived through bomb threats at the Tucson JCC and at their then-school.

“What’s exhausting isn’t one incident — it’s the accumulation. Lockdowns. Bomb threats at Jewish schools and JCCs. Active shooter drills that my kids now treat as routine. Now the Brown shooting. Each one adds another layer. - Erin, Somerville

Our kids never knew true safety

“I personally went to Brown, so now I’m feeling acutely the reality that really nowhere is safe. It leaves me, of course, completely without recourse. You can’t not live life, and you can’t not go places. And yet a study hall for finals is not safe. A college kid riding his bike across campus is not safe. College students expressing their right to free speech and political discourse are not safe.

“Do my sons feel the same? I don’t think they do, sadly. I don’t think they can experience the same loss because they grew up post-Sandy Hook, so they don’t know that churches and schools used to be safe.” - Amy, Lexington

“My daughter returned last night from her sophomore year at Lafayette. I’ve never felt more relieved to have her home. The shooting at Brown hit me hard — maybe because it’s close to home, my father went to Brown, and it’s a school, like Lafayette, where you just can’t imagine something like this happening. But it is increasingly obvious that no place is safe. My daughter was a first-grader during Sandy Hook, and I couldn’t stop crying over the loss of children the same age. Now, here we are again.

“There is so much to worry about when you send your child out into the world. We can’t control what happens. We trust her. But this kind of situation is not something we should have to worry about. The government is failing us by doing nothing about gun control.” - Mary, Concord

This is a problem growing out of control

“I know my child is nervous about going away to college and might choose a place closer to home where she could live at home while attending school. However, this really doesn’t make it much safer.

“Truth be told, gunmen are shooting up movie theaters, churches, and shopping malls, to name a few, so I’m not sure that I have a specific concern about college versus any other venues where people are vulnerable. And a lot of these guns have been acquired legally, so I don’t even know what to say about tighter gun control laws or security protocols. This seems like a problem growing out of control, and we are not adequately addressing it. When I was a kid, we had bomb scare drills because it was the Cold War. This is the new danger. But it’s everywhere and from within. - Laura, Falmouth

This is the new normal

“I’m part of Grassroots for Gun Violence Prevention, an organization I cofounded here in Massachusetts. I have a junior at Arlington High School, and although she’s not applying yet, Brown is her top pick and we were hoping to go visit soon. I think we’ll delay a bit. I could talk for days about gun violence prevention because I’ve been doing this for nine years, but even doing this work on a regular basis, sometimes it hits particularly close to home like this weekend.

What’s really sad is that my daughter is not even fazed by school shootings anymore. She’s got her plan for if it happens to her, and it’s sad that our young people have to plan for it. I admire that she won’t be deterred from going to college, and probably will still consider going to Brown, but we shouldn’t have to live this way. We all deserve better, no matter what school you go to. Schools should be safe places to learn.

It’s just devastating that my daughter’s dream school, Brown, is now marred by senseless violence and fear. I felt like I had to take her aside and let her know about the shooting and be prepared to console her. But, again, the sad part is she wasn’t even fazed.” - Angela, Arlington

“I have a child who is currently studying at UMass Boston and living on campus as a freshman. It is scary. This past fall, the school actually had a shelter-in-place and evacuation notice for the campus because of a suspected shooter. No one was harmed, and I don’t believe there was actually ever a threat, but it was one of the scariest days I have experienced. As parents, we found out via the news and then reached out to our child. He barely knew what was going on, only one text saying to shelter in your dorm.

“It lasted about an hour or two but eventually everything was cleared and he seemed totally unfazed. Can you imagine?! Kids are being trained for this now, and it’s totally unreal. We were in full panic but he was calm and just stayed quiet until police gave the all clear. I’m thankful he was calm but it’s irritating we live in a world where this is the new norm.

“We just try to remind our kids to be kind and respectful of everyone, but always know your surroundings. That day with the UMass Boston situation was very scary. We’re grateful it turned out to be not a real threat to the campus, but it puts things in perspective. Just because you’re in a surveillance area does not equate to a safe area anymore.” - Bea, Andover

“I am sad to say that the incident at Brown does not make me any more worried than I already am about various things to do with college kids — parties, unfortunate decisions, learning to be in the audience rather than the director of their lifetime plays. There’s a general feeling to me of it being all a terrible, horrible crapshoot: who is having a bad day and carrying a gun, who has a grudge and takes it out on your kids.

“The sad fact is that all of our kids in their teens and 20s have been dealing with ALICE drills and the constant terror for all their lives. They all know how to react. - Kristin, Weston

Home is safer than a campus

“My daughter is a student at a college in Providence, and we are very nervous about next steps. We went and got my daughter back home for Christmas break because of our anxiety around the situation.” - Caren, Medfield

“College is supposed to be the first time kids can really spread their wings and fly a little. Campus shootings make me wonder how far I really want them to fly.” - Sarah, Belchertown

We need to address mental health

“I’m feeling helpless and worried. This can happen anywhere, and unless we as a society address mental health, help men learn how to express themselves without violence, and do something about the insane number of guns available (and the ease of getting them), we really won’t be able to prevent this from happening. So I will hug my sons tighter, encourage them to be vigilant, and pray.” - Samantha. West Roxbury

title: Boston Music Awards 2025: Dropkick Murphys, ISHA!, and more win big. See the full list.
text:
“This means the world to us,” Brennan said while accepting the award at Wednesday’s ceremony, noting in his speech that “Boston is such a huge part of who we are.”

Dropkick Murphys, who haven’t secured any titles at the Boston Music Awards since 2012, also picked up wins for video of the year and song of the year (1 million+ streams) for the band’s politically-charged track “Who Will Stand with Us?” from the new album “For the People.”

While Dropkick Murphys led the field with three wins on Wednesday, Boston band Couch, who were nominated in five categories, took home two trophies, including live artist of the year and pop artist of the year.

Rising women hip-hop and R&B performers continue to dominate the new artist of the year category, with Lawrence artist ISHA! taking the 2025 title, shouting out “the Dominicans and the Haitians in the building” while accepting the award (she also performed at the event). The 2024 crown went to Dorchester R&B act Yanna G, while Mattapan rapper Nay $peaks won new artist of the year in 2023.

Rap also dominated the best album categories, with Boston rapper EXITFAME, who also performed at this year’s awards, winning album/EP of the year for “Last Shall Be First.”

“I grew up in Dorchester, Roxbury. And what makes you stay here is the pride of that,” EXITFAME told the Globe backstage at Wednesday’s event, noting how he wants “to bring an eye on the city” with his work.

Meanwhile, Salem rapper Token won the award for album/EP of the year (1 million+ streams) for “I’m Not Supposed to Be Here.”

“I was always insecure about growing up outside of Boston and being an internet kid,” Token said during his acceptance speech. “But where I’m from means a lot to me, and this means a lot to me.”

In a statement from Paul Armstrong, owner and producer of the Boston Music Awards, he praised this year’s nominees and winners for reflecting “the full spectrum of who makes music in Boston right now.”

“It’s been a difficult year in many ways, for a lot of people, and nights like this matter,” said Armstrong. “When things feel heavy, art is often what helps us see a way forward.”

He added, “Our hope is that the Boston Music Awards offered a little light, a sense of connection, and a reminder of the strength that comes from a creative community that truly represents everyone.”

The 2025 edition of the ceremony featured five new categories this year, including the inaugural Margaret Stewart Lindsay music nonprofit of the year award, which honors organizations supporting the creative community. The honor went to the Boston Music Project, a nonprofit that aims to support “the long-term social-emotional and musical success of Boston youth,” according to its website.

“The arts truly are the cornerstone of humanity, and especially right now,” said Chris Schroeder, executive director of the Boston Music Project, while accepting the award on stage. “They play a vital role in helping us to express, amplify, and shape the future that we all want to see.”

Also new for 2025 was the Afro/Caribbean artist of the year category, which took the place of the reggae/ska category. The award went to hip-hop and Afrofusion musician Echezona.

Additional genre-specific winners included Token (hip-hop); Yanna G (R&B); Lia Nicole (Latin); Megan From Work (rock); Hallelujah the Hills (alt/indie); Ezra Furman (singer-songwriter); GA-20 (blues); Samantha Rae (country); Freezepop (dance/electronic); DJ Real P (DJ); Jared Sims (jazz); TREE (metal); Haywire (punk/hardcore); Kier Byrnes & The Kettle Burners (Americana); Tiny Habits (folk); and Miranda Rae (vocalist).

The Boston Globe was honored as well, earning the award for publication of the year, with Globe contributing writer and music editor Victoria Wasylak winning journalist of the year.

title: A painful recovery ahead for Brown and the wider community
text:
I’m grateful to McGowan for addressing the naysayers and doom-mongers. But there’s more for us all to do. As local, state, and federal law enforcement and other Providence public officials did in tackling this case, let’s shut out the disrespectful commentaries and get to work — supporting our neighbors and helping to lead this country back toward the principles it was founded on.

Elizabeth Dorn

Watertown

Re “Research shows it was ‘very strange’ for an active shooter to just walk away” (Metro, Dec. 17): Although statistically improbable, there is precedent for the way the aftermath of the Brown University shooting played out. In October 2002, it took about three weeks before John Allen Muhammad and Lee Boyd Malvo were apprehended in the D.C. sniper killings. Law enforcement first believed they were searching for one killer, then realized there were two people involved, the older Muhammad reportedly having manipulated the teenage Malvo.

When we don’t have all the answers in an open criminal investigation, speculation and misinformation can run rampant. But just because something is statistically unlikely doesn’t mean it’s impossible.

Max F. Roberts

Natick

The writer teaches high school history, including a senior elective on law and society, which covers criminal behavior.

I was so moved by the articles on the two Brown University students who were killed in the campus shooting (“Two lives full of promise, cut short in a horrifying instant,” Page A1, Dec. 20). Ella Cook and MukhammadAziz Umurzokov, two of the best and brightest, were students with clearly purpose-filled futures.

What we lose with every school shooting is truly immeasurable, never mind forever devastating.

How soon can we elect candidates who will back strong gun laws to honor these incredible Americans we have lost? Not soon enough.

Jane Smith Curtis

Mashpee

The fatal shooting of the two students at Brown University is tragic. Those who survived face a harsh reality of their own.

In her Dec. 21 Ideas essay (“I’m a scholar of gun violence. Not even I can process what happened at Brown.”), Ieva Jusionyte writes, “Survivors, family members, activists work tirelessly, in a Sisyphean effort, to pass new laws, to make it safer for us to live in our communities.”

Sisyphus’s boulder was mythical. For the surviving victims of a shooting, the boulders are real. Survivors of violent crime face a lifetime of physical and emotional challenges they’d never anticipated. I know. I am one.

I was shot twice in the head and once in the arm. One of the slugs burned into my skull, where it remains, near my occipital lobe. I was left legally blind in both eyes and partially deaf in my right ear.

Amid enormous gratitude for life, and never one for the pity pot, I push boulders — seizures, nightmares, the inability to drive, etc. Sadly, the survivors of the Brown University shooting now face their own boulders, each with differing weight. Help them push. Family, friends, and faith make a lasting difference.

Frank Sullivan

West Roxbury

Re “Tragedy tests a steady leader at Brown” (Page A1, Dec. 21): For more than 40 years I chided a friend about his decision to attend Brown University. What was a semi-normal guy from Cleveland doing at a school we considered the most eccentric and “unusual” of the Ivies? His stories of reunions only added to the Ivy lore. Then some family members became associated with Brown over the years, and my opinion changed. I even visited the campus recently and became enamored with the school — the charm of its buildings, its brick walls and wrought-iron fences, its many gates and arches, its friendly students, and its relationship with the surrounding Providence community.

When I learned of the shooting and saw videos of the campus that I had come to appreciate as so peaceful and welcoming, I felt sorrow for students killed and wounded and their families. I feel for those traumatized by witnessing the carnage. And I fear the impact of this tragic event on what has made Brown unique to so many people, including me.

This Midwesterner admires how Brown’s president, Christina Paxson, is holding this entire community, inside and outside the Van Wickle Gates, close to her heart.

Stephen Gladstone

Shaker Heights, Ohio

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
