On hand will be such performers as David Coffin, David Keohane, Kristian Espiritu, Joshua Wolf Coleman, and Eliza Fichter. Dec. 12-28, with a “virtual encore viewing window.” Dec. 28-Jan. 11. Sanders Theatre, Harvard Square, Cambridge. 617-496-2222,boxoffice.harvard.edu

DON AUCOIN

Dance

GRAND KYIV BALLET The company returns to Boston for a one-night-only performance of its ballet “The Snow Queen.” Set to a score that includes music by Mozart, Vivaldi, Grieg, and Massanet, the ballet is an adaptation of Hans Christian Andersen’s familiar fairy tale, portraying the story of a young man whose heart becomes frozen after a tiny shard of a witch’s mirror catches in his eye. After being taken by the Snow Queen, his true love sets out on a perilous journey to find him and break the spell. Dec. 27. $47.58-$108.58. Emerson Colonial Theatre. www.grandkyivballet.com.ua/

THE SLUTCRACKER One more week to catch this sassy and irreverent take on holiday cheer. Though it’s set to the familiar music of Tchaikovsky, this version of “The Nutcracker” is definitely R-rated (18 and up). The bawdy story line transforms Clara and Fritz into a couple of sexually adventurous adults whose idea of Christmas magic is more naughty than nice, with a Dildo Prince and more tassels than tutus. Through Jan. 3. $38 and up. Somerville Theatre, Somerville. www.theslutcracker.com

DISNEY ON ICE This time around, the family-oriented skating show breezes into Boston with a production that ushers in a frosty blast with “Frozen,” then brings the heat with “Encanto.” Also, alongside characters from those two Disney hits will be Mickey Mouse, Minnie Mouse, Donald, Goofy, and other fan favorites. Through Dec. 29. $33 and up. Agganis Arena. www.ticketmaster.com

KAREN CAMPBELL

MARTIN PURYEAR: NEXUS Puryear represented the United States at the Venice Biennale in 2019 with a display of enigmatic sculptural works that, taken together, echoed the fractious unease of a country at war with itself, confronting old ghosts thought long laid to rest. So, what now? “Nexus,” not quite so pointed — it spans several decades of the artist’s 50-plus-year career, the first long-view survey in almost two decades — but it isn’t afraid to connect the obvious dots. Included in this show is “A Column for Sally Hemings,” made for that 2019 Venice display, which pays homage to the enslaved woman who bore Thomas Jefferson five children; in it, an iron rod topped with a leg shackle embeds in a fluted classical column, an emblem of a fire that never seems to go out. Through Feb. 8. Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, mfa.org

ALLAN ROHAN CRITE Two exhibitions celebrating Crite arrived this fall, “Urban Glory” at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum and “Griot of Boston” at the Boston Athenaeum. For Crite, who painted Roxbury and the city’s Black community with verve and affection for almost 80 years — he died in 2007, just a few years short of his 100th birthday — it’s about time. Along with it comes the first-ever scholarly text on his work, “Allan Rohan Crite: Neighborhood Liturgy,” from Princeton University Press. Crite was a passionate chronicler of both the trials and triumphs of urban Boston’s diverse and dynamic quarters for much of his life, and his official arrival in the canon is more than due. Through Jan. 19 (Gardner) and Jan. 24 (Athenaeum). Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, 25 Evans Way. 617-566-1401, www.isgm.org; Boston Athenaeum, 10½ Beacon St. 617-227-0270, bostonathenaeum.org

DAVID C. DRISKELL: COLLECTOR The late David Driskell, known more as an educator and advocate for centuries — yes, centuries — of lineage of Black art in America than for his own paintings, died in 2020 with an art collection that reflected his deeply held priorities. This exhibition, drawn from those personal holdings, puts on view, for the first time since his death, works that served as touchstones over a lifetime of advocacy and artistic production. Paintings from the 19th century onward by Black artists like Edward Mitchell Bannister, Loïs Mailou Jones, Romare Bearden, and Elizabeth Catlett hang with Driskell’s own, and help frame a legacy as much rooted in those he held up as his work itself. Through March 1. Portland Museum of Art, 7 Congress Square, Portland, Maine. 207-775-6148, www.portlandmuseum.org

MURRAY WHYTE

ESTEBAN DEL VALLE: THANKS FOR ALL THE CONDITIONAL LOVE Has capitalism, which in many ways runs on fueling and fulfilling desires in order to fill coffers, only left us feeling more empty? Del Valle’s satirical, color-drenched, semi-autobiographical paintings and drawings dive into how our access to so much deprives us of self-awareness and connections with others — those things that most sustain us and help us to grow. Through Jan. 17. LaMontagne Gallery, 450 Harrison Ave.www.lamontagnegallery.com

CATE McQUAID

JIMMY TINGLE: HUMOR & HOPE FOR HUMANITY The Cambridge-born satirist wraps up the year with his latest autobiographical show, offering a retrospective of his career going back to the ’80s comedy boom, and insight on current events. Dec. 26-28, 5 p.m. $38.95. The Comedy Studio, 5 John F. Kennedy St., Cambridge. www.thecomedystudio.com

PETER LIU “Growing up, my parents, they’d like to argue by pointing out all the negative traits that the other one had passed on to me,” says Liu. His dad would claim his mother’s ingrown toenails were the reason Peter can’t walk straight, and she’d counter by saying his astigmatism was why he can’t see. “Each of these insults is designed to hurt the other person. But every insult hurts me.” Dec. 27, 8 p.m. $29.50. The Comedy Scene, 23 Patriot Place, Foxborough. www.thecomedyscene.club

BOSTON COMEDY LEGENDS Lenny Clarke, Steve Sweeney, and Don Gavin were three of the biggest comedians in Boston in the ’80s, when stand-up comedy was gaining a foothold in local nightlife and the clubs were just springing up. It’s rare to see all three on the same bill these days, and the Friday show is already sold out. With Johnny Pizzi. Dec. 26-27, 7:30 p.m. $39.19. Giggles Comedy Club, 517 Broadway (Route 1), Saugus. 781-233-9950,www.princerestaurant.com

NICK A. ZAINO III

title: In West Roxbury, one volunteer has led the Salvation Army’s Red Kettle Campaign for nearly 30 years
text:
His effort has made him not only a fixture of his neighborhood’s holiday season, but also one of the longest-serving volunteer bell ringers in Massachusetts.

Nearly every year, Hennigan stands outside the Roche Bros. supermarket on Centre Street in West Roxbury. The location was his idea — he approached the store years ago, knowing it had a history of supporting community efforts, including food drives for Mary Mulvey Jacobson’s Families in Need, another organization with which he has long volunteered and now coordinates.

“They lean over backwards to make it work for us,” Hennigan said. “It’s a good partnership.”

But Hennigan didn’t set out to build a tradition.

Nearly 30 years ago, he was watching television when a news segment aired about the Salvation Army struggling to find volunteers.

That struck him.

“That shouldn’t be the case,” he recalled thinking.

At the time, Hennigan was juggling a full schedule. He was running his own insurance business in West Roxbury, serving on the board of the local YMCA, and raising two young children, both under the age of 3, with his wife.

Volunteering was always part of his life, he said — something he grew up with.

“I was always told by my parents that you do things for your community, for your neighbors, because it’s the right thing to do,” Hennigan said.

So when he saw the call for volunteers, he said, it wasn’t a question of whether he could help, but how — and how soon.

“It’s a natural instinct that I have, truthfully,” he said. “There wasn’t even another thought.”

The next day, Hennigan called the Salvation Army and offered to coordinate volunteers from West Roxbury.

When they asked him what days he wanted to help, he said he’d work every day of the season.

And he did.

That first year, Hennigan began making phone calls across the community — to friends, family members, neighbors, business owners, church leaders, and local officials — asking if people could give just one hour of their time and whether they knew others willing to do the same.

In the early years, Hennigan often filled in himself when volunteer slots went unclaimed, sometimes ringing the bell for multiple hours a day while still running his insurance agency. Today, still running his company, he continues to ring, but much of his time is spent coordinating others.

The red kettle season begins the first week of December and runs through Christmas Eve.

But for Hennigan, the work begins in November, when he pulls out his binder of names and phone numbers and begins making calls.

“If someone sees my name pop up in late November, they already know why I’m calling,” he said. “I’ve had people answer the phone and say, ‘What day do you need me?’ before I even ask.”

The ringing itself is simple. There are no scripted pitches or pressure tactics. Holiday music plays through a speaker, and a sign lists the volunteer on duty for each hour.

The daily setup and breakdown are Hennigan’s responsibility. Each morning, around 8:30 am, he heads to the Roche Bros. customer service desk to retrieve the kettle and stand and place them outside. Smaller items, including the speakers that play Christmas music, the signs, and bells, he stores at his home. At the end of the day, around 6 p.m., he returns to put everything away.

Among the volunteers Hennigan has recruited is Barbara Van Dyke, 70, a retired nurse practitioner who has volunteered at the kettle for more than a decade. Van Dyke first heard about the opportunity through her involvement with the West Roxbury Library, but she said it was Hennigan who kept her coming back.

“He’s always been an important person in the community,” Van Dyke said. “He’s generous with his time. Lots of energy. There’s very little that he doesn’t do.”

Over the years, Hennigan estimates hundreds of volunteers have filled shifts at the kettle. According to the Massachusetts division of the Salvation Army, Hennigan has raised more than $800,000 during his time, through his own shifts as well as ones that he’s filled with other volunteers.

Captain Shakai Drigo, 37, a social services supervisor and pastor with the Salvation Army’s Boston Kroc Center, said coordinating volunteers for the Red Kettle Campaign is often one of the most challenging parts of the holiday season. Hennigan’s long-running, community-based approach, he said, has made the Roche Bros. site the only one in West Roxbury to be consistently staffed year after year.

Earlier this year, Hennigan’s efforts were recognized with The Salvation Army’s Al MacLeod Outstanding Volunteer Award — an honor he insists belongs to the community rather than himself.

“They recognize me, but it’s really all the volunteers,” he said.

Some of the most memorable moments for Hennigan come not from large donations, but from conversations. He said people frequently stop to donate and share stories about receiving help from the Salvation Army.

“They tell me their families got food or clothing when they needed it,” he said. “That’s happened many times over the years. It makes your day.”

Hennigan’s now four children, all adults, grew up volunteering with him.

His daughter, Maeve Hennigan, 26, of Denver said some of her earliest childhood memories are of her and her siblings putting on their Santa hats and ringing the bells at Roche Bros.

“We were born into this organization,” she said, referring to the Salvation Army.

She said she can’t recall a time when her dad wasn’t doing something to help others. “He is never sitting still if he’s not working. If he has a spare second, he’s dedicating that to helping others. He’s always up and at ‘em. He strives to make the world a better place.”

Hennigan’s earliest memories of Christmas are also connected to the Salvation Army. He would visit downtown Boston before Christmas Eve with his family, and his mother would hand him and his sisters change to place in the red kettles.

Now, every Christmas, when the final bell rings and the kettle is packed away, Hennigan returns to his normal routine. But the break is temporary.

Come November, the binder comes back out — and the phone starts ringing again.

title: How two Boston teens are fighting the food waste crisis
text:
Her grandfather lived in China during the Great Chinese Famine, she said, and he witnessed extreme hunger and starvation.

“He would always make sure at the dinner table [that] I finished every last grain, and that’s something that I think is really instilled in me,” Sun said.

His words inspired her to volunteer at First Baptist Church in Jamaica Plain in 2022, where she cooked meals twice a week.

Along the way, she made a startling discovery: community businesses tossing out unsold goods at the end of the day.

“It just felt really rough to me, because I just spent so much time making food, but there was just perfectly fine food being thrown away on the same exact street, so I wanted to try to do something about that,” she said.

Sun and Hennessy, both 17, are seniors at Boston Latin School. Their campaign against food waste began when they were sophomores. The pair asked local businesses to give them the food instead of throwing it out at the end of the night.

They first approached Dunkin’ on Centre Street and then The Real Deal, a family-owned restaurant. And with those willing partners, NoVasta, Latin for “no waste,” was born.

It started out as a small school club whose members volunteer to collect food waste from local businesses and bring it to a drop-off center, such as the church. The club also organizes food drives and raises money to buy items in bulk from wholesalers like Costco.

Over the past two years, NoVasta has become part of the national Zero Waste Coalition. Club chapters have been started at other US schools and abroad.

NoVasta embraces the global goal of reduced food waste and passing legislation to halve food loss and waste by 2030.

“It’s given us a lot of hope to see that even though it’s such a big problem, there are a lot of people — whether it’s students or city councilors or people our age or restaurants — that are willing to work and find ways to contribute to this cause,” Hennessy said.

Nuvana Ivory, who has worked front of house at The Real Deal for two years, has seen Sun and Hennessy come in often to pick up food at the end of the night. The restaurant usually gives any excess food to staff or to homeless people in the area. But the girls’ initiative to eliminate food waste makes her feel good.

“I don’t like to see food go to waste,” she said. “To see the food go to a good cause and not be thrown in the trash is a good opportunity for us to help out.”

Food insecurity is a growing crisis in the United States, with approximately 13.5 percent of US households being food insecure in 2023, up from 12.8 percent in 2022, according to the USDA.

However, while food insecurity is on the rise, millions of tons of food are being thrown away each year, data show.

According to the US Department of Agriculture, food waste makes up between 30 and 40 percent of food supply. In 2019, 66 million tons of food waste were generated in the United States, according to the US Environmental Protection Agency.

The growing problem prompted Boston City Councilor Gabriela Coletta Zapata and others to propose an ordinance in 2023 to create a citywide food recovery program.

“More or less of what [is] safe to consume could go to neighborhoods such as East Boston, Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, High Park that remain underserved by a lack of grocery stores or forcing residents to travel to food pantries on their days off or when they have work,” Zapata said.

Programs to address food waste have been adopted in other cities, such as Washington D.C. Zapata has been working with Sun and Hennessy to try to implement a city-wide food recovery program, which would be established with the ordinance that councilors are working to pass.

“It would compel some of these large food generators to compile their edible leftovers, and then as an effort to utilize what is safe to consume at its highest possible use before it’s sent to be recycled or sent to the landfill,” Zapata said.

While NoVasta started as a school club, it has grown into an international initiative to “turn excess into access.” Through online forums and social media, Sun and Hennessy were able to connect with other high schoolers who noticed the same patterns in their communities: food going to waste while people were going hungry.

“[Students] saw the same overflowing dumpsters in their community, and they saw the same like empty hands on the street that were always just [a few] feet away. So every single student we talked to noticed the same issue in their own city, and they’ve sort of just been waiting for a catalyst to start it. And so we’re really happy that we were that catalyst for them,” Sun said.

title: Here are the 11 most exciting luxury hotels opening in 2026
text:
Big players like Aman aren’t all out of tricks, however, and in fact such established brands are still the options consumers trust most when they’re visiting a less familiar destination or planning a once-in-a-lifetime trip. The group’s opening in Mexico will help cement the rise of the eastern cape of Baja California, about 90 minutes from Los Cabos. It’s away from the thumping clubs on a less developed section of coastline that claims a rare amenity in this corner of Mexico: swimmable beaches. Meanwhile, Singita, the most renowned luxury safari camp operator in Africa, is finally planting its flag in one of the most desirable private concessions of Botswana’s wildlife-rich Okavango Delta at the end of 2026, a dream combination for safari connoisseurs.

When big brands come to big markets, they have to pull out all the stops. So in London, Waldorf Astoria will transform the landmark Admiralty Arch into the latest jewel in its crown — just one year after wrapping a jaw-dropping $2 billion, eight-year renovation of its New York flagship. But even then it may not be the biggest opening in town. The smart money is on Cambridge House, a Georgian gem overlooking Green Park that’s currently being converted by Auberge Collection. With so much early buzz, snagging a room the minute reservations open may be your best odds at getting in.

When: January

Where: Palm Beach, Florida

Palm Beach has its fair share of luxury hotels. But the Vineta is the American debut from Oetker Hotels, the European group behind Parisian palace Le Bristol. It’s a brand known for continental elegance, old-world glamour and impeccable service — qualities that aren’t typically native to South Florida. Now it’s setting up shop blocks away from the posh boutiques of Worth Avenue, in a Mediterranean-revival-style building that’s been standing for a hundred years.

Its extensive renovation has made for 41 spacious suites, with bedrooms decorated in soft pastels to fit the building’s heritage and pale-pink exterior. In a touch of whimsy, staffers will wheel bar carts around the hotel’s public spaces. One is dedicated to Champagne and another to poolside scoops of gelato. A third will be stocked with Barbara Sturm beauty products, delivering creams and serums to guests’ rooms so they can leave the hotel with not just a tan but also a radiant glow. Rooms from $1,497.

When: March

Where: Kyoto, Japan

It’s been three decades since homegrown Japanese luxury company Imperial opened a new property. That changes in spring 2026, with its update of a 90-year-old former theater in Kyoto’s famed Gion district. The main building has been respectfully preserved, with elements from the former performance space, including its distinct pillars and window frames, retained as visual focal points. A guests-only rooftop bar offers sweeping views of the cityscape and the lanterns’ glow on the streets below.

The Imperial’s 55 rooms use traditional materials such as Japanese cedar columns and tatami flooring, with design by local firms rather than imported big names, as has become the norm in town. The result is something more subtle, and more faithfully and authentically Japanese than the area’s shiny competition. From around $1,100.

When: Spring

Where: South of France

When French spirits entrepreneur Paul Ricard purchased Île de Bendor — off the coast of rosé capital Bandol — in the 1950s, it was just an empty plot. He transformed the stony island into a socialite playground where Russian cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin and artist Salvador Dalí would visit. Now the Ricard family is turning its vacation home into a destination for modern luxury travelers. There will be a 93-room hotel but also a little village with three restaurants, four bars, an art gallery and artisan shops open to the public.

Days on the 17-acre island can be spent playing pétanque, relaxing at the 1,200-square-meter (12,900-square-foot) spa or scuba diving (the hotel will have a dive center run in partnership with the Cousteau family). A ten-minute ferry will take guests to the mainland to explore Provencal vineyards, cobblestone villages and the region’s famed farmers markets. From around $600.

When: Spring

Where: Baja California, Mexico

Ultraluxe Aman is making a splash with its first Mexican hotel, with 18 casitas on a hillside along the quiet east cape of Baja California. Because Aman loyalists are often somewhat reclusive, choosing to hide away in their posh digs, each casita will include expansive views of the Sea of Cortez and the Sierra de la Laguna mountains, plus private pools flanked with plush loungers. The spa, one of the highlights of any Aman resort, will feature a modern temescal (sweat lodge), in a nod to local traditions.

One of the benefits of being here versus bustling Cabo is that the beaches of the east cape are very swimmable, with less strong currents, ideal for days spent exploring the gentle waters. Nearby is a golf course designed by the renowned Robert Trent Jones II, as well as 18 acres of organic farms and orchards to explore. Rates not currently available.

When: Second quarter

Where: Riyadh, Saudi Arabia

The futuristic overwater bungalows in Saudi Arabia’s glimmering new Red Sea development are getting fresh competition in an unlikely location: the busy, traffic-clogged capital. It’s here that the kingdom’s royal residence — built in 1943 as the home of the country’s founding father, King Abdulaziz Al Saud, and famous for its art deco architecture — will open to the public as a 70-room hotel. Historic spaces that hosted royal celebrations and state banquets will become reception suites, each one scented with King Saud’s favorite flower, the native Taif rose.

In another display of discretion, the spa is also made up exclusively of private suites, with each treatment room sporting its own changing area, sauna and steam room. And as part of the royal experience, guests will have palace hosts who cater to their every request, within reason. Rates not currently available.

When: March

Where: Charleston, South Carolina

Charleston has long been beloved for its gracious Southern architecture, miles of white flowering magnolia trees and rich Lowcountry cuisine — but now it’s one of the top 2026 destinations for the ways in which it keeps raising the bar. The Cooper, for instance, will be the first hotel in town to marry all the amenities of an urban resort with a waterfront location, making it feel almost like a beach retreat within the city itself.

Among its draws will be a 7,000-square-foot wellness center, five restaurants and a rooftop infinity pool, plus preferential access to a yearlong chef’s residence by Daniel Humm (of Eleven Madison Park fame) at sibling hotel Charleston Place. And of course, seeing the city from the water will be a unique experience worth prioritizing too: Guests will have access to a private marina with cruising vessels to tour the shoreline, as well as a water taxi to Daniel Island. From $950.

When: Spring

Where: London

London’s wildly competitive hotel market is getting a stellar new entrant, in a landmark building in Mayfair that was formerly home to a prince and a prime minister. The design of the 102 rooms and common spaces will channel the opulence of the Georgian era with intricate original ceiling designs, 19-foot-high ceilings and ornate fireplaces. They’ll overlook King Charles III’s current residence, with windows facing the greenery of the parks.

In keeping with its knack for decadent spas, Auberge is adding a wellness area inspired by ancient Roman bathhouses that’s set to span two floors, including a pair of heated swimming pools — a rarity in central London — and a relaxation area with a firepit. A new Major Food Group restaurant might not be the deciding factor in a booking for New Yorkers, but it will likely make Cambridge House a hot spot for Londoners in a similar way the new Carbone at the Chancery Rosewood has elsewhere in Mayfair. Rates not yet available.

When: May

Where: Cartagena, Colombia

Cartagena’s hotel scene — mostly composed of boutique spots in the new city, plus one stunning Sofitel behind the historic ramparts — is getting a big luxury upgrade this spring. Four Seasons, a brand still riding its White Lotus high, is taking over (and unifying) eight buildings including a 16th century San Franciscan temple and the 1920s Beaux Arts Club Cartagena, an old social hotbed. Inside will be 131 rooms and eight bars and restaurants, including a speakeasy and a steakhouse.

Guests can sign up for salsa lessons led by professional dancers, then cool down in one of the rooftop’s two swimming pools. As for the rooms, they’ll start at a spacious 388 square feet, many with balconies overlooking the old cloisters. Consider it the best of both worlds: old Colombian charm and all the modern creature comforts. Rooms from around $800.

When: June

Where: Florence, Italy

La Réserve’s first Italian hotel is located on the Via Santo Spirito, a street lined with Renaissance-era buildings and artisan workshops. It took a meticulous four-year renovation and a collaboration with celebrated designers Gilles & Boissier to transform the 600-year-old palazzo into a luxe hotel, but the result includes frescoed ceilings, ornate tilework, arched windows and the best of Italian craftsmanship, in a nod to the history and art-world heritage that defines Florence.

There are just six standalone apartments in one- to three-bedroom configurations. All have full kitchens and separate living areas, plus access to a gym, library and lounge. There’s also a roof terrace where you can sip on the region’s wines, as well as a “secret bar” to explore in the heritage building. Experiences will include Tuscan culinary adventures and the opportunity to play tennis at the owner’s Florentine house, truly making guests feel at home on the city’s storied streets. Rates not yet available.

When: Fourth quarter

Where: Oman

Rather than a single hotel, this is a trio of ultraluxe lodges forming a circuit — giving guests an easy way to explore an entire country in the most streamlined and amenity-rich way possible. (We’ve noted these circuits as one of the most compelling trends in travel right now.) The Malkai will have one tented camp in the sweeping sands of Oman’s desert and another in the coastal farmlands; the final lodge will be up in the jagged Al Hajar Mountains. The camps include spas and marble swimming pools in dramatic shades of dark red and beige. And unlike most hotels, these can’t be booked individually. Instead itineraries spanning all three lodges will last 4 to 10 days.

In a unique twist, guests will get paired with a personal so-called murshid, a butler who doubles as a driver. They’ll guide guests on every leg of their big Omani sojourn, shuttling them from lodge to lodge in Land Rover Defenders and arranging all sorts of adventures along the way, be it dune-bashing in the desert or snorkeling off Oman’s coast. Rates not yet available.

When: December

Where: Botswana

Singita has made its reputation as the king of five-star safaris without a lodge in Botswana, one of Africa’s most coveted destinations. So safari insiders are eager to see what the company can achieve now that it’s planting its flag in the famed Okavango Delta, a region made up of wildlife-rich islands, lagoons, grasslands and swamps. The specific area Singita has taken on — the privately managed, 400,000-acre Abu concession, where Wilderness Safaris long ran the iconic Abu Camp — teems with herds of elephants, lions and cheetahs. And its topographical diversity lets guests appreciate the animals from many distinct vantages, including wooden mokoro canoes as well as traditional open-top jeeps, offering a wider range of wildlife adventures.

Each of the lodge’s eight tents comes with its own private heated plunge pool, and there are ample outdoor decks to take in the clear skies. Expect a decadent level of luxury, even by the high standards that exist in the bush. As with most of Singita’s latest projects, Elela will have reliable Wi-Fi, in-room wellness treatments and a deep wine cellar for evening tastings. Plus, design will be as bold as the predators in the savannah: Singita’s aesthetic relies heavily on the works of top African artisans, including weavers, textilers and ceramicists who contribute to a colorful and local feel. All-inclusive rates from $4,500.

title: After decades as a pastor, lawyer, and advocate, Rev. Miniard Culpepper will take on a new role: Boston city councilor
text:
Now, Culpepper is getting ready to add a new line to his resumé. In January, he will be sworn in to elected office for the first time, representing Roxbury-based District 7 on the Boston City Council.

It’s one of the city’s most diverse and historically marginalized districts, and has faced immense turmoil in the last year. The council seat has sat vacant since July, when former councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson resigned after pleading guilty to federal corruption charges.

The council is often a launchpad for young politicians with ambitions for higher office, but Culpepper, 72, appears to be flipping that script. The council’s only new member will also be its oldest sitting member, and he comes to the body with decades of advocacy, legal, ministerial, and political experience.

Culpepper said his longstanding community work won him voters’ support.

“The community wanted a voice that they have heard and they can support and that they have confidence” in, Culpepper said.

Representing a council district is similar to leading a parish: They’re both 24/7 jobs, he said.

“Constituents, they call you when they have emergencies. Same thing with church folks,” he said. “What happens now is I don’t stop doing what I’ve been doing, in terms of helping people.”

The mission to serve has been a driving theme throughout his life, and is a thread of his family history, Culpepper said in a recent interview at his home on Seaver Street.

The house is a piece of history itself: His grandparents faced racism when purchasing it in the early 1950s, and were the first Black homeowners on the road, he said. In the 1960s, his mother and grandmother used the small building in the backyard as a day care. This year, it served as Culpepper’s campaign headquarters.

Culpepper remembers his grandfather sitting in the living room when he heard that Martin Luther King Jr. had been killed. The two had protested together, Culpepper said.

Hearing those stories as a child had a profound impact on him.

“How could you be part of a family that fought for civil rights and not have it as part of who you are?” Culpepper said.

Culpepper wants to bring those values to City Hall. He said he plans to push for an ethics committee on the council, a separate city agency focused solely on homelessness, and increased homeownership opportunities for Section 8 voucher holders.

After graduating from Boston Public Schools’ English High School in 1971, Culpepper earned his undergraduate degree from Brandeis University and got involved in politics while getting his law degree from Suffolk University.

He worked on Senator Ted Kennedy’s 1980 run for president and Bill Clinton’s White House bid in 1992. In Washington, D.C., Culpepper worked on Capitol Hill and earned a divinity degree from Howard University in 1988.

By 1995, Culpepper had moved from Washington to Milton with his wife and two young sons, and taken a job as a top lawyer for the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development. He also became the senior pastor at the Pleasant Hill Missionary Baptist Church, which his grandfather founded in 1939.

Contentious divorce proceedings between Culpepper and his wife briefly divided the church community in 1999, with some parishioners filing a lawsuit to bar Culpepper from church property, while others fiercely defended him, according to a Globe report from the time.

Culpepper’s ex-wife accused him of verbal and emotional abuse, while Culpepper got two restraining orders against her. A judge dismissed the parishioners’ lawsuit against Culpepper less than a month after it was filed.

In Boston’s Black communities and in many political circles, Culpepper is known for his work at HUD and for his civic leadership.

“He’s a very visible person; he’s out in the community a lot,” said Joyce Ferriabough Bolling, a native Roxbury resident and political consultant who’s known Culpepper for decades. “He brings a wealth of experience ... [and] has shown his love for the community.”

At HUD, Culpepper sued the Boston Housing Authority for alleged discrimination against tenants of color in the 1990s. It led the city to adopt new civil rights protections.

Culpepper also worked to curb youth violence, particularly after the death of 20-year-old Jahmol Norfleet, a onetime gang member who was shot to death in 2006. Norfleet was killed just months after he and other youth leaders, with the help of Black ministers, including Culpepper, brokered a peace deal between two rival gangs. Norfleet’s death inspired Culpepper to start the Trotter Park Peace Program, which provided activities and paid job opportunities for at-risk youth.

Antoine Goforth, now 39, was Norfleet’s best friend and also involved in a local gang. He said the Trotter Park Peace Program, and his relationship with Culpepper, changed his life. Not only did Culpepper work to get kids jobs and keep them out of trouble, he also developed relationships with them, listened, and earned their respect.

“Whenever we need help with something, he’d be the first person we’d call,” Goforth said. “If Reverend Culpepper wasn’t around, I’d probably be in jail or dead or something like that.”

Cedric White, a close friend and former colleague of Culpepper’s at HUD, said his dedication to advocacy and his community have not waned in the more than two decades they’ve known each other.

“He’s not one to sit around and be idle,” White said. “If there’s an issue that’s not right, he wants to be there to help the cause and stand up for the people.”

In recent years, Culpepper has rallied Black ministers to encourage their communities to get the COVID-19 vaccine, and started a small church farm to grow and distribute free fresh produce. He led protests against the closures of several Walgreens pharmacies in Black neighborhoods, and organized support for migrant families when the state had to temporarily house them in Roxbury’s Melnea Cass Recreation Center.

He also stayed involved in politics, praying over Senator Elizabeth Warren before debates during her presidential run in 2020. After weighing a run for mayor in 2013, Culpepper lost a race for state Senate in 2022.

He said he had no plans to run for office again, until community leaders urged him to run for the District 7 council seat last year.

Joseph Feaster Jr., who has known Culpepper since they worked on Kennedy’s 1994 Senate campaign, said Culpepper’s experience in politics and housing policy, plus his care for the community, will make him an effective councilor.

“Politics requires the ability to oftentimes compromise in order to get what you need to get done for the greater good,” Feaster said. Culpepper’s “going to be able to state his position, he will be able to articulate it well, but he’s also prepared to listen, and that’s the quality many don’t have.”

title: Dorchester man arrested on murder charge after Mattapan triple shooting that left woman dead, two injured
text:
A Dorchester man, charged with murder in connection with a triple shooting in Mattapan earlier this year that killed an 18-year old woman and injured two men, was arrested early Tuesday morning. An arrest warrant has been issued for a second suspect, authorities said.

At approximately 6 a.m., members of the Boston Police SWAT Team along with homicide detectives, served an arrest warrant at 260 Ruggles St. in Roxbury and took Dkhari Wornum-Brown, 22, into custody, according to a statement from Boston police.

He was arraigned in the Dorchester division of Boston Municipal Court Tuesday on charges of first-degree murder and carrying an unlicensed firearm, police said.

Judge Rebeca Figueroa ordered that Wornum-Brown be held without bail. His next court date, a probable-cause hearing, was set for Feb. 5, according to the Suffolk District Attorney’s Office.

Wornum-Brown was not the shooter, prosecutors said. An arrest warrant has been issued for the alleged gunman. Authorities did not disclose that person’s identity.

Wornum-Brown’s arrest stems from an afternoon shooting in Mattapan on Oct. 11. Police responded to a ShotSpotter activation at 2 Hiawatha Road and found three people suffering from gunshot wounds; all three were taken to local hospitals, authorities said.

According to prosecutors, five people were hanging out on the front porch when two men rode up on a scooter. Wornum-Brown drove the scooter, and the other man hopped off and fired off at least 21 rounds, striking three people. The shooter got back onto the scooter and the two men fled the scene.

Two of the victims were men who suffered nonlife-threatening wounds. But a third victim, 18-year-old G’Kiyah Lewis of Malden, eventually died of her injuries weeks later, police said.

“The violent death of G’Kiyah Lewis is a societal tragedy,” District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement Tuesday. “I’m grateful for the great investigative effort that brought someone forward to answer for this terrible crime and I urge the second suspect to turn himself in before he or anyone else gets hurt.”

Hayden extended his “deepest sympathies to G’Kiyah’s family and friends.”

Investigators used video, GPS tracking, and other circumstantial evidence to identify the alleged suspects, according to the district attorney’s office.

Lewis was a Malden High School senior who loved fashion, the beach, and having her photo taken, her mother, Rehema Grayson, had told The Boston Globe. She was hanging out with her boyfriend and other friends, her mother said, when a bullet went through her arm, grazed her heart, and lodged in her head.

She leaves behind two younger sisters, aged 7 and 15, her mother said.

After her death, Lewis’ organs were donated to three people, a 60-year-old woman and two men in their 40s, her mother said.

Faith leaders and community activists had demanded police action and urged residents to come forward with any information about her killing.

“None of our children should die in the streets,” said the Rev. Kevin Peterson, a community minister and public theologian at Grace Church of All Nations. “No blood should be in the streets of our community.”

Camilo Fonseca can be reached at camilo.fonseca@globe.com. Follow him on X @fonseca_esq and on Instagram @camilo_fonseca.reports. Tonya Alanez can be reached at tonya.alanez@globe.com. Follow her @talanez.

title: Mayor Michelle Wu, Boston city councilors to be sworn in for new term in office Monday
text:
“We will not appease or abet any threat to our city, and we will not wait for permission to build the world our families deserve,” Wu said. “Boston will be the proof that the nation we fought for is possible — a place where we take care of each other and take on the challenges that matter the most.”

Wu’s second inauguration, following a decisive reelection victory last fall, reaffirmed her considerable influence over Boston politics on a day that kept the face of city leadership largely unchanged and saw one of Wu’s allies elected City Council president. Wu was sworn in at Boston Symphony Hall by Sarah G. Kim, an associate justice of the Massachusetts Superior Court, as her two older children, sons Blaise and Cass, held a Bible beneath her hand. Wu then administered the oath of office to the 13 members of the council, 12 of them incumbents returning to office.

Wu’s remarks — which echoed her past pledges to improve Boston’s education system, tackle its affordability crisis, and protect the job sectors that power the city’s economy — underscored that continuity. Wu said she will spend the next four years continuing to improve school facilities and better city services. And, as the nation prepares to celebrate its 250th anniversary, Wu evoked American history as she promised to continue standing against a Trump administration that has repeatedly targeted the Democrat-run city.

“Right now, in some ways, the world feels helplessly stuck — like we know what problems need fixing, but we’ve lost faith we can fix them," Wu said. “Today, the forces we face aren’t British troops on the Common or ships in our harbor, but they demand no less ingenuity.”

Much of Wu’s speech centered on what her administration has already done. Wu said during her second term, she would continue to use “local government as the bedrock for getting results.”

Wu also took some shots at a Trump administration she said has “plundered our economy, ravaged our reputation, and destroyed the lives of our people.” She pledged to defend higher education, life sciences, hospitals, and clean energy — all sectors that the Trump administration has explicitly targeted or defunded.

Wu in the last year has earned support locally and attention nationally for sparring with the Trump administration. Still, her tone on Monday sounded somewhat milder than in some of her election year speeches, when she painted Boston as the defiant vanguard of the Trump resistance.

“God save whoever messes with Boston,” Wu warned in a speech last year. Her message Monday, though, sounded less provocative than defensive — guarded against economic uncertainty and threats from an unpredictable federal administration.

“This is certainly a moment where we have to make some tough choices about what comes next, and be clear that Boston and every community is having to do more with less. But we are going to keep doing more,” Wu told reporters.

Wu in Monday’s address said she plans to expand on some initiatives from her first term, but she did not propose major new programs. She pledged to make the country’s oldest public school system its best by “rightsizing our district” and investing in school facilities. Wu also said the city would “revisit school assignment” to make the process “simpler and more predictable.”

“We refuse to accept that accessing high quality education means crisscrossing our children all over our city rather than ensuring that, in every corner of Boston, the best school is just down the block,” Wu said.

She also touched on the city’s housing production and cost-of-living challenges, though she did not detail any specific new plans for tackling those challenges.

This week marks the official start of Wu’s second four-year term as mayor, and a new two-year term for the council. Monday’s event kicked off a week of planned community gatherings, including story times at libraries around the city, a gathering of faith leaders, and a celebration of small businesses.

Wu, the first woman and person of color elected to lead the city, sailed to victory in November. She appeared unopposed on the general election ballot after challenger Josh Kraft dropped out of the race following a dismal performance in the September preliminary.

A former city councilor who has long wielded influence over the body, Wu also helped council allies secure reelection in November. The panel appears likely to remain friendly to her policy agenda: Every incumbent councilor who sought reelection won in November.

Following Monday’s inauguration ceremony, the council elected Councilor Liz Breadon its new president, in a narrow 7–6 vote that followed a contentious debate. A 66-year-old physical therapist and immigrant from Northern Ireland, Breadon is the first openly gay female councilor and has been an outspoken advocate for LGBTQ+ rights.

Councilor Brian Worrell of Dorchester narrowly lost the election. The contest had been thrown into uncertainty over the weekend after a front-runner for the role, Councilor Gabriela Coletta Zapata, said she would not seek the presidency after all.

There is just one new face on the council this year: Rev. Miniard Culpepper, a longtime Dorchester activist, pastor, and former attorney for the Department of Housing and Urban Development, who was sworn in Monday. He represents Roxbury-based District 7, a seat that had sat vacant for months after former councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson pleaded guilty to federal corruption charges last year and resigned from the position in July.

While Wu has yet to detail her full agenda for the next four years, she has indicated one of her top priorities is making Boston Public Schools the “best major city school district” in the country.

It’s an ambitious goal and a daunting challenge: BPS’ persistent problems — including dropping enrollment numbers, decades-old facilities, and stubbornly low test scores — have vexed many of Wu’s predecessors.

Wu insists the district in her first term has made notable progress, while acknowledging that more work is still needed. However, Wu has not identified specific benchmarks or timelines she is targeting to determine success when it comes to improving academic outcomes.

While Wu focused many of her remarks Monday on Boston’s rich history, she closed on a more recent development:her daughter Mira’s first steps. Wu said Mira, who turns one next week, had tried to take a few steps on stage Monday morning, after her first attempt to walk last month ended in a fall.

“Some part of her already knows that progress takes courage — the willingness to take the next step when the ground isn’t certain,” Wu said. “Every one of us, from our earliest days, is living proof that last month’s impossible can become this morning’s milestones — that if we are only willing to try, with a little help from each other, we can build the future our families deserve.”

title: Roxbury teen among four suspects charged in group attack, robbery on Orange Line train, prosecutors say
text:
A Roxbury teenager was arraigned Monday in Boston Municipal Court in connection with a violent group assault and robbery aboard an MBTA Orange Line train earlier this month, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden’s office said Wednesday.

Mannice Mitchner, 18, pleaded not guilty to charges of unarmed robbery, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, and disorderly conduct on a public conveyance stemming from a Dec. 15 attack on an 18-year-old passenger, Hayden’s office said in a statement.

Mitchner is one of four teenagers who have been arrested in connection to the attack, prosecutors said. The other three are minors and their names were not released.

Judge Richard Sinnott revoked bail on several open cases involving Mitchner and ordered him to stay away from the victim as well as all MBTA stations and stops, Hayden’s office said.

Mitchner is due back in court Jan. 22 for a probable cause hearing, according to court records. His attorney could not immediately be reached for comment Wednesday.

Prosecutors say Mitchner was allegedly part of a group of seven teens who confronted the victim during the evening rush hour and participated in the assault while recording it on a cellphone.

The incident occurred about 5:45 p.m. after the group boarded an Orange Line train at Downtown Crossing. MBTA surveillance video allegedly shows the teens initiating a verbal confrontation with the victim that escalated into violence.

According to prosecutors, five of the teens allegedly punched the victim with closed fists, threw him to the ground, and continued to punch and kick him in the face and stomach. Mitchner is accused of approaching the scene with his phone out to film the attack and kicking the victim in the head.

Prosecutors said the group stole the victim’s shoes and cellphone before fleeing the train at the Massachusetts Avenue station. Two of the seven teens did not physically assault the victim, authorities said.

The victim told police he did not know any of the attackers, officials said.

“This was a frightening experience for this young man and for all the riders who witnessed it,” Hayden said in a statement, adding that surveillance cameras throughout the transit system play a key role in identifying suspects.

Prosecutors said Mitchner has open cases in multiple courts, including West Roxbury, Fall River, Roxbury, and Dorchester, involving charges such as breaking and entering, malicious destruction of property, attempted larceny, and receiving stolen property.

Three of the five juvenile attackers, along with Mitchner, have been arrested, Hayden’s office said.

Transit Police identified suspects through MBTA video footage and prior contacts with some of the juveniles. Additional arrests were made Dec. 16 and Dec. 19 with help from the Boston Police Department’s Youth Violence Strike Force, officials said.

The remaining juveniles are expected to be arraigned at a later date, Hayden’s office said.

Nick Stoico can be reached at nick.stoico@globe.com.

title: Years ago, Boston put bus lanes in the middle of this busy street. Has it worked?
text:
According to the T and the city, rush hour bus trips are quicker, cars speed less, and bus riders are pleased — proof that the lanes have been a “successful and impactful project,” in the words of a project summary published last February.

Attitudes among Roxbury residents and workers remain split. Some lane defenders welcome the prioritization of transit and find the lanes convenient. Some critics, however, said the lanes have sown confusion along the street, worsening safety.

Available data paint an ambiguous picture of safety improvements along the segment. The city says the number of crashes that caused injuries declined markedly. Boston police tallies indicate that vehicle collisions overall also declined on average, but only marginally. The T, meanwhile, said its buses have gotten into far more “major” collisions since 2021, an upswing that surprised some experts.

The T faulted the dangerous and illegal maneuvers of nonagency drivers for most of the crashes over the past couple of years. Only one incident, in 2023, “was considered preventable by the bus driver.”

“We are currently exploring updates to the bus lane design to make it more difficult for drivers to enter or cross the bus lane illegally,” the T said.

The agency said it’s already made some tweaks — enhancing physical barriers around platforms, banning left turns, and adjusting signal timing at some intersections, among other changes.

The T and the city plan to spend $37.3 million extending the lanes about a mile north to Ruggles. They intend to break ground in 2026, the T told the Globe.

Boston and the T also intend to carve out bus-exclusive street space along Blue Hill Avenue, in a not-yet-designed overhaul at one point priced at $44 million. The T said construction would begin in 2027 at the earliest, assuming the agency secures a still-pending Small Starts federal grant from the Trump administration worth about $80 million.

Columbus offers a rough template of how Blue Hill Avenue’s lanes may take shape.

From the sky, the lanes give the impression of a blood vessel, bound on either side by gray arteries of street and sidewalk.

There are eight stops in total, four in each direction — narrow islands wedged between the bus and general purpose lanes. The stops, outfitted with shelters, seats, barriers, and digital trip displays, are separated from the sidewalks by the shared lanes, much like some street-level Green Line stations.

Proponents promised that center-running bus lanes would free buses from thickets of traffic, improving their speed and reliability for a bus-reliant neighborhood.

Drivers bearing witness to the buses zipping by would, in time, ditch their cars and hop aboard. Confining the cars that remained to fewer lanes would enhance the street’s safety, according to advocates and some experts.

Stringing the bus lanes through the middle of the road, instead of connecting them to the curb, offers the added benefit of removing parked or turning vehicles from a bus’s path.

“It helps tremendously” with bus operation and reliability, said Zhan Guo, an urban planning and transportation policy professor at New York University.

Cities around the country have explored their potential benefits — from New York City to Eugene, Ore.

Bus lanes have recently attracted the scrutiny of the Trump administration, which this fall pumped the brakes on a bus lane project in New York City over its supposed impacts on freight traffic and emergency vehicles.

The Columbus Avenue rebuild cost $14.5 million, according to the MBTA. The corridor services three routes — the 44, 29, and 22, one of the T’s most popular, according to the agency.

The census estimates that about 30 percent of workers living in the 02119 ZIP code — encompassing much of Roxbury and Columbus Avenue — use public transit to get to work, about four times the state rate. About 28 percent of 02119 residents live below the poverty line, more than double statewide rate.

Expanding bus-specific street space is a pillar of the MBTA’s push to improve the popular service’s speed and reliability. Boston has publicly backed the effort, despite walking back bus lane installations in some parts of the city.

“The best bus-priority systems in the US have center-running lanes,” said Annie Weinstock, president of a New York consultancy specializing in bus infrastructure. “So it’s a very positive step that Boston has done that.”

Some in the Roxbury neighborhood greeted the revamp with skepticism that has only hardened since the lanes opened.

Working the checkout counter at Pina’s Grocery Store, a few yards from the dark red lanes, Maria Martinez griped about their impact on her car commute.

Martinez said she drove to work from Dorchester, a short journey that has been beset with “more traffic” since the buses ate up one lane along Columbus.

“We get to school late, we get to work late,” Martinez said in Spanish.

A city report from 2023 concluded that car trips along the nearly mile-long corridor took, on average, 20 to 40 seconds longer than they did prebus lane. Meanwhile, the study determined, bus lanes shaved around three to four minutes off bus trips during rush hour.

LivableStreets Alliance, a Cambridge transportation advocacy nonprofit, surveyed more than 150 Columbus Avenue bus riders in December 2021, shortly after the lanes went live. Around three-quarters of respondents reported faster and more consistent trips, according to a report summarizing the group’s findings. Just under one-quarter of respondents said they took the bus more frequently after the lanes were introduced.

It’s difficult to definitively pinpoint how exactly the Columbus lanes have impacted bus ridership.

“There is some evidence that with all things equal, [bus] speed increases can result in ridership increases,” said Weinstock, the bus infrastructure expert. “However, there are so many factors here and in other places that you really need to look at a lot [of] data before you can say definitively what caused what.”

Bus ridership plunged across the entire MBTA system during the pandemic — the early heights of which partly overlapped with the lanes’ construction — and has yet to fully recover. The T said the ridership recovery rate of the 22 bus has outpaced the agencywide average, but other lines without center-running bus lanes have also showcased strong rebounds. The 29 and the 44 buses, the other, less popular lines passing through Columbus, have shown weaker recoveries, according to data from TransitMatters, a research and advocacy group.

Still, some in Roxbury appreciate the bus lanes.

“They work well for what they’re meant to do,” said Sol Martinez Guevara, an employee at the Boston Public Library’s Egleston Square branch, a short stroll from where the bus lanes cease at Walnut Avenue and traffic begins to mingle again.

Despite typically biking to work from another part of Roxbury, Guevara appreciated what the lanes signaled about the city’s priorities.

“I feel like that’s just what makes more sense for being more of a public transit oriented city,” Guevara said.

Guevara’s colleague, Dorchester native Mikayla Willingham, largely agreed. She had, for a time, commuted by bus after the lanes were installed, she said.

“I feel like it’s convenient,” Willingham explained, acknowledging that confused or unconcerned drivers will sometimes trespass into bus zones.

For resident Luis Peña, that confusion feeds chaos.

“Boston City Hall’s worst expense has been to spend money on that,” Peña said in Spanish.

Vehicles barrel past the bus stops far faster than speed limits allow, he complained. Impatient drivers habitually veer into the bus lanes to slip around vehicles stationary in the right lane.

On a recent December day, some short bendable posts marking the lane-splits near bus stops were missing, snapped, or bore the marks of frequent beatings.

“It’s very unsafe,” said Peña, as he stood outside his friend’s store by the Weld Avenue stops, at times gesturing toward the road with his cane. “I don’t know why they did that and spent that money.”

The Police Department documented an average of 35.4 crashes annually along the corridor between 2015 and 2019, according to data shared by the agency. There’ve been, on average, 34.7 crashes annually along the stretch between 2022 and 2024. (BPD didn’t detail the types of crashes or their severity.)

The MBTA, meanwhile, documented 13 “major collisions” involving its buses along the Columbus corridor in 2023 and another 13 in 2024. The agency recorded only eight total major collisions between 2018 and 2022, four of them occurring in 2022.

The Globe in late November asked the T and the Transit Police for copies of the crash reports for each incident. Both agencies told the Globe to file a public records request for the documents. The Globe on Dec. 1 requested documentation for all crashes along the segment involving an MBTA bus between 2018 and 2024. The Globe later agreed to narrow the scope of its request to reports relating to the 34 collisions identified by the MBTA, but has yet to receive the reports.

More proactively identifying and punishing scofflaws could help reel in the rule-breakers, some experts said.

“More automated enforcement is a particularly powerful tool,” said Jeffrey Tumlin, a former director of transportation at the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency.

The agency, during Tumlin’s tenure, unveiled center-running bus lanes spanning a long stretch of Van Ness Avenue, a wide thoroughfare running through the heart of San Francisco. Buses experienced markedly fewer collisions along the segment once they began traveling through the lanes, according to an agency report published in April 2025.

Some drivers defied the rules of the new format, Tumlin said, but bus-mounted enforcement cameras helped keep them in line. The T plans to rollout a similar program in 2026.

Boston, meanwhile, maintains Columbus got safer. A July 2023 evaluation concluded that, on average, a larger share of vehicles — about 10 percentage points more — obeyed the corridor’s speed limit after the bus lanes came online.

It noted in a March report that the number of crashes resulting in injuries tumbled across the city in the years before and after the lanes opened. The decline in injury-causing crashes along the Columbus corridor was about 7 percentage points greater than the drop recorded on similar roads citywide, according to the report.

To Maha Aslam, a transit advocate in Greater Boston and bus lane believer, doubt and frustration and concern are understandable responses to drastic changes in a person’s environment.

“We see a lot of resistance from community members, because it changes the way they experience their neighborhood,” Aslam said.

She went on, “In general, people are antichange.”

title: Free skating in Dorchester sets family-focused tone for Wu’s second term
text:
Juliette Jacobs, 8,of Winchester, took a break from skating to explain what she liked most.

“You get to go fast while you’re roller blading around the corners,” she said, adding that she was happy the mayor had held the event “because we’re all having fun together.”

Her parents, Heather and Evan Jacobs, both 45, said events like this send a message about who the city is for.

“Living in an area that has such disparity in wealth, making events available to everyone gives everyone the opportunity to enjoy,” Evan Jacobs said. “It sends a message that you matter.”

The Dorchester event followed a similar free ice skating clinic Friday at the Frog Pond on Boston Common, part of a weeklong slate of family-oriented programming tied to Mayor Michelle Wu’s inauguration for a second term. The schedule also includes library storytimes, free museum days and youth-focused events across the city.

The focus on free, neighborhood-based events comes as Boston continues to grapple with a growing wealth gap, a divide that shapes which families can easily access arts, recreation, and cultural activities. Dorchester, long one of the city’s most diverse neighborhoods, has seen economic and demographic shifts that have put pressure on many families on the wrong side of that widening gap.

Florence Scott, an early-60s Dorchester residentwho brought her 16-year-old twins, Melaki and Myaja, said the skating clinic stood out for how it made young people feel included.

“It’s a positive outlet,” Scott said. “Especially for the teenagers.”

“They may not be exposed to this, and it’s right here. It’s right in the city,” Scott said. “It shows they’re investing in the future for the kids, because they are the future.”

Lorela Shehu, 32, attended the skating event with her husband, Jurgen Shehu, 34, and their 6-year-old son, JJ. The couple, who are originally from Albania, now live in Fenway, where Lorela is a graduate student at Boston University.

“I really appreciate that I’m raising him here,” Lorela Shehu said. “We’ve lived in other parts of the US, and that’s what I appreciate most about Boston, because of all these events and trying to engage families, which we didn’t see in other cities.”

“We kind of feel that we’re part of Boston,” she added. “It’s a good feeling to have.”

Toya Desarmes, 47, of Roxbury, said accessibility is not just about cost, but geography. Many kid-friendly activities, she said, require leaving the city altogether.

“If we bring more activities to the city that the kids have access to, whether it’s free or paid, something that’s local, so they don’t always have to go far,” Desarmes said. “They can use the bus or the train and get there.”

Her son, Alexander, 8, said he was “amazed” when he learned the skating was free. Asked why that mattered, he answered simply: “So everybody could have a chance.”

Noah Woodley, 19, of Milton, came with his girlfriend, Pulane Kgafela, also 19, of Norwood, and said the event felt different from anything he remembered growing up. He said he appreciated the mayor holding the skating clinic in Dorchester, a part of the city with many lower-income residents.

“I haven’t heard of mayors doing this type of stuff,” Woodley said. “Holding this in Dorchester speaks to what type of person she is. I think a lot of people in Dorchester and everywhere will appreciate it.”

Wu arrived midmorning, greeting families and watching skaters circle the rink. Asked what message she hoped to send by starting her second term with neighborhood-based, family events, Wu said the goal was to move beyond ceremony.

“We wanted to make sure that this wasn’t just about a fancy swearing-in ceremony downtown,” Wu said, “but that throughout the neighborhoods, families of every generation could come together and share in the excitement of what it means to build a community.”

“Times are really challenging right now,” she added. “So we have to double down on who we are as a community, and that means being the best city in the country to raise a family.”
