title: Hidden in a closet, a 200-year-old piece of Boston’s printing past emerges
text:
As Ahern helped extract the machine, broad smiles and compliments from movers and school staff greeted the press as it slowly emerged from its hideaway.

“Very cool,” cooed Ahern, who said the press will receive star treatment among the museum’s displays of printing’s centuries-long evolution.

“It’s really exciting to see a press like this pop up,” Ahern said. “In its day, this was printing technology. Our mission is to keep this kind of thing out of landfills.”

Its recent discovery at Franklin Cummings Tech, which is moving to Roxbury for the spring semester after 117 years in the South End, is a reminder of the school’s close association with Benjamin Franklin, the Boston-born printer and Founding Father whose generosity led directly to the college’s creation.

Franklin left 1,000 pounds sterling in his 1789 will to “the inhabitants of the town of Boston,” specifically for trade education, and noted that “good apprentices are likely to make good citizens.”

More than a century later, steel baron Andrew Carnegie matched Franklin’s gift on the condition that it be used for an industrial school and that the city donate the land. In 1908, with those conditions met, the school was dedicated as the Franklin Union.

Jackie Cornog, chief of staff at the college, said the press had been forgotten as Franklin Cummings prepared for its move to Nubian Square.

Amid the bustle, the press appeared — unmarked, untended, and unobtrusive — tucked into a corner of a small, cluttered space at the bottom of the college’s four-story main building.

The Museum of Printing soon showed interest. And Dana Thomson, Franklin Cummings’s facilities director, began hammering away to open a space wide enough to remove the heavy press from the basement.

The work culminated in its departure for the Merrimack Valley when four people, bending and straining, provided the muscle to lift the press into the van.

During a break in the move, Ahern noted that its hybrid design of wood and iron bridged a brief transition between completely wooden presses, which had been used for centuries, to machines made entirely of metal.

“Ramage was an innovator, and he was fine-tuning and tweaking the wooden presses, starting to change the design,” Ahern said.

The discovery of the press, which had been loaned to the college by the Bostonian Society many decades ago, is a reminder of Franklin Cummings’s educational mission, Cornog said.

“Being tied to history is so interesting, because this is just a building and we’re moving on,” Cornog said. “But in a sense, we’re still doing the same thing that we’ve done since the very beginning.”

Franklin’s presence is everywhere inside the main building’s expansive, marble-floor lobby. Murals of Franklin’s life ring the high walls, including one of Franklin at a printing press. Below them, a bust of Franklin, with moving tags attached, faces what once had been a steady stream of passers-by.

Franklin’s beginnings as a printer are what make the discovery so meaningful, Cornog said. More than 1,000 students a year gain skills in disciplines as varied as electricity, automotive repair, HVAC, and opticianry, which is the grinding and fitting of lenses for eyeglasses and contacts.

Franklin Cummings officials say they believe the school offered the nation’s first college-based auto-repair program, soon after Henry Ford introduced the Model T in 1908.

The college also was the scene of the first conference call, linking Boston, San Francisco, Chicago, Atlanta, Philadelphia, and New York in 1916, school officials said. And the first “telephoto” fax was sent from there in 1927.

Now, the printing press brings the school’s origins back full circle, she said.

“Franklin wanted other folks to have opportunities to become entrepreneurs in the trades,” Cornog said. “It’s something that started him out.”

Although Franklin moved to Philadelphia as a young man after a falling-out with his brother, his will showed he retained a lifelong affection for his hometown, where he was born in 1706.

The affection goes both ways. Cornog recalled with a laugh that when she placed the moving tags on Franklin’s bust, the building’s fire alarm suddenly began screeching.

“It seemed he was saying, ‘Either get the heck out or don’t leave,’ ” Cornog said.

title: Lawmakers of color have grown their ranks on Beacon Hill, but the Legislature remains disproportionately white
text:
The next chance to accelerate that change comes this year, with every legislative seat on the ballot in November. Candidates of color have made huge strides since redistricting in 2021, growing their caucuses to record numbers, and rising in the Legislature’s leadership ranks.

Still, those gains haven’t changed a firmly ingrained fact on Beacon Hill: The Legislature is 83 percent white in a state where just 68 percent of residents are. Advocates say the Legislature needs more lawmakers who share the lived experience of Massachusetts’ growing Black and Latino populations, particularly as amped up immigration enforcement, the state’s housing crisis, and the stratospheric cost of living are hitting those communities particularly hard.

The imbalance is not in race alone. Women make up a slight majority of Massachusetts residents, but are outnumbered by men more than 2-to-1 in the Massachusetts House and Senate.

“To no fault of a legislator in most cases, it’s hard to create all-encompassing policy when you yourself are not reflected,” said Celia Canavan, executive director of the Massachusetts League of Women Voters.

Of the state’s 198 sitting lawmakers, just five are Black women, said Miranda, who co-chairs the Legislature’s Committee on Racial Equity, Civil Rights, and Inclusion.

Miranda represents the progress candidates of color have made. In the 2022 election, she was one of a dozen lawmakers of color who won their seats for the first time. Now with 26 members, the Black and Latino Legislative Caucus has never been bigger.

But that caucus makes up just 13 percent of the Legislature, while Black and Latino residents make up 24 percent of the Massachusetts population, according to Census data.

If candidates of color realize new gains only after each decennial redistricting effort, Miranda said, it’d take decades to “get parity, to build the political infrastructure, to have more people stepping down and opening doors.”

“It will never be just about redistricting,” she said. “We have to actually change culture. . . . It actually takes grassroots support.”

Many of the obstacles are no secret. Massachusetts has some of the least competitive legislative elections in the country, meaning incumbents often face few, if any, challengers, and opportunities to run for an open seat are rare.

New candidates, regardless of race or ethnicity, have to quickly learn the basics of running a campaign: how to fundraise and navigate the state’s campaign finance rules, and also determine where to begin building support. That’s even more difficult when facing an incumbent who often enters the race with more money and experience.

For Black candidates in particular, “there’s no one there telling us how to do it,” said Reynolds Graves, founder of the 1866 Action Fund, which has run a super PAC supporting candidates of color. That has consequences, he said.

“Let’s use the [example of a] single Black mother in her mid-40s: When you don’t have that person in the Legislature advocating for her kids’ school funding, the community that might already have a skittishness about government or policymakers or politicians will feel even further out of place,” he said.

In the Latino community, there’s also the “complexities of that diversity” to consider, said Lorna Rivera, director of the Gastón Institute at UMass Boston, which is focused on issues affecting the state’s Latino population. In Massachusetts, that includes immigrants from 20 different countries, she said, all with distinct political and social histories that help shape voters’ choices at the ballot.

“We’re not a monolith,” Rivera said. “Let’s say there is a Latino running for mayor — it’s going to matter if [the candidate is] Dominican or Puerto Rican. And people don’t get that.”

The state’s last redistricting effort aimed to empower new candidates of color to win seats. After lawmakers redrew the map, voters sent the first Brazilian American women and the first Central American lawmaker to Beacon Hill. Last session’s legislative class was the most diverse in the state’s history, according to one state report. The State House added more lawmakers of color after the 2024 election.

The Black and Latino caucus alone has grown by more than 50 percent in less than four years.

“That was a direct result of intentional redistricting,” said state Representative Andy Vargas, the caucus’ president and the first Latino elected official in Haverhill.

Vargas also chairs the Joint Committee on Community Development and Small Businesses, alongside state Senator Adam Gómez, a Springfield Democrat who was the first Puerto Rican elected to the chamber. The panel’s first meeting in May was a “historic moment,” Gómez said. Vargas later said they are the first Latinos to co-chair a legislative committee in Massachusetts.

Policymakers warned then and now that redistricting alone is no panacea for diversifying legislative bodies. Out of Massachusetts’s 200 state legislative districts, there are now 39 so-called majority-minority districts, where most constituents are people of color. Many of those redrawn districts were intended to offer opportunities for new candidates of color to join the Legislature. Today, half are represented by white lawmakers, many of them incumbents who held the seats when the map was remade.

In some cities, the disparities are clear. In Lynn, where a plurality of people identify as Latino or Hispanic, four members of the city’s five-person State House delegation are white and none are Latino. Brockton, New England’s only Black-majority city, in November elected a Black mayor for the first time, but voters are still not represented by a Black state lawmaker. The city’s four-member delegation to the State House includes just one person of color, state Representative Rita Mendes.

“It takes time to mobilize and build political power within a district,” said Rahsaan Hall, president and chief executive of the Urban League of Eastern Massachusetts and a Brockton resident.

That said, at a time when the Trump administration has attacked diversity and inclusion initiatives and escalated immigration enforcement, “it’s all the more important to have people to speak truth to power and speak out to injustice because of the particular [lived] experience of those people,” Hall said.

Of course, lawmakers’ race or ethnicity doesn’t determine whether they can represent a community’s interests. In Chelsea, a small city where two-thirds of residents are Latino or Hispanic, voters since 2022 have sent Judith García to the House, where she is the chamber’s first Honduran American, and state Senator Sal DiDomenico, who is white, to the Senate.

DiDomenico has served in the chamber since 2010, though it wasn’t until the 2021 redistricting cycle that his already diverse district officially became majority-minority. The Everett Democrat said regardless of who’s living in his district, “my job is to show them that there are people in government who are fighting for them.”

Gladys Vega, head of the Chelsea-based La Colaborativa, said DiDomenico has done just that.

“He’s like a brother to me,” she said. “Redistricting is important because it reflects diverse communities, but most importantly, it’s who the leader is who represents your community, who sees you, regardless of your skin color. ... You also have to have leaders who get it. That’s what we’ve got.”

title: Boston’s Citgo sign survived sanctions and court battles. Now comes a post-Maduro test.
text:
A lawsuit against Boston Beer will put an unusual provision in Massachusetts’ noncompete law to the test.

RFK Jr.’s Health and Human Services Department dropped the number of vaccines it recommends for every child.

The New England Revolution took a big step forward in its quest for a new soccer stadium in Everett, after the Kraft Group and Boston Mayor Michelle Wu reached an agreement last week that aims to compensate the city for the expected impact on traffic and transit.

Follow the money: It’s the tried-and-true maxim for getting to the bottom of complicated or deliberately obscured events.

In the case of President Trump’s attempt at regime change in Venezuela, the money trail passes through Boston’s Kenmore Square, where the Citgo sign — an unofficial landmark and touchstone of city life — is planted atop 660 Beacon St.

You see, Trump used the sign’s owner, Citgo Petroleum Corp., as leverage in his extended campaign to oust Nicolás Maduro, Venezuela’s authoritarian leader.

That effort began with sanctions during Trump’s first term, including a freeze on the US assets of Venezuela’s state oil company, which owned Citgo, a Houston-based refiner and pipeline operator. The freeze has not affected the sign, but combined with other sanctions, it crippled Venezuela’s oil-driven economy, formerly the richest in Latin America.

But Maduro clung to power despite increasing US pressure, leading to Saturday’s stunning raid by US Army commandos that captured him and his wife, Cilia Flores, in Caracas. They were whisked away to New York to face charges related to cocaine trafficking.

The latest: Trump doesn’t intend to stop there. He and administration officials made clear over the weekend that steering a substantial chunk of Venezuelan oil revenues toward the US was a key objective behind Maduro’s removal.

The US will continue a military blockade of the country’s oil exports until the government stops drug trafficking and opens up the oil sector, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday. “What you’re seeing right now is an oil quarantine that allows us to exert tremendous leverage over what happens next.”

Trump’s view: The president left no doubt about what he wants to see next.

“We’re going to have our very large United States oil companies, the biggest anywhere in the world, go in, spend billions of dollars, fix the badly broken. . . oil infrastructure, and start making money for the country,” he said during a Saturday news conference.

“We’re gonna be taking out a tremendous amount of wealth out of the ground, and that wealth is going to the people of Venezuela. . . And it goes also to the United States of America in the form of reimbursement for the damages caused us by that country,” Trump said.

What’s at stake: Venezuela estimates its proven crude reserves at more than 300 billion barrels, the most of any country in the world.

The country was pumping about 3 million barrels a day in the mid-2000s. But after years of mismanagement under former president Hugo Chávez and Maduro, his successor, production has fallen to less than 1 million barrels, or about 1 percent of global output.

Oil prices were up slightly on Monday morning as investors weighed the fallout from Maduro’s capture. Shares of US energy companies, including Chevron, the only American company operating in Venezuela, jumped in trading.

Step back: When Venezuela nationalized its oil sector in 1976, it created Petróleos de Venezuela, or PDVSA, as the state oil company. The government opened up the sector in the 1990s to attract more foreign investment, but an exodus ensued after Chávez clamped down again.

While US sanctions took a toll, the state oil company, PDVSA had already been severely weakened by underinvestment, corruption, and the exodus of technical expertise.

Chevron held on — it’s been in Venezuela for more than 100 years. Operating with a special license, it accounts for about a quarter of the country’s output, with about half its production exported to the US.

Citgo’s role: PDVSA, seeking refining and distribution capacity in the US, bought a 50 percent stake in Citgo from Southland Corp. in 1986 and took full ownership four years later.

Trump’s first-term sanctions cut off Venezuela’s access to Citgo’s US operations, a reliable source of US dollars whose refineries were configured to handle PDVSA’s heavier grades of crude.

The US company’s parent, PDV Holding, has inhabited a legal netherworld: It’s been owned PDVSA but the US government recognizes a board of directors organized by the opposition-led National Assembly of Venezuela in 2019 after Maduro claimed reelection in a vote widely viewed as fraudulent.

After a series of mind-bending legal maneuvers — triggered when Venezuela and PDVSA stopped paying off debt and arbitration awards tied to nationalization — US courts ruled that creditors could go after the shares of PDV Holding. A Delaware judge then oversaw an auction of the shares, with proceeds going to creditors.

Amber Energy, backed by hedge fund Elliott Investment Management, won the bidding, but Citgo has appealed the decision.

The Iraq lesson: Trump’s plan to resurrect Venezuela’s oil sector echoes what happened after the US invaded Iraq in 2003 and toppled dictator Saddam Hussein.

Iraq’s crude production had fallen dramatically under sanctions and Saddam’s neglect. It took billions of dollars in investment and eight years to get output consistently back above pre-war levels.

In Venezuela, returning to peak production levels of the 1970s could require US companies such as Chevron and Exxon Mobil to invest about $10 billion a year over the next decade, Francisco Monaldi, an expert in Latin American energy at Rice University, told Bloomberg.

But before spending that kind of money, oil companies will want assurances of political and economic stability in Venezuela. Moreover, there is an oil glut and prices are near a five-year low.

Final thought: Cities Service, Citgo’s predecessor, put its sign up in Kenmore Square in 1940. The Citgo name appeared 25 years later with a new installation marking a rebranding.

The LED-lit sign is a reminder that oil still generates massive wealth despite political upheaval, environmental challenges, and real estate deals. (After 660 Beacon changed hands in 2016, a long-running lease deal was reached to keep the sign in place.)

Trump senses opportunity in Venezuela. Whether US oil companies will follow the money is another question.

title: Roxbury lawmaker tapped campaign for $6,500 in illegal personal spending, including on food orders and at a salon
text:
A Democratic state lawmaker from Roxbury spent nearly $6,500 out of her campaign account last year on personal expenses — including at a salon and on food deliveries — in violation of state law, according to public records and campaign finance regulators.

State Representative Chynah Tyler must pay the state $6,000 under a settlement agreement released by the Office of Campaign and Political Finance on Tuesday.

State regulators said they identified $5,664 in campaign money Tyler used for her “personal use.” That included at least $4,500 in spending last spring and summer that the five-term Democrat failed to document even after regulators asked for bills, invoices, and other records.

In addition, Tyler has already reimbursed her campaign account for $830 in other “erroneous personal expenditures” that she herself admitted to, including $223 at a hair-braiding salon, $100 on a AAA membership, and several Uber Eats orders, campaign spending records show.

The personal spending accounted for a significant share of her campaign costs in 2025, a nonelection year during which she reported spending just under $40,000. And between April and June, when officials said Tyler did not account for $4,500 in expenses, her campaign reported spending $6,190 in total, records show.

Elected officials and candidates are allowed to use their campaign accounts for a range of purposes as long as they can show it’s for the “enhancement of [their] political future” and is not “primarily for personal use.” Under those rules, state lawmakers have used campaign funds to pay for swanky dinners, visits to cigar lounges, and luxury car leases.

Campaign finance regulators said that Tyler’s failure to document thousands of dollars in purchases “creates a presumption that the expenditure was made for personal use.”

Officials said Tyler also broke a series of other campaign finance rules when she filed late disclosures, took donations exceeding state-mandated limits, and failed to “keep detailed records,” according to the settlement.

Tyler did not immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday. In a response included in the six-page agreement with state regulators, Tyler said she gave birth to a child in “winter 2025 and experienced limited mobility during that time, which impacted my ability to personally oversee certain campaign finance activities.”

She said that during that time, however, she continued to meet with constituents, “community leaders and other qualified professionals,” though she did not say how those meetings related to specific expenditures by her account.

“These meetings were in compliance with [campaign finance law], consistent with my commitment to transparency and adherence to all legal obligations related to campaign contributions and expenditures,” Tyler said in the statement.

Tyler was first elected in 2017 to succeed longtime representative Gloria Fox in a district rooted in Roxbury. She is currently the House vice chair of the Legislature’s committee on state administration and regulatory oversight, and in the past led the growing Massachusetts Black and Latino Legislative Caucus.

BISHOP ALLEN The brainy Brooklyn-via-Harvard indie pop act dusts off peppy, perky music-blogger-beloved tunes like the raucous “Middle Management” and the jittery “Ciick, Click, Click, Click” for their first run of shows in a decade. Jan. 15, 8 p.m. The Sinclair, Cambridge. 617-547-5200, sinclaircambridge.com

KEYSHIA COLE In 2005, this Oakland-born R&B belter released her debut, “The Way It Is,” a collection of songs about love and heartbreak that showcased her formidable voice and from-the-gut lyricism; this show will celebrate its 20th anniversary. Jan. 15, 8 p.m. MGM Music Hall at Fenway. crossroadspresents.com

CATE LE BON The Welsh avant-pop auteur’s latest project, “Michaelangelo Dying,” is a gorgeously prickly meditation on anguish and loss centered on her sturdy yet searching alto and saxophonist Euan Hinshelwood’s plaintive wails. Jan. 15, 8 p.m. The Sinclair, Cambridge. 617-547-5200, sinclaircambridge.com

MAURA K. JOHNSTON

ISABEL OLIART, SAMMY WETSTEIN AND ANNE HOOPER TRIO Oliart is the current US National Scottish Fiddle Champion. She’s joined by her teacher Anne Hooper and multi-instrumentalist Sammy Wetstein for a performance of traditional and original Celtic music. Jan. 10, 2 p.m. Free. Center for Arts at the Armory, 191 Highland Ave., Somerville. 617-718-2191, artsatthearmory.org

MICAH P. HINSON You could call Micah P. Hinson an indie-folk artist, but it’s probably more accurate to say, as one reviewer once did, that he resides firmly within his own universe. That universe doesn’t include trips to this part of the world very often, so catch him while you can. Jan. 11, 7 p.m. $15. The Rockwell, 255 Elm St., Somerville. www.therockwell.org

AVA NEAL Judging from the assured, hooky, jangly folk ’n’ pop collected on “Balance Beam,” an album this young Boston-area singer-songwriter released two years ago, she has a promising future. She’ll play music from that album as well as preview songs from an upcoming release this Sunday. Jan. 11, 8 p.m. $10. The Lilypad, 1353 Cambridge St., Cambridge. 617-955-7729, www.lilypadinman.com

STUART MUNRO

LUKE WINSLOW-KING Born in Cadillac, Mich., a resident of New Orleans for 15 years, and currently based in Calatayud, Spain, the blues and roots slide guitarist, singer, composer, and lyricist incorporates influences far and wide: from ragtime, Delta blues, and jazz to prewar American folk and Béla Bartók. Jan. 10, 8 p.m. $30-$32. Narrows Center for the Arts, 16 Anawan St., Fall River. narrowscenter.org

TIGER OKOSHI & TRULY TRUE Arts Wayland’s Berklee Faculty Series kicks off 2026 with renowned Japanese trumpeter and Berklee professor Okoshi and his chamber jazz band: vibraphonist Sam Cerra, violinist Louis Thélot, cellist Peter Sumner, and bassist Ferran Rico Andres. Jan. 11, 3 p.m. $20. First Parish in Wayland, 225 Boston Post Road, Wayland. artswayland.com

POINT01 PERCENT PRESENTS Two ensembles featuring adventurous local improvisors: guitarist Gabe Boyarin, violinist Phillip Rawlinson, pianist Anthony Coleman, and drummer Noah Mark perform a new work by Boyarin; three seasoned acolytes of Thelonious Monk — pianist Pandelis Karayorgis, saxophonist Allan Chase, and drummer Luther Gray — play pieces by the great man. Jan. 13, 7:30 p.m. $15. The Lilypad, 1353 Cambridge St., Cambridge. lilypadinman.com

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA The BSO opens 2026 with concert performances of Samuel Barber’s “Vanessa,” conducted by music director Andris Nelsons and starring Jennifer Holloway as the title character opposite Samantha Hankey as Erika, Anne Sofie von Otter as the Old Baroness, and last-minute additions to the cast Ganson Salmon and Patrick Carfizzi as Anatol and the Old Doctor respectively, stepping in for Pavel Cernovich and Thomas Hampson due to illness. The performances are presented in collaboration with Boston Lyric Opera, whose chorus joins the Tanglewood Festival Chorus for the evening (Jan. 10). Next week’s program opens with BSO principal flutist Lorna McGhee in Allison Loggins-Hull’s “Rhapsody on a Theme by Joni” (as in Mitchell), followed by Bernstein’s “Chichester Psalms” with the Tanglewood Festival Chorus and Tchaikovsky’s Piano Concerto No. 1 with fan-favorite pianist Seong-Jin Cho (Jan 15-17). Symphony Hall. 617-266-1200, www.bso.org

A FAR CRY x YEEMZ The Jamaica Plain-based string orchestra teams up with singer-songwriter and cellist Yeemz (Yi-Mei Templeman) for a casual and cozy show where audiences are encouraged to move about the space, grab a drink, and absorb the music. Jan. 9, 7:30 p.m., Somerville Armory; Jan. 10, 3 p.m., St. John’s Church, Jamaica Plain. www.afarcry.org

HANDEL AND HAYDN SOCIETY Artistic director Jonathan Cohen leads a program featuring the H+H Orchestra and soprano Carolyn Sampson in Mozart’s ecstatic religious piece “Exsultate jubilate” and Telemann’s mythological cantata “Ino,” with a side of Haydn’s Symphony No. 44, “Trauer.” Jan. 9, 7:30 p.m.; Jan. 11, 3 p.m. NEC’s Jordan Hall. 617-262-1815, www.handelandhaydn.org

A.Z. MADONNA

THE GREAT PRIVATION (HOW TO FLIP TEN CENTS INTO A DOLLAR) Nia Akilah Robinson’s play tells parallel stories of mothers and daughters, set on the same plot of land. The present-day parent-child pair work as counselors at a sleepaway camp in Philadelphia. The other mother and daughter are standing vigil in 1832 by the grave of their newly deceased husband and father. In an era when it was not uncommon for Black corpses to be illegally disinterred by white so-called “resurrectionists” and sold to medical schools, they are determined to protect him from grave robbers. Directed by Mina Morita, “The Great Privation” is a coproduction by Boston’s Company One Theatre and Washington’s Woolly Mammoth Theatre Company, featuring two actors from each city. The Boston-based performers are Marc Pierre and Victoria Omoregie. Jan. 9-31. At the Modern Theatre at Suffolk University, Boston. companyone.org

STOKELY & MARTIN Written and directed by Najee Brown, “Stokely & Martin” imagines a conversation in the afterlife between Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and Stokely Carmichael, a passionate advocate of civil rights who popularized the term “Black Power.” Stetson Marshall plays King, and Darren Paul portrays Carmichael. In Brown’s play, they “explore their ideological differences, personal struggles, and shared hopes for Black liberation,” according to press materials. Jan. 16-18. AtMulticultural Arts Center, Cambridge. https://multiculturalartscenter.org/stokely-and-martin/

JOB Josephine Moshiri Elwood plays Jane, a young woman on a leave of absence from her job as a moderator of online content, and Dennis Trainor Jr. plays Loyd, her psychiatrist. The conversation between patient and therapist brings them to some very dark places in this psychological thriller by Max Wolf Friedlich, which is directed by Marianna Bassham. Jan. 16-Feb. 7. SpeakEasy Stage Company. At Roberts Studio Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion at the BCA, Boston. 617-933-8600, www.speakeasystage.com

DON AUCOIN

SCREENDANCE ROADSHOW Formerly the Motion State Dance Film Series, this initiative co-curated by Ali Kenner Brodsky and Andy Russ launches its eighth incarnation with this East Providence presentation. Each season, the traveling short dance film series showcases an array of creativity by artists from around the world exploring choreography for the camera, screening the film program at a variety of venues around New England. This kickoff event also features a post-screening talk with the curators. Jan. 15. Free. Myrtle, East Providence, R.I. www.motionstatearts.org/about-screendance-roadshow

FIFTY FAVORITES / FIFTY SEASONS Jacob’s Pillow archivist extraordinaire Norton Owen put together a dazzling compendium of short clips from each of the seasons he has participated in over his remarkable half-century career at the festival. It’s a delightful trip down memory lane for those of us who’ve taken parts of the journey with him. For others, it’s a lively sampler. Annie B-Parson’s opening “occasion piece” from the launch of the new Doris Duke Theatre with a cast of veteran all-stars is priceless. Owen shares more in an online exhibit and podcast as well. https://danceinteractive.jacobspillow.org/playlists/fifty-favorites-fifty-seasons/#1

CONVERSATION IN MOVEMENT While there are few live performances this week, the Loading Dock Gallery continues its group exhibit exploring the relationship between dance and visual art. Captured motion in different media delve into a kind of visual kinesthetic dialogue that embraces form, color, and light. Participating artists include Nino Gordeladze, Dina Mordeno, Ed Porzio, and Johanna Tiemann. Through Jan. 31. Free. Loading Dock Gallery, Lowell. www.theloadingdockgallery.com

ONE MINUTE MOVEMENT SOLOS Mobius is presenting another round of its concert series of finished solos with a provocative twist — each is strictly one minute in length, not an easy task. Jimena Bermejo and Heather Kapplow curated this year’s edition, and the concert includes 18 different artists in a range of styles, from contemporary dance and performance art to a variety of multidisciplinary offerings. Jan. 10. $15. Lilypad, Cambridge. www.mobius.org

KAREN CAMPBELL

OF LIGHT AND AIR: WINSLOW HOMER IN WATERCOLOR Closing soon: “You will see in the future,” Homer once wrote, “I will live by my watercolors.” Not to diminish his grand oil paintings, many of them icons of American culture. But it only takes a moment with a handful of those watercolors to see what he means. Immediate, breathless, and intense, they often feel like stray thoughts captured and committed to paper in the brief moment before they flit away. Homer’s thoughts were rarely without gravitas — the curse of a life lived alongside conflict — and so, too, the watercolors, the largest collection of which is owned by the MFA. For the first time in decades — their fragility limits their exposure to light — 50 of them are out in the open together, an occasion not to be missed, nor seen again for a generation. Through Jan. 19. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, mfa.org

ALLAN ROHAN CRITE Ending soon: Two local exhibitions celebrate Crite, “Urban Glory” at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum and “Griot of Boston” at the Boston Athenaeum. For Crite, who painted Roxbury and the city’s Black community with verve and affection for almost 80 years — he died in 2007, just a few years short of his 100th birthday — it’s about time. Along with it comes the first-ever scholarly text on his work, “Allan Rohan Crite: Neighborhood Liturgy,” from Princeton University Press. Crite was a passionate chronicler of both the trials and triumphs of urban Boston’s diverse and dynamic quarters for much of his life, and his official arrival in the canon is more than due. Through Jan. 19 (Gardner) and Jan. 24 (Athenaeum). Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, 25 Evans Way. 617-566-1401, www.isgm.org; Boston Athenaeum, 10½ Beacon St. 617-227-0270, bostonathenaeum.org

HEW LOCKE: PASSAGES Last chance: Boston audiences will remember Locke from “The Procession,” an enormous still life parade of figures at the ICA’s Watershed last summer, mirroring the mass of diverse humanity that’s crisscrossed the globe since the advent of colonialism almost four centuries ago. This exhibition promises to both strengthen and clarify that movement, and its frequent injustices, as a lifelong theme for the Guyanese-British artist, as it draws on a quarter century of his work, right up to now. Through Jan. 11. Yale Center for British Art, 1080 Chapel St., New Haven. 877-274-8278, britishart.yale.edu

MURRAY WHYTE

MAGIC Maybe it’s the advent of AI, or maybe the uncertainty of the times, that has prompted the artworld to lean into mysticism and magic like spiritualists peering into a crystal ball. This group show features colored-pencil emoji drawings by Anna Von Mertens, whose art often examines astronomy and physics, along with psychedelic landscapes by Linda Nagaoka, hex-sign-like paintings by Lena McCarthy, and bright, glittery Rorschach blots by OH Projects. Jan. 10-Feb. 28. Drive-By Projects, 81 Spring St., Watertown.www.drive-byprojects.com

CATE McQUAID

CLOWN PEOPLE PODCAST LIVE TAPING Stand-ups Brieana Woodward and Al Christakis released their first episode of the “Clown People” podcast in 2022. At the Studio, they will tape their 200th official episode with guests Logan O’Brien, Trevor Dion, Gabi Hajos, and Cam Ohh, plus some games and interactive bits. Jan. 9, 9:30 p.m. $13.95-$18.95. The Comedy Studio, 5 John F. Kennedy St.www.thecomedystudio.com

BRIAN SIMPSON “Since I’m a young black man, everybody thinks that my biggest fear is racist cops,” says Austin, Texas, comic Simpson in a spot on Netflix’s “the Standups.” “I’m way more afraid of racist lifeguards.” Jan. 9 at 7 p.m. and Jan 10 at 6:30 p.m. and 9 p.m. $38.40. Laugh Boston, 425 Summer St. 617-725-2844, www.laughboston.com

BLACK COMEDY EXPLOSION Smokey Suarez will be the first headliner for the Black Comedy Explosion’s new night — it has moved from Wednesday nights to Thursday nights. Hosted by Jonathon Gates, music by DJ Wade. Jan. 15, 9 p.m. $15-$20. Carver Den, 80 Talbot Ave., Dorchester. 617-590-8334, Instagram @blackcomedyexplosion

NICK A. ZAINO III

title: Where to eat in 2026
text:
January is a time to celebrate fresh beginnings, and one way to embrace that spirit is by visiting new restaurants. There are a number of enticing openings off in the distance to anticipate. For instance, Michelin-starred chef George Mendes will open the tasting menu-focused Agosto in the South End in the summer, with bakery-cafe Baby Sister to follow (named after his son and daughter), while Danny Meyer Italian restaurant Ci Siamo expands from New York to the Seaport.

But in the here and now, diners can choose from sushi, Ethiopian cuisine, American comfort food, and beyond. In Back Bay, for the next month only, the lounge at Uni has been declared Lower Uni, offering four- and 10-course tasting menus. Korean mom-and-pop Park’s Kitchen, which offered takeout and delivery in Roxbury, has closed — to become a brick-and-mortar opening soon: Stay tuned for all your spicy rice cake and handmade dumpling needs. (In the meantime, check out the new Gangnam Spice, specializing in Korean fried chicken and more in Jamaica Plain.) And is it too soon to declare this the year of the neighborhood seafood restaurant? Lobster rolls are surfacing everywhere from Allston (at nouveau New England seafood shack Holdfast) to Watertown (read on).

Here are some restaurants to try in the coming days.

Get Food & Dining Headlines

The Globe's most recent food stories, delivered to your inbox every Wednesday.

Enter Email

Acapella by X

In the longtime Blarney Stone space, something new for Fields Corner: a nightspot with good food and live music, with a generous patio and valet parking coming down the road. Longtime friends Freddy Ureña (chef), Yancarlo Fernandez (general manager), and Anthony Cruz (front-of-house manager) are behind the venture, which offers a menu inspired by Ureña’s travels. Come for ceviche, dumplings, and grilled skirt steak with chimichurri sauce, plus cocktails (with some nice alcohol-free options for Dry January participants). Everyone is here, from babies to priests to friend groups dressed to impress.

1505 Dorchester Ave., Dorchester, 617-286-4620, www.acapellabyx.com

Ama at the Atlas

Three years ago, Comfort Kitchen arrived in Dorchester, with a menu that connected cultures, traced trade routes, and brought diners into its expansive worldview. Now, founding husband-wife team Nyacko Pearl Perry and Biplaw Rai and their Pearl & Law Hospitality group expand to Allston. At the Atlas Hotel, Ama is a salute to mothers and others who nurture us through food. (Rai is from Nepal; the restaurant’s name is Nepali for “mother.”) Ama, slated to open this month, features a menu that spans the globe, and the day. Breakfast might bring French toast flavored with Nepali spiced tea, lunch Senegalese-inspired yassa chicken salad sandwiches, dinner tamarind-glazed trout and Berbere-spiced fried chicken.

Atlas Hotel, 40 Western Ave., Allston, www.ama-boston.com

Black Cat Eatery at Wink & Nod

Chef Valentine Howell won a following at modern Greek restaurant Krasi in the Back Bay, then at his Black Cat popup at Jamaica Plain’s Vee Vee, which ended last March. Now Black Cat is on its second life, at South End culinary incubator-slash-speakeasy Wink & Nod. From shrimp ceviche to jackfruit empanadas to red snapper rundown in tomato-coconut broth, Howell’s Afro-Caribbean cuisine is bright and flavorful, a delight to eat and a wakeup for the palate.

3 Appleton St., South End, Boston, 781-435-0394, www.winkandnod.com

Boxfish

When chef Manita Bunnagitkarn moved her popular Cha Yen Thai Cookery across the street in Watertown, it opened up possibilities for the former space. Now it is Boxfish, where Bunnagitkarn offers a seafood-focused menu notable for its originality. Of course there is a lobster roll, the meat poached in brown butter and served on brioche with lemon aioli, as well as clam chowder, a fried fisherman’s platter, and linguine with clams. From there, it goes freewheeling with dishes such as grilled octopus with ube mashed potatoes; fettuccine with uni, brown butter, and nori; and an elegant pan-seared fillet of the day with tomato concasse and beurre blanc. If you’re feeling more surf than turf, try the Boxfish sandwich, featuring shaved ribeye with fontina and caramelized onions.

613 Mount Auburn St., Watertown, www.boxfish.food

Cactus Club Cafe

If you vaguely remember ripping it up at the Cactus Club on Boylston Street back in the day, don’t get excited. This is not a reincarnation of that. Cactus Club Cafe, which is on Boylston Street, is a Canadian export. It looks luxe, it opens for lunch and closes at midnight, and it has a crowd-pleasing menu comprising sushi, rigatoni Bolognese, miso caramel sea bass, burgers and steaks — and somehow much more, plus fun cocktails. If you want to get your OG Cactus Club on, don’t worry, there are tacos and margaritas here too.

500 Boylston St., Back Bay, 617-341-9428, www.cactusclubcafe.com

Cafe Sushi Nisei

Cafe Sushi, beloved in Cambridge, shuttered for dine-in service during the COVID era. Now it has reopened as Cafe Sushi Nisei (“second generation”), with a renovated dining room and sake bar. Brothers Seizi and Kenshi Imura continue to operate the restaurant, along with Seizi’s wife, Mindy Imura; the Imuras’ parents opened it in the mid-’80s and handed it down in 2007. Although the popular omakase menu Cafe Sushi once offered is no longer, the restaurant makes up for it with a focused menu of small plates, sashimi, nigiri, and rolls. Don’t miss the beautiful citrus salmon sashimi, with blood orange and fennel, or the madai nigiri with preserved yuzu.

1105 Massachusetts Ave., Cambridge, 617-492-0434, www.cafesushicambridge.com/nisei

Gato Exotico

Restaurateur Jason Doo is a nostalgist. His Harvard Square spot, Wusong Road, is an homage to classic tiki bars and Chinese-American restaurants like the one his parents ran, Bobo’s in Malden, when he was a kid. His new foray also reaches back to his childhood — spent hanging out at the very mall where he recently opened Gato Exotico. The CambridgeSide restaurant features a menu of guacamole, enchiladas, and tacos from chef Sergio Enriquez, plus drinks with names like the Tijuana Taxi and the Tres Leches Colada.

100 Cambridgeside Place, Cambridge, 339-229-8787, www.gatoexotico.com

Mesob Restaurant and Bar

Just a few blocks from the Eritrean Community Center in the South End is Mesob, featuring Eritrean and Ethiopian cuisine and named for the traditional woven basket on which shared meals are served. Start with sambusas, then move on to an array of fresh salads and platters of kitfo, timtimo, shiro, and more, served with the flatbread injera. Mesob also offers wine, beer, and cocktails.

1746 Washington St., South End, Boston, 857-305-3468, www.mesobrestaurantboston.com

Moona

For dreamy Middle Eastern fare — platters of labneh, hummus, and olives with pita; feta fritters; lamb kefta; grilled branzino — diners flock to Moona in Cambridge’s Inman Square. Now owner Mohamad El Zein has opened a new branch of the restaurant, nearby in Central Square: It is bigger than the cozy original, with more and new dishes to try. After you’ve feasted on monkfish shish and date molasses-glazed lamb shank with freekeh, try Arabic coffee and rose crème caramel or orange blossom labneh frozen yogurt with kumquat jam for dessert. Cafe service is coming soon.

750 Main St., Central Square, Cambridge, 617-665-5915, www.moonarestaurant.com

Devra First can be reached at devra.first@globe.com. Follow her on Instagram @devra_first.

title: Boston residents line up to get vaccinated at City Hall’s free clinic
text:
The last week of December saw a “very high” spike in flu cases, according to the Department of Health.

In the span of a month, flu cases in Boston rose from 133 cases at the beginning of December to 672 cases the last week of the month, according to the Boston Public Health Commission. During the same timeframe, the percentage of flu-like illnesses in emergency department visits jumped from 2.7 percent to 11.1 percent.

Those totals dipped slightly at the beginning of 2026, with 652 reported flu cases, 20 fewer than the previous week, and 10 percent of total emergency department visits, down by a percentage point less.

However, the totals for the beginning of the year are still above those during the same time in 2025, when there were 326 flu cases reported in the city, and 5.2 percent of emergency department visits due to flu-like illness.

Last year, flu cases statewide spiked around February.

The clinic on Wednesday, inside a room on the eighth floor of City Hall, was staffed with registered nurses from LCG Boston, a nurse staffing agency that runs vaccination sites across Boston. There were almost 30 people already registered within the first 30 minutes.

For Jordan Bordner, a city employee, the convenience of the City Hall location influenced his decision to get vaccinated.

”Everyone should get a flu shot,“ Bordner said. ”It helps you and also everyone that you work with and everyone that you live with.”

There are three more clinics planned for this month:

10 a.m.-2 p.m. Saturday, Josephine A. Fiorentino Community Center, 123 Antwerp St., Brighton

3-7 p.m. Wednesday, BCYF Hyde Park Community Center, 1179 River St., Hyde Park

3-7 p.m. Thursday, BCYF Perkins Community Center, 155 Talbot Ave., Dorchester

The registered nurses have been working in these clinics since September, vaccinating more than 2,500 individuals around Boston as of Dec. 23.

“It’s been quite a long, long season,” said Glendaly Avalo-Valdez, registered nurse with LCG Boston.

Since September, the city has held 27 clinics. Avalo-Valdez said individual clinics typically serve between 30 and 100 people. She has been operating vaccination clinics throughout the city, including Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, and Brighton.

Other people getting vaccinated, like Maya Lazar, had personal experiences that motivated them to get vaccinated. After Lazar lost her brother because of the flu, she believes annual flu vaccinations are essential.

“I suggest getting your flu shot every single year,” Lazar said. “Specifically, with the strain that’s going around this year, which is pretty bad. So everyone should get their flu shot, it just helps keep other people safe.”

The clinic is also an opportunity for those who weren’t able to get their vaccinations earlier in the season. Zoe Davis, a mom of 11-month-old twins, dropped into the clinic to get both her flu and COVID-19 vaccinations.

“I don’t have either shot so far, I’ve just been busy with my twins,” Davis said.

Davis said she hopes more people will get their flu shots, especially this year. While this year’s vaccine is a partial match to subclade K, doctors and public health officials say getting vaccinated greatly reduces a person’s exposure to severe illness, hospitalization, and death.

“From everything I’ve read, it definitely helps decrease symptoms,” she said. “I know it doesn’t totally prevent you from getting the flu, but I definitely am on board if it can make it better.”

On top of getting vaccinated, local doctors ask people to remember hygienic practices adapted during the pandemic.

This story has been updated to clarify the timing of the city’s flu and COVID-19 clinics.

title: 7 stories Globe journalists obsessed over in 2025 — and are following into 2026
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

Practically speaking, not much changed between Dec. 31, 2025, and Jan. 1, 2026. Still, the end of one year and the start of another offers a symbolic breather to look back at what’s happened and ahead to what’s next.

So with the new year in full swing, I asked my Globe colleagues which New England stories from 2025 they’re following in 2026. Some of their answers, like how Brown University adapts after a mass shooting and the guessing-games over Taylor Swift’s wedding, won’t surprise you. But here are seven other ongoing stories you may have forgotten about — or thought were behind us.

A jury found her not guilty last June in the death of her boyfriend, Boston police officer John O’Keefe. But as Globe express desk editor Hayley Kaufman points out, Read’s legal journey is far from over.

O’Keefe’s family has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against her, which is pending. Read has also sued investigators, alleging she was framed. As Hayley puts it, “More headlines to come.”

The prestigious Michelin Guide expanded into Boston last year and awarded a coveted star to 311 Omakase, Chef Wei Fa Chen’s Tremont Street sushi joint. This year, the city’s restaurant scene is poised to reap the rewards, says Chris Morris, who oversees food coverage.

The chance to compete for Michelin’s approval could spur chefs to take risks, persuade investors to back them, and serve Boston diners new delights. Chris predicts that will mean “more recognition for deserving, hard-working chefs; top-notch service; innovative menus; and a shared pride.”

Last year was big for women’s sports in Boston — so big that Massachusetts’ governor got personally involved in an effort to entice the WNBA’s Connecticut Sun here. Expect 2026 to make similar waves, says Katie McInerney, a senior assistant sports editor.

Here’s the lineup so far. On Jan. 20, the Women’s Beanpot hockey tournament will be held at TD Garden. In March, the NWSL’s Boston Legacy, the region’s newest franchise, will debut at Gillette Stadium. In April, the PWHL’s Boston Fleet will play its first game at the Garden. And after the Sun faced the Indiana Fever here in July, the league will likely return to Boston this summer. “Grab a ticket while you still can,” says Katie.

Sherry Naso died of cancer at 37 in 2024. Last year, her parents — both retired physicians — found themselves in Family Court fighting for the right to visit their granddaughter. It’s a complicated case centered on medical ethics and a grieving family. Lylah Alphonse, who oversees the Globe’s Rhode Island coverage, will be watching when the hearings resume next month.

Most of New England is politically blue. New Hampshire is different. While Massachusetts fought President Trump’s policies in court last year, Republican Governor Kelly Ayotte enacted conservative policies including bans on so-called “sanctuary cities” and transgender medical care.

Ayotte and the Republican-controlled state legislature are up for reelection this year, testing their staying power in a political environment shadowed by the president.

The struggles of New England health care providers occupied Globe reporters last year and will continue to in 2026. How will Trump’s Medicaid cuts affect Massachusetts hospitals? Can New Hampshire fix its labor-and-delivery desert? And will bankruptcy force the closure of two Rhode Island safety-net hospitals?

Okay, this story isn’t local. But it is top of mind for Lisa Weidenfeld, a Globe assistant arts editor. Last year, Lisa watched Disney temporarily yank Jimmy Kimmel’s show over his comments about Charlie Kirk’s assassination, CBS cancel Stephen Colbert’s late-night show, and politics seep into the Skydance-Paramount merger.

Lisa will keep following the interplay between the administration and TV companies this year, especially as Paramount maneuvers to buy Warner Bros. Discovery. Television “played such an outsized role in shaping his public image,” she says of Trump. “There’s something fitting (if still startling) about it proving to be such a battleground for his interests.”

Readers, let us know: Which stories from New England or beyond will you be following this year?

🧩 4 Across: Tossed | 🌧️ 38° A messy morning

Remembering John Axelrod: Mourners left flowers and handwritten notes on the Commonwealth Avenue Mall to honor the Boston philanthropist who was killed in a hit-and-run while walking his dog Tale there on Saturday. Neighbors remembered Axelrod as friendly, generous, and a lover of all dogs. Read his Globe obituary.

Money matters: Representative Seth Moulton, the Salem Democrat challenging Ed Markey, has out-raised the incumbent senator so far even though polls show Markey ahead. Meanwhile, the Red Sox and the Boston health tech company Whoop were among the donors to Mayor Michelle Wu’s inaugural celebrations this year.

Flu surge: The death toll in Massachusetts rose to four children, including Boston’s first reported child flu deaths since 2013. From getting vaccinated (no, it isn’t too late) to staying home if you’re sick, here’s how to keep yourself and others safe as cases rise.

Jan. 6: The Trump administration published a website that rewrites the 2021 attack on the Capitol. It falsely claims the 2020 election was stolen, blames Nancy Pelosi for the attack, and calls the pro-Trump mob “peaceful protesters” provoked by law enforcement. (CNN)

Criminal justice: A landmark ruling by Massachusetts’ highest court gave second chances to offenders convicted of crimes they committed when they were young. Here’s what some who have since been released are saying about their new lives.

Precarious majority: Representative Doug Lamalfa, a California Republican, died at 65. His death and Georgia congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene’s resignation further narrows the GOP’s slim margin in the US House. (KQED)

Legal issues: A Democratic state lawmaker from Roxbury unlawfully spent nearly $6,500 from her campaign account on personal expenses, including Uber Eats, records show. Meanwhile, a longtime Saks stylist for Boston socialites who is accused of stealing more than $400,000 is suing Saks, claiming the retailer retaliated against him for seeking employment elsewhere.

Last-minute deal: Outgoing Everett mayor Carlo DeMaria reached an agreement with Wynn Resorts, which operates the Encore Boston Harbor casino, on Monday, his last day in office. The deal clears the way for two hotels to go up opposite the casino and a new commuter rail stop behind it.

title: Boston music doesn’t need to be resuscitated. It needs a rebrand.
text:
In large part, that’s because the prevailing public notion of “Boston music” seems to be set in stone, as if its legacy is predetermined — and done. That — curses! — talent and opportunity are in limited supply here, and folks such as the Cars, Donna Summer, New Edition, and that sweet spot of alt-rock a lá Buffalo Tom, Letters to Cleo, and the Lemonheads, must have gobbled up most of it. Then the paltry scraps were just enough to fuel a few aughts success stories, like cabaret-rock outfit the Dresden Dolls, esteemed jazz bassist and Berklee alum esperanza spalding, and shimmering electro-pop act Passion Pit. In 2020, the Globe even published a story asking “where has all the music gone?,” which amplified this alleged death knell.

As a music columnist whose 4-inch boots are regularly sticking to the weathered floors of local clubs and dives, I know this is all bogus. Yet it’s a perspective I’ve often heard repeated in bar conversations, social media posts, and comment sections, to the point that it’s dangerously close to becoming a self-fulfilling prophecy.

In 2026, the concept of Boston music is overdue for a complete reimagining. The current implications of the phrase — that Boston’s mainly a rock city, and one with waning influence, at that — is outdated and incorrect. It also immediately tees up disappointment.

There are few cities with internet access (if any) where music consumption hasn’t become streaming-forward and algorithm-steered. Record label representatives often look for fresh faces on TikTok, judging an artist’s potential based on a viral hook instead of full performances and in-person panache. Certain acts monopolized the Billboard Hot 100 to the point where the chart had to change its rules to make room for new entries and force turnover. Releasing umpteen album variants — editions with bonus tracks, free autographs, alternate cover art, the blood of the artist’s first-born, you name it — is now one of the only ways musicians can move a significant amount of physical records. If Boston doesn’t “make ’em like we used to,” it’s because the 20th-century roadmap to success went out the window, nationwide, years ago.

Usually, the local music conversation — if it even gets that far — ends there, on a note that’s at best nostalgic, and at worst embittered about an issue that’s far larger than Boston. But the outlook gets better if you keep talking, and consider the reality that Boston just makes ’em differently now.

The newest roadmaps to success start in Boston and stretch to locales far beyond the city and its neighboring suburbs. The Mass Music & Arts Summit (organized by Boston nonprofit Beat The Odds) brought representatives from Warner Records and the streaming platform Audiomack directly to the Seaport last fall. Professionals from every pocket of the state’s music industry continue to pursue membership in the Recording Academy to forge connections with each other and the national music community.

Brockton’s a hotbed of activity, rooted in the success of Soundlab Recording Studios and Van Buren Records, a hip-hop collective comprising members like FELIX!, who seems poised to follow the path of recent Massachusetts hip-hop standouts such as BIA and Cousin Stizz. (He currently boasts more than 1.3 million monthly Spotify listeners.) In Salem, the nonprofit MOON is bringing together the North Shore music scene with its sober and all-ages venue Moon Base One, which you might recall from my coverage of its nifty “cassingle booth” last year.

There’s countless more examples that won’t fit here, although you’ll find a steady supply of them in my weekly music column, Sound Check (a shameless plug but a pertinent one nonetheless).

I’m not proposing that we paint over the past for this rebrand. Quite the contrary — the best boons for the scene’s morale come from juxtaposing different eras of the city’s music history, without one overshadowing another. Done right, that looks like R&B sensation New Edition and modern emcee Joyner Lucas receiving honorary streets in their respective hometowns of Roxbury and Worcester, less than two weeks apart last year.

Another prime crossroads of the city’s past and present: the Rock & Roll Rumble, the longest-running battle-of-the-bands-style competition in the country. The annual event has changed hands over the years, starting as a WBCN project, and is now helmed by Anngelle Wood via her online radio program, “Boston Emissions.” Every spring, a fresh crop of area bands who have never Rumble’d duke it out over the course of one month.

Founded in 1979, the Rumble is a true continuation of Boston music history, which has given rise to everyone from ’Til Tuesday (1983) to the Sheila Divine (1999), to Weakened Friends, the pride of Portland (runners-up, 2016). The Rumble took a break in 2025, but mentioned “a plan to return in 2026″ on social media last year. I sincerely hope it returns this spring.

There’s a saying that often surfaces in my work covering underrepresented communities: “If you can see it, you can be it.” The meaning, of course, is that representation in mass media reminds us that our aspirations aren’t impossible. If we can’t see Boston music — however you wish to define it — as something that’s still alive, then we’ve basically already closed the coffin.

And I really don’t want to write the obituary.
