title: A sanctuary for Black artists, born in the violent racial tumult of Boston’s past, finally gets its day
text:
What happened next might be one of the most catalytic moments in Boston’s urban cultural history, though it’s not as well known, or as much celebrated, as it ought to be. The end of Chandler’s South End studio also marked the beginning of the African American Master Artists in Residency Program (AAMARP) at Northeastern University, though even Chandler himself didn’t know it right away. A chance meeting, an empty factory, and a kindly gesture from a university dean coupled with Chandler’s fiery determination is the short version of the story; the much longer one, finally and for the first time, will get its clearest and most comprehensive treatment at the Institute of Contemporary Art when it opens “Say It Loud: AAMARP 1977 to Now” on Feb. 12.

An airing of decades of determination by an energized community of Black artists, inflected by activism, righteousness, and joy, the show features dozens of artists in the AAMARP orbit, now vital to the city’s cultural history: Ellen Banks, Marlon Forrester, John Wilson, Allan Rohan Crite, Benny Andrews,and of course, Chandler himself, who died last year at 84. Jeff De Blois, the ICA curator of the show, worked closely with Chandler as he pieced the story together, gathering personal histories, archival materials, and a lot of art. “One of the things that I was really drawn to was Dana’s idea that AAMARP is for everyone,” he said. “He wanted people to bring their families. Everything was a party. It was a joyous celebration.”

From the wreckage of Chandler’s studio to a squat former factory building in Jamaica Plain where AAMARP artists in residence still work today, there’s a long, unbroken line of continuous making, convening, celebrating, and doing, always centered on an active cohort of Black artists. The line has zigged and zagged, surely, from three locations and a standoff or two with the university. But today, on Atherton Street, 13 artists continue to carry the torch for a loose organization that honors its founder’s legacy as an activist, an advocate, and a champion for culture left on the city’s margins.

Its start sprang from a happenstance meeting in 1974 between Chandler and Gregory Ricks, then dean and director of the African American Institute at Northeastern University. Hearing of Chandler’s plight, Ricks offered him storage space in an unused building on campus, and then studio space, too. Chandler, mightily prolific, filled every inch offered, and quickly needed more. So Ricks took him to an unused college building at 11 Leon St. with 32,000 empty square feet and asked him how much he might require. Chandler, sensing the opportunity, replied quickly: All of it.

Official designations would come later. But with that answer, the program was born.

“He’d been thinking about how, in the name of Black self-determination, people could become organized; this was the opportunity to live up to those values,” said De Blois. “He convinced them to not only let him use the whole space but to give him a budget, and the budget then became the seed money for the founding of the residency program.”

Had Chandler’s South End studio not come to destruction, would it have happened at all? It’s hard to think not. Chandler was uniquely, irrepressibly resolute. In 1970, after years of agitating, he had finally goaded the Museum of Fine Arts into reluctantly dipping into the surging Black Arts movement that was seizing the country. Enlisting Edmund Barry Gaither, the newly-installed director of the fledgling National Center for Afro-American artists in Roxbury, Chandler pushed the famously non-confrontational MFA into an apex moment in the culture wars.

In the years after the murder of Martin Luther King Jr., the Black rights movement fractured into more militant strains, notably the Black Panthers. Running alongside that political disquiet was the Black Arts movement, a burgeoning cultural imperative to challenge polite society in music, in writing, and of course, in visual art. Unabashedly political, the Black Arts movement was breaking through and being seen at major museums around the country. But in Boston, staid, conservative, and famously racist, that moment had not come.

Chandler set out to change that. In January 1970, he sent a document to Perry Rathbone, then the MFA director. Its title: “A Proposal to Eradicate Instititional Racism at the Boston Museum of Fine Arts.” Among its many demands was an exhibition representing the Black Arts movement, which he shared with the local press. Under growing public pressure, the museum acquiesced. That spring, “Afro-American Artists: Boston and New York,” curated by Gaither, opened at the MFA, to immediate widespread acclaim.

Black artists, of course, had been working in Boston for decades. Allan Rohan Crite’s South End home was an informal artists’ club house, and John Wilson would become a major figure on the national scene. But AAMARP gave bricks-and-mortar permanence to a community of working artists whose place in the city was always precarious; it was their place to stand on, a home to be handed down through the generations.

In later years, AAMARP faced challenges. In 1993, after years of being funded as a program of Northeastern, its funding fell victim to severe budget cuts. The space would be maintained, but further funding, including Chandler’s pay as the program’s de facto head, were cut off. AAMARP would move twice, first to another underused Northeastern-leased building on Huntington Avenue in Roxbury, and finally to Jamaica Plain, to its current home on Atherton Street.

That’s not been without its challenges, either. In 2018, Northeastern moved to close that space down and issued eviction notices to the artists working there, citing liability concerns. A public spat ensued, quelled only when the school acquiesced and AAMARP was allowed to remain, though it remains in negotiations with the school to find a permanent solution.

Without funding and official affiliation with the school, AAMARP survives as it always has, through the sheer force of will of the artists and the community that surrounds it — in a way, an ongoing tribute to its founder, whose no-quit approach lit a fire that burns still.

“There was an entire Black art infrastructure across the country that existed separate from museums,” De Blois said. “We know its story in New York, in Chicago, in Detroit. AAMARP was a huge part of Boston’s story.” Finally, it’s being told.

SAY IT LOUD: AAMARP, 1977 TO NOW

Feb. 12 to Aug. 2. Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100, icaboston.org

title: Building a new Madison Park High School is a fine idea. Walking away from the community’s wishes isn’t.
text:
Planning Department chief Kairos Shen stunned a community meeting in Roxbury Monday night with the news that the city plans to abandon a deal with a development team led by HYM Investments and My City At Peace to build commercial laboratory space, affordable housing, and a cultural center on the site.

Building a new Madison Park is a great idea, and kudos to the city for moving it forward. It’s one of the best things the Boston Public Schools could do, a potentially transformative project.

It’s everything else that’s driving the controversy.

Community leaders have cried foul, accusing Wu of walking away from promises to bring economic development to Roxbury, and disrespecting the neighborhood by discarding the results of a years-long public process. The city maintains that rebuilding Madison Park offers significant community benefits of its own, and that development on the unused portions of the parcel will still be possible.

The developers’ proposal, approved by the city in 2023, was to use the proceeds from newly built lab space to fund its community-oriented projects, including deeply affordable home ownership and a cultural center to house Embrace Boston, the social justice organization responsible for the sculpture of Martin Luther King and Coretta Scott King on Boston Common.

In the city’s judgment, that project had become, as the bureaucrats say, unfeasible. Which is to say, the development team, led by veteran developer Tom O’Brien (HYM) and Rev. Jeffrey Brown (My City My Peace), was struggling to raise the cash to fund their ambitious plan.

It’s undeniable that this proposal — like lots of ambitious development plans around town — is stalled for lack of capital. But the developers say they thought the city was willing to be patient and work with them for a vision that promised sweeping benefits for the community.

They and their supporters find it especially galling that Wu has turned away from them while the Madison Park proposal is still in the early stages of a lengthy state approval process.

Wu said she understands the criticism, especially its timing. But it’s pretty clear that she believes the development plan that’s been approved is unrealistic, now and perhaps forever. And she said placing the new Madison Park on a parcel the city already controls could knock as much as $200 million from the cost of replacing the school — on land where nothing seems to be happening. She stopped just short of saying O’Brien’s proposal promises more than it can possibly deliver.

“I don’t want the city to wait around for another eight years, 12 years, seeing nothing happen here because the financial realities aren’t being acknowledged,” Wu told me.

She said she believes there will be plenty of room for economic development once the layout of the new school is established, which she estimated will take two or three years. (New schools in Massachusetts take as long as a decade to approve and build.)

“Once the layout is finalized, that’s when parallel planning for the economic development parcel can happen,” Wu said. “To say it can happen at the same time would be confusing and complicate the school planning process for a project that is not economically viable.”

But that would mean restarting the whole development process, years from now. And, what about the team that was already picked?

The loss of the parcel has to be especially stinging for Rev. Brown, a celebrated community activist. He’s been a Wu stalwart, traveling with her delegation to Washington last year when she testified before Congress, and figuring prominently in a video that played at her inauguration just last week.

Brown and O’Brien told me they are still hoping the city will work with them on an economic development proposal, which they insist the community wants and needs.

“The community has suffered through win-lose prospects for too long,” Brown said. “They deserve a win-win, and we want to deliver it for them.”

Almost everyone outside City Hall believes this process needs to slow down. And that Brown’s group should be part of any final project.

But we’re talking about a parcel that has been a political football for decades. Yes, building big things is a challenge now. But in boom times or bust, big projects in Roxbury always seem to be the ones that don’t materialize.

“I believe our community wants to see things done,” Wu said. “We’re going to see it through, so we’re going to have a brand new Madison Park and an economic development plan.”

If Wu really wants to make Boston “a home for everyone,” to quote her ubiquitous campaign tagline, she needs to do more in Roxbury than replace an existing school. I don’t think Wu is wrong: Parcel 3 needs rethinking. But there has to be a clearer timeline and process for deciding what will happen. Something a lot better than even more vague promises for someday.

MIT urban studies professor Karilyn Crockett wrote the definitive history of the community protests of the late 1960s and early ‘70s that killed the proposed highway project through Roxbury — and created Parcel 3 in the aftermath.

She told me Wu simply does not seem to grasp the history of city and state government overruling community desires in favor of their own judgment.

Crockett said there needs to be a true collaboration between City Hall and Roxbury residents on a path forward.

“Mayor Wu, you have some people who are trying to walk with you, instead of having this heavy-handed decision that just gets handed down,” Crockett said. “You don’t have the history to know that this is a decision that doesn’t feel like it’s meeting the moment.”

title: Annual MLK Day breakfast urges ‘community over chaos’
text:
The event’s emcee, WBZ-TV reporter and anchor Courtney Cole, said that choosing to come together across differences not only honors King’s legacy, but creates a “living symphony of purpose and possibility that will resonate for generations.”

State Senator Liz Miranda, born and raised in Roxbury, said King’s work reminds us that the “arc of the moral universe bends toward justice.” She said strength comes from community.

“As we move forward through 2026, let us do that with not only confidence but care for one another,” Miranda said. “Let us meet the challenges with more courage, meet the controversy with more compassion and the uncertainty with collective action.”

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu told the story of receiving a letter, two weeks after the birth of her daughter, Mira, requesting that she testify before Congress to defend the city’s immigration policies. In her appearance last March before the Republican-led US House Oversight Committee, Wu lauded Boston’s record as one of the safest cities in the country.

Wu said moments like that remind her that the fight for equality is not over, and it comes “from people who like to talk about Dr. King’s work like it’s finished.” Wu clarified, it isn’t.

“We’re reminded every day in our community that the civil rights movement is living, is needed, is being led by the people in our community,” Wu said. “Boston does not have the luxury of waiting. We need to be the community that presses forward even when it’s hard, especially when it’s hard.”

Imari Paris Jeffries, president and CEO of Embrace Boston, highlighted the relationship between King and Coretta Scott King, who met, fell in love and built a life together in Roxbury. Jeffries said the Roxbury YMCA has been a “home away from home” to so many people.

“Roxbury was and is Dr. King’s home, not just a stop along the way, but a place where he lived, where he rested, where he was held by a community while he was doing the work that demanded everything from him,” he said. “Home mattered because King made home and the world possible.”

Jason Price got the crowd on its feet, clapping and singing along to his stirring rendition of “A Change is Gonna Come,” before newly elected City Councilor Miniard Culpepper delivered the keynote address.

Culpepper, a Roxbury native, has a background as a civil rights lawyer and pastor. His grandfather marched with King and served as an NAACP leader.

Culpepper reminded the audience of a question King once asked: “Where do we go from here: chaos or community?”

While victories have been won, Culpepper said, justice is still unfinished. People, not laws, can change society, he added.

“Community doesn’t happen by accident,” he said. “It happens because people make community happen. In a city where inequality still shapes life outcomes, the YMCA stands as a living example that we can choose community over chaos.”

US Representative Ayanna Pressley and Boston City Councilors Ruthzee Louijeune, Henry Santana, and Julia Mejia were also in attendance.

Three awards were given out during the event: the Roxbury Legacy Award to Arnita Cooper, a longtime water aerobics instructor at the YMCA; the Community Champion Award to Mike Kozu, co-director of Project R.I.G.H.T. Inc.; and the Corporate Leadership Award to Comcast, which was accepted by Becca Fracassa, director of government and community affairs.

title: ‘Somebody is up there with binoculars.’ Parking is tops when it comes to Boston 311 calls.
text:
She estimates that it would cost her at least $400 a month for a parking spot. But, if she simply parks on specific streets in the neighborhood she knows to have relatively scant parking enforcement and eats the tickets she does get, she pays on average about $120 a month.

“I take a gamble,” she said.

Last year, 373 complaints were made to the city’s 311 system for 391-397 Congress St., making it the most complained about address in Boston for that time frame. Ninety nine percent of the gripes were related to parking.

Paige Maling, a 26-year-old who works in medical sales who was also at the dog park with her golden retriever that day, said she lives in a building that features $600 a month parking. That doesn’t necessarily guarantee her a spot, Maling said, as the parking garage is a mix of private and public parking. Sometimes there are no spots available. She’s not surprised that part of the Seaport is home to the most complaints in the city, and the vast majority of them deal with where people put their cars.

“Very frustrating,” she said of the parking situation in the Seaport.

For Khaled Eltokhy, an economist and PhD candidate at City University of New York whose research focuses on city governance, such grousing matters. When people know what their neighbors are complaining about, it deepens their understanding of their community, he said.

Eltokhy has collected 311 data from major American cities, organizing it into a website that displays neighborhood level statistics, including response times and complaint types. Put simply, the 311 data paints a portrait of a city’s day-to-day grind, including the difference in how quickly the city responds to problems neighborhood by neighborhood.

In Boston, according to Eltokhy, the fastest median response time to a 311 complaint came in the South End, at 2.2 hours. The complaints can run the gamut, from unshoveled sidewalks, to uncovered garbage cans, to potholes, to rodent activity, to, yes, drivers parking where they shouldn’t.

A spokesperson for Mayor Michelle Wu said the city is in the midst of upgrading and modernizing the 311 system, which means that the data set on Eltokhy’s website “doesn’t account for the full number of cases due to transitioning to the new platform beginning spring 2025.”

“Making Boston the best city for families means getting the basics right and delivering excellent city services every day,” said the spokesperson.

Median response times for Beacon Hill, downtown and the Financial District, and Back Bay all came in under 4 hours, according to Eltokhy’s analysis.

The slowest median response time was in Hyde Park, with 15.7 hours, followed by West Roxbury at 15 hours.

The Wu spokesperson said City Hall holds “departments accountable to specific standards for response time for each type of constituent service request based on the complexity of resolving an issue.” For instance, 80 percent of pothole cases should be closed within 24 hours. The expectation is the same for missed trash pick-ups.

Compared to other major American cities, Boston fares decently in how long it takes on average to respond to a complaint, ahead of Chicago, San Francisco, Austin, Texas, Los Angeles, and Philadelphia, but behind New York and Baltimore, according to Eltokhy. (Each city has its own criteria for 311 complaints.)

Parking complaints drive many of the grievances, but not all. An intersection near the area known as Mass. and Cass, the center of the city’s opioid crisis, had 201 complaints last year, with many of them involving requests for the disposal of syringes.

At 4-6 Greendale Road, a residence less than a five minute walk off Blue Hill Avenue in Mattapan, there were 156 complaints, most of them for poor conditions of the property.

Another address, 62 Kirkwood St. in Brighton, which historically has had a reputation as a party house for Boston College undergraduates known as Club Kirk, had 152 complaints, the data show. A review of that list shows neighborhood annoyances such as poor conditions of the property were the reason for the bulk of the 311 complaints, not partying. BC does not own the property. No one answered the door at that address one recent morning.

The second most complained about address in the city is 1138 Washington St., a Dunkin’ in the South End. Last year, 360 complaints were made. Almost all of them dealt with parking.

Stephanie Barbosa, a 45-year-old teacher, has lived in the neighborhood for 20 years and goes to the cafe every day. The staff know her food order: a toasted English muffin. She usually drives and described her parking calculus.

She will double-park in the bus lane or live-park at a meter without paying if she thinks she can get away with it. It’s often a call made purely on gut instinct, she explained. It helps if someone can stay in the car to move it if need be while she ducks into the Dunkin’.

There are some spots available on the other side of the street, but it’s residential parking only.

“If you don’t have a sticker, you’re getting a ticket,” she said.

On a recent day, small vignettes of city life unfolded as she exited the Dunkin’. Two large moving vans were parked nearby. With their ramps down, they took up six meter spots. A guy in a RAV4 parked in a spot directly in front of the Dunkin’. He threw on his flashers and didn’t pay for the meter.

Behind him, a work truck with a ladder on its roof double-parked. That vehicle was soon joined by a white pick-up truck, which pulled up behind the truck and also double parked.

Less than a block away, a driver idled in a Boston Transportation Department vehicle. Waiting.

“They’re ready to pounce,” said Roxanda Lockett, 42. She was there for her daily order: a butter pecan coffee. Iced, no matter the weather.

About a half-mile away in the same neighborhood is another block that is among the top frequent fliers for the 311 system. On Chandler Street in between Berkeley and Clarendon streets, parking also drives the complaints. For one address here, 311 received 257 complaints. Next door, there were 173 complaints.

In both instances, the vast majority of grievances dealt with parking. Here is a stately block of brownstones fit for a postcard. One condo is on the market for $1.3 million. It’s listed as a studio.

Diane Sutty, 67, lives across the street. She has called the neighborhood home for more than 30 years. She hasn’t had a car in decades, she said. She enjoys city living. She’s retired now but used to walk to her office where she worked in payroll.

“It’s not worth the hassle,” she said of owning a car.

She does occasionally rent a car. She recalled being dinged twice for briefly double-parking on the street. It’s maddening, she said. One time, she simply had to run up to her home to pick up a suitcase and bring it down to the car. She returned to a ticket waiting for her.

“Somebody is up there with binoculars, on the hotline,” she said, gesturing to the upper floors of the homes across the street. That morning, Sutty was walking around the corner, on her way to breakfast: pancakes at Thornton’s.

As if on cue, a white Transportation Department car pulled up across the street. A woman got out, took a photo of the license plate of a Honda HR-V, and slipped a ticket under one of its windshield wipers.

title: Looking back on the last 50 years with Boston’s Bicentennial photographer
text:
“They paid me a pittance, but it completely changed my career,” said Jones, who is still working at the age of 80. “It was interesting for this little nobody, and I took it to the extreme.”

Instead of simply photographing handshakes and historic sites, Jones journeyed into the neighborhoods, where he took his cameras to out-of-the-way streets to show what the Bicentennial meant to ordinary and marginalized Bostonians.

As the nation celebrates its 250th anniversary, Jones’s work from a half-century ago is receiving renewed attention.

A native of Washington, D.C., who moved to the South End in the late 1960s, Jones found his way to the Bicentennial celebration as a fledgling photographer with Boston 200, which managed the city’s commemoration of that anniversary.

“I’m an outsider, remember, and I’m just learning my craft,” Jones recalled.

The importance of the Bicentennial initially did not carry much meaning for him, Jones said. And in a city painfully divided by court-ordered busing to desegregate its schools, the promise of the Declaration of Independence could prompt celebration or cynicism depending on one’s address.

“I learned that the difference between the haves and the have-nots was far bigger than I had ever encountered,” Jones said. “I learned that Boston would be a complicated relationship for me going forward.”

That relationship became a close one with his adopted home, despite what Jones sees as a still-evolving conversation about race.

“I think a lot of the same problems exist. Some people are very resistant to Black people moving in,” Jones said. “But Boston has tried very hard. I find Boston to be a lot more capable of dealing with diversity.”

Fifty years ago, Jones recalled, “I couldn’t get hired for anything as a Black man, not even as an assistant. But think about it. I’ve now been in this business for 50 years as a photographer.

“Back then, I would not have believed it.”

Along the way, Jones’s self-taught photography has become part of the permanent collections of prestigious institutions such as Harvard University, the Boston Athenaeum, and the Boston Public Library, which holds more than 250 pieces of Jones’s work.

“The quality of Lou’s work over decades as a commercial, editorial, and fine-arts photographer is unmatched,” said Aaron Schmidt, the library’s curator of photography.

Through his lenses, Jones said, “I look at everything.”

That wasn’t always the case. Jones graduated with a physics degree from Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute and then worked briefly for NASA. Eventually, and ever since, he became captivated by the art and creativity of photography.

“I never thought for a minute I would be taking pictures,” Jones said. “I had no education in photography.”

The Bicentennial provided a springboard for his developing passion, even if Jones first regarded the work as only a temporary diversion.

“In the beginning, nobody knew what the Bicentennial was, but it got bigger and bigger and bigger,” Jones said.

“People started to get very, very into it. It was very palpable,” he added. “I suddenly realized I had access that I could not get in my normal life, and I thought, ‘I can leverage this.’ ”

Jones took his cameras into Roxbury, where he photographed street fairs and summer showers from open hydrants. And he looked for pictures at the St. Patrick’s Day parade in South Boston amid a mixed reception of taunts and curiousity.

“I was learning that Boston had these very segmented, segregated neighborhoods,” Jones said. “I was promoting the city, and at the same time, some people are saying we’ve been ignored.

“I saw that as my responsibility,” he added. “They needed more representation.”

Revolutionary Spaces, a nonprofit organization that stimulates civic dialogue through its management of the Old State House and Old South Meeting House, honored Jones last year with its Community Changemaker Award.

“Beyond the headline events and public figures, Lou captured intimate shots of ordinary people in all of Boston’s neighborhoods, documenting in a vivid fashion the complex relationship that Bostonians have with their city’s rich history,” said Nathaniel Sheidley, president of Revolutionary Spaces.

“His photographs remind us that who is seen, and how, defines how we remember the past, just as our memory of the past tells us who matters, and why. These lessons are more important now than ever.”

For Jones, the journey always has been about people, and it has been seasoned with innumerable, practical lessons about how to make those encounters happen.

To embed himself with one of the international Tall Ships during their Bicentennial parade into Boston Harbor, Jones didn’t wait for a city-brokered invitation. He wrote to the ship crews himself and found himself atop one of the dizzyingly high masts of the Christian Radich, a Norwegian ship, where he photographed a sailor climbing up the rigging.

Photographers with vertigo need not apply.

Jones also wouldn’t take no for an answer when Queen Elizabeth II, the first reigning British monarch to visit the cradle of the Revolution, toured the city with Prince Philip in July 1976.

He talked his way past security at the doors to the Old State House, where the queen addressed a crowd from the same balcony where the Declaration of Independence was first read to Bostonians.

And without seeking permission, he ducked past yet another stern-faced, security agent, who had been posted at the upper-floor entrance to the chamber that led to the balcony.

“I heard, ‘Where are you going?’ but just bent down, went under his arm, and never looked back,” Jones said with a laugh.

As the queen left the balcony, Jones recalled, he began walking backward in what he calls “the photographer’s two-step — “two steps, click; two steps, click.”

“All of a sudden, I hear a grumble,” Jones said. “I had backed Prince Philip into the corner bookcase! I thought I would hear, ‘Off with his head.’ ”

After a half-century, Jones hasn’t put his cameras away. Instead, he is preparing for yet another extended trip for his “panAFRICAproject,” which he describes as “redefining the modern image” of the continent.

It’s a project that reemphasizes Jones’s career-long interest in people — whether on Death Row in Texas or the side streets of Roxbury and South Boston — and his commitment to portray them with humanity, dignity, and context.

“I devour photography,” Jones said, reflecting on a long career unexpectedly jump-started by the Bicentennial.

Jones paused and smiled when asked what the nation’s 250th anniversary means to him.

“It means survival,” he said with a chuckle. “Fifty years is a long time.”

Luca Tirella and Kyle Sillars, Danvers — The senior duo dominated a 66-62 win over Peabody, with Tirella recording 20 points and 15 rebounds and Sillars amassing 23 points and eight boards.

“Playing D1 football and studying at a top tier school in the country has always been a goal of mine since I was a kid,” Chase wrote on social media.

▪ Andover boys’ hockey coach Kevin Drew has resigned midseason, according to the Eagle Tribune, which stated he declined to go into specifics but called it a “difference of opinion.”

Anthony Licciardello, the JV coach for the past decade, and varsity assistant Peter Loring will take over coaching duties for the remainder of this season before the school launches a full search.

Drew has coached Andover hockey for almost 12 years, five with the girls’ team and six-plus with the boys. He was 104-91-26 overall, with a 58-39-12 mark leading the girls and 46-52-14 for the boys, including a 1-6-1 record this winter. He led the girls to the 2019 Division 1 semifinals.

▪ Concord-Carlisle announced the hiring of Derek Robbins as its new baseball coach. Robbins, the football coach at Worcester Tech from 2019-22, has spent the last two years as an assistant in the Patriots’ program. A Marlborough graduate, Robbins works in campus safety at Concord-Carlisle. He has also served as a football assistant at West Boylston and Westborough.

Salem High is set to retire Evelyn Oquendo’s No. 24 jersey in a ceremony on Friday (5:30 p.m.). Oquendo will be the first female athlete in school history to have her number retired.

Oquendo, a 1997 inductee into the school’s Hall of Fame, was a standout basketball player, leading the Witches to an undefeated season in 1979-80 as the starting point guard. A 1982 Globe All-Scholastic, she led Salem to the 1982 North Regional championship.

She went on to become a three-time NCAA First-Team All-American at Salem State and a four-time MASCAC Player of the Year. Still the school’s all-time leading scorer with 1,738 points, her number was retired by Salem State in 2010.

Oquendo has worked as a physical education teacher at Collins Middle School in Salem since 2007 and coached the Witches’ girls’ varsity team from 2017-22.

title: Homelessness is rising fast among a surprising group: infants and toddlers
text:
Karian’s mother urged her to move back home to the Boston area and offered to house her and her daughters temporarily. Karian started working the night shift at a fast-food restaurant to save up for her own place while her mother and sister watched her children.

But in a city where fast-food wages aren’t enough to pay the rent, her efforts felt futile. And then, a month after moving in with her family, her mother’s landlord told her the apartment was overcrowded and she had to leave. Karian and her girls, then 7 years old and 8 months old, moved into a homeless shelter, where her depression and anxiety worsened.

“I tried my best, but it’s not their home,” said Karian, now 31.

Karian’s children had joined the growing ranks of very young children experiencing homelessness.

Between 2021 and 2023, the number of homeless infants and toddlers increased in 48 states and the District of Columbia. The most recent estimates found that in 2023 nearly 450,000 infants and toddlers in the United States were in families that lacked a stable place to live. That was a 23 percent increase compared to 2021, according to a report released last year by the nonprofit SchoolHouse Connection in partnership with Poverty Solutions at the University of Michigan.

The numbers could be even higher, experts worry, because “hidden homeless” children — those who are doubled up in homes with family or friends or living in a hotel — may not be captured in tallies until they start school.

High prices for diapers and formula, the exorbitant cost of child care, the rising cost of living, and rising maternal mental health challenges all contribute to the growing rate of homelessness among very young children, experts say. In 2024, one-third of infants and toddlers were in families that struggled to make ends meet, according to the nonprofit infant and toddler advocacy organization Zero to Three.

“We’re talking about families who have generationally been disadvantaged by circumstance,” said Kate Barrand, president and CEO of Horizons for Homeless Children, a nonprofit that supports homeless families with young children in Massachusetts. “The cost of housing has escalated dramatically. The cost of any kind of program to put a child in, should you have a job, is escalating.”

Housing instability is dire for anyone, but particularly for young children, whose brains are rapidly growing and developing. Studies show that young children who are homeless often lag behind their peers in language development and literacy and struggle to learn self-regulation skills, like being able to calm themselves when feeling angry or sad or transition calmly to new activities.

They also may experience long-term health and learning challenges. Early childhood programs could provide a critical source of stability and developmental support for these children. But SchoolHouse Connection found only a fraction of homeless children are enrolled in early learning programs, and the percentage who are has decreased over the past few years.

Karian and her daughters faced new difficulties after they moved into a shelter. Her older daughter had to change schools and left without getting to say goodbye to many of her friends. At her new school, her grades dropped. The baby developed a skin condition and there was a bedbug infestation at the shelter. Karian didn’t want to put her on the floor for tummy time.

“We were in a place where we couldn’t really make noise. I couldn’t really let them be kids,” she said.

In 2021, in response to ballooning child homelessness rates, Horizons opened the Edgerley Family Horizons Center, an early learning program that serves children from 2 months to 5 years old. While some families find Horizons on their own, many are referred by shelters around the Boston area.

The need is great: Edgerley serves more than 250 children, with a waitlist of 200 more. Karian’s younger child was one of those who got a spot soon after the program opened.

Inside Horizons’ large, light-filled building on the corner of a busy street in Boston’s Roxbury neighborhood, every detail is tailored to the needs of children who have experienced instability. Walls are painted in soothing blues and greens.

Each classroom has three teachers to maintain a low child-to-staff ratio. Many of the teachers are bilingual, and all of the educators are trained in how to build relationships with families and gently support children who have experienced trauma.

In the infant room, teacher Herb Hickey, who has worked at Horizons for 13 years, frequently sees infants who are hyperaware, struggle to fall asleep, can’t be soothed easily, or cling desperately to whichever adult they attach to first.

Every day, the teachers in the infant room sing the same songs to the babies. “When they hear our voices constantly, they know they’re in a safe space,” Hickey said. “This is calm.”

Teachers also follow the same familiar routines. The rooms are decorated simply, organized and filled with natural light. Teachers constantly scan the infants for signs of distress.

“We have to be even more responsive,” Hickey said. “When the child starts crying, we don’t have the convenience to say, ‘I know you’re hungry, I’ll get to you.’” He said teachers want even the tiniest babies to learn that “we’re not going to leave you crying.’”

Karian also received support. After graduating from a culinary training program, she now works a steady job as a cafeteria manager for a local school district, where she earns a salary with benefits. She has her sights set on eventually opening a restaurant.

She also has big dreams for her daughters, something that once seemed out of reach. She wants them to have ambition to “work towards something big,” she said. “I want them to have a dream and be able to achieve it.”

Experts say there are larger policy changes that could reduce the strain on families with young children: increasing the minimum wage, expanding child care options like Head Start, which saves a portion of seats for homeless children, and offering more affordable housing to low-income families, to start.

Providing more federal money to the programs that help poor families pay for child care could also help. Those programs require states to prioritize homeless children and give them the first opportunity to access that money.

But experts argue that these solutions shouldn’t need to exist in the first place.

“We should be able to come to an agreement as a society that we should prioritize keeping families with infants and toddlers in their homes,” said Melissa Boteach, chief policy officer at Zero to Three. “Babies shouldn’t be homeless.”

title: Amid federal rollbacks, Boston marks MLK Day with full houses
text:
“Every King event in the city this year is sold out, which is fantastic,” said Dr. Noelle Trent, president and CEO of the Museum of African American History. “But I also want people to come. I would say, just come. These events are meant to be shared.”

This year’s MLK Day arrives at a tense national moment, as the Trump administration continues to unwind federal diversity and inclusion initiatives and push for limits on how schools and museums teach about race. Many organizers say they feel a sharper-than-usual urgency: a celebration of King’s legacy in a political climate where that legacy is increasingly contested.

But in Boston — a city where King studied, met his wife, preached, and marched — the weekend is bursting with positive collective energy to commemorate the most well-known leader of the civil rights movement.

Since the start of his second term, the Trump administration has pursued a series of policies and executive actions aimed at reshaping how American history, race, and diversity are taught and publicly presented.

For Trent, whose museum is the nation’s oldest public institution dedicated to early African American history, the timing of this MLK Day feels unusually heavy, but also unusually necessary.

“We find ourselves in challenging times,” she said. “That is not new for the country. But this does feel more unique than any recent memory. It’s increasingly negative, very close to home. MLK Day is an opportunity to look up, to pause and remind ourselves that we’ve been through challenging times before and we’ve surmounted them because of people who exhibited courage, who got into what John Lewis called ‘good trouble.’”

Even without a ticket, many events remain accessible, including free admission to several museums, open-air gatherings at The Embrace memorial, and youth performances at the Museum of African American History’s Faneuil Hall.

This year marks the 40th anniversary of MLK Day as a federal holiday. The holiday was championed by Representative John Conyers, who introduced the first bill in 1968; early state observances began in the 1970s; Massachusetts adopted it in 1974; and all 50 states finally recognized it in 2000.

Each January, MLK weekend traditions kick off with Embrace Boston, the organization behind The Embrace memorial on Boston Common. Embrace hosts an honors gala recognizing civil leaders, artists, and changemakers advancing King’s vision of beloved community. The weekend continues with the annual MLK Breakfast and the Boston Children’s Chorus MLK Concert.

Embrace Boston CEO Imari Paris Jeffries said the holiday is not only about remembering King, but also about organizing for what’s ahead.

“People recognize the minimizing of MLK Day and Juneteenth, which are no longer part of the free days of the National Park Service,” Jeffries said. “People want to get together in [a] beloved community, and they want to prepare because 30 to 40 percent of the legislation attributed to Dr. King is already under attack. The Supreme Court is deciding what’s left of the Voting Rights Act and gerrymandering. These next two years will determine if democracy in America is going to survive.”

Jeffries said Bostonians “feel a chip on their shoulders because this is where Martin and Coretta met” in 1952, while he studied at Boston University’s School of Theology and she studied at the New England Conservatory of Music. While a student, King preached regularly at Twelfth Baptist Church in Roxbury, forging ties with local congregants and community leaders that would influence his later work in the Civil Rights Movement. The 1965 Freedom Rally was one of the first major civil rights marches in the Northeast, drawing 20,000 people to protest segregation.

In 2023, Boston unveiled “The Embrace,” a 22-foot bronze sculpture on Boston Common commemorating a moment between Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King after he won the Nobel Peace Prize.

“It has become an outdoor sanctuary,” he said. “Most protests in Boston start from there. Activations, vigils, youth gatherings, people come because it embodies belonging. Those arms could be yours or mine.”

Federal shifts also included Executive Order 14253, “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History,” which targets the Smithsonian and orders the removal of exhibits deemed to contain “improper ideology,” especially those highlighting systemic racism. The policy has already hit Boston. Last year, the Museum of African American History lost a three-year, $500,000 federal grant under the new guidelines.

Still, the Museum of African American History’s annual MLK tribute concert at Faneuil Hall is one of the few events that still has seats for free. The performance features the Boston Youth Symphony Orchestra’s Intensive Community Program.

But the heart of the event, Trent said, is the youth voice.

“A lot of times, when people look back at the movement, they look at the adults. They don’t highlight the children. Late Congressman John Lewis was in his twenties when he began. Civil rights pioneer Claudette Colvin was sixteen. Barbara Johns, who helped spark Brown v. Board, was a teenager. Young people stood up — sometimes without fully understanding the danger — and it changed the country,” she said. “Martin was only 32 years old.”

This year’s program includes Boston’s poet laureate, Emmanuel Oppong-Yeboah, a public school librarian, and several teen poets performing original work.

Kabria Baumgartner, Africana studies professor at Northeastern University, urges her students to return to King’s own writing, not just “I Have a Dream,” but also his speeches on poverty and income inequality because “his words resonate deeply in our current moment.”

Baumgartner said this year feels different, both because of the nation’s political climate and because 2026 marks the 250th anniversary of the United States, a milestone she sees as an invitation to read King alongside the founding documents he so often invoked.

“King called the Declaration of Independence a ‘promissory note,’” she said. “We should ask ourselves whether we’ve made good on those promises and why we’ve fallen short.”

As the federal government narrows what schools can teach about Black history, Baumgartner said, “American exceptionalism is a belief that must be interrogated.”

“In my classes, I teach radical abolitionists, youth reformers, and women’s rights activists — ordinary and extraordinary people who showed that American democracy is stronger through inclusion,“ said Baumgartner. ”As King said in 1963, ‘Now is the time to make real the promises of democracy.’ Now is still that time.”

When asked whether the museum would need to update its content in response to the current political climate, Trent said the opposite.

“We don’t need to add anything. We need to lift up the moments from the past that speak to the present,” she said. History, she added, is a tool for decision-making, not memorization. Her job, she said, is to stay “ten toes down as a truth teller” and give visitors access to the primary sources that show how earlier generations weathered similar storms.

As for Monday, Trent urged people to “choose one meaningful thing,” whether that’s a day of service or quiet reflection.

“You can’t get to everything anyway,” Trent said, laughing. “Pick one or two things that honor Dr. King. Pause. Reflect. That’s what matters.”

title: He’s Boston’s biggest social media food influencer. (But no, he’s not a stay-at-home dad, though he may wannabe.)
text:
You have a sizable following that some people can only dream of having. What brought you to Boston?

My girlfriend at the time, now fiancée, moved up for a biotech job in 2021, and then I followed her up in 2022. I started in Annapolis, Md.

Were you a food person in Annapolis?

This is new. I mean, I was eating a lot, but I was not recording myself. The foodie part started in January 2023.

How did this career unfold?

My best friend does DIY content in his house, and he was getting on me to just start doing content. Somehow, we just landed on doing food reviews, because I wanted to see where the good food was, because I was new to the area. I posted a video, and I think it got like 500 views. And I was like, “Oh, wow, I’m famous!” So I kept posting.

What was your first post, and why do you think it was so popular?

I went to Monica’s, the sandwich place in the North End. I think the premise was like: Is it worth it to pay $20 for a chicken parm sandwich? And I ended up saying yes, because the sandwich was delicious. But I think people related to the affordability aspect, talking through the food.

I think there’s a lot of people — and this is no shade to anyone, obviously — I think there’s a lot of people who kind of cover food and give you more of the aesthetic version. I was just really talking through how I was feeling as I was eating it. I think people related to that. Thank you to all those 500 viewers!

What had you been doing for work, and has this taken over as your full-time job?

At the time, I’d just started a job in consulting. I was a civil engineer by trade. As of August 2025, this is my full-time gig now.

For people who don’t understand how the world of influencing and social media works: How do you make money?

Pretty much all my money comes in through brand partnerships, which you’ll see labeled [in my posts] as paid partnerships. That’s if a larger brand wants me to promote a new product or new dish they’re selling. And some restaurants will pay to promote new locations and things like that.

Outside of that, I don’t charge any restaurant for any review. I pay for my food. I want that genuine, authentic experience. I am able to monetize a bit off of my viewership on TikTok and platforms like Facebook as well. Based on the amount of viewers you get, you get a certain amount per view.

How did you come up with the name wannabe stay-at-home dad? Are you a dad? Do you want to stay at home?

A part of the origin story is that the friend who was peer-pressuring me to do content, we were trying to think through ideas and different ways to do it. At first I was working remotely, and my partner was working in the office, so I was going to pretend to be a stay-at-home dad, or practice to be one. I filmed one video, and it was horrible. I was like: This premise is pretty stupid. So then we just started doing the food videos, and I didn’t have a chance to change my name. It had stuck. I don’t even have a child. … It’s an aspirational thing, totally.

Coming from Maryland, what was your take on the Boston food scene when you got here? How has your viewpoint changed?

I kind of pictured a ton of seafood, some Italian as well, because we had moved into the North End shortly after I got here. I thought those were the main things you’d be able to find. I think one misconception I had was I thought there would be a lack of diversity in Boston’s food scene.

I’ve actually learned that there’s a ton of different foods and different types of cuisines you can find here. You’ve just got to do a little bit of research. I feel like when people are recommending places to people visiting Boston, a lot of people will send you to the North End, and maybe you’ll even get some South End places.

But, similarly to finding more diversity, it was also finding more areas to go to — realizing how much good food is in places like Dorchester, Roxbury, and different areas like that. I kind of opened my eyes. I thought Boston was smaller. I didn’t realize, for example, how big Dorchester is. Dorchester feels like it stretches for miles.

What’s the best restaurant in your neighborhood? Where do you eat for pure pleasure?

I think this will be a popular pick: Rino’s in East Boston. I was a little worried when I first went because they’ve been on TV. It’s very popular. But it is truly an amazing Italian restaurant. I would say it’s the best restaurant over here.

There’s also a ton of great Latino food that you can find in the area, but I think Rino’s is top of the top.

What’s your go-to order?

I would try the chicken parm. If you just don’t want to cook one night and need to get the family fed, take chicken parm to go, put it on the table, and it’ll look like you cooked a big dinner.

And that’s similar with all their portions. Their gnocchi, their Bolognese, is incredible. Everything’s good. I’d say the chicken parm and the Bolognese are two that you’ve got to try.

What’s the most overrated restaurant in Boston, and the most underrated?

Overrated? I’d actually say Galleria Umberto in the North End. And this is not going to be received well. People love it because they have the $2 Sicilian slices. I lived down there for a bit. I tried it multiple times. I just couldn’t get it. And I’m not a big arancini fan, and people say the arancini’s great there. Not for me.

What restaurant do you wish more people knew about?

It’s kind of gotten popular now, but I want it to keep getting more recognition: Comfort Kitchen in Dorchester. I thought it was going to get recognized in the Michelin guide that came out: really great Caribbean food, amazing brunch, amazing dinner. Their jerk duck for dinner is incredible. It’s also really cool, their story. Part of the way they were able to get their brick and mortar is through a platform that allowed community members to invest. It’s a great group of people running it, and I love the food.

Best pizza?

Pizza Project in Brighton has the best pizza I’ve had right now. I feel like people are like, “Oh, it’s out of the way.” Brighton is not that far out of the way. Their pepperoni pizza with hot honey is incredible. And they have this vodka pizza with sesame seed crust, I think, that I’m excited to go back and try.

Best Chinese food?

Dumpling House in Cambridge. I’m a big takeout guy. I do a lot of Chinese takeout. We do huge orders. Obviously, dumplings, of course, are incredible. They’ve got great scallion pancakes.

What about tacos?

So people in East Boston are gonna get mad at me. I’ll say my favorite taco place is probably La Mesa in Chelsea. They do really good birria tacos. It’s between that and Taqueria Jalisco, which is a very popular one in East Boston. I go back and forth, honestly.

How do you decide where you’re going to visit? You try a wide range of places, and I’m guessing you don’t have a bottomless budget.

I wish the process was more refined. I’ll be honest with you. It’s a mix of, if I see a place that is trending, maybe it’s new, and I think people want to see my opinion about it, I’ll go there. So that’s based on things that are popping up in my algorithm. A big source for me is also Reddit. I check Reddit threads all the time. People will post: “Hey, coming to Boston for a few weeks. Where do I find the best burger or the best tacos?” And seeing responses of people who have lived here for a while has been really helpful to me, because I still feel like a tourist at times.

And most of my content is filmed in my car. I get a lot of affordable places. I’m doing a lot of takeout and stuff. That also informs the process.

Do you go in with the intention of ordering a certain item?

Usually, it’ll be a certain dish: I’ve heard this place has a great burger and also maybe try an appetizer. The other day I went to a place and had a great burger, and I got clam chowder because it was cold outside. I’ll try to get a little bit of a sampling of the menu, but most times I’m going in specifically for a certain thing.

How many times a week are you eating out?

I think I’m around four to five times. The way I try to mix it up, just healthwise, is I film a couple places in a day. That way I can take a day in between, or two days in between, to let my body not feel like crap.

How do you actually film yourself? Do you have someone who comes with you? Because this is very artfully done.

I appreciate that. The biggest compliment you can give me is to tell me that it looks artful.

Truthfully, I have this little phone holder in my car that I drop my phone on and then record myself in my driver’s seat. And then when I go out, if I’m sitting down somewhere, I have this little phone holder from Amazon that I can pop up, and then I have a light. I’ve got the classic influencer light that you see at a restaurant that annoys me. I have that, too. I try not to use it too much.

Do people see you coming and know who you are? Do you think you’re getting an objective experience?

If I’m doing takeout and stuff, I’ll try to put my order in ahead of time, just so I can grab it and go. But there’s been times now where I’ve sat down … I’m going to the table, sitting down, ordering, almost hoping no one recognizes me, because, again, my big thing is sharing that authentic experience. I want people who watch my videos to feel like it’s almost like they’re sitting at the table with me, and we’re talking about the food together. It’s not this specific influencer experience, where it’s not going to be the same if you go on your own.

What place has surprised you, in a good way?

I went to The Haven in Jamaica Plain. And that was a deep Reddit thread, where maybe two or three people had said, “Hey, their burger is amazing.”

I think it’s actually a Scottish restaurant. Their burger was incredible. It’s not that I thought it would be bad. I thought, maybe this is a neighborhood staple-type place, where people stand behind it, but it was actually a very good burger, one of the best burgers I probably have had in the area.

Let’s say you’re talking to someone who’s coming to visit for the weekend. Where are you sending them?

First off, I don’t believe you have to eat in Boston proper, right? Because I do genuinely think you can find some great places in Somerville and Cambridge.

I’m sending them to Pizza Project, because everybody comes up here thinking, “Boston’s pizza is terrible.” I think that it’s a great place to prove people wrong. I’m gonna send them to Bred Gourmet. They’ve got great burgers down in Dorchester. They have a location in Kendall Square as well. You can get a little taste of Southern cuisine. They’ve got po’ boys and things like that — some stuff maybe you wouldn’t expect to find in Boston.

And then here’s the one thing that I do think maybe is touristy of me to send them. I’m still gonna send them to the North End to get pastries, because I do genuinely think that’s still an experience. I might not send them to Mike’s Pastry, which, again, might be a controversial opinion, but I’ll probably send them to Modern Pastry for cannoli, because I do think that’s a genuine Boston experience, where the quality meets kind of the expectation.

What about a nice night out?

If you’re having a nice night out, trying to splurge, go to Grill 23.

I was going there with my fiancée. I was going to record, do a video. And I got so caught up in the food. As soon as they brought the bread out, I forgot. I never recorded anything. I just ate, and it was incredible. Now, I’ve got to try to figure out how to get another reservation.

What’s next on your list?

Oh my goodness, I’m forgetting the name of it. Sarma. Sarma is the name of the place I want to go because they have off-menu fried chicken that they serve occasionally. Every video I see of that, I’m like, that’s incredible. I love that idea, to have an off-menu fried chicken. I want to try that. And, of course, I’ve heard great things.

This is another trendy one, the Capri place … I just want to go to see if it’s the real deal. And just because it’s new, it is impossible to get a table right now. The honey bread that they do looks incredible.

What would be your last meal in Boston?

That’s really tough. I’m a big sandwich guy, so honestly, I’m going to go to Figaro’s in Chinatown. The steak and cheese with some chipotle mayo is probably my favorite. It’s so crazy because I put chipotle mayo on so many different things, and I never thought to put it on a steak and cheese until I had it there.

I’m gonna go to Square Deli in Everett and get their Grandma Flo pizza. It’s got homemade meatballs, ricotta. They have incredible pizza dough. I’m not gonna have any room left by the end of this day. By the way, I’m splurging completely. Let me see. I’m gonna go to Carmelina’s in the North End and get a chicken parm. Then, for dessert (I’ve already said the North End desserts; there’s so many other great bakeries) ... actually, I might skip dessert because I feel like I’ve gone too crazy.

Is there any food you hate?

I will never have a blue cheese dish on my channel. And I don’t like truffles. I feel bad, because a lot of places try to jazz up their fries with truffle fries … I can’t stand truffles.

Is there any type of food in the Greater Boston area that we don’t have?

Having some family from the South, I think it’s that Southern cuisine: your fried chicken, your plates like fried chicken, collard greens, mac and cheese, sweet yams, things like that.

Will you spin this career into something else? What’s the dream?

You know, before I was ever doing this, I was a die-hard Food Network and Guy Fieri “Diners, Drive-ins and Dives” fan, all those shows. My dream is to continue to do what I’m doing, but just doing it on a bigger stage and maybe even at the national level.

Interview was edited for clarity.

title: Dorchester teen charged with stealing man’s suitcase and throwing it onto MBTA tracks, causing explosion
text:
A Dorchester teenager is facing charges stemming from an alleged robbery at the State Street MBTA station last week that ended with a suitcase being thrown onto the tracks and igniting an explosion, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden’s office said Tuesday.

Addonis Reed, 19, was charged with obstructing or endangering a railroad, larceny from a person, unarmed robbery, disorderly conduct, and two counts of malicious destruction of property, Hayden’s office said in a statement.

Judge Mark Summerville set bail at $10,000 and revoked Reed’s bail for 60 days on two open cases at Reed’s arraignment Friday in the central division of Boston Municipal Court.

Reed was committed to Suffolk County Jail in lieu of bail and was ordered to stay away from the victim and all MBTA stops, according to court records. It was not immediately clear if he had obtained an attorney.

Prosecutors say the incident occurred at about 11:20 p.m. Jan. 14 at the State Street station at 200 Washington St. when five juveniles “engaged in a confrontation” with an MBTA rider, accusing him of photographing them. The victim denied the allegation, prosecutors said.

Authorities said Reed separated from the group and followed the victim. MBTA security footage allegedly showed Reed taking the victim’s phone and throwing it to the ground several times, breaking it into pieces, prosecutors said.

As the victim attempted to collect his belongings, Reed allegedly grabbed the victim’s suitcase and threw it onto the train tracks, prosecutors said. The suitcase struck the third rail, causing a large explosion and fire, the statement said.

The station was evacuated and train service was suspended as police, fire officials, and MBTA security responded to the scene, prosecutors said.

The victim told officers the suitcase contained two iPads, an Acer laptop, Apple AirPods, and chargers, with a total value of more than $3,000, according to the statement.

Transit police later identified Reed by reviewing security video and matching his description to an individual seen at the State Street station the following day, prosecutors said.

“This is an alarming set of facts, both with the fear that the victim must have experienced during the incident and the destruction of his property and subsequent station evacuation and shutdown in service,” Hayden said in the statement. “I’m grateful for the quick work of transit officers in identifying and arresting this defendant.”

Reed has two other open cases — one in the Roxbury division of Boston Municipal Court on charges of disorderly conduct, assault with a dangerous weapon, and assault on a police officer from December. Another, in BMC Central, includes charges of disorderly conduct, assault with a dangerous weapon, and assault on ambulance personnel from Jan. 6, prosecutors said.

Reed is scheduled to return to court Feb. 20 for a probable cause hearing, prosecutors said.

Nick Stoico can be reached at nick.stoico@globe.com.

title: Segun Idowu’s departure leaves a big hole in Wu’s City Hall
text:
“She’s in the last year of her life,” Idowu, 37, said Tuesday. “And I am seriously going to regret it if she dies and I have spent most of my days prioritizing this job, but didn’t actually get to spend time with her.”

Idowu’s specific role has focused on driving the city’s work on business development, especially small business development.

But, particularly in Wu’s first years as mayor, he also served as a primary conduit to the city’s Black leadership, much of which had distant relationships with Wu, if any at all.

Idowu had relationships with all the people his boss did not. The grandson of a prominent pastor, he practically grew up at Twelfth Baptist Church in Roxbury. Prior to joining the administration, he had run the Black Economic Council of Massachusetts, which promotes the development of Black businesses.

He leveraged a lifetime of relationships to build bridges between Black Boston and City Hall.

Within the administration, his portfolio ranged from greatly increasing the amount of business the city does with diverse businesses to boosting the city’s long criticized night life.

Over his tenure, the city has doubled the contracts awarded to minority-owned businesses and attracted companies like Hasbro and Eli Lilly. Also, it has awarded millions of dollars in grants to small businesses, and awarded liquor licenses that have opened restaurants and given entrepreneurs a long overdue financial stake in the city’s nightlife.

“I’ve got five departments under me, and when I came in, they were all operating in silos,” Idowu said. “They are unified under one vision, under one mission. They see themselves as part of each other, as opposed to distinct departments. They all work together. And I think that is really what has allowed us to be as successful as we’ve been in the last four years.”

Idowu’s time in City Hall was not without controversy. He was accused of misconduct last year after he allegedly propositioned a city employee whose boyfriend worked in his department. An outside investigation found no wrongdoing. But in an election year the allegations got traction, and his public profile visibly shrunk in the aftermath of the complaint.

Wu steadfastly stood by him at the time, and Idowu said that episode played no role in his decision to leave the administration.

“I’ve continued doing the work, continued getting stuff done, so I don’t see that it has had any impact,” Idowu said. “I mean, if I was going to leave as a result of all that, I would have left when it was all happening. But, I had no desire to go anywhere, and the mayor had no desire for me to go anywhere, because I did nothing wrong.”

Idowu is leaving at a delicate time for Wu’s relationship with the Black community. The mayor’s decision to try to build a new Madison Park High School on a parcel that had been committed to commercial development and other uses has been widely scorned in Roxbury. That’s just the kind of controversy Idowu used to help her navigate — or avoid altogether. Presumably, that work will now fall to other players in City Hall.

Idowu said his plans are to spend time with his family, before pursuing other opportunities. He’s often been mentioned as a potential candidate for office himself. But he deflects such speculation, saying he only knows that he plans to stay involved in the community.

“I’m not going to put anything off the table, but just to say that I don’t need elected office to make the city that I grew up in a better place,” Idowu said. “Wherever I am, I’m going to do something that benefits my people and my community.”

title: The palace intrigue over Segun Idowu’s departure shows that Wu has work to do mending fences with Black leaders
text:
But any time you read for family reasons, you have to wonder if that was the driving factor.

Now some of you will wonder if Idowu is leaving because of a lingering fallout from a City Hall scandal involving Idowu and two city staffers last year. An internal investigation cleared Idowu, who got to keep his job, while the others were fired. One of those former employees sued the city over her termination.

I don’t think it has anything to do with that. If that episode were the problem, Idowu would have left after Wu’s re-election in November, much as other Cabinet members, including chief of streets Jascha Franklin-Hodge, chief of staff Tiffany Chu, and chief communications officer Jessicah Pierre, departed after Wu’s first term.

No, what some say is that Idowu is leaving after a one-two gut punch from Wu to Boston’s Black business and civic leaders: On Jan. 5, city Councilor Brian Worrell lost the City Council presidency after the mayor’s council allies backed another candidate; then on Jan. 12 the city upset many in Roxbury when it announced it would scrap a long-planned lab and housing project on city-owned land to instead build a new Madison Park Technical Vocational School.

Idowu, the story goes, was fed up, and quit. Could it be that simple? Or are Black leaders projecting their own growing frustrations with the mayor? Those frustrations bubbled last February when Josh Kraft challenged Wu in the mayor’s race. Kraft — the longtime leader of the Boys & Girls Club of Boston and son of billionaire Patriots owner Robert Kraft — had hoped to capitalize on a recurring strain of dissatisfaction in Black neighborhoods over the quality of schools, rising property taxes, and a controversial redevelopment of White Stadium in Franklin Park. But Idowu stood by her then. Were Worrell and Madison Park really the last straws?

There was only one way to find out. On Tuesday, I asked Idowu if he’s unhappy, perhaps feeling sidelined as a second term begins. The short answer, he said, is no, but he also can’t control how other people are feeling about this moment for the Black community.

“We will always have those experiences,” he told me. “What matters is that we keep our eye on the ball and keep pushing towards progress.”

In other words, Idowu remains an ally of the mayor. You can understand why: she defended him during his darkest moments, amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Idowu maintains his departure has been a long time coming. He told the mayor a year ago — before the misconduct allegations emerged last spring — that he was unlikely to stay the full second term. At the time, his grandmother was in decline, losing mobility and nearing a point where she could no longer live independently.

Idowu’s grandparents helped raise him. He was away in college when his grandfather passed away, and this time he wanted to spend as much time with his grandmother, Frances Lawson, as he could.

Still, Idowu had hoped to give the mayor more time to find a successor and give himself more time to line up another job. He said he has been looking, and he’s hopeful that he will find something by the time he leaves City Hall.

Then he spent last weekend cleaning up his grandmother’s Dorchester apartment after she moved into a nursing home. It all became real: she was never returning and that he needed to make every day with her count. He realized he needed to step down sooner than later.

“I have the opportunity to actually be with her for however long she’s got left,” Idowu told me. “I will not forgive myself if I get the call that she passed away, and I haven’t seen her in two weeks because I’ve been in the office the whole time.”

Idowu made a name for himself as the chief executive of the Black Economic Council of Massachusetts. I got to know him as the thorn in the side of the Walsh administration, pushing the city to do a better job of giving contracts to more businesses owned by women and people of color.

When Wu was elected in November 2021, Idowu was among the first wave of hires she made to her Cabinet. Idowu spearheaded key economic initiatives, such as helping small businesses find retail spaces through the SPACE grant program, increasing supplier diversity for city contracts, growing the number of liquor licenses for restaurants, and helping to attract new companies like Hasbro to Boston. In a statement, the mayor hailed his efforts to spread prosperity across the city and help Boston recover from COVID-19.

“Under Chief Idowu’s leadership, Boston’s neighborhoods have become more vibrant, inclusive, and connected,“ she said. ”His work has helped Boston rebound from the pandemic as a thriving city where companies and their employees want to work and live.”

Idowu also serves as a critical liaison to the Black community, even more so after the departures of other senior Black officials including Pierre, planning chief Arthur Jemison, and environmental chief the Rev. Mariama White-Hammond.

That connection isn’t lost on Black leaders like Imari Paris Jeffries, chief executive of Embrace Boston, a racial justice organization that honors the legacy of Martin Luther King Jr. Some city officials do their job from downtown. Idowu made a point to get out to the neighborhoods.

”He balanced doing the job from City Hall and from the community,” said Paris Jeffries. “That made him acutely aware of what was happening. We hope the administration finds someone with the same connections to the Black community.”

Wu and Idowu may indeed be leaving on good terms, not over frayed relationships in Black business and civic circles. But given how quickly the chatter over his departure turned to those relationships, the mayor should take heed, and find a successor who will help to mend them.

title: Boston man, Hopkinton woman allegedly posed as bank customers, fraudulently withdrew more than $1.2 million, federal prosecutors say
text:
A Boston man and a Hopkinton woman who allegedly impersonated bank customers were arrested and charged with defrauding Citizens Bank of more than $1.2 million, according to the office of Leah B. Foley, US Attorney for Massachusetts.

William Shaw, 67, is accused of posing as a customer on 11 different occasions at Citizens Bank branches in Abington, Brookline, Concord, and West Roxbury, and fraudulently withdrawing more than $674,000, according to a federal indictment.

Shaw was arrested Wednesday. At an arraignment hearing in federal court in Boston, he pleaded not guilty to eight charges, four counts of bank fraud and four counts of aggravated identity theft, court records show.

A judge ordered that Shaw be held in the custody of the US Marshals Service until a bed opens up at the Barbara McInnis House, a South Boston respite care center for people experiencing homelessness, according to court filings.

Rosemary Parks, 59, was arrested Friday and made an appearance in federal court the same day. She pleaded not guilty to three counts of bank fraud and three counts of aggravated identity theft, according to court documents.

Parks was released on special conditions. She was ordered not to drink alcohol or take illegal drugs. She also must undergo a mental health evaluation, court records show.

According to charging documents, Parks impersonated a bank customer eight times and fraudulently withdrew more than $536,000 from Citizens Bank branches in Franklin, Roslindale, and Sturbridge.

The pair’s scheme lasted from at least December 2022 to March 2025, federal prosecutors said.

Shaw and Parks used fake driver’s licenses that showed their own photos but listed personal information that belonged to bank customers, Foley’s office said.

Shaw and Parks gave bank tellers withdrawal slips that listed the customers’ names and account numbers to withdraw cash and buy cashier’s checks, charging documents show.

Six men were arrested in July as part of a related investigation, Foley’s office said. The accused men allegedly were involved in a multi-million-dollar scheme that defrauded banks in Massachusetts, Connecticut and Rhode Island.

Parks and Shaw have status conference hearings scheduled for March 10.
