title: Requiem for a mama bear
text:
Charles had a big heart, a big smile, a big personality. But he was named after his father so he was always going to be Little Charles.

Pat Copney worked as a court officer at Roxbury District Court, where everybody called her Miss Pat. She was a mama bear at the courthouse, too, the one person you wanted to see, whether you were a lawyer, a judge, a cop, or just some random person who had the misfortune of appearing in court because you were a defendant or victim.

Her son’s empathy was hereditary. When he was in second grade at the Nathan Hale School, Charles wrote this: “When I grow up I will be a doctor. I care about people and I don’t want them to die. I want to work in an operating room. I want to work on arms. I want to work on legs.”

But Charles never got a chance to grow up.

Pat knew the streets could sometimes swallow kids whole, kids whose parents or guardians couldn’t take care of themselves let alone a child, unchurched kids and neglected kids who ran wild around parts of Boston, armed with guns and anger and no hope.

She was determined to protect Charles from those streets, those bad influences, those kids who didn’t grow up with the kind of nurturing love she showered Charles with.

But, and Pat knew this all too well, sometimes the streets prevail.

On April 20, 1991, three weeks short of what would have been the 11th Mother’s Day for her, four days after Charles’ joyous 11th birthday party, the streets prevailed: Charles was shot and killed as he played outside his Roxbury home, along with a 15-year-old named Korey Grant.

At the time, Charles, an innocent child playing outside his house, was the youngest victim of gun violence in the city’s history. Now, they shoot 2-year-olds.

After losing Charles, Pat Copney spent the rest of her life trying to save other mothers from the greatest heartache, from a pain that never goes away.

But mama bears don’t live forever. Pat Copney left this mortal, maddening world, and last week there was a celebration of her life at the New Hope Baptist Church in Hyde Park.

At the service, Rev. Kenneth Simms, the pastor at New Hope, reassured mourners that Pat was finally at peace.

“Earth has no sorrow that Heaven cannot heal,” Pastor Kenneth said, according to a video of the service the church posted on Facebook.

Pat Copney knew sorrow like few others.

In one of the tributes to her online, it was noted that “Pat was very stubborn, she stood strong in her beliefs, if she did not like something you were going to hear about it.”

She was stubborn in her belief in justice, and she believed she and her family did not receive justice, that the guy who murdered Charles evaded justice.

That guy was Damien Bynoe.

Bynoe was a 15-year-old aspiring member of the Orchard Park Trailblazers gang when he pulled a gun and shot Charles and Korey Grant.

What Pat Copney couldn’t get over, what she could never fathom, is what the cops told her where Damien Bynoe went after he murdered two boys.

“He went out for pizza,” Pat Copney told me one day, repeating it, as if she still couldn’t believe it. “He went out for pizza.”

What made it worse for Pat was when the case went to court, at the very courthouse where she worked, a judge named Paul McGill openly sympathized with the murderer instead of the murdered.

McGill suggested Bynoe was the real victim, that somehow something or someone made him pick up a gun.

McGill blamed the shooting not on Bynoe, who pulled the trigger, but his two teenage accomplices, who were unarmed. McGill refused to transfer Bynoe’s case out of juvenile court, but in one of the most convoluted pieces of legal reasoning in the history of the Commonwealth allowed the two unarmed accomplices to be tried as adults.

Damien Bynoe served just five years in a juvenile facility for murdering Charles and Korey Grant.

Pat Copney had to swallow that. But not for long. She channeled her outrage, all that anger, all that incredulity, and started talking to state reps and senators, buttonholing newspaper reporters, anybody who would listen about the injustice of someone escaping justice because of their age.

Less than one year after Charles was murdered, Pat Copney stood at the State House, looking heavenward, to the lost son who inspired her activism, after the Legislature passed the Copney-Grant bill, giving prosecutors the discretion to charge teenagers as adults.

Pat didn’t think all teenagers should be charged as adults. She worked in the legal system long enough to know that discretion is its greatest tool. She knew enough about the human condition to know some kids had bad breaks, and some kids just break bad.

Damien Bynoe broke bad. He got out of juvie at 21, then spent two decades in and out of a legal system that gave him break after break, In 2020, he was sentenced to 17 years in federal prison on gun and drug charges.

Pat Copney didn’t dwell on Damien Bynoe. Instead, she kept working against gun violence, teaming up with Charles’s pediatrician at Boston Children’s Hospital, a wonderful physician and human being named Judy Palfrey.

Charles’s plaque hangs in the registration area of the Primary Care Center at Children’s.

As the years went by, what comforted Pat most was knowing that one day she would be reunited with her son.

Knowing she is with Charles right now, fussing over his clothes, the two of them side by side in a realm far different and better than ours, Mama Bear and her Little Charles, together forever, well, as Pat Copney would say, “Praise God!”

title: Franklin Cummings Tech celebrates a new home, and a comeback
text:
“I remember driving by for decades and seeing this lot empty,” said Julius Rogers, a Dorchester native and cybersecurity student. Now, “I tell everyone I feel like I’m working at Google or a startup.”

But the formal opening of the building Thursday is also the culmination of a remarkable turnaround for a school that six years ago was struggling to stay afloat.

The then-Benjamin Franklin Institute of Technology was limping toward a merger with Wentworth that died shortly after becoming public knowledge. At the height of the pandemic, the technical school ran a $5 million deficit and laid off a third of its staff. Student enrollment plummeted. And many feared Franklin Cummings Tech would meet the same fate as over 80 colleges that have gone under since 2020, leaving a gaping hole in the kind of hands-on training that typically pays off in future earnings, particularly for lower-income people of color.

Then it didn’t: Bill and Joyce Cummings donated $12.5 million to the school and called for its renaming to Franklin Cummings Tech. The philanthropists considered a big gift to Harvard or MIT, but chose the two-year school precisely because of its focus on vocational training. That, in turn, ignited a wave of giving that surprised, well, everyone. In four years, the school raised $61 million from 700 donors, including $4 million from City Hall.

“It was amazing after that how they merchandised the fact that they had a Cummings grant,” said Bill Cummings, whose real estate business is based in Woburn. “We were astounded at how much it was.”

Most of the money went toward the new campus in Roxbury, a $75 million building with 68,000 square feet across three floors.

The funds also bolstered scholarships and academic needs as the school moved toward financial stability. It pared down the number of available majors from 22 to 10 to focus its resources on programs with the most potential, and the most student interest. Applications rolled in from longtime Franklin Cummings Tech strongholds — John D. O’Bryant School of Math and Science and Dearborn Academy, for example — as well as charter and private schools that see growing demand among graduates for technical education. In less than five years, enrollment doubled to almost 1,125 students. Staffing rebounded to pre-pandemic levels.

Seemingly overnight, Franklin Cummings Tech became the model for a style of vocational training the Trump administration (and much of the country) is clamoring for. Virtually no one is denied admission to the school, which has long taught mostly men of color, immigrants, and first-generation students. Nearly everyone receives financial aid, and tuition, now $9,500 a semester, has only climbed once in the last eight years. Its outcomes rival more prestigious colleges: Around 80 percent of Franklin Cummings Tech graduates quickly get jobs, with an average starting salary near $60,000, higher than the median income of the neighborhood where the school, and almost one in six students, now resides.

“That’s the joy of the work we’ve done over the past five years: We remain broad access. We’ve remained a majority-minority institution, and we’ve grown quite a bit,” said Franklin Cummings Tech president Aisha Francis. “And we believe there’s still more growth out there — that there’s still market share and demand for the education we offer.”

The renaissance extends not just to the school, but to the part of Roxbury around it.

Where Franklin Cummings Tech now stands was a vacant lot for two decades, after the hardware store Harrison Supply closed in the 2000s. Residents now hope that a wave of teachers and students will eat and shop nearby, and that fresh-faced graduates in biotechnology and business management, for example, staff new businesses that could grow in other major developments rising in the vicinity.

“This is a physical symbol of the absolute resurgence of Nubian Square that is actually in full bloom,” said Richard Taylor, a prominent Boston developer behind the unfinished mixed-used development Nubian Ascends. “This is a story of resiliency, persistence, and a vision to be realized and not deferred in this urban market. You can talk up change in a neighborhood. But to actually make it happen . . . oof.”

It took years, Francis said, and an intentional approach to both economics and architecture.

Forty percent of the construction contracts for the new building were awarded to minority business owners, some from Roxbury or Franklin Cummings Tech alums themselves. The campus hinges around a gleaming central staircase that threads through common study spaces stocked with sound-absorbing furniture. All but one classroom gets natural light, and much of what happens inside the school can be seen from outside. The shop where residents bring their cars in for repairs by automotive students, for the cost of parts alone, connects to a back street on the first floor. The lecturer in the robotics lab is observable from the sidewalk. And the optical shop by the front door — a training outpost for opticianry students that was tucked away on the former campus — will take drop-ins from the community.

“The visibility of the program is something we have been struggling with for the last few years,” said Rhiannon Raymond, an opticianry student in her final semester. “This puts us, literally, front and center.”

Hiding in plain sight throughout are homages to the school’s past and its people. A mural in the entryway depicts the facade of the old South End campus. The veneer cladding on the reception desk is really a collage of discarded chopsticks by a Charlestown business, ChopValue. And the sculptural spectacles affixed to the bike racks — another funky Franklin reference — were created by the Dorchester nonprofit Artists for Humanity. A third-floor ceiling installation depicting blue kites is also a nod to Franklin (and his kite-in-a-thunderstorm experiment), suspended between pieces of wood from the lumber supply company that once sat where the school is today.

Robert Kelchen, a higher education finance expert and professor at the University of Tennessee Knoxville, called Franklin Cummings Tech “a success story,” with an asterisk. Its turnaround is impressive, but is largely fueled by one-time donations, and the school only has $26 million in the bank.

“The one item to watch out for now is whether they are able to build an endowment out of this in case the supports soften from now on,” he said. “There’s always more to do.”

Maybe the biggest item on the agenda is salvaging the sale of the old South End campus, after a deal to turn it into a senior living community fell through in October. It left Franklin Cummings Tech with less cash on hand.

The sale imploded when what had been billed as an affordable housing development gradually transformed into expensive memory care units, costing upward of $10,000 a month, said Stephen Fox, a South End resident who was on the advisory group for the project.

“Talk about a bait-and-switch,” Fox said. “The whole project was beginning to take on a very different feel from what we originally hoped for.”

Related Beal, the development firm that had the site under contract but ultimately chose not to purchase the property, declined to comment. A joint statement with the school in the fall said the parties “could not agree on a viable business plan that would allow the project to move forward.” The purchase price was never made public, though the site is now assessed at $34 million.

Franklin Cummings Tech found bridge financing to fund the new building, the Boston Guardian reported, and still intends to sell the old campus. It is on the market with the permits for the senior living facility already approved, a spokesperson for the school said.

Francis, confident that a sale will work out, said there are already new bids.

That confidence extends to her as well. A doctorate in English literature and the first female president of the predominantly male institution, Francis seems an unlikely progenitor of its success. But “the leadership” was the reason that Cummings said he made his donation in the first place.

In that way, Francis may have something in common with Franklin, said Bithia Carter, president of the philanthropy nonprofit Give Black Alliance.

The Boston-born inventor and Founding Father gifted 1,000 pounds from his estate to Boston in 1790, specifically to support trade education, and designed the fund to mature in 200 years. Later in his life, Franklin became an ardent “education abolitionist,” dedicated to providing opportunities to all students like the ones who attend Franklin Cummings Tech today.

“He would smile down on this,” Carter said. “By the time he died, he had come to recognize that we need to invest more in all people and recognize their equal capacities. [Francis] is living out the legacy of freeing people, of teaching people to lead their own lives and giving them the tools to do that.”

title: A state-title winning hockey coach departs midseason, a 49-point night, and more Thursday night takeaways
text:
Before we dive into the rest of the day’s action, find our complete scoreboard here, and sign up for the weeklyVarsity News newsletter.

Roundups: Boys’ basketball | Girls’ hockey | Girls’ basketball | Boys’ hockey

League standings: Boys’ basketball | Girls’ hockey | Girls’ basketball | Boys’ hockey

▪ The Braintree girls’ indoor track team captured its first Bay State Conference championship by going 5-0.

▪ The Canton boys’ track team earned its first victory in two years, defeating Foxborough 58-42, with the help of wins from Joshua Saint Vil (high jump), John Martinek (55-meter hurdles and long jump), Sony Chery (55), Declan Monahan (300), and the 4x200m relay of Chery, Saint Vil, Angel Assad, and Ramson Madhel.

Nauset boys’ coach Connor Brickley will be taking over as Winchendon’s Director of Hockey, succeeding Jeff Pellegrini, who led the program for five years before departing for Masters Academy International.

Brickley will start at Winchendon immediately, but will continue coaching Nauset, the defending Division 3 champion, which is 10-1-2 and ranked No. 16 in the Globe’s Top 20.

Brickley, an Everett native, played 81 games in the NHL for the Panthers and Rangers after starring at Vermont. He has also coached with the Northeast Generals girls’ program.

“I am extremely excited to get to work with these amazing student-athletes,” Brickley said in a press release. “The Winchendon School has a great foundation and framework that will allow a seamless transition to continue tradition and bring the program to new heights.”

In his Winchendon role, Brickley will be head coach of the girls’ Elite U19 program, while providing “leadership and oversight for all hockey programming,” the school wrote.

“Connor Brickley is a leader who understands that athletics, at their best, are about far more than performance alone,” said Sean Duncan, Winchendon’s head of school. “He brings credibility, humility, and a clear commitment to helping young people develop the habits, discipline, and perspective necessary for success both on and off the ice. He is exceptionally well aligned with Winchendon’s mission and our emphasis on leadership and character education.”

▪ Phillips Exeter’s Jake Attaway, who led Hudson to a Division 6 Super Bowl title in 2024 during a record-setting career, has committed to play football at Merrimack. In his one year at PE, Attaway threw for 1,109 yards and 14 touchdowns, rushing for 598 yards and 10 scores to an All-NEPSAC honors. At Hudson, he set the state’s all-purpose TD record with 146 and became one of five players in state history with more than 10,000 total yards.

Merrimack lost last year’s starting quarterback, Central Catholic graduate Ayden Pereira, to Georgia State.

▪ King Philip senior Liam King has committed to play football at Union. The 5-foot-11-inch, 260-pound captain anchored the Warriors’ lines en route to a Division 3 Super Bowl title and 13-0 record.

▪ In addition to its new director of hockey, Winchendon announced a trio of college baseball signings that became official: Reed Buckler, a 6-1 catcher/first baseman, officially committed to Merrimack; Ryan Ruggiero, a 5-7 outfielder/lefthander, committed to Bucknell; and Tyler Marcoux, a 6-0 outfielder, commited to Northern Essex.

Shy Babb, Lynn Classical — The senior was monstrous down low, producing 26 points, 12 rebounds, and 5 blocks in a 74-56 boys’ basketball win over Medford.

Infinity Burns, Beverly — The junior cleaned up the glass, hauling in 16 rebounds to go with 7 points and three steals in a narrow 51-49 girls’ basketball win over Saugus.

Sloan Costa, Central Catholic — The sophomore goalie nearly single-handedly preserved a 1-1 draw with Acton-Boxborough by making 44 saves.

Charles Dobre, Revere — The sophomore powered a 68-62 double-overtime win over Lynn English with 25 points, 4 rebounds, and 4 steals.

Jackson Farrington, O’Bryant — The Tigers needed all of the junior’s 16 points, 10 rebounds, and 7 assists to slip past East Boston, 58-54, in boys’ basketball action.

Mackenzie Ilacqua, Quincy/North Quincy — While her sister, Riley scored once, the junior deposited four goals in a 6-3 girls’ hockey triumph over Plymouth.

Avery LeBlanc and Asuka Keough, Beverly/Danvers — LeBlanc, a sophomore, provided four assists and Keough, a junior, was the beneficiary, scoring twice and dishing two assists of her own as the Panthers won their first Colleen Ritzer Memorial Game win in five years.

▪ Fairfield senior attack Jake Gilbert, a Xaverian graduate from Foxborough, was a preseason All-CAA honorable mention for men’s lacrosse. Last season, he scored 29 goals with eight assists and was named All-CAA second team.

▪ Emerson senior Bri Frongillo, a Hopedale graduate, was named to the NEWBA weekly first team after a 2-0 week for the Lions in which she averaged 18.5 points, 4.0 rebounds, and 4.0 assists, highlighted by 27 points in a win over Salve Regina.

The only caveat is if one of the UMass Lowell hockey or basketball teams is still hosting playoff games, in which case the MIAA finals would move to Worcester State.

title: Developers push back on Wu plan to take Roxbury site for Madison Park high school
text:
But the developers said they have spent three years working with the Roxbury community to further the project, and have invested upward of $1 million, and would like the chance to continue.

“Since our selection in 2023, HYM and MyCAP have remained deeply committed to working in partnership with the City of Boston and the Roxbury community to ensure that P3 delivers meaningful, lasting benefits for the neighborhood,” they said in a letter to Wu on Thursday. “We have raised and invested substantial capital, advanced the project in good faith, and met our commitments to The Roxbury Strategic Master Plan Oversight Committee and the broader community despite significant economic and political headwinds.”

The developers are hosting a community listening session on Feb. 2 at Twelfth Baptist Church in Roxbury to discuss the decision — and they invited Wu and her staff to attend.

“Your participation would underscore the City’s continued commitment to partnership and to shaping a plan that reflects both community voices and municipal leadership,” wrote the Rev. Jeffrey Brown of My City at Peace and Tom O’Brien of The HYM Investment Group — last year, O’Brien had briefly considered challenging Wu for Boston mayor, but ultimately chose not to.

Kairos Shen, the city’s chief planner, announced at a Jan. 13 meeting of the RSMPOC that the city would not extend development rights, and would instead consider using at least a portion of the P3 site for a new campus for Madison Park. That project could cost more than $700 million and the city recently won initial approvals for state funding.

It was an abrupt reversal for a site that has remained undeveloped for 50 years, and one where past developers have had rights extended repeatedly.

Wu defended the decision on GBH radio on Tuesday, where she said the potential for state funding to rebuild Madison Park was “what everyone said would never happen” and made more sense than “prolonging a pipe dream” of a lab and affordable housing campus at P3. The economics of such a campus simply don’t work right now, she said, given that the region is grappling with a glut of lab space and little demand to fill it.

Meanwhile, the city expects replacing or renovating Madison Park’s campus is expected to be the most expensive school construction project in state history. Using P3 makes more sense, and would likely save money, compared with constructing a temporary building and rebuilding the existing Madison Park.

“We have a parcel of land that wasn’t going to be used for a feasible economic development plan under the current project proposal available to help us maneuver what the right layout is, to solve potentially some really challenging questions for Madison, and then have a school there moving forward that will spark an actually feasible economic development project,” Wu said on GBH.

Wu on GBH said HYM and My City at Peace’s pledge to build a lab campus subsidizing deeply affordable housing “hasn’t been true for some time.”

“It’s time to come to terms that those promises are not able to be delivered on by that developer,” she said. “Now we are finding a way to make something actually work.”

In their Jan. 22 letter, HYM and My City at Peace listed out “demonstrated momentum” of the P3 project, including a finalized project budget and pre-development budget, negotiating a term sheet with the city, and meeting with potential life-science anchor tenants.

“We disagree with the Mayor’s representation of our project’s viability,” Brown and O’Brien wrote. “Our vision has always been clear: to invest in the Roxbury community by creating deeply affordable homeownership and rental opportunities; good-paying jobs with viable, long-term career tracks; and meaningful equity participation in the development process by people of color and women.”

It’s unclear if Wu plans to attend the Feb. 2 meeting.

title: ‘Shirley has it wrong:’ When the mayor calls you out on the radio, you kind of have to respond
text:
It could be any number of things. Like the time I wanted Boston to host the 2024 Summer Olympics, or more recently questioned whether Boston really needs two soccer stadiums. Or maybe it was back when I told Market Basket employees to return to work rather than walk out in solidarity for beloved leader-in-exile Arthur T. Demoulas.

Nope. Wu was talking about my column on the future of a piece of city-owned land on Tremont Street in Roxbury that was supposed to become lab space, housing, and the new museum and policy center for Embrace Boston. Last week, the city pulled the plug on the long-planned project and instead decided to build the new Madison Park Technical Vocational High School there.

“Shirley has it wrong here, in terms of the initial framing,” Wu said on GBH on Tuesday. “It’s not true that the P3 economic development project isn’t happening because we chose to move forward with Madison Park. The P3 economic development project was not happening on its own.”

Well, that’s not quite what I wrote. But if I left that impression, allow me to clarify.

Normally I would just go on air to defend myself. Like the mayor, I’m a regular guest on GBH’s Boston Public Radio, but I didn’t want to wait until my next appearance.

I’ll try to do this in the nicest way because nobody wants to start a war of words with the mayor of Boston — well, aside from the occasional state senator or city councilor.

This is what I would say: I’m clear-eyed about why the original proposal stalled. The team the city picked to develop P3 — led by HYM Investment Group and My City at Peace — has struggled to line up financing because of a glut of lab space and soaring construction costs. But a lot of developers have had a hard time moving forward because of market conditions.

So I think moving Madison Park onto P3 is a really good idea, one that should be taken seriously, especially if the state might help pay for the $700 million school.

But where the mayor and I differ is the approach. The city wants to ditch the original P3 development team and focus first on planning Madison Park on the eight-acre parcel; it would then incorporate economic development on whatever land the school doesn’t need. The city is worried that involving another team might complicate and slow down its application for state money.

“It has to happen in the right order now, and we’re going to continue working on it so that we’re not just prolonging a pipe dream,” said Wu. “It’s time to come to terms that those promises are not able to be delivered on by that developer, and now we are finding a way to make something actually work.”

But should the city just cut ties with a development team that knows the site best? Why not give them the first crack at coming up with a new plan?

HYM and My City at Peace have been working closely with the neighborhood since, well, before they won development rights in 2023. The team has built trust with the neighbors, and built valuable partnerships, while Wu and the city barged in with an abrupt, top-down decision.

What’s more, I’m not convinced having HYM and My City at Peace involved could muck up the city’s request for state funding, given it’s still so early in the process.

It wouldn’t even be the first time HYM and My City at Peace considered putting a school on P3. Two years ago, the city asked the development team to look at whether a new John D. O’Bryant School of Math and Science could be built on the site and the answer was yes; it could be done faster and be less expensive than a publicly-managed project.

But the city decided it wouldn’t work. The mayor had also proposed relocating the O’Bryant from Roxbury to West Roxbury; that didn’t work either and was scrapped after vehement opposition from parents, teachers, and alumni.

What do I know?

Whether it’s the mayor saying so or by my own admonition, I do get things wrong from time to time.

I just think I’m right about P3.

title: Under Segun Idowu, City Hall focused on neighborhood development. Will Mayor Wu now pivot to downtown?
text:
For four years, Idowu did just that, launching new grant programs for local businesses, doling out liquor licenses in parts of town that have few, and connecting far-flung commercial districts to the resources of City Hall. Then, Monday, Idowu announced he will step down at the end of February, to care for his elderly grandmother.

Idowu’s departure comes at a precarious time for Boston’s economy, amid threats to some of the city’s core industries, concerns over the vitality of the Financial District, and declining values of commercial real estate that powers the city’s budget. Now, business leaders are wondering: Will Wu, and whoever she picks to succeed Idowu, continue the neighborhood-focused approach to economic development, or will they pivot to prioritize a downtown that’s still struggling to rebound from the COVID-19 pandemic?

It’s a push-and-pull faced by Boston mayors for decades, from Kevin White’s efforts to revive downtown and the waterfront, to Thomas Menino’s more neighborhood-centric approach, to Martin J. Walsh, who oversaw an era of building all across the city. But Wu, in an interview this week, said downtown and the neighborhoods isn’t an either/or question for her administration.

“That’s a false dichotomy,” Wu said.

“When we invest in downtown, it strengthens our neighborhoods, and when we open and fill neighborhood retail space that also strengthens downtown,” she said. “We need our residents, neighborhood businesses, our large corporations, [and] philanthropic sector all to not only coexist, but cooperate.”

As of now, Wu said, she does not have a replacement for Idowu lined up. Whoever she hires, she said, their top priorities will include filling still-empty storefronts and adapting to Boston’s changing economic landscape amid federal attacks on higher education, health care, and research.

“This continues to be a really challenging and really consequential moment for Boston’s future,” she said. “We are laser focused on driving down the commercial vacancy rates downtown and throughout our commercial areas, and [strengthening] our innovation sector and all the industries that have supported Boston’s economy for centuries and need to [continue to do so] for the next generation.”

That is a slight shift in tone for Wu, who four years ago campaigned on shrinking Boston’s racial wealth gap by investing in communities of color. Catering to downtown and big business interests were not as high on the agenda.

For some Boston business leaders, even that modest shift is likely to be welcome.

Jim Rooney, president and chief executive of the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce, said Idowu’s tenure has generally been good for the city at large. But he acknowledged that certain segments of Boston’s business community feel like City Hall has neglected the struggles of downtown and not done enough to make Boston’s business environment competitive.

“The view of the business community is that our [city and state] government partners should step up their game with respect to business attraction, retention, growth, expansion,” said Rooney. “And that not enough attention is paid or has been paid to those issues over time.”

The Wu administration has had some big business wins.Hasbro, Lego, and Eli Lilly all moved big facilities to Boston in the last four years, which Idowu said shows that big employers appreciate his and Wu’s “holistic” approach to economic development, prioritizing businesses across the city and improving residents’ quality of life.

“Our strategy was, for the benefit of the commercial cores of the city, it’s important that we have healthy, vibrant neighborhood economies,” Idowu said. “It is not cheaper to move a company to the city of Boston. So why are they doing that? It’s because it’s a place where their employees will want to be.”

Still, for much of her first term, Wu contended with a perception that she is less friendly to big business interests and traditional power brokers than her predecessors. That has played out in clashes over property tax rates on commercial buildings, and over affordable housing and green energy policies that critics argue has stalled new construction.

Those are challenges that Idowu’s eventual successor will have to confront, along with stubbornly high office vacancy rates. Then there are broad economic shifts that are hurting small businesses all over the city, including downtown.

Bessie King, who co-owns the Villa Mexico Cafe in the Financial District with her mother, Julie King, said they received grants from the city to help them survive the roughest parts of the pandemic. But since 2022 they’ve seen City Hall’s emphasis pivot elsewhere.

“They shifted to promoting new businesses or encouraging people to open new businesses without really helping the existing businesses that are trying to survive,” Bessie said.

Last summer, Julie King sent a letter to Idowu saying she was on the verge of closing her quarter-century-old lunch spot. The letter prompted the city to connect the Kings to a small business consultant, who is now helping them update their menu. But Bessie King said it shouldn’t have taken a desperate plea for them to get help. And time is running short.

“For us, 2026 is crucial,” Bessie King said. “If we do not make a profit this year, we will close.”

At the same time, other parts of the city are growing. From Dorchester and Roxbury to Mattapan and Hyde Park, new small businesses are springing up, says state Representative Chris Worrell. He gives a lot of credit to Idowu and a renewed focus from City Hall.

“We are becoming destination boroughs, communities, and that’s [due to] all the investment that Segun has seen into it,” Worrell said. “You see it far and wide when you go into the Black and brown areas of Boston, you see his handprint throughout the city.”

If that was Wu’s goal, Idowu was a natural fit for the job. As president and chief executive of BECMA, Idowu had focused on supporting Black-owned businesses, with the goal of helping marginalized communities build generational wealth. Under his leadership, BECMA and several other advocacy groups in 2021 filed a federal civil rights complaint against the city, after an audit found that just 1.2 percent of the $2.1 billion City Hall spent on contracts between 2014 and 2019 went to Black- and Latino-owned companies.

Then he joined City Hall, aiming to change the system from the inside.

“Segun took the role to be transformational,” said Nicole Obi, his successor at BECMA. “Under his leadership [at City Hall], we saw real progress, whether that was increased contracting with diverse businesses or expanded access to capital, or policies that helped businesses stabilize and grow. That was all by intention.”

Over four years, Idowu and the city nearly doubled the amount in city contracts that went to minority- and women-owned businesses, including a $17 million contract between Boston Public Schools and City Fresh Foods in 2022, the largest contract the city has ever awarded to a Black-owned business.

And when Beacon Hill granted Boston 225 new liquor licenses, Idowu worked to help minority-owned businesses in historically disenfranchised neighborhoods apply for them. He also launched the SPACE Grant program, which doled out COVID-era recovery funds to small businesses to help them move into empty storefronts, not just downtown but all over Boston.

Idowu tackled those efforts with the help of a critical tool: an unprecedented pot of federal pandemic relief dollars. Nearly one-10th of the $560 million Boston received in COVID recovery funds went to Idowu’s Economic Opportunity and Inclusion Cabinet, funding many of Idowu’s marquee initiatives.

Now that money is largely spent, and Wu has warned her department heads to prepare for modest budget cuts. Whoever follows Idowu won’t have the same resources to work with.

Still, Karilyn Crockett, an MIT professor of urban history, public policy, and planning who worked for City Hall for several years under Walsh, said she hopes Wu fills Idowu’s role with someone who will continue his efforts to address longstanding racial disparities in the city’s economic development efforts.

“These were hard-won or hard-fought battles,” Crockett said. “This is a moment to continue this focus and commitment and double down on it.”

For his part, Idowu said he is not at all concerned about leaving behind a vacuum of leadership, even with several major events around the corner, from the FIFA World Cup, Tall Ships, and the country’s 250th anniversary, which are expected to bring a wave of investment and tourism to the city.

“I have tremendous faith in my team,” Idowu said. “I would argue that we’ve been one of the most productive engines of progress in the city in many, many years ... and I think that the person who takes over is going to be standing on a very solid foundation.”

title: Brace yourselves: major winter storm arrives in Boston
text:
At least one storm-related death was reported when a plow truck backed into a married couple and killed a woman in an MBTA parking lot in Norwood, police said.

“This is the biggest storm we’ve seen in years,” Governor Maura Healey said Sunday at the State Emergency Operations Center in Framingham. “It’s going to snow until Monday night. It’s wicked cold already. Just hunker in ... look after your neighbors, take care of one another, and ride this one out.”

In Maine, a private jet with eight people on board crashed as it was taking off from Bangor International Airport about 7:45 p.m. Sunday, according to the FAA. It was not immediately clear if there were any fatalities or injuries.

The National Weather Service has issued winter storm warnings across Massachusetts, Rhode Island, and Connecticut through 8 p.m. Monday. NWS forecasters expected 7 to 11 inches during the day Sunday, followed by another 10 to 14 inches Sunday night as winds increased, gusting up to 28 miles per hour.

According to a regional roundup by the National Weather Service at 7 p.m., Lawrence, Smithfield in Rhode Island, and Manchester and Portsmouth in New Hampshire were experiencing “heavy snow.”

By about 10 p.m., Boston and most of the surrounding region was blanketed in more than a foot of snow.

Snow piled up to about 14 inches in Dorchester and about 15 inches in South Boston, according to the weather service. Outside of Boston, Braintree had about 16 inches of snow, Lowell had nearly 17 inches, Ipswich had just over 17 inches, Rehoboth had about 13.5 inches, Agawam had about 18 inches, and Pembroke got about 16 inches, according to the weather service.

On Cape Cod, a foot of snow was recorded in Sandwich and Brewster, according to the weather service.

Snowfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour were common at the height of the storm, between 3 and 11 p.m. Sunday, describing travel as “difficult to impossible.” Temperatures will remain frigid throughout, with highs in the mid-20s and wind chills dipping below zero in some areas. Forecasters expect snow to continue into Monday, with another 1 to 3 inches possible before tapering off.

The state’s response remains “laser-focused” on the hardest-hit areas of Massachusetts, particularly the South Coast and the Cape and Islands, where heavier, wetter snow has raised concerns about power outages, officials said.

Healey said it could take crews up to four hours to clear major roadways after the storm’s peak, though widespread outages were not anticipated for Greater Boston. “This is a fluffy snow, not the kind that weighs down lines,” she said.

As of about 12:15 a.m. Monday, the Massachusetts Emergency Management Agency reported 3,192 power outages in the state, most coming from Andover where there were 2,206 outages.

State Police reported 149 crashes, seven with injuries as of 8 p.m. Sunday. None of the crashes were fatal. The agency also reported 234 disabled vehicles and said it assisted 10 motorists.

A 47-year-old woman died after a snowplow operator backed into the woman and her husband in an MBTA parking lot in Norwood on Sunday afternoon, the agency’s Transit Police Department reported.

The woman’s 51-year-old husband was hospitalized with injuries that were not life-threatening. The 33-year-old driver of the Ford F-350 truck was a private contractor who remained on scene, transit police said.

Healey urged residents using space heaters, wood stoves, and fireplaces to do so carefully. “What we don’t need is for our fire departments to be taxed right now,” she said.

All nonessential state employees will work from home on Monday, and Healey urged private employers to follow suit.

More than 745 flights at Logan International Airport were canceled and 55 were delayed Sunday, according to flight-tracking website FlightAware.

Joshua Duncan, 45, who lives in Dallas, flew in for a friend’s wedding in Salem and was scheduled to return home Sunday evening, but was left stranded at Logan overnight.

“All anyone could talk about at the wedding was the storm,” Duncan said.

American Airlines initially told him his flight was still scheduled and planes would be de-iced, but by early afternoon, he was rebooked for Monday evening and placed on standby.

“I’ll wait it out. It’s not safe to drive, so standby is my last-ditch effort to get home,” he said, sitting near the ticket counters with a copy of “Tilt,” a book about a natural disaster he grabbed from a kiosk.

Around him, he said, the terminal buzzed with varying degrees of frustration. “People are slightly irritated. There’s a drunk young guy who DoorDashed liquor to the airport and is already intoxicated,” he said. “Air Canada, United, Southwest — they’re all still flying to some of the same places. American is canceled. I usually fly Southwest, but this one was a better fare.”

In Boston, Mayor Michelle Wu declared a snow emergency through Monday evening and activated a parking ban on major roads. Boston Public Works said it had 40,000 tons of salt available and more than 850 pieces of equipment deployed.

The state had pretreated major highways and positioned more than 3,000 plows and spreaders to keep pace with the storm. As of about 10 p.m., the state had 2,625 pieces of equipment deployed and implemented a 40 miles per hour speed restriction on Interstate 90 between the New York border and mile marker 110 in Soutborough.

Still, roads, especially bridges and overpasses, are likely to become slick and hazardous, and motorists are strongly advised to delay nonessential travel. Drivers should carry emergency supplies and flashlights if travel is unavoidable.

“With over a foot of snow forecasted statewide, we’re encouraging residents to avoid unnecessary travel,” said Massachusetts Highway administrator Jonathan Gulliver. “If you must travel, allow extra time, reduce speeds, and be mindful of snowplows and crews.”

Transit riders also faced challenges. The MBTA activated its winter weather plan, storing vehicles indoors overnight, and checking brakes and propulsion systems for ice buildup. Normal weekday service is expected Monday on the Red, Orange, Green, and Blue lines, while Mattapan Line service will likely be suspended and replaced with shuttle buses as snow conditions worsen, officials said.

Commuter Rail lines are operating on reduced storm schedules, running about one-third of regular weekday service, and ferry service from Hingham, Hull, Logan, and Boston will run hourly. Some bus routes are detouring to avoid steep hills and narrow streets.

Officials also emphasized support for people experiencing homelessness. Residents who need assistance can dial 211 to locate a warming shelter.

The Pine Street Inn nearly doubled its street outreach teams for the storm, deploying vans stocked with blankets, clothing, hot meals, and warm beverages. Almost 50 people were brought into its shelters overnight, and roughly 660 people were housed across its four Boston-area locations as of Sunday.

“Our shelters will be open around the clock,” spokesperson Barbara Trevisan said. “This is literally life or death for people in this coming week.”

Across the Commonwealth, 40 warming centers remained open, with Boston Centers for Youth & Families facilities activated during their normal hours. The city’s emergency shelters are operating 24/7, with amnesty for those with nonviolent restrictions when temperatures fall below freezing.

A fire in Roxbury displaced three adults, four children, and a dog Sunday afternoon during the storm when a fire broke out on the third floor of a three-family, triple-decker home. Nobody was injured, and the American Red Cross assisted in relocating the residents, the Boston Fire Department said.

Schools responded swiftly to the forecast. Boston Public Schools and at least 110 school districts across Greater Boston have announced schedule changes due to the winter storm. Nearly all are closed on Monday, with Brockton Public Schools closed through Tuesday.

As for universities, Tufts, Boston University, Emerson, and MIT are closed Monday. Northeastern University will be remote on Monday. Harvard University remains open.

At H Mart in Brookline, the storm’s practical impact played out in smaller ways. Cardboard boxes lined the store’s entrance, soaked by melting snow from shoppers’ boots. Shelves remained mostly well stocked, though the milk, ice cream, and frozen udon had been picked over.

Boston University sophomore Aidan Shen, who grew up in Los Angeles, said he and his Allston roommates were “not used to this weather at all.” They drove to the store Sunday to gather essentials and keep their pipes from freezing. “It’s definitely better to do it now than tomorrow, when grocery stores might be closed and people might not be able to get around,” he said, clutching a basket of rice, carrots, and ground meat.

City Hall and other Boston municipal buildings will be closed Monday. Trash and recycling collection will follow a modified holiday schedule. Mass General Brigham said hospitals will remain open with overnight accommodations available for staff.

title: Why stocks keep rising as the country rips itself apart
text:
Synergy Investments proposed converting an 11-story Downtown Crossing office building into 255 apartments in what would be the largest office-to-residential conversion yet in the city.

Seven people were killed when a private business jet crashed at Bangor International Airport in Maine on Sunday, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

Obamacare is now more expensive than the mortgage for these Americans.

The mood on Main Street is anxious. The frozen job market and the persistently high cost of living are the big culprits.

What’s more, there’s deep worry that democratic dysfunction has opened the door to authoritarianism — a fear stoked over the weekend by another killing of a protester in Minneapolis by federal agents.

But on Wall Street, optimism prevails, even if investors are occasionally rattled by presidential policy blunders such as undermining the Federal Reserve or alienating close allies with punitive tariffs.

Stocks are near record highs on the view that conflicts at home and abroad won’t derail the economy or erode US hegemony.

That view hinges on the durability of American exceptionalism — that the US economy and markets are uniquely resistant to long-term decline.

America will remain on top due to the country’s “unparalleled economic, human capital, and financial market strengths,” Goldman Sachs’s wealth management investment strategy group wrote in its recently released 2026 market outlook. Those traits, the authors said, are reinforced by “a system of checks and balances” and “remarkable resilience.”

Why it matters: Goldman, is one of the savviest financial firms in the world, and its annual market outlooks are closely watched by institutional investors managing trillions of dollars.

The firm says it’s offering a clear-eyed, nonpartisan assessment of the country’s economic and market prospects. Of course, Goldman and the rest of Wall Street make more money when their clients are bullish.

Still, understanding the reasons why money keeps flowing into stocks even as the world seems increasingly destabilized can help you make sense of the markets.

Step back: Fifty-six percent of registered voters believe the country is moving in the wrong direction, according to a New York Times/Siena poll released last week. Just 29 percent of respondents said the economy was in excellent or good shape.

Yet the Standard & Poor’s 500 on Friday was just 1 percent shy of its Jan. 12 record high. The index has climbed 15 percent since President Trump returned to the White House a year ago.

Goldman’s strategists acknowledge that after 2025’s chaos — tariff wars, a 21 percent market meltdown, and the longest government shutdown in history — some clients are asking whether it’s time to cut their US stock holdings.

No, they wrote, pointing to six previous periods since World War II when predictions of American decline proved wrong: after Sputnik in 1957, Vietnam and Watergate in the 1970s, Japan’s rise in the 1980s, the 2008-2009 financial crisis, and COVID in 2020.

It’s a fair point, though one could note that past recoveries don’t guarantee future ones.

The macro case: US preeminence will continue thanks to structural advantages that no presidential term can dismantle, according to Goldman.

America spends $940 billion annually on research and development — double China’s outlays, Goldman says. US labor productivity leads the world. The country has the deepest capital markets, the most Nobel laureates, and a culture that funds risk-taking without penalizing failure.

Moreover, the report argues the constitutional system is working — slowly, as designed — despite Trump’s efforts to erode the rule of law.

Courts have ruled against the administration in about one-third of the legal challenges to Trump’s executive actions, according to Goldman notes. The Senate rejected the Trump camp’s preferred candidate for majority leader. And state elections went against Trump-endorsed candidates from New Jersey to Florida.

The fundamentals: Trends for the primary drivers of the stock market — corporate earnings, economic growth, and interest rates — are positive, Goldman believes.

US equities aren’t in a bubble because valuations haven’t significantly deviated from fundamental earnings, the report contends. Elevated price/earnings ratios are supported by profit growth.

Worries about the high concentration of tech giants in the S&P 500 are overblown, the strategists wrote, because their profits justify the prices.

Goldman expects US earnings growth to nearly double that of other developed markets through 2030. It sees the Fed cutting interest rates by half a percentage point this year, and the economy growing by a solid 2.3 percent.

In the end, no other country rivals the US as an investment destination. That’s not just Goldman’s opinion, but a common tenet across the financial world.

To be sure: The US has real vulnerabilities, but Goldman argues they are manageable.

China has a chokehold on essential rare earth elements, but Western allies should be able to adapt over the “medium term.”

Rising government debt-to-GDP ratios must be monitored but aren’t at crisis levels.

Still, Goldman states plainly that “the greatest threat to US preeminence is an erosion of the country’s rule of law and system of checks and balances.”

After consulting constitutional scholars, Goldman’s analysts conclude both are holding — but the pace of executive orders (220-plus, triple that of any predecessor at this point in a term) is outstripping the speed at which courts and Congress can respond. The system works over months and years, not days.

Whether that lag creates lasting damage remains an open question.

Final thought: The market’s conventional wisdom is clear.

Tariff wars, foreign wars, and marauding Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents are bad. So is the ballooning federal deficit and Trump’s campaign to erode the country’s rule of law.

But, as Goldman argues, the center will hold and US exceptionalism will live on.

It’s an encouraging opinion. I hope it’s right.

“We are calling for an immediate deescalation of tensions and for state, local and federal officials to work together to find real solutions.”

— A letter released by the Minnesota Chamber of Commerce on behalf of more than 60 CEOs of Minnesota-based companies, after federal officers killed Alex Pretti on Saturday.

Help not wanted: Local employers added just 1,300 jobs in 2025 even after a modest pick-up in hiring in the final three months of the year, while the unemployment rate climbed to 4.8 percent from 4.1 percent.

By this point in the game, Brady has been an ambassador, strategic adviser, equity investor, official-user-of so many companies and products — Subway, Tag Heuer, IWC, Uggs, Aston Martin, Frito-Lay, FTX, Delta, Wheaties, Hertz, and so forth — that for the sake of space, it may be easier to list what he’s not involved with.

title: Boston digs out: Residents, work crews battle aftermath of historic snowstorm
text:
Southern New England was buried under 23 inches of snow during the storm, making it one of the region’s biggest in decades. The total ranked eighth on record and surpassed the Blizzard of 2005, when 22.5 inches of snow fell in Boston. Forecasters warned that bitter cold will continue through this weekend, limiting snowmelt, while meteorologists also monitored the potential for a nor’easter to develop late in the week.

In past winters, Boston has sometimes removed snow entirely from city streets, transporting it to designated snow farms, empty lots where it can safely melt. City officials have not yet confirmed whether similar measures will be used this year.

Boston Public Works deployed over 900 pieces of equipment to clear streets, Mayor Michelle Wu’s office said in a statement. Workers have focused on clearing intersections, crosswalks and curb ramps, and have coordinated with schools to keep bus routes open. Overnight snow removal operations continued Tuesday, with crews moving large piles to off-road locations. Space savers were set to be collected starting Thursday, along with regular trash collection, Wu’s office said.

Flynn said crews and contractors are limited in how long they can operate within a 24-hour period to ensure safety, noting that city officials have remained in close contact with the Public Works Department throughout the cleanup.

“Our city employees are doing a good job under very difficult circumstances,” he said. “It is the priority that we have to provide the necessary sleep for people that are plowing the streets and contractors. That’s also about public safety.”

The MBTA said service continued through the storm thanks to frontline workers, though delays and disruptions remain. Disabled trains and snow-related switch and signal problems affected the Red, Orange, and Blue lines, while the Green and Mattapan lines were running smoothly, the transit agency said. Many buses remained on snow routes Tuesday and paratransit service have been slowed by uncleared streets as crews continue snow removal efforts.

Similar snow removal efforts were underway in Cambridge on Tuesday, where the city deployed approximately 75 pieces of equipment since the start of the storm, and another 100 pieces were sent out via contractors, according to Jeremy Warnick, a Cambridge spokesperson.

Cambridge’s snow hauling operations began Tuesday night, taking snow to Danehy Park and, if needed, to a second location in Allston owned by Harvard University, Warnick said.

As cleanup continued, the impact of the storm remained visible on Boston’s streets.

In South Boston, plowed side streets were narrowed to single lanes, with parked cars nearly submerged beneath packed snow. Between vehicles, chairs, folding tables, and compost bins were pressed into service as space savers and dotted the curbside.

Sidewalks were even narrower, often incompletely cleared and blocked by snow piled at house entrances. Pedestrians clutched building walls to steady themselves on slick patches.

John MacDougall, a 26-year-old sales analyst and South Boston resident, opted to walk in the street rather than use the slippery sidewalk while returning to his C Street apartment from Stop & Shop.

“I just walked on the main roads, while cars are just blowing right by me,” he said.

MacDougall, who works remotely, said even short trips felt difficult after the storm. The grocery store is less than a mile from his apartment, but snow-covered sidewalks made the walk feel longer.

“The first day after the storm is pretty rough,” he said. “But getting people out here to clear these roads is dangerous for them, and I think they’re doing their best given the large amount of snow we got.”

A few blocks away on West Third Street, Brittani LeBlanc, 27, stood breathless after digging her Toyota Corolla out from a deep snowbank. Originally from Townsend, LeBlanc said she’s accustomed to winter weather, but this was her first major snowstorm living in the city.

“The hardest part is figuring out where to put it all,” she said.

“Somebody said to just put it on the street and they’ll come,” she added, “but I don’t know. I always feel bad doing that.”

LeBlanc said snow plows had passed regularly down her street for nearly 24 hours during the storm, though she had not seen them Tuesday. She credited her neighbors for doing a good job shoveling the sidewalk in front of their homes.

With another storm possible approaching, she offered simple advice.

“I definitely recommend to anybody who is parking to park in a garage spot,” she said, leaning against her open car door.

Flynn noted the importance of resident safety, particularly for seniors and people with disabilities. He urged residents to clear sidewalks, fire hydrants, and crosswalks to maintain access for pedestrians and emergency responders, and encouraged neighbors to help one another.

“And us neighbors help each other out,” LeBlanc said. “[My roommates and I] broke a shovel, and then somebody loaned us theirs.”

In Dorchester, similar scenes played out as snow plows passed through and residents shoveled sidewalks. A Public Works vehicle arrived on Gibson Street carrying salt, while a resident worked her way down the sidewalk clearing snow.

“You’ve got to help your neighbors,” she said.

Thomas McLaughlin, a 70-year-old retiree who previously worked in snow removal, treaded carefully along Gibson Street, noting it was “still hard to walk on” despite cleanup efforts.

“I’m very cautious because I don’t want to fall at this age and break anything,” McLaughlin said. “You take it for granted [that] it’s all soft and mushy, but it could be very slippery.”

Sunny Ortiz, a 27-year-old Roxbury resident who works for a commercial cleaning company, walked along Gibson Street toward a bus stop and said he had largely avoided public transportation due to delays.

Ortiz said he is grateful to the city’s street-clearing efforts.

“You don’t really want to wait 20, 30, 40 minutes for a train ride, so shout out to Mayor Wu,” he said. “The streets were still kind of clear, so I could go on the street and walk, [and] today, you could walk on the sidewalk.”

Ortiz said he had walked across much of Boston in recent days and didn’t mind seeing others enjoying the snow.

“We’ve got another one this week,” he said. “We’ll see how it is, just go day by day.”

title: Man charged with killing two at Carver birthday party called 911 immediately afterward, prosecutors say
text:
“Claims self-defense,” the dispatcher said.

Killed in the shooting were Jalen Pina, 20 and Benjamin Cowart, 27, prosecutors said. Two other men were wounded; their status Tuesday afternoon was not known.

Meuse told police he had been invited to the party but that “tensions flared” with some other guests over preexisting grievances, prosecutors said. Meuse said he saw one of the attendees reach for their waistband immediately before the shooting, prosecutors said.

Prosecutors said, however, that investigators found only a single gun at the club, a 9mm firearm with an illegible serial number.

Meuse is also charged with two counts of armed assault with intent to murder, two counts of attempted murder, and six firearms charges, according to court records.

His attorney did not immediately return a request for comment on Tuesday.

The birthday party was being held for a 7-year-old, one person in attendance told The Boston Globe. Dozens of guests, from toddlers to seniors, were at the club when Meuse allegedly opened fire shortly after 7 p.m.

Prosecutors said Meuse and the victims knew each other and that the shooting “was not a random act.” They did not say whether Meuse was related to any of the people he allegedly shot.

When officers arrived at the club, they found a desperate scene.

“We have a victim shot in the face, there seems to be another victim down,” a responder can be heard saying in a transmission. “Multiple victims. They need a couple of ambulances.”

Cowart was pronounced dead at the scene. Pina was taken to Beth Israel Deaconess Hospital in Plymouth, where he later died from his injuries, officials said.

A 28-year-old man was taken to Tufts Medical Center with injuries that were not life-threatening, and a 32-year-old man was taken to South Shore Hospital for undisclosed treatment.

Pina was a 2023 graduate of Middleborough High School, according to the school’s yearbook, and was voted “Most Musically Talented” as a senior. An aspiring rapper, he performed in Roxbury the day before his killing, according to his social media accounts.

An online fund-raiser said Pina’s stage name, “Buku Tensai,” means “a whole lot of greatness,” which organizers said “matched his soul.”

“Jalen was such a beautiful soul,” the appeal read. “A heart made of pure gold with a smile that could light up a room.”

Do Over Don’t, a Quincy recording studio, wrote on social media that Pina was “a pillar of our community.”

“Jalen was a soul that spread positivity and connected with many other creatives under our roof,” the studio wrote. “Many of our team members developed personal relationships with Buku outside of music over the years and we are blessed to have had him in our circle.”

Pina’s sister, Kayla Wells, wrote on social media Sunday that her brother’s death is “not making any sense.”

“I keep thinking this is a lie,” she wrote. “Some crazy dream I’m stuck in. I’m trying to wake up. But the truth is I am awake and you’re really gone.”

Pina was a cousin of the 7-year-old, she said.

Wells and other family members could not immediately be reached for comment.

Cowart, a 2016 graduate of Brockton High School, captained the football team his senior year, according to the Brockton Enterprise. In an all-scholastic profile that year, Cowart said his favorite player was Patriots tight end Chandler Jones and that he hoped to study sports management at Bryant or Merrimack universities.

“Benjamin was deeply loved and will always be remembered for his heart, his spirit, and the impact he had on everyone who knew him,” his family wrote in an online fund-raiser. “He brought light, laughter, and love into our lives, and his absence has left an ache that can never be filled.”

Material from previous Globe coverage was used.

title: Parents grapple with second day of school closures: ‘I’m looking at this as a safety measure’
text:
Cheryl Buckman, whose seventh-grade son attends Ruth Batson Academy in Dorchester, said she supported the decision to call off school for a second day.

Nearly 2 feet of snow dropped on Boston, and in her neighborhood, roads and sidewalks remained a sloppy mess, she said.

“There’s no way you can clear it all in one day,” Buckman said. “I’d rather they take the second day. I’m looking at this as a safety measure.”

Boston Public Schools have about 100 buildings to clean up before students return to school, and they need the time to do the work, she said.

Despite the time off, Buckman said her son hasn’t yet grown restless.

“He’s in seventh grade, you’d think he’d be locked into the electronics daily, but no, he’s been outside three times today,” Buckman said.

But for Eugenia Moorehead, a Nubian Square parent of two, the two-day closure made things difficult for her.

“We kind of depend on that school lunch,” Moorehead said. “I remember when we were kids, climbing over mountains of snow.”

“I don’t feel that this is worth it,” she said.

Moorehead said she also has neighbors asking her to watch their kids due to the snow day.

“People can’t afford this right now,” she said. “Child care and food, this is not OK.”

Moorehead’s son attends a school within walking distance, the Higginson/Lewis K-8, while her daughter goes to the much further Gardner Pilot Academy.

She’s confident she could’ve made it work, though.

“We would’ve gotten my baby to school,” she said. “I was born in Mission Hill, I went to school in Brighton, and we made our way to school.”

Jessica Thornton, a Beacon Hill mom, said she figures deciding to call a snow day must be a “difficult and nuanced decision.”

”It will hit some families much harder than others," she said in a text. “For us, I am pleased to have a snow day inside.”

Julianna Barrett, a Boston mother, weighed in on a Facebook post about the decision.

“Boston needs to be closed one more day it’s not safe and they have no where to stand for there buses, my child’s safety comes first!” she wrote.

A social media post by Newton school officials said, “we hate to miss the learning but are worried for student safety accessing sidewalks, schools and parking lots.”

Several parents responded, saying the decision made good sense to them considering the conditions of the roads Monday evening.

The superintendent of Reading Public Schools told families in an email Monday that he understands the decision isn’t “ideal” for them but the school grounds are not in a condition to safely open on Tuesday.

“Our DPW and Facilities teams have been working tirelessly around the clock on snow removal and site preparation, and we are incredibly grateful for their continued efforts and commitment to our schools,” Superintendent Tom Milaschewski wrote. “Despite this work, our buildings and surrounding areas are not yet in a position to open safely for students and staff tomorrow.”

“We recognize that additional closures are not ideal,” he continued. “However, the safety of our students, staff, and families remains our top priority and we must make decisions with that responsibility at the forefront.”

Milaschewski said he anticipated “a regular school opening on Wednesday.”

The situation was the same at Wakefield Public Schools, officials said in an email to families.

“The additional day will allow us to continue clearing and hauling snow away from parking lots and sidewalks to support a safe return for our students and staff,” the email said.

When calling a snow day, school leaders weigh many factors, such as timing and snow fall projections, progress on the cleanup of roads and sidewalks, and other factors.

They also have to consider the mandatory 180-day school calendar. Five snow days are built into the calendar. Any snow days over that limit have to be made up, usually at the end of the school year in June.

Some parents sparred on social media over whether a second snow day is a good or bad idea.

One commenter on Revere’s Facebook page assailed the decision to close for another day.

“This is ridiculous people have to go to work our kids need to be in school!” a poster said. “It’s not even snowing in the ’80s we would go to school in a blizzard this got to stop.”

Others balked at Bassett’s response.

“School isn’t daycare and it’s not the ’80s anymore,” one post said.

Shannon Larson of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Rachel Dratch heads to Broadway, and more news you might have missed
text:
On Feb. 21, Bostonians are stripping down for a good cause. The 2026 Cupid’s Undie Run, sponsored by the Children’s Tumor Foundation, will invite participants to run in their underwear to raise money for neurofibromatosis, a group of disorders that cause tumors to grow on nerve tissue across the body.

The run is more than a frigid round of exercise. Boston-based participants are invited to gather at noon at Lansdowne Pub where they will raise a glass for two hours before embarking on their (approximately) 1-mile run at 2 p.m. It’s been called “the pantless party with a purpose.”

Founded in 2010 by Brendan Hanrahan, Chad Leathers, and Bobby Gill, the first run took place in D.C. Leathers’ brother, one of the inspirations behind the run, was diagnosed with NF at 16 and became paralyzed in 2009. It was his brother’s story, among others, that pushed Leathers to be proactive in not only raising awareness about NF, but raising money to help find a cure.

Sixteen years later, Cupid’s Undie Run has grown into a nationwide event with more than 30 participating cities and raising $25.7 million since 2010. Just under a month out from this year’s run, Cupid’s Undie Run has already raised over $32K. Sign up as a runner or donate to a participant at join.ctf.org/event/2026-cupids-undie-run-boston/e705277.
