Writers invited to a weekend of literature and luxury

If you’ve always wanted to write a novel or screenplay, or even act in a film or play inspired by literature, a Boston staycation at the Mandarin Oriental hotel might be the launchpad for finally following your dreams.

From Feb. 27 to March 1, the hotel will debut what it’s calling “a literary and cinematic weekend experience. Local authors including Joseph Finder, William Martin, and Casey Sherman will be on hand, as will literary and casting agents. There will be panel discussions on plot, pacing, and getting published, along with many opportunities to share meals and cocktails, culminating in a special screening of “The Finest Hours,” a Hollywood product with deep Massachusetts roots.

The Globe recently published an ode to the mini-break, and increasingly hotels are providing fun programming to entice short-term visits. This one sounds positively delightful — it’s fair to say that it’s not cheap, though. According to the hotel, “the weekend experience is available beginning at USD 1,953 (excluding taxes and gratuity.) For reservations or more information, please call +1 (617)-535-8888 or email mobos-reservations@mohg.com.”

— Kate Tuttle

Rachel Dratch to star in ‘The Rocky Horror Show’ on Broadway

Get ready to do the Time Warp again, because “The Rocky Horror Show” is heading back to Broadway.

The latest revival of Richard O’Brien’s cult classic musical revealed its star-studded cast list this week, with Lexington native and former “Saturday Night Live” star Rachel Dratch joining the production as the show’s narrator. The Roundabout Theatre Company production is directed by Sam Pinkleton, who earned a Tony Award last year for his direction of “Oh, Mary!”, and stars Luke Evans, who makes his Broadway debut in the role of Frank-N-Furter.

Juliette Lewis will also hit the stage on Broadway for the first time as Magenta. Additional cast members include Tony nominees Andrew Durand as Brad and Amber Gray as Riff Raff, plus Oscar nominee Stephanie Hsu as Janet.

“The Rocky Horror Show” kicks off previews on March 26, with opening night slated for April 23 at Studio 54.

— Matt Juul

Jean Appolon Expressions celebrates new dance studio

Dance lovers braved the cold Tuesday to celebrate a ribbon-cutting at Jean Appolon Expressions’s new community space in Nubian Square. The new studio, dubbed the JAE Dance Center, is the Haitian dance company’s first permanent home.

“Having a physical home for JAE is more than a milestone, it’s the continuation of our aim to share movement that holds the power to heal, connect, and transform community,” artistic director Jean Appolon said in a statement. “We invite everyone, dancers, families, and neighbors, to make this space your own.”

The dance company said the new center, which is expected to be fully operational by winter of 2026, will host community dance classes, youth programs, and other offerings to local organizations and artists.

The new 2,800 square foot space was supported by the Mayor’s Office of Arts & Culture, the Barr Foundation, and New Atlantic Development, among others.

“We’re honored to support Jean Appolon Expressions in creating a new space that will contribute to the health and vitality of Nubian Square,” Mayor Michelle Wu said in a statement. “This ribbon cutting showcases what’s possible when we come together for the arts with sustained, meaningful attention and investment.”

— Malcolm Gay

title: Campaign over, Wu has to take on the messy work of running City Hall
text:
The pricey renovation of Franklin Park’s White Stadium as the new home of Boston’s women’s soccer team (a project I support) remains unpopular and under court challenge, awaiting a hearing before the Supreme Judicial Court.

It’s all a stark contrast from the heady days of a mere four months ago, when Wu walloped her well-financed opponent, Josh Kraft, by 49 points.

That race was largely driven by Wu’s fierce attacks on President Trump — conveniently, an old friend of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, Josh’s dad.

Right on schedule, the adrenaline jolt of the campaign trail has been replaced by the much more challenging day-to-day grunt work of running city government.

As the old saying goes, you campaign in poetry, you govern in prose.

Obviously, Wu remains a popular mayor. But popularity isn’t everything, and the problems are mounting.

Take Parcel 3, an 8-acre vacant lot in Roxbury that has been awaiting development for decades. Following a years-long community process, a popular development team, led by developer Tom O’Brien and Rev. Jeffrey Brown, was picked by the city to build on the parcel in 2023.

The plan included laboratory space, deeply affordable home ownership, and a cultural center that would house Embrace Boston, the social justice nonprofit best known for the “Embrace” statue on Boston Common depicting Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and Coretta Scott King.

Wu’s team clumsily announced the designation would be withdrawn later this month, with part of Parcel 3 to be offered up as the site of a new Madison Park Technical Vocational High School. Whatever isn’t needed for the new school will be offered for development at a later date, Wu has said.

Wu urgently needs a path out of her political problems in Roxbury, a community that is currently feeling seriously disrespected by City Hall.

Characteristically, she has insisted she has no intention of revisiting her decision. Bad idea.

Wu would be much better served by extending the designation for a year and working with the developers on a new plan that can be implemented in tandem with rebuilding the school. She insists her problem is with the plan, not the developers (O’Brien once toyed with challenging Wu in the last mayoral election). So why not work with them to find something that works?

More complicated is her tough relationship with leaders on Beacon Hill. Egged on by business leaders, who have resented Wu, with varying degrees of intensity, from day one, they have blocked many of her signature ideas, from tax relief to rent control to expanded free public transit.

Some of this is driven by centrist opposition to a progressive mayor’s politics. But just as much of it owes to Wu’s rocky relationships with leadership, including Senate President Karen Spilka and Governor Maura Healey.

Apparently, Team Wu’s current strategy is to challenge senators deemed as hostile. Former Wu aide Daniel Lander is running against veteran Will Brownsberger, while rumors continue to circulate Wu is seeking a candidate to oppose South Boston Senator Nick Collins, who has made a passion project out of killing her property tax proposal.

Collins, in particular, deserves the challenge. But even if successful, knocking off a couple of state senators won’t fix much. It could very well make even more enemies at the State House, where such challenges are always resented. Wu could gain two friends and make 10 more enemies in the process.

It’s important to note that Wu’s problems with State House leadership aren’t entirely her fault. Self-importance seems baked into these roles, along with an insulting belief that the mayor of Boston is some kind of subordinate. She is far from the first mayor to grapple with these relationships.

Still, the only real way forward for Wu is to find a way to mend some fences with Spilka and Healey because so many of her priorities run through Beacon Hill. That might not sound like fun for her, but dealing with adversaries is also basic politics. At some point, it becomes unavoidable.

Watching Wu during the campaign, it was clear that beating up on Trump and Josh Kraft was fun and invigorating. It also showcased Wu’s impressive political strengths. This year will be harder, with a different yardstick for success.

Welcome back to the grind, Mayor.

title: Community activist Monica Cannon-Grant to be sentenced for fraud ‘under the calculated guise of charity’
text:
In an appeal for leniency before learning her fate, Cannon-Grant told the judge she took ”full ownership” of her mistakes, but hoped she would also consider the good she had done for the community.

She told the judge she was “extremely proud” that, through her nonprofit, she had fed 80,000 people during the pandemic and helped others with rental assistance even while hers went unpaid.

The 44-year-old mother of six said it would have a devastating impact on her two youngest children, ages 4 and 7, if she were sent to prison, since they were already suffering from the tragic loss of their father.

Federal prosecutors had recommended an 18-month prison term for Cannon-Grant and portrayed her as a shameless fraudster who stole from people “under the calculated guise of charity,” according to a sentencing memo last week.

“A serious sentence in this case can restore faith in the system,” Assistant US Attorney Dustin Chao told the judge during Thursday’s hearing. “You don’t get to steal if you do good things. You don’t get a pass if you help the community.”

However, Cannon-Grant’s attorney, Emma Notis-McConarty, said it was important for the judge to recognize the good that she had done for so many people.

In a sentencing memorandum filed last week, the defense described her as “a loving mother, wife, and daughter who has dedicated her life to advancing social justice and serving communities in need.”

Cannon-Grant, who ran the nonprofit Violence in Boston Inc., pleaded guilty in September to 18 counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, mail fraud, and tax violations. In exchange, prosecutors agreed to dismiss nine counts related to allegations of mortgage fraud.

She was indicted along with her husband, Clark Grant, in 2022 on charges that they raised more than $1 million for their charity and received nearly $60,000 in pandemic relief funds to provide meals for people in need, but instead spent much of the money on themselves.

In March 2023, Clark Grant was killed in a motorcycle crash in Easton.

The initial indictment charged Cannon-Grant and her husband with three separate schemes: defrauding people who donated money to their nonprofit; illegally collecting an estimated $100,000 in pandemic unemployment benefits while she was working; and lying on a mortgage application.

Additional fraud charges were brought before Clark Grant’s death in 2023.

In 2019, Cannon-Grant’s nonprofit was awarded a $6,000 grant from the Suffolk district attorney’s office to take a group of at-risk young men to a retreat in Philadelphia.

Instead, prosecutors allege, Cannon-Grant and her husband used the money to take a vacation to Maryland, on dining at Bubba Gump Shrimp Co., Shake Shack, and other restaurants, and paying for car rentals, groceries, Walmart purchases, and visits to a Boston nail salon.

Cannon-Grant told the judge she grew up in deep poverty in Dorchester, with an abusive father, and frequently witnessed violence and crime.

She rose to prominence in 2020 after organizing a march in Franklin Park that drew thousands to protest the killing of George Floyd and other Black people at the hands of police. She formed a collaboration with a Dorchester restaurant to distribute more than 1,000 free meals a day to people struggling during the pandemic.

For those efforts, she was honored as a Bostonian of the Year by the Boston Globe Magazine and hailed as the city’s “best social justice advocate” by Boston Magazine.

She started her nonprofit in 2017, operating out of her Roxbury home, but by 2020, it had moved to a sprawling headquarters in Hyde Park.

Cannon-Grant’s lawyers estimated her “fraud-related conduct” involved about $224,000 in loss, and wrote that much of the money was used to “support underserved communities, families, and individuals” and advance social justice.

In a letter urging the judge to sentence Cannon-Grant to probation, Bishop William E. Dickerson II wrote that her organization “fed thousands of people during the Covid pandemic and hundreds of children received wonderful Christmas gifts.”

The death of Cannon-Grant’s husband “continues to be hell,” but she remarried last summer, her lawyers wrote.

Prosecutors allege that after Cannon-Grant collected nearly $400,000 from her late husband’s insurance policy, she made an urgent plea for donations to her GoFundMe account so she wouldn’t lose her home.

Yet, around the same time, prosecutors wrote, she spent almost $100,000 on travel and shopping, including $8,375 in purchases from Louis Vuitton, and trips to St. Thomas and Puerto Rico.

In court Thursday, Notis-McConarty said Cannon-Grant used the insurance policy money for funeral expenses and to support her family.

title: Can Boston still weather winter storms?
text:
In addition, the storm has strained or exhausted municipal snow budgets in Eastern Massachusetts. Officials in Framingham and Taunton, for example, now have exceeded their snow-removal budget for this winter, even as another storm is expected to strike the area this weekend.

One thing is certain: After several mild winters, the muscle, sweat, and community response needed to dig out from a big snowstorm have been tested anew, residents said.

“We need more plows on the road, a little more salt. There’s still a bunch of snow left over here and a bunch of snowbanks,” said Jay Jay Mosley, 30, of F Street. “All residents of Boston will appreciate it, especially here in Southie.”

In Cambridge, crews had already plowed all city-owned roadways and expected to complete sidewalk cleanup by the end of Thursday, spokesman Jeremy Warnick said Wednesday.

Nearly 200 pieces of equipment, including about 100 contracted units, were deployed during the storm, Warnick said. Overnight snow-hauling operations are expected to cost roughly $250,000 per night through at least Friday, he added.

Not everyone in Cambridge, however, could see a cleared street outside their windows.

Rob Yonkers, for one, still saw a storm-tossed sea of snow Wednesday, days after the biggest storm in four years had blanketed her side street in North Cambridge.

A city plow had come through Alberta Terrace only once, Yonkers said. And in its wake, cars had been buried in tall white bunkers, parking spaces vanished, and weary shovelers were forced to toss piles of travel-slowing snow into an already narrow road.

“A lot of the people on my street have given up, haven’t even tried to get their cars out anymore,” said Yonkers, a 30-year-old singer. “There’s just a huge snow pile in the street because no one knows where to put it.”

Following several years of mild winters, adjusting to a big snowfall can wreak havoc with the routine.

Where to toss the snow from driveways and sidewalks can be an awkward choice between courtesy and necessity. Patience wears thin all around. And public-works crews are prodding their muscle memory to stimulate old plowing skills.

“It’s like hit or miss,” Andrew Plifka, a 26-year-old South Boston resident, said of snow-removal efforts near his home on E Street. “Obviously, there’s a lot of snow, and there’s not many places for it to go. But the corners especially are pretty bad.”

Former Boston Mayor Marty Walsh said he recognizes the strain and challenges faced by both the city and its constituents in the aftermath of a big storm.

“It’s complicated, it’s hard, it’s not easy,” said Walsh, who lives in the Lower Mills section of Dorchester. “You have to think of a lot of things when a storm like this happens — canceling schools, plowing, emergency apparatus.”

“We’re watching the Patriots in the AFC Championship game” when the storm began Sunday, “and they’re out there working hard,” Walsh added.

Independent snow-removal contractors also have been helping residents dig out, including solo operators handling sidewalks, steps, and driveways in hard-hit neighborhoods.

Gabriel Ramos, a 27-year-old Malden resident, said he began clearing snow Sunday night and continued Monday as the heavy snowfall continued.

“I’m a one-man team,” said Ramos, an Army veteran who uses a snow blower and helped clear sidewalks, steps, small driveways, and cars.

Ramos, who works in IT, said snow removal is his winter side-job to earn extra money, and that residents appear to be adjusting to the irritation and inconvenience.

“I think everybody’s picking it back up again and getting used to the amount of snow that’s out there,” Ramos said. With another storm possible this weekend, the part-time snow warrior is prepared to take on more work.

The MBTA also has been plagued by slowdowns and interruptions, much to the dismay of commuters who have waited in bitter cold for less-frequent service.

At the Broadway station Wednesday, would-be riders huffed and grumbled after an announcement that the next Red Line train to Alewife would be delayed by nearly a half-hour because of a disabled train at JFK/UMass.

Among them was Jack Malespini, a 30-year-old who commutes to Massachusetts General Hospital. Service had been more reliable during the storm itself, he said, but delays had worsened since.

“Today is the worst for me,” Malespini said Wednesday.

But for some lifelong Bostonians, the scrambled routines and inconveniences of a big winter storm are to be expected in a traditional New England climate, all while warming temperatures might mean fewer of them occur.

“We’ve been walloped with the first significant snowstorm in four or five years, and maybe people forget about it a little bit,” said John Tobin Jr. of West Roxbury, a former Boston city councilor.

“I was out there shoveling and using muscles I hadn’t used, and didn’t realize I had, that had atrophied over the last four years,” Tobin said with a chuckle.

Overall, he added, the city’s cleanup seemed to go well.

“These men and women are out there busting their humps and are in their trucks for 12 and 14 hours at a time,” Tobin said. “It’s hard work.”

Amid the toil, and the dreary prospect of another round of digging, some residents looked ahead to reaping a reward on Feb. 8, when the New England Patriots face the Seattle Seahawks in the Super Bowl.

“Go, Pats!” Mosely, the South Boston resident, shouted as he shoveled. “Let’s go, Drake Maye. Let’s win a championship!”

title: Latin Academy won its 17th straight Boston City League swimming title, despite valiant O’Bryant effort
text:
Junior Jeremy Bradley wasn’t nervous going into Thursday’s Boston City League swimming championships. After all, Latin Academy had won the title 16 consecutive times, and this year was no different.

That composure showed in the pool at Madison Park High, where the Dragons extended their dynasty with a 17th city title in a row, scoring 120 points and winning six of the meet’s 11 coed events. O’Bryant (111 points) followed closely and East Boston (41) placed third.

“The whole energy on the Latin Academy swim team is so great that I think that’s the reason why we’re continuing to win,” Bradley said.

Bradley led the way with individual victories in the 50-yard freestyle (22.47 seconds) and the 100 free (49.59 seconds). He also contributed to wins in the 200 free relay (1:47.69) and the 200 medley relay (1:59.43), anchoring a balanced effort that Latin Academy coach Richard Mojica emphasized going into the meet.

“It was the team dynamic and the team that won that championship. Like I explained to them, ‘Jeremy can’t win the meet for you,’ ” Mojica said. “Second, third, fourth, those places are going to win.”

That proved true. Sophomore Marcus Ochoa won the 100 butterfly (1:03.97) by 10 seconds and took second place in the 200 free (2:11.99), and junior Kevin Anderson won the 100 breaststroke (1:13.18).

Bradley, who was named boys’ swimmer of the meet, said his development this season has been driven by technical and physical improvements under Mojica’s guidance.

“Specifically for the 50 freestyle, coach Richard has helped me work on it a lot, with my stroke. If you look at it from last year to this year, it’s completely new,” Bradley said.

Mojica pointed to Bradley’s development as emblematic of the program’s success.

“He started in lane six. He used to splash the officials when he dove in,” Mojica said. “His progression throughout the years, his focus on trying to get better, that was it. He went from being last to being first.”

O’Bryant kept it competitive, powered by junior Yiorgo Katsompenakis, who won the 500 free (6:06.69) and 200 free (2:08.81). Katsompenakis also helped anchor O’Bryant’s victory in the 400 free relay, keeping the pressure on Latin Academy.

“We got really close, the closest we have been in years, and we’re really proud that we’re working really hard,” Katsompenakis said.

O’Bryant also secured a win in the 100 backstroke courtesy of senior Carlita Rodriguez (1:09.68), who was named girls’ swimmer of the meet. Junior Dalyana Hamilton also took first in the individual medley (2:35.13).

title: As its budget struggles, Boston wants universities to contribute more money. Not all of them want to pony up.
text:
The $10 million ask was not a quid pro quo, but city officials knew their circumstances. Private real estate development that long buoyed the Boston budget has dried up, and the city needs new ways to bring in cash. Big-name universities and hospitals have deep pockets, they reasoned.

The question of how much colleges and hospitals contribute to the city budget is a long-running, dry, and often overlooked discussion on City Hall. But as both the city and its powerhouse institutions face financial struggles, it’s taking on added import. These backroom conversations raise a pressing question for the nation’s biggest college town: What does Boston owe its universities? And what do the universities owe Boston?

The answer started to dribble out in November, when Northeastern agreed to pay $2.6 million a year in cash and $37 million in community benefits by 2030, under Boston’s longtime “payment in lieu of taxation” program, or PILOT. Its terms are well below the initial $10 million ask, yet 40 percent more than the university previously paid.

In a press release, Mayor Michelle Wu touted the deal as a “new standard” for the wealthiest institutions at a time when “taxpayers need relief.”

It looks to be the first of several similar negotiations to squeeze more money from universities in Boston, ending a decade-long status quo where city officials rarely pushed nonprofits to boost their contributions.

For both the city and its schools, the stakes for PILOT have never felt so high.

Colleges are grappling with declining student enrollment and pressure from a White House targeting international students, controversial academic programs, and research funding that schools rely on to bolster the bottom line. Some have already eliminated staff positions and rolled back graduate and PhD enrollments to cut costs.

Boston University, for example, laid off 120 employees in July and offered buyouts to some tenured professors. It is now negotiating its cash and benefits contributions with the city. A spokesperson for BU said the school is “strongly supportive” of its partnership with Boston, but declined to comment on negotiations. In 2024, the university paid $18 million toward PILOT.

Universities argue higher payments would subtract from their “institutional capacity to support Boston’s most pressing needs” — including health care services, workforce training, and infrastructure investments, according to a December report from the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts.

Northeastern spokesperson Renata Nyul said the school made that point in its negotiations with City Hall.

“We emphasized that higher education is facing tremendous headwinds out of Washington,” she said. “And we appreciate the mayor’s team understanding those realities.”

But Boston can only afford to be so flexible. The city faces its second straight year of falling commercial property values, which fund a lion’s share of the $5 billion municipal budget. Projections show the value of office buildings and other commercial properties declining by 7 percent compared to the prior fiscal year.

The Wu administration — “stuck between a rock and a hard place” — is tapping every avenue for additional cash, said Travis McCready, an executive with real estate firm JLL who has previously worked for Harvard University and The Boston Foundation.

PILOT payments from 35 Boston nonprofit schools and hospitals power just one percent of the city budget. But many colleges are still adding dorms and classroom buildings that go untaxed.

“These decisions matter in the health and vitality of our city in this global economy,” McCready said. “These PILOT conversations have a gravitas to them that they just didn’t have 20 years ago.”

It might be less of an issue if universities did not own so much Boston land. Private nonprofits — of which colleges and hospitals are the largest — control nearly one-fifth of the city’s real estate value, according to a 2018 report from the Boston Municipal Research Bureau.

No school has grown quite like Northeastern.

Its real estate holdings in Boston have increased by 73 percent since 2000, from 5.1 million to 8.8 million square feet, according to institutional master plans filed with the city. Signs of that buildout abound: Northeastern’s futuristic six-story Interdisciplinary Science and Engineering Complex was hailed by architects as “the single most beautiful building” erected in Boston in 2017. New dorms have risen along Columbus Avenue, with another 23-story tower across from the Ruggles T station breaking ground last year. (On some of these projects, Northeastern has partnered with private developers, who do pay property taxes on the buildings.) And the university is rebuilding Matthews Arena into a pristine new athletics facility.

University leaders have long said the economic activity colleges generate far exceeds any costs the city recouped through the PILOT program. Colleges attract newcomers, create thousands of jobs, and give back to the city through myriad community benefits detailed in annual reports, they say.

In 2024, for example, Northeastern provided $32.2 million in grants and scholarships through city organizations, funneled $2 million toward upkeep for the Carter Playground in Roxbury, and paid for four co-op positions in the mayor’s office, among other contributions.

Taken together, Boston colleges created almost $1 billion worth of community benefits since 2018, according to a university trade group AICUM. Its president, Rob McCarron, said that sky-high figure excludes improvements that accompany all new construction, such as green space or sidewalks.

Before the early 2010s, Boston nonprofits simply struck one-off deals with the city assessor. That was when a committee formed by then-Mayor Thomas Menino created a formula where nonprofits contribute 25 percent of what their bill would be if their holdings were taxable.

Yet the PILOT agreements since are scarcely written down or signed. The requested contributions are based on real estate values assessed in 2009, and as payments are — and always have been — voluntary, city officials hold little leverage to ask for more. Already, most universities have ignored the Menino formula altogether, even as the scale and value of their real estate soars.

Now the city wants to craft five-year “bespoke agreements,” with each school, said Stephen Chan, senior adviser for partnerships at City Hall. They want the deals in writing and for community benefits to align with the city’s priorities.

The goal, a city spokesperson said in an email, is to “grow the PILOT program and establish a predictable schedule boosting annual community investment” — money that funds snow removal, road maintenance, and police dispatches.

To get there, the city is using whatever leverage it can. Both real estate leaders and higher education experts say the Wu administration tied Northeastern’s pricier PILOT deal to its new expansion plan. And a spokesperson for the Boston Planning Department acknowledged that a vote on that plan was delayed for several months while the city negotiated community benefits with the university and other stakeholders.

And the Northeastern deal pales in comparison to the revenue other cities have wrangled from universities, and to the amount paid by Boston’s nonprofit hospitals.

Yale University, for instance, paid New Haven, Conn., $135 million over five years after 2021, and Providence and Baltimore recently reached similar tax-replacement agreements with its colleges and hospitals.

“Boston being for all purposes a college town,” it should have “comparatively significant” PILOT revenue, said Davarian Baldwin, a professor at Trinity College in Hartford, Conn., who was involved in the New Haven negotiations. But “schools bully these cities because of the economics they bring.”

In May, amid Northeastern negotiations, 10 Boston community organizations signed a letter urging the university to do more, including increasing student housing and the money that flows into a fund that aims to reduce displacement in Roxbury — the latest chapter in a long-running battle between the school and activists decrying gentrification.

Armani White, lead organizer of the advocacy group Reclaim Roxbury, said he was “happy we have an agreement,” with a caveat.

“I feel like it doesn’t go far enough, but that is not necessarily on the mayor alone,” White said. “It is the university choosing not to give as much.”

Ultimately, the health of the city and the health of its universities are closely tied, and there’s only so far either side can push at the PILOT bargaining table. Jim Klocke, chief executive of the statewide advocacy group, the Massachusetts Nonprofit Network, said that as federal research funding flows away from Boston, leaving the region financially vulnerable, nonprofits can only afford payments to City Hall that are steady and still optional.

“There are giant rivers of research funding that have been cut off entirely,” he said. “It’s central to Boston and to societal goals like reducing illness, curing disease, and creating healthy communities around the world. How can we help each other navigate these waters together?”

title: From a lot of Masshole drivers to $1 million apartments: How a gas station’s demise represents a changing Boston
text:
In 1974, Morris’ son Stan moved the gas station to its current location, just a half-mile down Washington, and through the decades Hatoff’s became a Boston institution, sometimes serving drivers who belonged in one.

Cheap gas attracts, well, it just attracts, like flies to a light.

When I learned from Adam Gaffin’s terrific local news site Universal Hub that Hatoff’s was headed for the great cheap gas station heap in the sky, I jumped in my Subaru Crosstrek, still in my flannel pajamas and OluKai slippers, and drove from rural Vermont to the urban mecca of cheap gas, flooring it through Egleston Square, worried the pumps would be dry by the time I got there.

Alas, they weren’t. There is no official closing date. And it was impossible to tell if this was one last mad dash to Hatoff’s, because it was its usual crazy self. Like an open air market in one of those Indiana Jones movies, where anything can happen at any time, and probably will.

Drivers often approach a pump with their gas tank on the other side of their vehicle. This results in some drivers pulling three-point turns, to get their gas tanks lined up with the pumps, in a very tight space. This necessitates the kind of driving usually associated with the bumper cars at Canobie Lake Park.

But, still, it’s kind of amazing to observe the intricacy of the creative thinking and driving, like watching a ballet or a symphony, if the ballerinas, oboe players, and violinists were Masshole drivers.

I strategically placed my car at Pump 12, in the lane closest to Washington Street, facing Egleston Square, so I could make a quick getaway.

But, it turns out, Pump 12 was the slowest gas pump ever made. Pump 12 was eking gas with a velocity normally associated with pouring maple syrup on pancakes. It took forever. Well, it felt like forever, and it was frickin’ freezing.

Standing there, shivering in the cold, executing a fill-up with the speed of donating a pint of blood, I looked around Hatoff’s. In a city that is still very segregated, it may be the most integrated spot in Boston. There’s every kind of people, color, creed, city folk pumping good music, suburbanites pumping cheap gas.

Because everybody, no matter what they look like, no matter where they’re from, likes a bargain. And Hatoff’s remains a bargain when it comes to gas in the city.

After filling up, I drove down Centre Street in JP and noticed that Gibbs and JP Oil were selling gas for less than many places in the city, but not nearly as cheap as Hatoff’s.

Hatoff’s is slated to become — take a wild guess — housing. The $90 million project is aimed at building 230 apartments, the same kind of fate that engulfed the late and lamented Doyle’s, just blocks down Washington from Hatoff’s.

Doyle’s was a neighborhood tavern that dated back to the 1880s and was one of JP’s most enduring institutions.

It was depressing, frankly, thinking back to a Doyle’s where we toasted holidays and late friends from the Globe newsroom; where when my kids were young we met Cathy Mayo, a great JP lady, and her adopted son, Delmace, a disabled Haitian kid who grew up to become an elite para-athlete; where over all those years we shot the breeze with Gerry Burke Sr., the longtime proprietor of Doyle’s, who in the 1980s became the first publican to sell Sam Adams Lager.

Jim Koch, the Sam Adams founder, had just opened a craft brewery at the old Haffenreffer brewery on Amory Street. Gerry and Jim cut some JP kind of deal.

Doyle’s had the best collection of political memorabilia in the city. You’d half expect to see James Michael Curley, Kevin White, Ray Flynn, Tom Menino, and Marty Walsh come through the front door, arm in arm, as all those mayors, not to mention their coatholders, spent more than a little time in Doyle’s.

Doyle’s hosted more politicians and would-be politicians, the famous and the infamous, than any place in Boston, right up there with the Eire Pub in Adams Village in Dorchester.

Alas, that great JP bar where you could get a Pickwick Ale for short money is long gone, replaced by wood framing and blue tarp. The whole block is going to be transformed into 29 condominiums. Starting price? Well over $1 million. Six of the apartments are deemed “affordable.”

But, then, what the heck is affordable in the city of Boston?

It was a great relief to drive by the next block from Doyle’s and see the Midway Cafe is still going strong. Live music, great local musicians, good crowd. The Midway is JPAF, which means JP as ... well, I can’t print the rest.

There are places like the Midway and Hatoff’s and Doyle’s and, further afield, Simco’s, the hot dog kings in Mattapan, Sullivan’s on Castle Island, J.J. Foley’s in the South End, where the bartenders still wear ties, so many other places in Charlestown, Brighton, Allston, Roxbury, Dorchester, Beacon Hill, Hyde Park, Back Bay, Roslindale, West Roxbury, and East Boston that define neighborhoods and traditions. And with increasing regularity, the places that defined neighborhoods are giving way to condos and apartments.

The city’s biggest need, housing, is the biggest driver of change, and maybe that’s the way it has to be, the way it’s always been, the way it always will be.

But there’s also something to be said about losing the things and places and people that made Boston distinctive, neighborhoods that were ethnic and assimilated, places where people who don’t look like each other can, if only briefly, interact with civility and even joy, places where Joe and Nemo’s was valued over McDonald’s, where Vietnamese guys still fish off the pier on Castle Island while Southie guys in scally caps and hoodies walk by nodding approvingly.

It’s neither sad nor happy. It’s just what it is.

Cities change. Even Boston. Things change.

title: A day inside the Massachusetts department overseeing SNAP
text:
The changes could further strain an already overwhelmed system: Of the nearly 15,000 calls made on average each day to DTA in November, nearly 4,500 were unable to connect, according to DTA’s own statistics. Another 7,000 were answered by a voice assistant, and just under 3,000 people were connected to a call center.

Dany Rodriguez, a 41-year-old DTA caseworker, tries not to focus too much on the politics, or how overwhelming the need is. “I just want to help clients,” said Rodriguez, who has been at the agency for five years and handles about 220 clients who use SNAP, cash benefits, or both. “I want to be there for them, to support them.”

Rodriguez started her morning taking calls from clients. Some, she would be able to help. For many others, the needs were too great, and the problems too deep: decades of homelessness, persistent health issues, unemployment, economic marginality. Rodriguez could try, but she was limited by the tools at her disposal.

First, there was a woman who wanted to know if she could get part of her gas bill covered for the winter. Like many SNAP recipients, she works as a personal care attendant, and with her wages low — around $17-$22 an hour — she was finding the bill “is too much, I can’t do that.” Rodriguez replied that the application for the state’s Home Energy Assistance Program, which can cover winter heating bills for some low-income households, was already in the mail. The woman thanked her profusely.

Rodriguez went to call a mother of three, taking a deep breath before dialing the number. She had to tell the client that she was no longer eligible for a cash assistance program DTA oversees, since she now makes about $2,000 a month as a cleaner. Even with the income, the mother is financially strapped: She pays $600 a month for rent, plus $780 a month in child care. Her income is so low she’ll continue to receive $994 in SNAP, the max for a family of four.

Next, Rodriguez called a client to recertify his application, something all SNAP users are required to do every six to 12 months. Despite having an appointment, he didn’t pick up. The man is homeless, bouncing between family members. He’s also disabled. Rodriguez wasn’t surprised he missed the call. She rescheduled his appointment and mailed a notice to his mom’s house. If he doesn’t get back to her within 30 days, his case will close and he’ll have to reapply.

Through each phone call, Rodriguez remained composed. She never slouched, her breathing was steady. In over three hours, she took just one sip from her pink Stanley water bottle and didn’t touch the granola bar on her desk. Throughout the morning, she toggled between three screens, keeping color-coded calendar reminders as notes to herself alongside an unwieldy client database.

The Jackson Square office where Rodriguez works is new, created to take some of the workload off the much larger Nubian Square office just a couple miles down the road. One staffer described the client load there as a “deluge.” Just over one-quarter of the 34,454 people who visited a DTA office in November did so because they otherwise could not get through to staff.

Late morning, Rodriguez saw her first in-person client.

The visit was unexpected. The man showed up at reception, said he had been calling and had not gotten through. His case had been closed in October, when he started making too much money to receive any cash benefits. He still received some SNAP, though just $24 a month.

“What am I going to do, buy candy?” he told the receptionist, who popped her head into Rodriguez’s office. “I just want to give you a heads up,” she said. ”He’s mad!”

Rodriguez quickly reviewed his case, cross-referencing his name with work numbers shared by several agencies and employers. The man started working for a moving company in August where he was slated to have 40-hour work weeks at $22 an hour. But often, he only logged 20 hours, sometimes as few as six.

After sitting down in a corner chair, the client explained he lost his job just after Christmas and was now living in a shelter. He wanted to apply for cash benefits again. Rodriguez explained he had to first apply for unemployment, and only if that’s denied could he apply for cash benefits. He would need a termination letter and a new designation of disability from a doctor. On the other hand, without any income, his SNAP would go up, to $298 a month.

Rodriguez has an unusually intimate window into her clients’ lives. With this client, she learned about how his disability makes holding a job nearly impossible, which embarrasses him. When calling another client, she could hear the din of busy Boston outside: the rev of buses, the rush of traffic. She asked if anything had changed in his life. “Same situation financially, same situation, staying with family. I am still homeless.” She asked if he has any other income. “No. I wish.”

Chatting at the end of their call, the client asked whether it’s true that people can no longer use SNAP to buy sweets. “I don’t buy any myself, but you’re telling a mom you can’t buy her kids cookies?”

Rodriguez answered plainly, “We haven’t received any instructions about that.”

She has seen how news about SNAP changes can impact her clients. In the last year, she noticed fewer people coming to the office — many of Rodriguez’s clients are immigrants. “They’re afraid just to even walk out of their house,” she said.

“I love what I do,” she continued. “The political piece is something else. I try to avoid it.”

Rodriguez turned back to her computer, and clicked through her database, to see who needed help next.

This story was produced by The Boston Globe’s Money, Power, Inequality team, which covers the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston. You can sign up for the newsletter here.

title: Mayor Wu kicks off the 100th Black History Month in Boston in a yearly celebration
text:
Mayor Michelle Wu marked the start of Black History Month on Tuesday with the City of Boston’s annual celebration at City Hall, marking 100 years of Black History Month with speeches, performances, and a flag-raising that drew nearly 100 attendees.

Held on the third-floor mezzanine, the midday event transformed City Hall with a black, red, yellow, and green balloon arch framing the podium as people gathered to reflect on Boston’s past and future.

“Our history is being erased,” said Antonia Edwards, the community engagement chair for the city’s Reparations Task Force. “Any event that outlines [our history] is really a feather in a cap.”

According to the Association for the Study of African American Life and History the history of Black History Month dates back to February 1926, when Carter G. Woodson officially announced the second week of February dedicated to black history. Woodson was the second African American to earn a PhD from Harvard University. Fifty years later in 1976, the week officially became a monthlong commemoration to recognize the achievements, struggles, and contributions of Black Americans.

Janis McManus, an educational consultant and descendant of formerly enslaved people on both sides of her family, said that because of Boston and Cambridge there is a Black History Month because Woodson got the idea while working on his PhD at Harvard.

“You can study something every day in Black history,” McManus said.

The program began with opening remarks from Lori Nelson, the city’s senior adviser on racial justice, followed by a performance of the Black National Anthem, “Lift Every Voice and Sing,” by Zakiyyah, an artist and activist-scholar.

The Rev. Willie Bodrick II, senior pastor of Historic 12th Baptist Church, then led a prayer before delivering an impassioned address that drew repeated applause. During his speech he called for equity and justice for Boston’s Black community.

“Black history will save us,” Bodrick said.

Bodrick’s words touched Denise Washington, a lifelong Roxbury resident and an educator for Boston Public Schools.

“The part of the speech where he said, ‘We’re Black history’, resonated with me a lot,” Washington said. “History is today, it was yesterday, and it’s the future. We are history.”

Wu followed, acknowledging her colleagues before reflecting on Boston’s role in Black history. Referencing Sarah Roberts and the city’s legacy of segregated schools, Wu reminded the audience that “separate was never equal.” She also invoked the work of Martin Luther King Jr.

“This month should be a reminder of all that we have come through,” Wu said during her speech.

Amanda Shea recited her poem “Black Excellence,” the Black History Month flag was raised on City Hall Plaza. Afterward, the mayor read a proclamation officially declaring February 2026 as Black History Month in Boston.

For Rashad Morrison, an employee at the city’s equity and inclusion cabinet, the performances were the highlight.

“I really appreciated all the performances,” Morrison said. “It really captured the kind of essence of Black History Month.”

The event concluded with a reception, where attendees gathered over food and continued conversations. Edwards said moments like these are critical reminders of the realities behind Black history.

“We didn’t come here on our own,” Edwards said. “We just need as many allies as possible to acknowledge what happened.”

title: Trump’s $45 billion expansion of immigrant detention sites faces pushback from communities
text:
A proposed ICE facility just north of Richmond, Virginia, drew hundreds of people last week to a tense public hearing of the Hanover County Board of Supervisors.

“You want what’s happening in Minnesota to go down in our own backyard? Build that detention center here, and that’s exactly what will happen,” resident Kimberly Matthews told county officials.

As a prospective ICE detention site became public, elected officials in Kansas City, Missouri, scrambled to pass an ordinance aimed at blocking it. And mayors in Oklahoma City and Salt Lake City — after raising concerns about building permits — announced last week that property owners won’t be selling or leasing their facilities for immigration detention.

Meanwhile, legislatures in several Democratic-led states pressed forward with bills aimed at blocking or discouraging ICE facilities. A New Mexico measure targets local government agreements to detain immigrants for ICE. A novel California proposal seeks to nudge companies running ICE facilities out of the state by imposing a 50% tax on their proceeds.

More than 70,000 immigrants were being detained by ICE as of late December, up from 40,000 when Trump took office, according to federal data.

In a little over a year, the number of detention facilities used by ICE nearly doubled to 212 sites spread across 47 states and territories. Most of that growth came through existing contracts with the U.S. Marshals Service or deals to use empty beds at county jails.

Trump’s administration now is taking steps to open more large-scale facilities. In January, ICE paid $102 million for a warehouse in Washington County, Maryland, $84 million for one in Berks County, Pennsylvania, and more than $70 million for one in Surprise, Arizona. It also solicited public comment on a proposed warehouse purchase in a flood plain in Chester, New York.

Federal immigration officials have toured large warehouses elsewhere, without releasing many details about the efforts.

“They will be very well structured detention facilities meeting our regular detention standards,” ICE said in a statement, adding: “It should not come as news that ICE will be making arrests in states across the U.S. and is actively working to expand detention space.”

State and local governments can decline to lease detention space to ICE, but they generally cannot prohibit businesses and private landowners from using their property for federal immigrant detention centers, said Danielle Jefferis, an associate law professor at the University of Nebraska who focuses on immigration and civil litigation.

In 2023, a federal court invalidated a California law barring private immigrant detention facilities for infringing on federal powers. A federal appeals court panel cited similar grounds in July while striking down a New Jersey law that forbade agreements to operate immigrant detention facilities.

After ICE officials recently toured a warehouse in Orlando, Florida, as a prospective site, local officials looked into ways to regulate or prevent it. But City Attorney Mayanne Downs advised them in a letter that “ICE is immune from any local regulation that interferes in any way with its federal mandate.”

Officials in Hanover County also asked their attorney to evaluate legal options after the Department of Homeland Security sent a letter confirming its intent to purchase a private property for use as an ICE processing facility. The building sits near retail businesses, hotels, restaurants and several neighborhoods.

Although some residents voiced concerns that an ICE facility could strain the county’s resources, there’s little the county can do to oppose it, said Board of Supervisors Chair Sean Davis.

“The federal government is generally exempt from our zoning regulations,” Davis said.

Despite court rulings elsewhere, the City Council in Kansas City voted in January to impose a five-year moratorium on non-city-run detention facilities. The vote came on the same day ICE officials toured a nearly 1-million-square-foot (92,903-square-meter) warehouse as a prospective site.

Manny Abarca, a county lawmaker, said he initially was threatened with trespassing when he showed up but was eventually allowed inside the facility, where a deputy ICE field office director told him they were scouting for a 7,500-bed site.

Abarca is trying to fortify Kansas City’s resistance by proposing a countywide moratorium on permits, zoning changes and development plans for detention facilities not run by the county or a city.

“When federal power is putting communities on edge, local government has a responsibility to act where we have authority,” he said.

Kansas City is looking to follow a similar path as Leavenworth, Kansas, which has argued that private prison firm CoreCivic must have an operating permit to reopen a shuttered prison as an ICE detention facility.

As other ICE proposals have surfaced, officials in Social Circle, Georgia, El Paso, Texas, and Roxbury Township, New Jersey, all have raised concerns about a lack of water and sewer capacity to transform warehouses into detention sites.

Nationally, it remains to be seen whether local governments can effectively deter ICE facilities through building permits and regulations.

“We’re currently in a moment where it is being tested,” Jefferis said. ”So there is no clear answer as to how the courts are going to come down.”

The Democratic-led New Mexico House on Friday passed legislation banning state and local government contracts for ICE detention facilities, sending it to the Senate. Similar bills are pending in Hawaii, Massachusetts, New York and Rhode Island.

The Otero County Processing Center, 25 miles (40 kilometers) from downtown El Paso, Texas, is one of three privately run ICE facilities that could be affected by the New Mexico legislation. The facility includes four immigration courtrooms and space for more than 1,000 detainees. The county financed its construction in 2007 with the intent to use it as a revenue source, and plans to pay off the remaining $16.5 million debt by 2028.

Otero County Attorney Roy Nichols said the county is prepared to sue the Legislature under a state law that prevents impairment of outstanding revenue bonds.

Republicans warned of job losses and economic fallout if the legislation forces immigrant detention centers to close.

But Democratic state Rep. Sarah Silva, who voted for the ban, and said her constituents in a heavily Hispanic area view the ICE facility as a burden.

“Our state can’t be complicit in the violations that ICE has been doing in places like Minneapolis,” Silva said. ”To me that was beyond the tipping point.”

title: Kicking off the Olympics
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

Boy, do we need some joy these days. Fortunately, the Winter Olympics kicks off on Friday — and if you haven’t been paying attention, the Globe’s Matt Porter can help.

David Beard: Is the most common question you’re asked “Will this be the first US men’s hockey team since the 1980 ‘Miracle on Ice’ squad to emerge with a gold medal?” What are the chances for the men’s and women’s teams, and will two or three names be on our lips before this is over?

Matt Porter: This is the most talented men’s Team USA since 2002, when they won silver in Salt Lake. Going in, I’ll take the Americans’ defense and goaltending over Canada’s incredible forwards. It might not matter if Connor McDavid decides to take over. Similar idea on the women’s side. The US has had Canada’s number lately, and has the better team on paper, but Marie-Philip Poulin is the tournament’s most dangerous player. Two of Team USA’s best were raised in the Merrimack Valley: Jack Eichel, one of the NHL’s elite centers, and Caroline Harvey, a game-changing defender and possible No. 1 overall PWHL draft pick.

Lindsay Vonn, Lindsay Vonn: Can she do it, and what other skiers should we follow?

Vonn’s comeback is astounding. A gold-medal contender at age 41? Following a partial knee replacement? And a five-year retirement? She was looking ready — but last Friday’s crash at an Olympic tune-up in Switzerland leaves her status in doubt. Another one of the all-time greats, Mikaela Shiffrin, was favored in Beijing but landed nowhere near the medal podium. She was left with PTSD after a nasty crash 14 months ago. She looks excellent heading into Cortina. In cross-country, Wakefield’s Jessie Diggins, 34, aims for gold in what she says will be her last Olympics. And I’m always mesmerized by what the free skiers are doing. I could watch them all day.

Are there quirky sports we’ll be entranced with this time around? Bobsled and luge? Curling?

Curling will never beat the “shuffleboard on ice” rap, and why try? If you like taking a nap while watching golf, try it. The existence of the biathlon makes me wonder why they never tried horseback archery in the Summer Olympics. Sometimes I think I could do the skeleton if given the chance. Then I remember that I am made of bones.

Are there 1-2 amazing Olympians whose stories you already know we’ll be enraptured by? New Englanders to watch?

Not sure if or how much the Americans will be booed in Milan, but the skating world is rooting for 24-year-old Max Naumov. He made his first Olympic team less than a year after both of his parents (who were also his coaches at the Skating Club of Boston) were killed in a plane crash. Triumph over tragedy is a common Olympic story. Naumov has the chance to write one of the more memorable ones. (More New England Olympians to watch here.)

How long have you covered winter sports, and where’d you start?

It was November 2000, and my editor assigned me, a high school junior, to cover Gloucester High girls’ hockey. I didn’t want readers to know that my twin sister, Ashley, was on the team. Can’t play favorites. If I was writing about us, I would have mentioned that we started skating at age 2 and skiing at age 3 and had been in love with winter sports ever since. In the last 25-odd years, I have covered games and the people who play them in four seasons and on three continents. I’ve worked at roughly a couple hundred hockey rinks and played at a few dozen. title: One-third of BPS seniors risk not graduating high school in June
text:
It is unclear exactly how many of the students missing core classes could be prevented from graduating. Some schools and students are exempt from the MassCore requirement, such as those in vocational career programs, which is not reflected in the district data.

Boston added the core classes requirement after a 2019 study found graduates who completed the curriculum had far better odds of earning a college degree than those who did not. Around the same time, the Globe reported that even many of the district’s valedictorians failed to complete college, in part due to being underprepared academically. Some critics at the time warned that the requirement could instead lower high school graduation rates and wreak other damage.

The MassCore sequence includes four years of English and math; three years of science and social studies; two years of world languages; one year of the arts; and five electives. Prior to adopting MassCore, graduation requirements varied widely across the district’s dozens of high schools.

Absent action from the mayor-appointed School Committee, many Boston seniors who have failed to complete the MassCore standards will have to earn additional credits in summer school to graduate or return as fifth-year seniors next year.

Suleika Soto, 39, who has two children in Boston Public Schools, said Boston’s MassCore results show students are not getting enough resources to succeed academically.

“I really do feel like they’re setting up our poor kids for failure, which will impact them in their real life,” said Soto, who is an education advocate and college student in the South End. “There’s going to be a negative impact to them.”

Mary Tamer, executive director of the nonprofit education organization MassPotential and a former School Committee member under Mayor Thomas Menino, said the MassCore results are part of a broader problem regarding lagging academic outcomes in BPS, including MCAS scores and achievement gaps.

“It’s a failure of a proportion that is stunning, and why this is not being discussed at every single School Committee meeting is beyond me,” Tamer said of Boston’s student outcomes. “What are we doing for six-and-a-half hours a day when [the] majority of our students are not on grade level?”

In a statement, district spokeswoman Samara Pinto said the number of on-track seniors “will continue to increase as our seniors have opportunities in the coming months to complete required courses.”

“Boston Public Schools is committed to offering courses to our secondary schools that are aligned with MassCore,” Pinto said. “BPS is focused on reducing the opportunity and the achievement gap among racial and cultural student groups.”

MassCore completion rates vary dramatically by race and other characteristics.

Among last year’s graduating class, before the requirement kicked in, more than 60 percent of white and Asian students took all the required classes, compared with about 40 percent of Black, Latino, and low-income students, and students with disabilities and just one-quarter of English learners. Data released by the district last fall showed similar patterns continuing with the class of 2026.

Completion rates also varied wildly from school to school last year. At Charlestown High School, for example, just 15 percent completed MassCore, compared to 87 percent at Josiah Quincy Upper School in Chinatown.

Even the prestigious exam schools didn’t consistently get all students through the courses: Roxbury’s Boston Latin Academy reported a 93 percent completion rate, but the John D. O’Bryant School of Mathematics and Science, also in Roxbury, reported just 25 percent completion.

Ursula Allston, whose 16-year-old daughter attends Boston Day and Evening Academy, said she was heartbroken to learn of the district’s MassCore results. The state is a Mecca for education, Allston said, but BPS students are not benefiting from those resources.

“People come from all over the world to go to our colleges, and our kids within the BPS system can barely even get accepted or looked at because of the type of education that they received,” Allston said. “And I don’t understand how we are failing these kids this bad.”

John Mudd, a former member of the district’s English Learners task force, said the results for English learners underscored the failure to offer adequate support for those students in Boston.

“We’re cutting the legs out from under their ability to become productive members of society and support their families,” Mudd said. “We continue to undercut their opportunity to learn.”

Boston’s MassCore success rate had risen gradually from 2020 to 2024, hitting 50 percent for the first time in 2024. But the completion rate fell last year to 46 percent.

The district has said the school day schedule at many of the city’s high schools makes it difficult for students to complete MassCore.

More than half of the district’s high schools have six-period schedules, which only allows 24 units of study over four years. That is barely enough time during a student’s high school career to squeeze in enough MassCore-compliant classes before they graduate, the district said in a May 2025 briefing.

The schedule is set in part by the district’s collective bargaining agreement with its teachers. The latest contract, approved in the spring, included a process to move away from a six-period schedule and fit in more classes by the 2026-2027 school year, according to the district.

BPS declined to say exactly how many students could be prevented from graduating. Certain English learners and students with disabilities are also exempt from the requirement, as are the district’s alternative high schools for off-track students.

Boston’s district-level graduation requirement is distinct from the former statewide requirement that students pass the Grade 10 MCAS requirement, which voters abolished in 2024. It’s also distinct from the local measure the School Committee adopted in October to replace the MCAS, requiring at least a D- grade in five courses.

Boston’s MassCore outcome comes up short compared to peer districts such as New Bedford and Worcester, where high schoolers have near-perfect completion rates for those districts’ required courses.

In Worcester, a districtwide goal of increasing academic rigor has helped students complete the MassCore requirement, said Emily Lehman Miller, the district’s interim head of college and career readiness. For example, she said, the district allows students to count relevant college classes they’ve taken toward MassCore, adding flexibility.

As in Boston, some Worcester schools have had trouble fitting all of MassCore into their schedules. But with the district’s strategic goal of increasing rigor, administrators have reworked their schedules to fit in the needed courses.

“Schools are dealing with so many competing priorities,” she said. “Where are the hard choices going to come in because this is a priority?”

In New Bedford, which has 100 percent MassCore completion rate, the district added a series of other programs to help lay a foundation for its graduates attending — and succeeding in — college, Superintendent Andrew O’Leary said.

That includes offering more early college classes and encouraging more students to take PSAT and SAT exams and Advanced Placement courses to prepare them for college coursework.

“It’s an alignment of the expectations around MassCore,” O’Leary said.

Prior to MassCore’s adoption, BPS’s graduation rate had been on a long-term rise, from under 60 percent before 2009 to about 80 percent in recent years. But the district’s college enrollment rate has declined post-COVID after years of stagnation. Leaders have pointed to MassCore as one route to boost student success after graduation.

BPS leaders pushed for MassCore for more than a decade, with former superintendent Tommy Chang as far back as 2015 incorporating it into a plan to boost academic rigor. In 2021, in the depths of COVID, former superintendent Brenda Cassellius pushed the requirement through, with a five-year phase in, in the wake of a scathing state review of the school system. Cassellius declined to comment for this story.

Just one member of the School Committee at the time, Lorna Rivera, voted against it.

“Whenever we raise standards and adopt more rigorous curriculum, there are unintended consequences, collateral damage, such as higher dropout rates and lower graduation rates for the students who are most disadvantaged,” she said.

title: Hazmat team responds to Roxbury apartment building, residents briefly evacuated
text:
Residents of a Roxbury apartment building were briefly evacuated Thursday evening after firefighters arrived to investigate a of a “strange odor,” according to Boston fire.

A hazardous material team also responded to the building at 2465 Washington St., the department said.

The building was temporarily evacuated while firefighters worked to determine the source of the odor, the department said.

“Companies found a leak in the garage stairwell and determined this was the source of the smell,” Boston fire said.

Residents were allowed to go back inside after firefighters found the source and determined that it was safe, Boston fire said.

No injuries were reported.

title: Six years ago, winless Dedham had just three wrestlers on its roster. Now it’s in the mix for a D3 title.
text:
Six years later, there are two different Heaslip brothers wrestling, and the Marauders (16-4) are a frontrunner to win Division 3 states.

“I was never handed anyone who was good before. Every single person I’ve coached, it’s been personal,” Heaslip said. “I’ve seen them grow. Watching them grow is huge. [Some other coaches] can get a state championship team just like that.

“Completely rebuilding the program from scratch is what’s special to me. It’s because of me. I take some pride in that.”

Since 2009, at least one of eight Heaslip brothers has been in the Dedham varsity wrestling lineup, and there are more to come. Senior captain Falco (25-7 at 165 this season, 101-60 career) and freshman Rudolf (144 pounds) are the current entries.

“It’s not too much different except for the fact that [Finbar’s] my coach all the time instead of only in the wrestling room,” said Falco. “I come home and I still have my coach there. He’s telling me what to do. I’m grateful to have the extra time for wrestling.”

The Marauders enjoy back-to-back bulldozers in senior captains Ryan Talon-Kelly (25-2 at 132) and Manny Garcia (37-1 at 138). Talon-Kelly missed the better part of the past two years due to multiple injuries, but he worked with Garcia and his coaches to keep up.

“The journey has been great,” Talon-Kelly said. “I didn’t even want to start wrestling when I did. My dad convinced me. The day before . . . I said, ‘I don’t want to do this, don’t make me do this.’ I instantly fell in love with the sport and my teammates. I told my dad ‘Thank you so much for making me do this’ that day.”

He and Garcia work on different positions, tiring each other out and pushing to be the best they can be.

Garcia started wrestling freestyle in Puerto Rico when he was 9, but his family moved when he was 10 following Hurricane Maria. His family didn’t have the resources for him to wrestle until he got to high school, but joining the team quickly transformed his school experience.

“It’s been like a flip,” he said. “When I first came here I didn’t know how to speak English. I didn’t have a lot of friends. Throughout middle school I had one friend. I’d go home and have nothing in my life.

“I had a lot of fun learning about people and wrestling and getting better.”

The Marauders graduated no seniors last year, but benefit from a strong senior class this season. Outside of that group, sophomore Anthony Sateriale improved his 32-16 record last year to 32-4.

He’s wrestled since he was 5, and is looking to deliver what could be a dream result for the seniors.

“I feel really happy and proud to be a part of this team,” he said. “My coaches contributed to me as a wrestler and I’ve gotten 10 times better because of them.”

Heaslip said his starting 14 is a “mixed bag” but the “strongest group” he’s coached. Several wrestlers came into the year at the same weight and he had to sort that out to maximize the team’s potential.

Since last season, the message has been to carry themselves like champions in anything they do, and the month has finally arrived in which they can make that a reality.

“There were a lot of ups and downs during the offseason and the season. I experienced them myself,” said 120-pound junior captain Matthew Salas (22-14). “I was losing hope of a championship team, but now we’re in a position where we can win it all and we are going to win it all.”

title: ‘You cannot erase us’: Roxbury square renamed for historic Twelfth Baptist Church
text:
In the year since President Trump began his second term, his administration has removed Martin Luther King Jr. Day and Juneteenth from the National Park Service’s list of national holidays with free admission and ordered the agency to review materials related to slavery and racial injustice at certain sites. He has also issued executive orders targeting the National Museum of African American History and Culture and directing changes to content focused on slavery and racial history within Smithsonian institutions.

In Boston, after Trump signed a sweeping executive order directing federal agencies to end DEI initiatives tied to federal grants and contracts, Northeastern University removed language and initiatives from its DEI webpage and the Harvard Graduate School of Education closed its DEI office altogether.

But as crowds shivered through the unveiling of the bright blue “Twelfth Baptist Church Square” sign, churchgoers said the marker will help secure New England’s oldest Black Baptist congregation into public memory.

Historian and author Dart Adams said permanent recognition of the church’s past — including its role on the Underground Railroad and in shaping the early ministry of King — is essential to protecting its future.

“You can not erase us if we keep record of what we’ve done,” Adams said from behind the pulpit Sunday morning. “It’s our honor to have a marker declaring that Twelfth Baptist Church … is proof that Boston, especially Black Boston, will always survive and thrive.”

For worshippers packed into the pews, the renaming brought solace after what they described as a racially charged start to Black History Month, when Trump shared a social media video depicting former president Obama and former first lady Michelle Obama as apes.

Adonica-Curmazuela Chaplin, who officially joined the parish this week, said she hopes the renaming is a step toward recognizing Black history year-round, not just in February.

“If my history isn’t recorded and known, they will deny it like they’re trying to do it now,” said Chaplin, 79, of Roxbury. “We have leaders in Washington that refuse to tell the truth of our history. We can do it, but it has to be printed.”

The message echoed one expressed by Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, who sat in the chancel for more than two hours as Bodrick and other speakers addressed the congregation. It was the second time this month the two appeared together, following the city’s annual Black History Month celebration at City Hall, where Bodrick delivered an impassioned call for equity and justice for Boston’s Black community.

“What we’re here to do today is to make sure that as you’re going about your daily walk, not a single person will miss the reminder of the history that lives right here in this community,” said Wu. “Every month is Black History Month.”

Dozens of phones rose into the air as the crowd gathered outside the church, waiting for the brown paper concealing the new sign to be pulled away. The crowd cheered when a city worker climbed a ladder and sliced through the covering, revealing the marker.

Jaronzie Harris clapped as the sign came into view, exchanging excited words with fellow congregants. Having joined less than a year ago, she said the kindness and outspokenness of Twelfth Baptist members have insulated her from the rest of the world.

“I feel blessed to be in a community that’s pushing back on what the federal administration has been doing to censor the past,” said Harris, 38, who lives in Dorchester. “There’s erasure on a national scale, but it means a lot that the city is recognizing us and supporting us.”

Beside her, Violet Britton, a Roxbury resident who has attended Twelfth Baptist Church since she was a young child, stood in disbelief.

“My vocabulary isn’t extensive enough to explain how I felt,” said Britton, 81. “Something opened inside me.”

Speaking to the hundreds who gathered for his sermon, Bodrick urged worshippers to continue speaking openly about their struggles and perseverance. Assuming younger generations will automatically know the history that came before them, he said, is one of the “tragedies” of the modern day.

“We believe in memory, we believe in faith, we believe that truth prepares the next generation,” he said. “And we refuse to let the next generation walk into the future ignorant of their past.”

title: Roxbury development group splits over Madison Park high school plan
text:
As someone who grew up in Roxbury, Chanda Smart jumped at the opportunity to be part of the team to develop “P-3,” a vacant city-owned parcel spanning about eight acres on Tremont Street, across from the police headquarters.

But now that Mayor Michelle Wu’s administration has chosen to prioritize it for a new Madison Park vocational high school, Smart and her colleagues at OnyxGroup Development are saying in an open letter to the community that it’s time to walk away.

The residential development firm’s decision comes as another P-3 partner, Jeffrey Brown’s My City at Peace, is pushing ahead. Brown had planned to hold a listening session in Roxbury on Monday evening to galvanize support for the project. But as OnyxGroup notes in its letter, the “team is no longer on the same page” and advised Brown against holding the meeting.

The P-3 partners, also including Tom O’Brien’s HYM Investment Group, had envisioned building a complex consisting of labs and affordable housing at P-3, a site that’s been vacant for decades. However, in January, Wu and her planning director Kairos Shen announced they would let the developers’ designation for the project expire, citing the lack of interest in new lab construction and the need for a new Madison Park.

Smart said it was disappointing for her and her OnyxGroup partners, Shabnam Mashmasarmi and Carlos Castillo, but also a sign to move on. Exploring a way for a new high school to contribute to the site’s development is a direction that should be pursued, they note, in part because it would bring significant state funds to the community.

They say they’re sensitive to the historical context — the land was initially taken by eminent domain — but they disagree with continuing with the broader team’s existing plan for the site.

“We felt like, what was the point of having a listening session after the mayor has made her decision?,” said Smart, who also worked with Josh Kraft’s failed mayoral campaign last year. “This is difficult for us on so many levels.”

Now, OnyxGroup will focus its attention on Walnut Knoll, a 200-unit affordable apartment complex for seniors in Foxborough that it’s developing with Peabody Cos. and the nonprofit Affordable Housing and Services Collaborative. The first two buildings opened a few months ago, and Smart said she hopes to close on a construction loan for the third building in a few weeks. OnyxGroup will still consider other projects in Roxbury, including any future opportunities that may arise at P-3.

This is an installment of our weekly Bold Types column about the movers and shakers on Boston’s business scene.
