Chief executive Joanna Geraghty has had to navigate some turbulence as she charts a flight path to stability for JetBlue Airways.

She became chief executive two years ago after the federal government stymied the airline’s Northeast marketing partnership with American Airlines and its plan to buy Spirit Airlines.

Restoring JetBlue’s profitability meant trimming some routes, never a fun task. Then came the “tariff situation” after President Trump took office, dampening consumer demand, as Geraghty recalled in a conversation with Massport chief executive Rich Davey at the Boston College Chief Executives Club on Thursday. Then came a federal government shutdown and an Airbus safety recall.

From her perspective, it’s hopefully all blue skies ahead, by focusing on the customer experience, as it relates to everything from helpful personnel to free Wi-Fi.

“It’s been a rough couple of years for JetBlue,” Geraghty said. “We’re now emerging from some dark days. . . . We had a great [comeback] plan. We just need the macro backdrop to cooperate.”

JetBlue has now relinquished the top spot at Boston’s Logan Airport to Delta Airlines, as measured by the number of nonstops tracked by Massport. For example, for the fiscal 2026 schedule, Delta has an average of 149 daily flights planned at Logan, to 77 destinations, while JetBlue plans 122 daily flights, but to 78 destinations.

Davey may have had those numbers in mind when he asked Geraghty about the New York-based airline’s commitment to Boston. (Notably, Geraghty’s lieutenant, president Marty St. George, is from Boston.)

“Boston is our second home,” Geraghty responded. “We really want to be part of Boston’s community. We want to be authentically Boston. . . . We’re going to fight for Boston.”

A major player in Manhattan luxury real estate is now looking to “own” Boston, too.

Serhant, led by New York broker and TV personality Ryan Serhant, last week announced it has launched a new Boston office with some big names from rival agencies.

Founding members for Massachusetts include: Michael Carucci, from Gibson Sotheby’s International Realty; Antonio Khoury, from Compass Group; Jorge Sariego from Boston One Realty; and Kyle Farrell and Joe Albano (aka the “Prop Cousins”) from Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Chris Delaney, also from Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices, will be Serhant’s Massachusetts director.

Serhant said it’s starting in Boston with a roster of around 30 agents working out of a Back Bay office. Ryan Serhant grew up in Topsfield, and has had phenomenal success with his fast-growing firm in the nearly six years since its founding, now operating in 15 states.

Having a Netflix series about Serhant agents’ exploits in New York, “Owning Manhattan,” certainly hasn’t hurt.

Carucci, one of Boston’s most successful luxury home brokers, said his team was impressed with Serhant’s client-friendly technology.

“There aren’t a lot of brands that come around and get my attention, quite frankly, and Ryan’s did,” said Carucci, who joins as executive vice president of Serhant’s Massachusetts group.

Carucci said he leaves Gibson Sotheby’s on good terms with chairman Larry Rideout.

“It was 11 years,” Carucci said of his time with Gibson Sotheby’s. “We both did very well with the relationship. Me not being there is not going to affect our friendship at all.”

As to whether Serhant’s arrival might prompt a Netflix show around Boston real estate at some point, Carucci sounds doubtful: “I don’t think Boston’s that kind of market.”

title: How communities help us get through trauma
text:
There were 72 homicides in 2010, the year before I began my pastorate at Roxbury Presbyterian — many of them young men in the neighborhood. One of the dead, Jefferson Cory Johnson, was a member of my church. At 27, Johnson was a bright and cherished member of one of the church’s largest families, the first male in his family of his generation, active and respected in the community. He was father to two young girls and seemed headed for a promising future. Then one chilly night in May, he and his half-brother Justin Fernandez were ambushed on the street not far from Johnson’s home as they headed to a party. Johnson died, Fernandez was seriously injured, and their attackers were never found. Their families, the church, and the neighborhood were left in shock, confusion, and anger — emotional suffering that might never be addressed.

One of my first invitations as pastor of Roxbury Presbyterian was from Johnson’s mother, Debra Johnson, who asked me to pray at a community memorial service for him. The function room at the Salvation Army Kroc Center was packed. A large posterboard on an easel held a montage of images of her son: an adorable newborn baby in his mother’s arms, a young father holding his two children on his shoulders, the close-up of a fashion-model face, eyes gazing confidently at the camera lens.

Siblings, cousins, and all sorts of kinfolk and friends regaled one another with stories behind the pictures: how Cory Johnson inspired them and made them laugh, how he took care of them and loved them. On the surface, this family had put the worst behind them. But the sweet recollections, festive balloons, and good food did little to temper the grief and bitterness of their violent loss.

Trauma, in the words of Boston University theologian Shelly Rambo, is “the suffering that does not go away.” As a journalist, I was an expert in thrusting the microphone in the face of trauma survivors, recording that moving soundbite. But as a novice pastor standing face to face with this heartbroken community, I found myself speechless.

In fact, few of us know how to comfort or even discuss trauma and grief in our society or in our own lives. Amid ongoing violent events like the televised government killings and arrests of Minneapolis residents, including those protesting Immigration and Customs Enforcement, many of us feel speechless and powerless.

That is why, in response to Johnson’s death and that of so many others in our neighborhood, church members, mental health clinicians, and community members created Can We Talk…, a spiritually inspired, community based, clinically supported program in the basement of our church where people are invited to share their stories of pain and loss. Neither a church service nor a therapy session, the gatherings offer a good meal, artistic expressions, and a space where neighbors can learn the healing power of community.

The goal is not to fix anything. It’s about processing pain, accessing the spaces in yourself that are shut down, and allowing you to find “a way out of no way,” as we say in the church, in a community of love.

Healing in Can We Talk…, with gatherings created in 20 communities around the country, comes in surprising ways. Despite helping to create the program, Debra Johnson says she felt her emotional numbness would never go away. “I resigned myself to having to live this way, emotionally shut down the rest of my life,” she said. Now, after sharing her story for 11 years, she says, “The pain never goes away, but in this community, I am finding a way through.”

When we started the program, I had no plans to bring up the trauma of my own childhood. At 12, I lost my beloved father to a stroke a few weeks after he decided I would participate in the chaotic desegregation of public schools in my hometown of Little Rock, Ark. I was caught between a “seen but not heard” world at home and a world of racist bullying, harassment, and fights at school, and my silence and reckless choices masked the rage and confusion I didn’t know how to express. By the grace of God, I graduated high school and went on with my life, but I never addressed those crippling emotional wounds until one night, decades later, at a Can We Talk… gathering. I was so moved by someone else’s painful story, I decided to share my own.

We all have holes within, from those events and experiences that have shaken us deeply or left us feeling abandoned — experiences we’d rather not talk about, but should, because talking, mourning, and processing those hard parts of our life help us make sense of our pain and, just as importantly, help us find common bonds with others.

There is nothing more healing and hopeful than realizing how alike we all are. Creating healing spaces everywhere can help put us back on the road to restoring our deepest selves and our common humanity.

title: How Liz Walker found her higher purpose
text:
The following is a lightly edited transcript of the Feb. 12 episode.

Anna Kusmer: Welcome to Say More from Boston Globe Opinion. I’m Anna Kusmer.

If you lived around Boston in the 1980s or 1990s, you will probably recognize this voice.

Yes, that is the Liz Walker.

She was the first Black woman to co-anchor a TV newscast in Boston. In 2005, she left the news and went to church.

After TV, Reverend Liz Walker was the pastor of Roxbury Presbyterian Church. As a pastor, she found her higher calling, mixing faith with the power of talking. And between ICE raids, natural disasters and the mental health crisis, we need places to talk more than ever.

Her new project is called “Can We Talk.” Her book about the project, “No One Left Alone,” takes us into the church walls to sit beside grieving parishioners, healing together through conversation.

Welcome Liz, thanks for being here.

Liz Walker: It is an honor to be with you, Anna. Thanks for having me.

Kusmer: I want to talk about this new book and the project that inspired it. At the center of the book, as a young man named Cory Johnson. Can you tell me his story and why it became so important to your ministry?

Walker: Well, the first thing to tell you is that as a reporter, I covered this neighborhood often.

Roxbury, as we all know, is kind of the center of the — I hate to say Black, so I’ll say urban — community, and it’s a community that’s changing. When I went there in 2011, that neighborhood had been in the midst of what I’m going call gang violence, so that may not be accurate, but there was gun violence and lots of young people had died.

Seventy-five people had died between 2010 and 2011 in Boston. Many of them, most of them from Roxbury, and one of them was Cory Johnson. I had covered stories on shootings in that neighborhood, but I didn’t know the full story. You usually started on the news on a weekend.

Often, it was, “Another shooting in Roxbury, details at 11.”

So going back in as a minister and learning more about these young men who were dying, especially Cory because he was a member of the church and a promising young man. He had two children, two young girls, worked at the YMCA, worked in the community centers, and he was a typical youth, but he was really looking for a bright future. He and his brother went out to a party one night, and he didn’t come home. He was killed, and the murderer was never found. The circumstances have always been mysterious.

I wanted to know about Cory when I got to the church because I could see that his family was still grieving. I got there a year after he was killed.

Kusmer: One of your first events as pastor was like a one year anniversary of Cory’s death, and I think you were talking to his mother and that was that part of what inspired, sort of what came next?

Walker: Yeah. Because at this memorial service, a year after Cory was killed, and right after I got to the church, his mother asked me to pray at the memorial service. It was at the Boston Kroc Center in Dorchester, and the whole point of the memorial service was balloons and music. But underneath this, kind of party atmosphere and celebration, you could feel the pain.

There’s no way to go on when you — or at least there’s no way to go on in a healthy direction — when you haven’t dealt with some of the things that are holding you down. And this family was, and still is, trying to figure their way through this grief.

They’re a large family from Trinidad and Tobago. To see them try to put their best face on, in the wake of this violent death, broke my heart.

Kusmer: You say, and it really struck me in the book, that you didn’t know how to talk to someone whose loved one had been murdered when you were first talking to Debra at that event.

You were a journalist in Boston for decades, so obviously you literally knew how to talk to someone about hard things, but you felt like you were missing something in this new role.

Walker: Absolutely.

Kusmer: Can you talk about what you feel like you were missing?

Walker: Well, first of all, journalists, usually — now I’m old school and it may have changed in the last 5,000 years since I was on television — but you go to the scene of a horror show, or you go to the scene of a horrible situation and you usually say, “How did it feel?” which would make sense in a very kind of a superficial way.

But it’s really not quite the way to handle someone who just saw their love die.

So that’s what I mean about, what do you say?

And I think that in a culture that we have, we really don’t know how to address grief. What do we do? Do we come in and say, “He’s in a better place?” Do we come in and say, “You’re going to be all right?”

That’s not what you need to say. So that’s what I meant. I thought I knew what to say. I think we all think we know what to say, but in fact, talking in that way is not necessarily helpful. And so that was another part of this book: What do we say? How can we support our neighbors when they’re going through things?

And that’s what I learned, and that’s what I share.

Kusmer: So this project that came out of this realization is called “Can We Talk.” Can you describe what “Can We Talk” is, the sort of the form it took, and just what that actually looked like to be in the room there?

Walker: So we wanted to do something more than the usual fair, and I don’t say that with disrespect. When a person is killed or dies in our community, the church plans the funeral, the church works with the family, we talk to the police. We try to do everything we can to ease the burden of the family.

But what happens is after the funeral, maybe we bring covered dishes over, maybe we pray with the family, but at some point, life goes on for us. Life does not go on for the family. So this “Can We Talk” idea came from talking to mental health experts, funeral directors, and of course this family about, what would help you a little bit? After all of this is happening, how can we help you?

And talking really to psychologists because grief needs to be taken care of, it needs to be tended. Doesn’t mean it’ll go away, but it can be handled and managed so that you can cope, knowing that you are going through this.

So in talking to them, one of the ideas came up, “Well, why don’t we have something like Alcoholics Anonymous for people who are grieving?”

The similarity is only in the fact that this is a kind of a drop in group. It’s in the basement of the church. It’s not church, but it gives a safe — and we consider sacred — space for people to just release some of their pain.

These are gatherings we started monthly. We have food and we have a mental health worker on site who usually does it pro bono. We have companions — other people who have gone through trauma themselves, but have been trained in some basics of trauma education to identify what trauma is — identifying what you can do, as a neighbor, as a friend.

We tried it and the outpouring was amazing that first time. People just showed up. People heard we had a sign on the church wall outside, that was our only marketing plan.

People showed up and they talked about violence last week and about violence 20 years ago that they just were told to get over and move on, or they told themselves that.

But, it was always there because untreated trauma, any wound, needs at some point, light and air to heal. And if you don’t give it that, it can fester and it can get much worse.

Kusmer: The goal of this project, I think, maybe in a romantic sense we might think, “Oh, we want people to have these cathartic breakthroughs where they do relieve themselves of grief.”

But I think it’s not like that, you know? And I think of Debra, Cory’s mother, you kind of follow her throughout the book, her coming to these sessions.

What do you kind of define as progress for somebody who’s attending these events?

Walker: We had an event in New Bedford and Debra got up and spoke and so I listened to her very closely and I’ve watched her over the years, and she says that for her it is the ability to even talk about this incident that has given her a little space inside.

When Cory was first killed, she got a call in the middle of the night and she said she knew almost immediately something was wrong. When she got to the hospital, and this was back in 2010, and realized her son was gone, she said a part of her just shut down, just numb. There were no words for what she was going through.

Somehow over the years she kept working. She did what she had to do, but she never entered that space that was shut down. She said that went on for four years. So the idea of confronting your boogeyman, your darkness, your pain, your worst moment, it’s not about ending that moment, but it’s about finding a way through and then somehow integrating that into your life.

She will never be happy or get over Cory’s death. And she said that there are days now when she goes into a dark hole. She can’t help it, but she knows a way out.

The other thing she said that was very stunning to me, and it was nothing I even thought about, was that telling her story she sees now helps other people. And last night in New Bedford, it was extraordinary. People, probably about 30 or 40 people, were at this church and they listened to Debra talk, and then we tried a little, “Can We Talk” with them. And people started sharing things.

One man talked about being shot during busing and never having gone to the hospital. He was so ashamed. The things that we carry. So that’s what I think the healing is. A thing we talk about in Black religious tradition is God is a God of making a way out of no way. When you think there’s absolutely nothing, I’m going to be able to survive this.

Debra decided, “I’ll just have to live like this. I’ll have to live with this darkness. That’s just gonna be life.” And she says, a little of the darkness has lifted and she’s found a place to kind of deal with the death just a little easier.

So it’s not going to change. You’re right. It’s not big, but these are things.

I think one more thing you didn’t ask, but I’m going to tell you anyway, the idea of telling your story. We live in a culture, and this has always been the case, where other people define us, they define Cory: “at-risk young man, gang member.” That wasn’t who Cory was, so she gets to define who she is and who her son was.

Kusmer: And I imagine in a church setting where a lot of us might visualize a pastor speaking down to the congregation, this is maybe a new dynamic for a lot of people. They’re the ones speaking and they’re the lead, directing the conversation. I imagine that’s an interesting dynamic for you as well as a pastor.

Walker: I talk about these experiences in very dramatic terms, but it has been a life change for me because we are listening.

As a preacher, I love to preach. I could preach right now, but that’s not what you invited me for. But the goal here is to learn, to listen and to listen deeply because, part of the problem we’re in, the mess we’re in now is that so many people feel unheard. And that affects everything. And so this is a way for people to feel heard, to feel honored, to have dignity restored. And I’m not just talking about Black people or poor people or people of color. There are many people who just don’t feel heard. And this is a way to help kind of reach them and listen.

Kusmer: Liz, you grew up in Little Rock, Arkansas in the 1950s and 1960s, and you went to high school at Little Rock Central, which is famous for being the high school of the Little Rock Nine, where nine Black teenagers were sent to this all white school as part of integration after Brown v. the Board of Education. They were met with racist backlash. What was it like to be on the front lines of desegregation at such a young age?

Walker: I lived in the neighborhood around the school, at least within a mile of the school.

My brother and I have talked about this, “Are we just making this up or is this true?” But we remember the troops driving into — well, that’s a traumatic sight to see — government troops and guns and all these Jeeps and all that stuff.

So I think we do, I think that’s a real memory, not just imagination coming in when we were very young.

And then later my father, who was a part of the Civil Rights leadership in the city, wanted me to desegregate — be a part of the desegregation, the integration of these schools, because they did it in 1957 at Little Rock Central.

Then they shut down the schools and then they started it back up, grade by grade. And that’s how this was still going on all that time. So I was supposed to be in the seventh grade in 1963, and this was the year that they were desegregating the seventh grade. So they’d worked their way from the 12th grade down, and it was horrible.

Now, when the Little Rock Nine were in the news, the thing about them was, as horrible as their situation was, and it was certainly horrible, there were cameras, there was attention, there were interviews. They had Daisy Bates.

There was something to hold all of that chaos. By the time I got to the seventh grade, your father took you to the school or maybe you went with a group. I was not sent with a group. And you went and you were on your own. So there was no organized thing, at least not for me.

The reason I think I was not involved in that was right at the beginning of the school year, my father died.

So my family was thrown into its own personal chaos and the rules, whatever the rule, whatever he had in mind, who knows? But I felt very much on my own and so that was a traumatizing time for me. It was a time when puberty was coming, a time when most kids are thinking about dating.

It felt like the frontline of a war and there were only maybe in the whole school of 800 students, maybe 50 Blacks. I don’t think there were that many organized picnics or anything because I guess life just went on.

And, I really suffered from that, and other kids suffered from that, from being the only one in a class or being spit on. There were just all kinds of stories. I know that that has impacted me all my life, compounded by the trauma of losing my father.

And again, back in the day, there were no psychologists, there were no counseling services. You went to the funeral and my mother, my stepmother was grieving herself, she didn’t have time.

It was just shut down in my soul and has just begun to come up — of how I struggled with it since this program started. I tell people that and they look at me, but I think a lot of us hold our stuff to ourselves because we don’t know what to do with it, so we hold our pain inside.

Kusmer: What did the group, “Can We Talk,” unlock for you?

Walker: It unlocked the fact that I was not dealing with some issues. There was always this hole and it really came out in relationships, or the lack thereof, because I never went to a therapist. I never put a frame or a context around that time. I never even thought about the time I went through. You just got over it and moved on.

The year of 1963 was probably one of the worst years for this country. That was the year John F. Kennedy was killed. That was the year that the four girls were killed in Birmingham, Alabama. All hell had broken. We were in the Vietnam War. We look back on that time now as a defining moment in American history, and it affected all of us.

Kusmer: When I was a child growing up here in Boston, you were famous for being a local TV news anchor. What drew you to the calling of news?

Walker: Interesting. I have no idea. I wish I did. I think I always wanted to write, and I think one of the healing parts of my childhood was when I went to Central High School because by the time I got to Central, things had calmed down. One of the classes I took was journalism. I always liked to write little poems and things like that as a child, but I never thought that was going to amount to anything because I didn’t think it could. But I had a journalism teacher, Charles Lance. I was in his class and there was some project, and this was probably the 10th grade and he said, “You can write.”

Nobody had told me I could do anything, including my parents. When people say that to you, it can stick with you. That was kind of a way forward for me. I put everything into writing then.

Kusmer: What made you leave the anchor chair to go to Harvard Divinity School?

Walker: That’s another mystery in my life. I went to Sudan in 2001.

Kusmer: Is this a journalistic assignment?

Walker: I assigned myself this. Some people in Boston had been invited to go and observe and explore allegations of slavery in South Sudan. This was going on for decades, these allegations. And so a group went, and I was invited with them. I thought I’d do a documentary.

I went to my news director, and television news then, and now, was not looking at why we are gonna go all the way to South Sudan to do a story. “We cover local news.”

But I got mad and I decided, “You know what? I’m gonna do this myself.” So I took my own camera and it was on that journey that the people I went with Reverend Dr. Gloria White-Hammond and Pastor Ray Hammond, who are still two outstanding community leaders in Boston, medical doctors and ministers.

And I went with them and they kind of defined how I reacted to what I saw as a call. They said, “Oh no, this is God calling you. There’s something you should do.”

Kusmer: What in Sudan sort of created this shift for you?

Walker: I never had seen that kind of trauma, physical trauma. We went to villages where you could actually see the hollowed out piece where the bomb hit.

Kusmer: Wow.

Walker: Because this was the north against the south. I’d never been that close to that. I was never that close to a conflict, and so that kind of opened me up to the misery of the world.

Kusmer: Do you feel like you hit a wall with the tools of journalism? That then ministry felt like sort of an evolution of maybe what you had?

Walker: I do believe that I hit a wall of journalism because you sit there behind the camera and you’re watching this scene go on and this woman’s talking about gang rape and you’re thinking —

And telling the story is huge! This is important.

But remember, Hurricane Katrina hit, and when Katrina hit, people were waving white flags on rooftops that were covered with water and people were begging for help. And it seemed a little odd that TV cameras were just shooting that when I’m actually asking you to save my life. At some point there, the needs are beyond that idea of some objective and removed storyteller.

People are desperate for help, and your job is only to tell the story. I think storytelling is important, but sometimes you wanted —

Kusmer: — to do more.

Walker: I wanted to do more. That’s all.

Kusmer: Yeah, that makes sense. What do you think your dad would say if he knew you became a minister?

Walker: I wonder. I think he’d be going, “Girl…”

Kusmer: Why?

Walker: Well, I wonder if I became a minister because my dad was a minister and that’s all I remember.

I am not running around with some dramatic, “I’ve been called by God.” I kind of wonder was that just kind of trying to figure out what my dad was doing?

It has been the most satisfying role and it has been a role of kind of swimming in the deep end of the pool as opposed to on the side and taking the picture and really seeing the human condition, and seeing the commonality in it.

It crosses all kinds of barriers that you think. We have more in common. And you hear it and it sounds like a platitude, but it’s so true. That’s how I guess you get to platitudes. We have so much more in common as human beings than we think. And now when we are dividing the world into “us” and “them.” I think more than ever somebody’s got to say, “That’s not exactly what’s going on here, because we are all suffering.”

Kusmer: It’s funny because although you are technically a local celebrity, as a teenager, I was actually more in awe of your son because I went to Brookline High School with Nick. He was, and is, a phenomenal singer and actor. I still think about his performance in the musical “Ragtime,” which he was in as a senior.

Walker: Oh, that was huge.

Kusmer: Yeah. He was amazing in that. And I actually remember that he would walk down the streets next to Brookline High School, maybe he was walking home, and he would sing at the top of his lungs. I’m sure you remember that, too. And like an angel, the most gorgeous voice. First of all, you must be so proud of him.

Walker: I am very proud. I’m in awe of Nick. So many people remember him in Brookline walking down. I used to say, “Nick, be careful about that. People are gonna think you’re crazy singing at the top of [your] lungs.”

But that was his gift and he just did it.

Kusmer: Yeah. I mean, there’s so much in your book about humility, and I’m just curious about what you’ve learned from your son and your own parenting experiences.

Walker: Well, I’ve learned a lot from my son. I’ve learned that, you know, I wanted Nick to just be a regular kid that would just stay in the lines, because that’s what I wanted to do. And Nick had a sense of purpose early on. He wanted to sing and he only wanted to go to New York. And it wasn’t about, I look back now, I don’t think it was so much about fortune and fame. It was just about his gift.

Kusmer: Sharing his gift.

Walker: I really think so. That may be naïve.

So I learned that from him — the idea of purpose in our lives. And it is not an easy profession because there’s so many times of being down, so many times of being out. He was in “Hamilton” and that was huge, but he’s been struggling and hustling for a long time. And every victory is a big victory because he has been struggling and hustling. So, I talk a lot about purpose and trauma and grief can take us away from our sense of purpose.

And, “How do you restore that?” is important.

Kusmer: You have a whole chapter in your book about the power of music. I was wondering if you have a musical note to reflect on.

Walker: Oh, gosh. That’s a great, that’s such a great, great question. The song is “Golden.”

You know who I’m talking about — ”living my life like it’s golden.”

Kusmer: Jill Scott.

Walker: Jill Scott. I like Jill Scott, anything she does, because I love her voice. But that song is, you know, it’s just how we can take on a different kind of position and state of mind in life no matter what happens to you. It’s about just living your life, with swimming in the deep end, trying and taking risks, and not being afraid because there’s so much to make us afraid of everything.

And so “living my life like it’s golden” is a step out of that fear for me.

Kusmer: Liz Walker was the longtime pastor of Roxbury Presbyterian Church here in Boston. Her new book is called “No One Left Alone”, about the project “Can We Talk.” Thank you so much, Liz, for sharing with us. It’s been an honor to speak with you.

Walker: Anna, it’s been really delightful talking to you and I wish you the best.

Kara Mihm of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

Listen to more Say More episodes here and wherever you get your podcasts. If you like the show, please follow us and leave us a review. You can email us at saymore@globe.com.

title: For better or worse, Wu’s bet on White Stadium will define her legacy
text:
What about building a more modest alternative for the exclusive use of Boston schoolchildren and opposing teams — one that includes a regulation track, a field for high school football and soccer games, and a field house with lockers and showers? Opponents say that can be done for $29 million. But the Wu administration dismisses that option, saying the cost would be much higher than that, while producing no formal bids or cost estimates to back up such a conclusion.

It’s Wu’s way or the highway — and dare I say there’s something slightly Trumpian about that attitude?

Ignoring the critics, the cost, and legal arguments against it, President Trump demolished the East Wing of the White House in order to build a ballroom. After adding his name onto the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, Trump recently announced plans to rebuild it, no matter what detractors have to say about it.

Unlike the East Wing or the Kennedy Center, there’s no question White Stadium warranted demolishment. Built in 1949, it was once an urban jewel. After falling into extreme disrepair, it stood as a sad commentary on city priorities about Franklin Park and school sports.

Rebuilding it is now a legacy project that will define Wu’s mayoralty, and she appears to be willing to take the heat and risks that go with it.

The women’s soccer team could fail to gain a following, collapse financially, or exit Boston. Or it could be such a success that it needs a larger venue, like the professional soccer stadium planned for the New England Revolution in Everett. Either way, the Wu administration insists the city is protected.

As for cost, Wu now insists that it’s “locked.” However, in the Contrarian Boston, Scott Van Voorhis suggested that’s not accurate because guaranteed maximum price agreements don’t preclude or stop contractors from billing for change orders that would increase the cost. In the end, the public will eventually find out who is right about that, just like it did with the Big Dig.

To be fair, great vision often requires a great leap of faith. Past Boston mayors have taken on legacy projects that proved the skeptics wrong. Kevin White turned crumbling warehouses into Quincy Market, a popular tourist destination that revitalized downtown Boston, which is again in need of creative revitalization. Tom Menino championed a convention center in South Boston that spurred development of a new luxury neighborhood and entertainment district, known as the Seaport.

With White Stadium, Wu is looking beyond downtown, to a part of the city that could greatly benefit from attention and investment. According to Wu, the newly renovated stadium “will deliver the largest community benefits deal in Boston’s history.” With the city committed to $135 million, Boston Legacy, which will lease the stadium from the city, is putting in $190 million.

Construction is slated to begin at the end of March, and the project is expected to create more than 500 construction jobs. There are promises to share the work with local businesses in the neighborhoods surrounding Franklin Park, including Dorchester, Jamaica Plain, Mattapan, and Roxbury. Some $43 million in contracts are also allocated to minority and women-run businesses. It all sounds great.

The city still faces a legal challenge from the Franklin Park Defenders, who have joined the Emerald Necklace Conservancy to sue the city over the stadium plan, arguing that it’s an illegal use of park land. The case is now before the Supreme Judicial Court. For the plaintiffs, it is the last stand.

If the city wins, it will be Wu’s way, for better or worse.

Will it be all that she promised, from an investment in the future of Boston Public Schools to an economic boom for a long-neglected part of the city? Most of all, will it be what Boston student athletes need and deserve?

Because of the need to maintain pristine field conditions for the pro soccer team, high school football won’t be played there until November, the end of the season. Wu officials say high school soccer games can be played on the field. But questions are still being raised about how long high school games can coexist with professional games before field quality becomes an issue. As with the final cost, the truth about shared usage will eventually be known, too.

In the end, that truth will be Wu’s legacy.

title: How to entertain (or escape from) your children over February break
text:
Perks at Launch

Ah, yes, that venerable trampoline park where your kids lose their minds for hours while you doomscroll in between hiding from party parents you don’t know. But the kids; they love it! And during school vacation week, there are perks: Visit between Feb. 16 and Feb. 20, and get promos like $100 off any birthday party booking and a free one-hour jump pass. Truly makes the aroma of hand sanitizer and spilled soda worth it. www.themomentumenterprises.com

Culture at … the mall?

So your kids want to go to the mall. In a surreal twist, Michelangelo’s Sistine Chapel exhibition opens at Cambridgeside on Thursday, Feb. 12, with life-size displays of 34 of his frescoes. In my day, the mall’s most exciting exhibitions involved meat samples on sticks at the food court. Tickets are $28; less for seniors, students, and kids. Turn your teens loose at Sephora and pretend you’re in Rome. It’s open Wednesday through Sunday. www.cambridgeside.com

Pagu Lunar New Year

Last year, my 9-year-old and I took a cooking class at Pagu in Central Square. It was awesome: super hands-on, with pizza, chocolate cupcakes, and matcha cookies. Owner Tracy Chang manages to strike just the right balance in her (Michelin-recognized) Japanese-Spanish restaurant: elegant but not snooty. The place is named for the Japanese word for pug, after all. Anyway, this vibe makes it an ideal and tasty place to celebrate a fam-friendly Lunar New Year: lion dancing, drumming, and symbolic foods (Taiwanese beef noodle soup for longevity; steamed fish for abundance; mochi for progress). The celebrations are at doable times: Tuesday, Feb. 17, at 5:30 p.m.; Saturday, Feb. 21, at 1 p.m., and Sunday, Feb. 22, at 1 p.m. and 5 p.m. Kids under 8 are free. www.gopagu.com

Penguin Paramours at the New England Aquarium

Those of us who’ve finished “Heated Rivalry” might need a new spicy-icy love story. How about penguins? You can even take your kids to this show without wincing. “Penguins: A Love Story” spotlights penguin courtship and resiliency at the New England Aquarium, beginning on Friday, Feb. 13. Shot in Cape Town, South Africa, the story follows Lenny, an African penguin looking for his lifelong mate. On the other side of the beach, Fluffball, an orphaned penguin chick, is tended by humans at a penguin hospital. His surrogate mom feeds him sardines and teaches him to swim. Awww. The Aquarium itself is home to 51 well-loved penguins. www.neaq.org

T, the Musical

Do you really want to spend more time on the T? In this case, maybe: This musical parody of metro mishaps resonates for anyone who’s frittered hours on the Red Line, wondering if they’ll ever make it home again. Go to a matinee on Saturday, Feb. 21, at 2 p.m. with an appearance by Frank Edward Oglesby, for years the soothing voice behind MBTA announcements, which hopefully won’t trigger desperate memories. There’s even a scavenger hunt. The show runs through Sunday, March 1, at Davis Square’s Rockwell Theatre. www.tthemusical.com

Presidents’ Day Week at the JFK Library

The John F. Kennedy Presidential Library and Museum hosts programming throughout the vacation week, including a festival on Monday, Feb. 16, with offbeat attractions: There’s a “presidential pets” exhibit (did you know that Socks Clinton chilled in a Kitty Kondo?), a pet-themed state dinner, pet “Jeopardy!,” and actors portraying luminaries like John Adams and Calvin “Silent Cal” Coolidge (will this person have any lines?). There’s also the chance to sign a Declaration of Independence and contribute to a wish tree expressing your hopes for our country’s future. Kids under 17 are free. www.jfklibrary.org

Tarot for beginners

Speaking of the future: Hey, maybe it feels fraught right now. Who else but the Cambridge Center for Adult Education would come to the rescue with a virtual tarot tutorial? Log in, hide from your family for two hours, and learn the rudiments of the craft on Thursday, Feb. 19, at 7 p.m. The class comes complete with practice readings with journalist and astrological author Sally Cragin. www.ccae.org

Free Fun in Boston and beyond

Thanks to the Highland Park Foundation, tons of local attractions offer free admission throughout the week at spots like Brookline’s Jack Kirrane Ice Rink; the Wenham Museum; Boston’s Museum of African American History; the Eric Carle Museum in Amherst; the Rose Kennedy Greenway Carousel and Frostivus Ferris Wheel; and the City of Boston Winter Festival in Dorchester’s Franklin Park, with ice-skating, sledding, snow-shoeing, even archery. Check out the full lineup at www.highlandstreet.org/winter-camp.

Oh, if you do head out to Amherst, do yourself a favor and stop at the El Chapincito truck on Route 202 in Orange (164 Daniel Shays Highway). Yep, it’s in a Sunoco gas station parking lot. And, yep, it has tongue tacos and crispy mulitas, plus kid-friendly choices like chicken and beef quesadillas. Thank me later.

title: The new fare gates at South Station are annoying. They’re also part of the answer to a bigger problem.
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

For the past month, I’ve been conducting an experiment. Each time I passed through South Station to and from the Globe’s offices, I counted how many people needed an employee’s help getting through the new fare gates that divide the station’s arched concourse from its commuter rail platforms.

As readers who’ve gotten this newsletter before sunrise might guess, I take the train at odd hours and haven’t seen crowds jockeying to get through. But I have seen plenty of confusion: Two men searching for where to scan their app-purchased digital tickets to open the gates, a family negotiating a stroller through the barriers, a woman whose scanner didn’t work.

Yet despite the rocky rollout, transit experts say the gates are a small part of the effort to stanch the MBTA’s yearslong cash-bleed. For some, they’re a practical way to reduce the number of people who use the system without paying. For others, they’re a reason to radically reimagine what funding for public transit in Massachusetts could look like.

Fare evasion has costs, even if there’s no way to know exactly how much.

In 2016, analysts estimated that the T was losing up to $6 million annually to fare evasion on subways and buses. In 2019, analysts said the commuter rail could be losing between $10 million and $20 million. That’s a pittance compared to the T’s $3.2 billion total operating budget, but it still means less money for repairs, paying employees, and expanding services.

“Fare revenue is part of the pie,” said Caitlin Allen-Connelly of TransitMatters, which lobbies for better public transportation. “When the pie is not whole, it is a barrier and an obstacle to the T being able to deliver the level of service, the quality of service, that people need.”

Fare evasion conjures images of people jumping turnstiles, but it takes many different forms. Jim Aloisi, Massachusetts’ former transportation secretary who studies fare evasion at MIT, said it happens most frequently on buses. Sometimes it’s a protest against a late-arriving bus or a symptom of economic hardship. Other times, “evasion” isn’t really the right descriptor. Drivers sometimes wave riders through to prevent delays, and commuter rail conductors don’t always have time to scan everyone’s tickets.

Massachusetts decriminalized fare evasion in 2021, but cracking down on it can still recoup losses. The MBTA reported making $8 million more than it expected from fares at the start of the fiscal year. The bump coincided with deploying “fare engagement representatives” to remind riders to pay — and slapping those who don’t with escalating penalties.

The South Station gates reduce the need for conductors to manually scan tickets, which Aloisi called a minimally invasive, sensible way to reduce nonpayment. “The drill here shouldn’t be to obsess or focus about how much,” he said. “The drill should be where can we make cost-effective interventions that matter?”

Still, everything has costs. The MBTA paid $1.3 million for the South Station gates and $2 million to install them. Without knowing how much evasion they’re preventing, it’s impossible to know whether the gates will pay for themselves.

Gates can also become bottlenecks that slow commutes. “It is a tax on people if you’re stuck waiting in line,” said Jonathan Cohn, the policy director for Progressive Mass, which supports fare-free public transit. And that’s assuming they work; last month’s snow appears to have temporarily knocked the gates out of service.

The gates aren’t a panacea, either. If human conductors aren’t checking, passengers coming from more distant stops could buy cheaper tickets to scan, Allen-Connelly suggested. (Note: Officials say conductors will still check tickets on trains to verify travel zones, which carry different price tags for a lift home, depending on the length of the journey.)

Fare nonpayment is only a fraction of the T’s fiscal challenges, which include depressed ridership and stubborn operating deficits.

For Cohn, the fare gate debate is a chance to change how public transit works. “Whenever I see lots of money being put into combatting fare evasion, it always just ends up reinforcing to me why fare-free public transit is a good goal.”

Options to better fund the T include raising the state gas tax or implementing congestion pricing, which charges cars to use certain roads at peak times. Even experts who support the gates, like Aloisi, favor making certain bus routes free.

But even as experts look beyond, the new regime is settling in. During my commute yesterday, a conductor walked over, watched me activate my ticket, then walked away. He seemed happy to leave the scanning to the machines.

title: Can Wu end 50 years of failure at Roxbury site?
text:
The neighborhood should give her a chance to try — because despite the best of intentions, the city’s previous strategies clearly haven’t worked. And with the real estate market in the doldrums, there’s little downside: It’s not like developers are banging on the city’s door with other viable proposals for the site.

Indeed, absent some fresh thinking, P-3 would probably just remain what it’s been for a half-century: a weed-covered eyesore.

The parcel sits across Tremont Street from the Boston Police headquarters, a block from the Ruggles stop on the Orange Line. Until the mid-20th century, it was a mix of commercial and residential properties.

The city took the land by eminent domain and demolished the buildings in the 1970s to build a gigantic, 5,000-seat high school that was envisioned at the time. But that mega-school never materialized — the start of the cycle of overpromising and underdelivering on the site.

Since then, officials have eyed the empty site for a soccer stadium; a health care company headquarters; state office buildings; housing; a museum; and other uses.

One reason it’s been challenging to make projects click for the site is that in the past, the city has insisted that developers’ plans include a large share of income-restricted housing for sale or rent at below-market rates — which answers the community’s needs but reduces the profitability of any development on the site.

The latest failed plan involved a mix of lab space, income-restricted housing, and a museum. Since that proposal was hatched, though, the market for lab space in Greater Boston has deteriorated, and the developer was unable to attract financing before its authorization to develop the site ran out. In January, Wu stuck a fork in the project, describing it as a “pipe dream.”

In its place, Wu has proposed a sort of a real estate bank shot, taking advantage of the site’s proximity to Madison Park Technical Vocational High School, the city’s only vocational school.

Since well before the lab plan foundered, the city has been planning to build a new, modern Madison Park — a project that would benefit students across the city. But according to Wu, the school’s existing site made rebuilding there challenging.

“In our two years of looking at all the options for rebuilding the school, it became clear that working on a constrained parcel was going to dramatically increase the costs,” she said.

So she wants to redraw the boundaries of P-3, using some of the land for the new school — and, potentially, adding some acreage to P-3 after the old school is knocked down — and then use the brand new school to help attract private investment to the redrawn P-3.

“The order here is significant,” she said. “Getting Madison Park redeveloped as a world-class, top-notch feeder and pipeline will spark new interest” in the site, she said. Wu said the overall size of the reconfigured P-3 may end up being not very different from its current acreage, and that the exact boundary changes will depend on the final design of the high school.

Wu’s plan has run into opposition from neighborhood groups, who want to see job-creating commercial development on the P-3 site and bristled at what they saw as the lack of community consultation before Wu put Madison Park in the mix.

“People are disappointed because of the way the decision was made,” the area’s city councilor, the Rev. Miniard Culpepper, said. “We don’t have a lot of parcels that are ready for economic development.”

Culpepper says he wants the city to rebid the site. “Let different developers compete for that site, so we can get economic development done,” he said.

Wu says that’s likely just what will happen — after the borders are redrawn.

“We need to see what the boundaries actually look like and what the market will put forward at that point,” she said. Any use of the site at that point would go through all the normal community approval processes. She said the city would also be open to using public money to encourage economic development at the site.

Will Wu’s plan work? Maybe not: The reality is that the market is weak right now. It’s possible that even with a new Madison Park rising next door, no developer will be able to craft a plan that’s both financially viable and meets the neighborhood’s requirements for affordability.

But it’s hard to see a reason not to try — because development that meets the neighborhood’s needs has proven commercially nonviable under the current conditions, too.

At worst, Wu’s approach would leave the neighborhood right back where it started with P-3 — but with a nice new high school next door. At best, it will make the site attractive enough to private investors to finally unlock its long-wasted potential.

title: A costly labor mandate for Madison Park High School?
text:
When asked about the PLA, a spokesperson for the city wrote, “The City will pay workers the prevailing wage on the Madison Park project, like any other public construction project, as required by state law. By guaranteeing a steady supply of labor, the Project Labor Agreement helps to mitigate potential cost increases due to labor shortages or disputes.”

It’s hard to understand how excluding over 80 percent of the workforce will guarantee “a steady supply of labor.”

One need not look very far back to see the impact of PLAs in Massachusetts. In 2024, the Springfield Water and Sewer Commission decided it would use one to build a $325 million water filtration plant. As the project went out to bid, organizations representing nonunion contractors filed a lawsuit challenging the PLA.

In issuing an injunction to stop it, Hampden Superior Court Judge Michael Callan wrote, “The public benefits from an open, fair, competitive, and robust bidding process. The PLA requirement unnecessarily curtails that without legal justification.”

When the project was rebid without the PLA, the winning bid for electrical services alone was $15 million less than the one submitted under the PLA — a reduction of more than 35 percent.

The city’s Madison Park statement correctly notes that all employees on public projects — regardless of labor affiliation — earn the prevailing wage. PLA savings do not come from paying workers less.

Construction unions also argue that union work is of higher quality. But contractors must pass a state prequalification process to bid on public projects, and all trades workers in Massachusetts are subject to the same licensing, safety, and training requirements.

Perhaps the entities most harmed by PLAs are contractors of color and their employees — who remain overwhelmingly nonunion. In 2021, pro-union lawmakers had to set up a commission on participation by women and minority-owned firms — and bar bidders who had failed to hire enough such firms in the past — to secure a PLA on construction of a new Holyoke Soldiers’ Home.

During debate over the project, the Black Economic Council of Massachusetts wrote to legislative leaders arguing that PLAs usually require contractors to hire solely from union halls, where “most Black construction workers and other workers of color do not belong.”

Even pro-union elected officials are getting the message. In 2023, Governor Janet Mills of Maine, a Democrat, vetoed legislation that would have put PLAs on offshore wind projects, stating, “Most Maine workers in the construction industry — in fact, more than 90 percent — are not unionized. … [T]his could stifle competition, which could cut out thousands of workers and employee-owned businesses.”

The following year, Governor Gavin Newsom of California, a Democrat, vetoed a bill that would have put a PLA on a group of state university projects, writing, “The new requirements proposed in this bill could result in additional cost pressures that were not accounted for in this year’s budget.”

When public officials require Boston taxpayers to unnecessarily come up with more than 100 million extra dollars to build a school, you can’t help but wonder whether their commitment to fiscal responsibility amounts to anything more than lip service.

title: Why is this year’s St. Patrick’s Day parade going the opposite way? The answer goes back to 1776.
text:
Sound familiar? You’d be excused for forgetting that in years past, the parade kicked off at the Broadway MBTA Station and headed southeast, turning around up City Point, before heading west through Telegraph Hill and ending at Andrew.

Unless you’re particularly concerned about watching the parade go left-to-right rather than right-to-left, it may not seem like much of a change. (The one “real” change is an extra stretch tacked on to the end of the parade, a few blocks past the Broadway MBTA Station on A Street.)

But some locals are welcoming the decision — and, given the 250th anniversary of Evacuation Day (the withdrawal of British troops from Boston in 1776), celebrating its historical implications.

“The residents of Andrew Square are thrilled about this,” said Linda Zablocki, president of the Andrew Square Civic Association.

For starters, Zablocki said, it’s a return to tradition. Originally, the parade kicked off in Andrew Square and worked its way north toward Broadway. It was reversed in 1988 to start on Broadway and head south, the Globe reported.

But the change is especially poignant given that this St. Patrick’s Day will also be the 250th anniversary of Evacuation Day — the day the British army fled the city of Boston on March 17, 1776.

Over the winter of 1775–76, dozens of cannons captured from the British at Fort Ticonderoga in upstate New York were hauled over the Berkshires and across Massachusetts. George Washington, commander of the Continental Army, used the cannons to fortify the Dorchester Heights, atop what is now South Boston’s Telegraph Hill.

Under the cover of darkness, the colonists dragged the cannons from Roxbury to the peak of the heights. In the process, they marched through an area identified as the modern Andrew Square, up what are now Dorchester and Telegraph Streets — a march that closely mirrors the new climb of the parade.

“If that hadn’t happened, we’d all be speaking in a British accent right now,” Zablocki said.

City Councilor Ed Flynn, who represents the neighborhood, said the change was “fitting and proper” for the occasion, especially given the build-up to the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence later this year.

“We’re proud of our history in South Boston, and we recognize the historic time we’re in and the contributions made up at Dorchester Heights,” Flynn said. “It’s about celebrating not only Boston history, but American history.”

Flynn said that residents of Andrew Square had petitioned for the change in light of the anniversary, and that parade organizers viewed it as a “fair request.”

The South Boston Allied War Veterans Council, which runs the parade, did not immediately return a request for comment on Wednesday.

Zablocki also suggested the change would contribute to a more orderly atmosphere in Andrew Square; rowdiness, she said, tends to be worse at the end of the parade route than at the start.

“But that’s a problem everywhere in the city,” she added.

The St. Patrick’s Day parade, which has historically drawn roughly a million people into the city, has gained a mixed reputation among South Boston residents. Past parades have been criticized for rampant drinking, violent brawls, and other displays of public indecency.

That’s been the case for years — as far back as the 1970s, residents were bemoaning public drinking, the Globe reported. In 2016, then-Mayor Marty Walsh tried to shorten the parade route in the name of public safety, but his efforts were blocked by a federal judge who ordered the city to allow the event to proceed along its typical route.

Last year, police warned there would be “zero tolerance” for misconduct at the parade. Flynn acknowledged that the 2025 festivities were an improvement from previous years.

“We’re preparing and continuing to meet with city, state and federal officials,” he said. “This is not a Mardi Gras atmosphere.”

This year, parade organizers have also added a specific-place for “family-friendly viewing,” at Medal of Honor Park along Broadway.

“We wanted to make sure that families, and [especially] our military families, are respected,” Flynn said. “And that there’s an opportunity for them to watch the parade in a safe and healthy environment.”

The parade won’t be the only commemoration of Evacuation Day. On March 17, a procession of re-enactors and public figures will march through South Boston and re-dedicate the Dorchester Heights monument, a spokesperson announced on Tuesday.

The event, the spokesperson said, will culminate in celebratory cannon fire.

title: Boston to keep three MBTA bus routes free to ride through June, but long-term plan is unclear
text:
Wu extended the program for another two years in February 2024, again using federal COVID-19 funds to reimburse the MBTA about $340,000 per month for the program through the beginning of this March.

City officials said they have not spent all of the federal money they initially allocated to extend the program two years ago, leaving enough to fund the pilot through June.

But its future beyond that remains in jeopardy. The city, which is already facing budget challenges, has not publicly identified a sustainable funding source that could replace the dwindling federal money. On Friday, Wu’s office said the city is “discussing the long-term future of the program with the MBTA.”

The mayor had previously hoped that the results of the pilot program would spur the MBTA to fund and expand fare-free service. But the cash-strapped agency is staring down its own massive budget deficit, making any fare revenue it can bring in all the more important.

In a statement released by Wu’s office, MBTA general manager Phil Eng said the T has been “pleased to be able to support the City of Boston’s program,” but he did not indicate whether it would, or could, help extend the program past June.

A T spokesperson declined further comment Friday.

Speaking to reporters at unrelated event Friday, Wu did not clarify whether Boston intends to allocate money for the program in its budget for the next fiscal year. She said she has spoken with Governor Healey’s administration to discuss funding sources for the fare-free program.

“Free bus service is the best capitalist investment that you could make, because every transaction that is being made on that bus plugs directly back into our economy,” Wu said. “We’ll have to see how to make everything fit [in the city’s next budget], and whether there’s a way to come to some shared arrangement that recognizes how valuable the service has been for the MBTA overall.”

Uncertainty over what will happen to the program come July is raising anxiety among transit experts and advocates who want to see the city and the MBTA make the fare-free service permanent.

“We have been steadily gaining speed here, and we all know what happens when you slam the brakes,” said Seth Gadbois, a transportation attorney for Conservation Law Foundation, an environmental advocacy nonprofit. “The people who feel that whiplash first are low-income riders. So whatever the long-term [solution] is, these programs need to continue beyond the summer.”

Reggie Ramos, the executive director of transit nonprofit Transportation for Massachusetts, called the four-month extension a “reprieve.”

But she argued that Wu and other city officials have not publicly outlined a long-term plan, both for the fare-free program and the city’s other stated transportation priorities, such as the rollout of bike and bus lanes. Advocates say they also have not gotten any updates on other major transit projects, including plans to upgrade Columbia Road and Hyde Park Avenue.

“I cannot overstate how dismal outreach and community engagement has been from the city since late last year,” said Ramos. “Seeing all these safety infrastructure [projects] being unattended, being folded up, or taken away … is really, really disheartening, especially for a mayor who ran on a transportation platform.”

Implementing the fare-free pilot program in her first term was a key political victory and a marquee accomplishment for Wu, who has long championed providing fare-free transit.

Phineas Baxandall, director of research and policy analysis for the Massachusetts Budget and Policy Center, said what skeptics scoffed at as a “pie-in-the-sky promise” has been meaningful in the city.

“It had real results for a lot of people, and has been a model around the country,” he said.

Wu said Friday that ridership on the three free routes grew by 35 percent in the first year of the pilot, and ridership on all three is 16 percent higher than it was before the pandemic. Wu has also said that eliminating fares has also helped make boarding faster.

Analysis by the research and advocacy group TransitMatters, though, shows that the 23 and 28 buses ranked among the T’s slowest routes in 2024.

MBTA ridership largely plummeted during the pandemic. But in a March 2023 report, the city said ridership on the 23 and 29 buses rebounded sharply after the routes went fare free, recovering at a faster clip than the bus system as a whole.

The 2023 city report also notes that the vast majority of surveyed riders on the fare-free lines already took the bus before fares were removed, and about three quarters of respondents said they would’ve taken the bus even if they had to pay.

About 5 percent of respondents said they forewent cars trips because the bus was free.

Experts said eliminating fares on public transit produces a number of benefits, from increased ridership, to faster travel times. It also makes it easier for lower-income people to get around the city, whether for work, to see family or friends, or get to doctor’s appointments.

“People ride more when it’s cheaper. … that means improving their mobility, giving them opportunities to go places and do things, participate in life,“ said Peter Furth, a professor of civil and environmental engineering at Northeastern University. “​​The impact [of fare-free transit] is enriching people’s lives, it’s promoting economic inclusion."

Furth said he would like to see the city’s fare-free program continue, and expanded to additional bus routes, either paid for or subsidized by the MBTA.

The MBTA would not likely agree to that, said Brian Kane, executive director of the MBTA Advisory Board.

“Nothing’s free, someone always pays for it,” Kane said. “Given the fiscal conditions that the T is operating under, it’s just not money they can forgo, even on bus alone.”

He emphasized that the MBTA already offers cheaper fares to eligible riders. The T’s standard one-way bus fare is $1.70, but low-income and other eligible riders can qualify for a lower rate of 85 cents.

While the financial relief provided by the fare-free program could seem minor, for some, like Grove Hall resident Nico Nixon, every dollar matters.

“It helps people,” especially those scraping by, Nixon said. He spoke to the Globe while riding a 28 bus headed to Ruggles Station on Thursday morning, before the city announced it was extending the fare-free pilot.

Nixon said he was in between jobs and had come from visiting family.

“Obviously, I want all the buses free,” he said. “But let’s not get ahead of ourselves.”

title: The Boston accent melts her heart
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

Working in news can be kind of a bummer these days. Our democracy is teetering. New Epstein revelations besiege us daily. The weather is cold and gray.

Enter 84-year-old Sid McDonough, with one charming voicemail.

McDonough was the first reader to respond via voicemail to a recent piece by the Globe’s Beth Teitell documenting the death of the Boston accent. Assuming it would be a hotly debated topic, I invited readers to ring us up. But I was worried, with so much else going on, no one would actually call.

“Hi!” a cheerful gravely voice rang out on my laptop speakers. “I’m one of the few people I know who still drinks tonic.” (My colleague Rob DeCola, who made this all possible by lending his North Reading accent to our Boston Globe accent tip line, tells me that “tonic” is what old school Mass. natives call “soda.”)

“When I was in the Navy 60-odd years ago … my shipmates made fun of my accent, and I tried to lose it,” recalled McDonough, who grew up in various Boston suburbs before taking up residence in North Weymouth for 43 years. “After I got out and came back home, I realized my accent was a treasure.”

Reader, my battered heart melted.

It liquified further as more voicemails streamed in, nearly 50 in all, from as far away as California and Florida. The theme of almost all these messages was intense affection and pride for their accents.

" It’s sad to think that the Boston accent is disappearing. It’s like a warm Dunkin’ regular on a wicked cold day,” shared one reader. “Go Sox!”

A former Children’s Hospital nurse shared how a colleague once told her that every time she opened her mouth, she “sounded stupid.” She then told him that every time he opened his mouth, “he sounded like he was from New York, which was worse.” (Caller, I think we could be great friends.)

“I love my accent,” the retired nurse continued. “My father was a firefighter in Boston. My mother grew up in Roxbury. We all had Boston accents.”

Listening to these funny and moving messages, I understood better that the Boston accent is a symbol of family connection, a sense of identity and tied to place, a community. “If you put me in a room with kids I grew up with, it comes back instantly,” noted one reader.

Losing that generational link makes some native speakers sad. “It literally kills me,” mourned Katherine Loftus, the proud daughter of a Southie resident featured in Beth’s story, as she considered her kids lacking her distinctive R-less dialect.

Boston-born Stephanie McCloud connected her beloved accent to a broader regional ethos. “I love it, and I’m very proud of our take-no-prisoners type of attitude, and strong New Englanders who say what we think … but whenever we are friends, we’re friends for life.”

To someone like me, who moved four times by the time I was 14, that sort of geographic identity is downright alien.

I felt delight listening to these voicemails, waking up and listening to them immediately and sharing the best quotes with my colleagues. A reader named Leslie shared that once in Florida, “the girl behind the countah” asked her what country she was from. She loved it.

Frankly, this I’m-gonna-tell-you-exactly-what-I-think and be-exactly-who-I-am attitude is a balm in these confusing times.

So consider this my love letter to Greater Bostonians, with or without accents. I may not be one of you by birth, but I am in spirit, and the way my 8-year-old pronounces “mirrah” proves it.

Let me leave you with a few lines of the poem by Daria, a Roxbury native who wanted to correct those who “think there are no African Americans with Boston accents.”

Out of bed at half past six

grab onto your Dunkin’ fix.

Check the piggybank for quarters,

drive the rotary like martyrs.

We’ll ask about your mother.

Don’t start about your brother.

To hear Daria recite her whole poem in her beautiful accent, along with a selection of other voicemails we received, check out our collection here.

And I’ll keep checking the voicemail — (617) 798-0874 — to see if any of you share more anecdotes.

Read: How much longer will the music of the Boston accent linger?
