title: At Boston’s snow farms, blizzards meet a watery end
text:
Few people in Eastern Massachusetts and Rhode Island might share that sentiment, following two big, recent storms that have made this winter the snowiest in Boston in a decade. But more might be on the way early next week.

Thanks to the mechanical melters, thousands of truckloads of the white stuff have been transformed almost instantaneously into water at 14 “snow farms” from Hyde Park to East Boston.

“This is a tool in our tool kit now,” said Nick Gove, the city’s interim chief of streets. “And we’re going on the second decade of that. Both the state and the city got into snow farms in a big way in 2015,” which was known as “Snowmageddon.”

In that winter, which brought a record-breaking 110 inches of snow to the city, a snow farm in the Seaport in South Boston famously did not see its last clump of dirty slush disappear until July.

Gove doesn’t think Boston is due for a repeat, but he does believe the final bits of months-old snow will not become a puddle until late April.

“It’s been a long week, a long month,” Gove, who had been roaming the city, said in an interview from his car.

Despite the heavy snow this year, Gove said, the city has not had to ask the state for permission to dump any into Boston Harbor, a practice banned by the state Department of Environmental Protection in 1997. However, at the snow farms the melt is funneled down storm drains, which lead to a system that sometimes can get overwhelmed and discharge into rivers and streams.

Even for the harbor, officials left room for emergency exceptions.

“If we were to get another blizzard this size,” Gove said, “we would potentially be looking to ask” for that option.

By midafternoon Friday, the city had hauled 3,587 truckloads of snow, or approximately 59,344 cubic yards, to snow farms at locations ranging from Bunker Hill Community College in Charlestown, to the former Bayside Expo Center in Dorchester, to the old Edison power plant in South Boston.

The number of farms still being used has dropped by one, to 13, said Anne Roach, spokeswoman for the city’s streets department.

Front-end loaders, backhoes, and 10-wheel dump trucks have been put to work, Gove said, in an expensive, days-long effort to haul the snow to a medley of city, state, and privately owned sites.

The snow farms are dispersed throughout Boston to shorten the haul routes from each neighborhood. And with 802 miles of roadways, easier access to the snow farms makes a difference, Gove said as a warmer sun shined Friday.

“We’re now getting a good assist from Mother Nature — a lot of solar melt, which is a big help,” Gove said.

In West Roxbury off the VFW Parkway, the melter has been chugging away. Plenty of work had been done there by Friday afternoon, and plenty remained. A wall of snow about 400 feet long and 20 feet high waited for its quick transformation to liquid.

In a nonstop routine, a backhoe returned over and over to pluck bulging chunks of speckled snow from a steep, gray mound. Within minutes, the snow had been dumped into the melting tub, only to leave a minute later as a gushing stream of water.

A truck with reserves of diesel fuel was stationed nearby to keep the melter running.

“They’re very, very efficient,” O’Connor said, nodding toward an 80-ton-an-hour guzzler humming away in front of him.

Put in too much snow at once, O’Connor said, and an oversize load could gum up the works. Make it a bit less bulky, and the result will be a smoothly running, snow-chomping success.

“You’ve got to be patient,” O’Connor said.

Kevin Walsh of the Boston Water and Sewer Commission stopped by Friday to inspect the operation — an unending cycle of dump, melt, repeat — and took a few photographs.

“We’re making sure it goes into the storm drains,” said Walsh, adding that erosion-control measures are in place at each of the snow farms.

O’Connor said that a second melter was expected at the site, and that the melting would continue into the night. If all went well, O’Connor said, the rest of the snow might be gone this weekend.

And when might he sleep? “When we can.”

title: State revives long-stalled plans to redevelop Shattuck Hospital site at Franklin Park
text:
On Thursday evening, nearly 100 residents from neighborhoods bordering Franklin Park — including Jamaica Plain, Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan — poured into the Brooke High School auditorium in Mattapan for the first in a series of state-led public listening sessions on the future of the Shattuck Hospital campus.

Residents brought a range of competing visions for the site. Some want to restore the entire tree-lined expanse to open green space, with a meadow lined with paths to walk dogs and relax. Others propose new housing for seniors or military veterans. Still others long for a recreation center with a pool or ice rink, a place to socialize and help keep youths off the streets. Suggestions have also included a community garden, an urgent care clinic, and a 24-hour pharmacy.

For their part, officials in the Healey administration said they are committed to hearing all viewpoints and have no set plans for the site, effectively restarting community outreach efforts that began in 2018. But the Shattuck grounds are restricted under a 1949 state law for “public health” uses, and the state has already said it plans to issue a new request for proposals focused on supportive housing, a service that helps people out of homelessness and addiction by pairing stable housing with counseling, case management, and employment assistance.

For many residents who live next to the 527-acre Franklin Park, long considered the crown jewel of Frederick Law Olmsted’s network of public parks known as the Emerald Necklace, any proposal with the words “supportive housing” is a nonstarter.

“It’s going to be a fight,” said Louis Elisa, 76, who lives next to Franklin Park and heads the Roxbury-based Garrison-Trotter Neighborhood Association, during one of his regular walks through the park on Wednesday. “There is deep distrust that the state truly cares what people who live here think.”

Much of this distrust traces back to the last round of community discussions about what to do with the Shattuck site.

The state had called for 75 to 100 supportive housing units when it requested proposals in June 2021 for redeveloping the Shattuck. But the state received just one response, from a coalition of nonprofits led by Boston Medical Center. At 370 pages, that bid far surpassed expectations: It called for 446 treatment and emergency shelter beds and 405 units of supportive housing for individuals and families, as well as outpatient programs serving up to 400 people a day.

The grandiose plan faltered in part because of its size and timing. It was introduced amid mounting community reports of open-air drug use and discarded needles along the western edge of Franklin Park. Neighborhood groups largely blamed those problems on the 2022 opening of an 18-unit cottage village on the hospital grounds for people experiencing homelessness and addiction, arguing that the new housing drew illicit drug use to the park.

Public safety concerns were also heightened after Jean McGuire, a 91-year-old civil rights pioneer who was the first Black woman elected to the Boston School Committee, was stabbed multiple times in the fall of 2022 while walking her dog at the park. McGuire survived but the assailant was never caught.

The BMC-led plan also drew criticism from some addiction treatment specialists, who argued that housing hundreds of patients in one location was not therapeutic and echoed the outdated practice of isolating people in large state institutions, disconnected from society and support networks.

The state’s Executive Office of Health and Human Services said in a statement Wednesday that the earlier proposal, which would have cost $550 million, is “no longer feasible” because the BMC-led coalition behind the project was not able to identify a viable funding model.

Meanwhile, the state will work to relocate the Shattuck’s 268 medical and psychiatric beds to the East Newton Pavilion, a large medical facility in Boston’s South End that is under construction, in 2027.

Many residents still fear the state seeks to transform the land beside the storied Franklin Park into a catch-all repository for the city’s intersecting struggles with homelessness, untreated mental illness, and addiction.

“We are not against services and supports, but we are against dumping people behind a treasured park,” said Renee Stacey Welch, whose family has lived next to Franklin Park for five decades and is chair of the Jamaica Plain Neighborhood Council. “Who wants to live next to a community of active drug users?”

At the forum on Thursday, tensions occasionally flared as residents and park lovers sparred with several advocates pushing for more housing for those battling addiction, with speakers sometimes shouting at each other across the room. The debate carried on in the high school parking lot long after the meeting adjourned. “Why do all these programs have to be concentrated near our park?” said Shawn Nelson, a Roxbury resident, his frustration evident.

A coalition representing some 600 residents living near Franklin Park came to Thursday’s meeting armed with data and detailed maps of Boston showing their communities shouldering a disproportionate share of the city’s homeless housing.

Those residents had identified 167 facilities in Boston that provide supportive housing for people with substance use disorders, and estimate 70 percent of them are in the neighborhoods bordering Franklin Park. As a percentage of their population, the park’s adjacent neighborhoods have nearly five times as many supportive housing units as predominantly white neighborhoods of Boston, they calculated.

“We are witnessing a new form of geographic redlining: the hyper-concentration of statewide social burdens in majority-minority neighborhoods,” said Rory Coffey, a resident of Jamaica Plain and founder of the Coalition for Region-wide Services Beyond Franklin Park, or CORES, which did the property analysis. “True equity means every community in the state acts as a partner in recovery, so no single corridor is forced to become a sacrifice zone.”

Several members of a separate community coalition — which is calling for at least 200 units of supportive housing and substance use recovery services at the Shattuck site — also spoke up at the hearing. Wearing purple shirts saying “Our Neighbors Are Dying!,” they described the toll of the overdose crisis and the critical shortage of long-term supports for people struggling to maintain their recovery.

Shameeka Moreno, an addiction counselor from Dorchester and member of the coalition, described how access to supportive housing could have prevented the overdose death in 2023 of her 43-year-old cousin, who had long struggled with cocaine and alcohol addiction and was chronically homeless. “The number of people dying because they lack adequate support systems is astronomical,” Moreno said. “The situation is dire.”

Some of the community’s opposition to supportive housing is rooted in Franklin Park’s long history, and the way state and local officials have carved it up over time for various uses. Beyond the Shattuck Hospital, the park is home to a zoo, a large golf course, and a city parks maintenance yard.

Moreover, the city’s plan to redevelop the aging White Stadium on the other side of Franklin Park into a 10,000-seat stadium for a professional soccer team has upset some neighbors and park advocates, who argue it is an inappropriate infringement; conservationists are concerned it will lead to the removal of more than 140 trees from the park.

Today, 40 percent of Franklin Park’s land is inaccessible for free public use, according to the Emerald Necklace Conservancy, a nonprofit park stewardship group.

Former state senator Dianne Wilkerson, who lives a mile from Franklin Park in Dorchester, fondly remembers walking the park’s paths with her two young sons and taking in the vibrant colors of the annual Caribbean and kite festivals. On summer days, her children would fly their own kites and mingle with the men playing dominoes on the benches.

“That park has meant everything to this community, and we deserve a voice in shaping what happens here,” Wilkerson said.

State Representative Chris Worrell, a Democrat from Dorchester, has been among those pushing for a statewide strategy for addressing the critical shortfall of supportive housing.

“We want beautiful things too,“ Worrell said, referring to some of the ideas being floated for the Shattuck site. ”It’s not that my community is against [supportive housing] — but we already are bearing the brunt of it."

title: Life expectancy for Bostonians is increasing, but not for Black residents, new report shows
text:
In 2023, the city of Boston sounded the alarm over a stark 23-year life expectancy gap between people who live in Roxbury compared to those in Back Bay. A broader examination of the issue now shows a widening gap between all of Boston’s Black residents and other racial and ethnic groups — growing from 3.3 years to almost seven years in the past decade — according to new data from the Boston Public Health Commission.

At a press conference last week, Mayor Michelle Wu and public health officials announced the city is investing $2 million toward medical screenings and other preventative programs, including the launching of a Black Men’s Health Activation Summit in June, to help solve the issue.

“We cannot claim Boston as a beacon of health care, while entire communities are left in the dark,” Wu said at the Yawkey Boys and Girls Club in Roxbury. “A beacon that only shines for some is not beacon at all.”

The commission’s “Closing the Gap” report is part of Boston’s Long Live and Well agenda that studies how systemic racism has created a public health crisis. Public Health Commissioner Dr. Bisola Ojikutu said Boston’s health disparities have been longstanding and haven’t been updated since the Roxbury-Back Bay report in 2023.

“We promised to look very deeply at our data across the city,” Ojikutu said in an interview with the Globe. “This is part of fulfilling that promise.”

The new report found that while overall life expectancy in Boston has increased, it has declined for Black residents. According to the data, Black women in Boston had an average life expectancy of 80 years between 2022 and 2024, roughly six years lower than women of other races and ethnicities during the same timeframe. Black men had the lowest life expectancy of any major demographic group at 72 years, more than nine years lower than men of other racial groups.

Ojikutu said the findings are especially concerning because modeling shows the disparity will persist without major intervention.

“If we take no meaningful additional action to reduce inequities, 10 years from now the life expectancy gap will remain the same,” Ojikutu said during the press conference.

Ojikutu said there are three leading factors contributing to the gap: unintentional drug overdose; preventable and screenable cancers such as breast, colon, and prostate; and cardiometabolic diseases like heart disease and diabetes.

Last week, Wu announced a partnership with the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, in which Boston will invest $1 million to expand cancer screening and other prevention efforts in Black communities. The city is also committing an additional $1 million through the public health commission to support organizations focused on improving Black men’s health outcomes.

City leaders also introduced the creation of the Live Long And Well Advisory Council, composed of 30 community leaders from health care, nonprofit, and civic sectors. The council will help guide the city’s goal of eliminating race- and neighborhood-based life expectancy gaps by 2035.

Richard Claytor, 71, a member of the new council, said the research must focus on accountability, then lead to actual results.

“The goal for this group is to really put in something that sounds like the implementation of the recommendations, and follow up to make sure that all of the parties who are involved and engaged understand what the mission is,” Claytor said.

Community members in attendance said they hope the report leads to lasting change.

Saundra Owens-Skerrett, 77, of Roxbury said screenings are the main solution to help solve the life expectancy dilemma.

“We can now get all the help that we need from our doctors,” Skerrett said. “Years ago, we didn’t have the opportunity to get that type of coverage, and that’s how you can prevent or extend your life by getting things done early.”

A longer, more technical version of the report will be released in the coming months, along with additional studies “addressing unique challenges and health needs of diverse populations across our city,” Wu said.

Aayushi Datta can be reached at aayushi.datta@globe.com.

title: Mapping Boston: See how neighborhoods differ in race, income, and housing
text:
Dorchester remains by far the largest Boston neighborhood in both population and land area, with more than 126,000 residents — nearly a fifth of Boston’s total population. The next most populous neighborhood, Roxbury, has fewer than half as many residents, at roughly 50,000. Bay Village is the smallest, with about 1,600.

For this analysis, the Globe used neighborhood boundaries created by the city that align with census tracts, allowing for more precise comparisons across communities.

While Boston has been a majority-minority city since the turn of the century, many of its neighborhoods remain racially segregated, the latest data show.

In Mattapan, roughly 92 percent of residents identify as people of color, including about 70 percent who identify as Black. The overall racial composition has remained relatively stable over the past decade, though the neighborhood has seen growth in Haitian and Latino immigrant communities.

East Boston has the highest share of Latino residents, at just over half of its population. It also has by far the highest share of residents who identify as multiracial — about 43 percent, more than twice the next-highest neighborhood, Dorchester.

By contrast, the North End and Beacon Hill have the highest shares of white residents, each at nearly 90 percent.

Massachusetts is the richest state in the country, but Boston’s prosperity is unevenly distributed. The share of households earning more than $200,000 a year — the top income tier in census data — varies widely.

The Seaport, also known as the South Boston Waterfront, has the highest concentration of high-income households, with more than 40 percent earning above that threshold. The neighborhood is also one of Boston’s fastest-growing areas, filled with luxury towers, high-end offices, and new retail development.

Buildings in the Seaport account for roughly one-tenth of Boston’s property tax base. But rising sea levels and increasing flood risk threaten that concentration of wealth.

South Boston and Charlestown were long considered working-class neighborhoods, but now rank close behind Seaport in the share of wealthy residents — a dramatic transformation in recent decades. Mission Hill and Longwood have the lowest shares of high earners.

The share of children has been declining for years in Boston and across Massachusetts, contributing to a drop of about 70,000 public school students over the past two decades — an 8 percent decline statewide.

The highest concentrations of residents under 18 are clustered in the southern part of the city, including Dorchester, Mattapan, and West Roxbury, where children make up just over 20 percent of the population.

Longwood has the smallest share of children, at about 2.7 percent, along with other neighborhoods closer to downtown, such as the North End and Back Bay.

More than six in 10 housing units in Boston are renter-occupied, and renters are especially concentrated in the city’s densest and most student-heavy neighborhoods.

In Chinatown, more than 90 percent of occupied housing units are renter-occupied — the highest share in the city. Allston and Fenway are close behind.

In contrast, more residential neighborhoods on the city’s outskirts, including Hyde Park and West Roxbury, have renter shares of 40 percent or less.

Boston’s population has fluctuated in recent years, particularly during the COVID pandemic, but several neighborhoods have seen large infusions of Asian and Latino residents that are reshaping parts of the city.

Chinatown and East Boston have the highest shares of foreign-born residents — about 51 percent and 45 percent, respectively. In Chinatown, many foreign-born residents are of Asian origin; in East Boston, most are Latino.

Material from prior Globe stories was used in this report.

title: Photo gallery: High school tournaments firmly in spotlight
text:
STUDENT PHOTOJOURNALISM PROGRAM

Photo gallery: High school tournaments firmly in spotlight

Now this is what March is all about, athletes in all sports competing to be the best. Some might call it madness, but for high school sports fans across Massachusetts, it sure is a lot of fun.

With so much action happening each night, the readers are the big winners because the students involved in the Globe’s unique photojournalism program are on the scene, too.

Many of their pictures have already been featured in the Globe’s daily high school roundups, but they have submitted dozens more over the last week. Here below in this week’s photo gallery are more than 50 photos from games across the state, all taken by 17 student photographers.

The Globe’s sports photojournalism program is open to any Massachusetts high school student. It’s free to join and runs throughout the school year. To get started, just fill out the interest form here.

title: ‘Say It Loud’ at the ICA showcases art produced by Black artists in a historic Boston program
text:
Getting this far wasn’t easy, and neither is it all rosy right now for the African American Masters Artists in Residence Program, currently resident in a disheveled Jamaica Plain warehouse owned by its apparently-grudging, founding patron, Northeastern University. But let’s not let a relationship gone south sour a moment to be savored. There’s a story here, of determination, resilience, and no small amount of joy, and that’s where it starts.

“Dana Smiles,” a photo portrait of Dana Chandler — sun-drenched, mouth wide in toothy exuberance, eyes closed in genuine contentment, which hangs alongside the title wall, a tribute to the group’s founding firebrand. A living keeper of its history, he died late last year, after working closely with the ICA’s Jeff DeBlois putting the show together.

The photo, by Reggie Jackson, a member of AAMARP’s founding cohort in 1977 and now its executive director, is a direct line to the promise of early days: taken in 1976, when AAMARP was about to be born. Chandler, fast becoming the face of a rising community of Black artist-activists, was on the verge of willing it into being. An alliance with Northeastern’s Gregory Ricks, the director of its John D. O’Bryant African American Institute, would lead to many thousands of square feet in a university-owned warehouse, where AAMARP began its journey on Chandler’s foundational principles: to create space for Black artists in Boston, and to nurture a culture largely ignored by the city’s major institutions.

But Chandler — brash, gregarious, tireless, charming — found alliances all over. The early galleries establish the broad stage he set. One of the first pieces in the show is his “Pan-African Man‚” a sparse 1970 painting of a Black man in silhouette. Inside his head, his brain is neatly portioned into the three colors of the Pan-African flag: red, black, and green. Right next to the painting hangs Arnold Trachtman’s “Spirit of ’76 (Louise Day Hicks and Ted Landsmark),” from 1979, a kaleidoscopic, dark pop-art vision of the clash between Black and white during the city’s busing crisis. Hicks, a zealously anti-school-integration politician, looms crone-like over the scene. Landsmark, now a distinguished professor of public policy at Northeastern and a long-time civil rights champion, was the victim in the famous flagpole-lancing photograph taken at Boston City Hall in 1976. Trachtman was not Black, but his allegiance was clear. For Chandler and the AAMARP, the price of admission was radical politics and a hunger for justice. That much remains: L’Merchie Frazier’s “Ericka Huggins: Liberation Groceries,” 2019, is a recent take on a Black Panther Party luminary, cast in silky synthetics.

AAMARP has always toggled smoothly between art and politics; the exhibition is a vivid frame for turbulent local civic and political history across at least a couple of generations. One of the best works here is by Wen-ti Tsen, a Chinese-American artist and AAMARP confrere; called “Peaceable Kingdom,” 1971, its epic unfolds in multiple scenes across three hinged wooden panels. Inside, his take on the Quaker artist Edward Hicks’s famous vision of earthly harmony between man and beast. Framing it are eruptions of violent unrest: a murder suspect in the killing of three civil rights workers in Mississippi; American soldiers brutalizing a Vietnamese commando; another Vietnamese soldier, captured, confined, and howling in pain.

The piece first showed at the AAMARP because, really, where else? Tsen had lost his job teaching at the School of the Museum of Fine Arts because of his political bent, a reminder that within a city that prided itself on a veneer of gentility and intellectual heft, rougher notions of dissent were simply not welcome.

The city’s counter-cultural community found a home at the AAMARP where it could not anywhere else. For years, it thrived, holding exhibitions, performances, lectures, gatherings, and hosting Black luminaries from all over. Artmaking was its constant. Established senior artists like John Wilson and Allan Rohan Crite offered support and guidance. In a lovely moment here, Crite, a beloved painter of the everyday of Black Boston in Roxbury and the South End, lends his no-nonsense social realist style to a quilt-making collaboration with Susan Thompson. “Freedom, Justice, Equality,” 1989-2012, a bright scene of a street protest, is a marriage of their priorities and talents. Jackson, too, looked up to Crite; as the older artist made “An Artist’s Sketchbook of the South End: A Walking Tour about Black People” in 1977, Jackson photographed the same scenes and later superimposed them with images of sacred African objects to confer history and connection.

In art as in life, there’s a rupture here. In 1993, when Northeastern slashed AAMARP’s budget and fired Chandler, he made a 5,000-edition newsprint piece making a case for its value. It’s on view here too, its yellowed pages simmering with accusation and rage. In one glaringindictment, Chandler accuses the school of using AAMARP as a way to burnish its image among communities of color.

Northeastern left the program with free space but little else. In 2018, it changed the locks overnight and moved to evict them. Only an intervention by Mayor Marty Walsh stopped it, and the group remains in the building. But a palpable unease lingers, and a path forward together seems unlikely.

“Say It Loud” overflows with compelling, captivating, overlooked cultural history here. Remarkable works from its stored past are too many to count, and pull at the threads of a Boston that once was. A gathering of ebony-black felted soft sculptural figures in tribal finery by Barbara Ward have been revived here from their debut in a shop window at Filene’s Basement in the 1980s, put there as an anti-racism statement by the city’s Young Woman’s Christian Association. The epic scale of Bryan McFarlane’s “I Dream of African Souls,” 1986, is a somber ode to the ruptures of diaspora that were at the time just becoming fertile intellectual ground for artists and scholars both.

Even so, it all made me worry for its future. McFarlane has been a member of AAMARP since 1983, when a parallel cultural world was still much needed for Black artists mostly ignored by the mainstream. AAMARP “played an invaluable role in healing our communities of color,” reads a quote from McFarlane on the wall near his work. But what about now? That’s what AAMARP, in 2026, needs to figure out. In the exhibition’s last phases, next generation members of the group like Marlon Forrester and Khalid Kodi are on view, a hint at a future obscured by uncertainty.

Forrester makes powerful mixed-media work; his “Warrior Dance,” 2014, sets a sword-wielding figure amid a prismatic storm of abstract fields. Kodi’s work here is brand new, and makes a case: “Excessive Narrative: Echoes of Eden,” he calls it, made in 2025, a vibrant tableaux of bodies in fluid communion with rivers of shadow and color. It seethes with unease, but is just as certainly vital, dynamic, alive. The show may cover AAMARP, 1977 to now, but the question it asks is the real issue, hanging heavy in the air: What next?

SAY IT LOUD: AAMARP, 1977 TO NOW

Through Aug. 2. Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100,icaboston.org

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
SNÖÖPER Since 2019, this Nashville duo have been one of punk’s most gloriously odd presences, filling releases like last year’s “Worldwide” with brief, barbed cuts that delight in their in-the-red unpredictability. They open for Kalamazoo-birthed garage-punk lifers the Spits. March 7, 7 p.m. Middle East Upstairs, Cambridge. 617-864-3278, mideastoffers.com

VENDREDI SUR MER Swiss singer-songwriter Charline Simone Rosemonde Mignot makes pop gems that are both sonically chilly and alluringly cool — her latest album, “Malabar Princess,” includes the shimmery pop strut “Lola les yeux fermés,” the plush and detailed existential lament “J’irai en enfer,” and the spiky “Tout résonee.” March 7, 8 p.m. The Sinclair, Cambridge. 617-547-5200, sinclaircambridge.com

AMBER MARK “Pretty Idea,” the latest album from this soulful singer-songwriter, is a love letter to R&B’s evolution over the last few decades; selections like the bouncy pop-funk duet with polymath Anderson .Paak “Don’t Remind Me” and the strummy memory-lane trip “Cherry Reds” showcase her strong voice and savvy songwriting. March 8, 8 p.m. Royale. 617-338-7699, royaleboston.com

MAURA K. JOHNSTON

TÉADA Irish trad powerhouse Téada, which has been at it for a quarter-century now, brings its music to the ongoing Belleville Roots Music Series just ahead of St. Patrick’s Day.March 7, 2 p.m., 7 p.m. $40. Belleville Congregational Church, 300 High St., Newburyport. 978-503-7668.www.bellevilleroots.org

CHARLEY CROCKETT This prolific, dyed-in-the-wool country traditionalist is in the middle of releasing what he calls the “Sagebrush Trilogy,” three thematically linked albums that focus on “the wanderer” (“Lonesome Drifter”), “the rustler” (“Dollar a Day”), and “the outlaw” (“Age of the Ram,” coming out in April). March 8, 8 p.m. $49.50 and up. Roadrunner, 89 Guest St. 888-929-7849.www.axs.com

EILEN JEWELL While former Boston-area resident Jewell long since moved back to her native Idaho, she has frequently returned to play music that draws on country, folk, gospel, rockabilly, and more with ease. But she has announced that this could be the last visit for a while and maybe for always. That definitely puts some moment in this show. March 12, 7:30 p.m. $37. Bull Run Restaurant, 215 Great Road, Shirley. 978-425-4311.www.bullrunrestaurant.com

STUART MUNRO

GABE STILLMAN BAND The up-and-coming singer, guitarist, songwriter, and showman has been hailed by no less an authority than Alligator Records founder and president Bruce Iglauer as “one of the most promising young blues talents on the scene today.” March 7, 8 p.m. $32.95-$36.15. Spire Center, 25½ Court St. Plymouth. www.spirecenter.org

POINT01 PERCENT PRESENTS Two ensembles featuring adventurous local improvisors: a quartet comprising trumpeter Forbes Graham, pianist Chi Wei Lo, synthesist Andrew Neumann, and drummer Eric Rosenthal; plus Pandelis Karayorgis’s piano and electric Fender Rhodes trio, featuring his longtime collaborators bassist Nathan McBride and drummer Curt Newton. March 10, 7 p.m. $15. The Lilypad, 1353 Cambridge St., Cambridge. lilypadinman.com

KENNY WERNER TRIO New England Jazz Connections and Fenway Forward present the renowned piano master — a Guggenheim Fellow who’s played with everyone from the Thad Jones/Mel Lewis Vanguard Jazz Orchestra to the likes of Joe Lovano and Chris Potter — in a brilliant trio with bassist Greg Loughman and drummer Rafael Barata. March 12, 6:30 p.m. $10-$20. Newcastle Saranac Community Studio, 607 Columbus Ave., Roxbury. newenglandjazzconnections.com/concerts

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA Herbert Blomstedt leads the BSO and the Tanglewood Festival Chorus in a profound all-Brahms program, starting with the choral-orchestral pieces “Nänie” and “Schicksalslied” followed by the Symphony No. 4. March 5-7. Symphony Hall. 617-266-1200, www.bso.org

BOSTON BAROQUE Guest conductor Patrick Dupré Quigley makes his Boston Baroque debut leading Haydn’s “Lord Nelson Mass,” also known as the “Missa in Angustiis” — “Mass for Troubled Times.” The quartet of vocal soloists are all new to the company as well: soprano Lauren Snouffer, mezzo-soprano Alex Heatherington, tenor Alex Haji, and bass-baritone Philippe Sly. March 6, 8 p.m.; March 8, 3 p.m. NEC’s Jordan Hall. www.baroque.boston

THE DREAM THE DREAMERS DREAMED Boston-grown Black arts group Castle of our Skins collaborates with Vivo Performing Arts and the Boston Children’s Chorus to present a free all-ages concert, featuring a program of music for strings and voices inspired by the poetry of Langston Hughes. The Salvation Army Ray and Joan Kroc Corps Community Center. March 7, 3 p.m. www.castleskins.org

A.Z. MADONNA

YOU ARE CORDIALLY INVITED TO THE END OF THE WORLD! A comic drama by Keiko Green about a man named Greg who receives a diagnosis of terminal cancer and decides to spend his remaining days battling climate change, determined to save the planet. His wife, Viv, wants to “stop time,” huddle at home, and make the most of their limited time together. Narrating the story is Greg and Viv’s adult child, a nonbinary drag performer named M, who’s trying to figure out the meaning of it all as their world is turned upside down. Directed by Shawn LaCount. March 6-28. Company One Theatre, at Boston Public Library, Central Library in Copley Square. Companyone.org

ZABEL IN EXILE R.N. Sandberg is a dramatist of note, and his daughter, Megan Sandberg-Zakian, is a director of note who heads Boston Playwrights’ Theatre. The two have teamed up for the first production of R.N. Sandberg’s “Zabel in Exile,” about Armenian feminist writer and activist Zabel Yessayan. Set in 1937 in a Soviet prison, “Zabel in Exile” flashes back to episodes in Yessayan’s life, from her upbringing in Turkey to the Armenian genocide she witnessed and wrote about. With Sarah Corey as Yessayan and a cast that also includes Danny Bryck, June Baboian, Grace Experience, Anelga Hajjar, and Robert Najarian. Through March 8. Boston Playwrights’ Theatre. www.BostonPlaywrights.org

WAIT UNTIL DARK An adaptation by Jeffrey Hatcher of Frederick Knott’s suspenseful drama about Susan Hendrix, a blind woman in Greenwich Village in the mid-1940s who is terrorized by three hoodlums searching for a doll stuffed with heroin. “Wait Until Dark” premiered on Broadway in 1966, starring Lee Remick, and was revived in 1998 with Marisa Tomei making her Broadway debut. But it’s best known for the 1967 film version with Audrey Hepburn. Jenny S. Lee and Eliza Barmakian, who is legally blind, are splitting the role of Susan and will rotate performances. The hoods will be played by Paul Melendy, Bill Mootos, and Mamadou Toure. Directed by Weylin Symes. March 6-22. Greater Boston Stage Company, Stoneham. 781-279-2200, greaterbostonstage.org

THE ANTIQUITIES Jordan Harrison’s exploration of the perils of technology, set in a futuristic museum where AI curators show visitors various exhibits (from different time periods) in what director Alex Lonati calls “an effort to better understand what it meant to be human.” The cast includes, among others, John Kuntz, Kelsey Fonise, and Jesse Hinson. March 6-28. SpeakEasy Stage Company. At Roberts Studio Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion, Boston Center for the Arts. 617-933-8600, www.SpeakEasyStage.com

DON AUCOIN

BOSTON BALLET WINTER EXPERIENCE One of the don’t miss highlights of the dance season, this program offers a second chance to experience Crystal Pite’s extraordinary “The Seasons’ Canon.” Set to Max Richter’s evocative reimagining of Vivaldi’s “The Four Seasons,” this powerful, mesmerizing work features 54 dancers in ever-shifting patterns and sculptural configurations. The concert also reprises “Le Sacre du Printemps (The Rite of Spring)” by the company’s resident choreographer Jorma Elo. March 5-15. $36-$179. Citizens Opera House. www.bostonballet.org

CURTAIN CALL DanceVisions, Inc. presents a curated dance event that brings together a vibrant mix of choreographers and dancers from around the Boston area and Rhode Island. The program includes works by DanceVisions artistic director Margot Parsons, as well as Ballet Rhode Island’s Kathleen Breen Combes and Yury Yanowsky, plus Naoko Brown, Ruth Fentroy, Janelle Gilchrist, Kathy Hassinger, and Robert VerEecke. March 7-8. $25. Boston University Dance Theater. www.dancevisions.net

NAVA YUGA:THE NEXT CHAPTER The Boston-based Indian creative arts collaborative Souls of India gathers local and international artists for a showcase that illuminates the rich traditions of Indian classical music and dance. Hindustani music featuring Satyaprakash Mishra on tabla, Mani Akella on sitar, and Ria Dey on vocals creates the soundscape for original dance works by Souls of India performers Meghma Banerjee (Kathak) and Samadrita Bhattacharyya (Bharatanatyam and Rabindranitrya). March 7. $10-$25. Lesley University Marran Theater, Cambridge. https://events.ticketleap.com/tickets/souls-of-india/nava-yuga-the-next-chapter

BYCATCH Liquid Spine, a global dance initiative that aims to bring attention to the environmental needs of our water systems, gives the world premiere of this latest project. The new work for six dancers uses marine debris from area coastlines as expressive elements in an exploration of marine life entanglement, highlighting these ocean creatures’ fragility as well as their resilience. The performance is followed by a talk-back with the artists. March 8. Free, registration encouraged. All Seasons Barn at Wright-Locke Farm, Winchester. https://wlfarm.org/liquid-spine/

KAREN CAMPBELL

SPRAY: JULES OLITSKI IN THE 1960s Just opened: Olitski represented the US at the Venice Biennale in 1966 and was the first living artist ever to have a solo exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1969, but his long-ago star turn hasn’t been as enduring as New York abstract painting peers like Mark Rothko or Jackon Pollock. This exhibition is a chance to wonder why: A showcase of his signature spray-painted canvases from that era, rendered in mesmerizingly loose fogs of color, the show is a rare opportunity to contemplate his fade from renown to less-known. Through Aug. 9. Currier Museum, 150 Ash St., Manchester, N.H. 603-669-6144, currier.org

AN INDIGENOUS PRESENT Last chance: For a long time — and until very recently — “Indigenous” and “present” might have been regarded by the broader public as anathema. The dynamic culture of Indigenous peoples has survived years of assault, neglect, and disregard as archeology, but it’s risen in recent years to greater and greater prominence to arrive at a moment when its vibrance is undeniable. This exhibition takes in much of that arc: Spanning 100 years of art made by Indigenous people, it underscores cultural resilience over generations of hardship to arrive on triumph in the here and now. Through March 8. Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100,www.icaboston.org

DIVINE COLOR: HINDU PRINTS FROM MODERN BENGAL The mass printing industry in India has been alive for decades with wild color and flights of fancy depicting centuries of myths and deities that still play a central role in Indian life. Dismissed as art for their pervasive, throwaway ubiquity, this exhibition reexamines them in the context of not what they are as things, but what they represent, a dynamic culture rushing headlong to the future while holding fast to its deep ties to the past. Through May 31. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, www.mfa.org

MURRAY WHYTE

WHO WILL DRAW OUR HISTORY? WOMEN’S GRAPHIC NARRATIVES OF THE HOLOCAUST, 1944-1949 In the wake of World War II, Jewish women who survived the Holocaust picked up pens to draw and write about their experiences. The Hadassah-Brandeis Institute presents this exhibition, curated by art historian Rachel E. Perry, examining pictorial diaries and portfolios documenting life in camps and ghettos. Some were used as evidence in the 1961 war crimes trial of Adolf Eichmann, a key engineer of the Nazis’ “final solution.” Artist Lea Grundig wrote that after drawing her experience, “I could say of myself: I saw it.” Through April 30. Kniznick Gallery, Brandeis University, 415 South St., Waltham. www.brandeis.edu/hbi/artist-program/index.html

CATE McQUAID

ANDREW DELLA VOLPE The Boston comic was once asked to write a letter of recommendation to help a friend legally buy a gun. “Don’t get me wrong, I’m happy we’re starting to look into who gets guns these days,” he says. “I think we also need to look into who’s writing these letters of recommendation. Why do I care if you have one friend that believes in you?” With Tooky Kavanagh and Matt Fanikos. March 6, 7 p.m. $15-$27. The Rockwell, 255 Elm St., Somerville. www.therockwell.org

DAN SODER: THE GOLDEN RETRIEVER OF COMEDY TOUR Soder admits he was a weird kid, partly because he kept playing with action figures until he was 12, when he had already started smoking. “Do you know how hilarious of an overlap that is?” he says. “I would play with my G.I. Joes in earnest for 30 minutes and then go outside and fire up a Marlboro Red.” Early show is sold out. March 6, 7 p.m. and 9:30 p.m. $39.75-$74. Boch Center Shubert Theatre, 265 Tremont St.www.bochcenter.org

DAVID NIHILL: TAKING TANGENTS TOUR Originally from Dublin, Nihill moved to the States, and spent time in New Hampshire, where he was puzzled by open container laws. “A crime that you cannot commit in Ireland,” he says. “If you have a container, you’re gonna open it. That is the fundamental function of a container.” March 7, 9:45 p.m. $38-$70. The Wilbur, 246 Tremont St. www.thewilbur.com

NICK A. ZAINO III

title: Roxbury to commemorate 250th anniversary of Henry Knox’s Noble Train of Artillery march on Saturday
text:
Revolution 250, the organizing committee of the state’s celebration, has partnered with multiple community groups, including Boston 250 and Unitarian Universalist Urban Ministry, to celebrate Knox.

The event is part of Knox Trail 250, a statewide observance that has made its way across Massachusetts. Local communities have held celebrations on the date that Knox marched through, such as Feb. 8 in Framingham.

In the winter of 1775-76, Knox, a 25-year-old Boston bookseller, hauled away British cannons from Fort Ticonderoga to Boston. The cannons were positioned at Dorchester Heights, ultimately forcing the British troops to evacuate the city on March 17, 1776.

“You don’t get to declare independence without first commemorating Evacuation Day,” said Jonathan Lane, executive director of Revolution 250. “And you don’t get to Evacuation Day without telling the story of Henry Knox and his Noble Train of Artillery.”

Knox’s ties to Roxbury are significant. Before his expedition, he built fortifications in the neighborhood that caught the eye of Washington, launching his role as an officer in the artillery.

“Within a year, he was the Brigadier General of the artillery,” Lane said. “He has a meteoric rise, but that was Washington’s style.”

The events Saturday will begin at 2 p.m. with a procession from Fenway High School to John Eliot Square. Marchers will include colonial militia reenactors, patriots of color, a fife and drum unit, and the Hamilton-Garrett drumline. Two teams of Clydesdale horses will pull sleds and cannons, echoing Knox’s original winter trek.

Organizers said the event will stand apart from other Knox Trail events across Massachusetts and New York.

“We … wanted it to really feel true to what Roxbury has been and what it continues to be today as a the hub of Black Boston and a center of revolutionary thought and action,” said Alex Meadow, deputy director of partnerships in the mayor’s office.

Formal programs will be held at the Dillaway-Thomas House. Alongside Knox’s story, the programs will highlight Black patriots who fought in the Revolutionary War and explore the experiences of free, enslaved, and Indigenous people during the Siege of Boston. Black reenactors from the Living History Company and local historians, artists, and poets will participate as well.

A speaking program is planned to begin at 3 p.m. at the First Parish Church, recently reopened after a multiyear renovation. Mayor Michelle Wu is expected to attend and announce the launch of the Boston Historic Markers Program.

The event will conclude with a 15-minute light projection show as a part of the Boston Beacon initiative.

The Roxbury event is one of two Knox-related observances in Boston this month, alongside the annual Dorchester Heights ceremony on March 17. Both are part of Boston 250, the city’s public-private effort to mark its role in the nation’s founding. For Meadow, the theme running through Boston 250 is “everyday revolutionaries.”

“Henry Knox was a bookseller who went to Boston Public Schools,” Meadow said. “An important piece of this for us is through our events and through our programs, helping people realize that they hold power themselves.”

title: In fraught era, a play finds new relevance
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

It might be a little unexpected to lead our newsletter with a story about the theater, when news abounds. But stick with us.

Heartbroken by Hillary Clinton’s defeat in 2016, composer Shaina Taub kept working on a play to inspire, as Clinton put it in her concession speech, “all the little girls who are watching this.”

A decade later, Taub is bringing to Boston “Suffs,” her stirring Tony-winning Broadway musical of women suffragettes’ hard-won, century-old victory at getting the vote.

Surprisingly relevant

The story’s struggle seems fresher than ever these days, she tells James Sullivan, mentioning the Roe v. Wade reversal and up-to-the-minute, state-by-state struggles for maternal and reproductive rights. (Yesterday, Texans voted on a proposition that each person has the right to make their own health care decisions, including reproductive rights).

The Vermont native was raised on raucous, rebellious musicals like “Hair,” “Rent,” and “Les Misérables” — and summoned that spirit for the spirited song “How Long” after Trump took office in 2017.

“It’s an elegy that becomes this rallying cry,” Taub tells Sullivan.

A war on women?

While the national tour prepares to play Emerson’s Colonial theater from March 17-29, President Trump is trying to gear up support for a law, already passed by the House, that could strip tens of millions of American citizens of their right to cast a ballot.

In particular, the SAFE Act seeks to throttle mail-in voting and will make it harder for married women who have changed their last name to vote.

An estimated 69 million American women and 4 million men do not have a birth certificate that matches their current legal name.

Last year, the Pentagon had to clarify that Pete Hegseth supported women’s right to vote despite sharing a video that said otherwise.

The message of ‘Suffs’

“I’m not sure that Shaina could have known just how relevant her musical would become more than 10 years after she began working on it,” Sullivan tells me.

Sullivan was struck by Taub’s drive and uplift.

“She has taught herself to find energy in the fact that all movements for social progress are constantly subject to backlash and the frustrations of ‘one step forward, two steps back,’” he said. “I think it has been a conscious decision on her part not to give into despair.”

title: Boston has much work to do to close life expectancy gap
text:
In the Globe’s coverage of the Boston Public Health Commission’s new life expectancy data (“Boston moves to close life expectancy gap,” Metro, March 2), Mayor Michelle Wu observed that “a beacon that only shines for some is not a beacon at all.” The widening gap in Boston — nearly seven years between Black residents and other racial and ethnic groups, and 23 years between residents of Roxbury and those of Back Bay — is more than a public health statistic. It is a measure of whether our policies reach everyone.

Boston has earned recognition from AARP and the World Health Organization as an “age-friendly” city. This designation reflects thoughtful planning and engagement. But the health commission data demand a harder question: Friendly for whom?

An age-friendly label rings hollow if Black men in Boston can expect to live to only 72 — more than nine years less than men in other groups — and if preventable cancers, cardiometabolic diseases, and drug overdoses continue to cut lives short in neighborhoods long shaped by structural inequities.

What Boston needs now is not simply to be age-friendly, but age-responsive. Age-responsive governance would set measurable benchmarks, require transparent reporting, and commit to sustained investment beyond announcements. It would connect housing stability, addiction services, environmental justice, food access, transportation, and primary care into an integrated longevity strategy — with clear accountability for closing life expectancy gaps by 2035.

Boston is home to world-class medicine. The challenge is ensuring that excellence is not bounded by ZIP code or race.

If we truly aspire to be a beacon, the light must reach every neighborhood — and stay on.

Richard T. Moore

Uxbridge

The writer is a former Massachusetts state senator.

title: Reenactors commemorate Henry Knox’s 1776 winter expedition to haul cannons to Boston
text:
Saturday’s commemoration was the latest in a series of reenactments across the state leading up to the 250th anniversary of American independence in 2026. Organizers also used the event to recognize the contributions of Black Bostonians to the city’s history.

The celebration, part of the City of Boston’s Boston 250 Initiative, kicked off from Fenway High School with a procession of militia reenactors, a fife and drum corps, and the Hamilton-Garrett Drumline. The group marched to the church, where local historians reflected on Knox’s ties to the neighborhood.

Several speakers explored the lives of free, enslaved, and Indigenous people during the Siege of Boston. The experiences of Black Americans during the Revolution, said historian Dart Adams, are often left out of the narrative.

“Black Bostonians constantly feel erased,” Adams said.

The crowd applauded as he listed Black residents credited with shaping the city’s history. The cheering grew louder when Wu announced the city’s plan to invest $650,000 in an effort to “uncover the hidden histories” of Boston.

The funding will support the installation of more than two dozen historic markers and a program allowing community members to research and propose new ones, she said.

“This year we have an opportunity to shine a light in those spaces, on those sacrifices, on those individuals, and that collective action,” said Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll.

Revolution 250, the organizing group behind the state’s anniversary celebration, partnered with several community groups, including Boston 250 and the Unitarian Universalist Urban Ministry, to host the event. It was part of Knox Trail 250, a statewide observance in which communities hold events on the dates Knox passed through their towns.

Boston will host another Knox-related event this month, the annual Dorchester Heights ceremony on March 17. But several attendees found Saturday’s festivities especially meaningful for neighborhood residents, since many of the 250th commemorations have been held in other parts of the city.

“We’re so happy to see the history of this neighborhood being celebrated,” said Randy Foote, 77, who moved to the area in 1968 and taught history at Roxbury Community College. “It’s a tremendously historical place, but it gets forgotten.”

Foote, who said he’s “all about Henry Knox,” lives in a home that overlooks the area where troops positioned the cannons that ultimately forced the British evacuation.

His favorite moment of Saturday’s celebration came when he stepped inside the First Church. The Knox event marked the first gathering in the building since the completion of a multiyear restoration, and Foote was not the only one pausing to admire the fresh white paint and gleaming fixtures.

“I love seeing the horses and all, but seeing this church so beautiful and so alive is so heartwarming,” said Foote, who also leads tour groups along the Freedom Trail. “It just knocks me out what they’ve done.”

Though Saturday wasn’t the first time Foote had retraced the final leg of Knox’s route, the event gave many attendees a reason to explore it themselves. Some, despite years in the neighborhood, said they had never stepped inside the First Church.

Sean Burke, a Dorchester native, climbed the church steps for the first time wearing a 250th anniversary scarf and several patriotic pins on his cap. A self-proclaimed history buff, Burke said he attends reenactments whenever he can.

“You can’t go wrong with a live cannon demonstration,” said Burke, 38. “That’s always something you don’t think you’d hear in Roxbury. It’s usually a little more quiet.”

Burke has made several trips to Lexington and Concord over the past year and attended the lantern ceremony at Old North Church last April. He encouraged community members to get out and take part in events that highlight the country’s history, especially when they are happening close to home.

“It’s very fitting, in this time and political climate, to remember your history and to learn it,” he said. “Living here, we’re so blessed. It’s literally saturated with history. It’d be a shame for people not to partake.”

After the remarks, attendees inside the Putnam Street church turned their attention to a light show that illuminated the space. The immersive program highlighted the past, present, and future of Roxbury’s revolutionary spirit through light projections, live music, and multimedia art curated by local artists and historians.

“I love seeing the horses,” said Foote’s wife, Nel, 73. “But my actual favorite thing is seeing so many people come together in our neighborhood to acknowledge it.”

title: ‘It makes it feel like our needs aren’t as important.’ Disabled residents say Boston could have done better in removing snow.
text:
Jerry Boyd, 56, a West Roxbury resident who has cerebral palsy, uses MBTA RIDE, a door-to-door paratransit service, but said he couldn’t reach the vehicle in his motorized wheelchair when sidewalks weren’t cleared.

“I applaud the city on those efforts, but definitely more work needs to be done,” Boyd said. “We can’t be caught off guard in future winters like the city seemed to be this year.”

Curb cuts, sloped ramps built into sidewalks at intersections, are especially critical because they allow people using wheelchairs and other mobility devices to move safely from the sidewalk to the street.

“When we find curb cuts not shoveled out or sidewalks not with a wide enough path, it makes it feel like our needs aren’t as important,” Boyd said.

Councilor Ed Flynn called snow cleanup a civil rights issue.

“You judge a snowstorm on how accessible the streets and sidewalks are for persons with disabilities and seniors,” Flynn said.

The city did not respond to an interview request to address complaints from residents with disabilities. However, it defended its snow removal operations.

“We recognize the major impact that snow has on people with disabilities,” Disability Commissioner Kristen McCosh said in a statement. “We make every effort to maintain accessible paths of travel by ensuring that City resources are focused on sidewalks, curb ramps, and crosswalks.”

During the two major snowstorms, the city conducted targeted snow removal in priority areas, including Boston Public Schools locations, major thoroughfares, intersections, curb ramps, and public squares, according to Boston Public Works.

Crews have removed 10,444 truckloads of snow from city streets this season, 6,566 loads in January and 3,878 in February, according to Public Works. The Public Works Code Enforcement Division has issued 5,870 snow removal violations across both storms, the department said.

Of the 311 cases reported to the city each month, 59 percent in January and 53 percent in February were related to snow, according to Public Works.

“Every winter storm presents a unique set of challenges,” city spokesperson Michael Osaghae said in a statement. “We remain open to feedback and will continue to iterate on our snow removal strategies within our fiscal and staff constraints.”

Osaghae said the Boston Code of Ordinances requires property owners to clear snow, slush, and ice from sidewalks and curb ramps around their property. The ordinance requires a minimum 42-inch-wide path to be cleared for people using wheelchairs and pushing strollers.

“We need to have a finalized ‘who to go to’ when this situation is happening,” said Daniela Depina, 45, who is wary of stepping out of her Dorchester home and onto the icy, snow-ridden sidewalk.

Depina, who is visually impaired, has rescheduled medical appointments, skipped grocery store runs, and even paid someone to take her 11-year-old daughter, Mariah, to school, because the ground outside her home was not fully shoveled, she said. She called 311 after the January storm and said she didn’t get answers about who was responsible for clearing her sidewalk.

“I had to sit on my butt to get down my stairs, because that’s how bad it was,” said Depina, a disability peer advocate at the Boston Center for Independent Living. “If everywhere you call you’re getting the runaround, it’s almost feeling like the door is being shut.”

Gabrielle Mondestin, chief communications officer for the MBTA, said in a statement that its RIDE service is affected “even after the snow has stopped falling.” Drivers may struggle to pull over or park near a customer’s destination, and it can be difficult to deploy vehicle lifts when piled snow blocks the curb, she said.

Crystal Evans, 45, of Braintree, who has a neuromuscular disease and uses a ventilator to breathe, travels to Boston three to six days a week for health care. She gets medical transportation through her insurance company, but it has been unreliable, so Evans opts for the buses and trains.

Evans, who shoveled Braintree sidewalks using her motorized wheelchair in 2015, said piles of snow made the curb cuts inaccessible and crosswalk buttons impossible to reach from her chair.

“When we’re dependent on a sidewalk plow, then things like signs and light posts, the plows can’t navigate,” Evans said. “Then they just stop, back off, go into the street, and we don’t have that continuous path of travel.”

She said snowbanks left at traffic islands were another concern for her as she crossed intersections.

“As a wheelchair user, you don’t know if a car is going to come around the corner or not,” she said. “I’m lower than the snowbanks.”

William O’Donnell, 42, a peer support leader who lives in Quincy, was particularly fearful of having to walk into the street with Juno, his guide dog.

“The dog is trying to guide you around obstacles,” O’Donnell said. “Often, there’s not a straight way you can go, and then they have to dodge traffic, worry about getting you around the cars.”

When he walked in the street, O’Donnell said he could feel the heat of the cars traveling next to him, less than an arm’s length away. He suggested that if municipalities have to build snowbanks at the edges of the streets, they can keep them off of curb cuts or use melting machines to eliminate them.

Casandra Xavier, a 36-year-old disability advocate who was born with blindness and hearing loss, said city officials should take accessibility into account when clearing snow because they never know when they might need it.

“No one is exempt from acquiring a disability in this life,” she said. “We are not asking for a favor. We’re just simply reminding everyone of our rights as persons with disabilities, that we too should have access to our environment freely and comfortably.”

title: Many neighbors welcome supportive housing, treatment at Shattuck site
text:
Re “At Franklin Park, again a split over land use: Shattuck future fires fears of neighbors” (Page A1, March 1): Readers of the article about plans by the state to redevelop the Shattuck Hospital site may have been left with the impression that neighbors overwhelmingly oppose supportive housing and addiction treatment there. While there are some mobilizing against housing and treatment on the Shattuck campus, there is also a large, multiracial coalition, Housing and Health on Morton Street, that strongly supports housing and treatment at this site.

We are both members of this coalition, which sees Morton Street redevelopment as a crucial step in tackling our communities’ critical housing and health care needs. In contrast to the article’s framing, our group is made up not of “several advocates” but, rather, of hundreds of residents of Dorchester, Roxbury, Mattapan, and Jamaica Plain.

People of color or immigrants represent more than 70 percent of our coalition’s base. Member groups include African Community Economic Development of New England, Agencia ALPHA (serving Latino residents), New England Community Project (Dorchester), Reclaim Roxbury, and True Alliance Center (serving the Haitian community).

At the Feb. 26 listening session covered by the article, besides “calling for at least 200 units of supportive housing and substance use recovery services at the Shattuck campus,” as the reporter noted, we also urged the state to build on its earlier Vision Plan (from 2019-20), developed with a community advisory board, that incorporated substantial input from surrounding communities and identified key needs and priorities.

Shameeka Moreno

Dorchester

Clare Okalany

Roxbury

Moreno is an organizer with the Boston Tenant Coalition. Okalany is head of operations for African Community Economic Development of New England.

title: Wu backed off bike lanes last year. Now what?
text:
Over the last year, Boston Mayor Michelle Wu has quietly slowed the implementation of much of the street safety agenda of her first term. Residents deserve to know whether it’s a temporary pause or a longer-term shift in the administration’s priorities. Many Boston streets are still dangerous for motorists, pedestrians, and cyclists, and it would be unfortunate if Wu allows rancor over street projects like bus lanes or flex posts to block the kind of safety upgrades that are still needed across the city.

The dangers remain as clear as ever: Through the first half of last year, there were six road fatalities in Boston, according to the city’s dashboard. That includes four pedestrians.

In her first term, Wu spent serious political capital upgrading streets and intersections, through interventions like speed humps that slow down traffic and road reconfigurations to improve safety. For instance, she pushed through the stalled “road diet” on Centre Street in West Roxbury, addressing known safety hazards on a road where a pedestrian was killed in 2019 and many crashes involving pedestrians, cars, and bicycles have been recorded.
