A weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns.

Enter Email

The inclusion of bike and bus lanes, however, has been a sore spot in many neighborhoods and a potential political liability for the mayor. The bungled installation of speed humps on Allandale Street in Jamaica Plain and West Roxbury, which the city subsequently removed, created additional headwinds. So last year, facing a reelection battle against an opponent determined to make bike lanes a campaign-defining issue, Wu ordered a 30-day review of all street projects. Then she slowed the work of designers and planners in her Streets Cabinet, which since then has seen the steady departure of staff with street-safety expertise.

In an interview with the Globe editorial board, Wu denied adopting a more cautious approach and said street safety was a “constant focus” of her administration. “Ultimately, this is about balancing the tools that we have for the different uses of our streets,” she said. “We need more context-sensitive design, more engagement beyond just an individual street, but to the surrounding neighborhoods at large.”

The departures include former Chief of Streets Jascha Franklin-Hodge, who announced his exit in November; former Deputy Chief of Infrastructure and Design Julia Campbell, who stepped down from her role a month later; the Cabinet’s Chief of Staff Sarah Anders, who left in January; and Director of Transportation Policy and Planning Vineet Gupta, who retired this month.

Notably, the city has also stonewalled a public records request from the Globe editorial board originally filed in October that requested internal emails from the Streets Cabinet. The Globe appealed to the state supervisor of Public Records, who said in December that the city “must provide responsive records,” which it has not done. But the Globe has been told by people familiar with Streets Cabinet operations that many projects are now in indefinite limbo and that there is poor communication and a singular focus on uncontroversial day-to-day operations like street repaving rather than long-term street safety initiatives.

For example, 2024’s “Safety Surge” initiative, which aimed to install more than 2,000 bumps along Boston’s streets, has dramatically slowed. A series of traffic-calming projects for Lower Roxbury, which began its community outreach process back in 2019 and was supposed to be completed last year, has not yet been built. Egleston Square’s redesign is in a similar limbo. The Columbia Road Transportation Action Plan final designs were promised last year, but the website still lists the project in an early planning phase and lacks any upcoming events. Improvements from Boylston Street, between Brookline and Ipswich, were just delayed another four years.

Another project on ice is Hyde Park Avenue’s multimodal corridor. In 2024, after a pedestrian was killed near Forest Hills station, hundreds of residents and safety advocates demanded changes on that dangerous stretch of road. But since February 2025, despite comprehensive designs that have been ready for months, there has been no movement on Hyde Park Avenue’s transit upgrades. An SUV hit another pedestrian in September 2025. The victim sustained life-threatening injuries.

The election is over, and however much some residents may despise street safety interventions, Wu’s transit-friendly first-term record didn’t prevent her from winning reelection by a landslide. The 30-day review that kicked off this cautious approach ultimately recommended slowing down and building consensus. But the city applied this advice indiscriminately, hamstringing projects with years of community input alongside newer ones. Even if street upgrades change in priority and schedule, the mayor should let her specialists in street safety get back to work — or explain to constituents why she’s ignored their advice for more than a year. Above all else, if this change is permanent, Wu must articulate her new strategy to manage the dangers of Boston’s streetscape.

Editorials represent the views of the Boston Globe Editorial Board. Follow us @GlobeOpinion.

title: In a time of isolation and division, The Jar uses art to pursue the ‘most basic human thing,’ connection.
text:
Welcome to The Jar. Executive director Guy Ben-Aharon says the mission of the nonprofit organization, which he founded in 2019, is to inspire individuals to connect to folks like them and not like them through the arts. To that end, The Jar presents a variety of events designed to bring together disparate demographics into one another’s orbits in a way that invites curiosity and connection as a means of driving social change. It’s not just a way to understand differences, but to appreciate them.

“It’s intentionally joyful, a real moment of human connection at a time of real discord,” says Ben-Aharon. “The Jar is for adventurous, open-minded, direct humans who are longing for connection. And that comes in many shapes, sizes, beliefs, backgrounds, genders, sexualities — it crosses everything.”

The Jar’s prescriptive format quickly reassures skeptics and introverts. Each evening starts with a casual meet-and-greet over drinks followed by an artistic offering. Large performance-oriented programs might be held in area theaters. Other happenings are more akin to intimate salons, with smaller groups gathering in someone’s house for dinner and conversation, often provoked by a piece of visual art, a poem, or a reading. For this night of samba, led by former Boston Ballet dancer Irlan Silva, the theme is dance and how we relate to our bodies.

“I think of the small group salons as intimate and uplifting, while these larger events are all about this big communal energy,” says Samantha Tan, an executive leadership consultant who is the organization’s board chairman.

The structure is simple. The Jar’s signature “Convener Model™” was devised so that no one attends an event alone. You are either invited by someone you know (convened), or you are the one doing the inviting (a convener). Conveners buy a Jar of six tickets — all tickets are $10 for a three-hour evening of art, drinks, and food. Each convener invites a plus-one, two “usuals” they often experience culture with, and two “unusuals” intentionally chosen because they “may look, pray, love, or earn differently but who you would like to know better,” according to the website. That methodology creates a deeply diverse room of people open to experiencing a cultural journey together.

With an operating budget of $800,000 (98 percent philanthropy), The Jar presents roughly 25 programs a year in the Boston area with a slow rollout of events beginning in Los Angeles and New York as well. Programming ranges from new play readings to visual art, embracing both emerging artistic voices from around the world and esteemed superstars, like internationally-acclaimed cellist Yo-Yo Ma.

For the samba night, Silva led the group in a lively samba lesson, with most of the participants gamely trying the loose-limbed swings and fast footwork for the first time. After sharing his own personal journey from Rio to Boston, Irlan set the tone for what is the heart of each program, the “facilitated mixer,” an opportunity to share life experiences and reflections through three sets of provocations. Participants divide into small rotating groups of 4-8 people for conversations relating to the event’s theme, this night including: “What was a time your body betrayed you? Surprised you?” The experience requires a level of openness and vulnerability that can be both daunting and rewardingly cathartic, revealing and creating personal connections and understanding.

“People got to experience art and a story of someone’s life in the arts, they got to dance themselves, to feel first before they thought, then were invited to share more of themselves with folks like them and not like them,” says Ben-Aharon. “If there’s some magic sauce to The Jar, it is to go deep fast. People often share and hear stories they normally wouldn’t, and that’s a real gift at a moment when people feel so protective of themselves.”

He adds, “Everybody lives in a bubble. How can we expect to live and thrive in a multi-ethnic democracy by doing the same thing that has led to its destruction?”

Roxbury resident Courtland Townes III, who advocates for disability rights and access as deputy director for Boston Center for Independent Living, has been coming to The Jar events since the beginning and says he is always blown away by how open people are.

“I brought a friend I’ve known over 20 years and she talked about her struggles with ADHD. I did not know that about her, but she felt comfortable enough to share that at The Jar.” He cites upward of 20 new active social connections he’s made through The Jar, including friends he comfortably confides in.

In a divisive era fragmented by tribalism and isolation, Ben-Aharon says The Jar is an invitation for people to step out of their bubble and expand their worldview. “It is like an adventure for people willing to go somewhere they’ve never been. The reality is that it’s in their backyard. You meet people you ride the train with but never talked to. We reintroduce ancient social norms of gathering. It’s the most basic human thing.”

title: Boston pubs and restaurants that make you feel like you are in Ireland
text:
Sharon Carey

General manager, Carrie Nation

Where do you go?

There’s a little pub called The Druid and it’s amazing. It’s a little hole in the wall, and there’s just such an Irish vibe to it. It’s friendly, the staff are lovely, the food’s great, and it’s tiny. And also I’m a massive fan of Emmets. Another bar, the Brendan Behan, is really cool as well. I like the smaller little nooks and the little bars. It reminds you of a pub at home. The only thing missing is the fireplace, where you’re sitting by the fire on a cold winter night, sipping Irish coffee, chatting with your friends, having the craic.

What do you order?

Shepherd’s pie. You know us Irish and our meat and potatoes, right? Actually, I make it all the time. When you mash the potatoes, you have to use the Kerrygold Irish butter and the full-fat milk. Shepherd’s pie is technically lamb, but not gonna lie, I do use beef. My other half is definitely a Guinness drinker. He will get a Guinness whether we’re at The Druid or Emmets or The Dubliner. I love a good Irish coffee. Emmets does a good one. The Druid does as well.

What’s your hometown?

I grew up in a little town called Carndonagh in County Donegal. I came in 2005 to the US, for work, I suppose, excitement, I was young and wanted to travel. All them things. It’s a small town. It’s definitely got a little bit smaller. While I was growing up, I think there were something like 13 bars in our town, which is quite a lot for the size of it. That’s gone down in numbers a lot through the years. It’s very rural, an Irish little town. Everybody knew everybody, and if you didn’t know them personally, you knew their brother or sister or mother or granny. It’s definitely a close-knit community. It’s like that in Boston, as well, though. There’s such a huge Irish connection here, from all over. Everybody supports and tries to help each other out.

CJ Crawford

Bartender, The Druid

Where do you go?

The Druid!

What do you order?

The fish and chips and a pint of Guinness. Oh, and don’t forget the curry sauce. Make sure you say that.

What’s your hometown?

Liscannor in County Clare. It’s just in the shadow of the Cliffs of Moher, so it’s a lovely spot. It’s definitely somewhere you want to go, whenever you get here.

Mary Kiely

Director of operations and co-owner, The James, Essex

Where do you go?

If I was to think about my favorite Irish bar, I would probably say The Druid in Cambridge. The food menu is great, the Guinness is great, it’s a great people-watching place, and the music is great. It’s always a good time. I also really like Devlin’s and The Abbey, which are closer to my home, and Porter Cafe in West Roxbury.

What do you order?

I like to try fish and chips in most restaurants I go to, especially the Irish ones. What makes a good fish and chips, I think, is a light, crispy batter, the tartar sauce has to be really good, and crispy fries. I like Guinness, especially in March, and I also love a good Irish coffee. But usually I like to drink sauvignon blanc, French if they have it. Not really Irish! (Laughs.) We’ll be drinking a lot of Guinness this week.

What’s your hometown?

I grew up in Cork city. Cork is great. It’s a pretty big city with good nightlife and lots of restaurants. It’s a college town, so there are a lot of young people, and it’s always been kind of vibrant. My dad is from the country and I have aunts and uncles spread out all around the county of Cork; I spent a lot of time in Kinsale, and my cousin runs a pub in Drimoleague.

Aidan McGee

Chef and partner, The Dubliner and McGonagle’s

Where do you go?

I usually find Emmets Irish Pub on Beacon Hill is really, really good. It’s been around well over 20 years, and it keeps that small pub feel about it. It’s got that old-school Boston Irish vibe. You can get Irish cider in there. The bartenders are all Irish. It’s a very simple, homely kind of vibe, like I’d get sitting in my local in Donegal.

What do you order?

The sausage roll is my go-to if I’m just having a snack. We call it a sausage roll, here you call it pigs in a blanket. It’s nice, flaky pastry. It’s always fresh. I’m having the fish and chips if I’m extra-hungry. The fish and chips is really good.

What’s your hometown?

It’s in the northwest of Ireland, Donegal Town, right on the border to Northern Ireland. It’s an amazing place, very scenic, very rustic and rugged. National Geographic once voted it the most sought-after place, so we get loads of tourists coming from all over the world, but the locals never change. That hospitality is still there. The people are amazing. If your car breaks down, they’ll give you a lift or fix it for you. It’s that kind of country vibe. There’s very simply cooked fresh fish and loads of pubs that are just amazing. They don’t try to be anything they’re not. They’ve evolved, but they haven’t really changed.

Amy O’Sullivan

Server and bartender, Mr. Dooley’s

Where do you go?

I come right here into Mr. Dooley’s. That is the answer. If you ask me where I would like to go when I’m feeling homesick, it’s right in here. There’s very good Irish food in The Dubliner and McGonagle’s, too.

What do you order?

Beef stew and a pint of Guinness.

What’s your hometown?

Bantry, West Cork. It’s beautiful, stunning. Have you been? Well, you’ll have to do it now for your paper.

Dermot Quinn

Owner, Greenhills Bakery

Where do you go?

Obviously the Greenhills Bakery. Then you’ve got the Irish pubs. On St. Patrick’s week, we just find someplace with Irish music downtown. There’s The Banshee, another place down on Dorchester Ave. My wife (and Greenhills co-owner), Cindy Quinn, is from Holden. We met downtown in an Irish pub back in ’89. It’s not there anymore but it was up the street from Mr. Dooley’s.

What do you order?

We feature our Irish boiling bacon. That’s a favorite growing up. It’s like the rashers from Ireland, but boiled not fried. It’s a tradition in Ireland. Corned beef was not a staple in our diet growing up. It was either ham or boiling bacon. We boil it for like two hours and use the juices from the boiling bacon to make a white sauce, like a bechamel, with parsley. Then we serve it with cabbage and carrots and turnips and potatoes and stuff like that. We serve boiled dinner every Thursday, and we give out two slices of soda bread. Americans don’t really eat the white sauce, that’s more of an Irish thing.

What’s your hometown?

I grew up in County Offaly, out in the country. We grew up taking care of the farm. I’m one of 12 children. We had to fight for our space growing up. We fed the calves and pigs and did the farm work, sowed the potatoes, picked the potatoes, and took care of all the vegetables. My grandmother and mother always made the breads every day, made the butter, milked the cows and took the cream off the milk, then used the buttermilk to make the bread. It was a culture we grew up with. My grandmother passed away on Jan. 12, 1990. I had gone home to see her a month before. I said, “Granny, give me the recipe for the brown bread.” I came back not thinking I was ever going to use this recipe, then two months later I was trying it out in our apartment. There was a butcher shop in South Boston; we brought him down some brown bread and scones. He wanted more and more and more, then I had to rent a kitchen and it snowballed. We had our grand opening with Mayor Flynn 35 years ago.

Kevin Treanor

Owner, Chemist Cocktail Bar, Hugh O’Neill’s, The Merchant, and the Phoenix Landing

Where do you go?

I like the Phoenix Landing, where the Guinness I think is the best. Also The Druid, where I used to bartend. On St. Patrick’s Day, we give out real shamrocks that we order from a florist here in Cambridge.

What do you order?

I know it’s an American thing, but I do like my corned beef dinner. We didn’t have that growing up. A pint of Guinness and an Irish breakfast or corned beef dinner. At the Phoenix Landing, the Irish breakfast is one of our biggest sellers. We even have it on the main menu.

What’s your hometown?

I’m from Monaghan, Monaghan town. It hasn’t changed a whole lot. It’s very working class. The biggest manufacturer there now would be a company called Combilift: Those things that carry a forklift on the back of a truck, they come from Monaghan. It’s one of our claims to fame. The other is we have the biggest export of ducklings and mushrooms. It’s a nice, quiet spot. I love it, but people have never heard of it. I arrived here in San Francisco in the early ’90s and I didn’t know anything about St. Patrick’s Day. In Ireland, it was a religious holiday. We’d go to Mass and there was no drinking afterward. Now, of course, they do what the Americans do. I thought: People are celebrating St. Patrick’s Day like this? I thought this was fabulous, and I still do!

title: ‘More than just a game’: Free chess classes aim to reduce youth violence in Boston
text:
“I know we’re used to rushing, but this is a mind game. So we want to slow down and think,” Shaheed said. “Don’t move off of impulse.”

It’s a message that extends far beyond the chess board.

Organizers of Boston’s new Chess for Peace program are using one of history’s oldest board games to teach kids important life skills, including strategic thinking and conflict resolution. Their goals are to reduce youth violence and address the negative impacts of technology.

The program offers free chess classes Sunday afternoons in the basement of the Madison Park High School gym in Roxbury. It’s affiliated with a Boston Public Schools initiative that also includes basketball, boxing, yoga, rugby, and more, an effort to support families and keep students engaged throughout the week.

The 6-WON-7 program, which has grown significantly over the past couple of years, is about to mark its 100th Sunday, said Cory McCarthy, director of student support at Boston Public Schools. School administrators launched the program partly in response to reports about unruly teenagers causing chaos at the South Bay shopping center and elsewhere on weekends, McCarthy said.

“School should feel like a community,” he said. “It’s the forgotten piece in the academic journey. It’s a safety issue. It’s violence prevention, it’s youth development, it’s all part of student wellness.”

While violent crime has decreased overall, youth violence remains a concern in Boston, largely concentrated among small groups of teenagers and sometimes fueled by gang affiliations. Social media often plays a role, experts say, with kids posting threats or bragging about crimes they’ve committed.

As technology shortens our attention spans, encourages rash decision-making, and limits in-person interactions, playing chess can be a robust kind of antidote, said Renee Callender, a retired Boston police detective who spearheaded the program.

“It’s more than just a game. It actually mirrors life,” she said. “In the game of chess, like life, every action comes with consequences.”

During more than three decades on the police force, Callender saw firsthand how cycles of violence start and end. She also founded a nonprofit called Promoting Conflict Resolution, Inc.

She said the idea for the program came from watching a youth chess tournament on TV; she was impressed by how poised and attentive the players looked. Maybe this could help kids in Boston stay out of trouble, she thought.

“It’s not only about how to play but how to lose,” she said. “How to gracefully lose. How to be humble.”

Indeed, it’s all fun and games until your king is in check.

Jacquami eventually lost to his opponent, 7-year-old Filip Rancic, who said his winning strategy involved steadily advancing his pieces toward the middle of the board.

“Sometimes he wins, sometimes he loses. So that’s good for him,” said Filip’s dad, Milan Rancic.

“They need to learn to be patient enough to develop a strategy, and obviously avoid a tantrum when they lose — pretty much everything we want our kids to learn,” he added.

During the class, three sets of players sat across from each other at classroom desks, with Shaheed monitoring their games and offering instruction. Sometimes the clink of plastic chess pieces was the only sound in the room.

“I think I got checkmate,” exclaimed Henry Lee, 10, bouncing excitedly in his chair.

Shaheed inspected the board and confirmed — checkmate, indeed.

“Good game,” Lee said, reaching out to shake hands with his opponent, 11-year-old Jesus Beltran.

“Can you believe you just lost to a 10-year-old?” he asked, grinning.

Beltran laughed, rolled his eyes, and started setting up the board again; he had won the previous match. In addition to chess, the boys play soccer together. They agreed their friendship can easily withstand some lighthearted competition.

A few turns into the next game, Lee made a move he instantly regretted.

“Can I have that turn back?” he asked Beltran, who smiled and shook his head no.

“So often, they’re focused on just one piece,” said Rhodes Pierre, another instructor with the program. “I tell them to examine the entire board.”

Pierre, who grew up in Mattapan, has experienced firsthand the impacts of violence. His older brother was shot and killed in 1994 near their childhood home, about two weeks after he inadvertently witnessed another daytime shooting nearby. The case was later linked to a neighborhood drug gang, according to news reports at the time.

Pierre said he started playing chess in college and quickly came to appreciate the life skills it teaches.

“Giving people another outlet to express themselves without having to revert to violence, that’s a good thing,” he said. “Making people sit down and think. It’s a better avenue than what we have right now.”

While sprinkling in the basics of chess strategy, Shaheed sends a similar message.

“It’s about seeing the moves behind the moves,” he told the class. “It takes paying attention, hearing your own self think. Most games are won or lost because of focus.”

It’s something he personally learned the hard way, Shaheed said.

Now 45, he spent much of his youth caught in a cycle of poverty, crime, incarceration, and mental illness. From foster care and psychiatric institutions to jails and prison, he ended up playing a lot of chess.

The game took on a central role in his life, an overarching metaphor that changed the way he approached decision-making, Shaheed said. Especially when he found himself in a hostile environment, he would think about the moves available to him and their potential consequences. That finally helped him leave the streets behind and forge a new path.

“The easy money, it wasn’t working. It was almost like a setup — nothing made sense anymore,” he said. “I needed a better move.”

He still plays chess regularly with various partners he’s befriended around Boston. He said he hopes younger generations will find some of the same benefits he’s experienced.

“Chess is a game of distress, tribulations, defeat, obstacles, resistance, competition, sorrow, and conquest,” Shaheed wrote in his recently published book, “Games Over: The Real Story About Chess and Life.”

“And that’s what life is all about — overcoming barriers and making progress.”

title: The unsolved murder of Kendric Price, a beloved youth mentor gunned down on his childhood street in Dorchester
text:
“I’m not saying I can change the world,” Price told the Globe in 2012. “But I’m planning to make a difference one child at a time.”

He also coached basketball, first as an assistant coach at Roxbury Community College and University of Massachusetts Boston, and later as a head coach at Brooke High School.

In March 2019, Price was settling into his new job at Cristo Rey Boston High School and getting ready to move into a new apartment in downtown Boston when he was killed on Greenwood Street, the street he grew up on in Dorchester.

He was 32.

No one has ever been charged with his killing.

His mother, Carol Price, remembers the last time she saw him.

It was Friday night, and she cooked him one of his favorite dishes for dinner: sauteed chicken with onions, green peppers, rice, broccoli, and cheese.

“That day, he came home, he said he was tired. ‘But it’s a good tired,’ he said,” she recalled.

Price told his mother he was going to stay in and take it easy that night.

“He said he was not going out at all,” she said.

But for some reason, after his mother went to sleep, he changed his mind and decided to stop by a garage at 12A Greenwood St., just down the street from his mother’s house. The garage was a known party spot,according to Globe reports at the time.

“It was a party, an after-hours type of thing,” she said.

That’s where he was when gunfire broke out shortly before 3 a.m.

Officers found his body riddled with gunshot wounds, according to police. A police report did not indicate that anyone else was wounded.

For a long time, Price kept thinking that if she had only been awake, she could have stopped him before he went out the door.

“I beat myself up for a long time,” she said.

She still wonders who was at the party when her son was shot.

After her son was killed, many people came to her to show their support while she was grieving, she said. But no one spoke about what actually transpired that night, leading her to assume that witnesses did not come forward and “no one told the police anything.”

When she spoke to investigators right after his death, she pleaded with them to find out what happened and arrest whoever was responsible for taking her son’s life.

“Please do not let this become a cold case,” she said. “I want justice for my son.”

Seven years later, she is still waiting.

“I’d love for someone who knows something to please come forward,” she said. “This perpetrator has probably killed other people since. He needs to be held accountable.”

Carol Price doesn’t like using the word “anniversary” to describe the date of her son’s death. For her, March 2 is a “trauma-versary,” a day she relives the pain and anguish she felt when she learned she had lost her son.

Price had so many opportunities ahead of him and should have had a bright future, she said.

She recalled how busy he always was with school, sports, and other extracurricular activities. And that’s exactly what she wanted: for him to pursue his interests and stay out of trouble.

“I always thought, I don’t ever want the streets to get my son,” she said. “And unfortunately he went to a party, and that’s what happened.”

Carol Price still lives on the same street where her son was murdered and has to pass by the garage where he spent his last moments.

She can’t help but wonder what could have been.

“Kendric came back to Boston,” she said. “He chose to come back and help those who were left behind.”

So she tries to turn her pain into something productive, by giving back to the community like Price did.

She continues to run Big Business Network because it helps people and “reminds me of him,” she said.

Boston police say they continue to investigate Price’s murder.

“It’s an open and active investigation,” said John Boyle, a spokesperson for the Boston Police Department. “We urge anyone to come forward with information, no matter how little they think it is.”

Anyone with information about the murder of Kendric Price can call Boston police homicide detectives at 617-343-4470. Those wishing to leave an anonymous tip can call CrimeStoppers at 1-800-494-TIPS or text the word ‘TIP’ to 27463.

title: ‘It’s very dire’: Mass. Cubans reflect on worsening conditions in homeland
text:
He and his wife regularly send money to relatives so they can afford food, something he says many Cuban families abroad must do.

“We feel so sorry for them, and we cannot do anything for them other than help them out,” said Tarano, a retired financial officer.

The United States volatile relationship with Cuba dates to 1959, when Fidel Castro overthrew the government of Fulgencio Batista and established a communist state. That prompted a long-standing US trade embargo and triggered a massive exodus of Cubans.

Multiple US presidents have tried and failed to topple the regime. But many believe Cuba is facing one of its most vulnerable moments as the Trump administration pursues an aggressive posture in Latin America.

Alejandro de la Fuente, chair of the Cuba Studies Program at Harvard University, said the country imports more than half of the oil it needs to generate electricity, and disruptions in supply are causing the widespread blackouts and transportation breakdowns.

“This has a direct impact on ordinary people and on their daily lives,” de la Fuente, an educator who came to the United States from Cuba in 1992, said about the embargo and the pressure the government is facing from the United States.

He warned that the crisis could prompt a new wave of Cubans to flee. Punitive economic policies could ultimately create challenges for the United States by increasing migration flows.

Boston College student Armando Gonzalez, 20, grew up in Miami in its predominantly Cuban community. Gonzalez said that family friends who had visited Miami from Cuba told stories about food insecurity and the toll of rolling blackouts. While he sympathizes with those suffering, he believes the situation reflects the failure of the Cuban government and the need for political change.

“What the [United States] is doing is hard, but I think it’s needed,” said Gonzalez, treasurer for the Cuban American Student Association at BC. “The regime has to fall and fully be crushed.”

His father was born in Cuba and fled from the country in 1978. He and his family have chosen not to travel to Cuba because they believe tourism spending ultimately benefits the government rather than everyday people.

“We agreed never to support that,” he said. “We’d only agree to go to Cuba once the regime has fallen.”

For older members of the Cuban diaspora, the crisis is part of a much longer saga that began with the Cuban Revolution.

Miriam Gorriaran, a 78-year-old retired professor living in West Roxbury, left Cuba as a child in 1961 as part of a program that brought thousands of Cuban children to the United States when families feared government control over their children’s futures. She challenged the idea that international sanctions alone explain Cuba’s economic collapse, arguing that internal policies and government decisions have had a greater impact.

“The people [who] are in power don’t lack any goods,” she said. “The Cuban government is the one that has restricted the people from getting what they need.”

Gorriaran emphasized that Cubans in the United States have played a major role in keeping families on the island alive through money and supplies sent from abroad.

Alberto Calvo, a 79-year-old Newton resident, and his wife have been helping out relatives in Cuba. He said everything there is rationed, and now with the electricity and oil crisis, the situation is only worsening.

“It’s very dire,” Calvo said, a retired engineer and member of the Cuban Cultural Center in Boston, referring to the current situation. “People are struggling. It’s not getting better; it’s getting worse by the day.”

Calvo, who came to the United States in 1962, recalled experiencing shortages during his time in Cuba. But he blames the economic collapse on the failures of the Cuban system, rather than external pressure. The people, he said, have a “fear of retribution” if they speak up.

“People cannot protest because repression is there,” he said. “Not by the police but even by Cubans [who] are in favor of the government.”

De la Fuente said that beyond political outcomes, one of the most overlooked consequences of the economic pressure may be the growing inequality within Cuban society.

“A situation like this has fairly negative impact over all of Cuba, and Cubans,” he said. “The impact tends to hit disproportionately those who are at the bottom of the ladder.”

He said this crisis magnifies social differences in Cuba and generates an even greater “social polarization.”

Tarano, the Southborough resident, said he is uncertain what would happen if the government falls. He believes any future regime must ultimately come from within Cuba rather than imposed from outside.

“Cubans like Cuba for Cubans,” he said.

title: Roxbury seniors step it up with Alvin Ailey dance troupe
text:
Roxbury seniors stepped and swayed with a “teaching artist” from Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater in a class at Central Boston Elder Services on Wednesday afternoon.

Boston’s Vivo Performing Arts presented the “AileyDance for Active Aging” workshop, so residents could learn movements inspired by Ailey’s choreography, the arts organization said in a statement.

Ailey, based in New York City, “shares the African American cultural experience through performances, training, classes, and community programs,” the organization says on its website.

Amos Machanic, a former Ailey dancer, led about a dozen seniors through warm up stretches, dance elements, and mobility exercises, Vivo said.

The 60-minute class was part of a program by Vivo and the Ailey dance theater to bring active aging workshops to community centers throughout Boston from March 9 through 13, Vivo said in a flier for the program.

Ailey’s goal with the program is to “promote movement that can prevent injury due to inactivity or isolation, while encouraging participants to engage their imaginations and express their creativity,” the theater said.

The last two classes in the city will be on Friday at the Roxbury YMCA at 10 a.m. and at the Central Boston Elder Services at 2:30 p.m., Vivo said.

The workshops were planned in advance of the celebrated dance troupe’s spring visit to Boston.

Ailey will perform at the Boch Center Wang Theatre from April 30 through May 3, the dance company said.

title: Life expectancy gap between Black residents and other Bostonians has doubled over the past decade
text:
Community leaders say the loss of years for Black residents is fueled by systemic racism in Boston, which has led to community divestment and residential segregation.

“It’s always going to be different numbers for us, because the Black and Brown community is always overlooked,” said Lovelee Harvey, 56, a senior recovery coach at Metro Boston Alive, a nonprofit recovery center in Roxbury.

Over the last few months, the Boston Public Health Commission organized state mortality data by race and ethnicity to develop its life expectancy analysis, part of its “Live Long and Well” agenda, which examines how systemic racism has created this public health crisis.

A longer report containing more detailed data is expected to be released in April, said Dr. Bisola Ojikutu, executive director of the Boston Public Health Commission.

We broke down the “Closing the Gap” report, released Feb. 27; here are five takeaways.

The life expectancy gap is widening: Since 2013, Black residents maintained living around 78 years, while the rest of Boston’s life expectancy rose from about 81 to 85 years.

Black men, in particular, have the lowest life expectancy compared to all other groups, according to the report. Between 2022 and 2024, they lived about 9.3 fewer years than other men in Boston.

Black women have the lowest life expectancy compared to all other women, having lived about 6.4 years fewer than other women from 2022 to 2024.

“We think about the drivers of life expectancy, and we know that those are social and structural determinants of health,” Ojikutu said.

Black residents have maintained the lowest life expectancy of all major racial groups in Boston, at around 76 years in the latest period from 2022 to 2024, according to state data.

Meanwhile, Asian residents had the highest life expectancy of about 88 years from 2022 to 2024.

Life expectancy for all groups declined during the COVID-19 pandemic from 2019 to 2021, but have since rebounded.

The life expectancy gap between Black residents and other Bostonians has doubled over the past decade — from 3.3 years to 6.6 years.

“That should concern everyone,” said Winston Bodrick, executive director of the Roxbury YMCA and a member of the Live Long and Well Advisory Council, a new group of community leaders who will help guide efforts to close the gap. “Life expectancy is one of the most fundamental measures of how well the community is doing, so that was a real drawback for me.”

Ojikutu said the COVID-19 pandemic, during which Black residents lost more years of life than other groups, as well as a steep increase in overdose mortality, particularly among Black men, contributed to the gap’s doubling.

Unintentional drug overdoses — the product of substance use disorder and a drug supply that is frequently contaminated, such as with fentanyl — were the leading cause of premature death for Black men in Boston from 2022 to 2024. They have led the causes of premature deaths since 2020.

Negative stigma surrounding substance abuse may trigger feelings of shame for those struggling with addiction, discouraging them from seeking treatment, Ojikutu said. Greg Davis, a former heroin and cocaine user, said those feelings would only intensify his addiction.

“Each time those feelings kicked up for me, I sedated myself, which I believe is what’s going on with a lot of these folks who are still addicted,” said Davis, founder and president of Metro Boston Alive.

Davis added that many struggling with addiction don’t seek help because “they don’t trust the system.”

Now 41 years clean, Davis, 76, is exceeding the report’s average life expectancy for Black men.

Harvey, who described himself as a former “more user” — “If somebody had more, I would use it,” he said with a hearty laugh — overdosed more than 10 times during his active addiction. He recalled being angry about being given Narcan on multiple occasions, but now, he distributes Narcan on the streets every day.

Heart disease and cancer were nearly as significant, followed by homicide and several other health conditions.

Systemic barriers have contributed to these chronic diseases going unchecked, said Dr. Christopher Lathan, chief clinical access officer for the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and a member of the Live Long and Well Advisory Council. They are present in every stage of health care: prevention, screening and treatment.

Being unable to take time off work, or not having a primary care clinician at all, can hinder receiving a health screening.

“You can’t just stop your life and then focus on the cancer, which is what a lot of folks who have any means will do,” Lathan said.

Bodrick, of the Roxbury YMCA, said institutions like the YMCA play a “critical role” in addressing the life expectancy disparity by promoting physical health and wellness.

“We provide safe spaces for physical activity, youth development, community development, as well as preventative wellness programming,” Bodrick said. “These moments may look small, but together, I think they shape lives.”

Communities in Roxbury, Dorchester and Mattapan have the lowest life expectancies in Boston, Ojikutu said.

A 2023 report by the BPHC found a 23-year difference in average life expectancy between Roxbury and Back Bay. In Dorchester, that gap is approximately 20 years, and in Mattapan, the gap is approximately 18 years, Ojikutu said.

These neighborhoods are home to majority-Black populations, according to the Globe’s neighborhood census maps. Mattapan has the largest share of Black residents, with 69.8 percent, while Black residents make up 42.9 percent of Roxbury and 36 percent of Dorchester.

These are also not wealthy neighborhoods, according to the Globe maps. Only 8.9 percent of Roxbury households earn more than $200,000 a year, compared to 13.7 percent in Mattapan and 15.4 percent in Dorchester.

The city pledged on Feb. 27 to contribute $2 million toward medical screenings and other preventative programs to curb the widening life expectancy gap, adding to the $10 million investment from the Atrius Health Equity Foundation in 2024 focused on increasing economic opportunity in neighborhoods with lower life expectancies.

To reduce drug overdoses, Harvey said the community needs the right people to “educate in a loving, caring, culturally competent way.” He hopes the city will promote education and economical development, and give a “fair share” to underprivileged communities.

Lathan, of the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, said tackling food deserts and creating community health centers, among other efforts, can promote screenings and other forms of prevention.

“We have a government, both city and state, that’s really interested in trying to alleviate the barriers,” Lathan said. “Hope should not be restricted to just affluent communities. Hope should be accessible to all.”

title: As pressure mounted on transit plans, Wu imposed a new policy: nearly all streets projects must go through her
text:
That directive, which hasn’t been previously reported, has brought the vast majority of the city’s street projects involving design or infrastructure changes to a near standstill for the past year, according to 11 current or former cabinet employees. The slowdown has sent staff morale plummeting, those city workers said, and many of the cabinet’s top leaders have left City Hall in recent months.

“All these projects exist because someone asked for them,” said one Streets Cabinet employee, who, like 10 other former or current city workers, spoke on the condition of anonymity out of fear of retaliation from the administration. “These are going to be more promises that the city’s breaking. I think that’s what is breaking people’s hearts who are working for the city right now.”

The rollback of Wu’s street safety agenda has deeply frustrated transit advocates, who say City Hall is slow-walking, and potentially jeopardizing, projects that would deliver badly-needed safety improvements to key transit corridors.

Now, four months removed from Wu’s landslide reelection victory, some advocates are questioning Wu’s commitment to the transit priorities she championed in her first term, when she pushed for the city to install hundreds of speed humps and miles of bike lanes, and advocated for ambitious, if sometimes controversial, safety upgrades to dangerous roads.

In an interview with the Globe, Wu insisted that street safety continues to be a top priority, but that she also has to consider feedback from residents and other elected officials who felt the city had moved too quickly on earlier projects.

“Sometimes in the push for urgency and for speed of getting things done, things got lost in translation,” she said. “I intend to do better this term.”

Wu did not confirm she instituted the policy requiring her personal approval for advancing projects, but acknowledged she is “very involved” in the Streets Cabinet’s work.

Caitlin Allen-Connelly, executive director of the public transportation nonprofit TransitMatters, said the Wu administration did not respond for months to her organization’s repeated questions about the status of various infrastructure projects. TransitMatters is tracking at least 16 major projects that have not moved forward over the last year, Allen-Connelly said.

“There’s seemingly no explanation for why these projects are sort of on pause,” Allen-Connelly said. “When we’re not getting a response from the city, it begs the question: ‘Where’s the mayor?’”

Among the stalled projects are a $162 million plan to reimagine Blue Hill Avenue, another to overhaul Columbia Road, a yearslong plan to invest in Hyde Park Avenue, where a pedestrian was killed in 2024, and a project to extend a center-running bus lane on Tremont Street and Columbus Avenue.

Her administration’s “Making Neighborhood Streets Safer” program, which aimed to install at least 500 speed humps a year on city streets, has itself slowed to a crawl. For example, Boston installed around 600 in 2024. But last year, the city installed fewer than two dozen, according to estimates by five employees of the Streets Cabinet with knowledge of the effort.

As of Friday, Wu’s office did not provide data on how many were installed last year.

Wu said several street safety and infrastructure projects are still ongoing, including reconstruction of Congress and Sleeper streets in the Seaport, where a 4-year-old was hit by a pickup truck and killed in 2024, and a mammoth effort to overhaul Sullivan Square and Rutherford Avenue in Charlestown. She said the city has also made significant progress on other maintenance duties, such as repaving roads, repainting crosswalks, and fixing sidewalks.

Her close monitoring of the cabinet’s work has included attending meetings where she’s reviewed projects ranging from major changes to more minor ones, such as proposed locations for new speed humps.

Wu said she did so, in part, to ensure enough outreach had been done and that projects have the “full consensus of the community.”

Wu pointed to an incident last year when the city installed speed humps in a Jamaica Plain neighborhood, only to remove them later after nearby residents complained.

“Wherever possible, we need to be getting things right the first time,” Wu said. “Our role as a city is not to decide within City Hall what’s right for the neighbors and fight to force people to accept that.”

But transit advocates and employees within the department say some of the projects on pause have broad community support, and already went through years of design revisions and community engagement. That includes the Hyde Park Avenue project, they said, as well as the reconstruction of Harrison Avenue Ink Block, which is listed on a city website as under construction and set for completion this year, though the most recent update is dated January 2025.

“When the city engages the community, [and] asks them, ‘Hey, what do you need? How can we help you?’ And then it’s radio silence ... that’s the fastest way you can rupture trust,” said Reggie Ramos, executive director of the advocacy group Transportation for Massachusetts. She later added: “It feels like transportation is no longer a priority of the city.”

Wu heavily championed progressive transit policies during her 2021 mayoral campaign and has pushed through controversial projects, including bike lanes on Boylston Street. In 2023, the city also completed a redesign of Centre Street in West Roxbury with bike lanes and traffic calming measures, despite vocal opposition from some in the community.

Then, to many transit advocates, Wu changed her posture just as she began her reelection push, including walking back street design changes in response to criticism from prominent business leaders.

Early last year, amid public backlash over bike lanes and a political challenger in Josh Kraft aiming to capitalize on it, Wu ordered a 30-day review of all recent street infrastructure changes and had a controversial bus lane on Boylston Street removed.

Around the same time, administration officials began telling staff of the Streets operation to stop working on nearly all projects involving design or infrastructure changes, big or small, until Wu’s office gave them the go-ahead to continue. The edict left dozens of projects in limbo, 11 current and former Streets Cabinet employees told the Globe. Since then, they said they’ve received limited to no communication from Wu’s office on how to proceed.

Maha Aslam, transit and streets program manager of the nonprofit LivableStreets Alliance, said she had hoped Wu would allow work to resume on the stalled projects after she overwhelmingly won reelection in November.

“Unfortunately, that didn’t happen,” she said.

Meanwhile, Wu’s Streets Cabinet has lost much of its top leadership. Jascha Franklin-Hodge, the chief of streets and face of Wu’s transportation agenda, announced he was leaving the administration just days after the November election. The Streets Cabinet’s chief of staff and deputy chief of streets for infrastructure and design have also since departed, and the director of policy and planning has retired.

Now, advocates say they’re concerned the continued delays could mean some projects won’t happen at all. Two stalled projects, to redesign Maverick Square in East Boston and Roslindale Square, are backed by federal pandemic relief dollars that expire at the end of 2026, Allen-Connelly of TransitMatters said.

Wu said the city is aware of the funding deadline and that the projects “will get done.” But the websites for the initiatives indicate both are still in the planning stage.

Meanwhile, the Blue Hill Avenue project recently secured more than $80 million from a federal grant program. But according to LivableStreets, those funds, plus nearly $50 million in state and MBTA funds allocated for the project, are contingent on the design including a center-running bus lane, which is opposed by a vocal group of residents and some elected officials.

Four city streets staff members told the Globe they still haven’t received the green light from the mayor to continue working on the Blue Hill Avenue project.

title: Shattuck, take 2: Mass. still needs shelter beds at the JP hospital site
text:
The state last month resurrected an abandoned community planning process to redevelop the Lemuel Shattuck campus in Jamaica Plain, hosting the first official community meeting on the proposal in years. The aging hospital in Franklin Park, a grimy eyesore that serves prisoners and other vulnerable populations, is expected to close by 2027. Its 13-acre campus, which by law can only be used for public health purposes, offers a rare large-scale public redevelopment opportunity within the city of Boston.

Public health officials have long hoped to turn the campus into facilities for addiction treatment and supportive housing for homeless people — two things the state desperately needs. A previous, overly ambitious effort fell apart amid local opposition. Now, as the process starts back up, officials should consider the feedback of residents of Mattapan, Dorchester, and Roxbury, all of which are close to the campus. But this time they shouldn’t let neighborhood opposition stop development of the site to meet those broader public needs.

The plan to tear down the hospital, which was built in 1954, was first discussed in earnest in 2018. After a needs assessment to figure out what should go on the site, the state put out a request for an operator to run a modest 75 to 100 shelter beds at the site.

Boston Medical Center instead appeared with a 370-page, $550 million project that would have expanded the campus and added hundreds of treatment beds and supportive housing units.

The plan would have been a massive boost to addiction treatment efforts in Greater Boston, but the size of it caught residents of the surrounding neighborhoods off guard. In 2023, though, the project collapsed as community outcry grew.

With community coalitions already well-established during the years of the BMC proposal, the state now faces an uphill battle to convince residents that the renewed process is truly a clean slate, with no favored proposal. At the first listening session on Feb. 23, three state employees struck a conciliatory tone with community members who voiced their concerns.

If there are ways to mitigate the neighborhood impact of new facilities, officials should consider them carefully. But some critics want the state to turn the land back into a park, and that’s unrealistic given the legal restriction on the land. Officials will need to remain firm on the need for some form of treatment and housing facilities on the site.

There is no perfect place for addiction treatment or supportive housing, and communities across the city and region have battled plans to locate such facilities near them. But the Shattuck site has many advantages. The parkland surrounding the campus will offer some relief from direct abutters who would be most impacted by construction or traffic.

With the right mix of services, the Shattuck site could turn into a modern facility addressing a huge regional need. It will always be only part of the solution. As the initial needs assessment for the campus calculated, the number of supported housing units needed to house all chronically homeless people, homeless families, and people with substance use disorder and mental health conditions in Eastern Massachusetts is nearly 4,400. That was more than five years ago, and the numbers may well be worse now.

There are also plenty of opportunities to mix residents’ desires with development proposals — like incorporating new green spaces that respect the surrounding park land or reopening a long-closed day-care center on the campus.

The Shattuck Campus is currently the best option Greater Boston has for housing and addiction services. Despite City Hall’s reassurances that rebuilding the bridge to Long Island is still a feasible plan, the endeavor would cost hundreds of millions of dollars and likely take decades. The Shattuck campus, which already provides services to vulnerable people, is a much more feasible option to expand capacity for regional recovery and treatment options, and the state shouldn’t miss this opportunity to redevelop the site.

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
PRYVT This Discord-forged duo, whose second album, “BACK TO REALITY,” came out late last year, blends smooth grooves with smudged atmospherics to create hazy, hooky cuts that feel designed to accompany a late-night ride into space. March 20, 8 p.m. Warehouse XI, Somerville. get2thegigbos.com

DESTIN CONRAD Last year, this Tampa-born singer-songwriter released two albums: “LOVE ON DIGITALl,” a study of R&B’s last two-ish decades rife with highlights like the hiccuping “Delusional” and the psychedelia-dappled “Softside”; and “wHIMSY,” a release credited to his alter ego “MR. E” that frames his lithe tenor in jazz-club cool. March 22, 6:30 and 9:30 p.m. City Winery Boston. 617-933-8047, citywinery.com/boston

ROCHELLE JORDAN This forward-thinking Toronto belter plunged herself into the club’s deepest end on her stunning 2025 album “Through the Wall.” March 23, 7 p.m. Paradise Rock Club. 617-562-8800, crossroadspresents.com

MAURA K. JOHNSTON

Folk, World & Country

CASS MCCOMBS McCombs is touring behind his latest album, “Interior Live Oak,” a reflection (or refraction) of his bending back to his musical past; inspired by revisiting the early material collected on last year’s “Seed Cake on Leap Year” and working again with collaborators from those days, he’s conjured something as eclectic as ever while tapping the personal more than ever. He plays with full band; Jennifer Castle opens. March 21, 8 p.m. $25. Brighton Music Hall, 158 Brighton Ave. 800-653-8000, www.ticketmaster.com

RICH HINMAN AND COMPANY Rich Hinman continues to prove that there is no limit to what a pedal steel guitar can do with his periodic visits to this Cambridge subterranean nightspot. This time, he’s assisted by the formidable talents of Kevin Barry on guitar and lap steel, Zach Hickman on bass, and John Sands on drums. March 25, 8 p.m. $15. Lizard Lounge, 1667 Massachusetts Ave., Cambridge. 617-547-0759, www.lizardloungeclub.com

AFTERNOON BIKE RIDE This Montreal “trio of pals” (per their Instagram) has recently released “Running With Scissors,” a marvelous, seamless welding of ambient, folk, and indie strains that has at its heart a “poignant … exploration of life’s most tender and tumultuous moments” occasioned by band member Lia Kurihara serving for the past four years as caregiver for her father as he struggled with dementia. March 26, 8:30 p.m. $15. The Lilypad, 1353 Cambridge St., Cambridge. 617-955-7729, www.lilypadinman.com

STUART MUNRO

THE NEW BLACK EAGLE JAZZ BAND Among the world’s greatest traditional jazz bands, the seasoned septet plays early New Orleans, 1920s Chicago, and 1930s small group jazz, its wide-ranging repertoire encompassing blues, rags, spirituals, and much more. March 22, 3 p.m. $39. Groton Hill Music Center, 122 Old Ayer Road, Groton, grotonhill.org

LIL’ ED & THE BLUES IMPERIALS Showcasing his searing slide guitar and ebullient stage presence, Lil’ Ed and band have been major players on the Chicago scene for decades, and they bring the real, rollicking, house-rocking Windy City blues with them wherever they go. March 24, 7 p.m. $35-$65. The Music Room, 541 Main St., West Yarmouth, musicroomcapecod.com

ALLISON MILLER New England Jazz Connections and Fenway Forward present the renowned drummer, composer, and bandleader — who’s played with everyone from singer-songwriters such as Ani DiFranco and Brandi Carlile to the all-female Blue Note supergroup Artemis — with acclaimed guests trumpeter Jason Palmer and alto saxophonist Mark Zaleski. March 26, 6:30 p.m. $10-$20. Newcastle Saranac Community Studio, 607 Columbus Ave., Roxbury. newenglandjazzconnections.com/concerts

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA As the BSO players are rallying around music director Andris Nelsons in the wake of his abrupt dismissal, effective next summer; it’s a safe bet that they’ll be playing their hearts out even more than usual. Yunchan Lim takes center stage in Schumann’s Piano Concerto before Nelsons leads the orchestra in Tchaikovsky’s rarely performed “Manfred” Symphony (March 19-21). Symphony Hall. 617-266-1200, www.bso.org

BOSTON LYRIC OPERA With Anne Bogart’s three-person, two-singer staging of Mahler’s “Song of the Earth,” in an intimate chamber arrangement by 20th-century composer Arnold Schoenberg, BLO throws the doors open to its newly renovated rehearsal, performance, and community space in Fort Point. March 20-29. Opera + Community Studios. 617-542-6772, www.blo.org

VIKINGUR OLAFSSON Last year, the Icelandic pianist rocked Symphony Hall in a two-piano concert with Yuja Wang; now, he’s back on the same stage on his own, bringing a program of Bach, Schubert, and Beethoven that culminates in Beethoven’s Piano Sonata No. 30. Presented by Vivo Performing Arts. March 20, 8 p.m. Symphony Hall. 617-482-2595, www.vivoperformingarts.org

A.Z. MADONNA

ANGRY, RAUCOUS, AND SHAMELESSLY GORGEOUS Patrice Jean-Baptiste plays Anna Campbell, who made a name for herself as a young performer with a solo piece titled “Naked Wilson,” in which Campbell, in the nude, recited monologues by male characters from dramas by August Wilson. Anna is irate when she learns that a feminist theater festival plans to stage her signature piece, but with a younger performer named Precious “Pete” Watson (Yasmeen Duncan) whose primary acting experience is in pornographic films and exotic dancing. Pearl Cleage’s play is directed by Jacqui Parker, one of Boston’s most renowned actresses. March 20-April 12. At Lyric Stage Boston. 617-585-5678, www.lyricstage.com

(Barmakian, who is legally blind, is alternating in the role with Jenny S. Lee.) Once it gets past an overly expository and talky Act One, this “Wait Until Dark” turns into a nail-biter of a production. Director Weylin Symes handles the big, explosive moments and the small, chilling ones with equal skill. Paul Melendy, best known for comic roles, is genuinely menacing as a sociopath named Roat. Mamadou Toure, Amalia Tonogbanua, Bill Mootos, and Thain Bertin do solid work in supporting roles. Through March 22. Greater Boston Stage Company, Stoneham. 781-279-2200, greaterbostonstage.org

THE ANTIQUITIES Jordan Harrison (“Marjorie Prime”) has crafted a one-act play that examines the implications of artificial intelligence in an unblinking, here’s-the-road-we-might-be-on manner. His ingenious framing device is to set the action in the distant future, where AI curators take AI visitors on a tour of human history in a “Museum of Late Human Antiquities.” A series of brief vignettes, presented in nonlinear fashion, illustrate how humanity surrendered agency or had it taken from them. Under the direction of Alex Lonati, a nine-member, notably diverse cast delivers precise, disciplined performances, meshing together smoothly in a textbook illustration of how to generate maximum impact from an ensemble piece. DON AUCOIN

March 20-29. $42-$57. Woodman Center at Moses Brown, Providence. www.balletri.org

March 21-22. $30-$55. Boston Center for the Arts Calderwood Pavilion. www.bosoma.org

ALEXANDER DAVIS & SARA JULI The two adventurous dancer-choreographers split the bill on this upcoming evening of dance/theater works. Davis’s comedic “Gay Aesthetic: Based on a True Story” is fueled by his experience being asked to lose weight to fit the gay aesthetic of a dance project he hoped to join, provoking an examination of prejudices, expectations, and insecurities. “Sara Juli’s Midseason Mood” fuses dance with stand-up comedy in reflecting on the complexities of the female experience. March 21-22. $5-$50. The Dance Complex, Cambridge. www.dancecomplex.org

PULSE Urbanity Dance showcases a variety of new works choreographed by members of the organization’s select second company, Urbanity 2. The featured contemporary dance works explore tension/release and cycles of exchange, inviting audiences to reflect on relationships between repetition, connection, and the collective presence. March 21-22. $22-$75. Boston University Dance Theatre. www.urbanitydance.org

KAREN CAMPBELL

FRAMING NATURE: GARDENS AND IMAGINATION Just opened: A cross-cultural, collection-wide display of natural lushness to coincide with the 50th anniversary of the MFA’s “Art in Bloom” celebration, this show promises a gamut of garden-forward glory, both flora and fauna. But because I know you’re wondering: There are indeed Monets, so plan accordingly. Through June 28. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, www.mfa.org

EDMONIA LEWIS: SAID IN STONE Edmonia Lewis studied art in Boston in 1863 and then moved on to Rome a few years later — a feat for a woman artist in an era where few were taken seriously. But it was doubly so for Lewis, who was of mixed race, Black and Indigenous, a set of disadvantages in her time and place that could have sunk her career before it started. That it did not says a lot about her, and this show is a showcase for her gift of sculpting hard stone into flowing, lifelike effigies of a personal slate of concerns: abolition and social reform, and a dignified representation of Black and Indigenous people most often reduced in art of the time to cliche and disdain. Through June 7. Peabody Essex Museum, 161 Essex St., Salem. 978-745-9500, www.pem.org

MURRAY WHYTE
