title: A Roxbury man found a document that revealed a new chapter in his family history. He had no idea how rare it was.
text:
Haynes, who works as a operator on the MBTA’s Green Line, began exploring his family genealogy this winter after finding an original freedom paper belonging to one of his ancestors. The documents were proof that an African American person was free in the years before slavery was abolished. Without the papers, individuals risked being kidnapped and unlawfully sold into slavery.

Haynes’s ancestor’s document, issued in 1834, was passed down through generations to his grandmother, and stored in a hutch in his mother’s Roxbury home. He stumbled across it while cleaning, as he was dusting the contents of the old cabinet.

Issued nearly 200 years ago to 21-year-old Samuel Jones in Baltimore County, Maryland, the document identifies Jones based on his physical features.

It was signed by a court official certifying that Jones was “born free,” the document says. Thirty years later, in 1864, Maryland abolished slavery when it ratified a new state constitution. After the end of the Civil War in 1865, Congress ratified the 13th amendment abolishing slavery.

“I’m getting choked up, the fact that we have this and it’s tangible. ... I feel like I’m in an ancestral plane, at arm’s length from imagining what Samuel Jones looked like, what he sounded like,” said Haynes, 34.

In the early 1800s, African Americans — including many like Jones who were born free — carried their freedom papers on their person to protect against being captured and sold into slavery, according to historians. Original freedom documents are exceedingly rare, experts said.

“I’ve never held an original freedom paper in my hand before — I‘ve only seen them digitized,” said Lindsay Fulton, chief research officer at American Ancestors, a family history nonprofit in the Back Bay.

Archives at the University of Virginia in Charlottesville and an exhibit at the Senator John Heinz History Center in Pittsburgh house two of the largest collections of freedom papers, Fulton said. The National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington, D.C., also has freedom papers on display.

Samuel Jones would have stored his freedom paper somewhere safe after receiving it in 1834, Fulton said. When it was passed down to Haynes’s mother, it was in a smaller leather folder, and it’s been remarkably well-preserved.

“The reason these documents were so critical, and in many cases saved and passed down through generations, was because they are the key to avoiding enslavement or re-enslavement right after freedom,” said Kendra Field, chief historian of American Ancestors’ 10 Million Names project cataloguing identities of people enslaved in the US.

At first, Haynes said, he didn’t know where he could take the document to learn more about it. He considered traveling to the African American history museum in D.C., or reaching out to historians at the Museum of African American History on Beacon Hill.

In January, Haynes saw the American Ancestors building when he was on Newbury Street. When he showed researchers there the document, they immediately knew it was an stunning piece of history.

“We got so excited, because we were like, ‘That definitely looks real,’” Fulton said.

Field said the document is what historians call a certificate of freedom, because it was issued by a court. Other types of freedom papers include manumissions, which were issued by enslavers who voluntarily released someone from bondage, and lawsuits filed by people to become free, she said.

Samuel Jones’s certificate of freedom says he was 5 feet, 7 inches tall, he had a “light complexion” and “a small scar on his left hand.”

A Baltimore County Court wax seal dating from 1817 was stamped on the bottom left corner. The document isn’t made of paper, but rather parchment, which is more durable.

The document says Jones was “born free” in Anne Arundel County, which includes state capital Annapolis.

Because the document was issued in Baltimore County, it’s possible Jones got his freedom papers after moving away from his hometown to seek work at age 21, Fulton said.

It’s also possible Jones sought the document because he was in a new place with fewer relatives and connections, she said.

Haynes and other family members are researching their ancestry further after the discovery, tracing their lineage south of the Mason-Dixon line, which they didn’t know much about before.

“I’m proud that my son didn’t worry about what he might learn,” said Haynes’s mother, Michelle Kendrick. “Every family has a history, and he stepped into wanting to know his history and that’s a big step for anyone to take.”

Kendrick, 58, has lived in Roxbury her whole life, she said. The home of her grandmother, also in Roxbury, caught fire when Kendrick was a child and many family heirlooms were destroyed, she said. Jones’s certificate of freedom was salvaged.

“You don’t come across these type of documents every day,” Haynes said. “I’m just thankful she was able to save it.”

title: Teen charged in October shooting death of 61-year-old woman in Roxbury
text:
A teenager has been charged with murder in the October shooting death of Marie Molea, a Lynn native who had long struggled with mental illness and was killed not far from the Roxbury women’s shelter where she often stayed.

Boston police obtained a warrant against the teen on Wednesday, department spokesperson Sergeant Detective John Boyle said in a news release.

Officials didn’t release his name because he’s underage, but they identified him as a 16-year-old from Needham. They said he’s already in custody on unrelated gun charges.

Molea, 61, was found lying facedown next to a Washington Street bus shelter Oct. 13. She was later pronounced dead at the hospital.

The shooting took place a couple blocks from Rosie’s Place, a shelter and community center. Molea was a familiar face and beloved presence in the area, according to people who knew her.

Before she descended into severe mental illness and struggled to maintain housing, she was a devoted mother and school nurse. She grew up in Lynn, where she became captain of the cheerleading team and homecoming queen at Lynn Classical High School.

Police have released few details about how they identified her alleged killer.

The teen was initially arrested in late December after police found a loaded gun in his pocket while conducting a frisk in Roxbury.

Officers were driving on Dudley Street toward Warren Street when they saw the boy running at a full sprint toward Nubian Station, police said at the time. He “appeared hypervigilant and was observed swinging his left arm freely while keeping his right arm pinned tightly against his jacket, with his hand holding an object inside the front pocket,” police said.

The teen has been charged with murder, aggravated assault, and illegal gun possession in Molea’s death, according to police. He’s expected to appear in court for arraignment in the coming days.

Lea Skene can be reached at lea.skene@globe.com. Follow her on X @lea_skene.

title: Boston city councilors call for release of bodycam footage in fatal police shooting
text:
Stephenson King, 39, was killed March 11 after he allegedly tried to flee a traffic stop in a stolen car. Officials said he accelerated and struck a Boston police cruiser in the moments before police shot him.

“We are deeply saddened by this incident,” the councilors said. “Anytime we see a young man die in our community, it is a cause for serious concern.”

They also called on Boston’s Office of Police Accountability and Transparency, a civilian oversight agency, to conduct an independent investigation.

Boston police have released few details about the shooting; the department hasn’t disclosed the names of the officers involved or how many shots were fired.

On Wednesday, a department spokesperson referred questions to the Suffolk District Attorney’s Office, which is investigating King’s death. That office declined to comment on the councilors’ request.

King had committed a carjacking outside a pizza restaurant in Boston’s Mission Hill neighborhood, according to police. The mother of a restaurant employee was waiting outside to pick her up when a man approached her and demanded the vehicle, a manager told the Globe.

About 15 minutes later, officers stopped the stolen car less than a mile away at Linwood Square in Roxbury.

The driver ignored “multiple verbal commands” as officers approached the car on foot, then tried to drive away, Police Commissioner Michael Cox said that night at the scene, offering condolences to King’s family. A witness said the encounter escalated quickly.

In a phone interview Wednesday, Culpepper said his constituents want answers. He said they include Roxbury residents who witnessed the shooting, which occurred in his district.

“For something this serious, where there was loss of life, I think you have to be as transparent as possible,” said Culpepper, a Dorchester attorney and local pastor who was elected to City Council last year. “I want to see if the bodycam will verify what the eye witnesses told me.”

Culpepper said the overarching question is whether the shooting was necessary, “whether … the young man would still be alive” if police had handled the situation differently.

“I want to see what the officers said to the man while he was sitting in the car,” Culpepper said. “It’s obvious that he panicked.”

After the 2015 fatal police shooting of Angelo West, which also occurred in Roxbury, Culpepper said he was among a group of local clergy who were allowed to view the bodycam footage while the shooting was still under investigation. In that case, West shot a police officer in the face before other officers opened fire, killing him.

Culpepper said he believes the same protocol should be followed here. “The precedent has been set to bring in community leaders to see the bodycam,” he said.

title: Federal judge dismisses suit alleging discrimination of white, Asian students in BPS exam school admissions
text:
“BPS’s policy is lawful and fully consistent with legal precedent,” the spokesperson said. “BPS is committed to continuing to provide high-achieving students with strong learning opportunities at all of our schools and to partnering with families and school communities to ensure that young people from every neighborhood have equitable access to a high-quality, rigorous education.”

The Boston Parent Coalition for Academic Excellence Corp., a group of white and Asian families, immediately filed a notice advising of its intent to appeal the ruling in the US Court of Appeals for the First Circuit.

The group sought to block the district from continuing to use the admissions system the School Committee adopted in 2021 which divides the city up into socioeconomic “tiers,” where students compete within.

The lawsuit, filed in July in US District Court for Massachusetts, said the system used the tiers to reduce the proportion of white students admitted to the schools, violating their rights.

A hearing was held March 10 on the school district’s motion to dismiss the lawsuit.

The hearing focused on the differences between the district’s “Zip Code Plan,” which was in effect from 2020 until 2022, and “Tier System,” implemented in the 2022-23 admissions cycle, court records show.

The law firm representing the parents, Pacific Legal Foundation, filed a similar suit in 2020 after the School Committee voted to temporarily award seats based on grades and ZIP code. Federal courts ruled against the group, and the Supreme Court declined to take the case in 2024.

The coalition, represented by lawyers at the libertarian Pacific Legal Foundation, filed the current lawsuit last year.

US District Court Judge William G. Young dismissed the case, “solely on the basis that it is bound by the similarity of the present challenge to the First Circuit’s decision” in 2023, records show.

In his six-page order, Young said he was “duty-bound” to abide by previous court rulings on the matter.

While the two systems are different, they also possess similar fundamentals, Young said, adding that another court already had determined that there was insufficient grounds for an equal protection violation.

“Both plans are indisputably facially race-neutral” and do not result in an “aggregate disparate impact,” Young wrote.

Prior to the pandemic, admission to the three exam schools was determined in a citywide process based solely on grades and an entrance exam score.

Under the current admissions system, which has been repeatedly adjusted over the last few years, the city is split into four tiers based on socioeconomic measures, with students in each vying for one-quarter of the total seats.

Under the new system, the proportion of Grade 7 exam school invites going to white students declined from 40 percent for School Year 2020-21 to a low of 24 percent for 2023-24.

Students apply to enter the schools in Grades 7 and 9, and must have at least a B average to be eligible.

The wealthiest tier, Tier 4 (or Tier 8 in an earlier version of the system), has tended to have more applicants than the other tiers, but all tiers get the same number of seats.

Because the city’s white students are concentrated in Tier 4, which includes West Roxbury and Beacon Hill, they have lower odds of admission to their schools of choice, the lawsuit contended.

title: Ex-cons seek salvation through sandwiches in Lynn Nottage’s ‘Clyde’s’
text:
PAWTUCKET, R.I. — Approximately three-quarters of prisoners in the US relapse and get re-arrested within five years of their release. In the early 2000s, formalized culinary education was introduced into many of these institutions in an attempt to reverse this trend by offering a vocation in the perpetually understaffed restaurant industry.

Some establishments — like Edwin’s in Cleveland, All Square in Minneapolis, and the Haley House Bakery Café in Boston’s Roxbury neighborhood — were willing to hire, train, and support formerly incarcerated individuals with talent and the right temperament. Their success stories are the stuff of an Oscar-nominated documentary with the double entendre title “Knife Skills.”

But then there are eateries like Clyde’s, the fictional sandwich shop at a truck stop in Berks County, Pa., that resides in Lynn Nottage’s play of the same name. It offers dismal working conditions and its callous owner stands in the way of four formerly incarcerated kitchen staff members who are trying to reclaim their lives and invent the perfect sandwich.

Get Food Club

A weekly newsletter about food and dining, by Globe reporter Alexa Gagosz.

Enter Email

Nottage has made a career out of illuminating the lives of working-class people, typically in weighty, topical dramas. And she has earned Pulitzer prizes with “Ruined” (an unflinching portrayal of sexual violence and survival during a civil war in the Congo) and “Sweat” (which explores the desperate lives of union employees at a rustbelt steel factory). In “Clyde’s,” which opened on Broadway in 2021 and is getting its Rhode Island premiere at Burbage Theatre, the drama rides a wave of character-driven comedy and carries with it an overriding sense of optimism.

Under Jeff Church’s incisive direction, it does so brilliantly. The play is not particularly Pulitzer-worthy, but this production taps all that is deeply heartfelt and engaging in the work.

The sandwich shop’s kitchen staff consists of Rafael (Arturo Puentes), a playful and romantic recovering addict with a taste for things rich and hot; Letitia (Ashley Aldarondo), a feisty single mother who likes to mix savory and sweet; Jason (James Lucey), a quiet but hot-tempered new release, who prefers the classics with a sprig of something special; and Montrellous (Jason Quinn), a self-reflective mentor and true chef at heart. He gravitates toward the gourmet, building intricate combinations like fried quail egg salad with mint on oven-fresh cranberry pecan multigrain bread.

Creating the perfect sandwich is these ex-cons’ spiritual get-out-of-jail card from the prison of the mind built from years of incarceration, fortified by the tedium of the daily grind of short order cooking at Clyde’s, and reinforced by its hard-hearted owner’s abuse and blatant disrespect.

The play’s most charming and creatively rendered moments take place when these four stand at their workstation — realistically constructed by Trevor Elliott and appropriately distressed by Grey Rung — and exhibit their dream creations. Andrew Iacovelli bathes them in eureka-moment lighting when they list exotic ingredients as if reciting lines of forbidden poetry.

Their passion hits a wall when confronted by the shop’s cynical owner, Clyde (MJ Daly), who has no taste for their creative concoctions and no patience for their free-thinking. This is made perfectly clear when she puts out a cigarette in the jujed-up grilled cheese she is presented as a peace offering.

Church, who is also Burbage’s artistic director, knows on which side his bread is buttered, for he has anchored this ensemble cast with talented alumni. These actors deliver authentic and always interesting performances grounded in their respective characters’ dark backstory, which grows richer as the play progresses. Led by Quinn’s endearing portrayal of Montrellous, a gentle giant of a man, this troupe comes together to form a very believable makeshift family.

Aldarondo is the sole newcomer to the cast, though she is no stranger to the stage (her performance in last season’s “Someone Will Remember Us” at Trinity Rep was memorable). Her raw energy is the perfect counterpoint to all the vitriol that Daly so successfully dishes out as Clyde.

At the risk of overusing the running food metaphor, this play is a club sandwich of sorts — a multi-tiered creation with tasty layers of heartbreak, humor, and humanity. And it comes with a late arriving but most welcome side of redemption.

CLYDE’S

Play by Lynn Nottage. Directed by Jeff Church. At the Burbage Theatre Co., 59 Blackstone Ave., Pawtucket, R.I., through April 12. Tickets are $35, plus fees. 401-484-0355, burbagetheatre.org

Bob Abelman is an award-winning theater critic who formerly wrote for the Austin Chronicle. Connect with him on Facebook.

title: What these local companies can teach us
text:
Write to us anytime at startingpoint@globe.com. Your emails have turned into newsletters! To subscribe, sign up here.

An AI-powered weather forecasting company. A self-described podcasting conglomerate. A sticker company.

All are among New England’s 50 fastest-growing companies of 2026, according to the Globe and data and analysis firm Statista.

Starting Point alum Rob Gavin writes, “Some had the right products at the right time. Some built diverse lines of business. Some got lucky. But many also shared the important quality of vision: the ability to look to the future and be strategic even when the present demanded much of their attention.”

Among the “present” challenges: a slowing economy, rising energy prices, uncertain and changing tariffs. I talked with Rob to see how they did it.

David: Hey Rob, can you give me an example of a company addressing a current challenge?

Rob: SharkNinja, a Needham company the makes vacuum cleaners, blenders, and other consumer gadgets, was buffeted by one of the biggest challenges for businesses: tariffs. Most of SharkNinja’s manufacturing is done in Asia, so Donald Trump’s “Liberation Day” in April was anything but for the company. CEO Mark Barrocas told me that for eight days after the presidential announcement, leaders across the company did little else but brainstorm ideas to mitigate the impact of tariffs, ultimately coming up with some 1,500 possibilities.

Those ideas included negotiating with factories to hold down costs and analyzing each product to determine whether customers would tolerate price increases and, if yes, by how much. Despite the trade hoo-hah, SharkNinja reported that sales climbed 16 percent in 2025. Which I imagine was very liberating for Barrocas and his team.

What’s more important, a salient idea or solid execution of it?

You need both. If you don’t have the right product or service, all the execution and efficiency in the world isn’t going to get customers to buy it. Conversely, if you come up with a great idea, but can’t produce, market, or sell it effectively, it’s like the proverbial tree in the woods.

Do these businesses share a mix of optimism and stick-to-it-ness?

Definitely. No matter what was happening around them, these businesses had confidence in their products, their vision, and their people. In my reporting, I spoke with Brooke Thomson, the CEO of Associated Industries of Massachusetts, who noted a striking disconnect. AIM’s monthly survey over much of the past year has shown that local company executives have become more pessimistic about economic conditions — think tariffs, uncertainty, and rising costs — but remain optimistic about their own companies’ prospects. “People,” Thomson told me, ”believe in their companies, believe in the workforce, believe in their ability to deliver products and services.”

As you reported on these companies, was there something that really surprised you?

After hearing grumbling about the region’s tech sector losing its mojo, I was pleasantly surprised that the top three companies on the Globe’s list were young tech firms. Tenovi of Portsmouth, N.H., Salient of Falmouth, and HighByte of Portland, Maine, all have developed cutting-edge technologies that solve real problems for real people and real companies. A famous quote from Mark Twain comes to mind as people lament the state of our tech sector, but I’ll go with Monty Python: Not dead yet.

title: Mass. needs to thin its exploding deer population. Could Sunday hunting help?
text:
Write to us anytime at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

Hunters have long asked Massachusetts for three things. Now, they appear poised to get them, partly because the state needs their help to thin an exploding deer population.

On Thursday, Governor Maura Healey announced she will file legislation to allow the use of crossbows and reduce the minimum distance archery hunters are required from an occupied dwelling. The third change? Removing the ban on Sunday hunting — a holdover from the colonial “blue laws” that were established to make sure people went to church.

Massachusetts is one of only two states (hello Maine!) with an outright ban on Sunday hunting, and generations of hunters have lobbied to lift the prohibition, arguing that it halves the number of days many hunters can spend in the woods.

The changes were unanimously endorsed by the board of MassWildlife. The state conservation agency held five listening sessions and received more than 11,000 public comments. Seventy percent favor lifting the Sunday ban, according to a report.

Still, it’s a bold move in a state where less than one percent of residents hunt, and the subject of hunting is politically and emotionally fraught.

Calling Cotton Mather

“Hunting is one of our oldest traditions, and it’s still thriving,” Healey said Thursday at the Frances A. Crane Wildlife Management Area in East Falmouth.

“One of the funky things about Massachusetts is we have these ‘blue laws’ that go back to the Puritan times,” Healey said. “We stopped burning women at the stake, and allow people to drink alcohol. But we still have a ban on Sunday hunting. It doesn’t make any sense.”

Massachusetts has seen its deer population balloon in recent decades to a level far above wildlife management goals of 12-18 per square mile. In some areas of Eastern Massachusetts, that number is estimated to be 25-50.

Eve Schluter, the acting director of MassWildlife, said an overabundance of any wildlife population has a cascading influence. Too many deer, she said, have led to a spike in automotive collisions, impacts to agriculture, and concerns about deforestation. When deer consume too much ground vegetation, it damages the habitat for other animals and eliminates seedlings and saplings that would be the next generation of tree canopy.

Venison for all?

In 2022, MassWildlife allowed hunters to essentially kill an unlimited number of does in much of Eastern Massachusetts and the islands. That same year, they allowed hunters to donate the deer they killed, feeding families in need and keeping hunters in the woods long after their freezers are full of venison. The program has provided more than 100,000 meals, Healey said.

Continued concerns about forest damage has brought hunters unlikely allies, including Mass Audubon, which has said that some of its sanctuaries have up to eight times the number of deer they can sustain. A representative recently said that its “position has evolved in recognition of the severe damage to forests.”

The abundance of deer also raises concern about tick-borne illnesses, such as Lyme disease and alpha-gal syndrome. While thinning the herd won’t reduce tick levels alone, Schluter said, it will make other strategies to combat ticks more effective.

The main opposition to Sunday hunting has always been safety and sharing the land. Opponents argue it’s not too much to ask to have the woods free of hunters one day a week.

“It’s important to recognize those feelings of fear and discomfort that can result in less people going outside,” MassWildlife’s Schluter said. “There’s a perception, but it’s not supported by the data. ... All our hunters are required to take a safety course. Hunting is an extremely safe, regulated activity, and it can coexist with other outdoor recreation activities.”

title: City officials show support for Boston police, call for transparency as officer faces manslaughter charge
text:
On Saturday, a couple of other Boston city councilors spoke out about the incident, saying that with limited information available, it is “critical for transparency and accountability.” They also called for an independent investigation by a civilian agency.

“For someone to lose their life is always the last possible outcome anyone wants, including our Police,” Councilor John FitzGerald, who represents most of Dorchester and a part of the South End, said in a statement on Facebook. “While any allegation must be taken seriously, we must ensure fairness and due process. I stand with the Boston Police Department and our officers who serve honorably every day, and I remain committed to supporting both public safety and accountability.”

King allegedly carjacked a woman outside a Mission Hill pizza restaurant on March 11, according to the police. She was waiting to pick up her daughter, an employee of the store, when a man approached and demanded her vehicle, a manager told the Globe.

King was stopped at Linwood Square in Roxbury, about a mile away. According to a police report, the driver ignored verbal commands as officers approached on foot and tried to drive away.

O’Malley drew a department-issued Taser and shouted, “Bro, I’m going to [expletive] shoot you,” according to the report. King attempted to drive his vehicle forward and back, striking a cruiser behind him, “in an attempt to escape the police,” according to the report.

As King started to drive forward again, O’Malley drew his gun and fired three shots through the driver’s window, striking King, according to the report. He was taken to a Boston hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

O’Malley told investigators he fired because he feared for the life of another officer on scene.

Assistant District Attorney Ian Polumbaum said in court that O’Malley’s explanation wasn’t reasonable, pointing to witness testimony and footage from police body cameras, which have not been made public.

Councilor Ed Flynn wrote in an email statement that “As a city and society, we should not rush to judgment and immediately second guess a police officer.”

“While this criminal case goes forward, the City of Boston should not penalize Police Officer Nick O’Malley and his family by taking away his health care insurance and salary,” Flynn said.

Erin J. Murphy, Boston City Councilor at-large, shared a statement saying officers were responding to an unpredictable incident. She represents the whole city as a councilor-at-large.

“A life was lost, and that is always serious,” Murphy wrote. “But we also have to be honest about the full context. Public reporting shows this individual had a long criminal history, multiple open cases, repeated violations, and was out on bail at the time of this incident. That matters. It matters for public safety, and matters when we talk about what happened that night.”

The New England Benevolent Association, an organization that represents 5,000 law enforcement members across New England, called for O’Malley to be presumed innocent while the case moves through legal channels.

“The reality of modern policing is that officers are frequently placed into circumstances where hesitation can cost lives,” the organization wrote. “It is essential that this matter be allowed to proceed through the appropriate legal channels without the influence of public speculation or the rush to judgment that often follows critical incidents involving law enforcement.”

title: ‘We hold people accountable:’ Prosecutors send message with swift arrest of BPD officer, experts say
text:
But, she and other legal analysts said, bringing charges is just the first step. The question of criminal responsibility ultimately falls to a jury.

“Officers are under a lot of pressure, and it’s much easier to second-guess them in hindsight,” she said. “But the job is to use as little force as possible.”

Evandro Carvalho, executive director of Boston’s Office of Police Accountability and Tranparency, urged prosecutors in a statement to “pursue justice in a manner that is transparent, thorough, and fair.”

Carvalho said his office will suspend its review of the shooting until the district attorney’s prosecution is complete.

Stephenson King, 39, was killed in the March 11 shooting in Roxbury. He was trying to flee a traffic stop, driving a vehicle he had stolen about 15 minutes earlier when he committed an unarmed carjacking, according to police and prosecutors.

Just eight days later, officer Nicholas O’Malley was charged with voluntary manslaughter. He pleaded not guilty last week and was released on personal recognizance. O’Malley had told investigators he fired into the vehicle because he thought another officer was in danger of being run over, court records show.

Prosecutors didn’t mince words. Citing body camera footage and witness accounts, they said O’Malley’s actions were unreasonable.

The other officer “was in greater danger of being struck by those bullets than he ever was by the car,” Assistant District Attorney Ian Polumbaum said during the hearing.

King opened the car window at the command of police officers, but he didn’t turn the vehicle off or comply with other commands, according to a police report. Positioned outside the driver’s side window, O’Malley drew a Taser and shouted, “Bro, I’m going to [expletive] shoot you,” the report says. At that moment, King backed into the cruiser behind him, then maneuvered the car forward and back “in an attempt to escape the police,” according to the report.

As King started to drive forward again, O’Malley drew his gun and fired three shots through the driver’s window, according to the report. Almost immediately, O’Malley called over his radio that officers were involved in a shooting and the suspect “tried to run us over,” the report says. King was later pronounced dead at the hospital.

State law and Boston Police Department policy forbid officers from shooting at a moving vehicle unless there’s no other way to prevent “imminent harm to a person.”

While some praised the Suffolk District Attorney’s Office for acting quickly to bring charges, others sharply criticized the move.

“It’s just too fast. It’s unheard of,” said Larry Calderone, president of the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association. “It seems like a political statement and a rush to judgment.”

Police are frequently required to make split-second decisions, he said, and it’s unfair to condemn an officer for acting based on perceived danger. He accused prosecutors of “Monday morning quarterbacking.”

“I guarantee they have no idea how that police officer felt,” he said in a phone interview.

Calderone attended the arraignment accompanied by dozens of other Boston police officers, many in uniform, who filled the courtroom gallery in support of O’Malley.

Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden denied the accusations that politics were at play. He said O’Malley isn’t being treated differently from any other defendant.

Experts said it’s unusual for police officers to face criminal charges so soon after an incident like this. More commonly, the investigations take months or years, sometimes unfolding before a grand jury — and often ending in a decision not to prosecute.

Still a relatively new development in the history of law enforcement, the presence of bodycam footage likely contributed to the quick resolution here. Along with bystander cell phone videos, the footage has transformed police misconduct investigations in recent decades, said Tom Nolan, a former Boston police lieutenant and criminologist.

Boston police began a widespread implementation of body cameras in 2019.

The January fatal shooting of Renee Good in Minneapolis prompted calls to outfit immigration officers with body cameras. While the circumstances of the two shootings fundamentally diverge, Good was also driving away when an ICE agent shot into her SUV.

President Trump was quick to defend the agent, saying he shot in self-defense, repeating what has become a familiar refrain in the aftermath of police violence. But bystander video raised significant questions about the president’s account.

“Historically, the default position has been to defer to the judgment of the officer, unless there’s clear and convincing evidence to the contrary,” Nolan said, although that’s changing.

He commended Suffolk prosecutors for acting quickly based on the evidence they reviewed.

The last time a Boston police officer faced criminal charges for an on-duty shooting was more than 30 years ago. In 1991, officer James E. Hall shot and killed an unarmed Dorchester teenager following a foot chase. Hall claimed his gun accidentally discharged when he lost his balance, but he was charged with second-degree murder and ultimately convicted of involuntary manslaughter.

In a city with relatively low rates of gun violence, the Roxbury police shooting and subsequent response from prosecutors could serve as somewhat of a wakeup call, Nolan said.

“It will certainly cause some officers to have pause over whether or not they’re reflexively using force,” he added.

Convicting a police officer is a different story, however, according to criminal justice experts.

In 2022, a jury acquitted Reading police officer Erik Drauschke, who was charged with manslaughter for fatally shooting an unarmed man. Drauschke’s attorney argued the officer acted reasonably when faced with an evasive suspect who refused to show his hands.

“This is not going to be an easy prosecution,” Nolan said. “If this officer can convince the jury that he genuinely believed his colleague was in danger of serious bodily injury, he’s probably going to walk.”

title: It’s not just vaccines — parents are refusing other routine preventive care for newborns
text:
A recent study in the Journal of the American Medical Association, which analyzed more than 5 million births nationwide, found that refusals of vitamin K shots nearly doubled between 2017 and 2024, from 2.9 percent to 5.2 percent. Other research suggests that parents who decline vitamin K shots are much more likely to refuse getting their newborns the hepatitis B vaccine and an eye ointment to prevent potentially blinding infections. Rates for that vaccination at birth dropped in recent years, and doctors confirm that more parents are refusing the eye medication.

“I do think these families care deeply about their infants,” said Dr. Kelly Wade, a Philadelphia neonatologist. “But I hear from families that it’s hard to make decisions right now because they’re hearing conflicting information.”

Innumerable social media posts question doctors’ advice on safe and effective measures including vitamin K and eye ointment. And the Trump administration has repeatedly undermined established science. A federal advisory committee whose members were appointed by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — a leading antivaccine activist before joining the administration — voted to end the longstanding recommendation to immunize all babies against hepatitis B right after birth. On Monday a federal judge temporarily blocked all decisions made by the reconfigured committee.

One common thread that ties together antivaccine views and growing sentiments against other protective measures for newborns is the fallacy that natural is always better than artificial, said Dr. David Hill, a Seattle pediatrician and researcher.

“Nature will allow 1 in 5 human infants to die in the first year of life,” Hill said, “which is why generations of scientists and doctors have worked to bring that number way, way down.”

Babies are born with low levels of vitamin K, leaving them vulnerable because their intestines can’t produce enough until they start eating solid foods at around 6 months old.

“Vitamin K is important for helping the blood clot and preventing dangerous bleeding in babies, like bleeding into the brain,” said Dr. Kristan Scott of the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, lead author of the JAMA study.

Before injections became routine, up to about 1 in 60 babies suffered vitamin K deficiency bleeding, which can also affect the gastrointestinal tract. Today the condition is rare, but research shows that newborns who don’t get a vitamin K shot are 81 times more likely to develop severe bleeding than those who do.

Hill has seen what can happen.

“I cared for a toddler whose parents had chosen that risk,” the Seattle doctor said. The child essentially had a stroke as a newborn and wound up with severe developmental delays and ongoing seizures.

At a February meeting of the Idaho chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, doctors said they knew of eight deaths from vitamin K deficiency bleeding in the state over the preceding 13 months, said Patterson, who is president of the chapter.

Infections prevented by other newborn measures can also have grave consequences. Erythromycin eye ointment protects against gonorrhea that can be contracted during birth and potentially cause blindness if untreated. The hepatitis B vaccine prevents a disease that can lead to liver failure, liver cancer, or cirrhosis.

Even if a pregnant woman is tested for gonorrhea and hepatitis B, no test is perfect, and she may get infected after testing, said Dr. Susan Sirota, a pediatrician in Highland Park, Ill. Either way, she risks passing the infection to her child.

Parents give many reasons for turning down preventive measures, including fearing they might cause problems and not wanting newborns to feel pain.

“Some will just say they want more of a natural birth philosophy,” said Dr. Steven Abelowitz, founder of Ocean Pediatrics in Orange County, Calif. “Then there’s a ton of misinformation. … There are outside influences, friends, celebrities, nonprofessionals and political agendas.”

Abelowitz practices in an area with about an equal mix of Republicans and Democrats.

“There’s more mistrust from the conservative side, but there’s plenty on the more liberal side as well,” he said, “It’s across-the-board mistrust.”

Social media provides ample fuel, spreading myths and pushing unregulated vitamin K drops that doctors warn babies can’t absorb well.

Care refusals aren’t a new phenomenon. Wade, in Philadelphia, said she’s seen them for 20 years. But until recently, they were rare.

Twelve years ago, Dana Morrison, now a Minnesota doula, declined the vitamin K shot for her newborn son, giving him oral drops instead.

“It came from a space of really wanting to protect the bonding time with my baby,” she said. “I was trying to eliminate more pokes.”

Her daughter’s birth a couple of years later was less straightforward, leaving the infant with a bruised leg. Morrison got the vitamin K shot for her.

Knowing what she does now, she said, she would have gotten it for her son, too.

Doctors hope to change minds, one parent at a time. And that begins with respect.

“If I walk into the room with judgment, we are going to have a really useless conversation,” Hill said. “Every parent I serve wants the best for their children.”

When parents question the need for the vitamin K shot, Dr. Heather Felton tries to address their specific concerns. She explains why it’s given and the risks of not getting it. Most families decide to get it, said Felton, who has seen no uptick in refusals.

“It really helps that you can take that time and really listen and be able to provide some education,” said Felton, a pediatrician at Norton Children’s in Louisville, Kentucky.

In Idaho, Patterson sometimes finds himself clearing up misconceptions. Some parents will agree to a vitamin K shot when they find out it’s not a vaccine, for example.

These conversations can take time, especially since the parents doctors see in hospitals usually aren’t people they know through their practices.

But doctors are happy to invest that time if it might save babies.

“I end every discussion with parents with this: ‘Please understand at the end of the day, I’m passionate about this because I have the best interest of children in my mind and heart,’” Patterson said. “I understand this is a hot topic, and I don’t want to disrespect anybody. But at the same time, I’m desperately saddened that we’re losing babies for no reason.”

title: ‘So much more dire.’ Cuban-Americans in Mass. worry for those on the island amid humanitarian crisis
text:
Many people in New England are concerned about how to provide immediate relief to those on the island, with churches and local advocacy groups collecting donations and supplies. Others are worried that Cuba’s problems will continue as long as the US energy blockade that has halted oil shipments to the island over the past three months is in place.

Still more, like Gorriaran, are aware that some types of assistance will only go so far. Gorriaran, who serves as the secretary of Centro Cultural Cubano, a Massachusetts-based organization dedicated to preserving Cuban culture in the US, said imports into the country are under strict government control.

“Even when you send money ... the government will take a portion of that,” she said, adding that Cubans have resorted to buying food and essential appliances on the black market.

The waves of recent blackouts caused, at least in part, by the US energy blockade have left many of the nation’s 10 million residents struggling to keep food from spoiling. Hospitals have canceled surgeries. The leading university has reduced classes due to the power outages and transportation shutdowns. The most recent blackout is the country’s third big failure of its power grid since December.

“The people of Cuba haven’t just been struggling with a lack of electricity but food and so many other services,” said Marcela Betancur, the executive director of the Latino Policy Institute, a Rhode Island-based organization.

“Recently, it’s been so much more dire,” she added.

Kevin Whalen, 64, of First Baptist Church Jamaica Plain, said the church has partnered with its sister church in Cuba to coordinate aid and advocacy. The church has raised more than $10,000 to purchase medical supplies, which the Cuban church distributes to the local community.

“This medicine that was brought over was very quickly distributed into the community,” said Reverend Patricia Brennan, a Unitarian Universalist minister who helped transport the supplies during a recent trip to Cuba.

During a recent solidarity event, the church in Jamaica Plain gathered 54 signatures in support of a letter they wrote to the Massachusetts congressional delegation, asking them to stop the blockade and support a bill that would limit some trade embargoes on the island.

“We’re going to start something online so we can reach more people,” Whalen said.

Rubén Salinas Stern, 75, a former director of the Latino Center at Tufts University, has been donating and helping incorporate Cuban American perspectives into the church’s efforts.

“I’m trying to give support because the people in the church don’t have a lot of connections with Cuban Americans,” said Stern, a Cuban-born Massachusetts resident who left the island as a child.

Ramon Bueno, 73, commissioner of the Climate Action Commission in Somerville, said, “One of the areas that have been very successful before the pressures became so brutal is in the area of medicine.”

“That’s one of the areas that used to be one of the best working parts of the society, and that’s one area I can contribute to,” said Bueno, who came to the United States from Cuba in 1961.

On Saturday, a group of activists from Massachusetts Peace Action and Boston Cuba Solidarity Coalition gathered at the Park Street station in the Boston Common to protest the US oil blockade on the island.

Nalda Vigezzi, a lifelong activist with the Boston Cuba Solidarity Coalition, was at the protest waving a yellow sign in the air that read “Cuba is our friend, let Cuba live.” She said she has spent decades calling on the US government to end the 60-year-long economic, commercial, and financial blockade on Cuba.

“Denying Cuba food, medicine, basic necessities is abysmal and a crime,” Vigezzi said. “Cuba is not a threat to anybody and doesn’t threaten its neighbors; it’s just trying to take care of itself and its population.”

Dr. Tia Tucker, a 44-year-old physician at Cambridge Health Alliance who trained in Cuba, said she and her former classmates have organized efforts to send supplies and financial support to Cuban health care workers and students.

“We have kind of an unofficial alumni association, and we try to support our students and help them finish their training,” Tucker said.

Reverend Mark Pendleton, rector of Christ Church in Exeter, N.H., recently traveled to Cuba, bringing items such as medications and water-purification supplies. His church partners with a local church in Cardenas, Cuba, through Episcopal networks in New England and Cuba.

However, Pendleton said that fuel shortages forced his group to limit their visit to Havana, rather than traveling directly to their companion parish, which was a couple of hours away from the city.

In recent months, Pendleton’s church has received specific requests for medications such as Tylenol and Advil for both adults and children, due to mosquito-borne viruses that have been causing illness.

“We also brought down many solar-powered lanterns that are really invaluable when the lights go out,” Pendleton said. “We distributed over 45 of those.”

Yet despite aid efforts, the humanitarian crisis continues.

“To live off fire, what does that mean for health and hospitals?” said Betancur, of the Latino Policy Institute. “The humanitarian portion is incredibly concerning.”

Wire service materials were used in this report.

title: Hyde Park man who was allegedly armed with a butcher knife at Forest Hills MBTA station ordered held on multiple charges
text:
A man who was allegedly bothering people with a butcher knife at the Forest Hills MBTA station was ordered held Monday, pending a dangerousness hearing, prosecutors said.

Micah Martin, 29, of Hyde Park, is charged with 15 counts of multiple charges, including six assault and battery on a police officer, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden’s office said.

He is also facing four counts of assault and battery attempt to disarm a police officer; and one count each of armed carjacking, discharging a firearm within 500 feet of a building, assault with a dangerous weapon (knife), resisting arrest, disorderly conduct on a public conveyance, prosecutors said in a statement.

A plea of not guilty was entered on his behalf to all charges during his arraignment in Boston Municipal Court in West Roxbury, court records show.

Martin was ordered held without bail pending a dangerousness hearing March 30, prosecutors said.

He was arrested late Friday morning.

Officers responded to the station at around 11:15 a.m. and encountered the suspect, who was menacing passengers with a butcher knife, the Globe reported. A struggle ensued and an officer’s weapon discharged.

The suspect allegedly went for the officer’s weapon, the Globe reported. No one was injured when the gun went off.

Two officers struggled with the man and were able to take him into custody. . Both of the officers were taken to a Boston hospital for treatment of unspecified injuries.

The suspect was treated at the scene by Boston EMS first responders and was arrested by Transit police, the Globe reported.

title: Ex-community activist Monica Cannon-Grant ordered to pay more than $224,000 in federal fraud case
text:
Former Boston community organizer Monica Cannon-Grant was ordered by a federal judge Monday to pay more than $224,000, obtained by diverting donations from her now-defunct antiviolence nonprofit and illegally collecting pandemic relief funds.

US District Court Judge Angel Kelley sentenced the disgraced activist to home confinement and probation in January, and also ordered her to pay $106,000 in restitution and an unspecified forfeiture amount.

The judge Monday said Cannon-Grant must pay $224,063, an amount that reflects the proceeds from her crimes, according to a copy of the order.

The forfeiture amount includes roughly $181,000 in diverted donations, more than $33,000 in fraudulent pandemic unemployment benefits, and about $12,600 in rental assistance benefits, the order states.

Cannon-Grant, who ran the nonprofit Violence in Boston Inc., rose to prominence in 2020 after organizing a march that drew thousands to protest the killing of George Floyd and other Black people at the hands of police. She also collaborated with a Dorchester restaurant to distribute free meals to people during the pandemic.

She founded her nonprofit in 2017 out of her home in Roxbury, and by 2020 it had expanded to a headquarters in Hyde Park. Cannon-Grant, a mother of six, was widely praised for her work.

She was honored as a Bostonian of the Year in 2020 by the Boston Globe Magazine and hailed as the city’s “best social justice advocate” by Boston Magazine.

But in 2022, federal prosecutors charged Cannon-Grant and her husband, Clark Grant, alleging they raised more than $1 million for the charity and received nearly $60,000 in pandemic relief funds intended to feed people in need, then spent much of the money on themselves, including for vacations, car rentals, and eating out.

Clark Grant was killed in a motorcycle crash in Easton in March 2023.

In September, Cannon-Grant pleaded guilty to 18 counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud, wire fraud, mail fraud, and tax violations. In exchange, prosecutors agreed to dismiss nine counts related to allegations of mortgage fraud.

At her sentencing in January, Cannon-Grant told the judge she took “full ownership” of her actions, but said she was “extremely proud” of the nonprofit’s work during the pandemic.

title: Teen held without bail in October shooting death of 61-year-old woman in Roxbury
text:
A teenager was ordered held without bail Monday in the October shooting death of Marie Molea, a Lynn native who had long struggled with mental illness and was killed not far from the Roxbury women’s shelter where she often stayed.

During the brief arraignment Monday morning in Boston Municipal Court, prosecutors said investigators obtained “a significant amount of video” evidence that allowed them to identify a suspect in the brazen afternoon shooting: Jacob Donis, 16, of Needham.

But the hearing didn’t shed any additional light on a potential motive, leaving the circumstances of Molea’s death largely a mystery. Her family members attended the hearing, along with relatives of Donis.

A not guilty plea was entered on his behalf.

Donis was 15 at the time of the shooting, according to his attorney. The case is the latest in Massachusetts involving a juvenile defendant charged in adult court, a situation that has repeatedly led state lawmakers and jurists to consider questions of youth brain development and criminal responsibility.

Under state law, defendants 14 and older charged with murder are automatically prosecuted as adults.

Donis was allowed to remain hidden during Monday’s proceeding, standing behind a partially closed door. Judges sometimes allow defendants privacy based on their age or other factors.

It’s still unclear whether Donis had any prior relationship with the victim. Molea, 61, was found lying facedown next to a Washington Street bus shelter Oct. 13. She was later pronounced dead at the hospital.

The shooting took place a couple blocks from Rosie’s Place, a shelter and community center for women. Molea was a familiar face and beloved presence in the area, according to people who knew her.

Before she descended into severe mental illness and struggled to maintain housing, she was a devoted mother and school nurse. She grew up in Lynn, where she became captain of the cheerleading team and homecoming queen at Lynn Classical High School.

Her two adult daughters and first husband declined to comment after Monday’s hearing, saying only that they were shocked at how the case was unfolding.

Suffolk Assistant District Attorney Mark Lee said surveillance footage allowed investigators to track Donis’ path from his home in Needham to the shooting scene and back. He was riding one of Boston’s Bluebikes, the local bikeshare program, when he approached the bus stop on Washington Street where Molea was standing, Lee said.

Donis fired two shots; one struck Molea in the torso, according to prosecutors.

“In the process, Mr. Donis was captured on multiple surveillance cameras, some of which were high enough quality to permit an actual identification from his face,” Lee said.

Prosecutors announced the murder charge against Donis last week, but he was already in custody for unrelated gun cases.

The teen was previously arrested in late December after Boston police found a loaded gun in his pocket while conducting a frisk in Roxbury. Officers were driving on Dudley Street when they saw the boy running at a full sprint toward Nubian Station, police said at the time. Officers stopped him because he appeared to be holding something inside his front pocket, police said.

Judge James Coffey ordered him held without bail and set another court date for May. His family left the courtroom without commenting to reporters.

The defense will likely focus on his young age, brain development and mental state, his attorney, Stephen Weymouth, said after the hearing. While acknowledging the seriousness of the charges, Weymouth said the case highlights the inherent injustice of prosecuting someone so young as an adult.

“What I think is unfair is the fact that kids this age are charged with murder in the adult court,” he said. “That’s what I think is unfair.”

Weymouth cited research showing that people’s brain development continues well into young adulthood, which affects decision-making and impulse control. He said he plans to have Donis evaluated by a series of experts, including a psychiatrist, psychoanalyst, and neurologist.

title: CEO at Horizons for Homeless Children stepping down after 10 years
text:
“She has an unusual combination of passion and expertise in the organization’s mission ... with a fundamental understanding of the finances of a $15-million to $20-million organization, which you don’t always find,” said Michael Eisenson, cofounder of Horizons and also of private equity firm Charlesbank Capital Partners. “She’s a very effective leader with a style that makes people want to help her succeed.”

Barrand first got involved with Horizons as a volunteer in the late 1990s while working at Bank of Boston, one of the nonprofit’s corporate backers. She was impressed by the mission, as she got to see the circumstances of the young children that Horizons served, and pushed to join the Horizons board, where she stayed for around a dozen years.

She was working as a management consultant and executive coach in 2015 when someone on the Horizons board suggested she apply for the CEO job, even though she had never run a nonprofit, and had stepped off the board several years earlier.

“They thought I would be a brilliant candidate,” Barrand said. “I thought they were crazy.”

Initially, she intended to step in on a temporary basis. But once she got into the job, and saw both the need and the potential, she quickly realized it wasn’t going to be an interim appointment after all. She updated the nonprofit’s technology, refined its staffing, and made some crucial new hires. And she also went after any potential source of funding she could find.

Today, the nonprofit has an annual budget of about $20 million, roughly twice what it was when she took over a decade ago, with a staff of around 150. It serves more than 250 children, a 40 percent increase from 10 years ago.

Most notably, she presided over the construction of a new headquarters, consolidating Horizons’ three leased preschools into one location. It was built through a partnership with Lee Goodman of Watermark Development. Horizons’ space, named the Edgerley Family Horizons Center after benefactors Paul and Sandy Edgerley, is owned by the nonprofit through a condo arrangement. The 200,000-square-foot-plus building opened in 2021 in Roxbury, near Jackson Square.

Friends who know Barrand is about to retire have asked her what she’s going to do next. She doesn’t have an answer yet, except to say “I hope to do absolutely nothing other than some travel and visiting with a grandchild.”

But there’s a good chance she’ll stay involved in the issue of family homelessness in some way.

“The thing that keeps me going at this [is] the majority of people who are experiencing family homelessness are children under six years old,” Barrand said. “The fact that we allow that to happen in this country, with all the resources that we have, is shocking and appalling to me. That just keeps me going. We have got to do better.”

title: City councilors ask Boston police to update bodycam release protocols after recent shooting
text:
That hasn’t happened.

“In the nearly two weeks since, no body camera footage has been released to the public — leaving families without answers and threatening to unravel years of hard-won trust between law enforcement and the community,” Culpepper’s office said in a statement.

The councilors filed two pieces of legislation that would “establish greater transparency around the release of body camera footage by the Boston Police Department,” according to the news release. That includes a provision ensuring that law enforcement oversight entities have timely access to the footage.

Suffolk County prosecutors have repeatedly cited bodycam footage, along with witness accounts, in support of the manslaughter charge against Officer Nicholas O’Malley, 33, who pleaded not guilty last Thursday. He’s charged in the death of Stephenson King, 39, who was shot March 11 while he allegedly tried to flee a traffic stop in a stolen car.

Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said that his office wouldn’t immediately release the video.

“To do so would clearly compromise and imperil the ongoing investigation and the future prosecution of this most serious matter,” he told reporters outside the courthouse following O’Malley’s arraignment. “As we always do in every case, we will be guided only by the facts and the law as we continue to seek accountability and justice for Mr. King, his family, and the entire community.”

Hayden’s office also denied a public records request from the Globe seeking the footage last week, citing the ongoing investigation.

Local officials have taken a different approach in the past. After the 2015 fatal police shooting of Angelo West, which also occurred in Roxbury, a group of local clergy was allowed to view the bodycam footage while the shooting was still under investigation. In that case, West shot a police officer in the face before other officers opened fire, killing him.

In their legislation, Culpepper and Worrell said the department should implement a clear protocol that applies across the board. They also proposed a resolution that would symbolically call on Boston police to update its policies.

“Public confidence in law enforcement is strengthened when clear, consistent, and transparent policies govern the release of evidence following critical incidents,” the resolution reads.

After a lengthy debate Wednesday, the council adopted the resolution. The councilors also adopted a petition to have a hearing on the issue, referring the matter to the panel’s public safety committee.

“Right now, at the center of the anger and confusion surrounding the March 11 incidents are three families: the family of Stephenson King, the family of Nicholas O’Malley, and the family of the carjacking victim,” Culpepper said in a statement. “I am holding all of them in my prayers, but thoughts and prayers are not enough. These families and this city deserve real answers, and that is exactly what we are here to deliver.”

At a community meeting in Roxbury Wednesday evening, residents — including some who witnessed the shooting — expressed wide-ranging concerns about the city’s response.

Some echoed calls for Police Commissioner Michael Cox to release the footage. Others said they feel intimidated by an increased police presence around Linwood Square since the shooting unfolded in their close-knit residential community. They demanded more transparency from local officials.

US Representative Ayanna Pressley issued a statement Wednesday night calling for King’s family to have access to the footage.

“While justice would mean Stephenson’s life was not taken in the first place, we must have transparency and accountability. That means holding everyone involved to account,” she said.

title: Mayor Wu has been settling scores all winter. She could come to regret it.
text:
For 21 years, ladies have lunched in fancy hats for a good cause, raising a cumulative $11.5 million to help care for about 9,000 trees from the Fens to Franklin Park. The city explained it could not sign off on a week-long closure of a public park for a private function, and that any previous approval had been given in error.

Could there be another reason? Well, the conservancy dared to sue Wu to stop the redevelopment of White Stadium in Franklin Park. That’s where the city is helping to build a $325 million stadium that will be shared with Boston Public School students and the new professional women’s soccer team, Boston Legacy.

Some will argue that Wu is entitled to her grudges and has earned as many as she wants after trouncing Josh Kraft, her only real opponent, by 49 points in last year’s mayoral race. He felt so defeated, he dropped out after the primary.

But maybe this moment calls for something else: grace. Wu is one of the savviest politicians in the country, yet she acts like the only way to amass power is by settling scores.

Some slights have been purely political and at times border on petty. Skipping state Senator Nick Collins’s annual St. Patrick’s Day breakfast after he blocked Wu’s property tax plan on Beacon Hill last year doesn’t really hurt anyone. Nor does passing on the annual meeting of the Boston Municipal Research Bureau. Likely, few outside the city’s chattering class even noticed.

But sometimes grievances, like the one with the conservancy, take on a more vengeful tone, with potentially real-life consequences. For example, Wu seems to be setting her sights on unseating state Senator Will Brownsberger, who, along with Collins, helped kill her property tax proposal in the Senate.

A Wu senior aide, Daniel Lander, left her administration in January to challenge Brownsberger, a Democrat whose district covers Belmont, Watertown, and parts of Boston and Cambridge. Like Wu, Lander worked for Senator Elizabeth Warren; he lives in the Fenway, and he’s the son of Broad Institute founding director Eric Lander — the sort of candidate who’ll at least make Brownsberger work to keep his seat.

The political bloodletting picked up shortly after Wu was sworn in for her second term. Most of us can hardly remember developer Tom O’Brien’s short-lived mayoral aspirations last year, but one person who will never forget is Wu.

In 2023, the city had awarded O’Brien and his partners the rights to develop a $1 billion life sciences and affordable housing project on a long-vacant parcel along Tremont Street in Roxbury. Not anymore. When O’Brien’s development rights came up for renewal, Wu took the site back — rather than issuing the usual rubber-stamped extension — and says she wants to build a new Madison Park Technical Vocational High School there instead. O’Brien never got anything built, and he’s welcome to re-bid on whatever land is left over, if he wants.

Payback against political rivals is one of the unspoken perks of being mayor, and Wu clearly has learned from a master: former mayor Tom Menino. She was an intern in his administration while at Harvard Law School.

The late mayor kept a long list of political enemies, from developer Don Chiofaro to former city councilor Sam Yoon. Menino clashed with Chiofaro over the redevelopment of Harbor Garage, to the point that the developer packed away his plans until Marty Walsh took office, yet the glitzy skyscrapers he once envisioned are still just a dream. Yoon, who in 2009 became the first Asian American to run for Boston mayor, couldn’t find a job in Boston after he unsuccessfully challenged Menino. Yoon decamped to the Washington, D.C., area and remains there.

Some will say Wu is worse than Menino when it comes to retribution, but I don’t buy it. She’s just getting going. Menino had five terms to exact his revenge.

Dot Joyce, a former spokesperson and top aide to Menino, said Wu is simply “wielding the power of the office to deliver for the people of the city.”

“When a male mayor does this, you call them powerful,” Joyce added. “When she’s doing it, you call her petty or holding grudges.”

But at some point — hopefully sooner rather than later — Wu has to realize that she’s going to need friends, not enemies, if she wants to get anything done in this town.

Take, for example, that lawsuit the Emerald Necklace Conservancy filed, which will be heard by the Supreme Judicial Court in April. If the city loses on the issue of whether parkland can be used for private use, Wu will need two-thirds of the Legislature to approve a measure allowing her to proceed with a new soccer stadium. That means Wu will need allies in the Senate, and not just Collins and Brownsberger, but also Senate President Karen Spilka, another powerful figure Wu also sparred with.

There’s only one more week left in March, and this political madness should come to an end, too.

It’s time for Wu to get back to governing by building bridges, not tearing them down. Otherwise, her political vendettas will feel less like a power play and more like the pinnacle of pettiness, one that could come back to haunt her.

This story has been updated to reflect the parks that the Emerald Necklace Conservancy takes care of.

title: Thousands cheer as USS Massachusetts, America’s newest nuclear-powered submarine, is commissioned in South Boston
text:
“That is one heck of a boat,” she added with a big smile, echoing a submariner’s term for the vessel, a $2.8 billion high-tech marvel built in Virginia to roam the world’s oceans for 30 years.

The ceremony featured spirited marches and martial music, countless selfies with the Massachusetts, and an upbeat audience replete with hundreds of active-duty Navy officers in crisp dress uniforms.

“This is amazing. It’s been a long process,” said USS Massachusetts crew member Ana Barraza, 22, a sonar technician from El Paso. “It’s a little chillier than what I’ve been used to, however.”

The Massachusetts — a Virginia-class, fast-attack submarine — was christened in Newport News, Va., in 2023, launched in February 2024, and subjected to rigorous sea trials before arriving at Saturday’s commissioning ceremony.

The 377-foot ship carries 152 officers and sailors and is powered by a nuclear reactor that takes up more than half its length. Armed with torpedoes and Tomahawk cruise missiles, the Massachusetts can travel faster than 25 knots and dive deeper than 800 feet.

“May this boat always find safe harbor and deep water,” said US Representative Seth Moulton of Salem, a Marine veteran who cited the state’s pivotal role in founding the United States 250 years ago.

“It was Massachusetts that gave the Revolution its voice,” Moulton said.

Three Medal of Honor recipients attended the ceremony, including Thomas Kelley, a West Roxbury native and Navy veteran of the Vietnam War.

The submarine is the nation’s first warship to be called the USS Massachusetts since a decorated World War II battleship, built at the Fore River Shipyard in Quincy, was decommissioned in 1947.

That ship now serves as a museum in Fall River, a city that also lays claim to being the hometown of Edward Brennan III, the new submarine’s chief of boat and senior enlisted sailor.

The first USS Massachusetts was a wooden steamer, built in East Boston in 1845, that served in the Mexican-American War.

The large crowd, who sat facing the harbor on a chilly morning, included family members who had gathered in Boston from all over the country to celebrate with the crew.

One of them was David Forys of Highland, Ill., who boarded a plane for the first time in 25 years to share the moment with his 23-year-old son, a machinist’s mate second class assigned to the USS Massachusetts, who also is named David.

“He was inspired by a lot of his family” who served in the military, the elder Forys said, and sought an assignment on a nuclear aircraft carrier or submarine.

“I’m not aware of where they’re actually going” after the commissioning, Forys said. “But it’ll be far away from me. I live in the middle of the United States.”

The submariner’s brother Chris, an Army veteran, smiled at the thought of his sibling serving on a vessel that could remain submerged for months at a time.

“My brother wanted to one-up me,” Chris said, eyeing the ship. “This looks a lot more impressive than anything I’ve ever gotten close to.”

During the ceremony, Lieutenant Commander Joshua Hightower, the submarine’s executive officer, declared the Massachusetts to be “tested and battle ready.”

And at its conclusion, the crew boarded the USS Massachusetts, one by one. The first watch was set, the ship’s pennant was hoisted, and Naval Academy graduate Michael Siedsma announced he was in command.

title: Men talking
text:
Re “Why are the men around me doing all the talking?” by Judy Kugel (Ideas, March 22): When I attended Emerson College in the ’70s, we read communications studies that showed that despite the stereotype of women being chatterers, it was men who did most of the talking in social and business situations. It’s sad to me that 50 years later this hasn’t changed.

Women have been taught to be assertive, but have men been taught to ease up on their airtime?

Alice F. Stern

West Roxbury

The generalizations Judy Kugel makes about men in her senior community are akin to the sort of stereotypes for which others might be rebuked if they uttered them about women.

The “men talk about 90 percent of the time”? They “probably held leadership positions before retiring” and “miss being in charge”?

I have no doubt that the conversations Kugel refers to were indeed dominated by men, but I am confident she could have made her point without painting men with such a broad brush.

Michael R. Abend

Wayland

The men in Judy Kugel’s senior community may “talk about 90 percent of the time,” but this is hardly true in my age-integrated community, where all genders are equally talkative.

Men often get criticized for mansplaining, but women never get criticized for womansplaining.

Why can’t my fellow liberals realize that anti-male bias is still bias?

Felicia Nimue Ackerman

Providence

title: Girl Scout Daisies explore STEM, building with marshmallows, at Suffolk Construction
text:
Their biggest challenge?

Not eating the sticky-sweet construction materials.

“I builded [sic] a structure with toothpicks and marshmallows,” Chloe Beaulieu, 6, of Arlington explained. “We had a group and then everyone made a certain part.”

Suffolk hosted about 65 scouts who took part in the “Daisies Who Build” badge program at its main office in Roxbury.

The construction giant created the program with the Girl Scouts of Eastern Massachusetts to teach young girls about science, technology, engineering, and math, and introduce kids to careers in construction.

The Marshmallow Toothpick Tower Challenge is a fun way to get youngsters thinking about engineering.

“We have a big kind of mission to introduce Girl Scouts to new experiences and new potential careers,” Betsy Calkins, the director of program for the Girl Scouts of Eastern Massachusetts said. “Especially careers that are underrepresented for women.”

Suffolk and the scouts have worked together for the past five years to create STEM programs for Juniors, Brownies, and Cadets, but this year the organizations expanded to include Daisies, the youngest age group of Girl Scouts, Calkins said.

“Expanding the curriculum to the the younger age was really important . . . to start to combat the stereotypes that maybe start to take place of ‘this isn’t an industry for me,’” said Katherine Maloney, Suffolk’s director of corporate giving.

This month, 12 troops spent the day with women leaders at Suffolk, who gave the kindergarteners and first graders a tour and answered questions, according to Maloney.

Vanessa Beaulieu, Chloe’s mom and a troop leader, said it was special for the young girls to see women working in STEM fields.

“Exposure is huge — for the girls to get out there and just see other strong women doing different things and have different jobs," Beaulieu said.

While Daisies skipped around the building, volunteers walked the girls through the steps of a construction project, from designing and planning, to physically building structures.

“[On the tour] I learned that they usually build in very urban places,” Hannah Monzack, 6, of Lexington said. “Because there’s a lot of people there, which means there’s lots of buildings, which means they can’t build to the side, so they need to build taller.”

Beyond STEM, the girls got to check out Suffolk’s in-office hair salon, gym, and candy wall, which some girls happily sampled, Calkins said.

Making minimarshmallow buildings was the highlight of the day for many of the girls, including Monzack who created her very own “Mashmallow Palace.”

But, she admitted, “I was getting angry because I wanted to eat it.”

“Everyone was proud of what they created in the end,” Calkins said. “Even though some of them were eating the marshmallows that they’re supposed to be building with.”

Seven-year-old Catherine DePasquale, of Foxborough said she learned during the exercise that “we keep going if it falls.”

The scouts earned “Daisies Who Build” patches to commemorate their trip and celebrate completing the curriculum, according to Maloney.

The little scouts geared up for their visit by speaking to community members who work in STEM jobs, and trying on construction safety equipment.

Josephine Hemmings,7, of Arlington said that even though she didn’t go on the trip to Suffolk, she got to meet professionals and try on their gear to earn her patch.

“I really, really like how they build and how they design, and it’s cool that they make blueprints,” Hemmings said.

While she wants to be a singer, not an engineer or an architect, she learned from them that “you need to work hard and try your best,” Hemmings said. “Never give up, even if it is hard.”

Calkins said the Girl Scouts and Suffolk had to adapt the curriculum to be age appropriate for the young Daisies.

“When we’re working with the Daisies, it’s a lot more about sparking interest, getting them to see women in these roles and see these as potential careers, before they even have the experience of society telling them that women aren’t in these roles,” Calkins said.

DePasquale has set her sights on someday working at Suffolk.

Because “it looks like really fun to build and [the employees] said it’s cool to see the results,” DePasquale said.

Going forward, the Girl Scouts and Suffolk hope to create programs for high school-age scouts, Calkins said.

“So that’ll be obviously even more night and day from working with the Daisies,” she said." Where it’ll be really focused on those career paths."

title: Boston police officer faces charges for improper weapon storage, court records say
text:
A Boston police officer allegedly left his service pistol and taser in his personal vehicle and is now facing criminal charges for improper storage of the weapons, court records show.

Sean E. Cullen’s certification was also suspended by the state’s police oversight board, records show.

At his arraignment in West Roxbury Municipal Court on March 11, Cullen, 45, pleaded not guilty to a felony charge of improper storage of a large-capacity weapon and a misdemeanor charge of improper storage of a firearm, court records show.

He was released on personal recognizance and is scheduled to return to court April 15, records show.

His attorney, Keith J. Nicholson, could not immediately be reached for comment.

On Dec. 28, police went to Cullen’s home in West Roxbury home after he and his girlfriend got into an argument.

Officers smelled alcohol on his breath and a superior officer decided that his service weapons should be seized as a precaution, police said in a report.

Cullen handed over a shotgun he owned from a gun safe. He also reported that he had owned a .38-caliber pistol that he lost during a fishing trip but never reported that it was missing, police wrote.

Cullen then directed officers to his personal vehicle, where a fully loaded, holstered pistol was on the driver’s seat. A taser was found in his trunk.

The police department’s internal affairs division launched an investigation in January and concluded that Cullen should face criminal charges for his alleged mishandling of the weapons, records show.

A police department spokesman, Sergeant Detective John Boyle, said Cullen has been on administrative leave since March 16. Cullen has been a Boston Police officer for 12 years, officials said.

In suspending Cullen’s certification, the state’s oversight board ordered that his badge, uniform, and weapons be seized, records show.
