title: Faced with growing deer numbers, what’s a policy maker to do?
text:
In “Deer prudence” (March 26) the Globe’s editorial board argues that liberalizing hunting laws, and in particular authorizing Sunday hunting, is necessary to help control Massachusetts’ deer population. This is a plausible story, but with nearly 35 years’ experience engaging with communities on suburban deer issues, I think it’s probably wrong.

Massachusetts’ deer population has been growing steadily for the past 60 years. Also growing steeply have been the deer populations in most Northeastern and mid-Atlantic states and in suburbs clustered around cities in the South and Midwest. As the Globe notes, all of them have Sunday hunting and more liberal hunting rules. It hasn’t helped there, and it won’t help here.

Loosening hunting laws will improve recreational opportunities for the hunting 1 percent but will do nothing to ease public concerns surrounding deer. The Commonwealth should instead empower towns and cities to apply alternative deer population control and mitigation solutions to the problems associated with deer in their backyards.

Allen Rutberg

Holliston

The writer, an associate research professor in the department of infectious disease and global health, is director of the Center for Animals and Public Policy at the Cummings School of Veterinary Medicine at Tufts University.

Allowing Sunday hunting in the Commonwealth is a start to reducing the deer population and the spread of tick-borne diseases, but it is only part of the equation. Many towns and cities do not allow hunting on conservation land, where lots of deer live and seek safe harbor during hunting season. Other regulations around the state include restrictions against hunting on public lands in Wilmington and against hunting birds or mammals within the town of Bedford.

As for current limits on using crossbows, all hunters should be permitted to use crossbows, not just those with a permanent disability.

John Hauck

A good compromise for the use of natural lands would be to allow Sunday hunting only during deer season. Nonhunting nature lovers also contribute much to tourism and the economy. Allowing them one day a week in the woods to be worry-free of flying ammunition is not too much to ask.

title: Long-envisioned jazz club secures public backing to open in Roxbury
text:
MassDevelopment said it would provide a $380,000 equipment loan, with an additional $1.63 million in loan financing from M&T Bank and a $450,000 credit enhancement offered by the city. The Boston Foundation will guarantee financing through its Business Equity Fund.

The project is expected to create 26 new full-time jobs, officials said.

“This project demonstrates what is possible through the collaboration of public, private and philanthropic partners,” said Eric Paley, the state’s economic development secretary who also chairs the MassDevelopment board. “JazzUrbane Cafe will bring a new cultural destination to Nubian Square, expanding access to live music while adding to the neighborhood’s rich artistic tradition.”

JazzUrbane shares its name with a recording studio; both were founded by Bill Banfield, a jazz guitarist, producer, and professor emeritus at Berklee College of Music.

The club bills itself as a venue dedicated to spotlighting local and national artists “who define and celebrate the diverse cultural traditions that make Boston a unique and global city.” In addition to live music, it will also offer film screenings, dance, theater, and multimedia installations.

“We believe our company will be a force in contributing to how the next iterations of cultural development in Boston will be implemented,” Banfield said in the statement. “The JazzUrbane Cafe is positioned at the center of Nubian, in the heartbeat of the city, where we can serve and uplift the soul of our great city and be a temple for the entire community.”

It’s been a long road for the planned venue, which was first announced in 2019 by Mayor Marty Walsh as part of a renewed investment into the area, then known as Dudley Square.

The club received zoning board approval in 2022, with an eye towards a June 2023 opening; according to city records, however, it did not receive a liquor license until early last year.

The prospective club is already a member of the Ujima Good Business Alliance, a local development group that includes District 7 Tavern and the Dorchester Food Co-op.

“We are pleased that other actors in our ecosystem see the same immense promise and viability of this venture that we do,” Nia K. Evans, Ujima’s executive director, said in a statement.

At one point, JazzUrbane’s long list of backers also included Nia Grace, a restauranteur behind Grace by Nia in the Seaport and the new Uptown Social on Columbus Avenue. (Grace did not return a request for comment, nor did Banfield.)

The club is scheduled to open in May, Evans said.

Nubian Square itself doesn’t have much of a history of live music — unless you count church, said Byron Rushing, current president of the Roxbury Historical Society and a former state representative. But the nearby South End was once the hub of the city’s jazz scene, populated by clubs like Wally’s and its long-gone neighbors — Estelle’s, the Savoy, and the Hi-Hat, he said.

“With its location and historic facade, JazzUrbane will help shape the heart of Nubian Square,” said Orlando Watkins, chief program officer for the Boston Foundation.

The Bolling Building, renamed in 2015 after the first Black person elected president of the Boston City Council, once housed a well-known furniture store. The flatiron-style building — its decline, renovation, and eventual reopening — became a symbol of the rebounding fortunes of what was then known as Dudley Square.

title: ‘Comics have always been about community.’ Black voices find space at Comics in Color.
text:
“What’s great here is to see people who can give a legitimate voice of what [Black] culture is like,” said Davis, who owns a comic bookstore in Harvard Square.

More than 200 people attended this year’s festival, which featured several dozen Black artists who set up booths, spoke on panels, and advocated for an art form that has not always incorporated diversity into its milleu.

“The whole goal and premise of Comics in Color is to provide a space for people of color ... to tell their own stories in their own voice, so that their identities, their stories, and their experiences are represented,” said Marisa Luse, an organizer of the event.

According to Luse, Black representation in comic books and superhero tropes experienced a surge when Marvel released the first “Black Panther” movie in 2018, leading many people of color to embrace the art form for the first time.

“There’s definitely been people of color trying to get their stories out ... but it’s no longer a secret, right?” she said. “It’s not underground.”

Omari Malik, a 29-year-old artist from Brooklyn, N.Y., who owns a comic book publishing company, said he originally couldn’t envision a career for himself in the industry.

“A lot of Black people naturally gravitate to entertainment or even sports, because it’s a place where we can see ourselves easily,” he said. “I was seeking, wanting to find people like myself.”

Eventually, Malik discovered artists like David F. Walker, who helped create the DC Comic character Naomi McDuffie, a Black teenage superhero who becomes friends with Superman.

Malik said he could see “myself in those guys,” adding that it was “inspirational and let me know it was really possible.”

The original version of Black Panther, the superhero hailing from the mythical African nation of Wakanda, debuted in 1966 and was created by Marvel creative leader Stan Lee and artist Jack Kirby, according to the Smithsonian Institution.

Though it was groundbreaking at the time to have a Black superhero enter a pantheon typically reserved for white, transatlantic-sounding characters, Davis said the creators, who are both white, ultimately failed to accurately portray the hero as authentically Black.

“[They were] trying to have somebody write Black vernacular who had never spoken Black vernacular and didn’t know it,” said Davis.

Since then, major superhero companies like Marvel and DC have made strides in hiring Black artists to create Black characters.

In 1993, for example, DC signed a partnership with Milestone Media, a group of four Black artists who created new Black superheroes with progressive storylines.

For Davis, who grew up in Los Angeles, the first representative comic book he read was called “Love and Rockets,” a fictional series about punk rockers from Southern California.

“It was the first time you really saw a reflection of the non-white Los Angeles in a comic book,” Davis said. “I felt like I could know some of the people in this, or I’ve listened to some of the music that’s in the background of these stories.”

For younger artists, such as 24-year-old Zac Scandura, a Boston University student, diversity has always been par-for-the-course in comic book writing.

“Comics have always been about community,” he said. “There’s plenty of events like this everywhere in Boston.”

Scandura is part of a BU visual narrative program where students workshop their comic strips with professors and industry professionals.

The program is run by Joel Christian Gill, a leading Black artist in comics who in 2014 published “Strange Fruit,” a comic book about untold stories of African American history.

In a description of his 2023 BU College of Fine Arts exhibition, Gill wrote: “Comics have never been just for kids. Comics have never been only about superheroes.”

“Comics are a vessel for expression,” he continued.

In Roxbury on Saturday, Luce, the event organizer, said her 12-year-old son Coleman started making comics during the pandemic and has since finished six books.

“He’s got his latest book out there now, and so I just see the power in it and how enthusiastic people are,” she said. “That, to me, is inspiring.”

title: Bus lanes on Blue Hill Avenue still make sense
text:
Blue Hill Avenue has remained largely unchanged for the past 60 years, since the streetcar tracks that once ran down the center were removed. The roadway starts at Warren Street in Roxbury, bisects Dorchester and Mattapan, and is as wide as a highway, with four lanes of driving, two parking lanes, and an intermittent median strip. Double-parking, especially for businesses receiving deliveries, is an endemic problem with little enforcement.

City planners and designers have known for years that the most important upgrades for pedestrian and transit infrastructure just wouldn’t be feasible if buses remained reliant on curbside bus stops; there’s too much demand with double-parked cars, buses, pedestrians, cyclists, and businesses all vying for space — which is why the federal grant process has focused on the center-running approach.

Now, bolstered by federal money, it all boils down to those center lanes. Mayor Michelle Wu can either push forward with those plans, helping unclog some of the most high-traffic bus lines in the city and unlocking tens of millions of dollars for other improvements; or keep the roadway largely as it is, pecking at its problems through small initiatives like fixing sidewalks, adding lighting, and resurfacing the street.

Facing those two options, this editorial board stands where it did in 2022: in support of center-running bus lanes on Blue Hill Avenue. While this project will never reach unanimous community support, the center-running bus lanes maximize pedestrian safety, preserve the most amount of parking, and cut down the truly disastrous wait times for public transit during rush hour. Keeping Blue Hill Avenue largely unchanged would be its own form of failure; a crash requiring a Boston EMS ambulance happens every three days along the road, according to the city.

The most recent community feedback regarding the project was collected by the MBTA in 2024; while a sizable portion of community members strongly disagreed that the project would meet its goals, they were outnumbered by those who either somewhat or strongly agreed that the project would improve the roadway. The margins were slim, but those in agreement made up the majority.

In Denver, a former highway called Colfax Avenue is facing a dilemma similar to Blue Hill Avenue. Just like Blue Hill, Colfax Avenue is a major city thoroughfare hosting some of the highest-trafficked bus routes in the city. It suffers from clogged lanes, a lack of pedestrian infrastructure, and very little greenery. It also once hosted streetcar tracks and was left with little investment after they were torn out.

That 10-mile project began its buildout in 2024, giving Boston a model. The project in Denver includes small-business relief grants to offset the harms that ongoing construction can cause. With a new pot of cash, Boston should look into ways to support the small businesses that would face direct impacts during the most intensive construction phases.

Construction on the corridor will be a necessary disruption for meaningful change. Luckily, these impacts are something that smart city planning can mitigate. Understanding seasonal high times for businesses, factoring in Boston Public Schools transportation schedules, and even knowing the dates of special community events that provide bumps for local business can help mitigate the damaging impacts of construction.

There are other, local projects that provide a guide as well. The center bus lanes on nearby Columbus Avenue did drastically improve transit times for bus riders at a modest negative cost to drivers.

Any decision the city makes now is going to disappoint someone. Local City Councilors Miniard Culpepper and Brian Worrell, as well as other leaders, say the constituents they represent are against this plan. They believe their constituents deserve large-scale investment on their terms, and this project, like a previous attempt to rework the avenue under former governor Deval Patrick, is a mandate from outside the community.

But many residents do support it — the majority, if the T’s survey is to be believed. As the Dorchester Reporter has noted in its recent coverage, young people are largely in favor of improving this stretch. And while construction will strain the businesses that are the beating heart of this corridor, if they are supported, they will be able to benefit from an influx of investment, customers, and community growth brought by a safer main street.

title: Teacher age is not a liability in the classroom
text:
Contrary to the implication of Will Austin’s March 27 op-ed “Let schools keep their best young teachers,” (Opinion) age is not a liability. Having been a student, a teacher, and a parent in the Boston Public Schools, I have accrued a wealth of experiences, which I use to assist my current students in becoming their best selves.

Certainly newer and/or younger teachers make terrific contributions to our schools. I too was once a young teacher (in the dark ages before the internet). But I am a better teacher today than I was 30 years ago due in large part to the veteran teachers who helped me throughout my career.

Taking a “Children of the Corn” approach to education is as short-sighted as it is self-destructive. Imagine if hospitals terminated their most experienced doctors in the name of cost savings? The real question is why are we cutting student-facing positions in the first place?

Get College Town

A weekly newsletter packed with insights about higher ed from Globe journalist Hilary Burns.

Enter Email

School Committee Chair Jeri Robinson called for an audit. Let’s start there before we let go of any more teachers, whether young or old.

Michael J. Maguire

West Roxbury

The writer has taught in Boston Public Schools for over 30 years.

The implication of Will Austin’s article, “Let schools keep their best young teachers,” is that the best teachers are young teachers. As a retiree who spent a long and rewarding career in public education, I disagree.

It is energizing to see a new, young teacher in a classroom but it is special to observe a veteran teacher perform the job year after year. Years of service brings with it a depth of understanding that must not be ignored. Teacher salaries recognize the value of experience and advanced degrees.

Austin describes an education system that is failing; however, statistics show that the K-12 system in Massachusetts ranks first or second in the country. He implies that it is impossible to dismiss a veteran teacher; however, state law states that a teacher may be dismissed for “inefficiency, incompetency, incapacity, conduct unbecoming a teacher, insubordination or failure … to satisfy teacher performance standards … or other just cause.”

Are budget cuts demanding painful reductions in staff? Perhaps. But that is why reasoned layoff procedures were developed at times when cooler heads prevailed.

Ronald Suga

Plymouth

title: Put Blue Hill Ave. bus lanes to a vote
text:
And that shouldn’t be seen as a problem! We don’t all have to agree on things.

Still, the city does need to make a decision, relatively soon. So with millions in federal grants hanging in the balance, which side should the city disappoint?

Today’s Globe editorial urges Mayor Michelle Wu to go forward with the bus lanes, over the objections of some local lawmakers and businesses who worry about losing street parking:

“While this project will never reach unanimous community support, the center-running bus lanes maximize pedestrian safety, preserve the most amount of parking, and cut down the truly disastrous wait times for public transit during rush hour. Keeping Blue Hill Avenue largely unchanged would be its own form of failure; a crash requiring a Boston EMS ambulance happens every three days along the road, according to the city.”

If the city goes forward with the bus lanes, expect to hear complaints about Wu ignoring the neighborhood. Conversely, if the city pulls the plug, expect to hear complaints about Wu… ignoring the neighborhood.

So here’s an idea: hold a vote. Let the precincts Blue Hill Avenue bisects have a yes-or-no say on whether to accept the federal money for the bus lanes.

After all, if the question is, what does the neighborhood really want, then wouldn’t voting be the surest way to find out? Surveys and public meetings do not necessarily capture community sentiment reliably.

Neither does a vote, you say. And yes, turnout would likely be low.

But it would provide some needed resolution. And elected officials — almost all of whom owe their own positions to low-turnout municipal elections — would hardly be in any position to question the validity of the verdict.

There is some precedent for deferring questions to voters. In 2019, the city put a question on the ballot asking whether to rename Dudley Square as Nubian Square, then made the switch when majorities in that neighborhood backed the change.

Now, when I’ve written before in favor of referendums on transit projects, some readers felt it was a terrible suggestion to put engineering decisions to a popular vote.

I would agree if the question on the ballot were how to build a bus lane — experts should guide those details. But whether to build one is a public policy decision that seems legitimate for voters to decide.

There’s also an objection that in our interconnected road and transit system, nobody should be granted an absolute veto on what goes through their own backyard. Major roads and train lines have to go somewhere, but if every community could vote on individual projects within their borders, the result would be a smaller, poorer system for everyone. In this case, whatever happens on Blue Hill Avenue will affect people in Milton, people in other Boston neighborhoods, etc., so is it really fair to let just direct abutters have the last word?

Those are all interesting questions for political scientists to ponder. But in this case, voting wouldn’t just be a way to let residents have a say — it would be a way to at least reach a conclusive answer after so many years of dialogue that never have, and likely never will, yield a consensus.

This is an excerpt from Are we there yet?, a Globe Opinion newsletter about the future of transportation in the region. Sign up to get it in your inbox early.

title: City councilors call for changes to police bodycam policy as Boston officer faces manslaughter charge
text:
In the wake of a recent police shooting that resulted in a manslaughter charge against the officer involved, some Boston city councilors are dissatisfied with the department’s protocols governing the release of body camera footage in such cases.

Top police leaders didn’t attend a council hearing on the topic Tuesday afternoon, but the department’s legal adviser answered the council’s questions at length.

“The absence of Boston Police Department leadership raises a broader concern,” said Councilor Miniard Culpepper. “If we cannot have these conversations openly … with the people responsible for decision-making, then it becomes harder to build the very trust that body cameras were meant to strengthen.”

He called for a defined timeline and public-facing framework that would help standardize the process, among other changes.

The hearing came just three days after the latest deadly police shooting in Boston, which took place Saturday afternoon at an apartment building near Northeastern University’s campus. Police shot and killed a man experiencing a mental health crisis after he attacked first responders with a sword, officials said.

Last month, a Boston police officer fatally shot a carjacking suspect in Roxbury. Local prosecutors later charged the officer with manslaughter, saying his actions were unreasonable and unjustified.

In the immediate aftermath of the shooting, Councilors Culpepper and Brian Worrell called for the bodycam footage to be released. That hasn’t happened.

But Suffolk County prosecutors have repeatedly cited the footage, along with witness accounts, in support of the manslaughter charge against Officer Nicholas O’Malley. He’s charged in the death of Stephenson King, 39, who was shot March 11 while allegedly fleeing a traffic stop.

Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden has said his office isn’t releasing the video because it would “clearly compromise and imperil the ongoing investigation and the future prosecution of this most serious matter.” Prosecutors plan to present evidence to a grand jury as the case proceeds.

Dave Fredette, general counsel for the Boston Police Department, told councilors that state public records laws forbid release in this case, even though department policy gives the commissioner discretion under other circumstances. That’s partly because of the pending criminal charge and anticipated grand jury proceedings, Fredette said.

“Massachusetts statute will always trump a Boston police rule,” he said.

The council also recently adopted a resolution, without any specific recommendations, calling on the Police Department to update its policies governing bodycam footage release. Councilors reiterated that demand during the hearing.

Other cities across the country have established clear timelines, Worrell said. Oversight bodies, including Boston’s Office of Police Accountability and Transparency or OPAT, should also have faster access to the footage, he added.

OPAT Executive Director Evandro Carvalho, who also testified during the hearing, said the agency is closely monitoring the case. He previously said OPAT would suspend its review of the shooting until the district attorney’s prosecution is complete.

“If we’re going to rely on body cameras as a tool to build public trust, then the public needs to understand when footage will be released, who makes that decision, and what standards are being applied across the board,” said Councilor Erin Murphy.

Local officials have taken a different approach in the past, which councilors pointed out. After the 2015 fatal police shooting of Angelo West, a group of local clergy was allowed to view the footage while the shooting was still under investigation. In that case, West shot a police officer in the face before other officers opened fire, killing him.

But that situation differed from King’s death in that no officers were criminally charged, Fredette noted.

“Again, the public records request has to take a backseat to the criminal process,” he said.

Attorney Ben Crump, who’s representing the King family, said they’ll continue calling for more transparency.

“This family deserves the full truth, real accountability, and justice that is not delayed or denied,” he said in a statement Monday. “We will not stop fighting until they get it.”

title: ‘Pets shouldn’t be a privilege.’ As cost of living rises, demand grows for pet food pantries.
text:
YmaNini LaCourt wouldn’t know what she would do without her dog Mizzo, a small Chihuahua-mix with an adorable underbite.

But after losing her job during the pandemic, LaCourt has been working part time for less than $20 an hour, not nearly enough to cover her expenses, including food for a pet she describes as “part of me, part of my life, part of my world.”

LaCourt, 65, is among hundreds of pet owners increasingly turning to local pet food pantries to make ends meet. As the cost of living in the Boston area continues to climb, and with recent federal cuts to programs that help low-income Americans, including SNAP and Medicaid, more people would be forced to give up their furry family members without this kind of assistance, according to the food pantries.

“Pets are part of people’s families, and we’re really focused on keeping families together,” said Edward Schettino, president of the Animal Rescue League of Boston, which runs the Keep Pets SAFE program. SAFE stands for Supporting Animals and Families Everyday and its pantry serves pet owners in Dorchester, Mattapan, and Roxbury.

“When people struggle, pets struggle,” Schettino added.

Demand for the SAFE program and a statewide equivalent run by the Massachusetts Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (MSPCA) has surged this year compared to 2025, according to the nonprofits.

When money is tight, many pet owners sacrifice their own needs to buy a bag of kibble, animal advocates said. Some may feed their pet before eating a meal themselves.

Like LaCourt, many people in Massachusetts got pets during the pandemic to keep them company while spending more time at home.

Alyssa Krieger, director of community outreach for Boston’s MSPCA, said the group distributed 2.8 million pet meals across Massachusetts in 2024. In 2025, the number jumped to 3.5 million, she said.

Krieger said their clients typically get half of their pet’s monthly food from the program, visiting sites such as the Lawrence YMCA, Hyde Park’s Helping Plates and the Falmouth Service Center to pick up a bag of kibble provided by the MSPCA.

Pet owners seek out the program about two to four times per year, she said, and receive around $50 worth of food each time.

“People are using it when they really, really need it because life is nearly impossible in Massachusetts right now,” Krieger said.

Over the past several years, Krieger has talked to hundreds of pet owners at distribution sites in parks and parking lots. Often with their dogs in tow, the owners tell Krieger how thankful they are for the help.

“Those conversations really have taught me that pet ownership shouldn’t just be a privilege for people with a lot of money,” Krieger said.

In Boston, the ARL makes more than 25 deliveries per month, both to people’s homes and the offices of Action for Boston Community Development, a social services nonprofit, Schettino said.

The program focuses on dog and cat food, as well as cat litter. It also honors requests for food for birds, rabbits, guinea pigs, and other less common pets.

Monthly deliveries of about $80 worth of cat food and litter have helped Dorchester resident Betty Strickland pay off her 2019 Toyota Yaris, she said.

Strickland’s husband died in 2018 from health problems that began more than a decade earlier when he was shot in the stomach when their home was robbed, she said.

A friend decided Strickland needed a pet for company and gave her Leah, a long-haired white and tabby.

“She’s such a good kitty, I mean she’s so good, there’s certain things she knows not to do," said Strickland, adding that Leah provides “so much” company for her.

Because Leah had several teeth removed because of dental problems she developed as a kitten living on the street, she only eats canned cat food, said Strickland, 73.

Leah’s expensive taste, as well as her well-mannered behavior, leads neighbors to address her using a royal honorific.

The cat has her own kitchen chair, the only piece of furniture she’s allowed on.

“She really is a princess,” Strickland said.

Strickland’s monthly income, from her pension and Social Security, amounts to less than $2,000. Without the rescue league, she’d be spending nearly $100 a month on canned cat food and litter, she said.

“It makes it easier for me to spend money someplace else,” Strickland said.

Both Strickland and LaCourt receive housing assistance, which covers roughly two-thirds of their rent. A set percentage of their monthly income covers the final third.

LaCourt could work full time now, but she’s hesitant. The more she earns each month, the greater percentage of her income must go toward her rent. She already pays $1,000 toward the monthly cost of her two-bedroom apartment.

LaCourt’s 20-year-old daughter would contribute more to the household budget, but her hours at T.J. Maxx were recently cut to one day a week after her store on Newbury Street shut down and she was moved to another location.

That means that for now, the assistance is giving LaCourt’s family some much-needed peace of mind.

“I’d be lost without them, they’re so helpful,” she said.

title: Man arrested in Hyde Park stabbing was awaiting trial on other assault charge, court records show
text:
A Jamaica Plain man, arrested in connection with a Hyde Park stabbing incident on Monday, was awaiting trial on a separate assault and battery charge and serving probation for violating a restraining order, according to court records.

Henry Castro-Gerena , 32, was arrested in connection with Monday’s stabbing according to James Borghesani, a spokesperson for the Suffolk County District Attorney. Castro-Gerena pleaded not guilty to eight felony charges and one misdemeanor in West Roxbury Municipal Court Tuesday, records show.

He is being held without bail until a hearing on April 17 , which will determine whether he can be safely released into the community before trial, court records show.

The felony charges against Castro-Gerena included two counts of assault and battery resulting in serious bodily injury, two counts of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon causing serious bodily injury, one count of assault and battery on a person over 60 or with a disability causing serious injury, one count of assault and battery on a family or member of household, and two counts of assault with a dangerous weapon; in addition to a misdemeanor charge of threatening to commit a crime.

On Monday, police responded to a report of a stabbing around 10 a.m. at 135 Readville St. Two victims were subsequently transported to the hospital, one with “apparent stab wounds,” police said. Their conditions were unknown Monday.

Boston Police told The Globe they were later “made aware” the stabbing was a domestic incident.

Castro-Gerena had previously pleaded guilty in West Roxbury court on Dec. 30 to two misdemeanor counts of violating an abuse prevention order in a different case dating back to last April , according to court records. At that time, Judge John E. Garland , who also handled Tuesday’s arraignment, issued a suspended sentence with 18 months probation for those offenses.

Yesterday, Garland found that Castro-Gerena had violated his probation following his new arrest, court records show.

At the time of his arrest, Castro-Gerena was also awaiting trial in municipal court on one count of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon stemming from an incident last June, according to case files.

Material from prior Globe stories was used in this report.

title: House hunt stories: How three Boston-area buyers navigated the market
text:
The new year has brought significant changes to the housing market. The Warren Group reported an over 10 percent dip in Massachusetts single-family home sales, while the war in Iran has increased mortgage rates nationwide.

As house hunters face higher property price tags, here’s how three Boston-area buyers navigated the market.

Tara Flotta, her husband, and their three children recently moved from their house in Medway to a townhouse in Newton. They had a budget of $1.8 million.

Q: What was your house hunting experience like?

Tara Flotta: We were looking to cut down on my husband’s commute and my son’s commute. We had a budget in mind, but we had to increase it.

We really wanted to be in Newton because we wanted enough space. We’re at a stage of life where we have three older kids — one is graduating college, one is in college, and one is in high school in Brookline. So in five years, we may not need so much space, but we still need space for the time being. We thought Newton would probably give us the option of buying a single-family home, but we actually ended up buying a town house.

Probably the trickiest part of house hunting for us was the parking because you can’t park overnight in the winter in Newton, and we have five cars, so that really limited our options.

Q: What else were you looking for?

TF: We’ve lived through a lot of renovations. For our price point, any single-family homes that we came across required almost essentially a full renovation, and I wasn’t interested in living through more renovations. So finding something that was updated to our taste was important.

Q: How long did you search?

TF: We put our house on the market, and it sold in one weekend. We probably looked for houses for maybe six to eight weeks.

Q: How are you feeling about the space?

TF: The space is fantastic. It has a fully finished basement with a bedroom and a bathroom. My high school son loves that. If you asked my husband, he would say, I wish we did this much sooner, because he commuted an hour and 20 minutes each way for 25 years.

Originally from New York City, Ardelin de Jesus is a nurse who used to live with her two teenage children in the South End. She worked with the Boston Housing Authority’s First Home Program and the City of Boston’s Downpayment Assistance Program to purchase a house in Roslindale in October.

Q: What brought you to Boston?

Ardelin de Jesus: I came from the Bronx. It’s was very different. I mean, all my family is in New York. [Boston] was more calm, and when I got pregnant, I said, “Do I want to go back and raise my child over here?” I was thinking of moving to Puerto Rico because my mom was there, or staying in New York because my sister was there. But I said, No, let me just start by myself in a different place.

Q: When did you start to consider buying?

AJ: I came to Boston, I started from zero, and I had two children. I decided to work and go to school. When I finished school, I said, “OK, now I’m in a better place. Now is the time.”

My daughter is going to medical school, so I had to stay in Boston.

Q: What was the process like?

AJ: Everything was really expensive. We started looking for houses in December 2024, and we finally closed the deal on Oct.15.

Q: Were there any challenges?

AJ: The difficulty was mostly the budget.

There was a house that I did go for, and I put more money down than the person that got the house. I got upset. That was a setback that really broke me in the moment. My realtor, she told me, “That sort of thing can happen ... maybe they knew the buyer, maybe they knew the other realtor.”

Q: Were there certain features you were looking for?

AJ: The thing I said wasn’t negotiable was the parking. I wanted a two-bathroom because my daughter takes a whole hour in the bathroom.

Lakia Chambliss was born and raised in Roxbury but moved to Canton, where she lived for 11 years. With help from the City of Boston’s down payment assistance and the Family Self Sufficiency program [Section 8], she was able to move back to Boston in June and bought a home in Hyde Park, where she’s raising her 11-year-old daughter.

Q: When did you start to consider buying?

Lakia Chambliss: It’s always been a dream for me, but I started during the pandemic time back in 2020, that’s when I decided. Since we were stuck indoors and things like that, I was able to really buckle down and save more. And just keeping my credit in good standing.

Q: What was important to you?

LC: Neighborhood was a big one. I wanted to be somewhere where the environment was nice, the school systems, low traffic.

Q: What was your budget?

LC: I wasn’t sure of what I was going to be approved for. But when I finally got the OK through Boston Housing, I went to a lender, they gave me my ballpark, and that’s what I worked around, but I didn’t know going into it what my budget would be. I knew my credit was pretty good, my income wasn’t really up there, so I knew that was going to be like a little setback.

Q: How did the Boston’s programs come onto your radar?

LC: I’ve been with the Boston Housing Section 8 program for quite a while, since I was 21, and I’m 44 now. They do send notifications periodically of programs that they have. So when I saw the FSS program. I signed up for that because they put a certain amount of money into an account for you, and it builds over five years, and then you work with them towards your goals, like, if you want a new home, a new car, a new business, things like that. That was a big help, right there, that program. And then I always heard about Boston Housing having the homeownership program. I had to have a certain credit score, make a certain amount of money, and have a certain amount of money saved — I met all of those. So then I just went forward.

Interviews were condensed and edited for clarity.

title: In two long-vacant Downtown Crossing storefronts, Uniqlo and Teso Life get ready for their debuts
text:
The two stores — joining other budget-conscious neighbors like Primark, TJ Maxx, and Old Navy in the city’s stalwart shopping district — reflect an often-counted-out neighborhood learning to play to its strengths.

The COVID-19 pandemic wounded the real estate market in the downtown corridor — a key slice of the city’s property tax base. But that financial blow ended up giving the neighborhood an edge over pricier enclaves like the Back Bay or the Seaport in courting buzzy brands like Uniqlo and Teso Life. And those coups, observers said, are helping infuse the whole neighborhood with fresh energy.

“There’s this temptation to talk about the revitalization of the neighborhood . . . I don’t want to overstate it, but it’s kind of like, we’re already there,” said Noam Ron, of Hudson Group, one of the firms that bought 399 Washington last year. “We find ourselves no longer having to sort of apologize for Downtown Crossing.”

To be sure, downtown is still in recovery mode, with office vacancies well above pre-pandemic levels and foot traffic well below — though both appear to be steadily improving. Retail has been a notable bright spot, with a “single-digit number of vacancies” on Washington Street between City Hall and Chinatown, according to Michael Nichols, president of the Downtown Boston Alliance.

In addition to Uniqlo and Teso Life, Washington Street, a main downtown artery, is soon slated to welcome a new Skechers store, a hot pot restaurant, and an Italian sandwich shop. The retail vacancy rate in the greater downtown neighborhood was 1.6 percent in the last quarter of 2025 — down a tick from the same quarter in 2019, according to city data.

“I’m delighted it’s come as far and as fast as it has, given where we were two years ago,” said Nichols.

The rebirth of 399 Washington St. is a saga 20 years in the making. Once home to a string of clothing stores stretching back to the 1880s, the space has been without a retail tenant since Barnes & Noble moved out in 2006, unable to negotiate a new lease with its landlord. Out-of-state firms LaSalle Investment Management and L3 Capital purchased the building for $63 million in 2017, undertaking a major renovation as it prepared to court new tenants. Then the pandemic hit, robbing the neighborhood of much of its sought-after foot traffic.

That’s how, last year, the building ended up in the hands of Boston-based Hudson Group and New York-based Assembly Investments and Time Equities, for a cool $13 million — just a fifth of its previous price tag.

It was that rock-bottom rate that allowed the new owners to woo a tenant like Uniqlo “pretty immediately,” with an attractive rent price, said Ron. (Ron declined to specify what Uniqlo was paying for rent for the 10-year lease, citing confidentiality.)

“People constantly ask about the 20 years of vacancies, but it’s not rocket science,” he said. “We were fortunate enough to buy it at the right time, at the right basis, and we can pass that lower rent along to folks like Uniqlo.”

The retailer, which specializes in minimalist wares, handled much of the build-out of the 20,000-plus-square-foot space, taking care to preserve the brick ceilings, ornate columns, and central staircase linking the two levels.

“I just feel like bringing it to the area is going to bring a lot of traffic back,” said Alvin Spinkston, 29, a passerby who stopped by the almost-open store this week, wearing a tan Uniqlo trench coat. Growing up in the Roxbury area, he said, he used to go downtown frequently — not as much anymore. But that will change after the opening of the store, he said, which he patronizes often for its “great silhouettes.”

“This definitely got my attention,” he said, knocking on the store window, where mannequins posed in pastel ensembles.

From Uniqlo’s point of view, 399 Washington presented the opportunity to open up what Tomo Yasuda, director of real estate for Uniqlo North America, called a “key store” in Boston — larger than its Newbury Street and since-closed Faneuil Hall outposts, and more central than its other suburban Massachusetts locations. He said a flagship like this one, which will employ about 120 people, has the room to offer a wider selection, plus other services, like the Re.Uniqlo Studio, which can repair or recycle customers’ old Uniqlo duds or spruce them up with embroidery, and UTme!, a program that partnered with local artists to put their Boston-centric designs on T-shirts and tote bags.

“It was a perfect mix,” said Yasuda of the downtown area, pointing to the blend of office workers, tourists, and students. “The people are there, and there’s actually big spaces that we can really operate and show what we have to offer.”

It was a similar story over at the retail space in 459 Washington St., which also stood barren for years after the closure of former tenant Forever 21. In 2024, to avoid foreclosure, the property was taken over by the owner’s private lender. Marc Samwick, the founding partner of that lender’s New York-based parent company, said he connected with Teso Life “within days” of putting the approximately 20,000-square-foot, three-floor space up on the leasing market.

“We think this is really, almost, essentially, at the corner of Main and Main,” he said. “This is where you want to be.”

Like Uniqlo, securing a tenant like Teso Life, he said, required “a more flexible approach” compared to the previous owner. Part of that approach was setting a too-good-to-pass-up asking rent price — $37 per square foot, well below market value.

CY Kwok, general manager at Teso Life, said the brand had been looking to set up shop in Boston for three years, but had “never found the perfect site” before the Downtown Crossing space opened up.

“It has a lot to offer at that location,” he said. “We were looking at Newbury Street, but that area — it’s good, but it’s out of our budget, it’s way too expensive in terms of rent.”

For some consumers, the two retailers are more than just big-box stores.

“I like how it’s getting a lot more Asian representation,” said Kenzie Mao, a 20-year-old Suffolk University student, of the downtown neighborhood with Uniqlo and Teso Life moving in. “It makes us have more of a community.”

Last month, with the 10-year lease secured, Samwick decided it was time to sell the retail space, putting it on the market for $13.7 million. But that wasn’t an easy decision.

“We’ve thought about this longer and harder than others, because we really think that Downtown Crossing is — it has a very bright future in front of it," Samwick said.

That bright future is likely to come sooner because of the splash Uniqlo and Teso Life will make, said Whitney Gallivan, senior managing director and partner at Boston Realty Advisors, who helped broker the latest sale of 399 Washington.

“When a tenant comes to town, historically, they may say to us, ‘We only want to look in the Back Bay, in the Seaport,’ ” she said. “But if we can say, ‘Well, Uniqlo just opened up, and Teso, why don’t you take a look at this block on Washington Street, there might be a spot for you, and plus, you’re paying a lot lower rent than you are in the Back Bay,’ that’s going to help.”

title: Man killed by Boston police had history of mental illness, family says, demanding bodycam release
text:
The 39-year-old King had allegedly committed an unarmed carjacking the night of March 11 and was fleeing a traffic stop when Boston police Officer Nicholas O’Malley fired his service weapon, killing King.

Suffolk prosecutors quickly charged O’Malley with manslaughter, saying he wasn’t justified in shooting at the moving vehicle.

Several Boston city councilors and community leaders have also called on police to release the bodycam footage. But prosecutors and police have resisted, saying that would jeopardize the ongoing criminal investigation.

Crump, a civil rights attorney who also represented the family of George Floyd, said King’s mental health declined after his mother died from cancer in 2009.

Family members say they had been trying to get him adequate long-term treatment. They said he would cycle through the criminal justice system, sometimes receiving psychiatric medication while he was incarcerated, only to lose access to regular care after his release.

Recently, he was hearing voices and showing signs of intense paranoia, relatives said. Convinced that he was under surveillance, King would put tape over cellphone cameras, electric outlets, and even the emblems on his sneakers.

“That’s how bad it was,” said his father, Stephenson King Sr., a retired state corrections officer. “That’s why I was trying to get some help for my son.”

Hours before the shooting, King asked his father to call an ambulance because he’d been injured in an assault days earlier. Medics arrived and said they were taking him to the hospital.

“That’s the last time I saw my son,” said Stephenson King Sr., his voice strained with emotion.

Several family members, including two of King’s sisters, addressed the media during the news conference. They displayed a photo of King, smiling widely in a navy sweater and baseball cap, the way they want to remember him.

Police had pursued King after he allegedly committed the carjacking outside a pizza restaurant in Mission Hill. About 15 minutes after the reported carjacking, officers stopped the stolen car less than a mile away, at Linwood Square in Roxbury.

King then ignored verbal commands as officers approached the car on foot and then he tried to drive away, according to police. A nearby resident who witnessed the shooting told the Globe the situation escalated extremely quickly.

According to a police report, King opened the car window at the command of police officers, but did not turn the vehicle off. Positioned outside the driver’s side window, O’Malley drew a department-issued Taser and shouted, “Bro, I’m going to [expletive] shoot you,” according to the police report.

At that moment, King backed into the cruiser behind him, then maneuvered the vehicle forward and back “in an attempt to escape the police,” according to the report.

“Even though he wasn’t perfect, even though he struggled with mental illnesses, he did not deserve to be killed like this,” Crump said. “He did not deserve to be killed just because an officer had a rush to judgment.”

King’s family said they weren’t sure what happened after he was transported to the hospital earlier that day. If only his condition had been stabilized before being discharged, said his sister, Ebony King Gibson.

“He has been in and out of the system for a very long time, battling this thing, battling his demons,” she said.

When King was arrested in 2024 after police found him asleep in a stairwell with a loaded gun in his sweatshirt, he was drunk and suicidal, Gibson said.

“He wanted to take his life,” she said.

King’s death adds to a growing list of recent police shootings in Massachusetts that raise questions about whether mental illness played a role. On Saturday afternoon, a man experiencing a mental health crisis was killed by Boston police after he attacked first responders with a sword, officials said. He was identified as Jacob Graves, 29, a former student at Berklee College of Music.

Police in Weymouth and Westminster also reported deadly officer shootings last month.

Attorneys for the King family praised the district attorney’s quick decision to charge O’Malley.

But leaders of the department’s largest union have expressed outrage, saying it’s a slap in the face to law enforcement officers risking their lives every day. They pointed to King’s criminal history, which includes assault and firearms charges.

Also on Thursday, Boston attorney David Yannetti, who recently represented Karen Read, announced he’s been retained to represent O’Malley.

In the Read case, Yannetti said in a written statement, he “spent nearly four years zealously fighting a district attorney’s office that protected bad police officers while prosecuting an innocent woman.” Now, he plans to “zealously fight another district attorney’s office that is apparently choosing to protect criminals while prosecuting good police officers,” the statement said.

“Officer Nicholas O’Malley has always maintained a stellar record as a sworn Boston police officer,” Yannetti said. “He is an exemplary family man, a husband and a father to young children. He chose to become a police officer for all the right reasons.”

O’Malley told investigators he fired into the vehicle because he thought another officer was in danger of being run over by King, court records show. Moments later, O’Malley called over his radio that officers were involved in a shooting and the suspect “tried to run us over,” according to the police report. King was later pronounced dead at the hospital.

State law and Boston Police Department policy forbid officers from shooting at a moving vehicle unless there’s no other way to prevent “imminent harm to a person.”

Releasing the bodycam footage would allow people to see for themselves how the tragedy unfolded, Crump said. He questioned whether the video would have already been made public if it exonerated the officer and implicated King.

“We shouldn’t have two justice systems,” Crump said. “We should have equal justice for every citizen. Is that so much to ask?”

Boston City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, who has repeatedly raised the issue, called on Police Commissioner Michael Cox to at least let the family view the video.

“This is about whether Boston is serious about transparency when it matters the most,” said Councilor Brian Worrell. “We can’t have trust in the law without accountability.”

title: Is Rachael Rollins trolling everyone? Maybe ... maybe not.
text:
But just a short time before close of business Wednesday, Rollins sent everyone back to their original talking points when she took out nomination papers to run for her old Suffolk County position.

The comeback, it seemed, was on — though she would not comment Wednesday or Thursday on whether she actually was running.

Rollins’s sudden return is, in a way, not dissimilar to the five years the brash but calculating former progressive star prosecutor spent in the limelight.

This is a politician who won the district attorney’s office as a relative unknown, grabbed national attention with liberal policy platforms, and was appointed the top federal prosecutor in Massachusetts in 2022, making her the first Black woman to hold the post.

But she also was dogged by a series of escalating scandals, from allegations she inappropriately exerted her influence in a road-rage incident, to threatening to file a police report against a TV reporter outside her house, to her eventual downfall: trying, but failing, to influence the election to succeed her as DA by leaking confidential material to the press, and then lying about it, according to federal investigators.

And now, after three quiet years in which she took small steps toward rebuilding her reputation, Rollins is back — or so it appears. But how the voters of Suffolk County receive her remains to be seen, and a contest against incumbent District Attorney Kevin Hayden, a political foe, could answer weighty questions about the status of progressive policies in the current political moment, as well as the willingness of Boston voters to forgive.

First and foremost for Rollins, said former state senator Dianne Wilkerson, there must be a reckoning — a “public mea culpa.” Wilkerson, who herself went from Beacon Hill to federal prison for a bribery conviction, said Rollins would have to explain her past behavior, apologize, and take ownership of what happened — and be genuine and contrite while doing so.

”People have to see that it’s real," she said. But if she can connect with people, Wilkerson said, Rollins still would be a force. “I wouldn’t count her out.”

Rollins has drawn headlines since she splashed onto the Boston political scene in 2018, winning the DA’s office on a platform that drew national attention because she publicly cited a list of lower-level crimes that she would not prosecute. She was among the crop of staunchly progressive candidates across the country who won in major cities that year. Rollins drew pushback from police unions and some more conservative politicians, but while she was DA, some of her problems were more self-inflicted.

On Christmas Eve 2020, a woman said Rollins threatened her with a ticket and flashed the blue lights on her vehicle as they were both trying to exit the South Bay shopping center. She was ultimately cleared of allegations of a civil rights violation, but it garnered negative headlines, including after Rollins confronted a TV producer who went to her house to ask her about the incident.

Rollins also was a dynamic politician and communicator who made well-placed allies. In 2022, with the support of both of Massachusetts’ senators, then-President Joe Biden appointed her US attorney.

But in a twist that would prove to be her undoing, she was unable to leave local politics behind. Just a few months after her elevation, she attempted to meddle in the election to replace her in Suffolk County.

The Republican governor, Charlie Baker, had appointed Hayden, a moderate Democrat, as her interim replacement, and Hayden later sought a full term against Ricardo Arroyo, a progressive Boston city councilor. Rollins preferred Arroyo, an ally who promised to run the office in the vein she’d run it.

By late summer 2022, the campaign had devolved rapidly into one of the nastiest contests in recent local memory. And ahead of the Democratic primary that would effectively determine who won the seat, Rollins used her office to try to swing the election for Arroyo by leaking damaging information about Hayden, according to reports from federal investigations into her conduct.

By the next spring, she resigned a day before the release of two federal ethics probes, including one that found she sought “to create the impression publicly, before the primary election, that the DOJ was or would be investigating Hayden for public corruption.”

Investigators said Rollins also accepted two free tickets from the Celtics and solicited 30 free tickets from the team for a youth basketball program.

Rollins had maintained a fairly low profile since. She fought to maintain her law license, agreeing to a public reprimand from the Massachusetts Board of Bar Overseers in the wake of the DOJ investigation. In 2024, she took a part-time role at Roxbury Community College leading a program for formerly incarcerated people. As of February, she was still on the school’s payroll making roughly $110,000 a year, according to state data.

For some, including her predecessor as district attorney, the misdeeds of her past are disqualifying. Dan Conley, the county’s longtime district attorney, said Rollins is “unfit to hold an office that demands truthfulness, fairness, and public trust.”

“Through her actions, Rachael Rollins has shown that she lacks the two most fundamental qualifications for serving as district attorney: honesty and integrity. That’s not up for debate,” he said Thursday.

But Joyce Ferriabough Bolling, a longtime political strategist based in Boston, warned she could be “a formidable foe.”

“As far as Rachael goes, I think there’s still a lot of love for [her] here,” she said, noting that Rollins has “a core group of supporters who still like her style and commitment.”

Rollins would enter the race with almost $43,000 in her campaign account, more than the $29,000 Hayden reported on hand in March. She also needs to collect at least 1,000 certified signatures by April 28 to appear on the Democratic primary ballot, no small feat in less than three weeks.

The dynamics of the race are complex. Hayden, who personally and professionally has kept a lower profile than Rollins, faced his own issues in 2022, eventually having to pay a $5,000 ethics fine for a press release the office sent attacking Arroyo.

Rollins is to the left of Hayden politically, but the political lanes in this race are not entirely clear. The incumbent, for example, is fending off criticism on his right after he charged a Boston police officer with manslaughter in the fatal shooting of a man during a traffic stop. He’s increasingly allied himself with Mayor Michelle Wu, the most prominent progressive in the city, who hosted a fund-raiser for him last month.

The decision to charge the officer, Nicholas O’Malley, sparked swift backlash from the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, the city’s largest police union, which took to social media to call on “Anyone interested in running for Suffolk County District Attorney should start collecting signatures ASAP.”

Rollins is the second possible challenger to emerge: Linda Champion, a former Suffolk assistant district attorney, pulled nomination papers last week.

The range of candidates may offer voters a choice between progressive and more-moderate policies, “and we have to see if the electorate has changed in the last few years,” said state Representative Russell Holmes, a Mattapan Democrat who has pledged his support to Hayden. “Anybody in the race has a chance to win.”

title: The World Cup has become a crime
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

We’re a soccer family. It’s our thing. We watch all the big Champions League games (and every Manchester City game). We put up a bracket on the wall and meticulously track the scores of each World Cup game. We have a fish named after Norwegian striker Erling Haaland.

So when it was announced that the World Cup was coming to Boston, I promised my kids there was no way the world’s biggest sporting event was coming to our backyard without the Bakers showing up. Whatever it takes.

Here’s what it has taken: an absurd amount of money and uncertainty, and dealing with the criminal organization that calls itself the soccer governing body FIFA. I would ask the state to investigate this crime ring, but now they’re in on it!

Just the facts

To even have the opportunity to buy tickets to a game, you had to enter a lottery. Which I did, way back in the summer, and lost. I entered again and lost. The third time was a charm. I won! What did I win?

I was offered the opportunity to purchase four tickets to each of the games throughout North America (except the final). The problem is the actual draw had not yet happened. So your options were “Match 005” at “Boston Stadium.” And the seats were beyond expensive, even for the early group stage games featuring “who knows” against “TBD.” And you were not buying seats, you were buying tiers.

After going back and forth with my wife, discussing promises and overusing the phrase “once in a lifetime,” we basically said, “This will be the Christmas gift for the whole family, for the rest of time.” I closed my eyes, entered a credit card number, and bought four tickets for the first game in Boston, in Category 1 — which on the map was the entire lower bowl at Gillette Stadium — for the absurd price of $410 per ticket. Once in a lifetime. Once in a lifetime.

Complications ensue

Then we watched the match draw in December, kept our fingers crossed, and wound up with Scotland vs Haiti. Which, to translate that, is the #43 team in the world vs the #83 team. For $1,640. But hey, I’m sure the Scottish fans will show up in kilts and be drunkenly funny, and we’ll have good seats since we bit the bullet and paid for the top tier.

Wrong! News broke this week, to worldwide ire, that FIFA lied to everyone and reserved all the good seats for obscenely expensive “hospitality packages.” This was discovered when they finally released the seating assignments and put us lowly people, who paid what felt like Rockefeller money for Category 1, into the corners or behind the net.

In some cases, FIFA actually changed the stadium maps and put people who purchased Tier 1 tickets into what had been labeled Category 2 when they bought the tickets. And the ire also noted that none of the good midfield seats, which were on the map we were buying into, had appeared on the resale market, which meant no one had them. This was confirmed when FIFA on Thursday announced new hospitality packages featuring those exact seats.

Who ya gonna call?

I would call the state to file a criminal complaint, but they’re in on the gouging. They just announced the commuter rail to Foxborough will cost $80 per person. That ticket from South Station typically costs less than $20 round trip. Instead, I paid $175 for a parking spot, which is absurd, but is basically half what it would cost us to take public transportation.

When I had the chance to buy tickets in the lottery, I actually reached out to a few buddies and asked if they wanted some. “Who’s playing?” they all asked, and wisely passed when I told them I didn’t know, and then told them the price.

Except one friend, who bought four tickets to the second game. Which turned out to feature Norway. Which has Erling Haaland. Which is the name of our fish. And my wife dressed as him for Halloween.

And … he didn’t even make me go through it. He knew all this, and offered to switch games with us. You’re a good man, Kevin. Sorry I got you involved with FIFA.

Once in a lifetime, indeed.

---

title: New Edition doesn’t make the cut for 2026 Rock Roll Hall of Fame, despite leading fan vote
text:
The 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inductees were announced during Monday night’s episode of “American Idol,” and New Edition didn’t make the cut.

The Roxbury-raised R&B group was one of 17 performer nominees this year, marking their first Rock Hall nomination. Billy Idol, Phil Collins, Iron Maiden, Joy Division/New Order, Oasis, Sade, Luther Vandross, and Wu-Tang Clan were ultimately named members of the 2026 induction class.

The eight honorees will be celebrated during a Nov. 14 ceremony at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles. The presentation will air on ABC in December and be available to stream on Disney+.

This year’s inductees were revealed during the latest episode of “American Idol,” with Rock & Roll Hall of Fame members Pat Benatar and Neil Giraldo on hand to perform Benatar’s hit “Heartbreaker” and Johnny Cash’s “Ring of Fire,” plus serve as guest mentors for the show’s contestants. The evening kicked off with judge and season 4 “American Idol” winner Carrie Underwood performing “Rebel Yell” alongside Billy Idol and his frequent collaborator, Steve Stevens (who’s set to be inducted into the Rock Hall with Idol).

Get Starting Point

A guide through the most important stories of the morning, delivered Monday through Friday.

Enter Email

The current crop of “American Idol” hopefuls also performed songs made famous by past Rock Hall inductees, with highlights including contestant Rae Boyd singing “MacArthur Park” from Boston’s late Queen of Disco, Donna Summer, Braden Rumfelt’s rendition of “Superstition” by Stevie Wonder, and Daniel Stallworth’s funky take on “Livin’ on a Prayer” by Bon Jovi.

Despite coming up short for the 2026 induction class, New Edition, which formed more than 40 years ago in Boston’s Orchard Park housing projects, led the online fan vote ahead of Monday’s announcement, with the final results serving as a single ballot alongside the nominee ballots from an “international voting panel composed of over 1,200 artists, historians, and music industry professionals,” according to a press release. New Edition earned over a million fan votes, approximately 120,000 more than Collins, who placed second on the fan ballot.

In addition to this year’s performer inductees, the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame named recipients across additional categories, with the late Ed Sullivan earning the Ahmet Ertegun award. Linda Creed, Arif Mardin, Jimmy Miller, and Rick Rubin also will be honored with the musical excellence award, and Queen Latifah, MC Lyte, Celia Cruz, Fela Kuti, and Gram Parsons earned recognition as winners of the early influence award.

Along with New Edition, other 2026 performer nominees who didn’t make the cut include The Black Crowes, Jeff Buckley, Mariah Carey, Melissa Etheridge, Lauryn Hill, INXS, P!NK, and Shakira.

title: It isn’t sexist to say it: Rachael Rollins messed up
text:
The report also concluded that Rollins “knowingly and willfully made a false statement of material fact under oath” and generally “lacked candor.” According to the report, she also attended a Democratic Party fund-raiser featuring then-first lady Jill Biden “without required department approval and contrary to ethics advice she received,” a violation of the Hatch Act.

The US Office of Special Counsel also released a report of what it called her “egregious transgressions.”

When Rollins announced she would be resigning her position, her lawyer described the findings as mostly “minor process fouls.” Now that she appears to be launching a run against Hayden, she has taken to social media to suggest that as a woman, she is being held to a different standard than a man.

It’s true that Hayden paid a $5,000 civil fine for an ethics violation in 2024 after the state Ethics Commission found that he used his official position to try to discredit Arroyo. But Hayden also signed a disposition agreement in which he admitted the violation and waived his right to a hearing.

After taking responsibility for his actions, Hayden left it at that. Rollins is still trying to equivocate and deflect responsibility, and that’s a mistake.

As the first Black woman elected as Suffolk County district attorney and the first Black woman to become the region’s top federal prosecutor, she broke ground in many important ways. She pivoted away from punishment toward fighting the societal causes of crime and released a list of nonviolent crimes she said she wouldn’t prosecute. But over time, she gave critics of that approach too many weapons to use against her.

During her first run for Suffolk County DA in 2018, the Boston Herald first reported she had been charged with receiving stolen property while she was a college student. In response, her campaign said that the “minor” arrest did not affect her career as a prosecutor but has “informed how she views criminal justice reform.” The misdemeanor charge, which dated back to 1991, was eventually continued without a finding and dropped.

A stint as chief legal counsel at Massport from 2013 to 2015 ended with what CommonWealth Beacon described as “a puzzling coda” — a $175,000 severance agreement and a $45,000 education benefit that have never been explained to the public.

When Rollins was Suffolk County DA, a Dorchester resident filed a complaint alleging that Rollins threatened her and inappropriately flashed blue lights at her during a 2020 Christmas Eve confrontation at the South Bay shopping center. Then-Attorney General Maura Healey launched a review that found no civil rights or criminal violations, which is not the same thing as saying nothing happened. The matter was referred to the state Ethics Commission, which ultimately cleared her.

In January 2021, Rollins yelled at a television news crew that approached her in front of her home, seeking comment about the traffic incident. Telling them to “get out of here,” she added, “You know what I’ll do? I’ll call the police on you and make an allegation and we’ll see how that works out for you.” That from a prosecutor who listed trespass as a crime she wouldn’t prosecute in the name of criminal justice reform.

Some will say that because of race and gender, she was judged more harshly for reactions such as those connected to the alleged road rage incident. But I think she was also granted leeway because of her progressive agenda. The Globe, for example, endorsed her for DA, describing the charge of receiving stolen property as “a minor brush with the law as a college student” and emphasizing her ability to “push the office in new directions.”

With backing from Senators Elizabeth Warren and Ed Markey, who hailed her as a national leader in transforming the criminal justice system, Rollins was nominated by President Biden to be the region’s top federal prosecutor. Then came the scathing reports by two watchdog agencies about her conduct in that job.

The Massachusetts Board of Bar Overseers voted to publicly reprimand Rollins, with three of the 12 members finding the punishment too lenient and a fourth member recusing herself, the Globe reported at the time. When Rollins agreed to the public reprimand, she admitted to improperly disclosing confidential information to a Herald reporter about an investigation into Hayden. But still, according to the Globe report, she told the board she “erroneously thought she had discretion to disclose the matter without prior authorization pursuant to DOJ manual.”

She has been working at Roxbury Community College as executive director of a program focused on helping formerly incarcerated people for an annual salary of $96,000.

Does she deserve a second chance as a prosecutor? That’s up to the voters.

But she did mess up. Better to just admit that.

title: Top Spots to Live in Boston and Cambridge 2026
text:
Median single-family price: $704,343

Increase since 2020: 38.1%

Among the most affordable neighborhoods in Boston, Mattapan has plenty to offer beyond its prices. At the southern edge of the city, its single-family homes and triple-deckers — ranging from fixer-uppers to beautifully updated properties — make for a residential vibe. There’s the beloved hot dog stand Simco’s, the outdoor escape of Mass Audubon’s Boston Nature Center and Wildlife Sanctuary, and gardening workshops at the Trustees’ plant nursery, City Natives.

The area is home to many Haitian and other Caribbean immigrants, and those cultures are reflected in vibrant businesses and community organizations. Public transit access is a work in progress, but the MBTA is implementing a plan to modernize the iconic Mattapan trolley.

Median single-family price: $700,861

Increase since 2020: 32.3%

With its suburban vibes within city limits, Boston’s southernmost neighborhood is the best of both worlds: spacious houses and outdoor recreation — including the George Wright Golf Course — alongside a diversity of restaurants and other amenities. House hunters on a budget can find condos under $500,000 and single-family fixer-uppers for just a little more.

Median single-family price: $657,796

Increase since 2020: 24.3%

Often dismissed as a neighborhood for college students, Brighton has lots to offer for anyone who enjoys a range of dining options, night life, and access to the Green Line. With prices slightly lower than its cool-kid neighbor Allston, Brighton is popular with young professionals looking for urban energy.

Median single-family price: $836,757

Increase since 2020: 31.4%

Myles Duffey’s family moved from West Roxbury to the suburbs in the ’70s. Some 30 years later, he bought a house in the neighborhood that had never stopped feeling like home. “I always, in my heart, wanted to come back here,” he says. “This has proved to be better than I could’ve anticipated.”

With a tree-shaded residential feel and a taste of big-city bustle, West Roxbury has something for everyone. The shops and eateries along Centre Street — the Corrib Pub is big with locals, Duffey says — are reachable by foot from much of the neighborhood, and plentiful public transportation makes it easy to get to the rest of Boston. Billings Field, a hub of community activity, is in the middle of extensive improvements that should be completed this summer.

All of this adds up to a place with enduring appeal. “There is a lot of continuity and generational affection for the community,” Duffey says.

Median single-family price: $822,279

Increase since 2020: 19.3%

If you live there, you know it simply as “JP.” You’ll also know that the neighborhood’s reputation as a diverse and artistic area is well earned. Its lush green spaces — including Jamaica Pond — and historic homes make this a popular destination, but condos can still be found for under $1 million. And that signature JP spirit remains intact.

Median single-family price: $957,787

Increase since 2020: 9.2%

Mid-Cambridge is defined by historic homes, tree-lined streets, and a distinctively residential feel within the bustle of the city. Living in a neighborhood that includes parts of Harvard, residents can include some of the smartest neighbors to be found pretty much anywhere, and some of the best coffee and restaurants in the area.

Median single-family price: $1,194,318

Increase since 2020: 29.4%

Ask five different residents what the boundaries of North Cambridge are, and you’ll get five different answers, says Sage Jankowitz, a real estate agent and broker who was born in the neighborhood. What they all agree on, though, is that this wedge of Cambridge that runs from Alewife to Porter Square is a great place to live. “It’s very family-oriented,” Jankowitz says. “It has more of a community focus, and people know each other more there than in other areas of Cambridge.”

Parks dot the neighborhood, which is largely residential, with the notable exception of the businesses and restaurants along Massachusetts Avenue. The market is dominated by condos, though Jankowitz notes there are also quite a few two- and three-family properties and to a lesser extent, single-families. Many condos are in historic homes with traditional architectural details popular with buyers. Anything with stained glass or crown molding is sure to be snapped up in days, Jankowitz says. “They’re flying off the shelf,” he says.

Median single-family price: $1,207,402

Increase since 2020: 27.6%

One of Cambridge’s most densely packed districts, Wellington-Harrington packs a lot to like into a compact triangle of streets between Kendall Square and Inman Square. The largely residential area has a distinctly neighborhood vibe but is within easy reach of ice cream, cocktails, and bites in those commercial areas.

Median single-family price: $1,162,409

Increase since 2020: 17%

The crack of the baseball bat, basslines emanating from MGM Music Hall, rubbing shoulders at MFA Boston’s First Fridays events: The Fenway-Kenmore area is ideal for home buyers who want to be in the middle of the action. Add in the green space of the Fens and plenty of bars and restaurants — there is never a dull moment in the neighborhood.

Median single-family price: $1,710,485

Increase since 2020: 64.5%

Lauren Holleran moved to the Baldwin area for a house, a “classic Cambridge Victorian,” with high ceilings, beautiful architectural details, and enough room for her four kids. Once she got there, she discovered much more: an active community arts center, a park where neighborhood families gather, and a convenient location nestled between Harvard and Porter squares. “You know you’re in a city, but it feels residential,” says Holleran, a real estate agent specializing in Cambridge and Somerville.

If you think this sounds good, you’re not alone. Typically, an appropriately priced listing receives multiple offers and sells within 10 days, Holleran says. Families are particularly excited about the area, she notes, drawn by the top-rated Baldwin elementary school (living nearby doesn’t guarantee a spot, but does improve the chances). Would-be buyers need patience and good timing: “You will probably have to wait for a little while,” she says.

Median single-family price: $1,439,254

Increase since 2020: 54.8%

Prices are high and inventory low in this coveted Cambridge neighborhood tucked along the Charles River, and it’s easy to see why. It’s home to numerous parks, and foodies will love the proximity to the restaurants of Central Square.

Median single-family price: $2,129,783

Increase since 2020: 42.2%

Homes in this neighborhood come with the highest price tags in Cambridge, and it’s easy to see why. It combines the highlights of urban life — access to the restaurants and cafes of Harvard Square — with tree-lined streets and ample parks, including popular Fresh Pond Reservation. Listings include many beautifully updated historic homes that add richness and character to the area.
