Methodology: Determining the towns and cities on this list is an exercise in subjectivity, but one guided by the finite yet meaningful wisdom of supply and demand: Significantly increasing prices are a signal that many buyers are eager to call these communities home. We analyzed median home prices from 2020 and 2025 to find the biggest five-year increases across four price tiers for each region.

In the suburbs, we looked at single-family data from The Warren Group; for Boston and Cambridge neighborhoods, we used median home price data — including single-family, condo, and town house sales — from Redfin. In both cases, we excluded communities with fewer than 40 sales in 2025 — a slightly lower threshold than in years past, due to low sales volume. A small panel of journalists with real estate expertise collaborated to select our “May We Suggest” entries, our subjective picks of communities to consider.

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
ROMEO SANTOS & PRINCE ROYCE Last year, these two Bronx-born titans of the modern bachata scene surprise-released their first collaborative album, “Better Late Than Never.” Santos’s silk-lined croon and Royce’s pealing wail are well-matched to bachata’s chiming guitars and sturdy percussion and, as this record shows, to each other’s instruments; at this show they’ll join forces on their new music and their solo material. April 17, 8 p.m. TD Garden. 617-624-1000, tdgarden.com

HEAVENLY One of the ’90s most cleverly crushing indiepop acts, this English band paired chiming guitars and crisp rhythms with sweetly delivered, often devastating, and always clear-eyed lyrics; they returned earlier this year with the stellar “Highway to Heavenly,” the first album-length showcase for their pointed hookiness in three decades. April 19, 8 p.m. The Sinclair, Cambridge. 617-547-5200, sinclaircambridge.com

FEID The Colombian reggaeton mogul recently kicked off his label-boss era with the fast-paced, groove-heavy EP “FEID VS FERXXO.” April 20, 7 p.m. House of Blues Boston. 888-693-2583, houseofblues.com/boston

MAURA K. JOHNSTON

JAKE XERXES FUSSELL Fussell has made his name with the marvelous, singular treatment he gives to traditional folk material, but occasionally he’ll make his own contributions, as with the title song from 2024’s “When I’m Called,” which cops from a child’s list of things to do and not do: “I will answer when I’m called/ I will not breakdance in the hall/ I will not laugh when the teacher calls my name/ I won’t laugh when the teacher calls my name.” April 18, 8 p.m. $35.23. Center for Arts at the Armory, 191 Highland Ave., Somerville. 617-718-2191, artsatthearmory.org

TONY TRISCHKA Tony Trischka has had Earl on the brain of late; the current master of the banjo universe has spent his last two albums (“Earl Jam I” and “Earl Jam II”) paying homage to the all-time master (that would be Earl Scruggs). He’ll reprise that music live this Saturday, with the help of Michael Daves and the rest of his crack outfit. April 18, 7:30 p.m. $40. Belleville Congregational Church, 300 High St., Newburyport. 978-503-7668. www.bellevilleroots.org

YAGÓDY “Etho-drama” folk group Yagódy have the artistic and cultural aim of preserving the folk traditions of their native Ukraine — an act of preservation that they pursue in the midst of Russia’s attempts to destroy their country. April 19, 7:30 p.m. $38. Crystal Ballroom at Somerville Theatre, 55 Davis Square, Somerville. 617-876-4275. www.globalartslive.org

STUART MUNRO

TINSLEY ELLIS The Georgia-born bluesman, a razor-sharp guitarist and soulful singer, celebrates his new solo acoustic album, “Labor of Love.” April 17. $39.10-$43. Spire Center, 25½ Court St. Plymouth. www.spirecenter.org; April 22, 6 p.m. $32-$35. Chan’s, 267 Main St., Woonsocket R.I. chanseggrollsjazz.com; April 23, 8 p.m. $41. The Center for Arts in Natick, 14 Summer St., Natick. natickarts.org

JOHN PAUL MCGEE JAZZ TRIO Vivo Performing Arts presents the pianist and organist performing his signature “Gospejazzical,” a bracing and soothing blend of gospel, jazz, and classical music. April 18, 3 p.m. Free. First Church in Roxbury, 10 Putnam St. (John Eliot Square). vivoperformingarts.org

BILLY HART QUARTET Veteran drum master Hart has played with such legends as Stan Getz and Herbie Hancock. Recently, he’s been heard most often with his similarly seasoned colleagues The Cookers. For this gig, he helms a group of relative youngsters: tenor saxophonist Nicole Glover, pianist Ethan Iverson, and bassist Ben Street. April 23, 7:30 p.m. $30.15-$41.79. Regattabar, 1 Bennett St., Cambridge. regattabarjazz.com

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA Andrew Norman’s new two-piano concerto “Split” debuts to the world in the hands of Dutch piano brothers Lucas and Arthur Jussen, with the BSO under the baton of Finnish conductor Susanna Mälkki. The program also includes Ravel’s “Mother Goose” suite and Rachmaninoff’s “Symphonic Dances” (April 16-18). Next week, conductor Andrey Boreyko and pianist Evgeny Kissin join the orchestra for a double-feature piano concerto program, including Mozart’s Piano Concerto No. 12 and Scriabin’s Piano Concerto. (April 23 and 25) Symphony Hall. 617-266-1200, www.bso.org

VIVO PERFORMING ARTS PRESENTS PIANO Vivo, the new incarnation of Celebrity Series of Boston, presents two world-class pianists on back to back nights at New England Conservatory’s Jordan Hall. First up is French pianist Pierre-Laurent Aimard, performing the entirety of Book 2 of J.S. Bach’s “The Well-Tempered Clavier” (April 17). The next night brings British pianist Paul Lewis, visiting with his current touring project “The Mozart+ Initiative”; he pairs lesser-known Mozart sonatas with pieces by Poulenc and Debussy (April 18). NEC’s Jordan Hall. 617-482-2595, www.vivoperformingarts.org

TIME TO ACT Boston Conservatory at Berklee puts up the New England and collegiate premiere of the new opera “Time to Act,” by composer Laura Kaminsky (of “As One”) and director/librettist Crystal Manich. With the libretto written in the wake of the Parkland tragedy, the story is set in an American high school as students prepare for a production of “Antigone,” in the aftermath of a school shooting in a neighboring town. April 16-18. Calderwood Pavilion at Boston Center for the Arts. www.bostonconservatory.berklee.edu/events

A.Z. MADONNA

DIDO OF IDAHO Abby Rosebrock has reimagined the myth of Dido and Aeneas as a present-day dark comedy in which Parker Jennings (“Hedda Gabler”) plays Nora, a musicologist with a drinking problem whose affair with a married English professor, Michael (Mauro Canepa), leads to a confrontation with his ex-beauty-queen wife, Crystal (Ashley Lyon). Further sparks fly when Nora visits her estranged evangelical mother, Julie (Mariela Lopez-Ponce) and Ethel (Paola Ferrer), her roommate. Codirected by Brooks Reeves and Danielle Fauteux Jacques. April 17-May 10. Apollinaire Theatre Company. At Chelsea Theatre Works, Chelsea. 617-887-2336, www.apollinairetheatre.com

WHEN PLAYWRIGHTS KILL Inspired by a decidedly unfunny episode — the 2019 Faye Dunaway “Tea at Five” debacle in Boston — Matthew Lombardo has concocted a comedy that combines the broadness of farce with a welter of inside theater jokes. The cast is led by Beth Leavel, who is to playing divas what Olivier was to Hamlet, as a former movie star who refuses to learn her lines during an out-of-town tryout of a new, Broadway-bound play, and Matt Doyle as the homicidal playwright. Through April 18. Huntington Theatre. 617-933-8600, Bostontheatrescene.com

THE SECRET SHARER World premiere of a multimedia performance that blends music, dance, text, sound, and video projection in an adaptation of Joseph Conrad’s 1909 story about the bond that grows between a young ship captain and a stowaway who turns out to be the first mate of another ship — and stands accused of murder. Directed by Daniel Banks. April 24-May 3. Production by DNAWorks. Presented by ArtsEmerson. At Emerson Paramount Center, Jackie Liebergott Black Box. 617-824-8400, ArtsEmerson.org

GEM OF THE OCEAN August Wilson died in 2005 at age 60, less than a year after this allegorical and deeply spiritual play opened on Broadway. Set in a Pittsburgh home in 1904, its center is Aunt Ester (Regine Vital), a mystical “soul cleanser” who claims to be nearly 300 years old and lived through the horrors of slavery. She offers guidance to her home as a refuge for Solly Two Kings (Jonathan Kitt), who helped enslaved people escape on the Underground Railroad after he escaped slavery himself, and Citizen Barlow (Joshua Lee Robinson), who seeks absolution for ​a death he caused in his native Alabama​. Directed by Monica White Ndounou. April 16-May 17. Actors’ Shakespeare Project in partnership with Hibernian Hall. At Hibernian Hall. 617-241-2200, ActorsShakespeareProject.org

DON AUCOIN

KAIROS DANCE THEATER The Boston-based company, acclaimed for its rigorously physical and socially-attuned collaborative projects, presents a program of mixed repertoire that features a world premiere created with and set to music performed live by Grammy-nominated cellist Dave Eggar. The evening also includes the darkly comic “Tavernous,” which features live music by vocal ensemble Renaissance Men, and “husk/vessel,” co-created with choreographer Paula Josa-Jones. April 17. $47 and up. Global Arts Live at Institute of Contemporary Art/Boston. www.globalartslive.org

ABILITIES DANCE With “Intersections v5,” the company presents the fifth iteration of a series that honors BIPOC and deaf/disabled arts and activists. To highlight the intersections of life experiences and communities, the concert also includes voices that explore queer/trans and womxn/nonbinary identities, connecting creative artistry to bills before the Massachusetts Legislature. April 17-18. Free-$35. Multicultural Arts Center, Cambridge. www.abilitiesdanceboston.org

CHAVI BANSAL’S VIMOKSHA DANCE COMPANY Global Arts Live presents the troupe in a program that weaves together modern dance with traditional movement practices of India. Repertoire includes three distinct works, including a new piece inspired by the ancient Indian game Moksha Patam that explores “the mind’s journey from survival mode towards higher consciousness.” “Salt Soaked” highlights immigration stories from Rowes Wharf, and “Touched by Water” addresses gender disparity in India. April 18. $47 and up. Institute of Contemporary Art/Boston. www.globalartslive.org

BHOOMI: MOTHER EARTH Neena Gulati’s Triveni Ensemble offers a concert of Indian classical dance that reflects the profound connections between the natural world and the human spirit. Centered in the dance forms of Bharatanatyam, Kuchipudi, and Odissi, the production draws from the mythological and philosophical traditions of India to portray stories of creation, transformation, and devotion. April 18-19. $28.52-$33.85. Boston University Dance Theater. www.trivenidance.org

KAREN CAMPBELL

DERRICK ADAMS: VIEW MASTER Just open: Adams is a jubilant polymath with a very specific mission: “What can I reveal that has not been shown?” he told the ICA. “Black people — not entertaining, just being, living. Letting people deal with that as reality.” This show, his first-ever career survey, spans more than 20 years of painting, sculpture, installation, performance, and collage, all of it with a signature ebullience that celebrates the lives of his subjects and captures the joy of the everyday. Through Sept. 7. Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100, icaboston.org

DIVINE COLOR: HINDU PRINTS FROM MODERN BENGAL The mass printing industry in India has been alive for decades with wild color and flights of fancy depicting centuries of myths and deities that still play a central role in Indian life. Dismissed as art for their pervasive, throwaway ubiquity, this exhibition reexamines them in the context of not what they are as things, but what they represent, a dynamic culture rushing headlong to the future while holding on to its deep ties to the past. Through May 31. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, www.mfa.org

YINKA SHONIBARE: SANCTUARY Shonibare, a celebrated British-Nigerian artist known for his heady formal engagements with the messy, often brutal entanglements of colonial history, debuts a new installation in the US this winter with “Sanctuary City,” a suite of 18 tabletop architectural models of buildings with known histories as refuges for the vulnerable and persecuted. With inequity always buzzing in the background of the post-colonial world, the piece would never not be relevant; in the current roar of the American mass-deportation experience, it will be more resonant here and now than ever. Through Jan. 3, 2027. Rose Art Museum at Brandeis University, 415 South St., Waltham. 781-736-3434, brandeis.edu/rose

MURRAY WHYTE

WHERE DO I GO? لوينروح Photographer Rania Matar grew up in Lebanon and immigrated to the US as a young woman, fleeing the Lebanese Civil War in 1984. She travels to her homeland frequently and documents the lives of women who have faced recent economic collapse, the Beirut Port Explosion in 2020, and ongoing violence between Israel and Hezbollah. In these portraits, her subjects become anchors, holding space for their personhood in the midst of turmoil. Through May 31. Leica Gallery Boston,74 Arlington St.www.leicagalleryboston.com

CATE McQUAID

JENNY ZIGRINO Romance novels are instruction manuals, according to Zigrino, for any man who wants to know what women want. “It’s like, we just want you to say that you burn for us,” she says, “and to call us a good girl, and to be a grumpy cowboy billionaire that also is sometimes a gay hockey player and you’re a werewolf vampire that might kill us. Why is this hard?!” April 18, 7:15 p.m. $28.95-$33.95. The Comedy Studio, 5 John F. Kennedy St., Cambridge. www.thecomedystudio.com

RHYS DARBY: THE LEGEND RETURNS The “Flight of the Conchords” and “Our Flag Means Death” star uses sound effects in his act, and tried to use them in real life, faking the “beeps” at a self-checkout, just as an artistic challenge. But he was caught by a supervisor making one bad beep, and had to tell her, “Oh, I’m sorry. I’m from New Zealand. We usually do the beeps ourselves.” April 19, 7 p.m. $37-$51. The Wilbur, 246 Tremont St.www.thewilbur.com

SUSAN RICE When her niece signed her up for Silver Singles, Rice was reluctant. “Don’t you want to get married?” her niece asked. “No,” said Rice. “Nobody gets married for the first time at 70. No. Not unless there’s a verified pension and a diagnosis.”April 19, 7 p.m. $39.90. Laugh Boston, 425 Summer St. 617-725-2844, www.laughboston.com

title: Raspberries for $18 a pound? Why fruit in Mass. grocery stores can be so expensive right now.
text:
It’s not just gas stations where Massachusetts consumers are seeing erratic prices. It’s also in the produce section at Boston-area supermarkets: Some raspberries now cost as much as $18 a pound and blueberries as much as $14 a quart.

According to the USDA’s Consumer Price Index, food prices nationwide in February rose 3.1 percent over the previous year. Fruit decreased in price by 0.3 percent but is expected to rise 0.3 percent in the coming year.

President Trump campaigned on a promise of delivering cheaper groceries. Now, more than a month into a war with Iran, the United States is blockading the Strait of Hormuz, sending oil prices higher and driving up the cost of transportation.

Even when more New England produce becomes available in the coming months, buying local may not be a workaround, as farmers rely on oil products in their operations, from tractors to fertilizer.

Fruit is different from other foods, with price changes that can be more turbulent. Experts said a trio of factors — oil costs, labor shortages, and tariffs — could drive prices up.

Basically no fruit is in season in Massachusetts right now, so at the big stores, everything’s been shipped.

In a 13-store survey over the weekend, the Globe took a snapshot of Boston-area fruit prices. Trader Joe’s charged 23 cents per individual Chiquita banana. Sounds like a deal, but let’s do a little napkin math. A 6-ounce banana will cost 61 cents a pound at that price. If that banana weighed 4.16 ounces, as the USDA estimates it might, that would be around 88 cents a pound. The national average hit 67 cents in September. You could do better at Wegman’s, Market Basket, and Milton’s Fruit Center Marketplace, where bananas cost 49 cents per pound.

At a Brookline Stop & Shop, Cosmic Crisp apples cost 77 cents per pound with a coupon. The same apples were $2.99 per pound at the Roche Bros. in West Roxbury. Somerville’s Market Basket had Cortland apples for 99 cents per pound, while boutique grocer and wine shop Momma’s in Cambridge priced them at $6 a pound.

You can find the trademarked variety “Cotton Candy” green grapes for anywhere between $4.99 and $6.99 per pound, the latter at Milton’s Fruit Center. (There was a taste test, and yes, that name is descriptive.) The cheapest seedless grapes were at Brookline’s Stop & Shop for $1.69 per pound, and the most expensive at Formaggio Kitchen in Cambridge, where green table grapes were $10.95 per pound. (Nobody goes to Formaggio to bargain shop.)

With bags of grapes typically weighing in at 1.5 to 3 pounds, those prices mean that Massachusetts shoppers can expect to see their grape purchases ring up to almost $10 a bag at many local stores.

Formaggio is also where you can get a pound of anjou pears for $7.75. Move a decimal point and a few miles, and you’ll pay 79 cents for one at Trader Joe’s, or about $1.40 per pound depending on weight.

It may sound like cherry-picking, but pay attention to unit price.

At Roche Bros., a package of premium Oishii strawberries is just a dollar more than a clamshell of Driscoll’s, but by weight they’re considerably more: almost $15 per pound for the Oishiis compared to $5.99 for the conventional berries. A cantaloupe costs 99 cents at Star Market, but you’ll need $5 to take one home from the West Roxbury Roche Bros.

Fruit prices are more susceptible than those of other foods to fluctuations in supply and demand, said William Masters, professor of food economics and policy at Tufts University’s Friedman School of Nutrition Science and Policy.

“Whole fruit is mostly the price of the fruit itself,” said Masters. “It’s one of those rare grocery prices that actually goes up and down.”

Across all grocery items, Masters said, the more complex the packaging, the more expensive. “Shopping in the center aisles of a grocery store, it’s mostly brand costs, whereas when you’re shopping the periphery of the store, it’s mostly the product price,” he said.

People have taken for granted a substantial decline in the retail cost of produce, which since 2016 has dipped about 10 percent on average compared to the Consumer Price Index, as well as improvements in quality and variety, said Masters. From genetic innovation to improvements in distribution, we’ve come a long way from the days of the maligned Red Delicious apple.

“This has been a golden age for fruits and vegetables in America,” he said.

Rising labor and oil prices, plus tariffs, could bring that period to an end, said Masters. Labor shortfalls will make their mark by summer as the seasonal farm work gets underway, and oil prices are already having an impact.

The changes could hit Massachusetts’ mighty cranberry industry hard.

No one besides Wisconsin grows more cranberries than Massachusetts, which produces about 2 million 100-pound barrels annually (compared to 5 million in Wisconsin). Farmers contract with wholesalers for processing and distribution, who set prices based on supply and demand.

Most cranberries are made into juice, sauce, and nutritional supplements, said James Ross, a Cape Cod cranberry farmer. About 98 percent of his crop is sold wholesale, with just 2 percent sold direct to consumers.

“We had to pay a significantly higher price to fill up our tanks this spring compared to even six months ago,” said Ross. “If we had filled up midwinter, we would have been probably a little bit happier than where we’re at today.”

His operation uses diesel fuel and liquid propane to run pumps and motors, which power his irrigation system and guard against temperature fluctuation.

While Ross said he has some anxiety about fertilizer costs, one benefit to the cranberry being a native fruit here is that the peat bogs where they grow naturally contribute nitrogen, saving up to 50 percent in that type of fertilizer cost, compared to corn, soy, or wheat.

Unlike wholesale growers, local farmers have more flexibility to set their own prices, which could sway some shoppers to buy local instead.

“If supermarket fruit is coming up [in price], the prices might be coming closer to what’s being sold at your local farm stand,” said Karen Schwalbe, executive director of the Massachusetts Farm Bureau Federation. “Farmers are price sensitive. Their crops are perishable, and they want to move them so they can be competitive.”

For large-scale growers, higher retail prices do not necessarily mean bigger profits. In 2025, rising fuel costs, land costs, and weather contributed to a second consecutive year in which US apple growers failed to break even on production costs, reported US Apple, a national apple production association, this month.

“What the retailers charge is entirely up to them,” said Jon Clements, an extension fruit specialist at UMass Amherst. “I will say the apple growers are getting less and less of it.”

It costs more to farm here than in other parts of the country, said Claire Morenon, communications manager for Community Involved in Sustaining Agriculture, a nonprofit based in Deerfield. Oil costs impact heated greenhouses and refrigeration, she said. For farms that recently built new barns or added solar panels, tariffs added to the pain. It seems likely, she said, that locally grown food costs will increase.

Still, Morenon said, consumers can only bear so much.

“Shoppers are pretty price conscious, which makes a lot of sense, because obviously, everyone’s expenses are increasing in the current moment,” she said. “It’s not like wages are rising to meet them.”

As the New England growing season gets underway, Morenon said it’s worth it for fruit consumers to do a price comparison — taking into consideration that local farmers are stewards of the ecosystem — as they decide which apples and blueberries to buy.

“Money that goes to [farmers] circulates within our local economy,” Morenon said. “Locally grown food, especially when it’s picked fresh and it doesn’t have to travel as far to the grocery store, is really a special thing to be putting on your table.”

title: ‘There needs to be a rule’: Critics call for a bodycam release policy from Boston police
text:
But critics are skeptical, arguing that the discrepancy raises questions about whether authorities are picking and choosing when to be transparent.

Other cities have issued guidance and timelines to promote consistency. And the public has largely become accustomed to seeing the footage in high-profile cases nationwide, from the recent DUI arrest of Tiger Woods following a crash last month, to George Floyd’s death under an officer’s knee in 2020.

But without a specific policy dictating when bodycam footage is released following police killings, experts say, Boston is behind the curve.

“The reason we have policies is to eliminate decision-making in the moment of crisis. It’s hugely important to building public trust,” said Christine Cole, a Boston-based public safety consultant who’s advised police reform efforts across the country. “Policies also convey your values, your habits, your philosophy — to people inside and outside the department.”

Boston police said they’re committed to building and maintaining public trust while protecting “the integrity of investigations and prosecutions.”

“We are always reviewing our policies to ensure they include clear explanations of our processes,” department spokesperson Mariellen Burns said in a statement. “The goal is to demystify how and why we do things within the criminal justice system.”

Several Boston city councilors have recently raised concerns about the inconsistencies, calling for more transparency. On Wednesday, the council passed an order seeking bodycam footage in a host of cases, including King’s death and other police shootings.

“Why is footage shared in some cases but not others? Is that decision being driven by law and procedure, or is it influenced by pressure, timing, or public reaction?” Councilor Erin Murphy said during a recent hearing. “Because from the outside, without clear and consistent standards, it can start to feel selective.”

In an interview, Councilor Ruthzee Louijeune said other jurisdictions have addressed the issue through policy.

In New York, officials announced last month that they’d codified the practice of releasing bodycam footage within 30 days. The Milwaukee Police Department generally allows up to 15 days. In Baltimore, the police commissioner typically releases video roughly within a week.

Boston police were relatively late to roll out body cameras, which is probably why they’re lagging behind, criminal justice analysts said. The department began a widespread implementation of bodycams in 2019. Since then, police shootings and in-custody deaths have been a rarity in Boston; a higher volume of such tragedies has sometimes spurred policy changes elsewhere.

Dave Fredette, general counsel for the Boston Police Department, told city councilors last week that state public records laws forbid release in the case of King’s death, even though department rules give the commissioner discretion under other circumstances. That’s partly because of the pending criminal charge and anticipated grand jury proceedings, he said.

Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden has also declined to immediately release the video, saying it would “clearly compromise and imperil the ongoing investigation and the future prosecution of this most serious matter.”

But it’ll happen eventually, officials said last week.

“The body camera footage is subject to public records law, and will be released,” Mayor Michelle Wu told reporters. “It is a matter of at what point in the legal process is that appropriate.”

She said that generally the family would be allowed to view the footage before it becomes public.

In 2015, after the Boston police killing of Angelo West, a group of local clergy was invited to view surveillance footage of the shooting. West shot a police officer in the face at point-blank range before other officers opened fire.

Prosecutors and police then decided to release the video publicly while the investigation was still ongoing. Officials said they planned to continue that practice moving forward because it helped tamp down speculation and quell potential rumors.

Then-police commissioner William B. Evans said he supported the decision despite the difficult precedent it could set. “You can’t have it both ways,” he said at the time. “It can’t only happen when things are good. We’re going to have to do it when things are bad, too.”

City Councilor Miniard Culpepper has repeatedly cited the case in support of his recent demands for increased transparency.

“They have set a precedent,” he said during a news conference last week with the King family and their attorneys. “We’ve been pressing the Police Department because of the precedent they’ve already set.”

In addition to filing the order for bodycam footage passed by the council Wednesday, Culpepper proposed officially summoning Police Commissioner Michael Cox and his top deputies before councilors to discuss the department’s protocols, in what would be a rare flex of council authority. Culpepper withdrew the proposal, though, saying he recently spoke to Cox, who agreed to appear voluntarily.

King had long struggled with serious mental illness, according to family. He allegedly committed a carjacking about 15 minutes before police pulled him over. He tried to flee the traffic stop, which is when Officer Nicholas O’Malley fired at the moving vehicle, prosecutors say.

King’s father, Stephenson King Sr., said he wants to watch the video to see his son’s face and learn “what really happened.”

Attorney Ben Crump, who represents the family, questioned why Boston leaders aren’t being more transparent.

“I wonder if . . . they’re afraid of what’s going to be revealed once the body camera video is released,” he said.

Less than a month after King’s death, Boston police shot and killed another man, Jacob Graves, after he stabbed an officer with a sword during a mental health crisis at his apartment, officials said.

The Police Department also declined to release bodycam footage in that case, citing a state statute that says local prosecutors should “direct and control” death investigations. In response to a records request from the Globe this week, police said the Suffolk district attorney’s office “has said not to release the records.” The DA’s office hasn’t responded to a similar request. No criminal charges have been filed in that case.

A report released last year from the Police Executive Research Forum, a Washington-based think tank, recommends that law enforcement agencies proactively release bodycam footage from officer shootings and other serious incidents whenever “they can legally and ethically do so.” That “sends a powerful statement about their commitment to transparency,” the report reads.

However, there are many factors to consider, especially when criminal charges are involved, said PERF executive director Chuck Wexler. It’s never a decision to be made lightly, he said.

“You have the tension here between the public’s right to know and the district attorney’s investigation,” he said. “That puts the police department in a very difficult position.”

But a written policy would be a good start, analysts said.

“There needs to be a rule, something solid,” said Sam Harold, a youth public defender and chair of the city’s Civilian Review Board, which evaluates police misconduct complaints. “I don’t know the answer, but I think there has to be some clarity.”

Globe researcher Jeremiah Manion contributed to this report.

title: Boston man, 28, arraigned for alleged attack on Transit police officers
text:
A Boston man was arraigned Monday for allegedly attacking MBTA Transit Police officers last week, gouging one lawman’s eyes during the tumult, officials said.

Fritznel Jean, 28, pleaded not guilty in Roxbury Municipal Court to charges of assault and battery on a police officer causing serious bodily injury, two counts of assault and battery on a police officer, and mayhem, legal filings said.

He was ordered held on $100 cash bail, and his bail in a prior case out of Quincy was revoked for 60 days, records show.

His lawyer didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

The violence erupted around 8:20 a.m. Friday at Transit police headquarters, where officials were trying to process Jean before his court appearance on the Quincy case alleging shoplifting, said Suffolk District Attorney Kevin R. Hayden’s office in a statement.

Jean, who’d been arrested the night before, shouted that he wanted to go free when a police officer opened the cell door to escort him to the fingerprinting station, the statement said.

The officer told Jean he had to be booked and then brought to court for the Quincy case, but he remained uncooperative and was told to get back in his cell, authorities said.

“As the officer turned his back to open the cell door, Jean lunged toward the officer, jumped onto his back and bit him on the back of his head,” the statement said.

Hayden’s office said additional cops tried to intervene.

“During the struggle, Jean began to scratch and gouge the first officer’s eyes, causing significant facial injuries,” the statement said. “Another officer witnessed Jean grabbing the first officer’s face while driving his thumbs forcefully into the officer’s eye sockets.”

Jean allegedly tried to bite another officer’s hand before he was restrained, according to the statement.

Paramedics responded and evaluated all the injured officers.

“The first officer suffered severe bruising, burst blood vessels to both eyes, and a cut on his left bottom eye, requiring two stitches,” the statement said.

Hayden in the statement decried Jean’s alleged maelstrom of violence.

“This was an extraordinary burst of violence that hurt one officer and endangered all the others involved,” Hayden said. “I thank the officers for restraining this defendant before he could inflict more injuries and I wish the wounded officer a full and fast recover.”

Jean’s next hearing in the attack case is scheduled for May 12, records show.

Travis Andersen can be reached at travis.andersen@globe.com.

title: How a place becomes a Top Spot to Live
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

What do Mattapoisett, Milton, and West Roxbury have in common?

One has strong Cape-Cod vibes, another is nestled into Blue Hills Reservation, and the third is home to a decadent gelato shop that appears on the Globe’s Best of the Best list.

The answer? They’re all among the 47 communities in Greater Boston that appear on another big list, the 2026 edition of the Globe Magazine’s Top Spots to Live.

How does a town make this tally of the hottest places to call home? We hone in on communities where median home prices have increased the most over a five-year period, through analyzing data from The Warren Group and Redfin. Boiled down, it’s supply and demand: These are the places where people are lining up to live, driving up the prices. Rounding it out is our “May We Suggest” category, selected more subjectively by a small panel of experts.

The deep dive

We took a deep dive into each community to understand what’s driving the interest. There are the usual suspects: highly-rated schools, beaches or green spaces, public transportation.

We found some things rang true across all four pricing tiers, which started at under $750,000. There was a strong desire for community: places where neighbors jump in to help shovel during a snowstorm, or parents can gather as children romp on the playground.

Each has its own allure. “The entire town turns out, and it’s like a little bit of Norman Rockwell,” one resident said of their town. Another raved about theirs: “The community vibe is really strong.” And another: “We’ve tried to keep it a quiet little gem.”

Finances intrude

Sounds great, but anyone who’s peeked at Zillow or Redfin in the last year knows the market feels stuck in a frustratingly familiar place. Mortgage rates are still more than twice what they were in 2021. Owners paying low rates aren’t eager to jump back into the market. Low inventory is keeping competition — and prices — high. To acknowledge these realities, we added a new pricing tier — over $1.25 million.

Add in economic fallout from the Iran war, oil prices, and tariffs, and prospective home buyers are faced with daunting prospects. Still, experts and our data say there are reasons for guarded optimism. Inventory is one: The number of properties coming onto the market edged up in 2025. And the MBTA communities act may be starting to have an impact.

Woven with insights from experts and residents, Top Spots to Live 2026 guides buyers through this admittedly uncertain market. And even if you’re not house hunting, you may learn something about your own town — and the neighbors you may soon be welcoming in.

title: Columbus Avenue center bus lanes hit a dead end at Jackson Square
text:
In the April 6 editorial, “Bus lanes on Blue Hill Avenue still make sense,” the Globe contends that the new center bus lanes on Columbus Avenue “drastically [improved] transit times for bus riders at a modest negative cost to drivers.” This statement is only partially true, since this busway currently ends at the Jackson Square MBTA station and its northern half is yet to be built.

The unreconstructed mile or so from Jackson to Ruggles is a six-lane raceway with traffic often zooming by at speeds well beyond the posted limit, and with multiple accidents over the years, some fatal. As one who lives a block up Cedar Street, I have had a front-row seat to the frequent crashes in front of Roxbury Community College — one of them just after I had crossed Columbus Avenue on foot.

I was eager for the construction of the final mile of this busway and was frustrated to see its originally projected 2025 completion date come and go. Then I was appalled to read in StreetsBlogMASS last month that this project appears to have been indefinitely postponed.

Given what I have witnessed here over more than four decades, I find this delay inexcusable.

John Kyper

Roxbury

title: 26.TRUE Marathon offers community, comebacks, and culture beyond Boston’s main route
text:
Powder was one of 400 runners who participated in 26.TRUE on Saturday, a racing event designed as a more inclusive option to the Boston Marathon that takes the runner through the “real” city.

The event, which features a half and full marathon, was held for the first time during the COVID-19 pandemic when PIONEERS Run Crew, Boston’s first Black and brown-led running community, put together a race for runners who’d registered for the canceled Boston Marathon. It was supposed to be a one-time event, but garnered so much interest that it’s now in its sixth year.

Aliese Lash, an event organizer, said 26.TRUE is dedicated to celebrating predominantly Black and brown neighborhoods including Dorchester, Roxbury, Jamaica Plain, and Mattapan, which are usually overlooked during marathon weekend.

“These [neighborhoods] are historically underrepresented in running culture,” Lash said. “Something we care a lot about is how to make running more equitable and accessible to people of color and people who may not see themselves as elite, strong runners.”

Unlike traditional road races, 26.TRUE does not receive city-mandated road closures. Participants run on sidewalks and are encouraged to follow pedestrian rules. The marathon requires no qualifying standards, and runners register on a first-come, first-served basis and pay a $100 fee to cover overhead costs. Runners are able to complete 26.TRUE’s full or half-marathon options at their own pace without fear of having nobody left at the finish line.

This year 400 runners participated, the largest number in the event’s history, Lash said.

“We’re really centering it to be a tour of the city as opposed to a competitive race,” Lash said. “26.TRUE is so beautiful because the course itself gives runners a chance to really see the sights, smells, sounds, and culture of the parts of the city that we really love. This is what we call home.”

At the finish line, a block party was in full swing with a DJ, food trucks, and a recovery tent. Runners embraced family and friends and congratulated one another.

Near the finish line, Kelvin Velez stood holding a sign that read, “Jackie! Free tacos at the finish line!”

Velez said that Jackie is his “amazing” younger sister. While she’s not a regular runner, she always tries new things, he said.

“I’m the older brother, so I have her back, of course,” Velez said.

Later, when Jackie Velez crossed the finish line, she said completing the half-marathon was a personal goal of hers that she wanted to make by the time she turned 40 next month.

“This opportunity came, and I just signed up and started training,” she said.

Elsewhere at the block party, Whitney Polich greeted her friend Dylan Reyes, who had just completed the full route, with a sign reading, “Dylan runs on Dunkin!”

Reyes, of Boston, began running two years ago after reaching a low point in his life. He joined PIONEERS Run Crew and said the community helped carry him through.

The 26.TRUE route had excellent energy that kept him and other runners going, he said.

“You get to see so much of the historic parts of the city and so many people are out on their porches cheering,” he said. “It’s just a good vibe, everyone’s happy.”

Reyes is a fan of his friend’s poster, but he swapped Dunkin’ for a Modelo.

“No coffee now, but alcohol is great!” Reyes said, lifting his glass.

Volunteer coordinator Molly Ryan said the event’s 150 volunteers were essential to make 26.TRUE happen. Volunteers handle everything from bib pickup and registration to medal distribution and crowd support.

“Nothing would happen without the volunteers,” Ryan said. “It’s definitely a community effort.”

Powder said she plans to run the full marathon next year. Part of the reason she ran 26.TRUE was for its empowering community. Within the group, she’s seen runners become motivated to take risks like starting businesses and finishing school.

“Running is just the starting point, but the finish line is endless,” she said.

title: Head Start looks for help from Mass. in its mission to help young children
text:
In Massachusetts, roughly 1,300 slots for children across Head Start’s 28 agencies have been eliminated in the last three years because federal funding has plateaued over that time, while the cost of running the program continues to rise, according to the Massachusetts Head Start Association. Nationally, Head Start enrollment dropped from 1.1 million kids in 2013 to around 785,000 in 2022, according to research by the Annie E. Casey Foundation.

“If they didn’t get into a Head Start program, they would be sitting at home,” said Brittany Acosta, a Head Start parent in Dorchester.

It’s teachers are drastically underpaid, and there’s a serious need for a rainy day-type fund should the federal government shut down again, the association says. As they’ve done in years past, state lawmakers have offered to provide financial relief, but the Massachusetts Head Start Association’s request for 3 percent above the amount it received last year, an additional $4.6 million to help its staff keep up with the state’s rising cost of living, so far has not been allocated.

Last year, President Trump’s leaked budget proposal revealed he considered eliminating Head Start entirely. Then, in the summer, he cut off Head Start enrollment for immigrants without legal status. And during the fall’s government shutdown, four Head Start centers in Massachusetts closed because they couldn’t access their funding.

Trump’s latest budget proposal shows a fourth year without increasing funding for the program, which was established in the mid-1960s.

Michelle Haimowitz, executive director of the Massachusetts Head Start Association, said the program doesn’t want to eliminate more child slots than it already has, but paying teachers a competitive salary is equally important in order to keep them from leaving for higher paying jobs. Head Start teachers make under $50,000 annually compared to over $85,000 for the average Massachusetts kindergarten teacher.

“It’s an impossible choice,” Haimowitz said. “When we reduce the size of our programs, we’re not reducing the size of the need.”

Massachusetts is one of few states that supplements federal funding for Head Start, and last year it increased the program’s state grant from $5 million to $20 million, adding to the $189 million in federal aid it receives in this state.

“We can’t run a program without giving staff a raise for three years,” Haimowitz said. “Our next fight now is not just for survival, but it’s for thriving and growth.”

The Massachusetts House Ways and Means Committee on Wednesday released its budget, which doesn’t grant Head Start’s request of a 3 percent boost. But state Representative Christopher Worrell filed an amendment for additional funding. Worrell, whose district covers parts of Dorchester and Roxbury, said he loves Head Start’s embrace of culture, recalling one visit to a center where he could smell staff cooking stew chicken, a traditional Caribbean dish.

“I’ve been to dozens of schools throughout the district, and you don’t get that home-cooked meal,” Worrell said. “[The state is] stepping up and doing the best we can with what we have.”

At the Action for Boston Community Development’s Head Start and Early Head Start center in Dorchester, the children of Classroom 7 arrived one Monday morning and dove into bins of magnetic tiles before their teachers, Paola Polanco and Leolina Rasundar Chinnappa, served breakfast. Acosta dropped off her 4-year-old daughter, Violeta, before reporting to her teaching position at the center, where several other Head Start parents also work.

“It’s important for all Head Start parents to have the opportunity to give their child an experience in a learning environment before they actually start kindergarten,” Acosta said.

Beyond providing early education and care to children of low-income families, from birth to age 5, the program helps them access other resources, including mental health services, SNAP benefits, homelessness assistance, and employment opportunities.

It also serves as daycare for parents who might not be able to afford it, while they’re at work.

Research has shown the importance of preschool in a child’s development with one 2023 study, focused on Boston public preschools, finding that it improves student behavior and increases the likelihood of high school graduation and college enrollment.

For Rickencia Clerveaux and Christopher Mclean, the Dorchester Head Start center is the only place they feel comfortable sending their 3-year-old son, Shontz, who is on the autism spectrum. Shontz’s stimming — repetitive movements that stimulate the senses — has reduced, and his speech has improved since he joined the center in 2024, Clerveaux said.

His parents say he’s also come out of his shell. Mclean now drops his son off and gets a simple “bye” as Shontz joins his classmates, he said.

He and Clerveaux said they appreciate the specialized attention Shontz can receive from teachers, such as when staff identified that Shontz might have hearing issues. His parents were able to follow up with their doctor and get Shontz to have surgery to improve his hearing.

“It’s a safe net for parents,” Clerveaux said. “There’s so many ways that him being here helps him grow better.”

Without Head Start, Clerveaux said a lot of pressure would be put on parents to find care for their children, “knowing that they’re already struggling or not getting the ends to meet.”

“That’s a burden for everybody in the community,” she said. “If there’s no funding, there’s no daycare and parents cannot work.”

title: Educator caught in N.H. child sex trafficking sting sentenced to more than 13 years in prison
text:
Lancaster first responded to the ad at 7:21 a.m. on Nov. 14, 2024, initiating a back-and-forth conversation that continued into the afternoon, according to court records. He repeatedly asked undercover agents for reassurance that they weren’t with the police, then confirmed his intentions.

“I’ll be there at 3:15,” he wrote.

While in the hotel parking lot, Lancaster expressed nervousness about the transaction and sought further assurances that an undercover agent wasn’t working with law enforcement, according to an affidavit that prosecutors filed with the court. Then he confirmed he was ready to follow through with the planned encounter, and was arrested.

Lancaster was placed on administrative leave immediately, and the New Hampshire Department of Education suspended his credential eligibility within a week of his arrest.

Lancaster was convicted at the conclusion of a jury trial in May 2025 and detained pending sentencing.

Lancaster’s defense attorney, Charles J. Keefe, urged the court to impose a sentence of five years in prison followed by five years of supervised release, along with a $5,000 penalty. He argued the government had “enticed” his client to commit a crime that didn’t involve any actual children.

In the defense’s sentencing memorandum, Keefe wrote that a search of Lancaster’s phone and laptop “revealed that he had no demonstrated prior interest in underage girls” and that it was an agent who “pushed the conversation” at the hotel when Lancaster expressed reservations.

“Although the jury convicted him in this case, the evidence revealed someone appearing not to be fully committed to going through with the actual act,” Keefe wrote.

Lancaster’s wife and 10 other people, including fellow parishioners from a church in Lancaster, Mass., submitted letters of support ahead of his sentencing.

“The situation that led to his incarceration does not reflect who he truly is,” wrote his wife, Tamires Lancaster.

“Our family stands fully prepared to support him by providing a stable home, guidance, and encouragement as he moves forward,” she added.

The US attorney’s office in New Hampshire argued that a 15-year mandatory minimum sentence applies in this case. The prosecutors recommended that Lancaster be sentenced to nearly 20 years (235 months) in prison, followed by five years of supervised release.

In their sentencing memorandum, assistant US attorneys Matthew Vicinanzo and Anna Krasinski wrote that Lancaster’s plan was egregious, and the actions he took offer strong indications that he believed a real child was at the hotel awaiting his planned abuse.

“The conduct is all the more flagrant when considering that the defendant was employed as a teacher at Manchester West High School, that he worked with children every day, and that he was trained as a mandatory reporter of child abuse in his role as a teacher,” Vicinanzo and Krasinski wrote. “The defendant was in the process of negotiating to abuse a child that day while he was at work in a school building.”

Lancaster had testified that he intended to rescue the 12-year-old girl, but prosecutors said that testimony was inconsistent with his chat messages, his actions at the hotel, and his decision not to report the situation to law enforcement. The jury concluded his testimony was false, so a sentencing enhancement should apply, prosecutors said.

Judge Paul J. Barbadoro, at the federal court in Concord, N.H., ultimately imposed a sentence of 13.5 years (162 months) in prison, followed by five years of supervised release, according to a statement from prosecutors.

Prior to his job at Manchester West High School, Lancaster held a similar position at the John D. O’Bryant School of Mathematics and Science in Roxbury, Mass., according to court records. He served in the US Navy from 1999 until 2023, has a master’s degree, and had been enrolled in graduate coursework at Northeastern University when he was arrested.

title: Man dies, police officer wounded during exchange of gunfire in New Hampshire, authorities say
text:
A man died and a police officer was wounded during an exchange of gunfire during a traffic stop in New Hampshire Monday night, authorities said.

The fatal shooting in Ashland, a small town in the Lakes Region, is the latest in a series of officer-involved killings in New England in recent weeks.

During the Monday incident, officials said the man produced a gun when officers from the Ashland Police Department stopped his vehicle and “engaged in an exchange of gunfire with the officers,” New Hampshire Attorney General John M. Formella said.

There is no known threat to the public at this time, Formalla said in a statement.

One officer was shot and is being treated at an area hospital, he said.

The suspect died at the scene. His identity was not disclosed pending notification of next of kin.

An autopsy will be conducted by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

No other law enforcement officers or private citizens were injured during the incident, Formella said.

Per department protocol, the names of the officers who fired their weapons during the exchange are being withheld until the conclusion of formal interviews, Formella said.

Investigators are checking to see if cruiser cameras or police body cameras captured footage of the incident.

The recent string of fatal police shootings in New Hampshire and Massachusetts have raised scrutiny about how police respond to mental health and medical emergencies, particularly when officers are called to situations involving people in distress.

New Hampshire authorities this month said a man who died after exchanging gunfire with police in Raymond, N.H., fatally shot himself.

In early April, Boston police shot and killed a 29-year-old former Berklee College of Music student near Northeastern University. In March, officers fatally shot a 39-year-old man in Roxbury. Both men had struggled with mental health.

There were also deadly police shootings in Weymouth and Westminster in March. In three of the four incidents, authorities said the individuals were wielding a knife or sword.

There was another fatality Saturday when a 26-year-old man was shot and killed by police outside his Lexington home after his father called 911 seeking medical assistance for his son, authorities said. Police said the man advanced toward officers with a knife.
