title: 50 years ago this week, a radical group bombed the Suffolk courthouse in Boston, deepening the city’s turmoil
text:
“It’s inconceivable that somebody would put a bomb in a public place like that,” Narine, 88, said at his Brockton home.

The bombing, which investigators later linked to a broader series of attacks across New England in the months that followed, came at a volatile time in Boston, as the city grappled with racial tensions from school desegregation, economic decline, and deep uncertainty about the future.

Nearly two dozen people were injured in the blast, and while the attack has largely faded into history, for victims such as Narine the consequences have lasted for decades.

The explosion, fueled by at least six sticks of dynamite, ripped apart the courthouse’s second floor, just feet away from where Narine was in line.

“I was close to it . . . too close,” he said, sitting in his living room alongside his wife, Samali Kajubi.

Narine lost his left leg, and his left elbow was shattered so badly it no longer has a joint, he said. He suffered severe burns on his right leg that left deep scars.

Narine was rushed to Massachusetts General Hospital, where he awoke to find his right leg suspended in traction. His other leg was wrapped in bandages that were soaked in blood. A surgeon later told him he only survived the blast because he was in good physical shape.

The explosion knocked down parts of the ceiling, smashed walls and office partitions, and brought down large sections of marble.

In the immediate aftermath, authorities searched for a man who was seen running from the building after leaving a package, but the search was later called off after investigators were given conflicting descriptions of the suspect.

Narine said there was no sign of danger before the blast. He said he later learned that a warning call had been made to the courthouse before the explosion, but the building was never fully cleared, a lapse that Robert Allison, a history professor at Suffolk University, said reflected the lack of coordinated security protocols at the time.

The Globe reported that a courthouse operator had answered a telephone call from a woman who warned that a bomb would go off in 20 minutes. Allison said courthouse officials struggled to determine how seriously to take the threat, or how to respond, and did not order a full evacuation.

“Today, there would be a way of tracking where the phone call was made and who made it,” Allison said. “You couldn’t do that then.”

Court officials believed that if there were a bomb, it would be on the upper floors near a courtroom, and people on those levels were warned of the threat, according to Allison. But people on the lower levels were not notified.

“There was much less of a coordinated response,” he said. “These are things we learn through painful experience.”

Narine said there was no indication of a threat when he entered the courthouse and bounded up the steps to the second floor.

“One or two phone calls had been made, but nobody took the opportunity to say, ‘No, you can’t come in,’ ” he said.

Boston in the mid-1970s was a different city than it is today. Still reeling from the turmoil of court-ordered school desegregation and years of economic stagnation, the city “hadn’t yet figured out what it was going to do next,” Allison said.

The bombing happened just a day before a planned “March for Peace,” part of a broader effort by Mayor Kevin White to mark the nation’s bicentennial and project a sense of unity and renewal.

But the courthouse attack was only the beginning.

In the weeks that followed, radical groups launched a series of attacks across New England against symbols of authority, violence that investigators later connected to the courthouse bombing.

Explosions hit a power facility in Maine in May, and another courthouse in Lowell was bombed in June, injuring a custodian. On a single day in early July, bombs struck an Eastern Airlines plane at Logan Airport, a National Guard armory in Dorchester, and a courthouse in Newburyport. A post office in Seabrook, N.H., was also hit.

Over time, investigators focused on a group that included three figures who were allegedly tied to a radical underground network called the Sam Melville/Jonathan Jackson Unit, later to be known as United Freedom Front. The group allegedly carried out bombings and robberies along the East Coast in the 1970s and early 1980s.

“There was a proliferation of these left-wing groups that wanted to overthrow the government, and they didn’t have a whole lot of coordination among them,” Allison said.

For years, no arrests were made in the courthouse bombing. But more than a decade later, federal authorities launched a sweeping prosecution that charged the three with seditious conspiracy and racketeering tied to a string of bombings, including the attack on the courthouse.

The federal trial in Springfield lasted months, becoming the longest and most expensive trial in state history, the Globe reported. It seemed like a long-awaited chance for justice, but the jury was unable to reach a verdict, and a mistrial was declared in November 1989.

Prosecutors considered trying the case again, according to Globe reports from the time, but the defendants were already serving lengthy federal sentences for other bombings. A retrial would be costly and, in the government’s view, unlikely to change the outcome in a meaningful way.

The lack of a resolution is one reason the bombing has faded from modern memory, Allison said.

“You really can’t write history until you know the end,” Allison said.

Narine tried to find justice another way.

A jury found that courthouse officials had been negligent in their response to the threat and awarded Narine $1.5 million. But the state appealed and the award was overturned, apparently because Narine had not established which government entity at the city, state, or federal level was ultimately responsible.

“The court found that there was negligence,” he recalled. “But who was responsible for negligence? I didn’t prove that.”

Narine turned to state politicians for help, and at one point he was offered $100,000 by the Legislature, he said. But he refused, believing it did not properly compensate him for his loss.

The bombing changed the course of Narine’s life but didn’t diminish his ambition. At the time, he was attending Roxbury Community College at night while working days at Tufts University. He finished his degree and later continued his education at Boston University, where he studied creative writing and discovered a love for writing stories. He published a couple of books and built a life around reading and creativity.

Narine learned to walk with a prosthetic, but has faced chronic pain since the attack. He raised a family and has grandchildren now. He still drives; a few years ago he drove alone from Massachusetts to Philadelphia to visit a dying friend.

He said that he rarely thinks about the bombing, and that he “didn’t sustain anger over it.”

But Narine remains frustrated that what happened to him and others in the courthouse that day was never fully explained and over time largely forgotten.

“I lost my leg for no good reason,” he said. “Changed my life, absolutely, with a lot of pain behind it.”

Emily Sweeney and Jeremiah Manion of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Your guide to Vermont music (beyond Noah Kahan)
text:
It’s tricky to pinpoint the exact moment that Noah Kahan became Vermont’s poster boy. The Strafford-raised folk artist’s timeline is a blur of earth tones: the verdant mountains on the cover of his breakthrough album, 2022’s “Stick Season”; the camo-colored apparel of his L.L. Bean collaboration; the Kelly green walls surrounding him at Fenway Park, which he sold out twice in 2024 (and returns to for four nights this July).

Consciously or not, Kahan’s been signaling his role as the Green Mountain state’s latest music star, following in the footsteps of acts like Phish and Grace Potter. (The fact that he’s since pulled up stakes for Watertown, then Nashville, is beside the point — you can’t scrub the “Vermont woods” look off that hirsute mug.) His latest album, “The Great Divide,” arrives Friday, and includes material written “next to a pond” in the town of Guilford.

Kahan’s not the only one drawing inspiration from placid surroundings. With Vermont in the national spotlight once again, here’s a handful of performers from the state who’ve recently released new music and have upcoming performances in Greater Boston.

King Tuff, a.k.a. singer and guitarist Kyle Thomas, was enmeshed in Los Angeles’ 2010s music scene, churning out rock tunes that ranged from kaleidoscopic psychedelia to fuzz-coated rippers. But in recent years, the Brattleboro native returned to his home state, where he crafted his latest LP, March’s “MOO,” a sun-streaked collection of garage rock.

“Vermont is full of furniture makers, weavers, dyers, stonemasons, luthiers, quilters, blacksmiths, sign painters, popcorn farmers — tradespeople with very specialized skills who are just doing their own thing and making it work,” Thomas, who plays the Middle East Upstairs May 22, tells the Globe. “I find it really inspiring to be surrounded by people like that. I think of music as a trade as well.”

Another March offering from Vermont’s music scene is the latest LP from Burlington duo Dwight + Nicole, the longtime partnership of Dwight Ritscher and Nicole Nelson (who appeared on season 3 of “The Voice”). The group’s album “Day or Night” is a rich sampler of their pop-tinged blues and soul; perhaps their genre-blending flair is best described by saying that Mavis Staples and Melissa Etheridge are fans. In late June, the pair returns to Greater Boston — where they first linked up in the early aughts — to take the stage at Club Passim.

Another Burlington transplant is Lily Seabird, a Pennsylvania-raised artist who moved to the area “on a whim” when she was 19, not intending to stay past a season. That was eight years ago.

In the last three years, Seabird began putting all of her energy into her music career, yielding the albums “Alas,” and “Trash Mountain” (previously praised in this column as “heart-swelling alt-country”) and most recently, a frenzied folk single called “Demon in Me.”

“Burlington is a small town, and Vermont is pretty far from a lot [of things] — I’m not a skier or anything so I think being bored a lot has lent itself to making a lot of music,” says Seabird, who performs with Saintseneca at Lowell venue Taffeta May 16. “People here really like supporting the arts, too, I think more than the average place, so I’m really grateful for that.”

The tight-knit community is another advantage, she says, citing the satisfaction of witnessing the success of fellow VermontersRobber Robber, as well as Dari Bay, the project of Robber Robber’s drummer, Zack James. The acts are two sides of the same alt-rock coin. Robber Robber, who perform at Deep Cuts in Medford on May 23, streamline turbulent post-punk on the April album “Two Wheels Move the Soul,” while James’s latest work, the singles ”The Joke” and “We’re Gonna Be Okay,” can barely contain their mushrooming fuzz-rock riffs.

That’s just the tip of the Green Mountains’ music scene. Here are a few more artists to add to your palette of Vermont sounds: the liquid dream-pop of Acqua Mossa; Latin psychedelia by Sonido Mal Maïz; Burundian, Somalian, and Tanzanian musical traditions marbled with hip-hop from A2VT; and punchy post-punk delivered by THUS LOVE, my longstanding bet for Vermont’s “next big thing.”

GIG GUIDE

Alabama soul group St. Paul & The Broken Bones dropped their “Live at Southern Grooves” LP in February, and now bring the real deal to the House of Blues this Sunday; MIKA sprinkles starry-eyed pop from his new LP, “Hyperlove,” around the venue on Wednesday. On the heels of his new song with James Blake, “Doesn’t Just Happen,” English rapper and actor Dave performs across the street at MGM Music Hall at Fenway on Monday.

Also on Monday, two bands celebrate the big 4-0. Ohio’s rock shapeshifters the Afghan Whigs mark their 40th year together at Royale, while Cali ska-punks Fishbone trumpet the milestone anniversary of their debut album, “In Your Face,” at the Sinclair.

A pair of mini residencies from LCD Soundsystem and the Hold Steady, which both run Thursday through May 3, revive the early aughts New York music scene. LCD Soundsystem return to Roadrunner for a four-night takeover, while the Hold Steady’s stint at the Sinclair celebrates the 20th anniversary of the indie rock band’s third album, “Boys and Girls in America.”

Leading up to the residencies, London punks Cock Sparrer make an appearance at Roadrunner Saturday with their eighth and final album, 2024’s “Hand on Heart.” At the Sinclair, electronic-metal maven VANA visits on Sunday, and Georgia duo Lowertown drape the venue with their lo-fi rock experiments Wednesday.

A few Thursday showcases trumpet International Jazz Day, a UNESCO-backed initiative that launched in 2011. The Boston Jazz Foundation brings saxophonistsGodwin Louis and Jonathan Suazo to Union Church, with a focus on Suazo’s 2023 album, “Ricano.” Meanwhile, Detroit multi-instrumentalist Nina Ott leads her quartet, HUM, at Long Live Beerworks as part of the Roxbury taproom’s weekly jazz programming.

Drawing from the Well, a concert series programmed by the Irish Traditional Music Archive, makes its Boston area debut Thursday at the Somerville Theatre with sets from artists like Mass. native Aoife O’Donovan and West Kerry concertina player Cormac Begley. The series continues at the theater May 1 as part of the Tunes on the Charles Irish music festival, which runs Thursday through May 3 at venues like the Lilypad, McCarthy’s and Toad, and the Burren.

NOW SPINNING

Nine Inch Nails and Boys Noize, “Nine Inch Noize.” It’s a live album; it’s a studio album; it’s a reimagining of originals; it’s a clash of electro-industrial covers. “Nine Inch Noize” is all of the above, a melee of formats and genres orchestrated by Nine Inch Nails and German producer Boys Noize. Above all, the hodgepodge is a bone-rattling success — and a consolation prize for anyone who didn’t get to see the artists headline Coachella earlier this month.

BONUS TRACK

In case Thursday wasn’t busy enough, Lowell’s the Town and the City Festival launches that evening and runs through May 2. The multi-venue event, which sprawls across downtown Lowell, will feature 50-plus performers, including locals Vundabar, Grace Givertz, Future Teens, and the Wolff Sisters, as well as national acts like New York’s the Felice Brothers and Steve Wynn of the Dream Syndicate.

title: From spas to podcast studios, Boston’s apartment/condo building amenities are evolving
text:
“We’re not seeing a replacement of traditional amenities; we’re seeing an expansion of expectations,” said Shengchao Ying, a senior associate of research and analytics services at Greystar, one of the country’s largest apartment developers. “What’s changing is that residents increasingly want spaces that support how they live and connect day to day.”

Greystar’s 2025 Design Survey found that fitness centers and covered parking remain must-haves for more than 80 percent of renters. But layered on top of those basics is a growing appetite for amenities that blur the line between residential and hospitality.

At Gibson Point Apartments in Revere, developer Redgate transformed a former junkyard into a wellness-forward complex complete with outdoor saunas, cold plunges, a recovery room stocked with compression sleeves and vibrating massage guns, and a treatment room for massages and facials. The inspiration has roots that are more than a century old: the site once hosted a wellness retreat in the late 1800s.

“We don’t think it’s trendy,” Damian Szary, a principal at Redgate, said of the increasing emphasis on wellness. “We think it’s going to stick around for a while.”

What makes Gibson Point’s wellness program function, Szary said, is technology that eliminates friction points. Through a resident app called Elevate Living, prescreened service providers (physical therapists, personal trainers, and even estheticians) are bookable directly from a phone. Residents check availability and schedule an appointment in minutes, while the building avoids carrying the cost of full-time staff. The transaction happens directly between residents and providers while Redgate supplies the space. Apartments lease for $2,300-$4,400 a month.

But the wellness philosophy extends beyond equipment. At 273 Highland in Roxbury, Studio G Architects took a materials and design-driven approach.

“We think about wellness holistically — how a building is experienced, functions, and supports everyday life,” said Gabriela Shelburne, principal at Studio G. “That comes to life through healthier materials, abundant natural light, and shared spaces like the gallery-style gathering area that foster connection just as much as comfort.”

The affordable housing building serves households earning 30 percent to 60 percent of the area median income.

Coworking is another front in this amenities race, but the old model is dead. The conference room with a video setup that inevitably got colonized by one person has given way to something more intentional. Gibson Point features 13 individual glass pods with varied seating — including walking workstations — for a 300-unit building. They’re utilized all the time, Szary said.

Ying at Greystar echoed the shift: “Residents aren’t just looking for a desk, they want spaces that support real productivity, whether that’s private areas for focused work, strong connectivity, or adaptable layouts.”

For luxury condo buyers, the bar is higher still. At The EchelonSeaport, Cottonwood Group built out a PGA golf simulator and tech-enabled sports spaces that became a cornerstone of the sales pitch. The building is now 99 percent sold out. Units range from about 500 to 2,000 square feet and are priced at about $1,700 to $2,400 per square foot with fees ranging from $1.50 to $1.77 per square foot monthly. So, as an example, a 500-square-foot condo could be priced at $850,000 with a monthly fee of $750.

Angelica Nouhi, Cottonwood’s vice president of asset management, sees multisport simulators like those offered at The St. Regis Residences Boston as the next benchmark for residential amenities, alongside fully furnished guest suites that owners can book for visiting friends and family.

As for the broader trajectory, Greystar’s Scott Berka, senior managing director of brand and customer experience, sees amenity design evolving from individual features into something closer to community infrastructure.

“Overall, it points to a broader shift; amenities aren’t just about convenience anymore, but about supporting a more engaging, lifestyle-driven experience,” she said.

title: ‘You may be the first someday’: Ocasio-Cortez joins Pressley and Wu in Roxbury to champion more funding in early education
text:
“The country is better when we invest in our children,” Ocasio-Cortez, who is joining Pressley in Boston for a fireside chat Friday evening, told reporters after story time. [We’re] ”trying to make sure we invest in child care to every American, health care to every American, and making sure our teachers and our educators are dignified.”

Pressley singled out the Trump administration, which has requested raising defense spending to $1.5 trillion in its proposed 2027 budget, the largest such request in decades.

“We have an occupant in the Oval Office that says we have to fund a war that we don’t even know why we’re there, but we cannot afford to pay for child care,” Pressley said.

Trump’s budget proposal keeps funding to federal early education programs, including Head Start and the Child Care and Development Block Grant, the same as recent years, even as those programs struggle with rising costs. The proposal also eliminates the Preschool Development Block Grant Birth through Five program.

“We’re fighting wars. We can’t take care of day care,” Trump said at a private White House event April 1 ahead of a national address about the war in Iran, reported by the Associated Press.

“It’s not possible for us to take care of day care, Medicaid, Medicare — all these individual things,” Trump said. “They can do it on a state basis. You can’t do it on a federal.”

In Massachusetts, state and federally-funded early education programs support more than 111,000 children and families.

Head Start, a federal program founded in the 1960s, has eliminated 1,300 child slots in Massachusetts over the past three years as its federal funding has plateaued, and last year Trump threatened to eliminate the program. Head Start has looked to the state for additional support, and is advocating for an extra $4.6 million in grant funding this year to raise wages and adjust to the rising cost of living.

“I don’t think that the president’s administration right now is friendly to Head Start,” Ocasio-Cortez said. “There are some things that should not be on the table [to be cut], and Head Start should not be off the table.”

The state’s Commonwealth Cares for Children program supports more than 8,000 children, according to the Healey administration. At the local level, Boston Public Schools’ Universal Pre-K program offers free early education through partnerships with home- and community-based centers.

Research shows that investing in early childhood development results in significant gains in children’s health, cognition, and long-term learning.

Pressley said centers like Horizons, an independent, Massachusetts-based nonprofit, support some of the country’s “most vulnerable” families.

“So often, the children that have the greatest need are provided the least amount of support,” Pressley said. “Families are experiencing greater financial hardship and economic anxiety and vulnerabilities each and every day, because of the hostilities of this administration that are not focused on the things that matter most.”

Beyond the impacts on childhood development, Wu, Pressley, and Ocasio-Cortez said early education strengthens the workforce: Parents can leave their kids in good hands while they go to work, thus spurring the economy, they said.

Wu reminisced on a visit to Horizons that she and Pressley made as city councilors in 2017 to discuss the importance of providing child care to homeless families. She said Boston has seen increased public school enrollment since Boston Public Schools expanded its Universal Pre-K program, bringing in home- and community-based centers.

Wu said they don’t view early education, housing, and workforce development as separate issues.

“It’s really one in the same,” Wu said. “By taking care of what matters most, the impact then also ripples out across all of these areas.”

During the story time, young students bounced on their lily pad cushions as the elected officials took turns reading from “Ambitious Girl.” Pressley told the children what her mother always told her, “Don’t let anyone tell you who you are.”

“I am valued. I am loved. I have purpose, hope, and power,” the children said, affirming the words in the book.

“You have power,” one boy told his teacher in turn.

title: Nearly two years later, Roxbury Community College inaugurates its 18th president
text:
“We’ve got a number of things accomplished,” Jefferson said in an interview. “It was more of a celebration than it was inauguration.”

That approach was echoed by Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, who described Jefferson as a leader focused on action before recognition.

“[He] didn’t want to get celebrated until he’d actually done the work and could bring us all together with proof of that vision,” Wu said in her remarks.

Since taking office in July 2024, Jefferson has overseen a time of institutional change. Data from the state Department of Higher Education show the college’s enrollment grew 21 percent, from 2,694 students in fiscal 2024, to 3,281 students in fiscal 2025, which ended on June 30.

The college has also secured millions in grants, completed its reaccreditation process, and expanded programming in workforce development, STEM, health care, and clean energy.

Jefferson highlighted the completion of 22 projects in 16 months as a key milestone.

“That is a tremendous achievement,” he said with a smile. “We looked at where our college was and where it needed to go and what projects we need to do to get them there.”

Other initiatives include RCC Connect, a centralized “one-stop shop” for student services. The college has promoted dozens of staff members and improved IT systems.

In his inaugural address, Jefferson outlined a vision of RCC where students gain both academic credentials and practical experience.

“Our vision is to transform Roxbury Community College into a career-ready work college,” Jefferson said, talking about a model for students where every student has at least one paid learn-and-earn opportunity.

That vision is part of the college’s “Roxbury 2030″ strategic plan, which focuses on five priorities: purpose, people, place, programs, and partnerships.

“That’s what we’re doing, students at the center, faculty and staff are around that,” Jefferson said in an interview. “We just want to make sure that we’re providing economic mobility to our students.”

He said they are working on 18 projects following the theme, “transforming today for a better tomorrow.”

At the event, Israul Marrero, the interim chair of the college’s board of trustees, lauded Jefferson’s leadership and focus on student outcomes.

“I know that you will continue to prioritize student experience and will continue to work diligently to provide every student with personalized support needed for long-term success,” Marrero said.

RCC’s origins trace back to community activism in the 1960s when residents opposed the construction of Interstate 95 through Roxbury and instead advocated for an institution that would serve local educational needs.

Jefferson referenced the college’s history in his remarks, describing it as a college built on decades of community effort.

In 2021, RCC was recognized as a Predominantly Black Institution by the US Department of Education, the only one in the Northeast.

Much of the ceremony focused on RCC’s role in expanding access to higher education, particularly for minority students.

“Educational attainment and the economic mobility that comes with it is still too often determined by zip code, income, and race,” Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll said. “It’s exactly why institutions like RCC are so critical.”

For many attendees, the inauguration represented a sense of renewed stability after years of leadership turnover.

Jumaada Abdal-Khallaq Smith, a community volunteer with deep family ties to the college, said she admires Jefferson’s commitment.

“He promised not to leave,” Smith said, talking about the history of unstable leadership. “His consistency is very important ... people are feeling positive about that.”

Jefferson framed the college’s trajectory as a shift from instability to sustained growth, emphasizing long-term leadership and institutional trust.

“We want people to know that we’re here to stay,” he said.

title: A ‘distressing’ number of young Bostonians want out
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

Two years ago, the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce Foundation whipped the city into a frenzy by reporting that a fourth of 20- and 30-somethings were looking to leave here in the next five years.

An update to the study this week offers as much good as it does bad.

Today, 26 percent of the region’s youngest adult cohort are looking to move away from Boston. It’s a “distressing number,” the study says, though at least the outlook has not gotten much worse in the last few years.

Students, single people, and newer residents less than two years from their arrival to Boston are the most likely to leave. That said, fewer people (79 percent in all) are satisfied with their day-to-day lives in town.

Tell me why

The 600 people surveyed ranked job availability, the cost of rent, and safety as the most important factors when deciding whether to stay in Boston. And, shocker: They said local leaders should prioritize creating affordable housing and accessible health care options.

It follows a seemingly endless string of disheartening research about the ways Boston often delays adult milestones, which the Globe has covered over and over and over. Young people in Massachusetts have the fourth-lowest homeownership rate of anywhere in the country. And Bay State couples are typically older than those in all but one state when they get married and have kids.

Anna Giles, a self-certified “city girl” with no plans to leave, said “being in a central location for me is worth paying a little more in rent.” But she feels the same financial pressures as most other 28-year-olds who sacrifice financial security to keep pace with the cost of living.

“I make more money than I’ve ever made in my life,” she said, “but I still cannot save as much as I want to.”

Where are they going?

What is surprising from the Chamber survey is that the South is scooping up Boston’s leftovers. Of the respondents planning to leave Massachusetts, almost half are looking to the southeast and southwest. By comparison, 15 percent are looking to other Northeast states, and 11 percent are eyeing areas in New England.

Warmer and often cheaper, “the South seems to be an attraction these days,” Chamber President and CEO Jim Rooney said. Amber Haskell, the Chamber executive director, quipped that “the worst snowstorm we’ve had in years” might’ve also nudged people towards more tropical climes.

And yet...

There is some good news: Because of the sheer volume of young adults here, Boston still has the highest proportion of people under 34 of the largest American cities. They are having an easier time building community today than a few years ago, the study found. More and more are seeking on-the-job training to advance their careers, or exploring starting their own businesses. And even though complaints about the T abound, most people said they have an easy enough time getting around.

On Monday evening, I’ll be chatting with young Bostonians about how the city can slow outmigration and tackle its biggest challenges. They’ll be refreshments, a prize wheel, and a live art installation. If you care about people staying, or think about leaving yourself, RSVP here.

As Governor Maura Healey put it last month, “there’s work to do, certainly, but there are assets that this state has that other states just don’t.”

title: Police hunt for armed suspects in two bank robberies in Roxbury and Roslindale
text:
Police in Boston are investigating two armed bank robberies less than two hours apart on Tuesday morning.

Shortly after 10 a.m., two men robbed a Santander branch on Washington Street in Roxbury before fleeing on foot, police said.

Just before noon, a robbery was reported at a TD Bank on American Legion Highway in Roslindale. Two men entered the bank and demanded money from tellers at gunpoint, while a third suspect waited in a vehicle outside.

Police said the robberies are believed to be connected. The TD Bank location in Roslindale is about a half-hour drive south of the Washington Street Santander.

The men stole “an undisclosed amount” of money from the two banks, police said. They were still at large as of Tuesday evening.

One of the suspects in the Roxbury heist was described as light-skinned, approximately 5 feet 7 inches tall, and wearing a light blue Nike Tech hoodie. The other was wearing a black Champion hoodie with white lettering, police said. Both were wearing black pants, black face masks, and blue gloves.

They were last seen fleeing on foot on Harrison Avenue toward the Orchard Park area, police said.

Police said the men who entered the Roslindale bank were dressed similarly.

They drove away in a blue Toyota RAV4 with a Massachusetts license plate, registration 4MXN78, on American Legion Highway toward Cummins Highway.

Members of the public should use caution since the robbers are believed to be armed, police said.

In a statement, Santander said it was assisting law enforcement in the investigation.

“The safety of our team members and customers is our top priority, and we can confirm that they are safe,” the bank said.

A TD Bank spokesperson said they were “aware of the situation” and deferred further comment to law enforcement.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

title: Bees assemble: Woman unleashed a swarm of the stingers on deputies. Now she’s been convicted.
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

I’ve covered a lot of strange stories during my career at the Globe, but this incident is, by far, one of the most bizarre.

To understand the full story, you need to go back to Oct. 12, 2022, when a Hadley woman named Rebecca “Rorie” Woods was arrested in a beekeeper’s suit while allegedly trying to stop the court-ordered eviction of a resident who lived in Longmeadow. Here’s the story on TikTok.

Authorities alleged that Woods unleashed swarms of honeybees upon the sheriff’s deputies who were at the scene to enforce the eviction. It’s unclear what her relationship was to the resident who was being evicted from the 7,876-square-foot home at 49 Memery Lane, but she was placed under arrest outside of that house, wearing a beekeeper’s suit, which made for some interesting photographs.

Bees assemble!

I wrote that original story for the Globe, and at the time I reported that Woods had allegedly got out of an SUV and “began trying to open the lids to unleash” the bees from their hives, according to the Hampden County Sheriff’s Department.

“A Sheriff’s deputy tried to stop her, but as the agitated bees started getting out and circling the area, he pulled back,” the sheriff’s department said in a statement at the time. “She then smashed the lid, and flipped a hive off of the flatbed, making the bees extremely aggressive. They swarmed the area and stung several officers and other innocent bystanders who were nearby.”

Authorities also noted that Woods put on a professional beekeeper suit to protect herself, and allegedly carried a “tower of bees” to the front door of the home in an effort to stop the eviction.

Flight to Tennessee

Woods’s trial was originally supposed to start in August 2025, but then she fled to Tennessee. She was eventually returned to Massachusetts on a governor’s warrant three months later, according to the district attorney’s office.

Her trial finally began earlier this month, and on April 17, a jury found Woods guilty of four counts of assault and battery and two counts of assault in connection with the incident, according to Hampden District Attorney Anthony D. Gulluni’s office.

She was sentenced to six months in the House of Correction and was credited with 148 days of time already served, Gulluni’s office said.

After the jury returned the verdict Friday, Gulluni released a statement that said Woods’ attempt to disrupt the court-ordered eviction process in Longmeadow was “unlawful and absurd.”

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
NEWDAD This Galway trio, who released their second full-length, “After,” last year, makes moody, atmospheric gauze-gaze that spins into thrashy territory at its most intense moments. May 2, 7 p.m. Paradise Rock Club. 617-562-8800, crossroadspresents.com

DRY CLEANING One of the best post-post-punk bands of recent years, this London outfit released “Secret Love,” its stellar third album, in January; vocalist Florence Shaw’s fractured, elliptically melodic poetry is framed by jagged guitars and start-stop rhythms, creating a cracked-mirror vision of pop. May 5, 7 p.m. Paradise Rock Club. 617-562-8800, crossroadspresents.com

FAKEMINK London-based producer and MC Vincenzo Nischal Camille Bhatia has become one of the UK underground hip-hop scene’s breakout stars during his short career; his beats have the homespun intricacy of bedroom pop and the blown-out sonics of rage rap, while his rhymes feel free-associative and swaggering. May 5, 8 p.m. Roadrunner Boston. roadrunnerboston.com

MAURA K. JOHNSTON

TANYA DONELLY AND CHRIS BROKAW Two Boston vets join forces to venture into old-time music — and I mean really old-time; they’ve just issued a collaborative EP, “The Undone Is Done Again,” wherein they reimagine a handful of medieval madrigals. They’ll be joined by Elizabeth Steen to perform the EP Friday, along with some of their own material. May 1, 7:30 p.m. $35. First Church Congregational, 11 Garden St., Cambridge. 617-876-4275. www.globalartslive.org

KIMON KIRK AND SYD STRAW Boston expat Kirk is in the habit of returning to the area periodically to show us what he’s been up to musically. His latest visit this Friday brings two treats: First, he’ll be previewing an upcoming album, “Bikini Jardine;” second, he and his band will be backing up a set from the fabulous Syd Straw. May 1, 7:30 p.m. $15. Sally O’Brien’s, 335 Somerville Ave., Somerville. 617-666-3589. www.sallyobriensbar.com

LEAH BLEVINS Leah Blevins teamed up with Dan Auerbach to make her new record, “All Dressed Up,” and what resulted was a marvelous collection that mixes straight country (you want country hurt? Try “Lonely”) with timeless country-soul. She kicks off a tour in support of the album in Cambridge next Tuesday. May 5, 8 p.m. $20. The Lilypad, 1353 Cambridge St., Cambridge. 617-955-7729. www.lilypadinman.com

STUART MUNRO

HELLBENDER Helmed by saxophonist Jared Sims, the Boston Music Awards 2025 Jazz Artist of the Year, this fiery quintet boasts a compositionally canny and invigoratingly improvisatory spirit that takes the ball from 1970s Miles Davis and runs with it. Featuring guitarists Andrew Stern and Jeffrey Lockhart, keyboardist James Rohr, bassist Jesse Williams, and drummer Randy Wooten. May 1, 7:30 p.m. $30.15-$41.79. Regattabar. regattabarjazz.com

TIGER MOAN BATTLE OF THE BONES Singer and multi-instrumentalist Amy Kucharik and her vintage blues outfit hold a first Sunday residency featuring special guests. This time, it’s a duel between two local trombone talents: Tiger Moan’s own Tim Lewandowski and guest Sara Honeywell. May 3, 7:30 p.m. $20-$25. The Burren Back Room, 247 Elm St., Somerville. burren.com/music

THE EDMAR COLÓN QUARTET The accomplished Puerto Rican saxophonist, pianist, and composer — whose collaborators include Wayne Shorter, Teri Lyne Carrington, and The Boston Pops — fronts a first-rate band comprising keyboardist Maxim Lubarsky, bassist Oscar Stagnaro, and drummer Mark Walker. May 7, 6 p.m. No cover. Long Live Roxbury, 152 Hampden St. longlivebeerworks.com/boston

KEVIN LOWENTHAL

BOSTON SYMPHONY ORCHESTRA Dima Slobodeniouk leads the BSO in its final Symphony Hall concert of the spring season, featuring the Tanglewood Festival Chorus in John Adams’s majestic “Harmonium” and Beethoven’s beloved Symphony No. 9. April 30-May 3. Symphony Hall. www.bso.org

BOSTON LYRIC OPERA John de los Santos’s English-language production of Donizetti’s zany rom-com “Daughter of the Regiment” is around for one more weekend; last weekend’s opening proved the ample comedic chops of both the translated book and the excellent cast (standouts: Brenda Rae as Marie and Sandra Piques Eddy as Widow Berkenfeld). It’s well worth your time. Emerson Colonial Theatre. May 1, 7:30 p.m.; May 3, 3 p.m. www.blo.org

BACK BAY CHORALE The chorus’s 50th anniversary season concludes with Orff’s epic “Carmina Burana,” as the long-running community chorus teams up with singers, orchestra, and dancers from Boston Conservatory at Berklee as well as the Boston Children’s Chorus. Stephen Spinelli conducts. May 1, 8 p.m. Symphony Hall. www.bbcboston.org

A.Z. MADONNA

BEETHOVEN Valeriy Pecheykin’s play focuses on 17 crucial scenes from the life of Ludwig van Beethoven, underscoring the composer’s refusal to surrender in the face of his increasing deafness. Performed in Russian with English subtitles, it features live performances of Beethoven’s music and original compositions by Sarah Infini Takagi. Directed by Yana Gladkikh. May 1-10. Arlekin Players Theatre, Needham. 617-942-0022, www.arlekinplayers.com

SOMETHING ROTTEN! The enormous shadow of William Shakespeare (Jared Troilo) hangs over the playwriting and acting efforts of Nick Bottom (Ryan Mardesich) and his brother Nigel (Ohad Ashkenazi) in Elizabethan England. So Nick decides they should focus their efforts on a new genre called a … musical. With music and lyrics by Wayne Kirkpatrick and Karey Kirkpatrick, and a book by Karey Kirkpatrick and John O’Farrell. Directed by Ilana Toeplitz Ranson with musical direction by Katya Stanislavskaya. May 1-June 7. Lyric Stage Boston. 617-585-5678, www.lyricstage.com

GEM OF THE OCEAN What the late August Wilson always wanted us to understand is that emancipation is not the same as freedom. That’s a truth experienced firsthand by the characters in Wilson’s “Gem of the Ocean,” several of whom had formerly been enslaved and are now barely getting by in 1904 Pittsburgh. Under the direction of Monica White Ndounou, “Gem of the Ocean” does not disappoint for the most part, though it does suffer from Wilson’s compulsion to add one more digression, one more freewheeling monologue. Featuring Regine Vital as Aunt Ester, a mystical “soul cleanser”; Joshua Lee Robinson as Citizen Barlow, a young man who seeks absolution for ​a death he inadvertently caused in Alabama​; Jonathan Kitt as Solly Two Kings, who helped enslaved people escape on the Underground Railroad after he escaped slavery himself; and Kadahj Bennett as Caesar Wilks, a constable so iron-fisted he makes Inspector Javert of “Les Miserables” look like a dues-paying member of the ACLU. Through May 17. Actors’ Shakespeare Project in partnership with Hibernian Hall. At Hibernian Hall. 617-241-2200, ActorsShakespeareProject.org

SWEPT AWAY A musical about a 19th-century shipwreck and its aftermath, “Swept Away” is a should-see, maybe even a must-see, for, among other reasons: the variety and sheer energy of the indie-folk music by The Avett Brothers, coupled with the emotional directness of their ardent lyrics. The bravura direction by Jeremy Johnson, who stages scenes of stillness and tumult with equal deftness — the squall/shipwreck scene is a doozy — while smoothly transitioning among the musical’s radical mood shifts. The textured performances by the four principals: Peter DiMaggio as the ragged, haunted Mate; Christopher Chew as the curmudgeonly Captain; Max Connor as Little Brother, in flight from farm life and avid for adventure; and Bishop Levesque as Big Brother, a religious and initially starchy man locked in fraternal combat that conceals a deep love for Little Brother. Through May 23. SpeakEasy Stage Company at Wimberly Theatre, Calderwood Pavilion, Boston Center for the Arts. 617-933-8600, speakeasystage.com

DON AUCOIN

BILL T. JONES / ARNIE ZANE COMPANY “History of Collage,” which blended dance with music and spoken word to explore identity, community, and creativity, was the last piece Jones and Zane created together before Zane died in 1988. Last year, Jones remounted the work on members of his current company, and this weekend they bring “Collage Revisited” to Western Mass. as part of an ongoing legacy project. The concert also features “Story/,” set to the music of Franz Schubert. May 1. $20-$75. UMass Fine Arts Center, Amherst. https://arts.umass.edu/performing-arts/events/bill-t-jones-arnie-zane-company-2526

PANTOS PROJECT DANCE Under the direction of Kat Pantos, the company’s annual spring showcase, “without you,” examines the impact of time’s passage as it explores themes of love, loss, and friendship in new works by Carolyn Breton-Pantos and Marissa Masson. In addition to the professional company and the adult collective, called the ensemble, the concert highlights the pre-professional youth troupe MOVERS. May 2. $55. Boston University Dance Theater. www.pantosprojectdance.com

TONY WILLIAMS’ DORCHESTER DANCE FEST The dedicated Williams brings together a variety of artistic talent, including his own City Ballet of Boston, for a celebratory afternoon of music and dance, from ballet and modern to jazz. This free, family-oriented event is designed to highlight the creativity, spirit, and rich diversity of the community and beyond. May 2. Free. The Strand Theatre, Dorchester. www.cityballetofboston.org

BOSTON BALLET SPRING EXPERIENCE This upcoming mixed repertory program puts Boston Ballet’s versatility and artistic depth on full display through three very different works, including the return of principal dancer Lia Cirio’s “After,” featuring a life-size sculpture by John Farrell. Jerome Robbins’s “Dances at a Gathering” weaves together a masterful series of solos, duets, and group sequences set to piano pieces by Frédéric Chopin. William Forsythe’s 1992 “Herman Schmerman,” set to an electronic score by longtime collaborator Thom Willems, pairs the inimitable choreographer’s technical rigor with an edgy playful wit. May 7-17. $36-$239. Citizens Opera House. www.bostonballet.org

KAREN CAMPBELL

FRAMING NATURE: GARDENS AND IMAGINATION A cross-cultural, collection-wide display of natural lushness to coincide with the 50th anniversary of the MFA’s “Art in Bloom” celebration, this show promises a gamut of garden-forward glory, both flora and fauna. But because I know you’re wondering: There will be Monets, so plan accordingly. Through June 28. Museum of Fine Arts Boston, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, www.mfa.org

SAY IT LOUD: AAMARP, 1977 TO NOW The Black Arts Movement came to be in a critical time in 1960s and ’70s America as the civil rights movement had given way to more forceful ideas around Black rights. In Boston, those ideas found root in the African American Masters Artist in Residence Program, founded by the firebrand artist and activist Dana Chandler. This show charts the organization’s long evolution through decades of cultural and racial tumult, and its unwavering devotion to the cause of Black representation. Through Aug. 2. Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100, icaboston.org

AMERICAN IMPRESSIONISM In the mid-19th century, the Hudson River School of painters, led by Thomas Cole, adopted the heroic frame of their European Romantic forbears to craft a beatific vision of the American landscape that was often at odds with reality. While Americans fawned over their imagined idylls, Europeans were rushing headlong into Modernism as artists like Edgar Dègas and Claude Monet dropped Impressionism, frank and immediate, like a bomb into polite French establishment painting. It would take a while for the US to catch up, but they did, and with some masters of their own, many of whom you’ll see here: James McNeill Whistler, John Singer Sargent, and Childe Hassam, among others. Through June 7. Yale University Art Gallery, 1111 Chapel St., New Haven. 203-432-0601, https://artgallery.yale.edu/

MURRAY WHYTE

BOSTON UNIVERSITY MASTER OF FINE ARTS PAINTING THESIS EXHIBITION We’ve arrived at the sweet spot in the calendar for discovering new talent. Several MFA thesis exhibitions are open or opening soon. Besides BU right now, see work by artists from Massachusetts College of Art and Design at MassArt x SoWA (460 Harrison Ave.) through May 17. The School of the Museum of Fine Arts at Tufts University’s show runs May 5-17 at Aidekman Arts Center, 40 Talbot Ave., Medford. At Faye G., Jo, and James Stone Gallery, 855 Commonwealth Ave., through May 17.www.bu.edu/cfa/news/bu-art-galleries

CATE McQUAID

SAM JAY Now that we have been told aliens are real, former Boston comic Jay feels they are being a bit disrespectful, showing up in Vegas on a Sunday afternoon or at a mall in Miami. “I’m a ’90s kid, that’s not how my aliens roll,” she said a few weeks ago at the Melbourne International Comedy Festival. “This is how my aliens rolled — Iowa, cornfield, 3 a.m. One farmer.”May 2, 7 p.m. $37-$55. The Wilbur, 246 Tremont St.www.thewilbur.com

JOSH OCEAN THOMAS The New York comic says his mother can’t tell when a video is AI, which leads to some interesting conversations. She once called him in a panic, saying, “A man was just eaten on the subway by an octopus!” He said, “No, mom, that’s AI, and she’s like, ‘How do you know?’” May 1-2, 7 p.m., 9 p.m., and 11 p.m. $30. Goofs Comedy Club, 432 McGrath Highway, Somerville. www.goofscomedy.com

CERTIFIED GOLD The Comedy Studio’s signature showcase show features Matt McArthur, Holly Johnston, AJ Hapenny, Harrison Green, and Will Smalley on Friday and Green, Carolyn Riley, Sky Nockels, Zachary Morin, Dan Boulger, and Alex Giampapa on Saturday.May 1-2, 7:15 p.m. $29.95. The Comedy Studio, 5 John F. Kennedy St., Cambridge. www.thecomedystudio.com
