Before moving to Boston in 2017 to lead CMCB, Washington was based in Memphis, where he was a professor of bassoon at the University of Memphis and co-founded PRIZM Ensemble, a Memphis-based organization focused on chamber-music education for local youth. The H+H position represents a welcome “return to the performing arts” for him, at a time when many classical performance organizations are focused on attracting and retaining new audiences, he said.

“Everyone’s trying different things. They’re trying it with repertoire. They’re trying it with storytelling. They’re trying it with staffing. But no one seems to have found the perfect right answer, and I think in many ways there isn’t one,” said Washington. “You probably need some version of all of those things.”

But he thinks H+H is positioned well to “solve for a lot of things the entire sector is trying to solve for,” he said. “Because of its history, it has this core of people who are connected to it.”

Bass Dana Whiteside, a veteran member of the Handel and Haydn Chorus who served on the search committee, said he was excited about Washington’s style of leadership as well as the local connections he brings to the role.

“He’s very steeped in Boston; he knows the Boston landscape; he has a wonderful reputation and rapport civically,” said Whiteside, who works in urban planning and development in addition to his career as a professional singer.

H+H had been looking for a “great convener” as its next executive leader; someone who could engage and collaborate with musicians and staff as well as interfacing with donors, said Whiteside. Washington “has an understanding of the ways that board, staff, and other constituencies have to be fully engaged and involved in the work of taking an organization to the next level.”

Washington, who succeeds David Snead as president and CEO, is the first Black person to hold an executive leadership role at the 211-year-old ensemble, the oldest continually running performing arts organization in the United States. “I name publicly that I am Black; many of my social networks are Black, and that is absolutely who I am. And I’m also a bassoonist, and because of that, it means I have been in predominantly white spaces my entire life.”

As he sees it, that background gives him “a certain type of cultural fluency; multiple versions of language and culture and ways of being that I very much understand,” he said. “For me, this is a really great moment to be able to activate that cultural fluency in service of this music that I love. And when I say I love it, I mean, I’ve devoted my entire life to it. This is not a passion project, or something I do on the periphery … or something based on theory. I believe it because I live it.”

title: Two years ago, the city set aside $100 million to jump-start stalled housing development. It’s finally using it.
text:
But the project’s developers have two unusual equity partners that will make it work: The City of Boston and the Commonwealth of Massachusetts.

Through the Boston Accelerator Fund and the state’s Momentum Fund — both of which were created in 2024 to help jump-start stalled private sector housing projects — the city and the state are kicking in $10.5 million to get the project moving along.

“This partnership is a great example of what can happen when state, local and private partners work together toward a shared goal,” Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll said in a statement. “Projects like this help create more housing opportunities while investing in the long-term strength of neighborhoods like Nubian Square.”

The Nubian Square project will be the first private-sector development to receive funding from the city’s $100 million Accelerator Fund, which Mayor Michelle Wu has touted as a tool to help spark sluggish housing production in Boston.

The project is receiving $8.4 million from the city’s Accelerator Fund and $2.1 million from the state Momentum Fund — money that will be repaid once the project is built. (MassHousing is also offering a loan for the project from mortgage lender Berkadia.) The idea is that the funds will eventually be circular. Once the city and the state are paid back, the money can be reinvested in new developments.

The city’s Accelerator Fund for stalled private sector projects is part of a larger $110 million investment in 2024: $50 million was set aside to jump-start stalled apartment projects, $50 million was earmarked for the Boston Housing Authority’s $1.4 billion overhaul of Charlestown’s Bunker Hill public housing complex, and $10 million was set aside for a pilot program targeting new homeownership developments.

Both the Accelerator Fund and the state Momentum Fund, which is also $50 million, are administered by MassHousing, a quasi-state housing agency. While the funds are separate and financed by the state and city, respectively, deploying them together on projects in Boston increases the equity that stalled developments can tap into.

Prior to the Nubian Square project, the Momentum Fund had been used to help launch two projects outside of Boston, with more to come. The Residences at East Milton Square will total 92 apartments on a prominent street in Milton and is under construction with the help of $5 million from the Momentum Fund. The other is a 233-unit mixed-income project near the commuter rail station in Grafton, which received $9 million in equity from the state.

MassHousing eventually hopes to help finance the creation of more than 1,000 new multifamily units through the Momentum Fund.

Several developers have explored using Boston’s Accelerator Fund before the Nubian Square project, to no avail. One project, the 170-unit redevelopment of the former US Postal Service branch on Harvard Avenue in Allston, received approval to utilize the Accelerator Fund before the developer, Eden Properties, eventually landed on a different financing model.

And while builders have at times struggled to use the fund, the Nubian Square developers said it was critical to moving forward their project, which will also preserve the historic former Roxbury Boys Club building on the site.

“The takeout financing provided by the MassHousing Momentum Fund and Boston’s Housing Accelerator Fund is integral to the success of the project, and we are proud to be the first to put this state-city partnership to work,” said Jacob Vance, principal of SV+Partners.

title: Carjacking suspect killed by Boston officer had lengthy record with more than 17 criminal cases, court filings show
text:
O’Malley shot and killed a suspect in a carjacking in March. The swift decision to prosecute prompted outrage by the police union and law enforcement officials.

O’Malley, 33, has pleaded not guilty to manslaughter for the death of Stephenson King, 39, who was shot March 11 while he allegedly tried to flee a traffic stop in a stolen car. Prosecutors determined that O’Malley had no justification for shooting at a moving vehicle.

“It is disappointing that the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office is choosing to second-guess an officer whose only goal was to protect the public,” O’Malley’s lawyer, David Yannetti, said in an email to the Globe. “We will continue to vigorously defend this officer and this case.”

“The main issue in this case will be who the aggressor really was and whether Officer O’Malley acted in lawful defense,” Yannetti wrote in court filings.

On Wednesday, Yannetti filed several defense motions in the Roxbury division of Boston Municipal Court, in an effort to illustrate “King’s mayhem and reign of terror,” spanning nearly two decades and resulting in more than 17 criminal cases across Massachusetts, court records show.

Over the years, King has been charged with strangulation, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, carjacking, breaking and entering, gun charges, and resisting arrest, according to court filings.

At the time of his death, King was free on bail for at least three separate felony cases, and had active warrants for his arrest, court records said.

O’Malley is seeking King’s mental health, criminal, and court records from all of his past cases, recordings from police body-worn and dash cameras, the medical examiner’s file on King, along with statements taken from O’Malley and witnesses at the scene of the shooting.

O’Malley told investigators that when he shot King, he feared for his own life and for the life of another officer on the scene, believing his colleague was about to be run over.

Police had pursued King after he allegedly committed a carjacking outside a pizza restaurant in Boston’s Mission Hill neighborhood. About 15 minutes later, officers stopped the stolen car less than a mile away, at Linwood Square in Roxbury.

The driver ignored “multiple verbal commands” as officers approached and tried to drive away, police said.

King opened the car window, but did not turn the vehicle off. O’Malley drew his Taser and shouted, “Bro, I’m going to [expletive] shoot you,” the police report said.

That’s when King backed into the cruiser behind him, then maneuvered the vehicle forward and back “in an attempt to escape the police,” according to the report.

As King started to drive forward again, O’Malley fired three shots through the driver’s window, striking King, the report said.

King’s family has contended that he was experiencing a mental health crisis in the hours leading up to the deadly encounter.

In court filings, O’Malley’s lawyer, Yannetti, said King gave “O’Malley no choice that night.”

“Any suggestion that this shooting was precipitated by simply a ‘mental health crisis’ completely misses the point,” Yannetti wrote. “When facing an extremely dangerous threat, there is no time for a police officer to hold a counseling session on the street or to sit down to discuss the feelings of a menace who is intent on using a motor vehicle as a deadly weapon.”

“If a man is going to assault and carjack an innocent woman, then threaten the lives and safety of the public and a police officer, that man needs to be stopped — whether he is in his right mind or not,” according to O’Malley’s motion.

O’Malley’s next court date, a probable-cause hearing, is scheduled for May 21.

title: Police arrest 16-year-old boy with a loaded gun leaving a school in Jamaica Plain
text:
Boston police arrested a 16-year-old boy with a loaded gun after he led officers on a chase in Jamaica Plain Tuesday afternoon, law enforcement officials said.

He was not identified because he is a minor. He is facing several juvenile deliquency charges.

The police department’s Youth Violence Strike Force had been investigating the teen and followed up on a lead indicating that he was armed and in the vicinity of Community Academy, a small alternative high school at 25 Glen Road, police said Wednesday.

School officials referred all inquiries to the Boston Police Department. It was unclear if the boy is a student at the school for students facing challenges or trauma, or who have had code of conduct violations, or involvement in the courts.

Officers saw the teen leave the school at 2:10 p.m. As the boy was walking through a driveway at 21 Glen Road, an officer saw him “adjusting his front waistband in a manner consistent with carrying a concealed firearm,” according to a statement from Boston police.

“The juvenile then lifted his hoodie, allowing the officer to clearly observe a semiautomatic firearm tucked into his waistband,” the statement said.

When police attempted to stop the teen, he grabbed his waistband with his right hand and ran away. The boy threw his backpack, and tossed the gun under an SUV stopped at the intersection of Washington Street and Glen Road, police said.

The teen jumped several Jersey barriers while fleeing from police. He was taken into custody at 3368 Washington St., police said.

Police recovered the handgun and identified it as Smith & Wesson SD9. It had one round in the chamber, and the magazine contained an additional live round, the police statement said.

The Massachusetts Department of Youth Services issued a detainer for the teen following his arrest, police said.

He will be arraigned in West Roxbury District Juvenile Court on four delinquency charges, possession of a gun without a license, carrying a loaded gun, possession of ammunition without a firearms possession card, and possession of a large-capacity feeding device.

title: Person shot four times in Roxbury, Boston’s fifth shooting in four days
text:
A person suffered four gunshot wounds Tuesday night in Roxbury, the day’s second shooting in Boston and the city’s fifth episode of gun violence since Saturday night, officials said.

Shortly after 10:15 p.m., officers were called to the area of 58 Cheney St. for a reported shooting, police said in a report.

Officers found a victim who had been shot twice in his left arm and twice on the left side of his chest, police said.

The redacted report contained no information about the victim’s age. His name was also redacted.

“The victim stated that he had been shot in the back,” the report said, adding that his car, a Mercedes Benz, was parked on nearby Maple Street.

He “indicated that while sitting inside his vehicle, he observed a black vehicle approaching his location and [an] unknown individual began shooting at him,” police said.

The victim “immediately attempted to run away from the shooter, at which time he was struck in the back by gunfire,” police said.

Authorities said the victim described the shooter as wearing a black sweatshirt but couldn’t get a “good look” at him.

“Officers removed the victim’s clothing to assess the gunshot wound and determine whether there were any additional injuries,” the report said.

The victim was taken to Boston Medical Center for “further evaluations,” police said.

His condition wasn’t immediately available Wednesday afternoon.

“Officers canvassed the area and observed the victim’s motor vehicle had sustained damages consistent with gunfire,” the report said. “Officers observed apparent bullet holes in the front of windshield, along with shattered glass on the roof of the vehicle.”

The attack followed an earlier shooting around 1:20 a.m. Tuesday in the area of 25 Dacia St. in Dorchester.

Officers canvassed the area for suspects, victims, and witnesses. They recovered shell casings and projectile fragments and saw ballistic damage to multiple structures and a nearby vehicle, officials said.

Police contacted residents at both 25 and 33 Dacia St. and found they were not hurt.

Police were later notified that a shooting victim had been taken to an area hospital, where they are currently listed in critical condition but expected to survive, police said. The victim wasn’t identified.

Tuesday’s shootings continued a spate of recent gun violence in Boston that included a fatality, police said.

On Saturday night, a person was shot in Mattapan and later died, police said. Authorities identified the man as Michael Jacob, 30, of Randolph.

Shortly after 2 a.m. on Sunday, two people were shot while riding motor scooters down Geneva Avenue in Dorchester, according to a police report.

Both victims sustained injuries that were not life-threatening, police said.

Also Sunday, a man and woman were shot on Kingsdale Street in Dorchester. The woman remained in critical condition Tuesday while the man suffered injuries that are not believed to be life-threatening, police said.

No arrests have been made in any of the five shootings, police said.

title: A report found the Blue Hill Avenue redesign would speed bus commutes but slow car traffic. It was never released.
text:
“In relocating bus operations to the center of the roadway, the proposed project will greatly improve the travel experience for bus riders,” the report concluded. “The anticipated increases in vehicle travel time will encourage drivers to consider other modes of transportation and will ultimately help the City of Boston reach their mode shift targets.”

It’s not unexpected that the redesign plan — which is not final — would add time for drivers while reducing waits for bus riders. But the analysis puts numbers to a neighborhood concern that has been roiling for years. The data would have been helpful to see before the numerous hearings and meetings held on the project over the last few months, public officials and activists said. Two city councilors and one state representative who have been closely involved in the project said they had not seen the analysis until the Globe shared it with them on Thursday; some officials were not even aware it was conducted.

“To have to get it from you, it’s amazing,” said City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, who alongside many of his constituents has been a vocal opponent of the center-running bus lane. “We didn’t even know it was in existence.”

“I can’t say” there was an effort to hide it, Culpepper added, but “I can certainly say there wasn’t an effort to make it public.”

In response to Globe questions, MBTA spokesperson Joe Pesaturo said Thursday that “highly technical work products such as this early analysis are not generally posted publicly.” He added that the MBTA is still working with city officials to improve the Blue Hill Avenue design “with the goal of minimizing traffic impacts as much as possible.”

For years, transit planners have been pitching a center-running bus lane along Blue Hill Avenue from Mattapan Square to Grove Hall, a design they say would free up the bus to move faster and allow for badly needed safety improvements while having minimal impact on drivers. But that plan has never proven popular in the surrounding neighborhoods. Communities along the avenue rejected a similar plan, called the 28X, in 2009.

For Mayor Michelle Wu, the Blue Hill Avenue project has become a political quagmire, particularly as a vocal segment of Black voters expresses disappointment with her tenure. Critics from Mattapan, Roxbury, and Dorchester worry it would slow traffic and hurt businesses along the corridor.

“No one is disputing that it would be a good idea if the 28 would go faster,” said Dianne Wilkerson, a former state senator who has been actively opposed to the project. “We just think that there are some other ways to do it, rather than destroying the entire economic underpinning of the avenue.”

Some, however, particularly young transit riders, say a faster bus would be life-changing, allowing them to get to work, school, and recreation more quickly. Transit activists say the corridor, which is home to some of the city’s most diverse neighborhoods, deserves faster and more reliable ways to get around.

“This is about equity,” said state Representative Russell Holmes, a Mattapan Democrat who supports redesigning the avenue. “The road has been designed primarily for car drivers. ... But you’re trying to balance 40,000 car drivers and 40,000 transit riders.”

He acknowledged there might be some “tradeoffs” in the plan, including slower commutes for drivers, but said he is advocating for a design that will preserve two traffic lanes in each direction to keep cars moving. Holmes said he was aware the report was being done but had not seen it until this week.

“What’s driving our decisions is data and not emotions,” he said. “The existing conditions are horrible.”

City Councilor Brian Worrell, who also had not seen the report until Thursday, said government officials should be “as transparent as possible.”

“The fact that they’re not releasing the traffic study is telling me that the traffic study’s not good,” Worrell said. “We don’t know the plan because you’re not releasing all the information.”

Both the city and the MBTA had the report in their possession; both provided the report to the Globe on Thursday in response to separate public record requests. The project “has been a joint effort of the MBTA and the City of Boston in terms of community engagement, key design elements and traffic impacts,” said Pesaturo, the T spokesperson. He said the analysis cost the MBTA approximately $300,000.

Marcela Dwork, a spokesperson for Wu, said the report — which was dated Aug. 29, 2025, and received by the city in December — was “not yet vetted” and emphasized that “the design will continue to evolve.”

She did not respond to questions about whether the mayor supports the center-running bus lane as currently designed. At a council hearing last month, city transportation officials sounded noncommittal about the project’s future and said they would meet with the MBTA to discuss next steps.

“The City supports investing needed resources to deliver the highest quality of life throughout every neighborhood,” Dwork said in a statement Thursday. “The Mayor is in regular contact with and working closely with [MBTA General Manager Phil Eng] to incorporate community concerns into design details and get this important project right for the people who rely on this corridor every day.”

title: Just how angry is Black Boston at Mayor Michelle Wu?
text:
But as a report by the Globe’s Niki Griswold detailed this week, a recent community meeting at Roxbury Community College was heavy on criticism of Wu on a range of issues confronting Black Boston — some current, some grievances years old.

Former state senator Dianne Wilkerson headlined the event last month billed as a challenge to hold Black elected officials “accountable” for failing to aggressively advocate for the community’s concerns. City Council members who support Wu were put on notice that they should expect contested elections, or worse, if they continue to support Wu’s agenda.

The list of complaints included longstanding criticism of the renovation of White Stadium, as well as more recent concerns like the proposed center bus lane on Blue Hill Avenue.

But high on the list was Wu’s supposed sabotage of Brian Worrell’s bid to become president of the City Council. Worrell would have been the council’s fourth black president. But the council’s progressive wing — Wu’s usual allies, including several former aides — lined up behind Councilor Gabriel Coletta Zapata and didn’t back Worrell, even after Coletta Zapata’s bid fell apart the day before the election.

The machinations behind council president elections are mostly inside baseball, and the last election was no exception. Still, the bitterness behind Worrell’s defeat has shown staying power.

But more interesting complaints are the ones playing in the background. That Wu isn’t receptive enough to community input. That her inner circle doesn’t include enough Black voices. And that Wu isn’t the mayor some in Black Boston wanted in the first place.

In an interview, Wu said she believes some of the criticism comes with leading a city confronting major issues.

“We’re in a complicated moment with big challenges, and we’re in a smart, engaged city where all the easy solutions have already been implemented,” she said.

“So the problems that are left have bigger and harder issues to sort through, and it’s up to us to have those hard conversations and choose the places where we are going to decide to press forward together, even if it means doing something differently.”

Certainly, some of the criticism is deserved. Wu and her team botched the decision to change direction of the development of Parcel 3 in Roxbury, abandoning a longstanding community-backed plan in favor of designating that land for a new Madison Park High School. Building a new Madison Park is a great idea that will have a huge community benefit, but surely there was a better, more inclusive, way to navigate the neighborhood politics of the decision.

It played into the perception that many of Wu’s decisions are imposed, rather than reached through consensus.

White Stadium is also viewed by Wu’s critics as a community project the community never asked for, driven by a professional women’s soccer team — though Wu insists the driving force was the desire to create a first-class athletic facility for Boston Public Schools students (when they can use it).

Does the neighborhood really oppose it? Wu carried every precinct that borders Franklin Park, mostly by wide margins. If this project is so unpopular, why didn’t it have any traction as a campaign issue?

For some people, the biggest issue with Wu is one they are reluctant to air publicly: that they believe Boston’s first elected mayor of color should have been Black. Her supposed lack of responsiveness is especially galling, critics whisper, because there should be more solidarity.

I would argue Wu should be measured by what she does, especially as her second term unfolds. If her administration can deliver on its promises to spur development in Roxbury, improve the schools, and continue to drive down crime, that will be a great record on the issues that matter in Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan.

And in that sense, it’s good to know that Wu’s critics have no plans to stop pushing her. Landslide victories have been known to breed complacency. That’s something Black Boston rightly has no time for.

title: Teenager charged in double shooting in Dorchester ordered held without bail
text:
An 18-year-old was ordered held without bail after his arrest in connection with a double shooting in Dorchester on Sunday that left a man and woman wounded.

On Wednesday, police arrested Jaynell Sumler, of Dorchester, on two charges of assault to murder, and single charges for unlawful possession of a firearm and ammunition and discharging a firearm striking a building, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said Thursday.

Prosecutors allege that Sumler was inside 69 Kingsdale St. in Dorchester around 6:45 p.m. on Sunday when he shot a 42-year-old woman in the head. He then allegedly shot a 42-year-old man in the arm and leg, prosecutors said.

Witnesses identified Sumler, the boyfriend of the woman’s daughter, as the shooter, prosecutors said.

The woman remained at a local hospital on Thursday with life-threatening injuries, police said. The man’s injuries were not life-threatening, officials said.

Sumler was arraigned in Dorchester District Court on Thursday and ordered held without bail pending a dangerousness hearing on May 21, officials said.

“As if this set of facts isn’t tragic enough, the reality of these victims being shot on Mother’s Day adds another level of shock and sadness,” Hayden said. “I pray for the recovery of both victims and I believe a dangerousness hearing is perfectly appropriate in this act of terrible violence.”

Wednesday’s arrest marks the first apprehension in a series of shootings over the weekend. Across four days beginning Saturday, there were five shootings in Boston — three in Dorchester, one in Roxbury, and one in Mattapan.

The Mattapan shooting was fatal, killing Michael Jacob, 30, of Randolph.

That death increased the number of fatal shootings in Boston this year to two, compared with six at this time last year, according to police crime data.

title: ‘I am hoping some of those genes get passed down.’ Five residents of West Roxbury nursing home celebrate century of life
text:
Wearing a military cap, Lusardi, who served as an Army medic on Okinawa Island during World War II, sat at the table with his daughter and niece.

“He never bragged about it, he is just a great family guy,” said his daughter, Ann Hadayia, 65. “He is a hard worker, he never complained, always willing to help people, just everything that makes you live to 103.”

Hadayia and her cousin, Diane Butler, 73, joked that it was probably all the “red wine and salami” that helped Lusardi live so long.

For DeSantis, a longtime member of the Brookline Garden Club, it’s her love for gardening that “always kept her mind sharp,” her grandson, Nicolas DeSantis, said.

“She would always be going and doing stuff,” said DeSantis, 51. “It’s like mind over matter. It just overcomes your body. I am hoping some of those genes get passed down.”

State Senator Mike Rush, State Representative William MacGregor, and Emily Shea, head of the city’s Age Strong Commission, handed out citations to the residents for reaching the century milestone.

In Massachusetts, about 1 out of 3,000 people are 100 years or older, meaning there are around 2,200 centenarians living in the state, according to Dr. Thomas Perls, a geriatrician and director of the New England Centenarian Study at Boston University.

The right combination of genes plays an important role in longevity and becomes more important the older you get, Perls said.

“Interestingly, it isn’t really lacking genes that are associated with age-related diseases, but rather protective genes that slow down aging and decrease your risk for age-related diseases,” Perls said. “That’s not to say that some habits don’t play a strong role, for example, finding a centenarian who has a history of smoking is extraordinarily rare.”

Massachusetts residents have a much better chance of living to 100 than those in other parts of the country, thanks to better health care, education, and overall socioeconomic conditions, he said. But within that success are enormous disparities.

“Average life expectancy in Back Bay is 93, and you go three miles southeast to Dorchester, and it’s 26 years less,” Perls said. “I attribute that to structural and systemic racism, and all the things that go along with that in terms of determinants of aging-related diseases and disability.”

While some people might not want to live so long, assuming their health will be in decline at that age, getting older is worth celebrating, Perls said.

“Instead of it being the older you get, the sicker you get, I think it’s much more the case of the older you get, the healthier you’ve been,” Perls said. “I think it’s a very optimistic and enabling point of view about aging.”

Ng’s daughter, Jennie Ng, a real estate broker, said her father’s mind has faded over time. But there are still moments when he remembers the things that mattered most to him. Before entering the skilled nursing unit, Ng, a former owner of a Chinese restaurant, loved to swim and walk his dog.

“He is very kind and caring,” she said. “Sometimes seeing outside the grounds of the German Centre will remind him of his dog. He will say ‘Oh, Lucky is coming.’”

title: Roxbury Community College celebrates 50th commencement
text:
“Over 50 years ago, this campus rose from land once intended to divide a community,” Jonathan Jefferson president of the college, told the crowd, referring to the expressway that was originally meant to be built on the land but was halted because of community activism. “Today, it does just the opposite. It connects, uplifts, and transforms.”

The commencement, the second of Jefferson’s tenure, seemed to indicate the school appeared to be recovering from some of the problems that marked his predecessors’ terms and returning to its mission of supporting students through challenges both in and out of the classroom. In addition to having its largest number of graduates since 2019, Jefferson said nearly three-quarters of the graduating class earned honors, while more than 70 percent planned to either transfer to a four-year university or enter the workforce immediately.

Christelle Jean Louis, 27, who graduated with degrees in biological science and laboratory animal care, called Jefferson “a blessing for the school.” Other graduates spoke about how the college allowed them to accomplish their goals of earning a higher education degree later in life or preparing them for a four-year school.

Louis, a first-generation college student from Haiti who plans to transfer to Simmons University to pursue a nursing degree, credited tutoring services, advising, and campus resources with helping her succeed. She had always wanted to attend college but was unsure if she would ever get the opportunity.

“It’s a dream come true,” Louis said.

Hanuel Corbitt Jr., 20, who majored in health careers while also being a member of the college’s basketball team, said balancing athletics and academics required discipline and sacrifice.

“There were times where I had to sacrifice extra workouts for studying,” Corbitt, who maintained a 4.0 GPA throughout his time in college, said. “It was definitely strenuous, but it was worth it.”

Roxbury Community College was opened in the ’70s after years of activism by local community members to provide higher education to the Roxbury community. It was recognized as a Predominantly Black Institution by the US Department of Education in 2021.

Jefferson described the school as “a true highway for economic mobility,” and highlighted programs such as RCC Connect, a centralized one-stop shop for student services, along with workforce training opportunities and the school’s food pantry, known as the Rox Box, which helps students stay enrolled and to graduate despite financial and personal hardships.

“These are not just programs, these are your struggle,” he said. “They are part of the reason that you are here today, and they reflect a broader commitment to ensure that every student has the support they need.”

Suzanne Walsh, the commencement speaker and the president of City University in Seattle, talked about her failures in college and in her career and encouraged students to embrace uncertainty. She described the modern world as volatile, uncertain, and ambiguous, and argued that Roxbury Community College students were uniquely prepared to navigate those challenges.

“You are more than resilient,” Walsh said. “You are anti-fragile. You are uniquely ready to give back to your family, to your friends, and to your community.”

For many families in attendance, the ceremony represented generations of sacrifice and support.

Minister Brenda Womack, 72, attended to celebrate her niece, Zandra Banks, a Roxbury resident who earned her liberal arts degree after years of stopping and restarting college because of financial struggles and family responsibilities.

“She’s showing us that it’s never too late,” Womack said. “Once you set your mind to it, stay focused, you can achieve it.”

Banks, who is in her late 50s, paused her own education while raising her son, who graduated with a bachelor’s degree in business administration. Now, Womack said, he is supporting his mother as she reaches her own milestone.

Brandon Kelly, 32, attended the ceremony to celebrate his wife, Dawntayia Kelly, 31, who graduated with high honors in criminal justice while raising two young children. She is pursuing a career as a corrections officer.

“Whatever she needed, whatever I had to do, we got it done,” Kelly said, while wearing a “Proud husband of the class of 2026″ T-shirt. “That way, she’d be able to be here two years later.”

title: Don Mattingly settles into unexpected role as an interim manager, and the Phillies are better for having him
text:
“But I was here in 2004, too. That memory is not a great one,” he said, recalling his days as hitting coach of the Yankees when they couldn’t finish off the Red Sox in the American League Championship Series.

Mattingly didn’t join the Phillies as bench coach in January with any expectation of becoming their manager. Rob Thomson, who had the job, is one of his best friends in baseball.

His only aim was to offer advice to Thomson when needed and spend more time with two of his sons. Preston, 38, is Philadelphia’s general manager under president of baseball operations Dave Dombrowski. His youngest, 11-year-old Louie, also loves being around the game.

Then Thomson was fired late last month after a 9-19 start, and now Mattingly is managing again for the first time since he was with the Dodgers and Marlins from 2011-22.

“I’m enjoying it,” he said. “As a player, at the end of my career, it’s something that I felt like I wanted to do. The way it happened is not something you want, right?”

The Phillies started 12-4 under Mattingly and are working back into contention.

The schedule helped. After Mattingly took over, the Phillies played the Giants, Marlins, Athletics, Rockies, and Red Sox and won all five series. They had played their previous 13 games against the Braves and Cubs, winning twice.

The Phillies, who are loaded with lefthanded hitters, also faced righthanded starters in 12 of Mattingly’s first 16 games.

“Our guys are playing better now than they were before,” said Phillies major league field coordinator Mike Calitri, a Canton native. “I think we’ll be battling for something. There’s some excitement because we’re all going in the same direction.”

It helps that Mattingly’s stature as a player resonates in a clubhouse that includes Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber, Trea Turner, Zack Wheeler, and other stars.

“When they make the decision to make the change, you look at Donnie and the resume, that he played at such a high level and managed some good teams,” Schwarber said. “He knows what it takes. There were no drastic changes in what we’re doing. We know the group we have and what we’re capable of. We needed to start playing better, no matter who the manager was.

“But with him at the helm and having trust in us, there’s going to be some different things we’re going to try to do. There’s a lot of trust in him, and he has trust in us.”

Mattingly played 14 seasons in the majors, all for the Yankees, and has coached or managed at the highest level since 2004. He has yet to earn a World Series ring. This season may represent his last, best chance.

“I feel fairly comfortable,” Mattingly said. “Early on, it felt fast. Since then, it’s been pretty good. It helps when we’re winning. I’m glad to be in this seat.”

Pardon my cynicism, but it was refreshing — and a bit surprising — to hear interim Red Sox manager Chad Tracy say last week that he decides the lineup, not the front office.

“The final pen to paper is my call,” he said.

Tracy said he generally sits with bench coach José David Flores to come up with the lineup.

“I get ideas and hear other people’s thoughts about where will be a good day [to use] this guy or that guy,” he said. “That will always be the case. I have really good people around me that I trust to cover your blind spots.”

It can’t be easy. The Sox went into the weekend with the worst offense in the American League, a product of their lack of power and poor seasons from, among others, Caleb Durbin, Jarren Duran, Carlos Narváez, and Trevor Story.

Tracy had seven-plus years of experience managing in the minors before he was promoted. He said the level of information in the major leagues is far deeper, and there’s more video to use when making decisions.

“Similar information but a much wider [range] of what is actually available to you,” he said.

Minor league lineups are focused on development, not necessarily winning games.

“In the minor leagues, the construction of a lineup is who’s on the 40-man [roster] that’s immediately going to help us? Who are the top prospects that we need to see get in the batter’s box a lot?

“A guy hitting first vs. sixth could be the difference of 100 plate appearances in a year. All of that stuff is considered for getting guys the reps they need; making sure that 40-man guys who are going to come up the next day are ready to go.”

A few other observations on the Red Sox:

▪ Speaking of the lineup, how long do the Sox keep Duran batting leadoff? He has a .304 on-base percentage batting first over the last two seasons, with 100 more strikeouts (142) than walks (42).

That’s a 127-game sample size, too.

▪ Wilyer Abreu is off to a start that could merit down-ballot MVP votes.

The 27-year-old right fielder has a team-best .860 OPS and leads all American League outfielders with 11 defensive runs saved. Only Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong (13) has more.

Abreu won his second Gold Glove last season and has been even better this year.

“It’s hard to believe because he was so good before,” Tracy said. “Balls get hit, and it looks like he’s already taken four steps by the time you glance at him.

“He’s moving before the ball even comes off the bat. He’s just become very, very good.”

▪ You may have noticed Sox players on second base seeming to signal the batter what pitch is coming. With PitchCom, there are no signs to steal, but some pitchers give it away by how they waggle their gloves or if they show their grip too early.

That said, the Sox are mostly pretending, according to several opposing teams.

“Some of it’s real, and some of it’s just to make you think they know something,” Mattingly said. “We saw a lot of the same [signals] on different pitches, so it tells you they didn’t really have anything.”

▪ If the Sox wanted to fire Jason Varitek as game planning and run prevention coach, fine. That’s their right. Varitek was traded as a prospect and became a part-time player at the end of his playing career. He understands how the game works.

But the Sox claimed, “he has been reassigned to a new role within the organization.” Was that supposed to mollify the fans who have fond memories of Varitek from his playing days?

That wasn’t true. Like manager Alex Cora and the rest of the coaches who were fired, Varitek is a free agent and can join another team if he chooses.

In a NESN appearance, chief baseball officer Craig Breslow said Varitek has an “open invitation to stay in the organization as long as he wants.”

It would be out of character for Varitek to take some phony job and pretend all is well. If he wants to stay in baseball, there are teams that would value what he has to offer.

▪ Baseball America’s latest top prospect list has lefthander Payton Tolle eighth, with Double-A shortstop Franklin Arias soaring from 46th to 16th. Arias had a 1.072 OPS through his first 29 games this season.

(Yes, Tolle is still considered a prospect, but won’t be much longer.)

Two righthanders drafted last season — Anthony Eyanson (No. 48) and Kyson Witherspoon (73) — also made the list.

Three New England players are in the Top 100. Marlins Triple-A lefthander Thomas White (Rowley, Phillips Andover) is 11th. Dodgers High-A outfielder Mike Sirota (Northeastern) is 40th, and Cardinals Triple-A outfielder Joshua Baez (Boston, Dexter Southfield) is 57th.

Sirota was considered a potential first-round pick going into his junior season with the Huskies, but fell to the Reds in the third round of the 2024 draft. The Dodgers acquired him in a trade for infielder Gavin Lux prior to the 2025 season. He has since posted a 1.091 OPS in 89 games for the Dodgers.

Ryan Flynn is a baseball evangelist, bringing the game to places such as Australia, Guam, and New Zealand, undeterred by any obstacles.

He arrived in New Zealand in 2009 and helped build the national team to the point where it fell a game short of qualifying for the 2013 World Baseball Classic.

“It would have been one of the greatest upsets in baseball history had we advanced,” Flynn said.

Now he has taken on another big challenge: building up the baseball culture in Ireland.

Flynn was named chief executive officer of Baseball Ireland earlier this month. He is tasked with growing a grassroots program from the tee-ball level up while finding or developing players for the national team.

There are eight baseball clubs in Ireland, home to about 500 players. Gaelic football, soccer, hurling, rugby, and a few other sports are far more popular.

“That’s the kind of challenge I like,” Flynn said. “I want to go head-to-head and go after the best athletes and show a vision for the future.”

Beyond his Irish roots, the 55-year-old Flynn has an eclectic background that makes him a perfect fit for the job. He was born in upstate New York and played third base for St. Rose College. He has since visited 80-plus countries and lived in England, Hungary, the Netherlands, New Zealand, and Palau, a small island nation in the Pacific.

Flynn has a playbook for fundraising, building awareness, and engaging people. He has already spoken to Yankees general manager Brian Cashman and scheduled a meeting with Red Sox team president Sam Kennedy, among others.

“You have to work with the diaspora and raise awareness,” Flynn said.

Italy offers an example of what is possible. The Azzurri beat the United States in pool play during this year’s WBC, then knocked off Puerto Rico in the quarterfinals before losing 4-2 to Venezuela in the semifinals.

Most of Italy’s players were major leaguers of Italian heritage. But there were three natives on the roster, and baseball gained previously unprecedented attention in the country.

“Why can’t Ireland do that?” Flynn said. “The WBC had a huge impact in Italy in terms of interest in baseball.”

There have been 48 major leaguers born in Ireland, most of whom played in the late 1800s and early 1900s. The last was righthander Joe Cleary, who was born in Cork and raised in New York City. He appeared in one game for the 1945 Senators and allowed seven runs in one-third of an inning against the Red Sox at Washington’s Griffith Stadium.

If there’s a next one, it could be a player Flynn helps to discover.

The large Irish community in the Boston area could be a resource for Baseball Ireland, and Flynn is eager to hear from would-be supporters. Contact him at rflynn@baseballireland.com.

This is amazing. The Dodgers and Giants have played 2,602 times, going back to 1890. The Giants lead the series 1,292-1,291 with 19 ties … Good statistic from Mark Zuckerman of Nats Journal: The Nationals have lost 15 consecutive games when having a chance to get to .500. They beat the White Sox, 6-3, on May 14, 2024, to improve to 20-20, then lost the second game of a doubleheader. The Giants’ first baseman/DH is back to hammering pitches on the outside corner and using the whole field … Cal Raleigh is having a rough season. Despite all that time away, McClanahan is 4-2 with a 2.27 ERA through eight starts this season, and his four-seam fastball has approached 98 m.p.h. “I think that’s kind of what a lot of us thought was, it’s just going to take a little bit of time,” Tampa Bay manager Kevin Cash said. “We’re a month and a half in, pushing two months, and he’s definitely [going] in the right direction.” … Alex Verdugo, who has not appeared in a major league game since last July 1 with the Braves, is facing yet another career crossroads. The 30-year-old outfielder was released from his minor league contract with the Padres without having played a game and is expected to undergo season-ending shoulder surgery. Valenzuela had an incredible five shutouts in his first seven starts en route to winning the Cy Young Award and Rookie of the Year that season … No. 23 Boston College is playing for seeding in the NCAA Tournament, which would be its first since 2023. UConn, Yale, and Holy Cross are well-positioned to win their respective conference tournaments and claim automatic bids. Northeastern, which has made the tournament three times in the last five seasons, will likely have to get by Campbell in the CAA. The NCAA field will be announced on May 25 … Happy birthday to Brayan Bello, who is 27. The Red Sox righthander first joined the organization in 2017 when he was 18. Bello was one of 78 players who appeared in the Dominican Summer League for the Sox in 2018. Only he and center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela made it to the majors. title: Boston police Commissioner Cox: Cambridge shooter sentence ‘does not match the seriousness of the offense’
text:
“It doesn’t seem like the sentence matches the seriousness of the offense in any way, shape, or form,” Cox said Sunday. “Now the person comes out and almost does the exact same thing with a bigger gun and more bullets. It is troubling and the lack of accountability around that.”

Cox, who was not the Boston police commissioner in 2020, stopped short of directly criticizing the judge or parole authorities involved in the earlier case but repeatedly questioned whether the criminal justice system had adequately addressed the danger Brown posed.

“My job is not to criticize other people in their roles,” Cox said. “I don’t know all the factors that were considered, but clearly this person was really willing and able to offend again, and it didn’t really take long.”

The commissioner, who said he has been shot at before, described the emotional toll such cases take on police officers, particularly when suspects accused of violent crimes are later released and allegedly reoffend.

“It is disheartening,” Cox said. “You feel as though I’m putting my life on the line for what, when this person can get out pretty easily.”

On Monday, Brown’s alleged attack sent motorists fleeing from their cars and triggered a chaotic police response near Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Prosecutors say Brown fired 50 to 60 rounds from an “assault-style” rifle into traffic, striking two bystanders, before he was shot and apprehended by a Massachusetts State Police trooper assisted by an armed former Marine.

Brown pleaded not guilty Thursday from his hospital bed on video conference. He appeared heavily medicated during his arraignment. Officials said he was shot in the “lower extremities.”

Authorities said he had been reported suicidal and armed shortly before the shooting began. Brown, who suffered from mental health problems, was recently released from a psychiatric hospital and was reportedly using crack cocaine, according to court documents.

Cox said the Memorial Drive attack was “extremely scary” and praised both the responding troopers and the civilian who intervened.

“It’s a nightmare for the community, it’s a nightmare for law enforcement that has to respond to that as an active shooter,” he said.

The Memorial Drive shootout occurred during a recent spate of shootings in Roxbury, Mattapan, and Dorchester. Five shootings in just several days, including one fatal attack.

Cox defended the city’s public safety record while acknowledging public concern, maintaining that Boston remains among the nation’s safest large cities.

“Any act of violence is too many,” Cox said. “But our city is a safe city... sometimes we have a rush of things that happen, and then we do what we can and hold those folks accountable.”

Cox said Boston police have already made arrests in two of the recent shooting cases and are continuing efforts to identify and prosecute those responsible.

During Sunday’s interview, Cox also defended the department’s body camera policy, which received public criticism after Officer Nicholas O’Malley shot and killed a suspect in a carjacking in March. Under the current policy, bodycam footage is subject to public records laws but is exempt from release during an active investigation.

O’Malley was charged over the fatal on-duty shooting, meaning bodycam footage of the incident is not available to the public. He is the first officer charged with shooting and killing a suspect on duty in more than 30 years.

Some police departments across the country have adopted timelines requiring footage to be released within 30, 60, or 90 days, regardless of the status of an investigation. But Cox said those policies often contain exceptions that ultimately allow departments to withhold video anyway.

“There are certain things I think that we should do in the future, as far as transparency, as far as making sure people understand what our investigative processes are,” he said. “Putting things on the website so people can know what happens when someone is involved in a shooting, things of that nature, which we’re working on.”

O’Malley has pleaded not guilty to manslaughter for the death of Stephenson King, 39, who allegedly tried to flee a traffic stop in a stolen car.

title: Farewell and welcome: Boston College celebrates historic 150th commencement, the first for new Messina College
text:
More than 4,400 undergraduates and graduate students dressed in black caps and gowns and multicolored hoods and cords celebrated with cheers and big waves for their family and friends seated in the stands.

“You Boston College graduates of 2026 are more needed than ever,” said Leahy, who did not mention his planned retirement in his short remarks. “I pray that you strive to be forces for good and powerful examples for those around you, and that you bear fruit that will last.”

Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Holy See’s foreign minister, encouraged graduates to work for justice, promote dialogue, and never forget the poor and marginalized.

“Human dignity is granted or ceded, be it by the state, or government, or even popular consensus,” said Gallagher, a native of Liverpool, noting the 250th anniversary of the Declaration of Independence. “But rather arises from truths about the human person that precede all those things.”

He referenced the writings of theologian John Henry Newman, emphasizing the importance of community and human connection in education. Gallagher said Newman believed universities were shaped not only by classrooms and lectures, but also by relationships students build with one another.

“I would like to dwell briefly on the three verbs Newman highlighted: to respect, to consult, and to aid,” he said.

Gallagher and five others received honorary degrees from BC, the nation’s seventh-largest Catholic university.

After the ceremony, students retreated to other parts of campus to receive diplomas from their individual colleges, including arts and sciences, business, education, nursing and theology.

“We’re walking with all our friends in the sunshine, and that’s what BC has felt like for me,” said Charlotte Caine, 22, who received a degree in English and classics. “I’d like to continue feeling that way.”

Zaria Carter, a 21-year-old math major, teaches third- and fourth-graders at a local school and plans to continue doing so. She said a few years ago, she would have said she wanted to be an accountant, but she discovered a different path at BC.

“I’m really excited about the thought of being a teacher, and I was never really excited about being an accountant,” she said while walking to the ceremony. “BC has taught me to follow what makes me excited and passionate.”

The pride and emotion of the day extended to faculty and family.

“Today’s our 150th commencement ceremony, and so our [Messina College] students are part of that long, proud legacy,” said Thomas Wesner, a professor of business law who taught at Messina College.

Stefano DeZerega flew from San Francisco to watch his son, Nico Tomlinson DeZerega, get his bachelor’s degree in economics.

“I’m really grateful for all the experiences he had,” DeZerega said. “It’s a moment of optimism and exploration. I am very proud.”

Nancy Beltran was a proud aunt, there to see her niece, Katy Elena Meza, graduate with a nursing degree.

“She is the first grandchild in the family who is graduating,” Beltran said as she sat with their entire family. “We are all immigrants from Honduras, and honestly, I think we’re just very proud.”

About 100 Messina College graduates were welcomed into the BC alumni ranks during a ceremony on its campus in Brookline.

“Not many people can say that they were the first for their class,” said student speaker Truns-Winslie Paul. “We created a community where there wasn’t one yet, and we made it our own.”

Family members clutched balloons and cheered as students walked across the stage to collect their degrees.

About 40 students who earned a 3.4 grade point average or better will continue at BC for bachelor’s degrees. Others will head off to one of six colleges with which Messina has enrollment agreements: Bryant University in Rhode Island, Endicott College, Regis College, the University of Massachusetts-Boston, Worcester State University, and Albertus Magnus College in Connecticut.

Students took pride in being the first graduates of a program still finding its footing.

“We were the first class,” said Jose Builes Lemus, 19, a data science major who is from Colombia. “We were building everything together.”

Lemus, who is continuing at BC, said coming to the United States three years ago and entering a brand-new program was intimidating. But students learned to advocate to address some logistical challenges, such as transportation and campus resources, he said.

“Being able to help others that are coming behind me,” he said, “that was a good part of it.”

Brianna Amado, who graduated with an associate degree in applied psychology, said that they’re “setting the tone” for the upcoming classes.

“I’m happy to move on to bigger and better things,” said Amado, who will continue her education in psychology at the University of Massachusetts Boston.

Other Messina graduates reflected on how much they had changed since they first arrived on campus.

For Hodan Ahmed, a 20-year-old who will continue her education at BC’s nursing school, balancing demanding coursework with summer classes tested her.

“This semester specifically was really difficult for me,” Ahmed, who is from Roxbury. “But I have professors who were genuinely willing to help me outside of class time.”

Families who attended the ceremony at Alumni Stadium and at Messina are excited for their students’ future educational journey.

“They’re very excited,” Ahmed said about her family sitting in the stadium. “They’re really proud of me, which I see as obviously an accomplishment.”

Family meant everything to Ryan Pina Gonzalez, who graduated with a business degree.

“Without them I’m nothing, so it’s amazing having them here,” Pina Gonzalez said as he stood surrounded by his family after graduation.

“I’m so proud of him,” added his sister, Gianna Pina Gonzalez, “because I know how hard he’s worked to get to this point.”

Correction: Due to incorrect information from BC, an earlier version of this story incorrectly stated the name of Bryant University. The Globe regrets the error.

title: In a rare rebuke, Governor Healey’s latest Parole Board pick faces uphill battle
text:
In an interview on Saturday, Councilor Christopher A. Iannella Jr., of Boston, said DeMore’s nomination wasn’t put to a vote because he didn’t have enough support for confirmation. Nominees need a majority of the eight elected councilors, though Healey can tap Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll to break a tie.

Iannella said he opposes DeMore’s nomination, saying he’d prefer a nominee with expertise in mental health and substance abuse.

Councilor Paul DePalo of Worcester said Tuesday he would also vote against DeMore because he lacks expertise to evaluate whether a prisoner would be a good fit for parole.

Councilor Tara Jacobs, who represents Western Massachusetts, told State House News Service she would vote against DeMore and hoped Healey, a Democrat, would withdraw the nomination.

Yet Healey held firm, and then last week Tyler E. Brown IV, a parolee, allegedly shot and wounded motorists on Memorial Drive. The violence triggered fresh scrutiny of the Parole Board and harsh criticism of its performance from the state Republican Party and two GOP gubernatorial candidates hoping to unseat Healey in November.

When the Governor’s Council reconvenes on Wednesday, councilors voting on DeMore’s nomination will have to weigh unusually vocal opposition to his candidacy alongside public alarm over parole decisions at levels not seen since a parolee shot and killed a veteran Woburn police officer in 2010.

Late Monday, Healey’s office sent a letter to the Governor’s Council urging it to confirm DeMore’s nomination, saying it’s important that the Parole Board has diverse representation.

“It is imperative that — in all its functions — the Parole Board carefully evaluate the requests of its incarcerated individuals, the voices of victims and their family members, and public safety,” the letter reads.

DeMore is a cofounder and defense attorney at Henning Strategies, a Boston law firm, and a former prosecutor for the Suffolk district attorney’s office. He serves as a US Army Reserve captain who represents crime victims in the Judge Advocate General Corps. Reached Friday for comment, DeMore referred the Globe to Healey’s office.

The Parole Board has had a vacancy since last September when Tonomey Coleman, the panel’s acting leader, was nominated for a District Court judgeship.

The other Parole Board members confirmed for five-year terms during Healey’s tenure are Angelo Gomez Jr., a former parole supervisor who took charge of the panel in October; Rafael Ortiz and Edith J. Alexander, both former probation officers; and Sarah B. Coughlin, a licensed clinical social worker.

Healey also renominated Charlene Bonner, a forensic psychologist who joined the board in 2011 and was confirmed for a fourth term in 2023. Her credentials satisfy a state requirement adopted by the Legislature in 2014 that the board have at least one member with “experience in forensic psychology.”

Board members hold thousands of parole hearings annually, mostly in state prisons and county jails, and parole officers supervised nearly 3,000 people in 2024, the latest data available.

The institutional hearings resulted in votes for release for two-thirds of applicants from 2021 to last year, board figures show.

In 2024, the board’s workload grew significantly after the state Supreme Judicial Court banned life without parole for people who were convicted of crimes they committed when they were between the ages of 18 and 20.

Overnight, 210 offenders became eligible for parole for the first time, leading to closely watched hearings as people sentenced to life terms as far back as the 1960s lined up seeking release.

The board has issued decisions in 89 of those cases and granted parole to 65, or 73 percent, according to figures tracked by the Globe.

The parole rate between 2021 and last year for people serving life sentences was 59 percent, though the figures exclude six pending cases from 2025, the board said.

At DeMore’s hearing last month, six people, including a social worker and parole lawyer, testified against his nomination, arguing his prosecutorial background is at odds with the panel’s mandate to decide whether offenders have rehabilitated themselves and can safely rejoin the community.

More than 400 people have signed a letter urging the Governor’s Council to vote against DeMore, opponents said.

Among DeMore’s detractors is Stacey Borden, founder of New Beginnings Reentry Services, Inc. in Roxbury.

In an interview Saturday, Borden said the Parole Board needs a member who was previously incarcerated to provide more balance and insight into what parole candidates face.

She also took exception to DeMore’s testimony that his prosecution work was not a law enforcement role.

“The DA is absolutely law enforcement,” said Borden, who testified against DeMore’s nomination at his hearing.

Borden ran unsuccessfully in 2024 for the Governor’s Council, sharing her story about serving prison time for drug and financial crimes, and later earning a master’s degree.

“We do not need another punitive law enforcement person sitting on the Parole Board,” Borden said.

A former prosecutor hasn’t served on the Parole Board since 2022 when Gloriann Moroney resigned and became a District Court judge, Healey’s office said.

DeMore told the Governor’s Council that as a prosecutor, he worked in juvenile courts and collaborated with community partners to reach just outcomes for people with mental illness who were accused of crimes.

He highlighted his role in litigation before the SJC that led to the dismissal of more than 21,000 cases tainted by disgraced chemist Annie Dookhan. He also noted his work addressing drunken driving prosecutions undermined by unreliable breath tests.

“Service on the Parole Board represents an opportunity to use my diverse experience and marshal the many voices I’ve heard through the years to positively impact my community and to continue to lead with empathy and respect,” DeMore told the council.

A retired state judge and a formerly incarcerated person who now runs substance abuse and mental health programs for the city of Chelsea testified in support of DeMore.

Councilors Terrence W. Kennedy, of Lynnfield, and Tamisha Civil said they intend to vote for DeMore.

In the case of Brown, the alleged Memorial Drive shooter, Kennedy said DeMore might have scrutinized his parole request more closely.

“I fully support the governor in terms of not withdrawing the nomination. I think that would be a shame,” he said.

Councilor Mara Dolan, of Concord, said in an interview that “public safety must come first” but declined to comment on how she would vote on DeMore.

“When it can cost over $200,000 a year to keep someone in jail, we must be careful not to err on the other side and keep people in custody who do not pose a danger and have paid their debt to society,” she said.

Liam Lowney, executive director of the Massachusetts Office for Victim Assistance, said the Parole Board would benefit from a member well-versed in survivors’ experiences, though he said neither he nor his agency is taking a position on DeMore’s nomination.

title: How Boston’s World Cup organizers blew a sponsorship deal with Airbnb
text:
And if you’d like to subscribe to Power Play, please click here.

Featuring: Carlos Bueno, Martha Sheridan, Maura Healey, John Barros, Rose Staram, Jon Hurst, Robert Eugene, Jimmy Liang, Biplaw Rai, Douglass Williams, Jason Furman, Matt George, and more.

Here’s another tale about the gang that can’t shoot straight: Our vaunted World Cup host committee, Boston 26.

Last summer officials from Airbnb met with Boston 26 about sponsoring World Cup festivities as soccer fans descend upon the region for seven games this summer. The short-term rental giant, which is an official FIFA partner, had set aside $5 million to spend on World Cup programming at 16 host cities in North America.

On the same Zoom call, Airbnb brought up something they’re hoping to see happen in host cities: Relaxing short-term-rental regulations during the World Cup, to make it easier for people to rent out their homes, or what’s known as a special event exemption.

The meeting put Boston 26 on edge and they didn’t pursue a deal with Airbnb, for reasons that fairly sum up why local World Cup organizers can’t seem to get out of their own way.

According to a person knowledgeable about the call, the rationale went something like this: No way we’re approaching Mayor Michelle Wu. She was in the midst of a re-election fight against Josh Kraft, son of Robert Kraft, the driving force behind bringing the World Cup to Boston. Asking her to do a favor to help the World Cup? Awkward. Not only that, Wu, back when she was a city councilor, was the lead author of the short-term rental rules that Airbnb wanted to relax.

Then there was Meet Boston. The tourism agency is one of Boston 26’s biggest funders, and is itself largely funded by taxes on Boston and Cambridge hotels. Those hotels see Airbnb as a major competitor, and while Meet Boston CEO Martha Sheridan has touted the World Cup as an economic boom for the region, she presumably wants that boom to flow to hotels, not Airbnb hosts.

Moreover, at the time, Boston 26 was focused on securing seven-figure sponsorships. So its leaders, according to a person familiar with their thinking, decided it wasn’t worth alienating key allies for a slice of $5 million from Airbnb.

But Airbnb is keen on raising its profile this summer because soccer fans need a place to stay. Of the 164,000 tourists projected to visit Boston for the tournament, about 17,000 will stay in short-term rentals, according to a Deloitte study the company commissioned. Add in the nation’s 250th birthday on July 4, and Sail Boston’s parade of tall ships, and it’s shaping up to be a big summer.

In other words, Boston had leverage. And other cities, including New York, turned down Airbnb’s request to change their rules, yet still got Airbnb’s money for World Cup events.

It’s my understanding that Boston 26 did not think it was incumbent upon them to come up with a deal that would work for all involved. Meanwhile Airbnb was confounded by Boston 26’s tepid response, and moved on.

In the months since, Boston 26 has struggled with fundraising, securing a little more than $20 million in private donations from just a handful of companies.

Airbnb, meanwhile, has been delivering gifts to host cities like Santa Claus: more than $1.2 million to refurbish soccer pitches in San Francisco, Los Angeles, and Oakland, over $1 million for festivals and fields in New York and New Jersey, and over $1 million to Houston to expand green infrastructure and increase youth access to soccer. Philadelphia cleverly used Airbnb money to fund free subway rides home from its games (compare that with the $80 round-trip gameday fare on the commuter rail between South Station and Foxborough).

Airbnb even sent $250,000 to Rhode Island to help fund a summer of soccer celebrations. With Gillette Stadium about as close to Providence as it is to Boston, Ocean State 26 organizers gladly took Airbnb’s money.

Airbnb’s largesse makes me wonder if the company would take another look at supporting Boston’s World Cup festivities. After all, co-founder Nathan Blecharczyk, is a West Roxbury native and went to Boston Latin Academy. He’s still with Airbnb as its chief strategy officer and likes to support his hometown like the time he presented a $1 million gift to BLA.

So I asked an Airbnb spokesman, who said the company continues to look at ways to support host cities and is “open” to what more it can do in Boston.

Meanwhile, Boston 26 spokeswoman Julie Duffy said the committee welcomes partnership conversations and “our commercial team has reached out to explore what may be possible here.”

As for Meet Boston, Sheridan says she has no issues with a potential Airbnb sponsorship.

“Original discussions with Airbnb involved a Boston 26 staff member who has since departed the organization,” she said in a statement. “Meet Boston’s priority is to fill hotel rooms and we are confident that bookings are solid, so that is not influencing current discussions with Airbnb about a Boston partnership.”

This feels like the latest in a long string of misunderstandings around the World Cup, from who pays for security in Foxborough to FIFA holding up applications for local watch parties. But maybe there’s still time to make this relationship right. Perhaps it’s a chance to lower our cost of transportation to the games. Why should Philly be the only one?

Sounds like something we should pursue. Just don’t leave the negotiations up to Boston 26.

What do Raffles Boston general manager Carlos Bueno, Comfort Kitchen cofounder Biplaw Rai, and event planner extraordinaire Rose Staram have in common? They are all being honored Tuesday night at the Menino Convention & Exhibition Center for being among the “50 Most Influential People Of Color in Hospitality & Tourism.” We got a sneak peek of the list, compiled by Colette Phillips’s Get Konnected! networking group, as the region prepares to host a throng of tourists for the World Cup, a historic Fourth of July, and a parade of tall ships. John Barros is on the list as the interim executive director of the Massachusetts Convention Center Authority, as are hotel and restaurant GMs Gurkirat Singh of the Westin Copley & W Boston and Ezechiel Josma of Davio’s Northern Italian Steakhouse in the Back Bay. Restaurateurs who’ve reimagined dining also made the cut including Nia Grace of Grace by Nia, Park 54 Restaurant & Lounge’s Tasha Hull, JP Fuji Group’s Jimmy Liang, ZaZ’s Olrie Roberts, Mida’s Douglass Williams, Hue Boston’s Robert Eugene and Hermela Belachew, Andrew and Irene Li of Mei Mei Restaurant Group, and Brian and Patty Moy of China Pearl. Then there are the business owners who’ve focused on tourists like Jacqueline Church of Boston Chinatown Tours and Collin Knight, who runs Live Like a Local Tours. Congratulations to all, and good luck this summer!

We’ve heard from Associated Industries of Massachusetts that local employers have been downbeat for the past year. Now we have a new poll out today from the Retailers Association of Massachusetts showing consumers aren’t too happy, either. A pollster surveyed 608 registered voters a few weeks ago, via a web poll, and found only 36 percent believe things in Massachusetts are headed in the right direction, compared to 48 percent two years ago, and 59 percent in 2023. RAM president Jon Hurst says his business members regularly complain about taxes, health insurance requirements, and electric utility mandates, and he suspects consumers are starting to feel the pinch, too.

The Boston-based autonomous aviation startup Merlin has been banking on defense contracts, such as its work retrofitting a military transport jet made by Lockheed Martin. But now the publicly traded firm, led by entrepreneur Matt George, is branching out into commercial business as well, with a new collaboration with freighter lessor World Star Aviation. Merlin’s tech specializes in flying a plane with one pilot instead of two, or maybe someday, no pilot at all. So far, though, the pilots who fly our passenger airlines – Delta, JetBlue, and the like – seem to be safe from Merlin’s magic.

You-Do-It Development? One of the last vestiges of mid-century Americana along Route 128 will be preserved by developer Onyx Partners, which has acquired the former You-Do-It Electronics building in Needham, the one with the distinctive sign, to use as its headquarters. After more than 70 years of being run by the Achigian family, You-Do-It sold its last receivers and speaker wire in 2024. Onyx is redoing the building’s interior but has pledged to keep the You-Do-It billboard that sits atop its roof, a reminder of simpler times.

It was bound to happen: NIMBYs coming for data centers.

Municipalities all over the country, including in Massachusetts, are itching to pass ordinances to ban the hulking structures, which can be the size of a Walmart or even bigger, as our colleague Hiawatha Bray reported. A recent Quinnipiac University poll confirmed just how unpopular they are, with 65 percent of Americans saying they oppose the building of a data center in their community, citing concerns about electricity costs and water use, as well as noise.

The truth is, the data center boom has pretty much bypassed New England. Electricity is simply too expensive here. Still, we can understand why some towns are apprehensive about so-called hyperscalers coming here, even as other locales roll out the red carpet.

But the dearth of data centers has its downside: These are massive construction projects at a time when that sector is hurting locally. Harvard University economist Jason Furman has estimated that data center investment accounted for 92 percent of GDP growth in the first half of 2025.

And Governor Maura Healey knows the economic stakes are high for Massachusetts. In late 2024, she signed a measure that would exempt proposed data centers from state sales tax. And in April she pledged not to sign a moratorium on new data centers like one recently proposed in Maine. “That’s not going to help our economy,” Healey said at a New England Council meeting. “That’s not going to help our future.”

Take our survey here, and we’ll share the results on Friday.

Last Friday, we asked which company did Panera CEO Paul Carbone NOT help take public as a top executive. The most popular guess from our readers was Yeti Holdings, but it’s wrong: Carbone actually relocated to Texas to help Yeti with its 2018 IPO. The correct answer was Talbots, the Hingham-based apparel retailer owned by Sycamore Partners. Carbone did work there, but the timing didn’t work out for an initial public offering while he was there.
