title: Boston police officer indicted on manslaughter charge in connection with fatal shooting of carjacking suspect
text:
The now-suspended officer was released on personal recognizance following his March arraignment in Roxbury Municipal Court. The indictment moves the case to Suffolk Superior Court, where O’Malley will be arraigned at a later date, Hayden’s office said in a statement.

King was shot while he allegedly tried to flee a traffic stop in a stolen car. Prosecutors determined that O’Malley had no justification for shooting at a moving vehicle.

“It is disappointing that the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office is choosing to second-guess an officer whose only goal was to protect the public,” O’Malley’s lawyer, David Yannetti, previously said in a statement. “We will continue to vigorously defend this officer and this case.”

Yannetti, best known for his successful defense of Karen Read, added in court papers that the “main issue in this case will be who the aggressor really was and whether Officer O’Malley acted in lawful defense.”

Yannetti filed several defense motions in the Roxbury division of Boston Municipal Court in an effort to illustrate “King’s mayhem and reign of terror,” spanning nearly two decades and resulting in more than 17 criminal cases across Massachusetts, court records show.

Over the years, King has been charged with strangulation, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, carjacking, breaking and entering, gun offenses, and resisting arrest, according to court filings.

At the time of his death, King was free on bail for at least three separate felony cases and had active warrants for his arrest, court records said.

Yannetti is seeking King’s mental health, criminal, and court records from all his past cases, recordings from police body-worn and dash cameras, the medical examiner’s file on King, along with statements taken from O’Malley and witnesses at the scene of the shooting.

O’Malley told investigators that when he shot King, he feared for his own life and for the life of another officer at the scene, believing his colleague was about to be run over.

Police had pursued King after he allegedly committed a carjacking outside a pizza restaurant in Boston’s Mission Hill neighborhood. About 15 minutes later, officers stopped the stolen car less than a mile away at Linwood Square in Roxbury.

The driver ignored “multiple verbal commands” as officers approached and tried to drive away, police said.

King opened the car window, but did not turn the vehicle off. O’Malley drew his Taser and shouted, “Bro, I’m going to [expletive] shoot you,” a police report said.

That’s when King backed into the cruiser behind him, then maneuvered the vehicle forward and back “in an attempt to escape the police,” according to the report.

As King started to drive forward again, O’Malley fired three shots through the driver’s window, striking King, the report said.

King’s family has said he was experiencing a mental health crisis in the hours leading up to the deadly encounter.

In court filings, Yannetti said King gave “O’Malley no choice that night.”

“Any suggestion that this shooting was precipitated by simply a ‘mental health crisis’ completely misses the point,” Yannetti wrote. “When facing an extremely dangerous threat, there is no time for a police officer to hold a counseling session on the street or to sit down to discuss the feelings of a menace who is intent on using a motor vehicle as a deadly weapon.”

“If a man is going to assault and carjack an innocent woman, then threaten the lives and safety of the public and a police officer, that man needs to be stopped — whether he is in his right mind or not,” a defense motion stated.

But Assistant District Attorney Ian Polumbaum said in court in March that investigators determined O’Malley’s explanation wasn’t reasonable, citing witness testimony and footage from police body cameras.

The other officer, Polumbaum, said, “was in greater danger of being struck by those bullets than he ever was by the car.”

While the law affords police officers deference for split-second decisions, “we keep in mind the law and common sense,” he said.

Immediately after firing the shots, O’Malley called over his radio that officers were involved in a shooting and the suspect “tried to run us over,” according to the police report. He later told investigators he believed the other officer “was going to be crushed by the suspect’s vehicle,” according to the police report.

However, investigating officers concluded that O’Malley’s statement “was not factually true.” State law and Boston Police Department policy forbid officers from shooting at a moving vehicle unless there’s no other way to prevent “imminent harm to a person.”

In March, responding to a question from reporters about whether the officers should have allowed the suspect to drive away, Hayden said that “in this circumstance, that might have been prudent.”

Ben Crump, a civil rights attorney representing King’s family, said he welcomed the indictment.

“For months, Stephenson King Jr.’s loved ones have been grieving the devastating loss of a son, a family member and a man whose life mattered deeply, while also fighting for the transparency and accountability they deserve,” Crump said. “The arrest, manslaughter charge, and now this indictment against the officer involved sends a powerful message about the seriousness of this case.”

Crump said the family “knows that accountability cannot stop here. They deserve the full truth about what happened to Stephenson and a justice system willing to fully examine every decision that led to his death. We will continue standing beside them and demanding transparency, truth and justice every step of the way.”

Lea Skene of the Globe Staff contributed to this report.

title: Are AI school outcomes just another hallucination?
text:
As a 25-year veteran teacher, holder of both a master’s and doctorate in education, and the head of an intentionally small, independent school in Boston, I am deeply troubled by the motivations and supposed data-driven results of the Alpha School highlighted in “What critics get wrong about the Alpha School” (Opinion, May 13).

When the founders and supporters of these for-profit schools, many from the tech world or Ivy League institutions, talk about how students “crush” academics and optimize individualized learning, I am saddened by what is lost.

By focusing on computer-driven modules, students lose the moment of joy that is sparked after a struggling student eventually understands a concept in a classroom and is celebrated by their peers. By insisting that their “guides” are so much better than teachers, learners lose the reverence for teachers dedicated to their craft.

We do not need a one-size-fits-all model for K-12 education. Traditional classrooms do not work for all students. However, disrespecting the teaching profession and selling the idea that you need to learn more and learn faster negates the power of truly integrating skills and experiential learning, which ultimately prepares young people for this ever-changing world.

Maybe the strong test scores from AI schools have little to do with the Alpha School curriculum. Many studies show a strong correlation between SAT/ACT test scores and family income.

Any family that can afford $65,000 a year in K-12 tuition, as described in “Would you spend $65,000 to send your kid to an AI school?” (Opinion, May 13) certainly has the resources to ensure their students do well on any and all standardized tests. The school isn’t doing anything all that dramatic except taking credit, and charging, for a statistically expected outcome.

title: Roxbury’s Black Market to close at month’s end after failed bid to buy Nubian Square building
text:
“We’ve gone through a mortgage process, we’ve done deep dives, we’ve sat with financially savvy advisers, we looked carefully at the cost of the capital, the debt structure, the risk, the long-term obligations, and what it would truly take to bear the weight of this acquisition responsibly,” Kai Grant said in Friday’s video. “And after all of that, the hard truth became clear ... the level of risk required would place an unsustainable burden on us personally, financially, and operationally.”

The decision to close May 31 was not made “lightly,” she said.

When the Grants opened Black Market Nubian in 2017, it was hosted out of the first floor of a building on Washington Street and featured fashion, food, and craft vendors they hoped would gain traction in Nubian Square and help it grow. After COVID, they changed their business model, positioning Black Market as more of a cultural space and an arts and events venue. For five years, they have hosted an annual block party.

Earlier this spring, the Grants revealed they were in a dispute with their landlord and asked for community help raising $369,000 by the end of this month to buy the two-story building at 2316 Washington St.

Many were surprised the Grants didn’t own the building outright and instead had an option to buy it for $1.3 million. Others wondered why an organization that had recently been awarded an $823,000city contract for “creative placemaking” would struggle to keep its doors open. And some wondered why Madison Park, a longstanding Roxbury nonprofit, was at odds with a small business that seemed to share its mission.

In a statement Friday, Monica Dean, Madison Park’s chief executive, said the nonprofit was notified Friday afternoon that “the tenant had chosen to nullify the terms of the agreed-upon extension and vacate within the coming week.”

“This is an unfortunate turn of events,” Dean said. “Madison Park Development Corp. has worked diligently and in good faith to provide a path forward for Black Market.”

Dean said the nonprofit remains committed to its Nubian Square tenants and wishes the Grants “the best.”

City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, whose district includes the market, said in a phone interview Saturday that though the market is closing “physically,” it’s not closing “emotionally.”

“We’ll all work to keep it emotionally open,” he said. “The spirit of Kai and Chris will never stop.”

Nevertheless, he said the closure of the market is a loss of “an engine of economic development” for Boston’s Black community.

Imari Paris Jeffries, president and chief executive of Embrace Boston, a nonprofit dedicated to racial equity, said Saturday that the market likely struggled financially because the surrounding area lacked enough complementary businesses to generate consistent foot traffic.

“You can’t be out there by yourself,” he said. “We need multiple businesses at the same time happening, and ... that hasn’t happened yet.”

Jeffries said Nubian Square’s soon-to-be-opened Jazz Urbane Cafe, a jazz club with an attached restaurant, would have provided foot traffic that could have helped the market.

“It’s just sad,” he said of the market’s closure. “You need those types of things to make Nubian Square an attraction for people to go to as a tourist hub.”

Kai Grant told the Globe last month that their lease agreement with Madison Park “was supposed to be about becoming a model for equity and antidisplacement” that ensured artisans, founders, and microbusinesses could stay in Roxbury.

Dean told the Globe that Black Market had not upheld “their end of the bargain,” and the nonprofit would “put its own finances at risk if it continued to subsidize” the market’s lease.

The Grants owed $124,229.12 in unpaid rent accrued over 32 months between 2021 and 2023, according to records reviewed by the Globe.

The closure of the Black Market also highlights the tenuous status of Black-owned businesses and spaces in Boston.

A 2024 report from the Donahue Institute at UMass Amherst found that “business owners of color struggle to find capital,” particularly in Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, and East Boston.

Culpepper said the closure is “a product of this economy,” and emphasized that the venture was never intended as a “money-making venture.”

“If you look at the cuts in the city’s budget financially, the city is having challenging times. It’s not just Black Market, it’s even the city government,” he said, referencing Mayor Wu’s proposed budget cuts.

Jeffries said that although the loss of the market is a hit to the local culture and economy, there is still hope for the area.

“We’re pinning a lot of hope on Jazz Urbane to be successful,” he said.

Janelle Nanos of the Globe Staff contributed to this report.

title: Friday’s 11 HS sports takeaways, including new coaches at Nantucket and Newman and a fresh football co-op
text:
Then the games began and we had five Top 20 softball and baseball teams lose, including No. 2 Taunton baseball watching its nine-game win streak snapped by Brody Bumila and Bishop Feehan, even though the ace’s damage was limited to his bat.

Toss in four softball walkoff wins, a Woburn boys’ volleyball record matched, a pair of two-homer games, a no-hitter, a Top 5 five-set boys’ volleyball thriller, and the Boston City League outdoor track championships, and you’ve got another action-packed day.

Here’s everything you need to knowabout the upcoming postseason schedule, including Friday’s bracket releases.

▪ Woburn senior Trey Skumin matched the school record by racking up eight blocks while leading the Tanners to a 3-1 boys’ volleyball win over Lynn Classical. He added 15 kills.

▪ North Andover’s Lauren Lynch recorded both her 100th career hit and 100th career putout during a 5-4 loss to Andover.

▪ Roxbury Prep captured its first Charter School League baseball title, needing just five innings to beat Neighborhood House Charter, 17-7, with Rawen Perez leading the way with three runs scored and the win on the bump.

▪ Mt. Greylock boys’ lacrosse claimed its first Western Mass. Class C championship in three years with a 16-14 win over Hoosac Valley thanks to back-to-back goals from Brady Auger.

Three softball teams ranked between No. 8 and No. 16 faltered, two against ranked opponents, while two baseball teams in the Top 11 took an ‘L’.

No. 8 Somerset Berkley was taken down by No. 11 Middleborough, 10-4, with Taylynn Robinson dominating with a three-run double and four RBIs total. No. 13 Silver Lake ran into Marshfield sophomore southpaw Caroline Arruda, who mowed down 10 batters for the No. 17 Rams in a 4-1 upset. Unranked Danvers rode five Taylor Landry RBIs to a 13-7 win over No. 16 Georgetown.

Meanwhile, St. John’s Prep’s Collin Thornburgh spun a gem to shut out Xaverian, 1-0, striking out 11 and getting just enough offense from Brady Baldassare in the Pete Frates ALS Awareness game.

The Brody Bumila show got the best of No. 2 Taunton for a second time this year, except this time it was his bat, not his arm, that did in the Tigers. Bumila’s two doubles helped No. 5 Bishop Feehan slip past Taunton, 3-0, and snap its nine-game win streak.

The walkoffs came with regularity on the softball diamond Friday: Central Catholic junior Chloe Salerno connected for a two-run walkoff homer to defeat Tyngsborough, 4-2. Sophomore Ginger Thompson rapped the walkoff hit, scoring Ava Johnson as Triton walked off Revere, 8-7. Peabody freshman Claire Welton socked the walkoff hit in an 18-17 win over Austin Prep. Lynn Classical sophomore Jayden Barragan delivered a walkoff RBI single for a 7-6 triumph over Swampscott.

In the non-walkoff classification, Middleborough senior Tylor Zamora mashed a go-ahead homer in the top of the eighth inning to give the 11th-ranked Sachems a 2-1 win over No. 8 Somerset Berkley, and Masconomet junior Sydnee Vocino rapped a clutch two-out, two-strike hit in the top of the seventh to send Masconomet past Newton South, 12-7.

Georgetown’s Maddie Grant carried a big stick, homering twice, including a grand slam, to join Chelmsford’s Aidan Brackett in Friday’s two-homer club.

West Bridgewater enjoyed four blasts, one each from Emma Croce, Jillian Foley, Liliana Morales, and Alanna Fidalgo. The rest of the day’s round-trippers belonged to: Chelmsford’s Gavin Corbo, Central Catholic’s Chloe Salerno, Middleborough’s Tylor Zamora, Bishop Stang’s Bubba Garcia, Triton’s Katie Clemenzi, Bishop Fenwick’s Odin Garron, Archbishop Williams’ Alessandra Cautilli, Newton South’s Jonny Hunt, Nobles’ Ava Decourcey, and Peabody’s Lizzy Bettencourt.

Rolky Brea-Arias, St. Mary’s — The senior was a two-way force, firing a an eight-strikeout, five-hit shutout, then turning around and ripping an RBI triple in a 4-0 baseball win over Lynn English.

Gabriella Davis, Tewksbury — The senior fired a no-hitter for the Redmen, striking out three in a 12-0 softball win over Lynnfield.

Bubba Garcia, Bishop Stang — The junior was a beast out of the No. 9 spot, blasting a homer and ripping a double, scoring two runs, and driving in five during the Spartans’ 10-3 baseball win over Apponequet.

Maddie Grant, Georgetown — The Bentley-bound senior did all she could in a 13-7 softball loss to Danvers, cranking a grand slam in the third inning, adding a two-run homer in the fifth, and finishing with six RBIs on the Royals’ seven runs.

Lidia Miedema, Beverly — The junior was practically a one-person band in beating Essex Tech, 3-0, fanning five in a two-hit shutout while collecting two hits, including an RBI single.

▪ Nantucket has elevated coach Fernando Jones to head football coach. Jones served as head coach at Cyrus Peirce Middle School from 2022-24 and served as an assistant coach for Nantucket’s varsity, working with running and defensive backs.

Hailing from Manchester, Conn., Jones graduated from Williston Northampton, where he played running back and cornerback, before playing at Hobart. Jones, the director of operations for the Nantucket Boys & Girls Club, has also served in the Army National Guard.

“Nantucket Public Schools believes coach Jones’s unique blend of coaching experience, leadership, and community involvement makes him an outstanding fit to lead the next chapter of Whaler Football,” the school wrote in a statement.

Jones follows Coreese “Reese” Everett, who spent four years at the helm, culminating in a 9-1 season in 2025. He stepped down to move off island for family reasons.

▪ The Newman School has hired Justin Perron as its head boys’ basketball coach. Perron spent the last four years leading St. Mark’s, where he captured the 2026 Class B Large NEPSAC championship. Perron replaces Jackson Johnson, who departed for IMG Academy in Florida.

Perron, who also served as assistant athletic director at St. Mark’s, previously coached Northfield Mt. Hermon. He played guard at Framingham State, was an assistant at Mansfield and Franklin, then spent five years as an assistant at Clark.

▪ The Newman School also announced the hiring of Ramon Garcia as its director of strength. A former Bates men’s basketball star, Garcia is the owner of Elevate Fitness in Boston.

▪ Worcester Polytechnic Institute junior Naomi Boldebuck, a Billerica graduate, was named to the National Fastpitch Coaches Association Division 3 All-Region team, along with sophomore Lucy Latour, a Dighton-Rehoboth grad. Junior Sandy Fairbairn, a Norton graduate, made the second team for WPI.

Boldebuck went 16-4 with a 3.07 ERA, logging four shutouts and striking out 69 batters in 139 innings. Latour hit .500 with 66 runs, 17 doubles, 5 triples, 9 homers, 41 RBIs, and 23 steals, compiling a .576 on-base percentage and .842 slugging percentage in 48 starts. Fairbairn hit .398 with 19 doubles, 7 triples, 12 homers, 58 RBIs, 48 runs, and 14 steals.

▪ UMass Dartmouth sophomore Ancil Alexander, a Taunton graduate, earned All-American honors for the third time in his collegiate track and field career. He finished seventh at the Division 3 championships in the discus (167 feet, 5 inches) after winning the D3 New England championship.

▪ Millis and Norfolk Aggie announced a two-year football co-op agreement that will begin this fall. Millis will serve as the host school, welcoming Norfolk Aggie students to join the Mohawks.

The co-op, which has been approved by the MIAA and Mayflower and Tri-Valley leagues, comes a critical time for Millis, which was facing declining participation and no longer had a co-op with Hopedale. Thanks to the co-op, they plan to field a sub-varsity team.

“We are incredibly excited about this partnership and what it means for the future of football in Millis,” said Millis athletic director Derek Phinney in a statement. “Keeping our football tradition alive while prioritizing player safety is our top priority. By bringing in Norfolk Aggie student-athletes, we aren’t just saving our varsity program; we are rebuilding the foundation by offering sub-varsity levels again.

The new unified team will open its season Sept. 12 at Blackstone-Millville.

▪ Hingham will hold a track dedication Saturday to honor late coach Fred Jewett, who worked as an educator for 54 years and coached track at Hingham and Scituate for decades, winning 30 league and 11 state championships. He also had a 20-plus year career as a football coach.

The Hingham track will be named in his honor during a ceremony at 12:30 p.m., followed by a ribbon cutting and walk around the track.

title: TechBoston boys rise to Boston City League outdoor track title, Latin Academy girls win sixth in a row
text:
With 126 points, the Bears did just that, capturing the league title over runners-up O’Bryant (107 points).

“TechBoston is made of love,” said assistant coach Fatima Sidibe. “So when we show that, when we have that with each other, it makes these moments even better.”

The star emerging from the pack was senior captain Donte Robinson, who won the long jump (21 feet, 5.5 inches) and the 110-meter hurdles (16.51 seconds), adding a second-place performance in the high jump, scaling a season-best 6 feet. Not only did he earn 30 points and take home three medals, but he left with the boys’ MVP trophy.

“I’m very grateful,” said Robinson. “Right now our coach is in the hospital, so really everything we’re doing is for him, and, obviously, praising the lord because without him none of this would be possible.”

TechBoston’s first-year head coach Charles Dean has been outfor a week while dealing with an undisclosed health issue. His absence motivates the Bears, and Robinson, to continue and stand together.

“[Robinson] is somebody that you can put anywhere and he can perform to the highest extent,” Sidibe said with tears in her eyes. “I am so proud of him and his future endeavors and the lasting memory and impact he’s made on our team.”

On the girls’ side, Latin Academy continued its dominance, winning a sixth- straight outdoor title with 124 points, besting runner-up O’Bryant (109 points).

Latin Academy coach Laura Wiatt praised her distance team’s progress . The girls only won one individual event, with Anjuli Szydlo (14 minutes, 33 seconds) and Maya Friedman (14 minutes, 34.69 seconds) taking first and second in the 2-mile, but their depth and ability to compete in each event racked up the points for the Dragons.

“Today was a lot on our athletes’ mentals,” said LA assistant coach Imani Pressley, noting the meet was moved from Tuesday to Thursday to avoid the heat. “We have lots of gratitude and we are proud of them.”

Zariya Josaphat took home the girls’ MVP trophy for Green Academy, winning the 200 (27.83 seconds), 400 (1:02.12) and helping the 4x100 relay top the podium in 53.33 seconds.

“I underestimated myself a bit . . . but I’ve seen what I can do in contention and [did] what I have to do,” said Josaphat.

title: Prom is crazy expensive. This fairy-prom mother gives students their storybook dance for free.
text:
Over the last decade, Rapo’s charity,Giving the Glam, has helped over a thousand Massachusetts students afford the dance of their dreams. She gives high schoolers free ballgowns and suits expertly fitted by seamstresses; a glam squad for hair, nails, and makeup; and even a ride in a Ferrari with a police escort to the party.

As prices surge on everything fromtomatoes to coffee to beef, more parents can’t dish out the $1,000 it typically costs for a storybook prom. Teens are left scouring for gowns, borrowing outfits from relatives, and embellishing old dresses with tricks from TikTok. But people like Rapo are stepping in to fill an increasing need because they believe every student deserves that fairy tale.

Last week, prom festivities kicked off at midday at Rapo’s sprawling house in Dover, about 15 miles outside Boston. It was the big night for seniors at Cristo Rey, a Catholic high school in Dorchester that serves families with limited economic means.

In Rapo’s living room, two long tables were covered in an array of high heels, designer clutches, and men’s dress shoes. More tables held a rainbow of nail polish, lipsticks, and enough makeup to fill a stand at a Sephora. One at a time, 45 high school seniors rushed into the pop-up dressing room to try on bow-ties and necklaces covered in rhinestones.

“I never thought prom day would be like this,” said senior Abdiel Reyes. “It feels like I’m in the movies.”

Upstairs in a guest bedroom, Acosta had a fresh manicure and hair blowout when she slipped into a $600 gown that had been altered just for her. Like all the other teens, she will get to keep the dress.

“I feel like I’m glowing,” Acosta said.

Her mother, a social worker named Aracelis Acosta, was relieved when the school announced it was partnering with Giving the Glam.

“With everything being so expensive,” Aracelis Acosta said, “I wasn’t sure I could give her the prom she always deserved.”

One of the charity’s volunteers, who all wore black T-shirts with the nonprofit’s logo, knelt down before Acosta to help her adjust the straps on her black heels. Another volunteer, Josias Barbosa, closed his Loov Concept salon in Medford to curl and style students’ hair for the big night.

They were part of an army of 25 helpers who had traveled from as far away as Fall River and Nashua, N.H., to give students the royal prom treatment. Most of the volunteers grew up struggling in Brazil and want to help those who need a lift.

That’s what inspired Rapo to launch her charity. She grew up in Favela do Aço, a dense, low-income neighborhood in Rio de Janeiro, and she sees herself in today’s urban high schoolers.

“I want them to feel like a million bucks,” Rapo said.

The cost of prom has nearly doubled over the last 16 years, according to research by Jay Zagorsky of Boston University’s Questrom School of Business. The big ticket items include outfits, accessories, salon visits, and limo rides. Tickets to the dance can range from $30 to $150 in Massachusetts.

A number of local organizations work to make prom memorable on a budget. Anton’s Cleaners helps spearhead Belle of the Ball, which provides used prom dresses and accessories free of charge to higher schoolers.

Hundreds of girls referred by their schools flock to Hynes Convention Center every year to sift through thousands of donated gowns. A swarm of volunteers act as personal stylists, helping them find the perfect dress, shoes, and bag.

Demand has surged since the pandemic, according to Anton’s marketing director, Stephanie Littefield. They now invite 1,800 students to participate, up from 1,200 in 2019.

“Everything is expensive today,” Littlefield said.

The issue goes beyond cost, said Shauna King, a marketing teacher at Plymouth South High School. Students are spending more because they want their photos to meet the impossible standards they see online, King said.

King runs the Massachusetts chapter of Becca’s Closet, a national initiative that helps students find gowns. A dressing room built into Plymouth South High School allows students from all over the state to make an appointment and browse through donated dresses.

Rapo at Giving the Glam doesn’t rely on used outfits or do-it-yourself projects. The charity provides brand new gowns and celebrity quality makeovers. Rapo typically spends between $700 and $1,000 on each student, she said, and raises between $150,000 and $200,000 every year to make it happen.

“Helping kids afford the prom of their dreams isn’t about the money,” Rapo said. “It’s about teaching them to give back to the community.“

Earlier this month, Giving the Glam helped teens at Brockton High School, many of whom have lived in homeless shelters or were in foster care.

Marc Laviolette, 19, walked into the dance in a shiny pink suit that Rapo’s team helped him pick out. He said he never felt “so loved” by his classmates.

“They told me I should have been nominated for prom king,” Laviolette said. “I got my dream prom.”

title: ‘One of our best’: Boston firefighter killed battling three-alarm fire in Dorchester
text:
The fire broke out about 8 p.m. Saturday, and five residents were home at the time. All residents escaped safely without injury, though all were displaced.

The blaze spread through all three floors and burned through the roof, according to the Boston Fire Department, which said firefighters deployed “multiple ground and aerial ladders” to keep the flames from spreading to neighboring homes. Video posted to social media showed flames shooting from the roof of the building.

By 8:32 p.m., officials said the heavy fire had been “knocked down,” with crews continuing an aggressive interior and exterior attack to contain the blaze.

A mayday call went out for an injured firefighter. Minutes later, a second alert reported that the firefighter was being transported to a hospital under police escort, where he was later pronounced dead.

Fire officials said they could not provide additional details because an investigation into the fire and Kilduff’s death remained ongoing.

Early Sunday, rows of firefighters, police officers, and other personnel stood at attention as Kilduff’s body was loaded into an ambulance and taken from the hospital to the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

On Sunday night, despite steady rain, dozens of firefighters and police officers lined Albany Street outside the medical examiner’s office to honor Kilduff during a dignified transfer to a funeral home in West Roxbury. Flashing blue police lights and red firetrucks illuminated the street as a hearse carrying Kilduff slowly pulled away under escort.

Kilduff, a father of two, was a third-generation Boston firefighter and a US Marine veteran. He was remembered not only for his 24 years with the Boston Fire Department, but also for the compassion and energy he brought to volunteer work supporting families of fallen service members and first responders.

Kilduff — known as “BK” — was assigned to Rescue Company 2 and was a “quintessential rescue man,” Kelly said. He is the first Boston firefighter to die in the line of duty in more than a decade.

“He’s probably been to more fires than any firefighter currently employed by the Boston Fire Department and in this region,” Kelly said, adding the crew hasn’t slept since the fire.

On Sunday afternoon, firefighters at the fire station in Egleston Square hung black drapes from the bay doors and laid flowers on the ground.

The crew described Kilduff as the lifeblood of the station — “the guy that took care of everything” — who even kept retirees looped in to firehouse events.

On the floor near a fire rig was an outline of Kilduff’s shoes where he had left them the night of the fire, his initials “BK” inside.

“We gotta write ‘too big to fill’ on them,” Kelly said.

Inside the Rescue 2 break room on Sunday, the men who worked alongside Kilduff described him as the kind of rescuer who was either already at a trapped firefighter’s side, or sprinting toward them.

“That would be the only two modes BK would be in,” Kelly said.

Rescue 2 is a specialized company that responds to dangerous situations involving firefighters in distress. Kelly said Kilduff was among the few firefighters appointed directly to the unit because of his skill and experience.

Victor Gaybor, another Rescue 2 firefighter who was at the fire Saturday night, recalled his final interaction with Kilduff.

“We were on that fire floor in the back porch and like we always do, we take a moment and just bust each other’s chops a bit, we’d lighten the whole situation,” Gaybor said. “I went back downstairs to report to my lieutenant at the time, and what happened, happened. We just went out to see what we can do for BK.”

As they traded stories about Kilduff’s jokes and his “excellent” cooking, members of Rescue 2 team said they considered themselves family and felt as if they had lost a brother.

Kilduff’s two children were traveling and unable to reach the hospital Saturday night, Kelly said, adding that Rescue 2 would fully support the family.

Funeral arrangements were still being finalized Sunday, but union officials said services would likely take place this week.

“He’ll be buried with the highest honors available in the city and within our union,” said Sam Dillon, president of the Boston Firefighters Local 718.

On Saturday morning, before the fatal blaze, Kilduff helped rescue a homeless man “who was trapped in a confined space of an MBTA yard,” Kelly said.

Kilduff was also credited with helping save the life of a fellow firefighter who suffered cardiac arrest while battling a fire more than a month ago. Dillon said Kilduff rode to the hospital with the firefighter and performed CPR.

Michelle Caroline, a former volunteer coordinator for the Gary Sinise Foundation, said Kilduff became one of the organization’s core volunteers helping families of fallen military and first responders.

“He never backed down from a challenge and stepped in whenever or wherever needed,” Caroline said.

By Sunday afternoon, a small memorial had begun to take shape along the metal fence outside the home on Treadway Road. A photo of Kilduff smiling in his firefighter’s uniform sat above flowers, candles, toy firetrucks, and American and Irish flags.

Katelyn McCabe, 33, who lives across the street, said she spent much of Sunday helping build the memorial, including printing and framing a photo of Kilduff at a nearby Walgreens.

“Sometimes people say, ‘That’s what they signed up for,’ but you still expect them to come home,” McCabe said. She said her late grandfather served as a district fire chief in Boston.

McCabe said she came outside soon after the fire broke out and was there when Kilduff fell.

“I heard the impact, and then I heard ‘Mayday,’” she said. “I just can’t get it out of my mind.”

Nearby, a lone firetruck remained stationed outside the three-story home, where the charred interior was visible through shattered upper-floor windows.

Phat Dao, 56, was visiting a friend when he stepped outside Saturday night to find Treadway Road crowded with firetrucks as flames and smoke poured from the building.

Standing in the rain near Kilduff’s memorial Sunday, Dao said the firefighter’s death hit him hard because “he died helping people.”

“He’s a hero,” Dao said.

Kilduff’s father, who served as a Boston fire lieutenant, died in 2008, according to his obituary. The elder Robert Kilduff served as Local 718 vice president and founded the local’s Children’s Fund.

“Boston lost a hero,” Mayor Michelle Wu said in a statement Sunday morning. “The Kilduff family has given everything in service to this country and this city. ... Boston will forever honor Firefighter Kilduff’s dedication and service with the most profound gratitude.”

Boston Fire Commissioner Rodney Marshall said Kilduff was a “firefighter’s firefighter.”

“It’s going to stick with us for a long time,” he said. “There’s no routine fire, there’s no routine call. And you’re never truly safe until you get home.”

On Sunday morning, Governor Maura Healey ordered US and Massachusetts flags lowered to half-staff at all state buildings in honor of Kilduff.

“His death serves as a reminder of the dangers firefighters face every day when they put their lives on the line to keep our communities safe,” Healey said in a statement.

Edward Kelly, general president of the International Association of Fire Fighters, called Kilduff the union’s “unsung hero.”

“He did everything behind the scenes for our union,” Kelly said. “He mentored fire unions all throughout the state. He was just someone that left an indelible mark.”

The last two Boston firefighters killed in the line of duty were Lieutenant Edward J. Walsh Jr. and Michael R. Kennedy, who died in 2014 while battling a nine-alarm blaze in the Back Bay.

At the time, Kilduff spoke to the Globe about the somber rituals held to honor fallen firefighters, including the black shroud draped across uniform badges, the honor guard, and the bagpipes.

“It’s a show of respect for the family, and it’s a tribute from us as firefighters,” said Kilduff, then the director of operations for the Professional Fire Fighters of Massachusetts. “It’s really hard to explain, except to say that our job, if you break it all down to the bare bones, [is that] we show up at somebody’s really bad day and try to make it a little better.”

Globe correspondent Adam Sennott contributed to this report.

title: Scotland’s soccer connections to New England run deep
text:
Scotland opening World Cup play against Haiti in Foxborough on June 13 will act as a reminder of the country’s influence on soccer in the United States and New England.

In the first World Cup in 1930 in Uruguay, the US team was coached by Scotland-born Bob Millar, who moved to the United States to play for J&P Coats and the Fall River Marksmen in the American Soccer League. The lineup included Scotsmen Andy Auld, James Brown, Jimmy Gallagher, Bart McGhee, and Alexander Wood. They were among more than 80 Scotland-born players to compete for the US men’s national team, from Neil Clarke (1916) through Stu Holden (2008).

The Scottish accent on the US game goes back to its origins in the late 1800s. According to Iain Campbell Whittle of The Scots Football Historians Group, textile magnate William Clark can be considered the “father” of soccer in the United States. Clark founded the Clark ONT (Our New Thread) team in 1883 in Newark, and served as captain in its inaugural game. Clark’s team won the first three editions of the American Football Association Cup, forerunner of the US Open Cup, and several of its players competed for the first United States national team in 1885.

By the turn of the century, Scots probably outnumbered the English in soccer management positions and on the playing fields in New England. They kept the game alive year-round, setting up five-a-side games that emphasized precise passing at the Caledonian Games ($125 to the 1915 winner) in West Roxbury. They provided the backbone of the American Soccer League from 1921-31. The Boston & District League, one of the country’s top semi-pro leagues, listed 200 Scottish players on 1922 rosters, according to a Globe story. That’s along with the Boston area’s 10-team Scottish Clans League.

But the Scottish contribution — Whittle calls it “the Scottish inheritance” — transcends numbers. The Scots refined soccer, using subtle maneuvers to counterattack the direct, physical style of the English. Creativity and skill were emphasized, opening horizons for the game to expand. And the Scots didn’t just get style points — they outplayed England in the early years of the British Home Championship.

“There was disagreement over the best way to play,” said Tom McCabe, history professor at the University of Notre Dame in London. “You see the word scientific being used, and that means using geometry, angles, combination play, and, for that, it is the Scottish influence. Passing and moving, their particular brand of soccer. They were working class, in the mines, so they weren’t big, didn’t have the nutrition, didn’t do training on the side like English gentlemen, who were men of leisure and had a better diet, time to train. It’s an interesting turning point in the evolution of the game. Scots even talk about Enlightenment ideas of community and work. Where the English game was more dribbling and violent, Scots have to show up for work, so they’re passing and moving.

“They’re on to something there. They saw the game differently. It was not just played on festival days, but a weekly thing. You’ve got to go to work the next day. So, there’s that element, and it’s more beautiful, a game with a kaleidoscope of options, constantly changing — rather than boot it and chase it, and dribble till you lose it. Scots see passing and moving, that’s our innovation, we brought that to the global game.”

Soccer might not be the same without Scottish influence. The game, Whittle said in an email, “was invented in England but raised by us to what we know today, a global phenomenon. No Scots, no soccer.”

Andy Auld: Scored twice in US debut in 1925; played for Providence Clamdiggers/Gold Bugs in ASL.

Barney Battles: Dual international (United States, Scotland). Grew up in Charlestown, played for Bunker Hill Celtics, Boston Wonder Workers, Hearts (holds the club season scoring record with 44 goals).

James Brown: One goal for the United States in the 1930 World Cup, played for Manchester United, started soccer program at Brunswick School (Greenwich, Conn.).

Charles Burgess: Coached Harvard to 1913 and ’14 intercollegiate titles; as Woodland Golf Club pro, mentored Francis Ouimet.

Gordon Burness: Dual international (Canada, United States). Teamed with brother Harry on Boston Wonder Workers and Lusitania Recreation of Cambridge.

Bobby Clark: Scotland 1978 World Cup; Dartmouth coach, won 2013 NCAA title with Notre Dame.

Neil Clarke: One US cap. Won three US Open Cup titles, lost in 1918 final with Fall River FC.

George M. Collins: Boston Globe soccer editor (1917-50); managed US team in 1924 Olympics.

Tommy Fleming: Played for Fore River Shipyard; won four US Open Cup titles with Bethlehem Steel; ASL titles with J&P Coats, Boston Wonder Workers; coached Quincy High School to 1932 New England championship.

John Gilchrist: Scottish international; Celtic FC, Fore River.

Billy Gillespie: Played for, coached, and worked at General Electric in Lynn; ranks 10th on Manchester City all-time scoring list (132 goals).

Malcolm Goldie: One US cap; Bethlehem Steel, combined with Archie Stark (record 67 goals in 1925-26 season); coached MIT (1933-41).

Bill Harper: Scottish international goalkeeper; Arsenal FC; Boston Wonder Workers; Fall River Marksmen; New Bedford Whalers.

Joe Kennaway: Dual international goalkeeper (Canada, Scotland). Providence Gold Bugs, Fall River Marksmen, Celtic FC (1931-39). Coached Brown University (1946-59).

George Lambie: Refereed three American Cup, three US Open Cup finals.

Jackie Lyons: US international (1928 Olympics); Fore River.

Jock Marshall: Dual international (Scotland, United States), captained Scotland in early 1920s. Yale coach (1950-65), final game with Bulldogs was 6-3 win over Harvard on John Kerry hat trick.

Alex McNab: Dual international (Scotland, United States). Mentored 19-year-old Billy Gonsalves on Boston Wonder Workers front line in winning 1928 ASL title. McNab, Bill McPherson, and Gonsalves (considered among best all-time US players) combined to win six successive US Open Cup titles.

Alexander Meiklejohn: American FA treasurer, AFA Cup competitor; played for George Wright team on visit to Niagara for games of Canadian ice hockey/American ice polo (January, 1895); Brown University ice polo team center; captain All-Rhode Island XI v. Australia in 1913 cricket test match; Amherst College president (1912-23); 1963 Presidential Medal of Freedom.

Bob Millar: J&P Coats and Fall River in the ASL; played for the United States in 1925, coached the United States in the 1930 World Cup.

Tommy Muirhead: Scotland captain, played for Boston Wonder Workers in 1924, their initial season.

Steve Nicol: Scottish international, won 1984 European Champions Cup with Liverpool FC; Revolution coach 2002-11).

Andy Stradan: Converted a penalty kick in 1-0 win over Estonia in Paris, US Olympic team’s debut; played for Fisherville and Fore River.
