title: Is this Boston’s best new food hall?
text:
But Novo Marketplace is about more than food, Chen says: People are welcome to spend time here without buying anything. “We are building more of a community,” he says. “We want people to come out. We have board games, free WiFi, places to sit and hang out, and a stage for events.”

The space is large and airy, with tables to seat more than 250 people. Pop music plays in the background. This isn’t a fast food court; although the food is casual, many of the dishes and drinks are made to order. Customers take buzzers or numbers, then wander while they wait. Although a few stalls aren’t open yet, including Molly Tea and Noodle Lab, most of Novo is in business.

Here is what you’ll find — along with the best things to order — when you visit.

You’re not imagining things: There was previously a branch of this California-based Hong Kong-style cafe just a few steps away from Novo Marketplace. Now it’s inside the food court, serving rich beef stew, shredded chicken, and other specialties.

What to order: Hainan chicken ($14.99) is an excellent starting place, the slices of tender-skinned poached chicken served with yellow rice, cucumbers, and ginger-scallion sauce. Add on a milk tea for $3 more for the full Hong Kong cafe experience.

This chain started in China in 2022 and has expanded to more than 30 countries. It’s new to Allston, one of its latest landing spots. Sure, you could get something classic, like an Americano or flat white, but why would you when Cotti also offers honey-lemon sparkling cold brew, matcha-mango-coconut drinks, and blue-tinged cloud mousse lattes? Adjust the sugar level to your liking when you order. There are Hong Kong egg puffs and other baked goods, too.

What to order: The pandan coco latte ($6.49) is a layered drink of pale green and creamy brown, with pandan-flavored coconut milk on the bottom, and Cotti’s Gold Dark roast coffee and espresso on top. The coffee is satisfyingly bitter against the pandan and coconut sweetness.

Tall, airy souffle pancakes became an Internet trend a few years back, and they are Fluffy Fluffy’s specialty. Pancake makers whip egg whites, then cook the cakes low and slow and serve them in stacks topped with whipped cream and fruit, Nutella and banana, Oreos and cream, and more. There are also breakfast sets, Basque cheesecakes, and drinks — but it’s the fluffy, fluffy pancakes you’re here for.

What to order: Light, eggy matcha tiramisu pancakes ($16.50) come with whipped cream, a sprinkle of matcha powder, and strawberries, with a side of matcha cream for pouring.

If Hangover’s name obscures the fact that this business serves Istanbul-inspired street food, the Turkish flag and evil-eye talisman on the wall tip you off. You can build your own bowl with rice, beans, chicken or beef gyro, and other toppings. (Or get your fries loaded with gyro meat and sauces.) Panini come with egg and cheese, and also the spicy sausage sujuk. There are American classics like chicken salad sandwiches, and baklava for dessert.

What to order: Hangover’s specialty is the juicy bun burger ($6.99), or islak (wet) burger, a Turkish street staple for staving off regrets from a night of drinking. The seasoned beef patties are served on buns soaked in tomato-based sauce, a messy, squishy flavor bomb. Think of it as a Turkish dip.

This corner of Novo Marketplace is a Korean twofer. Park’s Kitchen previously gained a following at its takeout kitchen in Roxbury. This is the next chapter for the business, specializing in tteokbokki (rice cakes), fried chicken, fish cake skewers, and assorted snacks. Mumu’s Kimbap and Ramyun, as you might guess, offers kimbap (rice and seaweed rolls with various fillings) and popular varieties of instant ramyun, packaged noodle soups customers prepare themselves at the special ramyun machines on the counter.

What to order: Rosé tteokbokki ($17.99), a rich, smoky, spicy bowl of chewy, oblong rice cakes in creamy pink sauce with fish cake, bacon, and snappy little sausages, the whole thing topped in melted cheese. Pick a heat level, from mild to “insane.” Pair it with bulgogi kimbap ($11.99), stuffed with barbecue beef and vegetables.

Now, from the folks behind Hangover, something completely different: Liv serves smoothies, juices, and acai, mango, and coconut bowls. This is for the day after you stuffed yourself full of wet burgers. A healthful reset is just the thing, sometimes.

What to order: It’s hard to resist a juice called Better Than Botox (apple, cucumber, celery, spinach, and lemon, $13). But if you’re craving something more substantial, try a Hawaii bowl, with acai, blueberry granola, pineapple, banana, coconut flakes, and honey ($13).

A sister business to Lumi Vietnamese Bistro at the South Shore Plaza and Lumi Wok & Roast in Randolph, this branch specializes in fresh and fried spring rolls, vermicelli bowls, rice plates, pho, and banh mi. There’s also an alluring roster of Vietnamese coffee drinks.

What to order: Shrimp fresh rolls ($6.95) and a grilled pork banh mi ($10.95), filled with savory meat, pickled veggies, cilantro, and (if you want them) sliced chiles. Don’t forget a coffee topped with sweet egg or ube foam ($6.45).

At Mi-Nori, assorted push pops can be purchased and eaten — but they’re not ice cream push pops. The TikTok-trending tubes hold pre-sliced sushi rolls of your choice, from California roll to seared salmon truffle roll. The handle, a hollow plastic tube, is filled with soy sauce; pop open the cap at the end, sprinkle some on your sushi (careful not to spill), then use the handle to push the sushi out, bite by bite. It’s more than a gimmick; the sushi is fresh and delicious. You can also get sashimi, nigiri, regular rolls, and hand rolls.

What to order: A Lava Crunch push pop ($16), filled with rice, shrimp tempura, spicy crab, avocado, and fish roe, a satisfying mix of flavors and textures.

The smell of intermingling spices draws you to this Indian restaurant, related to Tabla outlets in Florida and beyond. Burnt-orange metal casseroles are on display, filled with butter chicken, palak paneer, Hakka noodles, and more; a friendly staffer is happy to offer samples. The Tabla chicken curry is rustic and fragrant, the vindaloo has real heat, and the biryani is studded with cardamom pods. I couldn’t tell you about vegetable korma, because the fellow behind the counter didn’t think it looked quite right and sent the batch back to the kitchen. Expect generous paneer in your palak, lively spicing, and pride of craftsmanship.

What to order: Tabla’s chicken tikka masala is more nuanced than many versions, and shrimp Madras curry is lively with mustard seeds and tamarind. If you like heat, try the vindaloo, with a mango lassi ($4.49) to cool the burn. Order in combos, from bowl ($10.99) to family feast ($54.99): The Royal Plate ($21.99) gets you three entrees, biryani, naan, and sweet gulab jamun (syrup-soaked fried dumplings) for dessert.

Indonesian food isn’t easy to come by in these parts. Tasya’s Kitchen changes that, serving Indonesian street food by way of New Hampshire. (The original Tasya’s, in Somersworth, is temporarily closed while this one gets up and running.) Come for fragrant, beautifully spiced dishes thrumming with lemongrass and coconut, as well as the ministrations of kind staffers who want to know if you like spicy food and where you might have eaten Indonesian cooking before. You’ll find Tasya’s signature nasi goreng, spicy fried rice with chicken or salted fish, egg, and toppings; variations on light, crisp fried chicken; and gado-gado, a salad of tofu and more that comes with thick, spicy peanut sauce.

What to order: Soto ayam ($17), chicken and glass noodle soup that’s bright yellow with turmeric, is a comforting elixir; apply lime and sambal sauce as you wish. Lontong sayur with chicken ($18) or beef rendang ($20) is a rich, spicy coconut curry with rice cakes and hard-boiled eggs.

This Chinese chain specializes in chicken, with nary a steak in sight. It comes in sandwiches, on skewers, as nuggets, and more. Skewered squid, fries, and other snacks are here, too. It has a following; this stand was doing numbers on a recent Friday night, the staff hoarse from calling out orders.

What to order: The signature spicy fried chicken breast ($6.99), flavored with your choice of sweet plum, chile, or fragrant, salty cumin. After the chicken is fried, staff cut it into bite-size pieces, then serve it in a bag with several long wooden picks to use for stabbing and eating.

122 Brighton Ave., Allston, www.novomarketplace.com. Open 10 a.m.-10 p.m. daily.

Globe correspondent Julian Flynn contributed to this report.

title: Varsity News: Breaking down the first week of the MIAA postseason
text:
Already, 13 state champions have been crowned:

Division 1 track: Lexington girls, St. John’s Prep boys

Division 2 track: Billerica girls, North Andover boys

Division 3 track: Canton girls, Walpole boys

Division 4 track: Duxbury girls, Newburyport boys

Division 5 track: North Reading girls, Weston boys

Division 6 track: Ayer Shirley girls, Abington boys

Girls’ golf: Walpole

The girls’ lacrosse and boys’ and girls’ tennis tournaments have reached the quarterfinals, while boys’ lacrosse is wrapping up its second round. Baseball started its second round Wednesday after softball got a jump-start Tuesday, and boys’ volleyball has just a couple of second-round matches remaining before the quarterfinal field is cemented.

The track Meet of Champions concludes Saturday, and another 31 championships will be claimed between June 11-14. Here’s the full schedule of championship dates and locations.

Hundreds of postseason games have been played, and if anything stands out it’s how remarkably well the seeding system works. To whit: Heading into Wednesday, of the 248 top-eight seeds across all tournaments, 234 were still dancing a week in.

In fact, boys’ lacrosse, which is in the midst of second-round play, has yet to lose a top-eight squad, with Division 3’s No. 9 Hanover and Division 4’s No. 9 Hamilton-Wenham being the highest-seeded squads to bow out heading into Wednesday’s slate.

Also falling out of the lacrosse brackets were No. 11 Advanced Math and Science, which lost to No. 22 Lynnfield, 16-12; No. 13 Westborough, which lost 8-7 to No. 20 Marblehead; and No. 15 Bishop Stang, which couldn’t overcome a late penalty in a 12-8 loss to No. 18 Dover Sherborn.

Let’s sift through the rest of the brackets for more upsets.

Girls’ lacrosse

Similar to the boys, the results have mostly followed seed, with a pair of major exceptions: No. 12 Franklin defeated No. 5 Bishop Feehan, 11-8, for the second time in 10 days in D1, and in D3 eighth-seeded Foxborough was eliminated by No. 9 Dover-Sherborn, 12-6, but that’s closer to a pick ‘em than an upset.

No. 19 Swampscott took out No. 14 North Reading, 9-8, in D3, and while it wasn’t an upset by seeds, it was a surprise to see two-time defending D3 champion Medfield, ranked 10th, take a 12-11 loss to No. 7 Scituate.

Boys’ volleyball

Last year, the upsets came fast and furious in the boys’ volleyball tournament, but this time around it’s been mostly chalk, with all 22 teams seeded in the Top 9 of either division still alive.

The highest seed to drop out thus far was D2’s No. 10 Granby, which fell to No. 7 Marlborough. No. 12 Springfield Sci-Tech was a 3-1 victim of No. 21 Norton, while also in D2, No. 14 Bellingham dropped a 3-1 match to No. 19 Dracut and No. 15 Veritas Prep fell to No. 18 Springfield International, 3-2. In D1, No. 15 Westford was taken down by No. 18 Arlington, 3-1, in the first round. Springfield International and Arlington were eliminated in the second round.

Softball

The fastpitch brackets have been a bit topsy-turvey, but still lacking in major surprises. On Sunday, No. 9 Andover became the first Top 10-seeded squad to relinquish its quest with a 7-2 loss to No. 24 Beverly. On Tuesday, No. 5 Wachusett was stunned by No. 12 Franklin, 3-2, becoming the highest seed bounced from the softball tourney thus far. Also in D1, No. 11 Needham dropped its first-round matchup with No. 22 Methuen, 7-1.

In D5, No. 12 Franklin County Tech ended No. 4 West Boylston’s 20-game win streak with 4-2 second-round win, No. 22 Holbrook tackled No. 11 Turners Falls, 9-5, but the only other results that went against seeding came in the 14 vs. 19 and 15 vs. 18 matchups: No. 19 North Attleborough over No. 14 Longmeadow, 6-5, in D2, No. 19 Narragansett over No. 14 Uxbridge, 5-4, in D4, No. 18 Agawam over No. 15 Marblehead, 6-1, in D2, and No. 18 North Reading over No. 15 Auburn, 10-8, in D3.

Baseball

We’ve arrived at where the action is. The baseball brackets have featured as many surprise results as all other sports combined, but that’s the nature of a sport where you can’t pitch your ace every game. Heading into Wednesday, six Top-10 seeded teams had been eliminated, including the No. 3 team in Division 1.

That would be Springfield Central, which was nipped by No. 35 North Quincy, 5-4, falling victim to a sterling pitching day from Max LaMonica (10 strikeouts in 5⅔ innings) and a two-run double from John Barron in the sixth.

No. 7 Taunton also couldn’t get out of the first round when it couldn’t figure out No. 26 Westford’s ace, Jared Welsh, in a 4-3 defeat, and No. 10 Shrewsbury was bounced by No. 23 Pope Francis, 4-3, in the first round. Those losses have set up a second-round matchup between No. 23 Pope Francis and No. 26 Westford, with the winner guaranteed a quarterfinal berth.

In Division 2, Monday was a rough day for the back half of the Top 10, as No. 6 Shepherd Hill, No. 8 Minnechaug, and No. 9 Hingham were all eliminated. Shepherd Hill lost, 5-4, to No. 27 Canton, Minnechaug was an 8-2 victim of No. 25 Masconomet, and No. 9 Hingham was undone by No. 24 Nashoba, 3-0, and Jake Schwartz’s four-hitter.

In Division 3, No. 22 Danvers defeated No. 11 Swampscott, 4-2; in Division 4 it was No. 22 Old Colony needing 11 innings to upset No. 11 Latin Academy, 1-0, and in D5 No. 20 Brighton got the best of No. 13 Madison Park, 13-8, reversing a regular-season sweep.

title: Boston police officer pleads not guilty to manslaughter in Roxbury fatal shooting
text:
Prosecutors also disclosed new details in court documents filed Thursday.

Dozens of Boston police officers filed into the courthouse Thursday morning to support their colleague. Several of King’s family members also attended the hearing, watching silently from the gallery; one of his sisters wiped away tears.

The swift prosecution marks the first time in more than three decades that a Boston police officer has been criminally charged under similar circumstances.

Prosecutors allege the officer wasn’t justified in shooting at the moving vehicle.

O’Malley, who joined the Boston Police Department about six years ago, told investigators he believed his partner was in danger of being run over.

State law and Boston Police Department policy forbid officers from shooting at a moving vehicle unless there’s no other way to prevent “imminent harm to a person.”

“Mr. O’Malley was not acting in reasonable defense of either himself, the other officer, or the general public,” said Suffolk Assistant District Attorney Ian Polumbaum, calling the shooting excessive.

O’Malley’s supporters have accused Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden of pursuing the prosecution to make a political statement.

“It is truly unjust that Nicholas O’Malley was forced to walk to a courthouse today, when he instead should be walking his beat in Roxbury — meeting, greeting, interacting with, and hearing the concerns of residents there as he always does,” his defense attorney, David Yannetti, told reporters after the arraignment.

In brief remarks during the hearing, Yannetti accused prosecutors of presenting a sanitized version of the facts. He sought to malign King, saying his violent behavior “left officer O’Malley with no choice.”

In recent court filings, Yannetti also documented King’s long criminal history, which includes assaults, breaking and entering, and gun charges.

Police pursued King after he allegedly committed a carjacking outside a pizza restaurant in Boston’s Mission Hill neighborhood; officials say he punched a woman in the face, forced her out of the car, and took off.

A short time later, a Boston police officer was heading to get dinner in his personal vehicle when he spotted the stolen car, prosecutors wrote in the court documents filed Thursday. Instead of broadcasting a message via dispatch radio, the officer called O’Malley’s cellphone, prosecutors said. O’Malley picked up that officer, and together they located the stolen car parked on Linwood Square in Roxbury. O’Malley then made a radio call saying as much.

Approaching on foot, the officers repeatedly told King to show his hands, turn off the car, and unlock the doors.

“King held up his empty hands and appeared to be speaking to O’Malley through the closed window, but did not unlock the doors or douse the engine,” according to prosecutors. He opened the driver’s side window slightly.

O’Malley drew his Taser and shouted, “Bro, I’m going to [expletive] shoot you,” according to prosecutors.

That’s when King backed into the cruiser behind him, then maneuvered the vehicle forward and back, essentially completing a three-point turn to get away, according to records. As he started to drive forward again, O’Malley “switched from the Taser back to his handgun and rapidly fired three times,” prosecutors wrote. The whole encounter lasted just 84 seconds.

In the moments that followed, O’Malley said over the radio that King had “tried to run us over,” according to the records.

“By this time sirens were audible from approaching police units that would have converged on the stolen car minutes earlier had they received timely word of its location,” prosecutors wrote.

King’s family has said he was experiencing a mental health crisis, hearing voices and showing signs of intense paranoia in the hours leading up to the shooting. Relatives said they’d been trying to get him adequate long-term treatment. They said he would cycle through the criminal justice system, sometimes receiving psychiatric medication while he was incarcerated, only to lose access to regular care after his release.

Along with some Boston city councilors and other community leaders, the family called on police to release bodycam footage of the encounter. But prosecutors and police have resisted, saying that would jeopardize the ongoing criminal investigation.

In an interview with homicide detectives during their investigation, O’Malley said he “did not know King or anything about his history, other than the reported carjacking described in the radio call,” prosecutors wrote in court documents. He said he initially planned to discharge his Taser through the small window opening, but he realized that wouldn’t be effective. He said he ultimately fired his gun to protect the other officer, who was positioned on the other side of the car, according to the records.

“I was fearing the worst,” O’Malley told detectives, believing the officer could get run over or crushed between vehicles, according to the records.

Prosecutors disputed his reasoning. They said the street was well-lit and the second officer was safely positioned.

“In fact, the second officer had holstered his own firearm” and tried to grab the car’s door handle, prosecutors wrote. They argued that when O’Malley opened fire, his partner was “at greater risk of being struck by the bullets than by the vehicle.”

They said that even if O’Malley thought his partner was in serious danger, “such a belief was not objectively reasonable.”

Police union leaders, however, are continuing to back O’Malley, reiterating claims that the prosecution is politically motivated.

“Make no mistake about it, he was treated differently because he’s a police officer. He is being scapegoated because he’s a police officer,” Larry Calderone, president of the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, told reporters after the hearing.

De-escalation requires compliance from the suspect, he said. “It’s unfortunate and horrible that we lost a life, but Nick O’Malley did what he should have done as a police officer.”

title: A crane operator gets in a jam, Pokémon cards are stolen, and goats get loose

Officer Bridges did his best to explain to mom crossing Walnut Street during school traffic time was dangerous, but we’re not sure she understood,” police wrote on social media on June 2. “Oh well, they’re safe now.”

Members of the Massachusetts Department of Fire Services Joint Hazard Incident Response Team and the state Department of Environmental Protection assisted firefighters in the Western Mass. town of Becket after local officials found some nitrate film dating back to the 1930s. “Film of this nature is highly flammable, especially in degraded condition, but fortunately these samples were safely disposed of,” state fire officials wrote.

At 10:40 a.m. May 23, Bridgewater police got a call reporting that a man wearing camouflage clothing was “possibly carrying a bazooka” in the area of South and Pleasant streets. The officer who responded to the call reported that the person was a landscaper with a leaf blower.

On May 22, Lincoln police got a call from someone reporting that goats were loose in the area of Mary’s Way. “An officer was able to gather the goats and return them to a nearby pen,” police wrote in the log entry.

At 8:52 p.m. April 18, someone reported to Saugus police that a backpack and box of Pokémon cards had been stolen out of his Honda Accord while he was in the Battleground Games & Hobbies store on Route 1. A similar theft was reported at the same location at 11:29 p.m. May 22, when Saugus police got a call from another victim who said roughly $2,000 worth of "Magic: The Gathering" trading cards were taken out of his Mazda Miata between the hours of 7:30 and 11 p.m. that evening. It seems these kinds of trading cards have become a favorite target of thieves lately. Back in November, more than $35,000 worth of trading cards were reported stolen from a shop in Mashpee, and similar robberies have been reported elsewhere.

Earlier this month, MBTA Transit Police shared video that showed an unruly Orange Line passenger jumping up and repeatedly kicking the window of a train. Police said it happened at around 5 p.m. on May 8 at Jackson Square in Jamaica Plain, and the man’s behavior obviously frightened other passengers. Police said after kicking out the window, he also assaulted a female before scurrying away. He was wearing a green baseball cap that was turned backwards, a dark olive green winter coat with a fur trim hood, and what appeared to be blue pants and white sneakers. title: The few, the proud, the actually contested races in Mass.
text:
A handful of races have the potential to get interesting this September and November — whether a result of unfinished business, intra-party combat, or a rare open seat. Here are a few we’re watching in a cycle where, as CommonWealth Beacon’s Chris Lisinski reported, three out of five seats are otherwise going uncontested:

THE REMATCHES: A pair of Democratic candidates who nearly pulled off primary upsets in 2024 are running it back this year.

In Cambridge, union leader Evan MacKay, who lost to six-term incumbent state Representative Marjorie Decker by just 41 votes, is giving it another go. MacKay, who made transparency a central issue in their last campaign, is once again trying to carve out space to Decker’s left. Decker and her supporters, meanwhile, have already been active. The Massachusetts Teachers Association was sending out mailers backing her a full year before the general election in November.

And in Springfield, public school teacher Johnnie McKnight is spoiling for a rematch against state Representative Bud Williams after Williams defeated him by 245 votes in their 2024 primary. Nicole Coakley, a mental health clinician, is also running in the Democratic contest.

THE OPEN SEATS: State Senator Patricia Jehlen’s impending retirement set off a game of musical chairs in the Camberville/Medford area.

The race to replace her in the district that covers all of Somerville and parts of Cambridge, Medford and Winchester has attracted a crowded Democratic field: state representatives Erika Uyterhoeven and Christine Barber, Somerville City Councilor Matt McLaughlin, Cambridge City Councilor Burhan Azeem, and Tom Hopcroft of Winchester.

That race has opened up competition down-ballot, too. Somerville City Councilor Ben Ewen-Campen and Olivia Gilligan-Corsetti, a former staffer for Governor Maura Healey, are both vying for Uyterhoeven’s seat. And three Democrats — Somerville City Councilor Will Mbah, software engineer Paul Ruseau, and Chris Oates, founder of the data analysis startup Legislata — are competing to fill Barber’s spot.

On the Cape, Brewster Democrat and school committee member Steve Leibowitz and Dennis Select Board vice chair Chris Lambton, who once appeared on “The Bachelorette,” are both seeking the Democratic nomination in the race to fill the seat currently held by state Representative Chris Flanagan, whose name isn’t on the ballot as he faces federal fraud charges. Joe Glynn, whose party is listed as “Gulf War Veteran” on the state’s candidate list, is also in that race.

In Western Mass., where former state Representative Natalie Blais’ seat has been open since she resigned for a job at UMass Amherst, unenrolled Whately Town Clerk Amy Lavallee will face whoever wins the Democratic primary between Corinne Coryat, Blais’ chief of staff at the State House, and Greenfield City Council President Lora Wondolowski.

THE PARTY CRASHERS: There are others looking to oust members of their own party.

Three Boston-area state senators are facing primary challenges. In addition to Nick Collins and Will Brownsberger — whose contests have drawn no shortage of attention amid disputes with Mayor Michelle Wu — incumbent Mike Rush is facing a challenge from Persis Yu, a non-profit executive running to his left.

In Plymouth County, Republican Mark Townsend, the chair of the Carver Select Board, is looking to take out first-term GOP state Representative John Gaskey, one of the Legislature’s most conservative members.

THE DEBATE DEBATE: A sign the US Senate primary between Senator Ed Markey and Representative Seth Moulton is finally entering a new phase: Markey is finally mentioning Moulton by name.

After Moulton spent the last handful of months hounding Markey for a debate, the 79-year-old senator threw down his own gauntlet Thursday. In addition to a mid-August debate and another that’s still to be scheduled, Markey is challenging Moulton to meet him on stage in western Mass. in late June or early July — about two months out from the Sept. 1 primary.

The challenge came with some trash talk. Markey targeted Moulton for “giving airtime to a MAGA multimillionaire in a fake debate,” an apparent reference to the mid-June debate scheduled between Moulton and GOP Senate hopeful John Deaton (and to which Markey was also invited but declined).

Moulton quickly accepted and hit back — hard: “No more hiding in Maryland,” Moulton wrote on social media. “I am ready to debate you every single week until the primary in September — if you can keep up.”

MIKE CHECK: Just because Mike Kennealy got bounced from the ballot doesn’t mean he’s done throwing elbows in the GOP primary for governor.

The former housing and economic development secretary jumped back into the Republican governor’s race Thursday — this time as a surrogate. Kennealy endorsed former Abiomed chief executive Mike Minogue, calling him “the only remaining Republican with a chance to defeat Governor Healey.”

The endorsement itself was a backhand to former MBTA chief administrator Brian Shortsleeve, a fellow Baker administration alum also running for the GOP nomination. But Kennealy, who failed to get enough support at the state GOP convention to make the ballot, also took a few direct shots in a lengthy post on X.

AI FAIL: AI keeps popping up in lawmakers’ and candidates’ digital campaign lit. The latest example: a since-deleted graphic that features an image of Republican state representative hopeful Larry Quintal in front of a capitol building that looks not-quite like the Massachusetts State House, with the words “Working for a better Maine” tucked in the bottom right corner.

Quintal called the mistake-riddled graphic “an oversight.” He’s looking for a rematch against state Representative Lisa Field (who faces her own primary) in the district that covers parts of Taunton and Easton.

BARS GET STOPPAGE TIME: Mass. House passes proposal to extend bar hours to 3 a.m. during World Cup, putting bill on fast track by Samantha J. Gross, The Boston Globe: The legislation would enable — but not require — bars and restaurants with liquor licenses to sell alcohol an additional hour past current closing times, starting Monday through July 31, albeit with the blessing of local licensing boards.

PRIVACY PUSH: House and Senate now united on need for stronger data privacy protections by Ella Adams and Sam Drysdale, State House News Service: The House on Thursday unanimously passed a major data privacy bill that would require affirmative consent before sensitive information can be sold or shared, ban the sale of precise geolocation data, create special protections for minors, and authorize enforcement by the attorney general and, in some cases, private individuals.

Here’s how the Globe’s Hiawatha Bray sizes up the bill: “a Swiss Army knife of privacy protection tools, some of them with teeth.”

MONUMENTAL MOVE: Park Service orders removal of ‘woke’ quotes at Boston’s Bunker Hill monument by Jake Spring, The Washington Post: The National Park Service has ordered the removal of three quotes at the Bunker Hill Monument in Boston commemorating a Revolutionary War battle because they have run afoul of President Trump’s policy seeking to scrub “corrosive ideology” from federal institutions, according to three people familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

At the monument on Thursday, the decision was met with confusion, per the Boston Globe’s Tonya Alanez and Chloe Pisani: “I don’t see the sense in removing them.”

LATEST ON O’MALLEY: Boston police officer pleads not guilty to manslaughter in Roxbury fatal shooting by Lea Skene, The Boston Globe: A Boston police officer pleaded not guilty to manslaughter Thursday in the fatal shooting of a carjacking suspect after recently being indicted by a grand jury in Suffolk Superior Court, the latest development in a polarizing case that has drawn outrage from the department’s largest union.

GAME PLAN: Boston to launch command center in Seaport during World Cup, Sail Boston by Diane Adame, GBH News: The city is planning a central command center in the Seaport to coordinate public safety, transportation, public health and emergency management for the World Cup and other tourist events this summer. The command center will operate on all World Cup match days, and will be partially active on days during Fan Fest events when there isn’t a match at Boston Stadium.

WORKING ACROSS THE AI-SLE: A Massachusetts Democrat negotiated an AI bill with a Republican. It ignited a political firestorm. by Tal Kopan, The Boston Globe: As Democratic Representative Lori Trahan worked to craft a bipartisan bill on artificial intelligence with California Republican Jay Obernolte, the resistance was fierce and swift — from her own side of the aisle. On Thursday, they unveiled the proposal, which would impose safety requirements on developers of AI, the result of weeks of negotiations. But the release did little to mute criticism of the bill, and Trahan’s involvement in it, illustrating the heightened politics of the issue.

title: Chelsea’s ‘Soccer Field Day’ stokes excitement before World Cup in Boston
text:
Soccer Field Day was part of a series of events surrounding the city’s Fiesta de Fútbol: From June 11 to July 19, Chelsea Square will transform into an outdoor watch party, complete with local food vendors, music, and other community programming. Unlike other watch parties in the Boston area, the broadcast feeds in Chelsea will feature Telemundo broadcasts with Spanish-language commentators. The programming is partially funded by a $175,000 state grant, one of a number of grants for World Cup watch parties across the state. The city will also host a free alumni tournament for graduates of Chelsea High School and Chelsea charter schools at Veterans Stadium on June 27.

“Soccer is so simple, it’s one ball, two nets, and if you don’t have two nets, you can use anything, and it speaks to the whole world, and so that’s why I think soccer connects to everybody,” Giuffrida said. “It’s accessible.”

Home to a diverse immigrant community that is largely from Latin America, Chelsea cherishes a strong soccer culture. Several youth programs, including Matias Soccer Club, founded by players from Colombian club Envigado, and the Escuela de Fútbol Infantil, work especially, though not exclusively, with immigrant children. And at a time of increased immigration enforcement in the Boston area, youth soccer programs in Chelsea and elsewhere can act as a refuge for children and parents alike.

Saturday’s Field Day event included players from the city’s youth soccer teams, Chelsea High School, and the nonprofit Soccer Without Borders, which uses soccer as a vehicle for positive change.

Alejandro Lopez, a parent and coach, played soccer as a kid in Highland Park over 30 years ago, and he’s been impressed with the growth of youth soccer in the city.

“Growing up in Chelsea, my whole life, we really didn’t have events like this for soccer,” he said as he looked across the turf. “It was a lot different, was real grass, and wasn’t maintained like it is today.”

Lopez said his daughter, Valencia Lopez, competed in her first-ever tournament through Soccer Without Borders, and the organization has even offered her a chance to escort one of the players onto the field during one of the games and to watch the match. She is already a soccer fan.

“My favorite team is Costa Rica, [El] Salvador and Puerto Rico,” she said.

The larger community is gearing up for the games, with excitement and some trepidation. As Soccer Field Day drew to a close, on Broadway, a main thoroughfare brimming with retail stores, restaurants and bars, Jaredy Ramirez, who was eating at Curly’s Restaurant, worried that the immigration crackdowns of the last year might sap the World Cup of some of its joy. The Trump administration has said those in the country legally have nothing to fear.

“A lot of people, from out of the country, they’re not coming because they see what is happening right now,” Ramirez said.

William Tejada, who said he watches 10 or 15 soccer games a weekend, said he was nevertheless excited for the upcoming matches. He got to go to a World Cup match in person back in 1994, when the US last hosted the games. Back then, he said, soccer wasn’t such a popular sport here.

“But now it is,” he said. “I think that was the beginning.”

He had free tickets then. Not this time, though, and with sky-high ticket prices starting in the thousands, he plans to watch the games from his TV.

Camilo Fonseca of the Globe staff contributed reporting.

title: Robert Coles, Pulitzer-winning psychiatrist who shaped public policy, dies at 97
text:
But Dr. Coles’s thoughts came with a quiet passion and a stunning velocity that shook the worlds of medicine and education, civil rights and American civic life.

“He added greatly to our understanding of children and the world they live in,” said Judith Palfrey, chief of the division of general pediatrics at Children’s Hospital Boston for more than two decades and a professor of pediatrics at Harvard Medical School. “He taught students of all ages through his books, and he studied the social determinants of health long before it became an important topic in popular conversation. He made these issues very accessible.”

Dr. Coles did so while helping to reinvent the professions of psychiatry and pediatrics and elementary and undergraduate education.

“His combination of brilliance and humility is what provided his lasting insights,” said David Greene, an expert in human development and psychology who is the president of Colby College. “He was open to hearing others and learning from them, not simply being the teacher or the expert. Seeing value in others and in their experiences seems to be a lost art, but he kept it very much alive and helped countless others recognize the power of the stories in us all.”

Dr. Coles’s acolytes and onetime teaching fellows are scattered across the country, a kind of diaspora sustaining the principal precepts of his teaching: the thoughts of children are significant; the lives of adults are empty without introspection and intervention in social problems; and people of all ages can profit by, as he would counsel his students, “putting your neuroses to work.”

One of Dr. Coles’s own neuroses — he might have called it his preoccupation — was to fill each moment not only with purpose but also with reflection.

“In an environment where everyone was ambitiously rushing around,” said one of those Coles graduate fellows, Gene Corbin, Harvard’s former dean for public service, “he created a space for students to reflect on who they were and their responsibilities to others and to society.”

When Corbin headed Harvard’s Phillips Brooks House Center for Public Service and Engaged Scholarship, he created an annual Robert Coles “Call of Service” Lecture and Award, a play on the title of a book Dr. Coles wrote that examines motivations for service.

Dr. Coles’s life ricocheted into unconventional, unpredictable, and unconnected directions. He was outspoken on issues of race and faith. He strayed into areas such as music (a book about Bruce Springsteen) and social activism (a book on the Catholic Worker leader Dorothy Day). He was as interested in the victims of polio as in the victims of racial discrimination (among the topics in the multivolume “Children of Crisis” that was awarded the Pulitzer in 1973). He published two volumes about the psychoanalyst Erik Erickson and one book illustrated by Norman Rockwell. He joined the poet-physician William Carlos Williams on medical house calls and hid the antiwar priest Daniel Berrigan from the FBI in his Concord home and the two produced “The Geography of Faith: Underground Conversations on Religious, Political, and Social Change.” He taught the novels of Dickens to law students and campaigned with Senator Robert F. Kennedy.

But his most evocative and enduring encounter may have been with a 6-year-old Black girl in segregated Louisiana, the best example of Dr. Coles’s devotion to what he called “in medias res,” Latin for “into the middle of things,” or, as he defined, it, “’in the midst of trouble,’ right in the midst of it.’’

Dr. Coles was an Air Force psychiatrist stationed in New Orleans when he learned about the integration crucible of Ruby Bridges, whose entry into the all-white William Frantz Elementary School in the autumn of 1960 triggered street protests and led the white parents to withdraw their children from the premises. He approached the local branch of the NAACP and asked to consult with the child, who was taught — in an otherwise empty first grade classroom — by an inspiring teacher from West Roxbury, Barbara Henry.

Henry said she did not know until years later the role Dr. Coles played for Ruby.

“A teacher told me there was some doctor involved with Ruby,” she said in an interview for this obituary. “I thought it was some kind of physical doctor.”

But Ruby surmised what Dr. Coles was up to.

“Every week Dr. Coles would come to my house with his tape recorder,” Bridges said in “Through My Eyes,” a book she wrote about her early life. “He would ask how I was doing, and I mostly told him I was doing fine. Then he would pull out crayons and asked me to draw pictures of myself or the school or some of the people in my life.”

She said she enjoyed the time with Dr. Coles, who also would write a children’s picture book about Ruby, “because an important man was coming to visit and color with me, and that made me feel special.”

Separately in “The Moral Life of Children,” Dr. Coles wrote, “Ruby had a will and used it to make an ethical choice; she demonstrated moral stamina; she possessed honor, courage.”

Moral stamina, honor, and courage were the touchstones of the creed of Dr. Coles, who was awarded a MacArthur “genius” award in 1981 and the Medal of Freedom, the highest civilian honor America bestows, by President Clinton in 1998.

“From Dr. Coles I learned the importance of staying committed to the things you love, the things you cared about, along with your professionalism,” said Brian Buckley, who took the Coles course in 1989, became a Coles teaching fellow a decade later, and eventually became executive director of the Southwest Native American Foundation. “He constantly told me how I could put my thoughts, insights, and ideals into action in practical daily life.”

For Dr. Coles in his own life, that meant a lifelong commitment to understanding how children thought and acted.

“There weren’t that many people around who were looking at the lives of children in such an open and deep way and who didn’t restrict the role of a doctor to just practicing medicine,” said Richard Goldstein, a pediatric palliative care doctor at Boston Children’s. “He really wanted to think about the insights a doctor might have for the world. He particularly cared about the moral lives of children.”

That inevitably drew him into religious waters. In his influential 1990 “The Spiritual Life of Children,” he argued that the seeds of religious practice were planted by parents who “talked about faith with them as children and practiced the faith in their presence.”

That constituted another break with the conventional thinking of the academic and medical milieu that Dr. Coles inhabited.

“Because he was a psychiatrist, he wrestled with the antireligious bias of his own profession,” said J. Bradley Wigger, a minister who teaches at Kentucky’s Louisville Presbyterian Theological Seminary and whose research was inspired by Dr. Coles’s work. “But he understood that religion could be a deep and powerful resource in the lives of children, particularly if they were in the hospital or going through trauma or other difficult circumstances.”

Though he possessed some of the instincts and methods of a reporter, Dr. Coles was not a journalist but a scholar, trusting the insights a child would share over an ice cream cone or in a school bus.

“He was an amazing listener,” said Goldstein, another Coles student who became a Coles teaching assistant and eventually a Coles collaborator, “and this technique started with Ruby Bridges.”

Dr. Coles was a rebel in a blue Oxford dress shirt, an iconoclast with a heterodox ideology.

“You mention his name to people in his field, and the word ‘maverick’ always comes up,” said Clark Power, a professor of psychology and education at Notre Dame. “He was at war with the establishment.”

In the days of rioting following the 1968 assassination of the Reverend Martin Luther King Jr., Dr. Coles challenged students who demanded institutional change through violence, suggesting that women in Black sections of Boston might not recoil at the presence of a white Irish-American police officer in their neighborhoods. He railed against what he called the “carefully well adjusted and certified” mandarins of his profession, arguing in “A Young Psychiatrist Looks at his Profession,” a 1961 broadside later collected in his 1995 “The Mind’s Fate,” that his colleagues — complacent if not burned-out — trafficked in “wordy and doctrinaire caricatures of life” with their “habits of talk [becoming] cluttered with jargon or the trivial.”

That was not the Coles way, though his upbringing was as conventional as his teachings were unconventional.

Reared in the Back Bay and Milton by a Jewish father from Leeds, England, and a mother from Iowa, he attended Boston Latin School and majored in English at Harvard before abandoning his dream of becoming a high school teacher, switching to the pre-med track, and, after graduation, enrolling in the Columbia College of Physicians and Surgeons.

The man who influenced so many was himself influenced by several people he encountered.

Before there was Ruby Bridges — whose passage in front of what he called in a later video “200 people waiting at 8:00 in the morning telling her they wanted to kill her” moved him deeply — he was shaped by childhood visits to the Museum of Fine Arts. There he encountered the Gauguin triptych: “D’où venons-nous? Que sommes-nous? Où allons-nous?” three searching questions (translated into “Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We Going?”) that his father told him was “the human story.” That notion would lead him to the conviction that the purpose of higher education was learning “how to live an honorable, a caring, and a decent life.”

Walker Percy was another important influence. Dr. Coles read Percy’s 1961 novel “The Moviegoer” — about a young man’s search for meaning — at a time when, Dr. Coles wrote, “I was somewhat lost, confused, vulnerable, and, it seemed, drifting badly.”

Dr. Coles credited Percy, who died in 1990, for giving focus to his life, saying, “I can scarcely imagine how I would have thought about either my own life or the lives of the children, parents, teachers I have met (in order to write “Children of Crisis”), were he to have decided, long ago, to keep his important and instructive thoughts to himself.” Dr. Coles would write Percy’s biography.

Dr. Coles was a constant presence in classrooms nationwide where psychiatry was taught.

“No one who studied psychiatry in the past half century failed to encounter Robert Coles,” said Charles Raison, a prominent psychiatrist and professor at the University of Wisconsin Madison and Emory University. “He realized the importance of childhood in adult development and the needs of children, and he knew that the things they thought about needed to be understood and studied. That was really a big deal, and it influenced the entire profession.”

His wife, the former Jane Hallowell, whom he married in 1960 and with whom he wrote the 1978 book “Women of Crisis: Lives of Struggle and Hope,” died in 1993.

In addition to Michael Coles, he leaves two sons, Daniel and Robert, and four grandsons, according to the Post.

In a 2008 article in the Journal of Catholic Legal Studies, Widener University Commonwealth Law School professor Greg Randall Lee wrote that Dr. Coles “would say that he has not so much performed research throughout his career as he has been a student of life,” adding, “He is not so much an author as a storyteller, which, in his own words, makes him a healer, because ‘healers make sense of stories.’ ”

Indeed, Greene, the Colby president, said that Dr. Coles’s book “The Call of Stories” “taught me to listen for stories instead of just to them.”

title: What’s boosting the Massachusetts tech pipeline? Colleges and universities, of course.
text:
Across the academic spectrum and around the state, education leaders are rolling out initiatives to prepare students for a world where the pace of change is accelerating rapidly. That will demand more flexibility, sounder judgment, and greater entrepreneurial energy from today’s graduates. It will also challenge academic and government leaders to ensure that more of those graduates build careers and companies in the Boston area and Massachusetts.

“The superpower has always been the university system,” says Aman Narang, CEO of restaurant-tech company Toast and an MIT alum. “The best thing Boston can do is keep these people around.”

For its part, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology is working to drive artificial intelligence forward in sectors where the region is strongest, from biotechnology and robotics to defense and clean energy. It’s also trying to broaden entrepreneurship through a “dorm-to-startup” push, creating a pipeline of support services — from hack-a-thons to venture funding — to help students to start companies between classes.

“We’re in the race, and we can dominate in some areas,” says Anantha Chandrakasan, provost at MIT, who is leading several of its new initiatives.

Trade schools are also stepping up. Franklin Cummings Tech, for example, is hosting “skills showcases” at its new Roxbury campus, inviting Boston-area employers seeking tech-savvy students who can operate high-tech machinery.

“Front-line hiring managers, CEOs, industry leaders, they get a sense of what our students know,” says Aisha Francis, the school’s president. “And we give students a chance to show their skills.”

Colleges and universities across the state are ramping up training and collaborations with employers in a range of fields as companies adapt operations and business models to artificial intelligence. Some schools in Massachusetts, including MIT, are carving out a specialty in applied AI — sometimes called “AI+X” — deploying the technology to help businesses, hospitals, and research institutions to supercharge productivity, innovation, and scientific breakthroughs.

But too few leading artificial intelligence companies are based in the Boston area, says Boston venture capitalist Jeff Bussgang, who teaches a Harvard Business School course on launching technology ventures. The region’s universities still act as talent magnets and launchpads for entrepreneurs, Bussgang says, but too many of the brightest students launch companies in other states.

“Let’s get back in the arena,” Bussgang says. “Let’s fight for the talent, not sit back on our laurels.”

One local company fighting for talent — and winning — is Blitzy, a Cambridge startup that raised $200 million in May to develop AI apps that help businesses revamp old software programs and write new ones.

Brian Elliott, the founder of Blitzy (which is backed by Bussgang’s Flybridge Capital Partners), says he finds it easier to recruit talented graduates of local colleges and universities for his 80-person company without having to hire in the shadow of Silicon Valley giants such as Google, ChatGPT developer OpenAI, and advanced chipmaker Nvidia.

Blitzy’s pitch, in part, is to offer people a chance to build careers with a growing company rather than jump from one California goliath to another.

“We think there’s a competitive advantage to being one of the most interesting companies to work for here versus trying to compete with the headquarters of Nvidia, the headquarters of Google,” says Elliott. “There are so many brilliant engineers and [commercial talent] here in Boston that we can attract. That’s allowed us to have a very loyal employee base.”

The innovations fueled by local universities aren’t limited to AI. Coming out of the MIT lab of scientist and engineer Yet-Ming Chiang, for example, are new products that are allowing batteries to store more electricity over longer periods, creating more opportunities for wind, solar, and other clean energy sources.

Students at Chiang’s lab and other MIT research centers are also working on innovations in microchips, critical minerals, fusion technology, and defense tech. All are examples of “tough tech” projects combining science and engineering, which Chiang says “are in the sweet spot of the Boston ecosystem.”

At Worcester Polytechnic Institute, meanwhile, student researchers are recycling batteries and transforming bamboo and other non-food plants into fuel. The school is tailoring its research, along with its undergraduate and master’s programs, to align with the needs of Central Massachusetts industries such as data storage, medical gear, and biomanufacturing.

Grace Wang, WPI president, says the state’s companies and research universities are creating a lane in Massachusetts for using AI to make robots, drug development, manufacturing, and supply chains more efficient.

But that can only work, she says, if colleges and universities instill the broad knowledge, curiosity, flexibility, and open-mindedness students will need to thrive in a fast-changing technological world.

“We educate our students purposely on the human skills,” Wang says, “the skills to work in a team, communicate effectively, critical thinking, dealing with the pace, ambiguity, and complexity of this world.”

title: Three MBTA bus routes to remain free through end of year
text:
Three MBTA bus routes will remain free to ride through the end of the year, Mayor Michelle Wu and the MBTA announced Tuesday, just weeks before the fare-free pilot program was again set to run out of funding.

Spokespeople for the Wu administration and the transit agency did not immediately make clear Tuesday how much the program’s temporary extension would cost.

City and state officials indicated that money used for the MBTA’s reduced fare program would cover the plan to temporarily extend the program for bus routes 23, 28, and 29, which go through Mattapan, Dorchester, and Roxbury. Wu’s office said in a statement that the reduced fare program “resulted in cost savings that are being applied to deliver this extension through the end of the year.”

City officials also said that they plan on “working this summer and fall on options for the fare free program in 2027.”

“There’s no such thing as free,” said Brian Kane, executive director of the MBTA Advisory Board. “It just means someone else is paying for it, and every trip on the MBTA is already significantly subsidized.”

Wu’s office on Tuesday touted the program’s success, saying riders have taken nearly 23,000 fare-free trips every weekday on the three bus routes since the start of the year. All-door boarding on the buses has cut times at stops by 20 percent, according to the city.

“We’re proud to partner with the MBTA to extend this successful program as we continue building a more reliable, accessible, and affordable transportation system across Boston,” Wu said in a statement.

Wu first eliminated fares on the three bus routes in March 2022, when she used $8 million in federal pandemic relief dollars to fund the program.

Then, in February 2024, Wu again used federal COVID-19 funds to reimburse the MBTA and continue the pilot program for an additional two years.

That money was set to run out at the end of February, but roughly a week before, city officials announced that enough of those funds remained to pay for the program through the end of this month.

Transit advocates have fretted over the program’s long-term future and from where officials could pull money to keep rides free on the three bus routes.

Seth Gadbois, a transportation attorney for the Conservation Law Foundation, applauded the extension of “this essential program.” But Gadbois said it feels “a little like we’re driving in circles when it comes to long-term solutions.”

“We bought four months of this back in February, and here we are buying six months more now,” Gadbois said. “Especially at a time when many transit advocates see the administration’s commitments to climate safety and justice missing from the budget, this is a promising and important step, but riders need and deserve more long-term certainty.”

Reggie Ramos, the executive director of the nonprofit Transportation for Massachusetts, said she was not surprised officials wanted to extend the fare-free routes through the end of this year, calling it a “wildly popular program that has proven to be a lifeline for that corridor.”

“Beyond the extension of this program, the real and critical questions are: How do we make programs like this sustainable and how do we ensure that the service these buses provide are at a level that is dignified and truly reliable?” Ramos said in a statement.

Transit advocates have pushed Wu and city officials to find a long-term, sustainable funding source to continue the program. In February, Wu’s office said the city is discussing the future of the program with the MBTA.

Supporters of the three fare-free routes have pointed to city statistics that show more than one-quarter of riders on the routes save $20 or more per month, savings they can put toward other expenses.

City Councilor Ruthzee Louijeune said the routes are used “ heavily by our working-class and Black and Brown residents.”

“We’re helping families save money, making it easier for people to get to work, school, and essential services, and continuing to build a more equitable and connected city,” she said in a statement provided by Wu’s office.

Niki Griswold can be reached at niki.griswold@globe.com. Follow her @nikigriswold. Chris Van Buskirk can be reached at chris.vanb@globe.com. Follow him on X @byChrisVan

title: In a shift, Airbnb will chip in to support Boston’s World Cup after all. What gives?
text:
Featuring: Sally Kornbluth, Siyu Huang, Julie Chen, Brooke Thomson, Ryan Durkin, Michael Nichols, Tim Berners-Lee, David Letterman, Corean Reynolds, Kathleen Joyce, Eneida Roman, Dieter Zetsche, and more.

For Governor Maura Healey, there’s been an important piece missing in World Cup planning: How to get free tickets into the hands of kids across Massachusetts.

Healey knows the power of sports and how it can change young lives. She lived it. Basketball took her from a small town in New Hampshire to Harvard University, and opened a whole new world for her.

So with the world’s biggest sporting event coming to town, Healey has been reaching out to see if any local organization would donate tickets, which easily cost several hundred dollars apiece. No dice. That just shows how hard it has been to drum up local support for the World Cup. Not even the governor could convince anyone to pony up for kids.

Then along came Airbnb. Three weeks ago, I reported how the short-term rental company had set aside millions of dollars to support World Cup programs in 16 host cities. Last summer Airbnb met with the local host committee, Boston Soccer 26, about a potential sponsorship here. Let’s just say it didn’t go as planned. Airbnb moved on, spreading their largesse from San Francisco to New York refurbishing soccer pitches and sponsoring festivals.

But my piece set off a flurry of calls from leaders wondering how much Airbnb wanted to play ball. And on Monday, Airbnb found a big way to help Massachusetts when Healey announced that the company is donating 1,104 World Cup tickets to local kids.

The agreement came together quickly. If the state could come up with a distribution plan, Airbnb would foot the bill. Community partners were lined up with the Massachusetts Alliance of Boys & Girls Clubs taking the lead on dispersing tickets to Foxborough’s seven games.

“I’m just really grateful to Airbnb for stepping up … when we asked them to do this, they said yes right away,” Healey told me. “This is just something I wanted to do from the beginning. It’s a big deal having the World Cup here. We know that not everybody’s going to be able to afford to get to these games.”

To be clear, this isn’t charity for Airbnb. It’s good business. Soccer fans need a place to stay, and Airbnb anticipates that the World Cup will be its biggest hosting event yet. A Deloitte study commissioned by Airbnb projected that 164,000 tourists would come from around the world for the tournament, and close to 10 percent would stay in a short-term rental.

Airbnb spokesman Ivan Valladares would not say how much the company is spending on the tickets other than it is a “significant investment.” But Airbnb, as an official FIFA partner, does get a little break because it can buy tickets at face value. The company has also given away tickets in bulk to youth in other host cities — Mexico City and in New Jersey and New York.

Valladares said Airbnb has been looking for ways to support host cities but ultimately relies on each region to tell them what’s needed. In Philadelphia, for example, the city prioritized free subway rides home from games, so Airbnb underwrote the cost for that.

“We have taken the lead of the host cities on these investments,” said Valladares.

Airbnb isn’t quite done with showing love to Massachusetts. After all, Nathan Blecharczyk, the company’s cofounder and chief strategy officer, grew up in West Roxbury and is a proud Boston Latin Academy graduate who gifted $1 million to the school.

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu has needs too. And despite Airbnb’s history of beefing with the now mayor, the company is expected to announce it will fund a $200,000 microgrant program for small businesses and neighborhood organizations to support their activities during our very busy summer of tourism.

So on the eve of the World Cup, the news is getting good.

What’s your take? Share in the comments here.

The Globe just dropped its fifth annual Tech Power Players list, highlighting the CEOs, founders, investors, and other leaders who are supercharging the Greater Boston technology scene. Some names have already been all over our newsletter including Whoop’s Ryan Durkin (who is spearheading the Massachusetts AI Coalition), Rapid7′s Corey Thomas (yes, he’s still there, as executive chairman), and state economic secretary Eric Paley (formerly of VC firm Founder Collective). Others on the list include MIT president Sally Kornbluth, University of Massachusetts-Lowell Chancellor Julie Chen, Franklin Cummings Tech Institute president Aisha Francis, and (finally) Tim Berners-Lee! Who’s No. 1? You’ll just have to read to find out. Alongside the list are thoughtful analyses on the edge that Boston has over Silicon Valley when it comes to AI, the role of colleges and universities in feeding the local tech workforce, and more.

Bartenders might not be excited by the new law that extends last call to 3 a.m. through July 31, but Downtown Boston Alliance president Michael Nichols is. That’s because the legislation signed by the governor on Monday includes a provision to create public social consumption zones, allowing people to walk around in a designated area with a glass of wine without flouting open container laws. Nichols piloted a version on Temple Place in 2023 and 2024, working with Boston nightlife czar Corean Reynolds and Boston Licensing Board chairwoman Kathleen Joyce. The street was shut down to cars, and a big screen was set up for a full day of Sunday tailgating starting with the Patriots game in London. For those who are wary of change, Nichols says: “This is something new to try, and I think there are probably just as many or more people excited about trying something new.”

Your next car might just be powered by solid-state battery technology developed at Greater Boston’s newest publicly traded company. Billerica-based Factorial is now trading on the Nasdaq Stock Market, following its merger last week with a special purpose acquisition company, or SPAC, affiliated with Cartesian Growth Corp. Factorial said the terms of the merger implies an equity value of $1.3 billion for the company. Leading the charge: chief executive Siyu Huang, executive chairman Joe Taylor and new board member Dieter Zetsche (or “Dr. Z” to me and you). Several big car companies are already invested. Among them: Mercedes-Benz, which took one of these Factorial batteries for a test drive last year and made it more than 700 miles on a single charge.

With the World Cup on its way to Boston, the Massachusetts Lodging Association and its PR firm, Hollywood Agency, put AI to the test by comparing answers from artificial-intelligence queries to some frequent questions to those offered by 13 veteran concierges at Boston hotels. Unsurprisingly, the concierges outperformed their robotic counterparts. The best clam chowder? Most concierges say the Sail Loft in the North End, while the robots picked more obvious choices: Union Oyster House and Legal Sea Foods. A good restaurant to visit without a reservation? AI says Neptune Oyster, but concierges know you could easily spend an hour on Salem Street waiting to get in. Maybe the worst advice: day trip destinations. The AI queries recommend the mansions of Newport, while most concierges suggest Salem or other spots on the North Shore. Seems like the robots have never driven to Newport in the summer.

Should the state Legislature make a 3 a.m. last call for bars permanent, instead of just for this summer? Take our survey here, and we’ll share the results on Friday.

Last week, we asked which talk show host met up with several business leaders at the annual Profile in Courage awards gala at the JFK Library on May 31. Readers primarily guessed Jay Leno, perhaps because of his Massachusetts ties. But the correct answer was David Letterman, who briefly hung out with Eneida Roman of We Are ALX, JD Chesloff of the Mass. Business Roundtable and Brooke Thomson of Associated Industries of Massachusetts.

It’s been two years since Jack Connors died, and Boston still misses the ad mogul-turned-philanthropist as much as ever. On Tuesday, one of his buddies, Eversource chief executive Joe Nolan, unveiled a new statue of Connors outside 200 Clarendon (aka the John Hancock Tower) where he once presided as head of ad agency Hill Holliday and then ran his family office from the top floor. The statue, funded by private donations, also drew Governor Maura Healey and Mayor Michelle Wu to the unveiling.

This newsletter was edited by Tim Logan and Greg Huang and produced by Diamond Naga Siu. Have a great week out there.

Have a question for the team? Email us at powerplay@globe.com.

title: How Franklin Cummings Tech president Aisha Francis is transforming the vocational school
text:
“It is a tough time in higher education, and we are not immune to the slings and arrows that are being aimed at so-called elite colleges,” Francis said. “It’s a call for us to be as creative as possible, as nimble as possible, and as collaborative as possible. Those are the hallmarks of our transformation over the past five years.”

In the latest episode of Bold Types, Francis sat down with Globe business reporter Janelle Nanos to talk about how her English PhD led her to lead a vocational school, why the job feels like part of her family history, and whether she’s managed to get any shut-eye lately. This interview was condensed and edited.

You became president of the then Benjamin Franklin Institute of Technology in 2021. Since that time, you’ve doubled enrollment, exceeded a $60 million campaign fund-raising goal, and established or expanded several majors. I’m curious if you’ve slept at all in the last few years.

I have slept [laughs]. I became president at a time when things were very different for the world and things were very different on campus. We have been very engaged here in this prospect of making trade and tech education accessible since 1791. When you do that work with folks who are first-generation and people who are not necessarily financially wealthy, it’s always work that can be precarious.

You have a PhD in literature. From an academic perspective, you may not expect someone with that sort of a background to lead a vocational school. I wanted to know more about what has driven you to this role.

Education, and education access, has always been a throughline. I come from a family of educators. And through some genealogy that I’ve been doing, I learned that I have a great-great aunt who actually was running a voc tech one-room school in the 1940s.

I do believe that there are things that you are called to do in this life. It’s really fate in some ways. I felt compelled by the mission of Franklin Cummings Tech at a point in my life when I wanted to work in higher ed administration and put the skills that I’ve amassed over my lifetime to bear for a community that I cared about.

Americans’ faith in higher ed is fading, with a recent Newsweek poll showing that nearly 60 percent of respondents said it wasn’t worth the cost. What’s your pitch for why vocational education can make a difference?

We were established as a college for people who were working and wanted to get an apprenticeship. But what we realized is that the work the students were doing to pay their way through college was completely disconnected from the automotive associate degree or from the cybersecurity degree that they were pursuing. That then made it such that their work and their degree were in competition. And we need work and the pursuit of education that leads to a good job to be complementary.

We can create more incentives for companies to create career exposure opportunities for students who are learning at all different levels. Our piece of that puzzle is to provide education that embeds industry-recognized credentials and to do our level best to make sure folks get in and get out in a very timely fashion.

Can you tell me more about the opportunities you’ve been able to introduce in your new building?

We teach HVAC and refrigeration and are making sure that our education is as comprehensive as possible and is as embedded with sustainability as possible. So our students are also learning about installation of heat pumps as well as traditional furnaces.

We are mostly focused on delivering certificate and associate degree education that leads to wonderful careers in our region and beyond. We have 10 tech and trade majors. These are the makers. These are the folks that help to operate and maintain our infrastructure, our built environment, our homes, and the buildings where we conduct our daily life.

Everyone I’ve talked to has said that this school exists because of the sheer force of your will. Tell me about the behind-the-scenes — the networks you’ve created and the relationships you’ve developed — to get some of Boston’s biggest names to look here and say: “This is where my money should go. This is where my emphasis should go. This is where my heart should go.”

There are a few ways to answer that question. First of all, I do believe that it is important to bring all of yourself to a big project, to an assignment if you will. And I think of my professional roles as an assignment. And so if I’m going to commit to something, I’m all in.

And I do think that the mission of the college is one that absolutely deserves to be championed from the rooftops. That the city on a hill should be as much about the folks who are educated at a Franklin Cummings Tech as it is about an MIT. Because these two are synergistic. One should not exist without the other.

title: Things to do around Boston this weekend and beyond
text:
LA MATINEE DE FUZZ This Sunday-afternoon celebration of the distortion pedal includes the pummeling Queens outfit Skeeter de Milo along with three Bay State bands: sludge-punkers BEDTIMEMAGIC, psych shredders Astrai Bitch, and euphoria-corevisionaries Sapling. Folk, World & Country

MAYNARD JAZZFEST The fifth annual edition of this musical jamboree will feature performances by master trombonist Brian Thomas and his funky big band, the BT Allstars; eclectic, Boston-based jazz sextet Subject2Change; and Arlington’s own scorching, horn-powered Latin group Gringo Kings. A.Z. MADONNA

Presented by ArtsEmerson at Emerson Paramount Center, Jackie Liebergott Black Box Theatre. 617-824-8400, ArtsEmerson.org

With a topnotch cast directed by Margot Bordelon, “Eureka Day” mines quite a few laughs from the spectacle of well-meaning progressives tying themselves in lexical knots as they try to process events that defy ideological pigeonholes. Lee’s play is, at bottom, an argument for humanity. And these days we can use as many of those as we can get. Through June 20. Production by CHUANG Stage. It features music and lyrics by Obie Award winner Dave Malloy (“Moby-Dick,” “The Great Comet”) and a book by Guggenheim Fellow Jen Silverman. Through July 12, $43 and up. Loeb Drama Center, Cambridge. www.americanrepertorytheater.org

KAREN CAMPBELL

AN EXQUISITE EYE: INTRODUCING THE ASO O. TAVITIAN COLLECTION Opening this week: The Clark Art Institute made a splash in 2024 when it announced it had received a coveted private collection from the Aso O. Tavitian Foundation, named for the late software billionaire who was also once a member of its board of trustees. A trove of 331 artworks by renowned European artists from the 15th to the 19th century — Peter Paul Rubens, Elisabeth Louise Vigée Le Brun, and Jan Van Eyck top the marquee — the gift came with a $45 million check to fund a curator to care for them and a new wing to house them. This summer the Clark offers a long look before its permanent home is set to be complete in late 2027. Through Feb. 21, 2027. Clark Art Institute, 225 South St., Williamstown. 413-458-2303, clarkart.edu

CELTIC ART ACROSS THE AGES Spanning almost three millenia, 800 BCE right up till now, this show takes a liberal approach to art made by Celtic people and their vast diaspora through the ages, stretching from Northern Europe to every corner of the globe. From the Iron Age through the Roman Empire to today, it attempts to weave connection across eras to both reveal lineage and unwind cliche. Through Aug. 2. Harvard Art Museums, 32 Quincy St., Cambridge. 617-495-9400, www.harvardartmuseum.org

AMERICAN IMPRESSIONISM Last chance: In the mid-19th century, the Hudson River School of painters, led by Thomas Cole, adopted the heroic frame of their European Romantic forbears to craft a beatific vision of the American landscape that was often at odds with reality. While Americans fawned over their imagined idylls, Europeans were rushing headlong into Modernism as artists like Edgar Dègas and Claude Monet dropped Impressionism, frank and immediate, like a bomb into polite French establishment painting. It would take a while for the US to catch up, but they did, and with some masters of their own, many of whom you’ll see here: James McNeill Whistler, John Singer Sargent, and Childe Hassam, among others. title: Find out how a World Cup ball works
text:
Aerodynamics applies not just to airplanes, rocket ships, and race cars, but even the subtle design of soccer balls that makes the inflated orb behave in ways we don’t always expect. If you’re in Seattle this week for a World Cup match or other adventures, don’t miss a presentation by sports physics expert John Eric Goff about what makes each World Cup soccer ball new and unique — and why some have generated controversy. “Soccer Science: Beautiful Physics in the Beautiful Game!” takes place June 14 (2-3:30 p.m.) at Seattle’s Museum of Flight (allow a couple of hours to take in this fascinating museum, which includes the original Boeing barn, old warbirds, artifacts from Apollo missions, and a flight hangar with historic Air Force One and Concorde planes). Goff, a visiting professor at the University of Puget Sound’s physics department, focuses his research on the aerodynamics of World Cup soccer balls. He’ll explain how the design of each World Cup soccer ball has subtle differences in surface texture and construction that affect how the ball moves through the air, and how experiments help connect ball design to what players experience on the field.

“The experiments are essentially the soccer-ball version of aircraft testing,” Goff, author of “Gold Medal Physics: The Science of Sports,” told the Globe. “We mount a ball in a wind tunnel, blow air past it at game-like speeds, and measure the aerodynamic forces on it. From those forces, we determine how much drag and lift the ball experiences and then use computer simulations to predict how the ball will fly.”

Soccer balls don’t come with smooth surfaces; they have surface textures (slightly raised patterns), seams, grooves, and a varying number of panels. The official 2026 FIFA World Cup match ball, the Adidas Trionda, has just four panels — the fewest number of panels for a men’s World Cup ball, said Goff. Air density also affects how a ball flies through the air, meaning it will behave differently at a higher-elevation stadium in Mexico City, for instance, versus near sea level in Boston, Seattle, or Vancouver. Goff will also explore AI’s role in modern ball technology and soccer officiating. Museum admission, which includes the presentation: Free for children up to age 4, $21 ages 5-17, $25 for age 65 and older, and $29 for age 18 and older. www.museumofflight.org

Festival shines spotlight on diverse people whose stories risk being erased

New England’s largest film fest celebrating people of color worldwide returns this week, running June 18-26 in person and June 26-July 2 online. The Roxbury International Film Festival (RoxFilm), now in its 28th year, helps amplify underrepresented voices and provide a platform for diverse stories. It opens with a screening of “Transforming the Beautiful Game: The Clyde Best Story,” directed by Dan Egan, a documentary that highlights the journey and impact of Clyde Best, the first Black soccer (or “English football”) superstar of the modern TV era who became a legend in the North American Soccer League; it runs June 18 at 7 p.m. at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, with Best in attendance to field questions after the screening.

RoxFilm includes more than 100 narrative, documentary, animated, experimental, and student-produced films from across the country (and from Boston Public School students and Lynn’s Raw Arts Program). Add to that question-and-answer sessions with filmmakers, panel discussions, networking opportunities, and filmmaker hangouts. Other film highlights include “Finding Your Laughter,” which follows Chicago comedian Arlieta Hall who uses stand-up comedy and improvisation as tools to support her mental health while caregiving for her father with Alzheimer’s disease (June 25), and “She Dared to Dream,” a portrait of US Representative Ayanna Pressley as part of a series of short films on June 21. The free Senior Lunch program returns to Hibernian Hall on June 23, with several screenings, including a showing of the new award-winning film “Pursuing Light: The Bill Strickland Story,” about the local New England Culinary Arts Training organization, and “Black History Begins with Love” by local author Irene Smalls.

“We are living at a time when stories about people of color are being erased — and that is intentional,” says Lisa Simmons, the festival’s artistic and executive director. “However, independent filmmakers are ensuring these stories are told in full, nuanced, and complex ways that reflect the richness of communities of color.”

Most in-person screenings take place at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, while the online version, RoxFilm@Home, includes screenings from June 26 to July 2. www.roxfilmfest.com
