title: Historical marker honors Boston’s desegregation movement at former School Committee headquarters
text:
“This historic marker is going to be dropped on a very well-traveled street,” said Lew Finfer, cochair of the Boston desegregation and busing initiative, during the event. “In 50 years, maybe somebody will say, ‘What was going on there?’”

One of the 14 demands presented in 1963 was the acknowledgment of unintentional segregation in public schools. The demand was fulfilled in 1974, when a federal judge recognized the segregation and ordered Boston Public Schools to begin busing students between predominantly white and predominantly Black communities. The ruling sparked protests and violence, and Black students faced harassment as they entered previously all-white schools.

Leola Hampton, a former student bused in 1974, described the fear and trauma Black students endured.

“For us, education was secondary to survival,” Hampton said.

She recalled bricks thrown through bus windows, shouted slurs, and the uncertainty of entering hostile schools.

“We were the casualties of desegregation,” she said, garnering supportive reactions from the audience. “In spite of all the ugliness we endured, we continue to persist, to dream, to thrive.”

Vernita Weller, daughter of Rev. Vernon Carter, a civil rights leader and pastor at a South End church, described his 114-day vigil for the Racial Imbalance Law in 1965. Carter launched the vigil outside the headquarters and spent over a hundred days sleeping on the sidewalk, demanding that officials address racial segregation and inequality in the public schools.

She recounted his endurance through harassment, exhaustion, and harsh weather to demand action from school officials.

“I’m so proud of what he contributed to this story,” Weller said.

Susan Batson, daughter of Ruth Batson, the late chairperson of the public education committee of the NAACP, who delivered the 14 demands, reflected on her mother’s role in challenging segregation in Boston’s schools. During the ceremony, she recalled accompanying her mother to committee meetings and watching her relentlessly push for change.

She called her mother a “tour de force” whose persistence brought attention to injustices officials ignored.

The growing recognition of Boston’s civil rights history feels like a continuation of her mother’s legacy, she said.

“For me, it’s a very, very powerful evolution of my mother,” Batson said in an interview. “I think she is working like crazy in heaven, or wherever she is, to make all of this happen.”

For some attendees, the marker represented a chance to recover a history that was often overlooked.

Klare Shaw, 71, was a kid when she saw her mother, Sarah-Ann Shaw, Boston’s first Black female television reporter, actively participate in Boston’s civil rights movement. She was glad she came to the ceremony to celebrate the movement’s unsung heroes.

“I’m glad that we are lifting up today’s history and keeping it relevant,” Shaw said, standing in front of the marker. “I hope that people will continue to be involved in advocating for the education they want for their families.”

Jeri Robinson, 77, chair of the Boston School Committee, now headquartered on Washington Street in Roxbury, said the event was both personal and professional for her. Robinson participated in desegregation-era demonstrations as a student and now oversees the same institution that activists once challenged.

Looking back at the demands made by civil rights advocates in the 1960s, Robinson said Boston has made progress but still faces inequality.

“We know there still are many inequities,” Robinson said. “We can continue to work to create an equitable opportunity for all.”

title: Running again for Suffolk County DA, Rachael Rollins is as defiant as ever
text:
As Rachael Rollins launches her improbable political comeback, her best defense may be a good offense.

At least that seems to be her modus operandi as she sat down for her first lengthy media interview since resigning as US Attorney three years ago amid two federal probes detailing “egregious” and “flagrant” ethical breaches.

“I will own that this entire situation when I was US Attorney was incredibly messy,” Rollins told me in a joint interview with GBH News’s Jim Braude. “I feel profoundly embarrassed. I feel shame, like remorse, about what happened.”

Yet Rollins can’t bring herself to say she did anything wrong — at least without knowing more about how the Department of Justice Inspector General and the Office of Special Counsel drew their conclusions that she violated the Hatch Act, which bars federal workers from partisan political activity, by attending a 2022 fundraiser with Jill Biden, and, separately, used her office to influence a Suffolk County District Attorney’s race.

“I concede they don’t think I was truthful,” said Rollins. “I believe I was.”

The 55-year-old Roxbury resident is emerging out of exile because she’s running for Suffolk District Attorney again – a role that catapulted her into political stardom in 2018. She was among the first in the nation to run as a progressive prosecutor, pledging not to pursue low-level crimes like shoplifting.

Today, Rollins likens herself to two defendants she had a hand in exonerating as DA and as US Attorney: Sean Ellis, who was found guilty of murder, and Gang Chen, an MIT professor accused of concealing ties to China. Both professed their innocence, and were ultimately vindicated.

She knows she’s asking a lot of voters to look past her transgressions — both of which involve improper use of political power. Keep in mind, all of this took place under friendlier times with President Joe Biden, who had appointed her to the role.

Still, Rollins remains characteristically defiant. She argues that scandals may not derail candidates the way they used to, drawing a parallel with Graham Platner, who easily won the Democratic senate primary in Maine on Tuesday, despite having a Nazi tattoo and allegations that he mistreated women.

“There’s righteous indignation that’s happening … that doesn’t mean I shouldn’t be held accountable,” said Rollins. “It’s just some of these things before used to be nonstarters, and now we’re in a world where they aren’t.”

So if Rollins — who blazed a trail as the first Black woman to serve as Suffolk DA and as US Attorney from Massachusetts — maintains she didn’t break the rules, then why did she resign her post as federal prosecutor? Why not stay and fight?

Rollins, who has spoken before about receiving death threats, said she had made up her mind to step down a couple of weeks before the federal probes were released in May 2023. Rollins said she had lost confidence that the US Marshal Service — assigned to protect her and her family — could provide adequate security, and another death threat was the last straw.

“Why am I fighting to stay in a place that does not care literally whether I live or die?” she recalled thinking.

Since leaving public office, Rollins has been teaching at Roxbury Community College and holding classes for incarcerated youth at Suffolk County House of Correction. Supporters urged her to run for Suffolk DA, she said, with momentum building after incumbent Kevin Hayden came under fire from the patrolmen’s union for filing a manslaughter charge against a Boston police officer for the shooting death of a carjacking suspect. The race has also recently drawn another Democratic challenger and local attorney Linda Champion.

“We were the most innovative and exceptional DA’s office in the country, hands down, and I believe we’ve lost that,” Rollins said. “We are lacking inspiration, we are lacking leadership, and we’re lacking transparency.”

And in what will likely be a familiar refrain as the campaign heats up, Rollins took a swipe at Hayden’s own ethical breach in the 2022 race. He paid a $5,000 fine after the state Ethics Commission found that he violated the conflict of interest law when used his official position to release information related to his opponent, then-Boston city councilor Ricardo Arroyo.

Rollins has always played by her own rules, and now she’s running on her own terms. Whether voters are ready to forgive and forget remains to be seen. But she’s ready to try again.

“When you ascend to the levels that I have, when you fall, it’s far,” Rollins said. “What I want is my daughter and my two nieces, who I’m the guardian of, to know that if you make a mistake, it’s okay … but you will pick yourself up, and you will continue moving forward.”

What’s your take? Join the conversation in the comments here.

Let the fireworks begin.

With Rachael Rollins trying to unseat Kevin Hayden, we should expect a no-holds-barred campaign. Remember Rollins was backing then-Boston city councilor Ricardo Arroyo in 2022, and it was her meddling in that race that ultimately drove her downfall as US Attorney. In response to the Rollins interview, the Hayden campaign issued a full-throated rebuttal:

“Rollins lied to federal investigators under oath, lied to and misled her own staff, lied to the public, and was eventually forced to resign in disgrace. The idea that she thinks the absence of a fine excuses her conduct – when federal investigators found that she engaged in the most egregious misconduct they had encountered – is ridiculous. But don’t just take our word for it, just search ‘Rachael Rollins investigation’ online and see for yourself.”

title: Seven high school tournament takeaways from Thursday, plus a national award for Brody Bumila
text:
Cohasset girls’ lacrosse captured its second title in three years, and fourth overall acrosse three divisions, by winning a rematch against Norwell in the Division 3 final, one year after they met in the D4 final.

In Division 2 boys’ volleyball, Wayland finally captured its elusive first title, in its fourth championship match appearance. And in rugby, it was all repeats, as the Belmont girls won their eighth in a row, the BC High boys completed a Division 1 three-peat, and the Hanover boys went back-to-back in D2.

Here’s Friday’s championship slate:

D5 baseball: No. 1 English High vs. No. 2 Georgetown, 4 p.m.

D3 softball: No. 5 Apponequet vs. No. 3 Joseph Case, 4 p.m.

D1 boys’ lacrosse: No. 1 Lincoln-Sudbury vs. No. 6 BC High, 4:30 p.m.

D1 boys’ volleyball: No. 1 Needham vs. No. 2 Brookline, 6 p.m.

D5 softball: No. 1 Advanced Math and Science vs. No. 3 Tyngsborough, 6:30 p.m.

D2 boys’ lacrosse: No. 2 Longmeadow vs. No. 4 Mansfield, 7 p.m.

D2 baseball: No. 4 Milton vs. No. 11 King Philip, 7 p.m.

And check out Nate Weitzer’s preview of Friday’s 48th Shriners Classic, a rare treat to see some of the state’s elite football players suiting up in June.

Cohasset flips the script in title-game rematch, capturing Division 3 girls’ lacrosse championship

Sandwich tastes glory with first girls’ lacrosse championship, taking down Ipswich in Division 4 final

Wayland finally rings the Bell by capturing Division 2 boys’ volleyball championship, its first

Scoring in bunches, BC High soars to third straight Division 1 rugby title

Great eight: Belmont secures another girls’ rugby title, but rest of state is catching up

St. Mary’s completes three-peat as Division 1 girls’ flag football champions, Fitchburg claims D2

Frustration lingers over Ipswich boys’ lacrosse team’s abrupt season-ending forfeit

Finn Bell, Wayland — With the final kill of a four-set victory over Westfield in the Division 2 boys’ volleyball final, Bell completed his career as the all-time kills leader in state history with 1,485. On Thursday, he slammed down a match-high 17, adding two blocks and an ace, to give the Warriors their first state championship.

Sophia Lafontant, St. Mary’s — The sophomore was named MVP of the Patriots Girls’ High School Division 1 Flag Football Championship as she led the Spartans to a third-straight title, 12-6, over Leominster.

Avery Regan, Cohasset — The Bucknell-bound senior led the way with three goals in the Skippers’ 9-6 triumph over Norwell in the Division 3 girls’ lacrosse championship game.

Elisabeth Stutzman, Sandwich — The junior scored a game-high three goals to lift the Blue Knights to their first girls’ lacrosse state championship with a 9-6 victory over Ipswich.

Bishop Feehan senior Brody Bumila has been named the Max Preps Male National Athlete of the Year. A two-season sensation, the 6-foot-9-inch senior led the Shamrocks to an epic Division 1 boys’ basketball run to the championship as the No. 14 seed, during which he averaged 41 points, 20 rebounds, and 3 blocks. He finished his basketball career with 1,365 points and was named Catholic Central MVP and a Globe Super Teamer.

The Texas-committed lefthander can also dial up his fastball to 101 miles per hour and has Feehan playing in Saturday’s Division 1 baseball championship as its ace pitcher. Earlier this season, he fired a 20-strikeout no-hitter.

Malden Catholic has removed the interim tag for boys’ basketball coach Mike Garrity, while hiring Sarell Sanders to coach its girls’ hoops team.

Sanders was the head coach at Medford, which she led to a tournament appearance and second-place Greater Boston League finish in her first season leading the program.

Previously, she was an assistant at St. Mary’s, her alma mater, earning a total of six state titles as a player and coach. She played Division 2 basketball at Caldwell and works as a physical education techer in Lynn.

“Coach Sanders is an outstanding leader who brings passion, energy, and a deep commitment to developing student-athletes both on and off the court,” said Malden Catholic athletic director Bill Raycraft in a statement. “Her vision for building a competitive program rooted in accountability, teamwork, and character aligns perfectly with the mission and values of Malden Catholic. We are excited to welcome her to the Lancer family.”

Garrity, who led the Lancers to a 15-7 record as interim coach in 2025-26, has been on the MC staff since 2020, and helped them win three state championships as the top varsity assistant.

Garrity, a former standout player at Somerville, had coaching stops at Danvers, Central Catholic, Fitchburg State, and with the Middlesex Magic and Mass Rivals AAU programs. He played collegiately at Anna Maria, Framingham State, and Salem State.

“I am incredibly honored and grateful for the opportunity,” said Garrity in a statement. “Having been part of this program’s success and growth, I have developed a deep appreciation for the tradition, commitment, and culture that make Malden Catholic unique.”

Leicester’s Owen Fadden has committed to play men’s soccer at New Hampshire. Fadden played for Intercontinental Football Academy of New England, part of MLS NEXT, for the last four years, including two years a steam captain. He graduated from the Center of Excellence this spring.

“Owen embodies the mentality and culture we want within our program,” said UNH coach Rich Weinrebe in a statement. “Defensively, he brings toughness, discipline and a strong understanding of the game, consistently showing the ability to read plays, compete in challenges and remain composed under pressure. His commitment to development, competitive nature and willingness to push himself every day will make an immediate impact on our environment.”

Charlotte junior third baseman Dawson Bryce, a Taunton graduate who also played at Merrimack, announced his transfer to Arkansas. Bryce was the preseason American Conference Player of the Year and was off to a strong start before getting injured. In 2025, he hit .340 with 14 homers and 17 doubles.

▪ The Mass Mutual Center will host the MADE Hoops Global Games, the first middle school basketball championship, this weekend.

The event will feature young athletes ages 10-14 competing under international rules. Participants hail from more than a dozen countries.

Tip-off is 3 p.m. Friday, with play continuing Saturday and Sunday. The event is free and open to the public.

▪ The Red Sox foundation will introduce its latest class of Red Sox Scholars on Saturday at Fenway Park before a 4 p.m. game against the Rangers.

Twelve seventh-graders from Boston Public Schools will receive $10,000 scholarships, mentoring, and professional support. The ceremony will also celebrate 24 Red Sox Scholars who are graduating from high school or college this spring.

This year’s Red Sox Scholars: Samanta Abad Garcia of Eliot Innovation, Emmanuella Barinda of English High, Ivy Circeo of Latin Academy, Khalil Elamin of Boston Latin, Angel Escoto of Hurley, Lucely Gonzalez of TechBoston, De’Andre Henderson of Roxbury Prep, Larry Kelley of Higginson-Lewis, Alanna Lopez of Hurley, Nepthalie Presume of New Mission, Adriel Romero of New Mission, and Anisa Sharif of Richard J. Murphy.

title: Accused thief of millions in jewelry from Jamaica Plain home will stay jailed for another month
text:
The prosecution is asking that Kisakye be detained until trial, or held on $250,000 cash bail, fitted with a GPS, and confined to his home because of the size of the amount allegedly stolen. Kisakye’s defense attorney, Andrew Stockwell-Alpert, asked that bail be lowered to $2,000 because the alleged incident involved no weapons and $2,000 is the maximum amount Kisakye’s mother, who is experiencing financial struggles, could pay.

He said Kisakye was no longer a flight risk.

“I would suggest to the court that he would not dishonor his commitment to his mother to not run away with the $2,000 bail, particularly with the GPS and home confinement,” Stockwell-Alpert said.

Kisakye was arrested in Miami last week and brought to Suffolk County, where he pleaded not guilty at his arraignment in West Roxbury District Court and ordered held without bail.

The alleged incident was reported on Nov. 19, when the homeowners called 911 worried that someone was lurking around the property, located inside a gated community on Allandale Road, according to the police report. Officers originally found nothing amiss, but discovered later that morning the back door was unlocked and the safe had been emptied.

Numerous items, including a 17-carat diamond ring worth an estimated $850,000, were allegedly stolen.

Detectives later obtained surveillance footage showing two hooded figures leaving the property around midnight, and began investigating Kisakye, according to the report.

Kisakye bought a one-way ticket to Uganda on Dec. 19 and departed the same day, declaring $54,000 in cash, according to the report. He later traveled to Miami, where he allegedly sold a stolen gold bracelet for $11,000, according to police.

On Thursday, Flaherty also approved a protective order to prevent Kisakye from accessing any evidence that involves personal and financial information about the alleged victims.

Prosecutor Alexander Jones said during the alleged incident, Kisakye knew the victims’ safe passcode because he knew their dates of birth.

He also alleged that Kisakye has, on at least two occasions, altered checks from the victims to be a higher amount than intended, and that there is evidence showing that Kisakye has done this with another alleged victim.

“The defendant has shown a pattern of targeting and victimizing elderly victims using financial information,” Jones said.

Kisakye started working for the homeowners as a home-care assistant in December 2023, according to a police report. He helped change the batteries in the basement safe last summer and has intimate knowledge of the property.

Kisakye had solicited a $10,000 loan from the homeowners to buy a new vehicle, but after depositing the money, Kisakye “never once returned to their home to work for them, nor has he ever spoken to them or reached out in any capacity,” the report says.

The police report said Kisakye has a long history of “thefts, check fraud and pawning jewelry.” Randolph police reports had already linked him to a stolen diamond ring and a residential burglary where an Xbox gaming system was stolen.

He had also made 14 pawn transactions between December 2024 and August 2025, according to the Boston police report.

A fingerprint at the crime scene was identified as belonging to Kisakye, police said, and GPS data placed him in the area of the home around the time of the burglary and on a suspected scouting visit about a month prior.

Boston police allege that after breaking into the Jamaica Plain home, Kisakye tried to sell the stolen jewels in various states before fleeing to Uganda “upon learning that investigators were inquiring about him.”

Detectives found suspicious activity in his financial transactions dating back years, including evidence he had opened accounts “in the name of a deceased individual for whom he had previously served as a caretaker,” according to the report.

Material from previous Globe coverage was included in this report.

title: Opponents of Blue Hill Ave. bus lane ask Trump administration to rescind $80m
text:
“The Wu administration’s unwillingness to listen to its most vulnerable residents continues a pattern of racist governance that Black Bostonians are all too familiar with,” Reggie Stewart, a Dorchester resident and chair of the Environmental and Climate Justice Committee of the Boston NAACP, said at a press conference Friday morning about the Blue Hill Ave. project. “We support better public transit, safer streets, and real investments in communities that have been neglected for generations, but investment does not mean forcing a harmful project onto Black neighborhoods after the people who live, work, worship, and run businesses there have said no to it.”

Residents are concerned the road redesign will decrease parking along Blue Hill Avenue, limit travel to one lane in spots, and remove trees along the thoroughfare, which could lead to more pollution and add to an already heightened rate of respiratory ailments among nearby residents.

What the community needs, according to the Coalition for Responsible Transportation Policy, which requested the revocation of federal funding, is for the city to lobby the MBTA to extend the Orange Line to Mattapan Square as well as beyond Forest Hills into Roslindale.

A light rail was supposed to be installed after the elevated Orange Line was taken down in the 1980s, coalition members said, but the Silver Line bus route was eventually added instead — one of many transportation-related “broken promises” to the Black community, they said.

Federal money for Blue Hill Avenue has been scrapped before. In 2009, the state withdrew an application for a federal grant for the 28X rapid transit bus line following significant opposition from the community.

In a statement, the Wu administration said the plan for roadway improvements would continue to evolve during the ongoing community process.

“The city is working closely with community leaders, residents, and the MBTA to deploy federally-awarded funds to make much-needed improvements to Blue Hill Avenue, beautify the roadway, speed up commutes, and expand opportunities for small businesses along the corridor,” city officials said in a statement.

The US Department of Transportation did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Russell Holmes, the state representative from Mattapan who supports the proposed developments around his neighborhood, pushed back against the idea that they were being built on the backs of the Black community.

“All of these developments are being done for Black people,” he said. “The rest of this city, it’s exploding in development, and for so long it felt like there was … nothing happening in the communities that I represent."

“Black people need to also be a part of this development and a part of this economic change that’s happening in Boston.”

But on Thursday night, city officials got an earful during a contentious meeting in Dorchester about the transportation plan for the White Stadium redevelopment in Franklin Park. Residents were upset at the plan to restrict parking on game days and require visitors to Franklin Park to request parking passes, according to the Dorchester Reporter, while people in surrounding neighborhoods would have to get resident permits to park in front of their homes.

“People like me, particularly Black people like me, who are homeowners, who pay taxes, cannot be anywhere around here celebrating birthdays, a regular cookout, a Little League team ... on game days,” one woman at the meeting said.

The city’s $325 million bid to redevelop White Stadium for a professional women’s soccer team is facing a legal challenge over whether it’s an impermissible use of a public park. The question before the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court is whether the project is a renovation of an aging facility or a new arena altogether.

Dorchester residents are also up in arms about a proposal from the state to build a campus for hundreds of people dealing with mental illness and addiction at Shattuck Hospital, adjacent to Franklin Park. One resident called the plan “a new form of geographic redlining” that would concentrate social burdens in the city’s majority-minority neighborhoods.

Speaking at the press conference about Blue Hill Avenue, Louis Elisa, president of the Garrison-Trotter Neighborhood Association said all those projects would be built “on the backs of the Black community.”

“Stop trying to fool people that this means anything to the residents of Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan,” Elisa said of the bus lane. “This proposed project, which will bring a lot of money to the city of Boston for construction, will do very little to improve the quality of life along Blue Hill Avenue.”

“Stop trying to destroy the Black community,” he added. “Stop the aggressive takeover.”

A project to improve sidewalks and add bike lanes to Cummins Highway in Mattapan, which has taken years and caused major disruptions, has added to worries about construction projects in the area.

The coalition opposed to the bus lane said the “last straw” was a meeting Mayor Michelle Wu held a few weeks ago about the Blue Hill Avenue revitalization without inviting community advocates or two city councilors, Brian Worrell and Miniard Culpepper, who have been critical of the project.

The coalition said Wu hasn’t met with residents or business owners in person about their concerns, despite the city holding 100-plus meetings about it in the past several years.

“I just want you to understand the extraordinary moment that we’re in, where a predominantly Black community … out of sheer frustration, have thrown up their hands and decided to prevail to the Trump administration for relief,” Dianne Wilkerson, a Dorchester resident and former state senator, said at the press conference.

Asking for the federal funds to be withdrawn, she said, is the only way to get the city to the table to discuss a plan that will help the community.

Globe correspondent Chloe Pisani contributed to this report.

title: Business groups and Mass. Teachers are battling again, this time over a federal tax credit
text:
Featuring: Peter Lynch, Steph Lewis, Diane Hessan, Juliana Azevedo, Mike Minogue, Tim Murray, Jim Klocke, Jon Hurst, Katie Everett, Max Page, Jorge Elorza, Rich Davey, Erin Murphy Rafferty, and more.

Here we go again. The business groups and teachers’ unions are starting to clash over something else now — and Governor Maura Healey is in the middle of the fracas this time.

The latest issue: a tax credit of up to $1,700 for K-12 scholarship donations. Give the money to an eligible nonprofit, starting next year, and you can subtract that amount from what you owe the feds — all of it, unlike a typical charitable tax deduction. Sounds great, right?

Well, don’t break out the checkbook yet. It’s not clear whether Massachusetts taxpayers will be allowed to participate, or if local schools and nonprofits will benefit. That is Healey’s call to make. And she has not yet said what she’s going to do.

That’s why a number of influential business and philanthropic groups this spring joined a coalition to make the case for the tax credit — a coalition spearheaded by Peter Lynch, one of Boston’s most respected investors and philanthropists, and his family foundation. (Time is of the essence, foundation executive Katie Everett argues, to get everything in place well before the new year.) This crew includes the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce, the Worcester Regional Chamber of Commerce, the Mass. Business Roundtable, and The Boston Foundation.

Congress required each governor to opt in, on behalf of their states. Thirty have said yes. But in the Northeast, New York’s Kathy Hochul is the only Democratic governor to offer support so far.

This gift is from the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” President Trump’s tax legislation from 2025 that’s despised in many circles for how it is ushering in significant cuts to health care and clean energy. (The name, “Education Freedom Tax Credit,” also has a MAGA ring to it.)

Adding to the intrigue: Healey’s likely Republican opponent, Mike Minogue, is among the outspoken fans.

The powerful teachers’ unions are decidedly not. On Wednesday, Massachusetts Teachers Association leaders Max Page and Deb McCarthy sent a letter to Healey arguing that this will be a big drain on public school resources, and should only be considered if private schools are excluded. (Fat chance of that happening.)

Page would like Healey to send a message to the remaining undecided Democratic governors. This tax credit, Page argues, is part of a Republican-led “voucher” movement to back government subsidies for private and parochial schools around the country. The new tax credit can help public school districts, too, but Page is skeptical. He describes the program as designed to draw kids away from public schools — and shrinking enrollment could hurt their budgets.

Meanwhile, the pro-side is gaining momentum. Supporters see this as an opportunity to direct anywhere from nearly $700 million to $2 billion a year in federal funds to worthy local programs. Why leave that on the table?

Charter-school advocate Education Reform Now, led by former Providence mayor Jorge Elorza, released compelling poll results on Friday. Two-thirds of Massachusetts voters support opting into the program, regardless of political party.

Among those cheering is Steph Lewis, chief executive of The Base in Roxbury. The tax credit, Lewis says, will help nonprofits like his close the gap between haves and have-nots, while spurring more local philanthropy. Jim Klocke, chief executive of the Mass. Council of Nonprofits, agrees: These funds could go to tutoring as well as after-school and summer programs, and maybe even launch a “new wave of education innovation” here.

Worcester chamber CEO Tim Murray notes that we, in Massachusetts, pay more to the federal government than we get back from Washington. He sees this tax credit as a way to buck that trend. Murray says this shouldn’t be a partisan issue, as some are making it out to be. Good luck with that.

So what’s Healey waiting for? A spokeswoman says Healey wants to first see official guidance from the US Education and Treasury departments. This week, Treasury offered a preview, but also said formal rules won’t be done until late September.

This could be a political quagmire, so it’s easy to see why Healey is being cautious.

Business and union groups warred over charter schools, the millionaires tax, the MCAS test. Which side will Healey take this time? At least both factions can agree on one thing: Neither wants to wait long to find out.

What’s your take? Join the conversation in the comments here.

Juliana Azevedo seems like a pro when it comes to consumer products. But now she’ll have to study up on Boston politics, too. Procter & Gamble just named Azevedo as the new head of its “Global Grooming” business – aka Gillette, to you and me. She’ll relocate from Geneva, where she runs P&G’s home care and professional business, to Boston to take over for Gary Coombe, who retires this fall after 40 years with the company. Azevedo, a native of Sao Paolo, will lead a team of 10,000 people around the world. That’s challenging enough. But the redevelopment of the company’s 31-acre campus along Fort Point Channel, and the construction of a new headquarters next door, will likely fall under her watch, too.

As Jon Hurst likes to say: Shop like jobs depend on it, because they do. The Boston Planning Department just put out a report showing which industries have grown in the city since 2019, and which ones have shrunk. Bad news for Hurst and the group he leads, the Retailers Association of Massachusetts: The retail sector has been hit hardest, shedding nearly 7,000 jobs from pre-pandemic times to 2025, while total employment in the city grew by more than 9,000 over those six years. Hurst’s best guesses about what’s behind the trend: government restrictions and messaging during COVID, less convenient parking options, and a surge in mobile commerce and delivery services. Plus: higher utility and health care costs, along with all those sales-tax-free stores just over the line in New Hampshire.

Video-tech company Brightcove is heading back to the public markets again, this time as part of a much bigger company, one with the “Matrix”-inspired name of Bending Spoons. The Italian software holding company just filed for an IPO in the US, to list with Nasdaq. Bending Spoons acquired Boston-based Brightcove more than a year ago, and operates it alongside the likes of AOL and Vimeo. Former Brightcove board chair Diane Hessan says Brightcove is different because it serves enterprise customers, with recurring business-to-business revenue. She points to the bigger story: Now, public investors need to decide whether they can make money by betting on Bending Spoons and its diverse array of software businesses.

The old Boston 2024 gang’s back. But this time they’re not rallying around Boston hosting the Summer Olympics. They’ve got World Cup fever and are behind what is destined to be the world’s biggest soccer ball. We’re talking, of course, about Massachusetts Port Authority CEO Rich Davey, and Suffolk Construction’s John Fish and Erin Murphy Rafferty. In 2015, as Boston was putting its Olympic bid together, Davey served as Boston 2024’s CEO, Fish was its chairman, and Murphy Rafferty was its chief operating officer. We all know how that ended: Amid local opposition, Boston pulled its bid. Now running Massport, Davey has another shot at being part of a global sporting event. That’s why on Massport-owned Piers Park in East Boston there is now a four-story-tall royal blue soccer ball — so big it can be seen by passengers flying into Logan International Airport. The inflated ball — which is vying to be in the Guinness World Records — isn’t cheap. It costs $300,000, and it’s not hard to figure out who’s footing the bill with Massport, Suffolk Construction, and design firm HNTB emblazoned on the ball.

The French national team, Les Bleus, is making Boston its home base during its World Cup run and practicing at Bentley University in Waltham. Which hotel is the team staying at? Click here to make your guess.

Bottoms up! On Tuesday, we asked readers to weigh in on whether a new law that extends last call to 3 a.m. should become permanent instead of ending July 31. Readers can drink to that but nearly as many wanted Massachusetts to bring back happy hour. In the last month, both Boston Mayor Michelle Wu and Governor Maura Healey have said they would support discounted alcoholic drinks because it would make Massachusetts more fun and attractive to young people.

This newsletter was edited by Greg Huang and Tim Logan and produced by Diamond Naga Siu. Have a happy weekend and maybe even watch some soccer.

Have a question for the team? Email us at powerplay@globe.com.

Delivered Tuesday and Friday.

title: For Boston’s Cabo Verdeans, finally, a seat at the World Cup table
text:
At the back of the pub, the cheers went up again when Coleta walked in, 23 minutes after kickoff, wearing the jersey of Cabo Verde’s national team.

“Traffic,” he said, rolling his eyes, taking a seat at the bar that Butler had saved for him. “There was an accident on the Expressway.”

Everybody nodded knowingly, because they’ve all been there before.

But, as a native of Cabo Verde, Coleta had never been in this position before: sitting down to a World Cup that includes the Blue Sharks, Cabo Verde’s national team.

Coleta is 62 years old. He works for the Massachusetts Convention Center Authority. He was born on Fogo, one of Cabo Verde’s islands. Fogo means fire in Portuguese, and the island has an active volcano. But like so many other Cabo Verdeans, Coleta and his family left the archipelago off the coast of West Africa for Boston not because they feared an eruption but because they longed for opportunity.

“I was 12 when I got here, to Boston,” he said. “Soccer was all I knew. It was my life.”

In high school, he played on one of those great Madison Park teams that won a city championship, then transferred to Boston Tech.

He played semi-pro, but any dreams of going beyond that broke down along with his gimpy right knee.

“It’s hard to explain today, but when I was a kid, soccer was everything in the Cabo Verdean community,” he said. “We didn’t play basketball, no baseball, no football. Now it’s different, Cabo Verdean kids are playing everything.”

With a population of around 500,000 people, and a diaspora that is estimated at 700,000 to 1 million, Cabo Verde never got near a seat at the World Cup table.

Portugal colonized Cabo Verde, and even after the island won its independence in 1975, the exploitation of natural resources extended to taking the island’s best players, Coleta said.

The last few generations, however, have produced young men who want to play for their country.

“We’ve got some really good players,” Coleta said, including those who qualify to play for the country through their parents. “We’ve got a guy, Pico Lopes, who grew up in Ireland and is the captain of Shamrock Rovers, right Ray?”

Butler, a native of Ireland who knows the League of Ireland well, leaned in.

“He’s a very good center back,” Butler said of Lopes.

The good people of Crumlin, the Dublin neighborhood where Lopes grew up, and where his Cabo-Verdean-born father settled, gave him a rousing send-off the other day.

Both Butler and Coleta like that symmetry, because the Irish and Cabo Verdeans share an immigrant history in Boston.

Marty Walsh, whose parents were from the Gaeltacht in Connemara, an Irish-speaking region, was the first Boston mayor whose parents’ native language was not English. He once told me when he looked at the Cabo Verdean kids playing basketball at the Boys and Girls Club in Dorchester near where he grew up, he saw Irish kids from a century before.

“Poor kids from a colonized island that couldn’t provide them jobs,” Walsh said. “A lot of them came to Boston to make a life for themselves and their families.”

The Irish struggled when first arriving in Boston in large numbers. But they assimilated and went on to run the town.

Immigrants from Cabo Verde faced similar struggles, but the community has become one of the most enduring and vibrant in the city.

In more recent years, many Cabo Verdeans who used to live in Dorchester have moved to Brockton, Coleta said, because the cost of housing in Boston continued to soar.

That means the Cabo Verde team is being cheered on in Brockton and Pawtucket and other places in New England as loudly as in Dorchester.

Cabo Verde plays its first game Monday, in Atlanta, against Spain, one of the favorites to win the World Cup, in what is billed as a David vs. Goliath matchup.

Coleta will be there, part of a group of 14 guys who grew up together in Dorchester, playing soccer on Franklin Field, where a slide tackle left the outside of your thigh looking like it had a run-in with a giant cheese grater.

As immigrant kids who grew up in Boston, they’re used to being underdogs.

“We grew up together. We played together. We scored goals together. But nothing can top this, watching Cabo Verde in the World Cup together,” Coleta said.

Coleta and his childhood buddies were at Cesaria’s, the Dorchester restaurant on Bowdoin Street, to watch the qualifying match when Cabo Verde punched its ticket to the World Cup last October.

“I would compare it to what Americans felt when the US hockey team beat the Soviet Union in the Olympics,” Coleta said. “It was more than just a game. It was a moment in history, a feeling you never forget, a pride bursting out of your chest. It was like the day my son was born, that feeling.”

Coleta and his buddies went back to Cesaria’s Friday, but it wasn’t a late night.

They had to get up Saturday morning for the flight to Atlanta, to cheer on the Blue Sharks, to remember where they came from, to celebrate where they landed, and to chase this idea, this crazy idea, that says anything’s possible.

title: City watchdog calls for Boston police bodycam release policy after two recent officer shootings
text:
After two recent fatal police shootings, Boston’s civilian oversight agency is calling for an updated policy that would require the department to release body-camera footage within a specific timeframe, increasing transparency in the wake of officer violence.

The recommendation was included in a memo sent last week from the city’s Office of Police Accountability and Transparency, or OPAT, to Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox. It called on the department to release bodycam footage to OPAT within seven days and publicly within 30 days.

That would bring Boston police more in line with other major law enforcement agencies across the country, many of which have similar policies.

OPAT’s memo, which separately addresses immigration enforcement concerns, is the agency’s latest effort to flex its authority. Created following the death of George Floyd and subsequent racial justice protests in 2020, the office initially struggled to get off the ground. More recently, it has encountered friction in its relationship with the Boston Police Department.

The memo echoes earlier demands from city councilors and community leaders. They raised the bodycam release issue following the March 11 killing of Stephenson King Jr., a carjacking suspect with a history of mental illness and violence. King was fatally shot by Boston police officer Nicholas O’Malley while fleeing a traffic stop.

Local prosecutors quickly deemed the shooting unjustified and charged O’Malley with manslaughter, but authorities have refused to release bodycam footage of the incident.

Both police and prosecutors argue that releasing the video could jeopardize the criminal investigation. They also haven’t released footage from another deadly shooting in April, when police opened fire on a man who stabbed them with a sword during a mental health crisis at his apartment building near Northeastern University.

However, the department has taken a different approach in the past. After a 2015 fatal police shooting in Roxbury, officials quickly released video of what happened and pledged to continue the practice.

Other agencies have clearly defined timelines and protocols.

In New York, officials recently codified the practice of releasing bodycam footage within 30 days. The Milwaukee Police Department generally allows up to 15 days. In Baltimore, the police commissioner typically releases video roughly within a week.

Boston police were relatively late to roll out body cameras, which is probably why they’re lagging behind, according to experts. The department began a widespread implementation of bodycams in 2019. Since then, police shootings and in-custody deaths have been a rarity in Boston; a higher volume of such tragedies has sometimes spurred policy changes elsewhere.

“In light of the recent killings of two Boston community members by on duty BPD officers, we are in the midst of an intense public dialogue” about police violence and bodycam release, OPAT’s Civilian Review Board wrote in the memo to Cox, which is dated June 8.

In addition to the proposed timeline, board members said the department should consult with “family members of the alleged victims and survivors” before making the footage public.

The memo also recommended policy changes pertaining to immigration enforcement.

“Boston’s commitment to civil rights and community trust requires that the BPD decouple its local policing activities from federal enforcement practices that undermine the Boston Trust Act and the principle of community-based public safety,” board members wrote. They called on the city to “adopt a precautionary approach — declining participation in federal programs that expand surveillance infrastructure or create indirect pathways for civil immigration enforcement.”

Specifically, the memo pointed to the Boston Regional Intelligence Center or BRIC, which critics argue facilitates unjust surveillance and racial profiling, including through the city’s gang database. It also shares data with some federal agencies.

Among other recommendations, board members called on the department to limit the collection and sharing of fingerprint information when someone is arrested on certain misdemeanor charges. They said local law enforcement should halt any practices that threaten to undermine the Trust Act, Boston’s ordinance that prevents local law enforcement from cooperating with requests by federal immigration authorities to detain people for possible deportation, unless the person is also wanted for a serious crime.

Lea Skene can be reached at lea.skene@globe.com. Follow her on X @lea_skene.

title: Eight ways to celebrate Juneteenth in Greater Boston
text:
Juneteenth lands on Friday this year, and opportunities to commemorate the holiday in Greater Boston will kick off Thursday and stretch through the weekend. From art-packed open houses to outdoor carnivals to live interactive game shows, here are standout ways to honor, remember, and celebrate with family, friends, and the neighbors you haven’t met yet.

MIT OPEN SPACE JUNETEENTH CELEBRATION Step outside and dance to live reggae music from the Roots Alley Collective with special guest Dion Knibb on Juneteenth Eve. Attendees can also look forward to ice cream, lawn games, food trucks, and more. June 18, noon-2 p.m. Kendall MIT Open Space, 292 Main St., Cambridge. Free admission. openspace.mit.edu.

JUNETEENTH FLAG RAISING AT CITY HALL The city of Boston invites community members to witness the official annual raising of the Juneteenth flag, a proclamation reading, and moment of silence on Thursday. The event will also feature keynote speeches from city leaders and live musical performances. June 18, noon. City Hall Plaza, 1 City Hall Square. Free. boston.gov.

HISTORICALLY BLACK PHRASES LIVE! FT JARRETT HILL AND TRE’VALL ANDERSON If you’re up for a friendly competition, then head to WBUR CitySpace for “Historically Black Phrases Live!” a live game show based on the event’s cohosts and coauthors’ book, “Historically Black Phrases: From ‘I Ain’t One of Your Lil’ Friends’ to ‘Who All Gon’ Be There?’” Audience members have the opportunity to play from their seats and compete to win prizes — followed by a signing with Anderson and Hill featuring Frugal Bookstore. June 18, 7 p.m. WBUR CitySpace, 890 Commonwealth Ave. $25, $10 for students. wbur.org

NEWTON JUNETEENTH CELEBRATION Celebrate Juneteenth with live performances, food trucks, and a New England Patriots skills and drills clinic at the 6th annual Newton Juneteenth celebration. Hosted by the Newton-based antiracist coalition Families Organizing for Racial Justice, attendees can shop from local vendors, meet Patriots cheerleaders, watch live African dance and poetry performances, and close out the night with a screening of “Black Panther.” Reggae Foods and Gourmet Kreyol, two food trucks serving up Caribbean cuisine, will be on location. June 19, 3-10 p.m. Hyde Community Center, 90 Lincoln St. Free, registration recommended. eventbrite.com

MFA JUNETEENTH OPEN HOUSE Admission will be free for all Massachusetts residents at the Museum of Fine Arts Boston for a special Juneteenth edition of its Open House. Ticket holders can challenge chess masters or play on a life-size board, create clay poem jars in honor of the holiday, watch live performances of Haitian song and dance, and of course, explore the museum’s galleries. June 19. 10 a.m.-10 p.m. 465 Huntington Ave. Free, Tickets required. mfa.org

WE CREATE THE WORLD In partnership with the Boston Ujima Project, the ICA is offering free admission plus all-day programming for a jam-packed Juneteenth celebration. In addition to the galleries, guests can peruse a zine fair, partake in a block-print workshop honoring notable Black printmakers, and sit in on screenings from the Roxbury International Film Fest. June 19, 10 a.m.-9 p.m. Institute of Contemporary Art, 25 Harbor Shore Dr. Free. Tickets required. icaboston.org

BROOKLINE JUNETEENTH CARNIVAL Celebrating the theme of “One Freedom, Many Flags!,” the Brookline Juneteenth Carnival is a free celebration of freedom and culture. Featuring waterslides, bouncy houses, Caribbean music, food, and more — it’s set to be one part fairground, one part block party, and a whole lot of fun. June 19, noon-4 p.m. Brookline High School, 115 Greenough St., Brookline. Free. eventbrite.com.

ANNUAL FRANKLIN PARK JUNETEENTH CELEBRATION The spirit of Juneteenth doesn’t have to stop after June 19. Head to Franklin Park’s Shattuck Picnic Area for an all-day celebration of Black freedom and community in one of the city’s most historic parks. June 20, 11 a.m.-7 p.m. Franklin Park Shattuck Picnic Grove. Free. boston.gov.

MUSEUM OF AFRICAN AMERICAN HISTORY Celebrate Juneteenth next to the African Meeting House, as MAAH hosts its annual block party all day Friday, featuring a local vendor lineup. Joy Street will live up to its name: guests can enjoy music, poetry performances, and art workshops. Friday, June 19, 10 a.m.-5 p.m. Museum of African American History, 46 Joy St. Free admission. maah.org/juneteenth/

title: Former postal worker admits to stashing years of undelivered mail in rented locker, officials say
text:
A former mail carrier with routes in Brighton, Dorchester, and Mattapan has admitted to stashing thousands of pieces of undelivered mail in a personal storage locker, federal prosecutors said Tuesday.

Khalea Turner, 29, of Hull, pleaded guilty Monday to one charge of obstructing mail, US Attorney Leah B. Foley’s office said in a statement. Turner, a former Postal Service employee, will be sentenced at a later date.

Between November 2022 and January of this year, Turner failed to deliver roughly 14,700 pieces of mail assigned to routes in the three areas of Boston , along with the Fort Point neighborhood, the statement said. Instead, he stored the undelivered mail in a rented U-Haul storage locker in Weymouth.

Investigators who recovered the mail on Jan. 9 found US passports, jury notifications, government checks, education documents, and immigration paperwork intended for customers on Turner’s routes, according to Foley’s office.

The case comes amid years of complaints about chronic mail delays and inconsistent Postal Service delivery across Boston, according to previous Globe reports. Some residents have said they could not rely on prescriptions arriving on time, while others report waiting weeks for bills and government documents.

In 2024, Senators Ed Markey and Elizabeth Warren, Representative Ayanna Pressley, and seven other members of Massachusetts’ congressional delegation pointed to reports of lost mail and delivery delays in Roxbury, Somerville, Brookline, and other communities as evidence of ongoing postal service problems, the Globe reported. Later that year, audits by the Postal Service’s inspector general found significant operational issues at mail facilities in South Boston and Fort Point, including mail left unprocessed for days and packages that were handled improperly.

Turner faces up to six months in prison, one year of supervised release, and a $5,000 fine for the obstruction of mail charge, according to the statement.

title: For dignitaries and CEOs, the World Cup is like the Super Bowl and Davos rolled into one
text:
For CEOs and dignitaries all over the globe, the World Cup is the Super Bowl and Davos rolled into one.

Before, during, and after the games in Foxborough, business and political leaders from around the world are converging on Greater Boston to network, strike deals, and forge partnerships. But how important is it, really?

Consider the itinerary of John Swinney, First Minister of Scotland (the country’s top elected official). He spent Saturday in a kilt and soccer jersey for the FIFA Fan Festival on City Hall Plaza and Scotland’s match against Haiti that night. The day before? He was all business — wearing a shirt and tie to visit Harvard, meet with Boston Mayor Michelle Wu and Governor Maura Healey, and participate in a roundtable on artificial intelligence.

“Sporting tournaments of this type are really significant ... they bring us all together,” Swinney said at the AI event held at Goodwin Procter’s Seaport office.

“It gives us the opportunity to construct a number of opportunities to develop partnerships and cooperation.”

That’s not lost on Jeevan Ramapriya, executive director of the Massachusetts Office of International Trade and Investment, and state economic secretary Eric Paley, who moderated the AI roundtable with two dozen business and government leaders. They’ve spent months scouting out the VIPs who are coming to Massachusetts for the World Cup. The playbook is a familiar one — highlight Massachusetts as a destination for innovation and startups — and then play the long game.

“Let’s build these relationships because nothing’s going to happen overnight,” said Ramapriya. “This is a process.”

Like the Scottish, the Norwegians are mixing soccer and business. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre arrived in Boston Sunday night for a round of meetings ahead of tonight’s match against Iraq, according to Hege Vibeke Barnes, managing director of Innovation Norway USA, the Norwegian trade and promotion agency.

Vibeke Barnes, who is based in New York, will also be at the Norway game, entertaining nearly a dozen American tour operators. “We have very good seats,” she noted.

And the economic opportunities between Massachusetts and Norway go well beyond tourism — extending into clean energy, life sciences, and the maritime industry. Norway is becoming a leader in electric boats; Vibeke Barnes thinks there’s a market here for that, too. Convening over the World Cup, she said, brings a bit of “joy” to “our business meetings and creates stronger relations.”

For the Ghanaians, soccer comes first — a match against England next Tuesday, followed by the Ghana–Boston Trade & Investment Summit in downtown Boston on Wednesday and then the Ghana Worcester Trade Fair in Worcester on Thursday.

The idea for the gatherings grew out of a March visit from a Ghanaian delegation to Worcester, which is home to one of the biggest Ghanaian populations in the US, said Rita Adubra Asante, a global business consultant who is organizing the events.

Kicking off the Ghana-Boston summit will be Ghana’s Ambassador to the United States, Victor Emmanuel Smith. He’s based in Washington, D.C., but has been spending time in Rhode Island where Ghana’s soccer team is practicing at Bryant University. Since becoming ambassador last year, strengthening economic ties with the US has been a top priority, in particular drawing investment to create jobs in the African country so that more young people will stay there.

“I’ll talk to anybody who wants to do business,” said Emmanuel Smith. “We need to help our country progress. We don’t want to go around cup in hand looking for help every time. Come, and let’s partner.”

Too often the economic payoff of hosting a World Cup is measured by the number of tourists, hotel rooms filled, or beers sold. Edinaldo Tebaldi, an economics professor at Bryant, thinks we’ve been using the wrong metric.

“The World Cup is much more than just this massive sports event,” said Tebaldi, who also serves as the university’s vice president of strategy and partnerships. “It’s a platform for global collaborations and partnerships … a catalyst for economic development.

That World Cup energy Boston is feeling? It just might be the spark our economy needs these days.

What’s your take? Join the conversation in the comments here.

Dan Conley is not running for Suffolk County District Attorney again. But he’s stepping into the heated campaign regardless. That’s because Conley has strong feelings about Rachael Rollins running for the office she succeeded him in eight years ago. Conley called up Shirley last week to dispute Rollins’s recollection of how she first entered the DA race in 2018. In a lengthy interview last week with Power Play and GBH’s Jim Braude, Rollins said her candidacy prompted Conley to resign. Conley said he chose not to seek re-election after 16 years – which was publicly announced weeks before Rollins declared her candidacy. Who cares at this point? Well, Conley, who today serves as special counsel at Mintz Levin, said it’s important to set the record straight, given that Rollins resigned as US Attorney amid two federal ethics probes. “It’s just another example of shooting from the hip and not being truthful with the public,” Conley said. “This is about her fitness for office.” (Rollins said she stands by her chronology.) In 2018, Conley supported Greg Henning, who lost to Rollins. This time he’s backing incumbent Kevin Hayden. Buckle up, this race could be a bumpy ride. In case you missed it, here’s the 22-minute interview that aired on Boston Public Radio.

There’s a new kind of CVS coming soon to Nubian Square. While a Universal Hub reader just reported that the Rhode Island-based drugstore giant is opening up on Warren Street, Boston business leaders already got a preview of sorts, courtesy of CVS Health chief executive David Joyner, when he spoke to the Boston College Chief Executives Club on June 4. Joyner explained that when the store opens this summer, it would be a new format for CVS in Massachusetts. CVS is shrinking the “front store,” as Joyner put it, and focusing on the “pharmacy experience.” “They don’t really have a front store, but it’s a pharmacist and a clinician,”Joyner said. “We can still meet the clinical needs of the population but not feel like you’re constantly trying to deal with the safety of running a front store.”

Keolis has a new joint-venture partner along for the ride in its bid to keep the MBTA’s commuter rail contract. A T spokesperson confirmed on Monday that Keolis has teamed up with Amey Ltd., a British consulting and engineering firm, for the bid; the two already run trains together in the United Kingdom. Demoted to “preferred subcontractor status”: train manufacturer Alstom, Keolis’ previous JV partner in the commuter rail bid. The Keolis-Amey partnership is one of three bidding teams competing for the job.

Let’s say you get offered the chance on short notice to buy a batch of World Cup tickets at a discount, what do you do? If you’re Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, you start working the phones to raise money. Much like Governor Maura Healey, Wu has wanted to get free tickets into the hands of locals. Last Monday Healey announced a deal with Airbnb, which donated more than 1,100 tickets to kids. Wu chose to use the city’s Airbnb money to fund grants to small businesses. Then last week Wu got her shot at tickets, too, when host committee Boston Soccer 26 offered a few hundred, at a reduced price. That set off a flurry of calls to raise more than $200,000, enough to secure about 500 tickets, plus transportation costs, in a span of 72 hours. Just about everyone who was called said yes, according to a city official. Donors included: Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts, the Boston Red Sox, Boston Legacy Football Club, Coca-Cola Beverages Northeast, Eastern Bank, Fidelity Investments, John Hancock, Puma, Related Beal, Whoop, Ron Druker and The Druker Company, Harpoon Brewery’s Dan Kenary and wife Julie, and philanthropists Barrie Landry, Alicia Cooney, and Stephen Quigley. The city is partnering with soccer, youth-serving, and cultural organizations to distribute the tickets.

When Governor Maura Healey announced a deal to save a group of former Steward hospitals two years ago, she said the fate of the shuttered Norwood Hospital would be dealt with at a later date. Norwood was different, after all. It was being rebuilt after a flood. Meanwhile, the need for health care services in that area remains great. You can’t blame local leaders if they’re restless.

Our colleague Jonathan Saltzman just reported that Mass General Brigham was in talks months ago with property owner MPT to buy the unfinished hospital — to no avail. (The price that MPT sought seems ridiculously high.) Meanwhile, Representative John Rogers and others are trying to build support for a bill that Rogers filed to help the Healey administration take it by eminent domain.

Healey may not need that bill. Reopening a half-finished hospital should fit the definition of a public purpose that’s needed for Healey to seize it. (Healey did it once before, with St. E’s in Brighton, now part of Boston Medical Center‘s health system.) What she does need is some money on hand to reimburse MPT for the value of the property, and a hospital operator willing to invest in this turnaround project and cover those site acquisition costs. Healey should consider calling up MGB to hash out some kind of deal that works for everyone.

No poll today. We’ll go right to the answer of last week’s quiz.

We asked readers which hotel the French national team, Les Bleus, is staying at, and most everyone got it right: the Four Seasons on Boylston Street. The World Cup favorites have taken over the luxury hotel while they practice at Bentley University in Waltham. Looks like readers are following the World Cup closely! But are you following closely enough to know where the Scottish and Haitian teams stayed this past weekend? Email us at powerplay@globe.com. First three readers with the right answer will get some Power Play swag.

title: Cambridge Health Alliance to reopen birth center after six-year hiatus
text:
“Standing here today, we didn’t know years ago whether this would happen,” said Decker, a former Birth Center patient, during an open house Wednesday. “During COVID, there were real questions about whether the center would reopen. But many people remained committed to the mission and making it equitable.”

More than 200 people attended the celebration , waiting in line for a tour. The building was operational for 22 years before closing, and since then, they’ve expanded to three delivery rooms, designed to resemble bedrooms rather than traditional hospital rooms. Two rooms have soaking tubs for water births, an option that medical professionals say can help with pain management and relaxation during labor. The facility also has exam rooms, cribs, a kitchen, a waiting room, an elevator, and a wheelchair ramp.

Birth centers offer a different model from hospitals: a home-like setting where midwives — licensed providers trained to support patients through pregnancy, labor, and the postpartum period — lead care for low-risk pregnancies. The centers typically offer longer appointments than hospitals, and many patients work with doulas, nonmedical professionals who provide physical and emotional support.

Midwives and doulas gave tours, many answering questions of expecting parents like “Do you have a birth stool? And a certified lactation consultant?” They replied yes.

Birth centers tend to have fewer patients, provide more personalized care, avoid medications during birth, and foster a culture of shared decision-making that empowers patients and reduces stress. They can administer IVs, but it’s not routine, midwives say. It’s also normal to be discharged 4 to 6 hours after giving birth with frequent follow-up visits. Patients who need to stay for 8 hours or longer will need to be transferred to the hospital.

At the same time, the centers have limitations. They are designed for low-risk pregnancies and do not typically include physicians or OB/GYNs as part of routine care. They also have restrictions on the procedures they can offer, including the use of epidural anesthesia and surgical interventions. If complications arise during childbirth, patients are transferred to a hospital.

The reopening comes as Massachusetts faces growing concern over maternal health access and outcomes. Hospitals across the state have shuttered 13 maternity units, totaling more than 100 beds, over the past decade. Maternal health inequities are widening despite years of state investment, with Black families disproportionately affected by complications and unequal access to care.

State leaders, including Governor Maura Healey, have pointed to birth centers as a lower-cost, lower-intervention alternative for people with low-risk pregnancies and have allocated millions of dollars in funding to support them.

Care will be led by certified nurse-midwives, supported by a team of 19 doulas who collectively speak 13 languages. Doula services are covered by MassHealth.

The Birth Center expects to deliver 100 babies in its first year, ramping up to about 300 by the fourth year. Hospital leaders said the center will be open to all patients but will place particular emphasis on serving vulnerable and underserved populations.

Samya Singletary of Boston, whose son is due on Halloween, enrolled at the CHA Birth Center when she was six weeks pregnant in March. She had some initial uncertainty about whether the facility would reopen in time for her delivery, but after touring the center Wednesday, those concerns had disappeared.

“I love my midwife here. I love that there’s no pressure, no monitors all over the place, and that I can feel relaxed and at home with good support,” said Singletary, 33. “I especially like the tubs and not feeling like I’m on a time crunch to push a baby out. I’m excited to come back when it’s time.”

Massachusetts currently has only one operating freestanding birth center, Seven Sisters in Florence, after a handful closed due to financial strain. The reopening of CHA’s Birth Center is expected to expand access to midwifery-led care in Greater Boston and comes as advocates push to grow the model statewide, with new birth centers planned in Roxbury and Worcester.

Neighborhood Birth Center, opening next year in Roxbury, and members of the Mount Auburn Midwifery Program also joined the open house to show their support.

During the last six years, CHA officials said they hired consultants to study whether the facility could safely resume deliveries and said it took several years to implement operational and infrastructure recommendations.

“I think this is a beacon of hope, not just for Cambridge, but for all of the other communities,” said Claire Laporte, vice chair of the Cambridge Health Alliance’s board of trustees.

CHA chief executive officer Dr. Assaad Sayah welcomed state and local leaders, including Decker, Representative Katherine Clark, whose congressional district includes part of Cambridge, Massachusetts Department of Public Health Commissioner Dr. Robbie Goldstein, and Cambridge Mayor Sumbul Siddiqui.

Goldstein said the Birth Center is special as it’s the oldest in the state.

“For decades, it had been a place where families have welcomed new life into the world,” Goldstein said. “Like so many institutions, this center faced enormous challenges during the pandemic, but today is not the story of a closure. Today is the story of renewal.”

title: You’ve got (ballot) questions. We’ve got answers.
text:
Ballot question campaigns face one of their last checkpoints Wednesday before they can officially get their proposal before voters this fall. Whether they actually do may be another matter entirely.

Campaigns have until the end of the day to turn their final batch of 12,429 signatures into local clerks, a hurdle most campaigns say they will clear.

But several questions are still tangled up in court. Others could get negotiated away on Beacon Hill before voters ever see them. One has already been knocked off completely. As of Wednesday morning, here’s the potentially record lineup of 11 measures currently barreling toward the ballot:

💸 Income tax cut: The business leaders behind a ballot question that would slash the state’s income tax from 5 percent to 4 percent say they have the signatures to get the question before voters.

It already seems to be popular with voters: 66 percent of the 500 registered voters in a Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll conducted last week said they support the question, compared to 21 percent who were opposed.

Not so much with labor unions or on Beacon Hill. House Speaker Ron Mariano expressed some interest in negotiating to keep the question off the ballot, where if approved experts estimate it could cost the state $5.1 billion in tax revenue. But lawmakers also passed legislation that would hold some other tax changes hostage if the question passes.

📈 Tax cap rewrite: It’s mostly flown under the radar so far, but this proposal, also pressed by business groups, could significantly reshape how the state crafts its budget.

The question would change the formula for Chapter 62F, the automatic tax refund rule you might remember from 2022 for delivering $3 billion back to taxpayers. That includes by counting revenue from the so-called millionaires tax in calculating what tax collections would be capped at before triggering a refund to taxpayers.

In other words, the law would likely be triggered more often — delivering taxpayers more money, but muddying the state’s budget-writing process.

🏠 Rent control: Supporters of a proposal to bring back a form of rent control say they’ve collected 33,000 signatures this round — more than twice what they would need — but two outside factors could still keep the question from going before voters this fall.

First, the courts: Opponents filed a lawsuit earlier this year claiming that the question was too ambiguous and the summary of it drafted by Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s office was misleading.

There’s also the possibility that proponents could strike a deal to keep the question off the ballot. The Globe’s Andrew Brinker has more on where those conversations stand.

🗳️ All-party primaries: After vowing to increase ballot access on her way out of the governor’s race in 2022, former Democratic hopeful Danielle Allen is back with a proposal to scrap traditional party primaries and replace them with a “top two” system for state elections in which every candidate runs in the same preliminary election, regardless of party affiliation.

The campaign says it has submitted 20,000 signatures this round, though the Supreme Judicial Court is still weighing a challenge from Democratic Party leaders on whether the proposal is constitutional.

📂 Public records: State Auditor Diana DiZoglio says the campaign she’s leading to subject the governor’s office and the state Legislature to the public records law has cleared the signature hurdle.

Don’t submit your records requests just yet, though. There’s no formal opposition to DiZoligo’s latest crusade, but the state Senate sought an advisory opinion from the SJC that left the door open for the Legislature to amend the ballot proposal if it passes.

And House lawmakers have already passed legislation intended to cut the ballot question off by subjecting the Governor Maura Healey to the current public records law while carving out new requirements for themselves that would allow the public access to a specific set of “legislative” records.

🌿 Marijuana legalization repeal: The state’s highest court cleared this one for the ballot late last week, and supporters say they’ve got the signatures needed to advance.

If it reaches the ballot, voters would decide whether Massachusetts should reverse course on recreational marijuana legalization a decade after it passed a separate ballot question creating the multibillion-dollar industry here.

☑️ Same-day voter registration: Secretary of State Bill Galvin is backing a proposal allowing voters to register on Election Day. No organized opposition has emerged so far, though the concept is not popular in the House.

🏘️ Starter homes: This is another measure that appears to be cruising toward November. The proposal would make it easier to build so-called starter homes across Massachusetts by changing zoning law to allow for development of single-family homes on smaller lots. Supporters say they’ve collected about 16,000 signatures and are already gearing up for a major advertising push after Labor Day, according to the campaign’s committee chair, Andrew Mikula.

🌊 Land and water conservation: We forgive if you totally missed this one. If passed, the proposal from the “Protect Water and Nature” campaign would redirect some of the sales tax on sporting goods into a conservation fund. So far, there isn’t any formal opposition campaign.

⚖️ CPCS collective bargaining: Another deep cut on the list.

The measure would give employees at the Committee for Public Counsel Services — the state’s public defenders agency — the right to collectively bargain. SEIU Local 888 Tom McKeever, whose union is one of two locals supporting the question, said the campaign is poised to clear the next signature hurdle.

📝 Gun law repeal: There’s also a measure targeting the state’s firearms law that is heading to voters through a slightly different process and doesn’t need to clear Wednesday’s signature deadline. That measure would give voters the final word on whether to keep or toss the sweeping gun-control law lawmakers approved last session.

TURNING THE PAGE: Mass. lawmakers strike deal on major reading instruction overhaul by John Hilliard, The Boston Globe: Massachusetts lawmakers announced an agreement Tuesday on a long-awaited overhaul of the state’s reading instruction requirements that will impose new mandates on school districts. The legislation, which still must clear each chamber and be signed by Healey, would mark a major increase in state oversight of local school districts.

FUELING DEBATE: At Massport’s urging, Healey signs tax break for sustainable aviation fuel by Jordan Wolman, CommonWealth Beacon: A supplemental budget bill Healey signed last week includes the state’s first foray into so-called sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, which is made from cooking oil, plant and animal materials, or synthetic fuel, instead of petroleum. Healey approved a $10 million tax credit for each of the next three years that’s meant to nudge airlines into adopting the nascent fuel despite opposition from some environmental groups.

SEA CHANGE: The House plans to vote Wednesday on its version of Healey’s environmental bond bill, but the chamber took a knife to some of the policy proposals and funding state senators included in the version they passed in April.

The nearly $3.1 billion bottom line in authorized borrowing is scaled down considerably from the state Senate’s $3.94 billion bond bill, and the House kept a controversial provision that would redefine when a shifting beach in Massachusetts is considered public. But it cut the Senate’s long-floated plastic bag ban. The Globe’s Kate Selig has more.

DEBATE DODGER: Missed last night’s US Senate debate? You’re not alone. Incumbent Senator Ed Markey also passed on the quixotic event that featured his Democratic primary challenger, US Representative Seth Moulton, and the all-but-certain GOP nominee, John Deaton. The Globe’s Anjali Huynh has four takeaways from the cross-party faceoff.

ENDORSEMENT ALERT: The Planned Parenthood Advocacy Fund of Massachusetts rolled out endorsements for legislative candidates on Wednesday, including for a few Democratic primary challengers. The group is backing Persis Yu in her bid to unseat West Roxbury state Senator Mike Rush, and Latoya Gayle, who’s challenging South Boston state Senator Nick Collins.

NO FARE: Most Mass. voters cool to congestion pricing, saying they oppose paying more to drive into Boston with less traffic by Chris Van Buskirk, the Boston Globe: An overwhelming majority of Massachusetts residents said they would not want to pay extra to drive to downtown Boston if that meant less traffic, dealing a blow to the idea of introducing congestion pricing in New England’s largest city, according to a new Suffolk University/Boston Globe poll.

Hillary Clinton Says Biden’s Re-election Bid Was a ‘Terrible Mistake’ by Tim Balk, The New York Times.

John Kerry calls Trump’s plan to end Iran war an attempt to fix his own mistakes by Samantha J. Gross, The Boston Globe.

Kraft Sports, Patriots sue Foxborough over licensing fees by Travis Andersen, The Boston Globe.

State’s mental health department should take over Bridgewater hospital, advocates say by Katie Lannan, GBH News.

Vineyard Offshore owes $1 million in rent, landlord says in suit by Anastasia E. Lennon, The New Bedford Light.

Worcester judge gave gift to crime victim. Now defendants want new trial by Brad Petrishen, Worcester Telegram & Gazette.
