title: The best things to do in and around Boston this weekend
text:
On tap this weekend: boogie down in Cambridge, celebrate Pride Month, plus World Cup fun continues. — Matt Juul

BOSTON FAN ZONE If you couldn’t get tickets to see Norway vs. France in Foxborough, you can catch all of the World Cup action at the Lawn on D’s watch party. If the match gets you in the competitive spirit, check out the event’s game selection, including cornhole, mini golf, and foosball. June 26, noon. 420 D St. 877-393-3393. signatureboston.com — Annie Sarlin

CAMBRIDGE CITY DANCE PARTY Shake off the week at the 26th annual Cambridge City Dance Party. Enjoy music from local DJs, interactive activities, and a sunset light show at this all-ages dance party. June 26, 6-10 p.m. Free. Central Square, 344 Broadway, Cambridge. cambridgeusa.org — Gitana Savage

QUEER HISTORY WEST END PRIDE PARTY In celebration of its new queer history exhibit, the West End Museum hosts a Pride-themed party at Dorchester Brewing Company. The event will be emceed by drag artist Axel Starcock and feature information on historic local LGBTQ activists, educators, and community spaces. June 26, 6:30-8:30 p.m. 1250 Massachusetts Ave. 617-723-2125. thewestendmuseum.org — AS

BOSTON GROWN-UPS MUSEUM If you’re having some summer camp nostalgia, the Boston Children’s Museum has the solution. Head to the museum for a special after-hours grown-ups-only night. Kick off the evening with a ride on the harbor in animal pedal boats, then keep the party going with a series of summer camp-themed activities, including tug-of-war, friendship bracelet making, and more. Food and drinks are also available for purchase. June 26, 7 p.m. $33.85. 21+. Boston Children’s Museum, 308 Congress St. eventbrite.com — GS

ROXBURY POETRY FESTIVAL Spend your Saturday channeling your inner poet at the Roxbury Poetry Festival. Sponsored by the Mayor’s Office of Arts & Culture, the event offers workshops, featured speakers, a slam poetry competition, and complimentary lunch at this free, daylong event. June 27, 10 a.m.-10 p.m. Free. Bruce C. Bolling Building, 2300 Washington St. boston.gov — GS

FAMILY FUN DAY Celebrate summer with bounce houses, magic shows, music, and more at Somerville’s 20th annual free Family Fun Day. The event will also include cornhole, soccer, basketball, and other games, as well as crafts like water bottle decorating and stuffed animal coloring. June 27, 1-4 p.m. 541 Broadway, Somerville. 617-625-6600. somervillema.gov — AS

SUMMER SATURDAY MOVIE NIGHT Who lives in a pineapple under the sea? Catch the Bikini Bottom gang at this free outdoor screening of “The SpongeBob Movie: Search for SquarePants” at Urban Park’s first Summer Saturday film of the season. Listen to music from a DJ before settling down on the lawn to watch SpongeBob’s adventures as he follows the Flying Dutchman and his ghostly pirate ship into the deep ocean. June 27, 4 p.m., movie starts at 6 p.m. 325 Main St., Cambridge. 617-491-0709. kendallcenter.com — AS

MAYOR WU’S WORLD CUP WATCH PARTY Keep the World Cup energy going at Boston Mayor Michelle Wu’s free watch party for the Colombia vs. Portugal match. Head to East Boston Memorial Stadium to cheer on your team. June 27, 7-10 p.m. Free. East Boston Memorial Stadium, 143 Porter St. boston.gov — GS

BOSTON FUNNY Tony V headlines the inaugural event in this planned monthly comedy series at the Royal Sonesta, under the Boston Funny banner. He’ll be joined by a host of Boston favorites, including Jimmy Dunn, Carolyn Plummer, and Will Noonan. June 27, 8 p.m. $28.52. The Royal Sonesta, 40 Edwin H. Land Blvd., Cambridge. bostonfunny.com — Nick A. Zaino III

BOSTON THAI TASTE Head to Boston Common for a festival honoring Thai culture. Sample dishes like pad thai, mango sticky rice, and papaya salad from food vendors, watch Muay Thai kickboxing, listen to DJ sets, and catch live performances of traditional Thai dance and Isan music. June 28, 11 a.m.-7 p.m. 139 Tremont St. nathikaevents.com — AS

5TH ANNUAL REVERE BEACH PRIDE CELEBRATION As Pride Month nears its end, celebrate in the sun at the fifth annual Revere Beach Pride Celebration. Enjoy drag and dance performances and do some shopping from a selection of local LGBTQ+ and ally organizations. June 28, 1-6 p.m. Free. Waterfront Square, between 400-500 Ocean Ave., Revere. revere.org — GS

48-HOUR ONE-ACT PLAY FESTIVAL The Rockwell hosts its second annual 48-Hour One-Act Play Festival, featuring theatrical performances from LGBTQ+ actors who, as the name suggests, only had 48 hours to conceptualize, write, and rehearse their material. June 28, 6 p.m. $18.87. The Rockwell, 255 Elm St., Somerville. therockwell.org — GS

KABOOM COMEDY AND VARIETY Boston has a small but mighty vaudeville/variety scene with occasional independent shows at different theaters. Kaboom is where they all perform on a regular basis, hosted by two of the most prominent variety acts, Alex Feldman and Colin Campbell. June 28, 7 p.m. $18.95-$29.95. The Comedy Studio, 5 John F. Kennedy St., Cambridge. www.thecomedystudio.com — NZ

ONE LONG EARRING The band is getting back together! Maybe. That’s the plan in this musical comedy about a fictional band reuniting after an ugly public breakup years ago at the Labia Majora Festival. June 28, 7:30 p.m. $50.25-$54.90. The Crystal Ballroom at Somerville Theatre, 55 Davis Square, Somerville. 617-245-2900, crystalballroomboston.com — NZ

JACOB’S PILLOW DANCE FESTIVAL The Berkshires summer dance event recently kicked off, with this weekend’s programming featuring performances from the Paul Taylor Dance Company (through June 28), Uppercut Dance Theater (through June 26), the School at Jacob’s Pillow’s Contemporary Ballet Performance Ensemble (June 27), and Shamell Pitts’s company TRIBE(through June 28). On June 27, Pitts will also host a “PillowTalk” discussing his inspirations behind “Touch of RED,” which the company will perform at the festival. Through Aug. 30. 358 George Carter Road, Becket. 413-243-9919. jacobspillow.org — AS

IN OLD AGE The widowed Abasiama Bassey (Ebony Marshall-Oliver), whom Boston audiences have gotten to know as a key figure in Mfoniso Udofia’s nine-play cycle about three generations of a Nigerian-American family, develops a late-in-life spiritual bond with Azell Abernathy (Marvin Bell), a gentle-spirited contractor. Directed by Dawn M. Simmons. Through June 28. Production by Front Porch Arts Collective. Presented by ArtsEmerson at Emerson Paramount Center, Jackie Liebergott Black Box Theatre, 559 Washington St. 617-824-8400, artsemerson.org

EUREKA DAY It’s a testament to Jonathan Spector’s skill that he managed to make his play as funny as it is while wading into the charged territory of mandatory vaccinations. That “Eureka Day” manages to (mostly) survive his wrongheaded decision to suddenly inject one character’s past tragedy into the mix is a testament to the play’s overall strength. With a topnotch cast directed by Margot Bordelon, “Eureka Day” mines quite a few laughs from the spectacle of well-meaning progressives tying themselves in lexical knots as they try to process events that defy ideological pigeonholes. Through June 28. Production by The Huntington. At Huntington Theatre, 264 Huntington Ave. 617-266-0800, huntingtontheatre.org

BAD BOOKS After discovering her teenage son with a book she considers obscene, a mother (Aimee Doherty) confronts a local librarian (Therese Plaehn). Matters quickly escalate, and soon the entire town is embroiled in the dispute. Sharyn Rothstein’s play is directed by M. Bevin O’Gara. Through June 27. Gloucester Stage Company. At Natti-Willsky Performance Center, 267 East Main St., Gloucester. 978-281-4433, gloucesterstage.com

ENSEMBLE ALTERA As the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence approaches, the Providence-based professional chamber choir debuts “Declarations,” an evening-length piece by composer Piers Connor Kennedy based on texts by a tapestry of American writers including Thomas Jefferson, Tracy K. Smith, Langston Hughes, and Iñupiaq poet dg nanouk okpik. June 27, 7 p.m., Old South Church, 645 Boylston St.; June 28, 3 p.m., First Baptist Church, 75 N Main St., Providence. ensemblealtera.com

ROCKPORT CHAMBER MUSIC FESTIVAL The Galvin Cello Quartet opens up the weekend early at the Shalin Liu Performance Center, featuring a free hourlong family concert Friday morning (perfect if the kids are out of school) — then, for the grown-ups and Broadway babies, Upstairs on Main hosts a Pride Month cabaret on Friday night with vocalist Thom Smoker and pianist Nick Place. Saturday begins with “The Nightingale’s Sonata” in the morning, narrated by Thomas Wolf and based on his book of the same name about violinist Lea Luboshutz; that evening, 2025 Banff Competition winners the Poeisis Quartet splash down with a new music-focused program. Sunday afternoon, violinist Augustin Hadelich (you’ve maybe seen him with the BSO) takes the spotlight with a mini-solo recital before intermission, Tchaikovsky’s “Souvenir de Florence” after. Through July 12. Shalin Liu Performance Center, 37 Main St., Rockport. 978-546-7391, rockportmusic.org

MAGGIE O’FARRELL Our critic adored O’Farrell’s new book, “Land” — even calling it better than her beloved “Hamnet,” the source material for the gorgeous recent film. Local readers will have the chance to hear from the author herself, in conversation with local superstar Celeste Ng (“Everything I Never Told You”), on Saturday. June 27, 7 p.m. $45.09 (includes copy of the book). First Parish Church, 1446 Massachusetts Ave., Cambridge. 617-661-1515, harvard.com

PAUL SIMON Solid Sound Festival isn’t the only major music event in Western Massachusetts this weekend. Paul Simon heads to Tanglewood for two shows — Saturday and Sunday — on his extended “A Quiet Celebration” tour, which visited the Boch Center Wang Theatre last summer. Read more about upcoming concerts in this week’s Sound Check. June 27-28. Tanglewood, Koussevitzky Music Shed, 297 West St., Lenox. bso.org

MUSEUM OF FINE ARTS: AMERICA AT 250 A celebratory occasion turned fraught and contentious by a radical turn in American government, the semiquincentennial this summer is shaping up to be yet another battleground in the daily culture war grind. At the MFA, there’s no backing down: It turned down a $400,000 federal grant for the full do-over of its just-opened 18th-century Art of the Americas galleries for fear of government interference, and has gone ahead with its vision of an inspiring, imperfect, still-in-progress democracy with much left to aspire to — a far more hopeful view than the simple-minded celebration the administration touts. Ongoing. Museum of Fine Arts, 465 Huntington Ave. 617-267-9300, mfa.org

LOOKING FOR AMERICA, FEATURING HANK WILLIS THOMAS Thomas will be best known to Bostonians for "The Embrace", the colossal bronze memorial to Coretta Scott King and Martin Luther King Jr. on Boston Common. But Thomas has spent a career contemplating the thornier elements of American history and culture, and this is the latest installment on the theme, in time for the country’s 250th. The exhibition will focus on collaboration and community, critical through struggle, and will include contributions from artists including Karinne Smith and Hector René Membreño-Canales, and his mother, the esteemed historian Deborah Willis. ThroughJuly 19. Ogunquit Museum, 543 Shore Road, Ogunquit, Maine. 207-646-4909, ogunquitmuseum.org

DANNY LYON: THE BIKERIDERS In creating one of the definitive documentary photography projects of the 1960s, Danny Lyons joined the Chicago Outlaws Motorcycle Club while still an undergraduate at the University of Chicago to capture his subjects from the inside. The result, a raw portrait of a subculture that helped define a generation of America, is now a totem of the form. Through Aug. 16. Currier Museum of Art, 150 Ash St., Manchester, N.H. 603-669-6144, currier.org

FIFA FAN FESTIVAL BOSTON Looking for another World Cup-themed event? Head to City Hall Plaza for the final days of the FIFA Fan Festival, the city’s central World Cup gathering spot. On Friday, you can catch Norway vs. France at 3 p.m. and Cape Verde vs. Saudi Arabia at 8 p.m., while Saturday’s games include Panama vs. England at 5 p.m., Colombia vs. Portugal at 7:30 p.m., and Jordan vs. Argentina at 10 p.m. A range of local food and drink offerings will also be available for purchase. Through June 27., Registration required. Boston City Hall Plaza, 1 City Hall Square, Boston. bostonfwc26.com — GS

BAMS FEST The multi-day celebration of arts and culture returned this week, with an array of programming to check out through the weekend. On Saturday, DJ Jazzy Jeff headlines the 2026 Play Playe event at Dorchester’s the Record Co., which invites the community to compete in a variety of board and card games, video game arcade, and spades tournament. The event also includes dance lessons and a vendor market. Other weekend activities include a Caribbean rave experience, an after-hours event at the Fuller Craft Museum, and slam poetry performances. Through June 28. Multiple locations. bamsfest.org — AS

title: A state official gave a grant to two young developers who sold him a house. Then came the shoddy work and fake invoices.
text:
Instead of getting full makeovers, the four buildings in Worcester and Pittsfield still had myriad problems: rickety stairways, deficient siding, peeling paint, nasty refrigerators and toilets, and a possible bedbug infestation, according to post-renovation inspections. Some low-quality kitchen countertops had been inexplicably painted over.

The lone tenant in the Worcester triple-decker targeted for renovation, 76-year-old Stephen Jenkins, called the modest improvements to his unit “some half-ass [expletive],” saying the developers relied on “sidewalk Willies,” or uncredentialed handymen.

Fraud is also at least partly to blame for the disappointing outcome, the Globe Spotlight Team found. At least nine subcontractors flatly denied doing the work attributed to them, for which the state paid nearly $580,000. Another two said they suspected the invoices the developers attributed to them were inaccurate. Only two subcontractors reached by the Globe confirmed they did the work on the invoices attributed to them and got paid for it.

Those misrepresentations were missed by officials at MassHousing, a quasi-state agency with a critical role in addressing the Commonwealth’s housing affordability crisis.

The agency executive who awarded the grants to the developers in Worcester and Pittsfield had a connection to them: He had purchased a home in West Roxbury from the same two men just six months before, paying $204,000 less than the original listing price, records show.

That executive, Tony Richards II, did not file a written disclosure about his relationship at the time, in apparent violation of state ethics laws. Asked about that lapse, MassHousing’s top lawyer initially told the Globe that Richards belatedly discovered the connection more than a year after making the grant awards.

But a Spotlight review of Richards’s emails shows he was corresponding with the developers about real-estate financing opportunities around the time of the home sale. After initially defending Richards, the agency’s lawyer, Colin McNiece, announced MassHousing would be hiring an outside firm to audit the entire matter.

In the meantime, Richards, who earns $255,000 as MassHousing’s vice president of strategic community investments, remains in his position, the agency said, though oversight of grants has been taken over by the legal department while the review is underway. The agency is also reviewing several grant programs under Richards’s purview.

Richards served as a deputy chief of staff to then-Governor Charlie Baker before joining MassHousing in 2021, just over a year before Baker left office. Shortly after taking office, Governor Maura Healey named him vice-chair of her Advisory Council on Black Empowerment.

Richards declined to speak with the Globe. He has retained a lawyer, Payal Salsburg of Smith Kane, according to MassHousing officials, but she did not return multiple messages seeking comment.

The developers who left a trail of shoddy work and bogus invoices, Gary Acquah and Reggie Woods, also did not respond to multiple requests for comment from the Globe.

Two ethics experts who reviewed the matter for the Globe said MassHousing did not properly address Richards’s conflict of interest when he made his bosses aware of it. Despite a number of red flags, including Richards’s conflict, the agency also failed to recognize the depth of the problems in Worcester and Pittsfield until after the Spotlight Team dug into the matter.

At first, the agency downplayed the Globe’s findings.

On June 9, MassHousing officials said Richards told them that when he was awarding the grants in 2023, he did not realize that four of the first seven went to the same people who had just sold him his house. He said that was why he failed to report the apparent conflict.

In that interview, Richards had made an innocent mistake, MassHousing said.

But the agency’s position changed after the Globe sought emails between Richards and the developers, which cast serious doubts on his claims. The messages make clear that Richards knew Acquah and Woods.

For instance, less than three weeks after Richards closed on the home, Acquah emailed him about an upcoming meeting of industry professionals to discuss obtaining pre-development capital, referencing a previous conversation between the two.

“Hey Tony, was this event the one you mentioned would be remote?” Acquah wrote. “Or is this one in person and where? Thanks, Gary.”

Days before, Richards had emailed MassHousing CEO Chrystal Kornegay asking for her approval of a list of 12 professionals under the heading “Equitable Business Kitchen Cabinet,” apparently a group of unofficial advisers. Acquah and Woods were included on that list.

MassHousing officials initially urged the Globe to drop its request for emails from the time period of the home sale. The Globe declined, and the agency subsequently turned over most of the emails.

Along with the emails, MassHousing released a statement saying the agency would hire an outside firm to audit the matter. About two dozen emails were withheld as privileged.

“Our initial review indicated that all grant award decisions were made in a manner consistent with grant criteria and aligned with the program’s stated objectives,” said McNiece, the agency’s chief legal and operating officer. “However, we have recently learned additional information that warrants further investigation.”

This week, when the Globe notified MassHousing that several subcontractors denied doing the work attributed to them, the agency said in a prepared statement it “takes allegations of potential fraud and noncompliance seriously and will thoroughly investigate any allegations brought to our attention.”

“MassHousing is committed to taking all necessary steps to respond to these allegations, including cooperating with law enforcement as appropriate,” the statement added.

Today, most of the 13 units the state paid Acquah and Woods $1.4 million to fix up are still in rough shape.

Jenkins, who lives on the second floor of the three-family in Worcester, said his unit has hardly been improved. While the first- and third-floor units are in better shape, the only occupants in the last three years have been squatters, Jenkins said.

Worcester officials had given Acquah a separate grant of $134,750 to fix up the triple-decker. The city now wants its money back because of his failures; the building was sold at a foreclosure auction in late March.

“It is definitely disappointing seeing the units not come to fruition, and seeing that opportunity not delivered to Worcester families that need affordable housing,” said Peter Dunn, the city’s chief development officer.

In both Pittsfield and Worcester, officials expressed concerns late in the process about whether the apartments will be able to be rented to people with Section 8 vouchers because of their condition, a frustrating outcome for a program that aims to help low-income residents.

Emily Baird, a tenant in one of the Pittsfield properties, recently showed reporters around her place. She pointed out how the porch is “really rickety,” while many doors don’t close right and “the floor is tilted every which way” because nothing is plumb.

But Baird, who said she struggled with homelessness before moving in, said she’s thankful for the place, imperfections and all.

Baird and her neighbors got a new landlord last year when Acquah and Woods sold the three Pittsfield properties.

The developers were supposed to retain control of the buildings under the terms of the Gateway Housing Rehabilitation Program — which ultimately gave away about $2.3 million, more than half of it to Acquah and Woods. The program had several aims: to boost “emerging” developers; to address blight in Massachusetts cities with weak markets; and to add quality affordable housing at a time when people are leaving the Commonwealth in droves over the cost of shelter.

While MassHousing mostly functions like a bank, selling billions of dollars in bonds to subsidize affordable projects, the agency has also been overseeing a growing array of state grant programs. It disbursed more than $100 million in grants last year.

Records show agency officials did not realize there were problems with the Pittsfield renovations until the grant money was gone. They had relied on photos and invoices from Acquah and Woods and signoffs from local officials.

But in the summer of 2024, they inspected the Worcester triple-decker and were appalled at what they found. The agency visited Pittsfield next.

“We are very disappointed with the quality of this construction and are concerned that these issues could affect your ability to successfully access MassHousing funding in the future,” wrote Richards, in a letter to Acquah.

It was shortly after those problems surfaced, in the fall of 2024, that MassHousing officials say they learned of Richards’s potential conflict.

McNiece, the agency’s lawyer, said Richards told Kornegay, the CEO, in October 2024 he had just realized the people who sold him his home were also the grant recipients in hot water over the sloppy renovations.

Richards told them he realized the connection when he was going through paperwork in preparation to have his private mortgage insurance canceled, officials said.

Kornegay referred Richards to McNiece, the lawyer said. McNiece said he determined that a formal written disclosure by Richards would have been “basically moot” at that point, since the grants were already awarded. So none was filed.

Typically, homeowners whose equity stake in their home is under 20 percent must carry mortgage insurance. Records show Richards put only 5 percent down when he bought his place. To increase his equity stake, Richards would likely have had to do one of two things: Put down more money or commission an appraisal showing his house was worth significantly more than he paid for it.

Regarding the Pittsfield properties, some of the invoices the developers submitted were “sloppy,” even amateurish, McNiece said, but officials eventually considered the issues closed in late 2024 after a back-and-forth with Acquah and Woods.

“We did dig into the invoicing and the work that was done,” McNiece said on June 9. “At the end of the day, the scope of work was completed. The quality of work was lacking.”

Had the agency dug a little deeper, officials might have noticed many obvious discrepancies on the invoices: Two different subcontractors were invoiced for installation of a roof on the same Pittsfield property. In another case, $20,000 appeared to have been added to materials costs on a receipt, without explanation. Another invoice catalogued repairs to a garage on a property that didn’t have one.

That puzzling contradiction was on an invoice purportedly prepared by contractor Michael Biancaniello. Contacted by the Globe, he was happy to clarify.

“I never set foot in Pittsfield,” Biancaniello said flatly.

Records show Acquah and Woods collected about $125,000 on invoices bearing Biancaniello’s letterhead. He said he never saw a dime of it.

Biancaniello said he does know the pair. He did a job for them in early 2022, fixing up a Colonial single-family house in Pascoag, R.I., he said. He vowed not to work for them again because they took so long to pay him, he said.

The invoice from the Rhode Island job, which Biancaniello shared with the Globe, was almost identical to one Acquah and Woods sent to MassHousing — the one that listed work on a phantom “garage” in Pittsfield.

Eight of the nine contractors who told the Globe they did not do the work attributed to them all said they had worked with Acquah and Woods in the past on smaller jobs.

“I’m super upset,” said Bruno Balles, who was shocked when the Globe showed him invoices for $160,000 worth of work on the Worcester property attributed to his company. He didn’t get paid nearly that much, he said, and the scope of the work was far smaller.

He said the documents Acquah gave MassHousing were “fake,” and he shared real invoices totaling $56,000. Balles’s signature did not match the ones on Acquah’s paperwork.

“It’s not only fake invoices and using my name,” Balles said. “He pretended that I signed those papers.”

Even after he revealed his relationship to the developers in late 2024, Richards continued to serve as the agency’s contact with Acquah and Woods. In letters to the two, Richards requested a series of fixes.

In December 2024, Richards said in a letter to the developers the grants for the three Pittsfield properties would be considered “closed.” He also suggested the developers might want to sell to someone more experienced — even though the terms of the grant program had envisioned long-term stewardship.

Asked why Richards continued to interface with Acquah and Woods, McNiece called the letters Richards sent out “miscommunications.” He added: “Tony was a signatory, but he didn’t have any involvement in any transactions at that time.”

Two ethics experts who reviewed the matter at the request of the Globe both criticized the agency’s handling of it. They said Richards should have filed a disclosure as soon as he made the conflict known — even if it was late — and that he should have been kept away from the matter after that.

“As soon as he recognized having had a commercial transaction with the grantees, that was the time to recuse and disclose,” Thomas Susman, a Washington-based lawyer and lobbyist who has written and lectured extensively on ethics, said by email.

Even a late disclosure has real value, Susman said, envisioning a scenario where ”an agency employee notices the disclosure and says, ‘Wait a minute. I saw Mr. Official at the Capital Grille having steaks and wine with the grantees right about the time the grants were made.’”

A situation like that, Susman said, would “suggest that maybe the ‘basically moot’ conclusion was premature.”

By June 2025, the developers had flipped the three Pittsfield properties. The $780,000 they received was enough for a profit in the hundreds of thousands of dollars, though that sum was $320,000 less than what the Commonwealth had invested into the properties.

In addition to the money they made on the Pittsfield sales, Acquah and Woods collected at least $139,000 in developers’ fees from MassHousing, a typical amount in such deals.

In July 2025, several months after the Globe began filing public records requests related to the Gateway Housing program, MassHousing officials started taking a harder line with Acquah and Woods.

An agency lawyer notified the developers they were in default on their Pittsfield grants because they had failed to get the city’s permission to sell the property.

On Sept. 2, McNiece sent a letter ordering the developers to return the $1.1 million that MassHousing invested in Pittsfield.

Acquah and Woods have not done so, and MassHousing officials conceded they’re unlikely to recover any of it.

Richards is well-known in local and state political circles.

He spent six years working for the local nonprofit Action for Boston Community Development, better known as ABCD, after graduating from Clark Atlanta University.

He left for a job in the Baker administration, where he spent four years, working his way up to deputy chief of staff. While working for Baker, he attended night school at Suffolk, earning a master’s in public administration.

Richards’s social media posts frequently highlight his connections to Baker, Healey, and other boldface political names, from Representatives Ayanna Pressley and Steven Lynch to Mayor Michelle Wu.

In 2017, the same year Richards went to work for Baker, Acquah and Woods started a development firm, Flex Investments, and focused on flipping small residential properties in and around Boston.

The duo had played football together at Holy Cross. Both then worked for technology firms and went on to get MBAs from Cornell, according to their resumes.

A Flex Investments slide deck from 2023 showcased various projects completed and under way in Boston, Worcester, and Western Massachusetts. Starting in late 2020, the pair went on an acquisition spree in Pittsfield, the largest city in the Berkshires. They soon owned nearly two dozen multiunit buildings, far more property than they had anywhere else.

The properties were cheap and rundown. It’s not clear if Acquah and Woods had a grand vision, but in the short run, many of their apartments were rented out, despite their bedraggled condition.

Closer to home, Acquah and Woods were trying to flip a five-bedroom, 2.5-bath house near Catholic Memorial, a prep school in West Roxbury. They’d bought it for $590,000 in early 2022 and taken out permits for $68,000 of improvements, according to records. The listing boasted of a “beautifully renovated” home with “granite, upscale cabinets and stainless appliances.” The asking price was $989,000.

Around the same time, Acquah bought himself a glitzy new condo in Boston’s upscale Seaport District for $2.2 million.

The West Roxbury house languished on the market, and Acquah and Woods reduced the price several times.

Eventually they relisted the property with Acquah as the seller’s agent, saving them from having to pay a commission. It eventually sold for $785,000, with the deal closing on Dec. 23, 2022.

The purchaser was Richards.

About seven weeks later, MassHousing announced the new grant program, to be overseen by Richards. Acquah and Woods, who had been corresponding with Richards, quickly became its biggest beneficiaries.

Days after Richards closed on his house, Baker named Acquah to the board of the Community Economic Development Assistance Corp., a quasi-public nonprofit known as CEDAC.

It is a prestigious appointment in the affordable housing world. It was one of Baker’s final acts as governor – in fact, the news was announced by Healey, who kept Acquah in the role.

Baker, now president of the National Collegiate Athletic Association, told the Globe through a spokesman that he doesn’t know Acquah.

The governor apparently got a recommendation via Chris Collins, a onetime rainmaker for Baker. Collins, a partner at First Atlantic Capital, which manages a large portfolio of multifamily housing, said through a spokesman that he had “offered a favorable impression” of Acquah when asked by the Governor’s Office of Boards and Commissions.

Several months after Acquah’s appointment to CEDAC, he and Woods applied for the Gateway Cities grants. On a slide deck, they listed Collins as a “partner and advisor” of Flex Investments, along with Collins’s business partner, Margaret Wagner.

Wagner, who was on the CEDAC board when Acquah joined, also said through the First Atlantic spokesman she had no involvement in Acquah joining the board.

The spokesman said Collins and Wagner “are not, and have never been, financially, formally, or programmatically affiliated with Flex Investments. They provided informal advice on a friendly basis, some of which was viewed as helpful and some of which was ignored.”

In addition, the spokesman said, the two “were not aware they had been listed as partners or advisers” to the firm. They did not lobby MassHousing or any other agency on behalf of Acquah and Woods, he said.

Acquah’s name recently disappeared from CEDAC’s website. Its executive director, Ethan Handelman, confirmed Acquah resigned June 5 without elaborating why, days after the Globe first sought comment from him about the MassHousing grants.

While Flex Investments is still listed on Acquah’s LinkedIn page, his profile now shows him as chief executive of a “cutting edge travel planning application” called Let’s Go Plan.

By late 2023, Flex had lost nearly all of the remaining properties in its Pittsfield portfolio to foreclosure. Acquah also is facing foreclosure at his Seaport condo, records show.

Woods has continued to buy property periodically, including a two-story home in Winchester he acquired for $965,000 at a foreclosure auction in early 2025.

When the Gateway Housing grant program was announced, Acquah and Woods were at the head of the line. Behind them were a young couple who saw the grant as a lifeline.

Taylor Dickerson and her then-fiance applied for funding after they bought a home in Brockton that badly needed repairs, including major electrical updates, plumbing, and new stair railings. MassHousing applications required local support, and theirs was backed by the Brockton Redevelopment Authority.

The couple seemed to check every box.

As children, Dickerson — who asked the Globe to use her middle name — and her husband moved frequently. Home is precious to the couple, and when they bought their first house, they were ecstatic. “I want stability,” Dickerson said. “I want to know there’s a space that’s ours, that we’re not going to get kicked out of.”

The couple went through a “rigorous” vetting process with MassHousing that took more than a year and included a binder full of contractor bids that they shared with the Globe.

Agency officials assured them they would be funded, they said, and the couple wound up spending roughly $90,000 on repairs. They took on sizable credit card debt and borrowed from family and friends, largely because of the promises they’d been made, they said.

In late 2024 — around the time the problems in Pittsfield and Worcester were discovered — they learned the program had been paused and they were out of luck. Dickerson was upset and let officials at MassHousing know it. Her husband, an optimist by nature, cried, she said.

“I had let myself be hopeful,” Dickerson said. “Then I was just really angry.”

title: Pioneering Black whaling captain and his wife now honored with monument on Nantucket
text:
“For people who are interested in whaling history, or interested in Black whaling captains, Absalom just sort of stands out,” Karttunen said in a phone interview Wednesday. “And of course, that’s why a lot of people come to Nantucket.”

Absalom Boston’s story is recorded in the first segment of “Nantucket’s Historic Coloured Cemetery: Stories Told by Nantucketers,” a documentary made by Karttunen and local historian Barbara Ann White.

The film was screened at the Roxbury International Film Festival on June 19.

Born in 1785, Boston made history for captaining an all-Black whaling crew on a six-month voyage in 1822, according to the filmmakers.

“That’s not common in Nantucket history — or in any history,” White said in a phone interview Thursday. “People here know about Absalom Boston. If you ask people on the street who they know from history that’s of African American descent on Nantucket, his would be the first name that would come to their lips.”

Boston was known for other deeds as well. Two decades after his trailblazing voyage, he sued Nantucket’s segregated public schools to comply with a statewide integration law so that his daughter, Phebe Ann Boston, could attend.

The Massachusetts Legislature in 1845 passed a law prohibiting discrimination in the state’s schools. But the Nantucket school committee still refused to admit Black students to two of the island’s grammar schools, the filmmakers said.

An overhauled Nantucket school board integrated the island’s school system in 1846, after more than a year of Black residents boycotting the segregated school system, and Boston dropped his lawsuit. Still, there are no records of Phebe Ann, then 18, attending one of the schools to which her father fought for her admission, Karttunen said. She died only a few years later.

Just three of Absalom Boston’s seven children survived him. The four that predeceased him and his first two wives are all buried in the Historic Coloured Cemetery on Nantucket, according to Karttunen.

“Unlike some families who have family plots with well-defined corners, the Bostons are a little bit scattered,” she said.

The cemetery commission put the new monument to Absalom and Hannah near Phebe Ann’s grave marker.

Absalom Boston was born to a family that figures prominently in the history of Nantucket’s Black community. His father, Seneca Boston, worked as a weaver. Seneca Boston’s house still stands on Nantucket and has been owned by the Museum of African American History, or MAAH, since 2001. His mother, Thankful Micah, was Wampanoag.

Meanwhile, Absalom Boston’s uncle, Prince Boston, was the first enslaved person on Nantucket to successfully sue for his freedom.

Hannah Cook Boston, the whaling captain’s third wife, was born to a prominent Black family in Dartmouth in 1795, according to Karttunen. After her husband’s death, she became the first woman to be a steamship stewardess on the S.S. Island Home, which traveled between Hyannis and Nantucket.

“That was a pioneering job because following her, at least four other women from Nantucket’s Black neighborhood, called New Guinea, also found employment as stewardesses on the steamships,” Karttunen said.

Hannah Cook Boston died in 1857.

In 2022, Absalom Boston was inducted into the National Sailing Hall of Fame. The Nantucket Whaling Museum has featured Boston in its tours for years, helping preserve his legacy on the island, White said. The Nantucket Historical Association owns an oil portrait of Boston believed to have been painted around 1835.

“There are not many portraits of African Americans before the Civil War, and the fact that we have one that was made of Absalom Boston speaks to his prosperity and his being well-known locally,” White said.

Neville Richen, a Nantucket resident since 1987, attended the Juneteenth ceremony at the cemetery. An actor, Richen has forged a special connection to Boston: He has portrayed him in reenactments and performances based on the whaling captain’s life. He helped narrate the story of the Boston family at the ceremony.

Richen said in a phone interview Thursday that he was glad the Bostons now have a headstone in the cemetery, but he believes more can be done to memorialize the couple and other figures of Nantucket’s historic Black community.

“I would have liked to have a pedestal and a plaque, but the headstone was good,” Richen said. “I like the acknowledgment.”

Karttunen hopes that the headstone will attract new visitors to the cemetery.

“People who come looking for something will be happy to find that there is a tangible monument there now,” she said.

title: Two Boston city councilors pitched a plan to extend the Orange Line. The map they used was full of AI-generated mistakes.
text:
The two said they had met with MBTA General Manager Phil Eng, also the state’s interim transportation secretary, who had been receptive to the idea. At a news conference, they shared a mock-up of one possible route: an Orange Line extension from Ruggles to Mattapan Square.

It didn’t take long, though, for observers to notice a few problems with the map the councilors presented.

For one thing, it’s missing the Charles River, and locates Aquarium station on a brand-new island in Boston Harbor. (Maybe the Zakim Bridge was dammed to flood the Financial District?)

That’s to say nothing of the lines themselves; the Green Line’s B branch has somehow added two Kent Street stops (the third, and the original, still marked correctly on the C branch), while the E branch seemingly runs express from Hynes Convention Center all the way to Heath Street. The Mattapan Line runs in reverse, and the Red Line’s Braintree branch has disappeared altogether.

Even the Orange Line seems somewhat bare bones, skipping three stops between Chinatown and Ruggles, and then running straight on (or rather, dipping slightly) to Forest Hills.

The slapdash mistakes pointed clearly to one culprit: artificial intelligence.

And as with anything that seems AI-generated, social media commenters were quick to poke fun.

“Green line stop consolidation has gone too far,” one commenter wrote on X.

“They evaporated Boston University,” another mused.

(Northeastern University, for the record, was also “evaporated.”)

The slapdash map has also raised more serious questions about the proposal. Caitlin Allen-Connelly, executive director of advocacy group TransitMatters, told WBUR that commuters on Blue Hill Avenue “deserve better than a concept that appears to have been assembled over a weekend.”

On Wednesday, Culpepper’s office acknowledged the map was produced by a large-language model, based on various hand-drawn proposals drawn up over the past several months.

Both councilors said the mistakes on the map did not detract from the merits of the proposal.

In a joint statement Wednesday afternoon, the two councilors characterized the map as a “conversation starter” with the MBTA “to make a case for why this should and could be studied.”

“The map we shared is just an initial vision of what’s possible, not a final plan,” the councilors wrote. “We leveraged AI to combine a number of iterative, hand-drawn maps to bring a vision to life during our meeting.”

Culpepper’s office said the proposed Orange Line stations in the mock-up were not randomly generated by AI, but deliberately selected over the course of several months of discussions.

The map, the councilors suggested, was just a visual aid. Only a formal prospectus from the MBTA, they said, would be able to “properly show constituents what rapid rail transit could look like in a corridor that has only ever been given bus options for half a century.”

“We left that meeting with an alignment from the MBTA that this was indeed possible,” they said.

In a social media post earlier Wednesday, Worrell acknowledged the map had been “upgraded” by AI, while sharing an earlier “handmade” proposal.

“No matter the map, the point remains the same: There is a gaping hole for rail in this section of Boston that aligns with economic, environmental and educational inequalities,” Worrell wrote.

The map shared by Worrell also gives a clearer idea where the proposed Orange Line stations would go: following Warren Street to MLK Boulevard and Grove Hall, before cutting down Blue Hill Avenue to Mattapan Square. (The Talbot Avenue and Morton Street stops, at least on Worrell’s map, would be west of the commuter rail stations of the same name.)

An extension of the Orange Line along the Blue Hill Avenue corridor would connect parts of Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan, predominantly Black neighborhoods, with the rest of the city. The MBTA said this week it’s committed to exploring the idea further.

Culpepper and Worrell said that a timeline or a cost estimate for the proposal would be available only after consultation with state experts.

The Orange Line pitch comes after fierce debate over plans to add a dedicated bus lane up the center of the frequently congested Blue Hill Avenue,. That plan has sparked deep opposition in certain quarters, with critics arguing it will worsen traffic and threaten small businesses along the corridor.

Culpepper and Worrell have emerged as vocal opponents of the proposed bus lane, although they said they did not explicitly address the issue with Eng on Tuesday.

Decades ago, a street car ran down Blue Hill Avenue all the way to Mattapan Square, but it was ripped out in the mid-20th century. In 2009, the state proposed, and residents rejected, an earlier plan for “bus rapid transit.”

“This ask for rapid rail options has been a core feature of our proposal since day one,” the councilors said in Wednesday’s statement. “The bus should always have been the floor, not the ceiling, for a community that has experienced over 40 years of transportation inequity and broken promises.”

Material from previous Globe coverage was used in this report.

title: ‘She’ll be known as a Bostonian’: Family and friends mourn woman killed in Mattapan carjacking crash
text:
A cousin said the crowd’s intervention is a testament to Janneh’s impact on those she met in Boston.

“She’ll be known as a Bostonian,” Ahmad Thorley, the cousin, said in an interview outside the Islamic Society of Boston Cultural Center in Roxbury, where the afternoon service was held.

“The fact of the matter is the people did not delay. They did not waste time. They went immediately,” he said. “That’s the humanitarian feeling of the community.”

Following the service, Janneh’s casket was put into a black SUV bound for John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York City. From there, her body was to be flown to Sierra Leone, where her parents and siblings live. They plan to bury her, Thorley said.

“Everybody that she touched and everybody that she talked to, surrounded herself [and] laughed with was able to give their last respects to her as she continues on to her journey back home to be buried,” he said.

Janneh was born in Sierra Leone and lived in Ohio before moving to Massachusetts in 2023, another cousin said.

On June 20, she took a bus to Mattapan Square to visit a bank to send money to her parents and then take a lesson at a driving school, Thorley said.

That’s when authorities allege Ibraim Matos drove a carjacked vehicle onto the sidewalk on Blue Hill Avenue, struck Janneh, and dragged her several hundred feet. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

Matos, 37, of Hyde Park, was arraigned last Monday in Dorchester Municipal Court, where he pleaded not guilty to murder and other charges.

He was ordered held without bail and sent to Bridgewater State Hospital to undergo an evaluation to determine his competency to stand trial. His next court appearance is July 10.

Thorley said he lives near the crash site and learned about the collision on social media, but initially did not know the victim was Janneh.

That day, Thorley said he had been at a cookout in Brockton celebrating his niece’s high school graduation. An aunt called him and told him the crash killed Janneh.

“The police had contacted her,” Thorley said. “She was crying.”

The deadly collision was part of a chaotic string of events that culminated with onlookers forcing Matos from the carjacked vehicle.

During the arraignment, a prosecutor said Matos was driving his own vehicle near Blue Hill Avenue and Woodhaven Street when he collided at about 2 p.m. with another car, abandoned his damaged Acura, and ran to a nearby car wash.

There, Matos allegedly yanked a woman out of her vehicle, got behind the wheel, and drove off again, traveling the wrong way on Blue Hill Avenue toward Mattapan Square.

As he approached traffic, a prosecutor said Matos “intentionally” drove onto a sidewalk filled with pedestrians, who desperately tried to get out of his way.

Janneh, who had just stepped off a bus, could not get to safety in time and was dragged “until her lifeless body was ultimately dislodged,” Suffolk Assistant District Attorney Ursula Knight said in court.

Matos then crashed into another vehicle and a bus before his car came to a stop and witnesses surrounded him, according to the prosecution.

Thorley said Janneh’s parents have seen video footage of witnesses restraining Matos.

Representatives from the funeral home handling Janneh’s services called her a “martyr,” he said.

“That could have been anybody,” Thorley said.

Janneh’s service came hours after more violence erupted near the crash site.

At about 1:45 a.m., gunfire activated a gunshot detection system along Blue Hill Avenue.

Officers found four people suffering from gunshot wounds, including one who was mortally wounded, Boston police said. A fifth gunshot victim went to a hospital outside Boston with “non-life-threatening injuries,” police said. He was later transferred to another hospital.

Thorley said Janneh relocated to Massachusetts because she had many relatives here and lived in Dorchester. A day before she died, she moved into their uncle’s home, he said.

A GoFundMe campaign to raise money for her burial costs had raised more than $12,000 by Saturday.

Mbalu Tarawally, one of Janneh’s aunts, said she hopes her niece is at peace.

“We need justice for Mabinty,” she said.

At Janneh’s service, mourners prayed to Allah to show her mercy and grant her forgiveness. Her closest relatives dressed in white.

A funeral program included a photograph of Janneh dressed in a white kaftan embellished with a red and green floral pattern. An emerald green head wrap offset her curly hair.

Pins featuring the same photograph were also distributed.

A cousin said Janneh enjoyed modeling and the photograph was from a shoot conducted on her birthday in April.

“She was loved,” said the cousin, who is also named Mabinty Janneh. “Every time she’s around everybody, she was so, so kind. Everyone can testify to that.”

She said her cousin was interested in travel and braided hair. Thorley said she worked in Boston aiding people with developmental disabilities.

Another aunt, Aminata Bangura, said her niece was loving.

“She loved everybody,” she said.

title: No. 1 NBA Draft pick and Brockton native AJ Dybantsa honored at Boston City Hall and State House
text:
As the first Massachusetts-born player selected No. 1, Dybantsa was honored by Wu and Governor Maura Healey during ceremonies at Boston City Hall and the State House.

Dybantsa came bearing gifts.

He presented Wu and Healey with No. 4 Washington Wizards jerseys.

“Since you’re now a Wizards fan,” he said.

He signed each jersey, “The City of Champs,” a message that wasn’t lost on Healey.

“You always make a point of honoring Brockton, mentioning Brockton, and thinking of the kids in Brockton in the work that you do,” she said. “And that’s something that’s really special about AJ. He’s going to have great success on the court, we know that.

“But he’s going to have great success off the court. And I think because of what you’re doing and what you’re supporting and funding and promoting with these kids, you’re setting these kids up for success in life. And that is going to be more important than any point you score in life.”

In February, Dybantsa launched the AJ Dybantsa Foundation with the stated mission of empowering youth and supporting the communities that shaped him, from Brockton to his father’s home country of Congo, and Jamaica, where his mother was born.

The foundation already has led multiple initiatives to support schools in the Brockton and Boston areas, including back-to-school drives, gear giveaways, academic development and math literacy programs, and care package distributions.

Healey presented Dybantsa with a citation recognizing his commitment as a Boston-born, Brockton-raised leader for students on and off the court.

“I’m psyched to see what AJ’s going to do, taking it to the next level,” Healey said. “I also think that having AJ out there is going to be an inspiration to so many other kids in the area. Kids from Brockton, kids from Greater Boston, kids around New England. He’s a kid who grew up here. He played here, he trained here. He worked out here. And he’s one of them. Obviously supremely gifted, but nevertheless, I think these kinds of things inspire our young people, and I think it’s going to continue to feed the quality and the level of players coming out of Massachusetts.”

Dybantsa also visited Wu’s office to offer advice to four Boston-area student-athletes, including Charles Allen Jr. of Madison Park and Jahmari Harrell of Cathedral, along with Tyrik Wilson, Boston’s youth sports initiative manager.

“Things like this are so dope to me because I’ve been on both sides of it,” Wilson said. “I was born and raised here and played with a lot of talented players and watched a lot of talented people grow around me. They all have good hearts, but not all of them take the time to come back, give back, and be present. It’s also a lot. So to really take that time and navigate through that and create foundations like AJ has and find ways to still give back and be around and go to your former high school is [special].”

Giving back always has been part of the vision Dybantsa had for himself.

“It just means a lot,” he said. “But it’s something I wanted to do. Not everybody’s going to do it, but I’ve been wanting to give back to my community, my family, since the start. They had my back since the start.”

title: ‘We cannot wait’: Wu’s bold move as Boston mayor targets state Senate foes
text:
While Wu has many allies in the House, her deteriorating relationships in the Senate have led her here, dropping the veil and endorsing first-time candidates running against those she views as thwarting one of her biggest priorities: a plan that would shift more of the city’s tax burden onto commercial real estate.

Perhaps no issue has more strikingly animated Wu’s bitter, nearly two-year-long battle with powerful Democrats in the Senate. It’s also the driving force behind her political moves now. She has endorsed both Lander and Latoya Gayle, one of the Democrats challenging Senator Nicholas Collins, another Wu antagonist.

Her decision to directly insert herself into races against sitting Democrats in her own city, and her unflinching public portrayals of Senate leadership, have prompted even her allies to question her tactics. Wu, fresh from a romp to reelection, is awash in political capital, but she also risks inviting further isolation from the power brokers who pull the legislative levers.

Wu said she isn’t worried about blowback.

“There are a lot of egos in politics,” she said in a recent interview at her City Hall office. “If the top criteria was to make sure that we get along with everyone and prioritize comfort in conversations and relationships, then we wouldn’t do anything at all.”

Wu repeatedly pushed her tax measure through both the City Council and the House, and in 2024 negotiated a compromise version of the legislation with business and real estate group leaders, who had initially opposed her plan.

But those organizations later walked back their support after data showed that residential tax bills would not jump as high as her administration had previously estimated, and feared commercial landlords would bear too much of the burden. Senators then killed the bill amid staunch opposition from Collins, and then the chamber denied it again this past winter as Collins and Brownsberger pushed alternative proposals.

“We were all disappointed by how that all played out,” said Representative Aaron Michlewitz, a North End Democrat, close Wu ally, and the House budget chief, who said his own property taxes have gone up the past two years. “What was very frustrating was that the bill could not even be advanced.”

That fight informs Wu’s new one. The mayor said that she personally didn’t recruit Lander or Gayle, but that the chamber’s moves to block her bills — and their “comfort of maintaining the status quo” — are driving why she’s targeting two sitting Democrats who represent her city.

“The question for all of us who are in leadership roles is: Are we going to throw up our hands and say this is bigger than we can manage? Or are we going to roll up our sleeves and try to find any and every way to make a difference for our constituents,” Wu said. “That’s what every election cycle is about.”

Senate leaders dispute that they’re the problem. Brownsberger said he is a collaborative partner on many issues, and pointed to endorsements he’s gotten from Governor Maura Healey, Attorney General Andrea Campbell, and several state representatives and officials.

“Most other local officials are endorsing me because they know what a great partner I am,” said Brownsberger, a Belmont Democrat who represents parts of Boston.

A spokesperson for Senate President Karen Spilka said lawmakers have delivered a myriad of progressive policies that benefit Boston and other residents, be it funding for tuition-free community college or free school meals.

“The question isn’t whether Boston should have a voice. It already does,” said Gray Milkowski, the Spilka spokesperson. The question, he said, is “whether every proposal that emerges from City Hall should become state law, or whether legislators have a responsibility to weigh different perspectives and sometimes take a different approach.”

Multiple efforts to reach Collins were unsuccessful.

Wu is not the first mayor to run into speed bumps on Beacon Hill, nor is she the first to pick political battles at the State House, where local officials are reliant on legislative approval for changes big and small.

While Wu has had some success, such as helping realize a dramatic expansion of liquor licenses in the city and getting her own appointee on the MBTA board, Boston has far less control over its own fate in the State House than other major cities across the country.

Tom Menino, the late and longest-serving Boston mayor, used to call members of the city’s legislative delegation to the mayor’s residence at the Parkman House or into his office overlooking Faneuil Hall to talk through his legislative agenda.

In his memoir, Menino recounted “haranguing” resistant state legislators to support in-district charter schools: “I put on my hot-under-the-collar act.”

“Hanging up on one rep, I told my press secretary Dot Joyce, ‘I’ll bet I gave him brown pants!’ " he wrote.

Former mayor Martin J. Walsh, who served in the State House from 1997 to 2014, ran a similar ground game as mayor, with the insider knowledge of a veteran legislator. But even he had setbacks, too, fighting unsuccessful battles to secure ambitious tenant protections, protect seniors from being displaced due to rent hikes, and move revenue to help fund Boston Public Schools.

Neither Menino nor Walsh played their cards like Wu has, however, in backing upstart challengers to sitting Democratic state lawmakers.

“You can point a finger at the Legislature and say, ‘I tried my hardest, but these people wouldn’t budge.’ You can work back channels and find a compromise,” said Keith Mahoney, who served as City Hall’s director of state relations under Menino. “Or you can stick to your guns and refile the bill and try a different approach.”

Boston lawmakers also view Wu differently than they did Menino or Walsh, said Representative Russell Holmes, a Mattapan Democrat who was first elected in 2010. Menino and lawmakers had a “father-son” relationship where he “pushed hard on us” to pass his legislation, he said, while Walsh felt like more of an “older brother” with the experience on Beacon Hill.

“She is making things harder in the Senate by running people against senators. It puts us all in the box when she does that,” he said. “The culture in the Legislature isn’t to go against your colleagues. . . . She doesn’t understand that.”

Senator Lydia Edwards, a Wu ally and former Boston city councilor, openly wondered if Wu’s endorsements constitute “normal politics” or “a division that can’t be mended.”

To be sure, the mayor’s not writing off all Beacon Hill incumbents being challenged in their primaries this year.

In January, she endorsed Senator Mike Rush, a moderate West Roxbury Democrat facing a progressive primary challenger in Hyde Park attorney Persis Yu. The race marks Rush’s first primary challenge since 2008.

While Wu has faced uphill battles in the Senate, the House is a different story. Speaker Ron Mariano, a Quincy Democrat; Michlewitz of the North End; and the chamber’s majority leader, Mike Moran of Brighton, all live in Greater Boston, and have had longstanding relationships with the mayor. In the Senate, Spilka is from Ashland in the MetroWest region, and Senate budget chief Michael Rodrigues is from Westport, near the Rhode Island border.

Wu said that in her experience, it’s not geography, but added that House lawmakers have shown more interest in collaborating. On the property tax issue, she said she personally called all 40 state senators.

“There was outright rejection or silence,” she said.

title: Welcome to Boston: Celtics introduce draft picks Chris Cenac Jr. and Dillon Mitchell to their new NBA home
text:
When Brockton native AJ Dybantsa was drafted first by the Wizards last Tuesday night, he made a brief stop to hug his longtime friend, Chris Cenac Jr., before walking up to the stage in Brooklyn to shake hands with NBA commissioner Adam Silver.

About two hours later, when Cenac was one of the last remaining players in the green room, the Celtics chose the Houston freshman with the 27th pick. Cenac, who grew close to Dybantsa after years of playing in the same elite basketball circuits, would at least have a reliable source for Boston recommendations.

“He’s going to be telling me some places to go to out here,” Cenac said with a smile.

Celtics draft picks introduced at Shamrock Foundation event

On Tuesday afternoon, Cenac and second-round pick Dillon Mitchell received an introduction to Boston by taking a tour around the city with a group of local children. Their final stop was the Reggie Lewis Center in Roxbury, where they also took part in group media interviews.

“It was a lot of fun,” Cenac said. “That was very welcoming, just being around the kids and the community. They’re pretty funny. They’re great people to be around, so it was a lot of fun.”

Cenac, a 6-foot-9-inch forward, said he recently had dinner with Joe Mazzulla, adding that the Celtics coach has already started giving him basketball advice. The draft picks also had dinner with president of basketball operations Brad Stevens on Monday night, and in the coming days they will start practicing with the summer league team before it departs for Las Vegas.

“Me and Chris landed [Monday] at like 3 [p.m.], and we went straight to the gym and worked out,” Mitchell said. “We worked out this morning. So, you could tell the type of culture is here just by how the first two days have been, just working out, getting around, meeting everybody.”

Cenac said he did not complete a workout with the Celtics, but had a good conversation with team brass during the NBA Combine in May. The 19-year-old compared himself to Wizards forward Anthony Davis and Jazz forward Jaren Jackson Jr., both defensive-minded players.

“I come in with the same attitude, the same energy every single day,” Cenac said. “I’m just going to give it all on my court when I’m on the floor.”

Mitchell, who played for three schools over four seasons, said he had a pre-draft workout with the Celtics, when Mazzulla preached about the importance of battling for offensive rebounds. But he first realized Boston was truly interested in him when he heard his name called during last Wednesday’s second round.

The 22-year-old, who was a Big East All-Defensive team choice at St. John’s, said he has studied the games of defensive-focused wings such as Jarred Vanderbilt (Lakers) and Jaden McDaniels (Timberwolves).

“I think for me [it] just comes down to just scouting, knowing what the other guy likes to do, and using what you do so great — my length, my athleticism — and just try to make plays,” he said. “It’s about possessions, trying to get extra possessions.”

title: Jaylen Brown’s legacy in Boston goes far beyond basketball. Now what?
text:
In a statement through a spokesperson, Brown said he plans to stay committed to his nonprofit work in Boston.

“Basketball can take you in different directions, but purpose doesn’t,” the statement said. “My work with the 7uice Foundation and Boston XChange was never about a contract or a jersey; it was about a promise I made to the people of Boston, and I’ll continue to keep that promise wherever my journey leads.”

But let’s face it. Boston will no longer be Brown’s priority. On and off the court, Philadelphia will be his new focus, as it should be.

And after 10 years as a Celtic, Brown was just finding his footing in the community and deepening his roots here — from running a summer program at MIT Media Lab for underrepresented kids to launching a nonprofit initiative to create $5 billion in generational wealth in communities of color.

Brown and his mother, Mechalle, who serves as president of his 7uice Foundation, understood the power and responsibility that comes with being a pro athlete with a mega contract.

Brown drove that point home in July 2023 when he signed his five-year, $304 million contract extension with the Celtics, the NBA’s biggest at the time, in front of about 100 students gathered at the MIT Media Lab for his summer Bridge program.

That same day he told Globe sports writer Gary Washburn about his bigger vision for the money: “I want to launch a project to bring Black Wall Street here to Boston. I want to attack the wealth disparity here.”

A year later, he launched Boston XChange, or BXC, a nonprofit initiative to close the racial wealth gap in Boston, working with MIT, Harvard Business School, Roxbury Community College, and the city of Boston to support entrepreneurs of color.

For the XChange’s first program, he partnered with then-Celtics teammate Jrue Holiday and his wife, Lauren, to fund an incubator and accelerator that awards up to $100,000 in grants to Greater Boston entrepreneurs working in the so-called creative economy. Think design, arts, media, entertainment, fashion, and culinary arts.

Lawyer Times, founder of Future Masters Chess Academy, received a $100,000 grant from the XChange in 2024, allowing him to expand his chess program to kids in Lawrence and other underrepresented communities. Times met Brown, who’s a lifelong chess player, early in his Celtics career, bonding over how chess and basketball can shape young people of color.

Like many Celtics fans, Times is in shock over Brown’s trade.

“It’s a shame,” he said. “This was a decision that was made under duress. It’s a good chess lesson that we need to make decisions when we are in a calm state.”

Times said he will see Brown next week at his four-day Bridge program at MIT, where another 100 kids will get exposed to science and technology.

“The amount of lives that he has affected is incalculable,” said Times. “I’m here to support him and do whatever I can to keep what he started going here in Boston.”

Malia Lazu, a Boston community organizer who served as a consultant to Brown’s XChange, said no one ever expected the superstar to build a Black Wall Street by himself.

“Jaylen was a catalyst for the Black Wall Street work that’s been happening in Boston,” said Lazu. “What has to happen now is that we have to continue doing the work, and hold some of the outsiders who got excited because Jaylen was in it, hold them accountable to continue to play [in] the Black economy that continues to look for a foothold.”

Closing the racial wealth gap always required more than one player. But it may be a long time before another steps up like Brown.

title: Revving the ‘economic engine’ of the state’s Black community
text:
BECMA filed a federal civil rights complaint in 2021 alleging the city discriminated against Black and Latino businesses. The complaint led to a more diverse slate of city contractors. The council also pushed state legislators to create benchmarks and pilot programs that benefited employers of color, and rallied Black business owners to testify about the need for more affordable housing.

In addition to its advocacy and policy work, the nonprofit has raised $13 million to support 700 Black businesses, offering grants, loans, and professional services. Since BECMA’s inception, there has been a surge in Black entrepreneurs, and more Black leaders are running corporations and foundations, local leaders say. Boston businesses run by and for Black residents have also popped up beyond the communities of Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan, where they’ve historically been concentrated.

“We are in places and spaces where we have influence and a little bit of power,” said Segun Idowu, the first president of BECMA, who went on to become the city’s chief of economic opportunity and inclusion before stepping down earlier this year.

Current president Nicole Obi has experienced the difference first hand. In the early 2000s, she ran a strategy consulting firm in Boston, flying around the country to serve major clients such as Visa and Volvo. But in those seven years, she got just one consulting job in Massachusetts, at an organization run by another Black woman.

“People outside of the place where I live can see the value of what I do, but I can’t work here,” Obi, who has two master’s degrees from MIT, remembers thinking at the time.

Now Obi leads an organization dedicated to making sure the local business community recognizes the value Black entrepreneurs bring.

Statewide, there are roughly 3,100 Black-owned businesses with employees, and increasing that number is key to building wealth, Obi said. The median wealth of Black employers is 10 times greater than that of all employed Black adults, according to Brookings Institution research.

Before BECMA, “the Black community was only viewed as a philanthropic opportunity and not as an economic engine,” said Teri Williams, president of OneUnited Bank and a BECMA cofounder. “It took us 400 years to get where we are, so 10 years is not a long time, but I do think that we’re on the right path.”

That path has become more difficult to navigate, however, as the country grapples with what Obi calls a “national retreat from equity,” since President Trump started ordering the elimination of DEI practices and cutting references to Black history.

Corporate and societal support for equity has been a roller coaster for much of BECMA’s tenure, starting with the COVID pandemic upending the economy, especially in communities of color, and the racial reckoning after the killing of George Floyd that led to a flood of support for Black-serving organizations.

When Obi took over in January 2022, support for the council’s work was at its peak. But the following year, when the US Supreme Court struck down affirmative action and the Heritage Foundation published Project 2025, support began to wane.

Today, with economic uncertainty gripping much of the country and a DEI backlash in full swing, conditions for Black business owners and nonprofits are as grim as they were during COVID, Obi said: “Things are bad.”

BECMA’s revenue dropped from $5 million to $4 million last year, due to a decrease in corporate donations, philanthropic gifts, and public funding. The nonprofit laid off a handful of staffers but managed to offer the same level of support to businesses by using the efficiencies of AI, Obi said, and has since gotten back up to 15 employees.

The nonprofit is also looking to use its new headquarters in Roxbury — its first permanent home — as an anchor for a “microgrid” to store solar power being generated around the neighborhood. This would allow BECMA, which has been zeroing in on clean energy, to generate revenue by selling power to the utility grid while lowering energy costs for those connected to the microgrid.

The support the council provides to businesses is crucial. Nationwide, firms owned by people of color are twice as likely as white-owned businesses to be denied loans at small banks and finance companies, according to a 2022 Federal Reserve report. BECMA found that for nearly 60 percent of the organizations it serves, BECMA is its sole source of support.

Businesses need to be “at the table” in order to fully benefit from the opportunities that exist, said Pratt Wiley, president of The Partnership in Boston, which cultivates the careers of professionals of color. But for centuries, that wasn’t the case.

“What BECMA does so well is making sure that the interests of Black businesses across Massachusetts are being advanced and are part of the agenda,” he said.

And this is good for everyone. BECMA has been an “invaluable partner” in spurring equitable economic growth and making Massachusetts more competitive, said Eric Paley, the state’s economic development secretary.

Nationwide, the number of Black employers in the United States grew by 62 percent between 2017 and 2023, according to the Brookings Institution. The number of overall employers increased by just 3 percent over the same period.

Still, the share of Black employers remained disproportionately low relative to their population size, accounting for only 3 percent of all employers despite making up more than 14 percent of the population.

Jeanette Velasquez joined BECMA after being laid off from a nonprofit during the pandemic and launching an accounting firm in Cambridge. In addition to helping her get a grant from National Grid, BECMA gave her a platform to promote her services and meet other local business owners, which opened the door to a bigger grant. Velasquez also has a contract with BECMA to provide financial services to child-care providers, hair salons, and property management companies that reach out for help.

“It has opened up many doors,” Velasquez said.

Despite all the progress, there’s still a long road ahead.

The share of contract awards going to businesses of color rose to 11.6 in fiscal year 2023, after BECMA filed its complaint, but it has fallen every year since, down to 6.4 percent so far in 2026.

BECMA members also tend to have less generational wealth than their white counterparts, Obi said, and the struggle to access capital and contracts has been amplified in this uncertain economic and political moment. At the same time, the traditional funding sources for BECMA and similar organizations have contracted.

To unlock the true potential of the Black business community, people need to understand that investing in it spurs economic development, Obi said. Last year, businesses supported by BECMA generated $11.70 for every $1 invested and created 146 jobs.

“It’s not charity,” Obi said. “It’s true value.”

This story was produced by the Globe’s Money, Power, Inequality team, which covers the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston. You can sign up for the newsletter here.

title: Jaylen Brown will always be part of Boston
text:
But the headliner was Clarke’s friend and idol, Jaylen Brown.

“We have a saying we like to say in our family, that energy lives forever,” Brown said that day. “And as long as we uphold his name and speak of his name in high spirits, Terrence is still alive. We wanted to honor him in the way he needs to be honored.”

Befriending a local kid with hoop dreams was nothing unusual for Brown. He has built a connection to the city that is truly rare for a star athlete.

That might explain why the news that Brown is being shipped off to the Philadelphia 76ers — an ancient Celtics rival — hits unusually hard for a sports transaction.

Every indication is the trade is wildly unpopular in this town, and no wonder. Brown was traded for onetime superstar Paul George, now 36, and a bunch of draft picks, spread out over the next few years.

Basketball nerds can spend the coming years debating whether the trade was wise or unwise, analytically justified or unjustified. But if you’re a Celtics fan, you’ve probably already decided that you hate it.

Brown is frequently and rightly lauded for the work of his 7uice Foundation, and his desire to address income inequality in the city. But that work, important as it has been, is just one measure of the many ways he showed up in Boston.

Mayor Michelle Wu — who described herself Thursday as cycling through “stages of mourning” in the wake of the trade — first met Brown that day at Vine Street.

They would go on to see a lot of each other, because his community projects were so active and varied, ranging from advocating for juvenile justice reform to being a champion for emerging small businesses.

“He helped pass legislation,” Wu said. “He would just show up unannounced to city parks where a local basketball tournament was going on. He invested in local entrepreneurs. I’ve been at MIT with him, at the MFA, at parks, and in community centers.

“My sense is that Boston respected his drive and his hunger to be the best and to take care of our community. That’s who we are as a city and that’s what he embodied from day one.”

When the Celtics — led by Brown and Tatum — broke through in 2024, winning the title, many were struck by the team’s close bond with the city, and Brown was a huge part of that relationship.

Brown’s divorce from the Celtics felt slow-moving at first, and then sudden. His outspokenness has always attracted its share of critics. His comments about last season being his best were, for my money, misinterpreted. As far as anyone has said publicly he never wanted out of Boston, the city he was drafted to as a 19-year-old, the place where he grew into an uncommonly thoughtful leader.

But those in power decided that he had to go. And just like that, ties that had been built over a decade dissolved overnight.

Or maybe not.

A video widely circulated online shows a 6-year-old fan crying about Brown’s departure. And Brown responding online, “it’s OK lil bro. We’ll always be friends.”

Apparently the Celtics, for whatever reason, soured on their onetime NBA Finals MVP. But Boston never did.

Though he was raised elsewhere, in many ways, Boston is where Brown grew up. And he’ll always be one of us.

title: Teaching a new generation about America’s founding is an exercise in hope
text:
But there are advantages to what Woodward called “the myth of America as the land of youth, always seeking renewal, a new greening, the eternal Peter Pan among nations.” Each new generation of Americans brings fresh interpretations to our founding stories and encounters our founding documents with expectations undiminished by disappointment. Woodward criticized people for blinding themselves to the gap between America’s myths and their contemporary reality. A more hopeful way to view that chasm is as a measure of America’s ambition.

Fifty years later, the country has reached another anniversary of the founding, this one marked in some quarters by self-doubt about America as a grand national project and in others by a defiant reaffirmation of American greatness that brooks no qualification. To make sense of the moment, I reached out to teachers from across the state, starting with those who had been recognized by the Gilder Lehrman Institute of American History as Massachusetts History Teachers of the Year. Some of them referred me to other teachers, and the result was a mix of responses from both teachers and students in small towns and bigger ones, from public, Catholic, and charter schools, from middle and high schools.

I asked the youthful and adult respondents three questions, and gave the teachers the option to reflect on how they teach the Revolution: What’s the most surprising thing you’ve learned about the American Revolution?
