What story from the Revolutionary era helped you understand what America became in the centuries that followed? And perhaps most importantly: What event from the American Revolution gives you hope for the future?

Their written responses have been edited for length and clarity.

Handing students the narrative

Early in my 25-year career, I taught the standard list of names, dates, and far-off battles. However, my summer job as a Freedom Trail tour guide with Hub Town Tours shifted my perspective. I saw how standing on the actual site of the Boston Massacre electrified visitors in a way a textbook never could. I knew I couldn’t bring every student to the Freedom Trail, but I realized I could bring the Revolution to them.

My colleague Matt Merten and I started in the local archives in Mendon and Upton. We found the “Mendon Resolves‚” a 1773 document written by local leader Joseph Dorr Jr. that used the language of “unalienable rights” a full three years before Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence. The Resolves were a response to the “Boston Pamphlet,” circulated by Samuel Adams’ Committee of Correspondence to build Colonial unity. Adams used these local responses to prove to the Continental Congress that this was a unified political movement, not just an unruly Boston mob. The Resolves showed our students that their town wasn’t just a passenger to history, but a driver of it.

After the Declaration of Independence was signed and ratified on July 4, 1776, it was sent to the printer John Dunlap, who made 200 copies of the document. It was then sent by horse and rider to all incorporated towns. Town leaders were asked to make a copy of the document for their records. With the help from our two town clerks, we were able to bring the Mendon Resolves and our towns’ handwritten copies of the Declaration of Independence, both dated July 17, 1776, to the school library, allowing students to examine them. It was the first time these documents had been together in 249 years!

Examining them side by side, students noticed the nuances of the handwriting and a unique additional paragraph at the bottom of the Upton copy explaining its presence in the records. They even deduced that the Mendon copy was likely penned by Joseph Dorr Jr. himself, noting it matched the handwriting of the Resolves appearing earlier in the records.

Then we handed the history storytelling to the students. Students created documentaries about historic locations in the two towns. Students who struggled with traditional essays shined as cinematographers and editors. Detail-oriented researchers were able to document a crumbling powder tower once used to house ammunition and weapons for the Continental Army at the Battle of Bunker Hill. The students who wrote the scripts used diaries and other primary source documents as well as information from the local historical society to create a vivid portrait of the roles Mendon’s Ammidon Tavern (now known as the Ammidon Inn) played as a shelter for war refugees, a prison for captured British soldiers, and a way station for spy Nathan Hale. And as an added benefit, these projects provided a chance for students to look up from their screens and pay attention to the spaces around them.

Researching and creating these historical narratives prepares students to be better citizens. I’ll never forget what a student told me while driving back from filming at the tavern: “I’m really glad we are doing this. I thought I lived in a ‘nothing’ town. It’s nice to know we actually did something during the Revolution.”

- Darcy Daniels, 2024 History Teacher of the Year, Nipmuc Regional High School

It was controversial

Many people didn’t actually want independence at first. Early in the conflict, quite a few colonists were still very loyal to King George III and hoped that their problems with Britain would eventually boil down without breaking away.

- Talia Murga, 10th Grade, Framingham High School

Both sides promised freedom

The most surprising thing I learned is that a lot of slaves joined the British because the British promised to set them free as long as the slaves fought on their side.

- Wesley Yazel, 8th Grade, Provincetown IB Schools

Small towns, big contributions

The most surprising thing that I learned about the Revolutionary War was the impact even the smallest towns had. In 1775 when residents of Concord heard the British were coming, they moved the supplies that they were hiding to the surrounding towns, including Mendon. The munitions they stored included gunpowder, cannonballs, and rifles, all things that were crucial to the fight.

The munitions were used when the militias marched to Boston where the British held control.

One man that stood out to me in my research was Captain Gershom Nelson, who led four companies of Mendon’s Minutemen to Roxbury in pursuit of the British on April 19, 1775. Later, our Minutemen marched to Boston to fight in the Battle of Bunker Hill. The grit that the untrained regular people had to march into battle with the professional army of the British is a testament to the strength of the American people.

- Matthew Joseph, 10th Grade, Nipmuc Regional High School

Ideas can come from anywhere

Mendon’s actions were not limited to just physically supporting the rebellion with men and materiel. The ideas Mendon’s leaders wrote about had wide-reaching effects that even shaped the Constitution. The Mendon Resolves were written before the Revolution started. The declarations that “all men have naturally an equal right to life, liberty, and property” and “that all just and lawful government must necessarily originate in the free consent of the people” are reflected in our Constitution today. They then ensured the Resolves would be “entered into the Town Book” so that their “children in years to come, may know the sentiments of their fathers in regard to their invaluable rights and liberties.”

I’ve learned to view not just Mendon, but all small towns, differently. No matter how small they seem, these towns’ individual stories and efforts reflect the ideals that founded the United States.

- Giacomo Grisanti, 10th Grade, Nipmuc Regional High School

A surprising hero

Henry Knox was just 9 years old when his father left his family and moved to the Caribbean, forcing the younger Knox to drop out of school and become an apprentice for a firm of booksellers. He read all types of books written by great men, including military histories, and he enlisted in the rebel army after the Battles of Lexington and Concord. Knox directed the American artillery at the Battle of Bunker Hill.

When Ethan Allen and the Green Mountain Boys captured Fort Ticonderoga, George Washington knew who to call on for help.

He asked Knox to do one of the most surprising feats of the American Revolution: move 60 tons of cannons 300 miles, from Fort Ticonderoga all the way to Boston. He rounded up oxen and men to haul all of the equipment over frozen rivers, the Berkshire mountains, and the rest of Massachusetts; my father and I drove some of the same route over February vacation. Knox said afterwards “I have almost seen all the kingdoms of the Earth.” Knox made it to Boston and helped Washington and the Continental Army deliver the first major victory of the war in Boston.

- Nolan Mias, Grade 7, Mater Dolorosa School, Holyoke

Why the basics matter

When I first started teaching American history, I was directed to study the historian Howard Zinn‘s works. He sought to illuminate the lived experiences of Americans in contrast with traditional celebrations of famous and influential political leaders. But I found that my students often had a poor understanding of the traditional American narrative in the first place.

Many students could not name the founding documents, identify key presidents, or describe important events such as early colonization or the American Civil War. Some students had deep knowledge of the histories of other nations or periods, but few knew much about early American history.

Over the years, I’ve collected a wide range of texts for students including primary, secondary, and tertiary sources, artworks, charts and graphs, and more. While primary source documents tend to be the most difficult for students to understand, they are also the most engaging. Reading both the Constitution and the private letters of the people who helped write it help students get a deeper sense of history.

The Declaration of Independence not only lists the specific grievances colonists had with the king and Parliament. Its sharp rhetoric helps students understand the political motives of the Founders. And its language echoes in later events; seeing those words and phrases again and again helps my students recognize the world the Revolution made.

But I haven’t forgotten Howard Zinn. I come back again and again to the stories of the Wampanoags, whose perspectives on the early colonists in New England help students see indigenous Americans as strategic and thoughtful rather than just victims of European colonization and American westward expansion. In different years we’ve also included Jason Reynolds’ and Ibram X. Kendi’s “Stamped” as a text to help students more deeply consider the way ideas such as “race” develop over time and influence periods such as the Revolution.

Every day, I am challenged to reflect on both what my students need and my own understanding of our history. The process is endlessly fascinating and rewarding.

- Michael Houle, Humanities Grade 10 teacher, Codman Academy, Dorchester

An important loss

Even though the Americans lost the Battle of Bunker Hill, they built ambition. Losing doesn’t always mean failure. It gives you a place to build from.

- Ella McGlashing, 10th Grade, Framingham High School

A hard winter

The story of Valley Forge helps explain what America later became. During the harsh winter of 1777-78, the Continental Army that was led by George Washington suffered from cold, hunger, and disease but continued to train and stay together. Their perseverance showed how the United States developed a national identity based on resilience and determination in difficult times.

- Talia Murga, 10th Grade, Framingham High School

A complicated man

There is one figure who encapsulated all of the words that come to mind when we think of the American Revolution: defiance, ingenuity, intrigue, leadership, passion, sacrifice, honor, betrayal. That person? The man remembered today only as a traitor, Benedict Arnold.

Arnold was flawed; so were all of our much-heralded Founding Fathers. We can debate which flaws were worse — treason or slave ownership, envy or hypocrisy — but there is no denying that these were imperfect men. Accepting this hard truth allows us to see Arnold’s significant achievements.

His contributions to the Revolution are the stuff of legend. His boldness, aggression, and bravery at Bemis Heights were a huge catalyst leading to the eventual French alliance that would help secure American independence at Yorktown. And his successes throughout the Northern theater of the war contributed to the British refocusing their military efforts on the Southern colonies, where American leaders such as Nathaniel Greene and Francis Marion would eventually help push the British toward the final surrender.

I watched the 250th anniversary of the capture of Fort Ticonderoga pass by with nary a mention of Arnold. I watched the anniversary of his courageous and daunting approach to Quebec pass with the same disappointment. His leadership at Montreal, his ingenuity at Valcour Island, his undaunting courage at Ridgefield, his heroic defiance at Saratoga, and his military prowess at Philadelphia get short shrift, too.

Recognizing Arnold’s achievements forces us to grapple with serious misjudgments by the Continental Congress, which disregarded his heroism, and even by George Washington, who failed in managing his most gifted general. Weighing Arnold’s legacy fairly gives us a chance to see the whole Revolution more clearly.

At the end of his life, Arnold was caught between American disgust and British distrust. As we celebrate 250 years as a nation, we should claim Benedict Arnold as the flawed American hero he truly is.

- Eric Wood, history teacher, Mater Dolorosa School, Holyoke

The Declaration’s limits

The Declaration of Independence is often treated as a sacred text. But “all men are created equal” only sounds revolutionary until you ask who was excluded by that sentence. Enslaved people, women, and Indigenous nations were not forgotten: They were deliberately left out of the category of “men,” and from the equality that was granted to white men.

The Revolution wasn’t just about breaking away from British control; it was about deciding who would be allowed to be a full citizen of the new nation.

In the centuries that followed, groups that were excluded from the Declaration had to argue their way into rights that were never intended for them. The Declaration mattered not just because it called for equality, but because it revealed the gap between America’s ideals and its reality. A gap that became a defining feature of the nation.

- Rana Muntasser, 10th Grade, Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School

An ongoing movement

When I first started teaching American history in 2012, I spent a lot of time focusing on major events and people of the American Revolution, especially local events such as the Boston Massacre, the Battle of Lexington and Concord, and the Battle of Bunker Hill. Over the next few years, though, I found myself standing in front of teenagers who wanted to talk about revolutionary movements happening in real time around them: Occupy Wall Street, Black Lives Matter, and #MeToo.

I understood the weight of my position in helping students unpack what felt like revolutionary moments to them (and me), though my ability to teach these moments was not always spectacular. I made mistakes, and students were quick to call me on them.

One such moment came after the 2016 presidential election. I, like many (but not all) of my students, was shocked by the results. I was teaching at an all-girls Catholic school in a more liberal-leaning setting, and the majority of my students felt upset, confused, and even scared. In an attempt to keep my own personal politics out of the classroom, I remember telling my seniors that if they were upset with the election results, they needed to move forward within our democratic society and be agents of activism, maintain hope, learn how history makes us understand the present, and make as much “good trouble” as possible.

It was not the response most were looking for, and dozens of students collectively wrote me a letter expressing their disappointment in my lack of visible reaction to the results.

It was a very hard time for me professionally and personally. I grappled with balancing my own feelings and the ethical responsibility I felt towards all students in my classroom — including those who might have quietly supported the president-elect. Should I have let students sit and cry for 55 minutes while I comforted them? No, and I stand by my decision not to do that. Should I have started teaching World War I that day? No, I shouldn’t have. I learned from that experience and approached elections very differently in 2020 and 2024 by guiding students through a structured lesson that covered the election results and provided space for reflection, questions, and conversation.

What I always came back to then, and what I find myself returning to now, are the foundational ideas of the Revolution. The women and men of the Revolution had beautiful, hopeful, and at times hypocritical visions of what America could be. The idealism of the Revolution, I believe, is still so necessary for us today.

The Declaration of Independence is my favorite document in American history. My love of the Declaration has not changed, but what has is the way I teach it not as part of the past, but as a living document that helps us understand the social contracts that govern our obligations to each other as citizens and the Age of Enlightenment’s ideas that are supposed to inform our lawmakers.

Individual stories and major events still matter in my classroom: Reading excerpts of interviews of enslaved persons and women of the Revolution bring vibrancy to the history and a greater understanding of the Revolution’s limits; asking students to create a declaration about something that matters to them today in the style of the Declaration of Independence brings history to life.

What is the sacred honor of citizens if not to uphold the self-evident truths this nation was built upon? I truly believe that young people today are excited and ready to discuss the nation around them and to take on those timeless responsibilities.

- Jenny Staysniak, 2025 Massachusetts History Teacher of the Year, Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School

Small sparks

The effect that “Common Sense” by Thomas Paine had gives me the most hope for the future. One man’s writing rallied and inspired so many people.

- Jon Gunn, 8th Grade, Provincetown IB Schools

Welcoming back loyalists

An event that gives me hope for the future took place after the Revolution. I was happy to learn that even after eight years of war, some patriots made efforts to welcome and reintegrate loyalists who fled the 13 colonies during the Revolutionary War and later asked to come home. George Washington hosted a British commissioner, John Anstey, to discuss compensation for loyalists who lost property. Alexander Hamilton wrote "Letters from Phocion, to the considerate citizens of New-York," arguing it was only just for New York to reintegrate the loyalists who had returned to America.

The wars and disconnection between different groups of people that I see today are almost suffocating. I can only hope that people look at history a little differently and take as an example efforts to welcome loyalists even after the Revolution. Maybe we can realize that there is no point in hating one another when it gets nobody anywhere, and it never has.

- Makaela Jenkins, 8th Grade, the MacDuffie School, Granby, Massachusetts

Pursuing the original promise

As a child of America, I was taught to view the American Revolution with pride. But the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence reminds me of the failures of our country.

The American government has racially profiled non-English speaking families, mistakenly detained American citizens for alleged violations of immigration law, and instigated violence that killed Alex Pretti and Renée Good for exercising their First Amendment rights.

The Declaration of Independence affirms America’s commitment to progress. In our country’s 250 years, we’ve come a long way. Children of all races have an inalienable right to equal education. No matter their race, sex, or religion, or the identity of the person they love, people have the right to marry. Women have the right to vote, to work, to birth control. Americans are able to lobby for our rights.

But America has so much more potential than what we’re seeing in 2026. I hope that the 250th anniversary of the Declaration will be a wake-up call for Americans: Our country needs to reaffirm our commitment to upholding the promises of our Founding Fathers. We have gone far too long allowing this country to fall short of its original promise.

title: ‘A literal life or death challenge’: Boston weighs mandating air conditioning for renters
text:
“I feel gross when I wake up,” she said.

The city of Boston, too, has put down a marker on the issue: In its climate strategy released this spring, the Wu administration said it plans to advocate for state-level policies that establish a temperature maximum. If Massachusetts were to set a statewide mandatory threshold, it would be the first state law of its kind in the country.

But when Boston might move forward with its idea is unclear, as are the political prospects of getting it adopted by Beacon Hill, where Mayor Michelle Wu has lost other battles with the real estate industry. A city official did not comment on whether Boston has begun lobbying for the temperature limit, or if there is an appetite among state leaders for such a policy.

In a statement, Chris Osgood, director of Boston’s climate resilience office, said, “The City will conduct additional analysis and public engagement to identify what options could work best for Boston.”

The Boston climate plan does not lay out specifics, such as what that temperature limit might be or how it would be enforced.

Proponents pointed to the state sanitary code, which sets health and safety standards for housing, as a pathway for setting a temperature maximum, since it already dictates a minimum for winter heating: at least 64 degrees at night and 68 degrees during the day. When landlords do not comply, renters can request a code enforcement officer or the local board of health to inspect the apartment.

Though nearly 90 percent of Massachusetts homes have some form of air conditioning, climate advocates said that number does not reflect apartments that are inadequately cooled or the renters for whom the cost of the unit is a significant expense.

Even with a temperature maximum in place, residents who pay for their own utilities would almost certainly have to shoulder the cost of air conditioning — at a time when electricity bills in Massachusetts, long among the highest, have spiked even higher in recent years.

Maria Landaverde, a mother of two who lives in Chelsea, said having a landlord install an air conditioning unit would be “great.” But her current electricity bill comes out to about $150 a month, and she can’t afford to spend more.

“I still have to pay the bill,” she said.

Boston’s climate plan also says the city intends to lobby for a state-level utility shut-off moratorium during heat emergencies, giving those struggling with energy costs time to work out a plan without losing their air conditioning in dangerously hot weather. Massachusetts already has a shut-off moratorium for winter that protects residents who demonstrate financial hardship from losing their heating.

Cities that have temperature maximums include Phoenix, New Orleans, and Dallas. While they are clustered in the hottest parts of the country, in December, the New York City Council passed a law requiring landlords provide cooling systems that can maintain indoor temps of 78 degrees upon request by 2030.

Lincoln Restler, the council member who sponsored the New York City legislation, said that just as with winter heating issues, tenants will be able to report problems with cooling by calling 311.

“It’s not pleasant on an extremely hot day to have a 78-degree temperature, but it does not pose a health risk to New Yorkers,” Restler said.

The Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors also passed an ordinance in August setting an 82-degree temperature maximum, with enforcement beginning in 2027, that applies to the unincorporated parts of the county.

Supervisor Lindsey Horvath, who coauthored the LA ordinance, represents a neighborhood that recorded a high of 121 degrees in 2020. She said there are tools property owners can use short of air conditioning to cool rental units, including improved ventilation, window upgrades, and roofs designed to absorb less heat.

“In some cases, some of those tools may be enough,” she said.

California also passed a law last year requiring homes to “be able to attain and maintain a safe maximum indoor temperature,” though it did not specify a number.

Governor Maura Healey’s office did not respond to a request for comment on whether Massachusetts would support a temperature maximum.

Any statewide proposal would also need the backing of other Massachusetts cities and towns. Julie Wormser, the climate chief in Cambridge, said the city is “beginning to take extreme heat as seriously as we have always taken blizzards.” Wormser said it would be helpful to have state temperature standards on an opt-in basis for municipalities to consider.

Some climate advocates said Boston should itself implement a municipal temperature maximum, which could be faster than going through the state. More than half of the city’s residents are renters.

City Council President Liz Breadon called the idea, which had not come up in her time on the council, “complicated, but worth a conversation.”

But the cost issues are not insignificant, according to Doug Quattrochi, executive director of the trade organization MassLandlords.

He said window air conditioning units are a stopgap and run to hundreds of dollars per unit, while installations of heat pump can cost tens of thousands of dollars for a single apartment; some old homes are also configured in ways that makes putting in cooling exceptionally difficult.

Quattrochi said increased funding for the Mass Save program, which offers incentives for energy-efficient upgrades, is the only way to reasonably carry out these changes while limiting how much landlords raise the rent. But the program’s financial future is in jeopardy as the Legislature debates a House proposal to dramatically cut funding for the program as a way to reduce utility bills.

“At MassLandlords, our mission is to create better rental housing, including cooler housing,” he said. “If we can find a way to work together to do it, let’s do it, but I don’t want another thoughtless solution.”

In the meantime, the current heat wave is especially tough on those without air conditioning. Climate advocates described working with residents who have turned to jerry-rigged solutions to stay cool, such as placing a bowl of ice in front of a fan or using aluminum foil-wrapped cardboard in their windows to reflect sunlight.

Last Saturday, climate groups hosted a workshop in Roxbury where they raffled off five air conditioners, drawing more than 60 residents to the event, said Kendra Beaver, director of climate justice at the Fairmount Indigo CDC Collaborative.

The same workshop last year gave away window units, but some residents who won didn’t have a car to transport the air conditioner or weren’t able to carry it up to their apartment. This year, the organizers had the units delivered to the winners’ homes.

Beaver said the experience underscored both the need for air conditioners and the barriers to getting them into homes.

“The demand is there,” she said. “There’s a lot more that we can do to make cooling accessible and affordable.”

title: ‘Enough is enough’: Weekend violence in Boston sparks calls for change, from more police to community investment
text:
“We are all saying today, enough is enough,” City Councilor Brian Worrell said Monday at a news conference in Roxbury. “We are calling for everyone to put down the guns, stop the community violence.”

He joined City Councilor Miniard Culpepper and others in calling for more resources to support grassroots organizations that work to reduce violence across Boston’s most historically underserved neighborhoods.

Culpepper said police are part of the solution, but real change comes from within impacted communities, and it doesn’t happen overnight.

Instead of taking a reactive approach, “we have to be consistent out there in the streets, promoting a culture of peace among our young people,” said Randy Muhammad, founder of 10,000 Fearless Peacemakers, a Dorchester-based group. “We need to be proactively in the community, building those relationships.”

Meanwhile, leadership of Boston’s largest police union decried a staffing crisis that has left the department lacking the manpower to properly respond to calls, especially on a busy weekend like July 4.

“Until we take back our streets, enforce the law, and have enough officers to do so, we’re just gambling that somebody won’t lose their life or get hurt,” said Larry Calderone, president of the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association. “That should be an embarrassment to the city of Boston elected officials and the leadership of this department.”

Calderone described an incident early Sunday in Dorchester when disorderly revelers threw fireworks at the police. A crowd of several hundred people was effectively blocking traffic at the intersection of Franklin Hill Avenue and Shandon Road.

“While officers were attempting to gain control of the crowd and restore order, numerous individuals threw beverages, miscellaneous objects, and ignited fireworks in the direction of responding officers,” according to a police report provided by the department.

Calderone said three injured officers were sent to the hospital for treatment.

He argued that reductions in overtime spending have exacerbated the problem.

The department’s massive overtime budget, long a point of contention among police reform advocates, regularly places officers among the city’s highest-paid employees. Department officials said during a City Council hearing in May that they were working to minimize overtime shifts without letting staffing drop below necessary levels.

A Roxbury resident told the Globe on Sunday that she had called the police multiple times about noise complaints as a raucous block party continued into the early morning hours, but a dispatcher responded that officers were busy. Gunshots broke out around 3:15 a.m. in the area, killing one person and injuring several others, according to police.

“We’re woefully understaffed. We’re outnumbered on the street,” Calderone said in an interview Monday.

However, Police Commissioner Michael Cox refuted the union’s complaints. He said there were many factors that contributed to the recent violence.

“The lawless behavior of this weekend is a combination of large crowds, alcohol, illegal fireworks and firearms, and we will hold those responsible accountable,” he said in a statement Monday evening. “There is no correlation between overtime and crime.”

Cox said his department remains focused on strengthening relationships with the community, ongoing efforts that help prevent crime. He also said they’re continually adding new officers to the force and rising to the challenge amid a slew of major events this summer, including World Cup games, the country’s 250th anniversary and an upcoming Tall Ships festival.

“Thanks to the work of our officers and partnership with the public, crime is heading in the right direction,” he said. “As we work through the duration of an incredibly busy summer, public safety and officer wellness are our priorities.”

Overall, gun violence in Boston is rare and homicides are down compared to this time last year. But the numbers lose meaning when residents feel unsafe, said Steve Wilson of the Ella J. Baker House Violence Reduction Taskforce.

“Right now, to people that look like me, it doesn’t feel like the safest city in America,” he said. “So the work’s being done, and we’re going to continue the work.”

City officials often tout a holistic approach to crime-fighting, which means addressing the root causes of violence and investing in impacted neighborhoods. Mayor Michelle Wu recently announced her latest summer safety plan, offering paid summer jobs to Boston Public Schools students.

In a statement Monday, City Councilor Erin Murphy said she’s requesting a hearing on the safety plan. She also joined Councilor Ed Flynn in calling for a public safety summit.

Officials have not yet identified either of the weekend homicide victims. No arrests have been announced in the shootings.

“This weekend’s violence is a heartbreaking reminder that every life lost leaves behind families and communities who are forever changed,” said Clementina Chery, president and CEO of the Louis D. Brown Peace Institute. “Every homicide creates a ripple that extends far beyond the crime scene, and adds another family to a club that no one wants to join.”

title: The big restaurant brands are coming for Boston
text:
Behind the boom is a fundamental shift in how Boston is viewed. Once considered an afterthought to New York or Chicago, Boston has become a must-stop for national hospitality groups. Some groups are even choosing Boston as the first city for expansion outside of their home market. Developers are increasingly recruiting them to anchor their swanky projects, while local investors are more apt to back brands with proven track records. Out-of-town restaurant executives see affluent, well-traveled diners, a growing population of young professionals staying in the city, and an opportunity to expand at comparatively lower costs than some of the country’s largest markets.

In short, some of Boston’s hottest new restaurants already exist elsewhere.

While walking into a restaurant space under construction inside the Four Seasons Hotel One Dalton Street, LPM Restaurants’ CEO Nicolas Budzynski said Boston was a better opportunity for his group’s expansion into the United States than Manhattan.

“We’ve been looking in New York for five years,” said Budzynski.

Boston offered a more attractive entry point with fewer operational hurdles and lower development costs than Manhattan. LPM Restaurant & Bar will open this fall with a French Riviera-inspired menu. It’s the company’s second location in the US, following its first in Miami.

“We rather favor affluent niche markets,” Budzynski said, “before going into larger cities.”

Not just any restaurant can afford to move into these premium locations. With developers increasingly viewing food as an amenity to elevate their properties, landlords are becoming proactive in courting restaurant powerhouses with proven track records instead of simply collecting rent.

“Landlords’ days of relying on scrappy, gritty startups with chefs might be over for now,” said said Ray Camillo, founder and CEO of Blue Orbit Restaurant Consulting, a national hospitality consulting firm.

That’s the case at Winthrop Center, a billion-dollar downtown skyscraper that partnered with New York chef John Fraser to run Vermilion, a steakhouse; The Lineup, a ground-floor food hall; and residents-only restaurant Winnie’s. The building’s developers “own the restaurants with me,” said Fraser. “It’s not a rent-type situation.”

“We are literally their partner,” said Fraser, who said he couldn’t have expanded to Boston without the arrangement.

While this new wave may give Bostonians access to restaurants once found only in New York or other far-away cities, local operators worry it could intensify competition for customers, workers, and real estate.

“If all of a sudden there’s too many of them, then it could certainly affect the Boston market in a negative way,” said Babak Bina, partner with Boston hospitality group BCB3, who explained that while he appreciates the outside investment, he’s concerned about the lasting effects on the dining scene.

In fact, the groups behind some of America’s most beloved restaurants, which have long been synonymous with New York City, are now planting roots in Boston.

Real estate investment company Highgate Hotels formed a partnership with Major Food Group — the team behind New York City destinations such as Carbone and The Grill — to open Contessa, a rooftop restaurant atop The Newbury Boston hotel in 2021. A year later, MFG opened Parm at Copley Place, a casual spot serving chicken parm and pizza knots.

Legendary New York restaurateur Danny Meyer and his Union Square Hospitality Group have opened two Daily Provisions locations, all-day cafés in Cambridge’s Harvard Square and in the Seaport District. A third is under construction in the Back Bay. Other than Boston, USHG has only opened Daily Provisions locations in New York City and Washington D.C.

“We only want to go into markets where we believe we could add six to eight Daily Provisions,” said Chip Wade, USHG’s current CEO. “Boston fit that market.”

Over the past four decades, Meyer founded many of Manhattan’s most beloved institutions, from Gramercy Tavern to Eleven Madison Park. In 2004, he also founded burger chain Shake Shack. Soon, USHG will also open Ci Siamo, the popular Italian concept that’s only ever been in Manhattan, in late fall on the second level of the Seaport’s newly renovated Commonwealth Pier.

There was a time when “Danny did not have the appetite to grow fine dining beyond New York City,” said Wade. “But Boston has grown over the past 15 to 20 years.”

New York chefs find Boston has lower saturation than Manhattan, said Rick Camac, the director of Industry Relations at the Institute of Culinary Education.

“There’s more opportunity in secondary and tertiary cities,” said Camac.

Canadian chain Cactus Club Cafe opened its first American outpost in Boston in December, followed by Miami in February. Boston has exceeded expectations, and now executives are scouting for spaces for a second location in the city, said company president Andrew Latchford.

National brands also have an easier time raising capital.

When the Chicago-based steakhouse chain Maple & Ash decided to open in Boston, the group assembled a roster of 11 local backers who were already familiar with the brand, said managing partner Danny Grant.

“They said, ‘I went to this one in Scottsdale. I went to this one in Miami. I was in Chicago. You guys are going to kill it in Boston. I want to be part of it,’” said Grant.

Others have found cheerleaders of Boston to help make up their minds.

For Dallas restaurateur Kevin Kelley, Boston had already been a required city for his fast-growing Southern restaurant chain, Kitchen + Kocktails by Kevin Kelley. A chance encounter with former mayor Marty Walsh and his wife, Lorrie Higgins, while vacationing in Turks and Caicos reinforced that decision. Walsh and Higgins touted Boston to Kelley, whom the couple described as a “class act” who was working on his laptop while sitting on a beach.

This fall, Kelley will open his restaurant in the former Salt Bae space in Back Bay, one stop in his ambitious national expansion plan.

As restaurant groups race to plant flags in Boston and dozens of other cities, operators like Kelley reject the idea that growth inevitably diminishes a brand’s appeal.

Asked whether there’s a point where a restaurant risks becoming so ubiquitous that it’s viewed more like the next Olive Garden or TGI Friday’s than destination dining, Kelley shrugged off the comparison.

“I don’t know if that’s a bad thing. I love Olive Garden,” he said. “I love concepts that have had that type of success.”

“It seems cool to create something that’s all the buzz and a one-off,” added Kelley. “But when you truly believe in hospitality, then why would you not want to serve the entire country?”

title: Auditor Diana DiZoglio says MassHousing program flagged by Spotlight ‘reeks of fraud and corruption’
text:
“MassHousing’s actions seem performative, at best, and more about protecting the institution rather than the public,” she said, adding that the program highlighted by the Globe “reeks of fraud and corruption.”

Whether another investigation has been or will be launched is unclear. Christina DiIorio-Sterling, a spokeswoman for US Attorney Leah B. Foley, said Foley’s office does not confirm or deny investigations.

A spokesperson for Governor Maura Healey, who appointed six of MassHousing’s nine board members, declined to comment and deferred questions to the agency.

A spokesperson for the state inspector general’s office also declined to comment.

A MassHousing representative referred the Globe to a previous statement announcing the internal inquiry and said the agency had no additional comment.

The Spotlight report revealed that MassHousing executive Tony Richards II awarded the bulk of the $2.4 million available in the Gateway Housing Rehabilitation Program to developers Gary Acquah and Reginald Woods just months after the duo sold Richards a house in West Roxbury. Records show Richards purchased the home for $204,000 less than the original list price.

Richards, a former aide to Governor Charlie Baker who serves as vice chair of an advisory council created by Healey, failed to disclose his relationship with the developers when he doled out the grants, a likely violation of state ethics laws.

MassHousing officials initially told the Globe that Richards wasn’t aware the grants were going to the same men who sold him his house. They said he alerted his bosses to the conflict when he realized it about a year later. But emails reviewed by the Globe Spotlight Team showed Richards interacting with Acquah and Woods in the months before and after the home purchase.

MassHousing officials have acknowledged the contradiction but have not said whether they believe Richards lied to them.

The developers’ work on properties in Pittsfield and Worcester had come under scrutiny from MassHousing officials in 2024, after inspections revealed that repairs had been poorly done or, in some cases, not done at all. The agency asked the developers to make several fixes and warned them they might no longer be eligible for grants.

But the Globe found Acquah and Woods submitted fake invoices bearing the names of at least nine contractors who told the Globe they never did the work attributed to them — apparent fraud that MassHousing failed to detect when it paid the bills. Following questions from the Spotlight Team, the agency announced an internal investigation by the Mintz firm into the Gateway Cities program and others under Richards’ purview.

Agency officials have declined to offer a timeline for when that review will be complete. Lawyers from the Mintz firm have already begun interviewing MassHousing employees at the agency’s Beacon Hill offices.

The Globe has repeatedly sought comment from Acquah, Woods, Richards, and Richards’s attorney. To date, none has responded.

Richards remains employed at MassHousing, where he earns a salary of $255,000 as vice president of strategic community investments. A spokesperson for the agency said the oversight of grants in his department has been taken over by the legal department while the outside review is underway.

Acquah, meanwhile, resigned from the board of the Community Economic Development Assistance Corporation when the Globe began asking questions about his dealings with MassHousing. CEDAC is a quasi-state nonprofit housing agency whose members are appointed by the governor.

Healey declined to comment on whether she will keep Richards as vice chair of her Advisory Council on Black Empowerment, a position she named him to shortly after she took office.

The Globe’s findings alarmed Representative Rodney Elliott, a Lowell Democrat and sponsor of pending legislation that would reshape the board at MassHousing and trigger a review of the agency’s spending of public money on affordable and low-income housing in the Gateway Cities. Elliott filed his bill before the Spotlight Team published its findings, but said the Globe report highlights an urgent need for “more oversight of the processes at MassHousing.”

“A full audit is required of all programs,” he said. “The more open, the more transparent the programs are, the better.”

Mintz, the firm conducting the review for MassHousing, has its own longstanding connections with MassHousing. Colin McNiece, the agency’s chief legal and operating officer, worked at Mintz for 11 years before joining MassHousing in 2019. Mintz has also served as bond counsel for the agency’s multifamily housing programs for more than 30 years, according to the firm’s website. Mintz helped the agency issue more than $1.3 billion in bonds over the last two decades.

For the Mintz audit to have real value, DiZoglio said, it’s important it be truly independent and open to public inspection, not subject to attorney-client privilege — citing as an example of the latter the report the Baker administration commissioned on the mismanagement at the Holyoke Soldiers Home that led to 76 deaths amid the pandemic. In that case, Baker’s office was the client of the firm of lawyer Mark Pearlstein, raising questions about whether Pearlstein was working for the governor or the public.

The Globe has requested a copy of MassHousing’s contract or letter of engagement with Mintz, but has yet to receive it. A spokesperson for the agency could not provide information about the cost of the contract, the timeline, or whether any of the firm’s findings would be privileged.

title: Rep. Ayanna Pressley is in a ‘situationship’ with America
text:
On this second episode of PATRIOTISM IS A VERB, Pressley discusses the verbs that are most patriotic to her: things like lawmaking, protest, and dissent. She also talks about the ways Black people have pushed America to be better since its founding.

The following is a lightly edited transcript of the July 9 episode of “Say More.”

Anna Kusmer: On Friday, two New Yorkers, two stark messages about the country on its big birthday.

Mayor of New York, Zohran Mamdani, and U.S. President Donald Trump. It’s like these two guys are having a boss battle for the soul of America. And it does feel like a battle, doesn’t it?

That’s the mess and the majesty of American democracy. It is the battleground for America’s soul, and the battle can be between the left and the right, but it can also be between activists and lawmakers.

I think at its most robust, democracy is rife with engaged activists reacting to the ways the country is falling short of its ideals.

This is “Say More” from Boston Globe Opinion. I’m Anna Kusmer. This three-part series is called “Patriotism is a Verb.” It’s a journey through my feelings of despair for my country to something else, some version of patriotism.

When thinking about the verbs of patriotism, democracy encapsulates so many: voting, lawmaking, campaigning. It’s so cliché, but I really try to remember not to lose sight of how lucky we are to have this system, as imperfect as it may be. And voting is important, but I think activists are the real engine of change.

There’s this moment from 2013 when President Barack Obama was giving a speech about immigration reform in San Francisco. From the risers behind the president, a man was yelling about record-high deportations happening under Obama. Obama asked security to let the protesters stay.

In the end, the immigration bill Obama spent years trying to pass died in Congress, and Obama shifted entirely to executive action, including more protections for Dreamers, undocumented people who came to the United States as kids. So I think those protesters were right to shout at Obama, and I’m glad he let them stay. I think Obama was right that reform takes more than shouting. But I also think the shouting helped push Obama to do more.

And of course, activism exists on the left and right side of the political divide, and within parties. I may not agree with the values of the right, but I do respect their right to protest. I want to believe that in a robust, self-realized society, the values of justice and equality will win out. For the second episode of “Patriotism is a Verb,” I knew I wanted to talk to a lawmaker who also embodies the spirit of activism.

Ayanna Pressley: We should hold elected officials accountable, but it’s not for us just to make demands. We have to do our part, too. And so part of that relationship, that symbiotic partnership, begins at that ballot box, but it doesn’t end there.

Kusmer: When I told Massachusetts Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley the idea for my series, she got it right away.

Pressley: I do believe it is a practice. It is a verb. Patriotism ultimately is something that exists not because of the legacy and history of this country, but in spite of it.

Kusmer: Pressley lives and breathes the values of democracy. She literally sells T-shirts on her website that say, “Policy is my love language.”

Lucky for her, she grew up in Chicago in the 1970s and 1980s, a hotbed of inspiring politicians.

Pressley: Growing up in Chicago exposed me to the likes of the Rev. Jesse Jackson and Harold Washington, the first Black mayor elected in the city of Chicago.

Female mayors to Black mayors, to ultimately Illinois’ election of the first Black woman elected to the United States Senate in Carol Moseley Braun.

Kusmer: But like so many children, her number one political role model was at home.

Pressley: If I’m being honest, my president was always my mother.

Kusmer: Pressley’s early worldview swirled around her mom, Sandra Pressley, and her neighborhood in Chicago, which was centered around mutual aid and Black pride.

Pressley: My first coloring books, my first flag that I ever had a relationship with was the Pan-African flag. My coloring books as a child were produced by “The Chicago Defender,” our Black newspaper. I was coloring in the images of children with Afros with solidarity fists raised.

Kusmer: Pressley says she got a great education at one of the best schools in Chicago, despite being one of the only Black students there. In U.S. history class, it was hard to feel proud of the country, considering nearly all the Founding Fathers owned slaves. When Pressley got a bit older, she developed her own ideas about what patriotism was all about.

Pressley: One of the most patriotic things I’ve ever bore witness to, that nearly brings me to tears every time I think about it, was Black custodians cleaning up the mess left behind by a white supremacist mob in the Capitol on the day of the insurrection.

We could not return to the House Chamber to finish our work. These so-called patriots that seized and stormed the Capitol to interrupt a peaceful transfer of power—so-called patriots, so-called. Those Black custodians cleaned up the mess left behind by this white supremacist mob, so my colleagues and I could return to that chamber and finish what we started. They’re patriots.

This is what it is to be in a relationship with America, which is why it feels like more of a situationship, that your heart breaks and in the same minute is made whole.

Because I can be laudatory about that, and acknowledge, that Black people have been the defenders of democracy, the architects of progress. They’ve been the patriots. Every time Black people are more free, everyone else benefits. Even when Black folks have not enjoyed our full citizenship, we have fought to liberate others. That is a fact. So I can stand on that history, on that business, and be patriotic and prideful about that.

But also, why did they have to clean? Why was the mess created in the first place? What those Black custodians did is as literal as it is metaphorical for our relationship with this country. We have been cleaning up the mess left behind by violent white supremacists, for everyone’s benefit. Their action made it possible for us to do our job, for everyone’s benefit.

Kusmer: One of Pressley’s favorite lines is, “Dissent is patriotic,” and I find her love of country completely sincere. And with that, I wondered how it must have felt when President Trump specifically called her out, along with other members of “the Squad” in Congress, accusing them of hating America. [He] never used any names, but we all knew who he was talking about.

Pressley: Of course I love this country, which is why I reserve the right to criticize it.

Again, patriotism is dissent. Because I agitate, because I organize, because I mobilize, because I litigate, because I legislate to get us closer to the promise and the ideals that we’ve espoused, to make them an actual practice.

See, people misunderstand righteous indignation, especially when it is coming from a bald Black woman. The righteous indignation that I display is rooted in a patriotism. It’s rooted in a radical love for humanity.

Kusmer: Yeah. For a lot of people who are on board with you about the idea of patriotism as dissent and these ways that you’re expressing patriotism, I think it’s still specifically really hard to celebrate July Fourth, a holiday that remembers the signing of the Declaration of Independence, which was only agreed upon because Northern states tabled the issue of abolition and let Southern states keep the institution of slavery.

I just think that’s really hard to celebrate. Do you struggle to celebrate July Fourth? Do you think about it differently?

Pressley: I didn’t need the federal government to make Juneteenth a federal holiday to celebrate it. I’ve been celebrating it for decades. We’ve been celebrating it for generations in Franklin Park, in Roxbury, which has its own patriotic history.

So I think Juneteenth has always been more, from a celebratory standpoint. [It’s been] my, our, July Fourth.

It’s a celebration of emancipation and freedom, and acknowledging the history of my ancestors and a more accurate telling of our history. I think against the backdrop of what’s happening right now, that is especially true.

Kusmer: You’re saying that Juneteenth is much more of a celebration for you than July Fourth. That makes me wonder what your relationship is with America 250 as even a milestone. Is that something that—

Pressley: Well, I told you I’m in a situationship with this country. So what happens when you’re in a situationship? We’re not gonna all sit here and pretend we’ve never been in a situationship. We thought it was a relationship, but it was a situationship. And so when people would ask you, ‘Are you in a relationship? Are you dating anyone?’ What would you say? ‘It’s complicated.’

So when it comes to America 250, it’s complicated. It’s complicated. The fact that I can, again, practice dissent is in and of itself a tribute to the freedoms I enjoy in this country, that I’m the beneficiary of. It is a testament and a celebration of the founding of our country that I can do that.

But that’s why I can say I’m “free-ish.” The fact that I can vote, the fact that I can own property, the fact that I can open my own bank account, the fact that I do have bodily autonomy, the fact that I could run for public office. That is proof of a level of freedom.

But I’ll say I’m “free-ish” because of the attacks on Black bodies, Black workers, Black voters, Black power, and Black progress. The way to undo centuries of harm, to disrupt that, is through lawmaking. We know what it is to experience in real time, in a residual way, legislated hurt and harm. I know we can legislate equity, healing, and justice. So the next 250 have to look different.

Kusmer: I’m trying to put this all together. Tell me if I’m wrong, but it seems like America 250 for you is not necessarily gonna be this big happy party, but it is a time to reflect on the country and on this complicated relationship you have with American patriotism, American history, the American project. Is that right?

Pressley: Though my first introduction to a flag was a Pan-African flag, because of my mother and that coloring book produced by “The Chicago Defender,” a Black newspaper, I also am a Fannie Lou Hamer Democrat who said, “The blood of my ancestors is drenched in that American flag,” that red, white, and blue. So I also deserve to claim that.

Little piece of history if you didn’t know: The Juneteenth flag was created by a Boston Roxbury artist, Ben Haith. Boston Ben.

And it was controversial to some that he chose to use the colors red, white, and blue in that flag. It’s a star to represent Texas, the Lone Star. It’s bursting. It’s like a nova to speak to a new horizon, freedom and a future. But he uses red, white, and blue in that design because this is stolen land, a country built by stolen hands. So we have every right to that flag, to that patriotism.

Kusmer: When you say, ‘Stolen land, stolen hands,’ that is so upsetting. It’s such an upsetting, true, but upsetting framing of American history.

But there’s so much to celebrate, too, in terms of the freedom fighting and the progress. So are these moments for you all about sort of not turning away from either truth about America in these moments of reflection?

Pressley: Yeah, I mean, embrace the whole truth, our whole history, as complicated as it is. And we shouldn’t shy away from that, not at all. Again, what is controversial about the truth? That is the truth. This is the season of “call a thing a thing,” if nothing else.

The thing is, violence is not something that can be contained. The harm in this moment is coming for everyone, and that is exactly why the path forward to survive and for the work of reconstruction is solidarity.

You cannot see attacks on majority-Black seats being represented by Black members of Congress or the defense of voting rights — all of this that we’re managing when it comes to the racial gerrymandering of districts, the attacks to disenfranchise and silence Black voters and voices — as just a fight for Black people to take on or just for Black people in the South to take on.

You can’t see the fight to extend temporary protected status as just a fight for immigrants’ rights advocates and our immigrant neighbors to take on. You can’t see attacks on bodily autonomy as just something for women to take on. It must be the work of all of us. We have to have a stakeholder in one another’s freedom.

That is the ultimate patriotism: to be in pursuit of each other’s collective safety, dignity, and the centering of each other’s humanity so that we can all experience our full citizenship. I want everybody to be free. And I am audacious enough in my radical dreaming to believe it is possible. And that is patriotism. That’s how I show up with it. That’s how I practice it.

I love this country, and so I reserve the right to criticize it and to do the work and to agitate to get it to live up to its promise.

Kusmer: Yeah. It’s an act of love.

Pressley: It is an act of love. It is an act of patriotism.

Kusmer: Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley is the U.S. representative for Massachusetts’ 7th Congressional District.

Pressley: That’s right. Respect on my name. The MA 7th.

Kusmer: Congresswoman Pressley, it is such an honor to speak with you about this topic. Thank you so much for coming in and for taking the time.

Pressley: Thank you.

Kusmer: Next week on “Patriotism is a Verb.”

U.S. history teacher Byron Williams discusses how to help young people with the ugliest parts of American history, and the beautiful parts, too. Tune in next week to our final chapter.

Kara Mihm of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

Listen to more Say More episodes here and wherever you get your podcasts. If you like the show, please follow us and leave us a review. You can email us at saymore@globe.com.

title: Six high school sports takeaways, including a CFL signing from Mansfield, coaching changes, and more
text:
▪ BC High FOGO All-American boys’ lacrosse star Jackson Ketchen has committed to Babson. The rising senior won more than 75 percent of his draws and scored twice in the state semifinals and final as the Eagles captured the Division 1 championship.

▪ Milton Academy junior Jon Cerullo, a Bridgewater resident who started his high school career at Roxbury Latin, has committed to play football at Williams College. The 6-foot-2-inch, 270-pound center and defensive tackle was named NEPSAC Class B honorable mention after helping the Mustangs win the Kevin Macdonald Bowl.

Wellesley sophomore quarterback Jack Cullinan is making the move to St. Mark’s and reclassifying to 2029. The 6-foot, 180-pounder was recently named Day 2 MVP at Showdown VIII at Bryant University — also attended by Tabor’s Peter Bourque, St. John’s Prep’s Chris Vargas, Hun School’s Lukas Prock (Wellesley) and Milton Academy’s Hudson Garrity, who became the youngest MVP in Showdown history.

▪ Alexandria Petit is making a professional move from Middleborough to Taunton to coach girls’ basketball. Petit led the Sachems to the Division 2 tournament and finished 9-10 in her only season at the helm. Now she takes over for Gretchen Rodrigues, who led the Tigers to a 9-12 mark and a Division 1 tournament appearance in her fourth season. Petit played at Point Park Park University and Ursuline College, where she later served as an assistant coach. She is an eighth-grade teacher in the Taunton district.

▪ Brookline assistant Julian Vesneske will take over the girls’ volleyball program at Acton-Boxborough. The former Brookline star from Holbrook played at Lasell and Emmanuel and served as an assistant at Newton South, Wellesley College, and UMass Boston. He was head coach at Roxbury Community College for one season and has served as player development coordinator and academy program director for the Lionheart Volleyball Club since 2024.

▪ Wayne Puglisi has stepped down as the athletic director at Andover High after 28 years with the school as a PE teacher, boys’ lacrosse coach, and AD since 2022.

“I am deeply grateful to the students, coaches, colleagues, families, administrators, and community members who have made my time in Andover so meaningful,” he wrote in a letter to families and staff. “Together, we have celebrated successes, overcome challenges, and built programs and relationships that I will always cherish.”

▪ Harvard officially announced its incoming 2030 hockey recruiting class Thursday, which includes Lincoln’s Justin Graft, who played at Rivers before joining the Cedar Rapids RoughRiders of the USHL, and Eli Heinze, a California native who played two years at Governor’s before joining the South Shore Kings of the NCDC. His father, Steve Heinze, played for Boston College and the Bruins and represented the United States in the 1992 Winter Games.

▪ MIT women’s basketball welcomed Newton North graduates Allie Danis and Nikki Rao to its Class of 2030. Danis, a 5-9 combo guard, committed in March, and Rao, a 5-8 guard, made her commitment official in December.

▪ Former Mansfield football star TJ Guy has signed with the Montreal Alouettes of the Canadian Football League. The 6-4, 250-pound defensive end/edge rusher from Brockton is coming off five years at Michigan, where he recording 66 tackles, 12.5 for loss, and 10 sacks in 48 games. He signed as an undrafted free agent with the Ravens but was never rostered. He joins a Montreal team that is off to a 3-1 start coming off a loss in the 112th Grey Cup last November.

▪ Boston Latin sophomore Elisa Maria Walker earned her first call-up to the El Salvador Under-17 national soccer team. Walker, who plays with the Scorpoins U17 ECNL club, will join El Salvador for training camp and two international friendlies against Honduras.

▪ A recent change by the National Federation of High School State Associations that expands the permitted bat weights for high school players is sparking controversy. The NFHS unveiled several major rule changes for baseball and softball, including an oversized (18 inch) bag for first base that can be used instead of the double bag, which will be required in 2027, and softball pitchers can now wear one-way communication devices to hear from coaches in their dugout.

But the most controversial is allowing bats with a “drop weight” of minus-4, minus-5, and minus-6 starting in 2028, which means a bat can weigh up to six ounces less than its number of inches. For example, a 31-inch bat can weigh as little as 25 ounces. Previously, the drop weight was only minus-3.

“Expanding the available drop-weight options provides younger and developing players with additional opportunities to build proper mechanics, confidence and skills while maintaining the safety and performance standards expected in education-based athletics,” said Elliot Hopkins, director of sports and liaison to the NFHS Baseball Rules Committee.

While the MIAA plays under NFHS rules for the most part, it does allow sports to make their own modifications. Look for the new bat weights to be discussed at the next MIAA baseball committee meeting in the fall.

title: A violent Fourth of July weekend reopened old wounds in Boston: ‘The antidote can’t be revenge’
text:
All the hard-earned wisdom of his elders wasn’t enough to save him. Neither was his own hard work and ambition. He had a college degree, a well-paying job, and a legion of supporters rooting for his continued success.

Despite decades of progress placing Boston among the safest major cities in the country, a violent Fourth of July weekend reopened old wounds. Two young men died and 11 other people were injured in five separate shootings, prompting immediate outcry from elected officials and community leaders alike. The holiday served as a painful reminder that gun violence remains a devastating force, its impacts heavily concentrated in historically underserved communities.

“When you look around, you’ll see soldiers that have done a lot of time, that have a lot of experience. And we’re the ones we need to turn to in these times,” said Stanley Greene, a longtime friend of Washington-Conway’s father who addressed a crowd of mourners Wednesday night in Dorchester’s Grove Hall neighborhood.

“We can’t allow these losses to take the fuel and allow us to self-destruct,” he said. “When we talk about breaking generational curses, this is how it starts.”

A therapist who earned a master’s degree in social work after struggling with addiction and other challenges, Greene had a clear message for the younger generation: “The antidote can’t be revenge” — even when hopelessness starts to creep in, even when it seems like you’re fighting a losing battle in an environment you can’t escape.

While he encouraged peace and healing, Greene said it’s no coincidence that violence is still concentrated in Boston’s Black neighborhoods, where tragedy so often hits close to home.

“Policies are the reason behind a lot of the challenges we’re dealing with,” he said.

Shootings in Boston used to be a lot more common. Between 1985 and 1995, the city recorded on average 97 homicides per year, with a peak of 143 in 1990, according to federal crime data analyzed by the nonprofit Murder Accountability Project.

Overall, the city has experienced a drastic drop in gun violence since then. Police have recorded nine fatal shootings so far in 2026, compared to 12 at this time last year.

But the numbers lose meaning in certain neighborhoods where crime is more common, residents say.

The other weekend homicide victim was Washington-Conway’s cousin, according to relatives. Police identified him as Travis Deonard Washington, 24, who was killed after gunfire broke out in the 500 block of Blue Hill Avenue shortly after midnight Sunday. Attempts to reach his immediate family were not successful.

“A lot of problems in our community are systemic. They put us in the condition that we’re in,” said Randy Muhammad of the Dorchester-based group 10,000 Fearless Peacemakers, also speaking during the memorial.

In the aftermath of the violence, local leaders quickly demanded a comprehensive response, including additional police officers on the streets and increased funding for anti-violence organizations.

While more affluent neighborhoods benefit from robust public safety resources and ample attention from local media and other stakeholders, residents of Dorchester, Roxbury, and Mattapan often find themselves overlooked, said Renee Callender, a retired Boston police detective who now runs the nonprofit Promoting Conflict Resolution, Inc.

“That’s the perception,” she said. “It feels like a lot of lip service, but what are we actually doing to help these families?”

Leaders of the city’s largest police union have long complained they’re hundreds of officers short. They said the events of last weekend exposed a full-blown staffing crisis as officers found themselves “outnumbered on the street.”

The police were facing a heavy call volume, especially after midnight Sunday.

Police Commissioner Michael Cox described a series of large late-night gatherings “involving both fireworks and firearms,” which he said have “no place in our city.”

The first shooting was reported around 12:30 a.m. in Dorchester, where four people were injured, one fatally. About an hour later, officers were trying to gain control of an unruly crowd, also in Dorchester, when disorderly revelers threw fireworks at them, according to a police report.

The Roxbury shooting unfolded around 3:15 a.m. Neighbors described a festive, raucous block party that devolved suddenly into chaos and terror as people ran for their lives. One resident told the Globe that she had previously called the police multiple times about noise complaints as the party continued into the early morning hours, but a dispatcher responded that officers were busy.

No arrests have been announced in the shootings, and police haven’t publicly identified any motives.

While the area around downtown and the Charles River Esplanade was adequately staffed for the Saturday night fireworks show, other districts needed more officers, said Larry Calderone, president of the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association. Instead, the strategy was “gambling that they can borrow officers from another station when they run out,” he said.

Calderone argued that recent reductions in overtime spending have exacerbated the problem. Department leadership has refuted that claim, saying there’s “no correlation between overtime and crime.”

During an appearance Wednesday on GBH’s Boston Public Radio, Mayor Michelle Wu said she and Cox believe the department is appropriately staffed. She also noted that homicides are down compared to last year. But, she said, “no matter how low a number is, any incident of violence is unacceptable in our city.”

“The hardest and heaviest part of my job is speaking to families who have gone through unthinkable loss,” she said.

City officials often tout a holistic approach to crime-fighting, which means addressing the root causes of violence and investing in impacted neighborhoods.

Washington-Conway was doing his part to change the narrative, making his community proud, loved ones said.

He played basketball at Charlestown High School, where he made lifelong friends. He later graduated from the College of St. Joseph, a small Catholic school in Vermont that’s since closed. He was among the last graduating class in 2019. A photo in the Rutland Herald newspaper features Washington-Conway waving to his family during commencement, looking sharp in a black cap and gown, his beard freshly trimmed, glasses perched on his nose.

After college, he started working for the MBTA, helping to monitor and maintain the tracks. He was making good money and enjoyed the work, his family said.

An amateur rapper, he recently released a music video under the rap name BIG BABY 6IIX.

He was most at home on the basketball court. He joined a local men’s summer league several years ago. His enthusiasm and dedication quickly made him stand out, said Coach James Webb, who helped establish the John Winthrop Basketball League in Dorchester.

“He was our gentle giant,” he said. “Some guys you just don’t see God taking away.”

Well over 6 feet tall, Washington-Conway was always easy to spot in a crowd, loved ones said.

“He was tall but soft,” said Jacque Jackson, a (notably shorter, he admitted) friend from high school. Smiling at the memory, he tilted his head skyward to demonstrate their difference in height. The two had recently reconnected in the neighborhood and enjoyed reminiscing about old times, Jackson said.

“Sometimes our environment gets the best of us,” Washington-Conway’s father, Chris Conway, said at the memorial.

Conway, a substance abuse counselor who runs a behavioral health nonprofit, also grew up in Grove Hall. He said his own father was killed before he was born. He spent his youth “running these streets,” before turning his life around and going back to school. He wanted to set a positive example for his son.

title: Mass. lawmakers roll the (tax) credits
text:
House lawmakers are now looking to sweeten the deal in an effort to bring more blockbusters (and the jobs they create) to the Bay State.

Tucked into the policy-packed economic development bill the House approved Wednesday night is a provision that would give filmmakers more breathing room to get some of their costs covered through the program, through which the state offers a 25 percent payroll credit for any project that spends more than $50,000 within Massachusetts.

Under current law, productions can only claim the payroll credit for work completed within a 12-month period. The proposal would extend that window by an additional year, a technical change with real recruiting value, industry experts say.

The current 12-month limit “has created issues for some productions who want to do post-production or visual effects here, who may choose not to because of the strict timeline,” said Chris O’Donnell, the business manager for IATSE Local 481, the union representing New England motion picture and studio mechanics. Extending the window to 24 months, as the House passed, could be particularly helpful for projects with longer timetables. (Think documentaries or TV series.)

Plenty of productions have already capitalized on the program in the past. Massachusetts has handed out millions in subsidies to multiple Academy Award nominees — a record-breaking $46.4 million tax credit to apocalyptic satire “Don’t Look Up,” in 2021 — and more than a few clunkers. The superhero flop, “Madame Web,” was made with the help of $23.7 million from Massachusetts taxpayers.

The pace appears slower in 2024, at least for now. The most recent available data show the state issued about $22.5 million in film tax credits for 2024, including roughly $4 million for “The Collaboration,” a yet-to-be-released drama about artists Andy Warhol and Jean-Michel Basquiat, plus more than $2 million for the movie “Aftermath,” which was filmed in Chelsea and Weymouth. That number could jump, however, since there are often applications still pending when the state releases its annual tax credit transparency report.

Supporters say the tax credits help pay for themselves by keeping production crews — and their paychecks — in Massachusetts. Extending the eligibility window would “enable projects to get finished and keep people here employed,” said Gary Crossen, the general manager of New England Studios.

There have also long been detractors of the program, charging it’s an inefficient use of taxpayer money. A state commission agreed in 2021, finding that the film tax credit program cost the state $100,000 per job created and concluding it was “not the best use of the state’s money.”

Lawmakers moved to extend it permanently that year, however, with some changes: The program also makes productions that spend more than 75 percent of their total budget in Massachusetts, or film at least 75 percent of the time in the state, eligible for a production credit and a sales tax exemption.

There’s no annual cap on the credit, and it’s transferable, allowing a production company to sell it to insurance companies, corporations, or even individuals.

State lawmakers now also want to credit where credits are due. The House also adopted an amendment during Wednesday’s debate that would require qualifying films to include a closing credit noting that the movie or show was “Proudly Made in Massachusetts,” alongside a logo designed and approved by the Massachusetts Film Office.

MAINE PROBLEM: Heartbreak and anger: With Platner out, unmoored Democrats in Maine confront conflicting emotions and a messy future by Sam Brodey, James Pindell and Sabrina Shankman, The Boston Globe: The dramatic collapse of US Senate hopeful Graham Platner — set into motion this week by a Politico story Monday afternoon in which a former girlfriend accused Platner of rape — has reshaped Maine’s nationally watched Senate contest in the most direct way possible. But the debacle could disrupt the race on a more fundamental level. In interviews with nearly a dozen Maine Democrats, from high-level officials to regular voters, it’s clear the emotions stirred by the Platner saga will linger for some time, and will even define how quickly the party can move forward.

NATIONAL OBSERVERS: The Justice Department plans to send election monitors to several New England cities this September, including Boston and New Bedford — a move Harmeet Dhillon, who runs the Justice Department’s civil rights division, described as routine.

But while federal personnel have, in fact, observed voting in several other Massachusetts cities in recent years — including during Republican and Democratic presidencies — Secretary of State William F. Galvin said a letter Dhillon sent to states laying out the DOJ’s plans was “far more adversarial” than what he’s seen in the past.

“We’ve had a long history of having observers from the civil rights division and others come and look at various locations,” he said, “and we’ve cooperated with them and encouraged them to observe. … This has a different tone to it.” Read more from the Globe’s Steven Porter.

WHERE THERE’S SMOKE: Galvin’s office confirmed Thursday that a ballot question asking voterswhether to repeal recreational marijuana legalization just barely cleared the last signature hurdle to make it onto the November ballot. Galvin’s office certified 12,551 signatures, just 122 more than the 12,429 proponents needed.

But on Wednesday, one opponent filed a challenge in a last-ditch attempt to keep the question from going coming before voters.

In the seven-page objection, Kevin Gilnack, the leader of a cannabis advocacy group, alleged that some unspecified number of signatures submitted by the campaign pushing the proposal should not to be counted because they were “obtained through fraudulent means,” were “not genuine,” or came from voters who later asked that their names be removed from the petitions.

It’s the second attempt from opponents to get the question tossed from the ballot, following last year’s allegations that the campaign hoodwinked some of the signers. The State Ballot Law Commission, which dismissed the last challenge, is set to hear arguments on the complaint Wednesday.

TRAGEDY ON TREMONT: Cycling advocate and Boston transportation planner fatally struck by car near Roxbury Crossing, family says by Bryan Hecht, Shannon Larson and Niki Griswold, The Boston Globe: Louisa Gag was an enthusiastic cyclist, regularly riding the winding streets of Boston. Her passion extended to her professional life, where she worked in City Hall as a bike-share and transportation planner to improve safety and accessibility on those very same roadways.

On Thursday morning, Gag was riding near Roxbury Crossing, an area known for its heavy and high-speed traffic, when she was fatally struck by the driver of a truck on Tremont Street, authorities said.

The crash sent shockwaves through the cycling community, where advocates recalled her effusive joy and wide-ranging impact. And it also hit close to home in City Hall, where Gag had been an intern for Mayor Michelle Wu when she was a city councilor.

WILD READ: Alleged union-busting, P.I. snooping, and forced urine tests: What is going on at Medford City Hall? by Danny McDonald, The Boston Globe: In December 2024, an unused syringe was discovered inside a trash bin at a Department of Public Works garage. Having heard rumors that on-the-job drug use was commonplace, Mayor Breanna Lungo-Koehn and other Medford officials decided to spring surprise drug tests on at least two dozen public works employees. What happened next is the subject of federal litigation, part of a pattern that Lungo-Koehn says is pushback against her efforts to modernize city government but which her critics allege is a hallmark of her tenure: acts they say are vindictive, morale crushing, and, at times, illegal.
