GOOD NEWS: Boston City Councilor Julia Mejia says she’s ‘in high spirits’ following medical episode during council meeting by Breanne Kovatch, The Boston Globe: Boston City Councilor Julia Mejia on Thursday said she is “stable, in high spirits, and focused on making a full recovery” a day after she appeared to experience a medical emergency during a City Council meeting. She said her doctors believe the event was brought on by dehydration and exhaustion.

DAYS LATE, NO DOLLARS SHORT: Healey signs $63 billion state budget with no new taxes, no new fees — and no vetoes by Samantha J. Gross, The Boston Globe: Governor Maura Healey on Thursday signed, with no changes, a $63 billion state budget plan that state officials said does not raise taxes and introduces a slew of new laws, including a panel to review how the state funds its local school districts and new protections for victims of sexual assault. The first-term governor, who is seeking re-election this fall, didn’t veto any of the spending lawmakers approved earlier this month, nor did she seek to amend any of various policy changes tucked into the plan, which hikes state spending by 4 percent over the budget Healey signed a year ago.

PSYCH! Beacon Hill starting to embrace pilot program for psychedelic mental health treatments by Chris Van Buskirk, The Boston Globe: Massachusetts legislators are moving to allow for the supervised use of psychedelic substances in some mental health care settings, embracing a proposal that supporters say would offer critical help to veterans suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder. The measure included in the House’s economic development bill — which still needs buy-in in the Senate and sign-off from Healey to become law — would create a five-year pilot program that would allow licensed mental health care clinics to offer on-site psychedelic treatments.

SNOW WAY: Healey administration vows to appeal as Trump rejects Massachusetts blizzard aid request by Kate Selig, The Boston Globe: President Trump denied Massachusetts’ request for emergency aid following a February blizzard brought record snowfall and hurricane-force winds to the state. The Healey administration said it plans to appeal the decision. Officials previously said that local governments and state agencies reported roughly $145 million in storm expenses, a significant fraction of which could be eligible for federal reimbursement.

Ahoy! Aboard the tall ship Mircea by Brian MacQuarrie and Stan Grossfeld, The Boston Globe.

Professional scab or essential backstop? Replacement nurses become a flashpoint in Brigham strike. by Marin Wolf, Sarah Rahal and Jonathan Saltzman, The Boston Globe.

Bill to protect health care workers from workplace violence set for Senate vote next week by Diane Adame, GBH News.

Thanks for reading The Scrum.

This newsletter was edited and produced by Matt Stout.

Have a question for the team? Email us at thescrum@globe.com.

Delivered Monday through Friday.

title: Tall ships arrive in Boston Harbor as part of Sail250 celebration. Follow live updates.
text:
By Chloe Craft, Globe correspondent

Across from the iconic USS Constitution, a humble blue tent housed a wealth of maritime history curated by the Naval History and Heritage Command, much of it highlighting the rich seafaring culture of New England.

“A lot of people don’t know that all the wood [of the USS Constitution] is all grown in its own forest in Indiana. Those trees are still used to make repairs or replace any deteriorating or rotting wood,” said Kim Ortega, 34, outreach coordinator for the Museum of the American Soldier in Chicago, one of 10 official Navy museums operating under the Naval History and Heritage Command.

“Seeing the ship today reminds me how the Navy works so hard to maintain the structural integrity and the beauty and majesticness of the Constitution for folks in the community of Boston, if not internationally, to enjoy,” she said.

Along with engaging the old salts — an affectionate term for sage elder mariners — Ortega said she has had plenty of memorable interactions with younger visitors.

“We had two boys, maybe 4 or 5 years old, come over and start spitballing questions left and right,” she said, pausing to laugh and pointing to postcards bearing vintage images of tall ships set out on a table. “They took one of each and asked, ‘Why do the ships look like this? Where are they going? What happened to them?’”

One of the postcards is a grainy black-and-white photograph from a World War II era PT boat, featuring the crew and the particularly famous commanding officer posing shirtless. That officer? Then-Lieutenant John F. Kennedy.

“One of our very popular images on our free postcards has been shirtless JFK, back when he was on the PT 109,” said Navy conservator Isabel Lobley, 30, from Maine.

“We’ve been giving a lot of these out, especially as it relates to Boston and Massachusetts. Everyone is like, ‘Is that JFK?’ And I say, ‘Yes, yes it is.’ You ought to take one too.”

The Naval History and Heritage Command pop-up will be in Charlestown Navy Yard, across from the USS Constitution, through Thursday.

By Bryan Hecht, Globe correspondent

For Robert Graves, 16, who sails for Nantucket High School, getting the chance to work on — and even steer — the 122-foot schooner Lynx is definitely a major upgrade.

The Lynx is a 2001 wooden ship that regularly commutes between its home port in Nantucket and Georgia, her crew said. Compared to some other ships in this year’s lineup, the Lynx doesn’t need assistance to be moved by another vessel and largely does all of its own sailing.

That means it needs more hands, too, like Graves.

He is part of a program through Egan Maritime Institute that helps get students on board sailing vessels like Lynx. It’s an interpretation based on a 19th century privateer that evaded the Royal Navy during the War of 1812.

“Part of our main mission is getting kids out on the water and getting them to see what they can do with their own two hands,” said crew member Nina Schiefelbein, 23.

Grave will be joining the crew for the next few days, his third time working on the Lynx, he said.

“It’s a great experience. I never thought I’d see this many tall ships all at once,” he said. “It’s kind of like a surreal moment.”

By Chris Van Buskirk, Globe staff

Passengers at Boston’s Logan International Airport got their own taste of the tall ships.

The height of some of the ships passing the end of major runways at the airport caused “temporary” delays, said a spokesperson for the Massachusetts Port Authority, the quasi-public agency that runs the airport.

“The delay program has ended,” the spokesperson said just after 4:30 p.m.

There were 325 delays at Logan as of 4:30 p.m., according to the flight tracker FlightAware.

By Ariela Lopez, Globe correspondent

As a volunteer liaison, Pat Cogan, 62, of Milton, will spend this week helping the crew of the tall ship Virginia settle in their Charlestown Navy Yard port.

He boarded the Virginia just after it docked to tell its passengers where they could go in the Navy Yard to use the bathroom or do laundry. He will also help control how many people board the ship at once when it opens to visitors.

Cogan said he retired a couple of years ago and has been looking for opportunities to take part in interesting events.

“I thought it was going to be a historic event and I just wanted to be a part of it,” he said. “I tried to volunteer for FIFA in Gillette, but didn’t make it. I’m trying to find things that I find interesting.”

Cogan does not consider himself a “boat person,” and clarified that he has no sailing experience.

“But I’ve always found these tall ships so beautiful, so I just thought it would be fun to be part of.”

By Ariela Lopez, Globe correspondent

On the Virginia, a recreation of a 1608 ship of the same name, the crew gathered to debrief the morning’s sail.

“Everything worked out,” said JB Smith, the ship’s 82-year-old captain. “We didn’t hit anything, nobody hit us. We did what we came here to do: Boston 250.”

The ship’s journey from its home port of Bath, Maine, to Boston for Sail Boston 250 is the farthest it has traveled since its launch in 2022, according to Matt Blazek, the interim director of Maine’s First Ship, which operates the Virginia.

Now docked in the Charlestown Navy Yard’s Pier 6, the ship’s crew left Gloucester Friday morning and arrived in Boston last night, docking in the Seaport.

While most of the crew plans to stay overnight in an Airbnb in the North End, Smith plans to stay on the ship, sleeping on his air mattress in the hull, he said.

Sailors wore clothes designed to imitate what a 17th-century crew might have worn.

They donned linen shirts and short pants, handmade by volunteers for the ship’s operating organization, Maine’s First Ship. Frances South, 69, also wore a colorful sash and a small satchel, in which she kept a rigging knife that she said a “guy in Maine” also handmade for the crew.

For South, the clothes and the knife testify to the ship’s ability to bring volunteers into the fold. The Virginia, whose home port is in Bath, Maine, was launched in 2022 after an 11-year volunteer-led recreation project.

“There’s always a guy in Maine, a woman in Maine, who does these amazing things,” she said.

By Chloe Craft, Globe correspondent

“Fiți bineveniți!” shouted 30-year-old Christina Goran from Romania, grinning as she hoisted a billowing Romanian flag. In an aside, she added, “That’s ‘welcome’ in Romanian.”

More than 100 people crowded at the end of Pier 4 in Charlestown Navy Yard at 3:30 p.m. to celebrate the arrival of the Mircea, a towering tall ship which is designated the official vessel of the Romanian Navy. As a tugboat carefully guided it towards the landing, a line of around 50 sailors in crisp white uniforms raised their hats with a shout, met with a chorus of cheers from those gathered on shore.

“We are very eager to welcome our friends from Romania who took a six-month-long trip to come here and celebrate 250 years of America with us,” said Liliana Oniță-Lenco, 62, of Revere.

Oniță-Lenco explained that she led a group representing the Association of Romanians in New England to welcome the Tall Ship.

“We are very excited for this beautiful ship to join us,” she said, pausing to speak a few words in Romanian to a nearby friend, who handed her an American flag that she unfurled with a smile. “Romania and America, together today!”

Before Oniță-Lenco could say another word, some of the ship’s crew members waved, drawing out another enthusiastic cheer from the crowd.

By Chloe Craft, Globe correspondent

A crew of enthusiastic Polish cadet sailors turned Pier 4 at Charlestown Navy Yard into the port city of Gdynia, as they exchanged words in their native language from aboard the tall ship Dar Młodzieży with Boston’s Polish diaspora, who were standing on the shore.

The ship, which will be open to boarding starting Sunday, is based at Gdynia Maritime University, where it serves as a training vessel for Poland’s future sailors.

“I am very pleased they’ve come over, and I challenge any non-Pole to pronounce the name of their ship,” said third-generation Polish immigrant Jan Tkacz, 81, of Charlestown, who pointed to the letters on the side of the vessel and sounded out, “Dar Mwohd-zee-jey.”

Tkacz said he previously taught English in Gdansk, a city not far from Gdynia, but that it was “heartwarming” to hear Polish spoken between the crew and their supporters in the states.

Second-year cadet Frank Gepner, 20, said he was pleasantly surprised to meet so many Polish diaspora after preparing to put his English lessons into practice.

“We prepared to visit something different since United States is quite far from us, and especially for me, since it is the first time here,” Gepner said. “But it’s really nice to see our Polish brothers and sisters over here.”

By Bryan Hecht, Globe staff

By Jaden Perry, Globe correspondent

With outstretched arms, Vivian Sanchez, 34, held up a red and white Peruvian flag as it unfurled with the breeze.

“Of course, we want to see all the tall ships, right? But me, especially, I want to see the one from my country, which is Peru,” Sanchez said. “I’m experiencing this amazing show [for] the first time in my life.”

Sitting beside her was her grandmother and 7-year-old daughter.

“We were sad because she had swimming classes,” Sanchez said in reference possibly missing Peru’s ship sail by because of her daughter’s class. “And then we just came here to check. And then look, this is an amazing view.”

Sanchez has lived in Boston for three years. Since then, she hasn’t been able to visit her country. For her, the incoming Peru tall ship was a nice reminder of home.

“I think these type of events just make people [come] together. Like, we are all in one heart,” Sanchez said as Peruvian ship began to appear in the distance.

By Camilo Fonseca, Globe staff

Between the foghorns and cannonades, spectators at Castle Island were treated to a non-stop parade of nautical themed music, booming from speakers mounted on the fort’s ramparts.

There were the obvious “sailing” hits: “Sailing” by Christopher Cross and “Sail On, Sailor,” by The Beach Boys. There were the rousing instrumentals: “Anchors Aweigh,” of course, as well as Hans Zimmer’s Pirates of the Caribbean theme. There were the songs that were, technically speaking, about water (Dr. John’s “I’m Gonna Go Fishin’“). There were even a few sea shanties in the mix.

It wasn’t just the park’s playlist. Peru’s BAP Union could be heard playing “The Star-Spangled Banner” as it neared the fort.

But what really got the crowd going was when the ship rounded the entrance to the inner harbor, blaring “I’m Shipping Up To Boston” by the Dropkick Murphy’s.

By Bryan Hecht, Globe correspondent

Andrea Pinilla, 52, and her family watched as crew members of the Chilean ship Esmeralda prepared the vessel for visitors on Commonwealth Pier in Seaport.

She said they regularly visit the ship whenever it is in Boston, where she lives, as well as at its home port in Valparaíso.

The Esmeralda was part of multiple previous Boston tall ships festivals, but has a controversial history in Chile, said Pinilla, who runs the local group Comunidad Chilena de Boston.

According to Amnesty International, Esmeralda was used to imprison and torture political prisoners under the military dictatorship of Augusto Pinochet in the 1970s.

However, for Pinilla, the ship carries happier memories. Over the years they have gotten to know much of the crew. With her was Lynette Trujillo, whose husband Carlos Pizzaro works as a machine repair technician on the Esmeralda.

The pair shared a joyful reunion when it docked earlier in the day.

“[For us] it’s a beautiful thing,” Pinilla said.

By Camilo Fonseca, Globe staff

Once the tall ships make the turn into Boston Harbor, Ryan Stranz has roughly a minute — maybe two, if he’s lucky — to put his impressions of their sails down on paper. Dipping his brush into a vial of black ink, his split second brush strokes are like trying to catch lightning in a bottle.

“It’s only here for a second, so you’ve got to make a decision and put the ink down in the way that makes the most sense to you,” he said. “Otherwise the boat’s gone.”

Stranz, who runs an art studio in Somerville, said he’s used to large-scale oil paintings and figure drawing. But with black watercolor ink, he said he’s able to work quickly and capture “all of the expressive gestures exactly as I mean them.”

“This is the stern of one of these large boats, the three-masted giants,” he said, the sea breeze whipping through the canvases in his hands. “And then this is one of those smaller ones. It just has some beautiful lines to it. It kind of steals the show from the large one.”

After running out of canvas, Stranz turned to anything else he can put his brush on — cardboard boxes, printer paper, even a greasy Sullivan’s lobster roll wrapper.

“My soul feels full being out here,” he said.

By Bryan Hect, Globe correspondent

Dozens of ship watchers flocked to the observation deck on the top floor of the Institute of Contemporary Art in Seaport — away from the heat — taking in the vistas of ships passing and docking, and crowds on Fan Pier.

For David Moy, 67, of Wellesley, the deck offered a nice place to rest while waiting for the American ship Elissa to pass through Boston Harbor.

“That’s my daughter’s name, so we’re excited to see that one,” Moy said as he adjusted his binoculars.

Admission to the ICA is free for all on Saturday, and hundreds more people thronged the grandstand steps behind the museum to watch the parade in the building’s shadow.

By Jaden Perry, Globe correspondent

Lou Jones, 80, had the picture perfect spot off the pier in East Boston. His camera, fit with a massive 600mm lens, was fixated right on the spot where the ships would emerge to the backdrop of the city.

Seeing that this is his fifth time visiting the passage of the Tall Ships, this is business as usual for Jones.

“I think it was more exciting then,” Jones said in reference to the 1976 Tall Ships event. At the time, he sailed on one of the ships from New York City to Boston.

“This is the first time I haven’t been on a ship for the Tall Ships’ visit,” Jones said. The Washington, D.C., native has been a photographer in Boston for the last 50 years. “I’ve done it so many times. I’m not going to say it’s boring, but I wanted to do it from a different kind of perspective.”

And a different perspective he got. The passing ships shored up memories from his experience back in 1976. Having seen the labor that crew members put into pulling the ropes as they tamed the wind with their sails, Jones thought back to his ancestors 300 years ago.

“It really shoved me back into history, and I think that that’s probably the most interesting part,” Jones said. “Literally having people sailing me, transporting me hundreds of miles on a ship that my forefathers sailed on just like that, that many years ago.”

By Thai Theodoro and Jaden Perry, Globe correspondents

Many spectators the Globe interviewed talked about how memorable the summer’s been, especially with the rareness of events such as the World Cup and, now, Sail Boston 2026.

“The history, the city, the charm with the World Cup and just everything all coming together — this is the coolest place to live,” Marissa Riveira, 40, of Winthrop, said at the Massport Marine Terminal.

Riveira attended Sail Boston in 1992 and 2017, but this year marks a first: bringing her two daughters, ages 5 and 11, to experience it for themselves. Riveira said she was most excited to introduce them to a piece of Boston’s history.

“We’re living in July, and we’re ready to see what August has for us,” she said.

As ships sailed through the harbor, Joseph Arjona-Sanchez, 27, sat with his wife under a heavily shaded part of Piers Park.

“It’s been a really good summer,” Arjona-Sanchez said sitting beside his camera, legs folded. “Between the World Cup and this it’s been a really fun few weeks.”

By Bryan Hecht, Globe correspondent

The Mayflower II, a reproduction of the pilgrim’s historic 17th century vessel, is one of over a dozen ships with home ports around New England, from Maine to Massachusetts.

It is a late addition to the Sail250 fleet, not appearing for the celebrations earlier in the summer in New York, Baltimore, Virginia, and New Orleans.

That’s because the bright brown and red merchant style vessel does not have its own motor, said deckhand Abby Connell. It took 10 hours just to move it by tugboat from Plymouth to Boston, she said, in what is the ship’s longest voyage since it was assembled in England and sailed across the Atlantic in 1957.

“We are absolutely thrilled to be able to bring her to a larger audience,” said Connell, a 22-year-old Plymouth native who works as a historical interpreter for Plimoth Patuxet Museums. “We always compare it to a sports car, you don’t want to keep her in the garage.”

Connell said the crew slept on the boat the night before the Parade of Sail, waking before dawn to join the flotillas in the staging area in Broad Sound.

As the ship prepares to board many new visitors, the only challenge that remains is correcting them to the fact that Mayflower is a 20th century reproduction and not an original 17th century merchant ship.

“We get that a lot,” Connell said.

By Jane Miller, Globe correspondent

Bringing a jubilant soundtrack to the tall ship procession, a group of shanty singers, “The Portermen” of Newburyport, could be heard singing old sailor tunes on the edge of Christopher Columbus park.

The five-member group slapped their knees as they sung “Bully in the Ally,” a traditional maritime tune that sailors would historically use to give rhythm to their work on deck. A baseball cap of money sat at the group’s feet.

“Most of our songs are traditional sea shanties that would have been sung on ships between 1780 and 1860,” Tim Fountain, 57, said.

None of the five Portermen, who frequently perform at maritime events, are sailors themselves. They were just drawn into the tunes and the community.

”It’s fun to lend some of the music that goes with that show,” said Steve Lichty, 63.

“As rough as we are,” Steve Lichty, 63, added with a chuckle.

By Bryan Hecht, Globe correspondent

Ruby Stith, 28, is a private contracted boat hand, or — as she calls it — “a professional boat hobo.”

She waited eagerly for the crew of the Mayflower II to disembark at Seaport to greet old friends.

Stith has sailed on numerous tall ships, her favorite being the USS Constitution which she helped man during Fourth of July celebrations earlier this month. She works primarily with California vessels, the Star of India in San Diego and the Bill of Rights in Chula Vista.

The sailing community, she said, is tight knit with everyone knowing each other, though crews are far flung across the globe for most of the year.

“Every time you leave a boat, it’s never gonna be the same,” Stith said. “To have them all in one space means you get to see all your friends that you probably thought you were never gonna see again.”

By Ariela Lopez, Globe correspondent

Kelly Mercier, 58, came to watch the tall ships from the Charlestown Navy Yard, where she is attending a patio party hosted by the restaurant on Pier 6.

Mercier, who grew up in Cambridge, said she remembers seeing the tall ships and the accompanying crew and cadet parade in 1976, America’s bicentennial, when she was 8 years old.

“I had to come back,” Mercier said. “Being the 250th just made it more special.”

Mercier said she arrived at the Navy Yard just after 8 a.m. to watch the USS Constitutional leave its pier to participate in the Parade of Sail. She heard the ship shoot its cannons.

“I guess this isn’t history,” Mercier said, “but it feels like history to me.”

By Thai Theodoro, Globe correspondent

At the Massport Marine Terminal, the sounds of the Navy Band Northeast’s Jack Tar Brass drifted across the waterfront, drawing visitors toward the stage. The band moved from New Orleans-style brass classics to 2000s pop hits as one of its members urged the crowd to “make some noise!”

Near the stage, Yinitza Vazquez, 50, of Lynn, danced through every song, twirling the skirt of her traditional Puerto Rican dress as the set shifted from one genre to the next.

“The tall ships create this unity in our hearts that everybody from the world can come and get together and be happy and sail,” Vazquez said.

She said she was especially excited to see BAP Unión, Peru’s tall ship and, at more than 378 feet long, one of the largest in the fleet.

By Camilo Fonseca, Globe staff

Sitting against the bricks of Fort Independence, Margaret Canty’s eyes lingered on a paper etching of a clipper ship, scanning for similarities with the billowing sails moving on the water before her.

Canty, of Dorchester, said she’d been gifted the detailed drawing by chance. She’d bumped into a young man holding the drawing while lining up to enter Castle Island. The young man said it was an etching of a ship that his ancestors had built in Boston’s shipyards, and took pride in describing its history and unique features.

At the end of the conversation, the young man offered Canty the drawing — a touch of generosity that she said deeply moved her.

“It was a goosebumps moment,” she said. “I felt like a kindergartner … like I was being handed a sacred relic.”

Canty, a lifelong Bostonian, said she couldn’t help but remember her experience as a young woman watching the tall ships, the first time they sailed into Boston Harbor in 1976.

“I was not in the most expansive state of mind back then,” she said. “Now I have a whole different perspective.”

By Ariela Lopez, Globe correspondent

As the Angelique, a 130-foot ketch with tanbark sails, docked in the Charlestown Navy Yard, Jasmine Thomas watched from the pier.

Thomas works on the Angelique at its home port in Camden, Maine. She was on board the ship during the Sail250 parade in New York City last week, and she said her boyfriend is currently firstmate on the ship — one of its 27 passengers.

“They usually do three-, four-, and six-daylong trips out of Maine, so it’s a real spectacular thing for her to make it all the way down here,” said Thomas, who was born in Falmouth, but grew up in Maine.

Thomas hopes Sail Boston attendees appreciate the Angelique’s rare red-colored sails and immaculate condition despite having been built almost 50 years ago.

“It’s really incredible to see so many people who still appreciate the old skill of sailing,” Thomas said. “Everything has become so modern and reliant on technology, and so to be able to still sail and travel such far distances under sail is really incredible.”

By Jane Miller, Globe correspondent

Eloise Cocci, 11, of Jamaica Plain sat peacefully next to the splash pad in Christopher Columbus park, watercolor painting in her notebook. She has been watching the tall ships with her parents since 9 a.m.

“I love how they’re all different sizes,” Cocci said, of the ships. “Some of them are so big, and the excitement grows throughout everyone when we see them.”

Cocci, who said she was inspired by Leonardo da Vinci, is painted a palm leaf.

“It’s a great time in the season,” Cocci said as she moved her paint brush across the page. “The waters are really calm.”

By Bryan Hecht, Globe correspondent

By 11 a.m., thousands have descended on Fan Pier Park, packing every swatch of green with picnic blankets and lawn chairs to take in the first flotillas of ships. More spectators gathered on balconies of nearby apartment buildings, while even more crowded the bridge into Seaport from downtown.

The views here are unbeatable, said Valorie Ortiz, 63, of Sterling, who came in from Central Massachusetts with her husband Stephen and two children.

“We just got so lucky to see them so close,” Ortiz said as the towering Mayflower II docked in its final berth just a few feet away from where she stood.

By Thai Theodoro, Globe correspondent

Vanessa Olaya, 25, of Miami, came to Boston with her family for Shakira’s “Las Mujeres Ya No Lloran World Tour.”

The tall ships, she said, were a welcome surprise.

At the Massport Marine Terminal on Fid Kennedy Avenue, Olaya watched the ships arrive with a Sail Boston teddy bear she named Theodore tucked beside her.

“I really like the vibe, and you get to see different cultures here as well,” she said. “It’s totally different for us [coming] from Miami.”

Olaya, who is Colombian, said she was excited to see Latin American countries represented among the international vessels.

“I would have never imagined that here in Boston I would see a Chilean or an Ecuadorian tall ship,” she said.

By Jane Miller, Globe correspondent

At the edge of Christopher Columbus Waterfront Park, people pitched their lawn chairs and staked out views of the tall ship flotillas as they sailed in front of the Long Wharf.

Barbara Mercer, 75, came all the way from Houston to see the ships. She watched from under her hot pink parasol as Esmeralda, the Chilean ship, passed by.

“I missed them in ’76,” Mercer said of the tall ships. “I’m not gonna be around for the next one, so I wanted to come jump on an airplane.”

The ship she’s most excited to see is the Elissa, a historical tall ship that’s usually docked in her neck of the woods, in Galveston.

“She’s the Texas tall ship,” Mercer said with a smile. “The last time she was in Boston was 1888, and she’s beautiful.”

By Bryan Hecht, Globe correspondent

Rich Bowers, 66, of Natick, and Val deOlloqui, 62, of Chattanooga, Tenn., traded a pair of binoculars on the steps of Fan Pier Park.

Both avid sailors, they said the park offered great offshore views of the ships making their approach with their sails up before docking.

“I just have a passion for sailing and the history of sailing,” said Bowers, who watched the ships pass the Cape Cod Canal earlier in the week and is taking his sailing team on an Adirondack sailing expedition next week.

deOlloqui, who comes from a Navy family with his grandfather serving as a vice admiral at Pearl Harbor, said he enjoyed watching the USS Constitution and other military vessels arrive earlier in the morning.

“My dad made models of some of these ships,” he said. “Square-riggers are particularly fascinating … [you won’t] see those just out sailing.”

By Jaden Perry, Globe correspondent

As morning stretched into afternoon, Andrew Leaper, 31, and Courtney Adams, 33, sat in a patch of grass at Piers Park over a picnic blanket, at the center of it all. Every now and then, horns wailed in the background and crowd applauded.

For Leaper, who lives with Adams in Jeffries Point, “seeing the neighborhood alive, like seeing everyone out, using the local space,” is his favorite part of the tall ships.

The pair have been engaged for a year and plan to take a ferry tour on Tuesday to learn more about the ships.

“Just learning about the history of the boats and the stories of the boats is really exciting,” Adams said while somewhat serenely taking in the breeze as she starred out into the water.

By Ariela Lopez, Globe correspondent

Louise Martin, from Cambridge, came to the Charlestown Navy Yard with her boyfriend and another friend to watch the ships come in.

A teacher, Martin said she stopped by her school this morning to pick up binoculars she uses in her classroom. She compared Sail Boston to the World Cup — both events were “for everybody.”

“It’s nice to come here because the ships are inclusive,” Martin said. “It’s a beautiful day to see the beautiful ships.”

Martin and her friends said they were especially excited to see the Portuguese ship, Sagres.

By Thai Theodoro, Globe correspondent

As the Chilean tall ship Esmeralda sailed past, spectators shuffled from one vantage point to another at Massport, eager for a closer look as the 371-foot, steel-hulled, four-masted barquentine approached the Marine Terminal.

Among them was Kathy Hogan, 71, of Boston, who arrived wearing her Sail Boston 2000 T-shirt.

“I was just pulling out some T-shirts, and I went, ‘Oh my God’,” Hogan said. “So I wear it proudly!”

The shirt brought back memories of Sail Boston 2000, which Hogan said remains one of her memorable life experiences.

“I came with four other people and myself, and it was raining! They had fireworks, and it was raining so hard that they wouldn’t go off,” Hogan said.

Hogan said this summer’s lineup of major events has reminded her why she loves living in the city.

“I’m thrilled. The fact that I got there, I saw the USS Constitution, I saw the Coast Guard,” she said. “It’s phenomenal, I’m just so proud of this city.”

By Jaden Perry, Globe correspondent

Sitting on a bench with his legs folded, Paul Lefkovith, 81, stared through his binoculars, fixated on the docked ships near Piers Park.

“I’m an avid sailor. I’ve sailed all my life,” Lefkovith said. At 13, he began learning how to sail at community boating on the Charles River. At 34, he decided to buy his own boat.

“I said the hell with the Charles River and bought my own first boat,” Lefkovith said, fitted in a sun hat, red shirt, and pearl-white socks pulled up to his knees.

A true son of the sea, Lefkovith owned a sail boat for 41 years. Every few years, he’d sell one off to buy a bigger one.

As a young man, Lefkovith, of Roxbury, was drafted into the Marines, and eventually started a career as an engineer. Once he retired, he and his wife would take months-long summer trips throughout the coast on his sailboat.

“I’ve cruised from Maine, MidCoast Maine, all the way to Long Island, Nantucket, Martha’s Vineyard, Block Island ... Sag Harbor,” he said.

As he spoke about his eventful life, fighter jets soared over the pier, juxtaposing his stories of life on the water. Putting on his reflective sunglasses, Lefkovith grabbed his binoculars, slung his backpack on his back, and walked further into the pier to catch a better view.

By Camilo Fonseca, Globe staff

As the first tall ships entered Boston Harbor, a cheer emanated from the crowd at Castle Island. But on the other side of Fort Independence, dozens of spectators bemoaned the fact that only the ships’ masts were visible.

Hundreds of people remained in long line late into the morning, many of them frustrated. Some reported waiting over an hour for the security checkpoint.

“It’s been a challenge,” said Ann Mariano, of Franklin, carrying a lawn chair and shuffling quickly to the edge of the island to see the ships.

Her husband, Mike Mariano, said he feared they already missed her favorite ships, the USS Constitution and Coast Guard training cutter Eagle.

The Marianos said left Franklin at 7 a.m.; they waited on shuttle buses at JFK/UMass for nearly 45 minutes. That was before reaching the security lines in the Castle Island parking lot, which nearly stretched back to William Day Boulevard.

“Now they’re just letting everyone through without really checking, probably because they were so backed up,” Mike Mariano said.

Despite the palpable frustration, the two said they were excited for the parade, as the boom of cannons echoed from the harbor.

“We’re going to have a great day,” said Ann Mariano. “This is Boston at its best.”

By Thai Theodoro, Globe correspondent

The American Society of Marine Artists was hard to miss at the Massport Marine Terminal. Members of the group positioned easels along the waterfront, each focused on their first strokes of paint on canvas as the tall ships arrived.

Patrick O’Brien, 66, of Baltimore, is the president of the society.

“A lot of people came from a great distance because this is an unusual event for us,” O’Brien said. “For marine painters, it’s the perfect experience.”

O’Brien has been painting since 1985. Over the years, he said, the USS Constitution has appeared on his canvas hundreds of times.

“As a kid, I used to stay at the dining room table and draw pictures of Civil War battles and Native American villages and Viking ships,” he said. “Now I’m in my studio all day, sitting there drawing these historic scenes.”

By Thai Theodoro, Globe correspondent

Stephen Bluto, 63, of New York, traveled to Boston after watching the vessels during Sail250’s stop in New York City.

Bluto, editor in chief of the Marine Art Journal by the American Society of Marine Artists, stood at an easel, painting the ships on his canvas. He said his passion for marine art comes from “a love of boats, a love of water.”

“This is such a great occasion for us,” he said.

Bluto said Boston has offered a much better experience than New York.

“The New York City one was all fenced off and they only let you in in like one little gate, and it was like a long line of people trying to get in,” Bluto said.

As a ship enthusiast, Bluto said he is especially looking forward to seeing the Amerigo Vespucci, an Italian full-rigged ship built in 1931, and ARA Libertad, the Argentinian tall ship built in 1963.

By Thai Theodoro, Globe correspondent

At the Massport Marine Terminal on Fid Kennedy Avenue, spectators raised binoculars toward the harbor as the water jets from the Fire Fighter — a fireboat built in 1938 — signaled the start of the Parade of Sail.

Moments later, the USS Constitution led the procession of tall ships into Boston Harbor.

Denise Paoni, 68, of Boston, came to watch with her children and grandchildren as part of an early birthday celebration.

“What I’m looking forward to is seeing the Amerigo Vespucci ship come in from Italy and all the ships really!,” Paoni said.

For Paoni, the event is especially meaningful because she attended the last Sail Boston in 2017. Now, she said, she’s excited to share the experience with her grandchildren, some of whom were not yet born when the ships last sailed into the city.

“We’re going to come back during the week and do some touring of the ships,” Paoni said.

By Jaden Perry, Globe correspondent

Tall ships are drifting into Boston Harbor. Before the heat gets too unbearable, visitors are finding their spots on the ledge in Piers Park, their feet dangling over.

A hot dog vendor rings a bell to catch the attention of early guests. Stickers that read “Shippin’ into East Boston” are being distributed. Sweet Italian ice is dished out before the main event.

People are starting to pack Piers Park, hauling bags and lawn chairs onto the dewey grass amid a salty smelling breeze.

By Laurie Fullerton, Globe correspondent

Along the way, you’ll likely hear plenty of nautical terms — and more than a few expressions you already use without realizing they began at sea.

Feeling under the weather. A project that’s dead in the water. Some office scuttlebutt. Being in the doldrums or back on an even keel. Even waiting until the sun is over the yardarm before celebrating with a drink. All of these phrases trace their roots to life aboard sailing ships.

“Dead in the water is a terrible place to be on the ocean, with no wind and going nowhere, and on land it means much the same, a plan or design that has no chance of succeeding or moving ahead,” said Eric Jay Dolin, local author of the bestselling book “Wreck of the Mentor.”

READ MORE

By Madyline Swearing, Globe correspondent

Visitors can view and tour the ships along the waterfront throughout the week, but the event’s highlight is the Parade of Sail on Saturday, when the majestic ships sail into the harbor. City officials and organizers urge visitors to use public transportation or walk.

City officials say road closures and parking restrictions will be in effect on the following streets in South Boston, Charlestown, East Boston, the North End, and Seaport throughout Saturday.

READ MORE

By Brian MacQuarrie and Stan Grossfeld, Globe staff

The wind finally had freshened to a sail-swelling 17 m.p.h. Thursday when a Romanian training officer pumped his fists, paced the deck, and exhorted dozens of naval cadets in a sharp, staccato voice to do what doesn’t come naturally to most people.

Climb high into the rigging of a tall ship. Shuffle along a spar more than 100 feet above deck and untie a furled sail. Do all this while rolling on the open ocean and standing only on a thin cable. But don’t worry, there’s a buckle for the spar.

“Be strong!” urged Stefan Scutelnicu, the Mircea’s senior sail-training officer.

“Hoo-rah! Hoo-rah! Hoo-rah!” the young cadets shouted before applauding and clambering aloft to masts that rise 144 feet over the scrubbed wooden deck.

And strong they were, climbing and working with a purposeful, fearless precision that smacked of age-old sailing choreography.

Dropping the Mircea’s sails was the pulsating prelude to a long race that began later Thursday among four “sister ships” that are headed to Boston for the tall ships celebration beginning Saturday.

The crew of the three-masted Mircea, the Black Sea-based training vessel of the Romanian Naval Academy, eagerly awaited the sprint north along Cape Cod from far south of Nantucket.

The “four sisters” also include the US Coast Guard training vessel Eagle, the Sagres from Portugal, and the Gorch Fock from Germany, all built in the 1930s in the same shipyard in Hamburg, Germany.

By Ariela Lopez, Globe correspondent

Fifty tall ships from around the world will sail through Boston Harbor on Saturday for Sail250, a maritime celebration of America’s semiquincentennial.

The vessels will then head to their assigned berths along Boston Harbor, where most will open to guests before departing the morning of July 16. The event is expected to draw millions of visitors.

Boston’s own USS Constitution, usually stationed in Charlestown, is the Parade of Sail’s oldest ship. Known as “Old Ironsides,” the vessel was built in 1797 and is the world’s oldest commissioned warship still afloat.

From a 19th-century British merchantman to a former floating prison, here are seven other ships to keep an eye out for in Boston Harbor.

By Thai Theodoro, Globe correspondent

Boston isn’t letting the holiday festivities sail away just yet. From July 11-16, the city is set to welcome more than 50 tall ships from 21 countries as it prepares to host Sail Boston, the grand finale of the nationwide Sail250 celebration.

The free, family-friendly event marks Boston’s role in commemorating the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States through Sail250, which will “bring in dozens of the most stunning, beautiful vessels from around the world, connecting our city to our heritage of seafaring,” Mayor Michelle Wu said during a press event Monday.

City leaders hosted one final preview on Monday to showcase plans for Sail Boston 2026.

“Massachusetts is excited to welcome the tall ships and the military vessels that will arrive and have already started arriving from around the world this week,” said Kate Fox, executive director of the Massachusetts Office of Travel & Tourism. “One of the world’s great maritime gatherings, Sail Boston will bring together history, culture, education, and international friendship in a way few events can.”

title: ‘More than just a cyclist’: Dozens mourn Boston transit planner killed while biking
text:
“She’s more than just a cyclist and an advocate,” Rose Frank, 36, who became friends with Gag in seventh grade, said. “Those were parts of her identity, but she’s such an amazing person in so many other ways, and we want to celebrate all of those ways.”

Gag, who grew up in Roslindale just minutes from the park, was a joyful and energetic child, said Mark Smith, 66, a neighbor who spoke at the event.

“She was the sweetest little girl with a big wide smile,” Smith said. “Whenever you were in her presence, you felt somehow special.”

Smith said Gag’s passion for giving back to her community likely came from her parents, Steve Gag and Laura Gang, longtime Roslindale residents who contributed greatly to developing the neighborhood. Steve Gag helped bring a farmers market to Adams Park, while Laura Gang was involved in the public library.

Gag’s loved ones said she grew up to become a generous person who cared deeply about her family and friends.

“Louisa showed up for people,” Molly Goodkind, 36, a childhood friend of Gag’s said during Sunday’s event. “We’ll never understand how she had time to be everyone’s go-to person.”

Gag, she said, would eagerly volunteer to cat-sit, even though she didn’t like cats. Another friend said she kept a spreadsheet of the birthdays of all the babies she knew.

“She was the person outside of my biological family who, if I needed something, she would be there in an instant,” Goodkind, who has known Gag since they were 2-years-old, said.

Gag’s friends said she was curious and remained open-minded, even though she held firm beliefs.

“Who do you know that was a vegetarian except for when it inconvenienced others? And of course, except for hot dogs, because according to Louisa, you can’t not have a hot dog at a barbecue,” Gag’s friend Danielle Shaked said, drawing laughs from the crowd, including Laura Gang, who dabbed at her eyes with a crumpled tissue.

Gag also found time for many hobbies, and was always trying new ones, her friends said. Beyond loving outdoor activities such as biking and hiking, she was passionate about sustainability and shopped secondhand or sewed her own clothes. She dabbled in photography, painting, and cooking.

Urban planning was one of Gag’s enduring passions, Goodkind said.

“In college, she created her own major,” she said. “I don’t remember exactly what she called it, but it was something like city and people.”

Gag attended college at the University of Rochester and later earned a master’s degree in urban and environmental planning and policy from Tufts University, according to her LinkedIn.

Before joining the city in 2022, Gag worked for LivableStreets Alliance, a Boston-based nonprofit that advocates for increased safety, equity, and affordability. She also interned for Mayor Michelle Wu when Wu was a city councilor.

Wu attended Sunday’s event, but did not speak. Like many other attendees, she held a yellow sunflower, one of Gag’s favorites, as she tearfully listened to the tributes.

While Gag didn’t like being the center of attention, her friends said she would have been grateful for Sunday’s event.

“She would be completely honored to know that she has impacted so many people,” Frank said, her gaze drifting over the people gathered in the park.

Under a small tent nearby, attendees crowded around a folding table, filling out remembrance cards. Dozens of bikes leaned against the park’s fences while more lay scattered in the grass.

This story was updated on 7/13 to reflect a new count of the number of people who attended the event.

title: What if Massachusetts had its own Plat-fall?
text:
The scramble got us wondering: What happens if a major-party nominee exits at the last minute in Massachusetts?

The short-answer is, nothing quite like Maine. When lawmakers passed a law last year moving up this year’s primary date to Sept. 1, they also rewrote the timeline for replacing candidates who withdraw after the primary, at least for this specific year.

Under the 2025 law, candidates have until noon on Sept. 4 — the Friday after the primary — to withdraw or file an objection against a nominee with the secretary of state’s office. If a vacancy opens up, the nominee’s party can fill it through an executive committee whose membership is determined by its state committee. That committee then has until 5 p.m. on Sept. 8 — just a week after the primary — to submit a new certificate of nomination to the secretary of state.

Part of the compressed timeline is because of Massachusetts’ notoriously late primary date. With just nine weeks between the primary and the general election, there simply isn’t enough time to remake the November ballots before they have to go out to voters.

“There is a limited window to replace people, because it’s about ballot printing now,” Secretary of State William F. Galvin said.

The timeline has also only gotten tighter as Massachusetts has expanded voting by mail. Applications for mail-in ballots go out to voters 45 days before each statewide election.

“It’s a very tight window,” Galvin said.

Massachusetts just doesn’t have much room for the kind of replacement campaign now unfolding in Maine, where primary voters had their say in early June.

Still, that doesn’t mean parties in Massachusetts have never had to improvise.

In 1986, Republicans pushed businessman George Kariotis to enter the race for governor after two other candidates — Royall Switzler and Gregory Hyatt — ended their campaigns amid separate scandals. Switzler admitted to lying about his military record, while Hyatt was accused of “bizarre behavior” in the workplace, submitting fraudulent nomination signatures, and accepting cash from an organized crime figure.

But because the deadline to qualify for the ballot had already passed, Kariotis was left to run a write-in campaign. Kariotis advanced to the general election, despite earning fewer votes than both Switzler and Hyatt, according to records from Galvin’s office. The Republican State Committee then had to hold a post-primary vote to solidify his position as the nominee, the Globe reported at the time.

Such a mess, unsurprisingly, didn’t do the GOP any favors. Kariotis got trounced that November by incumbent governor Michael Dukakis.

Two decades earlier, Democrats faced an even more unexpected vacancy after state Auditor Thomas Buckley died of a heart attack on the eve of the 1964 primary while running unopposed. Members of the Democratic State Committee voted to replace him with Thaddeus Buczko, who won that November.

BALLOT WHIPLASH: That’s not to say Massachusetts isn’t having its own ballot turmoil this year, too.

Michael Walsh, the state Republican Party’s endorsed pick for attorney general, could end up on the GOP primary ballot after all despite “substantial evidence” that he submitted forged signatures to qualify, reports the Globe’s Chris Van Buskirk.

Walsh owed his technical court victory to snail mail. Judge Jeffrey T. Karp wrote in a court ruling Friday that the state Democratic Party official, Adam Roof, who originally challenged Walsh’s place on the ballot did not correctly submit his objection under state law, which requires it to be sent via registered or certified mail.

Roof instead sent it by email and through first-class mail.

Karp, however, ruled that Anne Manning Martin, another statewide candidate facing allegations of submitting fraudulent signatures, should not be reinstated to the ballot. Shawn Oliver, a fellow lieutenant governor candidate who challenged her place on the ballot, had “complied” with state law in submitting his objection, Karp wrote.

Walsh’s spot on the ballot isn’t official yet. Lawyers for the State Ballot Law Commission — which issued the initial ruling removing him from the ballot after determining that hundreds of signatures he submitted were likely fake — filed an appeal with the Supreme Judicial Court late on Friday, according to David Mackey, an attorney for the commission.

Any decision will have to happen fast. Galvin’s office had asked the lower court to rule by Wednesday to give officials enough time to prepare Republican primary ballots for local clerks to send to overseas and military voters by Saturday.

SIX-TH PAC: Outside money is officially starting to flow into the race to replace US Representative Seth Moulton in the Sixth District.

The New Leadership PAC, a super PAC with a stated mission of “electing Democrats who fight,” spent nearly $270,000 on digital advertising and “media production” in support of former White House aide Dan Koh, one of six Democrats running for the seat.

The PAC started spending in the race Thursday, according to federal campaign filings, the same day Koh’s campaign last updated its red box to suggest supportive groups run ads “starting immediately.” (A red box is a public webpage that allows the campaign to whisper to a super PAC while circumventing campaign finance rules barring coordination between the two.)

Boston-based Sports betting giant DraftKings is the New Leadership PAC’s top donor with a $250,000 donation from late May. James MacKay, a construction company owner who maxed out to Koh’s campaign last year and gave another $3,500 this year, also donated $25,000 to the PAC, and Peter Palandjian, the CEO of Intercontinental Real Estate Corp., and another Koh donor, gave $50,000.

New Leadership PAC has spent some money in other races, too, running ads opposing Texas Representative Julie Johnson, a Democrat, who lost the party’s nomination to former Representative Colin Allred in a runoff election in one of Texas’s newly redrawn districts in May. It also supported Brooke Pinto, who lost the race to become Washington, D.C.’s delegate in Congress.

RHODE EXIT? How Dan McKee became one of America’s most endangered governors by Edward Fitzpatrick and Dan McGowan, The Boston Globe: Rhode Island Governor Daniel J. McKee is in danger of becoming just the second sitting governor in state history to lose his party’s primary, as sagging support within his Democratic base and the political fallout from a high-profile bridge closure have left his campaign in a precarious position.

JOB INSECURITIES: For Boston’s City Council staff, their jobs carry few protections or guarantees. by Niki Griswold, The Boston Globe: For most employees of the city of Boston, the vast majority of whom are unionized, sick time, vacation days, and set salary ranges for their positions are a given. But for Boston City Council staffers, almost none of those basic employment conditions apply.

First, they are all technically considered temporary workers; both their employment and biweekly pay must be publicly reauthorized by the council roughly every three months. The 13 councilors are not required to provide even a minimum amount of paid time off. Staff also are not eligible for overtime. There are no salary minimums or set pay ranges for council staff.

That leaves nearly every aspect of each staffer’s job to be dictated by the personal preferences and priorities of the individual councilor, which current and former council staffers say can lead to deep disparities, open staff to mistreatment, and, in rare cases, create an environment for criminal wrongdoing.

‘LOUISA SHOWED UP’: Dozens mourn Boston transit planner killed while biking by Allyson Chiu, The Boston Globe: Around 200 people clad in yellow — a color symbolizing pedestrian and bike safety — gathered Sunday afternoon to remember Louisa Gag, a bike-share and transportation planner for the City of Boston, who was fatally struck by a car while cycling near Roxbury Crossing last week.

RELATED: Crash that killed Boston transit planner sparks furor over road safety efforts by Diti Kohli, Niki Griswold and Ariela Lopez, The Boston Globe.

HOME RULES: The major bipartisan housing affordability bill Senator Elizabeth Warren played a key role in crafting automatically became law over the weekend after President Trump let the deadline to veto it expire on Saturday. The Globe’s Andrew Brinker has details on four of the bill’s biggest changes, and what they could mean in Massachusetts.

IN SOUTH CAROLINA: Sen. Lindsey Graham likely died after aorta tear, medical examiner says by Seung Min Kim, Mary Clare Jalonick and Meg Kinnard, The Associated Press: South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Trump’s closest allies in Congress who traveled the globe to advocate for a more aggressive U.S. foreign policy, died after a tear in his aorta, according to a preliminary medical examiner finding shared by his office. Graham, a Republican, had turned 71 years old just two days before dying on Saturday night.

Mass. scientists say Alzheimer’s, other research at stake in Trump funding shake-up by Allyson Chiu, The Boston Globe.

The gas is cheap. The Trump administration isn’t saying who’s paying for it. by James Bikales, POLITICO.

High schoolers are placing sports bets online. Experts warn of growing risks of addiction. by John Hilliard, The Boston Globe.

Ten communities in Massachusetts went ‘fossil fuel free.’ Then utilities spent $100M on natural gas infrastructure there. by Jordan Wolman, CommonWealth Beacon.

Some say Springfield courthouse decision smacks of typical Boston politics by Stephanie Barry, The Springfield Republican.

title: Blue Hill Avenue deserves rail, not another bus debate
text:
We have been left without the permanent rapid rail transit infrastructure that other communities take for granted. A look at the MBTA map shows a wide swath of Mattapan, Dorchester, and Roxbury with no rapid transit.

One can overlay maps of economic, environmental, and even educational inequality over this gap in the MBTA system. The lack of transit access has limited economic development and created more pollution for our residents.

Improvements to Blue Hill Avenue should never be conditional. Yet that is the choice being presented: Accept a plan for a center-running bus lane on Blue Hill Avenue, or continue waiting for long-overdue safety improvements. Routine infrastructure upgrades should not be used to pressure a community into accepting a proposal it has repeatedly opposed.

The absence of rail along Blue Hill Avenue is not an accident of geography. It is the product of decades of public policy that consistently underinvested in Boston’s Black and brown neighborhoods. In 1979, the MBTA studied expanding rapid transit to Nubian Square and along Blue Hill Avenue. Rather than advancing the project, planners prioritized investments elsewhere, such as Red and Green Line extensions and commuter rail expansions. Whether judged by the standards of the day or today’s understanding of equity, the result is unmistakable: Generations of residents were left without the rapid transit service other communities received.

An Orange Line branch, beginning at Ruggles, traveling down Blue Hill Avenue, and terminating at Mattapan Square, would cost billions of dollars and take years to build. That much is certain. But so is the need for that branch. Today, more than 30,000 riders depend on buses along Blue Hill Avenue every day. Imagine what that demand could become with true rapid transit. The Commonwealth invested roughly $1.1 billion to extend commuter rail to Fall River for a projected 2,500 riders. If that investment is justified, what is the appropriate investment for a road already serving more than 10 times as many people every day?

This is a double standard. When communities of color raise these transportation inequities or push for transformative investment, the conversation begins and ends with cost. Rail is too expensive, too ambitious, unnecessary because a bus already runs there. Some communities are told to dream big. Others are told to settle.

Rail serving Nubian Square and Blue Hill Avenue is not a fantasy. For decades, state and regional planners have examined major transit concepts for this corridor. The 2012 Roxbury-Dorchester-Mattapan Transit Needs Study evaluated rapid transit options linking Dudley (now Nubian Square), Grove Hall, Blue Hill Avenue, and Mattapan. The Urban Ring planning process envisioned rail connections through Ruggles and Nubian Square. The 2014 Fairmount Indigo Corridor Plan called for expanded rail service and expanded subway integration.

These studies were never intended to provide final engineering designs. But they did show something important: that residents and stakeholders had already done the work to build consensus around the need and that rail deserved serious consideration.

Yet, despite decades of planning and repeated acknowledgment of the corridor’s importance, the Commonwealth has never commissioned a comprehensive feasibility study to determine how a rail-based rapid transit replacement could actually be built, what it would cost, or what benefits it would deliver. Instead, those questions remain unanswered — not because rail was proven infeasible, but because the analysis needed to answer them was never completed.

Residents deserve to see a comparison of enhanced bus service, center-running bus lanes, and surface and underground rail. They deserve to understand the costs, construction impacts, effects on businesses and parking, travel time improvements, and displacement risks associated with each option.

That comprehensive comparison has never been presented.

Many residents along Blue Hill Avenue have said they do not support the current center-running bus lane proposal, and more than 2,100 residents signed a petition opposing the plan. Their concerns should not be dismissed as resistance to change or a misunderstanding of transit policy.

Today, policy makers are actively discussing the possibility of extending the Orange Line to Roslindale. If that corridor merits a study for rapid transit expansion, it is reasonable to ask why Blue Hill Avenue, one of the region’s busiest bus routes, has not received a comparable modern evaluation despite decades of existing plans.

The nearby Fairmount Line does not resolve the challenge. While it provides valuable commuter rail service, it does not directly serve the Blue Hill Avenue corridor, operate at true rapid transit frequencies, and, without the North-South Rail Link, cannot provide seamless through-service across downtown. It is an important part of the region’s transit network — but it is not a substitute for high-capacity rapid transit serving Blue Hill Avenue.

The next step is straightforward: The state should commission a comprehensive rail feasibility study; establish a timeline for funding, environmental review, and preliminary engineering; and allow the public to evaluate the alternatives based on evidence rather than assumptions.

Massachusetts is entering a new era of transportation investment. Service has improved, and Fair Share revenues have created billions of dollars for transit. That gives us the opportunity to think beyond incremental improvements, especially in communities that have waited generations for the investments others take for granted. After decades of deferred upgrades, Blue Hill Avenue deserves more than another bus debate. It deserves the same vision, analysis, and ambition that Massachusetts brings to every major transit investment.

title: ‘The time has come’: Blue Hill Avenue deserves proposed bus transit upgrades
text:
That was the first of many trips to Mattapan Station, many rides on the 28, many breakfasts at Brothers Deli, and many meetings about how the MBTA could improve the bus rider experience in a meaningful way. We proposed the 28X project, a plan for center-running bus rapid transit, or BRT, from Mattapan Station to Grove Hall, with bus priority features for the rest of the trip to Nubian Square. Using federal American Recovery and Reinvestment Act funding that had to be spent quickly, we had no time for meaningful public engagement. This gap in the engagement process was irreconcilable, and the effort failed that same year, but the idea remained alive.

Fast forward to today. Fast and reliable BRT along Blue Hill Avenue is finally within reach, with a strong federal funding commitment and active support from the MBTA, the city of Boston, bus riders, local youth groups, and transit advocates. Each day more than 30,000 riders use one of the bus routes using Blue Hill Avenue, and each day they collectively lose 3,000 hours of precious time due to traffic congestion and impediments like double parking. Bus rapid transit will change all that in this decade.

It puzzles and pains me to see two members of the Boston City Council, after several years of robust public engagement by the city and the T, actively oppose the project now, jeopardizing both the federal funding and the rare opportunity to significantly improve bus transit along this route. The councilors have proposed an alternative, their vision for a new Orange Line subway extension. The danger is that local residents may mistakenly believe that BRT conflicts with a future Orange Line extension. It does not.

A subway is a blunt mobility instrument, taking you from point A to point B with speed but none of the inherent flexibility provided by surface bus routes. Riders using the 22, 28, and 31 buses are reaching different destinations — each with different points A and B — and they will all be well served by the BRT corridor. The BRT plan would complement any future subway extension because each would serve different journey needs and patterns.

More than half the people traveling along Blue Hill Avenue during rush hour are bus riders. They are among the most transit-dependent passengers on the system. There is therefore substantial upside to benefiting bus riders in the short term while a subway vision wends its way through the lengthy, complex, and uncertain process of community engagement, design, engineering, and environmental review. Funding uncertainty is also inherent to the subway vision, because the federal money committed to the BRT project cannot be used for any other project or purpose.

How tall a mountain is this to climb? By comparison, the relatively simple and inexpensive Red Line/Blue Line connector has taken decades to advance to 30 percent design, and there is still no funding plan or construction commitment from the MBTA despite the economic and environmental justice benefits the project will provide. The Green Line Extension Project cost $2.3 billion and took nearly two decades to complete — and that is a surface and elevated light rail system built largely on existing or abandoned rail rights of way, not a complex subway project in the middle of a dense urban neighborhood.

There has never been an urban subway extension on the scale proposed by the councilors that has come to fruition in either a short period of time or at a politically feasible cost. We know little to nothing about the right path for an Orange Line subway extension (a 1978 study looked superficially at what were termed “generalized alternatives”), about soil or utility conditions, about constructability and potential property impacts from excavation, about surface street disruptions, about the right number of stops, or about an all-in cost estimate. Those issues will require decades to sort out, with no guarantee of success.

I assume the councilors are acting in good faith, but they are giving their constituents false hope. Their vision is not achievable in a reasonable time frame and faces many substantial challenges. In contrast, their constituents will benefit in the short term from the joint MBTA/city BRT plan. The bus riders who lived with suboptimal bus trips in 2009 continue to experience poor transit conditions. These riders have suffered long enough. BRT along Blue Hill Avenue will measurably improve transit access and pedestrian and vehicular safety along the route. The time has come.
