We want to hear from you.

title: Wu launches expanded free summer meal program in Boston with more locations
text:
Mayor Michelle Wu on Tuesday launched this year’s Boston Summer Eats program with an updated list of over 60 meal locations, including schools, libraries, community centers, and even an outdoor farmers market according to a news release.

Summer Eats is a federally funded food assistance initiative that provides healthy free meals to kids and teens throughout the summer months. This year’s program has expanded its scope from 33 meal locations last year to 62 across Allston, Brighton, Back Bay, Chinatown, Dorchester, East Boston, Fenway, Hyde Park, Jamaica Plain, Mattapan, Roxbury, South Boston, West Roxbury, Roslindale, North End, Charlestown, and Bay Village.

You can see the full list of spots here.

“In Boston, we believe in taking every possible step for access to fresh, healthy food. The Boston Summer Eats program ensures our young people get nutritious food even when school isn’t in session,” Wu said in a release.

“Summer doesn’t have to mean empty stomachs or worried parents,” added Erin McAleer, president of Project Bread, which is an program partner. “Summer Eats is a vital resource ensuring kids and teens in Boston and beyond have access to nutritious meals when school is out.”

Dorchester has the most meal locations at 13. The individual hours and operating days of each location vary, though the majority are open Monday through Friday, offering breakfast from 8:00 a.m. to 10 a.m. and lunch from 11:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m.

All meals must all be consumed on-site. “Grab and go,” options are no longer allowed due to updated federal regulations, officials said, though all meals will follow USDA guidelines and include milk, fruits, vegetables, grains, and proteins.

Many of the meals will be prepared at the Boston Public Schools’ Central Kitchen in Dorchester by BPS culinary staff, the release said.

The initiative is a partnership between the Mayor’s Office, Boston Public Schools, the YMCA of Greater Boston, Boston Centers for Youth & Families, and Project Bread and is open to all youths 18 and under.

Bryan Hecht can be reached at bryan.hecht@globe.com. Follow him on Instagram @bhechtjournalism.

title: Louisa Gag, cyclist fatally struck in Boston, recalled in obituary as a ‘beacon of kindness’
text:
Relatives of Louisa Gag, a bike-share and transportation planner for the city of Boston who was fatally struck Thursday while cycling near Roxbury Crossing, recalled her as a “beacon of kindness” in her obituary.

Gag, 36, who grew up in Roslindale and graduated from Boston Latin School before earning degrees at the University of Rochester and Tufts University, “worked tirelessly to improve the city she loved, devoting herself to making it more livable, enjoyable, and humane,” the tribute stated.

Gag was dedicated to her job at City Hall, her relatives said.

“While at the Boston Transportation Department, she grew the Blue Bikes program and engaged with many communities to make streets safer for all,” the obituary said.

She also had many hobbies and passions.

“Louisa also loved dogs, raspberries, leopard print, thrifting, ice cream, chocolate, sewing, and riding bikes. She was an avid reader,” the obituary said. “She brought the cleverest gifts to the Yankee swap. Louisa loved to play, especially cribbage, the Gag family favorite.”

In addition, Gag’s family said, she cultivated a deep love for the natural world.

“She found peace in nature, beginning in the Arnold Arboretum, evolving to winter hiking in the White Mountains, summers camping in Nickerson State Park on Cape Cod, and biking to Crystal Lake in Newton for a spontaneous swim,” the obituary said.

On Thursday morning, Gag was riding on Tremont Street near Roxbury Crossing when she was fatally struck by the driver of a truck, authorities said.

The crash stunned cycling advocates, who recalled her effusive joy and wide-ranging impact. And it also hit close to home in City Hall, where Gag had interned for Mayor Michelle Wu when she was a city councilor.

Wu said last week that Gag will be remembered as a “bright light” and “dedicated public servant.”

The crash occurred a short distance from Southwest Corridor Park. The driver stopped afterward, officials said.

Authorities haven’t identified the driver, who hasn’t been charged with any crimes. A spokesperson for the Suffolk district attorney’s office said Tuesday there were no updates on the investigation.

Gag had previously worked at the Livable Streets Alliance, a transit advocacy group, her obituary said.

“In lieu of flowers, please consider a donation to Livable Streets Alliance, www.livablestreets.info and designate your donation in memory of Louisa Gag," her obituary said.

The Massachusetts Vision Zero Coalition, a group working to prevent traffic fatalities, said it will hold a vigil for Gag on Thursday at 6 p.m. at City Hall Plaza.

The vigil will honor Gag’s life and call for “immediate, urgent action to create safer streets for all,” organizers said.

Material from previous Globe coverage was used in this report.

Travis Andersen can be reached at travis.andersen@globe.com.

title: Midwives break ground ceremonially for Boston’s first freestanding birth center in Roxbury
text:
“It’s about honoring the ancestors of this land as this is going to be a portal,” said Luana Morales, who set up a bed of flowers and presided over the ceremony. “It’s about respecting the people of this neighborhood with beauty, dignity, and integrity.”

Freestanding birth centers offer a different model from hospitals: a home-like setting where midwives — licensed providers trained to support patients through pregnancy, labor, and the postpartum period — lead care for low-risk pregnancies. The centers typically offer longer appointments than hospitals, have fewer patients, and most work with doulas, nonmedical professionals who provide physical and emotional support.

Some residents cited Roxbury’s high rates of maternal complications and the disproportionate risks faced by Black residents as reasons to establish birth centers as an alternative to hospital-based care. Neighborhood Birth Center’s founder Nashira Baril said her hope is that the center will fill a gap in maternal health care and address racial inequities within the health system by expanding access to comprehensive, insurance-covered midwifery care.

Board members hailed from Somerville to Salem, and many guests could be overheard saying “This isn’t just ceremonial, we’re actually breaking ground” and “It feels so real. It’s alive, not just a Zoom meeting.”

More than $10 million has been raised for the nonprofit birthing center, but more than $3 million is still needed.

“Boston has never had a freestanding birth center, despite well-documented poor outcomes and persistent racial inequities in perinatal health outcomes and growing demand for midwifery-led care,” said Baril, who has a master’s in maternal and child health from Boston University School of Public Health and serves on the state’s Maternal Health Task Force.

“Just hard hats and five shovels weren’t fitting for this occasion that has been years in the making. We invite everyone because that’s who it’s for,” she added.

Neighborhood Birth Center is being built on four parcels: 23 Kearsarge Avenue and 10, 14, and 18 Winthrop Street. There will be a two-story “home” center with four birth suites that will provide prenatal, birth, postpartum, newborn, and reproductive health services. Leaders say it’ll also serve as a hub for family education, postpartum support, community programming, and student midwifery training.

The center will serve more than birthing families but also plans to provide parenting classes, care for menopause, for people who want preventative services, or help with fertility. It will also have a community gathering space and host a house-in-residency for up to four training midwives learning at the center.

It is slated to open in the fall of next year.

Birth centers do have limitations, since they are designed for low-risk pregnancies and do not typically include physicians or OB/GYNs as part of routine care. They also have restrictions on the procedures they can offer, including the use of epidural anesthesia and surgical interventions. If complications arise during childbirth, patients are transferred to a hospital.

Neighborhood Birth Center is close to Warren Street and is nearby both Boston Medical Center and the Longwood Medical multiplex for quick transfers if needed.

Care will be led by certified nurse-midwives, supported by a team of doulas. Doula services are covered by MassHealth.

The groundbreaking comes as Massachusetts faces growing concern over maternal health access and outcomes. Hospitals across the state have shuttered 13 maternity units, totaling more than 100 beds, over the past decade. Maternal health inequities are widening despite years of state investment, with Black families disproportionately affected by complications and unequal access to care.

State leaders, including Governor Maura Healey, have pointed to birth centers as a lower-cost, lower-intervention alternative for people with low-risk pregnancies and have allocated millions of dollars in funding to support them.

Roxbury is especially meaningful for a center as it has among the highest rates of morbidity, along with Mattapan and Dorchester, said Jo-Anna L. Rorie, who has been a CNM for 37 years. She described how the neighborhood has to rely on BMC because Carney Hospital and St. Margaret Hospital closed.

“Roxbury is important because it has a rich history of Jamaican, African, and Caribbean immigrants and people from down south. This is where redlining took place, and birthing centers offer a feasibility for the community,” Rorie said.

Tara Register Curry, who lives across the street from the birthing center, said neighborhood residents are generally supportive of the birthing center, but not everyone understands its vision, she said.

“People need to look past just having a baby here,” said Curry, a mother of two girls. “This will be a place of community gathering, families seeking services and education, and providing that not just to the neighborhood, but to Boston. We go through more after having a baby, and this can be a safe place of support.”

title: Wu, City Hall remain reticent on key details in crash that killed Boston transit planner
text:
In response to multiple questions on Wednesday morning, Wu deferred to the ongoing investigation, saying she didn’t want to release any information that could jeopardize it.

“We need a full, transparent, comprehensive investigation about the facts of exactly what took place and what needs to be done to make sure that this never happens again,” Wu told reporters when pressed. “I know as soon as they are able, the appropriate authorities will share updates with Louisa’s family and with the general public.”

Boston police released a few more details Wednesday afternoon, specifying that the truck is a construction vehicle, specifically a Peterbilt 389 tractor trailer. Both the truck and Gag were traveling eastbound on Tremont approaching Parker Street when the truck “made contact” with Gag near the corner of the two streets.

Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden’s office said the investigation “will be comprehensive and will incorporate all aspects of the incident.”

Asked about why her Police Department isn’t putting out more information, Wu said, “I know as soon as they are able, we will make sure that they are sharing information with the public and with Louisa’s family.”

The 36-year-old Gag, an activist turned City Hall transportation planner, had worked for years trying to make Boston safer for cyclists and pedestrians only to become a victim of the very streets she was working to improve.

She was struck near the corner of Tremont and Parker streets near the Roxbury Crossing MBTA stop last Thursday. In the immediate aftermath, police gave a brief statement and released a short incident report.

Boston police first said they responded to a report of a pedestrian struck, though by the end of the day they clarified it was a cyclist. Police said emergency personnel pronounced the victim dead at the scene, and that the vehicle involved in the crash “has stopped.”

Later that day, the mayor wrote about Gag in a social media post in which she mourned her death and talked about her activism.

Investigations involving traffic crashes can take months. It took nearly one year for an investigation to conclude in criminal charges against the man accused of striking a child with a school bus in Hyde Park last year, though authorities released more information such as the name of the driver within a few weeks.

When a cyclist was struck and killed in September 2024 in Cambridge, State Police quickly released some general information about the mechanics of the crash — that the driver had lost control — though the investigation didn’t conclude until the following spring, when authorities filed criminal charges.

Gag’s family referred comment to lawyer Joshua Zisson, a local personal-injury attorney who focuses on cyclists. He declined to comment.

Gag grew up in Roslindale, graduated from Boston Latin School and earned degrees at the University of Rochester and Tufts University. She “worked tirelessly to improve the city she loved, devoting herself to making it more livable, enjoyable, and humane,” according to her obituary.

Hundreds attended a vigil for Gag on Sunday at Adams Park in Roslindale, and another memorial is planned by various bike groups for Thursday night at City Hall Plaza.

On Wednesday, Wu said, “We are devastated at tragic loss of someone who worked so hard and so brilliantly to ensure that the city of Boston would be a more vibrant and beautiful and welcoming, accessible space for everyone.”

The area of the crash has been a source of concern and frustration for cycling safety advocates in recent years. That section of Tremont has a painted bike lane as it approaches Parker Street that then transitions to a dotted line roughly 70 feet from a crosswalk.

Advocates have pointed to a 2023 city document relating to planning for an area around Parker Street that includes its intersection with Tremont. The presentation is largely focused on side streets rather than busy Tremont, but it still identified the stretch of Tremont as having “poor biking conditions.” It highlights that stretch in red, indicating the highest of four levels of “traffic stress” with bicycles.

Wu has said street safety remains a priority for her administration, and emphasized that work on many such infrastructure projects is ongoing. Wu’s office said last week the location of the crash was not covered under the Parker Street-area planning process and that there never were plans for a protected bike lane there.

Stacy Thompson, a transportation advocate who worked with Gag for years, said it’s not clear whether any particular proposed project would have directly affected driver or cyclist interactions on that stretch.

“We don’t know those answers yet,” Thompson said, adding that she looks forward to the police resolving a thorough investigation and providing more information.

But, she said, “That area has never been particularly comfortable and safe” for pedestrians or cyclists.

In 2025, there were 256 crashes in Boston that resulted in a cyclist being injured, according to the city’s “Vision Zero” database, which relies on data from Boston Emergency Medical Services. No fatalities were reported. Data on crashes involving cyclists in the city this year was not available.

The tragedy occurred during a time when some transit advocates have criticized Wu for stalling a number of street projects they said would improve public safety. One such area that’s been targeted for improvement is the busy intersection at Roxbury Crossing, a few blocks from the crash scene.

“The projects in and around that area would have changed driver behavior just generally,” said Galen Mook, executive director of MassBike.

title: The best things to do in and around Boston this weekend
text:
ICA’S VINYL NIGHTS The Institute of Contemporary Art hosts free vinyl nights throughout the summer. This Friday’s event will feature a launch party for Central On Air, Cambridge’s new internet radio station. Music selections will feature hip-hop/rap, R&B, freestyle, new wave, and indie-dance. July 17, 5-9 p.m. Free, but ticket required. Institute of Contemporary Art, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. icaboston.org — Daisy Levine

‘MALCOLM X’ The 1992 biopic from acclaimed director Spike Lee screens for free as part of the mayor’s movie nights series. Starring Denzel Washington, the film traces the life and legacy of the pivotal civil rights leader. Free popcorn will be provided while supplies last. July 17, 8 p.m. Free. Malcolm X Park, Dale St. at Regent St., Roxbury. boston.gov — Janira Skrbkova

BRIAN POSEHN It is strange times for Grandpa Metal, torch bearer for all things rock and nerd culture, and one of the stars of the upcoming “Big Bang Theory” spinoff “Stuart Fails to Save the Universe” on HBO Max. “I like Metallica and ‘Star Wars’ again,” he says. “But ever since Disney bought Metallica it’s so good.”July 17-18, 6:30 p.m. and 9 p.m. $41.74. Off Cabot, 9 Wallis St., Beverly. thecabot.org — Nick A. Zaino III

REVERE BEACH INTERNATIONAL SAND SCULPTING FESTIVAL World-class sand sculptors take over Revere Beach for the annual open-air festival this weekend. Beyond the sand art, visitors can enjoy amusement rides, fireworks, interactive activities, and more than 75 food vendors at this annual celebration. July 17-19. 350 Revere Beach Blvd., Revere. internationalsandsculptingfestival.com — JS

DUDLEY JAZZ FESTIVAL Jazz fans can enjoy an afternoon of free music, presented by Creative Cultural Arts, on Saturday. This year’s lineup includes the Fred Woodard Collective, Haneef Nelson Quintet, Kevin Harris Project, and Big Redd’s House, featuring Verna Hampton. July 18, noon-6 p.m. Shirley-Eustis House, 33 Shirley St.creativeculturalarts.org — JS

FESTIVAL BETANCES A cornerstone event for more than 50 years, Festival Betances is billed as New England’s longest-running Latino cultural festival. This year’s theme is “Boricua Legacy: Shaping America’s Story.” Stop by to enjoy a parade, food, music, and art. July 18, 12:30-9 p.m. RSVP for free on Eventbrite. Plaza Betances, 100 West Dedham St. ibaboston.org/events/festival-betances — DL

CHRIS GETHARD A constant advocate for artists and creativity, and the host of “Beautiful Anonymous,” Gethard is the beating heart of indie comedy, and often proves comedy can be simultaneously soulful and funny.July 18, 7:15 p.m. and 9:30 p.m. $29.95.The Comedy Studio, 5 John F. Kennedy St., Cambridge. thecomedystudio.com — NZ

‘WEIRD AL’ YANKOVIC Al has been writing silly music and parodies for 50 years, stretching back to his high school days, and he’ll be pulling from all over his catalog for this set, backed by a five-piece band.July 18, 8 p.m. $40-$198.60. TD Garden, 100 Legends Way. tdgarden.com — NZ

LEVITATE MUSIC AND ARTS FESTIVAL Featuring performances by Alanis Morisette, Caamp, and more, the Levitate Music and Arts Festival returns this weekend with plenty of music, plus food trucks, an artisan fair, and other fun activities. Read more about upcoming concerts and music events in this week’s Sound Check column. July 18-19, doors open at noon. Tickets start at $159. Marshfield Fairgrounds, 140 Main St., Marshfield. levitatemusicfestival.com — DL

COPLEY SQUARE VINTAGE FESTIVAL Courtesy of Select Markets and the Office of Youth Engagement & Advancement (OYEA), shop clothing, jewelry, temporary tattoos, and tooth gems at a vintage block party with offerings from more than 50 vendors. Visitors can enjoy free drinks, live music, and food trucks. July 19, noon-6 p.m. Copley Square. eventbrite.com — JS

BUYER & CELLAR Inspired by the strange-but-true fact that Barbra Streisand had a private shopping mall built in a basement on her Malibu estate, this comedy by Jonathan Tolins stars Victor L. Shopov as a struggling actor hired to work at the mall — which has only one customer. Directed by Daniel Bourque. July 18-Aug. 1. Hub Theatre Company. Club Café, 209 Columbus Ave. hubtheatreboston.org

A NEW ERA In Miranda Austen ADEkoje’s new drama about the Black suffragist movement in Boston, inspired by a real-life 1895 reform conference here of Black women from around the country, Patrice Jean-Baptiste plays Boston activist Josephine St. Pierre Ruffin, leader of an effort to outlaw lynching. Playing her fellow activists are Regine Vital, MaConnia Chesser, Frances Domond, Tolu Asade, Aislinn Brophy, Sydney Jackson, and Aliyah Harris. Directed by Summer L. Williams. July 18-Aug. 8. Company One Theatre. Strand Theatre, 543 Columbia Road. companyone.org

ESCAPE FROM NEW YORK On Saturday, the Brattle continues its tribute to the late actor Harry Dean Stanton with three of his films, including “Escape from New York.” John Carpenter’s 1981 sci-fi actioner stars Kurt Russell as the iconic eyepatch wearing antihero, Snake Plisken. It’s 1997, and Manhattan is now an inescapable maximum security prison. Plisken’s job is to sneak across the Hudson and rescue the US president (Donald Pleasance). Along the way, he meets Stanton’s power broker, Ernie Borgnine’s cab driver, Adrienne Barbeau’s badass with a gun, and most importantly, Isaac Hayes’s villain, the Duke of New York. The Duke of New York (A-Number One!) has the one movie prop I covet: a magnificent 1977 Cadillac Fleetwood Brougham with chandeliers on its hood and a disco ball on its rearview mirror. See the car, and hear composer Carpenter’s best theme. July 18, 4:45 p.m. and 9:30 p.m. Brattle Theatre, 40 Brattle St., Cambridge. brattlefilm.org

TANGLEWOOD BSO music director Andris Nelsons leads two programs this weekend in the Shed. Friday’s all-American program lines up a piece by BSO composer chair Carlos Simon, the Tanglewood debut of rising Boston-based violinist Keila Wakao in Barber’s Violin Concerto, and selections from Adams’s “Nixon in China” featuring baritone Thomas Hampson, soprano Renee Fleming, soprano Hye Jung Lee, and baritone John Brancy. Sunday afternoon promises early symphonies by Beethoven and Haydn alongside Shostakovich’s Piano Concerto No. 1 with Daniil Trifonov. But heads up for the film music buffs — Saturday’s guest conductor is Joe Hisaishi, whose name is revered on the level of John Williams among fans of the work of Japanese animation house Studio Ghibli (“Spirited Away,” “My Neighbor Totoro”). His Saturday evening program includes two of his own concert pieces as well as a suite from his score to “Princess Mononoke” (see if you can catch the Shostakovich shout-out) and Ravel’s Piano Concerto with Jean-Yves Thibaudet. And also, there’s several chamber music concerts at Ozawa and a plethora of offerings from the Tanglewood Learning Institute besides. Pack a few picnics. July 17-19. Tanglewood, Lenox. 617-266-1200, bso.org

BAROQUE SUMMER The Society for Historically Informed Performance (SoHIP) is winding up its summer season, while Aston Magna Music is just getting started. For its final concert of 2026, SoHIP presents the four-person Berry Collective, led by fortepianist Sylvia Berry, in a program of music from the final four decades of the 18th century. Aston Magna kicks off with an all-French program of sonatas and cantatas this weekend, and next week brings an assortment of Bach and Telemann. Aston Magna: July 16 and 23, Slosberg Music Center, Brandeis University, Waltham; July 18 and 25, Saint James Place, 352 Main St., Great Barrington. 888-492-1283, astonmagna.org; SoHIP: July 21, St. Anne’s-in-the-Fields, 147 Concord Road, Lincoln; July 22, The Chapel at West Parish, 210 Lowell St., Andover; July 23, Emmanuel Church, 15 Newbury St. sohipboston.org

BOSTON LANDMARKS ORCHESTRA Boston’s outdoor orchestra launches its summer season at the Hatch Shell with a “Best of Boston” program celebrating the city’s musical heritage. Dances from “West Side Story” by Bernstein, a symphony by William Grant Still, several miniatures by Leroy Anderson, and more. As always, it’s free. July 22, 7 p.m. DCR Hatch Memorial Shell, 47 David G. Mugar Way. landmarksorchestra.org

A HOT ROMANCE ABOUT SECOND CHANCES Julie Murphy’s latest novel, “Vera Stein Is Fine‚" is set at Starlight Palms, a retirement community favored by aging actors. Vera, age 40, goes there seeking comfort from her grandmother and a respite from her life’s disappointments; she finds far more than she bargained for, including senior citizens acting out sexually, and the inconvenient reappearance of one of her own lost loves. Murphy reads Monday at First Parish in Cambridge via Lovestruck Books & Cafe. July 20, 7 p.m. Tickets are $6.24, $37.74 with copy of the book. First Parish, 3 Church St., Cambridge. lovestruckbooks.com

BOTH SIDES OF THE LINE: CARMEN HERRERA & LEON POLK SMITH Closing soon: Friends, neighbors, and collaborators, Herrera and Smith, masters of crisp hard-edged abstraction, never quite got the recognition in life that they’re garnering posthumously. (Herrera, all but unnoticed much of her career, was a late life “discovery” for the cognoscenti. She enjoyed her first major museum show at the Whitney Museum of American Art in 2016, when she was 101.) This show puts them together for the first time, and conjures a little of the deserved glory that eluded them while they were alive. Through July 31. Addison Gallery of American Art at Phillips Academy, 3 Chapel Ave., Andover. 978-749-4015, addison.andover.edu

CELTIC ART ACROSS THE AGES Closing soon: Spanning almost three millennia, 800 BCE right up till now, this show takes a liberal approach to art made by Celtic people and their vast diaspora through the ages, stretching from Northern Europe to every corner of the globe. From the Iron Age through the Roman Empire to today, it attempts to weave connection across eras to both reveal lineage and unwind cliche. Through Aug. 2. Harvard Art Museums, 32 Quincy St., Cambridge. 617-495-9400, harvardartmuseums.org

YINKA SHONIBARE: SANCTUARY Shonibare, a celebrated British-Nigerian artist known for his heady formal engagements with the messy, often brutal entanglements of colonial history, debuted a new installation in the US with “Sanctuary City,” a suite of 18 tabletop architectural models of buildings with known histories as refuges for the vulnerable and persecuted. With inequity always buzzing in the background of the post-colonial world, the piece would never not be relevant; in the current roar of the American mass-deportation experience, it’s more resonant here and now than ever. title: Driver in fatal cyclist crash maneuvered around another vehicle
text:
She also promised a “full analysis” of the street design in the area of the fatal crash and beyond.

“I can’t stop thinking about Louisa. We owe Louisa more than our grief. We owe her action. We have to do better,” a tearful Wu told a crowd of cycling advocates who had gathered for a vigil outside City Hall Thursday evening. “And while I know the purpose of tonight is to focus on celebrating her life, I want you also to know that the city is taking action.”

Police have said little about the incident beyond that it remains under investigation. But the details newly disclosed on Thursday bring further clarity to a crash that has led to an intense debate over whether better safety protocols could have prevented it.

The two people who shared details about the fatal crash spoke on the condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak about the case.

The driver of the truck has not been identified and has not been charged with any crime. The new details do not indicate whether there was any wrongdoing. The driver stopped the truck near Tremont’s intersection with Melnea Cass Boulevard. Police spoke with the driver at that time.

The truck is owned by Allied Recycling and that morning had departed a demolition site at One Joslin Place, where a major hospital project in Boston’s Longwood area is underway.

In a statement, Allied Recycling confirmed its truck was involved and said the company is working with police “to determine what happened.” The company said it has turned over all information requested by authorities.

“We were deeply upset to learn of her death and mourn with the rest of the community,” a spokesperson said in a statement.

In response to a request to identify the driver, the spokesperson said: “While we are still trying to better understand the accident, the driver involved is one of our best — an experienced and responsible driver. Safety is of the utmost importance to our company and we continue to work closely with authorities."

Crash investigations often take months to resolve.

A lawyer for Gag’s family declined to comment on their behalf.

The death of Gag has triggered an outpouring of grief and anger from Boston’s cycling community. A popular evangelist for cycling, she worked as a bike-share and transportation planner for the city.

Gag, 36, grew up in Roslindale, graduated from Boston Latin School, and earned degrees at the University of Rochester and Tufts University. She “worked tirelessly to improve the city she loved, devoting herself to making it more livable, enjoyable, and humane,” according to her obituary.

Advocates and her City Hall co-workers — including Wu, for whom she was an intern years ago when Wu was a city councilor — remembered Gag as a kind, consistent, and committed friend.

At the vigil Thursday, friends and colleagues shared memories of Gag and her dedication to making Boston streets safer for cyclists and pedestrians. After a moment of silence, the talk at the vigil turned to action.

“I’m sad and I’m frustrated, but we aren’t helpless,” said Brendan Kearney, executive director of WalkMassachusetts and a part of the Massachusetts Vision Zero Coalition. “Look around here, we’re all connected to one person, from one crash. We’re going to make a difference and we’re going to keep showing up.”

Her death also put a harsh spotlight on Wu’s handling of street safety improvements, and led to criticism the city delayed many street infrastructure projects over the past year and a half, including some near the site of the crash.

Wu’s office said in a statement Thursday that, “We owe it to Louisa, her loved ones, and everyone who uses our streets to ensure a thorough, transparent investigation that establishes the facts and provides a clear understanding of exactly what happened. The City will continue working closely with the Boston Police Department and the District Attorney to support the investigation.”

The crash occurred near the office of Boston’s Cyclist Union, and members have said they’ve repeatedly raised safety concerns about cycling on Tremont Street.

That section of Tremont in Mission Hill is a tight, two-lane road running between two busy interchanges, Brigham Circle at one end and and Roxbury Crossing at the other. It has a painted bike lane delineated at times by solid lines and others by dashes. There are bus stops nearby and spots for cars to park.

The intersection of Tremont and Parker streets, where the crash occurred, was part of an area the city identified in 2023 as needing improvements. But the project does not appear to have advanced since then, and is on a list of those that advocates say were paused, or not updated by the city for more than a year.

Wu has said street safety remains a priority for her administration, and emphasized that work on many such infrastructure projects is ongoing. Wu’s office said last week the location of the crash was not covered under the Parker Street-area planning process and that there never were plans for a protected bike lane there.

At the vigil for Gag Thursday, Wu said she would assign two senior officials to the Streets Cabinet “to accelerate the policies, planning, and capital delivery work that will make our streets safer.”

The crowd of at least 200 had gathered at City Hall after riding bikes from the site of Gag’s death. They also delivered a blistering open letter to Wu demanding she take a series of actions to address street safety issues.

Titled “Enough is Enough,” the letter emphasizes that the majority of the signatures, tallying 4,000, are from Boston parents and residents who have pleaded with Wu for safety improvements for years.

Niki Griswold of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Man charged with shooting at Boston police officers had pending warrant for assault, records show
text:
The man who allegedly fired at police officers in Dorchester on Wednesday was wanted for an assault with a dangerous weapon and was recently declared mentally incompetent in another criminal case, records show.

Rasiel J. Carbuccia, 20, allegedly opened fire with a ghost gun at two officers near the intersection of Devon and Laredo streets around 9:11 p.m., police said Thursday.

Carbuccia was arraigned Thursday in Dorchester Municipal Court on multiple charges, including two counts of assault with a dangerous weapon, possession of a ghost gun, and illegal possession of firearms, records show. Not guilty pleas were entered on his behalf.

He was ordered held by Judge Thomas S. Kaplanes pending a dangerousness hearing set for July 28, records show.

In a statement Thursday, Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox praised the officers “for the immense bravery and professionalism they displayed.”

“This incident serves as a stark reminder of the dangers our officers face every day to protect this community,” Cox said.

The windshield of a marked police cruiser sustained ballistic damage, police said. Police later recovered a handgun with a spent shell casing jammed in the chamber, officials said. It had an extended magazine with 16 rounds. Police also recovered a bullet in the middle of the street where the incident originated, according to a police report.

After officers attempted to conduct a “subject stop,” near Devon and Laredo Streets, Carbuccia, of Jamaica Plain, allegedly opened fire and ran from the officers, leading to a foot chase over fences and through backyards that ended on Stanwood Street, the report stated.

Carbuccia was taken into custody. The ghost gun, a homemade weapon that does not have a serial number, was recovered on Devon Street, police said.

Two of the officers Carbuccia allegedly fired at were not physically injured but were taken to a Boston hospital for observation, police said.

“We are profoundly grateful that both officers escaped physical injury and were able to return home safely to their families at the end of their shift,” Cox said.

On July 6, a warrant was issued for Carbuccia’s arrest in Roxbury Municipal Court, where he was charged with one count of assault with a dangerous weapon. The warrant was still active on Wednesday night, records show.

According to court records, the state Department of Mental Health sought court permission in 2024 to treat Carbuccia with seven antipsychotic drugs without his permission. He was 17 and being treated at Boston Children’s Hospital on an in-patient basis, records show.

A judge agreed and his mother, Rosalba Carbuccia, was appointed as his guardian. She was tasked with ensuring her son was compliant with medication protocols, records show.

The order was extended in May 2025 after Carbuccia was examined by a doctor who recommended changes in his medication regimen, records show.

The mental health department stopped providing services in April 2025, according to court records, which provided no explanation for the termination.

Carbuccia was also facing a larceny case in East Boston from August and an assault and battery charge in Boston Municipal Court filed in November, records show.

Since being charged in both cases, Carbuccia was either being held on bail at the Nashua Street Jail or undergoing mental health care at the Solomon Carter Fuller Mental Health Center, according to court records.

In the East Boston case, he was found incompetent to stand trial in February and Suffolk District Attorney Kevin R. Hayden’s office eventually dropped the case, records show.

The second case is still pending. Carbuccia was released on personal recognizance on June 9, records show. His bail was revoked Thursday following the Dorchester arrest, records show.

Details of those incidents were not immediately available Thursday.

Nick Stoico of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Amid a fresh wave of young soccer fans, Boston-area programs meet demand with accessibility
text:
All of the city’s youth soccer programs, including the intramural soccer, street soccer, and free Soccer Without Borders program, have seen a boost in participation, he said.

“A super majority of these kids are not affiliated with any of our soccer organizations, and so this is really the first time they’re playing soccer,” Giuffrida said.

Chelsea’s not the only city riding the hype. Across New England, cities and towns are finding ways to capitalize on the energy the quadrennial World Cup has brought to North America. Some have worked to turn abandoned lots and unused public spaces to create vibrant hard-court pitches to attract new people to the sport and give current footballers space to play. Others are working to make the game cheaper — and in some cases free — for any kid who wants to play.

In Boston, parks and recreation director Mike Devlin said the World Cup has created an opportunity to introduce more kids to the game, and to “invest in quality playing fields, free and affordable recreation programs, and partnerships with local organizations that help remove barriers to participation so every child has the opportunity to play.”

From free seasonal soccer clinics to tournaments and leagues, Boston has a lengthy list of inclusive soccer programming for the city’s youth. Such programs are key to increasing access to the game, especially as the cost gap between city recreational programs and private soccer clubs widens.

A 2022 study by Project Play, a coalition that studies opportunity gaps in youth sports, found that parents spend an average of $1,188 annually on youth soccer programming — placing it among the most expensive youth sports to play in the United States. It has created a large access barrier for those who can’t afford to cough up that kind of cash.

Unlike the government-funded youth soccer clubs found in other countries, the US is dominated by a private pay-to-play model. That means parents tend to pay hundreds and sometimes thousands of dollars a year for their kids to travel and compete.

Anthony Rougier, founder of the Anthony Rougier Sport Foundation, knows better than most how much costs can hinder soccer talent in the United States. Before coming to Boston, Rougier, a native of Trinidad and Tobago, played professional soccer for over 20 years.

“With me coming to the US and getting into coaching, it was very strange for me,” Rougier said. “Even though I played professionally in England, China, and the US ... the pay-to-play model is such a harsh [model]. It’s difficult.”

That reality really struck in 2020 when coaching for the New England Football Club. The mother of one of his players couldn’t keep up with costs, putting her son at risk of leaving the team.

Seeing the passion in the player, and recognizing the opportunity that a successful soccer career could bring, Rougier covered the costs. Then, he founded the Anthony Rougier Foundation, a nonprofit that helps pay for young players while providing expert training to those aspiring to compete at a high level.

With the World Cup’s arrival, he said, more players are looking to compete. So now, Rougier is looking for more support and cohesion within the city’s soccer ecosystem, which would ensure the door remains open for soccer players trying to change their lives through their talents.

“We need to collaborate, so we can do more — not just for participation, but for everybody, to give everybody a chance," Rougier said. “Because that situation or circumstances will change a family’s life.”

Caroline Foscato is also working to help young players through the Soccer Unity Project, a nonprofit that serves over 1,500 Boston youth a year through free soccer programs, ranging from peewee clinics to travel teams. Through those programs, SUP scratches an itch that some parts of the city are still trying to reach.

But limited access means increased demand, and Foscato’s team has struggled to keep pace. Even with partnerships from the city of Boston, the Mayor’s office, Massachusetts Youth Soccer and Parks and Recreation, the problem still lingers.

“For the programming we’ve done on fields in Roxbury and South End, for a couple decades now, people they just keep coming, and we cannot serve everybody that’s coming,” Foscato said.

To remedy the issue, SUP is working to secure more corporate and philanthropic “sustainable partners” to invest in more quality, inclusivity-driven programs that support new players.

In Chelsea, Giuffrida has already begun to reel in some of that support, with local businesses expressing interest in funding the city’s soccer programs. With new money flowing in — and with more names on soccer sign-up sheets — his goal is to sustain that momentum well after the next World Cup champion is crowned.

“Having a vibrant town soccer program that is well tended to is critical to a player, it’s really community building and developing these kids,” Giuffrida said, championing accessible recreational programs. “To make sure [parents] at least have the option to put their kid in an affordable sports program or an affordable soccer program, I view that as one of the most primary responsibilities of government right now.”

title: MassHousing executive resigns after Spotlight investigation finds apparent fraud, ethics lapse at program he led
text:
The Globe found that the two developers who received the $1.4 million in grants — more than half the money given out in the program — had submitted fake invoices to MassHousing. At least nine subcontractors told the Globe they did not do the work the developers attributed to them nor were paid by them.

The developers, Gary Acquah and Reginald Woods, also had a connection to Richards that was not disclosed at the time Richards doled out the money. Just months before he approved the grants in 2023, Richards purchased a West Roxbury home from the developers for $785,000 — which was $204,000 less than the original asking price. Richards’s failure to disclose that relationship likely violated state ethics laws.

MassHousing officials told the Globe Richards had informed them of the connection about one year after the grants were awarded, after agency employees started to notice problems at the buildings Acquah and Woods were supposed to be renovating.

Colin McNiece, a lawyer for the agency, said he decided there was no need for Richards to file a written disclosure at that point because the money had already been given out. On Friday, an agency spokesman said that at the time, MassHousing consulted with outside counsel who advised there was no mechanism for reporting an ethics disclosure after the fact.

McNiece said that Richards told the agency he had not realized he had given the grants to the same people he bought his house from until late 2024, when he was seeking to get his private mortgage insurance canceled.

But emails from his MassHousing account, obtained by the Globe through a public records request, showed Richards exchanging friendly messages with the developers around the time of the home sale.

After turning over those emails, MassHousing officials announced that they were hiring an outside company, the Mintz law firm of Boston, to audit the Gateway Housing Rehabilitation Program as well as other grant programs under Richards’s purview. In the meantime, they said, Richards would remain in his role, although oversight of grants would be handled by the legal department while the Mintz review was being conducted.

Richards has yet to make any public comment about the matter. Neither he nor his attorney responded to the Globe’s request for comment on Friday.

A MassHousing spokesman said that Richards’s resignation was voluntary and that he did not receive a severance payment.

His resignation came one day after Governor Maura Healey told the Globe “the matter should be fully investigated,” her first public statement on the scandal. Healey had previously declined to comment on the Spotlight Team’s findings, but she spoke briefly as she rushed out of an unrelated event on Beacon Hill.

MassHousing is a quasi-state agency overseen by a board whose members are appointed by the governor, though their terms are staggered. Six of the nine current members of MassHousing’s board are Healey appointees.

Richards joined MassHousing after leaving the Baker administration in 2021. Shortly after taking office, Healey appointed him vice chair of her Advisory Council on Black Empowerment. When asked if Richards should remain in that post, Healey declined to answer directly.

“Look, as I’ve said, this matter should be fully investigated,” Healey said. “Certainly, I’ll take whatever steps are appropriate and necessary. But it should be investigated.”

The firm doing the internal investigation, Mintz, has had a business relationship with the agency for decades. It’s served as bond counsel for the agency for more than 30 years, according to Mintz’s website. McNiece worked at Mintz for 11 years before joining MassHousing in 2019.

The close connections led State Auditor Diana DiZoglio to criticize the agency and call for an independent investigation. DiZoglio said that because the Globe’s reporting raises concerns of “criminal conduct,” her office would defer to any possible civil or criminal investigation before having her auditors launch an inquiry.

title: Over 40 residents evacuated from South End building after fire breaks out
text:
More than 40 residents were evacuated from an apartment building in the South End after a fire broke out on its 20th floor, officials said Friday evening.

Firefighters responded at 5:18 p.m. to a report of a fire at 860 Harrison Ave., the Boston Fire Department said.

A second alarm was immediately sounded, and firefighters began evacuating residents, said Sharon Galloway, the department’s public information officer.

“Not that it was a huge fire, but to evacuate such a high building, it was more manpower,” Galloway said.

The 12-story building shares a main entrance and lobby with a 29-story sister complex at Northampton Street.

Residents were evacuated from the 20th and 21st floors of the building, the department said in a post on X at 6:56 p.m. Three residents were transported to a hospital for smoke inhalation, Galloway said.

She added that MBTA buses held the evacuated residents as firefighters extinguished the fire.

There is water damage to the building after the sprinkler system was activated, Galloway said. Officials have not confirmed how many residents can return to their units.

Three scooter batteries were determined to have caused the fire, which remains under investigation. Hazmat units were deployed to remove the scooters and batteries from the building, as the batteries can sometimes flare up again, Galloway said.

860 Harrison Ave. is an affordable housing development in the historic South End and Lower Roxbury neighborhoods.
