title: Roxbury library branch renamed in honor of Boston’s first black woman TV reporter
text:
As a reporter at WBZ-TV, Shaw covered stories largely ignored by other media outlets. From 1969 to 2000, she reported on issues such as Boston’s school busing crisis, the women’s rights movement, and Dorchester housing hearings.

Shaw was a lifelong resident of Roxbury. She died in 2024 at age of 90.

The Shaw-Roxbury Library was originally named after Thomas Dudley, a 17th-century governor of the Massachusetts Bay Colony whose family has been linked to the slave trade. The name was changed in 2020 to the Roxbury Branch. The request for a third name change originated from a petition from the community in 2025.

“She was a strong advocate for the library and a voice in its previous renovation,” David Leonard, president of the Boston Public Library, said at Saturday’s ceremony. “She could be equally warm and welcoming and connecting, but also would leave you in no uncertain terms about what she expected you to do for the community.”

Shaw’s long-time neighbor, The Rev. Mariama White-Hammond, said that while Shaw was not big on accolades she would feel deeply honored by the library’s name change. It was a place she visited regularly for years.

“The library was far more than the place where she picked up books. She was here all the time,” White-Hammond, pastor and founder of the New Roots AME Church in Dorchester, told the crowd. “She would stop by if she saw you. We would listen to this Walkman, which is not really what you were supposed to be doing in the library. So we were trying to hide it, but she would correct us, lovingly, right?”

Shaw was not only a voracious reader but a long-time activist. After her community organizing years in the ’60s she worked at Action for Boston Community Development, which supports low-income residents in Greater Boston, according to her obituary. She went on to become a contributing host on “Say Brother,” a public affairs program that focused on issues that mattered deeply to Boston’s Black community.

Shaw will be remembered as a reporter who showed compassion, said Catrina Cooley, 60, who watched the ceremony from a camping chair in the crowd.

After Cooley’s parents were struck and killed by a drunken driver in 1982, she recalled, Shaw came to the family home and sat on the couch with shocked and grieving relatives.

“She was very patient with us,” Cooley said. “She was one of the first Black reporters who we knew was going to tell the story, right.”

Wu’s office announced the name change in honor of Shaw in June 2025 after the BPL’s Board of Trustees voted with a vast majority in favor of the decision.

While Shaw “was deeply loved by the community,” some Roxbury residents had supported renaming the branch the Nubian Library to better reflect the surrounding district, and to honor Shaw and other civil rights and community leaders inside the building.

“We have been saying that there should be a wall of honor in the library,” Sadiki Kambon, lead organizer of the Nubian Square Coalition, said in a phone interview Saturday. ”Sarah-Ann’s name should be on there. They could name a room after her but not the entire facility.”

Leonard said trustees discussed the name “Nubian Library” twice.

“In practice, we actually like referring to it now as the Shaw-Roxbury branch of the Boston Public Library at Nubian Square because we think that respects both the service area for the library as all of Roxbury, but also recognizes that geographically we are located in Nubian Square,” he said.

Listening to the community was important to Shaw, White-Hammond said. When there was a community meeting at the library and Shaw happened to be in the building, she would never fail to stop by, she said.

“She’d sit down. She’d listen to what people were debating and talking about,” White-Hammond said.

“I think if we made it just about the moment and the name becomes totally ceremonial, she’d be annoyed,” she added. “But as long as we receive her name on the building and recognize that as an opportunity to continue that legacy, I think she’d be really proud.”

title: ‘Roxbury is love’: Unity Parade celebrates neighborhood pride, community leaders
text:
Mayor Michelle Wu joined Burton in honoring standout community leaders at the award ceremony before greeting recipients and posing for photos. She said the parade fills a long-missing role in celebrating Roxbury and Boston’s Black community.

“We get the chance to celebrate many cultures with festivals and parades in Boston, but this had been one that was missing for a very long time,” Wu said. “For Toy to step up, build a movement, and create a space for all of us to come together every year is really special. It builds momentum for all the work that happens every day in this community.”

Wu said the parade also recognizes the legacy of Roxbury residents who have shaped Boston’s history, including Sarah-Ann Shaw, Boston’s first Black female television reporter. The Shaw-Roxbury Branch Library was officially renamed to honor Shaw on Saturday, an event Wu also attended.

“If you look at every major movement for justice and change, Boston has played a role in that, and someone from Roxbury has always been driving the progress that we have to keep pushing for,” she said.

Wu wasn’t the only elected official at the event. State Representative Chynah Tyler, whose district includes Roxbury, received the Pillar of the Community Award.

“So much work goes into making sure that the legacy of Roxbury continues to live, so to be a part of that and to be able to be honored as a part of that, it means a lot to me,” Tyler said.

Several awards were named after well-known Roxbury residents, such as the Michael L. Bivins Community Hero Award. Bivins, a founding member of New Edition and Bell Biv DeVoe, remains active in the community and personally selected basketball coach and mental health advocate Al McClain for the award.

“I have known Mike [Bivins] since he was 10 years old, so for him to see me as a hero is unbelievable,” said McClain, 66, who works at the Boston Center for Youth and Families Tobin Community Center. “I want the kids in Roxbury today to see this [parade] and take away the love. The camaraderie, the way everyone gets along with one another, pass that on and it’ll make our streets safer.”

As participants lined up to march through Roxbury, McClain said he hoped the parade continues to grow.

“We want the whole of Roxbury to come out. We want these streets to be crowded,” he said.

Residents cheered from their front steps as parade participants walked the route and rode aboard a historic Boston trolley. Dance teams and a majorette group performed throughout the parade, while the Tempo International Rhythm and Steel band filled the streets with Caribbean music from an open-back truck.

City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, whose district includes Roxbury, waved from a car near the end of the procession. He said the parade celebrates the neighborhood’s historic contributions and, more broadly, “the greatness of Black people in the city of Boston.”

“This day is something that I prayed for for years. I always wondered, ‘Why does everyone else have a parade except Roxbury?’ and it felt like there was something missing in our community,” Culpepper said. “When Toy decided to do the Roxbury Unity Parade, I felt like my prayer was answered.”

Beside Culpepper sat Antonia Edwards, a paralegal and member of the city’s reparations task force. Edwards, whose family roots in Roxbury date to 1940, said the parade reflected the neighborhood’s “pride, legacy, heritage.”

“Roxbury is the heartbeat of the Blackness in Boston,” Edwards said.

Culpepper said Roxbury’s strength lies in its diversity, pointing to the neighborhood’s long history of welcoming newcomers.

“If you wonder why Roxbury is so diverse, it’s because whoever comes to Roxbury, we receive them with open arms and love,” he said. “Roxbury has always led the city of Boston in diversity, always.”

Asked what the parade means to the community, Culpepper summed it up in three words: “Roxbury is love.”

title: Man who beat woman, 87, to death in Roxbury in 1991 granted parole from life sentence
text:
A man who was 19 when he fatally beat an 87-year-old woman to death in Roxbury in 1991 has been granted parole from his life sentence, records show.

The state Parole Board on July 16 voted 4-2 to grant release to Dionicio Delvalle, 54, to a halfway house after six months in lower security, according to a ruling.

Delvalle had been convicted of first-degree murder in 2005 for the bludgeoning death of Maude Hinds, the ruling said.

First-degree murder normally carries a life term with no parole, but Delvalle became eligible to seek release after the state’s highest court in 2024 struck down such sentences for defendants aged 18 to 20 at the time of their crimes, records show.

The ruling said Delvalle killed Hinds on April 22, 1991, after she discovered him breaking into her apartment with his brother.

A first-floor tenant of the building discovered Hinds’s body that night in a common hallway, the decision said.

“She had been severely beaten, with injuries to her face and numerous fractures to her ribs and spine,” the ruling said. “A hammer and broken flashlight were found near her body.”

Her second-floor bedroom had been ransacked, and officials recovered fingerprint, blood, and DNA evidence from the crime scene, officials said.

Yet the case remained unsolved for years.

“Nine years later, the Boston Police Department matched fingerprints left on the window to Mr. Delvalle,” the ruling said. “Additionally, Mr. Delvalle’s DNA matched blood found on both the window and on Ms. Hinds’ clothing.”

Authorities said he initially denied involvement in the slaying, blaming the heinous attack on his sibling.

“Mr. Delvalle was interviewed and admitted that he had broken into the apartment building and ‘brushed’ by the victim as he made his escape,” the ruling said. “However, he blamed the murder on his brother.”

The ruling didn’t say what, if anything, had been stolen from the apartment.

In prison, Delvalle has made strides, the ruling said, participating “in programming that addressed his need areas.”

“Mr. Delvalle displayed positive institutional conduct with minimal disciplinary reports,” the ruling said. “Mr. Delvalle has also committed himself to occupational skills training with consistent employment in the metal shop as a welder.”

He is no longer blaming his brother for the murder, the ruling said.

“Mr. Delvalle accepted full responsibility for his actions and displayed insight into his decision making and actions following the offense,” the ruling said.

Officials said he has no diagnosis of mental health or drug issues.

“Mr. Delvalle has also provided employment opportunities upon release,” the ruling said. “The Board concludes that Dionicio Delvalle has demonstrated a level of rehabilitation that would make his release compatible with the welfare of society.”

Once he’s out, Delvalle must abide by several conditions, including staying off drugs and alcohol, submitting to electronic monitoring for the first six months, enrolling in mental health counseling, and having no contact with Hinds’s family, according to the ruling.

Delvalle remained incarcerated Tuesday at MCI-Norfolk, a medium-security facility, according to an online corrections database.

Travis Andersen can be reached at travis.andersen@globe.com.

title: First Literacy awards more than $34k in grants to support adult education across the state
text:
The recipients include nonprofits from Haverhill and Framingham, Roxbury and Worcester; half of them are repeat winners awarded a second year of funding to grow successful pilot programs.

“These pilot programs meet essential needs that are often not fundable through other sources,” said Terry Witherell,the organization’s executive director, in a statement.

Organizations receiving funding for a second year include the Boston Chinatown Neighborhood Center’s AI powered English learning program, Community Action, Inc.’s summer English learning program , Blue Hills Adult Education’s digital literacy intensive, and Salem’s The House of Seven Gables Museum’s career-centered English language learning class.

The organizations were awarded $2,703, $2,449, $3,371, and $2,500, respectively, according to the First Literacy website.

In addition to receiving a second year of funding, The House of the Seven Gables is partnering with Brockton Workers Alliance for its six-week intensive course.

Both organizations received $1,000 through a “Replication Grant” to expand the program and extend its opportunities to varying communities, according to the statement.

The Somali Development Center in Roxbury received the largest grant , totaling $7,140, to support adult immigrant learners, according to First Literacy’s website.

First Literacy said the learners, many of whom are from Afghanistan and Somalia, struggle with reading and writing in English, which limits their ability to succeed in English-language learning classes. The grant will pilot a program to use evidence-based literacy practices, including phonics, in supporting their needs.

Framingham Adult ESL Plus was granted $5,000 to help bridge the gap between the technical skills and English language proficiency of female students working in residential cleaning, according to First Literacy’s website. The seminar will prepare students for topics such as emergency response protocols and navigating client service agreements.

In Worcester, Senior Connection Inc. was awarded $4,500 to pilot a digital literacy and independence workshop for grandparents who serve as their grandchildren’s primary caregivers.

Julie’s Family Learning Program in Boston received $4,800 this year for a two-part pilot program on AI literacy. The pilot will see a mini-launch in summer before a full launch in fall.

“By investing in new approaches to Adult Basic Education, we can help educators address emerging needs, strengthen student outcomes, and remove barriers to learning for more adults,” Witherell said.

In addition to its annual grants, First Literacy provides free professional development workshops for instructors and scholarships for adults.

title: A multi-million dollar complex is being built in Mattapan. Local homeowners ask, why now?
text:
It’s the type of street where everyone knows everyone. The kind of place, older residents say, where you want to raise a family. Where football games are played at the park, and there’s neighborhood trick-or-treating. When Patricia Venter moved here decades ago, she liked that it seemed “nice and quiet.”

But last year, the explosions started. Months of sporadic dynamite blasts, followed by excavators clawing dirt and rock, disturbing the neighborhood and remaking the empty lot at the end of Culbert Street into what will soon become an affordable housing complex of 41 apartments.

Some in the city view the project as a much-needed addition to the housing stock in Boston, which continues to wrestle with an unrelenting housing crisis.

Not so on Culbert Street, where seemingly everyone loathes what’s happening and worries it’ll forever change the dynamic of the little enclave they beat the odds to build. They worry about parking, traffic, and how the size of the project will affect day-to-day life on Culbert.

Here may be a case study in how fraught building new housing can be in a city known for its stubborn resistance to change and well-documented history of racism. Experts say the region needs more housing of every stripe. Yet, there is a push and pull in neighborhoods throughout the region between the need for more housing and the fear of displacement, change, and what it will bring.

Such tension is even more fraught along Blue Hill Avenue, the longtime geographic spine of Black Boston that has for decades suffered from political disinvestment and is now undergoing large-scale change. The city is planning to inject $160 million into the corridor to add a center bus lane, plant more trees, and improve the crosswalks, a controversial plan that the city says will transform the boulevard’s transit infrastructure and revive the commercial corridor.

On Culbert, though, some of those changes are being met with heavy skepticism, with residents feeling as though this large housing project in particular is being foisted upon them, regardless of their objections.

Some residents here were content with the lot at the end of their street remaining empty. Others say they aren’t opposed to development of that space, but it is simply too large a building for their neighborhood. Critics say they’re being asked to shoulder an outsized burden in the city’s efforts to address the housing crisis.

Thousands of housing units have already been added to the corridor in recent years, including the new development under construction at the end of Culbert Street.

City officials acknowledge that the construction process can be hard on the neighbors, but the long-term benefits for those who need affordable housing are too great.

“Transforming a long-vacant site near public transit into 41 affordable homes is a meaningful investment in Mattapan’s future,” said Sheila A. Dillon, the city’s chief of housing.

Residents say the development is proof that the powers that be — developers and city government — are not listening to them.

The complaints are various: Dynamite has driven rats onto their properties, the commotion of heavy machinery has disrupted their day-to-day lives, and the influx of new residents will turn the tiny street into a parking lot.

Dane Fletcher, who grew up on the street and whose parents still live there, feels city authorities have downplayed residents’ concerns.

“Despite our earnest pleas to the city, we were blatantly bulldozed,” he said. “How can the city possibly make right the wrong that was done to the generation of residents that still live here?”

And there’s a wider question the city must contend with: How to develop the housing the city needs responsibly?

***

Patricia Venter and her husband, William, moved to Culbert Street in the early 1970s. At the time, Mattapan was still a predominantly white enclave, but those demographics were starting to shift.

In the 1930s, redlining kept Black residents and other racial and ethnic minorities out of certain neighborhoods, including Mattapan. Though it was outlawed in the late 1960s, discriminatory lending persisted for decades.

Then came the blockbusting. For decades, Mattapan had been predominantly Jewish, until real estate agents stoked fears of racial integration among white homeowners so they could buy their properties for cheap and, in turn, sell them to Black families at higher prices.

Change came rapidly: The neighborhood went from 78 percent white in 1970 to 70 percent Black in 1980.

“Jews sold their homes to unscrupulous speculators for less than market value, while [Blacks], eager to participate in the ‘American Dream,’ were forced to pay inflated prices,” wrote authors Hillel Levine and Lawrence Harmon in their book “The Death of an American Jewish Community.”

Nowadays, more than two-thirds of Mattapan’s residents identify as Black.

It is also a historically marginalized neighborhood. Yet, residents of Culbert Street managed to carve out a middle-class existence for their families.

Venter has fond memories of Culbert Street through the decades: birthday parties for her three boys and sports at the park. She understands that things change, she said, pointing out that two nearby churches used to be a grocery mart and a funeral home. But how that change is undertaken matters, she said.

“We were not given the proper consideration,” Venter said. “That’s a big project. I don’t think the humanitarian element was addressed properly.”

City officials acknowledge the challenges posed by construction in residential neighborhoods. But they also say the final project is a result of listening to community concerns about size and density: They reduced the scale from 48 to 41 units, added parking spaces, and created a special loading zone for delivery drivers.

And the units will be for working-class families, the city said, with units available for households making 30 to 60 percent of the area median income, or $49,000 to $97,000 for a family of four. Five other units are set aside for local homeless families.

“These new apartments, including one-, two-, and three-bedroom homes, will be within reach for Boston families who might otherwise spend more than half their income on housing, including residents transitioning out of homelessness and those working full-time at minimum wage,” Dillon said.

But that’s no comfort to those living through the construction. Esmie James, an 86-year-old retiree who has lived on the street for nearly 50 years, said that during one round of dynamite blasting, her furnace pipe exploded. The blasting is necessary because a prominent rock ledge dominated the site, leading some longtime neighbors to believe development there was impossible.

The months of wintertime blasting, which ended in late February, troubled residents because the neighborhood has a documented issue with natural gas leaks. National Grid reported 16 new leaks within a half-mile radius of the construction site between September 2025 and March 2026.

The city said proper precautions were taken, including a Boston Fire Department detail at each of the blasts and sniff testing for natural gas before and after each explosion.

Despite those safeguards, some residents report recent cracks in their foundations or their floorboards and cabinets becoming separated. They wonder aloud if the explosions caused them.

The company in charge of the blasting at the site, Maine Drilling and Blasting, did not respond to requests for comment. Fire and public safety officials have said that all the blasting that occurred was done within the city’s sound and vibration requirements, and such work is not uncommon in a region with so much ledge.

City officials parry other criticisms of the project, too, saying the plot was vacant and filled with trash before construction. There is a rodent mitigation plan in place, and the tree canopy has been maintained, all while building much-needed affordable housing on the site.

Multiple levels of government have invested in the project. The city has spent more than $2.4 million, while the state has invested $2.6 million, and state and federal tax credits for the initiative total $14.3 million. (Private lender financing tops $28 million, according to the city.)

The developer, Lincoln Avenue Communities, which specializes in affordable housing projects, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. During public hearings last year, developers framed the project as a win-win, saying that, because the lot was vacant, the proposal was “development without displacement.”

***

It’s an undeniable reality that cities change, and Blue Hill Avenue, a 4-mile-long thoroughfare that slices through Mattapan, Dorchester, and Roxbury, is no different. There are housing developments and sizable construction sites up and down the corridor.

Part of that change stems from the Blue Hill Action Plan, in which the city is seeking to sell about 30 small city-owned vacant lots along the corridor to local developers to build housing units, commercial property, or community spaces to revitalize the avenue. Many of the lots sat vacant for decades and had been seized by the city for tax liens.

The city’s Office of Housing says Boston remains committed to the plan, with the city owning 29 parcels along the corridor. Eighteen have designated developers, according to the city.

Between 2015 and 2025, nearly 2,000 housing units were built in the corridor, and the city spent nearly $70 million. It hasn’t been enough. Greater Boston continues to struggle with a housing crisis. Bostonians have relocated from the neighborhoods where they grew up to places well outside of the city.

Data show that Brockton, Randolph, and Avon now have the highest share of Black residents in the state. At the same time, Boston continues to lose Black residents, as more and more are priced out.

“I don’t think the question is if we need housing. We absolutely need more housing,” said Ruth Georges, a local community advocate. “I think it’s how we do that; that is still a question that has yet to be solved in a way that homeowners feel is intentional.”

State Representative Russell Holmes is among the politicians who do not want to see his constituents have to move out of the city. Holmes, a Democrat who lives in Mattapan, emphasizes the need for housing density along the avenue. It’s necessary to make the communities work, he said, to help ensure people can stay in the city if they want, and to support businesses there.

For Holmes, multiple things can be true simultaneously. He is happy with the number of units the Blue Hill Avenue project is adding to the local housing stock, but is critical of the way the proposal was “slammed onto the community.” The developers, he said, were not attentive to the neighbors’ needs. Most concerning for residents, he said, was the noise from the construction, as well as the construction vehicles associated with it. More conversation with neighbors, he said, could have smoothed over some of those issues.

Not all housing projects along the avenue have been met with stiff local resistance. If some residents point to the project at the end of Culbert as a case study in how not to effectively engage with stakeholders, there is another project that locals cite as a welcome addition to the neighborhood.

About a mile north of Culbert Street and the 1471 Blue Hill Ave. project on the corner, three buildings are currently under construction. They will house 30 condominiums to be sold at below-market rateS. (The project includes six parking spaces.) There’s also commercial space in each of the buildings, and during the planning process, community members heard pitches from various businesses, all of which were incentivized to have some sort of roots in Boston. Mattapan residents were able to recommend the ones they liked best.

During the permitting process, the developer, DVM Housing Partners, worked with a neighbor to grant them official access to a slice of land they had been using as a driveway for years, but was actually within the property lines of the redevelopment proposal.

In October, DVM also threw a block party and invited residents to celebrate the project.

For Neldine Torres, a nurse practitioner who serves on the board of the Greater Mattapan Neighborhood Council, that project exemplified responsible development.

“Any development project should probably take notes in terms of knowing how to engage with the community and listen,” she said.

The president and founder of DVM, Dariela Villon-Maga, knows the avenue well. She grew up in Grove Hall, currently lives in Mattapan, and has an office near Roxbury’s Nubian Square.

She explains the paradox of development in Boston’s Black and brown communities: After decades of disinvestment, investment can be viewed skeptically, particularly if it comes from a developer with no roots in the city. (Lincoln Avenue Communities lists four office locations on its website; none are in New England.)

People ask, “Who is this for?” she said. There are fears of gentrification and displacement.

Of course, people want nice amenities and housing in their neighborhoods, but there is also a level of paranoia that is justified, she said.

“External investment makes longtime residents ask, ‘What’s coming next?’” she said. “There’s a fear of ‘why now?’”

Back on Culbert Street, that fear has morphed into outrage.

David Venter has become the face of the opposition to the project, emailing city officials and developers, speaking out at public hearings, and penning a letter to the editor in The Dorchester Reporter.

Venter recently bought the house he grew up in from his mother so that she can live out her days there. He fears that the new apartments at the end of the block will undermine the feel of community that has developed over the decades.

“It really is a village,” he said.

He rejects the notion that the local opposition is grounded in NIMBYism. For him, the project is adding insult to historical injury. Decades of institutional racism shaped the neighborhood: redlining prevented Black people from moving there, blockbusting meant they had to pay a premium to buy there, and disinvestment kept home values low.

“You didn’t want us,” said Venter, who works in communications for a nonprofit home health care company. “You wouldn’t give us any loans for our houses. We had to do it on our own. We were self-sufficient.”

He paused. “Now this.”

title: Too many candidates are dodging the debate stage
text:
That is part of the work we have launched at Endicott College’s Center for Civic Participation. We inspire students to research an issue, argue it, hear the rebuttal, and productively engage people who see the world differently. These habits will produce citizens of character — and future candidates — who will welcome the stage rather than avoid it.

Having served in the White House under presidents of both parties, I have learned that a healthy democracy depends less on agreement than on the courage to show up and be questioned.

If we want leaders who debate, then we must raise citizens who can.

Jason J. Galui

Director

Endicott Center for Civic Participation

Beverly

I manage Republican Elizabeth Dionne’s campaign for Massachusetts state treasurer. I wanted to reach out after reading the Globe editorial on the importance of candidates participating in debates. We appreciated the position the editorial board took, and I thought readers should know what’s happening in the treasurer’s race.

In May our campaign sent Treasurer Deb Goldberg three separate letters asking for six in-person debates across Massachusetts. We have not received a response to any of them.

What makes that especially disappointing is that Goldberg’s office told Michael P. Norton with State House News, “The treasurer will review all invitations for debates by reputable news organizations interested in hosting.” To this point, though, there has been no indication that she’s willing to debate.

Your editorial made the point that voters deserve the chance to see candidates tested in public and to hear directly from them instead of relying on ads or social media. We couldn’t agree more. The treasurer’s office is responsible for managing billions of taxpayer dollars and plays a significant role in the financial health of the Commonwealth. Massachusetts voters deserve the opportunity to hear from both candidates before they cast their ballots.

Our candidate has made it clear from day one that she’ll debate any time, anywhere. We hope you’ll continue encouraging all statewide candidates, including the incumbent treasurer, to participate in the public discussions voters deserve.

Alex Hagerty

Belmont

I applaud your editorial “If candidates won’t debate, voters should wonder why not” for calling out GOP gubernatorial candidate Mike Minogue and incumbent US Representatives Jake Auchincloss and Stephen Lynch for not debating their primary challengers. I am wondering why my Democratic incumbent state Senator Mike Rush, who represents the Norfolk and Suffolk District, including Dedham, Norwood, Walpole, Westwood, and portions of Boston, is choosing not to debate his Democratic challenger, Persis Yu. Elected office holders have a civic responsibility to show up for debates, not just for scripted stump speeches, so that voters can make informed choices and hold them accountable.

Voters would also benefit from more in-depth media coverage of state legislative races, not just congressional and statewide offices. Major news outlets such as the Globe should put more resources toward educating voters about these elections that affect our state budget and policy priorities.

Roy Lincoln Karp

West Roxbury

title: After rebuke of last nominee, Healey floats another former prosecutor for Parole Board
text:
The Governor’s Council, the elected panel that must vote on her nomination, scheduled a hearing to question O’Leary for Aug. 12. O’Leary was not available Wednesday for an interview, Healey’s office said.

By nominating another former prosecutor, Healey signaled she remains committed to adding that perspective to the Parole Board after the Governor’s Council in May rejected her last nominee, Vincent J. DeMore III, a former Suffolk County assistant district attorney turned defense lawyer.

Healey wants the seven-person board to include a lawyer who has handled complex criminal cases and worked with victims — experience she says is missing from the panel, her office said Wednesday.

In a statement, Healey praised O’Leary for dedicating her career to state government service and public safety.

“As both a leader at the Parole Board and a former prosecutor, she understands the importance of making thoughtful, fair decisions that protect public safety while supporting successful reentry,” Healey said. “I know she’ll be a tremendous asset to the Board.”

O’Leary’s nomination must be approved by the Governor’s Council, a relatively obscure group of elected officials who represent eight districts from across the state.

The body rejected DeMore’s nomination by a 4-3 vote after some council members said they wanted a candidate with more experience evaluating prisoners’ fitness for integrating back into society.

Some criminal justice reform advocates also argued that adding DeMore would give the Parole Board a majority of members with a law enforcement background, given three others previously worked in probation and parole services. One councilor, Eunice D. Zeigler, didn’t attend the meeting when the vote was taken.

About a week before the vote on DeMore, a parolee allegedly shot and wounded motorists on Memorial Drive in Cambridge, generating fresh scrutiny of the Parole Board. But the incident didn’t shift opinions enough among councilors to secure his nomination.

On Wednesday, two opponents of DeMore’s nomination criticized Healey for tapping another former prosecutor.

“Why is Governor Healey doing this? Why does she think it’s OK to put a former DA on the board?” asked Stacey Borden, founder of New Beginnings Reentry Services in Roxbury and a former Governor’s Council candidate.

Borden said she prefers a nominee with a background in psychology or social work, or a person who was previously incarcerated.

“Maura Healey is not hearing the community,” she said.

Olivia Dubois, a social worker with a background working with public defenders, said she was also disappointed with Healey’s nomination.

“The Governor’s Council made it pretty clear they wanted a Parole Board member who had a deep understanding of reentry, mental health, substance abuse, and trauma,” she said.

A former prosecutor hasn’t served on the Parole Board since 2022 when Gloriann Moroney — who had been nominated to the board by Healey’s Republican predecessor, Charlie Baker — resigned to become a District Court judge. If confirmed, O’Leary would fill a vacancy left by Tonomey Coleman, who was nominated last year by Healey, and approved by the Governor’s Council, for a District Court judgeship.

O’Leary on Wednesday drew praise from others, including Julie J. Bernard, chief executive of the Flaschner Judicial Institute, who said O’Leary in 2014 helped to establish a drug court in Brockton District Court.

O’Leary was open to alternatives in incarceration and sentencing, said Bernard, who was the presiding justice in Brockton District Court when she met O’Leary.

“She’s fair-minded, reasonable, and I think she’d be an excellent choice for the Parole Board,” Bernard said Wednesday.

Criminal defense lawyer Michael A. Bergeron said O’Leary has a “unique ability to listen and look at the other side’s perspective and evaluate what was appropriate for each defendant.”

“She is more than qualified to make reasonable and fair parole decisions,” said Bergeron, a former supervising attorney for Pilgrim Advocates, Inc., a nonprofit organization that provides lawyers to indigent defendants.

Robert Sheketoff, a criminal defense attorney who has faced O’Leary in court, said she is smart, detail-oriented, and was attuned to his clients’ circumstances.

The Parole Board holds thousands of hearings annually, mostly in state prisons and county jails, and parole officers supervised nearly 3,000 people in 2024, according to data released by the panel in May.

Four people have joined the Parole Board under Healey, with three getting unanimous votes: Rafael Ortiz and Edith J. Alexander, both former probation officers; and Sarah B. Coughlin, a licensed clinical social worker.

The fourth, Angelo Gomez Jr., a former parole supervisor, was confirmed on a 6-1 vote. He took charge as chairperson of the board in October.

Healey also renominated Charlene Bonner, a forensic psychologist who joined the board in 2011 and was confirmed for a fourth term in 2023. Her credentials satisfy a state requirement adopted by the Legislature in 2014 that the board have at least one member with “experience in forensic psychology.”

title: Massachusetts Democrats are hitting the trail — and the road
text:
Pressley traveled last weekend to Tennessee to campaign alongside Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez for Justin Pearson, a Democratic state representative and one of the “Tennessee Three" who is running for the state’s open 9th Congressional District.

Warren has already been to Illinois to rally for Lieutenant Governor Juliana Stratton (now the state’s Democratic Senate nominee) and Evanston Mayor Daniel Biss, who topped the primary field in Illinois’s 9th Congressional District primary. She also stopped in New York City to campaign with Brad Lander in his successful bid to unseat Representative Dan Goldman. And she traveled to Maine during the spring to rally with Graham Platner before the end of his ill-fated Senate campaign.

Now, she’s heading west to stump for two Senate hopefuls. The Cambridge Democrat is headlining a rally in Minnesota on Friday with Peggy Flanagan, the state’s lieutenant governor, as she competes for the Democratic Senate nomination there against US Representative Angie Craig.

A Warren spokesperson said she’ll also hit the trail this weekend for Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Senate hopeful whom she endorsed Monday after her preferred pick, Michigan state Senator Mallory McMorrow, ended her campaign earlier this month. Next month, Warren is off to North Carolina to headline the state party’s “Unity Dinner” and campaign for Roy Cooper, the governor and US Senate hopeful.

Trahan has hit some of the country’s most competitive districts, campaigning in battleground districts for incumbents such as Ohio Representative Greg Landsman and Representative Kathy Castor in Florida. Trahan, the co-chair of the House Democratic Policy and Communications Committee, also helped fundraise for candidates in districts Democrats are looking to flip (Rebecca Cooke in Wisconsin and Bobby Pulido in Texas) and hold (Representative Susie Lee in Nevada).

Why log the miles putting their political clout on the line? Helping elect other Democrats can help members in safe-seats boost their credibility and branding beyond their districts. And many of the candidates they’re assisting are ideologically aligned, building up the bench of like-minded members with whom they can work.

Not that they aren’t lending a hand to some of their colleagues at home. Warren and Pressley both recently appeared in an ad for Senator Ed Markey as he tries to fend off a primary challenge from Representative Seth Moulton.

Representative Jim McGovern appears ready to cruise to reelection with no challengers, Democrat or Republican. But the rest of the Democrats’ delegation mates have their own races. Representatives Jake Auchincloss, Katherine Clark, Richard Neal, Bill Keating, and Stephen Lynch are all facing primary challenges from the left this year.

And none of the delegation’s current members have yet weighed in on the state’s only open congressional race in the Sixth District, where six Democrats are vying to replace Moulton.

SIGN NOT OF THE TIMES: Spotted at Rachael Rollins’s campaign headquarters in Roxbury: a campaign sign touting an endorsement from the Boston Globe’s editorial board, per a photo obtained by the Globe.

There’s just one catch: The Globe’s editorial board hasn’t endorsed in the Suffolk County district attorney’s race this cycle.

The sign, posted in a prominent spot above the front window of Rollins’s Centre Street campaign office, includes a quote from the newspaper’s 2018 endorsement, which described the then-political newcomer as “the best choice” in the five-person primary.

A spokesperson for Rollins’s campaign said in a statement that the team was “proud” of the 2018 endorsement, and that while Rollins has since updated the logo for her new campaign, “we love the vintage signs at our headquarters.”

Rollins, who resigned from her subsequent job as US attorney amid scandal three years ago, is now vying for the office against incumbentKevin Hayden and another challenger,Linda Champion.

“It’s an old sign, and we’re having new ones made,” the spokesperson said.

COMING SOON TO YOUR SCREENS: Patrick Roath, the Jamaica Plain attorney challenging Lynch in the Eighth District, is the latest congressional candidate to hit the airwaves.

Roath rolled out his first TV ad Wednesday, a 30-second spot that features footage of him from around the district, which stretches from South Boston to Easton.

“This moment requires urgency, and a conviction that we can actually change things,” Roath says in the ad. Lynch, who has been in office for more than two decades, is “not a bad guy,” Roath adds. “But he’s not the leader we need right now.”

Roath’s campaign declined to say how much money it’s putting behind the spot beyond describing it as a “six-figure” buy. The ad will run on broadcast and digital platforms.

LIT DROP: Roath’s campaign is also getting a hand from Leaders We Deserve, the PAC created by gun control activist David Hogg that helps challengers taking on sitting Democrats.

Mailers from the group, which endorsed Roath earlier this year, hit voters’ mailboxes this week labeling Lynch “MAGA’s favorite Democrat,” pointing to a vote he took (along with 74 other Democrats) to thank Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers, along with other law enforcement officials, as part of a 2025 resolution.

It’s a similar line of attack a pro-Markey super PAC has waged against Moulton, whose campaign framed the resolution as “broad” and the criticism over the vote as “misleading.”

Roath has regularly pitched himself as a more forceful foe to President Trump than Lynch, who is among the delegation’s most moderate members (but also an oft-critic of Trump, too).

NUMBERS GAME: The order of the record-tying nine(!) ballot questions Massachusetts voters will weigh this fall are officially set after a last-ditch effort to strike a proposal that would repeal the law that legalized recreational marijuana failed Tuesday.

The questions run the gamut:

Question 1: Expanding the public records law;

Question 2: Giving collective bargaining rights to Committee for Public Counsel Services employees;

Question 3: Overhauling the state’s primary elections system;

Question 4: Instituting Election Day voter registration;

title: ‘Should I just close everything?’: Why a restaurant owner’s tearful video went viral
text:
“What is all of this for?” he said, crying in the video. “You’re hoping that everything works out. Your hopes and dreams and all your sacrifices now will pay off.”

Pham and his wife, Yeanie Bach, originally an IT specialist and photographer, opened their first restaurant, Banh Mi Oi, in West Roxbury in July 2020. Since then, the two have opened a second Banh Mi Oi in Waltham, Greenhaus Cafe in Roxbury Crossing, Phinista Cafe in Fenway, Vang Coffee Bar in Quincy, and Yeanie’s Burgers and Social in Dorchester. They are hoping to open a second Yeanie’s in West Roxbury in the coming weeks.

Pham posted the video as a “PSA” to anyone looking to become a small business owner. “The entire company is literally on your shoulders,” he said in an interview with Boston.com. “Some days it gets really messy and it gets really heavy. There is no work-life balance.”

He never expected the video to go viral and receive an “insane” response in the comments — more than 4,000 on Instagram — and in his DMs, he said.

The video was “probably one of the lowest points of my life [and it] became one of the most heartfelt moments I’ve ever had,” he said in a follow-up video on July 17, thanking everyone for their words of support.

Pham believes the video resonated with so many people because they face similar struggles as business owners: paying off debt, supporting staff members, managing equipment issues, and ensuring customer satisfaction all while trying to invest back into the community.

The food industry is a particularly “hard” industry right now, Pham said. “There’s this really weird shift [in] mindset where food can’t be more expensive because people are making less money,” but then restaurants lose profits and risk potential closure.

In the video, Pham also shared that his main struggle is living 500 miles away from his wife and daughter and only getting to see them for one week every month. Pham lives in West Roxbury, but his wife moved to the D.C.-area so their daughter can grow up closer to family.

“I’m sacrificing being with my wife and daughter on my birthday. They’re 500 miles away,” he said in the video. “But I need to put the business first. I need to be here to make sure we are supporting the team.”

“Every time I come back to my daughter or I talk to her on FaceTime, she’s different. … Her hair’s a little bit longer, her face is different,” Pham said in the second video.

Although he continues to be apart from his family, Pham said he isn’t sure the sacrifice is “worth it yet.” He continued, “The only thing that keeps me going right now is the difference that we’re making in our neighborhood[s].”

title: Attorney general is probing MassHousing grant program highlighted in Spotlight investigation
text:
In late June, the Spotlight Team showed that MassHousing had awarded $1.4 million to two developers who submitted invoices bearing the names of at least nine subcontractors who later told the Globe they did not do the work attributed to them. The apparent fraud, for which developers Gary Acquah and Reginald Woods were paid more than half a million dollars, left the multi-unit buildings in Pittsfield and Worcester they were supposed to be fixing up in poor condition.

Acquah and Woods had a secret connection to Tony Richards II, the MassHousing executive who awarded them the money. Months earlier, he purchased a home in West Roxbury from the same developers for $204,000 less than the original asking price. Richards did not disclose the connection at the time, a likely violation of Massachusetts ethics laws.

When the Globe brought the matter to light last month, the agency paused Richards’s authority to disburse grant money and launched an internal review of grant programs he oversaw, though he remained on the payroll.

Last week, Richards voluntarily resigned from MassHousing and from his seat on one of Governor Maura Healey’s advisory councils. Neither he nor his attorney has responded to the Globe’s repeated requests for comment.

Healey, who appoints the members of the board that oversees the quasi-state agency, declined to comment on the scandal at first. When a reporter approached her three weeks later at a public event, she said the matter should be “fully investigated.”

For its internal review of programs under Richards, MassHousing tapped the Mintz law firm, which has done legal work for the agency for decades. The agency’s top legal officer, Colin McNiece, worked at Mintz for 11 years before joining MassHousing.

Last month, McNiece told the Globe that when Richards finally told his bosses about his relationship with Acquah and Woods, more than a year after giving them the grants, McNiece determined that there was no need to file a written disclosure because the matter was “basically moot.”

That decision was criticized by some ethics experts, who said a late disclosure would have been preferable to none at all.

A MassHousing spokesperson told the Globe last week that McNiece arrived at his opinion after he consulted with outside counsel for the agency. The spokesperson declined to comment about whether Mintz or some other firm offered that advice.

In part because of the close relationship between MassHousing and Mintz, State Auditor Diana DiZoglio has called for an independent government investigation. Earlier, she said her office might take it on, but on Thursday, she said her auditors will not get involved because federal auditing standards require her to defer to the attorney general’s investigation.

The controversy has sparked outcry from labor unions who seek to organize MassHousing’s workforce as a means of combating what they see as poor leadership. Thursday morning, a few dozen members from public sector unions demonstrated outside MassHousing’s offices in Beacon Hill. The activists called for reforms at the agency, including the passage of proposed legislation that could shake up the agency’s board and trigger a review of its spending in Gateway Cities.

Speaking into a bullhorn, Tom McKeever, president of SEIU Local 888, told the crowd that Richards’s recent resignation didn’t make MassHousing’s problems go away. He demanded an outside investigation.

“We believe there is more to see as it relates to fraud, misappropriation of money and criminal activity,” he said.

title: Pastor Chris Sumner, a light of faith who ‘left an indelible impact,’ dies at 64 of ALS
text:
“In essence, many believers interpret ALS not as a sign of God’s absence or indifference, but as an opportunity for an extraordinary work of grace, transforming their souls and deepening their relationship with the divine, despite the physical devastation.”

Mr. Sumner, who had been executive director of the Melnea A. Cass Recreation Center in Roxbury until he retired due to illness, was 64 when he died in his Hyde Park home on July 5.

A longtime Boston activist, he also managed Roxbury Heritage State Park and the Dillaway-Thomas House in his final job. Leadership roles in previous years included serving as executive director of the Ten Point Coalition, an organization of religious and community leaders.

Mr. Sumner “brought people together and made countless lives better,” Governor Maura Healey said.

“Massachusetts has lost a great community leader with the passing of Pastor Sumner,” she added. “Chris dedicated his life to lifting up others — with faith, compassion, and a deep belief in the potential of every young person and every neighborhood he served.”

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu said: “Pastor Chris had a rare gift of making everyone feel seen, whether through his steady encouragement, wise advice, or genuine friendship he offered so freely. He served as a dedicated mentor and champion for countless young people” — including many who went on to fill leadership positions in Greater Boston.

“Pastor Chris has left an indelible impact on our city and state that will be felt for generations to come,” Wu said. “I am grateful to have called him a partner and friend. May we carry forward his legacy, and may he rest in peace.”

Throughout Mr. Sumner’s life, family and friends said, he seemed to fill more hours than each day held, and that carried on to the end.

“Everyone has been amazed at how well I am doing,” he said at the April gathering. “God has had plenty of chances to take me home, but I believe I am still here because he has much more work for me to do.”

Along with having held leadership positions at various organizations, he devoted endless hours to being a father to his three daughters and a father figure to more people than he could count.

That was a role to which he had always aspired. He was raised by a single mother and never knew his own father.

His wife, Katani Eaton Sumner, recalled that when they were high school seniors — long before they began dating — she asked him one day as they walked home from basketball practice “what he wanted to be, and he said, ‘I want to be a good dad and a good husband.’”

In a Father’s Day tribute this year in The Bay State Banner, his oldest daughter, Kandice Sumner, president and chief executive of the Metco program, wrote that “my dad was everyone’s Dad, and there was enough of him to go around.”

“All of my friends wanted my dad for their dad,” she added in a phone interview. “My dad was our superman. I feel like I’m cutting it short by calling him a superhero. He was a magical human being on earth.”

Born on Nov. 9, 1961, Byron Christopher Sumner was the son of Annie Blanche Sumner, who raised him and his two sisters — one older, one younger.

The family moved a few times, but Mr. Sumner spent some of his youth in Roxbury and was delighted to have a view, from his Melnea Cass center office, of an area where he had lived.

A powerful athlete who grew to 6-foot-2 and 250 pounds, Mr. Sumner competed in baseball, track, and hockey, and later in life took to lengthy bicycle rides.

But he particularly loved basketball and played for the Titans, a Boston Neighborhood Basketball League championship team coached by the legendary Al Brodsky.

Having struggled with dyslexia, Mr. Sumner left English High School without a diploma but still landed basketball scholarships in Canada, playing for the University of Prince Edward Island and Acadia University in Nova Scotia, and garnering hoops honors.

Returning home after his college and semi-pro basketball career, he fell in love with Katani Eaton, proposing while she was a Brown University student. She was impressed by his intelligence and surprised he wasn’t bookish — due in large part to his dyslexia. At her encouragement, he pored through “The Autobiography of Malcolm X,” cover to cover.

“That’s the first book he ever read,” she said, laughing as she recalled that he’d tell people: “My wife made me read a book before she would go out with me.”

They married in 1985. He then earned his general equivalency diploma and went on to graduate with a bachelor’s degree from Springfield College and a master’s in social work from Wheelock College.

“I told him: ‘You’re going to be a role model for so many young Black men. You’ve got to go back and get your degree,’” his wife recalled.

Mr. Sumner went on to hold leadership positions at places including the Blue Hill Boys & Girls Club and the St. Stephen’s Youth Programs.

His reach exceeded his titles, though, the Rev. Ray Hammond of Bethel AME Church said in a video message played in April 2025 at a night of prayer at Jubilee Christian Church in honor of Mr. Sumner.

Hammond said Mr. Sumner was a mentor to many young people “who saw in you the living proof that early adversity can be a steppingstone to a great destiny.”

“His whole life is a miracle,” Katani Eaton Sumner, who worked for three decades in education, said.

In addition to his wife and his oldest daughter, Kandice, Mr. Sumner leaves his two younger daughters, Kortney of Pawtucket, R.I., and Kristian of Hyde Park; a sister, Cheryl of Jacksonville, Fla.; and two grandchildren.

Family and friends will gather for a visitation at 5 p.m. Friday in Jubilee Christian Church in Mattapan, where a celebration of Mr. Sumner’s life will begin at 6.

“One of my dad’s lasting legacies is the sacredness of joy,” Kandice said. “He would make everything joyful. And it wasn’t an effort. It was just him.”

Through Mr. Sumner’s own example, informed by his spirituality, he showed all he met how to navigate their own inevitable mortality, said Ron Hoffman, founder and chief executive of the nonprofit Compassionate Care ALS.

“Here was this extraordinary man, who was dancing his own dying,” Hoffman said. “That’s an unseen gift that Chris has given everyone who knew him and saw him — a gift to his family, his friends, his community, his church.”

title: In the Senate race, how old is too old and how much should one care?
text:
In response to Kelly Garrity’s article “Older voters not sure peers should run: Mass. Senate race highlights concerns on age” (Page A1, July 9), it’s too bad the Globe didn’t interview me. I’m a couple of months older than Senator Ed Markey, and I’m going to vote for him for sure. Representative Seth Moulton is using ageism to scare people away from voting for the better, more experienced person for the job. He used it eight years ago to challenge the leadership of Nancy Pelosi, then House speaker.

I had been a supporter of Moulton, both as a voter and financially, in his campaigns for the House. But his ageist attacks and his attacks against the trans community following the 2024 presidential election have turned me off from him. Democrats need the seniority in the Senate that Markey brings should the party take over the chamber after the midterms. From what I can see, he hasn’t lost a step, so there’s no reason to deny him another term.

Enter Email

I’m old enough to remember the phrase from the 1960s: “Don’t trust anyone over 30.” Of course that was a poor sentiment, as is: Don’t vote for Markey because he’s 80.

Herb Harris

Peabody

I am not sure that interviews with 15 voters who are 80 or close to it warrants the headline “Older voters not sure peers should run.” Consider me, at 88, the 16th interviewee, and I am voting to reelect Senator Ed Markey because I trust that he will pursue his progressive agenda. I am not so convinced about his opponent.

Lynn Gaulin

North Attleborough

As a man nearing 80, I am well aware of how quickly health can fail, as discussed in Anjali Huynh’s article “Senate race has liberals lamenting: Young candidates generate energy in other regions while Mass. lags, they say” (Page A1, July 20).

Many people refuse to face the realities of age and may fear letting go. Yet in politics, a feeling of being irreplaceable, that no one else could do the job as well, is damaging to our government and our democracy. President Biden is a noteworthy example, and his ill-fated reelection campaign is a major reason Donald Trump was elected again. Trump himself is 80 now and showing signs of decline.

I think of other examples, including Senators Dianne Feinstein and Mitch McConnell, Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, and many others past and present.

I agree with the 79-year-old voter from Hudson who said, “I would have preferred for Ed Markey to step down this year and become a mentor, an éminence grise to whoever was coming up.” I believe we in Massachusetts are fortunate to have a good younger candidate for Senate in Representative Seth Moulton. This is an important choice for us to make.

Markey, at 80, is running once again, after nearly 50 years in Congress. It’s likely he feels capable now, as he says, but much can change in three of four years. In a closely divided chamber, one senator’s seat could swing the balance of power across the aisle.

Randy Foote

Roxbury

title: What a bullet does to a body
text:
September 23, 1994, Burke, Virginia. After a high school football game, a fight broke out in a nearby park. Someone fired a .38-caliber handgun into the crowd. A stray bullet struck me in the throat. I was 17 years old.

I remember the warmth of blood soaking through my white shirt before I understood what had happened. I remember trying to speak and realizing I couldn’t. I remember my surgeon, Dr. Robert Ahmed, unlocking my gurney himself because he was dismayed at how long it was taking to get me to the operating room. I remember him leaning over me and saying, “Joe, I have to do this to save your life.” And I remember thinking about the pack of cigarettes in my pocket that my parents would kill me for if they found out — the kind of small, ordinary thought a teenager clings to in the middle of something enormous.

I survived. My windpipe was rebuilt. A vein from my leg was used to repair the carotid artery the bullet had torn open. In the hospital bed where I recovered, I made a decision that would shape the rest of my life: I was going to spend my life on the other side of the operating table. And for nearly two decades now, I have.

I am a trauma surgeon at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore. I have spent much of my career caring for victims of violence and sitting with families as they learn that their son, daughter, husband, or wife is not coming home. I know what a gunshot wound does to a windpipe because it happened to mine. So when I say that a new round of federal deregulation could cost lives, I am not speaking from a policy brief. I am describing what I have lived through and what I now spend my days trying to repair.

What should stop every American cold is this: The Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives is eliminating more than three dozen federal firearms regulations in what amounts to the broadest rewrite of its rules in agency history, and by its own admission, some of the changes could result in harm, “including potential mass casualty events.”

Note that that warning did not come from gun safety advocates or political opponents. It came from the agency itself. In its proposal for rule changes, the agency acknowledged risks in loosening restrictions on firearm access for people with documented histories of serious mental illness and in restoring access to stabilizing braces that allow pistols to be fired with greater accuracy and control, so that they function more like rifles. Devices of this type have been used in some of the deadliest mass shootings in recent years.

At the same time, the Justice Department has gone after states that have tried to curb gun violence. In May, Virginia banned the sale of AR-15-style rifles and capped magazines at 15 rounds; California barred the sale of handguns with a trigger design, common to Glocks, that makes them easy to convert into machine guns using aftermarket devices. Within weeks, the DOJ sued to overturn both laws, arguing they violate the Second Amendment. It is part of a pattern: Since September, the department has filed seven lawsuits challenging state and local gun laws designed to keep the most dangerous weapons off the streets. This is precisely why the legal defense work of organizations like Brady, where I serve as board chair and chief medical officer, matters as much now as the laws themselves: When the federal government turns litigation into a weapon against public safety statutes, someone has to be in court pushing back.

Enforcement against firearm dealers most likely to arm dangerous individuals has also sharply declined. After the Trump administration ended a zero tolerance policy for lawbreaking gun dealers earlier this year, federal license revocations for dealers who falsified records or failed to conduct background checks dropped dramatically.

Meanwhile, the public health infrastructure designed to understand and prevent firearm injury is being dismantled. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Division of Violence Prevention has been hollowed out by layoffs. Government-funded reports on strategies to reduce firearm injuries have quietly disappeared from federal websites. And Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health and human services secretary, recently told Congress that he does not consider gun violence a public health issue at all, calling it “a law enforcement issue and not public health.”

As a physician, I can say plainly: He is wrong. Nearly 60 percent of firearm deaths in America are suicides. You cannot arrest your way out of a mental health crisis. Public health is the framework that has helped reduce deaths from smoking, motor vehicle crashes, and infectious diseases. It works by identifying risk factors and implementing interventions before tragedy occurs, rather than simply responding to it afterward. Eliminating our ability to study gun violence does not eliminate gun violence. It only makes us less capable of understanding what works and less able to save lives.

I want to be precise about what these policies mean because policy language has a way of becoming abstract. A revoked license means a dealer can no longer sell guns illegally or irresponsibly. A restored license means that the pipeline may reopen. A stabilizing brace increases control and makes a weapon more deadly. For me, none of this is abstract. It is a Friday night in my trauma bay.

A couple of years ago, I operated on a 19-year-old with the same injury I survived at 17. I stood with his mother and delivered the devastating news that Dr. Ahmed never had to give mine. Those are the stakes of licensing rules, enforcement decisions, and regulatory exemptions. They are not abstractions. A specific family in a specific room on a specific night. And then another family. And another.

Although I did not grow up in a household with firearms, I’m not opposed to responsible gun ownership. And over the years of caring for patients, engaging with responsible gun owners, and working on firearm-injury prevention, I have come to understand both the culture surrounding gun ownership and the constitutional protections afforded by the Second Amendment.

But there is no interpretation of the Second Amendment that requires making it easier for someone in acute crisis to obtain a weapon or that demands we stop holding dealers accountable when they falsify records or ignore background check requirements. These are not questions about gun rights. They are questions about public safety.

We were building policies that were beginning to work. The Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, passed one month after 19 children and two teachers were murdered in Uvalde, Texas, was followed by declines in firearm deaths from their 2021 peak. States added their own protections on top of those federal measures — Illinois, for instance, banned assault weapons and high-capacity magazines in 2023, directly in response to the mass shooting at a Highland Park Fourth of July parade. (The Justice Department has since filed briefs in federal court arguing against that law’s constitutionality.)

For the first time in years, the trajectory was moving in the right direction.

Now the federal government is dismantling that progress on multiple fronts at once, even as its own experts warn of the consequences.

I did not need a government memo to understand what a bullet does to a body. I carry the scar. I have spent every year since my injury trying to ensure fewer families have to experience what mine did. I am asking Secretary Kennedy to walk through my trauma bay before deciding that this is not a health issue. And I am asking the officials who authored those warnings in the ATF’s report, and the members of Congress who can still act on them, to take those warnings as seriously as I take every patient who comes through my doors.

title: Seeking a path forward for Blue Hill Avenue
text:
Re “Blue Hill Avenue transit: Bus or rail?” (Opinion, July 13): The dueling op-eds in the Globe’s July 13 edition — “Community deserves rail, not another bus debate,” by Boston City Councilors Brian Worrell and Miniard Culpepper, and “Don’t jeopardize bus project waiting for rail,” by former state transportation secretary James Aloisi — show the chasm between a former bureaucrat and community leaders who point to decades of being told they should be grateful for crumbs instead of an objective analysis of transit options that could yield a full loaf.

Aloisi, who directs the MIT Transit Research Consortium, bizarrely says a subway is a “blunt mobility instrument” and focuses on the goal of improving “the bus rider experience.”
