Enter Email

The goal is to improve mobility for all. We need to look at alternatives and evaluate ridership, cost, environmental impacts, viability of construction, and other factors instead of pouring our energy into tinkering with the bus network.

Buses are the lowest-capacity mode with the least potential to shape land use and development. Why the fixation on buses? Because they are cheap to implement. Big thinkers like these city councilors have been told that buses are what you get. It’s long past time to see a study identify the best alternative for the corridor.

Anne McKinnon

Jamaica Plain

Amsterdam is an old city built around a canal system that makes straight roads practically impossible, but planners have engineered a practical solution that incorporates light rail, autos and light trucks, bicycles (lots of them), and pedestrians. Many of the major streets are configured as follows: sidewalk, bike lane, auto lane, tram, auto lane, bike lane, sidewalk. It would seem that the wide expanses of Blue Hill Avenue, Seaver Street, and Washington Street would be ideal for a similar configuration, incorporating light rail or Silver Line buses while connecting Nubian Square and Mattapan Square.

Lucius C. Michel

North Andover

I cannot overstate the need for presenting more study-based options for the Blue Hill Avenue corridor, including rapid transit, and notwithstanding the costs. Our community has working-class and lower-income families who are major public transit users.

Sentiments expressed by Councilors Brian Worrell and Miniard Culpepper are important, chief among them the history of unkept promises of transportation improvements for Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan.

I can still recall the neglected Orange Line slowly creeping around the Ferdinand Building into what was then Dudley Station because of the way the track leaned. It was still the best way to get to work downtown on time. Then it was gone altogether.

We know that plans of any kind will take years to be implemented. The road to gaining community agreement on a plan must be paved with a demonstration of ongoing commitment through action and investment, not one big gamble every 40 years that has as much of a chance of being a loss as a win.

Why not start spending the money that’s been set aside now on traffic infrastructure and enforcement improvements along the existing corridor, better bus scheduling, preparing businesses for changes, designing pollution controls, and other enhancements?

Laura Younger

Dorchester

The former state secretary of transportation needed a member of his staff to drive him to Mattapan Square so that he could assess “the poor quality of service on the 28 bus”? Seriously? I might have suggested a walk from the state office at Park Plaza to the Red Line at South Station, then a train to Ashmont, and then the Mattapan Trolley.

Paul Stewart

Quincy

title: Sea of Puerto Rican flags, street dancing, and more at Boston’s annual Puerto Rican parade
text:
“Seeing the families and the friends, they all come out and enjoy … It’s like a family reunion,” said Hector Pantoja, 40, a warehouse worker who has come to the event all his life. “[We] love each other.”

The parade is put on every year by The Puerto Rican Festival of Massachusetts, an organization founded in 1967 to promote belonging and cultural affirmation for Puerto Ricans in the area. It serves as the culminating event for the organization’s annual two-day Puerto Rican Festival, which in the past attracted more than 50,000 attendees, according to the organization’s website.

Massachusetts has the fifth-largest Puerto Rican population in the United States, according to 2023 data from the Boston Planning and Development Agency.

Near the front of the parade, just behind a group marching with a welcome sign, a tow truck decorated for Lulu’s Barbershop threw bags of candy towards the crowd. Elsewhere, a man dressed in Bad Bunny’s Super Bowl outfit waved at the crowd. Throughout the procession, several young dance groups, whose members wore long flowing skirts and cheer uniforms, twirled and jumped.

“It is a big deal. It feels like we’re back home,” Christina Colon, 34, a freelance UX/UI designer from Dorchester, said. “Honestly, it’s rough because I feel like Boston is slightly segregated … It does feel good because we don’t see this on a regular basis, especially when you’re at the inner, inner city like, let’s say, downtown.”

She added that this year, the parade seemed to include “more of our culture” such as “the dances, the history of it, some of the up-and-coming artists.”

Local politicians and activists attended the event, too. One group encouraging young people to consider a career in law enforcement marched in black shirts reading “Injustice everywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.”

Another group, standing on the back of a junk removal truck, carried red and black signs reading “No human being is illegal” and “No one is free when others are oppressed.”

Other groups walked in support of political candidates up for election, including a group for Massachusetts treasurer candidate Elizabeth Dionne and a group for Suffolk County district attorney candidate Linda Champion.

For community coordinator Veronica Bowens-Wiggins, 52, from South End, it was nice to see representatives in person rather than through a flier.

“They’re actually trying to give you a small token of who they are personally. And I think that’s important,” she said.

But for Myrna Santana, 50, who has been coming to the parade since childhood, the event was less about politics and more about community enjoyment.

“We always keep politics on the side when it’s [time] to have fun as family, as neighbors. … You just have to have fun as a community,” she said.

As the parade continued, a group of men on horses trotted by. One man pulled his horse to the side to greet three women with their iPhones out, filming, the horse’s nostrils getting up close to the cameras.

At the end of the procession, dozens and dozens of cars drove by, their doors opened or removed entirely— many balanced large speakers on their roofs.

But, even after the parade ended, festivities felt far from over. On building stoops, people sat, blasting music, waving flags, and chatting.

“People are going to be calling out of work tomorrow because it’s going to be a good night,” Jason Rodriguez, 30, from Jamaica Plains, said. “Puerto Ricans are very prideful people, so the fact that the community is this loud and this proud makes sense.”

title: Swimmer who drowned in Milford quarry identified as Boston teenager
text:
The swimmer who drowned over the weekend at a Milford quarry was identified Monday as a Boston teenager.

Yanick Rodrigues, 17, drowned at the Shadowbrook Quarries, while swimming with a friend Saturday, officials said.

His body was recovered on Sunday.

After immigrating from Cape Verde in 2016, Rodrigues attended Madison Park High School in Roxbury, where he was a star soccer player, according to a report by WCVB-TV.

His death comes less than a week after local officials issued a warning about the dangers of the quarries, a popular spot where swimming is forbidden.

On July 19, an 18-year-old woman fell about 12 feet from a ledge onto jagged rocks. The woman, who said she briefly lost consciousness after the fall, was found bleeding in several places, police said. She was flown to UMass Memorial Medical Center for treatment.

“While we’re thankful this incident did not have an even more tragic outcome, it serves as an important reminder that the Quarries are not a safe place for recreation,” Milford’s police chief, Robert Tusino, said in a statement last week.

“The steep rock faces, unstable terrain, and limited access for emergency responders create an extremely dangerous environment where a single misstep can have life-altering consequences for civilians and responders,” he said.

Other swimmers have drowned at quarries in Milford over the years.

In 2014, an 18-year-old from Providencejumped into Fletcher’s Quarry and did not resurface. The teen’s body was found a day later about 70 feet down and 10 feet away from the cliff. At the time, the death was the second at a local quarry since 2007, and the fourth in almost two decades.

Last summer, police said they would be cracking down on trespassing at local quarries by threatening thousands of dollars in fines.

Bryan Hecht can be reached at bryan.hecht@globe.com. Follow him on Instagram @bhechtjournalism.

title: State effort to seize Norwood Hospital by eminent domain advances in Legislature
text:
“We’re both very optimistic,” Rush, a West Roxbury Democrat, told the Globe, referring to himself and Rogers. “We’re both committed to rebuilding a hospital in the town of Norwood.”

A spokesperson for the Healey administration wasn’t immediately available for comment.

For roughly two years, the massive skeleton of the hospital has stood unfinished in Norwood, an unsightly symbol of the spectacular downfall of its disgraced and bankrupt former operator, Steward Health Care.

The bill would authorize the state Division of Capital Asset Management and Maintenance to take the 11-acre property from its owner, Medical Properties Trust, an Alabama real estate investment trust, to ensure public access to health care.

“We’re ecstatic that the Legislature is taking the lead in making this happen,” said Tony Mazzucco, Norwood’s longtime town general manager. “It finally feels like we’ve reached a turning point and we’re on the other side of this long journey to get a hospital back.”

A spokesperson for MPT said the company had no comment. MPT’s website said the company wants to set the record straight on Norwood Hospital, although it did not address the possibility of the property’s seizure. MPT says it did not abandon the construction project and that it “has finished the building as much as possible without having a new hospital operator in place.”

“MPT Built the Hospital with its own funds when it could have walked away,” its website reads. “Massachusetts Must Work with MPT to Finish the Job.”

Under the bill heading to the House, the process to use eminent domain would begin on Nov. 1. It would involve the state assessing the value of the unfinished hospital and soliciting bids from nonprofit hospital operators who would seek to buy or lease the property.

The Globe reported last month that Mass General Brigham held talks late last year and early this year with MPT to buy the construction site in the hopes of finally completing the project and reopening the hospital.

But MPT sought “flagrantly unreasonable” sums from Mass General Brigham, and the negotiations fizzled out, according to Rogers, who said he had personally encouraged both sides to make a deal. A Mass General Brigham spokesperson declined to comment on the latest development Wednesday.

Norwood Hospital has been closed since June 28, 2020, after a storm in the area dumped nearly six inches of rain in 90 minutes. Flooding destroyed the facility’s electrical room, cutting off power and forcing the evacuation of all patients. The damage was so severe that the hospital, which had about 200 beds, had to be razed.

Steward paid for that, then launched a $375 million project to rebuild the century-old institution. The steel framework of the hospital went up.

But in 2024, Steward, a for-profit national chain, ran out of money, stopped paying its bills, and collapsed in a bankruptcy that made headlines across the country. MPT paid to build a roof, install a heating and cooling system, and add windows and metal panels to seal the structure before winter, the Globe reported last year. Then the work stopped, local officials say. (MPT on its website said, “Construction has never been ‘paused.’”)

Because Norwood Hospital was closed when Steward declared bankruptcy, and its doctors and nurses had moved elsewhere, it wasn’t among the 31 hospitals nationally that Steward put up for sale. Norwood Hospital’s travails were overshadowed by the broader crisis provoked by Steward’s collapse.

It is the only one of eight former Steward hospitals in Massachusetts whose fate remains unresolved. It served an estimated quarter of a million people in a dozen nearby communities, and residents say they still intensely feel its absence.

MPT had bought Steward hospitals’ land and buildings in a sale-leaseback deal in 2016. The arrangement left the hospitals on the hook for excessively high rents, weakening them financially before life-threatening lapses in care occurred, a Globe Spotlight Team investigation reported.

The Spotlight Team in 2024 found a pattern of overpayment in MPT purchases of Steward real estate. Asked at that time about what appeared to be inflated hospital valuations, MPT’s then-spokesperson Drew Babin called the Globe’s findings “false and misleading” and said, “MPT stands firmly behind our rigorous underwriting process.”

title: ‘My family, we are all upside down’: Relatives mourn man killed on Boston Common as ‘beautiful son’
text:
“He never got mad, he never said no, he was never getting in people’s face,” Desrosiers said. “None of my boys ever get into an argument where it was heated or to a fight. We were very blessed.”

Sanon was beginning to build a life of his own after moving away from his childhood home to his own apartment in Norwood, Desrosiers said, when he was killed just after 5 a.m. outside the Boylston Green Line station, allegedly by a homeless man with a history of violence and mental health issues.

“My family, we are all upside down,” Desrosiers said, adding he wished he had been with Sanon that day to protect him. “I feel so powerless, because if I was there it would have been a different story.”

Sanon was a graduate of West Roxbury High School who worked various food service jobs and enjoyed playing basketball, Desrosiers said. He last worked at a Moroccan restaurant that closed in 2024 and was living off state assistance, Desrosiers said.

“He was a very helpful man. You have an issue, you need help? He’s going to be the first one to step up,” Desrosiers said. Sanon always called him “Mmai,” he recalled, because he couldn’t pronounce his name properly when he first came to live with him in 2004 after emigrating from Port-au-Prince.

Ashlie A. Jeremie, 27, the man charged with killing Sanon, had reportedly stopped taking the medication he was prescribed for a diagnosis of “bipolar disorder with psychotic features,” prosecutors said at his arraignment last week.

Jeremie was ordered held without bail and sent to Bridgewater State Hospital for a 20-day mental health assessment to determine if he can stand trial.

He had previously been examined by clinicians at Bridgewater last year in connection with an assault and battery case in Dorchester Municipal Court, records show, and had been released into the homeless shelter system from federal custody just 16 days before Sanon’s murder.

It remains unclear what led to the fatal encounter or why Sanon was on the Common so early in the morning.

Just over an hour before the attack, police had been called to Tufts Medical Center to remove Jeremie after he reportedly harassed staff members. Jeremie was later apprehended after assaulting a 21-year-old Boston University student with a stolen jackhammer bit in Chinatown.

For Desrosiers and other grieving relatives, the investigation so far has raised many questions about what happened to Sanon, and why his alleged attacker had been allowed to walk the street.

“They just talk to the same guy and let him go, and the same guy prior has a history of bad stuff,” Desrosiers said. “To me it’s negligence.”

While he had gotten his own place, Sanon lived only a short walk away from his parents’ house in Norwood and remained close with them and his brothers, whom he would talk with every day, Desrosiers said.

But in the week before his death, family members had lost touch with Sanon, who had only recently gotten a cellphone. Desrosiers was in Florida for his mother’s funeral and returned the day before his stepson’s death.

“All that’s a gray area, we don’t know what he was doing,” Desrosiers said, adding his stepson’s attacker was a “completely random person,” unknown to the family.

“For some reason he was so heated, so mad, [that he attacked] whoever was close to him at that time,” Desrosiers said. “Unfortunately, it was my beautiful son Jonathan. He didn’t even have a chance to run, a chance to fight. It could [have] been anybody.”

title: The best things to do in and around Boston this weekend
text:
JAWS Courtesy of the Boston Public Library, catch a free screening of 1975’s “Jaws,” directed by Academy Award winner Steven Spielberg and starring Roy Scheider, Robert Shaw, and Richard Dreyfuss. Known for its haunting score composed by the legendary John Williams, as well as its iconic New England setting (the movie was filmed on Martha’s Vineyard), the summer classic screens at BPL’s Charlestown location. July 31, 2 p.m. Free. BPL Charlestown, 179 Main St., Charlestown. bpl.bibliocommons.com — Daisy Levine

PARANORMAL CIRQUE SPECTER In a fusion of cabaret and theater, acrobats, illusionists, and performers bring a paranormal circus show to Boston, presented by Cirque Italia. No one under 13 is permitted at the show, while guests ages 13 to 17 must be accompanied by an adult. July 31-Aug. 3. Tickets start at $20. Suffolk Downs, 525 William F. McClellan Highway, East Boston. paranormalcirque.com — Janira Skrbkova

RAT CITY ARTS FESTIVAL A grassroots celebration of local artists, poets, and musicians returns to the Allston-Brighton area for its fifth year while also promoting neighborhood rodent mitigation. The lineup includes nu metal band Cheem and alternative rock band Makeout Palace. Aug. 1, 3-10 p.m. Free. Charles River Speedway, 525 Western Ave., Brighton.ratcityartsfestival.com — JS

SOULFUL BLISS Head to the Seaport this weekend for a celebration of music, culture, community, and joy. Organized by Boston-based event agency AfroDesiaCity, relive the R&B sounds of the ’90s and 2000s while enjoying live performances, DJs, art, community storytelling, and artisan markets. Aug. 1, 4-10 p.m. Viaduct Plaza, 9 World Trade Center Ave. afrodesiacity.com/event-details/soulful-bliss-2026-seaport — DL

KEVIN NEALON “Do you know what the most stressful job in the world is?” asks former “Saturday Night Live” cast member Nealon. “Air traffic controller. But not if you don’t take it seriously.” Aug. 1, 7 p.m. $45-$59.The Wilbur, 246 Tremont St. thewilbur.com — Nick A. Zaino III

ESTHER KU Ku started her stand-up career in Boston before appearing on shows like “Girl Code” and “Wild ’N Out.” She doesn’t get back to town often, and she is headlining with a great supporting group in Dan Crohn, Zach Stewart, and Chef Phil. Aug. 1, 9 p.m. $39.90. Laugh Boston, 425 Summer St. 617-725-2844, laughboston.com — NZ

ROARING TWENTIES LAWN PARTY Jazz, vintage vendors, and flappers take over Ipswich this weekend, creating a Gatsby-esque 1920s-themed summer bash. On hand will be music, dancing, contests, fashion parades, food and beverage vendors, and more. Aug. 1-2, 2-8 p.m. Tickets start at $52. Castle on the Crane Estate, 290 Argilla Road, Ipswich. roaringtwentieslawnparty.org — DL

DINE OUT BOSTON Meet Boston’s semiannual restaurant week returns this summer featuring multi-course fixed-price lunch and dinner menus across almost 200 participating establishments. Among the hot spots making their Dine Out debuts are Rosa y Marigold, Maple & Ash, and Fallow Kin. Aug. 1-15. Various locations.meetboston.com/dine-out-boston — JS

ZAC BROWN BAND AT FENWAY Joined by special guest Old Crow Medicine Show, Zac Brown Band returns to Fenway Park for the latest stop of its “Love & Fear Tour.” The concert marks the country group’s 15th time playing the beloved ballpark. Read more about the latest concerts coming to the Boston area in this week’s Sound Check column. Aug. 2, 7 p.m. Tickets start at $89. Fenway Park, 4 Jersey St. mlb.com/redsox/tickets/concerts/zac-brown-band — DL

HAVE FUN, BE YOURSELF In 2024, Andrew Mayer brought this one-person show to Edinburgh Fringe; now he is recording it as special. The story centers on Mayer’s struggles to stop resisting his nervousness and just be himself, played out in three dates over the course of six years, and the relief he felt at the end of that process.Aug. 2, 7 p.m. $20-$25. The Rockwell, 255 Elm St., Somerville. therockwell.org — NZ

TANGLEWOOD This weekend’s flagship event at Tanglewood is surely Saturday’s semi-staged performance of Mozart’s madcap “The Marriage of Figaro,” featuring music director Andris Nelsons on the podium, and an ensemble cast including baritone Michael Sumuel as Figaro, Nikola Hillebrand as Susanna, and Hanna-Elisabeth Müller as the Countess; in the director’s chair is James Darrah Black, who also stage-directed the Handel and Haydn Society’s excellent 2022 “Figaro” at Symphony Hall. Friday evening, Finnish composer-conductor Esa-Pekka Salonen visits the podium for a program of Wagner’s Prelude and “Liebestod” from “Tristan and Isolde,” Sibelius’s Symphony No. 7, and Beethoven’s Piano Concerto No. 5, “Emperor,” the latter featuring pianist Yefim Bronfman. Sunday, Nelsons ends his summer stint at Tanglewood with a visit from violinist Joshua Bell, performing Bruch’s “Scottish Fantasy,” and Tuesday afternoon into evening unites all the BSO and Tanglewood-based ensembles — and many more local groups too — as the grounds come alive for Tanglewood on Parade, this year curated by Yo-Yo Ma. Tanglewood, Lenox. 617-266-1200, tanglewood.org

BOSTON LANDMARKS ORCHESTRA Landmarks steps out of its usual Wednesday evening Hatch Shell timeslot this week, traveling to Jamaica Plain and Roxbury to present a program including Max Richter’s recomposition of Vivaldi’s “The Four Seasons,” Mozart’s Symphony No. 40, and several shorter pieces by Florence Price, William Grant Still, Gabriela Lena Frank, and Julia Perry. As with everything this orchestra does, attendance is free, but given the limited space of the indoor venues, online registration in advance is recommended. July 31, 7 p.m., Bethel AME Church, 100 Wachusett St., Jamaica Plain. Aug. 1, 3 p.m., Twelfth Baptist Church, 160 Warren St., Roxbury. landmarksorchestra.org

SAY IT LOUD: AAMARP, 1977 TO NOW Closing this week: The Black Arts Movement came to be in a critical time in 1960s and ’70s America when the civil rights movement had given way to more forceful ideas around Black rights. In Boston, those ideas found root in the African American Masters Artist in Residence Program, founded by the firebrand artist and activist Dana Chandler. This show charts the organization’s long evolution through decades of cultural and racial tumult, and its unwavering devotion to the cause of Black representation. Through Aug. 2. Institute of Contemporary Art Boston, 25 Harbor Shore Drive. 617-478-3100, icaboston.org

CELTIC ART ACROSS THE AGES Closing this week: Spanning almost three millennia, 800 BCE right up till now, this show takes a liberal approach to art made by Celtic people and their vast diaspora through the ages, stretching from Northern Europe to every corner of the globe. From the Iron Age through the Roman Empire to today, it attempts to weave connection across eras to both reveal lineage and unwind cliche. Through Aug. 2. Harvard Art Museums, 32 Quincy St., Cambridge. 617-495-9400, harvardartmuseums.org

SPRAY: JULES OLITSKI IN THE 1960s Closing soon: Olitski represented the United States at the Venice Biennale in 1966 and was the first living artist ever to have a solo exhibition at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in 1969, but his long-ago star turn hasn’t been as enduring as New York abstract painting peers like Mark Rothko or Jackson Pollock. This exhibition is a chance to wonder why: A showcase of his signature spray-painted canvases from that era, rendered in mesmerizingly loose fogs of color, the show is a rare opportunity to contemplate his fade from renown. Through Aug. 9. Currier Museum, 150 Ash St., Manchester, N.H. 603-669-6144, currier.org

DEAD GIRL’S QUINCEAÑERA In the premiere of a dark comedy by Haitian-American playwright and screenwriter Phanésia Pharel (“The Waterfall”), a teenage girl disappears during her quinceañera celebration, triggering an investigation by her three best friends in which they set about “interrogating suspects, spinning increasingly wild theories, and roasting one another along the way,” according to press materials. Directed by Melia Bensussen. Aug. 5-29. Coproduction by Barrington Stage Company, Goodman Theatre, and Hartford Stage. St. Germain Stage, 36 Linden St., Pittsfield. 413-242-6411, barringtonstageco.org

A NEW ERA Miranda Austen ADEkoje’s new play about the Black suffragist movement in 1890s Boston deftly avoids the trap of “message” art by telling a rich story full of complex, conflicted characters. The world premiere production from Company One focuses on the real-life Boston suffragist, journalist, and activist Josephine St. Pierre Ruffin (played here by Patrice Jean-Baptiste) as she tries to build coalitions without sacrificing her ideals. You can feel the ideas crackling as the drama builds. Through Aug. 8. Pay what you can. Strand Theatre, 543 Columbia Road, Dorchester. companyone.org

COMING OUT PERFECT Richard Mercado’s debut YA graphic novel, “Coming Out Perfect,” is autobiographical and extremely poignant, funny, and charming. His previous minicomic, “I Owe It to My Parents to Not Come Out” won accolades, and this more expanded version will win readers’ hearts. He’ll read at All She Wrote Books on Sunday. Aug. 2, 5 p.m. Tickets are on an income-based sliding scale and include a copy of the book. 75 Washington St., Somerville. allshewrotebooks.com

BETRAYAL The three lead performances are as exquisitely controlled as Shana Gozansky’s direction in this fine production of Harold Pinter’s 1978 drama of infidelity, which famously unspools in reverse chronology. In tracing the entwined lives of lovers Jerry (Michael Underhill) and Emma (Liza Giangrande, remarkable once again) and Emma’s husband, Robert (Tanner Efinger), Gozansky does not overdo the famed “Pinter pause.” But she does allow space within Pinter’s characteristically spare dialogue for meaning to take shape between the words as “Betrayal” winds its way backward from 1977 to 1968 in London and Venice. The production reminds us that there’s seldom anything small about Pinter’s small talk. Also featuring invaluable contributions from composer and sound designer Julian Crocamo. Through Aug. 1. Gloucester Stage Company. Natti-Willsky Performance Center, 267 East Main St., Gloucester. 978-281-4433, gloucesterstage.com — Don Aucoin

BUYER & CELLAR Inspired by the strange-but-true fact that Barbra Streisand had a private shopping mall built in a basement on her Malibu estate, this comedy by Jonathan Tolins stars Victor L. Shopov as a struggling actor hired to work at the mall — which has only one customer. Directed by Daniel Bourque. Through Aug. 1. Hub Theatre Company. Club Café, 209 Columbus Ave. hubtheatreboston.org — DA

title: What makes Boston so safe? Black pastors have different theories.
text:
There used to be a homicide in Boston, on average, every 58 hours. A man was found beaten and strangled to death in Savin Hill Park one Saturday afternoon in July, a pregnant woman found shot in the face on Neponset Avenue a few hours later. The year was 1990.

And at the forefront of fighting this vicious scourge of violence were Black clergymen, working with residents, advocates, and police to help bring about a huge dip in street violence, in what was eventually dubbed the Boston Miracle.

Now, more than three decades later, homicides in Boston are down nearly 80 percent from 1990, with fewer shootings and assaults than comparable American cities.

Those statistics beg the question: What makes a city safe?

It’s an inquiry with a multifaceted — and sometimes elusive — answer that keeps local ministers out on the streets on hot July evenings, talking to any stranger who will listen and some who won’t, and meeting with local police and other community leaders to dissect the problem in granular detail.

For Randy Muhammad, the solution to street violence in every era starts with being out on the streets. So on a recent Monday, he approached the type of crowd plenty of people would walk by and avoid eye contact. He sees an opportunity.

The group of men and women were hanging outside Ashmont T station. Some drank beers in brown paper bags, others nips of liquor. One guy rolled a joint. Another wore a balaclava obscuring his face despite the July heat.

Muhammad, senior minister for the Nation of Islam’s Muhammad Mosque No. 11 in Grove Hall, was on an hour-long peace walk through this section of Dorchester with about 30 others. The group walks the streets every Monday night.

“More unites us than divides us,” Muhammad tells those who are here. “We’re an example that we can come together, regardless of what neighborhood you come from.”

Boston, strictly by the numbers, is a safe American city. In 2024, The Economist declared it the safest major city in the nation, a distinction some, though not all, advocates scoff at. After all, if there are still shots being fired on your block, what good is that label?

Muhammad is acutely aware of this.

“It don’t feel safe to everybody,” he said, “but numbers don’t lie.”

This year, those numbers look like this: total shooting incidents in Boston for the year, as of July 19, were at 53, the same tally for the same time frame last year, but below the five-year average of 68. Homicides are down, both year over year and when compared to the five-year average: 13 so far this year, compared to 21 last year over the same period. The five-year average is 17. Those are a fraction of the killings that gripped so many neighborhoods decades ago.

While homicides are also down elsewhere in the US, the number of slayings in Boston is much lower than in cities of comparable size, like Baltimore and Washington, D.C., and much lower than smaller cities like New Orleans.

Among the Black ministers who have done this street-level outreach work, there is little consensus over what has kept street violence in Boston down.

Some credit police engagement with various communities, and the willingness of city officials, nonprofit advocates, and clergy to collaborate and identify shooters and would-be shooters and try to encourage them to choose a different life path.

Some church leaders offer a simple explanation: maybe a critical mass of the really bad guys are locked up or have been rehabilitated.

Others, among 10 clergy interviewed, hail the impact of after-school and extracurricular programming. Some highlight the importance of summer jobs.

“It takes a job to stop a bullet,” said City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, senior pastor of Pleasant Hill Missionary Baptist Church.

Yet others point to gentrification, suggesting that the escalating cost of living may have pushed out some would-be shooters. Some even cite the quality of hospitals, in keeping some gunshot victims from being another murder stat.

Or maybe it’s a combination of all of those factors.

* * *

It was not always this way. In 1990, Boston saw a record-breaking 152 homicides. The driver of that bloodshed was the introduction of crack cocaine in the late 1980s. As that market developed, so did turf-based gangs and the wars that went along with them, according to research from Christopher Winship, a sociology professor at Harvard University.

Boston had a street violence problem, and some people wondered aloud if that level of bloodshed was going to become a permanent reality.

It didn’t. Between 1990 and 1996, homicides in the city dropped about 60 percent. Many city stakeholders believe the decline in violence was driven, at least in part, by Black clergy, according to Harvard research, specifically a consortium of churches known as the Ten-Point Coalition.

Some faith-based leaders participated in Operation Ceasefire, an initiative from the mid-1990s that saw a “fully institutionalized collaboration” among various agencies, including Boston police and outreach workers. It focused on offering gang members ways out, and threatening them with federal sentences in prisons far from their families if they continued to be violent, according to past Globe coverage.

The dip in street violence during the 1990s was eventually called the Boston Miracle, and underpinning it was the street outreach work of Black ministers, who, in working with at-risk youth, “projected a sense of fairness.” Because people trusted them, the Black clergy created “an umbrella of legitimacy for fair and just policing.”

“The police cannot be effective if their activities are not perceived as legitimate by the community,” one of Winship’s research publications stated.

An outgrowth of that effort in the 1990s can still be seen in the basement of Roxbury’s Charles Street AME Church, every Wednesday morning. There, police, including members of the city’s gang unit, probation officers, sheriff’s deputies, representatives from the district attorney’s office, nonprofit staffers, and clergy convene to discuss crime in the city. These weekly meetings have continued since 1998, and some credit the collaboration fostered by such regular communication as helping prevent and mitigate street violence.

“That level of collaboration had never existed anywhere,” said the Rev. Eugene F. Rivers III, pastor at Azusa Christian Community, who founded the weekly meeting during the 1990s and was a leader in the Ten-Point Coalition.

Bishop John M. Borders III, of Morning Star Baptist Church in Mattapan, agrees that cooperation between the political, law enforcement, and pastoral classes of Boston is key. He recalls years in the early 1990s when he would preside over funerals for 25 to 30 murder victims.

“It was a way of life for me,” he said this summer. “It became personally exhausting and I suffered depression as a result of grieving with those families for so many years. So many deaths.”

One of those funerals would become the flashpoint for action and the partnerships lauded by so many in the city. In 1992, a funeral on a Thursday night for a 20-year-old victim of a drive-by shooting was interrupted when a group of young men stabbed a mourner.

Globe coverage of the violence paints a picture of hysteria and chaos: one person was chased through a parking lot and fired several shots from a handgun, one of which went through the open church door and lodged in a wall. Another mourner was pursued by youths up a church aisle toward the altar, almost tripping over the casket before being cornered in an alcove, where the assailants mauled him.

The funeral violence shook Boston, and prompted hundreds of clergy to come together. That spirit of collaboration continues to this day.

“It was the tipping point for the city,” Borders said.

Like Borders, Bishop William E. Dickerson II, senior pastor for Greater Love Tabernacle in Dorchester, has done hundreds of funerals for homicide victims. He grew up in Boston. He knows the city’s history of racism, including a stark racial wealth gap. One doesn’t have to be a scholar to see the link between affluence and reduced levels of street violence.

He has done street-level outreach and is not above getting confrontational to drive his points home, particularly during funeral services.

“You see your boy lying in the casket?” he demonstrated during an interview. “What y’all going to do? Go right back to the block?”

The Rev. Jeffrey Brown, associate pastor at Twelfth Baptist Church in Roxbury and a leader of the Ten-Point Coalition in the 1990s, did street-level ministry work throughout the worst violence of past decades and understood that locking people up was not going to be enough.

Collaboration was key. Sometimes, it meant police allowing clergy to work with gang members to get them on a better track rather than arresting them. Other times, it was city officials securing a job for a young person who was at risk of making some terrible choices.

Brown acknowledged that some people, no matter how they are approached, “are going to do what they’re going to do.” But he estimates that cohort to be a small percentage of those wrapped up in the criminal underground, say 2 to 4 percent.

His message to those embedded in street life was always the same: “The potential of your worth has yet to be seen.”

* * *

Back on the streets of Ashmont, Muhammad, the Nation of Islam minister, is handing out fliers promoting a mediation and conflict resolution hot line.

He’s wearing a bright orange T-shirt emblazoned with a quote from Louis Farrakhan, the Nation of Islam leader who attracted controversy in years past for antisemitic, homophobic, and misogynistic rhetoric. The quote itself is unobjectionable: “Making our communities safe & decent places to live.”

The idea behind events such as the peace walk is to build a rapport with community members, he said. That way, when it comes to disputes that could end in violence, his group can act as a neutral third party.

“We offer an exit ramp,” said Muhammad. Oftentimes, he said, “we’re the only voice of deescalation.”

Muhammad and others will talk to everyone they come across in their walks: men and women, old and young, Black and white. Some cajole strangers to join them on Mondays for the peace walk.

“We have to be vigilant, stay on it,” he said of street violence in Boston. “If you’re not out here being proactive, it just takes an instant . . . it can change.”

Jeremiah Manion of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: Boston at a Bargain: Donna Summer Disco Party, Salem’s quadricentennial
text:
Y2K ON THE WATERFRONT Brush off your cargo pants, butterfly hair clips, and neon tracksuits — AfroDesiaCity will bring its Soulful Bliss festival to the Seaport, and the theme is Y2K and the early aughts. The cultural nostalgia fest will include live performances by DJ Blicky, poets Osamase Ekhator and Herisa the Traveler, and headliner, Boston-bred rapper Nay Speaks. The daylong event will feature an artisan marketplace and gourmet food vendors, and marks the start of AfroDesiaCity’s trio of family-friendly festivities in partnership with Boston Harbor Now, including a Spectacle Island cruise on Sept. 19 and the tall ship on Oct. 10. Aug. 1, 4-10 p.m., Viaduct Plaza, 9 World Trade Center Ave. afrodesiacity.com/soulful-bliss

BORDER STREET BLOCK PARTY Eastie will celebrate the country’s diversity, arts, and flavors with the fifth annual Festival Viva Colombia. The community-centered neighborhood fest — hosted by Latin American nonprofit the Veronica Robles Cultural Center — will include live folkloric dancers and troubadours, artisan vendors, and authentic cuisine for an all-afternoon, full-family affair. Aug. 8, 1-8 p.m., 102 Border St., East Boston. givebutter.com/FestivalVivaCol2026

CURIOSITY WITHOUT A CURFEW Escape the heat and open your mind at SubSpace, the Museum of Science’s programming series for adults, where many of this month’s events center on the intersection of science and storytelling. Spoken word poetry explored through neuroscience, imagination and innovation optimized with an Afrofuturism lens, and a conversation on Haitian heritage and history — in partnership with the Toussaint Louverture Cultural Center — shed light on the living sciences around each and all of us. Various dates, Museum of Science, 1 Science Park. Registration required. mos.org/events

SECOND SHIFT AT THE SQUARE The Greenway’s Off the Clock series will pop up in Dewey Square this month. Dewey After Dark begins as the sun sets with two DJs, glow-in-the-dark face painting, and a blacklight “dance floor.” (The floor is Dewey Square.) Rixy’s electrifying “The Midnight Ride” mural provides the perfect on-theme backdrop for the occasion, but the aptly named Night Shift Brewery, which is seasonally on-site and will extend hours for the event, is just coincidence. Aug. 14, 7:30-10 p.m., Dewey Square, Boston. rosekennedygreenway.org/events/dewey-after-dark

BUG OUT Aspiring entomologists can join the Arnold Arboretum team on an insect safari in the Conifer Collection. Attendees of all ages will have access to digital microscopes, nets, and bug boxes as real-life bug experts help identify whatever creepy (or cute) crawlies you happen to find. The excursion is a drop-in event and we assume the plan is to set critters free once they’ve been ooh-ed and ahh-ed over and ID-ed. Our apologies to parents ahead of time should we be wrong. Arnold Arboretum. 125 Arborway. Aug. 15, 10 a.m.-noon. Registration required, rain date Aug. 16. arboretum.harvard.edu/event/all-ages-insect-safari-2

AN UN-RAGER Call it a night — before midnight. That’s the promise of High Street Place’s Home Before Midnight dance night. A (let’s be honest) millennial-centric DJ night that boasts throwback hits, a non-alcoholic drink menu, and a 6 p.m. start time. The downtown food hall’s vendors and bar will remain open, so dance breaks can be occupied by burgers, burritos, and bubbly. Aug. 15, 6-11 p.m., High Street Place Food Hall, 100 High St. highstreetplace.com

PLANT PARENTS, RISE UP It’s not too late to stretch your green thumb this summer. Long Live Beer Works is hosting what they’re calling a Swap & Prop — a BYOP (bring your own plant) event where attendees can clip and trade houseplant cuttings for propagation. Attendees are encouraged to also grab a pint with your fellow plant parents, but while cuttings are free, a drink will cost you some green. Aug. 16, 1-6 p.m., Long Live Roxbury Brewery + Taproom, 152 Hampden St. longlivebeerworks.com

OPENING ACTS This month, Global Arts Live presents live performances by Puerto Rican genre-benders (and Bad Bunny collaborators) Chuwi and highlife groove band Kotoko Brass to celebrate the Platform, the nonprofit’s soon-to-be performance home in Kendall. The outdoor concert series — which concludes with Rebirth Brass Band on Sept. 2 — will take place in nearby, picnic-friendly Termeer Square. Chuwi on Aug. 19, Kotoko Brass on Aug. 26; both at 6 p.m. 675 W Kendall St., Cambridge. globalartslive.org/events

BARTER SYSTEM REBOOT Givvy — a new, Boston-based networking platform — replicates its online model IRL with a regular in-person exchange, this month at Aeronaut Brewing Co. The idea is this: exchange your hard skills for someone else’s, e.g. your coding know-how for someone else’s plumbing expertise or your gift-wrapping prowess for use of a flatbed truck for an upcoming move. Organizers assure no cash should change hands and everyone starts on the same footing, so there’s no need to sweet talk your way to an ask. Aug. 26, 5:30-7 p.m., Aeronaut Brewing Company, 14 Tyler St., Somerville. luma.com/861nk7kg

The annual event — featuring ’70s dance floor lighting, glow sticks, and, of course, the soundtrack of Dorchester’s own Queen of Disco — starts before sundown and transports attendees to summers past under a glittering disco ball. DJ Vince 1 will keep things spinning, and revelers are encouraged to bring their own skates and their best moves. Aug. 28, 5-9 p.m., City Hall Plaza. boston.gov/calendar/donna-summer-disco-party
