title: For the sake of community and fun music, Boston Landmarks Orchestra performs its concerts for free
text:
Since Wilkins took over leadership, the orchestra has tried to attract audiences through what he calls a “strategy of participation,” he said.

“Partnerships, and collaborations, and invitations to communities who wouldn’t ordinarily think of symphonic music are very much front of mind.”

In other words, Landmarks is equally as likely to collaborate with the likes of the New England Aquarium, Brazilian drumming project Grooversity, and Haitian and Armenian dance companies as they are to pull in a Boys and Girls club or a local music education program such as Boston Strings Academy. American Sign Language interpreters are present at most Landmarks events. Some concerts even make haptic vests available, to provide a tactile experience of the music for deaf and hard of hearing attendees.

“We tend to program backwards. We first think of who we can get involved, and then we think, ‘What can we program to support that collaboration?’” said Wilkins. “I think it’s been really effective, and fun, and…the orchestra’s stretched artistically, because it’s playing some music orchestras don’t usually play.”

In the earliest years, concerts were slightly more formal and standard-repertoire driven “after the Arthur Fiedler model,” explained Paula Oakes, a violinist who has been in the ensemble since its second season.

Landmarks started regularly performing at the Hatch Shell in 2007, a handful of years after the Pops Esplanade Orchestra (in which several Landmarks players also play) scaled back its summer concerts in the city.

“It’s not a situation where it’s high-falutin’ classical music,” said trumpeter Dana Oakes, another longtime Landmarks player and Paula’s husband. “It’s a really good vibe out there.”

There’s little separation from the sights and sounds of the city, with cars driving along Storrow Drive on one side and joggers and dog walkers taking the Esplanade path on the other. Anyone can leave the concert and come back without consequence. It perhaps follows naturally that there’s barely any enforcement of the usual rules of orchestral concert hall etiquette, even those some might take for granted, such as sitting quietly while the orchestra plays.

It’s not unusual to see young children with batons in hand “conducting” the orchestra from a music stand near the Hatch Shell (cutely dubbed the “Maestro Zone”) or patrons wandering to a nearby ice cream truck mid-concert; or people listening while they play card games. With a much different atmosphere than Boston’s temples of music like Symphony Hall, the Hatch shell during these concerts feels like a gathering place, where people can choose to socialize in parallel with the music.

And that’s not even getting into the music Wilkins chooses. “With all due respect, Charles had a great concept for the orchestra, but this is something Charles would not have done: reach out to what would not be considered classical by any stretch, and somehow weave it into a program that’s seamless,” said Paula Oakes.

Landmarks’s repertoire mixes symphonies and other large-scale works from the standard repertoire with some film music, the Leroy Anderson-esque fare sometimes called “light classical,” orchestrations of genre-crossing modern tunes, and the occasional world premiere, such as 2018’s “Pegasus Promenade,” which was collectively composed by Gonzalo Grau and four students and alumni of East Boston arts program ZUMIX.

Paula Oakes admitted she doesn’t adore every piece she plays with Landmarks, but that’s not a negative in her reckoning. “It stretches your imagination, it stretches your technique,” she said.

Wilkins “made the programs we play much more challenging, and he just included so many different types of music as well,” Dana concurred.

Because Landmarks’s outdoor season is confined to the short New England summer, the orchestra has been making overtures towards performing more indoor concerts as well during and outside its standard performing weeks. This weekend, the orchestra brings a program including Mozart’s Symphony No. 40 and Max Richter’s recomposition of Vivaldi’s “Four Seasons” to churches in Jamaica Plain and Roxbury; next week, it’s back to the Hatch Shell for Verdi’s massive “Requiem” on the evening of August 5 with the One City Choir and Cantata Singers.

So far, the indoor audiences haven’t been as large as the lawn crowds on the Esplanade, but Wilkins sees it as “not as much about the numbers,” that being more important that people attend in the first place, he said.

“I think for the most part, people understand what our mission is,” he said. “I think it’s pretty obvious that we’re using great music to create community connection.”

Though a summer rainstorm soaked the Esplanade a few hours before showtime on July 22, that community connection seemed to be in abundance at the first concert of the season, which was performed to an all-ages crowd including a handful of multigenerational families and even a few dogs. Many brought sandwiches and other picnic fare; one ambitious group even brought their own table and spread out a Thai takeout feast. A young musician who had performed in the prelude concert happily added a Landmarks Orchestra sticker to the collection of Sanrio characters on her cello case. Couples wandered down the path holding hands, some lingering for a few minutes to listen, some content to enjoy the music as they passed by. A tattooed man in all black ate popcorn out of a plastic bag with chopsticks.

Landmarks season ”is one of my favorite times of year,” said state representative Jay Livingstone from the stage, naming the most crucial key to Landmarks’s success. “Anyone can come down the Esplanade and enjoy it.”

title: Sharing the streets and mitigating the risks
text:
That conclusion defies both compassion and empirical evidence. Protected bike lanes save lives — not every life, but neither do other public safety measures, from gun laws to vaccinations. A study of 12 cities found that bike infrastructure reduced deaths of all road users by 44 percent.

What about those on, as Vennochi puts it, “the side of business”? Research has found the economic impact of bike lanes to be positive or neutral. This is just one data point among many pointing to the benefits of a bike-friendly city for all Bostonians.

After a truck killed Louisa Gag, a transportation planner with the city, Mayor Michelle Wu reaffirmed her commitment to stalled transit projects. The city should fund and speedily implement them. Because no one, I trust, is on the side of deadly “stuff” happening on Boston’s streets.

Mary Battenfeld

Jamaica Plain

After weeks of excellent journalism in the Globe on the preventable death of Louisa Gag, Joan Vennochi’s “Safe streets in Boston require more than choosing sides” felt like a slap in the face. As Democratic state Representative Marjorie Decker of Cambridge said at the last Ride for Your Life event, street safety is a public health issue.

I never thought I would see the Globe publish a column basically accepting the status quo of loss and death when we have proven solutions to make our streets safer: fewer cars on the road, ways to get drivers to slow down, and protections from vehicles.

Somerville, which has invested in a range of traffic-calming measures, has accomplished its third year without traffic deaths. It’s not that streets can’t be made safer — Boston just lacks the political will to make changes. Studies show that protected bike lanes save lives. My question is: Why must we always require a human sacrifice to decide the time has come to build them?

Anne Griepenburg

Roxbury

As a driver, a pedestrian, and someone who gets around by bike, the refrain that cyclists don’t obey the laws is laughable. On a bike you get an up-close and personal demonstration, on a daily basis, that many, many drivers and pedestrians can’t be bothered to obey the rules. So I find it hypocritical that the expectation is that people on bikes should be different. Particularly when the potential for harm heavily skews to the cars.

mikebbruinsfans

BostonGlobe.com

Wouldn’t it be great if everyone obeyed our traffic laws, but that’s simply not the case. Enforce the rules, please!

munu12

BostonGlobe.com

Yes, Joan Vennochi, listening to others is important and necessary in a democratic society. We want people to “feel” heard. At the same time, let’s be clear: For a lot of people, being heard and consulted will never be sufficient if they don’t get what they want. When you make the roads safer for ALL — by narrowing them, eliminating some parking spaces to build bump-outs, installing a stop sign or a speed bump, constructing bus-only lanes, or adding protected bike lanes — there will be people who lose out. And those are first and foremost people who like to drive unencumbered. More important than having endless consultations that end up preventing change from ever happening, the city needs to experiment.

titpitina

BostonGlobe.com

Re “My bicycle could save the world … if you’d all just stop trying to kill me” by Rami Abou-Sabe (Opinion, July 21): Three cyclists — Louisa Gag, 36; Denise Olsen, 74; and Mark Salvador, 39 — have been killed on Massachusetts roads in July alone. They were more than statistics. They were loved ones who expected to make it to their destination safely.

As someone who relies on a bicycle and public transit rather than a car, these deaths feel personal. I bike 9 miles from my home in Malden to work in the Longwood area. Bike lanes make much of my route safer, but the danger lies in the gaps — where cyclists are treated as obstacles rather than fellow users of the streets.

That attitude, common in the comments people post on news stories following these tragedies, has real consequences. Pedestrians deserve sidewalks even though some jaywalk. Drivers deserve safe roads even though some run red lights. Yet cyclists are often denied infrastructure proven to save lives.

Helsinki went a full year without a traffic fatality. Somerville has gone three years without one.

Safe streets are not anti-car. They are pro-community.

We all deserve to get home safely, no matter how we travel.

Michael Hogan

Malden

As a kid and then for the last 25 years as an adult, I’d say riding my bike on the street is the most dangerous thing I do. If I were to ride in Boston, it would be much more dangerous. I don’t know how you guys do it. To me it’s just unacceptably dangerous, for all the reasons Rami Abou-Sabe outlined. I have decided to ride minimally on the streets of my rural town and take my chances with the deer and coyotes on trails. I really don’t like seeing aggressive cyclists alienating car drivers and giving the rest of us a bad name. That being said, too many behind the wheel are either clueless about cyclist (and pedestrian) safety or actually hostile toward them.

Hoping

BostonGlobe.com

Be careful out there.

coolbeanz

BostonGlobe.com

title: A second grant program overseen by MassHousing is a focus of fraud allegations and state investigation
text:
In the Vanderburgh case, a sprinkler installer told the Globe that Foote had done something similar, using a legitimate invoice from when the contractor previously did work for Foote to create phony ones for other locations where he did little or no work.

Steven DeLiberto of WAM Fire Protection said the bogus invoices on his letterhead featured his electronic signature — which he disavowed — and specified that various payments were due “forthwith.”

“I don’t use words like ‘forthwith,’” DeLiberto said, calling himself “just the sprinkler guy, moderately intelligent. … Nope, I leave that for reporters and highly educated college guys like Hunter. That’s for people who are smarter than I’ll ever be.”

After consulting with DeLiberto and conducting inspections in late 2024 and early 2025, MassHousing determined Foote “misrepresented” the extent of work completed at seven sober homes and told him to return the agency’s money. In three cases, inspectors found no work at all had been done, according to the letters, though the grants had been almost fully paid out based on invoices submitted by Foote and his associates.

All told, the agency demanded Foote and the associates give back more than $430,000. None of it has been returned to date.

Paul McMorrow, a MassHousing spokesperson, said the agency “takes allegations of potential fraud and noncompliance seriously.” He noted staffers took “immediate action” after identifying discrepancies in the sprinkler program in 2024, demanding the return of the money and referring the matter to the attorney general.

The sprinkler program and the problems with Gateway Cities grants were both referred to the Massachusetts attorney general, whose office confirmed to the Globe it is investigating both matters.

In an interview with the Globe, Foote denied any wrongdoing and said he doesn’t believe he owes the state anything. He acknowledged preparing the disputed invoices, but said if there were any inflated claims of progress, they were based on assertions from DeLiberto, whom he trusted at the time. He said he paid DeLiberto for all of the work listed on invoices and then billed the state.

Foote said he eventually completed all of the jobs, except for two where he determined sprinklers weren’t needed under local law, and spent hundreds of thousands of dollars of his own money to do it.

He said he submitted voluminous paperwork to MassHousing documenting compliance more than a year ago, but, “it’s been radio silence for a long time.” He did not share the paperwork with the Globe, which requested it.

The fire sprinkler grant program is the second program overseen by a now-former MassHousing official in which grantees have been accused of submitting — and receiving payment for — bogus invoices for work that was not performed.

The Globe Spotlight team reported in June that developers Gary Acquah and Reggie Woods, who received $1.4 million in grant money from MassHousing to rehabilitate blighted apartments in Worcester and Pittsfield, submitted invoices claiming more than $500,000 in work was done by at least nine subcontractors who said they didn’t do the jobs and weren’t paid for them.

Many of those subcontractors had done other work for Acquah and Woods, and they believed the pair used their earlier invoices as a template for fake ones.

Both programs were overseen by Tony Richards II, who resigned July 17 as vice president of strategic community initiatives for MassHousing. His departure came three weeks after the Globe reported he had steered the Gateway Cities grant money to Acquah and Woods months after they sold Richards a home in West Roxbury for $204,000 less than its original list price.

For the sprinkler program, MassHousing would not provide the Globe with contractor invoices and other records related to payments to Foote and his affiliates, citing an exemption in the public records law for documents that are part of an open investigation.

The Fire Sprinkler Safety Program was designed to cover most or all of the cost of installing sprinklers at sober homes around the state amid new regulations. The program offered up to $80,000 to sober homes that had been in operation for at least a year and certified by a nonprofit association.

But as with the grants in the Gateway Cities housing program, MassHousing did not inspect the sprinkler installations before it paid for the bulk of the work, a setup one watchdog group criticized.

“Any system of internal controls that relies on trust is not a system of internal controls,” said Mary Connaughton, director of government transparency at the Pioneer Institute, a right-leaning think tank. “Onsite inspections would obviously be the best solution.”

Connaughton added, “It would make sense for MassHousing to take a really close look at their policies,” especially because “this is the second kind of incident where this has happened.”

The seven homes where the state is disputing the payments are all linked to Foote, a Worcester entrepreneur who operates sober homes in Springfield, Taunton, New Bedford, and other locations and also offers franchising arrangements.

Foote acknowledged challenges with getting sprinklers installed at the nine properties for which he received grants. Ultimately, he told the Globe, work was completed at all but two, at a cost of more than $900,000 — significantly more than what he received from MassHousing. He said the scope of work at the two incomplete jobs had been scaled back for valid reasons.

Foote denied knowingly submitting fake invoices. He said the requests for payment he made on DeLiberto’s letterhead reflected the contractor’s assertions of how much work had been completed at the time. However, he declined to say how much he paid DeLiberto for work that he now alleges the contractor did not do. Foote has not filed a lawsuit seeking to recover money from DeLiberto.

What really matters, Foote said, is that the sprinklers were eventually installed.

“We’re ready to address any concerns,” Foote said. “But we need to know what they are and what we need to do about them. If it’s a permit closeout, we’ll close it out. We spent more money than was disbursed to us by a significant factor. It did take a long time, and it was very frustrating. But it all got done.”

DeLiberto, for his part, flatly denied Foote’s claims.

“He’s a worthless piece of [expletive] who continues to lie about everything,” DeLiberto said.

Moreover, in at least three cases, public records raise questions about Foote’s assertion that the work was completed satisfactorily. In Taunton, Deputy Fire Chief Robert Bastis told the Globe the city has not approved any sprinkler systems at two properties for which Foote received grants.

“From our perspective, there are no fire sprinklers, no building permits, no fire inspections” on record for those properties, Bastis said.

Likewise, in New Bedford, a permit application for a sprinkler system at a Vanderburgh sober home was rejected by inspectors with the city’s Department of Public Infrastructure in late 2024. No permit was ever approved, officials said.

Foote provided the Globe with documents showing a private firm had inspected those three systems in July 2025 and said there were “no deficiencies observed.” MassHousing’s contract with grant recipients says all jobs must be inspected and approved by municipal authorities. Foote did not respond to a question from the Globe about why some of the Vanderburgh jobs lacked such a designation.

Records show the firm that did the inspections, Tristar Fire Protection, has taken out a lien on Foote’s New Bedford sober home over unpaid bills of more than $16,000.

Since the problems were discovered in 2024, MassHousing has made some changes, according to agency officials, including “immediate re-inspection” of all fire sprinkler projects and new protocols requiring multiple inspections of such projects in the future.

Originally, the sprinkler program imposed no deadlines. The program’s current rules require work to be complete in 12 months, with the possibility of a six-month extension.

It does not appear MassHousing’s board, which is appointed by the governor, was made aware of the problems its staff discovered in either the sprinkler program or the Gateway Cities program. The Globe could not find records of any discussion in board minutes. Board Chair Jeanne Pinado declined to comment, deferring questions to the agency’s communications office. A MassHousing spokesperson also declined to comment.

Six of the board’s nine members were appointed by Governor Maura Healey, who has said little about the problems at MassHousing.

An internal audit by MassHousing published late last year made cryptic reference to recent “control improvements” to some programs under Richards’s oversight after management had “self-identified” shortcomings. McMorrow, the agency spokesperson, said it “has revamped grant application intake and evaluation processes, clarified design standards, created new grant closing checklists, improved invoicing and disbursement processes, and instituted mandatory third-party construction inspections.”

title: Boston Public Library welcomes new chef-in-residence
text:
Suman Shah’s journey has taken her from Bihar, India, her hometown; to Bombay; to Boston. And as of this month, she’s setting up shop at the Boston Public Library’s Nutrition Lab, where she has been named the new chef-in-residence.

Shah, the latest appointee to the BPL’s two-year-old program based out of the Shaw-Roxbury branch in Nubian Square, is the founder of Fork On a Road, an Ayurvedic-inspired maker of spice blends and vegetarian meal kits rooted in the ancient Indian practice of using herbs, spices, and food to support overall wellness. She’s also spent years teaching cooking classes that show people how everyday meals can nourish the body and even play a role in healing.

Her experience will carry over into this role, where she’ll lead conversations about cultural food traditions, and help community members build confidence in the kitchen and learn more about nutrition. Shah considers the work deeply personal: Her belief in food as medicine grew while caring for her aging parents, and became even more meaningful during her own recovery from cancer. Her classes will feature plant-based and vegetarian recipes, with an emphasis on making healthy cooking simple, flavorful, and culturally relevant.

Get Food & Dining Headlines

The Globe's most recent food stories, delivered to your inbox every Wednesday.

Enter Email

“I’m hoping to broaden people’s approach to food and cooking and open the door to a conversation,” Shah said. “And focus on flavor, which comes from spices.”

This year’s residency theme is “How We Gather,” and Shah plans to implement that by offering what she calls “gathering guidance”— how to bring people together, whether it’s around the dinner table or community events.

Throughout the year, the Nutrition Lab offers not only free, hands-on cooking classes, but also menu-planning assistance, one-on-one sessions, and guest speakers.

“The program is not just a resource for the four square blocks around the library,” Shah said. “It’s open to everybody in the city.”

The Nutrition Lab events begin in September and will be listed at bpl.org/nutrition-lab. The Shaw-Roxbury Library is at 149 Dudley St., Roxbury, 617-442-6186.

Ann Trieger Kurland can be reached at anntrieger@gmail.com.

title: Boston man arrested in shooting near Hyde Park restaurant that killed one, injured four
text:
Prosecutors released more details about the circumstances of the shooting in court, describing how investigators identified Derima in graphic videos that showed how a physical altercation escalated suddenly to shots fired. But some key questions still remain unanswered, including how many shooters were involved and what started the preceding fight.

The violence took place outside Little Haiti International Cuisine, which has recently drawn noise complaints and other concerns from neighbors.

One video showed Reynolds fighting with another unnamed person, who was apparently holding a gun and bleeding from his back, according to a police report. Sometime during the altercation, the gun was discharged into the air, and Reynolds fell to the ground, Suffolk Assistant District Attorney Ben Sabol said during the arraignment. While Reynolds was lying there on his back, Derima approached him, brandished a gun, and fired it “at least twice at his chest and torso area,” Sabol said. He said Derima’s clothing matched what the shooter was wearing in the videos.

Both Reynolds and Derima later arrived at Boston Medical Center for treatment of gunshot wounds, according to the police report.

Derima was arrested after being discharged from the hospital. During a brief interview with police, he admitted he was outside the restaurant when a fight broke out, according to prosecutors. “He did concede that there was gunfire that resulted in him also being shot that evening,” Sabol said.

Derima said his memory wasn’t clear because “he had been drinking and … lost a lot of blood since being shot,” the police report said.

Derima’s defense attorney, Anthony Ellison, firmly disputed the prosecution’s account and questioned where the fatal bullet came from.

“They got the wrong guy,” he said during remarks to reporters after the arraignment. He said more information will come out as the case proceeds.

“This is a live case. A lot of witnesses and a lot of evidence is going to be turned over, and we’ll get to the bottom of it,” he said.

Ellison noted some of Derima’s family members attended the hearing. Derima was allowed to hide behind a partially open door, meaning he wasn’t visible from the courtroom gallery.

In a statement Monday morning, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden thanked investigators “for such quick and effective work leading to this arrest of the man directly responsible for the killing.”

“Heinous acts like what happened a few days ago in Hyde Park show an utter disregard for the sanctity of life and tear at the fabric of our communities,” he said. “This investigation is continuing and we will hold anyone involved in this multiple shooting accountable for their actions.”

Police responded around 12:40 a.m. Monday to 1184 Hyde Park Ave., the address of Little Haiti International Cuisine. Boston police had been stationing officers outside the club on weekend nights around closing time because of complaints from the surrounding residential area.

City records show Little Haiti has also been brought before the Boston Licensing Board several times in recent years, including for allegations of operating after hours and over capacity.

The business expanded its operations in May 2025 to close at 1 a.m., records show. Posts on its Instagram account advertised a party starting at 4 p.m. Sunday with DJs, Haitian food, and no cover charge for women before 11:30 p.m.

In addition to Reynolds and Derima, three other gunshot victims were transported to local hospitals via ambulance, with one person “possibly being both stabbed and shot,” according to the police report.

At the scene Tuesday afternoon, a Boston police cruiser was stationed outside the restaurant and its entrance remained roped off with yellow crime tape. A bouquet of blue and white hydrangeas lay wilting on the sidewalk nearby.

In the immediate aftermath of the shooting, some local leaders have called for increased police staffing and more public safety resources.

“These complex cases require significant resources to investigate and prosecute,” leaders of the Boston Police Detectives Benevolent Society said in a statement Monday. The union called on department leadership to hire more detectives, saying the bureau is significantly understaffed.

“It is long past time to move on from campaign slogans and accept the reality for many Boston residents who no longer feel safe in their own neighborhoods,” said City Councilor Ed Flynn, also in a statement released Monday.

Similar demands also surfaced after a violent Fourth of July weekend that left two people dead and 11 others injured in gunfire.

While city officials have acknowledged the recent tragedies, they’ve also pointed to crime stats showing that violence remains relatively rare, especially compared to other major cities.

Boston has recorded 18 homicides so far in 2026, compared to 22 at this time last year, according to police data.

State court records show Derima has a criminal history that includes assault and domestic violence charges, most of which were ultimately dismissed by prosecutors. A warrant was issued last month for failure to appear in a credit card forgery case from 2024, records show. His next scheduled court date in the murder case is Sept. 4.

title: Beacon Hill’s biggest defender may be Healey
text:
Collins is facing two Democrats in September, most notably Latoya Gayle, a Michelle Wu-backed activist from Dorchester. Rush is confronting his first primary challenge since winning his Senate seat in 2010, this time from Hyde Park attorney Persis Yu.

Add those to the list of at-risk incumbents Healey is backing this cycle. She has already endorsed state Senator William Brownsberger, a Belmont Democrat facing another Wu-endorsed challenger, Daniel Lander. The governor, according to her campaign, has also lined up behind state Representative Marjorie Decker, who is facing a rematch from Evan MacKay, the Democratic Socialists of America-backed challenger who nearly ousted her in 2024. Earlier this week, Healey endorsed state Representative John Lawn, backing the veteran lawmaker in his primary against Newton City Councilor Alison Leary.

And she’s throwing her support behind state Representative Christine Barber in the crowded race to replace state Senator Patricia Jehlen.

None of those candidates are obvious underdogs, and most are the more moderate picks (relatively speaking) in their respective races. Backing them over insurgent newcomers is also reflective of the realities the Healey is facing in her role as governor. Even if lawmakers occasionally drag their feet on (or ignore) some of her legislative priorities, Healey needs like-minded allies in office in order to get her priorities passed — a circumstance she nodded to in statements Wednesday announcing several of the endorsements.

She said it’s a “privilege to work alongside” Barber. Her administration’s attempts to tackle the state’s high housing costs? She “couldn’t do it without legislative partners” like Collins. And Rush “has been critical in passing laws that help regular people,” she said.

It’s also a notably more cautious approach for the Arlington Democrat, who hasn’t always shied away from political risk. As attorney general, Healey was one of the first high-profile politicians to throw her weight behind Ayanna Pressley in her successful attempt to oust then-US Representative Mike Capuano, a 10-term incumbent.

Four years later, with her own gubernatorial primary all but wrapped up, she deployed her campaign operation to help lift Andrea Campbell to victory in the heated and expensive Democratic primary for attorney general.

Her strategy now sits in sharp contrast to Wu. The Boston mayor spent much of her first term using her political power to elect allies to the city council — which paid off when she needed votes to muscle through priorities or stop proposals in their tracks. Now, she’s seeing just how far that political operation can travel, backing Lander in a district anchored by Boston suburbs and Gayle in another that treads on territory in the city that hasn’t been particularly friendly to her.

Wu is simultaneously escalating a simmering power struggle on Beacon Hill, putting herself on the opposite side of legislative leaders — and now, Healey.

Whether Healey’s endorsements amount to more than a press release remains to be seen. She has a reelection campaign of her own to run, and it’s unclear how much time she’ll devote to, say, appearing at campaign events for legislative allies.

Healey is also notably passing on endorsing in what’s arguably the state’s most closely watched primary: the US Senate contest pitting Senator Ed Markey against Representative Seth Moulton.

“I have respect for both of them,” Healey told WBUR in June, “and that’ll be for the voters of Massachusetts to decide.”

IN OTHER ENDORSEMENT NEWS: House Minority Whip Katherine Clark is endorsing Brownsberger for reelection, the latest Democratic heavyweight to back the veteran state senator’s reelection bid.

The duo have a little bit of history: Brownsberger and Clark squared off in the 2013 scramble for the then-open Fifth Congressional District seat, a Democratic primary that Clark ultimately won. The two had served in the state Senate together for roughly two years to that point.

“Will is one of the most effective legislators I have had the privilege to work alongside,” Clark said in a statement shared by Brownsberger’s campaign. “He shows up, does the work, and never stops fighting for our neighbors.”

CROSSING PARTY LINES: Former governor and NCAA president Charlie Baker is still playing in Massachusetts politics — and not just on the Republican side.

Baker and former lieutenant governor Karyn Polito are headlining a Boston fundraiser for Democratic state Representative Chris Markey next week amid Markey’s run for Bristol County District Attorney, according to an invitation obtained by the Globe.

Markey does have a GOP opponent. Seth Aitken, a Swansea resident and attorney, launched his campaign last summer. But the Dartmouth Democrat and Baker have a history: Markey was one of a handful of Democratic state representatives who endorsed Baker during his successful 2018 reelection campaign.

PROGRE$$IVE CHANGE: Pressley is heading back to her hometown this fall to headline a fundraiser for Citizen Action/Illinois, a public interest group pushing progressive policies in the state.

Ticket prices for the Sept. 18 event in Chicago range from $250 to $10,000, according to a copy of the invite the Globe’s James Pindell got a hold of.

CHECK IT: A lot of accusations were lobbed during Markey and Moulton’s chippy debate Monday. WBUR’s Anthony Brooks fact-checked some of the biggest claims each candidate made — including Moulton’s Epstein files comments.

LOCATION, LOCATION, LOCATION: Suffolk DA candidates Linda Champion, Rachael Rollins defend their residency ahead of election by Gayla Cawley, Boston Herald: Suffolk DA candidate and Norfolk County homeowner Linda Champion said she moved to Boston in April, but didn’t achieve full occupancy until May. She confirmed to the Herald that she registered her campaign and took out nomination papers to run for Suffolk DA while using her new Hyde Park address before the home was issued an occupancy permit by the City of Boston.

Rachael Rollins, the former Suffolk County district attorney seeking the office again, is listed on the state elections website as being registered at a Roxbury address for the Sept. 1 Democratic primary, though property records show that she has declared her homestead or primary residence in Medford since 2003.

LOWELL REPORT: Massachusetts House primary spotlights Lowell’s growing Cambodian political influence by Trajan Warren, GBH News: In recent years, one Massachusetts House district in Lowell has become a contest of Cambodian leadership. This fall’s primary will be no different. Tara Hong, the 26-year-old incumbent, is a first-term state representative. He ousted state Representative Rady Mom in 2024 after trying to unseat the incumbent two years before, at age 22. But Sokhary Chau could keep Hong from a second term. The 53-year-old, a Lowell city councilor, was the first Cambodian to become mayor of an American city when he was chosen by the Lowell City Council in 2022.

SAFETY FIRST: Downtown attacks prompt civic leaders to hold new meetings on public safety by Jon Chesto, The Boston Globe: The mood seemed cautiously optimistic, maybe even hopeful, when civic and business leaders gathered at Emerson’s Cutler Majestic Theatre to discuss public safety in the downtown last October. The takeaway: Concerted efforts to address everything from shoplifting to drug dealing in Boston’s central business district seemed to be working.

But flash forward nine months, and the same old concerns are reemerging — concerns that could get in the way of ensuring downtown Boston is a thriving residential and commercial hub. Downtown’s prominent stakeholders in government, nonprofits, business, and law enforcement will gather again on Wednesday in the biggest summit to address the issue since that event at the Cutler last fall.

CAM COURTERS: Boston police, district attorney sued over fatal shooting video by Sean Cotter, The Boston Globe: A progressive advocacy group is suing the Suffolk County district attorney’s office and Boston Police Department, seeking the release of impounded video showing a police officer shooting a man to death earlier this year.

Lawyers for Civil Rights is seeking the release of the police body-worn camera footage showing the death of Stephenson King, a 39-year-old man Officer Nicholas O’Malley shot during a traffic stop on March 11 following a reported carjacking. The shooting led to a public outcry for more information — and to criminal charges. The Suffolk DA’s office announced a manslaughter charge against O’Malley less than two weeks after King’s death. It was the first time in three decades a police officer was charged with an on-duty killing.

WU ON STREETS: ‘I am furious’: Wu reflects on city planner killed while cycling, talks about street safety plans by Shannon Larson, The Boston Globe: The death of Louisa Gag, a Roslindale native who was responsible for helping improve roadways and expand city bikes, sparked furor from residents and cycling advocates. They demanded swift action from Wu, who ran for mayor as a champion for transit infrastructure, and said the tragedy could have been prevented.

“I’m never going to get over it,” an emotional Wu said on “Morning Edition” Tuesday. “I will always have Louisa on my heart as long as I am able to do anything to try to fix and improve our community.”

SPOT THE DIFFERENCE: In spring, Cambridge officials turned ShotSpotter off. Now, they’re turning it back on. by Spencer Buell, The Boston Globe: Depending on the audience, it was either a flip-flop under pressure, or a show of humility from elected leaders willing to give the public more say in how decisions are made.

This company should be in Massachusetts by Emma Platoff, The Boston Globe.

Nearly 15 years after student discipline reform, school suspensions in Mass. are falling. Are emergency removals taking their place? by Hallie Claflin, CommonWealth Beacon.

title: Paths for people with disabilities are a key element of safe streets
text:
We are members of Shared Spaces, a coalition convened by the Boston Center for Independent Living with WalkMassachusetts, MassBike, Boston Cyclists Union, Transportation for Massachusetts, and individual disability and deaf-blind advocates. Our mission is to promote collaboration and understanding of the challenges associated with shared spaces, such as bike lanes, sidewalks, crosswalks, and bus stops statewide. We are committed to advocating for safety and accessibility in the design of these spaces, focusing on the unique experiences of individuals with disabilities.

As we work to improve street safety in honor of Boston transportation planner Louisa Gag, who was killed last month when she was hit by a truck while cycling, we affirm that our streets must serve and protect everyone, especially the most vulnerable. That includes people walking, rolling, biking, using mobility devices, taking transit, and traveling by other forms of micromobility.

Safe, accessible street design is not a choice between disability rights and bicycle infrastructure. Protected bike lanes can and must be built while considering the need for accessible van ramps and accessible parking spaces, accessible sidewalks, safe crossings, accessible transit stops, and accessibly designed curb space.

By advancing solutions that reflect the principles of universal design and mobility justice, we can build streets that expand independence, improve safety, and ensure that everyone can travel with dignity. This work would honor Gag’s legacy.

title: 14-year-old charged with carrying loaded gun in Jamaica Plain
text:
A 14-year-old was arrested in Jamaica Plain Thursday after police found him carrying a loaded gun in his waistband, officials said.

The teenager is expected to be arraigned in West Roxbury Municipal Court on charges of carrying a loaded firearm without a license, assault and battery on a police officer, and vandalism, police said.

Around noon on Thursday, officers with the Youth Violence Strike Force watched the 14-year-old, who they had been informed was in possession of a gun, get into a vehicle outside his residence. When they pulled the car over on Centre Street, police noted that the teenager was breathing heavily as they approached the vehicle.

After he was asked to get out of the vehicle, officers found a loaded gun on the left side of his waistband, police said. Police identified and released the driver, while the 14-year-old was taken into custody.

Police said the teenager “tensed up,” when officers tried to take his phone during booking, leading to “a brief struggle” in which he “pushed an officer.” The teenager was eventually subdued, officials said.

title: Blame the red-hot Red Sox for a mild Mass. campaign season?
text:
At least, that’s one tongue-in-cheek theory from Secretary of State William F. Galvin, who suggested that voters may have more on their minds than September primaries.

“I don’t sense that there’s any great excitement about the election in September,” Galvin said in an interview Thursday. “Now, you can offer a lot of other reasons for that. … There are other things people are paying attention to. First, we had all the World Cup stuff. Now we’re getting the revival of the Red Sox. There are a lot of distractions.”

Whether baseball is actually siphoning off attention from politics is another question. But Galvin’s broader point reflects a reality of this year’s campaign season: With just weeks until voters head to the polls, there hasn’t been the same buzz that accompanied previous statewide primaries despite a handful of contested congressional races and a (sort of) nationally watched US Senate Democratic primary at the top of the ticket.

It’s an election cycle that feels “pretty flat,” Galvin said — and an unusually early pre-Labor Day primary that aligns with the annual Sept. 1 move-in rush across Greater Boston doesn’t help. That said, Galvin said he expects participation to land roughly where it has in past mid-term election cycles, which also didn’t set ballots ablaze.

As of Thursday morning, more than 570,000 voters had requested mail-in ballots, and roughly 46,000 had turned them in, according to Galvin. The number the state sent out is similar to 2022, the last statewide election year, when nearly 480,000 people ultimately voted by mail, accounting for nearly half of the 1 million ballots cast in those September primaries, according to data from Galvin’s office.

Galvin expects Republican and Democratic primary turnout this year is likely to resemble that year and 2018, despite the calendar shuffle. Lawmakers regularly move up the state’s primary to address logistical concerns tied to overseas and military ballots or to avoid primary day landing on religious holidays — a maneuver that this year is creating a campaign calendar that’s compressed even further.

Past primaries also featured marquee races that naturally drew more attention. In 2018, Senator Elizabeth Warren’s reelection campaign doubled as an unofficial preview of her eventual presidential bid. Four years later, while the governor’s race was largely settled before primary day, competitive contests for attorney general, lieutenant governor, and state auditor gave voters additional reasons to tune in.

Of course, in 2020, the US Senate primary between Senator Ed Markey and Representative Joe Kennedy III drew national attention and helped juice turnout, which topped 1.7 million that Sept. 1. The COVID-19 pandemic also prompted lawmakers to expand — and voters to embrace — mail-in voting that year.

The ballot this year is filled with challengers, but relatively few races have emerged as true toss-ups. None of the state’s six statewide constitutional officers, Galvin included, face any primary challenge, and even for the high-profile incumbents who do, voters say they’re having a hard time getting jazzed about their choices.

Take Markey’s challenge this year from Representative Seth Moulton. More than a dozen voters told the Globe’s Anjali Huynh and Samantha J. Gross that they’re either turned off or largely disinterested in the contest.

“People are just sick and tired and exhausted from the last couple of years,” said Lynn Chenevert, 65. “You just put your head in the sand and pretend it’s not happening.”

THE ACE UP HIS SLEEVE? Republican gubernatorial hopeful Brian Shortsleeve spent the opening stretch of his campaign putting some distance between himself and Charlie Baker — the popular former governor who elevated Shortsleeve to lead the MBTA, but who some Massachusetts Republicans view as a liability in a GOP primary.

Now, with less than four weeks until the Sept. 1 primary against fellow GOP hopeful Michael Minogue, Shortsleeve is embracing the Baker brand.

Shortsleeve’s campaign on Friday rolled out an ad leaning hard on the candidate’s ties to the former governor, whose approval ratings routinely topped national rankings.

The spot, dubbed “Roll Up,” packs in nearly as much Baker as it does Shortsleeve, featuring photos of the duo shaking hands at a press conference, standing shoulder-to-shoulder for the camera, and sitting around a conference table looking suitably serious. (Baker, to be sure, hasn’t endorsed Shortsleeve nor has he gotten involved in the gubernatorial primary.)

“The T was in crisis and Charlie Baker called me,” Shortsleeve, a venture capitalist who served as the MBTA’s chief administrator, says in the 30-second spot.

It would be an obvious general election pitch; Baker left office four years ago still broadly popular with Massachusetts voters. But in a Republican primary, the calculation is trickier.

Baker spent his final years in office openly feuding with the conservative wing of the state GOP and breaking with the national party as President Trump’s rise reshaped it. He ultimately opted against seeking reelection and fighting through a primary against a Trump-aligned Republican. And even out of office, he’s continued to dabble in Massachusetts politics — and not always on the Republican side.

Which may help explain why Shortsleeve wasn’t always eager to campaign as Baker’s political heir. Pressed earlier this year on whether his politics more closely aligned with Baker or former Governor Mitt Romney — another moderate Republican whom Shortsleeve long supported — Shortsleeve told WBUR that he was his “own man.”

His new ad, which Shortsleeve’s campaign says it’s putting $1 million behind, also milks Shortsleeve’s last name for all it’s worth. It includes the phrases “long sleeves” and “no sleeves,” and Shortsleeve says he’s a guy who’s been “rolling up [his] sleeves.” It then pivots to his a résumé reel: He pitches himself as a Marine veteran and MBTA budget-slasher who Baker recruited to help get the T’s finances under control.

OPENING ARGUMENTS: Suffolk County district attorney candidates face off in fiery forum by Griffin Gonzalez and Mike Pescaro, NBC10 Boston: Three candidates for Boston’s top prosecutor faced off in a tense forum Thursday in Roxbury. Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden, former Suffolk County District Attorney Rachael Rollins and former Suffolk County assistant district attorney Linda Champion made their cases to voters ahead of the Democratic primary.

“You only know Kevin because I left to become your U.S. attorney,” Rollins said Thursday.

“This person left her job, and now she wants it back, cause nothing else worked out for her, and it didn’t work out for her because of her lack of ethics and integrity,” Hayden fired back.

COURTHOUSE CONTROVERSY, CONTINUED: Attorney General urges judge to allow courthouse construction to move forward by Jeanette DeForge, The Republican: Attorney General Andrea J. Campbell is urging the courts to reject a demand to stop the state from entering into a contract with the selected developer for a new Springfield courthouse, calling the complaint of a flawed bidding process a “fever dream of imagined malfeasance.”

In a strongly worded brief filed late Wednesday, Campbell asked for the request for a preliminary injunction be rejected so the work to build a new courthouse can move forward. She disputed the argument that one of the principals in the Liberty Junction team selected as the preferred developer had a conflict of interest, so the project should not have been considered.

John Barros, the head of the Massachusetts convention center authority who was involved in the winning bid, said last month that he was “divesting” from the controversial $2 billion contract.

POT HOLE: Newton ordered to repay over $2m to marijuana companies after it spent the money on unrelated projects by Yogev Toby, The Boston Globe: A judge this week ordered Newton to pay back the $71,734 it spent on “Officer Leo,” a golden retriever who helps keep kids off drugs, along with another $2 million it collected from licensed marijuana companies.

The city, the judge ruled, improperly spent the money on projects unrelated to regulating their businesses.

BLUES TRAVELER: ‘Blue Line, best line’ no more? Delays, downed wires are testing the T’s long-steady subway. by Diti Kohli, The Boston Globe: Once the darling of a beleaguered system for its reliable service, the six-mile track between downtown Boston and Revere has been hamstrung by persistent problems with overhead wires and the electrical power system.

Passengers have been diverted from stalled trains at least four times this summer. A small fire broke out in July. And one rider escorted from a train Monday told a local television station they saw a “shower of sparks” and smelled “burning metal” from a downed cable.

LANE CHANGE: Lynn’s mayor says redesign of Lynnway is a safety issue. Commuters call it a ‘nightmare’ by Diane Adame, GBH News: The state-funded Route 1A project, which was first introduced in May 2025, is a partnership between the MBTA and state transportation and recreation agencies. The project proposes cutting the number of lanes from six to four and adding bus and bike lanes.

Quabbin Reservoir towns take funding fight to Beacon Hill amid extended drought by Jordan Wolman, CommonWealth Beacon.

Littleton shut down Flock surveillance cameras on public roads. Without telling the town, Flock turned them back on. by Yogev Toby, The Boston Globe.

title: ‘The new club is working out’: Boston gyms, fitness studios see soaring membership
text:
In 2017, JET Boston started with a few machines, many dumbbells, and a hope that embracing personal training, not a traditional gym model, would allow the business to boom.

Now, after a pause for COVID-19, that plan seems to be working. The original JET location in the Back Bay has closed, but facilities in the South End, Nubian Square, and Brooklyn have opened. The South End studio expanded in May to include pilates and strength conditioning equipment, costing $25,000 and aiming to retain hundreds of members.

Five years after the pandemic decimated health clubs, the industry has come roaring back to a point where many owners say they are on the verge of turning new applicants away. In Massachusetts, more than 150,000 more people were gym members last year than in 2021, according to industry data.

The reasons for the rebound are many. The fading of COVID-era sensitivities helped propel many fitness enthusiasts from home treadmills to public clubs. Employers’ return-to-office plans have led many employees to look for spots near work. And health-conscious young people are bringing a whole new generation of customers into the gym.

Geoffrey Janey, founder and owner of JET Boston-Brooklyn, said some of his young gym-goers are intermingling expensive lifestyle choices like high-end workouts with weekend nights out on the town.

“It’s almost like the new club is working out,” Janey said.

Since 2019, membership has grown 20 percent at Healthworks, GymIt, and Republic Fitness, making it the highest on record, according to Mark Harrington Jr., president of Healthworks Group, which operates the three gym franchises.

Healthworks has been trying to construct new gyms and expand its current locations, but it’s a difficult feat, he said, pointing to how a successful gym should be in a pedestrian-dense district and tends to require a large, costly build-out.

Even when gyms make their best attempt to persuade people to switch, loyal gym-goers often won’t leave.

Selhadin Yasin, 25, doesn’t plan on leaving any time soon from the Planet Fitness in Downtown Crossing. Yasin, an accountant, pays $15 per month for unlimited access to gym equipment.

“It’s all I need,” he said.

A few blocks away, Jeff Bissinger, a 33-year-old who works in finance, frequents Equinox for an hour or two most mornings for amenities like a steam room and personal trainer. Bissinger pays around $500 per month and lives nearby.

“It’s stupid. It’s very expensive,” Bissinger said. “But I value investing in health and wellness, and this is incredibly convenient for me.” (Equinox, a premier gym chain with five clubs open in Boston, declined to comment.)

In 2025, there were 1.9 million fitness-facility members across Massachusetts. That number is the same as in 2019, according to the Health and Fitness Association, a trade group that represents gyms. Meanwhile, the number of commercial health clubs and studios remains around 1,700 — about the same as in 2019.

Buoyed by such high demand, some of Boston’s priciest gyms cost hundreds of dollars per month even for memberships that don’t include all amenities.

Bene Stroud, a 29-year-old who works in marketing, did deep research on Equinox’s fitness instructors and their techniques before putting down almost $300 per month.

A private fitness instructor, Stroud moved from Florida around two months ago and has tried other Boston gyms. Those she frequented didn’t open early or have savvy instructors, she said.

But other operators may have somewhat lower prices, niche workout classes, and special events — providing a middle ground between low-cost and higher-end gyms.

“We’re not running it like a [private equity] firm,” said Giampaolo Nicosia, managing partner of SoWa Health and Wellness, referring to some ritzy high-end gyms.

When SoWa opened in September 2023 in the South End, it had 400 memberships. Now, it has more than 2,000 gym-goers, each paying $190 per month — the same rate as when it opened. But management will cap memberships when lines for equipment become too long, Nicosia said.

Nicosia has noticed that there’s almost no space for large gyms to come to town, and attracting customers from small boutique studios is difficult. “Most of Boston is pretty saturated right now,” he said.

Elsewhere, Planet Fitness gyms recorded $1.3 billion revenue in 2025, up 12 percent from 2024. Memberships also grew by a net 1.1 million, according to a report from February. Now, it has over 21 million members worldwide.

New York Sports Club, formerly operated as the chain Boston Sports Club, has three locations in Greater Boston after a whirlwind of legal headaches and bankruptcy erupted in 2020.

At six of Beacon Hill Athletics Clubs’ seven locations, around 35 percent of gym-goers are Gen Z, and referrals grew 10 percent year-over-year from 2024 to 2025.

Because more young people are spending on health and wellness, making gyms more of a one-stop shop has become more important than ever, said marketing coordinator Jeremy McCabe.

Household spending on alcohol is hanging around 40-year lows, and Gen Z’s spending growth for gyms is over double that of alcohol, according to a February report from Bank of America.

“People know what they want,” McCabe said, “and what they can get out of their dollar.”

title: Massachusetts Lottery touts online gambling success, retailers think otherwise
text:
“The system wasn’t broken before,” said Robert Mellion, executive director of the Massachusetts Package Stores Association, which represents alcoholic beverage retail stores headquartered in the state. “A better way doesn’t mean that you necessarily do it.”

Bracken said he doesn’t expect all lottery players to migrate to the app, which was built with some $2.5 million the state approved in 2024 for start-up costs. Instead, he believes online-exclusive users will make up a subsection of players, with the rest playing online and in person.

More than 24,000 players have made bets on the app, according to Mass. Lottery officials. The new platform offers just over 7 percent of all Mass. Lottery games online, including draw games like Mass Cash, Powerball, and a number of slot machine-style instant win games. All lottery games are still found in stores.

“Retailers in the commonwealth, obviously, they are the cornerstone of our lottery operation. They’ve been with us since the start,” Bracken said. “We value our partnerships and our relationships with our retailers.”

Before launching online, Massachusetts residents spent more on the lottery per capita than any other state. On average, Bay Staters spend about $839 a year on the lottery.

“We’ve been there for them since the beginning, and now they can simply just bypass us and sell direct to consumers,” said Joe Dion, owner of Dion’s Fine Wine in Newton and Waltham. “It’s just not right.”

Retailers that sell lottery tickets get a small cut from every sale: a 5 percent commission from every ticket sold, and a 1 percent commission from winning tickets.

Because they only receive a modest commission, ticket sales aren’t what most retailers are worried about. Instead, it’s the foot traffic the lottery brings to their stores. A pack of chips, a few drinks, maybe a bottle of alcohol. All of that contributes to a retailer’s profit when customers walk in to play the lottery.

“Those loss of sales are going to have negative impacts on our members, not only lottery sales but on their ancillary sales,” said Ryan Kearney, vice president of the Retailers Association of Massachusetts, a retail advocacy nonprofit.

Some business are already struggling, said Mellion with MassPack, as consumers are spending less in stores partly because of the Trump administration’s tariffs on goods, less alcohol consumption, and the affordability crisis.

“Whatever those reasons may be, the state just decided that they’re gonna give [shoppers] one more reason not to step into a brick and mortar store,” said Ryan Maloney, owner of Julio’s Liquors in Westborough.

Ying Huang, a marketing professor at the University of Massachusetts Lowell, said it’s reasonable for store owners to be nervous about the digitization of lottery sales.

“This is like a typical concern in the retail industry over the past decades,” Huang said. “Even with Walmart going to Walmart e-commerce, of course, that will take some sales from the Walmart physical store.”

Huang’s solution: create an omnichannel marketing system, in which products are promoted both online and in stores. For the lottery, this could look like exclusive events for in-store players that are promoted online.

To ensure sales are sustained both online and in stores, Bracken, of Mass. Lottery, said his team is considering the omnichannel model along with other exclusive in-person games. Wellion agrees with the solution, but said it should have been rolled out in tandem with online gaming to avoid retailers’ possible profit loss.

Meanwhile, Bracken said the state continues to onboard new retailers. At present, Mass. Lottery has over 7,200 locations selling lottery games across Massachusetts, making it the state with the most ticket sellers per capita, per square mile in the country.

“Access to the lottery has never been greater as it is in the commonwealth,” Bracken said.

For some, easy access is the concern.

On a recent Wednesday at Fort Point Market in Seaport, Moses Shin, 39, held a stack of Numbers Game tickets in his hand as he fed them to a machine.

Shin said he spends a moderate $10 a week in tickets. With the lottery now available at his fingertips, he said he’s choosing to avoid the app out of fear of catching an addiction.

“[I would] not be able to control myself,” Shin said.

Janelle Patrick, 48, stood in Mission Hill Liquors in Roxbury zoned in on the more than 15 red Numbers Game tickets strewn across the counter. She crossed out numbers to place her bets. Slip by slip, she handed them over to the cashier for scanning.

“I mastered this [expletive], man. It’s sickening,” said Patrick, who has played since 2016 and is studying for a masters in psychology at the University of Massachusetts Boston. She hopes to one day use her experiences to help others addicted to gambling, and is set to graduate next May.

“I picked up one of the worst addictions,” she said. “One of the worst addictions, meaning this is worse than drugs.”

Because of the easy accessibility, Patrick warned that online gambling would exacerbate addiction, especially in lower-income communities.

There’s no definitive data on whether online lottery will increase addiction, said Marlene Warner, CEO of the Massachusetts Council on Gaming and Health. But she understands the concern, considering the rise of other gambling sites.

“They go online and now they have more access, and you can gamble faster,” said Warner, whose nonprofit helps residents overcome addiction to consumer activities, including gambling. “There’s the ability to just place wagers that much faster, and that does become problematic rapidly.”

To avoid the pitfall that is 24/7 access to the lottery, Bracken of Mass. Lottery said the app has integrated a number of safeguards. An on-screen timer counting play time, a 30-minute pop-up and mandatory cool down time are just some of the ways Mass. Lottery is trying to curb addictive habits.

There’s also voluntary self-exclusion, which blocks people from using the app. So far, Warner said more than 20 people have self-excluded.

Dr. Timothy Fong, a psychiatrist and co-director of the gambling studies program at the University of California Los Angeles, said such safeguards could help people become aware of how much they’re spending.

“That’s a very different experience than going to the gas station five times a day,” Fong said, “and it’s highly unlikely that vendor is gonna say ‘This is the fifth time you’ve been here this week or today, I’m not selling you a scratcher.’”

title: Biotech entrepreneur Greg Verdine scores a victory after leasing big office in Watertown
text:
LifeMine has developed a radically new drug for organ transplants, one that avoids the kidney damage caused by the drugs in use over the past three decades. Two of Verdine’s other startups, VidaVinci and DoveTree, are also in the building.

Verdine estimates around 70 people work in the building at one of the three startups today, including LifeMine’s new chief commercial officer Yves Zinggeler (recruited from Vertex Pharmaceuticals), leaving plenty of room for future growth.

“I’m a big believer that real estate can be transformative,” said Verdine, a chemical biologist. “This was intended to be transformative for Watertown Square. It can also be transformative for [our] companies.”

The building offers floor-to-ceiling glass windows with Charles River views, along with a gym, restaurant, and parking. Verdine said he believes employees are happier to work in a beautiful building, and it can have a strong impression on potential investors. “For us,” Verdine said, “it has been a good luck charm.”

Verdine has been behind the launch of a long line of biotechs over the years, most with the intent of finding new approaches to treating otherwise untreatable conditions — or, as he puts it, drugging the “undruggable.” They include Wave Life Sciences, which announced promising data for an obesity treatment last December, and cancer drug maker Parabilis Medicines (formerly FogPharma), which raised $670 million in its June IPO, a new record for a VC-backed biotech.

Verdine often gets asked how he balances all of his various ventures. The key, he said, is picking the right executives to take over, as he did with Parabilis chief executive Mathai Mammen, formerly at Johnson & Johnson. Most of Verdine’s time now is focused on his three startups at 66 Galen.

“I had to learn to reprogram myself from an academician to someone running a biotech company,” Verdine said, and then added, half-jokingly: “[Now] I’m learning how to transition from control freak to judicious delegator . . . in my advanced years.”

The Community Music Center of Boston is relying on millions of dollars in donations to buy and renovate a new home in Roxbury’s Nubian Square.

Now, it’s getting another $1 million, this time from the Barr Foundation, to ensure the nonprofit music school can offer robust programs after the new place opens in January, and to strategize for its future.

It is wrapping up the extensive renovations on the 15,000-square-foot building at 2164 Washington St., which was most recently home to an art gallery. CMCB will keep its leased location in the South End after it opens up in Nubian Square.

To cover the $23 million purchase price and renovation costs, the school raised $11 million in philanthropy, worked with TD Bank, the National Community Investment Fund, and BlueHub Capital to obtain $9 million in proceeds from state and federal tax credits, and will borrow another $3 million.

Zach Sheets, the school’s chief advancement officer, said his 50 or so colleagues are looking forward to playing their part to bolster Nubian Square’s growing arts scene.

“To be able to own [our own building],” Sheets said, “and be a cornerstone institution has been huge for us.”

Rob Waldron has a new ally in his quest to make us all history buffs like him.

Well, actually, the new role for Megan Costello is a bit broader, but certainly it’s on her to-do list: now that Waldron and his wife Jen Waldron have named her the new chief of staff for their family firm Waldron Civic LLC.

Costello might be best known in Boston for her work in the Walsh administration: She led then-mayor Martin J. Walsh’s office of women’s advancement from 2014 through mid-2018, before getting her master’s in public administration from Harvard Kennedy School. She returned to work for Boston in early 2021, as a senior adviser in the schools superintendent’s office.

Now joining the Waldrons, Costello will serve the city in a new way. Waldron had led educational software firm Curriculum Associates until retiring at the start of 2025, and since that time has used some the money he made by trying to bolster the public’s interest in history. Most notably, he sponsored a video contest for eighth graders this past spring called “We Declare! Challenge.” Much of the Waldrons’ charity work is done through a fund they established at the Boston Foundation.

Costello will help oversee the Waldrons’ portfolio of public work that includes improving first-generation college access, high-quality early education, the well-being of children from low-income families, and, of course, public history access and engagement.

“I really love the big dreams that Rob and Jen have,” Costello said, “and look forward to helping them piece it all together.”

Elias Torres hired Andrew Bialecki as one of his first engineers at the marketing startup Performable in 2010.

Now, it’s Bialecki’s turn to do the hiring.

Klaviyo, the marketing-tech firm that Bialecki now leads as its co-chief executive, has acquired the technology created by Agency, the AI customer management startup that Torres led, and hired Agency’s 25-person team. Torres becomes Klaviyo’s chief product officer, and will work closely with Bialecki at the Boston headquarters.

Torres will oversee all of Klaviyo’s agentic AI products, including its “Composer” and “Customer Agent” businesses, reporting directly to his buddy who runs the place, “AB.”

Klaviyo and Agency already had a business relationship, but Bialecki decided it made more sense to bring their work entirely in-house. The deal terms, which were not disclosed, came together quickly, Torres said, in large part because of the level of trust he has with Bialecki.

Torres was one of Bialecki’s first angel investors and can’t help but wish now that he had put a little bit more into Klaviyo at the time. (The firm is worth $5 billion today.)

Torres and his business partner David Cancel stayed in touch with Bialecki over the years, after HubSpot acquired Performable in 2011 and Bialecki cofounded Klaviyo with Ed Hallen the following year. Torres and Cancel went on to found Drift, a firm that’s now part of Salesloft.

“I have told my team this is a very small world,” said Torres, a native of Nicaragua who moved to the United States for college. “You can never know [when] it’s going to be a full-circle moment.”

Investors liked the fact SharkNinja raised its revenue outlook for the year. But consumers were more interested in something else: the Needham company’s new microwave oven.

Chief executive Mark Barrocas talked about both on an earnings call last week; the company’s stock is up around 10 percent since its better-than-expected quarterly report card came out on Aug. 5.

Best known for its Shark vacuums and Ninja blenders, SharkNinja is regularly expanding into new and adjacent categories, such as the release last month of the Ninja Crispi Microwave and Air Fryer.

To some extent, the surge in sales can be attributed to SharkNinja taking more of its distribution work in-house. Barrocas said the constant product development and innovation also helps.

With the microwave, SharkNinja applied its air fryer technology to solve a common complaint among users: their food can get soggy when heated or reheated. It is the 40th “subcategory” of home appliance that SharkNinja has entered.

“That’s a category that has had no innovation over the last 20 years,” Barrocas said in an interview. “In its first week on social media, it had over eight million impressions. When we hit on something that is a real consumer problem [and] we start putting content on social media, it resonates. Consumers are saying, ‘Why hasn’t anyone done this before?’”

title: Darryl ‘God’ Whiting, Roxbury crack kingpin, dies in prison
text:
Darryl Whiting was 71. He died of natural causes on Aug. 1, according to a one-page letter notifying US District Judge Denise J. Casper, chief judge of federal courts in Massachusetts, of Whiting’s death.

The letter was entered into Whiting’s court record on Monday.

Whiting had been serving out his life term at Federal Correctional Institution Schuylkill, a medium-security men’s prison in Minersville, Pa. He died at the Geisinger Medical Center in nearby Danville, Pa., the letter signed by Warden A. Cruz said.

“Despite being incarcerated for more than three decades, Darryl was deeply loved by his family,” Sandra Ganz, Whiting’s former federal assistant public defender told the Globe in a telephone interview Tuesday night. “He had six kids, and he’s a grandfather who’s incredibly close to his niece, his sister, and his brother.”

“Daryl’s life sentence, imposed in 1991, was a relic of draconian and mandatory sentenching schemes,” Ganz said.

Whiting ruled the crack trade in the Orchard Park housing project in Roxbury in the late 1980s and early ‘90s, grossing millions of dollars. His group, known as the New York Boys, forcibly removed residents from the project and used their apartments to store and sell drugs, prosecutors said.

Whiting had been locked up since his arrest Dec. 21, 1990.

He was sentenced Oct. 21, 1991 to life without the possibility of parole for running a criminal cocaine enterprise.

A decade ago, Whiting made a bid for early release, arguing that sentencing laws for drug crimes had changed, making it so that a life term was no longer the mandatory penalty for his convictions.

Whiting lost his bid largely due to his self-published e-book, “Takin’ It to Another Level.” The novel came out in June 2013.

Federal prosecutors initially supported Whiting’s request for a reduced sentence, as part of the office’s general support of shorter sentences for drug crimes, but later withdrew support after learning that Whiting had written a novel that glorified his life of crime.

Prosecutors said Whiting’s book showed a likelihood that he may return to criminality. The main character had the same name as Whiting and was serving a life term for running a continuing criminal enterprise. The fictional Whiting was released from prison after 20 years because of a change in the law and took revenge on former associates who testified against him.

At a February 2016 hearing on his release, Whiting choked back tears as he pleaded for mercy.

“I’m sincere in trying to be, in wanting to be, a productive member of society,” Whiting told the judge. “I just want a chance.”

Whiting also inspired a 1999 movie called “In Too Deep,” starring rapper LL Cool J as a Cincinnati gang lord who goes by the alias “God.”

Whiting renewed his bid for release in December 2024. His federal assistant public defenders wrote in court filings that during Whiting’s three decades in prison, he had embarked on a journey of personal growth, completing courses in history, economics, business, and screenplay writing, as well as vocational courses in barbering, Spanish, and computer skills.

US District Judge Patti B. Saris on Dec. 1, 2025, reserved ruling on Whiting’s release until after the US Supreme Court issued its opinion on a case with similar issues. Saris still had not issued a decision at the time of Whiting’s death.

“He died still in the fight,” Ganz said, adding that she believes “that had he been sentenced today, and had the court had the full and complete picture of his life history, and the benefit of expert opinions related to his work of fiction, Daryl could have died free.”

If released, Whiting had hoped to live with his sister, an ordained minister, her husband, and their adult children in Corona, N.Y. He had plans to revive his relationship with his six children and live out his remaining years, peacefully and free, his lawyers wrote.

Whiting was born in New York, the youngest of seven children. His father died when he was an infant, leaving his mother, maternal grandmother, and aunt to raise him, according to court filings.

Whiting was the adored baby of the family with few restrictions and little discipline. A pattern of incarceration began when Whiting was 12 with a stint in juvenile detention that was repeated into his teens and adulthood and eventually saw him imprisoned at Rikers Island, court records said.

Whiting arrived in Boston in 1987. He was flamboyant and known for his stylish dress, diamond rings and luxury cars. He portrayed himself as a role model and treated the children who worked for him to new sneakers, leather coats, and motor scooters, the Globe reported.

Whiting also owned and ran several business in Roxbury, including a barber shop, video store, and the Crown Social and Recreational Hall which were used to recruit youth to work for him and as fronts for his drug deals.

Whiting was convicted by a Boston jury after a month-long trial in which former colleagues testified to being recruited by Whiting when they were young. They also testified about the violence Whiting used to discipline those within his organization. A single mother who relied on welfare told jurors that Whiting supplied her with drugs so he could use her apartment to sell drugs.

Whiting testified too, telling jurors he considered himself a community-minded entrepreneur and role model for young people who came to his social hall, barbecues, rap concerts and outings to amusement parks. Whiting said he knew some of his associates were dealing drugs, but he wasn’t involved in it.

title: The 2026 midterms are turning into ‘dropout season’
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

This summer, there’s no “tune in” or “turn on.” For politicians of all stripes, it’s just the third element of that 1960s hippie catchphrase:

Drop out.

Dropping out, or calls to do so, seems like the defining characteristic of the 2026 midterms, the Globe’s James Pindell writes. Many reasons have prompted the calls for the candidates to quit.

“Some of it was based in political strategy. Several exits were caused by a male candidate’s unacceptable past behavior toward women,” Pindell writes.

And some calls to quit, such as dueling efforts to oust Democratic and Independent Senate candidates in Montana, were based on polling that said one or the other could possibly defeat the Republican candidate — but both would lose to the GOP if they both stayed in.

Who’s gone?

North Carolina’s Representative Chuck Edwards gave up his Republican seat after an ethics report detailed widespread — and very cringey — sexual harassment events on his own staff, Pindell writes.

Maine Democratic Senate nominee Graham Platner dropped out over allegations that he raped a former girlfriend. Allegations of sexual misconduct prompted Democrat Eric Swalwell to leave the California gubernatorial race.

Ahead of yesterday’s contentious race for Wisconsin governor, three Democratic candidates had dropped out. Then one of them resumed the campaign.

Who’s still in?

In choosing to stay in, Ohio Representative Max Miller pointed to Trump’s persistence in running despite Trump’s negative publicity — over his infidelities, 34 criminal convictions, and reported sexual assaults. Miller’s contentious divorce comes with allegations he broke the collarbone of his 2-year-old daughter and committed significant domestic abuse.

Also not quitting: Kentucky’s Mitch McConnell, despite the fact he hasn’t been seen in person or even heard by voice since he went to the hospital in June.

As Pindell writes, there are three more months to November’s general elections — so dropout season could roll deep into fall.
