title: The therapy team on call for the trafficked women of Mass. and Cass
text:
“But with Abby, she was my one constant person for nine years that I could depend on,” McKenzie said, referring to Abigail Judge, a clinical and forensic psychologist who cofounded the nonprofit, the Boston Human Exploitation Advocacy Team, or HEAT.

Other groups designed to support housing needs and substance use recovery oftentimes don’t address trauma from sex trafficking, advocates said. Meanwhile, organizations helping trafficking victims frequently don’t have the bandwidth to address drug use, according to social workers.

Flying under the radar of clinics meant to help homeless Bostonians, unhoused women who are trafficked and use opioids, as was the case for McKenzie, are exposed to overdose risks and physical violence from abusers. Since 2024, nine women trafficked around Mass. and Cass died from homicide or overdose, according to data collected by HEAT.

The intersection of Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard has long been a hub for sex trafficking because unhoused people who use drugs there are in survival mode, said Katie Koh, a street psychiatrist with Boston Health Care for the Homeless Program.

“A lot of people use drugs in the first place to cope with the adversity and pain they’ve experienced throughout their life, and their addiction can lead them to make decisions they wouldn’t make in the absence of using substances,” Koh said.

Women who use intravenous opioids at Mass. and Cass become targeted by traffickers who exploit their basic needs for shelter, substances, and food. Victims who work with HEAT said they’ve also used fentanyl and heroin to numb the trauma of being sexually exploited.

Without safe housing and facing criminalization and stigma surrounding their drug use and the commercial sex trade, the women become trapped in a coercive web, said Jessica Loftus, a clinical social worker who helps trafficked women at two Boston hospitals.

“When you have a criminal history and you have really complex medical and mental health needs, you get ruled out of accessing services, which perpetuates the problem and prevents you from getting to a place where stabilization is possible,” Loftus said.

Judge and Sandra Andrade, a Roxbury District Court senior peer advocate, launched HEAT in 2020 after working at a Massachusetts General Hospital clinic helping women like McKenzie. After they realized that only a sliver of women from Mass. and Cass checked in, they took their work to the streets. Via sidewalk outreach, they invite women to HEAT’s nighttime safe space, called “the spot,” which feels like a cozy, underground bunker.

Relying mostly on grant funding, including a recent anti-trafficking grant from FIFA, Judge provides victims with psychotherapy, and Andrade navigates them through legal obstacles.

“The ‘spot’ isn’t only temporary respite and safety, it‘s a community based on what I know from a clinical perspective about trauma recovery and what Sandra knows in her bones from lived experience,” said Judge, who has remained on the faculty at MGH.

When a woman calls the phone numbers on her wristband, Judge and Andrade accompany her to the hospital in the middle of the night, meet her at the police station, or shepherd her through a court hearing.

“I go to court with them, because a lot of them don’t like to walk in, there’s a lot of anxiety, or fear of [withdrawal] because they’re in active addiction,” Andrade, 46, said.

When the Boston Police Department Human Trafficking Unit refers victims to resource groups, HEAT is their first call, according to Sergeant Detective Marc Sullivan. Since 2024, the unit has sent more than 120 victims to Judge and Andrade.

South End residents formed a group to build community buy-in for HEAT, which has quickly become Boston’s most effective advocate for commercial sexual exploitation victims, said Jim O’Connell, founder of Boston Health Care for the Homeless.

“We knew about the drug trade, but we were not aware of how many people were really being trafficked,” O’Connell said. “What Abigail and Sandra did on Mass. and Cass quietly and under the radar was really astonishing.”

Like many women who work with HEAT, McKenzie said she was first trafficked as a teenager, at age 15, after meeting the son of a local “pimp” in downtown Boston.

For the next 15 years, McKenzie said life was a blur of paid “dates,” physical abuse, and a “full-blown” drug addiction.

She met Judge at MGH in 2017 while receiving treatment for endocarditis, an infection of the heart, which she suffered from using intravenous drugs.

“I’d probably be dead if it wasn’t for Abby,” McKenzie, 39, said in an interview.

Now, McKenzie is on Sublocade treatment and other medications for PTSD.

“Abby has been the most essential part of my health care,” said McKenzie, who lives about seven miles northwest of Boston with her father and son. “With the trauma and PTSD, it’s really hard to not live in the past, but Abby’s helped me focus on the present.”

Another woman who accesses HEAT’s resources said in a written testimonial filed to city officials last year that she was first sexually trafficked as a child by her own mother.

“The amount of support and understanding I feel from Abigail and her team is something I have never experienced in my life,” wrote the woman, who signed her initials, “SM.”

Women such as SM can also find support at Boston hospitals that have social workers trained to help.

But many victims avoid health care settings, said Amy Farrell, director of Northeastern University’s School of Criminology and Criminal Justice.

Women describe feeling a “very static” underlying stigma from doctors and nurses, she said.

“They are often treated as people who are not worth helping or somehow responsible for their own victimization,” Farrell said.

Social workers at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Brigham & Women’s Hospital can help, usually when a patient checks in for more than one day.

“I think we do, unfortunately, miss folks who come through the emergency department,” said Loftus, the clinical social worker.

When many women return to the streets after a medical crisis, they find themselves in the situations that landed them in the hospital.

But on Tuesday and Friday nights, women who work with HEAT come inside at “the spot,” which has an address that isn’t listed online.

The space has a large dining table, a soft couch, a kitchen, and a clothes closet. Women can shower and get daily essentials such as deodorant, toothpaste, and hair ties.

During recent evenings, women laughed as they ate watermelon cubes, green grapes, and frosted sugar cookies while blasting hip-hop music on their phones.

When they’re with Andrade and Judge, women are surrounded by pastel portraits painted by a former client who is now an accomplished artist. They vent about drama that’s unfolded on the streets and reflect on their relationships, both good and bad, as well as deaths in the community.

Andrade and Judge are on track to help more women this year than last, to expand weekly hours at “the spot,” and to acquire a mobile van. They hired a third staff member in June.

“People seem to help women a lot when they’re clean, but what about when they’re actually going through things?” Andrade said. “Our women sustain being clean and being in housing because they have support now, when things are really shady.”

title: ‘There is no uptick’ Police Commissioner Cox addresses city violence and safety concerns ahead of large Dominican Parade
text:
The press conference, which Cox said is the first to be held before one of these events, comes just two years after five people were shot at the same festival.

Officials said that disorderly behavior won’t be tolerated at the parade , which regularly draws tens of thousands of visitors. The route goes from Hyde Square in Jamaica Plain to Franklin Park. It will begin around noon and result in various road closures along Centre Street, Perkins Street, Columbus Avenue, and Walnut Avenue, city officials announced.

Various other festival and parade gatherings in Boston have been marred by violence.

Just last month, a teenager was arrested for opening fire at a Puerto Rican Festival also held in Franklin Park, though no one was injured, police said.

At the Caribbean Carnival heritage festival in 2023, eight people were shot when gunfire broke out between two rival groups, catching civilians in the crossfire. This year’s festival is set for next month.

In 2022, a man was fatally shot at the same event, and the early morning hours before the parade were the backdrop for fatal shootings in 2015 and 2014 as well.

Cox said that Sunday’s parade route is “part of the area where we have had discharged firearms, certainly over the summer,” but that “this year we’re looking to improve.”

He said that lessons have been learned from past incidents and the upcoming festival was planned with a focus on addressing safety “blind spots.”

More officers will be on the ground this year, Cox added, and visitors are asked to leave the area immediately following the event.

Last year’s Dominican Parade was held without any violent incidents.

“We do a lot in general to try to curtail” violence, he said. “For the most part, we’ve probably done a decent job doing that, but … anytime violence happens, it’s not a good thing. It’s not something we plan for, but the fact is that it does occur."

Sunday’s event also comes as community concerns have mounted following a string of various shooting and stabbing deaths in the city.

A man was fatally stabbed during rush hour Wednesday at South Station, while various fatal shootings have occurred throughout the city in recent weeks.

In July, Jonathan Sanon of Norwood was also fatally beaten outside an MBTA Green Line station on Boston Common, prompting civic leaders to hold a forum on improving safety.

In total there have been 20 homicides in Boston this year, police data show, compared with 24 at this time last year.

Cox emphasized that the South Station stabbing, which police have said was not a random incident, like a domestic violence stabbing that also took place near North Station on Thursday, follow a pattern that is true of most of the recent violence in Boston.

“Usually it’s related to people who know each other and choose to engage in some type of altercation,” he said, adding that violent crime is “down in every category except for two, which is aggravated assaults and domestic assaults.”

So, “we don’t have an uptick,” in violence, Cox added. “What we have is an uptick of reported events ... [and] isolated incidents in different parts of the city.”

title: A mega-merger could drive up Massachusetts energy bills
text:
Featuring: Rebecca Tepper, Caitlin Peale Sloan, Ed Markey, Richard Levitan, Julian Cyr, Tito Jackson, Jason Waddleton, Martha Sheridan, Michael Nichols, Brian Golden, Cecelia Lizotte, Jen Faigel, Paul Dama, Beth Healy, Greg Huang, Tim Logan, and more.

Most of the public debate around the pending NextEra-Dominion megamerger is happening in the Southeast, where the companies have extensive electric utility operations.

But now it’s taking shape here, too. Rebecca Tepper, Governor Maura Healey’s energy secretary, is speaking out about the Healey administration’s concerns, saying the merger could result in serious cost impacts for New England ratepayers. As if we didn’t have enough reasons to worry about our utility bills.

She raised her concerns in a statement to me, as requests pile up to intervene in the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s merger review. In recent days, the state Department of Public Utilities, the state attorney general’s office, and the New England States Committee on Electricity all filed motions to be included in the case — and those are just the ones representing Massachusetts. Then, on Monday, Senator Ed Markey urged FERC to reject the merger outright, citing affordability and antitrust concerns.

NextEra and Dominion aren’t household names in New England. Neither company owns a utility here. But they do have something that’s quite valuable: our last two nuclear power plants.

Dominion owns Millstone in Waterford, Conn., the region’s biggest power plant. Guess who is number two? NextEra’s Seabrook, in New Hampshire. Together, they provide a quarter of New England’s electricity.

Should the merger go through as planned, a single company (NextEra) would control the region’s two biggest power stations — also its last remaining nuclear plants.

It’s easy to see why Tepper is concerned. She is calling on FERC to “heavily scrutinize the impacts this merger may have on ratepayer bills, market power, and reliability.”

The merger lands on our doorstep as New England warms up to nuclear power again, thanks to its reliability and low carbon emissions. In 2018, Connecticut officials orchestrated long-term contracts to financially support the two power plants, after Dominion threatened to close Millstone.

Those contracts expire in 2029 — right around the corner in infrastructure-planning terms. As a result, Governor Ned Lamont’s administration is knocking on Healey’s door, looking for help in a new multi-state procurement of green energy; the contracts will likely again support one or both nuclear plants.

Meanwhile, Beacon Hill lawmakers have embarked on closed-door negotiations to resolve differences between two sprawling energy bills. Among the disputed items: the House wants to end a state law that requires a statewide vote before nuclear construction happens — effectively a ban on new nukes — while the Senate version doesn’t lift the requirement. No one expects a new reactor similar in scale to the shuttered Pilgrim or dismantled Yankee Rowe, near the Vermont border. Local fights would be too fierce. But maybe the bill opens the door for compact “microreactors,” like ones being sold by Radiant, to supplant backup diesel generators.

Of more importance to the New England grid: the future of Millstone and Seabrook. Ensuring they stay open for the long haul is crucial to keeping our lights on.

The Conservation Law Foundation’s Caitlin Peale Sloan worries about the negotiating power the new company would have for future contracts. “When Millstone first put its hand out to Connecticut, they had a lot of leverage,” she said. “And now that leverage is going to grow.”

There’s another reason for concern with NextEra at the helm. The Florida-based company became Public Enemy No. 1 on Beacon Hill as it fought a power line from going up through western Maine — first quietly, then quite publicly. NextEra didn’t want the competition from Canada’s hydropower that would come along the new line for Massachusetts. The project officially finished in January, but its cost grew by more than 50 percent, to $1.6 billion, because of the delays. Massachusetts ratepayers picked up the tab.

Could NextEra use its increased might in the region to thwart other competitors? Boston energy consultantRichard Levitan says it’s likely. “They have a history,” he says, “of not playing well in the giant New England sandbox.”

Others in the industry speak in more favorable terms, echoing the two companies’ talking points. One insider suggests to me that NextEra might be more likely to invest in New England, such as with a new small modular reactor at one of the existing sites, if it has a bigger scale here. NextEra, per its usual MO, didn’t respond to my request for a comment; a Dominion spokesperson reminded me that Connecticut ratepayers are saving a ton of money now with those nuclear contracts.

On balance, though, the NextEra-Dominion combo is generating skepticism around here. With no local regulated utility involved, state officials here have no say in ultimately deciding the merger’s fate. But they’ve got a voice. And, as the documents piling up at FERC show, they plan on using it.

What’s your take? Join the conversation in the comments here.

The White Stadium waiting game is going to take a little longer now. In case you are living under a Roxbury puddingstone boulder, a revamp of the Franklin Park fixture is being pursued by Mayor Michelle Wu and the Boston Legacy FC soccer team but also challenged in court by the nonprofit Emerald Necklace Conservancy. The issue, now before the Supreme Judicial Court, could hinge on whether the stadium site should be deemed parkland, which would require Wu and the soccer team to get approval from the state Legislature to host a business there. The SJC heard oral arguments back on April 8. But this week, lawyers for all sides were informed that the court is waiving its standard “130-day guideline” to resolve the White Stadium debate. What’s taking so long? Are the judges closer to shutting the project down, too busy with stopping ballot questions, or just spending a little extra time on the Cape?

The consensus at a summer economic roundtable convened Wednesday by Mayor Michelle Wu was clear: Make 3 a.m. last call and social districts permanent. Those were measures the Legislature temporarily passed to help bars and restaurants take advantage of the throngs of tourists and fans visiting for World Cup, Fourth of July, and Sail Boston. We hate to be a party pooper, but only social districts – allowing municipalities to create designated public drinking areas – made it to a conference committee as part of the Senate’s “fun agenda.” That means extending last call for an extra hour is dead until next session, according to state senator Julian Cyr. While lawmakers were not enthused, business leaders and bar owners who gathered at Roundhead Brewing in Hyde Park for the mayoral roundtable – including Apex Noire’s Tito Jackson, The Haven’s Jason Waddleton, Meet Boston CEO Martha Sheridan and Downtown Boston Alliance president Michael Nichols – value the 3 a.m. option.

Think it’s hard getting homes built in Boston? Sometimes, it’s even harder in Newton. Just ask Brian Golden. The former head of the Boston Planning & Development Agency is now on the Newton City Council, and he gave his first speech to the full council the other night. The issue in question: whether the council should approve replacing a two-family house with four attached single-family homes in Newtonville. Golden said he agrees with some arguments on both sides, but in the end favors more housing: “It is impossible for me to lose sight of how important it is to grow the number of units not just in Newton but in the commonwealth,” Golden said. “All along the socioeconomic spectrum, we need more units.” A passionate plea, but apparently it wasn’t enough. The special permit didn’t get the two-thirds majority vote that city officials say it needed.

It’s an email no restaurateur wants to write: “I Don’t Want This To Become Our Farewell Letter.” But that’s what Suya Joint founder and chef Cecelia Lizotte sent Wednesday to a local food email group run by Jen Faigel’s CommonWealth Kitchen. Lizotte revealed she has considered closing her West African restaurant with locations in Roxbury and Providence due to rising food and labor costs and heightened fears about ICE that have kept immigrant customers home. (Her brother Paul Dama, who works with her, was detained and released by ICE last year.) Suya Joint also bet big on the World Cup, staffing up and activating its food truck, but it didn’t pay off. The poignant letter was Lizotte’s way of telling her network that she needs help to survive – including booking catering, hiring the food truck, and hosting private events. “We are not looking for a handout. We are looking for opportunities, partnerships, resources, and a bridge through an extraordinarily difficult period.”

The Federal Reserve Bank of Boston released this week its much anticipated follow up to its landmark “Color of Wealth” report from 2015. The new analysis, years in the making, takes a deeper dive into family wealth by surveying more than 5,000 Massachusetts residents. One data point that caught our attention because it wasn’t studied last time: About one in six families expect to receive an inheritance in the future. It’s another way to look at generational wealth and the ability for families to pass on their assets. The study found that only 3.7 percent of Latino families and 4.3 percent of Black families expect to receive one, compared to 18.6 percent of white households and 13.1 percent of Asian American households.

It didn’t take long for the progressive Massachusetts Budget & Policy Center to seize on that part of the Fed study as a reason to keep the estate tax. Their argument: proceeds from the tax — which is expected to bring in more than $700 million a year — could be used to address economic disparities. MassBudget will have a fight on their hands: Major business groups say the estate tax is driving wealthy people out of the state, and they want it eliminated. This issue could be the next big tax-related showdown when lawmakers start their new two-year session in January.

In Tuesday’s edition, Jon wrote about how so many tech companies are moving into the Financial District that maybe it should be renamed. Not so fast, say our readers. They like retaining the moniker, plus a lot of banks and investment firms are still there.

Changes are coming to the Boston Globe business desk: Editor Brian McGrory announced new roles for business editor Greg Huang and deputy business editor Tim Logan. Starting in mid-September, they’ll be senior assistant managing editor for storytelling and deputy managing editor for local news, respectively. Meanwhile, Beth Healy, WBUR’s managing editor for local news, will be returning to the Globe to lead the business section.

Today’s edition was edited by Aaron Pressman and Andy Rosen, and produced by Jack Osmond.

title: At a hot Salem Porchfest, a thirsty Dan Koh
text:
“I’m going to be honest with everyone here, we need the most help with this song,” Koh, clad in a sweat-soaked “Harvey Milk Supervisor” shirt, told the smattering of spectators, who gamely clapped along to the popular folk-country song “Wagon Wheel.”

This is the sort of humbling exercise that only a candidate for office — and perhaps only a particularly thirsty candidate for office — is willing to endure. And Koh, in the closing days of a six-way race to replace US Representative Seth Moulton may be among the thirstiest.

After narrowly losing the open Third District Democratic primary in 2018, Koh once openly considered challenging US Representative Lori Trahan, the Westford Democrat who edged him in that 2018 race. He ultimately passed, and his hometown of Andover was later carved from the Third and pushed into the Sixth District amid the state’s 2021 redistricting process.

That shuffling proved serendipitous this year. After Koh quietly considered challenging Moulton, the seat opened up when the Salem Democrat mounted his own challenge to US Senator Ed Markey. A chance for Koh’s thirst to be quenched.

This time around, is there anything he wouldn’t do to win?

“This is going to sound corny, but compromise Democratic values against Trump,” Koh said in a post-performance interview.

There’s plenty that he is willing to do — beyond, literally, playing to the crowd.

The former Biden administration official and Boston City Hall alum has leveraged his connections, big and small, to build a dominant war chest, topping the field in fundraising at roughly $4.5 million through June. The next closest candidate, Lynnfield fintech executive John Beccia, ended June having raised about $3.5 million, though nearly $3 million of that has come from his own pocket.

The next closest fundraiser, state Representative Tram Nguyen, isn’t in the same financial stratosphere. Three other candidates — Topsfield’s Jamie Belsito, a former state lawmaker; software engineer Bethany Andres-Beck; and Mariah Lancaster, a veterinarian and former Congressional aide — are also running in the Democratic primary.

Add Koh’s own fundraising to the more than $700,000 a super PAC has already spent to send mailers and air digital ads on his behalf, and he’s enjoyed a huge cash advantage.

Whether that means he also has a huge advantage in general . . .

“There is definitely some anti-Dan sentiment,” said Essex County Register of Deeds Eileen Duff, a Democrat who has yet to endorse in the race. “But I think how non-stop he is shows tenacity more than just blind ambition.”

Koh has been here before. He looked, at times, like the favorite in the 2018 race before he fell to Trahan by razor-thin margin, losing the Democratic nomination by 145 votes after a recount. Which may be why the second-time candidate spent a sweltering Sunday in Salem, performing for just a handful of people.

For at least one Sixth District voter, it worked.

“When my husband told me Dan Koh was performing, I was like, ‘He’s actually playing music?’” said Tanya Shallop, a Salem resident who was, until Sunday, undecided on who she would back.

“I mean, I wouldn’t hire him as my wedding singer,” she said. “I had actually been on the fence, but it was so endearing and kind of vulnerable, and I really like that about him.”

Shallop then added. “I know that sounds ridiculous.”

LOCATION, LOCATION, LOCATION: Three Boston-area state Senators facing challenges from their left are getting a six-figure boost from the real estate lobby.

The Massachusetts Association of Realtors’s super PAC is putting more than $104,000 in digital ads and mailers alone behind state Senators Nick Collins, William Brownsberger, and Mike Rush, newly filed disclosures show. All told, the super PAC reported dropping $131,000 in recent days in its first batch of spending this election cycle.

Collins and Brownsberger are each facing Mayor Michelle Wu-backed challengers in Latoya Gayle and Daniel Lander, respectively. (Juwan Skeens is also challenging Collins.) Rush, a moderate West Roxbury Democrat who has Wu’s endorsement, is facing a progressive primary challenger in Hyde Park attorney Persis Yu.

Of their challengers, only Lander has so far gotten help from an outside group. The Massachusetts Teachers Association’s associated super PAC recently spent $25,000 to air digital ads on his behalf, according to a campaign finance disclosure filed Tuesday.

UNREALISTIC SQUAD GOALS: Flyer with AOC, Pressley called ‘misleading’ in Providence council race by Patrick Anderson and Colin Hogan, The Providence Journal: Campaign flyers linking New York congresswoman and potential presidential candidate Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to a Providence City Council race are heating up one of the most closely watched local elections this year.

The flyers from Ward 1 City Councilman John Goncalves’s reelection campaign showing him with Ocasio-Cortez and Massachusetts US Representative Ayanna Pressley do not claim an endorsement from either member of the progressive “Squad” of House members. They say “Councilman John Goncalves Delivers Progressive Results” beside a photo of the incumbent between a smiling Ocasio-Cortez and Pressley.

“The congresswoman has not endorsed Councilor Goncalves,” a spokesperson for Pressley’s campaign said Thursday. “The Councilor approached her at an event and took this photo. Using this photo on campaign materials is misleading and unprofessional and he should set the record straight with voters.”

HEAT CHECK: Massachusetts appoints first-ever chief heat officer by Kate Selig, The Boston Globe: Governor Maura Healey on Thursday announced the appointment of the state’s first-ever heat resilience officer. Katie Schlick, a Biden administration alum who previously worked as an environmental planner in Connecticut, will collaborate with state government and local communities to combat the deadly consequences of extreme heat.

The new heat chief position is fully funded by The Boston Foundation, a community foundation that has made climate change a priority. It has committed to funding the position for at least two years. Some climate advocates were concerned to see the position paid for this way, raising questions about the state’s investment in the role and its permanence.

KRATOM CRACKDOWN: Healey announces crackdown on kratom, an unregulated ‘gas station drug’ by Chloe Craft, The Boston Globe: Healey on Thursday also announced several new moves to crack down on the sale of kratom, an unregulated, opioid-like substance. Kratom is widely available in gas stations, smoke shops, and convenience stores in several different forms such as powders, capsules, tablets, and gummies.

Under an emergency order from Department of Public Health Commissioner Robbie Goldstein, all forms of kratom will be temporarily placed into Schedule I — the drug class with the highest potential for abuse, which also includes heroin, LSD, and ecstasy — under Massachusetts law.

GREEN LINE’S RED LIGHT: The Green Line is shut down, and will be again soon. Take a look at what the T is fixing. by Diti Kohli, The Boston Globe: Green Line riders, already fatigued by a string of summer T shutdowns, should gear up for more. Regular Green Line service resumes Monday after the current nine-day diversion ends, but large swaths of the line will close again the weekend of Sept. 19. That will be followed by two nine-day shutdowns that will spill into October and November, T spokesperson Joe Pesaturo said. The exact dates and stations affected were not yet available.

HARVARD PASSES LEGAL TEST: Federal judge dismisses Trump administration’s antisemitism lawsuit against Harvard by Michaela Towfighi, Camilo Fonseca and Brooke Hauser, The Boston Globe: One of the more explosive lines of attack President Trump launched against Harvard University hit a dead end on Thursday when a federal judge in Boston dismissed the administration’s lawsuit that alleged the university violated civil rights law in its treatment of Jewish students.

The dismissal offers a reprieve for Harvard, as the Trump administration continues to scrutinize the university from all fronts, recently opening an investigation into its financial aid practices for foreign students and suing the school over alleged racial bias in its admissions policies.

STOPPAGE TIME: SJC delays White Stadium ruling, and Boston Legacy won’t commit to timeline for hosting games there by Michael Silverman, The Boston Globe: An extended wait for a ruling from the state Supreme Judicial Court on the fate of a rebuilt White Stadium has cast doubt on whether the venue will be ready to host Boston Legacy home games next year as planned.

Workers were on site Thursday at the ambitious, controversial, and expensive — $325 million in private and public dollars — new Franklin Park home for Boston Public Schools Athletics and the NWSL team. The foundations of the two grandstands are in place, as are steel girders and elevator shafts — all viewable via the web and live cameras at the site. The pace of progress, however, is up in the air, with the seven-member court needing extra time to issue a ruling on the case, which was heard in early April.

Police Commissioner Cox addresses city violence and safety concerns ahead of large Dominican Parade by Bryan Hecht, The Boston Globe.

Mass. will help fund gender-affirming care for youth after federal government backs out by Hannah Reale, GBH News.

Seeing the future? Massachusetts wants to see your license by Hallie Claflin, CommonWealth Beacon.

Housing Bank Legislation Fails Again At State House by JohnCarl McGrady, Nantucket Current.

Flock announces changes amid backlash over its license plate reader network by Sarah Rankin and Claudia Lauer, The Associated Press.

title: Man accused in stabbing near North Station was pulled off victim by good Samaritan, prosecutors say
text:
The suspect in a domestic violence incident near North Station last week stabbed his girlfriend repeatedly and only stopped when a Good Samaritan pulled him off the victim, authorities said Monday.

Daudy B. Martinez was arraigned Monday from a Boston hospital where he is recovering from self-inflicted injuries sustained Thursday in a building on Causeway Street, according to Suffolk District Attorney Kevin R. Hayden’s office.

Martinez, 51, was ordered held by Judge James W. Coffey pending a dangerousness hearing sought by Hayden’s office. He faces multiple charges, including armed assault with intent to murder and domestic violence, subsequent offense.

Hayden’s office provided new details during the arraignment. Martinez, prosecutors said, got into an argument with a woman identified as his 44-year-old girlfriend.

“During the course of that fight, the defendant pushed her to the ground and proceeded to stab her at least four times,” the prosecutor said. Police “observed her to have blood running down her face from a head wound and bleeding to the back of a leg.”

The woman was rushed to a Boston hospital where officers learned she had stab wounds to her forehead, her left hand, her chin and neck area, and behind her left leg, the prosecutor said.

On-scene officers reviewed surveillance video that captured Martinez’s alleged assault, the prosecutor said.

Martinez “doesn’t stop until an unidentified female comes up behind him and pulls him off the victim,” the prosecutor said.

The victim is hospitalized for treatment of her multiple injuries, the prosecutor said.

Officers pursued Martinez, allegedly still armed with a knife, into a nearby restaurant. When police ordered him to drop the knife or be tased by them, Martinez injured himself with the weapon, the prosecutor said.

Martinez pleaded guilty to domestic violence charges in West Roxbury Municipal Court in 2021 and was sentenced to two years in Suffolk County House of Correction, court records show.

He completed a two-year probation period last October, records show.|

John R. Ellement can be reached at john.ellement@globe.com. Follow him @JREbosglobe.

title: Darryl Whiting, once a crack-dealing ‘God’ and the scourge of Roxbury, has died. Here’s what locals say about his ruinous legacy.
text:
“I’m not a romantic; at the end of the day, his legacy is [expletive] crack cocaine,” said Jamarhl Crawford, who grew up in Roxbury and dealt drugs as a teenager, before becoming a community activist and organizer. “He was just a crack dealer.”

Whiting, for all his imprint locally, was not from Boston. He came here from New York in the 1980s and took over the Orchard Park housing development in Roxbury, eventually turning it into his personal trap house. There, he preyed upon the weaknesses of drug-addicted mothers surviving on government assistance to gain the use of their apartments to move significant amounts of narcotics.

“Basically, he came into Orchard Park, got rid of the old dealers, and either you were buying from him or selling for him,” said Crawford.

The operation was 24-7, with Whiting’s organization eventually becoming the largest supplier of cocaine in Roxbury, authorities said at the time.

By the time his New York Boys organization was dismantled by law enforcement in the early 1990s, the group was grossing more than $6 million a year in drug sales and controlled about $11 million in local real estate, according to federal court testimony. Whiting owned and operated a video store, sneaker shop, and barbershop, all on Warren Street in Roxbury, as well as the Crown Social and Recreation Hall on Geneva Avenue in Grove Hall.

At one point, Whiting’s organization had about 75 members, according to court testimony from someone who worked for him, including women who acted as drug mules, bringing hard drugs from New York to packing houses in Boston. There were also people who processed and packed cocaine, runners, and street-level sellers, all ultimately answering to him.

His rise in the Boston underworld inspired LL Cool J’s character in the 1999 crime thriller “In Too Deep.” And some of Whiting’s tale has become blurred with fiction locally.

Some observers from his era have suggested that Whiting was the one person most responsible for bringing wholesale amounts of crack cocaine to the streets of Boston. Others are adamant that that is an urban myth, a reductive oversimplification, and a fundamental misreading of Boston street life during the 1980s.

Whatever the reality, a Boston police commissioner once described him as “an evil person.” To the head of the US Drug Enforcement Administration office in Boston, he was “a piece of trash.” A different investigator labeled him “a city’s worst nightmare.” Newspapers dubbed him a criminal mastermind.

The head federal prosecutor in Boston once gave his case higher priority than that of New England Mafia boss Raymond “Junior” Patriarca.

His larger-than-life story sometimes had elements of a Hollywood noir script.

During one court appearance, he announced to the gathered press, “Call this the second trial of Jesus Christ!” He once struck a cop with a ring shaped like a ram’s head. Police said he went by many names: God, G, Rah.

Taking down his operation was a massive undertaking: In 1990, 250 federal agents and police raided locations in Roxbury, including Orchard Park, Dorchester, and Mattapan, arresting 18. Whiting was already behind bars when that happened, serving an assault and battery sentence at the Deer Island House of Correction.

Ultimately, Whiting became the first person in Massachusetts to receive a life sentence for selling narcotics.

The Rev. Eugene F. Rivers III has worked on street violence prevention and mitigation in Boston for decades. To him, Whiting was among the dominant underworld forces that circulated hard drugs throughout Black Boston, ripping apart families and ruining lives.

“There wasn’t anybody comparable to what he was doing,” Rivers said this past week.

Whiting’s rise to the top of the Boston drug trade corresponded with a historic spike in street violence in the city. In 1989, there were 100 homicides in the city. The next year, the number was 152. Such street violence, according to researchers, was fueled by the crack cocaine trade and the turf-based conflicts it fostered.

Rivers said Whiting’s organization was part of the milieu that increased the bloodshed on the streets of Boston.

“There was no question about that,” he said.

Like so many underworld figures, he leaned into the Robin Hood trope, projecting an image of someone who cared about Black communities in a city that had a very real history of racism.

He once put on a free rap concert for more than 1,000 teenagers at Dorchester’s Strand Theatre. There were also free trips to amusement parks for youths, Christmas parties, Easter egg hunts, barbecues, weekend brunches, and gifts of sports equipment. One registered nurse testified in court that his Grove Hall club doubled as a day care center for homeless mothers and offered youth programs and health care counseling.

But for one retired Boston police officer who grew up in Orchard Park, Whiting’s legacy is no different from James “Whitey” Bulger, the mobster who lorded over South Boston’s underworld for years and corrupted the local FBI office. Crack turned their home into a “zombieland,” they said.

Speaking on the condition of anonymity because they feared reprisals on their relatives, the former cop said it’s true that Whiting would buy people groceries and pay their bills when they were tight on money. But once he did someone a favor, that meant they owed him. For the Orchard Park native, Whiting was a “wolf in sheep’s clothing.”

“He did all that, but he had his own agenda,” said the retiree. “He was helping himself. He was making his money.”

Court testimony painted an even darker and more violent picture. One former member of his organization said under oath that discipline was instilled with violence, saying he was beaten on Whiting’s command at least three times.

A woman testified she became addicted to crack after agreeing to let Whiting’s gang use her apartment to set up a drug-dealing operation. The woman said she earned $350 a week for allowing drugs to be processed and packaged in the apartment she shared with her two small children. She also admitted to torturing a suspected informant on behalf of Whiting’s gang, saying the person was burned on the forehead with a curling iron “for a long time.”

Boston political consultant Joyce Ferriabough Bolling recalled feeling “horrible for the Orchard Park community” during Whiting’s heyday, which was marked by rampant and brazen drug peddling in and around the development that was colloquially known as “OP.”

“I wondered why the police or somebody in authority didn’t move on closing down God’s in-your-face operation,” she said.

His legacy is a dark one, according to Ferriabough Bolling, as it took at least two generations to clean up the crack scourge in Boston.

“I hope he made his peace with the real God,” she said.

Jeremiah Manion of Globe staff contributed to this report.

title: The generational challenge that actually may be tightening in Mass.
text:
A new poll — commissioned by Leaders We Deserve, the progressive group putting its firepower behind Eighth Congressional District candidate Patrick Roath and other younger, progressive challengers — shows a tightening race in Roath’s primary against US Representative Stephen Lynch.

The survey of 469 likely Democratic primary voters in the district found Roath, a 39-year-old Jamaica Plain attorney, trailing Lynch by seven percentage points, 43 percent to 50 percent. The remaining 7 percent were undecided.

As with any internal survey, caveats apply. The poll, which was conducted on Aug. 5-6, had a margin of error of plus-or-minus 4.53 percent, according to a polling memo shared by Leaders We Deserve. The PAC, founded by gun control activist David Hogg, also has a vested interest in boosting Roath, a first-time candidate trying to unseat a more well-known, moderate incumbent in Lynch, 71.

A poll Roath’s campaign paid for from February found him lagging Lynch by 26 percentage points. There’s been no independent public polling of the race so far.

Still, if the latest numbers hold, those results paint a picture of a race that’s far closer than the matchup between US Representative Seth Moulton and US Senator Ed Markey in the party’s US Senate primary, according to a new University of Massachusetts Amherst/WCVB poll.

Of the 445 Democratic primary voters surveyed, 54 percent said they would vote for Markey, 80, compared to 28 percent who said they’d back Moulton, 47, if the Sept. 1 election were held today. Another 17 percent were still undecided. Throw in those who said they are leaning toward one candidate or another, and Markey’s lead grows wider: 60 percent for the incumbent, versus 32 percent for Moulton.

Markey’s edge in the new poll is far wider than the one he had in a University of New Hampshire poll conducted in late June that showed the Malden Democrat leading Moulton by just 6 percentage points.

“We’ve seen primaries across the country where you have the establishment candidate versus the progressive challenger or upstart, but in this instance, we have a little bit of a different story,” said Tatishe Nteta, the UMass Poll director. “The incumbent [Markey] is viewed as a more progressive candidate. The challenger is viewed, at least by the electorate, as a much more moderate candidate.”

Moulton, he added, “is going to need a miracle or a Hail Mary to really change the dynamics of this race.”

In the Eighth District, it’s a different story. Roath has positioned himself to Lynch’s left on an array of issues from healthcare to immigration.

Still, Lynch holds several advantages in the race. He ended June with a $1.2 million war chest, more than doubling the $460,000 Roath had on hand. Lynch has also fended off progressive challengers in the past, defeating Robbie Goldstein, now the state’s public health commissioner, in 2020, and Democrats Brianna Wu and Christopher Voehl in 2018.

Lynch is also running — literally — at least in his latest digital ad, a 15-second spot that shows him jogging along the beach in South Boston.

DEBATE GUYS: The two Republican candidates for governor aren’t expected to face off in a debate ahead of their Sept. 1 primary, though not from a lack of trying on one of their parts.

So, in a spirit of civic discourse, the Globe’s Chris Van Buskirk tried to create one — or the closest thing to a debate without having Michael Minogue and Brian Shortsleeve on the same stage. Read their answers to Chris’s questions (edited for clarity and length) here.

THE STATUS KOH: A debate coursing through Democratic Party is playing out in Mass. 6th District and its crowded primary field by Anjali Huynh, The Boston Globe: As Democrats here and elsewhere try to pitch voters on the need for wholesale change, Sixth District congressional hopeful Dan Koh is leaning on his years spent inside government offices — and on his famous former bosses — to help deliver the message.

Koh and former US Labor Secretary and Boston mayor Martin J. Walsh spent Wednesday shaking hands and giving hugs among the crowd attending a concert-in-the-park series. The same week, Walsh, who also campaigned for Koh during his unsuccessful 2018 bid in the Third Congressional District, visited seniors and attended a canvass with Koh. Then on Thursday, Koh, the former White House aide, released a new television ad featuring smiling cameos from former President Joe Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris.

Walsh said he plans to be out “as much as I can be” in the days before the Sept. 1 primary, calling himself “a friend helping a friend.” Still, he and Biden are the type of surrogates few can trot out — and perhaps that others aren’t clamoring to campaign alongside.

PAC ATTACK: With just over two weeks to go before the primary, another Sixth District hopeful is dropping the gloves. Lynnfield fintech executive John Beccia’s campaign is out with a new digital ad titled “Fine Print,” knocking Koh for, among other things, support he’s seen from a super PAC that has taken money from sports betting giant DraftKings.

SPEAKING OF OUTSIDE SPENDING ... Another super PAC waded into the Sixth District race late last week. The Save America Fund, a Rhode Island-based super PAC, shelled out almost $44,000 on behalf of state Representative Tram Nguyen, according to federal campaign filings.

Sound familiar? That’s the super PAC that Nguyen donated nearly $200,000 to last year using funds from her state campaign account.

SETTLED: MBTA to pay nearly $500,000 to chief communications official whose hair GM Phil Eng pulled in ‘insensitive’ incident by Diti Kohli, The Boston Globe: The MBTA will pay nearly $500,000 to Gabrielle Mondestin, the T’s chief communications officer whose hair general manager Phil Eng admitted to — and apologized for — pulling at a 2024 dinner, according to a settlement agreement released Friday by the transit agency.

Mondestin will resign from the agency on Sept. 18 with a $495,000 settlement, ending a strange saga in which Eng repeatedly acknowledged that his actions nearly two years ago toward Mondestin, who is Black, were “insensitive.” The agreement does not include an admission of wrongdoing by Eng, who also serves as the state’s interim transportation secretary under Governor Maura Healey. Both Mondestin and Eng signed the deal on Aug. 7, according to a copy provided to the Globe.

SOMERVILLE’S BIG BRAKE: Somerville has gone 4 years without a traffic death. Here’s how New England’s densest city did it. by Diti Kohli, The Boston Globe: While other communities in Massachusetts have had to confront traffic deaths, from highway drivers to cyclists, serious crashes in Somerville dropped by 50 percent in 2025 from the year before.

But the most effective traffic calming strategy in the region’s most densely populated city can also easily become a cultural firestorm: slowing down cars.

TRAIN DREAMS: Kennedy School researchers tout benefits of proposed North-South Rail Link by Travis Andersen, The Boston Globe: The ambitious project has been discussed for years and comes with a hefty price tag should it ever get rolling.

ALLEGED LAW(RENCE) BREAKER: Lawrence mayor arrested on federal charges of wire fraud, money laundering by Sean Cotter, The Boston Globe: By mid-2021, hundreds of thousands of dollars in personal bills were coming due for Brian DePeña, and, according to authorities, his campaign for Lawrence mayor needed money, too. DePeña, according to federal prosecutors, turned to a source of cash that he had access to thanks to his tire dealership: low-interest, high-dollar loans the federal government was offering to businesses to help dig out from the coronavirus pandemic.

His requests grew to more than $1.6 million, according to court documents. But instead of putting the money into his business as he was required to, authorities say DePeña used it to pay down personal debts and also steered $90,000 to his campaign committee. FBI agents arrested him at his home Friday morning. DePeña, still the sitting mayor of Lawrence, is facing felony charges of wire fraud and money laundering.

His lawyer, Carlos Apostle, said the mayor has seven children and is receiving treatment for a prostate issue, and therefore isn’t a flight risk. As they bolted from the pack of reporters and cameras, DePeña and the lawyer piled into an orange Dodge, which the lawyer threw into drive and immediately drove into the back of a parked white sedan. He took down the car’s information, yelled at the assembled press, and left.

READ MORE: Lawrence mayor’s arrest a ‘step back’ for a city with a long history of political scandal by Chris Van Buskirk, The Boston Globe.

NOW WATCH THIS DRIVE: Mass. Democratic Party leader attended awards gala in Boston before he was charged with drunken driving, footage shows by Samantha J. Gross, The Boston Globe: Steve Kerrigan, the chairman of the Massachusetts Democratic Party, was driving home from a community health centers gala in Boston when he was pulled over after crossing marked traffic lanes in a “pretty egregious” fashion and arrested on drunken driving charges, bodycam footage from the June incident shows.

Kerrigan later admitted in court that prosecutors had enough evidence to convict him after he was arrested in Southborough on June 13, and lost his license for 45 days. He told police that he had two IPA beers before dinner, several hours before he was pulled over around midnight about 18 miles south of his home in Lancaster.

Higher education commissioner stepping down in September by Sam Drysdale, State House News Service.

‘Give us more of that socialism’: Markey, Warren rally Democrats in Holyoke by Samuel Gelinas, Greenfield Recorder.

This tiny Mass. town is fighting a proposed battery park, saying it could harm Boston’s drinking water. Some officials disagree. by Danny McDonald, The Boston Globe.

title: Why is Rachael Rollins casting Michelle Wu as Boston’s Trump?
text:
Rollins is trying to make a political comeback after resigning in disgrace three years ago as the top federal prosecutor in Massachusetts, and she seems to be betting that there’s enough dissatisfaction with Wu that yoking the current Suffolk DA, Kevin Hayden, to the mayor might be enough for Rollins to win her old office back.

In Rollins’s telling, the problem isn’t Wu’s policies — it’s just that she has too much power.

“I support Mayor Wu. I think she can be a great mayor,” Rollins said. “I just don’t want her to be in charge of my Boston City Council, or my DA. She controls everything right now. So, for me, I just feel like we need an autonomous DA.”

If the Trump administration decides to launch an immigration enforcement operation in Boston, she wondered, “Who do you want at a podium? Do you want Kevin Hayden, who can’t make a decision without speaking to Mayor Wu, who, by the way, is now about to control all three branches of municipal government?” (Rollins argues that because DAs are the gateway to the judiciary, controlling the DA amounts to controlling the judicial branch.)

Rollins’s loaded, hyperbolic attack seems, on its surface, like a cheap political calculation. But the attack has an identifiable audience.

A vocal network of Black neighborhood and civic leaders have clashed with Wu over the redevelopment of White Stadium in Franklin Park and Parcel P3, and the redesign of Blue Hill Avenue, as well as other projects, often accusing her administration of asking for communities’ feedback only after decisions have effectively been made. Rollins appears to be betting that frustration with Wu can be converted into votes against Hayden.

Boston political strategist Jacquetta Van Zandt told me there’s “something distinctly Trumpian” about Wu’s tactical approach to opposition, though not about her ideology. Van Zandt served as a senior communications advisor to Josh Kraft, whose 2025 bid for mayor collapsed after Wu trounced him by a stunning margin in the preliminary election — 72 percent to his 23 percent.

“I think Rachael is making a legitimate political argument when she is asking people to examine Kevin Hayden’s relationship with Mayor Wu,” Van Zandt told me. But “having the mayor’s support and being controlled by the mayor are two different things,” she said. If Rollins can show that Hayden made prosecutorial decisions at Wu’s request, Van Zandt noted, “that’s serious.” But if the two elected officials merely agree and partner on public-safety policy and work together, “that’s not being a puppet, that’s government.”

Reggie Stewart, a director of the Roxbury Neighborhood Council, called Black civic opposition to Wu “a coherent, real thing,” animated by multiple projects and a shared belief that the mayor simply does not listen to critics.

And yet, Rollins’s Black political base exists independently of that opposition, according to Stewart, who is not supporting any of the Suffolk DA’s candidates publicly as of now. “Maybe the anti-Wu sentiment is the icing on the cake, but I don’t believe that’s what makes Rachael popular,” Stewart said. “Her Black supporters support her because they support her, not because they oppose Wu. Those two things just happen to intersect.”

To be sure, Rollins has offered no evidence that Hayden is controlled by Wu, and none emerged in my reporting. In an interview, Wu didn’t directly respond to Rollins’s accusation but she defended her partnership with Hayden by citing the city’s falling crime and violence.

“I’m proud to support District Attorney Hayden because he has been steady, thoughtful, and innovative in his work,” Wu said. “He’s built relationships, is competent, drama-free, and has been leading that office in a way that has helped achieve the results that we’ve seen.”

As for an anti-Wu constituency in Black Boston, the mayor’s defenders point to her decisive victory over Kraft in last fall’s preliminary to rebut those claims: The mayor won three out of four votes in Wards 12 and 14, which are regarded as the heart of the city’s Black community.

True, but that is not necessarily proof that the underlying frustration is imaginary. Elections measure choices and voters were choosing between Wu and Kraft, a challenger whose campaign never really gave dissatisfied Black voters a compelling reason to defect.

“It was like, ‘anti-Wu, okay, great. We agree. What will you do differently?’ And the [Kraft] campaign just couldn’t answer that question,” Stewart said.

There’s actually a lesson for Rollins in Kraft’s failure. Anti-Wu sentiment may give her an audience but it can’t substitute for evidence that Hayden has surrendered his office’s autonomy. Rollins has found a provocative way to frame the race: If Wu is Boston’s Trump, then she is running as the resistance. But calling Hayden a puppet is not the same thing as proving that he is one. And running against Wu is not the same as making a strong case for Rachael Rollins.

title: White Stadium victory frees Wu’s second term from a political thicket
text:
It all adds up to a big win for Wu, who has faced more than a year of allegations that she was stuffing an unpopular and possibly illegitimate idea down the throat of a community that didn’t want it. The prospect of losing must have been nightmarish for her.

It’s fair to say that White Stadium was an unlikely choice for a crusade. The stadium has been a mess for years, but somehow it became a mess everyone had learned to live with. Plans to improve it had been floated and discarded without fanfare or outrage. It was as though everyone had decided it wasn’t great, but it was good enough.

Politically, it didn’t help Wu that the catalyst for this project was bringing a women’s professional soccer team to Franklin Park. Though Boston Legacy FC has committed to paying $190 million of the cost of the $325 million project, the claim the city was somehow selling out the community around Franklin Park resonated in some quarters. Many would argue that Wu could have chosen a more worthy cause for a 2 ½ year dogfight.

For my part, I became an advocate for restoring White Stadium years ago. Unlike some so-called advocates, I’ve toured White Stadium multiple times and was shocked by its decrepitude. I supported construction magnate John Fish’s idea of renovating it in 2013 - which died a quiet death after Mayor Thomas M. Menino left office before it could be realized. And I’ve never changed my mind that a new White Stadium would be a great benefit for the young people of Boston.

I give Wu’s courtroom adversaries, the Emerald Necklace Conservancy, great credit for its deep concern about Franklin Park. It fought this battle for principled reasons, and the finished product will be better for its advocacy.

Of course, no ruling will change the fact that a large and vocal contingent of neighboring residents are uneasy with the White Stadium renovation.

It’s up to the city to prove the many remaining issues of access can be resolved without placing an undue burden on residents. Wu should expect to be held to her promises this will be an economic engine for Roxbury, Dorchester, and Mattapan, beginning with the awarding of contracts to renovate and operate it. And that this will be a facility for Boston Public School students first, and for a soccer team second.

Those are the reasons this project is worth it.

As for Wu, it’s fair to say the start of her second term has been a slog. After her resounding victory in the mayor’s race last year, Wu immediately became the target of criticism. Black activists have argued that she is both too inaccessible and too inflexible. Progressives say she isn’t going far enough in pushing their issues. Even cyclists are bitterly critical, even though Wu is literally the first champion of their causes to occupy the mayor’s office.

But wins like Tuesday’s offer an opportunity to reset. Instead of debating what happens if Wu loses the White Stadium case, the conversation can now move to what the renovation can bring to Boston. It can dampen the talk that she’s damaged politically, or headed to some other work opportunity.

The truth is that Wu, for better or worse, is the same person who destroyed Josh Kraft a year ago, the same person who has never, in fact, had a single close race in her political career.

We might not know for years whether White Stadium was a visionary idea or a lousy idea. But what we know today is that Wu took a considerable political risk, stuck to her guns, and won.

title: ‘Full steam ahead’: Wu takes victory lap after end of White Stadium legal battle
text:
The SJC’s decision eliminated the final legal hurdle for the controversial project, effectively clearing the path forward for construction to continue. The redeveloped stadium, which the city is partnering with the professional women’s soccer team Boston Legacy FC to deliver, will be the new hub for Boston Public Schools athletics and the home stadium for the women’s soccer team.

The city committed to covering $135 million of the project’s estimated price tag. Boston Legacy FC is expected to pay about $190 million.

Officials from Boston Legacy FC, top City Hall staff, and local and state leaders joined Wu on Thursday to celebrate the SJC’s decision.

“We are charting a course that teams and cities around the country are already looking to,” Wu said at a news conference behind the William J. Devine Golf Course clubhouse, situated on the other end of Franklin Park from the stadium.

The project has generated substantial scrutiny and opposition over the past three years, as critics raised concerns about the project’s rising price tag, the city’s partnership with a private entity, and the decision to locate a professional sports complex in Franklin Park.

Wu has framed the project as an extraordinary opportunity to overhaul the more than 75-year-old dilapidated stadium and give Boston Public Schools students and city residents access to a professional-grade sports facility, without taxpayers having to shoulder the full cost.

She said “generations” of Boston Public Schools families have been asking the city to renovate the aging stadium. “Our Boston kids deserve the very best, and as a city, we can never apologize for fighting to give it to them,” she said.

But the project’s opponents, who filed the initial lawsuit to stop the project in February of 2024, argued it violates constitutional parkland protections, and that the neighborhoods around Franklin Park are not an appropriate place for a professional sports stadium.

The Supreme Judicial Court ruled Wednesday that the stadium site is a school facility, not parkland, and therefore not subject to those protections.

Still, even with that legal victory in hand, it remains unclear when the stadium will be finished and ready to host games and practices, either for students or professionals.

Wu did not directly answer questions Thursday about the project’s timeline and target completion date, but said construction work is happening on the site six days a week and meeting planned milestones.

She indicated that the lawsuit over the project had caused some delays.

“It’s undeniable that the litigation process has been a distraction and took significant resources and time and energy,” Wu said. “So we are evaluating closely, and we’ll be working to really fully assess what that means for the remainder of the schedule.”

Wu and Boston Legacy FC owner Jennifer Epstein on Thursday also did not answer questions about whether the professional women’s team plans to host any home games at White Stadium during the 2027 National Women’s Soccer League season, which begins in February.

The team is currently playing all of its home games this season at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough.

Work on the stadium began in early 2025 with the demolition of the old facility, and on Thursday, construction appeared to be back in full swing.

The sound of clangs, beeps, and crashes filled the air as excavators rumbled across the site. Two red cranes towered over dozens of laborers in hard hats and fluorescent T-shirts and vests, helping lift long metal rods.

As construction continues, a group of elected and community leaders that make up the White Stadium Neighborhood Advisory Council will finalize transportation plans for the 20 Boston Legacy FC game days, Wu said.

Residents can share their input on traffic management plans, including game-day parking restrictions, at four community meetings the city is planning to host in Roxbury, Jamaica Plain, Mattapan, and Dorchester this fall.

title: Roslindale woman allegedly assaulted parents of her former boyfriend while wielding a baseball bat, prosecutors say
text:
A Roslindale woman was charged with felony home invasion after allegedly breaking into the home of a former boyfriend wielding a baseball bat and assaulting his parents, authorities said Wednesday.

Alyssah G. Harrison, 19, pleaded not guilty in West Roxbury Municipal Court on Wednesday to single counts of home invasion, assault with a dangerous weapon, assault and battery, and malicious destruction of property, court records show.

She was released on personal recognizance by Judge Maureen Flaherty, ordered to comply with a restraining order, and stay away from the home, the alleged victims, and witnesses, records show. A pretrial hearing is scheduled for Oct. 2.

Harrison’s lawyer, Patrick Kelly, declined to comment on Thursday.

Prosecutors allege that Harrison used a baseball bat to smash through the door of her former boyfriend’s house before trying to steal money from a safe on the second floor, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden’s office said.

“It’s not hard to imagine the fear these homeowners must have experienced when their peaceful day at home was suddenly turned chaotic and violent by an armed intruder,” Hayden said in a statement.

Around 1 p.m. on July 22, police responded to a call from a security office for a property near Highcrest Road and Highcrest Terrace stating that a distressed resident had reported a woman was inside his home vandalizing the property, prosecutors said.

The resident said that he was home with his wife when the woman whom they recognized as their son’s former girlfriend, came to the front door and swung an aluminum baseball bat, shattering a glass screen and entering the home.

When the man and his wife tried to approach Harrison, she allegedly pushed the woman and punched her in the face. Harrison then threatened the couple, holding the bat in “a cocked position,” and proceeded upstairs to a second-floor bedroom where the couple said they heard her rummaging through drawers.

At that point, the husband left the home to contact security, while the wife tried to remove Harrison from the bedroom.

According to a police report, the husband appeared at the security desk holding a baseball bat, though it is unclear whether it was the same bat Harrison allegedly used or when he may have gained possession of it.

Upstairs in the house, the wife told police she got into a fight with Harrison, causing her to flee, prosecutors said. The couple declined medical attention, police said.

The wife told police she didn’t know if Harrison had stolen anything, but didn’t see anything in her hands as she ran off. Harrison’s former boyfriend told police he believed she had targeted the upstairs safe, prosecutors said.

When speaking to police, the wife said Harrison only entered one of two upstairs bedrooms, although her husband later told officers that she had told him she’d seen Harrison enter both bedrooms.

When police told the husband that his wife only reported seeing Harrison entering one room, he became “visibly upset” and walked away.

title: With White Stadium ruling, some win, some lose
text:
Featuring: Karen Mauney-Brodek, Jennifer Epstein, Bill Keravuori, Robert Kraft, Miceal Chamberlain, Mike Firestone, Adam Chapdelaine, Dianne Wilkerson, John Holland, Mary Veronica McGuff, Richard Henning, Santi Garces, Jessicah Pierre, Lacey Rose, Stéphane Bancel, Noubar Afeyan, and more.

When the Supreme Judicial Court heard oral arguments in the White Stadium fight in April, it looked like opponents might have a shot.

The questioning at times seemed more antagonistic to the Wu administration and Boston Legacy FC than to the Emerald Necklace Conservancy, the plaintiff aiming to stop their stadium project.

However, the justices ended up siding with Mayor Michelle Wu this week. They decided rebuilding White Stadium to share with a pro sports team — as well as related work nearby in Franklin Park — won’t violate the state constitution’s parkland protections.

Their ruling will affect many constituencies, in and outside of the city. Here’s a rundown of where they stand.

The mayor: It’s a big vindication for Wu — who staked considerable political capital on this — and her advisers from the Rose, Goulston & Storrs, and WilmerHale law firms. Wu plowed ahead with the controversial $325 million project despite the litigation. (The price has gone up a bit in two years.) The city committed to an eye-popping $135 million, to rebuild one grandstand area. Boston Legacy is covering the rest.

The Kraft Group: Boston Legacy has played at Gillette Stadium in the team’s first year, and theoretically could use the Everett stadium that Robert Kraft and Jonathan Kraft are pursuing for the Revs once that’s done. But the Kraft Group actually rooted for Wu’s project by filing a surprising legal brief in support in March. A stated reason: generating more interest in soccer. The Krafts need Wu on their side, as they build their own stadium on Boston’s doorstep.

Emerald Necklace Conservancy: Guess who is not on Wu’s good side? The conservancy, led by Karen Mauney-Brodek. The nonprofit sees itself as a city partner in supporting Emerald Necklace parks. But the city recently denied a permit for its spring fundraiser. Could its home at the Curley House (another George White legacy building) be next?

Boston Legacy/Able Co.: Team lead owner Jennifer Epstein calls the ruling a “tremendous victory” for the city’s schools, “the Franklin Park community,” and pro women’s soccer in Boston. Left unsaid: It’s also a win for Able Co., the firm led by Bill Keravuori, Epstein’s husband. Able is developing the team’s portion of the stadium, and is involved with another city project in Nubian Square.

Bank of America: Miceal Chamberlain and other local BofA execs can breathe easy. They agreed to a $100 million-plus financing deal for Boston Legacy’s portion a year ago. (The team has not said whether the bank will chip in more after the costs shot up.)

The governor: Maura Healey steered clear of this imbroglio — until this summer. Several of her top aides, such as Rebecca Tepper and Phil Eng, recently met with a group of stadium opponents. Among them: former state senator Dianne Wilkerson, who took to social media on Wednesday saying: “This doesn’t mean the City can do anything they want. Much more to say later. For now, just know we’re not done!”

Environmental groups: Several expressed concern the project could weaken the constitution’s Article 97, which requires state legislative approval for changing the use of parkland. (The SJC ruled this was fulfilled with votes in 1947 and 1950.) However, many prominent environmental organizations — including Mass Audubon and the Conservation Law Foundation — sat this one out.

Mass. Municipal Association: The group representing cities and towns essentially had an opposite fear, that a ruling against Wu could make it harder for municipalities to convert their own land for different uses. “We feel strongly it protects all cities and towns,” executive director Adam Chapdelaine said of the ruling.

Local businesses: How much of the stadium business will trickle down to the neighborhoods abutting the park? Ed Gaskin, executive director of Greater Grove Hall Main Streets, says now is the time for a plan ensuring an economic benefit comes to his area, and not just congestion from soccer fans passing through.

Olmsted Network: The national coalition that supports the work of famed landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted lodged an amicus brief supporting the conservancy, an ally. “Disappointing is not a strong enough word,” said president Sue Breitkopf, adding that the real losers are neighbors whose use of Franklin Park will be interrupted, particularly on game days.

George White: Speaking of historical figures, it’s hard not to wonder what White — a philanthropist and “antibacterial soap magnate,” to quote the SJC — would think of all this fighting over the stadium that bears his name. Maybe it’s time for the “Angel of Peace,” as the memorial to White in Forest Hills is known, to get to work.

What’s your take? Join the conversation in the comments here.

The Poor Clare Nuns aren’t the only ones anxiously waiting for the city of Boston to approve the long-stalled redevelopment of their Jamaica Plain monastery – so are the sisters of the Monastery of Christ the King. The order, located in Florida, merged last month with the Boston nuns so they can retire together in Westwood, where the Poor Clares have relocated. But there’s no room at the inn. As our colleague Catherine Carlock wrote earlier this year, the nuns can’t expand their Westwood home until they finalize the sale of the old monastery on Centre Street, which is contingent on the Boston Planning Department approving developer John Holland’s plan to build 158 apartments and condos. The big hang-up: Concerns over how new housing would impact the Arnold Arboretum next door. But after three years, patience is wearing thin. Michael Perry, Minister Provincial of the Franciscan Friars — a bishop-like figure for the sister orders – asked for the project to move “as expeditiously as possible” in an Aug. 11 letter addressed to sister leaders Mary Veronica McGuff and Leanna Chrostowski, with Boston Archbishop Richard Henning copied in.

Will UNITE HERE Local 26 roll the dice and go on strike at the Encore Boston Harbor casino? The union wraps up strike authorization votes today as it steps up the pressure on casino operator Wynn Resorts before their contract expires at the end of the month. The union represents nearly 1,200 workers at the Everett casino and hotel. (Another 230 Teamsters members are also planning to vote to authorize a strike today). The union says it wants workers at Wynn’s fancy casino to earn wages and benefits similar to contracts it has won at other Boston hotels recently. Surely, Local 26 argues, with all the profits Wynn makes from the casino, the company can afford it. (A Wynn spokesperson said it’s committed to reaching a fair agreement, one that works for employees and keeps the business strong for the long term.) Our bet: a deal gets done before the union workers walk out.

The City Hall-to-Harvard pipeline keeps growing. Santi Garces, Boston’s chief information officer for the past four years, is the latest to leave Mayor Michelle Wu’s administration for her alma mater. Garces departed recently to become a senior fellow at Harvard’s Bloomberg Center for Cities to study and teach on the future of government, artificial intelligence, and innovation. He’ll find a familiar face there: Jessicah Pierre, Wu’s former chief communications officer, who started in February to lead the center’s communications team. Across campus, they might bump into Lacey Rose, former communications chief for the Boston Planning Department, who in July decamped to Harvard Law School to run media relations. We bet they won’t be the last to hop the Red Line northbound.

It’s a great day if you own Moderna stock. CEO Stéphane Bancel and chairman Noubar Afeyan are certainly among those cheering the company’s cancer-treatment news. Both have watched their substantial stakes in the Cambridge biotech dwindle in value since hitting pandemic-era peaks in 2021. The breakthrough announced on Wednesday with Merck, its business partner, sent shares soaring, nearly tripling their value in one day. Even after a slide today, Bancel’s stake is now worth around $4 billion, assuming he still owns more than 30 million shares in stock and exercisable options, per the company’s March proxy. Afeyan, meanwhile, holds about 7 million shares. Today, Moderna’s shares are trading above $130 but they are still a far cry from the $400-plus we saw five years ago.

With Santander completing its $12 billion acquisition of Webster Bank today, the merger raises a number of questions. What’s going to happen to the spacious branch Webster opened nearly 20 years ago in the former home of the Boston Stock Exchange at 100 Franklin St.? At the time, the Connecticut-based bank was trying to make a big impression in Boston, so it opened a branch with soaring 32-foot-high ceilings, a throwback to the old days when bank executives thought they needed a cavernous lobby to be taken seriously. (This building was originally home to Boston Safe Deposit and Trust.) Christiana Riley, head of Santander US, and John Ciulla, formerly Webster’s CEO and now Riley’s top lieutenant, both say they know it’s a beautiful location but no decisions about branch closings have been made.

We asked our readers which Boston pub was visited by the actors who played the hobbits in the Lord of the Rings trilogy recently while in town for a fan convention. The hint: the pub’s name was mentioned in a song that they sang in one of the movies. Turns out our readers know their Nazguls from their necromancers: Half of the respondents got the answer right: the Green Dragon, near Faneuil Hall.
