title: Hip-hop therapy is uncommon in the US. This Roxbury nonprofit wants to change that.
text:
In the 2010s, CSR adopted a program called Beats Rhymes and Life (BRL), an initiative that uses hip-hop clinics to address mental health and community wellness for children and young adults. These clinics, which last about 10 weeks each semester, involve writing workshops, hip-hop education, and other exercises that build communication skills.

CSR currently uses the program to work with clients between the ages of 14 and 24 who may not want to receive treatment through traditional therapeutic services.

Artist coordinators and registered local clinicians create programming that is hip-hop inspired and addresses issues students might be experiencing at home, such as substance abuse and depression. Staff use tools like a visual “hip-hop timeline” and songwriting exercises to teach students how the genre has been used to address oppression in Black and brown communities for decades.

The program is the first of its kind in Massachusetts, and similar programs are extremely uncommon in other parts of the country. Representatives from CSR say that shouldn’t be the case.

According to Stephanie Sabins, the lead clinician for BRL, the creative process in therapy creates opportunities for “healthy risks” and helps people understand themselves.

“Some of the best conversations I’ve ever had with youth are in these groups,” she added.

Sabins, who has worked in the program for five years, thinks hip-hop therapy is still making its case as a respected approach to improving mental health.

“We are actively decolonizing therapy,” said Candice Watch, BRL’s director. “Storytelling is actually what hip-hop has always been, and that is an actual form of therapy.”

Therapy doesn’t have to look like the traditional medical model, Watch explained. She said using an already known form of cultural expression — such as hip-hop — is sometimes more effective than talk therapy or other clinical treatments.

Each cohort is encouraged to write about whatever they want in their songs. Heartbreak, stress, and grief are among the many topics. That creative autonomy helps participants develop social skills, creativity, and self-assurance.

Students like Luis “Louie” Colon are reaping the benefits.

Colon, a 22-year-old Roxbury native, started the program in the spring. He struggled with public speaking and, at times, connecting with and relating to his peers. BRL changed that.

He said BRL is one of “the only things I really had where I can be with my peers, laugh, joke, and have fun.”

When Colon’s not in BRL sessions, he’s pursuing a career in photography and visual art. Making time for his personal life is difficult. Dwindling support for artistry leaves Colon feeling like he’s fighting an uphill battle and often alone.

“We all go through the same stuff, but being here, I was happy,” he said.

Clinicians say that relatability is crucial in participants’ mental health.

Alan-Michael Chest is a Massachusetts-licensed mental health counselor and musician. He incorporates music and culture into his practice.

“Music offers vulnerability without judgment,” Chest said.

At age 7, Chest wrote his first rap: a song about struggling to understand crime in America. He said the creative process must be a part of therapy: “It’s really meeting a client where they’re at, and it’s really changing the framework for therapy altogether.”

BRL reaches participants through local grassroots organizations and city programs that work with youth at risk, such as Spoke Art and You Got This Center. Several programs can’t pay for partnerships with CSR, or can’t give kids stipends to participate, which makes getting people to participate in the clinics more challenging. When BRL loses participation numbers, the program itself is at risk; a portion of BRL’s grant funding is based on the number of young people it serves.

In 2021, BRL built a studio in a van to bring the program to prospective artists’ backyard. Budget cuts have kept the van off the streets because it needs repairs.

For staff, demonstrating to the public that BRL offers an important model for therapy is a challenge, but one that keeps them inspired.

Michael “Big Mike” Mendes, BRL’s main teacher-artist, has been making music and drawing since he was a kid. Growing up in Dorchester and coming from a Cape Verdean family, art has always been how he communicated best.

Mendes said BRL’s mission isn’t making artists, but introducing a new channel of healthy expression. He believes hip-hop is a key path to inspire new leaders.

“Through rapping and teaching people how to rap, we’re getting them to find their confidence, have conversations that they’re not having, and develop healthy relationships with adults,” he concluded.

This article has been updated to correct the names of Michael “Big Mike” Mendes and Luis “Louie” Colon, Colon’s age, and how many years Stephanie Sabins has been with BRL. The caption has also been updated to reflect correct event information.

title: In defense of the Liberty Tree Mall
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

In America, by law, everyone has a mall. That accident of proximity you are referring to when you utter the phrase: “My mall.”

Mine is the Liberty Tree Mall in Danvers, and I feel some duty to defend its weirdness as it has become much-maligned in recent days, thanks to a new song about it by Phoebe Bridgers that is called, simply, “Liberty Tree.”

Bridgers is from California, though it is no great mystery how she was introduced to my mall, for she is in a relationship with the comedian and filmmaker Bo Burnham. And the Liberty Tree is also his mall, which I know because back in 2009, when Burnham was an 18-year-old who’d become a YouTube sensation singing funny songs in his childhood bedroom in Hamilton, I spent quite a bit of time with him for a Globe Magazine profile.

When I asked him to show me around his life, he took me to the Liberty Tree Mall. “This is where I was conceived,” he told me in the parking lot.

So what on earth is this song about? To understand, I did the unthinkable. I went inside the Liberty Tree Mall, which most people avoid unless they are going to the movie theater or going to church. (See: my story from last year about Netcast, the mini-megachurch that is slowly taking over the mall.)

Clue No. 1: Beyond Dippin’ Dots

Long ago, the mall transitioned to big-box retailers positioned along its periphery, leaving the inside as some sort of strange ghost town with a Marshalls. I don’t like the way it feels. No, I love it.

Liberty Tree Mall… Bridgers sang as I inserted my earbuds just inside the main entrance.

In the photo booth… Ok, I see it right in front of me.

This place is dying…

Wrong! I pause the song and approach a man fixing an iPhone at a workbench overlooking the photo booth.

Who you calling ‘dying’?

“I’ve been here 15 years now, and I wouldn’t say it’s dying,” Kyle Barvaro, the owner of Tech Center, tells me. “It’s been dead the whole time.”

Correct. And that’s the eerie magic of this place, I tell myself as I take a deep breath and walk to the start of the dystopian Kohl’s corridor. What is the opposite of claustrophobia? That’s what I feel as I look at the hangar-sized hallway, with exactly zero storefronts, that leads to a Kohl’s you need binoculars to see.

You know what, I’m not going down there. I’ll just stop and take a photo.

This place is dying… We don’t care if we’re living proof...

Wait, am I dead? I think I’m already dead. When I stopped to take that photo, I swear there was no one in the corridor. But is that a figure in the distance? I’m definitely dead. This is awesome, but I’m going back to the photo booth.

I’m sticking out my tongue/And liftin’ up my shirt

Not gettin’ any younger, honey/But if we don’t try, how can we be sure?

Wait, is this a love song? What happened in that photo booth? Is this really where Burnhams are made?

You were made in the image of God

But you look like your mom in this picture of us

Fallin’ in love that night after our fight

This is a song about falling in love at the Liberty Tree Mall? Then why has the Internet been using it as an excuse to pile on my mall, making all these easy jokes about how creepy it is. Bridgers has it right; this is a love mall. There are deep emotions in this place, a palpable feeling of yesterday, of the time before malls were turned into these Disney-fied small towns.

And the past is lookin’ brighter all the time

See! She gets it. And while one should never read song lyrics literally, this California girl wrote the perfect song about my mall. Or at least the first half of the song is. I didn’t quite follow the second half about running through an airport.

Is that the Kohl’s corridor? I could see how it feels like an airport, but I’m not going down there.

title: Joshua Báez’s skill and hard work makes Cardinals’ debut star a victory for Boston baseball community
text:
Báez started his high school career at Cristo Rey High in Dorchester, then transferred to Snowden International School in the Back Bay.

His emerging baseball talent led Báez to Dexter Southfield in Brookline for the 2020 season. That season was canceled by the pandemic, but Báez continued to improve.

Báez played summer ball for The BASE in Roxbury and embraced their commitment to academics, ultimately committing to play for Vanderbilt.

There weren’t many ballfields in the greater Boston area that Báez didn’t play on at some point.

“The first time I saw him take batting practice, my jaw dropped,” said Dan Donato, who coaches baseball and hockey at Dexter Southfield and is the brother of former Bruins winger and Harvard coach, Ted Donato. “He had massive power. He was somebody who could hit 20 home runs in his sleep.”

And a powerful right arm, too. Major League teams saw Báez as almost a perfect draft pick because if he didn’t hit, he could move to the mound and take advantage of his 98 mile-per-hour fastball.

Craig Breslow, then working for the Cubs, was among the scouts and team officials who came to watch Báez play in 2021. But he fell into the second round after an inconsistent senior season.

The Red Sox were interested, but had the fourth pick that season and used it on Marcelo Mayer. Their mistake was taking University of Florida outfielder Jud Fabian early in the second round. He didn’t sign.

The Cardinals took Báez with the 54th pick. His apprenticeship in the minors was longer than expected — 452 games over parts of six seasons — because of injuries and a high strikeout rate. But Báez had a strong 2025, and it continued with Triple-A Memphis this season.

“[The Cardinals] told him a few weeks ago that he was a big part of their future. And once he was called up, they wanted him there for good,” Donato said.

Donato played in the minors for the Yankees, Mariners, and Rays from 1995-98, reaching Triple-A. He knew a five-tool player when he saw one, having shared the field with Derek Jeter and Bernie Williams, among others, during spring training.

“Josh ran a 6.31 60 [yard dash], and Bernie Williams was 6.7. In the outfield he’d go the gap as smooth as Ceddanne Rafaela and make a throw right to the bag,” Donato said. “He had all the skill, and he worked harder than anybody I had ever watched.”

Báez came of age at a time when baseball talent in the Boston area was at a high level. Boston College outfielder Sal Frelick was a first-round pick in 2021. Maryland’s Sean Burke, who played at St. John’s (Shrewsbury), was a third-round pick that year.

Future All-Stars Ben Rice, Cam Schlittler, and Shane Smith also emerged during that period.

“There were always pitchers from the Northeast, but there are more indoor facilities now, and players can work on baseball all year. For somebody like Josh, that was huge,” Donato said. “It’s different now than when I was coming up. It’s super competitive now. In our league, we have pitchers throwing 88-93.”

Landmark days are nothing new for Báez. He hit four home runs for Memphis on June 16, the third anniversary of his father’s passing. His mother, Yris, was at the game.

José Manuel Báez, known as “El Bronco” in the Dominican Republic, was an accomplished semi-pro baseball and softball player known for his power. His son promised him he would make it to the majors, and he did.

Báez was 0 for 17 in the four games after his debut. He came off the bench on Wednesday, singled to end his skid, then drew a walk. On Friday in Philadelphia, he blasted the first pitch he saw for a two-run homer.

“He’s going to be fine,” Donato said. “He’s shown what he’s made of.”

Without fail, new Red Sox catcher Adley Rutschman makes it a habit to meet the pitcher as he’s coming off the mound at the end of an inning to offer a few words of encouragement.

The exchange usually comes along the baseline and lasts only a few seconds.

“I really don’t know when it started, but I’ve always done it,” Rutschman said.

It’s a habit he picked up from his father. Randy Rutschman was a catcher at Linfield University in Oregon who later coached and played semi-pro ball in the West Coast League.

“He kept playing after college just because he liked baseball so much,” Rutschman said. “I think I was 6 when he stopped playing, but I remember him doing that with the pitchers.”

Rutschman said his message is usually something along the lines of, “Great job, let’s keep it going,” or “We’re going to get through this,” if it’s a rough inning.

Rather than wait until they get to the dugout, Rutschman says what’s on his mind right away.

“It’s different, but I like it,” Payton Tolle said. “He takes care of the pitcher.”

A few other observations on the Red Sox:

⋅ According to Baseball Reference, Wyatt Olds was the 23,757th player to appear in a major league game when he pitched for the Sox on Monday.

The 27-year-old righthander got the news that morning, too late for any of his family or friends from Oklahoma to get to Fenway Park. But his wife and four-month-old son were there.

Olds had started to wonder if the day would ever happen. He was drafted in 2021 out of the University of Oklahoma, and this was his third season in Triple-A and sixth in the minors. Olds also had not been pitching particularly well of late for the WooSox.

But he struck out James McCann and Jordan Lawlar, both swinging, on nine pitches, then retired Tim Tawa on a weak groundout.

“The Lord works in crazy ways,” Olds said. “Just happy to be here. I’m glad I did this with the Red Sox.”

His new teammates celebrated the occasion in the clubhouse. As Triple-A manager, Chad Tracy was accustomed to telling players they had been called up. But until this year he had not watched any of his players make their debut in person.

“It’s really cool,” Tracy said. “To be part of that is a lot of fun.”

When he took the mound in front of a sellout crowd, Olds said he remembered his college coach, Skip Johnson, always saying to take big moments one pitch at a time.

“That was all I was thinking, just make the next one,” he said. “He really imprinted that on us. It worked for me.”

Olds had a ball and a lineup card to take back to his family. He couldn’t stop smiling as he spoke about his day.

“I told the guys that was the most fun I ever had in my life,” he said.

⋅ The Sox set a major-league record winning 15 consecutive games against teams with a winning record before Wednesday’s loss against the Diamondbacks. Joe Cronin and the 1933 Washington Senators were the last team to record 14 straight victories against above-.500 foes.

⋅ Tanner Houck said in spring training that his goal was to return from Tommy John surgery this season, even though the Sox thought it was unlikely. It still might be a long shot, but Houck is moving closer to a minor league rehabilitation assignment and could be a relief option before the year is out.

Houck has a 2.68 ERA in 33 career relief appearances in the majors, with 9.6 strikeouts per nine innings.

⋅ He’s never made the major leagues, and it doesn’t seem likely he will this season, but Triple-A Worcester outfielder Braiden Ward is sure an interesting player.

The 27-year-old leads the International League with 53 stolen bases in 60 attempts. He also has been hit by a pitch 28 times, the most in the minors. Ward has scored 64 runs and had a .362 on-base percentage.

⋅ The “Sell the team” chants at Fenway Park have dissipated, but there is a chance John Henry and FSG could sell Liverpool.

According to reports from England, the investment group that purchased an approximately 38-percent stake in the club earlier this month has the option to acquire a controlling interest over the next year.

That alliance, called 1892 Holdings, includes British-Indian billionaire Amit Bhatia, Jeff Bezos, and Facebook co-founder Eduardo Saverin.

FSG sold its interest in the Pittsburgh Penguins last year after four years of ownership. Henry also owns the Globe.

The passing of Tommy John earlier this month sparked a discussion about if he should be in the Hall of Fame, given the combination of a successful career and having ulnar collateral ligament reconstruction surgery named after him.

Everybody in baseball, from the amateur ranks on up, knows about Tommy John even if they aren’t familiar with all the details of this career.

But when it comes to the Hall of Fame, less is more.

Only players, managers, team or league executives, and umpires can be Hall of Famers. Broadcasters and writers are honored by the Hall every year with awards voted on by their peers but aren’t inducted.

Still, they are recognized on the stage and have their moment in the spotlight. It’s special.

The late Dr. Frank Jobe changed the course of the game in 1974 when he performed what was revolutionary surgery on John by replacing his elbow ligament with a tendon from his left wrist.

Jobe was recognized by the Hall during the 2013 induction ceremony with John in attendance. One of Jobe’s proteges, Dr. Neal ElAttrache, spoke. Jobe passed away less than a year later. They had their moment.

The Hall has also given out the Buck O’Neil Lifetime Achievement Award since 2008, “to honor an individual whose extraordinary efforts enhanced baseball’s positive impact on society, broadened the game’s appeal, and whose character, integrity and dignity are comparable to the qualities exhibited by O’Neil.”

O’Neil was a player and manager in the Negro American League, and later a revered scout and coach. He was the first recipient of the award, which is given every three years.

Roland Hemond (2011), Joe Garagiola (2014), Rachel Robinson (2017), David Montgomery (2020), Carl Erskine (2023), and Bill White (2026) have been honored in the years since.

Ballpark architect Janet Marie Smith should also be on that list, along with notable coaches — Dave Duncan, Leo Mazzone, and Ron Washington come to mind — scouts, and others in the game who don’t fit neatly into a particular category.

The Cubs went into the weekend with a five-game lead in the National League wild-card race. Pete Crow-Armstrong is having an MVP-type season with 32 home runs and 31 stolen bases through 129 games. He’s already at 7.8 bWAR. Alex Bregman has played a big role, too. He has a .964 OPS and 25 RBIs in 32 games since the All-Star break while playing Gold Glove-level defense at third base. After a slow start, Bregman is again leading another team to the postseason. “You can’t fake it through 162 games,” Cubs manager Craig Counsell said. “It’s a credit to how he works every single day.” … The Diamondbacks gave Ketel Marte a seven-year, $116.5 million extension before the 2025 season, the kind of contract that is essentially a partnership with the player and a sign of trust. It helps explain why manager Torey Lovullo looked so exasperated and angry at Fenway Park on Monday when he didn’t know where Marte was. Marte just didn’t show up for the game and didn’t give any explanation. “There was very little coming back,” Lovullo said when asked what Marte had told the team. Marte was placed on the unpaid restricted list and was later moved to the injured list because of a knee issue. Diamondbacks CEO Derrick Hall, who was in Boston, called the latest situation “bizarre” and said the team wanted an explanation. Marte also was on the restricted list last season when he returned to the Dominican Republic without permission after his home in Arizona was broken into during the All-Star break … The Mariners have been a wreck, but entered the weekend only three games out of a wild-card spot. The odds are against them, but 13 of Seattle’s final 15 games are against the Angels, Athletics, and Rockies. Cal Raleigh was somehow 5 of 48 with 18 strikeouts in his first 16 games this month … Jordan Walker won the Home Run Derby and has hit five home runs for the Cardinals since, blasting his 27th of the season Friday night … Duquette Consulting, owned by former MLB executive Dan Duquette, is collaborating with Lorenzo Garmendia and Gradum Gswing — the hitting development company Red Sox third baseman Caleb Durbin employed to help turn his season around after a slow start. The goal is to bring the company’s model to other MLB players and teams. Durbin worked directly with Garmendia at the company’s facility in Waltham. Gswing has centers in nine states … Received an email a few days ago from an online sportsbook listing prop bets for the Little League World Series. It included over/under odds on strikeouts for specific pitchers. How does anybody think that is a good idea? Meanwhile, MLB’s Field of Dreams Game in Iowa earlier this month was played on a field with advertisements for FanDuel and BetMGM on the outfield fences. That was unintentionally amusing. If you recall the film, one of the main characters is the ghost of Shoeless Joe Jackson, who wants to play ball again after being banned for fixing the 1919 World Series … Happy birthday to Mike Boddicker, who is 69. The righthander was 39-22 with a 3.49 ERA over 83 games for the Red Sox from 1988-90. The Sox sent Brady Anderson and 21-year-old prospect Curt Schilling to the Orioles for Boddicker at the ’88 trade deadline. Boddicker had a 2.63 ERA down the stretch to help the Sox win the division by a game over the Tigers. The Sox were then swept by the Athletics in the ALCS, with Boddicker taking the loss in Game 3. Boddicker left the Sox as a free agent. In all, he played 14 seasons and won 134 games, and a World Series with Baltimore in 1983 when he pitched a three-hitter in a 4-1 win over the Phillies in Game 2.

title: A Market Basket-inspired cabaret show is coming to Boston
text:
Crank up the yacht rock and let the air-conditioning flow: Boston cabaret and bar Jacque’s (79 Broadway St.) will host two Market Basket-inspired drag and burlesque shows on Wednesday, Sept. 23.

The spectacle, called “Market Rate,” is a tribute to New England’s iconic grocery store. Tickets go on sale today at 2 p.m.

The two-hour performances will include “a small rotisserie chicken-eating competition,” according to co-organizer and producer Gnat, who says the concept originated as a joke among friends but quickly took off.

“The thing about New Englanders is that they love New England, and love to hate it, and hate to love it,” Gnat says. “You bring in a niche reference, and folks immediately connect to that representation. I mean, just look at the most recent Noah Kahan tours — the lyrics that reference Boston [and] New England landed so strongly with the New England audience at the Fenway stops.”

While Noah Kahan is certainly no Arthur DeMoulas, Gnat does note that New England has a long history of locally themed drag and burlesque shows. In 2025, Jacque’s hosted “MBTGay: A Transit Drag Show.”

Approximately 60 performers auditioned for the Market Basket homage, with a dozen or so making the more-for-your-dollar cut. Selected performers include standup comic Andi Van Dyke and burlesque performer Stabitha Christie. The show includes two acts, with an intermission.

“You can expect drag, burlesque, and maybe even some live singing,” says Gnat, who notes that a pre-show playlist spotlights tunes one might hear whilst cruising the aisles.

This is a different kind of drama for the beloved chain, which most recently made headlines when longtime CEO DeMoulas was ousted by Market Basket’s board of directors.

This evening has a more benevolent angle: It benefits a few food charities. Jacque’s will accept monetary donations for Haley House, the West Roxbury Food Pantry, and the Allston-Brighton Food Pantry at both performances. The shows are 21-plus.

Reps for Market Basket had no comment about the performance. Get tickets at https://posh.vip/e/market-rate.

It’s been almost a week since Karen Solomon, last pictured in grainy surveillance video shared by police, walked around the corner of an animal clinic in Worcester’s Columbus Park neighborhood and disappeared into thin air.

The 58-year-old mother of two is wanted by police for the slaying of her husband, 57-year-old Kurt Solomon. The veteran Worcester police officer was found dead at the couple’s Wildwood Avenue home early last Tuesday.

Solomon, police said, is armed, dangerous, and still at large.

Her mysteries also run deeper than her disappearance.

From founder to fugitive

Before she wound up the target of a massive police manhunt, Solomon spent decades as a highly respected law enforcement advocate.

She’s the founder of a nonprofit advancing police and first responder mental health awareness and suicide prevention, and wrote two books detailing the personal struggles officers face on the job.

For former colleagues, friends, and neighbors, the turn of events has been hard to reconcile with the woman they said they knew.

Yet Solomon’s work leaves a trail of interviews and collected writings offering clues.

In a 2023 interview with The Guns & Yoga podcast, she described her husband as being initially hesitant about her advocacy work, describing him as reserved and not wanting the spotlight.

Describing her work, she implored anyone feeling lost to seek help.

“You can fix anything … please don’t think suicide is your only option,” Solomon said on the podcast. “I know it’s incredibly difficult to ask for help ... but it’s going to make everything easier after that.”

In an interview last year commemorating a new memorial for first responders and military veterans who died by suicide, Solomon described her own mental health struggles, saying she sought counseling for “compassion fatigue,” brought on by her advocacy work.

She said she had previously attempted suicide three times.

“Every time I’ve said, ‘No, no, I’m not going to hurt myself,’ and I did,” Solomon said.

The morning of

Investigators have declined to comment on whether Solomon is believed to be alive or when she was last seen.

Kurt Solomon died from injuries inflicted by a “sharp object,” police said, but officials have not shared more details. Karen Solomon is wanted on charges of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon causing serious bodily injury, police said.

Dispatch recordings show that Karen Solomon made the 911 call to police, reporting a “male laid out in her backyard, unknown breathing,” around 5:30 a.m. When officers arrived, she was not there.

Worcester District Attorney Joseph Early has said other people were “involved at the house” during the incident, but he hasn’t elaborated.

Combing the pond

The manhunt so far has brought battalions of law enforcement down on a residential Worcester neighborhood where neighbors said tight community bonds are common and violence is rare.

Officials spent days canvassing the animal clinic and local woods and combing the waters of Coes Pond, a reservoir near where security video spotted Solomon on Tuesday morning.

For the community, the investigation has turned life upside down, particularly in the secluded neighborhood where Kurt Solomon grew up and lived his life, according to a family obituary.

“I just want it to end,” neighbor Karen Avedian said.

title: Boston health officials lift cyanobacteria advisory on West Roxbury part of the Charles River
text:
The Boston Public Health Commission (BPHC) has lifted an advisory on a cyanobacteria algae bloom in the West Roxbury part of the Charles River but another warning on a bloom downstream near the Massachusetts Avenue Bridge is still effect.

On July 21, the BPHC warned residents to avoid contact with the West Roxbury area of the Charles River, from Kendrick Street in Needham to Spring Street.

As of Tuesday, officials announced that the advisory for this West Roxbury part of the Charles River had been lifted.

“The concerns were originally raised, as all of these start, because somebody looked at the water and said, ‘My, that looks green’,” said Shoemaker.

Testing in the West Roxbury part of the river revealed that cyanobacteria had been growing as mats on the riverbed, said Shoemaker.

According to the advisory put out by the BPHC, contact with cyanobacteria may cause a plethora of serious health problems, including gastrointestinal issues, respiratory irritation, and in very severe cases, death.

The state continued monitoring the site and conducted two water tests, which as of Monday, showed that the bloom had cleared, said Shoemaker.

A separate health advisory, announced August 20, still remains active for the cyanobacteria bloom located near the Massachusetts Avenue Bridge, in what is called the Charles River’s “lower basin,” said Paul Shoemaker, Director of the Environmental and Occupational Health Division.

“We have not yet reached the stage where things have started to look visually clear for the state to even begin to take the first of its tests,” said Shoemaker.

Shoemaker said that it will be at least another week and a half to two weeks before he could see the advisory being lifted for the lower basin.

According to the Charles River Watershed Association (CRWA), this is the third consecutive year that the Charles River has experienced a cyanobacteria bloom.

“Cyanobacteria blooms are fueled by excess phosphorus from stormwater runoff and warmer water temperatures,” Carly Sherman, communications manager at the CRWA, wrote in a message to the Globe.

“There’s concerns there around climate change and shifting weather patterns that give us more of those long, dry, hot summer days with bright sunshine,” said Shoemaker.

“As the climate changes and average water temperature gets warmer, the rate at which cyanobacteria reproduces increases,” Amanda Darby, a fellow at the CRWA, wrote in an email to the Globe.

The coming fall season, with cooler temperatures, should bring the river some reprieve, said Shoemaker.

Jane Miller can be reached at jane.miller@globe.com.

title: The Massachusetts primary races we’re watching
text:
By Joan Vennochi

What do President Trump and Boston Mayor Michelle Wu have in common?

Both have a zeal for endorsing candidates of their choice to try to control election outcomes — and with that zeal, the confidence to test their own clout.

State Senators Nick Collins and Will Brownsberger, both Democrats, now face Wu-backed primary opponents because they did not support the mayor’s proposal to shift some of Boston’s property tax burden from residents to commercial property owners. Daniel Lander, a former Wu aide, is taking on Brownsberger, while Latoya Gayle, a community activist and first-time candidate is challenging Collins with Wu’s blessing.

While these contests do test the power of insurgency against incumbency, because of Wu’s involvement, the debate has focused more about the role that Boston lawmakers should play in pushing the mayor’s agenda. There is palpable tension between Wu and the two senators, especially Collins, who during the fight over her property tax legislation accused Wu of using “fear and manipulation” in her ultimately unsuccessful bid to get the proposal through the Legislature.

After serving eight years in the House, Collins won election to the state Senate in 2018 and now represents a district that includes South Boston, Dorchester, the South End, Chinatown and parts of Roxbury, Mattapan and the Back Bay. Brownsberger, a 20-year veteran of the Legislature, is a key part of Senate leadership, and represents a district that includes parts of Boston and Cambridge, along with all of Watertown and Belmont. Sounding less than eager for this fight with Wu, Brownsberger recently told the Globe editorial board, “I’m not quarreling with the mayor. The minute we can have peace in the valley, I will embrace peace in the valley.”

But peace does not seem to be Wu’s priority right now and, in a way, that’s understandable. Her power is at its height. She ran unopposed in her 2025 reelection campaign, after she bested challenger Josh Kraft by 49 points in the preliminary election and he dropped out. She has a track record of success when it comes to endorsing Boston City Council candidates. Watching congressional candidates backed by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani sweep to victory may have also encouraged her to test her own political muscle.

Yet the stakes are different for Wu than they were for Mamdani. If either Gayle or Lander win, she gets credit. But that credit won’t win Wu any more friends in the Senate or any more support on Beacon Hill for her tax proposal. Indeed, it may produce the opposite.

But she’s all-in with Lander and Gayle, just like Trump is all-in with Darline Graham, naming her interim US senator in South Carolina after her brother, longtime Senator Lindsey Graham, died suddenly last month. Trump then backed her in Tuesday’s special run-off election.

At least Trump’s backing of Darline Graham is motivated partly by his loyalty to her late brother. Wu’s backing of Lander and Gayle is strictly a matter of payback politics.

Is there no way to build bridges instead? Wu seems to share Trump’s view that there isn’t.

By Abdallah Fayyad

What interests me in next week’s Massachusetts primaries? There is, of course, the Democratic Senate primary between Senator Ed Markey and Representative Seth Moulton. There’s the race for Suffolk County district attorney, pitting the incumbent Kevin Hayden against his controversy-prone predecessor, Rachael Rollins, and Linda Champion. And there’s the Republican gubernatorial primary that will give us a temperature check on the post-Jim Lyons Massachusetts GOP.

But the primary result that I’m especially eager to see will come from the Eighth congressional district. The current Democratic representative, Stephen Lynch, is the kind of incumbent that up-and-coming Democrats have been trying to oust. At 71, he’s older than the average House member, he’s been in Congress for a quarter of a century, and he’s more conservative than the party’s base. Meanwhile, his challenger, Patrick Roath, is an energetic 39-year-old lawyer who is knocking Lynch for votes that haven’t aged well — like his opposition to the President Barack Obama’s Affordable Care Act.

Polling in congressional primaries isn’t easy, and there have only been a couple in the Eighth. These polls, which aren’t independent, show that the race is tightening. In February, a poll sponsored by Roath found that he was trailing Lynch by 26 points. But earlier this month, a poll by a PAC affiliated with Roath found that he’s only down by 7 points. Some close observers are calling the race a toss-up.

Given the dearth of independent data, it is possible that Lynch might cruise to reelection, or that Roath could manage an upset. And while Roath, who served in Governor Deval Patrick’s administration, is still the underdog, he has a lot going for him. A relative unknown just a year ago, he’s been active on the campaign trail compared to Lynch, who has run a relatively quiet campaign. And since Lynch first got elected to Congress, the Democratic base has drifted away from his style of politics and is looking for younger and more progressive candidates. Voters also want spirited fighters who can do more to stand up to Trump, and Roath is hoping to convince just enough of them that he’s in better shape to do that than the incumbent.

Earlier in the race, in an apparent dig at Roath, Lynch said, “Nowadays, kids get up in the morning, and they think they see a member of Congress in the mirror — no experience, no leadership, no accountability.” Next week, we’ll see whether voters agree with Lynch, or whether they think it’s time for a new kid on the block.

By Kara Bettis Carvalho

I’ll be following three races closely on Sept. 1. First up: the GOP gubernatorial primary, because the outcome will reveal the state of moderate Republicanism in Massachusetts.

The two candidates, Mike Minogue and Brian Shortsleeve, are similar in some ways — both are military veterans who advocate growing jobs and support cutting government waste and taxes. But their differences underscore some of the lasting tensions in the state Republican Party.

Minogue, a wealthy biotech executive and philanthropist who is backed by the state GOP, contributed generously to President Donald Trump’s inaugural fund and is conservative on social issues, including abortion. Shortsleeve, a venture capitalist who managed the MBTA under former Governor Charlie Baker, falls more comfortably in the traditional New England Republican camp, supporting abortion rights, for instance.

Polls have shown Minogue comfortably ahead, and his allies have pressed his opponent to drop out of the race. While Minogue touts his party’s support, Shortsleeve argues that he has a more realistic chance of unseating Governor Maura Healey, in no small part because of Minogue’s opposition to abortion. (Healey is not facing a primary challenge.)

Second: I’ll be watching the Democratic primary in the Fourth Congressional District, which includes towns from Brookline to my city of Fall River. Like many races nationwide, Democratic voters in the Fourth will choose between a more moderate Democrat, Representative Jake Auchincloss, and one with more left-wing values — Jason Poulos.

Auchincloss has not faced a primary opponent since he was elected to replace Representative Joe Kennedy III in 2020. He is a former Marine and Newton City Councilor who has garnered a reputation for working pragmatically across the aisle and sometimes criticizing his party’s progressive wing.

Poulos, a Sherborn resident and AI researcher, is running on a more progressive platform that includes canceling student debt and providing universal basic income. Though he has said he is a member of Democratic Socialists of America, he also contends that he is not running as a democratic socialist in this race. Voters can judge for themselves what that means.

Third, I’m watching the Republican primary for the First Bristol and Plymouth District State Senate seat, which covers the South Coast towns of Fall River, Somerset, Swansea, Westport, Freetown, Rochester and Lakeville. It’s the only contested Senate Republican primary in the state, and by some accounts the first time the district has had a contested Republican primary seat in decades.

Gabriel “Boomer” Amaral, a realtor from Fall River who lost the mayoral race in 2025 by 225 votes, is running against Somerset resident Manny Silva, a former information technology manager who works as a pastor. The outcome could hint at the type of red shift the South Coast has seen in recent years, evidenced by Fall River voting for Trump in 2024. While both candidates are conservative, Amaral has expressed frustration with the left’s focus on “social justice issues” and says he wants to help working-class families. Silva has talked about improving government transparency and reducing taxes.

For either man, unseating the Democratic incumbent, Senator Manuel Rodrigues, will be a steep challenge. Rodrigues, a 16-year incumbent who is chair of the powerful Senate Ways and Means Committee, is unopposed in the Democratic primary and has raised $225,000 in campaign contributions. The two Republicans, meanwhile, have less than $30,000 between them.

title: Boston police commissioner says officers will be on alert for Caribbean celebrations; urges people not to bring weapons
text:
Scooters are also prohibited, and the roads around Franklin Park will be closed to traffic and parking.

The Caribbean Carnival, a parade that begins at 1 p.m. at Warren Street and MLK Jr. Boulevard in Roxbury, will travel up Blue Hill Avenue before reaching Franklin Park, Cox said.

The event will have a firm cutoff time of 6 p.m., he said.

The carnival is preceded by another parade, known as J’ouvert, which begins at 6:30 a.m. at Shattuck Hospital, cutting through Franklin Park before ending at 10 a.m. at the parking lot of the Franklin Park Zoo.

In previous years, the morning procession has been the backdrop for various violent incidents, most notably in 2023 when eight people were wounded from gunfire between two rival groups.

Mayor Michelle Wu and community leaders denounced the violence at the time.

That followed fatal J’ouvert shootings in 2015 and 2014, which also happened in the hours just before or during the parade.

After the 2023 shooting, officials changed the parade route to avoid Talbot Avenue, where some of the previous shootings had taken place, Cox said. Now the festivities cut through Franklin Park, he said.

“Since we’ve moved it from Talbot Avenue, I don’t think we’ve had any incidents associated with it,” Cox said.

The carnival has also been marred by violence. In 2022, a man was killed when a gunman drove into a crowd and opened fire as people dispersed from the event following an earlier verbal altercation.

The shooter was later sentenced to 15 years in prison, the Globe reported.

Cox said police will continue to implement safety measures during the carnival.

Ahead of the city’s annual Dominican Parade on Aug. 16, Cox made a similar pledge, saying police would be out in force to prevent violence.

After that event concluded, police near Franklin Park apprehended a 20-year-old Dorchester man who was allegedly trying to conceal a loaded gun.

Police reported no violence during the parade.

Cox said that the training that helped officers make that arrest will prove critical again Saturday.

“The goal is for people not to bring [guns] here in the first place,” he said. But “our officers are trained on how to both observe folks that might be having them and then more importantly how to retrieve it from them in a safe way.”

Addressing a rise in stabbings in the city, Cox said that officers are aware of the threat.

“If you think there are a lot of guns in the world I would say there are exponentially more knives,” he said. “You can make a weapon out of anything. The reality is it’s a choice, and that’s what we’re trying to tell people — don’t make that choice.”

John R. Ellement of the Globe Staff contributed to this report.

title: MassHousing report confirms fraud findings in Spotlight investigation, says exec lied about conflict
text:
Mintz’s conclusions largely echo the Globe’s reporting, from the inconsistencies in Richards’s explanations on how he knew the developers to the apparent fraud in the projects the developers were supposed to be completing with the public’s money.

After reviewing several years’ worth of emails and interviewing several of Richards’s subordinates, the Mintz team concluded Richards was “untruthful” about the extent of his relationship with the two developers, Gary Acquah and Reggie Woods, who received $1.4 million in grant money from Richards’s department.

The two sold Richards a West Roxbury home in December 2022 for $204,000 less than the original listing price. Months later, in early 2023, Richards approved the grants, which were supposed to cover renovations to four apartment buildings in Pittsfield and Worcester.

The Mintz report concludes there is no evidence Richards used his position to secure a discount on the house. It also says there is no evidence the grants awards were improperly influenced by Richards, though he and his boss, MassHousing chief executive Chrystal Kornegay, had the final sign-off.

Acquah and Woods left a trail of shoddy and incomplete repairs at their properties. According to the Mintz report, in October 2024, the state’s Office of Inspector General began seeking records related to the awards a few months after MassHousing had taken notice of the poor work.

That investigation had not been previously reported. A spokesperson for the inspector general said Thursday that she could not confirm or deny the existence of an investigation.

At the time, MassHousing’s top lawyer, Colin McNiece, immediately alerted Richards about the state investigation, according to the Mintz report. Four weeks later, Richards told McNiece and Kornegay that after after reviewing his paperwork he realized the developers were the same pair who had sold him his home.

Richards’s claim of a sudden discovery was contradicted by one employee who told Mintz’s investigators that Richards had told her around the time of the 2022 sale he was aware the home sellers also did business with MassHousing.

MassHousing’s board held a special meeting Thursday to discuss the inquiry. Shortly after, the agency published the report on its website. MassHousing chair Jeanne Pinado said in a statement the report details “failures of ethical disclosure and a disheartening lack of candor by a former employee toward Agency leadership.”

“The review also identified weaknesses in MassHousing’s administration and oversight of the Gateway program,” Pinado said. “MassHousing takes responsibility for those shortcomings and welcomes all recommendations for strengthening program controls and oversight.”

The Mintz report also confirmed fraudulent invoicing in the grant program that was first brought to light by the Globe in June.

Acquah and Woods submitted fake invoices to trigger payments for work that was either done poorly or not at all. But in interviews with the Globe, at least nine subcontractors denied doing work attributed to them, for which Acquah and Woods collected reimbursement. Two more said invoices the developers attributed to them were inaccurate.

Several of those contractors also confirmed the inaccuracies with the Mintz investigators.

As the Globe investigated Richards’s conflict of interest, MassHousing officials initially defended him. They urged the Globe to drop a public records request for his emails from the time of the home sale, saying it would be overly burdensome to collect and review them.

McNiece, the agency’s top lawyer, earlier told the Globe then that Richards had come clean about his conflict as soon as he became aware of it.

However, the emails the Globe sought and obtained showed Richards corresponding warmly with Acquah and Woods about real-estate financing opportunities through MassHousing around the time of the home purchase.

The emails led MassHousing’s leaders to change their posture. Days before publication of the Globe’s first story, McNiece told reporters the agency would be launching an internal audit of programs under Richards’s purview.

Mintz’s email review found communications between Richards and Woods as far back as 2019, when Richards was serving as a top aide to then-governor Charlie Baker. Investigators wrote that the professional relationship between Richards and the two developers began as early as 2021, and deepened in 2022 and 2023. Richards began working at MassHousing in September 2021.

Three weeks after the Globe report was published, Richards, who earned around $255,000 annually, voluntarily resigned. He and his attorney have not responded to multiple requests for comment since June.

The Mintz report outlines discrepancies in what Richards told Kornegay and McNiece, two of the top leaders at the agency.

In August, Spotlight detailed a second instance of apparent fraud in a separate grant program under Richards’s oversight. The grants funded the installation of fire sprinkler systems in sober homes across the state.

In that case, MassHousing officials had directed sober home operator Hunter Foote to return more than $400,000 that officials said he improperly billed for even though the work was incomplete. In addition to sending Foote demand letters, they referred the matter to Attorney General Andrea Campbell.

Mintz did not examine the fire sprinkler program in its inquiry.

Campbell’s office confirmed it is investigating both programs. None of the disputed money has been returned, and Foote denies he did anything wrong.

Critics, including state Auditor Diana DiZoglio, note Mintz has close ties to MassHousing, having served as the agency’s bond counsel for more than 30 years. McNiece, the agency’s top lawyer, worked at Mintz for 11 years before joining MassHousing.

title: Can we please end the rancor over White Stadium now?
text:
The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court was as clear as clear could be in a unanimous opinion, written by Justice Gabrielle R. Wolohojian, ruling that the stadium may be located in Franklin Park, but it is not protected parkland — and hasn’t been for 75 years.

“We conclude that the 1947 and 1950 statutes collectively establish the Legislature’s unequivocal intent to extinguish the stadium parcel’s status as parkland,” the court found. “The 1947 statute demonstrated the Legislature’s willingness to divert parkland to the White Fund for nonpark uses, and the 1950 statute showed the Legislature’s recognition and approval of the stadium parcel’s new status as a school ground.”

The court also rejected the opponents’ contention that “the construction and improvement of pedestrian and vehicular pathways and utility lines to the stadium” — everything necessary to make the facility accessible to student athletes and to the fans of the women’s professional soccer team that is footing the lion’s share of the costs — would change the nature of the park and the way it is used.

“But pathways, including vehicular pathways, are ordinary elements of a park landscape,” the court found.

End of story.

But this is Boston, where political battles often take on a life of their own.

Neighborhood groups, including the Emerald Necklace Conservancy and the Roxbury Neighborhood Council, which were filing the lawsuit, are vowing to fight on, insisting they support “a smaller but fully public project that would be better for Boston’s students, the public and local residents.”

But without political support at City Hall for their idea — and there is none in the Wu administration — that fight is dead in the water. The contracts and lease agreements are already signed.

The bulldozers have long since cleared away everything but the art deco clamshell wall, which is to be integrated into the new structure, and construction proceeds apace.

At some point it behooves parties on all sides to set aside the rancor and work to ensure that the facility will provide all that was promised to Boston Public School kids — first-rate playing fields and tracks, good seating for their fans, state-of-the-art locker rooms, classrooms, and facilities they can be proud of.

Sure, the now $325 million facility isn’t the bargain-basement price it was when it was first proposed in 2023. Back then city taxpayers were picking up only $50 million of the total $100 million project. Now the city is on the hook for $135 million, with Boston Legacy picking up $190 million of the new tab.

The team is also expected to pay more than $62 million in rent, maintenance, and other improvements to the park over the 10-year period of the initial lease.

A community benefits package during and after the construction phase means local businesses will also benefit. The city said some $52.4 million in contracts have already been awarded to local firms, including women and minority-owned businesses.

The timeline for completion remains something of a mystery — the line on the city’s own website for “Expected year to be completed” still reads “To be determined.” City officials have indicated an updated estimate is just weeks away. And the project is now on a six-day work week schedule.

With construction equipment beeping and clanging in the background during Wu’s post-decision news conference in Franklin Park last week, the mayor noted that the litigation “has been a distraction” and did result in some delays.

But “our Boston kids deserve the very best, and as a city, we can never apologize for fighting to give it to them,” she said, adding, “As a government our job is to take those big swings, even when they’re hard, even when they’re complicated, even when they require really creative partnerships and legal documents and leases.”

The facility itself will be open to the community “every day,” Wu assured.

Meanwhile, City Hall will have a continuing obligation to make sure it keeps costs in check to protect taxpayers.

And there’s still an important role for community groups and parents of BPS students to play in the days ahead. Someone needs to hold the city’s feet to the fire on a workable transportation plan for Legacy game days in what will be an 11,000-seat facility.

Even more importantly, parents and community leaders need to make sure BPS students do indeed get what has been promised to them. City officials say that students will get “first crack” at the stadium as soon as it’s done. And post-season high school football games — which will be possible when the Legacy season ends in mid-November — are guaranteed in the lease agreement.

Making sure those promises are kept is an important role for people who insist they care about the city’s student athletes. Now they need to show they care about those kids more than about carrying on the fight.

title: Anthropic’s Beacon Hill spending spree
text:
Now, as Rush fights for his seat in Tuesday’s primary election, he’s getting some direct help from Anthropic employees. Over the course of the last three weeks, donors who identified as working for Anthropic have donated nearly $7,000 to Rush’s campaign as he looks to fend off a challenge from his left in attorney Persis Yu.

He’s not alone in getting such largesse. More than a dozen Democratic legislators have benefitted from a burst of donations from Anthropic staff this month, a Globe review of campaign finance records found.

Between Aug. 7 and Wednesday, Anthropic employees collectively poured almost $123,000 into the campaign coffers of sitting Massachusetts politicians, the state Senate Democratic leaders’ political action committee, and the state Democratic Party, which pulled in $25,000 alone, data show.

The money is flowing in as Beacon Hill lawmakers negotiate that bill that could set some of the country’s most rigorous rules for AI development. There’s also a wider national battle waging between Anthropic and its chief competitor, OpenAI. Both companies have turned to local lobbyists to help push their priorities, though records don’t indicate that OpenAI workers are similarly trying to beef up lawmakers’ campaign accounts.

Each company backed the Senate’s broader effort to put new guardrails on AI development, but they differed on how far those rules should go.

While OpenAI wanted to bring the Senate’s plan in line with existing laws in states such as California, New York, and Illinois, Anthropic wanted state lawmakers to tighten safety measures even further through Rush’s proposed language.

While Anthropic ultimately prevailed in the Senate, with the bill now in closed-door negotiations between House and Senate leaders, there’s no guarantee the language that emerges will look the same as the one senators approved.

So about those donations: The tens of thousands of dollars in contributions all come from a dozen different employees, many of whom donated the same amounts on the same days to the same candidates.

Much of all the money that’s poured into legislators’ campaign coffers came on the same day — Aug. 12, when 10 employees donated a combined $63,428.

“Employees’ donations are personal and not company-directed,” Danielle Cohen, an Anthropic spokesperson, said in an email.

The biggest recipients have those with the most power to influence the legislation. Senate President Karen Spilka, House Speaker Ron Mariano and state Senator Barry Finegold each took in almost $10,000 from Anthropic staff since Aug. 7. House budget chief Aaron Michlewitz received almost $9,000, followed by Rush, state Senator William Brownsberger, and state Representative Mark Cusack, who took in just under $7,000 apiece.

Finegold and Michlewitz are among the negotiators on the economic development bill.

Donors also handed out checks to some of the candidates in each chamber who are facing competitive primaries, including Brownsberger and Rush. In the House, state Representative John Lawn, facing a primary from Newtown City Councilor Alison Leary, took in almost $5,000 from Anthropic employees. Both Governor Maura Healey and Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll also benefited from the spending spree, pulling in exactly $5,000 apiece.

LET’S UN-PAC THAT: In a matter of days, a recently created super PAC has put more than $100,000 into state Representative Marjorie Decker’s reelection bid, a breathtaking sum for a state House race.

The so-called Progressive Cambridge IE PAC reported dumping almost $113,000 into digital ads, mailer, and mobile billboards as Decker vies for the Democratic nomination against Evan MacKay, the second-time candidate who lost to Decker by 41 votes after a recount two years ago in the left-leaning district.

The PAC has only reported three donors so far. Two service employee unions — SEIU Local 509 and the SEIU state council — put a combined $35,000 into it, and another super PAC, the so-called Boston Opportunity IE PAC, donated $85,000. The Boston Opportunity PAC has been largely dormant for years: It hasn’t reported raising any money since 2022, and its biggest backer is also a union, the United Association of Journeyman Apprentices Of The Pipe Fitting Industry, which donated $100,000 to the group in 2021.

To put all that money into perspective, MacKay has reported spending roughly $60,000 total so far this year. They’ve likewise gotten a hand from an outside group, albeit on a (much) smaller scale: The Massachusetts Teachers Association’s super PAC put $8,000 behind their bid.

Decker isn’t the only potentially vulnerable incumbent getting a last-minute assist from a super PAC, either. The Citizens for an Affordable Massachusetts IE PAC, which was created in July, dropped more than $43,000 on mailers and digital ads boosting state Senator Nick Collins, who’s facing a challenge from the Boston Mayor Michelle Wu-backed Latoya Gayle and another challenger, Juwan Skeens.

Among that group’s top funders: Cox Engineering, a Randolph-based mechanical contractor ... and yet another super PAC, this onewith ties to former Boston mayor Martin J. Walsh.

WALSH WATCH: Speaking of Walsh, the former US Labor secretary is wading into another Democratic primary beyond Boston’s borders.

Walsh is endorsing Middlesex District Attorney Marian Ryan in the Democratic primary pitting her against challenger David Solet, the Cambridge Democrat who served alongside and under Ryan for more than 20 years in the DA’s office.

Ryan “is a strong, common-sense leader who never forgets who she works for,” Walsh said in a statement shared by Ryan’s campaign. “She stands up for victims and working families, holds violent offenders accountable, and understands that first-time offenders deserve a chance to get their lives back on track.”

Walsh has thrown his weight around in a handful of races across the state this year. He’s backing his former City Hall chief of staff, Dan Koh, in the open Sixth Congressional District race, and Brownsberger as the Belmont Democrat faces a challenge from former Wu aide Daniel Lander.

Walsh also endorsed former “Bachelorette” contestant Chris Lambton in the open race on Cape Cod to replace outgoing state Representative Chris Flanagan, who is facing federal criminal charges.

ROUND 2 FOR KRAFT VS. WU? This time last year, Josh Kraft was fighting for his political life in a longshot bid to unseat Wu. But the disastrous end to that campaign hasn’t stopped Kraft from getting involved in this year’s closely watched races — often opposite Wu, the Globe’s Jon Chesto and Shirley Leung reported Thursday.

The longtime nonprofit leader and son of billionaire Patriots owner Robert Kraft has been maxing out on donations: $1,000 each to Brownsberger and Collins, the state senators who are being challenged by candidates Wu is endorsing. Kraft also gave $1,000 to Linda Champion’s bid for Suffolk County District Attorney as she tries to topple incumbent Kevin Hayden, who has been endorsed by Wu.

MAKING A WU-TURN: ‘I’m not a puppet.’ For Lander and Gayle, Wu’s backing against state Senate incumbents comes with boost — and tough questions. by Niki Griswold and Chris Van Buskirk, The Boston Globe: At forums or debates, Lander and Gayle have had to vouch for their independence, and even motivations for simply running. Collins, a South Boston Democrat, has used Wu’s endorsements as something like fodder, arguing voters don’t want a “blind loyalist” to City Hall. Business leaders have questioned whether Wu’s influence in Brownsberger’s district outside Boston is a help or perhaps a hindrance.

SOCIAL CONSTRUCT: Markey taps online influencers as Moulton hits on age and tech by Ella Adams and Katie Castellani, State House News Service: Influencers are taking to social media to vouch for US Senator Ed Markey in his reelection campaign — in both paid and unpaid ways — as Representative Seth Moulton continues to use the 80-year-old incumbent’s age as a talking point in his attempts to unseat Markey.

GREENER PASTURES: Healey’s Cabinet-level climate chief to resign, taking job leading Vermont law school by Samantha J. Gross, The Boston Globe: Melissa Hoffer, a former Biden administration official whom Healey tapped as the nation’s first Cabinet-level climate chief, is leaving her administration to lead the Vermont Law and Graduate School as its next president. She will begin her new role on Dec. 1, the school announced Thursday.

BURSTING A HOUSING BUBBLE: MassHousing report confirms fraud findings in Spotlight investigation, says exec lied about conflict by Joey Flechas and Gordon Russell, The Boston Globe: Former MassHousing executive Tony Richards II repeatedly lied about his professional relationship with two real estate developers who sold him his home and later received grants from him, according to an investigative report released Thursday.

PRIMARY QUESTION: Secretary of State William F. Galvin — who oversees the state’s elections, including Tuesday’s primary — said he isn’t taking a public position on a ballot question that would fundamentally change that very type of election.

But he had some thoughts. The proposal to implement a so-called top-two system — in which the top two vote getters in a state primary would advance to the general election regardless of their party — would likely “wipe out” third parties in Massachusetts, Galvin warned. The system is pitched as a way to make primaries less ideological and enhance voter’s rights, he said, but at least in California, which uses it for statewide elections, the results have been “mixed.”

“I don’t think anyone is terribly satisfied with what we currently have,” the Brighton Democrat said of the state’s primary system. But, he said, there are heavy questions left to be answered. “Is it going to be more complicated? Is it going to restrict groups that might have been able to run more as third parties? Those are all questions.”

It’s not just your imagination: Congress is historically dysfunctional, and it’s actually worse than you think by Tal Kopan, The Boston Globe.

Boston Legacy FC won’t play at White Stadium until 2028 by Emma Healy, The Boston Globe.

You’re moving next Tuesday. And... voting? Here’s what renters on the move should do. by Renuka Balakrishnan, GBH News.

title: ‘We get to celebrate everyone’: Boston’s 53rd Caribbean Carnival brings large crowds and flair to Franklin Park
text:
Boston’s 53rd annual Caribbean Carnival once again brought large crowds Saturday to the streets in and around Franklin Park for a full day of festivities.

The J’ouvert parade kicked things off on Circuit Drive early in the morning, then headed to Franklin Park Road, before ending on Blue Hill Avenue.

David Cabrera of Revere, representing the island national of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, wore a colorful vest and hat. He said the rhythmic and thunderous music was the only thing keeping parade watchers and participants awake after the J’ouvert’s 5:30 a.m. start.

“This music is just crazy, it’s nonstop ... Caribbean music is the best in the world,” Cabrera said. “A lot of people don’t even drink here. They’ve been awake since 6:30 in the morning, 5:30 in the morning, and the music is the only thing that’s been keeping them up. I’ve been here since 7 a.m.”

The main event, the Caribbean Carnival parade, started coming down Martin Luther King Boulevard in Roxbury in the afternoon, before traveling up Blue Hill Avenue and ending at Franklin Park.

Spectators lined up and down the route, with Caribbean-themed street food and clothing vendors set up on every corner.

Michelle Carter, a chef instructor and CEO of her own business, Michelle Green Thumbz, was selling food with her family along the route. Carter says Caribbean culture remains strong in Boston.

“A lot of us migrated from the South back in the ’60s. So we’re an intricate part of this community for close to 60-something years,” Carter said.

Now with three generations of her family living in this area, Carter says the Caribbean Carnival is tradition.

“It’s part of our memories, what we are fond of, and culturally, it aligns with what our purpose is in life,” Carter said. “That’s all beauty, health, dance, song, costume, and the flair of it. It just speaks artistry, and that’s what it brings ... and we get to celebrate everyone, just to be free for this one day.”

The parade featured trucks for various Caribbean nations, each having its own music and costumes, from places such as Trinidad to Jamaica.

Hundreds of locals were dressed for the occasion in colorful outfits — flag capes, bandannas, lighted-up tops, and all other types of expressive clothing representing their cultures.

Toward the end of the Carnival route, in Franklin Park, dozens of food vendors were serving up an array of flavors.

Ruddy Barros, of Cape Verde Taste, was selling Cape Verdean food such as shish kebabs, cachupa stew, and an octopus dish. Flore Thompson, of Hartley’s Jamaican Restaurant, cooked up different kinds of rice; vegetables like cabbage, beans, broccoli, and plantains; and an array of meats such as curry chicken, sweet chicken, jerk chicken, jerk pork, and sweet spicy wings.

Thompson said she can’t count how many people she knows who attend Carnival each year.

“The funny thing is, rain or shine, they’re here. Rain or shine, we’re here,” Thompson said. ”I can’t give you a number. All I can tell you is it’s a large."
