title: Lindsay Clancy trial spotlights need for postpartum awareness, resources
text:
Ashleigh Owens, a Belmont mother who experiences depression, anxiety, and ADHD, said she took part in such programs and saw the benefits. She and her husband, Spencer, were nervous about having children because of her mental health history, but they wanted to raise a family.

“I just got this motherly feeling, and I just knew I was ready to have kids,” she said.

Preparation didn’t spare her entirely from postpartum depression and anxiety, she said, but it helped. Owens, 31, is now a mother to a 4-year-old daughter and 20-month-old twin girls.

“There are some days that are harder than others, but at the end of the day I know that it was worth it,” Owens said.

Among all women, it’s common to have some level of postpartum mood changes. About 85 percent of mothers experience “baby blues,” according to the Maternal Mental Health Leadership Alliance, a national nonprofit advocacy organization. Up to 8 percent report experiencing anxiety disorders, while 14 percent experience depression.

According to trial testimony and legal documents, Clancy began seeking treatment for anxiety, depression, insomnia, and exhaustion about three months after her youngest child, Callan, was born. Over the course of five months, Clancy received 30 prescriptions for 13 different drugs but didn’t experience consistent relief from her symptoms.

A 2018 study found that women with a history of depression are 20 times more likely to experience postpartum depression than women without that history.

That doesn’t mean all women who have a history of mental illness will suffer serious illness if they become parents. And though she reported previous bouts of anxiety, Clancy wasn’t diagnosed with a mental illness until after the birth of her third child.

But preparation with health care professionals, a strong support system, and strategizing for stress reduction and healthy sleep during the postpartum period can improve the chances of avoiding a crisis and resolving symptoms more quickly, advocates said.

One other factor: Perinatal women with mental health conditions are less likely to reach out for assistance, a reluctance that could stem from a lack of insight into their own condition, the stigma attached to mental illness, or fear that admitting to difficulties could cause them to be reported as a risk to their children.

“We want to normalize talking about mental and emotional health,” said Wendy Davis, chief executive of Postpartum Support International, a perinatal health organization based in Pennsylvania. That means “making plans to support emotional and mental wellbeing just the same way we talk at every appointment about blood pressure, nutrition, childbirth, accident prevention.”

She emphasized finding a peer support system, ideally making connections with other women who have experienced postpartum challenges.

In Massachusetts, advocates say, finding help can be a challenge, with access varying depending on where a new parent lives, who her provider is, and whether the program is recommended by community members. There does not appear to be a public clearinghouse of postpartum depression support groups operating in Massachusetts.

The Department of Public Health directs families to several group directories — including MCPAP for Moms, Postpartum Support International, and Jewish Family & Children’s Service — while also suggesting parents look to hospitals, libraries, and community organizations.

That decentralized system can pose challenges, particularly for mothers seeking in-person or culturally specific support.

“I don’t think there are enough, honestly,” said Stephanie Crawford, founder of Roxbury-based Propa City Community Outreach, which supports families affected by pregnancy and infant loss and works with mothers across Massachusetts.

Crawford was one of 35 organization leaders who applied for DPH funding to “address mental health conditions and substance use disorders among perinatal individuals.“

Five organizations were chosen: Monumental Beginnings (Falmouth Together We Can), Building Stronger Beginnings (Cooley Dickinson Hospital, Moms Do Care – Northampton), Vital Connections (Boston), Worcester RISE for Health, and the Haitian Mental Health Network and William James College. They’ll each receive $44,000 annually over the next five years.

Davis emphasized that people should seek out virtual groups if one isn’t available locally. Her organization offers hundreds of national online support groups, she said.

Expecting mothers who had treatment for mental health conditions in the past or are receiving treatment currently should consult health care professionals about perinatal care. That could include a psychiatrist, doctor, or other health care provider, said Dr. Michelle DiBlasi, director of inpatient psychiatry at Tufts Medical Center.

A major question, experts said, is whether to continue taking medications for mental health care during pregnancy and breastfeeding. A lot of the most common medications for depression, anxiety, or bipolar disorder are safe for pregnant and new mothers, but the specifics should be discussed with a doctor.

“It needs to be a conversation between the provider and the patient, ideally even before the person gets pregnant, about what the plan would be,” DiBlasi said.

Owens, the Belmont parent, began seeing a therapist in high school, and had conversations with both a therapist and a psychiatrist before her first child’s birth. With the exception of a prescription for ADHD, Owens stayed on medication during her pregnancy and while breastfeeding, she said.

“A healthy mom is better than a mom who’s struggling,” she said.

She still experienced symptoms of anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder after her first birth, she said.

“I was checking on breathing all the time, what she’s eating. When she started foods, I would worry about if she was choking,“ Owens recalled. ”I felt like that anxiety consumed my life.”

After her twins were born, she said, her anxiety was replaced by depression and difficulty connecting with her babies, she said.

“I felt like sometimes they weren’t my children and they were just children I was taking care of,” she said.

She was able to talk about those feelings with a therapist, who told her they were normal. As time passed, she has gotten better at connecting with her youngest children, she said.

Her experience during her first pregnancy also made her better at managing her stress after her twins’ births. She and her husband took shifts overnight that allowed each of them to get four solid hours of sleep. Her mother was involved immediately after the births of the twins, she said. And Owens became more comfortable telling people she wasn’t ready for visitors.

Now, she said, she still struggles with periods of depression, but finds comfort in communicating in those moments.

“The most important thing is telling someone how I feel,” she said. “It’s still a work in progress.”

title: Boston puts its hands up for annual Donna Summer Disco Party
text:
On the dance floor Friday night, friends stood in little circles. An elderly man took a woman’s hand, spinning her around and around. “Boston, put your hands up in the air!” the DJ instructed the crowd. “Are you having a good time?”

“You cannot be from Boston and not love Donna Summer,” said Shameeka Brown from Roxbury, who said she is in her 40s. “I don’t think we take enough advantage of all of these things … there’s all age ranges. It’s nice. Even the teenagers are out here, and it’s hard to get teenagers to do anything with anybody over 20.”

Behind the dance floor, people lined up to skate across a little roller rink constructed from colorful plastic tiles. One man skated off the rink and across the surrounding bricks. He wore a disco ball on his head.

“They call me Disco Bob,” Bob Naftal, 66, from Burlington, said. “They could be laughing with me or at me as long as they’re laughing, you know?”

Naftal has been skating for over thirty years. He’s been attending the Donna Summer Disco Party for over ten years. “Nice to see you again,” one woman told him as she walked by. Another group of women approached, asking to take a picture.

“You put this outfit on, every beautiful woman wants to take a picture with you,” he joked. “In all seriousness, it’s important to put a smile on somebody’s face, especially in these times … I skated with a guy who was 90, and he actually passed away at 90, but he was skating a month before he died. And if God’s good to me, I hope I’m doing that too.”

On the bricks behind the DJ booth, a group of women started a game of Double Dutch, swinging two fluorescent jump ropes in the air. A young girl jumped in, expertly hopping between the ropes. A dad pushed a stroller through the crowd. A man walked a large, fluffy dog. All across the plaza, friends sat chatting, eating, and people-watching.

“I feel like Boston doesn’t have enough events like this, to be honest,” Emma Sikora, 25, from South End, said. “All the people here are just so fun, and everyone just comes to have a good time.”

Sikora’s mom rallies a group to come out to the party each year.

“She just loves to dance, and she loves sparkles, and she loves disco music,” Sikora said. “She stokes the fire more than I do, but I try. I try to keep up.”

As the night dimmed, a set of lights turned on, washing the crowd in red. Glow sticks illuminated necks and heads and wrists. People continued to rush to the dance floor. On the edge, Kelly Cronin, 37, from Melrose, swayed side to side while balancing her 10-month-old daughter on her hip.

“She likes to dance already. She bops to the music,” Cronin said.

Cronin’s other daughter, age 3, likes to dance too. She picked out the perfect outfit: a pink dress with cascading sequins and a mini tiara.

“I like to have my girls out, and not worrying, and dancing like nobody’s looking, and just having fun. If everyone’s happy and safe, just keep going, you know?” Cronin said. “Groove on.”

title: Ozempic hypocrisy: You’ll be shamed if you take GLP-1s, shamed if you don’t
text:
Uh, it looks like it’s already too late.

Just ask Traci Finkel, 37, an executive assistant at Boston Children’s Hospital, who’s been dealing with pressure to lose weight since childhood, when her sister was taken bikini shopping while her outing was to Weight Watchers.

“It’s almost like people are in​ a cult,” she said of those using GLP-1s. “The drugs are [messing] with people’s minds. It reminds me a lot of the diet pills in the ‘80s. Just do this easy thing, and you don’t have to do anything else.”

Or Ashley L., 37, a bartender and server from Malden who knows she has weight to lose but who wants to do it naturally, and to say “[expletive] you” to the co-workers badgering her to take a weight-loss drug.

“The ladies I work with, they’ve all taken GLP-1s, and they’re like, ‘What are you waiting for — do you want to stay like that forever?’” she said, requesting that only her last initial be used for privacy reasons.

And Jun Ni, a railroad project manager from West Roxbury, who describes herself as “larger,” and puts off medical care because she dreads her doctor’s relentless pressure to start on a GLP-1.

“I’ve worked through shame and body-image issues, and I don’t have any health issues,” said Ni. “It feels predatory.”

It seems hard to believe, but the “Ozempic era” is only a few years old. In 2021, views for TikTok videos tagged with #Ozempic were a mere 2 million, according to a history of the drug’s rise by the Medical University of South Carolina. In 2023, the views hit 1.2 billion, the school reported.

The society-wide makeover it enabled was so intense that at the 2023 Oscars, host Jimmy Kimmel joked about it from the stage. “Everybody looks so great,” he said. “When I look around this room, I can’t help but wonder ‘Is Ozempic right for me?’” And a cosmetic dermatologist coined a term to describe the look: “Ozempic face.”

By now, it’s so widespread that restaurants, marriages, and seamstresses are feeling the impact. “Smaller portions, more protein: How GLP-1s are quietly changing chain restaurant menus,” read an NBC news headline. “Fat jabs to unleash divorce boom,” The Telegraph reported. “Size Doesn’t Matter, Fit Does: Introducing David’s Fit Guarantee™," read the David’s Bridal press release.

But not everyone wants to use the medications (and some patients with certain pre-existing conditions have been advised not to for safety reasons).

For starters, even with insurance, the drugs can come with high costs, “and,” said Finkel, “you’re supposed to do it for your whole life.”

Many people don’t want to risk the known and unknown side effects — which can be as temporary as nausea or as long-lasting as eye damage. Others say they want to repair their emotional relationship with food at its source.

Virgie Tovar, host of the “GLP-1 Truth Serum” podcast and an expert on weight-based discrimination, says the new weight-loss drugs have unleashed “peak weight stigma or fat phobia.”

Because conversation about weight has now been “medicalized,” it’s given friends, family, and even strangers the self-appointed right to meddle, she said, as she captured the thinking: “It’s my job to step in if someone has a disease they’re not treating because GLP-1 ads are using that language.”

“But I don’t think it’s about health,” she said. As evidence, she pointed to the fact that people are being shamed whether or not they take a weight-loss drug.

Meghan Garcia-Webb, a medical doctor who runs a boutique weight-management practice in Newton, hears those very challenges from patients in her practice.

“You are policed if you are too thin,” she said (cue the frenzy around Ariana Grande). “If you lose weight, people say inappropriate things to you. And if you accept yourself as you are, people ask why aren’t you taking these meds?”

Given our pre-GLP-1 obsession with weight and dieting, it would have been hard to imagine things getting even more bonkers, but Lauren Beckham Falcone, the WROR radio host, captured the heightened madness.

She lost weight a little while ago, she said, and wanted everyone to know she did it without the use of drugs. But now that she’s gained the weight back, she’s insulted because she thinks others are thinking that she’s not using a drug. “It’s the new embarrassing life status: She’s not taking the shot.”

title: Hyde Park man sentenced to 16 years in prison for 2025 shooting that wounded police officer
text:
A Hyde Park man will serve at least 16 years in state prison for a 2025 shooting that wounded a Boston police officer, officials said Tuesday.

Daiquan Rice, 32, was convicted by a jury last week of assault and battery with a firearm, carrying a firearm without a license, and carrying a loaded firearm without a license, Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden’s office said in a statement.

Judge Mark Hallal Tuesday sentenced Rice to 12 to 13 years in state prison for the assault and battery and four to five years for firearm possession, to be served consecutively, the statement said.

Hallal also sentenced Rice to two years of probation for carrying a loaded firearm without a license with the conditions that he obtain a GED or equivalent degree and complete a violence prevention program, the statement said.

“This is an appropriate sentence for such a reckless and dangerous action,” Hayden said. “I’m so grateful that the officer survived and was able to overcome his injuries. We will never relent in prosecuting anyone who harms or attempts to harm our law enforcement officers.”

Rice was convicted of several prior firearm-related offenses out of Suffolk Superior Court, where he received a seven-to-10-year prison sentence with three years of probation to follow, the statement said.

Rice was on probation and parole at the time of the 2025 shooting.

On Sept. 12, 2025, at about 12:45 a.m., officers were patrolling the area of Washington and Dudley streets to address complaints about quality-of-life issues in Nubian Square, including complaints of people congregating in and around the African American Veterans Memorial Park, the statement said.

Officers reported several people in the park and one person standing away from the group smoking, the statement said. The park has posted signs indicating it closes at dusk and prohibits smoking.

Officers approached the person smoking, later identified as Rice, and he began walking in the opposite direction. Rice fled down Washington Street when officers exited their cruiser, the statement said.

Officers followed as Rice turned right onto Archer Terrace toward Kenilworth Street. Rice shot an officer in the arm during the pursuit, which prompted police to return fire, the statement said.

Rice and the officer were taken to hospitals with wounds that were not considered life-threatening, Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox told reporters near the scene on Sept. 12, 2025.

Police recovered a loaded firearm with a large-capacity magazine, the statement said.

Three additional officers were treated for non-life-threatening injuries at local hospitals, according to past Globe coverage.

“This is another example of the amount of guns that are out there,” Cox said. ”We’re very lucky and fortunate that there was no loss of life here."

title: Mass. voters casting ballots in primary elections for US Senate, governor, and more. Follow live updates.
text:
By Kaitlin Lewis, Globe Staff

Incumbent Kevin Hayden will win the Democratic primary for Suffolk district attorney, according to the Associated Press.

Hayden’s victory marks a failed political comeback for Rachael Rollins, a former Suffolk district attorney who, after leaving the post for US attorney, resigned in 2023 amid an ethics scandal. Hayden was appointed to replace Rollins as district attorney by former Republican governor Charlie Baker in 2022.

READ MORE

By Emma Platoff, Globe Staff

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu appeared with state Senate candidate Daniel Lander Tuesday night as he celebrated a close margin in his challenge to incumbent William Brownsberger.

Wu, who had been one of Lander’s highest-profile backers, called the results “a real reflection of the energy on the ground,” even as the contest remained too close to call.

Asked whether her support had influenced Tuesday’s Senate races, she demurred.

“Your vote is deeply personal,” Wu told reporters. “Everyone thinks about that in their own unique way.”

In another race, Wu’s chosen candidate, Latoya Gayle, lost to incumbent Senator Nick Collins. Asked whether she was disappointed in the result, Wu called Gayle’s showing “an incredible accomplishment” for a first-time candidate.

“That is a process that takes time,” she said.

By Kaitlin Lewis, Globe Staff

US Representative Stephen Lynch will win the Democratic nomination in the Eighth Congressional District, the Associated Press projected, staving off a challenge from progressive Patrick Roath.

The contest was the latest example of a younger candidate challenging an established Democrat. Lynch, 71, is running for a 13th term in Congress. Roath, a 39-year-old attorney and former aide to ex-governor Deval Patrick, accused Lynch on the campaign trail of clinging to “politics of the past.”

With Lynch’s projected win, all congressional Democratic incumbents running in Tuesday’s primaries safely moved on to November.

READ MORE

By Emma Platoff, Globe Staff

First-time candidate Daniel Lander said Tuesday night that his closely-watched challenge to state Senator William Brownsberger was “within double digits.”

“While I wish tonight we were ready to say we had a decision, it is so, so close,” Lander said.

A longshot running against a two-decade veteran of the state Legislature, Lander framed that tight margin as a major victory.

“Tonight, we have already sent shockwaves on Beacon Hill,” Lander said.

He appeared with Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, one of his most high-profile supporters and his former boss. Wu said Lander had “crushed” it in Boston.

By Niki Griswold, Globe Staff

State Senator Nick Collins of South Boston declared victory Tuesday night over challenger Latoya Gayle, a first-time challenger backed by Mayor Michelle Wu.

Collins told the Globe that city election results obtained by his campaign show that he achieved a “decisive” victory, which he said demonstrated that his constituents are looking for an “independent” representative in the state Senate, who is willing to compromise. Gayle had already conceded to her supporters.

“I love this city, I love this state, and I want to make sure that it has the type of representation that can represent everybody,” Collins said as he addressed a crowd of cheering supporters at Florian Hall in Dorchester.

Just after 11 p.m., Collins said Gayle had not called him to formally concede, but said, “it was not a close election.” That said, he implied that he appreciated the competition.

“Sometimes you have to dust off the cleats,” Collins told the Globe in an interview. “Nobody owns a seat, and I think it’s made me a better senator. It’s tested my team and brought out the best in the district.”

Collins acknowledged that Wu’s endorsement and support for Gayle made for a challenging re-election race, but argued that ultimately his message resonated with voters.

“My prerogative is to not prioritize the zero sum, [but] to try to find common ground, which requires compromise, and I can work with anybody who has that mindset,” he continued. “It can’t be about rigid ideology and purity tests. … You can have disagreements with being able to work on other issues.”

READ MORE

By Kaitlin Lewis, Globe Staff

Incumbent Representative Richard Neal will win the Democratic primary in the First Congressional District, the Associated Press projected, fending off a challenge from political newcomer Jeromie Whalen.

Whalen, a high school teacher, ran on a more progressive platform than Neal, who is seeking a 20th term. But Whalen’s campaign was not without hiccups, including reports of a past drunk driving arrest that he acknowledged on social media just 10 days before Tuesday’s election.

READ MORE

By Kate Selig, Globe Staff

In a surprise 11 p.m. announcement, state Senator Will Brownsberger told the crowd of supporters gathered at Donohue’s Bar and Grill in Watertown that the vote count had turned in his favor. He said the campaign previously did not have all the ballots from Belmont.

“We’re actually up by a [expletive] 1,000 right now,” he said.

The crowd erupted in cheers.

By Kaitlin Lewis, Globe Staff

Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, who endorsed Markey’s reelection bid over Moulton, said in a post on X that Markey “knows that, at a time of massive income and wealth inequality, Congress must take on the billionaires and fight for working families.”

Representative Ayanna Pressley, who also endorsed Markey, posted a photo of her and the senator on her X account to congratulate him. Pressley won the Democratic primary for the Seventh Congressional District after running unopposed.

“Tonight, Massachusetts sent a clear message: we want Democrats who will defend our communities and never back down,” Pressley wrote.

READ MORE

By Tal Kopan, Globe Staff

As local news flashed the current margin of the Lynch race on the screen — with Lynch up 57 percent to 43 percent — a huge cheer went up at Lynch’s watch party.

Until now, the event has been fairly muted, with roughly four dozen supporters in attendance. But the jump in Lynch’s lead noticeably excited the group.

By Sterling Davies, Globe Correspondent

Latoya Gayle officially conceded her race for the 1st Suffolk state Senate seat against incumbent Nick Collins. This came after Gayle made a speech to her supporters, thanking them for their commitment throughout her campaign.

By Kaitlin Lewis, Globe Staff

Dan Koh, a former Biden White House aide, will win the Democratic primary for the Sixth Congressional District, according to the Associated Press. Koh was projected to prevail over a crowded primary field vying for the nomination to fill Seth Moulton’s House seat.

One of his opponents, state Representative Tram Nguyen, was backed by Representatives Ayanna Pressley and Lori Trahan.

READ MORE

By Sterling Davies, Globe Correspondent

As Senator Nick Collins appears to pull ahead in the race for the 1st Suffolk state Senate seat, Latoya Gayle made an appearance at her watch party in Dorchester.

“The results are not what we wanted, but that’s not why I’m crying,” Gayle said, shedding a few tears. “He said that I made him be a better state senator, and I hope he means that. We ran one hell of a race”

Gayle noted that the fight isn’t over for her, thanking the organizations and nonprofits that stood by her and hoping they continue working towards what her campaign envisioned.

“This wasn’t a race about me. This was a race about us. Yes, and we’re still gonna keep fighting for the things that matter to us,” she said. “And I’m sorry I couldn’t get us over the finish line.”

With her family present and supporters cheering her on, they popped cider, and said a toast to the campaign’s work.

“We can do hard and brave things. And so let’s just keep doing hard and great things together,” Gayle said.

“We can still fight because I’ve meant every word that I said on this campaign, and I care about all of you, and I care about our community, and I care about our city.”

By Kaitlin Lewis, Globe Staff

The senator highlighted several of his campaign promises while on stage, including “Medicare for all,” protecting abortion rights, and tackling cost-of-living issues like childcare.

“It is a future we can realize through a bold, transformational, progressive agenda,” Markey said.

Markey also took shots at President Trump and painted a picture of growing up in Malden and watching his parents make “sacrifices” for him and his brothers. He attacked the Trump administration for cutting social programs that he said will help “boys and girls” that grew up like him.

“Donald Trump brings out the Malden in me every single day,” he said.

READ MORE

By Emma Platoff, Globe Staff

Even after incumbent state Senator Will Brownsberger indicated he “might have lost” his Democratic primary on Tuesday, his opponent, first-time candidate Daniel Lander, had yet to take the stage.

“Continue to hang tight,” a supporter, Josh Wolfson, told the upbeat crowd at Peka Restaurant in Brighton. Wolfson is the Massachusetts state director for the Working Families Party, which had backed Lander alongside a slate of legislative candidates. Wolfson said votes were still being counted.

Lander has yet to appear at the party, where a couple dozen supporters gathered beneath neon lights to hope for victory.

By Jim Puzzanghera, Globe Staff

There was some nervousness early among about 100 supporters of US Representative Richard Neal at his election night party as numbers from liberal areas showed his opponent Jeromie Whalen in the lead.

But that dissipated and a big cheer went up when results from Springfield, the biggest city in the First Congressional District showed Neal in the lead.

The 19-term veteran is poised to chair the powerful Ways and Means Committee if he wins re-election and the Democrats take the House majority. And that means a lot to Neal supporter Brian Ahern, 73, of Springfield.

“I was saying to somebody I know who was with Whalen, ‘If everything goes according to plan, Richie’s going to be head of Ways and Means and it’s a two-year term,’ “ said Ahern, sipping a beer and wearing a Neal t-shirt. “It’s going to take your guy one year to find the men’s room in the Capitol.”

By Kaitlin Lewis, Globe Staff

Markey said that he spoke with Moulton and thanked him “for a hard fought campaign.”

“I told him that I look forward to talking with him about how to build a better future for everyone that we are both committed to,” Markey said.

By Kaitlin Lewis, Globe Staff

Markey spoke to a cheering crowd gathered in downtown Boston and touted his win as a “progressive movement fueled by young people demanding more from their leaders.”

“Young people will show us the way,” the 80-year-old senator said. It was a direct response to Moulton’s campaign, which pitched voters on generational change.

By Kaitlin Lewis, Globe Staff

The Associated Press has made projections in a handful of US House races in Massachusetts, and others are still too close to call.

In the Fourth District, the Associated Press projected a win for US Representative Jake Auchincloss over progressive Jason Poulos. House Minority Whip Katherine Clark also fended off primary challenges from two different candidates, the Associated Press projected.

In Boston, Representative Stephen Lynch was leading his progressive challenger, Patrick Roath, with about 20 percent of the votes counted. Roath’s campaign hinged on pushing for younger leadership in Congress. Lynch, 71, is running for a 14th term.

With 30 percent of the votes counted in the First District, AP data showed that Representative Richard Neal was starting to pull away from Jeromie Whalen, a high school journalism teacher whose campaign was rocked by reports of a past drunk driving arrest.

In the wide-open Sixth District, former Biden White House aide Dan Koh and state Representative Tram Nguyen were leading the crowded field to replace Seth Moulton.

By Amanda Kaufman, Globe Staff

By Kate Selig, Globe Staff

In a candid speech delivered to a crowd of supporters at Donohue’s in Watertown Tuesday night, state Senator Will Brownsberger said the results were “not looking that good tonight.”

“We might have lost,” he said. “I’m not quite saying that yet, but as is my way upfront, that’s what I’m seeing out there.”

He thanked his supporters who had gathered hoping for a different result. He said, “You’ve been so good to me, and —”

A woman called out from the crowd: “You’ve been good to us.”

Daniel Lander’s team has not commented on race results yet.

By Tal Kopan, Globe Staff

Stephen Lynch’s election night watch party was slowly getting going as early results rolled in. After a last-minute change of venue, a group of his volunteers, supporters, friends, and family occupied a back room of the hip Southie bar The Playwright.

Chafing dishes held sliders and finger food and Lynch signs adorned the walls as most of the noise came from the active patrons at the bar and pop music playlist. TV screens showed US Open Tennis, the Red Sox game, and NBC’s America’s Got Talent, as perplexed bar staff couldn’t identify a news channel showing results to put on instead.

As results trickled in and the lead changed with different batches, it was unclear if Lynch’s backers were following closely. Some looked at phones and others mingled as they passed the time.

Quincy Mayor Thomas Koch said he thought Lynch was in a good position.

“I thought he did a good job,” Koch said. “I was I was impressed with the mailings. I thought he defended his position pretty well. It’s crazy times … and in a Democratic primary, it’s very dangerous to somebody who’s moderate because you get a lot of the extreme left that come out and vote in the primary. [But] I feel good about Quincy.” edited by me

By Kate Selig, Globe Staff

As early results ticked in, supporters of Senator Will Brownsberger gathered at Donohue’s Bar and Grill in Watertown — over chicken tenders and fries — and were cautiously optimistic that their candidate would prevail.

Donna Palombo, 51, of Brighton, said Brownsberger has a leg up over his opponent with his experience and track record of helping constituents. She is the vice chair of the Ward 21 Democratic Committee, which Brownsberger’s challenger Daniel Lander chairs.

When Palombo was completing a master’s degree at the Boston University School of Public Health, she reached out to Brownsberger’s team for the senator’s opinion on a topic she was researching for an assignment: getting full-time care for older people. Brownsberger called her directly.

If Brownsberger were to win, she said, it would show that “your life experience matters.”

By Sterling Davies, Globe Correspondent

After polls closed, Latoya Gayle supporters and volunteers trickled in to Sweet Teez Bakery to join her official election watch party. With tables full of snacks, sweets, and refreshments, Boston locals are anxious to see how Gayle will fare against incumbent Nick Collins for the state Senate seat representing the 1st Suffolk District, based in South Boston and Dorchester.

One volunteer even made cookies with Gayle’s face on them to hand out.

Shirley Jones, a longtime Dorchester resident, has known Gayle for over 20 years, so choosing to volunteer for her came with zero hesitation.

“When she told me that [she would run], I was like, ‘You know what? You’re already doing the work. It’s nothing new,’” Jones said. “Latoya decided to run for 1st Suffolk Senate because she knew the community needed someone who would stand up and provide for them what they weren’t getting.”

By Emma Platoff, Globe Staff

The closely-watched state Senate race between incumbent Will Brownsberger and challenger Daniel Lander is still “too early to call,” a Lander ally told a crowd of his supporters at a restaurant in Brighton Tuesday evening.

Josh Wolfson, Massachusetts state director for the Working Families Party, which has backed Lander as part of a slate of legislative candidates, told a room of several dozen Lander supporters that he had just spoken with the campaign and that votes were still being counted.

The mood was upbeat at Peka Restaurant as attendees munched on empanadas and chips with guacamole. Blue Lander signs decorated the brick walls.

The race between Lander, a first-time candidate, and Brownsberger, a stalwart of state Senate leadership, heated up this summer after Boston Mayor Michelle Wu, Lander’s former boss, endorsed him in the race. Wu waded into two closely-watched state Senate races, in both cases targeting Democrats who have opposed her top legislative priorities.

By Kaitlin Lewis, Globe Staff

At his campaign’s watch party in Dorchester, Moulton briefly took the stage to concede the Senate Democratic primary and told supporters that he called US Senator Ed Markey “to congratulate him on his victory.”

“He has my full support as our Democratic nominee and we must stand united to protect our democracy and defeat Donald Trump,” Moulton said.

Moulton also thanked his family, his staff, and supporters, and said he “could not be prouder of the fight we put on.”

“We didn’t achieve our goal tonight but I am confident that because of this campaign, others will be inspired to buck the system when told to wait their turn,” Moulton added.

By Kaitlin Lewis, Globe Staff

Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren hailed Markey’s projected victory with a “double woohoo” on social media. The senior Massachusetts senator, Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, and US Representative Ayanna Pressley were among the progressives who backed Markey’s reelection bid.

Warren said in her post that Markey was “the best partner in the Senate that money can’t buy.”

“Always proud to fight the good fight alongside [Markey],” she added.

By Kaitlin Lewis, Globe Staff

The Associated Press projected that the 80-year-old incumbent would win the primary roughly half an hour after polls closed.

Of note, Markey was up by roughly 40 points in Worcester against Seth Moulton in the minutes before the AP issued its projection. As the Globe’s Sam Brodey points out, Worcester was one of the closest jurisdictions in Markey’s 2020 win against former representative Joe Kennedy III, who ultimately won the city with 52 percent of the vote.

By Chris Van Buskirk, Globe Staff

Mike Minogue, a former medical device company executive who poured millions of dollars of his personal wealth into the Republican primary for Massachusetts governor, will win the contest, the AP projected. He’ll face Governor Maura Healey, a Democrat, in November.

READ MORE

By Sam Brodey, Globe Staff

Supporters of Representative Seth Moulton gathered in Dorchester as initial results roll in for Massachusetts’ US Senate primary election — and it did not take long for discouraging news to roll in for this crowd.

Not long after polls closed at 8 o’clock, Senator Ed Markey was posting strong results in several jurisdictions.

Inside an event hall at the Plumbers Local 12 building in Dorchester, friends, staff, and supporters of the Salem Democrat had been chatting and clutching drinks from the bar as an upbeat pop playlist played from speakers.

As results came in, supporters gathered in front of a wall where a projector displayed NBC News’ live coverage. The room grew quieter as analyst Steve Kornacki announced that his network has called the race in favor of Markey — barely a half hour after polls had closed.

Minutes later, the Associated Press projected Markey as the winner.

Moulton is expected to speak to the crowd later in the evening.

By Sam Brodey and Samantha J. Gross, Globe Staff

US Senator Ed Markey is projected to win the often-bitter Democratic Senate primary against US Representative Seth Moulton, according to the Associated Press.

By Samantha J. Gross, Globe Staff

As the clock ticked closer to 8 p.m., Senator Ed Markey’s supporters and staffers filtered into a rooftop ballroom at the Omni Parker House in downtown Boston.

The crowd snacked on cheese and crackers while they watched NBC News’ Steve Kornacki analyze the Senate race on TV. Among them was Sarah Zahed, 74, who lives next door to Markey in a Malden senior living building.

The two met earlier this year while she was passing out literature in her neighborhood, she said.

“He said ‘where are you going?’” she recalled. “Then he said ‘I want to take a picture!’”

Zahed, who moved to Malden from California in 2015 to be closer to her grandchildren, said she likes Markey’s focus on environmental issues and his promise of a “Green New Deal.”

“I’m a very strong believer that we have to save the planet,” she said.

By Kaitlin Lewis, Globe Staff

Massachusetts Governor Maura Healey won the Democratic gubernatorial primary, according to the Associated Press, sending the first-term governor to the November ballot for reelection.

Healey ran uncontested for her party’s nomination. She will face the winner of the Republican primary matchup between Mike Minogue, a former medical device company executive, and Brian Shortsleeve, a former MBTA executive under former Republican governor Charlie Baker.

By Kaitlin Lewis, Globe Staff

Polls are now closed in Massachusetts’ state primary. Voters who are in line may remain in line and can still cast their ballots.

The Globe is tracking live election results for races up and down the ballot. You can find results for all races here.

By Globe Staff

By Anjali Huynh, Globe Staff

David Hogg ruffled feathers among Democrats when he pledged to put millions of dollars toward taking on longtime politicians within his own party in a bid to push younger, liberal candidates into office. His biggest test case may come Tuesday.

The 26-year-old gun control advocate’s organization, Leaders We Deserve, has put half a million dollars toward unseating US Representative Stephen Lynch, the Eighth District’s 71-year-old unapologetically moderate incumbent who’s become one of Hogg’s top House targets this cycle.

Hogg is funneling time and resources behind Patrick Roath, the 39-year-old lawyer and former Deval Patrick aide challenging the congressman. Hogg earlier this year headlined a fund-raiser for Roath in Dorchester, walked with Roath and college students along the Freedom Trail, and has papered the district with mailers. On Sunday, Hogg knocked doors in Roslindale with Roath, personally pitching that Roath would bring more fight against the Trump administration to Washington.

“This race is not about Stephen Lynch’s age — it’s about his track record,” Hogg told roughly 40 Roath supporters in Roslindale, including state Representative Sam Montaño, Boston City Councilors Enrique Pepén and Ben Weber, and members of the Boston Teachers Union.

READ MORE

By Anjali Huynh, Globe Staff

US Representative Seth Moulton has spent years helping fellow candidates with military service backgrounds get into Congress. Some are returning the favor in the biggest political fight of his career.

Earlier this month, New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill trekked to Greater Boston to participate in a roundtable on veterans’ issues alongside Moulton, but also to help boost the Marine veteran in the waning weeks of his primary challenge against US Senator Ed Markey.

Her “full circle” appearance, as she put it, came after Moulton aided Sherrill through his Serve America PAC when she first ran for Congress in 2018. Several Serve America alums have backed Moulton in the final weeks of his Senate campaign, as polls show him trailing Markey by double digits — including among veterans, a University of Massachusetts Amherst/WCVB poll found.

In July, four of Moulton’s House colleagues — Pat Ryan of New York, Chrissy Houlahan of Pennsylvania, Seth Magaziner of Rhode Island, and Derek Tran of California — endorsed him after all of them were backed by Serve America during their own runs.

READ MORE

By Chris Van Buskirk, Globe Staff

US Senator Ed Markey called in the progressive cavalry Saturday to convince voters that his ideologies should matter more than his age in his race against Representative Seth Moulton, who has made generational change a key pitch in his challenge to the 80-year-old incumbent.

During a rally at a Dorchester union hall only days before the state’s primary election on Tuesday, Markey fielded some of the nation’s most well-known progressive lawmakers to make the case that his track record in Washington should earn him another term in the Senate. That included Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, who described Markey as someone who is “prepared to stand up to the greed, the irresponsibility, the arrogance of the billionaire class.” Senator Elizabeth Warren called Markey a “progressive, a fighter that Massachusetts can depend on.”

“Are you ready to elect someone who has got the guts to stand up to giant corporate executives, to billionaires, to Republicans, to the president of the United States, and say enough screwing American families, we are here to fight back?” Warren said at the union hall.

READ MORE

By Sean Cotter, Globe Staff

Just over four years ago, Kevin Hayden was a little-known name in Boston’s political circles. Then-Governor Charlie Baker had tapped Hayden, then the director of the state Sex Offender Registry Board, seemingly out of nowhere in January 2022 to serve in the high-profile role of Suffolk district attorney and to fill out the term of Rachael Rollins, who left to become Massachusetts US attorney.

Hayden secured the position on his own that fall following a closely contested, brutal election in which he defeated a scandal-plagued opponent. Hayden also faced an ethics violation himself for using the office for mudslinging during the race, and his victory was widely credited to the opposition his opponent faced as much as an endorsement of him.

Now, the onetime appointee of a Republican governor is the unlikely favorite of the Boston political establishment, heading into a winner-take-all Democratic primary with the endorsement of Mayor Michelle Wu, the city’s most prominent progressive Democrat.

In that contest, voters for the first time will have an official say on Hayden with a full term on which to judge his track record as district attorney: They can send him back to office, or return to the progressive platform of Rollins, who is challenging him, or go with another candidate in Linda Champion, who is vowing changes from both of her would-be predecessors.

READ MORE

By Jackie Kucinich, Tal Kopan, and Sam Brodey, Globe Staff

For weeks, Representative Seth Moulton and his team have been pushing a narrative that his Democratic primary opponent, Senator Ed Markey, was somehow implicated in the Epstein files. Markey and his campaign have vehemently denied any association with the disgraced financier, calling the insinuation “reprehensible.”

On Aug. 12, Moulton doubled down on his claims during an interview on Boston Public Radio. Host Jim Braude asked whether Moulton regretted asking Markey during their second debate earlier this month “why would [Markey] even take a meeting with a lobbyist on behalf of Jeffrey Epstein.” Moulton said no.

“He met with a lobbyist hired for hundreds of thousands of dollars by Jeffrey Epstein to try to get his sex trafficking friend, this guy you are talking about in Senegal, out of prison,” Moulton said. Pressed by Braude for more details, he dodged by saying, “if you look at the emails, it’s very clear.”

The Globe looked at the emails, fact checked the Moulton campaign’s claims, and spoke to the lobbyist who has been at the center of the allegations. The short version is, it’s not as “clear” as Moulton would like voters to believe.

READ MORE

By Chris Van Buskirk, Globe Staff

Mike Repetto, 64, of Reading, said he decided to back Michael Minogue in the Republican gubernatorial primary race because Governor Maura Healey, the Democrat incumbent, is “spending money like a drunken sailor.”

“There isn’t fiscal responsibility,” Repetto said as he ate pizza and drank a beer.

Repetto said he went to a Minogue rally at the Kowloon Restaurant in Saugus last week, where he said Minogue’s message was “very clear.”

“He wasn’t decrying his competition so much as he was trying to say what he was going to do,“ Repetto said. “It’s easy to just say negative things about somebody, but you know, he put it out there that he had an eight-point plan on going forward with things.”

Repetto was one of hundreds of Minogue supporters who packed a beer hall in Medford on Tuesday about an hour before the polls closed in Massachusetts. Minogue is running for the Republican nomination to take on Healey in November against Brian Shortsleeve, a former MBTA executive under former Governor Charlie Baker.

Ken Doran, 73, of Lawrence, said he supported Minogue “because I believe in what he has to say.”

“He believes in a lot of things that I do, and it’s time we got a new governor,” Doran said.

Minogue won the Massachusetts Republican Party’s endorsement in April, and Shortsleeve has since feuded with party activists, who have tried to push him out of the race and to line up in support of Minogue’s candidacy.

Amy Carnevale, the chair of the Massachusetts Republican Party, said party members are “really excited to turn the chapter and focus on the general election.”

“We want to be talking about Maura Healey’s failures — a failure on the economy, failure on affordability, failure on energy issues,” she said at Minogue’s primary night event.

By Jim Puzzanghera, Globe Staff

Jeromie Whalen, a high school teacher from South Hadley looking to upset US Representative Richard Neal in the Democratic primary, spent election day the way he’s spent most days during the campaign: driving around the First Congressional District in Western Massachusetts in his signature yellow van.

“I’m feeling good. We put in a year and a half of work and we have a lot of people out,” Whalen, 39, said as he stood with volunteers in a light rain greeting voters outside the Greenleaf Community Center in Springfield about 6 p.m. His campaign dispatched about 200 volunteers to polling places around the district, he said.

“From the get-go, this has been: can organized people beat corporate money?” Whalen said between waving to cars and responding with a thumbs up when drivers honked their support. “And this is the referendum that we have today.”

Whalen said he has not taken corporate political action committee money, in contrast to Neal. It’s been one of Whalen’s pitches to voters as he tried to paint Neal, 77, a top House Democrat first elected in 1988, as being out of touch with his constituents.

After starting the day greeting voters in South Hadley at 7 a.m., Whalen traveled around the district Tuesday. He said he didn’t plan to stop until the polls closed.

“I’m going to keep on cranking until 8 o’clock,” he said.

By James Pindell, Globe Staff

If you pay attention to just one race during the Massachusetts primary today, make it the Massachusetts 8th Congressional District Democratic primary.

The race features longtime incumbent Representative Stephen Lynch, 71, against lawyer and former Deval Patrick aide Patrick Roath, 39. The district includes parts of Boston and stretches south to Brockton.

Unlike the other races today, this one cleanly follows the national script for Democratic upsets in 2026: Roath is the younger, more progressive and well-funded challenger. Lynch has tried to avoid giving his opponent much attention while calling his old political band back together.

There has been no independent public polling in the race, so it’s anyone’s guess where things stand. Lynch has faced plenty of challengers from the left before and dispatched them easily. But this one feels different. Roath has built a better campaign than any of Lynch’s previous challengers, and the national mood among Democrats has lined up neatly with what Roath is selling.

READ MORE

By Tal Kopan, Globe Staff

As he fights to stave off a younger, more progressive challenger, Representative Stephen Lynch projected confidence Tuesday as he greeted volunteers at a West Roxbury precinct.

Despite the slow trickle of voters amid drizzle in the lunchtime hour, Lynch said he wasn’t concerned about turnout.

“It doesn’t bother me that it’s a little bit light here,” Lynch said. “It’s probably a result of most people voting by mail because it’s the Tuesday before Labor Day. … I think we’re gonna do well. I like my chances.”

It wasn’t clear from voters if he’s right.

Emily Engler, 47, an IT consultant from West Roxbury, said she backed Lynch’s challenger because of his more progressive positions. But she said the argument for generational change was more complicated, as she also backed Senator Ed Markey, 80.

“I feel like we can have better representation than we’ve had from [Lynch], and so I was happy to have an alternative that felt like a good alternative,” Engler said.

By Samantha J. Gross, Globe Staff

US Senator Ed Markey and his wife, Dr. Susan Blumenthal, voted late Tuesday morning at the Irish American Club in Malden. The two walked into the polling location hand in hand, waving at a small group of supporters who gathered across the street.

“Please get out and vote, everyone across the Commonwealth,” Markey told reporters outside the hall. “We need to hear your voice. We need to have your vote be counted today.”

He added that he was feeling “very, very gratified by the response” from voters so far, including a few who dropped by to see the Senator despite voting elsewhere in Malden.

“I just came here because I thought Ed Markey was going to be here!” said Helen Weitz, 74, of Malden.

By Sam Brodey, Globe Staff

Representative Seth Moulton, accompanied by his wife Liz and two young daughters, cast his ballot late Tuesday morning at his local polling site, the Mayor Jean A. Levesque Community Life Center in Salem.

Speaking to reporters afterward, Moulton said his feeling as his US Senate campaign draws to a close echoes how he felt 12 years ago, when he pulled off an upset win over a Democratic incumbent, former Representative John Tierney.

“I got a very similar feeling to today, where the polls said we were behind, but the energy on the ground, the voters who were just walking up to me… everyone wants change,” Moulton said. “They want new leadership, and I understand that frustration in Washington because I live it. It’s not fun. It’s not good. We need to do better.”

Moulton told reporters his day started around 4:30 in the morning, and he and his team have been making their way to polling sites and businesses, largely within his North Shore-based congressional district. Strong support from his home region, which he has represented for over a decade, would be a huge boost if he hopes to overcome Senator Ed Markey.

A steady trickle of voters made their way inside the building to cast their votes. As the rain paused, Moulton and supporters held signs and waved to passersby on the sidewalk outside the community center.

The congressman plans to do “just more crisscrossing the state” before polls close tonight.

By Matt Stout, Globe Staff

Federal officials sent a dozen polling monitors to sites in Boston, New Bedford, and Lowell for Tuesday’s primary, the Department of Justice said.

The presence of monitors is fairly routine. Federal personnel have observed voting in several Massachusetts cities in recent years, including during Republican and Democratic presidencies. In July, Harmeet Dhillon, an assistant attorney general for civil rights, announced plans to dispatch monitors to more than a dozen jurisdictions in six states, including Massachusetts and New Hampshire.

On Tuesday, Department of Justice officials said they had deployed 80 monitors to eight states across the primary election season. That includes the 12 monitors in three Massachusetts cities, where officials said they would “ensure transparency, ballot security, and compliance with federal law.”

The move, while common, had stoked concerns among some Democrats who have objected to the pressure campaign the Trump administration has been waging to exert more influence and control over how states manage their elections.

That environment aside, Secretary of State William F. Galvin said at a news conference Thursday that the state has “never had an issue in the past” with the DOJ monitors.

“They’ve told us where they’re going, we told them what we expect, but they’ve always understood that they could observe but they couldn’t interfere,” said Galvin, an eight-term Democrat. “That’s still the rule as far as we’re concerned.”

By Matt Stout and Audrey Tomlin, Globe Staff

On a dreary Election Day, the question is not just who voters will pick in the state’s primaries on Tuesday, but also: How many actually will bother?

Those casting ballots Tuesday were met with steady rain in several parts of the state, and in some cases, few lines at their morning polling places. In Boston, many are also navigating the annual Sept. 1 move-in churn, and the primary’s timing — six days before Labor Day — could mean some are simply trying to enjoy the last gasp of summer before the school year begins.

“I was so unsure. I waited until the last-minute,” Jeanne Blois, an 81-year-old independent voter from Wakefield, said as she ducked under an overhang at her polling location. She said she ultimately voted for US Representative Seth Moulton in the state’s US Senate Democratic primary over incumbent Ed Markey, but she didn’t do so confidently.

“I didn’t think there were a whole lot of good choices,” she said. “I think we’re in trouble. And I did my best.”

Secretary of State William F. Galvin said he expected 800,000 voters to cast a ballot in the state’s Democratic primaries, and another 280,000 to do so in the Republican races.

Should those projections hold, nearly half of voters weighing in during the state primaries have already made their choices. Entering Tuesday, roughly 464,600 voters already voted early or by mail in the Democratic primary while 91,000 submitted a Republican ballot, according to Galvin’s office. Those account for about 11 percent of the state’s registered voters.

Those in Boston who waited until today to vote will likely have to dodge rain drops throughout the afternoon. Local weather can have a “significant” effect on whether voters show up, according to a 2023 study that found that election day rainfall reduces turnout by 0.95 percentage points per centimeter on rain. And that can impact so-called marginal, or young, voters the most, the study found.

By 9 a.m., about 33,500 had cast ballots around Boston, according to city data. That actually was about double the number who did so by the same point during the last statewide primary in 2022, when roughly 85,000 ultimately people voted in Boston and about 1 million did statewide.

Outside the Jackson Mann Community Center in Allston on Tuesday morning, a few people stood outside campaigning for various politicians including Suffolk District Attorney candidate Linda Champion, Governor’s Councillor Mara Dolan, and state Senate candidate Daniel Lander in the rain.

They wore clear plastic rain ponchos and carried umbrellas, waving their signs and their hands at passing cars.

By Chris Van Buskirk, Globe Staff

Governor Maura Healey cast her ballot in the primary election Tuesday morning. Who she voted for beyond herself, however, was unclear.

Healey would not say who she voted for in the state’s marquee US Senate Democratic primary between Senator Ed Markey and Representative Seth Moulton. But speaking to reporters after casting her vote, the governor criticized the Republicans hoping to unseat her, Michael Minogue and Brian Shortsleeve.

“My opponents … voted for Trump, funded Trump, think that Trump is doing a really good job,” Healey told reporters outside an elementary school serving as a polling location. Minogue and Shortsleeve have acknowledged voting for Trump.

Minogue has also donated money to a super PAC that backed Trump’s successful 2024 campaign, federal election records show. But both candidates have also tried to distance themselves from the president.

Minogue cast his ballot earlier in the morning at his polling location in Hamilton. He said people “are ready for a change” in the governor’s office.

“We are tired of the political establishment. We need a new kind of governor that’s going to serve the people,” he said, according to an audio recording provided by his campaign. “Massachusetts is working for some, but not everyone.”

Shortsleeve was scheduled to cast his vote at 11:30 a.m. near his home in Osterville, according to his campaign.

Minogue has led Shortsleeve in polls heading into the primary election. Healey, however, has remained the frontrunner ahead of the November general election, with surveys showing the governor leading both men by double digits in hypothetical matchups.

By Samantha J. Gross, Globe Staff

It was a moment that Representative Seth Moulton’s Senate campaign had likely been waiting for. In the last televised debate between Moulton and Senator Ed Markey, the 80-year-old incumbent answered a question about his use of artificial intelligence in a way that felt rather, well, grandfatherly.

“I use whatever is inside my iPhone or my iPad, whatever comes up,” Markey answered.

In the moment, and the days afterward, Moulton pounced. On stage, he cast Markey’s response as evidence of the need for “a new generation of leaders to regulate these technologies.” His campaign quickly spread the clip on social media and sent out a press release post-debate. Then came a digital ad recapping the moment, titled, “The future is now.”

But while Moulton, 47, has made Markey’s age a central part of his “pass the torch” campaign, those potentially viral clips illustrating his argument on the need for generational change have been otherwise rare. Markey, across three debates, regularly jostled with his younger challenger, lobbed well-rehearsed retorts, and, last week, was quick to note his support from even younger representatives.

It’s all left some experts to question: Will the message ultimately break through?

READ MORE

By Kelly Garrity, Globe Staff

Do you want to be a Democrat or Republican? Massachusetts voters are increasingly picking door No. 3: neither.

Both major parties shed thousands of voters over the past 18 months, according to new data from Secretary of State William F. Galvin’s office. And the share of registered voters affiliated with each party has slipped, too. Democrats now make up about 24 percent of the state’s more than 5.1 million registered voters. Republicans have fallen below 8 percent, their lowest share since at least 1948.

In turn, the state’s already outsized proportion of unenrolled (or independent) voters has hit a new high, accounting for just over 67 percent of the state’s total.

That means there are even more voters who can opt to pull either a Democratic or Republican primary ballot on Tuesday. Galvin said at a Thursday news conference that he expects turnout for the primaries to be similar to, if not slightly exceed, that from the 2022 primaries.

READ MORE

By Globe Staff

Michael Minogue, a candidate in the Mass. Republican gubernatorial primary, cast his vote this morning in Hamilton.

By Globe Staff

Polls have opened across Massachusetts as voters look to cast their ballots in many primary races. See all the races voters are weighing in on across the state today.

Find your local polling place here.

By Anjali Huynh, Globe Staff

On the campaign trail in April for Massachusetts’ Eighth District congressional primary, 71-year-old Representative Stephen Lynch talked Trump cuts and term limits with seniors at Braintree’s Elder Affairs. Later that same day in Boston, his 39-year-old Democratic challenger, Patrick Roath, barreled down the perilous ‘Cop Slide’ on City Hall Plaza alongside a firebrand Gen Z gun violence activist.

The age and style differences between the two candidates underscore a key dynamic animating the Democratic Party, even in safe-blue corners such as Massachusetts: Whether a tested old-guard or a youthful but inexperienced vanguard is best to meet the moment, both in terms of the party’s own struggles to connect with voters, and in confronting the Republican opposition.

Lynch is pitching that his 25 years in the House and seniority on committees position him to deliver for his district and respond to a Trump-led White House. Roath, meanwhile, is singling out aspects of Lynch’s moderate record to argue that a fresh perspective is urgently needed to fight the Trump administration.

READ MORE

By Sam Brodey and Kelly Garrity, Globe Staff

The outcome of Massachusetts’ Democratic Senate primary may hinge on whether it’s hit with a late injection of something the race has lacked: urgency.

Since the beginning of the race, Democratic voters have largely been tuned out of the contest between incumbent Senator Ed Markey, of Malden, and challenger Seth Moulton, the congressman from Salem.

The choices haven’t exactly galvanized primary voters. And with Democrats desperate to win a check on President Trump in the 2026 midterms by defeating Republicans elsewhere, the stakes of a blue-state Senate primary have seemed comparatively minor.

As Markey bets it all on consolidating the most engaged of the core party base, Moulton is counting on a groundswell of support from outside the usual corners — which would require generating strong voter turnout.

READ MORE

title: The four races I’m watching Tuesday night
text:
West Roxbury’s Michael Rush is seeking a ninth term in the state Senate, representing Dedham, Norwood, Walpole, Westwood, and parts of Jamaica Plain, Roslindale, West Roxbury, and Hyde Park. (I live in the district.)

A Navy veteran, Rush has served on Beacon Hill since 2003, when he was elected state representative. His first opponent in 16 years is Persis Yu, a Hyde Park attorney, social worker, and first-time candidate challenging him from the left on affordability and State House transparency.

Rush, the Senate Majority Whip, has the backing of the Democratic establishment, including Mayor Michelle Wu. The Dorchester Reporter noted that Rush supported Wu’s tax proposal, while the mayor endorsed challengers to senators who opposed it.

Yu has been a strong fund-raiser. Meanwhile, Globe political reporter Kelly Garrity noted that Rush and other Massachusetts politicians received contributions from Anthropic employees after Rush offered an AI-safety amendment that the company supported and the Senate adopted.

Rush has no apparent campaign website and according to published reports did not debate Yu or show up at a candidate forum with her. He seems to be running on a low-engagement strategy. Voters must decide whether that reflects confidence born of experience or avoidance.

State Senator Patricia Jehlen’s retirement opened a crowded contest over who can best continue her progressive legacy in a district that includes Somerville and Medford, and parts of Cambridge and Winchester.

Four candidates are running: state Representatives Christine Barber and Erika Uyterhoeven, Cambridge Vice Mayor Burhan Azeem, and Somerville City Councilor Matt McLaughlin. (A fifth, Tom Hopcroft, ended his campaign too late to have his name removed from the ballot.)

The contenders have similar progressive priorities. The disagreement centers on how to wield power on Beacon Hill. Barber, endorsed by Jehlen and Governor Maura Healey, argues that legislative experience and coalition-building produce results. Uyterhoeven emphasizes transparency and a willingness to challenge Beacon Hill leadership. Azeem highlights his municipal record, particularly on housing, while McLaughlin calls himself “the working-class” candidate.

Following the money, the Abundant Housing Massachusetts Independent Expenditure PAC reportedly spent $93,000 supporting Azeem, fueling the debate over outside spending. In the end, the race may reveal less about ideology than about which style of progressive leadership voters want.

Six days before the primary, federal prosecutors charged state Representative Francisco Paulino of Methuen with pandemic relief loan fraud and money laundering. They allege that Paulino fraudulently obtained more than $700,000 in pandemic unemployment benefits and business loans before entering the Legislature. Paulino pleaded not guilty.

Paulino, who’s seeking a third term representing parts of Lawrence and Methuen, has refused to drop out, saying that he expects to clear his name. Healey called the allegations “very disturbing.”

His challenger, Lawrence City Councilor Celina Reyes, was already campaigning on greater transparency and accountability on Beacon Hill. A child-care provider and union organizer, Reyes has struggled to fund-raise. The timing of the federal charges complicate the race — by the time Paulino was arraigned, many voters had already cast their ballots. Still, the remaining voters must determine how much unresolved criminal allegations should matter when choosing their representative.

In the 2024 Democratic primary, state Representative Marjorie Decker defeated Evan MacKay by just 41 votes. Two years later, MacKay is back.

Decker, who has represented the Cambridge district since 2013, argues her experience and relationships have delivered results for her constituents. Healey and US Senator Ed Markey have endorsed her. MacKay is a former Harvard labor organizer supported by the Democratic Socialists of America, campaigning again on legislative transparency and challenging Beacon Hill’s concentration of power. They’re both staunch progressives, but their debates have exposed differences over policy approaches.

MacKay entered the rematch with stronger fund-raising than two years ago, while outside groups have spent large sums supporting Decker. The results on Tuesday should settle the question: Did the 2024 razor-thin margin reflect momentary dissatisfaction with Decker or a more durable demand for change?

No Republican or independent candidate is officially running in any of these four contests. Barring a successful write-in campaign, Tuesday’s Democratic primaries will determine who will represent these districts in the State House. That means a relatively small share of the electorate will decide four consequential questions about ideology, political power, and experience.
