title: At a Dorchester cemetery, elderly Black women were buried in unmarked graves. Now, there’s an effort to memorialize them.
text:
On Wednesday evening, an art installation was unveiled at the site and the names of the 133 women known to have been buried there were read off during a ceremony. Eventually, the group plans to install permanent memorials with the women’s names.

Nearly 100 people filled the pews of the cemetery’s chapel, as violinist Adrian Anantawan performed as they arrived for the 5 p.m. ceremony.

“We cannot change the circumstances of the burial, but we can change what happens now,” said Diana Lam, president of the Boston Women’s Heritage Trail. “We can speak their names, we can honor their lives, we can tell their stories, and we can ensure the future generations know that these women were here.”

The project began when Joyce Linehan, a former aide to ex-Boston mayor Martin J. Walsh who lives in Dorchester, walked her dog past the burial site and noticed it was marked only by a stone inscribed with the name of the Home for Aged Colored Women. She wondered who was buried there and started asking questions.

Linehan’s friend Karilyn Crockett, also a former city official and a professor at MIT, then launched a multiyear research project that led to the discovery of the buried women’s names and shed light on a mostly forgotten chapter of the city’s history.

“These women were building a city for us and with us at a time [when] they were not given credit or recognition for that at all,” Crockett said.

The women lived in a segregated elder home on Beacon Hill between 1860 and 1944. They were domestic servants and suffrage activists. They were congregants at Twelfth Baptist, then known as the Fugitive Slave Church. Some had been born into Southern slavery and moved north after the Civil War.

They were not welcome at the nearby Home for Aged Women, where the residents were white and mostly Protestant. The homes were only a few blocks apart. Their burial sites were even closer — literally adjacent plots at Cedar Grove. But only one had headstones. The residents of the Home for Aged Colored Women were buried, and then their names — or at least their burial sites — were largely forgotten.

In 2024, Rita Steele, a data analytics professional and avid genealogist, was trying to trace her family tree to its Native American roots. She thought her fourth great-grandmother, Sarah Smith, who died in Boston in 1890, might provide the link.

“So I used one of my successful research strategies (reverse address search) of the address on her death certificate,” Steele said by text message. She assumed the Beacon Hill address was a family home. But instead, “it came back with the name for the Home for Aged Colored Women.”

That discovery led her to a blog post by Linehan about the Dorchester burial site. She got in touch with Linehan and Crockett and has been involved in planning the memorial ever since.

Crockett’s research has proceeded on a parallel track. After learning of the burial site from Linehan, she assigned her MIT graduate students to research the home. The cemetery had handwritten note cards listing the women’s names in its archives. Then they found the home’s records in the archives of the Massachusetts Historical Society.

What emerged was an unusually intimate portrait of the women’s lives. The records showed “who was an avid reader, who was a vegetarian, who didn’t like who,” Linehan said. “There was gossipy stuff in there.”

For Crockett, the research also challenged the assumption that Black Bostonians, especially elderly Black women, must have been isolated, only marginal participants in the life of the city. Eliza Gardner, who received financial assistance from the home, was a prominent public speaker and member of Black political organizations, Crockett said. She was once featured in The Woman’s Era, a newspaper founded in Boston in 1894.

Other women were part of migrations to New England. Some came from Canada, others from the American South.

Annie B. Merrick was born into slavery in North Carolina in 1848, according to Crockett. She moved north and then lived in the Home for Aged Colored Women beginning in 1923. She died at Boston State Hospital in 1941.

Smith, Steele’s ancestor, was born in Newport, R.I., around 1799. Her father had been enslaved and fought in the Revolutionary War. Two of Smith’s brothers were abolitionists who worked with Frederick Douglass. Steele and Crockett are still trying to learn more about Smith herself.

Steele traveled from her home in Maryland to attend the ceremony. “There’s tons of work to be done,” she said. “I hope this is a flicker of light for someone.”

The women, including her ancestor, Smith, are buried in two plots — the one next to the white women’s burial ground and a second one that was used when the first filled up.

The temporary memorial is a “collage” of flowers and women’s portraits formed into a single figure to “reflect both the individuality of each woman and her presence in a greater community,” artist Ekua Holmes said.

The Roxbury-born artist entered the chapel to applause. She drew inspiration from Ellis Wilson’s “Funeral Procession” painting, she said.

The installation will remain there for a year while the nonprofit Boston Women’s Heritage Trail raises money for a permanent memorial that includes all of the women’s names.

Robert MacEachern, who runs the cemetery, estimates the memorial will cost more than $100,000. The past two state budgets earmarked $45,000 combined for the project. A grant from the city of Boston paid for Holmes’s work but is not funding the permanent memorial.

When Steele first learned of Smith’s burial place, she found the circumstances “very disturbing and disappointing.”

“No one knew who they were walking by,” she said. “Like they didn’t mean anything to anyone. . . . But I am so proud that their names are finally being restored.”

Correspondent Madyline Swearing contributed to this story.

title: Wu endorsed in three contested state Senate races. Two of her candidates lost, the last race is still too close to call.
text:
Wu downplayed the outcome of the primary in an interview Wednesday, noting that she backed two first-time candidates who took on entrenched incumbents.

“Every election matters, and every year matters for getting things done, and that’s what we saw in the results from yesterday,” Wu said. “We had first-time candidates who started with no name recognition, taking on incumbents, and really outperforming expectations.”

In addition to Lander, Wu backed education activist Latoya Gayle, also a first-time candidate, in her unsuccessful bid to unseat state Senator Nick Collins of South Boston.

Wu has publicly clashed with both Collins and Brownsberger in recent years, and her endorsement of their challengers raised eyebrows as an attempt to oust her political adversaries on Beacon Hill.

Wu also endorsed state Senator Michael F. Rush of West Roxbury, an eight-term incumbent who lost to attorney Persis Yu in a district that includes Dedham, Norwood, Walpole, Westwood, and parts of Jamaica Plain, Roslindale, West Roxbury, and Hyde Park.

On Tuesday, Gayle lost to Collins by roughly 10 percentage points. And Yu unseated Rush by winning 51 percent of the vote to Rush’s 49 percent.

Lander and Brownsberger, though, remain neck and neck. As of 6:30 p.m. Wednesday, Lander had 12,132 votes — a mere three votes ahead of Brownsberger, who tallied 12,129 according to the Associated Press.

The candidates have until 3 p.m. Thursday to request a districtwide recount, in a race where more is riding on the outcome than just who will represent a district that covers swaths of Boston, Cambridge, Watertown, and Belmont, in the state Senate. Neither candidate responded Wednesday for comment.

Wu took a risk spending her political capital backing newcomers against well-established incumbents, said Erin O’Brien, a political science professor at the University of Massachusetts Boston.

“People are going to do the tally,” O’Brien said. “If you endorse and the person loses, it goes against your tally.”

Still, O’Brien argued it would be premature to assume that the losses are a reflection that the mayor’s influence or popularity are waning.

“Wu’s a variable,” O’Brien said. “She’s not a determining force.”

But on a night where most incumbents across the state retained their seats, Rush’s loss, especially with Wu’s endorsement, was a notable outlier.

The result reflected the broader trend across the country as Democratic voters showed an increasing appetite for generational change and progressive leadership, according to David Hopkins, a political science professor at Boston College. Yu, who defeated Rush, ran to his left.

“There is clearly this increasingly mobilized progressive vote in Democratic primaries here in this state, as well many other places around the country,” Hopkins said. “Some Democratic incumbents are facing serious competition, sometimes for the first time in many years, or the first time in their career.”

On Wednesday, Rush’s campaign did not respond to a request comment. Wu defended her endorsement of the West Roxbury Democrat, who faced a progressive challenger who espoused many of the same talking points as Lander and Gayle.

Still, Rush “has often been the first to call and ask what Boston needs in the state Senate,” Wu said. “He has moved issues and funding for us quietly and effectively, and I wish he would still be in a position to help serve our community, [but] the voters have spoken.”

In an interview in the wake of her loss against Collins, Gayle said that the 10-point margin in her race shows that Boston voters’ are scrutinizing incumbents’ records and demanding urgency from elected leadership.

“The people are watching,” Gayle said. “It’s important that when you show up to the State House, when you volunteer for this job, that you are listening to the people and and pushing the policies, the budget, the things that the people actually need and want.”

“Because your seat won’t be safe,” Gayle said, ”if you’re not.”

title: Roxbury needed a pharmacy. CVS says it has the answer. But is it enough?
text:
Insurance reimbursements, labor, and real estate costs have squeezed margins as drugstores have lost market share on everyday retail to competitors, including Amazon. Meanwhile, executives have said shoplifting has become an increasing concern.

CVS isn’t alone in experimenting with a smaller drugstore footprint. Walgreens has also tried smaller-format stores that are about 20 to 25 percent of the size of their typical stores, said Neil Saunders, managing director at GlobalData Retail, a retail consulting agency.

At the same time, drugstores’ basic retail business has also weakened, Saunders said. Dollar stores have eroded their convenience advantage, while Amazon and Walmart have made it easier to have goods delivered. Meanwhile, drugstores often charge more than Target and Walmart for the same everyday items.

Pharmacy chains “have kind of have lost the battle on retail,” said Saunders. “They don’t really want to do that on pharmacy.”

In Roxbury, CVS tried a new path: bringing back the pharmacy without the drugstore. It’s one of roughly 20 such concepts that CVS plans to roll out in cities nationwide. The Boston move triggered mixed feelings, with some arguing it represents an inequity.

Rahsaan D. Hall, president and CEO of The Urban League of Eastern Massachusetts, said CVS should be praised for returning a pharmacy to the community, but added the company was “creating a two-tier retail experience.”

“Residents in one community can browse products, compare ingredients and prices, and purchase ordinary household necessities while residents in another community, made up of a completely different racial and socioeconomic demographic, cannot,” said Hall. “That difference deserves a level of scrutiny.”

The new format comes after a string of pharmacies, including Walgreens and CVS, have pulled out of the neighborhood over the last decade. In fact, the community lost five drugstores since 2017, with only one family-owned shop — Kornfield Pharmacy — left standing.

Renewed pharmacy access fills one major gap in Roxbury. But CVS isn’t filling another: the loss of a local drugstore where residents can pick up toiletries, food, and other everyday necessities. For a neighborhood that has lost pharmacies and drugstores, is it enough?

“I’m glad there’s a new pharmacy here, but I wish they sold retail goods,” said Alex DiMario, 38, who lives near the new store. “There’s not enough real convenience stores in the neighborhood.”

CVS, headquartered in Rhode Island, calls this model a new answer to an old problem of how to put pharmacies back into communities where access has become increasingly challenging.

“People [have been] taking the bus to go pick up their prescriptions,” said Siddharth “Sid” Tenneti, the senior vice president and interim president of CVS’s pharmacy and consumer wellness division. “This is our attempt to be a health care answer to the community.”

The first pharmacy-only CVS opened earlier this year on Chicago’s West Side, a dense and diverse neighborhood. Others opened in Houston, Detroit, Birmingham, and Washington, D.C. CVS is also opening a dozen new traditional stores and more than 30 pharmacies inside Target stores across the United States.

Chris Ribeiro, the founder of retail strategy firm Starlight Analytics, said this format signals a broader shift in the economics of retail drugstores, particularly in places with high rents.

“The question to ask is whether prescription revenue alone is enough to justify even these smaller footprints,” Ribeiro said.

Michelle Fenstermaker, the executive strategy director of consulting firm Landor, is blunt about the industry’s future: “The era of the monolithic, one-size-fits-all, 14,000-square-foot corner drugstore is officially over.”

Rite Aid, which operated more than 5,000 stores at its peak, is now defunct after filing for bankruptcy twice. To survive, Walgreens has also closed underperforming stores, cut corporate positions, and invested in technology such as prescription-filling robots.

Walgreens’s small-format stores, which the company first began testing in 2019, mostly offer Walgreens-branded health-related products. As of 2024, Walgreens had reportedly opened about 100 mini drugstores nationwide.

At the same time, pressure from competitors seems to be coming from everywhere: Club chains, such as Costco, have continued to grow and compete with drugstores’ convenience-based demand for beauty and hygiene products, said Jeremy Bowman, a retail analyst for investment research company The Motley Fool. Online pharmacies, such as Amazon, GoodRx, and Hims & Hers Health Inc., have also exploded, said Bowman.

The vast majority of Roxbury has long qualified as a pharmacy desert — meaning a poorer, urban area with low car-ownership rates, where the nearest pharmacy can be at least a half-mile away. In contrast, many white and wealthier residents in the Back Bay can walk to two or three pharmacies within a half mile.

The disparities extend beyond convenience. Pharmacy access is among the factors that health experts say can worsen health disparities. The average life expectancy in Roxbury is 68, 23 years fewer than in the Back Bay. And the neighborhood has higher rates of chronic diseases.

At 3,000 square feet, the new CVS store is less than half the size of the company’s urban stores in the area.

The format comes as CVS has restructured its portfolio in recent years: Coming out of COVID, the company closed 900 stores, while theft is one complication in “certain markets,” CVS CEO David Joyner has said. Merchandise is often locked behind glass to deter theft, a practice Joyner has acknowledged creates a “horrible customer experience.”

For years, customers of CVS, and its competitors, have complained about having to wait for employees to unlock everything from toothpaste to deodorant. Some analysts have warned that the practice has undermined the convenience factor that’s supposed to be the stores’ selling point.

Joyner didn’t want security guards in every store where there’s a high theft rate, he said during a talk at the Boston College Chief Executives Club in June.

One solution, he said, was to roll out pharmacy-only stores like the one in Roxbury — “where we can still meet the clinical needs of the population, but not feel like you’re constantly trying to deal with the safety of running a front store.”

City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, a longtime Roxbury pastor, said he disagrees with Joyner. When he protested against Walgreens closing in Roxbury, Culpepper presented data that showed theft wasn’t as high as executives made it out to be.

“I challenge the CVS executive to cite the data that supports his statement,” said Culpepper.

Hall said while he understands theft is an issue broadly, CVS’s response to “the behavior of a small number of people should not be to punish an entire neighborhood by removing resources from everyone.”

The new Roxbury store can order products for customers and deliver them to their homes free of charge.

Lauren Beitelspacher, a Babson College marketing professor, said she expects dollar stores to try to fill the in-person retail void.

“However, I do think that establishing yourself as a leader in the health care and wellness space in a neighborhood that doesn’t have access is a way to really build up brand loyalty,” said Beitelspacher.

title: Photos show Gloria Steinem through decades as a leading voice of the women’s movement
text:
Photos show Gloria Steinem through decades as a leading voice of the women’s movement

Gloria Steinem, the celebrated author and activist who became one of the most visible symbols and potent voices of the US women’s movement and a fierce advocate for feminist causes throughout her life, has died. She was 92.

With her trademark streaked hair parted down the middle and large aviator glasses, Steinem, a co-founder of Ms. Magazine, was a hugely recognizable presence wherever she went. And she went everywhere: Much of her life as an advocate was spent on the road, speaking at college campuses and community centers, at rallies and marches.

She died Wednesday at her home in New York City, according to her and her foundation’s social media pages.

title: Financing plan for the T’s Fairmount Line could give the entire system a jolt
text:
The clock is ticking for the MBTA to put the finishing touches on an unusual financing deal within the next few weeks — one that could help determine the entire commuter rail system’s future.

The T is in final negotiations with several private-sector partners to finally redo the Fairmount Line, with battery-powered cars to replace the diesel dinosaurs that rumble through the heart of the city.

They’re working with the familiar faces at commuter rail operator Keolis, and some new ones at the table. This will be the first time the T has relied on a third-party financier — in this case, British infrastructure firm Rock Rail — to buy new commuter rail vehicles on its behalf.

The T board blessed this in June, agreeing to spend $765 million over 15 years to cover the cost of leasing and maintaining seven four-car trainsets that run on electric batteries. The cars will be made by Stadler in Utah, and start showing up for testing in late 2029.

This isn’t only about righting a wrong for Boston’s poorer neighborhoods, by offering trains that arrive at 20-minute intervals. The ramifications go well beyond the Fairmount’s nine-mile corridor through Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, and Hyde Park.

General manager Phil Eng sees this as a model that could be replicated as he looks to put the entire commuter rail system on track for electrification, another long-awaited change. What works in Boston’s urban neighborhoods might also work in suburban outposts. The Fairmount purchase is a test run; the deal includes options to procure as many as 96 more new cars, the equivalent of 24 trainsets, for other lines.

Another reason to watch Fairmount: politics. Keolis is in a race to keep its coveted job as the commuter rail operator. By coincidence, bids for the new contract are due later this month. It was once thought delivering an electric train in time for Governor Maura Healey’s reelection campaign in 2026 would give her bragging rights — and maybe help Keolis with its case that it should stick around.

That timing turned out to be wishful thinking. But at least Healey can brag about the financing, right?

Whether this helps the French company’s bid, we may never know. T officials structured the Fairmount financing so a different operator, or even the T itself, can take over the lease.

The more traditional route would be issuing bonds for new trains. But the T says it would have had to cancel or reschedule other critical projects to do so. Plus, Rock Rail takes on some of the risk; lease payments don’t start until these machines are in service.

An upgraded Fairmount has been on the arrivals board for years, thanks to pressure from neighborhood advocates and politicians, along with the Conservation Law Foundation that fought for mitigation to offset Big Dig impacts.

The T did add four stations to Fairmount’s three preexisting ones and its South Station and Readville terminals. And the cost to ride was also cut, to the same price as the subway.

What about subway frequency? A plan from Deval Patrick’s administration to buy self-propelled diesel-powered units was scuttled after Charlie Baker took over, though the T did trim headways in 2020 under Baker.

Finally, we have a plan to go electric — even though it will take four more years to see it in action. T officials decided each car should be wheelchair accessible (in part to adhere to a 2006 legal settlement), not just one per trainset. That drove up costs, and delayed delivery.

In June, board member Mary Skelton Roberts chastised T executives for the delays, and a failure to keep the community apprised. Folks, she said, have been waiting for these trains for ages.

Some still won’t be fully satisfied. City councilor Brian Worrell says the neighborhood might be better served by overhead wires the whole way, instead of batteries, making the line even more like a subway. (The trains will use overhead lines to recharge, but for only a small section.) Worrell has been in the news along with councilor Miniard Culpepper pushing their own transit proposal for the area, an Orange Line extension along Blue Hill Avenue; he says it could augment, not replace, the electrified Fairmount trains.

Kimberly Lyle, head of the Dorchester Bay Economic Development Corp., says she’s just happy to see meaningful progress. Her neighbors deserve a quick commute downtown, and cleaner air, as much as anyone in Boston.

Now, finally, the T is poised to deliver on that promise — and put the wheels in motion for bigger changes down the line.

What’s your take? Join the conversation in the comments here.

Republican Mike Minogue is already shattering records for self-funding, pouring $15.8 million into his gubernatorial bid, according to state campaign filings. So who did he surpass? Venture capitalist Chris Gabrieli previously topped the list of self-funders after putting $15.1 million into two unsuccessful gubernatorial and lieutenant governor bids during the 2000s. Former lieutenant governor Kerry Healey was right behind him after spending $11.8 million only to lose the 2006 governor’s race to Deval Patrick. Labor lawyer Shannon Liss-Riordan also bet big on herself, but her $9.3 million wasn’t enough to become attorney general in 2022. Of the top five self-funders, so far only Bain Capital cofounder Mitt Romney – who spent $6.3 million to run for governor in 2002 (equivalent to $11.9 million today) – came away with a win. Kerry Healey, who is now executive chair of the independent Forward Party, said campaign finance reforms are needed. “Whether campaigns are self-funded or funded by others, there is simply too much money spent on politics,” she said.

Welcome to Massport, Taidgh McClory. The real estate consultant was sworn in this week by Governor Maura Healey as the newest member of the Massachusetts Port Authority’s board of directors. Also in attendance at the State House ceremony: board chair Patricia Jacobs, chief executive Rich Davey, and board member Sean O’Brien. McClory takes over for Warren Fields, a Charlie Baker appointee whose seven-year term expired in 2025, but was asked to stay on for another year. Davey says he wanted someone else with real estate experience to take over for Fields, and he reached out to former board member Duane Jackson and Weld-era transportation secretary Richard Taylor for suggestions. Independently, both suggested McClory, who worked at Millennium Partners and CBRE before launching his own firm. He won’t have much time to ease into the unpaid role, with the first board meeting scheduled for next week.

If only lawyer David Lurie were still here to savor this victory. The town of Nahant just won big at the Supreme Judicial Court today, in its years-long fight with Northeastern University over the fate of East Point. The town has a waterfront park there, including an easement over land Northeastern owns. In 2018, the university unveiled plans to expand its marine science campus there, to the chagrin of those in the town. The town then used its eminent domain authority to seize access rights, essentially blocking the expansion. Northeastern sued, saying this was an illegal use of the authority simply to block a project, and a Superior Court judge agreed. But the SJC today overruled that decision: Protecting a park fits as a public purpose for eminent domain. Lurie represented the Nahant Preservation Trust in the case, but died in 2024 before he was able to see it through fruition; former colleague Harley Racer kept the fight going.

Congrats to readers Dr. Jeff Lowenstein and David Ball. Both had more than a feeling for the right answer when we asked the question about where bandleader Tom Scholz worked while putting together rock band Boston’s blockbuster debut album, which came out 50 years ago. The employer was Polaroid, which all but disappeared in bankruptcy more than 20 years ago. It’s been such a long time since we used a Polaroid camera.

Rest in power, Gloria Steinem. The feminist icon and cofounder of Ms. Magazine passed away on Wednesday at age 92. Generations of women have Steinem to thank for her lifelong advocacy for equal rights. There would be no women CEOs, governors, or mayors without her. But her greatest legacy, perhaps, is this: The fight for women’s rights is never done. We can’t let up. She never did.

Today’s edition was edited by Greg Huang, Tim Logan, and Aaron Pressman, and produced by Diamond Naga Siu.

Have a question for the team? Email us at powerplay@globe.com.

Delivered Tuesday and Thursday (in summertime).

title: Yu who? Meet the progressive who pulled off a Boston-area upset
text:
Her insurgent campaign flew largely under the radar outside of the district stretching from West Roxbury into Boston’s southern suburbs, despite Mayor Michelle Wu coming to the moderate incumbent’s defense in the very district in which she lives.

That was due, in part, to Wu’s other electoral pursuits: The second-term mayor backed two first-time candidates who were trying to take down sitting senators, including one of Rush’s fellow Senate leaders.

“People outside the district didn’t know what was happening,” said Rob Orthman, a Yu backer and co-director of Progressive West Roxbury/Roslindale. “And we were perfectly fine keeping it that way. We did not want to raise attention to this to suddenly start seeing, you know, all the money and support for the incumbent start to flow in.”

Yu was one of a tiny percentage of candidates Tuesday to successfully take out an incumbent by running to their left.

With no Republican on the ballot in November, she effectively clinched the Norfolk and Suffolk seat with her primary victory, taking out not just an eight-term incumbent but also Senate President Karen Spilka’s handpicked majority whip.

So who is this first-time candidate turned (likely) senator-elect — and how did she turn a quiet primary challenge into Tuesday’s biggest down-ballot shocker?

Yu jumped into the race last year, motivated in part by President Trump’s reelection in 2024. In the current political climate, “we need to have steadfast leaders who are protecting our rights, especially on abortion access, especially on LGBTQ+ issues, and especially on immigrant rights,” she said.

But the campaign wasn’t simply a referendum on social issues. Much of her pitch centered on affordability concerns, and, according to Yu, frustration with what voters saw as a Legislature that wasn’t getting enough done. Lawmakers’ resistance to a voter-approved law giving the state auditor the authority to probe the Legislature often came up organically on the trail, Yu said.

“There was a dissatisfaction with the status quo,” the Hyde Park Democrat said. “And people want to know what is actually happening in the Legislature.”

Yu, a Boston Public Schools parent and mother of two, had been active on Boston’s Ward 18 Democratic Committee, but first popped up on Orthman’s radar last spring, he said, as she met with progressive groups around the district to test the waters on a potential state Senate bid.

A consumer protection attorney, “she always likes to say [that] she’s sued the last few presidential administrations on behalf of student loan borrowers, both Democratic and Republican,” Orthman said.

Her campaign was up against some early headwinds. While Rush started off with a cash advantage, Yu outraised him during the campaign, pulling in a little over $156,000 since the start of last September, compared to Rush’s roughly $148,000.

Rush, an Iraq War veteran who first won his seat in 2010, also had some serious institutional support from both Wu and Governor Maura Healey.

The mayor’s support for the more moderate Rush normally would’ve been somewhat surprising. But Rush helped shepherd Wu’s closely watched property tax shift legislation on Beacon Hill, pushing an amendment that the Senate ultimately rejected in January.

That denial prompted Wu to put her political power on the line by backing challengers to Senators Nick Collins and William Brownsberger, and turning those races into something of a proxy war. But her presence was less notable in Rush’s region — and ultimately, didn’t seem to sway voters in her city.

Yu outperformed Rush in Boston, according to unofficial results, earning 57 percent of the vote in the city while Rush carried parts of the district beyond.

“The kind of voter who is highly engaged and supports Michelle is unlikely to be swayed to vote for Rush by her endorsement,” said Matt McCloskey, a Yu volunteer focused on elections data. The district itself changed as well when state lawmakers crafted new maps in 2021, McCloskey said.

“It’s definitely an easier district for a progressive to win now than it would have been in 2020,” he said.

Then there was another notable moment days ahead of the election: When Rush skipped a debate set up by the Dedham and Westwood Democratic town committees, apparently to present a check for state funding in another town in the district.

The move handed Yu and her supporters a ready-made cudgel to hammer Rush heading into the home stretch of the campaign.

Rush has not commented publicly since the loss, and efforts to reach him Thursday were not successful.

Yu, however, said she spoke to Wu briefly Wednesday, and the mayor “was very gracious.”

“It’s a good place-starting conversation, and I definitely look forward to having further ones in the future,” Yu said.

Wu, in a statement, said she offered Yu her “full partnership and support,” and that she looked forward to “working with her as my new state senator to deliver on a shared agenda for the district and the city.”

Notably, Yu isn’t pitching herself as some type of Wu agitator. Case in point: She said that she, too, is supportive of the mayor’s tax shift proposal.

DOWN FOR A COUNT: Back to one of those other Boston-area state Senate races ...

The still too-close-to-call Brownsberger-Daniel Lander contest appears to be headed for a recount.

With just four votes separating the two, per unofficial tallies as of Friday morning, both the Belmont Democrat and the Wu-backed Lander requested a recount, the Globe’s Niki Griswold reports.

It’s a quick turnaround for everyone involved. Brownsberger and Lander had until Thursday afternoon to file their requests. If their petitions advance, local election officials have to complete the recount by 5 p.m. next Friday.

TRUMP BUMP: Trump hails Ed Markey win in Mass.: ‘I couldn’t stand Moulton’ by Sam Brodey, The Boston Globe: Speaking at a White House dinner for Republican candidates Wednesday night, Trump hailed what he called Senator Ed Markey’s 30-point “landslide” win over US Representative Seth Moulton in Tuesday’s primary election.

ABORTION ON THE (2028) BALLOT? Antiabortion activists launch effort to suspend new Mass. abortion law, put repeal before voters by Chris Van Buskirk, The Boston Globe: Antiabortion activists in Massachusetts filed paperwork with the state launching a bid to suspend and eventually seek the repeal of a law that makes it easier for women to receive an abortion later in pregnancy. That move sets up a potential ballot battle in 2028, and more immediately, kick-starts a scramble to stop the law before it can even take effect.

CHANGING LANES: More parking, fewer bike lanes: City of Boston, T release new Blue Hill Avenue redesign by Diti Kohli, The Boston Globe: Residents and politicians have for years railed against the city of Boston’s plan to reconfigure Blue Hill Avenue and the impacts that proposed bus and bike lanes could wrought on the busy corridor through the heart of the Black Boston.

Now, city officials and the MBTA say they’ve funneled those concerns into a new design that preserves a controversial center-running bus lane, but significantly expands the portions of the boulevard that would have two traffic lanes on each side, while shrinking the amount of proposed bike lanes.

A LITERAL POWER PLAY: The Globe’s Jon Chesto and Shirley Leung have a look at the unusual financing deal that would grease the wheels for an overhaul of the Fairmount Line — and which in turn could help determine the future of the entire commuter rail system.

The T is working with some familiar faces (commuter rail operator Keolis) and some new ones (British infrastructure firm Rock Rail) in an effort to electrify the line that runs along a nine-mile corridor through Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, and Hyde Park, they reported in Thursday’s edition of Power Play.

BREAKING BAD: This Boston firm owes $100,000 because Beacon Hill delayed a Trump tax break. It’s not alone. by Larry Edelman, The Boston Globe: Thousands of Massachusetts businesses — it’s impossible to say exactly how many — may be facing large tax bills as a result of the state’s decision to “decouple” from the R&D deduction provision in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the GOP’s massive tax and spending bill that President Trump signed in July 2025.

Local companies can still claim the full R&D deduction, which reduces taxable income, for 2025 and again this year. But they cannot do so on state returns, leaving them with higher taxable income — and a bigger Department of Revenue tax bill. A Department of Revenue spokesperson didn’t respond to a request for comment.

title: A Zillow search led to a startling pattern on a quiet street in Roxbury
text:
Write to us at startingpoint@globe.com. To subscribe, sign up here.

About a year ago, I opened Zillow and started messing around with the website’s interactive map. I stumbled upon one street in particular, in Roxbury: Montrose. The home valuations were noticeably varied, from several hundred thousand to over $1.2 million. What was going on?

Using land records, I learned that the $1.2 million home had been sold just about two years before, for $525,000, by a long-term resident to two Boston restaurateurs, who had turned it into a freshly renovated, gleaming duplex.

I wanted to know more: About the seller, the buyers, and what the home’s reincarnation might tell us about Boston’s overheated housing market.

So I headed to Montrose and started knocking on doors. I met older residents who said they were struggling to hang on, amidst rising taxes and constant pressure from real estate agents. And I met newer residents who were thrilled to gain a foothold in a vibrant, diverse community with a rich history and new, attractive amenities.

Something different in play

It soon became clear that this wasn’t a classic story of gentrification as it’s often told: Some white people were moving in, but so were people of color, who worked in academia, business, for non-profits. And some of the long-term residents were thrilled they could get up to a million bucks on old properties that were becoming onerous to care for.

But there was a real sense of loss, too. The woman who originally sold the $1.2 million house told me she couldn’t afford to hang onto it, even though she had planned to pass it down to her children, and felt pressured by developers who didn’t give her a fair price.

I learned that many of the older residents had faced liens, foreclosures, and debt. Our data editor, Yoohyun Jung, pointed out that this part of Roxbury faces one of the highest risks of displacement in Boston. As one long-term resident, Silvery Richardson, told me: “Each time something sells, the calls and the paperwork start coming.”

How it happens

Everyone talks about gentrification. But you rarely get the backstory of how it actually happens. This week, we offer you an intimate portrait of one block facing drastic change, told through the people who have lived there.

There are tensions here, but there’s also humor — one resident told me, “you’ve gotta be careful about juice places!”

You’ll also get a real sense of the stakes. One woman, who first moved to the neighborhood, stopped in the middle of our interview. “I’m not going to talk it up,” she said. “I don’t want even more people to move here.”

title: Persis Yu's blueprint for challenging entrenched power on Beacon Hill
text:
Yu’s account of the upset — in which Democratic primary voters ousted a senator who has served on Beacon Hill since 2003 — is not a magic formula. But it does show how a credible challenge to entrenched power gets built: You show up early and often, you give voters a compelling reason to fire the incumbent, and you run against him on purpose, and not simply because the seat opened up.

Yu, the deputy executive director and managing counsel for Protect Borrowers, a national nonprofit group that fights predatory debt, was clear-eyed about how she made an invisible race visible. “We had an incredible ground game. We were everywhere, we were out in every single community multiple times a week,” Yu told me. “I connected with families of all kinds across the political spectrum.”

Yu treated campaigning as a conversation rather than a pitch, she said. “Once you connect with people as people, and as families, the labels kind of disappear.” It’s why she believes “Democrats as a whole” need “to get better at just talking to people.”

It sounds embarrassingly basic, but this is Massachusetts, the land of the low-competition political culture. In those conversations, Yu drew a contrast between her stances and Rush’s record. For example, Rush voted against expanding access to reproductive health care in 2020 (although he has voted for the major reproductive-rights bills since.) And he was perceived as absent from the district: He declined Yu’s debate requests, skipped a town hall in August, and canceled a Dedham-Westwood forum by email the day of, citing a scheduling conflict.

She was also gathering intelligence from voters. On doorsteps, at community events and parks, Yu kept hearing about an issue she had not expected to carry much weight: the stalled audit of the Legislature.

Lest we forget, in 2024, 72 percent of voters in the state approved Question 1, granting state Auditor Diana DiZoglio explicit authority to audit the Legislature. House and Senate leaders spent the year and a half that followed refusing to comply, until a Supreme Judicial Court order this past May forced the Senate to hand over a narrow set of financial records while still reserving its constitutional objections. As Senate majority whip, Rush was part of the leadership that dragged its feet on the audit.

“People were really worked up about it. ‘The only thing I care about is the audit. I’m a single-issue voter. Where do you stand on the audit?’,” Yu said, recalling what she heard from voters. Yu had entered the race talking about transparency as a principle, but door-knocking taught her that the state auditor fight had given some voters a concrete way to understand it. “They said, ‘I voted for this, and you haven’t done it,’ and that felt unfair.” And Rush’s seniority and leadership post meant he had “more unique ownership of this issue.”

In a way, the audit was a symbol of the deeper dysfunction of the Legislature: Lawmakers answer to leadership because they so rarely face a challenger at the ballot box. That dysfunction was part of why she decided to challenge Rush in the first place.

“One of the reasons why I ran against an incumbent is because I think it’s important to show that it can be done,” Yu said. “Even if I lost by [the same] margin, it’s still a huge statement … by voters here of a desire for change — but also, it’s the change that they want.”

Yu ran on the proposition that competition moves power “out of the hands of leadership and back into the hands of voters,” as she put it. Winning proved that an entrenched incumbent could be beaten. Governing will test the harder part of her argument: whether a candidate elected by challenging Beacon Hill can enter it without becoming insulated from the voters who sent her there.

Yu offered one measurable promise: “I can always put my votes [out]. I can be transparent about where I stand on things. I can hold town halls in my community and provide feedback about the process. People will know what’s happening because we’re going to tell them what’s happening.”

I need your advice about my advice. In the coming months, the Globe will be launching a new advice column written by… me. Do you have a favorite advice columnist? What kind of questions would you have? I want to hear your ideas for what topics I should tackle. And of course, if you already have questions I could answer, send them to me at marcela.garcia@globe.com.

title: Teacher urges young voters to focus on local, state races
text:
Re “Here’s how to get your son to vote” (Opinion, Aug. 31): John Della Volpe’s excellent op-ed is a subject close to my heart. I have taught government and civics in high school, at a community college, and at a county jail. I urge all of my students to vote, but I emphasize that it is not about the national political circus that they see on TV, where so much is just for show and power. Rather, I advise, pay heed to the local and state elections, where you and your vote can make a real difference.

For my men in jail — and indeed for the jail itself — politics is local, as is government. For example, educational and reentry programs are directly important to them and their situation, as is the district attorney race this fall.

I also tell my students that city councilors and state lawmakers are based nearby and that students can get to know them, work on their campaigns, get involved in other ways, and become an agent rather than an object of politics and government. I tell them that candidates seeking office may be their neighbors and that, for the most part, they are good men and women trying to do their best for the community.

Remember that in 2019 Julia Mejia won her Boston City Council seat by a single vote. Voting and participation do matter at this level.

Randy Foote

Roxbury

title: ‘Not realistic’: Why many musicians feel they can’t make it in Boston
text:
Since moving, he’s earned six Grammy nominations and released six albums. He’s on a cross-country tour and has 120,000 monthly listeners on Spotify.

Lacossade is one of many Boston musicians who felt they had to leave town to seek fame and fortune. Artists say the music industry in Boston has always been tough — and is only getting tougher.

Since the pandemic, the obstacles for local musicians have multiplied. A slew of performance venues have recently closed, including Thunder Road, ONCE Lounge, and Hennessy’s Bar. At a time of tight budgets, government funding for arts programs has also been slashed.

One of the largest cuts in Mayor Michelle Wu’s $4.9 billion spending plan for the next fiscal year was to the Mayor’s Office of Art and Culture fund, which supports programs for local musicians and artists such as Beat the Odds, Boston Music Project, and the Roxbury Concert Series.

In January 2023, Allston’s Sound Museum, a studio and rehearsal space, was bought out to be turned into biotech labs, displacing hundreds of musicians. The organizers of this year’s BAMSFest, an annual arts festival, decided to save money by getting rid of music performances. That closed a huge door for rising local artists, as each year around five music acts were selected to perform.

Lacossade started in local Boys and Girls Clubs’ studios and studied audio engineering at the University of Massachusetts Lowell. He’s lived in New York and Atlanta and said his fan bases are stronger in those cities than in Boston. With the cost of living here continuing to soar even as resources and opportunities erode, it’s increasingly difficult to make it in Boston as a creative.

“As much as I would love to live in Boston full time, it’s just not realistic,” he said.

His first Atlanta apartment, which he shared with two roommates, only cost him $550 a month and allowed him to save money while trying to make it in the industry. (That would be much tougher in Boston; the average rent for a three-bedroom apartment is now nearly $5,800 per month.)

City officials say the issue isn’t a shortage of artists, but a dearth of infrastructure — performing venues, affordable housing, and grants — to support them.

“We are producing talent, but it’s seemingly hard to keep them here,” said Kenny Mascary, a member of the Boston Art Commission. “We have a $15 billion sector here in Boston, but it’s invisible.”

He told the Globe that less than 1 percent of the new construction approved by the Boston Planning & Development Agency in the last decade was for creative or cultural uses. Meanwhile, over a quarter of Boston residents say they earn their main income from creative work, according to a 2026 city-conducted report.

Sophia Perez, a recent Berklee College of Music graduate, faces a similar dilemma to Lacossade’s. She likes Boston, but constantly tosses around the idea of moving to New York or even Spain to break into the music industry. She moved here with dreams of becoming an R&B singer-songwriter, and thought she’d get a jump-start from attending a renowned music school.

“I left with my degree not knowing what to do,” she said. “I studied songwriting, and I don’t think there [were] any opportunities for songwriting or singing.”

It’s been over a year since Perez graduated, and she spends most days balancing work at a coffee shop with performing gigs, booked through an agency, playing with a band at weddings and corporate events. Those jobs help pay her bills, but after factoring in costs for her music — studio time, engineers, and musicians — it’s hard to make ends meet.

To record her upcoming album, Perez has been seeking grants and searching for venues where she can perform her music. She also wants to build a community with rising musicians. She feels stuck.

Several local artists say that since there’s little of the pie to go around for them, Boston has developed what some refer to as a “crabs-in-a-barrel” mindset, where there’s less camaraderie and mutual support and more unhealthy competition.

Lisa Bello, Boston’s 2009 Female Vocalist of the Year, is a member of the Recording Academy, the nonprofit responsible for Grammy selections. She has been working as an artist for over two decades, and over that time, as an artist and mentor for rising acts, she has witnessed Boston’s music industry change.

“We complain because the OGs that have been in [the industry] 15-plus years know that there were pockets of time where we were fully supported in the city,” Bello said. She believes that time is over.

She said a main turning point was Live Nation’s increasing domination of some of Boston’s most prominent performing venues over the past 20 years through ownership or other management agreements.

When major entertainment corporations control key spaces like Brighton Music Hall, MGM at Fenway, and Citizens House of Blues, getting booked is harder for smaller local artists who may not generate the revenue an out-of-towner could.

“If you’re a new artist here, you’ve got to go through a gamut to even get on stage,” Bello said.

The closures of performance venues heighten competition in ways that ripple beyond the community of area musicians.

Clay Ferno, the publicist and event producer for the Cambridge rock club Middle East, said he prioritizes local acts for the club’s five venues in Central Square, but space is still tight.

“When venues close down, it hurts us because it increases the demand on the room,” he said. “We don’t have enough rooms to sustain those bands.”

As city leaders and nonprofits take stock of the challenges, they are hopeful that Boston can still be a home for musicians.

Mascary said the city is partnering with the Boston Housing Authority to develop new affordable housing and rehearsal space for artists by the end of 2026. He also wants to restore funding to the Mayor’s Office of Art and Culture.

The Record Co., a nonprofit that offers low-cost studio and rehearsal spaces in Dorchester and Roxbury, is working against what many artists see as bad vibes in Boston’s industry. When the Sound Museum closed, many of those artists found new homes with The Record Co.

The nonprofit has also received city grants, but after watching such support fluctuate, CEO Bobby Boyd said the organization hopes to be sustainable without government assistance.

A Dorchester native, he thinks Boston can be like New York and Los Angeles as a place to start a successful music career. Boyd said support for local artistry “should be critical infrastructure,” not an afterthought.

“When we exercise our creative genius,” Boyd said, “that’s when we’re at our best.”

title: ‘I wear Boston through and through’: WNBA player Taina Mair enjoys an emotional homecoming
text:
When she finally returned to Boston last week, the city made sure she knew how much she meant.

Roxbury Prep, one of the launching pads that lifted Mair from Dorchester to the WNBA, hosted a homecoming last Friday, filling the gym with everyone from starstruck students to proud former coaches.

Mair’s mother, Mercy Pineda, sister Trayana, and brother Talik shared emotional messages. Her mother and sister held back tears. Her brother couldn’t.

“She always said, ‘Ma, I’m going to go out there and I’m going to do what I need to do,’ ” Pineda said. “And that’s what she’s doing. And I’m proud.”

State Representative Chris Worrell presented Mair with an official citation and award. Then City Councilor Brian Worrell declared Sept. 4 “Taina Mair Day” in the city.

Mair was overwhelmed, but also honored to be an example for kids who were sitting where she once sat.

“I don’t even know the word for it, but I’m so grateful,” she said. “This is something that, as a kid, you dream of. When you go away and you do great things, and you come back home and the city shows you nothing but love.

“It’s a top-tier feeling. I’ve never felt like this in my life and I’ve won plenty of championships, I’ve won a lot of things in my life, but this is something different.”

Emma Simmons, principal of Roxbury Prep’s Dorchester campus, coached Mair in middle school and remembered the packed gyms for middle school games. She also remembered Mair working as relentlessly in the classroom as she did on the court — the combination set her apart at an early age and sets an example to this day.

“If you ask, I’d say, 25 percent of our kids right now, what do you want to be when you grow up, they’d say basketball player, football player,” Simmons said. “And she’s one of the only ones that I was like, ‘Oh yeah, you’re going to get there.’

“I just feel grateful that she’s coming back to Roxbury Prep and she sees us as a home and that my current students can look up to her and see her as a real inspiration.”

From AJ Dybantsa, who took Brockton everywhere he went on his journey to becoming the NBA’s No. 1 pick in June, to Veronica Burton, a star at Newton South who’s now the reigning WNBA Most Improved Player and the engine for the Golden State Valkyries, Mair joins a growing list of players carrying Boston-area basketball onto the sport’s biggest stages.

The closest example Mair had when she was growing up would’ve been Roxbury native Shey Peddy, but Mair was 15 by the time Peddy made her WNBA debut in 2019.

“I feel like I didn’t really have anybody, to be honest,” Mair said. “That’s why me coming back is pivotal for the youth. Just being able to be the person that they can look up to and see they can reach these heights.”

Mair signed a player development contract with the Storm in May that allows her to practice and travel with the team, but limits her to 12 regular-season games. She’s played nine this season, six since late July, putting up her most productive night on Aug. 23 in a loss to the Dallas Wings (6 points in 13 minutes).

With the WNBA season coming to a close at the end of the month, Mair said she already has plans to sharpen her game in the offseason in Poland.

“There’s really levels, and you can see it,” she said. “When you get to the pros, there’s a bigger gap because these girls have been playing for 20-plus years and they know their role, they know what they have to do.

“But I think just coming in, figuring out how to adjust my play style, just being a little more physical, understanding that when you get a shot it needs to be knocked down. You’ve just got to be sharper.”

But on a day dedicated to her, Mair was proud to be an example of what’s possible.

“I wear Boston through and through,” Mair said. “Everywhere I go, I’m like, ‘I’m from Boston.’ You can’t tell me nothing. This is the city where I came from, I grew up here, born and raised.

“So to be able to have that is a special gift for what I’ve done for my city. Just being a role model — or trying to be one — I think having that kind of solidifies me as who I am as a person and who I’m trying to be.”

Outlook: After closing out last season with three consecutive wins, Hamilton-Wenham is looking to take another step forward under second-year coach Mike Flynn, a retired NFL lineman and former Super Bowl champion for the Baltimore Ravens. Senior Anthony Folger is back at quarterback, leading the offense next to classmate Andrew Baum, the team’s bruising 6-foot, 195-pound starting tailback. Junior Joe Flynn (6-1, 185) will be a big target in the passing game and provide a steady presence in the secondary, while seniors Jake Collins (6-2, 230) and Harrison Esker (6-0, 230) supply veteran leadership to the line. After introducing a spread offense last preseason, Flynn said the Generals have experienced a much smoother start at this year’s camp. “We already have everything in that we’ve done in the past,” Flynn said. “The biggest thing is having our whole (offensive) system in and knowing what we’re trying to do.”

Season opener: Thursday, Sept. 10, 6 p.m., vs. Brighton

League: Boston City

Coach: Rocco Zizza (19th season). Career: 113-75.

Last year’s record: 8-3

Strengths: Veteran offensive line

Concerns: Inexperience at quarterback

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: All-Scholastic QB Jack Shapiro, the reigning Boston City League Player of the Year, has graduated. But the Dragons hope increased numbers and a seasoned offensive line can pave the way in defending their BCL title. Junior tailback Jayden Ramirez returns behind a veteran O-line that includes seniors Tyrell Brown (6 feet, 260 pounds), Loc Hoang (6-1, 260) and Michael Macneil (6-0, 200). “We bring back four starters on the line, so that will be our strength this year,” longtime coach Rocco Zizza said. “Our line will be solid with the most experience.” With three sophomores vying to be the starting QB, Latin Academy will be inexperienced behind center, though senior Mizzyah Nevarez (WR/DB) will provide a playmaker outside in the passing game. The Dragons will play their home games at Clifford Field in Roxbury while White Stadium undergoes renovations.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 6 p.m., vs. Weston

League: Commonwealth

Coach: Zack Swale (2nd season). Career: Career 1-10.

Last year’s record: 1-10

Strengths: Veteran offensive line

Concerns: First-year QB learning new system

Offense: Spread

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Second-year coach Zack Swale is counting on senior Janzel Trinidad, who racked up 1,000-plus all-purpose yards, including 900 on the ground, to be a force. Trinidad will run behind a veteran line that includes seniors Kaidyn Rivera (6 feet, 1 inch, 205 pounds) and Matt Poirier (6-1, 190), junior Declan McComas (6-7, 300) and sophomore Jayden Rivera (5-6, 280). Seniors Jimmy McGonigle, Jayvin Lao (LB) and Teddy Chege (WR/LB) will provide veteran leadership in the middle of the defense, and senior Maric Nthala (6 interceptions last season) is a star in the secondary. Senior Robby Thibeault, a transfer from St. Thomas Acquinas, will start at quarterback and free safety. “We knew last year was probably going to be a rebuild, but this year we have 14 or 15 seniors, which is going to be huge for our leadership and accountability,” Swale said.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 7 p.m., vs. Chelsea

League: Cape Ann

Coach: Nick Brougton (1st season). Career: 0-0.

Last year’s record: 7-4

Strengths: Experience at skilled positions.

Concerns: New faces on O-line.

Offense: Spread

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Nick Broughton, a 10-year assistant at Marblehead who is a math teacher at Beverly, is a head coach for the first time, replacing five-year coach Joe Grimes. Although Broughton must replace All-Scholastic quarterback Zach Hurd, the Hornets return senior Noah Cohen (WR/DB) from last year’s playoff team. Junior Nick Glass starts behind center, and Broughton expects junior Anton Gilson (WR/DB) to make an impact in the coach’s new spread offense. Junior Blake Leschinsky (6-1, 235) will lead an O-line full of fresh faces. “It’s been really awesome to see how smart they are and how much we’ve been able to get in so quickly,” said Broughton. “We are changing to the spread – the kids are picking it up pretty quickly, and when they make a mistake they learn fast.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 6:30 p.m., at Newburyport

League: South Shore

Coach: Matt Triveri (22nd season). Career: 175-59.

Last year’s record: 7-3

Strengths: Big, experienced linemen

Concerns: New backfield, team depth

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: The Falcons must replace their entire backfield, including 1,500-yard rusher Daniel Alade. But coach Matt Triveri is optimistic in the players that have returned. “There’s talent here,” he said. “We’ll be able to match up athletically with anyone we play. We have size up front, it’s just going to come down to how many mistakes we make.” Mashpee will rely on seniors CJ Jennings (6 feet, 1 inch, 320 pounds), Coti Wieden (6-0, 240) and Keneil Mattis (6-2, 260) to impact both lines of scrimmage, in particular in front of first-year junior QB Anthony Foss. “He’s a dual threat with an enormous arm,” said Triveri. Foss inherits massive targets out wide in seniors Aarian Brown (6-4, 185) and Jacoby Spinola (6-1, 175). Sophomore Benton Davies and senior Jayden Williams line up in the backfield with senior fullback Aiden Amaral.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 6 p.m., at Martha’s Vineyard

League: Boston City

Coach: Kevin Gadson (19th season). Career: 102-79.

Last year’s record: 1-9

Strengths: Cohesion at quarterback, receiver.

Concerns: New offensive line.

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Coach Kevin Gadson hopes his Tigers can rebuild on the fly after graduating the majority of last year’s starters on both sides of the ball. Senior Jackson Farrington returns at quarterback and punter with a familiar target in senior Gementri Williams (WR/TE/LB). But Gadson said the rest of the lineup will feature new starters. “We’re really rebuilding,” Gadson said. “We lost a lot of seniors, and those are the only two back.” Gadson said he is encouraged by the youth movement and the program’s numbers (40-45 have signed up), but the Tigers will need to answer plenty of question marks to return to their 2023 form when they last captured the Boston City League title. “We’re teaching and building the young players’ confidence, consistency and discipline,” he said. “That will lead to personal and team success on the field and in life.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 18, 4 p.m., vs. Boston Latin

League: South Shore

Coach: Nick Liquori (10th season). Career: 61-35.

Last year’s record: 5-6

Strengths: Offensive line and rushing attack

Concerns: Limited experience at key positions.

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: After back-to-back seasons without recording a South Shore League victory, coach Nick Liquori hopes this is the year the Bulldogs break through. “We have a lot of guys back,” Liquori said. “It’s a little more veteran than it has been the past couple years.(Winning a league game) has been our big focus this preseason to turn that around.” Rockland returns one of the most dynamic tailbacks in Eastern Mass., senior Marvelous Pleasant, who gave opponents fits throughout the season -- including a six-touchdown performance in a 58-56 loss to East Bridgewater. Seniors Jack Phillips (5 feet, 11 inches, 275 pounds), Jack Reardon (6-2, 190) and Jake Levy (6-3, 225) anchor the O-line alongside junior Cam Campanile (5-8, 195) in front of junior Dustin Ayer, who replaces graduate Hayden Hatch at QB. Junior receiver Patrick McDonagh returns after a breakout sophomore campaign alongside classmate Justin Kiser.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 7 p.m., vs. Dennis-Yarmouth

League: South Coast

Coach: Brendan Costa (1st season). Career: 0-0.

Last year’s record: 4-7

Strengths: Speed and athleticism

Concerns: Learning a new offense

Offense: Read option

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: For the second time in consecutive years, the Warriors will start a season with a first-year head coach; but again, it is a person that they are familiar with. The team’s offensive coordinator the past three seasons, Brendan Costa steps in for Matt Brown, a longtime Seekonk assistant who will return to that role this fall. The Warriors graduated impact players at key positions, but Costa loves the talent he has inherited. “I think this could be the most athletic team I’ve seen us have since I’ve been here,” he said. “We have a lot of athletes in different places, so our job is to get the ball to them in space.” Seniors Hunter George (6 feet, 2 inches, 210 pounds) and Marcus Amaral and junior Gabe Bonafiglia will be the featured backs in Costa’s new option offense. Senior JP Gibson (6-2, 255) anchors the line, with junior Lucas Escaler making his starting debut at QB.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 6:30 p.m., vs. Old Colony

League: Mayflower

Coach: Matt Doyle (8th season). Career: 41-35.

Last year’s record: 7-6

Strengths: Veteran linebackers, running back

Concerns: Coming together as a team

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Coach Matt Doyle hopes the Vikings can rebuild on the fly after advancing to the MVADA Small final last year, a 30-24 loss to Cape Cod Tech. Junior Dillon O’Brien, a three-year starter, returns at tailback alongside senior Jayden Fraser. Seniors Will Traynor and Brendan Fennessy and junior Jason Cutter will be favorite targets in the passing game. Junior James Aikey will make varsity debut at QB behind an offensive line that returns junior Bobby Medico (5 feet 8 inches, 200 pounds) and seniors Aiden Jones (5-8, 190) and Owen Collins (5-10, 190). Defensively, Jones and fellow senior inside linebacker Joe Humphries, moving from the outside, are the anchors. “There’s a lot of returning guys, but we also lost a lot of guys,” Doyle said. “As hard as they’ve worked, you really see if they can play as a unit once you face an opponent.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 7 p.m., at Nashoba Valley Tech

League: South Coast

Coach: Justin Kogler (8th season). Career: 108-42 overall (54-18 at West Bridgewater).

Last year’s record: 9-2

Strengths: Speed and athleticism

Concerns: Players taking on larger roles

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Replacing 20 graduates is never easy, but West Bridgewater coach Justin Kogler recognizes the cupboard is not bare. The Wildcats return an influx of veterans, spearheaded by senior linebacker Gage Turner (6 feet, 225 pounds), who racked up 100 tackles last fall. Seniors Jonathan Chervil (CB), Kevin Kearton (WR) and Jacob Bettencourt (WR/FS) all return with big-game experience at the skill positions, while seniors Naithan Gomez (6-0, 260), Cole Seckinger (5-10, 210) and Calvin Pike (6-0, 190) and Ben Kneeland (5-10, 210) return on the line. Turner is expected to receive carries in the backfield, but Kogler said he’ll also count on juniors Jake Callahan and Salake Woodbury to help fill the void left by the graduating of star back Ty Holmes. Senior captain Nick Navin, a starter at linebacker the past two years, replaces grad Ryan Nunes at QB. “We’re not big, but I think overall our speed and athleticism should be pretty good,” Kogler said.

text:
