Here are the 38 Eastern Mass. players you need to see this season

Sign up for Varsity News, our free weekly newsletter

League: Mayflower

Coach: Kazeem Adediran (5th season). Career: 15-24.

Last year’s record: 4-6

Strengths: Effort, coachability

Concerns: Depth

Offense: Pro set

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: In his fifth season, Kazeem Adediran is not letting numbers shake his confidence in his team. Losing players to neighboring schools has been a consistent problem. But this season, Atlantis Charter has a reinvigorated sense of determination, leaning on the Patriots motto: “we all we got, we all we need.” With a strong arm, and elusive running ability, junior quarterback Kaleb Pacheco will pilot the offense. Serun Pitt, a versatile junior, is top target as a back and receiver. Though depth issues remain persistent, Adediran knows his team has the talent to get to where they want to be. “I have high, high hopes,” he said. “I’m pushing championship-level play every single game and making sure that this community is proud of all the hard work they’re putting in on a daily basis.”

Season opener: Saturday, Sept. 12, 12 p.m., at Hope (R.I.)

League: CMAC

Coach: James Caprarella (3rd season). Career: 10-10.

Last year’s record: 6-5

Strengths: Defensive skill positions

Concerns: Young offensive and defensive lines

Offense: Spread

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: In his second season, James Caprarella guided BMV to the program’s second league title. This season, however, the Chargers are on their own, no longer hosting a co-op with Hopedale. Senior captains Nate Oliveira and Karson Cournoyer spearhead a defensive unit looking to establish an identity, generate turnovers, and earn second-chance opportunities. “They’re the cornerstone of our defense,” said Caprarella. “They really empower the rest of the team to follow their lead.”

Season opener: Saturday, Sept. 12, 12 p.m., vs. Millis

League: South Coast

Coach: Anthony Fulmine (1st season). Career: 0-0.

Last year’s record: 8-3

Strengths: Skill positions, defensive edge

Concerns: Lack of depth

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: In his first season, Anthony Fulmine is determined to build on the success of a squad that advanced to the Round of 8 in the playoffs. “My expectation is that we’re going to finish the season better than where we are right now and build it from there,” he said. The Canalmen will lean heavily on defensive edge Malachi Coelho, a 6-foot-4-inch, 230 pound senior. Malachi’s brother, Osiris, a junior, will run the offense. Despite a small roster and the depth concerns that come alongside it, Fulmine is confident that his players have the talent needed to continue their success. “It’s a war of attrition.”

Season opener: Saturday, Sept. 12, 12 p.m., at Burncoat

League: Boston City

Coach: Randolph Abraham (15th season). Career: 75-65.

Last year’s record: 3-6

Strengths: Sizeable offensive line, strong defense

Concerns: A 20-player roster, new QB

Offense: Spread

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: A fixture with the Brighton football program since 2004, 15-year coach Randolph Abraham is emphasizing quality over quantity. “I expect us to be competitive,” he said. “We have a group of tough young men who have been coming out to work every day and leaving it out on the field.” Fielding a roster of just 20 players, Abraham believes he still has the talent on the field to make a run, especially on the defensive side. Senior outside linebacker Gavin Dodson returns after an injury-riddled season to lead a gritty defensive front. Junior Mason Soohoo is making the transition from running back to quarterback. Desipte a struggle to recruit new players to the program, Abraham has faith that hard work will pay off with a good season.

Season opener: Thursday, Sept. 10, 6 p.m., at Hamilton-Wenham

League: Mayflower

Coach: Calvin Castillias (4th season). Career: 15-18.

Last year’s record: 9-4

Strengths: Leadership, experienced team, good chemistry

Concerns: Offensive line

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: Last year, Cape Cod Tech defied the odds. After a 1-4 start, the Crusaders ran the table with seven straight wins, the culmination a 30-24 win over South Shore Voc-Tech for the MVADA Small title. This season, with a roster stocked with returnees, the goal is bigger. “The goal is to win the big one: the state championship,” said coach Calvin Castillias. Senior quarterback Daniel Handville directs the attack complemented by a talented back, senior Thomas Allen, and junior receiver Jordan Wilson, who according to coach Castillias “can go up and get it with the best of them.” Tech was a surprise a year ago. Can the Crusader make another run?

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 6:30 p.m., vs. Monomoy/JP II

League: Catholic Central

Coach: Derrick Beasley (9th season). Career: 28-41.

Last year’s record: 5-4

Strengths: Depth, offensive and defensive lines

Concerns: Linebacker depth

Offense: Spread

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Depth was a concern last season at Cathedral team. This season it is an advantage, with the Panthers hosting Roxbury Prep and Neighborhood Charter in a co-op. With 50-plus players, coach Derrick Beasley said his team has the numbers to do damage in the Catholic Central league. “If we can compete and maintain a high competition level, we can cement ourselves back in the league again,” he said. Leading the way is 6-foot-2-inch junior quarterback Keyon Lungelow-Hilaire. Junior receiver Josiah Anthony Reid has the ability to make plays downfield.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 6 p.m., vs. Triton/Ipswich

League: Boston City

Coach: Ryan Conway (11th season). Career: 37-59.

Last year’s record: 4-5

Strengths: Speed and depth at running back

Concerns: First-year quarterback, inexperience

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: In his 11th season, coach Ryan Conway is confident that his Blue & Blue will pack a punch in the backfield. Seniors Manuel Carrion and Freddy Anderson, along with junior Savion Bowden combine speed with high physicality. With a first-year quarterback following the graduation of Lovenson Pierre, the trio will see a lot of reps, with the ability to make a difference. “I want to minimize turnovers and make sure we’re playing smart, physical football,” said Conway. “I see that they can be a really, really good team.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 6 p.m., vs. Randolph

League: Mayflower

Coach: Fran Cass (3rd season). Career: 49-76 (including 2018-23 at Wareham).

Last year’s record: 0-5

Strengths: Experienced coaching staff

Concerns: Small roster

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Seeking its first win since 2023, the Holbrook/Avon co-op again will compete with low numbers. But Fran Cass’s club did not make strides offensively a year ago, increasing their output by 35 points. He and his staff will continue to recruit students, stirring up interest in the program.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 18, 6 p.m., vs. Cardinal Spellman

League: South Shore

Coach: Michael O’Donnell (10th season). Career: 54-45.

Last year’s record: 4-7

Strengths: Athleticism, experienced offense

Concerns: Depth

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: With a wealth of senior leadership, the Pirates after determined to make a run at one of the top 16 seeds in Division 8, and a playoff spot. Senior quarterback Tegan Bellew will have fellow seniors Landon Manfredi and Tristan Lofgren lining up at receiver. Senior Nate O’Hare and sophomore PJ Riviecchio return in the backfield. With many of the offensive pieces returning, the experience and chemistry built last season will hopefully fuel a turnaround.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 6 p.m., at TechBoston

League: CMAC

Coach: Michael Luks (2nd season). Career: 7-5.

Last year’s record: 7-5

Strengths: Skill players, rushing attack

Concerns: Youth, inexperience, quarterback

Offense: Spread

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: In his first season, Michael Luks guided the Framingham-based Broncos to their first winning season in at least two decades. But this year he wants to keep building where he left off. “We started a winning culture last year, you just want to keep raising that bar each time,” he said. The attack will be led by junior back James Kilgallen, who racked up 1,000-plus yards rushing in a breakout season. Fellow junior Hunter Duran, who also starts at corner, will also see reps at wide receiver to give sophomore quarterback Kelton Fertel, a first-year starter, another weapon. Building off last season with a younger team, Luks has just one simple goal in mind: “win more games.”

Season opener: Saturday, Sept. 12, 12 p.m., vs. Murdock

League: Commonwealth

Coach: Marcus Taylor (1st season). Career: 0-0.

Last year’s record: 5-6

Strengths: Defense, depth

Concerns: New coach, high expectations

Offense: Spread

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: With Jim Rabbitt departing after a storied 10-year run for Wakefield, Marcus Taylor has high expectations for his first season as head coach: a trip to Gillette Stadium. “They’ve been a very successful program in the past, we just need to get over that hump now,” said Taylor, a 2018 Lynn Tech grad who wants to foster a defensive identity of stopping the run. He believes KIPP has the foundation pieces on defense, led by 240-pound senior defensive lineman Carlos Sanchez and the Rosa brothers, juniors Joshua and Noah Rosa. “In order to win you have to stop the run,” said Taylor, who previously served as an assistant at Lynn Tech and Bishop Fenwick. On offense, KIPP will be led by quarterback Elai Machado, a 6-foot-3-inch, 200-pound senior who already has established chemistry with his top receivers, senior Aavian Pena and junior Ryan Reynoso.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 6:30 p.m., at Salem

League: Commonwealth

Coach: James Runner (17th season). Career: 65-75.

Last year’s record: 4-4

Strengths: Returning skill positions

Concerns: Inexperienced defensive line

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Once again, the Tigers are determined to make a playoff run. “We just like to compete and play very well,” said coach James Runner. To reach the postseason, Tech will lean on the leadership of their fourth-year stalwarts, in particular junior quarterback Jadiel Ortega, a gold medalist with the 15U US boys’ flag football national team. The junior twins Anthony and Tyler Brown, both track standouts, will be major playmakers. With Anthony at slot receiver and Tyler at nickelback/safety,t their names will be prominent. “If we’re one of the top teams in the division, everyone should be nervous to play us,” said Runner.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 6 p.m., at Malden

League: Tri-Valley

Coach: Don Shumaker (2nd season). Career: 3-7.

Last year’s record: 3-7

Strengths: Returning letter winners, plus players from Norfolk Aggie.

Concerns: Undersized offensive line

Offense: Spread

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: Don Shumaker expects the Mohawks to qualify for the playoffs, a belief enhanced with a new co-op agreement with nearby Norfolk Agricultural (Walpole). One addition from Aggie: Jason Barry, a 6-foot-2-inch, 300-pound two-way tackle who has the speed to play linebacker. Barry will be a pivotal piece protecting four-year starting quarterback senior Owen Caulfield. Shumaker believes the newly established co-op could be a game-changer for his squad. “They really matured over the offseason,” he said. “The intensity, the focus, and the maturity is so much better than last year. That could be because of the numbers.”

Season opener: Saturday, Sept. 12, 12 p.m., at Blackstone-Millville

League: Commonwealth

Coach: Rob Flynn (3rd season). Career: 9-10.

Last year’s record: 6-5

Strengths: Experience, leadership

Concerns: Offensive line depth

Offense: Spread

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Buoyed by a winning season, and stability, the Mustangs are rejoining the Commonwealth Athletic Conference after a four-year absence. “We know we’re going to need some of our younger guys to step up,” said coach Rob Flynn. “We want to compete in our league, make it competitive, and get a win on Thanksgiving.” Though they’ll need help from the underclassmen, Flynn will lean on his senior captains. Senior QB Gus Stillman is back under center, and classmate James Leonard to surpass 1,000 total yards after falling 4 yards short last season. Senior tackle Jackson Whight will protect Stillman’s blindside.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 6:30 p.m., at Southbridge

League: Commonwealth

Coach: Danny Kelly (5th season). Career: 34-13.

Last year’s record: 8-3

Strengths: Experienced skill positions, senior quarterback and running back

Concerns: Young offensive line

Offense: Double wing

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: The Vikings, the top seed, were derailed by Randolph, the eventual champion, in the Division 8 semifinals. Now fifth-year coach Danny Kelly and Nashoba Tech feel they have something to prove. “They’re not satisfied with being in the top four,” said Kelly. “It’s a great accomplishment but they understand we have to work a lot harder to get past it.” The Vikings return senior QB Nick Sloboda and running back Jayden Garshong performing double-duty on defense in the secondary. “They’ve been two great three-year starters for us,” said coach Kelly. “They really anchor our offense and defense.” Sloboda and Garshong will be sharing running responsibilities help fill the void left by the transfer of Zack Deschenes (Suffield Academy). But they will be lining up behind a young offensive front, led by 6-foot-4, 290-pound Deacon Carson.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 7 p.m., vs. South Shore Voc-Tech

League: Mayflower

Coach: Brandon Mendez (12th season). Career: 72-45.

Last year’s record: 4-7

Strengths: Skill positions

Concerns: Offensive and defensive line depth

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: The 4-7 finish last fall was a disappointment. But coach Brandon Mendez expects that another season of development for his underclassmen skill players to be a game-changer. The centerpiece will be junior back Will Ciavarro in a run-heavy dual wing scheme. “I expect him to shoulder a lot of the load,” said Mendez, who will also experiment with the spread, noting that he has quarterbacks who can “sling it.” That includes the healthy return of senior quarterback Cole Correia. “For us it’s about improving week in and week out,” he said. “We always want to play with a lot of energy, enthusiasm, and physicality.”

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 6:30 p.m., at Seekonk

League: South Shore

Coach: Jonathan Marshall (7th season). Career: 38-22.

Last year’s record: 12-0

Strengths: Size, championship experience

Concerns: Graduation departures, youth at skill positions

Offense: Double wing

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: Off an undefeated season, and the program’s second Division 8 Super Bowl title, coach Jonathan Marshall emphasized that he wants his players to “elevate.” Seniors, particularly All-Scholastic Mekhi White, keyed last year’s run to Gillette. Marshall expects this year’s class to do the same. That starts with Santos Santiago, who is making the shift from defense to quarterback. He’ll be lining up behind a massive line, led by 260-pound guard Aidan Davis, a senior captain, along with fellow guard and captain Diego Perez. Brandon Belony, a 6-foot-3-inch, 300-pound tackle, mans the left side. Junior tight end Sebastian Vasquez (6-2, 260) also helps with protection. “If I was a young skill player on this team, I’d be excited to play behind this line,” said Marshall.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 6 p.m., at English High

League: Boston City

Coach: Jason Seapker (2nd season). Career: 2-7.

Last year’s record: 2-7

Strengths: Senior skill players

Concerns: Depth, with the graduation of 20 players

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Artificial turf

Outlook: To improve on last year’s win total, coach Jason Seapker is preaching consistency. “If we can get consistent with what we do, then I think we’ll be OK,” he said. TechBoston graduated 20 players, but retains an experienced group of seniors on offense. Those leaders, headlined by wide receiver Tray French, a member of the 2024 Boston City team, as well as backs Ezra Boyd-Wallace and Jaeden Duperval, will be pivotal. Their contributions will have a major impact if TechBoston can take a run at a city title.

Season opener: Friday, Sept. 11, 6 p.m., vs. Hull

League: Mayflower

Coach: Joe Ellia (1st season). Career: 4-5.

Last year’s record: 4-7

Strengths: Run game, team chemistry, depth

Concerns: Secondary

Offense: Wishbone

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: With a solid line up front and a strong contingent of backs, first-year coach Joe Ellia and the Rams have high expectations. “These guys have great chemistry,” said Ellia, a 2004 grad who was named the interim coach in Week 3 last year. ”They have what it takes to be special. They have what it takes to go to the Voke playoffs down the road, to win the Mayflower [Athletic Conference], to win on Thanksgiving Day. They love playing football together.” Senior right guard Jared Chadwick (6 feet, 4 inches, 300 pounds), junior left guard David Duca (6-1, 260), and senior captain and tight end Tyson Munk (6-1, 225) will be anchors on both lines of scrimmage. Senior fullback Austyn Tucker (6-4, 200) returns and James Perry is a first-year starter at quarterback. Eight-plus players attended tryouts, which bodes well for the future.

Season opener: Saturday, Sept. 12, 11 a.m., vs. Sandwich

League: Mayflower

Coach: Cy Bariteau (3rd season). Career: 9-13.

Last year’s record: 6-5

Strengths: Returning players, line, depth

Concerns: Injuries, young secondary and receivers

Offense: Multiple

Playing surface: Grass

Outlook: The foundation for success is on the line. Senior Donovan Leonardi (6-3, 330), a three-year starter, is at right guard, joined by senior left tackle Cullen Bird (6-0, 220), junior center Danny Gavin (5-11, 210), and senior right tackle Jevani Lopes (6-2, 230). His brother, Jesiah Lopes (6-3, 223), a freshman, is the newest addition at left guard. Sidelined with a broken ankle last season, senior back Ty-Rell Pires (5-9, 220) spent the offseason bulking up. Three-year starter Amare Rose (6-3, 180) returns at quarterback and will be among the driving forces to guide a skilled, but young group of receivers. “What we preach is our goal is to go 1-0 every week,” said coach Cy Bariteau. “It might sound cliche, but right now the team set out and they’re buying into it.” It may be a youth movement, but Bariteau says the group is physical and eager to learn.

title: How does an MBTA Green Line operator make it on $73,000 a year?
text:
“Everybody always says, ‘Hey, the T is a good job. They have good benefits, pension, all that,’ ” he said.

After a training class to learn the ins and outs of operating the light rail, Conveniencia took to the tracks. “It’s muscle memory now,” he said.

Conveniencia bounces between the line’s branches on an often-changing schedule, which is how he likes it. “You’re always seeing something different,” he said, including the cast of characters that boards his trollies. He strives to be the friendly face of an often-unfriendly transit system, taking pride in helping riders navigate diversions, giving tourists directions, and holding the doors for people he sees running to catch the train.

“I know I’m helping everybody get to where they need to go,” he said.

The earnings: Last year, Conveniencia earned about $73,000. Without a college degree or a professional passion, “I didn’t think I would be making this much,” he said. “I’m grateful to be in the position that I’m in.”

And he will soon get a raise. At the end of the month, he said, his roughly $36 hourly wage will grow to about $41, a pay bump built into the MBTA’s union contract. Under the current bargaining agreement, he can expect to make about $49 an hour after he’s been with the T five years.

But those numbers are just on paper. Conveniencia’s biweekly paychecks currently come out to around $1,700 to $1,800, depending on overtime, he said. Deductions for health insurance (about $230), union dues (about $50), and the MBTA retirement fund (about $300) each cut into his take-home pay.

The steady pay, plus the promise of a pension, means Conveniencia is inclined to stay with the MBTA for the long haul. Plus, he knows the job has stability in a topsy-turvy labor market.

When it comes to the T, “I don’t think AI is going to take over,” he said.

The expenses: Conveniencia pays $1,500 a month in rent for an income-restricted studio apartment in Mission Hill, which he found through Metrolist, a city database. It’s a big discount, with the normal rent for such a unit topping $3,000, he said. Utilities, meanwhile, are all on him. He tries to budget at least $300 a month for gas, electricity, Internet, and water.

As for transportation, he sticks to riding the T — his badge gets him free rides — and the occasional Bluebike. Until late last year, he drove a Honda Civic, which cost $800 a month between the car payment and insurance, he said. But in November, he got into an accident, and decided to give it up.

About once a month, Conveniencia goes to Stop & Shop or Price Rite for a big grocery trip, and his last one cost about $200, he said. On workdays, he tends to eat fruit or toast for breakfast, bring leftovers or fruit to work to avoid buying lunch, and turn to simple dinner recipes.

“My meals will pretty much always consist of rice, some type of meat, and beans,” he said.

One more regular expense? “I work in the public, and I just want to make sure I look my best at all times,” he said, so he spends $35 on a weekly barbershop visit.

The debt: While Conveniencia now tries to keep his regular expenses to a minimum, he wasn’t always so prudent.

After getting his first credit card at 19, he began swiping with abandon, recalling dropping “like, $1,000″ on hauls of trendy clothing, or high-end sneakers, his kryptonite. “When I do shop, I kind of go crazy,” he said.

Eventually, he said, he racked up close to $10,000 in credit card debt. “The bulk of it was really just pointless purchases,” he said, plus the ensuing interest and late fees. When his cards maxed out, he turned to the “buy now, pay later” service Klarna, which breaks up purchases into smaller installments. Earlier this year, for instance, he paid for an $860 laptop in four $215 chunks.

“Everything’s at your hands,” he said. “It’s hard to break out of the habit.”

But, finally, he did, once he realized he wanted to buy a house one day, and with the milestone of his 25th birthday approaching.

He made it his mission to free himself of credit card debt by his March birthday, promising himself a trip to the Dominican Republic, where his family is from, if he could do it. Once he no longer had his car to pay for, he began funneling around $1,500 a month to dig himself out of the financial hole, he said.

“I had to cut down on everything,” he said — and he means everything. “I was dating at the time, and basically, I just had to say, ‘I can’t afford to be in a relationship right now,’ ” he said.

In the end, he pulled it off, and booked the Caribbean getaway — on a debit card.

Now that Conveniencia is back in the black, “I feel like a weight’s been lifted off my shoulders,” he said. But the experience left its mark. He limits using credit cards and removed them from his phone’s Apple Pay — while still trying to improve his credit score — and resists Klarna.

“I kind of scared myself,” he said. “I’m still kind of recovering from that.”

The outlook: For Conveniencia, that recovery means unlearning the bad habits that he observed growing up, where “everybody around me maybe drives a really nice car, but might not have enough money to afford the really nice car,” he said.

Don’t get him wrong — he still splurges occasionally, such as on a $220 pair of Nike Jordan shoes or, yes, on a date, where he always expects to spend at least $100. But these days, he tries to follow a simple maxim: “If you don’t have the money to do what you’re trying to do, just don’t do it,” he said.

Beyond that, he’s taking steps to improve his financial literacy, such as reading up on starting a Roth IRA account.

“I was living reactively,” he said. “Now I’m trying to live proactive, so I don’t have to react to my bad decisions.”

The goal: Like so many Boston residents, “my goal is to buy a home,” Conveniencia said. No one in his family owns their home here, he said, and he wants the security of knowing he won’t “get priced out of my city.”

He took one of Boston’s homebuyer classes, which qualifies him for financial assistance programs. “After a year of saving, I want to see how much I’ve saved and see where I can go from there,” he said.

He currently has about $2,500 in his savings account, he said, and he is currently trying to set aside $1,000 a month — money that once went toward paying off debt — with the hope of accumulating at least $12,000 by next September. “Is that possible? I’m not sure,” he said.

It’s something he feels good about working toward. The idea of taking out a mortgage? Not so much.

“I worked so hard this year to get rid of my debt, to now get into a debt of 30 years,” he said. “Granted, at the end of those 30 years, I’ll have something, but I’m like, ‘Man, does it ever end?’ ”

title: Boston and the MBTA redesigned Blue Hill Avenue, again. Opponents warn the changes are ‘not a done deal.’
text:
A vocal movement of opponents warned Thursday: “This is not a done deal.”

Roughly three dozen people called for the elimination of the proposed center-running bus lane in a protest march down Blue Hill Avenue before the meeting. Business owners at the meeting raised concerns that changes to the street, and parking, will spell doom for their storefronts. And dozens of public commenters accused public officials of, once again, not listening to the people of Black Boston, arguing that changes to the avenue will be the harbinger of gentrification.

When Bishop John Borders III asked opponents of the project to stand, half the room rose.

“They have a meeting, but they don’t really listen to us,” said Cynthia Grant Carter, 54. “What’s wrong with what we got?”

The $163 million trove of public money set aside for Blue Hill Avenue would not only go toward adding the bus lane, but also narrowing pedestrian crossings, planting 200 trees, and replacing street lighting — beautification and safety improvements many agree are sorely needed.

The latest proposal preserves roughly 11 of the existing 14 miles of car-travel lanes from Grove Hall through Mattapan Square and increases the total number of parking spots to 717 from 675. It separates some parts of the thoroughfare for car travel during rush hour and parking in off-peak periods.

In the meeting, Wu cited conversations with more than 3,000 people, saying they informed how City Hall and the T created the latest redesign, block by block.

“This is part of a big-picture plan to put dollars where they need to be to ensure we have equity throughout the city and opportunity in every neighborhood,” she said.

In the meeting, just five residents spoke to say they back the plan; two others raised concerns about the pullback of some proposed bike lanes in the latest design.

Carmen Blyden, director of community organizing at Bikes Not Bombs, said she “supports the project” but asked for additional bike parking on the avenue. Tony Baez, a cycling advocate, made the final remarks before public comment was cut off nearly an hour after the meeting’s scheduled 8 p.m. end time.

“I support this project today, just like I did a year ago,” he said. “We are asking drivers to give up 20 seconds, so that bus riders can get 15 minutes.”

But few meeting attendees were otherwise on board.

City councilors Brian Worrell and Miniard Culpepper called for “real alternatives” to the plan, including a feasibility study on bringing rail back to the corridor. The two councilors have proposed extending the Orange Line subway beneath the street, though Wu’s office has warned it “would take many years ... and likely well over a billion dollars in federal investment.”

There’s been long-standing frustration among residents about decades of neglect on the avenue dating to the 1950s, when the streetcar trolley along it was eliminated.

The MBTA previously committed to looking into a rail expansion, and Eng — serving as both the leader of the T and the state’s interim secretary of transportation — said on Thursday that the bus lane “does not preclude future discussions of rail.”

Public officials said Thursday the changes announced last week would immediately make the corridor safer. Blue Hill Avenue is frequently congested and accident-prone, with a crash requiring emergency medical services every three days on average, according to city data.

Justin Rodriguez, a 33-year-old Dorchester resident, said the center-running bus lane would be an “interference” to his commute as a regular bus rider. And frankly, he said he isn’t inclined to trust public officials, even when it comes to repaving sidewalks.

“If the idea didn’t come from people who are here every day, where did it come from?” Rodriguez asked. “These projects happen. We are never asked.”

Muhammed Uddin, owner of American Food Mart on Blue Hill Avenue, said the congestion and parking impacts he believes the center-running bus lane would hurt his business, which opened in 2024.

“It’s going to slow down everything,” Uddin said. “You want the street widely open.”

Dana Dowell, a lifelong Mattapan resident, said she’s “for beautifying our neighborhood and better infrastructure.” But not like this.

“This decision is being forced down our throat,” she said.

Still, some residents hope City Hall backtracks entirely and leaves their neighborhood untouched.

Gwendolyn McLaurin lives around the corner from Blue Hill Avenue and regularly takes the 28 and 31 bus. She believes the city and state should simply back off. No bus lane, no new rail line, no touching the sidewalks.

“There’s already not enough room for everybody. It’s not fair,” she said. “It should stay the way it is.”

Two open houses where public officials plan to share the block-by-block redesign will take place on Monday and Sept. 22 in Dorchester and Mattapan respectively. A final town hall is planned for Sept. 30, which Wu also plans to attend.

Correction: A previous version of this story misidentified Tony Baez’s job. The Globe regrets the error.

title: 15-year-old Latinas are including their love of soccer and dance in quinceañeras
text:
As I approached my own 15th birthday more than a decade ago, I thought having a quinceañera meant following all its traditions or not having one at all. If only I could’ve seen my niece’s celebration — eight years later — which began with her in a lilac gown and soccer cleats, and ended with her and her cousins playing soccer behind the outdoor dance floor.

The quinceañera’s roots trace back centuries to the Indigenous civilizations of the Maya and Aztec people; the ceremony honored a young woman reaching maturity. In the 1500s, Spanish missionaries and colonizers settled in the Americas and adapted the ceremony to reflect Roman Catholic beliefs and European court traditions, which led to the addition of a Mass, crowns, and elaborate gowns.

Evolving to celebrate the broader sense of womanhood, the event gained in popularity, spreading farther into South America, the Caribbean, and, eventually, the United States. Over time, different countries developed their own unique practices.

Even within my family, the associated traditions have changed since we came to the United States from Peru nearly 40 years ago. Nine years after Angelica’s magical quinceañera, I got my chance to be part of another prima’s court celebration in Connecticut.

The birthday girl (who, like the event, is also called the quinceañera, or quince), traditionally has a court of 14 girls, called damas, symbolizing each year of her life so far. Each dama has a gentleman escort, or chambelán.

Today, though, traditional courts are rarer. “Back in the day, when we had our quinces...it was still a thing to have 15 damas,” says Karla De La Rosa, founder of the Quinceañera & Sweet 16 Expo of New England, an annual Rhode Island trade show attended by about 250 people. “Now, some [people] don’t even have them.”

Madrinas (godmothers or female sponsors) and padrinos (godfathers or male sponsors) act as mentors to the quince, participating in the ceremony and helping out financially with specific items for the event. A relative or close friend gives the brindis (toast), paying tribute to the relationships within the quinceañera’s life and the community she has built.

In my family, there’s a moment during the celebration where we form a line to dance with the birthday girl and offer her our congratulations. However this custom came to be, it’s our way of expressing togetherness.

Pedro Aguirre and Raúl Garcia II had dreamed about what their daughter’s quinceañera would be like since she was born. The couple, who live in Roxbury, began saving for the celebration when she was still an infant.

This past June, they hosted Luna Garcia Aguirre’s long-awaited celebration, themed “A Night Under The Moon,” at The Cedars Center in Jamaica Plain. The ballroom, decorated in glittering black and gold, featured an elaborate throne at the front. Pedro and Raúl watched their daughter glide across the ballroom in a gold and black gown, greeting their friends and family as mariachis played. “It does truly become a celebration of the woman you see her becoming,” Pedro says.

“As Guatemalan and Mexican men, we knew that it was important to continue that with her in front of our family that maybe didn’t expect us to hold certain traditions,” Raúl tells me. “And sometimes, when we do some things, they end up being a little different — because we are different also.” Some relatives who chose not to attend Pedro and Raúl’s wedding 22 years ago were there to watch them present their daughter — to celebrate Luna and share their story as a family with this loving community they built together over the years and across regions.

“It meant so many different things to me,” Luna says. “Being Latina, it was such a good moment for me to really feel that aspect of myself and my community” — including, she emphasizes, “family” not related by blood.

Luna’s chosen madrinas — Pedro’s eldest sister and Raúl’s cousin — gifted her traditional Mexican accessories from Veracruz: a headband, hairpiece, and skirt. In Spanish, both women spoke about what an honor it was to watch her become the wonderful young woman she is. “It just made me feel so thankful,” Luna says. “I was so emotional.”

Although more than half of the guests were not Spanish speakers and had never attended a quince before, the emotions behind the speakers’ words were evident. Pedro says there was not a dry eye under that sparkly moon.

“I know there’s a lot of history attached to the quinceañera. It’s probably a little antiquated, but we just thought, Let us make it our own, let’s have a party, let’s pass on a tradition,” Pedro says. “We get to redefine it.”

For their father-daughter dances, both dads surprised Luna with pop songs they chose — orchestral covers of “Complicated” by Avril Lavigne and “The Only Exception” by Paramore — and they each got a turn to waltz with their daughter.

Luna’s quinceañera included a court, and the traditional ceremony of the changing of her shoes (more on that later). But she personalized moments to reflect herself at this stage in her life and omitted parts, including the Catholic Mass before the celebration, that she doesn’t identify with.

She chose to focus on female empowerment: An all-women mariachi band performed, and her court consisted solely of six damas (no chambelanes). “She wanted it to be about her and her girls,” Pedro says.

Across the country, designated themes for quinceañeras have become a big trend, industry professionals say, though some stick with the more traditional quince, including a white gown and simpler, classic decor.

Jynia Laury, who goes by Nia, transported guests to the world of Alice in Wonderland in Holyoke in 2024. After watching the Disney movie as a child, she’d fallen in love with the character of Alice. Vivid flowers and butterfly decorations created an enchanting garden setting in the ballroom, and “drink me” potions and “eat me” cookies set the scene for Nia to make her appearance in an Alice-inspired, shimmering, sky-blue gown.

Born in Colombia, Nia’s mother, Lori Goshea, was adopted by an American family and raised on Long Island. She didn’t get to have a quinceañera, but hoped to continue Colombian traditions with her daughter.

It took Lori and Nia eight months to plan the whimsical celebration for more than 150 guests. Nia, now 17, had a specific vision and talked it through with her mother — which traditions to keep and what she wanted to do differently.

Nia and her mom danced to “Blue” by Beyoncé — the artist’s tribute to her own daughter — in a meaningful parent-child moment. For the father-daughter dance, Nia glided across the floor holding a photo of her father, who is incarcerated, adorned in a gold frame. “She came up with the idea,” Lori says. “The father-daughter dance was really sad, touching. ... She looked up to him, growing up.”

Nia says she felt a powerful sense of “being celebrated ... getting a little bit older, maturing, and surrounding myself with family.”

On the morning of July 20, 2024, my mother’s backyard in Connecticut metamorphosed into an outdoor ballroom for my niece Kayley Rodriguez’s Sweet 16. The ivory tents were set up, the glossy dance floor in place; all that was left were the decorations. Then the torrential downpour began. We all rushed outside to hold the tents down, working together for about 40 minutes. It was some true family bonding.

Kayley was the first in our immediate family to have such an event; my mother, sister, and I were either too shy or couldn’t afford a quince or Sweet 16. And we had waited an extra year to save up for Kayley’s celebration, which is why it included numerous quinceañera traditions. We weren’t going to let rain get in the way.

The sky was completely clear the rest of the day. Family and friends watched tearfully as Kayley waltzed with her father, then her mother and sister, and participated in the changing of the shoes and the crowning ceremony.

During the “changing of the shoes,” the father or a father figure ceremoniously replaces the quinceañera’s slippers with high heels, symbolizing her transition into womanhood. Now, young women are swapping their slippers for sneakers — or exchanging their high heels, as everyone looks on, for a customized, bedazzled pair of Jordans or Nikes.

Surrounded by soccer fans in my family and circle of friends, it’s no surprise that I know not just one but two young women who traded in their soccer cleats for glittering high heels at their parties. For the crowning, as the tradition goes, a tiara or crown is placed on the quinceañera’s head by her parents, godparents, grandparents, or another close relative. Kayley got a traditional tiara from her dad, but at my cousin Angelica’s celebration, she received a necklace and ring from her madrina and padrino.

After the formal waltz by the court and the father-daughter dance, there’s el baile de sorpresa (surprise dance), choreographed and performed by the birthday girl along with her court. This tradition usually includes modern dance styles chosen by the quinceañera. At the quince for another one of my cousins, the surprise dance included hip-hop moves and ended with two of her damas waving the Peruvian and Puerto Rican flags in honor of her heritage. Luna’s blended disco, R&B, pop, norteño, and other genres.

As special as quinceañeras are to many young Latina and Hispanic women, plenty of us never had one. The most common reason I’ve heard is the cost. But financial barriers are nothing new. Like Pedro Aguirre’s sisters, who longed for a quinceañera, none of my aunts was able to have one. None, that is, except my tía Gladys Salcedo, who had hers in Lima in 1976. Growing up, Gladys felt excitement at turning 15. With 10 children to provide for, my grandparents postponed Gladys’s event until they had enough savings for a modest dress, a cake, and plenty of food. At 17, she celebrated her quince in a short-sleeved, baby blue dress, surrounded by her friends and family.

Here in the States, today’s price tags range from about $2,000 for a small-scale celebration to as much as $60,000 for something extravagant, according to New Dawn Photo, a quinceañera photography and videography business based in Dallas -Fort Worth that analyzed 80 actual budgets. New Dawn Photo is also behind a Facebook group called Quinceañeras on a Budget, set up for people to exchange planning advice and tips.

In New England, quinces usually run from $8,000 to $15,000, De La Rosa estimates. Catering, venue, and photography expenses add up quickly on top of formal wear for the family.

Operations specialist Celeste Ribeiro Hewitt at Spinelli’s, a popular venue with branches in East Boston and Lynnfield, says she has noticed quinceañeras becoming smaller in size in recent years, after peaking before COVID. “I would say, post-COVID, the way people celebrate things in general are a little bit different,” she says. The East Boston location services about 24 to 30 quinceañeras a year, either in-house or for catering. “They happen almost as frequently as weddings, and that’s multiple per month.”

Instead of a party, some parents offer a trip as quieter way to celebrate. My mother and I drove along California’s coast for my 15th birthday — the most meaningful trip I’ve taken to this day.

Maybe when I reach 50, decades from now, I’ll decide to have a cincuentañera, like some women who didn’t get a big celebration of womanhood in their teens are doing now.

I asked my cousin Angelica what her quince means to her, over a decade later. “What stands out [was] the unity I was able to have with my family, the experience alone, how beautiful everything was, and how beautiful I felt,” she says. “And how I was able to enjoy that with friends and family.”

title: Erica McLaughlin to lead Cabot Corp. as it looks to expand into battery sector
text:
McLaughlin joined the company’s accounting department in 2002, back when Cabot was one of the few major businesses with offices in what is now known as the Seaport. Formerly with KPMG, she has gradually risen up the ranks at Cabot, before becoming chief financial officer in 2018, working closely with Keohane to set Cabot’s strategy and ensure it is carried out.

“Cabot has been a great place to develop and to move into new roles,” McLaughlin said. “I feel quite good about what I’m inheriting.”

As chief executive, McLaughlin will lead a global workforce of 4,100 people, with around 10 percent of that number based in Massachusetts: at the Boston headquarters, a research center in Billerica, and an inkjet plant in Haverhill. The publicly traded company reported nearly $4 billion in revenue last year, and its current market value is around $4 billion as well.

When she takes over at the end of the month, McLaughlin will be the ninth chief executive in the company’s 144-year-old history — and the first woman in the role.

“To be able to lead this company is a great honor for me,” McLaughlin said. “Evolving the company, as we think about this ‘next generation economy’ — batteries, energy storage, the buildout of data centers. . . . I really look forward to building [Cabot} into a greater company over my tenure.”

The biotech industry is in full swing, with deals activity happening at a breakneck pace and investors’ dollars pouring into new treatments. But there’s one important segment getting left behind: early-stage firms.

That’s why Governor Maura Healey and her economic development secretary, Eric Paley, huddled with a few dozen chief executives of young biotechs last week at MassBio’s headquarters in Kendall Square. Also on hand: Kirk Taylor, chief executive of the quasipublic Mass. Life Sciences Center, through which many of the state subsidies for the biotech sector flow. Healey later told reporters that state officials should consider increasing the state assistance available for early-stage biotechs, given the financial challenges they face.

Paley and Taylor are updating the strategic approach for the Mass. Life Sciences Center, and want to use the input they gleaned to tweak its incentives. The hope is to come up with more grants for these younger biotechs, in particular to support them through expensive clinical trials, as well as working with another quasi-public, MassVentures, to help commercialize more university research.

“Massachusetts has an unbelievable pipeline of research,” Paley said. “We’re not getting enough of it out of the labs.”

For Ben Pope, founder of MelliCell, a Newton biotech working on a pill to treat the Fragile X syndrome that can cause autism, it was refreshing to hear state officials so engaged on these issues. “I really appreciate them recognizing,” Pope said, “that our success is what will drive Massachusetts to continue to dominate in this space.”

Rich Davey will find out later this month how Logan Airport scores on the latest JD Power ranking of customer satisfaction.

But the Massachusetts Port Authority chief executive just received a different kind of evaluation, from Massport’s board of directors. Last week, the board unanimously approved a 6 percent raise, bringing his salary for this fiscal year to $481,000, and awarded him a bonus equal to 10 percent of his salary.

Since returning to Boston from New York City Transit two years ago, Davey says he’s been focused on improving the customer experience at Logan, while balancing security and safety. The most well-known evaluation of airport customer experience comes from analytics firm JD Power, which last September ranked Logan 10th in its mega-airport category.

Davey won’t be satisfied until Logan is in the top five. Toward that end, Massport revamped many bathrooms, improved food options, and launched a popular remote terminal program in Framingham (with a similar project in the works for Braintree), among other changes.

The numbers of flights and passengers are relatively steady this year compared to last year, so far, per Massport’s statistics. But from the metrics that board chair Patricia Jacobs is looking at, Davey is flying high. “The results speak for themselves,” Jacobs told Davey before the vote, “nothing short of spectacular.”

When brothers Ronn Garry and Randy Garry started chatting about a succession plan for Tropical Foods, their grocery store near Nubian Square in Roxbury, they thought about selling to a competitor. They worried, though, about what might happen to Tropical’s 100 workers if a chain bought Tropical. So the two brothers decided to sell it to the employees instead.

To help line up financing, Tropical turned to Apis & Heritage, a foundation-backed investment firm that specializes in arranging employee buyouts to protect blue-collar jobs. Now the company’s newly created Employee Stock Ownership Plan holds a majority stake, with a trustee overseeing the shares for the ESOP.

Tropical’s new board will feature two seats for Washington-based Apis & Heritage, one for Ronn Garry, and one for an outside adviser. Ronn Garry said his brother will exit in six months, while he’ll leave in around 18 months, after helping to find a general manager to replace him. He plans to stay on the board for five years.

Choosing the ESOP route gives employees a stake in the company’s future while also ensuring stability after the brothers’ departure.

Rumors had circulated that the brothers had put the business up for sale, so employees were nervous when they headed over to the nearby Residence Inn in waves for meetings on Aug. 31. The relief, Garry said, was palpable when they were told not only was no one losing their job, but they’re now going to be owners in the company.

“By the end of the day, when the last group came in, and they heard from the previous groups what was going on, . . . it was a very different feeling,” Garry said. “This is such a great solution, and such a great thing for us and the community. This is real wealth-building in Roxbury.”

For one glorious evening Lisa Lobel and Angela Peri mingled among Hollywood stars, as they received their first Emmy award, for casting work behind the hit series “Widow’s Bay.”

It was a long road to the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles for Lobel, Peri, and their firm Boston Casting. When they started the firm three decades ago, the bulk of TV and movie work in Greater Boston consisted of brief exterior shoots. But business picked up after state lawmakers adopted and later expanded the state’s film tax credits.

Lately, Lobel, Peri, and their local colleagues have been busy with shows and movies such as “Julia,” “Coda,” “The Holdovers,” “Tony,” “Kevin Can F**K Himself,” and “Dexter: New Blood.”

Then there’s “Widow’s Bay,” Apple’s horror-comedy set in a coastal New England town. Its first season was shot in Massachusetts last year. Lobel says Boston Casting handled more than 80 speaking roles for the show, which stars Matthew Rhys as the titular town’s mayor. Boston Casting worked with casting director Allison Jones, a Needham native who made it big in Hollywood. They shared the Emmy win with Jones and Emily Buntyn, a casting associate at Jones’s namesake firm.

The Emmy awards are spread over three nights; casting was up on night two, on Sept. 6.

“Widow’s Bay” is the kind of quirky show that might not have clicked if not for the genuine New England locales — and genuine New England supporting actors. “The feeling of the New England coastal town is really special,” Lobel said. “You have to live here, and live it, to know how to make it feel real.”

title: The new owners of Tropical Foods in Roxbury? The employees.
text:
When brothers Ronn and Randy Garry started chatting about a succession plan for Tropical Foods, the grocery store they own on the outskirts of Nubian Square in Roxbury, they thought about selling to a competitor — maybe one of the big regional chains.

They worried, though, about what might happen to Tropical’s 100 workers if a chain purchased the company. So the two brothers decided to sell it to the employees instead.

To help line up financing for the deal, Tropical turned to Apis & Heritage, a foundation-backed investment firm that specializes in arranging employee buyouts to protect blue-collar jobs. Now the company’s newly created Employee Stock Ownership Plan holds a majority stake, with a trustee overseeing the shares for the ESOP.

A board of directors will be set up in the coming weeks, one that will feature two seats for Washington-based Apis & Heritage, one for Ronn Garry, and one for an outside adviser.

Ronn Garry said his brother will exit in six months, while he’ll leave in around 18 months, after helping to find a general manager to replace him. He plans to stay on the newly assembled board for five years.

Both brothers are looking for a break from the grind of the past 30 years in which they worked through many holidays and often got up at 5 a.m. Their goal, he said, was: “how we could step back and not have to work those hours but still keep Tropical Foods the way it is.”

Choosing the ESOP route gives employees a stake in the company’s future while also ensuring stability after the Garry brothers’ departure. In five years, Garry said, Apis & Heritage will sell its remaining stake back to the company as well, presumably at a profit. Individual employees, meanwhile, will be granted equity over time based on their longevity with the business.

The Garry brothers have owned the store since 2006, when they bought out their father, and moved into the new 26,500-square-foot location in 2015.

Rumors had circulated through the ranks that the brothers had put the business up for sale, so employees were understandably nervous when they headed over to the nearby Residence Inn in waves for meetings on Aug. 31. The relief, Garry said, was palpable when they were told not only was no one losing their job, but they’re now going to be owners in the company.

“By the end of the day, when the last group came in, and they heard from the previous groups what was going on, ... it was a very different feeling,” Garry said. “This is such a great solution, and such a great thing for us and the community. This is real wealth building in Roxbury.”

title: Former White House official talks federal health cuts, reform during Future of Medicine Summit
text:
Cuts to federal aid are pushing the health care system to the brink at the expense of ordinary Americans, a former White House health official said Tuesday morning.

Dr. Ashish Jha, who was the White House’s coronavirus response coordinator in the Biden administration, said during a discussion at the Globe’s third annual Future of Medicine Summit that the effects of health care reforms designed to root out fraud and waste have been “overstated.” More people are being left behind by rising costs, he said.

“For 20 years we’ve said health care spending is unsustainable, and yet we’ve somehow managed to sustain it,” Jha told Globe editorial writer Shira Schoenberg during the summit’s first discussion Tuesday morning. “I actually think we are now at a tipping point that may make it less tenable to continue on that path.”

Jha said he saw a shift in American health care after the One Big Beautiful Bill Act passed and left fewer people with coverage even as new, increasingly expensive medical advancements push forward.

“We have got to get our act together on figuring out how to make health care more efficient,” Jha said. “Or we’re going to be in a place that we are not going to be happy.”

But Jha called for a “uniquely American” solution to rising costs, rather than adopting socialized medicine as some other countries have done. He mentioned opening up more competition and allowing for more options, including physician-owned hospitals.

“Finding the villain and blaming the villain is very fun politics, but it doesn’t actually make for very good policy,” Jha said. “Everybody is just maximizing the incentives we have created for them.”

Jha and Schoenberg also discussed a 2023 Boston Public Health Commission report that found average lifespans in Boston’s wealthy Back Bay neighborhood were nearly 25 years longer than residents in Roxbury. Jha said those results reflect a systemic loop “where social factors drive health outcomes” and vice versa that health policy makers play a role in breaking.

“Making health care cheaper, more accessible, higher quality is a very important part of the intervention,” he said.

In addition to better health policy, Jha also spoke on “extraordinary benefits” of using AI in health care to lower costs.

Jha, co-founder of BioRadar, an AI-powered biological threat detection technology, said health care administration would benefit from using AI to streamline bureaucracy, though he’s mostly seen it used by insurance companies and providers to automate and appeal denials.

“AI’s got a lot of possibility,” he said. “But we’ve got to drive it that way.”

Jha previously proposed multiple reforms, both market-based and policy-based, in his Globe Opinion series, The Cost Cure, which he brought up during his discussion with Schoenberg.

“I think there’s broad consensus in the policy world, and now we just have to get our political leaders ... to adopt these things,” Jha said. “Because if we do, they actually can substantially lower health risk.”

The Future of Medicine Summit focuses on medical breakthrough and innovation, and featured multiple conversations on post-pandemic preparedness, topics in public health, and biotechnological advancements. Jha was one of the conference’s headliners.

title: Boston scraps overdue reparations report led by former Tufts professor accused of poor research
text:
The city did not say whether it will seek another team of historians to take up the work, but said the money “will be redeployed to support” other priorities of Boston’s Task Force on Reparations.

Task force chairman Joseph D. Feaster Jr. said committee members also concluded the information compiled by Tufts researchers could not be authenticated or used in the group’s final report.

He added that a subcommittee led by the Rev. Mariama White-Hammond is looking into other options for completing the research. Without that examination of the 320 years the Tufts team focused on, Feaster said, it will be difficult to move forward with presenting the city with recommendations on reparations.

“This is a major setback [and] it could prove fatal,” Feaster said Tuesday. “The task force doesn’t feel that they can come with . . . a recommendation without having that body of knowledge.”

Feaster added that he does not anticipate the task force will hold community meetings until either the group has research to present or it has made other decisions about next steps.

The city first passed an ordinance in 2022 to review possible reparations for Black Bostonians, and set a deadline to release research by the end of 2023 — a deadline it missed by nearly three years.

In that time, Boston set aside $500,000 to hire two teams to research 400 years of slavery and racism, each assigned to produce reports spanning different time periods in Boston’s history.

One report, written by experts at Northeastern University and detailing discrimination against Black Bostonians after 1940, was submitted months ago, although it has not been publicly released. The city said it will be released in the near future.

The second report, led by Greenidge, Kendra Field, and Kyera Singleton, would have covered slavery and its legacy in Boston from the early-17th century to the mid-20th century. It was due to the task force by the end of June. The city said the report was never completed.

Antonia Edwards, a member of Boston’s task force on reparations, told a community group Monday night that task force members ”felt like the credentials were compromised.”

“If the lead researcher lost her credentials and that she was no longer valid for Tufts, then it’s [in] the best interest not to present this to the community,” Edwards said at a community event about reparations at the Shaw-Roxbury library.

The Tufts report came under question in July after The New York Times published a story on allegations made by other scholars that Greenidge had factual errors and mis-cited credits in her 2022 book about the Grimkes, a prominent slaveholding family from South Carolina whose family members were also abolitionists.

Tufts, it turns out, knew about the allegations since at least December 2022, about 13 months before Greenidge was selected by Boston to research reparations. But the revelations came as a surprise to Boston officials, who were left scrambling to figure out next steps.

The book, ”The Grimkes," was released in 2022 by Liveright Publishing, an imprint of W. W. Norton, and received glowing reviews, including from the Globe.

In 2024, Myra C. Glenn, a retired professor of American history at Elmira College, raised concerns about Greenidge’s book, saying she often “lacks the evidence to substantiate many of her major claims,” and further said the book “is also riddled with factual errors and repeatedly omits needed endnotes.”

Glenn also noted the book asserted some of the letters from the Grimke sisters are held by the University of Michigan’s archives. The university, Glenn said, does not possess those letters.

After a review of the allegations, Tufts officials alerted the book’s publisher and it was pulled off its website. Tufts officials would not say when they finished their review, or when they informed the publisher of their findings. The university told the city in October 2025 that Greenidge was placed on leave.

Greenidge, who was an associate professor in the Department of Studies in Race, Colonialism, and Diaspora, was placed on leave in October 2025. She no longer works for Tufts.

“I feel sorry for the sister, that’s for sure,” said Feaster. “Her whole career has been decimated as a result of this.”

Adrian Walker of the Globe staff contributed to this report.

This story was produced by the Globe’s Money, Power, Inequality team, which covers the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston. You can sign up for the newsletter here.

title: Residents will weigh in on proposed game-day parking plan around White Stadium, officials say
text:
The decision about resident parking protections around White Stadium on Boston Legacy FC game days will be put in the hands of the neighborhoods surrounding Franklin Park, according to city officials.

A survey will ask residents for their opinion on the city’s proposed parking protections in their area, which would go into effect on game days for the National Women’s Soccer League team at White Stadium, city officials said Tuesday evening.

“The neighborhoods decide,” Mayor Michelle Wu said Tuesday evening to around 40 Roxbury residents at the Bruce C. Bolling Municipal Building. “What we do as a city is we put in the policy that we believe best reflects the consensus and decisions and needs of our residents, and then we continue to evaluate.”

The Roxbury meeting was the first of four that will be held with residents and business owners of the neighborhoods surrounding Franklin Park to share the new transportation plan and request their input on parking restrictions.

For five hours on game days — including two hours before kickoff and one hour after games conclude — the city proposed a “resident parking protection zone” stretching 0.75 miles from the stadium entrance, which residents will vote on.

The survey asks residents whether they approve of the resident parking protection zone, as well as proposed protections for general parking inside Franklin Park, including for golfers and visitors to its zoo.

The results of the survey, which closes Oct. 24, will be shared with neighborhood associations in Roxbury, Dorchester, Jamaica Plain, and Mattapan, which will ultimately vote whether to add the parking restrictions, officials said.

Officials also shared the city’s broader plan to promote public transportation by fans. Boston Legacy FC will fund the operation and enforcement of the plan, according to the city.

There is no spectator parking at White Stadium, officials said.

On game days, the city will provide free shuttles at MBTA stations and at satellite parking lots outside Boston. It will also use a parking lot on Seaver Street as a pickup and drop-off area for game attendees using ride-sharing services like Uber and Lyft.

The city is also upgrading bike and pedestrian pathways around Franklin Park to allow for stadium access.

The renovation of White Stadium drew harsh criticism from opponents concerned that the involvement of Boston Legacy FC, a for-profit sports team, would illegally allow a private company to profit from public parkland and improperly limit the public’s access to the facility.

In August, the city’s $325 million plan to renovate White Stadium was backed by the Supreme Judicial Court when it rejected a lawsuit trying to halt the project, ruling the overhaul does not violate a state law that protects public parkland.

The ruling also ended a yearslong lawsuit to stop the project brought by the Emerald Necklace Conservancy, an environmental nonprofit, and a coalition of residents living in the neighborhoods surrounding Franklin Park.

The renovated stadium will serve as a new hub for Boston Public Schools Athletics and become the home stadium for Boston Legacy FC.

The stadium will still be owned by the city and primarily used by students and Boston residents, officials said at Tuesday’s meeting. The current lease agreement allows Boston Legacy FC to use the stadium for up to 20 home games and 20 practices each year.

Still, Roxbury residents have many concerns about game day operations, ranging from the sale of alcohol to the impact on other community events.

“If someone shows up from out of town and they’re not aware it’s game day, they can have their car towed,” said Louis Elisa, 77, a Seaver Street resident and cofounder of the Franklin Park Coalition, which aims to preserve the historic green space.

“You’re not allowing the people who’ve been in this community, taking care of this park, taking care of this community, to live freely and enjoy themselves,” Elisa said.

Tony Brewer, who lives a few doors down from Elisa, said in an interview that solving the resident parking issue is essential before White Stadium opens.

“We don’t have to fight about it,” Brewer said. “We just need to come up with ways of resolving it in a peaceful manner.”
