title: Mayor Wu needs to build bridges on Beacon Hill
text:
In the most recent Democratic primary, Wu took her best shot at removing two of those legislators, Senators Will Brownsberger of Belmont and Nick Collins of South Boston. She targeted these two influential senators largely because they had opposed her legislative proposal to shift more of the city’s tax burden to the already hurting commercial sector.

Meanwhile, she endorsed Senator Michael Rush of West Roxbury, who had supported her home rule petition on the tax shift, only to watch him lose to newcomer Persis Yu in what is Wu’s home district.

Brownsberger bested Wu’s former aide and endorsed candidate, Daniel Lander, by a 35-vote margin. Collins won his South Boston-based district handily over Wu’s choice, first-time candidate Latoya Gayle.

Having failed to defeat the incumbents, Wu should try working with them. As state Senator Robyn Kennedy, Democrat of Worcester, said: “If the mayor wants to pass legislation in the Senate, it’s not about running races against individual senators, it’s about building relationships with all 40 senators. My phone line is always available if she wants to start doing that.”

Wu’s response?

“My job is to get things done for the residents of Boston and to stand up for the city’s interests,” she told the Globe editorial board Tuesday. “I don’t have the time or the capacity to do the job of [winning over] our state Senate. It’s the role of the Boston delegation to advocate for the city’s needs and get things done for our home community.”

Well, no. Boston’s representatives are elected officials in their own right. Their job is to do what they think needs to be done for their community and the state — not what the mayor tells them.

An unrepentant Wu had no olive branch to offer to the Senate — although she said she has spoken to Brownsberger, Collins, and Yu since the election. But she did concede that in the future “the city needs to do a better job of defining our own agenda and be clear when that agenda is not being heard.”

There’s little doubt that the mayor’s agenda for next year will include one more attempt at shifting the city’s tax structure and revisiting her version of a rent stabilization bill. A real estate transfer fee, something the city has been trying to get from Beacon Hill for the past eight years, would have put $200 million in a housing development fund had it passed when it was first proposed, she said, indicating it’s still on her list.

This editorial board hasn’t supported the tax shift or rent stabilization proposals. But the transfer fee could be a valuable tool.

Like countless mayors before her, Wu also chafes at the restrictions imposed by state law on cities and towns that require legislative approval, whether it’s changing the structure of the city’s development agency (still not approved by the Legislature) or closing hours for bars, which when lifted statewide during the World Cup, Wu added, were a huge boost to Boston’s economy.

But until those laws change, working with the Legislature is unavoidable.

“The Legislature is a people business. The more bridges you build, the more successful you’ll be. The more bridges you burn, the less successful you’ll be,” said Senate Ways and Means Chair Michael Rodrigues last week during the Boston vote recount in the Brownsberger race.

Senator Adam Gomez of Springfield sounded a similar theme, noting that even had Wu been successful at ousting Brownsberger, then what?

“You still have to be able to organize and whip votes,” he added.

Interesting that it was lawmakers from the state’s two other major cities — Worcester and Springfield — who had to remind Wu that all political power doesn’t stop at the Boston city limits.

Only six of the 40-members of the Massachusetts Senate represent districts that include parts of Boston. In the 160-member House, Boston is represented by 16 legislators.

But Wu insists she has no trouble dealing with House leaders, alluding to a compromise reached with that branch over the tax shift bill last year.

“Our experience in the Senate has been that it [the same tax bill] never even gets released from committee,” she added. “That’s not compromise and it’s not acceptable.”

That gets to a broader level of legislative dysfunction and a lack of transparency that is as frustrating to the general public as it is to the mayor.

On that score, Wu’s not wrong.

Look no farther than the dozen conference committees still at work since the Legislature otherwise went into hiatus on July 31.

Wu can’t solve the Legislature’s internal squabbles or single-handedly cure its dysfunction. But she can attempt to build bridges in the Senate that will make such dysfunction irrelevant. The future of her own legislative agenda depends on it.

title: Botox and a brownstone? Boston-area real estate agents are hosting lavish open houses.
text:
“The host feels so good because the guests are saying, ‘Oh my God, this is the best showing we’ve ever been to,’” said Cervasio.

She was hired to turn a realtor’s open house into a curated event. During the COVID pandemic, agents couldn’t host open houses for about two years. That happened at the beginning of a cycle of volatility in the real estate market that continues to shift due to everything from wars and oil prices to elections and housing shortages.

“It’s been an uphill battle, at least on the sales side,” said Sarah Maguire, principal of the Aronson Maguire Group at Compass. “So we started to have to get very creative.”

Throughout Boston, real estate agents are getting savvier when it comes to getting potential buyers and their agents through the doors of open houses. But a free glass of cheap wine and a cheese board doesn’t pull the weight that it used to. As a result, agents are going to tremendous lengths to curate custom events that engage the community, attract unlikely guests, and satisfy builders who want to see a successful return on their investment.

Realizing that free beers and a gift certificate weren’t going to do the trick, Maguire’s team leaned into special events. To highlight a new build in Dorchester, it hired Red Oyster to walk around the open house shucking oysters with pails of empty shells hanging from their matching aprons. The event was a hit.

“They were running around literally shoving oysters down people’s throats with all the accouterments,” said Maguire. “People loved it.”

For another listing that went up between Thanksgiving and Christmas, Maguire needed to drum up interest for three units in a Jamaica Plain development.

“It’s the absolute worst time to sell anything,” said Maguire. “We’re like, what the hell are we going to do? No one’s buying anything. Rates are through the roof.”

Maguire and her team came up with the idea of hosting a holiday market inside the development featuring local makers from Jamaica Plain, West Roxbury, and Roslindale. Vendors sold everything from knitted hats to homemade dog treats throughout the three units. Ultimately, the sale of the units set price records.

“Our sellers need to see that we’re trying to do everything we possibly can to get people through the door,” said Maguire, who has also hosted open houses featuring bouquet-making bars, Botox, a gelato stand, and a tarot card reader.

When the builder of Diana Lannon’s listing told her they wanted the open house for a recently constructed $2.8 million home to be “something like the ones on ‘Million Dollar Listing,’” the popular Bravo real estate show, she knew she had her work cut out for her.

“The reason 100 people show up to an open house on ‘Million Dollar Listing’ is that they’re going to be on TV,” said Lannon, an agent with Gibson Sotheby’s Realty. “I needed to get the most attention on this property.”

But the $2.8 million listing was on the pricier side for Sudbury, and it was in the middle of January, when getting people to leave their homes is tough. Lannon knew she’d have to come up with an unusual idea to reel in attention from people in neighboring suburbs and the city. Knowing a new medspa was opening in town, she came up with the idea for a “Botox and Bubbles” event. She paid for the first few units of Botox and asked interested people — who were invited to the open house on Paperless Post invitations — to sign up ahead of time.

“People from the local area were going to come, but I needed people from the city,” Lannon said. “I needed agents who have higher-end buyers that are selling their $1.5 million or $2 million condo in the city, and want to come to the suburbs, but they want something brand new and luxury.”

There were a few negative reactions. Lannon even received a few “nasty” emails. But on the day of the event, attendees were greeted by champagne and a spread of food from Baker’s Best in Needham. The fireplace glowed, and music played in the background. The medspa was set up in the home office, so guests could get injections in privacy. For a broker open house that typically yields eight agents, around 40 people came through the door, including agents from nearby towns like Wellesley and Lexington.

“They never would have come if I didn’t do that,” she said.

So is investing the time — and significant money — in turning an open house into a custom event worth it?

“It depends on what it is that you’re trying to sell,” said Maguire. “What’s the product? What’s the price point? Where’s the location? Sometimes we have to do these things to appease our sellers. The potential commission that we’re making from it has to be enough for us to cover the cost. These things cost thousands of dollars. The risk has to be worth it.”

title: Protesters made a makeshift bike lane where a cyclist was killed. Some fear it made a dangerous stretch worse.
text:
In an anonymous note posted to a nearby pole, the protesters who created the lane said it was meant as a practical response to improve biker safety and to raise awareness about stalled infrastructure improvements under Mayor Michelle Wu.

But after a man riding an electric scooter was struck by a driver who ran a red light near the same intersection on Wednesday, City Councilor Erin Murphy says she wants the tape removed, saying it may have made the street, which cyclists have complained about for years, even more dangerous.

“Privately installed changes to traffic patterns that have not been reviewed or approved by City engineers can create confusion and potential safety risks,” Murphy wrote to Chris Osgood, the city’s interim chief of streets, after she unsuccessfully tried to have the City Council hold an emergency hearing on the makeshift lane.

Her emergency order was filed past deadline, but is on the agenda for next week’s meeting, she said.

Murphy’s comments drew a sharp response from cycling advocacy groups, who said her focus on the unsanctioned bike lane distracts from the need for prompt safety upgrades.

“Whether or not it’s the right thing to do, it was a thing that I guess folks decided to do because safe streets are not happening fast enough,” said Tiffany Cogell, interim executive director of the Boston Cyclists Union, which is located a block from the makeshift bike lane.

“If you push people hard enough, long enough, they are going to find ways to activate the answers and the actions that they’re calling for,” she added.

Cogell said her group was not responsible for the duct tape bike lane, which appeared Aug. 30, and she wasn’t sure who was.

The lane runs along one side of the street, heading downhill on Tremont Street toward Roxbury Crossing, where it appears to block a portion of a parking space before continuing across a crosswalk at the intersection, taking up roughly half a dozen car lengths in total.

Bike advocates have used such protests, known as “tactical urbanism,” in Boston for years to show where city infrastructure is lacking and push for change, said Maha Aslam, transit and streets program manager for LiveableStreets Alliance, where Gag worked for a time.

“Inherently, a bunch of residents coming together to make themselves feel safer while they’re biking down the street is OK,” Aslam said.

In 2015, cyclist Jonathan Fertig used potted plants to create a temporary bike lane divider near the site of a crash that killed a biker on Massachusetts Avenue. Officials later replaced the pots with plastic posts.

Since then, activists have lined roadways on a number of occasions to form “human bike lanes,” beginning with a 2017 protest for upgrades to the Congress Street Bridge.

“Tape on a street isn’t going to make it more unsafe than it already was,” Cogell said, urging Murphy and others to “focus on making those infrastructure improvements happen rather than trying to drum up hearings and legislation that will vilify people who have been asking for something for years to save lives.”

Zachary Yaro, a 32-year-old member of the Cyclists Union who rode past the makeshift lane on Thursday, said the markings are “an improvement over nothing.”

He said the design mirrors many bike lanes he’s seen in Somerville, making the outrage over it feel “like a distraction from the actual issue.”

As other bikers rode through the intersection on Thursday, many followed the lane marked off by dozens of white and green tape strips, though some drivers cut through it as they made right turns.

Murphy said her concern over the bike lane was raised by Wednesday’s crash, in which the driver was issued a citation for failing to stop or yield, police said. The scooter rider is recovering from his injuries, city officials said.

Murphy was added to an email chain that day by a resident imploring her, Osgood, and other City Council members to remove the unsanctioned bike lane citing safety concerns, she said.

The resident previously emailed Osgood on Aug. 30 about the tape. Marcela Dwork, a spokesperson for Wu, said Friday that was when officials were notified about it.

Dwork added the city responded to that inquiry the day it was sent, promising to remove the lane. A copy of the resident’s correspondence shows they emailed again on Sept. 11 asking why it was still there.

In her letter, Murphy asked Osgood to evaluate whether the makeshift lane may have contributed to the latest collision. But dashcam video of the incident, shared with the Globe by a witness to the crash, appears to show the crash happened in the middle of the street.

The scooter rider was attempting to cross Tremont when a gray sedan sped through a red light, crashing into him near the center line and sending him flying through the air, the video showed.

In a call Friday, Murphy said even though the bike lane didn’t influence the crash, unapproved road changes still make city streets less safe.

“This area needs attention, and we can’t just let people take it into their own hands,” she said.

On a pole a few feet away from the bike lane, the anonymous note titled “If Wu Won’t, We Will!” said protesters had created the lane after Gag’s death in July because “knowledgeable and skilled street designers,” did not step in to ensure “the same tragedy didn’t befall anyone else.”

“Unfortunately, Mayor Wu hasn’t let them do their jobs since early 2025,” the note said. Wu began requiring her personal approval on many street infrastructure projects last year, leading to substantial slowdowns.

Following Gag’s death, Wu committed to installing more concrete bike lane barriers and making other road improvements, also pledging to have street officials receive more input on how to speed safety projects.

Murphy expressed some sympathy with the protesters.

“They obviously felt that nobody was listening to them,” she said.

On Friday, the cyclist’s union said that they agreed with Murphy’s call for a professional solution and that they look forward to attending her hearing to voice their concerns.

City officials added that they have continued evaluating safety along the intersection and Tremont Street corridor and will continue to work with residents, local leaders, and advocates on improving safety in the area and enforcing traffic laws.

On Friday morning, the lane remained in place, although a city worker on a bike arrived around 9 a.m. to take photos and measurements.

Wu officials said the city plans to remove and replace the tape once they’ve finalized design changes for the area, which are being developed by the city’s Streets Cabinet.

In the meantime, bikers say they plan to hold officials to account if they don’t follow through.

On Thursday night, 59-year-old Nathan Phillips, a professor at Boston University, stopped his bike at the intersection to add red tape to reinforce the bike lane design.

The color was “fitting for the blood that has been shed,” he said.

“If they remove it, I’d be someone who’d come right back out and put it down again,” Phillips added, before riding away.

Niki Griswold of the Globe staff contributed.

title: UMass Boston seniors to teach public health in high schools through a partnership led by Mayor Wu
text:
Wu said Boston’s concentration of universities, hospitals, and research institutions has not, by itself, guaranteed an adequate pipeline into public health careers.

“We have the best academic and healthcare institutions in the world,” Wu said. “We conduct more medical research here than anywhere else in the world, and we’re going to fight for every dollar of NIH [National Institutes of Health] funding and to sustain that, but maintaining that edge and continuing to lead the world in not only healthcare but public health means making sure we are closing the gaps within our community and investing in the next generation of leadership.”

The announcement was held at UMass Boston and was attended by the university provost, chancellors, city council members, teachers, and students. City Councilor John FitzGerald, whose district includes parts of Dorchester, said the arrangement could also help Boston continue to retain workers trained in the city.

“About 80 percent of undergraduates stay in Boston after. That means the training that we do and the education that we’re giving are staying in our city,” he said.

The partnership comes as health departments nationwide confront persistent workforce problems. A survey of nearly 5,000 public health workers conducted in March found growing concerns about burnout and retention. The Public Health Workforce Interests and Needs Survey asked employees what’s changed since 2024, and 35 percent said their feelings of burnout had worsened, including nearly half of workers aged 35 and younger. Among that group, 31 percent said they planned to leave their organization within the next year.

One in four workers also reported that their opportunities for advancement had worsened since 2024.

Boston Public Health Commissioner Dr. Bisola Ojikutu said, “We’re at a pivotal moment for public health across the country,” pointing to unstable federal funding, difficulty recruiting and retaining workers, and challenges ranging from infectious diseases and substance use to mental health and persistent health disparities.

“Similarly, academic institutions are also facing significant challenges that threaten the pipeline of public health leaders, scientists, educators, and practitioners that our country desperately needs,” Ojikutu said. “This is the time for us to join forces.”

The UMass Boston initiative is the first workforce project to emerge from Boston SPHERE —Strengthening Public Health-Academic Partnerships in Education, Research, and Equity — a broader effort bringing together the Boston Public Health Commission with more than 30 colleges, universities, research centers, and academic medical centers that was announced last Friday.

Participants include Mass General Brigham, Boston Medical Center, Boston Children’s Hospital, Beth Israel Lahey Health, Harvard, MIT’s Broad Institute, Boston University, Northeastern, Tufts, UMass Boston, Fenway Health, the Massachusetts League of Community Health Centers, and the Massachusetts Department of Public Health.

Ojikutu said the coalition has three broad goals: developing a more diverse pipeline of public health workers, getting research and new technologies into practical use more quickly, and using that work to reduce racial and other health disparities.

The need for a larger workforce is not unique to Boston. Public health agencies nationally have struggled for years with turnover and staffing shortages. One analysis cited by the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials estimated that state and local health departments would need 80,000 additional workers to provide basic public health services.

UMass Boston launched its Urban Public Health department in 2022. The program has 65 students entering their second, third, and fourth years and expects enrollment to grow to 100 with this fall’s incoming class. Students study epidemiology, environmental health, biostatistics, data science, health systems, and health communication.

Seniors applied for the city program last spring and were selected by the Public Health Commission. During the fall, they will be trained in adolescent health, health education, facilitation, community engagement, and public health practice. In the spring, they will teach high school students under commission supervision.

“Now, we’re currently in the training semester,” said Althea Laci, 23, a UMass Boston senior from Quincy who hopes to work in public health policy. “We are learning how to develop curriculum and navigate conversations that can be sensitive. It’s a lot of practice, practice, practice.”

Massachusetts requires public schools to provide health education, but districts have discretion over the curriculum. Parents can also opt their children out of lessons. The city health commission launched a Health Resource Center Program in 2010 to provide materials to teach students about sexual health, mental health, substance use, and health equity.

Trinity Stinson-Salmon, a 21-year-old senior from Brockton, said she was eager for a chance to work directly with young people while figuring out where she fits within the broad public health field.

The program gives students “a more hands-on avenue” than a traditional classroom experience, she said.

“We get to have in-person experiences, learn from professionals, but also we get to learn more about ourselves and what we can do.”

Students who do not want to teach can pursue other capstone placements in areas such as policy, health communication, and data analysis, said Patricia Janulewicz, chair of UMass Boston’s Urban Public Health Department.

title: ‘I’m not your neighbor’: In Southie, a few blocks away is a world apart
text:
West Broadway marks the dividing line between the affluent, where the median family income is more than $250,000, and the underprivileged, where it’s just $60,000. It’s one of the starkest contrasts in Greater Boston, which is among the most income-segregated metropolitan areas in the country and has experienced some of the largest increases in income divergence in recent years, according to new research by the MassINC Policy Center. This polarization has increased more in Massachusetts than in any other state since 2020.

That means fewer neighborhoods with an array of income levels. The rich are clustered with the rich, the poor with the poor.

This separation can limit access to relationships and resources that spur upward mobility, the report states, perpetuating inequities across generations.

Massachusetts also has one of the highest levels of income segregation between school districts, generating a lawsuit in May. This indicates that these sharply divided levels of economic mobility will continue, said Ben Forman, director of the policy center.

“The more the economy produces inequality, the more people sort themselves out,” Forman said.

In West Broadway public housing, home to nearly 1,500 people, some residents play bingo in the West Broadway Task Force building, competing for prizes such as detergent and dish soap. Most tenants stick close to home, said Luz Leon, the task force secretary, who has lived there for more than 20 years. But now that the Family Dollar on West Broadway has closed, Goodwill is one of the only affordable places to shop among a sea of high-end stores.

Leon, 51, is grateful for donations of diapers and Christmas gifts from wealthier residents, whom local nonprofit leaders praise for their generous contributions, but she’s highly aware that they occupy an entirely different space.

“There is a line,” she said. “They can help, but we know our place.”

The seclusion that results from inequality also perpetuates it, said Steven Durlauf, director of the Stone Center for Research on Wealth Inequality and Mobility at the University of Chicago. Where children grow up can determine what school they go to, which resources are accessible, how much crime they’re exposed to, and whom their role models are.

It also has a profound impact on how long a person lives. In 2023, the Boston Public Health Commission found a 23-year difference in life expectancy between an area in Roxbury, where the median family income is around $60,000, and one in Back Bay, where it’s more than $250,000.

“There is extremely powerful empirical evidence that neighborhoods matter,” Durlauf said. “They mold people.”

Indeed, low-income people who have contact with well-off residents are more likely to go to college and have higher earnings, recent research shows. And these cross-income interactions also help prosperous people “understand America as a whole,” Durlauf said.

But as the rich keep getting richer, they’re becoming more isolated. The increase in income segregation in Greater Boston over the past four decades has been driven mainly by the rise of high-income households, according to a 2025 Boston Indicators report.

South Boston was solidly working class when public housing was built there in the 1930s and ’40s. But when the waterfront started transforming in the early 2000s, the city allowed luxury developers to pay into an affordable housing fund rather than put those units onsite, and the “white, wealthy waterfront” was born, said Donna Brown, executive director of South Boston Neighborhood Development Corporation, who has lived in the neighborhood since 1989.

The gentrification spread, as young college graduates started snapping up apartments near the beach and the T, driving up rents and pricing out working families.

“Everybody benefits from a neighborhood that is safer and nicer,” Brown said.

But it’s unclear how much that’s helped low-income residents.

Sister Margaret Lanen, 86, came to South Boston as part of the Sisters of Notre Dame and has lived in West Broadway housing since 1975. She likes to go walk by the water at Castle Island but stays away from the Seaport, where the unfairness of the economy is on full display.

“There’s so much money available to people who have money,” she said.

Soaring costs make it more challenging for people to work their way out of subsidized housing because they can’t afford to rent nearby, said Kenzie Bok, administrator of the Boston Housing Authority. But West Broadway public housing residents are a “force,” she noted, particularly leaders who pushed to create a community garden and build mini soccer pitches open to the neighborhood.

At Fourth Presbyterian Church on Dorchester Street, the congregation is a striking blend of low-income and affluent families. This connection builds empathy and openness, said the Rev. Burns Stanfield, who has been a pastor at the church for 35 years. But he mourns the loss of school-age children as parents increasingly leave for the suburbs.

“Nothing brings out altruism like kids,” he said. “We get better restaurants, we have better coffee, but it seems like less investment in the community as community.”

Income segregation is “extraordinarily hard” to fix without policy solutions, said Durlauf, at the University of Chicago, because parents who can afford to live anywhere want to provide the safest, most-resource-rich environment for their children.

Meier, the South Boston resident, saw this happen as his wife’s Harvard Business School friends left the city for Wellesley after they had children. Meier, who has a PhD in mechanical engineering and is currently a stay-at-home dad, and his wife, the CEO of a small energy company, have no plans to leave.

“It just seems like the American way is to segregate yourself off and set up neighborhoods that are insulated,” he said. “We want our children . . . to understand how the world actually works.”

Sharp income divides aren’t confined to cities. Some affluent suburbs — including Wellesley, Lexington, and Sudbury — contribute greatly to the Boston area’s income segregation. In one census tract in Natick, the median family income is $209,000, according to MassINC data; in an adjacent tract in Framingham, it’s just $49,000.

The high cost of living in Massachusetts, coupled with high rates of income inequity, mean that lower-income households have to grapple with prices shaped by one of the country’s most expensive markets armed with disproportionately low spending power.

“We’re all shopping at the same mall, we’re all shopping at similar grocery stores,” said Rachel Vingsness, executive director of the Natick Service Council, which assists low-income residents. “The cost for everyday living is the same regardless of where you live and what your income and financial situation is.”

Take kids’ sports, she said, where children from well-off families pay to play in club sports year-round and end up dominating school teams that used to be accessible to everyone.

“It’s just getting harder and harder,” she said. “I’m not sure people fully understand what’s happening right in their community or in the community next door to them.”

This story was produced by the Globe’s Money, Power, Inequality team, which covers the racial wealth gap in Greater Boston. You can sign up for the newsletter here.

title: In its 60th year, Metco is a success, Boston families say — but remains frozen in time
text:
For over 60 years, more than 20,000 predominantly Black and Hispanic children have made similar long journeys to distant schools in wealthier, mostly white suburbs, where they have thrived in higher performing classrooms.

Yet despite indisputable evidence of its academic achievements, Metco remains a Civil Rights-era experiment frozen in time. Its enrollment is roughly what it was when President Jimmy Carter was in office and not a single suburb has been added to the program in nearly a half-century, including some of Boston’s immediate neighbors.

“Metco has shown us that this works, that it is worthy, that it is necessary, that it needs to be expanded,” said Karilyn Crockett, an MIT assistant professor of urban history, public policy, and planning. “There’s more to do.”

Critics such as Crockett question why, after six decades, Massachusetts still relies on a modestly sized, voluntary desegregation effort instead of a bolder, comprehensive solution. The systemic inequities that gave rise to Metco remain in Boston, where classrooms almost entirely serving students of color still lag behind their largely white suburban counterparts.

An expensive housing market reinforces those longstanding racial divisions by limiting where families can afford to live, leaving many city students without access to the same quality of public education available in the suburbs.

Since the first buses rolled out of Roxbury and Dorchester for the suburbs on Sept. 8, 1966, Metco has changed lives by offering Boston students a shot at an education in a wealthy school district.

The benefits are unmistakable. Students have better attendance, are more likely to graduate from high school, are more likely to attend college, and earn more in their careers, researchers have found.

But the sacrifice is real. Generations of Metco students have gotten up earlier, traveled farther, arrived home later, and ultimately had to work harder to obtain the same education as their suburban classmates. They’re outsiders in their own schools and have endured racism, classism, and more from what often is a cultural exchange that runs only in one direction.

“We see where they live, but they don’t come to see where we live,” said Vanesa Morales of Dorchester, who bought a used Hyundai to drive her Black daughter on nights and weekends for school activities in Wayland. “They don’t really get to know the people in Boston.”

The voluntary state program enrolls 3,200 K-12 students, about 5 percent of the Boston public school enrollment, in 33 suburban communities. But many of Boston’s immediate neighbors don’t participate, forcing some students to travel as far as Sudbury, Marblehead, and Scituate.

Among Boston’s closest neighbors, three — Brookline, Newton, and Needham — participate in Metco. Other nearby wealthier, majority-white suburbs such as Milton, Watertown, and Winchester do not.

Some cities elsewhere do things differently. In Raleigh, N.C., and Louisville, Ky., for example, sprawling school systems encompass both the city and suburbs, broadening the access for students to classrooms beyond where they live.

But Massachusetts assigns students into school systems based largely on municipal borders, and Boston and its suburbs remains racially segregated.

Boston has some strong — and even excellent — schools but quality varies widely. More than 14,000 Boston students attend schools that rank among the state’s lowest-performing.

For most, the higher performing, and largely white, suburban schools remain out of reach unless a family has the money to move.

The stasis is so entrenched that a group of families from Boston and other local cities sued the state in May, demanding education leaders impose more racial integration in public schools. One solution offered in their complaint: expand Metco.

“School segregation deprives all students of the benefits of learning with and from each other in racially and economically diverse schools,” the families said.

Education has always been one of the most powerful engines of upward mobility. It’s why Metco students are willing to travel so far. For the trip to Reading, Daniella packs yarn with her textbooks so she can knit hats and mittens on bus rides that take an hour to get there in the morning and even longer on the way home.

The journey adds to the work, but it has been worth it for Daniella, who has excelled in Reading, according to her mother, Kemeisha Daley.

“It’s a commitment,” Daley said. “If you want it to work, it will work.”

One day last spring, Brodi Morales began his commute before 6 a.m. with a long walk from his Dorchester home to his bus stop. After one ride, he transferred to a second bus for the 15-mile drive to Wellesley High School. His body is so attuned to the long journey that he naps and can wake up just as the driver approaches the school.

“It doesn’t even feel like two hours for me,” Morales said. “I legit sleep on the bus.”

Morales stood outside a largely empty Wellesley High. It was a little after 7:10 a.m., and it took another 20 minutes before the local students began to arrive. Where the yellow bus had left Morales, a fleet of late-model Cadillacs, BMWs, and Mercedes arrived driven by Wellesley parents, a virtual auto show of luxury vehicles dropping off his classmates.

On the chilly morning of Sept. 8, 1966, when buses left Roxbury and Dorchester with 220 youngsters bound for six suburbs, the Globe featured a photo of one under the headline, “History is made in Massachusetts.”

At the time, Paula Jackson was among students from Roxbury headed to Wellesley Senior High School. Now using her married name, Paula Davis, she remembers her mother learning of Metco that summer and becoming intent on enrolling her studious 16-year-old.

Wellesley was welcoming, but breaking down barriers proved hard. Her classmates offered polite smiles but remained distant. Davis was the only Black teen in a roomful of white students.

“My classmates did not know how to relate,” Davis said, “to a person who looked like me.”

But the education in Wellesley was far more rigorous than at Brighton High, set in a building with a new gymnasium, cafeteria, and natural light pouring into classrooms from large windows.

Over time, Davis built friendships. She still has a book of newspaper clippings from back then. In one, a photo shows her smiling with her classmates out on the school lawn. She went on to study business at Aquinas Junior College and worked as a property manager in the Boston area. But she still keeps her high school diploma in like-new condition from when she was awarded it on June 7, 1968.

“It was worth it,” said Davis, now 76. “despite the struggle.”

Metco began after the Boston School Committee resisted desegregating and refused to address inequities facing Black students. Before court-ordered busing nearly tore Boston apart, Metco offered a limited, voluntary solution that sent willing students to suburban schools.

Six decades later, the program formally known as the Metropolitan Council for Educational Opportunity is funded by the state with an annual budget of about $31 million. It is administered by the nonprofit Metco Inc., which also oversees a program that buses about 100 students from Springfield to nearby suburbs.

Boston Metco’s most notable alums include CNN anchor Audie Cornish, Boston’s first acting Black mayor, Kim Janey, and Michael Bivins and Ronnie DeVoe, members of the 1990s bands New Edition and Bel Biv DeVoe. DeVoe, who cohosted a fund-raiser to mark 60 years of “changing lives and creating opportunities,” described himself as a Metco kid from Newton North.

When the nonprofit needed a new leader last fall, Metco named Kandice Sumner, who attended schools in Weston, where she was the high school’s first Black female class president. Sumner’s mother is a Lexington Metco graduate.

“In an ideal world, Metco shouldn’t have to exist, because the things that cause it to exist no longer are a reality,” Sumner said. “This practical world needs Metco.”

Metco is often cast as a gift to Boston students of color, presenting them with access to suburban schools, said Malcolm Cawthorne, a Brookline native who serves as the town’s director of Metco. But the program was also intended to benefit children in the suburbs.

“The root of this,” Cawthorne said, “was to make our districts richer, and make our districts better.”

When suburban and urban students meet halfway, the binds can be transformative. Take the decades-long friendship between Anthony Jones, who is Black and originally from Roxbury, and Jim McCann, a white native of Sudbury.

“My life would definitely be missing something,” McCann said, “had I not met my lifelong best friend through Metco.”

Both men served as the other’s best man at their respective weddings.

The pair met while playing football at Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School, where they graduated in 2004. Their families bonded over dinners while they were in school. Jones sees McCann’s father as a mentor; McCann’s children think of Jones as Uncle AJ.

“This is beyond school friendships, this is family,” Jones said. “The most important thing that happened to me was getting into that Sudbury school.”

But the pressure of making Metco work most often falls to Boston residents whose children are enrolled in the program.

Instead of a cultural exchange, it’s often the job of Boston children and parents to build connections with host communities: planning long commutes and late nights to make time for afterschool sports, to friends hanging out, to meetings between parents and teachers.

“The Metco experience is not for the faint of heart, especially in parenting,” said Christopher Worrell, a state representative from Dorchester who graduated from Lincoln-Sudbury Regional High School in 2004. His own children now attend public schools in Newton.

Beyond the commute, racism has been a stubborn part of Metco’s history. Two Boston families filed federal civil rights complaints in recent years alleging discrimination in Melrose and Marblehead. Over the decades, countless other instances of bigotry haven’t resulted in complaints to the federal government.

Abriana Morales, a 2010 graduate of Wayland High School through Metco, described daily prejudice that caused a “mental strain” for families. If a Black boy, for example, played sports, he’d likely be embraced by a suburban school. A Black boy in the chess club? Not so much, she said.

And for Black girls, the pressure is even higher, Morales said. Some get called “loud and ghetto,” she said. If they stand up for themselves, Black girls especially risk being shut down by white peers, she said.

Morales is a teacher at a charter school in Boston, and her brother, Brodi, is the Metco student at Wellesley High whose bus dropped him off last spring a few minutes before the parade of luxury cars.

Brodi’s mother is Vanesa Morales, who bought a used Hyundai when her daughter attended Wayland schools through Metco. Morales enrolled her children in the program because of the topnotch education, she said, but that comes at a cost.

In Wellesley, Brodi said, stereotypes circulate about the Boston neighborhoods where he and other Metco students live. Because of the stigma, Brodi doesn’t always volunteer that he’s enrolled through Metco, and said even some of his teachers don’t know.

Brodi is from a multi-ethnic family: his mother is Hispanic, his sister Black, and he is white.

His mother wants her son to be proud of where he is from.

“I don’t want Brodi to go into Wellesley,” Vanesa Morales said, “and then look down on Boston.”

On a late spring afternoon, Brodi recalled chatting with some Wellesley teens when the topic turned to Dorchester. They didn’t know Brodi lived there, he said, and one of them described it as a dangerous neighborhood.

Brodi didn’t say anything, but the remark stung. He told the story in front of his sister, Abriana Morales, during a recent visit, and she pressed him about that moment in Wellesley.

“That’s your opportunity,” she said, “to be like, ‘I live in Dorchester.’ ”

As they talked in the family’s Dorchester kitchen, a poster on the wall listed “12 things to always remember.” Everyone’s journey is different, read one. Another said: Judgments are not about you.

Brodi considered his sister’s point. His friends wouldn’t care he’s from Dorchester, he argued, so why bring it up?

“It shouldn’t matter,” Brodi said, “where you live.”

title: Results are in from city survey aiming to amplify experiences of Black men, boys in Boston
text:
The summary of the report was released last week.

Among the other disparities faced by Black men and boys locally are shortfalls in education, health issues, access to mental health services, criminal legal exposure, and lack of awareness about available services, the report said.

“The evidence is clear on what Black males identify as most urgent and on why existing resources are often not experienced as reachable or trustworthy,” the summary of the report said. “The next step is not more fragmentation.”

In a statement, Frank Farrow, executive director of the Office of Black Male Advancement, said the first phase of the study “represents a critical milestone in our commitment to advancing equity for Black men and boys in Boston.”

“This is not just a report, it is a road map,” Farrow’s statement said. “Our focus moving forward is to translate these insights into targeted strategies, stronger partnerships, and real outcomes that expand access, build trust, and create pathways to prosperity.”

The findings of Phase 1 will be used to frame future planning, reporting, and actions across departments to reduce barriers and level the playing field for Black men and boys in Boston.

The report documents “the voices and experiences of our residents to guide priorities across departments,” Wu said in the statement. “I’m grateful to the Office of Black Male Advancement, the Black Men and Boys Commission, the Tury Institute, and every resident who contributed to this critical effort. We look forward to continuing our work together to build on Boston’s progress.”

More than 2,000 Boston residents participated in the study. Their feedback was combined with information gathered from citywide survey data, stakeholder interviews, deliberative engagement sessions, and community outreach.

“As a Roxbury native and former city councilor, I’ve long believed that Boston must take a hard, honest look at the inequities facing Black men and boys, and act on what we find,” Tito Jackson, former chair of the Black Men and Boys Commission, said in the statement.

“During my time as chair of the commission, advancing this equity study was about building accountability and grounding our work in the lived experiences of our community,” Jackson said. “Phase 1 delivers on that vision.”

The priorities highlighted in the report include pathways to careers and living-wage jobs, housing affordability, access to transportation and childcare, and mental health support that fit with Black men’s lived experiences.

For Black boys, the report recommended improvements to education quality, mentorship, community safety, and minimizing exposure to criminal courts.

Bindu Kalesan, chief executive officer of the Boston-based Tury Research Institute, said this “consequential project ... centers the lives, experiences, and needs of Black male residents in Boston.

“We hope the findings will inform and move the needle towards accountable action toward structural equity,” Kalesan said in the statement.

Maddrey Goode, chair of the Black Men and Boys Commission, said the study “puts real voices and real experiences at the center, and what we’re hearing is clear: Our communities are navigating systems that weren’t built with them in mind.”

“As the new chair, my focus is on building on the progress of my predecessor,” Goode said in the statement. “How do we close the gaps, rebuild trust, and make sure Black men and boys can actually see and feel the impact of this work in their daily lives? That’s the standard we’re holding.”

The second phase of the study will be completed over the next year. It will provide a detailed set of recommendations and will provide a citywide resource guide, covering 150 resources across 50 city departments, along with an asset map of services available to Black male residents in Boston.

title: MBTA buses to begin using automatic cameras to ticket vehicles blocking bus lanes, stops
text:
With fines topping $100 for some infractions, the program represents a crackdown on bus lane laws after years of complaints.

Starting Jan 1., parking in a bus stop will automatically bring a $100 fine, while drivers recorded committing a moving bus lane violation will first receive a warning followed by escalating penalties, beginning at $25 for a first offense and maxing out at $125 for four or more violations over 180 days.

Fines are similar for commercial vehicles, though they begin at $50 for the first bus lane violation.

“This program is about keeping buses moving, but also about keeping people safe,” said Phillip Eng, the MBTA’s general manager and the state’s interim transportation secretary. “When bus lanes and stops are blocked, thousands of riders are impacted and lose time out of their schedules every day.”

The warning period, which begins Oct. 1, will be piloted along Boston’s SL4 and SL5 bus routes, which run from Nubian Square to Downtown, officials said.

These will also be the first targeted for fine enforcement as well, though officials said they plan to install the cameras across all bus routes in early 2027.

The driver notification process will mirror existing systems for HOV lane violations, officials said, adding that bus stop violations trigger immediate fines due to “creating an immediate threat to safety and accessibility.”

License plate information is read by cameras without any intervention from bus drivers, according to the MBTA, although employees will review footage to confirm violations before mailing tickets to the address connected to each driver’s registration.

In-state vehicles will receive mailed warnings or tickets within 14 business days, while those registered in other states and countries will receive theirs within 21 business days, officials said.

Drivers may submit an appeal within 60 days, officials said.

The cameras will not be used to track vehicles, the MBTA said. The data collected cannot be shared or used outside the lane enforcement program and will be deleted after 120 days.

In accordance with state law, the MBTA has also said it won’t use recorded data to identify drivers, passengers, or the contents of a vehicle, and will redact footage of these elements before using it to issue a notice.

The contract for the cameras was awarded to third party vendor Hayden AI over the summer, following a 30-day demonstration, an MBTA spokesperson said.

The use of automatic license plate cameras on MBTA buses was authorized under a 2025 law; the MBTA adopted the regulations in October.

Tickets will not be issued in certain situations where drivers may legally use bus lanes and stops, officials said, such as making way for emergency vehicles, temporary stops in bus lanes while parking, and making legal turns in bus lanes, provided drivers have given buses the right of way.

title: Boston sues Trump administration over $20 million grant for street safety upgrades in Roxbury
text:
The money was earmarked for the Roxbury Resilient Corridor project, which had planned for a number of improvements to Melnea Cass Boulevard, Malcolm X Boulevard, and Warren Street. The project fulfilled all the RAISE grant criteria, including by prioritizing a historically disadvantaged and underinvested area, the city said.

The $20 million would have gone toward installing safer sidewalks, pedestrian crossings, and bike lanes; addressing needed road maintenance; adding better stormwater management to reduce flooding; and improving bus service, according to the lawsuit.

“Boston earned this competitive grant to meet community needs and address long-needed infrastructure upgrades,” Wu said in a statement Monday. “The City of Boston will continue to fight back against lawless federal attacks, and we urge the court to reverse the Trump administration’s illegal actions and restore these critical funds for Roxbury.”

The city is arguing the Transportation Department illegally revoked the funds for “overtly political” reasons. According to the lawsuit, city staff spent hundreds of hours since 2022 to meet the requirements for receiving the federal funds, and did not receive any indication the money would be canceled. The city then received a brief letter from the Transportation Department in September 2025 saying the project “no longer aligns with DOT priorities” because it included electric vehicle chargers.

The letter did not offer the city a chance to respond or appeal the decision, the lawsuit said. The department also sent similar letters to other cities set to receive RAISE grant funds, including Albuquerque. In October 2025, the city offered to remove the EV charging stations from the project, but the federal government still did not agree to release the funds, according to the lawsuit.

“DOT grants typically involve a lengthy iterative process between the time the grant is awarded and the ultimate signed agreement, and DOT has consistently engaged in this process as a good-faith partner with the City,” the lawsuit said. “Prior to 2025, DOT had never abruptly withdrawn an award from Boston.”

The Department of Transportation is reviewing the lawsuit, and “remains committed to ensuring that taxpayer dollars are spent wisely and in ways that benefit all Americans,” a department spokesperson told The Boston Globe in a statement Monday.

US Representative Ayanna Pressley, who had advocated for the Biden administration to back the project in 2022, slammed the reversal in a statement Monday.

“These funds are an essential investment in Roxbury and the unlawful cancellation of this grant is more evidence of [Secretary of Transportation] Sean Duffy and Donald Trump’s contempt for the people we serve,” Pressley said.

“Our shared constituents should be able to get where they need to go and public transit is a public good,” she continued. “The law is on our side here and this lawsuit is a critical step in defense of this project that our office fought hard to secure funding for.”

Without the federal dollars, the city “was forced to suspend” the project, according to the lawsuit.

“For decades, Roxbury has waited for significant investments to improve our roads and sidewalks, add more trees and public spaces, and keep our families safe,” said the Rev. Willie Bodrick II, senior pastor of Twelfth Baptist Church on Warren Street, in a statement. “These federal funds are critical in delivering much needed improvements, making it easier for everyone but especially our kids and elders to breathe clean air and get to where they need to safely in their community.”

Last year, Boston joined a group of municipalities in a federal lawsuit against the Trump administration after the White House moved to withhold $3.6 billion in federal grants to address homelessness and improve public transit.

title: A recall is brewing in Lawrence
text:
“These cases are taking his mind away from being a mayor. It’s too much going on in his life, and we need to have the city keep running,” said Sarah Perez Marquez, one of the residents leading the recall effort. “If he doesn’t resign, this is our only option.”

DePeña pleaded not guilty to the felony wire fraud and money laundering charges in August. Federal prosecutors accused him of fraudulently obtaining more than $1.6 million in pandemic relief loans, money they say he then used to pay down debts and bankroll his successful 2021 mayoral bid.

Then on Thursday, a new slew of charges dropped. Campbell’s office charged DePeña with 14 counts of distributing a wiretapped communication and one count of witness intimidation. Her office said DePeña, after installing private security cameras for his City Hall office, recorded a hallway conversation between two employees, and then distributed that video to 14 people.

DePeña’s attorney didn’t respond to questions Sunday, but the second-term mayor previously brushed off questions about whether he should step aside after the federal indictment was unveiled, saying “of course” he could still be mayor.

Controversies have repeatedly dogged the mayor since he took office almost five years ago. In 2023, DePeña’s former chief of staff was charged, and later convicted, of possession of child pornography. And just last year, DePeña’s opponent in the 2025 mayoral race, Juan “Manny” Gonzalez, accused the incumbent’s supporters of ballot harvesting and submitting batches of absentee ballots on behalf of voters, prompting Secretary of State William F. Galvin to “take over” supervision of the city’s elections department. DePeña went on to win another term by fewer than 1,000 votes.

The latest round of charges, if true, would be a “shame to the city,” said Lawrence City Council President Jeovanny Rodriguez. At 89,000 residents, Lawrence is a Latino-majority city that has long been a gateway for immigrants from the Dominican Republic and a hub for Puerto Ricans.

“A lot of people are here to work and pay their taxes as part of the American dream, and they deserve a certain quality of service from the local government,” Rodriguez said.

While he didn’t directly call for DePeña to step down, the mayor “should consider the time and the effort that this is going to take for him to fight all those [charges],” Rodriguez added.

Recall efforts, while relatively rare across the state, are something of a rite of passage in Lawrence; DePeña would be at least the third straight elected mayor to face such an effort.

In 2011, some residents tried to recall then-mayor William Lantigua, who was plagued by his own swirl of legal controversies during his single term. Lawrence residents also twice attempted to recall Lantigua’s successor, Dan Rivera, who ultimately stepped down in 2021 for a job leading MassDevelopment, a quasi-public state agency that helps finance development around the state. Each attempt died before making it to the ballot because those pushing the efforts failed to collect the required signatures to set up a special election.

Those looking to recall DePeña, however, aren’t deterred by the hurdles ahead. To trigger a recall election, they first have to submit an affidavit to the city’s clerk signed by 100 Lawrence voters. Then the clock starts: They’d have 30 days to collect signatures from around 6,500 Lawrence voters, per the process laid out in the the city’s charter.

Supporters of the recall are aiming to file the affidavit this week, Perez Marquez said, and they already have 150 volunteers on board to collect the necessary signatures.

Still, she’s hoping it won’t actually come to that.

“Hopefully, when [DePeña] sees that this is for real, he will resign,” she said. “Because this is a bad mark for Lawrence.”

Is a recall the right move? Let us know what you think here.

EXIT STAGE LEFT: 2026 might be the year the campaign debate began to disappear by James Pindell, The Boston Globe: For decades, the fall televised debate served as the defining civic ritual of American politics: an unscripted, 60-to-90-minute job interview under unforgiving studio lights. Yet across the 2026 electoral map, this time-honored tradition is quietly collapsing.

COMMON INTERESTS: One Commonwealth, the non-profit Governor Maura Healey and Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll launched in 2024 to bolster the state’s housing interests, is throwing its weight behind a ballot question that would reshape zoning laws to make it easier for developers to build single-family homes on smaller lots.

Question 7 is “a common sense step to ensure our communities have room for the next generation of families and is a tool to create opportunities for home ownership,” Kate Kelly, the group’s executive director, said in a statement. Healey herself endorsed the question last week.

PLAYING THE CHARLIE CARD: Former Republican governor Charlie Baker hasn’t endorsed his party’s nominee for governor in Massachusetts — and hasn’t said if he will before the Nov. 3 election. But that isn’t stopping Michael Minogue from borrowing the NCAA president’s name, image and likeness in an attempt to link himself to the popular former governor.

Minogue on Friday night posted a photo of himself standing shoulder to shoulder with Baker in front of a display for Abiomed, the company Minogue once led.

“When Charlie Baker was governor, people wanted to move to Massachusetts. I was running a business and was able to recruit employees from around the country. That’s not the case today,” Minogue captioned the photo. “When I’m governor, I’ll build on Charlie’s legacy and make Massachusetts the best place to live, work, and raise a family.”

Neither Minogue’s campaign nor Baker responded to questions Sunday about the post or the potential for a Baker endorsement.

MONEY TRAIN: It cost $1 billion more to run the commuter rail than the T contracted. The bill is about to get bigger. by Diti Kohli, The Boston Globe: The T has so far paid at least $5.2 billion to French transportation company Keolis to run its 300-some miles of regional commuter rail service — nearly $1 billion more than the $4.2 billion T leaders estimated when the contract was inked more than a decade ago. The escalating costs offer a glimpse into just how expensive it could be to keep trains moving under the T’s next contract.

SMILE! YOU’RE ON CAMERA: MBTA buses to begin using automatic cameras to ticket vehicles blocking bus lanes, stops by Bryan Hecht, The Boston Globe: Starting this week, drivers illegally blocking bus lanes and bus stops will be recorded by newly installed automatic cameras on the vehicles traveling along routes in Roxbury, the South End, Chinatown, and Downtown, officials said. Drivers will receive tickets at the start of next year. With fines topping $100 for some infractions, the program represents a crackdown on bus lane laws after years of complaints.

DEMOLITION MAN: How Doug Burgum became Trump’s go-to-guy for D.C. construction projects by Julian E.J. Sorapuru, The Boston Globe: President Trump has spent much of his second term directing an overhaul of Washington’s iconography in his image. And Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum is the one he turns to to make it a reality. From the Triumphal Arch to the Garden of American Heroes to the “US Open-caliber” golf course — and, of course, the troublesome Reflecting Pool — Burgum has a hand in it all.

FIELD OF SCHEMES: Trump administration considers building baseball park in Grand Teton National Park by Jake Spring and Stephanie Apstein, The Washington Post: The Trump administration has scouted locations in Grand Teton National Park to build a baseball park to host an MLB game, according to two other people familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to the media.

HISTORY RE-MAKER: Trump is using the government to wage an unprecedented American history culture war by Julian E.J. Sorapuru, The Boston Globe: In addition to his attempts to control the Smithsonian, Trump has also directed initiatives to filter what parts of America’s story are celebrated in monuments and on federal lands. Meanwhile, thousands of cultural organizations across the country have had their work interrupted and threatened in an effort to force historical narratives bankrolled by government agencies to align with the president’s cultural sensibilities.

He’s slashing quality at nursing homes. The state is letting it happen. by Kay Lazar, Neena Hagen, and Tricia L. Nadolny, The Boston Globe.

Saint statues to be kept from ‘prying eyes,’ Quincy mayor told staff by Peter Blandino, The Patriot Ledger.

How much leeway should officials have to deny gun licenses? SJC will decide. by Jennifer Smith, CommonWealth Beacon.
