title: Violent Boston employee arrest has two city councilors calling for overhaul of mayor’s hiring protocols
text:
Two Boston city councilors are calling for an emergency hearing to tighten up the Wu administration’s employee screening and hiring protocols, in light of the latest city worker arrest that involved a violent confrontation with a state trooper.

Councilors Erin Murphy and Ed Flynn plan to introduce an order for a hearing at Wednesday’s City Council meeting “regarding immediate reforms to background checks, sex-offender screening, and ongoing suitability reviews for City of Boston hiring and employment.”

“In recent months, there has been a surge of troubling incidents involving City of Boston employees, including fights and other violent or criminal behavior, raising serious concerns about the adequacy of pre-employment screening, continuous monitoring and suitability policies,” the councilors’ hearing order states.

“The pattern of incidents in recent months underscores a serious gap in safeguards, suggesting additional cases may exist undetected, and requiring urgent policy reform to ensure public trust and safety,” the councilors’ order went on to state.

Murphy and Flynn referenced reports of the latest city employee arrest, involving what they described as a “violent confrontation” with a State Police trooper in South Boston.

The confrontation that led to the arrest of Nasiru Ibrahim, a 25-year-old property management employee for the city, occurred on July 30, but it didn’t come to light until last Friday, when it was first reported by WCVB-TV.

Ibrahim “was placed on unpaid administrative leave immediately after the city became aware of the allegations against him,” the mayor’s office said. He was paid $13,651 last year, per city payroll records.

“We are a city that holds all of our city workers to incredibly high standards,” Mayor Michelle Wu told reporters Monday. “That means on the clock, but also off the clock.”

Wu said the city is reviewing why Ibrahim was hired in the first place, given his criminal record that involves a past gun and drug arrest. Wu also mentioned the city’s commitment to its reentry services, which provide a pathway for ex-convicts to get hired by City Hall.

“We have many programs that the city has created to ensure that individuals get a second chance, who have done their time, who have put in the work to support themselves and take care of their own lives and are reentering our community have a pathway where it’s appropriate,” Wu said.

The councilors’ hearing order raises questions as to whether the mayor’s hires of Ibrahim — who tased a State Police trooper during the traffic stop — and a registered Level 3 sex offender, who worked for the parks and recreation department for most of this past year, were appropriate reentry opportunities.

The incident that led to Ibrahim’s arrest was documented in a State Police report, and captured on police body and cruiser dash cam footage, obtained by the Herald through Boston Municipal Court.

Per the police report, State Trooper Matthew Hickey chose to conduct a traffic stop after observing a 2014 Jeep Compass with “excessively dark window tint on the front windows” in the vicinity of Old Colony Avenue and Preble Street, which Hickey described as a high-crime area in South Boston.

After pulling the Jeep over on Old Colony Avenue, the trooper wrote that Ibrahim identified himself as a City of Boston employee who was in the area to pick up his daughter after getting off work. He was wearing a hat and T-shirt with a Boston property management logo, the police report states.

The trooper wrote that he detected an “odor of raw marijuana emanating from the vehicle,” and that Ibrahim’s nervousness, which was “unusual” for a typical traffic stop, “intensified” after he asked Ibrahim if he had previously been arrested, the police report states.

Per the video and report, Ibrahim said he was arrested on “all types of nonsense,” when he was a juvenile. When asked by the trooper whether he had been arrested on firearms offenses, Ibrahim said, “Yeah, but nothing recently. Not in like the last five years.”

The trooper wrote in his report that the situation escalated after he asked to search a visible backpack in the vehicle, based on Ibrahim’s “nervous demeanor,” “darting eyes,” and his admission to a prior gun offense.

When the bag was on Ibrahim’s lap, Trooper Hickey wrote in his report that after he asked to feel its contents and reached for the backpack, “Ibrahim abruptly yanked it away toward the passenger side and then placed the vehicle into drive in an attempt to flee.”

The police body cam footage captured the chaos, with Trooper Hickey diving headfirst into the Jeep and pleading with Ibrahim, “Stop! Stop dude! You’re going to make this worse!”

Hickey wrote that he wrestled with Ibrahim and was able to put the vehicle back into park, but the city employee then put the Jeep back into drive, “still attempting to flee.”

While struggling with Ibrahim inside the vehicle and attempting to put it back into park, the trooper wrote that he pleaded with the driver, saying, “You’re going to (expletive) kill someone, dude! You’re going to (expletive) kill somebody,” the report states.

As Ibrahim continued to try to place the Jeep into drive and flee, the trooper wrote that he drew his taser as he was “fully inside the vehicle and feared for my life,” along with the lives of others in the pedestrian-heavy area.

Trooper Hickey wrote that he deployed the taser into Ibrahim’s stomach. Ibrahim was then able to grab it and tase the trooper, who was forced to drop it to prevent the suspect from driving off, the report states.

“I felt an intense electric current surge through my upper torso, causing excruciating pain,” the trooper wrote in his report, adding that he punched Ibrahim twice in the face and “fish-hooked his mouth in an attempt to twist his head and gain control of his body.”

At that point, Ibrahim conceded defeat and an off-duty Boston Police officer rushed over to help Trooper Hickey take him into custody, per the report.

While there was “nothing of note” in the backpack, the trooper wrote in his report that he recovered a loaded firearm “equipped with a machine gun conversion device, commonly known as a ‘Glock switch” that converts a semi-automatic pistol into a fully automatic weapon.

The gun had been wrapped in a Boston property management sweatshirt that Ibrahim had allegedly been sitting on during the traffic stop. Ibrahim does not have a license to carry a firearm in Massachusetts, the report states.

Ibrahim, of Norwood, was arrested on 12 charges. Seven were firearms offenses that included a violation with a prior violent/drug crime, assault and battery on a police officer with serious bodily injury, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, resisting arrest, and two motor vehicle offenses.

He was arraigned in South Boston Municipal Court on July 31, and ordered held on $75,000 bail with GPS and home confinement if released. His next court date is Sept. 5 for a probable cause hearing, the Suffolk District Attorney’s office said.

Ibrahim’s attorney, Peter Marano, said the traffic stop that led to his client’s arrest was “questionable.” He said it was unusual for a trooper pulling over a vehicle for a “bogus” tinted windows civil offense to ask about what’s inside a bag in the vehicle, and question the driver about whether he had a prior firearms offense.

Marano also argued that his client, a black man, panicked when a white state trooper “aggressively” dove into the vehicle, which made Ibrahim try to drive off.

“I don’t know what it’s like to be a black man stopped by white state troopers, but I’m quite certain the level of fear and nervousness, given what’s going on, is kind of high,” Marano told the Herald. “Diving into a window head-first of a car that never really moves over window tint. I mean, that’s a little over the top.”

Marano said there are “significant constitutional issues” with the traffic stop.

“He’s pled not guilty and we’re going to let the system play it out, because this stop is very, very questionable, to say the least,” Marano said.

The incident is the latest in a string of allegations that have been made against city employees.

Jacqueline Cherisme, 34, a housing supervisor with the Boston Public Health Commission, was the latest city employee to be arrested last month in connection with a deadly shooting that occurred on April 19. Cherisme was placed on unpaid administrative leave by the commission.

Last month, the Herald reported on how a Wu administration official was placed on unpaid leave but is still employed by the city months after being arrested on felony assault charges.

Daunasia Yancey, 33, of Jamaica Plain, was arrested and charged with assault and battery and assault and battery with a dangerous weapon on April 11, after allegedly attacking the ex-wife of her then-girlfriend in a Roxbury home during a dispute the former spouses were having over the return of a birth certificate.

Yancey is the deputy director of Mayor Wu’s office of LGBTQ+ Advancement.

In May, Marwa Khudaynazar, chief of staff for the Office of Police Accountability, and her boyfriend, Chulan Huang, neighborhood business manager for the Office of Economic Opportunity and Inclusion, were arrested following a domestic dispute that occurred in Huang’s Chinatown’s home.

Both were placed on unpaid leave immediately after their May 15 arrests and arraignments and fired by the city days later, on May 20.

In that instance, Wu cited the two employees trying to invoke their “official status” as city employees “to try to prevent the consequences of a police interaction,” rather than the incident itself as being the reason for their terminations.

title: Boston City Council to hold Mass and Cass emergency declaration hearing after blocked vote
text:
South End residents are expected to “pack the room” at a long-anticipated public hearing that the Boston City Council plans to hold on the city’s open-air drug market at Mass and Cass, which has spilled over into surrounding neighborhoods.

Councilor John FitzGerald has scheduled an off-site Council hearing at the Hampton Inn and Suites at 811 Massachusetts Ave. It will be held on Sept. 4 at 6 p.m.

The hearing is focused on a resolution put forward by Councilor Ed Flynn that seeks to declare a public health and safety emergency at and around the intersection of Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard, an area that’s become known as Mass and Cass or Methadone Mile.

“We plan to pack the room,” said Brian McCarter, a resident of the South End, which has been hit particularly hard by the open-air drug use, dealing, and related violence that’s spilled over from Mass and Cass into surrounding neighborhoods.

FitzGerald previously told the Herald that he had initially been targeting the South End for an off-site hearing, but ran into difficulty with the availability of the location and Wu administration officials set to participate in the discussion.

The scheduling difficulty was part of broader criticism from FitzGerald, Flynn and Councilor Erin Murphy, who accused Mayor Michelle Wu and her Council allies of putting hot-button hearings on the backburner until after the Sept. 9 preliminary election, to avoid issues that may be politically risky for the mayor.

Councilor Sharon Durkan, a former employee and ally of the mayor, blocked an immediate vote on Flynn’s resolution this month, thus sending it to a hearing. When doing so, she said an emergency declaration is not necessary as it would not lead to any additional funding to address the addiction and homelessness crisis.

FitzGerald, chair of the Public Health, Homelessness and Recovery Committee, said he had been targeting Sept. 4 initially for the hearing, but had been asked by the Wu administration to hold off on scheduling it until after the primary.

In a prior statement, he described the request, due to what he said was a lack of Wu administration availability, as an “egregious overreach of a manufactured excuse not to hear the issues before our city.”

FitzGerald said Friday that South End residents urged him to hold the hearing “sooner rather than later,” given the “rapid downturn of the situation,” in terms of why it was ultimately held before the preliminary election. He said there would be more coordination to get administration officials to attend a subsequent hearing.

Flynn spoke Thursday of the public pressure put on the Wu administration and other city councilors.

“I think it was due to residents in the South End and Roxbury demanding accountability from city councilors and the administration,” Flynn said. “They didn’t want to wait until after the election. They put a lot of pressure on the City Council. The administration did put a lot of pressure on City Councilor FitzGerald not to hold it, but I respect Councilor FitzGerald and his work to get it scheduled.”

Flynn added, “Residents deserve to be heard. That’s true in the South End and Roxbury. We need to listen to them and the best answers don’t come from here at City Hall. The best answers come from the residents.”

The hearing also comes amid criticism from Flynn, FitzGerald and other elected officials who represent the area and have called for the city to rethink its current approach to tackling crime, homelessness and drug use in the area.

Flynn has called the city’s plan, which began with clearing the tent encampment at Mass and Cass two years ago, a failure.

Since tents were cleared on Atkinson Street in November 2023, residents and some elected officials have stated that the open-air drug use, dealing and related violence has migrated, and, therefore, worsened in surrounding neighborhoods.

Flynn’s emergency declaration proposal comes at a time when the spillover from Mass and Cass has become particularly prevalent in the South End, according to residents there, who have been calling for more policing, and even the deployment of the National Guard.

The mayor has dismissed calls for a military response to tackle the issue, but has said the city is deploying more public safety resources in the area.

According to Flynn’s office, reports of serious public safety issues have “significantly escalated” in the past several weeks. Those incidents include car and business break-ins, along with multiple intruders who have entered and stolen from South End residents’ homes.

Residents taxed by Mass and Cass spillover in their neighborhoods are forced to side-step discarded needles and human defecation, which has left them frustrated and fearful for their public safety, Flynn’s office said.

“The status quo of crime and violence spreading from Mass and Cass can’t continue,” Flynn said Wednesday in a statement. “We need zero tolerance when it comes to public drug dealing and drug use, human trafficking, crime and assaults. On public health, we need a treatment-first approach for those battling addiction, and detox programs to address underlying mental and behavioral health issues.”

Mayor Wu has already come out in opposition to an emergency declaration at Mass and Cass and its surrounding neighborhoods.

“The city is using all levers of public health, public safety, and public works resources, in partnership with the community, providers, and the state, to end congregate substance use and the criminal activity that supports it,” Wu spokesperson Emma Pettit said in a prior statement. “Declaring a local public health emergency does not unlock any additional authority or resources.

“What is needed is continued coordinated, compassionate response to eliminate public drug use and address barriers to treatment, shelter and housing. This work is urgent and we are focused on concrete solutions,” Pettit added.

FitzGerald, in a statement issued Wednesday, said he sees the hearing, while focused on the emergency declaration proposal, as the “first in a series of hearings around the complex substance abuse, mental health and homelessness issues, specifically in the South End and its surrounding neighborhoods.”

“With this first hearing, we intend to hear directly from our residents and get a baseline understanding of what is being done today,” FitzGerald said, “and then have subsequent hearings to give the administration the opportunity to respond to the issues that are brought up.”

title: Boston preps for chaotic college move-in weekend: ‘Do not get Storrowed’
text:
Boston Mayor Michelle Wu said the city is taking steps to alleviate issues that may arise when college students begin to move into their new residences this weekend.

City officials estimate that more than 150,000 students will be attending colleges and universities in Boston this school year.

“Move-in day is a special tradition in Boston,” Wu said Friday at a press conference in Allston, one of the Boston neighborhoods that is expected to house many students this year. “All that activity also means a lot of coordination, and it can feel a little hectic every day in this period throughout our neighborhoods.

“That’s why our administration has been hard at work to make sure that our students and families can move in as smoothly as possible.”

City officials said there will be on-street parking restrictions in Allston, Fenway, Mission Hill and Roxbury to help provide parking spaces for vehicles being used to help students move into their new dorms and apartments.

To lessen traffic congestion, the city’s Inspectional Services Department is not granting construction permits in those areas for the long weekend move-in period, which extends from Friday to Labor Day on Monday, the mayor’s office said.

The Boston Transportation Department has issued more than 4,500 moving truck permits across the city this month, with more than 2,500 issued for Aug. 29 to Sept. 1, according to BTD Deputy Director Nick Gove.

Wu warned students and families to be mindful of low bridges that U-Haul and other box trucks have been known to strike on Storrow Drive and Soldiers Field Road in Boston and Memorial Drive in Cambridge.

“If you are driving a truck, do not get Storrowed,” Wu said. “We want to make sure you keep all of your stuff and do not need to get removed from under the bridge.”

State officials have already warned movers driving trucks to avoid those collision-prone areas during college move-in season.

The day’s press conference also included preparations that city officials said will benefit college students and year-round residents beyond move-in weekend.

“At Inspectional Services, we’ve been working diligently to ensure a smooth transition with minimal disruptions to our neighborhoods,” ISD Assistant Commissioner Jessica Thomas said. “Throughout the week, ISD will deploy more than 60 staff members throughout the neighborhoods known to have a high turnover rate.”

The 60-plus ISD inspectors will conduct walkthroughs of areas heavily populated with students including, but not limited to, Allston, Brighton, Back Bay, Fenway, Mission Hill and Beacon Hill, the mayor’s office said.

“These teams will distribute flyers and brochures, conduct on-the-spot inspections, ensure residential trash has been properly disposed of, and verify that rental units are clean, sanitary, and free of hazards that may endanger the health and safety of all occupants,” Thomas said. “We urge property owners to take extra care in preparing for the tenant transitions.”

College students are advised to put out their trash by 6 a.m. on the day of pickup, or after 5 p.m. the day before to cut down on rat activity, register their vehicle with the city should they be looking to park on resident-only streets in their neighborhood, schedule their mattress disposal separately as it isn’t part of regular trash pickup, and call or log an online complaint to 311 to report any problems.

“If you’re moving to Boston, download 311,” City Councilor Sharon Durkan said. “One of the most fun things to do is report your neighbors for things that they shouldn’t have done.”

College students will receive a number of benefits from the city and its partnering organizations this year, including $9 Boston Red Sox tickets, and free admission to the Museum of Fine Arts, Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, Institute of Contemporary Art, and New England Aquarium, Wu said.

Students will also see their admission discounted at JFK Library and Museum, Paul Revere House, and Museum of African American History. They will further benefit from catching a show for as little as $20 at the Boston Ballet, Huntington Theater and Boston Symphony Orchestra, the mayor said.

For transportation, Bluebikes offers students a 55% discount on annual passes, and the MBTA, for a limited time, is providing free rides after 9 p.m. on five Fridays and Saturdays this fall, as part of its extended late night T service, officials said.

Wu also referenced the fraught political situation between the federal government and sanctuary cities like Boston, in her remarks.

“A quarter of our students come from all over the world, and while there are some right now who are targeting and threatening international students and trying to insert their own agenda of fear and division in Boston, we are a home for everyone, and we’re making sure that all of our students and city residents live in a welcoming community for all,” Wu said.

“We will continue to work with our university partners to communicate directly around these issues,” the mayor said, “and do everything possible to make sure that Boston is a home away from home.”

title: Legendary Boston R&B group celebrated with ‘New Edition Way’ (Photos)
text:
Saturday was “New Edition Day” in Boston in honor of the legendary R&B group founded in the city’s Roxbury neighborhood in 1978.

“It is an honor to welcome home Roxbury natives New Edition to celebrate their global impact, from our communities here in Boston to the music industry worldwide,” said Mayor Michelle Wu ahead of the celebration.

The day began at 10 a.m. at the corner of Ambrose and Albany streets, when Wu unveiled that Dearborn Street would be named “New Edition Way.” Then, at 11 a.m., the community celebrated with a block party on the newly named street in honor the group, whose members are Ronnie DeVoe, Bobby Brown, Ricky Bell, Michael Bivins, Ralph Tresvant and Johnny Gill.

The block party’s location at Orchard Gardens was symbolic, as the members of the group grew up there when it was known as Orchard Park.

“I am truly grateful for the privilege of being made a permanent fixture in our city that has played such a significant role in shaping our lives and career,” Bell said.

Bobby Brown said “Boston is where it all began for us. This honor means the world to me.”

title: Pols & Politics: Tania Fernandes Anderson hands out endorsement ahead of sentencing
text:
Ex-Boston City Councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson is getting all her ducks in a row ahead of her sentencing on federal corruption charges next week, including by endorsing a candidate in the crowded race for her former District 7 Council seat.

Fernandes Anderson, convicted in May on two public corruption charges tied to a $7,000 City Hall kickback scheme, said last week that she is endorsing Said Abdikarim for Boston City Council District 7.

“Said embodies the work ethic, compassion, and courage our community needs,” Fernandes Anderson said in a statement last Wednesday. “He demonstrates unwavering integrity and prioritizes the needs of District 7 residents.

“At this crucial time, we need a leader who is deeply connected to the community and unafraid to hold the government accountable,” Fernandes Anderson said. “Said listens with humility and acts with boldness. If you want a dedicated public servant who will lead with courage and compassion, I urge you to vote for Said Abdikarim. Together, we can ensure that District 7’s voice remains powerful and respected.”

It’s unclear whether Fernandes Anderson’s endorsement, which came about a week before her sentencing is set to take place in federal court Friday, will help or hurt Abdikarim in the District 7 City Council race.

Eleven candidates are running for District 7, which includes Roxbury, Dorchester, Fenway, and part of the South End. The Sept. 9 preliminary election will whittle the field down to two candidates. Fernandes Anderson resigned on July 4, and the seat is currently vacant on the Council.

Fernandes Anderson, 46, pleaded guilty on May 5 to two public corruption felony charges that were lodged against her in a federal indictment last December, when she was also arrested by the feds outside her Dorchester home.

Four other charges were dropped as part of a plea deal she entered into with federal prosecutors in early April.

Fernandes Anderson doled out a $13,000 bonus to one of her Council staffers, a relative but not an immediate family member, on the condition that $7,000 be kicked back to her. The handoff was coordinated by text and took place in a City Hall bathroom in June 2023, the federal indictment states.

U.S. Attorney Leah Foley has recommended that the ex-councilor be sentenced to a year and a day in prison and ordered to pay $13,000 in restitution.

The two charges Fernandes Anderson was convicted on, wire fraud and theft concerning programs receiving federal funds, can carry respective sentences of up to 20 and 10 years in prison. Both carry fines up to $250,000. – Gayla Cawley

Another Republican emerges with eyes on 2026 U.S. Senate campaign…

A Republican who chairs the Westport School Committee and unsuccessfully ran for a state legislative seat in 2024 is considering running against U.S. Sen. Ed Markey next year.

Christopher Thrasher, a 40-year-old South Coast attorney and self-described public policy advocate, formed an exploratory committee this past week, a move he said will allow for a “testing the waters period” to engage voters and evaluate the feasibility of a campaign.

Thrasher took aim at Markey’s age and the Massachusetts Democratic Party for “refusing to pass the torch to a new generation.”

“No matter your personal political persuasion, the one thing most every American can agree on is that the status quo cannot hold. That is why I have decided to begin the process of exploring a run for U.S. Senate in 2026,” he said in a statement this past week.

Thrasher is just the latest in a series of Republicans who have started to debate running against Markey, a 79-year-old who was first elected to public office in the early 1970s and has served in the U.S. Senate since 2013.

Nathan Bech, a former town councilor from West Springfield, previously told the Herald he is also considering a run against Markey. John Deaton, who unsuccessfully ran against U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren last year, has also floated himself as a candidate.

Thrasher said elected officials need to “find new ways of addressing systematic failures in our government, and to embrace a new era of leadership that can restore hope and offer a renewed faith in the American dream.”

“I look forward to hearing from Massachusetts voters in the coming weeks and to taking these first steps toward making the dream a reality for every generation,” he said.

Thrasher is no stranger to running for elected office.

He ran a write-in campaign last year to secure the Republican nomination for the 8th Bristol House seat, a district that covers Westport and parts of Acushnet, Fall River, and New Bedford.

Thrasher lost by 261 votes in the general election to Rep. Steven Ouellette, a Democrat from Westport, according to state election data. A recount in late November confirmed the loss. – Chris Van Buskirk

title: BPS back to school: Officials aim to get more kids in classes as year kicks off
text:
BPS and city officials are gearing up for the start of school Thursday, personally reaching out to chronically absent students and sharing information with families.

“We’re trying to make sure our students are healthy, supportive, nourished and opened up to every possible opportunity,” said Mayor Michelle Wu at the BPS central office Wednesday. “And that all starts today.”

Wu, Superintendent Mary Skipper and volunteers with the BPS Re-Engagement Center headed out Wednesday morning to knock on doors and talk to families with students who have a history of chronic absenteeism or are at risk of dropping out.

BPS students from grade 1 to 12 will return to classes Thursday, while kindergarteners are scheduled to start on Monday.

Over the last four years, chronic absenteeism has dropped 10% across BPS schools. Chronic absenteeism is defined as missing 18 school days in a year for any reason.

Chronic absenteeism in high school remains “slightly above” pre-pandemic levels in the upper 40th percentile, though elementary school rates have leveled in the upper 20th percentile, Superintendent Mary Skipper said.

“There’s so many reasons why our students sometimes struggle to go to school,” said Skipper. “Mental health, sometimes they’re working, sometimes they have to bring an income in, or they’re taking care of other siblings. There’s lots of reasons that prevent them from being able to go that’s not just as simple as they don’t want to.”

The mayor and superintendent first visited the Roxbury home of a 19-year-old student who struggled transferring after her school closed. The student committed to returning Thursday, Skipper said, as district staff work with her principal and mom.

“It is about individual families,” said Wu. “It is about individual students, and how we can provide that targeted, individualized support for everyone.”

Wu also spoke to the “fear” in some families as ICE actions ramp up around the country, citing examples of families avoiding basic necessities like going to a doctor’s appointment or personally driving kids to school.

In a message to parents concerned, Wu reiterated that the city is “a home for everyone.”

“We do not ask about immigration status when it comes to registering for school, taking out a library book, taking advantage of any of the programs that we have, from kids through seniors and every generation in between,” the mayor said.

The officials also spoke to wide-ranging preparations for the new school year, from facilities updates to new bilingual programs to new food services.

Three new BPS school buildings are opening this year, Wu said, the Carter School in Roxbury for students with special needs, the Sarah Roberts Elementary School in Roslindale where the Sumner and Philbrick schools will be merged, and the PJ Kennedy School in East Boston.

The district is also launching nine new bilingual education programs this year, as well as updated literacy program material at all schools, the mayor said.

On-site cooking from scratch has been integrated at “nearly every school in the district,” Wu said, and those without room for a kitchen will be supported by the reopened Central Kitchen in Dorchester. For school meals, over 15% of the food will be sourced from Massachusetts or New England as of this year.

title: Josh Kraft parts ways with top advisors to his Boston mayoral campaign ahead of preliminary election
text:
Boston mayoral candidate Josh Kraft is parting ways with two key advisors who have helped to shape his campaign, due to strategic differences, in a shakeup that’s taking place just days before next week’s preliminary election.

The Kraft campaign and married West Roxbury couple Will Keyser and Eileen O’Connor of Keyser Public Strategies “mutually parted ways” earlier this week, a Kraft campaign spokesman said on Wednesday night.

“Josh is grateful for the professional leadership and support that Will and Eileen have provided to guide the campaign,” Kraft campaign spokesman Max Baker said in a statement. “Earlier this week, a mutual decision was made to part ways based on strategic differences as the campaign narrows to two candidates.

“Josh looks forward to reaching every Bostonian with his vision for how to bring better housing and more opportunity to the city,” Baker added.

Keyser and O’Connor have been Kraft’s top advisors since his campaign launched in February, typically appearing separately or together at all of his press events and public appearances.

The campaign shakeup comes less than a week before the Sept. 9 preliminary election, which political observers expect will narrow down the field of four candidates to Kraft and Mayor Michelle Wu. Both are Democrats.

Polls suggest Kraft is far behind the popular progressive incumbent mayor, however, with the latest polling from Suffolk University revealing in late July that he was 30 points behind Wu, in terms of being the preferred candidate for voters.

A statement from Keyser Public Strategies provided by O’Connor does not get into specifics about the separation.

“We are grateful for the opportunity to work with Josh,” the Keyser Public Strategies statement said. “We deeply respect and admire his many years of community service work, and wish him the best in his mayoral campaign.”

Keyser previously worked as director of communications in Sen. Ted Kennedy’s office, and later as a key strategist to Gov. Charlie Baker’s winning campaign, while O’Connor worked on Congresswoman Lori Trahan’s campaign, according to their respective biographies on the firm’s website.

Max Baker did not respond when asked whether another consulting team would be stepping into their former roles on the Kraft campaign.

title: Long-shot candidate outshines Michelle Wu, Josh Kraft in Boston mayoral forum
text:
Long-shot candidate Domingos DaRosa stole the show at Tuesday night’s mayoral forum, which featured education, immigration and home-ownership topics seen as key issues to voters representing the Black faith community.

It remains to be seen how much DaRosa’s performance before a packed crowd at the Bethel AME Church in Jamaica Plain will translate to the polls in next week’s preliminary election, which political observers expect will narrow down the field to Boston Mayor Michelle Wu and her principal challenger Josh Kraft.

“I think Domingos owned the room tonight,” State Rep. Russell Holmes told the Herald after the roughly hour-long forum. “I think he did a very good job.”

The Mattapan Democrat said, however, that DaRosa didn’t necessarily elaborate on how he would bring about a change in city government, and people considering voting for him still have to learn more about where he stands on the issues.

“I didn’t hear that very clearly, but folks were very attracted to him,” Holmes said, citing DaRosa’s connection to the city.

Asked whether he thought his message would be able to resonate effectively with voters to make an impact in a mayoral race where money has been such a factor, DaRosa said he’s optimistic that voters will connect with a candidate who has a similar economic background.

“The majority of Bostonians are living paycheck to paycheck,” DaRosa said. “Most Bostonians are renting. So people understand the struggle, and that’s what I bring to the table. It shouldn’t be about how much money you have in the bank, but that’s what seems to be the norm for politics.

“We’ve learned from the presidency what that does and how that takes away the integrity of what this process should be,” he added.

DaRosa, a 48-year-old community activist who lives in Hyde Park, urged voters to do their research on the four candidates, three of which participated in Tuesday’s forum, to “see who fits the lifestyle that you’re looking to have and what they’ve been doing to improve the city.”

Despite his strong performance Tuesday, DaRosa remains a long-shot candidate, according to political observers and the latest Suffolk University poll, which revealed in late July that he was the preferred candidate for just 3% of respondents, compared to Wu, at 60%, and Kraft, at 30%.

DaRosa’s finances — roughly $1,600 cash on hand as of the end of August— are also a blip compared to the fundraising Wu and Kraft have been able to pull in during the race. Wu, the 40-year-old first term mayor, has more than $2.4 million cash on hand, per the state Office of Campaign and Political Finance.

While Kraft’s campaign spending has left him far less cash on hand — $147,740 reported with the OCPF as of the end of July — the 58-year-old third son of the billionaire New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft and longtime philanthropist has already put $2 million of his own cash into his campaign. He said on a recent radio appearance that he anticipates he will dip back into his bank account.

On Tuesday night, the three candidates were asked to weigh in on education, immigration and homeownership, but in a way that the forum’s moderators said were surveyed as being most important to the Black faith community.

For education, that meant asking candidates whether they would commit to renovating the Madison Park Technical Vocational High School in Roxbury, even if funds were not made available through the Massachusetts School Building Authority, commonly known as the MSBA.

Wu and Boston school officials said early this year that construction was expected to start on the Madison Park rehabilitation this summer, but there has been little movement since that time. City officials are seeking state funding for the project, which Wu said at Tuesday’s forum will cost more than $700 million.

“We will get there — I guarantee you that,” Wu said of the rehab.

Kraft used the question to get in a dig at the mayor’s spending on the public-private rehab of White Stadium, a $200 million project that has taxpayers on the hook for $91 million and counting. Boston Public Schools student-athletes are expected to share use of the facility with a professional women’s soccer team.

“Under my watch, we will finally fix and give Madison Park High School what every student, teacher and alumni there deserves: the best vocational school in Massachusetts,” Kraft said. “I will redirect money from the school capital budget, perhaps money going to White Stadium now, and prioritize the long-awaited renovation of Madison Park.”

Kraft, who opposes the mayor’s White Stadium plan, drew loud applause for his reallocation response.

DaRosa, a Madison Park graduate, was able to connect more with the crowd than Wu and Kraft on the question, by speaking of a larger issue in the area, the city’s open-air drug market at Mass and Cass. He said the issue is about more than funding. It’s about the need, he said, to provide inspiration for kids to go to Madison, in spite of their exposure to the crime and lawlessness that festers nearby.

“I want you guys to understand Madison is the gem and will be the gem,” DaRosa said. “And we’ll get the money from all the weed we’re selling in Boston.”

His remarks drew laughter, prompting one woman in the crowd to jest, “talk about a reallocation of funds.”

All three candidates gave similar answers on the remaining two questions, by saying they would commit to continuing the city’s sanctuary protections for illegal immigrants, by limiting local cooperation with federal authorities amid the Trump administration’s threats to flood the city with ICE agents; and reducing the racial homeownership gap.

The fourth mayoral candidate, Robert Cappucci, was unable to attend due to what event organizers said was a family emergency.

The preliminary election is next Tuesday, Sept. 9.

title: Wu administration planning police crackdown at Boston’s Mass and Cass amid crime surge
text:
The Wu administration plans to flood the Mass and Cass area with many of the 100 new Boston police officers who graduated from the academy last month, to crack down on the crime and drug use that’s spread like wildfire to other neighborhoods.

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu’s coordinated response team announced the city’s updated plan to address the open-air drug market at Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard in a five-page memo to the City Council on Wednesday.

The memo touches on plans to increase police deployments to the hot-spot areas of the South End, Newmarket and Nubian Square, without getting into specifics about how many officers currently patrol those areas and how many new ones will.

“Our plan combines continuous enforcement with direct pathways to divert individuals into treatment and away from the area through voluntary services, judicial diversion, and compulsory screening,” the memo states. “Our efforts target the drug use, drug dealing and congregation at the core of our public safety and quality of life challenges.”

The mayor’s updated plan to tackle open-air drug use at Mass and Cass and its surrounding neighborhoods, initially rolled out last February, comes at a time when residents taxed by spillover from that area have been begging for a police crackdown in their surrounding neighborhoods.

Residents, particularly in the South End, have been outspoken about what they see as a lack of police resources — citing the lack of, or slow response, to their 911 calls or 311 reports, after witnessing drug deals and crime, having to side-step needles or human defecation, or experiencing home break-ins.

Since tents were cleared on Atkinson Street in November 2023, residents and some elected officials have stated that the open-air drug use, dealing and related violence has migrated, and, therefore, worsened in surrounding neighborhoods.

South End residents have been calling for more policing, and even the deployment of the National Guard. The mayor has dismissed calls for a military response to tackle the issue, but previously said the city is deploying more public safety resources to the area.

The memo provides the first sense of what those additional resources will look like, with what city officials are calling a significant deployment to the Mass and Cass area. Many of the 97 new police graduates from Aug. 22 will be deployed, as part of prolonged effort to tackle outdoor drug use and addiction, the memo states.

Last month, the city also added a bike patrol in the police department’s D4, or South End, district. Portable cameras “for real-time monitoring of high-impact areas based on 311 and 911 call volumes” have been added by the city. A new flusher truck has been deployed to enhance street cleanings amid reports of filth, according to the memo.

The memo also includes two other notable updates to Wu’s Mass and Cass plan.

The city has created a new weekly case management “Hub table,” which was modeled on successful BPD Hub tables and aims to “connect individuals with substance use treatment and recovery programs,” the memo states.

The mayor’s team is also taking steps to reduce the public safety risk of discarded needles — an issue that gained significant traction after it was reported that a 4-year-old boy had to undergo HIV-prevention treatment after stepping on a needle while playing outside in South Boston in June.

The city is cutting down on needle distribution hours at AHOPE, ending weekend services and limiting distribution to clients. At the same time, the Boston Public Health Commission has increased outreach services for needle collection, from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m., to 5 a.m. to midnight. Syringe pickups take place through “proactive sharps sweeps of parks and schools every morning and afternoon,” per the memo.

A Public Health Commission spokesperson declined to say how many needles the city and its partner organizations distribute to drug users on a weekly basis, but indicated those questions will be answered at a Thursday City Council hearing.

Other changes, per the memo, involve city instruction to third-party organizations to “end tent and meal distribution outdoors and instead direct individuals who need assistance to authorized indoor programs.”

The memo indicates that the updates to the city’s approach to Mass and Cass are aimed at building on the mayor’s plan to end outdoor drug use in Boston.

“Open substance use in any part of Boston is illegal,” the memo states. “As we have built up a coordinated citywide response to shut down encampments, decrease overdose mentality, and continue to strengthen the continuum of care, our focus is now on ending congregate substance use in Boston and the criminal activity that supports it.”

The City Council and “residents of Boston” were delivered the memo on the eve of a long-awaited off-site Council hearing on Mass and Cass, which will take place at the Hampton Inn and Suites at 811 Massachusetts Ave. at 6 p.m. Thursday.

The hearing is responsive to a resolution filed by Councilor Ed Flynn, who is pushing for the city to declare a public health and safety emergency at and around Mass and Cass. The mayor, per her office, opposes such a declaration.

“It’s beyond time for zero tolerance for any criminal activity in Boston, including reform in our court system,” Flynn said in a statement. “Residents deserve to live in a safe and healthy neighborhood.”

The Herald has learned representatives from the Boston Police Department, coordinated response team and Public Health Commission will be attending on behalf of the Wu administration.

title: Boston distributes 80,000 needles to drug users per month, inflaming Mass and Cass tensions
text:
Tension in a packed Boston City Council hearing on how Mass and Cass spillover is taxing surrounding neighborhoods boiled over when a top Wu administration official said the city hands out more than 80,000 needles per month to drug users.

The admission came amid a back-and-forth between Councilors John FitzGerald, Ed Flynn and Boston Public Health Commissioner Bisola Ojikutu, who said the city handed out 14,500 needles last week and distributes 81,112 on average per month to drug addicts.

Amid audible gasps from the hundreds of people in attendance at the Hampton Inn and Suites at 811 Massachusetts Avenue on Thursday night, Ojikutu defended the city’s harm reduction approach as key to fending off HIV and other diseases that are commonly spread through shared needles during drug injection.

“If you consider the number of times someone is using fentanyl — it’s 10 to 15 injections per day,” Ojikutu said. “We are trying to decrease the risk of HIV exposure.”

She said the city’s Public Health Commission has identified a cluster of HIV cases in the Boston region. Most of the more than 200 HIV cases in the region are connected to Mass and Cass drug injection, Ojikutu said, adding that the number would be higher without the city’s harm reduction approach.

Despite the city’s continued commitment to that approach, Ojikutu said the city’s monthly needle distribution has decreased by 22% this year, compared to last year. But she said, when pressed by Flynn and FitzGerald, that distribution numbers are actually higher than 81,112 per month when accounting for the number of needles that are given to drug users by both the city and its partner organizations.

The back-and-forth on needle distribution further inflamed tensions among residents in attendance, many of whom reside in hot-spot areas for Mass and Cass spillover like the South End, Roxbury and Nubian Square and were forced to stand outside the meeting room in the hotel lobby as the room was at capacity early on.

Angry residents

Residents and business owners took to the mic to speak of the drug use, dealing, filth, and related violence that have become common in their neighborhoods. Residents and some elected officials have said the spillover has worsened since those problems migrated from Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard after the city cleared the Atkinson Street tent encampment in November 2023.

Some residents spoke particularly to the city’s needle distribution, likening it to enabling drug use in the city, while pointing out what they see as hypocrisy with law-abiding citizens and taxpayers getting pinched for simple parking violations while drugs are openly used and dealt on city streets without consequences.

Referencing the 1980s crack epidemic, Rob Zochowski said the city’s decision to hand out needles was an outdated approach from that time period.

“Don’t give out needles,” Zochowski said. “We are creating a false bottom for people. They have no incentive to change.”

Zochowski said that if he doesn’t pay his property taxes, the city will move to put a lien on or take away his home, but yet, people are allowed to use drugs and defecate on the street.

Liz Jacobson also hit on the different standard of accountability in the city, quipping that it is allowing drug use, but “if I double park in the South End for 20 minutes, I will get a ticket.”

When addressing councilors, she also referenced the “temperature” in the room, saying that it speaks to the frustration felt by residents of the South End and other hot-spot spillover areas, after years of dealing with the same problems.

Emergency in neighborhoods

Other high-tension moments occurred when FitzGerald stated the Council wouldn’t be taking any action that evening on the resolution that sparked the hearing, which was a push from Flynn for the city to declare a public health and safety emergency at Mass and Cass, and when Ojikutu reiterated the Wu administration’s stance, which is that it opposes such a declaration.

Ojikutu said the city has only declared a public health emergency once in its history, for COVID-19, and that such a declaration does not unlock any additional funding to address the humanitarian crisis at Mass and Cass, the region’s epicenter for the opioid epidemic, and would limit public process like the night’s hearing.

Residents and some elected officials strongly disagreed with that assessment.

“Being out of compliance with the state’s sanitary code at this stage is evidence enough we are in a state of emergency,” state Sen. Nick Collins, a South Boston Democrat, said in a statement to the Herald. “Whether it’s discarded needles in parks or blood and human waste on sidewalks and people’s doorsteps, it is all unsanitary and out of control.

“State law empowers the Boston Public Health Commission and City Council to respond to this public health crisis with extraordinary action. A declaration of emergency would empower the city, without delay, to be commandeer a facility for treatment that has proven to be unattainable thus far; marshall city employees to perform tasks that may be outside their job description like responding to the discarded needle proliferation; or request emergency funds from the state.”

Emilie Schleer, a 37-year-old mother of two, spoke of the brazen break-in that occurred at her South End home in July, when a homeless woman squatted in her residence while her family was away for the weekend. The woman slept and bled in her bed, bathed, ate her family’s food, and stole her jewelry, she has said.

Schleer said that there was another attempted break-in at her Worcester Square home on Wednesday night, while taking a shot at Mayor Wu’s frequent claim that Boston is the safest major city in the country.

“We’ve been told that it’s getting safer, but we really have an administration trying to redefine what safety is,” Schleer said. “We need laws that are followed and real consequences that actually mean something.”

Linda Zablocki, a South Boston resident, said she is “disgusted with the way the city has taken care of this problem.” She said the city is enabling drug use and crime to continue, and, referencing involuntary commitment, said it was incumbent on a functioning society to take care of people who can’t help themselves.

“Mass and Cass has done nothing but spread through the neighborhoods,” Zablocki said. “Now it is a cancer everywhere instead of just one area.”

Enough is enough

Frank Baker, a former Dorchester-centric District 3 councilor who is running for an at-large seat, said, “The party has to stop. It’s either arrest or Section 35.”

Wu administration officials defended the city’s approach to tackling the issue, speaking of the hundreds of homeless people who have been connected to low-threshold housing over the mayor’s first term, the 55 people on average from hot spots who have been connected to treatment since March and the 32 people the city has petitioned for Section 35, or involuntary commitments.

Police representatives also referenced the 467 drug-related arrests in the South End, Roxbury and other hot-spot neighborhoods for open drug use in 2025, an increase of 85% over 2024.

The Wu administration also announced this week that it was deploying many of the 97 new police academy graduates to areas impacted by the Mass and Cass crisis, as part of the mayor’s plan to end outdoor congregate drug use.

When peppered about why the city isn’t taking a harder line with arresting or involuntarily committing drug users, Kelly Young, director of the city’s coordinated response team, said it was key to address each person on a case by case basis, in order to save lives.

“There is no in between with the disease,” Young said. “It’s jail, institution or death.”

title: Tania Fernandes Anderson sentenced to 1 month in prison for Boston City Hall bathroom kickback
text:
Former Boston City Councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson was sentenced Friday to one month in prison, $13,000 in restitution and three years of probation.

She was also hit with a $200 special assessment.

The former councilor pleaded guilty in May to two public corruption charges tied to a kickback scheme federal authorities said she carried out in a City Hall bathroom.

She spoke in federal court in the Seaport saying she wanted to “ask God for forgiveness for every time I have fallen short.”

“I feel disgusted, like I can’t forgive myself,” Fernandes Anderson, 46, said.

Through tears, she added: “I didn’t want to speak today because I didn’t want to say the wrong thing. I don’t want you to think that I’m portraying myself as a victim. … I’m not an arrogant person as the media portrays me. I’m certainly not above reproach. I take full accountability.”

Her attorney asked for probation while the U.S. Attorney’s office sought a year and a day behind bars.

Judge Indira Talwani said sentencing guidelines called for 0-6 months based on the ex-councilor’s criminal record. The judge, who was appointed to U.S. District Court by former Democratic President Barack Obama, added the government was seeking “above that threshold.”

“It’s serious,” Talwani said. “Maybe it was low-hanging fruit because you thought you could get away with doing it, but it is a breach of the trust we put in public officials.”

Fernandes Anderson pleaded guilty to charges stemming from an allegation that she gave one of her staff members — a relative but not immediate family member — a $13,000 bonus on the condition that $7,000 be handed back to her. The handoff took place in June 2023 inside a City Hall bathroom, according to authorities.

Authorities said Fernandes Anderson’s tenure as a city councilor — that paid her $120,000 — was “marked by anything but true faith and allegiance to her constituents and to the City of Boston.”

“Tania Fernandes Anderson was elected to serve her constituents but instead, she deliberately used her elected position as a Boston city councilor to serve herself,” U.S. Attorney Leah Foley said in a statement. “From Boston’s City Hall to the Massachusetts State House, to local and state public officials, this office will continue to aggressively root out and expose public corruption.

“Massachusetts taxpayers deserve an honest government and accountability,” Foley added. “As federal prosecutors we have no fear nor favor, and there will be no blind eye or separate justice system for the powerful. The rule of law does not make exceptions for anyone, including someone like Tania Fernandes Anderson.”

Assistant U.S. Attorneys John Mulcahy and Dustin Chao, when arguing for the government’s recommended year-long sentence, sought to draw parallels between Fernandes Anderson’s case and past Massachusetts public officials who were convicted on corruption charges. They cited former state Sen. Dianne Wilkerson, who spent two years in jail, and ex-Boston City Councilor Chuck Turner, who was sentenced to three years, among others.

Talwani was not swayed, however, saying that the Fernandes Anderson kickback did not constitute a bribe, as it was initiated by the former councilor as a way to get additional funds, rather than by someone else who was trying to get her to do something in exchange for the cash.

Wilkerson was convicted after she was infamously shown stuffing $1,000 in cash bribes into her bra in a photo that was released by the feds. Turner, the last Boston city councilor to be probed by the feds, was convicted for pocketing a $1,000 bribe from an informant who claimed to be seeking a liquor license.

Prosecutors had argued that the Fernandes Anderson kickback was tantamount to an imperfect or unofficial bribe, but that the evidence didn’t allow the government to officially charge her in such a way.

Talwani disagreed. Nor was the judge swayed by prosecutors’ arguments that Fernandes Anderson’s actions since her arrest and federal indictment last December, conviction in May, and resignation in July, were indicative of a lack of proper remorse on the former councilor’s part.

Mulcahy and Chao had cited Fernandes Anderson’s media interviews, her defiance of calls from the mayor and five councilors to resign for months after her arrest, and the latest use of her public platform to endorse a City Council candidate seeking her former seat. The endorsement, prosecutors argued, was indicative of Fernandes Anderson trying to lay the groundwork for her return to a position of public trust.

Prosecutors also said the lengthier sentence would have served as a deterrent, putting elected officials on notice of such consequences should they be busted for future corruption.

Fernandes Anderson’s attorney, Scott Lauer, on the other hand, pointed to the more than 100 pages of letters of support that were submitted by community members and several elected officials ahead of the sentencing as indicative of the ex-councilor’s character and impact on others.

The letters sought to portray Fernandes Anderson as someone who had overcome the odds and a difficult upbringing to reach her position. While Talwani was sympathetic to that argument from the defense, she mentioned that was why the ex-councilor’s conviction and betrayal of the public trust was all the more “heartbreaking.”

Fernandes Anderson was the first Muslim-American, African immigrant and formerly undocumented person to be elected to the Boston City Council. She resigned in disgrace on July 4 from her Roxbury-centric District 7 seat, roughly a year and six months into her second term.

When speaking with reporters outside the courthouse after her sentencing, Fernandes Anderson blasted the media at length for what she saw as an unfair portrayal of her during her time in elected office, but kept her remarks brief when asked what she thought about being sentenced to jail.

“Everything,” she said, “happens for a reason.”

title: Disgraced ex-prosecutor Rachael Rollins advises Boston’s White Stadium opponents to keep up the pressure
text:
Disgraced former U.S. Attorney Rachael Rollins has waded into the White Stadium debate, by urging opponents of Boston’s public-private rehab plan to keep up the pressure on the mayor and city officials who support the project.

Rollins’ remarks were responsive to an email chain that includes residents who oppose the city’s professional soccer stadium rehab plan, elected officials and journalists. The chain began with criticism over what some residents see as the City Council president invoking a procedural rule to shut down debate over the potential for shifting to an alternative community-led and fully-public proposal.

The ex-U.S. attorney and Suffolk district attorney advised project opponents late last month to take advantage of this “finite opportunity” in the election cycle, by capitalizing on the vulnerability of city politicians seeking reelection.

“Politicians are usually only vulnerable when they are up for reelection,” Rollins wrote. “Many start listening more and being present more in communities. Currently our district is the only one out of the nine that does not have a designated city councilor. We are at a significant disadvantage. So our community needs to step up.”

She was referencing the vacancy in the City Council’s Roxbury-centric District 7 seat, which was previously held by Tania Fernandes Anderson who resigned in disgrace in early July after her conviction on two public corruption charges. Fernandes Anderson was sentenced to a month in prison in federal court on Friday.

Rollins also resigned in disgrace, in May 2023, after she was scorched in two federal reports that found she abused her position as the state’s top prosecutor, for, in part, trying to influence the outcome of the Suffolk district attorney’s preliminary election in favor of ex-City Councilor Ricardo Arroyo. Rollins was found to have leaked false information to the media about DA Kevin Hayden, among other offenses.

She landed on her feet and now works part-time at Roxbury Community College, where she was hired early last year. She is paid $109,852 as a special projects administrator focused on developing a program for formerly incarcerated people, according to the state comptroller’s office.

After moderating a high-profile panel discussion hosted by Boston mayoral candidate Josh Kraft late last month, Rollins is now wading into the White Stadium debate, by advising critics of the public-private rehab plan championed by Kraft’s opponent, Mayor Michelle Wu.

“I am happy that New Edition is getting a street named after them in Roxbury this weekend,” Rollins wrote, “but I want the City of Boston to care just as much that Roxbury: lost two Walgreens and is now a pharmacy (desert) for residents without vehicles; bears the brunt of the opioid crisis for our region as Mass and Cass is in Roxbury; has the highest number of abandoned properties and vacant lots in Boston; is a food (desert); and has the lowest life expectancy rate of any neighborhood in Boston according to the Boston Public Health Commission.”

Rollins advised White Stadium opponents that “everyone is watching now as the primary and general elections approach.”

“You can demand answers and accountability from a politician and still vote for them,” she wrote. “This isn’t about anti or pro any candidate. It is about fairness, access and opportunity.”

Opponents of the city’s public-private rehab are pushing for an alternative, fully-public rehab of White Stadium for Boston Public School student-athletes, who would share use of the stadium with a new National Women’s Soccer League team, beginning in spring 2027.

The Emerald Necklace Conservancy and community members unveiled an updated alternative rehab plan for the stadium that they say can be rebuilt for just $64.6 million, compared to the city’s roughly $200 million plan. Under today’s plan, taxpayers would be on the hook for the city’s half, at $91 million and counting.

Rollins closed her email by taking a swipe at the Wu administration’s focus on potential traffic and parking impacts that may tax Boston’s Charlestown neighborhood, as a result of the Kraft Group’s planned Everett soccer stadium, while turning a blind eye to those same concerns related to White Stadium.

“And don’t even get me started on the hypocrisy of Boston demanding a seat at the table for the Encore casino in Everett and now again with the potential New England Revolution stadium in Everett due to the crippling traffic impacts to Charlestown making Boston a host community resulting in a surrounding community agreement,” Rollins said, “while ignoring that exact same argument from the host communities of Roxbury, Dorchester and Jamaica Plain about White Stadium.

“But,” she said, “I digress.”

title: Editorial: Bostonians caught in crossfire of Wu — Trump fight
text:

title: Boston police officer shot in arm in shootout with suspect in Roxbury
text:
A Boston Police officer and a suspected criminal were both injured in a shootout in Roxbury early Friday morning, police say.

“We’re extremely, deeply proud of the officers for what they do daily and we’re very, very lucky and fortunate that there was no loss of life today,” Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox said from the scene.

According to a Boston Police Department statement, officers approached a group of “suspicious individuals” in the park at Dudley and Washington streets in Roxbury at around 12:45 a.m. Friday. Upon their approach, one member of the group fled and officers pursued.

When officers rounded Kenilworth Street, according to the BPD statement, the suspect fired at them and the officers fired back. One officer was shot in the arm, according to Cox, and the suspect was shot “multiple times.”

Both the officer and the suspect were taken to separate hospitals to be treated for non-life-threatening injuries.

“Tonight is another reminder of the kinds of risks our officers face 24 hours a day,” Mayor Michelle Wu said from the scene. “I am incredibly proud and thankful for their service and all that they put into taking care of our community members and making sure everyone is safe.”

Police say that the suspect is under arrest at the hospital. Police say they will release more information later. A BPD spokesman says the injured officer’s name will not be released.

This is a developing story.

title: Boston’s newest school proving a success despite proximity to Mass and Cass
text:
Students and parents at Roxbury Prep say they are seeing “new possibilities” at the charter school, just weeks into its first year, despite the building’s close proximity to the opioid-addled Mass and Cass.

Roughly 950 middle- and high school students are still acclimating to the new 83,000 square-foot building, but they say the community here is “strong,” which they believe is a critical tool in ensuring a successful future.

“We have a very strong community; we are all united under one building,” senior Zidane Nogueira told the Herald. “It’s going to impact my learning positively just because we have so many labs, so many resources that make us successful.”

Nogueira has been at Roxbury Prep since the sixth grade, building a “strong foundation” with a “strong group of people.” The new building in the mostly industrial neighborhood of Newmarket is a result of consolidating the charter school’s previous campuses in Mission Hill, Hyde Park and Nubian Square.

Demand for the grades 6-12 school, which typically sees over 90% of its graduates enroll in college, grew for the new facility, with a waitlist for admission as evidence, Principal Chelsea McWilliams told the Herald.

Students, staffers, and parents alike have all connected their excitement for the new space to a full regulation-size gymnasium, performing arts spaces and “state-of-the-art” science labs – amenities that the previous campuses lacked.

Abigail Adedeji, a senior on the volleyball team and student council, said the science labs allow her to gain hands-on learning experience. She’s also pretty psyched about the new cafeteria, which accommodates students across the school’s various grades.

“Having this huge building, and having a lot of community, it helps me because I now have more support from my teachers,” Adedeji told the Herald. “I can go to the gym, the weight room, everywhere and just hang out.”

Elected officials and school representatives held a pomp-and-circumstance and ribbon-cutting on Friday, continuing to pave the way for an upbeat environment.

Newmarket, which overlaps Dorchester, Roxbury, South Boston and the South End, has long grappled with Mass and Cass and the relentless spillover of open-air drug use, violence, and public sex.

Roxbury Prep is just blocks away from the intersection of Melnea Cass Boulevard and Massachusetts Avenue. Officials have pointed to the success of the Mason, a full-inclusion elementary school that has served the community for decades.

School leaders say that when the public charter network has opened buildings across the city since its founding in 1999, the crime rate tends to drop in the respective neighborhood.

Nayeli Castillo drives her ninth-grade son, Angel, to school from their home in Malden.

Castillo said her son, who is on an individualized education plan, is performing much better than he did in public schools, writing essays and conducting multiplication and division. All of which have helped his self-esteem, she said.

The mother says she believes school officials, in partnership with local law enforcement, are doing an “incredible job” in creating a safe learning environment, both from the inside and outside.

“I know some of the security guards by name — that is how integrated they are,” Castillo told the Herald. “I am in this area all the time at all different hours. I live all the way in Malden … and I travel to bring my son to this school because it is worth it. I have never felt that he is in danger.”

Jessica Gonzalez, a mother of a seventh-grader, echoed Castillo.

She said that she’s already starting to see a tangible difference in her son, Amori, at the new Roxbury Prep just weeks after the first day, on Aug. 25. Amori is feeling more pride at the school and is running for president of the student council — an opportunity he didn’t consider at his former campus.

“Having the new building specifically in this environment,” Gonzalez said, “is bringing new possibilities to the community.”

title: Exam school admissions debate reemerges ahead of new policy recommendation
text:
The exam school admissions debate split the BPS community across the city once again, as the superintendent and School Committee members take steps towards new policy changes this fall.

“Our district goal remains the same, to create an equitable and transparent policy that ensures all students have an opportunity for a seat at one of the exam schools within the city this time around,” said Superintendent Mary Skipper before the School Committee on Wednesday. “However, it’s important to me that we have a stable policy that will be left alone for a period of years.”

BPS officials presented on public comment on three proposed avenues to alter the current controversial exam school admissions structure at the meeting. The district will offer “recommended adjustments to the policy based on public feedback and our analysis” at the next school committee meeting, Skipper said.

Following the superintendent’s recommendation, the committee will vote on whether or not to adopt any changes.

The exam school admissions policy has been tweaked every year for five years changing the structure at the elite BPS high schools, Boston Latin Academy, Boston Latin School and the O’Bryant School.

Under the current iteration, seats are distributed evenly across socio-economic tiers based on neighborhood, and students are awarded extra points based on factors like attending a school with an over 40% economically disadvantaged population, living in DCF care and homelessness.

Of the three proposals up for debate, the first option would consider removing the school-based extra points and removing or altering the housing-based points.

The second would alter the four socioeconomic tiers. Instead of distributing the number of seats based on the number of children within each tier, the seats with be distributed based on the number of applicants in each tier.

The third would consider adding a “citywide round,” allowing for students with the highest composite scores to compete for 20% of seats outside of tiers.

BPS officials presented on simulations of admissions under each policy option in a special June meeting, before the public comment period began.

Skipper said Wednesday BPS aims to leave the next policy in place for “ideally three” years.

Within the public comment period, district officials said they received hundreds of participants and many responses from mainly BPS students and families.

The “themes” of public comment were broken down by option. For the school-based option, some families saw the advantage as a “departure from merit” or “poor proxy for individual

socioeconomic need,” while others saw them as a “tool to account for historical

resource disparities among schools” or incentive to stay in diverse BPS schools.

In the tiers option, BPS staff said, some of those in favor noted it “addresses the wide disparity in minimum composite score across socioeconomic tiers” or adjusted the approach to the actual applicant pool rather than Census numbers. Those opposed commented that it would complicate the process regularly and make “invitations less geographically representative.”

Regarding the city-wide option, some criticized it would hurt the impact of the tiers and “disproportionately benefits” higher socioeconomic students, while others said it could guarantee the “highest-achieving students” a seat and send a message that all students interest have a shot.

More public comments from all sides of the issue came in during Wednesday’s meeting, with more opponents of all proposed alterations joining in.

“I agree with the critics that all applicants should have a shot at an exam school seat,” said Roseanne Tung, former member of the 2021 Exam School Admissions Task Force. “However, the solution should not backslide on equity gains. Yet the three simulations do exactly that.”

Tung argued all three simulations would result in lower invitations for “the lowest socioeconomic tier, multilingual learners, former English learners, students who are economically disadvantaged, students from BPS-sending schools and BPS students applying to BLS” and increase “white students, students from the highest socioeconomic tier, and students who do not attend BPS elementary schools.”

Peter Alvarez, Madison Park alum and BPS parent from West Roxbury, testified in favor of Option C, saying “it’s really important to have 20% of students across the city to obtain admission to the exam schools” and “low income students can go to any school in the city.”

“Equitable for students, regardless of where they happen to live or go to school,” Alvarez said. “We can’t have students getting a 97.4 composite score and not being admitted, and that’s the case under the current policy. And under C the highest non-admitted score goes down to 93.5.”

Several school committee members questioned the policy options Wednesday, including new member Rachel Skerritt, who served on the original 2021 Exam School Admissions Task Force.

BPS officials are expected to present on the subject again at the Sept. 25 School Committee meeting.
