title: Boston mayor’s $325M White Stadium rebuild hammered by residents, councilors after latest cost hike
text:
Opposition to the city’s now $325 million public-private plan to rebuild White Stadium for a pro soccer team has intensified following the latest taxpayer cost update, and exposed the mayor’s fractured relationship with the Black community.

Residents and city councilors who oppose the project, which now has taxpayers coughing up $135 million to cover the city’s costs, forcefully pushed back on Wu administration officials’ insistence that new costs announced last month are final and that the city had no other choice but to pursue a public-private stadium rehab. Construction began this month.

The project was first announced two years ago as a rebuild that would cost taxpayers $50 million for the city’s half of construction, while records first reported by the Herald last year showed that the city’s private soccer investment partner was given a head start in the public bidding process for the renovation.

“I think we hear the frustration from the community because the beginning process did not include their thoughts and it was never an option,” City Councilor Brian Worrell said Monday at a Council hearing. “It wasn’t a private stadium versus a public option. I think that’s an ultimatum our community hears too often.

“It’s like, you’re either going to go with this option or you’re not going to get the investment inside of your neighborhood, when it’s looking at Blue Hill Ave. or it’s looking at White Stadium,” Worrell said.

Worrell said the debate over White Stadium — which is set to house a new National Women’s Soccer League team, Boston Legacy FC, that will share use of the facility with Boston Public Schools student-athletes — is not the first time the city has had a conversation around a soccer stadium. But the talks have played out differently, he said.

“Past conversations stopped short of bringing a soccer stadium to the Bayside Expo Center because of community voice and elected officials pulling back, so it just kind of unfortunately reaffirms to certain communities that government is not working for them,” Worrell said.

Similarly, residents from the majority-Black communities of Dorchester, Mattapan and Roxbury that surround Franklin Park’s White Stadium, spoke of how they felt like their voices have been silenced by the Wu administration and how the mayor’s plan has been pushed through over their objections.

Reggie Stewart, a member of the District 7 advisory council, said residents in majority-Black communities will be voting in future elections based on where Mayor Michelle Wu and city councilors stand on what they consider to be broken promises and commitments to those communities.

Stewart cited, for example, the city’s recent removal of an economic development designation for a parcel in Roxbury referred to as Parcel P3, that the mayor now wants to use to build a new Madison Park Technical Vocational High School.

“For many residents, the decision-making processes around issues such as Parcel P3, White Stadium, Blue Hill Avenue, and other development choices are not being treated as routine planning matters,” Stewart said. “They’re being viewed through the lens of Boston’s racist history of urban renewal, where Black homes and businesses were destroyed and decisions regarding the future of vulnerable residents were made without them.

“The mayor is unilaterally making decisions and declarations regarding Madison Park and Parcel P3, breaking decades-old agreements and fracturing an already fragile trust with the Black community,” Stewart added. “Many rightly see this as a continuation of a long-standing pattern of racist governance on the part of this administration.”

Stewart said that right now, “when it comes to trust with Black Boston, city leadership, frankly, is skating on the thinnest of ice, and I would argue that the ice is cracking underneath your feet.”

That dynamic was at play at the hearing, which was chaired by Councilor Sharon Durkan, one of the mayor’s closest Council allies, who chose to turn a community panel of project opponents invited by Councilor Julia Mejia into a brief segment for public testimony. The decision heightened tension.

Many of the panelists invited by Mejia are part of a group of residents who call themselves the Franklin Park Defenders. The group joined the Emerald Necklace Conservancy in filing a lawsuit against the city that seeks to block the project.

Mejia was criticized by some of her colleagues, including Durkan, last term for holding hearings that elevated the voices of stadium opponents suing the city.

“For me, I’m not about supporting billionaires, so I’m really concerned about who’s going to be benefiting here,” Mejia said in a dig at the wealthy soccer investment group.

The Defenders allege that the city’s plan constitutes an unconstitutional privatization of public parkland, and favor a high-school-only rehab that they have estimated will cost $64.6 million.

A Suffolk Superior Court judge sided with the city last spring, but the case was appealed and is set to be heard by the state’s highest court later this year.

Wu administration officials defended the stadium plan, saying that the city could not afford the rebuild without a private investment partner.

A public-only stadium would cost taxpayers “well over” $135 million, according to Diana Fernandez Bibeau, deputy chief of urban design for the city’s planning department. She mentioned a high-school-only soccer stadium rebuild in Seattle is projected at $150 million.

City officials also insisted that the $135 million taxpayer cost for the city’s half of the rebuild is capped, and protected by a guaranteed maximum price contract, that includes built-in contingencies — but copped to the possibility of unforeseen circumstances driving up the cost even further.

“We’ve committed to do a project that has been decades of years in the making, that no one has taken on because it’s been so difficult to achieve,” Fernandez Bibeau said. “In this moment, we have tried to find a creative solution to bring investment into a Black and brown community … We are finally delivering on decades of students that have wanted this work done.”

title: Boston luxury home sales lead councilors to probe whether City Hall is giving the rich a tax break
text:
Two record-setting home sales in Boston’s most affluent neighborhoods have the Boston City Council looking to probe city assessment practices that may be under-assessing the value of luxury homes and giving a tax break to wealthy owners.

City Councilor Miniard Culpepper said he was compelled to put forward a hearing order “to review discrepancies between market value and tax assessed value for residential properties” in city assessing practices after seeing reports about a recent $21 million sale of a Back Bay home that was assessed by the city at $12.5 million.

“Property taxes are one of the most important ways the city funds essential services, and the fairness of that system depends on assessments accurately reflecting market conditions,” Culpepper said last Wednesday at a City Council meeting. “However, recent sales suggested some properties, especially high value homes, are being assessed far below the actual sale price.

“At the same time, some lower-priced homes appear to be assessed at or even above their sale price, raising concerns about whether the current system is applying valuation practices consistently across different segments of the housing market,” Culpepper added. “Ensuring that property assessments are accurate and equitable is essential to maintaining public confidence in our tax system and making sure that the responsibility of funding city services is shared fairly across all homeowners.”

The sale of 59 Commonwealth Ave., an 11,500 square-foot Back Bay home, was recorded on Nov. 24, per the Suffolk Registry of Deeds, and set a record on the luxury market that stood until last month’s $22 million sale of a Beacon Hill home.

The 9,412 square-foot Beacon Hill home at 46 Chestnut St. sold on Feb. 17 for far beyond the city’s assessed value of $5.26 million. The same home had sold for $8.9 million on Sept. 1, 2023, when it was assessed around $3.8 million, city assessing records show.

At a time when the average single-family homeowner was hit this year with a 13% tax hike, Culpepper said the hearing he requested will focus, in part, on reviewing city practices that appear to be under-assessing luxury homes and overassessing homes in less affluent neighborhoods.

“An analysis of residential sales indicates that luxury homes in Boston are assigned a tax assessed value averaging roughly 68% of their sale price, suggesting that some high-value properties may be valued significantly below their actual market value for tax purposes,” Culpepper’s hearing order states.

His order cites unspecified data examining the top 20 luxury property transactions in the City of Boston that show reported under-assessments totaling roughly $35.43 million in 2024 and $43.65 million in 2025, in terms of the city’s assessed value for those luxury homes and the price they sold for on the real estate market.

By contrast, Culpepper cited the sale of a single-family home in Roslindale that sold for roughly $430,000, but was assessed a higher value by the city, of $489,000, or “about 114% of its sale price.”

Assessed value determines how much a homeowner pays in property taxes, meaning that the higher a home’s value, the higher the property taxes.

Such discrepancies are “raising concerns regarding the accuracy and consistency of high-value property assessments and the potential implications for equitable property tax administration in the City of Boston,” Culpepper’s order states.

When asked by the Herald whether he thought the city was intentionally giving a tax break to certain affluent property owners, Culpepper said, “That’s why we’re going to have a hearing to find out exactly how they go about assessing homeowners.”

“I have concerns about whether the current system is applying valuation practices consistently across different segments of the housing market,” Culpepper told the Herald.

Culpepper, who represents District 7, which includes low-income neighborhoods like Roxbury and Dorchester, said he hears constant concerns from his constituents about not being able to afford property taxes.

“So we want to look and see whether they’re being over-taxed because they’re over-assessed, and we won’t know until we really look closer at this and get some data,” Culpepper said.

He said he supported Mayor Michelle Wu’s stalled legislation that would have allowed the city to increase commercial tax rates to lower taxes for homeowners. He called on the state Senate, which has repeatedly killed the bill, to take a vote on it, when asked whether the city should move on to an alternative tax relief option.

A vote was taken by the Senate on the mayor’s bill in January, and it was overwhelmingly defeated. The Senate voted, 33-5, to defeat an amendment filed by state Sen. Michael Rush that closely mirrored the language in Wu’s legislation.

Nick Collins and William Brownsberger, two Boston senators who led the push to kill Wu’s tax bill in late 2024, put forward alternative tax relief measures that were approved by the state Senate, but not the House of Representatives, which passed the mayor’s legislation three times.

Councilor Erin Murphy, who has been pushing for the mayor to move to a “Plan B” for tax relief, said she signed on to co-sponsor Culpepper’s order because the Wu administration failed to provide “good reason” for why certain neighborhoods were seeing assessing discrepancies during a similar Council hearing held last year.

“It didn’t seem equitable,” Murphy said, adding of the abatement process, “The other fear that many residents have is if you file for them to come and check, it could inadvertently negatively impact you in the other way. So sometimes people are afraid for us to check to make sure that they did it right.”

The city was sued in December by a watchdog group that alleges the city has been inflating the assessed value and taxes of commercial properties that file abatements, a practice the group has slammed as retaliatory and unlawful.

Mayor Wu’s office did not respond to a request for comment on Culpepper’s order, which was also co-sponsored by Brian Worrell, and referred to the Council’s Ways and Means Committee for a hearing. All 13 councilors signed on to the order.

title: Police community rallies around officer charged with manslaughter
text:
The police community is continuing to rally around an officer charged with manslaughter in connection to an fatal on-duty shooting of a carjacking suspect in Roxbury earlier this month.

A GoFundMe for Boston Police Officer Nicholas O’Malley’s family had raised more than $370,000 by early Sunday evening.

“The O’Malley family is facing an incredibly difficult time due to unforeseen circumstances, and they need our support now more than ever,” the fundraiser page said. “With two young children depending on them, the financial road ahead is uncertain.”

The donations will go toward the family’s “essential expenses,” the page added.

O’Malley, 33, was released on personal recognizance after being arraigned in Roxbury District Court Thursday. Some 50 officers attended that arraignment, filling the courtroom during the proceedings, then forming a blue line outside to prevent photographers and journalists from approaching O’Malley and his family as they left.

On Thursday, the same day as the arraignment, the State’s POST Commission suspended O’Malley’s law enforcement certification. The suspension order did not state a reason for the suspension, just that the board had received “sufficient evidence” according to its statute, “thus requiring immediate suspension of the Respondent’s certification.”

Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said that his office had probable cause to arrest and charge O’Malley for shooting Stephenson King three times during an interaction with police after King allegedly committed a carjacking. He called the prosecution a matter of justice.

Following the fatal shooting, O’Malley and the department said that King, 39, had tried to ram the stolen vehicle into the responding officers.

But body camera footage reviewed by the DA’s office shows that wasn’t accurate, a prosecutor said at the arraignment.

“Neither officer was in the path of the car,” Assistant District Attorney Ian Polumbaum said, telling a judge that the incident “didn’t warrant deadly force.”

Instead, Polumbaum said that King was only trying to flee from police when he moved the car in reverse and forward repeatedly, backing into a police cruiser, against the commands of the officers.

O’Malley had told investigators that he feared the other officer who responded to the incident would be crushed by the vehicle.

Polumbaum said that the other officer was “in more danger of being stuck by [O’Malley’s] bullets than by the suspect’s car.”

President of the Boston Patrolman’s Association Larry Calderone argued that the DA was “Monday morning quarterbacking,” not fully understanding how dangerous the officer may have perceived the situation.

On Saturday, the association posted “Help Wanted” notes to their social media, telling “anyone interested in running for Suffolk County District Attorney” to start collecting signatures before the April 28 deadline.

Meanwhile, the reaction from city councilors has been mixed.

Ed Flynn, representing District 2, said that he’d donated to O’Malley’s gofundme and encouraged others to do the same.

“As a city and society, we should not rush to judgment and immediately second guess a police officer,” he wrote in a statement following O’Malley’s arrest.

District 3 councilor John FitzGerald and at-large councilor Erin Murphy both issued similar statements urging the public not to rush to conclusions following the charge.

Murphy also wrote that she supports the release of the body camera footage from the shooting, “so the public can better understand what happened.”

“But even with hindsight, we should be careful not to assume we would have acted differently,” she added.

“Officer Nicholas O’Malley has served this city with an excellent record and is widely regarded as a dedicated officer. From everything we know, he was doing the job we ask our police officers to do, responding to a dangerous situation to protect others,” she wrote.

City Councilors Miniard Culpepper, of District 7, and Brian Worrell, of District 4, in a statement days after the shooting, said that they want the body camera footage to be released.

“As this case moves forward, we remain grounded in the principles that define our justice system — the presumption of innocence and the guarantee of due process,” they wrote. “We are still hopeful to see bodycam footage of the incident and will continue to ensure that this process unfolds with transparency, accountability, and fairness that our communities deserve.”

title: Man killed by Boston Police in carjacking confrontation has history of resisting arrest
text:
The carjacking suspect shot and killed by a Boston police officer earlier this month has a history of resisting arrest — a charge dropped under the policies of previous District Attorney Rachael Rollins.

Stephenson King, 39, of Dorchester, was shot and killed by a Boston police officer a little before 10 p.m. on March 11 in Roxbury.

Police say he did not comply with their demands and gunned his vehicle at officers as he attempted to flee, putting officers at risk and necessitating them to shoot him. The officers were placed on administrative leave as the shooting was investigated by the Suffolk District Attorney’s office.

The next week, prosecutors filed manslaughter charges against Boston Police Officer Nicholas O’Malley for King’s death. O’Malley, 33, pleaded not guilty in Roxbury District Court, where his arraignment was attended by some 50 fellow officers and the head of the police union.

Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association President Larry Calderone told the media outside the courthouse that, to his knowledge, it had been decades since a Boston Police officer was charged for an on-duty death, and that “We shouldn’t be standing here.”

Prosecutor Ian Polumbaum said in court that O’Malley’s interaction with King “didn’t warrant deadly force” as body camera footage showed he was attempting only to flee the scene and showed no indication he was gunning the vehicle at officers. Shooting a fleeing suspect is against Boston Police policy and against the law, he said.

Body camera footage has not been released for public view by request of both the prosecution and the defense — and despite the Boston City Council’s repeated attempts to have it released. For now, the story is told only in competing narratives.

Criminal history

What is public is King’s criminal history, which includes a 2019 case for a similar incident involving officers approaching his vehicle and him not complying with their stated commands. In this incident, he physically resisted his arrest, according to the police report.

On Oct. 21, 2019, a Massachusetts State Police trooper spotted a 2004 Hyundai Elantra registered to King, who at the time had three warrants for his arrest: one for possession with intent to distribute Class D and B drugs, along with firearms charges; another for assault and battery, destruction of property and violation of a protection from abuse order; and one more for threat to commit a crime.

The trooper, who was in the Beachmont area of Revere, called a Revere Police Department detective as he began his pursuit from an unmarked vehicle, according to the police report. That detective and another Revere officer joined in the pursuit in their own vehicles and the three attempted to pull King over, but he didn’t pull over immediately.

The trooper positioned his vehicle in front, blocking King’s forward movement and the Revere officers pulled in behind him, according to the report. King allegedly backed his vehicle at slow speed into the detective vehicle’s bumper. The police told King to stop his vehicle and get out, but King did not comply, the report states, so they moved in to physically extract him.

“King who was still smoking a cigarette was refusing to exit the vehicle and was holding onto the steering (wheel) with the other hand,” the report states. “King who is 6’ tall and weighing more than 200 lbs used his body size to prevent the officers from getting him out of the vehicle.”

The Revere detective pulled at King from the driver’s side, ripping King’s jersey shirt in the process, as the trooper pushed at him from the passenger side, the report states. King was extracted but “still struggling” with the police until they got him to the ground and he gave up, stating “that he was done fighting,” the report states.

Light touch

The incident came at the end of 2019 and was in the early stages of court hearings when the COVID-19 pandemic started changing everything.

Rescheduling orders due to the “State of Emergency surrounding the Covid-19 virus” began in the case in March 2020 and continued until Sept. 15, 2020, when prosecutors dropped the case.

Prosecutor John Blazo, working under the orders of then-DA Rachael Rollins, submitted a “nolle prosequi” — a formal disposition meaning the charges were dropped.

Instead, prosecutors entered into an agreement that King apologize to the arresting officer and complete community service — though even that was negotiable in the era of COVID.

“The defendant wrote and submitted a letter of apology to the officer, but was unable to complete the community service hours due to the COVID-19 pandemic,” the nol. pros. notice, dated Sept. 11, 2020, states. “Specifically, the defendant cares for his 80-year-old grandmother, who due to her age and health, is particularly vulnerable to the virus.

“In lieu of the community service, the defendant has provided a letter documenting the type of care and assistance he provides for his grandmother,” the notice concludes. “Accordingly, the Commonwealth is satisfied that the defendant has complied with the aforementioned conditions and, therefore, continued prosecution of this case would not serve the interests of justice.”

The Rollins tenure

Rollins’ tenure as DA from January 2019 to January 2022 was marked by her controversial “no prosecute” list, which featured 15 crime types ranging from shoplifting and trespassing to drug possession and resisting arrest — like King’s case — that her office would not prosecute.

title: Boston Public Schools parents call out bus issues continuing to mire certain schools
text:
Despite early improvements in bus on-time performance this school year, BPS families came out to the Boston City Council Tuesday to share how some routes and school communities are still being hit hard by regular failures in bus performance this year.

“This past year has been the worst by far in relation to buses being late or canceled,” said BPS mom Laurie Murphy, whose children attend Hernandez K-8 School in Roxbury. “From the data I’ve seen, our bus route alone is over 20 days — 21 counting today actually — of either cancellations or significant delays this school year.

“That is a month of school,” Murphy added. “In the past five weeks alone, we’ve had nine cancellations or delays over 40 minutes. Imagine at 7 a.m., and you’re getting your children ready for school only to get another alert, ‘There’s no bus.’ ”

Tuesday’s City Council emergency hearing order, filed by lead sponsor Councilor Erin Murphy, examined “chronic school bus delays and special education transportation failures.” The hearing featured parents, noting the concentration of issues at schools including the Hernandez K-8, Horace Mann School for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing, and Edison K-8.

BPS Executive Director of Transportation Dan Rosengard spoke to a surge of school bus timeliness issues through the winter and several ongoing and upcoming steps, including the implementation of $500 fines for every “blown trip” included in the latest Transdev contract.

BPS will begin fining the transportation provider in liquidated damages assessed for the “blown trips,” any trip that goes uncovered or is over an hour late, starting for the month of March, Rosengard said, along with punitive measures.

One parent said their student’s route has gone uncovered for seven days or about 15% of scheduled rides since February break. Another said her kid’s bus is late “at least three days a week,” noting today it came one hour and 18 minutes behind schedule.

Parents and school speakers asked for a long list of changes throughout the hearing.

Some items of focus included an audit of the Zum app, a metric of reported data showing the “family experience,” reimbursement for all parents forced to use rideshare services to get their students to school when there are delays or cancellations, more reliable bus aide staffing and assistance for special education students, better communication when there will be delays and cancellations, and more.

“The current state of BPS transportation is a not a logistical hiccup,” said South Boston parent Cheryl Buckman. “It’s a systemic failure, compromising the safety and stability of our families.”

Rosengard noted that live GPS updates are available via Zum and alerts can be personalized through the app. When a bus route is uncovered, he said, the district calls schools right away and sends a “push notification” to families.

Reimbursement is also available for families of students with transportation required in their IEP when the bus is canceled or significantly late and they have to use rideshare or other alternatives, Rosengard said. There’s also a reimbursement mechanism for undocumented families.

Rosengard noted that on-time performance (OTP) was the “highest on record” for BPS in the mornings and afternoons at the start of the school year and continued to be high in the fall. January and February saw a “decline” as snow storms piled up, he said, but OTP returned to historically high levels in March, averaging 93% in the morning and 88% in the afternoon for the month.

“This is not nearly enough,” Rosengard said. “Even at that 95% target level, nearly 1,000 students would be arriving late to school every day. And if you are a student on one of the buses that is consistently arriving late, the system is failing you, whether OTP is 95% or 99%.”

BPS officials stated that there has been a “very concerning regression” in the number of uncovered trips each day since December.

There have been several steps taken so far, Rosengard said, including route consolidation and increases to driver hiring, with 25 drivers currently undergoing training. March has seen “some improvements so far,” with morning uncovered trips half what they were in the prior three months.

City councilors brought up the upcoming budget process, asking for more information on transportation services as they consider the spending.

“Through the few BPS budget hearings we’ve had so far, $200 million budget for transportation,” said Murphy. “That’s $10,526.32 we’re spending per student on the bus, and thousands of them are not getting reliable or service at all. So how do we defend that?”

title: Boston Police officer charged with manslaughter on leave with pay, pending indictment
text:
Boston Police Officer Nicholas O’Malley is on administrative leave with pay after he was charged with manslaughter in connection to an on-duty shooting of a carjacking suspect. But that could soon change.

If a grand jury hands down an indictment, bumping the manslaughter charge to the Superior Court, Massachusetts law dictates that his suspension go without pay, a BPD spokesperson confirmed to the Herald.

O’Malley was arraigned in Roxbury District Court on March 19 and released on personal recognizance. Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said they have brought the charge to a grand jury.

“In line with civil service laws, officers who are charged with a crime are placed on paid administrative leave,” according to a BPD spokesperson. “If an officer is indicted, per the statute, the officer’s status is unpaid administrative leave.”

The only officers not subject to this law are state troopers who can still take pay after being indicted. The four troopers charged with manslaughter for their alleged involvement in the 2024 death of a trooper trainee are all suspended with pay even though they were indicted earlier this year, the Herald previously reported.

In 2025, O’Malley made $218,156.91 total, including overtime and details with a base pay of $123,037.90.

Since the arrest, some community members have rallied around O’Malley and his family. A GoFundMe for the officer has raised over half a million dollars.

“We’re 100% behind him and his family,” Boston Police Patrolman’s Association President Larry Calderone said.

The officer’s arrest marked outrage from the union, its members, and several officials who have said the charge was rare and unjustified.

Following the arraignment, Calderone told the press while standing in front of about 50 BPD officers who’d come to support O’Malley, that this was the first time a city police officer had been charged for an on-duty shooting in decades.

O’Malley shot and killed Stephenson King after King allegedly assaulted a woman and stole her car in Roxbury on March 11.

According to police reports and accounts from the prosecution, King did not fully comply with commands issued by O’Malley and another officer when they approached him in the allegedly stolen vehicle.

King would not roll his window down all the way or turn off the car.

When O’Malley said, “Bro, I’m going to f***ing shoot you,” while holstering his gun in favor of a Taser, the report said, King backed into the cruiser parked behind him, and moved forward and backward, according to a police report based on body camera footage.

As King moved forward the last time, O’Malley opened fire.

O’Malley told investigators that he feared for his partner’s life, but the DA’s office said that body camera footage shows his partner was not in danger of being hit and that King was only trying to flee.

title: South Boston high school baseball team gifted caps amid city’s budget crunch: ‘Bush league’
text:
Community leaders had to step up over the weekend to buy baseball hats for a South Boston high school varsity team due to a budget crunch at the Boston Public Schools, which led to criticism about the city’s spending priorities.

Bob Ferrara said he received a phone call last Friday night that left him “beyond disgusted” — the school district hadn’t delivered baseball hats to the Excel High School team ahead of their opening day game, which was scheduled for Monday.

Ferrara soon learned that the hats wouldn’t be coming on time, if at all, from BPS — which in January paused hiring and spending to try to close a $53 million budget gap for the current fiscal year, which ends on June 30. The school district has proposed a budget with more cuts for next fiscal year, amid Boston’s larger financial difficulties, which have the city facing a $48.4 million budget shortfall this fiscal year.

“I’ve been coaching youth sports and high school sports for a long time in the city, so this is a disgrace,” Ferrara, 62, told the Herald Tuesday. “You put a team that you know has nothing and send them on a field without baseball hats on. That’s bush league. That’s unacceptable.

“The mayor is spending $130 million helping a private entity with a soccer team, and they can’t come up with money to make sure these kids have hats on time?” Ferrara added.

Ferrara was referring to the city’s $325 million public-private plan to rebuild White Stadium for a professional women’s soccer team that has taxpayers coughing up $135 million for the city’s half of the renovations. The taxpayer cost was initially projected at $50 million when the project — which will see BPS student-athletes share use of the rebuilt facility — was announced two years ago.

After learning of the Excel High School team’s predicament, Ferrara said he worked over the weekend to ensure new hats would be made and arrive on time for their first varsity baseball game of the season.

Ferrara said he made a call to a “South Boston fixer” and his former youth football coach, Robert Pacitti, who then called his friend, David Moynihan, who owns The Spot, a Southie store that does clothing printing and embroidery. Moynihan offered to make the hats free of charge.

The hats were embroidered with an “SB” logo within 48 hours, and Ferrara said he dashed out on Monday to hand-deliver them to the team in time for opening day, which was played at Madison Park Technical Vocational High School.

“They couldn’t believe it,” Ferrara said of the team. “They couldn’t believe we pulled this off.”

Ferrara said he doesn’t know how much the hats set back the store owner, who did not respond to the Herald’s request for comment. He estimated that it “wasn’t a tremendous amount of money.”

“It’s just the little stuff that falls through the cracks,” Ferrara said. “The way I operate is 1,000 little things. You let one thing fall through the crack, what about the next thing? I’m beyond disgusted that I get pulled into this stuff because it seems like I’m one of the few people who can make things happen. It’s pathetic.”

BPS did not immediately respond to the Herald’s request for comment.

Ferrara, who said he worked for Josh Kraft’s mayoral campaign last year, criticized what he described as the city’s “new way” of doing things, which has led to “filthy” streets and a lack of basic city services.

“We’re totally reinventing the school system, because everything new is better, right?” Ferrara said. “You can’t fix what’s old.”

South Boston’s Excel High School is closing at the end of this school year, as part of a BPS reconfiguration plan. The district’s plans call for renovating the high school and opening a so-called anchor school to occupy the building in the future.

Boston City Councilor Erin Murphy, who has repeatedly voted against the school budget, criticized BPS for failing to provide baseball caps to the Excel team. She recalled pressing for answers after school transportation issues hampered the same varsity baseball team and left players stranded on game days two years ago.

“Now, to hear that this same team is being told there are no funds for baseball caps is deeply frustrating and completely unacceptable,” Murphy said in a statement, “and it speaks to a problem I’ve been raising for years. Boston Public Schools is now operating with a budget of roughly $1.7 billion, and we are spending well over $30,000 per student.

“Yet when you look at athletics, the investment reaching students is still less than $100 per student. That disconnect is exactly what we are seeing play out here. When a school team cannot get something as basic as hats for opening day, it is not a funding issue. It is a prioritization and accountability issue.

“Athletics are not extras. They are part of a well-rounded education and critical to student engagement, attendance, and school pride. We cannot continue to talk about record spending while failing to deliver for students in the most basic ways,” Murphy added.

The councilor thanked the South Boston community for stepping up to provide the caps, but said it should have never come to that. She added that community support “should never be a substitute for a system that works.”

“Our students deserve better,” Murphy said, “and along with Councilor Ed Flynn, we will be demanding answers from BPS on how this happened and how we ensure it does not happen again.”

title: Boston man accused of sexually assaulting MBTA bus driver; Mass. school bus driver to face criminal charges
text:
A 41-year-old man with multiple convictions for violent offenses dating back to 2005 is now accused of sexually assaulting an MBTA bus driver.

Police officers last Thursday met with an MBTA bus driver who said a man — later identified as Jamaica Plain man Michael Vandenbroeke — sexually assaulted her while boarding the bus at the Massachusetts Avenue and Washington Street Silver Line stop.

Vandenbroeke boarded the bus and picked up a bottle of perfume that the driver had dropped. As Vandenbroeke went to hand her the perfume bottle, he allegedly grabbed her face, poked her in the eye, placed his hand on her chest, and groped her breast.

The driver said she moved Vandenbroeke’s hand away and yelled at him. Vandenbroeke then sat at the back of the bus, getting off a few stops later. The incident was captured on surveillance video from the bus and reviewed by police.

Cops posted still photos of Vandenbroeke. He was identified and arrested on Monday at the Nubian Square station.

“The women and men who operate MBTA buses and trains are instrumental in transporting our workers, consumers, visitors and students throughout the metro Boston area day in and day out and they deserve our praise and our gratitude,” Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden said.

“An incident like this is an intolerable affront on them and on everyone who uses public transportation,” he added.

Vandenbroeke was charged with indecent assault and battery on a person over 14, assault and battery on a public employee, and disorderly conduct on a public conveyance.

The judge ordered Vandenbroeke held on a $500 bail. He will return to court April 21 for a pre-trial hearing.

Mass. school bus driver accused of distracted driving, other offenses

A school bus driver is expected to face criminal charges, as officials accuse the operator of distracted driving and using inappropriate language while young students were on the bus.

Norfolk Police were investigating an incident involving a school bus driver transporting students to the H. Olive Day School (Pre K-2) and Freeman-Kennedy School (grades 3-6) on Wednesday morning.

The bus driver — who’s employed by W.T. Holmes Transportation — is accused of distracted driving and using inappropriate language, according to officials.

Once school officials were notified about the incident after students arrived at school, administrators contacted the School Resource Officer with Norfolk Police, who launched an investigation.

The driver will no longer operate a bus for Norfolk Public Schools.

As a result of the investigation, Norfolk Police was filing an application for criminal complaint in Wrentham District Court — charging the driver with multiple driving violations and other offenses related to his conduct.

“Nothing is more important to us than the safety of our students,” said Norfolk Superintendent Ingrid Allardi. “We take any situation involving student safety seriously and address concerns right away to make sure our students feel safe and supported at school and on their way to and from school.”

The bus driver’s identity was not immediately released because the court hadn’t issued a criminal complaint yet.

“The Norfolk Police Department takes every report concerning student safety very seriously,” said Chief James Barrett. “We are working with the school to review the situation and will follow the proper legal procedures as the case moves forward.”

The incident remains under investigation by the Norfolk Police Department.

title: It’s not just vaccines — parents are refusing other routine preventive care for newborns
text:
By LAURA UNGAR, AP Medical Writer

One day at an Idaho hospital, half the newborns Dr. Tom Patterson saw didn’t get the vitamin K shots that have been given to babies for decades to prevent potentially deadly bleeding. On another recent day, more than a quarter didn’t get the shot. Their parents wouldn’t allow it.

“When you look at a child who’s innocent and vulnerable — and a simple intervention that’s been done since 1961 is refused — knowing that baby’s going out into the world is super worrisome to me,” said Patterson, who’s been a pediatrician for nearly three decades.

Doctors across the nation are alarmed that skepticism fueled by rising anti-science sentiment and medical mistrust is increasingly reaching beyond vaccines to other proven, routine, preventive care for babies.

A recent study in the Journal of the American Medical Association, which analyzed more than 5 million births nationwide, found that refusals of vitamin K shots nearly doubled between 2017 and 2024, from 2.9% to 5.2%. Other research suggests that parents who decline vitamin K shots are much more likely to refuse getting their newborns the hepatitis B vaccine and an eye ointment to prevent potentially blinding infections. Rates for that vaccination at birth dropped in recent years, and doctors confirm that more parents are refusing the eye medication.

“I do think these families care deeply about their infants,” said Dr. Kelly Wade, a Philadelphia neonatologist. “But I hear from families that it’s hard to make decisions right now because they’re hearing conflicting information.”

Innumerable social media posts question doctors’ advice on safe and effective measures like vitamin K and eye ointment. And the Trump administration has repeatedly undermined established science. A federal advisory committee whose members were appointed by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. — a leading anti-vaccine activist before joining the administration — voted to end the longstanding recommendation to immunize all babies against hepatitis B right after birth. On Monday a federal judge temporarily blocked all decisions made by the reconfigured committee.

One common thread that ties together anti-vaccine views and growing sentiments against other protective measures for newborns is the fallacy that natural is always better than artificial, said Dr. David Hill, a Seattle pediatrician and researcher.

“Nature will allow 1 in 5 human infants to die in the first year of life,” Hill said, “which is why generations of scientists and doctors have worked to bring that number way, way down.”

Vitamin K and other measures prevent serious problems

Babies are born with low levels of vitamin K, leaving them vulnerable because their intestines can’t produce enough until they start eating solid foods at around 6 months old.

“Vitamin K is important for helping the blood clot and preventing dangerous bleeding in babies, like bleeding into the brain,” said Dr. Kristan Scott of the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, lead author of the JAMA study.

Before injections became routine, up to about 1 in 60 babies suffered vitamin K deficiency bleeding, which can also affect the gastrointestinal tract. Today the condition is rare, but research shows that newborns who don’t get a vitamin K shot are 81 times more likely to develop severe bleeding than those who do.

Hill has seen what can happen.

“I cared for a toddler whose parents had chosen that risk,” the Seattle doctor said. The child essentially had a stroke as a newborn and wound up with severe developmental delays and ongoing seizures.

At a February meeting of the Idaho chapter of the American Academy of Pediatrics, doctors said they knew of eight deaths from vitamin K deficiency bleeding in the state over the preceding 13 months, said Patterson, who is president of the chapter.

Infections prevented by other newborn measures can also have grave consequences. Erythromycin eye ointment protects against gonorrhea that can be contracted during birth and potentially cause blindness if untreated. The hepatitis B vaccine prevents a disease that can lead to liver failure, liver cancer or cirrhosis.

Even if a pregnant woman is tested for gonorrhea and hepatitis B, no test is perfect, and she may get infected after testing, said Dr. Susan Sirota, a pediatrician in Highland Park, Illinois. Either way, she risks passing the infection to her child.

Why are parents refusing routine care?

Parents give many reasons for turning down preventive measures, like fearing they might cause problems and not wanting newborns to feel pain.

“Some will just say they want more of a natural birth philosophy,” said Dr. Steven Abelowitz, founder of Ocean Pediatrics in Orange County, California. “Then there’s a ton of misinformation. … There are outside influences, friends, celebrities, nonprofessionals and political agendas.”

Abelowitz practices in an area with about an equal mix of Republicans and Democrats.

“There’s more mistrust from the conservative side, but there’s plenty on the more liberal side as well,” he said, “It’s across-the-board mistrust.”

Social media provides ample fuel, spreading myths and pushing unregulated vitamin K drops that doctors warn babies can’t absorb well.

Doctors in numerous states say parents refusing vitamin K shots often also decline other measures. Sirota, in Illinois, encountered a family that refused a heel stick to monitor glucose for a baby at high risk for having potentially life-threatening low blood sugar.

Care refusals aren’t a new phenomenon. Wade, in Philadelphia, said she’s seen them for 20 years. But until recently, they were rare.

Twelve years ago, Dana Morrison, now a Minnesota doula, declined the vitamin K shot for her newborn son, giving him oral drops instead.

“It came from a space of really wanting to protect the bonding time with my baby,” she said. “I was trying to eliminate more pokes.”

Her daughter’s birth a couple of years later was less straightforward, leaving the infant with a bruised leg. Morrison got the vitamin K shot for her.

Knowing what she does now, she said, she would have gotten it for her son, too.

Doctors and parents want ‘the best for their children’

Doctors hope to change minds, one parent at a time. And that begins with respect.

“If I walk into the room with judgment, we are going to have a really useless conversation,” Hill said. “Every parent I serve wants the best for their children.”

When parents question the need for the vitamin K shot, Dr. Heather Felton tries to address their specific concerns. She explains why it’s given and the risks of not getting it. Most families decide to get it, said Felton, who has seen no uptick in refusals.

“It really helps that you can take that time and really listen and be able to provide some education,” said Felton, a pediatrician at Norton Children’s in Louisville, Kentucky.

In Idaho, Patterson sometimes finds himself clearing up misconceptions. Some parents will agree to a vitamin K shot when they find out it’s not a vaccine, for example.

These conversations can take time, especially since the parents doctors see in hospitals usually aren’t people they know through their practices.

But doctors are happy to invest that time if it might save babies.

“I end every discussion with parents with this: ‘Please understand at the end of the day, I’m passionate about this because I have the best interest of children in my mind and heart,’” Patterson said. “I understand this is a hot topic, and I don’t want to disrespect anybody. But at the same time, I’m desperately saddened that we’re losing babies for no reason.”

title: Police Blotter: Shots-fired call suspects and early morning nudist
text:
Police have released the names of the three men arrested Thursday — one of them outside the South Bay jail — following a shots-fired call and barricaded standoff in Roxbury.

David Carrasquillo, 24, of Roxbury, is charged with three counts of assault and battery attempt with a firearm and discharging a firearm within 500 feet of a building. He was the one arrested after police located his vehicle on the Massachusetts Avenue Connector outside the South Bay House of Correction.

Everything began when a BPD sergeant stopped at a red light at the intersection of Dearborn and Dudley streets at about 1 p.m. heard multiple gunshots and saw a suspect, identified as Carrasquillo, run toward a vehicle and then take off toward Melnea Cass Boulevard. The sergeant called in the vehicle’s description and direction of travel and police pulled him over and arrested him outside the jail. They say he had a Smith and Wesson M&P M2.0 handgun stuffed into his waistband.

Police then reviewed video footage from the area of where the gunshots were heard and say they saw Carrasquillo fire his weapon at three others across Zeigler Street. Two of them allegedly returned fire. Police say they found ballistic evidence around the area and located the other suspects holed up inside 121 Zeigler St.

It was declared a barricade situation and the SWAT team and negotiators were called out until the suspects surrendered.

Eliel Pena, 19, of Roxbury, and David Ortiz, 19, of Boston, were arrested and charged with multiple firearm and assault and battery counts.

Early-morning nudist

The Bedford, New Hampshire, community helped local police crack the case of a man seen walking around the neighborhood in the nude during the early morning hours.

While photos from home surveillance systems were initially released in the police department’s request for help identifying the man, those photos were no longer there when police updated to say they had identified the man and that he “has been in contact with the police.”

The department said that officers responded to the area of Elizabeth Way and Connie Court on Thursday at around 5 a.m. for reports of a nude man walking up a driveway. Further investigation determined that the man had walked up several driveways between 2 and 3 a.m.

Commenters on the police department’s social media updates suggested that the man could have been sleepwalking.

‘Habitual’ crack dealer arrested

The Boston Police Department says officers arrested a man they described as a “habitual drug dealer” whose activity has “plagued the area of New Market Square.”

Darmayne White, 51, of South Boston, was arrested Thursday at around 10:20 a.m. when they say they saw him “hand to two other individuals an unknown item from his rear pocket” and that he had a noticeable “large plastic bag inside the rear of his pants.” These observations led police to conclude it was a drug deal.

Police say that a search of White revealed 23 individually wrapped baggies of crack cocaine hidden within the larger bag seen stuffed down his pants. He was arrested and charged with intent to distribute Class B drugs.

Incident Summary

The BPD responded to 234 incidents in the 24-hour period ending at 10 a.m. Friday, according to the department’s incident log. Those included three robberies, five aggravated assaults, one residential burglary, one auto theft and 16 instances of miscellaneous larceny.

Arrests

All of the below-named defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty.

— Johanna Gratini, 23 Caltha Road, Brighton. Unlicensed operation of a motor vehicle.

— Dominique Thomas, 9 Reddy Ave., Hyde Park. Assault and battery.

— Felix Sanchez, 129 Redlands Road, West Roxbury. Operating a motor vehicle in violation of license class.

— David Carrasquillo, 27 Lakeside Ave., Quincy. Assault and battery attempt with firearm.

— David Ortiz, no listed address. Assault and battery with firearm.

— Eliel Pena, 121 Zeigler St., Roxbury. Assault and battery attempt with firearm.

— Lionel Horbas, 59-29 Myrtle Ave., Ridgewood, New York. Fraud scheme: Obtain property over $250 by trick.

— David Goodrich, 35 Creighton St., Jamaica Plain. Breaking and entering for a misdemeanor.

— Venel Dameus, 444 Harrison Ave., Boston. Operating a motor vehicle in area closed to travel.

— Curtis Britton, 42 Oakwood St., Hyde Park. Armed robbery.

— Devallon Emmanuel, 40 Lincoln Road, Brooklyn, New York. Number plate violation: concealing identification.

title: Gaskin: Making good on police reforms 5 years on
text:
Recent events underscore the stakes. In March 2026, Boston police shot and killed a carjacking suspect in Roxbury — a case that has since led to a manslaughter charge against an officer and ongoing disputes over the release of body-camera footage. When even the most high-profile cases leave the public with unanswered questions, it raises a deeper concern: whether the city’s oversight system is functioning as intended. Even in a relatively safer city, when serious incidents occur, the system can still struggle with transparency and accountability.

Five years after Boston promised sweeping police reform in the wake of the 2020 protests, the public still lacks clear evidence that those reforms are working.

In the aftermath of nationwide protests over policing and racial justice in 2020, Boston convened the Police Reform Task Force to examine the policies and practices of the Boston Police Department and recommend reforms to improve transparency, accountability, and community trust. The task force — made up of civic leaders, legal experts, clergy, and community representatives — spent months reviewing research and hearing from residents.

The result was a sweeping set of reforms that Boston’s political leadership pledged to implement.

Among the most significant changes was the creation of the Office of Police Accountability and Transparency (OPAT). The agency oversees two key bodies: a Civilian Review Board that investigates complaints from residents and an Internal Affairs Oversight Panel that monitors the Boston Police Department’s disciplinary process. Together, these institutions were designed to create an independent system of civilian oversight capable of strengthening both police legitimacy and public trust.

At the time, the reforms were widely praised by residents, policymakers, and the media. Boston appeared ready to build a modern system of accountability.

But the real question today is simple: Did Boston actually implement the reforms it promised?

Reports from news outlets and community advocates indicate that OPAT and other oversight bodies continue to face resistance when requesting information or cooperation from the police department. According to reporting by GBH News, officers have at times declined to participate in OPAT interviews, limiting the agency’s ability to independently investigate complaints.

Disciplinary recommendations issued by the Civilian Review Board are advisory rather than binding. Police officials have argued that some oversight requests conflict with existing procedures or legal protections for officers.

But without transparency about how these conflicts are resolved — and without a clear process for addressing them — the credibility of Boston’s entire reform framework is at risk.

Police reform ultimately succeeds or fails on a single question: does the public believe the system is fair and transparent?

Trust is not built through speeches or press conferences. It is built through accountability and transparency.

That is why the Boston City Council should act now.

The Boston City Council should hold a public oversight hearing bringing together the officials responsible for implementing the city’s police reform framework: Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox, leadership from the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, and the heads of the city’s oversight bodies — including OPAT Executive Director Evandro Carvalho, Civilian Review Board Chair Sam Harold, and Internal Affairs Oversight Panel Chair Anthony Fugate.

Such a hearing would serve several important purposes.

First, it would allow the public to understand whether the tensions between the police department and the oversight system stem from policy disagreements, legal constraints, or simple resistance to reform.

Second, it would allow city leaders to determine whether Boston’s current laws or ordinances need to be strengthened. If civilian oversight is to mean anything, its findings must carry real authority.

Members of the original Police Reform Task Force should also be invited to testify regarding whether the current system reflects the reforms they intended.

Third, it would reaffirm a basic principle: police reform is not about weakening law enforcement. It is about strengthening trust between the police and the communities they serve.

Transparency also requires addressing another longstanding concern: delays in responding to public records requests.

Improving access to public information was one of the core promises of Boston’s reform process. If the public cannot obtain timely information about how the oversight system functions, the promise of reform risks becoming largely symbolic.

Recent events illustrate why transparency still matters. On Sept. 11, 2025, an unidentified man died following a “brief struggle” during an encounter with Boston police at a Bay Cove Human Services facility in Mattapan. The incident was referred to the Suffolk County District Attorney’s office for investigation. Yet months later, the public still knows very little about what occurred. The man’s identity has not been publicly confirmed, and Boston City Councilor Brian Worrell called for the release of police body-camera footage citing conflicting accounts of the encounter.

This example underscores the larger issue facing Boston’s reform effort. Oversight systems only build public trust when they produce transparency. When critical information remains unavailable months after a death following a police encounter, it reinforces the perception that the oversight framework is not yet delivering the accountability residents were promised.

Boston is not alone in facing these challenges. Cities across the country that pledged reform in 2020 are still struggling to translate those commitments into fully functioning oversight systems.

But Boston should strive to lead.

Five years ago, Boston promised residents a system of civilian oversight that would make policing more transparent and accountable.

When a man can die following a police encounter and the public still does not know what happened — or even who he was — it is clear that promise remains unfinished.

Because in the end, police reform is not about politics.

It is about trust.

And trust, once promised, must be delivered.

Ed Gaskin is Executive Director of Greater Grove Hall Main Streets and founder of Sunday Celebrations

title: Police Blotter: Shoplifting suspects arrested in Prudential Mall, teen found with large-capacity firearm
text:
A man and woman were arrested after allegedly stealing over $1,700 in merchandise from shops on Newbury Street and in the Prudential Mall, according to Boston Police.

At about 6:40 p.m. Friday, police states they received a report of shoplifters in the Alo store in the Prudential building. The two suspects were reportedly seen “concealing multiple items into a bag and exited the store,” BPD said.

The pair left the store as responding officers were involved with another shoplifting incident, police said.

Later the same day, police received another report of the suspects allegedly stealing from the Alo store on Newbury Street, BPD stated. The male suspect, later identified as Floyd Summerville, 55, of Bronx, New York, exited the store. The female suspect, identified as Tiphaine Jones, 45, remained inside.

Summerville was reportedly stopped on 279 Dartmouth Street and put into handcuffs, at which time officers “recovered stolen merchandise,” police said.

Officers also found a key fob and vehicle parked on Dartmouth Street, recovering more allegedly stolen merchandise inside, Boston Police said. The total merchandise added up to $1,726, according to BPD.

Jones was stopped as she exited the store and arrested, during which she allegedly provided officers with multiple names, police stated. Her identity was determined during the booking process.

Both suspects were charged with larceny over $1,200 and conspiracy. Jones faces additional charges of receiving stolen property over $1,200 and providing law enforcement false ID information.

Ghost gun seized

After 9 p.m. on Friday, Boston Police also took several juveniles into custody after finding a large capacity firearm on one and engaging in an altercation with a group teens.

Police with the Youth Violence Strike Force responded to a report of a large party around 5 Metcalf Court in Jamaica Plain, where they found about a teen boy seated with about eight people. As the responders approached in a cruiser, the juvenile male stood and began walking away at a “fast pace,” police said.

When officers exited the car, the teen reportedly broke into a “full sprint,” BPD said, and another individual followed him. One of the teens “was seen clutching the left side of his jacket while running,” police stated.

The pair entered a doorway at 5 Metcalf Court, BPD said, where police caught up and prevented them from closing the door.

The officers conducted a pat frisk, allegedly finding a firearm from one suspect’s jacket, police said.

When they put the boy in handcuffs, the second teen “attempted to interfere, refused to comply with orders, and struck an officer,” according to police.

Police said the group became “combative” and the situation escalated, leading to a third individual to allegedly attempt “to assault officers.” The three suspects were taken into custody, BPD said.

The recovered firearm was identified as an alleged ghost gun equipped with a large-capacity extended magazine loaded with ten rounds.

One 16-year-old male was charged with delinquent unlawful possession of a firearm, large capacity feeding device and ammunition and carrying a loaded firearm and is expected to be arraigned in West Roxbury District Court. The two other teens will be summonsed to West Roxbury District Court on charges of assault and batter on a police officer and disorderly conduct.

Incident Summary

The BPD responded to 241 incidents in the 24-hour period ending at 10 a.m. Sunday, according to the department’s incident log. Those included eight aggravated assaults, one residential burglary, two thefts from a vehicle, one auto theft and 17 instances of miscellaneous larceny.

Arrests

— Denise Banks, 43 Georgetowne Pl, Hyde Park. Operating under the influence (OUI) alcohol.

— Brenda Poliskey, 41 Bowdoin St, Boston. Drug possession class B.

— Wesley Williams, 256 Spruce, Chelsea. Drug distribute class B.

— Moses Collins, 79 Devon, Dorchester. Assault and battery with a dangerous weapon.

— Vincent Durbano, 94 Library St, Chelsea. Shoplifting by asportation.
