title: Gaskin: $1 billion Mass Save cut will cost us more
text:
Massachusetts faces a decision that will test whether we are serious about both climate leadership and economic equity.

Last winter, a grandmother in Roxbury faced a choice too many families know well: keep the heat on or keep food on the table.

After a Mass Save energy assessment, her home was insulated, drafts sealed, and her heating system upgraded. Her monthly bills dropped — not temporarily, but permanently. For the first time in years, she wasn’t choosing between survival and stability. What changed was not her income, but her energy burden. The system around her finally worked the way it was supposed to.

That’s what’s at risk.

A provision in the Massachusetts House’s energy affordability bill, H.5151, would cut roughly $1 billion from Mass Save. Supporters call it ratepayer relief. But for families like hers, it is something else entirely: the removal of one of the only tools that actually lowers costs for good.

To understand why this matters, it helps to remember who Mass Save has historically served — and who it has not. For years, energy efficiency programs disproportionately benefited wealthier homeowners — those with the time, capital, and access to take advantage of rebates, upgrades, and incentives. Renters, low-income households, and communities of color were often left out, not because they didn’t need help, but because the system was not designed with them in mind.

Only recently did that begin to change. In 2022, Massachusetts became the first state in the country to adopt an equity performance incentive, explicitly holding the system accountable for reaching low-income households, renters, and communities of color. This was more than a policy tweak; it was a structural correction. It signaled that access mattered as much as efficiency, and that outcomes should be measured not just in kilowatt-hours saved, but in who benefits.

That progress was hard-won. It required advocates, policymakers, and leaders on the Energy Efficiency Advisory Council to push the system to serve communities it had long overlooked.

Now, just as those gains are beginning to take hold, we are cutting the program.

This is not a matter of trimming excess. Administrative and marketing costs represent only a small share of Mass Save spending. A $1 billion reduction will not come from bureaucracy; it will come from the program’s core — fewer incentives, fewer projects, and fewer families served. In practical terms, it means more families living in drafty apartments, more renters locked into inefficient systems they cannot control, and more households stuck paying high utility bills month after month.

It also means fewer opportunities to modernize the state’s aging housing stock, particularly in environmental justice communities where older buildings are more likely to be energy inefficient. These are not marginal improvements. Weatherization, insulation, and efficient heating systems can reduce energy use in meaningful ways, lowering both costs and emissions. Cutting these investments slows progress on both fronts.

Supporters of the cuts argue that they will lower bills in the short term. That argument is appealing — but incomplete.

Energy efficiency is one of the only tools that reduces costs permanently. When you cut it, you are not eliminating expenses; you are postponing them and often making them worse. Demand rises, infrastructure costs increase, and households remain exposed to volatile energy prices. Utilities must still meet that demand, often through more expensive generation or expanded infrastructure, costs that ultimately flow back to ratepayers.

And like many policies that prioritize short-term savings, the consequences will not be evenly distributed. Households with resources will find other ways to adapt — through private upgrades, newer homes, or alternative energy options. Low-income households will not have those options.

There is another consequence, less visible but just as important. Mass Save has become a quiet engine of workforce development across Massachusetts, supporting thousands of jobs in construction, energy services, and building trades. In recent years, it has also opened doors for small businesses and contractors who had historically been excluded, particularly those owned by people of color.

Through partnerships and workforce investments, including those connected to the Massachusetts Clean Energy Center, the program has helped build a more diverse clean energy workforce. These investments recognize that the transition to a clean energy economy is not just about technology — it is about people. Who gets trained, who gets hired, and who gets to participate in the economic benefits of that transition all matter.

A $1 billion cut does not just reduce energy savings. It reduces opportunity. It means fewer contracts for small businesses, fewer training opportunities, and fewer entry points into an industry that is supposed to define our economic future.

At its core, this is not just an energy decision. It is a choice about who benefits from public investment — and who does not.

The Legislature now faces a clear test. It can treat this as a simple budget adjustment, or it can recognize what is being undone. Mass Save, particularly in its current form, is one of the rare programs that lowers long-term costs, advances climate goals, and expands access at the same time. It reflects an understanding that affordability, sustainability, and equity are not competing priorities, but interconnected ones.

To cut it now, just as it begins to reach communities long left out, sends the wrong signal at exactly the wrong moment. It suggests that equity is conditional, that it can be set aside when budgets tighten, rather than treated as a core measure of success.

Massachusetts should not balance its books on the backs of the very people it has only recently begun to serve. We should be expanding what works, not scaling it back.

Ed Gaskin is Executive Director of Greater Grove Hall Main Streets and founder of Sunday Celebrations

title: Humbled by honor, Chris Nilan headed to Massachusetts Hockey Hall of Fame
text:
Chris Nilan clearly remembers the first time he put on skates.

He was 5 years old and his father Henry brought him, his sister Susan and brother Stephan to the Rexall drug store parking lot at the end of Gardner Street in West Roxbury where he grew up. There was a giant puddle in the parking lot that had frozen over and that’s where he took his first spin. He remembers on that cold and sunny day constantly falling down and getting up and loving every minute of it.

“That’s where the match was lit for me,” Nilan told the Herald earlier this week.

Nilan would graduate from that puddle to Catholic Memorial to Northeastern to the great hockey palaces of his day, the Montreal Forum, Madison Square Garden and Boston Garden.

And on Saturday night at the Sea Crest Beach Resort in Falmouth, he will be inducted into the Massachusetts Hockey Hall of Fame with a stellar class that includes former Bruins and Massachusetts natives Jay Miller, Mike Mottau, former Northeastern coach Jim Madigan and builder Larue Renfro.

“I wouldn’t have ever thought I’d be asked to be in something like this, being a player like myself. Believe me, I’m honored to be in it,” said Nilan. “When I think of being in it, I think of my mom (Leslie) and my dad who sacrificed so much when I was a young kid to get me involved in hockey, getting the equipment and then let me follow that passion I had to one day want to play in the NHL. And to be recognized in this way, it is truly an honor for me. Guys like myself, guys like Jay Miller, guys like Terry O’Reilly don’t usually get asked to be part of things like this. It’s awesome.”

There is a certain symmetry that goes along with Nilan and Miller going into the Hall together, of course. They combined for 4,766 penalty minutes in their respective careers – and that was just the regular season. Nilan and Miller spent a lot of those minutes punching each other, Nilan as a Canadien and Miller as a Bruin, during the 1980s iteration of the ancient rivalry. They have long since become friends.

“Let’s just say it’s apropos,” said Nilan. “I think it really nice we’re going in together. We should be able to have a few laughs together. Both going in the same year is cool. Jay did his job, and I did a job and O’Reilly did a job. A lot of guys did a job that other guys couldn’t do or wouldn’t do. And that was hockey back then. And all those guys that are in the Hockey Hall of Fame in Toronto and the US Hockey Hall of Fame, let’s face it, if they didn’t have those type of guys around … I’m not saying they wouldn’t have had the success that they did, but it sure made it a lot more comfortable for them.”

Nilan admits that there was a time when an honor like this might not have had registered with him. He has been open about his battles with addiction and has said getting sober has opened a whole new world for him.

“The emotion of (this honor) is so much more meaningful,” said Nilan. “When I was struggling with the other stuff, you do all you can do to take care of yourself. Your not worried about much else. When you’re sick and you’re in a bad place like I was, I quite frankly could have probably cared less. And this does hit a lot.”

Another honor he was tickled about when he was speaking with the Herald on Thursday was the fact that he was going to be the torch bearer prior to the Canadiens-Lightning Game 6 on Friday night, an honor that had previously gone to Serge Savard and Yvan Cournoyer in that series. Not bad company.

“A kid from Boston, to have that honor? I think of my mom and dad (who passed away in 2024 and 2021, respectively), they would be beside themselves to be able to see that,” said Nilan. “And my daughter Colleen and son-in-law Sean are driving up for it and they’re driving back down to be there at the Hall of Fame. It’s so cool to be a part of that and to be a part of the tradition. When I think about my sobriety, good things have come into my life because of it. If I wasn’t sober, if I didn’t clean my life up, I would have never been able to experience any of this, at all. It’s awesome. Beyond words.”

Nilan has lived full time in Montreal for the past 15 years and has been spending his time as an ambassador for the Barry. F. Lorenzetti Foundation for mental health. It was through that foundation that he developed a one-man show called “Knuckles” about his life, career and struggles. He’s performed the show five times as a benefit for the foundation and is in talks to do a few more.

Clearly, the 68-year-old Nilan has a story to tell. His advice to young players just entering into the NHL?

“Just follow your dreams and keep the ego in check. Keep the ego in check. You get knocked on your ass pretty quick,” said Nilan. “My dad always told me ‘Keep your goddamn feet on the ground. Don’t ever think you’re a big cheese.’ I think I adhered to that pretty much. I had my issues, obviously, but I think I was always there for the fans. I liked the fans and I’m still that way today. That’s what the game’s all about. We wouldn’t have this game if we didn’t have the fannies in the seats. To kids today, the one thing I’d say is you don’t know how fast it goes. You’re retired a lot longer than you’re a hockey player. You just never think it’s going to end. But, boy, it ends. And you think you’re ready, but you never are.”

title: Police Blotter: Lawrence crash victim suffering from gun shot wound dies
text:
Police are investigating the death of a 20-year-old woman who was involved in a crash while suffering from a gunshot wound, according to the Essex County District Attorney’s Office.

The crash occurred around 9:21 p.m. Thursday on Erving Ave. in Lawrence.

Police responded to the scene and discovered that two 20-year-old occupants of a 2014 Jeep Cherokee involved in the crash were suffering from gunshot wounds.

The young woman was transported to a local hospital where she pronounced dead Friday, a statement from the DA’s office said. The young man was also transported to the hospital in critical condition.

Both the shooting and the crash are being investigated by the Mass State Police, the Lawrence Police, and the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

Fatal fire breaks out at retirement community

An elderly adult and dog died in a fire in Pepperell Saturday, according to officials.

Firefighters responded to Maple Leaf Village, a retirement community, around 2:50 a.m., according to the state department of fire services. When they arrived on the scene, a mobile home was engulfed in flames.

Firefighters entered the home, but couldn’t find any occupants. After attacking the fire from the outside, they later found an older adult who lived in the home dead, as well as a dog.

The Office of the Chief Medical Examiner is still determining the cause of the victim’s death.

“On behalf of the Pepperell Fire Department, I want to express our condolences to the family that lost a loved one,” said Pepperell Deputy Fire Chief John Rose. “This is a sad day for them and our community.”

The cause of the fire is also being investigated.

Athol man busted for allegedly selling fentanyl

Boston Police arrested a 40-year-old man from Athol Saturday after recovering 32 grams of fentanyl.

Officer said they saw Keith Curtis using drugs via a glass pipe near 700 Boylston St. around 3:50 p.m.

According to BPD, when the officers approached Curtis, he pushed an officer away and attempted to flee.

After “brief struggle,” the suspect did flee but was caught quickly by additional officers arriving on the scene, BPD said.

Police said they recovered the fentanyl after a search of the suspect and charged Curtis with trafficking a Class A drug and resisting arrest.

title: Boston Mayor Wu taps new parks commissioner, creates new leadership job amid budget crunch
text:
Boston Mayor Michelle Wu appointed Diana Fernandez Bibeau, who has been overseeing her administration’s contentious $325 million rebuild of White Stadium, as the city’s new parks and recreation commissioner.

Wu announced Monday that Fernandez Bibeau will be the first Latina to lead the parks and recreation department, and will work concurrently as the city’s deputy chief of open space, a newly created position by her administration — beginning on June 1.

The new leadership position comes at a time when the city has frozen some spending and delayed hiring for the remainder of this fiscal year to try to close a $48.4 million budget gap. The mayor has proposed a $4.9 billion budget for next fiscal year with a 2.1% increase, the lowest rate of growth since the Great Recession in FY10. Wu created 301 new positions in her first three years in office, 97 of whom earned more than $100,000.

Fernandez Bibeau, who already works for the Wu administration as deputy chief of urban design for the planning department, will not be taking two salaries for her new roles. Compensation is determined based on the senior-most role occupied, which in this case would be deputy chief of open space. The post pays roughly $190,000, the mayor’s office said.

Fernandez Bibeau was paid $204,235 as deputy chief of urban design last year, a job she began in 2022. She replaces Interim Parks Commissioner Cathy Baker-Eclipse, who was paid $156,539 last year, per payroll records.

“I’m thrilled to appoint Diana Fernandez Bibeau as commissioner of parks and recreation and deputy chief of open space,” Wu said in a statement. “Diana brings years of experience as a dynamic problem solver and visionary designer, grounded in deep personal connection to the communities we serve and the role of public spaces connecting us all.

“Her leadership will build on Boston’s legacy stewarding the nation’s oldest and most beautiful park system,” Wu added. “I am deeply grateful for the leadership of Interim Commissioner Cathy Baker-Eclipse over the last year and look forward to our continued work creating beautiful, welcoming and resilient open space where every resident feels at home.”

Fernandez Bibeau is the latest leadership hire for Wu in recent weeks, despite her administration stating in March that it would be pausing hiring to try to close a $48.4 million budget shortfall by June 30, the end of the fiscal year.

Wu last week hired a new press secretary Marcela Dwork, who held the same role for Middlesex District Attorney Marian Ryan and left her job at strategic communications and public relations firm Denterlein to work for the mayor.

She also tapped Veronica Yoo, a former spokesperson for U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, as her new chief of communications earlier this year.

Fernandez Bibeau has been overseeing the city’s contentious public-private rebuild of Franklin Park’s White Stadium for shared use by a new National Women’s Soccer League team, Boston Legacy FC, and Boston Public Schools student-athletes.

Taxpayers are picking up the city’s costs, which have nearly tripled, from $50 million to $135 million, since the project was announced two years ago.

Fernandez Bibeau has testified on behalf of the Wu administration at City Council hearings on White Stadium and a Suffolk Superior Court trial that ruled in favor of the city, and against a community lawsuit that seeks to block the project. The ruling was appealed, and the case is now being weighed by the Supreme Judicial Court.

The mayor’s office said Fernandez Bibeau brings more than 15 years of experience in the public and private sectors to her new dual roles, “including a substantial design portfolio to advance equity, sustainability, and resilience through Boston’s built environment.”

Prior to joining the Wu administration, she practiced landscape architecture and design at Sasaki for more than seven years, working on several significant projects including the Frederick Douglas Memorial in Roxbury and coastal resiliency efforts in Charlestown and East Boston.

Wu’s office said “she will also be making history as the first Latina to serve as commissioner of the Boston Parks and Recreation Department,” where she will lead more than 300 full-time staff and the stewardship and programming of 2,200 acres of permanently protected open space.

Her hire follows that of Rodney Marshall, who Wu appointed last month as the city’s first Black fire commissioner.

“Parks are my passion,” Fernandez Bibeau said in a statement. “As an immigrant, they were the first spaces where I felt welcome, sparking my dream to become a landscape architect. I’m eager to build on the parks department’s legacy of excellence by bringing a renewed perspective to how we grow, protect, and program our parks.

“I look forward to delivering on Mayor Wu’s vision — ensuring Boston’s public spaces are exceptional, safe, and welcoming for everyone,” she added.

Fernandez Bibeau immigrated from the Dominican Republic as a young child, and considers it to be a formative experience. She graduated with a degree in landscape architecture from Temple University, lives in West Roxbury, has three children, and enjoys gardening with her husband, Devin Bibeau.

Mayor Wu formally announced the appointment Monday at a press conference at Mozart Park, where she also shared plans to connect open spaces throughout Boston to realize Frederick Law Olmsted’s vision for a completed Emerald Necklace park system.

title: Police Blotter: ‘Operation Safe Scooter’ in Roxbury recovers 10 scooters, mopeds
text:
As a result of “Operation Safe Scooter,” Boston Police said they confiscated ten moped/scooters for motor vehicle law violations Monday.

The operation took place around 4 p.m. and was in response to “ongoing public safety concerns regarding the use of these vehicles” on Shirley Street in Roxbury, according to the department.

“The Boston Police Department remains committed to improving traffic safety and will continue to conduct enforcement operations across the city,” the department said in a statement.

The department urged anyone with information about illegal activity related to scooters and mopeds to reach out to BPD.

The operation took place the same day that Governor Maura Healey filed new legislation to regulate e-bike, scooters, and mopeds, known as “micro-mobility devices.”

A statement from Healey’s office said that the law would create a “first-in-the-nation, speed-based framework,” that allows lower speed e-bikes to largely operate like bikes while higher speed bikes, scooters, and mopeds will be limited to riders 16 and older. Drivers of the faster mopeds, e-bikes, and scooters will have to get insurance and register.

The law would also set more restrictions on where high speed devices can operate and give the Registry of Motor Vehicles more control to regulate new technologies without waiting for legislation to pass on Beacon Hill.

“Micro-mobility is already a part of how people get to work, school and around their communities, but right now, the rules are unclear and inconsistent,” Healey said in a statement. “We are seeing too much reckless behavior, more crashes and close calls, and too many people, especially pedestrians and young riders, are at risk.”

Remains of missing Hanson woman found in Plymouth

The Plymouth County District’s Attorney’s Office announced human remains found off Route 3 belong to a Hanson woman who went missing more than six years ago.

A hunter found the remains in a wooded area in Plymouth on March 6, the DA’s office said.

The office contacted the FBI, who was able to match DNA from the remains to Sandra Crispo, a woman who was reported missing by her family after they couldn’t get in touch with her in August of 2019.

Hanson Police, the Mass State Police, and the DA’s office “conducted an extensive and exhaustive investigation into her disappearance,” after Crispo was first reported missing, the DA’s office said.

The investigation remains ongoing and anyone with information was asked to reach out to the Hanson Police Department or the Mass State Police.

Dorchester man sentenced to up to 40 years for abusing foster kids

A judge sentenced a 46-year-old Dorchester man to between 28 and 40 years in prison for abusing two foster children in his care, according the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office.

Taryl Ford, 46, was convicted last month on four counts of aggravated rape, two counts of indecent assault and battery on a child under 14 and one count of disseminating obscene matter to a minor.

Ford’s mother had fostered 34 children over the span of 11 years, while Ford lived in the building and acted as an approved secondary caregiver for the kids, the DA’s office said.

The first victim was abused starting when he was five years old for about a year and the second was abused from age seven to eight. A third child was shown porn by Ford, the DA’s office said.

During the sentencing hearing on Monday, the victim impact statements described how Ford’s crimes profoundly impacted their lives.

One of the victim’s mothers said that Ford “is the monster that lives under the bed but never stays under the bed.”

Because Ford’s mother fostered so many children, prosecutors believe there could be more victims, and the DA’s office encouraged anyone with more information to reach out.

“These courageous victims eloquently described the lasting impacts of this serial abuse on them. And, to their enormous credit, they also expressed their concern for other children who may have been hurt,” Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden said. “We hope anyone else who may have been abused by Taryl Ford will contact authorities. They do not have to bear this pain alone.”

title: Police Blotter: Man charged in 2023 Caribbean festival shooting sentenced to life
text:
A Dorchester man charged with participating in a harrowing shooting at a festival that left eight people injured was sentenced to life in prison Thursday.

Gerald Vick Jr., 33, was convicted of carrying a firearm without a license (second offense), possession of a large capacity feeding device, and possession of a machine gun, according to the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office.

The DA’s Office said that Vick was also charged as a habitual offender because of convictions for two prior crimes, leading a judge to issue a mandatory life sentence. He will have the possibility of parole in 15 years.

Before Vick was supposed to face trial at the end of 2024, the DA said he removed a GPS bracelet and fled the state. He was apprehended six months later in Georgia.

The shooting at the 2023 J’Ouvert parade, a Caribbean festival, took place on Aug. 23 and was observed by officers and caught on surveillance footage, the DA’s Office said.

Officers saw a confrontation between two groups of men, and as they approached, shots rang out. Eight people were injured but no one was killed.

Vick was among the group of men and arrested on the scene that day, according to the DA. Police found a sear switch that was capable of holding 24 rounds; five of the shell casings recovered on the scene were found to have been fired from the gun.

Two other men, Dwayne Francis, 31, and Sebastian Monteiro, 22, were also charged in connection with the shooting. Francis is scheduled to be tried on June 1, while Monteiro was sentenced to four years in prison.

“This was a brazen, unconscionable act of violence made all the worse by being committed in the middle of one of our city’s proudest cultural events, attended by thousands,” Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden said in a statement. “I’m grateful for the time and care these jurors took in reviewing all the evidence and testimony before reaching their decision to hold Gerald Vick accountable for his reckless actions.”

MS-13 gang member sentenced for role in 2010 Chelsea murder

A MS-13 gang member was sentenced Thursday to 15 years in prison by a federal judge for his role in a 2010 Chelsea murder.

Adam Rodriguez, 35, had already pleaded guilty to conspiracy to participate in a racketeering enterprise for his involvement in the killing of Joaquin Aguilar, of Allston.

Rodriguez and other members of the local syndicate of the MS-13 conspired to kill Aguilar because they believe he was a member of a rival gang, the U.S. Attorney’s Office said in a statement.

Aguilar was found stabbed to death under a Chelsea on-ramp. According to the U.S. Attorney, Rodriguez was among the individuals who led the victim to the secluded area, where he was hit over the head and stabbed multiple times.

A secret recording of a gang meeting showed Rodriguez getting disciplined from leaving Massachusetts after the crime without permission, the statement said.

Man shot, killed in car in Holyoke

The Hampden County District Attorney’s Office is investigating a fatal shooting in Holyoke Wednesday night.

Officers responded to ShotSpotter activity near Suffolk St. just before 9:30 p.m. and found a man suffering from a gunshot wound sitting in a vehicle.

The victim was transported to a local hospital where was later pronounced dead, the DA said.

The office indicated that the suspects may have tried to rob the victim but noted that the investigation is on-going.

Bristol DA identified New Bedford homicide victim

A 31-year-old man was found shot in a vehicle in New Bedford last Wednesday night.

The Bristol County District Attorney Office identified the victim as Steven Coan, of New Bedford.

Police responded to ShotSpotter activity around 11:30 p.m. in the area near Achushnet Ave. and Russell Street, the DA said in a statement.

When they arrived, Coan was suffering from several gunshot wounds in his car. He was transported to the hospital but died a short time later, the DA said.

The shooting is being investigated by the DA, the Mass State Police, and the New Bedford Police.

title: Police Blotter: Quincy man injected harmful black-market Botox at Milton spa
text:
A Quincy man admitted in federal court that he was injecting clients of his Milton spa with black-market Botox, which led many of those customers to suffer some serious medical effects.

Rodrigo de Medeiros Siqueira, 33, the proprietor of Rodrigo Beauty at 464 Granite Ave. in Milton, pleaded guilty in federal court in Boston to one count of misbranding of a drug after shipment in interstate commerce with the intent to defraud or mislead, a charge that carries a maximum sentence of three years in prison. U.S. District Court Judge Richard G. Stearns scheduled sentencing for Aug. 12.

The case against Medeiros Siqueira began June 1, 2025, when a physician reported to the Massachusetts Department of Public Health (DPH) a patient who was suffering from botulism and who reported having received injections of generic Botox at Rodrigo Beauty, according to a law enforcement affidavit filed to support the charge. Botox is a brand name for Botulinum toxin, which is used as a cosmetic treatment for wrinkles.

Then similar reports started rolling in.

Of the six types of botulism — infant botulism, food-borne, wound-associated, adult intestinal toxemia, inhalation, and iatrogenic — botched botox injections can create the last one, according to the affidavit.

This iatrogenic type of poisoning, the affidavit explains, “is caused by botulinum toxin circulating in the blood and producing effects remotely from the injection site … (which) can lead to life-threatening symptoms, including: blurred or double vision, drooping eyelids, slurred speech, and/or difficulty swallowing or breathing.”

When confronted by U.S. Food and Drug Administration agents, Medeiros Siqueira said he had obtained the legitimate and FDA-approved Botox brand Daxxify from another spa operated by two licensed nurse practitioners, according to the affidavit. Those nurses told investigators no such thing had occurred. Revance, the maker of Daxxify, also said they had no record of Medeiros Siqueira.

“Manufacturers of other commonly used FDA-approved botulinum toxin products likewise reported that there is no record of Medeiros Siqueira or Rodrigo Beauty ever having purchased their products,” the affidavit states.

Investigators said that it appears that Medeiros Siqueira, who is not certified or licensed to perform Botox injections and is therefore not legally permitted to obtain legitimate Botox products, obtained his wares from less-than-legitimate sources. Investigators say people often purchase alternative products from other countries like China and South Korea both because these are “typically significantly less expensive than FDA-approved” products and because they do not require licensure.

Federal authorities ask that anyone who believes they received an illegal injection from this man or at his spa should fill out the questionnaire at the FDA’s website at https://www.fda.gov/inspections-compliance-enforcement-and-criminal-investigations/criminal-investigations/oci-vw-assistance-rodrigo-beauty.

Illegal immigrant gets to 2+ years for selling ghost guns

An illegal immigrant from El Salvador who was residing in Chelsea was sentenced to more than two years in prison and will be subject to deportation after pleading guilty to selling ghost guns to gang members.

U.S. District Court Chief Judge Denis J. Casper sentenced Melbi Ovidio Ortez, 41, to 27 months in federal prison on the firearms violations. Ortez is subject to deportation after serving his sentence.

Ortez was arrested in June 2025 and in February pleaded guilty to one count of engaging in the business of dealing in firearms without a license and one count of distribution of and possession with intent to distribute a controlled substance.

Prosecutors say that Ortez is an 18th Street Gang associate known to sell guns and drugs to members of the gang. Over a single month last year, from April 3 to May 2, prosecutors say, Ortez sold four pistols, two with defaced serial numbers, making them untraceable ghost guns, and more than 100 rounds of ammunition from behind his house in Chelsea. Those guns were a Glock 9mm, a Sturm and Ruger .22 revolver, a Glock .40, and a Colt .380. He also sold cocaine.

title: Governor Healey, Mayor Wu to co-invest Boston, state funds to build 110 new homes in Roxbury
text:
Gov. Maura Healey and Mayor Michelle Wu announced plans to combine $10.5 million in city and state funds to build 110 new apartments in Roxbury, and will co-invest millions more to advance other Boston housing projects.

The money to advance construction of new homes at 20 Malcolm X Blvd. will be drawn from Healey’s momentum fund and the city’s housing accelerator fund, to support a development led by SV+Partners and Trax Development.

Healey’s office said the project aims to transform an underutilized parking lot in Roxbury’s Nubian Square into a mixed-income housing community with affordable and market-rate apartments, public space and neighborhood amenities.

“Our administration is committed to building more housing, lowering costs and creating more opportunities for people across our state, and that requires new partnerships and innovative financing tools,” Healey said in a statement. “We created the momentum fund to help move housing projects into construction faster.

“By bringing together state, local and private investment, this partnership will help transform an underutilized site into new housing, create jobs and support the future of Nubian Square,” Healey added. “This is exactly the kind of collaboration we need to help unlock more housing production and create more opportunities for people across our state.”

Officials described the Roxbury housing project as a “first-in-the-nation state and local co-investment.”

It’s the first to leverage city and state funds through a new partnership that will see the city invest $50 million from a $110 million housing accelerator fund created by Wu last year, alongside the state’s momentum fund, created though Healey’s Affordable Homes Act, to support several housing projects across Boston.

Both funds are effectively aimed at spurring housing production for projects that have already been approved, but lack the financing to move forward. Boston is the first co-investor in Healey’s momentum fund.

The Roxbury development will include a six-story mixed-income building with 22 affordable rental homes and 88 market-rate apartments. Amenities will include a sixth-floor sky deck, rear courtyard, fitness center, resident lounge with kitchen, co-working space and game room. It will also create a nearby MBTA bus stop.

“This project will prevent displacement and add more housing for older adults, working families and longtime residents of Nubian Square,” Wu said in a statement. “As families face increasing pressure on household budgets and growing housing costs, I’m excited to join efforts with Gov. Maura Healey and the state in this innovative partnership to strengthen our communities by building more housing.”

title: Boston carjacking suspect had at least 17 criminal cases before cop shot, killed him: Attorney
text:
An attorney for the Boston police officer accused of manslaughter in the on-duty shooting of Stephenson King says the carjacking suspect had an “extensive history” of violence, including at least 17 criminal cases.

David Yannetti, representing Officer Nicholas O’Malley, 33, has filed a slew of discovery motions in the case — requesting records of King’s complete criminal history, including all arrests, charges, dispositions, and pending matters from any jurisdiction.

“Information available to the public reflects that Stephenson King had an extensive documented history of violent conduct,” Yannetti states in a motion filed in Boston Municipal Court’s Roxbury division on Wednesday, “including seventeen or more criminal cases across Massachusetts courts, prior instances of resisting arrest while in a vehicle and ramming police vehicles, strangulation charges, firearms offenses, assault charges, and domestic violence.”

O’Malley shot and killed King, 39, during an encounter on March 11.

The case has pitted the Boston Police Department against Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden.

King allegedly assaulted a woman and stole her vehicle in Roxbury. When O’Malley and another officer approached him while he was parked in the Boston neighborhood, he didn’t fully comply with their orders, according to police reports based on footage of the incident.

According to O’Malley, after King backed into their cruiser, the officer feared his partner would get hit, but according to prosecutors, King was only trying to flee the scene.

O’Malley was charged with and has pleaded not guilty to manslaughter, and Hayden said his office has brought the matter to a grand jury.

“The identity of the first aggressor,” Yannetti states in the motion, “and specifically who escalated this encounter to the level of deadly force, is the central disputed issue in this case.”

Under procedural requirements, Yannetti mentions, O’Malley is “entitled to introduce evidence of specific acts of prior violent conduct that the victim is reasonably alleged to have initiated, regardless of whether the defendant was aware of such conduct at the time of the incident.”

Yannetti, who came to fame as an attorney for Karen Read, is requesting all criminal, court and law enforcement records into King’s criminal past. The defense is also seeking a court order for prosecutors to preserve video and audio recordings of previous police interactions with King.

“These motions reflect a portion of our initial investigation into the many past violent acts of Stephenson King,” Yannetti said in a statement.

The defense will address the motions next Thursday during a probable-cause hearing.

The Herald previously reported in late March that King had a history of resisting arrest, including an incident in October 2019, when a Mass State Police trooper tried to pull him over, but King did not comply.

King had three warrants for his arrest at the time.

King’s family has said he was suffering from mental health issues at the time of his death.

“Any suggestion that this shooting was precipitated by simply a ‘mental health crisis’ completely misses the point,” Yannetti said in his statement on Wednesday.

“When facing an extremely dangerous threat,” he added, “there is no time for a police officer to hold a counseling session on the street or to sit down to discuss the feelings of a menace who is intent on using a motor vehicle as a deadly weapon.”

title: Boston’s low cash flow has Council critics backing off $325M White Stadium opposition: ‘Economic opportunity’
text:
After deadlocking last year on a vote to halt the White Stadium demolition, the Boston City Council now appears to be more supportive of the project, due to the revenue it may bring to a cash-strapped city.

Councilor Julia Mejia was forced to abruptly reverse course Wednesday, when it became apparent that she didn’t have the votes for a resolution calling for the city to pause construction at White Stadium until the Supreme Judicial Court issues a ruling in a community lawsuit that seeks to block the $325 million public-private plan.

“What sense does it make for the city to continue moving forward with permanent construction, while the highest court in the Commonwealth is still deciding whether this project even has the authority to properly move forward?” Mejia said at the City Council meeting. “This is a $325 million project involving public funds, a private partnership, and long-term consequences for Franklin Park, BPS students, taxpayers and the surrounding communities.”

Mejia was able to drum up support from nearly half the Council in January 2025, when her resolution to halt demolition was defeated by a 6-6 vote. Now-Council President Liz Breadon, who would have cast the tie-breaking vote, was absent.

The landscape appears to have changed nearly a year and half later. Mejia’s call for a pause on the pro soccer stadium rehab was challenged even by longtime critics of the project like Councilor Ed Flynn, who said he would vote against it, despite his lingering concerns about the city’s “lousy” community engagement process.

“The reason I’m voting against this proposal is, the city is struggling financially and economically,” said Flynn, who voted to halt demolition last year. “We do need economic development taking place in the city. … I would have a difficult time right now asking for economic development to be stopped, especially when there’s no economic development or little economic development taking place.”

Freshman Councilor Miniard Culpepper, who represents Roxbury and other neighborhoods impacted by the project, said he supports the public-private development “because of the real economic opportunity it can bring to the community and to black and brown businesses, not only during construction, but through the long-term operations of the stadium.”

“Rather than pausing the project, we should be using the remaining phases of construction, including the Grove and South Crescent portions of the project, as opportunities to secure as many contracts for minority businesses as possible,” Culpepper said.

“The Supreme Court will issue a decision in due course, and until then construction should continue to move forward,” Culpepper added. “Delaying this project now risks slowing economic opportunities and undermining momentum at a time when we should be ensuring that the promised benefits actually reach the communities and businesses they were intended to support.”

Taxpayers are on the hook for the city’s half of the costs, which have nearly tripled from $50 million initially to $135 million earlier this year. The escalating price tag has long been a point of contention for the project. The soccer team, Boston Legacy FC, is paying more than $190 million for its portion of the rehab costs.

Councilor Brian Worrell, who voted to halt stadium demolition last year, requested that Mejia settle for a hearing, rather than a vote on her resolution, that would focus on how the taxpayer dollars being spent on the project are impacting the minority workforce and businesses.

Mejia then abruptly changed course, saying that she was willing to entirely scrap her resolution’s language and swap it with Worrell’s request as an amended measure, that the Council could then vote on.

“Everything and anything that deals with processes, protocols and procedures, we always find ways to kick the can down the road,” Mejia said. “We’ve had hundreds of hearings as it relates to White Stadium, and we have not received the type of answers and information … regarding some of these outstanding questions.”

Worrell agreed to put forward his request as a formal amendment, leading to a nearly 40-minute recess in the meeting to draft a new resolution. This caused massive confusion among Council members.

Apparently Mejia agreed to abandon her call for a vote during a second, shorter recess, after Culpepper asked why the Council was being asked to vote on a resolution on the minority benefit language rather than defer action on a hearing order, given that Worrell had asked for a hearing.

Breadon, the Council president, said after a second recess that Mejia had requested that a vote be skipped, without elaborating. Breadon referred the amended resolution to the Council’s Committee on Labor and Workforce Development.

Boston Legacy, a National Women’s Soccer League expansion team, is set to begin playing home games at White Stadium next year, after construction delays forced it to play its inaugural season at Foxboro’s Gillette Stadium this year.

title: Police Blotter: 18-year-old charged in Chelsea stabbing; Mass. Appeals Court affirms Brockton robber’s life sentence
text:
An 18-year-old was arraigned for charges related to the stabbing death of a young man in Chelsea, the Suffolk County DA stated Wednesday.

Jose Joel Umana Janes, 18, was arraigned in Chelsea District Court on Tuesday on a murder charge in connection to the fatal stabbing of 25-year-old Eduardo Rosales López in Chelsea on March 19, the DA said. Janes was ordered held without bail.

“This case pulled together dogged investigative work and available surveillance technology to identify suspects in a terrible burst of violence that ended a young man’s life,” Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said. “I extend my deepest sympathies to the family and friends of Mr. López.”

On the evening of March 19, López and another man were allegedly walking down Everett Avenue when he had a brief interaction with Janes and four other men, according to court records reported by MassLive. The group allegedly chased López and the other man down the street, before they fled in separate directions and López was caught.

The 25-year-old was then assaulted, fell to the ground and was stabbed several times, and the group fled the scene, with Janes allegedly running in a different direction.

Another one of the alleged attackers, Sergio Josue Castellanos Cerrato, 18, was arrested on the night of the stabbing and previously arraigned on murder charges. He was ordered held without bail.

Investigators tracked Janes through “various sources of surveillance footage,” the DA said, and positively identified him through still images.

“Consistent with Cerrato, Janes is alleged to have chased López and stabbed him with a long, fixed bladed knife after López fell down in the middle of the street,” the DA’s office stated.

Janes will return to court on June 12 for a probable cause hearing.

Appeals Court affirms life sentence

On Tuesday, the state Appeals Court affirmed the convictions of a man found guilty of attacking a Brockton woman in her home in 2013, the Plymouth DA announced.

Brian Vines, 51, was found guilty on charges including armed assault with intent to rob a person 60 years or older, assault and battery on an elder causing serious bodily injury, armed robbery and more in relation to a violent 2013 incident.

The Appeals Court affirmed his convictions Tuesday and denied his motion for a new trial, overruling claims that there were issues with the judge not excusing a juror for cause and the defense counsel was ineffective.

In June 2013, Brockton Police were called to a home on Brookfield Drive for a report of a woman attacked in her home, finding a victim in her 60s “badly beaten and lying in a pool of blood in her kitchen,” the DA said. The victim was beaten and stabbed multiple times, including a slash to her throat.

The woman reported her attacker was Vines, who attended school with her sons, the DA stated. Vines had arrived at her home and asked for her son’s phone number, the victim reportedly told police, before putting her in a chokehold with a gun to her back.

Vines demanded all her money, the woman reportedly said, and then demanded her ATM card and PIN number. He then used a weapon to beat her, stabbed her in her back several times and slit her throat, the DA said.

The defendant was arrested days later after being linked to debit card use, and DNA testing confirmed blood on his clothes, the DA stated.

“I applaud our state Appeals Court for their work on this matter, and I’m grateful to them for keeping Brian Vines in prison, where he belongs,” Plymouth DA Timothy Cruz said. “Vines spent decades preying on vulnerable women and the community is far safer with him incarcerated.”

title: Police Blotter: Boston stolen scooters and death suspect convicted of rape
text:
Boston cops were really burning rubber on the illegal scooter issue this week.

During yet another targeted enforcement of illegal moped and scooter activity in the city, this time on Kenberma Road in Dorchester, police arrested three teens and recovered nine vehicles, which they say were stolen.

“The investigation was a result of ongoing public safety concerns as well as quality of life issues regarding the use and storage of these vehicles in the Dorchester area,” the Boston Police Department wrote in a statement announcing the arrests.

Police arrested Kevin Afonseca Varela, 18, of Jamaica Plain; Jayden Theodat, 18, of Roslindale; and a 16-year-old juvenile of Dorchester after allegedly finding the trio in a basement scattered with stolen scooters and mopeds at 11 Kenberma Road.

Members of the BPD’s Youth Violence Strike Force — the gang unit — say they saw significant in-and-out moped and scooter activity at that address and moved in. After gaining access to the basement, “officers observed several mopeds in various states of repair as well as an overwhelming odor of gasoline emanating from the mopeds.”

Police say that none of the vehicles were registered and “all of them showed signs of being stolen with exposed wiring and damaged ignitions.”

Man suspected of women’s death convicted of rape

A man who had been set to plead guilty in the 2021 death of one woman was convicted of multiple counts of rape against two different women.

A Boston jury on Friday convicted Rinnyers Pena, 47, of Dorchester, of drugging for sexual intercourse, strangulation, two counts of rape and two counts of photographing an unsuspecting nude person.

Pena is also charged in the death of 38-year-old Alenny Matos, who had been investigated as a missing person beginning on Jan. 27, 2020, until May 9, 2020. On that day, a woman walking her dog in the area of Enneking Parkway within the Stony Brook Reservation in Hyde Park discovered a body in a trash bag, which was then identified as Matos through dental records.

Pena was scheduled to plead guilty to disinterring a body in the Matos case on April 29, but withdrew his plea halfway through the hearing, according to the Suffolk DA’s office. That case will go to trial at a later date.

Police say that Pena had been in contact with Matos by cell phone two days before she was reported missing and a subsequent investigation suggested that he had picked her up from her Dorchester apartment on Jan. 26, 2020, and drove her to his Norton Street residence in Dorchester.

It was Pena’s cell phone that also sealed the case against him regarding the rapes.

While investigating the Matos case, prosecutors say, police found a series of photographs on Pena’s phone. One set depicted a 21-year-old female who appeared “unclothed and unresponsive or incapacitated on Pena’s bed” as well as photos of him doing inappropriate things with her while she was in that state. Another set on a second phone showed something similar with another female victim.

Prosecutors say that Pena confined the first victim in a locked room at a Roxbury rooming house against her will and plied her with opioids to facilitate his sexual abuse of her.

title: Police Blotter: Chelsea man burned children with lighters, heated forks, DA says
text:
A man is being held without bail on charges that he physically abused young children in both Chelsea and Revere, including burning one with a cigarette lighter.

Kener Bautista-Zepeda, 19, is charged with four counts of reckless endangerment of a child, three counts of assault and battery on a child with substantial injury, two counts of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon on a child under 14, two counts of strangulation or suffocation, and one count of assault and battery. A Suffolk County grand jury indicted him on the charges earlier this week.

Bautista-Zepeda was arraigned on the charges Friday morning in Suffolk Superior Court. Judge Catherine Ham ordered him held without bail, an order that will be reviewed in a dangerousness hearing scheduled for May 28.

The charges stem from two distinct relationships.

The first involves Bautista-Zepeda’s romantic partner and the child they share in Chelsea. The woman told police on March 12, 2025, that Bautista-Zepeda had physically assaulted her and that as he pushed and punched her, their 2-year-old child began to cry. Bautista-Zepeda then allegedly took a cigarette lighter and used it to burn the child on his upper back, causing a burn mark that prosecutor Allyson Portney described as the size of a nickel.

Then came another instance of alleged child abuse last month in Revere. A mother of a 3-year-old took the child to Boston Medical Center for treatment for wounds including what appeared to be burn marks on the child’s arm caused by a heated fork, according to the Suffolk DA’s office.

Revere Police responded to the hospital and took the woman’s statement. She told them that Bautista-Zepeda had regularly babysat her child. After she noticed the wounds, the mother installed a camera in the child’s bedroom. Prosecutors say the camera recorded damning evidence of Bautista-Zepeda’s assault on the child at around 11 a.m. on April 3.

The recording, as Portnoy described it, depicted the child walking toward Bautista-Zepeda “with his arms outstretched as if to be picked up. Bautista-Zepeda then lifts the child with both hands above his own head and forcefully throws the child down onto the bed.”

As the child cried in pain, Portnoy continued, Bautista-Zepeda punches the child in the abdomen three times and then mounts the child and “places both hands over the child’s mouth and nose, bearing his weight down onto the child through his arms and holding the child down by the neck.

“The child is seen on the video struggling to breathe for approximately nineteen seconds as Bautista-Zepeda held his hands over the child’s mouth and nose,” Portney said.

2 men charged in Boston armed bank robberies

Federal prosecutors have now charged two men with the robberies of two Boston banks last month.

Angel Gonzalez, 25, is charged with bank robbery by force and violence with a deadly weapon and aiding and abetting. His alleged co-conspirator Steven Harris was charged earlier in the month.

The pair is accused of robbing first the Santander Bank branch located at 2189 Washington St. in Roxbury at around 10:11 a.m. on April 28 and then the TD Bank branch at 930 American Legion Highway in Roslindale just before noon the same day.

Surveillance footage from the banks shows brazen robberies with the suspects walking into each bank branch already holding pistols.

In one still of the first robbery, Subject-1, who law enforcement identifies as Gonzalez, is shown holding one female bank employee by her collar as she kneels and he places his pistol to the back of her head.

An affidavit supporting the charges says this is the branch manager, who he allegedly “dragged … from her office to a bank teller station, threatening to shoot her” unless the pair got their money.

The would-be robbers aborted their plan when new customers came into the branch, according to the affidavit. The pair then fled the scene in a light-blue Toyota Rav4 with Massachusetts plates.

They found more success an hour and a half later at the Roslindale TD Bank branch, where they allegedly stole around $3,000.

Kickin’ it on the T

The MBTA Police is asking for the public’s help in identifying a man who went haywire and scared passengers on an Orange Line train.

Police shared a video of the man on a train car, apparently around the Jackson Square station, lifting himself onto a bar and then forcefully kicking out one of the car’s windows.

title: Battenfeld: World Cup crowds to test T safety
text:
Just in time for the FIFA World Cup to arrive at the “safest city in the country,” the MBTA is dealing with a terrifying string of crimes on the problem-plagued T, which officials are pleading with riders to take to the matches.

A suspect this week was charged with kidnapping after he allegedly tried to nab a toddler from his stroller and told the mother “I’ll (expletive) kill you; you understand me? I’ll shoot you… Look, he wants to come with me. Look at the way he’s looking at me. He wants me.”

“No user of public transportation should have to experience an episode like this, particularly a parent with a young child,” Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement.

Just what soccer fans want to hear.

Earlier this month a violent man acting in an “antisocial” manner kicked in a window on an Orange Line train and attempted an “unprovoked” attack on a passenger.

And MBTA police several months ago warned the public about an attacker with a large knife attempting to stab people on a bus at Forest Hills. During a struggle, an officer’s gun was discharged but luckily did not hit anyone.

Six people were taken to the hospital in that incident.

“This was a violent person armed with a butcher knife,” police said.

Again in May, police said a man attacked another man and slashed him in the neck at a Roxbury MBTA station.

Last December, in another horrifying unprovoked incident on the T, a group of teens assaulted and filmed an attack and robbery on an 18-year-old rider attempting to board an Orange Line train at Downtown Crossing – a neighborhood plagued by violent crime.

An 18-year-old suspect was charged with assault and battery with a dangerous weapon and unarmed robbery. Police said the teen attackers punched the victim repeatedly and threw him to the ground, then one suspect recorded the attack with his phone then kicked the victim in the head just for good measure.

“This was a frightening experience for this young man and for all of the riders who witnessed it,” Hayden said. “These arrests and prosecutions should serve as warnings to other potential transit offenders – surveillance cameras are in place throughout the system and you will be seen and caught.”

The attacks came as public officials and lawmakers have been planning to deal with throngs of visitors for the World Cup, which is slated to start next month with seven matches in Foxborough at Gillette Stadium.

Hundreds of thousands of people will be descending on the Boston area soon. Boston Mayor Michelle Wu and T officials are strongly urging fans to take mass transit to the matches, including a special $90 Commuter Rail train that runs to the stadium pitch.

Some officials fear the rowdy crowds that take the T could cause safety problems on the trains.

The ancient T system has been plagued with crime and maintenance problems for decades, earning a reputation as one of the worst mass transit systems in the nation.

But Wu has continually bragged that Boston is the “safest major city” in the country, despite evidence and high-profile crimes that show it is not.

The Trump administration last year sent a letter to the MBTA demanding to know what the agency is doing to stop crime on the subway, train and bus system. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy cited assaults on the bus system last summer, including one in which someone shoved a senior woman. In another case a suspect attacked someone with a belt.

Duffy speculated that the federal government could take over South Station, similar to the way the federal government took over crime-plagued Union Station in Washington, D.C.

T GM Phil Eng responded to that letter, claiming safety is a “core component in everything” the agency does, spending hundreds of millions of dollars to upgrade security infrastructure.

But the perception in the public remains that the T is not a safe or reliable mode of transportation, especially in Boston.

And crime is not the only problem facing officials preparing to welcome the World Cup matches to Massachusetts. Wu has been only lukewarm on the World Cup and is feuding with state officials on their plan to shut down Summer Street near South Station on days of the matches.

A number of communities in Massachusetts have also complained that FIFA, the organization running the World Cup, is refusing to grant permits to hold watch parties for the games.

title: Suffolk DA to discuss fatal Boston cop shooting for first time in invite-only community meeting
text:
Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden plans to speak to the community for the first time about his office’s manslaughter case against a Boston cop who fatally shot a carjacking suspect, but on an invite-only basis.

Hayden said the meeting will be held Wednesday afternoon at the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office in Boston, and will be open only to community representatives who receive an invitation. The media will be barred from attending.

“On March 11, 2026, Stephenson King Jr. was shot and killed by Officer Nicholas O’Malley while attempting to flee from officers in Roxbury,” Hayden wrote. “On March 19, 2026, we, the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office, charged Officer O’Malley with Mr. King’s death.

“We recognize that many members of the community have interest surrounding the circumstances of Mr. King’s death,” Hayden added. “On May 20, 2026, a Suffolk County Grand Jury indicted Officer O’Malley on a voluntary manslaughter charge in connection with Mr. King’s death.

“With the conclusion of the grand jury proceedings, we believe now is the appropriate time to invite community representatives to attend a meeting with our office and the Boston Police Department about this incident and matters of transparency around officer-involved shootings,” Hayden further wrote.

Hayden’s invite, obtained by the Herald, appears to apply to community leaders, rather than typical residents, given that he states, “As a member of the community who represents others, your presence is important.”

The DA’s decision to charge O’Malley, 34, before a grand jury indictment was criticized by the local police community, including the head of the city’s largest police union, the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association.

It marked the first time a city cop has faced criminal charges for an on-duty death in “approximately 30 years,” according to Larry Calderone, president of the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association.

Hayden, who is up for reelection this year, has also faced criticism for withholding body camera footage of the fatal shooting.

The footage of the shooting has not been released to the public despite a number of filed public records requests and calls from officials to do so, with Hayden and Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox citing the ongoing criminal proceedings and an investigatory exemption in the public records law.

The Boston City Council held another hearing on the police department’s policy for releasing body camera footage tied to officer-involved shootings on Friday.

Cox, who blew off a similar hearing last month and agreed to appear at this one after the Council threatened to subpoena him, repeated his stance on why his department was not releasing the footage tied to the King shooting.

“If there’s anything that’s going to interfere or potentially jeopardize our ability to hold people accountable in the criminal justice system, that is not going to be released. It is not going to be shown. It’s not going to be shared. … The second that we’re done with that (investigation), it will be released.”

Boston City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, who has called for the footage to be released since the shooting took place, disagreed.

“I’ve said it before, and I’ll say it again, when footage is delayed or withheld, especially in moments of crisis, it creates confusion, frustration, and a loss of trust in the very institutions we are working to strengthen,” Culpepper said.

Hayden’s office told the Herald after Wednesday’s indictment that the footage has already been shared privately with the family of King, 39, and that it contradicts O’Malley’s account, that he was acting appropriately in a deadly situation.

The invite does not state whether community representatives will view the footage.

“We appreciate your understanding as we moved forward appropriately and responsibly in the aftermath of a tragic event before meeting with the community,” Hayden wrote. “Our office is committed to maintaining the integrity of this case and ensuring privacy and respect for all involved, including the family and loved ones of Mr. King.

“While there may be legal limitations on what can be discussed publicly, we remain committed to transparency, respectful engagement, and maintaining trust with the community throughout this process,” Hayden said, adding, “This meeting is invitation only and will be closed to the media.”

title: Boston EMS leader John Gill dies at 61
text:
John Gill, a longtime leader of Boston Emergency Medical Services, has died. He was 61.

Gill, who died Saturday, served with Boston EMS for what would have been 40 years next month, having joined on June 25, 1986, according to the agency.

He was promoted to paramedic in 1991, to deputy superintendent in 2003, and to his final role as superintendent-in-chief — the department’s second in command under Chief James Hooley — in 2020.

“John faithfully served this department for nearly 4 decades, dedicating his entire career to the mission of providing the highest standard of prehospital care to the people of Boston,” Boston EMS wrote in a statement announcing his passing.

“John’s decades of service, leadership, and institutional knowledge leave an enduring mark on Boston EMS. We extend our heartfelt condolences to his loved ones, friends, and colleagues as they remember his life and his longstanding dedication to the department,” the statement continued.

During his career, Gill served on Ambulance 13, Ambulance 5, and Paramedic 16, according to Boston EMS, “where he built a reputation for reliability, depth of knowledge, and dedication to operational excellence.”

Gill’s obituary says that he was “a long-standing member of Knights of Columbus” as well as a founding member of the department’s Honor Guard and instrumental in establishing the Boston EMS Relief Association.

Visiting hours are scheduled for May 28 from 3 to 7 p.m. at Robert J. Lawler & Crosby Funeral Home in West Roxbury. A funeral the next day is for family and friends.

Gill’s family asks that donations be made in his memory to “benefit and support EMT’s furthering their education and pursuing certification as Paramedics in the city of Boston. Donations may be mailed to BEMSRA PO Box 290668 Charleston, MA 02129.”

title: Massachusetts Gov’s Council is slammed for ‘outrageous’ vote to reject ex-prosecutor from Parole Board
text:
Bay State DAs are ripping into the Governor’s Council after the members denied a former prosecutor from joining the Parole Board, calling the council’s vote “outrageous” as they choose “politics over public safety.”

The Governor’s Council last week voted 4-3 to reject Gov. Maura Healey’s nominee Vincent DeMore for the Parole Board.

DeMore, who served 12 years as a prosecutor in the Suffolk DA’s office along with seven years as a criminal defense attorney, would have been the lone ex-prosecutor on the Parole Board — which has been releasing dozens of first-degree murderers from prison.

Now after last week’s denial of DeMore, the Parole Board still does not have a member with a prosecutorial background. That is not sitting well with local DAs.

“The Parole Board as currently constituted is in desperate need of a prosecutor’s perspective, and this was a missed opportunity to balance out this board,” Plymouth DA Timothy Cruz said. “This is what happens when people choose politics over public safety.”

After Governor’s Councilor Christopher Ianella voted against appointing DeMore last week, Ianella said the Parole Board needed more members with backgrounds in social work and psychology — “social science backgrounds.”

The Parole Board already has members with those perspectives, Cruz noted.

“The board has a forensic psychologist, a licensed social worker, members from parole and probation,” the DA added. “Vincent DeMore was more than qualified to serve on the board. We needed his character and experience as a seasoned prosecutor to help the board make fair and just parole decisions.

“For victims and witnesses, their families and communities impacted by crime, parole decisions need to made with representation from a prosecutor, someone who has fought and advocated for victims and public safety,” Cruz said.

‘Go too far in ensuring public safety’

Governor’s Councilor Mara Dolan after last week’s vote said she voted against DeMore out of fear that he may “go too far in ensuring public safety.”

The council vote comes at a time when the Parole Board has freed dozens of criminals convicted of violent felonies, including first-degree murder. The Parole Board granted early release to alleged Cambridge mass shooter Tyler Brown from his already light five-year sentence for shooting at police officers.

“It is outrageous that a well-qualified candidate would not be approved for a position on the Parole Board simply because he was a ‘former’ prosecutor,” Bristol DA Thomas Quinn said. “Although there are other factors to consider, public safety needs to be a top consideration in all parole decisions, especially for those defendants with a history of violence.

“There have been a number of questionable decisions made by the Parole Board which highlights the need for change within the Board itself,” the DA added. “This includes the release of many defendants convicted of first-degree murder. The citizens of the Commonwealth deserve a Board with a balanced approach that puts their safety and welfare at the forefront. That clearly is lacking.”

In addition to his background as a prosecutor and criminal defense story, DeMore currently serves as a Special Victims Counsel in the JAG Corps — where he works closely with victims of crime and represents them in military court proceedings.

Healey was urging the council to approve DeMore, underscoring both his prosecutorial experience along with his current work as a victim’s advocate, saying the Parole Board is in need of a new member with this background.

The governor is now back to the drawing board, assessing new candidates for the position.

The annual pay rate for Parole Board members is $157,533 — up from $155,405 last year, according to the statewide payroll database.

Parole Board members

Healey previously nominated Charlene Bonner, Sarah Coughlin, Angelo Gomez, Rafael Ortiz, and Edith Alexander to the Parole Board. The other member is James Kelcourse.

Bonner: She’s a certified designated forensic psychologist, who also has expertise in substance use disorders. She has more than 30 years of experience in the diagnosis and treatment of mental health and substance use disorders.

Coughlin: She’s a licensed clinical social worker, an alcohol and drug counselor, and a certified recovery coach supervisor. She has experience in violence prevention and restorative justice.

Gomez: His career spans roles as chief parole supervisor, deputy chief parole supervisor, field parole officer, probation officer, correctional officer, and court procedures clerk.

Ortiz: He has served as a probation officer in Central Massachusetts for more than three decades, with a focus on juveniles and emerging adults.

Alexander: Her career began at Perrin House Community Services in Boston, where she ran a residential program for new and expectant mothers in recovery. She was a longtime probation officer at the Roxbury Division of Boston Municipal Court.

Kelcourse: He’s an attorney with a background in criminal defense and civil litigation. He also served four terms in the Massachusetts House of Representatives.

SJC’s Mattis ruling

Scores of first-degree murderers have had Parole Board hearings in the last year following the state Supreme Judicial Court’s Mattis ruling involving “emerging adults” who were initially sentenced to life without parole.

The SJC in 2024 ruled that those convicts who were 18 to 20 years old at the time of the murder cannot be sentenced to life without parole.

This court ruling made more than 200 inmates eligible for parole hearings.

title: ‘This is a big void’: Robert “BK” Kilduff remembered for his love of family, firefighting
text:
A few weeks ago, Boston Firefighter Robert Kilduff was busy arranging for members of the department to attend the dignified transfer and services of a State Police Trooper killed on the job.

Now, his friends and colleagues are left to figure out how to organize Kilduff’s own send off after he died fighting a fire in Dorchester over the weekend.

“I’ve reached for my phone three or four times to call him,” said Sam Dillon, the president of the Local 718, the Boston Firefighter’s union. “We’re planning his services, we’re trying to take care of his family… We’re gonna get it done, I just don’t know how we’re gonna do it without BK.”

Kilduff, known to his friends as “BK” or sometimes Bobby, was always the person to turn to in moments like this — he had boundless energy, a level head, and a deep well of generosity, several union leaders who called Kilduff their friend told the Herald.

Ed Kelly, the General President of the International Association of Fire Fighters, had a picture on his phone of Kilduff standing next to the widow and baby of young Army Sgt. Shane Duffy, a Taunton native killed in the war in Iraq in 2008. Kilduff, a Marine himself, had helped organize the services.

“This is the epitome of what he did, he just showed up when people needed help,” Kelly said.

“Bobby knew you needed his help before you did,” Rich MacKinnon Jr., president of the Professional Fire Fighters of Massachusetts, added.

Kelly said he’d felt that especially after his son, now 16, was diagnosed with cancer at 4 years old.

Kilduff created a website and a social media campaign to start a prayer chain for Kelly’s son. “I would credit all the prayers that my son got for helping to save his life,” Kelly said.

Kelly had originally worked with Kilduff’s father, Robert Kilduff Sr., who was his vice president at the Local 718 after Kelly was first elected president in the early 2000s. Kilduff Sr. was a father-figure to Kelly, and after he died from a job-related cancer he’d developed after years of firefighting, the younger Kilduff stepped up and became his “right hand.”

And Kilduff did everything, worked late, sometimes slept in his office, always took things off other people’s plates. They joked that they won’t really know the true extent to Kilduff’s responsibilities until the coming weeks and months.

“We’ll know when the rent doesn’t get paid and lights go off,” Jay Colbert, a friend of Kilduff and his family and the VP of IAFF’s District 3, joked.

Somehow, though, between the job, the union, and all the work he did for the community — Kilduff also volunteered for the Gary Sinese Foundation helping the families of fallen first responders and veterans — Colbert said Kilduff still managed to always be there for his family.

“He was the quintessential on-the-scene dad,” Colbert said. “Big Disney guy because his kids liked Disney.”

“I think Bobby liked Disney, too,” Colbert added with a smile and a laugh.

They said that Kilduff’s two children, Mason, 22, a Marine, and Hanna Jane, 24, who is in education, take after him and have shown incredible resilience.

In addition to the more than $60,000 raised by both the Greg Hill Foundation and the Professional Fire Fighters of Massachusetts for them, Kelly said that the Tunnel to Towers Foundation, created in honor of a firefighter who died in 911, has said it will pay off the mortgage on Kilduff’s home and the kids’ student debt.

Kelly said they were “completely overwhelmed” and relieved about the stress that they took off their shoulders.

Kilduff is also survived by his longtime girlfriend, who Kelly said, “lost the love of her life,” as well as her daughters who are 12 and 14 years old and Kilduff adored.

The fallen firefighter’s services are scheduled for next week. The wake will be held from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. at Avila Church in West Roxbury on Sunday and the funeral will start at 10 a.m. the next day at The Cathedral of the Holy Cross on Washington St. in Boston.

“This is a big void… this is a big, big hit,” Colbert said. “Everybody likes to lionize people that pass away and say all nice things, and a lot of times it’s true, but this is — we cannot overstate what BK meant to us.”

title: Police Blotter: East Boston couple threw wood, sprayed water at victims in alleged racial assault
text:
Noise coming from an East Boston restaurant didn’t sit well with a neighboring husband and wife who allegedly sprayed water and threw pieces of wood at a group of patrons and now face assault charges.

East Boston Judge Debra DelVecchio has ordered Arielle Raso, 37, and her husband, Gregory, 39, to stay away from Tertulia’s Cafe at 26 Porter Street, where an alleged racial assault unfolded Monday night.

Around 8:30 p.m., city police officers returned to Tertulia’s for a reported assault. Less than two hours earlier, BPD had responded to the cafe for a noise complaint from the Rasos, who live next door.

Officers told the couple to contact them again if the noise persisted after 11 p.m. When police returned to the Porter Street restaurant at 8:30, a female alerted them of a verbal altercation between the Rasos and her party.

“The victim said the Rasos complained about the noise and told the victims, who are Hispanic, to ‘get out of this country,’ ” the Suffolk DA’s office said in a release. “They also used racial slurs and threatened to kill the victims.”

The Rasos are accused of breaking off a piece of a shared fence, throwing pieces at the group, and striking a child. The couple also allegedly sprayed the victims with a hose.

“All of the victims reported being hit by water,” the Suffolk DA’s office said. “While interviewing the victims, officers heard Arielle Raso admit she sprayed the group with a hose and heard her say ‘I will kill you, I don’t give a [expletive],’ followed by ‘I’m [expletive] done with all those [multiple racial expletives].’ ”

Arielle Raso, arraigned in East Boston BMC on Tuesday, has been charged with seven counts of assault and battery, seven counts of civil rights violation, seven counts of threatening to commit a crime, and one count of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon on a child under 14.

Gregory Raso has been charged with seven counts of assault and battery, seven counts of civil rights violation, and one count of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon.

“The assaults on this group were terrible alone, but the injection of such vile racial rhetoric makes this incident even more appalling,” Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement. “Our office will not—and our society must not—allow such actions to go unnoticed and unpunished.”

Delvecchio set bail at $750 each, also ordering the Rasos to have no contact with the victims or any restaurant patrons. The Rasos will return to court on July 28 for a pretrial hearing.

Shooting outside a bar near TD Garden

The Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association is sounding off after a shooting outside a popular bar near TD Garden sent patrons frantically searching for cover.

City officers responded to a shots-fired call in the area of 100 Legends Way, the address listed for the Garden, at about 10:50 Tuesday night.

Responding authorities noted they discovered ballistic damage to a parked vehicle and a shattered door at Hotel Indigo, 280 Friend St.

Sullivan’s Tap, at 168 Canal St., posted a video on Instagram showing patrons running for safety after the gunshots. The establishment reported that no one inside was hurt.

The Police Patrolmen’s Association called the incident a “BRAZEN downtown Boston shooting.”

“This is NOT what a safe city looks like,” the union stated on social media on Wednesday. “The numbers don’t lie. Fewer cops means more crime. More crime means LESS SAFETY for EVERYONE.”

No arrests have been made amid the ongoing investigation.

Those included one robbery, six aggravated assaults, four commercial burglaries, one residential burglary, four larcenies from vehicles, 19 instances of miscellaneous larceny, and one auto theft.
