title: Police say multi-million dollar JP heist case of caretaker turned crook
text:
Millions of dollars of fine jewelry — diamond, gold, pearls — disappeared from a safe in the basement of a Jamaica Plain residence last November.

Six months later, police say the man who stole the rings, watches, bracelets and necklaces once worked in the JP home as a caretaker.

Cory Kisakye, 27, of Randolph was arrested Tuesday in Miami, Florida, according to Boston Police.

He was arraigned in West Roxbury District Court on charges of unarmed burglary, breaking into a depository, and larceny from a building.

The incident took place on Nov. 19, around midnight, when two suspects broke into the Allandale Rd. home and looted a locked safe room containing designer jewelry, including Tiffany and Co., Piaget, Chopard, and De Grisogono pieces, police said.

The individual items were valued between $1,000 and $850,000, “with the total loss estimated to be in the millions,” BPD said.

Surveillance footage showed the suspects entering the basement. The victims reported to police that Kisakye worked for them as a caretaker previously and knew the combination to get into the safe.

BPD said that finger print from the crime scene and GPS data puts Kisakye at the scene around the time of the burglary.

Following the break-in, police said Kisakye traveled to Miami and began pawning expensive jewelry.

In December, he boarded a plane to Uganda declaring $54,000 in cash as he left. “Investigators believe he fled to avoid prosecution,” BPD said.

But Kisakye eventually returned to Florida where he was detained earlier this week.

BPD said that officers in their Fugitive, Special Investigations, and Latent Prints Units along with district detectives worked with Randolph Police and Florida law enforcement.

title: Family of fallen Boston firefighter reflects on legacy: ‘My dad was kind of the best’
text:
Robert “BK” Kilduff Jr.’s son and daughter say they were always aware of the dangers of firefighting, but they also knew that their father saved countless lives.

The pain of losing their father is raw, a week after Kilduff died when he fell out of a window while battling a roaring three-alarm blaze in Dorchester last Saturday night.

“It’s unbelievable,” BK’s son, Mason Kilduff, 22, said. “You can never expect it. It’s always on the back of your head, like it’s a ‘what if,’ especially with this job.”

Mason added that his father always set up arrangements for firefighters to mourn fallen first responders, no matter if they died in the line of duty or off the job.

“You never really expect it to happen to you,” BK’s son added, “but we were always aware of the dangers of the job. But I always think about the amount of lives that he saved, himself, … it is unbelievable.”

On Friday, Mason, a Marine; his sister, Hanna Jane Kilduff, 24, studying education; and their father’s longtime girlfriend, Jess Spruell, visited the Boston Fire Rescue 2 station. There, they opened up about their hero’s life and the legacy that he leaves behind.

“He loved his job,” Hanna Jane said. “He loved the people he worked with. He was really proud of the work that he did.”

Just hours before responding to the Dorchester house fire, Kilduff, a 24-year veteran of the force and third-generation firefighter, assisted in a technical rescue, saving a man trapped in an MBTA elevator shaft.

At the scene, Kilduff and his crew stopped flames, shooting through the roof of a three-decker on Treadway Road, from spreading to adjacent houses, saving property and possibly even more lives.

A mayday was called after Kilduff reportedly fell from a third-floor window.

“I always knew that my dad was kind of the best,” Mason told reporters inside the fire station his father worked out of, “whether it was saving lives in a fire, all the volunteering stuff that he did. We were talking about it last night, the lives that he saved that he didn’t know he saved.”

“Being the guy someone could go to,” Mason added of his father, “he didn’t even know that person needed someone to talk to. He was that guy all of the time.”

Though firefighting proved to be one of Kilduff’s main passions, his family said that they will always remember what he did off the job, as a volunteer, as a longtime partner, and as a father.

Outside his job, Kilduff volunteered for the Gary Sinise Foundation, supporting veterans, first responders and the families of fallen heroes across the country.

“He was a hero outside of just being a firefighter,” Hanna Jane said. “I know that people have talked about him as a coach, as a mentor, and obviously as a father. I mean, in every facet of his life, he was always looking to help the people around him. You could be a hero in a lot of ways. He was a hero in all of them.”

Now, the community has rallied to support Kilduff’s family. The Greg Hill Foundation and the Professional Fire Fighters of Massachusetts have raised over $90,000 in separate fundraisers. The Tunnel to Towers Foundation has also said it will pay off the mortgage on Kilduff’s home and the kids’ student debt.

Hanna Jane spoke about how she and her father took a trip to Disney World last year. Mason laughed about how he and his father landed on a Duck Boat with Patriots players in the Super Bowl rolling rally parade after the team beat the Seahawks in 2015.

Spruell reflected on how BK, her longtime boyfriend, surprised her family by flying across the country to see her two daughters in Seattle.

“I think making memories was really a priority to him,” Hanna Jane said. “That’s something he always instilled in us: If you have the opportunity to do something, if you’re mulling over a trip that you want to take that you want to do with your family, you should always say yes because you never know how much time you have left with them.”

The fallen firefighter’s wake will be held from 3 p.m. to 7 p.m. at Avila Church in West Roxbury on Sunday, and his funeral will start at 10 a.m. on Monday at The Cathedral of the Holy Cross on Washington Street in Boston.

“I just want to emphasize how much he loved being a dad,” Spruell said. “He was so strong for them. And I got to see the other side of what he had to do to be the best dad, and I’m just so proud of him. I’m going to miss my best friend.”

title: Wake for fallen Boston firefighter draws hundreds
text:
Hundreds of people lined up outside St. Theresa of Avila to pay their respects to the family of fallen Boston firefighter Robert “Bobby” “BK” Kilduff at his wake Sunday.

Kilduff died while fighting a three-alarm blaze at home in Dorchester May 23. All five residents made it out safely.

As a procession of firefighters and first responders delivered Kilduff and his family to the West Roxbury Church, members of the community stood along the route in the rain, including a little boy in a firefighter’s costume. Afterwards, a line formed down the block, waiting to get inside.

A large America flag hung from Ladder 29 over the scene.

Since his death, the third generation firefighter, union leader, and father has been remembered both for his love of his family and his job.

His kids Hannah Jane, 24, and Mason, 22, said despite all the lives he saved and the effort he put into the community, Kilduff somehow always found time to make memories with them, whether that was a trip to Disney or attending a Pats Superbowl parade and ending up on a duckboat with some of the players.

“I always knew that my dad was kind of the best,” Mason told reporters during a firehouse interview last week.

“I just want to emphasize how much he loved being a dad,” Kilduff’s longtime girlfriend Jess Spruell said. “He was so strong for them. And I got to see the other side of what he had to do to be the best dad, and I’m just so proud of him. I’m going to miss my best friend.”

Fundraisers for Kilduff’s family have raised more than $100,000. The Tunnel to Towers Foundation, created in honor of a firefighter who died in 911, has said it will pay off the mortgage on Kilduff’s home and the kids’ student debt.

For Kilduff’s funeral Monday, firefighters from across the country are expected to attended, along side several elected officials including Boston Mayor Michelle Wu.

Kilduff was known for his own work organizing firefighters to make sure they’d attend the services of other first responders. “He just showed up when people needed help,” Ed Kelly, the General President of the International Association of Fire Fighters said of his late friend and colleague.

Kilduff’s funeral services will begin at 10 a.m. at The Cathedral of the Holy Cross on Washington St. in Boston.

title: A 17-carat diamond ring, $10,000 loan, and one-way ticket to Uganda: Inside the multi-million dollar JP jewelry heist
text:
After borrowing $10,000 from his elderly employers last August, home-care assistant Cory Kisakye never worked again for the couple or returned to their Jamaica Plain townhouse — until he allegedly broke in and stole a 17-carat diamond ring three months later.

According to police reports and court records, Kisakye, 27, of Randolph, used his insider knowledge of the couple’s home to break in, unlock their safe, then make off with large diamonds, gold, watches, and pearls.

Kisakye was arrested after police said he fled to Florida — and briefly Uganda — following the alleged crime. He was arraigned on charges of larceny from a building, unarmed burglary, and breaking into a depository. He will be back in West Roxbury District Court for a dangerousness hearing Thursday.

His lawyer, Andrew Stockwell-Alpert, told the Herald that he was communicating with the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office about the hearing, and what other issues might be discussed in court.

In addition to the 17-carat rock, estimated to be worth $850,000 alone, the safe also contained a 4.9- and 11-carat diamond rings, two Piaget watches (valued at $20,000), De Grisogono block earrings (valued at $18,000), and two of the couple’s wedding bands, the documents noted.

When the couple, who are in their late 80s, spoke with police, they said that Kisakye had once helped change the battery to the safe and had access to the code. They also told police about the unpaid loan.

After the defendant cashed the $10,000 check, which was supposed to help him pay for a new car, according to the report, the couple said he “refuses to answer their phone calls and has never attempted to repay them.”

Two months after he abruptly stopped working for the victims and a month before the crime, GPS data from a rental car showed Kisakye returned to the area with the intent, the report said, “to conduct a dry-run and/or reconnaissance mission for the November burglary and jewelry heist.”

GPS data from his cellphone as well as a fingerprint found on a Bloomingdale’s bag left in the safe after the burglary placed him at the scene of the crime, according to court records, although investigators noted that they believed he had at least one accomplice on the night of Nov. 18.

Surveillance footage shared by the victims showed two hooded individuals leaving the townhouse just before midnight. Only Kisakye has been charged in connection to the break-in.

There were 46 items in the safe, some of which Kisakye allegedly pawned and sold to feed a substantial gambling habit. According to the police reports, he “spent a significant amount of time at Encore,” in Everett.

He made 55 trips between October 2024 and December 2025, the report said, with a total cash in of more than $142,000.

A few weeks after the burglary, Kisakye sold an $11,000 18kt gold Italian bracelet to a shop in Miami, Florida, using his Massachusetts driver’s license as an ID during the transaction, the reports said. When police showed a photo of the piece to one of the victims, she immediately recognized the bracelet as hers.

Kisakye allegedly made several queries using ChatGPT after the burglary, the reports said, including:

“Can you estimate carats of diamond in picture… how much is 3 ct like that worth”

“What kind of tiffany bracelet is this”

“How much is this diamond worth worst case scenario if its natural”

In addition to the allegation surrounding the November heist, the documents noted that according to Randolph Police reports, Kisakye was also involved in two prior incidents involving a stolen Xbox and a stolen 1.8-carat ring.

Between Dec. 2024 and Aug. 2025, prior to the alleged crime, the report said Kisakye had made 14 pawn shop transactions, including selling jewelry, silverware, Cartier sunglasses, and a PS5, in which he made $9,670.

Kisakye was between Massachusetts and Florida following the break-in, until purchasing a one-way ticket to Uganda on Dec. 9. The report said police believe Kisakye might have been tipped off to the investigation by someone he sold gold to.

It isn’t clear when or why Kisakye returned to the U.S., but Boston Police said he was taken into custody on May 26 in Miami.

title: Boston adds new park as World Cup makes a mark in the city, beyond the matches
text:
As excitement mounts for the World Cup, youngsters in South Boston are already looking to the future, even after the matches, as they’ve been gifted a community soccer park to enjoy the game they love.

Two adjacent mini-pitches with professional-grade artificial turf, a financial education learning center, and other space for community events, comprise Southie’s Visa Street Soccer USA Park – a hub of energy within the West Broadway Boston Housing Authority development.

The World Cup is set to bring people from around the world to Greater Boston for all kinds of soccer fun – the seven matches themselves at Boston Stadium in Foxboro and watch parties across the Bay State.

The community soccer park unveiled in Southie is part of an initiative that Street Soccer USA CEO Lawrence Cann is spearheading with financial backing from Visa and Bank of America to build 26 such hubs across the 11 U.S. host cities.

“I don’t want to say fear, but our concern was that the World Cup would arrive in the United States, and we’d see it on the TV screens and in the stadiums,” Cann said, “but it wouldn’t leave a legacy here in communities, like where we are today.”

“We’re not only building here,” he added, “but we’re building in every U.S. host city, places like this, where communities can come together and have access to soccer.”

Over 150 kids and families got a glimpse of the fun-filled future that will stem from the Southie community park on Wednesday: interactive soccer clinics, local food vendors and other family-friendly programming.

Each of the two pro-grade artificial turf fields measures 76 feet by 52 feet, featuring rebound boards and perimeter netting, with 12-foot-by-4-foot goals.

Caroline Foscato, president of Soccer Unity Project, founded her nonprofit in 2008 when she launched free soccer programming for youth on fields in Roxbury and the South End. Since then, the organization has served kids from all over Boston and over 100 schools.

Foscato couldn’t help but smile when thanking the creators of the Southie community soccer park.

“We have all been talking about building a legacy from the World Cup and how we can take this powerful moment coming to our city and country,” she said, “and do something.”

“You have stepped up,” she added, “and that is huge.”

title: Boston Mayor Michelle Wu reinstates LGBTQ deputy director after assault arrest
text:
Boston’s LGBTQ+ deputy director is back on the city payroll after being placed on unpaid leave following her felony assault arrest last year, Mayor Michelle Wu’s office confirmed while calling her a “valued” team member.

Daunasia Yancey, 34, of Jamaica Plain, appeared alongside Wu at Monday’s Pride flag raising ceremony, where she introduced herself as deputy director of the Mayor’s Office of LGBTQ+ Advancement.

That appearance raised some eyebrows, given her past widely publicized legal troubles.

Wu also acknowledged Yancey as a member of that office at the flag raising ceremony. Her office confirmed Yancey’s reinstatement on Wednesday.

“The city is proud to serve LGBTQ+ residents and will continue to lead this work in the face of rising discrimination and violence targeting the community,” city spokesperson Veronica Yoo said in a statement. “Ms. Yancey is a valued member of the team who was reinstated to her position following resolution of a legal matter.”

Wu’s office did not state when her reinstatement became effective. Yancey was placed on paid leave on April 15 of last year, after disclosing her arrest to the city. She was placed on unpaid leave on May 7 last year, “once the city” said it “was able to obtain more specific information,” and remained employed by the city.

Yancey was arrested and charged with assault and battery and assault and battery with a dangerous weapon on April 11, after allegedly attacking the ex-wife of her then-girlfriend in a Roxbury home during a dispute the former spouses were having over the return of a birth certificate.

Court records show the felony assault and battery with a dangerous weapon charge was dismissed on July 10 of last year, and the misdemeanor assault and battery charge was continued without a finding on that date.

On that date, Yancey entered a plea colloquy, and she changed her plea to admission of sufficient facts, which was accepted by the judge. She was ordered to stay away from the victim and enter into and complete anger management, court records show.

The mayor’s office statement indicates that resolution was satisfactory enough to lead to Yancey’s reinstatement to her high-ranking position.

Yancey, who founded the Boston Black Lives Matter chapter in 2014, was paid $69,398 last year, when she was on unpaid leave for part of the year. She was paid $116,571 in 2024, per city payroll records.

The assault that led to her arrest allegedly occurred after Yancey accompanied her partner to the Roxbury home of her partner’s ex-wife, in order to pick up her belongings, according to the police report.

A dispute arose when the ex-wife of Yancey’s partner was unable to produce her ex-spouse’s birth certificate, as it was locked in a safe and she couldn’t find the keys at the moment, the police report states.

The situation allegedly escalated when Yancey’s partner tried to take the locked safe with her, and her ex-wife “grabbed it back and prevented that from happening,” the police report states.

“The victim stated that after her ex-wife attempted to take the safe from her, the ex-wife’s new girlfriend/suspect, Daunasia Yancey … intervened, physically assaulting her,” the police report states. “According to the victim, the suspect grabbed her, and threw her out of the bed.

“The victim also stated that the suspect (Daunasia) took the locked safe from her and slammed her into the wall,” the report continued. “The victim also stated that the suspect had punched her in the neck.”

Wu’s office said last July, upon the revelation of Yancey’s arrest and continued employment, that employees are placed on paid leave upon arrest, per city policy.

“If those charges are related to an employee’s job function or violate the public trust, they may be terminated or immediately placed on unpaid leave until the case is decided or until the job function can no longer be held vacant, whichever comes sooner,” the city said at the time. “Once the case is resolved or facts are confirmed, the city will take appropriate employment action up to and including termination.”

title: Police Blotter: BPS employee assaulted at Mel King South End Academy
text:
A student and school employee were taken to the hospital following an assault at Melvin King South End Academy last week, Boston Police confirmed.

Last Tuesday, officers responded to Mel King Academy at 90 Warren Ave, where a student assaulted an employee of the school, a BPD spokesperson said.

The student and employee were taken to local hospitals, the police said, where the employee was treated for “non-life-threatening injuries.” The student was reportedly sent for evaluation.

The small South End academy is a therapeutic public day school serving students with a primary disability of emotional impairment who need a high level of support.

No arrests were made following the incident, the BPD spokesperson said, and the incident remains under active investigation.

Suspect in JP jewelry heist held without bail, again

Corey Kisakye, a home-care assistant accused of stealing millions of dollars worth of jewelry from his former employers’ home, was held without bail pending a dangerousness hearing that was continued to next week.

Kisakye was arrested and arraigned at the end of May after a months-long investigation into an alleged break in at a Jamaica Plain home safe in November.

According to documents, Kisakye used the information he had from his time working for the owners of the home, a married couple in their late 80s, to break into the townhouse, open a safe in the basement, and steal the jewelry. Among the items taken were 4.9, 11, and 17 carat diamond rings, police reports said.

Kisakye’s lawyer Andrew Stockwell-Alpert said that he asked the court for additional time before making a decision on whether or not his client would be deemed dangerous, explaining that he was looking to see if there is a place Kisakye could stay pre-trial.

Stockwell-Alpert said he would be arguing that his client should be confined to home and wear a GPS monitor instead of being jailed even if he is deemed dangerous.

“It’s up in the air right now,” he said.

Kisakye will be back in court via Zoom Thursday at 9 a.m.

Fatal fire in Swampscott apartment

A Swampscott woman died in a fire at her condo Thursday morning, the Essex County District Attorney Paul F. Tucker confirmed.

title: Ex-US Attorney Rachael Rollins says Michael Proctor defendants should review cases
text:
Former U.S. Attorney and Suffolk DA Rachael Rollins is urging criminal defendants investigated by disgraced and former cops Michael Proctor and Sean Goode to have their attorneys review their cases.

“EVERY SINGLE DEFENDANT that had one of these 2 (poop emoji)stains on their case needs to contact CPCS or their lawyer,” Rollins posted on X Friday. “If you are Black, Latino, Jewish, Female, an Immigrant & Proctor or (No)Goode were involved with your case — DEMAND A NEW TRIAL. Can you say Brady/Due Process violations?”

Rollins served as Suffolk DA until she was appointed U.S. Attorney for Massachusetts during the Biden administration. She was confirmed following a contentious Senate vote, with a tie broken by Vice President Kamala Harris. Rollins resigned in May 2023 after two federal reports found evidence of corruption.

Rollins, who currently works a $104,289 job at Roxbury Community College, according to Comptroller records, is running for her old job as Suffolk DA.

Proctor and Goode exchanged deeply offensive text messages displaying “entrenched and unrepentant hatred for women, Black Americans, Asian Americans, Jews, Hispanics, Arabs, and gay people,” according to a lawsuit filed Thursday by Karen Read.

Proctor, a former Massachusetts State Police trooper assigned to the detective unit at the Norfolk DA office, served as the “case officer” for the investigation into Read for the murder of her boyfriend, Boston Police Officer John O’Keefe, in January 2022. O’Keefe’s body was found frozen on the front lawn of a Canton home owned by a fellow Boston cop and Goode, who resigned days ago from the Canton Police Department, was one of the first cops on the scene.

Read’s attorneys over two trials and again in the new lawsuit have alleged widespread police conspiracy to frame her for O’Keefe’s murder. Read was ultimately acquitted of the charge last summer.

“If I had handled the Karen Read trials & the ‘suicide’ of Sandra Birchmore the way my former colleague did, I would’ve been fitted with an iron scold’s bridle & paraded through Government Center,” Rollins had posted about Norfolk DA Michael Morrissey immediately following reports of the Read lawsuit. “Now these texts? And no elected has called for his resignation? $223K until 1/4/27.”

Morrissey’s office has come under fire regarding both the Read case — which garnered national media attention, including network specials and an HBO/ID docuseries — and the Birchmore case.

Birchmore was found dead in her Canton home in February 2021 and local authorities labeled it a suicide and moved on. But federal authorities weren’t so sure and in September 2024 filed charges against Matthew Farwell for her death.

Farwell, a Stoughton cop at the time, allegedly groomed Birchmore starting when she was 12 years old and then killed her when she told him she was pregnant with their child. A superseding indictment also charges him with the death of the unborn child. Farwell has pleaded not guilty.

Rollins also took aim at the background check system for these two agencies.

“As DA, I personally interviewed the Boston Police Detectives & State Troopers for my Homicide Unit. Looked at IA files & complaints,” she posted Friday. “Talked about race & bias. Majority of my homicide victims were Black & Latino; most of my BPD & MSP candidates looked like Proctor & (No)Goode.”

title: Police Blotter: Ex-Tyngsboro daycare worker gets 21+ years in prison for making child porn
text:
A woman who produced pornography of at least three toddlers at a Tyngsboro daycare for the sexual gratification of her trans-woman partner — a former New Hampshire state representative — was sentenced to more than two decades in federal prison.

“Lindsay Groves was every parent’s worst nightmare: a predator hiding in plain sight, in the place they brought their children every morning so that they would be safe and happy while the parents were at work,” federal prosecutors Anne Paruti and Jessica Soto wrote in a sentencing memorandum.

U.S. District Court Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV sentenced Groves, of Hudson, New Hampshire, to 21 years and 10 months in federal prison on Thursday. Groves pleaded guilty last October to three counts of sexual exploitation of children and one count of distribution of child pornography. She will have to register as a sex offender.

Groves immediately filed notice she was appealing the sentence.

Her co-defendant, Stacie Marie Laughton, 41, of Nashua, N.H., a former New Hampshire State Representative, pleaded guilty last November to three counts of sexual exploitation of children and has yet to be sentenced.

Prosecutors had recommended a sentence of 35 years in prison to be followed by five years of supervised release.

Prosecutors wrote that Groves, a teacher at the since-shuttered Creative Minds daycare in Tyngsboro, “took advantage of her access to children to feed the sexual desires of her then-girlfriend,” Laughton.

“In the midst of an ongoing text-based conversation where Groves and Laughton discussed their mutual sexual interest in the children and what they would like to do with the children, the defendant followed through on what they had discussed,” prosecutors wrote.

“She took them into the bathroom, where no one would see what she was doing, and she created graphic imagery of the children’s genitals with her cell phone. She then sent the photographs to Laughton, and the two used the images to fuel their sexually-motivated conversations,” prosecutors continued.

In all, the feds say Groves traded 2,500 text messages with Laughton and that these messages discussed child exploitation at length and included sexually explicit images of children in her care. Prosecutors say she used bathroom breaks and “naptime” routines as opportunities to record the children.

Excerpts from the pair’s text message conversations included in court documents are for the most part extremely explicit, including detailed descriptions of desired activity with the children pictured in the images.

Prosecutors summarized the messages sent over a five week period leading up to their arrest as demonstrating “an active relationship in which they discussed past sexual encounters, explicit descriptions of sex with each other and others, and indicia of their personal relationship. … The messages also included the discussion about and transfer of child pornography featuring Minors 1, 2, and 3, all of whom were at the time three-year-old students at the childcare facility.”

The gravity of the crimes was made apparent not just in the details provided in court documents but by how family members of children at the daycare reacted when the perverted duo appeared in court for their arraignments.

“I want to (expletive) kill that (expletive),” a tearful woman cried from the gallery at the close of the first hearing in federal court in Boston on June 28, 2023.

“You need to rot in jail!” the woman screamed as a group of people with her tried to calm her down.

title: Boston Police Blotter: Teen arrested after ghost gun falls from waistband
text:
Boston Police arrested a 17-year-old after a ghost gun allegedly fell out of his waistband during a foot chase.

Officers said they noticed a group including the suspect in the parking lot area of Monsignor Reynolds Way around 6 p.m. on Friday while they were patrolling the Cathedral Housing Developments.

When the officers entered the parking lot, they said they saw the group start to disperse.

The teen suspect “began walking away in a hurried manner with long strides,” BPD said, and kept looking back at officers as he “quickened his pace again.”

He continued to look back at the officers before starting to record them — then he took off towards East Brookline Street and Washington Street, BPD said.

As the teen was running, police said he clutched his waistband. Officers then saw a firearm fallout and heard it hit the ground, according to the department.

The 17-year-old was arrested, and police said they identified the firearm as a 9mm loaded ghost gun.

The suspect’s fanny pack also allegedly contained 30 grams of fentanyl pills, six grams of crack cocaine, and a knife.

Officers charged the suspect with carrying a loaded firearm without a license, possession of a large-capacity feeding device, possession of a firearm in the commission of a felony, possession of ammunition without an FID card, trafficking fentanyl, and possession with intent to distribute Class B drugs.

The suspect is expected to be arraigned in Boston Juvenile Court.

Police looking for suspect in Museum of African American History arson

Both the Boston Police and National Park Service are investigating an incident involving arson and vandalism at the African Meeting House on Beacon Hill.

The incident occurred in the early hours of Wednesday morning, according to NPS, who said video footage showed a person opening a package outside the building, removing what was inside, and burning some of the objects in the alley next door.

The crime was reported to Boston Police by an employee of the Museum of African American History which operates the historical site, according to an incident report.

Materials inside the package were for Juneteenth, the employee told police.

The report noted that the incident was a suspected hate crime, motivated by “Anti-Black or African American” bias.

According to NPS, the meeting house is the oldest still existing Black church in America.

title: Column: For ‘Ferris Bueller’s Day Off’s’ 40th anniversary, we found the real Ferris Bueller
text:
Ferris Bueller is a lifelong Republican.

He holds a conservative view of the U.S. Constitution. I know because we spoke the other day. Ferris Bueller was fun to talk to and extremely charming and, despite what the movie suggests, he was thoughtful. Ferris Bueller owns a sheep farm in the Hudson Valley of New York, and he produces his own maple syrup. He has also remained close to the major seats of power in this country for several decades. He served on the transition team during Donald Trump’s first term and worked with Brett Kavanaugh for George W. Bush, he wrote speeches for George H.W. Bush and represented — Ferris Bueller being a trial lawyer now — George Ryan, the former governor of Illinois.

Ferris Bueller didn’t want to talk politics, though.

He said John Hughes (a rare Hollywood Republican conservative) didn’t make political films.

None of which is why I have such mixed feelings about Ferris Bueller, as in the fictional character played by Matthew Broderick, the rascally folk hero of “Ferris Bueller’s Day Off,” which premiered 40 years ago this June and since become a Chicago touchstone.

Still, I was uneasy explaining my ambivalence to Ed McNally.

See, McNally IS Ferris Bueller.

Or rather, he very probably is. Director John Hughes never said flatly that McNally was the basis for the Ferris Bueller character, but McNally believes he was at least a major component in a thinly-veiled composite, and frankly, the evidence is compelling. McNally and Hughes grew up on the same street and attended Glenbrook North High School together. McNally’s best friend back then was a kid named A.C. Buehler, though it was McNally who had such a talent for skipping class that Glenbrook’s principal launched a crusade to catch him. In the film, Ferris skips nine days of school. McNally skipped 27 days. On one of those days off, he “borrowed” his father’s prized possession — a purple Cadillac — and put 113 miles on it, then, as the fictional Ferris does with a red Ferrari, McNally lifted the car onto jacks and ran it backwards, hoping to reverse the odometer.

So, how is Ferris Bueller… er, uh, Ed McNally, 40 years later?

“My life, on certain levels, turned out about the way you might think Ferris’ life would turn out,” he said.

McNally went from almost a month of skipping classes and the wrath of the Glenbrook administration to Yale University, the University of Notre Dame and the London School of Economics. Then he was suspended a year from Yale because of his talent for pranking — including stealing several prized possessions of Harvard and planting a totally fake story about a Yale kite-flying team in the New York Times. A decade later, as a traveling scholar in China, while riding in a motorcycle sidecar, he was arrested with John Burns, the Times’ Beijing bureau chief, accused of espionage and expelled from the country.

“On some level, it all kind of tracks,” McNally said. “It’s about what you’d expect of Ferris. Like the movie, I guess it’s been a mixed bag of the consequences of exuberance.”

He later became an assistant attorney in the Southern District of New York; and George W. Bush’s first general counsel for Homeland Security; he’s now a law partner at the Manhattan-based firm Kasowitz, which has represented Trump and conservative commentator Bill O’Reilly.

Frankly, I can’t help but think of Tracy Flick, the overachieving anti-heroine of “Election” (1999), played by Reese Witherspoon as an intense, rule-bound Ferris. She spends much of the film certain of her place in the high-school meritocracy, and a thorn in the side of her teacher, played (serendipitously enough) by Matthew Broderick. But in the final minutes, we see her in Washington, years later. Broderick’s character is attending an educator’s conference and happens to spot Tracy getting into a politician’s limo. As he narrates, he remembers her relentlessness, he feels sorry she let ambition rule her life, but soon that annoyance veers into jealousy, his voice rises: Where is she going, why is she in a limo — “and who the (expletive) does she think she is?” He throws his drink at the car window, panics and runs off. Faced with the Ferrises of the world, all we can do is rage.

Indeed, Jeanie, Ferris’ sister (played by Jennifer Grey), expresses this very same irritation with her brother, blurting: “Why should he get to do whatever he wants, whenever he wants? And why should everything work out for him? What makes him so (expletive) special?”

Eventually, everyone gives in to his charms.

Even Cameron (Alan Ruck), Ferris’ best friend, who’s domineered by Ferris from the start, who should seethe with righteous anger by the end of the film, says: “It is possible to stop Mr. Ferris Bueller.” Then he takes the fall for Ferris Bueller.

All of which is why I want to build a case against Ferris, why I think Chicago should move on, rethink Ferris and stop shouting “BATTER, BATTER, BATTER SWING BATTER” at Wrigley Field in honor of Ferris and his pals and their day off. But I’ll be generous here and say, in a world now run by Ferrises, at least the kid believed in something. Everyone knows: “Life moves pretty fast. If you don’t stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.” It’s been a senior quote in generations of yearbooks.

Everyone’s knows the basic plot, in so much as there is one: Ferris fakes a cold, convinces his mom and stays home from school; talks his best friend Cameron into stealing his father’s Ferrari; jailbreaks girlfriend Sloane (Mia Sara) from class; then everyone spends a day as Chicago tourists (Sears Tower, Wrigley Field, Art Institute of Chicago, the Loop), discussing their distracted parents and futures and sidestepping trouble, including the humorless principal Ed Rooney (Jeffrey Jones).

McNally, though, sees more, a broader Tao of Ferris.

He can imagine both the prosecution, and the defense, of Ferris.

He says he’s used Ferris’ outlook on life “every single day.” One line in particular hits hard: “You realize if we played by the rules right now, we’d be in gym?” “That is a lesson that should be part of everyone’s day,” McNally said. “Sure, you have to work for a living, and sure, you have to pay taxes, but if you’re lucky enough to have a backyard to BBQ or a hill to ski down somewhere, do it — our lives are filled with gym classes to avoid.” He also sees a recognition that “your situation doesn’t have to be what it appears.” He said, “It’s what I do for a living. I defend a lot of CEOs and politicians facing serious consequences, and my job is not only to protect and defend them but to help them see beyond their current situations. I will have CEOs crying in my office, and they think the world has come to an end.” He wants them to picture a different outcome.

On the other hand, Ferris Bueller, he agrees, is irresponsible.

“You goad a friend into stealing a prized car, you drive it recklessly, then you cause it to be ultimately damaged beyond recognition — which would have been catastrophic for Cameron and his family. And what happens to Ferris? Nothing. Which always felt a little too easy.”

Therefore, my case against “Ferris Bueller’s Day Off” is such:

No. 1: We need to stop thinking of the character Ferris Bueller as a hero, a spontaneous defender of freedom and Chicago, but as the entitled sociopath he proves himself to be. Despite a therapeutic motto about life moving fast and needing to stop and look around or miss it, he avoids introspection himself.

No. 2: How else to explain a teenager — played then by a 23-year-old actor — who bullies a clearly depressed friend with a strict father into stealing their father’s jewel? And after that car is destroyed, Ferris leaves his friend to accept the blame? True, Cameron says he could have stopped Ferris; yes, Cameron admits he must face his father, who we learn only loves the car and doesn’t take enough time to appreciate his wife or son. But it’s a cheap excuse for Ferris, who runs home and faces no consequences at all.

No. 3: Similarly, the film itself treats Cameron’s depression, and need to assert himself, as flavoring to lend the story weight, only to discard it when things turn real.

No. 4: Worse, Ferris has the nerve to advocate for a father-son dialogue for Cameron and then races home before his parents learn he’s lying about being sick. Mind you, he’s already faked his way into eight other days off. So who is the one with a phony relationship here? Who is the one so eager to keep parents happy that he baby-talks them while bundled beneath his sheets?

No. 5: Who really needs the intervention here?

No. 6: Who’s the one reframing manipulation as friendship?

No. 7: A privileged child of the North Shore — although the exteriors of his home were filmed in California — Ferris is clearly the product of generational wealth, his bedroom a hub of tech. Yet his ongoing complaint is that he got a computer for his birthday, not a car. You get the sense that no matter what happens to him, he’ll have a future anyway. (One of the odder things about “Ferris Bueller’s Day Off” is that, unlike the other teen movies that John Hughes made in the mid-1980s, there isn’t a middle-class kid in sight.)

No. 8: Ferris Bueller is anti-education and classist. Why does he avoid school? To miss a test on socialism and a lecture on the problems with Reaganomics. The first person he meets after he steps out of the North Shore is a parking garage attendant in the Loop (played by Richard Edson, who, incidentally, was Sonic Youth’s first drummer). And the first thing he thinks to say: “Do you speak English?” Ferris leaves the Ferrari with the attendant and his coworker, who promptly take the car joyriding.

No. 9: Tabloid-wise, “Ferris Bueller’s Day Off” did not age well. Jeffrey Jones, who spent the movie hunting a teenager, pleaded no contest in 2003 to hiring a teenager to pose nude and later received five years of probation and was required to register as a sex offender. Also, Broderick and Grey, despite playing siblings, were secretly dating — a relationship that went queasily public in 1987 when the pair were vacationing in Northern Ireland and Broderick crashed a rental car, killing a mother and daughter.

No.10: No matter how universal the film’s themes of cutting loose and living in the moment sound, it has a habit of punishing anyone who shows responsibility. Plus, the movie is misnamed. It’s Cameron’s story. He’s the only character with any contours, the only one with a soul. Ferris, in comparison, is basically Bugs Bunny as a cult leader, and unlike Cameron, he’s also a conformist, responsible to nothing but his parents’ approval.

And now I will pull this stick out of my backside and admit:

When I was 15, when “Ferris Bueller’s Day Off” premiered, I saw it on opening weekend and loved it. I believed deeply in it. Like a moviegoer who peels out of a parking lot after a “Fast and Furious” sequel, it was life-affirming, albeit briefly. Like a cinematic fortune cookie. Yes, teens SHOULD cut loose. Yes, self-respect IS hard won. Ferris was just trying to get a friend to look beyond his parents’ materialism — a ubiquitous ‘80s theme.

Forty years on, it’s obviously a fantasy of freedom, the parents (distant figures in Hughes’ teen movies) as cartoons, Ferris himself more attitude than person. On paper, Ferris — rule-breaking, anti-authority, contradictory — should be a classic anti-hero. He confesses to the camera, breaking the fourth wall, that his relationship with Sloane is doomed. Hughes left clues suggesting he once intended a more bittersweet character: He cut a scene in which Charlie Sheen’s juvenile delinquent explains that Ferris tried to save him from delinquency, better explaining Ferris’ demand to save Cameron. The movie’s novelization even includes a scene at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange where Ferris seems more self-aware, railing: “How is it that just 50 miles from here there are farmers working their asses off from dawn to dusk and they’re going broke while these guys act like jerks for six hours a day and get rich?”

Alas, the Ferris we know is a visionary of sorts. He shows an early understanding of sampling technology, he grasps the power of digital ghosting. (It’s how he fakes out the adults.) Ferris will have a future. Today, he would be teaching us how generative AI can allow everyone their own day off — while steering around that part about losing your job.

In summation:

“Ferris Bueller’s Day Off” is a love letter to Chicago and its suburbs, starring downtown and Highland Park and Winnetka and Northbrook. It has been a wellspring for Movies in the Park, and an inspiration for out-of-towners who reenact its scenes for Instagram. Along with “About Last Night,” which opened a few weeks later, it shifted the city’s cinematic profile from the South Side of “The Blues Brothers” to a glossier, gentrifying North Side, a provincial view of Chicago as the heart of the world.

All flattering, no doubt.

The Art Institute — which has long had a “Be Like Ferris Bueller” tour, easily its most popular self-guided tour, according to a spokesperson — gets a close-up for the ages, a breezy two-minute walk-through pitched just right, as lovely and dreamy as a lazy day.

Revisiting ‘Ferris Bueller’s Day Off’ filming locations 40 years later

But that scene is sandwiched between a lurching Looney Tunes that periodically casts aside its silliness and begs to be taken seriously. Nobody wants to see Bugs Bunny get caught, and no one wants him to pause to offer life advice either. By chance, summer also marks the 75th anniversary of “Catcher in the Rye” and Holden Caulfield, another tale of a teenager of privilege who took time off and avoided his family. Like Ferris, Holden has no use for school or authority figures. He rants famously against the “phonies” of the world. You might assume they would have plenty to discuss, but I bet Holden would hate Ferris, who sidles up soundlessly to power to grab what he wants, who extracts exactly what he wants from those closest, then leaves them to clean up.

I asked Ed McNally if Ferris Bueller would have a future in the White House.

And like Ferris Bueller, he sidestepped without quite dodging.

He said of the presidents he’s worked closest with — Bush 1, Bush 2, Ronald Reagan — “all were easy laughs with a light touch, none of which diminished their seriousness of purpose.” He said of all his years in Washington, of the people with power he’s known, “no one was as humorless and unsympathetic as Ed Rooney — and by that, I mean the original Ed Rooney who chased me.”

Myself, I’m ready to convict Ferris.

And McNally?

If The Man Who Was Ferris Bueller had to defend Ferris Bueller, he knows exactly how he might do it.

“The main defense, I think, is that there is really no dark heart there. Even when things go awry for Ferris, there is no malicious intent. He is trying to bring light and laughter to the days of everyone he encounters. Unlike, say, Al Capone, he is all goodwill and light heart — and so what jury is not going to let this guy get off? All I would have to do, really, is have one juror hold out on Ferris’ behalf, and that I would have.”

Besides, the statute of limitations probably expired anyway.

title: ‘Her last days are coming for her’: Alleged cyberstalker charged for online harassment
text:
A Rhode Island man has been charged with stalking after he allegedly spent a year and a half harassing a Boston woman online, according to the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office.

Space Vixaisak, 23, sent threatening messages to the alleged victim, found her and her parents’ personal phone numbers, and posed as her online, the DA’s office said.

Judge Nicholas Brandt ordered Vixaisak, who is also charged with violating a harassment prevention order, to abide by the conditions set by the order and to maintain no contact with the victim or her family at his arraignment at Roxbury District Court last week.

He is scheduled to be back for a pre-trial hearing Aug. 26.

The 20-year-old victim walked into a Boston Police station last December to report that a person known online as “Space Vegas” had been harassing her via TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, Facebook, and other platforms since the previous February, the DA’s office said in a statement.

The victim told police she’d never met the person, who was later identified as Vixaisak, but he “continually messaged her,” writing thing like, “I need you to love me and let me love you,” the statement said.

During the course of the alleged harassment, in addition to finding her and her family member’s phone numbers, Vixaisak also learned where she lived and went to school, according to the statement.

She told the police that she had to block more than 900 accounts on TikTok and Instagram believed to be created by the suspect, and the DA said that BPD was able to use location data from those accounts to trace them to Vixaisak.

The account created by the suspect to impersonate the victim was a tool to get more information about her via a friend, the DA’s said.

Police were also shown multiple screenshots of threatening messages to the victim, including, “I told you to love me … now you’re going to have to watch your back every time.”

Vixaisak also allegedly sent a message to a victim’s family member saying, “Hey tell your daughter. Her last days are coming for her…if she doesn’t love me or I’ll find her.”

Despite being issued a harassment prevention order by the victim in January, the DA said that Vixaisak kept messaging the victim daily.

According to the DA, in 2021, Vixaisak was charged with cyberstalking a different victim, leading him to serve one year of probation and be enrolled in a mental health program.

“Social media is a vital part of many lives in our digitalized society and it can be used in positive ways or, as the facts indicate here, in unsettling and disturbing ways,” Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement. “Our citizens are entitled to peaceful existence in all aspects of their lives, including their engagement with social media.”

title: Boston Police Blotter: Officers break up fight at World Cup watch party
text:
Three men were arrested after a fight broke out during a World Cup watch party at a Downtown bar Monday night.

Boston Police officers responded to Estella Restaurant on Temple Street around 5:44 p.m, according to a police report. The restaurant was in the news earlier this year after it hosted an afterhours party for the New England Patriots, leading the establishment to have its liquor license suspended for a day.

The officers were responding to a radio call for an assist, the report said, and by the time they arrived, they knew that the restaurant was hosting a watch party for the Cape Verde vs. Spain World Cup game.

They also knew that the Transit Police had reported two parties in the bathroom, which the report noted had already led to “multiple arrests.”

When they got to the scene, the officers saw a large crowd inside and outside the restaurant, the report said, with officers seeing two people engaging in a verbal dispute.

They officers tried to de-escalate the argument and separate the individuals.

Khalea Turner, 29, of Hull, stuffed the mail in a U-Haul storage locker he rented instead of stuffing it in people’s mail boxes, a statement from the office said. The practice went on for about three years between November 2022 and January 2023.

Turner was supposed to deliver mail to the neighborhoods around Boston, including in Brighton, Dorchester, Mattapan, and Fort Point, according to the U.S. Attorney. Among the undelivered mail, recovered by law enforcement in January, there were passports, jury notifications, government checks, and education and immigration paperwork.

title: Police Blotter: Karen Read case Canton cop Sean Goode gets decertified
text:
Another police officer involved in the Karen Read investigation has had his law enforcement certification suspended.

This time it is Sean Goode, the Canton Police sergeant who recently resigned just ahead of Read’s lawsuit that revealed obscene and racist text messages he shared with ex-State Police Trooper Michael Proctor.

“The Massachusetts Peace Officer Standards and Training Commission hereby suspends the law enforcement certification of the Respondent Sean Goode,” the Commission wrote in its order. “The Commission voted to suspend the Respondent’s certification upon determining that it is in the best interest of the health, safety, or welfare of the public.”

Goode was supervisor of the Canton PD overnight shift when Boston Police Officer John O’Keefe’s body was discovered on the front lawn of another Boston cop’s house on Jan. 29, 2022.

Read’s attorneys expressed a belief during the first of Read’s two trials that Goode, whose testimony was rather limited, was “more of a straight shooter” than other police on the scene in those early hours of the investigation.

That understanding appears shattered after Read successfully obtained text messages shared between Goode and Proctor, the lead investigator of the case that led to Read being charged with O’Keefe’s murder, that painted a picture of two heavily biased and corrupt cops.

Proctor was placed on administrative leave immediately after the first trial ended in mistrial. His time on the stand led to a cross-examination that revealed a slew of wildly offensive text messages he sent to colleagues and even old high school buddies showing clear bias against Read from the start. Proctor was fired after the second trial concluded with Read’s acquittal on all charges save for drunken driving. Proctor at first fought for his job back but ultimately dropped that battle.

The biases of police investigating her laid the foundation for the defense theory of a local conspiracy to frame Read for O’Keefe’s murder and to protect others who were actually responsible.

The lawsuit Read filed earlier this month uncovered much deeper bias than even that revealed by Proctor’s time on the stand. It has also created a mad dash for defense attorneys representing clients investigated by these cops to get all the sordid details to see if the materials could help free their own clients.

“They are not officers who occasionally voiced an offensive remark,” Read’s attorneys wrote of Proctor and Goode in the lawsuit complaint. “They are men whose written and recorded communications — sent to one another and to a circle of like-minded friends over the course of a decade — establish entrenched and unrepentant hatred for women, Black Americans, Asian Americans, Jews, Hispanics, Arabs, and gay people.”

title: Battenfeld: Michelle Wu’s unlikely nemesis — ex-con Dianne Wilkerson — emerges as political force
text:
Boston Mayor Michelle Wu now has an unlikely nemesis – former state Senator and ex-convict Dianne Wilkerson, who has emerged as a political force and no-holds-barred critic of the Wu administration.

Wilkerson, who pleaded guilty to eight felony counts of taking $23,500 in bribes in 2010, has been posting on social media and sending media emails blasting Wu on everything from co-opting Juneteenth for political purposes to the White Stadium project to the city’s redesign plan for Blue Hill Avenue.

Wilkerson, who ran for her old seat in 2022, is trying to mobilize Boston’s Black community in what could be an attempt to put together a powerful voting bloc in a future election. So she is a threat to Wu and has the potential to embarrass her nationally.

Wilkerson says she is “absolutely not” interested in running for political office again but is motivated to speak up for her community in Roxbury, Dorchester and Mattapan, which she says has been ignored by Wu.

“I am in a place where I can say what I want and need to say without fear of retribution, which has become a hallmark of her mayoralty and quieted so many people,” Wilkerson said in an interview. “I don’t have a contract. I don’t need a contract.”

Wu’s administration has tried to marginalize Wilkerson by pointing out her extortion conviction and questioning whether residents really listen to her. Wilkerson became infamous nationally because of the feds’ picture of her stuffing the bribes into her bra.

But Wilkerson said she will not go away and won’t change her hard-charging style of confronting Wu. And because of Wilkerson’s credibility in the Black community, she represents more of a threat to Wu than Councilor Ed Flynn, who is routinely ignored by Wu.

“It’s not about throwing bombs for me,” she said. “If I don’t feel Roxbury, Dorchester and Mattapan are getting their due I will say something.”

Wilkerson’s chief complaint is something Wu critics often point to – the mayor’s seeming inability to listen to opposing views and meet with residents like those affected by the White Stadium project in Franklin Park.

“When you called (former Mayor) Marty Walsh he called me back,” she said. “This woman does not do that. If you criticize anything she does you become the enemy. It’s scorched earth.”

Wilkerson, now 71, said she’s been working with Boston mayors since Ray Flynn in the 1980’s and her criticisms are not personal.

“I just deal with facts and that’s what’s driving the Wu cabal so crazy,” she said.

Wilkerson and others most recently appealed to the Trump administration to stop Wu’s plan to turn Blue Hill Avenue into a one-lane street by creating a center lane for buses only. They asked the Trump Department of Transportation to withdraw $80 million in funding for the project.

Wilkerson said she went to the Trump administration to “protect” the Black community – months after Wu said she would protect the city from Trump.

“I am extremely well aware I have an enormous amount of respect from people within this community so it’s driving them nuts,” Wilkerson said. “I don’t have a contract with the city. I don’t want one. They can’t control me in a way they are threatening other people.”

Wilkerson’s latest complaint is about Juneteenth, which Wu and Gov. Maura Healey are turning into a political event in Franklin Park.

“I think it is beyond the height of insult for the mayor and governor to be inviting people to come to Franklin Park to celebrate Juneteenth in the park that you have refused to discuss with the community. What kind of chutzpah does that take?”

title: 16 Boston community center pools open for summer following repair work
text:
With one more pool now open, all but a handful of the city-run community center pools will be operational this summer – after years of maintenance projects had over half closed just a few years ago.

“I know this moment has been a long time coming, so we’re so excited that it’s here,” said Mayor Michelle Wu at the opening of the Hennigan Pool in Jamaica Plain on Monday. “It is really because of years of advocacy, feedback, and community participation in shaping all the different parts of this, that now the Hennigan is back and better than ever.”

This summer, 16 city pools are expected to be open for the summer, according to Boston Centers for Youth and Families: BCYF Condon, BCYF Charlestown, BCYF Clougherty, BCYF Draper, BCYF Flaherty, BCYF Hennigan, BPS Madison Park, BCYF Mason, BCYF Marshall, BCYF Mattahunt, BCYF Mildred, BCYF Perkins, BCYF Paris Street Pool, BCYF Quincy, BPHC South End Fitness Center, and BPS Umana. BCYF Curley Beach will also be open.

Of those, eight have been fixed under the current administration, Wu said, noting “there was a lot of work that we had to dig out from.”

Just three years ago, over half of the city-run public pools were closed for maintenance, sparking widespread frustration during a scorching summer.

Still more work is coming. BCYF pools at Curtis Hall in Jamaica Plain, Mason in Roxbury, and the Mirabella in the North End are still scheduled for upgrades, with Curtis Hall set to close on Friday and Mirabella already shuttered this season.

“We’re going to work as quickly as we can,” Wu said of Curtis Hall. “We need some HVAC upgrades, flooring repair, adding new benches on the pool deck, updated locker rooms, fresh paint, and much more. So, we’re hoping to have it ready in time for next summer, when Jamaica Plate will have two pools online for the first time of a long time.”

BCYF Blackstone in the South End and Holland in Dorchester pools remain listed as currently closed, with no scheduled openings this season.

Public officials heralded widespread work from local advocates and officials in getting pools open for this summer, noting the importance of community cooling sites across neighborhoods as temperatures rise.

The open BCYF pools are free to the public but operate with certain protocol, including requiring registration, only Boston residency, children under eight to be accompanied by an adult, no more than three children under 12 per adult, and more.

The city also invested $114,892 in “Swim Safe” grants this summer season, funding the expansion of free beginner swim lessons for young people across 11 nonprofits. In total, Boston officials estimated over 700 children and teens will receive free swim lessons through the grants.

Chief of Human Services José Massó asked the crowd gathered for the reopening of the Hennigan pool on Monday to raise their hands if they could swim.

“For the folks that did not raise your hand, no worries, do not fret,” Massó said. “This pool is for you, alright. And for the adults in the room, it’s never too late to learn how to swim. It’s a critical skill that I believe everybody should have.”

After a few speeches, Wu, local state Rep. Sam Montaño, City Councilor Ben Weber and a line of excited kids dove into the brand new pool, landing with a giant splash.

“After years of deferred maintenance, this has not been an easy task, but the mayor has stuck with the project,” said Massó. “And each summer we get a little closer to our goal of having all of our pools open.”

title: Boston city councilors pitch MBTA subway alternative to contentious Blue Hill Avenue bus lane redesign
text:
Two city councilors who oppose Boston’s Blue Hill Avenue redesign plan met with MBTA brass to pitch an alternative Orange Line extension through that corridor, but the T says it’s instead studying a connection to the mayor’s Roslindale neighborhood.

A MassDOT spokesperson revealed the DOT and MBTA Orange Line extension study plans Tuesday evening, presenting a stark contrast to what Councilors Miniard Culpepper and Brian Worrell proposed in a meeting earlier in the day with MBTA General Manager and MassDOT Secretary Phillip Eng.

Culpepper and Worrell have proposed extending subway service on the Orange Line from Ruggles station in Roxbury to Mattapan Square via the Blue Line Avenue corridor, an area they described as a “train desert.”

While the councilors described their meeting with Eng as “productive” when speaking with reporters at the state transportation building late Tuesday morning, the T and MassDOT later revealed that the state is already studying the feasibility of an Orange Line extension in Boston, but in a completely different direction.

The direction MassDOT is studying would extend the Orange Line from Forest Hills station in Jamaica Plain to the Roslindale Village commuter rail station. Roslindale — like the extension area proposed by the councilors — lacks a subway connection. It also just so happens to be where Mayor Michelle Wu lives.

“MassDOT, through its Office of Transportation Planning and in collaboration with the MBTA, is conducting a study to determine the feasibility of expanding transit service between the Forest Hills Orange Line station and the Roslindale Village commuter rail station,” MassDOT spokesperson John Goggin said in a statement in response to an inquiry about the councilors’ proposal.

“This study will be funded through Fair Share funding. The study will seek to analyze scenarios for future rapid transit between Forest Hills and Roslindale Village, including potential alignment for Orange Line service or more frequent commuter rail service.

“The study will also evaluate criteria such as ridership, accessibility, social equity, cost, and economic and land use impacts. The study team expects to release a report detailing analyses of each service scenario by fall of 2026,” Goggin added.

When asked whether MassDOT’s plan differed from what the councilors met with Eng about on Tuesday, Worrell told the Herald, “Yes.”

Worrell didn’t respond, however, to further questions nor acknowledge a comment about the study area being where the mayor lives, rather than the corridor Wu is moving forward with a center-running bus lane and redesign plan he opposes.

Mayor Wu’s office indicated that it opposed the councilors’ proposal, and plans to move forward with the city’s $162 million redesign plan for Blue Hill Avenue, despite persistent community opposition.

“The city is always looking to expand public transit access for our residents in partnership with the MBTA,” city spokesperson Michael Osaghae said in a statement. “However, digging new miles of subway tunnel under city streets would take many years of evaluation and likely well over a billion dollars in federal investment.

“Today, Boston has an opportunity to deliver more immediate improvements and beautification of the Blue Hill Ave corridor with nearly $150 million secured in state and federal funds.

“As we continue to work with community members to incorporate feedback into the proposed project design, we are focused on ensuring improvements to speed up commutes, expand opportunities for small businesses along the corridor, and boost quality of life for families in our neighborhoods,” Osaghae added.

City officials have stated that federal funding — including the latest $80 million infusion — allocated for the Blue Hill Avenue corridor is contingent upon completion of the transit project the city applied to the feds for, which includes the contentious center-running bus lane.

Culpepper and Worrell contend that’s not necessarily the case. The councilors said they learned from their meeting with Eng that roughly $22 million of the $80 million in federal funding allocated to the city is not tied to the center-running bus lane, and can be used for other purposes, such as beautification and safety.

“What we have seen across the country is that rail has been used for that federal grant, so there’s other cities that have used that same federal grant to extend or install rail, so that is the ask,” Worrell said at the media briefing. “That’s a possible way that we can get funding for this new proposed Orange Line extension.”

The councilors say the city and MBTA can do better than bus service for Boston’s predominantly Black communities of Roxbury, Mattapan and Dorchester — where their proposed Orange Line extension would run through — which “have been promised world-class transit” for “nearly 40 years.”

Staff for the councilors distributed a fact sheet to reporters ahead of their press briefing that stated Culpepper and Worrell, “alongside local advocates, are drawing a line: they’re not anti-transit, they’re pro-justice — and they refuse to accept a process that treats buses as the ceiling for their community’s transit ambitions.”

Culpepper said, however, that they didn’t ask Eng to pause plans for the center-running bus lane, despite their opposition and their plan being pitched as an alternative.

“We didn’t get into that part of the conversation,” Culpepper said when asked if Eng committed to taking the contentious bus lane off the table.

Worrell added, “We were focused on presenting our proposal and the data around why we believe the Orange Line extension is a better fit for this corridor. That was the focus of the meeting today.”

The councilors said the funding breakdown for the city’s Blue Hill Avenue redesign project consists of an $80.3 million Federal Transit Administration Small Starts grant, $38.4 million from the Massachusetts federal match, $18.2 million from the City of Boston, $14.9 million from a federal RAISE grant, and $10.7 million from the MBTA Capital Investment Plan.

title: Boston councilors’ MBTA Orange Line extension plan for Blue Hill Avenue slammed
text:
A plan from two Boston city councilors to extend the MBTA Orange Line below Blue Hill Avenue to replace a contentious center-running bus lane has drawn backlash, with one transit advocate saying it’s not “a serious transit proposal.”

TransitMatters Executive Director Caitlin Allen-Connelly didn’t mince words Wednesday when asked what she thought about a plan Councilors Miniard Culpepper and Brian Worrell pitched Tuesday to MBTA General Manager Phillip Eng.

“I don’t think it’s a serious transit proposal, if they’re proposing something that looks like a concept that they assembled over the weekend with an AI-generated map that’s proposing a multi-billion-dollar rail investment without any discussion of operations or cost or timelines or how it even fits into the existing transit network,” Allen-Connelly told the Herald. “I don’t think it’s a serious transit proposal at all.”

Allen-Connelly said there are “obvious errors” in the map Culpepper and Worrell distributed Tuesday showing their proposed Orange Line subway extension, which the councilors envision as being from the Ruggles station in Roxbury to Mattapan Square via the Blue Hill Avenue corridor.

The bigger problem with the plan, Allen-Connelly said, is that it’s presented as an either-or situation that would take decades and billions of dollars to accomplish, while leaving riders grappling with congestion the center bus lane seeks to resolve — if that lane were to be scrapped for the rail extension, as the councilors prefer.

“It would take decades to plan, fund, design, and build, and the people riding Blue Hill Avenue, the buses there, they need improvements now,” Allen-Connelly said, explaining that roughly 40,000 riders use the corridor daily. “The conversation should be about, what can we do today in the short term to improve speed and reliability, and not about a hypothetical project with no plan for implementation.”

She added that bus and rail improvements “are not competing ideas,” as pitched by the councilors.

“When you do have successful bus priority, it often helps build the case for future rail investments, so higher ridership, faster trips, a stronger corridor performance make it easier to justify a larger capital investment down the road,” Allen-Connelly said. “So, if our goal is eventually bringing higher capacity transit to Blue Hill Avenue, improving bus service is one of the most important steps you can take to set that up for success.

“Transit riders,” she added, “deserve real solutions and not distractions.”

Worrell on Wednesday responded to the criticism, which has also been prominent on social media, by posting “the handmade map of the Orange Line proposal that we asked AI to ‘upgrade’ to its other form.”

“No matter the map, the point remains the same: There is a gaping hole for rail in this section of Boston that aligns with economic, environmental and educational inequalities,” Worrell wrote on social media.

He cited and linked to a 1979 report that he said showed the Orange Line extension to be feasible along the Blue Hill Avenue corridor, but said “our community was deemed not worthy of such an investment.

“Meanwhile, investments downtown and in Cambridge and Somerville have moved forward,” said Worrell, who represents Mattapan, Dorchester, and parts of Jamaica Plain and Roslindale.

Worrell and Culpepper contend that the city and MBTA can do better than bus service for Boston’s predominantly Black communities of Roxbury, Mattapan and Dorchester — where their proposed Orange Line extension would run through — which “have been promised world-class transit” for “nearly 40 years.”

They both oppose the city’s $162 million redesign of the Blue Hill Avenue corridor, which is being supported by more than $80 million in federal funding. Mayor Michelle Wu’s office said Tuesday the councilors’ proposal “would take many years of evaluation and likely well over a billion dollars in federal investment,” and added that the city is moving forward with the bus lane redesign.

Worrell maintains that the city should change its approach.

“The end goal here is … to provide these communities with equitable transportation,” Worrell said. “The majority of these residents are not ditching their car for a center-running bus lane to nowhere, but they will for a one-seat ride to downtown.”

A MassDOT spokesperson said Tuesday that the DOT and MBTA is already studying the feasibility of an Orange Line extension in Boston, but in a different direction, from the Forest Hills station in Jamaica Plain to the Roslindale Village commuter rail station. The study is funded through Fair Share funding.

Roslindale, like the extension area proposed by the councilors, lacks a subway connection.

title: Police Blotter: FBI seizes 23 drones over Boston Stadium World Cup airspace
text:
Law enforcement seized nearly two dozen drones flying in the restricted airspace over Boston Stadium and World Cup events, the Boston FBI says.

“The FBI is reminding the public to leave your drones at home,” the agency posted to X. “Temporary Flight Restrictions are in effect, and violations may result in enforcement action.

In all, the FBI and its law enforcement partners — which were not named in the statement — have seized 23 drones as of June 11.

The Federal Aviation Administration in May launched “No Drone Zones” for FIFA World Cup 2026 stadiums, fan events and base camps, supported by the Drone Expedited and Targeted Enforcement Response (DETER) program launched a month earlier.

“This program will further deter violations by ensuring swift enforcement action and reinforce the agency’s commitment to protecting the National Airspace System,” FAA Chief Counsel Liam McKenna said when announcing the DETER program in April.

The program prohibited drones “within a 3-nautical-mile radius and up to 3,000 feet above ground level around the stadiums.”

That program is itself part of President Trump’s Executive Order 14305 of June 6, 2025 — the Restoring American Airspace Sovereignty order.

The order targets “unmanned aircraft systems,” or drones, which Trump’s order says “offer the potential to enhance public safety as well as cement America’s leadership in global innovation.” But the order states drones also pose risks: “criminals, terrorists, and hostile foreign actors have intensified their weaponization of these technologies, creating new and serious threats to our homeland.”

$3 billion Russian fraud scheme busted in New England

A “transnational criminal organization” with a base of operations in Russia and elsewhere in Eastern Europe bought up established durable medical equipment companies to run them as shells to fraudulently rip off Medicare to the tune of $3 billion.

That’s according to U.S. Attorney for New Hampshire Erin Creegan, who announced the arrests of two men from the country of Georgia.

“These charges expose the staggering scale of fraud and money laundering that Transnational Criminal Organizations are willing to inflict on our health care system and the people of New Hampshire,” Creegan said Thursday. “This was not a local scheme. It was a transnational operation that stole the identities of New England patients and doctors to defraud our health care system of nearly $3 billion in intended losses and then launder those proceeds internationally to escape detection.”

Kakha Bendeliani, 48, and Goga Danelia, 37, are charged with conspiring to commit money laundering in connection to the scheme.

While the men allegedly used their shell companies to bill Medicare for nearly $3 billion, they ended up netting significantly less — $12.5 million — before their alleged fraud scheme was exposed.

In order to make the scheme work, the organization put up real people as the nominal heads of the once-legitimate businesses while actually orchestrating the scheme from afar, according to the indictment returned on June 17. They then stole the identities of hundreds of thousands of Americans in order to bill Medicare for fake medical expenses.
