title: Boston developer claims City Hall is trying kill his plan to rehab Roxbury’s Nawn Factory
text:
A developer claims the City of Boston is trying to kill his plan to reimagine Roxbury’s Nawn Factory as a dance studio, by withholding designated funding and clawing back his approval to proceed with the $7 million project.

Jonathan Smalls, a local performance artist and former software engineer for the U.S. Department of Commerce, said the city’s opposition to his redevelopment plans for the Nawn Factory site stems from the Wu administration’s preference for the other applicant he beat out during the bidding process five years ago.

He compared the city’s response to his project to the $325 million White Stadium redevelopment for a professional women’s soccer team, which has been championed by the mayor and advanced by the city over community opposition. Boston is contributing $135 million to the public-private rehab.

“Meanwhile, just a few miles away, my project does enjoy strong support from the community,” Smalls told the Herald. “Everyone is very excited to see just a regular Roxbury resident, somebody who has grown up from the area, have an opportunity to build something that will welcome members of the community with open doors at all hours, and Boston city staff have made clear in no uncertain terms that they will allocate $0 to support that effort.”

Smalls cited an internal city memo that states the Wu administration is leaning against extending the development designation that was first granted for Smalls’ project in June 2022, due to lack of financial feasibility. The designation was extended for six months in March and is set to expire in August.

“At this time, the project does not have the necessary financing, permitting or designs to move this project into construction,” city planning officials wrote in the memo to the Roxbury Strategic Master Plan Oversight Committee, a community advisory body that selected Smalls’ bid over Historic Boston in December 2020. “Given the current status … the project will not be able to advance to closing by the designation expiration in August 2026.”

Smalls asserts, however, that the city “has taken steps to defund my work and reissue” the request for proposals.

He said the city applied for and received an $800,000 state grant that he claims was supposed to be designated to the bidder selected for the Nawn Factory development, but it was never released to him, as he says was “legally required.” Instead, it was later sent back to the state.

“That was really challenging and unexpected,” Smalls told the Roxbury oversight committee at a February meeting. “We don’t really have an explanation for why city staff would apply for funding and then not apply it to the project.”

He said he’s had to pay $150,000 out of pocket thus far to advance the project. The city memo puts his plan’s projected cost at $6.5-$7.2 million.

Smalls went back to the White Stadium comparison, and referred to past reporting by the Herald on public records that showed that the city’s private soccer investment partner was given a head start in the public bidding process.

The records included internal emails between the city and Boston Unity Soccer Partners that revealed negotiations to rehab White Stadium for a pro soccer team were underway long before the city sent out a public request for proposals. When the RFP went out, it very closely resembled the framework discussed between the investor group and the city. The soccer group was the sole bidder.

“In my case, Boston city staff similarly designed an RFP for the Nawn Factory to favor Historic Boston, Inc.,” Smalls said. “The major difference here seems to be that I managed to spot the RFP in time, submitted a qualifying submission, and was ultimately selected.”

Historic Boston, which has long advocated for preservation of the Nawn Factory, had pitched a mixed-use space to revitalize the vacant, two-story brick building as home to the Wellness Collaborative and a Roxbury History and Orientation Center. Smalls is planning a dance studio and fitness center.

Smalls claims favoritism is at play, given that two people who have since joined Mayor Michelle Wu’s cabinet, Brian Swett, the city’s chief climate officer, and Kathy Kottaridis, director of historic preservation, previously served in leadership positions with Historic Boston.

“I believe that this suggests a pattern of Michelle Wu directing public resources to her political allies, and seeking to minimize community input to avoid resistance to advancing private goals,” Smalls said.

Wu’s office denied assertions that the city has a preferred developer under consideration for the Owen Nawn Factory site. The city says it has spent more than five years working consistently and patiently with Smalls to support the project, which included securing land for development, granting and repeatedly extending designation four times, providing ongoing technical assistance, and obtaining state funding for site preparation.

Her office said the $800,000 MassWorks grant awarded to the city in 2019 for site preparation at the Nawn Factory was rescinded by the state for lack of progress. It said Smalls has applied to many funders for predevelopment, construction and permanent financing, but has been unable to secure any commitments due to the project’s lack of progress and business operating plan.

“The city shares the Roxbury community’s desire to see the Nawn Factory building redeveloped as a vibrant cultural and community hub, and we continue to believe in this site’s potential,” city spokesperson Veronica Yoo said in a statement. “We will continue to work closely with community members and the leadership of the Roxbury Strategic Master Plan Oversight Committee to advance a financially feasible development plan that supports the revitalization of Nubian Square.”

The city appears to have moved on, but Smalls said he’s set on fulfilling his vision for the site.

“I expect to be given more time to complete the project,” Smalls said. “It may turn into a legal battle, but that remains to be seen and that is not the preferred course.”

title: Boston Police Blotter: Three men injured in Theatre District shooting
text:
Three people were shot in the Theatre District Monday night, according to Boston Police.

Officers responded to an address on Tremont Street around 10:49 p.m. for a report of multiple people shot, BPD said in a statement.

Police said they found three men with non-life threatening injuries and were treated at a local hospital.

“It appears there is no arrest,” a BPD spokesperson said.

Boston City Councilor Ed Flynn mentioned the shooting in a letter to Mayor Michelle Wu regarding what he said was a lack of consideration in the decision to extend last call to 3 a.m. at more than 100 local bars.

“The Boston Police Department has longstanding issues of understaffing, overstretched resources, forced overtime and looming retirements… They privately expressed to me that they are overwhelmed with the recent rise in violent crime,” Flynn wrote. “Just last night around 11 p.m., there was a triple shooting outside of The Tam in the Theater District, steps away from the Emerson College campus, the Boston Common, and several hotels.”

Flynn said that first responders and community members deserved more say and urge more consideration of the trickle down effects of the summer’s big events.

Idaho man sentenced to federal prison for cyberstalking Mass. academic

A man from Idaho was sentenced to two years in federal prison for cyberstalking a local professor, according to the Massachusetts U.S. Attorney’s Office.

Edward John Kay, 54, will also serve three years of supervised release and was ordered to pay more than $16,000 in restitution, according to a statement from the office.

Kay met the victim when he took an online class with her last year. After a Zoom meeting with the professor and one virtual class, “Kay became fixated on the victim, dropped the course, and proceeded to harass and intimidate the victim over email and LinkedIn,” the statement said.

The messages swung from professions of love to threats. In one message, the defendant wrote to the victim, “I miss you-truly, deeply- with all of my heart and soul. That day I saw you on Zoom…You were the most beautiful thing I have ever seen. Not just appearance. Everything. Your presence. Your mind. Your light. To gain you…and then to lose you like that? It devastated me.”

In a post on Linkedin, he wrote a poem, referring to the victim as a mouse in a maze who needed to be burned, the office said.

After he was arrested, Kay told police he wanted to live with the victim and her child in a compound in Wyoming. In total, he sent more than 80 “harassing communications,” according to the office.

title: Boston Police Blotter: BPD Commissioner advises no illegal fireworks, heat safety ahead of July 4th
text:
It’s hot out, the city is on the cusp of the Fourth of July, and Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox has some advice and warnings for residents who plan on celebrating.

At the season opening of the Frog Pond spray pool in Boston Common, Cox said officers in stations around the city are there to help people who might be feeling the heat.

In addition to staying hydrated and in cool spaces as much as residents can, Cox said, “Don’t partake in the alcohol,” saying it can make heat-related symptoms worse.

He asked residents to say something if they see something, noting that scooter thefts, street takeovers, and aggravated assaults are up, even though homicides and other crimes are down compared to this time last year.

Cox suggested residents keep GPS devices like AirTags on their scooters to help police find them if they’re stolen. He also asked Bostonians to be on the lookout for troves of improperly stored scooters or large gatherings of people on scooters.

“We’ve also found that a lot of these large gatherings of scooters, they tend to be stolen across the board,” he said.

He also asked that residents call 911 when they see large, afterhours parties.

“The parties are not just a nuisance, they’ve been the center of some of the most extreme violence that we’ve had traditionally in the city,” the commissioner explained.

To discourage some of that behavior, Cox said some parks and streets would be closed this summer.

With America’s 250th birthday on Saturday, he pleaded that people not set off illegal fireworks.

On top of being against the law, “The most important thing people need to understand is that they’re dangerous,” he said. “Every year people lose fingers, toes, and they can lose their life dealing with fireworks… Let the professionals handle it.”

Lakeville drowning victim identified

Police were called to the pond around 5:46 p.m. for a report from a boater that two people on a jet ski tipped over, and one of them did not resurface.

The office is investigating the incident and noted that the victim did not have a life jacket on at the time.

title: Gaskin: Opposed to White Stadium? Blame Marty Walsh
text:
Some people have wondered why White Stadium became the first and only serious choice for Boston’s new professional women’s soccer stadium.

It was not because Franklin Park has easy traffic access, or because the surrounding neighborhoods have ample parking, or because the environmental and public-land questions were minor, or because the economic impact on Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan and Jamaica Plain had already been independently established.

So why White Stadium?

One possible answer deserves public scrutiny: the tax incentives may have been too valuable to ignore.

Opportunity Zones were created under the 2017 federal tax law signed during the Trump administration to encourage private investment in lower-income communities through capital-gains tax advantages. In 2018, Gov. Charlie Baker nominated Massachusetts’ Opportunity Zone census tracts, based in Boston on recommendations from the Walsh administration, including tracts that covered the Franklin Park area.

The stated local logic was defensive. Boston officials were worried that Opportunity Zones could fuel gentrification by attracting private capital into vulnerable neighborhoods. So rather than nominate every eligible tract, the Walsh administration selected a smaller number, including tracts with significant public ownership or public control. WBUR reported at the time that some Boston Opportunity Zones included land largely off the table for redevelopment, including Franklin Park, cemeteries, open space and public housing.

But that logic had a serious flaw.

If the whole purpose of an Opportunity Zone is to attract private investment, and the most valuable asset inside the zone is public land, then the pressure does not disappear. It shifts. Instead of speculation through ordinary private parcels, the pressure moves toward monetizing, leasing, commercializing or redeveloping public assets.

White Stadium may now be the case study.

At the time, I remember hearing that Franklin Park had been included in an Opportunity Zone and thinking that such a decision should never have been made without a serious community process. Franklin Park is not unused land on a map. It is Boston’s largest park and a shared resource for Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, Jamaica Plain and the entire city. If a federal tax designation could make private investment in or around the park more attractive, residents deserved to know before a stadium deal was moving forward.

There was another cost to that decision.

At the time, John Kingston III, then running for U.S. Senate, was talking about launching a $100 million Opportunity Zone Fund to help redevelop Roxbury and parts of Dorchester. That was exactly the kind of investment Opportunity Zones were supposed to encourage: capital for raw land, abandoned buildings, underused commercial corridors and neighborhood redevelopment.

But when the Opportunity Zone geography was drawn around Franklin Park, public open space and other land largely unavailable for ordinary redevelopment, the incentive for that kind of neighborhood investment was weakened. The tax benefit did not disappear. It was redirected.

The Opportunity Zone program could have been used to help unlock long-neglected parcels in Roxbury and Dorchester, support local ownership, create jobs, build housing and strengthen commercial districts. Instead, Boston placed federal tax incentives around public assets that were supposedly protected from development.

Years later, the most visible private investment opportunity emerging from that geography is not the redevelopment of abandoned buildings in Roxbury. It is a professional sports stadium in Franklin Park.

The public deserves to know whether any part of the White Stadium/Boston Legacy investment has been structured to take advantage of federal Opportunity Zone tax benefits.

Opportunity Zone benefits can be extremely valuable. If an investor makes a qualifying equity investment through a Qualified Opportunity Fund and holds it long enough, the gain on that investment’s appreciation may be excluded from federal capital-gains tax after 10 years.

Consider the growth in women’s soccer franchise values.

Boston reportedly paid a $53 million expansion fee for its NWSL franchise. Current NWSL valuations show the upside: Angel City at about $335 million, Kansas City Current at $315 million, Bay FC at $208 million, and the average NWSL team at about $184 million.

Now do the simple math.

If a qualifying investment tied to Boston women’s soccer rose from the $53 million expansion-fee level to the current NWSL average of $184 million, that would be about $131 million in appreciation. At a 23.8% federal capital-gains rate — 20% capital gains plus the 3.8% net investment income tax — the potential federal tax avoided on that appreciation could be about $31 million.

If the value rose to something closer to Angel City’s $335 million valuation, the appreciation would be about $282 million. The potential federal tax benefit could be roughly $67 million.

Boston says the White Stadium deal includes more than $190 million in private capital investment and tens of millions more for operations and maintenance.

The public has been told this project is about students, women’s sports, community benefits and the revitalization of a neglected stadium. Those may all be part of the story. But they cannot be the whole story if private investors may also be positioned for major tax advantages from a public park and public-school stadium.

Boston can support women’s sports and still demand transparency. Renovating White Stadium and asking hard questions about private financial benefits are not contradictory positions.

The tax benefits would flow to investors. The traffic, parking pressure, disruption and loss of park access would fall on Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan and Jamaica Plain.

That is why disclosure matters.

Ed Gaskin is Executive Director of Greater Grove Hall Main Streets and founder of Sunday Celebrations

title: Police Blotter: Merrimack River too contaminated for July 4th fun, tests show
text:
Portions of the Merrimack River downstream from Haverhill will likely be unsafe to use through the July 4th weekend due to dangerous fecal bacteria levels, though the data shows improvement.

Haverhill found two breaks in its 42-inch sewer pipe following excessive rains in the final days of last month, causing some 8 million gallons of wastewater to spill into the Merrimack River.

Testing of seven river sites downstream of the city showed increasing site contamination until a diversion pipe was installed Wednesday. That day’s sampling still showed six of seven test sites contaminated, but the situation appears to have lessened, with three of seven sites contaminated at Thursday’s testing, the most recent available.

Those sites with dangerous levels of fecal bacteria are Amesbury, Deer Island to the Newburyport Harbormaster’s Pier — this last being seven to eight times the safety limit.

The Merrimack River Watershed Council stressed in a statement that testing takes 24 hours, so no one should assume that the data can show “whether it is safe or unsafe at these locations today.”

“MRWC recommends that people do not engage with the Merrimack River downstream of Ferry Park in West Newbury, including Newburyport Harbor, until further testing can validate that it is safe to do so,” the Council wrote in its statement. “Unsafe conditions will likely extend through the July 4th Weekend. MRWC defers to the state and its testing for determinations at ocean facing beaches.”

Framingham woman is ex-girlfriend from Hell

A Framingham woman is charged with stalking and threatening to kill her ex-boyfriend — and threatening to chop “into little pieces” any cops who would stand in her way.

“If you date another girl, I will kill you,” Emma Hammond allegedly told her ex after grabbing him by the neck outside a Back Bay restaurant last week.

Hammond, 31, was charged in Boston Municipal Court with two counts of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon and one count each of stalking, strangulation or suffocation, assault and battery on a family or household member, assault and battery on a police officer, and resisting arrest.

Judge Paul Treseler set bail at $200 and ordered Hammond to have no contact with the alleged victim.

Hammond and her alleged victim had only dated for about a month before he ended things. He told police that she then bombarded him with phone calls, in-person harassment at his apartment, and frequent appearances at this restaurant. Then Facetime calls from an unknown number threatened his death if he dated anyone else, with displays of guns and machetes.

Boston police responded to the Dartmouth Street restaurant a little before midnight on June 26 for the allegation of her choking him. She was gone when they arrived so they took the man’s statement and left — only to be told she had returned.

When officers arrived to arrest Hammond, she became combative, prosecutors say. She allegedly kicked, flailed her arms, and spit in one officer’s face. When finally handcuffed, she expressed suicidal statements and told officers that she “wish[ed] [she] had a gun to shoot [them],” and that she would “chop [the officers] into little pieces and put [their] bodies in a box because [her] family was part of the Mafia.”

Teen boy charged with shooting teen girl in Boston

A 14-year-old boy faces numerous gun charges, including assault and battery by discharge of a firearm, related to the shooting in May of a 14-year-old girl in Dorchester.

Police responded to Milton Avenue a little after 8 p.m. on May 6 for a report of a person shot. Inside a residence there, they found the victim suffering from a gunshot wound, according to a Boston Police Department statement. She was transported to a hospital where she has remained in recovery.

At the same home, police allegedly found two teen boys attempting to escape through a rear door. The officers say they found a pistol with an extended magazine in the backpack of one of the boys. Police that day arrested him on firearm and ammunition charges. Following an investigation, the boy was then charged in connection with the girl’s shooting.

Since all parties are juveniles, none was identified in the police statement.

I-495 shutdown identities released

The identities of the two men who died in Tuesday’s shooting in Berlin and the subsequent standoff on Interstate 495 in Lowell have been released.

The victim has been identified as Nicholas Ferreira, 35, of Haverhill, and the suspect as Edward Pyne, 43, of Salem, New Hampshire, according to published reports citing the Worcester County District Attorney’s Office.

title: Celtics’ Jaylen Brown trade leaves Boston fans, community feeling bankrupt: ‘A huge void’
text:
Jaylen Brown came to Boston in 2016 as a raw lottery pick out of California; he leaves a decade later, following a stunning trade to Philadelphia, as an NBA champion and an essential piece of the city’s social fabric.

“What this trade does is show young fans what sports heartbreak is,” Celtics superfan Chris Soldani told the Herald. “There is now a huge void, and a lot of people don’t know how to process this situation.”

Look no further than Randolph for proof. Immediately after learning about the trade, 6-year-old Giovanni “Gio” Jean cried uncontrollably while wearing a No. 7 Celtics jersey autographed by Brown.

His mother, Gigi Durand, captured the moment on video as Gio sobbed, “You are my favorite player in the whole NBA.” Holding up a handmade sign pleading for his idol to “come back one day,” the youngster asked his mother to mail it.

The footage went viral, racking up over 10 million views and drawing a direct response from Brown: “It’s ok lil bro,” he posted, adding a heart emoji. “We will always be friends.”

That instinct to connect directly with the fan base is exactly what drew superfans like Soldani to Brown.

In early May, Brown invited Soldani — known as “Caveman on Causeway” — and several others onto a Twitch livestream he hosted just after the 76ers eliminated Boston. The stream stirred controversy as the longtime Celtic described last year as the favorite of his career despite playing most of it without Jayson Tatum.

Soldani called the bond “one of the most unlikely connections.”

Under the blockbuster deal, Boston sends the 29-year-old 2024 Finals MVP to their bitter Atlantic Division rival for 36-year-old veteran Paul George and four draft picks. Fans say it will take time to overcome losing a superstar who doubled as one of Massachusetts’ most impactful civic anchors.

“With all the impact that Jaylen has on the city, and the youth, and putting money into the city,” Soldani said, “it truly bankrupts the city as a community.”

This spring, Boston Magazine ranked Brown the eighth most influential Bostonian, detailing his work hosting fundraising bowling events and education fairs in Roxbury.

That legacy echoes across local sports talk radio as fans process the gamble taken by front-office architect Brad Stevens — a decision complicated by reports that Brown feels his decade of service ended without the mutual respect he earned.

Gov. Maura Healey noted on social media that it’s “hard to imagine” the Celtics without Brown. She added, “You’ll always have a home in Boston.”

In 2019, Brown founded the 7uice Foundation, a nonprofit providing healthcare, education, and digital literacy resources to underserved youth through its STEM-focused Bridge Program camp.

The work recently drew criticism from the Massachusetts Fiscal Alliance, a state watchdog, after lawmakers approved a $700,000 state earmark for the charity.

“Jaylen Brown is expected to earn roughly $60 million this year,” the Alliance posted. “If he wants to support charitable work through his foundation, that’s commendable. But why are Massachusetts taxpayers being asked to subsidize the private foundation of a multi-millionaire?”

In 2024, Brown also launched the Boston XChange with teammate Jrue Holiday, an incubator aiming to generate $5 billion in wealth for communities of color by providing $100,000 in funding to 10 local businesses annually.

Superfan KJ Green, creator of the “Green Runs Deep” brand, cut straight to the raw reality: “I want to (expletive) die right now.”

Green, who also appeared on the May livestream, praised Brown for making fans feel seen and knowing them by name. “This guy cared about using his platform to build other people up,” Green said. “He helped so many businesses in Boston get to the next level.”

For special education teacher Kaiya Santos, who partnered with Brown in 2023 to redesign a basketball court at Fenelon Street Playground in Dorchester, the loss is personal. “It was clear that the project was not just about beautifying a court,” Santos told the Herald. “It was about the role the space would play in the community. Boston will miss him.”

Mayor Michelle Wu thanked Brown for “shifting the energy” and always “showing up” for the city, even as he became a “Celtics great.”

“We won’t forget the looks on young players’ faces as you pulled up unannounced to tournaments in the park,” Wu posted, “or the hope and determination of entrepreneurs and students reaching for their dreams through the opportunities you made possible. Because of your example, kids in Boston know that faith, consistency, hard work pays off.”

For now, the city seems unwilling to let go: Brown’s larger-than-life posters still hang untouched inside the TD Garden ProShop and throughout the busy North Station concourses.

title: ‘Enough is enough’: City councilors call for ‘public safety summit’ following holiday shootings
text:
Two city councilors are calling for a “Public Safety Summit” following a deadly Fourth of July night in Boston.

“Enough is enough… I am outraged,” City Councilor At-Large Erin Murphy wrote in a statement after news that two people were killed and eleven others were injured in five shooting incidents that began late Saturday night. The shootings occurred in Roxbury and Dorchester.

Murphy wrote it was, “heartbreaking, unacceptable, and a stark reminder that the status quo is not working.”

She called on Mayor Michelle Wu to brief the full council on an updated Summer Public Safety Plan and to convene a citywide “Public Safety Summit” that would include elected officials, neighborhood organizations, violence prevention advocates, first responders, and residents, as well as state and federal partners.

“We cannot continue reacting after tragedy strikes,” Murphy wrote. “Boston residents deserve action, not talking points. They deserve fully staffed police shifts, safer neighborhoods, and leaders willing to put differences aside before more lives are lost.”

In a letter to Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox, District 2 City Councilor Ed Flynn also called for a summit “to address violence and crime in Boston.”

“It’s clear we need a new, comprehensive public safety plan that includes hiring hundreds of police officers every year,” Flynn, whose district includes parts of Downtown, the South End, and South Boston, wrote.

Murphy noted that she, too, has been calling for hiring more officers.

Both councilors had also spoken out last week after another spike in city violence that included an assault on a police officer and a triple shooting.

Murphy, Flynn, and the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association had said that staffing issues were in part to blame for a recent uptick.

“I hate to be the person who told them so,” BPPA President Larry Calderone said, “each week, the city is becoming more violent.”

In addition to the shootings, two people we also stabbed during the same time period, while other crimes like larceny, rape, and aggravated assault are seeing an upswing so far this year. Calderone said the department hasn’t been fully staffing shifts or hiring enough new officers to replace retirements.

At a press conference to address the July 4th violence, Cox pushed back on criticism that there aren’t enough officers on the streets.

“Contrary to the word out there, since FIFA, we’ve got many, many officers working, probably far more than any other time period,” Cox said. “We had a lot of people working, that being said there were a lot of parties last night… that kind of volume, we’re probably not used to.”

District 7 Councilor Miniard Culpepper, who represents parts of Fenway, Roxbury, Dorchester, and the South End, told the Herald in an interview that it was a “terrible night for everyone.”

Culpepper said that, “all hands, all people need to be working on this problem.”

“All of us will work on peace in the city,” he said, adding that he expects to work with Murphy and Flynn. “We want a peaceful summer.”

Culpepper, a pastor who has worked in the community to decrease violence, wants to see a return to a focus on peace, mutual respect, and community policing.

“They can’t arrest their way out of this,” Culpepper said, explaining that he believes seeing clergy and community members out with the police, working together, is better than just seeing more police on the streets. “Strong community policing works best.”

Calderone agreed that he’d like to see Boston Police return to a community policing approach.

He said that community policing means, “the same officer, on the same beat, in the same neighborhood,” explaining that right now, “we don’t have the bodies.”

title: Two killed, 11 others injured in July 4 shootings across Boston
text:
Two people were killed out of the 13 shot in Boston during what Mayor Michelle Wu called a “long and difficult” July 4th night.

Boston Police responded to five separate shootings, with most of the incidents occurring in Roxbury, the department said. The victims have not yet been identified.

Officers were also injured by fireworks during the overnight response, Police Commissioner Michael Cox said at a press conference Sunday to address the violence.

In a video obtained by the Herald, officers are responding to a large and loud crowd, when a firework gets tossed right next to an officer. The firework explodes, someone screams, and people can be seen lying on the ground after the light flashes and the smoke clears.

“Fireworks, firearms, and alcohol — bad combination,” Cox said, “and that’s what you saw around these events.”

He noted that the Fourth of July is always the peak of the year in terms of call volume for Boston and likely all major American cities.

Still, he said, “it was a very high volume.”

“It was a long and difficult night last night,” Wu said. “Our first responders and community safety teams were out throughout the night. This is a busy time of year, and when we see firearms present at large gatherings, that is never, never a recipe for peaceful celebrations.”

Wu said that her thoughts were with those impacted by the violence, especially the families of the victims, and that there has been and will continue to be trauma services available to community members.

She noted that prior to Saturday night, the number of shootings and shooting victims were down in Boston compared to the same time last year.

As of June 28th, Boston Police crime stats showed that 50 people had been shot, five fatally, down 14% from the same period in 2025, and down more than 20% from the five year average.

“We’re still at historic low numbers overall,” she said, “but that is never something we say to suggest that our work is slowing down or finished.”

Wu faced criticism last week after doubling down on rhetoric that Boston was still America’s safest major city, after an uptick in violence that included a triple shooting the weekend before. She held her stance despite calls from some city councilors and the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association for more officers on the street to address the increase in crime.

Although she said that numbers were low, Wu said, “We will not be satisfied until there is no violence anywhere in the city of Boston.”

Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said his office is investigating the incidents and asked for anyone with information about the shootings to come forward.

“Last night was obviously a challenging one,” he said. “We need the community’s help and support.”

Officers responded to the first shooting of the night on Fayton Street in Roxbury around 11:54 p.m. The victim’s injuries were life-threatening, and he was transported to the hospital, BPD said, adding that no arrests have been made.

Then, at 12:36 a.m., officers saw someone with a gunshot wound near 500 Blue Hill Ave., ultimately discovering three victims, who were all transported to the hospital.

One victim was pronounced dead at the hospital, and the others have non-life-threatening injuries, according to BPD. A fourth victim from the same incident also admitted themselves to a hospital with a non-life-threatening gunshot wound.

At the same time, another person admitted themself to the hospital for a non-life threatening gunshot wound from a separate incident on Horadan Way.

Just before 2 a.m., officers responded to Draper Street in Dorchester for another person shot with non-life threatening injuries.

The last shooting occurred back in Roxbury around 3:14 a.m. Officers arrived at an address on George Street and found three victims who’d been shot. One person was pronounced dead at the hospital, another was transported with life-threatening injuries, and the third had non-life threatening injuries, police said.

Officials applauded police and EMS for their work. Hayden called it an “extraordinary effort,” and Cox said they’d done a “tremendous job,” despite the challenges.

“There was no question about who was supposed to do what, where, it was just a lot to respond to,” Wu said of night.

She noted the stark difference between the start of the “incredible” day and celebrations for America’s 250th birthday, with the violence that took place later.

“Our first responders do such hard work, they put their all into this,” Wu said. “Everyday they save lives, whether it’s a big holiday weekend or not, they are there for our community.”

title: ‘Right now, it doesn’t feel like the safest city in America’
text:
Officials and residents are asking for resources to make Boston safer after a chaotic and violent July 4.

Thirteen people were shot, two fatally, in five separate incidents that occurred throughout the city Saturday night into Sunday morning. Additionally, two people were stabbed and officers were assaulted by fireworks. No arrests have been made and the Boston Police Department has not released the names of the victims.

City Councilors Erin Murphy, who represents the city at-large, and Ed Flynn, of District 2, filed a resolution calling for a public safety summit.

“After another deadly holiday weekend, we cannot simply issue statements and move on. Boston deserves answers, accountability, and a real plan,” Murphy wrote in a statement.

In addition to the summit, the resolution also calls for Mayor Michelle Wu and Boston Police Commissioner to brief the city council on their “Summer Safety Plan” and to hold a collaborative review with stakeholders, including community leaders and residents.

District 7 Councilor Miniard Culpepper, who represents parts of Roxbury, where most of the shootings occurred, said that he’d work with the councilors on a summit.

“We’re going to work with anyone who works for peace,” Culpepper said at a press conference Monday outside the Roxbury branch of the Boston Public Library to discuss the need for additional, preventive resources for the community.

“For now, it compliments it,” Culpepper said of Flynn and Murphy’s plan and his. “We hope that it all comes together.”

Asked if more cops should be on the streets, something the other two councilors have advocated for, Culpepper responded, “I leave that to Commissioner Cox, but I do know part of the answer to the question is the community. When we have community policing, it’s when we have peace.”

Culpepper said that he’d like to see a “supplemental budget for peace,” saying, “I pray that we look at more money to fund the groups that do the work every day.”

He stood with several members from anti-violence community groups, as well as faith leaders and District 4 City Councilor Brian Worrell, whose constituents also include Roxbury residents.

“We are calling on everyone to put down the guns, stop the community violence,” Worrell said at the press conference. “This is not normal.”

For a successful plan to be in place, Worrell said, “it needs to be everyone at the table,” including the people standing around him and others who care about the neighborhood.

Minister Randy Muhammad, the founder of Boston’s chapter of the 10,000 Fearless Peacemakers, called on the community to help step in.

“To the community, I’m calling on us, because elected officials and the police have their job to do,” he said, “but it’s all of our responsibilities to make our community a safe and decent place to live.”

He said that he respected the work of the police, but that their work often comes after violence happens.

“Let’s invest not only in the after,” Muhammad said, “but let’s invest in those that are doing the work to prevent the crisis.”

Steven Wilson Jr. of the Ella J. Baker House noted continued rhetoric about the city’s safety stats.

“We keep saying these things, and we keep hearing these things: ‘This is the safest city in America,’” Wilson said. “Right now, it doesn’t feel like the safest city in America. Right now, for people who look like me, it doesn’t feel like the safest city in America.”

Culpepper spoke about the irony of how the more the phrases about Boston being the safest and most peaceful city get discussed, the more budgets for safety and peace get cut.

“We need to talk about the reality of the situation,” Culpepper said.

Local resident Purple Reign said she attended the press conference while one of her family members, who’d been shot over the weekend, was in surgery.

She said that work had to be done in the neighborhood to prevent the violence from happening to being with, namely promoting job and educational programs for young people.

Reign expressed frustration with ongoing gun violence.

“When you leave the house with a gun, that’s premeditated,” she said. “You’re not going to sit for dinner, you’re not going to read poetry.”

She also noted that prevention and policing have to work together. “I believe in Black Lives Matter and I believe blue lives matter,” she said.

During a different press conference earlier in the day, Wu had said she was working closely with Commissioner Cox in the aftermath of the violent weekend. Responding to a question about department staffing levels, she said during her tenure, Boston Police Academy classes were the largest they’d ever been.

“We’ve added hundreds of new officers to the force,” she said.

She also mentioned the city’s crime stats.

“We are still at historic lows compared to any point in our history, now that does not mean that we are easing off in any way,” Wu said. “We will not be satisfied in the city until our numbers are zero.”

title: Osborne: Situational awareness key to a safe summer
text:
There’s a lot going on in America this summer: Festivals, parades, fireworks, family vacations and the 2026 FIFA World Cup, which is bringing millions of fans to stadiums, city streets and watch parties nationwide.

Most public events take place without incident. However, history reminds us that large gatherings can also attract criminals and, in rare cases, terrorists.

We all remember the headlines. In 2017, the Route 91 Harvest Festival in Las Vegas became the site of the deadliest mass shooting in modern U.S. history. Sixty-one people lost their lives, more than 400 were wounded by gunfire, and hundreds more were injured. In 2022, seven people were killed and dozens more injured during the Fourth of July parade attack in Highland Park, Ill.

These tragedies underscore a simple reality: preparation matters. In an emergency, seconds matter.

During my years working alongside law enforcement agencies worldwide to combat human trafficking, I spent much of my career focused on security, threat awareness and public safety. Today, as a certified instructor with the U.S. Concealed Carry Association (USCCA), I teach individuals and families practical skills to help them recognize potential threats, stay calm under pressure and respond effectively during emergencies.

Fortunately, staying safe does not require living in fear. It simply requires awareness.

At public gatherings, sporting events, festivals, holiday celebrations and while traveling, people should strive to remain in a relaxed but alert mindset in which they remain aware of their surroundings and attentive to potential problems.

Before attending a large event, discuss a simple emergency plan with your family. Take a photograph of your children before leaving home in case you become separated. Designate a meeting location in advance. Teach children that if they cannot find you, they should seek help from a uniformed police officer, firefighter, medic or event staff member. Pay attention to public safety announcements and follow instructions from law enforcement and event personnel.

The goal of situational awareness is not to create anxiety or ruin fun. Quite the opposite. Preparedness allows us to recognize potential threats early and respond effectively if necessary. Awareness builds confidence. Preparation provides peace of mind.

At USCCA, I teach a simple framework for situational awareness: SAFE.

S — See the threat. Look up from your phone and pay attention to suspicious behavior, unattended bags, unusual disturbances or individuals who appear to be monitoring people or locations.

A — Assess the danger. Determine whether the situation presents a legitimate risk to you and your family and consider what actions may be necessary.

F — Find a safe place or exit route. Know where the nearest exits, emergency personnel, and safe areas are located before you need them.

E — Emotional control. Stay calm. Clear thinking can save lives.

America’s summer traditions are worth celebrating. With a little preparation, we can fully embrace the moments that bring us together while protecting ourselves and the people we love.

Matt Osborne is a certified instructor for the U.S. Concealed Carry Association/InsideSources

title: Boston City Council calls for ‘immediate’ public safety briefing from Mayor Wu after July 4 violence
text:
The Boston City Council passed a resolution calling for a “public safety summit” and review of the mayor’s summer safety plan in light of the July 4th gun violence that rocked the city, killing two people and injuring 11 others.

The Council approved the resolution, 11-0, on Wednesday, and later referred a related hearing order to committee for further discussion.

“Over the Fourth of July holiday weekend, multiple shootings occurred across the city of Boston, resulting in 13 individuals being shot and two people being killed, while officers also faced dangerous conditions, including fireworks being thrown and shot at them during public safety responses,” Councilor Erin Murphy, the resolution’s lead sponsor, said.

“These incidents are not isolated, but part of a larger and deeply concerning pattern that demands a clear, coordinated, and accountable response from city leadership,” Murphy added. “The people of Boston want us to work together to keep every neighborhood safe, and they want to see that we’re committed to taking proactive steps to prevent violence before tragedy strikes.”

Murphy and co-sponsor Councilor Ed Flynn’s resolution calls for a citywide public safety summit to evaluate current strategies, identify opportunities for improvement, and develop additional recommendations to reduce violent crime, support first responders, and improve public safety in all Boston neighborhoods.

It also calls for the Council to be briefed on the city’s summer safety plan by Mayor Michelle Wu, Police Commissioner Michael Cox, and other relevant public safety officials, which the resolution says should be “immediate.”

Murphy and Flynn, who have been calling for increased police staffing levels to counteract violence, state in their resolution that the Council briefing on the city’s safety plan should include information on police deployment, staffing levels, violence prevention, and intervention efforts, among other priorities.

“It’s clear we need a new comprehensive public safety plan,” Flynn said. “Staffing levels are dangerously low. Shifts are not filled, impacting public safety in every neighborhood. We have also witnessed frequent assaults against police officers.

“We know police officers are frequently working 16 hours a day, mandatory overtime. We also know morale is low in the Boston Police Department. Police officers know they’re not supported or appreciated here at City Hall,” Flynn said.

He added that the city needs to “respect our police officers,” and recognize that because, “we’re not providing the level of police officers that are needed across the city of Boston, public safety is negatively impacted.”

The Council also referred a similar late-file hearing order that was sponsored by Councilors Miniard Culpepper, Brian Worrell and Henry Santana and called for the city to consider a community-based summer safety plan to the Public Safety and Criminal Justice Committee for further discussion.

Earlier this week, Culpepper and Worrell, who both represent parts of Roxbury, the neighborhood where last weekend’s holiday gun violence largely took place, convened a press conference with faith leaders to call for more community policing and violence prevention.

“The recent acts of violence across our city, most of which occurred in my district, are heartbreaking. Every resident deserves to feel safe in their neighborhood, and we cannot and will not normalize what has happened,” Culpepper said. “It’s heartbreaking to see violence resurface in communities that have fought hard to move forward.”

Culpepper said community leaders and organizations that have spent years cultivating trust in Boston neighborhoods that experience a “disproportionate share of gun violence” should have a “seat at the table from the very beginning,” rather than have their input on the city’s safety plan be viewed as an afterthought.

“Now is the time to come together as one city,” Culpepper said, “to incorporate community organizations’ expertise into the city’s summer safety strategy.”

title: Editorial: What it takes to be ‘the safest city in America’
text:
Boston is the safest city in America — until the shooting starts.

Thirteen people were shot, two fatally, in five separate incidents that occurred throughout the city Saturday night into Sunday morning. Additionally, two people were stabbed and officers were assaulted by fireworks.

In late June, a Boston Police officer tried to arrest a man in Dorchester, but a crowd intervened, throwing drinks and objects at the officer before the suspect got away.

This spike in city violence has officials and residents sounding the alarm for the community.

“Right now, it doesn’t feel like the safest city in America. Right now, for people who look like me, it doesn’t feel like the safest city in America,” said Steven Wilson Jr. of the Ella J. Baker House.

This is not Boston’s first rodeo — recall the faith-based group Ten Point Coalition, an integral part (with the Boston Police) of the “Boston Miracle” of the 1990s, a period in which violent crime dropped by 79%.

That took coordinated effort, organization, support services and a lot of dedicated people. That success story can, and needs to be, repeated.

City Councilors Erin Murphy, who represents the city at-large, and Ed Flynn, of District 2, filed a resolution calling for a public safety summit.

“After another deadly holiday weekend, we cannot simply issue statements and move on. Boston deserves answers, accountability, and a real plan,” Murphy wrote in a statement.

More police on Boston streets is always top of mind after incidents such as these. But District 7 Councilor Miniard Culpepper, who represents parts of Roxbury, noted that a plan must include more.

“I do know part of the answer to the question is the community. When we have community policing, it’s when we have peace.”

Culpepper said that he’d like to see a “supplemental budget for peace,” saying, “I pray that we look at more money to fund the groups that do the work every day.”

Culpepper shouldn’t have to pray for needed funds, they should be on the table now.

Violence is a public health crisis, and Boston needs to treat it as such. Remember how we handled COVID? The Boston Foundation established the COVID-19 Response Fund in 2020, to, as it explains on its website, “rapidly deploy flexible resources to organizations in Greater Boston that were providing critical basic needs to communities disproportionately affected by the coronavirus outbreak.”

There’s an outbreak of violence in Boston, and we need a similar fund, or funding in general, to address it. It won’t go away on its own.

Minister Randy Muhammad, the founder of Boston’s chapter of the 10,000 Fearless Peacemakers, said that he respected the work of the police, but that their work often comes after violence happens.

“Let’s invest not only in the after,” Muhammad said, “but let’s invest in those that are doing the work to prevent the crisis.”

The situation on Boston streets can get better, or it can get worse. We can be “the safest city in America,” or we can have that boast belied by news of yet another shooting.

The ball’s in City Hall’s court.

title: Boston Police ordered in for ‘mandatory overtime’ during Sail Boston Saturday
text:
The Boston Police will be going all hands on deck for Sail Boston this weekend.

“With the department ordering all officers of all ranks in for mandatory overtime beginning at 5:45 am this Saturday; we feel our voices being heard,” he said. “However, with the Tall Ships, a labor strike by the MNA at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and our normal calls for service throughout the city, we are still very concerned.”

Sail Boston, an international tall ships festival, comes on the heels of a chaotic and violent July 4 that left two dead and 11 others injured in five separate shootings.

The Herald reached out to Boston Police for comment but did not hear back before press time.

Following the uptick in violence, city councilors Ed Flynn and Erin Murphy are also asking to beef up BPD staffing.

“We cannot continue reacting after tragedy strikes. Boston residents deserve action, not talking points,” Murphy wrote in a statement. “They deserve fully staffed police shifts, safer neighborhoods, and leaders willing to put differences aside before more lives are lost.”

On Wednesday night, the Boston City Council unanimously approved a resolution calling for a safety briefing for the councilors and a public safety summit with stakeholders in different roles from around the city to weigh in on how to address the violence.

Councilors Minard Culpepper and Brian Worrell have said they’d like to see resource go towards the community groups that do non-violence work. They also said that residents of neighborhoodss that have been most impacted by the violence, like Roxbury where four of the five Fourth of July shootings took place, should be at the table when discussing solutions.

“If we all come together, that’s how we’ll win,” Culpepper said.

title: Bottoms up: Boston Mayor Wu, City Council want 3 a.m. last call, public drinking zones to stick around
text:
Mayor Michelle Wu and the City Council want to keep the party going in Boston after the World Cup ends, and are pressing state lawmakers to extend 3 a.m. last call hours and public drinking zones through the summer.

Wu and the Council on Wednesday spoke favorably about a special state law that loosened nightlife restrictions in Boston for the international soccer tournament, by allowing the city to set later last call hours at bars and restaurants, and implement two downtown social districts where people can legally drink outside.

“We’ve had no incidents,” Wu said on GBH’s Boston Public Radio. “The businesses have reported huge gains, and people have been having a great time. I think it’s really important that with all that’s happening in the world, there are spaces where people can come together and have fun.”

With the temporary provisions set to expire July 31, city officials are exploring ways to make the changes permanent, which would require Beacon Hill to sign off.

“We would very much advocate for that,” Wu said. “It should be on cities to be able to make those decisions, and we are going to continue to advocate for keeping the momentum going. It’s not just World Cup and summer events, but all throughout the year, there’s something happening in Boston.”

In the meantime, the Council, by an 8-2 vote Wednesday, passed a resolution backing a state Senate bill that seeks to keep the public drinking zones and later bar hours in place through August, or the “rest of the summer” as councilors put it.

“More than 200 establishments now participate, and two social districts operate downtown,” City Council President Liz Breadon, the resolution’s lead sponsor, said. “Residents and visitors have embraced the extended hours and social districts. We’ve hosted the Tartan Army and other World Cup visitors with great success.”

The city’s two social districts opened last month at Union and Marshall streets in downtown’s Blackstone Block Historic District and on Temple Place in Downtown Crossing, where people can purchase booze from restaurants and drink outside.

Breadon said “the summer is just getting started,” and pushed for state lawmakers to pass a bill co-sponsored by state Senators Barry Finegold and Julian Cyr that now sits in the Committee on Economic Development and Emerging Technologies.

The Senate bill, Breadon said, would “keep the fun going and allow cities and towns to continue the program through August.”

Both Breadon and Wu cited the potential economic benefits from keeping looser drinking restrictions in place in Boston.

Cyr, a Democrat who represents the Cape and Islands, said Thursday that the bill would actually continue the program for a longer period of time, through Labor Day on Sept. 7.

“I think there’s been a real recipe for change in Massachusetts this summer, and I want to figure out how we can hold onto that,” Cyr told the Herald. “It makes abundant sense for us to extend this through the end of the summer. Also, I’ve been a longtime proponent of a local option happy hour. We should do that as well.”

Boston’s sleepy nightlife scene has come alive in recent weeks, as soccer fans from around the world have flocked to the city for the World Cup. The Scots, known as the Tartan Army, were a particular force, with some local bars reporting that they ran out of beer due to round-the-clock Scottish drinking.

“I think it’s encouraging to see Massachusetts embracing so much fun this summer,” Cyr said. “Let’s find a way to keep it up.”

City Councilor Brian Worrell made similar arguments last month when he proposed a home rule petition that would allow for last call hours to permanently be extended from 2 a.m. to 3 a.m. in Boston. If approved by the Council, the legislation would advance to Beacon Hill for consideration.

Worrell, who spearheaded a prior legislative effort that brought 225 new liquor licenses to Boston, said last month that his proposal is about boosting revenue and keeping the city competitive, akin to nightlife offerings from other major cities that allow for later last call hours like New York, Washington D.C. and Miami.

“I think we are a fun city, but there’s an opportunity to be a little more fun,” Worrell told the Herald. “We want to be an area that continues to attract young people.”

The push to keep the temporary nightlife parameters in place past July 31 has its detractors, with criticism centering around public safety concerns and police staffing constraints, in light of last weekend’s chaotic and bloody July 4 violence that left 13 people shot, two fatally.

Larry Calderone, president of the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, the city’s largest police union, said Thursday that the union is “100% against” extending 3 a.m. last call hours, given that the police “can’t manage the calls that we have now.”

“As the police commissioner himself recently stated on the record, booze and big crowds are a bad combo that lead to more trouble,” Calderone said in a statement. “And, really, we couldn’t agree with him more. Extending last call from 2 a.m. to 3 a.m. is a bad idea that invites and encourages bad behavior and the elected officials pushing the measure should think long and hard about the undeniable negative consequences associated with excessive alcohol consumption.”

Ed Flynn and Erin Murphy, the two councilors who have joined the BPPA’s call to beef up police staffing levels to counteract violence, voted against Breadon’s resolution to extend looser drinking regulations, while Miniard Culpepper, who represents Roxbury, where most of the July 4 shootings took place, abstained from taking a position by voting “present.”

title: Federal appeals court upholds Illinois assault weapons ban, overturning lower court ruling
text:
A federal appeals court in Chicago on Thursday upheld Illinois’ 2023 assault weapons ban, overturning a lower court decision and delivering what could be a short-lived victory to Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker.

In a 2-1 decision, a three-judge panel of the U.S. 7th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled the Illinois law, which also prohibits high-capacity ammunition magazines, is “consistent with our regulatory tradition” and does not violate the Second Amendment right to bear arms.

“Whatever else may be contributing to America’s mass-shooting epidemic, the record makes one thing clear: The more people killed, the more likely it is that the killer used an assault weapon and large-capacity magazines,” Appellate Judge Amy St. Eve, who was nominated to the court by President Donald Trump, wrote for the majority.

The majority opinion from St. Eve and Judge Frank Easterbook, a nominee of Republican President Ronald Reagan, sends the case back to U.S. District Court in southern Illinois with instructions to rule in favor of the state of Illinois.

The ruling represents a significant victory for gun control groups and leading Democratic officials, including Pritzker, who pushed for the ban on a long list of high-powered semiautomatic weapons and high-capacity ammunition magazines after a mass shooting at Highland Park’s Fourth of July parade in 2022 that killed seven people and injured dozens more.

“Illinois will continue banning assault weapons and high-capacity magazines capable of inflicting mass casualties,” Pritzker said in a social media post. “A victory in the fight to end gun violence that helps keep our communities safe.”

Attorney General Kwame Raoul, whose office is defending the state law, called the ruling “a win that enhances public safety in Illinois.”

“We have seen the damage that assault weapons and large-capacity magazines can inflict, and these weapons of war have no place in our communities,” Raoul said in a statement.

The longevity of that victory remains in question, however, after the U.S. Supreme Court indicated last week that it would take up legal challenges to similar laws in Cook County and the state of Connecticut.

Firearm industry groups that are involved in the legal challenge to the Illinois law said they were disappointed, though not surprised, by the ruling from the 7th Circuit and expressed confidence that the Supreme Court would ultimately rule in their favor.

“There is absolutely nothing new here,” said Dan Eldridge, president of Federal Firearms Licensees of Illinois, an advocacy group for gun dealers that has been part of the litigation.

Eldridge noted Thursday’s opinion relied on much the same reasoning the appeals court had used in previous cases involving assault weapons bans.

“It’s just regrettable that they chose to sit on it until after the Supreme Court was out of session,” he said.

The National Shooting Sports Foundation said in a statement that it planned to appeal to the high court and anticipated justices would overturn the Cook County and Connecticut bans based on previous rulings that pared back gun restrictions.

The challenge to the Illinois law is based on landmark Second Amendment cases decided by the high court, including the 2022 decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen. In that case, the 6-3 conservative majority ruled that modern gun laws must be rooted in the nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation. Key to that determination is whether gun laws are historically consistent with laws on the books in the 18th century, when the Bill of Rights was ratified.

In its 44-page opinion, the appeals court found it was “appropriate to take a more nuanced approach to the historical inquiry” and that differences between the Illinois law and past rulings cited in the legal challenge were “less material in light of the dramatic technological changes and unprecedented societal concerns that have taken root since the Founding and Reconstruction eras.”

Attorneys in Raoul’s office have argued the prohibited weapons are not considered “arms” under the Second Amendment and that they possess the same qualities as military weapons that are not commonly used for self-defense.

While the appeals court’s ruling assumes the weapons in question are “arms,” it found that “legislatures have long imposed restrictions on particularly dangerous weapons, and the (Illinois law) is but another chapter in that story.”

Illinois Deputy Solicitor General Sarah Hunger argued during the September oral arguments that the prohibited guns, particularly AR-15s, should not be typical for civilian use and that if the courts say it’s constitutional for the government to ban automatic weapons, the same principle applies to semiautomatic weapons.

“Mass shootings are a very specific type of event and this law was enacted to prevent this type of shooting,” Hunger said during the hearing.

In challenging the law, gun rights groups, including the National Shooting Sports Foundation, cited the Bruen case to argue Illinois’ ban on many semiautomatic guns — requiring the trigger to be pulled once per round — is too broad because it doesn’t protect guns that are commonly used by law-abiding citizens, including AR-15- and AK-47-type guns that are subject to the Illinois ban.

The court’s majority rejected the argument that widespread use of the guns necessarily conferred constitutional protection. As historical precedent, the court pointed to 19th-century restrictions on Bowie knives, which were upheld in courts despite the fact that the weapons “were both widespread and used for lawful purposes.”

“As the Reconstruction-era judicial decisions cited earlier demonstrate, our ancestors regulated particularly dangerous weapons for sufficiently specific similar reasons as Illinois is regulating AR-15s and large-capacity magazines,” the majority opinion says.

In his dissenting opinion, 7th Circuit Chief Judge Michael Brennan, another Trump appointee, argued that, despite weighing “perhaps the most comprehensive trial record in any Second Amendment case to date,” the majority was repeating a previous error it made in a preliminary ruling upholding the law. That decision, with the same split, came in a group of cases that also included similar bans in Chicago, Cook County and Naperville.

“Our Nation’s enduring traditions forbid governments from prohibiting firearms commonly owned for self-defense. Because the people have overwhelmingly chosen the AR-15 rifle and its magazine as their weapon of choice, they are protected by the Second Amendment,” Brennan wrote in a dissent that ran seven pages longer than the majority opinion.

While the Trump administration is not a party to the case, Harmeet Dhillon, the U.S. Justice Department’s assistant attorney general for civil rights, argued before the 7th Circuit in September that the nation has a “strong interest” in ensuring that the Second Amendment’s right to bear arms is “not relegated to a second-class right.”

Dhillon’s participation in oral arguments was an indication of just how far the Trump administration is willing to go to fight Illinois’ gun ban. Pritzker, who is running for a third term as governor and has been an outspoken opponent of Trump, has repeatedly defended the law as constitutional, reasonable and necessary.

Aside from the president’s administration inserting itself into the legal fight, Justice Clarence Thomas, who has long been part of the U.S. Supreme Court’s conservative wing, indicated in court papers in July 2024 that the Illinois weapons ban is “highly suspect” and the high court should accept the full case if it comes back for review.

Pritzker, who is considered a potential contender for the 2028 Democratic presidential nomination, signed into law the ban on so-called assault weapons in January 2023, six months after the mass shooting in Highland Park. The law prohibits more than 100 semiautomatic rifles, handguns and shotguns, high-capacity magazines and other accessories, and requires gun owners who possessed these weapons prior to the ban to register them with the Illinois State Police.

The gun ban has withstood a number of legal challenges.

U.S. District Judge Stephen McGlynn, nominated to the bench by Trump during his first term, granted a motion from gun rights groups in April 2023 to temporarily block the enforcement of the gun ban. His ruling was overturned later in the year by the 7th U.S. Circuit, which found in a 2-1 vote “there is a long tradition, unchanged from the time when the Second Amendment was added to the Constitution, supporting a distinction between weapons and accessories designed for military or law-enforcement use, and weapons designed for personal use.”

But at that time, the appeals court noted its opinion dealt only with a preliminary injunction from the lower court and did not “rule definitively on the constitutionality” of the state and local laws at issue.

Chicago Tribune’s Olivia Olander contributed.

title: Boston named the most collision-prone city ahead of crash that killed city worker
text:
Ahead of a fatal crash that killed a city employee this week, a report from a major car insurance company listed Boston as the “riskiest,” most collision-prone city in America.

Allstate’s 2026 America’s Best Drivers Report states that Boston drivers are 189% more likely to be involved in a crash than the national average.

Hub motorists average less than four years between collisions, per the report, which was released this month and ranks the 200 largest U.S. cities based on auto claims data. Massachusetts has three cities ranked in the bottom 10, more than any other state.

“Where you drive plays a role in your risk, but how and when you drive matters just as much,” said Laura Hoffman, Allstate’s vice president of auto design and telematics, in a statement.

Boston, at 200, was listed the riskiest city for the second year running. Two other Massachusetts cities, Worcester and Springfield, were only a few spots behind Boston for risky driving conditions, at 197 and 196, respectively, per the report.

The Bay State’s capital city was found to be riskier than seven other cities that ranked in the bottom 10 for driver safety: Washington, D.C. at 199, Baltimore at 198, Glendale, Calif. at 195, followed by Providence, Rhode Island; Sunrise Manor, Nevada; Los Angeles and Philadelphia.

Boston’s collision-prone conditions, with drivers averaging 3.76 years between crashes, can be costly, with accidents leading to higher insurance prices and the need for repairs, the report states.

At the top of the list for safest cities is Brownsville, Texas, with drivers going nearly 15 years between collisions. Texas and Colorado lead the best drivers list, with five of the 10 top cities for safety coming from those two states.

The top 10 after Brownsville is Fort Collins, Colorado; Boise, Idaho; Laredo, Texas; Cary, North Carolina; Madison, Wisconsin; McAllen, Texas; Colorado Springs, Colorado; Eugene, Oregon; and Olathe, Kansas.

Drivers in the top 10 cities average 12.51 to 14.99 years between crashes, while drivers in the bottom 10 cities average between 3.76 to 6.12 years, per the report.

The report lists distracted driving as a contributing factor to crashes in Boston, with it joining other major metro cities like Miami, Chicago, and Washington, D.C. for elevated phone use.

Other crash factors cited as impacting cities ranked by Allstate include speeding, hard braking, and nighttime driving.

Boston has also consistently ranked among the worst cities for traffic in the country, and throughout the world.

Allstate’s report was released less than a week before a fatal crash rocked the city, after the bicyclist struck and killed by a person driving a truck on Tremont Street was identified as a Boston City Hall employee.

Louisa Gag, 36, was a transit advocate and planner for the city’s Transportation Department, who, according to Mayor Michelle Wu, worked to make Boston “streets, neighborhoods, and public spaces safer.”

“I am absolutely devastated by this unfathomable loss for our community and our city,” Wu said in a statement after Thursday’s fatal crash. “Louisa led programs and improvements that made our streets safer, our communities stronger, and our residents’ daily lives better.”

Gag was hit between Brigham Circle and Roxbury Crossing around 8:19 a.m. She was pronounced dead on scene, police said, and the truck involved stopped. The incident is under investigation by Boston Police and the Suffolk DA’s office.

At an April hearing, Boston city councilors and transit advocates hammered the Wu administration for delaying transportation projects, saying that its inaction has cost the city millions in federal grant funding and put cyclists and pedestrians at risk.

The Council hearing was focused on three orders that were reactive to a reported change in policy by the mayor that resulted in, per one order, the city’s participation in “numerous transportation projects” being “indefinitely paused.”

Tiffany Cogell, executive director of the Boston Cyclists Union, said at the April hearing, “Every day of inaction is a day that federal and state dollars slip through our fingers or get transferred to another project.”

“It’s a day a cyclist is endangered, a day a disabled resident is stranded,” Cogell added. “The pause on Boston’s transportation projects is a regional crisis.”

Transit advocates also protested the $4.9 billion city budget this year, as proposed by Wu, for similar reasons ahead of last month’s approval by the Council.

The Massachusetts Vision Zero Coalition, which advocates for the reduction of traffic injuries and deaths, said Thursday that Gag “was a champion for safer streets, a vibrant part of the planning and advocacy community, and a person dedicated to fixing the very system that failed her.”

title: Boston Police Blotter: Man charged in Burger King brawl
text:
A man faces several charges after allegedly yelling racial slurs, beating up a customer, and lunging at an employee at an East Boston Burger King, according to the Suffolk District Attorney’s Office.

Patrick Donovan was charged with assault and battery causing injury to a person over 60 or disabled person, assault and battery, disorderly conduct, resisting arrest, assault, and vandalism, the DA’s office said in a statement.

He was arraigned in East Boston District Court and released on personal recognizance on condition that he stay away from the Burger King and area where the incident allegedly occurred.

According to the DA, Donovan started yelling at an employee after ordering food late one night at the end of June at Maverick Square. Then, he allegedly lunged at the employee and grabbed her arm, before pushing another customer and punching them in the faces while yelling racial slurs.

The DA said that there is surveillance footage of the incident.

Officers caught up with Donovan at the Maverick MBTA station, where he allegedly took a swing at them, but didn’t make any contact, the DA’s office said.

“Our workers deserve to be safe in their workplaces and our consumers deserve to be safe in their shopping or dining places, without exception,” Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden said in a statement. “Beyond that, none of our citizens or first responders should be subjected to racial slurs. These appalling words have no place in Suffolk County or anywhere else in our society.”

Donovan will be back in court Aug. 7 for a pre-trial hearing.

Man arrested for allegedly smashing cars with stick, cinderblock

Boston Police arrested a man in East Boston for allegedly smashing cars with a wooden stick and cinderblock Sunday night.

Officers responded to Sumner Street around 5:13 p.m. for reports of a person vandalizing parked cars in the area, police said.

When officers arrived, they saw a person matching the description of the suspect carrying a wooden stick and placed them in custody.

Witnesses told them that the suspect had taken a wooden stick that was holding up a recently planted tree to smash the windows and side mirrors of the vehicles, according to BPD.

Police said they also saw a cinderblock at the scene that was likely used to break glass.

Revanth Kumar Mahesh, 27, of Roxbury was arrested, BPD said, but during the booking process, officers found a U.S. permanent resident card and Social Security card with false information that did not match his identification.

Mahesh faces several charges, including forgery, and is expected to be arraigned at East Boston District Court.
