title: Boston Mayor Michelle Wu slammed for stalled streets projects after city transportation planner’s death
text:
A Boston City Hall vigil will be held Thursday for the city transportation planner struck and killed by a truck driver while riding her bicycle last week, with speakers set to honor Louisa Gag and push for safer streets.

The vigil will be held at 6 p.m. on City Hall Plaza, exactly a week after lifelong Boston resident, Gag, 36, was fatally struck on Tremont Street between Brigham Circle and Roxbury Crossing.

“Members of the Massachusetts Vision Zero Coalition, Louisa’s colleagues and community members will gather to remember her and call for urgent action to prevent further deaths from traffic violence,” a media advisory states.

Ahead of the event, “parents, families and neighbors of Boston” wrote an open letter to Mayor Michelle Wu that began with the letterhead, “Enough is enough” and, as of Wednesday evening, was signed by more than 3,800 people.

“For years, we have told you, in public and to your face, that continued delay on street safety would cost lives,” the letter said. “Last week it cost the life of Louisa Gag, a transportation planner in your own administration, a person who devoted her career to making our streets safe.

“Louisa was killed on her bicycle blocks from an intersection your administration has studied and stalled. She was not the first. We have been losing neighbors to these streets for years, and we have been warning you, specifically and repeatedly, that more deaths were coming,” the letter adds.

Stacy Thompson — a board member for the transit advocacy group LivableStreets Alliance who worked with Gag before she was hired by the city — said Wednesday that she and other organizers of the vigil are coordinating with the advocates who wrote the open letter, many of whom are coming to the event.

Thompson said city employees who worked with Gag at the Boston Transportation Department will be speaking at the vigil. She said there hasn’t been any pushback from the Wu administration about the City Hall event, despite the adversarial nature of part of the planning messaging about the city’s lack of street safety.

“Two things can be true at once,” Thompson told the Herald. “Louisa was a valued member of the Boston Transportation Department, and everyone inside City Hall wants to remember her and mourn her loss. We are absolutely partnering with the city on that. They’re welcoming that. They also know that it is our right to be angry and demand more.

“Because of who Louisa was, it’s not as simple as the city is on one side and the advocates are on another side. I think that there’s a real sense, even beyond the borders of Boston, that we all have to do more, and that is the spirit that we’re showing up in together.

“We’re doing both things at once: remembering Louisa and we’re calling to action,” Thompson said. “The city knows that’s going on, and of course they’re not stopping us because they loved Louisa too.”

title: Boston Mayor Wu vows to restart stalled street safety projects, recommit to bike lanes after city transit planner’s death
text:
Boston Mayor Michelle Wu said the city will conduct an analysis of road design at the corridor where her transportation planner was killed by a truck while on a bike and will recommit to bike lanes and other street safety projects.

Wu made a surprise appearance at a community vigil held Thursday night on City Hall Plaza for Louisa Gag, a 36-year-old city transportation planner and lifelong resident who was fatally struck exactly a week earlier on Tremont Street between Brigham Circle and Roxbury Crossing.

“We owe Louisa more than our grief,” Wu said through tears. “We owe her action. We have to do better. … I can share today that to complement the law enforcement investigation of the facts of the crash, we will do a full analysis of street design too, and build this in as a standard practice, one that we hope can be a model everywhere. My vision is that everyone should get to grow old in our city.”

Wu, who has been under intense political pressure from transit advocates to recommit to stalled street safety projects since Gag’s death, said her administration would be taking steps to beef up bike lane protections and restart work citywide.

“We’ve already stepped up enforcement of blocked bike lane, crosswalk and other double-parking violations, mapped out a plan to install or replace protected bike lane infrastructure,” Wu said, “and I’ve assigned two senior members of my team to the streets cabinet full-time to accelerate the policies, planning and capital delivery work that will make our streets safer.”

Wu said she would share more in the days to come on efforts to revamp street safety, when speaking at the vigil organized by Vision Zero Massachusetts, an organization that advocates for the reduction of traffic injuries and deaths.

Of Gag, Wu said, “She devoted her life and career to building a Boston where every resident and every visitor could move through our city safely, with comfort, dignity and confidence — and she was killed on her streets.”

The mayor’s plans to recommit to street redesigns, bike lanes and other pedestrian-oriented accessibility improvements comes after transit advocates have hammered her administration for months over delaying transportation projects.

Advocates and city councilors said at an April Council hearing that the Wu administration’s inaction has cost the city millions in federal grant funding and puts cyclists and pedestrians at risk.

The criticism intensified over this past week, following Gag’s death, as reflected in an open letter delivered to Wu ahead of the vigil with the letterhead, “Enough is enough,” and 4,000 signatures from “parents, families, and neighbors of Boston.”

“For years, we have told you, in public and to your face, that continued delay on street safety would cost lives,” the letter said. “Last week it cost the life of Louisa Gag, a transportation planner in your own administration, a person who devoted her career to making our streets safe.

“Louisa was killed on her bicycle blocks from an intersection your administration has studied and stalled. She was not the first. We have been losing neighbors to these streets for years, and we have been warning you, specifically and repeatedly, that more deaths were coming,” the letter adds.

The letter called for Wu to unpause every stalled street-safety project within 30 days with a set date for the beginning of construction, restore the street safety and transportation funding cut in her $4.9 billion city budget, and build projects fast and refine them later rather than waiting for perfect design and unanimous consent.

It also called for Wu to hire a “permanent, qualified” chief of streets with a broad, public mandate to eliminate traffic deaths, and be accountable by publishing a public timeline for every high-crash corridor, including Tremont Street and Hyde Park Avenue, with a named official responsible for each.

Stacy Thompson, a transit advocate who worked with Gag during their time together at LivableStreets Alliance, said ahead of the vigil that there isn’t enough information available about the crash to determine whether the fatality could have been prevented had the city made improvements to the corridor that were stalled.

“That information doesn’t exist yet, but what we can say is we know the conditions now, whether you’re walking, biking or driving, don’t feel good, and there’s an opportunity to improve them along with many other roadways in the City of Boston,” Thompson told the Herald.

The mayor’s office said Friday that the Wu administration has built nearly 20 miles of protected bike lanes, more than doubling the prior existing bike lane network.

The city added that its focus ahead is for the growing bike network to be protected and connected, by tackling key missing links and transitioning to more permanent, resilient infrastructure to be safe, well-maintained, well-integrated into the aesthetics of Boston’s neighborhoods, and built to last.

Wu, who was sharply criticized during last year’s mayoral race for worsening street safety and traffic by implementing bus and bike lanes, appeared to be nervous about speaking at the vigil where she was surrounded by bike groups and other transit advocates angry at her for pausing bike lane infrastructure.

“I really struggled with whether I should come here tonight or not, whether it would help the healing that is so needed for a community in such grief and pain, and whether I would be able to get out any words out at all,” Wu said. “I’m here for Louisa. … Louisa loved Boston and knew it had to be better.

“I can’t stop thinking about Louisa, but especially about the Boston that she wanted to live in, the city that she was working toward to build every day, the city that she would have built over the next few decades if she could,” Wu added. “That is the city of Boston that we will make real.”

title: Longtime Boston police officer charged with assault and vandalism, Massachusetts POST Commission suspends his certification
text:
A longtime city cop has been charged with assault and vandalism, as the Massachusetts POST Commission suspends his police certification.

Meanwhile, a Mass State Police trooper who retired with a dishonorable discharge has had his certification suspended.

Boston Police community service officer Mark Loewen was arraigned this week in West Roxbury BMC on two counts of assault and battery, and one count of vandalism stemming from a domestic incident last weekend.

The veteran cop — who has been with BPD for more than 25 years, and who made headlines in 2001 after killing a drug suspect — pleaded not guilty to the charges. He was released on the condition that he stay away and have no contact with the two alleged victims.

Following the arraignment earlier this week, the Massachusetts POST Commission (Peace Officer Standards and Training Commission) suspended Loewen’s law enforcement certification.

The POST Commission cited “evidence that the Respondent engaged or may have engaged in criminal conduct.”

Loewen was ordered to “immediately surrender” his agency-issued gun, cruiser, uniform, blue lights, Taser, and more.

BPD has assigned Loewen to paid administrative duty.

The Herald reached out to BPD for the police report involving Loewen, but the records are sealed under “the so-called statutory exemption to the public records law.”

“The records, which include an incident report are being withheld in their entirety because said records involve officers responding to an alleged incident of domestic violence and as such, the Department is prohibited from releasing them by statute,” BPD wrote in its response to the Herald. “The statute prohibits public disclosure of all records containing allegations of domestic violence.”

Loewen denies the allegations, according to his attorney.

“Mr. Loewen has been a well-respected Boston Police Officer for over 25 years,” his lawyer, Pete Pasciucco, told the Herald.

“He denies the allegations,” his attorney added. “We will let the court process play out and look forward to clearing his name.”

Over the years, Loewen has been disciplined for misconduct. In 2001, he was suspended for up to 5 days for improper firearm usage or storage. That discipline was held in abeyance, according to the POST Commission.

Then in 2018, he was accused of conduct unbecoming, and that allegation was sustained.

Loewen made headlines in 2001 after shooting and killing a drug suspect, in what the Herald called a “scene straight out of an action flick.”

During the chaotic incident, the undercover cop was sprawled across the roof of a speeding car when he fired his pistol through the sunroof and killed the suspect near North Station. The shooting was later ruled justified.

Then more than a decade later, Loewen received the Jeremiah Hurley medal of honor award — which recalls a Boston cop who died while trying to detonate a bomb in Roslindale.

Loewen last year made more than $300,000, according to City of Boston payroll data.

His total take-home pay of $315,340 was broken down to $132,977 in base pay, $133,341 in detail pay, $36,197 in overtime, and $12,823 in other pay.

Last year, the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association gave a shoutout to Loewen for a community street hockey event.

“We appreciate Rep. Bill MacGregor organizing this wonderful event,” the union wrote. “The kids had a blast and our officers did, too. The District E-5 Community Service Office — including Elvis Garcia and Mark Loewen — were happy to interact, engage with and safeguard all who participated in the Bill MacGregor Street Hockey Event at Fallon Field in Roslindale. Officers were there to cheer on the athletes, assist with traffic and connect with neighbors about things happening in the community.”

Also last year, the state representative posted about Loewen when he attended Opening Day at the Jason Roberts Challenger League.

“Thank you to the Boston Police Department Area E-5 for always being involved and volunteering. We all appreciate that Officer Loewen is a better Officer than pitcher,” MacGregor wrote.

Mass State Police Trooper Ryan Hennessey

The POST Commission also recently suspended a statie’s law enforcement certification.

Mass State Police Trooper Ryan Hennessey retired from MSP with a dishonorable discharge, as he was the subject of an internal affairs investigation.

“The Commission voted to suspend the Respondent’s certification upon determining that it is in the best interest of the health, safety, or welfare of the public,” the Commission wrote.

The Herald asked Mass State Police about the internal affairs investigation into Hennessey.

“The investigation was into alleged violations of department policies,” a spokesperson for Mass State Police said in a statement.

The Herald has filed a public records request to seek more information on the investigation.

title: Massachusetts’ high-stakes $1B race to sustain World Cup glory: ‘A tipping point’
text:
As the World Cup concludes, local insiders agree that a nearly billion-dollar dual-pronged stadium push is the key to sustaining soccer’s momentum across Greater Boston.

Following a massive economic surge, the question facing the Commonwealth is clear: How does Massachusetts capture this month-long, cross-cultural energy to cement soccer’s place at the forefront of the region’s sports landscape?

The answer lies in abandoning Gillette Stadium in Foxboro for a “more accessible” future home, according to executives from the city’s professional soccer teams, the MLS’s New England Revolution and the NWSL’s Boston Legacy FC.

All seven World Cup matches in Foxboro sold out, drawing a combined total crowd of nearly 450,000. But the authentic, rowdy atmosphere from the international fanbases has not been present during the Revolution season so far.

Ahead of the tournament break, the Revolution saw home attendance plummet by 16% from prior campaigns, with 18,610 fans per match, the Sports Business Journal reported in late May.

Cathal Conlon, the Revolution’s vice president of marketing and public relations, has acknowledged that playing in a nearly 66,000-seat NFL stadium is a roadblock to the Revolution gaining more passionate fans.

“We’ve had this circled as a potential tipping point for the growth in the game since the bid was awarded,” Conlon told the Herald of the World Cup’s impact on the growth of soccer.

“You take our average crowds, and you put them into a building designed to have that capacity,” he added, “and it just changes the dynamic. It is hard to generate that full passion in a venue that has so many empty seats.”

To carry the World Cup momentum forward, the team is aggressively courting casual fans. Last week, the front office launched a marketing campaign titled “Thanks World, We’ll Take It From Here,” featuring Revolution and U.S. Men’s National Team goalkeeper Matt Turner, fresh off his second FIFA World Cup.

The long-term remedy to changing soccer culture here, the team says, is the Everett stadium project: A privately funded, 25,000-seat venue slated to be built on a decommissioned power station site along the Mystic River.

Last New Year’s Eve, the Kraft Group reached a $91.7 million community impact agreement with Everett and a separate $48 million mitigation package with Boston. The pacts are the backbone of the project’s blueprint.

The $500 million plan is navigating the formal Massachusetts Environmental Policy Act review process.

Boston-based sports attorney Joe Rosen believes an urban shift is mandatory for MLS to have a fighting chance in survival against European league giants.

“You can’t change the fact that they don’t have the best players in the world, but they still have very good players,” Rosen told the Herald. “What you can change is where they are playing these games. If you can make this a more energetic, familial, closer space, like it is in Europe, that’s going to go a long way.”

To prove his point, Rosen highlighted NESN broadcaster Tom Caron, an investor and part-owner of the Portland Hearts of Pine, a professional soccer club based in Maine. The team plays its home matches at a stadium that features a capacity of 5,500.

“All of their games are sold out. It’s crazy, even when it’s cold. A lot of it has to do with the venue,” Rosen said. “This is the most popular sport in the world. These types of projects are ways to capitalize.”

Fans agree that atmosphere is everything.

Cameron Corey, a longtime youth soccer coach who plays recreationally in Boston, believes casual supporters won’t commit to a diluted matchday experience.

“People want to see themselves in the team; they want to see themselves in a winning team,” Corey told the Herald. “They don’t want to see themselves in a team that fills up half of Gillette Stadium.”

Paul Romeo, owner of the Koko Fit Club in Needham and a self-described “typical Boston sports fan,” added: “We are kind of spoiled here in Boston. If the Revs are middling, it’s going to be tough to get a fanbase that’s really behind them.”

Leaving Foxboro has sparked a culture clash.

Kirsty DiSipio, a West Roxbury resident and board member of the Parkway Soccer Club, warned that ditching the suburbs could alienate traditional tailgaters, and moving to the city could cause a traveling nightmare.

“There aren’t enough parking spaces for tailgating,” DiSipio said of the Everett site, “and tailgating is a huge part of the full Revolution experience. … It’s going to be too much of a hassle as opposed to just driving over to Gillette. They’re going to lose a lot of people.”

As the Revolution look north to Everett, Boston’s new NWSL expansion franchise, Legacy FC, is laying foundations in the heart of the city.

The club drew 30,000 fans to its inaugural home opener at Gillette Stadium in March, but the franchise is actively preparing for its permanent move.

Construction is progressing on the $325-million redevelopment of White Stadium in Franklin Park. The 11,000-plus-seat venue, slated to open in 2027, is a public-private partnership funded by $135 million from the city and $190 million from the club’s female-founded ownership group.

The massive project is currently navigating a pivotal legal challenge before the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court.

Spearheaded by the Emerald Necklace Conservancy and nearby residents, opponents argue that the shared-use lease effectively privatizes public parkland, violating Article 97 of the state constitution. The City of Boston maintains that the venue remains a public facility.

Amina Bulman, Chief Revenue Officer for Boston Legacy FC, sees an accessible urban stadium as the ultimate tool to invite new demographics into the fold.

“Right now, it’s not that easy to be a soccer fan in the United States; it could be challenging to get to venues in person,” Bulman said. “The more that we can lower the barriers to accessibility for professional soccer, the more we’re going to see the growth of this sport take off.”

In the meantime, the Legacy are looking to capitalize on the soccer wave.

On Sunday, the team will host a “Global Celebration of Soccer” at Centreville Bank Stadium in Pawtucket, where fans can watch the World Cup final on the big screen, immediately followed by a live NWSL clash against the Washington Spirit, led by USWNT star Trinity Rodman.

“So many Bostonians got a taste for global soccer culture,” Bulman said, “and we have the opportunity to build on that in our own backyard.”

Soccer advocates stress that true accessibility requires addressing the sport beyond the professional gates.

In Massachusetts, the dominant youth system remains a costly “pay-to-play” model where elite year-round club fees can exceed $15,000 annually.

“Money is a major barrier. It can feel really exclusive, beyond just the economics,” said Lindsey Whitford, a director at Soccer Without Borders who spent years leading community youth programs in Boston.

Whitford told the Herald that the financial burden includes steep tournament travel logistics, leaving many urban neighborhoods completely unserved.

In Chelsea, for example, there is currently no city-run recreational soccer league for youth. To combat this, Soccer Without Borders is partnering with officials to launch a dedicated initiative this fall to recruit youth, ensure they feel welcome, and leverage the post-World Cup climate.

Warren Zola, a Boston-based sports lawyer, agrees that massive private stadium investments must serve as the primary anchors of broader infrastructure. He warns that the region’s civic fundraising model requires a complete structural overhaul.

“If Boston wants to be a soccer city, the civic infrastructure for these events can’t be dependent on one-time fundraising that falls short,” Zola told the Herald. “It’s that the city, state, and private sector all need to stand in a partnership model.”

Zola added that establishing that framework and investing in recreational hubs with better-maintained pitches and indoor winter access are what separate short-term host cities from true, enduring soccer capitals.

“When the next big soccer movement comes, we’re not scrambling to raise a couple of dollars here and there,” he said. “The Marathon doesn’t need a new fundraising campaign every April – the infrastructure exists. We need that same kind of standing partnership for soccer.”

title: Another Boston police officer faces suspension from Massachusetts POST Commission
text:
Another city cop is facing a suspension from the Massachusetts POST Commission.

Boston police officer Tyraun Barboza’s law enforcement certification has been suspended by the state’s Peace Officer Standards and Training Commission (POST Commission).

BPD a couple years ago sustained misconduct allegations against Barboza — including him viewing/sharing graphic adult websites and/or recordings of unsuspecting women.

“The Commission voted to suspend the Respondent’s certification upon determining that it is in the best interest of the health, safety, or welfare of the public,” reads the POST Commission’s suspension order for Barboza.

Last week, longtime Hub cop Mark Loewen had his police certification suspended after he was charged with assault and vandalism. The Boston Police community service officer was arraigned last week in West Roxbury BMC on two counts of assault and battery, and one count of vandalism stemming from a domestic incident.

The POST Commission in its suspension order for Loewen cited evidence that he “engaged or may have engaged in criminal conduct.”

Meanwhile, Barboza two years ago faced three misconduct allegations from Boston Police, and the department sustained each of the allegations.

The “conduct unbecoming” misconduct included: viewing/sharing graphic adult websites and/or recordings of unsuspecting women; accessing CJIS (Criminal Justice Information Services) for no legitimate law enforcement purpose; and traffic enforcement options — failure to cite an unlicensed motor vehicle operator.

Boston Police suspended him for 30 days for those sustained misconduct allegations. Barboza’s 30-day working suspension included 10 days without pay.

In the POST Commission suspension order, Barboza was ordered to “immediately surrender” his agency-issued gun, cruiser, uniform, blue lights, Taser, and more.

He’s currently on paid administrative duty with Boston Police.

Last year, Barboza had a total take-home pay of $161,764. That was broken down to $116,051 in base pay, $21,702 in overtime, and $23,210 in Quinn education bonus pay through the Police Career Incentive Pay Program.

Barboza in 2022 graduated with a degree in criminal justice from UMass Lowell, where The Lowell Sun spoke to him on graduation day. Barboza told the Sun that he achieved his degree while working his job as a Boston cop and while being a full-time parent to his three kids.

“My advice would be to never quit,” Barboza said on graduation day. “Never put a cap on your goals and what you want to obtain. We’re here until we go in the grave.”

In 2017, he graduated from the Boston Police Training Academy.

“It’s about neighborhood policing,” he told WBUR at the time. “You want to bridge the gap between civilians and police force. You know, you gotta go in there with a positive mindset no matter how tough the job is. That’s one of the things I’m looking forward to is trying to help bridge that gap.”

title: Boston, US Army announce coastal flooding and sea level rise protection plan
text:
Hundreds of thousands of Bostonians live at risk of worsening coastal flooding, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) states in a draft report set to be released this week outlining massive projects to defend the city’s waterfront over coming decades.

“More than 40% of our residents now live in areas at risk of coastal flooding, including some communities who are more than a mile away from the ocean,” Mayor Michelle Wu said Monday. “Without action, we risk $54 billion in damages to our homes, hospitals, businesses, roads, and other critical infrastructure by the end of the century. And that’s why over the past decade we’ve been working with our local, state, and federal partners to build a climate-ready Boston, and it’s why once again we’re turning to the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to help us defend our city.”

The drafted Boston Coastal Storm Risk Management Feasibility Study details over 20 infrastructure projects along 16 miles of the city’s 47-mile coastline to mitigate potentially catastrophic sea level rise and coastal flooding over the coming decades, city and Army officials said Monday.

The study, commissioned to allow Boston to access a 65% federal cost-share for construction of the baseline protection infrastructure, is set to be released in full on Friday. The city and Army are seeking public feedback on the draft, before the release of a final report scheduled for 2028.

The USACE study will “drive one of the biggest investments in our waterfront, more than twice the size of the Boston Harbor cleanup,” Wu said.

Officials outlined the impact of mounting coastal flooding and sea level rise at Langone Park in the North End, built on a sea wall to help the neighborhood withstand flooding.

About one-sixth of Boston is built on filled tidelands and is in “danger of flooding due to sea-level rise and extreme weather,” the city stated. Along with about 284,000 residents in areas at risk of coastal flooding, about 20,000 buildings are at risk of severe flooding, the USACE findings show.

Neighborhoods including Dorchester, Roxbury, the South End, Back Bay, Beacon Hill, East Boston, Charlestown, and Allston are expected to feel impacts, as well as access to hospitals, the MBTA, I-93, the Mass Pike, Logan Airport, and more.

Already 24 severe storms have triggered federal or state disaster declarations in Boston since 1991, and 14 have caused major flooding.

“The reality of this is, after looking at it, doing nothing is not a viable solution,” said Lt. Col. David MacPhail, deputy commander of the USACE New England District. “We have to do something to mitigate this. Without action, the cost of public safety and economic viability from the coastal flooding will be compounded and untenable.”

The study assesses Boston’s “people, the ecosystems of the area, the property, and the critical infrastructure,” MacPhail said, and plans for interventions including seawall improvement, flood walls, berms, levees and surge barriers – a “lattice work of almost puzzle pieces” to build resilience in the 47-mile coastline.

The construction would ultimately close 20 long-term coastal flood pathways, which are inland areas that could flood during extreme weather events. These pathways were identified “by the federal government as key areas of risk that could compromise the safety and economic future of both Boston and the country at large,” city officials said.

At the same time, MacPhail added, there has been effort to “maintain the character and charm” along the Boston Harbor with elements like harbor walks, urban furniture, and other betterments.

All together, the projects are estimated to cost over $10 billion over the next few decades, not including upgrades like green spaces and outdoor recreation expected to be added in, city officials said.

If Boston takes no action, the USACE estimated, the city is projected to lose $54 billion by the end of the century – with about $4 in residents’, businesses’, and the public sector’s avoided disaster losses for every $1 invested.

One study published in the Nature Climate Change journal in June found floods that historically had a 1% chance of striking a coastline in a year are now about 12 times more likely, on average.

Wu said that the city would “have a much better idea” of cost, phasing, funding sources and more following the 2028 final study release.

The Boston Green Ribbon Commission launched a one-year study to identify funding sources for the 35% of the projects non-federal cost share.

City officials urged residents to take part in public comment on the projects from July 24 to Sept. 18, along with an upcoming series of community meetings and webinars.

“If you live or work in Boston or have an interest in Boston, we really do want to hear from you,” said Boston Chief Climate Officer Brian Swett. “Your voice can not only help us protect Boston for generations to come, but also expand your access to green spaces and recreational opportunities right here along the Boston Harbor.”

title: Boston City Council pressures Mayor Wu to provide street safety updates after transit planner’s death
text:
Two Boston city councilors are pushing for a change in city law that would require Mayor Michelle Wu to report street projects annually as Wu faces criticism for stalling road work before a city employee was killed by a truck.

Councilors Enrique Pepén and Liz Breadon filed an ordinance this week that would mandate the city administration to provide annual reporting of street safety projects, with an eye toward improving pedestrian accessibility and achieving the city’s Vision Zero goals of eliminating all fatal and severe crashes by 2030.

“There is a need for greater transparency and accountability in Boston when it comes to transportation and streets projects,” Pepén said Monday in a statement posted to social media. “This ordinance is about creating transparency and ensuring residents have clear information about the transportation projects they care deeply about and impact their daily lives.”

The filing, set to be introduced at Wednesday’s Council meeting, comes after hundreds of bike and transit advocates descended on City Hall Plaza last Thursday for a vigil to honor Louisa Gag, a transportation planner for the city who was killed by a truck while riding a bicycle earlier this month.

Gag, 36, was fatally struck on Tremont Street between Brigham Circle and Roxbury Crossing, an area that transit advocates say was “blocks away from an intersection” the Wu administration had “studied and stalled” for improvements.

“We have been losing neighbors to these streets for years, and we have been warning you, specifically and repeatedly, that more deaths were coming,” transit advocates wrote last week in an open letter to Wu signed by 4,000 people.

Wu vowed at last week’s vigil that the city would conduct an analysis of road design at the corridor where Gag was killed and recommit to bike lanes and street safety projects that she has been hammered for pausing in the wake of Gag’s death.

While the criticism reached a breaking point after the fatality, it had been mounting for months. Advocates and city councilors said at an April Council hearing that the Wu administration’s inaction has cost the city millions in federal grant funding and puts cyclists and pedestrians at risk.

Pepén and Breadon’s ordinance filing states, “It is important for residents to understand how the city uses taxpayer funds to finance the fulfillment of its commitments with short- and long-term projects.”

The annual reporting should include “regular updates on project progress, budgets, timelines and overall status,” Pepén said.

“By providing public annual updates, the city can better track progress, identify challenges, and remain accountable for delivering safer streets for every neighborhood,” Pepén said. “We believe residents deserve to know how projects are moving forward and what steps are being taken to improve the streets in their neighborhoods.”

Wu told reporters Monday that the city already provides updates on street safety and transportation infrastructure projects on the city website, but stopped short of saying the ordinance proposed by the two councilors wasn’t necessary.

“The work that we do has to be clear, has to be urgent, and we already have all the information up on the city website, the status of all the projects,” Wu said. “I can certainly continue to share that information with councilors and the community, but most important is that the work is done and it’s done right.”

While the ordinance will likely be referred to a Council committee for a hearing, Pepén and Breadon, the Council president, will be seeking approval Wednesday for a resolution that calls for the city to recommit itself to its Vision Zero 2030 goals.

Pepén is also co-sponsoring a hearing order filed by Councilor Ben Weber “to review the status of Boston’s citywide bike network plan.”

title: Boston man who strangled 87-year-old woman to death has been granted parole
text:
A convicted murderer who beat and strangled to death an 87-year-old woman during a break-in has been granted parole.

Dionicio Delvalle is the latest “emerging adult” teen killer who the Massachusetts Parole Board voted to release from prison.

Delvalle had been sentenced to life without parole in 2005 after he was convicted of first-degree murder for killing Maude Hinds in 1991.

But Delvalle became eligible for parole two years ago when the state’s Supreme Judicial Court ruled that “emerging adults” who were 18 to 20 at the time of the offense could not be sentenced to life without parole.

That court ruling has led to hundreds of parole hearings for convicted murderers, including Delvalle.

He was 19 years old in April of 1991 when he beat and strangled to death the 87-year-old woman, who was described as a spunky woman and a “bouquet of life,” according to Herald reports in the wake of Hinds’ death.

Hinds had discovered Delvalle breaking into her Roxbury apartment with his brother. The 4-foot-11 Hinds was punched, kicked and stomped to death when she crept down a back staircase after hearing a suspicious noise.

The first floor tenant of the apartment building later found Hinds’ lifeless body in the common hallway of the building. She had been severely beaten, with injuries to her face and numerous fractures to her ribs and spine.

A hammer and broken flashlight were found near her body.

Her second-floor bedroom had been ransacked, and her bedroom window was broken. There were fingerprints and blood evidence on the window. Also, DNA evidence from blood on the window matched DNA from blood on Hinds’ clothing.

Nine years later, the Boston Police Department matched fingerprints left on the window to Delvalle. His DNA also matched blood found on both the window and on Hinds’ clothing.

Delvalle was interviewed and admitted that he had broken into the apartment building and “brushed” by the woman as he made his escape. However, he blamed the murder on his brother.

Then earlier this year, Delvalle appeared for the first time before the Parole Board. He’s now 54 years old, and he has served 25 years behind bars.

“Mr. Delvalle participated in programming that addressed his need areas,” the Parole Board wrote in its ruling. “He appears to have benefited. Mr. Devalle displayed positive institutional conduct with minimal disciplinary reports. Mr. Delvalle has also committed himself to Occupational Skills training with consistent employment in the Metal Shop as a welder.

“Mr. Delvalle accepted full responsibility for his actions and displayed insight into his decision making and actions following the offense,” the board wrote, later adding, “Mr. Delvalle has a strong support system and release plan to assist with successful re-entry. Mr. Delvalle has no diagnosis of Mental Health or Substance Use Disorder. Mr. Delvalle has also provided employment opportunities upon release.”

Delvalle’s sister and two of his friends pushed for his release, while the Parole Board heard opposition to parole from a Suffolk County District Attorney prosecutor.

The Parole Board ultimately decided: “The Board concludes that Dionicio Delvalle has demonstrated a level of rehabilitation that would make his release compatible with the welfare of society.”

title: Comic-Con 2026: Hollywood’s coming to town. These are the celebrities set to attend this year
text:
For the celebrity-obsessed, Comic-Con is like Christmas in July — when Hollywood comes to town with a sleigh filled with celebrities.

The official day-by-day schedules released last week have given us a peek into what this year’s Comic-Con holds for us, with names ranging from John Cena and George Takei to Rebecca Romijn and Kate McKinnon.

With what appears to be a big Hollywood presence throughout, we expect more high-wattage names to leak in the coming days.

Adria Arjona

Hot off the “Star Wars” series “Andor,” Puerto Rican actress Adria Arjona will hit the scene at Comic-Con to promote the A24 action thriller “Onslaught.” The film, which premieres in September, is about a rogue group of genetically engineered super soldiers. Arjona has been involved with a range of other fan-favorite TV and movie projects recently, including “Hit Man,” “True Detective” and “Fortnite.” Ballroom 20. Thursday, July 23, 5:30 to 6:30 p.m.

Jessica Biel

You may have first known her in the 1990s for “Seventh Heaven,” but now, Jessica Biel has carved out a place as a TV and film star, not to mention Justin Timberlake’s better half. On the way to a leading role in Apple TV’s upcoming “Matchbox The Movie” with John Cena, Biel recently starred in Amazon Prime’s “The Better Sister” alongside Elizabeth Banks. “Matchbox The Movie,” based on the Mattel toys by the same, should find a good home at Comic-Con surrounded by action figures and toys of all kinds. Hall H. Saturday, July 25, 2 to 4 p.m.

Alex Borstein

The “Family Guy’s” Lois Griffin will be in the house Saturday, July 25, when Alex Borstein drops by Ballroom 20 for a 45-minute panel on what’s next for the long-running animated sitcom created by Seth MacFarlane. Besides voicing Lois, Borstein has kept herself busy acting in films and TV, including “The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel,” for which she’s won two Emmy awards. Created in 1999, “Family Guy” is expected to unveil exclusive footage and drop some announcements at this panel, which will also be attended by actors Seth Green, Arif Zahir and Jennifer Tilly as well as supervising director Peter Shin, and showrunner and executive producer Rich Appel. Ballroom 20. Saturday, July 25, 1:30 to 2:15 p.m.

John Cena

The wrestler-turned-actor John Cena will definitely not be undercover when he makes his appearance in Hall H as part of the “Matchbox The Movie” panel on Saturday, July 25. The Apple TV film, inspired by the Mattel toys, stars Cena as an undercover CIA agent. The movie, which premieres on Oct. 9 on Apple TV, also stars Jessica Biel, Sam Richardson, Teyonah Parris, Arturo Castro, Corey Stoll, Bill Camp, Danai Gurira and Golshifteh Faranhani. Hall H. Saturday, July 25, 2 to 4 p.m.

Kyle Chandler

Most famous for playing Coach Eric Taylor in the NBC drama “Friday Night Lights,” actor Kyle Chandler steps into the DC universe in the HBO-produced series “Lanterns.” Chandler plays Hal Jordan. He’ll appear on a panel on Friday, July 24, with Aaron Pierre (John Stewart), Garret Dillahunt (William Macon), Poorna Jagannathan (Zoe), and co-creators Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof and Tom King. Expect never-before-seen clips and exclusive chatter about the upcoming series, set to air in August on USA. Hall H. Friday, July 24, 1:30 to 2:30 p.m.

Common

One of the buzziest panels of the weekend will be Apple TV’s two-hour event featuring “Silo,” “Matchbox the Movie,” “Dark Matter,” “Mayday” and “Widow’s Bay.” Common — an Academy Award-, Emmy- and Grammy-winning rapper, actor and author — will join the cast of “Silo” to discuss the latest season and other details from behind-the-scenes. He’ll be joined by other series stars: Graham Yost, Rebecca Ferguson, Ashley Zukerman, Jessica Henwick and Alexandria Riley. Hall H. Saturday, July 25, 2 to 4 p.m.

John Cusack

If you fell in love with John Cusack in 1987’s “Gross Pointe Blank,” 1989’s “Say Anything” or 2000’s “High Fidelity,” here’s your chance to see the actor up close and personal. He’ll be at Comic-Con on Friday, July 24, to sign copies of the book “Momo,” illustrated by Ignacio Noé. Simon & Schuster describes the book this way: “Two fugitives form an uneasy alliance on a mission tied to none other than Jackie Gleason — yes, that Jackie Gleason — and quickly find themselves in way over their heads. What follows is a surreal collision of pulp sci-fi, occult mystery, and dark humor, packed with bizarre encounters, buried secrets, and forces far beyond their control.” Autograph Area AA04. Friday, July 24, 4:30 to 5:30 p.m.

Guillermo del Toro

Two decades after Guillermo del Toro brought us “Pan’s Labyrinth,” the Oscar-winning filmmaker will make a Comic-Con appearance in what’s considered the primetime of the annual convention: the five o’clock hour on a Friday in Hall H. The Mexican director will be joined by actors Doug Jones (Pale Man, Faun) and Ivana Baquero (Ofelia) as well as Oscar-winning cinematographer Guillermo Navarro. The film will be re-released in October, so expect sneak peeks. Lots of it. Hall H. Friday, July 24, 5:15 to 6:15 p.m.

Seth Green

Seth Green, the man behind Adult Swim’s “Robot Chicken,” will be on another panel on Thursday. Green is definitely well-known in Comic-Con circles as a multi-hyphenate: actor-producer-director-writer-comic. He made his acting debut in 1984’s “The Hotel New Hampshire” and has appeared in countless films and TV shows since, including the “Austin Powers” movies and “Buffy the Vampire Slayer.” At this year’s Comic-Con, he’ll appear on a panel about the art of visual storytelling with a sneak peek inside the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art. He’ll be joining Matthew Senreich, with whom he formed Stoopid Buddy Stoodios, the Lucas Museum’s senior curator and head of film programs Ryan Linkof, and DC president, publisher, and CCO Jim Lee. Hall H. Thursday, July 23, 4:45 to 5:45 p.m.

ENHYPEN

Expect some ear-piercing squeals from Ballroom 20 on Thursday morning when the K-pop sensation ENHYPEN graces the stage for some vampire talk. The panel, aptly called “Bite Me: Calling All Vampires,” will feature members of the ENHYPEN talking about the “Dark Moon” franchise. They’ll be joined by familiar faces from the “Twilight” series — director Catherine Hardwicke, Ashley Greene (Alice Cullen) and Peter Facinelli (Dr. Carlisle Cullen). TV guide senior writer Damian Holbrook will moderate the panel, followed by an audience Q&A. Ballroom 20. Thursday, July 23, 11:15 a.m. to 12:15 p.m.

Kevin Feige

His name might not be recognizable to the general public, but in Comic-Con circles, especially those in the Marvel fandom, he is definitely an A-lister. Kevin Feige is the president and executive producer of Marvel Studios and the chief creative officer of Marvel. And since 2007, he has been the primary producer for the Marvel Cinematic Universe. Feige and his Marvel cohorts are taking the main stage Saturday night — as in, Hall H — for the biggest presentation of the entire convention, marking Marvel’s return to Comic-Con. Its next big release, “Avengers: Doomsday,” is set for a Dec. 18 opening. Since no celebrity names have been released, we’re expecting some major surprises. Marvel knows how to put on a show, so this should be no exception. Hall H. Saturday, July 25, 5:30 to 6:30 p.m.

Nathan Fillion

Nathan Fillion is such a Comic-Con staple that he’s even had a massive advertisement of his face on the side of a downtown San Diego building. He’s been there the last two years for “The Rookie” and returns this summer to discuss the show’s ninth season. Fillion is also known for “Castle,” “Big Mouth,” “Superman” and “Peacemaker.” Indigo Ballroom. Saturday, July 25, 1:45 to 2:45 p.m.

Chris Kattan

The star of “Saturday Night Live” and “A Night at the Roxbury” is headed to Comic-Con with a new comedy project celebrating the culture of live music. Much of the filming for the upcoming “Concert Heroes” took place in San Diego, so it’s a fitting place for the cast and crew to share some behind-the-scenes stories and exclusive clips. The movie also features Elizabeth Daily, famous for playing the voice of Tommy Pickles in “Rugrats” and ” Buttercup in “The Powerpuff Girls.” Indigo Ballroom, Saturday, July 25, 11:15 a.m. to 12:15 p.m.

Matthew Lillard

Horror fans will already know Matthew Lillard as an ongoing star in the “Scream” franchise, including the most recent “Scream 7.” Now, he’s back to bring to life another beloved horror character, Stephen King’s “Carrie,” in an Amazon Prime Video series of the same name, debuting in October. Lillard, also known for playing Shaggy in the “Scooby-Doo” franchise, will play the schol principal in “Carrie.” The show will be the subject of a Saturday panel, “Meet the New Class of Carrie.” Ballroom 20. Saturday, July 25, 5 to 6 p.m.

Mike McCready

The Pearl Jam, Mad Season and Temple of the Dog guitarist joins the wave of musicians getting into graphic novels. McCready will join a panel titled “Mike McCready’s Alternative History of Grunge” to discuss “Farewell to Seasons,” which seeks to capture the ’90s grunge scene explosion with illustration through comics. The founding member of Pearl Jam also contributes to the pop culture world by scoring TV and film projects. Indigo Ballroom. Thursday, July 23, 12:30 to 1:30 p.m.

Kate McKinnon

“Saturday Night Live” mainstay Kate McKinnon will hit Comic-Con hard as part of a panel for “Heads Will Roll,” the hit comedy series she created with her sister, Emily Lynne. The sisters promise to “take you behind the scenes” of their hit Audible Original comedy series on Saturday, July 25. “Kate and Emily will share the creative chaos of building their absurd medieval world … where a raven turns into a toad, queens face demonic reproductive deadlines, and nothing goes according to plan,” organizers say. Room 5AB. Saturday, July 25, 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.

Jeffrey Dean Morgan

Actor Jeffrey Dean Morgan, who plays “Negan” in the super popular “The Walking Dead” franchise, will join the cast and producers of AMC/AMC+’s “The Walking Dead: Dead City,” set to return July 26 for its third season. Morgan, who also is an executive producer for the series, will be joined by Lauren Cohan (executive producer; “Maggie”), Jimmi Simpson (“Dillard”), Aimee Garcia (“Renata”) and Seth Hoffman (showrunner and executive producer). A sneak peek of the season’s first episode is expected. Hall H. Friday, July 24, 11:45 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.

Rebecca Romijn

Rebecca Romijn first captured the hearts of the nerd community in the role of Mystique in the early 2000s in the “X-Men” movies, and now she’s at Comic-Con for another beloved franchise: “Star Trek.” On Saturday, a special 60th anniversary celebration will include Romijn and other cast members from “Star Trek: Strange New Worlds.” They’ll be joined by other icons of Trek history, such as Michael Dorn, Jerry O’Connell and Robert Picardo. In the latest Paramount+ original series for the franchise, “Strange New Worlds,” Romijn plays the role of Una Chin-Riley. Hall H. Saturday, July 25, 12:30 to 1:45 p.m.

Dan Stevens

The acting range of Dan Stevens, known to many as the heartthrob of “Downtown Abbey,” includes everything from the horror anthology series “The Terror” to the Beast in the live action version of “Beauty and the Beast.” Now he’s joining the cast of a new action thriller, “Onslaught.” He’ll play a scientist in the film about a group of genetically engineered super soldiers. The movie hits theaters in September, but attendees of the “Onslaught” panel will get to see footage debuting to the public for the first time. Ballroom 20. Thursday, July 23, 5:30 to 6:30 p.m.

George Takei

No celebration of “Star Trek” history would be complete without the legendary George Takei. A frequent star at Comic-Con, Takei played the character of Sulu in the 1960s “Star Trek” TV series and has contributed to many other movies, series and podcasts in the franchise. Takei is considered a television pioneer for representation of Asian Americans in media and is also and author and activist. He’ll join Romijn and other “Star Trek” legends at a 60th anniversary celebration. Hall H. Saturday, July 25, 12:30 to 1:45 p.m.

Lisa Whelchel

If you’re a child of the 1980s, Lisa Whelchel — aka Blair Warner — will be a familiar face at this year’s Comic-Con. The actress will attend the convention as part of a panel for MeTV’s hit show, “Collector’s Call.” Whelchel is host of the show about collectors and their amazing collections. She’ll be joined by Neal Sabin, vice Chairman of MeTV; and “Collector’s Call” experts Rob Klein, Jennifer Klein and Matt Weinhold. Room 6DE. Friday, July 24, 10 a.m. She’ll also be in Autograph Area AA04 from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. after the panel.

title: Boston Police Blotter: Fugitive team arrests suspect wanted for Dorchester murder
text:
Boston Police said members of their fugitive unit arrested a suspect wanted for a Dorchester murder Wednesday.

Officers arrested Justin Ferrer, 23, of Dorchester, just before noon in the area around 1931 Dorchester Ave., on a warrant for murder, the department said.

Ferrer was charged in connection to the shooting death of 22-year-old Giovanni Bala, also of Dorchester, on May 22.

Bala was found by police suffering from a gunshot wound on Bowdoin Street at 1:05 a.m. He was transported to the hospital, where he was pronounced dead.

BPD said it was still actively reviewing the case, and urged anyone with information to come forward by calling the Homicide Unit or staying anonymous via the tip line.

Mattapan man arrested for alleged drug trafficking at Mass and Cass

An alleged drug dealer who sold little baggies marked with alien faces was arrested near Mass and Cass Tuesday, according to Boston Police.

Brandon Hamler, 37, of Mattapan, faces several charges, including trafficking between 18 and 36 grams of fentanyl, distribution of Class B substances, both methamphetamine and Adderall, and possession with intent to distribute a Class B substance (also methamphetamine), the department said in a statement.

Police said Hamler engaged in “hand-to-hand exchanges” in the parking lot of a gas station on Southampton Street for about 30 minutes around 2 p.m.

Officers stopped Hamler and other individuals who they saw interacting with the suspect. Police said they found narcotics on the others and Hamler, who also allegedly had a “large quantity” of suspected drugs on him and an undisclosed amount of cash.

During a search of Hamler, officers recovered 31 individually packaged bags of suspected fentanyl that total about 19 grams. They also said they recovered 20 little bags of suspected meth, and pills police believe are Adderall.

BPD shared a photo of what they recovered, showing the packages marked with green alien faces.

Boston Police officers working on the Neighborhood Engagement Safety Team made the arrest as a part of an ongoing initiative to improve quality of life issues near Massachusetts Avenue and Melnea Cass Boulevard. The team also works with clinicians and members of the Mayor’s Office Coordinated Response Team.

“This collaborative approach combines enforcement with substance abuse alternatives, housing resources, and mental health support for individuals in the area,” BPD said.

Hamler was transported to Nashua Street Jail and is expected to be arraigned at Roxbury District Court.
