title: Boston man arrested in deadly July 4 weekend shooting held without bail
text:
Family members of a 24-year-old gunned down during a violent July 4 weekend filled a courtroom Wednesday afternoon for the arraignment of his alleged killer, another 24-year-old accused of doing the shooting.

Catrelle Davis has been charged with murdering Travis Washington in the early morning hours of July 5. Davis allegedly shot the victim while he was standing with a group of people celebrating the holiday on Blue Hill Avenue in Roxbury.

Three other people were shot during the same incident, but none of the others’ injuries were considered life-threatening. Davis has not been charge in connection to those other injuries.

A warrant was issued for Davis and he was arrested Wednesday around 4:35 p.m. in the area of Maple Street and Sonoma Street in Dorchester, according to Boston Police.

Assistant District Attorney Nathan McGregor asked that Davis be held without bail because of the strength of the evidence in the case. The prosecutor said “the entire thing” was caught on video, and “quite clearly” showed the shooting and that Davis was the aggressor.

He asked the court to impound the videos as evidence, which the defense didn’t object to.

Davis was held without bail and will be back in court Sept. 22 for a probable cause hearing.

McGregor also noted that a grand jury investigation into the homicide was ongoing.

People who appeared to be family of Davis were allowed to leave the courtroom first after the hearing, with the large crowd for Washington, wearing pins and t-shirts with his face, filing close behind.

The victim’s family members declined to comment to a reporter after meeting with the prosecutor at Dorchester District Court, following the arraignment.

“Every homicide is a societal tragedy, and the tragedy is magnified when the victim is a young person just getting started in life,” Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement. “I extend my deepest sympathies to Travis Washington’s family and friends, and I thank all of the investigators for their tireless work resulting in Catrelle Davis’s arrest.”

Washington was one of two young men killed over in the early hours after the Fourth of July.

Christopher Washington-Conway, 29, was killed in a triple shooting on George Street, also in Roxbury, according to Boston Police. The department has not announced any arrests in that case.

In total, 13 people were shot in five incidents that occurred that night.

The spike in violence led to calls for a public safety summit as well as more resources for the police department and local anti-violence community groups.

According to the latest crime data, which was published Monday, the total number of victims shot in Boston is up from the same time last year, while shooting fatalities are slightly down.

Between Jan. 1 and July 19, 2025, 12 people were shot and killed in the city, compared to nine so far this year. The department does note that information is preliminary and subject to change.

title: Boston Mayor Wu unveils street safety plan that prioritizes cyclists, cracks down on drivers
text:
Boston Mayor Michelle Wu released a street safety plan that prioritizes cyclists while cracking down on drivers seen as putting them at risk in response to intense pressure from bike activists following a city worker’s traffic death.

The new plan unveiled on Friday follows the mayor’s vow last week to recommit to stalled street safety projects and bike lanes at a transit advocate-led vigil for Louisa Gag, a 36-year-old city transportation planner who was fatally struck by a truck driver while riding her bicycle earlier this month.

“We remain devastated by the loss of Louisa Gag,” Wu wrote in a letter outlining her plan. “Louisa loved Boston and devoted her life to making our city better every day.

“I know many Bostonians are personally mourning this unfathomable loss while also continuing the fight for safer streets — a movement shaped by Louisa’s leadership, creativity and compassion,” Wu added. “Residents deserve clarity about our vision for streets that are safe, beautiful, and family-friendly.”

Wu said the city will look to provide protection to cyclists by encasing bike lanes in concrete barriers — similar to what’s been built on Congress Street — replacing the flimsy plastic flex posts that have been separating bike and car lanes citywide and are, per the mayor, “creating unacceptable risks for bike commuters.”

The city has added roughly 20 miles of bike lanes under the Wu administration, but the effort stalled after criticism during last year’s mayoral race that bike lanes were worsening traffic, creating hazards, and hurting the bottom line for businesses.

Other plans call for ramping up construction for the “thousands of curb ramps and hundreds of miles of sidewalks that need to be built or fixed” after “years of deferred maintenance.”

The city intends to target those upgrades on areas that are most urgent and used, with a particular focus on “ensuring that children can walk and bike safely to the places where they gather, play and learn” — such as school zones, libraries, parks, playgrounds, and community centers, Wu said.

Other plans call for cracking down on motorists who double park or block bike lanes, crosswalks or sidewalks, with fines and technology that allows for and encourages more rapid reporting of violations and subsequent enforcement.

Wu said Gag was killed by a large truck, which has prompted the city to crack down on truck safety. She said trucks and other heavy commercial vehicles are to blame for the majority of fatal traffic crashes involving cyclists over the past decade.

A city truck-side ordinance is already on the books to regulate truck safety for city-owned and contracted vehicles, but Wu said the city needs protections for all trucks and large commercial vehicles on Boston streets.

“In the coming months, we will work to advance more comprehensive truck-safety legislation, strengthen side-guard enforcement, review city routes used by heavy commercial vehicles, and assess additional safety measures to prevent future crashes,” Wu said.

Police have not identified the truck driver who fatally struck Gag on the morning of July 9 nor pressed charges.

Gag was fatally struck on Tremont Street between Brigham Circle and Roxbury Crossing, an area that transit advocates say was “blocks away from an intersection” the Wu administration had “studied and stalled” for improvements.

Wu vowed at last week’s vigil that the city would conduct an analysis of road design at the corridor where Gag was killed — Tremont Street in Mission Hill — and recommit to bike lanes and street safety projects that she has been hammered for pausing in the wake of Gag’s death.

Her letter on Friday states that the corridor review will be aimed at identifying “important fixes.”

Wu said she plans to convene a group of advisors to review the effectiveness of her Streets Cabinet, and has taken steps to enhance operations by appointing two of her senior staff members to oversee the cabinet full-time. She identified them as Chris Osgood, the city’s senior advisor for infrastructure and former chief of streets, and Tali Robbins, her deputy chief of policy.

The plans were framed by Wu as advancing the city’s Vision Zero goals of eliminating all fatal and severe crashes by 2030.

“Boston should be a city where every resident and visitor can move comfortably and confidently,” Wu said. “We will carry forward Louisa’s legacy by working to make this vision a reality.”

title: Massachusetts Senator Nick Collins undercuts Boston Mayor Michelle Wu on tax relief amid feud
text:
State Sen. Nick Collins fired the latest shot in his ongoing feud with Mayor Michelle Wu by tucking a property tax relief clause into the economic development bill to blunt Boston’s “unnecessary tax increase on homeowners.”

Collins said his property tax relief amendment, which would expand senior tax exemption eligibility and provide rebates to Boston homeowners using city surplus funds, was unanimously approved by the state Senate.

“The purpose of the senior property tax exemption is to support seniors on fixed income who deserve tax relief to ease the burden of the city’s unnecessary tax increase on homeowners,” Collins said from the Senate floor. “In addition, the legislation would authorize the city to issue rebates to homeowners to mitigate unnecessary tax increases levied by the city year after year.”

Collins, a South Boston Democrat, said his amendment to the proposed state economic development bill would expand eligibility of the senior property tax exemption and triple the benefit to $1,500.

It would also provide tax rebates to homeowners using funds from what Collins called the city’s “substantial surplus,” or reserve fund, “to the tune of $1.7 billion that was built up by the taxpayers and that rating agencies suggest the city is stockpiling for small businesses.”

Collins said the amendment would also triple the personal property tax exemption to help businesses “survive the unnecessary tax increases levied on them also by the city, year after year.”

The senator — who has been in the mayor’s crosshairs since his late 2024 move to block her signature tax shift legislation and is facing a primary challenge from a political newcomer backed by Wu — suggested that any opposition from City Hall to the Senate-approved tax relief amendment he proposed would be political.

“These policies, the city is already on record in support of, including passage of the Boston City Council,” Collins said. “For the city to be against it now, they’d have to be for it before they were against it.”

The amendment, co-sponsored by Republican Senate Minority Leader Bruce Tarr, is the latest shot fired in the state Senate’s battle with Wu over how to provide property tax relief to homeowners.

Wu has publicly blamed Collins for the failure of her tax shift bill, citing his procedural move to block a vote multiple times before it was ultimately killed by Senate President Karen Spilka due to lack of support.

The bill sought to provide a tax break to homeowners by increasing commercial tax rates. It was passed by the City Council and House of Representatives three times, but stalled in the Senate.

Wu has endorsed Latoya Gayle, a political newcomer and community activist challenging Collins in the Sept. 1 Democratic primary. She has also endorsed her former senior aide Daniel Lander in his bid to knock off William Brownsberger, the President pro tempore of the Senate and the other senator Wu blames for killing her tax bill.

Collins and Brownsberger put forward alternative property tax relief bills that they argue won’t have the same harmful effects on the economy.

Their legislation was approved by the Senate in January but drew opposition from the mayor, who called their bills “costly alternative Senate proposals that require sacrificing needed funding for city services.”

Collins said his new amendment to the Senate version of the state’s economic development bill marks the second time this session that the Senate has moved to approve property tax relief measures.

While Wu has blamed the Senate for this year’s 13% average tax increase for homeowners, due to their failure to approve her legislation, Collins said the city’s “unfair” assessment practices are to blame.

“Finally, the part of the legislation that hits at the heart of why Bostonians continue to see tax increases year after year is due to the city’s unfair assessing practices,” Collins said. “The facts are these: the city is giving wealthy homeowners in Back Bay and Beacon Hill a tax cut by under-assessing their property dramatically.

“At the same time, these unfair assessing practices by the city are hammering the middle class, taxing them to the max or more — communities like Dorchester, Roxbury, Mattapan, South Boston, the South End,” Collins added. “It does not make any sense, and it’s wrong.”

Collins said that, recently, a home in Back Bay valued at $20 million was assessed by the city at $12.5 million. He added that a property on Beacon Hill that sold for $20 million was later assessed by the city at just $5 million.

Meanwhile, in the working class neighborhood of Roslindale, a home that sold last year for $435,000 was assessed later by the city at $485,000, leading to higher property taxes, Collins said.

The senator said the city’s assessment practices have already led to a lawsuit filed by the Pioneer New England Legal Foundation on behalf of commercial property owners who allege the city added assessed value — and therefore, higher taxes — following abatements, and are seeking restitution.

“It is the reason the city’s assessor recently resigned in disgrace,” Collins said, referencing Nicholas Ariniello’s abrupt departure. “This will cost the city. … But while the former assessor skips town, taxpayers will suffer.”

Collins said his amendment seeks to counter “unfair” city assessing practices by giving property owners an additional 75 days to file abatements and “keep their existing assessment intact before their dispute is resolved.”

The senator said, “It’s clear that the city needs assessment reform.”

title: Blindsided family of slain 87-year-old Boston woman ‘in shock’ as Mass. Parole Board frees killer: ‘Wait, but he got life!’
text:
Shocked family members of a slain 87-year-old woman, who was strangled to death during a break-in, were blindsided when they found out in the Herald that her murderer was granted parole.

Roxbury’s Maude Hinds was beat and strangled to death by Dionicio Delvalle in 1991. He was 19 at the time of the killing, and the first-degree murderer was sentenced to life without parole in 2005.

Hinds’ family members left that trial 21 years ago thinking Delvalle would never see the light of day, but a state court ruling two years ago gave him and other “emerging adult” killers a chance for parole.

George Greenidge, the great-nephew of Hinds, told the Herald that family members had no idea about the parole eligibility for Delvalle. So when Greenidge saw the Herald’s article this week about Delvalle’s parole, he screamed.

“Oh my God! This lady looks just like my sister! Oh no! It’s my great-aunt!” Greenidge told the Herald as he recalled his live reaction to seeing the news.

“Wait, but he got life!” Greenidge added. “What are you talking about?… We all are in shock!”

Hinds in 1991 had discovered Delvalle breaking into her Roxbury apartment with his brother. The 4-foot-11 Hinds was punched, kicked and stomped to death when she crept down a back staircase after hearing a suspicious noise.

The first-floor tenant of the apartment building later found Hinds’ lifeless body in the common hallway of the building. She had been severely beaten, with injuries to her face and numerous fractures to her ribs and spine.

“I was 18 when this happened, in school in Atlanta, and my friend called me saying they’re killing old women in Roxbury. Then my Dad calls me and says it was Aunt Maude!” Greenidge recalled. “The whole city was in mourning over this.”

Delvalle was sentenced to life without the possibility of parole, but he became eligible for parole two years ago when the state’s Supreme Judicial Court ruled that “emerging adults” who were 18 to 20 at the time of the offense could not be sentenced to life without parole.

That court ruling has led to hundreds of parole hearings for convicted murderers, including Delvalle. He’s now 54 years old, and has served 25 years behind bars.

The Parole Board granted his release, saying he benefited from programming and “accepted full responsibility for his actions.”

The Parole Board did not hear opposition from Hinds’ family members.

“We had no clue that this was happening,” Greenidge said. “We all would have been there at the hearing for victim-impact statements. We are devastated.

“The Parole Board saw that an elderly Black woman didn’t have anyone there who cared for her, who loved her,” he added. “She was absolutely beloved.”

Greenidge reminisced on Hinds’ big smile, her love of dancing and how much she gave to the Roxbury community. She loved going to church.

“No one could make a better fishcake delicacy than Aunt Maude,” Greenidge said.

The Greenidge family is well known in the city. His great-uncle and namesake, George C. Greenidge, filed a landmark discrimination complaint in 1953 involving the Pullman Company. The company ended up agreeing that in Massachusetts, it would no longer restrict hiring for porters and conductors based on race, color, creed, national origin, or ancestry.

Nine years after Hinds’ killing, the Boston Police Department matched fingerprints left on the window to Delvalle. His DNA also matched blood found on both the window and on Hinds’ clothing.

Delvalle was interviewed by police and admitted that he had broken into the apartment building and “brushed” by the woman as he made his escape. However, he blamed the murder on his brother.

“He kept on saying it was his brother,” Greenidge said. “Now he says it was him, and now he can get out. What the hell!”

He vows to push for “Maude’s Law” for community impact statements to complement these parole hearings.

“So this never happens again,” he added.

The Parole Board has a Victim Services Unit to support families during the parole process. The Unit advises family members about opportunities to participate in hearings, including submitting victim impact statements and testifying at parole hearings.

The Unit did talk with a descendent of Hinds about Delvalle’s parole eligibility after the Mattis “emerging adults” court ruling.

However, further attempts to contact the family member with specific details about the parole hearing were apparently unsuccessful.

“Following the Mattis decision, Parole recognized the need for an unprecedented research initiative to identify, notify, and counsel hundreds of surviving family members regarding their rights in the newly created parole eligibility process,” a spokesperson for Parole Board said in a statement to the Herald. “The Victim Services Unit worked with the District Attorneys’ Offices, and the Department of Correction to identify family members using a number of sources (e.g., state records, media reports, open source information).

“In this case, after significant research, the Victim Services Unit identified and spoke with a direct descendent of Ms. Hinds regarding the case and the Mattis decision,” the spokesperson added. “Victim Services Staff also made attempts to contact that family member regarding the parole hearing and the opportunity to attend, testify, or submit a victim impact statement for the Board’s consideration.”

Boston City Councilor Ed Flynn’s father was the mayor at the time of Hinds’ murder.

“I do not agree with the decision by the Massachusetts Parole Board to release the perpetrator of this violent, ruthless, fatal attack on Maude Hinds, an 87-year-old woman, in her own home,” Flynn said. “When someone commits homicide, we can’t stand in the way of justice for the victim and their family or respect for the rule of law and society.

“It’s critical that officials communicate with the families of victims prior to a public release date and the actual scheduling of a parole hearing as well,” he said. “Additionally, I will file a City Council hearing order to examine the services the City of Boston provides to families of victims of violence, including homicide, and to identify ways we can better support and respect them in the pursuit of justice.”

title: Boston Puerto Rican Parade marches historic celebration to Franklin Park
text:
The 59th annual Puerto Rican parade and festival brought out the masses to celebrate the one of the fastest-growing and storied cultural populations in the region over the weekend.

The Puerto Rican Festival took over Franklin Park throughout the day Saturday and Sunday, with the annual parade marching through Columbus Ave. in Roxbury all the way to Franklin Park.

The parade kicked off at noon Sunday, showcasing the cultural pride of Puerto Ricans in Massachusetts with a wide array of “fabulous floats, colorful dance troupes, singers, dancers, and appearances by distinguished honorees,” festival organizers said.

The festival was first organized in 1967 in the South End neighborhood, the organizers said, when Jorge “Chico” Muñoz and other formed the original festival committee to “create an event that would promote a sense of belonging and cultural affirmation for Puerto Ricans living across the Commonwealth.”

The first festival took place in Blackstone Park with about 2,500 in attendance, the committee said, launching a annual tradition for decades.

The two-day festival has drawn over 50,000 participants, organizers said, calling Puerto Ricans the “fastest-growing ethnic population in New England and the United States.”

Artists set up live performances throughout the weekend, while vendors sold Puerto Rican food and cultural crafts and merchandise at the festival. The event also hosted carnival rides and activities for attendees of all ages, along with a informational health expo for the community.

title: Ex-Boston Children’s Hospital nurse arraigned on charges of assaulting 2 minors
text:
A former Boston Children’s Hospital nurse accused of assaulting two teenage boys in his care was arraigned in Suffolk Superior Court on Monday.

“These boys were assaulted and taken advantage of in their most vulnerable states with their parents out of sight,” Suffolk ADA Madeline Berry said. “These are cowardly, heinous acts before you.

“Boston Children’s Hospital is supposed to be a place members of the public can trust to ensure that their children’s safety is the utmost priority, and (the defendant) has instilled fear in the community with the allegations against him today,” the prosecutor added.

John Tam, 33, of Hopedale, was indicted by a grand jury in early July on four counts of indecent assault and battery on a person 14 years or older, and four counts of indecent assault and battery on a patient by a health care provider.

Tam also faces charge in Marlboro District Court regarding a third alleged victim who was a patient while he worked at the UMass Memorial Medical Center in Marlboro. The adult patient was similarly in an “extremely vulnerable position for defendant to take advantage of,” prosecutors said.

The defendant was previously tried in Roxbury District Court, which resulted in a mistrial. The Roxbury case will be dismissed now that he has been indicted in Suffolk Superior, the DA’s office said.

Suffolk Clerk Magistrate Michelle Pierce released Tam on personal recognizance Monday with conditions of no employment in health care and no unsupervised contact with anyone under 18.

“He has been on personal recognizance in both cases for some period of time,” Pierce said of his cases in Roxbury and Marlboro. “There have been no defaults, no violations of conditions of release, and he appeared pursuant to a summons today, knowing that an indictment was pending.”

On Sept. 19, 2022, the first victim underwent chest surgery at Boston Children’s. The 15-year-old boy was waking up from anesthesia when he found his PACU nurse, identified as Tam, allegedly inappropriately touching his genitals, “prompting victim number one to say, ‘Don’t touch me down there,’ ” Berry said.

The alleged victim had underwent multiple visits and surgeries for cancer and was having a mass removed from his chest to determine if the cancer had returned, the prosecutor noted.

On Jan. 2, 2025, a 16-year-old boy was having a similar surgery under anesthesia at the hospital and under Tam’s care.

Tam allegedly gave the victim and his mother discharge instruction, Berry said, including “specific instructions against sexual activity of any kind.” The nurse then allegedly sent the mother out to collect her car and wait, while he took the boy in a wheelchair to a lobby-level single-stall bathroom, locking the door behind him.

Tam then proceeded to allegedly sexually assault the patient for about eight minutes, inappropriately touching him and offering to show him pornographic material on his phone.

Video shows Tam wheeling the victim into the bathroom and out about nine minutes later, the DA’s office said. He then allegedly took the boy to his mother waiting in the car.

The victim allegedly learned the nurse’s first name, and told his mother what happened in the bathroom as soon as they were alone. The mother alerted hospital staff, and Boston Police were called.

“He waited until his patients were emerging from anesthesia in hopes they would not remember or notice,” Berry said. “A child who was 15, a 15-year-old cancer patient, and a child who was a 16-year-old nervous kid recovering from surgery.”

Tam’s defense attorney pointed to the hung jury in the Roxbury case, as well as a former hospital investigation into Tam in 2022.

“They did not pursue anything,” the defense said of the investigation. “The alleged victim’s family didn’t want to. They were contacted. The hospital looked into it. Surgeons had spoken, too. Nothing came up out of that.”

Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden warned the public these “may not be isolated incidents,” adding “we want to assure parents that any information they provide will be thoroughly and sensitively investigated.”

The DA urged parents whose children may have encountered Tam at Boston Children’s Hospital or at his prior workplaces, including Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and UMass Memorial Medical Center Worcester and Marlboro campuses, to contact local law enforcement or Children’s Advocacy Center to report any instances that they’re concerned about.

Hayden said Boston Children’s Hospital has “been fully cooperative with this investigation,” thanking them for their support Monday.

“At Boston Children’s Hospital, our patients’ and their families’ safety and well-being are our utmost priority, and we continue to cooperate with the investigation and prosecution,” Boston Children’s Hospital said in a statement.

Survivors of child abuse and exploitation and non-offending caretakers can contact Children’s Advocacy Center of Suffolk County at 617-779-2146, or the Child Protection Unit at the Suffolk DA’s Office at 617-619-4300 for support resources. Anyone who suspects child abuse should contact the DCF Child at Risk Hotline at 1-800-792-5200, the DA said.

“I can only imagine what they’re going through,” said Hayden. “I can tell you that we as an office, Children’s Advocacy Center, and everybody will be in support of them, their families, and the entire community as it relates to this.”

Tam will return to court on Sept. 18 for a pre-trial hearing.

title: Five shot overnight in Hyde Park, 1 dead, hits on National Night Out
text:
Five people were shot in Hyde Park just after midnight today, and police report one victim has died.

The shooting was reported in the area of 1184 Hyde Park Avenue, and police said that upon arrival they discovered the five gunshot victims. They were all taken to the hospital, where one has died. That address is home to the Little Haiti International Cuisine restaurant, according to online listings.

“This remains a preliminary and active investigation,” police added, with detectives on the case.

The call first came in at 12:38 a.m. with District 18 officer responding immediately, police said. All five victims were observed “suffering from gunshot wounds,” police said.

At-Large City Councilor Erin Murphy posted early today that after “waking to reports of five more people shot” it ramps up the “urgency” of a briefing she’s calling for at this week’s council meeting on the summer’s public safety plan.

“Every councilor represents residents who deserve to know their elected officials are informed, included, and working together to keep out neighborhoods safe,” Murphy added in her social media post.

Televised video of the shooting scene shows police have taped-off a crime scene on Hyde Park Avenue from the AutoZone to a nearby gas station. It appears from evidence cones set up that the shooting was outside.

This all hits as the Boston Police and Mayor Michelle Wu are set to take part in the annual National Night Out.

title: Hyde Park rocked by mass shooting that left 1 dead, 4 injured: Boston ‘violence is officially out of control’
text:
Hyde Park was left reeling Monday after investigators said someone went to a restaurant and “started shooting up the place,” leaving one dead and four others injured in the latest act of violence rocking Boston.

MORNING UPDATE: Arrest just announced in Hyde Park shooting.

The mass shooting occurred just after midnight at Little Haiti International Cuisine, a creole restaurant located at 1184 Hyde Park Ave., according to police.

Police Commissioner Michael Cox said Monday that there was no update beyond what his department disclosed early that morning, which was that officers discovered five shooting victims upon arrival. They were all taken to the hospital, where one person died.

No other fatalities were reported by Cox, who provided no update on the condition of the four who remain alive. He added that the incident is under investigation, and while no arrests have been made and details have remained scarce early on, “We are pretty confident that we’re going to figure out what occurred there.”

“I’m fairly sure our investigators will spare no expense or leave no detail undone to make sure that we hold that person accountable,” Cox said.

Cox’s remarks came during an appearance with Mayor Michelle Wu at a National Night Out public safety event.

Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said it’s unclear whether the incident was a targeted attack, but he said it was certainly not a random occurrence.

“No reason to believe it was random,” Hayden said. “It’s not like someone just went into the restaurant and started shooting up the place. Whether it was targeted or not at the specific individual, that’s a different question.

“It remains under investigation, but we’re making good progress, and we’re going to continue to do what we do in every single case, which is treat it like the most important case at any given time, because that’s what it is,” Hayden added. “We’re going to keep pressing hard to make sure every community in Boston is safe.”

Cox described the incident as an “isolated” occurrence, but suggested that there may be some retaliatory violence taking place. He urged residents to keep their cool following the latest attack.

“For the residents there, we just want to encourage people to certainly stay cool, calm and collected under the conditions that we’re seeing a pattern of isolated incidents throughout the city, where people are having skirmishes, whether it’s in their homes or businesses,” Cox said.

“I know it’s summertime. It’s still warm, but there’s resources out there to help people,” Cox added. “There’s one of the biggest resources of calling us if there’s any kind of dispute or problem of any sort.”

The brazen shooting sent shockwaves throughout Boston, intensifying calls from the city’s largest police union for more cops on the street to counteract the summer violence that is tarring the mayor’s “safest major city” claim.

“5 SHOT. 1 DEAD in Hyde Park. The violence is officially out of control,” the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association posted on X Monday. “The fact that this incident took place less than 700 feet from a police station is alarming and should have all concerned.

“Safest city in America? Something needs to change. Let’s start with BPD staffing levels,” the BPPA added.

Councilor Ed Flynn went further, saying that it’s time for Mayor Wu to ditch her safest major city claim, which he called “tone deaf,” in light of the “fourth mass shooting in the city in just over a month.”

“With all this activity that has since happened in such a short period of time, it is tone deaf if we continue to downplay residents’ concerns on violent crime,” Flynn said. “It is long past time to move on from campaign slogans and accept the reality for many Boston residents who no longer feel safe in their own neighborhoods.”

Boston needs “a larger police presence,” Flynn said, “but we also need a Massachusetts criminal justice system that values justice for survivors of crime, their families and law enforcement by holding people accountable when convicted for their own criminal wrongdoing, actions and behavior.”

At-Large City Councilor Erin Murphy posted early Monday that after “waking to reports of five more people shot” it ramps up the “urgency” of a briefing she’s calling for at this week’s council meeting on the summer’s public safety plan.

This all hits as the Boston Police and Mayor Wu are taking part in the annual National Night Out, which puts the focus on community policing.

Alongside Cox and Hayden in West Roxbury, Wu said, “I know the city is safe,” while pointing to crime statistics from the police department that show the city is “still at historic lows” for homicides and violence.

“That is no comfort to residents who have experienced the unimaginable, and we will not be satisfied or let up until we have eliminated violence from Boston,” Wu said.

Wu stuck to her safest major city claim, saying, “I say that on purpose, and I say that even though it would be easier not to say those words, but it’s important for us to remind all of our city teams, and our community that we hold ourselves accountable to the highest possible standards.”

She also joined Cox in defending police staffing levels, pointing to a recent recruiting class of 100-plus officers. Cox said there is no correlation between the recent uptick in violence and the number of cops on the streets, and does not believe more cops would have prevented it.

“But there is a core connection between community policing, working with people in the community, and making sure you address the core drivers of violence and crime,” Cox said. “That’s what we’re trying to do always.”

Cox said the department was at ideal staffing levels of 2,600 officers back in the 1980s, but “our crime rate was off the charts,” with an average of 100-plus homicides a year.

“The fact is, we do a tremendous amount with the officers we have because we are way more efficient and effective,” Cox said.

BPPA President Larry Calderone shot back, “People aren’t interested in the department’s 30-40 year old statistics on crimes. They’re worried about being a victim of a violent crime today; like being shot, robbed or physically assaulted.

“And,” Calderone said, “most people feel safer when they see police officers in the neighborhood deterring crime, and making them less susceptible to becoming a victim.”

title: Rachael Rollins blasts Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden after his office was sued for withholding police shooting video
text:
Rachael Rollins blasted DA Kevin Hayden after a new lawsuit was filed against the Boston Police and Suffolk DA’s office seeking to force the release of body cam footage tied to a shooting that left a city cop charged with manslaughter.

“It’s a shame that people have to sue for transparency; politicians and our leaders talk a lot about equity and access until it applies to them,” said Rollins, who is vying to unseat Hayden, in a statement Tuesday.

Rollins said that she would do things differently if elected district attorney, by implementing a “30-day release policy for critical incident footage.”

It would aim to “restore public trust and ensure that the residents of Suffolk County are informed by facts rather than speculation following police-involved shootings and major use-of-force events,” claims Rollins, an ex-Suffolk DA who resigned as U.S. Attorney amid a federal ethics probe that found she abused her position.

“Transparency, trust, and accountability are not just campaign slogans; they are the building blocks of a fair justice system,” Rollins said. “For too long, the delay in releasing vital footage has created a vacuum filled by uncertainty and grief. My administration will treat the public as partners in safety.”

Rollins was reacting to a lawsuit filed in Suffolk Superior Court Tuesday by Lawyers for Civil Rights that alleges BPD and Suffolk DA’s office are failing to comply with public records law by withholding police body camera footage tied to a March 11 shooting.

The Roxbury police shooting led to the death of carjacking suspect Stephenson King, 39, and a manslaughter charge filed against the 34-year-old Boston cop who fired the shot, Nicholas O’Malley.

The prosecution from Hayden’s office moved to place the body camera footage under a protective order during a July 23 hearing. Suffolk Superior Court Judge Joshua Wall said then that the order was granted to avoid depleting the “jury pool by distributing evidence well before trial.”

Lawyers for Civil Rights said Tuesday the footage should be released immediately.

“Few records implicate a greater public interest than footage of a police officer taking a life,” LCR senior attorney Victoria Miranda said in a statement. “The public has a right to see what happened. Every day that BPD and the DA’s office refuse to release the footage is another day the community is denied the transparency and accountability the law demands.”

Boston Police declined to comment due to pending litigation. The Suffolk DA’s office referred comment to the DA’s motion for the protective order.

Hayden wrote that the order is intended “to protect the integrity of the expected trial and reduce potential prejudice to both O’Malley and the Commonwealth.”

His order states that release of body cam video before trial would “expose the jury pool not just to the footage of the homicide itself, but to a barrage of inadmissible commentary about it.”

“The Commonwealth therefore seeks to avoid a global pretrial airing of the homicide,” Hayden wrote, adding that the video shows “core elements of the case.”

Linda Champion, a Suffolk DA candidate backed by the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association — which has criticized Hayden for charging a cop in the fatal shooting — told investigators Tuesday to “release the tape.”

“Under my administration,” Champion said, “the policy will be, after all witness interviews are completed and the officer has been arraigned on the charge … the Suffolk County District Attorney’s Office will release all body cam footage unless prohibited as a matter of law.”

title: Police Blotter: Boston man arrested for Dorchester fatal shooting
text:
Boston Police arrested a 23-year-old man for the Wednesday morning shooting on Blue Hill Avenue in Dorchester.

Billy Thien Huynh was arraigned Thursday in Boston Municipal Court’s Dorchester division in connection with the fatal shooting of a 20-year-old man at 564 Blue Hill Ave. on Wednesday. Boston Police on Thursday identified the victim as Victor Armani Arias Rivera, of South Boston.

“This was a brazen, brutal shooting that took a young man’s life and showed yet again how illegal guns in the hands of people willing to use them are a menace to our city,” Suffolk District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a morning release from his office announcing the arrest.

“I grieve for the victim’s family and I thank the Boston police detectives, prosecutors from my office and members of the public for all their efforts leading to such a quick arrest,” Hayden continued.

Huynh faces charges of murder and several firearm-related counts, including carrying without a license. The suspect was ordered held without bail Thursday.

On Wednesday at about 10:14 a.m., police were called to an apartment on Blue Hill Ave. in Dorchester, where they found Rivera suffering from a gunshot wound to the upper torso, the criminal complaint states. Rivera was pronounced dead an hour later at Boston Medical Center.

According to a witness statement, the complaint says, the suspect arrived at the apartment on a motorcycle, left briefly and then returned with a second man and a young girl in pink on an electric bike. Huynh was allegedly questioning Rivera and a witness about a missing bike, the document states.

Huynh allegedly pulled a gun, the police reported of witness statements, and when Rivera said, “I don’t have your bike,” shot him. The second man with the child reportedly yelled, “Why did you do that,” the complaint states.

“After a short exchange of words, the defendant fired at least two rounds into the top half of his body, ultimately resulting in his death,” said ADA Ashlee Mastrangelo. “The defendant fled the scene on a motorcycle and was later picked up by an Uber in Quincy and turned over to the Boston Police Department.”

The second man allegedly told police Huynh was staying at his house when they received word Huynh’s stolen bike was at Blue Hill Ave. near Seaver St. and went to help him retrieve it. With his daughter present, the witness allegedly told police, “they were not trying to get into any violent altercations.”

After the shooting, the complaint details, the second man left with his daughter and met with his partner. Together, the pair called to tell Huynh he “needed to turn himself in,” ordered him an Uber to take him to BPD headquarters, and met him there, telling officers the defendant “made a bad decision.”

“When the defendant was confronted with that statement, he said, ‘I guess I shot somebody. I was out riding. I guess, I had just snapped, blacked out, and just, now it’s like, I realized what I did and I came in,” Mastrangelo said of a police interview with Huynh.

Following the incident Wednesday, BPD Superintendent Paul McLaughlin said the shooting was one in a string of violent incidents in the city that “are very alarming to the public and to us.” He said they had assigned “a lot of detectives” to the case.

The Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, the department’s largest union, stated in a social media post that this is the latest example why the city needs more officers.

“Broad daylight violence, in addition to being incredibly brazen, is especially concerning for all who live in the city,” the union posted on X. “If bad guys aren’t thinking twice about shooting people at 10:15AM, that’s a problem.”

Huynh will return to Dorchester District Court on Sept. 4 for a probable cause hearing.

Dorchester shooting suspect arrested

A 32-year-old suspect was charged with murder in connection with the fatal shooting of a man in Dorchester in July, Boston Police reported Thursday.

Hensly Dominique Jeanty, of Dorchester, was arraigned on counts of murder and several firearm charges in Dorchester District Court following his arrest Wednesday.

The charges stem from a July 15 shooting at 15 York St. in Dorchester. At 11:53 a.m. on the date, the criminal complaint states, police responded to the area and found a man shot, identified as Breidy Martinez, 29, of Dorchester.

Martinez was pronounced dead on the scene, according to the court documents.

Police tracked a black Jeep Grand Cherokee from the scene of the shooting to Roxbury on July 15 using video footage and witnesses, finding Jeanty allegedly operating the vehicle, the complaint states. The evidence indicates Jeanty “operated or was an occupant” of the vehicle as it moved from the crime scene to Roxbury, the police reported.

The footage, witnesses and cell phone records allegedly show another person in the car “prior to, during and after” the shooting, the complaint continues. The second individual identified as an occupant or driver was identified as 26-year-old Dradae Montissol.

One occupant of the car was the driver and the other allegedly shot Martinez, police allege.

Montissol also faces identical charges of murder and firearm counts, the criminal complaint states.

Boston Police stated the incident remains under active investigation and anyone with information is urged to contact Homicide Unit detectives at 617-343-4470.

title: Suffolk DA debate turns nasty between Kevin Hayden and Rachael Rollins as past scandals resurface
text:
The long-standing vitriol between Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden and Rachael Rollins was on full display during a Roxbury debate where the two took swipes over each other’s past ethics lapses and records as the county’s top prosecutor.

A third candidate, Linda Champion, sought to portray both of her opponents as unfit for office, and drew jeers for accusing the rowdy pro-Rollins crowd of treating a serious debate as a form of entertainment.

“I think you guys all find this very entertaining,” Champion said. “But the reality is, the position of the district attorney is a serious role. We work to protect you. We work to protect victims. We work to make tough decisions.

“The reason I’m running is because the individuals that I see do not have the temperament,” Champion said, adding, “The temperament of the district attorney has to be held, and the position has to be held in high regard. This is not a game.”

The digs came early and often between Hayden and Rollins — who both ignored the rules of the debate that prohibited personal attacks.

“You only know Kevin because I left to become your U.S. attorney,” Rollins, who preceded Hayden as Suffolk DA, said. “So, I feel personally responsible when my phone still rings and people say we can’t get a return call from the DA’s office.

“We’ve seen four mass shootings in the last five weeks, and we’re getting thoughts and prayers from this DA. I don’t want your thoughts and prayers. I want an active leader, not a passive person. I want somebody who knows what they’re doing, who is confident and qualified, and who two of the six police departments haven’t turned their back on.

“The MBTA Police and the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association have an issue with this DA. I’m going to ask for your vote. I want my job back,” Rollins added.

Hayden hits back

Hayden fired back by portraying Rollins as an opportunistic social climber who had one foot out the door as Suffolk DA.

“We are in community all day, every day,” Hayden said. “In addition to that, I didn’t leave my post after three years. I didn’t have one foot out the door for three years looking for something bigger and better.

“This person left her job and now she wants it back because nothing else worked out for her, and it didn’t work out for her because of her lack of ethics and integrity, because she lied to federal investigators,” added Hayden, whose words were drowned out by loud boos and jeers from the crowd at Hibernian Hall.

Rollins then pointed out to the moderator that she said no personal attacks would be allowed before going on to attack Hayden.

“You heard his voice quivering because he’s uncomfortable. He’s not used to standing up. He’s not a leader,” Rollins said. “I have never lied to federal investigators. If somebody doesn’t know the difference between an allegation, a ruling, or a judgment, you don’t deserve to be a lawyer.”

Hayden was appointed by former Gov. Charlie Baker to replace Rollins as Suffolk DA in January 2022, after Rollins was appointed the Massachusetts U.S. Attorney by former President Joe Biden.

Rollins had been elected Suffolk DA in 2018, and drew controversy during her tenure for implementing a so-called do-not-prosecute list for low-level crimes like shoplifting. The list drew criticism during her confirmation process for U.S. attorney for Massachusetts, where she was narrowly confirmed by the Senate, with then-Vice President Kamala Harris casting the tie-breaking vote.

Rollins was alleged to have tried to influence the outcome of a nasty Suffolk DA’s race in the fall of 2022 in favor of her preferred candidate and fellow progressive, ex-Boston city councilor Ricardo Arroyo, by leaking damaging non-public Department of Justice information about the more moderate Hayden to the media.

She was U.S. Attorney at the time, and resigned her post as the state’s top prosecutor in May 2023 amid a federal ethics probe and allegations that she abused her position.

The probe was sparked by Rollins’ attendance at a Democratic National Committee fundraiser headlined by then-First Lady Jill Biden in July 2022, in potential violation of the Hatch Act, which limits political activities of federal employees, as first reported by the Herald.

Rollins probed by DOJ

The two federal reports from the Department of Justice and Office of Inspector General stated that Rollins faced further discipline from the feds if she did not promptly quit.

Rollins said at the debate, however, that while she quit upon the release of the two federal reports, the allegations weren’t the reason she stepped down.

“I wish I had exercised better judgment at that time, but I also made clear that I left not necessarily because of the OIG investigation, but because my family and I were being threatened, and I am a crime victim,” Rollins said. “No job is worth anyone having their life threatened over, and I happily stepped down because I love the office that I worked in as U.S. Attorney.”

Rollins insisted that she had clearance to attend the DNC fundraiser, and then reframed her other allegations around attempting to influence an election as a way to expose corruption in the Suffolk DA’s office, headed by Hayden at the time.

“Kevin used the Suffolk County DA’s office for his own personal gain four days before the election,” Rollins said. “Three days after the election, I gave the Herald a document to say, we will look into this person, and that’s what it was.”

Hayden was issued a state ethics violation in April 2024 and agreed to pay a $5,000 fine for violating conflict-of-interest law by allowing his office to issue an official press statement aimed at discrediting his primary opponent days before the election.

The State Ethics Commission found Hayden was aware of, and took no action to prevent, his office staff from releasing a statement that undercut claims made publicly by Arroyo, who stated investigators had deemed decades-old sexual assault allegations against him unfounded.

“I admitted to that, and I took responsibility for that because that’s what leaders do,” Hayden said. “I didn’t change my story. I didn’t try to duck and dodge from it. Something happened under my watch that should not have happened, and I took responsibility for that and moved on.”

Rollins was issued a public reprimand by the state board that oversees her law license last fall for the same disclosure outlined in the federal reports, which she admitted to, per records from the Massachusetts Board of Bar Overseers.

BBO records show that Rollins admitted to improperly disclosing sensitive Department of Justice information to a Herald reporter about a possible criminal investigation into Suffolk DA Hayden’s handling of a police misconduct case, and her office’s recusal from the matter, while Hayden was running for election.

The disclosure Rollins was disciplined for by the Mass BBO did come three days after Hayden won the primary over Arroyo, but the Herald had held off on publishing damaging information Rollins had been leaking to the Boston Globe and Herald about Hayden until after the primary.

Hayden went on to run unopposed in the general election, and is now running for a second term.

Police body-camera video

While the 2022 Suffolk DA primary that ignited the Rollins-Hayden feud led to most of the fireworks, it was actually Hayden, rather than Rollins, who was on the hot seat for much of the night over his decision not to publicly release police body camera footage tied to a March 11 fatal police shooting of a carjacking suspect.

Hayden has faced criticism from the community, and as of this week, is being sued along with Boston Police for choosing not to release the footage ahead of trial.

The DA has also been slammed by the city’s largest police union, the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, for taking the rare step to charge a city cop. Hayden charged Nicholas O’Malley, 34, who fatally shot Stephenson King, 39, with manslaughter.

O’Malley’s initial attorney said his client should not have been charged ahead of the grand jury indictment. The BPPA says it’s the first time a city cop has been charged with an on-duty death in roughly 30 years, and is actively backing Champion in the race.

Champion and Rollins both called on Hayden to release the tape, and claimed that they would be more transparent about footage around use-of-force incidents.

Hayden, who has been publicly backed by Mayor Michelle Wu, repeated his stance that it would be unfair to both the prosecution and defense to release evidence in a homicide case ahead of a jury trial.

Hayden and Rollins attacked each other over their respective records as Suffolk DA. Hayden took credit for Boston’s record-low homicide rate during his time in office, while Rollins accused his office of “almost exclusively” prosecuting Black and Latino youth.

Hayden focused on his diversion efforts, through his services over sentences program, while Rollins spoke of her “first-in-the nation” discharge integrity team, which she said was more independent from police during her tenure as DA.

“People do not trust the police, particularly when they discharge their gun and kill one of us or harm one of us, for the police to do their own investigation,” Rollins said.

Lone debate

Champion, who ran unsuccessfully for DA in 2018, the race that Rollins won, was largely spared from personal attacks, though Hayden accused her of being in the “pocket” of the BPPA, the city’s largest police union, questioning her ability to be independent as the state’s top prosecutor.

“We cannot go backwards to where we came from and we can’t go forward with uncertain leadership that’s in the hip pockets of the BPPA,” Hayden said. “We need an independent leader that knows how to do the job, that knows how to do it fairly and justly without regard to who the defendant is or what the circumstances are.”

Champion countered, “Eight days, you drag an officer out his house and you arrest him. The district attorney said, ‘Because I saw the evidence.’ So, if you saw the evidence, let us see the evidence.

“I think we deserve more than people who want to weaponize the legal system, who want to put people in jail who are not deserving of being in jail,” Champion said of her two opponents. “Let’s go in a new direction.”

This week’s forum was likely the only time the three candidates will meet ahead of the Sept. 1 Democratic primary that will decide the winner of the DA’s race.

title: Buy Nothing Project: Members give and receive. No cash ever changes hands
text:
ST. PAUL, Minn. — My tech-gadget giveaways have made me a neighborhood rockstar.

The cardinal Buy Nothing rule: Everything is free.

My Amazon Kindle Oasis e-book reader? It’s free. My Logitech MX Mechanical Keyboard? No charge. My Google Pixel tablet with companion speaker/charging dock? Es gratis.

“I actually got a (high-tech) baby scale from you when I was pregnant,” Sacha Brown of St. Paul told me in a Facebook comment earlier this month, to jog my memory. “It came in handy because my son had severe jaundice and we needed to monitor his weight.”

I give, and I receive. In a “gratitude post” last year, I gave thanks for items I obtained from Buy Nothing members. These include a digital bathroom scale, a Timbuk2 messenger bag and a Titleist brim cap.

My latest acquisition: a hardcover copy of Caro Claire Burke’s popular novel “Yesteryear.” This book got me out of my reading slump, and I’ve already thrown it back into the Buy Nothing pool for someone else to enjoy.

Founded in 2013 by friends Rebecca Rockefeller and Liesl Clark in Bainbridge Island, Washington, Buy Nothing has over 14 million users exchanging 2.6 million items a month in over 50 countries, according to the group’s website, buynothingproject.org. It calculates that about 162,000 tons of waste are diverted from landfills each year.

“Every single day, I am moved by what I see happening here,” Clark wrote in a June blog post. “Whether you come to Buy Nothing simply to witness the authentic expressions of gratitude that fill our feeds, or you are actively giving and asking to help our gift economy thrive. We see you. Your presence matters, and your participation is the heartbeat of this community.”

In addition to the Facebook network, which you can quickly find by searching “Buy Nothing Project” from your Facebook profile, there also is a website/phone app combo. (The Facebook sites and the app/site duo stand apart, somewhat confusingly.)

Users’ stories

Buy Nothing members have many reasons for using the service.

“As a member of Buy Nothing for the past six years, I’ve made connections with folks in my community, saved money, helped the environment and gotten rid of clutter that I no longer need!” said my neighbor Jenna Haack Ramirez.

Her favorite examples:

Plastic eggs: I needed plastic eggs for a classroom activity, but didn’t want to buy new plastic just for one-time use. I put in a request and found a neighbor just two blocks away who wanted to give me a bagful of plastic eggs that she was no longer using.

Hair gel: I bought a new hair gel for $14, used it once, and realized that it wasn’t for me. Nobody in my house was going to use it, I couldn’t return it to the store, but throwing it in the trash would have felt wasteful because it was practically new. I posted it and had a neighbor who was excited to have it!

Baby bathtub: A couple in my neighborhood received two baby bathtubs at their baby shower, and wanted to give one away. I was pregnant and thrilled to receive a brand new tub for free, especially because the cost of preparing for a newborn can get excessive. I used the tub for a full year, and I was able to pass it along to a cousin who used it for her baby, as well.

“I love seeing items posted, then reposted months later. I believe some items have been used by multiple people in the community,” Haack Ramirez said.

Bonnie Harris of St. Paul said, “Last fall I completed my transition to owning practically zero things and moving in with my partner. Since most of his things are of much higher quality I was able to purge through my Buy Nothing group, and it became a joyful exercise in letting go, removing negativity, and giving back.”

Her examples:

Recording equipment: A young woman starting her own podcast channel got the expensive equipment that a former agency that fired me bought for me.

Kitchen equipment: A person moving to the Twin Cities for the first time came and took almost everything out of my kitchen. I ended up making a new friend.

Bicycle: A young couple got my Trek bike and now could go on joint bike rides together.

Furniture: An immigrant family now has my couch and dining room table and chairs.

Here are more stories via Facebook or email:

“I love Buy Nothing!” Reagan Carpenter said. “I’ve furnished a whole apartment. 2 actually! One in Merriam Park and the other on West 7th! (Buy Nothing) is my favorite thing about Minnesota, actually!!”

“I’ve had some fun interactions,” said Stacy Sommerhauser Gianino of Highland Park. Like “gifting my Cherished Teddies figurine collection to a nonprofit for adults with disabilities that was going to use them for bingo prizes, and giving my shot glass collections from college to an up and coming bartender.”

“We moved from Charleston to St. Paul,” Sacha Brown said. “We moved with items we couldn’t use in our new house, and we needed many new things due to the drastic climate change. Buy Nothing allowed us to acquire items that we couldn’t find, like snow pants, because we waited until the last minute.”

“I once gave some winter coats to a student at Macalester. (He was a freshman and had never experienced winter),” said Kim of Macalester-Groveland. “A year later, he responded to a post on a bed I was gifting. He was moving from the dorms to an apartment, and I was happy to see him flourishing in Minnesota!”

Then there’s Buy Nothing Barb of Vadnais Heights:

“I want to tell you about my mother (Barbara Zurfluh Sandquist),” said Gayle Gammel. “She is 85 years old. A couple of years ago I got her on to this wonderful (Buy Nothing group). She fell in love. Starting clearing out her place and posting right and left.

“Then a dear friend’s wife passed away who had a hoarding habit,” Gammel said. “My friend would bring over bin after bin of new or slightly used stuff. My mother was in her glory! She set up shop in her spare room. Turned the bed into a photo studio and posted away. Every time he dropped off more stuff she squealed with delight.”

Admins on alert

Each Buy Nothing group on Facebook is supervised by a team of administrators who are sometimes fiercely protective of their domains. When I asked an admin of my group whether I could reach out to members in my Pioneer Press capacity, she politely but emphatically said no.

Admins enforce a rule of thumb: That people should belong to only one Buy Nothing group on Facebook. Those who break this rule are dubbed “frequent flyers,” said admin Cassie Hagen of Macalester-Groveland.

For enforcement purposes, admins are shadow members of adjoining groups on the lookout for frequent flyers, said Anya Benham of Macalester-Groveland.

Admins get to be users, too. “Gosh, when I walk into my house, there isn’t a place that I can look where there isn’t something I got from Buy Nothing,” Benham said.

Facebook admins are often oblivious to Buy Nothing’s phone app/website combo, which seems to exist in a parallel universe.

“I don’t know a ton,” said St. Paul admin Georgia Nesbitt.

I, too, am ignorant of the app, so as an experiment I put a bag of chocolate chip cookies up for grabs. I had a few takers — though this took a while. Seems legit, I concluded, though I’m not abandoning my Facebook group and “All Star Contributor” status anytime soon.

I am struck, for instance, how Buy Nothing is hawking paid “pro” accounts with added features for $4.99 a month (with “enterprise” accounts costing even more).

Isn’t free the whole point of Buy Nothing?

title: Police Blotter: Would-be Boston renters face rise in scams
text:
Remember: if you’re asked to pay in gift cards, it’s a scam.

The Boston Police Department is warning those seeking housing in the city’s tough rental market of a rise in scams.

Scammers are posing as landlords or agents and posting fake listings — or copied and pasted listings for real properties that are no longer available — onto the likes of Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, and other legitimate websites and pressuring potential renters to send money upfront, sight unseen.

That money, the police say, is requested “frequently via wire transfers, gift cards, or cryptocurrency, for application fees, deposits, or first month’s rent without ever seeing the property.” On top of that, the scammers will ask for sensitive personal information in a potential bid at identity theft.

The police say that an apartment seeker can help themselves to avoid these scams by being skeptical of any such requests, being wary of prices that seem too good to be true, never allowing oneself to be rushed to payment, and perhaps do some sleuthing by searching the internet for the rental company or landlord’s name alongside keywords like “complaint,” “review,” or “scam.”

If you’ve already been scammed, file a report with your local police station, which for the city can be found on Police.Boston.gov, reporting the listing on the website where you found it, and filing a report with both the Federal Trade Commission at FTC.gov and the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center at IC3.gov.

title: Boston Police Blotter: Serial shoplifter gets up to three years behind bars
text:
A man who pleaded guilty to several Home Depot heists was sentenced to up to three years behind bars this week, according to the Suffolk DA’s office.

Jeramie Croft, 42, of Boston, was sentenced Tuesday to between 2.5 to 3 years in state prison after pleading guilty to larceny over $1,200, larceny over $1,200 by a single scheme (two counts), malicious destruction of property (three counts), and being a common notorious thief.

The prison sentence is to be followed by two years of probation, and Croft was ordered to stay away from victims and the locations that he stole from.

According to the DA’s office, Croft targeted Home Depot stores in West Roxbury and the South Bay Mall.

Through a series of thefts from February to June last year, Croft stole $7,000 worth of merchandise in eight incidents that were caught on surveillance footage.

He stole drills, nail kits, wire, circuit breakers, and, in at least one instance, a wheelbarrow — which Croft used to carry other lifted loot from the store, according to the statement.

Croft has more than 80 convictions on his rap sheet, including more than 20 shoplifting charges, the DA said.

“We take great care to provide rehabilitative services to offenders when appropriate, but some individuals require a much different approach. Mr. Croft is one of those individuals,” Suffolk DA Kevin Hayden said in a statement. “He presents a clear threat to our retail community and this prison sentence is entirely justified by his repeated offenses.”
