title: Gaskin: Data centers should help fund energy justice
text:
Gov. Maura Healey should use the current pause in Massachusetts’ data-center tax exemption to direct her administration to create a statewide data-center strategy that links new development to host-community protections and sustained investment in the Commonwealth’s highest-priority energy-justice neighborhoods.

First, every host community should have an environmental master plan showing how data-center development will affect land, electricity, water, transportation, air quality, emergency response, workforce and climate goals. The developer should finance that plan and its implementation over time as a required community benefit.

Second, Massachusetts should create a linked plan to transform its highest-priority Green Zones: neighborhoods carrying the greatest household energy burden, environmental damage, poor health outcomes and historic underinvestment.

The financing mechanism should be a Data Center Energy Justice Linkage Fund.

Under the proposal, the host municipality would keep 100% of its property taxes, PILOT payments, infrastructure reimbursements, mitigation payments and community benefits.

The host bears immediate effects — land use, traffic, water and sewer demands, emergency-response costs, noise, backup generators and eventual decommissioning — and should not have to surrender its compensation.

The host-community master plan would make those benefits strategic rather than episodic. Instead of negotiating a road improvement here, a workforce promise there and a short-term payment somewhere else, the community would establish a long-range plan for what development should accomplish.

That plan could include grid and water infrastructure, air and noise monitoring, renewable energy, resilience, local hiring, minority-business participation, environmental remediation, housing protection and decommissioning. Annual community-benefit payments could finance it over the facility’s operating life.

The developer would also pay a separate statewide assessment equal to 15% of the facility’s property-tax obligation before abatements, exemptions or negotiated reductions. It would not come out of the host community’s share. It would address burdens that do not stop at a municipal border.

Those burdens include increased electricity demand, pressure on transmission and generation resources, competition for clean power and the danger that infrastructure costs will be shifted to other ratepayers. A company should pay the full cost of serving its own facility.

But paying for its substation or water line does not repair inequities already embedded in our energy system.

The statewide fund should go first to neighborhoods with the highest household energy burdens. Energy burden is usually measured as the percentage of household income spent on electricity and heating. The proposed index would also examine energy costs as a share of disposable income. A $400 monthly energy bill does not have the same meaning for a wealthy household as it does for a family choosing among heat, food, medicine and rent.

In a December 2023 Boston Herald column, I argued that Massachusetts needed better targeting of environmental-justice money. The state’s environmental justice designation is based principally on income, minority population and English-language isolation. Those criteria identify communities that may face exclusion, but they do not adequately rank qualifying neighborhoods by cumulative environmental damage.

The Northeastern University team described in that column developed an Environmental Justice Impact Scoring system using public-health, demographic and emissions data. Its factors included significant gas leaks, gas-leak age, roadway carbon emissions, pollution proximity, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, life expectancy, existing environmental-justice criteria, energy burden and population.

That framework should be updated to identify Data Center Energy Justice Priority Areas, or Green Zones. Energy burden and energy insecurity — including arrearages, shutoff notices and disconnections — should receive the greatest weight. The index should also consider inefficient housing, repairs that prevent weatherization, extreme heat, outages, air pollution, asthma, proximity to energy infrastructure, historic redlining, tree canopy and access to earlier clean-energy programs.

Each highest-priority Green Zone should receive a funded transformation plan with measurable capital projects: weatherization, electrical upgrades, roof and moisture repairs, efficient heating and cooling, community solar, energy storage, tree canopy, cooling centers, resilience hubs, pollution monitoring and neighborhood-scale clean-energy infrastructure.

This is not an untested concept. Boston has used development linkage since the 1980s. Large commercial projects pay fees supporting affordable housing and job training across the city. Growth in Downtown and other high-development districts has helped finance housing in neighborhoods including Roxbury.

In this light, 15% is not radical. It is a reasonable starting point that should be confirmed through a nexus and economic-feasibility study. The study should calculate attributable statewide costs, evaluate what projects can reasonably pay and compare rates from 5% to 25%. A per-megawatt minimum should prevent an enormous energy user from making a small contribution merely because it is located in a low-tax municipality.

The Commonwealth should phase the assessment in — 10% in the first year, 12.5% in the second and 15% thereafter —and review it every five years. Payment should be a condition of receiving or retaining the state data-center tax exemption.

At least 60% of annual spending should go to communities in the highest tier of combined energy burden and environmental harm.

Data centers may become an important part of Massachusetts’ innovation economy. But the Commonwealth should not permit one facility at a time and hope the pieces add up to a strategy.

The host community should have a funded environmental master plan and keep everything negotiated for hosting the facility. The developer should make a separate contribution to the broader Commonwealth. And the highest-priority Green Zones should receive sustained investment capable of transforming homes, infrastructure and neighborhood conditions over time.

That is how growth becomes a tool of repair.

Ed Gaskin is Executive Director of Greater Grove Hall Main Streets and founder of Sunday Celebrations

title: Boston Police announce safety plan for Dominican Parade
text:
Boston Police officials announced safety precautions for the upcoming Dominican parade and festival this Sunday, informing people of “highly visible” police presence and rule enforcement in the wake recently publicized violent crime during summer holidays like the Puerto Rican Festival and Fourth of July.

“It’s a family fun event in which you come and enjoy yourself and have a good time,” said Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox. “But we encourage you also to make sure that you follow all the rules associated with large events and know what the expectations are.”

The Dominican Parade will march through Jamaica Plain and Roxbury, starting along Centre Street at 11 a.m. on Sunday. The parade lands in Franklin Park, where the the festival will feature live performances, vendors and food throughout the day.

BPD officials and organizers gathered at police headquarters in Roxbury on Thursday to discuss the safety preparations in place, including a large police presence, parking enforcement and more.

“There’ll be large crowds, and that being the case, people should know that there’s really no parking in the area,” said Cox. “So they can seek alternate forms of transportation or ways to get to the park. We highly encourage taking public transportation to the event, as parking will be very, very difficult to come by.”

Police will be enforcing parking rules in the residential area around Franklin Park, Cox said. A full list of parking and road closures, some going into effect Saturday, will be available at BPDnews.

Cox said there has been an uptick in police at the festival from a couple years ago, adding “we try to learn from every event that happens to less the likelihood of anything bad happening the next year.” In 2024, five people were shot during the Dominican Festival.

Police will be enforcing rules including no public drinking, no use of illegal drugs or marijuana, no weapons of any kind, no fireworks and no disruptive or disorderly behavior, Cox said. Car, scooter or other unauthorized vehicle meetups in the area are “highly discouraged,” the commissioner added.

Vehicles in the area with speakers above the legal limit will be “addressed, ticketed, and potentially seized if after ticketing you don’t comply with our instructions,” Cox said.

At the end of the evening, Cox noted, the park will close and people will be asked to leave immediately.

“And, as always, if you see something, say something,” Cox said. “There will be police officers all about the area. So, if you need police help or you have a concern, please contact one of the officers that will be there with you.”

Boston Parks Commissioner Diana Fernandez Bibeau said the festival will be taking lessons learned from recent events.

“We’re really excited to ensure that we have an incredibly wonderful, joyful event with community members,” Bibeau said. “And are here to work in partnership with the Boston Police Department, our park rangers, and our entire park staff to ensure that this event is a success.”

title: Dominican parade and festival bring out community pride, officials highlight safety preparations
text:
Dominican Bostonians came out with booming beats and joyful dancing for the 40th annual Dominican parade and festival, as city officials highlighted preparations to keep everyone safe at another highly attended summertime event.

“This is one of the most beautiful days of the year, every year,” said Mayor Michelle Wu as the spirited parade lined up to start in Jamaica Plain on Sunday morning. “We get to celebrate with our Dominican community, culture, heritage, multi-generational fun. And we start with a parade here in Jamaica Plain, proceed to Franklin Park where there will be a festival, concert.”

The 40th Dominican parade kicked off in Hyde Square in Jamaica Plain at 11 a.m. Sunday, winding through Roxbury to Franklin Park, where organizers hosted a festival through the evening.

Safety “has to be the first concern” anytime families are out, Wu said, highlighting the safety plans reviewed with law enforcement, organizers and community members ahead of the event.

City officials hosted a safety briefing ahead of the parade and festival on Thursday, highlighting a heightened and strategic police presence. The preparations follow a string of high profile violent incidents around celebrations including the Fourth of July and Puerto Rican Festival this summer, as well as an incident in which five people were shot around the Dominican parade and festival two years ago.

“It’s rare that the event itself is ever an issue,” said Wu. “It’s often following or sort of gatherings that are not sanctioned by the organizers. So everyone should just have fun, but remember that we’re in a community together. That where you are is also where someone else lives, and so we ask you to take care of that place just as you would your own home, and make sure that this is a reflection of all of the beauty of our community.”

Boston police reported no incidents at the event as of Sunday evening.

Local resident Bolivar was out holding Dominican and Puerto Rican flags along Centre Street to honor his heritage as the parade passed through Sunday – one of dozens of residents waving the country’s red, blue and white flag and decked out in Dominican pride. Bolivar, standing with his young relative Silas, said he’s come to the event every year.

“It’s been good out here,” said Silas. “There’s been a lot of people that we know and see around.”

The parade featured booming speakers fixed to cars with the Dominican flag across their hoods; colorful dancers twirling batons, hoops and pom poms to the beats; local organizations trumpeting support for the community and more.

Community pride was evident across parade, crowd and businesses that opened their doors along the route, with one float featuring a man with a giant flag jumping on top of a minivan.

“The Dominican community is huge here,” said Dominican Jamaica Plain resident David, standing with a flag draped around his shoulders with his family. “We’re happy to be here and be out today with everyone.”

title: Prosecutors: Good Samaritan thwarted domestic stabbing near Boston’s North Station
text:
Prosecutors said the man who allegedly stabbed his girlfriend repeatedly last week near North Station only stopped the attack because he was pulled off the victim by a Good Samaritan.

Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden’s office released more details on a double stabbing that occurred late last Thursday morning, where a man, Daudy Martinez, 51, is accused of stabbing his 44-year-old girlfriend multiple times before stabbing himself to the point where he sustained life-threatening injuries.

Prosecutors outlined the gory details of the broad daylight domestic violence that occurred in the area of 44 Causeway St., during a Boston Municipal Court arraignment that was held Monday via Zoom from Martinez’s hospital bed.

Martinez is facing one count of armed assault to murder, four counts of assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, one count of assault and battery on a family or household member (subsequent offense), and one count of assault and battery on a family or household member, according to the DA’s office.

Prosecutors said police responded to a report of a stabbing in progress last Thursday and found the female victim screaming in Spanish, with blood running down her face from a head wound and on the back of her leg.

The woman told police she had gotten into a fight with her boyfriend, who “pushed her to the ground and proceeded to stab her at least four times.” Police then observed that she had stab wounds on her forehead, left hand, chin and neck, and behind her left leg, prosecutors said.

“The police were able to recover some video from the scene where the defendant can be seen attacking the victim and stabbing her multiple times,” a prosecutor said. “The defendant doesn’t stop until an unidentified female comes up behind him and pulls him off the victim.”

The woman was taken to Massachusetts General Hospital for treatment.

When police responded to the scene, they were directed to go inside an unidentified restaurant, where Martinez was allegedly “wielding a knife.”

“When the police approached him, he began stabbing himself and slashing his own neck,” a prosecutor said of Martinez. “He dropped the knife when police threatened to deploy their tasers on him.”

Prosecutors said Martinez was taken to the hospital with life-threatening injuries. The victim is “recovering from her injuries,” the prosecution added.

Martinez was previously convicted for assault and battery on a family or household member out of West Roxbury Municipal Court, prosecutors said.

He was held without bail pending a dangerousness hearing set for Wednesday.

title: Police blotter: 124 forged credit cards, moped sweep and Roslindale home invasion
text:
Boston Police have arrested a 27-year-old man on charges of possessing 124 forged debit cards.

The department says it also seized an “undisclosed amount” of cash inside a vehicle that officers pulled over in Brighton on Tuesday, in the area of Harvard Avenue and Brainerd Road.

Officers pulled the vehicle over after it failed to stop at a red light, and they reportedly recognized the operator, Nicusor Lazar, who was wanted in connection with an ongoing ATM card fraud investigation.

“Officers approached the vehicle and the operator provided an Italian driver’s license and a bank card with the same name,” the BPD said in a release. “As officers were speaking with the operator, they observed a large stack of US currency bundled together in the center console as well as numerous credit/ debit cards in the cup holder.”

Investigators determined that the Italian driver’s license and bank card were fraudulent.

Lazar did not possess a valid license to operate a motor vehicle within the U.S.

Lazar was expected to be arraigned in Brighton District Court on charges of Money Laundering, two counts of Uttering, Identity Fraud, Forgery of an RMV Document, and Furnishing a False ID to Law Enforcement.

Home invasion

A West Roxbury judge has released a Roslindale teenager who allegedly vandalized property and unleashed other violence at her ex-boyfriend’s home.

Boston Municipal Judge Maureen Flaherty released Alyssah Harrison, 19, on personal recognizance and ordered her to stay away from the victims, witnesses and home.

Harrison, charged with home invasion, assault and battery, assault and battery with a dangerous weapon, and malicious destruction of property, is set to return to court for a pretrial hearing on Oct. 2.

The rampage unfolded on July 22 when Harrison allegedly broke the glass screen of her ex-boyfriend’s front door in Roslindale with an aluminum baseball bat, according to a report that the victim provided to BPD.

The victim alleged that Harrison entered his home, pushed his wife and then punched her in the face, threatening them both with the bat.

“Harrison then ran up the stairs into a bedroom on the second floor and began opening drawers and the closet, as if looking for something,” the Suffolk DA’s office said in a release. “The male victim left the home to contact property security, and the female victim followed Harrison upstairs, where she attempted to physically remove Harrison from the room, resulting in a fight.”

Harrison then allegedly fled the home.

“It’s not hard to imagine the fear these homeowners must have experienced when their peaceful day at home was suddenly turned chaotic and violent due by an armed intruder,” DA Kevin Hayden said in a statement. “Our victim witness advocates are trained in trauma and acquaintance violence scenarios and will provide all the support these victims require as the case moves forward.”

Moped sweep

A targeted enforcement operation in Dorchester and Roxbury seized 31 mopeds, with officers issuing summonses for 12 individuals.

Officers and detectives in Roxbury partnered with members of the BPD’s auto theft unit to crack down on the mopeds that reportedly violated auto laws in the areas of Blue Hill Avenue and Warren Street.

“The initiative was organized in response to ongoing public safety concerns regarding the use of these vehicles in the Dorchester and Roxbury neighborhoods,” the department said in a release.

“The Boston Police Department remains committed to improving traffic safety,” it added, “and will continue to conduct enforcement operations across the city.”

Incident Summary

The BPD responded to 311 incidents in the 24-hour period ending at 10 a.m. Wednesday, according to the department’s incident log. Those included one robbery, three aggravated assaults, one commercial burglary, one residential burglary, one larceny from a vehicle, two auto thefts, and 25 instances of miscellaneous larceny.

title: Gaskin: Boston must innovate homeownership boost
text:
Boston knows how to innovate.

We do it in life sciences, high tech, medicine, biotech, artificial intelligence, climate research, robotics, finance, and higher education.

But when it comes to homeownership, our imagination gets small.

For too many young people and working families, homeownership no longer feels like a life goal. It feels like a fantasy. Not because they lack ambition, but because the math has turned brutal.

Depending on the measure used, the typical Boston home is selling below but approaching $1 million. Redfin recently put Boston’s median sale price at about $852,000. Zillow put Boston’s average home value at about $786,000. Across Greater Boston, the median single-family home price has already crossed the $1 million mark.

So when people say buying a home in Boston costs “around a million dollars,” they are not far off. Once interest rates, closing costs, bidding wars, taxes, repairs, and moving costs are included, the barrier feels even higher.

The result is a city where working people can pay high rent for years but still struggle to buy.

Boston has useful tools. The First-Time Homebuyer Program provides down-payment assistance. ONE+Boston offers discounted fixed-rate mortgages, down-payment and closing-cost help, and no private mortgage insurance for eligible buyers.

If Boston wants to remain a city where working people can build wealth, not just pay rent, we need to lead in innovative home financing the same way.

Around the country, people are experimenting with paths from exclusion to ownership. Boston should study them, adapt them, improve them, and build its own versions.

Napoleon Wallace’s work offers one model. Through Partners in Equity, Wallace and his colleagues help Black, Brown, and women-owned businesses buy the commercial buildings where they operate. The larger insight is that many people can handle monthly payments but cannot overcome the upfront capital barrier. Patient, shared-equity capital can help close that gap.

That same logic applies to Boston homeownership. Many renters already pay $3,000 or $4,000 a month. They are not financially irresponsible. They are cash-constrained, blocked by down payments, closing costs, credit repair, and competition from wealthier buyers. Boston should help them convert some of that burden into equity.

John Wallace’s work in Pittsburgh offers another lesson. Through church-led “withintrification,” the goal is neighborhood improvement without neighborhood removal. Instead of waiting for outside investors to drive up prices, residents, churches, small businesses, and local institutions gain control of land, property, and development from within.

In Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan, Hyde Park, East Boston, and Roslindale, the question is not just how to build more housing. It is whether the people who held these neighborhoods together can still own a piece of their future.

Arlo Washington’s work in Little Rock, Arkansas, offers another lesson. Washington, featured in the Oscar-nominated documentary “The Barber of Little Rock,” built People Trust to respond to what he saw as a credit desert. His model grew out of a barber school and expanded into community lending, financial education, and capital access for people traditional banks often overlook.

Boston should ask: where are our credit deserts? A city serious about homeownership needs CDFIs, credit unions, neighborhood lenders, and trusted community institutions at the table.

Bernard Garrett’s story, dramatized in the 2020 film “The Banker,” offers a historical lesson. In the Jim Crow era, Garrett used banking and real estate strategy to get around racist barriers to property ownership. His methods came from a different time, but the lesson remains: access to banking power determines access to ownership.

The Dearfield Fund for Black Wealth offers a contemporary model. It provides down-payment assistance to first-time Black homebuyers. When the homeowner sells or refinances, the fund is repaid and receives a small share of appreciation, allowing the money to help the next family. This is recyclable capital, not charity.

Ben Slayton’s Legacy Home Loans offers another lesson: representation in mortgage lending matters. Who designs the product, explains the terms, understands the borrower, and is committed to closing the racial homeownership gap all matter.

None of these models should be copied blindly. Some need changes to fit Massachusetts law, Boston’s housing market, and consumer protection standards. But that is innovation: study what exists, test what works, reject what harms, and build something better.

Boston should now create a Homeownership Innovation Fund. Bring together the city, CDFIs, credit unions, local banks, hospitals, universities, unions, employers, churches, community development corporations, foundations, and responsible private capital.

The fund should test shared-appreciation down-payment assistance, patient-equity funds, community land trusts, employer-assisted homeownership, church-led development, and neighborhood lending. It should focus on residents close to ownership but blocked by front-end costs — families who can afford monthly payments but cannot assemble $80,000, $100,000, or more just to compete.

Any new model must have guardrails. Boston should not invite predatory rent-to-own schemes or speculative investor products under the banner of innovation. Programs must have plain-language terms, capped investor returns, independent counseling, public reporting, anti-displacement goals, and a clear path to full ownership.

Financing is not a substitute for housing supply. Boston still needs more housing, faster permitting, smarter zoning, more family-sized units, and protection against displacement. But supply alone will not close the ownership gap either. If new housing is built but only high-income buyers can purchase it, Boston will still lose the middle class and widen the racial wealth gap.

If we can lead the world in high tech and life sciences, we can lead the country in creating new paths to homeownership. The question is not whether every Bostonian will own a home. The question is whether Boston will remain a city where ordinary families still have a fair shot.

Right now, too many do not.

Ed Gaskin is Executive Director of Greater Grove Hall Main Streets and founder of Sunday Celebrations

title: Pressley speaks on murder at Boston home, defends $2B state contract awarded to husband’s firm
text:
Congresswoman Ayannna Pressley has opened up about the homicide at a Boston home owned by her husband and defended the $2 billion state contract his company was awarded.

Pressley answered the Herald’s questions on the hot-button issues of the homicide, which is under investigation, and the contract on the Springfield judicial center that is subject to a lawsuit following a campaign event for Sen. Ed Markey at Roxbury Community College.

Pressley defends husband on $2 billion state contract

Pressley jumped to the defense of her husband, Conan Harris, when asked by the Herald if the $2 billion state contract awarded by the Massachusetts Division of Capital Asset Management and Maintenance (DCAMM) to a partnership that includes his Boston-based firm, CoJo Partners, was fair and appropriate. Harris co-owns that partnership with Massachusetts Convention Center Authority interim Executive Director John Barros, who has since divested his interest in it.

The congresswoman distanced herself from her husband’s finances, adding that she is “proud” of Harris.

“I don’t have any unique insights on that. My husband and I met later in life. We got married later in our life. We keep our finances and everything completely separate,” Pressley said. “What I will say is I’ve always been proud of my husband and what he has done. He is the American dream. He’s overcome a great deal. He has made great contributions (to society).”

The contract awarded to the partnership that includes CoJo Partners, called Liberty Junction, is facing a lawsuit to stop it in its tracks by two of ten losing bidders: New England used car magnate Jeb Balise and real estate conglomerate Dinesh Patel, who filed the suit on July 9 under their respective business entities USPB JV, LLC and Tower Square, LLC.

The legal battle over the contract comes amid backlash that such a lucrative contract was awarded to a company owned by two men with notable political connections and possible conflicts of interest.

Attorney General Andrea Campbell’s office is defending DCAMM in the civil suit. The office filed a scathing response earlier this month, calling the suit “nothing more than a fever dream of imagined malfeasance.”

The Massachusetts Fiscal Alliance says Pressley’s stated ignorance of the Springfield contract only raises “more red flags” over the deal.

“If the contract was won on meritocracy, it shouldn’t be hard for the Congresswoman to explain why. Saying I don’t know over and over is doing nothing to help their family’s defense,” MassFiscal Executive Director Paul Craney told the Herald.

DCAMM announced the contract was awarded to Liberty Junction in a July 2 press release — the last business day before the Independence Day weekend. The agency maintains it awarded the contract based on the recommendation of the Massachusetts Trial Court in an effort to finish the project “as quickly as possible.”

Gov. Maura Healey has defended the contract, saying it is the “best deal for taxpayers,” something disputed by another losing bidder.

The two Republican candidates for governor are also slamming Pressley, with Brian Shortsleeve and Mike Minogue both blasting the appearance of corruption in Massachusetts politics – something they say Healey is complicit in.

“The first rule of Massachusetts politics: the insiders win. The proposed $2 BILLION Springfield courthouse is what happens when political insiders make the deals and hard-working taxpayers foot the bill,” said Mike Minogue. “As governor, I’ll fight to stop insider deals and bring transparency and accountability back to the Commonwealth. Massachusetts is working for some, but not all. This $2 billion deal is proof Maura Healey is failing us.”

“When Ayanna Presley was confronted on her husband’s shady business deals with Maura Healey even she distanced herself from the scandal,” added Shortsleeve. “Our state is plagued with corruption. We need an overhaul top to bottom and I look forward to delivering that.”

Ayanna Pressley’s net worth has exploded from an estimated $12,500 during her time as Boston City Councilor in 2018 to a whopping $8 million in 2024, according to Open Secrets. She receives a congressional salary of $174,000.

According to Pressley’s financial disclosure report, the congresswoman has listed several homes with estimated value between $1 million and $5 million.

Homicide at Boston home

Pressley also spoke on the July 18 murder committed at a rental property in Mattappan owned by Harris.

“A tragedy occurred at a rental property that my husband owns, not our home,” Pressley said.

“We are parents to an 18-year-old girl that we just dropped off at college two weeks ago. And my heart goes out to this family, because that little girl had dreams and they will never become a reality. That is what people should be focused on: grieving with that family and centering that young girl,” she continued.

The state Office of the Chief Medical Examiner ruled the death of 18-year old Yoseliani Ann Marte Ocasio a homicide late last month. Ocasio was discovered at Pressley and Harris’ 25 Malta Street address in Mattapan by responding officers with a single gunshot wound.

Police officials clarified that the property owners are not involved in the investigation.

“There is absolutely nothing that indicates any connection to the owners of the property,” Chief of Internal & External Communications Mariellen Burns told the Herald.

title: Election primer: A look at the key races in the 2026 September primary
text:
Massachusetts voters prepare to decide on several key races in the September 1 primary election.

From the Republican gubernatorial race and a clash for the U.S. Senate to key races for seats on Beacon Hill and the battles for District Attorney in Suffolk County and beyond, here’s what voters need to know.

Republican gubernatorial — Minogue vs. Shortsleeve

On the Republican ballot, Massachusetts voters will have the chance to decide who takes on Gov. Maura Healey in the general election in November: Mike Minogue or Brian Shortsleeve.

Minogue, a billionaire and first-time political candidate, brings a wealth of experience from the private sector who for nearly two decades led the medical technology company Abiomed, acquired by Johnson & Johnson in 2022.

Shortsleeve served as the chief administrator and later the acting general manager of the MBTA under former Gov. Charlie Baker. He calls himself a “turnaround specialist” in campaign materials from his experience improving this agency.

Both candidates served in the U.S. military. Shortsleeve served in the Marine Corps and Minogue as an Army Airborne Ranger and West Point graduate.

Minogue has hung his hat on the landslide victory he captured at the Massachusetts Republican Convention, taking home 70% of the vote from delegates. Shortsleeve made the ballot by a hair, just squeezing by the 15% delegate vote threshold.

Minogue has ignored requests from the Shortsleeve campaign to participate in primary debates and has focused on taking on Healey in the general election.

On the other hand, Shortsleeve has centered his campaign around attacking both Healey and Minogue, which has earned him some criticism from fellow Republicans.

The two candidates share many ideas about the commonwealth’s future, but the abortion issue may be what separates them most. Shortsleeve is pro-choice, while Minogue says he is pro-life.

The abortion issue has regained importance in deep-blue Massachusetts after Healey this month signed into law a controversial bill that removes all restrictions on abortions after 24 weeks gestation.

U.S. Senate — Markey vs. Moulton

The Democratic primary race between Sen. Ed Markey and Congressman Seth Moulton is less separated by political visions, but something else: age.

Moulton has centered his campaign around promoting himself as the “fresh face” Capitol Hill needs to replace the aging establishment — a group epitomized by Markey, who has served in Congress for 50 years. He was first elected to the U.S. House in 1976 — two years before Moulton was born.

Markey has countered this by highlighting the need for someone with his experience in Washington, while also pushing his record of fighting for liberal Democratic values during his lengthy tenure.

With few real political differences between the two, Markey and Moulton have resorted to mudslinging. They have exchanged accusations of insider trading and accepting campaign donations from corporate PACs. They’ve also railed against President Trump, with Markey and Moulton mentioning the president frequently during their three summertime debates.

Markey has remained the frontrunner in the race, according to polls, starting with a sizable 19-point lead over Moulton in polls taken back in November. Moulton had considerably closed that gap over the spring and summer months, but a recent UMass Amherst/WCVB poll gave Markey a massive 30-point advantage in August.

The primary winner will face Republican candidate John Deaton in the general election.

8th Congressional District — Lynch vs. Roath

Longtime Congressman Stephen Lynch is facing a primary challenge from Democratic candidate Patrick Roath.

Lynch was first elected in 2001, replacing the outgoing former Congressman Joe Moakley. He has held various House committee assignments during his tenure, currently serving as a ranking member of the House Oversight Committee.

Lynch’s campaign paints him as a proven, experienced, “common sense” candidate that will stand up to Republicans and President Trump. Like Sen. Markey, the 71-year old Lynch is fending off attacks from Roath on his age and his 25 year stay on Capitol Hill.

The younger Roath, 39, is promoting himself as a “voting rights advocate and attorney” who will serve as a younger, fresher face to “take on Trump’s authoritarian agenda and deliver bold solutions for working families.” Roath also boasts his resume, which includes serving as an aide to former Gov. Deval Patrick and former President Obama.

“I’m running against a member of Congress who’s been an elected official since I was five years old, Roath told CNN News Central last month. “Isn’t it time for the next generation to get someone new in there to do something a little different and that’s more tailored to what the times require?”

Lynch has countered these attacks with highlighting Roath’s Connecticut upbringing, as well as his political support from private equity groups and the pharmaceutical industry.

1st Congressional District — Neal vs. Whalen

Voters in western Massachusetts will face a similar situation in the 1st Congressional District: an aging Democratic incumbent trying to hold onto his seat from a younger, more progressive challenger.

Longtime Congressman Richard Neal is running to defend his seat against 39-year old high school teacher Jeromie Whalen.

Neal, who paints himself as a “lunch-bucket” Democrat, was first elected to Congress in 1989 after serving as Springfield Mayor for five years prior. Currently, the 77-year old Neal serves as a ranking member of the House Ways and Means Committee — which he chaired until 2023.

Whalen holds both a bachelor’s degree and Ph.D. from UMass Amherst, degrees he earned in 2011 and 2018, respectively. He has worked as a high school teacher and for the nonprofit local community media outlet.

In addition to going after Neal’s age and over 35 years in Congress, Whalen has zeroed in on Neal’s acceptance of campaign donations from corporate PACs. Whalen promotes himself as an “everyman” candidate who will provide a fresh start and more progressive perspective on Capitol Hill, particularly highlighting his support of Medicare For All against Neal’s opposition to it.

Neal is fending off attacks on his age and lengthy tenure by promoting the need for his vast wealth of political experience and representation of western Massachusetts. Otherwise, Neal has adopted the classic incumbent playbook by not mentioning Whalen’s name or responding to any attacks launched by him.

Neal and Whalen will participate in a televised debate next week on WWLP-TV.

State Senate: First Suffolk — Collins vs. Gayle

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu’s failed push to increase commercial tax rates has taken center stage in a state Senate race between incumbent Nick Collins and his challenger Latoya Gayle.

Collins, a South Boston Democrat, led the effort to kill Wu’s tax shift bill in the Senate two years ago. Wu in turn went on the offensive this year and campaigned fiercely against him by endorsing his primary opponent and lobbyist, Gayle.

The race has escalated a years-long public feud between Wu and Collins, with the two trading jabs over what Wu has characterized as Collins’ move to block Boston homeowners from seeing a tax break through her stalled legislation.

Wu’s bill, which Gayle supports, would have shifted more of the city’s property tax burden from homeowners to commercial property owners for several years.

Collins last month undercut Wu on the matter by tucking a property tax relief clause into the state’s economic development bill to blunt what he called “Boston’s unnecessary tax increase on homeowners.”

His alternative tax relief clause was passed unanimously by the state Senate, leading Wu to slam Collins for being “an obstacle, not a partner” on tax relief.

Gayle, a political newcomer, is vying to unseat Collins. He was first elected to public office in 2010, to the House of Representatives, and has held his First Suffolk Senate seat in 2018.

State Senate: Suffolk & Middlesex — Brownsberger vs. Lander

It’s the battle of Boston mayors in the race between political newcomer Daniel Lander and the state Senate’s President pro tempore William Brownsberger, as Wu’s influence beyond the city will be tested in the race.

Wu is backing Lander, a former senior aide in her administration, in his bid to unseat Brownsberger, who co-led the push to kill her signature tax shift bill in the state Senate in late 2024.

In a shot at Wu, former Mayor Marty Walsh has endorsed Brownsberger, who is also backed by Gov. Healey and Attorney General Andrea Campbell.

Lander, who supports Wu’s tax bill, has touted an endorsement from U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a mentor of Wu. He worked as a senior political advisor for Warren’s 2020 presidential campaign.

Lander has cast the race as trying to change the “broken” status quo of Beacon Hill, by trying to oust Brownsberger, whom he calls its “architect.”

Brownsberger is facing his first challenge since winning his Senate seat in a 2011 special election. He has touted his experience, and has been praised for his ability to work with other legislators “to get things done,” as Walsh put it.

Brownsberger, a Belmont Democrat, represents neighborhoods beyond the Hub. His Suffolk and Middlesex District seat includes Watertown, Belmont, as well as the Fenway and Allston-Brighton neighborhoods of Boston, and West Cambridge.

Suffolk District Attorney — Hayden vs. Rollins vs. Champion

A nasty Suffolk District Attorney’s race simmers in the long-standing vitriol between incumbent Kevin Hayden and his predecessor Rachael Rollins. A third candidate, Linda Champion, has sought to cast herself as a steady alternative.

Hayden and Rollins took swipes at each other over their past ethics lapses at a rowdy debate in Roxbury earlier this month.

Rollins resigned in disgrace from her post as the Massachusetts U.S. Attorney in May 2023 amid a federal ethics probe that found she abused her position by leaking confidential information that was damaging to Hayden and lying about it to federal investigators.

Two damning federal watchdog reports found that Rollins leaked confidential Department of Justice information during her time as U.S. Attorney in an effort to influence the Suffolk DA’s race in favor of her preferred successor and fellow progressive, ex-Boston City Councilor Ricardo Arroyo.

Hayden won the 2022 Democratic primary over Arroyo and ran unopposed in the general election that year. He is seeking a second, four-year term.

Rollins claimed during the debate that she resigned as U.S. attorney not because of the federal ethics probe, but because she was receiving death threats, calling herself a “crime victim.”

She called the findings of the federal probe “allegations” while pointing to a 2024 state ethics violation Hayden was hit with related to that same primary race with Arroyo, for which he paid a $5,000 fine.

Rollins has faced a different scandal this time around, amid her bid to reclaim her old job as Suffolk DA.

Suspicious signatures out of Chelsea were flagged on Rollins’ nomination papers, a matter Rollins said she is looking into and AG Campbell said should lead to her removal from the ballot, if “she fraudulently got on the ballot.”

Hayden has been slammed by the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, over his decision to charge a city cop with manslaughter following a fatal police shooting of a carjacking suspect. The BPPA has endorsed Champion, a prosecutor who ran unsuccessfully for Suffolk DA in 2018, the race Rollins won.

The DA has also been criticized by community and elected leaders for choosing not to release the related police body camera footage before the homicide trial.

Champion said during the debate that both of her opponents are unfit for office.

title: MBTA announces Orange, Green, Red line closures in September
text:
The MBTA announced a new slate of closures on the Green, Red and Orange lines and Commuter Rail, as well as more station closures and service changes, in September to accommodate a host of ongoing infrastructure projects.

“The MBTA is reminding riders that service outages such as these are a critical and necessary part of maintaining the infrastructure improvements that took place as part of the 2024 Track Improvement Program while also making further system upgrades and modernizing the MBTA’s infrastructure,” MBTA officials stated of the work.

Upcoming planned MBTA closures include: the Orange Line between Forest Hills and Back Bay from Sept. 10 to 14, and the Red Line between JFK/UMass and Ashmont from Sept. 19 to 20.

On the Green Line from Sept. 19 to 20 and Sept. 26 to Oct. 4, all branches will see closures: the B branch between Government Center and Babcock Street, C branch between Government Center and Kenmore, D branch between North Station and Kenmore, and E branch between Heath Street and North Station.

Commuter Rail service will be out on the Framingham/Worcester Line between Framingham and South Station from Sept. 19 to 20; Needham Line between Needham Heights and South Station from 11 p.m. on Sept. 18 to end of service Sept. 20; New Bedford/Fall River, Greenbush, and Kingston lines between South Station and Braintree Sept. 19 to 20.

Orange Line and Red Line closures

The Orange Line closure will accommodate the Ruggles Station Improvements Project to improve subway, Commuter Rail and bus service at “one of the most used stations in the network,” the MBTA said, with concrete repairs at platforms, along stair walls and the Ruggles Street Bridge.

The Red Line closure will likewise allow for bridge work at the Ashmont branch, including repairing columns on the Savin Hill Bridge and installing shielding at the JFK Bridge, T officials said.

Free, accessible shuttle buses will replace both lines along the closure, the MBTA said, reminding riders to “budget ample extra travel time.” Riders in need of accessibility accommodations can also request van service via station personnel or a station call box if they prefer.

T officials also noted Orange Line riders can consider Commuter Rail service as an alternative during the closure.

The Red Line will operate regular and increased frequency weekend service along the Braintree branch during the planned closure.

Green Line station and line closures

The Green Line closure will allow for “critical signal upgrades within the central Green Line tunnel,” T officials said, noting that the over 100 year old line’s signals updates will create safety and reliability improvements.

Free, accessible shuttle buses will run on portions of the B, C and D lines, while E line riders can use the 39 bus with additional buses running to add capacity. Riders can use Orange Line service between Back Bay and North Station, T officials said.

Additionally, on the Green Line Symphony station will remain closed through 2029, Brandon Hall on the C branch will be closed through Oct. 4 and C branch inbound trains will bypass Dean Road from Sept. 14 to Oct. 9.

Blue Line changes

The Blue Line will also see slight changes for one weekend from Sept. 26 to 27, allowing the “Maintenance of Way team” to perform switch work and spot tie replacements at and near the Wonderland stop, the MBTA said.

The trains will operate on a single track between Revere Beach and Wonderland during the weekend, meaning riders will need to board all trains at Wonderland on the outbound platform. Though service will operate between Bowdoin and Wonderland, every other train will terminate at either Wonderland or Orient Heights, the T said.

Commuter Rail closures

On the Framingham/Worcester Line, the closure will allow for Worcester Line track and signal improvements in Wellesley, the MBTA said, enabling potential future upgrades like all-day, 30-minute “Zonal express” bi-directional service to Worcester and local bi-directional service to Framingham.

Free, accessible shuttle buses will replace the service, with four different routes between Framingham and South Station but no stops at Wellesley Farms and Lansdowne. The line will be fare-free during the change.

The Needham Line closure, allowing for parts of the West Roxbury Parkway Bridge Replacement and South Station Signal and Track Improvements projects, will not have shuttle bus replacement. MBTA officials outlined bus service along the 35, 36, 37 and 59 routes and Orange Line service alternatives, reminding riders again to budget for extra time.

The New Bedford/Fall River, Greenbush, and Kingston lines closures will serve the bridge work along the Red Line’s Ashmont branch. Riders were encouraged to use Red Line subway service between South Station and Braintree (via Quincy Center) for Commuter Rail connections beyond Braintree or Quincy Center.

Of the outages, T officials noted the work “cannot be performed during the overnight hours when the MBTA does not operate, and would be extremely inefficient and costly if planned during single weekend outages.”

“Closing a section of the transit system for multiple days is the most efficient way to perform the MBTA’s routine maintenance, revitalization efforts, inspections, and upgrade work, and combines the efforts of multiple contractors and the MBTA workforce around the clock 24/7 to maximize productivity,” the MBTA said. “This work is necessary and continuous to maintain the reliable service riders count on.”

The T also recently announced a $140 million federal FRA investment for the Haverhill Double-Track Project, intended to have a “transformative impact” on Haverhill Commuter Rail Line and region. The project is projected to improve capacity and reliability for the Commuter Rail, Amtrak, and freight service on the line “while supporting the Commonwealth’s goal of advancing regional rail,” T officials said.

title: Rachael Rollins touts endorsements from ex-cons in bid for Suffolk DA
text:
Ethically challenged Rachael Rollins, who pledged she would never accept campaign cash or endorsements from police unions, has been rolling out a series of endorsements from ex-cons backing her bid for Suffolk District Attorney.

“After 52 years of incarceration, I know that Rachael’s integrity, fairness and commitment to justice are impeccable,” reads one endorsement posted last week by Paul Robinson.

Robinson was convicted alongside a co-defendant for two counts of first-degree murder and two counts of assault with intent to rob in 1969. In 2022, the Suffolk DA’s office agreed to reduce Robinson’s first-degree murder conviction to manslaughter, leading him to be released with his time deemed served.

Since the beginning of last week, Rollins has posted six endorsements from men who served time in jail, some of whom claim they were wrongfully convicted by the Suffolk DA’s office for the crimes they were incarcerated for.

Criminal defense attorney Rosemary Scappichio’s website states grand jury testimony showing Robinson’s co-defendant was the shooter in the incident was suppressed for more than 50 years.

Other ex-cons said Rollins, who resigned as Massachusetts U.S. Attorney in May 2023 amid a federal ethics probe that found she abused her position, advocated for their release from prison during her time as Suffolk DA.

Rollins is vying to reclaim her old job as Suffolk DA, which she was elected to in 2018 but left after she was appointed U.S. Attorney by former President Joe Biden. She is facing her successor, DA Kevin Hayden, and Linda Champion, a local prosecutor who worked in the Suffolk DA’s office.

Two damning 2023 federal watchdog reports found that Rollins leaked non-public Department of Justice information to the media during her time as U.S. Attorney in an effort to influence the 2022 Suffolk DA’s race in favor of her preferred successor, ex-Boston City Councilor Ricardo Arroyo.

“I endorse Rachael Rollins because I experienced firsthand her belief in accountability, rehabilitation, and second chances,” said convicted murder Thomas Koonce. “As Suffolk District Attorney, she considered the circumstances of my conviction and the decades I spent transforming my life while incarcerated.”

Koonce spent 30 years in prison for the 1987 murder of Mark Santos, and was released in 2022 after his sentence was commuted by former Gov. Charlie Baker following a vote by the Parole Board. At his commutation hearing, Koonce said he took “full responsibility” for taking Santos’ life.

Rollins “put her support in writing, advocating for my clemency before the Advisory Board of Pardons and urging the board to recommend that Gov. Charlie Baker grant my petition,” Koonce wrote. “At one of the most important moments of my life, she stood behind the person I had worked to become.”

At a time when her opponents have been touting the support of heavy-hitters in Boston — Mayor Michelle Wu for Hayden and the Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association, the city’s largest police union, for Champion — Rollins’ decision to play up endorsements from ex-cons has raised some eyebrows.

“Criminals love Rachael Rollins,” one person commented on an endorsement from Stephen Pina, who was convicted of first-degree murder for the 1993 fatal shooting of a man in Boston.

Pina was released from prison in 2022 after serving 28 years, but was not exonerated. He maintained that he was wrongfully convicted. A judge found that prosecutors and police withheld evidence in his case. The Suffolk DA’s office opted not to seek a retrial in the case against him earlier this month.

Hayden’s office sought to keep Pina’s conviction in place, but was ultimately forced to drop the case, saying in a court filing, “Given the current state of evidence, the Commonwealth has determined that it would be unable to sustain its burden of proof at trial,” per a Boston Globe report.

Other comments on Rollins’ endorsement posts ranged from, “Is this satire?” to “Next up: Monica Cannon Grant?!?” Others questioned if the ex-cons are “her base voting block?” saying, “Criminals for Rollins has a nice ring to it.”

Rollins, who drew controversy during her time as Suffolk DA for implementing a so-called “do-not-prosecute list” for low-level crimes like shoplifting, defended her decision to tout support from the formerly incarcerated while vying for a position that is responsible for prosecuting criminals.

“I am proud of my record in seeking justice for victims and helping the wrongfully accused,” Rollins said Tuesday in a statement to the Herald. “I have dedicated my life to public service. But like people, the government doesn’t always get it right.

“One in 3 people in the United States has a criminal history. In Massachusetts, your criminal history does not preclude you from voting, so long as you are not serving a sentence for a felony conviction.

“Exonerees are not ‘ex-cons.’ In fact, they have procedurally been brought back to innocence. If the former DA’s wrongfully convicted all of these people, the work of my administration corrected all of that unconstitutional, unethical and at times criminal conduct,” Rollins added.

Rollins, who signed a pledge in 2020 promising never to accept endorsements from police unions in the wake of George Floyd’s death at the hands of a white Minneapolis police officer, said she would rather have the support of the formerly incarcerated than “political elites.”

“Having the support of the people instead of political elites means the world to me,” Rollins said. “I am just as proud to have the support of these resilient people as I am to have the support of city councilors in Chelsea, community organizations, victims of domestic violence and survivors of homicide.”

After her federal ethics scandal, Rollins landed a job at Roxbury Community College, where she works as an executive director for a program focused on curriculum and services for the formerly incarcerated, particularly women of color.

She is paid an annual salary of $109,852 for the full-time position, and is also being paid $13,623 for a part-time faculty role at RCC, per state payroll records.

title: Gaskin: Mayor Wu, do the right thing with White Stadium
text:
The Massachusetts Supreme Judicial court has settled whether White Stadium can move forward. It has not settled whether the project will be successful, equitable, environmentally responsible, or meet the needs of Boston Public Schools students. Those questions are now the City’s responsibility. The “right thing” consists of two things: completing the studies necessary to make White Stadium successful and getting all stakeholders on board.

First, do the studies.

I understand why the administration may have hesitated to undertake some of these studies earlier: any negative finding could have become another argument for stopping the project. That is no longer the issue. White Stadium is going forward, so the studies can now identify potential problems early enough to develop solutions.

Start with transportation and parking. The City has proposed plans, but no objective, independent analysis has determined whether they are adequate. We need studies that establish the size and scope of the problems and whether the proposed plans are sufficient.

There should also be an environmental impact study, whether one is legally required or not. You cannot bring as many as 10,000 people into Franklin Park for professional soccer games up to 22 times a year and assume there will be no environmental impact.

An independent economic-impact study is equally important. I have argued that White Stadium should be viewed as an economic-development opportunity for Roxbury, Dorchester, Mattapan and Jamaica Plain. A professional sports franchise can create jobs, contracts, tourism spending and opportunities for nearby businesses, but Boston will not maximize that opportunity, in a way that is sensitive to community needs without intentional planning connecting the stadium to surrounding neighborhoods and businesses.

We should know how much economic activity White Stadium is expected to generate, where spectators will spend money, what jobs will be created, what those jobs will pay and how nearby businesses can capture some of that spending. The study should also examine property values, commercial rents, housing costs, gentrification and displacement. If public investment makes the neighborhoods around Franklin Park substantially more valuable, homeowners should benefit rather than be pressured to leave because of higher property taxes; renters should not face higher housing costs as the project’s principal economic effect on them; and local businesses should not help create a more attractive district only to be priced out. The analysis should also tell us who captures the value White Stadium creates — workers, neighborhood businesses, homeowners and residents, or primarily outside contractors and property owners.

There also needs to be a serious return-on-investment analysis. Typically, ROI would be part of the business case for building a stadium, but that was not done here. Boston is investing $135 million, and taxpayers should understand what they are receiving; even if the ROI is negative, people need to know because that reveals the true cost of the project.

We also need to settle whether the facility can adequately serve both professional soccer and Boston Public Schools. Critics have questioned whether professional soccer and high school football can effectively share the same field and whether soccer requirements will limit BPS use. What facilities do BPS students need, what will White Stadium provide, where are the conflicts or gaps, and what are the solutions?

The City should also explain how White Stadium fits into Mayor Wu’s broader vision for Roxbury and Dorchester, including the P3 parcel, Madison Park Technical Vocational High School, the proposed Blue Hill Avenue bus project, Franklin Park, Nubian Square, housing and transportation. How do these projects fit together, and what is the City’s larger vision for this part of Boston?

Second, bring in the stakeholders.

The Boston business community should be first to step forward. Where is the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce? A $325 million sports project should be of obvious interest to the region’s business community, as should the travel, tourism and hospitality opportunity. Thousands of people will be coming to professional soccer games, and hotels, restaurants, attractions and other businesses should have a stake in helping Boston maximize that opportunity.

The park and environmental stakeholders should also be at the table. The Emerald Necklace Conservancy, Franklin Park Defenders and others who raised concerns about Franklin Park should still be advocating for the park, helping determine what environmental indicators are monitored and what mitigation occurs if problems emerge. So should neighborhood organizations such as the Garrison Trotter Neighborhood Association and the Roxbury Neighborhood Council, which supports renovating White Stadium for BPS students while advocating for Franklin Park protection, equitable access, transparency and accountability.

If as many as 10,000 spectators are going to arrive at Franklin Park on game days, residents, transportation planners, MBTA officials, parking experts, Boston police and neighborhood businesses should work together before the first game to identify problems and test solutions. BPS parents and students, teachers, coaches, youth organizations, civic institutions, educational and financial institutions, and economic-development organizations should also have a role.

Their involvement should include implementation and monitoring. That monitoring should establish before-and-after measures for things such as noise, air quality, litter and park use so Boston can determine whether conditions improve, worsen or remain unchanged.

The measure of success should not be whether the stadium is completed or professional soccer succeeds. It should be whether Boston can demonstrate that the public investment improved the park, served BPS students, strengthened surrounding neighborhoods and created benefits shared across the city.

White Stadium needs to become an important Boston asset for the citizens of Boston — all citizens, not just some of them.

Ed Gaskin is Executive Director of Greater Grove Hall Main Streets and founder of Sunday Celebrations

title: Boston Police Blotter: Man shot dead in Roxbury
text:
A man was shot dead on Warren Street in Roxbury over the weekend, according to Boston Police.

Officers responded to a radio call for shots fired around 9:23 p.m. Saturday, the department said in a statement. When they arrived at the scene, officers said they found a man suffering from multiple gunshot wounds.

The man was taken to the hospital, where he was later pronounced dead, police said.

The department has not identified the victim.

BPD’s Homicide Unit is investigating the death and urging anyone with information to reach out at 617-343-4470 or anonymously via the CrimeStoppers Line.

Prior to Saturday’s shooting death, there have been 13 shooting victims killed in Boston since the start of 2026, according to preliminary crime statistics.

title: Massachusetts marks International Overdose Awareness Day with thousands of flags remembering those lost
text:
Over 20,000 purple flags waved on Boston Common Monday morning, marking each Massachusetts life lost to an overdose since 2013 as the state observed International Overdose Awareness Day.

“Today these purple flags not only ask something of us, they demand something of us, especially those of us in government,” Gov. Maura Healey said. “They ask us to not look away. They ask us to keep fighting, and they ask us to do everything that we can so that this field, as poignant as it is, doesn’t grow any larger.”

In honor of the day kicking off a campaign of awareness for National Recovery Month, families, loved ones and survivors joined city and state officials on the Common to mark each overdose death in Massachusetts from 2013 to 2025, creating a sea of solemn purple in the park.

The state reported about 978 opioid-related overdose deaths in 2025, a 27% decline from 2024 and the first time the fatality count dropped below 1,000 in over a decade.

Since the “devastating peak” record high of 2,364 of the overdose deaths in 2022, the state has seen yearly declines resulting in a nearly 60% drop by 2025.

Public Health Commissioner Robbie Goldstein cited the state’s treatment and recovery investments and harm reduction resource efforts, saying we’ve seen “firsthand progress is possible.”

“What we are doing together is building a Commonwealth where people struggling with substance use are met with dignity, compassion, treatment, recovery, support and the opportunity to live — to live well, to live safely and to live fully,” Goldstein said.

In Boston alone, nearly 3,000 residents have died of opioid-related overdoses since 2015. The city recorded 120 opioid overdose fatalities in 2025, according to Boston Public Health Commission data. The 2025 fatality count marked the lowest in a decade.

The city’s trend followed the state’s, with a 29% year-over-year drop in 2025 and 56% drop from the fatal overdose peak of 272 in 2023. Non-fatal overdose hospitalizations likewise fell in Boston, from a peak of over 1,600 in 2017 to 523 in 2024.

“As we honor the lives lost and reflect on the devastating impact of the opioid crisis on Boston’s families and communities, we must remember that every overdose death is preventable,” said BPHC Commissioner Bisola Ojikutu. “We are making progress, but our work is far from over. By putting naloxone within reach, expanding access to evidence-based treatment, and strengthening trusted community-based harm reduction services, we are saving lives.”

Ojikutu said the city would “continue working with urgency, compassion, and without stigma to ensure that every person living with substance use disorder has the opportunity to recover.”

BPHC runs a number of support initiatives, including inpatient treatment at the Mattapan Recovery Campus, AHOPE harm reduction services, PAATHS treatment services, Community Overdose Response Grants for neighborhood organizations providing support, and the Family Overdose Support Fund to support families hit by overdose financially.

The commission has also partnered to provide 16 naloxone, known by the brand name Narcan, kiosks and 7 public health vending machines in recent years. BPHC provides a Narcan Map showing locations to find the life-saving treatment throughout the city.

Boston will continue National Recovery Month events throughout the month, with Nubian Square Recovery Day on Sept. 17 at the Roxbury Boston Public Library branch and Recovery Month Celebration Day Sept. 24 at the Common’s Parkman Bandstand.

Crouching to put stakes in the ground Monday morning, families and loved ones added names and messages to or about those who’d died on the flags.

One Massachusetts state representative who’s son died of an overdose eight years ago remembered his struggle to find treatment covered by his insurance.

“He was thrown out of programs for drinking and smoking,” said Rep. Kate Donaghue. “Why do we punish people for showing the symptoms of the disease? What if we had more beds and better quality treatment? What if an overdose prevention center had been available? What if our prisons and jails were not our largest treatment providers?”

More information about Boston support services can be found at boston.gov/recovery. Massachusetts support services can be found at mass.gov/opioid-overdose-prevention.

State House News wire service reporting was used in this article.

title: Police Blotter: Fake Massachusetts ‘nurse’ sentenced to 3+ years for pumping clients full of fake Botox
text:
The owner of a Massachusetts spa who falsely advertised herself as a nurse and injected hundreds of clients thousands of times with fake Botox and knock-off fillers will be heading to prison.

U.S. District Court Judge Julia E. Kobick this week sentenced Rebecca Fadanelli, 40, of Stoughton, to three years and 10 months in federal prison. Fadanelli’s crimes netted her more than $1 million in payments from more than 900 afflicted clients of her Skin Beaute Med Spa, with locations in Randolph and South Easton.

“This was not a mistake or a one-time lapse in judgment. Rebecca Fadanelli built a business on deception and repeatedly put profit ahead of the health and safety of the people who trusted her,” U.S. Attorney Leah Foley said following the sentencing.

“Her victims were left with infections, facial paralysis, vision problems, scars and the lasting fear of not knowing what was injected into their bodies,” Foley continued. “As cosmetic injections and med spas continue to grow in popularity, this case underscores a serious and growing public health threat: counterfeit products and unlicensed providers can cause devastating harm.”

Fadanelli, arrested and charged in November 2024, pleaded guilty in April to four counts of importing merchandise contrary to law, two counts of selling or dispensing a counterfeit drug and two counts of selling or dispensing a counterfeit device. In addition to her prison term, she will have to pay $1,001,562 in restitution to her victims and be monitored by authorities for two years following her release.

Federal prosecutors, who asked for 57 months of prison, say Fadenelli administered knock-off Botox, Sculptra and Juvederm from China and Brazil at her business. From March 2021 to June 2024 she performed more than 2,700 botulinum toxin and dermal filler injections and 1,085 filler appointments.

“Many of these procedures resulted in adverse health effects, with multiple clients ending up in the hospital. When clients complained to her about these results, the defendant showed a callous disregard for their health, dismissing their concerns, claiming to be ‘a professional . . . doing everything right,’” prosecutors wrote in their sentencing memo.

“This lack of accountability, much less remorse, has persisted throughout the course of these proceedings. Rather than own up to her crimes, and notwithstanding her guilty plea, the defendant has continually sought to avoid the consequences of her actions, including by continuing to deny the essential facts underlying her offenses of conviction,” prosecutors continued.

The defense asked that Kobick sentence Fadanelli to 10 months in prison, arguing that “Ms. Fadanelli should not be defined by this case.”

They add that Fadanelli, who was born in Brazil and moved to the U.S. in 2004 at 17 years old, had a troubled upbringing and troubled relationships but has worked to improve life for herself and her children. They also say that while Fadanelli admits she was not licensed to perform these injections, she has been trained on the procedure and “her training would be sufficient

to inject cosmetic substances in Brazil.”

The defense sentencing memo shows a medley of educational certificates Fadanelli earned, amassing 168 of them, they claim, while at Wyatt Detention Facility since her arrest in 2024 and that she has a reentry plan and an offer of employment at a steak house in Stoughton. She also plans to seek employment as a Portuguese interpreter.

Incident Summary

BPD responded to 532 incidents in the 48-hour period ending at 10 a.m. Friday, according to the department’s incident log. Those included two robberies, 12 aggravated assaults, one residential burglary, four thefts from a vehicle, two vehicle thefts, and 34 instances of miscellaneous larceny.

title: Highlights of Boston’s fall classical music season
text:
We’ve got solo pianists on deck. We’ve got symphony orchestras on the calendar. We’ve even got an all-cello orchestra.

It’s going to be a busy and beautiful season for classical — and classical adjacent — music so let’s dive right in with a few highlights of the fall line-up.

Opening Night with the BSO, Andris Nelsons, and Yo-Yo Ma

Sept. 17, Symphony Hall

The Boston Symphony Orchestra opens its season — the final with Nelsons after the board decided against extending his tenure — with the maestro leading the group through Edward Elgar’s epic and devastating Cello Concerto. Riding the wave of Elgar’s emotions with Nelsons and the BSO will be the always awesome Yo-Yo Ma. The program also includes Brahms’s final symphony and Arturs Maskats’ Tango. bso.org

“William Tell”

Sept. 25 – Oct. 4, Emerson Colonial Theatre

You know the overture, now take in the full sweep of this story of the folk hero’s fight for freedom over a despot. The Boston Lyric Opera presents a big, bold new production (11 principals, 54 musicians, 40-person chorus) of Rossini’s final opera that is a wonderful first dive into French-language opera. If you’re already a fan, you’ll want to know that the great George Gagnidze will be in the title role. blo.org

“The Art of Living”

Oct. 2 & 4, Symphony Hall

The Handel and Haydn Society kicks off its season with Handel’s “L’Allegro, il Penseroso ed il Moderato.” That’s “The Cheerful, the Thoughtful, and the Moderate Man” to you and me. A pastoral ode based on the poetry of John Milton, the performance will be delivered with help from H+H favorite, soprano Joélle Harvey, and include contributions from Massachusetts poet laureate Regie Gibson. handelandhaydn.org

Weber/Beethoven/Brahms

Oct. 11, Symphony Hall

After nearly a half century of Benjamin Zander passionately leading the Boston Philharmonic Orchestra, the organization will shutter following this season. Help Zander and his ace musicians go out with a booming cheer.
