title: Boston Mayor Wu sticking with center bus lane for Blue Hill Avenue over opposition: ‘Not safe’
text:
Boston Mayor Michelle Wu’s latest positive spin on the city’s $163 million redesign of Blue Hill Avenue didn’t do much to tamp down the community’s fierce opposition to a center-running bus lane that highlights the project.

Wu held an invite-only virtual press conference last week, which the Herald was not invited to attend and included an updated look at the city’s contentious redesign for Blue Hill Avenue. The major 4-mile street serves as Boston’s central spine, stretching through Roxbury and Dorchester and ending at Mattapan Square.

While Wu released a statement to the rest of the media several days later that said “community input has been critical to shaping a design that responds to the needs of the neighborhoods along Blue Hill Avenue,” critics of the plan say that’s not the case and the project has been rammed through over neighborhood opposition.

“The MBTA and the city has told us that they’ve been involved in meaningful engagement with the community, but from day one, only one option has been presented: the center-running bus lane,” Boston City Councilor Miniard Culpepper, who represents Roxbury, said last Thursday in a video posted to Facebook.

Culpepper said the planned center-running bus lane would create a “dangerous” situation for passengers who have to walk across the street to get on board.

“This is the only option that we have been given,” Culpepper said. “Our community deserves to be at the table, and not on the table when it comes to decisions that affect our daily lives, our livelihoods and our neighborhoods in the long-term. No center-running bus lane down Blue Hill Avenue. It’s just not safe.”

Reggie Stewart, a community organizer and former Roxbury-centric Council staffer, said the mayor’s community engagement process has been about giving residents a chance to help design a project the city has already decided to implement, rather than giving the community a chance to “reject the central policy choice.”

“This entire Blue Hill Avenue ‘community engagement’ process is a masterclass in political gaslighting,” Stewart posted to Facebook last Friday. “The central question has never simply been about where to put parking spaces, trees, loading zones or bus stops.

“The central disagreement is over the center-running busway itself. Yet that decision remains off the table while residents are invited to debate the details around it,” Stewart said.

He added that the Wu administration’s way of rolling out the information in a series of back-to-back meetings in affected communities over the next two weeks, beginning on Thursday, is “racist governance.”

Stewart said the rollout is designed to “distract, disperse, exhaust and overwhelm a coalition that is beginning to coalesce over shared concerns” about projects impacting Black communities: Blue Hill Avenue, White Stadium and Parcel P3.

“This is racist governance,” Stewart said. “And we need to get comfortable applying that word to what the Michelle Wu administration is choosing to do.”

A social media flyer is being distributed ahead of Thursday’s community meeting at Mattapan Town Hall that states a standout is being organized at the location with attendees encouraged to say “Hell no to center bus lane on Blue Hill Avenue.”

The flyer states that the project will worsen congestion by removing vehicular traffic lanes to allow for the center-running bus lane, hurt local businesses, make the area dangerous for all road users, and waste public funds.

Wu’s office distributed a press release Saturday that defends the center-running bus lane as a way to improve travel times for the 40,000 daily bus riders who travel on Blue Hill Avenue and ease congestion for all road users.

Her office said the design also includes a two-way, sidewalk-level bike path on the west side of Blue Hill Avenue, separated from traffic, to provide neighborhood cyclist connections to Franklin Park.

The latest updated design revealed last week to the city’s preferred media outlets “incorporates significant changes based on community feedback” from what was originally presented by the city two years ago, per Wu’s office.

Those changes include maintaining at least two general travel lanes in the majority of the corridor, a net increase in parking, including local parking solutions for high-demand areas like Morning Star Baptist Church. It also reflects additional investment in Blue Hill Avenue’s streetscape, with six miles of new sidewalks, 200 new accessible curb ramps, new street lighting, and 200 new street trees.

“This is a true once-in-a-generation opportunity to deliver on improvements that will enhance the quality of life and economic opportunity for our residents, small businesses, and community,” Wu said in a statement.

Roughly $124 million in local, state and federal funds have been secured for the project. Construction is set to begin in 2028.

title: Man found guilty in 2021 Lowell killing
text:
LOWELL — Nearly five years after a burst of gunfire left 30‑year‑old Stedman Tucker dying in the passenger seat of a Toyota RAV4, the man accused of pulling the trigger has been convicted of first‑degree murder and ordered to spend the rest of his life in prison.

On Aug. 27, a Middlesex Superior Court jury found 27‑year‑old Wesley Lindor, of North Andover, guilty of killing Tucker in the parking lot of the Barker Avenue Apartments in October 2021.

On Aug. 31, Judge Kenneth Sallinger imposed the mandatory sentence of life without the possibility of parole to Lindor. Court documents show that in addition to the murder conviction, Lindor was also found guilty of carrying a firearm without a license and was sentenced to not less than four years and not more than five years.

“Wesley Lindor took something so very special to us,” Tucker’s sister, Jasmine Tucker, said in a statement provided to The Sun. “My parents only son, my sister and I only brother. We will never get him back.”

A Lowell Police incident report states at about 6:15 p.m. Oct. 22, 2021, Stedman Tucker, a Lowell resident, had been sitting inside the parked RAV4 when Lindor approached the vehicle, exchanged brief words with him, opened the passenger‑side door and shot him three times — once in the arm and twice in the chest — before driving away.

Stedman Tucker was rushed from the scene by emergency crews and later pronounced dead at Lowell General Hospital.

The Lowell Police and the State Police detectives interviewed witnesses, reviewed surveillance video and collected forensic evidence, including fingerprints on the car door handle, cell phone activity, spent shell casings and bullet fragments.

That evidence led them to identify Lindor as the suspect and ultimately to a Boston residence, where he was taken into custody weeks after the killing.

He was indicted in Middlesex Superior Court on the murder charge in December 2021.

Court documents previously showed Lindor had a criminal history and several pending cases in multiple courts at the time of his arrest, including firearm charges in the Roxbury Division of Boston Municipal Court, trespassing charges in the South Boston Division and larceny from a person charges in Attleboro District Court.

In her statement, Jasmine Tucker described Lindor as a coward for having shot her brother “without a word or a chance to even react,” adding that he had every opportunity to stop himself before ultimately pulling the trigger.

“May his family now feel his absence FOREVER,” Jasmine Tucker said. “Every birthday, holiday, and even day to day may they feel his absence. May Wesley be reminded of his cowardly actions on October 22, 2021, everyday as life on the outside will go on without him.

“Nobody won here,” she continued. “Two families have lost here just in a different way. I pray my family and I will be able to find the strength to live every day and carry Stedman in our hearts forever.”

Stedman Tucker’s obituary states he was a Lowell High School graduate and later went on to attend Middlesex Community College. He was a member of Calvary Baptist Church in Haverhill. He worked as a chef and had a love for music.

“Blessed with a musical gift since early childhood, Stedman played both the piano and drums with precision and ease,” the obituary states.

Attorneys Tracy Nina Firicano and Moya Reece Gibson defended Lindor at trial. They were not immediately available for comment about the case’s outcome.

The prosecution was handled by Middlesex Assistant District Attorneys Christopher Tarrant and Whitney Williams.

Follow Aaron Curtis on X @aselahcurtis, or on Bluesky @aaronscurtis.bsky.social.

title: Police blotter: Massachusetts restaurateur pleads guilty to paying employees under table
text:
A Massachusetts restaurateur has pleaded guilty to federal charges of paying employees in cash while failing to withhold and pay more than $500,000 in employment taxes.

Marios Michalakis, 44, of Westwood, faces up to five years in prison after he pleaded guilty in federal court in Boston on Tuesday to paying employees in cash “under the table” and failing to pay over $580,000 in taxes owed to the IRS and the state Department of Revenue.

Michalakis ran the scheme at Amelia’s, which he owned and operated in Stoughton, and Sofia Italian Steakhouse, in West Roxbury, from at least January 2016 through December 2022, according to Massachusetts US Attorney Leah Foley’s office.

The restaurateur failed to withhold income taxes, Social Security taxes and Medicare taxes from employee wages.

Michalakis pleaded guilty to six counts of failing to collect, report and pay over federal employment taxes.

His sentencing is scheduled for Dec. 8, when he could face up to five years in prison, three years of supervised release and a fine of $250,000 or twice the gross gain or loss, whichever is greater, together with restitution.

Fraud

A Dominican illegal immigrant has been sentenced to a year in prison for receiving over $300,000 in federally funded benefits.

Juan Felipe Chalas, 58, reportedly used the name, birthdate and Social Security number of a United States citizen to apply for and receive Massachusetts driver’s licenses, U.S. passports and other benefits.

In total, he defrauded over $25,000 in Social Security disability benefits, more than $12,000 in SNAP benefits and over $266,000 in MassHealth benefits, according to Massachusetts US Attorney Leah Foley’s office.

Judge Leo T. Sorokin sentenced Chalas to one year and one day in federal prison, to be followed by two years of supervised release. Chalas was also ordered to pay restitution of $304,932 and is subject to deportation upon completion of the imposed sentence.

More fraud

A Dominican national living illegally in Dorchester has pleaded guilty to using a stolen identity of a U.S. citizen to obtain over $80,000 in MassHealth benefits.

Manuel Antonio Baez, 52, allegedly used the stolen identity, including the citizen’s Social Security number, when he represented himself as a U.S citizen on an application for healthcare benefits. He also submitted an affidavit falsely alleging the same.

Baez ultimately obtained over $80,000 in MassHealth benefits using the stolen identity. The defendant also committed drug offenses in the name of the U.S. citizen, including a 2018 conviction for trafficking heroin and a 2007 conviction for possession with intent to distribute a Class B substance.

Baez was arrested and charged this past May with one count of falsely representing a Social Security number, one count of making false statements relating to health care matters and one count of aggravated identity theft.

He has been held since his arrest.

title: Gaskin: Racial wealth gap won’t close by itself
text:
Eleven years ago, the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston published one of the most startling economic statistics associated with this city. In The Color of Wealth in Boston, the median net worth of U.S.-born Black households in Greater Boston was $8. For white households, it was $247,500.

This August, the Boston Fed gave us another warning. Its 2025 Massachusetts Economic Conditions and Household Opportunity Survey estimated median family net wealth at $549,200 for white families, $7,800 for Black families and $1,200 for Hispanic families. The two studies cover different populations and cannot be directly compared, but no one can conclude from those figures that the underlying problem has been solved.

What may be most disturbing is that the report received news coverage and responses from economic-justice organizations, but nothing resembling the sustained civic alarm these figures deserve. No public five- or ten-year target. No annual racial-wealth scorecard. No institution or leader publicly responsible for results. We risk treating one of Massachusetts’ largest economic disparities as background noise.

Some in Black Boston remember Councilor Chuck Turner, Sen. Dianne Wilkerson and State Rep. Mel King. Turner helped drive Boston’s resident-jobs policy. Wilkerson pressed institutions on minority banking, businesses and access to opportunity. King made community control and economic development central to his work.

They could get in the faces of decision-makers and make clear that exclusion carried a political price. That pressure sometimes produced results, but it did not permanently change procurement systems, lending practices, development networks or institutional incentives. Decisions changed faster than systems did. That is one reason a much smaller group is refighting battles that should have been settled decades ago.

Massachusetts and Boston have enhanced supplier-diversity programs, homeownership initiatives, entrepreneurship programs and commitments from banks, foundations and universities. But programs are not the same as a comprehensive strategy with numerical goals, timetables, assigned responsibility and public accountability.

Greg King of TSK Energy Solutions has put his finger on part of the problem. Executive Order 599 directs state agencies to promote supplier diversity, but King argues that participation means little unless it changes the competitive structure.

Supplier diversity is not uniformly scored in every procurement. Winning bidders’ diversity promises are not always converted into enforceable contract obligations. The public cannot consistently compare promises with what certified firms were actually paid, nor does the system consistently measure whether diverse subcontractors become prime contractors or participating firms grow.

The Seaport provides the clearest Boston example. By 2017, more than $18 billion in public investment had helped transform the district. At the time, Black developer and restaurateur Darryl Settles said: “I don’t know one person of color that has made any money from the development of the Seaport. Not one.”

Then Massport changed the rules. Diversity became 25% of the evaluation criteria for the project that became the Omni Boston Hotel. The winning team included Black co-developer Richard Taylor, minority-owned firms and $7 million in equity from minority investors.

The Omni does not disprove Settles’ warning. It helps prove his point. The market did not suddenly discover Black developers and investors. The rules changed, and the outcome changed.

That lesson matters because another extraordinary wave of investment is underway. White Stadium represents more than $325 million in public and private construction. Madison Park Technical Vocational High School is estimated at roughly $680 million to $720 million. The Blue Hill Avenue center-running bus lane project is $163 million. Franklin Park has $28 million in dedicated investment. Nubian Square projects include approximately $160.7 million at 135 Dudley St., $20.4 million at 40-50 Warren St. and $10.8 million at 75-81 Dudley St. That brings the pipeline to more than $1.388 billion at the low end and more than $1.428 billion at the high end, before other housing and infrastructure projects are counted.

The World Cup and Tall Ships brought crowds, spending and headlines about an economic boom. Preliminary city data estimated roughly $83 million in Boston spending during the second half of June, while bars, restaurants, hotels and short-term rentals reported substantial gains.

But here is the racial-wealth question: How much went to Black-owned businesses?

Before the World Cup, African immigrant business owners reported difficulty obtaining grants and securing vendor opportunities. The city’s subsequent survey showed many hospitality businesses gaining customers and revenue, but the publicly reported results did not tell us how Black-owned businesses performed.

Tall Ships did better in one important respect. Boston Harbor Bites brought together more than 40 local vendors, with organizers reporting that 65% were minority- or women-owned. That is the kind of intentional intervention we should learn from.

Economic impact is not the same thing as wealth creation.

The question for this nearly $1.4 billion pipeline of neighborhood development should extend beyond how many Black vendors receive contracts. How many subcontractors become prime contractors? How many firms gain bonding capacity and working capital? How many entrepreneurs acquire equity? How many businesses buy the real estate they occupy?

We do not need another decade of studies telling us the same thing. Mayor Michelle Wu, Gov. Maura Healey and the region’s business, philanthropic, banking, university, hospital and Black business leadership should establish a measurable racial wealth strategy. Set targets for homeownership, business growth, capital, contracting and asset ownership. Publish an annual scorecard. Assign responsibility for results.

Boston will continue creating enormous wealth. The question is whether we will keep counting how much money moves through the economy — or finally measure who gets to build the wealth, own it and keep it.

Ed Gaskin is Executive Director of Greater Grove Hall Main Streets and founder of Sunday Celebrations

title: Boston announces 1,600 ‘learn-and-earn’ school year jobs for high schoolers
text:
Boston high school students can apply for over 1,600 school year jobs through the city’s new public-private partnership program – as the city continues seeks additional partnerships to reach their goal of 2,000 “learn-and-earn” jobs available for teens.

“Today, I’m proud that we are now at more than 1,600 jobs for the upcoming school year, almost where we were last year, more than 80% of our goal,” Mayor Michelle Wu announced Monday morning. “And we are not going to stop until we meet and surpass that goal. But today, we are launching 1,607 jobs across the employers who are in our coalition for every working student to have access to an ecosystem of professional mentorship, leadership training, and wraparound job supports.”

In June, city officials announced an expansion and redesign of their sponsored school-year job opportunities for students ages 14 to 18, branching out to invite private sector and other partners to invest as budget constraints hit the city.

Building on the SuccessLink program, which connected over 1,700 students with school year jobs in the 2025-26 year, the city intended to provide 2,000 job opportunities in the coming year through the new partnership to reach roughly 10% of all BPS high schoolers.

On Sept. 30, students will be able to find and apply for the learn-and-earn jobs at boston.gov/futurebos, Wu announced at New Mission High School in Hyde Park Monday.

Current employer partners include the YMCA of Greater Boston, Boys and Girls Clubs of Boston, Artists for Humanity, Boston Private Industry Council, the Greater Boston Chamber of Commerce Foundation, the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston, Suffolk Construction, State Street, Eastern Bank, Citizens Bank, Bank of America, John Hancock, Dana Farber, P&G Gillette, Mass General Brigham, Liberty Mutual, Roxbury Community College, Emmanuel College, Boston Children’s Hospital, and Beth Israel Leahy Health, Wu listed.

The program currently includes 400 publicly-funded Boston City Youth Corps jobs, 340 privately-funded positions with partner organizations and 663 direct employer hires.

“If you are an employer who is still yet to join us and eager to get started, we still need your help,” Wu urged. “We need you to help us close the gap to the rest of that goal and beyond.”

The city is also reviving the Redshirts youth program, building on the old program that paid students to clean and beautify their neighborhoods. The renewed program will employ 400 young people through the Boston City Youth Corps, said City Councilor Gabriela Coletta Zapata, who sponsored the return.

“What I love about this new iteration of the program, young people will still help beautify their community, but they will have the voice in identifying what their neighborhoods need, and importantly, their jobs will connect them to actual career pathways,” said Coletta Zapata, listing examples of positions in IT at Boston Public Library; urban forestry, climate resilience, or park stewardship through the Parks Department; healthcare experience at the BCYF lifeguard program; and facilities management, business, or property management at Boston Housing Authority.

The beautification component will be youth-led, Coletta Zapata said, aiming to instill students’ “ownership” of their neighborhoods.

“When a young person can walk past a park, a library, a community center, or a neighborhood space and say, ‘I helped make that better,’ we are cultivating the next generation of people who will care for and lead the city, and hopefully future city employees,” the councilor added.

Wu said the administration has taken a “big swing” on the summer job program, tripling funding for summer youth jobs and raising overall funding for youth jobs from $11 million in fiscal year 2022 to $25 million in fiscal year 2025. In the last summer, nearly 11,000 Boston students held program summer jobs, including 6,000 funded by the city.

While the city was able to help fund the school-year jobs with “expanded budgets and federal support,” the mayor said, “this year, national fiscal pressures required us to be really creative.” The new “stronger, more sustainable ecosystem” brings in private sector, nonprofit and institution employer to provide opportunities, she added.

“It is so important that they’re getting those experiences and those impressions, getting mentors, learning tangible skills, and getting paid at the same time,” BPS Superintendent Mary Skipper said. … “We are going to have 2,000 students get these school year jobs. That is something that doesn’t happen in other cities, but it’s happening here in Boston.”

title: Battenfeld: Mike Minogue shifts strategy to focus on Healey failures
text:
Mike Minogue is shifting the focus of his campaign to Maura Healey and her scandals and failures — not himself — as he seeks to make the gubernatorial race competitive.

While Minogue’s early ads are heavy on the GOP nominee’s background and personality, the new ads barely mention the biotech CEO — instead painting incumbent Democrat Healey in a harsh light.

“Are you better off than you were four years ago?” the ad says, repeating a line made famous by Ronald Reagan’s campaign against Jimmy Carter.

The ad goes on to blast “insiders” benefitting from the Healey administration and shows headlines from a litany of scandals and missteps.

Minogue’s ads and campaign web site deliberately fail to mention he’s a Republican — instead calling him a “new kind of governor.”

It’s an effective ad which counters the feel-good spots and anti-Trump ads that Healey is running.

The shift to focusing on Healey may be deliberate and also necessary because Minogue’s business record has a major blemish.

His Danvers-based company, Abiomed, was forced to pay a $3.1 million fine by the U.S. Attorney’s office to resolve kickback allegations that came from a company whistleblower that it paid for “lavish” meals for physicians to induce them to use Abiomed’s heart pumps.

The alcohol-fueled meals came at some of the nation’s most expensive restaurants like Spago in Beverly Hills and Eleven Madison Park in New York City.

“Health care companies seeking to boost profits by wining and dining physicians must be held accountable,” said Special Agent in Charge Phillip Coyne, with the Inspector General of the Department of Health and Human Services.

The company’s sales representatives allegedly padded the number of attendees at the meals and used fake names like “Mike Anesthesia.”

At the time, Abiomed said in a statement that they were “putting this matter behind us to focus on our heart recovery mission…”

The allegations have not yet become an issue in the campaign but expect them to become a major part of Healey’s arsenal as she seeks to dent Minogue’s reputation.

Healey, in contrast, wasted hundreds of millions in taxpayer funds in benefits fraud and to pay for meals and lodging for illegal migrants.

A super PAC backing Minogue is also hitting Healey now so she’s getting a double-barreled attack focusing on her record as governor for four years.

“After four failed years of one-party control, Healey refuses to take accountability or take any blame. That’s why it’s time to fire Maura Healey,” the ad says.

Minogue is facing a double digit deficit in the polls and needs a major boost with unenrolled voters and disaffected Democrats in order to close the gap.

His ads seemed to be focused on that target group, because Republican voters now make up less than 8% of the electorate.

title: Tuskegee Airman legend Woody Woodhouse honored as new Hanscom Charitable Foundation emeritus chair
text:
At 99 years old, living legend and former Tuskegee Airman Brigadier General Enoch “Woody” Woodhouse II added a new title to his lengthy resume – being honored as the emeritus chair of a local credit union charity supporting veterans and military members.

“Here today for the first time, I am speechless at being honored by so many good Massachusetts people, so many friends,” Woodhouse said to a full State House hall, earning countless laughs and a standing ovation from the crowd with his trademark humor and stories. “I’m overwhelmed.”

Woodhouse gathered with other veterans, local officials, gold star families and more in the State House’s Nurses Hall on Wednesday morning to be recognized for the new position as Emeritus Chair of the Hanscom FCU Charitable Foundation.

The Littleton-based credit union charity aims to “empower financial readiness of military and veteran communities to support their overall wellness,” Hanscom states.

Numerous speakers heralded Woodhouse’s storied life of service, noting his exceptional impact on the military community, state and nation.

A Roxbury native, Woodhouse enlisted at 17 years old and served as a member of the Tuskegee Airmen or 332nd Fighter Group, deployed during World War II as the first Black aviator group. He went on to a wide-ranging career, studying at Yale Law School and Boston University, teaching physics and chemistry at Roxbury Memorial High School, working as a State Department courier, serving as assistant corporation counsel for the city of Boston, and working in private legal practice, before going on to speak to and inspire countless others well through his retirement.

Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll delivered a governor’s citation for Woodhouse on Wednesday, noting wryly it is far from the local legend’s first state commendation.

“You see what I mean when I say he is a true force of nature,” said Driscoll, after reading Woodhouse’s accomplishments. “The Commonwealth thanks you for your honorable service and lasting impact. We congratulate you on this latest appointment of your amazing career.”

Hanscom Federal Credit Union President and CEO Peter Rice spoke about the charity’s mission, citing housing, small business financing, fraud and more issue hitting the veteran and military communities hard.

“We want to help bring the entire community together: public leaders, nonprofits, housing partners, together with a financial institution,” said Rice. … “That brings me to Brigadier Gen. Enoch ‘Woody’ Woodhouse, who has the widest leadership across matters at this particular moment.”

At 73 years old, Rice said, Woodhouse’s 99 years makes the credit union’s history the “youngsters in the relationship,” saying his fight for and belief in his country was “in our own smaller way, the same spirit that created Hanscom.”

When Rice asked him to take the position, Woodhouse said in his address, he told him, “Great, it’s an honor.” When Rice added it was unpaid, Woodhouse recalled with a characteristic wide grin that he said, “What else is new?”

Woodhouse shared stories and advice with the crowd, from lessons of trusting your instinct to do the right thing to the importance of just keeping going.

“Woody was fought all of the fights,” said Rice. “He served a country that didn’t always extend him the same rights, dignity, and opportunities enjoyed by others. He experienced discrimination firsthand, and he still served. He still made positive change. He still believed.”

title: Police Blotter: Ex-Massachusetts police chief pleads guilty to misusing his office
text:
Former Methuen Police Chief Joseph Solomon, who a city-ordered report said ran his department like “a ‘Don’ of an organized crime family,” has pleaded guilty to 17 state charges related to the misuse of his position of authority.

“Massachusetts communities rely on their police chiefs to make the best decisions for the safety and security of residents. Former Chief Solomon broke that trust by misusing his authority to elevate unqualified officers, putting residents’ wellbeing at risk,” said state Attorney General Andrea Campbell, whose office prosecuted the case.

Solomon was indicted in September 2023 on seven counts of obtaining unwarranted privileges in violation of the civil service laws, six counts of civil service law violations, two counts of perjury by written affidavit, and single counts of uttering a forged document and procurement fraud.

Solomon pleaded guilty to those charges on Friday. He was sentenced to 2.5 years in the House of Correction, with 30 days to serve and the balance suspended for three years. He will lose his city pension, license to carry a firearm, and a private investigator’s license.

Central to the case against Solomon was his promotion of part-time officers — notably Sean Fountain — into full-time officers in a way that circumvented civil service laws. He and Fountain claimed, for instance, that the latter was a graduate of a police academy when he was not.

A report commissioned by the City of Methuen and issued in late May 2023 by the STIRM Group stated “the current investigation does not paint Solomon in a positive light. His leadership style is that of a ‘Don’ of an organized crime family that leads through humiliation, fear, intimidation, and retaliation.”

Even before that, however, the case against Solomon was made in part in the 153-page “Leadership Failures in Methuen Police Contracts” report issued by the state Office of the Inspector General in December 2020.

“I want to acknowledge the hard work and diligence of the prosecution teams from the Attorney General’s Office and the Essex District Attorney’s Office for bringing this case to resolution,” Inspector General Jeffrey Shapiro wrote in a statement following the guilty pleas. “So-called public servants who enrich themselves at the expense of the people they swear an oath to serve must be held to account, no matter how long it takes.”

title: Police Blotter: Feds seek more info on ex-Malden school employee accused of exploiting Michigan teens
text:
Federal investigators are seeking more information about a now-former Malden school employee charged with sexually exploiting two minor Michigan girls into submission to him.

Federal investigators arrested Anthony Lamont Fowlkes, 40, at his home in Malden last week on multiple charges related to the sexual exploitation of a child, child pornography, and interstate threats with intent to extort.

“Fowlkes has held positions of trust and HSI wants to identify any other potential victims/survivors,” U.S. Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) New England wrote on Saturday, adding specifically that he had been employed in the Linden STEAM Academy in Malden.

They ask that anyone who believes their child was affected by Fowlkes to contact the agency at HSI-Fowlkes-Investigation@hsi.dhs.gov.

Fowlkes’ two alleged minor victims were friends who lived in Waterford, Michigan, a northern suburb of Detroit.

A Detroit-based HSI agent, in an affidavit supporting the charges, described Fowlkes as soliciting nude images of the girls and exploiting his possession of these images to force the girls into submission to him as their master. The affidavit asserts that at all times Fowlkes knew the girls were underage.

“Idky (I don’t know why) I had to ask. You know you’re supposed to send them,” Fowlkes allegedly texted the first of the two 16-year-old girls on July 30 when she didn’t send him nudes fast enough in the morning.

This first victim, according to the affidavit, would in the same conversation introduce Fowlkes to a friend.

“She ready to be claimed like I have over you?” Fowlkes asked, and he was assured that the second girl was.

But it wasn’t to be, according to the affidavit. She broke contact with him and blocked him but, through the first girl, Fowlkes threatened to post the nude images she had shared with him online if she didn’t get back in touch. title: Boston announces UMass urban public health internship partnership
text:
Boston city officials announced a new partnership with UMass Boston to provide Public Health Commission internships for college students, who will then teach high school students through the program.

“This very special partnership between the Boston Public Health Commission and the UMass Boston Urban Public Health major gives us the skills and the opportunity to teach,” said UMass student Gabriela Gonzalez at the announcement event Monday. “Through this senior capstone, we will work directly with public health professionals learning to teach sexual health education and relational health in a way that is medically accurate, equitable and comprehensive. These skills are of great value to us as we grow as advocates and future public health scientists.”

Through the Boston Public Health Commission and UMass Boston partnership, college seniors in the first class of the three-year-old degree program will receive training with the city commission in the fall semester before moving on to teach at Boston high schools in the spring semester.

The new program builds on the BPHC SPHERE, or “Strengthening Public Health-Academic Partnerships in Education, Research, and Equity,” program that aims to “unite public health leadership and academia.”

The SPHERE program has formed a Boston Area Health Education Center in partnership with the UMass Medical School to grow the workforce and the Health Resource Center program to promote adolescent health, as well as an upcoming “AI Insight to Impact Innovation” project with the National Coalition for Health AI.

“This is actually a first of its kind initiative,” said BPHC Commissioner Bisola Ojikutu. “I’ve asked around, and I haven’t seen this in any other city where the bulk, almost all of our research institutions throughout Boston, even into greater Boston, are actually joining forces. It’s more than 30 institutions, from community colleges, to universities, to research centers, to academic medical centers, all working towards specific goals.”

Ojikutu called this a “pivotal moment for public health across the country,” citing federal funding cuts, persistent challenges with recruitment and retention, pipeline challenges in academic institutions, and “increasingly complex threats from infectious diseases to substance use disorders to mental health needs and longstanding, persistent, pervasive health inequities.”

The UMass Boston students participating in the BPHC year-long internships were selected by the commission and are currently receiving training in “adolescent health, health education, facilitation, community engagement, and public health practice” in the fall semester.

For the spring, the students will teach health education with BPHC supervision at participating high schools, including Roxbury Prep, Boston Prep, and Academy of the Pacific Rim.

The UMass Boston Urban Public Health department launched in 2022 and offers bachelor’s in environmental health, biostatistics, health care systems, urbanization and more, currently serving 65 students and expanding to over 100 in the fall semester.

“By bringing together UMass Boston, Boston Public Health Commission, and our Boston schools, we are giving our young people the chance to connect with public health leaders, gain meaningful hands-on experience and share trusted information with their peers and communities,” said Mayor Michelle Wu. “We are excited to build on this partnership and create a healthier, more connected Boston for years to come.”

The officers arrived in the area of 76 Weaver Way — which like all streets mentioned in this report are part of the same housing development — and found “a large group of individuals congregating near numerous illegally parked vehicles … all appeared to be teenagers, and they were drinking in public, smoking marijuana, and even urinating in public.”

When the cops exited their patrol car, five people hurried from the group and the officers pursued them. The police report goes in-depth on the trials of two police officers trying to keep up with five allegedly high and drunk teens and young adults.

The physicality begins when some of the group start to use their bodies to block the path to Jahmere Antenor, who police say had a gun — a black Polymer 80 Glock with laser attachment and extended magazine without a serial number — in his waistband. An officer “had to physically toss (the interlopers) out of the way,” according to the report.

The two initial cops continue to struggle with the group trying to block the arrest when, finally, backup arrives and the two additional officers “were able to safely tackle Antenor to the ground.” This, the report alleges, riled up the crowd who began “screaming and verbally abusing the officers … in an attempt to intimidate and add confusion to an already hectic scene.”

When officers cuffed another alleged delinquent, Isaiah Morel, 20, for underage drinking, his brother, Samuel Morel, 22, “continued to accost officers” and began pushing them forcibly, according to the police report. State prosecutors say that not only did de Vargas neglect her husband, leading to his death, but also claimed to be his “ex-daughter-in-law” to bypass MassHealth regulations preventing spouses from serving as personal care attendants that collect funding from the MassHealth program. During her alleged fraud, the taxpayer-funded state program doled out some $135,000 to her based on her submitted timesheets.

But the allegations extend beyond mere neglect, as prosecutors with the state attorney general’s office said that the husband arrived at Lawrence General Hospital extremely emaciated and with more than 10 pressure wounds — at least eight of which were considered severe. He died from sepsis — due to infections to these wounds — four days after arriving at the hospital. title: Boston Mayor Wu sues Trump administration for rescinding Roxbury’s $20M federal transit grant
text:
Boston Mayor Michelle Wu filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration that alleges it unlawfully rescinded a $20 million grant awarded in 2022 for Roxbury street upgrades because the project no longer aligns with federal priorities.

“We’re fighting for every dollar of investment to improve quality of life for Roxbury residents, commuters, and businesses,” Wu said Monday in a statement. “Boston earned this competitive grant to meet community needs and address long-needed infrastructure upgrades.

“The City of Boston will continue to fight back against lawless federal attacks, and we urge the court to reverse the Trump administration’s illegal actions and restore these critical funds for Roxbury,” the mayor added.

The city’s lawsuit alleges the grant withdrawal by the U.S. Department of Transportation was politically motivated. It said the reversal was based on a “small” portion of allocated funds that were set aside for electric vehicle charging, which goes against the Trump administration’s stated energy priorities.

“In September 2025, after three years of grant planning, DOT abruptly and without warning withdrew the city’s award,” the city’s lawsuit filed against DOT and its Secretary Sean Duffy in federal court, states. “In a brief letter, DOT stated that the agency’s priorities ‘presently include: promoting traditional forms of energy and natural resources,’ and ‘ensuring that taxpayer dollars are used efficiently.’

“DOT then claimed to have reviewed the city’s grant in light of these priorities and determined that the grant was ‘inconsistent’ with them ‘because of the project’s inclusion of EV charging infrastructure,’” the lawsuit went on to state.

The city’s filing states the DOT’s decision to withdraw the funds was unexpected, given that “less than 1%” of the planned project costs would have gone towards EV charging infrastructure, and DOT itself had encouraged the city to include that initiative when applying for the grant to improve its chances of winning the funds.

The $20 million in funding for the project was awarded to the city by the Biden administration in 2022, as part of the Rebuilding American Infrastructure with Sustainability and Equity, or RAISE grant program.

The grant was set to fund the Roxbury Resilient Corridors project, including state of good repair, safety, transit, accessibility and traffic flow improvements to Melnea Cass Boulevard, Malcolm X Boulevard, and Warren Street.

The city contends that the funds were clawed back in September 2025 due to the federal government’s shifting political priorities that occurred under the second Trump administration.

“DOT’s withdrawal of the Boston grant award did not occur in a vacuum,” the lawsuit states. “On Jan. 20, 2025, the president issued an executive order titled ‘unleashing American energy.’

“The executive order included plans to ‘terminate the Green New Deal,’ and instructed federal agencies to ‘consider the elimination of unfair subsidies and other ill-conceived government-imposed market distortions that favor EVs over other technologies,” the lawsuit added.

The city said the federal government’s budget office issued a memo the following day that “instructed federal agencies to freeze … funds that would support EV projects and other environmental sustainability priorities established by Congress.”

The lawsuit claims that the Wu administration offered to remove the funding it designated for EV charging infrastructure to allow the Roxbury project to move forward, but was told by the feds in early January that it “remains canceled.”

The city contends that by withdrawing the grant, the Trump administration’s Department of Transportation acted against the instruction of Congress, which created the grant program and its application eligibility parameters.

U.S. Rep. Ayanna Pressley, who represents Roxbury and advocated for the grant funding, issued a statement that said, “These funds are an essential investment in Roxbury and the unlawful cancellation of this grant is more evidence of Sean Duffy and Donald Trump’s contempt for the people we serve.

“There was no good reason to rescind these funds,” Pressley added. “DOT should reverse course so we can move this project forward, improve the daily lives of commuters, and enhance the climate resilience of at-risk communities — just as Congress intended.”

The city claims it has been irreparably harmed by the loss of funds, given that it was relying on the federal grant to pay for roughly 60% of the Roxbury street upgrade project, which is estimated to cost just shy of $34 million. It was thus “forced to suspend the project,” per the lawsuit.

A USDOT spokesperson issued a statement that said the department is reviewing the city’s lawsuit.

The spokesperson added, “DOT remains committed to ensuring that taxpayer dollars are spent wisely and in ways that benefit all Americans.”

title: Boston City Councilor Sharon Durkan decries being made into ‘clickbait’ villain for blocking late-file orders
text:
Boston City Councilor Sharon Durkan railed against the media for turning her into a “clickbait” villain for relentlessly blocking late-file matters before blocking a late-file order aimed at funding police and firefighter cancer screenings.

Durkan’s move to block the hearing order, filed late by Councilor Erin Murphy, continued the months-long feud between the two councilors, which boiled over at Wednesday’s City Council meeting.

“I do think there has been a politicization of late files,” Durkan said. “I have been used as clickbait. I have some threats that are actually in my DMs right now from something that happened last week. I think it’s really, really important that we actually prioritize the work and stop trying to make villains of certain people.”

Durkan has been blocking Murphy’s late-file orders on a near-weekly basis since around this past April.

The feud garnered renewed media coverage last week, when Murphy was left steaming after Durkan blocked her latest request, while allowing another matter filed late by a different councilor to move forward.

Murphy accused Durkan, a close ally of Mayor Michelle Wu, of singling her out. Murphy, who is seen as an antagonist of the mayor, said Durkan’s actions have been “unprofessional” and “obviously personal.”

“Councilor Durkan is playing games with my filings, and delaying work on issues Boston residents care about,” Murphy said last week, adding that the Council “rules should not be weaponized to obstruct my work.”

At Wednesday’s meeting, Durkan for a third straight week blocked a late-file order from Murphy, while allowing a late matter from other councilors to move forward.

This time, Murphy was calling for a hearing to review city funding for first responder health screenings, in response to comments made by the head of the Boston Police detectives union, who said at a Monday Council hearing that the union, not the city, covers the cost of its members’ preventative screenings.

Per Murphy’s filing, Boston Police Detectives Benevolent Society President Robert Griffin testified that his union relies on roughly $50,000 in fundraising and about $60,000 of its own union funds to provide health screenings for members.

“This testimony brought specific information about the union’s funding burden to Councilor Murphy’s attention after the filing deadline for the Sept. 30, 2026 Council agenda, prompting this late-filed request for an emergency hearing to obtain answers and identify reliable funding for essential health screenings and wellness support,” Murphy’s order states.

Her order would also review city funds for EMS and firefighter screenings.

Murphy has previously stated that “late files are an established part of the Council’s rules and process for matters that arise after the Monday 10 a.m. filing deadline and could not have been reasonably anticipated.”

Durkan objected to Murphy’s order, which means she will have to file it again for next week’s meeting. But Durkan allowed a late-file resolution from Councilors Miniard Culpepper and Henry Santana calling for the city to provide “immediate relief for businesses devastated” by Monday’s six-alarm fire in Roxbury.

The reason for her disparate actions, according to Durkan, is that Culpepper’s late-file order adhered to her understanding of what should constitute exceptions to the state’s open meeting law, which requires that agenda items be publicly noticed 48 hours before a public body meeting.

Durkan has stated that her blocks are procedural, not political or personal, and that she believes only late files that are “true emergencies” should be accepted.

“I just want to support my colleague, Councilor Culpepper,” Durkan said. “The way that we should think about emergencies is something unexpected, unplanned, and a crisis, which I believe this is.

“It is so important to me that everyone know that any time I have blocked a late file matter, it has not been about the person who is putting it forward. It has been about the contents and not feeling like it was an emergency,” Durkan added.

Durkan took a dig at Murphy, however, for “filing 50%” of late-file emergency orders over the past year, adding after Council President Liz Breadon tried to cut her off, “I will not be silenced on this because I think that transparency and accessibility should be of top concern to everyone in this body.”

Murphy said her late file on first responder health screenings adheres to the definition of what constitutes an emergency, as dictated by Council rules, and should have been allowed.

“I would like to reference Rule 46,” Murphy said. “It does say that the emergency needs to be written into anything filed late per open meeting law under circumstances where such filing was unable to be anticipated prior to the filing deadline, so that is the reason.

“It’s not always the content, but it’s that you could not anticipate it,” Murphy said, adding that she found out about the information from the police detectives’ union after the Council’s filing deadline.

Councilor Julia Mejia had sparked the day’s nearly 40-minute debate by questioning whether Murphy’s order was an emergency and required immediate action, or a hearing to be held ahead of next week’s Council meeting.

Mejia said she saw the Roxbury fire order as having greater urgency, and sought clarity from Breadon on what constituted an emergency, to prevent the situation from generating further “headlines” that lead people to believe the Council is “not supporting certain things because we’re allegedly blocking them.”

“I need to know how we’re going to be moving forward because these late files occupy a lot of oxygen and space and time and political theater, and I think that we need to get real about what the business of our council is,” Mejia said.

Ultimately, the debate ended with Murphy’s order being blocked by Durkan, leading Murphy to point out that the matter could have been resolved within two minutes, had her order simply been taken up and referred to a Council committee for a future hearing.

Murphy said she sees an emergency “any time any city employee has to put their hand in their own pocket to get cancer screening for wellness.”

title: Gaskin: Hard questions for Mayor Wu about Blue Hill Ave.
text:
The City has been working on plans to improve Blue Hill Avenue since the Deval Patrick administration. By 2022, we already knew the major concerns. Residents and businesses were worried about traffic, church and general parking, access, and imposing one solution on very different sections of Blue Hill Avenue. The political signal was equally clear: four of the five candidates running for the state Senate seat now held by Sen. Liz Miranda opposed the proposal then under consideration.

It should not have taken four years to address those concerns, but it has.

The new design takes a more block-by-block approach, preserves at least two general travel lanes through most of the corridor, produces a net increase in parking, responds to high-demand locations, and proposes new sidewalks, lighting, pedestrian crossings and nearly 200 trees. That is real progress.

The City listened, and the plan improved. Now it is time to answer the next set of questions.

1. What about business interruption?

Better design and better communication do not answer the hardest question facing businesses that will live through years of construction: What happens when construction costs them customers and revenue?

It is one thing to tell a business owner construction is coming. It is another to compensate that owner when customers cannot reach the store, parking disappears, entrances are obstructed or people decide getting there is too inconvenient.

During previous work on another section of Blue Hill Avenue, some businesses lost months of revenue when access became difficult. For a small business operating on narrow margins, several bad months can be enough to put it out of business.

So the City should answer directly: Will businesses receive compensation for documented revenue losses? How will losses be measured? Which businesses will qualify? Will a dedicated business-interruption relief fund be in place before construction begins?

2. How good will the BRT actually be?

Bus Rapid Transit has internationally recognized standards. The Institute for Transportation and Development Policy evaluates dedicated right-of-way, busway alignment, off-board fare collection, intersection treatment, platform-level boarding and other elements. Gold-level BRT requires at least 85 points.

Using that standard, how would the proposed Blue Hill Avenue design score?

Publish the projected scorecard. If Boston is making a generational investment in Blue Hill Avenue, excellence ought to be the starting point.

3. Why does the project end at Warren Street?

The problems on Blue Hill Avenue do not suddenly disappear at Warren Street. Businesses between Warren and Dudley Street have already endured disruptive utility construction, with some coming dangerously close to being put out of business. Earlier transportation planning considered a Dudley-to-Mattapan BRT corridor. The current project stops at Warren Street.

If extending the project farther now is impractical, tell us whether there will be a Phase II, whether it will extend to Nubian Square or perhaps Ruggles Square, and what the timetable will be.

Residents and businesses should know whether Boston intends eventually to complete the corridor.

4. Why shouldn’t Blue Hill Avenue become a model environmental corridor?

Communities along Blue Hill Avenue already carry significant environmental-health burdens. If Boston is reconstructing a major corridor through these neighborhoods, the street and streetscape should incorporate better environmental design.

That should include substantially better stormwater management: rain gardens, bioswales, infiltration areas, permeable surfaces where practical, additional tree canopy and other green infrastructure that captures and absorbs water closer to where it falls.

These measures can reduce runoff, relieve pressure on drainage infrastructure and improve the streetscape. The project should also expand public EV charging where appropriate in commercial districts.

5. What is the larger traffic-management strategy?

Redesigning Blue Hill Avenue is not the same thing as managing traffic.

What is the City’s strategy for reducing the number of vehicles competing for limited roadway space during the busiest periods? Better enforcement and signal timing matter, but the City should also examine better transit service, employer transportation programs, stronger rapid-transit connections, parking policy and, where appropriate, demand or congestion pricing.

There is also the question of induced demand. If roadway changes make driving easier, additional trips can eventually consume some of that new capacity.

So if traffic demand itself is not reduced, are we simply rearranging the same number of vehicles within a different street design?

And what happens to surrounding neighborhoods? If drivers avoid congestion on Blue Hill Avenue by cutting through residential streets, we have not eliminated congestion. We have moved it.

The City should explain its assumptions about future traffic volumes, how much reduction in vehicle demand is necessary for the design to work, what happens if that reduction does not occur, and how side-street diversion will be measured and addressed.

A transportation project of this scale should not depend on traffic behaving the way planners hope it will.

Finally, show us your work.

Publish the traffic projections at major intersections, the parking inventory and the assumptions behind travel-time estimates. Tell us how reduced demand, induced demand and traffic diversion are modeled.

Establish MBTA service standards, because an expensive bus lane is not rapid transit if the bus does not come. Make certain center platforms work for seniors and people with disabilities.

And establish the measures by which the project will be judged before construction begins: bus travel times, intersection delay, crashes, parking availability, side-street traffic and business impacts. Establish the baseline now, measure the same things after construction and publish the results.

The City deserves credit for listening and changing the design. But listening cannot be the finish line.

Ed Gaskin is Executive Director of Greater Grove Hall Main Streets and founder of Sunday Celebrations

title: There is another marathon in Boston this weekend called "26.True" and runners of all abilities are welcome
text:
As many make their way into the city of Boston for the 130th Boston Marathon, did you know there's another very special marathon taking place on Saturday, April 18th?

It's called 26.True and it's hosted by the Pioneers Run Crew. Their goal is to build community with every step.

High-knees and hugs, lunges and love. It's all a part of the weekly warm-up for Pioneers Run Crew at The Marshall Community Center in Dorchester.

Pioneers Run Crew

Pioneers Run Crew, founded in 2017 as Boston's first Black and Brown-led running community, is getting ready to host their sixth annual 26.True Marathon this weekend.

"There's the other marathon that happens the following Monday every year and that race will always be loved. That race is so significant and historic to the community. But what we're creating is different and I feel really, really proud to be a part of that," said Aliese Lash, a captain of the Pioneers Run Crew and a Race Director of 26.True Marathon and Half Marathon.

The hard work that goes into preparing for this race can't be ignored, especially since 26.True is entirely volunteer led, but neither can their love for running and their love for each other.

"Six years is a huge milestone. It just makes me think of when we first started, our first year, Lash said.

She explained to WBZ's Courtney Cole that the idea for the race was born during the pandemic. Seeing a gap and filling the need, when the Boston Marathon was canceled for the first time in its history, PRC decided to host their own marathon.

One that would center around equity, accessibility and celebrating the rich history and culture of neighborhoods in the city of Boston.

"I've always loved the quote, 'You can't be what you can't see.' And the power of representation in our neighborhoods in particular, especially when it comes to health and wellness," Lash said.

With a background in Clinical Social Work, Lash told Cole she cares greatly about the public health impacts of running.

"If we're going to change some of the cycles of what health and wellness looks like in our community—it starts with inspiring the next generation," said Lash.

Jaia Peabody is glad to be a part of the mission.

"I like showing people that there's a different outlet. Showing kids that there are other things to do. It's not just for a certain demographic or for a certain community. You can get out there and run, you deserve to be out there and run, and I know that it means a lot to them to see people who look like them doing this. That's incredible to me," Peabody said.

400 runners expected at 26.True Marathon

This race started with just about 30 runners in 2021. This year - they're expecting 400.

One of the goals here — to making running accessible. That means runners of all abilities are welcome, their marathon is not timed, and everyone will get the chance to break the finish line tape.

"I'm ready. I'm ready to do my 26. I'm finishing regardless, that's what I keep telling myself," Peabody said confidently.

After runs in the rain, cold and the snow, Peabody, a rising leader in the crew, says nothing can stop her now.

For Lanisha Harrison, her second time around is about connecting with the community. She ran the Boston Marathon two years ago, two months pregnant.

"To see people that look like you, it gives you more of an inclination to actually go outside and do it. And we see it all the time when we're running through the community. People are stopping their cars, they're yelling, cheering us on. It actually pushes us to go on further as well," Harrison said.

Marathon through Boston neighborhoods

As an ode to the city, 26.True will take runners through Roxbury, Jamaica Plain, Dorchester and Mattapan.

The course is 13.1 miles; runners will run the course once to complete the half marathon and twice for the full.

"We didn't realize how much traction it would gain and how meaningful it was for people to experience that course. People will say how special it was to run by their childhood home, to run by their churches, to run by these areas that were so prominent for them," Lash told Cole she reflected on the upcoming run.

Normalizing running by and through Boston neighborhoods we know and love.

"I think that's what makes it especially impactful. A lot of us have said it's really hard to go into spaces where you don't see yourself reflected. But here, there is someone that's like you. You see it, whether they're your age, whatever that commonality you share. When you see them outside doing what do you think you couldn't do, it's inspiring," said Sharon Lee, a captain of Pioneers Run Crew and a Race Director for 26.True.

If any of this leaves you feeling inspired, maybe wanting to learn more about Pioneers—Run, don't walk. They'll meet you there.

"We're here to support people, to help them explore and motivate them and inspire them to do the hard things," Lee said.

"We welcome everybody. All ages, no matter where you are in life. Please come, please spend time with us, you are welcome. You belong," Peabody said.

If you're looking for a way to support on Saturday, Pioneers would love for you to pull up.

The Finish Line Block Party will be at Malcolm X Park - right on the corner of Dale and Washington Streets.

title: Violent 4th of July weekend in Boston leaves 2 dead, 13 injured in separate shootings
text:
The Boston Police Department is investigating a total of five shootings that left 13 victims early Sunday morning, including two dead, as the city celebrated the 4th of July.

Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox blamed the violent Independence Day on large neighborhood gatherings that included illegal fireworks and public alcohol consumption.

Deadly Boston shootings

Just after 12:30 a.m., police were called to Blue Hill Ave. in Roxbury for a shooting. Three victims were taken from the scene to an area hospital by ambulance. One person did not survive.

A fourth person later walked into the hospital. All three surviving victims have non-life threatening injuries, police said.

Hours later around 3:15 a.m., police were called to George Street in Roxbury for another shooting.

Three people were hospitalized, and one was pronounced dead. Police said the second person has life-threatening injuries, and the third victim is expected to survive.

About an hour after the initial response, three more victims went to the hospital on their own with non-life threatening injuries.

"It's a long summer"

Cox said police dealt with an "unusually high volume of calls and serious incidents throughout the city."

"We're asking the public, it's a long summer. We're at the beginning of the peak of the summer. Large amounts of people gathering, fireworks, firearms and alcohol is a bad combination," Cox said. "And that's what you saw around these events. We're asking you as the summer goes on, think twice before you want to throw late-night parties. Because we will certainly doing all that we can to be shutting those down."

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu echoed Cox's message to the community.

"It was a long and difficult night last night," Wu said. "This is a busy time of year and when we see large gatherings with firearms present, that is never, never a recipe for peaceful celebrations."

Officers hit with fireworks

In addition to the shootings, Cox said officers responding to several incidents suffered injuries when they were hit with fireworks.

The Boston Police Patrolmen's Association posted body camera video from the incident, saying they are "beyond outraged."

Union president Larry Calderone said the incident happened during a street takeover party in Mattapan. He said three officers were taken to the hospital, where they were treated and later released.

"They can be as small as a firecracker, and other times they're throwing M-80s or something worse. So I'm not quite sure what that was in the video, whether it was thrown, planted, shot at them. But the video speaks volume. Officers were hurt," he said.

Calderone relayed to WBZ-TV about how a veteran police officer described Saturday night into Sunday morning.

"This was the most horrific night that he has experienced in his 14.5 years as a Boston police officer working midnights. And that should speak volumes for anyone who sees this video," Calderone said.

title: Boston donut shop has had customers coming back for fresh donuts and coffee for 40 years
text:
A donut shop in Boston's West Roxbury neighborhood has been serving up freshly-made donuts and coffee for decades.

At Anna's Hand Cut Donuts, you're immediately greeted with the smell of hot coffee and donuts still hot from the fryer. Owner Kosta Keskinidis has been part of the community for the last 40 years.

In business for 40 years

"Everybody knows me," said Keskinidis.

"You can come in here and get a donut, a fresh donut, freshly made donut with the best ingredients and a nice hot cup of, you know, real coffee," a customer told WBZ-TV.

"We've been coming here for over 60 years and we're still coming here," said a customer at Anna's Donuts.

Keskinidis got his start in the donut-making business decades ago when he worked for Dunkin.

"I started when I came to the United States, I worked for somebody, he teach me for a year and then I started working for Dunkin Donuts and then I have the opportunity to buy this place," said Keskinidis.

"The secret is love"

What sets Keskinidis apart from the rest if that he gets up at 2 a.m. every morning to make his confections by hand. He even put WBZ-TV's Jordyn Jagolinzer to the test to help him make jelly donuts.

When asked what his secret is, Keskinidis said, "The secret is love. I work with love."

"West Roxbury is very fortunate to have this establishment," said a customer at Anna's.

Earlier this month, Anna's Donuts got a certificate from Boston for being an age and dementia-friendly business.

title: Man in ski mask tried to lure Boston student into van during morning recess, police say
text:
Boston Police are investigating what they're calling an "attempted abduction" outside the Dudley Street Neighborhood Charter School in Roxbury on Thursday morning.

According to a police report, a female student was playing on the playground during morning recess when a light-skinned man with hazel eyes in a ski mask spoke to her from a gray, scratched-up minivan. She told police he offered her money and asked her to come in the van.

When she screamed, school administrators responded and the man drove away.

The incident happened at the intersection of Shirley and Dudley Streets.

"This morning, an individual unknown to the school community attempted to engage with a student who was in the recess yard," an email sent to parents from the school began.

Several parents showed up to school early to pick up their kids due to safety concerns after receiving the email.

"They said there was nothing to worry about," one mother said. "They are trying to make it sound like a very small incident. But child abduction is a very big incident."

Two mothers spoke with WBZ-TV anonymously after they claimed school employees told them not to speak with the media about the incident.

"When they tell you to make no comment when it's your child, it's a big deal," one mom said. "How are they going to keep our children safe?"

"It could've been [my son] or any other kids and y'all are downplaying it like it's nothing. It is something," another mom said. "My son is autistic, so he can't speak for himself, so yeah, I'm coming to get mine. If they want to keep their kids, that's fine, but for my sanity, I'm coming to get my baby."

One other mother said she felt her child was safe at the school, saying, "They have good protection."

WBZ-TV reached out to the entire board of the charter school for comment, but didn't receive a reply. No arrests have been made.

title: Supermarket chain to open 2 stores in former Christmas Tree Shops, Big Lots locations in Massachusetts
text:
Two shuttered retailers are set to become supermarkets in southeastern Massachusetts.

Big Y announced Thursday that it's opening grocery stores in Fairhaven and North Dartmouth. The Fairhaven Plaza location used to be a Big Lots, and the Faunce Corner Center store in North Dartmouth was a Christmas Tree Shops.

"These new stores will allow us to better serve families in the South Coast region," Big Y VP of real estate and development Mathieu L. D'Amour said in a statement.

The supermarkets will open sometime in 2027. Hiring details and a grand opening date will be announced in the next few months.

Most Big Y stores are concentrated in the Springfield area and Connecticut, but the chain has 10 locations in the state east of Worcester. Big Y opened new stores in Westboro and Uxbridge earlier this year.

Big box store closures in Massachusetts and around the country in recent years have created opportunities for other retailers to move into vacant storefronts.

Christmas Tree Shops, the bargain outlet that started on Cape Cod more than 50 years ago, went bankrupt and closed all of its stores in 2023. The old North Dartmouth location is being used temporarily this holiday season as a "Spirit Christmas" pop-up.

Another Christmas Tree Shops in Falmouth has been transformed into an Aldi supermarket. Others have been taken over by Ocean State Job Lot.

Big Lots closed all of its Massachusetts stores last year amid financial turmoil. Just last month, an Ollie's Bargain Outlet moved into a former Big Lots location in Fitchburg.

It hasn't always worked out for supermarkets that move into old retail stores. The Fresh Market, which moved into an old Bed Bath & Beyond store on Route 9 in Framingham less than a year ago, is already closing.

A competing grocery store chain, Trader Joe's, opened two new stores in Newton and West Roxbury this fall.

title: Boston artist John Wilson's work now the subject of Museum of Fine Arts exhibit celebrating humanity
text:
A late Boston artist that got his start in the Roxbury neighborhood now has his work gracing the walls of the Museum of Fine Arts as part of a new exhibition.

Welcome to Roxbury: the geographic center of the city, the heart of Black Boston, and the birthplace of artist John Wilson.

"His life came out of that community very deeply, and it produced this—at least for me—this magnificent representation of human beings," said Roy Wilson, John's son.

Importance of family

John Wilson was born in 1922, to immigrants from British Guyana.

Although his career took him to many places, Including Europe and Mexico, family was always important to him. He went on to marry his wife Julie and they had three kids: Erica, Rebecca and Roy.

Roy Wilson invited WBZ-TV into his childhood home in Brookline.

"I just have this vision of him doing anything to protect us. And I always knew that about him - that he'd be there in the end for you - whatever it took," said Wilson.

John Wilson passed away in 2015 at the age of 92, but the memories that Wilson made with his father are still very much alive.

"Well - one thing is - he was upstairs working a lot. When I went to the show, it was kind of impressive… seeing all the stuff that he had been working on in his studio for so many years—to see it all in one place!" said Wilson.

New MFA exhibit

That place? The walls of The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

One hundred and ten of his works grace the walls; paintings, prints, drawings, sculptures and illustrated books—all on display in the exhibition "Witnessing Humanity: The Art of John Wilson."

"The self-portrait was an incredibly important part of John Wilson's work and throughout his six-decade career, so much of his work is focused around portraits of himself, his family, and his friends," said co-curator Edward Saywell. "And a lot of that has to do with his reclaiming, the dignity and the gravitas of the portrait for Black Americans."

Saywell, one of the four co-curators of the John Wilson exhibit, told WBZ-TV that as an art student, Wilson never got to see himself in art history books or exhibitions.

"And when he did see representations of Black Americans, all too often he described them as caricature-like or dehumanized. And one of the threads that you see throughout the entire exhibition is incredible humanity and empathy that he imbues in all his portraits—whether it's a portrait of himself or a portrait of a family member or a friend," Saywell explained.

John Wilson spent more than six decades creating artwork that challenged viewers to not just look...but see.

"The works speak to, not only key political and civil rights moments over those six decades, but they speak to what life was like in Roxbury growing up in the 1940s," Saywell said.

Works displayed in Roxbury

Long before Wilson's works were in the MFA, they were on display in the neighborhood that helped shape him. One of those works sits on the campus of Roxbury Community College, called: "Father and Child Reading." A 7-foot tall bronze sculpture that honors the fond memories John Wilson had of his father reading to him.

"I know that he was very dedicated to the idea of being a father, in acculture, that in some ways, made it difficult to be an upstanding man," said Wilson.

The other work, a very well-known piece called "The Eternal Presence", more affectionately known as "The Big Head." The monument, described by the artist himself as, "an image of universal dignity."

"For him, putting it in Roxbury was as important as the piece itself. And attaching it to the ground, no pedestal, in his home community—was as important as anything else about the piece. And the fact that people come once a year to polish it and to refinish it, was completely moving to the man. It was the highest compliment he could imagine being paid," said Saywell.

That piece sits on the campus of the museum of The National Center of Afro-American Arts.

"My sincerest hope is that any visitor is going to see an extraordinary Boston artist who should be on the national stage and are going to come away, hopefully seeing work that speaks to them in one way or another," Saywell shared.

"That we are as magical, as strong, as thoughtful, as human, as any other people on the planet," Wilson said when asked about what he wants visitors to feel leaving his father's exhibit.

John Wilson's impact is also still felt by students and staff alike at Boston University, where his inspiration and instruction as a professor continues to reverberate.

The exhibition at The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston will be on display through June 22 – and then it will travel to The Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York in September.

title: Boston bike activist Louisa Gag hit by truck, killed while cycling to work at City Hall, mayor "devastated"
text:
Louisa Gag, a Boston bike activist who was dedicated to making streets safer for cyclists and pedestrians, was killed in a crash in Roxbury Thursday.

The 36-year-old was riding her bike on Tremont Street near Roxbury Crossing when she was hit by a truck just after 8:15 a.m. The driver stopped at the scene.

The Massachusetts Vision Zero Coalition, which works to reduce traffic deaths in the state, said Gag was on her way to work at City Hall at the time. She died at the scene.

Gag began working for Mayor Michelle Wu's office as a policy fellow before becoming a transportation planner for the city of Boston. She dedicated her career to ensuring that the city was safer and more accessible, according to the mayor. Gag had previously worked at Livable Streets Alliance, a nonprofit transportation advocacy group in Cambridge.

In a statement, Wu said she was "heartbroken" by Gag's sudden death.

"I am absolutely devastated by this unfathomable loss for our community and our City. I will miss her terribly," the mayor said. "Our hearts are with her family, friends, colleagues, and all whose lives she touched as a beloved daughter of Roslindale and a bright light in our community."

The Zero Coalition called for action in the wake of Gag's death and said that she was "dedicated to fixing the very system that failed her."

"Fatalities are a heartbreaking reminder of the safety gaps in our infrastructure. Inaction and needless delays have consequences. Changes must be made to dangerous streets before we lose a community member, not after," the coalition said in a statement.

Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said that his office is investigating Gag's death. No charges have been filed at this point in the investigation.

title: Boston brewery turns into family-friendly jazz club once a week
text:
Once a week, a craft brewery in Roxbury transforms into a jazz club. Thursday nights are jazz nights at Long Live Roxbury.

For more than a year now, the taproom has hosted some of the best talent in the area.

"Nothing can compare to going to a live room with people that are there paying attention to you, " said pianist and Berklee College of Music professor Zahili Zamora.

She is a repeat performer at Long Live Roxbury, telling us, "It's creating a big community of all the musicians in Boston that are just eager to play and show their artistry and share their artistry with other people."

Free event

Michael Feldman, the CEO of Feldman Geospacial, owns the Roxbury building.

He says, "When people arrive, they feel like they're in some kind of an art center. And then they come in and they're at this old 1856 brick and beam beautiful building that coincidentally did manufacture pianos back in the 1800s."

Feldman helps curate the music for the free family-friendly event, that's held weekly.

"You can't bring your kids to many jazz venues because they're ticketed events, they're 21 or over," Feldman says.

"But this is a way for parents from the neighborhood to come unwind, bring their kids, have a beer, get something to eat. They have board games that the kids will play with. And these kids, without even knowing it, they're being exposed to some of the best musicians in Boston."

Establishing a sense of community

Co-owner of the brewery, Jessica Debry, says "It's been amazing to see the caliber of people coming into the space… having a taproom that's open to the public and being able to host events allows for us to not only offer a good product, but also build community."
