Oliver D'Agostino, 37, told his own story at the press conference, describing years living outdoors near Mass. and Cass while struggling with addiction, and cycling in and out of detox before finally entering sustained recovery with the help of the city's outreach workers.

Young said since Sept. 15, the CRT has placed "close to 480 people in inpatient substance use treatment."

"We have not turned a single person away that's wanted treatment," she added.

The Working Group is made up of community leaders, including those within the Newmarket Business Improvement District and South End Forum. Moran, FitzGerald and Young have met with the community group over the last six months since Wu requested they develop recommendations for a new approach at Mass. and Cass.

Asked whether she supports the program, Mayor Michelle Wu said in a statement: "Alongside partners in community, public health, and across government, Boston is working to ensure strong pathways into recovery and quality of life in every neighborhood, including an end to outdoor substance use. I thank the Working Group for carefully reflecting the shared progress of the many city departments engaged in our Coordinated Response Team, for their strong endorsement of the Boston Police Department's NEST initiative, and for highlighting more opportunities to meet our shared goals. The City is focused on active preparations for warmer weather and continuing to engage with all stakeholders on our coordinated approach."

A Specialty Court to 'Complete the Cycle'

The most novel element of the recommendations is the proposed specialty court, which would centralize cases involving people repeatedly arrested for drug-related offenses at Mass. and Cass and divert them into treatment before traditional arraignment.

"We want to call it a specialty court. And ultimately, the core of this work is diversion," Young said. "We want people to be diverted into the treatment and the help that they need."

The goal, Young said, is "more of a centralized system for these people that we're seeing over and over again, because most of them, or a lot of them, I should say, are already involved with the judicial system. So we want to leverage that to increase the likelihood that they will stay on the pathway to recovery."

Working Group Chair Stephen Fox described the approach as a long-sought integration of previously disconnected systems.

"We believe that we have found a magic sauce," Fox said. "Being able to use public safety, public health and judicial initiatives together in an integrated fashion."

Fox pointed to retired Judge Kathleen Coffey's homelessness specialty court held at Pine Street Inn as proof of concept.

"That's why we're saying that we need to have that component at the judicial piece in order to complete the cycle," he said. "So recovery at the front end, public safety all through and then judicial initiatives and judicial reform within it."

'You Are Going to Get Clean'

While speakers emphasized compassion Wednesday, they also made clear the plan would place clearer boundaries around open drug use at Mass. and Cass.

Sue Sullivan, executive director of the Newmarket Business Improvement District, framed the plan as a balance between recovery and neighborhood safety.

"There are those who would say that what we are doing, pushing people to try to choose recovery, doesn't work," Sullivan said. "Some would say that when individuals are incentivized to go into recovery, 50% will fail, and they will be more vulnerable when they come back out on the street. The reality is that on the streets, 0% are getting better, and many overdose daily. We cannot stand by and continue to let this happen."

She argued that pairing long-term case management with removing people from street-level drug activity "will work to improve the quality of life for everyone."

FitzGerald was even more direct about the cultural shift he hopes to see.

"If you are coming to Mass. and Cass, if you're coming to the South End, you are going to get clean, right?" he said. "It might not be the first time we see you, maybe not the second time, but at some point, if you keep coming down here, you're going to end up on the road to recovery."

D'Agostino on Wednesday recounted his first encounter with CRT workers.

"At the time, I was convinced they were undercover cops, disguised as parking authorities," he said. "I was suspicious, but when I asked around the other guys said, 'No, that's Erica. She's from CRT. She's cool.' That word 'cool' was the foundation of trust that eventually saved my life."

He described relapsing after years of sobriety and living "like a piece of cattle" on a bike path near a Boston Water and Sewer facility.

"They respected the line. They knew if they pushed too hard, I'd be gone," he said. "When I decided to finally pull the trigger and ask for help, Tommy was right there. He got me into detox time and time again."

After a brain bleed landed him in the hospital, D'Agostino said CRT staff showed up repeatedly.

"That was the turning point," he said. "I realized these strangers care more about me than I cared about myself. It was time to hold myself accountable."

Budget and State Role

Pressed on the cost of the recommendations, Moran acknowledged the group does not yet have a precise estimate.

Major expenses include expanding the teams on the street, establishing the specialty court — "it needs to be bespoke to what we need," he said — and investing in short-term sober housing, "two months, for example, 150 people."

Those are "the building blocks," he said.

Moran noted he sits on the House Ways and Means Committee as lawmakers begin work on the fiscal year 2027 budget. The committee's budget is expected in April.

"We're gonna have to do this quickly, but we have the building blocks. We just need to figure out a better concept of those hard dollars," he said.

He said state leaders, including the governor and attorney general, have copies of the plan, and emphasized that "the state invests a lot in Mass. and Cass."

FitzGerald said he has pushed to explore a more regional response, acknowledging that many individuals at Mass. and Cass are not Boston residents.

"There is a need to be a good neighbor and ask for that approach," he said.

title: Boston-area community grocery nonprofit closing all its stores: ‘we cannot continue'
text:
[This story first appeared on Boston Restaurant Talk.]

A local group of nonprofit community grocers that help provide food to those in need is ceasing operations.

According to a Facebook post from the business, Daily Table is shutting down all of its markets, with the post saying the following:

With heavy hearts, we share that Daily Table will be closing our doors within the next few days. This was not an easy decision. For the past 10 years, we have had the honor of serving neighborhoods across Greater Boston, working alongside our community to make affordable, nutritious food accessible to all. We are proud to have served over 3 million customers, returning over $16 million in savings to the community while removing the barriers to healthy food. The past several years have been particularly hard; navigating the challenges of COVID-19, plus the pressures of facing historically high levels of food price increases, to the current uncertain and difficult funding environment, sustaining Daily Table has become increasingly difficult. Without immediate funding to bridge us through 2025, we cannot continue. After careful consideration, we have come to the heartbreaking conclusion that we can no longer continue operations.

Please know that due to the urgency of the situation, we were unable to individually reach out to all of our longstanding partners, and we apologize if this news comes as a shock. We understand that this comes at a time when other food access resources and organizations are at risk, which makes this news even more difficult to share. We hope that those who have been generous to Daily Table will continue investing in other organizations to meet the ongoing need.

The note refers customers who may be in need of support to this link within the City of Boston website: https://www.boston.gov/departments/food-justice/food-resources

A note on its website says that Daily Table's markets in Dorchester, Roxbury, and Salem will close after business hours on Sunday, May 11, while the market in Cambridge's Central Square, will remain open through Monday, May 12. (Another store had been in Mattapan but it closed at the beginning of the year.) The website for Daily Table can be found at https://www.dailytable.org.

title: Boston officer moves to dismiss manslaughter charge in deadly shooting
text:
A Boston police officer who's been charged in the deadly shooting of a carjacking suspect in Roxbury has asked a judge to dismiss the case or appoint a special prosecutor.

Officer Nicholas O'Malley's lawyer, Karen Read attorney David Yannetti, said that District Attorney Kevin Hayden had prevented the officer from getting a fair trial by holding a press conference after O'Malley's initial arraignment in the killing Stephenson King Jr. following a report of a carjacking on March 11. O'Malley pleaded not guilty then, and again after a grand jury brought a manslaughter charge against him.

"This is a rare case of a district attorney's office second-guessing the actions of an officer trying to prevent a violent carjacker from hurting someone else," the motion says, adding that the press conference that Hayden gave after O'Malley was charged prejudiced the officer "and poisoned the jury pool against" him.

Hayden's improper conduct continued, according to O'Malley's lawyer, by having a private meeting with community leaders to discuss the case.

Members of the community have been demanding that body-worn camera footage of the shooting be released, which Hayden's office hasn't done, though a legal advocacy group filed a lawsuit seeking to compel the release of the footage earlier this month.

Asked for comment, a spokesman for Hayden's office said in an email, "We consider the motion to be without merit and we will respond in the appropriate forum."

Prosecutors have said in court that O'Malley and another officer located a stolen vehicle after a report of a carjacking on March 11, approaching the car and issuing commands for King to show his hands. Investigators said King showed his hands but did not unlock the vehicle, or open it.

O'Malley allegedly made a comment about shooting King, according to prosecutors, at which point King backed the vehicle up a few feet into an unoccupied police cruiser. As King was finishing a three-point turn to drive away, prosecutors said, O'Malley fired three shots into the driver window and door, all three of which hit King; at least one of them caused his death.

The commonwealth contended in court that O'Malley was not acting in reasonable defense of either himself, the other officer or the general public: "The shooting was excessive, and that's what brings us here."

Yanetti responded in court that the defense has a very different view of the evidence in this case, arguing that the prosecutors had presented "a partial version of what happened" that was "sanitized quite a bit."

According to Yanetti, the evidence in this case shows that a mother was in Roxbury picking up her daughter when a violent carjacker entered the car, punched her in the face, ordered her out of the vehicle and stole her vehicle.

O'Malley was doing his job when he came across that stolen vehicle, with the carjacker, "a violent man," still inside.

Yanetti conceded that King showed his hands once after several commands, but then hid them again, ignoring "lawful order after lawful order after lawful order until he made the decision to smash that stolen car into a police cruiser and then he showed he had no care in the world about who he endangered or who he hurt as he was trying to escape a scene for the second time."

"He left Officer O'Malley with no choice," Yanetti said. "This will be a very highly contested case. We don't agree with the commonwealth's decision in this case to charge it. We vehemently feel that this is not an appropriate charge and we look forward to our day in court."

O'Malley was released on his own recognizance.

Dozens of police officers showed up in court to support O'Malley.

"It's unfortunate and horrible that we lost a life. But Nick O'Malley did what he should have done as a police officer, and every police officer would do standing behind me," Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association President Larry Calderone said after the hearing.

title: Boston officials aim to curb shoplifting
text:
Boston city leaders are expanding their efforts to reduce shoplifting, urging businesses to report every incident.

The push comes as part of Boston's broader "Safe Shopping Initiative," launched last year.

Shoplifting is up 15% in Boston compared to last year, according to police data. Officials said the increase is partly due to more businesses speaking up rather than staying silent.

"We want everything to be reported so that we can know how to formulate the best approach," said Mayor Michelle Wu during a press conference Tuesday at the Boston Police Headquarters in Roxbury.

Retail-heavy neighborhoods, like Downtown Crossing, have become a focus of the city's efforts to improve safety and boost foot traffic for local businesses.

One business that opened just a few months ago, City Liquors, has already seen its share of theft.

"We definitely had our fair share of instances," said store manager Christopher Whitter. "A kid came and pushed one of our employees, took the vape and ran out the store."

City leaders are partnering with retailers, law enforcement and prosecutors to focus their enforcement on organized theft and habitual offenders. They said first-time shoplifters could be directed toward resources instead of jail.

"Our focus is on repeat and violent offenders that are impacting retail theft," said Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden.

Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox said authorities' goal is to build a stronger system of accountability through better reporting.

"While we recognize that we will not eradicate shoplifting, we are working together to encourage better reporting and eventually lead to a reduction of crime in general in this area," Cox said.

The Retailers Association of Massachusetts estimates that stores across the state lose approximately $2 billion a year to theft of all kinds.

As the city expands its program, Whitter hopes these measures will make his store — and others — more inviting for customers.

"Our safety comes first, then everything else," he said.

title: Gunman due in court in shooting that left 1 dead, 1 hurt in JP
text:
The teen arrested in connection with a deadly shooting Monday night in Boston's Jamaica Plain neighborhood appeared in court Tuesday.

The incident unfolded at the Mildred Hailey Boston Housing Authority Apartments on Centre Street in Jamaica Plain around 9:30 p.m. Monday, police have said. Officers could be heard shouting "Shots fired" and "Man down!" in police radio audio.

Officers were patrolling the apartment complex when they heard multiple shots fired, officials said. Officers found a man who'd been shot, who was pronounced dead after being taken to a local hospital. He was identified Friday by police as 19-year-old Quami J. Clarke, of Boston.

Edwin Vinales, a 19-year-old from Boston, was found carrying a gun and arrested on outstanding warrants and firearms violations, police said. They said he was seen running from the shooting scene and tossed a semi-automatic gun with an extended magazine capable of holding more than 10 rounds of ammunition.

As of right now, Vinales is not charged with the shooting itself.

"Officers did observe Mr. Vinales discard a firearm as he fled and did recover that firearm, leading to the charges before the court today," a prosecutor said in court Tuesday.

The crime scene stretched blocks away to Heath Street, where officers also roped off a crime scene. They said multiple weapons were found on scene.

"At this time we're dealing with a very large and active crime scene that spreads out through most of the development," Boston Police Deputy Superintendent Paul McLaughlin said Monday night.

Vinales pleaded not guilty at his arraignment in Roxbury District Court Tuesday afternoon to charges of unlawful possession of a firearm, unlawful possession of a large capacity firearm and unlawful possession of ammunition. He was ordered held without bail and is scheduled to return to court on Sept. 30.

His attorney cautioned in court Tuesday against tying his client to the deadly shooting.

"They have to produce evidence with regard to that shooting," his lawyer said.

People who live nearby said it was shocking seeing how quickly how many officers descended on the neighborhood.

“We were up in the window and we just saw a ton of cop cars, like a SWAT team, not an ambulance, like an EMT guy like breaking down the door materials," one resident said. "I didn’t see any of that, but they definitely had a lot of people with a lot of stuff to take someone down.”

A memorial had been set up in the neighborhood on Tuesday afternoon for the man who died in the shooting.

title: Boston police officer charged with manslaughter in fatal shooting of carjacking suspect
text:
A Boston police officer has been charged with manslaughter in connection with the deadly shooting of a carjacking suspect last week.

Nicholas O'Malley, 33, of Boston, was arrested Thursday morning and was arraigned in Roxbury District Court in connection with the fatal shooting of Stephenson King, 39, of Dorchester, on March 11. He entered a not guilty plea and was released on personal recognizance, with a condition that he surrender any firearms in his possession.

Court paperwork said the manslaughter charge against O'Malley is for "assaulting and beating Stephenson King when they knew or reasonably should have known that the battery endangered human life." Police reports included in court documents also detail how O'Malley shot King three times even though neither he nor his partner were in danger of being struck by his car and King was not armed.

Listen to our new podcast, Uncovering the News, wherever you get podcasts.

The matter will be put to a grand jury, Suffolk County District Attorney Kevin Hayden said Thursday.

The defense pushed back, calling the arrest "election-year tactics" and defending his client's actions.

Local

In-depth news coverage of the Greater Boston and New England area.

"They can say whatever they want about my client being able to see where his partner was because his body worn camera could see it. But that body-worn camera does not have human adrenaline, that body-worn camera is not worried about not seeing somebody's hands. That body-worn camera isn't worried about going home safe at night," defense attorney Kenneth Anderson said. "My client's perception is what matters here and he stands by his actions. I think at the end of this case, he's going to walk away as an innocent man."

Hayden denied that the election was a motivation for the charges and said officials would not be releasing the body camera footage.

"Neither my office nor the Boston Police Department will be releasing any further evidence, including any body-worn camera footage to the public. To do so would clearly compromise and imperil the ongoing investigation and crucial prosecution of this most serious matter," Hayden said outside court after O'Malley's arraignment.

[Read the full contents of the police report here.]

Police responded to Linwood Square just before 10 p.m. last Wednesday after a carjacking on Tremont Street in Mission Hill.

Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox said at a press conference held that night that the officers approached the vehicle on foot, giving multiple verbal commands, and the suspect did not comply.

"At some point, the suspect accelerated his vehicle, striking a Boston police cruiser in an attempt to flee. Officers discharged their weapons, hitting the suspect," Cox said.

The suspect was transported to an area hospital, where he was pronounced dead. He was later identified as King.

A Boston police spokesperson said the suspect had tried to hit the officers with the vehicle.

Hayden said at the time that the officers involved in the incident were taken to a hospital to be treated for any trauma they experienced, but that they were not believed to have been injured.

Police said at the time that the incident was under investigation by the Suffolk District Attorney's Office, per protocol.

Boston City Councilors Miniard Culpepper and Brian Worrell said in a statement Monday they were closely monitoring the situation, and that it was important to fully understood what happened and ensure that appropriate measures are being taken.

"First and foremost, our thoughts and prayers are with the family of the man who lost his life. We are deeply saddened by this incident. Anytime we see a young man die in our community, it is a cause for serious concern," the councilors said in a joint statement. "We also want to make sure that Boston Police officers are able to do their jobs safely while maintaining the trust and safety of the community they serve."

Culpepper and Worrell said they were calling for the body camera footage to be released, arguing it's critical for transparency and accountability.

"We are also hopeful that the Office of Police Accountability will work alongside this investigation to help ensure public trust as the facts come to light,” they added.

Court documents released Thursday reveal new details about why O'Malley was charged in the incident, with a police report dated March 19, showing investigators determined there was probable cause to believe that O'Malley committed the crime of voluntary manslaughter based on "physical evidence and numerous witness interviews," specifically that he "1) committed an act intended or likely to cause death, 2) did cause Stephenson King's death, and 3) was not acting in proper self-defense or defense of another."

The officers involved in responding to the carjacking were both wearing Body-Worn Cameras, police report shows.

"As captured on their BWC's as well as partial witness statements, both officers, firearms drawn, began to yell commands to King such as: show me your hands, shut off the vehicle and unlock the vehicle. King did show the officers his hands at times, did partially open his driver's window, but did not shut off the vehicle or unlock the doors," the report said.

The report said O'Malley, outside the driver's window and while holstering his gun in favor of a Taser, then shouted to King: "Bro, I'm gonna (expletive) shoot you." King immediately put the car in reverse and backed into the cruiser behind him.

King then maneuvered his vehicle forward, reverse, and forward again in an attempt to escape police. At the moment when the vehicle began to move forward the last time, the police report said O'Malley again drew his gun and fired three shots at King through the driver's window.

An autopsy performed on King on March 13 determined that he had been struck by three projectiles, two of which were recovered from his torso. Investigators found a third projectile in the passenger's area of the carjacking victim's vehicle. No weapons were recovered from the vehicle or King's body.

The report said that after he fired his gun, O'Malley did broadcast that officers were involved in a discharge and that the suspect "tried to run us over." Based on the body camera footage and interviews of officers, the report said that statement was not found to be "factually true."

During his interview with investigators, O'Malley said he fired his gun because he thought the other office with him was going to be crushed by the suspect's vehicle. But the report said the body camera footage "revealed that such a belief was unreasonable, and that neither officer was in danger of being struck by the vehicle at the time of Officer O'Malley's discharge." An eyewitness who observed the incident also said that neither officer was in the path of the vehicle as it drove away.

"At no time in his attempt to flee did Mr. King drive at the officers, nor were either officer in the path of Mr. King's vehicle when Officer O'Malley open fired," Hayden said Thursday.

The report said that although the law allows police officers to use deadly force when reasonably necessary, it also says that police "shall not discharge any firearm into or at a fleeing motor vehicle unless, based on the totality of the circumstances, such discharge is necessary to prevent imminent harm to a person and the discharge is proportionate to the threat of imminent harm to a person."

Boston Police Patrolmen's Association President Larry Calderone said that the rank and file are outraged by the charges.

"Try being an officer in two seconds to process all that information. To give verbal commands, pull a taser, and go to that next piece of equipment. Make the right decision all the time," said Calderone.

Calderone said O'Malley has been on the Boston Police Department for close to six years and has never had any issues on the job.

O'Malley was released with no bail set after prosecutors asked for it to be set at $25,000.

The Massachusetts Peace Officers Standards and Training Commission — the agency that oversees police certification in the state — has suspended O'Malley's status while the case is pending.

I think at the end of this case, he's going to walk away as an innocent man."

Hayden denied that the election was a motivation for the charges and said officials would not be releasing the body camera footage.

"Neither my office nor the Boston Police Department will be releasing any further evidence, including any body-worn camera footage to the public. To do so would clearly compromise and imperil the ongoing investigation and crucial prosecution of this most serious matter," Hayden said outside court after O'Malley's arraignment.

Hayden says his investigation found the use of force unjustified.

“O’Malley fired through the driver’s side of the car striking Mr King three times and killing him just as he drove away,” said Hayden.

What happened on March 11?

The incident happened earlier this month after police say O’Malley and another officer spotted a stolen car on Linwood Square in Roxbury. According to court documents, the officers pulled their cruiser up behind King who was parked up against a curb. They instructed King, who was in the driver’s seat reclined, to show his hands. Investigators say King showed his hands at times and opened the door partially when O’Malley yelled, “Bro, I’m going to [expletive] shoot you.”

That’s when investigators say King put the car into gear and went back and forth trying to escape.

“At no time in his attempt to flee did Mr King drive at the officers nor were either officer in the back of Mr. King’s vehicle when Officer O’Malley open fired,” Hayden explained.

[Read the full contents of the police report here.]

O’Malley’s defense attorney said an officer’s perception of deadly force can be different for each officer.

Reaction

Boston Police Patrolmen’s Association President Larry Calderone says the rank and file are outraged by the charges.

“Try being an officer in two seconds to process all that information. To give verbal commands, pull a taser, and go to that next piece of equipment. Make the right decision all the time,” said Calderone.

O’Malley was released with no bail set after prosecutors asked for it to be set at $25,000.

Peace Officers Standards & Training – the agency that oversees police certification in the state – has suspended the officer’s status while the case is still pending.

O’Malley’s union president says the officer has been on the Boston Police Department for close to six years and has never any any issues on the job.

Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox said Thursday this is a difficult day for the department and the city.

“We remain committed to our mission of building trust while reducing crime and fear of crime with those we serve," Cox said. "We rely on the integrity of the criminal justice system in what we do every day, and this case will be no different. On behalf of the Boston Police Department, we want to extend our sympathies to all of those impacted.”

Margo Lindauer, an attorney and law professor, says she's surprised at how quickly the officer was charged.

"It is very rare that police officers, even if they are charged, are found guilty by a judge or jury," she said.

Activists, including Sadiki Kambon of the Black Community Information Center, are pointing to race, as O'Malley is white and King was Black.

"He's our George Floyd here in Boston," Kambon said Friday. "We're talking about a Black man who was apparently assassinated by a white police officer."

He said that while King acted inappropriately, he believes O'Malley should be in jail while awaiting trial.

"He shot and killed a Black man, and he's home with his family right now, probably contemplating his legal defense, and of course the police union lining up behind him," Kambon said.

Was deadly force necessary?

Police in Massachusetts go through use of force training every year — but retired Newton Police Chief John Carmichael is worried that this could make officers hesitate in dangerous situations.

"If you're involved in a deadly force type of situation that trauma is with them now for the rest of their lives," he explained. "We're expecting them to do a job and you have to make sure that they're covered when they do it."

"It's a little unusual for this to take place so quickly and get to the point where we are right now," he added.

Carmichael says investigators look at whether deadly force was really necessary.

"This all goes back to 2022 when the Peace Officer Standards and Training commission created the new guidelines for use of force here in Massachusetts."

That law specifically states that police can't fire at a moving car unless someone could get hurt.

"If someone's life is in imminent threat or serious bodily injury or that of the officer, then they can still apply the use of deadly force," Carmichael said.

Calls for body camera footage to be released

Court documents say the body cam shows neither officer was in the car’s path — but the video hasn’t been released, not even to elected officials.

Boston City Councilor Miniard Culpepper wants the video made public to see if what witnesses say lines up — and give the community some clarity, saying they are traumatized by what they saw.

"The precedent has been set that the commissioner has brought in community leaders. In this case Councilor [Brian] Worrel and myself were looking to see it," Culpepper said. "It bothers me in that situation that we end up with a young man who lost his life through poor decision making by the police officer."

Culpepper, who says he hasn't seen anything from the body camera, is calling for a clear policy on when that footage will be released — if not to the public, then at least to public officials.

"Why not release it, because releasing it well will answer a lot of unmet questions," Lindauer said.

title: Boston police officer shot by man during shootout near Roxbury park
text:
A Boston police officer was wounded during an exchange of gunfire with a man being chased on foot early Friday morning in Roxbury, not far from Nubian Square, officials said. The man was shot as well; both are expected to survive.

The police department confirmed the incident started when officers saw a group of suspicious people loitering in the park at Dudley and Washington streets in Roxbury around 12:45 a.m. As officers approached to see what was going on, one man ran away, with officers chasing after him.

As the man turned onto Kenilworth Street, police say, he fired at the officers, striking the one officer in the arm. Police returned fire, hitting the suspect multiple times.

Both the officer who was struck and the suspect were taken to separate area hospitals for treatment of non-life threatening injuries.

Four other officers were also taken to the hospital, police said. It wasn't immediately clear why.

Gunfire rang out during the shootout and was picked up by a nearby Ring doorbell camera. The homeowner said she was shaking, and that she was even more unsettled after learning what happened.

The suspect was under arrest at the hospital, according to police, who identified him Friday afternoon as Daiquan Rice, 31. He faces an attempted murder charge, as well as gun and drug charges. It wasn't immediately clear if he had an attorney who could speak to the charges.

Police said they recovered one high-capacity firearm with an extended magazine from the man at the scene of the shooting, as well a rock-like substance in two plastic bags that fell from his pocket.

The identity of the officer who was shot will not be released, police said.

City officials including Mayor Michelle Wu and Police Commissioner Michael Cox both responded to the scene and spoke about gun violence and the dangers that officers face every day.

"This is another example of the amount of guns that are out here, but we're extremely and deeply proud of officers for what they do daily, and we're very very lucky and fortunate that there's no loss of life today," Cox said.

"Another reminder of the kinds of risks that our officers face," Wu added. "It's just not okay for violence to be happening anywhere in the City of Boston."

The incident was under investigation by the firearms discharge investigative team, according to police, who said investigators were still on scene hours after the shooting.

title: Boston police seek Roxbury woman missing since last weekend
text:
Police are searching for a Boston woman who has been missing for over a week.

The Boston Police Department said Monday that it was searching for 50-year-old Maria Ines Goncalves of Roxbury, last seen on Maywood Street on Dec. 21.

Goncalves is described as being a Black woman, about 5 feet tall and 145 pounds, with brown eyes, short black hair and a thin build.

When she was last seen, police say she was wearing a black hat, a black jacket, grey cargo pants and sneakers with red and white.

Police say Goncalves is reported to have mental health complications.

Anyone with information is asked to call 617-343-4275 or dial 911. Anonymous tips can also be left by calling 1-800-494-TIPS or by texting "TIP" to 27463.

title: Boston police sergeant charged with aggravated rape of a minor
text:
A longtime Boston police officer has been charged with aggravated rape of a minor and other charges, according to the Suffolk District Attorney's Office.

Paul Downey, 58, of West Roxbury, was arraigned at 2:30 p.m. in Boston Municipal Court, but as no attorney was available to represent him, the judge didn't allow prosecutors to state the details of the case. Downey stood with his back to the courtroom for the duration of the brief hearing.

Resources for victims of sexual assault are available through the National Sexual Violence Resources Center and the National Sexual Assault Telephone Hotline at 800-656-4673, and Massachusetts provides this list of statewide and resources for sexual assault survivors.

A not guilty plea was entered on Downey's behalf on four counts of aggravated rape of a minor, two counts of sexual conduct with a child under 18 and two counts of electronic enticement of a child for sexual activity. He was ordered held without bail overnight pending a hearing Tuesday, when a defense attorney is expected to be available.

According to the commonwealth's statement of facts, around March 26 Downey connected with a 14-year-old boy through the Grindr dating app, then took the conversation to Snapchat. Downey allegedly agreed to pay the teen for oral sex. Prosecutors say Downey then picked the victim up, took him to a parking lot near the South Bay mall, and raped him. Downey allegedly paid the victim $50.

Prosecutors say Downey continued to message the victim and eventually asked to meet again for sex. He is accused of meeting the teen again on May 11, driving to the same parking lot and raping the victim, paying $80.

Snapchat records helped identify Downey as a possible suspect through an IP address. The victim also provided information, including a physical description and possible license plate number, which was similar one on a vehicle driven by Downey. The victim further identified Downey through a photo array, prosecutors say.

Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox issued a statement following Downey's court hearing, saying "These charges are obviously very troubling and our thoughts are with any alleged victims. We have faith in the Massachusetts State Police and the SCDAO to conduct a thorough investigation. The officer was immediately placed on administrative leave."

Downey has been with the Boston Police Department since 1991 and his current rank is sergeant.

No further details have been released.

title: Boston police sergeant charged with raping 14-year-old boy to appear in court
text:
A Boston police sergeant accused of raping a 14-year-old boy he met on a dating app was back in court on Tuesday morning.

Paul Downey, 58, of West Roxbury, was arraigned Monday in Boston Municipal Court, but as no attorney was available to represent him, the judge didn't allow prosecutors to state the details of the case. Downey stood with his back to the courtroom for the duration of the brief hearing.

Resources for victims of sexual assault are available through the National Sexual Violence Resources Center and the National Sexual Assault Telephone Hotline at 800-656-4673, and Massachusetts provides this list of statewide and resources for sexual assault survivors.

A not guilty plea was entered on Downey's behalf on four counts of aggravated rape of a minor, two counts of sexual conduct with a child under 18 and two counts of electronic enticement of a child for sexual activity. He was ordered held without bail overnight pending a hearing Tuesday, when a public defender would be available.

At Tuesday's hearing, Downey again mostly stood with his back to the courtroom, but occasionally looked to the side, his face covered with a mask. A judge ordered him held on $250,000 cash bail, as requested by prosecutors. They said they were asking for such high bail because of the seriousness of the charges and because Downey has significant resources, having earned in the area of $280,000 last year.

Downey's public defender, Victoria Campbell, had asked for $40,000 bail, saying Downey and his family couldn't afford anything higher.

According to court documents, Downey connected with a 14-year-old boy through the Grindr dating app around March 26 and then took the conversation to Snapchat. Downey allegedly agreed to pay the teen for oral sex. Prosecutors say Downey then picked the victim up, took him to a parking lot near the South Bay mall, and raped him. Downey allegedly paid the victim $50.

In court Tuesday, prosecutors revealed that the child said in a Snapchat message to Downey ahead of that meetup, "That's too low. I'm 14, you know, I'm young, and you're asking me to commit a crime."

Downey allegedly responded, "How about $80?"

Prosecutors said Downey continued to message the victim and eventually asked to meet again for sex. He is accused of meeting the teen again on May 11, driving to the same parking lot and raping the victim, paying $80.

Video surveillance images allegedly showed Downey's vehicle parked at the South Bay mall on March 26 for about 10 minutes, around the same time the victim texted his friend saying, "He's here."

Snapchat records helped identify Downey as a possible suspect through an IP address. The victim also provided information, including a physical description and possible license plate number, which was similar one on a vehicle driven by Downey. The victim further identified Downey through a photo array, prosecutors say.

Downey has been with the Boston Police Department since 1991 and his current rank is sergeant.

Boston Police Commissioner Michael Cox issued a statement Monday, saying "These charges are obviously very troubling and our thoughts are with any alleged victims. We have faith in the Massachusetts State Police and the SCDAO to conduct a thorough investigation. The officer was immediately placed on administrative leave."

title: Meet the people behind Boston Public Library's free cooking classes, spice bank
text:
The Boston Public Library serves up more than just books. Inside its Nutrition Lab in Roxbury, residents can explore new recipes and learn how to make simple, nutritious meals — free of charge.

Kayla Tab is the chef-in-residence this year, helping people build confidence in the kitchen through nutrition literacy and more.

"They have a lot of fun getting their hands dirty, learning new things, and also just spending time with people in their community and getting to know new faces. We get to cook together and we get to eat together," Tabb said. "The more that people are aware of and comfortable with different types of vegetables, different proteins, cooking them, it becomes a lot easier for them to do that at home for themselves."

The lab offers hands-on classes and demonstrations to anyone in the city.

"My classes right now have been in the evenings on Monday nights," said Tabb. "I like to include a lot of cultural and historical information about what it is that we're cooking and the country of origin."

The California native said creating a delicious meal doesn't have to break the bank.

"I also try to make sure that the ingredients that at least show up in my recipes and in my classes are also pretty accessible," Tabb explained. "Sometimes there are extra ingredients for people to take home and try it out themselves. That's the beauty of cooking from scratch too. Your money can stretch a lot further."

The Boston Public Library also has a "spice bank" to help people access seasoning.

"That was kind of a gap I saw in food pantries," said nutrition literacy coordinator, Stephanie Chase.

It's an effort she hopes will inspire others to embrace cultural identity without having to worry about cost.

"If people are curious about food, if you're using a food pantry and you're wondering about a spice or a culture, that's kind of an inroad into learning more about another part of the world," said Chase.

Tabb's classes may be filling up -- but she's just getting started.

"Food is so much more than just health and calories in and calories out. It's also about enjoyment, it's about connection and all of these things," said Tabb. "Coming to a class at the Nutrition Lab gives you an opportunity to explore those things, to reinforce those ideas and also just to be reminded that everybody's doing the best that they can. But there's also space for people to help you out and help you grow and progress and things like that."

title: Woman charged in daylight stabbing of 65-year-old at Boston park
text:
A woman has been charged with first-degree murder in a daylight stabbing at a Boston park last month, prosecutors said Monday, sharing new details about the killing.

Rasheedah Hughes was ordered held without bail after her arraignment in Boston Municipal Court's Roxbury courthouse Monday, according to the Suffolk County District Attorney's Office. She's accused of killing Celia Simmons on Saturday, Nov. 16, at Ramsey Park.

Simmons, who's been remembered as a caring member of the community, is believed to have been killed after a fight that escalated. Prosecutors say that Hughes brandished a boxcutter and that Simmons hit her with her cane, and that Hughes left, only to come back with what was witnesses called a large knife.

Hughes allegedly stabbed Simmons repeatedly — the 65-year-old's stabbing was reported about 12:48 p.m. and officers found her stabbed multiple times.

Investigators identified Hughes through interviews with witness, video and more, according to prosecutors. Police said over the weekend that she was arrested Friday afternoon on Hammond Street, which leads to Ramsay Park.

It wasn't immediately clear if she had an attorney who could speak to her murder charge — the 40-year-old is due back in court Jan. 23.

"This appears to be a middle-of-the-day altercation that went to the very worst of extremes," District Attorney Kevin Hayden said in a statement. "As we see time and again, this type of quick, careless decision-making ends lives and ruins others. My sympathies go out to the family and friends of Celia Simmons as we begin the process of seeking accountability for the person charged with her death."

Nichole Powell has told NBC10 Boston that Simmons, whom she met while living in a shelter, didn't deserve what happened to her.

"She's a good person. She's a decent lady," Powell said.

title: Snow piling up at Boston's ‘snow farms' as students return to school in city
text:
The snow emergency and parking ban in Boston have been lifted, and students are returning to school in the city today thanks in part to the city's so-called "snow farms."

More snow is expected Wednesday on the heels of the 17 inches Boston got during the blizzard, but Wu said Tuesday that a significant amount of snow had been cleared overnight, and large-scale removal was underway.

“Thank you to all our City workers for the nonstop hard work to keep everyone safe, and thank you to our residents for doing your part,” Mayor Michelle Wu said in a statement Tuesday announcing the updates. “Because of the intensive efforts during this extended period, including operationalizing large-scale daytime snow removal for the first time ever, we’ve been able to get ahead of more snow expected [Wednesday] with major thoroughfares clear and passable."

In addition to the cleanup efforts by city teams, there were citywide snow shoveling meet-ups on Tuesday, which brought together volunteers to help clear sidewalks, curb ramps, and areas of concern during snow emergencies.

"We continue to remind all property owners to clear their sidewalks so neighbors can safely navigate the streets," Wu added. "Thank you for continuing to be a good neighbor, and stay safe.”

The city has 14 snow farms, and what happens is dump trucks pick up snow from the city and bring it to one of the properties like the former West Roxbury High School site to get it out of the way.

"We're piling the snow away from intersections mid block and then they'll get taken overnight. Usually we only do removal overnight because it involves getting large trucks there and the front loaders and that can really disrupt traffic," Wu explained.

Crews have already removed 165 loads totaling 4,620 cubic yards of snow, according to Wu. They were continuing to create snow piles around schools Tuesday in preparation for the night's snow removal operations.

Wu says the snow farms can handle all of this snow, so there's no need to dump in the Boston Harbor.

But it's been all hands on deck to clear it out, even the National Guard helped out by shoveling snow at bus stops and on sidewalks in the city.

So what happens to the snow at the farms now? Melting operations, which were paused for the blizzard, will begin at a number of the city’s snow farms again to create more space for the removal efforts.

But the city is also looking at other options. Next Tuesday, City Councilor Ed Flynn is holding a hearing on buying snow melting machines. Councilors will also discuss other snow removal strategies.

Boston isn't alone in having nowhere to put the snow. In Brockton, where more than 30 inches fell Monday after 20 inches fell in another storm a few weeks ago, crews have been working around the clock to dig people out.

Major thoroughfares are clear, but smaller streets have been a problem, with vehicles getting stuck.

Mayor Moises Rodrigues, who has been in office for under 50 days, says it's been chaotic.

"We're operating minus 80 pieces of equipment," he said. "We can't create equipment. And the city itself cannot go out and buy enough of those equipment, because what happens in the offseason is when you don't have snow, it's personnel -- it costs a great deal of money to keep a city running, so people need to understand that now, we've got all hands on deck."

Rodrigues explained that in past years, the city would have up to 160 pieces of equipment, but that it has been down for years due to lost contractors.

He said that while a travel ban is in place, people are still traveling, complicating the cleanup process.

"We can't clean streets if cars are in the streets," Rodrigues said. "We can't clean streets if cars are not obeying the rules and the regs."

The mayor added that the city is considering canceling school through the end of the week.

title: Person shot in Jamaica Plain, victim flees scene on MBTA bus
text:
A person was shot in Boston's Jamaica Plain neighborhood on Tuesday morning and fled the scene on a bus before police were able to locate them.

Boston police said they responded to the area of 64 School St. around 9:30 a.m. for a report of shots fired. The victim had apparently taken a bus from the scene and got off at Humboldt Avenue and Seaver Street. MBTA Transit Police were notified and responded.

Boston police officers assigned to Roxbury ultimately located the victim suffering from a gunshot wound. The victim was taken to a local hospital and is expected to survive, police said.

A crime scene was located at Dixwell Street and School Street, police said. No arrests have been made and the investigation is ongoing. A photo from the scene showed about a half dozen Boston police officers gathered in the street at the shooting scene, with at least one bullet mark on the ground in front of a local restaurant.

title: Student stabbed inside high school in Boston, 2 schools briefly placed in safety mode
text:
Police are investigating after a student was stabbed inside a high school in Boston's Roxbury neighborhood on Wednesday.

Boston police said officers responded to Madison Park High School at 75 Malcolm X Boulevard, shortly after noon on Wednesday for a report of a person who had been stabbed in the building.

Upon arrival, officers found a 17-year-old male suffering from a minor stab wound. He was taken to a local hospital and is expected to survive. Boston Public Schools confirmed the victim was a student at the school.

Police said preliminary investigation indicates that the incident occurred in a common hallway inside the school

The suspect fled out of the school. No arrests have been made, and police said their investigation remains active.

Aerial images showed police searching the area around the school with K9 units.

A text message alert sent to parents said that Madison High School and the nearby O'Bryant School were placed in safety mode because of a security issue. Parents were advised not to come to the school.

Boston Public Schools said in a statement just before 2 p.m. that school operations had returned to normal.

"The safety of our students and staff is our highest priority, and we are taking this incident very seriously. Our district crisis response team will be at the school today and for the rest of the week to support our school community," the statement said.

title: At work with a Boston veterans outreach team: ‘I do therapy sessions on the street'
text:
This Veterans Day, communities across Massachusetts honored the men and women who have served our country with pride.

At the State House, people gathered for the annual Veterans Day Ceremony to thank the nation's heroes.

"Today is a day of reverence, it's a day of respect. It should also be a day of celebration," said Gov. Maura Healey. "Veterans will continue to inspire and they will continue to keep this nation on course."

In Quincy, that spirit of freedom was on full display as a parade marched through the city. In West Roxbury, German Centre Skilled Nursing celebrated 15 years of its annual Veterans Day Program honoring its more than 25 residents who bravely served.

But beyond the day's celebrations, so many veterans also rely on year-round support. That's where Pine Street Inn's Veterans Outreach team comes in.

"We don't ever expect people to come to us. We bring the services to them," said Amanda Proctor, a clinical supervisor. "So it's their space and so it's about really slowly developing rapport with someone and being consistent."

The team helps unhoused veterans access benefits, medical care, mental health care and permanent housing. They also help bring clients to medical appointments.

On Tuesday, Proctor met with Miguel, an Army veteran whom she has been working with for 12 years.

"Just support," said Miguel when asked how Proctor has helped him over the years. "Support in every way that she can."

Proctor says the key is showing up consistently for the people who showed up for our country.

"Just want to bring everything to them. We'll sit on the sidewalk and do a housing application or disability benefits claim," Proctor added. "I do therapy sessions on the street and work on treatment plans. Just everything that could happen in an office happens outside."

The team will also bring their clients supplies, including food, water, hygiene products and clothing. Donations are always welcome.

"We want to go beyond just survival," said Proctor. "We want to get to thriving, where people are reconnected to community and finding their purpose in the world."

title: Potentially harmful algae bloom in part of Charles River, Boston health officials say
text:
Health officials in Massachusetts are warning people and their pets to avoid part of the Charles River due to a potentially harmful cyanobacteria algae bloom.

The Boston Public Health Commission alerted residents Friday to the finding that is impacting the Charles River Lower Basin downstream of the Massachusetts Avenue Bridge.

Staff from the Massachusetts Department of Public Health conducted the assessment of the pond and identified the presence of cyanobacteria exceeding DPH guidelines for recreational waterbodies in the state.

Cyanobacteria, also known as blue-green algae, produce toxins that can make people and pets sick, according to health officials, who urged residents to avoid contact with the water and any areas of algae concentration, even on shore. It can sometimes make the water look like pea soup or paint. Toxins may be present within the algae cells or in the water.

Tips

Avoid direct contact with the water and impacted shoreline, including swimming and other water activities.

Do not allow dogs to swim in or drink the water. Pet owners should call their veterinarian immediately if an animal develops symptoms such as vomiting, staggering, drooling or convulsions.

These symptoms present themselves soon after exposure. Dogs have been known to eat the scum that washes ashore and lick scum out of their fur.

If you, your child, or your pet comes in contact with the water or algae on the shoreline, rinse off immediately.

Local

In-depth news coverage of the Greater Boston and New England area.

The primary concern for people is ingesting water containing blue-green algae while swimming. A secondary concern is direct skin contact and inhalation of water droplets. For dogs, the primary concern is the ingestion of water containing blue-green algae or scum that has washed ashore or gotten onto their skin or fur.

Health officials say contact may cause skin and eye irritation, and inhalation can cause respiratory irritation and exacerbate pre-existing respiratory conditions. Ingestion can cause acute gastrointestinal symptoms, such as vomiting and diarrhea.

If the blue-green algae are producing toxins, the health effects can be more serious, especially for children and small pets due to their smaller body weights. These health effects can include issues with the functioning of the liver, kidneys, and/or neurological systems. In severe cases toxins produced by blue-green algae can result in death.

In Massachusetts and in many other states, canine deaths have been documented due to the ingestion of harmful algae. A woman told NBC10 Boston last month that her 16-year-old dog, Dobby, died just hours after a swim at Millenium Park in Boston's West Roxbury neighborhood. Veterinarians say cyanobacteria is likely to blame.

When will this advisory be lifted?

Harmful algae blooms are most common in the summer months when warm sunny conditions promote algae growth. They can last for weeks in the summertime or may disappear quickly. The Mass. DPH will continue to monitor cyanobacteria algae levels in the area and will conduct sampling for laboratory analysis once the bloom has dissipated.

The advisory cannot be lifted until two rounds of samples collected a week apart are below the threshold of 70,000 cells/milliliter of water.

Anyone who would like more information can contact the Boston Public Health Commission's environmental and occupational health division at 617-534-5965.

title: What to know about the Charles River's potentially harmful algae bloom
text:
Massachusetts health officials are warning people and pets to avoid part of the Charles River while they look into a potentially harmful cyanobacteria bloom.

The Massachusetts Department of Public Health on Tuesday issued an advisory for the river between Kendrick Street in Needham and Spring Street in West Roxbury. The affected area includes Cutler Park and Millennium Park.

Warning signs are now posted at access points along the river.

“I just noticed them and people have been talking about them where I live,” dog owner Brian Drayton said.

The advisory is changing how some dog owners use the area.

“He was just trying to get near the water and last time we went for a walk with him, we actually allowed him to drink some of the water. So now we pulled him away from the water and tried to keep him safe,” dog owner Angie Almonte said.

The warning comes after a dog died from liver failure following a possible exposure to algal toxins near Millennium Park. State health officials have not confirmed that cyanobacteria caused the dog’s illness or death.

The type of algae suspected in the area may be difficult to spot, said Marielena Lima, river science program manager for the Charles River Watershed Association.

“I’ve heard anecdotes from the dog owner saying, you know, the water looked clear, and that is possible with benthic cyanobacteria blooms,” Lima said.

Benthic cyanobacteria grow along the bottom of a body of water. Lima said that is different from the blooms people commonly see on the Charles River.

“Normally the kinds of cyanobacteria blooms we see in the Charles are more in the water column, so they’re towards the surface of the water and that’s why you see a green haze or scum on the top of the water surface,” she said.

Warm temperatures, sunlight, excess nutrient runoff after rainfall and stagnant or slow-moving water can promote cyanobacteria growth, according to the Department of Public Health.

“The way the temperatures have risen, we’re gonna get more and more of this so it’s something you sort of expect after a while,” Drayton said.

Some cyanobacteria can also produce toxins that may make people and animals sick. Exposure can cause skin and eye irritation, respiratory problems, vomiting and diarrhea. More serious cases can affect the liver, kidneys or nervous system.

People should avoid swimming, kayaking or coming into contact with the water or shoreline in the affected area. Pet owners should not allow animals to swim in or drink from the river.

Anyone who comes into contact with the water or algae should rinse off immediately. Pet owners should call a veterinarian if an animal develops symptoms such as vomiting, staggering, drooling or convulsions.

State health officials collected water samples Wednesday to test for cyanobacteria cells and toxins. Laboratory results are expected Thursday, and officials will issue updated recommendations after reviewing them.

title: Chelsea plans '39-day party' for World Cup, but still awaits FIFA license
text:
UPDATE (Tuesday, May 26, 2026): The city tells NBC10 Boston that its FIFA license has been approved.

With 20 days remaining before the start of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, the city of Chelsea, Massachusetts, moved ahead with plans for a 39-day celebration despite still waiting for approval to show tournament matches publicly.

City officials launched promotional campaigns for watch parties, soccer events and family activities planned throughout the tournament. Leaders said they expected the World Cup festivities to bring tourism dollars to local businesses while encouraging residents to gather in public again.

Chelsea City Manager Fidel Maltez noted 70% of the city is comprised of a Latino population, and 53% are foreign-born. He said immigration enforcement activity over the last year had hurt businesses and kept many residents from spending time downtown.

"We walked our streets in fear. We felt like we couldn't come outside. Our business owners complained about how our downtown was decimated," he said.

Maltez said the city hoped large public gatherings and increased local police presence would help residents feel safe during the tournament.

"Anytime that there was a large gathering, [ICE] shied away from it," he said.

The city has planned several English and Spanish watch parties in Chelsea Square and other activities tied to the World Cup.

Beginning June 11, Chelsea Square will be transformed into an outdoor gathering space for the tournament. Visitors can expect an outdoor large-screen viewing experience, local food vendors, music and community programming showcasing the cultures and traditions of the city's diverse community.

Chelsea Sports Tourism Director Charlie Giuffrida said officials wanted to create opportunities for local families and youth soccer players during the tournament.

"We want to make sure our youth soccer ecosystem and all of our community has some amazing things to do to capitalize on what's going to be, probably, one of the best summers North America's seen in a long time," said Giuffrida.

Maltez said the city allocated nearly $500,000 in combined state and local funding for the celebrations.

However, organizers said they still had not received FIFA licensing approval to broadcast matches during public watch parties.

"It's definitely scary that we're weeks away and we don't have a license yet," said the city's civic designer, Omar Miranda, who applied for a license several months ago.

Several other cities and towns hosting World Cup watch parties were also still waiting for FIFA approval, including Worcester, Brockton, Everett and Lexington.

Even if the license does not arrive in time, organizers said the city still planned to move forward with festivities.

"They're going to watch it in our businesses if they have to. We're just going to have a space for them to have fun and enjoy the celebrations," said Miranda. "Licenses or not, we're going to have a 38-, 39-day party here at Chelsea Square."

The City of Chelsea posted a watch party calendar on its website and is kicking off "Fiesta Fútbol" on Saturday with other public activities to follow:

Adult Soccer Tournament: 10:30 a.m. Saturday, May 23, at Highland Park, 45 Willow Street, Chelsea

The City is accepting 16 teams for an 8v8 double-elimination tournament. Teams are encouraged to play as their home or favorite nations — including Honduras, El Salvador, the United States, Mexico, and others — and wear culturally-themed gear. Pre-registration is required at recreation.chelseama.gov.

Soccer Field Day — Youth Soccer Community: 10:30 a.m. – 2:30 p.m. Saturday, June 6 at Highland Park, 45 Willow Street, Chelsea

Open to the entire Chelsea Youth Soccer Community, Soccer Field Day will feature mini soccer matches, a skills competition, inflatables, local vendors, and more. Families can learn about local soccer programs and register on-site. No pre-registration required.

Alumni Soccer Game: 10 a.m. Saturday, June 27 at Veterans Stadium, 299 Everett Ave, Chelsea

Chelsea soccer alumni ages 18 and older are invited back to the field for a friendly competition and a celebration of community pride. All are welcome, including those who attended private, vocational, or other schools. Players register by graduating year or decade and are grouped accordingly. Games are continuous 7-v-7 format beginning at 10 a.m.

title: ‘Not good': Closed pools make waves in Boston
text:
With summer underway and temperatures rising, several pools in Boston remained closed Monday, as many people looked for ways to cool down.

"That's not good, not good at all," said Keneth Jackson when he heard his community pool was closed for the summer. "I usually go every day, especially when it's hot."

Of the city's nearly 20 community pools, at least four of them will be closed for the entire summer for repairs and renovations. Boston Centers for Youth and Families operates three of those: the Holland in Dorchester, the Perkins in Dorchester and the Blackstone in the South End. Boston Public School's Madison Park in Roxbury is also closed for the summer.

"The Blackstone, unfortunately, the whole school needs to be rebuilt, so they won't invest in fixing the pool," said at-large City Councilor Erin Murphy. "But we definitely have neighborhoods that feel as though pools aren't open for them, so we have to address that."

Murphy held hearings over the winter in an effort to have more pools be ready to open in the summer.

In an email to NBC10 Boston, a Boston Centers for Youth and Families representative said the Hennigan in Dorchester is expected to open later in the summer. BCYF Mirabella in the North End and BCYF Condon are opening Tuesday. BCYF Mildred Avenue is also slated to open in July.

The Clougherty Pool in Charlestown just reopened over the weekend after a two-year, $35.5 million renovation project.

"It's a wonderful asset in the city. We should definitely have never let it get to that level of disrepair, so it did cost us a lot of money," Murphy said.

Mayor Michelle Wu said that, over the past three years, more than five pools have reopened under her administration and, by the end of the year, there will be more pools open in Boston that there have been in over a decade.

"We always do things as quickly as possible but on a schedule that can make sure that pools are open in the neighborhood. If we're going to close one to make repairs, hopefully another one is up and running so it's near enough in that vicinity," Wu added.

title: Man arrested after Dedham gas station employees assaulted, car stolen
text:
Two store employees were assaulted and a car was stolen from the same gas station in Dedham, Massachusetts, in three separate incidents on Saturday.

Dedham police say officers were dispatched the first of three times to Sam's Express, located at 2 Washington Street, around 9:09 a.m. for a report that a man had entered the store and assaulted an employee. A customer intervened, according to police, and escorted the man out of the store before police arrived on scene.

Responding officers tended to the victim, gathered evidence, canvassed the area and shared information about the incident with Massachusetts State Police, MBTA Transit Police and Boston Police.

Police were sent back to the gas station around 5:37 p.m. for another report of assault and battery on a second employee, who denied medical assistance from first responders.

Officers were unable to locate the suspect again, but a Boston police officer was able to identify him, police said.

At 10:44 p.m., police responded to the gas station for a third time after a customer reported that his vehicle had been stolen from the area of the gas pumps after he walked away from his vehicle to pay for gas.

The stolen vehicle was seen traveling on Washington Street towards Boston, according to police. Based on evidence obtained at the scene, investigators believed the car thief was the same person from the previous two assault and battery incidents.

An arrest warrant was obtained on Sunday to charge the suspect with two counts of assault and battery, trespassing and larceny of a motor vehicle.

Boston police were able to arrest John Laurent, 35, at his West Roxbury residence, police said, and he was transferred to the Dedham Police Department for processing.

The stolen vehicle was found in the area of 4975 Washington Street in West Roxbury, police added.

Laurent is due in Dedham District Court on Monday. It's unclear if he's obtained an attorney, or why he targeted that Dedham gas station repeatedly.

Further information was not immediately available.

title: Ex-Boston City Councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson sentenced in corruption case
text:
Former Boston City Councilor Tania Fernandes Anderson was sentenced Friday for wire fraud and theft involving federal funds, several months after she pleaded guilty in the federal corruption probe.

Federal Judge Indira Talwani sentenced Fernandes Anderson to a month of incarceration with three years of supervised release. The former councilor was ordered to pay $13,000 in restitution.

Fernandes Anderson spoke in court before the sentence was announced, telling the judge, "I can't forgive myself," "I'm sorry for everything" and "There is no excuse."

Speaking outside of court after the sentencing, Fernandes Anderson criticized news coverage of her.

"The reason why I don't talk to you is because you never report accurately on Black people," she told the media after her sentencing. "You're always causing some sort of trouble."

Prosecutors had sought a sentence of one year and one day in prison, followed by three years of supervised release and $13,000 restitution. Her public defender asked for probation and community service.

“Tania Fernandes Anderson was elected to serve her constituents but instead, she deliberately used her elected position as a Boston City Councilor to serve herself,” U.S. Attorney Leah B. Foley said in a statement Friday. “From Boston’s City Hall to the Massachusetts State House, to local and state public officials, this office will continue to aggressively root out and expose public corruption. Massachusetts taxpayers deserve an honest government and accountability. As federal prosecutors we have no fear nor favor, and there will be no blind eye or separate justice system for the powerful. The rule of law does not make exceptions for anyone, including someone like Tania Fernandes Anderson.”

Fernandes Anderson, who was arrested and indicted last December, pleaded guilty on May 5 to one count of wire fraud and one count of theft concerning a program receiving federal funds. In exchange, prosecutors dropped four wire fraud counts against the 46-year-old lawmaker, who in 2021 became the first African immigrant and Muslim-American elected to the council.

The guilty plea was a result of accusations that in 2023, Fernandes Anderson funneled a $13,000 bonus payment to a relative on her staff -- more than twice as much as the combined bonuses she gave to the rest of the staff.

The staffer received about $10,000 after taxes and withdrew the money in several bank transactions in May and June of 2023, before exchanging texts to meet Fernandes Anderson in a City Hall bathroom that June 9, where the staffer gave Fernandes Anderson $7,000 of the money in cash.

Prosecutors said Fernandes Anderson was facing personal financial difficulties that year, partly because the Massachusetts State Ethics Commission told her it would fine her $5,000 for hiring immediate family members. Council members aren’t permitted to hire immediate family members as paid staff.

Fernandes Anderson, who served as the city councilor for Boston's District 7, which includes Roxbury, Dorchester, Fenway and part of the South End, was first elected to a two-year term in November 2021 and won re-election in November 2023.

She submitted her letter of resignation to the city council in June, with her last day in office on the Fourth of July.

Fernandes Anderson has previously apologized to her constituents for her actions, telling NBC10 Boston in May, "I'm deeply sorry for all of the pain that you have endured. I'm deeply sorry for everything, every hardship that this has caused for you."

The former city councilor will have to report to prison to start serving her sentence at some point before mid October.

The Associated Press contributed to this report

title: New indictment for ex-Boston police sergeant charged with raping boy, 14
text:
A grand jury has indicted a former Boston police sergeant on charges he raped a 14-year-old boy he met on a dating app, prosecutors said Friday.

Paul Downey, a 57-year-old from West Roxbury, was previously charged in Boston Municipal Court, and a not guilty plea was entered on his behalf.

The grand jury's indictment elevates the case to Suffolk Superior Court, where he's due next Friday to face the new counts of aggravated rape of a minor, sexual conduct with a child under 18 and electronic enticement of a child for sexual activity. Grand juries review prosecutors' allegations and decide whether or not the evidence is sufficient to bring charges.

Resources for victims of sexual assault are available through the National Sexual Violence Resources Center and the National Sexual Assault Telephone Hotline at 800-656-4673, and Massachusetts provides this list of statewide and resources for sexual assault survivors.

Downey, who joined the force in 1991, was still with the Boston Police Department when he was first charged. Commissioner Michael Cox said at the time, in a statement, "These charges are obviously very troubling and our thoughts are with any alleged victims. We have faith in the Massachusetts State Police and the SCDAO to conduct a thorough investigation. The officer was immediately placed on administrative leave."

Downey resigned in July, a police representative said Friday.

According to court documents, Downey, whose age was previously given as 58, connected with a 14-year-old boy through the Grindr dating app around March 26 and then took the conversation to Snapchat. Downey allegedly agreed to pay the teen for oral sex. Prosecutors say Downey then picked the victim up, took him to a parking lot near the South Bay mall, and raped him. Downey allegedly paid the victim $50.

In court, prosecutors revealed that the child said in a Snapchat message to Downey ahead of that meetup, "That's too low. I'm 14, you know, I'm young, and you're asking me to commit a crime."

Downey allegedly responded, "How about $80?"

Prosecutors said Downey continued to message the victim and eventually asked to meet again for sex. He is accused of meeting the teen again on May 11, driving to the same parking lot and raping the victim, paying $80.

Video surveillance images allegedly showed Downey's vehicle parked at the South Bay mall on March 26 for about 10 minutes, around the same time the victim texted his friend saying, "He's here."

Snapchat records helped identify Downey as a possible suspect through an IP address. The victim also provided information, including a physical description and possible license plate number, which was similar one on a vehicle driven by Downey. The victim further identified Downey through a photo array, prosecutors say.

At his June hearing, Downey again mostly stood with his back to the courtroom, but occasionally looked to the side, his face covered with a mask. A judge ordered him held on $250,000 cash bail, as requested by prosecutors. They said they were asking for such high bail because of the seriousness of the charges and because Downey has significant resources, having earned in the area of $280,000 last year.

Downey's public defender, Victoria Campbell, had asked for $40,000 bail, saying Downey and his family couldn't afford anything higher.

title: Family of Boston man shot and killed by police holding news conference today
text:
The family of a man shot and killed by Boston police last month and their attorney, Ben Crump, held a press conference Thursday "to demand justice, transparency and full accountability," including the release of body camera video from the incident.

Stephenson King Jr., 39, was shot and killed by police responding to a carjacking on March 11. The Boston police officer who shot King, Nicholas O’Malley, 33, of Boston, is now facing a manslaughter charge.

"We're standing here for a reason — because we want justice for Stephenson," said Crump, a well-known civil rights and personal injury attorney whose previous clients have included the families of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor. "We refuse to let them sweep this under the rug. We refuse to let them act as if Stephenson's life didn't matter."

'We want everybody to understand that transparency is good for everybody. If the officer did nothing wrong, then we should be able to see it on the video. If the officer did something wrong, we should be able to see it on the video. Consequently, if Stephenson did something wrong, we should be able to see it on the video. Because transparency is good for all of us. It's good for the family, it's good for the Boston Police Department."

Crump said King struggled with mental health issues, and his family had tried to get him help earlier in the same day that he was shot and killed, saying that he was in a paranoid state. He was brought by ambulance to a hospital but somehow got out later in the day.

"Let it be known that just because you're having a mental health crisis doesn't mean you should be sentenced to death, and that police officer on the side of that street was the judge, the jury and the executioner," he said.

"We want to make sure police are not allowed to operate with impunity," Crump added. "He should have been given due process also, the same due process they're asking for Officer O'Malley, we want that same due process for Black people in Boston."

King's father, his father's fiancée and his three sisters also spoke at Thursday's press conference.

"My son wasn't perfect, but he was a great son," said Stephenson King Sr., a retired corrections officer. "He did a lot of things that made me happy and made his family happy... He shouldn't be dead. I tried to get some help. To see my son gone the way he's gone is very brokenhearted for me, personally. I apologize if I seem a little angry, but I am. I'm hurt, disappointed in everything that has happened."

He explained why the family believes it's so important to see the video of what happened.

"Was he scared? Was he looking at he wants to make it back home? Officers saying what he's saying to them and he's panicking that he's going to die," said King said.

"That day I put my son in an ambulance, I wasn't expecting him to be dead the same night," he added. "I want justice for my son. Everyone in this world should want justice like this for anything that happened to their family."

On the other side of the case, attorney David Yannetti, the original defense lawyer in the Karen Read case, announced Thursday that his law firm will be representing O'Malley going forward.

Yannetti wrote in a statement the DA prefers to "second guess the split-second decisions of police officers and punish them for trying to protect the public."

"We will not rest until Officer O'Malley is rightfully acquitted," he added.
