title: Cheverus profiles: Carolyn Caveny of St. Katharine Drexel Parish, Dorchester
text:
DORCHESTER -- On the tabernacle behind the altar of St. Katharine Drexel Parish in Dorchester is a symbol that is not often found in Catholic churches.

It is an image of a slender bird. Its feet are pointed forward, but its delicately curved head is pointed backward. This image, the sankofa, originates from the country of Ghana in West Africa. Sankofa is the Akan word meaning "retrieve." The word's pictorial symbol is a bird that is moving forward but looking back, always remembering its past. It is a fitting symbol for the Black Catholic community that St. Katharine Drexel represents.

"It's a symbol from God," said Carolyn Caveny, who has served as executive assistant to the parish for almost a decade.

Caveny, 86, has been part of Boston's Black Catholic community for over 50 years. She has seen the parishes of St. John-St. Hugh, St. Philip, and St. Francis de Sales in Dorchester and Roxbury merge to become St. Katharine Drexel in 2005. Before that, she was a Sister of St. Joseph of Carondelet, one of only a handful of white sisters teaching in Boston's predominantly Black Catholic schools during the racial tensions that gripped the city in the 60s and 70s. She was a woman religious for over 40 years before separating from the congregation in the 2000s in order to serve the Church in lay ministry. She is still close with the sisters, who remain an important part of her life. Like the sankofa, she looks back on her life and tries to understand where God has taken her.

"What I have seen and heard is that God has blessed me," she said. "I have had an extraordinary life, and I don't try to figure out why I came in 1971 to St. Joseph Community School. I don't try to figure out why I'm a member of a Black Catholic parish."

Caveny admits she can be "a little hard-headed" at times, but she has done her best to cooperate with the Holy Spirit. She knows she's "not going to be messing around with God's mysterious gifts."

For her contributions to St. Katharine Drexel, Caveny was among 150 people who received the Cheverus Award in 2025. The annual archdiocesan awards, named after Boston's first bishop, honor those who have given long-time service to the Church.

"She has worked tirelessly to help make St. Katharine Drexel what we are today," wrote Father Oscar Pratt, the parish pastor, when nominating Caveny for the award. "I can think of no one more deserving of this award."

For her, the award was not only for herself but for all of St. Katharine Drexel Parish.

"The recognition of dedicated service to God's people, in a real sense, is the dedicated service of the parishioners here to each other, and also to our outreach as it relates to social justice," she said.

She is part of a five-person team that meets every two weeks to discuss happenings in the parish, and a member of the 10-person team responsible for the upcoming Drexel Village housing project, which will provide 217 units of affordable housing on the site of the St. Katharine Drexel Parish Center in Roxbury. The generosity of the parish has become "evident" to her.

"I'm not talking about financial generosity alone," she said. "I'm talking about how people care about what happens to other people."

Caveny grew up in an all-white community in Syracuse, New York.

"Segregation was alive and well," she said. "It still is."

She first came to Roxbury in 1971, a few years after she professed her vows, to work on her master's degree in philosophy at Newton College of the Sacred Heart. She said her vocation was "God's invitation at that particular time."

"I didn't know at that time that was a mysterious gift," she said.

Sister Sylvia Thibodeaux of the Sisters of the Holy Family, one of the oldest Black religious orders in the U.S., enlisted her to teach seventh and eighth grade at St. Joseph Community School. St. Joseph, St. John, and St. Francis schools were set up in Boston as an initiative of the National Black Sisters' Conference. Most of the students, and most of the sisters teaching them, were Black.

"I was welcomed, I was taught, I was loved," Caveny said. "I had expectations. And the first thing I noticed, the first thing that intrigued me, was Black spirituality."

She now considers Black spirituality to be "a precious gift" in the Church.

"In Black spirituality, there is no dualism, so you can be happy and sad at the same time," she said. "You can also hope in the midst of despair, and the continued fight for freedom continues through the teachings, through the lives, the faith, and hope of the ancestors."

Her work in the schools coincided with Boston's desegregation busing crisis and extreme tension between the city's Black and white residents.

"It was very clear within a couple of months that the children and youth I had in seventh and eighth grade were absolutely my focus," she said. "In that school and the other two schools, you were expected to thrive."

One of her former students is now a parishioner at St. Katharine Drexel.

"What stands out for me is the success of all of these young people coming from these three schools," she said.

During weekly meetings at St. Joseph's, students would say "the African Pledge." Since Caveny was white, she wasn't sure if she should say the Pledge along with her students. Eventually, she had no problem saying it. The community had welcomed her as one of their own. The Pledge went, "We will work, study, and listen, so we may learn, so we may teach."

Teaching children was Caveny's lifelong calling. In 1988, she became director of student support services at Emmanuel College. She led the TRIO Student Support Services Project for first-generation college students from "economically disadvantaged backgrounds." Disliking that label for students in need, she changed the program's name to Success for the Self-Determined Student. She later served Emmanuel as an assistant dean of academic advising, where her interest in social justice and anti-racism advocacy continued. After leaving Emmanuel, she fell and broke her wrist in three places. That didn't stop her from volunteering at St. Katharine Drexel.

"I am determined," she said.

Caveny still lives in Roxbury. Seeing how much the neighborhood has changed over the past half-century has been "bittersweet."

"In some ways, the effects of racism are still alive and well," she said. "They're alive and well in housing situations, they're alive and well in school systems, they're alive and well in how people are not represented to the degree that they should be in the Church, in the city, in the state, etc."

A woman in the neighborhood once asked Caveny, "Are you Catholic?"

Caveny replied that she is Catholic "with a small c," referencing the word's meaning as "universal."

"I follow the teachings of Jesus," she told the woman, "the poor Jew from Nazareth, who excluded no one."

title: Archdiocese finalizes plans for National Eucharistic Pilgrimage
text:
BRAINTREE -- Since May 24, a small group of perpetual pilgrims has been on a Eucharistic pilgrimage along the Eastern U.S. in celebration of the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, passing some of the holiest and most historic sites in the country until July 5.

The One Nation Under God National Eucharistic Pilgrimage will visit the Archdiocese of Boston from June 26 to 28. On June 26, the pilgrims will stop for Divine Liturgy at Our Lady of the Annunciation Melkite Cathedral in West Roxbury, then go down to Pilgrim Memorial State Park in Plymouth for adoration beside Plymouth Rock. A procession will take the Blessed Sacrament from the park to Downtown Plymouth for a Mass at St. Peter Church celebrated by Archbishop Richard G. Henning. On June 27, a 2.5-mile procession will take the Blessed Sacrament from Boston Common along the Freedom Trail and some of the most hallowed sites in U.S. history, concluding with adoration at Bunker Hill in Charlestown. Later that afternoon, there will be a Votive Mass of the Sacred Heart celebrated by Archbishop Henning at the Cathedral of the Holy Cross. The original plan for June 28 was that the archbishop would celebrate Mass on the Lexington Battle Green, but he will now be celebrating Mass at St. Brigid Parish instead. A procession will then bring the Blessed Sacrament to the Battle Green, where the Revolutionary War began, for adoration. Throughout the weekend, the perpetual pilgrims will be visiting young adult communities in the archdiocese's parishes. They will also attend Mass at Regina Cleri, Boston's home for retired priests.

Devotions throughout the weekend will take place in many languages. Representatives from the Archdiocese of Boston's African, Asian, Brazilian, Hispanic, and Polish communities, among others, will participate in the processions. Members of the archdiocese's Filipino Catholic community will provide first aid and nursing support during the processions, representing the prominence of Filipino Americans in Boston's healthcare industry.

"Their participation beautifully reflects the spirit of accompaniment, service, and compassionate care that lies at the heart of our Eucharistic witness," said Wendy Mejia, Archdiocese of Boston director of multicultural ministry.

Mejia said the weekend's devotions will honor the history of contributions that immigrants have made to both the U.S. and the Catholic Church throughout their shared history.

"While we speak many languages, come from different cultures, traditions, and languages, we are united by our faith in the real presence of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist," she said.

In a video posted to the Archdiocese of Boston's website, Archbishop Henning compared the pilgrimage to Paul Revere's ride. Rather than warning that "The British are coming," the archbishop said the pilgrimage's message is a hopeful one: "Jesus is coming."

"This pilgrimage is an invitation to place our lives, our communities, and our country under the sovereignty of Christ, to truly be one nation under God," he said.

When the pilgrimage makes its way through New England, Ben Wallace plans to join the pilgrims as much as he can. Wallace, 30, lives in New Hampshire but attends daily Mass at Holy Rosary Shrine in Lawrence. Much of his education in the faith took place in the Archdiocese of Boston, in parishes such as St. Leonard of Port Maurice in Boston's North End and St. Mary of the Assumption in Brookline. The pilgrimage will pass these churches, as well as ones where he and his family received their sacraments.

"It feels like this really sweet, nostalgic farewell to the region before I go wherever God is leading me," Wallace said.

In August, Wallace will become a postulant for the Franciscan Friars of the Renewal. The order's "super radical, Eucharistic, contemplative life" appealed to him. Everything the friars do flows from the Eucharist, and Wallace, who spends much time in adoration, wants the same for himself.

"The Lord had more in mind for us at his Eucharist than just a symbol," he said. "He had his very presence there."

He also wants to help people like his brother, who struggled with addiction before dying of an overdose in 2021. Wallace, who had drifted from his Catholic faith, had no one to turn to after his brother's death.

"I felt a lot of despair, and from that point, I was grasping for answers," he said.

A month after his brother died, Wallace had a vision of Christ on the cross. Waking up, he thought to himself, "Oh boy, this is all real. Jesus is real."

He started attending a Protestant church, then returned to the Catholic Church, wanting the real presence of Jesus in the Eucharist.

"Jesus is here," he said. "He's present in his Church, and he wants us every single day we can, to go to church every day. Why wouldn't we do that if we really believe that Jesus is who he says he is?"

He said the pilgrimage comes at "a really interesting time in our country," with the 250th anniversary and the U.S. bishops consecrating the nation to the Sacred Heart of Jesus.

"This feels like an absolute way of bringing our Lord through the streets and hopefully bringing more souls to Christ," he said.

More information on the pilgrimage and events is available at bostoncatholic.org/national-Eucharistic-pilgrimage.

title: Harvard Catholic Center alum takes helm at Black Catholic news outlet
text:
CAMBRIDGE -- As a journalist, Sheila Hodges wants to tell the stories of people who have often been misunderstood -- prisoners, homeless people, immigrants, and the like. Pope Francis called them those on "the peripheries."

Black Catholics like herself, she said, are also often misunderstood. As a group, they are more diverse than most people realize, including immigrants from Africa and the Caribbean among their numbers. Their liturgical traditions, including Gospel music, dancing, and verbal outcries during Mass, are equally diverse.

Hodges said almost all Black Catholics can relate to the experience of talking about their faith to non-Catholic Black people who are surprised that Black Catholics even exist.

"In general, I think there can be a misunderstanding, or lack of understanding the experience of being Black and Catholic," she said. "I think there historically have been a lot of challenges living within the intersection of those two identities."

Hodges, 24, is the new CEO and editor of the Black Catholic Messenger, an independent nonprofit online publication written by and for Black Catholics. Founded in 2020, the Messenger, according to its website, wants to "reiterate that Black Catholic advocacy is entirely compatible with Church teachings," while challenging the stereotype of Black Catholics as "exotic or even pitiful."

Hodges has always dreamed of heading her own media company. As an elementary schooler, she was a TV host for the school news crew and idolized Oprah Winfrey. Eventually, her dream evolved to heading her own Black Catholic media company.

"It's honestly so surreal to see the fruits of my prayer and that God, he recognizes that I have this desire and he fulfilled it," she said.

Boston, Hodges said, was where she received her formation. She attended Harvard Divinity School and received a master's degree in theological studies in 2026. She took classes with seminarians at St. John's Seminary in Brighton. At the Harvard Catholic Center, she was surrounded by people of every description -- students, professors, young professionals, and families -- all wanting to understand their faith.

"They're constantly having reading groups and various talks on very nerdy theological topics, but once again, I think what's cool is, no one finds these things weird," she said.

She led the HCC Women's Group and started the Verbum Dei Gospel reflection group for people in their 20s. Both of those ministries inspired the kinds of stories she wants to tell in the Messenger.

"I have been exposed to so many riches within the Catholic Church, and I think my desire is for everyone to have access to those things," she said.

Hodges will soon be moving from Boston to Washington, D.C., to be close to Catholic institutions like the USCCB, Catholic University of America, and Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception. Her "deepest regret" has been not getting to visit St. Katharine Drexel, the Archdiocese of Boston's Black Catholic parish in Roxbury. She hopes she can visit it before she moves to D.C., or when she comes back to Boston. She wants the Messenger to feature the testimonies of Black Catholics -- how they found the faith and how they are living it.

"I want to hear from Black Catholic FOCUS missionaries," she said. "I want to hear from the Black Catholic lawyers, the Black Catholic moms. How are they living their faith day by day?"

She also wants to start a regular faith formation column featuring spiritual reflections by Black Catholic priests and religious, especially for Black Catholics who don't have access to their own parishes and communities. The priests and religious would also answer common questions non-Catholics have about the faith.

"I think, particularly given the history of race relations in this country, I think it's very inspiring that Black people have clung to the Catholic faith despite all the difficulties and despite all the obstacles," she said.

When she first came to Boston, the only Black people she saw were doormen. She was shocked, so she went up to one of the doormen and asked, "Where are all the Black people?" The doorman explained that high rents and gentrification have effectively segregated the city.

"Despite all of that, I genuinely have felt so loved by the Catholic community here," she said.

Hodges grew up in Orange Park, Florida. She attended St. Catherine of Siena Parish there. The parish was diverse, with large Hispanic and Filipino communities. She also attended St. Pius V, a historically Black Catholic parish in Jacksonville, where she was an altar server.

"I grew up in a single-parent household," she said, "and although that came with its challenges, I would say the biggest gift in that is that I had my mom, who was such a role model of how one ought to connect the Catholic faith with their daily lives."

Her mom taught her to see God every day and everywhere. While studying communications at the University of Pennsylvania, Hodges was the West Philadelphia beat reporter for the student newspaper.

West Philadelphia has a reputation for violent crime, but Hodges wanted to go deeper than that. She wrote about Black-owned businesses and other topics that humanized the neighborhood's residents. When reporting on gun violence, she didn't want to simply write "this person got shot." She focused on community members trying to stop the violence, and reframed shootings as a public health epidemic. Her goal was to bring "a bit more empathy and nuance" into the conversation.

"There was a strong desire in me to connect my gift for storytelling with Catholicism," she said.

She interned with Ascension Press and contributed to Penn Epistle, the university's Christian journal. In 2023, she met Nate Tinner-Williams, co-founder of the Black Catholic Messenger, at a U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops listening session for Black Catholics in New Orleans. Tinner-Williams invited her to join the Messenger's Board of Directors.

"I think he saw all the wonderful ideas I had and the passion I had for the publication, and I think that ultimately led everyone to have a lot of confidence in nominating me for the position," she said.

Hodges spoke to The Pilot on Aug. 1, her first day on the job. To handle the responsibility, her spiritual director gave her this advice: when talking about her life, instead of saying "I" or "me," to say "we."

"God is doing this with me, and so that has made all of this a lot less daunting," she said.

title: Report: Federal aid helped Catholic schools avoid pandemic learning loss
text:
BRAINTREE -- As schools across the U.S. see lagging test scores since the COVID-19 pandemic, especially in low-income districts, Catholic schools across the Archdiocese of Boston are seeing spectacular gains, some as high as 20 percent, in math and language proficiency.

A report by the Archdiocese of Boston Catholic Schools Office analyzed 11 of the 14 schools that received educational resources purchased by COVID-era Emergency Assistance to Non-Public Schools (EANS II) funds allocated by Congress in 2021. The Massachusetts Department of Elementary and Secondary Education allocated $13,819,692 worth of resources to 14 Catholic schools in the archdiocese. Ninety-nine percent of that money was used, with each school selecting the resources it needed.

"We were very grateful that the federal government recognized that all children, regardless of where they attended schools, needed that help," said CSO Associate Superintendent for Government Programs Mary Goslin.

Due to income restrictions for EANS eligibility, the 11 schools analyzed in the CSO report are all located in diverse, working-class urban areas with large immigrant populations. The vast majority of the schools are predominantly non-white, with four being over 90 percent students of color.

In several schools, the majority of students speak English as a second language (ESL). Districts with low-income ESL students have struggled the most since the pandemic, but the schools that received EANS funding have bucked the trend. The 11 schools -- Cheverus in Malden, Immaculate Conception in Revere, Lawrence Catholic Academy in Lawrence, Mission Grammar in Roxbury, St. Anthony in Everett, the three campuses of St. John Paul II Catholic Academy in Dorchester, St. Pius V in Lynn, St. Theresa of the Child Jesus in Somerville, and Trinity Catholic Academy in Brockton -- saw an overall increase in standardized math test scores.

Many of the individual schools saw significant increases in language test scores. In summer 2025, leaders and staff from EANS schools attended a CSO symposium. There, Goslin recalled, staff said the resources provided by EANS reminded them "of the reason that Catholic schools are there."

"The reason why they stayed open was to help the students and help the families feel like somebody cared about them, and that they were one big community for another," she said. "That was what empowered them to make a difference."

That, she said, is why the schools are avoiding a decline in test scores. While public schools in Massachusetts moved online, the 11 schools were meeting in person with the help of resources provided by EANS. As private schools, they could make their own decisions on how and when they would safely reopen. Coming to school in masks and sitting six feet apart, students went out for recess and interacted face-to-face with their friends and teachers.

"They were able to forget about the fact that COVID was out there because they were with their friends," Goslin said. "They were eating with their friends, they were playing with their friends, they were learning with their friends, and families were greatly relieved knowing they were well cared for."

EANS funds were divided into five sectors -- curriculum and resources, instruction support, mental health, teacher training, and furniture and technology.

The CSO found that the 11 schools that received those resources saw a 10 percent overall increase in enrollment between 2021 and 2026. Four schools saw their enrollment jump by 20 percent. Ten of the schools have students on waitlists to attend. More students are now receiving financial aid. The schools received Chromebooks, iPads, educational coaches, mental health counselors for students, outdoor play equipment, robotics programs for STEM learning, new textbooks, teacher training, learning software, and social-emotional learning programs. Teachers were taught new strategies for analyzing student data and tailoring learning to children's individual needs, including for students learning English.

Additional staff members kept class sizes small, and technology allowed students to keep up with school if they were at home sick. Thanks to their tutoring and counseling program, Mission Grammar's language scores are higher than the national average. Both of Trinity Catholic Academy's campuses now have their own special education teacher. Cheverus received tricycles and volleyball nets for recess.

The strategies implemented in the 11 EANS schools will be studied for potential use at other schools in the archdiocese.

"They select the highest quality of resources, but they don't have funding to be trying out new programs all the time," Goslin said of the schools. "And this gave them the chance then to test new programs out, programs that they normally wouldn't have had access to."

With the report, CSO wants to show how EANS resources protected students from learning loss. In the future, additional resources could further improve Boston's Catholic schools. In 2025, President Trump signed the Educational Choice for Children Act, which offers tax credits to support scholarships at private schools. Taxpayers would be able to set aside up to $1,700 each year for a tax-deductible donation to a scholarship fund. Those scholarship funds could provide resources to Catholic schools in the Archdiocese of Boston -- if Gov. Maura Healey decides to opt into the federal program in January.

"In our Catholic schools, we have proved that we are able to support our students using those EANS resources, and we would be able to support our students all the more through this federal tax scholarship," Goslin said.

She said many students are attending Boston Catholic schools from scholarships, and "flourish" thanks to them.

"To be able to continue to support them and give them more support would be a real gift," she said. "So we're hoping that the governor will opt into this to benefit all families, not just those in Catholic schools."

title: Early 20th-century archdiocesan Department of Education records
text:
The Archive Department is currently processing a number of collections from the Department of Education, now known as the Catholic Schools Office in the Archdiocese. We began by looking at the oldest collection we have from the Department of Education, which turned out to be reports and correspondence from the supervisor of schools, spanning 1918 to 1934.

The reports from parochial schools took up 13 banker's boxes and consisted of one folder of reports per year per parochial school, organized by town. We rehoused the reports, collating all the years into one folder for each school. This left just 10 boxes of material after we discarded the old, acidic folders that were covered in coal dust -- a sign that they had probably been stored in a furnace room at some point in time. Alongside the reports, there was also correspondence spanning 1920 to 1921 from the first diocesan supervisor of schools, Father Augustine F. Hickey. Thankfully, the reports and correspondence themselves were in good condition, and rehousing the materials gave us an opportunity to glean information about the administration of parochial schools in the early 20th century.

The reports for each school include monthly attendance, June examination grades, lists of textbooks, and a record of which teachers had attended continuing education classes over the summer. The existence of the reports themselves shows a formalization of education in the archdiocese, which began under the leadership of Archbishop O'Connell. They also share important information about the nature of schooling at the time.

The attendance reports show how many classes were held at each school, how many boys and girls were in each teacher's class each month, and how many left to work or to attend public schools. Though the reports from the 1922-1928 school years are missing from our collection, we know that they must have existed, because statistics on parochial school attendance were still published diligently in the National Catholic Directories for those years. For example, in 1924, there were a total of 88,129 children in parochial schools, 1,683 teaching sisters, 65 teaching brothers, and 74 lay teachers.

Teachers had greater freedom in their classrooms than today to choose what subjects they taught, and how often. The eighth-grade June examination reports and lists of textbooks show what subjects were being taught at each school, though arithmetic, English, and religion were core subjects. Correspondence shows that their decision was often a response to the needs of the students from their parish community, such as where they were likely to attend high school. For example, in 1921, Cheverus Commercial School in Roxbury taught bookkeeping, office training, commercial law, and commercial geography to their second-year "commercial grade."

Archbishop O'Connell prioritized the establishment of parochial schools throughout the archdiocese for the benefit of Catholic children, but also to bring Catholics to the center of American public life, in part by teaching American values and civic consciousness. This was especially true for the many parochial schools that served immigrants. At this time, there were only a handful of Catholic high schools, so most parochial students would go on to enter public schools. In one letter to Sister M. Teresa of Holy Rosary Italian School in Lawrence, Father Hickey said, "You will understand, I am sure, that it is a matter of vital interest to me to have your children go to the public schools thoroughly equipped in the English language ... and familiar with some of the fundamentals of American history."

The correspondence also shows how Father Hickey and the teachers defined and honed the education offered in the archdiocese. In 1915, the communities running the Catholic schools created the first common curriculum for the archdiocese. In 1919, they began to issue uniform exams to all grammar students. To prepare for this, Father Hickey asked school superiors for their exams in arithmetic, spelling, English, and music, to use as model questions. Additionally, he frequently received requests to share samples of exams, course outlines, and report blanks with other diocesan supervisors of schools who were forming their education programs.

At that time, there was freedom in curriculum, and there was also no standardization of credentials for private or public school teachers. Anticipating the future, Father Hickey suggested that religious teachers should have high school diplomas and, if possible, have graduated from a normal school, as teaching schools were once called because they taught "norms" for education.

In a letter to Sister Mary Clare of St. Joseph in Fitchburg, Father Hickey said, "It is a splendid idea for you to do all in your power to increase the educational opportunities of the sisters in your community. Whatever you do in this respect will improve the character of the work done in the classroom at the present time and will prepare your sisters for whatever the future has in store for us," meaning the much-discussed possibility of legislation requiring certification to teach in Massachusetts.

The small file of correspondence shows Father Hickey's great interest in the daily work of teachers, the theory and improvement of their education, and the political movements affecting Catholic education in the United States. He cared for the details and the grand ideas. In one letter to a beleaguered sister, he advised, "Remember the great and large purpose of our work for education. Whatever our shortcomings and difficulties, we are forming great Christian characters and we are making a conspicuous contribution to the life of the Church in this country and to our national life as well. A constant appreciation of this fact will make us more patient with ourselves and with others when the daily grind becomes almost unbearable."

In the early 20th century, primary and secondary education was just taking the shape that we recognize today. The reports and files of correspondence from the Department of Education illustrate the effort of diocesan leaders, teachers and religious to professionalize and bolster parochial schools within the larger, still-evolving context of American education.

SAVANNAH MILLER IS AN ARCHIVIST OF THE ARCHDIOCESE OF BOSTON.

title: Father John E. Sheridan, senior priest, chaplain at Regina Cleri
text:
Raised in the Garden City, Newton, and in its Mary Immaculate of Lourdes Parish, Father John E. Sheridan is an alumnus of Newton South High School and archdiocesan seminaries. He is the eighth of the nine children of the late Denis and Elizabeth (Henebury) Sheridan born on Jan. 30, 1964. He has four brothers: Denis, James, Mark, and Patrick; and four sisters: Catherine Carver, Elizabeth Harris, Ellen Geary, and Mary Martin.

On June 16, 1990, Cardinal Bernard Law ordained him and other members of the Class of 1990 to the priesthood at Holy Cross Cathedral. He celebrated his First Mass at Holy Name Church, West Roxbury, the following day.

The cardinal also gave him his first assignment as parochial vicar at St. Joseph (French) Parish, Salem.

Over the next 36 years, he would receive additional assignments, all of them to archdiocesan parishes, pretty much across the archdiocese in each of the pastoral regions except Merrimack.

Cardinal Law gave him the following assignments after Salem: parochial vicar, St. Ann in Dorchester's Neponset section (1996-1998); St. Cecilia, Ashland, with chaplaincy at Marian High School Framingham (1998-2002); and his first assignment as pastor at St. Matthew, Dorchester.

title: Father Charles J. Higgins, pastor in Danvers, Kingston, and Weymouth
text:
One of Boston's well-known priests and one with extensive service to the priests of the archdiocese, as well as to her parishes, Father Charles J. Higgins became a senior priest on Feb. 1, 2026.

He was born on July 12, 1949, in Milford, then one of the most eastern towns of the Springfield Diocese! He was one of two children of the late Charles and Mary Rita (Slavin) Higgins. He has one sister, Linda Lucier.

He was raised in St. Joseph Parish, attended local schools before going to the newly established Xavierian Brothers High School, Westwood. He was in the first graduating class, Class of 1967, and the first of several XBHS alumni to be ordained priests for the archdiocese. He spoke highly of his high school and especially the Xaverian Brothers faculty. "The education we received from the Xaverian Brothers touched all aspects of a person's life," he told The Pilot in a previously published interview.

He entered archdiocesan seminaries following high school, first to Jamaica Plain at Cardinal O'Connell, then to Brighton for philosophy at St. Clement Hall, and then across the field to St. John for theology.

title: Father Sean M. Connor, served as pastor in Dorchester, Weymouth, and Braintree
text:
Born in the "Boxer City," Brockton, on Sept. 19, 1965, Father Connor was one of the children of the late Myles and Sarah (Coyne) Connor. He was raised in Marshfield and recalls his early relationship with the parish priests of his home parish, St. Ann. He named the late Fathers Patrick Gilmore and Leo Cormier as influences on his sense of priestly vocation.

He attended local schools of Marshfield, graduating from its high school in 1983 and subsequently graduated from Northeastern University with a bachelor of science degree in criminal justice.

His father had been a police officer in Milton, and in some way, the "law enforcement gene" proved dominant. He served as an officer in the police department of Marshfield for 10 years before the vocational tug he had experienced earlier pulled him towards the priesthood.

In 1995, after a period of reflection and a Cursillo Retreat at Stonehill College, he entered St. John Seminary. Six years later, after philosophy and theology study, he was ordained to the priesthood at Holy Cross Cathedral by Bernard Cardinal Law on May 26, 2001, a member of the first class of priests of the new millennium for the archdiocese.

His first assignment was a brief one, two days shy of a year as a parochial vicar at St. Francis Xavier Parish, Weymouth. He was even more briefly a parochial vicar at Immaculate Conception Parish, Marlborough, from June to October 2002.

title: Celebration of Priesthood highlights unity, service
text:
BOSTON -- Priests don't just fall out of the sky, says Jesuit Father Jack Butler, Boston College's new president.

Nor do they hatch from eggs or get manufactured in a factory. Instead, he explained, they are formed by loving, faith-filled families like his own. They are formed by parents who teach them right from wrong, encourage them, forgive them, and show them how to pray and take them to Mass.

"Our parents gave us wisdom, and told us how proud they were of us and the fact that they were behind us and that we could do it," he said.

Seeing how his relatives comforted each other in times of mourning inspired his own devotion to the sacrament of the sick. When his twin died in the womb and when his grandparents died, priests were there. When he struggled with dyslexia at his Catholic high school, priests told him, "You can do it because all things are possible."

"Priests didn't learn how to be priests by going to the seminary," he said. "The seed was there when moms and dads and coaches and teachers, the lay people that helped raise us, taught us about love and hope and forgiveness. Taught us about integrity. Taught us about who and what we could be."

Father Butler spoke to an audience of over 1,400 people, including 230 priests, at the 18th annual Celebration of the Priesthood Dinner, held at the Omni Seaport Hotel in Boston on Sept. 16. The annual dinner raises funds for the Clergy Trust, which provides healthcare to active and senior priests in the Archdiocese of Boston and funds Regina Cleri, the archdiocese's residence for senior priests. This year's dinner, at which Father Butler was keynote speaker, raised over $2 million.

"It's amazing to me that this room is filled with people who have put aside tonight and given out of the generosity of their heart for the Clergy Trust fund," Father Butler said.

Throughout his ministry, he has seen laypeople support, even form, their priests. In return, the priests serve them.

"Every time you let us baptize your child, every time there's a congregation to preach to, any time you call us to go to your house to anoint somebody, or there's a difficult time, and you just want to talk," he said. "We would not be able to flourish without the people of God."

He thanked the priests at the dinner who, like the Virgin Mary, answered God's call to serve.

"Every priest in this room, thank you for your courage, thank you for standing up, thank you for your yes, thank you for ministering to us, thank you for walking with the people of God, and I beg you, please don't leave us alone," he said.

Cardinal Sean P. O'Malley delivered the invocation, as well as a memorial to Ann Carter, who served as his advisor and led communications for the Archdiocese of Boston. She later became a consultor to the Vatican's Dicastery for Communication and an advisor at the Vatican's 2019 Meeting on the Protection of Minors. Carter died of cancer in March. The cardinal remembered her fondly for the behind-the-scenes service she provided the archdiocese, and her ability to authentically listen to others. He called her "a great friend, a good Catholic, and a consummate professional."

"All of us who knew her will remember her warmth, her laughter, her generosity, her friendship," he said. "She reminds us all that her example of kindness and common sense are the heart of effective communication."

The theme of this year's dinner was unity, and the Clergy Trust presented a video spotlighting three parishes and pastors overseeing culturally diverse parishes that are united by their Catholic faith: Father Richard Fitzgerald of St. Columbkille in Brighton; Father Thomas Macdonald of Holy Name Parish in West Roxbury; and Father Matthew Westcott of the Catholic Tri-Parishes of Brockton.

"These three men and their stories are just a small subset of the wonderful guys who serve throughout this archdiocese,"said Bishop Robert Reed, the evening's emcee, "offering the grace of the sacraments, and as they said so many times, creating unity in Christ Jesus."

In her remarks, Clergy Trust Board Chair Sharon McNally led a round of applause for her predecessor, Jim MacDonald, who had to step down after being diagnosed with ALS. She said he was facing the disease "with courage, conviction, positivity, and grace."

"This event is not just a crucial fundraiser for the Clergy Trust," she said. "It's also an opportunity for us to pay homage to the wonderful priests who do so much for us."

Clergy Trust Executive Director Mike Scannell presented Father William Joy with the St. Joseph the Worker Award. Scannell explained that the award goes to "those who give freely and completely of themselves in order to help the mission and serve those in need."

As a young priest, Father Joy served the working-class Charlestown community at the height of racial tensions during the desegregation busing crisis. He spent his ministry helping parishes going through challenges, visited the sick in healthcare settings, and was a longtime supporter of Catholic Relief Services, a ministry which took him to sites of war and famine around the world. He also served on the Clergy Trust Board of Trustees.

"For any of you lucky enough to know Father Joy, you can attest that he has done all of this while staying true to his name, serving with true joy," Scannell said.

Upon receiving the award, Father Joy spoke very little about himself but instead acknowledged all those he wished to thank. He said he was accepting the award on behalf of "many, many priests," who were also worthy to receive it. In preparation for receiving the award, he thought about how Isaiah compared God to a potter forming clay. Father Joy said his family, the religious sisters and Jesuits who educated him as a youth, and the faculty of St. John's Seminary were among the many "potters" who formed him. As priests age, he said, Regina Cleri and the Clergy Trust aid in their continual formation. He asked Joan Smith, the Archdiocese of Boston's benefits coordinator, and Regina Cleri Clinical Director Christine Lilley to stand and be recognized.

"They're there for us whenever we need them," he said, adding, "These are the faces that take care of us. These are the faces that are there for us."

Taking the podium to deliver the benediction to conclude the evening, Archbishop Richard G. Henning described Father Butler's address as "awesome," adding that he was looking forward to "Father Jack's" installation as president of Boston College in October.

"Your choice to be with us tonight is an expression of your love for your brother priests, but it's also an expression of your love for the Church of Boston," he said.

The archbishop thanked Father Butler, his family, and the Jesuits who formed him, as well as Bishop Reed for emceeing the dinner. Most of all, he thanked Clergy Trust, its supporters, and the priests themselves. He was proud to announce that the Archdiocese of Boston will welcome 22 new seminarians this year.

"Your presence here tonight witnesses to your love of your priests, our priests," he told those at the dinner. "The very work of the Clergy Trust is motivated by love and finds its concrete expression in the compassionate care of our priests, especially when they face the challenges of illness and age."

title: Does Boston deserve its troubled reputation around race and sports?
text:
When cricket gained popularity in Boston in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, Black immigrants from the West Indies became some of the top players. Based in Boston and neighboring Cambridge, their teams competed against all-white squads in the Massachusetts Cricket League. By the early 20th century, Black teams were dominating the league. The 1931 final was played between two such teams – Windsor and Standard.

Not exactly the narrative you may be accustomed to hearing in the land of Dunkin’, Big Papi and Brady, eh? And perhaps not a narrative that fits easily into the story of race and Boston sport, with its recognizable highs (the Boston Celtics drafting the NBA’s first Black player in Chuck Cooper in 1950, and making their longtime star Bill Russell the league’s first Black coach in 1966) and lows (the Boston Red Sox being the last Major League Baseball team to integrate, with Pumpsie Green in 1959).

Yet this is exactly the kind of narrative that co-editors Robert Cvornyek and Douglas Stark were looking for in their recently released anthology, Race and Resistance in Boston: A Contested Sports History. Published in time for Black History Month, with a foreword by the New England Patriots’ three-time Super Bowl champion Devin McCourty, the book sheds light on Black sporting achievements in Boston that may be lesser-known to the broader community.

“These stories resonate within the African American community,” Cvornyek says. “They never left the community. We would never say we discovered these stories.”

Stark adds: “You always hear about the Red Sox as the last team to integrate. On the other side, you hear about Bill Russell and the Boston Celtics and how progressive they were … If you’re in Massachusetts, that’s a large narrative about race and sport in the city, two polar opposites. I think Bob and I tried to find a kind of counter-narrative, a more complete story.”

The book’s chapters span 150 years of Boston history, and include examinations of Black athletes in lesser-covered Boston sports such as soccer, boxing, golf and tennis. Even when it comes to the national pastime, there’s room for a reappraisal. There’s similarly comprehensive treatment of better-known names such as Russell and Willie O’Ree – in 1958, the latter became the first Black player in the NHL with the Boston Bruins. O’Ree’s Canadian roots are explored by Canadian-born historian, documentarian and publisher George Fosty.

Several chapters address intersectionality – one, by Texas Christian University journalism professor Jaime Loke, looks at fans’ differing reactions to the coming-out narratives of men’s basketball player Jason Collins (overwhelmingly positive) and women’s basketball player Brittney Griner (largely negative).

And then there’s the chapter on cricket, authored by Texas A&M University history professor Violet Showers Johnson.

“The cricket piece comes out of the CLR James tradition, looking at cricket as a form of resistance,” Cvornyek says. “Professor Johnson did a wonderful job with that.”

This chapter goes beyond describing the great Black teams and players. It explores their wider social milieu in the West Indian immigrant community – such as worship at St Cyprian’s Episcopal Church and identification as part of a British global community that went unrecognized by at least one British colonial official. In the Massachusetts Cricket League, there was a degree of equality. There were Black umpires and even a Black league president, although segregated rosters and unequal field conditions persisted.

As the editors explain, the idea for their project arose during the Covid-19 pandemic and the Black Lives Matter movement.

“Bob’s platform is the academic world,” Stark says, noting Cvornyek’s career as an emeritus history professor at Rhode Island College and his own experience in the worlds of preservation and interpretation. “My background is public history, museums, sports museums. We leveraged all of our contacts in these areas.”

Among the earliest they reached out to was Joseph Cooper, the inaugural chair of sport leadership and administration at the University of Massachusetts Boston, where he is also a special assistant to the chancellor for Black life as well as an associate professor.

“His response was, ‘this book has to be written, it’s not out there,’” Stark says. And, Stark says, “I think what makes the book unique among books on race and sport is that you don’t find one focusing on a particular city.” He calls the book’s subject “one particular northern city with sort of a troubled, racist past.”

“The question is always, is Boston the most racist sports city?” Cvornyek says. “I don’t think it’s a good historical question, it’s not something we talk about in the book. But it’s out there.”

As he explains, “The whole notion of Boston as the cradle of liberty, people see Boston as a fairly liberal city. On issues of sports, it’s simply not the case.”

Cvornyek cites Russell’s description of Boston as a “flea market of racism – specifically regarding the fans. One of the ways we sort of take a look at Boston’s troubled racial history is through a multitude of sports, sports figures and fans.”

One chapter in the anthology, authored by critic and literary historian Bijan Bayne, looks at an especially controversial moment from the city’s history – the busing crisis of the 1970s, in which a court order mandated desegregation in the Boston public school system. As Bayne relates in the chapter, he grew up in the predominantly Black Boston neighborhood of Roxbury before leaving as a youth with his family for Washington DC. He notes the racist white mobs who protested outside Boston schools that were compelled to admit Black students.

Arguably best remembered for the protests that gained national attention and stained Boston’s reputation as a liberal city, busing had unintended consequences for Black student-athletes, according to Bayne. Some left the Boston public schools for alternatives in affluent suburbs through a program known as Metco, which remains in existence. Or, like many white classmates, they went to Catholic schools.

“As these transitions unfolded, sports went on,” Bayne writes. “Children who grew up on Bobby Orr, John Havlicek, and Carl Yasterzemski weren’t going to be stopped by relocation – they were disheartened maybe, and feeling displaced, but far from inactive.”

The chapter concludes with a look at the glittering high school basketball career of future hall of famer Patrick Ewing of Cambridge Rindge & Latin, who went on to play college ball for John Thompson at Georgetown and was the top NBA draft pick in 1985 by the New York Knicks. Throughout the chapter, Bayne maintains a sense of balance regarding race and sports in Boston.

“There are bigoted fans and all-white school enclaves and communities across the United States,” he writes. “While not perfect, Boston has been a place for Black athletes from all over the world to showcase their gifts – long before and long after the busing mandate.”

Get ready for more explorations of less-chartered terrain: The anthology is the first in an intended multi-volume series.

“We don’t feel this is the end for us,” Stark says. “It’s sort of the beginning.”

title: Boston sues Trump administration over infrastructure grant withdrawal
text:
Boston has sued Donald Trump’s administration over the withdrawal of a $20m grant for infrastructure improvements in the latest example of cities across the country mobilising against the federal government.

Boston is challenging a decision by the transportation department to cancel funding for a project on the basis that it included a small allocation for electric vehicle charging.

The grant was awarded to Boston during Democrat Joe Biden’s presidency under the Rebuilding American Infrastructure with Sustainability and Equity (Raise) programme.

The city argues the Roxbury Resilient Corridors project would improve safety, public transport, accessibility and traffic flow. Three streets identified for improvements are in the top 3% of Boston’s streets in terms of concentration of traffic injuries and fatalities. They are in an area classified by the transportation department as one of “persistent poverty” and a “historically disadvantaged community”.

Boston says the department gave a single reason for withdrawing the grant in September last year: it included electric vehicle charging infrastructure. However, the city contends this accounted for less than 1% of the project’s costs.

The lawsuit argues that the decision was unlawful and overtly political and contradicted the purpose of the Raise programme, which Congress established to support infrastructure projects promoting sustainability, safety and technological innovation, including in underserved communities.

Michelle Wu, the mayor of Boston, said: “We’re fighting for every dollar of investment to improve quality of life for Roxbury residents, commuters and businesses.

“Boston earned this competitive grant to meet community needs and address long-needed infrastructure upgrades. The City of Boston will continue to fight back against lawless federal attacks, and we urge the court to reverse the Trump administration’s illegal actions and restore these critical funds for Roxbury.”

The Democratic congresswoman Ayanna Pressley, whose Massachusetts district includes Roxbury, said: “These funds are an essential investment in Roxbury and the unlawful cancellation of this grant is more evidence of Sean Duffy and Donald Trump’s contempt for the people we serve.”

She added: “There was no good reason to rescind these funds – DOT should reverse course so we can move this project forward, improve the daily lives of commuters, and enhance the climate resilience of at-risk communities—just as Congress intended.”

The lawsuit argues that federal agencies cannot change the terms of a programme established by Congress to reflect changing political priorities. The case, City of Boston v Duffy, names the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, and was filed in the US district court for the district of Massachusetts.

Boston city says it will have filed nine lawsuits against the administration once the latest case is included, eight of them in partnership with the Public Rights Project.

Toby Merrill, litigation director at the Public Rights Project, which is providing pro bono legal counsel to Boston, said: “Boston lost a $20m infrastructure grant over electric vehicle chargers that represented a fraction of 1% of the funding – infrastructure the federal government itself encouraged.”

Cities including Chicago, New York and Los Angeles and states across the US have brought a series of lawsuits against the administration over federal funding decisions and other policies since Trump returned to the White House.
